### Series Title Page

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age up to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, most diligently corrected; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the very extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the material treated; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with others possessing some authority and weight in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one, of subjects, by consulting which everything that each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other, of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture.*

*The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if the following matters are considered: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the exceedingly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection itself—single, systematic, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time assembled in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.*

**FIRST SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# The Complete Works of Marius Mercator

## [Column 0009]

### Notice Concerning This Latest Edition

At the very threshold of this volume we have thought it appropriate to detain the reader for a little while, so that, once informed about the arrangement we have followed in this new edition of Mercator’s works, he may begin his reading both more efficiently and more pleasantly. As for the author’s character and period, and for the kind, quality, and number of his writings, since the notices that follow provide more than enough evidence, it is proper to refer diligent readers to them. Nothing remains for us to say except something about the relation of our edition to the preceding editions and, so to speak, its typographical arrangement.

Many editions of Mercator’s works have indeed thus far been published, though not all with equal approval from learned men. Among them the principal places are occupied by Garner’s edition, printed in 1673; Baluze’s, published in 1684; and finally Galland’s, which appeared in 1772. These editions are so connected with one another that each derives from the preceding edition not only its origin but also the particular kind of usefulness in which it excels. Galland, with only a few corrections and notes added on his own account, reproduced Baluze’s work, rightly holding his predecessor’s scholarship and accuracy—*ἀκρίβεια*—in high esteem. For, besides the fact that nowhere else can one find a fuller text, drawn from various copies most carefully collated and elucidated by exceptionally perceptive annotations, the very name of Baluze, who rendered outstanding service to the republic of letters, lent considerable authority to this edition.

On the other hand, if anyone examines the matter more closely, he will easily discover that Baluze’s edition owes the greater part of its praise and reputation to Garner’s, of which it should be considered a recension and almost a necessary appendix. Baluze himself seems to acknowledge this, since he repeatedly directs the reader back to it. Be that as it may, since we are going to follow Garner’s footsteps in this edition, we refrain from discussing the annotations of that most learned man, which are distinguished not only by their almost infinite number but also by their exceptional learning, since, as it seems to us, no one exists who would begrudge him this praise.

Since, however, some people blame him for dividing the entire collection of Mercator’s works into two parts, so that the monuments relating to the history of the Pelagians are included in the first and those relating to the Nestorian heresy in the second, we gladly seize the opportunity to defend him against this accusation. We believe that such a division introduces much clarity and not even the slightest confusion. We shall therefore employ it all the more willingly in our edition, since it offers itself most conveniently at this point in the Patrology, where we are about to resume, as though by looking backward, the history of the heresies that most recently struggled against the Church. This is especially appropriate because the struggles of the Pelagians and Nestorians against the Catholic faith receive considerable illumination from the extensive and learned dissertations with which each part of Garner’s edition is furnished.

From this it can easily be inferred that we intend to provide men of letters with an edition of Mercator’s works complete in every respect, provided that we reproduce Garner’s text, division, and notes in full, while also incorporating whatever corrections or annotations have been added through the work of both Baluze and Galland.

> **[Note: Column 0009]** It should nevertheless be noted that we have deliberately omitted certain Greek fragments which Marius Mercator extracted from Saint Cyril and translated into Latin, but which Garner’s work printed alongside the Latin text. We refer the reader to the works of the holy bishop, which are to be printed in Greek in the second series of the Patrology.  
> **[Column 0010]**

Intending, therefore, to follow this course, we collated the three editions mentioned above with the greatest care. Whenever they differed from one another, we recorded the variant reading either below the page, when the matter required some explanation, or in the text itself within brackets, always adding the name of the author from whom it had been taken. The reader will also find the author’s name attached to the other notes.

> **[Note: Column 0010]** If we have contributed anything of our own in the notes, it will easily be recognized by this mark: **EDITOR**.

Unless Garner is responsible for it, whatever appears without another name is to be attributed to him.

## [Column 0011]

# General Preface of the Reverend Father Garner to All the Works of Marius Mercator

## Prologue

There are altogether six things, learned reader, that it is useful for you to know in advance before you approach the works contained in this volume.

First, concerning the author himself, whose name appears to have remained unknown down to the present day.

Second, concerning the works, which are now being brought to light for the first time.

Third, concerning our study and labor: partly in correcting manuscript codices; partly in supplying observations wherever necessary; and partly in distributing the works according to a suitable arrangement.

Fourth, concerning those matters which, although previously unknown, are now learned for the first time from this author with regard to the Coelestian and Nestorian heresies.

Fifth, how Mercator’s works came into our hands.

Sixth and finally, what remains of the letter sent by Saint Augustine to Mercator.

## Chapter One  
### Marius Mercator: Who Knew Him, When He Lived, His Origin, and His Character and Authority

The works of Marius Mercator are now appearing in the light for the first time. He was certainly an ancient author and a contemporary of Augustine; yet until now he was so unknown even to learned men that he was not mentioned by name either by Gennadius, otherwise a careful cataloguer of ecclesiastical writers of the same period, or by other Fathers, whether his contemporaries or those of nearly the same age.

Perhaps someone will wonder at this silence, or even wish to interpret it unfavorably and therefore place less confidence in Mercator, as though he were falsely claiming to belong to his period and, emerging like a shadow from the grave, were attempting to mock minds stunned by novelty. “How,” such a person will say, “could an author equal to the noblest writers have remained hidden for so long, even amid the decay and darkness of libraries? How could he have escaped the curious diligence of men of our time and their tireless zeal in examining the monuments of antiquity?”

But, leaving aside for a while what should be said about Gennadius, and another reason for doubt, of which there will be a more suitable occasion to speak toward the end, Mercator’s name is certainly not as unknown as it might appear. Augustine and Possidius remembered him, and those two may count for the equivalent of many.

### Augustine

“Concerning those, however, who will be caught up in the clouds, in a certain letter which I wrote **TO MY SON MERCATOR**, beginning: ‘Without a doubt, it is very well known to you …’ when he had consulted me about certain questions of the Pelagians, who deny that death is repaid for sin, insofar as I have argued the matter under the Law, etc.” (*Book on Eight Questions of Dulcitius*, question 3).

### Possidius

When Possidius was listing Augustine’s works or letters against the Pelagians, equal in number to books, he wrote in seventeenth place:

“Likewise, one letter to **MERCATOR** against the same men.”

These words will be sought in vain in the ordinary editions of the index usually placed at the beginning of Saint Augustine’s works. They are found only in the first edition, which John Ulimmerius, a canon regular, separately prepared and published at Louvain.

It may be inferred that Mercator flourished from approximately the year 418 to 450 of Christ, because he received a letter from Augustine in 418; in 429 he presented the *Commonitorium* against the Coelestians to Theodosius; at the beginning of 431 he opposed the anathemas of Nestorius; at the end of 431 he wrote the *Book of Subnotations* against Julian; and finally he mentioned both a letter written by Theodoret to Domnus of Antioch and a sermon preached by the same man in the Church of Antioch after the death of Saint Cyril in 444, as well as the Eutychian heresy, which grew powerful after those times and was condemned in 451. All these points must be confirmed by suitable arguments.

First, then, that he received letters from Augustine in 418 is established as follows. Part of that correspondence is contained in the book on the eight questions of Dulcitius, in which the *Enchiridion to Laurence* is mentioned; in the *Enchiridion*, Jerome is praised as already dead. Since Jerome died on the day before the Kalends of October in 420, it must be admitted that the book on the eight questions of Dulcitius was not written before the year 420.

Augustine, however, states that it was written in a year in which Easter Sunday fell in March. He says:

“So far as I can see, I was not slow in answering your questions. For at Easter of this year, in which the Lord’s Day was the sixth day before the Kalends of April, I received from Carthage the letter of your affection. After those holy days I immediately went to Carthage, where the multitude of business, which cannot be absent from that city, allowed me to dictate nothing. But after I returned from there, having completed fifteen days among our people, who compelled me after my long absence to attend to other matters—for three months later, when I was permitted to return, I did not delay replying to these things—you sent me questions which I had already treated in various little works of mine, and from those same works I supplied either my solution or at least my discussion.”

## [Column 0013]

Since, therefore, during the entire period extending from the year 419 to 430, when Augustine died, Easter did not fall in March except in the year 422, the book must be said to have been written in that year. There is no reason to postpone it to 430 unless it is postponed at the same time to the month immediately preceding Augustine’s death. The holy Doctor states that he replied to Dulcitius at least three months after Easter, and consequently either at the beginning of July or at the end of June.

Neither possibility is consistent with the facts. For the book to Dulcitius is mentioned in the second book of the *Retractations*, completed before 428, and Hippo Regius had already been under siege for three months when Augustine died.

If, then, the book on the eight questions was written at the time just stated, Augustine’s letter to Marius Mercator was certainly sent several years earlier—probably immediately after Zosimus pronounced his judgment against Coelestius and Pelagius—and therefore belongs at least to the year 418, in which Zosimus died on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.

At that time Marius must already have possessed some reputation, since he questioned the most celebrated bishop in the whole world, a man overwhelmed with business, about matters of the highest importance. He not only deserved a response—and one so carefully composed that Augustine himself praised it as though it were a prior judgment on questions of faith—but was also asked in turn to inform the teacher of the Church if he should devise anything concerning the question. These are Augustine’s words:

“If you have heard or read anything settled and defined by a reasonable and complete discussion, or if you should even be able to hear, read, or devise anything further concerning this matter, I ask you not to hesitate to send it to me. For I confess to your charity that I love learning more than teaching.”

Second, that Mercator presented the *Commonitorium* to Theodosius in 429 is clearly established by its title itself:

“An example of the *Commonitorium* which, concerning the name of Coelestius, was delivered by Mercator in the Greek language not only to the Church of Constantinople but also to many most religious men; it was also offered to the most pious prince Theodosius, ever august, and was translated from Greek into Latin by the same Marius Mercator, servant of Christ, in the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius, illustrious men. Through this *Commonitorium*, once the most disastrous error had been recognized, by imperial command Julian, its defender and follower, together with his other associates and participants, and later Coelestius, were expelled from the city of Constantinople; and afterward, at the Council of Ephesus, they were condemned in the presence of 275 bishops.”

As the consular lists show, the consuls in the year 429 were Florentius and Dionysius.

Third, the period in which the *Book of Subnotations* against Julian’s words was written can easily be inferred from the fact that Augustine is mentioned in its preface as though already dead, while the Council of Ephesus is not mentioned—even though it would have been particularly appropriate to mention it, if truth permitted, since Julian and his associates were condemned there.

This work was therefore composed at the time of the Council of Ephesus, as will be demonstrated more fully in the notes. At that time Mercator received from Bassula, a deacon of the Church of Carthage, the composite work of Augustine and Julian. Augustine died in the year 430, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September. The council began the following year, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July.

Fourth, the same method can establish the period when Mercator wrote his refutations of the impious anathemas of Nestorius. As is clear from the title of the twelfth sermon, Nestorius, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, both Augusti, received with Cyril’s letter twelve Catholic anathemas, to which he opposed twelve of his own, as the title of the contradictions written by Mercator shows. Mercator certainly wrote them before Nestorius’s deposition, since no mention is made of that deposition, although, if it had been permissible, both the time and place would have required frequent mention of it.

This work was therefore composed in 431, before the council began. For the year designated by the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III is the year 430 of Christ.

Fifth, the period when Mercator wrote against Theodoret is plainly shown not only by the refutation of the Nestorian heresy, in which the Eutychian heresy is also mentioned, but by these words in the title against Theodoret:

“Likewise, from the acts composed against Domnus, bishop of Antioch, in which that same Domnus is accused because, in his presence, the most wicked Theodoret dared publicly in the Church, after the death of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, of holy memory, while insulting his blessed repose, to utter the following …”

These acts were composed at the second Council of Ephesus, the so-called Robber Council, in which, under the presidency of Dioscorus, Domnus was deposed in 449, Theodoret was condemned, and Eutyches was acquitted.

Mercator therefore wrote against Theodoret either in that same year or in the following one, since he must be considered to have written before the Council of Chalcedon, at which Theodoret, after anathematizing Nestorius, was received back. He would not have dealt with a man received by the Church in the same way as with Theodoret, an opponent of the Council of Ephesus.

Finally, one may infer either that Mercator did not live to the year 450, when the Council of Chalcedon was held against Eutyches, or that from that time he committed nothing to writing that has come down to us. For if he had learned that Theodoret had been received by so great a council after receiving a proper confirmation of his faith, this man, himself thoroughly Catholic, would certainly have called him a Catholic bishop in a different manner from that customary in the works we possess.

So much for the period in which Mercator flourished. We now turn to his origin.

He was certainly born in the West among the Latins. For in the preface to the sermons of Nestorius he testifies that, stirred by the fervor of faith, he translated from Greek into Latin certain blasphemous statements of that heretic addressed to the people, so that they might be known and avoided by the faithful who shared his language.

Nevertheless, he was moderately skilled in the Greek language. He wrote in Greek the *Commonitorium*, which was read by the Church of Constantinople and by the Emperor himself, and he translated from Greek into Latin nearly all the works that we are now publishing.

## [Column 0015]

Although it cannot be determined with certainty from his writings from what region he originated, unless my conjecture deceives me, he was either from Campania, Apulia, or that part of Italy which faces Sicily. For he knows the private and domestic affairs of the Campanian Coelestius and the Apulian Julian in a way scarcely possible for anyone who was not from the same city or at least the same province.

That Coelestius originated in Campania we demonstrate both in the notes to the *Book of Subnotations* and in the dissertation on the authors and principal defenders of the heresy that took its name from Pelagius. Augustine shows that Julian was born in Apulia when he addresses him in these words:

“Do not despise the Punic man who warns or admonishes you, puffed up by earthly descent. For it is not because Apulia gave you birth that you therefore think the Punic people must be defeated by race, since you cannot defeat them in mind.” (*Sixth Book of the Unfinished Work against Julian*, chapter 18).

How private, moreover, are the affairs of these two men that Mercator reports! He says that Coelestius was born of a noble family, was a eunuch by a defect of nature, served among the scholastic auditors, heard Rufinus the Syrian at Rome in the time of Anastasius, and left the City in 408, and so forth.

As for Julian, Mercator says that he was regarded as the son of Memorius by Juliana, a woman of rank; yet that he was believed by his nurse to have been substituted, as the offspring of a female household slave, for the child of such parents; that he was wholly devoted to reading Petronius and Martial, obscene authors, and had thereby acquired license in speaking and writing; that after the death of his parents he kept two sisters under his guardianship and trained them according to the same disciplines; and that he was forced to remain silent by one of them, to whom he had reproached the ruin of her chastity by recalling an offense, and so forth.

Another fairly weighty conjecture may be added: in Sicily and the neighboring provinces there was less discussion of the grace of Christ than of original sin and of death incurred through sin. Marius treated this one question and asked Augustine to teach him about no other. Indeed, he thought that all the others should be referred back to it.

This is clearly evident partly from the *Book of Subnotations* and the collected fragments, whether from the sermons of Nestorius against the Pelagians or from the book of Theodore of Mopsuestia against Saint Augustine; and partly from Augustine’s letter to Marius, a considerable portion of which we possess.

I do not think that Marius was ever a bishop, or even a presbyter, or perhaps even a deacon. Certainly he was not a bishop or presbyter when Augustine wrote to him and called him “son.” Who does not know that at that time bishops, when speaking of other bishops and presbyters, or even deacons, customarily called them brothers, fellow bishops, fellow presbyters, and even fellow deacons? Whenever they spoke of laymen, however, they called them sons.

In such an obvious matter one need consult only Augustine: concerning bishops, when he writes to Aurelius, Coelestine, and others; concerning presbyters, when he writes to Jerome, Paulinus, and others; concerning laymen, when he writes to Hilary, Prosper, and others. Certainly, when he speaks of Julian the deacon in his letter to the bishop Memorius, he calls Memorius his brother and fellow bishop, while he calls Julian his son and fellow deacon.

Marius was not a bishop at the time of the Council of Ephesus, to whose Fathers he presented his *Commonitorium* against Coelestius and Julian. If he had held episcopal rank, he would undoubtedly have sat among them; but that he did not sit among them is clear from the names of the bishops, which are recorded repeatedly.

He was not a bishop, nor even a presbyter, when he sent the *Book of Subnotations* to Pientius, whom he calls “venerable presbyter.” In accordance with the custom of the period, he would certainly have called him either brother or fellow presbyter if he had belonged to the same order.

Finally, he held neither rank when, around the year 446, he composed his refutation of Nestorianism and closed the book with these words:

“We have necessarily believed that both forms of depravity—Nestorian and Eutychian—creeping through the ignorance of very many people, were exposed by the discourses of our most blessed Father John, bishop of the city of Tomi in the province of Scythia, and so forth.”

In those times, bishops—especially living bishops—were addressed in this way only by those who were counted either among the lower clergy or among the laity.

I am therefore easily led to believe that he lived as a layman; or, if not throughout his whole life, as I nevertheless think, at least for as long as he wrote the works that have reached us. The evidence already brought forward persuades me of this. The conclusion is further strengthened by the observation that he everywhere and repeatedly calls himself “a servant of Christ.” Laymen were accustomed both to call themselves and to be called by others “servants of Christ.”

Thus Prosper, in his *Chronicle*, calls Constantius, that noble layman and enemy of Pelagian impiety, a servant of Christ. In the letter to Capreolus, Vitalis and Constantius are likewise called laymen, and there are many others, as learned readers know.

Accordingly, the entry in Possidius’s index should be corrected, where, through the fault of the copyists, we read: “to Mercator the bishop, one letter against the same men.” It should read: “to Mercator, one letter against the same men.” The confusion was not difficult between related words, especially if, as often happens, *Epist.* and *Episc.* had been abbreviated.

If someone should say that Mercator perhaps became a bishop after the periods we have mentioned, let him note first that Possidius did not extend his life beyond the year 450; and second, that those to whom Augustine wrote were customarily designated by Possidius with no other titles than those they held at the time of writing, even if they later received much higher honors.

Thus, in the very passage under discussion, Possidius lists two letters to Sixtus the presbyter, although Sixtus later, while Possidius was still alive, rose to the supreme pontificate. Since Marius was not a bishop at the time when he received Augustine’s letter, he could certainly not have been called a bishop by Possidius. The error was made by the copyists.

I suspect—and the suspicion does not seem rash to me—that Mercator served at Rome among the scholastic auditors, and that Julian had him in mind when he complained that, to bring him into hatred, they were stirring up “common soldiers, scholastic auditors, young men released from monasteries, and men from every sort of clerical crowd.”

By “commoners” I understand Constantius of Vica—this is how the reading should be understood; by “soldiers,” the comes Valerius; by “scholastic auditors,” Mercator; by “young men,” James and Timasius, to whom the book *On Nature and Grace* is addressed; and by “clerics,” the deacon Paulinus, accuser of Coelestius. All these men, inflamed by zeal for the faith, attacked the Pelagians.

Moreover, whether in the *Commonitorium*, the *Subnotations*, and the *Contradictions*, or even in the prefaces to the Greek works that he translated into Latin, Mercator consistently employs the language of the forum. Add to this the fact that he knew the secret matters of Coelestius the scholastic auditor, which suggests some association and perhaps a sharing of office.

Nor should the fact that he may have lived permanently as a layman make him seem to possess lesser authority, at least in that part of the Catholic faith which he undertook to defend. I have sometimes observed, not without great wonder, that God, who loves to resist the proud through the hands of the humble, opposed to the three heresies of Pelagianism, Nestorianism, and Massilianism—hereses which the Fathers especially accuse of pride—first of all laymen, so that, as the Apostle says, he might confound the strong through the contemptible things of the world and overthrow the inflated power of a kind of Pharaoh through the weak.

Certainly Constantius, a man from Vica—for this is how the text should be read—who lived at Rome, was the first to oppose the Pelagians. The first to detect Nestorius’s deception and reveal it to the clergy, attaching a written protest to the doors of the church, was Eusebius, who at that time was either, in Theophanes’ words, *σχολάστικος τῆς βασιλίδος Κωνσταντινουπόλεως*—“a scholasticus of the empress-city Constantinople”—or, according to Nicephorus, a rhetorician, or, as Leontius writes, a forensic judge.

Two laymen, Hilary and Prosper, were the first to resist the presbyters of Massilia. They warned Augustine in letters which a later age esteemed so highly that it joined them to the final labors of the great Doctor of grace as though they were their equals.

Why, then, should we not understand that the same providence of God raised up Mercator, so that a layman himself might complete the work begun by a layman? Certainly, through his *Commonitorium*, he expelled the Pelagians from Constantinople and Ephesus. He presented Nestorius as worthy of execration to the West, partly through a letter published for the general public and through his contradiction of the impious anathemas, and partly by presenting the Greek documents in Latin.

From this one may see how important are the works we are now publishing. For the three things that ordinarily establish confidence in authors commend Mercator in an extraordinary way. He wrote about Julian, Coelestius, and Nestorius, matters which he partly witnessed and partly himself carried out. He published his writings at a time when anyone could have condemned him for falsehood if he had reported anything contrary to the truth. What he wrote and published agrees so closely with the writings of other ancient authors that, just as Marius receives authority from the ancients, so in turn he pours light—and indeed much more light—into writings of the ancients that would otherwise be obscure.

Mercator is also greatly commended by the fact that Augustine himself asked to be taught by him about an exceedingly difficult question, as was mentioned earlier:

“As for the question of the resurrection, concerning those who are believed not to die but to pass from this mortality to immortality without an intervening death, a more careful inquiry must be undertaken. If you can devise anything settled and defined concerning this matter, I ask you not to hesitate to send it to me. For I love learning more than teaching, and so forth.”

# Chapter Two  
## The Works of Marius Mercator

Although the works we possess prove Marius Mercator to have been a most courageous defender of the Catholic faith against the Coelestian and Nestorian heresies, he nevertheless appears in them to have gathered rather the established materials of a case by which a judgment might be carried out than to have composed treatises from which the minds of readers might be instructed in the doctrine of the faith.

In my judgment, this was the reason why he gave his writings the titles *Commonitorium*, *Subnotations*, and *Contradictions*, rather than calling them books. Yet although he translated far more from Greek than he composed by his own labor, he was accustomed to attach prefaces to the works he translated. These prefaces are often more useful for ecclesiastical history than the lengthy treatises of other writers.

All these materials have been excerpted from two ancient codices, one Vatican and the other Bellovacensian, both of which possess the credibility appropriate to their age. The former was transported from the Heidelberg library to the Vatican; the latter is preserved by the venerable chapter of the distinguished Church of Beauvais. Both are of excellent quality, though the Bellovacensian is more carefully corrected. Each appears to be approximately eight hundred years old, as may be inferred from the form of the script.

The Palatine manuscript had been seen by the most learned Lucas Holstenius, who extracted from it certain passages found among his papers in the possession of the eminent Cardinal Francesco Barberini and transmitted here through the work of the Reverend Father Possinus.

The venerable chapter of the Church of Beauvais kindly allowed us to use the Bellovacensian manuscript, with a generosity that can never be praised sufficiently.

The works of Mercator contained in both codices are so confusedly and carelessly scattered, and so mixed with other materials, that the learned Holstenius believed that everything contained in the Vatican manuscript, including the old translation of the Council of Ephesus itself, should be attributed to the same author.

Although this opinion is defective in one respect—for the creed of Theodore of Mopsuestia was translated once by Marius and in another form by the old interpreter—it is nevertheless not wholly without plausibility, whether because of the authority of so great a man or for other reasons that we shall present in their proper place.

Although we intend to distribute all these materials systematically into two parts, they nevertheless seemed to us to require presentation in the form in which they occur, and even with the titles and words by which each item begins or ends in the Bellovacensian manuscript. That manuscript is far superior to the Vatican one, so that the reader may more easily understand what has been done by us.

## [Column 0019]

That codex has two parts. One contains the Fifth Synod; the other bears the following title, added by a more recent hand:

**THE SYNOD OF EPHESUS, WHERE THE HERESY OF NESTORIUS IS CONDEMNED TOGETHER WITH ITS AUTHOR**

The following materials then appear.

I. Here begins the letter of Anastasius, bishop of the city of Rome, to John, bishop of Jerusalem, concerning the name of Rufinus. Opening: “It is indeed characteristic of proven affection,” etc. Closing: “Let him see where he can be absolved.”

II. Here begins [the work] concerning the faith of the same Rufinus. Opening: “Because of the veneration,” etc. Closing: “Let them be anathema, as being done daily by God.”

III. Memorandum for the reader against the heresy of Pelagius and Coelestius, and also against the writings of Julian, by Marius Mercator, servant of Christ. Opening: “The question against the Catholic faith,” etc. Closing: “We convict and lament.”

IV. Book of Annotations. Opening: “Now Julian’s words,” etc. Closing: “A ridiculous mouse is born.”

V. Marius Mercator, servant of Christ, sends greetings to his fellow servant and reader. Opening: “The Greek discourse is Theodore’s,” etc. Closing: “One God in the Trinity, always and for ever.”

VI. Another letter. Marius Mercator, servant of Christ, sends greetings to his fellow servant and reader. Opening: “This is the doctrine of Paul of Samosata and Nestorius, no less impious than vain,” etc. Closing: “He was condemned.”

VII. Another item. M. Mercator, servant of Christ, sends an equal greeting in the Lord to his fellow servant and reader. Opening: “Of Nestorius, formerly bishop,” etc. Closing: “Beauty is pleasing.”

VIII. Now follows the first discourse on impiety in the Church, delivered to the people, in which he unhappily fell and disastrously collapsed concerning the Lord’s Incarnation. Opening: “The doctrine of piety is,” etc. Closing: “For ever and ever. Amen.”

IX. Another treatise. Opening: “As for the insults of the heretics against me, I think,” etc. Closing: “Thus all will be made alive in Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever.”

Opening: “The preceding teacher, sweet to us,” etc. Closing: “The God of peace will be with you.”

Opening: “Against whose perverse,” etc. The first discourse delivered, translated by us from Greek into Latin word for word. Opening: “With many and frequent storms of anguish,” etc. Closing: “And the remainder, which does not pertain to the present matter.”

XIX. Another discourse of the same man on Adam, publicly delivered in the Church. Opening: “The sun indeed above the earth,” etc. Closing: “Restoring her from there.”

XX. Another discourse of the same man on the passage written: “I will give you all these things, if you fall down and worship me”; its beginning is: “In another discourse,” etc. Closing: “And cast him down.”

XXI. Another treatise of the same man to the people on Adam. Opening: “And the instruction of the hearers who seek me,” etc. Closing: “In Christ, to whom be glory for ever.”

XXII. Now follows a copy of the letter of the same Nestorius replying to Coelestius, translated from Greek into Latin. Opening: “To the honorable and most religious,” etc. Closing: “Most religious brother.”

XXIII. Another copy of the Memorandum concerning Coelestius, delivered in Greek not only to the Church of Constantinople but also to many most religious men; it was likewise presented to the most pious emperor Theodosius, ever Augustus, and translated from Greek into Latin by the same Marius Mercator, servant of Christ, in the consulship of Dionysius and Florentius, most illustrious men. Through this Memorandum, once the most disastrous error had been recognized, by imperial command both Julian, its defender and follower, together with his other associates and participants, and later Coelestius were expelled from the city of Constantinople; and at the Council of Ephesus, where 275 bishops were present, they were condemned. Opening: “A certain eunuch named Coelestius,” etc. Closing: “They were received.”

[Col. 0021]

XXIV. Another item: the chapters of Nestorius’s blasphemies, in which he contradicts the letters sent to him by the holy Coelestine, bishop of the city of Rome, and Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and attempts, by answering the twelve chapters of the faith sent to him in very brief arguments, to refute them. Opening: “Now, concerning Bishop Cyril,” etc. Closing: “It absolutely cannot be anything.”

XXVI. Excerpts from Nestorius’s own book. Opening: “In quaternion XVI,” etc. Closing: “To have preached to the people.”

XXVII. Names of the bishops who signed. Opening: “Cyril,” etc. Closing: “Here end the names of the bishops who attended the synod against Nestorius, numbering 193.”

The same Theodoret’s preface to the five books which, instigated by the devil, he composed against blessed Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, and against the holy Council of Ephesus, by which Nestorius was condemned. Opening: “Before the assembly convened at Ephesus,” etc. Closing: “Assuming the designation of its nature.”

XXXI. Theodoret sends greetings in the Lord to my truly God-loving lord and venerable holy Father Nestorius. Opening: “Because urban society and service to you,” etc. Closing: “We greet you most warmly.”

XXXIII. Letter of Theodoret to Andrew of Samosata. Opening: “The distinguished man Aristolaus,” etc. Closing: “Giving strength.”

XXXIV. To Himerius, bishop of Nicomedia, among other matters. Opening: “We make our intention clear,” etc. Closing: “Clinging to your footsteps.”

XXXV. To John of Antioch, after he learned that John had condemned Nestorius’s doctrine, following other matters. Opening: “Let it not be hidden from your holiness that afterward,” etc. Closing: “Contains the Apostolic [teaching].”

Another excerpt from the acts composed against Domnus, bishop of Antioch, in which Domnus is accused because, while he was present, that most impious Theodoret had dared publicly to say the following in the Church, after the death of Cyril, of holy memory, bishop of Alexandria, insulting his blessed repose. Opening: “No one now [is] nobody,” etc. Closing: “They proclaim God.”

XXXVII. From the second codex of the fourth book of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, folio ten, against Saint Augustine, who defended original sin and argued in Catholic fashion that Adam had been made mortal through transgression. Opening: “With so many things existing,” etc. Closing: “To endure experience.”

XXXVIII. Another passage of the same Theodore from some other book against the Lord Jesus Christ and his Incarnation. Opening: “For he also says,” etc. Closing: “Had been made.”

Opening: “To the religious and God-beloved fellow priest Nestorius,” etc. Closing: “Let him be anathema who is life-giving as God.”

XLIII. Scholia of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten. Opening: “What is Christ?” etc. Closing: “With the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever.”

# CHAPTER III. What We Have Contributed to the Edition of the Works of Marius Mercator

Since Mercator’s works are so diverse and have been scattered so recklessly here and there through the manuscripts, it seemed necessary first to restore them to order. Nothing appeared more convenient than to divide them into two parts: the first would contain everything pertaining to the Coelestian heresy; the second, everything pertaining to the Nestorian heresy.

It also seemed appropriate to attach notes to each work, chiefly historical or philological rather than dogmatic—notes that would illuminate otherwise obscure passages and would be drawn from authors already known in their own right. Even so, they would generally be drawn only from those who lived in the same period as Marius, or who themselves played a role in either of the two controversies, namely, the Nestorian and the Coelestian heresy.

It also seemed appropriate to add certain other materials—such as collections from Nestorius, Theodore of Mopsuestia, and others—even though they are not found in Marius, to the other materials diligently collected by Marius: partly so that other matters might be confirmed by them, and partly because, although they may have the weight of notes, they could not be inserted without considerable loss of method and concision.

# CHAPTER IV. A Sample of What First Becomes Known from the Works of Marius Mercator

Mercator transmitted little about the doctrines of the faith, but much about the history of the Coelestian and Nestorian heresies—matters that until now either had not been adequately explained by any writers or had not been committed to memory at all. They can conveniently be divided into two parts, corresponding respectively to the two heresies, although not everything can now be presented: for how could it be done without producing a book of considerable size? A sample must therefore be given, to stimulate the reader’s appetite.

## § I. A Sample of Matters Pertaining to the Pelagian Heresy

Besides what others have left in writing about Pelagius, his disciple Coelestius, and their follower Julian, or about the condemnation of those same heretics—first at Carthage by Aurelius, when the deacon Paulinus accused Coelestius; then at Diospolis in Palestine, when the bishops Eros and Lazarus accused Pelagius; afterward in two provincial councils, those of Carthage and Numidia; later at Rome by Innocent and Zosimus; then in the plenary council of Africa; finally at Constantinople by Atticus, at Rome by Coelestine, and at Ephesus by the Fathers who condemned Nestorius—

besides these matters, I say, which have hitherto either been explicitly transmitted or at least indicated by Augustine and other writers, Mercator now teaches the following for the first time.

The Pelagian, or rather Coelestian, heresy—which he pursues as a single movement—took its origin among the Syrians, especially in Cilicia, from Theodore, bishop of the town of Mopsuestia. From there it was first brought into Rome under Anastasius by a certain Syrian Rufinus; hence the popular opinion concerning Rufinus of Aquileia is disproved. It was handed on to Pelagius, the teacher of Coelestius, and was disseminated by Coelestius. With Julian and other bishops lending their support, it gained strength in Italy, aided by the strategies, letters, and books published by Julian.

Not only Julian but also Theodore of Mopsuestia wrote against Saint Augustine, the defender of original sin; and many other matters besides are now revealed. It is better to report these individually as they relate to the persons who played their respective parts in this affair.

Theodore, therefore, bishop of Mopsuestia, was the first in Cilicia to raise the question against the Catholic faith. He defended the view that the ancestors of the human race, Adam and Eve, were created mortal by God; that no later human being had been harmed by their transgression, but that they had harmed only themselves and made themselves guilty before God—nothing else whatsoever. Mercator is the first to teach this.

Julian met Theodore in Cilicia before composing his final work against Saint Augustine, and in his books he extravagantly praised him as his teacher. Mercator is also the first to transmit this fact.

At that time Theodore wrote five books against Saint Augustine, who defended original sin. Mercator presents substantial fragments of them, from which it is certain that these are precisely the five books of Theodore of Antioch against those who assert that human beings sin by nature and not by will—books that Photius reports having read. Before Mercator, this was entirely unheard of; nevertheless, it is extraordinarily useful for history, for correcting Photius, and for overturning common opinions.

Immediately after Julian’s departure from Theodore, a council of the bishops of Cilicia Secunda was convened, and Theodore himself condemned Julian, although not sincerely. This council too had not previously been known.

A certain Syrian Rufinus, Mercator writes, first brought the heresy against original sin to Rome under Anastasius. Being a crafty man, he wished to avoid the odium of so wicked an error; he therefore instructed Pelagius to be somewhat bolder and urged him to write. Thus two common opinions are overturned: one concerning Rufinus of Aquileia as Coelestius’s teacher in this matter; the other concerning Pelagius as the author of the heresy, when he was only its disseminator, or at most a timid and covert transmitter. How much light this sheds upon Pelagian history!

Pelagius, instructed by the Syrian Rufinus, soon wrote commentaries on the Apostle Paul.

[Note: [Col. 0029] We have already had occasion to publish these commentaries; if you wish, consult volume XXX of our *Patrologia*. EDITOR.]

He published them long before the devastation of the City by the Visigoths. Marius presents fragments from them, especially the passage containing the objections of those who deny the transmission of sin. Through Mercator’s assistance, both the authorship of the commentaries and the time at which they were written are established, and many historical conclusions follow.

After Pelagius had deceived the Fathers at Diospolis, he was condemned and expelled from Jerusalem by a later synod presided over by Theodotus, bishop of Antioch, with the same accusers, Eros and Lazarus, pressing their case. Concerning this matter, Theodotus and Praylius of Jerusalem, who had previously favored Pelagius, sent a letter with the acts to the bishop of the City. No one except Mercator mentions this council; yet how important is it to know for understanding Pelagian affairs!

At this same council, as at Diospolis, certain passages from writings addressed to a widow were brought forward. Mercator identifies her by name and presents fragments of the books much more extensively than they are found either in Jerome or in Augustine. Thus light is shed on what is reported concerning this matter in the book *On the Proceedings in Palestine*.

Coelestius was indeed noble by birth and a legal scholar of that period, but, being a eunuch by a defect of nature, he was born so from his mother’s womb. From the time of Anastasius onward he attached himself to Pelagius, who taught him the heresy received from Rufinus. By his incredible loquacity he drew many over to his side. Apart from Mercator, no one has transmitted this; yet it overturns several popular conjectures concerning Coelestius’s origin, the birth of the Pelagian heresy, and related matters.

Accused at Carthage by Paulinus, the deacon of Saint Ambrose, and excommunicated by Aurelius, he fled to Asia and became a presbyter at Ephesus. Mercator transmits this, thereby providing considerable illumination for the history.

Later he was condemned not only by Atticus at Constantinople, with letters sent to the principal sees, but also by Pope Zosimus, who ordered all bishops to sign his formal letters. Much concerning this double condemnation is either newly taught or brought out of obscurity.

Finally, with Mercator pressing the matter—he presented his Memorandum to the emperor Theodosius in the year 429—Coelestius was expelled from Constantinople once again. He wrote to Nestorius and received from him a consolatory letter, which Mercator presents.

Concerning Julian, apart from certain domestic matters hitherto unheard of, though not without interest—for example, that he was the son of Memorius by Juliana, a most honorable matron; that he was of servile birth, though believed to have been substituted by a nurse in place of a legitimate child; that he was excessively devoted to reading the books of Petronius Arbiter and Valerius Martial; and that he had two sisters, entrusted to his guardianship after their parents’ death, whom he did not sufficiently restrain—or at least one of them—from the ruin of chastity—Mercator is the first to teach facts of greater importance.

He was ordained by Saint Innocent, the pontiff, as bishop of the town of Eclanum, near the Ampsanctian marsh. Thus the popular question concerning the location of his bishopric is resolved.

As long as the holy bishop who ordained him lived, he remained in a sincere confession of the faith, at least outwardly, and condemned Pelagius and Coelestius. But immediately after Innocent’s death he revealed his mind and openly refused to subscribe to the condemnation of those same heretics, as though it had been wrongly carried out. He wrote to Pope Zosimus, the condemner, attempting to mock the Apostolic See with ambiguous language and maliciously twisting the meaning of the five condemned propositions. Fragments of these letters are preserved by Mercator and by no one else.

He also wrote several books. Of these, he composed the last eight against Augustine’s second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* in Cilicia, at the house of Theodore of Mopsuestia, and published them after crossing the sea, during a long journey with other deposed bishops. This becomes known for the first time through Mercator’s report.

Although Nestorius had received Julian and Coelestius into friendship together with the deposed bishops, and had given them hope of absolution, he nevertheless delivered four discourses in the Church against them, with Julian and his companions listening, and in defense of death as a punishment inflicted upon Adam for sin. Marius Mercator presents these discourses, almost complete and previously unknown, together with a letter in which Nestorius replied to Coelestius after receiving the denunciatory letters of the holy Coelestine and Cyril, and, by his own example, consoled his friend, who had been expelled from Constantinople.

Mercator is the first to report that the letter which Zosimus sent concerning the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius to all the bishops of the world was extremely long and comprehensive. It contained, evidently, every point of the accusation and the entire case both of Pelagius and of Coelestius. He also reports that it was sent to the Eastern Churches, to the diocese of Egypt, Constantinople, Thessalonica, Jerusalem, and also Carthage, so that it might be signed by all the bishops, with the penalty of deposition proposed for those who refused. This wonderfully illuminates the history.

For three points are thereby understood which would otherwise create difficulty. First, what was meant by “the greater Churches” in the Roman world; second, that what was written to all the bishops of the world was transmitted to the bishops of the greater Churches so that they might communicate it to the bishops of the lesser Churches; finally, that the letter of the emperor Honorius to Aurelius of Carthage did not command Aurelius himself to obtain the signatures of all the bishops of the world, but only those of the Africans.

Two councils were convened in the case of the Pelagians, previously unheard of: one at Antioch under Theodotus, attended by Praylius of Jerusalem; the other in Cilicia, at which Theodore of Mopsuestia was present. Both are now known for the first time from Marius Mercator. The former was held in the year 417, the latter around the year 424.

## § II. A Sample of Matters Pertaining to the Nestorian Heresy

Among those who played roles in the Nestorian case, Marius Mercator mentions Nestorius, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret, and Eutherius as standing against the Catholic faith; and, on behalf of the Catholic faith, Cyril and the Fathers of Ephesus. Concerning them he teaches many things that until this day were either uncertain or entirely unknown.

The discourses of Nestorius were unknown. Mercator presents them translated by himself into Latin; in them the heresiarch enclosed the entire poison of his error.

Two letters of Nestorius were likewise unknown: one to the heretic Coelestius, mentioned above; the other to Saint Coelestine, the pope, written shortly before he received the letters of condemnation. This letter is very different from the two other letters that Nestorius wrote to the same man, one concerning the Pelagian case and the other concerning his own.

It was likewise unknown from which books of Nestorius the excerpts had been taken that either Peter, chief of the notaries, presented to the Ephesian Fathers for condemnation, or Saint Cyril refuted in his five books of contradiction, or in his *elenchus* (“refutation”). Mercator names and publishes the individual books and discourses.

It was also unknown which pestilential treatise of Nestorius Cassian refuted in seven books *On the Incarnation*, especially in the seventh, where he adduces substantial fragments. Mercator teaches that this was the first discourse, entitled “On the Virgin Birth,” and that it was the original cause of all the disturbances.

It was no less unknown which book of Nestorius on the Incarnation was mentioned by Gennadius; which homily on the Incarnation was referred to by Theophanes, Cedrenus, and Nicephorus; and which dreadful absurdities were recalled by the author of the letter attributed to Theodoret and addressed to Sporatius. From Mercator it is clear that this was the very first discourse, whose beginning is drawn from the words: “The doctrine of piety,” etc.

Until now scholars have doubted on what occasion Proclus delivered that celebrated panegyrical address *to the Theotokos* (*eis Theotokon*) in the Church, with Nestorius presiding, as the authors of that period report. It is plainly gathered from Mercator that it was delivered to refute the first discourse of Nestorius, and that Nestorius refuted it by an extemporaneous address and by other discourses afterward, which Marius presents complete.

It was uncertain, though not entirely unknown, which discourse of Nestorius Saint Cyril had in mind in his letter to the clergy residing at Constantinople, when he wrote that its beginning was: “The insults of the heretics against me,” etc. From Mercator it is perfectly clear that this was Nestorius’s seventh discourse, than which none is either more pestilential or more lengthy. It also becomes clear that the letter was not addressed to the Constantinopolitan clergy, divided by mutual hatreds, as the common edition states, but to Cyril’s own representatives who were managing the affairs of the Alexandrian Church at Constantinople.

Hardly anyone could understand what Theopemptus, one of the bishops who delivered the denunciatory letters to Nestorius at Constantinople on Sunday, had reported to the Fathers at Ephesus when he said that, after receiving the letters, Nestorius had publicly proposed in his sermon the same doctrines as before, and doctrines much worse than those. Mercator makes this clear by reporting the two later discourses, which the enraged Nestorius filled with blasphemies—one delivered on Saturday, 13 December, and the other on the following Sunday, in the year 430.

It was not indeed obscure that Nestorius had set his anathemas against those written by Cyril for the Catholics; but the time at which he composed them was unknown. Since they existed only in Latin, it was also unknown through which translator they had reached us. Mercator teaches both points: he not only translated them himself but also refuted them in a lengthy and learned contradiction. These are a few of the many matters concerning Nestorius contained in the notes.

As for Theodore of Mopsuestia, besides the excerpts from the five books against Saint Augustine mentioned earlier, many passages from his fifteen books *On the Incarnation*, different from those found in the Fifth Synod and in Facundus of Hermiane and Leontius the Scholastic, are now published for the first time from Mercator’s collection.

Mercator’s testimony also defends the Fifth Synod against Facundus of Hermiane’s calumny that it attributed an impious creed to Theodore of Mopsuestia. For Mercator not only translated this creed from Greek into Latin but also overturned it in a learned refutation.

[Col. 0033] What Theodore of Cyrus’s faith was before the Council of Chalcedon has been disputed contentiously by learned men. Many, following Agobard, preferred to believe more charitably that he had fought against the truth for the sake of truth, and that he had agreed with Nestorius or disagreed with Cyril more in words than in conviction. But Mercator, producing documents that had previously been unknown, proves the man to have been a supporter of the Nestorian heresy—not merely one who retained it in his mind, but one who openly professed it until the year 447. For he excerpted very extensively from the five books that Theodore composed against Saint Cyril and the Council of Ephesus; indeed, he also reported passages from letters and sermons that plainly refute Theodore’s defenders. Mercator supplies all this, hitherto entirely unknown, and it is now published for the first time.

Now also, through Mercator’s assistance, the sermon of Eutherius, a not insignificant adherent of the Nestorian party, is read for the first time. It is mutilated, certainly, and its preface is, as it were, severed at the beginning; nevertheless, it is not without value, since from it the author of that work can clearly be identified which Photius attributes to Theodore in twenty-seven books, and of which twenty-one books are found in the second volume of the works of Saint Athanasius. For although the first six books may belong to Theodore, the others certainly belong to Eutherius. The sequence of the books and the connection of one with another demonstrate that they all have the same author; and the information Mercator has supplied is scarcely surpassed in usefulness for the history of those times.

Moreover, the number of the Fathers assembled at Ephesus, which previously had been reported differently by different authors on the basis of rather slight conjecture than probable reasoning, is now stated definitely by Mercator in more than one place as 274.

Cyril’s letter which, in the commonly circulated editions of the Council of Ephesus, is said to have been written to the clergy of Constantinople, who were fighting among themselves in mutual dissension, bears this title in Mercator: “Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, to his clergy stationed at Constantinople.” As Mercator’s translator presents it, it differs astonishingly from the commonly circulated Greek and Latin editions alike. It contains things that establish its own credibility, demonstrate that the Greek text is corrupt, and disclose many hidden mysteries of the history.

These, then, are only a very few of the many things that can first be learned from Mercator with almost no reasoning, by simple inspection. Those conclusions, however, that are established by certain arguments—although there are many of them, and although they are highly useful, indeed necessary, for illuminating the history—ought not to be set down here, but in the observations, lest the preface become longer than the rules permit.

Regarding the observations, I should like to inform you, reader, before I finish this preface, that I deliberately made them almost entirely historical or philological, as I have already said. The doctrines of faith at issue in Mercator’s works are few in themselves and, especially after so many definitions of the Church and explanations by learned men, seem to me to present either no difficulty or very little. We wanted the observations to be of such a kind that the material found in Mercator would confer authority upon the accepted writers, while at the same time borrowing credibility from them in return. For we compared this work of Marius, whatever its extent, with all authors of the same or approximately the same period, and we did so with such painstaking labor that no one who has dealt with the Nestorian and Coelestian controversy has escaped being read through carefully and inquisitively more than once.

## CHAPTER V. How the works of Marius Mercator came into our hands

I do not think it will be unwelcome to the scholarly reader if, before bringing this preface to an end, I briefly explain how Mercator’s works came to me and how I happened to undertake their publication.

Father Peter Possinus had sent to Father Philip Labbe, at the command of the most eminent Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Francesco Barberini, a *Commonitorium* of Mercator—whose author was then unknown, but whose work nevertheless seemed worthy of being inserted into the second volume of the Councils, under the year 412. As soon as the indefatigable collector of the councils received this treasure, he shared it amicably with me, knowing that I was possessed by no ordinary zeal to gather everything bearing upon the history of the Pelagian heresy.

While we read through it together with delight—the “little golden monument,” as he himself called it, of antiquity—it happened by chance that we opened a manuscript codex of the distinguished Church of Beauvais. At the same moment the name of Marius Mercator met our eyes, and, as we immediately turned over various little works, indeed even the *Commonitorium* itself sent from Rome appeared before us. I can scarcely express the joy with which this filled me.

When Possinus learned of this good fortune through our letters, he himself more carefully consulted the codex preserved in the Vatican Library, which had once belonged to the Count Palatine of the Rhine; from it he sent a transcript of what we had indicated was contained in the Beauvais manuscript.

Relying upon the great and unquestionable assistance of these two codices, Labbe was preparing an edition of Mercator’s works. It was, however, mutilated in large part and without notes; for, overwhelmed by the immense labor of the general councils, he could neither investigate what lay hidden in confused and disordered form nor examine attentively the individual passages that called for clarification.

An unexpected death forestalled the man’s undertaking and was the reason that the work was offered to me as though bequeathed by his will. I accepted the offer all the more willingly because, although I was unequal to him in talent and far inferior in learning, I nevertheless had more leisure than a man occupied with the business of seventeen centuries, and could more readily devote myself both to investigating what the disordered arrangement of the codices concealed and to reflecting more carefully upon certain obscure passages in the observations.

For some time, however, the image of my friend kept appearing before my mind while I was working through the codices and held me back from hastening. His loss had not been fully assuaged by mourning before, nor has the passage of time yet brought sufficient consolation.

For again and again, as though Marius were reminding me, I recall how great the deceased man’s virtue was as an example; how great the gentleness of his character in companionship; how great his intelligence, memory, and breadth of learning; how indefatigable his labor in study; how ardent his zeal for the faith in persecuting heretics; how mild his patience in enduring the slanders of the envious; and how frank his freedom in bearing witness to the truth.

The loss of these qualities was in itself enough to produce no slight grief and the deepest longing. Yet both would have been increased by the further thought that death, before his years were mature, had begrudged us the enjoyment of so many gifts—unless, because virtues supplied the number of years lacking, death had seemed to us not so much death as the fullest crown of a life rich in merits.

For Labbe had embraced religious virtues when scarcely more than a boy, and had borne the yoke of Christ almost before adolescence. From this came such innocence throughout his life, such integrity of character and devotion to God, as modesty could not conceal, however much his other virtues might impede it; nor could human praise on earth adequately reward him, but only God’s munificence in heaven.

His virtue was assisted in its purity by an insatiable desire for knowledge and a mind perpetually attentive to every branch of learning. When was he ever at leisure? What part of the honorable disciplines did he leave untouched in which, once he wished to engage, he did not excel? He despised none, however humble, because he knew that all were capable of advancing the glory of God. Indeed, at times he descended from the loftiest summit of divine subjects even to grammar, remembering Christ’s command that little ones not be kept away from his teaching.

His study was matched by a labor that we could all admire, though no one could imitate. You would have thought that the man was invigorated by what weakens others, and relaxed his mind through what strains theirs. To those who examined his museum after his death, it seemed almost miraculous that he had written more with his own hand than others are accustomed to read, and had made so many annotations on nearly every author that he could deservedly be called a library of libraries.

Yet he was not therefore one of those for whom paper takes the place of a brain and all learning exists only in writing. His memory was extraordinarily capacious in breadth, tenacious in permanence, ready in usefulness, and felicitous to the point of wonder. I appeal as witnesses to all who made habitual use of him. Who ever asked him about historical matters without his immediately and readily bringing before them the time, the persons, and every relevant detail? Who asked him about humane letters without his reciting, as if from a book, the names of authors, their conflicting opinions, and the arguments by which each either defended itself or refuted another? Who consulted him about theology—scholastic, polemical, or moral—without his answering almost to the envy of scholars?

Yet beware, whoever you are who read this, lest you entertain the opinion—no less insulting than false—that Labbe should be counted among those whom, as the common proverb has it, a happy memory serves in place of intelligence.

Nature had bestowed upon him so liberally every gift of intelligence—those useful for shaping and arranging the forms of things, those for penetrating subtly into the innermost parts of the sciences, those for the delights of poetry, and those for unraveling the knots of history—that I often believed, when others considered the matter more attentively, that his intelligence had taken the place of his memory. He handled both the exposition of matters and the recitation of a speech from memory with such felicity.

He was born at Bourges, among the Bituriges, to parents of the highest nobility, in the year of Christ 1607, on 10 July. He lived forty-four years in the Society of Jesus, with an enduring reputation both for piety and for learning. He was approaching his sixtieth year when he was consumed by a continuous fever lasting fifty-eight days. He died on 16 March 1667. His death matched his life: pious and tranquil. He may even be said to have foreseen it, since, while his disease raged, he poured forth the following verses to Christ hanging upon the cross and to the Blessed Virgin. They seemed to belong here as the epitaph, like the final voice of a swan singing before its own funeral.

### Prayer to Christ

[Col. 0035]

While the fever burned my marrow,

And I endured troubled nights,

And troubled days,

Fasting, wakeful, heavy, harsh,

Unpleasant to me, burdensome to others,

These things, Christ, we offered to the Father and to you—

To you whom, hanging from the shameful beam,

Through the whole night and through the whole day,

I continually behold,

Soothing my sufferings with your sufferings,

And your sufferings with mine.

And whatever I have endured, and whatever the harmful force

Of disease still threatens that must be endured,

I dedicated, and dedicate, to your love,

A languishing victim. Nor do I cease to ask

That, when my final light shall come,

The final day for a mortal,

For a Christian the one day of true concerns,

The one repose from vain concerns,

A day to be feared by the people, by kings, by all—

The day which was once your single concern,

Which, Arsenius, you wanted to preside over

Everywhere among your cares—

When that day shall come, and deep night

Shall close my eyes for a long time,

And my body, laid out and carried by the pious hands of the Fathers,

Shall be delivered as food to the worms of the earth,

And from the dreadful blast of the trumpet

Shall be summoned from its urn before the severe Judge,

Be an everlasting light to my soul;

Command it to fly immediately to you,

To embrace you and remain in your embrace,

And, together with you, with the Father

And the Holy Spirit,

To sit in realms above the stars with you.

### Prayer to the Virgin

[Col. 0037A]

And you, too, whom I have so often called upon,

Amid the burning heat of fever,

Virgin Mother of Christ, and our Mother as well.

For I remember that you were my mother,

My mother from earliest childhood even to my gray hairs,

Leading me by the hand through every step

Of an age consecrated to you and to your Son;

Sheltering me in your bosom through all

The rough places of a sterner life,

And the burdens of more arduous study,

Which you watered, as it were, with your milk.

This one thing I now ask: that you, who were always a gracious mother

To me while I lived, Virgin,

May also be a mother when death is in danger.

Receive the final breath of one who lies here;

May this breath follow you to the stars,

It which on earth always followed

Mary as its guide and Mary as its patroness.

## CHAPTER VI

[Note: [Col. 0037B] This work is not found among Augustine’s writings as they are now reckoned, nor was it found there even when either Bede or Peter of Tripoli wrote commentaries on Paul. For a passage from it is cited, yet not as from a letter, but as from a book addressed to Dulcitius. Nevertheless, no prudent person will doubt that it is Augustine’s letter to our Marius Mercator, since it has testimony from Augustine in an unquestionably authentic work, and its name, date, and subject agree with our Mercator. For in Augustine’s time Mercator was especially attacking the Pelagians because they denied that the death of all human beings had been imposed as a punishment in return for the sin of our first parent.

I infer that the letter was extremely long, not only because Augustine and Possidius list it among letters equal in length to treatises, but also because, although it contained a response to several matters raised by the Pelagians, the portion that survives treats at length only one incidental question—or rather objection—and that in itself not of the greatest importance. [Col. 0037C]

We established in the first chapter that the letter was written before the twentieth year of the fifth century, but how much earlier? Someone might perhaps believe that this cannot easily be determined, since the words “Although I no longer think that they say that, even if Adam had not sinned, he would have been mortal in body”—which, solely because of the expression “no longer,” seem to indicate some particular period—could be true whenever the letter is said to have been written: whether after the Council of Carthage in 412, after the Council of Diospolis in 415, after Zosimus’s decree sent to all the bishops of the world in 418, or finally after the universal African synod of that same year. For in all these assemblies the opinion of Coelestius, which is under discussion, was condemned. Nevertheless, the words cited unquestionably refer to the period following Zosimus’s decree and the African synod. Both were more widely known than the other two councils, namely Carthage and Diospolis, and Augustine seems to be speaking of a condemnation that would have been well known to Mercator and the Pelagians.

[Col. 0038B] Indeed, I suspect—and not altogether rashly—that the words beginning the letter had approximately this meaning: “You undoubtedly know very well what was issued by Pope Zosimus to all the bishops throughout the world against the errors of the Pelagians,” and so forth. For Augustine wrote something similar to Optatus at about the same time. I also conjecture that Mercator questioned Augustine about the Pelagian controversies in the same way that he was later questioned by Hilary and Prosper about the controversies of Marseilles: not so much about what should be thought concerning the matter itself, since it had already been decided, as about how either to meet the objections by which the Pelagians wished to defend themselves or to dissolve the objections with which they troubled the Catholics.

The subject is clear from these words of Augustine: “Concerning certain questions of the Pelagians, who deny that death was imposed in return for sin.” The question was how one might meet the objections of the Coelestians, who cited various passages of Scripture to prove that death comes upon human beings not because of the merit of guilt but by a necessity of nature. Above all, they cited the passage in which the Apostle seems to teach (1 Thess. 4:16) that not everyone will die, but that some will pass immediately from mortal life to immortal life. From this they proceeded to prove that not all are held liable for the sin of the first man, since justice requires a common punishment to be repaid for a common guilt.

The passage from the First Epistle to the Thessalonians was supported by another from the First Epistle to the Corinthians, where the Apostle says: “We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51). From this it is evident that the Pelagians did not use the commonly received Latin edition of the New Testament, but rather the Greek. For Jerome notes (Epistle 152, near the end) that what is read in the Latin codices—“We shall indeed all rise, but we shall not all be changed”—is not found in the Greek volumes. Instead, they read either “We shall all sleep, but we shall not all be changed,” or “We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.” Pelagius himself makes the same observation in his Commentary (Preface, chapter 1).]

### Part of the letter written by Saint Augustine to Mercator

It is established that Augustine wrote Mercator a long and weighty letter, both because Possidius counts it among his works and because Augustine himself borrowed from it the solution to a difficult question.

The passage of the years—or some other hidden cause—has deprived us of the entire letter. The portion that survives is found in the book *On Eight Questions of Dulcitius* (Augustine’s Works, vol. IV), where Saint Augustine answered Dulcitius’s questions in such a way that, for seven questions, he supplied either a solution, as he himself puts it, or at least his own discussion, drawing upon earlier little works.

He solved the first partly from the book *On Faith and Works* and partly from the *Enchiridion*; the second from *On the Care to Be Had for the Dead* and the *Enchiridion*. To the third he wrote as follows:

1. “Your third question is whether we should believe that judgment will take place immediately at the Lord’s coming, or after an interval of time. You say that, since we read that in the days of his coming those who remain will be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and will thus always be with the Lord, you wish to know whether judgment will immediately accompany his coming, and whether those who are caught up into the clouds will be released into death—unless perhaps we ought to understand the transformation itself as taking the place of death.

2. “To your question, in which you ask whether judgment should be believed to take place immediately at the Lord’s coming, I think the faith of the Creed is sufficient. In it we confess that Christ will come from the right hand of the Father to judge the living and the dead. Since this is the very reason for his coming, what else will he do immediately upon coming except that for which he will come?

3. “As for those who will be caught up in the clouds, in a certain letter that I wrote [Note: [Col. 0039A] From this passage we have concluded that Mercator was neither a bishop when Augustine wrote to him, nor a presbyter, indeed not even a deacon. Otherwise the holy man would have called him either a fellow bishop—which all bishops of that age customarily did when speaking of their colleagues—or a fellow presbyter, which they did for the most part—or a fellow deacon, a form that Augustine uniquely made a practice of using when the person in question was a deacon, as is clear from his letter to Memorius, whose son Julian he calls a fellow deacon (Epistle 131).] to my son named MERCATOR, which begins: [Note: [Col. 0039A] If the subject was Zosimus’s decree against Pelagius and Coelestius, as a substantial conjecture indeed suggests, it may be concluded from this passage that Marius Mercator wrote to Augustine from a place where the judgment was widely known—that is, from the city of Rome, where the decision of the Apostolic See was read before a very large gathering of the people and accepted by the signatures of the city’s clergy.] ‘You undoubtedly know very well,’ and so forth, when he had consulted me about certain questions of the Pelagians, who deny [Note: [Col. 0039A] The seventh dissertation will establish how subtly Mercator perceived the secret of the entire Pelagian heresy and how learnedly he questioned Augustine about the root from which all the subsequent doctrines arose, so that, once the root had been cut out, the rest might easily be removed. There, I think, it will become clear that from the Pelagian error concerning death not being imposed as punishment for sin, nearly countless other errors were propagated.] that death was imposed in return for sin. To what extent I discussed the matter, read in what follows.” [Note: [Col. 0039B]

Bede, it is believed, transferred this entire passage into his commentary on chapter 4 of the First Epistle to the Thessalonians, from the words, “The Apostle said, when he was speaking,” as far as the words, “to live without having tasted death.” He then adds from the twentieth book of *The City of God* the solution to the same question, though not in the same sense:

“It is commonly asked whether those whom Christ will find alive here, whose person the Apostle represented in himself and in those who were then living with him, will never die at all, or whether at the very moment when they are caught up with those who rise in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, they will pass with extraordinary speed through death into immortality.

“For it cannot be said that it is impossible that, while they are being carried upward through the air, they should in that interval both die and come to life again.
