For when he says, ‘And so we shall always be with the Lord,’ this should not be understood as though he said that we would always remain with the Lord in the air while dying, since he himself certainly will not remain there, but will pass through the place as he comes. We shall go to meet him as he comes, not remain with him there. Rather, we shall always be with the Lord in this sense: wherever we are with him, we shall possess everlasting bodies.

“Toward this interpretation—that we should believe that those whom the Lord will find alive here will, in that brief interval, both suffer death and receive immortality—the Apostle himself seems to press us when he says: ‘In Christ all shall be made alive’; while elsewhere, speaking of the resurrection of the bodies, he says: ‘What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies.’ How, then, will those whom Christ finds alive here be made alive in him through immortality, even if they do not die, when we see that the words ‘What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies’ were spoken for this very reason? Or, if we correctly say that only those human bodies are sown which, by dying in whatever manner, return to the earth, as is also contained in the divinely pronounced sentence against the transgressor, the father of the human race—‘You are earth, and to earth you shall go’—then we must admit that those whom Christ will find not yet departed from their bodies when he comes are not included either in the Apostle’s words or in those from Genesis. For they will be caught up into the clouds above and therefore will not be sown, since they neither go into the earth nor return to it, whether they experience no death at all or die for a little while in the air.

“But another consideration arises. The same Apostle says, when speaking to the Corinthians about the resurrection of bodies: ‘We shall all rise,’ or, as other codices have it, ‘We shall all sleep.’ Since resurrection cannot occur unless death has preceded it, and since in that passage we cannot understand sleep except as death, how will all either sleep or rise if so many whom Christ will find in the body will neither sleep nor rise? If, therefore, we believe that the saints who will be found alive when Christ comes and will be caught up to meet him in the air will, in that very rapture, depart from mortal bodies and immediately return to the same bodies made immortal, we will encounter no difficulty in the Apostle’s words—whether where he says, ‘What you sow is not made alive unless it dies,’ or where he says, ‘We shall all rise,’ or ‘We shall all sleep.’ For they too will not be made alive through immortality unless they die, even if only for a little while; and therefore they will not be excluded from the resurrection, which is preceded by sleep—brief indeed, but not nonexistent.

“Why should it seem incredible to us that the multitude of bodies should somehow be sown in the air and immediately there come to life again immortally and incorruptibly, when we believe what the same Apostle says elsewhere with complete clarity: that the resurrection will occur in the twinkling of an eye, and that the dust of the most ancient corpses will return to limbs destined to live without end with such ease and such immeasurable speed?

“Nor should we think that those future saints will be exempt from the sentence pronounced upon humanity, ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall go,’ merely because their bodies, when they die, will not fall to the earth. Rather, just as they will die in the very rapture, so they will rise again while being carried through the air. For ‘to earth you shall go’ means: in this state, having lost life, you shall go to what you were before you received life; that is, lifeless, you shall be what you were before you were animated. For God breathed the breath of life into Adam’s face when the man had been made a living soul. It was as though he were told: ‘You are animated earth, which you were not; you shall be lifeless earth, as you were,’ just as all the bodies of the dead are before they decay, and as those bodies will be if they die, wherever they die, when they are deprived of the life they will immediately receive again. Thus they will go to earth, because from living human beings they will become earth, just as what becomes ash goes into ash, what becomes old goes into old age, and what becomes a potsherd from clay goes into a potsherd; and in six hundred other ways we speak in the same manner. But how what we now conjecture as best we can with the limited powers of our reasoning will actually occur—we shall then be able to know.”

I thought this passage, though lengthy, ought to be included because, when compared with another passage, it shows how difficult Augustine regarded the question, since he more than once professed before Mercator that he preferred to listen to those more learned than himself. Certainly, in the book *The City of God* he seems inclined toward the opinion of the Fathers Origen, Chrysostom, and Jerome, who say that some will be found alive at Christ’s coming and will not die, but only be changed. In writing to Mercator, he follows the opposite position and carried along with him the greater part of the theologians who adhere to Saint Thomas (*In IV Sententiarum*, distinction 43). For the Master, [Col. 0041A] after teaching that Jerome and Ambrose were in conflict with one another—through a popular error he named Ambrose instead of the deacon Hilary—denied that human judgment could determine which position was more truthful.] 

Those, then, I say, about whom the Apostle spoke when he said concerning the resurrection of the dead, “And we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:16), do indeed raise a question, but on account of themselves, not on account of these others. For even if they themselves are not going to die, [Note: [Col. 0041A] That is, the Pelagians, of whom he says shortly afterward: “But whichever of these interpretations is more truthful and clearer may be found,” and so forth.] I do not see at all how this helps these men, since things can be said about them such as were said about those two—namely, Enoch and Elijah.

4. “But, so far as the words of the blessed Apostle are concerned, he does seem to assert that at the end of the world, when the Lord comes and the resurrection of the dead is to take place, some will be found not dead but alive, and will suddenly be changed into that immortality which is also given to the other saints. They will be caught up together with them, as he says, in the clouds. Nothing else has seemed correct to me whenever I have wished to reflect upon these words. Yet I would rather hear from those more learned, lest the Apostle should be found saying even to those who think that some will pass into perpetual life without death preceding: ‘Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies.’

5. “For what of the statement found in most codices, ‘We shall all rise’? How could this happen unless we all die? There is no resurrection unless death has preceded it. And the reading found in some codices, ‘We shall all sleep,’ compels and permits us to understand this much more easily and clearly. If anything similar is found elsewhere in the sacred books, it likewise seems to urge us to believe that no human beings will attain immortality unless death has preceded it. Therefore, when the Apostle said: ‘And we who are alive, who remain, will not precede those who have fallen asleep; for the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord’ (1 Thess. 4:16), I would, as I said, like to hear from those more learned concerning these words. Even if they can be explained to me in such a way that it may be understood from them that all human beings who are now living or will live after us are destined to die, [Note: [Col. 0041A] I do not remember reading that Augustine treated this question elsewhere than in the twentieth book of *The City of God*. I therefore have no doubt that the words now brought under examination refer to this passage. Augustine did not compose the twenty-two books of *The City of God* all at one time, as he himself teaches (*Sermon 2 on the Words of the Apostle*). He began them after the devastation of the city by Alaric, in answer to the pagans who attributed Rome’s fall to the Christian faith, and completed them before the death of Marcellinus, to whom he sent the entire work. He therefore composed them from the year 411, after Rome’s devastation, to the year 413, when Marcellinus was killed by the faction of Heraclian.] I am willing to correct whatever I have at some time thought differently about this. For we ought not to be unwilling students of teachers; and certainly a crooked man is better corrected than a hard man broken. Yet through the matters we have set down, our weakness or that of others may be exercised or instructed, without any canonical authority being established in them.”

6. “But if no other meaning can be found in these words of the Apostle, and it becomes clear that he intended what the very words seem to proclaim—that at the end of the age and at the second coming of the Lord there will be people who are not stripped of the body but clothed over with immortality, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life—then this interpretation will unquestionably agree with what we confess in the rule of faith: that the Lord will come to judge the living and the dead. By “the living” we should not here understand the righteous, and by “the dead” the unrighteous, although both righteous and unrighteous will be judged; rather, we should understand as living those whom his coming will find not yet departed from their bodies, and as dead those whom it will find already departed from their bodies.

7. “If this is established, the words ‘What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies’ (1 Cor. 15:36), and ‘We shall all rise,’ or ‘We shall all sleep’ (ibid., 51), will have to be examined to determine how they may be understood without contradicting the opinion that some are believed to live forever in their own bodies without tasting death.

8. “But whichever of these interpretations is more truthful and clearer may be found: what relevance will it have to the case of these people, whether all are punished by the death they owe, or whether some are spared this condition? For it remains certain that not only the death of the soul but also the death of the body would not have followed if sin had not preceded it, and that by the more wondrous power of grace the righteous will rise again from death to eternal blessedness than if they had never entered into the experience of death.

9. “Let this be said sufficiently concerning those about whom you wrote to me, although I no longer think that they say that, even if Adam had not sinned, he would nevertheless have been mortal in body.

10. “As for the question of the resurrection, however, because of those who are believed not to die but to pass from this mortality into immortality without death intervening, careful inquiry must be made; and [Note: [Col. 0042A]

From these words we previously established how highly Augustine regarded Mercator: from him he was willing to be taught despite being a layman; as an older man, by a younger man; and concerning a question that he confessed to be exceedingly difficult and obscure, so that he wished to hear those more learned.

Yet, to say frankly what I think about the matter as a whole, I cannot sufficiently wonder why Saint Augustine (Preface, chapter 2) asked Mercator to send him anything concerning this question that he had heard, read, or might yet hear, read, or be able to devise by a rational and complete argument that was settled and definitive.

Had Jerome not already answered inquiries about this matter from different people twice? Once, indeed, for Marcella of Rome, but more briefly (Epistle 59); and a second time for the Egyptian monks Minerivus and Alexander, in a learned letter [Col. 0042B] (Epistle 119), in which he embraced, even citing the actual words, whatever the most distinguished Greek writers had thought while treating this subject: Origen, Theodore of Heraclea, Acacius of Caesarea, Diodore of Tarsus, Apollinarius, and Didymus. Was there then such scarcity or neglect in Africa of Greek codices, even the most distinguished ones? Could only a few people at that time read in Greek the treatises that had not yet been translated into Latin? Or were Jerome’s own works so unknown in Africa, although they were spread throughout the entire world, that they were scarcely possessed even by the learned?]

If you have heard, read, or even now are able to hear, read, or devise anything concerning this matter that is settled and definitive through a reasonable and complete argument, I ask you not to be unwilling to send it to me. For—I confess this to your charity—I love learning more than teaching; and we are admonished of this also by the Apostle James, who says: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak” (James 1:19).

11. “Therefore, in order that we may learn, the sweetness of truth ought to invite us; in order that we may teach, the necessity of charity ought to compel us. Rather, we should pray that this necessity may pass away, by which one human being teaches another, and that we may all be taught by God (John 6:45). Yet even when a human being seems to teach us, we are still taught by God when we learn the things that pertain to true piety, because ‘neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth’ (1 Cor. 3:7). Therefore, if God did not give the growth, the Apostles would not be planters and waterers; how much less am I, or you, or any people of our time, when we imagine ourselves to be teachers!” [Note: [Col. 0043]

P.S. This preface was already under the press when I happened by chance upon a letter of Pope Pelagius II to Elias of Aquileia concerning the Three Chapters, which Gregory the Great calls a book and which he himself is said to have written in the pope’s name while he was still a deacon. While reading its twentieth chapter, I found twelve excerpts from the writings of Theodoret. From them I learned, first, that the author of the letter—whether that author was Pelagius or Gregory—had read the works of Marius Mercator, at least the part in which he wrote against Theodoret; for the same words are reported both from the letters and from the refutations of the anathemas and other books. Second, I learned that the letters to Himerius and the two Alexanders, which Mercator presents, are Theodoret’s. Third, that the *Pentalogus*, or *On the Incarnation against the Council of Ephesus*, is rightly attributed by Mercator to Theodoret. Fourth, that something is missing from Pelagius’ letter; for after Theodoret’s words have been quoted, the following is read from the refutation of the tenth anathema: “And again”—as though to show that he had grown toward divinity by successive stages—“in the same work he adds,” etc. Since a fragment from the second book *On the Incarnation* is immediately cited, it is beyond doubt that something else had previously been quoted. I believe it was the passage which Mercator has from the first book.

Thus we have one, or even two, supreme pontiffs bearing witness to Mercator’s works—not indeed by naming the author, but, what is more important, by turning part of his works to their own purposes and inserting it into a decretal letter.

We could also introduce a fourth witness, the deacon Liberatus, who in chapter four of his *Breviary* reports in Latin certain passages from Cyril’s first letter to Nestorius, which are found word for word in Mercator’s translation.

[Column 0043]

## Baluzius’ Preface

Before our own age no one had been found who mentioned the works of Marius Mercator, although it is clear that certain ancient writers used them. The first to know of them was the very learned Lucas Holstenius, prefect of the Vatican Library. After his death, among his papers were found certain excerpts from them, including the *Commonitorium concerning the name of Caelestius and other heretics of that opinion*. This was sent by the Reverend Father Possinus, a priest of the Society of Jesus who was then in Rome, to the Reverend Father Philippe Labbe, who was at that time engaged in producing the most extensive edition of the Councils.

At the same period Labbe had borrowed the very old codex of the acts of the Fifth Council from the library of the distinguished Church of Beauvais. In it he also discovered the works of that same Mercator, including the *Commonitorium*. Having learned this, he sent Possinus a list of the works of Mercator found in the Beauvais codex, asking him at the same time to investigate whether the same or other works existed in the codex from which Holstenius had made his copies. Possinus accordingly went to the Vatican Library and there, among the codices which had belonged to the Palatine count, found an old copy of the works of Marius Mercator. From it he sent copies of those works which he had been told were contained in the Beauvais manuscript.

Labbe, being a man of expansive spirit and eager for work, had decided to publish them; but death intervened and left this task to another. That man was the Reverend Father Jean Garnerius, also of the same Society, who for many years had taught theology with the highest distinction at the Paris College and possessed abundant and important resources for preparing and embellishing an edition of works containing very much material against the heresies of Pelagius and Nestorius. He therefore published them here in Paris in 1673, divided into two parts. In the first he placed what concerned the Pelagian controversy; in the second he placed the controversy concerning the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, which Nestorius attacked. He added extensive annotations and dissertations, filled with great learning, which shed much light on the writings of Marius Mercator.

In the same year the Reverend Father Dom Gabriel Gerberon, a Benedictine monk, publishing under the name Rigberius, arranged for part of the same works to be printed at Brussels, using the copy he had obtained from the Vatican Library. This consisted of the *Commonitorium against the heresy of Pelagius and Caelestius, and also against the writings of Julian*, together with the works that follow it, up to the third sermon of Nestorius against Mary the Mother of God. For this edition ends with the second sermon, which begins: “Indeed, insults …” There follow the very learned annotations of the same distinguished man on these works of Marius Mercator.

I shall briefly explain on what occasion I undertook to treat this subject and what I accomplished in revising the works of Marius. In 1677, when I was seriously considering publishing the first volume of a new collection of the Councils—the volume issued the following year—and had noticed that Labbe mentioned an old copy of the Fifth Council from Beauvais, I became eager to obtain it. I willingly acknowledge that I succeeded through the kindness of the very learned Godefroid Hermant, a canon of that Church.

When I examined it, I found the works of Marius Mercator joined to it, and immediately compared them with the editions of the distinguished scholars. From this comparison I learned that Garnerius had changed the order of the old copy, for the reasons mentioned above; that he had also altered many things while attempting to remedy corrupt passages; and finally that he had omitted several matters which seemed to me highly important.

I further learned that the Beauvais codex was very faulty and mutilated, and that another copy was therefore needed so that corrupt passages could be corrected and omissions restored. For this reason, on 26 November 1677, I wrote to the eminent cardinal, very learned man, and devoted friend of our studies, Girolamo Casanata. I asked him, as a favor to me, to have the Vatican codex containing the works of Marius Mercator copied and sent to me.

He replied as follows on 15 March of the following year:

“Several matters occur to me which I must write in order to satisfy your requests. That codex of Marius Mercator, the Palatine-Vatican copy, compared with the Brussels and Paris copies, has been found to differ greatly from both. The first of those volumes is only a small part of it. In the second, although it is larger in bulk, much is missing, and what it contains is read in an entirely different order. Accordingly, work was immediately begun so that I might satisfy your wishes by having the Vatican codex copied in full.

“Since everything contained in the Brussels edition agrees entirely, in substance and order, with the Vatican manuscript, I judged that it would be pointless to spend time transcribing those portions and thereby delay your wishes with wholly useless labor. I thought it better to begin the work where Rigberius stopped, as you will learn from the gathering which I am sending you; I shall soon give you more. This codex is full of barbarous and truncated words. Although I could easily have supplied or corrected them by conjecture, I deliberately left them untouched, knowing that you would prefer a genuine and completely faithful copy of that codex, whatever its condition.”

We therefore now give you, reader, the works of Marius Mercator as they are read in the ancient copies of the Church of Beauvais and the Vatican Library, and with such fidelity and care that we have retained even the errors of the ancient scribes. The distinguished Jean Garnerius believed that the Beauvais codex was far superior to the Vatican. I, however, have discovered that the Vatican is much better than the Beauvais copy—not only because it is sometimes more correct, but also because it contains certain things which were plainly omitted by the person who copied the Beauvais manuscript. Examples include the titles of certain excerpts from Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Diodore of Tarsus, and Eutherius of Tyana.

Because these titles were absent from the Beauvais codex, Garnerius fell into inextricable difficulties and, to use Pliny’s expression, “twisted the minds of observers.” It would be desirable for other, older and more accurate copies of the same author to be found, with whose help the passages mentioned above as corrupt could be corrected. Meanwhile, until almighty God grants this benefit to mortals, make use of these copies, whatever their condition.

It remains for us to say something about the author himself: who he was, what his origin was, and what studies he pursued. The distinguished man whom I mentioned shortly before, the first to publish the works of Marius Mercator, believed that he was from Campania or Apulia, or from that part of Italy which faces Sicily. His reason was that Mercator knew the domestic and private affairs of Caelestius and Julian—whom he maintained to have been respectively Campanian and Apulian—in a way scarcely possible for anyone except a fellow citizen or at least a fellow provincial.

That argument, however, does not establish necessary certainty. Jerome himself, although he was from Stridon—that is, a Dalmatian—described the life of Paul of Thebes and of Hilarion of Palestine as though they were his countrymen; and he knew the origins and birthplace of Vigilantius, a Gaul, as though he had belonged to the same city and province. All things are full of examples of this kind.

Therefore, since I too may conjecture, I believe that our Mercator was an African. First, I think he was the same man as the disciple of Saint Augustine, since our Mercator openly professes himself a devoted student and admirer of Augustine. Second, his manner of writing is extremely similar to the style of the African writers of that age. Finally, Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, occasionally used his words in composing his books in defense of the Three Chapters.

The very learned scholar correctly concluded that Mercator flourished from approximately 418 to 430, since he received a letter from Augustine in 418 and somewhere mentions the Eutychian heresy, which was condemned in 451; the same distinguished writer establishes this with several arguments. Yet, in my opinion, he is mistaken in believing either that Mercator did not live beyond 450 or that from that time onward he committed nothing to writing which has come down to us.

For since it is clear from the material reported on page 355 that he wrote after the name “Eutychians” had come into use—that is, some time after the Council of Chalcedon, which condemned the impious doctrine of Eutyches—it is evident that he wrote some time after 451, the year in which that council was held.

But Mercator severely attacks Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus. He would certainly not have done so if he had known that Theodoret had been received by so great a council after making an adequate profession of faith. From this it may be inferred that Mercator did not live until the time of the Council of Chalcedon, or at least that he committed nothing from that period to writing which has come down to us. Thus argues the very learned scholar.

I, however, conclude with complete certainty from this that Mercator survived the Council of Chalcedon, because, as I said earlier, he mentions the Eutychians—yes, the Eutychians, whose name was not heard in the Church of God before the time of the Council of Chalcedon. From his attack on Theodoret, therefore, it seems to me that only one of two conclusions can be drawn: either Mercator wrote these things against him—as I readily believe—before the Council of Chalcedon was held, or, if he wrote afterward, the proceedings of the council reached him late, so that he was not aware of Theodoret’s reception.

Although none of the ancients cited the works of Marius Mercator, it is nevertheless perfectly clear that they were known in antiquity. The scholia of Cyril of Alexandria *On the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten* have come down to us from no other source than Mercator’s translation. Moreover, the testimonies of the Fathers reported at the Council of Ephesus against Nestorius are also found, in the same translation, in codex 1868 of the Colbert Library.

In addition, Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, and Pelagius II in his third letter to the bishops of Istria often used Mercator’s words, and used them precisely in the form in which his works appear in the ancient codices. This proves that they were already corrupt at that time, and no one should be surprised that we possess them today in an extremely corrupted state.

[Column 0047]

## Historical-Literary Notice on Marius Mercator

*(From Schoenemann’s* Bibliotheca Historico-Litteraria Patrum Latinorum, *vol. II.)*

### § I. Life

Whatever is commonly debated concerning the homeland, place, social condition, and more precise dating of the life of the man whose name only began to revive toward the end of the last century rests on conjectures which are not indeed implausible, but are nevertheless not free from controversy.

Garnerius believed him to have originated in Campania, Apulia, or that part of Italy which faces Sicily. He had no other reason than that Mercator knew the domestic and private affairs of Caelestius and Julian—whom he maintained to have been respectively Campanian and Apulian—in a manner scarcely possible for anyone except a fellow citizen or at least a fellow provincial.

Gerberon, by contrast, who at the same time worked on a substantial portion of his writings, judged him to have been an African. He based this conclusion on the comparatively harsh style of Mercator’s writing, on his thorough knowledge of the proceedings of the African Church and possession of copies of them, and also on his being an especially devoted student of Saint Augustine and a vigorous defender of the grace of Christ and its ordering.

Baluzius likewise indicated that this opinion appealed to him. He weakened Garnerius’ argument chiefly by Jerome’s example: although Jerome himself was from Stridon or Dalmatia, he described the life of Paul of Thebes and of Hilarion of Palestine as though they were his countrymen, and knew the origins and birthplace of Vigilantius, a Gaul, as though he had belonged to the same city and province.

Baluzius thought he had found a new argument for his position in the fact that Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, sometimes used Mercator’s words when composing his books in defense of the Three Chapters.

Both Garnerius and Gerberon recognized that Mercator was neither a priest nor a bishop but a layman, since his works bear no mark of any ecclesiastical rank. Indeed, he declares that he obeyed the instructions of a certain presbyter Pientius, addressing him not with the greeting of a fellow priest or brother but merely with that of a venerable presbyter.

Baluzius, agreeing with Garnerius, dated Mercator’s flourishing from approximately 418, since the letter which he received from Augustine appears to belong to that year. Against Garnerius, however, he held that Mercator did not cease to live or write before 450. For since he mentions the Eutychians, whose name was not heard in the Church before the time of the Council of Chalcedon, he thought it necessarily evident that Mercator wrote some time after 451, the year in which that council was held.

He did not consider the argument derived by Garnerius from Mercator’s attack on Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, to be an obstacle. Garnerius had inferred that Mercator would not have made such an attack if he had known that Theodoret had been received by so great a council after making an adequate profession of faith, and from this had concluded that Mercator had not lived until the time of the Council of Chalcedon, or at least that he had committed nothing from that period to writing which has come down to us.

Baluzius argued in response that Mercator’s attack on Theodoret establishes only one of two possibilities: either Mercator wrote these things against him before the Council of Chalcedon was held, or, if he wrote afterward, the proceedings of the council reached him late, and he therefore did not know of Theodoret’s reception.

Mercator appears to have begun his skirmishes against the Pelagians at Rome during the time of Pope Zosimus, when their opinions were being debated amid various movements of feeling. He is thought to have sent to Africa from Rome the books he had composed on that heresy and to have received Augustine’s letter there.

Afterward, whether prompted by an impulse of his own mind or by Augustine’s advice I do not know, he went to Constantinople to prevent the errors of Julian and his followers—who, having been expelled from Rome, had turned there—from taking root. Having achieved this, and having delivered his *Commonitorium* in 429 to the younger Theodosius and the clergy of Constantinople, he soon involved himself with equal ardor in the dispute initiated by Cyril against Nestorius. As in the earlier controversy, he gathered the more forceful statements of both heretics and orthodox, which contended through various writings, together with his own outcries against Nestorius, from which he seems scarcely to have desisted before the end of his life.

### § II. Writings

All the writings of Marius Mercator which survive today are directed toward refuting the Caelestian and Nestorian heresies. Most were composed not so much through original labor as by translating Greek materials into Latin, collecting them, and excerpting them from the writings both of the adversaries and of those who had opposed them. They functioned as instruments of the controversy, by which readers could be instructed in the matters belonging to right faith and prepared to pass judgment on the impiety of those who held perverse opinions.

We shall give a list of them according to Baluzius’ edition, which follows the order of the Vatican codex.

1. **The *Commonitorium against the Heresy of Pelagius and Caelestius, and also against the Writings of Julian*.** Its full title is: *A Commonitorium for the Reader … by Marius Mercator, Servant of Christ.* It contains excerpts from Julian’s writings, everywhere followed by Mercator’s own responses or *Subnotations*. Garnerius judged it to have been written in 431.

Garnerius gave this work the title *Book of Subnotations to the Presbyter Pientius*. He believed it consisted of two parts: one serving as a preface under the name *Commonitorium*, the other comprising the work itself under the title *Subnotations to Julian’s Words*. Garnerius divided the latter into nine chapters. Eight correspond to the excerpts which Mercator undertook to examine from Julian’s books; he numbers eight, unlike Baluzius, who distinctly presents only seven excerpts and includes in the sixth what Garnerius makes chapters six and seven.

The ninth, beginning with the words “You have, I believe,” on page 30 of Baluzius’ edition, he says contains a reconsideration of the question of death’s entrance into the world through sin. He also supplied throughout Augustine’s words on each of Julian’s statements, which Mercator had not added in his notes.

2. **The Refutation of the Symbol of Theodore of Mopsuestia, or Exposition of Theodore’s Perverse Faith, with Mercator’s Preface.** In Garnerius it is found in volume II, pages 250–253; the preface appears twice, in volume I, page 95, and in volume II at the corresponding place.

3. **Comparison of the Doctrines of Paul of Samosata and Nestorius.**

4. **Five Sermons of Nestorius against Mary the Mother of God.**

5. **Nestorius’ Letter to Cyril of Alexandria.**

6. **Cyril of Alexandria’s Letter to Nestorius.**

7. **His Second Letter to Nestorius.**

8. **His Letter to His Own Clergy.**

9. **Excerpts from the Codices of Nestorius.**

10. **Four Sermons of Nestorius against the Pelagian Heresy.**

11. **His Letter to Caelestius.**

12. **Mercator’s *Commonitorium concerning the Name of Caelestius*.** Its full title is:

*Copy of the Commonitorium which Mercator delivered in Greek concerning the name of Caelestius, not only to the Church of Constantinople but also to very many religious men; also presented to the most pious prince Theodosius, ever august; translated from Greek into Latin by the same Marius Mercator, servant of Christ, in the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius, most illustrious men. Through this Commonitorium, once the most fatal error had become known, by imperial command Julian the defender and his follower, together with their other associates and partners, and later Caelestius himself, were expelled from the city of Constantinople; and afterward, at the Synod of Ephesus, they were condemned in the present matter by the judgment of 275 bishops.*

The year designated here by the consuls is 429, when the document was first presented to Theodosius. Garnerius and Norisius believe that it was translated into Latin later, after the Council of Ephesus had been celebrated in 431.

13. **The Chapters of Nestorius’ Blasphemies**, in which he contradicts the letters sent to him by the holy Caelestine, bishop of Rome, and Cyril of Alexandria. He responds in very brief arguments and refutes the twelve chapters of faith which had been sent to him; these were translated into Latin and refuted by Mercator under the name “the Catholic.” Garnerius assigns the beginning of this book to the start of 431.

14. **The Ephesian Synod against Nestorius**, that is, excerpts from the acts of this synod which seemed especially damaging to Nestorius. Garnerius omitted them entirely, but compensated for this to some extent with a careful account of Nestorius’ affairs over eight years, from his ordination to his deportation. He derived this account from the descriptions both of all the proceedings of the Council of Ephesus and of its individual parts.

In this account he states that many things are confusedly arranged even in the best editions and orders that they be placed differently. He marks with asterisks many more passages which are missing, although they belong no less to this council and are even more necessary.

15. **Cyril of Alexandria’s Apology against the Easterners.**

16. **His Apology against Theodoret.**

17. **Fragments of Theodoret, Theodore, Diodore, and Ibas.**

18. **A Fragment of Eutherius of Tyana.**

19. **Nestorius’ Letter to Pope Caelestine.**

20. **Cyril’s Synodical Letter to Nestorius.**

21. **His Scholia on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten.** Garnerius assigns these final collections of acts against the Nestorian heresy to the year 446.

The books of Marius Mercator against the Pelagians have perished, as we learn from Augustine’s Letter 193. If, however, we follow Dupin, they still survive in Augustine’s books of the *Hypognosticon*.

[Note: Dupin, *On Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. III, p. 256. Garnerius held the opposite view. In a special dissertation he destroyed this suspicion as soon as it arose and maintained that the same books belonged to Sixtus the presbyter, successor of Caelestine in the Roman see; see chapter 6, dissertation 6, in vol. I of the works of Marius Mercator, pp. 357–365.]

### § III. Editions

Before the time of Clement X, the name of Marius Mercator was entirely unknown. For although it is clear from the examples of Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, and Pelagius II that certain passages from his writings had been read approximately a hundred years and more after his death, no ancient writer cited Mercator’s works, and among later writers not even his name was heard.

Lucas Holstenius deserves the credit for having almost entirely rescued this author from the oblivion in which he lay buried. Holstenius had brought so many distinguished monuments of ecclesiastical history out of the Vatican cloisters; from the Palatine-Vatican codex he also recovered the acts of Mercator, which are so useful for the history of the Pelagian and Nestorian controversies.

Holstenius does not appear to have thought of publishing them, and perhaps did not believe that everything contained in that codex belonged to the same author or translator. Nevertheless, he gladly showed his friends what he had excerpted and perhaps shared it with them.

Thus Henry Norisius relates in his *Pelagian History* that Holstenius showed him, in the presence of Christian Lupus, Mercator’s *Commonitorium concerning the name of Caelestius*, which had been presented to Theodosius. I do not know how much time passed before Cardinal Bona encouraged Norisius, while he was preparing the work just mentioned, to read the booklets of Marius Mercator, which were entirely unknown to him.

Bona also affirmed that he had arranged for copies to be made and sent to France, where they came into Gerberon’s possession.

[Note: I had originally written this from conjecture, but I learned that it was not false from the French work *Literary History of the Congregation of Saint Maur* (Brussels, 1770, quarto), in the Life of Gerberon, p. 329.]

This, however, does not seem to have happened before all the same materials had been discovered in France by Philippe Labbe and Jean Garnerius in a certain Beauvais codex.

Cardinal Barberini had sent the *Commonitorium concerning the name of Caelestius*, together with certain other excerpts from that codex found among the papers of Holstenius after his death in 1661, to Philippe Labbe, who had just begun his extensive collection of the general councils. The sender was the Reverend Father Peter Possinus, a priest of the Society of Jesus.

At nearly the same time Labbe had borrowed the very old codex of the acts of the Fifth Council from the library of the chapter of the Church of Beauvais. In it he also found the works of Mercator, including the *Commonitorium*. Once he had learned this, he sent Possinus a list of Mercator’s works, instructing him to investigate whether the same or other works existed in the codex from which Holstenius had drawn his materials.

When Possinus promptly carried this out and found in the Roman copy everything which had been reported as contained in the Beauvais book, I believe that Mercator’s name finally became more widely known at Rome and that his works began to be read and commended.

Norisius not only reproduced this entire *Commonitorium* from the codex just mentioned in his commentaries; he also turned most of Mercator’s other writings concerning Pelagian affairs to his own use, frequently inserting the very words and citing the pages of the codex.

When copies made from the Vatican codex had been sent to Labbe at Rome, he began preparing an edition of these works. Unexpected death, however, overtook him and left the task to his close friend Jean Garnerius, a fellow member of the same Society and doctor of theology at the Paris College.

Garnerius had long examined the history of the Pelagian heresy with exceptional devotion and had shared in his friend’s good fortune in discovering this literary treasure. Equipped with the resources of the two codices and with considerable learning, he devoted himself to Mercator’s work.

When he realized that Labbe, overwhelmed by his enormous labor on the councils, would have published these works without notes and in the form in which they appeared in the codices, Garnerius, having leisure and love for this part of ecclesiastical history, began not only to observe more carefully each matter requiring explanation but, above all, to prevent the works from appearing mutilated in large part.

He thought this would happen if each item were copied in the same sequence and order as that preserved in the codices. Since he saw the acts of the Pelagian and Nestorian heresies mixed together and not coordinated even by the bond of the years in which they had been composed, he convinced himself that this was the fault of the copyists and that they had badly separated and even torn the materials apart.

He therefore separated the two bodies of material, divided them into two volumes, distinguished them with very extensive annotations and dissertations filled with great learning, and, in certain places where he thought it necessary, joined them together differently. He published them at Paris in 1673, in folio.

In the same year, at Brussels, Dom Gabriel Gerberon, a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur publishing under the name Rigberius, issued in duodecimo a portion of Mercator’s works copied from the Vatican codex and furnished with choice notes.

But since Garnerius’ edition, because the text was frequently interrupted by his annotations, was less convenient for use and was judged insufficiently faithful because of the liberties he had taken in arranging it, while Gerberon’s edition, though excellent, contained only a small portion, the man of immortal memory Stephen Baluzius undertook a new and complete edition.

He followed the same path by which Labbe and Garnerius had earlier proceeded, namely, the study of the councils; but he was supported by the same codices and by learning far more exact and extensive. His edition appeared at Paris in 1684, in octavo. Everything was presented in the same order in which it is found in the Vatican codex, with the greatest fidelity, including the faults of the writing, and with critical notes. It was received with the applause of all learned men.

Andreas Gallandius recently arranged for it to be reprinted in the Venetian *Bibliotheca Patrum*. At the same time, with commendable zeal and sound judgment, he endeavored to remove all the textual faults which had in part been left by Baluzius deliberately.

## The Seventeenth Century

### 1671

Paris, at the expense of the Society of Ecclesiastical Printers established by royal command; folio.

*Marius Mercator, Servant of Christ: Commonitorium concerning the Name of Caelestius, Pelagius, and Julian, and Their Heresy; Written under the Consulship of Florentius and Dionysius, Most Illustrious Men*, in *The Holy Councils Published in the Royal Edition*, prepared through the efforts of Philippe Labbe and Gabriel Cossart, priests of the Society of Jesus, vol. II, pp. 1512–1517.

To the title cited above Philippe Labbe added the following notice:

“Lucas Holstenius copied this from the Palatine Library of the Vatican. After his death, at the command of the most eminent Cardinal Francesco Barberini, the Reverend Father Peter Possinus of the Society of Jesus sent it from Rome. We, having furnished and illustrated it with various testimonies of Saint Augustine and other ancient writers, have prefixed it to the following councils and letters of the Roman pontiffs as the most accurate brief account of the Pelagian heresy, from which anyone may draw much material relevant to history.”

It begins: “A certain Caelestius …” Scholia are added in the margin, and there is also appended Philippe Labbe’s observation on the excellence of this short work.

### 1673

Brussels, printed by Lambert Marchant, under the sign of the Good Shepherd; duodecimo.

*The Acts of Marius Mercator, Disciple of Saint Augustine, Doctor of the Church, with Notes by Rigberius, Franco-German Theologian.*

The following works now appear for the first time from the Vatican codex:

1. *Commonitorium for the Reader against the Heresy of Pelagius and Caelestius, and also against the Writings of Julian*, beginning: “The question against the Catholic faith …”

2. *The Creed of Theodore of Mopsuestia*, translated from Greek into Latin by Marius Mercator and refuted, with a prologue prefixed.

3. *A Letter of Marius Mercator refuting the perverse doctrines of Paul of Samosata and Nestorius.*

4. *Another letter attacking the blasphemies of Nestorius*, with a preface.

5. *The First Sermon of the same author*, translated by Mercator.

6. *The Second Sermon of Nestorius*, translated by the same.

Gerberon’s preface is remarkable for its brevity. Here it is in full:

“For a long time reports had circulated that certain works of a Marius Mercator, a disciple of Saint Augustine the Doctor, still remained unpublished. When I inquired more carefully where they might be found, friends informed me that one copy was preserved by a Father of the Society of Jesus at the Clermont College, and another was in the possession of a certain monk of Saint-Germain of Paris.

“Having abandoned all hope of obtaining anything from these men, who were extremely protective of their manuscripts, I finally, through the assistance of the distinguished H. N., obtained from the Vatican Library a transcription of writings of this kind. I judged that they should be published, illustrated with both historical and doctrinal notes.”

The notes, which occupy most of the book, are filled with the most accurate learning and are exceptionally well suited to illustrating these acts. In them Gerberon discusses the author, admittedly by conjecture but with considerable probability.

### 1673

Paris, at the establishment of Sébastien Marbre-Cramoisy, printer to the king, on the Rue Saint-Jacques, under the sign of the Storks; folio.

*All the Extant Works of Marius Mercator, Contemporary of Saint Augustine.* Published for the first time through the efforts of Jean Garnerius, priest of the Society of Jesus, who also added notes and dissertations.

We shall speak later about the codices from which this new collection was prepared, namely the Vatican and Beauvais codices. It is impossible, however, to list each of the booklets contained in it without first discussing Garnerius’ work.

He believed himself entitled to change the order in which the individual works are preserved in the codices, or, as he himself put it, to restore the scattered and randomly dispersed materials to their proper order. He thought he had arranged them conveniently by dividing them into two parts, the first containing everything related to the Caelestian heresy and the second everything related to the Nestorian heresy.

He further appended to each work historical or philological notes, especially explaining obscure passages from authors contemporary with Marius and involved in both controversies, the Caelestian and the Nestorian heresies.

Finally, he added to the other materials collected by Marius certain things not found in Marius himself, such as collections of passages from Nestorius, Theodore of Mopsuestia, and others. He did this partly to confirm other matters through them and partly so that they might serve as explanatory notes which could not be inserted without sacrificing brevity or coherence.

With these preliminaries, we shall not hesitate to present an index of everything contained in the volume: both Mercator’s works and the notes and other additions of Garnerius.

## FIRST PART

It contains:

1. A general preface and a fragment of a letter written by Saint Augustine to Marius Mercator, with notes.

2. The *Commonitorium concerning the name of Coelestius*.

3. Notes appended to the *Commonitorium* chapter by chapter, together with two brief dissertations: the first on Pope Zosimus’s vindication in the case of Coelestius and Pelagius; the second on the *tractoriae* of the supreme pontiffs.

4. The *Commonitorium to the reader against the heresy of Pelagius and Coelestius*, and also against Julian’s writings.

5. Notes on the *Commonitorium*, or preface to the book of *Subnotations*.

6. The book of *Subnotations* on certain statements of Julian addressed to the presbyter Pientius.

7. Notes appended to each item.

8. The *Commonitorium*, or [Col. 0054D] prologue to the Creed of Theodore of Mopsuestia; the Creed itself, with Marius Mercator’s refutation, has been assigned to the second part.

9. Notes on the *Commonitorium*, or prologue.

10. Extracts from five books of Theodore against Saint Augustine, translated by Mercator.

11. Photius’s Codex 177, concerning Theodore’s five books.

12. Notes on the extracts and on Photius’s codex.

13. Mercator’s preface to Nestorius’s treatises against the heresy of Pelagius and Coelestius.

14. Notes on the preface.

15–22. Four sermons of Nestorius against the Pelagians, the last of them on the words, “I will give you all these things, if you will fall down and worship me,” translated by Mercator, with notes appended to each; among these notes is a brief dissertation on the time of solemn baptism.

23. Sermon IV, the same sermon in its entirety in Greek and Latin [Col. 0055A], formerly attributed either to Chrysostom or to Asterius (from volume VII of Savile’s edition of the works of John Chrysostom, p. 301), together with a new translation.

24. Two letters of Nestorius to Saint Coelestine on behalf of the Pelagians, by an uncertain translator.

25. Notes on both letters.

26. A letter of the same Nestorius to the Pelagian Coelestius, translated by Marius Mercator.

27. Notes on that letter.

[Note: This, then, is how Garnerius describes the sequence of the contents of the first part in the general preface, chapter 3. In reality, however, the arrangement is very different. For immediately after books 7 and 8 of the *Subnotations* there follow three letters written by Nestorius in the Pelagian case, on pages 65–72; then, on pages 73–94, the four sermons of Nestorius with Mercator’s preface—that is, everything listed under numbers 13–23. Finally, Mercator’s preface to Theodore’s Creed follows with the extracts from Theodore’s books, and thus occupies the end of numbers 8–12.]

In the first appendix:

28. Anastasius’s letter to John of Jerusalem concerning the name of Rufinus.

29. Historical notes on Anastasius’s letter.

30. Rufinus’s profession of faith, translated by Marius Mercator.

31. Notes on Rufinus’s profession of faith.

In the second appendix:

32. Seven dissertations:

- The first, on the earliest authors and principal defenders of the heresy that took its name from Pelagius, down to the words of the *Commonitorium* in the *Subnotations*: “A question contrary to the Catholic faith,” and so forth [Col. 0055B].

- The second, on the twenty-four synods held in the Pelagian case, the last of them being the Council of Ephesus, down to the words of the *Commonitorium*: “By priestly statutes.”

- The third, on the imperial enactments in the Pelagian case, down to the words of the same *Commonitorium*: “By imperial commands.”

- The fourth, on the subscriptions exacted by pontifical and imperial authority, down to the words: “Strengthened by the subscriptions of the Fathers.”

- The fifth, on the professions of faith issued by the authors and earliest defenders of the Pelagian heresy, down to Mercator’s words addressed to Julian: “Now hear also you,” and so forth.

- The sixth, on the books written by defenders of the faith against the same heresy during the lifetime of Saint Augustine; here the defense of Orosius is vindicated and the author of the books of the *Hypognostica* is disclosed, and so forth [Col. 0055C], down to the words: “Saint Augustine composed different books at different times,” and so forth.

- The seventh, on the Coelestian heresy—how from a single opinion it grew into something like an immense multitude—down to Mercator’s words: “To one most impious opinion,” and so forth.

## SECOND PART

The second part is divided into four books, whose contents are as follows.

At the beginning there is a historical preface embracing the whole case of Nestorius and the events from his ordination to his death.

### Book One

Book One contains thirteen sermons of Nestorius, translated by Mercator; one sermon of Proclus; three letters together with four of Saint Cyril; one letter of Mercator concerning Nestorius’s heresy; and extracts from Saint Cyril’s works on Nestorius’s writings, and so forth.

They follow in this order:

1. Mercator’s preface to various sermons of Nestorius on the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0055D].

2. Notes on the preface.

3. Sermon I of the impious Nestorius on the Incarnation of the Word, or on the virginal birth; it is preserved only in Latin.

4. Notes on the same.

5–6. Sermons II, on doctrine, or *Theognosia* (Θεογνωσία), and III, apparently against the Arians and Macedonians, in Greek and Latin.

7. Notes on Sermon III.

8. Marius Mercator’s letter on the distinction between Nestorius’s heresy and the doctrines of Paul of Samosata, Ebion, Photinus, and Marcellus [Col. 0056A].

9. Notes on this letter.

10. The homily of Proclus in Greek and Latin against Nestorius, apparently translated by Marius Mercator.

11. Notes on the same.

12. Sermon IV of Nestorius, his first extemporaneous sermon against Proclus.

13. Notes on the same.

14. Sermon V, in Greek and Latin, on the God who was born and on the Virgin *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος), his second sermon against Proclus.

15. Sermon VI, his third against Proclus, on statements in the Apostle’s Letter to the Hebrews.

16. Sermon VII, partly in Greek and Latin, against those who, on account of the union, either put the divinity of the Word to death or deify the humanity.

17. Notes on Sermon VII.

18. The first letter of Saint Cyril to Nestorius, in Greek and Latin, translated by Mercator.

19. Notes on the same, together with Nestorius’s reply.

20. The second letter of Saint Cyril to Nestorius, in Greek and Latin, translated by Marius.

21. Notes on the same.

22. Saint Cyril’s letter to his representatives residing at Constantinople, in Greek and Latin, translated by Marius.

23. Notes on this letter, which differs greatly from the corrupt form in which it is read in the published books.

24. The *Commonitorium* inserted into the letter, in Greek and Latin.

25. Nestorius’s second letter to Saint Cyril, in Greek and Latin, translated by Marius.

26. Notes on the same.

27. Four sermons of Nestorius—VIII, IX, X, and XI—in Greek and Latin.

28. Saint Cyril’s third synodical letter to Nestorius, containing twelve anathemas, in Greek and Latin, translated by Marius.

29. Notes on Saint Cyril’s third letter.

30. Nestorius’s letter to Saint Coelestine, supreme pontiff, in Latin only, translated by Marius.

31. Notes on the letter, together with a brief dissertation on matters relating to the Council of Ephesus [Col. 0056C].

32. Sermon XII of Nestorius, delivered in the church where he received the denunciatory letters of Coelestine, bishop of Rome, and Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, on 7 December.

33. Notes on the same.

34. Sermon XIII, delivered on the following day, on the knowledge of piety.

35. Extracts from various books or treatises of Nestorius, chapters selected by Bishop Cyril, translated by Mercator.

36. Extracts from a book of Nestorius read at the Council of Ephesus, in Greek and Latin.

37. Other extracts collected from here and there, differing from those of which information is available elsewhere.

### Book Two

The contents of Book Two are:

1. Twelve chapters of Nestorius’s blasphemies, in which he contradicts the letters sent to him by Saints Coelestine, bishop of Rome, and Cyril of Alexandria, and attempts, by replying with very brief disputations [Col. 0056D], to refute the twelve chapters on the faith that had been sent to him; together with Marius Mercator’s refutation.

2. Notes on Mercator’s entire work.

3. An exposition of the anathemas, being Saint Cyril’s reply to the objections raised in the name of the Easterners by Andrew of Samosata, translated by Marius Mercator.

4. Notes on the same.

5. A second exposition of the anathemas, being Saint Cyril’s reply to the criticisms of Theodoret, translated by Marius Mercator [Col. 0057A].

6. Notes on the second reply.

7. Saint Cyril’s complete scholia on the incarnation of the Only-Begotten, previously published in incomplete form, translated by Marius Mercator.

8. Notes on certain chapters of the scholia.

### Book Three

Book Three contains:

1. Extracts from the books of Theodore of Mopsuestia on the Incarnation of the Word, translated by Marius Mercator.

2. Notes on the extracts.

3. Collections from various works of the same Theodore, found in the Fifth Synod, in Facundus of Hermiane, Leontius the Scholastic, and other authors, useful for understanding the Nestorian heresy.

4. Extracts from the five books that Theodoret wrote against Saint Cyril and the holy Council of Ephesus, translated by Marius Mercator.

5. Notes appended to the extracts wherever necessary [Col. 0057B].

6. Theodoret’s letter to Nestorius, translated by Marius Mercator.

7. Notes on the same.

8. Another letter by the same author, sent to Constantinople in support of the Nestorians, translated by the same translator.

9. Notes on the same.

10. Another letter by the same author to Andrew, bishop of Samosata, translated by Mercator.

11. Fragments of two letters from Theodoret to Himerius, bishop of Nicomedia, translated by Marius.

12. Notes on the preceding letters.

13. A fragment of a sermon delivered by Theodoret before Domnus of Antioch after the death of Saint Cyril, translated by Marius.

14. A fragment of a sermon delivered by Eutherius against Saint Cyril, translated by Mercator.

15. A refutation of Nestorianism, in Greek and Latin, and Marius’s epilogue.

### Book Four

Finally, Book Four contains two dissertations.

The first is on Nestorius’s heresy and other errors for which he may be regarded as suspect, and on the books that he himself wrote in support of the heresy.

The second is on the synods convened in the case of Nestorius, from the time when the disturbances began until the peace of the Churches.

He had intended to add a third dissertation, on the books published at the same time by defenders of the faith against the Nestorian heresy; this is in fact promised in the table of contents. Nevertheless, so as not to enlarge still further by its length the bulk of this volume, which already seemed to have grown large enough—and since it also needed to be enriched with several documents that he was expecting from elsewhere—he decided that it should for the present be omitted. Because its subject would be related to the matter that would have to be treated while assessing Theodoret’s books, he decided to defer it instead to the supplement concerning Theodoret [Col. 0057D].

[Note: It appeared in folio at Paris in 1684, after Garnerius himself had died, under the title of volume V of the works of Theodoret edited by Sirmond at Paris in 1642. Yet not even a trace of this dissertation appears in it.]

From this table of contents everyone can understand with what zeal and learning Garnerius cultivated both parts of Mercator’s writings [Col. 0058A]. He thereby certainly deserved the esteem in which these labors have always been held by learned men. Yet, as regards Mercator’s own text, and also some other brief works that Garnerius inserted, and as regards the fact that he tore these separate works apart according to his own sole judgment rather than arranging them, he fell so far short of securing the agreement of others that he instead incurred severe criticism from even the most learned man in this field.

[Note: Father Garnier—this is Tillemont’s judgment in the *Mémoires ecclésiastiques*, volume XV, p. 142—gave the public everything he had been able to find in one manuscript of the Vatican and another belonging to the chapter of Beauvais, which he valued much more highly than the other. He arranged them in the order that seemed best to him. He added certain other pieces found in the same manuscripts, and appended a great number of notes and dissertations, among which one often has difficulty finding the text of his author. He was free to place Mercator’s works wherever he wished. But it seems to me that he even separated the different parts of one and the same work.]

Cotelerius’s judgment is not far removed from this. In his notes on the *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graeca*, volume III, p. 602, where he attempts to emend several passages of Mercator’s edition by Baluze, he says:

> “I pay no attention to another edition of Marius Mercator, apart from Baluze’s, because its editor, Garnerius—a man of venerable memory—is accustomed, as a bad example, to make his ingenious conjectures into the text.”

See also what we noted in volume I of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 644, while discussing the writings of Anastasius, pope of Rome, concerning the same man’s boldness in establishing Rufinus’s profession of faith.

Nor should one think it unjust to complain that Garnerius was excessively hostile in spirit toward the authors and defenders of those heresies. In this connection, one should especially consult what the most distinguished Joannes Ludovicus Schulze, an ornament of the University of Halle, set forth in his dissertation on Theodoret’s life and writings, prefixed to volume I of the new edition of Theodoret’s works. There nearly the whole of this portion of Garnerius’s work, which concerns the case of Nestorius and Theodoret, is subjected to rigorous examination [Col. 0058B].

In the general preface, chapter 1, Garnerius discusses Marius Mercator, his age, origin, location, talent, and authority; in chapter 2, his works; in chapter 3, what Garnerius himself contributed to the edition of those works; and in chapter 4 he presents a specimen of what first became known from Marius Mercator’s works. Chapter 5 explains how Mercator’s works first came into Garnerius’s hands.

He dedicated the work to the dean, canons, and chapter of the Church of Beauvais, in a letter dated Paris, 8 January—the feast of Saint Lucian, apostle of Beauvais—in the year 1673.

### 1673

Padua; in folio. Marius Mercator’s *Commonitorium against the Pelagians*—the work mentioned above under the title *Concerning the Name of Coelestius*—in Henry Noris’s *Pelagian History*, which first appeared that year and place, Book II, chapter 6. In the copy whose title states that it was reprinted according to the Paduan exemplar, the relevant passage is on pages 125–128. Add Noris’s works, edited by the Ballerini brothers in 1729, volume I. He likewise asserts that he received this work of Marius from Holstenius, transcribed from a Vatican manuscript.

### 1677

Lyons, at the house of the Anissons; in folio. *Acts of Marius Mercator*, and so forth, with Rigberius’s notes, in the *Bibliotheca Maxima Patrum*, volume XXVII, pages 129–173.

### 1684

Paris, at the printing house of François Muguet, printer to the king and to the most illustrious archbishop of Paris; in octavo. *Works of Marius Mercator*. Stephen Baluze of Tulle corrected and illustrated them against the authority of ancient manuscript codices.

What works of Marius are included in this principal edition, and in what order, has been explained above.

As for the occasion on which Baluze undertook the treatment of this subject, he writes as follows:

> “When in the year 1677 I was seriously considering publishing the first volume of the new Collection of Councils, which was issued the previous year, and noticed that Labbeus had mentioned an old copy of the Council of Beauvais V, I was inflamed with the desire to possess it. I willingly acknowledge that I obtained it through the good offices of the most learned Godefridus Hermant, a canon of that same church.
>
> “When I examined it, I found together with it the works of Marius Mercator, and immediately compared them with the editions of the most distinguished scholars. From comparison with the old exemplar I recognized that Garnerius had changed the order, had altered many passages while attempting to apply a remedy to corrupt readings [Col. 0059B], and had finally omitted some things that seemed to me of great importance.
>
> “I also recognized that the Beauvais codex was very faulty and mutilated, and that another exemplar was therefore needed so that corrupted passages could be corrected and omissions restored. For this reason, on 26 November 1677 I wrote to the Most Eminent Cardinal Hieronymus Casanata and asked him to have the Vatican codex containing Marius Mercator’s works copied for my sake and sent to me.”

He complied with the requests of this man, who had rendered such distinguished service to these studies, and replied on 15 March of the following year in a very courteous letter, from which we shall later extract several details concerning the character of that codex.

After Baluze had reproduced the letter in full, he continues:

> “We therefore now give you, reader, the works of Marius Mercator as they are read in the ancient exemplars of the Church of Beauvais and of the Vatican Library, and with such fidelity and diligence that we have retained even the errors of the ancient scribes.
>
> “The distinguished John Garnerius considered the Beauvais codex far superior to the Vatican. But I have discovered that the Vatican is much better than the Beauvais, not only because it is sometimes more correct, but also because it contains several things that were plainly omitted by the person who copied the Beauvais codex. These include, for example, the titles of certain fragments extracted from Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Diodore of Tarsus, and Eutherius of Tyana.
>
> “Since those titles were absent from the Beauvais codex, Garnerius became entangled in inextricable difficulties; and, to speak with Pliny, he so tortured the ingenuity of observers. It would be desirable for other, older and more accurate exemplars of this author to be found, by whose help those passages that we have said are corrupt could be corrected.”

This is what he says about the method of his work.

He then turns to the question of the author, his homeland, and his studies, treating it briefly but in such a way that he establishes more correctly certain matters that Garnerius had presented without sufficient caution.

The notes have been removed to the end of the volume, with numbers written in the margins referring to the pages concerned. They are not numerous but are of great importance; nearly all are critical, and in hundreds of places they correct Garnerius [Col. 0060A].

Finally, there is an index of subjects.

The edition is dedicated to the same Cardinal Hieronymus Casanata, to whom we have learned that a large part of it is owed.

### 1690

Paris; in folio. Marius Mercator’s *Commonitorium against the Pelagians*, in the Benedictine edition of Saint Augustine’s works, volume X, part II, appendix.

### 1700

Antwerp; in folio. Marius Mercator’s *Commonitorium against the Pelagians*, in Saint Augustine’s works, Benedictine edition prepared by John Clericus, volume X, part II, appendix, columns 46–48.

## EIGHTEENTH CENTURY

### 1772

Venice, from the printing house of Giovanni Battista Albritius; in folio. *Works of Marius Mercator*. From the edition of the distinguished Stephen Baluze, now revised anew, restored in many places, and illustrated, in Andrea Gallandi’s *Library of the Fathers and Ecclesiastical Writers* [Col. 0060B], volume VIII, pages 615–737.

Baluze’s notes have been added at the foot of the page, since he assigned the lower margin to his own notes, scattered there with a liberal hand. Nearly every one of them seeks to correct the text, and the attempt usually succeeded, especially through comparison with the Greek texts of Cyril and Theodoret.

Nor did he neglect what learned men had contributed elsewhere to the correction or illustration of Mercator—for example, Noris in his *Pelagian History*, Cotelerius in his notes on the Greek monuments, Constantius in his notes on the letters of the Roman pontiffs, Merenda in his notes on the works of Damasus, and others.

The pages of Baluze’s edition to which the notes refer are indicated in the margin; beneath the text, as in the other parts of this *Library*, the biblical passages are carefully marked [Col. 0060C].

In the Prolegomena, chapter 19, p. XXXIII, there is an excellent dissertation on Marius Mercator, composed with judgment and diligence.

## MANUSCRIPTS

The entire record of Marius Mercator, and all the surviving remnants of his acts that we now possess, have been recovered from only two manuscript codices. It is therefore plainly an error found in Gallandi, otherwise a most accurate scholar, that Baluze corrected this author with the help of three manuscript books.

The first in the order in which they began to be used was the Vatican codex; the second was the Beauvais codex. Both were approximately of the same age—about eight hundred years old, as Garnerius writes may be inferred from the form of their script—and both were of excellent quality, although the scholar just mentioned judged the Beauvais codex far superior to the Vatican. Baluze disagreed, insisting that the Vatican deserved the palm over the Beauvais, and proving it with several examples [Col. 0060D].

### I. Vatican Codex

The Vatican codex formerly belonged to the Heidelberg Library.

To it is owed the first *Commonitorium* of Mercator published by Labbeus. It was soon examined again according to the list of works that Labbeus had found in the Beauvais codex; Garnerius had this comparison available to him.

At the same time, one complete portion of it was copied in continuous sequence and sent to Gerberonius, who published it faithfully.

For Baluze’s benefit, Cardinal Casanata arranged for a third comparison and transcription. On that occasion he wrote the following to Baluze concerning it:

> “That codex of Marius Mercator, the Palatine-Vatican codex, when compared with the Brussels and Paris printed editions, was found to differ greatly from both. The first of those volumes contains only a small part of the work. The other—the edition of Garnerius—is larger in bulk, but many things are missing from it, and what it contains is read in a completely different order.
>
> “Therefore work was immediately undertaken so that, by transcribing the Vatican codex in full, I might satisfy your wishes. Since, however, everything contained in the Brussels edition agrees entirely in both substance and order with the Vatican manuscript, I decided not to spend time transcribing those portions and thereby prolong your wishes with wholly useless labor. I thought it better to attack the work where Rigberius stopped.
>
> “This codex is full of barbarous and mutilated expressions. Although I could easily have supplied or corrected them by conjecture, I deliberately omitted to do so, knowing that you desired a genuine and completely faithful copy of that codex, whatever its condition.”

### II. Beauvais Codex

The Beauvais codex belongs to the chapter of the Church of Beauvais.

This book once attracted Labbeus, to whom it had been lent to assist his Collection of Councils; he therefore asked his Roman friends to compare it more accurately with the Vatican codex.

Garnerius, who gives it first place, presented in chapter 2 of the general preface to all Marius Mercator’s works a synopsis of his works and of the other brief writings connected with the same subject, as they lie in the codex.

He generally observes that it has two parts. One contains the Fifth Synod; the other bears a title added by a more recent hand: “The Synod of Ephesus, where the heresy of Nestorius is condemned together with its author.”

Finally, Baluze himself examined the codex.

# FIRST PART OF THE EXTANT WORKS OF MARIUS MERCATOR, CONTAINING MATERIAL RELATING TO THE PELAGIAN, OR RATHER COELESTIAN, HERESY

[Col. 0061]

# MARIUS MERCATOR’S *COMMONITORIUM CONCERNING COELESTIUS, PRESENTED TO THE EMPEROR*

Its title in the ancient exemplars is:

## Copy of the *Commonitorium* Given by Mercator in Greek Concerning the Name of Coelestius

[Note: By this name, which is found everywhere among writers of that period, including the Greeks, a kind of memorial booklet is meant. It is not, however, a booklet intended to aid someone’s memory, in which sense Augustine understood the term (*Retractions*, Book I, chapter 5) and Vincent of Lérins (*Commonitorium*); nor is it a brief set of instructions given to someone, as occurs more than once at the Council of Ephesus and in civil law. Rather, it is a document containing materials by which the importance of some case may be assessed either by a judge or by others.

It was first published by the distinguished Philip Labbeus in volume II of the Councils, p. 1552; then by the learned Henry de Noris, *Pelagian History*, Book II, chapter 6 [Col. 0064A]; and afterward, together with the remaining works of Marius Mercator, by Father Garnerius. BALUZE.]

A copy of the *Commonitorium* concerning the name of Coelestius was given by Mercator in Greek, not only [Col. 0065] to the Church of Constantinople but also to many most religious men.

[Note: Coelestius was named, and not also Pelagius, because the matter concerned condemning the man who was stirring up disturbances at Constantinople. After Pelagius’s condemnation, he had either withdrawn to his homeland, as some have incorrectly thought, or rather remained in some part of Palestine, which I consider more likely. I say “in some part of Palestine,” for Mercator reports that he was driven from the holy and venerable places of Jerusalem by a later synod presided over by Theodotus, bishop of Antioch (*Commonitorium*, chapter 3).]

[Note: Nor was it presented to the bishop of Constantinople, partly because the Constantinopolitan clergy had for the most part separated from their bishop as he preached heresy, and partly because Nestorius, who then occupied the see of the imperial city, was attached to the Pelagians (Cyril, in his letter to Coelestine, Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 14). Hence Cassian says (*On the Incarnation*, chapter 3): “By his intercessions he fosters the complaints of the Pelagians, and by his writings maintains their cause, because he subtly—or rather, as I should say, deceitfully—patronizes them and gives wicked support, with wicked affection, to an evil akin to his own; knowing, namely, that he is of the same mind and spirit, and therefore grieving that a heresy akin to himself has been separated from the Church.” Hence also Saint Coelestine says (in his letter to Nestorius, Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 18): “A just condemnation, though they call it unjust, expelled these heretics from their sees; we do not think it surprising that they found rest there: for they found an impious preaching in comparison with which they judge themselves innocent.” And shortly afterward: “What have those to do with you who were condemned for denying these things? Those who agree in matters adverse to themselves never meet without suspicion; indeed, they would be expelled if they likewise displeased you.”]

[Note: Namely, monks and laymen, but especially the fathers of the monks, or archimandrites, of whom there were many at Constantinople and in the neighboring regions. The Coelestians were setting snares for all of them, so that, if they could not draw the unwary into their party, they might at least gain a reputation for piety through association with religious men. See what Gennadius writes about Julian (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 45), namely, that by almsgiving he enticed many religious men and joined them to his heresy.]

It was also presented to the most devout emperor, Theodosius, ever august [Note: Theodosius the Younger—whom the Fathers of Ephesus more than once called a new Constantine—burning with remarkable zeal for the Catholic faith, issued at Constantinople a law against all heresies to Florentius, praetorian prefect of the East, on 30 May, in the consulship of Felix and Taurus (*Theodosian Code*, Book V). Nestorius, it is believed, was its author, but at the same time he most impiously abused the religion of the most pious emperor in order to clear a path for his own heresy through the destruction of the others (Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitorium*). It is worth observing that, among the many names of heretics enumerated in the law, the Coelestians are not named, though above all they ought to have been, because Atticus had formerly condemned them in that very imperial city; but it is reasonably believed that Nestorius himself framed the law so as to exempt friends who would be useful to him.]; the same document was translated from Greek into Latin by that same Marius Mercator, servant of Christ [Col. 0065C], in the consulship of the most illustrious men Florentius and Dionysius.

[Note: This consulship fell in A.D. 429, the seventh year of Pope Coelestine, the twenty-second of Theodosius, and the fifth of Valentinian, as is clear both from the consular fasti and from chronological history. But a serious doubt arises: is the *Commonitorium* said to have been first presented to Theodosius under these consuls, or was it then rendered into Latin after having been presented many years earlier in Greek both to the emperor and to Atticus, bishop of Constantinople? We followed the former view in the first dissertation on Julian’s booklet; the latter nevertheless seems not improbable. I should almost adopt it, if Mercator himself did not keep me with the former view: when speaking of Theodotus, bishop of Antioch (*Commonitorium*, chapter 3), he signifies that he was dead. Theodotus died in 428, as Theodoret relates (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 39). Still more strongly do the words that immediately follow, “at the present time,” press the point; for they show that the Latin translation was made during the Council of Ephesus.]
