in the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius, most illustrious men. Through this *Commonitorium* the most disastrous error was brought to light [Note: As far as I know, that command does not survive. It is not found in the Theodosian Code, nor in any writer of this period [Col. 0066A].

It ought to have been addressed to Florentius, prefect of the East, if it was an appendix to the law issued against all heresies in the preceding year.

But someone may object: Why should it not be said to have been addressed to Nestorius, just as in the same case we read of two commands being issued (*Appendix to the Theodosian Code*, no. 6)—one to Aurelius of Carthage by Honorius, the other to Patroclus of Arles by Caesar Valentinian?

What prevents us from believing this is that, when imperial laws are examined, one can observe that only those laws whose execution belonged to ecclesiastical office were addressed to bishops; laws requiring the power to coerce criminals by penalties were addressed to prefects.

The words of Mercator make clear that the command now under discussion belonged to the second category. The law said to have been sent by Valentinian to Patroclus was in fact addressed directly to Amacius, prefect of the Gauls; but it was arranged that Amacius should summon the bishops through Patroclus and, unless they were corrected by ecclesiastical means, compel them by the prefect’s edict, after twenty days, to leave their sees and be exiled from Gaul.]

By an imperial command, therefore, both Julian the defender and his follower [Note: Noris reads “his followers,” who published this *Commonitorium* of Marius transcribed from the Palatine codex in *Pelagian History*, Book II, chapter 6; the distinguished Gallandi omits “and his follower.”], together with their other associates and accomplices,

[Note: Julian, in the name of eighteen bishops, wrote a profession of faith to Zosimus, supreme pontiff, which we have published. In the name of the same men he also wrote a letter to Rufus of Thessalonica, which Augustine refuted in the three later books addressed to Boniface. Seven of that number seem to have surpassed the others in prominence, since their names have been preserved: Julian, Turbantius, Florus, Orontius, Fabius, Persidius, and Marcellinus (*Letters* I and II of Nestorius to Saint Coelestine, Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapters 16 and 17, and Part II, Act 5, in the synodical letter to Saint Coelestine).

Among these, four were more notable: Julian, who led the army; Turbantius, to whom Julian sent the first four books against Saint Augustine; Florus, to whom the later eight were sent; and Orontius, at whose urging Annianus translated the first eight homilies of Chrysostom on Matthew.

Augustine reports that Turbantius returned to the Church after renouncing the heresy, in these words (*Unfinished Work against Julian*, Book I, chapter 2): “Would that you might imitate Turbantius after those writings of yours, and after those praises of yours in which you say that he, conspicuous for the great splendor of his virtues, has been freed from your error.”

From this passage it appears that Turbantius was freed from error at the time between Julian’s writing of his final work and Augustine’s reply. Julian would not have adorned with such praises a man who, as he claimed, had already departed from the Catholic faith and returned to Manichaean filth.]

and later Coelestius himself, after being driven from the city of Constantinople, likewise at the Synod of Ephesus [Col. 0066C; source boundary].

[Note: Julian and his companions were condemned in the ecumenical council, although it is said that they had previously been acquitted by schismatics. Gregory the Great mentions this acquittal (*Register*, Book V, letter 14; Book VI, letter 61; Book VII, letter 48). He writes that the schismatics had defined the matter of Adam’s soul by saying that it had not died in sin, because the devil does not enter the human heart; and that anyone who said this was to be anathema.

He recounts this history more fully elsewhere and reports that in many codices the acts of the Catholic council had been confused with those of the schismatics, thereby creating error for many. But in the acts as they now exist, nothing of the kind is found.

We shall show in the second part what the whole matter was and shall overturn the popular opinion concerning it.]

[Note: The number of Fathers assembled at Ephesus has until now been uncertain. Mercator does not contradict himself when, in his preface to the sermons of Nestorius against the Pelagians, he numbers only 274; for an error could easily have crept into either passage through the carelessness of copyists, who may have omitted the second I in one place or inserted an I before the V in the other.

Nevertheless, several things might seem to contradict Mercator: the Cresconian collection, which numbers 190 Fathers; the common edition of the councils, in which only 153 are recorded as having subscribed; the synodical letters, which say merely that more than 200 bishops assembled; and the acts of later councils, where mention is made only of 200.

But Cyril supports Mercator in his letter to the Alexandrians, when he says: “More than 200 bishops are assembled here, nearly 300, give or take” (Part II of the Council of Ephesus, Act 1).

Nor does he contradict himself when he writes in his letter to the Constantinopolitan clergy: “The bishops who pronounced this sentence against him were more than 200 in number.”

The reason is that when Nestorius was deposed in Act 1, the representatives of the apostolic see had not yet arrived, and many of the Eastern schismatics had not yet crossed over to the Catholic side. From these—whether those newly arriving or those returning to the faith—the number of bishops who formulated the canons toward the end of the council could have been formed.

This question will be discussed again in the preface to the sermons of Nestorius against the Pelagians.]

By the judgment of two hundred and seventy-five bishops, they were subsequently condemned in the present case.

[Note: [Col. 0067B] From these words I infer, as was just said, that the *Commonitorium* was translated from Greek into Latin at the time of the Council of Ephesus, so that it might be delivered to the legates of the apostolic see and to Bassula himself, the Carthaginian deacon, for conveyance to Italy and Africa together with the letters and canons of the Ephesian synod.]

[Col. 0067]

# HISTORICAL PREFACE TO M. MERCATOR’S *COMMONITORIUM* ON THE NAME OF COELESTIUS

[Col. 0061]

The bishops expelled from the West, having despaired of obtaining from the apostolic see what they most earnestly desired—namely, either that the whole case be reconsidered, or that they themselves be restored to their sees without a lawful subscription—turned their attention toward Constantinople, to see whether by some means they might draw the bishop of the imperial city over to their side, or at least convert the emperor’s patience, wearied by their petitions, into compassion for them.

They had already attempted, through suitable agents, to influence Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, by the devices of Coelestius, and Sisinnius, Atticus’s successor. Their efforts with both had failed: Atticus, being a teacher of the Catholic faith—“not unequal to so great a see” (Coelestine, Letter to Nestorius, part I of the Council of Ephesus, ch. 18)—did not even allow the obstinate heretics to remain in the city; while Sisinnius, following the example of his predecessor, defended his own flock against the wolves’ snares. Both were truly successors of blessed John, and both wished only the faith they had found to be preached.

But when they saw that Nestorius had been appointed in place of Sisinnius, and understood that he possessed great influence with the emperor and considerable power among the courtiers—for Theodosius had summoned him from Antioch as one fit to fill Chrysostom’s see, and he had bound the courtiers to himself partly by gifts, partly by his reputation for holiness, and partly by his eloquence—they conceived great hope that through his assistance they would gain access to the palace and bring their complaints before the emperor, as though, in orthodox times and on behalf of the orthodox faith, they had suffered danger through calumny and underhanded dealing (in Nestorius’s letters to Saint Coelestine).

Two things especially encouraged this hope. First, they had Theodorus of Mopsuestia as a teacher in common with Nestorius; second, they were joined by fellowship in heresy. Nestorius had learned from Theodorus the impiety for which he was seeking an opportunity to speak; and the Pelagians, together with him, denied that the Blessed Virgin was Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*, “God-bearer”).

Indeed, Nestorius received Julian, the bishops associated with him, and Coelestius himself into his friendship. He showed no reverence either for the judgment of the apostolic see, by which they had been condemned, or for Honorius’s edict, by which they had been proscribed. Rather, he dared to promise them acquittal and, as a pledge of his good faith, first undertook to ensure that the Pelagians would not be arrested under Theodosius’s law against all heresies (*Theodosian Code*, book 16, title 5, law 65). Then, through the courtiers, he arranged for them to be admitted to the emperor’s hearing, allowing them to fill the palace with their complaints; he also permitted them to attend the sacred mysteries in his church. Finally, when he sent letters to the supreme pontiff Coelestine, he subtly—or, to speak more accurately, in Cassian’s words, “with a wicked affection he wickedly supported a wickedness akin to his own” (*On the Incarnation*, book 1, ch. 3).

As a result, they were no longer regarded by everyone, as before, as heretics. Some, moved by an inopportune compassion, said that they suffered only from the indignation of the Roman pontiffs, not from the injustice of their cause; others said that they deserved no protection, since they had been expelled from the West because of their obstinate heresy; while the rest, ignorant of what had happened, neither acquitted them altogether nor condemned them (in Nestorius’s letter to Saint Coelestine).

When Mercator saw that not only the Church of Constantinople but also the imperial court was divided over this matter, and understood that men distinguished for their religion were wavering about which side to take—men who would nevertheless cause great prejudice against the good cause if they did not join it—he wrote the *Commonitorium*, first in Greek and then in Latin, concerning, as he says, the name of Coelestius. He intended thereby to explain the whole sequence of events and make clear to everyone that these turbulent men really were heretics and had deservedly been driven from the West.

To accomplish this more effectively, he brought forward the principal documents of the entire dispute. With public testimonies and ecclesiastical records, he presented, as it were in summary, the councils held throughout the world, the order and procedure of the judgments, the condemnations issued by the supreme pontiffs, the imperial edicts by which the Church’s judgments were strengthened, the common consent of the whole Church in condemning heretics, the indulgence of the apostolic see in receiving those who returned from error, and many other matters of the same kind. From these materials the truth would be evident to all, and the Pelagians themselves might be called back to a better mind.

This work has five parts. The first embraces Coelestius’s case and the manner in which it was handled at Carthage, Constantinople, and Rome. In the second, Pelagius’s mind and error are exposed from his own undisputed books. The third contains the condemnation of both heretics, whether that issued from the two supreme pontiffs, Zosimus and Innocent, or that pronounced by the Fathers of the Diospolitan synod. The fourth shows that both heretics held exactly the same opinion, and that the condemnation of one therefore applies to the other. Finally, the fifth takes up Julian, partly so that he might explain any complaint or question he had, and partly so that, following the example of those who repented, he might return to the Church.

It is remarkable how many aids to the Catholic cause are brought forward in this single little book; but it is regrettable that so few of them have survived to our time. Mercator mentions—or rather, when he presented the *Commonitorium*, had before him—copies of the pamphlet sent by Paulinus to Aurelius against Coelestius; the acts of the Carthaginian council under the same Aurelius; Atticus’s letters to the churches of the major sees concerning Coelestius’s condemnation; the acts of the Roman council under Zosimus; and Zosimus’s letters to all the bishops of the world; Pelagius’s commentaries on the Apostle Paul’s letters; Pelagius’s books to the widow; the letters and pamphlets of Eros and Lazarus against Pelagius; the synodal letters of the councils of Carthage and Milevis to Saint Innocent; Innocent’s replies to both councils; the acts of the Diospolitan synod under Eulogius and even those of the Antiochene synod under Theodotus; and the letters of Praylius, who no longer commended Pelagius but condemned him. Of these, however, little now remains. Fragments of some survive, but they are exceedingly small. Even the commentaries on the Pauline Epistles were interpolated by Cassiodorus; of the rest nothing remains except their memory and our longing for them.

What the outcome was, and what effect was produced by such painstaking concern on behalf of the Catholic faith by a man inflamed with apostolic zeal, Mercator himself explains in the title of the *Commonitorium* in these words:

“Through this *Commonitorium*, after the most disastrous error had been recognized, by imperial command both Julian, its defender and follower, together with his other associates and companions, and afterward Coelestius himself, were expelled from the city of Constantinople; and subsequently, in the synod of Ephesus, they were condemned in the present case by the judgment of two hundred and seventy-five bishops.”

But since this work touches upon almost the whole twenty-three-year history of Pelagianism, and also recounts many matters either previously unheard of or known only to the most learned, it seemed worthwhile to do two things in the notes: first, to bring all the historical material into conformity with a chronological account; second, to strengthen Mercator’s authority by the testimony of the ancients. Both tasks, however, will be treated more briefly than the nature of the subject might perhaps require, since, if God wills, we shall one day discuss these and all similar matters more fully in the Pelagian history that we have in hand.

# CHAPTER ONE

## Coelestius’s case, and how it was handled at Carthage, Constantinople, and Rome

[Col. 0067A]

**1.** [Note: We have set out this man’s entire history in the dissertation on the authors and defenders of the Pelagian heresy; consult that work (Dissertation 2).]

A certain Coelestius, [Note: Mercator says this again (*Preface to the Subnotations*): “Coelestius attached himself to Pelagius, a man noble by birth and at that time a scholarly auditor of the courts; but, owing to a defect of nature, he had been born a eunuch from his mother’s womb.” Although this has hitherto been unheard of, it can nevertheless be confirmed by Orosius’s authority, who writes in his *Apology* as follows (ch. 12 of our edition): “And our mutilated man, smooth on the forehead, double-eyed, does not consider a defense necessary for himself in the head, who presumes possibility in the flesh.” We have treated this passage more fully in the dissertation just cited. Certainly the words “mutilated” and “smooth on the forehead” indicate a eunuch, although there is some difficulty, which is resolved in the place already mentioned.]

born a eunuch from his mother’s womb [Col. 0068A], a disciple and auditor of Pelagius, [Note: Unless the correction that has been supplied is adopted, but the text is read as it stands in both manuscript codices—“A certain Coelestius, born a eunuch from his mother’s womb, having gone forth as a disciple and auditor of Pelagius about twenty years earlier,” etc.—it will be uncertain whether the number of years belongs to his departure from the City or to Coelestius’s instruction under Pelagius. Coelestius had already attached himself to Pelagius when the two were living in Rome and were being taught by Rufinus the Syrian that sin is not transmitted by descent (*Preface to the Book of Subnotations*). This occurred under Anastasius, as Marius intimates. Since Anastasius ceased to live in the year 402, and Mercator was writing in 429, twenty-seven years had elapsed. Moreover, Coelestius wrote against the transmission of sin before Pelagius composed his brief expositions on Paul’s Epistles. The author of the *Predestinate* testifies that Pelagius had his attention directed to Coelestius’s writings when he reported the arguments of those who opposed the transmission of sin (*Book 1, heresy 88*). Mercator writes that Pelagius completed these expositions before the first devastation of the City (*Commentary*, ch. 2). having gone forth from the city of Rome about twenty years earlier, [Note: He departed with Pelagius before the City was besieged by Alaric, and therefore about May of the year 409. came to Carthage, the metropolis of all Africa, and there, in the presence of Aurelius, bishop of that city, was accused by a certain Paulinus, [Note: Baronius believes, and not without the strongest reasons, that this was the same Paulinus who accused Coelestius and who, at Augustine’s request, wrote the *Life of Saint Ambrose*—indeed, the same man who in 401 was sent to Carthage by Venerius, bishop of Milan, to Aurelius. the deacon of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, [Col. 0069A] by means of a written accusation concerning the matters set out below, as appears from the record of the proceedings into which that pamphlet was inserted; we have copies of those proceedings in our hands. - That Adam was made mortal, and that whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.

[Note: By “Fathers” are meant the primates, or senior bishops, of the provinces. Thus Augustine calls Victorinus, the senior of Numidia, a Father. In Mauritania, Numidia, and the other provinces, the bishop who had first been ordained among all the bishops, whatever city’s see he held, presided over the others, summoned councils, gave judgment, and so was accustomed to be called an elder. Hence, when Innocent replied to the Fathers of the Council of Milevis, he addressed his letter to “Silvanus the elder,” etc. (in Augustine, Letter 181).]

What prevents them from being understood—or perhaps what requires them to be understood—as referring to the sentence of excommunication pronounced by Innocent against Pelagius and Coelestius, rather than to the sentence previously pronounced by Aurelius? This is confirmed by the African Fathers, as Prosper reports (*Against the Collator*, ch. 10): “We determined that the sentence pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius through the venerable bishop Innocent, from the see of blessed Peter, should remain in force until they openly confessed,” etc.]

Concerning Coelestius’s appeal to the apostolic see, Jerome, Augustine, and Orosius are silent; but, besides Mercator, Zosimus bears witness when addressing the bishops of Africa (*Letter 3 to the Africans*): “We wish,” he says, “to deliberate with you concerning the man who, as you yourselves write in your letters, was accused before you and came to our see by his former appeal, not refusing judgment, so that he might assert his innocence.” Paulinus the Deacon also bears witness in his pamphlet to Zosimus (in Baronius, under the year 418), when he explains why he had not attended the trial, although summoned by Basiliscus the subdeacon, because Zosimus had already begun the judgment:

“At the apostolic see,” he says, “I could do nothing, because the man who had appealed to that see was absent, although he ought certainly to have pursued the merits of his appeal—especially since, when the appellant does nothing, even according to human laws, the one who has once prevailed is always in the superior position.”

Finally, Facundus of Hermiane bears witness (*Book 7, ch. 3*): “Coelestius, whom Zosimus himself had examined in the proceedings after he had been convicted in the Church of Carthage and had appealed to the apostolic see.”

The learned Petavius used this testimony of Facundus to resolve the difficult question of how the apostolic see, the first, as Prosper says (*Book 3 of the Dogmatic Poems*), and Innocent, the first, as Facundus writes (*On the Heresy of the Pelagians*, ch. 1, no. 15), could have condemned the Pelagian heresy when Aurelius had proscribed it at Carthage five years earlier. Petavius holds that Aurelius’s sentence was suspended by Coelestius’s appeal and therefore treated as null while the judgment was pending.

But what then becomes of the Diospolitan synod, which preceded Innocent’s sentence by nearly fourteen months? Or how could the appeal suspend the sentence of the Carthaginian synod when the appeal was either neglected, as Marius relates, or certainly extinguished by the passage of time, since more than five years elapsed between Aurelius’s sentence and Innocent’s decree?

This knot must therefore be untied in another way. Baronius (*Year 412*, no. 36) has recourse to the condemnation of Jovinian and Rufinus by Innocent’s predecessors, as though Prosper had called this “a branch cut off at the root.” But Prosper was speaking of something altogether different from the later condemnation: namely, the condemnation that followed after the poison scattered by the British serpent, and that would occur when:

> When mad error spread such things widely,  
> and drew inexperienced ears  
> by deadly fictions.

Perhaps someone will think that Prosper committed a chronological error and placed Innocent’s sentence before the acts of the Diospolitan synod. But how could a man of such diligence make such an error concerning so recent a memory?

I therefore think that the knot has hitherto been sought, as the saying goes, in a reed. Prosper did not wish to say that the heresy had been condemned by the apostolic see before it was condemned by other bishops, for that is plainly false. Rather, after comparing the West and the East, he wished to say that it had been suppressed on the one side by the first see of Peter, which is at Rome, and on the other by the Eastern Fathers who gathered at Diospolis.

Nor did Facundus wish to say that Innocent was the first of all bishops to condemn Pelagius, but the first of the supreme pontiffs—which is entirely true.]

From that sentence he believed an appeal should be made to the judgment of the Roman bishop; [Note: Observe: first, that Coelestius was condemned in the council of the proconsular province convened at Carthage because of the heresy he had spread there, and that he was therefore subject to the judgment of Aurelius, the primate; second, that, after being deprived of communion by a lawful council, he appealed to the apostolic see, and that the African Fathers made no objection to the form of the appeal; third, that the Fathers of the Carthaginian and Milevitan councils, together with the five most distinguished bishops of all Africa, requested in their synodal letters that Innocent, after hearing the case at Rome, confirm by his authority the sentence previously pronounced in Africa; fourth, that they even asked him to summon Pelagius from the East and, after reconsidering the proceedings of the Palestinian synod, determine whether Pelagius had been acquitted justly or unjustly; fifth, that Coelestius, after his appeal had been extinguished by the passage of time, was fully restored by the supreme pontiff, while the accusers were summoned to appear before the apostolic see on an appointed day, and yet the African Fathers made no objection to the pontifical commands or accused him of usurping authority; sixth, that once the case had been brought before the supreme judge, nothing whatever was attempted in Africa against the accused except that it was determined that Innocent’s sentence should remain unharmed and intact; seventh, that eight canons were enacted against the error in a plenary council, but that they attacked only the error, which had long before been proscribed by Innocent, and did not touch the persons whose case was being disputed before the supreme head of the Church; eighth, that Zosimus’s letter, by which both the Pelagian error and its defenders were condemned, was accepted by the Africans as a rule of faith to be subscribed by all bishops who wished to prove themselves Catholic; ninth, that all these events occurred at a time when the controversy between Zosimus and the Africans concerning appeals in disciplinary cases is thought to have been more intense. So constant was it then, and so universally acknowledged, that which Saint Innocent wrote: “Whenever the matter of faith is under discussion, the bishops must refer only to Peter, that is, to the author of his name and honor” (Letter to the Fathers of Milevis, numbered 181 among Augustine’s letters).]

but soon afterward, with the appeal itself disregarded, [Note: Until the present day, the only fact known from the letters of the Carthaginian and Milevitan councils to Saint Innocent was that Coelestius had fled from the city of Carthage into Asia and had there attained the presbyterate; it was not known in what church he had attained it. M. Mercator teaches that he reached Ephesus and sufficiently demonstrates that he was ordained by Heraclides, the predecessor of Memnon; at that time Heraclides presided over the church of Ephesus. This sheds light on Prosper’s verses (*Poem on the Ungrateful*, ch. 2), which many learned men interpret, not without chronological error, as referring to the general Council of Ephesus:

> I pass over how greatly famous Ephesus was stirred  
> by a well-directed tumult, and would not allow  
> the vessels of wrath, the blasts of disease, and the seeds of death  
> to remain in its beds.

Since the subject is the expulsion of the Coelestians from the city of Ephesus in a tumult, before Augustine’s death—which occurred nearly a full year before the Council of Ephesus—the tumult mentioned must have been raised while Augustine was alive. For the following verses, in which the living Augustine is mentioned, show that the poem *Against the Ungrateful* was composed while the holy doctor was still alive:

> Or could the holy council have proceeded  
> toward another end, in which Aurelius was leader  
> and Augustine its intellect? He, whom the grace of Christ,  
> watering him with a more abundant horn, gave as a light to our age,  
> himself kindled from the light. For God is his food,  
> his life, and his rest; and his sole delight  
> is the one love of Christ; the one honor of Christ is his.  
> And while he attributes no good to himself, God becomes for him  
> all things, and wisdom reigns in the holy temple.

It should also be added that the tumult at Ephesus occurred at approximately the time when Atticus expelled the Coelestians from Constantinople and when they were driven out of Sicily. Thus Prosper sings in the passage just cited:

> What shall I say, and why speak of the great care  
> that the good and learned bishop Atticus  
> exercised in the great city of Constantinople,  
> refuting the envoys of the heretics  
> by the ancient faith? From there the impious hearts,  
> although they concealed themselves beneath a covering appearance,  
> bore the torments of judgment and silent rejection.  
> I pass over how greatly famous Ephesus was stirred  
> by a well-directed tumult, etc.

[Col. 0073C]

> And by what faith burning Trinacria  
> drove the viperous troop from its own shores.

Since both expulsions occurred, as no one denies, before Augustine departed this life—and Atticus died five years before Augustine—the Ephesian tumult must also be referred to this period. Moreover, no ancient writer records that the Coelestians were expelled from Ephesus in a tumult at the time of the council; rather, they withdrew of their own accord when the Easterners were escorting Nestorius away. From this it may be inferred that, after they had entered into fellowship with Nestorius’s supporters and obtained from them an acquittal together with some confirmation of their doctrine, matters proceeded as we have already said. On these matters, however, consult the dissertation on synods.]

he proceeded to Ephesus, a city of Asia, and there dared, by underhanded means, to seek a place in the presbyterate.

[Note: Norisius reads “of the presbyters.” GALLAND.]

**3.** [Note: Mercator reports that after several years Coelestius came from Ephesus to Constantinople and was condemned there by Atticus. If only he had counted the years! How greatly this would have assisted the chronology of such a history. Prosper’s verses concerning Coelestius’s condemnation by Atticus are those we quoted earlier. Augustine also writes as follows (*Against Julian*, book 3, ch. 1): “Far be it from me to challenge you to single combat, you whom, wherever you appear, the army of Christ, spread everywhere, defeats—he who defeated Coelestius at Carthage, when I myself was not there, and again at Constantinople, so far from the African regions; he who defeated Pelagius in Palestine,” etc.

Finally, there are these words of Coelestine, writing to Nestorius (*Part I of the Council of Ephesus*, ch. 18): “Why are the things then done against these men [the Pelagians] being investigated, when it is certain that the acts carried out there by Atticus, then the Catholic bishop, were sent to us? Why did Sisinnius of holy memory not investigate these matters? Clearly because, under his predecessor, he had approved that they had been justly condemned.”]

But at what time Atticus passed judgment on Coelestius is difficult to determine. For that he had done so before both of Zosimus’ judgments—that is, not only the second, in which Coelestius was openly condemned, but also the first, in which the crafty heretic could appear to have been acquitted to some extent through the pontiff’s extreme leniency—is indicated by Mercator’s words (Commentary, ch. 1, no. 5):

> “Nevertheless, the aforesaid Coelestius, expelled from here also—from Constantinople—hastened to the city of Rome under Bishop Zosimus of holy memory.”

For afterward Mercator speaks of Zosimus’ first judgment and of the letters sent to the African bishops in Coelestius’ favor. It follows that Atticus’ judgment took place during the interval between Aurelius’ judgment and Zosimus’ judgment. Since the former was held at the beginning of 412 and the latter around May 417, the intervening period was certainly five years and several months. Indeed, since Coelestius, expelled from Constantinople, hastened to Rome under Zosimus, and since Zosimus began his episcopate either on 19 August, as Baronius holds (under the year 417), or—what seems more probable to others—on 2 April 417 (the ancient Martyrology of Bede), Atticus’ judgment itself, or at least Coelestius’ expulsion, must have fallen in the first months of Zosimus’ episcopate, and, as I think, in April or May.

These points appeared to the learned Labbe (vol. II of the General Councils) to exceed credibility, because he believed that the words quoted from Coelestine’s letter to Nestorius had to be understood as referring to records sent by Atticus to Coelestine himself, who began his episcopate in 423. Yet the pontiff could have written those words even if the records had formerly been sent to the apostolic see while his predecessors occupied it.

But two matters certainly cause me much greater difficulty. First, no one is recorded as having been expelled from an episcopal see, or from any other city, on account of the Pelagian heresy before the constitution of Honorius issued at Ravenna on the day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, Augusti—that is, on 13 April 418. Second, if the records of the judgment held concerning Coelestius had been sent by Atticus to Rome, and indeed to Carthage and the other sees, before Zosimus had concluded the case, it is not apparent why the African Fathers—who gathered arguments for condemning the heresy from every quarter—would have made no mention of such records and so significant a precedent. Likewise, how could Augustine have failed to mention Atticus’ records until he wrote against Julian in 422, when he had often had suitable opportunities to do so?

I see only one possible answer: perhaps the writing from Constantinople to the other Churches did not take place immediately after the judgment, but one or two years later, as often happened. In that way everything can be reconciled without much difficulty.

Once this chronology has been established, I think we should say that Coelestius fled from Carthage to Asia in 412; remained for some time at Rhodes to spread his error, as Jerome suggests (Preface to book IV on Jeremiah); then proceeded to Ephesus around 414, where he obtained the presbyterate; after three years went from Ephesus to Constantinople, from which he was expelled after Atticus’ sentence in 417; and from Constantinople hastened to Rome under the beginning of Zosimus’ pontificate. But I shall discuss these matters more fully in the dissertation on the synods.

Afterward, several years later, under Atticus, bishop of holy memory, he went to Constantinople, where, having been exposed in similar matters, he was expelled from that noble city through the great zeal of that holy man, with letters sent concerning him to Asia, Thessalonica,

[Note: Someone might suppose that the letters sent by Atticus were addressed to the Churches mentioned for particular private reasons: to Asia because Theodorus of Mopsuestia was teaching there the same doctrines as Coelestius, being also the teacher of Pelagius, as John Maxentius reports (In the Second Confession of Faith); Mercator agrees with him in more than one passage, as will be said in the preface to the Subnotations; and to Thessalonica because Rufus presided there. Julian, writing in the name of eighteen bishops, had attempted by his cunning to test Rufus and, if possible, draw him over to his side, as Augustine says (Book I to Boniface, ch. 1). They might likewise be thought to have been sent to Carthage because Coelestius had first been condemned there and because, very probably, Atticus had received letters from that city. It might also appear that letters were sent to Rome, as Coelestine testifies in his letter to Nestorius, in the words quoted shortly before.

Yet, whatever force this explanation may possess, another reason need not be sought beyond the fact that in those places there were certain greater sees to which, according to ecclesiastical custom, the records of judgments were sent when their knowledge concerned the whole Church, by means of synodical letters, of which we shall speak in the third chapter.]

and Carthage, sent to the bishops; we are prepared to produce copies of them.

### 4

Nevertheless, the aforesaid Coelestius, expelled from there also, hastened with all speed to the city of Rome under Bishop Zosimus of holy memory. There, when questioned on the basis of the records—which records we possess—he was to some extent frightened by the judge; yet by his frequent answers and statements he sowed hope,

[Note: This is the reading of the Benedictine edition following Baluzius. Norisius instead has “spread the seed,” which may be more correct. Shortly afterward he reads “by kindness.” Galland.]

promising that he would condemn those articles on which he had been accused at Carthage. For this too

[Note: Paulinus agrees with Mercator in the booklet cited earlier, where Zosimus is reported as pressing Coelestius with these words (in Baronius, under the year 418, no. 12): “So then, do you condemn all those things contained in Paulinus’ booklet—that is, concerning the questions?” And elsewhere: “Do you recognize what sort of letter the apostolic see sent to the brethren and fellow bishops of the African province? Do you condemn everything we condemned, and hold what we hold?” And again: “Do you condemn all those things that have been circulated concerning your name? I do not want you to lead us around by evasions. Do you condemn all those things that Paulinus either brought against you or that have been spread abroad by report?”]

he was indeed ordered more insistently to do so [Baluzius adds: “and it was more vehemently expected of him that he should do so”]; and for that very reason

[Note: Augustine says (same work, ch. 7): “The venerable Pope Zosimus dealt with a man whom the wind of false doctrine had inflated, so that he would condemn those things brought against him by the deacon Paulinus and assent to the letters of the apostolic see that had proceeded from his predecessor of holy memory. But he refused to condemn the deacon’s charges; nevertheless, he did not dare resist the letters of blessed Pope Innocent. Rather, he promised that he would condemn everything that that see condemned. And thus, like a madman, so that he might rest as though gently soothed, he was nevertheless not yet thought to have been released from the bonds of excommunication. But after a period of two months, until a reply could be sent from Africa, an opportunity for recovering his senses was granted him under the leniency of a medicinal sentence.”]

he was judged worthy of some consideration through the humanity of that holy priest; and thus

[Note: Whether the author means the first or the second of the three letters that Zosimus sent to the African bishops in the Pelagian affair is not worth investigating more closely. Both greatly favor Coelestius, though the second was written in Pelagius’ interest. What could be more advantageous to Coelestius in these words? What more suitable for assisting his stratagems? The pontiff says (Letter 2 to the Africans): “After the presbyter Coelestius was heard by us, and clearly expressed what he thought concerning the faith, he also strengthened by repeated professions the same things that he had set forth in his booklet.” And afterward: “Behold, we have received the letter of Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, who was ordained bishop in the place formerly occupied by the holy Bishop John, and who intervened as an energetic supporter of Pelagius’ case. Pelagius himself also sent his letters in great abundance, containing his defense. In them he fully set forth, without any disguise, what his profession of faith followed and what it condemned, so that the snares of every interpretation might cease. They were read publicly. They contained everything equal and formed according to the same meaning and opinions that Coelestius had previously advanced.” A little later: “How astonishing that such men of unblemished faith could also have been branded! Is there any place in which the grace or assistance of God has been omitted?” Then, after listing the accusers’ faults and criticizing the Africans’ haste, he says: “Let it be a joy to you to recognize that those whom false judges charged have never been separated from our body and from Catholic truth. Certainly what our expectation desired has shone forth: that they should condemn what must be condemned and follow what must be followed.” Finally, referring to the Gospel father rejoicing at the son’s return (Luke 15:21), he says: “How much greater is this overflowing joy of faith—that those about whom false reports have been spread are not dead and have not perished?”

It may be useful to note two matters incidentally. First, the second letter is read as dated 21 September, and the third 21 March, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus XII; but the first lacks the month and day and gives only the consuls Honorius XI and Flavius Constantius. Why does it lack a date? Is it because none was actually found in the Vatican manuscript? Or was one that perhaps existed deliberately omitted because it would have conflicted with Baronius’ theory concerning Innocent’s death and Zosimus’ accession, which he placed in another period?

Second, the three letters first published from the Vatican manuscript in the Annals under the years 417 and 418 could have appeared to Cappellus (in his book On Appeals) to be forgeries. Now, however, Mercator establishes their credibility sufficiently, so that there is no need to resort to the unwelcome defenses of Vossius, who here, in the manner of heretics, seized an opportunity to attack the supreme head of the Catholic Church (Book I, The Pelagian Heresy). Nevertheless, we shall dispute Cappellus in the dissertation on the synods, where we shall present Zosimus’ letters purified of the errors with which they had previously teemed.]

he earned a certain letter full of kindness from him to the African bishops.

[Note: That pertinacious and at the same time crafty heretic, although he had been proscribed almost everywhere throughout the world by both ecclesiastical and imperial decrees, nevertheless claimed that he was suffering undeserved persecution on account of the Catholic faith. He alleged that he had been heard in person by Zosimus in a legitimate council, where his accusers had been rejected as infamous and lying; that the judgment of the African bishops had been criticized as contrary to the canons and rash in itself; that his own faith had been acquitted; that his booklet had been pronounced Catholic; and that letters concerning the whole matter had been sent to Africa, which he produced. He then replied concerning what happened afterward, claiming that all the proceedings had been conducted by deception, through the faction of powerful men and fear imposed upon the Roman clergy; and that Pope Zosimus himself had acted improperly through the counsel—or rather the force—of factionalists. He said that the final sentence against absent men had been issued partly because of the pontiff’s own fear and partly through the devices of the Africans, who, through Alipius, had corrupted not only court officials by gifts but had also wearied Honorius with prayers that, in those circumstances, were terrifying—Honorius, who at that time feared everything, with Africa scarcely yet settled after the disturbances of Stilicho and Heraclian. What effect these claims had even at Constantinople, upon the minds of many and especially at court, is shown by Nestorius’ letters to Coelestine, mentioned earlier.]

which he has abused, or continues to abuse, to deceive many ignorant people.

### 5

When the bishops from Africa replied, explaining the whole case that had taken place among them,

[Note: The author distinguishes two kinds of records: those drawn up with Coelestius present and those drawn up concerning him. The former belong to the Carthaginian council of 412; the latter to the second Carthaginian council and the council of Milevis in 416. Coelestius was present at the first Carthaginian council; at the others, the Fathers of the Carthaginian council themselves testify (in their synodical letter to Saint Innocent) that judgment was rendered solely on the basis of the booklets or letters of Eros and Lazarus. Zosimus appears to criticize this method of judgment (in his first and second letters to the African bishops) as contrary to the canons. Along with the records, Paulinus’ booklet was also sent, containing the accusation against Coelestius, as is clear both from Augustine (On Original Sin, chs. 5–6) and from another booklet of Paulinus to Zosimus (Zosimus’ Letter 3 to the Africans). The bearer of all these documents was Marcellinus, a subdeacon of the Church of Carthage. Norisius previously reads “with him, namely concerning him.” Galland.]

and also sending the records of what had then been drawn up with him or concerning him,

[Note: Augustine relates the same history: “When so many and such important ecclesiastical letters were passing back and forth between the apostolic see and the African bishops, and even records concerning this case had been drawn up at that see while Coelestius was present and answering, he replied that he agreed with the letters of Pope Innocent of blessed memory, by which the entire doubt concerning this matter had been removed. And so that this might be made fuller and clearer, letters were awaited from Africa, where his craftiness had become somewhat more evident. When those letters afterward arrived, they stated that it was not enough for slower and more cautious men that he confessed generally that he agreed with Bishop Innocent’s letters; rather, he had to anathematize openly the errors that he had set forth in his booklet. Otherwise, if he did not do so, many people of limited understanding might believe that the poisons of faith in his booklet had been approved by the apostolic see, because that see had said that his booklet was Catholic, rather than corrected because he himself had replied that he agreed with Pope Innocent’s letters.

“Then, when his presence was demanded so that either the man’s deceit or his correction might be made clear through definite and lucid answers, and no ambiguity might remain for anyone, he withdrew and refused the examination. It should no longer have been postponed, as it was, for the benefit of others, if the obstinacy and madness of exceedingly perverse men could not benefit from it. But, God forbid, if Coelestius or Pelagius had then been judged in the Roman Church in such a way that those doctrines of theirs which Pope Innocent had condemned in and together with them were pronounced worthy of approval and adherence, then this would rather have been a mark of misconduct to be branded upon the Roman clergy.”

This entire passage seemed worth transcribing, although somewhat lengthy, because we learn several things from it:

1. From the time Zosimus began to reconsider Coelestius’ case—which the Africans believed Innocent had already concluded—many ecclesiastical writings of private individuals, as well as records of synods, were sent back and forth; scarcely anything of these remains.

2. As some think, a continuous synod of bishops may have remained at Carthage for almost an entire year, from the time the case began to be agitated until it was finally completed by Zosimus’ tractoria, by which Pelagius and Coelestius were condemned. This point is necessary for reconciling, and even understanding, many matters belonging to the history of the entire affair.

3. From the records drawn up by Aurelius with Coelestius in 412 and sent to Rome, the matter had been judged and largely concluded by Zosimus. Paulinus the deacon also testifies to this in his booklet.

4. Coelestius employed such craft that he insisted he generally assented to Innocent’s letters and that no more explicit condemnation of the writings was necessary, especially of the booklet in which he had explained his own opinion, since it had been called Catholic by the Roman see.

5. The Africans firmly resisted this and even demanded that he be compelled openly to anathematize the errors he had set forth in his booklet.

6. Zosimus summoned the man from the African council to a hearing and pressed him sharply—even personally, through frequent and forceful questioning—to disclose his mind through definite and lucid answers. Coelestius, however, in order not to do so, either fled from Rome or concealed himself among his supporters under the pretense of flight.

7. Innocent condemned the Pelagian doctrines in and together with their proponents. This was one of the forms in which heresies were condemned in the earliest period, and it was both better and safer. For the other method, by which propositions are proscribed, so to speak, in the abstract, is less useful for preventing heretics from continuing to mock the less perceptive through their evasions and from tiring others out by their tergiversations. See what we have said in the dissertation on subscriptions (Dissertation 5, On Subscriptions in the Pelagian Affair).]

was summoned to a fuller hearing so that he might hasten to fulfill what he had promised—that is, so that, after condemning the aforesaid articles, he might be absolved from the sentence of the African bishops by which he had been deprived of communion. He not only failed to appear, but also

[Note: Augustine had said that Coelestius refused and withdrew from the examination; Mercator adds that he fled from Rome. The deacon Paulinus testifies to the same thing as Augustine: “At that time,” he says in his booklet to Pope Zosimus, “that is, at Rome, I could do nothing, because the man who had appealed to the apostolic see was absent, although he ought certainly to have pursued the merits of his appeal.”]

fled from the aforesaid city of Rome. For this reason he was

[Note: By these writings he means the letter that he will call the tractoria in chapter 3. It does not survive in its entirety, at least it has not yet been published. Some fragments remain in Augustine (Letter 190 to Optatus) and in the appendix to Coelestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul. Augustine writes as follows: “To use the words found in the letter itself of the most blessed Bishop Zosimus:

> ‘The Lord is faithful in his words, and his baptism, in reality and in words—that is, in work, confession, and the remission of sins—holds the same fullness for every sex, age, condition, and class of the human race. For no one is made free except one who is a slave of sin; nor can anyone be called redeemed except one who was truly captive beforehand through sin, as it is written: “If the Son makes you free, you will be truly free” (John 8:36). Through him we are spiritually reborn; through him we are crucified to the world; by his death the bond contracted through the propagation of sin, introduced by Adam and transmitted to all of us and to every soul, is broken—the bond in which none of those born is not held liable before being freed through baptism.’”

In the appendix to Coelestine’s letter are these words:

> “All the efforts, works, and merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him from any other source than from what he himself has given.”

To this opinion the authoritative rule of Pope Zosimus of blessed memory directs us. Writing to the bishops of the whole world, he says:

> “We, however, moved by God—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—have reported everything to the conscience of our brethren and fellow bishops” (Appendix to Coelestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul, ch. 8).

And afterward (same work, ch. 4):

> “When the same teacher spoke to the bishops of the whole world concerning the assistance of divine grace, he said: ‘What time intervenes in which we do not need his assistance? Therefore, in all actions, cases, thoughts, and movements, he must be entreated as helper and protector. For it is arrogance for human nature to presume anything for itself, while the Apostle cries out: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers and authorities of this air, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12). And again, as he himself says (Romans 6:24–25): “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.” And again: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty; but I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10).’”]

### Defense of Pope Zosimus in the Affair of Coelestius

It will be useful, I think, to examine Zosimus’ case at this point, since some vehemently accuse him concerning the affair of Coelestius, while others defend him—not all, however, with sufficient regard for the dignity of the matter.

Those who accuse Zosimus bring four charges against him, each apparently very serious. First, after a man had been condemned almost everywhere throughout the world—and certainly in seven provinces: at Carthage, Diospolis, Antioch, Constantinople, again at Carthage, in the province of Numidia, and at Rome—after his appeal had been extinguished, after he had attempted to deceive the whole world by fraud, and after his wicked stratagems had been exposed, Zosimus thought that the case should be reopened, disregarding the sentence of his holy predecessor.

Second, he pronounced Catholic the booklet in which Coelestius openly denied original sin and concealed Christ’s grace through malicious evasiveness; indeed, he seemed to acquit the person of both heretics.

Third, he charged the African bishops—among whom Aurelius, Augustine, Alypius, Evodius, Possidius, and others, the holiest and most learned bishops in the entire world, stood out—with harsher letters, accusing them of inconsiderate zeal, intemperate curiosity, violation of the canons, credulity toward unworthy accusers, precipitate judgment, and wounded charity.

Finally, he brought atrocious charges, in angry language, against the two holy bishops of Gaul, Eros and Lazarus, the accusers of Pelagius—men who perhaps suffered persecution for justice, and certainly were forced by violence to abandon their sees. In his second letter to the Africans he treated them as though they were storms and tempests of the Church, bearing names made shameful by their deeds and condemnations: one of them had at some time been convicted of calumny and had burst into the priestly throne almost sprinkled with the blood of an innocent man; the other, an accomplice in murder, had caused chains to be placed upon presbyters who contradicted him; and both had supported the tyranny of Constantine.

Even those who have attempted to excuse Zosimus do not deny these facts: among the ancients, Augustine, Mercator, Facundus, and any others; among more recent writers, Baronius, who produced Zosimus’ letters in the Annals as witnesses for the prosecution, and the rest generally who treat this argument—except those who have thought the letters forged.

Facundus offers this excuse (Book VII, ch. 2): neither the Palestinian bishops nor Zosimus should be considered heretics by the Church because they thought well of heretics; rather, they should be judged and honored as Catholics according to the merit of their faith, since the uncomprehended cunning of the wicked ought not to be counted as a crime against the simple. But what does it mean to accuse, if this is to excuse? Zosimus was not a heretic—no one has yet made him guilty under that name—but this simplicity, I think, does not sufficiently absolve the act of the supreme pontiff, a judge reopening a case made so distinguished by so many precedents.

Augustine uses a much better defense (Book II to Boniface, ch. 3). He says that the minds of Pelagius and Coelestius, although corrupted by a wicked error, were not contemptible, and seemed rather to require diligent correction than easy condemnation; for that reason they were treated somewhat more leniently than the strict discipline of the Church demanded. After immediately explaining everything that took place between Zosimus and Coelestius, he concludes with these words:

> “Since the letters of the most blessed Pope Innocent, responding to the letters of the bishops, likewise condemned among the Africans this error which these men are attempting to persuade others to accept; and since his successor, Pope Zosimus, never said or wrote that what they think concerning infants must be held; moreover, since he constrained Coelestius, who was trying to clear himself, through repeated interventions to assent to the aforesaid letters of the apostolic see—certainly whatever was dealt with more leniently in the meantime concerning Coelestius, provided the firmness of the ancient and most robust faith was preserved, was a most merciful urging toward correction, not a most destructive approval of depravity. And the fact that Coelestius and Pelagius were afterward condemned by the same priest with renewed authority was the reason for producing the severity that had necessarily been interrupted for a short time, not a betrayal of a truth previously recognized, nor a new discovery of the truth.”

Yet this method of defense, however much it absolves Zosimus from the charge of heresy—and even from betrayal and imprudent leniency—is not, to speak frankly, complete in every respect. It neither adequately addresses each individual charge nor responds to the arguments brought against him. It will therefore be worthwhile to examine the entire matter more carefully.

First, the holy pontiff should not be blamed for granting Coelestius a hearing or for accepting Pelagius’ letters and booklet. Although Innocent had condemned both men, he had nevertheless tempered his sentence by expressly ordering (Letter 30) that, if they should ever recover their senses after laying aside the error of their false doctrine and condemning the things by which they had condemned themselves through their own misconduct, the Church should not deny them the customary remedy—that is, its place of refuge.

It was therefore lawful, indeed necessary, to hear men who said that they had laid aside their error, agreed with Innocent’s letters, produced testimony from the bishop of the see of Jerusalem, and, through an appeal—even though not pursued within the lawful period—were restored in full by the supreme authority of ecclesiastical law. In addition, they had not been condemned by lesser sees or by councils of bishops through a definitive sentence, but under a ruling suspended at the discretion of the supreme pontiff.

Next, although Coelestius’ booklet openly attacked original sin, about which Pelagius had remained silent, and although it also contained an obscurely formulated discussion of the grace of God, Augustine nevertheless appears to have been able to call it Catholic for the following reason (in the passage cited immediately above): it belonged to a Catholic mind to submit one’s doubt or opinion to correction by the judgment of the apostolic see. First, let us hear both heretics, and then Augustine.

Pelagius says in his statement of faith:

> “This is the faith, most blessed pope, in which, if something has perhaps been stated less skillfully or with too little caution, we desire to be corrected by you, who hold both the faith and the see of Peter.”

Coelestius says likewise in his booklet:

> “I have not established these things with the fixed authority of one defining a doctrine. Rather, what I have received from the source of the prophets and apostles I offer for approval to the judgment of your apostleship, so that, if perhaps—as happens among human beings—some error of ignorance has slipped in, it may be corrected by your sentence.”

Augustine says (Book II to Boniface, ch. 3):

> “When Coelestius had set this concerning original sin in his booklet, among those matters only about which he confessed that he still had doubts and wished to be instructed, the will to be corrected was approved in a man of very keen intellect who, if corrected, would certainly have benefited many, not the falsity of the doctrine. For that reason his booklet was called Catholic: it was characteristic of a Catholic mind that, if one happens to think in some way other than truth demands, one should not define that opinion with complete certainty, but reject it once it has been exposed and demonstrated.”

As for the letters written to the African bishops, I admit that they could contain something of the leniency extended even to the heretic himself. Nevertheless, it must not be denied that they have a strong appearance of justice, if someone should reasonably believe that the Africans had sinned in their judgments.

Should not Aurelius, when Coelestius appealed to the apostolic see, have granted him letters of appeal? Yet he did not. Should not the records have been sent immediately to Rome? They were sent, I admit, but only after almost five full years.

Furthermore, if anything was judged concerning Pelagius at the second council of Carthage—as many think, and not implausibly infer from the words of the Fathers writing to Innocent—the judgment against the absent Pelagius was instituted solely on the letters of absent accusers, or even on Orosius’ report. He had never been legitimately heard in Africa, something that Cyprian himself, the ancient canons, and the custom of the Church regarded as unlawful.

If nothing was judged, but the matter was merely referred to the apostolic see—which can scarcely be maintained—or if Innocent’s sentence alone was approved, as appears to have been done much more cautiously in the councils attended by Augustine, nevertheless it is scarcely excusable that no one was sent to Rome—not even the deacon Paulinus, who could have convicted Coelestius, then present, through adequate documents.

Moreover, the pontiff could have interpreted the action as arising from some estrangement or at least agitation of minds because of the controversy concerning appeals that had arisen at that time. Add that Zosimus could plausibly accuse the Africans of excessive and precipitate zeal: in a matter as important as the defense of Catholic doctrine, they had credulously believed Eros and Lazarus, wandering men and bishops without sees, deprived of communion by an apostolic sentence because they had seized priestly offices by force, with the support of a tyrant, while presbyters resisted and clerics were thrown into chains, and after the city had been handed over and occupied.

Finally, concerning Eros and Lazarus: since the memory and case of both are obscure, and since the writers of this period maintain a profound silence concerning Lazarus, I would rather believe the supreme pontiff concerning Eros—especially since he is writing to an entire diocese—than the chronicler Prosper, who perhaps, indeed almost certainly, is different from Prosper of Aquitaine. Even if he was not a different man, he may have been inclined, given his favorable disposition toward the Africans and the condemners of Pelagius, to insert into his Chronicle what was said about Eros’ holiness through an inclination of will rather than through a careful examination of the facts.

Yet because the history of Eros and Lazarus—or rather, a clear view of their lives—can contribute greatly to the vindication of Saint Zosimus, I have thought it appropriate to gather here what is found scattered among various authors.

Those two bishops were Gallic not by origin but by see. Although they were foreigners, they occupied bishoprics in Gaul (Zosimus’ second letter to the Africans): Lazarus the see of Aix, Eros that of Arles. Both acted in turbulent times, and both through the power of the tyrant Constantine.

Lazarus was condemned at the Council of Turin by Proculus because of the slander he had brought against Saint Britius. Yet afterward, for reasons unknown, he was ordained by Proculus bishop of Aix. Relying on the tyrant’s patronage, he burst into the priestly throne that was still almost stained with the blood of his innocent predecessor and remained in it under the shadow of the priesthood for as long as the tyrant’s imperial image endured. Accordingly, after the destruction of his patron, he voluntarily withdrew from that position and condemned himself by his own resignation. These are the words of Saint Zosimus (same letter).

Eros was first a disciple of Saint Martin and later a supporter of Constantine’s faction. Through the same favor by which Lazarus seized the see of Aix, Eros himself invaded the Church of Arles. The presbyters resisted his invasion, and the clergy opposed him courageously; nevertheless, after casting many of them into chains and prison, he compelled them to serve both the circumstances and himself.

He ordained the tyrant Constantine as a presbyter after Constantine had laid aside the imperial purple. But soon afterward, when Count Constantius had taken the city of Arles by force and the tyrant had been killed on the road while being led to the emperor Honorius, Eros was expelled from the city by the people, and Patroclus was appointed in his place through Constantius’ favor.

A close connection existed between the two men, although it is uncertain whether because they shared a homeland or for some other reason; they also shared a great and continuous community of affairs. Were they not both disciples of the same Martin? Certainly they shared the same plans, supported the same tyrant, were ordained by the same Proculus against the will of the Churches, were expelled from their sees by the same storm, and sailed back and forth with the same purpose, seeking support and clearly unwilling to accept their deposition. They were also the accusers of Pelagius: first absent at Diospolis and acting through booklets, then present at Antioch, and finally before the African Fathers through letters delivered by Orosius.

What became of them after they fled to Palestine—perhaps their native land—I believe to be unknown. This alone is certain: they rendered the Church very great service, whether from zeal for the faith or from some other motive, when they exposed the two extraordinarily deceitful heretics, Pelagius and Coelestius, who were trying to conceal themselves among the Catholics, and delivered them up to the Church for judgment. Yet, even if they served divine Providence in this matter, the words written by Saint Zosimus do not thereby cease to be true: that they became storms and tempests of the Church, and by their acts and condemnations made their names objects of shame; for the wicked have often been cast into the sea by storms and tempests.

Although the case of men of this sort is so perplexed that very weighty authorities accuse them on one side and excuse them on the other. John of Jerusalem first accused them at the Synod of Diospolis, but Augustine immediately excused them in no slight discourse; for these are his own words (*On the Proceedings in Palestine*, book 16): “Whatever Bishop John said about our absent brethren—whether our fellow bishops Eros and Lazarus, the presbyter Orosius, or others whose names are not stated there—I believe that he understands it not to avail to their prejudice. For if they had been present, they might perhaps, far be it from me to say it, have convicted him of lying; but they might instead have recalled something that he had forgotten, or pointed out where the Latin interpreter had misled him. And if not through an intention to lie, certainly through some difficulty arising from an insufficient understanding of a foreign language—especially because the whole matter is conducted in written records; records which are usefully established so that the wicked may not lie and the good may not forget anything. But if anyone should raise any question against our aforementioned brethren on this account and summon them to an episcopal judgment, they will defend themselves as they are able; what need is there for us to trouble ourselves, when not even the judges themselves wished to pronounce anything on the matter after the account given by our fellow bishop?”

Zosimus subsequently accused them in letters to the Africans, as we have seen; Prosper excused at least Eros in his *Chronicle*, in most honorable terms: “Eros,” he says, “a holy man and a disciple of the blessed Martin, while serving as bishop over the town of Arles, was driven out by the people of that city though innocent and subject to no accusations. Patroclus was ordained in his place, a friend and intimate of Constantius, master of the soldiers, whose favor was sought through him; and this affair was the cause of great dissensions among the bishops of that region.”

He was condemned in very extensive, or very lengthy, writings, in which the very chapters of which he had been accused are included, and the whole case is narrated, both that concerning the aforementioned Coelestius and that concerning his teacher Pelagius, still more depraved. [Note: [Col. 0082D] Norisius prefers the reading *videretur esse*, “it would seem to be,” rather than *narratur*, “is narrated.” GALLAND.] We possess copies of these writings here, and we suggest that similar and identical documents were sent to the Eastern Churches—to the diocese of Egypt, Constantinople, Thessalonica, and Jerusalem—and to their bishops. [Note: [Col. 0082D] Marius lists the principal sees to which it was customary to write concerning matters that were to be made known to the whole Church. He omitted Rome, where Zosimus was seated, and Carthage, to which Augustine says that special letters were sent. The principal sees were Rome, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem, Constantinople, Carthage, and Thessalonica. Under Rome were included the Westerners; under Alexandria, the Egyptians; under Antioch, the Easterners; under Jerusalem, the Palestinians; under Constantinople, the Asians, except for the autocephalous Churches; under Carthage, the Africans; and under Thessalonica, the Macedonians.]

## CHAPTER II. On Pelagius’s doctrine, as it is known from his writings

### 1

The reason why Pelagius too was condemned together with him [Bal. *isto*, “that man,” for *ipso*, “him”] is as follows. The aforementioned man dared, before the sack of the city of Rome, to compose commentaries on the Apostle Paul and to publish them among those whose friendship he relied upon. [Note: [Col. 0083B] Below (chapter 3): “After the sack of the city of Rome, Pelagius lived in Palestine.” The sack of the City referred to occurred under Alaric, king of the Goths, in the year of Christ 410.] [Note: [Col. 0083B–D] These *Commentaries*, as already mentioned, are found in volume 30 of our *Patrology*, and in volume 11 of Jerome’s works. EDIT. They were long thought, at least by the less sharp-sighted, to belong to the holy doctor, I suppose because of the preface, which some, though without justification, think bears his name. There were also those who attributed them to Primasius and Sedulius; but this opinion has become obsolete. No learned person now doubts that they are the work not merely of some Pelagian—as Bellarmine and other learned men thought—but of Pelagius himself. Besides Mercator, this is plainly taught by two writers of the same age, who also testify that they read them. The author of the *Praedestinatus* says: “Pelagius himself writes as follows in his commentary on Romans, while treating the passage where the Apostle says: ‘Through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death, and thus it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Rom. IV, 12). Touching upon Coelestius, who first wrote against the transmission of sin, he says: ‘Those who oppose the transmission try to assail it as follows: “If Adam’s sin harmed even those who did not sin, then Christ’s grace also benefits even those who do not believe.” They add this as well: “If baptism takes away that original sin, those born of two baptized persons ought to be free from this sin. For how can they transmit to their descendants what they themselves did not possess?”’ We have set down these words as written by Pelagius himself.” Augustine says: “After very few days I read certain writings of Pelagius, a man, as I hear, holy and of no small Christian advancement, which contained very brief expositions of the Epistles of the Apostle Paul; and there I discovered, when he came to the passage where the Apostle says that through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and thus passed into all human beings, an argument of those who deny that infants bear original sin.” And later, explaining the Apostle’s words, “Adam, the type of the one to come,” he says: “Pelagius himself expounded this in more than one way.” And on the Apostle’s words, “For the unbelieving husband is sanctified,” etc. (1 Cor. 7:14): “Either it is to be understood as we have elsewhere, and Pelagius too, while treating the same Epistle to the Corinthians, expounded it,” etc. And in another book: “He also interwove other execrable statements of his which Pope Zosimus attached to his letters, written for circulation throughout the Catholic world, as you may read; there Pelagius, as though expounding the Apostle Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, argues and says: ‘If Adam’s sin harmed even those who did not sin, then Christ’s righteousness also benefits those who do not believe,’” and other such things, all of which, with the Lord’s help, were refuted and demolished in the books we wrote on the baptism of infants (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*). “And indeed in those purported expositions he did not dare to make the objection in his own person; but he said it there where he was widely known and where what he thought and said could not be concealed.” And again, in another book: “Do you think you have discovered why an infant is baptized? Say why it is exorcised. Certainly the saying of your author Pelagius was considered great and unanswerable: ‘If Adam’s sin harmed even those who did not sin, then Christ’s righteousness also benefits those who do not believe’” (*Unfinished Work*, book 1, chapter 54). Many other passages scattered here and there in Augustine are read in such commentaries. Yet this very explicit passage must not be omitted: Augustine says, “There are certain expositions of the Epistle written to the Romans which are said to be Pelagius’s, where he maintains that what is written, ‘It is not of one who wills or runs, but of God who shows mercy’ (Rom. 9:16), was not said in Paul’s own person, but that Paul used the voice of one questioning and reproving when he said it, as though it certainly ought not to be said.”] [Note: [Col. 0084C] Jerome is an especially weighty witness to how cautiously Pelagius disclosed his thought (*Letter to Ctesiphon*): “The Eunomians, Arians, and Macedonians, distinct in name but united in impiety, cause us no labor; for they say what they think. This heresy alone is ashamed to say publicly what it does not fear to teach in secret. The silence of its masters is voiced by the frenzy of its disciples.” See what we said in the dissertation on the constitutions of the emperors (Appendix, dissertation 4).] [Note: [Col. 0084C] See Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 1, chapter 1 and following, and *On Original Sin*, chapter 21. GALLAND.] He thought that he was explaining individually the words or meanings of the Apostle.

In the Epistle to the Romans, therefore, when he had come to the passage where the chosen vessel speaks in this way: “Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death, and thus death passed into all human beings” (Rom. 5:12), he believed that it should be explained as follows. [Note: [Col. 0084C]

Cassiodorus says of this book: “The eighth canonical codex contains the Epistles of the Apostles. But in the thirteen Epistles of Saint Paul I found, at the very beginning of my writing, annotations which were so widely known and circulated among everyone that they were said to have been written by the most learned man, Pope Gelasius of the city of Rome. This is what those usually do who wish to defend defective works by the authority of a glorious name. But from the preceding readings it became clear to us, after careful reconsideration, that although they are extremely subtle and very brief in expression, the poisons of the Pelagian error have been sown there. And so that the heretical error might be kept far from you, I purged the first Epistle to the Romans with all the care I could; the others, written in a parchment codex, I left for you to correct. This will easily be accomplished, since the example of what precedes makes the imitation of what follows bolder.”]

From this we learn, first, that at that time these annotations were in the hands of many because of their brevity and subtlety; second, that they were attributed to Saint Gelasius, bishop of the City; finally, that Cassiodorus himself carefully cleansed those on the Epistle to the Romans of the poison of Pelagian error, so as to provide his own monks with an example for correcting the others—though it is uncertain whether they actually carried this out. They are therefore sought in vain in the commonly circulated editions, which Augustine, Mercator, and the author of the *Predestined One* report as full of Pelagian error. For it is credible that the common editions were taken from those copies which Cassiodorus handed down to his monks and the monks transmitted to their successors.

What is read in the annotations on chapter 7:9 is likewise suspect: “When there was no law, sin was dead; those who assert that sin comes to us from Adam through transmission are insane.” For what could more openly conflict with the Catholic faith concerning the propagation of sin from Adam? Or how could a man who had cleansed the exposition of this Epistle with such care, and who was thoroughly Catholic, have left behind such impiety? It is futile to say that Cassiodorus was speaking either of personal sin—which would be an Origenist delusion—or of the transmission of another’s sin through the transmission of soul together with body, which seemed to some an obvious madness. I therefore consider it more probable that the passage, after being cleansed by Cassiodorus, was again defiled elsewhere by a copyist.] 

We possess his book and produce it to convict his error.

### 2

Thus he himself says:

> “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death.” He used an example, or an image, he says, because just as, when sin did not exist, it entered stealthily through Adam, so also, when righteousness did not remain in anyone, life was restored through Christ.

### 3

> “And death passed into all human beings.” Since those who sin likewise die, he says. For death did not pass into Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob, concerning whom the Lord says: “For all live to him” (Luke 20:38). Here, he says, he calls all dead because, on account of the multitude of sinners, the few righteous are not excepted, just as he says there: “There is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 52:2, 4). And again he says: “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:11); or certainly it passed into all those who lived according to human custom, not according to the heavenly one.

### 4

And shortly afterward:

> “But death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not transgressed in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. 5:14). Either, he says, when there was no one to distinguish between the just and the unjust, death thought that it ruled over everyone; or it reigned over those who transgressed a commandment, like Adam—that is, over the sons of Noah, who were commanded not to eat a living creature’s soul in its blood, and over the sons of Abraham, who were commanded to be circumcised—but also over those who, beyond the commandment, had disregarded the natural law. [Note: [Col. 0085D] “Had sinned.” Thus reads the Bellovacensis codex. The Vaticanus and earlier editions have *praevaricaverunt*, “had transgressed.” But we preferred the reading of the Bellovacensis book because it agrees with the Vulgate version of this Pauline passage. BALUZ.]

### 5

> “Who is the form of the one to come” (ibid.).
