For just as Adam, he says, was formed by God without sexual intercourse, so Christ proceeded from a Virgin, with the Holy Spirit as creator; or, as some say, the form is by contrast—that is, just as the former is the head of sin, so the latter is the head of righteousness. [Bal. *ex*, “from,” instead of *a*, “by”; Bal. adds *ut*, “that”; Bal. omits *etiam*, “also.”]

### 6

> “But not as the transgression, so also the gift” (ibid. 15), so that, he says, equality should not be supposed in the comparison.

### 7

> “For if, through the transgression of one, many died, much more did the gift and grace of God abound to many through one man, Jesus Christ” (ibid.). “Grace,” says the Apostle, “was more powerful in giving life than sin was in bringing death, because Adam killed not only himself but also his descendants, whereas Christ delivered both those who were then in the body and those who would later come into being.” [Note: [Col. 0085D] What follows is absent from the commonly circulated editions, and there is no doubt that Cassiodorus deleted it because it was like an inconvenient episode and was otherwise full of heretical argumentation.]

### 8

Here the attentive Catholic reader should note what he says: “Adam harmed not only himself but also his descendants.” Hold fast to his earlier definition: by “descendants” he does not here mean all human beings everywhere and altogether [Bellov. “not all human beings altogether and everywhere”], but only those who, by imitation, are likewise guilty of transgression through their sins and their own actions, as Adam was. [Note: [Col. 0086C] Norisius reads *quia*, “because”; this seems correct. GALLAND.] These, without doubt, are themselves found to be his great-grandchildren and descendants.

### 9

[Note: [Col. 0086C–D] Augustine also reports these words (*On the Merits of Sins*, book 3, chapter 2), as does the author of the *Praedestinatus* (book 1, heresy 88), whose words deserve notice: “Touching upon Coelestius, who first wrote against the transmission of sin.” Vincent of Lérins agrees (*Commonitorium*): “Who before his monstrous disciple Coelestius denied that the whole human race was bound by the guilt of Adam’s transgression?” He denied it in writing, I say; for Coelestius himself confessed at the Carthaginian trial under Aurelius that he had received this error from Rufinus. From this conclude either that the five books written by Theodore of Mopsuestia against defenders of original sin were unknown to the author of the *Praedestinatus* and to Vincent of Lérins, or that they were written later; this will be considered in the notes on those books.] 

> “But those who hold against the transmission of sin,” he says [Note: [Col. 0086D] Norisius and Baluzius read *aliter*, “otherwise”; Garnerius, *acriter*, “vehemently.” Shortly afterward, with Norisius and the manuscripts, we have restored: “If sin, they say,” a reading confirmed by what follows: “Then they say . . . they add this.” Baluzius has “he says.” GALLAND.], “try vehemently to attack those who defend its transmission. ‘If Adam’s sin harmed even those who did not sin, then Christ’s righteousness also benefits those who do not believe,’ they say, ‘since the Apostle says that through one person people are liberated, even more than they had previously perished through one person.’
>
> “Then they say: ‘If baptism cleanses that ancient and timeworn sin, those born from two baptized persons ought to be free from this sin; for they will not be able to transmit to their descendants what they themselves did not possess.’ [Bal. *habuerunt*, “possessed,” instead of *habuerint*, “will have possessed.”]
>
> “They add this: ‘Since the soul is not transmitted by descent, [Note: [Col. 0086D] Norisius places such words in parentheses and prints them in another typeface, as follows: “‘This argument of Pelagius,’ he says, ‘If the soul is not transmitted by descent (as indeed it is not), but only the flesh possesses the transmission of sin, then only the flesh deserves the punishment.’ We have printed it in this way so that the assertion inserted there in parentheses may be attributed not to Pelagius but to Mercator himself. For Augustine, in book 3 of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 3, reports Pelagius’s words as follows: ‘If the soul is not transmitted by descent, but only the flesh, then the flesh alone possesses the transmission of sin’; and in chapter 10 he commends Pelagius for this: ‘Observe, I beg you, how the circumspect Pelagius (for I transcribed the words just quoted from his book) understood the difficulty in which the question concerning the soul is involved. He does not say, “Since the soul is not transmitted by descent,” but “If the soul is not transmitted by descent”; and he adds that he speaks hesitantly rather than confidently.’ Moreover, even without that parenthesis, the same opinion of Pelagius was condemned in Zosimus’s encyclical letter, as Augustine testifies in Epistle 157 (now 190), to Optatus: ‘For Pelagius’s argument on this matter, which among his other condemnable statements was also appended to the letters of the apostolic see, runs as follows: “If the soul is not transmitted by descent, but only the flesh possesses transmission,” and so forth.’ From this it is clear that, in the question concerning the origin of the soul—which was extremely prominent in that age—Mercator agreed with Jerome, namely, that the souls of all human beings are created by God, unless we say that those words were inserted into the *Commonitorium* by another hand. For Mercator was an exceptionally devoted student of Augustine’s doctrine. I therefore believe that, in this difficulty, he suspended his assent with Augustine rather than adhering to the doctrine that souls are created.’ Thus far the very learned man; Tillemont also adopted his view, vol. 15, p. 857, note 2. GALLAND.] as neither is it, but only the flesh possesses the transmission of sin, then only the flesh deserves the punishment. For it is unjust that a soul born today, not from Adam’s substance, should bear another’s sin, so ancient; indeed it is reasonable that God, who forgives personal sins, should not impute another’s.’” [Note: [Col. 0087C] “Should impute one.” Thus Henricus de Noris edited it, and this is also found in the ancient books. Labbeus and Garnerius restored *non imputet*, “should not impute.” The reading of the ancient books is confirmed by Augustine, Epistle 157, to Optatus, where, in reporting Pelagius’s words, he writes: “For there is no reason to allow that God, who forgives personal sins, should impute one that belongs to another.” BALUZ.]

### 10

And again, in another discourse of his, Pelagius said: [Note: [Col. 0087C]

It can scarcely be conjectured which other discourse is meant, unless by this name another passage from the *Commentaries* is understood. For of all the books published by Pelagius before this time—besides the *Commentaries*, four or five were published, namely, the work *On the Trinity*, the letter to Paulinus, the little book *To the Widow*—whether it was one book or two—the *Book of Testimonies*, and perhaps the book *On Nature*—hardly any can accommodate a discussion of this material except through an irrelevant addition.

Augustine supports this conjecture in book 3 of *On the Merits of Sins*. After having completed two books on Adam’s mortality through sin, on the baptism of infants, and on the sinlessness of certain people, he writes to Marcellinus in the third book, chapter 1, that after only a few days he had read some writings of Pelagius containing very brief expositions of the Epistles of the Apostle Paul, and that there he had discovered an argument of those who deny that infants bear original sin. He then reports the words, “But those who hold against transmission,” and refutes them in the six following chapters (chapters 2–7). Immediately afterward, in three additional chapters, he cites what Mercator says was contained in another discourse of Pelagius and refutes it, without mentioning any other book (chapters 8–10). Unless my opinion deceives me, therefore, Pelagius did not set out the arguments of those who opposed the transmission of sin in only one place, but once in chapter 5, where the first part of the objections had been gathered, and again in chapter 7, where the second part had been gathered. Neither passage, I admit, is found in the commonly circulated copies, because, as I have said, Cassiodorus deleted both; but he deleted the second in such a way that the words “Those who assert that sin comes to us from Adam through transmission are insane” were not so completely obliterated that an unlearned copyist could not read and transcribe them.]

There is no denying that the very words under discussion are also found in Augustine’s second book *On the Merits of Sins*. Someone might therefore conclude that they were taken from elsewhere rather than from the *Commentaries*, since Augustine had not read them before completing that book. But from this I conclude that one of two things must be admitted: either the material that Marcellinus sent to Augustine for discussion was largely excerpted from Pelagius’s *Commentaries* on the Epistles of Paul, at least insofar as it touches on original sin; or Mercator’s reading is corrupt and must therefore be emended, so that *iterum jam sermone suo Pelagius* should be read—“Pelagius is now speaking in his own discourse”—as though he were saying that Pelagius had until then spoken in another’s discourse but was now speaking in his own. Augustine, however, does not greatly support this emendation, since throughout these books he teaches that Pelagius always spoke in another person’s voice.]

> “If a sinner,” says Pelagius, “begot a sinner, so that his infant’s original sin might be forgiven in the reception of baptism, then a righteous man ought to beget a righteous man. If parents, after their conversion, are not harmed by their own sins, much less can their sins harm their children through them.” [Note: [Col. 0088C] Augustine, book 2 of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 9, reports this passage with the words “so that the guilt of original sin in his infant might be forgiven.” BALUZ.] [Note: [Col. 0088C] Augustine, in the same work, chapter 27: “Nor should this escape notice: ‘If their own sins do not harm parents after their conversion, how much less,’ they say, ‘can they harm their son.’”]

> “If it happened that the first man was the cause of death, then through Christ’s coming it ought no longer to be the case that we die.” [Bal. *fecisse*, “to have caused,” instead of *fuisse*, “to have been.”] [Note: [Col. 0088C] Augustine, in the same work, chapter 38: “Therefore those who say, ‘If it happened through the sin of the first man that we should die, then through Christ’s coming it ought to have happened that we believers should not die,’ add, as though giving a reason: ‘For the transgression of the transgressor did not harm us more than the Savior’s incarnation or redemption benefited us.’”] [Note: [Col. 0088D]

Augustine, in the same work, chapter 33: “But those who say: ‘If this bodily death had occurred because of sin, surely we would not die after the forgiveness of sins which the Redeemer has granted us.’”

Someone may perhaps ask why Pelagius’s own words are not the same in Augustine as in Mercator, although the sense is identical in both places. I believe that Mercator faithfully copied Pelagius’s words, which were not especially elegant, whereas Augustine expressed their meaning in better language. Here I cannot conceal a thought that has often occurred to me: that the letter to Demetrias and the books that follow were composed in Pelagius’s thought, indeed, but in the words either of Anianus or of Julian.

The testimonies of the ancients lead me to this opinion. Jerome wrote that Anianus was “copiously fed” so that he might furnish ringing words for another’s blasphemy. And, while mocking Pelagius’s unlearned eloquence, he raises a substantial suspicion that Pelagius’s Latin had been begged from others. Addressing Pelagius, he says in *Dialogue 3 against the Pelagians*: “You and your disciples commonly swear that two chapters of discourse and praise are not yours, although the splendor of your style plainly shines in them, and the elegance of their expression is so great that, proceeding at a tortoise’s pace, you do not dare publicly to profess what you teach and sell secretly. O happy man! No one writes books except your disciples, so that whatever seems displeasing to you may be declared not yours but another’s! And who could possess such great talent as to imitate the charm of your speech?” And shortly afterward: “Ah! You have begun to be excessively eloquent—to say nothing of being a polished speaker—since your disciples have become teachers.”

For this reason Bede, in the preface to the *Song of Songs*, did not hesitate to attribute to Julian the book *On the Institution of a Virgin*, addressed to Demetrias, virgin of Christ. He also reports its beginning and reproduces the errors scattered here and there.

But Orosius is clearest of all, in his *Apology*, chapter 20. Addressing Pelagius, he says:

> “For even in that most laboriously composed letter of yours we could scarcely understand these very things: I mean the letter which, as I hear, you, a most modest man, did not blush to write to Demetrias, a girl consecrated and holy, teaching, as I believe, reverence for chastity under the story of Joseph lusting after his mistress. There you wrote: ‘When his mistress was frequently spurned, she laid closer snares for the young man; in secret and without witnesses, her shameless hand seized him.’ You have woven an inappropriate story into the most obscene language. Yet we ought not to attribute what is said neither suitably nor decorously to you, since neither did your birth give you the opportunity to be educated in more honorable studies, nor did it naturally follow that you should possess understanding; rather, it should be attributed to those writers of yours who compose miserable thought in the most miserable language and expose you to be read amid laughter, as though it were the title of a confession.”

Even if these testimonies, so manifest, were lacking, reason and experience would nevertheless demonstrate the point. First, almost nothing is more childish than the *Commentaries* on Paul, and nothing is more eloquent than the letter to Demetrias. Second, the reading of Scripture in the *Commentaries* is often different from that in the letter; the author of the letter frequently twists and rearranges the Apostle’s words. Moreover, the *Commentaries* sometimes bristle with solecisms, whereas the Latin of the letter is purer, for that period. Finally, a man who was indeed talented but barbarous wrote the *Commentaries*, while the letter was written not merely by an eloquent orator but by a polished speaker. Thus Pelagius was rightly called “the most mendacious of men.” For he lied even in his name, making himself Latin from a Scot; he lied in his manner of life, since he was something like a monk; he lied in the character he assumed, changing it according to circumstances; he lied in the ambiguous words he habitually used; and he lied in the title of his books, to which, as Orosius says, he attached another’s name.] 

> “If death had arisen through Adam’s sin, we would never die after the forgiveness of sins which our Liberator granted us. Adam’s sin was therefore more powerful in killing absolutely all human beings than Christ’s grace was in saving, since the latter benefited not everyone but only those who believe. For not all who are born from Adam are also reborn in Christ.” And so forth.

## CHAPTER III. On the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius, especially Pelagius, both by the Roman pontiffs Innocent and Zosimus, and by the Fathers at Diospolis and Theodotus, bishop of Antioch

### 1

[Note: [Col. 0089D]

Augustine agrees with Mercator in writing to Optatus (Epistle 190). Although the passage is somewhat lengthy, it seemed worthwhile to transcribe it in full, since it can contribute much faithfulness and clarity here:

“When Pelagius and Coelestius had emerged as either the authors or at least the most ardent and notorious advocates of the new heresy, they were condemned throughout the Christian world by the vigilance of episcopal councils, with the assistance of the Savior who protects his Church, and also by the two venerable bishops of the apostolic see, Pope Zosimus and Pope Innocent, unless they corrected themselves and also performed penance. We have taken care to send you examples of the recent writings that proceeded from that see, both those addressed particularly to the Africans and those addressed universally to all bishops, lest they perhaps have not yet reached your Holiness. They were sent by those brethren to whom we entrusted these letters, so that they might forward them to your Reverence.

“These men are not heretics merely because they say that souls do not derive their origin from that first sinful soul—a statement which perhaps can be made true in some sense, or may be unknown without damage to the faith. Rather, they attempt to draw from this the conclusion for which they are judged plainly heretics: that the souls of infants derive nothing evil from Adam which must be expiated by the washing of regeneration.

“For Pelagius’s argument on this matter, which among his other condemnable statements was also appended to the letters of the apostolic see, runs as follows: ‘If the soul,’ he says, ‘is not transmitted by descent, but only the flesh possesses the transmission of sin, then only the flesh deserves the punishment. For it is unjust that a soul born today, not from Adam’s substance, should bear another’s sin, since there is no reason to allow that God, who forgives personal sins, should impute one that belongs to another.’

“If, then, you can assert such a novelty of souls without any propagation, and so forth. For, to use the words found in the very letter of the blessed bishop Zosimus: ‘The Lord is faithful in his words, and his baptism, in reality and in words—that is, in deed, confession, and forgiveness of sins—maintains the same fullness in every sex, age, and condition of the human race. For no one is made free except one who is a slave of sin; nor can anyone be called redeemed except one who had previously truly been captive through sin, as it is written: “If the Son makes you free, you will be truly free” (John 8:36). Through him we are spiritually reborn; through him we are crucified to the world. By his death, the bond of obligation contracted by propagation through the death introduced and transmitted from Adam to all of us is broken for every soul; and no one at all among those born is free from liability under it before being freed through baptism.’”

In these words the ancient, firmly established, certain, and clear Catholic faith of the apostolic see is so evident that it would be wicked for a Christian to doubt it.]

From all this—both what has now been cited from Augustine and what has been brought into the text from Mercator—we learn matters of considerable usefulness for the history of Pelagianism:

1. Augustine doubted, and not without reason, whether Pelagius and Coelestius were the authors of the heresy called after them, or merely its defenders, although they were its most notorious and vehement advocates.

2. These heretics raised the question of the origin of souls because, from the premise that the soul was not transmitted by descent but only the flesh was, they seemed to themselves to be able to conclude that original sin was not transmitted.

3. They were condemned throughout the whole world by the two bishops of the apostolic see. Since Augustine asserts such a thing of no other judgment, the universality of the condemnation signifies the supreme authority of the apostolic see.

4. Zosimus’s letter to all the bishops of the world concerning the Pelagians was very lengthy and, above all, didactic, since it contained both the arguments of the heretics and the grounds of Catholic doctrine.

5. The words that have been discussed up to this point, presented as excerpts from Pelagius’s *Commentaries*, are cited by Zosimus, Augustine, Mercator, and the author of the *Predestined One*, all writing while Pelagius was still alive and Coelestius was still causing disturbance.]

All the chapters written above are contained in that letter of the bishop Zosimus, of blessed memory, which— [Note: [Col. 0090D]

The very learned Labbeus preferred that it be written *tractatoria*, and I would not strongly object, on account of the didactic form in which Mercator, and indeed Augustine, described the letter written by Zosimus, unless this consideration drove me in the opposite direction: that in no place, except where the text is corrupt, do the ancients mention a *tractatoria* letter, whereas they frequently mention a *tractoria*.

I do not deny that Zosimus’s letter may have been called a *tractoria* for a different reason from that in which this term is ordinarily understood—whether in the Code [Title: *On Tractoriae and Statives*], where a diploma authorizing public transport, the provision of transport supplies, and soldiers’ letters of leave and testimonials are called *tractoriae*; or in ecclesiastical law, where a *tractoria* is the letter by which bishops were summoned to a synod by the primate. For the letter was, in its entirety, both a decretal concerning doctrine and a denunciation of the sentence passed against Pelagius and Coelestius. That both these kinds of letter were formerly called by the name *tractoria* can easily be established by definite testimonies of the ancients (in Augustine, Letter 217; the First Council of Africa; and elsewhere passim).

For that a decretal letter was called a *tractoria* is clear from the passage commonly cited from the Council of Telepte. When the council was discussing a letter of Pope Siricius, the bishops said: “Let the letter of Siricius, of venerable memory, be read, so that we may know what its text contains.” When it was handed over, the notary Privatus said: “A copy of the *tractoria* of Siricius, bishop of the city of Rome,” etc. (Volume II of Labbe’s edition of the General Councils, p. 1577). These letters, which the Fathers ordered to be read, were neither letters summoning bishops to a synod, nor did they announce a sentence pronounced against an accused person; nor were they letters of dismissal or recommendation for clerics. Rather, they contained the nine statutes of the Apostolic See, formerly sent from the Roman council to the bishops of Africa.

Now that a denunciatory letter was likewise called by the same name *tractoria*, two testimonies of Augustine plainly demonstrate. He reports the sentence passed by the Maximianists against Primianus in these words (Sermon 2 on Psalm XXXVI):

“We have judged it expedient that all the holy fellow priests, all the clergy, and all the peoples who remember that they are Christians should be admonished by this our *tractoria*, so that all may carefully shun his communion, since he has been condemned. For he himself will have to give an account of his destruction, if he attempts to violate this decree of ours by refusing to hear it. It has indeed pleased us and the Holy Spirit that time be reserved for those slow to repent, on the condition that those fellow priests or clerics who, forgetful of their salvation, have withdrawn from the communion of the aforementioned Primianus from the day of his condemnation—that is, from 8 Kalends of January—or at least from the communion of Primianus after his condemnation, be bound by such a sentence,” etc.

Writing to the Donatist bishops, he says as follows (Letter 43):

“But if they do not do this, their depravity and perversity will there also become known; and when a *tractoria* has been sent throughout the whole world concerning them, wherever Christ’s Church has already been extended, their communion will be cut off by all the Churches, lest any error arise in the chair of the Church of Carthage.”

I am not unaware that the printed copies, in both passages, have *tractatoriam* in place of *tractoria*. This prompted Francesco Bernardino Ferrarius, in his work on ancient ecclesiastical letters, to entitle the second chapter of the second book “On *Tractatoriae*” and to establish two kinds of them: one kind consisting of letters of excuse, by which someone summoned by a primate to a synod through a *tractoria* would offer an excuse before him on grounds of illness or some other impediment; the other consisting of denunciatory letters, by which other Churches were informed of a sentence passed against someone in an ecclesiastical judgment. The most learned Labbe agreed with Ferrarius (Volume II of the General Councils, pp. 1517 and 1577). For that reason, both at the Council of Telepte and especially in Mercator’s *Commonitorium*, he wished the word to be written *tractatoriam* rather than *tractoria*, contrary to the evidence and authority of all the manuscript copies.

Both men could, without much difficulty—for both were exceptionally learned—have been brought back to the correct view concerning each kind of letter. As for the letters of excuse, this could have been done partly from canon 76 of the African Church and partly from chapter 20 of Book VII of the *Capitularies* of Charlemagne; for in both places it is commanded that the excuse itself be subscribed to the *tractoria*. The African canon reads:

“It has been decided that whenever a council is to be assembled, the bishops who are hindered neither by age, nor by illness, nor by any other serious necessity should attend in due measure; and that this be announced to the primates of each of their provinces; and that two or three groups be formed from all the bishops; and that, from each group in turn, however many have been selected should attend the day of the council with the utmost urgency. But if they cannot attend, they shall record their excuses in the *tractoria*; or, if some necessities should perhaps suddenly arise after the arrival of the *tractoria*, unless they give an account of the impediment to their primate, they must be content with the communion of their own Church.”

The Greek interpreter omitted these words—“They shall record their excuses in the *tractoria*, or, if some necessities should arise after the arrival of the *tractoria*”—but the cited chapter 20 supplied, or rather explained, them abundantly. For it contains the following:

“It has been decided that whenever a council is to be assembled, the bishops and presbyters who are hindered neither by age, nor by illness, nor by any other serious necessity should attend in due measure; but if they cannot attend, they shall record their excuses in the *tractoria*.”

As for denunciatory letters, both men could likewise have been dislodged from their opinion: Labbe by both of Mercator’s manuscript copies, the Vatican and Beauvais manuscripts; Ferrarius by both of Augustine’s testimonies concerning the Donatist controversy cited above. In the better-quality manuscript copies (the Code [Title: *On Tractoriae and Statives*]), these passages do not have *tractatoriam* but *tractoria*, as Jacobus Gothofredus observed.

Before I leave this subject, however, I think the reader should be informed of the following:

1. Ferrarius thought that *tractoria* came from *trahere*, “to draw,” but it actually came from the stretch of the public road (*tractus viae publicae*) along which those possessing a diploma of public transport traveled. Certainly, once the word *tractoria* passed from the civil sphere into the Church, by what reasoning could imperial letters—whether letters of leave or soldiers’ testimonials—be called *tractoriae*?

2. In the time of Hincmar of Reims, the very authorizations that bishops gave to presbyters to perform their duties at a synod, whenever the bishops themselves could not attend in person, were also called *tractoriae* (see among the ancient formulas collected at the end of Volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*, formulas eleven and twelve, pp. 651 and 654).

3. The same name was sometimes also given to a letter by which a bishop summoned to a synod, when unable to attend, communicated his opinion in writing to the synod. Of this kind is the *tractoria* of Prudentius of Troyes, who could not attend the ordination of Aeneas, bishop of Paris.

4. Finally, in the place cited earlier, Gothofredus wrote, when he wished to criticize Ferrarius, that bishops, when summoned to a synod by *tractoriae*, were indeed received on the road by the faithful with Christian charity; but that this was neither commanded nor contained in the *tractoriae*, and, in fact, cannot yet be sufficiently proved from any passage. He had certainly not seen the Roman *Book of Offices*, which contains the formulas of two *tractoriae*: one that the supreme pontiffs customarily gave to someone sent on ecclesiastical business, and another that they gave to those returning from Rome to their homeland. From these he could probably have inferred, not implausibly, what ought to be thought concerning those summoned to a synod. Since, as far as I know, the formulas themselves have not yet been published, I thought they should be transcribed from a manuscript code approximately eight hundred years old.

**FIRST TRACTORIA, GIVEN TO A PERSON SENT ON ECCLESIASTICAL BUSINESS**

“The usefulness of ecclesiastical affairs does not admit delay. Therefore we have sent our notary of our holy Church to our most excellent son, the king. We exhort you to have your charity procure for him, without delay, horses with which he may easily reach the neighboring city, so that the undertaking entrusted to him may, with God’s favor and your assistance, speedily attain its fulfillment.”

**SECOND TRACTORIA, GIVEN TO THOSE RETURNING TO THEIR HOMELAND FROM THE THRESHOLDS OF THE APOSTLES**

“The bearers of this letter, having, in accordance with their devotion, presented themselves at the thresholds of the blessed chief apostles, have asked that, released by us, they may return to their own homes. Therefore we command that, without hindrance, you offer them assistance and provision and release them, so that, refreshed by your aid, they may return safely and guiltlessly to their own homes. For their support on the journey, provide assistance and men, undoubtedly awaiting from the God who rewards all good things a return of the favor to you.”

The *TRACTORIA* by which Coelestius and Pelagius were condemned was reinforced by the subscriptions of the holy Fathers, after it had been sent both to Constantinople and throughout the whole world.

[Note: It is worthwhile to consult what we shall say about Zosimus’s *tractoria* in the dissertation on the Subscriptions (Dissertation 5, Appendix 2). There, after this very passage and another cited above—which establish that in the Pelagian controversy no confession of faith other than Zosimus’s *tractoria* had to be subscribed, just as in the Eutychian controversy there was none other than the letter of Leo the Great to Flavian—we gather six points from two testimonies of Marius, to which authors of the fifth century, especially Augustine, wrote statements agreeing.]

[Note: From this we learn how ancient the custom is that, whenever some heresy emerged, a subscription to its condemnation was required, at least from bishops—partly to demonstrate each person’s faith, and partly to strengthen among the people the sentence of the superior see.]

Now he first turns to Julian, whom he will later attack with great force.

[Note: We have written, for the benefit of learned readers, an account of the life, character, and deeds of this wicked heretic in the dissertation on the Authors and Defenders of the Pelagian Heresy (Dissertation 2, Appendix 2). The passage may be consulted with some profit. For the moment, however, it will be useful to note in advance what we learn from Mercator (*Book of Notes*, chapter 6, no. 9).

At that time Julian dared to send a letter to the Apostolic See, having refused, together with the whole Church throughout the world, to condemn Pelagius and Coelestius (Dissertation 6, chapter 46). In it he gave, in the name of eighteen bishops, the reasons for their refusal to subscribe. These were the reasons ordinarily offered by those who do not respect the authority of the Church: namely, that the men against whom charges of condemned doctrines were being brought had themselves condemned, in their own writings, the things falsely alleged against them; that they had suffered an undeserved sentence while absent and unheard; that even the accusers themselves had not been present at the trial, nor had the defendants been given an opportunity to defend their case against the accusers; that the supreme pontiff had judged the case through partisan zeal and by subterfuge; that since a subscription takes the form either of testimony or of judgment against the accused, conscience, because of fear of God, did not permit the bishops either to give testimony or to exercise judgment against men who had not been heard; and finally, that it was wicked rashly to judge men who profess themselves Catholics, especially since charity commands that in doubtful matters one should think the better of each person, and since the Apostle establishes for bishops the rule of judgment when he says: “Do not accept an accusation against a presbyter except on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (1 Timothy 5:19). See the letter itself, first published by us, in which Julian, in a heretical spirit, asks either that the case not be pressed—which he calls avoiding the stirring up of scandal and disturbance of the Church’s peace—or that a hearing before a plenary synod be granted (Dissertation 6, on the Letters Published by the Defenders of the Pelagian Heresy).]

Julian and the other accomplices, refusing to subscribe and unwilling to make themselves of one mind with those same Fathers, were not only—

[Note: The Church’s practice was constant, from the time when Christians were set free by the Christian emperors, that, partly for the eradication of heresies whenever they persisted too stubbornly, and partly for the coercion of either their authors or their patrons when they acted as factions, both powers ordained by God—the ecclesiastical and, namely, the imperial—should act in concert.

When Marius writes that these bishops were deposed and expelled from all Italy both by laws and by statutes, he clearly shows that he is speaking of one *tractoria* of Zosimus and one or another sanction of Honorius.

Equipped with the combined strength of both powers, Boniface, Zosimus’s successor, deprived of office and expelled from Italy those who stubbornly followed or supported the heretics. Hence Prosper (*Against the Collation*, chapter 41): “Then their machinations were broken; then they collapsed among their partners and leaders in arrogance—the Semi-Pelagians—when Pope Boniface, of holy memory, was rejoicing in the devotion of the most pious emperors and was using against the enemies of God’s grace not only apostolic but also royal edicts.”

Prosper’s words remind me to give, briefly—and I hope the reader will not find this unwelcome—an account of what the emperors established against the Pelagian heresy from the time when it first seemed to arise until the point at which it could be believed to have been either completely extinguished or overthrown, after the Council of Ephesus, when peace was restored to the Church.

The first constitution was issued by Honorius to Palladius, *praefectus praetorio*, at Ravenna on the day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, concerning the expulsion from the City of the leaders of the accursed doctrine, Pelagius and Coelestius, and concerning the forcible bringing of their followers before the competent judge, to be condemned, after lawful proof, to inexorable deportation into exile.

The second was sent by the same Honorius to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, at Ravenna on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta. It concerned the demand from all bishops—some of whom stubbornly refused it—that they subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius already issued long before; and it concerned punishing obstinate bishops by the loss of their episcopates and depriving each of them of communion with his own see forever.

The third is the constitution of the emperor Constantius to Volusianus, *praefectus urbi*, concerning the expulsion of Coelestius from the City. There is considerable controversy concerning its date and place.

The fourth is the constitution of Valentinian Caesar to Amatius, *praefectus Galliarum*, issued at Aquileia on the seventh day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus XI and Valentinian Caesar. It concerns the summoning, through Patroclus of Arles, of various bishops who followed the abominable error of the Pelagian and Coelestian doctrine. Unless they corrected their errors within twenty days, during which they were to be granted an opportunity for deliberation, they were to be expelled from the Gallic provinces, their sees being taken from them and assigned to others who were more faithful.

The fifth is Theodosius’s constitution after receiving Mercator’s *Commonitorium*, concerning which we have spoken under the title *Commonitorium*. You will search for all these documents in vain in the Theodosian Code, whether in the version abridged by Annianus or in the version that Gothofredus, in a remarkable fashion, expanded into six volumes. But these matters will receive their own dissertation in due course (Dissertation 4, on the Imperial Constitutions in the Pelagian Controversy).]

They were deposed and deprived of office by imperial laws, but also—

[Note: As I said, Mercator speaks of one *tractoria*, that of Zosimus, or perhaps also of the decree of Innocent, whose promulgation this *tractoria* in some sense was, as is clear from Gennadius (*On Illustrious Men*, chapter 43). It is nevertheless remarkable that, during the nineteen-year period in which the Pelagian heresy appeared to possess some strength, more than twenty-four synods were held. These will receive a separate dissertation (Dissertation 3, on the Synods Held in the Pelagian Controversy during the Time of St. Augustine). For the present, a synopsis of the synods, distinguished according to their dates, should be placed here in advance.]

**SUMMARY OF THE NINETEEN YEARS**

1. First Synod at Carthage, concerning Coelestius (A.D. 412).

2. Assembly at Jerusalem under Bishop John (A.D. 415, July 30).

3. Synod of Diospolis (in the same year, in December).

4. Second Carthaginian Synod (A.D. 416, in September).

5. Synod of Milevis (in the same year, in October).

6. Synod of five bishops at Carthage (in the same year, in November).

7. First Roman Synod under Innocent (A.D. 417).

8. First Synod of Constantinople under Atticus (A.D. 417, toward the end of the year).

9. Synod at Antioch under Theodotus (at the same time).

10. Second Roman Synod under Zosimus (in the same year).

11. Third Carthaginian Synod (in the same year).

12. Universal African Synod (A.D. 418, on the Kalends of May).

13. Third Roman Synod under Zosimus (in the same year, in July).

14. Second Universal African Synod (in the same year, July 17).

15. Third Universal African Synod (in the same year, in August).

16. Fourth Universal African Synod (A.D. 419).

17. Synod in Cilicia against Julian (A.D. 423).

18. Fourth Roman Synod under Celestine (A.D. 424).

19. Second Synod of Constantinople, concerning the bishops expelled from Italy because of the Pelagian heresy (A.D. 425).

20. Fifth Universal African Synod, concerning Leporius (in the same year).

21. Gallican Synod under Honoratus (A.D. 427).

22. English Synod at Verulamium (A.D. 429).

23. Fifth Roman Synod under Celestine (A.D. 430).

24. General Council of Ephesus (A.D. 431).

by priestly statutes, and driven out of all Italy; of these, many—

[Note: Possidius (*Life of St. Augustine*, chapter 18): “Those men of the great Apostolic See—Innocent and Zosimus, holy pontiffs—at different times marked out those same Pelagians and cut them off from the members of the Church. In letters sent to the Churches of Africa and of the East and West, they decreed that all Catholics should anathematize and avoid them. repented, were corrected from the error just mentioned, and returned as suppliants to the Apostolic See, where they were received and restored to their Churches.

**2.** The aforementioned Coelestius and Pelagius do not appear to have been condemned at that time for the first time by Zosimus of holy memory, but by his predecessor, Innocent of holy remembrance, by whom Julian also had been ordained.

[Note: Here we first learn who ordained Julian. Augustine, Prosper, Gennadius, Bede, and others had handed down that he held the episcopate, but they had been entirely silent about his ordainer, and even seemed to disagree about the see. Mercator clearly teaches both points (consult the dissertation on Julian’s Life and Character; also consult the notes to Mercator’s preface to Theodore’s Symbol).]

After their condemnation, Julian—

[Note: Chronologists raise no question concerning the year in which St. Innocent died. For it is certain that he was still alive on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, when he replied to the two synods, the Carthaginian and the Milevitan, and to the five bishops from whom he had received letters, after the consulship of Theodosius VII and Junius Quartus Palladius, a man of senatorial rank, as the Corbie copies have it; or in the consulship of Honorius XI and Constantius II, as appears in some printed editions.

It is also certain that Innocent was not alive on the eighth day before the Kalends of October of the same year, at which time his successor Zosimus was writing his second letter to the African bishops. But it is not equally clear in what month and on what day he died, since the authorities disagree. Nevertheless, a definite chronological indication is necessary for constructing the history of Zosimus; therefore we must try to establish the matter by arguments and conjectures.

That Zosimus began to hold office before Easter in A.D. 417 is concluded from these words of Paschasinus of Lilybaeum to St. Leo (among St. Leo’s letters, 63):

“Let not a single day placed farther away frighten us, lest, while avoiding this, we fall into error, as happened in the time of my lord, your predecessor Zosimus, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus XI and Constantius II. For when it was being avoided that Easter should fall on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, it was celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of April—that is, a common year was treated as an embolismic year—and a very serious error arose, to such an extent that this truth was demonstrated by the sure ministry that is administered through the gift of the Holy Spirit.”

Since, then, in A.D. 417 Easter was wrongly celebrated on March 25, although it ought to have been celebrated on April 22, and since this error occurred during Zosimus’s time, as Paschasinus reports, Zosimus certainly began to hold office before March 25. Thus Innocent died not on July 28, as Baronius thought and many have believed, but on March 12, as Bede, Ado, the ancient Roman Martyrology, and others have it.

What is more, a letter of Zosimus concerning the privileges of the Church of Arles is found, dated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Honorius XI and Constantius II, and this letter is certainly not spurious. This is clear both from Baronius, who inserted it in his *Annals* and confirmed it by the authority of Gregory the Great, and from Sirmond, who collated it in Volume I of the *Councils of Gaul*, adding a note concerning its date—perhaps omitted by Baronius because it was inconvenient. Zosimus, therefore, must be said to have been seated before March 24.

But on what day? This is a great and difficult question. First, Anastasius recorded that Innocent’s see remained vacant for twenty-two days. How, then, could Zosimus have taken office before March 24, if Innocent died on March 12?

Furthermore, Prosper states that Zosimus’s pontificate lasted one year, nine months, and either eight or nine days, as variant manuscripts have it. He must therefore have begun on March 27, since Zosimus, as everyone agrees, died on December 26.

Mercator then teaches that Julian, from the condemnation of the Pelagians by Innocent, persevered until Innocent’s death in sincere faith and in communion with the one who condemned him. What an excellent praise of perseverance—not to have departed from the faith for forty-three or forty-four days! For no more time elapsed between the condemnation, which took place on the third day before the Kalends of February, and March 12, when Innocent died.

Finally, all Zosimus’s letters that pertain to A.D. 417—except one concerning the privileges of the Church of Arles and the first one concerning Coelestius—are found dated in September. Hence someone might perhaps suspect that so active a pontiff had not held the Apostolic See for long before that time.

To make clear what I conjecture concerning this matter, so obscure and perplexed, I believe first that almost nothing of importance for the present question can be gathered from Zosimus’s letters, since it is certain that many letters, including the most famous *tractoria*, have perished. The letters now extant were collected for the most part in Gaul from the archive of the Church of Arles and cannot be compared with other manuscripts, so that it may be discovered whether there is any error in the chronological notation.

Second, I think that the argument derived from Mercator has no greater strength. For although three letters of Innocent concerning Pelagius and Coelestius were sent to Africa toward the end of Innocent’s life, nothing prevents us from saying that the council at which the supreme pontiff instituted proceedings against both heretics and passed sentence took place three months earlier, since the Africans’ letters arrived at the Apostolic See toward the end of October. Thus Julian, though unwillingly, was able to restrain himself for nearly five months and not vomit out the poison he held concealed in his breast.

Indeed, I think that a reason for confirming our assertion concerning the time of the holy pontiff’s death can be derived from these very letters of Innocent. Since Gennadius teaches that Innocent wrote a decree against the Pelagians to the universal Church, which his successor promulgated, I conclude that Innocent did not survive long after the letters were sent to Africa, but that death intervened and prevented him from sending the decree to the other Churches of the East and West. He certainly would have had enough time to do this had he not died on the fourth day before the Ides of March, as the ancient martyrologies have it, but on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, as Baronius prefers.

Moreover, I hold that whenever Prosper and Anastasius contradict each other, greater credence should be given to Prosper, who wrote about matters not only of his own time but also about matters placed before his eyes and observed with great care, than to Anastasius, who, being more than four centuries removed from the events, transcribed what he committed to writing neither with the greatest diligence nor from the most reliable authorities.

Therefore, although learned men—and Baronius above all, repeatedly and everywhere—usually detract from Anastasius’s credibility, I think that it should be withheld from him in this matter, where he conflicts with Prosper concerning the period during which the Roman See was vacant after Innocent’s death. Indeed, I cannot sufficiently wonder why learned men have so readily agreed with a man whom almost every life of the pontiffs accuses of falsehood.

I therefore think we should stand by Prosper’s statement that Zosimus’s pontificate lasted one year and nine months; but an error must have entered the number of days. Otherwise Zosimus would have to be said to have become pontiff on March 27, which is disproved by the testimony of Paschasinus and of Zosimus himself.

I therefore suspect that, through the fault of the copyists, the notation of the decade was omitted and IX was written in place of XIX. Once this numerical correction is made, everything will easily be consistent; otherwise it is entirely ἀσύστατα—‘incoherent’ or ‘without foundation.’ First, it will be found that Zosimus began to hold office on March 17; second, the date attached to the letter concerning the privileges of the Church of Arles will not be accused of falsification; third, the date of Innocent’s death—the demonstration of which occasioned this entire discussion—will remain certain; and finally, the popular opinion will be refuted, while the proper credibility is granted to Bede, Ado, and the ancient Martyrologies, which celebrate the memory of St. Innocent on March 12.]

remained in his communion and persevered in the true opinion until the death of the aforementioned Innocent, and, while communicating with the person who had condemned those men, himself also undoubtedly condemned Pelagius and Coelestius.

[Note: These statements may appear to agree with the words of Nestorius, who wrote to St. Celestine concerning the Pelagians (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 16):

“A certain Julian,” he says, “and Florus, Orontius, and Fabius, claiming that they were bishops of the Western regions, often approached both the most pious and most celebrated emperor and bewailed their cases, as though, being orthodox in orthodox times, they had suffered persecution. They often lamented the same things before us, and, although often rejected, did not cease doing the same, but persist day after day, filling everyone’s ears with tearful cries.”

And in Letter 2:

“I have often written to Your Blessedness concerning Julian, Orontius, and the others, who usurp episcopal dignity and make a very public approach to the most pious and celebrated emperor. They wear us down with frequent laments, as though, being orthodox in orthodox times, they had been cast out of the West,” etc.]

What he now wants, or what he complains about, we do not know.

[Note: Norisius is unknown. — GALLAND.]

**3.** The reason why they were condemned by Innocent of holy remembrance was as follows.

[Note: Consult the dissertation on Pelagius’s Life and Character (Dissertation 2, on the Authors, etc.). There we showed that he left Rome either before the siege, when the City was in the greatest alarm, or after the siege had been lifted but before either of the two sackings. He came from Rome to Sicily, and from there, after three years, to Hippo and then Carthage, at the time when the conference between Catholics and Donatists was being prepared; finally, from Carthage he hurried to Palestine, as Augustine teaches (*On the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 22).]

After the devastation of the city of Rome, Pelagius was living in Palestine. Certain zealous bishops found—

[Note: Erotes and Lazarus, Gallican bishops—the former from Arles, the latter from Aix, as we said earlier. The opinions of the ancients concerning them are so varied that the truth can scarcely, if at all, be distinguished, whether this resulted from the schemes of the Pelagians or from the inherent perplexity of the case. — Erotes and Lazarus, bishops of the second Narbonensis. See the most illustrious Peter de Marca in his dissertation on the Ancient Collections of Councils, p. 361. — BALUZE.]

certain books of his in which many and various things appeared to have been written against the Catholic faith.

[Note: Concerning Pelagius’s writings, Gennadius says the following (*On Illustrious Men*, chapter 42):

“Before he was exposed as a heretic, Pelagius wrote for earnest students three necessary books on the faith of the Trinity, and, concerning practical conduct, one book of *Eulogies* from the divine Scriptures, marked out by an index of chapters in the manner of St. Cyprian. After he had been proclaimed a heretic, he wrote things favoring his heresy.”

This is not entirely true, for he wrote several works before he was exposed as a heretic, and those works favored his heresy. Besides the *Work on the Trinity* and the *Eulogies*, he wrote books of Expositions on the Epistles of Paul, two books *To the Widow*, and a letter to Paulinus; for he was not exposed as a heretic until after the sack of the City, before which he had published these works. Indeed, Jerome (*Dialogue 1 Against the Pelagians*) cites quite a few passages from the *Book of Eulogies* in which the heresy is plainly contained. Augustine too (*On the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapters 3, 4, 5, and 46) testifies that the propositions which the Gallican bishops presented for condemnation at Diospolis were extracted from these same *Eulogies* and from the books *To the Widow*. See the dissertation on the First Authors, etc.]

These books were sent with letters to the Fathers and bishops in Africa, where, after three councils had been assembled, the books just mentioned were read.

[Note: Only two councils seem to have been held in Africa—the Carthaginian and the Milevitan—at which the books mentioned here could have been read before Innocent’s sentence was issued. This difficulty cannot be resolved in any other way than by counting among the two councils just mentioned the assembly of the five bishops who wrote privately to Innocent. For Innocent’s reply is also addressed to them; and those five bishops, the most learned men in all Africa, not unjustly appeared to Mercator to possess the weight and authority of a complete council. See the dissertation on the Synods Held in the Pelagian Controversy.

Three synodal letters were consequently written to Innocent, which occur among Augustine’s letters as numbers 175, 176, and 177, although the last is not properly synodal but a private letter. — GALLAND.]

From there, reports were sent to Rome, together with the books themselves, and the Apostolic sentence of the replying pontiff was issued to the aforementioned councils. It deprived those same men, Coelestius and Pelagius, of ecclesiastical communion; copies of their writings are in our hands.

**4.** While Pelagius was still staying at Jerusalem—

[Note: He means the Diospolitan council of fourteen bishops, whom Augustine lists (*Book I Against Julian*, chapters 5 and 7). It was held at Lydda, which is Diospolis, in December A.D. 415, as the letter of the presbyter Lucian (*On the Discovery of the Relics of St. Stephen*) demonstrates. In it, with Eulogius of Caesarea presiding, the letter of the absent bishops Erotes and Lazarus was read, by which Pelagius was accused. But the slippery heretic deceived the Fathers through an untrustworthy interpreter, since they did not sufficiently understand the Latin language, and thus secretly obtained his own acquittal; nevertheless, he was compelled to anathematize the impious doctrines, whether his own or those of Coelestius.

Those who confuse this synod with the assembly of presbyters held under Bishop John at Jerusalem on July 30 of the same year have read Augustine’s book on the Proceedings in Palestine and Orosius’s apology very carelessly. For Augustine testifies that Orosius did not attend the synod, whereas Orosius asserts that he formed a major part of the assembly.]

Jansenius of Ypres (Lib. I, *On the Pelagian Heresy*) therefore unlearnedly seizes this opportunity to criticize Orosius’s apology, as though it had been composed by someone ignorant of the circumstances of that time; but we have refuted his accusation, as well as Vastellius’s not especially apt objections and John of Jerusalem’s insufficiently firm defense, in their proper place (*Dissertation 3, On Synods*, etc.).]

He was accused before the synod and at first, by evasive conduct,

> For what benefit is it to you, Augustine says (*Book I Against Julian*, ch. 5), that you weave together—I know not by what art of perplexity—certain handles and hooks, so that simple matters may not be exposed and made clear? And shortly afterward: “By these clouds Pelagius thinks he has deceived that judgment of Diospolis; and you wholeheartedly approve this wickedness, laughing that so many bishops were mocked by him” (see *Dissertation 5, On Subscriptions*, etc.).

covering himself with certain ambiguous professions, and pursuing equivocal points or giving equivocal answers; he seems at that time to have deceived the hearing of the bishops.

### 5.

But afterward, when he had been clearly exposed,

[Col. 0099D]

by the Gallic bishops, undoubtedly, Heros and Lazarus, who had previously accused Pelagius at the synod of Diospolis by means of a written indictment alone—for they had been unable to attend because of the illness of one of them—and, having realized that he had deceived the Fathers, afterward personally pressed the matter before Theodotus, bishop of Antioch, so that the judgment of Diospolis concerning Pelagius’s person might be reconsidered (Augustine, *On the Proceedings in Palestine*, ch. 1).

Certainly those two bishops were still in the East when Orosius returned to Africa in 416. From there, through Orosius, they sent a letter to the African Fathers, explicitly mentioned in the synodal letter of the Council of Carthage

[Col. 0100B]

to Saint Innocent:

> When, according to custom, we were coming to the Church of Carthage, and a synod had been assembled from among us on account of various matters, our fellow presbyter Orosius delivered to us a letter from our holy brothers and fellow priests, Heros and Lazarus. We have decided that its contents should be appended here. After it had been read, we recognized Pelagius and Coelestius as the authors of an utterly wicked error, which all of us must anathematize (Letter 26 among Innocent’s Letters, our volume XX).

They are also mentioned in the synodal letter of the Council of Milevis:

> Pelagius, as letters sent by certain of our brothers report, is said, while staying at Jerusalem, to have deceived some persons (ibid., Letter 27).

Indeed, they were still residing there in the following year, when Zosimus wrote to the Africans:

> As for the letter of Heros and Lazarus, sent in the earlier report, it is entirely evident that this was dispatched with a zeal for the faith that was too hasty (Letter 1 to the Africans).

And in another letter to the same persons:

> It was grievous that Lazarus and Heros should be the footmen of their own letters. Did they not know that your affection would report the matter to the Apostolic See? They would have sailed here by the shortcut of calumny. When the matter concerns resigning from a bishopric, they traverse seas and lands and omit no means of support; but when the reputation of innocent men is struck, they, as idle and delicate people—whether accusers or witnesses—abuse letters in their chambers and beds, and by their lusts these two plagues cloud all Africa and the whole calm of Catholic serenity.]

while the accusers were pressing their charge, by a later synod,

[Col. 0100C]

I do not remember reading that anyone named it explicitly, except Marianus Victorius (*Preface to Jerome’s Letter to Ctesiphon*), although perhaps he substituted the Council of Antioch for that of Diospolis. For he says:

> Pelagius, vomiting forth these and other opinions, when many admonished him, fearing condemnation, first recanted; then, falling back again into the same and worse errors, he was condemned by the synod of Antioch, and likewise by Innocent I and Zosimus, the supreme pontiffs, etc.

Photius nevertheless makes a fairly clear reference to it. The passage in which he does so, if corrected—as it certainly ought to be—decisively confirms Mercator’s statement. He writes as follows (*Bibliotheca*, codex 54):

> Moreover, this Pelagian or Coelestian heresy flourished not only in the East but also spread through the West; and at Carthage in Africa it was detected and convicted by Aurelius and Augustine and publicly condemned in various councils. Those who agreed with them were expelled, as heretics, from the Church, in the time of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, and Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, by the Roman, African, and other bishops of the West.

Where the Greek reads, *ἐν τοῖς χρόνοις τοῦ Θεοφίλου τοῦ Ἀλεξανδρείας* (“in the time of Theophilus of Alexandria”), one should read *ἐν τοῖς χρόνοις τοῦ Θεοδότου τοῦ Ἀνθιοχείας* (“in the time of Theodotus of Antioch”). For it could not have happened that the Pelagians were expelled from the Church in Egypt during Theophilus’s time, since they had scarcely become known in the West in 412, the year in which Cyril succeeded Theophilus; whereas the statements in question agree remarkably well with Theodotus of Antioch, who held the synod mentioned by Mercator at almost the same time that the Africans wrote from Carthage and Milevis to Innocent (see *Dissertation 3, On Synods*).]

which was presided over at Antioch by Theodotus,

[Col. 0101A]

“of holy memory,”

[Col. 0101B]

Theodotus is famous throughout the East. In 411 he succeeded Alexander in the episcopate of Antioch. He was a man distinguished by gentleness, a pearl of continence, and richly adorned by careful discipline of life, as Theodoret says (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, ch. 37). He brought the Apollinarists back into the Church, from which he expelled the Messalians without hope of return at the Council of Constantinople. He died in 427, according to Theodoret (*at the end of the entire History*), after sixteen years in the episcopate; hence one may refute Nicephorus, who assigns him only four years. We have discussed at length the synod over which he presided in the case of Pelagius.]

and, after being exposed, was expelled even from the holy and venerable places of Jerusalem. This is attested by the writings sent by that same holy Theodotus to the most reverend bishop of the city of Rome,

[Col. 0101B]

In my opinion, those writings in question were sent to Innocent, but were received by Zosimus after Innocent’s death (*Dissertation 3, On Synods*). The reason for this opinion is as follows. Zosimus, as has often been said, wrote two letters to the Africans in favor of Coelestius and Pelagius, in the year in which he began to preside, namely 417: the first, according to Baronius, in an uncertain month; the second afterward, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. In the latter he mentions a libellus received from Pelagius together with a commendatory letter from Praylius. The libellus was sent to Innocent, whom Pelagius did not yet know to be dead, as Augustine testifies (*On Grace and Original Sin*, ch. 30). Since it is therefore reasonable to believe that Pelagius sent the letter and libellus for no other purpose than to influence Innocent, so that, if anything were attempted against the acquittal at Diospolis in the council which he saw the Gallic bishops urging before Theodotus, the judgment given at Diospolis concerning his person would not be reconsidered at Rome, it may reasonably be judged that the later writings of Praylius and Theodotus were directed to that same Innocent, whose death had not yet become known in the East.]

and of sacred memory,

[Col. 0101C]

Theodoret says (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, ch. 37):

> At Jerusalem, after the death of that admirable John, a man named Praylius, whose character beautifully answered to his name, assumed the governance of that Church.

Zosimus says (*Letter 2 to the Africans):

> We have received the letter of Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, who was ordained bishop in the place of the former Saint John and who intervened as a most energetic supporter of Pelagius’s case, etc.

These words would seem to conflict with Mercator unless we had first mentioned the synod of Antioch and said that Praylius had written two letters to the Apostolic See concerning Pelagius: the first dedicated to the memory of his predecessor John, and the second to the truth.

John, whom Praylius succeeded, died on 10 January 417 and left behind a doubtful reputation, however admirable Theodoret calls him, for two principal reasons: he was believed to have favored Origen and Pelagius excessively, and he maintained enmity with the very holy men Jerome and Epiphanius—or rather, he displayed toward them wholly undeserved hatred.]

The writings sent by Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, bear witness to this; we possess copies of them as documentary evidence.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Common Opinion and Condemnation of Both Heretics

### 1.

Among the articles of accusation that were then brought against Pelagius himself, this too was included, along with other abominable propositions:

[Col. 0101D]

At Diospolis the same propositions were brought against Pelagius (*On the Proceedings in Palestine*, ch. 11) as had earlier been brought against Coelestius at Carthage:

1. that Adam was made mortal and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin;
2. that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race;
3. that the Law leads to the kingdom in the same way as the Gospel;
4. that before Christ’s coming there were human beings without sin;
5. that newly born infants are in the same condition in which Adam was before the transgression;
6. that neither through Adam’s death or transgression does the entire human race die, nor through Christ’s resurrection does the entire human race rise again.

Augustine says that Pelagius replied to these charges as follows:

> Concerning the fact that before the Lord’s coming there were people without sin, we say that before Christ’s coming some lived in holiness and righteousness, according to the tradition of the Holy Scriptures. As for the remaining propositions, even according to their own testimony, they were not spoken by me, and I ought not to give satisfaction for them; nevertheless, for the satisfaction of the holy synod, I anathematize those who hold or have ever held such views.

By these words Pelagius seems to refute Mercator, who accuses him of agreeing with Coelestius in this proposition: “The Law leads to the heavenly kingdoms in the same way as the Gospel.” But, as he lied in many other matters, so here too Mercator later proves him to have been guilty of falsehood.

I have sometimes been exceedingly surprised that Augustine, nowhere, as far as I remember, called this proposition—“The Law leads to the kingdom of heaven in the same way as the Gospel”—to examination. Was it because it was not thought to contain a serious error? Why, then, is it attacked so sharply by Mercator in the *Commonitorium*, which ought to have included only the gravest matters? Or was it because it does not differ from the proposition examined at length, “The kingdom of heaven was also promised in the Old Testament” (*On the Proceedings in Palestine*, ch. 5)? This is the more probable solution.

For what Mercator complains of in Pelagius—his equating the Law with the Gospel—is precisely what Augustine, after a sufficiently lengthy discussion, reproaches him for in these words:

> How, then, would the sons of promise, the sons of the free Jerusalem in heaven, the eternal Jerusalem, not rightly be disturbed, when this distinction, apostolic and Catholic, seemed to be removed by Pelagius’s words, and Hagar in some way seemed to be equated with Sarah?

And afterward:

> Therefore, to express as briefly as I can what I think about this matter: just as the Old Testament suffers injury if it is denied to be from the good and supreme God, so also the New Testament suffers injury if it is equated with the Old.

What was also included was this proposition, which his disciple Coelestius held:

> “Infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.”

### 2.

We have also stated above that the following proposition was held by Coelestius and was consistent with his teacher’s doctrine:

> “The Law leads to the kingdom of heaven in the same way as the Gospel.”

Pelagius openly confirms and asserts this in certain of his writings.

### 3.

Finally, there is a libellus of his, which we possess, addressed to a certain widow,

[Col. 0102D]

This is the widow whom Jerome first accused Pelagius of addressing flatteringly (*Dialogue 3 Against the Pelagians*, near the end):

> Concerning this swelling of pride and that audacity in prayer which bursts forth, when, writing to a widow, you declare how the saints ought to pray: “For he,” you say, “rightly raises his hands to God,” etc.

And afterward:

> Flattering the widow in the same way, you are not ashamed to speak of a piety that is found nowhere, etc.

Then at the Council of Diospolis (*On the Proceedings in Palestine*, ch. 6):

> After this it was alleged that Pelagius had written in the same book of his that a person can be without sin if he wishes, and that, writing flatteringly to a widow, he had said: “Let piety find in you,” etc.

Pelagius replied:

> We did say that a person can be without sin and keep God’s commandments if he wishes. God gave him this possibility. But the remaining statements that they have attached are neither in our books nor have we ever said such things.

After hearing this, the synod said:

> Since you deny that you wrote such things, do you anathematize those who hold them?

Pelagius answered:

> I anathematize them as foolish, not as heretics, since this is not a dogma.

Augustine says:

> When we were reading this defense of Pelagius in the little document that we had previously received, certain holy brothers were present. They said that they possessed Pelagius’s exhortatory or consolatory books written to a certain widow, whose name was not given, and they advised that we should investigate whether the statements he denied might perhaps have been written there, since they themselves claimed not to know this. Then, when those books were read from the beginning, the statements in question were sought and found. Those who produced the codex asserted that for nearly four years they had possessed these books as Pelagius’s books and had never heard anyone doubt that they were his. Since we recognized that the faith of God’s servants, which was entirely known to us, could not lie about this matter, it seemed that we ought rather to believe that Pelagius had lied in the episcopal judgment—unless we should suppose that, even many years earlier, something had been written under his name but not by him.

Several points should be noted from this. First, the widow’s name was not given in the codex that Augustine had read in his presence; but although it was absent from one copy, it may have been present in others. Second, this widow may in fact have been called Livania; or perhaps, as the most learned Labbe thought, her name was, by an anagram, Juliana, and she was either the mother of Demetrias—which is less probable—or, more credibly, a relative of Julian of Eclanum. Mercator testifies that she was called by that name (*Book of Subnotations*, ch. 4).

Claudius Menard, who in the first edition of the *Proceedings in Palestine* added variant readings and scholia in the margin, believed that she was the celebrated Melania known as “the elder,” who supported the party of Rufinus of Aquileia. But I do not sufficiently understand what argument could have supported his opinion. Two considerations certainly weaken it. Jerome (*Dialogue 3 Against the Pelagians*), when he mentions this widow, would by no means have omitted the name Melania if the book had been written to her. And Augustine (*in the passage from the Proceedings cited above*) testifies that in the codex containing Pelagius’s books—whether exhortatory or consolatory—the widow’s name was not given. If she had been Melania, her name would certainly have been included, since the woman’s nobility would have enhanced the book’s value.

Moreover, Pelagius seems to have written two books *To the Widow*: one consolatory, from which the passages cited by Jerome in his dialogue and by the Council of Diospolis were taken; and another exhortatory, from which Mercator made his excerpts. The reader will not find it unwelcome if fragments of both are reproduced—not here, lest the law of the notes be violated, but in the dissertation on Pelagius’s life and character.]

containing an exhortation, addressed to the widow Livania. It reads as follows:

> “It is fitting,” he says, “for Christ’s handmaid to follow simplicity—not that which is more foolishness than simplicity, but that of which Scripture says [Baluzius: “Scripture says”]: ‘Every blessed soul is simple’ (Proverbs 11:27, according to the Septuagint). Elsewhere Scripture says: ‘Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them’ (Deuteronomy 27:26). From this,” he says, “it is shown that true simplicity is not the kind that, with senseless security, disregards God’s commandments, but the kind that keeps the precepts of the Law with wise fear. For since Scripture says that the one who does not remain in the things written is cursed, by contrast it does not wish the one who has not kept all the commandments to be considered blessed. And if every simple person is blessed, then the simple person is the one who has fulfilled all the commandments of the Law.”

[Col. 0104B]

The Vulgate edition has: “The soul that blesses shall be made fat, and he who waters shall himself be watered” (Proverbs 11:25). The Septuagint has: *ψυχὴ εὐλογουμένη πᾶσα ἁπλῆ, ἀνὴρ δὲ θυμώδης οὐκ εὐσχήμων*, that is, “Every blessed soul is simple, but an impetuous man is dishonorable.” Jerome (*Apology Against Rufinus*, near the end) has: “Every blessed soul is a simple man; an impetuous man is dishonorable.” The Vulgate edition agrees far more closely with the Hebrew text.]

### 4.

No Catholic who has read this passage can doubt that he asserts what has so often been stated above:

> “To the kingdom of heaven, the books of Moses send people in the same way as the Gospel.”

Nor can he avoid the difficulty by interpretation. And because he indiscriminately used the word “Law” in that most impious chapter—if by it he meant the Mosaic Law, whose testimony concerning the curse he quoted,

[Col. 0104C]

For if everyone who does not remain in the things written in the Mosaic Law is cursed, then certainly no part of the Law ought still to be disregarded. But if this is so, we must still bear the yoke of the whole Law, even though the Apostle cries out that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law (Galatians 3:13).]

This manner of speaking signifies that Mercator means the subscription to Zosimus’s *Tractoria* must be made. At that time the Church required such a subscription, as has often been established by the unquestionable testimony of the Fathers. For now, one example from Julian himself, writing to Saint Zosimus, will suffice: he refused, in the name of eighteen bishops, to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius. ## MARII MERCATORIS LIBER SUBNOTATIONUM IN VERBA JULIANI (C)

## ADMONITION ON THE FOLLOWING BOOK OF MARIUS MERCATOR’S SUBNOTATIONS

[Col. 0107]

This work was divided by Mercator into two parts. One received the title *Commonitorium to the Reader*, because it serves as a preface; the other, *Subnotations on the Words of Julian*, is the work itself. Both contain many remarkable things: the first especially matters relevant to history; the second, matters concerning doctrine, although it also reveals certain things about Julian that had remained unknown down to the present day.

Here a single question is proposed for treatment in itself: the mortality of Adam through sin. Other matters are touched upon as appendices—original sin, the baptism and redemption of infants, and so forth. Hence Mercator says (*Commonitorium*, or Prologue to this book, part I):

> The entire substance of Julian’s foolish and more than impious labor seems reducible to one perverse proposition: namely, that the transgression of Adam and Eve did not make them mortal.

And later (*at the end of the Book of Subnotations*):

> You know that in this dispute between us concerning mortality—specifically, the mortality of the human race, which through the first transgressors of the divine command has spread generally through their offspring, continues to spread, and will continue to spread to the end—the whole of your case is constructed.

Something concerning the date can, I think, probably be inferred from this. Mercator wrote after the death of Theodore of Mopsuestia, as is clear from these words (*at the beginning of the Prologue or Commonitorium*):

> From Theodore, formerly bishop of the town of Mopsuestia;

and indeed after the death of Saint Augustine:

> Augustine, bishop of holy memory, at various times, etc.;

and also after his response to Julian’s final work had become known. For Mercator says (*in the same work, near the end*):

> Saint Augustine overturned the first four of Julian’s books in his six books; he also attached his own responses to the eight later books, one response to each chapter. When the work of both men had come into our hands, etc.

Since Theodore died in 427 and Augustine in 430 (Theodoret, at the end of his *Ecclesiastical History*), and since the *Unfinished Work* could scarcely have reached Mercator, who was situated in the East, before the deacon Bassula arrived at Ephesus—who, as is plausible, brought this work together with the letter of Capreolus, bishop of Carthage, as the sacred testament of that most holy man dying in defense of grace—the truth does not seem far from this: Mercator composed the *Subnotations* toward the end of 431, when the synod was held at Ephesus, but collected them into a single book at the urging of Pientius in the following year. For what happened to Mercator was doubtless what usually happens to curious minds: he eagerly read the long-awaited work as soon as he received it, annotated it after reading it, and at the appropriate time gathered the *Subnotations* together into one volume.

The reader should observe three things here. First, although we have divided the Subnotations into eight chapters, we have followed Mercator in this respect, since he proposed to examine the same number of excerpts from Julian’s books. We have distinguished the individual chapters, and the Commonitorium itself, by various numbers, so that if we should at some time need to cite any of them, they may be found all the more easily the more numerous the identifying indications are. [Note: [Col. 0107] We thought these responses should be relegated to the end, so that the text might be more convenient. EDIT.]

Second, although Mercator did not append Augustine’s response to each of Julian’s excerpts, we have added it, so that the responses of both doctors, set alongside one another, may shed reciprocal light.

Finally, nowhere—whether in Mercator or in other authors of the same age—is there found, independently, so much obscure material relating to the history of the Coelestian movement. One may therefore rightly call this little work *The Revealed Mystery of the Coelestian Heresy*.
