—a man indeed of noble birth and, in those days, an *auditorialis scholasticus* [Note:

A *scholasticus*, whom Mercator calls *auditorialis*, is called *forensis* by the Council of Sardica (canon 10): “If a rich man or a forensic advocate is thought worthy of becoming a bishop, he shall not be appointed until he has performed the ministry of lector, deacon, and presbyter.” Augustine also calls him a legal expert (*Treatise 7 on John*): “Those who have a case and wish to petition the emperor seek a learned lawyer to compose their petitions.” The term *scholasticus* is frequently mentioned by the ancients.

It should be noted that an advocate for public cases, and for the churches and cities, was called a *defensor scholasticus* (Book II of the Code, *On Advocates Who Extort Money*), and received this designation from the cities. Thus Eusebius, later bishop of Dorylaeum, is called by Theophanes a *scholasticus* of the imperial city when he opposed Nestorius (*African Church Canons*, canon 97). Likewise Severus, to whom Ferrandus wrote a letter (p. 132 of the Dijon edition), whose subject is “That our Lord Jesus Christ is one of the Trinity,” is called a Constantinopolitan *scholasticus*, etc.

The expressions *auditorialis scholasticus* are sometimes used together by writers and sometimes separately, but with one and the same meaning. Examples of the separated usage are found everywhere. Augustine used the combined form (*Book V against Julian*, chapter 4), addressing Julian: “You attack the forensic advocates and say that they will shout against me, ‘O the times! O the customs!’” Elsewhere (*Book II of the same Work*, chapter 10): “Were Irenaeus, Cyprian, Reticius, Olympius, Hilary, Gregory, Basil, Ambrose, and John stirred up against you out of the common dregs of the petty shopkeepers, as you jest in Tully’s manner, to your disgrace? Were they soldiers? Were they forensic advocates? Were they sailors, tavern keepers, silk workers, cooks, butchers? Were they dissolute young men from among the monks? Finally, are these men from any sort of crowd of clerics?”

I cannot remain silent about what I have inferred from these words, and perhaps not implausibly: namely, that while saying these things Julian intended Valerius the Count, who was a military man; Constantius, who was a townsman and from the lowest ranks of the people; Marius Mercator, whom he meant by the name “forensic advocate”; James and Timasius, young men who had professed the monastic life; and Paulinus, Coelestius’ accuser, who belonged among the deacons—all fierce persecutors of the Pelagian heresy, all bound to Augustine by some special obligation, and all organized and dispatched by the leader of the Catholic host against the faction hostile to Christ.

If this conjecture is not wholly contemptible—as indeed it is not—does it not seem to follow from it that Mercator served among the forensic advocates, and specifically at Rome, and that for this reason he knew every detail concerning Coelestius all the more distinctly, since through their professional association he had, as often happens, investigated his life and character more frequently? Certainly, his entire method of procedure seems to me to come from the courtroom. What is more exact than the *Commonitorium* according to the rules of forensic accusation? What is more consistent with the custom by which such men read books while annotating them?

Nor does it seem wholly unreasonable to suppose that Marius Mercator was born at Rome—or, as I am more inclined to think, in Campania—and that he was not only Coelestius’ professional associate but also his fellow countryman. In the notes on the *Commonitorium* we made Coelestius a Campanian, and we had substantial reasons for doing so. Baluzius.]

—but, having been born a eunuch through a defect of nature. Instructed by Pelagius, he absorbed this most impious view in a purer form and, [Note:

It is scarcely credible how many Coelestius drew over to his side. Augustine, writing about him to Hilary (*Letter 157*), says: “Those who share his error are more numerous than we can hope; and wherever they are not refuted, they seduce others into their sect as well. Thus they multiply, so that they do not know where they will break out,” etc.

The Fathers of the Council of Carthage: “Many who are said to be, or to have been, their disciples do not cease in every way to affirm these evils, by which they attempt to overthrow the foundations of the Christian faith” (*Letter 175*).]

with incredible loquacity, made many participants and accomplices in this madness of his.

### 5

[Note: That Coelestius was bolder than Pelagius in openly proclaiming his opinion is attested by Jerome (*Letter to Ctesiphon*): “The fury of the disciples exposes the silence of the teachers.” Augustine (*On Original Sin*, chapter 22): “Between this man and Coelestius, in the question of baptizing infants on account of original sin, what difference is there except that the one was more open and the other more concealed; the one more obstinate and the other more deceitful; or certainly the one freer and the other more austere? For he did not wish to condemn in the Church of Carthage what he later confessed himself to hold in the Roman Church, and he professed himself ready to be corrected if, as a human being, error had crept into him. But the other condemned that doctrine as contrary to the truth, lest he himself be condemned by Catholic judges, and later reserved it for defense—or condemned it deceitfully, or interpreted it cunningly.”]

For he dared to disseminate his sense openly and publicly among the people in these words, namely:

[Note:

Observe, reader, the chapters in which Mercator says that the Coelestian heresy is contained. Observe likewise those in which Augustine (*On the Proceedings at Palestine*, chapter 11) and other writers of the same age contain it.

The author of the books called the *Hypognosticon* (*Preface*): “The blasphemy of this wicked doctrine is of the following kind: Adam would have died whether he had sinned or not; his sin harmed no one except himself; moreover, a human being can fulfill whatever he wishes through free will, as though he were sufficient for himself, or even receive grace from God according to the merits of his works; sexual desire is naturally good, and there is nothing shameful in it; the children of the baptized do not carry original sin, nor will they perish from eternal life if they depart from this life without the sacrament of baptism.”

The author of the book called the *Praedestinatus* (*Book I*, heresy 28): “Then they presented Coelestius with their books, in which he said that human nature itself was sufficient for perfection; that is, that a human being could exercise such great righteousness that he could even be without sin, if he wished; that Adam had been made mortal and would have died whether he sinned or not; that the Law had been sent to the kingdom just as the Gospels had; that infants were to be baptized for the remission of sins solely because of the universal rule of the Church; and that Adam’s sin had harmed nothing in the human race. Whether before or after they were condemned by the universal Church, they did not cease writing that a human being could be without sin, that Adam had harmed nothing in the human race, that the Law had been sent to the kingdom just as the Gospels had, and that infants were not baptized because they might possess original sin, since nature had been so well made by God that it was sufficient for itself to be free from sin.”]

“Adam was made mortal, and whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.

[Col. 0115A]

“Because Adam’s sin harmed only himself and not the human race.

“Because infants who are born are in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression.

“Because the whole human race does not die through Adam’s death [Baluz. “may not die”], since the whole human race does not rise through Christ’s resurrection.

“Because infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.”

[Note:

This is the doctrine in question: that no sin was transmitted from Adam to his descendants. Moreover, what Mercator skillfully did in his questions concerning original sin, Prosper did in questions concerning grace. Thus he says (*Letter to Rufinus on Free Will*): “It is too well known to require a narrative how the Pelagian heresy attempted to destroy the Catholic faith by its doctrine, and with what poisons of impiety it wished to occupy the innermost parts of the Church and the very vitals of Christ’s body. Yet one of its blasphemies, the most wicked and subtle seed of the others, is that they say the grace of God is given to a human being according to his merits.”

The teacher Augustine had preceded both disciples, not only in words that could be established by many testimonies, but especially in deed, when he wrote two books on the entire heresy for Albina, Pinianus, and Melania: one, *On the Grace of Christ*, against Pelagius; the other, *On Original Sin*, against Coelestius. By this division he also showed what we have often noted: that both heretics defended the whole impiety, but that one adopted one part as his own and the other the other part more emphatically.]

These five chapters generate one single, most impious and abominable doctrine.

He added moreover: “That a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments, since before Christ’s coming there were people without sin.

[Col. 0116A]

“And because the Law sends people to the kingdom of heaven in the same way as the Gospel.”

### 6

These and similar doctrines pleased Julian himself and his other fellow conspirators. When these doctrines had become known and exposed, and had been condemned by ecclesiastical authority together with the persons mentioned above, [Note: He speaks of the number of books not absolutely but comparatively, as they say, estimated with reference to the subject. For apart from the four books with which Julian attempted to answer Augustine’s first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, as Mercator will shortly say, and the other eight with which he attacked the second book of the same title, Julian does not seem to have written anything else on this question—unless someone wishes to count among the books his letters to Rufus of Thessalonica, or perhaps has in view the book *On Love*, the *Commentaries on the Song of Songs*, and the treatise *On Constancy*, which Bede mentions (*Preface to the Song of Songs*).]

and when they had also been defended by Julian in a multitude of books, he consented to be numbered with Pelagius and Coelestius as a third person in the condemnation. [Note:

The *Tractoria* of Zosimus, which contained the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius, made no mention of Julian; nor was he mentioned in the eight canons that the African Fathers issued against the same heretics at the universal council. Yet afterward they were never condemned without Julian being numbered among them.

The first condemnation is contained in the acts of Saint Celestine at the Roman Council against Coelestius, Pelagius, and Julian, which were read and approved at the Council of Ephesus (*Part II of the Council of Ephesus*, act 5, in the synodical letter to Pope Celestine).

The second occurs in Gelasius’ letter to the bishops established in Picenum (*Letter 7*): “We have proved that Pelagius, Coelestius, Julian, and many other men of oratorical eloquence were convicted in this assertion, and that they were struck both by ecclesiastical constitutions and by imperial commands.”

These words, “both by ecclesiastical and imperial commands,” give Mercator great illumination and credibility, for no imperial command against Julian is found except the one mentioned by Mercator as having been issued by Theodosius after the *Commonitorium* had been presented. See the notes on the title *Commonitorium*.

The third is found in Photius (*Codex* 54): “John, bishop of Alexandria, condemned in his *Apology* addressed to Gelasius, bishop of the city, not only the Pelagian heresy but also Pelagius himself and Coelestius, together with Julian, who was found to have succeeded them in this same sect.”]

### 7

[Note: [Col. 0116C] When the holy defender of the faith had written one book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* to Count Valerius, Julian replied in four books. From these the Count sent Augustine certain excerpts, which Augustine refuted in the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, believing them to be accurate. But when he received the books themselves and found that the excerpts did not correspond sufficiently to the books, he answered Julian’s four books in a most painstaking work of six books (see *Retractions*, book II, chapter 53). Meanwhile Julian set eight further books against Augustine’s second book; the holy doctor, now dying, again answered in his final work, as though with a swan song. A more careful account of Julian’s books will be given in the dissertation on the defenders of the Pelagian heresy. For the present, one point only should incidentally be noted: the four books written by Augustine to Boniface *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians* are commonly thought to have been written against Julian, whom Augustine himself also believed to be the author of both letters. In fact, however, the first was against Coelestius, as the author of the letter to the Roman clergy which is refuted; the other three were against Julian, who, although he admits that the letter to Rufus of Thessalonica is his, denies the other, and Augustine does not dispute this (*Unfinished Work*, book I, chapter 17).]

Then, in opposition to his childish audacity, Bishop Augustine, of holy memory, composed various books at different times. From all of these Julian selected one of the two first published to Count Valerius [Note: Augustine mentions this matter in *Retractions*, book II, chapter 53. Baluzius.] and undertook to refute it in four books completed by himself and addressed to Turbantius [Note: He was indeed a bishop, but of an uncertain see. After attaching himself to Julian for some time, he later returned to the Catholic faith. Hence Augustine, addressing Julian (*Unfinished Work*, book I, chapter 1), says: “Would that you might imitate Turbantius after those writings of yours, and after those praises of yours in which you call him conspicuous for the great splendor of his virtues, once he had been freed from your error.”]. To the second he boasts that he replied in eight final volumes sent to Florus [Note: Julian’s first work consisted of four books written against Augustine’s first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. Galland.], pretending that he was completely unaware of many other works of that holy man composed on the subject. [Note: His final work consisted of eight books against Augustine’s second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. Galland.]

### 8

[Note:

The work contained in those eight books was called *Unfinished* when only its first two books had been published by the distinguished Claudius Menardus (Paris, 1627). It is now called *Finished* by many after the other four books had been added by the distinguished Jerome Vignerius (Paris, 1655). Vossius (*On the Pelagian Heresy*, book I, chapter 6) would prefer it to be called *The Book of the Disputation*, on the authority of Gennadius, whose words are (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 45): “Attempting to defend the heresy of Pelagius, he wrote four books against Augustine, its opponent, and again seven books. There is also a book of disputation in which both defend their respective sides.”

The older title should be retained, as is suggested by the words in the catalogue of Possidius, published by Ullimerius (Louvain, 1564): “Against Julian’s second response, the *Unfinished Work*” (*Preface to that final Work of Augustine*). These words are absent from the other commonly circulated editions. It was therefore once surprising why Vignerius thought that this title had been introduced only after Menardus’ edition and had consequently entered Possidius’ catalogue. For Ullimerius’ edition preceded Menardus’ by more than sixty years.

It is worthwhile to investigate the matter a little more carefully and, unless I am mistaken, to demonstrate clearly that Possidius’ opinion must be retained. Either Augustine received only Julian’s first five books, because military disturbances prevented the others from being sent, or, if he received them all, he died while answering the sixth. Thus both statements will be true: what Possidius wrote, that this work was unfinished, and what Prosper the chronicler recorded (*Chronicle*, under the consuls Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III), that Augustine died while responding to Julian’s books amid the assault of the besieging Vandals, at the very end of his days, and persevering gloriously in the defense of Christian grace.]

Augustine therefore writes to Quodvultdeus (the letter prefixed to the *Opus Imperfectum*): “I am replying,” he says, “to Julian’s books, eight of which he published after the four to which I had previously replied. For when the brother Alypius had received these at Rome, he had not yet transcribed them all when he did not wish to let pass the opportunity that had presented itself, by which he sent me five of them, promising that he would soon send the other three and pressing me strongly not to delay my reply. Compelled by his insistence, I have consequently had to proceed more slowly with the work I was undertaking, so as not to neglect either work—one by day, the other by night—whenever I was granted relief from the other occupations that kept coming upon me from one side and another.

“I was engaged in a highly necessary task, for I was revising my own little works . . . and had already completed two volumes . . . There remained the letters and popular treatises, which the Greeks call homilies. I had read many of the letters, but had not yet dictated anything from them, when these books of Julian also began to occupy me. I have now begun replying to the fourth of them. When I have explained that one and replied to the fifth, if the three have not arrived in the meantime, I plan, if God wills, to begin what you request, working on both at once: this work and that concerning the revision of our little works, dividing them between the hours of night and day.”

From these words it may be concluded that the holy teacher had not yet received Julian’s three later books at the time when, having begun his reply to the fourth, he was writing to Quodvultdeus. He was writing, moreover, after completing the two books of the *Retractations*, as he himself testifies. Yet he had scarcely completed them, according to Possidius (*Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 28), when the Vandals invaded Africa, laying waste everything with sword and fire and making hostile not only the land but also the sea.

Since the Vandals crossed into Africa in 427, defeated Boniface in 428, and he withdrew to Hippo Regius, the most strongly fortified city in all Africa, while the Vandals were ravaging all Mauretania and Numidia and holding the harbor of Hippo closed; and since Augustine died, while Hippo Regius was being besieged by the Vandals, in the third month of the siege, in the year 430, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, it is highly probable—if not entirely certain—that, with communication cut off, Julian’s later books could not have reached Augustine.

And certainly, before his death, the holy defender of the faith composed the book *On Heresies*, although he had promised to write it only on the condition that the three later books, which he was expecting from day to day, did not arrive.

Moreover, upon examining more attentively the books edited by Vignerius, one might reasonably suppose either that Augustine replied to Julian’s fifth book in two of his own, or that Augustine’s fifth and sixth books may be joined into one. For whereas the transition from one of Julian’s books to the next is sufficiently clear in each case, in this place it is either absent or somewhat less distinct.

Yet someone might not unreasonably conclude from the following considerations that all eight books reached Augustine. First, according to Prosper and his copyist Gennadius, it was believed down to the present day that Augustine died while replying to Julian. But if the former opinion is correct, he must have replied nearly two full years before his death. Second, the sixth book is not so lacking in a preface—which is explicit in the other books—that it cannot readily be distinguished from the fifth, as is evident to anyone who examines it carefully. Finally, if Julian’s fifth book is answered by Augustine’s fifth and sixth books, then either Augustine failed to assign one book of his own to each of Julian’s books, although he did precisely that in the first four, or Augustine’s fifth and sixth books must be combined into one; and in that case it would grow so large that it would be almost twice the length of the largest of the others.

These arguments have a not implausible answer. For Prosper’s testimony is outweighed by Possidius’s authority: Prosper recorded what he heard while far away, whereas Possidius, being present, committed to memory what he observed with his own eyes. Further, if the second argument has any force, then by the same right the sixth book ought to be divided into three—short books, certainly, but nevertheless sufficiently distinct by their own prefaces and by the variety of their subject matter. Finally, if the argument based on the unequal lengths of the books has any force, the sixth should not be separated from the fifth, lest the fifth by itself barely exceed half the length of the second.

Whatever the case may be—whether Augustine received all eight books or only five, and whether he replied to the whole of six or stopped in the sixth—it is certainly established that he neither replied to all of them nor completed the work, and that Possidius rightly called it *Imperfect*. Therefore there was no suitable reason for changing the title *Opus Imperfectum*, nor any reason why the ancient title should not be retained, unless perhaps, with Gennadius, one prefers the title *Altercation* because of the form of disputation.

### Eight later books

**Note:** Augustine (*Preface to Book II of the *Opus Imperfectum*): “It happened that, under the same title, I also wrote the second book, against which Julian composed another eight with excessive loquacity,” and so forth. From this it may be concluded that Julian’s eight later books were not written against Augustine’s first reply, which comprised six books, as some have thought, including men of no little learning, but against the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, in which he refuted the excerpts sent through Valerius. Thus, to Augustine’s two not very lengthy books Julian replied with fourteen books that were certainly not short.

He wandered about with dreadful loquacity, wishing to display himself as more eloquent and learned, and, after countless insults—

**Note:** Augustine (*Book I against Julian*): “Your insults and abusive words, which burning anger breathed out in four books,” and so forth. Elsewhere, in the *Opus Imperfectum* (Book II, chapter 58), when the impure heretic had made some shameful and obscene accusation against the most holy man, Augustine replied with the greatest restraint: “Do you not fear what is written: ‘Nor will the revilers possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 6:10)? For you would not utter such vile insults, which help you in nothing, unless you spoke out of a desire to revile.”

—which, as we mentioned above, he had learned from Pelagius and Coelestius to his own destruction, he impudently—or rather, by that point, impiously—defended the insults and disgraceful abuse that he had hurled at the holy man named above.

Although, just as in the first four books—

**Note:** This was their method and the technique they employed, as had all heretics throughout the preceding ages, but especially the Pelagians. Hence Augustine says (*Book I against Julian*, chapter 1): “First I ask you”—he is addressing Julian—“why you boast that you have replied to my book, at least in appearance, when in your four books, by criticizing one of mine, you have not even touched a quarter of it, and have made such leaps in passing over my arguments as though you entirely despaired of there being any reader of either work—both mine and yours—who could detect this. Finally, even the few points in which, as I have said, scarcely a fourth of my volume is contained—points which, considering them weaker, you attempted to overthrow and trample beneath the noise of your four larger volumes, as though beneath the charge of chariots—are shown to remain unshaken when compared with the far more numerous points that you feared to touch. It is almost unnecessary to demonstrate this. Those who wish to know it should rather be reminded not to shrink from reading both works: what I wrote and what you wished to answer.”

The five bishops to Innocent (*Letter 177 among Augustine’s letters): “The issue is not one Pelagius, who perhaps has now been corrected—would that this were so!—but the many who, by arguing noisily and dragging along weak and uninstructed souls as though they had been defeated, while exhausting those who are firm and steadfast in the faith by the very force of their disputation, have already filled every place.”

he kept turning over the same matters, always the same, and, finding no prudent solution, filled more sheets or pages with injuries and insults than with any sound argument concerning the true faith. And although the matter could have been treated with the greatest brevity and on the authority of the Holy Scriptures and divine revelation, he composed an enormous quantity of distorted and wholly unnecessary material, from which he could forge impieties while accomplishing absolutely nothing. For he accomplishes nothing who devotes himself to impiety.

### 9.

The holy bishop Augustine, often mentioned above, diverted the first four of Julian’s books with his own six; and, by attaching his individual replies to the individual chapters of the eight later books as well, he blunted—indeed, shattered—his vain and leaden daggers with the hammer of Catholic truth.

**Note:** Thus the better manuscripts read. In Baluz’s edition the reading is mistakenly *ex suis libris* (“from his own books”). The author is referring to Augustine’s first work against Julian, consisting of six books. — Galland.

When the work of both men had come into our hands, I read and understood it with particular care—

**Note:** Baluz omits *studiosius perlegi et intellexi* (“I read and understood it with particular care”).

—for the entire substance of Julian’s foolish and more than impious labor appears reducible to one perverse opinion:

**Note:** Just as Julian undertook in his books to defend one particular aspect of the Pelagian heresy, so Mercator thought one particular aspect ought to be attacked. He consulted Augustine about precisely this one issue, as may be inferred from the relevant portion of the reply found after the general preface.

“Namely, that Adam and Eve’s transgression did not make them mortal, nor did their guilt pass by an original succession to their descendants; rather, only by imitating them does the person who has despised the divine commandments become guilty.”

### 11.

As I said, after I had read the whole work with particular care, I too replied, briefly and as far as my abilities allowed, by adding *Annotations*—

**Note:** *Annotations*, that is, replies placed beneath Julian’s words, as Augustine had done. — Baluz.

—to his books wherever the opportunity required, so that the reader, after hearing the trumpet of so great a father and teacher, may not disdain to take up our own humble reed pipe and may understand, in its entirety and with the utmost brevity, that Julian expended empty and rather boastful labor, together with the height of impiety, in preparing his innumerable books.

**Note:** He wrote annotations only on the first two books, certainly for no other reason than that these alone dealt with the question of Adam’s mortality and the existence of original sin—the one issue that Mercator had undertaken to contest—while he was not greatly concerned with the remaining matters, which belonged to another subject.

### 12.

Since you too, venerable presbyter Pientius, ordered me to gather into one body these same *Annotations* that I have mentioned—

**Note:** It was customary in those times that when one presbyter addressed another, he called him either “brother” or “fellow presbyter.” From this passage it may reasonably be concluded that, when he wrote this, Mercator was neither a bishop nor even a presbyter. He wrote after Augustine’s death, in 431 or perhaps 432.

—you were not unaware that in complying with your command we would incur the abuse of that slanderous and unbridled tongue. But what can the barking of a rabid dog accomplish against those who are bound outside the Church?

**Note:** That is, “against.” — Baluz.

Let us glory in becoming participants and companions of so many men and so many ecclesiastical teachers, shining throughout the whole world, against whom he hurls insults so unheard-of, so unspeakable, so obscene and atrocious.

**Note:** Augustine (*Book against Julian*, chapter 5; see also chapter 7): “Have Pelagius and Coelestius such influence with you”—he is addressing Julian—“that you dare not only to abandon so many and such great teachers and defenders of the Catholic faith, both ancient and near to our own age, whether at rest or still living, but even to call them Manichaeans? I wonder whether this will ever be able to come from your own mouth, although the perversity of your error compels you to cry it out. Yet it is remarkable how great a distance there is in a man’s face between his forehead and his tongue, so that in this matter the forehead does not restrain the tongue.”

### 13.

I know, of course, that he will also be angry with us over the order of the chapters and will raise against us a more than usually empty clamor of words, accusing us, naturally, of having no order at all in our statements against him. As we have already said, we have placed or inserted the *Annotations* among his perverse opinions in scattered form—

**Note:** Mercator did not wish to call his *Annotations* a book. He called them *Commonitories*, together with the materials that he either translated from Greek or excerpted from Latin authors, by which the Coelestians and Nestorians were to be convicted. This, I think, was the reason why Gennadius did not list him among ecclesiastical writers, nor did the other ancient and more recent cataloguers of ecclesiastical authors: consequently he was almost buried in oblivion, with no record of his name itself, had Augustine not mentioned him. There may, however, have been another reason why Gennadius omitted him, namely, Mercator’s hatred of the Pelagians and Gennadius’s enthusiasm for them.

—and we have composed no book against him.

### 14.

Let him take care of us:

> “. . . to fill the wax tablets  
>   
> in the middle of the crossroads . . .”  
>   
> *(Juvenal, Satire 1)*

**Note:** No ancient writer failed to reproach the Pelagians for abusing logical technique while neglecting the testimonies of Holy Scripture, which are nevertheless necessary for settling controversies of faith. Augustine (*Book I against Julian*, chapter 1): “Are we, my son Julian, Manichaeans? I ask: what will you answer? With what eyes will you look upon so many holy Fathers? What arguments will occur to you? What Aristotelian categories? With these you wish to leap upon us like a skilled debater, seeking to appear polished; but what edge of glass or leaden daggers among your arguments will dare to be drawn out in their presence? What weapons of yours will not flee and leave you naked? And elsewhere (*Book III*, chapter 2): ‘Where is your acuity, by which you think you have mastered both Aristotle’s categories and the other cunning devices of dialectical art?’ And again (the same book, chapter 7): ‘You see how dialectically you have said nothing, and certainly through no fault of dialectical discipline how far you have strayed from its path. You seem to use the words of that art for the purpose of puffing yourself up and stunning the unlearned, wishing to appear to be what you are not. Even if you were what you claim, in the manner in which these matters must be argued you would be nothing; but now you are both inept and ignorant, whereas then you would be an inept practitioner. Yet you advance into the contest as though laden with the sharp darts of dialecticians and boast of leaden daggers.’ And elsewhere (*Book III of the *Opus Imperfectum*, chapter 32): ‘These are the men whom, harassed by urbane wit—or rather vanity—you despise because they cannot judge doctrines according to Aristotle’s categories, as though you, who complain most loudly that examination and episcopal judgment are denied to you, could find a council of Peripatetics in which a dialectical judgment might be pronounced concerning the subject and the things that are in the subject against original sin, and so forth. If this dialectic, which does not build you up but puffs you up and makes you as ridiculous as you are boastful,’ and so forth.”

We refute, convict, and lament his deviations from Catholic truth by the divine utterances of Scripture—

**Baluz adds:** “our [Scriptures]”—

not by the art of sophistry.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

### CHAPTER ONE

Now the words of Julian from his first book to Florus, chapter 111, are as follows.

**Note:** In the editions of Menardus and Vignerius the division of the chapters is the same as it formerly was, when Mercator read Augustine’s *Opus Imperfectum*—that is, immediately after the death of the holy teacher. This should not seem surprising, since Augustine’s replies to Julian’s words divide each of his books into its own chapters.

**Note:** Chapter 112: Thus the older books and Gerberon’s edition read. But because Augustine’s books against Julian are numbered 111, Garnerius amended the number here as well. Shortly afterward, on page 8, he likewise substituted 16 for 17, and made similar changes elsewhere. — Baluz.

> “But let them hasten to him who cries, ‘My yoke is easy, and my burden is light’ (Matthew 11:30), who, in his immeasurable goodness, grants forgiveness even to the wrongdoer and, by renewing and adopting it, makes better the innocence that he creates good.”

**Note:** Mercator repeats these very words of Julian in chapter 8 of this work, and Augustine repeats them in Book III against Julian, chapter 3. This particular expression was not Julian’s alone, however, but was common to all the other Pelagians. Hence the author of the books of the *Hypognosticon* speaks in this way with a Pelagian (*Hypognosticon*, Book V, toward the end): “We baptize,” you will say, “both adults and little children for the remission of sins, as we have sometimes heard from you. And when we say to you in reply, ‘Then there is sin in little children which is remitted to them in holy baptism,’ you answer, ‘None. They are baptized only for adoption as children. Grace has in them something to adopt; the water has nothing to wash away. But they are immersed for the remission of sins solely because of the formula of the creed, so that the received custom may be preserved,’” and so forth.

**Editorial note:** After this Garnerius adds Augustine’s reply, which reads as follows:

> “Augustine: These are the very people whose liberator you begrudge them, while denying that they possess the evil from which they must be liberated. How, then, can you consistently and faithfully answer that you do not begrudge human beings the Lord Jesus Christ as their liberator, when you rather act stubbornly and faithlessly to prevent people from believing that infants can be saved by him, just as he saves his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21), for which reason, as we learn from the Gospel, he was called Jesus? Therefore you will not be able to teach that you do not begrudge Christ as liberator to human beings, since you cannot in any way demonstrate that infants are not human beings.”

### 1. Reply

In response: He renews all by creating, certainly, but he does not regenerate all, except those alone of whom he himself says: “Unless someone has been born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5). Or, as he likewise says: “Unless someone has been born again” (the same passage, verse 8).

Thus you are suspected of fraud and deceit, because nowhere throughout your entire work does any mention of renewal appear to have seemed necessary to you; rather, your mind always turns to the language of innovation.

**Note:** It is nevertheless certain that the Fathers did not always use such precision. Augustine too used the term “innovation” when he said: “Just as, therefore, an already existing soul is created by an innovation of righteousness, so an already existing soul is fashioned by the shaping of doctrine” (*Letter 166*). The Fathers of Milevis also used it (*Synodical Letter to Saint Innocent*): “They obstinately maintain that children will have eternal life even though they are renewed by none of the sacraments of Christian grace.”

Nor was Julian averse to the word “regeneration” when speaking about baptism, although Mercator wishes it to have the same force as “renewal.” He speaks as follows (*Book V of the *Opus Imperfectum*, chapter 9):

> “We testify both by our conduct and by our words that all must be reborn through baptism; but not so that, by the granting of this benefit, they should appear to have been lawfully seized by the devil. Rather, those who are works of God should become God’s pledges; those who are born in a lowly condition, though not harmfully, should be reborn in a precious condition, though not calumniously; those who proceed from God’s institutions should be advanced by God’s mysteries; those who bring the works of nature should receive the gifts of grace; and their Lord, who made them good by creating them, should make them better by renewing and adopting them.”

It is certain that there is a very great difference between innovation and renewal. For something is understood as “innovated”—as everyone knows—when it never existed before and has recently come into existence; whereas something is “renewed” when it already existed and has reached old age, and, if it is restored, is said to have been renewed.

### 2.

Nor can it easily be proved—

**Note:** So far as I know, Scripture did not use this expression when speaking of baptism; but David said concerning repentance: “Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me” (Psalm 50:12). Jeremiah also said: “Convert us, O Lord, and we shall be converted; renew our days as from the beginning” (Lamentations 5:21).

—that divine Scripture used this expression, namely “innovation”; rather, its language concerning “renewal” is extremely frequent.

### 3.

Hear the Apostle Paul, though unwillingly, saying: “As the truth is in Jesus, put away from you, according to your former manner of life, the old man who is corrupted according to the desires of error; but be renewed in the spirit of your mind”—

**Baluz reads:** “in the spirit”—

“and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in the righteousness of holiness and truth” (Ephesians 4:22–24).

Again, the same apostle says: “But when the kindness and humanity of our Savior God appeared, not from works of righteousness that we performed, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us most richly in Christ” (Titus 3:4–6).

Again, the same apostle says: “Although our outward man is being corrupted, the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).

### 4.

Next, hear who are also adopted. Hear, I say, not me but the Apostle Peter:

> “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for adoption, so that you may proclaim the virtues of God, who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light” (1 Peter 2:9).

Do you hear what he says? Do you perceive what he proclaims? He plainly says that those who have been called out of darkness into that wonderful light are adopted so that they may become God’s people for adoption. Consequently, unless someone has been called out of darkness into that wonderful light, he does not deserve to be considered a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, or a people for adoption.

### 5.

Will you perhaps say—and order us to say—that only adults, who are called out of darkness into that wonderful light as sinners, become God’s people, whereas infants, who from their very birth are placed in the light and are strangers to darkness, because, as you wish, they have merely been innovated and not renewed from some oldness of sin, are not part of God’s people?

Who among Christians could tolerate you saying such things? Who would not shudder at you and flee from what you write as from deadly poison?

## CHAPTER II

Likewise, in Book II, chapter 16, Julian’s words:

> “But the feeble defense of your opinion multiplies sins rather than diminishing them. This itch of the wretched and of those who are voluntarily declining can contribute no weight against the very principle of truth. But because they assert that this is confirmed by certain passages of Scripture, especially by the Apostle Paul, they call it natural sin, and so forth.”

**Note:** When the Pelagians argued against Catholics about the transmission of sin from Adam to his descendants, they preferred to call that sin “natural” rather than “original,” so that they might arouse greater hostility toward the Catholics among the less educated, insofar as they seemed, at least verbally, to have a closer affinity with the Manichaeans, who asserted that human nature was evil.

Pelagius (*Booklet of Faith*, section 7): “Apart from the sole stain of sin, which is not natural.”

Julian (*Booklet of Faith*, part II, section 10): “Since, therefore, we have first spoken of the goodness of nature, of blessing, and of the honor of marriage, we consequently reject natural sin—or whatever other name it is called—lest we inflict an injury upon God the Creator of all things by maintaining that something could have been made by him with sin, and by charging the testimonies of his Scriptures with falsehood.”

When Julian had said, “You must admit that the natural sin which the Manichaean invented—but which you call original by changing the name—has perished,” Augustine replied (*Book V of the *Opus Imperfectum*, chapter 9): “We call it original sin rather than natural sin more significantly, so that it may be understood to derive not from a divine work but from human origin,” and so forth.

This is what is commonly said in the schools: the stain of sin should not be called natural in Adam’s descendants if “nature” is understood as substance, which is God’s work; although it is truly natural if “nature” is understood as origin, for it is contracted by being born.

**Editorial note:** Augustine’s reply in Garnerius reads:

> “Augustine: Why do you not admit that a heavy yoke could not have been imposed by the omnipotent and just God upon the children of Adam from the day they came forth from their mother’s womb without any merit of sin?” (Ecclesiasticus 40:1).

Baluz omits this here, as above.

### 1. Reply

In response: No one says that nature, or that what is natural, is sin; rather, one says “original sin.” And it exists in nature, not—

**Note:** “Outside what is born.” Thus the ancient books and Gerberon’s edition read. Garnerius restored “outside nature.” But this emendation was unnecessary, since the sense is clear without it. — Baluz.

—outside nature. Yet it may not absurdly or improperly be called “natural,” though not “nature”; for, being deceived yourself, you deceive those whom you can.

There is some difference between “original” and “natural.” Although what is natural can also be called original, it does not follow that what is originating must be acknowledged to be natural in every respect. Consider an example: nature is every human being, of whatever age, sex, or condition; origin, however, is what makes one a senator, a member of the municipal council, a slave, a tenant farmer, or a barbarian. These are not names of nature but of an originating condition.

Thus we do not say that sin is nature or natural; rather, we say that it is the cause of origin, which has been subjected to servitude through sin.

### 2.

Although, as we have already said, it cannot exist except in the nature in which it exists—unless you are so mad as to seek it outside that nature—or unless it has of itself its own substance or nature, in which case the Manichaean, who impiously raves that the nature of evil possesses and holds the primacy of its own right, status, and origin, will devour you as one who thinks in this way.

## CHAPTER III

Likewise, somewhat farther on in the same chapter, Julian’s words:

**Note:** “It has therefore been shown.” Garnerius restored: “It has therefore been shown.” The difference is of very little importance. I nevertheless record it because, since our reading is found in Mercator’s ancient copies and in Saint Augustine, there was no reason to change *ergo* into *igitur*. — Baluz.

> “It has therefore been shown that nothing can be proved through the Holy Scriptures that justice cannot uphold; for if the law of God contains the perfect form of justice, nothing contrary to it—that is, injustice—is permitted through it to acquire the power of virtue. Consequently, what reason condemns cannot be vindicated by authority.”

**Note:** Mercator creates a difficulty for the reader, for he appears either not to have grasped Julian’s meaning—Julian denies that something can be vindicated by authority when reason proves it false—or to have read the sentence with a negation, roughly as follows: “What reason does not condemn—that is, does not prove—cannot be vindicated by authority.” The reader will easily notice, if he reflects for a moment, that the affirmative meaning favors Julian more, while the negative meaning favors Mercator.

Julian himself, however, as Augustine reports (*Book I against Julian*, chapter 7), whenever something had to be proved, wished the following order of arguments to be observed: first reason, then Scripture, and finally the authority of holy men. He speaks as follows:

> “Since it is therefore plainly clear that this is the sound and true opinion, which reason has defended first, then the authority of the Scriptures, and which the learning of holy men has always celebrated—holy men who did not attribute authority to truth by their own agreement, but received testimony and glory from their participation in it—let no gathering of the lost disturb any prudent person.”

**Note:** Garnerius has:

> “Augustine: He used a single reply to the whole connected statement, being more concerned with the doctrine itself, which had to be dealt with on its own, than with the incidental words that Marius perhaps subjected to a more subtle and overly meticulous examination.”

### 1.

In response: I wish you could prove by your reasoning the virgin’s giving birth, or conception without sexual intercourse—

**Baluz reads:** “without sexual mixture”—

and also that God became man and was brought, through the progression of the ages, to the cross. Since no human reasoning establishes these things, the authority of the divine utterances vindicates them through faith.

### 2.

It is therefore a matter for ridicule—or rather for lamentation—in your case that you say: “What reason condemns cannot be vindicated by authority.” Who, however, could count the many and frequent testimonies of Scripture against this miserable little declamation of yours—testimonies in which, since reason can investigate nothing, we have recourse to faith, so that eternal salvation may be sought through the authority of faith?

## CHAPTER IV

Likewise, in Book II, chapter 58, Julian’s words:

> “Or if perhaps, since your doctrine cannot stand otherwise, you answer that Adam conceived and gave birth from himself, no one will doubt that the Apostle did not mean this. But you have shown what you wish to happen to your own sex.”

**Note:** Garnerius has:

> “Augustine: Do you not fear what is written: ‘Nor will revilers possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 6:10)? For you would not utter such vile insults, which help you in nothing, unless you spoke from a desire to revile.”

### 1. Reply

**Note:** Mercator endured Julian’s obscene insult less patiently than Augustine did. His bile was inflamed by the dignity of the most holy old man, which had been violated by one who least of all ought to have violated it, since Augustine had loved him uniquely as the friend of his own father; and by a shamelessness unbecoming even to a layman, much less to a bishop. He therefore answers the fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself (Proverbs 26:5). Hence in this chapter—and also in the following one—he reveals many private secrets of Julian, many matters concerning the corrupt character of a man who pretended to piety, and many things that could bring shame even to a forehead that was not especially hard.

In response: Shame on you, most wretched man, for such obscenity from a vulgar—or rather, mimical—tongue. You deserve to hear the acclamations of the common people:

**Note:** This form of acclamation and voice of applause was common in earlier times, even in honorable praise. Concerning the Fathers at Ephesus, after the letters of Saint Celestine had been read in the council, the following is recorded (*Council of Ephesus*, part II, act 2, edition of Labbe, p. 618): “All the most reverend bishops acclaimed together: ‘This is a just judgment. To the new Paul, Celestine; to the new Paul, Cyril; to Celestine, guardian of the faith; to Celestine in agreement with the synod, the whole synod gives thanks. One Celestine, one Cyril, one faith of the synod, one faith of the whole world.’” For it is certainly great praise for someone to excel so far among others that no one else is considered equal to him.

> “You alone, you alone—”

**Note:** On Philistion the mime-writer, whom Jerome mentions (*Apology II against Rufinus*).

Scaliger, commenting on these words of Eusebius (*Notes on Eusebius*, p. 64, column 2, under the word “Philistion”), observed several points worth recording:

> “Philistion the mime-writer, a Magnesian by nation, was famous at Rome.”

He says that there seem to have been two Philistions. The first was a writer of mimes, according to the testimony of Suidas. For the phrase *κωμῳδίας βιολογικάς* should be interpreted in this way, since *βιολόγοι* are mimes and actors in comic performances, such as the Atellan plays among the Romans.

He was from Prusa—or from Nicaea, as the epigram on him testifies:

> **Ὁ τὸν πολυστένακτον ἀνθρώπων βίον**  
> **Γέλωτι κεράσας Νικαεὺς Φιλιστίων**  
> **Ἐνταῦθα κεῖμαι λείψανον παντὸς βίου·**  
> **Πολλάκις ἀποθανών, ὧδε δ’ οὐδὲ πώποτε.**
>
> “I, Philistion of Nicaea, who mingled laughter  
> with the much-lamented life of human beings,  
> lie here, a remnant of an entire life;  
> having often died, but never before in this way.”

According to Suidas, he lived in the time of Isocrates—or, as other copies have it, of Socrates.

The second Philistion was a Magnesian by nation and was likewise both a writer and actor of mimes. He is the one now under discussion, whom Martial mentions: “the mimes of the ridiculous Philistion.”

Epiphanius, in his work against Ptolemy (*Heresy* 33), says:

> **Οὔτε γὰρ τῶν παλαιῶν τραγωδοποιῶν τις, οὔτε οἱ κατεξῆς μιμηλοὶ τὸν τρόπον· οἱ περὶ Φιλιστίωνα, λέγω, καὶ Διογένη τὸν τὰ ἄπιστα γράψαντα etc.**
>
> “For neither was any of the ancient writers of tragedies like this, nor were those who followed imitators in this manner—those, I mean, associated with Philistion and Diogenes, who wrote incredible things,” and so forth.

Marcellinus also mentions him more than once, in Book XXX:

> “And the judges tolerate men trained by the jests of Philistion and Aesop more readily than those produced by the discipline of that Aristides the Just and of Cato.”

Jerome, in his work against Rufinus, says:

> “And, as though it were a mime of Philistion or Lentulus, or a trick of Marullus”—  
> **Correction:** “Marcellus”—  
> “fashioned in elegant speech.”

Sidonius, *Letter 2 of Book II*:

> “The actors are absent, ridiculous in dress and features, whose multicolored cosmetics imitate the furnishings of Philistion.”

Cassiodorus, *Letter 51 of Book IV*:

> “Even the mime, who is now regarded merely as an object of mockery, was discovered with such ingenuity by Philistion that his performances were committed to writing.”

I think that the Philistion of Nicaea, for whom the epigram quoted above survives, is the same person as this man, and that Suidas is mistaken in saying that he lived in the age of Isocrates or Socrates. For Nicaea was founded by Antigonus after Alexander’s death and was called first Antigonia and then Nicaea, many years after the deaths of Isocrates and Socrates. Therefore there is no doubt that there was one Philistion, a writer of mimes, not two. Thus Scaliger.

The Greek epigram has been rendered into improvised Latin as follows:

> **Nicaenus ille miserias hominum graves**  
> **Condire risu callidus Philistio**  
> **Cinis hic sepultus jaceo: saepe mortuus**
>
> “That Philistion of Nicaea, skilled in seasoning the grievous miseries of humankind with laughter, lies here as buried ashes: often dead—”

Life throughout, but not previously by such a death.

That Nicaean Philistio, by birth,  
who tempered the miseries of humankind with jokes,  
here I lie; whatever remains of my life,  
long since extinguished—often dead before,  
but never in this way.

I, Nicaean Philistio, was able to mingle  
human life with laughter  
and join jokes to tears.  
Now I lie lifeless forever. For what the theater  
often gave, this tomb gives once only: death.

] Philistio, [Col. 0127A] one

[Note: [Col. 0127B]

I once wondered whether the reading should instead be *Lucilius of the Latins*, whom Jerome mentions in these words (*Epistle* 80): “Lucilius too is censured because he runs along with an unregulated foot; his wit and charm are praised.” This is the poet whom Horace calls “muddy,” and whom Pliny says was the first to sharpen the satirist’s style; for that reason Quintilian calls him the prince of satirists. I also wondered whether Mercator might have indicated that disreputable iambic poet Lucullus, whom Cicero mentions in his letter to Atticus (*Book I, Epistle 16*); but Jerome removed all doubt and ordered that the reading be retained in these words (*Apology II against Rufinus*): “It may happen that, even if you have heard the truth from me, another person ignorant of the matter may say that you composed it, and that it is, as it were, a mime of Philistio or Lentulus and a trick of Marullus, contrived in elegant speech.”

But who, then, is that Lentulus among the Latins who is compared with the Greek Philistio? ## 2. You, most truly—

[Note: [Col. 0127D]

Lake Ampsanctus lies in the middle of Italy among the Hirpini, where sulfurous waters gush forth. Because they are enclosed on every side by woods and narrow ravines, they emit so poisonous a vapor that those who approach too closely are killed by it. Cicero says: “We see how various are the kinds of land, some part of which is even deadly, as at Ampsanctus among the Hirpini” (*On Divination*, Book I).

Virgil describes the valley of Ampsanctus in these verses (*Aeneid*, Book VII):

> There is a place in the middle of Italy, beneath high mountains,  
> famous and remembered by report in many lands,  
> the valley of Ampsanctus; on both sides the dense foliage  
> of the grove presses it into darkness, and in the middle a rushing torrent  
> gives sound among the rocks and whirls through its entire course.  
> Here a dreadful cavern and the breathing-holes of savage Dis  
> are shown; and, with Acheron broken open, a vast chasm  
> reveals its pestilential jaws, and so forth.

Servius, commenting on this passage of Virgil, says: “Ampsanctus has sulfurous waters, made more oppressive because they are surrounded by woods. The entrance to the underworld is said to be there because its heavy odor kills those who approach it, so much so that victims were not sacrificed around this place but died from the odor when brought near the water.” He mentions victims because, as Pliny records (*Book II, chapter 93*), “among the Hirpini, at Ampsanctus, near the shrine of Mephitis, those who entered the place died.”

These matters have been cited in order to restore a passage that is thoroughly corrupt, where Julian insolently rants against Saint Augustine as follows (*Unfinished Work*, Book I, chapter 4): “Here you, most devout priest and most learned rhetorician, breathe forth something more mournful and more horrible than either the valley of Conscen”—as it appears in Menardus; “Conscensis” in Vignerius and Paludanus—“or the pit of Avernus; indeed, something more wicked than the very worship of idols that was practiced in those places.”

The text is corrupt throughout. It should read either “the valley of Ampsanctus” or “the pit of Avernus,” and so forth. For among the ancients there is no mention of any valley called Consentina, Conscensis, or Cossensis, nor even of a valley of Compsa—although Compsa is a city among the Hirpini—from which something foul was exhaled and in which some unspeakable and dreadful worship of idols was practiced. Near Lake Ampsanctus, however, there was a temple of the goddess Mephitis, and those who approached it were killed. There were the valleys of Ampsanctus, which Virgil mentions; there was also, in the valleys, the pit of Avernus, or a cavern near the temple of Mephitis; and finally there were the goddess Mephitis’s dreadful rites. All these facts remarkably suit the comparison by which Julian, after charging the holy teacher with detestable sacrilege and abominable blasphemy, says that Augustine exhaled something more mournful and horrible than either the valley of Ampsanctus or the pit of Avernus could breathe forth—indeed, something more wicked than the idolatrous worship practiced in those places.]

the most loathsome stench of your neighboring spring at Ampsanctus, [Col. 0128C] the most noxious vapor of Lake Avernus, [Col. 0129A] and finally the pestilential vapor of the Atabulus of your province [Note: [Col. 0128C] He calls the spring at Ampsanctus Julian’s “neighboring” spring because Eclanum, or Aeculanum—the city whose bishopric Julian held—lies only a few miles from Lake Ampsanctus. On this basis, according to Mercator, the opinion of those who assigned Julian a bishopric in some other place is refuted.] [Note: [Col. 0128D] Everyone knows that the name Avernus was customarily used in several senses. Properly, it was the Campanian lake near Baiae, from which sulfurous vapors rose upward, so poisonous—or so thin—that passing birds either were killed by their malign power or were unable to withstand them because of their tenuity. Hence the name *Avernus*, from Greek ἄορνος, “without birds.” The name was then transferred to signify any cleft in the earth from which, as though from the underworld, a foul and harmful vapor would corrupt the vital air and bring destruction upon human beings. Thus Julian himself, in the passage corrected above, speaks of “the pit of Avernus” for the cleft near the temple of Mephitis from which a vapor of foul odor burst forth.]

the Atabulus, pestilential to your province, [Note: [Col. 0129A] Here Mercator indicates what Augustine plainly teaches: that Julian was born in Apulia. The Atabulus is a wind peculiar to Apulia, and from it the region is also called Apulia. Horace mentions it in these verses (*Satires*, Book II, Satire 5):

> Then Apulia’s famous mountains  
> are pointed out to me, which the Atabulus scorches.

Porphyrion, explaining this passage, says that Atabulus is so called *παρὰ τὸ τὴν ἄτην βάλλειν*, that is, “from inflicting harm.” According to Pliny (*Book XVII, chapter 24*), it is extremely cold; if it blows around the winter solstice, it burns everything, drying it out with cold so that no later sun can restore it. See also Gellius, *Book II, chapter 2*.]

has inflated you; [Note: [Col. 0129B] *A breath or vapor.* What was said shortly before about the Atabulus confirms our reading, which we received from the Beauvais manuscript. Other editions have *halitus* (“vapor”). BALUZ.] and with so many diseases swelling within you, made diseased—indeed, insane—you belched out these things, vomited out these things, exhaled these things. And if only you had exhaled your vital breath—for that would have been more beneficial to you—before you uttered such obscene and disgraceful things with your mouth wide open! [Note: [Col. 0129B] I remember having read somewhere in Augustine that Julian had poor health and was accustomed to suffer from illness; Mercator explains the causes, or rather the nature, of his disease. It was leucophlegmasia, caused either by the malign vapor of the Atabulus, the wind that assails the Hirpini from Apulia, or by the spring at Ampsanctus, which reduces and gradually extinguishes innate heat. Hence weakness of the vital organs, belching from the stomach, vomiting, and foul vapors produced by undigested food, as physicians report.]

## 3. What stage-player—

[Note: [Col. 0129C] If the word is not invented, it may signify an actor speaking obscene words on stage, which I strongly suspect. It may be corrupt, as though *Turpio* had been substituted for *Turpilius*, the comic poet who died on the day Cicero was born. *Turpio* means one who speaks shameful things, as the most learned Charles Du Fresne, Lord of Cange, correctly explains this passage in his glossary. BALUZ.]

what Turpio, what Durio— [Note: [Col. 0129C] The word *Durio* may also be invented to designate a man with a forehead so hardened that shame could not soften it. What if *Curio* should be restored in place of *Durio*? Curio was, as Valerius Maximus testifies (*Book IX, chapter 1*), the most wicked son of an excellent father; he contracted six hundred times a hundred thousand sesterces in debt, to the notorious disgrace of the young nobles. At that time two generations lived under the same roof: one, the father’s most frugal generation; the other, the son’s most depraved one. The comparison between Julian and Curio, the son of a good father, would certainly not be inappropriate. *Durio* means a man with a hard and calloused forehead, an impudent man, as it is read in the same glossary. BALUZ.—*Durio.* It often happens that *c* and *l*, joined together, form a *d*. Thus here, “What … durio?” where Garnerius is in great difficulty. If you read *clurio* or *cluria*, everything becomes clear: *cluria* and *clura* mean πίθηκος (“ape”) in the glosses. Hence it became a very familiar insult for all people depraved in body and mind, who were called “ape-like” and “clurine cattle.” But if you do not accept this, understand *durio* as a hard-mouthed, γελωτοποιός (“buffoon”), who was accustomed to expose himself on stage to the insults of slaps. WESSELING, *On the Ancient Roman Itinerary*, p. 383.]

or what Sannio— [Note: [Col. 0129D] Cicero says (*On the Orator*, Book II): “What can be so ridiculous as Sannio, who is mocked by his mouth, expression, imitated movements, voice, and finally by his very body?”—*Sannio*: a class of mimes who arouse the people to laughter through gesture, movement, and voice. BALUZ.] would publicly utter such things with the avowed license of shamefulness? Would chaste matrons, honorable and well-dressed men, read you? But if they remember decency and modesty, they will shudder and flee from you like a monstrous viper, such as the hydra is said to have been.

## 4. Are you the son of Bishop Memorius, of holy and blessed memory? Were you brought forth from the womb of Juliana, a lady of the first rank, than whom nothing more honorable could be found among the most venerable matrons? Far, far be it from me to dare believe this of you.

[Note: Among Augustine’s letters is one addressed to Memorius, Julian’s father, in which he says of Julian: “Indeed, I do not dare say that I love him more than you, because that would not be true. Yet I dare say that I miss him more than you. It may seem strange that I should miss more one whom I love equally; but this is because I have greater hope of seeing him. For I think that, if he comes to us at your command or with you sending him, and does what befits a young man, especially one not yet occupied by weightier cares, he will bring you yourself to me unencumbered.” From this may be seen the wicked disposition of the mad heretic, who answered a man of such stature, and so great a friendship attested in such tender words, only with insults and abuse. But this is the inborn spirit of heresy: with faith, to violate every law.

It is commonly believed that Memorius governed the Church of Capua. Hardly any reason is offered for so great credulity except that Baronius and Bellarmine thought so, themselves readily trusting either Prosper, who calls Julian a Campanian, or Gennadius, who seems to make him bishop of Capua. They therefore inferred that Memorius, being noble by birth, governed the noble Church of Campania and that he preceded his son both in episcopal office and in see.

But anyone may readily see how slight such conjectures are. First, the variant manuscripts of Gennadius cannot establish this with certainty. Next, Prosper’s epigram against Augustine’s detractor has an obscure meaning, which we shall explain in its place (*Dissertation II on the Authors and Defenders of the Pelagian Heresy*, in the eulogy of Coelestius). Next, Julian derived his origin not from Campania but from Apulia, as Mercator teaches with Augustine. Next, he held not the Church of Capua in Campania, but that of Eclanum among the Hirpini, as Mercator testifies. Moreover, from Paulinus’s verses in the epithalamium of Julian and Ja one might not implausibly infer that Memorius’s church was subject to Beneventum, to which Capua certainly was never subject. For when the holy poet had ingeniously summoned from heaven Aemilius, Ja’s father, so that he might bestow a heavenly blessing at the altar upon the spouses led there by Memorius, Julian’s father, he sings:

> Rise, Memor, reverence your father, embrace your brother:  
> in Aemilius each has one name for you.  
> Both younger and elder are Memor: a wondrous gift  
> and work of mighty God—here the younger is the father.  
> Later-born, he is the elder, because as priest he bears  
> the apostolic dignity, grey with age in his heart.  
> Memor is both son and brother, and rejoices that the father  
> common to himself and to his children is present.

These words show plainly enough that Aemilius was younger in age than Memorius but greater by the prerogative of his see. We have already shown that primates were called fathers by the other bishops of their province, not only in Africa but elsewhere too (*Notes on chapter 1 of the Commonitorium*). Therefore, if conjecture may be indulged where ancient authors with greater occasion to speak are silent, I should almost think that Memorius presided over the Church of Eclanum and that his son succeeded his father there. For Eclanum was under Beneventum; nor does any other reason seem to explain why Julian, though held in such high repute for learning, was put over so undistinguished a church, unless he had already served in it under his father.

Before leaving this passage, it is worth observing that Julian did not marry before the year 408. He married after the death of Aemilius, Ja’s father; and Aemilius was still alive in 407, if, as is very likely, he is not different from the man sent by the Apostolic See to Constantinople in the affair of John Chrysostom, whom Metaphrastes calls bishop of Beneventum.]

[Note: Here for the first time the name becomes known of the woman who bore Julian. One may reasonably suppose her to be the very widow to whom Pelagius is said to have written a book of consolation after Memorius’s death.---Juliana. Garnerius suspected that she was that widow; but afterward, on reconsidering the matter, he abandoned this opinion in favor of the view that the widow to whom Pelagius wrote was Juliana, wife of Olybrius. We shall discuss this more fully below, at p. 140. BALUZ.]

I should rather believe you the son of their household slaves, fraudulently substituted for them—as has often been said to have happened—and this your own excessive impudence and obscenity of speech rather confirms; or, if that is not so, no one who knows the holy character, holy life, and manner of life of those persons, and has carefully examined your language in these writings [Baluz.: *hisque*, “and these”], will doubt that they have degenerated in you.

[Note: Mercator hints that a rumor had at some time been spread abroad that the son of household slaves had been substituted to noble parents in place of a legitimate child, and that Julian’s conduct confirmed the rumor. Nothing, certainly, could be more abusive, insulting, and arrogant; this fault readily attaches to household slaves, but scarcely to sons of noblemen.---Garnerius here and below thinks that Mercator hints at a rumor that Julian had been substituted for his parents. But, in my judgment, Mercator’s words have another meaning. Rhetorically he says only that Julian’s character differs so greatly from that of his parents that one may suspect him to have been substituted for them, as is often said to occur, or otherwise that they have degenerated in their son. BALUZ.]

## 5. After the death of these holy persons, you deservedly trained your two sisters in such disciplines as those of your mouth. We know, we know what one of them retorted or reproached you when you rose with excessive severity to ruin her modesty; and you at once fell silent, not daring thereafter to inflict upon her grief any further vexation from your censure.

[Note: They had lived chastely under the discipline of their most holy parents. Hence Augustine offered a good wish for the whole household, as truly a house of God: “May you all dwell forever in the help of the Most High—you who dwell united in the house: father and mother, brothers of the sons, and all children of one Father, mindful of us.” But after their parents’ death, the sisters, following the example of their brother, who after long dissimulation was now living according to his own nature, fell away from domestic holiness.]

[Note: That Julian did not live very chastely, even after the dissolution of his marriage and during his episcopate, is suggested, besides Mercator, by Augustine himself: “According to you, when spouses have ceased to have intercourse, they will no longer be spouses; therefore, lest this happen, let the aged do, as far as they can, what they did when young, and let them not spare their bodies, though worn out by age, from that act in which even you, while professing continence, take excessive delight.” Elsewhere: “You labor so faithfully on behalf of the lust you have undertaken that you suffer violence unless you place it, such as it is now, even in paradise—not saying that it was made such there because of sin, but that it would have remained such even if no one had sinned, so that in that peace it might be fought against, or, lest it be fought against, satisfied whenever it arose. O holy delights of paradise! O the brow of whatever sort of bishops! O the faith of whatever sort of chaste persons!”

The author of the *Hypognosticon* says: “You would not proclaim lust a natural good if, considering the virtue of chastity, you chastised your bodies as Paul did. Instead, sporting with shameless brow, you praise its movement in public with such wanton speech that it is evident to all what you do in private—if indeed those who are not ashamed to praise such things publicly choose any privacy.” A little later: “Lust is a good generative heat, and there is nothing in it of which one should be ashamed; for if it is called evil, marriage will now be condemned, since without it offspring cannot exist. Let your beloved ones, most chaste assailants, observe, as much as they please, what so delights you to praise; or, if it does not please them, why do you urge them to find it pleasing, and why is chastity assailed by you? Why do you proclaim good what you experience as hostile in yourselves? I ask you, blush. No one ever delights to call good and adorn with praises what is hostile to himself.”

Relevant also is Bede’s report from Julian’s second book *On Love*, where Julian philosophizes most foully about the nature of milk, so that it would be horrible to quote it all.

Indeed, Jerome reproaches the Pelagians for excessive familiarity with their, as he calls them, Amazons: “You have deceived many, especially those who cling to women and know that they cannot sin.”

On this occasion I think two points should be noted: first, that Jerome seems to hint at Coelestius’s eunuchism; second, that Iprensis charged Pelagius with intemperance in pursuing feasts and, to prove it, adduced the testimony of Isidore of Pelusium, who once reproached some such thing to Pelagius, an aged monk. But Iprensis, as he commonly does in his *Pelagian History* whenever he does not borrow from Ussher the heretical matter he writes, erred twice here: first through rashness, judging Pelagius to have been the only monk of that name then in the world, although Augustine plainly says that there was also another Pelagius of Tarentum; again through lack of historical inquiry, thinking that Pelagius had spent some time in Egypt before his condemnation, which altogether conflicts with the chronology derived from Augustine.

He might have cited the much more reliable witness Paul Orosius, who says to Pelagius: “Perhaps you have a special confidence in carrying that burden because, nourished by baths and feasts, you carry broad shoulders and a stout neck, displaying fatness even upon your brow, as it is written: ‘For he stretched out his hand against God, and strengthened himself against the Almighty. He ran against him with uplifted neck, armed with a fat neck. Fatness covered his face, and grease hangs from his sides’ (Job 15:25). But such persons cannot be those to whom Christ always speaks in their hearts: ‘Strive to enter by the narrow way, for broad is that which leads to death’ (Luke 13:24). And the apostle Paul admonishes: ‘Make no provision for the flesh in its desires’ (Romans 13:14). The truth of Christ is in me, because I grieve greatly for you; for, according to the judgment of my blessed father Augustine, this is not the confidence of a healthy man but of a madman.”

But Jansenius saw that he would damage his own case if he credited Orosius’s authority concerning Orosius and accepted the *Apology*; because it is contrary to his own position, he considers it spurious, after the fashion of those whom Jerome and Augustine accuse of a kind of licentious judgment by which they rejected even books of Scripture unfavorable to themselves.]

[Col. 0133A]

# CHAPTER V. Likewise, in the same book, chapter LIX: Julian’s words.

“It was not said, ‘The two shall be in one human being,’ but, ‘The two shall be in one flesh’ (Genesis 2:14); by which name of union that pleasure and lust of those who unite, which affects the sensation, overwhelms the limbs, and, as that prudent man understood, strives to make one flesh, is shown to have been instituted by God and implanted in bodies before sin.”

[Note: [Col. 0133B] Augustine’s response, according to Garnerius:

“Augustine: If lust could alone effect that the two might be in one flesh—that lust which you have embraced, such as you now praise and assail it, which you confess to be shameful and yet love so without shame, and even dare to endow with possession of paradise—then in no way could ‘the two shall be in one flesh’ be understood also of Christ and the Church. For you do not stray so far from the way of truth as to dare impute this lust to the union of Christ and the Church. But if Christ and the Church can be two in one flesh without this lust, so also could husband and wife, had no one sinned, be joined not by shameful lust—of which he blushes who has no blush in praising it—but by charity, which deserves praise, and be two in one flesh for the purpose of begetting children. Hence, when the Lord says, ‘Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh’ (Matthew 19:6), he certainly did not say, ‘They are no longer two [feminine], but one flesh.’ What, then, are no longer two, except human beings? Just as Christ and the Church are not two Christs but one Christ. Thus it was also said to us: ‘Therefore you are Abraham’s seed’ (Galatians 3:29), whereas it was said to him: ‘To Abraham and to your seed,’ which is Christ (ibid., 16).” EDIT.]

## 1. To this.

[Note: [Col. 0133C] Again Mercator is compelled, as in the poet, to hear a man saying what he ought not say, just as one hears what one does not wish to hear.]

You speak elegantly, buffoon, in your usual manner, and in the manner in which [Note: [Col. 0133C] I do not remember reading that either Petronius or Martial published comedies; one wrote the *Satyricon*, the other epigrams. Mercator’s words therefore refer to the books of these men, especially Martial’s first book, which took its name from the amphitheater. He nevertheless preferred to mention the theater rather than the amphitheater because it suited an indecent man, and because the theater was the proper stage of indecency, as Tertullian excellently teaches in these words (*On Shows*, chapter 20): “Do we pursue madness outside the boundaries of the circus; indecency outside the limits of the theater; insolence outside the stadium; mercilessness outside the amphitheater?” and so forth. Anyone who wishes to shudder at the impurity of the ancient theater should read chapter 17 of the same book.---Garnerius says here that he does not remember reading that either Petronius or Martial published comedies, and therefore that these words refer to their books, particularly Martial’s first book, which took its name from the amphitheater. Mercator is using rhetoric here and has transferred a general name to this context, as Martial too used it in the preface to his first book: “Let Cato enter our theater.” BALUZ.]

Petronius Arbiter’s and Valerius’s theater you have disgraced. [Note: [Col. 0133D] By both names he means the impure men mentioned earlier, Petronius and Martial. The former had *Arbiter* as his cognomen, while the latter’s agnomen was *Valerius*; although, if we believe Valerius Maximus, there was also a certain Valentinus Valerius among the Romans who wrote love verses full of the most shameless license.]

It is established that in those progenitors of the human race there was implanted in their nature [Note: [Col. 0133D] The author did not use the term “lust” in a bad sense, following the example of Sallust, whom he greatly admires.
