Rather, he used it to signify the innate human desire to procreate, which in itself is indifferent and is counted among goods or vices according as it is restrained by a bridle or allowed free rein. Augustine, however, imitating Cicero, never, as far as I remember, used this term in a good sense; nor could he, since he defined lust as the desire of the mind by which any temporal things are preferred to eternal goods (*On Lying*, chapter 7). Elsewhere he says: “Although there are lusts for many things, nevertheless when ‘lust’ is spoken of without specifying the object, the mind generally understands only that by which the shameful parts of the body are aroused” (*City of God*, Book XIV, chapter 15), and so forth. Elsewhere again: “What food is for the health of a human being, intercourse is not for the health of the race, and neither is without carnal pleasure; yet when this pleasure is moderated and brought into natural use by temperance restraining it, it cannot be lust. This is said because lust is not good and right use” (*Retractations*, Book II, chapter 22).]

a lust that divine Scripture customarily calls—not, as you wish, “lust”—but “the desire of the flesh,” concerning which they would fulfill the words: “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28). And also: “He shall cling to his wife, and they shall be two in one flesh” (Genesis 2:23). But if they had kept the divine commandment, there would not have arisen for them that immodest, hostile, and importunate goad, when its activity is not being sought—the activity which, as it now exists, drags by its force and often hurls even great vessels from the citadel of chastity. Therefore, since it is not such as it had naturally been divinely given solely for the sake of producing offspring—as indeed it is not—it has been corrupted. [Col. 0134B]

[Note: Augustine and his followers—Mercator, Fulgentius, Bede, and others—consistently held that the lust of the parents is the vehicle by which original sin is transmitted, having been made ferocious through the disobedience of the first human beings and propagated into their descendants like a kind of hereditary disease. How, however, can original guilt, which exists in the higher part of the soul, be transmitted through lust, which belongs to the lower part? Mercator correctly explains this in words that seem to have been borrowed from Augustine: “If it is not such as it is—and indeed it is not—the desire of the flesh that was divinely given naturally for the sole purpose of producing offspring has been corrupted; and when, through its own corruption, it generates, what is born from corruption is corrupted and rightly needs Christ as physician and restorer.”

Saint Thomas may shed light upon a truth that is not equally clear in itself to everyone; this is his teaching (*Summa*, I–II, questions 81 and following). There were two parts to original justice, by which God freely endowed the human being from the beginning, wishing to create him upright. One was the part by which the higher part of the soul was subject to God; the other was the part by which the lower part remained subject to the higher for as long as the higher itself clung to God. The former was charity; the latter was the bridle of concupiscence. Both were freely bestowed upon Adam, and both would also have been freely bestowed upon his descendants if Adam had abstained from eating the forbidden fruit. Insofar as this condition concerned Adam’s will, it was a kind of obligation; insofar as it concerned God, it was a commandment; insofar as it concerned both, it was a covenant. Augustine often mentions this covenant, especially when he demonstrates original sin from the passage in Genesis: “The male whose flesh of his foreskin has not been circumcised, that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant” (Genesis 17:14).

This doctrine of the covenant passed, as if by tradition, from the Fathers to the scholastics, none of whom holds another view without incurring the charge of rashness. Its proper understanding refutes, in Catholic fashion, Michael Baius’s empty and naturalistic fantasies about the elevation of humanity into fellowship with the divine nature. Finally, its truth convicts the critics of the schools either of negligence in reading Augustine’s books, of slowness in understanding them, or of bad faith in interpreting them.

Original sin, then, being a defect of original justice, as Saint Thomas defined it, must consist of two parts: one material, namely, the unrestrained force of concupiscence; the other formal, namely, the privation of charity. Augustine calls the former a vice, disease, sickness, and evil of nature; the latter he calls sin and guilt. Guilt is removed by the power of the sacrament, while the vice remains for the struggle. It either increases through sinning or diminishes through right action, according as the creature is sweetened by the habit of sinning or God becomes sweeter through a life of good conduct.

Just as the two parts of original justice were mutually joined, so that they were once a single benefit in innocent Adam and would have been a single benefit in his innocent descendants, so the absence of both parts, which was a single loss in sinful Adam, is a single evil in his descendants until they are reborn in Christ and become new human beings.

Therefore, when a righteous man begets children, because he begets from what has been left for the struggle, he transmits sin along with the vice into his son; for things arising from their principles resemble those principles.

This is the meaning both of the comparisons Augustine sometimes uses and of the metaphorical expressions by which he explains the matter. He says that the parents’ seed has been corrupted; that the sick arise from the sick; the uncircumcised from the circumcised; wild olive trees from grafted olives; sinners from the righteous—because in generation the flesh is transmitted, and receives a soul deprived of the bridle of original justice and lacking the other part of justice, namely charity, until it receives that part through the sacrament of Christ.

A certain author devoted much effort to this question, yet made scarcely any progress, because he preferred to say something contrary to the scholastic doctors rather than agree with the holy teachers Augustine and Thomas concerning the covenant established between God and Adam. He was therefore forced into certain absurd conjectures: about corrupted parental seed, about Adam’s bodily constitution being corrupted by sin, about a hidden and diseased quality introduced by the serpent’s breath, and other similar fictions, which are unjustly attributed to Augustine.

But why was it necessary to bring back into its former darkness a question that, when it first arose, was somewhat obscure but was later illuminated by the labor of the doctors and by the Church’s understanding? Was it so important to defend obstinately, after it had been condemned by three supreme pontiffs, the opinion “that fellowship with the divine nature is natural to the human being,” that belief in original sin should almost be perverted into a doctrine scarcely less blasphemous than that of Illyricus? What could be clearer than the teaching of Saint Thomas, whose *Summa* Jansenius calls “Augustine contracted and bound, in a fixed proportion, to natural arguments?”]

When it generates through this corruption, what is born from corruption is corrupted, and therefore [Baluz.: *juri*, “by right,” for *inde*, “therefore”] needs Christ as physician and restorer.

# CHAPTER VI. Likewise, in the same book, chapter LXIII: Julian’s words.

“He did not say that sin passed over, but death; death, to be sure, imposed by the severity of judgment, the avenger of transgression; pursuing not the seeds of bodies but the vices of morals.”

[Note: [Col. 0136C] Augustine’s response, according to Garnerius:

“Augustine: In that passage where it is said, ‘Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed through to all human beings,’ it appears ambiguous whether sin, death, or both are said to have passed through all human beings. But what the truth of the matter is now clearly demonstrates. For if sin had not passed through, every human being would not be born with the law of sin that is in the members; and if death had not passed through, all human beings, insofar as they belong to the condition of mortals, would not die.

“But when the Apostle says, ‘in whom all sinned,’ in whom is this understood except Adam, in whom he says that they also die? For it was not just that punishment should pass over without guilt.

“Turn wherever you will: you will in no way overthrow the foundations of the Catholic faith, especially since you yourself contradict yourself. Now you say that not sin but death passed over, although earlier you said that the Apostle emphasized not two human beings but one in order to teach that sin passed over by imitation, not by generation. What is this that you now say: not that sin passed over, but death?” EDIT.]

1. On this point, you utter fool, you have struck yourself with your own dagger: for you wish not sin, but death, to pass through the seeds, although you say that death was “inflicted by the severity of judgment, as the avenger of transgression.” Let the answer be made to you from your own words. What has this to do with posterity, all of whom without exception have died, are dying, and will die—that death, namely, which has passed through all human beings, and which, as you say, is the avenger of transgression? For the other claim is laughable: you say that death, which you declared to be the punishment of sin, alone passed into the race, without that which was the cause of so great an evil. Behold the remarkable defender of God’s just judgment, who transmits the punishment of the ancestor to posterity, although they do not possess the cause of his punishment!

It is pleasing, however, that you add: “Pursuing not bodily seeds, but moral vices.” [Col. 0136A] As though you were commanding rather than teaching that no one has died, is dying, or will die except one who has proved an imitator of Adam’s transgression. Are you not ashamed of such enormous foolishness? Was there, is there, or will there at least be no one—according to the definition of your master Pelagius, which you have defended in so many books—in accordance with which you both declare that “a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments”?

Thus, as we were saying, even according to your own position, throughout so many centuries there has been no one who, being found free from this imitation of yours, did not deserve to undergo in himself that punishment of Adam which you say is “the avenger of transgression, and which has been commanded to pursue not the seeds but the vices of character.” And surely those whom you say “can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments” ought to be without vices. Finally, according to you, so many thousands of infants are born, have been born, and will be born without any vice at all. Why, then, are they punished with this death [Baluz.: “this”], which was inflicted by the severity of judgment as the avenger of transgression [Baluz. omits “of transgression”], although neither its cause followed them nor, as you say, did it pass into any of them?

[Note: “Any fallen person.” This is the reading of the old books and of Gerberon’s edition; Garner, however, restored “of them.” BALUZ.] [Col. 0136D]

[Note: The passage is especially noteworthy because it shows that Julian defended Pelagius’ position concerning human sinlessness and the powers of nature for keeping God’s commandments by means of many books. But which books does Mercator mean? For this subject is treated neither in Julian’s earlier nor in his later work against Saint Augustine. Is the letter to Demetrias to be attributed to Julian, as Mercator’s author? Or the book *On Nature*, the three books *On Free Choice*, and other works of that kind, composed in Julian’s words according to Pelagius’ sense? Or should we also attribute to him, as we have elsewhere conjectured, the *Book of Arguments*, in which both questions are discussed and defined according to Pelagius’ view? See Dissertation 2, in the eulogy of Pelagius.]

3. Here, so to speak, the splendid definition of your fellow disciple Caelestius fell from your hands: “Since Adam’s sin harmed him alone, and not the human race.” [Col. 0137B]

[Note: The words that follow deserve somewhat closer attention. They show how highly the Pelagians esteemed themselves and their own party. Yet they are not found in Augustine’s third book of the earlier work, which answers Julian’s third book to Turbantius, but in the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 3; they are said to be excerpts from the preface to the whole work. They read as follows:

“Our teachers of the present age, most blessed brother, and the authors of the wicked sedition that still burns, have resolved to reach insults and destruction against men whose holy pursuits consume them through the ruin of the whole Church, not understanding how much honor they have conferred upon those whose glory they have shown could not have been overthrown except together with the Catholic religion.” For if anyone says either that human beings possess free choice or that God is the creator of those who are born, he is called a Caelestian and a Pelagian. Thus, lest they be called heretics, they become Manichaeans; and while fearing a false disgrace, they incur a true crime, like wild animals surrounded by wings so that they may be driven into nets. Since reason is lacking to them, they are pressed toward genuine destruction by an empty fear.”]

This Caelestius is one of those concerning whom, in the first of the four books of your work addressed to Turbantius, you say:

“Our teachers of the present age, most blessed brother Turbantius, and the authors of the wicked sedition that still burns, have resolved to reach insults and destruction against men whose holy pursuits consume them through the ruin of the whole Church, not understanding how much honor they have conferred upon those whose glory they have shown could not be overthrown except together with the Catholic religion.” [Col. 0137C]

[Note: Pelagius made this same complaint against Jerome, who, in the preface to his *Dialogues*, written, I think, at the time when John of Jerusalem had imposed silence on both parties and forbidden either side to accuse the other of heresy—indeed, had accused the Catholics of envy toward Pelagius. He says:

“To those who say that I have written this work inflamed by the torches of envy, I shall reply briefly: I have never spared heretics, and I have labored with every effort to make the enemies of the Church my own enemies also. Helvidius wrote against the perpetual virginity of holy Mary; was I driven by envy to answer him, whom I never saw in the flesh? Jovinian, whose heresy, O Pelagius, you now revive, disturbed the Roman faith in my absence; he was so inarticulate and foul in speech that he deserved pity more than envy. I answered him as best I could . . . Everyone chatters what he thinks; I alone am bitten by the glory of all, and so wretched that I even envy those who deserve no envy. Therefore, to prove to everyone that I hate not people but errors, and that I do not seek the disgrace of anyone, but rather grieve for those who are overthrown by knowledge falsely so called, I introduced the names Atticus and Critobulus, through whom I might express what both our side and the opposing side thought . . . But if anyone cries out that he has been falsely defamed, and boasts that he shares our views, he will prove his agreement with the true faith when he openly and without deceit condemns what is opposed, lest he hear the prophetic saying: ‘And in all this her treacherous sister Judah has not returned to me with her whole heart, but falsely’ (Jer. 3:7). It is a lesser sin to follow an evil which one has thought good than not to dare defend what one knows with certainty to be good. Those who cannot endure threats, insult, and poverty—how shall we conquer the flames of Babylon? LET NOT A FEIGNED PEACE REMOVE THE WAR IT HAS PRESERVED. I do not wish to learn perfidy through fear, since Christ has left the true faith to my will.”]

Have you so completely forgotten friendship [Baluz.: “friendships”]? Is this how you have learned to defend? Or do you now yourself need a patron, and have those who had prepared you as their defender been deceived?

4. You will no doubt claim that I have said these things as though I had failed to understand how clever and eloquent you are. If you persuade yourself of this, you will be greatly deceived. I understood you: I know what absurd opinions you hold against the steadfastness of the faith; I remember the verbal evasions you now employ here; and, if you will bear with us a little, we shall prove this.

5. You evidently take advantage of the simplicity of Christians who happen to read these books of yours. These are your own words, surely:

“Death, however, passed to all human beings, not sin, having been inflicted by the severity of judgment as the avenger of transgression.”

Let me hold you here for a little while; let me profitably spend some time with you here. I ask whether you are speaking simply and not, like Loxias to Croesus and Pyrrhus, in a dilemma [Greek *dilēmma*, “a dilemma”], as though you were the one spirit of error [Baluz.: “and you now speak in the spirit of error”]. How can you impose the name “Traducianist” upon Catholic Christians, as you please and still may? For even death itself, which you attribute to them, has come and will come, according to your own preference, only through passage or transmission; and you wish it to be a punishment without anyone’s deserving the punishment.

[Note: This word is found in Rufinus of Palestine’s *On the Faith*, chapter 53:

“When they ask us,” he says, “whether God begot the Son or not, and receive from us the answer, ‘He begot him,’ they immediately add a question of the following kind, which the Greeks call a *dilemma*: ‘Unwillingly or willingly?’”

Moreover, since, so far as I know, this word is not found in other authors, I am strongly led to believe that Mercator rendered Rufinus’ book into Latin. But on this matter elsewhere at greater length (Dissertation 2, on the authors and defenders of the Pelagian heresy).]

[Note: This passage is corruptly read in the Beauvais manuscript: “As though you were placing Acresus and Phirus, you too now, one spirit of error,” and so forth. It has been corrected both from the Vatican manuscript and especially from Jerome, who writes to Pammachius and Oceanus about heretics as follows (*Letter* 84):

“When they begin to be pressed, and must either subscribe to them or leave the Church, you may see remarkable turns: they regulate their words, alter their order, and compose ambiguous statements so that they hold both our confession and that of their opponents, so that the heretic hears one thing and the Catholic another—as though Apollo of Delphi, also called Loxias, had not uttered oracles to Croesus and Pyrrhus in the same spirit, though at different times, deceiving them by the same trick. For example, they say: ‘We believe in the future resurrection of bodies.’ If this is said properly, it is a pure confession; but since there are heavenly and earthly bodies, the orthodox hearer thinks ‘body’ means flesh, while the heretic recognizes spirit,” and so forth.

Loxias is another name for Apollo, who, because he gave ambiguous, twisted, and oblique responses, was called Loxias. Among the Greeks, *loxos* (λόξος) means “oblique,” although others give different explanations for the name; on this subject consult Macrobius in *On the Gods*. What Apollo of Delphi answered obliquely to Croesus when he was planning an expedition against Persia, and to Pyrrhus when he was preparing to move against the Romans, is widely known.]

[Note: By this name the Pelagians habitually branded all defenders of original sin, but Augustine above all. Julian was not the only one to make this insult; Annianus did so as well in both letters prefixed to his translations of Chrysostom’s homilies into Latin. Writing to Orontius, to whom he was sending the homilies on Matthew, and after praising that great teacher’s eloquence and falsely claiming agreement between his views and Pelagian doctrines, he says:

“How great a consolation arises for us when we see that, in so learned and illustrious a teacher of the East, the truth which the Traducianist attacks in us is upheld—a truth which blessed John, in all his books, guards, arms, and kindles as protected on every side, so that he seems not so much to have instructed his present disciples as to have prepared aids for us against the attack on the true faith! How great is he against necessity! How greatly he rises in defense of free choice! How, everywhere in harmony with our books, while preserving the right of the will, he commends the supports of divine grace! How he sets forth the most splendid Vessel of Election against the darkness of all vices and as the mirror of every virtue!”

A little later, explaining the subject of the individual homilies, he says:

“Sixth, he resolves all those questions by which the Traducianist, resisting blessed Paul, stains him with the obscurity of vices, so that he may supposedly reconcile sins to his faithful by the apostolic example.”

He is evidently alluding to what the Pelagians maliciously used to allege against Catholics, as though they said that the Apostle Paul, or all the apostles, had been polluted by unrestrained lust. Note the perpetual slander of Caelestius and Julian against Catholic teachers: that by their doctrines they encouraged moral corruption and loosened the reins of concupiscence.]

6. To escape these difficulties, which you yourself have created—being more talkative than eloquent—you repeat and explain in what follows that here you were speaking of the death by which Adam was punished after his transgression: not the death that destroys bodies, but the death that comes upon the soul through crimes and contempt of God and is eternal, since it draws one to eternal punishment. Holy Scripture also signifies this death:

“The widow who lives in pleasure is dead” [Baluz.: “who acts in pleasure”] (1 Tim. 5:6).

And in the Gospel:

“Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. 8:22; Luke 9:60). [Col. 0139B]

You will say that this is the death I declared to have passed, and to pass, into Adam’s posterity—not into absolutely everyone, but only into those who, like him, became imitators of his transgression and forgetful of the divine commandments. But that other death, you will say—the dissolution of the body, or the separation of the soul from the body—would have existed in Adam even if he had not sinned.

7. Hence came those celebrated definitions of your fellow soldier and fellow disciple Caelestius, and of Pelagius, master of both of you, which, together with their authors, were long ago condemned throughout the world by ecclesiastical authority:

“Adam was made mortal, so that whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die; and since Adam’s sin harmed him alone and not the human race; and since infants are in the same state in which Adam was before his transgression.” [Col. 0140A]

[Note: We have shown in the case of Pelagius and Caelestius (Dissertation 5) that the condemnation ought to have been subscribed against the persons rather than against their doctrines; that the form of subscription was prescribed by the supreme pontiff and the law by the emperors; and that not only clerics but also laypeople were bound by that law. All truly Catholic people rendered obedience so religiously that Prosper rightly sang (*Poem on Ingenuousness*, chapter 9) that this heresy had been condemned by the councils and by the hand of the whole world.]

8. From this also arose that final statement of yours, which you did not fear to bring forward to your own detriment:

“Infants, even if they die unbaptized, possess eternal life.”

And that still more than sacrilegious assertion [Baluz.: “sacrilege”]:

“Nor does the whole human race die through Adam’s death, because the whole human race does not rise again through Christ’s resurrection.”

9. These, surely, are the magnificent decisions of your school; these are the dogmas of the Christian learning, as you call it. But we Christians do not call them doctrines of truth.

“To the people, your finery. I know you within and on the skin.” (Persius, *Satire* 3.)

What does it profit you, as the same poet says,

“To keep a crafty fox in your reeking breast?” (The same, *Satire* 5.) [Col. 0140B]

[Note: It was the characteristic of the entire Pelagian faction to think that nothing concerning their position should be said without disguise and an artful complexity. Jerome had charged them with this before Mercator (*Letter to Ctesiphon*):

“The Eunomians, Macedonians, and Arians, separated by names but united in impiety, cause us no trouble; for they speak what they think. This is the only heresy that is publicly ashamed to say what it does not fear to teach in secret,” and so forth.

Augustine says likewise (*Against Julian*, book 1, chapter 5):

“What does it profit you that by some art of perplexity you tie together I know not what handles and hooks, so that simple things may not be exposed and clear things may not shine in the light?” and so forth.

Innocent says (*Letter to the Council Fathers of Carthage*):

“Instructed—or rather destroyed—by the sophistries of words, disputing under the appearance of the Catholic faith, they exhale a pestilential poison.”]

I shall indeed drag you out of your most twisted and foul pits, by careful investigation, into the light, so that you may be exposed to the Christian peoples.

10. Listen now, both you and those who have thought it worthwhile to read both you and me, to what you yourself once pronounced against this most impious, most perverse, most shameless, and most insolent opinion of yours. I mean in your letter, which at that time you dared to send to the Apostolic See, [Col. 0140C]

[Note: Julian admits (*Imperfect Work*, book 1, chapter 17) that he sent two letters to Pope Zosimus, but denies that the other, which was addressed to the Roman clergy, was written by him. Augustine does not strongly contradict him, although he had previously refuted it as Julian’s in the first book addressed to Boniface.]

[Note: This establishes the time at which the letter was sent—namely, when Julian refused to join the universal Church in condemning Pelagius and Caelestius. The council took place after Zosimus’ *Tractoria* had been sent to all the bishops of the world, after May 418. Since Zosimus saw Julian’s letter, as Mercator reports, and Zosimus died on 26 December of that same year, as is the settled opinion of all, it must be acknowledged that the letter was sent in the intervening period.]

when you refused to condemn Pelagius and Caelestius together with the universal Church throughout the whole world. Before that letter reached the bishop of that holy Roman Church, it was circulated through almost all Italy by the agency of certain people whom you had deceived, and, as though it were something remarkable, was conveyed to the ears of many. There, among other things, you say:

[Note: Julian himself says in his *Booklet of Faith*:

“We thoroughly detest anyone who asserts that the whole human race does not die either through Adam or rise again in its entirety through Christ.”]

[Note: Observe that in the earliest period of the Church the general restoration of the human race in Christ was as universally accepted among all the faithful as the general ruin in Adam. Even the heretics did not dare to speak openly in opposition to this, but employed a distinction between “all” without exception—that is, simply, *haplōs* (ἁπλῶς)—and “all” in some particular class, that is, *kata ti* (κατά τι).]

“Who, then, is the one who asserts that the whole human race does not die through Adam’s death and that the whole human race does not rise again through Christ’s resurrection? He is opposed to the Apostle, who says: ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ’ (1 Cor. 15:22).”

11. We know and understand by what fraud and deceit you say and think “all” means: not absolutely all human beings, that is, the whole human race, but all those who chose to become imitators of Adam. And concerning the resurrection through Christ, which that Apostle declared, you must similarly say, without doubt, that not the whole human race whatsoever will rise, but only the righteous and holy, those who have imitated Christ’s righteousness and holiness. [Col. 0142A]

Yet it is established that absolutely everyone will rise through Christ, although some will rise to the kingdom and others to judgment.

[Note: I say, let this be established among Catholics. For Theodore of Mopsuestia appears to have thought otherwise (*Fragment 4 from book 5 against Augustine*):

“Who,” he says, “could be so mad as to believe that so great a good—the resurrection—would become the occasion of infinite punishment for those who rise, for whom it would have been more advantageous never to rise at all than to endure, after the resurrection, the experience of such great and such terrible evils under endless punishments?”]

And you add:

“It is therefore rightly rejected whoever contradicts this opinion, which says: ‘Through a human being came death, and through a human being the resurrection of the dead’ (1 Cor. 15:21).”

Likewise:

“Adam’s sin harmed him alone and not the human race.” And this opinion, you say, “is rightly refuted by us; for it must be believed that it harmed not him alone but the human race.”

12. [Note: Saint Leo (*Letter* 8) notes this perpetual fraud of the Pelagians and warned Nicetas of Aquileia to guard against it when receiving people who said they wished to return from this heresy to the Catholic Church:

“Let them condemn in explicit professions the authors of their proud error, and let them detest whatever the universal Church has abhorred in their teaching. Let them declare, in full, explicit, and personally signed statements, that they embrace and approve in every respect all the synodal decrees which the authority of the Apostolic See has confirmed for the eradication of this heresy. Let nothing obscure or ambiguous be found in their words, since we know this to be their trick: in whatever portion of the detestable doctrine they distinguish themselves from the company of the condemned, they think that none of their opinions has been lost. Although they pretend to reject and renounce all their definitions, as though to facilitate their evasion, they accept this entire art of deception unless it is understood,” and so forth.

The holy pontiff considered this warning so important that he threatened the bishop of so great a see with severe punishment if he failed to take care:

“Let your affection not doubt that, if—which we do not suppose—the things we decree for the protection of the canons and the integrity of the faith are neglected, we shall be moved still more strongly. For the faults of those in lower orders are attributable to no one more than to negligent and careless rulers, who often nourish a great pestilence while pretending not to apply the harsher medicine.”]

Here too, despite preserving for yourself—as you suppose—the meaning of your most perverse and tortuous doctrine, you could not conceal from us what you are doing. For those whom you wish to teach, though few in comparison with the whole race, are nevertheless the human race.

Likewise:

“You say that infants are in the state in which Adam was before his transgression; I count this among the undisciplined questions.”

[Note: This formula is taken from the Second Letter to Timothy, 2:23, where the Apostle warns his disciple:

“Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they generate quarrels,” and so forth.

It is remarkable how much Julian liked the expression “undisciplined questions,” since he used it frequently (*Booklet of Faith*, part 3, no. 22):

“If there are any such matters,” he says, “which either oppose the Catholic faith or belong to undisciplined questions, we condemn them with a similar curse.”]

No learned person is unaware of the distinction the ancients made between dogma and a question, opposing one to the other in such a way that, under the Catholic faith, it is permissible to dispute a question on either side, but not permissible to dispute dogma.

[Note: I observed that the Pelagians once did what all heretics usually do: so that they would not seem to be fighting the Church, they falsely boasted that their disagreement concerned not dogma but merely a question. Caelestius first dared to do this at the Council of Carthage, as Augustine reports in these words (*On Original Sin*, chapter 4, and elsewhere):

“Now it is necessary to examine the point by which, wishing cunningly to avoid the odium of heresy, they assert that this is a question beyond the danger of faith, so that, if they are proved to have deviated in it, they may seem to have erred not criminally but, as it were, civilly.”

Thus Caelestius spoke in the ecclesiastical acts at Carthage:

“Concerning the transmission of sin, I have already said that I have heard many within the Catholic Church destroy it, and others affirm it, although this is a question, not a heresy.”

And in the booklet delivered at Rome:

“If questions beyond the faith have arisen, concerning which there is disagreement among many, I have not, as the author of any dogma, established them by a definitive authority; rather, we submit for the judgment of your apostolate what we have received from the fountain of the prophets and apostles.”

That all the Pelagians commonly proclaimed this is attested by the author of *Predestination*:

“We are distinguished by a question, not by communion” (*Book 1, Heresy 88).]

You say, therefore, that infants who are born today are not in every respect in the state in which Adam was before sin, although it cannot be denied that they, like him, are God’s work.

13. [Note: Mercator exposes Julian’s most shameless quibble. In a matter so serious—giving an account of his faith to the supreme pontiff in a public document, with the whole Church waiting—he nevertheless played with an inept ambiguity of words, having a Catholic dogma on his lips and something ridiculous in his heart. Has anyone perhaps said of him what Augustine said of Pelagius? “By these clouds he thinks he has deceived the judgment; and you, with your whole head, applaud this wickedness, laughing that so many bishops have been mocked by him” (*Against Julian*, book 1, chapter 3).]

We know perfectly well what state you say and understand this to be, while imagining that you preserve your meaning: not, of course, the state of the soul before sin, but the condition of smallness and littleness in which infants are born.

Be sure to remember that you have just said nothing here about unbaptized children who, if overtaken by death, supposedly possess eternal life—a most false claim, because Christ neither wills nor willed this, despite what your utterly senseless audacity commands and teaches.

You add likewise:

“Adam was also made mortal, so that whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died” [Baluz.: “would have been going to die”];

and you said that this too was not supported by reason.

“For it must be believed,” you say, “that he was indeed made immortal, but that, if he had not sinned by tasting the tree of life, he could have acquired the power of immortality.” Therefore it was wrongly stated that “whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.”

[Note: The same reading is found in both the Vatican and Beauvais manuscripts, and again in Mercator (*Book of Subnotes*, chapter 8), where more of Julian’s words are quoted. Yet the sequence of the argument seems to require that *mortal* be substituted for *immortal*, as follows:

“For it must be believed that he was indeed made mortal, but that, if he had not sinned by tasting the tree of life, he could have acquired the power of immortality.”

Such a correction is demanded by the Pelagian doctrine: that Adam was made mortal and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin.

Nevertheless, I think the reading of both manuscripts should be retained. First, because it permits a reasonable meaning: Adam was made immortal, but only in such a way that, if he had not sinned by tasting the tree of life, he could have acquired the power of immortality. Second, because from Augustine we learn that some Pelagians, driven by the force of Catholic arguments into such difficulties, not only admitted that Adam had been made immortal, since Scripture says, “God made man indestructible” (Wis. 2:25), but, because they obstinately wished to retain their opinion that infants and Adam had an equal origin, asserted something even more remarkable: namely, that all Adam’s descendants are born immortal and do not die except through the merits of their sins, just as Adam did.

This obscure passage of Augustine, understood by few, will receive light from both of Mercator’s testimonies. It reads as follows (*Sermon 7 on the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 6):

“Some of them argue as we have heard: ‘Absolutely all people die according to their merits; for there would be no death unless it came from sin.’ This is said very well and truly: there would be no death unless it came from sin. But when I hear this, I praise it because I look to that first death and to the sin of that first human being. For I hear the Apostle: ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ’ (1 Cor. 15:21). ‘Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Rom. 5:12). For all were one. Thus I hear you saying that human death comes from sin. ‘No,’ you say. And what do you say? ‘Does God now create every human being immortal?’ What a remarkable novelty! What do you say? ‘Absolutely,’ you say, ‘God creates every human being immortal.’ Why, then, do little infants die? . . . Answer me: why do they die, if all human beings are born immortal and die because they sin? What do you think could be said? What ears could endure it? ‘They sinned too’ . . . For if they did not sin, you say, they would not die,” and so forth.]

14. So that you may not accuse me of having slandered you, or so that neither anyone else nor you yourself may later say that you did not hold these defined opinions, listen again to what is preserved in your own words in the book under discussion.

**CHAPTER VII. Words of Julian from the same book, chapter 66.**
“Therefore, according to the Apostle, sin entered through one man, and through sin death, because the world saw him as both guilty and liable to the condemnation of everlasting death.” [Note: [Col. 0144D] Baluzius, on the authority of old books, substitutes *destinatum* (“destined”) for *obnoxium* (“liable”). EDIT.] “Certainly, you soon said something else [Baluz. omits *aliud mox*], and you denied that sin had entered this world through that one man, whereas now you confess that it did enter. “But death passed to all human beings, because one pattern of judgment encompassed all transgressors of the succeeding age. Yet [Baluz. adds *ais* (“you say”)] this death is permitted to rage neither against the saints nor against any innocent persons, but spreads only over those whom it sees to have imitated the transgression. Although that transgression was not made natural, it was nevertheless a pattern of sin; and therefore, although it does not burden those being born, it accuses those who imitate it. Judicial death, however, passes in him in whom all sinned, but by free choice.” [Note: [Col. 0144D] Augustine’s response, as reported by Garnerius:

“Augustine: This is what you say—the proposition that was brought against your heresiarch Pelagius in the episcopal judgment at Palestine: that Adam was made in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died. For you do not wish to admit that this death, by which we all die, concerning which it is said, ‘From a woman sin had its beginning, and because of it we die’ (Eccli. XXV, 33), passed originally from sin into all, lest you be compelled to confess that sin also passed originally into all. You perceive how unjust it is that punishment should have passed over without merit. Nevertheless, what you are trying to overthrow is so thoroughly Catholic that the one against whom this was brought, unless he had condemned it, would certainly have left that judgment condemned.

“Therefore both this death, by which the spirit is separated from the body, and that which is called the second death, by which spirit and body will be tormented, passed, so far as the merit of the human race is concerned, into all human beings. But the grace of God, through him who came to remove the kingdom of death by dying, by that resurrection whose example preceded in him, does not allow death to reign. This is held by the Catholic faith; this is held by the judges whom Pelagius feared; this is not held by the heretics whom Pelagius sowed . . . And if you have forgotten the heavy yoke that weighs down those being born, we nevertheless do not cease reminding you . . . In vain you try to twist straightforward words and obscure what is clear: all sinned in the one in whom all die. That one is Adam; and if infants do not die in him, they will certainly not be made alive in Christ. But because, just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ (I Cor. XV, 22), those who wish to pervert these words are overthrown by them while the words themselves remain.” EDIT.]

[Col. 0145A] 1. In response to this: If this is judicial death [Baluz. omits *mors* (“death”)], by which Adam was punished, and if it is itself the death that passed and continues to pass to his descendants—not, as you say, to absolutely everyone, but only to imitators—what or what sort of death will that other death be, which separates soul from body? Here, pressed hard, you will say: “Natural, because Adam would have died whether he sinned or did not sin.” Behold a Christian pedigree! [Note: [Col. 0145C]

Mercator will later repeat this same point at greater length (Chapter 2, no. 6). He spoke ironically in the words we are explaining, in order to chastise the insolent boasting of the Pelagians. Although they were wholly engaged in persuading others of their new doctrine, they falsely claimed that they were transmitting nothing in teaching except what they had received from their ancestors; indeed, through intolerable slander, they did not blush to accuse the defenders of the Catholic faith of novelty.

Thus Pelagius (Book *On Nature and Grace*, chapters 61 and following) attributed his opinion concerning impeccability to Lactantius, Hilary, Ambrose, Chrysostom, Sixtus the false martyr, Jerome, and Augustine himself. Thus Coelestius (in the *Book of Faith* that he presented to the Apostolic See) boasted that he was offering for approval by the judgment of Zosimus the things he had received from the source of the prophets and apostles. Thus Julianus (Book I of the *Imperfect Work*, chapter 59) reproached Augustine for novelty: “This is not the faith”—the faith by which original sin is believed—“handed down and founded in antiquity, except in the councils of the wicked, inspired by the devil, brought forth by Manichaeus, celebrated by Marcion, Faustus, Adimantus, and all their followers, and now, to our profound grief, spewed forth by you in Italy.”]

Behold the ancient ecclesiastical tradition! But surely you see how, contradicting yourself [Baluz. has *contrariis* (“contradictory statements”)] in your own statements, you tear yourself to pieces like a viper, while with more clatter of words than with any declamations you expend your empty effort.

2. I should like to question you more closely about what sort of death you think this is, since you allow at least one of those deaths to pass to others. So tell me what the death is that, in your judgment, passes onward. Is it substance or nature, or is it something accidental to a thing? [Note: [Col. 0145D]

On this occasion it will not be out of place to say something about the author of the *Book of Definitions*, or *Reasonings*, to which Augustine replies in the book *On the Perfection of Justice*. At one time the holy Doctor doubted whether those reasonings were Coelestius’s or belonged to someone else from the same faction. At that time he indeed acknowledged that they were said to be Coelestius’s, and he did not think that what he had sufficiently perceived in another work was alien to Coelestius’s ability; nevertheless, he seemed inclined to attribute them rather to one of his followers than to Coelestius himself.

I am not particularly reluctant to adopt this latter opinion, but I add that I conjecture they were written by Julianus. He too was a follower of Coelestius, of the sort Augustine intended when he spoke of the author; he was also a friend of the Sicilians, among whom the book was circulating; and either Augustine did not know him, or rather he ought not to have named him because he had not yet openly revealed himself. He also constructed the reasoning in question in a manner not unlike the others contained in the book, and he was often accused by Mercator, and very frequently by Augustine, of enjoying the use of dialectical method in treating questions.

The author of the *Definitions* did use such a method, and used it with complete precision. First he proposes the question at issue—whether a human being can exist without sin; then, through sixteen reasonings, he establishes the affirmative side; afterward he confirms by testimonies from Scripture what he had established by reasoning; finally he responds to the objections of the Catholics and, as a kind of crown, sets before his opponents certain little questions which, as he says, are to be proposed to his own side.

Two considerations strengthen the conjecture. First, throughout all these sixteen reasonings, and indeed in the Scriptural testimonies appended to them, the single conclusion established is that a human being can exist without sin. But Mercator reports that this very definition of Pelagius was defended by Julianus in published books (chapter 6 of that work, no. 2): “According to the definition of your teacher Pelagius, which you have defended in so many books, by which you both determine that a human being can exist without sin and easily keep God’s commandments.”

Second, there is scarcely one among those sixteen reasonings that Augustine does not report as having been composed by Julianus, nor any Scriptural testimony of which Julianus had not made abusive use elsewhere. Moreover, the reasoning with which Mercator is now concerned is the fourth in the *Book of Definitions*, with only this difference: here it is presented at greater length, whereas there it is stated more briefly. It runs as follows (*On the Perfection of Justice*, reasoning 4): “It must be asked what sin is: an act or a thing. If it is a thing, it must have an author; and if it is said to have an author, someone other than God will already seem to be introduced as the author of some thing. But if it is impious to say this, it must be acknowledged that every sin is an act, not a thing. If it is an act—or rather, because it truly is an act—it can be avoided.” The fourteenth reasoning is also related: “It must be asked: if human nature is good—which no one except Marcion or Manichaeus will dare deny—how is it good if it is not possible for it to avoid evil? For who doubts that every sin is evil?”

Notice here that Marcion is joined with Manichaeus, as Julianus commonly does. This is clear both from the preceding note and from another passage in which the heretic addresses Augustine as follows (*Imperfect Work*, Book III, chapter 53): “Who are you, who, driven on by the heat of Marcion, rush into the destruction of equity? You who, under the censorship of your tongue, still slippery with the mysteries of the Manichaeans, constrain both the judgments and the commandments of God?” And so forth. This is also a significant confirmation of the conjecture.] 

We remember that, at the time when I was present in the city of Rome, you were discussing this among some of the simpler people in the presence of the leaders of your utterly mad error. [Note: [Col. 0146D] *Gerberonius*: “with the associates.” GALLAND.] You used to ask them: “What is sin—is it something evil or something good?” “Evil,” they would of course answer you. To this you would add: “Is God the author and maker of this evil?” “Far be it, far be it!” they would exclaim to you [Baluz. *exclamatur*, “is exclaimed”]; “far, far be this madness from us!” Even the most impious Manichaeus did not dare profess this. Although he neither believes nor professes that God is the author of evil, he most wickedly demands that evil have its own beginning from eternity, its own essence, and its own nature. You then immediately declared that it must be asked “whether sin is substance, or nature, or something accidental.” When Christian simplicity hesitated somewhat at this, you proceeded in the following manner: “Sin can in no way be substance or nature; for if it were so [Note: Gallandius, following Baluzius, prints *si* (“if”) in place of *sic* (“thus”), and notes that Gerberonius has: ‘because, if it has a nature.’ EDIT.],” you said, “it would have God as its maker and author, since there is no nature that God did not create. But since it has already been established that God is not the author of evil [Note: Baluzius directs that *Deum* (“God”) be corrected in the errata; Gallandius adopts his correction. EDIT.], sin is therefore neither substance nor nature, and it has been made perfectly clear that it is evil. Since, you say, it is not substance, it is to be believed by no right or reasoning that it can pass from substance into substance, or from nature into nature—that is, into the human being.” And you concluded: “Therefore it is wrongly and foolishly believed that sin is transmitted from Adam.”

3. Therefore, as I said above, allow me to question you by this same route and along the same lines of argument, so that you may teach us by answering. This death, at least the death that belongs to the soul and is eternal, which the transgressing Adam received and transmitted to his descendants, and which you define as passing only to however many imitators—not to absolutely all human beings generally, as the Apostle says, but to a very few imitators—for you make no mention of that other death which separates the soul from the body: is this death some substance or nature, or a certain thing accidental to substance?

If you still have any light within you, you will answer and say that it happened to the substance of nature and cannot be called substance, since it was given as punishment first to the transgressor and afterward to the human race. “No prudent person,” you will say, “would call punishment substance or nature.” At this point, however, you will immediately be caught in your own snares. It has been clearly established that in no way can that judicial death, which, because it is punitive [Baluz. adds *quae* (“which”)], is no substance, and which you transmit at least to Adam’s imitators among his descendants, pass from substance into substance, or from nature into nature [Baluz. has *vel natura, quod* (“or from nature, which”)], that is, into the human being.

[Col. 0148B] 4. Do you see, [Note: [Col. 0147C]

The Author not unjustly returns to Julianus what Julianus himself had previously imposed upon the Catholics with the greatest injustice (*Against Julianus*, Book I, chapter 7), in these words: “Since it is therefore perfectly and clearly evident that this is the sound and true opinion, which reason first fortified and afterward the authority of Scripture, and which the learning of holy men has always celebrated—men who nevertheless did not confer authority upon the truth by their own agreement, but received testimony and glory from their association with it—let no one prudent be disturbed by the conspiracy of the ruined.”

Saint Augustine immediately testified how grievously he had endured that disgraceful statement. He says: “Observe into whose assembly I have introduced you. Here is Ambrose of Milan, whom your teacher Pelagius praised with such great commendation that he said the Roman faith shone especially in his books, and that among Latin writers he appeared as a kind of splendid flower, so that not even an enemy would dare criticize his faith or his most pure understanding of Scripture. Here also is John of Constantinople, whom you placed among the learned and saints as pre-eminent in this very discussion of yours to which I am replying. Here is Basil, whose words—not relevant to the matter now at hand—you thought would somehow help you. Here also are the others, whose great agreement ought to move you. This is not, as you write with your slanderous pen, a conspiracy of the ruined. In the Catholic Church they shone through their zeal for sound doctrine; armed and girded with spiritual weapons, they waged vigorous wars against heretics; having faithfully completed the labor of their stewardship, they fell asleep in the bosom of peace.”

And afterward: “Will you call such great agreement among Catholic priests a conspiracy of the ruined? O words worthy of a teacher of the Church! O lesson useful for all ages!”]

—you distinguished teacher of the ruined and dialectical disputant—do you see where you have fallen? Do you now at least perceive how far you have strayed from the path of truth? But for the moment, if you retain any old shame [Baluz. has *ullus* (“any”)], let these things suffice for you. If God grants the means of life and gives me time to review these very fine books of yours and reread [Baluz. omits *ad* (“to”)] that very wise letter of yours, then, when God wills, we shall answer you again. [Note: [Col. 0148C] Either the author to whom he promised the labor did not undertake it, or the completed work has not come down to us. By “very fine” books he means ironically the last eight books against the second book of Augustine’s *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. Likewise, he calls “very wise” the letter which, although it had been written to the supreme pontiff, did not reach him before it had been circulated throughout Italy by trustworthy men and by men who captured people’s minds.] In the meantime I shall bring forward [Baluz. has *proferamus* (“we shall bring forward”)] other statements of yours, which we avoid with profound abhorrence.

## CHAPTER VIII  
Also from the third book of the four books published to Turbantius, near the beginning of the third chapter: Julianus’s words. [Note: [Col. 0148C] What Marius reports, Augustine quotes in exactly the same words in Book III of the earlier work, chapter 3. Therefore one of two things must be admitted: either Marius extracted what he reported not from Julianus’s books but from Augustine’s, or Augustine replied to the whole of Julianus’s work in such a way that he refuted book by book and chapter by chapter. The latter seems to me much more credible, partly because Marius reports passages found in Augustine with only slight alterations, not otherwise than an author ordinarily binds together passages in a more extended discourse; partly because Augustine suggests this unmistakably when he says (*Imperfect Work*, Book I, chapter 2): “Against those four books of yours I have written six books.” After recalling the Catholic doctors, which I explained in two volumes, I assigned the following four books to your four individual books.]

[Col. 0148C] [Note: [Col. 0148D] Baluzius has *Quia gratiam* (“because grace”). EDIT.]

“We say that the grace of baptism is not to be changed according to circumstances, because it dispenses its gifts according to the capacity of those who approach it; and therefore Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0148D]

When Catholics were severely accusing the Pelagians of denying that Christ was the Redeemer of infants, and when that accusation, as was proper, strongly disturbed the minds of the faithful, fraudulent men, in order to remove this odium from themselves, did not shrink from using the word “redeemer.” Indeed, they confessed that infants are baptized for the remission of sins. Nevertheless, lest they appear to have abandoned their position, they denied that this confession implied that infants who were baptized were infected with original sin.

After Pelagius had said (*On Original Sin*, chapter 18) that neither he nor any impious heretic had ever said what he had proposed concerning infants, he added: “For who is so ignorant of evangelical teaching that he would not only try to affirm this, but could even lightly say or think it? Who is so impious as to wish infants to be excluded from the kingdom of heaven, while he thinks that they are baptized and reborn in Christ?” Then, after inserting a testimony from the Gospel that no one can enter the kingdom of heaven unless he has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he says (*ibid.*, chapters 19–20): “Who is so impious as to forbid a child of any age the common redemption of the human race, and to prevent him who was born for uncertainty from being reborn into perpetual and certain life?”

Coelestius (*in the confession presented at Rome*): “We confess that infants ought to be baptized for the remission of sins, according to the rule of the universal Church and according to the teaching of the Gospel, because the Lord established that the kingdom of heaven cannot be granted except to the baptized. Since infants do not possess the powers of nature for this, it must necessarily be granted through the generosity of grace. We do not say that infants are to be baptized for the remission of sins in order to appear to confirm sin as transmitted by descent, which is very far from Catholic understanding; for sin is not born together with a human being, although afterward it is practiced by the human being, because it is shown to belong not to nature but to the will. It is therefore fitting to confess the former, lest we seem to make different kinds of baptism; and it is necessary to guard against the latter, lest, under cover of the sacrament, evil should be said to be transmitted by nature to a human being before it is committed by that human being, to the injury of the Creator.”

Julianus (*Imperfect Work*, Book I, chapter 51): “I am not unaware that, when we say these things, it must be disseminated about us that we do not think the grace of Christ the Lord necessary for infants. This greatly and deservedly offends Christian peoples, if they do not regard us as the authors of statements intrinsically wicked. For in that way they would neither incur the crime of believing false things about their brethren nor prove themselves zealous in their love of the faith. Therefore this part of our position must be fortified against the assault of vanity, and by a brief confession we must speak to those who whisper error.

“We therefore acknowledge the grace of baptism to be useful to every age to such an extent that we strike with eternal anathema all who think it unnecessary even for infants. But we believe this grace to be rich in spiritual gifts: abundant in many benefits and venerable in virtues, it heals according to the varieties of infirmities and the differences among human conditions, being at once the giver of remedies and the source of gifts. When it is applied, it is not to be changed according to circumstances. For it already distributes its gifts according to the capacity of those who approach it. Just as all the arts, according to the diversity of the materials they receive for cultivation, themselves undergo either diminution or increase, although remaining always the same and consistent in one form and being adorned by manifold effects, so also, according to the Apostle, the one faith and one baptism are multiplied and expanded in their gifts, yet are not changed in the order of the mysteries.

“But this grace is not opposed to justice, which washes away the stains of iniquity; it does not create sins but cleanses them; it acquits the guilty and does not accuse the innocent. For Christ, who is the Redeemer of his own work, continually increases his benefits toward his image through his generosity; and those whom he made good by creating, he makes better by renewing and adopting them. Therefore whoever thinks that this grace, through which pardon is given to guilty mortals, ought to be denied to some, deserves the hatred of all good people.

“Christ, who is the Redeemer of his own work, continually increases his benefits toward his image, and those whom he had made good by creating, he makes better by renewing and adopting them.” [Note: [Col. 0150B] Augustine’s response, as reported by Garnerius:

“Augustine: Is this the whole reason why you do not think that an accusation ought to be brought against you concerning the baptism of infants—as though any one of us had said that you deny that infants ought to be baptized? You do not say that they ought not to be baptized; but, in accordance with the greatness of your wisdom, you utter marvelous statements: ‘They are baptized in the sacrament of the Savior, but they are not saved; they are redeemed, but they are not liberated; they are washed, but they are not cleansed; they are exorcized and exsufflated, but they are not rescued from the power of the devil.’ These are the monstrosities of your opinions, these the unexpected mysteries of your new doctrines, these the paradoxes of the Pelagian heretics, more marvelous than the Stoic philosophers.”

“For you fear hearing the following if you make such statements: If they are saved, what was sick in them? If they are liberated, what was held in them by the bond of slavery? If they are cleansed, what uncleanness was hidden in them? If they are rescued, for what reason were they under the power of the devil, since they were not guilty through their own iniquity—unless they possess what you deny, original sin?

“And you deny this not in order to assert that they are saved, free, and clean, subject to no enemy—for your false testimony before the true Judge does not help them in any way—but so that, while they remain in an evil antiquity, you may pursue a new vanity. For the true opinion is not yours but that of the one who said: ‘Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God’ (John III, 6).

“But you, excellent lovers of that life which is to be eternal with Christ, think it no punishment for the image of God to be excluded forever from the kingdom of God. Yet if you said that this was a small punishment, these would not be the words of a blessed lover of that kingdom but of a wretched despiser. If, however, you admit that it is at least a small punishment—which is in fact a great one—that the image of God is not permitted to enter the kingdom of God, I beg you to open whatever eyes you have and see by what justice this punishment is to be inflicted on a child whom, with your eyes closed, you deny to be liable to original sin.

“I omit mentioning the evils that nearly all infants suffer in this very transitory life and how the statement is to be explained: ‘A heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all’ (Exod. IV). Such evils would certainly not be inflicted by the just and omnipotent God upon his image—evils in which infancy cannot be said to be exercised in virtue—if no evil merits were drawn from parents.

“You entirely pass over these evils of infants—not those that you deny them to have, but those that all of us see them enduring—and you pay no attention to them. There, most eloquent man, you roam beyond the bounds and exercise your ingenuity and your tongue in praising nature. This nature, fallen into such great and evident miseries, needs Christ as Savior, Liberator, Cleans­er, and Redeemer—not Julianus, not Coelestius, not Pelagius as its praiser.

“You would not confess that this nature is redeemed in infants unless Coelestius, unable to endure the Christian voice, had confessed this in the ecclesiastical proceedings at Carthage. But I ask you: how can this redemption be understood unless it is redemption from evil by him who redeemed Israel from all his iniquities? For wherever redemption is mentioned, a price is understood as well. And what is this price except the precious blood of the spotless Lamb, Jesus Christ?

“Concerning this price, why should we ask anyone else, if it has been poured out? Let the Redeemer himself answer; let the merchant himself say: ‘This is my blood,’ he says, ‘which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins.’ Continue, continue, and say as you do: ‘They are baptized in the sacrament of the Savior, but they are not saved; they are redeemed, but they are not liberated; they are washed, but they are not cleansed; they are exorcized and exsufflated, but they are not rescued from the power of the devil.’ Say also: ‘Blood is poured out for them for the remission of sins, but they are not cleansed by the remission of any sin.’ What you say is marvelous, what you say is new, what you say is false. We are astonished at the marvelous, we guard against the new, and we refute the false.” EDIT.]

[Col. 0150A] 1. First I should like you to teach and prove where the captivity of infants came from—infants whom you admit to be God’s work but deny to be guilty—so that they should need a redeemer. No one offers the price of redemption for a free person without cause.  From what old condition, moreover, are these infants to be renewed—or, as you prefer, innovated—if they are, as you say, the image of God, yet have not been disfigured by the ancient foulness of their forefather Adam?

2. But I shall press you more closely concerning the baptism of infants, so as to prove to you that, according to your own definitions, you really think they have no need of it, and that you merely say that they ought to be baptized in words, in order to deceive the simple, while in fact you deny it through the propositions of your disputations. For if, according to you, their condition at birth is immaculate, from what are they to be cleansed when they are washed? And since, as you maintain, they are born liable to no guilt of origin [Baluz. has *rebus* (“things”) for *reatu* (“guilt”)], from what are they to be liberated, so that Christ may truly and properly be Jesus for them as well—for “Jesus” is rendered in Latin as “Savior”? And since they carry no defect of their generation, from what are they to be regenerated?

3. Finally, leaving aside innumerable other considerations, this must be said against you. If infants at birth have received, as you say, the condition of innocence and purity that Adam possessed before sin; if no stain of that same forefather has touched them and no contagion has defiled them; if, as they grow [Baluz. has *ut credens* (“as believing”)], with the free choice of the will that remains in nature until the final end of life, they never fall away from the innate or congenital goods belonging to them, then why was the baptism of Christ necessary for them?

[Col. 0152A] 4. [Note: [Col. 0151D] This was the escape-route of Pelagian wickedness. Men of bad faith distinguished eternal life from the kingdom of heaven, saying that infants ought to be baptized in order to attain the kingdom of heaven, but not likewise in order to possess eternal life, which they would possess even if they died without baptism. For, they said, when Christ imposed the law of baptism, he mentioned not eternal life but the kingdom of God. He said: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 3).

“To refute this sophistry of the false teachers, the holy Fathers brought forward Christ’s words imposing the command to eat his body and drink his blood, where he mentions life: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves’ (John VI, 54). They showed that this command could be fulfilled neither except by the baptized nor by adults alone. Thus they concluded that no one can possess eternal life without baptism, as Mercator is about to say.

“Someone might wonder why, in a matter so easy, the issue was once treated with such labor, since the whole dispute could have been settled from Matthew, chapter XXV, where Christ treats the kingdom of heaven and eternal life as the same thing. For after he had said in verse 34 to those who would be at his right hand, ‘Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,’ and in verse 41 to those at his left, ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels,’ at the end, gathering together both statements, he says: ‘And these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.’]

Or perhaps you will say that it is for the sake of the kingdom of heaven and adoption as sons? [Note: [Col. 0152D] The order of the words seems disturbed here. The words “this condition of preserved nature,” as they stand, yield no tolerable sense; but they will produce a suitable sense if restored in this way: “For why would such a condition of preserved nature, and such holiness of life subsequently acquired through their own acts, not admit them into that kingdom or adopt them as sons?”]

Why would such a condition, and such holiness of life subsequently acquired through their own acts, of preserved nature not admit them into that kingdom or adopt them as sons? [Baluz. adds *vel*, “or.”] But let them hear, as though from some gatekeeper and ever-watchful bishop, these words as they rush forward: “Unless someone has been born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 6). [Baluz. adds *item*, “likewise.”]

5. But [Baluz. *Et*, “And”] let us examine baptism itself: what its power is, and how many and how great are its powers and causes of effects. The Apostle Paul says of it: “He who redeemed us saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal” (Tit. III, 5). Therefore it is salvation, redemption, and renewal. Will there then be no punishment for unbaptized infants—not to have salvation, redemption, or renewal; finally, not to enter the kingdom of heaven (John III, 6); not to be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God’s love (Col. I, 13); not to eat the Lord’s flesh and drink his blood (John VI, 54)? Concerning this sacrament the Savior’s voice says: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI, 54). Certainly, without any evasion, no one claims this without baptism, nor does anyone become a participant in that sacrament.

6. [Note: [Col. 0152D] Augustine treated the same argument (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 20): “Let doubt now be removed; let us hear the Lord, not the suspicions and conjectures of mortals. Let us hear the Lord—not, indeed, saying this about the sacrament of washing, but about the sacrament of his holy table, to which no one properly approaches unless baptized: ‘Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves,’ and so forth” (John VI, 54).]

Do you order us, as you usually do, even here to evade the issue by saying that this statement about taking the Lord’s flesh and blood is not general but particular, addressed, that is, only to those who were physically present and to whom he was then speaking? Let Christians hear this—let them hear it if you rush forward with such an argument—and let them reply to you that, by this method, you declare the Lord’s Supper, at which, with the apostles alone, he solemnly declared [Note: Baluzius has *contitus* and Gallandius *constitus*; Gallandius notes the passage is corrupt and, with Gerberonius, reads *contestatus* (“having solemnly declared”). EDIT.] the sacraments concerning his own body and blood to be observed.  [Note: [Col. 0153C] Baluzius has *contitus*; Gallandius has *constitus*, adding: “Baluzius passes over this corrupt passage. Read with Gerberonius: *contestatus*.” EDIT.] Do you pronounce that the command belonged to those men alone and did not extend to anyone else—either to someone who was not present at that supper then or to all of us, their descendants?

Do you see by what snares and in what straits you are being strangled when you deny that the bond of origin—concerning which Christ has absolved the entire human race and every age only through these sacraments, in which the washing of regeneration and renewal comes first—is a great evil, a great punishment, and an unavoidable condemnation?

### 7.

When these points are brought together against such great and manifestly impious audacity of yours, it is clear that you, as a follower of Caelestius—who defined that “infants, even those not baptized, possess eternal life”—deny that infants ought to be baptized; but, as I have already said, merely play with words, while in reality you openly hold impiety with pagans and Jews.

[Note: “Merely play with words.” Gerberonius printed *tantum verbis includere*, “to enclose [it] only in words”; Galland reports the advised, grammatically awkward reading *tantam verbis includere*, “to enclose so great [a matter] in words.” The supplied note gives no explicit noun for *tantam*.]

[Note: Mercator makes Caelestius the author of the wicked doctrine that infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life (*On the Proceedings of Palestine*, ch. 11). Pelagius, indeed, openly denied at Diospolis (*On Original Sin*, ch. 12) that he had ever said this; rather, to satisfy the synod, he added that he anathematized those who held or had ever held such views. Nevertheless, Augustine demonstrates that there was no difference in this respect between Pelagius and Caelestius, except that the former was more outspoken and the latter more covert; the former more obstinate and the latter more deceitful; or certainly, the former more open and the latter more crafty. For Pelagius was unwilling to condemn in the Church of Carthage what he later confessed that he held at Rome, declaring himself ready to be corrected if error had crept upon him as a man; Caelestius, however, condemned that doctrine as contrary to the truth lest he himself be condemned by the Catholic judges, while later reserving it for defense—either condemning it deceitfully or interpreting it artfully.]

### 8.

[Note: Mercator lists twenty-two names by which Christ’s beneficence toward humankind is signified: giver of life, savior, illuminator, redeemer, liberator, mediator, propitiator, physician, reconciler, circumciser, merciful one or compassionate one, testator, comforter, advocate, adopter, regenerator, justifier, transferer from darkness to the kingdom, cleanser or expiator, eraser of the bond, life, refresher or restorer. He explains each from Scriptural testimonies. The passage is especially noteworthy: scarcely another Father treats the subject more fully, since Mercator gathers here what others usually give separately.]

To prove this more clearly than daylight, listen to the names by which, together with their proper causes, Christ’s benefits toward the human race are signified, and from which you make infants strangers, declaring that the Lord Christ Jesus himself owes them none of these things and has bestowed none of them upon them.

[Note: Namely, you exclude them from this consideration: that infants have no need of Christ’s baptism. Marius proves this by arguments whose force no one can evade except one who either diminishes the authority of all Sacred Scripture, as the pagans do, or rejects the Gospel and the apostolic writings, as the Jews do. He derives these arguments from the names by which Christ’s benevolence toward human beings is signified, but in such a way that it is evident that these names do not apply to infants if they do not need Christ’s baptism, by which they are cleansed from the stain of sin.]

### 9.

Christ is, whether you wish it or not, the giver of life. I shall ask: of the soul and of the body? Although unwillingly, you will admit this. I shall repeat the question: of every age without exception? You will answer: of every age. I shall press you more closely: and of infants? You will say: even of them.

[Note: Garnerius has in the margin: “Of a little child.” EDIT.]

But listen; I shall tell you in what manner—and, so to speak, by what method—he gives life.

“God,” says his herald and chosen instrument, the apostle Paul, “who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us in Christ, by whose grace we have been saved” (Eph. 2:4).

What do you think now? He has included and named infants among them. Are they outside this mercy and love because they are not dead in sins, and do they await you, that most worthless gatekeeper, to admit them to mercy for the giving of life only when he has ceased to show mercy to sinners, so that he may give them life in some manner different from others?

### 10.

[Apparatus: The text has *De Salvatore* (“Concerning the Savior”); Baluzius reads *quod de Salvatore* (“that concerning the Savior”). He also reads *ad* for *apud* (“to” for “with/before”) Zacchaeus; omits *tu* (“you”) after *hinc*; and omits *nostris* (“our”) from “for our sins.”]

But, for the sake of brevity, let us pass from this to another title: he is the Savior. Concerning the Savior, it is written in the Gospel: “Today a Savior has been born for you in the city of David” (Luke 2:11). Hence also, in the Greek expression, *Jesus* properly means “salvation”; and to Zacchaeus: “Today salvation has come to this house, since he too is a son of Abraham” (Luke 19:9). Again: “The Son of Man has come to seek and to save what was lost” (ibid., 10).

[Note: Garnerius has in the margin: “Correct, you say.” EDIT.]

Since you undoubtedly declare that the flocks of infants have not been lost, they are neither saved nor sought. Listen to this, then: concerning the lost sheep, sought and found, he says the same; and likewise concerning the *dragma* or bundle that had been lost (Luke 15).

[Note: Mercator reads Greek *drágma* (δράγμα), not, as in the common manuscripts, *dragmēn* (δραγμήν), and accordingly translates it as “bundle,” although he suspected that something deeper and more recondite might perhaps lie hidden here, because in certain small coins of former times a sheaf of grain or a bundle was represented. I recall having read this at some point in ancient writers on monetary matters. Yet this conjecture may be subtler than it is true.]

Again the apostle Paul says: “The saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (1 Tim. 1:15).
