Therefore, you excellent teacher, drive away the crowds of infants, so that those who are not lost may not run to him who came to save what was lost (Luke 19:9); who did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance (Luke 5:32); who baptizes for the remission of sins (Acts 2:38); who seeks the sheep that has gone astray (Luke 15:4); who seeks the drachma—that is, the bundle—that had been lost (ibid., 8); who died for sinners (1 Cor. 5:3); who poured out his blood for the remission of sins (Eph. 1:7); who was handed over for the sins of human beings (Rom. 4:25); who was wounded because of our iniquities (Isa. 53:5); who bore our sins in his body upon the wood (1 Pet. 2:24); who, like a sheep for slaughter, was offered for our sins (Isa. 53:7); who erased the bond of debts (Col. 2:14); who, according to the apostle Peter, suffered, the just for the unjust, so that he might bring us to God (1 Pet. 3:18); whose blood, according to the evangelist John, cleanses us from every offense (1 John 1:7); who, while we were still weak, died for the ungodly at the appointed time, as the apostle Paul says (Rom. 5:6); who, in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh because of sin, as the same Paul testifies (Rom. 8:3); who reconciled us to God the Father from a state of offense, as the same Apostle says again (Rom. 4:10); who gave himself for our sins, and one died for all, so that he might rescue us from the present evil age (Gal. 1:4).

And what end will there be if we list here everything from which this excellent teacher drives away an innumerable multitude of infants?

### 11.

That he illuminates us, the apostle John says as follows: “But if we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from every offense” (1 John 1:7).

I ask: with what ears and with what countenance do you hear that we are cleansed from every offense by the blood of Jesus, the Son of God, when you keep infants—whom, as you say, have no offense—from this most holy blood?

### 12.

That he is the Redeemer, listen: “Giving thanks,” says the Apostle, “to God the Father, who has made us fit to share in the lot of the saints in light, who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption, the remission of sins” (Col. 1:13).

Do you think that, weighed down by so deep a sleep, you will awaken and hear what he says, and recognize with what shame you spoke of infants: “Christ, who is the redeemer of his own work”? For this great herald says that those have been redeemed and are being redeemed who have been drawn, or are being drawn, out of the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of the love of God’s Son, and that the gift of redemption cannot be obtained except with the remission of sins.

Listen still, whether you wish to or not, and unwillingly: “He gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from every iniquity and purify for himself a people zealous for good works” (Tit. 2:14).

Therefore drive infants away from here, since they are not redeemed from the iniquity that they do not possess, nor cleansed, since, as you say, they have nothing from which they need to be cleansed in order to be joined to God’s people, zealous for good works. And if we pursue everything in this chapter concerning redemption, when shall we finish showing the abyss of your utterly empty impiety?

I therefore think it more suitable, in order to avoid prolixity, to heap together as many names as we can for the Savior’s benefits and to append brief and scattered testimonies of Scripture concerning a few of them—benefits from which your impiety attempts to exclude infants—so that it may be evident to everyone what kind of person you are, how harmful you are, and how hostile to sound and correct faith.

### 13.

That Christ is the liberator, the mediator, and the propitiator: tell me the reason for his mediation on behalf of an infant whom you deny has any cause of offense. You would also have to explain the access to propitiation for one whom you determine to have no fault for which God might grant forgiveness and propitiation.

[Note: Garnerius has in the margin: “Correct to read, ‘whose [fault] has been forgiven.’” EDIT.]

[Col. 0156B]

### 14.

That he is the physician, who is necessary only for those who are ill (Mark 2:17).

### 15.

[Apparatus: Baluzius adds *post paululum* (“a little later”) before the third Pauline citation.]

That he is the reconciler, listen to Paul saying: “For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life” (Rom. 5:10).

Again, the same Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their offenses against them” (2 Cor. 5:19). And again he himself: “Not only this, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation” (Rom. 5:11).

With what countenance do you refuse to have infants belong to this reconciliation?

### 16.

That he is the circumciser—you will hear this in what follows. For the moment, give this infant the foreskin whose existence you deny to him, so that he may be circumcised.

### 17.

[Apparatus: Baluzius reads *dilectis* (“beloved [ones]”) for *delictis* (“offenses”).]

That he is the shepherd, but he receives no sheep into his fold without first circumcising it. He certainly circumcises this one, which is dead in offenses and in the foreskin of its flesh, and he came to the lost sheep (Col. 2:15; Matt. 15:24).

### 18.

That he is merciful and compassionate, listen to the apostle Paul: “We too,” he says, “were children of wrath, like the rest. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ” (Eph. 2:4).

### 19.

[Apparatus: Baluzius reads *qui quos vel* (“who, whom, or”) for *quis quos et* (“who [adopts], whom, and”), and *ne* (“lest”) for *ut* (“so that”) in Peter’s citation.]

That he is the testator, the comforter, the advocate, the adopter or adoptive father. Who adopts whom, and what sort of people he adopts—for you have become altogether too deaf—let Catholic Christians hear the apostle Peter saying:

“But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for adoption, so that you may proclaim the mighty works of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Pet. 2:9).

### 20.

[Apparatus: The text has *prima origine* (“first origin”); Baluzius reads *generatione* (“generation”). Its difficult question reads *aliis, qui bene se habent, et, ut tibi placet, in generatione*—literally, “for others, who are well, and, as pleases you, in generation”—rather than supplying a familiar formulation. Baluzius reads *alicui* (“to someone”) for *aliis* (“to others”) and omits *in* (“in”). The accompanying note reports *aliqui bene* (“some [are] well”) and, with Gerberonius, *alioqui bene se habente* (“otherwise, if he is well”).]

That he is the regenerator, but he regenerates no one except one who contracted a defect in his first origin [or: generation]. What need is there of regeneration for others who are well and, as you maintain, are in a generation that furnishes a just ground for regeneration? Or what is there in them that ought to be amended or corrected, unless perhaps something is corrupt?

[Note: Baluzius prints *aliqui bene* (“some are well”), but notes that, with Gerberonius, it is better to read *alioqui bene se habente* (“otherwise, if he is well”), as in the present translation. EDIT.]

### 21.

That he is the justifier or one who justifies, listen to the apostle Paul: “As truth is in Jesus: put off, according to your former manner of life, the old human being, who is corrupted according to the desires of error. Be renewed in the understanding [*sensum*; Baluzius: *sensu*, ‘in the understanding’] of your mind, and put on the new one [*eum*; Baluzius: *hominem*, ‘human being’], who was created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. 4:23).

What will those whom you declare to have been clothed in no old age do if they listen to you? They will not approach the renewer; they will not put him on, having laid aside their old condition, so that they may be renewed in the spirit of their mind.

### 22.

[Apparatus: The text has *sortis sanctae* (“of the holy lot”); Baluzius reads *sortis sanctorum* (“of the lot of the saints”). Later Baluzius reads *et* (“and”) for *sed* (“but”).]

That those who have been baptized are transferred from darkness into the kingdom, listen to the apostle Paul:

“Giving thanks,” he says, “to God the Father, who has made us fit to share in the lot of the saints in light, who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption, the remission of sins” (Col. 1:13).

I ask: with what mouth—or rather, with what shamelessness—did these matters appear to you otherwise, lest you be crushed by the truth of so great a light and by the weight of Christian reasoning?

Therefore you will also separate infants from this passage, lest those who, according to you, are innocent and established in the light by the merit of their innocence appear to be drawn out of the power of darkness.

[Note: This entire section, up to the word “darkness,” had dropped out of Garnerius’s edition; we have restored it from Baluzius. EDIT.]

But, most senseless of mortals, they are transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God’s love neither otherwise nor earlier than after they have first been drawn out of the power of darkness, and unless they possess redemption—that is, the remission of sins.

And note here the word “redemption,” which you too will mention and concede, although I do not know what fabricated redemption you mean. But the Apostle says that redemption is nothing other, in the first place, than the remission of sins.

### 23.

That he is the cleanser or expiator, listen to John the Baptist: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

What, I ask, does this Lamb signify here except a sacrifice for sins? Certainly he is offered for his own—for those whose sins he expiates when he is offered—and he is offered daily in his sacraments, granting remission of past and present sins.

[Note: Notice here the testimony of a very ancient writer in support of the propitiatory sacrifice of the Mass for past and present sins. This truth was so universally acknowledged at that time that scarcely any writer of that age failed to mention it.]

### 24.

[Apparatus: Baluzius reads *idem* (“the same”) for *item* (“likewise”) before Paul’s citation.]

Do you therefore order infants, who are guilty of no sin, to say that this victim was of no benefit to them, although it is recognized as having been slain solely for sins or for sinners?

Rather, you must hear what the herald of this victim proclaims later in the Epistle: “The blood of Jesus, the Son of God, cleansed us from every offense” (1 John 1:7).

Paul likewise says: “He gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from every iniquity and purify for himself a people zealous for good works” (Tit. 1:24).

Where will you turn? Where will you flee in order to avoid these snares?

Do you see, most shameless man, that the blood of this victim is cleansing from sins and also redemption from every iniquity, by which he prepared for himself a people zealous for good works? Yet with an iron face and a heart of stone you separate infants from the people of God, who, having been expiated and redeemed, rejoice in so many and such great divine rewards.

### 25.

[Apparatus: Baluzius supplies *est* (“is”) in the heading, “that [Christ] is the eraser of the bond.”]

That he is the eraser of the bond, listen to the apostle Paul:

“And you, when you were dead in offenses and in the foreskin of your flesh, he made alive with him, *dolens* (‘grieving’) the bond which was against you in decreed judgments, which was contrary to you; taking it from the midst, he fastened it to the cross; stripping himself of flesh, he led the principalities and powers publicly in triumph, triumphing over them in himself” (Col. 2:14).

What will you assert here, excellent teacher? Does he erase in baptism even the bond of infants? Or, since they have no bond—neither their own nor their father’s—do you not care to admit them to this grace of the giver?

Let Catholic Christians hear here what you think, and whom they ought to understand you to be; I leave the judgment to them.

### 26.

[Apparatus: In the opening quotation the source note says that the words through *ejus est* (“is in his Son”) had also dropped from Garnerius’s edition, as Baluzius observes. In the subsequent Gospel citation Baluzius reads *et* (“and”) for *aut* (“or”), adds *est* (“is”) after *leve* (“light”), and—following the Bellovacensis manuscript—reads *lene* (“mild”) where the text has *mitis* (“gentle”).]

That Christ is life, listen to the apostle John:

“And this is the testimony: God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son does not have life” (1 John 5:11), “but the judgment of God remains upon him” (John 3:36).

Come now, rash man: permit an infant to possess this life without baptism. You have become stuck here, I believe, and, by remaining stuck in the same mud, you are paying one debt with another.

[Note: That is, you increase the interest; you add evil to evil. BALUZ.]

If, therefore, without this sacrament he does not possess life, the judgment of God remains upon him. How is this so? I do not ask; let the intelligence of the readers understand.

### 26.

That the Lord refreshes and restores, in the Gospel:

“Come to me, all you who labor or are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:28).

[Note: Here and shortly below, Baluzius has *gentle* or *mild*, following the Bellovacensis manuscript. EDIT.]

Will there be any doubt here that no one should hasten to that preacher except one who is worn out by labor under some burden, so that, once it has been laid down, he may take his gentle and humble-hearted master’s light yoke upon himself?

And what else is this burden except, as we have said, the burden of sins? Since, as you delight in asserting, infants have no such burden, they should not listen to this preacher—whom the Greeks call the *Ecclesiastes*—nor concern themselves with taking up his gentle and light yoke, because they have no burden to lay down.

Is it not sacrilegious for Christians to hear such things? And is it not a severe punishment that you still suffer such chatter through the negligence of priests?

# CHAPTER IX. Reconsideration of the Question of Death’s Entry into the World through Sin

[Col. 0159A]

### 1.

You have, I believe, something that touches and goads you; but if you are stirred up again, I know that, by God’s gift, you will be bound still more tightly so that you may not be stirred up any further.

[Col. 0160A]

### 2.

[Apparatus: The text has *qua enodata* (“when which has been unraveled”); Baluzius reads *quae enodata* (“when these things have been unraveled”).]

Nevertheless, for the sake of necessary consideration, let us return to what was said above, examining more closely what you think about the punishment that the transgression of our foreparents deserved by divine judgment; and, by bringing you back to this question, I shall once again expose your abyss.

[Note: *Teneam.* This is the reading of the Bellovacensis manuscript. Garnerius printed *veniam*; Gerberonius, *te ducam*. What if we read *tendam*? BALUZ.]

When this has been unraveled, and when the authority of the divine Scriptures has pressed upon your throat, you will know that you have supplied arms to the pagans and Jews in all your books,

[Col. 0161A]

[Note: This same charge Mercator had previously leveled against Julian (ch. 8, no. 6), in the sense that we explained. Among recent writers on Pelagian history there is one who attempted to distinguish four stages of Pelagianism, each succeeding the other so that that monstrosity, like the mythical Proteus, first assumed the form of paganism, then semipaganism, then Judaism, and finally semichristianism. In the first, he says, no mention at all was made of divine grace; in the second, mention was indeed made of it, but of a grace that did not differ from nature; in the third, the grace of doctrine and of the law was added to nature; in the fourth, true grace of God was admitted, but as a handmaid of free will, not its guide, as it ought to have been. This author holds that the first three stages preceded the condemnation of the heresy by Zosimus, and the fourth followed that condemnation; that the former were devised by Pelagius, the latter by Julian. He holds that the first existed at the very beginnings of Pelagianism, before the faithful resisted the error that was lifting its head; the second, when the heretics first attempted, under the opposition of the faithful, to disguise it with an empty appearance of words; the third, after the condemnation by Saint Innocent.

Yet just as nothing pleases those ingenious minds, admiring themselves, more than such fabrications, nothing flatters the proud more sweetly, and nothing more easily deceives those who love themselves, so nothing could have been said that is more futile or more contrary to history than this distinction.

[Col. 0159C]

To demonstrate this, I establish five points which, in my judgment, are fixed with certainty by their chronology.

First, that Pelagius wrote a letter to Paulinus in the year 405, and to Demetrias in 413; that he wrote commentaries on Paul’s Epistles in 403, or at least before the devastation of the City by the Goths, which occurred in 410; and that he wrote the book *On Nature* before 411 (*Dissertation on the First Authors, etc.*, ch. 4).

Second, that Caelestius was judged at Carthage by Aurelius in 412; Pelagius at Diospolis in December 415; both at Rome by Innocent in January 417; and both again at Rome by Zosimus around May 418 (*Dissertation on the Synods Convened in the Pelagian Affair*).

Third, that Augustine wrote nothing against the Pelagians before 412, but earlier dealt with them only in sermons and conversations, as occasion arose, without naming them; that at that time he delivered Sermon 13 on the words of the Apostle; and that he wrote to Hilary in 413 or 414 (*Dissertation on the Writings of the Defenders of the Faith, etc.*, ch. 2).

Fourth, that Caelestius presented to Aurelius at Carthage a short statement of his faith in 412 (Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ* and *On Original Sin*; Zosimus’s second letter to the Africans); that a similar statement was given to Zosimus at Rome in 417; that it consisted in almost the same words as the confession sent by Pelagius to Innocent and, after his death, delivered to Zosimus and scarcely short of being approved; that Augustine criticized nothing in either statement that concerned the Trinity or the Incarnation, but only what concerned original sin, which Caelestius openly denied, and grace, which Pelagius explained in ambiguous words; and that Caelestius was praised for confessing Christ as the redeemer of infants.

Fifth and finally, that the beginnings of the Pelagian heresy—if its stages must be distinguished—or rather its infancy, existed at Rome before Pelagius fled from there because of the approaching Goths (see the notes on the Commentary and on Mercator throughout); that its adolescence was in Sicily, where teacher and pupil remained for two years and more; that its mature age was partly in the East, partly in Africa and elsewhere, down to the times of the supreme pontiffs Innocent and Zosimus; and that its remaining period began when Julian undertook the defense of a desperate cause.

With these points established, I ask first in what sense that author with whom we are now concerned wishes to define paganism, and semipaganism, Judaism, and semichristianism; whether according to what was handed down by the Fathers, or according to something fabricated at his own discretion.

If according to what was handed down by the Fathers, the distinction of four stages disappears. For the Fathers define paganism as ignorance both of the true God, who is the most holy Trinity, and of the Lord’s Incarnation, through which the mediator was sent; semipaganism as ignorance of Christ, who is substantially God-Man; Judaism partly as hatred of Christ, whom the Jews crucified, and partly as devotion to the Mosaic rites, which they ordered to be retained; and, finally, they confuse semichristianism with Judaism. Yet Augustine never accused the Pelagians of such an error against the Catholic faith, whether concerning the most holy Trinity, the Lord’s Incarnation, or the abrogation of the Mosaic rites.

But let those four stages be defined, even if no Father ever did so, by denial or confession of divine grace. I ask this man again what grace of God he wishes to be understood.

Does he mean that supreme grace which is eternal life in the kingdom of God? The Pelagians confessed this from their earliest beginnings.

Or the singular grace by which Christ the redeemer was given to humanity? They confessed that too, even before the devastation of the City.

Or the grace by which the baptized are adopted as children of God? Pelagius himself confessed this long before he departed from Rome.

Or the grace by which we are helped to act piously through the revelation of truth? Pelagius mentions divine illumination before 404, when he wrote to Saint Paulinus.

Or the grace by which the will is moved by the Holy Spirit and prepared by the Lord to act holily? I admit that the Pelagians were unwilling to confess the necessity of such grace, but maintained that, if it were ever given, it was given by God either on account of merits or merely to make action easier and more ready.

But again I ask the adversary: on whose authority, and at what initial time, does he think the Pelagians held this view of grace?

“Julian,” he says, “devised this opinion after the condemnation by Zosimus,” that is, in 418. But on what grounds and with what confidence does he say this, when Augustine records that Caelestius wrote that God’s grace is given according to our merits—not merely that this was objected to Pelagius at Diospolis, but that the same charge had been brought against Caelestius when he was first accused at Carthage by the deacon Paulinus—and when the Diospolitan synod and the condemnation by Zosimus were preceded by more than two years, and the Carthaginian judgment by five full years?

Moreover, Augustine, in Sermon 13 *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapters 1, 11, and 12, argued against the Pelagians without naming them before 412, when he first began to write against them by name, because they said that, with the grace of God, what could be accomplished without grace—though with greater difficulty—could be accomplished more easily. Yet at that time no judgment of Aurelius, Innocent, or Zosimus had preceded it, and there was no mention of Julian.

[Col. 0161B]

I would also gladly ask the inventor of these stages what he thinks the Pelagians—who define the assistance of grace as illumination of the mind—have in common with the Jews, who proclaim the law of Moses and the divinely prescribed ceremonies.

Does he confuse the Gospel, which is the doctrine of Christ, with the Mosaic law? Does he suppose that the Jews believed they were justified and acted holily by the external law alone? Or has he finally convinced himself that the Pelagians understood Mosaic law by the word “law”?

The first is impiety; the second, ignorance; the last, ἀνιστορισία—lack of historical knowledge. All of it is incredible negligence in handling Augustine’s works. EDIT.]

as weapons—but truly weapons of lead; for they could have no power to overthrow faith in Christ.

### 3.

[Apparatus: Baluzius reads *Et* (“and”) for *Sed* (“but”), and *iterum iterumque* (“again and again”) for *iterum* (“again”). Later he reads *arbitratur* (“he judges”) for *arbitratus* (“having judged”), and *intentasque* (“and [being] intent,” a feminine/plural inflection) for *intensusque* (“and [being] intent,” masculine singular).]

But let us examine again what these things are, and of what kind, in which—tell me, please—this man’s error is an inexplicable labyrinth. What are these unsolvable problems of the Theban monster?

[Note: Since Julian, in ambiguous words and with a superficially Catholic appearance, concealed a heretical meaning and attempted to deceive not only the simpler among Catholics but even the apostolic see itself, Mercator aptly compares him with the Sphinx, that monstrous beast which, according to the fables, posed riddles to the unwary people at Thebes and harshly punished those whom it deceived. See again what was said in the notes on ch. 6, no. 9 and following.]

In your letter, which, as we have mentioned, was sent to Pope Zosimus of holy memory, you disapprove and condemn anyone who thinks that Adam was made mortal, and that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died. You say that this too is unsupported by reason: “For I believe,” you say, “that he was indeed made immortal, but that, if he had not sinned by tasting of the tree of life, he could have attained the power of immortality.”

You add that the person who contradicts the Apostle’s preaching must rightly be rejected, when he says: “As in Adam all die, so in Christ all shall be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22). Immediately you add this other testimony: “Through one man came death, and through one man the resurrection of the dead” (ibid.).

When a simple Christian hears this, believing that no deception or fraudulent argument is being introduced, he regards it as excellent and as his own teacher, in the manner in which the Church is accustomed to be instructed by the apostles, and eagerly hastens to hear the rest of that same Apostle’s discussion which you pursue in this matter.

[Note: Both manuscripts have the text in this form, though scarcely with any plausible meaning. It may be corrected as follows: “Believing that no deception or fraud is being introduced, in the manner in which the Church is accustomed to be instructed by the apostles, he regards him as excellent and as his own teacher and, intent on hearing the rest of that same Apostle’s discussion in this matter, hastens onward.”]

A similar passage is found in the letter of the five bishops to Innocent. At its beginning, concerning Pelagius’s use of the name “grace” in a sense different from that customary in the Church, and concerning the bishops at Diospolis, who understood his words according to the Church’s custom, it says as follows (Letter 177 in Augustine):

“In the East, where he resides, ecclesiastical proceedings are said to have taken place by which he is thought to have been cleared. If the bishops there pronounced him Catholic, we must believe that this happened for no other reason than that he said he confessed the grace of God and declared that a person could live justly by his own labor and will, while not denying that God’s grace assists him in this. On hearing these words, the Catholic bishops could understand no other grace of Christ than that which they were accustomed to read in God’s books and preach to God’s peoples.

“They understood the grace of which the Apostle said: ‘I do not nullify the grace of God; for if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing’ (Gal. 2:21)—without doubt, the grace by which we are justified from iniquity and saved from weakness, not the grace by which we were created with our own will. For if those bishops had understood him to mean the grace that we possess even with the impious, with whom we are human beings, while denying the grace by which we are Christians and children of God, who could have patiently listened to him—not merely as a Catholic priest, but as anyone at all—or tolerated him before their eyes?

“Therefore the judges are not to be blamed, because they heard the word ‘grace’ according to ecclesiastical custom, not knowing what such men habitually scatter either in the books of their doctrine or in the ears of their followers.”

But you, having one thing hidden in your heart and another ready on your tongue, a new and excellent disputant, now introduce this into your work, composed after so long a time in Cilicia.

[Note: These words are Julian’s own: “Because you earnestly demanded it—indeed, commanded it by the authority of your fatherland” (he is addressing the Pelagian bishop of Florence), “that I should oppose the book of the African writer which Alipius, that household servant of his sins, recently brought to Count Valerius, my response has consequently become longer” (*Unfinished Work*, book 1, ch. 6).]

[Note: From this we also learn that Julian’s final work against Saint Augustine was composed in the presence of Theodore of Mopsuestia, the author of the Caelestian heresy. Mercator teaches this in several places, especially in the prologue to the *Annotations*. See the notes on that same passage.]

### 4.

[Apparatus: Baluzius omits the second *in* (“against”) in *nec in sanctos, nec in innocentes* (“neither against saints nor against any innocents”). The final note reads *nostri* (“our”) for *noti* (“known”) in “wiser than the known world.”]

Therefore, by the necessary repetition of the chapter, let us examine again what new and unheard-of matter you have brought back from having traversed the sea and surveyed the East.

[Note: These matters were discussed in chapter 1 and are found in book 2, chapter 66, of the *Unfinished Work*.]

“You say, therefore, that according to the Apostle sin entered this world through one man, and death through sin, because the world saw that he was both guilty and destined for the condemnation of perpetual death.”

You add:

“But death alone passed to all human beings, because one form of judgment also encompassed all transgressors of the remaining ages. Yet this death is not permitted to rage against any saints or innocents; rather, you say, it spreads only among those whom it sees to have imitated the transgression. Although that transgression was not made natural, it was nevertheless a pattern of sin; and therefore, although it does not burden those who are born, it accuses those who imitate it. Judicial death, however, passes upon that in which all sinned, but by free will.”

These, then, are the more plausible and clearer expressions of the doctrine; but what has become of the definitions stated earlier?

[Note: This concerns the time when Julian wrote the letter to Zosimus mentioned in chapter 6, no. 9 and following. In that letter he expressed the contrary view, at least verbally: “Whoever asserts that the whole human race does not die through Adam’s death, nor does the whole human race rise through Christ’s resurrection, contradicts the Apostle, who says: ‘As in Adam all die, so in Christ all shall be made alive’” (1 Cor. 15:22).]

Is there some hidden and profound matter that perhaps must be explained to us by the Brahmans, the Gymnosophists, or the Hyperboreans, or by whatever other peoples there may be who are wiser than the known world?

[Note: Baluzius corrects the reading to *nostri*. EDIT.]

### 5

Let us then come to this more recently defined point: that it was held that sin entered through one human being, and death through sin; but that death alone passed into all human beings. I ask you not [Baluz.: “I do not wish you to”] to abuse the slowness or limited capacity of my mind. You say that two things entered, sin and death; but you maintain that death alone passed into human beings [Baluz.: “all”], though not into all human beings whatsoever. You are exceedingly foolish: for if sin entered and did not pass through, where did that which entered remain? I suppose that it is to wait for its companion [Note: [Col. 0163B] “Waiting for a companion.” In the Beauvais manuscript, *exspectandam sociam* (“a female companion is to be awaited”) was first written, but afterward corrected as we have restored it. Gerberon printed *exspectandum socium* (“a male companion is to be awaited”), thereby confirming our reading. Garner printed *exspectandum sociae*, which makes no sense. BALUZ.], until it goes out, and that this will happen once some business has been completed.

But if we are serious—and there is no laughing matter in so great a subject—then, by your own reasoning, if sin could enter, it passed through; whereas if it could not pass through, neither did it enter. Did it enter in order to stand still? And if it is absurd even to say this, it passed through; and where could it pass except into all human beings [Baluz.: “to have passed through”]? Moreover, you will never be able to explain how imitative sin, as you please, has passage, while original sin has none. These things cannot be read without laughter—indeed, without tears [Note: [Col. 0163C] Baluzius, following the Beauvais manuscript, reads “I cannot read.” EDIT.]—because you deserve to be mourned rather than laughed at by Christians. Let us therefore leave it to those who read you, if they are Christians and prudent persons, to decide what they ought to think of your emptiness.

For who, from your preceding proposition, could even suspect that you thought otherwise than all those who, with Pope Zosimus of blessed memory presiding, condemned Pelagius, Coelestius, and you concerning all those points about Adam which earlier had been rejected and condemned by you, and which now, as though gathered together and stored away, have deserved to be received into your faith?

[Note: [Col. 0163C] It is therefore evident from Mercator’s testimony that a council of bishops was held at Rome under the presidency of Zosimus, and that from it a letter was sent to all the bishops of the world containing the whole case and condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius. I have further observed—something I cannot pass over—that in the matter now under discussion no condemnation was issued either by the supreme pontiffs or by bishops of the greater sees, except in a synod of bishops (see the dissertation on synods convened in the Pelagian controversy).

From this understand that the Pelagians’ complaint concerning subscriptions extorted from simple bishops sitting in their own places, without an assembled synod, and Augustine’s reply at the same time (*To Boniface*, book IV, final chapter), concerning very many heresies condemned without an assembled synod, must be understood of either a plenary synod of one whole diocese, such as Africa or Egypt, or an ecumenical synod of the entire Christian world. That Augustine indicates this in many other places is certainly shown by *Against Julian*, book II, final chapter, where, after citing and explaining the opinions on the five questions, as they were then called, of Irenaeus of Lyons, Cyprian of Carthage, Reticius of Autun, Olympius the Spaniard, Hilary of Poitiers, Gregory Nazianzen, Basil of Caesarea, Ambrose of Milan, John of Constantinople, Pope Innocent, and Jerome the presbyter of Stridon, he says: “As though you, who complain most of all that examination and episcopal judgment are denied you, could find a council of Peripatetics,” etc. These bishops are learned, weighty, holy, and most vigorous defenders of truth against chattering vanities; in their reason, standing, and freedom—the three goods which you attributed to a judge—you can find nothing to despise. If an episcopal synod were assembled from the whole world, it would be remarkable if so many such persons could easily sit there: for these men did not live at one time, but God himself distributes his few stewards, faithful and superior to many others, through different ages, distances of time and place, as pleases him and as he judges expedient. Thus you see these men, gathered from diverse times and regions, from East and West, not into a place to which people must sail, but into a book which can sail to people, etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0164C] This passage might suggest that Julian was expressly condemned by Zosimus along with the other two heretics, were the contrary not evident from the *Libellus of Faith*, the letter to Rufus of Thessalonica, and almost innumerable passages in the works of both Julian and Augustine. For in these writings the former, conscious of his condemnation, and the latter, knowing and certain of its public character, speak very differently. He is therefore called condemned either because he in fact held the same views as those condemned, or because, lying under suspicion of heresy, he was compelled to condemn in writing what the Apostolic See had proscribed and to declare his mind on these matters. When [Col. 0164D] he failed to do this and obstinately showed himself opposed to the Catholic faith, he was afterward deprived of office.]

[Note: This passage could give rise to the suspicion that Julian was explicitly condemned by Zosimus along with the other two heretics, unless the contrary were evident from the libellus of faith, the letter to Rufus of Thessalonica, and almost innumerable passages in the works both of Julian and of Augustine. In those writings, the former, conscious of his condemnation, and the latter, fully aware and certain of its public character, speak in a very different manner. He is therefore said to have been condemned either because in fact he held the same opinion as those who were condemned, or because, being under suspicion of heresy, he was compelled to condemn in writing what the Apostolic See had proscribed and to declare his mind concerning these matters. When he failed to do so and obstinately showed himself opposed to the Catholic faith, he was later deprived of office.]

### 6

Next, concerning this question—namely, death—let us see what the universal Church (which in Greek we call *catholic*) says and believes, and what she teaches her children: by what death she knows Adam and Eve to have been punished after their transgression. Was it that death which separates the soul from the body, which we know and see to be common to the entire human race from that time onward? Or was it that which is said to affect the soul and is eternal, concerning which it is written: “The widow who lives in luxury is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:6); and again: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. 8:22); and whatever other passages can be brought forward for this interpretation?

[Note: Nestorius (*Sermon 2 Against the Pelagians*, part 2): “He who struggled with the author of mortality and redeemed life from both kinds of mortality—for a twofold mortality was advancing against us: one, which happened to mortal nature made subject to death through sin; the other, which comes through the rejection of knowledge. For ignorance of God bears the likeness of the insensibility that results from death—thus the devil became the author of both deaths. Christ, striking him down, lifted our life from both kinds of death: he raised the soul by life-giving commandments, and by the resurrection restored and renewed what is mortal. For when the one who had caused the fall has been cast down, that which he had caused to fall is raised up.”]

There is no doubt, then, that they were punished by both deaths, and that Christ brought a remedy for both. For since through the laver of regeneration and renewal he remits sins, and is to bestow immortality through the resurrection of the flesh—which we now possess in hope through faith—upon all at one and the same time, we must believe that the forefathers of the human race were condemned in no other way than by a twofold death, and that both deaths pass into their race.

### 7

But since this most learned teacher believes and attempts to teach that this bodily death was natural to them and is likewise natural to us, and that it has never passed through sin nor can pass through the generative seed, let us see, as I said, what the apostle Paul meanwhile believed and proclaimed concerning it.

For when writing to the Corinthians about the resurrection of the body, to which this death—that is, the dissolution of the body or the separation of the soul from it—is opposed, he speaks at greater length as follows:

“Now I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel which I preached to you, which you also received, in which you are being saved; by what manner I preached it to you, if you hold fast to it—unless indeed you believed in vain. For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures” (1 Cor. 15:1–3).

[Note: Marius takes the opportunity to bring forward an argument against Julian from these words of the Apostle: “Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. 6:3), and so forth. Since the Apostle was addressing the Romans, many of whom had received the sacrament of baptism from infancy, and nevertheless said, “all of us who were baptized,” he included by such universal language even those who had been initiated through baptism before attaining the use of reason. Augustine uses the same testimony repeatedly and everywhere (*Against Julian*, book I, chapter 6; book VI, chapters 3 and 5; *Unfinished Work*, book II, chapters 135 and 222).]

Come, madman, declare—if you dare—that the death of Christ, who died for sins, does not apply to the little ones whom you defend as being without sins, or that they are not baptized into Christ’s death.

“And that he was buried,” he says, “and that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he was seen by Cephas, and afterward by the eleven. Then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once, of whom many remain to the present, while some have fallen asleep. Then he was seen by James, then by all the apostles. Last of all, as to one untimely born, he was seen also by me; for I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty; rather, I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me. Whether therefore it was I or they, so we preached, and so you believed. But if Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? If there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen. But if Christ has not risen, then our preaching is empty, and your faith also is empty. We are even found to be false witnesses of God, because we have testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise. For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised; but if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile, and you are still in your sins. Therefore those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are more pitiable than all people. But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep; for since death came through a human being, through a human being also comes the resurrection of the dead. And just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive, but each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ, who have believed in his coming; then the end, when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Cor. 15:4–26).

Again, shortly afterward, the same Apostle says:

“Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed. At the last trumpet—for the trumpet will sound—and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” [Baluz. adds: “But when this mortal body has put on immortality”]. “Then will be fulfilled the saying that is written: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your contention?’ (Hos. 13:14). The spur of the flesh is sin, and the power of sin is the law; but thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid., 51–57).

### 8

Have you heard, most insane man? Do you perceive—now at least—with singular shamelessness and rabid fury? “Through a human being came death,” he says. What death is this, tell us, which is proclaimed to have passed through a human being? Is it yours, or that which the Church knows has already been conquered by Christ’s resurrection and is to be conquered in us also at the end?

But, I warn you, lend your ear and hear what follows:

“For just as in Adam,” he says, “all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.”

Who has ever doubted that here the Apostle understood any vivification other than the resurrection of the flesh, which is to come for all human beings?

Do you therefore command that only a very few should rise, and that death should have been conquered—and at the end be conquered—only in those who imitated Adam in his transgression, into whom this death of yours (for it must always be called yours) was able to pass, and not in all human beings whatsoever who derive their origin from Adam and Eve, the first transgressors, from the mortality—not innate in them, but acquired through sin—that came from them?

And what is the point of this herald’s lengthy yet sound and salutary teaching of so many words on this subject, if you, a new spirit—may God avert it [Baluz. adds: “of error”]—are to be heard?

[Note: Augustine testifies that the Pelagians made this accusation against Catholics, as though they believed that all would rise in the same bodily glory because all died for the same reason.]

Nor will you have any opportunity to slander us, as though we said and believed that an equal resurrection—that is, one of identical merit—must be granted to all. For although all die by one death, their outcomes are different, as the Apostle’s evident statement teaches us: “Each in his own order.” And again: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed.”

### 9

Let the reader, I ask, repeat what I said immediately above against you, where I stated that our forefathers were punished by both deaths, and let him see what I meant concerning this point; then let him thrust into your throat that cornerstone of yours, which has been placed for you as an offense and a stone of stumbling.

### 10

Yet hear further what will provoke you to still greater madness against us and the Church of God:

“Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you. For the love of Christ,” he says, “constrains us, judging this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and rose again” (2 Cor. 5:13), “so that he might be Lord of both the living and the dead” (Rom. 14:9).

Be silent! No one has died, or is going to die, except through Adam—but only by way of punishment; no one will rise except through Christ, though one will rise to reign and another to undergo eternal punishments: “Each,” as Scripture says (1 Cor. 15:23), “in his own order.”

[Note: The words of this sentence have been disturbed and confused. They can be restored as follows: “Provided that, as we have often said, and as together with the Apostle we protest against you, no human being whatsoever, at any age at all, has died except in Adam, and no one who is to be restored to life in the flesh will be so except through Christ.”]

Provided, as we have often said, and as together with the Apostle we protest against you, that no human being whatsoever, at any age at all, has died except Adam, and that no one who is to return to life in the flesh will do so except Christ.

### 11

You should also remember that we hold, and regard as certain in our faith [Baluz.: “our faith … as begun”], what we have said above as best we could concerning the two deaths: one, which affects the soul, Christ did not possess—

[Note: Another calumny of the Pelagians: as though Catholics, in defending original sin, uttered some injurious blasphemy against Christ and said that he had been polluted by sin through the necessity of birth. See what was said both in the notes to the *Libellus of Faith* written by Julian and in the notes to the excerpts from Theodore.]

—we pray that no one should say or think this in utter madness, because he was not born as all other human beings are, from carnal pleasure; rather, a new generation, without lust, was present in him, from an immaculate virgin, both before and after childbirth.

[Note: In explaining why Christ was free from original sin, the ancient Fathers agree with Mercator, among them the author of the books of the *Hypognosticon*, book I. For all of them, Augustine alone may suffice (*Against Julian*, book V, chapter 15): “What are you struggling through such great arguments to reach the precipice of impiety, so that, because Christ was born from Mary—whose virgin flesh, like that of all others, had been propagated from Adam—Christ’s flesh should differ in nothing from sinful flesh, and the Apostle should be believed to have said without distinction that he was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh? (Or does the heretic maintain that there is no sinful flesh at all, or, if there is, that because Christ came from it, Christ’s flesh also came from it?) Rather, you insist that there be no sinful flesh, lest this also be true of Christ. What, then, is the likeness of sinful flesh if there is no sinful flesh? But you said that I had not understood this apostolic statement, and yet you did not explain it, so that under your instruction we might know how anything can be like something that does not exist. If it is madness to say this—and plainly Christ’s flesh is not sinful flesh but is like sinful flesh—what remains for us to understand except that, with this flesh excepted, all other human flesh is sinful? Hence it is clear that the concupiscence through which Christ did not wish to be conceived produced a propagation of evil in the human race. Although Mary’s body came from that race, it did not transmit that concupiscence into the body which was not conceived through it,” and so forth. A little later: “Christ’s flesh therefore drew mortality from the mortality of his mother’s body, because he found her body mortal. But he did not draw the contagion of original sin, because he did not find the concupiscence of intercourse. If he had received from his mother not even mortality, but only the substance of flesh, his flesh would not merely have failed to be sinful flesh; it could not even have been the likeness of sinful flesh.”]

Pay attention, reader. The other death, namely the separation of the soul from the body, he voluntarily accepted, although it was not owed to him. If he had not been killed by the crime of the Jews, it could have happened that, after reaching a long old age—since this had once been pleasing to him—he would voluntarily have accepted it, dying undeservedly for us—that is, for the debt which we contracted in Adam and for our own sins which we added.

Nevertheless, no Christian should doubt that all the prophecies concerning him, including his being handed over to the cross through the murderous fury of the Jews, had to be fulfilled.

### 12

Now go to perdition with this magnificence of your words, runaway! No one listens to you barking in your madness; no one follows you as you stray from the Church; no one agrees with such insanity.

Concerning mortality, which was given to the human race as a punishment for the transgression of our forefathers, which has passed into nature through the generative seed and will continue to pass into it until the end, when it will be said at the sound of that divine trumpet, “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your contention?” (Hos. 13:14)—concerning this mortality, together with the entire Church of God,

[Note: The teachers who preceded Julian and Coelestius, and who were regarded by the Church as occupying the place of parents and masters in matters of faith, taught with unanimous agreement that bodily death entered the world through Adam’s sin and passed into the human race together with guilt. Because of the inseparable connection between the question of the cause of death and that of the transmission of sin, the statement of Vincent of Lérins in the *Commonitorium* should be understood in this sense: “Who, before Coelestius, that prodigious disciple of Pelagius, denied that the whole human race was bound by the guilt of Adam’s transgression?”

It is worthwhile to set forth the tradition of the Fathers from the time of the apostles down to Julian, so that Theodore and his disciple Julian may be refuted.

The Apostle Paul: “Through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin, death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). And: “If Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of justification. But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (ibid., 8:11–12). And: “Since death came through a human being, through a human being also comes the resurrection of the dead. And just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:21–22).

Justin Martyr, speaking of Christ (*Dialogue with Trypho*): “Just as he did not endure birth or crucifixion because he needed them, but for the sake of the human race, which through Adam had fallen into death and the serpent’s deception,” and so forth.

Irenaeus (*Against Heresies*, book V, chapter 16, from Augustine’s version): “Just as the human race was bound to death, so let it be released by the Virgin, with the balance of virginal disobedience being set against virginal obedience. For even now, while the sin of the first-formed human being receives correction through the correction of the Firstborn, and the serpent’s cunning is conquered through the simplicity of the dove, we have been released from the bonds by which we were bound to death. Just as through the defeated human being our race descended into death, so again through the victorious human being let us ascend into life; and just as death gained the palm against us through a human being, so again let us gain the palm against death through a human being” (ibid., chapter 21).

Athanasius (*On the Incarnation of Christ*): “He who had to answer for Adam’s disobedience and, after judgment had been completed, had included a twofold punishment in his sentence, spoke thus concerning the earthly body: ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall return’ (Gen. 3:19); and thus, in accordance with the Lord’s decree, the body departs into the earth. But to the soul he said, ‘You shall surely die’ (ibid., 2:17). Hence the human being is torn into two parts and condemned to depart to two places,” and so forth.

Gregory Nazianzen (*Oration 42*): “After he had forgotten the commandment he had received and had been overcome by that bitter taste, through the envy of the devil and the assault of the woman—whom the devil both found more susceptible because of her weakness and employed because she was more suited to persuasion (O my weakness! For it is the weakness of my first parent)—he was expelled at once from the tree of life, from paradise, and from God himself because of sin; he put on coats of skin, namely, flesh that was thicker and mortal; he first recognized his shame and hid himself from God. Yet even here he gained something from death and the cutting off of sin, so that evil might not be immortal; thus punishment itself passed into mercy. For this is how I judge God to inflict punishments,” and so forth.

Gregory of Nyssa, *Against Eunomius* (oration 1): “The Lord came to seek and save what had perished. What had perished was not the body, but the whole human being composed of soul and body; or, to speak more accurately, the soul had perished before the body. For disobedience of choice, or of will, is not a sin of the body; choice belongs properly to the soul, from which every calamity of nature had its beginning, as God’s wholly truthful threat bears witness when it says that on the day they touched the forbidden fruit, death would immediately cleave to them.

Since the human being is a twofold composite, death appropriately performs in both parts the deprivation of the twofold life in the one who dies. The death of the body is the extinction of the instruments of the senses and dissolution into the kindred elements; but the soul that has sinned will itself die. Sin is alienation from God, who is the true and only life.

The first-formed human being therefore lived for many centuries after the transgression, but God did not lie when he said, ‘On the day you eat of it, you shall surely die’ (Gen. 2:17). For on the very day on which he became alienated and turned away from true life, the sentence of death against him was established and confirmed; afterward, as the years passed, bodily death overtook Adam.”

Epiphanius (*Against Heresies*, book II, heresy 64, number 24): “The body could have lived forever and become immortal if it had not been forbidden to taste of life.” And afterward: “Therefore God willed him to be mortal and condemned him to death. For those coats of skin signified this,” and so forth.

Chrysostom (*Homily 10 on Romans 5*): “How did death enter and gain dominion? Through the sin of one. What, then, does ‘in whom all sinned’ mean? When he fell, even those who had not eaten from the tree became mortal from that time onward,” and so forth. “When Adam sinned, his body also became mortal and subject to suffering,” and so forth (*Homily 12 on chapter 7*). “Together with death entered a multitude of passions. For when the body became mortal,” and so forth (*the following homily*).

Theophilus of Alexandria (*To Autolycus*, book II): “Let someone ask: Was the human being created mortal? Certainly not. What, then? Immortal? Not that either. For from the beginning of his creation he was made neither mortal nor immortal. If God had made him immortal from the beginning, he would have made him God; if he had formed him mortal from the beginning, God could plainly have seemed to be the author of human death. It is therefore evident that the human being was made by God neither mortal nor immortal, but, as we indicated above, in some way a participant in both: so that, by keeping God’s commandment, he might attain immortality and, receiving this reward, might at last himself become like God. But if he turned toward sin and became disobedient to God, he would become the author of his own death,” and so forth.

To these let Nestorius be added, although he was a disciple of Theodore, yet in this respect more reverent toward the tradition of the Church than his teacher: “The devil,” he says (*Sermon 2 Against the Pelagians*), “brought forward that deed of ownership [*chirographum*] which is contrary to nature, written as follows: ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall go’; and from this he pressed on, consuming the generations of human beings through death,” and so forth.

Such was the tradition of the Eastern Church, which ought to have instructed Theodore, Julian’s teacher; and such is that of the Latins, which refutes Julian’s shamelessness.

Tertullian, addressing the soul (*On the Testimony of the Soul*, chapter 3): “You pronounce Satan in every aversion, rejection, and detestation. We call him the angel of wickedness, the craftsman of every error, the corruptor of the whole world, through whom the human being, deceived from the beginning so as to transgress God’s commandment and therefore handed over to death, thereafter made the whole race infected from his own seed and the inheritor of his own condemnation.”

And elsewhere (*On the Soul*, chapter 50): “By the public judgment of the whole human race, we declare death to be owed to nature; this is what God’s voice stipulated, this is what everything that is born has pledged.”

Cyprian (*On the Good of Patience*), explaining the sentence pronounced by God upon Adam, guilty of violating the commandment: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which alone I had commanded you not to eat, cursed shall the earth be in all your works. In sorrow and groaning you shall eat from it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall produce for you, and you shall eat the plants of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken, for you are earth and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:17 ff.). “By the bond of this sentence we are all bound and constrained until, death having been removed, we depart from this world,” and so forth.

Hilary the deacon (*On Romans 7*): “How does sin dwell in the flesh, when it is not a substance but the transgression of what is good? Because the body of the first human being was corrupted through sin so that it could be dissolved; the corruption of sin itself remains in the body through the condition of the offense, retaining the force of the divine sentence pronounced upon Adam. This is the sign of the devil’s law, at whose prompting Adam sinned,” and so forth.

Ambrose (*On Paradise*, chapter 7): “Disobedience was the cause of death, and therefore the human being himself is the cause of his own death, since he does not have God as the author of his death.”]

we have sworn allegiance to this understanding of the divine Scriptures and to these words, together with our fathers, the illustrious teachers of the Church.

### 13

With due reverence and honor, of course, for Augustine, bishop of holy and blessed memory, who with his pastoral staff drove you away from the Church, expelled you, and crushed you, let the following also be known or observed by anyone who wishes: after reading your entire work, as I said above, I have scattered these remarks wherever seemed appropriate and have attached or applied them to certain chapters of your fragments [Baluzius prints *fragorum* and notes that this reading is consistently found in Mercator’s manuscripts.] in the manuscripts that I have read.

### 14

Nor should you mock the great brevity of this little work of ours, since you ought not to boast about your numerous books, which display more dreadful loquacity than anything worthy of consideration.

I do not want you to pretend ignorance in this matter. For you know that in the question at issue between us—namely, the mortality of the human race, which through the first transgressors of the divine command has passed generally through the generative seed, continues to pass, and will continue to pass until the end—your entire cause is consumed, as though it were tied to the strongest possible stake.

When a prudent and Christian reader perceives that this cause of yours—or rather, this cause in you—has been extinguished, he will recognize that absolutely nothing remains for you to mutter or to say further, whether on this same subject or elsewhere [Baluz.: “nothing further, or from which”]. And concerning your whole discourse, which you boast to be the height of eloquence, he will judge that the following saying applies to you more aptly and appropriately than to the person of whom it was spoken:

[Note: Marius portrays Julian through the words of Sallust, whose author Julian greatly admired and whom he loved to quote repeatedly in his books. Marius could have cited still more, had the limits of his discourse permitted, since all these characteristics suited him so well: “He was born of noble family, possessed great strength of mind and body, but had a wicked and depraved character; his spirit was bold, deceitful, changeable, a simulator and dissimulator of every matter; burning with desires, he had eloquence enough but little wisdom; his spirit was vast, and he always desired immoderate, incredible, excessively lofty things” (Sallust, *The Conspiracy of Catiline*).]

“Enough eloquence, too little wisdom. His vast spirit desired immoderate, incredible, excessively lofty things.”

But concerning your opinions, by which you are exalted in your wandering and vanity, a wise voice from another age will pronounce and apply to you this saying: “The mountains have labored, and a ridiculous mouse has been born.”

# THE TRANSLATIONS OF MARIUS MERCATOR OF VARIOUS SHORT WORKS WRITTEN IN GREEK IN THE CASE OF THE PELAGIANS

## I. THREE LETTERS OF NESTORIUS

### NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING THREE LETTERS

Two questions seem to me to require investigation concerning these three letters: first, whether they certainly have a known author; second, by which translator they were rendered into Latin.

No one can rightly doubt that all three were actually written by Nestorius, although no Greek text of any of them survives. For Coelestine, Cyril, Cassian, and Marius Mercator mention them, and their authority makes the matter certain.

Coelestine, in his letter to the clergy and people of Constantinople (*First Council of Ephesus*, chapter 19): “Nestorius, as though he had forgotten the reverence due to the virginal birth and to the divinity of Christ, our God and Savior, and the common salvation of all, makes impious pronouncements and persuades people to avoid them. The writings which he himself sent to us with his own signature have revealed this, as has the report of my holy brother and fellow bishop Cyril, sent to me through Possidonius the deacon.”

And to John of Antioch (ibid., chapter 20): “These matters reached us amid the grief of the faithful. They have been made public in the books which he himself had sent. And, what is stronger proof, these matters were communicated to us in letters bearing the author’s own signature, so that there can no longer be any doubt.”

And to Nestorius himself (ibid., chapter 18): “Some time ago we received your letters, to which we were unable to give any reply in the midst of our pressing circumstances. For they had to be translated into Latin; and although late, we are now doing so,” and so forth.

A little afterward: “Now, having considered both the complaint of the aforesaid brother against you and your letters, finally translated and containing manifest blasphemy.”

Cyril, speaking about Nestorius to John of Antioch (ibid., chapter 21): “I had advised him by letter to refrain from those wicked and perverse questions and to follow the faith of the Fathers. But, thinking that I had written these things out of hatred, he was so far from paying any attention at all to the one who, out of charity, had prescribed these things to his piety, that he hoped, by holding and expressing such opinions, he could also insinuate himself into Roman ears and forestall them . . .

“For in a lengthy letter, filling it with certain absurd doctrines, and sending it to my lord Coelestine, the most devout bishop of the Roman Church, he added among other things the following against those who disagree with him: ‘They call the sacred Virgin Mother of God without horror’ (*Epistle 1*, part 4). He also sent some quires of his expositions, and so forth.”

A little afterward: “When the letters were read in the council, especially those in which there could be no room for trickery—for they bear his signature.”

And to Juvenal (ibid., chapter 24): “Thinking that he could draw the Roman Church over to his opinion, he wrote to my lord Coelestine and inserted into these letters the perversity of his doctrines; he also sent many expositions,” and so forth.

Cassianus (*On the Incarnation*, Book I, chapter 3): “For this is the reason why, by his intercessions, he nurtures the complaints of the Pelagianists and supports their causes in his writings.” And elsewhere (Book II, chapter 2): “You say, then—whoever you are, heretic—that God was born from a virgin, yet deny that Mary, the mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, can be called Θεοτόκος (*Theotókos*), that is, ‘Mother of God,’ but say that she is Χριστοτόκος (*Christotókos*), that is, merely ‘Mother of Christ,’ not of God. ‘For no one,’ you say, ‘gives birth to one who existed before her’ (Epistle 1, part 5).” And again elsewhere (Book VII, chapter 7): “Your second perversion, or blasphemous calumny, or calumniating blasphemy, is this: you say, ‘The birth must be ὁμοούσιος (*homoousios*) with the one who gives birth,’ which is not different from the preceding statement. For it differs in wording more than in substance and kind; since, when the birth of God is under discussion, you say the same thing when you say, ‘a more powerful being could not have been born from Mary,’ as you said above (Epistle 1, part 4), ‘one existing earlier could not have been generated.’”

It is certain that the third epistle was translated into Latin by Marius Mercator. The question can concern only the first two: whether they had Cassianus as their translator, or Dionysius Exiguus, or someone else.

The case for Marius is supported by the great similarity of the Latin in these two epistles and in the third. It is also supported by the fact that the statement, “They make the divinity of the Only-Begotten die together with the flesh,” and so forth, occurs in the same words in Cyril’s letter to the clergy residing in Constantinople, which Marius translated. Finally, it is supported by the fact that the epistles use expressions otherwise familiar to Marius, such as *praedicatio*, *praedicatissimus*, and so forth.

The case for Cassianus, however, is supported by the fact that he read these same epistles as having been sent by Saint Leo, then archdeacon; and that he read them at the very time when Saint Celestine says that they were translated. It is likewise supported by the fact that he quotes fragments from them in words no different from those now read in the epistles.

Perhaps someone might attribute this translation to Dionysius Exiguus, relying, as it might seem, on the testimony both of Cassiodorus and of Dionysius himself. Cassiodorus wrote that the Council of Ephesus had been rendered into Latin by Dionysius; Dionysius himself suggests that Cyril’s orthodoxy and Nestorius’s impiety had remained unknown to Latin speakers down to his own time, and that for this reason he undertook to translate Cyril’s synodical letter.

But letters of this sort were rendered into Latin in the year 430, indeed in 429, since the supreme pontiff writes that they had been translated before his response to Nestorius’s letters, and complete sentences from them are read in Cassianus’s work, which was composed at this time. Dionysius, however, lived a full century later, for he was alive in the year 533. Moreover, Cassiodorus, like Isidore Mercator, understood by the expression “the Council of Ephesus” only Cyril’s synodical epistle with its twelve anathemas. Finally, since Dionysius flourished after even the Fifth Synod, at a time when the Ephesian material had long since been translated into Latin, he either slipped in his wording through carelessness when writing the foregoing, or he was referring to the Nestorian impiety that had revived in his own time.

Setting aside this opinion, I would readily incline to Cassianus’s side, were it not that the humility of diction found in these Latin epistles seems insufficiently compatible with the elevation and grandeur of style that shine forth in the seven books *On the Incarnation*, and also in those fragments that Cassianus translated into Latin from Nestorius’s sermons. Nor do the two statements brought forward on the opposite side adequately prove the point at issue, since they were translated literally from the Greek; and it is natural that the same things should be expressed in the same words by everyone.

Nor do I think that they were translated by Mercator, since at the time when they were translated he was staying in Constantinople, where he presented his *Commonitorium* to the emperor toward the end of the year 429.

It remains, then, that they should be said to have been rendered into Latin by some other unknown person. This nevertheless does not prevent their being cited here. Although the first two are not found in our manuscript codices, I judged that they should nonetheless be appended to the third because of their affinity of subject; that they should be published in a more corrected form than before, so that readers may understand them; and that they should be placed in the common volume of Nestorius’s works, in order to serve the convenience of certain scholars.

[Note: [Col. 0173] Baluzius omits these epistles. — Editor.]

[Note: [Col. 0173A]

Nestorius divided it into two parts: one concerning the cause of the Pelagian bishops, the other concerning his own. Celestine replied to both, but at greater length to the second, because it contained the very matter for which the entire epistle had been written; for Cyril clearly indicates that the cause of the Pelagians had merely provided the occasion.

Cyril called it lengthy when he wrote to John of Antioch, measuring it, I think, not so much by the number of words as by the magnitude of its subject, since in a brief summary it contains the whole venom of Nestorian impiety. He also sent with it to the supreme pontiff several booklets of his expositions, as though they were commentaries on the epistle. Finally, after these letters had been read at Rome, he added that, since the open subscription left no room for calumny, an explicit sentence had been pronounced against Nestorius by the holy Roman synod.

Cassianus therefore calls this very statement a “blasphemous calumny” or a “calumniating blasphemy,” because Nestorius at once levels a calumny against the Catholics, as though they held the same view of the Lord’s Incarnation as Apollinaris and Arius, and pours forth blasphemy against the most holy Virgin, whom he denies to be Θεοτόκος.

The time at which it was delivered can be inferred from the circumstances. When Nestorius sent it, he had already openly offered the faithful the poison of his doctrine in many sermons and, as he says, had endured many conflicts on that account. Indeed, by force or promises he had compelled many, both clergy and monks, to agree with him, and the report of what had taken place at Constantinople had spread widely throughout the world. These events could not have occurred before the end of the first year of his episcopate or the beginning of the following year, which was 429. The epistle was therefore sent around the Paschal season and delivered through Antiochus, an illustrious man, to Saint Celestine, together with the booklets of expositions.

Since it had hitherto appeared in an extremely corrupt form, it has been corrected—though perhaps not with complete precision, which may not have been possible because Greek manuscripts were lacking—by comparing the relevant passages of various authors, especially Cassianus. It has at least been corrected tolerably enough to be understood, something no one had previously accomplished.]

# FIRST EPISTLE OF NESTORIUS TO CELESTINE, POPE OF THE CITY OF ROME

[Col. 0173A]

## 1

[Note: [Col. 0174A] This passage was extremely corrupt in the common edition: “We owe one another fraternal conversations, so that, with concord prevailing among us, we may fight the devil, the enemy of peace.” Some attempted to correct it by placing in the margin: “With unanimity prevailing among us, we may attack,” and so forth. Our reading gives a much better sense: “We owe one another fraternal conversations,” that is, sincere reports concerning what is happening among each of us, “as though true concord according to the Scriptures” (Proverbs 18:19) “were prevailing among us”—that is, dominating, κρατούσης (*kratousēs*)—“so that we may fight against the devil, the enemy of peace.]

“We owe one another fraternal conversations, [Col. 0174A] so that, with true concord prevailing among us according to the Scriptures, we may fight against the devil, the enemy of peace. Why this preamble?”

A certain Julianus, [Col. 0175A] together with Florus, Orontius, and Fabius, claiming to be bishops of the Western regions, repeatedly approached both the most pious and most renowned emperor and lamented their cases, [Note: [Col. 0175C] This was the old complaint of almost all heretics, which Augustine both reports and refutes (Book I against Julianus).] as though, in orthodox times, they had suffered persecution at the hands of orthodox men. Repeatedly lamenting the same things among us, and repeatedly being rejected, they did not cease doing the same thing, but persist day after day, filling everyone’s ears with tearful voices.

[Note: [Col. 0175B]

These were bishops expelled from Italy because they refused to subscribe to the condemnation of Celestius and Pelagius, as Celestine, Marius Mercator, and the Fathers of Ephesus relate (Part II of the Council of Ephesus, Act 5). At first they numbered eighteen; in their name Julianus wrote an epistle to Rufus of Thessalonica and a book of faith to Pope Zosimus. Augustine refuted the epistle in three later books addressed to Boniface; we publish the book of faith.

Of these bishops, Turbantius returned to the Church. It is credible that certain others did likewise, if we accept the testimony of Possidius and Mercator. Among the Ephesian Fathers, besides the four mentioned above, Persidius and Marcellinus are named specifically (in the synodical epistle to Celestine).

It is sufficiently clear which Church Julianus governed; it is uncertain which Churches the others governed, except that either all or most of them were Sicilians. Julianus dedicated the first four books against Augustine to Turbantius and the later eight to Florus, just as Annianus dedicated to Orontius the homilies of Chrysostom on Matthew that he had translated into Latin.]

## 2

“We did indeed address them in the manner appropriate to them, since we did not know the true character of their case. But because we need a clearer knowledge of their grounds, so that our most pious and Christian emperor may not repeatedly suffer trouble from them, and so that we, ignorant of their causes, may not be divided in defending their case, [Note: [Col. 0175C] This passage is splendidly illuminated by Saint Celestine’s reply (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 18): ‘For a few days of our life,’ he says, ‘after the impious and repeatedly condemned doctrine of Pelagius and Celestius, the Catholic faith enjoyed peace, when East and West, united in a single judgment, struck them and the followers of their opinion with their weapons,’ and so forth. Near the end he says: ‘These heretics also, concerning whom you wished us to advise you, as though unaware of what had been done, were expelled from their sees by a just condemnation because they were making unjust statements. And afterward: Why are the actions then taken against them being investigated, when it is certain that the actions of Atticus, then the Catholic bishop, were sent from there to us?
