Why did Sisinnius, of holy memory, not investigate these matters? Clearly because, under his predecessor, he had approved that they had been justly condemned. Let the wretched men lament that they were deceived by the hope they placed in men, when, because of communion with them, only repentance could now help them. You are beginning to learn about them, if previously you knew nothing.’]

“be pleased to grant us knowledge of them, so that some people, through ignorance of the justice of the truth, may not be disturbed by misplaced compassion, or may not regard the canonical indignation of your Beatitude against them—which has perhaps been approved on account of their religious sects—as something else. For the novelty of sects deserves no defense from true shepherds.”

[Note: [Col. 0175D] From this we conclude (*On Synods*) that these men were condemned first by Zosimus, then by Boniface, and finally by Celestine. The last point is clearly demonstrated by the words of the synodical letter of the Fathers of Ephesus to Celestine (Part II, Act 5): “After the commentaries on the proceedings concerning the deposition of the impious Pelagians and Celestians had been read in the holy synod, and concerning what your Piety decreed and established regarding them,” and so forth.]

## 3

“Accordingly, since we too have discovered here among certain people no slight corruption of orthodoxy, [Note: [Col. 0176B] Nestorius certainly did not use restrained anger against the presbyters, monks, and laymen who opposed him, but savage fury, which Basil the archimandrite and other holy monks described almost in their own blood in their petition to Theodosius (Council of Ephesus, Part I, chapter 30). Many will perhaps not believe what we suffered at his hands. Indeed, in order to learn thoroughly whether the things we had heard about him were true or false, we went up to the episcopal palace at his command and invitation. Rejected once and again until another time, we finally saw him emerge and say, ‘Explain briefly what you want.’ But after he heard from us that what he had taught was not consistent with the true faith, he immediately ordered us to be arrested. We were then brought before the tribunal by a crowd of attendants beating us; there we were stripped like wicked criminals, and, naked and bound, we were shamefully thrown to the ground and beaten with rods, and kicked. Finally, in the church, we suffered such things unjustly at the hands of that unjust man—things that not even clergy, monks, or archimandrites, indeed not even men of the lowest rank, experience in a civil court. After being tormented there for a long time and wasting away from hunger, we were kept under guard for a considerable period. Nor did his fury rest content with this. Through some deception we were handed over to the city prefect, loaded with irons, and dragged to prison. Then we were brought out again, bound with chains as before, and presented at the praetorium. Since no one at all was present there to accuse us, we were again led by the attendants to the place of the accused; after being brought back there, we were again struck in the face by him. Finally, in a carefully composed speech, he deceitfully assented—as later became clear—to the statement that the natural Son of God had been born from holy Mary the Mother of God, adding that there was also another son. In this way at last he dismissed us.]

“we daily use both anger and gentleness toward the sick. For this is no minor disease, but one akin to the corruption of Apollinaris and Arius. They indiscriminately mix the union of the Lord in man into a kind of blending, to such a degree that certain clergy among us—some through ignorance, others through a heretical deception formerly concealed within them, such as occurred frequently even in the time of the apostles—are sick like heretics, and [Note: [Col. 0176D] This passage was extremely corrupt in the published manuscripts, and no sense could be extracted from it except with great labor. It read as follows, even in the learned edition of Labbe: “They openly blaspheme God the Word, ὁμοούσιον to the Father, as though he had taken the beginning of his origin from the virgin Χριστοτόκος, and, having been built together with his temple and buried together with the flesh, they say that he mixed the same flesh after the resurrection, but that it passed into the nature of the deity. In brief, they refer both the divinity of the Only-Begotten and the origin to the flesh joined to it, and they make it die together with the flesh; but they blaspheme that the flesh joined to the deity passed into the deity, in the very expression ‘deification.’”]

“openly blaspheme, saying that God the Word, ὁμοούσιος (*homoousios*) with the Father, as though he had received the beginning of his origin from the Virgin Χριστοτόκος (*Christotókos*), was built together with his temple and buried together with the flesh; and they say that the same flesh did not remain after the resurrection, but passed into the nature of the deity. In brief, they refer the divinity of the Only-Begotten to the origin of the flesh joined to it and make it die together with the flesh; but they blaspheme that the flesh joined to the deity passed into the deity,” [Col. 0177A]

[Note: [Col. 0177B]

This passage shows how truly Socrates wrote (Book VII, chapter 32) that Nestorius was extremely ignorant and that the cause of such ignorance was his neglect to study the writings of the ancients. For the Fathers never shrank from the word “deification” or similar expressions. To mention only those whom a presbyter of Antioch and a bishop of Constantinople could not have been permitted to ignore, the Fathers of the Council held at Antioch in 266, writing to Paul of Samosata, said:

“διόπερ καὶ τὸ ἐκ τῆς Παρθένου σῶμα, χωρῆσαν πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος σωματικῶς, τῇ θεότητι ἀτρέπτως ἥνωται καί τεθεοποίηται.”

“For this reason, the body from the Virgin, having received bodily the whole fullness of the divinity, has been united to the deity without alteration and has been deified.”

Gregory of Nazianzus (*Oration* 51, which is the first epistle to Cledonius):

“τὰ γὰρ ἀμφότερα ἐν τῇ συγκράσει, Θεοῦ μὲν ἐνανθρωπήσαντος, ἀνθρώπου δὲ θεωθέντος, ἢ ὅπως ἄν τις ὀνομάσειε.”

“For both are one in the commingling: God having become human and man having been deified, or however one might name it.”

The deacon Rusticus translated it thus: “For these two are one by commingling, God having become human and man having become divine, or whatever one may call it.”

The same Gregory (*Orations* 58 and 42):

“προελθὼν δὲ Θεὸς μετὰ τῆς προσλήψεως ἓν ἐκ δύο τῶν ἐναντίων, σαρκός καὶ πνεύματος, ὧν τὸ μὲν ἐθέωσε, τὸ δὲ ἐθεώθη.”

“God, proceeding together with that which he assumed, became one from two opposites, flesh and spirit, of which he deified the one, while the other was deified.”

And elsewhere (*In an Iambic Poem*):

“οὕτω τὸ θεῶσαν καὶ θεῶθεν εἷς Θεός.”

“Thus the deifying and the deified are one God.”

John Chrysostom (*Tome V, Homily 162*):

“ἀλλ’ αὐτοῦ πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἐλθόντος, καὶ ἡμῶν φύσιν ἀναλαβόντος, καὶ θεώσαντος τὸ πρόσλημμα, etc.”

“But when he himself had come to us, assumed our nature, and deified what he had assumed, etc.”]

“using that very word ‘deification,’ which is nothing other than corrupting both.”

## 4

[Note: [Col. 0177D] This passage too was corrupt: “But they have dared to call the Virgin Χριστοτόκος, while in a certain way calling her Θεοτόκος; for, when they call her Θεοτόκος, they do not shudder, although those holy Fathers, beyond all praise, are read to have said nothing more concerning the holy Virgin at Nicaea than that our Lord Jesus Christ was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.”]

“But certain people have dared to call the Virgin Χριστοτόκος (*Christotókos*); yet, when they call her Θεοτόκος (*Theotókos*), they do not shudder, although those holy Fathers, beyond all praise, are read to have said nothing more concerning the holy Virgin at Nicaea than that our Lord Jesus Christ was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. I say nothing of the Scriptures, which everywhere proclaimed the Virgin as the mother of Christ, not of God the Word, through both angels and apostles.”

[Note: [Col. 0177D] Cyril cites this passage of the epistle in his letter to John of Antioch, as stated above.]

## 5

“For this reason, I think that the preceding report has informed your Beatitude how many conflicts we have endured, especially since you should also note that we did not contend without reason, but that, by the grace of the Lord, many were corrected.” [Col. 0177B]

[Note: [Col. 0178B] This passage admitted no intelligible sense. What suitable meaning could be extracted from it? It read: “Many of those who were perverse, departing from us because they themselves and the birth ὁμοούσιος to the one who gives birth … which has been entrusted with life: that union in man is the union of the Lord’s humanity, joined together from the Virgin through the Spirit.” Cassianus helped to correct it when, referring to this epistle, he says (Book VI *On the Incarnation*, chapter 13, and Book VII, chapter 3): “But you use as a great proof of your faithlessness and impiety for denying and persecuting the Lord God the statement that ‘the birth must be ὁμοούσιος with the one who gives birth.’”]

“Many of those who were perverse, learning from us that the birth must be ὁμοούσιος (*homoousios*) with the one who gives birth, [Col. 0178A] because there is no blending of God the Word with man, but a union of the creature and of the Lord’s humanity, joined to God from the Virgin through the Spirit.”

## 6

“But if someone proposes the name Θεοτόκος (*Theotókos*) on account of the humanity born and joined to God the Word, and not on account of the woman who gave birth, we say that this term is not appropriate for her who gave birth. For a true mother must be of the same essence as that which is born from her. Nevertheless, the term can be tolerated on account of the consideration itself, and because this word is used of the Virgin only to indicate that the inseparable temple of God the Word came from her—not because she is the mother of God the Word; [Note: [Col. 0178C] Cassianus reports and refutes this statement in the following words (Book VII, chapter 2): “Thus, to destroy the faith in the sacred birth, a new serpent hisses in the Church of God: ‘No one gives birth to one who existed before her.’ First, then, I think that you do not know not only what you are saying, but also where you are saying it from. For if you knew or understood the source of your statement, you would certainly not assess the birth of the Only-Begotten God by the language of a mortal opinion, nor attempt to prejudice him who was born outside the conception of human origin by human definitions. See the rest through to the end of the chapter.”]

“for no one gives birth to one who existed before her.”

## 7

“These things, I think, have been indicated by the preceding report. We too, however, explain what happened and demonstrate by the facts that we wish to learn about the case of the men mentioned above with a brotherly disposition, not from an intrusive desire for curiosity, since we also relate our own affairs, as brothers to brothers, mutually making known to one another the novelty of the sects, so that the beginning of my letter may be entirely truthful. For when I began this letter I said that we owe one another fraternal conversations.

“I and those who are with me salute all the brotherhood that is with you in Christ.”

[Note: [Col. 0178D]

In this epistle, as in the first, Nestorius partly pleads the cause of the Pelagians before the supreme pontiff and partly his own. He complains that he had repeatedly sent letters about the matter but had received no reply. From this complaint, if it is true, one may conclude that Nestorius sent not merely the two epistles we possess, but more, because the Pelagians were importunately demanding it and pressing their own case with unremitting effort.

The time at which it was sent is easily determined from the circumstances. Several letters preceded this one, and the first of all was written in 429 around the Paschal season. This letter must therefore belong to the end of the same year. It could not have been delayed longer, since Mercator’s *Commonitorium*, presented in Constantinople when Theodosius and Florentius were consuls—that is, in 429—contains the entire case of Celestius, Pelagius, Julianus, and the other bishops. How could Nestorius have been unaware of the Pelagian case after the *Commonitorium* had been presented to Theodosius and published at Constantinople? Or why would he have sought information far from the city of Rome when he possessed there the matter confirmed by suitable documents?

From this one may also infer the reason why Mercator wrote the *Commonitorium*: namely, both to inform the emperor about the case of Julianus and Celestius, which Nestorius wished to conceal, and to demonstrate to everyone how he was lending assistance to a disastrous error hostile to the Catholic faith.

It was delivered by Valerius the chamberlain, just as the first was delivered by Antiochus, distinguished men of the court. Nestorius had won their support with money taken from the poor, while the Pelagians had corrupted them by their own devices. I infer that this Antiochus, whom Celestine calls an illustrious man, was the same man who in 430 held the prefecture of the praetorium and then the consulship with Bassus. I likewise infer that Valerius, who was chamberlain at the time he carried Nestorius’s letters, held the consulship with Actius in 432. The reason for these inferences is that, at this time, communications necessarily had to pass between Theodosius, residing at Constantinople, and Placidia, the mother of the scarcely ten-year-old Valentinian III, residing at Ravenna—not merely by letters but especially through illustrious men who knew the secrets of state and were experienced in public affairs, while the barbarians were miserably tearing the Roman Empire apart. The Franks and Goths were ravaging Gaul, the Visigoths Spain, and the Vandals Africa; the loyalty of Aetius, commander of both military forces, was uncertain; the defection of Count Boniface was open; and the intentions of many powerful men who were contemplating tyranny were suspect.

Nor should it seem surprising if such distinguished men lent their assistance to Nestorius by carrying letters, booklets of sermons, and the complaints of the Pelagians. That cunning heretic, before exposing his impiety openly, had corrupted the minds of the powerful and deceived them as though with the spell of a false sanctity, so that the power of those whose favor had given him the authority to teach together with his see might suppress the efforts of the holy men who opposed him. The court, as often happens, preferred to defend a known impiety rather than admit its own error in making the choice.]

# SECOND EPISTLE OF NESTORIUS TO POPE CELESTINE

## 1

“I have often written to your Beatitude concerning Julianus, [Col. 0179A] Orontius, and the others who usurp the episcopal dignity and make very frequent approaches to the most pious and most renowned emperor, cutting us down with their repeated lamentations, as though they had been cast out from the West in orthodox times. But up to now we have received no letter from your Veneration concerning them. If I had one, I could answer them and give a concise reply to their words.

[Note: [Col. 0180C] This is a noteworthy passage, since it can often serve as important evidence. For, as Mercator relates (*Subnotations*, chapter 6, no. 5), the spirit of all heresies, in every age and every place, is one and the same.]

“For now, from their uncertain statements, no one knows where to turn: some call them heretics and say that for this reason they were cast out from the Western regions; but they themselves swear that they have suffered calumny and endured danger because of their orthodox faith, through false accusation. We are gravely ignorant as to which of these claims is certain. For to sympathize with them if they are truly heretics is a crime; yet not to sympathize with them if they are suffering calumny is harsh and impious.”

## 2

“Therefore, may your soul, most loving of God, deign to instruct us, since until now we have been divided between these two impulses toward them, namely hatred and compassion. We wish to be taught what judgment we should hold concerning them. [Note: [Col. 0180C] The text of the common edition read *defecimus*, entirely incorrectly. In the margin of Labbe’s edition of the councils it was changed to *detinemus*, which is still not correct. The verb is *differimus*, which suits the passage and is approved by authorities of better Latin.]

“For day after day we defer action concerning these same men, waiting in hope and expectation of your Beatitude.”

## 3

“For, most venerable one, as you know, the investigation of a pious sect is not a trivial matter, nor is the testing of those who undertake it insignificant. Much labor is also being expended here by us as we strive to root out from the Church of God the utterly filthy impiety of the wicked doctrine of Apollinaris and Arius. [Col. 0180A]

[Note: [Col. 0180C] The text required correction, since the common edition scarcely yielded any sense: “For I do not know how certain people among the ecclesiastics, receiving some image of blending from the deity and humanity of the Only-Begotten, are sick with the sickness of the aforesaid heretics,” and so forth.]

“For I do not know how certain ecclesiastics, conceiving from the deity and humanity of the Only-Begotten a kind of image of blending, are afflicted with the disease of those heretics: they dare to pour the passions of the body over the deity of the Only-Begotten, they falsely claim that the immutability of the deity has passed into the nature of the body, and they confuse the two natures—which are worshiped in the one person of the Only-Begotten through a supreme and unconfused union—by the mutable blending of their natures.

[Note: [Col. 0180D] This passage must also be carefully noted and numbered among those cited in the notes to Nestorius’s second sermon. For it simultaneously displays the subtle and malicious mind of the man who conceals his error under the confused ambiguity of Catholic terms, as heretics commonly do; and it warns Catholic minds that the words of heretics must not be rashly trusted, but that their faith must be examined and tested against the definite formula of confession proposed by the Church.]

## 4

“Blind men, who neither remember the exposition of those holy Fathers nor see them openly crying out against this: ‘We believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.’ [Col. 0180B]

[Note: [Col. 0180D] This sentence in the common edition admitted no sense: “For this expression, in the name which signifies both natures, that is, Christ, is ὁμοούσιος with the deity of the Father. But the humanity was born at a later time from the holy Virgin, who, because of the union with the deity, is worshiped equally by angels and men.”]

“For this expression, ‘in the Lord,’ signifies both natures. For Christ is ὁμοούσιος (*homoousios*) with the deity of the Father; but the humanity, born later from the holy Virgin, is, because of its union with the deity, worshiped alike by angels and human beings.”

## 5

“Consider, then, what this man, who here is wearied by so many labors on account of the wickedness of the sects, must suffer again if he does not know the case of the men mentioned above and fears excessively that, through ignorance, he may introduce here some addition of the heretics. Therefore I ask that your holy soul be zealous in every way to grant knowledge concerning the men mentioned above, especially since the most faithful intermediary of the letters, [Col. 0181A] Valerius the chamberlain, can personally explain their troubles to your Beatitude.

[Note: [Col. 0181A] The title “chamberlain,” when used simply by reputable authors, means the superintendent of the sacred bedchamber, such as those whom the French call *les premiers gentilshommes de la chambre*. Before Theodosius, chamberlains had indeed ranked among the highest dignities, but below the urban and praetorian prefects, the masters of the cavalry, the counts of the consistory—that is, the counts of the sacred largesses and of private affairs—the quaestor, and the master of offices. They were later placed among the counts and made equal to the first three, in favor of Macrobius, as stated in the law issued at Constantinople by Theodosius to Florentius, Urban Prefect, on the eighth day before the Ides of November, under the consulship of Honorius XIII and Theodosius X, Augusti. This was the year 422.]

“I and those who are with me give the greatest greetings in Christ to all the brotherhood that is with you.”

[Note: [Col. 0181B] It is reasonable to believe that Nestorius wrote to Celestius not as to one of his friends, but as to the leader of the entire faction, which, since it had many bishops, could increase the number of Eastern bishops from whom John of Antioch would assemble a council in Nestorius’s favor. I infer that he wrote after Celestius had been expelled from Constantinople by imperial decree. He was expelled in 429, as we saw in the *Commonitorium*.]

# THIRD EPISTLE OF NESTORIUS TO CELESTIUS, IN REPLY

[Note: [Col. 0181C] It follows that Celestius must first have sent a letter to Nestorius indicating how grievously he resented his expulsion from the imperial city and, I think, complaining that Nestorius had until then deceived him and his companions with a vain hope of absolution; indeed, he must have demanded that a safe place of retreat be secured for him.]

“To the honorable and most religious presbyter Celestius, Nestorius sends greetings in the Lord.”

## 1

“Do not take it badly, venerable one, that you are suffering at the hands of those who ought to inflict the things that are inflicted, especially those who assert the truth and avoid communion with those who are defiled or who defile others. [Col. 0181C]

[Note: [Col. 0181C] These words are spoken in the manner of heretics, who commonly complain that they suffer from others the evils that they themselves inflict upon Catholics with the greatest wickedness (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 30). See, concerning this matter, the petition of Basil, Thalassius, and the other most holy monks to the emperor Theodosius. From it you will learn how savagely the raging heresiarch, abusing the power of courtiers and magistrates, acted against the Catholic servants of God.]

“For even the sufferings that existed before our time were pleasing to the saints; and those sufferings were temporal, but the truth was eternal. Thus John the Baptist, reproving Herod for his sin—indeed, reproving a man who was king—was condemned to death; but he did not fear, for he had Christ as his head, and that head could not be cut off. Thus Paul and Peter too were killed in this manner. And what more need be said? [Note: [Col. 0181D] Saint Celestine treats this passage splendidly near the middle of his epistle to the clergy of Constantinople, most of whom had been expelled from the Church and even thrown into prison because they had bravely defended the Catholic faith. [Col. 0182A–B]]

“Thus it has always been: piety advancing through various trials.

## 2

“Therefore, do not abandon the truth and betray it (since [Note: [Col. 0182B] This passage was doubtless obscure and compelled us, contrary to our usual practice, to insert certain words in order to make the meaning clear.)”

The reason for inserting these materials is readily apparent from the following. Celestine convened a synod at Rome in the West, from which the supreme pontiff sent letters to various bishops: to Nestorius, threatening deposition unless he revoked his errors within ten days; to Cyril, authorizing him to depose the obstinate man in due form; and others to John of Antioch and Juvenal of Jerusalem, by which they were informed about the entire matter. After receiving these letters, Cyril likewise convened a synod at Alexandria. From there he announced the judgment of the Apostolic See by letter both to John and Juvenal, and also to Nestorius—but to the other two bishops before writing to Nestorius. John therefore immediately thought that Nestorius ought to be warned, so that he might take precautions for himself and forestall Celestine’s sentence by a voluntary recantation. But Nestorius, in the proud spirit of one who rejects a friend’s warning, spurned the counsel. Thus, by “the council of the West” is meant the Roman council, presided over by Celestine; by “the Alexandrian” council, Cyril’s council together with him; and by “the writings,” Cyril’s letter to John and John’s letter to Nestorius. These matters will receive clarification partly from Celestine’s judgment and partly from John’s words.

“Understand clearly,” Celestine says, addressing Nestorius, “that this is our judgment: unless you proclaim concerning Christ our God what the Roman, Alexandrian, and entire Catholic Church believes—and what even the holy Church of Constantinople, down to your own time, has held most faithfully, in accordance with the faith expounded at the Council of Nicaea—and unless you renounce and condemn in an open written confession, within ten days counted from the first day on which this summons is made known to you, that impious novelty by which you strive to separate what venerable Scripture joins together, know that you have been cast out from communion with the universal Catholic Church and are wholly unfit for any of the functions of priestly authority.”

“Because our sins,” says John, “have opened a great door to ecclesiastical disturbances, I am therefore compelled to explain to your Charity what has most recently been written to me from Rome and Alexandria. For the Alexandrian clergy brought us, with great eagerness, various letters concerning your piety: some from the most devout bishop Celestine, and the rest from the most holy bishop Cyril. In sending copies of these, I earnestly ask your Charity to read them in such a way that no disturbance of mind may arise from them, since from such disturbance exceedingly harmful disputes and seditions frequently spring,” and so forth.

From these materials it is evident that Nestorius wrote to Celestine toward the end of October or the beginning of November 430. He wrote after receiving John’s letter and before receiving Celestine’s; he received Celestine’s letter through four bishops on 8 December. Nor could he have received John’s letter before the date mentioned, since John himself could not have received Celestine’s letter addressed to him—first carried to Alexandria by the deacon Possidonius and then sent from there to Antioch together with Cyril’s letter—until at least three or four months later.

[Col. 0183A] Letters sent to the bishops by the council of the West and by the Alexandrian council, together with many replies, made our judgment clear to us),

[Note: [Col. 0183A] That is, to the thoughtful or learned, in the customary idiom of authors of that period. Thus Saint Innocent used *imprudentes* to mean “the unlearned”: “These examples are then better presented when we are dealing with those who are known to be unlearned in such matters.”]

that is, to the thoughtful members of the same orthodox confession:

[Note: [Col. 0184A] By this name he calls the impiety that denies that the blessed Virgin is *Deipara*, Θεοτόκος, “Mother of God.”]

for perhaps, with the Lord cooperating, something useful may result for the Churches of the true faith.

[Col. 0184A]

[Note: [Col. 0184A] He calls the bishops and other supporters of Celestius “brothers”—those who were doing everything possible at Constantinople to defend themselves, with the support of the East, against the judgment of the West. Nestorius continues to deceive the wretched exile with some remaining hope.]

We greet the entire brotherhood.

And in another hand:

“May you be preserved safe and courageous, and pray earnestly for us; may you be granted to us, most religious brother.”

[Col. 0183]

## II. NESTORIUS

[Note: [Col. 0183C] Someone might suspect that these were the very treatises which Nestorius sent to Saint Celestine through Antiochus, together with at least two sermons on the Virgin’s childbirth, by which he proved his faith concerning original sin to the supreme pontiff. For it is attested not only by Cyril but also by Celestine that some such writings were sent. “Nestorius,” he says, “preaches and persuades others with abominable things concerning the Virgin birth, as is also revealed by his writings sent to us by him with his own subscription, and by the report of the holy father and fellow bishop Cyril, sent to me through his son, the deacon Possidonius. After reviewing all these materials, we found a great and to-be-avoided perversion in his impious preaching,” and so forth. (Letter to John of Antioch; letter to Juvenal of Jerusalem; letter to the clergy of Constantinople.) And writing to Nestorius: “We have read the contents of the letters and the books which we received when my illustrious son Antiochus delivered them. In these, after investigation, he was detected and apprehended by us,” and so forth. Near the end: “We have read how well you hold the doctrine of original sin; how you assert that nature itself is indebted, and that he who descends from the race of the debtor pays the debt deservedly,” and so forth.]

But this suspicion is not merely slight; it is also groundless. For the holy pontiff learned Nestorius’s view of original sin in fact from the second sermon, which begins: “The insults of the heretics indeed …” The words he used were taken from no. 15, where Nestorius speaks as follows: “So that just kindness may be shown, not gifts bestowed indiscriminately and arbitrarily without judgment, Christ therefore assumed the person of the indebted nature, and through it paid the debt as a son of Adam; for it was necessary that the one paying the debt should be descended from the race of him who had once contracted it,” and so forth.]

# TREATISE AGAINST THE HERESY OF PELAGIUS OR CELESTIUS

[Note: [Col. 0183B] This note is printed at the foot of column 183, but its callout letter, a, does not appear in the text.]

[Note: We shall speak more fully about him in the second part of Mercator’s Works. For the present, what Vincent of Lérins says in the *Commonitorium* (chapter 16) is sufficient: “To open a way for his own heresy, he attacked the blasphemies of all the heresies.” This helps us understand the purpose with which the deceitful heretic attacked the Pelagians, although he had admitted them into his friendship, and the intention with which he prompted the emperor Theodosius to issue a decree against all heretics and impure persons (*Theodosian Code*, law 65, *On Heretics*, and *On Pimps*, book II).]

Reader, if you should wish to consult these laws, observe that among the heretics who are individually designated by name, Apollinarians and Manichaeans in particular are listed. The Pelagians are entirely passed over in silence, although they ought especially to have been named in a decree renewing earlier statutes, since they had been condemned by Atticus, expelled from the imperial city by imperial authority, and rejected by Sisinnius, whose orthodoxy they had tested after Atticus’s death. But Nestorius favored the Pelagians and was already considering how to make the Catholics odious, as though they held the same views as Apollinaris concerning the Incarnation of the Word and the same views as the Manichaeans concerning grace and free will.

[Note: [Col. 0184B] Although very brief, this note nevertheless confirms many things that were doubtful, clarifies obscure matters, and teaches what was previously unknown. It had been doubtful which city Julian governed; it asserts that he governed Eclanum. It had been doubtful how many Fathers assembled for the ecumenical council; it counts 274. It had been doubtful in what respect Nestorius agreed with the Pelagians; it denies that he agreed with them concerning original sin. What Celestine and Cassian had written about Nestorius had hitherto been obscure; this note sheds light upon it. It had been unknown what happened to Celestius after his condemnation and in what part of the world he lived, and likewise where Julian and the deposed bishops were. It had equally been unknown how close the relationship was between Nestorius and Celestius. Finally, it had been unknown that Nestorius possessed treatises against the Pelagians in his own Church, and that these same heretics had been condemned twice by the Council of Ephesus. All these things are taught here for the first time.

The reader must necessarily be warned that we have added this title, because the heading of the following work was lacking in the ancient copies. BALUZ.]

## PREFACE OF MARIUS MERCATOR

[Col. 0183B]

### 1.

Although Nestorius thought and taught correctly against the corrupt and impious definition of Pelagius and Celestius,

[Note: [Col. 0184C] Mercator repeats the same point shortly afterward: “Against whose distorted opinions, apart from his own impiety, which brought him all the way to condemnation, he [Nestorius] thought and taught most correctly.” Celestine agrees with Mercator. After the words just quoted, he continues as follows: “Who are those who agree with you, who were condemned for denying these things? Things opposed to one another never come together without suspicion. They would have been expelled if they had likewise displeased you.”]

nevertheless he judged Julian, formerly bishop of Eclanum,

[Note: [Col. 0185A] Namely, the bishops who had been deprived of office—Persidius, Marcellinus, Florus, Orontius, Fabius, and others—who are mentioned partly in Nestorius’s two letters to Celestine and partly in the acts of Ephesus. That Florus is the man to whom Julian wrote his final work, against the second book of Augustine’s *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, just as he had dedicated his first work, attacking Augustine’s first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, to Turbantius.]

together with his associates, the standard-bearer and champion of this heresy,

[Note: [Col. 0185A] Mercator asks: “Or were those who prepared you for themselves as a defender deceived?” (*Book of Subnotations*, chapter 6). And indeed, in book I addressed to Turbantius, Julian compared himself with David, fighting for God’s cause, and Augustine with Goliath, the monster of gigantic savagery. We have cited Augustine’s passage in the notes to the *Subnotations*.]

who had long before been deprived and deposed by ecclesiastical judgment,

[Note: [Col. 0185B] Julian, together with the others, had been condemned nearly twelve years earlier because he refused to attend the assembly when the whole Church throughout the world was condemning Pelagius and Celestius. These are Mercator’s words. But the sentence of deposition had been carried out by Celestine nearly five or six years earlier, namely after the edict of Valentinian III. See what is said in the notes on chapter 3 of the *Commonitorium* concerning the imperial edicts and their date. See also what we have discussed at length in the dissertation on the authors and defenders of the Pelagian heresy.]

[Baluz.: “formerly deprived by apostolic judgment.”]

to be received meanwhile into friendship, promising him hope of absolution. He also consoled Celestius by his letters, copies of which we have appended.

[Note: [Col. 0185B] Hence the reproach of Celestine in his reply to Nestorius, which we quoted shortly before. Hence Cassian’s words (*On the Incarnation*, book I): “By his intercessions he encourages the complaints of the Pelagianists, and in his writings he asserts their cause; he subtly—or, to speak more truthfully, stealthily—patronizes them and supports, with a shameful affection, the shamelessness akin to himself, knowing that he shares their mind and spirit. He therefore grieves that a heresy related to himself has been separated from the Church,” and so forth.

By “intercessions” he means Nestorius’s letters on behalf of the Pelagians, whose heresy he called related or akin to the Nestorian heresy—not because the Celestians denied original sin, concerning which Nestorius perhaps held the correct view, but because the Pelagianists asserted that grace is given according to merits. This is clear both from Cassian’s preceding words, from those quoted by Mercator—“apart from his own impiety”—and finally from Prosper’s epitaph on the Nestorian heresy. We shall discuss this question at length in the second part of Mercator’s works.]

### 2.

Whether he did this through malice or folly cannot easily be known: although, against whose distorted opinions—apart from his own impiety, which brought him to condemnation—he thought and taught most correctly, he nevertheless had them as friends and considered them deserving of encouragement and indulgence through the hope of a vain promise; and they, together with the aforesaid patron, were condemned again and again at the Council of Ephesus by 274 bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0185C] It was recently observed in the Notes on Vincent of Lérins, p. 451, that ancient opinions differ regarding the number of bishops who attended the first Council of Ephesus held against Nestorius; the more probable opinion seems to be that there were 200, or about 200. Marius Mercator, however, both here and below on p. 132, gives a much larger number, writing that the bishops of that synod were 274 or 275. Garner adopted this opinion as true; and in order to confirm it he employed the reading of an old Greek manuscript reported by Labbe in vol. III of the *Councils*, p. 573:

> ὑπὲρ τούς διακοσίους, ὡσεὶ τριακοσίους ἥττω ἢ πλείω

Garner translates this: “We bishops are assembled here, more than two hundred, nearly three hundred, more or less.”

But this was taken from Cyril of Alexandria’s letter to the clergy and people of Alexandria, in which the Roman editors printed:

> ἦμεν δὲ οἱ συνελθόντες ἐπίσκοποι ὡσεί διακόσιοι ἥττους ἢ πλείους

That is: “We bishops who assembled were about two hundred, more or less.” Since those most learned men neither could nor wished to conceal that Commelin had printed *ὑπὲρ τοὺς διακοσίους*, omitting the words *ἥττους ἢ πλείους*, they placed that reading in the margin, thereby attesting their good faith in this matter. Labbe had intended to retain the marginal variant readings of earlier editions; hence, through the printers’ carelessness, the Roman marginal reading—Commelin’s—was joined to the reading which Labbe produced from an old manuscript of the Séguier library, and that monstrous reading was thus formed.

Deceived by this, therefore, and then led by Mercator’s authority into an opinion remote from the common view, while overlooking and disregarding the testimonies of Cyril and of the bishops of the Ephesian synod—testimonies to which, as Baronius says in discussing this very matter, everyone would say greater weight should be given—Garner maintained, contrary to the belief of every age, that the bishops of that synod were nearly 300. Yet the testimonies of the bishops of the Ephesian synod plainly teach that those present did not exceed 218. I know that the reading on which Garner relies is found in part in two Greek manuscripts of the royal library, in which, instead of *ὑπὲρ τοὺς διακοσίους*, which is Commelin’s edition, or *ὡσεὶ διακόσιοι ἥττους ἢ πλείους*, as the Roman editors printed it, there is written *ὡσεὶ διακόσιοι ἥττους ἢ πλείους*. Nevertheless, I judge that reading false, because it conflicts with all earlier antiquity, as Garner himself admits, and also because it is contrary to the Greek manuscripts used by Commelin and by the Roman editors. It was introduced by persons who had seen copies of the Council of Ephesus in which the number of bishops had grown to 300 or about that number—copies, that is, like those which came into Mercator’s hands.

The marginal reading which printers’ carelessness introduced into Labbe’s edition, by joining Commelin’s reading with the new one supplied by Labbe, is moreover ridiculous. For what could be judged more ridiculous than to make Cyril write that at this synod there were more than 200 bishops—that is, nearly 300, more or less? For one who says “more than 200” plainly says “about 200,” so that the number cannot greatly exceed 200; just as Pliny, in book XIV, chapter 4, saying that wines made in the consulship of L. Opimius, in the 634th year from the founding of Rome, still lasted for about 200 years, did not mean to say that they lasted for about 300. For from the 634th year after Rome’s foundation to the death of Vespasian, under whom Pliny wrote, only 199 years intervened, as everyone knows. In the same way, one who says “nearly 300, more or less” leaves far behind the number 200, which certainly is included within 300.

Accordingly, to return to the point from which we necessarily digressed in investigating the truth, it may also be proved that the bishops of the Ephesian synod numbered only 200 or about 200: Baronius testifies that in the Cresconian collection of the Vatican library, 190 bishops who attended the Ephesian synod are named and counted; the same number occurs in the Greek manuscript of the royal library which we cited on p. 508 of vol. I of the new collection of Councils. Add that Marius Mercator, after setting out the names of the bishops who delivered the sentence of condemnation against Nestorius, sums them up on p. 218 and says that 193 bishops attended the synod against Nestorius—though only 190 are found there. From all this conclude, as we said at the beginning, that the more probable opinion is the one which holds that the bishops of the Council of Ephesus were 200 or about 200. BALUZ.]

### 3.

Now, therefore, with that same Julian and his accomplices established in the city of Constantinople, and while Nestorius was listening to him expound publicly in the Church,

[Note: [Col. 0187A] That is, teaching in the Church. Hence Vincent of Lérins (*Commonitorium*, chapter 40): “So that no one may rashly suppose that the holy and catholic agreement of those blessed Fathers can be disregarded, the Apostle says in the First Letter to the Corinthians (12:28): ‘And God has appointed some in the Church, first apostles’—of whom he himself was one—‘second prophets,’ such as Agabus, whom we read about in the Acts of the Apostles; ‘third teachers,’ who are now called expositors, whom this same Apostle sometimes also calls prophets, because through them the mysteries of the prophets are opened to the peoples. Whoever despises these teachers, whom God has distributed through times and places in his Church, when they agree in one judgment concerning Christ within the meaning of Catholic doctrine, despises not a human being but God. Would that those who slander scholastic teachers would read this.”]

his first sermon was delivered,

[Note: [Col. 0187B] It is apparent from this that the sermon was delivered by Nestorius not merely before his deposition, as no one could reasonably deny, but also in the second year of his episcopate, and at a time when the Pelagians had not yet been expelled from the imperial city, since they too were present while Nestorius was listening to Julian teaching in the Church. Nestorius himself testifies in his preface that he had already been flooded by many and repeated rains of anguish, and the solemnity of baptism was approaching, as is stated in no. 12—that is, Lent.

Since Socrates writes (*History*, book VII, chapter 29) that Nestorius was ordained in 428, amid the greatest joy and thanksgiving of all, on 10 April, that is, on the eighth day before the Ides; and since Easter fell that year on 22 April, the 27th of Pharmuthi, as Cyril teaches (*Paschal Homily* 5)—that is, thirteen days after Nestorius’s ordination—it must be admitted that this sermon was not delivered in 428. In that year Nestorius was not yet immersed in great rains of anguish before Easter; rather, he was enjoying the congratulations of all.

Nor can the sermon be assigned to 430, since the Pelagians, who heard Nestorius teaching in the Church, were expelled from Constantinople immediately after Mercator submitted his *Commonitorium* to the emperor. The *Commonitorium* was submitted in 429 (Mercator, in the title of the *Commonitorium*).

This opinion is confirmed not only by the chronological reasoning already explained but also by the Church’s custom. Catechumens used to enroll their names at the beginning of Lent, so that they might be counted among the *competentes*, as may be inferred from the Council of Laodicea. The argument may also be drawn from the letters either which Nestorius sent to Saint Celestine in 429 concerning the Pelagian cause, or which Saint Celestine sent in reply to Nestorius on 11 August 430. Celestine replied later and gives the reasons for the delay at the beginning of his letter; nevertheless, in replying he mentions the Pelagians as though they either still actually existed at Constantinople or as though he did not yet know that they had been expelled.

Since the Pelagians were expelled from Constantinople either at the end of 429 or at the beginning of 430, as is established from Mercator, it follows that the sermon [lacuna] was delivered before the Pelagians in the Church of Constantinople in the second year of Nestorius’s episcopate.

But in what month or on what day? Someone might conjecture that it was delivered *ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγελισμῷ τῆς ἁγίας Παρθένου*—that is, on the Annunciation of the Holy Virgin, 25 March. First, because of these words of Nestorius: “I see you stretched out toward divine matters, taking up this disposition, which does not grow sluggish amid the cycle of so many festivals, whose common origin is the advent of the Lord’s goodness.” For the advent of the Lord’s goodness is celebrated especially on that feast. Moreover, nearly the whole sermon is devoted partly to explaining the angelic greeting and partly to comparing the childbirths of the blessed Virgin and Eve. Finally, the day of the Annunciation fits well with the time when the solemnity of baptism was near. For if Easter fell on 7 April, as is established from Saint Cyril (*Paschal Homily* 17), only twelve days would have intervened between the feast of the Annunciation and Holy Saturday, on which baptism was celebrated.

Yet two matters may make this conjecture uncertain. The first is the first canon of the tenth Council of Toledo, which orders that the feast of the Mother of God—namely, the Incarnation or Annunciation—be celebrated throughout Spain on 18 December, eight days before the Nativity of the Lord:

“This appears to have been instituted not without the example of an ancient custom, which is known to be observed in different parts of the world. For in many Churches far removed from us in distance and territory, this custom is known to be retained.”

What Churches could be distant in territory except the Eastern ones? For the African, Gallican, and Italian Churches commemorated the Annunciation on 25 March, as may be gathered from Chrysologus and others.

Indeed, scarcely any ancient writer who lived before the sixth century speaks openly about the time at which the feast of the *Εὐαγγελισμός* was celebrated in the Church of Constantinople. This is partly because in those earlier times the Annunciation perhaps was not yet counted among the *ἑορταὶ κυριακαί*—the solemn or panegyrical festivals at which formal homilies were delivered—and partly because the ancients did not always understand the *Εὐαγγελισμός* in the sense that some now do, as having occurred on a fixed day and being commemorated by an annual feast.

Thus Baronius, in the *Martyrology* under 25 March, when he asserts that Augustine says (*On the Trinity*, book IV, chapter 5) that the Annunciation, according to the tradition of the Fathers, was celebrated on 25 March, says more than Augustine actually indicates. For Augustine writes there only that the ancients handed down that on that day, when the angel announced it, the Incarnation took place.

I know that these words are attributed to Gregory Thaumaturgus (*Oration 1 on the Annunciation*, translated by Combefis):

“Today the choirs of angels resound with joyful melody in divine praises, and the splendor of Christ’s advent shines upon the faithful. Today the true sun of righteousness has shone upon us, illuminating us with bright light,” and so forth.

These words appear to place the Annunciation in spring.

I also know that the following words are either Chrysostom’s or at least are attributed to him (in Combefis, *Bibliotheca Concionatoria*):

“When, after the cold winter, the warmer weather of spring has dawned, the earth likewise produces green grass,” and so forth. “Come, then: when the heavenly true Sun, Christ, has arisen for us from the virginal womb,” and so forth.

But neither Bellarmine considers the three orations of Thaumaturgus on the Annunciation certain, since they differ greatly from his genuine works; nor does Savile list the sermon attributed to Chrysostom among the authentic ones.

Finally, I know that Anastasius, bishop of Antioch, also called the Sinaite (*Sermon 1 on the Annunciation*), speaks openly of 25 March, as does the emperor Leo concerning springtime. But both lived in later periods, about which there is scarcely any question; our concern is with the earlier period, before Nestorius occupied the see.

The second matter makes the conjecture doubtful. Since this sermon of Nestorius is entirely about Genesis chapter 3, which contains God’s sentence against sinful Eve, it ought to appear to have been delivered at the beginning of Lent. At that time, sermons on the beginning of Genesis were delivered in the Church, as we infer from the homilies of Chrysostom and other Greek Fathers. The first homily on Genesis is entitled:

> λόγος παραινετικὸς εἰς τὴν εἴσοδον τῆς ἁγίας τεσσαρακοστῆς

“An exhortatory discourse on the entrance of the holy Forty Days.”

The homily that follows the seventy-seventh on Genesis is likewise entitled:

> ἐν ἀρχῇ τῆς τεσσαρακοστῆς εἰς τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν οὐρανόν

“At the beginning of Lent, on ‘In the beginning God made the heaven,’” and so forth. Other homilies found in various authors are similarly entitled, “On Adam.”

Although these considerations may create difficulty and some uncertainty, it is nevertheless reasonable to suppose that the *Εὐαγγελισμός* was formerly celebrated at Constantinople at the same time as in later centuries, since the ancients mention no change and several substantial arguments lead to this opinion.]

translated by us from Greek into Latin word for word.

## FIRST SERMON

### Treatise on Adam, delivered publicly in the Church

[Col. 0189A]

It was delivered by Nestorius in the second year of his episcopate, in the great church, at the beginning of Lent, after the departure of the Catholics, before a large gathering of his own followers, with the Pelagians listening. Its subject was the punishments inflicted by God upon the human race because of Adam’s sin and their removal through the Incarnation. Scarcely anything more eloquent is found among the Greeks. It may conveniently be divided into twelve parts.

### 1.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Before beginning to annotate Nestorius’s treatises, the Jesuit—worthy of commendation no less for piety than for learning—prefaces them with these few words:

“Neither is it useful, nor does it seem permissible, to illuminate the sermon of a heretical man with notes other than those by which either the history of the times or the practice of the Church, insofar as Nestorius touches upon it, may be made clearer. For I would not wish to draw even doctrines that are pure—as some of these are—from an impure source, when the purest sources are open in other Fathers.” EDIT.]

Since this sermon was delivered in 429, at the beginning of Lent, before Proclus delivered his panegyrical oration on the Virgin Deipara, Nestorius seems at that time to have been suffering the anxieties which Cyril mentions in his letter to Celestine (*Part I of the Council of Ephesus*, chapter 14):

“There was a certain bishop named Dorotheus at Constantinople, holding the same opinions as Nestorius, a man exceedingly devoted to flattery for the sake of gain and, as it is written, so ready with his tongue that he went as far as rashness. While the people were gathered in large numbers in the church and the most reverend Nestorius was seated in the chair of the Church of Constantinople, Dorotheus rose and dared to shout in a loud and exalted voice: ‘If anyone calls Mary Deipara, Θεοτόκος, let him be anathema.’

“Immediately a great outcry and withdrawal of the entire people followed, for they no longer wished to share communion with those who possessed such a mind and such an opinion. Indeed, even at this very time the people of Constantinople—except for certain frivolous and empty-headed persons and those who merely flatter him—are abstaining from the assembly. Almost all the monasteries and their archimandrites likewise abstain; a large part of the senate also abstains, fearing that Nestorius himself and those whom he had brought with him from Antioch might pour forth some perverse doctrine and thereby cause damage to the faith.”

Moreover, Eusebius, although at that time still merely a layman conducting legal cases, nevertheless dared to publish a public protest against the bishop of the imperial city in the following form (*Part I of the Council of Ephesus*, chapter 13):

“I adjure and implore, by the holy Trinity, all who receive this document to display it to the bishops, presbyters, deacons, and readers, and also to the laypeople living in Constantinople, and to distribute copies of it among them, for the evident confusion of the heretic Nestorius, who holds precisely the same opinions as Paul of Samosata, condemned by Catholic bishops with an anathema 160 years ago.”

Add to this the deed of that simple monk mentioned by Basil the deacon and archimandrite in his petition presented to the emperor (*ibid.*, chapter 30):

“Finally, a certain simple monk, driven on by vehement zeal, came forward into the middle of the church. While the assembly was being celebrated, he tried to prevent the herald of impiety, because he was a heretic, from entering. But Nestorius had him beaten and handed over to the high officials; after he had again been torn by lashes and publicly beaten, with a herald loudly preceding him, he expelled him into exile,” and so forth.

These events deeply affected the mind of a man whom Basil portrays with the following colors:

“Nestorius tries to frighten people by threats, attacks, exiles, and crafty and wicked schemes. To make his madness and impiety more firmly established, he undertakes indiscriminately whatever can be devised. He does not fear God; he respects no human being; he venerates no bishop; he honors no priest, cleric, holy monk, or devout layman; he fears no punishment decreed for the wicked; finally, he respects no law imposed by the ministers of divine wrath upon those who provoke it. Inflated by pride, through which he regards everyone as insignificant, relying upon money and the influence of certain corrupt men—and, to speak frankly, relying upon your own authority as well—he does these things,” and so forth.]

Flooded by many and repeated rains of anguish, and turning these matters over within myself, I draw breath again in your beloved hearing. For, having set aside the anxiety of grief, I recover from you that joy which comes from seeing you stretched out toward divine things and taking up this disposition, one that does not grow sluggish amid the cycle of so many festivals,

[Note: [Col. 0190D] These and other passages, as was his custom, Nestorius took from Chrysostom, whose words are as follows (*Homily on Saint Philogonius*):

“The feast of all feasts, most worthy of veneration and awe, is approaching. If anyone calls it the metropolis of all feasts, he would not be mistaken. And what is this feast? Christ’s birth according to the flesh. For from it the feast of the Epiphany, holy Easter, the Ascension, and Pentecost derive their origin and foundation. If Christ had not been born according to the flesh, he would not have been baptized—for that is the feast of the Theophany; he would not have been crucified—for that is the feast of Easter; he would not have sent the Holy Spirit—for that is the feast of Pentecost. Thus, as though from some fountain from which different rivers have arisen, these feasts were born for us,” and so forth.]

whose common origin is the advent of the Lord’s goodness.

[Col. 0191A]

### 2.

Before this, the entire human race had been placed in grief and lamentation, beneath that sentence whose curse cried out against its origin:

[Note: [Col. 0191C] This passage from Genesis, together with the other passages concerning the punishment of the first parents’ sin, is discussed by Julian and Augustine alike. Julian evades the authority of Scripture; Augustine presses it forcefully.]

Julian. It was not said to the woman, “Pains will arise in you,” or “I will generate groans for you,” as though their sensation were instituted after the transgression; rather: “Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows”; by this He showed that what he promised, in the person who had sinned, was already present in the natural order—not to create it, but to multiply it; for things are never multiplied unless they already exist. Thus, in this order, the groans of childbirth, which had been instituted according to nature in human bodies just as in animals, are not created in Eve but increase, so that, with the peculiar magnitude of their excitation, she might be afflicted by pains, etc.

Against Augustine: “We say that the pain of childbirth is the punishment of sin, for we know that God said this without any ambiguity; and that He said it only to the transgressor of His commandment; and that He said it for no other reason than that He was angry that His commandment had been transgressed” (*Sixth Book of the Unfinished Work*, chapter 26.]

“Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows and your groans” (Genesis 3:16). For this reason the Lord’s coming, and the announcement of so many blessings, is the first announcement of joy: “Hail, full of grace” (these words were spoken to the Virgin); “the Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28), because “the Son of God will be called holy from you” (ibid., 35). “With you,” he says, “and from you”: with you, namely, through the coming of the Godhead; from you, through the human form assumed from her.

### 3

Therefore, when you hear, O pagan, of an infant placed in a manger and wrapped in swaddling clothes, do not take offense at the flesh that is seen, but consider the dignity of that infant,

> **[Note: [Col. 0191D]]**  
> Nestorius might, on account of these words, have appeared catholic, unless it were otherwise established that he was accustomed to conceal heresy beneath opinions that seemed orthodox. For nearly the same expressions occur in the Council of Ephesus and in Mercator; yet neither the Fathers nor Mercator accepted them as having been spoken in a catholic sense. Nestorius had said: “So that you may know how great was the union of the Godhead, when even the Lord’s flesh was seen in an infant—for the infant was the same as the infant’s Lord. You praised the expression, but do not praise it too carelessly; for I did not say that the same one was an infant and the inhabitant of the infant.” Flavian, however, bishop of Philippi, to whom the Fathers assented, after these and similar statements had been read out by the notary, said: “The words of Nestorius are dreadful and blasphemous, and our ears can no longer endure being polluted by them.”
>
> Hence Mercator writes: “Who, moreover,” he says (*Against the Twelve Anathemas of Nestorius*), “could calmly endure this other delirium of his, by which he says that Christ Jesus is his own Lord? These are his words: ‘I say this so that you may know how surpassingly excellent and supreme a certain union existed even in the infant himself, when the Lord’s flesh was seen. For he himself was the infant and the Lord of that very infant.’ Who has ever been said to be his own lord? But in wishing and attempting to introduce a fourth person and substance into the holy Trinity, he is marked by astonishing stupidity and stained with the blemishes of impiety.”

—the mother who gave birth to him, begetting him in respect of his Godhead, while he was formed humanly in her and divinely formed her; wrapped in swaddling clothes according to the flesh, yet by the providence of the Godhead containing all things; suckled according to the nature of the body, yet, by his divinity, lavishly granting the nourishment of milk to all who are born.

### 4

Perhaps it was on account of such a gift that Gabriel cried out to the Virgin: “Hail, full of the grace of God.” For as soon as Christ, the Lord of all, was born into this life, he dissolved the entire account of sorrows, and, changing the accursed fruits of nature, released that birth which had once been condemned in bodies. He also erased the decree of that sentence which is born together with nature, namely: “Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows and your groans. In sorrows you shall bear children” (Genesis 3:16).

### 5

But the statement “you shall bear children” was indeed a blessing of fertility.

> **[Note: [Col. 0192D]]**  
> Baluze more correctly has this passage as follows: “[lacuna] blessing. For the providence of increase is generative. ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.’ In sorrows, etc.” —EDITOR.

“Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28); for the providence of increase is generative. But “in sorrows you shall bear children” displays the fruit of sin. For just as eating is a life-giving gift bestowed upon the human race by the Creator—for before sin, God’s ordinance concerning food spoke to the first-formed man: “Of every tree that is in paradise you shall eat for food” (Genesis 3:16)—so “in sorrows you shall eat” entered through the curse. For God did not say to Adam: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and because you ate, therefore I condemn you”; rather: “Because you ate from the tree concerning which alone I had commanded you not to eat, therefore in the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (ibid., 3:17).

> **[Note: [Col. 0192D]]**  
> Baluze has *indoloriae* and adds the following note: “The ancient books have *in alolore*. Certainly, in the Beauvais manuscript it is written *indolorie*, but the letter *i* was deleted in antiquity. We find *indoloriam* in Sidonius, in the preface to the epithalamium composed for Polemius and Araneola, where he says that the word is Cicero’s. See Sirmond and Savaron there.” —EDITOR.

For the first delights of the first-formed man were without pain and entirely free from the labors of agriculture. Likewise, concerning the procreation of children, after the sin God did not say to Eve simply, “You shall bear children,” but “In sorrows you shall bear children.”

### 6

For marriage is a gift of divine goodness, the abundance of nature, a mechanism resisting death, which consumes all things; a bridle of chastity against lust; the power of blameless pleasure. But the multiplied groans of women in childbirth are the punishment of sin.

### 7

To give birth is not a curse; for a blessing would not be turned into a curse. But to give birth in sorrow: this burden is drawn from that curse after sin. To give birth with nature pierced by the pains of labor; to waste away in anguish; to endure the fear of bitter delivery; sometimes to expel premature fetuses; occasionally for pregnant women to exceed the times established for childbirth and carry the burden of the womb longer; to waste away often together with the fetuses themselves; sometimes even after the birth to remain anxious lest what has been born should fail, through some want, to enjoy the nourishment of milk; to take care that it suffer no adverse desire; that it not crave some fruitless instruction; that it not be harassed by the attacks of demons; that it not be worn down by a disease of such a kind as scarcely to admit health; that it not at some time be snatched away into poverty beneath someone’s bitter yoke: of all these sorrows nature’s discourse is a brief teacher: “In sorrow you shall bear children.”

### 8

This misery is pitiable: for what had been prayed for and desired later becomes something to be fled. They become betrothed because they desire to have children, and they bear these children in sorrows. They desire offspring, yet cry out against the passage of the months in which they are carried. They wish and rejoice to become mothers, yet, goaded by the burial of those who have been born, they complain that the day of their childbirth was the cause of their present sorrow—confirming it, as it were, with their lamentations: “In sorrows you shall bear children” (Genesis 3:17). What is born and what gives birth share in this sentence: one gives birth in sorrows, while the other is born in sorrows.

### 9

But the compassionate Lord did not despise those offspring of nature who had been condemned. Coming into the woman’s womb, he transformed in that mother the customary process of childbirth and changed the laws of delivery—for he had prepared the childbirth of the holy Virgin to be free from sorrows—and he granted to human nature an unmarried mother, neither rejecting the offspring of marriage nor despising it. In this way Christ, when born, deigned to transfer earthly life into a heavenly mode of living.

### 10

For nature was bound by a most bitter sentence. What sentence is more bitter than this? “Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows and your groans; in sorrows you shall bear children” (Genesis 3:16); and again: “Cursed is the earth in your works; in sorrows you shall eat your bread all the days of your life” (ibid., 17); and again: “It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (ibid., 18). Each of these obtained healing in no other way than by bringing to each wound the remedy that was contrary and most closely suited to it.

### 11

Consider, then, the release granted by Christ from all these sad sentences. “Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows and your groans”: he resolved this through the words, “Hail, full of grace” (Luke 1:28).

“In sorrow you shall bear children”: he resolved this through what is written, “Blessed is the fruit of your womb” (ibid.).

“Cursed is the earth in your works”: he resolved this through, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace” (Luke 2:14).

“The earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you”: he resolved this through the crown of thorns placed upon his head (John 19:5), for they deserved to be uprooted because they had come so near to such a head.

“In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread”: he resolved this through what he says: “The bread that I shall give you is my flesh, which I shall give for the life of the world” (John 6:52).

He resolved what had been said against us to the serpent, “You shall watch his heel,” through what was said: “I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions” (Luke 10:19).

He resolved the nakedness that arose after sin through the incorruptible garment of the glory of the resurrection.

### 12

No catechumen has any share in any of these things.

> **[Note: [Col. 0193C]]**  
> This passage prompts me to say something about the widespread opinion of certain people who believe that, formerly in the Church, baptism could be celebrated on only two days, namely Easter and Pentecost, and was forbidden on the other days unless necessity compelled it (Vicecomes, book 1, *On the Ancient Rites of Baptism*, chapters 19 and following). I admit that this practice prevailed in the Western Church, at least on this side of the sea, and not merely prevailed but was also sanctioned by laws. Yet I maintain that in the Eastern Church, especially at Constantinople, the matter stood otherwise, and that there were three solemn days of baptism: the Feast of Lights, that is, Epiphany, Easter, and Pentecost.
>
> **[Col. 0193D]** I infer this first from the oration which Nazianzen delivered on the day after the Feast of Lights (*Oration* 40), in which he vehemently attacked those who postponed baptism from one solemn day to another: “You offer this excuse and that, and excuse excuses that are sins: ‘I await the day of the Lights; I regard the feast of Easter as more important; I shall await Pentecost.’ It is better to be baptized with Christ, to rise to life with Christ on the day of the resurrection, and to honor the coming of the Spirit. What then? The end of life will come on a day you do not expect, and at an hour you do not know,” etc. It is useful to consult Nicetas on this passage.
>
> If anyone, however, thinks with Pamelius (*Notes on Tertullian’s Book on Baptism*) that the Feast of Lights was the *Hypapante*, which we call the Purification of the Virgin, when people proceed with candles, let him read the beginning of the aforementioned oration and compare it with the preceding one (*Oration* 39), entitled “On the Holy Lights.” Let him also attend to these words near the end: “Christ is illuminated; let us be illuminated together. Christ is baptized; let us descend together, so that we may ascend together,” and the rest—which fit the *Hypapante* not at all, but Christ’s baptism most perfectly—and he will abandon that opinion.
>
> I infer this next from the already cited *Oration* 39, which begins: “Holy is the day of the Lights, to which we have come and which today, by divine favor, we have celebrated. As the beginning of my Christ—that is, of the true light that enlightens every human being coming into the world—it possesses baptism and also accomplishes my purification. Therefore hear the divine voice: ‘I am the light of the world’ (John 8:12); and consequently, approach and be enlightened.” **[Col. 0194D]** “It is the time of regeneration; let us be born from above,” etc.
>
> I infer it third, partly from the *Spiritual Meadow* (chapter 214), where mention is made of the solemn baptism celebrated at Epiphany and divinely confirmed each year by a miracle; and partly from the iambic quatrains of Damascene on Epiphany, in which there is a very extensive mention of baptism customarily performed on that day.
>
> I infer it fourth from the fact that, among the Greek canons, none is found, so far as I know, that assigns only two days to baptism. Hence I almost conclude that different practices prevailed in different particular churches; for Basil (*Exhortatory Sermon on Baptism*) seems to state, with some clarity, that in his Cappadocia only two days were observed. Certainly, in Thessaly baptism was permitted only at Easter, a practice criticized by Socrates (book 5, chapter 21) and Nicephorus (book 12, chapter 34) as something abnormal and harmful to the salvation of many.
>
> **[Col. 0195A]** I infer it fifth from the fact that all the canons so diligently gathered by Vicecomes to prove that baptism could be conferred on only two days belong to the Western Church—and not even to all of it, but only to the Church on this side of the sea—as anyone can easily understand if he consults either the Cresconian collection, which contains the decrees of Siricius to Himerius of Tarragona, of Leo to the bishops of Sicily and Campania, and of Gelasius to the bishops of Lucania, or considers what is reported as prescribed by other pontiffs and by the Councils of Gerunda (chapter 4), Toledo XVII (chapter 2), Paris II (book 1, chapter 33), Meaux (chapter 44), Tribur (chapter 12), Mainz under Rabanus (chapter 3), and others.
>
> Finally, I infer it from the letters of Saints Siricius and Leo themselves. When they wished to prevent the custom of the Greeks, which was spreading in Sicily and other neighboring regions of Italy, from spreading more widely—and indeed to prevent another, far more corrupt custom from being introduced, by which some celebrated solemn baptism for a mixed multitude even on the anniversaries of the apostles and martyrs—they unquestionably acknowledged that one practice was customary among the Greeks and another among the Latins.
>
> When it was said that baptism was solemnly celebrated in the Western Church on only two days, the Church on this side of the sea was excepted. This was done on account of the African Church, in which a different practice seems to have been observed at different times—not only in different provinces but also in the Church of Carthage itself. For Tertullian (*On Baptism*, chapter 19) mentions only Easter and Pentecost when he lists the days of baptism; indeed, he excludes the others in these words: “Moreover, every day belongs to the Lord; every hour and every time is suitable for baptism. If solemnity is at issue, it makes no difference to grace.” But Victor of Utica (*Book 2 of the Vandal Persecution*) recounts that a great miracle occurred at the Epiphany baptism: a blind man was divinely instructed to go on that day to Eugenius of Carthage. After the bishop had blessed the font in which those approaching the faith were to be baptized, he touched the eyes that nature had closed, and opened them after they had been washed with water. This happened exactly as it had been revealed, and all who had gathered for the solemn baptism were amazed at so great a miracle.]

Since the time of baptism is approaching, it is good to admonish these people briefly, so that they do not deprive themselves of such gifts,

—prevented by death; indeed, lest they themselves should also be plunged into the very evils, and into evils as great as those to which Adam was subjected. For each person will carry away with him the penal sentences pronounced against nature. For he has not been made

## SERMON II

Another sermon of the same author to the people, concerning Adam.

Why this sermon is placed second here, although it is fourth in the manuscript, will be explained in connection with the following sermon. It appears to have been delivered in the same year and place, and on a Sunday, since the preceding sermon was delivered on the preceding Saturday. The Pelagians heard him discussing how the entire human race had been bound by Adam’s sin and entirely restored by Christ’s coming. The sermon is eloquent, although toward the end it becomes lighter and more youthful in style. It has no heading. It is divided into twelve parts.

### 1

The desire of my listeners, who await instruction, moves me, and my weakness urges me more strongly toward silence; nevertheless, the force of illness is overcome by the duty owed to the priestly office.

### 2

> **[Note: [Col. 0197C]]**  
> Much is undoubtedly missing here, concerning either the formation of man from the mud of the earth, or at least his placement in the paradise of delight, or even the command given by God to abstain from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For all three are mentioned not only in Genesis 3, before the account of the animals brought to Adam, but also in section 3 of this sermon, where Nestorius, addressing Adam, says: “You were made from dust; you dwelt in paradise; you lived amid an abundance of delights,” etc.]

Then, with the command already given, as though demonstrating from it the progress of human nature in wisdom, he brought animals before Adam’s sight. Adam assigned each of them names appropriate to its nature, improvising each name and pouring forth, as it were, the sources of names. God indeed was calling things that did not exist as though they existed (Romans 4:17). Adam, however, called things that had not yet been called as though they were already being called.

### 3

> **[Note: [Col. 0197C]]**  
> After explaining the fall of the proud devil and the envy conceived against man, whom he calls the image of God’s second creation, Pope Gelasius writes: “With the same impulses,” he says (*Short Treatise against the Pelagians*), “he attacks the man living in security by which he himself, relying wickedly on his own exalted position, had fallen from the heights to the depths. Hence that happiness of paradise could not remain with the first human beings. Hence the integrity of that first creation: while he trusted so greatly in himself, as though he did not need the one who had created him; neither gave thanks for what he had received, which he is nowhere remembered to have done; nor asked assistance for preserving what he had taken possession of; nor, when the tempter’s approach had knocked, did he devoutly hasten to consult God; rather, amid prosperity, he entrusted himself to his own will. Without the Creator’s protection, he was easily exposed to the deceiver’s snares, and, consequently broken into transgression of what was forbidden, he encountered the condition of the death that had been decreed and was rightly subjected to an appropriate punishment. For he had neither been devoted to retaining the good nor guarded beforehand against the evil that had been foretold, while, through an ambition for greater power, presuming that he would, so to speak, be God, he fell into the pits of the enemy’s persuasion. And although, had he remained grateful to his Maker in the proper order, he could have attained perpetual communion with the supreme Godhead, having been rightly frustrated by an abundant promise without the duty owed to the supreme divinity, he could not attain divinity,” etc.
>
> Although this passage is longer, it seemed worth including partly because it contains the opinion of this period concerning the grace of prayer, and partly so that catholic truth might be transmitted not through the sacrilegious mouth of Nestorius but through the more sacred mouth of a supreme pontiff.]

O Adam, how much thanksgiving for such great gifts did you fail to render to my God! You were formed from dust; you dwelt in paradise; you lived amid an abundance of delights; free from pains, you enjoyed pleasure; riches flowed to you without any care; you were also God’s disciple; you became the first recorder of names; the wild nature of the beasts stood before you, more obedient to reason; you issued a law in assigning names to the animals; you conversed in mutual speech with the Creator.

### 4

> **[Note: [Col. 0198C]]**  
> It appears that a narrative had been inserted here concerning both the sin committed by disobedient Adam and the sentence pronounced by God—not only against the guilty parents themselves, but also against the children who would become children of wrath by nature. Yet because of this sentence human beings did not immediately die; rather, they became mortal, in the manner often stated by Augustine.]

And a little farther on in the same place: The angels, offended by the corruption of sinners and perceiving that our punishment was being delayed, were greatly disturbed. They approached God and cried out: “Do you wish us to go and gather up the weeds?” (Matthew 13:28).

### 5

The demons, meanwhile, either hoped for the conflagration of the whole world like that of Sodom, or awaited a flood, as in the time of Noah, with even greater expectation.

> **[Note: [Col. 0198C]]**
