> After mentioning demons, he speaks of the devil in the singular, following the custom of the holy Fathers, who commonly use that name for one of the fallen angels. Christ called him “the ruler of this world,” “the power of darkness,” and Satan (John 12:31; Luke 23:53; Mark 1:13; Matthew 25:41); he said that fire had been prepared for him and his angels, into which he orders the accursed to go when he represents the form of the final judgment.
>
> Augustine likewise calls him “the ruler of the impious city” and “the head of the wicked.” He is commonly called Lucifer, and is believed to hold authority over the other demons, either by the privilege of a superior nature or by a certain tyranny after the unjust defection of the others whom he enticed.
>
> He is also believed to have attacked the parents of the human race personally, with a fury gathered against the image of God the avenger, whereas, as the Fathers relate, he usually acts through the ministry of demons. Out of envy, he is likewise said to have personally attacked Christ in the desert and to have implanted in Judas’s soul the plan of betraying the Lord, etc.
>
> He is the one whom the Apostle John presents as fighting in the form of a dragon with Michael as his rival and being bound by the victor (Revelation 12:7). John says that he is “the accuser of our brothers before the presence of our God day and night” (ibid., 10), and that from this he received the name “devil.”]

But the devil produced that document which is against nature, written as follows: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19).

> **[Note: [Col. 0198D]]**  
> The Fathers note that immediately after the curse was pronounced upon the serpent, by which it was ordered to eat earth, God said to the human being: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go.” The allegorical meaning of these words was thereby indicated: namely, that human beings are consumed and destroyed by the devil because of sin, not only in spirit but also in body, insofar as God permits. Hence Nestorius, following other interpreters, adds: “And from that time he persisted in consuming human generations by death.”]

And from that point he persisted in consuming human generations by death.

### 6

Thus, when we had been deprived of better hopes amid such great difficulty, the greatest reconciliation of nature came about. For the Mediator of the world and of God is born—not like Jeremiah or any other prophet, who were despised, but one who possesses the Godhead joined to himself as the giver of whatever he wishes; not the mediator of one nation, like Moses of the Jews, but, as Paul says: “One God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0199B]]**  
> Someone might suspect that Nestorius betrayed his own heresy here, by which he asserted two sons and two persons in Christ, joined only by a moral connection. For he seems to admit a human person, in whom Christ is seen and appears, and to say that Christ is called God only through his conjunction with the Godhead—which is pure Nestorianism. Yet the statement could be understood catholically: namely, that he is truly both man, because of the human form assumed by the Word, through which he appeared to us, and God, because of the form or nature of God joined to the human form. Nevertheless, it is credible that the cunning heretic spoke with heretical intent.
>
> It will nevertheless be useful here to explain certain statements both of Cyril and of Nestorius, which, through their unusual character or obscurity, may cause difficulty. Someone less attentive to these matters might perhaps think that Cyril reproved Nestorius for precisely what is the formula and, as it were, password of catholic doctrine, while Nestorius in turn approved and claimed as his own what Cyril pronounced in the most catholic manner.
>
> When Cyril, therefore, was explaining Nestorius’s opinion, he says (*On the Correct Faith to Regina*, section 13): “Some people, I do not know in what manner, assert that this name ‘Christ’ applies to the Word of God the Father even separately and by himself—that is, they conceive of him mentally as existing apart from the flesh. Then they contend that it likewise applies to him who was born from the holy Virgin, insofar as he too is considered to subsist separately and independently. Finally, they teach that it belongs to both together, as though to one, by reason of the conjunction which, as they themselves say, binds them together into one person. For among them there is truly no account of a union according to nature. Although they present this one path of the mystery as clear and safe from every error, this feigned confession is not sincere but full of black poison and deception,” etc.
>
> And writing to Nestorius (*Letter 2*), while expounding the catholic position, he says: “We assert that the Word, having united to himself according to hypostasis a body animated by a rational soul, became man in an indescribable and incomprehensible manner and became the Son of man, not through will or good pleasure alone, nor as in an assumption of a mere person (*οὐδὲ ὡς ἐν προσλήψει προσώπου μόνου*),” etc.
>
> **[Col. 0200B]** But Nestorius, replying to Cyril (*First Part of the Council of Ephesus*, chapter 9), appears to have spoken in catholic terms. “Because,” he says, “the Apostle was about to mention death, lest anyone should infer from this that God the Word was passible, he adds the name ‘Christ,’ which denotes both natures—the passible, I mean, and the impassible—in one person, so that the same Christ may be conceived without danger as both most passible and impassible: the former according to the human nature, the latter according to the divine.”
>
> And a little later (ibid., section 2): “But in this I praise you: that you proclaim the distinction of the natures according to the reality of divinity and humanity, and their conjunction in one person; that you affirm that God the Word had no need at all of a birth from a woman; and that you expressly declare that the divinity could not suffer. For these statements are truly orthodox and most opposed to the vain opinions of all heretics concerning the Lord’s natures.”
>
> **[Col. 0200C]** The entire difficulty is easily resolved if only two points are observed. First, the word “person” can be understood—and in fact is sometimes understood by the Fathers—in a theological sense, if one may speak in that way, as the hypostasis of a rational nature; and at other times in an almost forensic sense, as one who possesses the right and authority to conduct affairs. Second, there is a great difference between natures being joined or a nature being assumed, and persons being joined or a person alone being assumed. If persons are joined or only a person is assumed, the connection is, as they say, merely moral; but if natures are joined or a nature is assumed, a substantial connection also intervenes. To assume someone’s person, however, it is enough for that person’s appearance to be taken on, his role to be performed, and his place to be occupied; but if a nature is truly said to be assumed, there must be a “natural and substantial union” (*ἕνωσις φυσικὴ καὶ οὐσιώδης*).
>
> In the passages cited above, therefore, Nestorius used the word “person” in a forensic manner. Thus, although in reality he said that the natures had been joined according only to affection and the “sharing of authority” (*κοινωνία τῆς αὐθεντίας*), it is not surprising that he should at the same time have affirmed that they had been joined in one person—namely, the Word assuming the form of a human being and communicating his dignity to it. Nor is it surprising that for this reason Cyril reproved him as a heretic. Otherwise he would deserve praise as a catholic if he had used the word “person,” as Cyril did, in the theological sense. Furthermore, he wished the persons of the two natures in Christ to be joined, and called this conjunction a “personal union” (*προσωπικὴ ἕνωσις*), because one enjoyed the right and honor of the other. But Cyril rightly attacked this kind of conjunction, which Nestorius called *synapheia* (*συνάφεια*, conjunction or connection), with great force.]

Man: the person in whom he is seen and appears; God: through the joined nature of the Godhead; the mediator, taking up the cause of our nature against the devil.

7. He brought forward the sin from Adam as a bond of indebtedness [Col. 0199B]; Christ, by contrast, from flesh without sin, was intent on canceling this debt; he annulled the condemnation that had proceeded through Eve against the whole nature; Christ, however, referred to the mortification [Baluz.: justification] that had come upon the human race through blessed Mary; he alleged Adam’s intemperance concerning food in paradise [Baluz.: the food of the intemperate]; Christ, on the contrary, showed that human nature, having been given vinegar to drink in him, was without any sin.

8. He canceled everything that the devil alleged against us and proclaimed victory in this case, saying: “Now is the judgment of this world” (John 12:31). “In me,” he says, “this world is judged; through my Incarnation it is conquered. Now,” he says, “is the judgment of this world, and the prince of this world will be cast out” (ibid.), as a wicked calumniator from the judgment—bringing forward a canceled bond of indebtedness and maliciously attacking those who owed nothing [Col. 0200B].

9. But this benefit is conferred upon all by the necessary sacrament of the saving bath: for whoever has been washed in baptism becomes the domestic, fellow-member, and familiar of him who canceled that bond, and together with him becomes an inhabitant of heaven. “For where I am,” he says, “there also is my servant” (John 12:26).

10. The catechumen, however, remains a debtor, as a stranger to the one who canceled the bond; [Note: [Col. 0201B] This almost poetic fiction contains more rhetorical artistry than sincere theology, although something not unlike it is also read in authors better than Nestorius.] when his soul has departed from the flesh, the devil, interposing himself among the angels who are escorting souls, says: “Why are you carrying off this soul of mine, which is standing here? You are violating my right; you are invading my possession; you are attacking my debtors.” And if what happens among human beings also seems applicable here, this better argument concerning catechumens will prevail, with the devil adding: “They close the doors of the churches to them on earth, but you come forth from heaven to receive them. You are attempting, O angels, to use force against my right” [Col. 0201B].

11. “What, it seems, do you have in common with catechumens? They have not been reborn of water and the Spirit, so that they may be led by you into the kingdoms of heaven. They have not renounced the inheritance that is subject to me. [Note: [Col. 0201B] He alludes to the provisions found in Book XII of Justinian’s Code, title 51, and in the Theodosian Code, under “Public Transport,” *angar* [and] *parangar*. *Evectio* is permission to make use of the public transport, granted either by the emperor or by the prefect of the praetorium to persons who had held civil or military office. The public transport, which Spartianus calls fiscal and Nestorius royal, was a service established at fixed places along the public road for carrying out public necessities. Those who supervised it in a province were called *curiosi*; those stationed at individual places, *stationarii*; and those on the road itself, *deductores* or custodians. Nestorius therefore compares baptism with the granting of *evectio*, passage into a better life with the public or royal transport, those baptized with persons distinguished by rank, the angels who guard souls with the *deductores*, and the devil with the *curiosi*.] Not possessing royal transport, how will they complete their journey by royal conveyance?”

12. But now these allegations of the devil against human nature have fallen silent, and that baptized nature confidently cries out against him: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ” (Ephesians 2:6), to whom be glory forever.

## SERMON III. Likewise, another sermon of the same treatise, publicly delivered in the church; its opening is “The sun indeed ...”

[Note: [Col. 0201C] Up to this point it had been asked who was the author of this treatise. Savilius, following Fronto Ducaeus, indeed thought it was falsely attributed to Chrysostom (vol. VII of Chrysostom’s Works), but did not disclose whose it was. Combefis called it the work of Asterius (vol. II of the *Bibliotheca Concionatoria*), because of the similarity of its diction. Mercator attributed it to Nestorius, and his testimony is not doubtful, since he was present when it was delivered, translated the published text into Latin, and excerpted from it many passages with which, on the testimony of its own advocate, he refuted the heresy of Coelestius. Even if Mercator’s testimony were entirely lacking, the speech itself could sufficiently reveal its author, or at least accuse him of Nestorian impiety, since it speaks more than once of Christ as though he were a mere man. Combefis noticed this well; I therefore wonder how he could attribute to Asterius, a thoroughly Catholic man, so impious a sermon.

“First observe, reader, that in Savilius’s Greek text the passages are joined together which are separated in Marius, with the customary words of excerptors inserted between them: ‘and afterward,’ and ‘after some intervening matter.’ These insertions, however, may have been made more frequently than was appropriate through the sole fault of copyists. Next observe that the sermon which is one continuous piece in Savilius is divided into two by Mercator; and that a separate beginning, along with many other things absent from the Greek, was attached to the latter. I nevertheless think it may reasonably be said that either Mercator, or rather a copyist, appended an excerpt of the first sermon to a fragment of the second. If this portion is restored to its proper body, as certainly it should be, it will remove all confusion or doubt.

“Finally, observe that the titles of the sermons, whether through the carelessness or ignorance of the copyists, have been so confused that, unless they are restored from other passages and even by conjecture, perpetual confusion will result. I therefore believe that Nestorius delivered two sermons on Adam and two on Christ’s struggle with the devil. The true title of the first was: ‘A treatise on Adam, publicly delivered in the church,’ beginning ‘Although many ...’; of the second: ‘Likewise, another treatise of the same author, addressed to the people, on Adam’; of the third: ‘Likewise, a treatise of the same author publicly delivered in the church,’ beginning ‘The sun indeed ...’; and finally of the fourth: ‘Likewise, of the same author, on the passage written: “I will give you all these things, if you fall down and worship me,”’ beginning ‘In another sermon.’ Thus Garnerius. Baluzius agrees with him, except that he has in the title of the third sermon ‘... a treatise on Adam ...’ and regrets that Garnerius did not indicate on what authority he asserts that Mercator was present in the church when Nestorius delivered it. EDITOR.]

It seemed that this sermon, as well as the following one, ought first to be transcribed as it is found in the excerpts of Marius, and then in full, as it appears in volume VII of Chrysostom’s Works edited by Savilius; for there is some difference between them, which will afterward provide a not implausible basis for conjecture.

1. The sun, having risen higher above the earth and traveling from the East all the way to us, changes night into day, dispels sleep, and restores us to our tasks; but the light of the knowledge of God rouses the mind from the sleep of indolence, illumines its thoughts, and raises them toward virtues. It will always be desirable for this light to shine upon us; and if someone does not see this visible sun, he still lives, since even a blind man lives, possessing knowledge of the sun only through hearing. But souls that do not know God are entirely dead without the sun, even though someone may suppose them to be alive. Of such the Lord also says: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22).

2. [Baluz.: And after some intervening matter, there:] [Note: [Col. 0202D]

He understands Christ, who overcame both deaths contracted through Adam’s sin: the spiritual death, namely, separation of the soul from God; and bodily death, namely, the soul’s separation from the body. It should be noted, however, that Nestorius defines the former not by the deprivation of love, as he ought to have done, but by the deprivation of knowledge: “If souls,” he says, “do not know God, they are entirely dead without the sun,” and so forth. A little later he says: “For a twofold mortality was raging against us: one, affecting the mortal nature made through sin; the other, which occurs through the rejection of knowledge,” etc.

“From this a serious suspicion has arisen in my mind: Nestorius differed to some extent from the Pelagians concerning original sin, but agreed with them entirely concerning inward grace. For although he acknowledged that human nature had been made mortal through sin, and that the devil was the author of both deaths and the progenitor of mortality—which was Catholic—he nevertheless asserted that Christ lifted our life from both forms of mortification: raising the soul by life-giving commandments and restoring the body through resurrection. Here one may see what is entirely Pelagian: the establishment of God’s grace in law and instruction alone. Indeed, after carefully reading all his sermons and excerpts from his books, I find nothing that supports the true grace of God, but very much that opposes it, as will be observed in its proper place.]

But he who wrestled with the author of mortality redeemed life from both mortality [Baluz.: and mortality from both life]. For a twofold mortality was raging against us: one affecting the mortal nature made through sin; the other occurring through the rejection of knowledge. For ignorance of God bears the likeness of the insensibility that results from death. Thus the devil became the author of both deaths; but Christ, having struck him down, lifted our life from both forms of mortification: raising the soul by life-giving commandments and, through the resurrection, restoring and renewing what is mortal. For when the one who caused the fall has collapsed, what he had caused to fall is raised up.

3. [Baluz.: And after some intervening matter, there: This] [Col. 0203B] [Note: [Col. 0203C] The Greek has *τῷ βίῳ*, that is, “to the living” or “to mortals”; for *βίος* sometimes signifies mortals and the human race, that which exists among the living. The author of the book *On the World*, attributed to Aristotle, used it in this sense when he wrote: *συνεπιμαρτυρεῖ δὲ καὶ ὁ βίος ἅπας, τὴν ἄνω χώραν ἀποδούς Θεῷ*, that is, “all mortals also bear witness, assigning the region above to God.”]

An image of this struggle has been left for the living. Where? Look at the desert. There the divine nature raised this one up, terrifying the tyrant through the image of a tyrannicide, by crushing the tyrant in the desert [Baluz.: by wearing him down].

4. Likewise, after some intervening matter in the same place: He gave human beings nourishment through food and stability to the body through sustenance. [Note: [Col. 0203D] Does he allude to threats from the people, who were angered by his impiety? He mentions these at the beginning of that sermon against the Catholics, which begins: “I consider the insults of the heretics against me like the laughter of infants, and their threats of drowning in the sea, together with their desire for disturbances and the new schemes of persecution that are being directed against me,” etc.]

But divine Scripture taught me that God surpasses the limits of nature. For I remember the voice of God crying out, teaching that human beings should not fear hunger and the desert, but should even answer there: “Let God bring help, and let bread perish, because God is life-giving even without food; flesh too will live without nourishment if God commands it to live.” Thus, it is written (Matthew 4:4), and thus I believe, placing my confidence in the divine utterances; nor do I await the life that comes from food alone.

5. Likewise, after some intervening matter in the same place: By the means through which Adam offended, Christ reconciles. Formerly [Baluz. “Since”] he had fallen through unbelief and food, not believing God, and he fell when he ate; Christ, coming from faith and self-restraint [Baluz.: beginning with faith and from self-restraint], begins therefrom, restoring nature from the point at which it had collapsed.

## SERMON IV. Likewise, of the same author, on what is written (Matthew 4:9): “I will give you all these things, if you fall down and worship me”; its opening is “In another sermon,” etc.

1. In another sermon, as my tongue presses me onward, the teacher mentioned earlier reminded me that I owe you an account of the Lord’s struggle and constrains me to repay it. [Note: [Col. 0204C]

By the title “teacher” he means the person who taught the people in the church before the bishop; his sermon was ordinarily followed by a brief address from the bishop, either approving what had been said, as happened more frequently, or correcting it, as sometimes occurred.

That teacher was generally one of the presbyters. Thus Chrysostom taught at Antioch before Flavian; Nestorius likewise there before Theodotus; Anastasius at Constantinople before Nestorius; and Augustine at Hippo before Valerius, performing the duty of instructing the people.

Nevertheless, bishops of lesser sees sometimes taught the people in larger churches before the presiding bishop. Thus Augustine frequently preached at Carthage while Aurelius listened; Theodoret at Antioch before John; Proclus of Cyzicus and Dorotheus of Martyropolis at Constantinople while Nestorius presided, and so forth.

At times even other bishops from a different diocese delivered addresses. Epiphanius certainly did so at Constantinople in the presence of Chrysostom, and at Jerusalem in the presence of John. Paul of Emesa did so at Alexandria before Cyril; and even then the address of the presiding bishop did not fail to follow the sermon of the visiting bishop—indeed, it sometimes reproved it. This is demonstrated both by John of Jerusalem’s example in instructing Epiphanius and by Nestorius’s example in censuring Proclus.]

2. [Baluz.: Among other things, and below:] I am grateful to those who remind me [Baluz.: to the one reminding me], and I have great confidence in discharging the debt. For he who canceled the bond of sins on our behalf will also repay before you the debt I contracted concerning this same struggle [Col. 0204B].

3. Likewise, after some intervening matter in the same place: When the devil saw the heat of faith in his heart, then the harmful flatterer attacked and contrived nocturnal visions. Taking possession of the sleeper’s sense, wearied by drowsiness, he addressed him as an angel of light. Once he had placed chariots before the eyes of the man already awake, he also sent a clearer voice through the air, saying: “It is right, O man, to receive the judgments of God and his treasures.”

4. Likewise, after some intervening matter in the same place: By the same art he suspected that he might also ensnare the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0204D] “To ensnare.” Garnerius had printed *irritare*, “to provoke,” because the Bellovacensis manuscript reads *inritare*. We have restored *inretire*, “to ensnare,” because the Vatican manuscript reads *inritire*. No one can fail to see that our edition is better. BALUZIUS.]

All those events then taking place were prefigurations of all future events and defenses for the Church that was to be built. For just as human nature took its foundation in Adam, and collapsed when that same foundation fell, becoming subject to the hand and power of the devil who cast Adam down, so, with the faith of the Church having the Lord Christ as its foundation, the strength of that foundation remains immovable, secure, and unshaken in the firmness of its head, and cannot be torn away.

5. Likewise, of the same author, in the same place, among other things and below: “I will give you all these things,” he said to the Lord, “if you fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:9). “You prophesy only in part, unwillingly, O devil; for you will restore to the Lord the world that you had unjustly assigned to yourself in slavery—but beaten, not worshiped. Do not imagine that you are speaking with Adam. For by a promise he lured Adam and persuaded him that he would become God, and by this persuasion he cast him down. Now also he was promising Christ omnipotence, thinking that he would cast him down through the hope of exaltation. But he deserved an answer worthy of rejection: ‘Go away, Satan; you shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’” (ibid. 10).

6. Likewise, in the same place, among other things and below: “And behold,” he says, “angels came and ministered to him” (ibid. 11). Let us therefore also render service to the Lord with the angels. Let us leap into heaven while fulfilling angelic ministry on earth; let us support [Baluz.: subject] the soul of others without tiring. Let us love with all our strength the one who raised up our fallen nature; let us worship him who cast down and overthrew our implacable enemy.

## ANOTHER VERSION OF SERMONS III AND IV, COMBINED INTO ONE

[Col. 0205C]

On the words: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.” Matthew 4.

Likewise on the words: “The devil took him up onto a very high mountain,” etc. Ibid.

1. Just as the sun, rising above the earth and driving its chariot toward us from the East, dispels night, awakens sleepers, and restores them to their tasks, so the radiance of divine knowledge commands the mind, as it were, to awaken, pours light upon its thoughts, and rouses us to virtues. This light, shining upon us, is more desirable than the solar light. For even if you lack sight of the sun, you can live—as the blind actually do, knowing the sun only through hearing—whereas souls not illuminated by the sun of divine knowledge are dead, although they may appear to live. Concerning them also comes that word of the Lord: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22).

2. But he made us free from both these deaths, he who wrestled with the author and father of death. For a twofold death falls upon us: one that the condition of mortal nature brings with it; the other that the loss of divine knowledge inflicts, depriving us of all perception of heavenly things and making us exceedingly like the dead. The devil is the craftsman of both these deaths. When Christ broke and struck him down, he drove both deaths away from nature: the soul was raised by saving instruction, while the mortal body was restored through the power of the resurrection. Thus, when the one by whom we had been crushed lay prostrate, we who had previously been tottering and overthrown shall thereafter stand and be raised up [Col. 0206A].

3. A memorial and image of this struggle, which Christ undertook with the devil, was left for the human race, so that, by gazing upon it, it might raise its strength and courage. But where is that image? Look at the desert. Grace has hung it there, as it were, and displays the tyrant, cut down as though in a painting and terrified by Christ in the wilderness. Thus we see the arena: the desert; the combatant: the devil, provoking Christ’s hunger; and finally the three encounters of Christ with the enemy, with three answers, according to the law of the contest, which requires combatants to join hands three times.

4. Come, then, let us review the threefold struggle. “If you are the Son of God, say that these stones should become loaves.” The devil began his struggle with the Lord from this point. Christ answered him: “Man does not live by bread alone,” and thus made himself safe and unharmed by the enemy. “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down”: here is the devil’s second attack. “You shall not tempt the Lord your God”: those words defeated the force and demand of the adversary. “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me”: thus the struggle was begun for the third time. In it the Lord, like an experienced athlete, drove the troublesome and badly fighting adversary, the devil, from the arena and the field of contest: “Go behind me, Satan; it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”

5. Contemplate this struggle so that you too may learn to wrestle and become a disciple from being a spectator. Christ’s first fight with the demon teaches you to fight against pleasures. Hunger gave rise and occasion to the contests—hunger, I say, that hard desire, like the manner of an unrestrained tyrant; hunger, the cause and beginning of the pursuit of pleasures. For the appetite for food does not tolerate restraint, especially when the belly sees a pleasure set before it that cannot be refused. Since many could neither moderate nor restrain this appetite, they were driven to deny that providence exists, as though God did not care for the hungry.

The devil drives Christ toward this obstacle, hoping that, stimulated by hunger as a man, he may easily be dashed against it. For he did not know that God had been united to man; nor would he have approached God as one who was hungry. For how could he, knowing him to be God, have asked him for food, when he knew that his own nature was free from hunger? The one whom he saw as a man he addressed as a man: “If you are the Son of God, say that these stones should become loaves.” A curious examiner of the divine adoption in Christ, and a provider of food worse than hunger itself, he had once implanted in human beings the false hope of attaining divinity through the fruit of the forbidden tree; now he provokes Christ’s hunger in the same way, pointing out the desert, where there was nothing except stones, so that the place itself, increasing despair of finding food, might instill the disturbance of distrust in his mind and remove from him the filial affection toward God the Father.

6. But come, let us examine the tempter and inspect the traps he sets in precisely these words. “If you are the Son of God,” he says, “say that these stones should become loaves.” “Son of God,” he says, “you were recently called when you were baptized. I heard the voice proclaiming: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’ (Matthew 3). I mocked that address as full of flattery and magnificent jest, and as conferring an honor both trivial and hardly worth the effort. Meanwhile you rejoiced inwardly and already persuade yourself that you are that beloved one; in your presumption you exult as though you were in heaven itself and preferred above all others by God and his favorite.

“But what father should be considered one who has no care for his hungry son? What kind of advocate and protector is one who does not feed his clients? Yet you have now continued fasting for forty days, while your father has shown no concern about your hunger, calmly observing your hunger of many days without the slightest compassion. What a parent who truly loves his son—one who does not even give bread to his hungry child! What an excellent son, whom not even his father feeds in the extremity of hunger! Let him show his love for you, give bread, and nourish his hungry son in the desert. He can change stones into loaves. Ask this of him now, when you are nearly exhausted by hunger. If you obtain this favor from him, I refuse nothing that would prevent you from being the Son of God and from rightly glorying in that name; but before you obtain it, do not arrogate such a great name to yourself.”

7. What honor devoid of true honor, and humanity most inhuman! He shows compassion in order to kill; he feigns care while preparing destruction; he offers poison in the sweetest cup of praise. The crafty one incites Christ to distrust, provokes him to ask for food—not in order to relieve his hunger, but so that, once lured and incited to ask, he may then drive him, as one who distrusts, to commit some sin against God, as though the one who had earlier said, falsely, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

8. What does the Lord Christ say to this? He does not immediately reveal the God hidden within him, lest he frighten away the prey; instead, as one of the common mass of human beings, he replies: “For it is written,” he says, “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.”

“The scarcity of food,” he says, “does not greatly disturb me. It is neither strange nor unexpected that I should hunger here in the desert, nor do I ask that loaves come forth from stones. There are many ways by which God provides for us, and many kinds of means by which he supplies our needs. He gave human beings food for eating, dishes appropriate to flesh and body; yet sacred Scripture has taught me that he is not confined within the boundaries and limits of nature. Nor has that divine utterance escaped my memory which admonishes human beings not to be anxious about hunger, since God provides for it abundantly.

“Therefore, do not pretend to care for one who is hungry, nor show me the desert in order to bring me to despair. God will surely provide, even if no loaves are available. Indeed, he can preserve our life without food, and flesh will live without bodily nourishment when God commands it to live. Thus it is written,” he says, “and thus I believe, relying on the divine words; nor do I think that my life is dependent upon and suited to food alone” [Col. 0208A].

9. Thus Christ, in reconciling us to the grace of God, used the same things through which Adam sinned against God. For since Adam fell into sin through unbelief and the eating of forbidden food—he fell because of disbelief and gluttony—Christ, who had come to restore nature, begins with faith and temperance.

Therefore, laying aside what was like a mask, the demon prepares to wage open war against him by his customary arts. “Before this child was brought forth into the light,” he says to himself, “I plotted an ambush against the offspring through suspicion of adultery. Frustrated in that hope, I then attempted, through Herod’s agency, to surround and destroy him after he was born. That prey also escaped me. I was defeated as long as I fought with another’s hand; now I shall wage war myself. O blind desire for battle! He was defeated by one scarcely born, and now he attacks him after he has become a man. Come, then, demon, join hands with the man; test him again and once more make trial of his strength.”

10. He had already been subdued and broken in the first encounter, when he approached the hungry man—as you have heard, this was how he was defeated. But now, eager to repair the defeat he had suffered, he doubles his strength and boldness. Since he had used the first device in vain and without effect and had not been able to deceive the hungry man, he employs another contrivance.

“Nothing was accomplished for me by that first fraud, which had nevertheless overthrown Adam. I shall abandon it and cease trying to lure him through the desire for food. He appears to have mastery over pleasures, since, when the pleasure of eating was set before him, he could not even be induced to ask for bread to relieve his many days of fasting; he is incapable of being conquered by these bodily weapons.

“I have found a more cunning way of fighting. I have at hand a hook sweeter than anything else: glory. Mortals ordinarily pursue nothing more eagerly than this. It contains not only an abundance of allurements with which to entangle them, but also a double reward for one’s efforts, since vanity is joined to madness and recklessness, and almost everyone inflamed by the desire for glory rushes headlong into conceit and exaltation.

“There is also a reason why this man may seem more desirous of glory. It is easy for one who has now remained fasting for so many days to think rather boastfully of himself. I shall tickle the man; I shall approach him as though he were some righteous man and provide an opening for vainglory, using some sentence from the Psalms that I shall pretend was pronounced long ago for his sake. Thus I shall lure him with a deceitful question.

“A suitable place for putting the question will be some precipitous location. I shall seize him and drag him to the pinnacle of the temple; and when he has taken his seat upon the highest summit, I shall opportunely suggest this: ‘If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down; for it is written that he has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’

“Clearly one of two things will happen: either he will believe my words or reject them. If he accepts my speech in a favorable sense and flatters himself as righteous, it will be easy for him to hurl himself down, as I propose. Thus he will throw his body from the summit; and if he dies from the fall, I shall mock the dead man. If he nevertheless survives, he will at least have received a blow from me in the form of vainglory, having been induced by my speech to throw himself rashly down.

“But if I see him refusing and declining, I shall call him into hatred and resentment before God, as I once did Job, slandering the dignity and benefit of divine adoption that he has violated, in this way: ‘I recited to him the sentence written by you; I spoke the words by which you promised him certain salvation, and yet he hesitated to throw himself into the abyss below. It is evident that he has no trust at all in your promises. How, then, did you call him your son when he has so little faith in your words?’”

11. Christ was not ignorant of what the adversary was contriving. He permits himself to be dragged along and follows just as one man follows another. But when he has reached the summit, the demon prepares to utter the words he had devised: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.”

Let us answer the devil who speaks: “If you believe it to be proper to that man who rejoices in God the Father that, even in danger and in a fall, he should remain entirely free from harm and peril, you have here the means of making evident what you seek. For it is precisely this that shows him to be the Son of God: although the one who stands beside you, under your blow and in your power, is present, you do not cast him down or hurl him headlong, although you have long desired to do so. You can do nothing except urge and persuade him to fall; you cannot force him.

“What does it mean,” he says, “that you do not throw yourself down of your own accord? Come, then, cast yourself down without hesitation; throw yourself down. For it is written that he has commanded his angels concerning you, lest you strike your foot against a stone.”

In saying this, the enemy showed that he did not know that the one to whom he was speaking was God. For if he had known him to be God, he would not have urged him to fall from the summit. He knew that God was neither lowered by any height nor surpassed by any level surface, but that he rises with the highest things and is equal to them, while he extends equally with things that are level and flat; thus he is free from every danger of stumbling, and it is possible for a human being to strike his foot, but not for God himself. These words of the devil therefore prove that he was dealing with Christ not as with God.

12. Let us now hear the meaning and intention of his words. “You said a moment ago,” he says, “‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.’ I myself have praised your faith in God. But since another word of God is the one that testifies that he has commanded his angels concerning you, lest you strike your foot against a stone, show that you add faith in God’s word and throw yourself down, confident that no harm or danger will result.

“Here is a suitable precipitous place to establish that you are the Son of God; here is a fall that will prove God’s care for you. For if, after throwing yourself down from here, you rise up safe and unharmed, that voice which proclaimed you the Son of God will unquestionably be true, since God previously promised you that he would entrust you to the care of angels, so that they might guard you in all your ways.”

13. From a fragrant vessel you bring forth ointment, O devil, and renew an old story. A certain lion killed by Samson had a honeycomb in its mouth, although it lay dead and stinking. You, like that lion, drip honey drawn from the Scriptures out of your mouth, while you yourself, struck down by the Lord’s answer, lie prostrate.

“For it is written,” he says, “‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’”

Christ neither refused to throw himself down nor consented to do so. If he had refused to cast himself down, he would have given the devil an opportunity to accuse him, as though he distrusted God’s words; but if he had consented, he would have appeared more arrogant and more inclined to ostentation. Therefore he gave an answer by which he seemed neither to agree nor to refuse: “You shall not tempt,” he said, “the Lord your God.”

He did not say, “You shall not tempt me, your Lord.” For if the devil had heard this, he would not afterward have attacked him as a man with the promise: “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me.”

What, then, did he answer? “I embrace the words of the Psalms as true, and I place my hope entirely in God, who promises that he will not fail to help. I know that the care of human beings has been entrusted to angels; but not if human beings throw themselves headlong, not if they lay violent hands upon themselves, not if they rashly tempt God.”

14. Thus the devil was defeated and thrown down for the second time; he rises to the third temptation. The following sermon, if I complete it, will have to explain the sequence of this third temptation, and I shall repay the entire debt which I bound myself to discharge by my promise, as though by a bond. The payment of this debt is exceedingly pleasing both to me and to you, but bitter and hateful to the devil alone, since the price of his rashness is paid by his own defeat.

I certainly see that two payments of the promised sermon have now been made. The third remains to be weighed, and, in my opinion, it is more serious and difficult than the others: namely, the devil’s third device, third in sequence but first in cunning and gravity. Though last in number, it easily takes first place among the others on account of its craftiness. In the earlier temptations his wickedness had to be endured. He was not urging an open revolt from God; rather, by misusing divine testimonies and Scriptures and by presenting Christ with the words “If you are the Son of God,” he fought impiously against God while concealing his art beneath the appearance and pretext of piety.

15. In this third temptation he reveals naked rage and malice, and displays wickedness stripped of every disguise. He demands that he be worshiped by the one whom everyone worships; and, from what he has already heard from Christ, he comes to hope that he can extort worship from him. For when he saw the Lord speaking entirely from the oracles of faith and denying that God should be put to the test, he thought him inclined to believe and not especially inclined to labor anxiously in examining and proving the things proposed to him. Accordingly, he advances with a most beautiful arrangement of appearances, as though he were about to strike his mind and eyes with the novelty of the spectacle. “The devil,” says the sacred text, “takes him to a very high mountain and shows him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory.” He sketches an imaginary image and, imitating the pictures and forms of things made from air, constructs an unordered mass representing the world and fabricates the splendors of a shadowy kingdom, evidently thinking that by the empty brilliance of this image he could induce Christ’s readiness to believe and lead him into error. Yet he does not even understand that he is fighting against himself while urging Christ to this worship. He should rather promise him all the wealth of the world, lest he fall down and worship him.

Nevertheless he continues: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.” Whoever does not believe Paul’s assertion that the greedy person is a worshiper of idols should listen to the father of idols himself testifying that Paul’s words are true: “Whoever worships me,” he says, “to him I will give what belongs to others.” Is not, then, whoever possesses what belongs to others a client and follower of the devil? For he himself promises that he will give away what belongs to others, giving to some in such a way as to harm others, and distributing nothing but his own stolen goods.

[Col. 0211B] 16. His generosity toward Christ has this purpose: by promising such great gifts, he gently induces him to fall down before him. “This man,” he says, “cannot be led by the pleasure of food or tickled by the sweetness of empty glory. He has shattered the two most reliable weapons I possess for fighting; I must seek another, more powerful weapon. The desire to rule is present in all human beings: no one refuses to make profit and acquire property if the opportunity arises; greed is like a wound fixed in every person’s mind. I shall draw this arrow from my quiver.

“Where, then, shall I strike the man? What place will assist my plan? If only I had encountered him on some lofty mountain! A higher position gives an easy view in every direction. From there I could readily have placed before his eyes the fertility of the plains; I could have displayed the treasures of kings for him to behold; I could have set before a single gaze all the pomp and grandeur of life—some things showing as they really are, others fashioned by art. Since human nature is so easily ensnared by gifts and profit, if it sees the splendid and distinguished things of the earthly sphere, it will immediately leap toward possessing them; greedily it will seize the wealth displayed to it and be driven by the most vehement desire to have it. It will accept a shadow in place of reality, and the mere appearance of things will make a person believe, since in every other respect he is highly pliable in believing.

“Ask for bread,” I was saying; he rejected it, having no doubt that he would be fed by God even without bread. Throw your body downward, I urged; he dismissed these words, denying that God should be put to the test. I shall now approach him with this empty display and pomp of things. I shall certainly deceive him and persuade him to fall at my knees, as though he were being tested by God himself. He will believe, I said—a man not at all difficult or stubborn when it comes to believing. Then, once I have mocked him after deceiving him, I shall send him away.”

17. Aware of this brilliant deliberation, Christ continued with him to the high mountain. The devil begins to unfold the frauds he had planned: he places before his eyes an imaginary image of various things. Christ neither reproves nor rejects his skillful cunning, but, as though unaware of the fraud, observes it. Thinking that he had conquered by deception and the illusory nature of the spectacle, suspecting that his opponent had been captured by the appearance presented, and drawing as though a certain inference concerning the rest of his victory, he pours out grandiose lies in exaggerated words—words suited to one who would be ruler and arbiter of the world.

“All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.” “Do you not see,” he says, “O man, the vastness of the world? Do you not perceive how numerous and how great these possessions are? Are you not stirred by the sight of almost innumerable kingdoms? I am their lord. These palaces are distributed among human beings according to my will and granted to them as dwellings. I readily set you above all the rest and judge you worthy to rule alone over the whole world. Receive from me the authority and strength by which you may be equal to governing the world. In return for such great gifts, give me this one thing: worship me. All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.”

18. “In part, at least, you will fulfill the prophets’ words, O devil, though unwillingly: you will indeed give back the world that you oppressed under an unworthy slavery; but you will not likewise take away the worship due in adoration; rather, you will receive the punishment of scourging. Do not think that you are conversing with Adam. Adam he enticed with the hope of divinity and, having wrongly persuaded him, ruined him. Now he likewise offers Christ dominion and sovereignty over all things, hoping in the same way to persuade him and make him fall by the magnitude of his promise.”

He received the answer he deserved: “Get behind me, Satan; for it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’ Depart, Satan.” Here he rightly and entirely calls him “Satan” by name, just as a master, calling a slave who is hiding by his name, thereby indicates that the slave is not concealed. “Away with you!” This is a gentle and mild expression, yet, as can be seen, it is also threatening and resembles the voice of an indignant master, as though he were saying:

“You have labored in vain to conceal your fraud. Your mask has been removed; you have despaired of victory. Now you wish to charm and flatter me with gifts; now you are negotiating my sale; now you are using the language of a traitor. You have undertaken the ill-timed plan of buying me. Wait for your associate and accomplice in the bargain, Judas. Depart for the present, while I undergo the cross that awaits me. Depart, I say; you will not buy me now. Away with you! Keep your gifts for the traitor. This one thing you will now receive from me: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’ Do not seek to divide the service of human beings with God or claim it for yourself; they are indebted to him alone.”

19. “Then,” he says, “the devil departed from him.” Great indeed and renowned was Christ’s victory in this final struggle. Just as a noble and strong champion lifts up his lofty opponent and then throws him down from on high and crushes him, so Christ the Lord broke the devil, who had been led up onto the mountain and lifted up by empty hope, by hurling him down from that same lofty hope.

20. The wonder of this victory roused the astonished angels and gathered them around the victor as a heavenly guard. “And behold,” he says, “angels came and ministered to him.” Let us imitate the angels, offering Christ worship and service equal to theirs; let us commend our devotion to heaven and perform on earth the ministries of blessed minds. Let us place our soul in those hands that cannot be defeated; let us love the restorer of fallen nature; let us embrace him who cut through the strength and sinews of the common enemy, and let us accompany the victory that vindicates our glory with unceasing remembrance. Let us exult over the prostrate devil, and, tearing away his shameless head, let us cry out with one voice and from the depths of our hearts:

“You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.”

To him be glory and power forever and ever.

[Col. 0213]

## III. THE CREED

[Note: He was once called Antiochene from his homeland, and more often Mopsuestene from the see that he held. (Mopsuestia is a town of Cilicia Secunda under the metropolitan see of Anazarbus and in the diocese of Antioch.) He was closely associated with John Chrysostom because of their common homeland, life, and studies under Diodore of Tarsus. He held the episcopate for thirty-six years and died in 428. He had many disciples, but three especially famous ones: John, bishop of Antioch; Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople; and Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus.]

OF THEODORE OF MOPSUESTIA AND HIS REFUTATION

### PREFACE OF MARIUS MERCATOR

[Col. 0213B]

[Note: In this preface Mercator teaches many things, but especially three that, down to the present day, have either been uncertain or unknown: first, that the creed he interprets truly belongs to Theodore—a fact denied by Facundus of Hermiane, who in this matter is less trustworthy than Marius; second, that Julian and his associates went to Theodore of Mopsuestia so that they might be instructed by him, as by the teacher, or rather the parent, of the Celestian doctrine, against Augustine, the most vigorous defender of the Catholic faith, before Julian composed his second work; finally, that a synod was held in Cilicia Secunda in which Julian was condemned by Theodore himself soon after his departure from the province.]

Marius Mercator, servant of Christ, sends greetings to his fellow servant, the reader.

1. [Note: This preface might seem not to be separable from its discourse and therefore ought to be assigned to the second part of the works of Marius Mercator, to which the creed of Theodore of Mopsuestia belongs as the source of Nestorian impiety. In my judgment, however, it should also be assigned to the first part, since it contains quite a few matters concerning Julian and Pelagian history—indeed, far more than concern the Nestorian affair. Yet, so that neither part might lack material proper to it, I have thought that nothing need be noted here except what pertains to the Pelagian matter.

The preface has altogether four parts. In the first, Mercator discloses his purpose in translating Theodore’s Greek discourse. In the second, he narrates Julian’s journey to Cilicia and the reason why he visited Theodore. In the third, he mentions the condemnation of that same Julian at a synod of the province of Cilicia Secunda. The fourth is occupied by the epilogue.

The time at which either the prefatory letter was written or Theodore’s creed was published in Latin will be discussed in the second part of the works of Marius Mercator.]

The Greek discourse belongs to Theodore, once bishop of the town of Mopsuestia, [Note: Namely, of Cilicia Secunda, according to the division made by the emperor Constantine. In this province, under the metropolitan see of Anazarbus—which was later also called Justinianopolis—eight bishoprics were counted: Aegeae, Castabala, Epiphanea, Flavias, Irenopolis, Alexandreia, Rhosus, and Mopsuestia, as is established by the Council of Mopsuestia, held by command of Justinian in 553 (reported in the fifth session of the Fifth Synod).] in the province of Cilicia. I have therefore attempted, to the extent of my ability, to transfer it into Latin, word for word, [Col. 0214B] wishing to insinuate into Latin ears that its perverse and Catholic-faith-opposed understanding of the Lord’s dispensation, an understanding sufficiently estranged from the truth, by which it wrongly deceived Nestorius, once bishop of Constantinople, must be avoided in every way and not followed.

2. I also wish to warn [Note: Julian is discussed in the notes to the preceding treatises. Concerning his see, since the matter has been called into question, something should be noted. Pontacus learnedly remarks in his notes that Prosper’s Chronicle, where it speaks of Julian, has different readings in different manuscripts. Hence different scholars, following different readings, have held different opinions concerning Julian’s episcopate. We have reconciled them all to some degree, at least the older opinions, under the guidance of Mercator (*Dissertation 2 on the authors and defenders of the Pelagian heresy*).

I said “the older opinions,” for it has not been possible to reconcile those among the more recent writers who, with the very learned Chifletius (*Pauline Illustrated*, part II, chapter 29), make Julian bishop of Atella, or who, with the learned Vignerius (*Preface to Part II of the Supplement to the Works of St. Augustine*), make him bishop of Caelia—certainly against the evidence of the better manuscripts and the clear testimony of Mercator, the most trustworthy of all the authors in this matter.

Both of them argue against the episcopate of Eclanum, which we establish in the second dissertation, using an argument that seems to me far from strong: the former because Julian is called Campanian by Gennadius, Prosper, and Bede; the latter because Augustine is said to have written that he was born in Apulia. Yet Eclanum is neither in Apulia nor in Campania, but among the Hirpini. Let it be, however, either Atella in Campania or Caelia among the Apulians of Peucetia.

The argument drawn from Julian’s homeland is weak. For how many bishops were made bishops in their own cities? Augustine was certainly not born at Hippo, nor Aurelius at Carthage, nor Innocent and Zosimus at Rome, nor Paulinus at Nola; nor were the other illustrious bishops of that period born in the cities whose churches they governed.

Nor is there greater force in what is taken either from Gennadius’s words (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 45): “Julian, a Campanian bishop, a man sharp in intellect,” and so forth; or from Prosper’s verses (*Epigram against the detractors of St. Augustine*):

“Or the Britons of the sea nourished this man with their own grain,

or the hearts of this Campanian swell with Campanian grass”;

or from Bede (*Preface to the Song of Songs*): “The minor works of Julian, bishop of Caelane in Campania.”

First, the commonly circulated manuscripts of Gennadius do not have the word *Campanus*, “Campanian,” but *Capuanus*, “Capuan”; neither word appears, according to Chifletius himself, in the manuscripts of Corbie and Jura. Indeed, the Corbie manuscript reads: “Julian, a man sharp in intellect,” and so forth; the Jura manuscript: “Julian, a bishop, a man sharp in intellect.”

Next, how is it established that Prosper—if it is Prosper—speaks of Julian in the verses cited, rather than of Celestius, who may have been Campanian? For two epigrams are circulated as having been written against Cassian, supposedly as a detractor of Saint Augustine, in which Cassian is alleged to have been associated with someone. Yet the genuine Prosper scarcely reproaches Cassian for association with Julian, but reproaches him greatly for association with Pelagius and Celestius. Moreover, whoever the poet may be, he accuses the detractor of arrogance in attacking a man renowned throughout the whole world. Cicero’s famous saying about Campanian arrogance is well known; therefore the subject is not Julian the Apulian but Celestius the Campanian.

Finally, Bede preferred to say that Julian was a bishop of Eclanum “of Campania” rather than “of the Hirpini,” partly because Campania and the Hirpini are neighboring provinces and Eclanum is situated scarcely anywhere but on the very border of the two; partly because Campania was much better known than the Hirpini. Indeed, when the name Campania is taken in a broader sense, the Hirpini themselves are included under it.]

I also wish to warn that Julian, a heretical Pelagian or Celestian, formerly bishop of the town of Eclanum, followed Theodore—having traversed lands, crossed the sea, and surveyed the East, he made his way with his associates and companions, his fellow travelers and sufferers (*συνταλαιπώροις*), with great exertion, as to a teacher renowned for proclaiming Christian doctrines—in order that he might be confirmed by him in defending and following the Pelagian or Celestian heresy [Note: Julian first professed an open defense of the Celestian heresy in his *Book of Faith* (*Dissertation* 6, chapter 6). He later explained the reasons for undertaking it especially in two places. First (*Unfinished Work*, book II, chapter 11):

“Now, after it began to be offered as a remedy and authority was added to pleasure, so that vice—the all-powerful queen of minds, the destroyer of honor, and the unconquered captor of every soul—might rage with the assent of almost the whole world, the defense of truth has become for us all the more honorable and all the more difficult. For against headlong peoples who are hostile to their own remedies, the rarity of those who administer medicine has little force. What, then? Shall we, out of regard for them, sound the retreat, avenge our insults by silence, and laugh at the shipwrecks of others from the harbor of conscience? Yet this hatred is opposed, first, by the benevolence we owe to the human race; next, by the faith we have in God, who, beyond that which often lifted up the ruins of desperate times [possibly: ‘even if he often lifted up the ruins of times that had been despaired of’], nevertheless rewarded with eternal recompense the steadfastness—which he willed to be practiced even to the hour of death—even if it were to produce no immediate result. Therefore, rejoicing in this consolation of faith, let us apply ourselves to the work we have begun,” and so forth.

In the latter passage (*Unfinished Work*, book III, chapter 10):

“We are asked why we do not agree that sin is natural. We answer: because it has no appearance of probability, much less of truth; no appearance of justice, no appearance of piety; because it makes the devil appear to be the creator of human beings,” and so forth.]

and hence, as though better instructed, might compose those eight volumes—which he considers extremely prudent—against the Catholic faith rather than against Augustine of holy memory.

[Col. 0216A] 3. Let the aforementioned Julian therefore recognize from this translation, if he is not reluctant to read it, that while the evil faith by which, as we have said, Theodore deceived Nestorius along with himself remains evident, Theodore is even more opposed to Julian and to his doctrine, concerning which he composed books in a wickedly swollen and diseased spirit; and let Julian recognize that, after his departure from Cilicia, he was also condemned by Theodore with an anathema at an assembly of the bishops of his province.

[Note: The silence concerning the assembly of the bishops of Cilicia Secunda is remarkable down to the present day, since there is no mention of it in any other writer and Mercator’s account is not very extensive. It is touched upon only in these few words: “and that, after his departure from Cilicia, he was condemned by him with an anathema at an assembly of the bishops of his province.” We must therefore use conjectures to investigate the time, cause, place, and name of the Fathers; this has been done with some probability in its proper place (*Dissertation 3 on synods in the Pelagian controversy*).]

4. Therefore let him not become angry or resentful toward us if we expose and refute him as alien to the Catholic faith and rightly condemned, together with Theodore, whose boundless praises he expounds in his books and whose authority he boasts of relying upon in his error; and let us mourn him, because he deserves mourning more than persecution with hatred.

[Note: Julian does praise Theodore in his final work, but briefly, and ranks him with Saints John Chrysostom and Basil the Great in these words (*Unfinished Work*, book III, chapter 113):

“I omit those things which the holy Scriptures—those things brought forth by the prophets, the evangelists, and the apostles—and the disputants shining with Catholic soundness, John, Basil, Theodore, and their like, have commended: that it is far more laborious to commit crimes than to avoid them.”

Augustine replies to these words:

“If only you held the faith of these men, you would not deny sin in infants.”

By these words the holy teacher may seem to place Theodore among the defenders of original sin, and not yet to have known what Theodore had written on that subject against the Catholic faith.

Nevertheless, this whole passage is burdened in my judgment by no slight suspicion, partly because it joins Theodore, still living, to two other Fathers who had long since died—a thing that scarcely occurs; partly because Theodore was not, even at that time, so unblemished in reputation in other matters of faith that Augustine should have commended him without some qualification.

The learned Vignerius suggested that *Theodoretus* might perhaps be read instead of *Theodorus*. But even if Theodoret held sound doctrine concerning original sin—a question I do not now raise—I still cannot see clearly how a recently created bishop, and not very advanced in age, certainly still among the living, could rightly be numbered with men and teachers so holy who had long since died.

What if *Diodorus* should be read instead of *Theodorus*? He had died long before, still enjoyed a great reputation for learning, no question had yet been raised concerning his writings, and nothing beyond the celebrity of his name had yet reached Augustine, since his writings had not yet been translated into Latin.

If anyone approves this conjecture concerning the name, let him go on to conjecture that Theodore himself received from his teacher Diodore the heresy that he later transmitted to Julian, first through others and afterward himself. We shall examine this matter more carefully in the second part of Mercator’s works.

Amid such uncertainty, until a new light appears, the old reading must be retained, at least because of Mercator’s authority: he testifies that Julian lavished endless praise upon Theodore. This is especially so since the text of Julian reported by Augustine agrees with Mercator, if it is accepted as it stands in the printed books. It shows both how Julian boasts in his error of relying upon Theodore’s authority and how immense is the praise of a man ranked with Chrysostom and Basil. Meanwhile Vignerius’s text should be corrected, and *protulerunt* (“brought forth”) restored in place of *pertulerunt* (“endured”).]

## EXPOSITION OF THEODORUS’S PERVERSE FAITH

Those who are now being instructed for the first time in the clear understanding of ecclesiastical doctrines, or who have decided to turn from heretical error to the truth, ought to be taught what we believe.

(And the rest, as reported in the latter part. The final words of the creed are:)

[Col. 0218A] “Let everyone who thinks contrary to these things be anathema.”

(Mercator’s refutation follows:)

“Rather, we Catholics say to you, who have uttered such things with your most impure mouth and most wicked tongue: may you and all who agree with you be perpetually anathema,” and so forth.

(Mercator then continues:)

“Let us establish from his writings, which we have translated from the Greek, what sort of bad faith the aforementioned Theodore also possessed.”

## FIRST EXCERPT OF THEODORE

From the second codex, book four, folio ten, against Saint Augustine, who defends original sin and teaches in accordance with the Catholic faith that Adam was made mortal through transgression.

[Note: Theodore of Mopsuestia … book four … against Augustine … and Adam made mortal through transgression.—

1. *Theodore of Mopsuestia.* He wrote almost without limit, but two works in particular are full of errors: one concerning the Incarnation of the Word, which he in reality abolished; the other against Saint Augustine, defender of the Catholic faith in which original sin is believed. From the second work Marius excerpted what is now published.

When I examined this entire little work more carefully, I realized that I was dealing with an exceedingly obscure subject, one neither commonly known nor even heard of by the writers of Pelagian history themselves. I therefore thought it necessary, although with considerable labor, to investigate everything in approved authors that might bring light to the matter. Nor did the labor disappoint my hope; rather, it surpassed my diligence incredibly. I collected a good deal which, although it may perhaps seem excessive, I nevertheless judged should be presented in view of the subject and the place—not merely in the form of a dissertation, as someone might have advised, but with observations attached to each word of the title, so that brevity might be served as far as was permissible and nothing worthy of notice might be omitted. Let the reader therefore accept with goodwill these not inconsiderable notes on a short title; the novelty of the subject will doubtless remove the weariness of reading.

2. *Book four.* This work was contained in five books altogether, although Mercator mentions the third and fourth. Nor do I think it different from the five books that Photius says he read, under this title: “Five books of Theodore of Antioch against those asserting that human beings sin by nature, not by will” (*Codex* 177). Nor do I doubt that the excerpts found both in Vigilius’s *Constitutum*, without a designation of the books; in the fourth session of the Fifth Synod, under this title—“From the book of Theodore of Mopsuestia: that God introduced death, and from book five concerning creation, or that God made good and evil,” and so forth; and finally in Leontius Scholasticus (*Against the Nestorians and Eutychians*, book III, no. 28)—belong to the five books read by Photius.

I have therefore thought that both the complete codex of Photius, since it contains many things worth knowing, and the excerpts I have mentioned should be presented: not merely as fragments related to those of Marius—which would itself be sufficient reason for presenting them—but also as certain complements, from which much light may shine either upon the Marian excerpts or upon the history.]

## FROM THE LIBRARY OF PHOTIUS, CODEX 177

The work of Theodore of Antioch, who was bishop of Mopsuestia, as we gather from some of his letters, was read under this title: “Against those asserting that human beings sin by nature, not by will.” [Col. 0218A] This disputation is completed in five books, which he wrote against Westerners infected with this contamination. He says that the author of this heresy arose from there, that he was now living in the regions of the East, and that he had composed books on the heresy recently devised by him and sent them to his countrymen at home, so that by this method he had already drawn many of them over to his opinion and had even imbued entire churches with those absurd doctrines.

He calls the author of those books Aram—whether this is his name or surname is uncertain. He says that this man also added a fictitious fifth Gospel, pretending that he had found it in the libraries of Eusebius of Palestine. He further rejected the version of the divine Old Testament produced by the Seventy translators when they met together, as well as the interpretations of Symmachus, Aquila, and others, and dared to prepare a certain new version of his own. For he had not, like them, been accustomed from childhood to the Hebrew language, nor had he learned the meaning of sacred Scripture; he had merely placed himself under the instruction of certain Hebrews of degraded status and from this had undertaken to compose his own edition.

The principal doctrines of that sect are approximately these:

[Col. 0218C] Human beings sin by nature, not by will. By “nature,” I mean not that nature with which Adam was endowed and in which he was created at the beginning—for they assert that this nature was good and the good work of God—but the nature he acquired after sin, when through transgression and sin he exchanged the good for the bad and the immortal for the mortal. In this way, they say, those who had previously been good by nature also became wicked by nature, and acquired sin in their nature rather than in their will.

The second doctrine is derived from this: infants, although newly born, are not free from sin, since because of Adam’s transgression a nature established in sins is propagated to all his descendants as a sinful nature, to use their expression. He says that they also cite: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities” (Psalm 50:7), and passages of the same kind; and that they invoke the holy baptism and communion of the sacred body, which are bestowed even upon infants for the remission of sins, as support for their own opinion.

[Col. 0218D] Moreover, no mortal is righteous. This too follows from what they posited at the beginning: “For,” says the Prophet, “no flesh shall be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142:2), and similar passages.

Fourth—O blasphemous and impious words!—not even Christ, God, is free from wickedness, since he assumed a nature infected with sins. “Although,” he says, “in other blasphemies of theirs as well one may observe that they attribute human nature to him not truly and naturally, but only figuratively.”

Fifth, they assert that marriage—or at least the desire for intercourse and the emission of semen, and everything similar by which the human race is propagated through succession—are works of the perverse nature into which Adam fell through sin, and that by the defect of that nature he then took upon himself the whole swarm of all evils.

These are the doctrines of the sectarians.

Theodore is right, then, to detest and reject these very doctrines and at times to refute their absurd and blasphemous opinions excellently and forcefully. He also adapts the proper meanings to the passages of sacred Scripture that they abused, so as thoroughly to convict their ignorance. Yet this is not his consistent practice. For he seems to us in many respects to be giving birth to the sect of Nestorius, and at least concerning the end of punishments to be muttering the opinion of Origen.

But when he further asserts that Adam was mortal from the very beginning of his formation, and that God, in order that we might hate sin, pretended that death had been imposed as a punishment for sin, I do not think that he offers any sound doctrine; rather, he seems to expose himself to many accusations if anyone demands reasons for it, however sharply such an opinion may, as he himself perhaps said, fight against the heretics. For if something fights against what is worse, it is not immediately good; evil too fights against itself. Only if something is plainly in harmony with right reason and manifestly with the sacred writings should it finally be accepted, even if no heresy dares resist that doctrine.

Nor would I count among the doctrines of truth, as a carefully considered statement or one known to the Church of God, his assertion that there are two remissions of sins: one concerning sins committed, and the other—which, I do not know who could call a remission, although that is what he calls it—sinlessness itself, or no longer sinning. For, as is evident, we must use several explanatory expressions to clarify this new remission of sins. What correct speech calls “sinlessness,” he calls the perfect and most complete remission of sins, and the total destruction of sin.

What, then, is this remission of sins, and where did it take place, and from what did it originate? “It began,” he says, “to reveal itself from the time when Christ the Lord assumed flesh and gave himself to us as a pledge. It is granted perfectly both on account of good works and in that restoration which will take place after the resurrection of the flesh; in order to attain it, both we and newly born infants are baptized.”

So far, what has been said is sufficiently splendid, and almost commands everyone to yearn for the end. Speak, then, about what follows—and what does this mean? We offer you attentive ears. What, I ask, is this perfect remission of sins? “We shall no longer sin after the resurrection,” you say. What an immense hope you have cast us down from! Without now asking how it can properly be called a remission of sins, I shall ask only this briefly: consider what you are saying. Does Christ therefore seem to you to have become human and been nailed to the cross so that you would not sin there after the resurrection? Did those who departed this life before Christ came into the world sin there? And if perhaps we are not baptized, do you think that we—and infants as well—will still sin there? What then? Will all unbelievers again in the future age steal, commit fornication, act impiously, and practice robbery, fulfilling every wicked desire of their hearts? For you do not find sufficiently just punishments even for the things they committed here, however serious they may be. But I have already shown sufficiently why this remission of sins itself cannot be approved.

Perhaps, however, he was led to this conclusion without even intending it, merely to untie the knots of those who ask uncertainly: “Why do children participate in the most holy mysteries? Why are they judged worthy of baptism, unless they too abound in sins, since sin is already implanted in nature itself?” For these sacraments are bestowed for the remission of sins.

Yet he ought to have resolved that question in another way—although it admits many other means of resolution—and, after considering the absurd consequences that follow from this remission of sins itself, he ought not to have fabricated anything of this sort in such a monstrous manner.

Thus far Photius. The six fragments that follow are taken from the fourth session of the Fifth Synod, in which, besides Theodore’s impious creed and excerpts from the books of Saint Cyril against the same man, seventy-one passages collected from various works of Theodore and full of blasphemy are numbered.

[Col. 0220B] Theodore, from the third book of his commentary on creation, where he says that God taught sin and introduced death (No. 56).

“Because Adam did not obey, he was afterward subjected to death; and we have been taught that this happened because of disobedience, although even apart from disobedience it was brought about by the Creator for our benefit: we have all been instructed in sin.”

The same Theodore, from the fourth and fifth books of his commentary on creation, in which he also says that both good and evil were made by God (No. 57).

“Therefore he did not inflict death upon human beings unwillingly and contrary to his own judgment; nor did he grant sin access for no useful purpose. For he was certainly not unable, had he been unwilling, to prevent this from happening; rather, because he knew it to be useful for us—and indeed for all rational beings—that the worse and inferior should first gain access, and that afterward these should be abolished while better things were introduced. [Col. 0220C] For this reason God divided creation into two states, the present and the future: in the latter he would lead everything to immortality and immutability, while in the present he temporarily leaves us in mortality and mutability. For if he had made us immortal and immutable from the beginning, we would have had no distinction from irrational beings, since we would not have known our proper good; and, ignorant of mutability, we would have been ignorant of the good of immutability; not knowing death, we would not have known the gain of immortality; ignorant of corruption, we would not have praised incorruption; not knowing the burden of sufferings, we would not have marveled at freedom from suffering. To put it briefly, and not make a long speech: if we had not experienced evils, we could not even have earned knowledge of those good things.”
