The same author, in the same work, asserting that angels, human beings, and demons are likewise evil (No. 58).

“Now it is necessary that all rational beings together—[Col. 0220D] I mean the invisible beings and ourselves, whose body is mortal but whose soul is in every respect like those same invisible and rational substances—should here undergo the present mutability, so that we may be instructed in the best teaching of religion [Col. 0221A] and trained in benevolence.”

The same author, abolishing judgment and saying that all things were made mutable and mortal, and that again all things will immediately after the resurrection be immutable and immortal, after the likeness of Christ (No. 59).

“What pleased God was to divide creation into two states: one, the present, in which he made everything mutable; the other, the future, when, renewing all things, he will transfer them to immutability. He showed us the beginning of this in the dispensation of the Lord Jesus Christ: although he was one of us, he raised him from the dead and made his body immortal and his soul immutable. By this he demonstrated that the same thing will happen with respect to the whole of creation.”

The same author, from the fourth book of his Commentary on Creation (No. 60).

[Col. 0221B] “Once it has been firmly established that, just as through the resurrection we shall have an incorruptible body and an immutable soul, so too the invisible and rational natures will attain immutability, it follows that they are now receiving conversion, as is shown by the many tens of thousands of demons who have repeatedly been converted, but that then they will be with us in immutability.”

The same author, from the fifth book of his Commentary on Creation, saying that God, knowing sin to be advantageous for human beings, arranged for it to occur (No. 61).

“For he knew that they would certainly sin; yet he permitted this to happen, knowing that it was advantageous for them. For it was not possible that he who, after making beings that did not previously exist, had shown them to be masters of so many things and had set before them such great goods that they might enjoy them, should prevent access to sin if he knew that this was advantageous for them. Indeed, it was not otherwise possible for us to learn about sin, the distress of sufferings, and inferior things, and to have our weakness demonstrated in these matters, so as to display the greatness of the immutability that he would afterward grant us, unless these things had been arranged by God in the beginning in such a way that, through comparison and experience, we could know the greatness of those infinite goods. For this reason, since he allowed sin to enter as something that would benefit us, he found great assistance in its struggle.”

Leontius, after making many objections to Theodore, says: “These are small matters” (Book III *Against the Eutychians and Nestorians*, vol. IV of Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, p. 75). “But add this for me: that Adam’s sin was fabricated, and that God was its author, so that a most unjust judgment against Adam—who had not sinned but had been condemned through slander—and his banishment might become a just and plausible cause for redeeming the world. Did Christ not come because of this root of evils, and of the rest of humanity’s subsequent impiety, in order to save Adam, like a good Shepherd saving a sheep snatched away and gone astray from a flock of a hundred?”

I shall briefly touch upon what is reported from Photius, Leontius, and the Fifth Synod [Col. 0221D], weighing each item more carefully and stating what I have either conjectured or established by reasoning. Some of these matters are certain to me, others doubtful.

It is certain, although many think otherwise, that Theodore did not write the work in question against the Manichaeans, who say that human nature is evil. For he wrote against Westerners infected with the error he attacks; its author had his homeland in the West, was still living in the regions of the East, and had drawn entire churches over to his opinion. These and many other details that follow do not fit Manichaeus, who, having been born in the East, had long since perished and was not accepted by whole churches, and so forth.

It is likewise certain that those are mistaken who think that Theodore’s work attacked the Origenists. The same arguments apply against them, and Origen was never accused—indeed, could not have been accused, even by malicious opponents—of any of the five doctrines censured by the man of Mopsuestia, except perhaps insofar as he defended it together with the Catholics, though not in a Catholic manner, because of his preconceived opinion that souls had been precipitately confined in bodily prisons to undergo punishment for preceding sins.

It is equally certain that, when Theodore’s opponent is described, Jerome is indicated by eight unmistakable marks. He is said to have been born in the West, to have been established in the East, to have sent books from there to his fellow countrymen, to have fabricated a fifth Gospel—namely, the Gospel according to the Nazarenes—to have found it in the library of Eusebius, to have attempted a new interpretation of the Old Testament, not to have been imbued with knowledge of the Hebrew language from his earliest years, and to have learned it from a low-born Hebrew, namely Bar-Chaba.

Finally, it is certain that the five doctrines Theodore attributes to his opponent are precisely those which the Celestians imputed, partly truthfully and partly through slander, to Catholic defenders of original sin and especially to Saint Augustine: that human beings possess sin by nature—not the nature created by God, but one corrupted by the first parent; that infants are baptized for the remission of sins; that no mortal is righteous, that is, without sin; that Christ himself was not free from sin; and that marriage and its use are the work of a corrupted nature.

What follows is less certain. First, I think that Theodore’s work was composed when Julian was staying in Cilicia; but Theodore lied both about the date, as though he were writing while Jerome was still alive, and about the opponent, whom for three reasons he represented as someone other than Augustine: to favor Julian, who was using Theodore’s influence among his own people; so as not to incur the hatred of the whole Church, from which he knew Augustine was highly esteemed; and so as not to irritate the court of either empire, where he had learned—perhaps from Julian himself—that Augustine possessed very great influence.

Next, I think that this work was entitled *Commentary on Creation*, against those who asserted that human beings sin by nature, not by will; and that one part of the title should be taken from the Fifth Synod, the other from Photius.

I also think that, since the complete work consisted of five books, the first was devoted to explaining the doctrines that Theodore undertook to attack and to disparaging their author through slander; the second to praises both of God the Creator and of rational creation; the third to assembling arguments against the mortality of human beings contracted through the sin of the first parent; the fourth to attacking the Catholic faith concerning original sin and the reason why infants are baptized; and the fifth to resolving the arguments of the Catholics, especially those concerning original sin. I am led to this opinion partly because this arrangement appears intrinsically suitable and can be gathered with some clarity from what survives; partly because the Celestians customarily began their disputation with praises of the Creator and of creation; partly because Mercator excerpted from the third book what concerns human mortality and from the fourth what concerns original sin; and finally because what is reported in the Fifth Synod from the fifth book, and what Photius reports from the end of the work, plainly belong to resolving the difficulties raised by those who inquire, as Photius puts it.

### 3. Against Saint Augustine, etc.

Photius appears to object, as was just stated, and seems to report that Theodore called Jerome rather than Augustine “Aram,” that is, accursed or cursing; but this is only an appearance. For his words do not rule out Mercator’s opinion. Why could Theodore not also have lied, as I have already said? Why could he not, without lying, have first written the same books against Jerome while Jerome was still alive—and indeed immediately after publishing the three dialogues—and then have issued them, slightly altered, against Augustine after being confronted by Julian? Finally, why could he not have given one work either two forms or two titles, under one of which it appeared to Mercator, under the other to Photius?

Indeed, since both holy men—I mean Jerome and Augustine—defended the Catholic faith not only with one spirit but also with the same scriptural testimonies and arguments, whoever attacked the faith could properly be said to have argued against both.

Certainly Jerome, when he once congratulated Augustine on the hatred he had incurred from the Pelagians, proudly declared that he shared it. Such was the fellowship of the teachers of the Church, such the communion of truly evangelical men: “Courage,” he says (*Epistle* 195, in Augustine), “in your virtue; you are celebrated throughout the world. Catholics honor and venerate you as the restorer of the ancient faith; and, what is a sign of greater glory, all heretics detest you and persecute me with equal hatred, so that those whom they cannot kill with swords they may kill by their wish.”

Another conjecture could also be proposed, one that is plausible in itself and supports the other: namely, that these books were in fact written against Augustine after the books *On the Merits and Remission of Sins* had been composed, as Mercator correctly understood; but that they were published, at least in the East, later under the fictitious appearance of being directed against Jerome. This was because Jerome’s fame was greater in the East than Augustine’s, and because a Greek work would more readily be received and read by Greek-speaking people, especially in places where Jerome was highly renowned but also considerably envied: partly among certain monks, both Origenists and followers who rivaled Rufinus; partly, and especially, among the presbyters and bishops who were friends of John of Jerusalem; and partly among otherwise good men who were advancing the Pelagian cause, as though it were being pursued with greater force than the matter warranted.

I therefore think that Theodore wrote this work at the request of the Pelagians, against Augustine’s books *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, especially the first and third; but that he published it, perhaps with some portions altered, so that it might answer Jerome’s dialogues and his letter to Ctesiphon. Indeed, I almost assert that Marius Mercator translated from Greek not merely the four fragments that we present, but the entire work—at least in the form in which it fought against Augustine.

The first part of my opinion—that Theodore undertook this labor against Augustine’s books *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*—is supported by Mercator’s title: “Theodore of Mopsuestia, from the fourth book of the second codex, folio ten, against Saint Augustine, etc.” Augustine’s first and third books deal with the questions of Adam’s death through sin, original sin, and the baptism of infants; and Photius reports that the five books he read concerned sin, the baptism of infants, and the sinlessness of adults.

The second part—that the books were published against Jerome, though perhaps somewhat altered—is sufficiently indicated both by Photius’s words concerning the author whom Theodore attacks under a fictitious name, and by the certain fact that the Pelagians responded both to Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon and to the three dialogues. Among that faction it was either customary or established almost as a law to leave nothing written against them unanswered; indeed, they sought either to deter their opponents from writing by threats of response or, if they could not do so, to overthrow them by a multitude of books.

[Col. 0224A] Finally, I infer the third part from these words of Marius: “But let us demonstrate from his writings, which we have translated from Greek, how perfidious the aforesaid Theodore also was.”

### 4. And Adam was made mortal through transgression

As I have often said, Mercator wished to press one question especially forcefully against the Pelagians. He asked Augustine about this matter, either exclusively or above all, and obtained a response from him. From Theodore’s books and Nestorius’s discourses he excerpted nothing except what concerned the same question. He reduces the whole matter to this as its central point, and rightly so, of Julian’s final work against Saint Augustine. Finally, in the four excerpts before us he argues only that Theodore asserted that human beings had not been made mortal by sin, while at the same time claiming that the Catholic doctrine was wrongly inferred from Scripture (excerpt 1), conflicted with divine justice (excerpt 2), and violated the laws of wisdom (excerpt 3).

### 5. Speaking in a Catholic manner

Augustine had used the celebrated scriptural testimony, “On whatever day you eat, you shall surely die” (Genesis II, 17), to prove that human mortality arose from sin. Theodore first argues that Augustine improperly used such a testimony: for God, he says (in the second part of the excerpt), should be understood to have threatened death to disobedient Adam no otherwise than he later threatened it to the Jews in the Law, and than people commonly threaten sinners—that is, not the very possibility of dying, which everyone possesses innately, but the experience of death, which all dread.

Then he argues that the sentence of God condemning the guilty should be understood in the same sense (Part III, 4 and 5) both where it concerns death [Col. 0224C] and where it concerns labor and cultivation of the earth. Yet the latter expression certainly does not mean that Adam was then first assigned to labor itself, but to labor not yielding an adequate return. For immediately after his creation he is said to have been placed in paradise “to work it and keep it” (Genesis II, 15). Therefore the former expression likewise does not mean that after sin human beings immediately became subject to death itself, but to violent death and death suffered before its appointed time. For, since the human being was made from earth and by a fatal necessity will return to earth, God said, “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Genesis III, 19), not “You shall become earth because you have sinned”—which he would certainly have said if he had then first made him mortal, since in ordinary speech to be earth means precisely to be dissoluble, and therefore mortal.]

[Col. 0219A]

### 1.

[Note: [Col. 0220D] Theodore had undoubtedly prefaced this with arguments drawn from the formation of the human being out of clay, by which he would prove that the human being possesses a dissoluble and therefore mortal nature. For his disciples, thoroughly faithful followers of their teacher, were accustomed to argue from this passage in Genesis as the starting point of their discussion: thus Rufinus the Syrian in his little book *On the Faith* (chapter 29 and following), and Julian in his final work against Saint Augustine (Book III of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 30). I would not improperly call this the marrow or substance of Theodore’s five books, composed in Cilicia in Theodore’s own presence (Mercator, book *On the Notes*).]

With so much existing to demonstrate that Adam was formed from earth in such a way that he was altogether mortal, he wished to direct the discussion toward the appropriate food and was thereafter unable [Note: [Col. 0220D] Henry of Noris printed *volens*, as it stands in the Vatican manuscript that he used. Baluzius.] to perceive the truth, joining special pleading to a seductive lie in place of true doctrine [Col. 0223A] [Note: [Col. 0224C] He seems to attack Augustine as though Augustine had substituted the devil’s words for God’s words. For if the Hebrew text and the Latin Vulgate are consulted, and even the Greek of Symmachus, the tempter used the plural number when urging sin, whereas God used the singular when giving the command to abstain from eating the fruit. The Septuagint, however, also translated the Hebrew text with the plural number; Ambrose believed that some hidden mystery lay concealed in this passage (Book *On Paradise*, chapter 5).], and so forth.

[Col. 0224A] 2.

[Note: [Col. 0224D] From this passage in Genesis Augustine formerly concluded (Book *On the Merits of Sins*, chapter 2) that bodily death had been brought about by sin. Those who say that Adam was created so that he would die even without the merit of sin, by the necessity of nature rather than as punishment for fault, plainly try to refer the statement in the Law, “On the day you eat, you shall surely die” (Genesis II, 17), not to bodily death but to the death of the soul that occurs in sin, and so forth. The passages bearing on this subject in Book XIII of *On the City of God*, chapter 23, and Book XI of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 23, should be read. Symmachus translated it thus: *θνητὸς ἔσῃ*, “you shall be mortal,” a translation that Jerome prefers to the others.]

God does not say, “You shall be mortal,” but “You shall surely die” (Genesis II, 17); although they were by nature mortal, he threatened to inflict the experience of death, which he also delayed bringing to completion in accordance with the custom of his own benevolence. For just as, when he says, “Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed in return” (Genesis IX, 6), he does not say that whoever kills a human being will be mortal, but that he is worthy to be condemned to such a death, so here too he said, “You shall surely die”—not that they would then become mortal, but that through transgression they would incur the sentence of death [Note: [Col. 0225C] Baluzius has “for transgression.” EDITOR.].

### 3.

But observe also the divine sentence that God appears to impose upon Adam after the sin. For he says (Genesis III, 17): “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I had commanded you, saying, ‘From this alone you shall not eat,’ you ate from it: cursed is the earth in your works; in sorrow you shall eat of it all the days of your life. It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the grass of the field; and in the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth.”

By these words he threatened that Adam would have a life full of hardship, thereafter obtaining from the earth with labor the fruits by which he would be nourished and sustained, and no longer having, as before, such abundant provision as he had enjoyed from the plenty of paradise. For God did not impose cultivating the earth as a punishment, as though he were transferring human beings from an immortal nature into mortality, since he had also assigned paradise to him “to work it and keep it” (Genesis II, 15). Rather, in place of the former abundance and delight of paradise, he threatened that his sustenance from the fruits of the earth would be laborious.

[Col. 0225C] For, having been made wholly mortal [Note: [Col. 0225C] Baluzius has “as mortal,” and notes: “Thus the old books. Garnerius omitted the word ‘as’; Noris changed it to ‘so.’ EDITOR.”], he then needed the fruits of paradise, just as now he seeks the fruits of the earth; and, deprived as punishment of his former delights, he is chastised by this most sorrowful and laborious way of life.

[Col. 0226A] 4.

Therefore, in conclusion, he appropriately added, “For you are earth, and you shall return to earth” (Genesis III, 17), thereby also indicating the mortality of nature. He did not give this name to the earth because an immortal being, now for the first time beginning to receive a sentence of death, had become subject to it—as the most learned defenders of original sin, or rather the remarkable fathers of sin, assert—but because divine Scripture indicated that this name properly belongs to one who was mortal by nature from the beginning. Scripture frequently applies this term to human beings to display their corruptible and dissoluble nature. “For he remembered,” it says, “that we are dust; a human being’s days are like grass, and like a flower of the field, so shall he flourish, because the spirit has passed through him, and his place shall know him no more” (Psalm CII, 15).

It means that we are all corruptible and dissoluble, like grass that blooms briefly and soon perishes. For we live only a short time, and afterward arrive altogether at nonexistence. Abraham likewise says, “I am earth and ashes” (Genesis XVIII, 27), as though he were saying, “I am not worthy to converse with so great a God, being made from earth and destined in every respect to become this.” He therefore ought rather to have said, “You shall become earth, and you shall return to earth,” if human nature were only then first becoming mortal.

## SECOND EXCERPT OF THEODORE

From the second codex, book three, four leaves before the end of the book.

### 1.

[Note: [Col. 0225C] Theodore attacks the Catholic doctrine of human mortality, or chiefly for this reason: the sentence of God would be unjust if he imposed such a great punishment for such a sin, when one person’s fault was being expiated by all; Scripture denies that this is just. A serious punishment, namely death, would follow a slight fault, namely eating the fruit; equity forbids this. God’s wrath would extend to all, including the many who were saints—Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, and so forth—while the merits and virtues of so many great men resisted it in vain; this conflicts with divine clemency. The first righteous man, Abel, would have suffered the first vengeance for another’s injustice; it is impious even to think this. The devil, the first author and instigator of sin, would nevertheless have continued immortal; this is contrary to reason. Enoch did not die, although he was far inferior in virtue to Moses, the prophets, the apostles, and the other martyrs celebrated by Paul: “of whom the world was not worthy” (Hebrews XI, 38). What justice, then, would there be in God, or how would he show no partiality, if one of Adam’s descendants, though less holy, were rescued from death while holier persons were condemned? If death is the punishment of sin, Christ, who was most holy, ought rather to have been exempted from the common necessity than Enoch, who possessed lesser righteousness, in accordance with the laws of divine wisdom.

From this he concludes that mortality is natural to human beings, and that God wisely established it, since it is useful for us to strive from mortality toward immortality, so that we first bear the image of the earthly and mortal Adam, and afterward that of the heavenly and immortal one. Christ himself demonstrated by his example that one must progress from the imperfect to the perfect: first he submitted to the necessity of nature and the law, being born of a woman, increasing in stature, circumcised, presented in the temple, obedient to his parents, and finally dying. Then he showed himself Lord of nature and the law, when he rose immortal from the tomb and, established at the right hand of the Father, possesses power over all. In addition, Theodore argues that, because the Word assumed mortality together with nature but did not assume sin, it follows that mortality belongs to nature, whereas sin belongs solely to the will.]

But that remarkable defender of original sin could perceive none of these things [Baluz. “foresee”] [Note: [Col. 0226D] It is uncertain to which of the two teachers the sentence refers. For the reproach that follows—namely, that this defender of original sin had not learned the sacred writings from infancy—could refer to Jerome, as is evident from Photius, but fits Augustine better according to Theodore’s intention, whether he is speaking ignorantly or rather maliciously. The same is true of the statement about the attempted movement of power. Julian chiefly brought both charges against the most holy teacher through slander; he reported them to Theodore concerning Augustine, first in writing from the West and afterward in personal conversation in Cilicia.], since he had not been trained in the divine Scriptures at all, nor, in accordance with the blessed Paul’s words, had learned the sacred writings from infancy (II Timothy III, 18). Yet, whether he was declaiming about scriptural meanings or about doctrine, he frequently and shamelessly uttered many absurdities, specific and general, about the Scriptures themselves and about many doctrines [Note: [Col. 0226D] Noris: “he proposed”—namely, things contrary to the doctrines of Scripture itself, which he shamelessly set forth in several places. BALUZIUS.], . For the exercise of power [Baluz. “movement of power”] prevented anyone from speaking against him, and only those who possessed knowledge of the divine Scriptures criticized him silently. [Note: [Col. 0227B] Augustine responds to this complaint of Julian the slanderer in words most worthy of notice: “Do not use that most wretched argument which all heretics use, whom the laws of Christian emperors restrain from pernicious license. For all such people say what you have said: that the party which, in discussion, substitutes terror obtains no assent from the prudent but extorts blind assent from the fearful.”]

Against which book, finally, was Theodore directing his attack when he wrote that Augustine had most recently said that God, in anger, had consigned Adam, guilty of disobedience, and all his descendants to death? Was he referring to the fourteenth tractate on John, on the words “The wrath of God remains upon him,” where Augustine says: “All who are born possess the wrath of God—but what wrath of God? The wrath that the first Adam incurred. For the first human being sinned in this way and heard, ‘You shall surely die’; that man became mortal, and we began to be born mortal; we were born with the wrath of God”? Or rather to the exposition of Psalm CI, on the words “From the face of your wrath and indignation,” where Augustine addresses God: “That is your wrath, Lord, in Adam: the wrath with which we were all born, to which we were joined by being born; wrath from the propagation of iniquity, wrath from the mass of sin, according to what the Apostle says: ‘We too were once children of wrath, like the rest’ (Ephesians II, 3); and whence the Lord says: ‘The wrath of God remains upon him’ (John III, 35).” Or finally to the commentary on Psalm XXXVII, where he says: “By nature punishment was made for us, from the vengeance of the first human being; what was punishment has become nature for us.” Hence the Apostle says, “We too were once children of wrath,” that is, bearing vengeance, and so forth.

Yet, although these passages indicate to some extent the wrath of God that Theodore mentions, they scarcely fit the word “most recently,” if the dates of Theodore’s writing are considered. Augustine delivered or wrote the tractates on John and the expositions of the Psalms either before the Pelagian heresy arose or at least before he composed the three books *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*; yet Theodore published the work whose excerpts we have before us approximately twelve years after the publication of those books.

Therefore, unless I am mistaken, Theodore was referring to the *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, where these words are read (chapter 25): “For the Lord had threatened the human being with the punishment of death if he sinned, granting him free will while nevertheless ruling him by command and terrifying him with destruction; and he placed him in the happiness of paradise, as though in the shadow of life, so that, if he preserved righteousness, he might ascend from there to better things.”

Then, after he had become an exile through sin (chapter 26), “he also bound his offspring, whom he had corrupted in himself as in a root by sinning, with the punishment of death and condemnation, so that whatever offspring was born from him and from the wife who had been condemned together with him, through whom he had sinned, would contract original sin through carnal concupiscence—in which a similar punishment was repaid for disobedience—and through various errors and sufferings would be drawn to that final punishment, without end, together with the rebellious angels, its corrupters, possessors, and companions. ‘Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Romans V, 12). For in that passage the Apostle called the entire human race ‘the world.’”

The words first cited contain both the wrath of God threatening, the vengeance of punishment, and the sentence of death imposed upon all. Moreover, Augustine composed the *Enchiridion* after Jerome’s death, and therefore after the year 420. Theodore wrote the five books with which we are now concerned against Augustine about the year 423.]

But most recently he fell into this novelty of doctrine [Baluz. “returned to”], saying that God, in anger and fury, had decreed Adam to be mortal and, because of his one offense, had punished all human beings, even those not yet born, with death. In arguing thus he neither fears nor is ashamed to entertain concerning God ideas that no one has ever attempted to entertain even concerning human beings of sound judgment and some concern for justice [Note: [Col. 0228C] Noris: “would judge.” BALUZIUS.]; [Note: [Col. 0228C] The testimonies Theodore cites (Part II, nos. 11 and 12), whether from the prophets or from the Apostle, were used by Julian in his book *On the Faith* when he argued against original sin. He says: “Since, therefore, we have already spoken of the goodness of nature, of blessing, and of the honor of marriage, we consequently reject natural sin, or whatever other name it may be called, lest we inflict an injury upon God the Creator of all things by claiming that anything could have been made by him together with sin, and lest we accuse the testimonies of his Scriptures of falsehood. For they say in the Old Testament: ‘The fathers shall not die for the sons, nor the sons for the fathers; each shall die for his own sin’ (II Kings XIV, 6). And another prophet says: ‘Why do you use this proverb in the land of Israel, saying: The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children’s teeth are set on edge? As I live, says the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son, they are all mine. The soul that sins, it shall die’ (Ezekiel XVIII, 2). Again: ‘The son shall not bear the iniquity of his father, nor the father bear the iniquity of his son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him’ (ibid. 20). And there: ‘I shall judge each of you according to his ways, house of Israel, says the Lord’ (ibid. 30). And the Apostle says: ‘We must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil’ (II Corinthians V, 10). Again: ‘Each of us shall give an account of himself to God’ (Romans XIV, 12). And elsewhere: ‘Each of us shall bear his own burden’ (Galatians VI, 5).”]

nor did he remember that divine utterance which says that this proverb would no longer be spoken in Israel: “The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” [Col. 0227B] because these are the words of Adonai [Col. 0228A] the Lord: “The teeth of those who have eaten the sour grape shall be set on edge” (Ezekiel XVIII, 2) [Note: [Col. 0228D] Thus the Bellovacensis manuscript. The Vatican manuscript has “were numbed.” Noris has “are set on edge.” Shortly afterward the Vatican manuscript has “shall be set on edge.” BALUZIUS.], thereby showing that God does not punish one person in place of another, as some mistakenly think, but that each person will give an account for his own offenses.

### 2.

Blessed Paul likewise adds statements agreeing with these: “God,” he says, “who will render to each according to his works” (Romans II, 6); and, “Each of us shall bear his own burden” (Galatians VI, 5); and, “Why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ” (Romans XIV, 10).

### 3.

But that remarkable man imagined that, because of one sin [Note: [Col. 0228D] “Sin of such magnitude.” The old books have the reading as we printed it. Henry of Noris restored: “He judged that Adam’s sin had so moved God with fury that he wished to subject him to a terrible punishment.” Garnerius instead has: “sin of such magnitude,” and so forth. BALUZIUS.], God had been moved by such fury that he subjected him to the most atrocious punishment and promulgated the same sentence against all his descendants [Baluz. omits “and”]—among whom no one could easily count how many righteous persons there had been. Above all, he ought to have considered how wholly incongruous it would seem that Noah, Abraham, David, Moses, and the countless other righteous should be made liable to punishment because of one offense, one sin consisting in tasting the fruit of the tree [Baluz. “the approved fruit of the tree”]; and that God should extend his wrath beyond the bounds of justice [Baluz. “has extended”], so that [Note: [Col. 0229D] This is the reading of the Bellovacensis copy. The Vatican manuscript reads “of all whose.” From this Noris produced “of the descendants.” BALUZIUS.] he would cast aside all the virtues of so many righteous people and consign them to so great a punishment because of Adam’s one sin.

### 4.

For even if he considered nothing else, he ought at least to have judged consistently concerning Abel [Baluz. “if he considered nothing else, at least concerning Abel in a consistent manner”], who, being the first righteous man, was the first to die—and, if God had established death as the punishment of human beings, how could it not have been the height of impiety for the one who had caused the sin to live, and for Eve, the discoverer of wickedness, to live with him as well? I pass over the devil, who has continued thus far in immortality; yet the first righteous man, the discoverer of virtue, and the first to undertake the care of divine worship, was struck by the punishment of sinners before them all [Note: [Col. 0229D] Baluzius corrects *pene* to *poena*, supported by the ancient books. EDITOR.].

5. It was necessary, moreover, for that most learned man to consider carefully Enoch also, who did not die. For he was not endowed with such virtue or piety that he surpassed everyone—Moses, I mean, and the prophets and apostles, or all the others of whom the most blessed Paul says: “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. 11:38)—so that, while they had died, he alone should continue without experiencing death. Rather, from the beginning God [Baluz.: God had determined this] had determined within himself that mortals should first become mortal, but afterward rejoice in immortality, he himself arranging that this should happen for our benefit.

6. And a little later: “God,” he says, “showed these same things more plainly when he transferred Enoch and made him immortal. For if God introduced death as the cause of punishment through sin, and had not long ago determined this within himself, dispensing everything ineffably for our sake according to his own wisdom, Enoch certainly would not have existed as immortal, while the Lord Christ would have undergone the experience of death.”

7. And a little later: “For this reason,” he says, “the Lord became the author of all good things for human beings, so that, just as Adam was the initiator of the first and mortal condition, so he himself, being the initiator of the second and immortal condition, might first preserve the natural characteristics of the former Adam: while he is born from a woman; while he is wrapped in swaddling clothes; and while he gradually receives the increments of age.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] For the Italian edition of Luke is defective: in it the words “and grace” immediately dropped out. BALUZ.]

“For Jesus,” he says, “was advancing in age, wisdom, and grace before God and human beings” (Luke 2:52); while he receives circumcision; while, according to legal custom, he stands before God in the temple, is subject to his parents, and is devoted to the lawful manner of life. Thus also, to complete the remaining matters, he finally accepts death, as a tribute owed to nature: so that, dying according to the law of human nature and rising from the dead by divine power, he might become the beginning for all human beings who receive death according to their own nature, so that they might rise from the dead and be transformed into an immortal substance.

8. For just as we have all been made conformed to Adam according to the present condition, so in the future we shall be conformed to the Lord Christ [Baluz.: according to the flesh]: “For he will transform the body of our humility so that it may be conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:21); and, “As was the earthly, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly; and just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:48–49). He demonstrates that, having become participants in Adam’s first condition, we necessarily also attain participation in the future condition of the second Adam, Christ the Lord, according to the flesh: since he arose from this same nature and assumed everything that belonged to nature; and therefore he endured death, so that, by accepting the death of nature and rising from the dead, he might perfect nature as free from death.

9. He accepted death for this reason, but by no means sin; rather, he remained wholly free from it. What belonged to nature—that is, death—he unquestionably assumed; but sin, which did not belong to nature but to the will, he accepted in no way.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] The opponents of original sin reached the conclusion that Christ was not without sin by reasoning of the same kind. Augustine, concerning Julianus (Book 5 Against Julian, chapter 9, elsewhere chapter 15): “Why do you labor, with great arguments, to arrive at the precipice of impiety, so that, because Christ’s flesh was born from Mary—whose virgin flesh, like that of everyone else, had been propagated from Adam—there should be no difference between it and sinful flesh, and the Apostle should be thought to have said without distinction that he was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh? [The heretic either maintains that there is no sinful flesh at all, or, if there is, contends that because Christ came from it, Christ’s flesh too is from it.] Rather, you insist that there be no sinful flesh, lest this also be true of Christ.” Theodore, in Photius (Codex 177): “Fourth [O blasphemous and impious words!]: that not even Christ, God, having assumed a nature infected by sins, should be pure from wickedness.”]

But if sin had existed in nature, then, according to the eloquence of this most learned man, he would necessarily have assumed sin, since sin would have existed wholly in nature.

[Note: [Col. 0230D] Theodore argues that no one can prudently affirm that there had been any divine intention to grant Adam immortality immediately from his origin, if God is said to have foreknown everything, including the sin Adam was going to commit; for that would detract either from divine wisdom or from divine power. “What kind of wisdom is it,” he says, “to grant something as an exceptional benefit for only six hours? Or what kind of such great power is it seriously to will that a human being be immortal, yet not prevent him from being dragged by the devil into death?”]

## THIRD EXCERPT FROM THEODORE

From the second codex, from the third book, folio eighteen.

[Note: [Col. 0230D–0231B] Undoubtedly the passage has been disturbed by a scribal fault; it should be restored thus: “Did God not know that Adam would sin? But since this too is the answer of these most learned men—that it is utterly mad even to entertain this in thought—it is evident,” etc.]

1. “If,” he says, “God truly knew that Adam would sin, and this too is the answer of these most learned men—that it is utterly mad even to entertain this in thought—it is evident that he knew both that Adam would sin and that, on that account, he would undoubtedly die. How, then, is it not the height of madness to believe that he first made him [Note: [Col. 0231B] Although he acknowledges that *immortal* is the correct reading, Baluze nevertheless retains *mortal*, which all the other books have. EDIT.] immortal for six hours [Baluz.: six hours]—for that was the interval from his creation until the [Note: [Col. 0231B] Thus the Vatican manuscript; but the Bellovacensis has *commixtionem* (“mingling”). Henry de Noris, thinking that something was lacking here, added the word *peccati* (“of sin”). I readily believe that *comestionem* (“eating”) should be read. BALUZ.] commission, since on the sixth day he was made from the earth and, after eating contrary to the divine command, was expelled from paradise—and then showed him to be mortal after the sin?”

2. “For it is certain that, if he had wished him to be immortal, not even the intervening sin would have changed God’s judgment; for he did not make the devil mortal from immortal, even though the devil is the source of all evils.”

## FOURTH EXCERPT FROM THEODORE

From the second codex, from the third book, folio twenty-five.

[Col. 0232A]

1. “For,” he says, “he will not bestow upon those who, from Adam until the coming of Christ the Lord, lived in such impieties and injustices as the blessed Paul expressed in his own words—as has been made clear above from his statements—the great reward of resurrection, if he hands them over to punishments without end and without correction. For where will resurrection now be regarded as a gift, if punishment without correction is inflicted upon those who rise?”

[Note: [Col. 0232B] Theodore, I think, as though astonished that Augustine should fight with such force to assert immortality for innocent Adam, attempted to prove that immortality is not to be reckoned among goods in itself, but among the *adiaphora* (indifferent things), and is not to be considered of great value unless joined with freedom from sin and the reward of blessedness—since it must also be granted to the impious, to increase their punishment; yet it would certainly not be granted if it were as great a good as the defenders of original sin assert.]

2. And a little later: “Who is so mad,” he says, “as to believe that so great a good should become the material of unending punishment for those who rise, for whom it would have been altogether more useful not to rise than to endure, after the resurrection, the experience of such great and such evils under infinite punishments?”

# FIRST APPENDIX TO THE FIRST PART OF THE WORKS OF MARIUS MERCATOR

Containing Pope Anastasius’s Letter to John of Jerusalem concerning Rufinus of Aquileia, and the Profession of Faith consisting of twelve anathemas, which a certain Rufinus published.

[Col. 0231]

[Note: [Col. 0231C] Jerome mentions this in his *Apology Against Rufinus*, addressing him as follows: “Why, when you are going to translate heretical material, do you place before it, in their defense, a book as though it were that of a martyr, and thrust upon Roman ears what the whole world shuddered at when it had been translated? Or, certainly, if you interpret it in order to accuse him of heresy, do not alter anything from the Greek, and bear witness in your preface to this very fact, which Pope Anastasius most prudently expressed in his letter written against you to Bishop John.” Jerome mentions it also, or rather Theophilus of Alexandria, praised by Justinian, mentions it in his letter to Menas, as will soon be said.

Rufinus accused Jerome of either having written or forged the letter. Hence Jerome says above: “In the letter of holy Pope Anastasius you proved slippery and confused; you find no place on which to plant your foot. For now you say that it was composed by me; now that it ought to have been sent to you by the person to whom it was sent. Again, you accuse the writer of injustice.” And shortly afterward: “If you suspect that I forged the letter, why do you not seek it in the archives of the Roman Church? Then, when you discover that it was not given by the bishop, you may hold me guilty of an evident crime, and need not oppose to me little bundles of cobwebs, but bind me with the strongest and most solid net.”

It is found in several places: namely, in volume 9 of Jerome’s works, among the letters of the supreme pontiffs; in Baronius under the year 402; and in more recent collections of councils. Everywhere, however, it is much less carefully corrected than in the present edition, which is based partly on the Bellovacensis manuscript and partly on the Vatican manuscript.

It is especially famous because it contains much ecclesiastical history, but even more of the apostolic vigor by which the supreme pontiff proscribes the books *On First Principles* (*Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*), chastises Rufinus the translator, condemns Origen the author, terrifies readers with imperial edicts, and accuses the bishop of Jerusalem of being a supporter of Rufinus and Origen, seriously warning him not to allow himself to be mocked by a defender of error.

The distinguished author of the *Annals* thought that it was issued in the year 402; but this opinion cannot stand. For since Anastasius died on 27 April 402, as Baronius himself establishes from the chronicles of Marcellinus and Prosper, how could so many and such extensive events have occurred within four months—almost all of them winter months, and not even complete months—as necessarily must have happened and are certainly known to have happened? First, the letter was sent from Rome to Jerusalem; then Rufinus, who was residing at Aquileia, received news from Syria of what the letter contained; then Rufinus requested that a copy of the letter be sent to him from Syria; then Jerome, who was in the East, learned of Rufinus’s request and mentioned it in his *Apology*, which he published there afterward, while Anastasius was still alive. Could it have happened that within four months, with the sea stormy and closed to navigation, someone traveled twice from Italy to Jerusalem and twice from Jerusalem to Italy? Moreover, Jerome himself attests to all these matters in the following words (*Book 3 of the Apology Against Rufinus*): “In the letter of holy Anastasius you proved slippery”; and afterward: “You produce a letter of Siricius, already sleeping in the Lord, and disregard the words of Anastasius, who was still alive,” and so forth.

The letter must therefore have been issued in 401. This is not a conjecture but Jerome’s explicit testimony. When writing the *Apology* in 402, he says: “Suppose that I forged the letter of the previous year; who sent to the East the things recently written? In them Pope Anastasius adorns you with such profuse praises that, when you read them, you begin to wish to defend yourself rather than accuse us.”

To avoid this argument, Baronius maintains that two letters from Anastasius concerning Rufinus were issued: one to Rufinus himself, which was a summons; the other to John of Jerusalem, which condemned Rufinus. The first, in 401, seemed to Rufinus to be forged; the second, in 402, is said to be the one referred to by the name of the writings recently sent to the East. But I cannot understand how this coheres with what Jerome left written in the same passage: namely, that Rufinus claimed that the very letter he was awaiting from Jerusalem had been forged by Jerome. He was not awaiting the letter that he had received and in which Anastasius said that Rufinus had translated Origen’s books and handed them over to the simple people of the Roman Church, so that he might himself destroy the truth of the faith which they had learned from the Apostle. Almost these very words occur in the letter to John.

I do not fail to recognize what appears, at first sight, to support Baronius in Jerome’s *Apology*: “Since you do not approve our letter, you also say that the letter of Pope Anastasius is supported by a similar fraud, concerning which I answered you previously. If you suspect that it is not his, you have grounds for accusing us of falsehood before him; but if it is his—as the letter of this same year against you proves—you strive in vain and falsely to accuse as false a letter which is false, when from his true letter we demonstrate that ours is true.” From this it can be gathered that at least two letters were issued by Anastasius against Rufinus: one in the year Jerome was writing, that is, 402; the other in the preceding year, that is, 401. But since both were sent to the East, and neither was addressed to Rufinus, but both to John of Jerusalem, I am astonished how Baronius’s conjecture can be supported by this. Indeed, I think it is clear from this very passage that the letter now under discussion was issued in 401; for the later letter, which is understood by the reference to the writings sent to the East, had already reached Jerusalem when Jerome wrote.

Anastasius, bishop of the city of Rome. Anastasius succeeded Siricius on 14 March, in the consulship of Honorius IV and Eutychianus, that is, in 398; he died on 27 April, in the consulship of the two Augusti Arcadius and Honorius, that is, in 402, after having held office for four years, one month, and several days.

To John, bishop of Jerusalem. That John held the see of Jerusalem for a full thirty years: that much time elapsed between the death of Saint Cyril, whose successor he became, and the accession of Praylius, whom he had as his successor. He favored both the Origenists and the Pelagians, perhaps less from intellectual conviction than from an inclination of the will, because he understood that Rufinus, the defender of Origen, and the monk Pelagius were adversaries of Jerome, toward whom he was already hostile for personal reasons. Jerome was not the only one to accuse John; Innocent, Augustine, and Orosius did so as well, and in such a way that, in the judgment of the learned, the recent vindications of Vastel have not yet succeeded in removing the accusation.

Replying. Namely, to the letter in which John had apparently consulted the pontiff about Rufinus and asked what he thought; in reality, however, he was excusing Rufinus and bringing Jerome—against whom he was already angry for other reasons—under accusation, both of envy and of hatred toward a presbyter who, as John thought, was distinguished by recognized holiness and exceptional learning. This is indicated by Anastasius’s words: “Rufinus, concerning whom you have deemed it appropriate to consult me, has the divine majesty as the judge of his conscience.” And later: “But since the complaint of the common people about Rufinus troubles you, so that you pursue certain persons with vague suspicions,” and so forth.

Concerning the name Rufinus. The name is used for the matter at issue, in a mode of expression customary among writers of that period, though not unknown in a better age. The Rufinus mentioned is that widely renowned presbyter of Aquileia, at first Saint Jerome’s friend and companion in study, but later his hostile enemy, when he translated the books *On First Principles* into Latin and revealed himself as an Origenist.

After twenty-five years of travels in Egypt and the East, during which he accompanied the elder Melania, he returned to the West in 397 and brought to Rome, as Jerome puts it, “a ship full of his blasphemies” (*Apology* 2). For he carried with him the book *On First Principles* and other works composed by himself, and offered the Romans poison in a golden cup. Troubled by the odium resulting from this act, he withdrew to his homeland; from there he wrote an *Apology* to Anastasius, the supreme pontiff. He also wrote three extremely venomous books of invective against Jerome. He remained at Aquileia until, when the Visigoths were ravaging the countryside and the city, he was forced to flee to Sicily, where he died in 411.

He left behind an uncertain reputation: some praising him as a saint, others cursing him as a heretic.

[Col. 0235B] He was certainly condemned before his death by Anastasius, at the accusation of Jerome’s friends; he was also condemned after his death by Gelasius, because he had held a view contrary to Jerome’s concerning free will. I do not wish to decide this dispute. Perhaps, however, someone may believe—not altogether rashly—that, on account of the very great praises bestowed on Rufinus even by supreme pontiffs, Anastasius’s condemnation was merely a threatening one and, for just reasons, did not later become a formal judgment. Gelasius’s decree certainly does not concern the person but the books, just as books have often been condemned without prejudicing the holiness of men whose conduct was highly approved. Perhaps, likewise, the suspicion was not without cause. I do not recall Jerome’s bile against Rufinus being inflamed by zeal for the faith. See, reader who loves truth, Gennadius and the other cataloguers of ecclesiastical writers where they discuss Rufinus.]

# LETTER OF ANASTASIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME, REPLYING TO JOHN, BISHOP OF JERUSALEM, CONCERNING THE NAME OF CAELESTIUS

(C)

[Note: [Col. 0231] Although this letter contains nothing directly related to the Pelagian heresy, it nevertheless has much worthy of attention and is of no small importance for history. For that reason it seemed that it should not be rejected altogether as extraneous, but rather relegated to this final position, although it occupies the first place in the manuscript codices. Nor do I think that Mercator himself prefixed it to his works, since it has no bearing either on the Pelagian or on the Nestorian matter; rather, it was added by some not very learned compiler who, knowing no Rufinus other than the one from Aquileia, immediately encountering the name Rufinus placed before the anathemas, thought that both works belonged to one and the same Rufinus.]

[Col. 0231C]

1. It is indeed a sign of approved affection that one priest should speak laudably of another priest. Therefore, in return for the great praise that you have undeservedly and most abundantly bestowed upon me, just as I give thanks for your love, so my favorable speech continually pursues, in a manner, the splendor of your holiness and those virtues which you possess in the Lord. For you shine conspicuously with the brilliance of your praises, most excellent man of all, so that speech cannot be equal to your merits. Moreover, I am so carried away by the encouragement of your titles that I shall not cease to dare even what I cannot fulfill.

2. This too belongs to your praises: you praised me so highly for the serenity of that heavenly disposition. For the distinguished order of your episcopate, shining throughout the whole world like a radiant light, has brought even to us the brightness of your splendor. You attribute everything to friendship in my case and leave nothing to examination; or, if you praise me justly, you too must be praised in like measure. I therefore beg you, for both reasons, to stop praising me to myself: for a double consideration restrains you, lest false praise inflict pain upon the feelings of your fellow priest, or true praise kindle his embarrassment.

3. But to return to the matter: Rufinus, concerning whom you have deemed it appropriate to consult me, has the divine majesty as the judge of his conscience; before it, with the full duty of devotion, he himself sees how he ought to prove himself.

[Note: [Col. 0235C] Namely, whether he translated Origen’s books *On First Principles* either in order to spread the heresy or for some other reason, and also whether he sincerely and from the heart detested Origen’s errors, or detested them maliciously and merely with his lips. The previously cited words of Jerome are relevant here: “Why, when you are going to translate,” and so forth.]

4. But before he translated Origen’s works into our language, our interest did not know either who Origen was or to what utterances he had proceeded; but what my intention is, I shall briefly discuss with your holiness concerning this matter.

[Note: [Col. 0235D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “But Origen, whose compositions he transferred into our language, before [the translation of the book *On First Principles*] who he was and into what words he proceeded, our purpose does not know,” and so forth. The Bellovacensis manuscript has: “But Origen . . . or who he was and into what words he proceeded,” and so forth. The common reading is: “Origen . . . before, who he was and into what words he proceeded, did not know our purpose,” and so forth. The passage, as it stands in all the codices, requires an Oedipus. For what do the words “did not know our purpose” mean? I have no doubt that the first exemplar from which the other codices were copied had the order of these two words—*purpose* and *interest*—disturbed, and that, when one word had been written above the other, especially at the ends of lines, the careless eye of the copying scribe was deceived, as often happens. The passage is clear if restored as follows: “But Origen, whose compositions he transferred into our language, before [the translation of the book *On First Principles*]—who he was and into what words [of impious doctrines] he proceeded—our interest did not know; but what my intention is, when I speak with your holiness,” and so forth. For the ancients testify that Origen was unknown to the Latins before Rufinus’s translation—not entirely, since Jerome, at Damasus’s request, had previously rendered several homilies into Latin for the Romans to read, but insofar as the errors in the books *On First Principles* were so dense and so impious.]

5. It must therefore be conceived in the mind that he who, through the works of Origen translated into our language, exposed them by his reading to the people of our city introduced into pure minds, as it were, a cloud of blindness, and sought to dissolve the faith established by the tradition of the apostles and the elders as though through wandering byways.

[Note: [Col. 0236C] We corrected this passage with no little labor, since it was no less corrupt than the preceding one. The Vatican and Bellovacensis codices read: “That he revealed to the people of our city through the reading of Origen’s translated works, having cast over pure minds a kind of cloud,” and so forth. The old printed books read: “That he who revealed to the people of our city through the translated reading of Origen, raising and casting in pure minds, as it were, a cloud, wished to dissolve, through wandering turns, the faith established by the tradition of the apostles and the elders,” and so forth. The sense, if there is any, is entangled throughout; but it becomes clear after our correction.]

6. At this point I am inclined to say: What will this translation into the Roman language accomplish? I approve it if it accuses the author, exposes his deed as detestable, and reveals him as hateful to the people, so that the one whom reputation had long since bound may at last be held by justified hatred. But if the translator himself gives assent to the errors of such great evils and exposes impious doctrines to the people for reading, he has constructed by the labor of his work nothing other than a means by which, at the prompting of his own will, he might overthrow these things—which alone, which first, and which as the true faith among Catholic Christians have been maintained from the apostles down to the present time—by the title of an assertion.

[Note: [Col. 0236C] The common codices corruptly read: “This faith, which alone and which first among Catholic Christians is now held as true from the apostles onward to the present time, he might overthrow under the title of an unexpected assertion.” We have corrected it, unless I am mistaken, correctly, by comparing the codices with one another.]

[Col. 0236B]

7. Far be this from the Catholic discipline of the Roman Church. It will certainly never happen that we admit by any means what we rightly and deservedly condemn. Therefore, what is spread throughout the whole world, through the providence of Christ our Lord, will deign to approve that we cannot accept at all those things which stain the Church, overthrow approved morals, wound the ears of those standing by, and arrange quarrels, anger, and dissensions.

8. Moved by this consideration, we have condemned the writings and errors of Origen. But since the translator has not sufficiently cleared himself, either by his preface to Origen’s books or by the apology sent to us—indeed, perhaps he actually agrees with the same errors—we summoned him to Rome for the judgment of the apostolic see, and when he refused to come, we included him under the same sentence. We wrote the letter of condemnation to our brothers Venerius and Chromatius. You will be able to confirm from what follows how carefully our humble self sent that letter to our brother and fellow bishop Venerius.

[Note: [Col. 0236D] The common codices, contrary to the authority of the manuscripts and without any plausible sense, read: “Therefore know what kind of letter our humility has written with more careful attention to our brother and fellow bishop Venerius and sent, and I have made this conscience for myself, that I do not labor under an unnecessary fear,” and so forth.

I suspected—and not lightly—that there had once been a lacuna in which words expressing the sentence of condemnation issued against Origen and Rufinus, or at least a mention of that sentence, had been omitted, approximately in the form that we have supplied in different type. I draw the reasons for this suspicion from the following. First, all writers say that Anastasius condemned the errors of Origen. Jerome alone may stand for all, writing to the virgin Demetrias and referring to this letter (*Letter 6, On the Preservation of Virginity*): “When you were still a little girl, and the bishop Anastasius, of holy and blessed memory, was governing the Roman Church, a savage storm of heretics from the regions of the East attempted to pollute and undermine the simplicity of the faith praised by the voice of the Apostle. But the man of richest poverty and apostolic concern immediately struck down the harmful head and silenced the hissing mouths of the hydra.”

If Anastasius condemned Origen, he ought apparently not to have kept silent about it when writing to a bishop suspected in the name of those same errors, and certainly favoring Rufinus, who was suspected as well. Further, the words “has preceded the form of my sentence up to this point” clearly indicate that mention of a sentence had already been made. Jerome later writes (*Book 2 Against Rufinus*) that Anastasius sent letters by which he pursued Origen throughout the whole world, and that, after receiving them, he compelled Chromatius of Aquileia and Venerius of Milan to convene synods in which, with an identical judgment and therefore with an identical spirit, they denounced the heretic Origen to the people. Finally, the supreme pontiff sufficiently shows that Rufinus was condemned by him in these closing words: “Let him himself see where he can be absolved.”]

9. Therefore let the man who translated it keep this conscience to himself; I do not suffer needless alarm, nor am I troubled by empty fear. For my part, I shall not lack concern to preserve the faith of the Gospel among my people and, through letters as extensive as I can make them, to address the members of the body spread through different regions of the earth, so that no source of profane interpretation may creep in and, by casting its darkness over devoted minds, attempt to weaken them.

[Note: [Col. 0237B] The holy pontiff calls all the faithful parts of his body, in the same sense in which later Celestine, himself the head of the universal Church, wrote to the clergy and people of Constantinople (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 19): “Although we are far away, when we learned that our members were being torn apart by the perversity of doctrine, with paternal concern burning within us, we burned for you in another’s fire, although among the Churches of God, which everywhere are joined into the one bridal chamber of Christ, nothing is far away and nothing is considered foreign. Since, then, you are our inmost parts, we rightly tremble lest the insinuation of an evil teacher divert your faith from the path of truth,” and so forth.]

10. I could not remain silent about this as well, which I rejoice has happened:

[Note: [Col. 0237C] Jerome mentions the imperial replies against the Origenists in these words: “The imperial replies ordering that the Origenists be expelled from Alexandria and Egypt were drafted at my prompting” (*Book 1, Apology Against Rufinus*). There is no mention of them in the Theodosian Code, nor, I think, anywhere else except in these two passages.

I am surprised that Justinian does not mention them in his letter to Menas of Constantinople, where the condemnation of the Origenists by Anastasius is discussed. But since Justinian’s letter has been mentioned, it will not be useless to note in passing three matters relevant here.

First, the words mentioning Anastasius, the supreme pontiff, do not belong to the emperor, as some learned men have thought, but to Theophilus of Alexandria. They run as follows: “Let us also hear the holy Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, from a discourse written to certain monks who agreed with Origen. For he says: ‘Therefore, anathematizing Origen and the other heretics, following our example and that of Anastasius, bishop of the holy Roman Church, who, renowned for his ancient struggles, was appointed leader of that most noble people, and whom the synod of all the blessed bishops of the West follows, since it accepted and approved the judgment pronounced by the Church of Alexandria against the impious man.’”

Second, Justinian sent his letter not only to Menas but also, as he says, to “the most holy and most blessed Pope Vigilius of elder Rome and patriarch,” and to all the other most holy bishops and patriarchs, namely, of Alexandria, Theopolis, and Jerusalem, so that they too might take measures in this matter.

Third, the patriarchs were ordered to send copies to other bishops and also to the superiors of monasteries. For these are the emperor’s words: “We have given this letter to your Blessedness, exhorting you to convene an assembly of all the most holy bishops who now reside in this imperial city, and of the God-beloved superiors of the holy monasteries here, and to ensure that all of them, in their own writings, anathematize the impious and God-opposing Origen, also called Adamantius, who was a presbyter of the most holy Church of Alexandria, together with his wicked and impious doctrines and all the chapters set out below. Send copies of what your Blessedness has done for this purpose to all the other most holy bishops and to the superiors of the venerable monasteries, so that they too may anathematize Origen and his criminal doctrines, together with all who will be declared heretics, by their own signatures. In the future, however, let no bishops or superiors of monasteries be appointed unless, together with all the other heretics who are customarily anathematized in published documents—namely, Sabellius, Arius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Eutyches, Dioscorus, Timothy the Cat, Peter the Hoarse, Anthimus of Trebizond, Theodosius of Alexandria, Peter who was of Antioch, Peter who was of Apamea, and Severus formerly of Antioch—they first anathematize the aforementioned Origen, who was afflicted with the madness of the pagans and Arians, together with his detestable and impious doctrines. Everyone must be warned that no one may dare to defend such a heretic or his interpretations, but that each person must hate, reject, and anathematize them with all his heart and all his mind.”

From these matters we learn five things worth knowing:

1. how encyclical letters of pontiffs and emperors were sent throughout the entire world—or, as others put it, to all the bishops of the world—namely, by being addressed directly to the bishops of the principal sees;

2. that, in order for the prescriptions contained in the letters to be carried out, synods of their dioceses had to be convened by the bishops of the principal sees, and that these bishops then informed each of the lesser bishops what had to be done, sending them copies of the letters they had received;

3. that copies of the commands were also sent to the superiors of monasteries and that, whenever a heresy was to be condemned with greater solemnity, a subscription was required from them in the name of the entire monastery;

4. that at that time no one was placed in charge of a Church or monastery without first, by his own subscription and in published documents, pronouncing an anathema not only against the doctrines of the heretics but also against the heretics themselves;

5. that such a subscription was required by which each person testified that he wished to defend neither the condemned person, nor the books, nor the doctrines, but that he “hated, rejected, and anathematized all these things with all his heart and all his mind.”]

Replies have been issued by our most blessed princes, by which every person serving God may be recalled from reading Origen; and the one whom profane reading has exposed as guilty has been condemned by the judgment of the princes. Thus far has the form of my judgment proceeded.

[Note: [Col. 0238D] It is well known what distinction exists between imperial sanctions, or constitutions, and replies or rescripts: the former were issued by the emperors as if on their own initiative; the latter were given in response either to consultations by magistrates or to the petitions and written requests of others. If, therefore, the imperial sanctions mentioned by the pontiff were replies, they must have been sent after the petition presented to the emperor Arcadius by Theophilus through his envoys in 400. From this follows the chronology of the time at which we said Anastasius wrote to John (see Palladius, *Dialogue on the Life of John Chrysostom*). Since he speaks of the imperial replies as something very recent, he must have written in 401, if the replies were issued at Constantinople in 400 and became known to the pontiff after being sent from there to the West at the beginning of 402.]

11. But since the complaint of the common people about Rufinus troubles you, [Note: [Col. 0239B] He seems to be speaking of Jerome and Jerome’s friends, Pammachius, Oceanus, and Marcella, who in fact contributed greatly to advancing the condemnation of the Origenists—not, however, driven by hatred of Rufinus, as John supposed, but by abhorrence of the errors that, from reading the book *On First Principles* (Περὶ Ἀρχῶν), had filled Catholic minds with horror. See Jerome’s Letter 64, which is Pammachius and Oceanus to Jerome; Letter 65, Jerome to both; and Letter 78, Jerome to Pammachius and Marcella; for these shed light [Col. 0239C] on this otherwise rather obscure passage.] so that you persecute certain men on vague suspicions, I shall correct this opinion of yours by an example from divine Scripture. [Col. 0240A] 12. [Note: [Col. 0239C]

This passage has been corrected, since it was read corruptly in the common printed version, contrary to both manuscript codices: “Know that Rufinus translated into Latin and approved with his own judgment the statements of Origen, and he is no different from one who gives assent to another’s faults. Nevertheless, I wish you to know,” etc.

[Col. 0240A] Toward the end Rufinus himself must be heard, speaking in his own defense to the supreme pontiff and offering whatever explanation he could of his conduct, while turning the charge against Jerome, of whose envy he complains maliciously: “When, at the request of the brothers,” he says (*Apology to Pope Anastasius*), “I translated certain works of Origen from Greek into Latin, I think everyone understands that I am being blamed here solely out of spite. If there is something displeasing in the author, why is it turned against the translator? In the Greek text it says that I was asked to make it available to Latin readers; I supplied Latin words for Greek ideas only. Therefore, if there is any praise in those ideas, it is not mine; and likewise, if there is blame, it is not mine.”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore, I beg you, holy, venerable, and blessed Father, let no one, on this account, manufacture envy against me; let no one employ factions and slanders, which may not be done in the Church of God. For where will simplicity and innocence be safe, if not here?

“I am neither Origen’s defender, nor his advocate, nor his first translator. Others had undertaken this same work before me; I did it last, at the request of the brothers. If it is ordered that this not be done, the order must be observed in the future. If those who acted before the order are blamed, let the blame begin with the first.

“For, apart from the faith I have set forth above—that is, the faith held by the Roman Church, the Alexandrian Church, and our own Church of Aquileia, and preached at Jerusalem—I have neither held, nor do I hold, nor will I hold any other faith concerning this man; and if anyone believes otherwise, whoever he may be, let him be anathema. But on the day of judgment those will give an account who, moved solely by envy and spite, generate stumbling blocks, dissensions, and scandals among the brothers.”]

Therefore, dearest brother, setting aside every suspicion, know that Rufinus translated into Latin and approved with his own judgment the statements of Origen, and that he is no different from one who gives assent to another’s faults. Nevertheless, I want you to hold this firmly: he is regarded by our party as so alien that we wish to know neither what he is doing nor where he is. In the end, let him see for himself where he can be absolved.

[Col. 0239]

THE FAITH OF RUFINUS. [Note: [Col. 0239] It is remarkable how many secrets of doctrine—both historical and dogmatic—this very brief booklet contains, so that it could at least be set alongside, if not preferred to, great volumes. It therefore seemed that it ought to be illuminated by more careful notes, laboriously gathered; and it needed no ordinary elucidation, so that the riches which its small size concealed as though wrapped up in it might be unfolded. It has moreover been relegated to the appendix for the same reason as Anastasius’s letter, to which it is appended in the manuscript codices, although it occupies the second place after that letter. For it contains little about Pelagian history and much about a different matter, namely, the Origenist controversy. In those times, as must be demonstrated in the notes, questions arising from Origen’s books *On First Principles* (Περὶ Ἀρχῶν), which the presbyter Rufinus of Aquileia had recently translated into Latin, were being heatedly debated, especially in the region where this booklet was written. But these matters will become clear from the notes, in which certain popular opinions must be overturned and some Origenist teachings, insufficiently known even to the learned, brought to light.] (G)*

[Col. 0239C] Because of our reverence for the holy places, [Note: [Col. 0239D]

From this it is clear where that little *Faith* booklet was published: namely, at Jerusalem or Bethlehem, where an immense multitude of presbyters and monks gathered, partly because of the sanctity of both places, and partly because of Jerome’s reputation and the charity of noble women who supported the servants of God from their own resources.

The question of its date is more difficult, but the conjecture must nevertheless be drawn from the following considerations. It was certainly published before Nestorius was condemned; otherwise the third anathema would have mentioned not only Paul of Samosata and Photinus but also Nestorius. It was likewise published before Pelagius was condemned, for otherwise how could the second anathema have spoken so sparingly about the assistance of divine grace? It may therefore seem to belong to the time of Anastasius, when the Origenist controversies were being debated with intense passion, especially in the East, while the Pelagian controversies were, as it were, taking shape.

Indeed, I scarcely hesitate to think that it should be assigned as far back as the pontificate of Siricius, when the East was disturbed by the mutual disagreement of two great men, Saint Epiphanius and John of Jerusalem—the former attacking Origen, the latter defending him. For two distinguished presbyters joined those great bishops, together with a large crowd: Jerome, who followed Epiphanius, and Rufinus, who followed John. The choirs of monks adhered so closely to Jerome that they would not communicate with John (see Jerome’s Letter 61, *Against the Errors of John*); and, with the presbyters divided into parties, a lamentable schism was tearing apart the Church of Jerusalem. It may therefore reasonably be said that the booklet was published around the year 398.

The title indicates that a certain Rufinus was its author; the form of its diction shows him to have been a Latin; and the sequence and arrangement of the manuscript codex seem to point to the presbyter of Aquileia. Someone might think of the presbyter of the province of Palestine whose *Booklet of Faith* was published by P. Sirmond; another might think of the presbyter Rufinus whom we read was sent by Jerome from the holy places to Milan in the year 400. For, when the records of those times are being examined, three presbyters of this name come to mind, whether they lived at Jerusalem or in neighboring churches; and they present themselves so insistently to the curious mind that suspicion may arise concerning every one of them. For as heresies emerged day after day, especially in the East and at Jerusalem because of the multitude of people converging there, each person had to prove his faith to those whose communion he sought, since many concealed heresy under an appearance of piety.

The authority of Mercator—or rather, of both codices containing Mercator’s works—primarily favors Rufinus of Aquileia. In both codices the anathemas are inserted between Anastasius’s letter and the annotations on the words of Julian, in such a way that, although the first place explicitly mentions Rufinus of Aquileia and the later place mentions the Rufinus who taught Coelestius and is commonly believed—even by the most learned—to have been from Aquileia, the anathemas are given no other title than this: “Here begins the Faith of the same Rufinus,” namely, the Rufinus mentioned in both works.
