It also favors him that, according to Jerome (*Letter to Ctesiphon*), Rufinus of Aquileia was very sympathetic to Origen and not unsympathetic to the Pelagians, while this booklet is almost entirely concerned with questions raised both by Origen and by Pelagius. Finally, it favors him that nearly everything condemned here was rebutted by Rufinus of Aquileia, both in his *Apology to Pope Anastasius* and especially in his two *Invectives Against Jerome*.

Yet there are very strong arguments to the contrary, and they are not few. For if the man of Aquileia had ever made this recantation, how could it have escaped Jerome, especially in those early days when a close relationship and harmony of spirit bound the two together? How could it not have been reproached to him, especially by a more irascible man who did not remain silent even about lesser matters, after their friendship had been dissolved? Moreover, the final anathema attacks those who say that souls existed before they entered bodies, rather than being created daily by God, following the example of the first man. Yet Rufinus, in his *Apology to Pope Anastasius*, confessed when already an old man that he still did not know the truth and left it to God to know: “What is true concerning the three opinions about the origin of souls that had then become prevalent,” one of which was that “after bodies have been formed in the womb, God creates souls and infuses them every day.”

Add also that the Rufinus the Syrian whom Mercator mentions in the preface to the *Annotations* is very different from the Rufinus of Aquileia, who held sound views concerning original sin, as has been established by incontrovertible arguments against popular credulity.

Nor does the argument drawn from the *Apology* and the *Invectives* suffice. Rufinus of Aquileia was compelled everywhere—both before the judge Anastasius and before his accuser Jerome—to dispel the charge that he agreed with Origen in matters of doctrine.

Furthermore, the argument taken from Mercator’s authority, since it rests partly on the word “same” and partly on the placement of the booklet after Anastasius’s letters, accomplishes very little. Who could prove that Mercator placed Anastasius’s letter there where it stands in the manuscript codex? Who would not see that this was done by an incompetent copyist who, knowing of only one Origenist Rufinus, attributed everything belonging to the various Rufinuses to him because of the commonness of the name?

[Col. 0242B] I therefore think—not implausibly—that the author of this booklet was that third Rufinus (if indeed he differs from the second), whom Jerome sent as a presbyter to Milan and Rome, certainly to arouse Venerius and Anastasius against the Origenists, as we have shown in the notes on the preface to the *Annotations*. The basis of this conjecture is that, besides the name, the time, place, country, and other circumstances of this sort agree. For a Latin from the Bethlehem retreat was sent in the time of Anastasius, a man who was conducting an important affair with the Westerners—that is, energetically pursuing the matter against the Origenists—who knew their errors more deeply because he had himself been infected by them, and who pursued the heretics with all the greater ardor because he knew that, by openly professing hatred of them, he had to be more securely freed from suspicion of his former association with them (see what we noted in the preface to the *Annotations*).]

We came to Jerusalem [Col. 0240C] and Bethlehem and learned [Col. 0241A] that very many brothers were scandalized by us, because they had heard that we professed many heretical things and things contrary to the faith of the Church.

[Col. 0242A] Therefore, with God as our witness, we testify that we formerly held through error some of the things written below, and now condemn them; [Note: [Col. 0242B]

This entire condemnation is contained in twelve anathemas. Concerning them, if they are considered as a whole, I think three matters deserve especially careful attention. First, they all attack a doctrine which, although contrary to Jerome’s teaching, was not equally proscribed by all the other Fathers. For the twelfth anathema, directed against those who say that souls existed before they were born and were not created daily by God together with the body, would not have been accepted by Augustine, who never dared in his own time to settle this question as though it were already certain. It must therefore have been a confession that was not public in any Church, but rather private and proper either to some group of clergy or to a monastery. It must likewise be understood that the word “anathema” was not taken in its usual sense, as a canonical curse, but in another general sense, as the condemnation of some statement. Thus, when Pelagius was ordered at Diospolis to reject certain statements as a matter of compliance, the synod said: “Since you deny that you wrote such things, anathematize those who hold them.” Pelagius replied: “I anathematize them as foolish, not as heretics, since this is not a dogma.” Then the bishops judged, saying: “Now, since Pelagius has anathematized the foolish statement inserted here,” etc. (*Book on the Proceedings of Palestine*, ch. 6).

Second, all the anathemas attack Origen and the heresies that arose from his source—those of Paul of Samosata, Arius, Apollinaris, and Photinus. Indeed, nothing is condemned that Jerome had not at some time charged against Origen. Hence one would be neither rash nor imprudent in believing that the author of the anathemas was a disciple of Jerome and wrote at a time when the sharper conflict between Jerome and John of Jerusalem had not yet died down—that is, before the year 394. Indeed, he may even have published this profession in Jerome’s own monastery, at holy Bethlehem, in order to clear himself of suspicion of heresy and prove himself worthy of admission into the Catholic assembly.

Finally, in that period many professions of faith like this one were made by various people, if not in their definitions, at least in the questions on which each person expressed his own opinion, some favoring Origen and others fighting against him. Thus Rufinus of Aquileia composed his *Apology*; Rufinus of Palestine, his *Booklet of Faith*; the Fathers, better than either of them, their expositions of the creed; and Gregory Nazianzen, his anathemas against the Apollinarians.

Now, if the individual anathemas are considered separately, it will certainly seem worthwhile to provide notes on each of them, drawing both from Origen himself and from other confessions, or even from the writings of Jerome and others against the Origenists, so as to demonstrate that Origen is attacked by all these thunderbolts.]

but that the other things with which we are falsely branded we have neither said nor say, while, on the contrary, we have set forth and condemned the things that we suspect in others.

[Col. 0244A] 1. [Note: [Col. 0243A]

The entire anathema concerns the punishment that God is going to inflict—not only upon the devil, the demons, and the impious, which is the first part, but also upon Christians who follow the right faith yet are sinners, which is the second. The punishments of the former are called eternal, which is wholly Catholic; those of the latter temporal, which, although it pleased great men in former times, is nevertheless condemned as erroneous by others. As for the first part, concerning demons and the impious, Origen taught it so consistently and everywhere that everyone has attributed to him, as a characteristic heresy opposed to Catholic doctrine, the doctrine which all have reported as contained in the work entitled *On First Principles*. Jerome, warning Avitus about the errors to be avoided while reading these books, says (*Letter 124*): “He mixes everything together, so that the devil can become an archangel, and again the devil can return into an angel.” And shortly afterward: “He says that the demons themselves, and the rulers of darkness in some world or worlds, if they wish, can be converted to better things, become human beings, and thus return to their original beginning—provided only that, after enduring punishments and torments for either a long or a short time, they may, having been instructed in human bodies, return once more to the heights of the angels.”

Rufinus of Aquileia not only removed many things from the books *On First Principles*, especially these passages, but also, in order to remove from himself suspicion of agreement with Origen, said (*In the *Apology to Anastasius*): “If anyone denies that the devil is to be consigned to eternal fires, let him receive a share of eternal fire with him, so that he may feel what he denied.”

As for the latter part, concerning Christians, Jerome transmitted it when he was refuting Pelagius’s seventy-second proposition, which asserted that at the day of judgment the wicked and sinners should not be spared but should be burned in eternal fires. For, after a lengthy discussion in which he responds to the scriptural passages cited by Pelagius, he concludes with these words (*Dialogue 1 Against the Pelagians*): “If Origen says that all rational creatures are not to be destroyed, and attributes repentance to the devil, what is that to us, who say that the devil, his satellites, and all the impious and transgressors perish forever, but that Christians, if they have been overtaken in sin, are to be saved after punishments?”

Marianus Victorius tries to apply Jerome’s statement to the fire that the Church calls purgatory, by which either lesser stains contracted by the just are burned away or punishments for more serious crimes, remitted through justification, are paid. But he does clear violence to Jerome’s resistant text. Jerome distinguishes the sinners of whom he speaks only from those impious persons whom he defines as people who have no knowledge of God, such as the Gentiles, or who have departed from it, such as heretics. But although the following passage may contain some obscurity, it certainly does not: “Just as we believe that there are eternal torments for the devil and for all deniers and impious people who said in their heart, ‘There is no God’ (Psalm 13:1), so we judge that the sentence of the Judge concerning sinners and impious people who are nevertheless Christians, whose works must be tested and purified in fire, is measured and mingled with mercy.”

These words seem to exclude the more indulgent than truthful objections of Sixtus of Siena and Francisco Suárez. For moderation in the sentence is set against eternal torments, and by the term “impious Christians” cannot be meant those whose sins have been remitted through justification, since through justification people cease to be impious. Moreover, the history of the controversies of that period entirely removes credibility from the opinion of those two doctors.

And what of Augustine? In my judgment, he had Jerome in mind when he wrote (*Enchiridion*, ch. 67): “Some believe that even those who do not abandon the name of Christ, who are baptized in his washing in the Church, and who are not cut off from it by any schism or heresy, will be saved through fire, no matter how many crimes they commit, if they neither wash them away by repentance nor redeem them by almsgiving, but persist in them most obstinately until the final day of this life—saved through fire, although punished not with eternal fire because of the magnitude of their crimes and wickedness. But those who believe this and nevertheless are Catholics seem to me to be deceived by a certain human benevolence, for when consulted the divine Scripture gives a different answer. I have written a book on this question entitled *On Faith and Works*,” etc. For he wrote a book on three questions: “When I had received,” as he says (*Book II of the *Retractations*, ch. 38), “from certain brothers—laymen indeed, but devoted to the study of the divine words—some writings which so distinguished faith from good works that they argued that without faith one could not attain eternal life, but that without good works one could.”

At the beginning of the book he explains the three questions he undertook to treat: “Some people think that everyone should indiscriminately be admitted to the bath of regeneration that is in Christ Jesus our Lord, even if they are unwilling to change a bad and disgraceful life, marked by the most obvious crimes and wickedness, and have openly declared that they will persevere in it. For example, if someone clings to a prostitute, he should not first be instructed to leave her and then come to baptism; rather, while remaining and intending to remain with her, he should be admitted and baptized, and should not be prevented from becoming a member of Christ even if he continues to be a member of the prostitute. Only afterward should he be taught how evil this is, and, once baptized, instructed to change his conduct for the better. They consider it perverse and backward first to teach someone how a Christian ought to live and then baptize him; rather, they think the sacrament of baptism ought to come first, followed afterward by instruction in life and conduct, and that he will act beneficially if he wishes to hold and preserve this instruction. But if he does not wish to do so, and, while retaining the Christian faith without which he would perish eternally, remains in any crime and impurity, he will be saved as through fire, as one who has built upon the foundation that is Christ—not gold, silver, and precious stones, but wood, hay, and straw, that is, not just and chaste conduct but wicked and immoral conduct” (1 Corinthians 3:12).

Now, I think that the laymen from whom Augustine received these writings should be understood as none other than admirers of Jerome—either the tribune Marcellinus or the noble Romans who had fled to Palestine and had often consulted Augustine about ecclesiastical questions. Nor do I think that any writings other than those which Jerome published, either in his commentary on Isaiah or in his commentaries on Paul’s Epistles, were sent by laymen. There he openly treated two of the three questions and seemed to indicate the third, but in such a way that he adopted the position which Augustine, without naming him out of reverence for so great a man, was nevertheless compelled to refute with strong arguments.

Indeed, when Jerome later treated the third question at greater length, Augustine was again compelled to write in defense of the Catholic faith (*Dialogue 1*, cited partly in the *Enchiridion* and partly in Book XXI of *The City of God*, ch. 17 and following); but he did so after Jerome’s death, since he both feared offending him and revered his doctrine and holiness.

[Col. 0245A] From these facts it is plainly evident in what sense Jerome spoke about the question commonly proposed—namely, in the sense in which it was customarily debated by Catholics. It is also evident that he cannot more plausibly be said to have spoken in the Catholic sense concerning purgatorial fire than Origen himself, whose footsteps he follows very closely. Thus, something human occurred in this matter—something which must be acknowledged—to this great doctor of the Church, because of certain preconceived opinions arising from his earlier reading of his old master.

Origen, however, did not mean by the name “purgatorial fire” what the Church now ordinarily means; rather, he meant the punishments of hell themselves, by which Christian sinners would eventually purge their crimes, as though faith could be kindled into love by flames. It is worthwhile to note this, in order to understand the statements of the Fathers when some of them appear to hold an opinion concerning purgatorial fire. For they do not deny the fire confessed by the Church, but the fire devised by others after Origen.

Some believe that Jerome could also have received this doctrine from Gregory Nazianzen, whose teaching he proudly acknowledged as his own (*Oration 39*). For, when Gregory reviewed the various kinds of baptism, he mentioned last the baptism of fire, which, as the final baptism of all, would consume gross matter as hay and destroy every lightness of vice.

Yet there would be nothing to prevent these words from being interpreted of purgatorial fire as the Church understands it, unless the commentator Nicetas led the teacher’s meaning in another direction. For he represents Gregory as speaking to the followers of Novatian in this way: “If we do not bend you, we shall shed tears for you, as for those afflicted with an incurable disease; for you will be baptized with eternal fire, which consumes earthly and gross matter like hay, to use the words of Isaiah. That is, it tortures those who serve gross and obscene bodily pleasures, people made light and dry by sin, yet does not consume them,” etc.

There are also those who would regard Gregory of Nyssa as suspect of the same doctrine, as learned men have observed. Photius certainly writes as follows about Theodore of Mopsuestia (*Codex 21*): “He confirms and openly proclaims the heresy of Nestorius, especially in the third book; but he also fantastically fabricates the restoration of sinners.”

Nor is it surprising that these and other very ancient Fathers held such an opinion. For they were not deceived only by a certain human benevolence, as Augustine says (*Book on Faith and Works* and Book I of *The City of God*, ch. 17), but also by a preconceived belief that the supremely good God, who loves Christ, could not destroy people who had put on Christ through true faith. Hence Ambrose, after teaching that Christ is the head of the faithful and that the members are joined to the head by faith, says (*On Psalm 118*, discourse 20): “Keep this head, you human serpents; guard it, and with an upright life salvation is secure. For no one can perish whose Christ has not been taken away. Where there is faith, we have both a beginning and an end. Where there is faithlessness, there is neither beginning nor end.”

Besides this Syrian Rufinus, Paul Orosius adhered to Jerome, attacking precisely what Pelagius had been charged with by Jerome (*Apology*, ch. 13): namely, that all sinners, together with the impious, are to be condemned eternally. Mercator also adhered to him (*Commonitorium*, ch. 4), as we have shown in its proper place; and even John of Damascus, at least in part, in his *Oration for the Faithful Departed*, if that work is not spurious.

How the error of such great men ought to be refuted is demonstrated by Augustine (*Book on Faith and Works*). How it does not favor the heretics of our own times, we have explained in the notes on Mercator’s passage. Finally, how we undertook this investigation—not from a foolish desire to reproach the Fathers, but from a sincere pursuit of truth—will easily be judged by anyone who understands well that we must oppose the spirit of our age, in which each person often establishes the Father whom he venerates as a certain rule of truth according more to affection than to reason.]

Those who say that the devil, the demons, and the impious—that is, Gentiles, Jews, Samaritans, and all heretics (except Christians who follow the right faith and are sinners)—will at some time be spared, and that their punishments will not be eternal, let them be anathema.

[Col. 0246A] 2. Those who say that any holy man, and [Note: [Col. 0246A]

It should be observed that the terms “prophetic man” and “apostolic man” indicate someone perfect and holy, whether he lived before Christ, like the prophets, or after his coming, like the apostles. For the men of both classes were the most perfect of their own age.

It should likewise be observed that, from the time when this faith was written—that is, before the year 400—the question of ἀναμαρτησία, that is, of the powers of free will by which a human being can be without sin if he wishes, had already been raised in the East. For this reason Jerome said in the year 413 that the Pelagian heresy was reviving (*Preface to Book IV of the Commentary on Jeremiah*), when he wrote that it had long before been alive but could have seemed extinguished, though unburied. For the same reason Photius (*Codex 54*) left it written that this heresy was born in the East and flowed from there into the West.

Moreover, what Rufinus says—“to be able without the help of God,” etc.—must not be passed over without notice, for it is precisely what Pelagius was saying: that a person can do so if he wishes, as we have often indicated.

Origen gave occasion for this anathema (*Book III of *On First Principles*, chs. 4 and 6), when he exalted the power of free will in both directions to such an extent that, for attaining perfection in virtue, he denied that it needed any assistance other than law and instruction. Hence Jerome (*On the Letter to Ctesiphon*) lists Origen among the teachers of Pelagius “concerning sinlessness and impassibility” (περὶ τῆς ἀναμαρτησίας καὶ ἀπαθείας)—something he certainly would not have done if Origen had said that divine assistance, or the diffusion of charity by the Holy Spirit, was necessary for attaining sinlessness. Nevertheless, a more explicit statement must be brought forward when Origen’s opinion concerning the soul of Christ, progressing by its own merits into the name of God, is explained.]

a prophetic or apostolic man can be perfect without the help of God, let them be anathema.

3. [Note: [Col. 0246C]

In both parts the anathema attacks Origen, although each part separately condemns one of the mutually contrary heresies of Apollinaris and Paul of Samosata. Since one of them, so to speak, sinned against the truth of the Lord’s Incarnation by excess and the other by deficiency—the former deliriously imagining a transformation of the divine Word into a human being, the latter refusing a substantial union of the natures—both could seem to have arisen from Origen, so confusedly, or rather inconsistently, did he speak about so great a mystery. [Col. 0246D] He was certainly of one mind with Apollinaris when he said (*Book II of *On First Principles*, ch. 6): “The mind had turned toward the Word before the creation of the world, and, having fallen from heaven at the fullness of time, existed in Christ in place of a soul”; indeed, he said that it had been changed into a human being. He erred with Photinus when he asserted (*ibid.*) that Christ’s soul—by which name he understood the human being whom, following Plato’s manner, he defined as a soul using a body—had been deified by merit of virtue and works. He spoke with the Catholics, provided that one softened a single word, when he uttered these statements (*Preface to *On First Principles*): “Jesus Christ, who came, was born from the Father before every creature. After he had served the Father in the creation of all things—for through him all things were made (John 1:3)—in the last times he emptied himself, became human, and was incarnate, although he was God; and he remained what he was, God, while assuming a body like ours,” etc.

From this anathema understand that the Eutychian and Nestorian heresies arose from others and received their names from others. For both are condemned in this booklet, published before Nestorius and Eutyches were born. Therefore, in my judgment, one should not listen to those who suspect that the following words were added to the *Book of Faith* composed by Pelagius: “We likewise execrate the blasphemy of those who attempt to assert in a novel sense that, from the time when he assumed flesh, everything belonging to divinity passed into the human being, and again everything belonging to humanity was transferred into God; so that, by this confusion, both substances—divinity and humanity—appear to have been emptied, something no heresy has ever dared to say, and both to have been changed from their proper state.” For none of the ancients, before Eutyches was born, failed to mention that error according to which the Incarnation was said, through Apollinaris—or rather according to the opinion of certain Apollinarians—to be a transformation of the divine Word into flesh and, conversely, of flesh into divinity.

Understand likewise how Origen, Paul of Samosata, Photinus, and others who asserted that Christ progressed into the name of God by merit and virtues preceded Nestorius, by a different route, in denying that the holy Virgin was Θεοτόκος—that is, “God-bearer.” For what was born from her was certainly not God at the moment of birth, if he progressed into this name by merit. Origen’s case may nevertheless seem different from that of the others, since he imagines certain eternal merits, or at least merits preceding time, by which the mind became worthy, before it came into a body, to be joined to the divine Word.]

Those who say that Christ, the Son of God, God the Word, was changed into a human being, so that God the Word ceased to be; or that a mere human being was born from Mary, who, according to Paul of Samosata and Photinus, progressed into the name of God through merit and virtues, let them be anathema.

4. [Note: [Col. 0247C]

Although, as far as I know, no one has charged Origen with attributing ignorance of the final day to Christ, I scarcely doubt that Rufinus here directed the anathema against him, though unjustly and, if I may put it so, through a suspicious slanderous accusation. For in the first part it fights against the Arians, who attributed such ignorance even to the divine Word; in the second it condemns those who deny such ignorance to the human mind joined to the Word—something Origen did (*Book II of *On First Principles*, ch. 6). He imagined that the mind, while it was in heaven before the creation of the world, had turned perfectly toward the Word and embraced all mysteries; but that, when it descended in time into a body, in which it served in place of a soul, it descended in such a way that, unlike other souls, it lost nothing through its descent from its former perfection, either of knowledge through being overshadowed or of will through cooling.

There are therefore two parts to the anathema: one concerns Christ insofar as he is the Word; the other concerns the same Christ insofar as he is human. The first asserts that the day of judgment is known to the Word, which the Arians denied; the second acknowledges that it was unknown to the human being, concerning which the Fathers of old did not hold a single opinion.

Although all commonly fought against the Arians, some nevertheless maintained that Christ, insofar as he was human, truly did not know the final day. For this reason they customarily used a distinction and said that Christ knew the day of judgment θεϊκῶς, “divinely,” but did not know it σαρκικῶς, “according to the flesh.” In this way they seemed both to contradict the Arians, as faith required, and to preserve the sense of the Gospel statement, which they said was obvious to everyone.

Several Fathers, including men of great authority in the Church, held this opinion: Eustathius of Antioch, in Facundus of Hermiane (*Book VI Against the Arians*); Athanasius (*Book XI*, ch. 1); Basil (*Oration 4 Against the Arians* and near the end of the *Book to Serapion*); Gregory Nazianzen (*Letter 391 to Amphilochius*); Cyril of Alexandria (*Oration 36*); Theodoret (*On Anathema 4*); Hilary (*Book IX On the Trinity*); Ambrose (*Book II On the Faith*, ch. 4); Fulgentius (*Book I to Thrasamund*, ch. 7); and quite a few others.

Nevertheless, the position of contemporary theology is constant: Christ, even insofar as he was human, did not lack knowledge of the final day of judgment while he lived among mortals. That statement—that not even the Son knew that time—must be understood not simply [Col. 0248B] of knowledge in general, but narrowly of the particular knowledge that he was sent to communicate, in accordance with Christ’s words: “For I have not spoken from myself, but the Father who sent me himself gave me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak,” etc. “Therefore, the things that I speak, just as the Father has said to me, so I speak” (John 12:49).]

Those who say that what is written—“But concerning the day and hour no one knows, neither the angels nor the Son” (Matthew 24:36; Mark 13:33)—is true according to the blasphemy of the Arians, and not on account of the dispensation of the assumed flesh, let them be anathema.

**5.** [Note: [Col. 0248B]]

This anathema strikes not only the Arians and Macedonians, but also Origen, the original father of both errors, whom Epiphanius above all, and Jerome, reported to have held utterly absurd and impious views about the Trinity in his books *On First Principles* (*Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*). The former should be consulted in heresy 64 and in his letter to John of Jerusalem; the latter, when sending Avitus his translation of the books *On First Principles*, warned him to remember while reading that he had to walk among scorpions and serpents, since those books contain very many detestable things. Among them is the following, immediately in the first volume (Letter 124):

Christ the Son of God was not born but made; God the Father, because of His invisible nature, is not seen even by the Son; the Son, who is the image of the invisible Father, when compared with the Father, is not the truth; among us, however, who cannot receive the truth of almighty God, an imaginary truth appears, so that the majesty and greatness of the greater may in some way be understood as circumscribed in the Son.

And later:

He gives the example of two statues, one large and one small: one filling the world and being, by its magnitude, in some way invisible, the other falling within the range of sight; he compares the former with the Father and the latter with the Son.

He calls God the almighty Father good and of perfect goodness; but he says that the Son is not good, rather a certain breath and image of goodness, so that He is not called simply “good,” but with an addition, “the good Shepherd,” and so forth. In dignity and honor he places the Holy Spirit third, after the Father and the Son. Although he says that he does not know whether the Spirit was made or unmade, he later expressed his view of Him by affirming that nothing except God the Father alone was unmade. He also says that the Son is lesser than the Father because He is second after Him, and that the Holy Spirit is inferior to the Son; that He dwells in each of the saints; [Col. 0248D] and that, in this order, the power of the Father is greater than that of the Son and the Holy Spirit, while the power of the Son is again greater than that of the Holy Spirit; and consequently that the power of the Holy Spirit Himself is greater than that of all the other things called holy.

The things that Jerome then charged against Origen, and later Justinian as well, together with many others of the same kind, you will seek in vain in the books we possess, since they were interpolated by Rufinus and purged of heresies opposed to the Nicene faith. Would that either Origen’s Greek text itself, or at least Jerome’s Latin translation, which he sent to Avitus, had reached our own time!

Rufinus of Aquileia certainly professed views contrary to Origen. “Concerning the Trinity,” he says (*Apology to Anastasius*), “we believe that it is of one nature, one divinity, and one and the same power and substance,” and so forth.

Rufinus of Palestine develops the same point at greater length (*Booklet of Faith*), as do certain other heretics of nearly the same period. They used the confession of *homoousios* (*ὁμοούσιος*, “of the same substance”), which at that time was almost the badge of Catholic faith, to deceive the simple and draw the unwary into their own errors.]

Those who say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the holy Trinity—are of different substances from one another and not of one power and nature, let them be anathema.

[Col. 0249A] **6.** [Note: [Col. 0249A]]

None of Origen’s defenders contradicts the Catholics who accuse the books *On First Principles* (*Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) of the dogma condemned here. Hence Epiphanius writes (Letter 51, in Jerome):

What Catholic could endure this with equanimity? Which of those who adorn their faith with good works could bear to hear Origen’s doctrine and instruction, and believe his splendid preaching: “THE SON CANNOT SEE THE FATHER, NOR CAN THE HOLY SPIRIT SEE THE SON”? These things are written in the books *On First Principles*. We read them in these words, and this is how Origen spoke: “For just as it is incongruous to say that the Son can see the Father, so it is inconsistent to suppose that the Holy Spirit can see the Son.”

The Origenists plainly resorted to astonishing evasions when they were no longer being pressed on behalf of their teacher, but were required to speak for themselves: whether the Son saw the Father, and whether the Holy Spirit saw the Son. [Col. 0249B] Hence Jerome, addressing his speech to John of Jerusalem (Letter 51):

You are charged with the fact that your teacher, whom you call a Catholic and defend vigorously, said: “The Son does not see the Father, and the Holy Spirit does not see the Son.” And you say to me: “The Father is invisible, the Son is invisible, the Holy Spirit is invisible”—as though angels too were not invisible to our eyes according to their nature. And shortly afterward:

The question is “whether the Son sees the Father,” and you say: “The Father is invisible.” The issue is “whether the Holy Spirit sees the Son,” and you answer: “The Son is invisible.” The matter under discussion is “whether the Trinity sees one another”; human ears cannot endure so great a blasphemy, and you say: “The Trinity is invisible.” You wander into other praises and launch into arguments about matters no one is asking about; you lead the hearer elsewhere so that you will not speak about what we are asking.

Rufinus of Aquileia found another such *kresphýgeton* (*κρησφύγετον*, “evasion”): he argues that Origen used the verb “to see” in the sense of the faculty of sight (*Invective 1 against Jerome*), since Origen was arguing against the Anthropomorphites and Valentinians, who gave God a body. But no one who consults Origen himself will fail immediately to despise this quibble as worthless—even ridiculous.]

Those who say, in whatever manner and in whatever sense, that the Son does not see the Father, let them be anathema.

[Col. 0250A] **7.** [Note: [Col. 0249C]]

Epiphanius writes in his letter to John of Jerusalem, preserved by Jerome:

Who could tolerate Origen saying in the books *On First Principles* that the souls of angels were in heaven, and that after they sinned in the heavenly places they were cast down into this world and confined, as it were, in these bodies as in tombs and graves, to pay the penalties of ancient sins; and that the bodies of believers are not temples of Christ but prisons of the condemned? And later:

Although he is accustomed to affirm such nonsense and delusions through a perverse interpretation of Scripture, saying something other than what is true, as in: “Before I was humbled, I sinned” (Psalm 118:67); and: “Return, my soul, to your rest” (Psalm 114:7); and also: “Bring my soul out of prison” (Psalm 141:8). And elsewhere: “I will confess to the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 114:9), and so forth.

Jerome treats this same matter at great length (Letter 51), exposing and dissolving John’s evasions and tricks in his response to Epiphanius, as he calls them. But since the discussion is too long, it should perhaps be omitted here, and something more concise should be supplied from elsewhere.

Jerome therefore introduces the heretics arguing as follows (Letter to Demetrias):

“If the judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves” (Psalm 18:10), and if there is nothing unjust with God, reason itself compels us to believe that souls once existed in the heavenly places and, because of certain ancient sins, were condemned to human bodies and, so to speak, buried in them; and that we are paying in this valley of tears the penalties of ancient sins. Hence the Prophet also says: “Before I was humbled, I sinned” (Psalm 118:67), and: “Bring my soul out of prison” (Psalm 141:8), and so forth.

This impious and criminal doctrine once circulated in Egypt and the regions of the East, and now, as though hidden in the pits of vipers, it circulates among many and pollutes the purity of those regions, and so forth.

But since Jerome mentioned divine justice, under cover of which Origen attempted to hide himself, it will not be out of place to explain how, on this account, the holy man formerly suffered slander from Rufinus of Aquileia (*Invective 1 against Jerome*), as though he had reproached another for a sin of which he himself was guilty.

In his commentaries on the Letter to the Ephesians, after explaining the reason for divine election, which is called grace, he was about to explain another, which they call justice, and wrote as follows:

Another person, who attempts to demonstrate that God is just because He chooses each person not through any prejudice arising from His foreknowledge but according to the merit of the elect, says that before the visible creatures there were other invisible ones, among which were souls that, for reasons known only to God, had been cast down into this valley of tears, and so forth.

But Rufinus’ inept cavilling, which abuses the patience of readers, is refuted sufficiently by the passage itself, since Jerome is explaining there not what he himself thought but what someone else thought. He himself repeatedly testified to this, pleading the law of commentaries that prevailed at that time.

If anyone wishes to know more carefully by what stages, according to Origen, souls are hurled down from the height of angels all the way to human bodies, let him read Book II of *On First Principles*, chapter 8, and Jerome’s Letter 61, shortly before its middle.

But observe, reader, into what absurdities so great a man as Origen—the teacher, as he was called, of the East and doctor of the Church—fell because of that premature judgment by which Augustine himself was once driven astray: that GOD’S ELECTION IS NOT OF GRACE BUT OF JUSTICE.

For, since he did not think that the causes of distinction could be attributed to God, lest anything unjust should be found in Him, he placed them partly in human beings, whom he saw born into infinitely unequal and different conditions. He attributed the whole matter to the unequal merits of individuals, so that those whose merits were better might be chosen for a better lot, and those whose merits were evil for a worse one—as though, in Augustine’s former statement (*Book II to Simplicianus*), no one were chosen over another unless he were already different from him.

Since he understood from elsewhere that no one could reasonably be said to be judged according to subsequent merits, he concluded that certain antecedent merits had to be found.

Accordingly, he first thought that souls had existed before they fell into bodies. Then, since the time of their priority could not be determined without rashness, he supposed that they had existed at least throughout the whole age of the world, and that all had been created simultaneously, with a certain spiritual world of souls existing before the sensible world.

Among them, he said, was also the soul of Christ, equal by nature to the others but far superior in the pursuit of virtue. It had joined itself with such devotion to the divine Word—that is, to Wisdom, the parent of all virtues—that the bond of union became indissoluble. Consequently, that soul advanced by its merit and virtue into the status of God.

He wished this entire merit to arise solely from the powers of free choice, so that God, the common parent of all and goodness and justice itself, would not create any distinction among equals. Thus he thought that each soul could do what Christ’s soul had done, and that no soul could rightly begrudge another a good that lay within its own power.

This may be what later became the dreadful blasphemy of Theodore of Mopsuestia: “I do not envy Christ because He was made God; for what He was made, I can become, by the powers of my nature.” This was certainly the heresy of the Pelagians, if Cassian is to be believed (*Book I on the Incarnation*, chapter 4), as well as the writer of the epitaph of the Nestorian heresy, among the works attributed to Prosper—though perhaps they are mistaken.

Now, since Origen believed that souls existed for so long without bodies, equal by nature and differing only in merits, he thought it followed that bodies had to be conceived as something foreign to human beings, introducing manifold difference, dulling the powers of souls, and impeding their movements. For this reason he wished “man” to be defined, in the manner of Plato, as “a soul using a body.” He also wished the soul, although previously it had been merely a mind, to receive the name “soul” only when it put on a body.

But since Origen could form no conception of the mind that he imagined separated from the garment of the body and devoted for exceedingly long intervals to spiritual activities, other than the conception impressed upon our minds by angels—for we define angels as minds separated from bodies and perfect without them—he made the human mind angelic in nature.

Indeed, he decided that the whole universe consisted entirely of three things: divinity, minds, and matter (*hyle*). If any further diversity is observed, he traced it all to the merits of wills and the justice of God. He held that the lowest part of the world was constructed from denser matter by the angry hand of God into a valley of tears, while the highest was formed from the finest particles of matter by God’s other, benevolent hand into the kingdom of the blessed, and so forth.

From this there arose four notions. First, the descent of souls from the height of angels into bodies, some being cast down—namely, the guilty—while others were sent voluntarily and, since they possessed virtues, served divine Providence in governing the rest. Second, the transformation of souls into demons through crimes, and into angels through what may be called degrees of virtue. Third, the reciprocal transformation of angels and demons. Fourth, that all these names—minds, souls, angels, and demons—signify not natures but merits, or rather conditions arising from merits.

Finally, it seemed to him that from all rational creatures—which, considered in themselves, are pure minds and are reckoned in one order—there arose a general kind of embodiment (*ensōmatōsis*, *ἐνσωμάτωσις*) once they were distinguished by degrees and names; so that every diversity arises from the variety of bodies, whether finer or denser.]

Those who say that our souls fell from the height of angels into these bodies because of certain ancient sins and perform penance in this world, adducing the testimonies “Before I was humbled, I sinned” (Psalm 118:67), “Bring my soul out of prison” (Psalm 141:8), and other similar passages, let them be anathema.

**8.** [Note: [Col. 0251D]]

This entire anathema attacks the heresy of the Apollinarists. The author of the *Predestined One* says (Book I, heresy 55) that they deny “a perfect man in Christ,” but hold that the assumption of flesh took place in such a way that divinity was within the man in place of a soul. They also most contentiously assert that the flesh and the Word are of one and the same substance, wishing to teach that the words “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14) mean that something of the Word was changed into flesh. Moreover, they affirm that nothing was assumed from Mary’s flesh in the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. A synod at Antioch acted against Apollinaris.

There were two Apollinarians. As Socrates says (Book II, final chapter), they first said that the soul had not been assumed by God the Word in the dispensation of the Incarnation; [Col. 0252A] then, apparently brought to repentance and correcting themselves, they added that a soul had indeed been assumed, but that it did not possess a mind, since God the Word occupied the place of the mind in the assumed man.

Before both of them, Apelles had held that Christ possessed a body of some heavenly substance. Although Origen may appear to have reproved him verbally, he could in reality be thought to have followed him because of his own notion concerning the descent of souls by the mystical ladder of Jacob—as Jerome jokes—and the assumption of different bodies according to the various regions of the world, as though according to different steps. See Tertullian, chapter 51, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*.

The Arians too, before Apollinaris, had held that the Word served Christ in place of a human mind. Although they may have learned this error elsewhere, they could nevertheless have received it to some extent from Origen, since he devised something akin to it: namely, that Christ’s soul or mind, before descending into a body, had once been transformed into the Word, as some interpret him.

That Origen opened the way to this entire class of heretics may be inferred from the fact that his opinions—whether deliberately obscure or inconsistent according to the character of his intellect—gave those devoted to the Catholic faith grounds for attributing to him, not implausibly, the things that Pamphilus is believed to have attempted to refute (*Apology for Origen*). Above all, they could accuse him of saying that everything done by the Savior had occurred *dokēsei* (*δοκήσει*), that is, only apparently and allegorically, and not also according to the events reported in the historical narrative.]

Those who say that our Lord and Savior did not come in our nature, but was of a different and higher substance, whether heavenly; and that He did not assume the whole of what comes from Mary; or that He did not possess a human soul; or that He possessed a mind without sin, let them be anathema.

**9.** [Note: [Col. 0252C]]

The dogma addressed here is so proper and distinctive to Origen that, unless it were already generally acknowledged, one could transcribe a large part of the books *On First Principles* wherever they discuss the world, and indeed rational creatures. Many testimonies could also be drawn from Epiphanius’ letters to John of Jerusalem, and from Jerome’s letters to Avitus and Pammachius, as well as from Jerome’s books against Rufinus and Rufinus’ books against Jerome.

Hence Augustine writes (*Book on Heresies*, heresy 43):

There are also other dogmas of Origen that the Catholic Church has entirely rejected. In these matters he is neither falsely accused nor capable of being excused by his defenders, especially concerning the purification and liberation, and then, after a long period, the return to the same evils, of the entire rational creation. For what Catholic, learned or unlearned, would not shudder violently at the purification of evils that he describes? He says that even those who ended this life in the greatest depravity, crimes, sacrileges, and impieties, and finally the devil himself and his angels, are purified and liberated after very long periods and restored to the kingdom and light of God; and that again, after very long periods, all who have been liberated relapse and return to these evils. He says that these alternations of blessedness and misery in rational creatures have always existed and will always exist. Against this most empty impiety, and against the philosophers from whom Origen learned it, I have argued most diligently in the books *On the City of God* (Book XXI, chapters 17 and following).]

Those who say that, after many ages and periods which human thought cannot comprehend, there will be a restoration of all things to their former state, and that everything will return to its original principles, let them be anathema.

**10.** [Note: [Col. 0252D]]

This too was a doctrine handed down by Origen, more briefly in the books *On First Principles*, but at greatest length in his book *On the Resurrection*: that human beings would not rise in the same body in which they had lain; for after the resurrection the members serving the preparation of food or the generation of offspring would not remain, nor flesh, bones, and other such things, which either burden the body, make human beings subject to death, or obstruct the nobility of the soul.

Jerome demonstrates this at great length (Letter 51), using Origen’s own words (Book II of *On First Principles*, near the end):

“When we have advanced so far that we are no longer flesh and bodies—perhaps not even souls—but mind and sense brought to perfection, with no cloud of disturbances darkening our understanding, we shall behold rational and intelligible substances face to face.”

Jerome translated these words in his letter to Avitus; Rufinus corrupted them in the commonly circulated manuscripts.

Moreover, the book *On the Resurrection* has perished and is entirely lacking except for the fragments Jerome cites in Letter 61, which you should consult.]

Those who say that after the resurrection we will not have the same bodies, but certain airy and spiritual bodies, not of the same nature as those in which we were buried, though incorruptible and immortal, let them be anathema.

**11.** [Note: [Col. 0253B]]

The dogma condemned here differs little from the preceding one. Origen transmits it in Book II of *On First Principles*, chapter 5, from which Jerome extracted the following, writing to Avitus what must be avoided (Letter 124):

“If everything will live without a body, all bodily nature will be consumed and reduced to nothing, although it was once made from nothing; and there will be a time when its use is again necessary.” And shortly afterward: “We will be without bodies when we have been perfectly subjected to Him [Christ].” And in the same place: “When all have been subjected to God, all will lay aside their bodies, and then the whole nature of bodily things will dissolve into nothing.”

Observe that in nearly all passages where “nothing” (*nihilum*) occurs, “matter” (*hyle*) ought to be restored. For Origen considered the matter from which bodies were created and into which they must be dissolved to be everlasting and, as they say, coeternal with God. This can easily be confirmed both from the testimonies of the ancients and from Origen himself.

Observe also in this anathema, as in the ninth, the mention of a remarkable notion by which Origen imagined that all things were created by God in a single state, from which rational natures later departed through their own movements. Nevertheless, they were to be recalled to that state by various changes and alternations, whether of individual creatures or of the sensible worlds themselves. When they had returned to it, an everlasting peace would immediately arise after periods so long that to us they seem to have the character of eternity.

From this it may be inferred that Origen never really called creatures absolutely eternal, nor the changes of creatures absolutely everlasting, but only eternal and everlasting in relation to us, for whom the interval between beginning and ending is incomprehensible.]

Those who say that, after the end of the resurrection and after many ages, bodies will be abolished and return to matter (*hyle*), so that we will be souls alone without bodies, as we were previously, let them be anathema.

**12.** [Note: [Col. 0253C]]

Origen consistently and explicitly taught in the books *On First Principles* that souls existed before they were enclosed in bodies. No defender of his has dared to deny this—not even Pamphilus, who is believed to have defended him (*Apology for Origen*). Pamphilus thought he had defended Origen sufficiently in this respect after showing that, in Origen’s lifetime, nothing had yet been defined by the Church concerning this question. It was therefore permissible for anyone to follow whichever of the three widespread opinions concerning the origin of souls he preferred: that souls had either pre-existed bodies, [Col. 0254A] or were created daily by God, or were transmitted by parents.

Accordingly, contrary to his usual practice, he fought the latter two opinions with numerous arguments, as though, once they had been overthrown, the Origenist position would be established.

Jerome called the view of daily creation an ecclesiastical dogma (Letter 51), and responded at length to the objections commonly raised against it, including those already raised by Pamphilus. Nevertheless, he was never able to win Augustine over to his own side (*Book II of the Retractions*), nor could he prevent Augustine from remaining doubtful about the matter until the end of his life.

Rufinus of Aquileia likewise remained doubtful until that point in his life. Thus, after recounting various opinions on the question in his *Apology*, he says:

“With God as my witness, I declare that up to the present I hold nothing certain or defined concerning this question.” And shortly afterward: “I confess that I still do not know, apart from what the Church plainly teaches: that God is the creator both of souls and of bodies.”

Rufinus of Palestine writes (*Booklet of Faith*, chapter 26):

Thus, those who believe that souls are particles of God, and likewise those who say that souls were made before bodies, appear to be far removed from piety. Hence the impious Origen, captivated by the error of the pagans, and so forth.

Pelagius writes (*Booklet of Faith*, number 16):

We believe that souls are given by God, and we say that they were made by Him, anathematizing those who say that souls are, as it were, a part of the divine substance. We also condemn the error of those who say that souls sinned previously or lived in heaven before they were sent into bodies.

It will be useful to note several things here.

First, from the contradiction between the two Rufini—namely, the author of the anathemas and Rufinus of Aquileia—it is certain either that Mercator was mistaken when he believed that the anathemas had been written by Rufinus of Aquileia (a view I can scarcely bring myself to entertain), or, much more plausibly, that the error arose from scribes, so that Anastasius’ letter was placed before this confession of faith because the name of Rufinus, which had been placed before the anathemas, was mistakenly understood by ignorant copyists to mean Rufinus of Aquileia.

Second, the Pelagians themselves, who must be distinguished from the Massilians, strongly attacked both Origen’s opinion concerning the pre-existence (*proýparxis*, *προΰπαρξις*) of souls and the opinion concerning their transmission from parents, which Jerome attributed to many Westerners. They therefore stood so firmly by the third position that they seemed thereby to attack the doctrine of original sin more certainly, as though it could not stand at all unless it rested on one or the other of those opinions.

Third, the view of the daily creation of souls was not as firmly established as it is now until after the eighth century. Gregory the Great testifies that in his own time the question was still uncertain and commonly debated on both sides. He writes as follows (*Book IX, Letter 53 to Secundinus*, chapter 6):

“Let your most sweet charity know that a considerable inquiry concerning the origin of the soul has been debated among the holy Fathers; but whether it descended from Adam or is certainly given to each individual remained uncertain. They confessed that the question was insoluble in this life, for it is a difficult matter and cannot be comprehended by man,” and so forth.]

Those who say that souls existed before they were born, and that they are not created by God daily together with the body, according to the example of the first man, let them be anathema.

[Col. 0255]

# SECOND APPENDIX TO THE FIRST PART OF THE WORKS OF MARIUS MERCATOR

Containing seven dissertations, in which the whole history of Pelagianism is set forth and many popular opinions are refuted.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0255] At one time I intended to write, as an appendix to the first part of Mercator’s works, a history of the Pelagian heresy. I would have included everything that I had either now learned for the first time from my author or diligently gathered from other writers of the fifth century and had at hand. I was restrained, however, not only by the nature of history itself, which demands greater freedom of composition and more leisure free from teaching duties than I possess, but also by the character of the material to be treated, which, because of its complexity, requires a freer style of writing.

For the laws of history do not permit *ta kritika* (*τὰ κριτικά*, “critical discussions”) to be mixed into narratives, although that would have been necessary; nor could the critical discussions be omitted without diminishing the labor undertaken in preparing an accurate edition of Marius Mercator’s works.

I therefore preferred to encompass in dissertations rather than in a history whatever I had to say about matters relating to the Pelagian controversy. I preferred this, I say, not only for the reason I have given, but especially because this entire kind of disputation has a closer affinity with the scholastic disputations in which I have grown old, and because it does not wish to be adorned with any elegance of expression other than that by which each person ordinarily explains his own opinion simply and openly.

Since the whole work we are undertaking has been undertaken for the purpose of explaining Mercator’s statements, and since Mercator has transmitted nothing concerning Pelagian affairs beyond the death of Saint Augustine, or at least beyond the Council of Ephesus, it seemed appropriate to confine the dissertations to that same period of years and to touch on nothing except what occurred from the rise of the heresy that received its name from Pelagius to its condemnation by the Fathers at Ephesus. It also seemed appropriate to place at the beginning of each dissertation the words of Mercator that occasioned it.

Since, however, it is of great importance for our undertaking to understand what the heresy in question was, from what parents it arose or by what patrons it was defended, by which synods it was judged by the Church, by what imperial enactments it was proscribed, and how it was condemned throughout the entire world; and finally, by what confessions it was asserted by the heretics and by what books it was refuted by defenders of the Catholic faith, seven dissertations were needed altogether.

The dissertation that investigates the heresy’s origin and growth—especially the phase called Coelestian and attacked by Mercator—had to be placed last, so that it might serve as a kind of completion and fruit of the others. The first will therefore show which parents the heresy acquired and who its principal defenders were; the second, by which synods it was judged; the third, by what imperial sanctions it was proscribed; the fourth, how, in Prosper’s words (*Poem Against the Ungrateful*), it was condemned “by the hand of the world”; the fifth, by what booklets the heretics attempted not so much to explain their faith as to conceal it; the sixth, by what books the Catholic Fathers defended the Catholic faith; and the final dissertation, in what prodigious manner the heresy grew from a slender root.

For I think that in these seven dissertations I can encompass the entire Pelagian controversy as it was conducted in those times, and confirm it with such manifest documents that, although many popular opinions concerning individuals must be overturned—for I do not intend to treat the doctrines—the reader will not lay aside his preconceived judgments without great pleasure when he sees the truth emerging from its darkness for the first time under the guidance of a most authoritative author.

No dissertation will fail to contain a great deal that is new and hitherto unknown. To offer a taste of the matter, the final dissertation will show the origin of the whole Pelagian heresy and its growth from a single little question into a prodigious multitude of parties. The first will plainly refute the popular error that Rufinus of Aquileia was Coelestius’ teacher. The second will present more than twenty-four councils convened in the Pelagian controversy during Augustine’s lifetime. The third will disclose with what industry Augustine, through friends and emperors, exerted pressure and moved the imperial court in defense of the Catholic faith. The fourth will encompass the entire history of the subscription required in this controversy. The fifth will publish for the first time the *Booklet of Faith* sent by Julian to Zosimus, the supreme pontiff. The sixth will bring forward the authors of the books *Hypognosticon*, *Questions on the New and Old Testaments*, *Commentaries on the Letters of Paul*, and others, marked by unmistakable identifying features.

# FIRST DISSERTATION: ON THE FIRST AUTHORS AND PRINCIPAL DEFENDERS OF THE PELAGIAN HERESY

On these words of Mercator:

“The controversy against the Catholic faith, among certain Syrians and especially in Cilicia, was raised long ago by Theodore, formerly bishop of the town of Mopsuestia,” and so forth (*Preface to the book of Subnotations*).

[Col. 0257]

## CHAPTER ONE

The purpose of the dissertation, and incidentally concerning Paul of Samosata, who might appear to someone to be the first author of the Pelagian heresy.

[Col. 0257A]

What happens to heresies also happens to rivers: people commonly think they arise where they receive their name, although they often trace their origin farther back and flow from distant springs whose nature they retain. This is plainly visible in very many sects, and clearly in the one that received its name from Pelagius and Coelestius.

The common people think that it arose from those from whom it took its name; learned people either openly disagree with this or assent to it hesitantly. Certainly Augustine—a matter that once caused me considerable astonishment—when writing in the name of the Fathers of Milevis to Saint Innocent concerning Pelagius and Coelestius, did not simply call them the authors of the detestable heresy, but added the words “as they report.” It was as though he did not wish to guarantee the opinion of the multitude and did not think that he should affirm what he understood to rest on slight arguments.

[Col. 0257B] My astonishment increased because, in his letter to Optatus, Augustine himself wrote that those same men were either authors of the new heresy or, at any rate, its most vigorous and notorious promoters. He was evidently inclined to attribute to them alone the defense of a heresy received from other authors, and not to make them its parents, lest he follow the opinion of the multitude, which was not sufficiently weighty.

He says the same thing in his book *On Original Sin*, so that his wavering may appear consistent. “The authors of this perversity,” he writes (chapter 22), “are either said to be, or even proved to be, Pelagius and Coelestius; or, if they are not its authors but learned it from others, they are nevertheless proclaimed its advocates and teachers, through whom it spread and grew more widely, by their words, their writings, their appropriate signs, and the reputation arising from all these and becoming increasingly widespread.”

This consideration prompted me to attempt, with greater effort, to discover by whatever means I could where this doubt had arisen in Augustine’s mind. For it was not enough for me that I had read in Jerome [Col. 0257C] (*Letter to Ctesiphon*) about Origen, Rufinus of Aquileia, Evagrius of the Hyperboreans, Jovinian, Palladius, Priscillian, the Manichaeans, the Euchites, and other heralds of ἀναμαρτησία (*sinlessness*), whom someone might reasonably call the forerunners of Pelagius in this respect. For in those passages of Augustine from which my astonishment arose, the subject is two other Pelagian questions, quite different and of the greatest importance: whether the grace of God is given on the basis of merits, and whether Adam’s sin injured him alone. I therefore thought it necessary to ask further from whom Pelagius and Coelestius had learned both parts of their error concerning these two controversies, if indeed they were neither its authors nor, so to speak, its parents.

While I was investigating more ardently where light might emerge in so obscure a matter, I encountered, as I searched the monuments of antiquity, Theodore of Mopsuestia in John Maxentius, and, in Sirmond’s collections, Rufinus, a presbyter of the province of Palestine. Both are found in Marius Mercator, an author whom no one investigated the affairs of the Pelagians more inquisitively, and no one reported them more briefly or distinctly.

First we must discuss these two parents of the Pelagians; then the four most ardent defenders of their doctrines, Pelagius, Coelestius, Julian, and Annianus. Annianus is less well known to the general public because he wrote little under his own name, although perhaps more under another’s.

## CHAPTER II  
### On Theodore, Bishop of Mopsuestia, the First Author of the Coelestian Heresy

[Col. 0258A] I confess that formerly the origin of Pelagian impiety seemed to me to have to be traced farther back, namely to Paul, who was sometimes called “of Samosata” by the name of his homeland, and sometimes “of Antioch” from the see of that illustrious city, which he had occupied despite his humble origins. For he held impious opinions about Christ, on account of which he was corrected by the bishops at the first Council of Antioch and then deposed at the second. He maintained, namely, that Christ was not true God but a mere human being, upon whom the effective Word of God—he absurdly imagined it to be something uttered, resembling our own word, and ἀνυπόστατον (*without independent subsistence*)—had descended just as upon the other prophets, though in greater abundance and with more excellent operation. He further said that this man, by his works, had merited such great grace, though not to the extent that someone else could not attain the same, provided only that he wished to strive.

The first two parts of this error—that Christ is a mere human being and that the Word of God descended upon him—are known to all theologians. Concerning the third, somewhat less familiar point, that he merited this grace by his works, we have the following testimonies of the ancients.

Dionysius of Alexandria, writing to Paul, says:

> Hear and understand, in opposition to what has been said by you, and consider what you say: a human being honored by God with greater graces according to God’s good pleasure, especially when he proved more acceptable to God by leading a diligent life, and so forth.

A synod of Arians held at Antioch in the year 344 declared:

> Because we confess one God alone, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and one only-begotten Son, we do not on that account deny that Christ was God before the ages, as do the disciples of Paul of Samosata, who assert that after his Incarnation he became God through progress in virtue, because he was a mere human being.

(*In Athanasius, On the Synods.*)

Athanasius writes:

> Is that man Christ like other human beings, or is he God clothed in flesh? If he is an ordinary human being, and like other human beings, let it be granted that, as a human being, he makes progress. This, however, is the opinion of the Samosatan, which you foster with all your heart and strength, repudiating it in name because of human considerations.

(*Oration IV against the Arians.*)

[Col. 0258C] Yet since testimonies of this sort are not especially explicit, and do not concern Paul in such a way that they cannot be redirected to his disciples, I do not think they should be given much credence—especially since the epitaph of the Pelagian heresy, on account of whose interpretation I had been inclined toward the opinion I mentioned, can be interpreted in another way, as we shall show in the second part of Mercator’s works.

## CHAPTER II. On Theodore, Bishop of Mopsuestia, the First Author of the Coelestian Heresy

From the time of Paul of Samosata, that poison which the impure enemy of Christ had breathed out infected the Church of Antioch almost continuously. Heresy was not extinguished at the same time as its head was cut off; rather, once the teacher had been driven out, the disciples remained—more pernicious in proportion as they were more skilled at deception, and outwardly closer to the Catholic faith. It is credible that they were not altogether concealed, since, according to Athanasius and other writers, they were commonly recognized and called disciples of Paul, and some of them periodically caused trouble for the Church.

Theodore surpassed the others in impiety. Photius called him “the Antiochene” from his homeland, while others called him “the Mopsuestian” from the city whose church he governed for thirty-six full years. He transferred the poison received from Paul into Nestorius and the Pelagians, so that Nestorius was called “the son of Theodore of Raithu, Theodore’s descendant, Paul’s grandson” (*The Great Library*, vol. II), and John Maxentius wrote that Theodore of Mopsuestia had been the teacher of Pelagius, Coelestius, and Julian (*Profession of Faith*, vol. IV of the same Library).

Since we must discuss this man in the later part of Mercator’s works, where fragments of the books he composed are to be presented, three matters must now briefly be investigated in relation to our present subject: first, on account of which errors he could rightly be called the parent of the Pelagian heresy; second, from whom he received those errors; third, to whom he subsequently transmitted them.

He is said to have held three principal errors, from which others depended either entirely or to a greater extent. He taught that Christ had been a pure and simple human being, differing from the rest only in that God the Word operated in him more effectively than in the others. He then said, so it is reported—although this will later have to be examined—that by the merits of his works and the powers of his free will this man had attained such great grace that he was called the only Son of God (*Fifth Synod*, session 4). Finally, he denied that the Son of God had come to remove original sin, since he acknowledged no such sin, but said that Christ had come so as to benefit all by example and instruction (*in Mercator’s excerpts*).

Facundus of Hermiane opposed the Fifth General Council in almost twelve complete books, in order to remove from Theodore the charge of the first error. But the council prevailed, and, victorious, secured the acceptance by the whole Church of its judgment against Theodore and against two defenders of Theodore, Ibas and Theodoret.

Mercator may be regarded as a witness to the second error when he reports Theodore as saying:

> I do not envy Christ because he was made God; for what he himself was made, I too have been made, because he belongs to my nature.

(*Collections from Theodore’s books.*)

The passage must be corrected on the basis of the tenth session of the Council of Chalcedon, where mention is made of a statement attributed to Ibas of Edessa, which Theodore, his teacher, commonly proclaimed:

> I do not envy Christ, who was made God, since I too, if I wish, can become so.

(*Council of Chalcedon*, session 10.)

For in those times the expression “I, if I wish, can” meant nothing other than that the matter under discussion could be accomplished by the powers of free will. Hence Jerome charged Pelagius (*First Dialogue against the Pelagians*), as did Orosius in his *Apology* and the Palestinian Fathers, with having denied the necessity of divine assistance for fulfilling the commandments, because he had written in his book *Eulogies* that a human being could keep God’s commandments if he wished.

Augustine says:

> That proposition was not approved, because it appeared to have been placed by him in his book as though this lay solely within human power through free will. For this is what he was accused of having thought when he said, “if he wishes.”

(*On the Proceedings at Palestine*, ch. 39.)

Theodore himself clearly reveals the third error in the five entire books he wrote against Saint Augustine. We received excerpts from these books through Marius Mercator under the following title:

> From the fourth book, folio ten, of Theodore of Mopsuestia’s *Second Code*, against Saint Augustine, who defended original sin and argued in Catholic fashion that Adam had been made mortal through transgression.

[Col. 0259D] We have said more on this subject in the notes to those excerpts, where we showed that Photius had mentioned these books. It will be worthwhile to consult Photius’s passage, and the notes themselves as well.

The first error Theodore received from Paul of Samosata, as everyone admits, though through Diodore, whom he heard teaching at Tarsus and from whom he could likewise have received the other two. For the second is clearly found in the surviving fragments from Diodore’s books, while the seeds of the third seem to appear in the work *Against the Mathematicians* preserved by Photius. It is preferable, however, to make Theodore himself the author of both later doctrines, and to apply to this matter what Photius says:

> The Coelestian heresy flourished in the East and was also spread in the West.

Greek: Κελεστιανὴ αἵρεσις ἤκμασεν ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ· διεδόθη δὲ καὶ ἐν τῇ δύσει.

[Col. 0260A] Theodore transmitted the first doctrine to Nestorius, as Cyril writes in his letter to Succensus; the second perhaps to the monk Leporius, as may be gathered partly from Prosper and partly from Cassian; and the third to Rufinus the Syrian, and through him to Pelagius and Coelestius, according to Mercator. I say that he transmitted the first both orally and in writing, the second only in writing, and the third by oral instruction alone. Nestorius heard Theodore speaking and drew poison from his books. Leporius, since he was born in Gaul, learned the Eastern errors only through writings. Finally, since Theodore did not write about original sin until old age, or at least until questions concerning it had openly arisen, he could have instructed Rufinus only by word of mouth.

Marius Mercator briefly weaves together the entire history of the origin, homeland, parents, propagation, and defenders of the Coelestian heresy:

> A question against the Catholic faith, raised long ago among certain Syrians, especially in Cilicia, by Theodore, formerly bishop of the town of Mopsuestia, is still secretly gnawing away among a very few of them. It is not openly brought forward, but is retained within the churches by those who whisper about it as though they were Catholics:
>
> “The progenitors of the human race, Adam and Eve, were created mortal by God; and they did not injure any of their descendants through their own transgression, but harmed only themselves. They made themselves guilty before God of the commandment, and no one else at all.”

This foolish question, no less hostile to the true faith, was first brought to Rome under Anastasius, of holy memory, supreme pontiff of the Roman Church, by a certain Rufinus, a Syrian by nationality. Being clever, and protecting himself against the odium of the matter, he did not dare to put it forward on his own. Instead, he deceived Pelagius, a monk by race from Britain, and thoroughly imbued and instructed him in the impious vanity mentioned above.

Soon afterward, when Pelagius dared to compose commentaries on the Apostle Paul and came to the most famous passage in the Epistle to the Romans, which reads:

> Therefore, just as through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so passed into all human beings, and so forth

(Rom. 5:12), he declared there that only those were guilty and held liable to that transgression who wished to imitate Adam in transgressing God’s commandments—not all those who had been generated from his seed through successive generations.

From this point he argues at greater length about the passages that follow in the Epistle, and declares that no human being at all had been injured, or is injured, through generation by Adam’s sin and transgression:

> But by imitation, he says, because that first man sinned within the human race; and he becomes guilty and liable who imitates him by his own will—not by being born, but by sinning.

Coelestius, noble by birth and at that time a legal scholar, but rendered a eunuch by a defect of nature from his mother’s womb, attached himself to Pelagius. Instructed by the Pelagius just mentioned, he absorbed this most impious opinion in a purer form and, with incredible loquacity, made many people participants and accomplices in his madness. He dared openly and publicly to disseminate the same opinion throughout the peoples in the following formulations:

> Adam was made mortal, and whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died; Adam’s sin injured him alone and not the human race; infants who are born are in the same condition in which Adam was before his transgression; just as the whole human race does not rise through Christ’s resurrection, so the whole human race does not die through Adam’s death; infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.

These five propositions generate one single, most impious and unspeakable opinion.

He further added:

> A human being can exist without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments, because even before Christ’s coming there were human beings without sin, and because the Law leads to the kingdom of heaven in the same way as the Gospel.

These and similar propositions were also pleasing to Julian and the rest of his fellow soldiers. Once they had become known and exposed, and had been condemned by ecclesiastical authority together with the persons mentioned above, they were defended by Julian through the sheer number of his books.

Before concluding what must be said about Theodore, a certain likeness of him must be sketched, so that the entire portrait may later be painted in its proper colors. The acts of the Fifth General Council provide the outlines.

By nature he possessed an intellect capable of learning, but deceitful, changeable into any form, eager for novelty, and impatiently desirous of glory. His eloquence, which he cultivated through the arts of rhetoric, was said to have been so powerful that he could persuade not only the common people but even others of almost anything.

In public sermons, composed entirely to please, he said one thing; in private, whether in his chambers or in books, he said another. He did not entrust these books indiscriminately to everyone, but only to those whom he sometimes compelled by oath to keep the secret most carefully. Meanwhile, if something should either have slipped out in the course of speaking or have been deliberately uttered that was not received by the listeners in the way Theodore wished—whether it might provoke hostility among the learned or complaint among the faithful—he immediately retracted the statement in evasive language. He was ready to fabricate anything and bold enough to lie, so as to retain the reputation of a Catholic teacher and not lose the opportunity to spread poison within the Church.

Thus, as long as he lived, he enjoyed an illustrious, or at least not a bad, reputation even among praised and holy men.
