But after his death people first began to have doubts; then, when the impiety of his pestilential books had been disclosed, the Fifth General Council proscribed the man’s memory. Time, which is the parent of truth, uncovered the falsehood that the skill of his followers, the power of his supporters, and fear of the authorities had wrapped in certain shadows that appeared religious and sacred.

## CHAPTER III  
### On Rufinus, Whom Coelestius Acknowledged as His Teacher

We cannot fail to list among the parents of the Pelagian heresy a certain presbyter Rufinus, since Coelestius acknowledged such a man as his teacher at the Council of Carthage, and Mercator wrote that Pelagius had been instructed by someone similar. But we must investigate more carefully who this presbyter Rufinus finally was.

Coelestius himself, accused by the deacon Paulinus before Aurelius and the bishops assembled at Carthage, explained certain words that he had previously uttered:

> I said that I was uncertain about the transmission of sin, but in such a way that I would agree with the one to whom God had given the grace of knowledge, because I had heard different things from men who were certainly presbyters established in the Catholic Church.

When Paulinus, who was questioning him, asked for the names of those presbyters, he replied:

> Saint Rufinus, a presbyter at Rome, who stayed with Saint Pammachius. I heard him say that there was no transmission of sin.

This gave rise to the question we are investigating: who was that Rufinus whom Coelestius mentioned?

An opinion became fixed in the minds of many and prevailed, partly through the passage of time and partly through authority—whether that of those who held the opinion, who were important men, or of the Fathers whose testimonies are produced and appear at first sight to be clear—that the Rufinus whom Coelestius said he had heard was the same as the presbyter of Aquileia, who was known throughout the Church because of his companionship with the traveling Melania and his published books, and also because of the enmity he carried on with Saint Jerome and his stubborn defense of Origen.

I may perhaps not easily uproot this opinion from the minds of learned men, because it has struck such deep roots. Even if I could, I would still dare to do so only very cautiously, out of the respect with which, as is proper, I regard the authors and those who follow them. Nevertheless, I shall honestly state what I think and submit for judgment by more learned men nine arguments which, even if they do not openly demonstrate the contrary to the common opinion, certainly create a considerable difficulty for me, and will do so for all who are willing to approach the matter honestly.

Marius Mercator says that the Rufinus mentioned in the ecclesiastical trial before Aurelius, and who taught Coelestius to deny the transmission of sin, was a Syrian (*Preface to the Subnotations*). Rufinus, Jerome’s rival, was Italian if we believe Palladius (*Lausiac History*); according to Jerome, he originated from a town in the territory of Aquileia. We must believe both, since the man must have been very well known to each: to Palladius because of their shared errors, and to Jerome because of their disputes and almost mutual hostility.

Mercator speaks of Rufinus, the teacher of Coelestius, as of a man who was not very well known:

> A certain Rufinus, a Syrian by nationality, and so forth.

The whole world knew the Aquileian because of his reputation for learning, his reputation for holiness, and his association with Melania.

The Aquileian brought into the city, in the thirteenth year of Siricius, a ship full of his blasphemies, as Jerome writes (*Against Rufinus*, book II). The Syrian first brought to Rome, under Anastasius, the question hostile to the true faith concerning original sin, as Mercator testifies in the passage cited shortly afterward.

The Rufinus whom Coelestius praises stayed at Rome with Saint Pammachius. But Pammachius was so devoted to Jerome that, far from allowing Rufinus of Aquileia to remain with him and treating him as a friend, he aroused Jerome against him and moved Anastasius to condemn him.

Rufinus, the teacher of Coelestius, was at Rome when he taught that there was no transmission of sin (Augustine, *On Original Sin*, ch. 4). The Aquileian, once he had departed from Rome, did not return there—not even for the trial, however insistently Anastasius summoned him—but withdrew to Aquileia, which he did not leave before the barbarians devastated his homeland.

Rufinus of Aquileia is indeed accused by Jerome as the forerunner and teacher of Pelagius, but in the same way as Jovinian, Evagrius Ponticus, and all the others whom he mentions in his letter to Ctesiphon: only with respect to the part concerning ἀπάθεια (*passionlessness*) and ἀναμαρτησία (*sinlessness*). With respect to the other matter, concerning the transmission of sin, he was not even suspected. But the teacher of Coelestius taught his disciples that there was no transmission of sin.

Indeed, since the Aquileian supported Origen, there was little reason to prosecute him as guilty of denying original sin, since Origenists sinned in this matter almost by excess: they believed, namely, that souls were thrust into bodies as into prisons, where they paid the penalties due for sins committed in an earlier life.

Paulinus made no exception against the Rufinus whom Coelestius mentioned. He could certainly have brought many charges against the Aquileian, especially this one: that he had been condemned by the Apostolic See on account of heresies and had died under that condemnation. Nor could Paulinus have been ignorant of the sentence of condemnation, since Venirius at Milan, at the same time that Anastasius did so at Rome, struck the Origenists with an anathema, and Paulinus had not yet been sent from Milan to Carthage.

Coelestius seems to indicate quite clearly that the Rufinus whom he praises was still alive at the time of the trial; otherwise he would have called him “holy” and “of blessed memory.” But the Aquileian had died in Sicily already a year or even two earlier, as can be demonstrated partly from Jerome’s books and partly from many other arguments.

Finally, the Rufinus who taught Coelestius was a presbyter established in the Catholic Church at the time when he taught—that is, he was in communion with the Apostolic See. The Aquileian had been deprived of communion by Anastasius before the year 402, in which Baronius thinks Anastasius wrote his letter concerning Rufinus to John of Jerusalem.

Who, then, was that Syrian Rufinus who, while living at Rome, taught Coelestius and Pelagius to hold an opinion contrary to the Catholic faith concerning original sin? I shall confess, with embarrassment, that I have nothing I wish to assert forcefully, because of the long-standing prejudice concerning the Aquileian. Nevertheless, I suspect—and perhaps someone will convert this suspicion more boldly into an opinion, and then into certainty—that this was the very man whom Jerome (*Letter 81, to Rufinus*) sent to Milan to Venirius in the year 399, ordering him to pass through Rome so as to greet his friends, chief among whom was Pammachius.

Why should he not, after returning from Milan to Rome, have stayed with Saint Pammachius? After Pammachius had embraced a more perfect life under Jerome’s guidance, he delighted in receiving monks as guests, especially those whom he knew to be welcome to his friend Jerome. Why, I say, should Rufinus not have stayed at Rome while the judgment against the Origenists, and especially against Rufinus, was being prepared, so that he might both instruct and press Pammachius?

For a strong suspicion may arise that he was sent to Milan for the purpose of inducing Venirius to condemn the Origenists, just as one may conjecture that Paulinianus was sent to Aquileia to summon Chromatius to the same counsel. Certainly Jerome writes that Anastasius, Venirius, and Chromatius issued a unanimous judgment against the Origenists (*Apology against Rufinus*, book II). Nor would anyone judge rashly if he thought that those three bishops had been stirred up by Jerome against the entire faction of treacherous men, the Origenists who were hostile to him.

This seems to be the meaning of Rufinus’s words of complaint (*Apology to Anastasius*):

> This is the central point: those who were sent from the East to lay traps for me have tried to disgrace me not only through a perverse interpretation but also through the corruption of words.

Those whom he complains were sent are undoubtedly Vincentius, Paulinianus, Eusebius, and Rufinus. Jerome writes of them as follows (*Apology II against Rufinus*):

> Yet I wish to know what those poisoned darts are which you complain that we hurled behind your back. The presbyters Vincentius, Paulinianus, Eusebius, and Rufinus: Vincentius came to Rome long before you; Paulinianus and Eusebius departed after the year of your voyage; Rufinus was sent two years later in the matter of Claudius; all either on account of family property or because of another man’s danger to life, and so forth.

Shortly afterward, however, he does not deny that these men had vigorously acted against Rufinus of Aquileia. For he says:

> It was not, it was not, I say, our plan, but God’s providence, that men sent to fight against something else should fight against the rising heresy and, after the manner of Joseph, relieve the future famine by the ardor of faith.

I shall add something further, since permission has been granted not merely to suspect but also to conjecture, and almost to divine, that this very Rufinus was the author of the *Book of Faith* which Father Sirmond published from the Corbie manuscripts. The name, homeland, rank, learning, and age all agree.

Both Rufini were Syrians or Palestinians; both were presbyters; both opposed original sin; both lived before the Pelagian heresy; both came to Rome under Anastasius; both were hostile to Origen; both firmly pronounced that souls are created in bodies, although the most learned men still doubted this matter or at least held it more cautiously.

Indeed, I suspect—to say nothing more assertive—that the twelve anathemas which we first brought to light were written by this same Rufinus, whether Jerome’s associate or disciple, as we have shown in the notes to those anathemas.

Whatever kind of intellect Rufinus, the teacher of Coelestius, possessed, Mercator clearly reveals in his *Preface to the Subnotations*, where he says:

> This foolish question, and no less hostile to the true faith, was first brought to Rome under Anastasius, of holy memory, supreme pontiff of the Roman Church, by a certain Rufinus, a Syrian by nationality. Being clever, and protecting himself against the odium of the matter, he did not dare to put it forward on his own, but deceived Pelagius, a monk by race from Britain, and thoroughly imbued and instructed him in the impious vanity mentioned above.

From these words it is clear that Rufinus lived, or rather taught, during the pontificate of Anastasius. But someone may perhaps doubt when he wrote his exposition of the faith: before he taught Pelagius and Coelestius, or afterward, in order to strengthen his disciples. It may also be doubted whether he himself first issued such an exposition in Greek and later in Latin. Nevertheless, I am almost certain that the *Book of Faith* was written by Rufinus before he came to Rome; and I am entirely certain that Julian not only saw it but transferred a large part of it into his own books. Hence I am almost inclined to think that Julian was the Latin translator of the Greek work.

Of the three matters I have said I suspect, someone may perhaps affirm them more confidently as certainties. First, that the Rufinus who was Coelestius’s teacher should not be separated from Jerome’s disciple will be established by the arguments brought forward for this purpose. These arguments are certainly neither easily resolved nor weakened by contrary reasoning.

For Jerome admits that he sent a certain presbyter Rufinus from Syria or Palestine into Italy to Venirius during the time of Anastasius, and ordered him on the way to greet his friends at Rome, among whom Pammachius was prominent; he also admits that this Rufinus acted vigorously against the Origenists and against Rufinus of Aquileia himself, and so forth. Since the name, status, homeland, time, place, lodging with Pammachius, and other circumstances agree; and since there is also the testimony not only of Mercator, who asserts that Rufinus brought the Coelestian heresy from Syria under Anastasius and transmitted it to Pelagius and Coelestius, but also of Coelestius, who confesses that he received his error from the presbyter Rufinus residing at Rome with Saint Pammachius, two Rufini can be imagined—one sent by Jerome, the other the teacher of Coelestius—only rashly.

Someone may object that it could have happened that a heretic attached himself to Jerome, that most holy and most vigorous defender of the Catholic faith. That this could indeed have happened is shown especially by the fact that, like Augustine, Jerome at times complained that impure men harboring error lay hidden among his own followers under a sheep’s skin.

Moreover, since among Jerome and Jerome’s disciples the settled opinion was that there was no transmission of souls, one of the disciples, neither especially intelligent nor sufficiently Catholic, could easily have concluded from this that there was likewise no transmission of sin. Augustine himself, although superior in intelligence and faith, everywhere testifies that he suffered such great difficulty in grasping the transmission of sin, if souls are not propagated in the same way as bodies.

Indeed, all the Pelagians defended the one transmission as connected with the other. At that time it was not easy to separate the two, since faith in original sin had not yet, at least in the East, been released from its obscurity, and the Church had not yet proscribed the contrary doctrine.

Second, that the author of the *Book of Faith*, recently printed by the work of Father Sirmond, is none other than the teacher of Coelestius can be established in the same way as the first point. For the argument drawn from the name, homeland, status, and so forth, is useful for establishing both. It is all the stronger because the author of the book is stained with all the filth of Pelagianism—or rather Coelestianism—and equipped with all the devices later defenders used, so that it plainly appears that the teacher preceded his disciples.

The Coelestians taught that original sin could not be believed without attributing iniquity to God, since God forgives the impious their own sins but imputes the sins of others to the innocent. They taught that each person sins for himself and no one for another; that each must be judged by his own works and no one by another’s; that infants, in whom there is nothing except the work of the Creator, cannot be condemned by a just God even if they die without baptism; that when baptized they are not cleansed from a sin they did not possess, but, from being good, become better and are made coheirs of Christ; that there is no transmission of souls, lest there also be a transmission of sins; that God, both in the beginning when the first human being was created and every day when individuals are conceived in their mothers’ wombs, makes the human being in his own image, so that the stain of sin is not natural; that Christ came only to go before us by example and instruction; and that human death did not arise from sin but from the condition of nature.

Rufinus of Palestine transmits these and similar doctrines:

> They are insane, he says, who condemn the whole world to iniquity and crimes through one man, Adam. For those who say this either declare God unjust or at least judge the devil stronger than God, because the devil was able, through the transgression of Adam and Eve, to make evil the nature that God created good—if, that is, through the transgression of the first man Adam and his wife Eve, all human beings are liable to sin, and so forth.

(Chapter 39.)

Since every human being possesses free will, each will be considered deserving either of the highest praise or of blame according to the quality of his deeds. In the same way, on the day of judgment each will either be justified or subjected to punishment, as blessed Paul also teaches when he says:

> For we must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his body according to what he has done, whether good or evil.

(1 Corinthians 5:10.)

That children are not punished for their parents, nor parents for their children, God taught plainly again when he said to the prophet Moses:

> Fathers shall not die for sons, nor sons for fathers; each shall die in his own sin.

(Deuteronomy 24:16.)

Certain people, through ignorance of the divine Scriptures, dare to break out into a wicked and unjust statement about Christ, asserting that he assigns children who have not been baptized to the punishment of eternal fire, which Scripture commonly calls Gehenna. Let them learn from the divine Scriptures that the punishment of eternal fire has not been prepared for the innocent, who are entirely ignorant of sin, but for those known to have transgressed God’s law.

And shortly afterward:

> Children, as the divine Scripture itself has thoroughly taught, being entirely innocent, having had no experience whatsoever of wickedness, and being ignorant of the distinction between good and evil, are not at all handed over to the punishment of eternal fire, since eternal fiery punishment has been prepared for the impious and sinners. Let these children, then, be dismissed together with their ignorance.

Infants receive baptism not on account of sins, but so that, having a spiritual birth, they may be created in Christ, so to speak, through baptism, and become participants in the kingdom of heaven, as the blessed Apostle teaches in these words:

> If anyone is a new creation in Christ.

(1 Corinthians 3:17.)

And again:

> But if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and coheirs of Christ.

(Romans 8:17.)

And later:

> Infants who are not in sins also deserve the grace of baptism, so that, created in Christ by a new generation, they may also become coheirs of his kingdom, according to blessed Paul: “If anyone is a new creation in Christ.”

(Chapter 48; 1 Corinthians 3:17.)

There are some who, seized by madness, say that the soul of the woman Eve was taken from the one soul of the first man Adam. Others say that souls were transmitted from Adam alone, together with the emission of seed, into all those born from him; and others that they came from Eve alone, and so forth.

[Col. 0265D] The Lord made only the human being according to his image and likeness, as Moses teaches when he says:

> And God said: Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness.

(Genesis 1:26.)

And shortly afterward:

> That it is God who forms those things for which seeds are cast into the womb, just as he also gives life to the various things sown by farmers in the earth, blessed Job bears witness when he says to God: “Your hands made me and fashioned me.”

(Job 10:8.)

Christ therefore became human so that, having condemned sin in the flesh, he might leave us an example of how each person ought, after overcoming fleshly vices, no longer to be deceived by the devil’s deceptions.

That Adam and Eve were created mortal in body, as I have said, is attested by Moses when he says:

> And God planted a paradise in Eden, toward the East, and placed there the human being whom he had fashioned; and from the earth he brought forth every tree beautiful to look upon and good for food, and the tree of life in the middle of the paradise, and the tree for knowing good and evil.

(Genesis 2:8.)

God would never have planted the tree of life in paradise if Adam had been created immortal according to the flesh, and so forth.

Having therefore been instructed by many witnesses that this common death is not an evil, let us now declare that those who call death evil are far from the truth. We say instead that God granted the first man Adam, for his good, both sweat and labors, which he would endure from the earth.

What more is there to say? No path afterward trodden by the Pelagians, no method employed for fortifying error, no device for bringing calumny against the Catholic defenders of original sin, was left unanticipated by Rufinus, so that Augustine may seem to have had him in mind when he reviews the devices by which the Pelagians were accustomed to mock the minds of simpler people (Book IV to Boniface, chapter 2; and Book II Against Julian, chapter 1, and elsewhere throughout).

I would even dare to add this, which in my [Col. 0266B] judgment settles the matter: Julian’s little book, if not in every respect, at least in the part concerning original sin, was copied almost word for word from Rufinus. Certainly the same testimonies from Scripture are brought forward; the same arguments are handled in the same manner, so that Rufinus’s book may be called a kind of source of the Coelestian heresy and Julian’s, as it were, its arsenal.

I add something rather more unusual: Augustine says that certain Pelagians asserted (Sermon 7 on the Words of the Apostle, chapter 6) that all human beings are now created by God immortal in the same way as Adam once was: “For all die according to their merits, and there would be no death unless it came from sin.” Marius Mercator reports something identical, or closely related, as having been written by Julian in a letter to the supreme pontiff, when Julian wished to conceal his error concerning Adam’s mortality beneath deceptive interpretations. Rufinus taught precisely this long before such questions had been raised in the West—both what Augustine reported and what Julian wrote.

[Col. 0266C] These arguments may perhaps move someone to object and lead him to doubt whether Rufinus’s book was written at the time we have stated—that is, before Pelagian heresy had been debated in the West—or afterward, when, after minds had been educated by a long controversy, some writer might have been able to encompass in his speech all the trickery of one side. Yet the date of the book can be shown to be certain from this: it was written not only before the times of Nestorius and Eutyches—for otherwise, among the erroneous doctrines concerning the Incarnation of the Word, the names of both heretics would not have been omitted, just as neither the errors of Photinus, Apollinarius, nor the Arians were omitted—but also before the controversies concerning the grace of Christ had arisen. For so important a subject could not have been left untouched.

It therefore belongs to the period when the questions concerning the Arians and Origen were being debated in the East, for the whole book is occupied with them. Those controversies were especially heated in the time of Siricius, as is easily understood from the writings of the Fathers published then, in which scarcely any other subject is treated. [Col. 0266D] Moreover, Mercator reports that controversies concerning Adam’s mortality, the baptism of infants, original sin, and other doctrines so carefully treated by Rufinus arose at that time.

Now, as to what we conjectured thirdly—that the twelve anathemas which we published from Mercator’s manuscript were also composed by the same author—perhaps no one will doubt it who considers more attentively that they were composed by a Coelestian, concerned with the same questions, at the same time, by a certain Rufinus, who had lived at Jerusalem and Bethlehem, and who had held the same views as Jerome—whether Jerome was correct concerning the origin of souls, and so forth, or was likewise in error concerning the salvation through fire of sinful believers, and so forth—as is clear from the observations we appended to the anathemas.

## CHAPTER IV. Pelagius, from whom the Pelagian heresy was named

Pelagius, who, with Coelestius and Julian as his assistants, put forward the doctrine bearing his name against the grace of Christ [Col. 0267A] (Prosper, in the *Chronicle*), is said by certain writers on English affairs (in Usserius, *On the Ancient Beginnings of the British Church*, chapter 8) to have been called Morgan in his native language, as though “man of the sea.” But, so that the barbarous character of the name might not offend Roman ears, he is said to have removed it, changing the native word into a Greek word of the same meaning, one long since adopted by the Latins.

Augustine writes (Letter 186) that, to distinguish him from another man called Pelagius of Tarentum, he was surnamed Brito; by this name he is also called by Prosper the Chronicler (*Chronicle*). But because the name Briton, British, and Britannic, which Orosius uses (*Apology*), was common to several provinces, it happened that some reported him to have originated from Lesser Britain, which is Armorica and has native Britons; others from England, which the ancients once called both Albion and Britain; and others from Scotland or Ireland, which were reckoned under the name of the Britains. But since at that time Armorica had not yet [Col. 0267B] acquired the name Britain, and the Romans did not commonly distinguish the other three provinces very carefully from one another, this alone is certain: that this “white dog,” as Jerome calls him (*Preface to Book III of the Commentary on Jeremiah*), was brought from the Britains beyond the sea, weighed down by Scottish porridge.

Polydore, Bale, Dempster, Cantelupus, Caius, and Ranulph of Chester, together with the author of the life of Saint Alban, further report certain details concerning his homeland in Wales, his having shared Augustine’s birthday, a doctorate from Cambridge, the prefecture of Bangor, and the governance of more than two thousand monks (*English History*, Book III, century 1; *British Writers*, chapter 38; *History of Scotland*, Book XV; *Cambridge History*; *History of Cambridge*, Book V; *Polychronicon*, Book IV, chapter 32). But no learned person will fail to pardon these things easily to lovers of fables, and will at the same time judge that they must be relegated to the tales of Merlin.

Jerome depicts the man as large in body. For, speaking of Rufinus of Aquileia, he says ([Col. 0267C] *Preface to Book III on Jeremiah*): “He himself, though mute, barks through a white dog, large and corpulent, who can rage more with his heels than with his teeth. For he has the offspring of a Scottish race from the neighborhood of the Britons.” Hence, in the first dialogue, he addresses Pelagius in this way: “You yourself, who puff yourself up before us with Cato’s pride and swell with Milo’s shoulders,” and so forth. Elsewhere, however, he makes him not merely large but also fat in body: “Recently an unlearned slanderer burst forth, who thought my commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians ought to be criticized; and he does not understand, snoring in excessive stupidity, how to read commentaries, and so forth; nor does the most senseless man, weighed down by Scottish porridge, remember, and so forth.”

Orosius agrees with Jerome (*Apology*, chapter 27), addressing Pelagius in these words: “But perhaps you derive a special confidence for carrying that burden from the fact that, nourished by baths and banquets, you bear broad shoulders and a sturdy neck, even displaying fatness on your forehead, as it is written: ‘For he has stretched out his hand against God and strengthened himself against the Almighty. [Col. 0267D] He ran against him with an erect neck and armed himself with a fat neck. Fatness covered his face, and lard hangs from his sides’” (Job 15:25).

He is commonly believed to have professed the monastic life; but that he did not rise to a higher rank is established by the certain testimonies of the ancients. In those times, if someone had been adopted from the monastic order into the clergy, he was thereafter called not a monk but by the name of his clerical rank. Therefore, whoever retained permanently the designation either of monk or of layman is thereby shown to have remained in the lay order. Since Pelagius is called a layman both by Orosius (*Apology*, chapter 3), shortly before the Council of Diospolis, and by Zosimus in 417, and is also called a monk either by the Fathers of Diospolis (*Letter 2 to the Africans*) in 415, by Augustine in 417 in his book *On the Proceedings in Palestine* (chapters 19 and 20), and in *Heresy* 88 in 426, and by Mercator in 432 (*Preface to the Subnotations*), while no ancient writer calls him either bishop [Col. 0268A] or presbyter, he must certainly be believed to have remained among the laity. Therefore the claims made by Bale (*Century 1*, chapter 38) and Prateolus (*Catalogue of Heresies*, Book XIV, chapter 14) concerning Pelagius’s episcopate are rightly despised by learned men, especially since he produced his heresy when already an old man—not because we accept the opinion of certain people that Pelagius was denounced by Isidore of Pelusium (Letter 314), for that conflicts remarkably with the chronology, but because he composed commentaries on the Pauline Epistles before the sack of the City in 408, or even before 404, when his body was growing old and his strength failing, as he himself says in the preface.

Although I do not think it inappropriate to state frankly what once caused me to doubt Pelagius’s monastic status, namely these words of Augustine (*On the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 35): “After many ancient heresies, a new one has now arisen, not from bishops, or presbyters, or any clerics whatever, but from certain people who were, as it were, monks, against the grace of God, and so forth.” Why did he [Col. 0268B] say “from certain people who were, as it were, monks,” and not simply “from certain monks”? Is the word *as it were* superfluous and to be deleted in order to correct the reading? Yet manuscripts of better quality resist such an emendation. Or, although Pelagius and Coelestius displayed a religious way of life in their outward dress, were their morals nevertheless not very consistent with it? But Augustine himself denies that they were such men (*Letter 140*): “They would easily have been despised, but they lived continently and conducted themselves commendably in good works.” Or, having professed the coenobitic life, did they nevertheless live outside the monastery? Yet at that time not all who were called monks lived in coenobia; nor, if they had wandered about viciously, would they have been held in such high esteem by all good people—Augustine, Paulinus, Julia, Demetrias’s mother, and others.

It remains, therefore, to suppose that Pelagius truly was a monk, though not in the sense in which the name monk is usually used to designate a coenobite or even a dweller in the desert. Rather, he was a monk in the sense in which people were called monks in former times [Col. 0268C] who, after spending some time in retreat far from the crowd, cultivating their minds through works of penitence and piety and meditation on divine things, came forth in clothing arranged for piety and displaying contempt for the world, so that they might form others in a stricter discipline of conduct than they themselves had embraced.

Indeed, at that time people of three kinds were reckoned under the name of monks: some lived in monasteries and were called coenobites; others lived in deserted places and were called hermits, or solitaries; others lived in their own houses and were sometimes called philosophers by the Greeks, but commonly monks by the Latins. Thus Pammachius, Paulinus, and very many others practiced the monastic life in their own homes according to the rule of evangelical perfection. So too did both Melanias and Demetrias, as well as Terasia, the wife of Paulinus, and many other Roman women who professed a religious life outside the desert and the coenobia. Pelagius, therefore, appears to have been a monk, though not of the first or second kind, but only of the third. Such men customarily went about either [Col. 0268D] wearing the *pallium*, or in dark clothing, or in some other modest bodily dress that gave the appearance of inward virtue and contempt for the world.

By nature he had received an exceptionally strong, swift, and acute intellect, as Augustine says (*On Nature and Grace*, chapters 6 and 35), at once ardent, vehement, and quarrelsome; nor could even Roman culture or association with honorable men and noble women teach him out of his native disposition. Hence his exhortations to the good life were vehement and in a certain sense fiery, but in them he retained a method of teaching lacking restraint and arrogantly dictatorial, in keeping with his people’s character. Hence he dared to interpret the evangelical counsels in such a way that he did not recommend them, as was proper, but transformed them into commands. Hence Christian perfection was subjected to the harsh necessity of laws. Hence those opinions, contrary to common sense and insolent, found in Jerome’s *Dialogue* and throughout Augustine: [Col. 0269A] that one ought never to swear at all; that the display of clothing and ornaments is opposed to God; that a Christian ought to possess such patience that, if someone wished to take away his property, he should gladly surrender it; that a rich man living in his wealth cannot enter the kingdom of God unless he sells everything he owns, and that it does him no good if he happens to perform good works from those riches.

These were Pelagius’s methods when disseminating his heresy (*Letter to Ctesiphon* and *Dialogue*): he did not openly entrust his mysteries to the public, but only to trusted ears; if any of his doctrines escaped into public view, he openly denied what he taught in private rooms; if the error had to be put forward openly, he introduced another person’s identity; if compelled to speak in his own name, he presented the matter timidly, like someone asking to be instructed; if he was proved from books to have made some assertion, he blamed the books, saying either that they were not his or that they had been stolen before they were corrected; if he happened to be pressed on the basis of admissions he had made, he interpreted his statements in obscure and superficially Catholic language; if necessity required it, he agreed with some condemnation issued by the Church, willingly [Col. 0269B] condemning everything but, as he said, “in the Church’s sense”—that is, in the sense he would later invent according to his own will; if at some point he had to explain his faith, he would expound at length on many matters about which he had not been questioned, while saying either nothing or something ambiguous about the actual issue. He imitated serpents, which, as Orosius says (*Apology*, chapter 1), “when, merely to protect their head, they expose the rest of their body to cutting and injury, consider that no harm has been done so long as that one part of themselves is free from danger, the part that contains within it their many poisonous tongues, even if all their limbs are cut off.”

Why, however, did he not teach publicly, but only in private rooms and among friends? Besides the reasons common to almost all heresies, there was this particular one: his speech was barbarous. For although, if we believed the books that bear his name—especially the letter to Demetrias—he might reasonably appear eloquent, indeed almost offensively so when compared with men of the same age born in more cultivated soil, [Col. 0269C] it is nevertheless a plausible, if not certain, opinion that the barbarous speech of a foreigner who was otherwise intelligent and rich in reasoning was assisted by the Latinity of more polished men. Thus Jerome called Pelagius a wretch who could not even slander him in his own words (*Preface to Book IV of the Commentary on Jeremiah*).

Those more polished men were chiefly three (*Letter 201* in Augustine): Coelestius, who changed from a disciple into a teacher; Annianus, who was abundantly supplied so that he might furnish the tinkling and beggarly words of another’s blasphemy; and Julian, to whom Bede therefore attributes the letter to Demetrias (*Preface to the Song of Songs*, chapter 5).

Orosius was aiming at Annianus when he said (*Apology*, chapter 2): “There stands also a most savage Goliath, swollen with pride and puffed up with carnal power, confident that he can do everything by himself: his head, hands, and entire body moreover are clad in an elaborate outfit, and behind him he has his armor-bearer, who, although he himself does not fight, nevertheless supplies every support of bronze and [Col. 0269D] iron.”

He was also aiming at Julian—or perhaps again at Annianus—when he thought certain expressions from the letter to Demetrias deserved criticism: “In that most laboriously polished letter of yours,” he says (*ibid.*, chapter 26), “we could scarcely understand these very things. This letter, this letter, I say, to the girl Demetrias, who, as I hear, is sacred and holy—you, a most modest man, were not ashamed to write it, teaching, I believe, reverence for chastity beneath the guise of Joseph’s lusting after his mistress, and so forth, weaving together an inappropriate story in the most obscene language. Yet we ought not to charge you with this, which is expressed neither suitably nor decorously; for neither did your birth grant you the opportunity to be educated in more honorable studies, nor did nature produce you with understanding. Rather, the fault belongs to those dictators of yours who write a wretched mind in the most wretched language and expose you to be read with laughter, as though your title were one of disgrace.”

Jerome was aiming indiscriminately at certain people [Col. 0270A] when he said to Pelagius (*Dialogue 3 Against the Pelagians*): “You customarily swear to your disciples that these two chapters, of prayer and praise, are not yours, although the splendor of your style plainly shines in them, and the elegance of your speech is so great that, proceeding at a tortoise’s pace, you do not dare publicly to profess what you teach and sell in secret. Happy are you, then, for no one except your disciples writes books, so that whatever appears displeasing to you, you may claim is not yours but someone else’s! And who could be of such great talent as to imitate the charm of your speech?”

There is no single consensus about who his teachers were. We have counted two: Theodore of Mopsuestia and Rufinus the Syrian. Others, however, usually enumerate the following on the basis of Jerome (*Letter to Ctesiphon*): Rufinus of Aquileia, Evagrius Ponticus, Sextus the philosopher, Jovinianus, Priscillian, Mani, Palladius of Galatia, the Gnostics and Euchites, and Origen, whom Jerome calls Pelagius’s *archaios* (ἀρχαῖος, “ancient one”) and beloved companion (*Dialogue 3 Against the Pelagians*). [Col. 0270B] Yet, if we listen to Jerome, they should be called not so much teachers as forerunners; indeed, they preceded him only in defending sinlessness or *apatheia* (ἀπάθεια, “passionlessness”), so that arguments directed against them could rightly be turned against the Pelagian claim of *anamartēsia* (ἀναμαρτησία, “sinlessness”).

Jansenius of Ypres did not make much progress (*Book VI on Pelagian Heresy*, chapter 17) when he wished to show that not only the doctrine of impassibility was a branch of Origen, but also the principal parts of Pelagianism—that is, the five headings to which he promises to reduce the whole of that heresy: free will, its natural possibility, the law of nature and of Moses, grace and merit, and predestination. On these, he says, as on hinges, the whole Pelagian heresy turns. For just as he was carried along in the entire matter more by a preconceived opinion than by judgment, so he did not see that in Origen he was condemning things plainly found in Jerome himself, while condemning as untouched those things that the exceptionally keen and sharp-sighted accuser of Origen had passed over. [Col. 0270C] I therefore think that what he produced should be disregarded, since it is twisted toward meanings belonging to others. Yet this is no reason to defend Origen’s position, for he was a man of doubtful faith while alive and of no better reputation after death.

Pelagius handed on the doctrine he had received from wicked teachers to worse disciples. Among these two excelled in depravity: Coelestius and Julian. The former was more capable of managing affairs craftily, since he came from the forum; the latter was better at handling questions, having been trained in dialectic. Both were confident in their speaking ability; both were bolder than their timid teacher and therefore more harmful to the Church.

I have called Julian a disciple of Pelagius, but I do not agree with Bede, who writes that Julian was instructed by Pelagius even as a young boy (*Preface to the Song of Songs*). How could that have happened, when during the earliest years of his life he lived at Capua with his father, Saint Memorius? I do not deny that he could have been taught when he was already a presbyter or deacon, during the two or three years in which Pelagius remained in Sicily [Col. 0270D] before sailing from Syracuse to Africa and from Hippo to Palestine. Nor is it incredible that Julian was in Sicily at that time, as though in a place safe from the Visigoths and agreeable because of his friends.

There is insufficient agreement among writers about the time when the heresy named after Pelagius first arose. Usserius reviews the opinions of individuals (*On the Early Beginnings of the British Church*, chapter 8). But just as they rest on slight or even nonexistent arguments, they can easily be dismissed, especially in view of what Marius Mercator teaches (*Preface to the Book of the Subnotations*): namely, that the heresy arose in Syria, especially in Second Cilicia, under the influence of Theodore of Mopsuestia, toward the end of the fourth century; that it was brought to the West by Rufinus the Syrian and handed over at Rome, under Anastasius, to Pelagius, at the latest in 400 or the following year; that Pelagius then transmitted it to Coelestius; that at nearly the same time Coelestius first committed it to writing in books that have perished, and afterward Pelagius did so in commentaries [Col. 0271A] on Paul’s Epistles before the sack of the City; indeed, that it was spread in private conversations throughout the long period during which Pelagius and Coelestius remained at Rome, and that they were believed by many—even by the supreme pontiff himself—to have persuaded them of their views; that afterward it was disseminated in Sicily in 409 and 410 and carried from there to Africa, where it was first condemned at Carthage, in a council of bishops under Aurelius, in 412, before the forty days preceding Easter.

The individual events of Pelagius’s life must now be briefly recounted in chronological order. He came to Rome, as is credible, not from the Eastern regions, as some assert without adequate reason, but from his homeland, while Damasus occupied the apostolic see—that is, before 384, the year of Damasus’s death. Since this may appear paradoxical, it must be established by weighty arguments. He certainly left the city of Rome in 408 or 409, as is established in the notes to Mercator’s *Commonitorium*. He had been there not only in 405, when he wrote to Saint Paulinus [Col. 0271B] (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 35), but also under Anastasius, according to Mercator (*Preface to the Subnotations*), when he was being instructed by Rufinus the Syrian. Indeed, he lived there for a very long time, as Augustine says (*On Original Sin*, chapter 21), an expression that signifies more than a decade. Pelagius therefore lived at Rome in the time of Siricius, while Anastasius held the pontificate for scarcely more than four years and died in 402.

But that he had come there before Siricius himself occupied the see is established by the fact that he was on familiar terms in the City with Jerome, who nevertheless withdrew from there to the East in 385, immediately after Damasus’s death, in order to avoid the hostility that had been stirred up against him among the Roman clergy. Jerome himself testifies to this familiarity between himself and Pelagius (*Preface to Book IV of the Commentary on Jeremiah*), when he writes of Pelagius without naming him:

“The heresy has begun to revive and not only to hiss in the regions of the West but also in those of the East; it stains many and grows day by day, [Col. 0271C] while they teach in secret and deny in public. I, who had long remained silent and swallowed my grief in silence, have been compelled by the frequent complaints of the brethren to answer it.” And afterward: “These men avoid public exposure and whisper in the corners of the lost; they grieve as though on behalf of their own people, while they fear to confess that these things are theirs. When we have spoken generally against vices and heretics, they complain that they themselves are being attacked, and, after concealing their indignation for a long time, they declare the evil of their conscience. But if we must beware lest, by cutting down the most arrogant heresy with a spiritual sword, we seem to injure an OLD RELATIONSHIP: then must we endure the crosses of betrayed faith,” and so forth.

For where could an old relationship between Pelagius and Jerome have been formed, if not where familiarity was possible? And where else could familiarity have existed between men present together than in the City? Pelagius had never been in the East before 412, nor Jerome in the West after 394; and both could have stayed in the City and enjoyed one another’s company at the time we have mentioned, since [Col. 0271D] Pelagius lived at Rome for a very long time (Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapter 21).

There are indeed some who claim that Pelagius remained in the East while Chrysostom was in exile at Arabissus and that he visited the monks in the Egyptian deserts before falling into heresy (Jansenius, *Book I on Pelagian Heresy*, and others). But they arrived at this opinion because they were deceived either by Chrysostom’s letter to Olympias concerning the fall of the monk Pelagius or by Isidore of Pelusium’s reproach to a certain monk named Pelagius [Col. 0272A] for his lust for wandering and his craving for banquets. They were deceived, I say, through thoughtlessness; for at the very time Chrysostom was in exile, Pelagius was living at Rome with his reputation intact and free from suspicion. Indeed, he was regarded as holy and as a Christian making considerable progress (Augustine, *Book III on the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapters 1 and 3). Therefore, it must be the fall of another monk of the same name that Chrysostom lamented, and another man bearing the same name whom Isidore reproached, since before he revealed his heresy Pelagius was loved, because of the appearance of his piety, by very holy men—Jerome, Augustine, Paulinus, and others.

While he still possessed either an unimpaired faith—if indeed he ever possessed one—or at least the reputation he was pursuing, he appears to have written the three books on the Trinity mentioned by Gennadius (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 42), in order, I believe, to display his faith and how greatly he rejected the Arians. This was the chief mark of orthodoxy (*tēs orthodoxias*, τῆς ὀρθοδοξίας) in that period.

Under Anastasius he heard Rufinus the Syrian at Rome, as Mercator reports, and probably wrote the book *Eulogies*, or *On Practical Conduct*, to demonstrate his ascetic discipline and holiness of life. Yet Jerome, together with the two bishops who accused him, Erote and Lazarus, detected in it the seeds of his future impiety (*Dialogue 1 Against the Pelagians*).

At the same time, through his vehement and ardent exhortations, as Augustine says (*On the Proceedings [Col. 0272B] in Palestine*, chapter 25), he drew many people—Coelestius above all, a scholarly student of the forum—to a stricter life, but at the same time infected him with the error he had received from Rufinus the Syrian.

In 405 he sent a letter to Saint Paulinus (Mercator, *Preface to the Subnotations*), with whom he enjoyed great renown for learning and piety. As he later boasted in a letter to Saint Innocent, that letter, contained in three hundred verses, confessed nothing other than the grace and assistance of God and that we can do absolutely no good without God. Augustine shows, however, that the letter was not free from poison (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 35).

At the same time, unless perhaps earlier, he composed commentaries on Paul’s Epistles, in which he attacked original sin under the guise of another person (Mercator, *Preface to the Subnotations* and *Commonitorium*).

Around this same period he wrote a letter to Bishop Constantius, which must have been full of doctrine and elaborated with the greatest care, [Col. 0272C] since, in writing to the supreme pontiff, he praises it as a witness to his faith (Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 36).

He also appears to have written to the Widow—I think Julian’s mother and the wife of Saint Memorius—two books either of consolation or exhortation (Mercator, *Commonitorium*). At one point he falsely claimed that these were not his, although he could easily have been refuted by the testimony of trustworthy men (Augustine, *On the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 6).

To the same or a nearby period belongs what Augustine reports as having occurred at Rome between a bishop and Pelagius, on the occasion of words that the bishop himself had placed in his confessions while praying to God: “Give what you command, and command what you will.” When the bishop recalled these words, Pelagius could not bear them. He contradicted him with some agitation and almost quarreled with the man who had quoted them (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 20).

To this period also belongs what Augustine records concerning the speeches and controversies Pelagius held at Rome [Col. 0272D] (*On Sin*, chapter 21), from which it could be understood what he concealed in his books and what Pope Zosimus appended for reading to the letters he had composed for circulation throughout the Catholic world.

In 408 or 409 he withdrew from Rome with Coelestius to Sicily, as though to a safer place from the barbarians devastating Italy. For Mercator writes that approximately twenty years had passed when he presented his *Commonitorium* in 429 since Coelestius had left Rome. Since Coelestius left together with his teacher, and could not have departed while the Goths were surrounding the City either during the first or the second siege—or even during the intervening period, when they were ravaging everything with iron and fire, especially in the part of Italy facing Sicily—Pelagius must certainly be said to have fled when the immense panic caused many people to leave Rome in 408.

He spent about two years at Syracuse in Sicily, or even nearly three, [Col. 0273A] with his disciple, and scattered seeds of error that later grew with an unhappy yield, so that the monk Hilary had to consult Augustine (*Letters 156 and 157* and *On the Perfection of Righteousness*) about how an evil spreading so stubbornly and widely could be uprooted.

I believe that the book *On Nature* was written there. In it Pelagius defended human nature, against the grace of God by which the ungodly are justified and by which we are Christians, with as much argumentation as he could muster (Augustine, *Book II of the Retractions*, chapter 22). Augustine refuted this book—sent to him by Timasius and James, devout and respectable young men who had formerly been disciples of Pelagius but had been converted to the true faith—in a work entitled *On Nature and Grace* (Augustine, *On the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 23, and Letter 181).

In 411, at the beginning of spring, he landed with Coelestius at the harbor of Hippo (*On the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 22). I believe that he did so in the hope of winning over, if possible, Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius, and [Col. 0273B] later abusing his friendship in order to spread his error more safely. But perhaps Augustine was away, which gave Pelagius the opportunity to write, so that he might greet in a letter the man whom he could not address in person. Augustine replied (*On the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 28), but afterward was compelled to interpret the letter in order to show how unjustly Pelagius had produced it before the judges at Diospolis as a letter of recommendation for himself.

Both men proceeded from Hippo to Carthage. There they began to enlarge the heresy, already disseminated by the people who had conspired with them in Sicily, using their customary methods: namely, saying very little openly, not directly attacking the ancient faith implanted in people’s minds, but either circumventing simpler people through deceitful and captious questions or deceiving the more cunning through a false eagerness to learn.

After a brief stay, he sailed from Carthage to Palestine, leaving his disciple in Africa. Thus Augustine says [Col. 0273C] (*On the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 22):

“To speak especially of myself, I first learned of the name of Pelagius, who was absent and established at Rome, together with great praise of him. Later, reports began to reach us that he was arguing against the grace of God. Although I was grieved by this, and it was told to me by people whom I trusted, I nevertheless wanted to learn of something of this kind from him himself, or from one of his books, so that, if I began to refute him, he could not deny it. But after he came to Africa, while I was absent, he was received on our shore—that is, the shore of Hippo. There, as you know, absolutely nothing of this kind was heard from him, because he left sooner than had been expected. Later, as I recall, I saw his face once or twice at Carthage, when I was wholly occupied with the care of the conference we were to hold with the heretical Donatists. But he himself was also hurrying overseas. Meanwhile these doctrines were being heatedly discussed by the mouths of those who were regarded as his disciples.”

In 412 he began to make disciples for himself at Jerusalem, as in other places, and even to court the favor of Bishop John (*Letters 177 and 179*) [Col. 0273D], employing no other methods than those by which he was generally believed to have deceived Saint Innocent at Rome: namely, a feigned appearance of piety, the profession of a stricter life, ardent exhortations to perfection, the secret transmission of his mysteries, perpetual dissimulation, and so forth (Jerome, *Letter to Ctesiphon*).

In 413 he wrote a letter to the virgin Demetrias, consecrated to God. Although he later produced it in his letters to Saint Innocent as an open testimony to his sincere faith, Augustine nevertheless showed that it was full of error (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 37). It is surprising, however, that the letter did not reach Africa, or at least Augustine’s hands, before 417, when Augustine, having received Pelagius’s letter to Saint Innocent, wrote to Julia, Demetrias’s mother, warning her against the poison ingeniously concealed in it.

In the same year Ctesiphon, an illustrious man and, as can be gathered [Col. 0274A] from Jerome’s letter (*Letter to Ctesiphon*, prefixed to the three dialogues), scarcely not deceived by Pelagius, whom he supported with his wealth, consulted Jerome about the question of *anamartēsia* (ἀναμαρτησία, “sinlessness”), which was splitting the Church of Jerusalem into factions. The most holy defender of the faith replied at considerable length for a letter, though briefly in proportion to the importance of the subject, so that he was compelled to promise a fuller treatment, which he later supplied in three books of dialogues.

In that letter to Ctesiphon, although Jerome indicated Pelagius by unmistakable signs, he nevertheless thought it best to refrain from naming him, lest he appear to be attacking the person of a complaining man rather than the heresy itself. The final words deserve notice because of their usefulness for every age:

“I beg and admonish you and the assembly of that holy and illustrious household not through one man—or, at most, three little men—to admit the filth of so many heresies, or, to put it mildly, their disgrace; so that where virtue and holiness were once praised, there the shame of diabolical presumption and the filthiness of the most sordid association may be found. Let those who furnish resources to men of this kind know that they are gathering a multitude of heretics, making enemies of Christ, and nourishing his adversaries; and that they vainly profess one thing with their tongue when they are proved by their hand to feel another.”

In the spring of the year 415, Orosius came to Palestine. Augustine had sent him from Africa to Jerome (Epistle 166) to inquire about the origin of souls. He found the Church of Jerusalem divided by factions and so heated by disputes that some were called by the name of Pelagius and others by the name of Christ, as Jerome writes (Epistle to Ctesiphon). After staying for some time at Bethlehem with the holy old man, he was summoned to Jerusalem to the assembly which Bishop John convened, having gathered the presbyterate, on July 30 in the case of Pelagius. What took place there Orosius recounts at length in his *Apology* (chapter 3 and following); among many other proceedings contrary to custom [Col. 0274C], he complains that the layman Pelagius sat among the presbyters at the bishop’s command.

In December of the same year, a synod of fourteen bishops was held at Diospolis, in the Palestinian city of Caesarea, with Eulogius presiding. There the Fathers, deceived by the machinations of John of Jerusalem, who favored Pelagius, and by Pelagius’s own lies, condemned the heresy but acquitted the heretic (Augustine, *Book on the Proceedings in Palestine*, passim). The grounds for the acquittal were the interpreter’s bad faith, Pelagius’s evasive condemnation of anything and everything, and the numerous letters of bishops, filled with praise of Pelagius, which the fraudulent heretic produced.

In the year 416, Orosius returned to the West and brought to the Africans letters from the bishops Heros and Lazarus, accusers of Pelagius. These letters were intended to rouse them to defend the faith, which was endangered in the East by the deceits of the heretics. A letter was also circulated among the people through the machinations of the Pelagians, said to have been written by Pelagius to a presbyter who was his friend. In it [Col. 0274D] these words were inserted with the utmost shamelessness:

> “The verdict of the fourteen bishops has approved our definition, in which we said that a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments, if he wishes.”

This statement covered the mouth of contradiction with confusion and separated from one another the whole society conspiring for evil (the synodal letters of the Fathers of Carthage and Milevis to Saint Innocent; *Book on the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 30).

Likewise, Pelagius sent Augustine, through a certain citizen of Hippo, an Eastern deacon, a little document defending his position (*ibid.*, chapter 32). All these things were the reason why Aurelius held a council at Carthage with sixty-eight bishops and Sylvanus one at Milevis with forty. Their proceedings were reported to the apostolic see by Bishop Julius in synodal letters, to which the five bishops Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Possidius, and Evodius added fuller letters (in Augustine, Epistles 233, 92, and 95).

[Col. 0275A] In the same year Pelagius published four books *On Free Choice*, compelled to do so in order to escape the odium attached to the denial of God’s grace and to conceal a heretical meaning beneath words outwardly Catholic. He published them after the Council of Diospolis, held at the very end of 415, and before he sent his letters to Saint Innocent in the year 417 (Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 41).

At about the same time, Augustine wrote to John, bishop of Jerusalem, concerning Pelagius (Epistle 237), and, at the request of many bishops, asked that an account of what had taken place at Diospolis be sent to the West. In this letter mention is made of two young men seduced by Pelagius, of the book *On Nature* written by Pelagius, of Augustine’s reply to it, and of John’s having been deceived by Pelagius.

In the year 417, a synod was convened at Rome in January by Saint Innocent. The reports of the Africans were read there, and in turn decretal letters were sent to the Africans, containing the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius.

[Col. 0275B] In the same year Pelagius suspected—correctly—that a synod was being prepared at Antioch to review the proceedings at Diospolis. He therefore sent to Saint Innocent, whom he had not yet heard was dead, a statement of his faith together with letters; he also sent a letter from Praylius, who had succeeded John in the see of Jerusalem, entirely in his own commendation (Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 41). When Zosimus received these after Innocent’s death, he may be thought to have experienced something human when, rather too hastily favoring Pelagius, he wrote back to the Africans (Zosimus, Epistle 2, to the Africans).

In fact, a synod was convened in the East by Theodotus of Antioch. Mercator mentions it in these words (*Commonitory*, chapter 3):

> “While Pelagius was staying at Jerusalem, he was accused before the synod. At first, by evading the issue, covering himself with certain ambiguous professions, pursuing uncertainties, and giving equivocal answers, he seems to have deceived that hearing of the bishops. But [Col. 0275C] afterward, when he was clearly detected and the accusers pressed their charge, he was exposed by the later synod over which Theodotus of Antioch, bishop of holy memory, presided; and he was expelled even from the holy and venerable places of Jerusalem,” and so forth.

Around the middle of April 418, Zosimus convened a council at Rome. After receiving letters from the Africans and the machinations of the heretics had been exposed, he sent a letter to all the bishops of the world. Once it had been received everywhere and signed by the whole world, as Prosper says, the Pelagian error was proscribed.

In the same year, on the day before the Kalends of May, the emperor Honorius at Ravenna issued a decree to Palladius, the Praetorian Prefect, ordering that Pelagius, Coelestius, and the other participants in the same error be expelled from Rome and banished throughout the empire.

While these events were taking place in the West, Albina, Pinianus, and Melania informed Augustine by letter from the East that they had dealt with Pelagius and asked him to condemn in writing whatever was said against him. They reported that, in their hearing, he had said:

> “Anathema to anyone who either thinks or says that the grace of God, through which Christ came into this world to save sinners, is [Col. 0275D] not necessary—not only for each hour or each moment, but also for each one of our acts; and may those who attempt to take it away suffer eternal punishments.”

(*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 2 and following.)

Augustine showed that this profession was not merely suspect but also treacherous (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 2 and following).

In the year 419, Augustine published two books against Pelagius, one *On the Grace of Christ*, the other *On Original Sin*. He sent both from Carthage to Albina, Pinianus, and Melania, although Albina, Pinianus, and Melania had not yet departed for Egypt after leaving Jerusalem, while Zosimus’s *tractoria* had already reached Africa. They departed in the year 420, whereas the *tractoria* of Zosimus reached Africa around July of 418.

[Col. 0276A] After this period there is a profound silence concerning Pelagius. I suppose that the reason is that, after Theodotus’s sentence, he withdrew from the holy places where he had been expelled and retired to some more remote part of Palestine, where he lived in obscurity and died worn out by old age. For he must then have been more than seventy, since he wrote his commentaries on Paul around the year 404, when his body was already failing (in the preface to Heliodorus), and therefore was at least sixty years old. Moreover, he had lived familiarly at Rome with Jerome, evidently as his equal or as one not much younger. Jerome, however, left the city in 385 and had almost reached his ninetieth year when Theodotus condemned Pelagius. Add that old men of heavy build and burdened with fat, such as Pelagius was, scarcely complete eleven periods of seven years of life, if we believe the physicians, especially when they are severely afflicted by adversity, as men of an excessively proud spirit tend to be—and Pelagius was such a man.

[Col. 0276B] Nor do I think that those who assert that he returned to his homeland should be heeded (Jansenius of Ypres, book 1 *On the Pelagian Heresy*). They base this on what Constantius the presbyter left written (*Life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre*): that at the council of Verulamium Pelagius stood on one side and Christ on the other. Yet they bring no testimony from the ancients in support of their view, nor can they answer Prosper the Chronicler, who records that in Britain the Pelagian heresy was disseminated by Agricola, son of Severianus and a Pelagian (under the year of Christ 429). Prosper would certainly not have been silent if it had been spread by Pelagius himself. Nor, finally, do they see that Constantius’s words must be understood figuratively, Pelagius and Christ being named as representatives of their respective parties, from whom those parties took their names.

[Col. 0276C] No one understood Pelagius’s particular heresy better than Augustine, because of his continual defense of the faith; no one explained it more clearly or briefly, because of the force of his understanding. To Augustine, I think, must be attributed what no learned person now denies: the eight canons commonly called the Milevitan canons. For they were issued in the universal African council,

> “whose mind and genius was Augustine,”

as Prosper says (*Poem on Ingratitude*, chapter 2).

Of these canons, the first two concern Adam’s sin and the baptism of infants; three others concern the grace of God through Christ; the remaining ones concern impeccability. All concern the absolute rule of Catholic faith. It is therefore lamentable that Catholic teachers, abandoning this rule, sometimes accuse one another of Pelagianism when their passions grow heated, whether through party spirit or the ardor of disputation, and often accuse one another precisely where both parties follow the rule of orthodoxy (*ὀρθοδοξία*) handed down by Augustine and received by the Church.

Pelagius wrote many books and still more letters to various people. Their catalogue can be compiled nowhere better than from Jerome, Augustine, Orosius, Mercator, and Gennadius. They are as follows:

[Col. 0276D]

**Three books *On the Trinity*.** Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 42.

**One book of Testimonies or Eulogies.** Jerome, *Dialogue 3 against the Pelagians*; Augustine, *Book on the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapters 1 and following, and book 4 *To Boniface*, chapters 8 and 10; Orosius, *Apology*; Gennadius, at the place cited.

**Thirteen books of Expositions on all the Epistles of Paul.** Augustine, book 3 *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapters 1 and 12; *Book on the Proceedings*, chapter 16; Mercator, *Commonitory*, chapter 2, and preface to the *Subnotata*; the author of *The Predestined*, heresy 88; Cassiodorus, *Divine Readings*, chapter 8.

**A letter to Paulinus.** Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 85.

**A letter to Constantius the bishop.** Augustine, *ibid.*, chapters 34 and 36.

**One book *On Nature*.** Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 1; book 2 of the *Retractions*, chapter 4; *Book on the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 33; and elsewhere throughout.

[Col. 0277A]

**Two books *To the Widow*: one consolatory, the other exhortatory.** The Synod of Diospolis, *Book on the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 6; Jerome, *Dialogue 3*; Mercator, *Commonitory*, chapter 4.

**A letter to Augustine.** Augustine, *Book on the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 26.

**One book to Demetrias, *On the Institution of a Virgin*.** Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, chapters 22 and following, and Epistle 264; Orosius, *Apology*, and so forth.

**Four books *On Free Choice*.** Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, chapters 3, 4, 5, 13, and 29.

**A Defense of His Faith to Augustine.** Augustine, *Book on the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 32.

**A letter to a certain presbyter and friend, *On the Proceedings at Diospolis*.** Augustine, *Book on the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 30.

**A statement of faith to Innocent, together with letters.** Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 30, and elsewhere throughout.

It should be noted that of all these works, whether books or letters, nothing survives intact except the statement of faith [Col. 0277B], the book *On the Institution of a Virgin*, or letter to Demetrias, and the Expositions on the Apostle’s Epistles. Even these, however, Cassiodorus interpolated in some places in a pious attempt to preserve them.

The fragments of the remaining works, collected with no little care, seemed best relegated to the end: partly to prevent the dissertation from growing beyond measure, and partly to make the mind of the man more easily discernible. His words are sometimes ambiguous in themselves, and are then especially difficult to understand when they are read detached from one another and mixed with Augustine’s writings, not without some effort and with the mind already prejudiced in Augustine’s favor.

## CHAPTER V. Coelestius, the Disciple of Pelagius

Coelestius, who through the error of copyists is called Coelestinus by Gennadius (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 44), was indeed a disciple of Pelagius. But he surpassed in boldness the man from whom he had received the poison of heresy, so that he spread the plague far more widely; indeed, he almost obscured the name of his teacher in the East and gave his own name to the Coelestian heretics.

It is easier to overturn the widespread opinion concerning the country from which he originated than to determine the truth with certainty. The first person, so far as I know, to make him a Scot and a fellow countryman of Pelagius was Baronius (under the year of Christ 410, no. 61), prompted by a certain testimony of Jerome. The others accepted Baronius’s view without investigating the matter, including the historians of Pelagianism, Usserius (*On the Early British Church*, chapter 8), Jansenius (*Book on the Pelagian Heresy*, at the beginning), and others, who ought nevertheless to have examined the issue more carefully.

Jerome’s testimony is as follows (preface to book 3 on Jeremiah):

> “The mute man barks through the white dog, a large and corpulent creature, one who can rage more with his kicks than with his teeth. For he has the offspring of the Scottish race, from the neighborhood of the Britons, who, after the fashion of the poets’ tales, must be struck with a spiritual club like Cerberus, so that, together with his master Pluto, he may be silenced in eternal silence.”

[Col. 0277D] Usserius argues that three men are mentioned here: first, the man who barks mutely through the white dog; second, the white dog himself; third, the man called Pluto, who has departed this life in such a condition that he may rightly be believed to exist among the dead. He therefore takes the mute man, barking through another’s mouth, to be Pelagius, born among the Britons; the white dog, Coelestius, from the neighborhood of the Britons—that is, of the Scottish race; and Pluto, Rufinus, who, having been condemned by the supreme pontiff, had already died.

The conjecture is strengthened by the objections which Jerome frequently directed against Pelagius: that he spoke through another’s mouth; that he sent biblical letters against Jerome; that he had learned his error from Rufinus as his teacher; that he had recalled from the underworld a heresy buried there; and so forth.

[Col. 0278A] But the passage concerns Rufinus of Aquileia. Although Rufinus had died in Sicily nearly three years before Jerome wrote these words, he seemed still to live in Pelagius, the defender of *apatheia* (*ἀπάθεια*) and *anamartēsia* (*ἀναμαρτησία*), and through Pelagius to rage against Jerome with his accustomed slanders. Thus the mute and dead Rufinus barks through the white dog, the Briton Pelagius—large and corpulent, being weighed down by the porridge of the Scots—who must be slain with a spiritual club like Cerberus, so that he may be silent together with his master; that is, with Rufinus his forerunner, who was given the name Pluto, so that the allusion might refer partly to the master of Cerberus and partly to the death of the unfortunate Rufinus, as Jerome himself interprets it, who had perished under an anathema.

[Col. 0278B] What is added to support the conjecture is certainly weak. First, although Pelagius may have used another’s style in writing, he nevertheless taught the heresy in his own voice. Furthermore, Pelagius was not the only one who sent biblical letters to seduce people’s minds in the provinces, nor is it absurd to say that Rufinus sent them through him. Finally, far from strengthening the conjecture, the name Pluto which Jerome attached to Rufinus weakens it, as is clear from what has preceded.

I therefore suspect that Coelestius was either a Roman or at least a Campanian, certainly born in a province of Latin speech. He was both a courtroom scholar and a man of distinction among the Romans, exceptionally eloquent, and he wrote ascetic little books to his parents which were commonly read by Latins. These four facts scarcely fit a man born among barbarians.

Prosper’s verses, as they are said to be, concerning Augustine’s detractor seem to me to refer to this:

> “Either the Britons of the sea fed this man on their own grain,  
> or the Campanian grass swells his heart.”

For I cannot agree with those—although there are many—who understand the second verse of Julian, since Julian was not a Campanian but an Apulian, as Augustine testifies (*Sixth Book of the Unfinished Work*, chapter 18), nor is he usually counted among the followers of Pelagius, whereas Coelestius certainly is.

[Col. 0277C] [Col. 0278C] That Coelestius was of noble birth and earned a place among the courtroom scholars we learn only from Mercator (preface to the *Subnotata*, no. 4). Nevertheless, it cannot rightly be called into doubt, because of the authority of the witness. Hence someone might reasonably hesitate over what Gennadius wrote (chapter 44): that when still a young man, Coelestius gave his parents three letters in the form of little books, written “from the monastery,” and necessary for everyone who desires God—unless perhaps the words “from the monastery” indicate not the place from which the letters were written but their subject. For it surpasses all belief that a courtroom scholar could either have been made out of a monk, or have been a monk before the age of twenty-seven, the age at which a person ceases to be called a young man.

Mercator alone likewise reports that he was born a eunuch from his mother’s womb through a defect of nature (*Commonitory* and preface to the *Subnotata*). We have nevertheless brought forward from Orosius something noteworthy on this matter. We established with sufficiently probable arguments that the mutilated man whom Orosius calls “light in the forehead” (*Notes on the Commonitory* and on the preface to the *Subnotata*) was none other than Coelestius. This may also be connected with the fact that Vincent of Lérins calls Coelestius monstrous (*Commonitory*, chapter 34). A eunuch is indeed a monster; for what other reason would he have called him so?

[Col. 0278D] The popular opinion has become no less established, on Baronius’s authority (under the year of Christ 405), that he professed the monastic life than that he came from Scotland. Yet Baronius himself does not explain what moved him to think this, nor do the others who followed his footsteps with closed eyes. Three considerations may occur to someone reflecting on the matter.

Augustine says that this heresy arose not from bishops or presbyters or any other clerics, but from certain monks (*Book on the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 35); and it arose from Pelagius and Coelestius. Gennadius, moreover, states that Coelestius, while still a young man, wrote three letters “from the monastery” (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 44). Finally, he was Pelagius’s companion as a monk. Frequently present at the house of Pammachius, which was called a lodging-place for monks, he preached that a rich man could be saved only by throwing away his riches. These facts, in the case of a man who professed monasticism, provide either certain evidence or at least a not implausible suspicion.

[Col. 0279A] Yet Augustine himself on one occasion called Pelagius a monk, but never Coelestius. Indeed, none of the ancients applied that name to Coelestius—not Orosius, not Mercator, not the Fathers of the councils, nor the supreme pontiffs, who would certainly have done so just as they did with Pelagius if the matter had really stood thus.

Furthermore, how could Coelestius, as a young monk, have become a courtroom scholar; or have moved from the forum into a monastery, with the matter remaining unmentioned or even unknown to Mercator, who was so eager to investigate every smallest detail?

[Col. 0279B] Finally, the statement attributed to Augustine—that this heresy arose from certain monks—does not press the argument very far, since the better and nearly all the manuscripts read “from certain people resembling monks.” We interpreted this wording in the account of Pelagius. Nor does Gennadius’s statement compel the conclusion, for the matter has already been sufficiently discussed. As for Coelestius’s intimacy with Pammachius, among whom were many who professed and practiced a holier life, what need is there to say anything, when it is hardly surprising that a senator converted to a better life should be frequently visited by a former advocate of causes who had likewise been converted?

Before giving himself over to the wicked discipline of Pelagius, he practiced law in the forum, as befitted a courtroom scholar (Mercator, at the place just cited). Thus, by becoming an advocate of heresy from an advocate of causes, he confirmed by his example what Tertullian himself and others had once demonstrated: that when men from the legal profession applied themselves to matters of faith, a few benefited the Church, but more harmed it. They did so all the more perniciously because they perverted the tools of the forum—by which I mean eloquence, shrewdness, and diligence—into instruments of deception and related vices.

[Col. 0279C] The man possessed by nature a sharp intellect, a bold spirit, and a changeable, factious disposition.
