When these qualities were joined to the experience of the forum, which is the parent of cunning, and to the training of a teacher exceptionally skilled in fraud, he attempted and almost accomplished things commensurate with such instruments.

First, he quickly seized command of the whole army after having been Pelagius’s recruit. Then the doctrines which his teacher, fearing condemnation, entrusted only to barbarous speech and faithful men as though they were mysteries, Coelestius himself made public openly and eloquently—sometimes in books, sometimes in letters sent into the provinces through men instructed in impiety. He did not merely publish them among the masses; he also defended them in episcopal tribunals and even before the apostolic see itself. Finally, he personally tested the African, Constantinopolitan, and Roman Churches, attempting, if possible, to draw those principal sees into the error’s camp—something he very nearly accomplished.

[Col. 0279D] He adopted a compressed, pointed, brief style of speaking, wholly dialectical. By means of frequent and minute questions he was accustomed to press his opponents and to suspend simpler minds in admiration of his acumen when they became entangled in the snares of syllogisms. From an indication of this style, which he had perceived elsewhere, Augustine seems to have detected the author of the definitions to which he replied in his book *On Perfect Justice*. For this reason he attributed them to Coelestius, and not implausibly, since Coelestius used the same form of writing—somewhat obscurely in the fragments of his statement of faith, but most clearly in his letter to the Roman clergy. Jerome, however, preferred to say (*Epistle to Ctesiphon*) that Coelestius did not run, as his followers boasted, through the thickets of syllogisms, but through the briars of solecisms. Yet he did not prove his opinion by examples, as he ought to have done.

It is now useful to arrange Coelestius’s actions as though in annals, from the time when he attached himself to Pelagius until the time when he seems to have been buried in silence. I think that no one knows in what year of Christ he began or ended his life. Nor is there any explicit mention of him [Col. 0280A] either before he attached himself to Pelagius and wrote against the transmission of sin, or after he was condemned by the Council of Ephesus.

Nevertheless, someone may plausibly conjecture that he was born around the year 370, for this reason. He was among the courtroom scholars at the time when he attached himself to Pelagius; he attached himself to Pelagius after Pelagius had received the heresy from Rufinus; and Rufinus had come to Rome before the year 400. Since scarcely anyone can plausibly be said to have made a name for himself as an advocate before the age of thirty, Coelestius’s birth may therefore be assigned to that year or to an earlier one.

Around the year 400 he studied under Pelagius, and at that time he may have appeared, having put on the cloak, to profess the monastic life. This was not unusual in those days, since others, even men of the highest rank, such as Pammachius and Paulinus, professed monasticism in their own homes. Nor is our own age without examples of men, even from the forum, who lived the life of monks although they were not actually monks.

[Col. 0280B] At that time, I think, Coelestius wrote letters to his parents “from the monastery,” that is, concerning the discipline of a stricter life, in which he explained the reasons for his decision. He was imitating Tertullian, himself a man from the forum, who, after putting on the cloak, wished to give an account of it in speech and writing (*On the Pallium*).

Around the year 402 he wrote a book against the transmission of sin. Vincent of Lérins seems, in my opinion, to have remembered it in these words (*Commonitory*, chapter 34):

> “Who, before Pelagius’s monstrous disciple Coelestius, denied that the whole human race was held bound by the guilt of Adam’s transgression?”

[Col. 0280C] The author of *The Predestined* refers to it still more explicitly (book 1, heresy 88):

> “Pelagius himself writes the following in his Commentary on Romans, while discussing the passage in which the Apostle says, ‘Through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death’ (Romans 5:12). Referring to Coelestius, who first wrote against the transmission of sin, he says these words: ‘Those who oppose the transmission …’”

Since Pelagius explained Paul’s Epistles long before he fled the city out of fear of the impending Alaric, and since he fled before the first siege, which took place in 409, we must admit that Coelestius wrote around the time indicated, provided that he composed his book against the transmission of sin before Pelagius’s expositions.

In the year 408 or 409, he accompanied Pelagius, who, fearing the Visigoths threatening the city, withdrew to safer regions of Sicily. They spent two years or somewhat more on that island, at Syracuse, and Coelestius also infected many bishops with his heresy. Since this date is of great importance for the history of Pelagianism, yet has not hitherto received sufficient clarification, it must be established by certain arguments, so that it may subsequently be used without danger of error.

[Col. 0280D] It is certain and beyond doubt that many people in Sicily embraced the Pelagian heresy. Jerome testifies to this (preface to book 4 on Jeremiah):

> “The heresy of impassibility and impeccability has begun to revive and to hiss not only in the regions of the West but also in those of the East; it has stained many people in certain islands, especially Sicily and Rhodes, and it grows day by day, while they teach secretly and deny publicly.”

The monk Hilary, writing from Syracuse to Augustine, says (in Augustine, Epistle 156):

> “I ask you to deign to instruct my ignorance concerning what certain Christians at Syracuse explain: that a person can be without sin and can easily fulfill God’s commandments if he wishes; and that an unbaptized infant overtaken by death cannot perish on account of guilt, because he is born without sin.”

Prosper writes (*Poem on Ingratitude*, chapter 2):

> “And wherever Trinacria, aflame with faith,  
> drove the viperous host from its own shores.”

Julian himself, when he sent a statement of faith to Zosimus, the supreme pontiff, in the name of the Sicilian bishops who refused to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius, wrote the statement of faith. The conclusion of that document reads:

> “Here ends the statement of faith of S. I. C.”

[Col. 0281A] Furthermore, Augustine’s words clearly enough indicate that Coelestius himself personally taught the heresy in Sicily. In the preface to his book *On Perfect Justice*, writing to Eutropius and Paul, Augustine says that he was replying to definitions brought from Sicily and said to be those of Coelestius. He also says that Coelestius, although he was then reported not to be there, nevertheless had followers in Sicily whom he had instructed personally, and from whom those who brought the definitions had learned the author’s name. Add to this that the great and stubborn loyalty of the Sicilian bishops toward Coelestius and Pelagius, which Julian’s statement of faith reveals, could scarcely have arisen from anything other than continued association and intimacy.

[Col. 0281B] No one who believes Mercator will agree with Jansenius of Ypres, who wished Coelestius, after being struck with an anathema by Aurelius, to have fled to Sicily. Indeed, no one should doubt that he came to Sicily before he was condemned and never returned there afterward. For Mercator accurately describes the wanderings of this restless man (*Commonitory*, chapter 2):

> “Coelestius, in no way content, but rather resisting the proceedings by which he had frequently been heard, was deprived of ecclesiastical communion. He believed that he ought to appeal from this sentence to the judgment of the Roman bishop. But, immediately disregarding that appeal, he made for Ephesus, a city of Asia, and there dared, by stealth, to seek a place in the presbyterate. After some years, under Bishop Atticus of holy memory, he made for Constantinople, where, being detected in similar matters, he was expelled from that illustrious city through the great zeal of that holy man. Letters concerning him were sent to the bishops in Asia, Thessalonica, and Carthage, copies of which we are prepared to produce, since we possess them. Yet the aforesaid Coelestius, expelled from there as well, hastened with all speed to Rome under Bishop Zosimus of holy memory.”

[Col. 0281C] Three points of the greatest importance may be gathered from this. The first, which is our principal concern here, is that Coelestius was not in Sicily after the judgment at Carthage, and that the common opinion on this matter is therefore false. The second helps to illuminate Orosius’s *Apology*: Coelestius was not at Jerusalem, either when Pelagius was secretly teaching the heresy or when the synod was held at Diospolis. The third refutes recent writers on Pelagian history, who maintain that the man whom Orosius calls Pelagius’s “arms-bearer” was different from Coelestius but was nevertheless Annianus, the deacon of Celeda, whom Jerome says supplied the words of another’s blasphemy (Epistle 201, among Augustine’s letters).

[Col. 0281D] Two considerations, finally, suggest that Coelestius spent approximately three years at Syracuse in Sicily. First, he attached many people on that island, including bishops, to himself and his party so completely that they later preferred to persist obstinately in their position rather than retain their sees and communion with the Church. Who could believe that this was accomplished in a short time, especially by a foreigner who was not immediately believed by every kind of hearer, but only by those whose loyalty experience had confirmed? Second, he did not reach Africa with his teacher until the famous conference between the Catholics and the Donatists was expected. Since Pelagius sought refuge overseas at no other time than the one we have indicated, both men must have spent the entire intervening period, which lasted more than two years, somewhere along the way. But where else could they have been except in places where they left unmistakable traces of themselves?

[Col. 0282A] In the year 411, probably in the spring, Coelestius arrived at Hippo with Pelagius, and both proceeded to Carthage. There they began to enlarge, by their accustomed methods, the heresy already disseminated by the men in Sicily who had conspired with them beforehand. When Pelagius soon departed for Palestine, Coelestius remained behind and insinuated himself into the friendship of the clergy. He either found them already imbued with his doctrines by his forerunners, or made them participants and accomplices in his madness through his incredible loquacity. His success was encouraged partly by the eloquence of the teacher, partly by the curiosity of the hearers, partly by the novelty of the questions, and even by hatred of the Manichaeans, whom he almost persuaded the less intelligent to regard as akin to the Catholic defenders of original sin (Mercator, *Commonitory*, chapter 1).

Relying on this favor among the clergy, on the appearance of piety, and on his reputation for learning and eloquence, he dared to hope for, indeed even to seek, a place in the presbyterate of the principal Church of all Africa, but in vain (Augustine, *Book on the Proceedings*; Mercator, *Commonitory*). Those among the clergy who possessed the greater zeal for the faith opposed his attempt, moved, I believe, by Augustine, who was already acting vigorously against the new error, sometimes in private conversations and sometimes in sermons to the people (Augustine, book 2 of the *Retractions*, chapter 33).

The faithful clergy did not merely oppose these unworthy attempts. Paulinus, once a deacon of the Church of Milan, acting on behalf of all good men, presented Aurelius with a written accusation charging Coelestius especially with five doctrines, which will be discussed at greater length in the dissertation on the synods. [Col. 0282B] Aurelius did not hold judgment until after the conference had been completed on June 8 and Augustine had departed from Carthage. Augustine had not taken part in the episcopal judgment; when he later returned, he reviewed what had been done in his absence, as he himself testifies (*Book on the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 11).

In the year 412, therefore, when Aurelius had, as usual, convened the council of the proconsular province before the Lenten season of Easter, Coelestius was accused by Paulinus before the bishops. He was condemned and deprived of communion until he cleared himself of the charges. The chronology is established in the dissertation on the synods. Jansenius of Ypres must therefore have been mistaken when he writes that this judgment was constituted by the bishops gathered for the conference.

During this period Coelestius did not submit to the judgment of the judges. Instead, having appealed to the apostolic see in order to evade the sentence, he fled from Africa to Asia and withdrew to Ephesus, where, by his customary methods, he insinuated himself into the presbyterate, probably being ordained by Heraclides, the predecessor of Memnon (Mercator, *Commonitory*, chapter 1).

[Col. 0282C] At this city he taught the heresy to many people, through whose assistance he infected the neighboring islands, especially Rhodes, as Jerome testifies (preface to book 4 on Jeremiah). But when the people of the Coelestian party could no longer contain themselves at Ephesus, the Catholics were rightly aroused and expelled them in a tumult, as Prosper says (*Poem on Ingratitude*, chapter 2):

> “Vessels of wrath, breaths of disease, and seeds of death.”

By these names I believe he meant both those who had absorbed the error and those who, as though by contagion, infected others, but especially Coelestius himself, the first author of the destructive plague. These events occurred during the four years from 412 to 416.

[Col. 0282D] Someone might doubt whether he ever stayed at Jerusalem with Pelagius because of these words of Orosius (*Apology*, chapter 2):

> “The most savage Goliath of pride still stands, swollen with carnal power and confident that he can do everything by himself. His head, hands, and entire body are dressed in an elaborate array. Behind him he has his arms-bearer, who, although he does not himself fight, supplies every support of bronze and iron.”

Many understand Coelestius by the term “arms-bearer.”

Yet Mercator’s authority tells against this, for when he described Coelestius’s flight from Africa and the journey that followed, he made no mention of Jerusalem, although otherwise he most certainly should have done so, whether because of his association with Pelagius or because of the events at the Council of Diospolis. Indeed, Jerome never mentioned Coelestius as a man whom he had seen; nor was any speech delivered either at the Jerusalem gathering or at the Synod of Diospolis concerning Coelestius as though he were present, or even as though he were someone who, while staying in the province, could easily be summoned. From this point the reason for doubt brought forward above is decisively refuted: Orosius is speaking of Pelagius’s armor-bearer as one who was present, whereas Coelestius was absent.

In the latter part of 416, or rather at the beginning of 417, under Atticus of holy memory he sought the city of Constantinople; there, having been detected in similar matters, he was expelled from that venerable city through the zeal of that holy man. Thus Mercator relates (*Commonitorium*, chapter 1). From this we concluded that a synod was held at Constantinople at that time. I think that Coelestius fled then for two reasons. The first was that, having been expelled from Ephesus, he wished to bring a complaint before a greater see concerning the injury done to him—for Ephesus was then in the diocese of Constantinople. The second was that, realizing that the proceedings at Diospolis were not approved at Rome and that the apostolic see was being urgently pressed by the Africans to pronounce sentence of condemnation against him and his master, he wished to test whether he could in some way obtain the protection of New Rome against the power of Old Rome and thereby somewhat avert the anger of the West through the favor of the East.

In 417, around midsummer, [Col. 0283B] after being expelled from Constantinople, he quickly fled to Rome, as soon as he learned, evidently, that Innocent had died and that Zosimus had succeeded him. He had perhaps found Zosimus friendly when he was acting at Rome, and, being a Greek, he hoped that Zosimus would be more favorably disposed toward his errors, which he had drawn from the East (Mercator, *Commonitorium*, chapter 1).

What he did with the new pontiff in that year is related by Mercator, Augustine, Facundus of Hermiane, and Zosimus himself in his third letter, which is the first addressed to the Africans in Coelestius’s case. Coelestius presented a document in which he promised to submit in every respect to the judgments of the apostolic see; by this trick he obtained something resembling a provisional absolution, and so deceived Zosimus that, in his favor, the pontiff sent harsher letters to the Africans and ordered those who openly accused him to come to Rome by the second month, and so forth. See what has been said in the dissertation on the synods and in the notes on Mercator’s *Commonitorium*.

In 418 [Col. 0283C] four events of great importance for the history of Pelagianism occurred. First, after many writings had passed back and forth and after the Africans had exposed Coelestius’s frauds, the supreme pontiff, finally instructed in the truth, issued a definitive sentence and sent a letter throughout the world. Once it had been subscribed by all the bishops, it utterly overthrew the heresy and its defenders. We have reported the synod from which the pontiff’s decree was sent in the dissertation on the synods under the month of May.

Second, on the day before the Kalends of May, the emperor Honorius wrote at Ravenna to Palladius, the praetorian prefect, concerning the expulsion from Rome and from the entire empire of Pelagius and Coelestius together with their supporters.

Third, at the subsequent plenary African council, held in June, eight canons were enacted, which the common people call the Milevitan canons.

Fourth, after the sentence of the apostolic see and after the Roman clergy, led by the presbyter Sixtus, had pronounced an anathema against the Pelagians, Coelestius wrote a letter to those of his own party who were then in Rome. In it he accused the remaining clergy of treachery, because, through fear of the imperial command, they had withdrawn from the sentence which, in their earlier proceedings, they had followed as though it were Catholic, and had thereby given the whole world an example of subscribing not merely to the condemnation of the Pelagian doctrines that they had previously approved, but especially to the condemnation of their authors, [Col. 0283D] whom they had formerly honored.

In 419, after Augustine had received through Alypius from Boniface two letters of the Pelagians, he replied in four books addressed to that same Boniface. In the first of these he refuted the letter to the Roman clergy, which he thought had been composed by Julian. Julian later denied that it was his, and Augustine did not strongly oppose him in his denial. In the notes to Julian’s little book we have restored this letter to its true author, Coelestius.

In 420, on the fifth day before the Ides of June, the emperor Honorius again wrote at Ravenna to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, concerning Pelagius and Coelestius, but especially concerning the compulsion of certain obstinate bishops to subscribe to their condemnation. These bishops either supported the heretics’ perverse arguments by silent consent or failed to destroy them by public opposition. He ordered that they should be punished by the loss of their episcopates and, once expelled from their cities, deprived of communion forever.

[Col. 0284A] Aurelius received the emperor’s letter at the time when he was holding that universal council at Carthage at which the eight doctrinal canons were confirmed. From there, on the Kalends of August, he wrote to the bishops of the province of Byzacena and of Arzeguitana. Sending them copies of the imperial constitution, he explained from whom and for what reason a subscription was required: from everyone, namely, both those whose synodal proceedings already contained a subscription and those who had been unable to attend that plenary council of all Africa. Since everyone’s subscription had been complete in the condemnation of the aforementioned heretics, there was absolutely no reason why any suspicion of dissimulation, negligence, or perhaps hidden perversity should rightly remain concerning anyone.

In 421, the emperor Constantius sent Volusianus, the urban prefect, a decree concerning the expulsion from Rome of those who showed hostility toward the piety of God, so that they would not have permission to remain even within the hundredth milestone. “Moreover, we order that Coelestius also be expelled from the city more and more completely. For it is certain that, once such men have been removed from our midst, grace and concord [Col. 0284B] retain their ancient stability. If anything of this kind should hereafter be reported, know that the office of Your Eminence must be subjected to the death penalty. For our commands do not permit negligence in their execution to remain unpunished.”

From these words one may conclude that Honorius’s earlier sanction had not been carried out because of the negligence of the urban prefect; and that Coelestius either did not in fact flee Rome when he withdrew from Zosimus’s judgment, but hid among powerful people, especially women, or returned safely to Rome after the storm had died down, with the urban prefect conniving—since he was devoted to profane rites. The same may also be concluded from Volusianus’s edict:

“Until now, the secret retreats friendly to criminals have hidden Coelestius, the disturber of the divine faith and of the public peace, from judicial action. Now the laws and edicts will pursue him even while absent. Above all, residence in the Eternal City is denied him, so that, even if he should stay in the neighboring regions, he may not escape the death he deserves,” and so forth.

[Col. 0284C] Prosper is to be understood as referring to this decree of Constantius (*Book Against the Collation*, chapter 41), when he writes that Boniface, enjoying the Catholic devotion of the most pious emperors, had used against the enemies of grace not only apostolic edicts but also royal ones.

In 422 and the following two years, it is credible that Coelestius accompanied Julian when Julian went to Cilicia to see Theodore of Mopsuestia. It is scarcely possible to doubt that sectarians had gathered with this bishop to deliberate on the affairs of their party, that they had shared their plans, and indeed had composed through common labor the eight books which Julian brought back from Cilicia and published against Augustine’s second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, thereby conspiring against the Catholic Church.

In 425, at Aquileia on the seventh day before the Ides of July, Caesar Valentinian issued a constitution to Amatius, the prefect of the Gauls, against various bishops who followed the wicked error of the Pelagian and Coelestian doctrine. He ordered that they be summoned by Patroclus, bishop of Arles, and that, unless they corrected their errors within twenty days of the summons, they be expelled [Col. 0284D] from the regions of Gaul and a more faithful priesthood substituted in their place.

In 426, or perhaps in the preceding year, the event occurred that Prosper records in these words (*in the place cited immediately above*):

“Celestine, the pontiff of venerable memory, to whom the Lord granted many gifts of his grace for the protection of the Catholic Church, knowing that the condemned are owed not an examination at trial but only the remedy of repentance, ordered Coelestius, who was requesting a hearing as though the matter had not been examined, to be expelled from the boundaries of all Italy. So inviolably did he judge that the statutes of his predecessors and the synodal decrees had to be preserved that he would in no way permit the reconsideration of what Coelestius had once deserved to have severed.”

The same year, 426, another event also occurred, which Pope Celestine himself seems to indicate in his letter to Nestorius. The Pelagian bishops, led by the presbyter Coelestius, attempted to win over Sisinnius, Atticus’s successor, who had died the previous year. The attempt failed, however, because Sisinnius judged that the acts of his predecessor had to be religiously [Col. 0285A] preserved.

In 428, after Nestorius had been appointed in the place of Sisinnius, Coelestius conceived the hope of restoring his position completely, relying on the assistance of a bishop who enjoyed great favor with the emperor and was bound to him by many obligations. He therefore began, together with the bishops who were exiled with him, and especially with Julian, the foremost of the others, to use his usual devices at court (Nestorius, Letter 1 to Saint Celestine), so that certain people might be disturbed by an ill-considered compassion and might regard the canonical indignation of the apostolic see—which had been established against them on account of religious factions—as something else.

In the same year, unless perhaps in the following one, Nestorius delivered in the Church of Constantinople the sermons against Coelestius’s error concerning original sin, concerning the debt contracted by the whole of human nature through Adam and discharged through Christ. Mercator translated these sermons into Latin, and we have illustrated them with notes in their proper place.

In 429, Nestorius wrote to Pope Celestine on behalf of the Pelagian bishops and therefore on behalf of Coelestius.

[Col. 0285B] Marius Mercator presented his Greek *Commonitorium concerning the name of Coelestius* not only to the Church of Constantinople but also to many highly religious men, in order to show them that “men who shamelessly lie” were claiming to suffer persecution for the Catholic faith in orthodox times and to endure danger, through deception and slander, on behalf of the orthodox faith. He also presented it to the emperor Theodosius, so that, by exposing the truth, he might restrain the emperor’s mind, which the devices of Nestorius were inclining toward the Pelagian party, and indeed drive it in the opposite direction. This he actually accomplished: once the disastrous error had been recognized, an imperial order expelled from Constantinople first Julian, its defender and adherent, together with his other associates and accomplices, and later Coelestius himself.

In 430, Coelestius was condemned at Rome together with the other obstinate men in the council at which Celestine dealt with the entire affair of Nestorius.

[Col. 0285C] Coelestius also complained to Nestorius, apparently because he had not been defended sufficiently by Nestorius against the imperial order by which he had been commanded to go into exile. Nestorius sent him a consolatory letter, which we received through Mercator and have illustrated with notes; in it the chronology is calculated through specific arguments.

In 431, after Mercator had presented the *Commonitorium* to the Fathers gathered at Ephesus, and after the proceedings sent from Rome by Celestine against the Pelagians had been read, Coelestius was condemned, together with Julian and the other bishops involved, by the judgment of 275 bishops, although he might have appeared to have been acquitted in the schismatics’ little council.

After the time of the Council of Ephesus, the ancient writers make no further mention of Coelestius. Perhaps he soon died, overcome by grief and unable to endure the collapse of his plans; perhaps, following the example of his master, he hid himself away in some secluded place, lived unknown, and perhaps did penance; or perhaps, finally, he followed Nestorius to the monastery of Saint Euprepius near Antioch, [Col. 0285D] and, after peace was restored to the churches, experienced the same fate as Nestorius.

Jansenius of Ypres—or whoever else he may have named—is astonishingly mistaken when he either considers it uncertain where Coelestius was after Celestine’s sentence and Valentinian’s edict, or thinks that he returned to Britain with Pelagius and attended the synod held at Verulamium, where he disputed with Saint Germanus. For we know with certainty that he was in the East in 429, the year in which the synod at Verulamium in England took place, and that he was still there in the following year, indeed even in the year after that.

No ancient writer, so far as I know, has transmitted when or how he ended his life. Indeed, there are no arguments by which one might even guess, or cautiously suspect, what would be fitting for master and disciple—men supremely arrogant toward God—in accordance with Moses’ saying about the impious violators of sacred things: “They went down [Col. 0286A] alive into the underworld, the earth closing over them, and they perished from the midst of the assembly” (Numbers 16:33).

Only two works published by Coelestius survive intact: the book *Ratiocinations* and one confession of faith. Of the others, almost nothing remains except their memory among ancient authors and isolated fragments scattered through various works of Augustine.

If we believe Gennadius (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 44), before he embraced the Pelagian doctrine—indeed, while still a young man—he wrote three letters to his parents from the monastery, in the form of little books, necessary for all who desire God. Their moral instruction contained nothing of the vice later revealed in him; rather, it was wholly an exhortation to virtue.

He also wrote a book against the transmission of sin before Pelagius himself completed his commentaries on the Epistles of Paul, as the author of the *Predestined* reports (*Book I of the Heresies*, 88).

He likewise wrote a book whose chapters 1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 12, and 13 are mentioned [Col. 0286B] in the book *On the Palestinian Proceedings*, chapters 13, 14, and 18. This appears to have been different from the preceding work. For everything cited from it pertains to *apatheia* (ἀπάθεια, “freedom from passion”) and *anhamartēsia* (ἀναμαρτησία, “sinlessness”), whereas the other work was directed against original sin. It is highly credible that the material alleged concerning Adam’s sin was drawn from this same book, if indeed a book divided into parts contained a different type of argument.

Augustine attributes to him, though with hesitation, the definitions or *ratiocinations* sent to him from Sicily, to which he responds in his book *On Perfect Justice*, addressed to Paul and Eutropius. Some think that Jerome supports this view when he says (*On the Letter to Ctesiphon*):

“One of his disciples—indeed now his master, and leader of the entire army—running through the thickets of solecisms, not, as his followers boast, through the brambles of syllogisms, philosophizes in this way,” and so forth.

Nevertheless, what Jerome immediately adds undoubtedly belongs to the book discussed in the *Proceedings*; and the whole book of *Ratiocinations* is contained in Augustine’s reply.

[Col. 0286C] He presented two little books of his faith: one at Carthage, when he was accused by Paulinus; the other at Rome, when he attempted to deceive the apostolic see. Until now it has been believed that nothing remained of either except two fragments of one of them preserved by Augustine. But in the fifth dissertation one of them will be presented intact, as it appears in Zosimus and Augustine.

Finally, he wrote a letter to his supporters who were then in Rome. In it he made the clergy of the Roman Church guilty of treachery and requested a hearing, evidently a full synodal hearing, as was his custom. Thus he says (*in Augustine, Book I to Boniface*):

“Either let a hearing be granted, or let these very bishops who are now in disagreement condemn [me],” and so forth.

The bishops he names were certainly those who, with Zosimus presiding, pronounced the sentence of condemnation at the Roman synod in 418.

[Col. 0286D] Some also attribute to him two letters: one concerning the dutiful and prodigal son, beginning, “Of all the questions from Scripture …”; the other concerning knowledge of the divine law. Both are found together with the former among Jerome’s works (*Vossius, Book I of the Pelagian Heresy*). The doctrines compel us to admit that both were written by a Pelagian, but their style and manner of expression forbid us to call them works of Coelestius.

## CHAPTER VI. On Julian, Bishop of Eclanum

That most boastful defender of the Pelagian—or rather Coelestian—heresy, Julian, was born in Apulia. For this reason, when Julian became arrogant and reproached Augustine for having been born in Africa, the holy doctor rebuked him in these words (*Book VI of the Unfinished Work*, chapter 18):

“Do not, puffed up by your earthly lineage, despise this Punic man who gives warning or admonition. It is not because Apulia gave you birth that you therefore think the Punic people must be defeated by your race, whom you cannot defeat in mind.”

He came from an illustrious family, but he seems to have obscured the brilliance of his lineage [Col. 0287A] by the manner of his life. Thus Fulgentius, in Vignerius (*Supplement, Part II, preface*), writes:

“It was not enough for him”—Julian, puffed up by his earthly lineage—“to add the fasces of the Aemilii to his father’s nobility; he disgracefully stained them with a degenerate heresy.”

His father was Memorius, or Memor, who is believed later to have become bishop of Capua. Augustine is witness to this everywhere; Paulinus is also a witness in his epithalamium for Julian and Ja (*Poem 14*), where he sings:

> Lead your children, noble Memor, before the Lord’s altars,  
> and commend them in prayer with your sanctifying hand.

Finally, Mercator is a witness; he was the first to report the mother’s name (*Subnotebook*, chapter 4):

“Are you the son of Bishop Memor, of holy and most blessed memory? Were you born from the womb of Juliana, a woman of the highest rank, than whom you would find no one more honorable among the most reverend matrons? Far be it, far be it from me to dare believe this of you.”

Mercator reports that a rumor had been spread among the people [Col. 0287B] that, instead of being the legitimate child of noble married parents, Julian had been shamefully substituted by someone as the son of household slaves (*ibid.*):

“Were you born from the womb of Juliana, a woman of the highest rank, and so forth? Far be it, far be it from me to dare believe this of you. I would sooner believe you the son of their household slaves, substituted for them, as has often been said.”

He had two sisters, whom he instructed in his own methods—certainly not the best ones—after the death of their most holy parents. Mercator bears witness to this in the same passage:

“After the death of those holy people, you rightly instructed your two sisters in such doctrines taught by your own mouth. We know, we know what one of them said or reproached you with when you, excessively severe, rose up against the downfall of the more modest woman (*pudioris*); and then you immediately fell silent, not daring to inflict any further burdens of your censure upon her grief.”

He was serving as a lector in his father’s church when he married. [Col. 0287C] Hence Paulinus writes (*Epithalamium for Julian*):

> Let the cleric love a wife made beautiful by Christ’s favor,  
> and love the beautiful woman with the light of his heart;  
> and let the lector learn from the heavenly story  
> the woman made by divine gift for the aid of her husband.

He married Ja, a consular virgin, the daughter of the illustrious Aemilius, later bishop of Beneventum.

Augustine writes concerning his wife (*Book III of the Unfinished Work*, chapter 79, and *Book III Against Julian*, chapter 14):

“You, then, with what shamelessness do you deny the shameful thing—concupiscence? Against this very thing, since you now willingly praise it, I wonder whether you fight faithfully. When you joined yourself to your wife, although you desired the pleasure granted for use without fearing anything, nevertheless you sought privacy out of shame.”

Concerning Ja, Paulinus gave poem 14 the title: “Epithalamium for Julian, son of Bishop Memor, and his illustrious wife Ja.”

The words of Fulgentius cited earlier—“to add the fasces of the Aemilii to his father’s nobility”—are to be understood as referring to Aemilius and his consular dignity.

He entered into marriage while his parents, Memor and Juliana, were still alive, but, I think, after Aemilius’s [Col. 0287D] death. For Memor gave the nuptial blessing, as is reported from Paulinus. Writing to Memor after Julian had become a deacon, Augustine blesses the whole family and the mother as follows:

“May you all dwell forever in the protection of the Most High—you who dwell as one in a house: father and mother, brothers of children, and all the sons of one father. Remember us.”

As for Aemilius’s death, I disagree with the most learned Vignerius, who thinks that he survived. The verses of Paulinus that Vignerius cites to prove that Aemilius, being present, imparted the nuptial blessing to the couple seem to me to establish the opposite, since they cannot be understood of bodily presence, but only of assistance and divine power. They are as follows (*Epithalamium for Julian*):

> May the bishop father himself bless you; may he himself [Col. 0288A]  
> lead the sacred songs before choirs resounding with hymns.  
>   
> Lead your children, noble Memor, before the Lord’s altars,  
> and commend them in prayer with your sanctifying hand.  
>   
> But what fragrance comes wafting through the air into my nostrils?  
> From where has an unexpected light struck my eyes?  
>   
> Who is that man approaching from afar with peaceful steps,  
> whom the abundant grace of Christ accompanies?  
>   
> Whom does a blessed company of heavenly nurslings surround,  
> presenting the likeness of an angelic host?  
>   
> I recognize the man whom divine fragrances accompany,  
> and upon whose face the splendor of the stars (*siderum*) shines.  
>   
> This, this is the man of the Lord, rich in the abundant  
> gift of Christ: Aemilius, the man of heavenly light.  
>   
> Rise, Memor, venerate your father, embrace your brother;  
> in Aemilius, one name belongs to both of you.  
>   
> Memor is both younger and older—a wondrous great  
> gift and work of God: the younger is here the father.

[Col. 0288B] What brought about the dissolution of this marriage—whether the common decision of the couple or Ja’s death—I do not know. It is certain, however, that it was dissolved before Julian’s parents died. For Augustine wrote to Memor when Julian was already a deacon, as follows (*Letter 131 to Memor*):

“The preceding five books will scarcely seem worth knowing to our son and fellow deacon Julian, since he too is now serving alongside us,” and so forth.

At that time deacons were not permitted either to remain married or, at any rate, to make use of marriage, as is clear from Siricius, Letter 1, chapter 7; Innocent I, Letter 2, chapter 9; Letter 3, chapter 1; and elsewhere.

Augustine held Julian very dear, at least at the time when the holy man wrote to Memor (*Letter 131*). The writer’s words are full of the tenderest affection:

“As for him”—Julian—“I do not dare say that I love him more than you, because I would not be speaking truthfully; nevertheless, I do dare say that I desire him more than you. It may seem strange how I can desire more greatly one whom I love equally. But this is brought about in me by the greater hope of seeing him. For I think that if, at your command or through your sending, he comes to us, he will also do what is fitting for a young man, especially since he is not yet occupied with greater cares, and will bring you yourself to me with greater ease.”

[Col. 0288C] Yet how does Augustine call him a young man when he acknowledges him as a deacon, given that in those times ecclesiastical law prohibited the ordination of deacons before the completion of the twenty-fifth year (*Third Council of Carthage*, canon 16)? Perhaps, when the elderly Augustine was writing to the elderly Memor, Julian, who was somewhat older than twenty-five, could be called a young man in comparison with both of them. The same usage applies when, after he had become a bishop—and indeed had passed his thirty-fifth year—the most holy man called him “a most confident young man” (*Book II Against Julian*, chapter 8). He addresses him in the same way in these words (*Book III*, chapter 27):

“Your books show, young Julian, that you cannot find what to say against my books and are seeking accusations which you may noisily and emptily heap upon us.”

Thus the Fathers of the Council of Reims call Armentarius, who had been ordained bishop, a young man.

Nevertheless, if age is assessed according to ancient custom, an easier solution to the question presents itself. Formerly, a person was called a boy up to the age of twenty-one; [Col. 0288D] an adolescent up to twenty-eight; a young man up to forty; a man up to sixty-three; and thereafter an old man (*Censorinus, On the Birthday*, chapter 14). On this reckoning, someone who was serving as a deacon could rightly be called an adolescent.

This also incidentally clarifies the meaning of the canon of the Council of Carthage, which orders that a lector, once he has reached the age of puberty, must either marry or vow continence:

“Likewise it was decided that lectors, once they have reached the age of puberty, must be compelled either to marry or to vow continence.”

The Fathers did not understand this as the beginning of puberty, which occurs in the fourteenth year of life, but as completed puberty, which occurs in the twenty-first year. For, apart from the absurdity of compelling someone by ecclesiastical law either to contract marriage or to vow chastity as soon as he reached the age of fourteen, a lector in those times was certainly not ordained before the age of eighteen, which is mid-puberty. Thus the law concerning lectors applied only to those who had passed beyond mid-puberty and attained full puberty. [Col. 0289A]

He was made a deacon before his parents’ death. For Augustine, writing to Memor (*Letter 101*), calls Julian a fellow deacon and at the same time mentions that his mother was still living.

The learned Vignerius is wrong, however, when he thinks Augustine’s letter corrupt and believes that *commilitonem* (“fellow soldier”) should be read instead of *condiacono* (“fellow deacon”), as though Augustine had written the preface to the work he calls *Perfect* before the marriage had been dissolved, rather than at the time when Julian, already free from marriage, was devoting himself to study—more to secular studies than to sacred ones, contrary to the duty of a man committed to ecclesiastical service.

Mercator teaches that Julian was ordained [Col. 0289B] by Innocent (*Commonitorium on the Name of Coelestius*, chapter 3), but he indicates neither the date of the ordination nor the rank. I think that the ordination occurred in 416 or even earlier. Innocent died on 12 March 417. Therefore, since Julian, from his ordination until Innocent’s death, “continued,” in Mercator’s words, “in a sincere position,” and remained in communion with the condemner of Pelagius and Coelestius, he himself must undoubtedly have condemned those men as well. Some period of time must therefore have elapsed between Julian’s ordination and Innocent’s death. For who can be said to have persevered in something in which he has spent no *axiologon tempus* (ἀξιόλογον *tempus*, “a significant period of time”)?

I also think that this ordination should be understood, according to the custom of the ancients, as an episcopal ordination. For it is clear from Augustine, Mercator, and the two letters that Julian himself sent to Zosimus that, during the time of Zosimus—who succeeded Innocent and governed the Church for scarcely sixteen months—Julian was already among the bishops.

The authors seem to disagree about the city whose episcopate he held. [Col. 0289C] Gennadius says that it was Capua (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 45); Gelasius says Celanum (*Decree of the Holy Roman Church*); Bede says Celanum (*preface to the Song of Songs*); Peter the Deacon says Edanum (*Book on Grace*); Vossius says Eclanum or Atella (*Book on the Pelagian Heresy*); and Vignerius says Celanum, in the place cited repeatedly above.

Mercator, who could not have been ignorant of the location of the episcopate and who deserves no less confidence than anyone else—being Julian’s contemporary and fellow provincial, and, as his opponent, exceptionally well informed—declares him bishop of Eclanum. At the same time he settles the dispute, with the agreement, indeed, of both contending sides (*Preface to the Symbol of Theodore*). He has Prosper in actual agreement with him, since the better manuscripts read *Eclanensis*, as Pontacus and Scaliger noted (*Notes on Prosper’s Chronicle*). Gelasius and Bede also agree with him, for in both authors the error of a copyist, who transposed a single letter, changed *Eclanensis* into *Celanensis*. Finally, Paul the Deacon agrees for the same reason: the letters *cl* had coalesced into *d*.

[Col. 0289D] Nor does Gennadius disagree, since the better-quality manuscripts make no mention of the place and do not read the word *Capuanus* (“Capuan”), but instead read in some copies, “Julian, a man keen in intellect,” and in others, “Julian the bishop, a man keen in intellect.”

This opinion is further demonstrated by these words of Mercator addressing Julian (*Subnotebook*, chapter 1):

“The foulest stench of your fellow-countrywoman, the Ampsanctine spring, has inflated you most truly.”

For Eclanum was situated near Ampsanctum; in the *Itinerary of Antoninus* it is called Eclanum. Hence we find the Eclanian territory in the *Book on Boundaries*, and the commonwealth of the Eclanians in inscription 446 in Gruterus.

Eclanum was once an episcopal city among the Hirpini, between Campania and Apulia, twenty miles distant from the metropolitan city of Beneventum. It is now called Frigento and is joined to the bishopric of Avellino.

From this it is clear that Julian was born before the year 386 of Christ. [Col. 0290A] At that time no one could legally become a bishop, or even a presbyter, before the age of thirty. Therefore, if Julian had reached the age of thirty when he was ordained by Innocent, who was exceptionally strict in observing the canons, he must have been born before 386.

Concerning the time when he attached himself to Pelagius or Coelestius, scarcely anything else may be conjectured beyond what we said in the account of Pelagius. These words of Bede seem to indicate that he had been instructed by Pelagius from early childhood (*Book I on the Song of Songs*, chapter 5):

“Indeed, Jerome himself, in the dialogue of Atticus and Critobulus, which he published while Pelagius was alive, would have overcome and crushed his faith—or rather his faithlessness—with divine utterances, while Julian, still a little boy under him, was being nourished as a basilisk in the serpent’s cave.”

But unless Bede’s statement is understood in a manner adapted to the meaning of the prophet Isaiah [Col. 0290B] (chapter 11:8), and contains some mystical significance, it conflicts astonishingly with the chronology. When Jerome wrote the dialogues, Pelagius was in Palestine, while Julian was in Rome and scarcely less than a bishop.

Bede may therefore be said to have spoken appropriately of Julian as a recruit of error who, after being instructed by Pelagius through his disciples, grew secretly, as one who loved to hide in a serpent’s cave, and later became a teacher of impiety all the more harmful because a basilisk spreads a worse poison than a serpent.

He was keen in intellect, as Gennadius reports (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 45), and devoted careful attention both to secular and to sacred literature, but more to secular literature—indeed to such an extent that he was excessively devoted to wearing away at the more licentious poets.

Gennadius also bears witness to his study of sacred literature (*ibid.*). Augustine likewise testifies to his excessive love of secular literature (*Letter 101*). Concerning his reading of impure poets, Mercator writes (*Subnotebook*, chapters 4 and 5):

“You speak elegantly, like a buffoon in your customary manner, and in the manner in which you have reviled the theater of Arbitrius and Valerius,” and so forth.

By nature he possessed a great aptitude for eloquence, [Col. 0290C] as his writings show. Thus he could rightly appear renowned for his speech, as Gennadius says (*ibid.*), indeed a certain Roman Demosthenes, as he himself and his supporters liked to claim. Yet the great power of his eloquence degenerated into loquacity through the faults of boastfulness and abuse. Both Mercator and Augustine accuse him of this repeatedly and everywhere.

Before he revealed Pelagius’s impiety in himself, he was distinguished among the teachers of the Church, according to Gennadius (*ibid.*). From this one may infer that Julian wrote far more than the works that contained his error. Yet not even the memory of those writings survives, unless perhaps they include his commentary on the Song of Songs, whose preface was the little book *On Love*, or his books *On Constancy*, which Bede mentions, like the preceding work (*Book I on the Song of Songs*). Nevertheless, both works are not merely written in the Pelagian spirit but filled with it. Bede accuses the first of Pelagian error, and no one who has read the second would acquit it.

He wrote two letters to Zosimus, as he himself admits, [Col. 0290D] but he denies that the letter sent to the clergy of the Roman Church was his—the letter that Augustine refutes in Book I to Boniface. His words are as follows (*Book I of the Unfinished Work*, chapter 1):

“Augustine also mentions a letter which he says was sent by me to Rome. But we were unable to recognize from the words he quoted what writing he was referring to. For I sent two letters to Zosimus, formerly bishop of that city, concerning these questions, but at a time when I had not yet begun my books.”

Observe two points here. First, Julian wrote twice to Zosimus concerning the Pelagian questions. Second, he wrote at a time when he had not yet begun those books—namely, the four books mentioned in the letter attributed to him, in which he fought against Augustine’s first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*.

He also wrote a letter to Rufus of Thessalonica, [Col. 0291A] not only in his own name but in the name of eighteen Pelagian bishops. He himself testifies to this when the impure man addresses Saint Augustine in these words (*Book II of the Unfinished Work*, chapter 178):

“By such an argument nothing is indicated except your impiety—namely, the impiety by which you believe that the propagation (*tradux*) of souls, formerly condemned in the profanities of Tertullian and Mani, is the same as that of bodies. This is so wicked that, when it was charged against us in the letter we sent to the East, you now try to repel it by denying it in the books you recently sent to Boniface.”

He also wrote twelve books against Augustine’s two books *On Marriage and Concupiscence* in defense of his own heresy: four, namely, against Augustine’s first book, and eight against the second. For when Augustine had sent Count Valerius, before whom the Pelagians were slandering the Catholics as though they condemned marriage, a book by which he might repel the slander, Julianus offered four books in reply to this work (Book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 53). When Augustine had refuted from these certain excerpts that Count Valerius had sent into Africa through Alypius, he poured forth against this same Julian, with extraordinary prolixity, those eight books in Book II of *On Marriage and Concupiscence* [Col. 0291B]. Augustine answered them in his final work, which Possidius called incomplete in the *Index*, Gennadius called an “altercation” in the passage often cited, and Vignerius called complete in the preface to that same work.

From this one may refute not only Gennadius and Honorius of Autun, who seem to distinguish that work from the *Altercation*, but especially also certain more recent writers who suppose that Julianus repaid Augustine’s six books with eight books of his own, and that Augustine answered those eight books in his final work. For Julianus does not appear ever to have read—as Mercator reports (*Preface to the Book of Notes*)—that Augustine had written six books against his four.

He inclined more toward the party of Caelestius than toward that of Pelagius; that is, he argued against the Catholic faith less concerning the grace of God than concerning original sin. This is evident not obscurely from the four books just mentioned [Col. 0291C], and it is manifest from the final work, in which he raises, by himself alone, only the following questions: Whether Adam’s sin harmed all his descendants in such a way that they are born liable to sin; how this sin is transmitted; whether even the children of the faithful perish eternally if they are not baptized; whether diseases and other evils of that kind, and death itself, originated from Adam’s sin; whence evil comes, and by what means it was introduced into God’s work; how Catholics differ from Manichaeans on this matter and on the origin of sin; what concupiscence is, whence it arose, what powers it possesses, and whether it is evil in itself; and so forth. Of the grace of Christ he speaks scarcely at all—even when Augustine forcibly draws him into the subject.

Now it seems appropriate to arrange in chronological order everything we have prefaced, so that the remaining matters may be treated by the same method.

Julianus was therefore born, at the latest, in 386; became a lector in 404; married in 407; attained the diaconate in 411; was elevated to the priesthood in 416; and remained constant, at least outwardly, in the profession of the Catholic faith until 417, when Innocent died, on the day before the Ides of March. Out of reverence for Innocent, Julianus remained in office, as Mercator explains (*Commonitory*, chapter 3). Augustine, however, writes that Innocent warned Julianus, so that, if he had not rejected the warning, he would certainly not have fallen into heresy.

The events that Mercator reports concerning Julianus disputing at Rome seem to belong to the year 417. He gives them in these words (*Book of Notes*, part II, chapter 8):

> For we remember how, at the time when you were present in the city of Rome and were attacking the Church together with the associates of this most insane error of yours among certain simpler people, you used to ask: “What is sin? Is it something evil or something good?” You were answered: “Certainly, something evil.” To this you added: “Is God therefore the author and maker of this evil?” “Away with it, away with it!” they exclaimed, and so forth.

There also undoubtedly belong here the words in which Julianus himself boasts of the reason why he undertook the defense of the afflicted Pelagian heresy [Col. 0292A] (*Against the Two Books of the Unfinished Work*, Book II, chapter 10):

> Now, after the dross of the most impure doctrines began to be offered as a remedy against the Manichaeans, and authority was added to the pleasure, so that, with almost the whole world consenting, that all-powerful queen of minds, destroyer of decency, and unconquered captor of every soul—shamefulness—might run riot, the cause of defending the truth became for us all the more honorable because it became all the more difficult. For truth and the speech of those who administer remedies have little power against headlong peoples hostile to their own remedies. What, then? On their account shall we sound the retreat, avenge our insults by silence, and from the harbor of conscience laugh at the shipwrecks of others? Yet this hatred is contradicted, first by the kindness we owe to the human race, and then by the hope and faith we have in God. Apart from the fact that he has often restored the desperate ruins of the ages, he has also rewarded with eternal recompense the steadfastness that he wished to be exercised even until the hour of death, although it might achieve no immediate result.

In 418 he wrote three letters: one to Zosimus, fragments of which Mercator reports (*Book of Notes*, chapter 7, no. 9) [Col. 0292B]; another to the same person, namely, the *Booklet of Faith*, which we published first in Dissertation 5; and a third to Rufus of Thessalonica, which Augustine refutes in the three later books—II, III, and IV—of his work addressed to Boniface. The latter two he issued not only in his own name but also in the name of eighteen Sicilian bishops.

There is nothing to prevent these bishops from actually having been Sicilians, even though they are said to have been expelled from Italy at the Council of Ephesus (see Sirmond, *On Advent*, chapter 5), since Sicily was at that time included under the name of Italy.

On this occasion that passage in the synodal report of the Fathers of Ephesus to Saint Celestine should incidentally be corrected (Part II of the Council of Ephesus, act 5). The passage concerns the bishops who had joined the party of John of Antioch on behalf of Nestorius and had pronounced the sentence of deposition against Cyril and Memnon:

> “With them also were the Pelagians and Caelestians, and certain of those expelled from Thessaly: καὶ τῶν ἀπὸ Θεσσαλίας ἐκβεβλημένων τινές.”

It should instead read: “and certain of those who had been expelled from Italy: καὶ τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰταλίας …”

At the beginning of 419, or toward the end of the preceding year, he composed four books against Augustine’s first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. For, as he himself testifies (*Book I of the Unfinished Work*, chapter 16), he had not yet begun these books at the time when he sent the two letters to Zosimus. He sent them, as Mercator explains (*Book of Notes*, part IX of chapter 7), when he refused to join the entire Church throughout the world in condemning Pelagius and Caelestius. He was not summoned, however, before Zosimus’s *Tractoria* had been sent to all the bishops of the world. Since it was sent around the end of May 418, and since Zosimus died on 26 December of that same year, Julianus must have replied to Zosimus in 418, when the latter was already ill, and must consequently have composed the four books against Augustine at the time just specified.

Add that, even if they had perhaps been prepared earlier, he does not seem to have published them until the middle of 419; and [Col. 0292D] even then not openly, but secretly, after the Pelagian manner, and only among trusted associates. Hence it happened that the complete work could not immediately be obtained, but only excerpts, and not particularly reliable ones, which Alypius brought to Augustine after receiving them from Count Valerius. The books themselves came into the hands of Bishop Claudius only after another year and after a careful search (*Letter to Claudius*, prefixed to Book I *Against Julianus*, and elsewhere throughout).

A much stronger argument, however, is supplied by these words of Augustine addressed to Julianus: “Remember, certainly, how you insultingly bring up the disagreement of the Roman people concerning the appointment of a bishop, and call it God’s vengeance” (Book VI *Against Julianus*, chapter 4). From this we understand that Julianus wrote during the disagreement in which, after the death of Zosimus, some contended for Boniface and others for Eulalius as pontiff (Baronius, under the year 419). Therefore, since the disagreement lasted from 27 [Col. 0293A] December 418 until 8 April of the following year, it must be admitted that the books in question were composed during that period.

In 421, expelled from Italy, he either fled to Sicily or, more probably, to the East. The expulsion is indicated by these words of Prosper (*Against the Collation*, chapter 41):

> When Pope Boniface, of blessed memory, was rejoicing in the Catholic devotion of the most pious emperors and was using not only apostolic but also imperial edicts against the enemies of God’s grace—for what does it mean to use edicts except to put them into execution? Or what edicts can be understood except those three, one issued on the day before the Kalends of May under the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, Augusti and consuls; another on the fifth day before the Ides of July under the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta at Ravenna; and the third issued under the consulship of Constantius, Eustachius, and Agricola? Or what else were those edicts ordering, except the expulsion of Pelagius and Caelestius and the deposition of the bishops who refused to subscribe to their condemnation?

The following verses of the same Prosper may perhaps refer to the place of his flight (*Poem on the Unbelievers*, chapter 2) [Col. 0293B]:

> I pass over how great a tumult stirred  
> Illustrious Ephesus, not suffering within her walls  
> The vessels of wrath, the breath of disease, and seeds of death  
> To remain; and with what faith the land of burning Trinacria  
> Drove the viperous host from its own shores.

Although, since they were expelled from Italy—or rather from the whole West—it is more credible that they proceeded to the East, as will be said later.

Finally, the time of the flight is established with certainty both by the words of Prosper concerning Boniface that we have quoted and by what follows.

In 422, expelled from the West, he went to Cilicia, to Theodore of Mopsuestia, the first author and parent of the Caelestian heresy, so that, after conferring with one another about their affairs and forming a conspiracy, they might fight against Augustine with united forces.

Mercator’s testimony on this matter should be heard [Col. 0293C], since he alone has informed us of the history (*Preface to the Refutation of the Creed Composed by Theodore*):

> At the same time I wished to warn Julianus that this man—formerly bishop of the town of Eclanum, now a Pelagian or Caelestian heretic—had followed Theodore. After traversing lands, crossing the sea, and surveying the East, he hastened with his associates and companions, with great effort, as to a teacher renowned for proclaiming Christian doctrines, so that Theodore himself might confirm him in the Pelagian or Caelestian heresy which he had undertaken to defend and follow. From there, as though better instructed, he might compose those eight volumes, as he supposes, most prudent, against the Catholic faith rather than against Augustine of blessed memory.

And in the final chapter of the *Annotations*, addressing Julianus:

> With one thing shut up in his heart and another ready on his tongue, a new and excellent disputant, you now thrust this into your present work, composed after so long a time in Cilicia. Therefore, by the necessary repetition of the chapter, let us examine again what new and unheard-of thing you brought back from there, after crossing the sea and surveying the East.

From these statements I conclude that Julianus remained for some time in Cilicia with Theodore, and that there he composed his final work, contained in eight books, and then brought it back from there into the West.

Moreover, that Theodore also wrote against Augustine is demonstrated by the considerable fragments preserved by Mercator from five books that Theodore himself composed against Augustine. They bear this title: “Let us establish, from the writings of Theodore translated by us from Greek, what sort of bad faith the aforesaid Theodore possessed.” And shortly afterward: “From Theodore of Mopsuestia’s fourth book of the second codex, folio ten, against Saint Augustine, who defends original sin and teaches in Catholic fashion that Adam was made mortal through transgression,” and so forth.

In 423 a synod was held in Cilicia at which Julianus and his heresy were condemned, while Theodore of Mopsuestia himself at least verbally consented to the condemnation. Thus Mercator writes (*Preface to the Refutation of Theodore’s Creed*):

> Let the aforesaid Julianus recognize from this translation, if he is not unwilling to read it, that, while that bad faith remains with the aforementioned Theodore by which we said that he had deceived Nestorius along with himself, Theodore is also more opposed to Julianus and to his doctrine, concerning which, swollen with evil pride and unsound in mind, he composed books; and let him recognize that, after his departure from Cilicia, he too was condemned by Theodore with an anathema in the assembly of the bishops of his province, and so forth.

In 424, as I suppose, Julianus returned from the East to Italy. His only reason for returning was that, on the one hand, a vehement longing for his lost episcopate held him, while on the other a vain hope of reopening the entire case soothed him. For when he learned that Pope Boniface, by whom he had been deposed, had died, and that the emperors Honorius and Constantius, by whose edicts he had been compelled to live in exile, had also died; when he further learned that Boniface had been succeeded by Celestine, a man far gentler than his rival Sixtus, he dared to hope for some change in circumstances. But hope deceived the daring man. For, as Prosper says (*Against the Collation*, chapter 31) [Col. 0294B]:

> Pope Celestine, of venerable memory, to whom the Lord granted many gifts of his grace for the protection of the Catholic Church, knowing that those who have been condemned are owed not judicial examination but only the remedy of repentance, ordered Caelestius, who was requesting a hearing as though the matter had not been examined, to be expelled from the whole of Italy. He judged that the statutes of his predecessors and the synodal decrees must be preserved inviolate, and therefore would by no means permit the reopening of what the man himself had deserved to have severed.

At that time, moreover, not only Caelestius but Julianus too was again expelled from Italy by Celestine. Julianus himself admits this in Nestorius’s letter to Celestine, which contains the complaints of the expelled men, in these words (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 16):

> A certain Julianus, and Florus, Orontius, and Fabius, claiming that they were bishops of the Western provinces, repeatedly approached both the most pious and most renowned emperor and bewailed their cases, as though, being orthodox, they had suffered persecution in orthodox times.

And shortly afterward:

> Let them not suppose that the canonical indignation of Your Blessedness, which was perhaps rightly directed against them on account of their sectarian beliefs, means anything other than this (ibid., chapter 17), and so forth.

And in Letter 2:

> I have often written to Your Blessedness concerning Julianus, Orontius, and the others, who arrogate episcopal dignity to themselves and make very frequent approaches to the most pious and most renowned emperor, cutting us down with continual lamentations, as though they had been cast out of the West in orthodox times.

In 425, as I suppose, he was expelled from Constantinople itself by Atticus, together with Caelestius and the other bishops—Orontius, Florus, Persidius, Marcellinus, Fabius, and others. For Prosper sings of Atticus (*Poem on the Unbelievers*, chapter 2):

> What should I say of the great care he exercised in the imperial city,  
> Constantinople, where the good priest Atticus, with learned speech,  
> Refuted the ambassadors of the heretics with the ancient faith?  
> From that city, then, the impious hearts,  
> Although they concealed themselves beneath a covering of outward form,  
> Endured the silent torments of rejection.

The words of Celestine to Nestorius should be understood in the same sense (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 18):

> These heretics too, concerning whom you wished to consult us as though unaware of what had been done, were expelled from their seats by a just condemnation, although they uttered unjust things. We do not think it surprising that they found rest there, and so forth.

Why, however, are the things then done in that place being investigated, when it is certain that the actions of Atticus, then the Catholic bishop, were transmitted from there to us?

For it is evident from the same source (chapters 16 and 17) that those bishops whose names Nestorius had placed in his letters were expelled from the imperial city by Atticus. He had indeed listed Julianus, Florus, Orontius, Fabius, and others.

In 426, fleeing once more from Italy to Constantinople, Julianus, as I infer, published the eight books that he had until then shared only with trusted associates after bringing them from Cilicia [Col. 0295A]. Two considerations support this conjecture.

First, Atticus died on 10 October of the preceding year, and Sisinnius succeeded him in the see of Constantinople on 28 February of this year. He was, as Marcellinus puts it, “a man of holy simplicity and simple holiness” (*Chronicle*, indiction 9, under the consulship of Theodosius XII and Valentinian II). He therefore seemed to Julianus a suitable man to be deceived by the arts, hypocrisy, and falsehood of heretics, and, once deceived, to placate the emperor’s attitude toward men who called themselves orthodox and who claimed to have suffered persecution in orthodox times through a surreptitious pretext on behalf of the Catholic faith (Letter 2 of Nestorius to Saint Celestine). Yet his hope again failed him, since Sisinnius consistently followed in Atticus’s footsteps, as Celestine explains (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 17).

Second, Augustine, after receiving the first five books of Julianus’s eight from Alypius, had already begun answering the fourth when he wrote to Quodvultdeus in the letter prefixed to his book *On Heresies* [Col. 0295B]. Quodvultdeus was urging him to compose a commentary on the heresies, while Augustine was simultaneously pressing forward, allotting time both to the reply Alypius was urging and to the revision of the books, whose completion he ardently desired. He wrote to Quodvultdeus, however, in 427.

In 428, when Nestorius, the disciple of Theodore, had assumed the governance of the Church of Constantinople, Julianus came to the imperial city with his associates, full of hope, in order, through the assistance of the new bishop, to bend the emperor’s mind by means of their complaints.

Nestorius himself bears witness to his arrival and complaints in both letters to Celestine on behalf of the Pelagians; their words have been cited under the year 426 (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapters 15 and 16).

The chronology is also supported both by the aforementioned letters, the first of which we demonstrate in our notes on Mercator to have been written in this year, and by the edict issued at Constantinople on 29 June under the consulship of Felix and Taurus against the heretics (Book XV *On Heretics* of the Theodosian Code) [Col. 0295C]. In that edict all their names are carefully listed, except those of the Pelagians.

Nestorius was the one who prompted the emperor to issue the edict. For, as Vincent of Lérins says (*Commonitory*, chapter 16), in order to open an entrance for his own heresy, he attacked the blasphemies of all the heresies. And, as Cassian writes (*On the Incarnation*, Book I, chapter 3), “he supported a depravity akin to his own with a depraved affection,” knowing that he shared the same opinions and the same spirit, and therefore grieving that a heresy related to him had been separated from the Church. Indeed, he was already then considering increasing the number of those on his side by adding the Pelagians, which he actually accomplished at the Council of Ephesus. Accordingly, as Mercator says (*Preface to the Treatise of Nestorius against the Pelagians*), he judged that they should meanwhile be received into friendship, promising them hope of absolution, and so forth.

In 429, Mercator presented the emperor Theodosius with a *Commonitory* against the error of Caelestius and Julianus and against the other bishops who followed them. After receiving it, the emperor expelled Julianus, Caelestius, and the others from Constantinople (Part I of Mercator’s works). This is shown by the title of the *Commonitory*:

> A copy of the *Commonitory* which, concerning the name of Caelestius, Mercator composed in Greek and presented not only to the Church of Constantinople but also to many most religious men, and which he also offered to the most pious prince, Theodosius, ever Augustus. It was translated from Greek into Latin by the same Marius Mercator, servant of Christ, in the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius, illustrious men.

The *Commonitory*, by making the most destructive error known, led to the imperial order by which both Julianus, its defender and follower, together with his other associates and companions, and afterward Caelestius himself, were expelled from the city of Constantinople; and they were subsequently condemned in the Council of Ephesus by the judgment of 275 bishops.

In 430, Celestine held a synod at Rome concerning Julianus and the other bishops who supported Caelestius. From it he replied to Nestorius in letters issued on 11 August [Col. 0296A]. Nestorius received them in the church on Sunday, 7 December, delivered by the hands of four bishops—Theopemptus, Daniel, Potamon, and Macarius (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 17; Part II, act 2). These facts are clearly established partly by our dissertation on synods, partly by Celestine’s letters, partly by the report of the bishops in act 1 of the Council of Ephesus, and partly by the title of the sermon delivered in the church on the sixth day after the letters were received. It reads as follows in Mercator (Part II of Mercator’s works):

> Sermon of Nestorius delivered in the church in which he received the letters of Celestine, bishop of Rome, and Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, concerning the denunciation, on 7 December, in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, Augusti, on the sixth day after he received the letters.

In 431, Julianus and his associates were condemned at the ecumenical Council of Ephesus, although he had earlier appeared to have been acquitted in the assembly of the schismatics.

Gregory the Great mentions that acquittal (*Register*, Book V, Letter 14, and Book VI, Letter 61). He writes that the schismatics had defined the matter of Adam’s soul by declaring that it had not died in sin, because the devil does not enter into the human heart, and that anyone who said this would be anathema. Elsewhere (*Letters*, Book VII, Letter 48) he recounts the history at greater length and explains that in many manuscripts the acts of the Catholic synod had been mixed together with the proceedings of the schismatics. In the proceedings of this kind that are now extant, however, nothing of the sort is found.

The fathers of Ephesus themselves mention the condemnation, in addition to Mercator in the title of the *Commonitory*, both in the canons and in the report to Saint Celestine, in these words (Part II of the Council of Ephesus, acts 5 and 7):

> After the commentaries of the proceedings concerning the deposition of the impious Pelagians and Caelestians had been read in the holy synod, together with the things decreed and established concerning them by Your Piety, we too judged that these decisions must remain solid and firm, and we all determined the same thing with you, regarding them as deposed.

In 432, Celestine replied concerning the condemned Caelestians in three letters issued after the synod: one to the Fathers of the synod, another to Maximianus, bishop of Constantinople, and a third to the clergy of that city (Part II of the Council of Ephesus, chapters 20, 22, and 23). They are dated the Ides of March, under the consulship of Flavius, Aetius, and Valerius, and contain the procedure for receiving heretics who returned from this heresy to the Church.

In 439 the events narrated by the chronicler Prosper occurred, as follows (*Chronicle*, under the consulship of Theodosius XVII and Festus):

> At this time Julianus of Eclanum, the most boastful defender of the Pelagian error, whom an intemperate desire for his long-lost episcopate had been driving, employing many devices of deception while presenting the appearance of correction, attempted to insinuate himself into communion with the Church. But Pope Sixtus, vigilantly confronting these plots at the urging of the deacon Leo, allowed no opening for his pestilential efforts. Thus he caused all Catholics to rejoice at the exposure of the deceitful beast, as though the apostolic sword had then for the first time cut down the most arrogant heresy.

In 440, Vignerius writes in the preface to the *Final Work* that Julianus arrived at the island of Lérins [Col. 0296D] and there drew Abbot Faustus over to his own error, after Faustus had received him kindly and supported him for several months. But I have not yet been able to determine whose testimony he cites for this. Is it that mysterious codex of his, which remains completely hidden? Or the testimony of other authors who could be consulted? Whatever the source of that testimony, I will not easily grant it credence.

For if Julianus came to Lérins, it was certainly after his second expulsion from Italy by Pope Sixtus, at which time, struck by all the thunderbolts of the Church and expelled by all the prohibitions of the rulers, he wandered like another Cain. But at that time Faustus had been appointed abbot in succession to Maximus, a most holy man, because of the sanctity of his conduct. How, then, could a man of unimpeachable reputation have supported an infamous person for several months? How could the holy abbot have associated familiarly with a heretic—as would have been necessary in order to enter into fellowship in error? How could this have happened without provoking the complaints of so many holy monks and of Vincent, who otherwise detested Julianus [Col. 0297A]?

Furthermore, if any smoke of the Pelagian error clung to the people of Lérins—and it certainly did—it was not blown there by Julianus’s association but by Cassian’s, and indeed many years earlier, as may be gathered from Vincent’s *Commonitory*.

Finally, when Faustus, long after these events and after becoming a bishop, wrote his books *On Grace and Free Will*, how could he have attacked the opponents of original sin—with whose leader, Julianus, he knew the movement to be identified at that time—with such vehement language as this, if he had formed an alliance in error with Julianus? (*On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 2):
