> But perhaps you will say: “When you argue these things, you will be found to condemn marriage.” It is not so. The institution of marriage began with blessing; the generation of corruption began with transgression. The flesh, subjected to the curse, stained undefiled beds, and the spirit of pride corrupted the simple affection; and just as it lost the privilege of immortality, so it lost the gift of purity. It is not the grace of marriage that is called to account, but the injury of obscene passion. Gold itself is not accused, but whatever fraud and iniquity mixed into refined gold as an adulterant—just as the author of wickedness infected with pestilent corruption the spirit of Pelagius, which God had created for better pursuits, and so forth.

Vignerius, being learned in only a few matters, might perhaps have been able not merely to resolve these arguments by force of intellect but also to challenge them by the testimony of that codex of his, which is rightly desired.

Historians usually refer to the year 444 what is found in the author of the book *On the Promises and Predictions of God* (Part II, chapter 6), attributed to Prosper:

> In Italy too, while we were staying in Campania, when Pope Leo—who must be named with venerable and apostolic honor—was overthrowing the Manichaeans and crushing the Pelagians, especially Julianus, and so forth.

In 447, Saint Leo prescribed the manner in which those who returned from the Pelagian or Caelestian heresy to the Catholic faith were to be received. Thus he writes to Nicetas of Aquileia (Letter 86):

> Let them condemn in explicit professions the authors of their proud error, and let them detest whatever the universal Church has abhorred in their teaching. Let them declare, in full, explicit statements subscribed in their own hand, that they embrace and approve in every respect all the synodal decrees which the authority of the apostolic see has confirmed for the destruction of this heresy. Let nothing obscure be found in their words, nothing ambiguous; for we know this to be their trick: in whatever small part of their detestable doctrine they distinguish themselves from the fellowship of the condemned, they consider that none of their opinions has been left unsaved. And while they pretend, for the sake of slipping away, to disapprove and reject all their definitions, they evade this by every art of deception unless they are understood, and so forth.

In 454, or perhaps the preceding year, Julianus died in an obscure town of Sicily, where, after traversing the world, he had settled like the fugitive Cain and, having been a bishop, had for some time taught children as a schoolmaster [Col. 0297D]. Concerning the place I have no other witness than Vignerius, who writes as follows in the frequently cited preface:

> He certainly lived until the time of blessed Fulgentius, who calls him another Cain, that is, a fugitive and an exile from every place. Finally, he died in an obscure Sicilian village among the Pelagians, having been a schoolmaster after serving as a bishop. When he died, they placed over his tomb an inscription that was still being read in the ninth century:
>
> **HERE RESTS IN PEACE JULIANUS, CATHOLIC BISHOP.**

Concerning the date, Gennadius says (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 45):

> This Julianus, by distributing alms to all his needy people in a time of famine and hardship, enticed many—especially noble and religious persons—into associating with his heresy under the appearance of compassion. He died while Valentinian, the son of Constantius, was emperor.

From this testimony it may be concluded that Julianus died not merely before 455, when Valentinian was killed, but around 453. I think Gennadius’s words must be interpreted as though he had written “while Valentinian was still reigning,” that is, a few years before he ceased to reign.

Vignerius accuses Gennadius of monstrous error if Julianus lived into the time of Saint Fulgentius. He promises that he will establish this by certain proofs drawn both from Fulgentius and from other writers, and that he will also affirm several other matters of this kind which are unknown to many.

The learned man understands by the name Fulgentius the books that that holy bishop wrote against Faustus, books that he had in a manuscript codex while he was alive. But the codex must have been corrupt. For Fulgentius was born in 464 (*Life of Saint Fulgentius*, chapter 1), undertook the governance of the Church of Ruspe in 504 (chapter 17), completed his books against Faustus shortly before the death of Thrasamund and his return from exile to Africa, which occurred in 522 (chapter 28), and died in 529 (chapter 30). He must therefore be said to have flourished midway between his birth and death, that is, around the year 480.

[Col. 0298B] Since these facts are certain, I ask: To what period of Fulgentius’s life is Julianus said to have survived? To the time of Fulgentius’s death, or even to the time when he was writing against Faustus? To the time of his maturity, or of his birth? If to the time of his death, Julianus would have prolonged his life to the age of 143, since that many years separate Julianus’s birth from Fulgentius’s death, Julianus having been born in 386 or even earlier and Fulgentius having died in 529.

If to the time when Fulgentius was writing, Julianus would have lived to the age of 136. If to the time of Fulgentius’s maturity, Julianus would have died older than one hundred, as the calculation of the years shows. If to the time of Fulgentius’s birth, then Gennadius did not err monstrously, but at most by nine years. For Julianus may be said to have died one year before Valentinian, that is, in 455, while Fulgentius was born in 464. In this matter, however, greater credence should be given to Gennadius than to Fulgentius or to another writer of the same age, since Gennadius was nearer in time and was writing about matters that he would almost have had before his eyes.

[Col. 0298C] Julianus therefore seems to have lived at least sixty-eight years, to have disturbed the Church for thirty-eight years, and finally to have perished miserably—a restless and proud man, plainly, as the Lerinian says (*Commonitory*, chapter 40), “unworthy, while he lived, of being regarded by God among those united in faith and made equal in humility,” a fate than which none more bitter can be imagined. Accordingly, after setting forth the Apostle’s statement, “If anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14:38), he says this concerning a teacher of spiritual matters who prefers his own opinions to those of everyone else and withdraws from the judgment of all:

> We see that this happened, in accordance with the apostolic threat, to that Pelagian Julianus, who either neglected to incorporate himself into the judgment of his colleagues or presumed to remove himself from it.

We have already spoken of Julianus’s writings.

## CHAPTER VII. On Annianus, Deacon of Celeda

Thus far, among the defenders of the Pelagian heresy, we have listed a certain Annianus. We mentioned him both in the preface and in the encomium of Pelagius. Jerome preceded us (Letter 20, among Augustine’s letters) when he replied to Alypius and Augustine. He wrote:

> You ask whether I have replied against the books of Annianus, the pseudo-deacon of Celeda, who feeds most abundantly in order to furnish frivolous words to another’s blasphemy. You should know that I received the books themselves, sent in sheets by our holy brother the presbyter Eusebius, not long ago; and thereafter, either because illnesses were pressing upon me or because of the death of your holy and venerable daughter Eustochium, I grieved so deeply that I almost considered them unworthy of attention. For he remains stuck in the same mud and, apart from tinkling and beggarly words, says nothing else. Nevertheless, we have taken great pains that, while he tries to answer my letter, he might expose himself more openly and make his blasphemies known to everyone. Whatever he denies having said in that miserable synod of Diospolis, he professes in this work, and it is no great task to answer the most foolish drivel. But if the Lord grants me life and we obtain a sufficient number of copyists, we shall reply in a few little essays—not to convict a dead heresy, but to refute his ignorance and blasphemy by our own arguments. And your Holiness would do this better, lest I be compelled to praise my own work against a heretic.

We have quoted Jerome’s words as they are commonly read in printed editions, although they ought to be corrected, as will be seen later. They have given rise to a question in which learned men have perhaps engaged more diligently than successfully: Who, precisely, was the man under discussion? Was he the translator of the fifteen homilies of Chrysostom, whom Sigebert confused with Annianus the illustrious man (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 70)? Was he Pelagius himself, who had assumed a false name, as seemed to Jansenius of Ypres? Was he a certain Valerianus, who tried to draw Cyril over to the Pelagian side, as Baronius thinks? Or was he Julianus himself, as has occurred to more than one person?

Before these and related questions are resolved, we must take account of the characteristics by which Jerome identifies the man about whom he writes. He calls him Annianus [Col. 0299B] and says that he was a deacon of Celeda. He also says that he was being fed very abundantly so that he might furnish frivolous words to another’s blasphemy; that he wrote in tinkling and beggarly language on behalf of the Pelagian party; and that he did so after the heresy had died and been strangled, at the time when Jerome himself and Augustine were still alive. We must see to whom these seven features ultimately correspond.

### § I. On the translator of Chrysostom’s fifteen homilies, what kind of man he was, and so forth

There are many homilies of Chrysostom that were formerly rendered into Latin. Fifteen are now under consideration: namely, the first eight on Matthew, prefixed by a letter from Annianus to Bishop Orontius, in which he testifies that he translated these very homilies into Latin; and seven on the praises of Paul, likewise prefixed by a letter from Annianus to the presbyter Evangelus, to whom he sends the work translated by him.

The translator of both the eight and the seven homilies [Col. 0299C] is one and the same person. Apart from the fact that scholars acknowledge this, it is clearly demonstrated by the same name being placed at the head of both works, the same style in both, the same opinions, the same zeal on behalf of the Pelagians, and the same hatred toward Augustine, whom he calls by the name of “Traducian” and “Manichaean,” a designation circulated among the Pelagians.

As for the name Annianus, the eyes report it; as for the style, anyone with literary taste can judge it. The conformity of the opinions is shown by this one example. The man who writes to Orontius, speaking of Chrysostom, says:

> “Thus throughout he agrees with our opinions, so that he may be believed to have instructed even those whom he never saw at all in the complete understanding of the Scriptures.”

But the writer of the letter to Evangelus says:

> “So that he may appear not so much to have instructed his present disciples as to have prepared for us aids against the assault upon the true faith.”

How great is his opposition to necessity! How vigorously he rises in defense of free choice! How everywhere he sings in harmony with our books!

[Col. 0299D] Both letters accuse the translator of the two groups of homilies of zeal for the Pelagians—and the first letter accuses him of especially ardent zeal. The first is addressed to Orontius, one of the bishops expelled from Italy because of the Pelagian heresy; the second to Evangelus, a presbyter of the same faction. In the first, the writer declares that he is suffering temptation together with the bishop for the sake of the faith; in the second, the author says that he receives consolation from the presbyter because he sees that, through a learned and distinguished teacher of the East, the truth which the Traducian attacks in his own writings is being asserted.

Moreover, both letters are filled not only with insults against the Catholics, and especially against Augustine, but also with the opinions and techniques of the Pelagians: namely, with praise of human nature and of free choice, with an exaggerated assertion of the possibility of fulfilling God’s commandments, and so forth.

Add to this that in the letter to Evangelus, after the subject of each of Chrysostom’s homilies on the praises of Paul has been set out, we read:

> “In these homilies he presented that holy teacher, the Chosen Vessel, in various ways as a mirror of every virtue, resolving all those questions by which the Traducian, while claiming the blessed Paul, stains him by darkening him with vices, so that he might, by the apostolic example, commend sins to his own faithful.”

He is evidently alluding to the slanderous charge which the Pelagians habitually brought against the Catholics, and especially against Augustine—as though they said that the Apostle Paul, or all the apostles, had always been polluted by uncontrolled lust (Book I to Boniface, chapter 8).

Furthermore, that translator was neither a bishop nor a presbyter. For he calls Orontius “father,” and Evangelus “holy presbyter”; if he himself had been a bishop, he would surely have called the former “fellow bishop,” and if he had been a presbyter, the latter “fellow presbyter.” He would have called both “brother” if he had occupied the same rank as either, as was customary in those times.

He wrote during the lifetime of Augustine, when Orontius also lived and when the Pelagian heresy—Augustine and his associates pressing the matter vigorously—was being attacked with increasing force, indeed being strangled and already dying. Thus he addresses Orontius (in the preface to the homilies of Chrysostom on Matthew):

> “Amid the storms of temptation which we endure together for our love of the faith, you draw me away both from grief and from lethargy, and restore to literary study my spirit, which was wasting away through anxiety.”

A little later he adds:

> “Especially at this time, when, under the pretext of certain excessively difficult questions, there is an unusually insolent obstruction to the building up of morals and ecclesiastical discipline, blessed John rises everywhere with such force and eagerness—both in his other works and in this one also—that, by interpreting the Evangelist’s words, he seems to be fighting with us for evangelical perfection. For what does he impress upon people more than the nobility of their nature, which is praised by the unanimous agreement and assembly of all right-thinking men against the madness of Manichaeus? It is praised either to glorify the admirable Creator, or to arouse zeal for virtue, or to chastise the vices of pleasure, and so forth.”

[Col. 0300C] From this Sigebert is plainly refuted, for he confused with the translator of the homilies on Matthew the distinguished man by whom the Theodosian Code was either abridged or the abridgment made by another was revised and approved at the command of Alaric. Sigebert says:

> “Annianus, a distinguished man, at the command of King Athalaric”—he should have said Alaric—“published one volume of the laws of the Emperor Theodosius, and, at the urging of Bishop Orontius, translated the book of John Chrysostom on Matthew from Greek into Latin.”

He is almost an entire century out of date. The translator of the homilies wrote while Augustine was alive, that is, before the year 430, in which Augustine died. The distinguished man who worked on the Theodosian Code performed that service in the twenty-second year of Alaric, which was A.D. 506.

## § II. On the translator of Chrysostom’s homily to the newly baptized

Besides those fifteen homilies mentioned above, there is another addressed to the newly baptized, concerning which Julian disputed with Augustine (Book I against Augustine). Julian also used this testimony when, in writing to Pope Zosimus in the name of eighteen bishops, he seemed to remove original sin. The Greek text no longer survives. It was once seen by Augustine, who reports two fragments, especially this one (Book I against Julian, chapter 6):

> διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τὰ παιδία βαπτίζομεν καί τοι ἁμαρτήματα οὐκ ἔχοντα

“For this reason also we baptize infants, although they do not have sins.”

From these words Augustine accused Julian, or rather the translator, of fraud, because he had translated them:

> “For this reason also we baptize infants, although they have not been defiled by sin,”

as though he had wished to imply that Chrysostom denied, contrary to the faith of the Church, original sin.

But let us hear Augustine (in the same place):

> “Comparing them—infants—with adults, whose personal sins are forgiven in baptism, John said that they ‘do not have sins,’ not, as you yourself rendered his words, that they ‘are not defiled by sin,’ while you plainly wished it to be understood that they are not defiled by the sin of the first man.”

[Col. 0301A] “Yet I will not attribute this to you, but to the translator, although in other manuscripts containing the same translation one reads not ‘by sin’ but ‘by sins.’ Hence I wonder whether someone from your number did not prefer to write the singular number, so that it might be understood as the one sin of which the Apostle says: ‘Judgment indeed was from one offense unto condemnation, but grace from many offenses unto justification’ (Romans 5:16). There, by ‘one,’ he wants only one offense to be understood. Since you are unwilling to believe that infants are defiled, you say that they do not have sins—not ‘sin.’ What John said was intended to prevent people from understanding personal sins. Or, since the same translation reads ‘sins’ in other manuscripts, you preferred to say that they were not defiled by ‘sin,’ so that the one sin of the first man might come to mind. But let us not act on suspicions. Let this be regarded either as a copyist’s error or as a variation in the translator. I shall set down the very Greek words which John spoke: διὰ τοῦτο, and so forth.”

From Augustine’s words I conclude, first, that as early as the period when Augustine was writing—he was writing in the year 421—there were already different readings of this translation in different manuscripts. Nevertheless, in the book of the Faith which Julian published, the wording is exactly as Augustine charged. Second, this translator belonged to the number of the Pelagians. Third, he himself wrote before the disputes between Augustine and Julian began. Those disputes began in A.D. 418, when Julian first composed four books against Augustine’s earlier work On Marriage and Concupiscence. Finally, the translator of this homily is none other than Annianus, who translated the others: the style is the same, the Latin is the same, both works are the labor of a Pelagian, the period is the same, and nearly all the other circumstances are the same.

Therefore I conclude—and in my judgment neither rashly nor obscurely—that the translator of the homily under discussion is none other than that Annianus who wrote the two letters: one to Bishop Orontius, prefixed, as stated above, to the eight earlier homilies of Chrysostom on Matthew; the other to the presbyter Evangelus, [Col. 0301C] which serves as the preface to the seven homilies of the same Chrysostom on the praises of the Apostle Paul.

## III. That the deacon Annianus is not different from the translator of the homilies

It must now be demonstrated—this being the principal reason for undertaking the inquiry—that Annianus, whom Jerome mentions, is not a different person from the translator of the homilies, but one and the same. The matter is easily established. The name is the same, Annianus; the ecclesiastical rank is the same, below that of a presbyter; the disposition is the same, inclined toward the Pelagians and hostile to the defenders of the faith; the period is the same, during Augustine’s lifetime; the reason for writing is the same, to serve the Pelagians; and the time of writing is the same, after the heresy had been strangled and was dying, when the heretics bitterly hated those whom they thought had deprived them of the freedom to teach their error and whom, since they could not kill by the sword, they sought to destroy by wishing them dead, as Jerome says (Letter 20 among the Augustinian letters).

This also dispels the conjecture of Jansenius of Ypres (Book I On the Pelagian Heresy), which I know has pleased certain others: namely, that Annianus, whom Jerome and Augustine mention, was none other than Pelagius using a false name. For, to pass over other considerations for the moment, Pelagius, if we believe Augustine in his book On the Proceedings at Palestine and Orosius in his Apology, knew so little Greek that at Diospolis he was forced to answer Greek-speaking men through an interpreter; whereas Annianus knew Greek very well, as his translations demonstrate.

An objection may be raised from the statement of Jerome which led Jansenius of Ypres to his conjecture. In the place cited shortly before, Jerome says:

> “We acted so that, while attempting to answer my letter, he might reveal himself more openly and disclose his blasphemies to everyone; for whatever he denies having said at that wretched synod of Diospolis, he professes in this work.”

It therefore seems to follow [Col. 0302A] that the pseudo-deacon of Celeda is the very man who denied at Diospolis what he later professed in the work composed against Jerome—that is, in Jansenius’s conjecture, in the four books On Free Choice.

But the objection has its solution in Jerome’s preceding words. First, Jerome says that the pseudo-deacon was abundantly fed so that he might supply the words of another’s blasphemy. Whose was that other man’s blasphemy, if not Pelagius’? Second, the books which Annianus composed against Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon were sent by the presbyter Eusebius to Jerome in the East in A.D. 419, the year in which the holy virgin Eustochium passed happily to God. At that time Eusebius was in the West and Pelagius in the East. How, then, could Jerome, who was in the East where Pelagius’s books On Free Choice had been published, have needed to receive them from the West?

Furthermore, the four books On Free Choice were not a small work; yet the books which Jerome received in separate sheets must not have been large. Again, Augustine replied to the four books On Free Choice at the end of A.D. 418. But in A.D. 419 no answer had yet been made to Annianus’s books, and Alypius and Augustine were asking whether they ought to reply at all.

Moreover, it was impossible to answer Annianus’s books without heaping praise upon Jerome. Augustine was silent about Jerome in his book On the Grace of Christ; he would certainly not have been silent if an opportunity had arisen, as it did in his book On Nature and Grace—not only because Jerome was personally his friend, but also because of Albina, Pinianus, and Melania, to whom he was writing and who, through the common bond of their relationship, embraced both defenders of the faith.

Finally, Annianus’s books became known to Alypius and Augustine in Africa before they became known to Jerome in the East. Jerome did not receive them until shortly before Eustochium’s death, which occurred on September 28, A.D. 419. But Alypius and Augustine had already written to Jerome about them through the presbyter Innocentius, who is said to have been sent by the African synod to Cyril to seek the Nicene canons and who consequently departed from Africa toward the end of May A.D. 419 (Augustine, On the Grace of Christ). Those books, therefore, were not written by Pelagius, since Pelagius was in the East in A.D. 418 and had published his books On Free Choice even earlier.

How, then, is the difficulty contained in Jerome’s statement to be resolved? I suspect that one word is missing from the commonly printed editions of the letter in question and that the whole passage should be corrected as follows:

> “He remains stuck in the same mud and, apart from his tinkling and beggarly words, says nothing else. Yet we acted vigorously so that, while attempting to answer my letter, he might reveal himself more openly and disclose his blasphemies to everyone. For whatever Pelagius denies having said at that wretched synod of Diospolis, this man professes in the present work.”

Thus everything fits together easily; otherwise the details are ἀσύστατα, “incoherent,” and plainly contradictory to the truth. Nor is there any lack of a basis for the emendation. Jerome seems to compare Annianus with Pelagius and to accuse Annianus of remaining stuck in the same mud as Pelagius and of saying nothing else, but only saying the same things more eloquently and elaborately.

This also refutes the opinion of certain people who thought that Annianus was none other than Valerianus, who crossed from Italy to Alexandria in order, if possible, to introduce the Pelagian heresy into that most distinguished Church. By insinuating himself into Cyril’s friendship, he attempted in Egypt what Caelestius had attempted in Africa and Sicily, Pelagius in Rome and Jerusalem, and Julian in Constantinople and Thessalonica. The Pelagians, indeed, tried by deception either to incline or to draw every important see into their faction.

Yet although this conjecture receives considerable support from the letter in which Eusebius, apparently Bishop of Cremona, warns Cyril to beware of Valerianus—and, as Baronius believes (Annals, under A.D. 417, no. 15), had previously informed Jerome that Annianus the deacon had written the response to his letter to Ctesiphon—I can scarcely be persuaded to believe that the servant of Count Valerius, whom Eusebius portrays as a ventriloquist, devoted to his belly, and infamous for other vices, was numbered by the ancients among ecclesiastical writers.

Nevertheless, a person may perhaps not be far from the truth if he understands the Valerianus mentioned by Bishop Eusebius to have insinuated into Count Valerius’s mind the Pelagian calumnies against the defenders of original sin and to have prepared excerpts from Julian’s four books against Augustine which were not particularly faithful.

I say “Valerianus,” the man mentioned by Bishop Eusebius. For the other Eusebius, from whom Jerome received the books of Annianus the deacon, was certainly not a bishop but only a presbyter. Jerome himself writes that he received those books from “the holy brother Eusebius the presbyter” (Letter 201 among the Augustinian letters).

A further, and not insignificant, suspicion is likewise refuted: someone might have thought that Annianus the deacon of Celeda was none other than Julian, who himself supplied his Latin to Pelagius and, if we believe Mercator, was hired by the Pelagians to defend their faction. Why should he not have used a false name and written in the West, so that Eusebius might send his work to the East and so that it might reach Augustine in nearby Sicily before reaching Jerome, who was settled at Bethlehem? Julian was certainly no mean scholar of Greek, since Gennadius calls him learned in both Greek and Latin (Book On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 45).

Yet it is not credible that Julian either hired himself out to the Pelagians, since he was wealthy in his own right, or translated the homily to the newly baptized, since that translation already possessed authority before the controversies arose; or that he wrote other books on behalf of his heresy which neither he himself, nor Mercator, nor Gennadius mentions; or that he published anything in Sicily which Augustine, because of its proximity, would not have known thoroughly; or, finally, that he wished to use the name of the deacon of Celeda, which would have involved him in conflict with Jerome, who considered it a matter of glory to attack openly and scornfully the most distinguished teachers of the Catholic Church.

## § IV. Other matters concerning Annianus the deacon of Celeda

Having established these points concerning the person of Annianus, we must next inquire into Celeda—whether it was his homeland, from which he originated, or the Church in which he ministered. Annianus was certainly of Latin nationality, as he himself testifies in his letter to Evangelus:

> “You ordered me to translate into our language certain passages from the works of the blessed John,” and so forth.

Since, then, he was a Latin and a friend of Julian of Apulia, Caelestius of Campania, and other Pelagians from that region or its vicinity, what prevents us from supposing that he too was a Campanian, from the town of Celenna or Celena? An error could easily have entered Jerome’s text, especially in the case of a name that was not very well known. Certainly Ortelius admits that, apart from Jerome, he knows no one who uses the name Celedensis. We have also seen more than once in manuscripts (in the geographical Thesaurus) that the letter N is formed in such a way that it could readily be changed into D by a reader lacking close attention. But since Celena is said to have had no Church, Annianus must have been called Celenensis from the place not where he ministered but where he was born.

Although this conjecture has no little appearance of truth, I am not inclined to accept it readily. Jerome’s letter to Mark, a presbyter of Celeda, holds me back; for I can scarcely believe that an error has entered this passage as well. If no error has entered it, we must admit that there was a Church of Celeda. For, as I think, it is difficult to find among the ancients any example of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon receiving his designation from anywhere other than the Church to which he was attached.

It is uncertain whether he was the deacon of Bishop Orontius and a minister of the same Church as the presbyter Evangelus. This cannot be determined from the testimony of either letter. Indeed, there may perhaps be some presumption in favor of the negative view. If he had served in Orontius’s Church, or in the same Church as Evangelus, then, among the reasons he gives for obeying the commands of Orontius and Evangelus, he would surely not have omitted one that is obvious to everyone: namely, that it is right for a deacon to obey both his bishop and his presbyter.

I have almost no doubt that he is the very man whom Paul Orosius calls Pelagius’s armor-bearer (Apology, chapter 2):

> “The most monstrous Goliath still stands, swollen with pride and puffed up by carnal power, confident that he can do everything by himself—his head, hands, and entire body equipped with an elaborate array—and behind him he has his armor-bearer, who, although he himself does not fight, nevertheless supplies every support of bronze and iron.”

Nor do I doubt that he is one of those writers of dictation of whom Orosius speaks. After reproaching Pelagius for the shameless statement contained in his letter to Demetrias, Orosius continues:

> “Although we ought not to attribute to you what is expressed neither appropriately nor decorously—for neither your birth gave you the opportunity to be educated in more honorable studies, nor did you naturally acquire the ability to understand—it should instead be attributed to those writers of dictation of yours who set down a wretched thought in the most wretched language and expose you to be read amid laughter, as though you were a title of disgrace” (same work, chapter 25).

Accordingly, someone might reasonably conjecture that the eloquent letter was written with Pelagius’s ideas but in Annianus’s words.

Indeed, I do not doubt that he was that malicious interpreter who, both at the assembly of presbyters before John and at Diospolis before the Fathers, expounded in Greek Pelagius’s answers, which Pelagius gave in Latin, though not with sufficient fidelity. Orosius complains about this in the case of the assembly, and Augustine in the case of the Council of Diospolis.

Orosius, however, creates a difficulty when he accuses the interpreter of ignorance of one or the other language, a charge which no one could rightly bring against Annianus. He says (same work, chapter 3):

> “Because of the incompetence of an interpreter unknown to us, whom the distinguished and religious men, the presbyters Posserius and Avitus and Domninus the former magistrate, very often refuted when he was either interpreting perversely, suppressing a great deal, or suggesting one thing in place of another.”

But what is charged against the interpreter is less ignorance than dishonesty. Therefore I interpret the ignorance attributed by Orosius as the malicious cunning of a man wishing to deceive: he pretended not to have sufficiently understood what he was attempting to distort, thus securing an affected excuse if he were challenged.

What he wrote, whether on his own initiative or while translating another’s work, can to a large extent be established from what has been said. It is nevertheless worthwhile to display the individual works in summary, collecting what remains of them at the end together with the works of the other Pelagians.

**Homily to the newly baptized.** Volume V of the works of Chrysostom in the Latin edition, and volume II of the Greek-Latin edition.

**Letter or book to the virgin Demetrias.** It is found scattered everywhere and was formerly Letter 142 among the Augustinian letters. But every somewhat more learned age has recognized that it is neither Augustine’s nor Jerome’s, although it is found in the appendix to volume II of Jerome’s works.

**Books against Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon.** Nothing survives of them except the memory preserved by Jerome, Letter 24 among the Augustinian letters and Letter 98 among the Hieronymian letters. The letter of Alypius and Augustine to Jerome, in which they were mentioned, has also perished.

**Letter to the presbyter Evangelus**, prefixed to the seven homilies of Chrysostom on the praises of Paul. Volume V of the Greek-Latin edition, volume III of the Latin edition, and volume VI in Bede.

**Letter to Bishop Orontius**, prefixed to the eight earlier homilies on Matthew. Volume I of the Commelinian edition and volume II of the Latin edition.

It should be observed that among the homilies of Chrysostom whose ancient translator is said to be unknown, there are many—if not nearly all—which may be attributed to Annianus without rashness, for two principal reasons. First, they appear to have been rendered into Latin in a style similar to that of the works whose translator is certainly known to have been Annianus. Second, they are concerned almost entirely with subjects which, although treated by Catholics in a sound sense, were habitually twisted by the Pelagians in support of their heresy.

# CHAPTER VIII. On the author of the book of Questions on the New and Old Testament

In the fourth volume of Augustine’s works there is a book On Questions of the Old and New Testament which is commonly believed—and is certainly said by Jansenius of Ypres (repeatedly in his book On the Pelagian Heresy)—to be full of Pelagian errors. Hence it is of the greatest importance for the matter under discussion, indeed it is necessary, to investigate carefully whether this is really so. For if that widespread belief is not without probability, it must be said that the heresy which later took its name from Pelagius was already flourishing at Rome around the year 373, and that it had a different parent from Theodore of Mopsuestia. Mercator would therefore have written falsely (in the preface to his book of Notes) that this doctrine hostile to the true faith was first introduced into Rome by a certain Syrian named Rufinus in the time of Anastasius. For the author of the Questions writes that he had published his work in the city long before those times.

Some attribute the entire work to Hilary the deacon, to whom the Commentaries on the Pauline Epistles falsely attributed to Ambrose are also said to belong. Both works appear to have been written at the same time, in the same style and with similar doctrine. Indeed, if any credence were to be given to the Louvain scholars, Bellarmine, and Jansenius of Ypres, the same Pelagian errors would be scattered throughout both works.

For my part, I do not deny that the Questions and the Commentaries are disfigured by certain errors, but I can scarcely agree that they are infected with Pelagianism. The arguments usually brought forward to prove this are either understood in a sense foreign to the passage, or are ambiguous in themselves, or at least do not depart far from the opinion of the Fathers, including those whom Augustine praises as teachers of the Catholic faith. The arguments which refute this charge of error, however, are so open and so clear that almost the testimony of the eyes alone is sufficient to absolve the author of both works. It is therefore worthwhile to examine more carefully both this book of Questions and the aforementioned Commentaries—first the Questions, then the Commentaries.

As it was published by the Louvain scholars in the appendix to the fourth volume of Augustine’s works, the volume of Questions consists of four parts. The first contains forty-seven questions from the Old Testament; the second, fifty from the New Testament; the third, thirty drawn indiscriminately from both; and the fourth, sixty-five likewise from both.

[Col. 0305D] The first three parts may be regarded as forming a single complete work. The fourth contains nothing except an interpolated repetition of the first and second parts. It was not included in the edition of Saint Augustine’s works prepared at Basel by Erasmus. Many years later it was added by Jacob Haemerus from what he calls a very ancient manuscript of the Victorine Library in Paris. Indeed, it appears to have been written by a man who had more leisure than either learning or judgment and who, after reading another work, perhaps wished to test what he himself could add. He added a great deal, certainly, but neither anything good nor anything expressed in good language. This entire part should therefore rightly be omitted as material of either no value or very little value. I am surprised that the Louvain scholars did not notice this.

The principal questions concerning the earlier work are therefore three. First, whether the whole work, whoever its author may finally prove to be, is so filled with Pelagius’s errors that its author ought for that reason to be called a complete Pelagian and the most faithful interpreter of the Pelagians—so much so that he surpassed Pelagius himself in presenting the integrity of Pelagianism and explained Pelagian mysteries more accurately than anyone else. Second, whether the work called by the single name Questions is really one work. Finally, who its author was, when he wrote it, and where.

## § I. Whether the volume of Questions on the Old and New Testament is polluted by the errors of the Pelagians

There are people who assert this, and they are neither few nor obscure: the Louvain scholars, Bellarmine, Jansenius of Ypres, and other censors of books. Erasmus, however, in his judgment, although he brought many charges against the author of this work in order to detract from whatever authority he had hitherto possessed, said nothing at all about Pelagianism. He certainly would have said so if he had thought he saw anything of the kind. For what stronger argument could he have used to establish the point he was chiefly asserting—that the book of Questions was not composed by Augustine, the conqueror of Pelagius and the Pelagian heresy?

[Col. 0306B] In this matter I agree with Erasmus, both because the author of the Questions openly overturns all the foundations of the Pelagian heresy, and because the arguments brought against him are partly ambiguous, partly assumed without proof, partly not presented with sufficient accuracy or fidelity, and in every case consist of things commonly said by the Fathers at that time.

The Pelagian heresy, as it was set out by the ancients and condemned by Pope Zosimus, consisted of five doctrines: that Adam would have died even if he had not sinned; that by his sin he harmed only himself and not his descendants; that a human being could, through free choice—as though he were self-sufficient—fulfill whatever he wished, or even that God grants grace to each person on account of the merits of works; that sexual desire is a natural good; and that infants do not inherit original sin.

Against these five points, however, the author of the Questions thinks as any wholly sound Catholic would have thought, at least in his own age or a neighboring one—for example, Chrysostom, Jerome, and others.

[Col. 0306C] Against the first point, concerning Adam’s mortality:

**QUESTION VI.** It was said to Adam and Eve: “On the day when you eat, you shall die”; and certainly they did not die immediately, but after a long interval of time. Yet because they had already lost the hope of immortality, the future death was called present, since it had already begun to be held in hope.

**QUESTION XIX.** God made the human being such that, so long as he did not sin, he would flourish in immortality, so that he himself would be the author either of life or of death for himself. By guarding himself from sin, he would rejoice that through his own labor he was immortal; but once he had become negligent, he would attribute to himself the fact that he had begun to be mortal.

**QUESTION XXXIV.** Life and death are from God in this sense: he gave a law which promises life to those who keep it, but death to those who despise it—the death called the second death. When he assigns to each person what he deserves, from him come either acquittal unto life or guilt unto death. He is therefore not the inventor of death but its judge, because sin is the author of death. How, then, could God make death, since he does not know how to sin? Yet when he repays sins, death is said to be from him, although it does not come from him but from the one who sinned.

**QUESTION CXVI.** The devil is the author of death, since he was found to have sinned in the death of the Savior and lost his blood along with all of us. For just as through one sinning Adam he held everyone in death, so through one who did not sin he lost everyone.

Against the second point, that Adam did not harm his descendants by his sin:

**QUESTION XLVII.** The prophet spoke in general terms in order to signify that we need God’s gift, so that both sinners and the righteous might be understood to await God’s mercy: sinners on account of their own offenses, so that they might be snatched from the jaws of death; but the righteous, having been absolved from their father’s sin, because the sentence pronounced in Adam, by which all were held, had been erased.

**QUESTION LXXXIII.** The devil triumphed over the human being; the defeated man subjected his race to sin.

**QUESTION CXII.** And he continues: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities.” By adding this, he recalls the cause of the weakness of the human race, because it is easy for a human being to sin, so that he may mitigate the judgment of the judge concerning himself. He mentions the first fault, through which Adam, by transgressing, made the human race liable to sin. By conceiving iniquity through the persuasion and deceit of the enemy, he subjected all his seed to iniquity, so that all who were born from him by transmission would be liable to sin. Therefore he added: “And in sins my mother conceived me,” so that the transmission of sin from Adam would impede those conceived and born from him from living a good life.

Against the third point—which was not a simple one but at least a twofold claim, concerning sinlessness and the assistance of grace—the author thought in such a way that he openly opposed the first part of the Pelagian error, while on the second he expressed his opinion with precision, almost with excessive care, in agreement with the Fathers of his age.

On sinlessness:

**QUESTION CIX.** Human nature, because it does not possess the perfection of divinity, advances through exercise and struggle, becoming better when it conquers more often than it is conquered. For if it acted in such a way—which is impossible—that it never sinned, it would become better than God. May that never be! A nature which can sin, just as it can refrain from sinning, would, if it always conquered, have to be preferred to that nature which does not sin because it is incapable of suffering.

**QUESTION CXII.** The heart can be pure if it sins neither within nor without—that is, neither in action nor in thought. But because it is almost impossible for this to be maintained in every respect, it must at least be maintained in the matter of God, which is the principal concern. Let the pure heart also be guarded in the sacrament of God and Christ, while the faith is kept inviolate; for it is said elsewhere: “Who can boast that he has a pure heart, or that he is free from sins?”

**QUESTION CXV.** No one can be found who always does what is good, and so forth.

There are two questions concerning divine grace: one concerning what is commonly called habitual grace, which is inherent righteousness and the pledge of adoption; the other concerning actual grace, by which we perform works of piety. Concerning the former, what could have been stated more precisely—even in the sense of the schools—if one sets aside the terminology?

**QUESTION CXXV.** This is the sign of believers, that they are sons of God: when they receive him—the Holy Spirit—they dare to call themselves sons of God. For unless they possess the sign of divinity, they cannot be called sons of God. Nevertheless, no one is a true Son of God in such a way as to be wholly from the Whole, as Christ is. Through adoption, however, they become sons of God, so that, receiving the Spirit of Christ, they are called sons of God through him, by virtue of what is from God—the Spirit whom they possess within themselves. For in sons, even though they are adopted, the substance of the father ought nevertheless to be seen in some degree. In the world, because created things are imperfect, human beings who are adopted as sons receive no pledge from their human adoptive parents, but only the name. God, however, because he is perfect, does more: he gives his Spirit to those who are adopted, through whom they appear to possess some reality of adoption by him, since names without realities are empty.

Concerning actual grace, Augustine teaches that it is given by the Holy Spirit to the humble and to those who do not presume upon themselves, on account of faith’s merit. This grace itself is also the gift of God, enabling the performance of every act of piety and the conquest of temptations; it grants even the ability to do divine things and is a certain heavenly light and spirit of righteousness. The author of the Questions teaches all these points with extraordinary clarity.

### QUESTION 123

If he had been made perfect, so that he needed nothing, he would not have been a man but God, nor would he have been deceived and transgressed. To possess the Holy Spirit, however, is beyond the nature and perfection of man, so that he may be able to do the things that belong to God. Here we have an explicit exposition of divine grace: its cause, namely, possessing the Holy Spirit; its necessity, namely, that one should need nothing; its supernatural character and gratuitousness, namely, that it is beyond human nature and perfection; and its efficacy, by which it grants the ability to do divine things, so that one may do what belongs to God.

Later, concerning the same gift of the Holy Spirit:

“This gift was also promised through the prophets, so that it might then be given when the mystery of God was to be revealed in triumph, death having been conquered, so that creation might know that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God.” Hence the Evangelist says: “The Spirit,” he says, “had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39). For this glorification consists in his being recognized, through his power, as what he testified about himself; because this glorification bestowed the gift that had been promised through the prophet Joel. For God says: “In the last days I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh,” and so forth (Joel 2:28). And the Apostle says, among other things: “But when the kindness and humanity of our Savior God appeared, not from works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (Titus 3:4–7). The Apostle confirmed what had been promised through the prophet Joel, because, after Jesus had been glorified, God fulfilled it by pouring out the Holy Spirit upon those who believe in Christ.

### QUESTION 111

Whoever has faith in God always seeks his help.

### QUESTION 112

For the Lord always wishes his servants to flee to his help. And later:

“Their hearts were illuminated by a flash from heaven, so that they might see God’s providence in Christ.” And later:

“Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts”: that is, to entreat mercy with a good disposition of mind. He does not ask only concerning past matters, but is also concerned about the future, so that the sinner, intent on hating sin so that he may not sin, may be helped by God through the spirit of righteousness, which he prays may be established in his inward parts; that is, so that a new spirit may be placed in him for this purpose, to guard him from sins, lest he be compelled to do what he knows he does not wish to do. He can possess a clean heart in this way: if he sins neither inwardly nor outwardly, that is, neither in deed nor in thought.

### QUESTION 115

For if the fear of God is in the mind, neither flesh nor blood, neither rulers nor powers, would prevail, because, by God’s support, they persecute them in such a way that, although they suffer, they are nevertheless not overcome. But if we were not in possession of our own power, how could the Lord say: “Ask, and it will be given to you”? For everyone who asks will receive (Matthew 7:7). If, then, whoever wishes to ask will receive, it is no longer true what is commonly said: “We do not have what we want, but what has been given.” For the will is stirred up by the Savior to ask and to receive what it has asked for.

They say that these things are matters of fate, so that whether one asks or does not ask, one nevertheless obtains by fate whatever is either bad or good. But the Lord, excluding this, says: “Daughter, your faith has made you well” (Matthew 9:22). It is no longer something produced by fate when faith receives a benefit. And again: “If you believe,” he says, “all things are possible for the one who believes” (Mark 9:22). He placed merit, certainly, in the will, because goodness belongs to faith, not to nature. Faith, however, is something added, which arouses the will to exercise itself; and because faith is not present in nature, the will—which is present in nature—places merit before God once it has received faith.

### QUESTION 119

When the Apostle prayed that temptations might cease from him, the Lord said to him (2 Corinthians 12:9): “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.” Then he continued: “When I am weak, then I am stronger”; and, he says, “I rejoice in my tribulations, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.” If necessity drives us to God’s help, how much more should security do so?

Why should I pursue the rest? Certainly, to have thought so openly about grace in those times was neither the mark of an unlearned man nor of one preparing the way for Pelagianism.

Moreover, in opposition to the fourth Pelagian doctrine—that lust is a natural good—which of the Fathers, greater than Augustine, thought more clearly?

### QUESTION 112

Therefore he added (Psalm 50:7): “And my mother conceived me in sins,” so that the transmission of sin from Adam might be an impediment to those conceived and born in living a good life, and consequently that mercy should not be denied to one who supplicates, because he has an enemy hostile to him, who persuades him to sin. For through sin, after the first man had been subjected to him, the devil received power to mingle himself with his flesh and to suggest pleasures through a certain subtlety of sins, by which he strips the captured man of life. Recalling this, the teacher of the nations says: “But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind.”

Finally, against the fifth doctrine, which concerns original sin, besides the points already brought forward against the second doctrine:

### QUESTION 112

So that those who hope in the promised salvation may be freed from every sin, they will be freed through Christ not only from their own sins but also from Adam’s sin, which has reached everyone through transmission.

### QUESTION 127

Rebirth does not accuse birth but reforms it; and what is reformed is shown to have been well established from the beginning. Therefore, by being reborn, we are changed according to a plan, having received the cleansing of the body, so that we may be restored to Adam’s original state. The body was stained by the sin of the soul; when it has been restored and improved through the plan of faith, we are washed, so that, just as it had been polluted through contempt of God, so it may be cleansed through obedience, escape the sentence pronounced upon Adam, and be able to rise again. Therefore, if sin began with the soul, why is the body not accused, since in the cause of Adam’s sin there was not bodily desire, but the soul, enticed by hope of divinity, transgressed God’s command, so that its body might be subjected to sin, **and human beings might be born under sin**?

Can these be the words of a man who, in transmitting Pelagianism in its pure form, often surpasses even Pelagius? Of one whose work teems with Pelagian doctrines from beginning to end? Of one who has explained the Pelagian mysteries more accurately than anyone else? Of one whose doctrine concerning original sin is sheer Pelagianism, and the basis and foundation of that entire heresy?

We must next consider what the accusers bring against the author of the Questions—provided that we first observe that throughout almost the whole work, whenever the opportunity arises, this author attacks people of three kinds: the Manichaeans, who deliriously maintain that human nature itself is evil; the Mathematicians, who subject human wills to fatal necessity; and those who equate the Law with the Gospel and assert equal dignity for both—something the Pelagians later asserted. Had the critics with whom we are dealing considered these three matters a little more carefully, they would certainly have refrained from accusing a man whom they ought to have judged, among the defenders of the Catholic faith, precisely in the matter for which they accuse him.

## § II. The objections of the Louvain theologians, Bellarmine, and Jansenius against the author of the Questions concerning original sin

Those whom I have named bring two objections against the author of the Questions concerning original sin: one from Question 13, the other from Question 80. In both cases they make him guilty of denying original sin. Bellarmine alone makes the first accusation:

“So that the excessively impious crime of the Sodomites might be recognized, their sin reached even to the death of their own children, lest any trace of their origin should remain. Was provision not made for them, lest, if they lived long, they should follow the examples of their fathers? For they are free from Gehenna, having been killed in another’s cause.”

The three accuse him together on the second point:

“Neither are those who are born sons of God, nor sons of the devil.”

From these testimonies they derive their argument for accusing him. For they say that no Catholic says that infants who perish before attaining the use of reason, without any sacrament of faith, are free from Gehenna; and likewise that no one denies that we are born children of wrath—and, as they themselves think, therefore children of the devil.

But I plainly see no reason why the author can be accused from these passages of denying original sin. As for the first, he speaks generally of infants, all those who had not yet attained the use of reason when they were destroyed in the conflagration together with their fathers. Many of these, if not all or nearly all, had been cleansed from original sin by the sacrament of the most ancient Law, since the inhabitants of the Pentapolis, however unspeakably they lived, nevertheless worshiped the true God.

Moreover, even if he is speaking of infants still bound by such sin, he certainly does not mention every kind of Gehenna—that is, every kind of punishment—but only that punishment which was owed for the detestable crimes of their parents. The infants plainly do not suffer that punishment, but another exceedingly mild one, which, although eternal, is not the punishment inflicted on account of their parents’ sins, but on account of the guilt of the first man, which the author plainly teaches was transmitted to his descendants. For what else do these words mean?

“He mentions the first guilt, from which Adam, by transgressing, made the human race liable to sin.”

And these:

“The righteous, absolved from their ancestral sin, with the sentence pronounced upon Adam erased, by which all were held,” and so forth.

As for the second point, I scarcely think the accusers read attentively the passage from which they took their testimony. For the entire passage is directed against the Manichaeans. Since they considered human nature evil, and therefore believed it to have arisen from an evil principle, they consequently said that we are born children of the devil. Thus, when the author denies precisely what the Manichaeans affirmed—namely, that human beings are born children of the devil—he does not depart from the Catholic faith. For he explains whom he calls a child of the devil (Question 13):

“He who is born and is imbued with evil habits, so that he pursues those things which are hostile to the Creator, asserting many gods and that sacrifices should be offered to them, as though they were the rulers of the world.”

Therefore, he does not attack the Catholic doctrine that we are by nature children of wrath (Ephesians 2:3), but only the Manichaean doctrine that human nature is so evil that it cannot even receive virtue.

Indeed, no Father, so far as I remember, said that Adam’s descendants, through original sin, become children of the devil. They called them only captives, slaves, liable, placed under his power, and by other such terms—expressions signifying necessity rather than will. Following this view, the author of the Questions was nevertheless more subtle than the others in this respect: distinguishing the meanings of “son” and “slave,” he denied that Adam’s descendants are born children of the devil, while openly confessing that they are born slaves.

In this way he avoided both impieties: that of Manichaeus, who says that nature is evil, and that of Pelagius, who denies that there is any sin of origin. By taking the middle path, he adhered to the Catholic faith.

I am surprised that Bellarmine did not consider the basis of this more subtle distinction. For no one is called another’s son except one who has either been begotten by him or voluntarily adopted by him. Every sonship is either natural, which comes about by necessity, or adoptive, which comes about by will. That human beings are begotten by the devil is a Manichaean blasphemy; that they are adopted by him is manifest insanity.

The devil is indeed called the father of the impious, but in the sense in which Abraham is called the father of believers: through voluntary imitation. Thus Augustine says (Letter 89): “He is called the father of the impious, just as our father Abraham is called our father, because of imitation of faith, not because of the origin of the flesh. For this is why it was said of the devil himself: ‘Those who belong to his portion imitate him’” (Wisdom 2:25).

## § III. The objections of the Louvain theologians and Jansenius of Ypres concerning the help of divine grace

The Louvain theologians have gathered many charges into almost a single word. They say that, toward the end of Question 115, the author “Pelagianizes in the manner of Julian,” as can be seen in Bede, chapter 6 on the Song of Songs. At that place Bede, believing the letter on the education of the virgin addressed to Demetrias to have been written by Julian, extracted from it twelve points to bring against Julian.

In my judgment, however, the shorter and more general an accusation is, the less equitable and the more suspect it becomes. The author of the Questions does indeed acknowledge that the human will is free. But, apart from the fact that everyone must acknowledge this, in opposition to the fate of the Mathematicians—which he attacks in that Question—he says that the will, with God’s assistance, conquers even the powers of the air.

He likewise acknowledges that we are in possession of our own power and can have what we wish; but at the same time he teaches that this will is stirred up by the Savior to ask and receive what it has asked for.

He also acknowledges that we are saved by the merit of faith, and that faith receives the benefit it has sought. But he warns that faith is received as a gift bestowed from elsewhere—that is, descending from the Father of lights.

Finally, he acknowledges that the human being possesses in his nature the seed of faith, but asserts that this is nothing other than the fact that creation understands, and almost sees, the Creator from the things that have been made.

Since the discussion has turned to the seed of faith, we must answer Jansenius of Ypres on behalf of the author of the Questions, since Jansenius raises a dispute concerning the seeds of virtues and the law naturally implanted in us. For what will he do with Basil’s teaching (in the Rules, and elsewhere): “We bear within us the virtues of all the commandments that we have received from God”? What will he do with Chrysostom, who writes the following (on chapter 2 of the Epistle to the Ephesians): “You see that by nature we possess the seeds of virtue, and that each one of us has within his nature an implanted knowledge of virtue”? What will he do with Jerome, who asserts (on chapter 2 of Galatians) that no one lacks within himself the seeds of wisdom, righteousness, and the other virtues?

What will he do with Augustine, who devoutly confesses before God (Confessions 2.4) that the law of God is written in human hearts, which not even iniquity itself can erase? What will he do with that same Augustine when he denies (On the Spirit and the Letter) that the image of God in the human soul has been so worn away by the stain of earthly desires that no final traces, as it were, have remained in it?

Someone might say: when these statements are written by the holy Fathers, they present a plausible opinion to kindly readers because of the preconceived authority of the writers. Let it be so. But why does the authority of the Fathers have a presumption in its favor on this point? Because, I suppose, elsewhere they expressed their view of divine grace in clear and Catholic language.

But the author of the Questions also expressed his view of divine grace, like the Fathers, in clear and Catholic language, as has been shown. Why, then, is their authority presumed, but not his? Why is there not equal weight and force on both sides? Especially since the author of the Questions surpasses the four Fathers mentioned in age, and is himself the one whom Augustine calls holy and invokes as a witness to the Catholic faith against the Pelagians (Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians 4.4).

Moreover, does he explain his view of the seeds of virtue and faith in any other way than Augustine does? Anyone who compares the passages of the two authors will easily understand this. For what Augustine says—that the ability to have faith belongs to human nature—the author says by stating that faith exists only potentially in human nature.

Finally, however much the Pelagians may have held that the seed of faith and righteousness exists in human nature, one who uses the same words as the Fathers should not immediately be called a Pelagian. For words can contain a meaning not rejected by the Church, and ambiguous words should not be interpreted in the worse sense whenever they are uttered by an otherwise Catholic author, such as the writer of the Questions has been shown to be.

Who would call someone a Pelagian because he denied that souls are transmitted by generation, praised the saints of the Old Testament, defended marriage, rejected the fate of the Mathematicians, attacked the Manichaeans, and so forth, simply because the Pelagians did these things in defense of their own heresy?

Who would condemn the Fathers whom Augustine excuses—those who once spoke more freely, before the heresies arose, in such a way that heretics later abused their words for a foreign meaning? The Pelagians certainly abused the words of other writers, and likewise the words of this author. This was the cause of the popular opinion that he held Pelagian views: the Pelagians spoke using his words.

## § IV. Four objections concerning the state of the first parents

Concerning the state of the first parents before the fall, Jansenius of Ypres brings four charges against him (On the Heresy of the Pelagians 2.7).

First, in Question 23 Adam is said to have been created earthly, without the Holy Spirit, without adoption as a son of God, and without righteousness—and therefore, as Jansenius himself interprets it (chapter 8), without habitual grace.

Second, in the same Question Adam is likewise said to have been devoid of both understanding and all knowledge when he was created (chapter 14).

Third, the author of the Questions is said to have held that the woman would have experienced a small amount of pain in childbirth if she had not sinned, but that this was increased by sin; and likewise that Adam, after he sinned, was not simply condemned to labor, but was recalled to that for which he had been made and to his original institution, with the cost of labor, so that the earth would not respond to him without effort.

Fourth, he is said to have acknowledged natural righteousness and to have defined repentance as a return to that same righteousness (On the Heresy of the Pelagians 4.12).

To begin with the first point, someone might immediately—and rightly—complain that the author of the Questions bears the reproach of Pelagianism precisely where he suppressed the heresy before it was born. For in the passage from which the objection is taken, he vigorously defends the grace of adoption proper to the New Testament against those who equated the Old Testament with the New. He also carefully explains the nature, properties, and causes of the grace by which we do what belongs to God, against the proud advocates of free will.

Since both of these offenses belonged to the Pelagians, it is truly astonishing that a sensible man could accuse the author now under discussion of associating with the enemies precisely where he attacks and defeats them most vigorously.

Against those who said that no greater gift had been granted to human beings through Christ’s coming than had formerly been granted to their ancestors—and especially to Adam—he argues in such a way as to make Adam’s case the same as that of the other ancestors, while distinguishing both from believers, whose condition he wishes to be entirely different.

After proposing the question in these words—“Did Adam, when he was made, receive the Holy Spirit as it is now given to believers?”—he concludes with these words:

“And therefore the Holy Spirit was not in the ancient saints as he now is in believers.”

And later:

“Those, therefore, who think that Adam or the others possessed the Holy Spirit do not know what kind of gift of God they have,” and so forth.

He therefore admits that the Holy Spirit was formerly with human beings. For he says:

“It is not doubtful that the Holy Spirit was with the prophets and righteous men: with the prophets for the sake of administration; with the righteous for the sake of holiness.”

He denies only that the Spirit was in them as he is in believers after Christ was glorified. He thus raises a question about the mode of presence, by which the Holy Spirit was present in different ways at different times; he does not raise a question about the presence itself, which he assumes to have existed at all times as an indisputable fact.

Accordingly, he answers the question by employing a subtle distinction: the Holy Spirit was formerly with the righteous, but is now in the righteous. This manner of speaking signifies nothing other than what Augustine says (Sermon 185): that the Holy Spirit is present to his believers no longer merely through the grace of visitation and operation, but through the very presence of his majesty.

He follows the opinion of the Fathers (Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 44), according to which the Holy Spirit was formerly in the righteous κατ’ ἐνέργειαν (*kat’ energeian*), that is, only in respect of operation, but is now οὐσιωδῶς (*ousiōdōs*), that is, through his substance. Formerly he made the righteous holy, but as servants; now he makes them holy as adopted sons of God. Formerly he consecrated human hearts to himself as houses; now he consecrates them to himself as temples.

Although this doctrine is not easily understood by ordinary people, it is commonly defended by Athanasius (Against the Arians 2), Gregory of Nazianzus (Oration 44), Chrysostom (Homily 4 on Acts and elsewhere), Cyril of Alexandria (Treasury 34), Augustine (Sermon 185), and nearly all the others who interpret John’s statement:

“But this he said of the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive; for the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39).

But the author of the Questions said that Adam was made earthly, a term that signifies pure nature. He may indeed have said this verbally, but he did not say it absolutely; he said it only by comparison with the heavenly Adam, who is Christ, and with those spiritual and heavenly human beings who, having received the Spirit of Christ, have been appointed heirs of God and coheirs of Christ.

The author admirably explains this (Question 123):

“After Jesus had been glorified, God fulfilled the promise by pouring out the Holy Spirit upon those who believe in Christ. And this is what it means to become an heir of eternal life: to receive the Holy Spirit. Since the Spirit is eternal, whoever receives him possesses eternal life; for he is the pledge of immortality. Whoever receives him and remains in his love, when this life has been completed, goes on to heaven to the one whose Spirit he possesses. For it is incongruous that one who departs this life possessing the Holy Spirit should be held in the underworld. His Spirit in a human being is the sign of Christ’s victory, by which he conquered death, so that one in whom his Spirit is may not be held in the underworld. And therefore the Holy Spirit was not in the ancient saints as he now is in believers, because when they departed from the world they were in the underworld,” and so forth.

If the Holy Spirit was with Adam—as he truly was, if we believe the author—Adam certainly lacked neither righteousness nor habitual grace. For the Holy Spirit worked both in him. He did not, however, work adoption as a son of God in him, concerning which the Fathers speak—unless perhaps Athanasius is an exception. For they distinguished in a certain way these two things, which are usually confused: being pleasing to God and being God’s adopted son.

Indeed, they carefully distinguished between being a son of God, which signifies a particular kind of love, and being an adopted son, which, in addition to love, indicates the right that the author of the Questions shortly explains.

They carefully observed that before Christ no righteous person is called in Scripture either a son of God by adoption or a temple of God—not even Adam, when he was innocent. He is called either merely a son, as when Israel is called the firstborn son (Exodus 4:22), or a servant, although righteous and holy.

This must be understood of an eminent kind of sonship, belonging to individual persons, and not likewise to the whole nation, lest the Fathers seem to have spoken carelessly in scholastic fashion and to have contradicted the Apostle himself, who attributes the adoption of sons to the Israelites (Romans 9:4).

I speak of an eminent sonship by which the Holy Spirit is communicated no longer merely κατ’ ἐνέργειαν (*kat’ energeian*), through operation, but οὐσιωδῶς (*ousiōdōs*), through substance, as Nazianzen says (Oration 44); by which not merely the fragrance of balsam enters the sacred vessels, but the very substance of the sacred ointment flows into them, as Augustine says (Sermon 185); by which a human being is established not merely as dear and pleasing to God—which is the condition of divine grace—but as an adopted son in Christ, the natural Son.

Because of this excellence, even John the Baptist, than whom no greater has arisen among those born of women, is less than the least in the kingdom of heaven, if we believe Cyril (Treasury 12). Through this sonship the saints are finally given not merely a pledge, but an earnest of paternal and fraternal glory: namely, the Spirit of life and immortality. Finally, they do not receive again a spirit of slavery in fear, but the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15).

The second charge is dissolved much more easily than the preceding one. To answer it, one need only see what the author’s purpose was and with whom he was contending. He was contending with those who thought that Adam’s perfection was restored in believers, so that this restoration contained no gift beyond what Adam had received.

They therefore thought that the first man had been given the Spirit of adoption when he was made, and they sought to prove their opinion from the fact that Adam had been created perfect, and that our sanctification was nothing other than a return to Adam’s original state.

Against them he argues as follows. First, in order for someone to be called perfect, it is not necessary that he need nothing; otherwise he would be perfect as God is. Second, Adam can be called perfect in his own kind, as can anything else, even though he possesses nothing beyond human nature and perfection—such as possessing the Holy Spirit—and knows nothing except what he learns by learning. Third, through sanctification believers are not merely restored but also improved, a point he develops at length. Finally, God gave new gifts to human beings when he established the kingdom of his Son among us.

In the last place, these new gifts are nothing other than what the Evangelist says: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become sons of God” (John 1:12).

As for the third charge, it is not worth answering at length. What the author says, whether concerning Eve’s pain in childbirth or concerning Adam’s agricultural labor, increased by sin, was accepted partly from Hebrew words. One of these signifies not only “to multiply” but also “to increase”; the other, according to learned men, is said to refer both to conception and to pains.

What is increased is something that either already exists to some extent or would otherwise have existed in the future. The statement was also accepted partly from a common opinion of the ancients, which Chrysostom transmitted in writing.

When he had said that Adam was commanded to guard and cultivate paradise, he added the reason (Homily 14 on Genesis):

“For if he had been entirely free from labor, he would immediately have fallen from excessive leisure into laziness,” and so forth.

Augustine agrees (On the Literal Meaning of Genesis 8.9):

“What objection is there,” he says, “if we believe that the human being was placed in paradise so as to practice agriculture, not with servile labor, but with an honorable pleasure of the mind?”

The fourth charge may rightly, and indeed ought to, be disregarded. It was taken from two passages, one of which is in that part of the Questions which we have shown to be spurious; the other is attributed to the author, although it belongs to the opponents whom he attacks.

Even if authority were established for both passages, nothing could be concluded except through an unjust prejudice, since the expression “natural righteousness” can bear a Catholic meaning. Thus Augustine says (Against Julian 4.3) that the vices themselves bear witness to the goodness of nature—that is, of what is according to nature. The author of the appendix to Celestine’s letter, writing on behalf of Augustine, says that in Adam’s transgression all human beings lost their natural possibility and innocence—that is, what they had received at their origin.

Certainly, the author has the following words in Question 80, from which that idle interpolator whom we mentioned copied almost everything:

“If he should repent and think according to his nature, turning himself toward the Creator, he will be a son of God.”

It is as though he said: If he detests idolatry and believes in God, who made heaven and earth, from whom he naturally understands himself also to have been made (Augustine, On Nature and Grace 2), he will be a son of God, and so forth.

## § V. Whether the entire work of the Questions has one author, and what his period was

At the very beginning we rejected as spurious the portion commonly called the second part, which was added by James Hemeraeus. We are therefore inquiring only into the earlier part, which itself is threefold, as we showed at the beginning: whether it has one and the same author throughout; or whether the first two sections, which are genuine Questions, were written by an author different from that of the third, which consists more of sermons and treatises.

Someone might perhaps think that there was not one author because the author of the first part says that he wrote approximately three hundred years after the destruction of Jerusalem by Vespasian, whereas the author of the third part claims to be writing in the sixth thousandth year of the world, as the common manuscripts indeed read.

Since the destruction of Jerusalem occurred in the year of Christ 70, and the sixth thousandth year of the world, according to the common computation of the Greeks, is the year of Christ 459, eighty-nine years must necessarily have elapsed between the periods of the two works.

Moreover, in the earlier work scarcely anything is found deserving of criticism, except what is said about Jephthah—for who could accuse as criminal and wicked, without qualification, the man whom Paul praises?
