In the later work there are many things that are wholly false, such as the material concerning Melchizedek; inappropriate, such as the sermons; rash, such as the definition of the future age of the world and the criticism of the canon of the Mass; barbarous, such as *diffamia*, *deterioratur*, *saxonitia vestis*, and *sanctimonium*; and unlearned, such as the claim that Easter (*Pascha*) was so called from the Passion.

Against this, however, stands Jerome’s authority, if indeed he is writing to Evagrius about the deacon Hilary. For he indicates that the later work, which consists of Questions on the Old and New Testaments mixed together, is by the same author in these words (Letter 126):

“You sent an anonymous and masterless volume—ἀνώνυμον καὶ ἀδέσποτον (*anōnymon kai adespoton*)—and I do not know whether you removed the name from the title, or whether the writer, wishing to avoid the danger of disputation, did not wish to acknowledge his author.

“When I read it, I understood that the famous question concerning the priest Melchizedek had been developed there through many arguments (Question 109), in an attempt to teach that the one who blessed so great a patriarch was of a more divine nature and should not be regarded as one of human beings.

“At the end he even dared to say that the Holy Spirit came to Abraham, and that the Holy Spirit himself was the one who appeared in the form of a human being. But how the Holy Spirit brought forth bread and wine and received the tithes of the spoils which Abraham had brought back after defeating the four kings, he entirely refused to touch upon. You ask me to explain what I think either of the writer or of the question.

“And later:

“Certainly you will not accept that spiritual interpreter of yours, who, unlearned in language and knowledge, pronounced with such arrogance and authority that Melchizedek was the Holy Spirit, thereby confirming the truth of what is sung among the Greeks: ignorance produces confidence; learning produces fear.”

The entire question may therefore seem obscure, both because of the conflict among the arguments and because, in addition, the same Questions are treated in the third part in the same words as in the earlier parts. Nor does the same gravity of expression and purity of doctrine shine equally in both, qualities scarcely compatible with one man unless he repeatedly forgets himself or deliberately wishes to appear different from himself.

Nevertheless, the opinion that has long prevailed must be retained: both works are to be attributed to one and the same author (Question 97). He claims both works for himself with sufficient clarity when he says in Question 125:

“This is the end, for the remaining matters contained in the indivisible unity of the Trinity have been treated more fully in the little book composed against Arian impiety.”

And in Question 106:

“What it means to be made according to the image and likeness of God, although we have discussed it elsewhere, this passage and subject nevertheless require us to say it again here.”

He had said the same thing in Question 21, in the same sense and in the same words.

The opposing arguments have little force. The chronological argument is introduced through an error, as will be demonstrated later. We must also frankly admit that certain blemishes occur in these Questions and that the Latin is not of the highest quality.

Nevertheless, the argument drawn from this contributes to proving the unity of the author, as will be clear to any reader. As for the period of the work, it can be recognized without difficulty from various indications.

The author says that he is working on the work approximately three hundred years after the destruction of Jerusalem by Vespasian. Since Vespasian captured Jerusalem in the year of Christ 70, the author must have published his work around the year 370.

Nor does the statement in the common manuscripts that he wrote in the sixth thousandth year of the world present an obstacle. An error has entered the text, and VI must be corrected to IV, as will be shown in the following chapter.

He then argues against the Jews and the Manichaeans throughout almost the entire first part; against the Novatians on repentance, Question 102; against Eusebius of Emesa on Melchizedek, Question 109; against the pagans in defense of the Christians, Question 114; against the Mathematicians on fate, Question 115; against Eusebius of Caesarea on the Holy Spirit, Question 125; against those who defer baptism, Question 126; and against those who condemn marriage, Question 127. These were questions being debated with great intensity as the fourth century was drawing to a close.

He then refutes the arguments of Photinus with both force and subtlety, addressing him as though he were still alive. Photinus died in exile in Galatia in the year 376, after having first been condemned at Sirmium in 350.

Finally, he argues against Apollinaris and the other enemies of the Lord’s Incarnation, certainly no less vehemently than against the other heretics, since he was an especially ardent defender of Christ’s divinity. He therefore wrote before this heresy had either become known or been condemned in the West. It was condemned by Damasus at Rome in the year 373.

Then he mentions the devastation of Pannonia, as though it were a recent disaster: “Pannonia,” he says, “was so utterly destroyed that it could have no remedy,” and so forth. This devastation occurred in the year 351, when the forces of the whole empire were brought together against one another.

Next he mentions a certain notable calamity suffered not long before. “Behold,” he says, “we know that Italy and Africa, Sicily and Sardinia, suffered from famine.” That famine raged in the year 363. He further mentions Sardinia as his homeland; he may therefore be regarded as a Sardinian.

Finally, he responds to those matters, arguing with the pagans about what Julian the Apostate reproached the Christians for; and, in turn, he indirectly censures—without naming him—the impious things Julian was doing in his abominable [Col. 0316B] assemblies, so that he seems to have been accommodating himself to the times. We may therefore conjecture that he wrote shortly after Julian’s death, that is, around the year 365, when the times had not yet become sufficiently settled and the affairs of the pagans had not yet been utterly ruined.

From these considerations it may be gathered that the *Work of Questions on the Old and New Testament* was published by a certain Sardinian, around the year 370, during the pontificate of Damasus.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Author of the Commentaries on Paul’s Epistles, Formerly Attributed to Ambrose

In our own age no learned person is unaware that the *Commentaries* in question were falsely attributed to Saint Ambrose; but not everyone likewise knows that this was already being done from the year 550 onward, even by great men, and that the charge of false attribution therefore does not belong to a later period.

### § I. On the Author’s Name and Identity

[Col. 0316C] The true author of this work has been carefully investigated. Until he became known—if indeed that was the issue at stake—some preferred to call him “Ambrosiaster.” But I am surprised that this was attempted by those who boast of having devoted themselves assiduously to reading Augustine’s works, since Augustine himself, in one and the same passage, twice names Hilary (Book IV *To Boniface*, chapter 4):

“Thus,” he says, “Saint Hilary understood what is written: ‘In whom all sinned.’ For he says: ‘In whom, that is, in Adam, all sinned.’” Then he adds: “‘It is manifest that all sinned in Adam, as in a lump. For he himself was corrupted through sin, and all whom he begot were born under sin.’ Thus writes Hilary,” and so forth. These words are read verbatim in the *Commentaries* on the fifth chapter of Romans, section VII.

The Hilary whom Augustine praises cannot have been either an obscure person or a recent writer. For in Augustine’s time his *Commentary* was commonly in everyone’s hands, and the Pelagians could neither diminish its authority because of the age of its author, who had written before the Questions arose, nor evade it because of the celebrity of his name. He wrote, as he himself expressly testifies, during the pontificate of Damasus. For he says (*On chapter III of the First Epistle to Timothy*):

“Although the whole world belongs to God, the Church is nevertheless called his house, whose ruler today is Damasus.”

Damasus ceased to live in the year 384, on December 11.

I cannot sufficiently wonder what reason Jansenius of Ypres had for asserting (*Book VII on the Pelagian Heresy*, chapter 4) that Hilary wrote the *Commentaries* at approximately the same time as Jerome wrote his *Dialogues against the Pelagians*. For no fewer than thirty years elapsed between the death of Damasus and the publication of the *Dialogues*; yet Hilary published the *Commentaries* many years before Damasus’s death. Furthermore, how could Augustine, in the year 419, have praised books as already possessing authority when they had first appeared only four years earlier, [Col. 0317A] or thereabouts? Finally, if the author of the *Commentaries* is the same as the author of the *Questions*, as will later be demonstrated, it is impossible for the *Commentaries* to have been composed at approximately the same time as the *Dialogues*, since the *Questions* were prepared around the year 365.

Perhaps for the same reason the Ypres scholar thought that the author of the *Commentaries*, whom he calls Ambrosiaster, had borrowed something from Pelagius’s *Commentaries* in order to explain the Apostle’s celebrated statement, “Therefore it is not of him who wills,” and so forth. For Pelagius did not compose his brief *Expositions on Paul* before the year 400, but approximately at the time when Innocent I began to occupy the see.

Since this is so, we must next investigate which Hilary was the author of the *Commentaries*. He was certainly not that monk of Syracuse who consulted Augustine about the Pelagian Questions in the year 413; nor the bishop of that name to whom Augustine wrote in the year 416, after the Pelagian heresy had been condemned by two African councils; nor [Col. 0317B] the bishop of Arles, nor the lay author of the letter to Augustine concerning the remnants of Pelagius. All of these lived long after Damasus.

Nor was he that unconquered conqueror of the Arians, Hilary of Poitiers. Although, as most think, he lived under Damasus, it can scarcely be plausibly maintained that, in extreme old age, he elaborated so extensive a work. Even if this argument failed, the great Hilary would be sufficiently disqualified as its author by the considerable differences in style, in the version of Scripture used, and also in doctrine.

Nothing, therefore, can be asserted more credibly than what Bellarmine says (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Ambrose”): the writer of the *Commentaries* was none other than Hilary the deacon. Along with Eusebius of Vercelli and other defenders of Athanasius, Hilary was expelled from the council of Milan, which was controlled by the Arians, and sent into exile in the year 355. He is said to have fallen into the heresy of those who rebaptized; from this, in my opinion, he repented before his death. He also appears to have been reconciled with the Apostolic See, [Col. 0317C] which explains why he speaks honorably of Damasus, and to have died in peace. For this reason Augustine could call him “saint.”

### § II. On the Doctrine Contained in the Commentaries

Those who, disregarding Augustine’s authority in praising Hilary, disparage him under a fictitious name as a disseminator of many heresies, a complete Pelagian, and overflowing with Pelagian errors, may consider with what reverence for Augustine, or with what argument, they advance such claims. Certainly, if we believe Augustine, the Pelagian doctrines were chiefly contained in four questions:

Whether the whole human race is held liable to Adam’s sin;

Whether grace consists only in the law and instruction;

Whether faith is a gift of God;

Whether human beings die not on account of the deserts of guilt but by necessity of nature.

On each of these points Hilary held the Catholic view.

Regarding original sin transmitted from the first parent to his descendants—that is, the sin of all in Adam—the testimony of Augustine cited above is sufficient. By this one testimony the issue ought to be settled, and anyone who boasts of being Augustine’s disciple ought to be thoroughly refuted. For in writing these words Hilary clearly indicated how the statement “In whom all sinned” was to be understood. Augustine’s entire demonstration against the opponents of original sin depends upon that understanding. For after the holy man had argued at length from the Apostle’s passage, he says:

“It remains, then, that all are understood to have sinned in that first man, because all were in him when he sinned. Hence sin is contracted by birth, and unless one is reborn it is not removed; for Saint Hilary also understood it in this way,” and so forth.

Regarding grace, this statement is especially excellent, among many others:

“Thus it may appear that this gift is bestowed neither through the merit of those who are saved, nor through that of those by whom they are called, but by the grace of God through the faith of Christ” (2 Timothy I).

Regarding faith as a gift of God:

“For it is faith that gives salvation” (1 Timothy II). Unless the whole mind receives it by its will, it will not only profit nothing but will also harm. For the grace of faith has this power: toward those devoted to it, it pours divine healing; toward those who are not devoted to it, it brings the disease through which the whole person perishes.

Finally, concerning the claim that human beings die because of the sin of the first man, he states, in the words following the sentence cited by Augustine (*On chapter V of the Epistle to the Romans*, section VII):

“For by transgressing he lost God’s beneficence, becoming unworthy to eat from the tree of life, so that he would die. Death, however, is the dissolution of the body, when the soul is separated from the body.”

I know that certain statements have been criticized—for example, that the second death, which is Gehenna, was not passed on to Adam’s descendants through Adam’s sin (*On chapter V of Romans*, chapter 2), but only the first death, which is the soul’s separation from the body; that, guided by nature, the Gentiles believed in Christ (*chapter VI*), and recognized that believing was proper to their nature; that God assists good efforts (*On chapter II of Philippians*), so that willing is ours but bringing it to completion belongs to God; that God accepts one of two equals on the basis of justice and rejects the other [Col. 0318B] (*chapter IX of Romans*); that predestination depends on foreknowledge of faith (*ibid.*); and that God wills all human beings to be saved, provided that they also will it (1 Timothy II).

But since almost all these statements have been advanced by other Fathers, especially Chrysostom, in nearly the same words and concerning the same passages of the Apostle, why are they not softened by a similarly charitable interpretation in Hilary’s case? Indeed, they do not greatly require such charity, provided that, as is proper, one gives credence to the common judgment of approved authors rather than to someone’s preconceived interpretation.

For, besides Augustine’s testimony that Hilary held the Catholic view concerning original sin (*On chapter VII of Romans*, on the words “But occasion…”), the following statement also demonstrates it:

“The devil rejoices that he holds the human being in this condition both because of Adam’s sin and because of the person’s own sin,” and so forth.

Therefore, when Hilary denies that the second death, which is in Gehenna, is transmitted from the first parent to his descendants—that is, the punishment of sense, as they call it, is not repaid by God for original sin—his view does indeed conflict with some. Nevertheless, it has many adherents, both among the Fathers and among the theologians of the ancient school, including the Angelic Doctor himself.

Hilary says that the Gentiles believed, guided by nature; Chrysostom says the same. Both speak Catholicly, since neither set nature in opposition to the help of God, but to the Mosaic law. Both commonly taught what they had received from the Apostle: namely, that nature was for the Gentiles, just as the law was for the Jews, a pedagogue leading to Christ.

Furthermore, when Hilary teaches that good efforts are assisted by God, he simultaneously teaches that they are stirred up by God, who gives faith. When he says that willing is ours, he does not exclude the help of grace, but rather the necessity imposed upon the will.

That God acts through justice—or, which is the same thing, through judgment—even when he chooses one person over another, is Augustinian. That predestination to glory, which they call absolute, is based on foreseen works, is Ambrosian. That God wills all to be saved if they will it—that is, if they consent to prevenient grace—is Catholic.

### § III. Whether the Author of the Questions and the Commentaries Is One and the Same

All learned people commonly say that the author is one and the same. There are three certain arguments for this common opinion, since the author of both works wrote at the same time, to the same effect, and in the same words.

The chronology is clear from the following. The third part of the *Questions* was written before the year 363, and the first part after the year 367; the *Commentaries* were written around the year 370, during the pontificate of Damasus, as has been shown. Since Damasus died in the year 384 and began to occupy the see in the year 367, both the first book of the *Questions* and the brief *Commentaries* could have been written at approximately the same time, or at least during the same period of the author’s life.

The *Questions* and the *Commentaries* contain so many passages expressing the same view that it would be endless to cite them all. It is easy, however, to offer examples; for the present, two will suffice.

**Question.** “Why is the man the image of God and not the woman, when man and woman are one flesh?” Man and woman are indeed of one substance, both in soul and in flesh; but the man is greater in rank because the woman is from him, as the Apostle says: “The head of the woman is the man” (1 Corinthians II, 3). For causation made the man greater, not substance (*Question 24*).

**Commentary.** Although man and woman are of one substance, nevertheless, because the man is the head of the woman, he is said to be placed before her, so that he is greater by causation and order, not by substance. The woman, therefore, is inferior to the man; for she is his portion, since the man is the woman’s origin. She is from him and therefore appears subject to the man (*On chapter II of 1 Corinthians*).

**Question.** “This is why the Apostle Paul says: ‘In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware’” (2 Timothy II, 20). He said this concerning Hymenaeus and Philetus, who, although they belonged to the Church, held a perverse view concerning the resurrection, just as some members of the Corinthian Church denied the resurrection. But Novatian understands this great house to signify the world, not the Church, so that he need not maintain that within one Church there are both bad and good, the clean and the unclean—a view that, I think, can easily be overturned. In one house, all are under one name. Although they differ in conduct, they are nevertheless designated by the one name and profession of their master. This world, however, contains people of different professions, so that they profess to have different gods and lords. You see, therefore, that this could not have been said of the world but of the Church, in which people dwelling under one name differ in conduct, and so forth (*Question 102*).

**Commentary.** He signified that there are different kinds of people in the Church: some good and outstanding, whom he wishes to be understood as gold; some merely good, whom he designates as silver; and others who are not good, whom he calls wooden and earthen vessels. I think this is beyond dispute. For this is demonstrated in the Corinthian Church by the Apostle’s frequent language of rebuke; now it is openly evident in our own Church, and it is confirmed by clear readings in the temple of Jerusalem, which was a type of the Church. For the Sadducees were there, and Hymenaeus and Philetus sprang from their root. After the Apostle had spoken of their erroneous opinion, he immediately added this, so that it would not be surprising to see dissenting people in the Church. For in the Corinthian Church, of which I have spoken, there were also some who dissented and denied the resurrection.

“But the mad Novatus, in order to flatter his own error, teaches that this should be understood differently, so that the great house is believed to signify the entire world, because it contains a diversity of people. Yet it is clear that the Apostle used the example of a wealthy and prosperous household, which, although it is well supplied, nevertheless has wooden and earthen vessels. In the same way, the Church, although it is called holy, nevertheless contains both vicious people and people who hold perverse opinions, as I mentioned above. He shows that they deserve condemnation, but not that they will perish; rather, they are to be purified by fire, because they are necessary in some respect to the household” (*On chapter II of the Second Epistle to Timothy*).

[Col. 0319D] He frequently used the same words in both works. Since this is clear in the preceding example concerning the woman, it would be pointless to cite others, which will occur to anyone who pays even slight attention while reading. In both works, certainly, *diffidentia* is used for unbelief; the verb *praevaricari* is barbarously used with an active ending; and the verb *meliorare*, along with many other expressions, although unusual, nevertheless appears either familiar to the author or deliberately adopted by him.

I see that two objections may be raised: one against the chronology established above, and the other intended to prove a difference of opinion. The author of the third part of the *Questions* says that he wrote in the six-thousandth year of the world, which, according to the Greeks, was the year 459 of Christ. Thus more than eighty years separate him from the period of the author of the *Commentaries*, who wrote during Damasus’s lifetime. Furthermore, in *Question 109* Melchizedek is said not to have been a human being, whereas in the *Commentaries* on chapter II of the Epistle to the Hebrews this is asserted.

But as regards the date, it was easy for an error to enter the numbers through the transposition of letters, and the computation of the years of the world according to the Greek method may seem suspect when made by a Latin author. Why, then, could “six-thousandth” not have been written for “four-thousandth,” with “thousandth” used for “millenary”? In this way everything is readily reconciled, since the *Questions* would have been written, according to the Latin reckoning, in the fourth millennium of the world. This conjecture is all the more probable because so many additional considerations, which we examined earlier, confirm it.

The difference of opinion—that the author of the *Questions* denies that Melchizedek was a human being (*Question 109*; *Commentary on chapter VII of Hebrews*), while Hilary affirms it—would create a greater difficulty unless it were established that Hilary wrote nothing on the Epistle to the Hebrews. The same is true of Jerome, Pelagius, and every other Latin author of that period; those learned in the matter are aware of it. Someone therefore supplied a commentary explaining the first ten chapters of the Epistle, partly from Chrysostom and partly from Jerome. No one should therefore be surprised if contradictory statements concerning Melchizedek are read in this work and in the *Questions*, since Jerome refutes them in that very epistle, from which the interpolator borrowed even the words themselves.

[Col. 0320C] From what has been argued thus far in both of the preceding chapters, I conclude that Hilary—who is said to have come from Sardinia, is usually called a deacon, and is commonly known as a Luciferian—wrote these two works, whose examination was undertaken in this and the preceding chapter.

I conclude further that he was unjustly disparaged under another person’s name, although he has his own name, by which Augustine mentioned him once and again. He was likewise unjustly accused of either the Pelagian or the Coelestian heresy, since he plainly opposed both and was praised by Augustine as a witness to the Catholic faith concerning original sin. Nor can he be called an interpreter of Pelagius or Coelestius, since he preceded both by a considerable period and agreed thoroughly with the highly Catholic Fathers of his own age.

He also possesses as much authority for bearing witness to the affairs of his own time—that is, of the declining fourth century—as any other Latin author, except perhaps Ambrose. Finally, Mercator was correct in saying that the heresy which later acquired the name either from Pelagius or from Coelestius arose from Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia. This was what had to be demonstrated in both chapters.

# DISSERTATION II. ON THE SYNODS HELD DURING THE LIFETIME OF SAINT AUGUSTINE IN THE PELAGIAN CONTROVERSY

In these words of Marius Mercator: “They were deposed and deprived of office not only by imperial laws but also by ecclesiastical decrees,” and so forth (*Commonitorium*, chapter 3).

[Col. 0319]

[Col. 0319D] Although Mercator, in the words of the *Commonitorium* just quoted, was speaking of a single *tractoria* of Zosimus, or even of the decree of Innocent, it will nevertheless not be irrelevant, nor, I believe, of little use to the history of Pelagianism, to review briefly the twenty-four synods which the ancients are said to have held concerning the Pelagians, up to the death of Augustine or the convocation of the Council of Ephesus. The period in question lasted no more than nineteen years, during which the heresy of Pelagius and Coelestius seemed either to exercise or retain some degree of strength.

Someone may wonder that so great a multitude of bishops met so many times in so short a period and for the destruction of a single sect, yet that the unfortunate growth could not be uprooted despite such immense effort. But just as that impiety was nearly the most pernicious of all heresies, since it attempted to tear up the foundation of Christian piety—namely, the humility of human beings under God—so none resisted the Church more stubbornly. For it had seized the citadel of human nature and freedom itself and defended itself tenaciously from that position.

## I. SYNOD: Held at Carthage by Aurelius against Coelestius, under the Augusti Honorius IX and Theodosius V, in February of the year of Christ 412

After the Pelagian heresy had been detected in Africa, a synod was held at Carthage by Bishop Aurelius in the case of Coelestius, who was attempting to insinuate himself into the presbyterate, partly through his reputation for learning, partly under the appearance of piety, but chiefly through the efforts of his supporters (*Augustine, On Original Sin*, chapter 2 and following). This was the first of all, and it seems to have been a kind of rudimentary exercise for the Church as she learned to triumph over the monstrous error.

The date is easily established by comparing two testimonies of the ancients: that of the Carthaginian Fathers and that of Augustine.

In the year 416 they wrote to Saint Innocent in these words (*Letter 175, in Augustine*):

“When, according to custom, we were solemnly coming to the Church of Carthage, and a synod of us had been assembled from various causes, our fellow presbyter Orosius gave us letters from our holy brothers and fellow priests, Heros and Lazarus, the text of which we have decided ought to be appended here. After reading them, we recognized Pelagius and Coelestius as the authors of an entirely wicked error which all of us must anathematize. Hence it came about that we requested [or: thought] that what had been dealt with here at the Church of Carthage concerning Coelestius nearly five years earlier should be reviewed,” and so forth.

Augustine likewise wrote in *On the Proceedings at Palestine*, chapter 11, addressing Aurelius:

“These matters were brought forward in such a way that your Holiness and the other bishops with you said that they had heard and condemned them at Carthage. As you recall, I myself was not present there; but later, when I came to Carthage, I reviewed the proceedings.”

From these statements three things are clear:

1. Two synods were assembled at Carthage in the same case. The later one, from which the letter to the supreme pontiff was sent, met approximately in September, since the Nicene canon prescribed that synods should then be convened. It was held in the customary and solemn manner—that is, according to the prescription of the canon.

2. Nearly five years, not a full five years, elapsed between these two Carthaginian synods.

3. Augustine was not present at the earlier synod.

The earlier synod was therefore held not immediately after the conference with the Donatists, which was completed on June 8, as some have thought—for otherwise Augustine would have been present, since he played a major part in the conference—but after September. If it were placed close to the time of the conference but before September, it would have to be admitted that more than five years, rather than nearly five years, elapsed between the two synods. If it is assigned to September itself, it must likewise be admitted that a full five years intervened between this earlier synod and the letter written by the later one.

It therefore remains that it be assigned to the remaining months of 411 and the beginning of the following year, 412, so that it may be said to have been gathered in the customary manner—that is, according to the Nicene canon—before Lent. Thus it becomes clear both why Augustine was not present, since after the conference he went to his own people and did not return to Carthage until after the Easter celebrations, and how nearly five years elapsed between the two synods, since only three or four months were lacking to complete the five-year period.

The number of bishops who assembled is uncertain. Augustine says that many gathered, not only in the words just quoted but also in the following passage (*On the Proceedings*, chapters 11 and 35):

“When this heresy had deceived very many and disturbed the brothers whom it had not deceived, a certain Coelestius, holding such opinions, was brought to judgment before the Church of Carthage and condemned by the judgment of the bishops.”

Orosius says (*Apology*, chapter 3):

“I explained to your assembly, as best I could, that Coelestius, already attempting to insinuate himself into the honor of the presbyterate at Carthage, had been exposed, heard, convicted, confessed, and rejected by the Church while very many bishops were judging him, and had fled from Africa.”

A little later he adds:

“I immediately continued: The African synod rejected this in Coelestius.”

Marius Mercator says (*Commonitorium*, chapter 1):

“On all the chapters written above, the Fathers and bishops of that region, on the basis of copies of the synodal proceedings, resisted Coelestius and ordered that he condemn them, because they contained heretical opinions.”

The author of the *Predestinatus* says (*Heresy 88*):

“A certain Paulinus, deacon, defender and procurator of the Church of Milan, opposed him and brought forward before the assembly of priests many chapters contrary to the Catholic faith, which Coelestius failed to condemn.”

From these four testimonies, and especially from the last three, someone might suspect that this synod was not insignificant—indeed, that it was not merely Carthaginian but, as Orosius says, African; that is, it may have been composed either of the whole African diocese or of several provinces, since, according to Mercator, the Fathers and bishops assembled for it.

The meaning of “Fathers”—whether it refers to the primates of the provinces, or elders—could perhaps be understood from the first action of the Carthaginian conference, number 46. There Aurelius mentions “my Fathers and brothers” while speaking of the election of seven legates from the universal council of the Catholic Church to attend the conference. This would in some measure support the opinion of those who believe that the judgment concerning Coelestius was held at Carthage by the Fathers assembled for the conference—unless a clear argument stood against it.

Coelestius was accused by Paulinus, whom Augustine simply calls a deacon; Mercator calls him the deacon of Ambrose, bishop of Milan, of blessed memory; and the author of the *Predestinatus* calls him the deacon, defender, and procurator of the Church of Milan.

The six charges were brought forward, as Augustine reports them (*On the Proceedings*, chapter 11, and *On Original Sin*, chapter 11), together with Marius Mercator (*Commonitorium*, chapter 1). The author of the *Predestinatus* gives them in these words (*Heresy 88*):

“They presented him with his books, in which he said that human nature itself could suffice for perfection; that is, that a person could exercise such great righteousness that he could even be without sin, if he wished; that Adam was made mortal and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin; that the law led to the kingdom just as the Gospel did; that infants ought to be baptized for the remission of sins. Therefore, according to the rule of the universal Church, we confess that Adam’s sin did no harm to the human race.”

All these charges were brought against Coelestius for condemnation.

Augustine was not present. But as soon as he came to Carthage, he reviewed the proceedings, of which he transmitted nothing to us except a fragment and part of the little treatise published by Coelestius at Rome and cited in the ecclesiastical proceedings.

The surviving portion of the proceedings, as preserved by Augustine, reads as follows (*On Original Sin*, chapters 3–4):

“We have transcribed the following words of his [Coelestius] from the ecclesiastical proceedings at Carthage.

“Bishop Aurelius said: Let the following charges be read.

“And it was read:

“‘That Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race.’

“When this had been read, Coelestius said:

“‘I said that I was uncertain about the transmission of sin; nevertheless, I consent to the person to whom God has granted the grace of knowledge, because I have heard different things from those who are certainly presbyters established in the Catholic Church.’

“Deacon Paulinus said:

“‘Tell us their names.’

“Coelestius said:

“‘The holy presbyter Rufinus at Rome, who stayed with Saint Pammachius. I heard him say that there is no transmission of sin.’

“Deacon Paulinus said:

“‘Is there anyone else?’

“Coelestius said:

“‘I also heard many others say it.’

“Deacon Paulinus [Col. 0323A] said:

“‘Tell us their names.’

“Coelestius said:

“‘Is one priest not enough for you?’

“And after some other matters, Bishop Aurelius said:

“‘Let the remaining charges in the treatise be read.’

“And it was read:

“‘That infants who are born are in the same condition in which Adam was before the transgression,’ continuing to the end of the shorter treatise inserted above.

“Bishop Aurelius said:

“‘Coelestius, did you at some time teach, as the deacon Paulinus has said, that infants who are born are in the same condition in which Adam was before the transgression?’

“Coelestius said:

“‘Let him explain what he meant by “before the transgression.”’

“Deacon Paulinus said:

“‘You must deny that you taught this. There are only two possibilities: either deny that you taught it, or now condemn it.’

“Coelestius said:

“‘I have already spoken about it. Let him explain what he meant by “before the transgression.”’

“Deacon Paulinus said:

“‘Deny that you taught those things.’

“Bishop Aurelius said:

“‘I ask what I am to gather from this objection. I say: Adam, placed in paradise, was first made indestructible, as it is said, and afterward, through transgression of the commandment, was made corruptible. Is this what you are saying, brother Paulinus?’

“Deacon Paulinus said:

“‘Yes, lord.’

“Bishop Aurelius said:

“‘The question is whether the condition of infants who are baptized today is such as Adam’s condition was before the transgression, or whether they derive from the same origin of sin from which they are born and thereby bear the guilt of the transgression. This is what the deacon Paulinus wishes to hear.’

“Deacon Paulinus said:

“‘Whether he taught this or not, let him deny it.’

“Coelestius said:

“‘I have already spoken about the transmission of sin. I have heard many people established within the Catholic Church destroy it, and others also affirm it, although this is a matter of dispute, not heresy. I have always said that infants need baptism and ought to be baptized. What more does he ask?’”

The outcome is taught by the four authors cited in the passages quoted above. To them may be added the Fathers of the Carthaginian council:

“Coelestius was exposed and repeatedly heard; indeed, he was convicted, confessed, and rejected by the Church—that is, struck with an anathema and deprived of communion—until he openly anathematized the charges brought against him” (*Synodal Letter to Innocent*, in Augustine, Letter 182).

The obstinate heretic did not submit to this sentence, but appealed to the Apostolic See in order to evade the judgment. He nevertheless fled to Ephesus, a city of Asia, disregarding the appeal, where he was ordained presbyter through subterfuge, as Mercator relates in chapter 1 of the *Commonitorium*.

## II. SYNOD: Convened by John, Bishop of Jerusalem, in the Case of Pelagius, under the Augusti Honorius X and Theodosius VI, on July 30 of the year of Christ 415

Orosius reports the proceedings of the second synod, which was convened at Jerusalem in the case of Pelagius by Bishop John in the year 415 (*Apology*, chapter 3). Augustine mentions it in these words (*On the Proceedings at Palestine*, chapter 14):

“Saint John, bishop of the Church of Jerusalem, used this testimony. When asked what had taken place in his presence before the judgment, he himself related it to our fellow bishops who were presiding with him at that judgment. For he says that when certain people were whispering and saying that Pelagius claimed that this could be accomplished without the grace of God—that is, that it was possible for a human being to be without sin, as he had said above—he brought this charge against him:

“‘The Apostle, laboring greatly, but not according to his own strength, rather according to the grace of God, said: “I labored more than all of them, yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me”’ (1 Corinthians XV, 10).

“And again:

“‘It is not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy’” (Romans IX, 16).

“And this:

“‘Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain’” (Psalm CXXVI, 1).

“‘And we said many other similar things from the holy Scriptures,’ he says. But when they did not accept what we were saying from the holy Scriptures and continued to whisper, Pelagius said:

“‘I too believe this. Let him be anathema who says that, without God’s help, a human being can advance in every virtue.’”

The testimonies of both authors just cited clearly establish the place and the presiding authority.

The date is established as follows. First, this synod necessarily met during the period extending from spring of the year 415 to December of that same year. Orosius played a major part in this synod, and it was mentioned at the Council of Diospolis. Orosius arrived in Palestine in the spring of 415, and the Council of Diospolis was held in December of that same year.

Furthermore, when Orosius came, as was his custom, on the first day of the dedication festival to wait upon John, he was rejected by him on the grounds that at the synod he had blasphemously said that a human being could not be without sin even with God’s help. Since the first day of the dedication festival was September 14, as Nicephorus reports (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VIII, chapter 50), and since it was the forty-seventh day after the synod, as Orosius writes (*Apology*, chapter 4), the synod must have been held on July 30.

This was an assembly of presbyters alone, not of bishops—at least not bishops who had been compelled by law, though perhaps they had been summoned amicably. For at that time John had no authority to compel them, since he possessed neither a diocese nor even a province. He was counted as belonging to the diocese of Antioch and was subject to the bishop of Caesarea, the metropolitan of all Palestine.

That gathering therefore consisted either only of the presbyterate, which I consider more likely, or also of neighboring bishops. John is said to have taken two such bishops, Eleutherius of Sebaste and Eutonius of Jericho, to recover the relics of Saint Stephen and transfer them to the holy city, according to Lucian (*Letter on the Discovery of Saint Stephen*).

Pelagius gave occasion for the assembly. He had by then spent nearly three full years in Jerusalem and, by his customary methods, had won some members of the clergy to his side, especially Bishop John himself. Even if he had not infected John’s mind with his error, he had bound his heart to himself so completely that he easily persuaded the bishop—who was already hostile toward Jerome because of the Origenist controversy—that the holy old man opposed him not out of zeal for the faith but out of envy.

Hence disagreement arose among the presbyters: some favored Pelagius, following the example of their bishop; others fought against him, led by Jerome, who had carefully investigated the meaning of the slippery heretic and exposed it to the Catholics for their examination. Serious disturbances of mind consequently arose on both sides. John, not indeed to calm them, but to prevent them from harming Pelagius, assembled a meeting of the presbyters and attempted, if he could find some means, to impose silence on the opposing parties.

Orosius, a Spanish presbyter whom Augustine had sent to Jerome to be instructed by the teacher of the East concerning the origin of souls, summoned from his retreat at Bethlehem, sat among the presbyters. When they asked him what had been done at Carthage with Coelestius, he openly related what Augustine had answered, whether to the questions of Hilary of Syracuse or in his book *On Nature*. It is uncertain whether he also read aloud the acts of the Council of Carthage itself. Certainly he read Augustine’s letter to Hilary, and said that he had heard two things from Pelagius: first, that a person could be without sin if he wished; second, that he could easily keep God’s commandments. Both doctrines had been condemned by the Africans.

Pelagius, whom John had ordered to be admitted and to sit among the presbyters, although he was a layman, objected that he had not said that this could happen without God’s help. The bishop gladly accepted the qualification and, after confirming it with testimonies from Scripture, attempted to force Orosius to accuse him, since he himself was the judge. But when an altercation arose, and many argued that the same man could not be both advocate and judge for a single heretic, and that a case which had arisen among Latins ought to be debated by Latin judges, this sentence was finally pronounced: the parties and letters should be sent to the blessed Innocent, Roman pope, and all should follow whatever he decided; but in such a way that the heretic, silence having been imposed upon him, should remain silent for the time being, and that our people should refrain from insulting a man who had been convicted and put to shame (*Apology*, chapter 3).

But it is better to hear Orosius himself speaking in his own words (see *Apology*, sections 3 and 4). For what he says may reflect the position of those who convened the assembly.

> “I was staying in Bethlehem, entrusted by Father Augustine so that I might learn the fear of the Lord, sitting at the feet of Jerome. From there, summoned by you, I came to Jerusalem. Then, at the command of Bishop John, I sat down together with you in your assembly. Immediately you all asked my lowliness that, if I knew anything had been done in Africa concerning this heresy which Pelagius and Coelestius had sown, I should report it faithfully and plainly.
>
> “I briefly explained to your gathered company, as best I could, that Coelestius, already seeking to insinuate himself into the dignity of the presbyterate, had fled from Africa after being exposed, heard, convicted, confessing, and detested by the Church at Carthage, while many bishops were judging him. I also explained that blessed Augustine had given a full response to Pelagius’ book, when Pelagius’ own disciples had exposed it and requested an answer. I further stated that a letter of the aforementioned bishop was in my hands (*Letter 89 to Hilary*), which he had recently sent to Sicily and in which he reported many questions raised by the heretics. You also ordered me to read it there, and I did so.

> “At this point Bishop John requested that Pelagius be brought in. Out of respect for his fatherly standing, and for the usefulness of the proceedings—for you thought that, while present, he could be refuted more effectively by the bishop—permission was granted for him to be admitted.

> “Once Pelagius had been admitted, you all unanimously asked him whether he acknowledged that he had taught these things to which Bishop Augustine had replied. Immediately he answered: ‘And who is Augustine to me?’ When everyone cried out that he was blaspheming against the bishop, from whose mouth the Lord had granted healing to the unity of all Africa, and that he ought to be expelled not only from that assembly but from the whole Church, Bishop John immediately ordered him—a layman, plainly guilty of manifest heresy—to sit in the midst of the presbyters and among Catholics. Then he said: ‘I am Augustine,’ so that, assuming as it were the person of one who was present, he might more freely forgive on the authority of the man who had been injured and calm the minds of those who were grieving. We immediately said to him: ‘If you assume Augustine’s person, follow Augustine’s judgment.’

> “Then that same bishop said to us all: ‘The statements being read were directed against others. Or do you think that Pelagius is to be indicated?’ But if they concern Pelagius himself, state what you say.’ With your approval, I replied: ‘Pelagius told me’ (*Book of Eulogius*, title 100) ‘that he teaches that a person can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes.’ Pelagius replied in your hearing: ‘I cannot deny that I both said this and say it.’ I immediately continued: ‘The African synod condemned this in Coelestius. Bishop Augustine recoiled from it in his writings, as you have heard. He now condemns it in his response to Pelagius’ own writings. Blessed Jerome has also condemned it—Jerome whose eloquence the whole West awaits like fleece awaits dew, for many heretics have already been struck down along with their doctrines when he opposed them—and he condemned it in his letter recently addressed to Ctesiphon. Likewise, in the book he is now writing, he refutes it in an exchange composed in the form of a dialogue. For this is the slippery task of holding the dragon by the hook, so that it cannot escape (Job 40:19).

> “Bishop John, however, listening to none of this, tried to compel us to admit that we were accusers, while he himself was the judge. Everyone repeatedly answered: ‘We are not this man’s accusers. Rather, we are informing you what your brothers and our fathers thought and decreed concerning this heresy, which a layman is now publicly preaching, lest he disturb your Church—especially the Church to whose protection we have fled—without your knowledge.’ But when he repeatedly tried, under the pretense of instructing us, to lead us toward some kind of profession, he said that the Lord had said to Abraham, ‘Walk before me and be blameless’ (Genesis 17:1), and that Zechariah and Elizabeth had both been pronounced righteous before the Lord, walking in all the Lord’s commandments blamelessly (Luke 1:6). Many of us knew that he had taken this statement from Origen.

> “I answered him: ‘We are sons of the Catholic Church. Do not demand of us, Father, that we dare to be teachers above teachers or judges above judges. The fathers whom the whole Church throughout the world approves, whose communion you rejoice that we [variant: you] adhere to, have decreed that these doctrines are condemnable. It is right for us to obey those whom they approve. Why do you ask sons what they think, when you hear what the fathers decree?’

> “After he had argued at length, and while our proceedings were often either distorted or suppressed—because of the incompetence of an interpreter unknown to us, whom the eminent and devout presbyters Posserius and Avitus, and Domninus [variant: Domnus], a former military commander, repeatedly refuted for either mistranslating, omitting very much, or substituting one thing for another—Bishop John said: ‘If he had said that a person could do this without God’s help, it would be a very wicked and condemnable statement. But now, since he adds that a person can be without sin, not without God’s help, what do you say? Do you perhaps deny God’s help?’ I replied: ‘With you and the aforementioned men as witnesses, and as those who are now bearing witness, anathema to anyone who denies God’s help. I certainly do not deny it, especially since I have argued against the heretics precisely on the contrary.’

> “Then, after we had understood the judge and exposed the interpreter, we cried out that the heretic was a Latin, that we were Latins, that the heresy was more familiar to Latins, and that it ought to be debated by Latin judges. Since he was almost shamelessly thrusting himself forward as judge, although we were not accusers, and was both a single and a suspect party, many had to say: ‘No one can be both the advocate and the judge of a heretic.’ After many other matters had been discussed, Bishop John pronounced his final sentence, ultimately confirming our request and intention: that the parties and letters should be sent to the blessed Innocent, Roman pope, and that all should follow whatever he decided; but that the heretic Pelagius should remain silent for the time being, silence having been imposed upon him, and that our people should refrain from insulting a man who had been convicted and put to shame. We all agreed to this sentence. After giving thanks, making peace, and completing a prayer as a testimony to peace, we departed.

> “Now, forty-seven days later, when, on the first day of the Encaenia, as was my custom whenever I was present, I ran to attend Bishop John, I immediately received from him, in place of a greeting, the mark of a false accusation. For he said to me: ‘Why do you come to me, you who have blasphemed?’ He wished, I believe, to imply: ‘Do not touch me, because I am clean and without sin’ (Isaiah 65:5). But, conscious of nothing, I asked when, in whose hearing, or in what form the statement had been made that could be charged as blasphemy. The bishop replied: ‘I heard you say: “A person cannot be without sin even with God’s help.”’”

Thus far the acts.

I know that some have thought otherwise, such as Jansenius of Ypres (*Book I, On the Pelagian Heresy*) and Wastellus (*Book II of the Vindications*), who have attempted to cast suspicion on the credibility of the *Apology*, alleging that it sins against history, as the former thinks, and against the Catholic faith, as the latter thinks. But no one among the learned now agrees with them. The former did not sufficiently distinguish the assembly at Jerusalem from the synod at Diospolis, although this would have been easy for anyone who heard Augustine’s testimony immediately afterward. The latter scarcely seems to have seriously accused the author of the *Apology* of Novatianism and Nestorianism. Both, moved not by reason but by emotion, rejected the common understanding because this distinguished little book, by its authority—that is, by the authority of a man instructed in Catholic doctrines by both Jerome and Augustine, each an eminent teacher of the faith—was inconvenient to their own positions.

## III. SYNOD

Collected at Diospolis by Eulogius of Caesarea against Pelagius, under the Augusti Honorius X and Theodosius VI, on 20 December in the year of Christ 415.

Because John feared that, if Pelagius’ case were handled at Rome before the apostolic see, as had been decided in the assembly of the presbyters, the judgment of the Church of Carthage concerning Coelestius would be confirmed and Pelagius’ stratagems exposed, and that the crafty man would receive a sentence worthy of his errors, he wished to forestall the matter and occupy the mind of the supreme pontiff. Accordingly, he had a synod convened by Eulogius, bishop of Caesarea and primate of the province, gathering several bishops whom a malicious interpreter could easily deceive because they were ignorant of the Latin language.

[Col. 0327B] At Lydda, therefore, which is Diospolis, in the province of Caesarea of Palestine, fourteen bishops assembled: Eulogius of Caesarea, John of Jerusalem, Ammonianus, Porphyrius of Gaza, Euthonius [in the letter of Lucian: Eleutherius] of Jericho, another Porphyrius, Fidus, Zosimus, Zoboenus of Eleutheropolis, Nymphidius, Chromatius, Jovinus, Eleutherius of Sebaste, and Clematius.

The synod was held in the year of Christ 415, in the thirteenth year of Innocent, supreme pontiff, under the Augusti Honorius X and Theodosius VI, on the twentieth day of December, as is concluded from the letter of the presbyter Lucian concerning the revelation of blessed Stephen, in the following manner:

Lucian says (*Appendix to volume X of Augustine’s Works*):

> “On the day of Preparation—that is, Friday, the third day before the Nones of December—in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius for the tenth time and Theodosius for the sixth time, at the third hour of the night, as though I had fallen into an ecstasy, I saw a man, and so forth. On another day of Preparation the Lord Gamaliel appeared to me in the same manner, and so forth. Then, in the third week, on the same day and at the same hour, the aforementioned man came, and so forth. When I awoke, I went to the city, to Saint John the bishop, and when I had reported to him everything that I had seen, he wept for joy when he heard it and said, and so forth: ‘Go, dig in the heap that is in that very field, and if you find anything, report it to me.’ And so he dismissed me, and so forth. We turned toward the tomb, and while digging we found three coffins, and so forth. Immediately I reported it to the bishop, who was in Lydda, which is Diospolis, conducting the synod. He took with him two other bishops, Eleutherius of Sebaste and Eleutherius of Jericho, and they came to the place, and so forth. With psalms and hymns they carried the relics of blessed Stephen into the holy Church of Sion, and so forth. The relics of the Martyr were transferred on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.”

Thus far Lucian.

From this the time of the council, indeed almost the precise day, can be determined. For the first revelation occurred on 3 December, the second on the 10th, and the third on the 17th. John was in Jerusalem on the 18th, when Lucian approached him. On the 19th or 20th Lucian dug, found the relics, and went to Lydda, where John was conducting the synod, and from which he returned before the 25th. The council must therefore have been held between the 20th and the 23rd.

When Augustine received the long-awaited acts of this council, he composed a book *On the Proceedings in Palestine* for Aurelius of Carthage. The passages that follow were taken from it, with Augustine’s comments removed.

When the synod had assembled at Diospolis and Pelagius had been brought into the assembly, among the matters read from the written document the first charge brought against Pelagius was that he had written in one of his books that no one could be without sin unless he possessed knowledge of the Law. After it had been read, the synod said: “Did you publish this, Pelagius?” He replied: “I did say it, but not in the sense in which they understand it. I did not say that a person who possesses knowledge of the Law cannot sin, but that knowledge of the Law helps one not to sin, as it is written: ‘He gave the Law for assistance’ (Isaiah 8:20, according to the Septuagint).” The synod said: “What he has answered is certainly not alien to the faith.”

The synod said: “Let another chapter be read.” In the same book it was read that Pelagius had said that everyone is governed by his own will. After it had been read, Pelagius replied: “I said this also because of free choice, for God is the helper of the person who chooses good; but when a person sins, he himself is at fault, as one possessing free choice.” The bishops said: “This too is not alien to ecclesiastical doctrine.”

It was also read that Pelagius had stated in his book that on the day of judgment the wicked and sinners should not be spared but should be burned in eternal fires. Pelagius replied: “I said this according to the Gospel, where it is said of sinners: ‘These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life’ (Matthew 25:46). And if anyone believes otherwise, he is an Origenist.” On hearing this, the bishops approved the Catholic judgment.

Next Pelagius was charged with having written in his book that evil does not even enter into one’s thoughts. Pelagius replied: “We did not put it that way, but said that a Christian ought to strive not to think evil.” The bishops approved this answer.

Another passage was read, in which he had written that the kingdom of heaven was also promised in the Old Testament. Pelagius replied: “This can also be proved from the Scriptures. Heretics deny it in insult to the Old Testament. I followed the authority of Scripture and said so because it is written in the prophet Daniel: ‘And the saints will receive the kingdom of the Most High’ (Daniel 7:22).” After this answer had been received, the synod said: “This too is not alien to the Catholic faith.”

After this Pelagius was charged with having said in the same book that a person could be without sin if he wished, and with having written flatteringly to a widow:

> “May piety find a place with you where it has nowhere found one; may justice, a stranger everywhere else, find a home in you; may truth, which no one now recognizes, become your intimate and friend; and may the Law of God, which nearly all people despise, be honored by you alone.”

And again to the same woman:

> “How fortunate and blessed you would be if the justice which is believed to exist only in heaven were found on earth in you alone.”

And in another book addressed to her, after the prayer of our Lord and Savior, while teaching how the saints ought to pray, he said:

> “That person raises his hands worthily to God; that person pours out prayer with a good conscience who can say: ‘You know, Lord, how holy, innocent, and clean from every wickedness, iniquity, and robbery are the hands that I extend to you; how just and pure, and free from every lie, are the lips with which I offer my supplication to you, that you may have mercy on me.’”

In response Pelagius said: “We did say that a person can be without sin and keep God’s commandments if he wishes. God gave him this possibility. But we did not say that anyone is found who, from infancy to old age, has never sinned. Rather, after turning away from sins through his own labor and by God’s grace, a person can be without sin, though this does not make him incapable of turning away again afterward. As for the remaining statements they have brought forward, they are not in our books, nor have we ever said anything of the kind.”

The synod said to him: “Since you deny having written such things, do you anathematize those who hold them?” Pelagius replied: “I anathematize them as foolish, not as heretics, since this is not a dogma.” The bishops said: “Now that Pelagius has anathematized the foolish language attributed to him, correctly answering that a person can be without sin with God’s help and grace, let him answer the other chapters as well.”

Next Pelagius was confronted with the doctrines reported as having been found in the teaching of his disciple Coelestius: that Adam was created mortal and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin; that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race; that the Law leads to the kingdom in the same way as the Gospel; that before Christ’s coming there were people without sin; that newborn infants are in the same state in which Adam was before the transgression; and that the whole human race does not rise through Christ’s resurrection. These charges were presented as matters that had also been heard and condemned at Carthage by Aurelius and his fellow bishops.

Some other chapters were then brought forward, with Augustine’s name mentioned, which had been sent to him from Sicily when the Catholic brethren there were being troubled by such questions. They were these: that a person can be without sin if he wishes; that infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life; and that baptized rich people, unless they renounce everything, are not credited with whatever good they may appear to do and cannot possess the kingdom of God.

To these charges Pelagius replied: “That a person can be without sin has already been stated. Concerning the claim that there were people without sin before the Lord’s coming, we also say that some lived holy and righteous lives before Christ’s coming, according to the tradition of the Holy Scriptures. As for the remaining statements, they were not made by me, according to their own testimony, and I ought not to answer for them. Nevertheless, for the satisfaction of the holy synod, I anathematize those who hold or have ever held such doctrines.”

The synod said: “The present Pelagius has given a sufficient and proper answer to these aforementioned chapters, anathematizing those that were not his.”

Next Pelagius was charged with saying that the Church here on earth is without spot or wrinkle. He replied: “We said this in the following sense: the Church is cleansed from every spot and wrinkle by the washing, and the Lord wishes it to remain so.” The synod said: “This also pleases us.”

Next the contents of the various chapters of Coelestius’ book were brought forward, more according to their meaning than their wording, for Coelestius develops them at greater length. Those who had produced the written charge against Pelagius said that they could not set out all the material at that time. Thus, in the first chapter of Coelestius’ book, it was said to be written that we do more than what is commanded in the Law and the Gospel.

Pelagius replied: “They presented this as though it were ours. We said it, however, according to the Apostle, concerning virginity, about which Paul says: ‘I have no commandment of the Lord’ (1 Corinthians 7:25).” The synod said: “The Church also accepts this.”

Other capital charges from Coelestius’ book were then brought against Pelagius. In the third chapter Coelestius was said to have written that God’s grace and help are not given for individual acts, but are found in free choice or in the Law and teaching. He was also said to have written that God’s grace is given according to our merits, because if God gives it to sinners, he appears unjust. He added these words:

> “Therefore grace itself has been placed in my will, whether I should become worthy or unworthy. For if we do everything by grace, then when we are overcome by sin, it is not we who are overcome but God’s grace, which wished to help us in every way and was unable to do so.”

He is also said to have written:

> “If it is God’s grace when we overcome sins, then it is also to blame when we are overcome by sin, because it either could not or did not wish to guard us completely.”

To these statements Pelagius replied: “Those who say that these are Coelestius’ statements must see to it themselves whether they are his. I have never held such views, but I anathematize anyone who holds them.”

The synod said: “The holy synod accepts you, since you condemn these reprehensible statements in this way.”

Next, from the fifth chapter of Coelestius, Pelagius was charged with affirming that every person can possess all virtues and graces, and with removing the diversity of graces taught by the Apostle. Pelagius replied: “We did say this, but they criticized it maliciously and incompetently. We do not remove the diversity of graces; rather, we say that God grants every grace to the person who is worthy to receive them all, just as he granted them to the Apostle Paul.” The synod said: “You have also understood the gift of graces consistently with ecclesiastical teaching and with the meaning of the holy Apostle.”

After this it was charged that the sixth chapter of Coelestius’ book states that the children of God cannot be called such unless they have become entirely without sin; that the seventh chapter states that forgetfulness and ignorance are not subject to sin, because they occur not according to the will but according to necessity; that the tenth chapter states that free choice does not exist if it needs God’s help, since each person has it in his own will either to do something or not to do it; and that the twelfth chapter states that our victory comes not from God’s help but from free choice. The latter was said to be expressed in these words:

> “The victory is ours, because by our own will we took up arms; conversely, defeat is ours, because by our own will we refused to arm ourselves.”

He also brought forward the testimony of the Apostle Peter that we are partakers of the divine nature, and constructed the following syllogism: if the soul cannot be without sin, then God too is subject to sin, since the soul, which is a part of him, is subject to sin. In the thirteenth chapter he says that forgiveness is not granted to penitents according to God’s grace and mercy, but according to the merits and labor of those who have become worthy of mercy through repentance.

After these passages had been read, the synod said: “What does the present Pelagius the monk say concerning these chapters that have been read? For the holy synod and the holy Catholic Church of God condemn them.”

Pelagius replied: “I say again that these statements also are not mine, according to their own testimony, and that I am not required to answer for them, as I have said. Those which I have acknowledged as mine I affirm to be correct. But those which I have said are not mine I condemn according to the judgment of the holy Church, pronouncing anathema on anyone who opposes or contradicts the teachings of the holy Catholic Church. For I believe in the Trinity of one substance, and in all things according to the teaching of the holy Catholic Church. But if anyone thinks otherwise than this, let him be anathema.”

The synod said: “Now that we have been satisfied by the answers of the present Pelagius the monk, who has agreed with pious teachings and rejected and anathematized what is contrary to the faith of the Church, we confess that he belongs to ecclesiastical communion and to the Catholic Church.”

Thus far the acts.

The two Gallican bishops, Eros and Lazarus, brought the accusation—not personally and orally, since the illness of one of them prevented both from being present, but by sending a written statement containing two heads of accusation, one against Pelagius and the other against Coelestius (*On the Proceedings*, chapter 35). The excerpt was taken from only two of Pelagius’ books, *Testimonies* and *To a Widow*—remarkably, not from his *Commentaries on Paul*. The material concerning Coelestius was taken partly from his books and partly from Hilary’s letter to Augustine. Augustine summarized everything as follows:

> “In this,” he says (*On the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 35), “the whole of this heresy consists:
>
> 1. That Adam was created mortal and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin.
>
> 2. That Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race.
>
> 3. That the Law leads to the kingdom in the same way as the Gospel.
>
> 4. That newborn infants are in the state in which Adam was before the transgression.
>
> 5. That neither through Adam’s death or transgression does the whole human race die, nor through Christ’s resurrection does the whole human race rise.
>
> 6. That infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.
>
> 7. That baptized rich people, unless they renounce everything, are not credited with whatever good they may appear to do, and cannot possess the kingdom of God.
>
> 8. That God’s grace and help are not given for individual acts, but are found in free choice and in the Law and teaching.
>
> 9. That God’s grace is given according to our merits, and that grace itself has therefore been placed in the human will, whether a person becomes worthy or unworthy.
>
> 10. That the children of God cannot be called such unless they have become entirely without sin.
>
> 11. That forgetfulness and ignorance are not subject to sin, because they occur not according to the will but according to necessity.
>
> 12. That free choice does not exist if it needs God’s help, because each person has his own will either to do something or not to do it.
>
> 13. That our victory comes not from God’s help but from free choice.
>
> 14. That, from Peter’s statement that we are partakers of the divine nature, it follows that the soul can be without sin in the same way as God.
>
> 15. That forgiveness is not granted to penitents according to God’s grace and mercy, but according to the merit and labor of those who have become worthy of mercy through repentance.”

The judges approved Pelagius, who denied that all these matters, together with any arguments inserted to confirm them, were his own and anathematized them; they therefore declared that, by rejecting and anathematizing them, he had condemned doctrines contrary to the ecclesiastical faith.

Pelagius thus deceitfully stole an acquittal from Greek-speaking men, to whom he gave ambiguous answers through an interpreter who was not entirely faithful. Augustine repeatedly makes this accusation against Pelagius himself and against other Pelagians (*On the Proceedings*, *On the Grace of Christ*, and elsewhere).

Although Augustine praised this synod magnificently, and although it is commonly celebrated by everyone as the Church’s first victory over the Pelagian error, Jerome nevertheless calls it pitiable: partly because Pelagius deceived the Fathers, diverting the condemnation he deserved through repeated lies; partly because, after sending letters to the provinces (Letter 24 in Augustine), he persuaded not a few credulous people that his doctrines had been approved; and finally because Pelagius’ followers, growing insolent, proceeded to such audacity that, after forming a band of criminals, they inflicted the most wicked slaughter on God’s servants and handmaids attached to the care of the presbyter Saint Jerome, killed a deacon, and burned the monastery buildings. Only a more strongly fortified tower, by God’s mercy, scarcely protected Jerome himself from this attack and assault by the impious (*Augustine, On the Proceedings*, chapter 35).

[Col. 0331C] The holy old man may have been referring to this synod—or rather to the assembly of the presbyters—when, indignant that silence was being imposed on the defenders of the faith while the enemies dared everything, he uttered a fitting sentence, or rather a vow:

> “May a feigned peace not take away what war has preserved” (*Preface to the Dialogue against the Pelagians*).

## IV. SYNOD

Convened by Aurelius at Carthage against the absent Pelagius and Coelestius, under the consuls Theodosius Augustus VII and Junius IV Palladius, around the autumn of the year of Christ 416.

The fourth synod, the second Carthaginian synod in the case of the Pelagians, was convened by Aurelius in the year 416, around the autumn.

Sixty-eight bishops of the proconsular province attended; their names are listed in the synodical letter to Innocent, which will shortly be discussed.

The date can be established partly from Innocent’s reply to the synodical letter, given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus XI and Constantius II, and partly from canon 73 of the African code, provided that it is read as it stands in Greek:

> “It was decided that the same day should be observed for the council as had been established at the Council of Hippo—that is, the tenth day before the Kalends of September—and that it should be written to the primates of each province, so that, whenever they convene a council in their own territories, they may observe this day.”

The year is readily known from Innocent’s letters, and the month and day from the canon. For the pontiff replied at the beginning of the following year, and the Fathers write that they had assembled at the Church of Carthage according to custom—that is, at the time which Aurelius himself had established fourteen years earlier.

This canon has always caused me difficulty. Although the Greek reads:

> δεῖ γὰρ καὶ γραφῆναι πρὸς τοὺς πρωτεύοντας πασῶν τῶν ἐπαρχιῶν, ἵνα ὅτε παρ᾽ ἑαυτοῖς σύνοδον προσκαλοῦνται ταύτην τὴν ἡμέραν φυλάττωσιν

—that is, “For it must also be written to the primates of all the provinces, so that whenever they convene a synod in their own territories they may observe this day”—these words seem to mean that the primates were to convene their own synods on the specified day.

The Latin text, however, which is certainly the original and more deserving of confidence, gives an entirely different and opposite sense: namely, that the primates should not obstruct the appointed day of the plenary council by holding their provincial synods, so that the bishops might come freely to it on the tenth day before the Kalends of September. Since the Greek text appears to command that provincial synods be convened on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, while the Latin forbids this, the disputed word φυλάττωσιν—“they may observe”—must be interpreted to mean that the day of the tenth before the Kalends of September is to be preserved free from impediments.

Since this meaning is entirely straightforward, it might at once seem to weaken the force of the argument just advanced. Yet it rather confirms it, if we appeal to the original source, namely, the fifth canon of Nicaea, which subsequent ages treated as an established rule for convening synods. It reads as follows:

> “It was decided that councils should be held twice each year in every province, so that, with all the bishops of the province assembled together, such questions might be examined in common”—namely, questions concerning those rejected or excommunicated by a bishop. “Let councils be held: one before the forty days of Easter, so that, every disagreement having been removed, a perfectly pure offering may be made to God; and the second around the time of autumn.”

That this canon cannot refer to universal councils of an entire diocese is proved by the authority of the ancients, as well as by the following consideration: since cities of lesser sees were often separated from a city of a greater see—for example, Antioch or Alexandria—by immense distances, nearly the whole year would have had to be spent traveling back and forth, while a synod was to be held twice each year. The canon therefore applies only to provincial councils, which history shows were once convened everywhere at those fixed times and which custom still causes to be convened.

I therefore think that it can correctly be inferred from the canon of the African code cited in support of the argument that, around the tenth day before the Kalends of September, certain primates formerly used to convene provincial synods. Otherwise the Fathers would have enacted without reason a law preventing private assemblies from obstructing the time of the universal council. Others held their councils around the time of autumn, that is, toward the end of September, so that when the delegates returned from the universal council, they could report to their fellow bishops of the province what had been handled in common. The custom of the former was approved; that of the latter rejected.

“But,” you will say, “provincial synods ought to have been convened not in the month of September, but on the tenth day before the Kalends of September—that is, one month earlier—for delegates were sent from provincial synods to the universal council, as can be gathered from several of the African canons.”

The matter is otherwise. In the earlier synod, which preceded the forty days of Easter, delegates were chosen and prepared themselves so that, as soon as the summons of the primate of all Africa arrived, they could go to the appointed place. After returning from the universal council, they were to report what had been done at the later autumn synod.

Since we have digressed, the reader should be reminded in passing that the Fathers of Nicaea and the Africans established the time for holding synods within the interval extending from Pentecost to the Nativity of Christ, and from the Nativity to the forty days of Lent. They wished the bishops to attend the synods in large numbers, but did not want anyone to be absent from his own Church during the more solemn feasts, at which either baptism was celebrated—as at the Resurrection of Christ and Pentecost—or the coming Easter was announced—as at the Nativity.

This observation is useful for determining the date of synods when it is recorded in less conspicuous chronological indications. It never fails unless some extraordinary necessity is pressing.

The bishops had various reasons for assembling, but the chief was this: after learning from Orosius’ report and from the letters of Eros and Lazarus how greatly Pelagius had deceived the Fathers at Diospolis, and how much harm the affairs of the Catholic Church would suffer from this apparent acquittal, they thought that the evil had to be confronted and the authority of the apostolic see invoked.

They reviewed what had taken place there with Coelestius nearly five years earlier, so that the Fathers might appear not to judge openly in opposition to the canonical prohibition against judging absent persons, but merely to confirm, by the judgment of the whole province and the supreme authority of the apostolic see, what had formerly been done when he was present.
