Therefore they wrote a synodical letter to the supreme pontiff, in which they set out only two doctrines of the Pelagian error: the one concerning the necessity of divine grace for works of piety, and the other concerning the baptism of infants, for the removal of original sin. These, indeed, are the two principal points of nearly everything which the deacon Paulinus had charged against Coelestius at the earlier council.

*(Garnerius next gives the synodical letter of the Council of Carthage. Since we have already published it among the letters of Pope Saint Innocent I, see it there, namely in volume XX of this Patrology, column 564.)*

## V. SYNOD

Convened at Milevis by Silvanus the Elder, or Primate of the Province of Numidia, against the same heretics, under the same consuls, around the end of October in the year of Christ 416.

At almost the same time and for the same reason—namely, on account of Pelagius and Coelestius—the fifth synod was held by sixty-one Fathers of the province of Numidia in the city of Milevis. Silvanus, the senior of the province, presided, and by that right was the primate and president of the council. These matters, however, must be explained more distinctly and clearly.

As I have said, it was held at almost the same time as the Council of Carthage. The Fathers indicate that some interval intervened when they write in the synodical letter that they imitated the bishops of the province of Carthage, whom they had learned to have written to the apostolic see concerning this matter. See Letter 94, which is Augustine’s letter to Bishop Hilary.

They acted for the same reason, which they explained in words that make these two points the heads of the whole heresy:

> These are the two things, they say, by which they endeavor utterly to overthrow everything on which our being Christians depends, and by which faithful hearts are sustained: that God should not be asked to be our helper against the evil of sin and for the performance of righteousness; and that the sacrament of Christian grace does not aid infants in attaining eternal life.

They clearly meant Pelagius and Coelestius, whose names they reported in the following manner:

> The authors of this most pernicious error are said to be Pelagius and Coelestius. We preferred that they be healed within the Church rather than, their salvation having been despaired of, be cut off from the Church, if no necessity compelled it. One of them, namely Coelestius, is also said to have attained the presbyterate in Asia. Your Holiness will be better informed by the Church of Carthage concerning what happened a few years ago in his case. Pelagius, however, as the letters sent by certain of our brethren report, is said, while established at Jerusalem, to be deceiving some people.

Note concerning the words “whom we preferred within the Church,” and so forth: according to this council, whose mind was Augustine’s, the authors of the heresy had not been deprived of communion. They could not rightly have been so deprived, not only because both were absent from the judgment and were said to be accused solely through the written statements of their accusers, but also—and especially—because, since the entire matter had been referred to the supreme judge, his decision had to be awaited.

“By sixty-one Fathers”: that many names are mentioned in the synodical letter, among whom three distinguished men were present: Augustine, Alypius, and Possidius.

“In the city of Milevis” (Collation 8). This does not mean that Silvanus, as senior of the whole province and therefore its lawful primate, had summoned the bishops to his own city by an official summons. For he did not preside over the Church of Milevis, but over the Summensian, or Zamensian, Church, as can be seen in the subscriptions to the mandate read in the first session of the Carthaginian conference. Rather, Milevis was more convenient for assembling the Fathers, since it lay almost in the middle of Numidia, as may be conjectured. For this city, although so celebrated—whether because councils, even plenary councils, were held there, or because of Optatus, its bishop—is not found, so far as I know, either in descriptions of ancient Africa, in the Itinerary of Antoninus, or in the old histories, except where it is named in connection with councils and Optatus.

Some think that Milevis is the same as Mileum, which Antoninus mentions in his Itinerary and whose location is shown on the maps of Ptolemy, although the name is somewhat corrupted, between Cirta Julia and Sitifis. They support this opinion by the fact that at the fifth synod Bishop Restitutus is said to have been from Mileion in the province of Numidia, and by the close resemblance between the names Mileum and Milevis. Ferrarius holds this view in his *Geographical Lexicon*, and says that the city is now called Mela, but that formerly it was an episcopal see under the archbishop of Carthage. These points, however, have their difficulties. The Church of Milevis was in the province of Numidia, which formerly had its own primate; it was not in the proconsular province, whose capital was Carthage. Furthermore, in the *List of the African Provinces* published by Father Sirmond, Benenatus of Milevis is listed among the bishops of Numidia, while Patera of Milianum is listed among the bishops of Caesarean Mauretania; yet Milianum appears to be the same as Mileum. Moreover, an error could have crept into Restitutus’s subscription in the eighth conference of the fifth synod, since in all the other conferences he is said merely to be of the African province. Finally, Ortelius, an especially learned geographer, distinguishes Milevis from Mileum, and Ferrarius gives no reason for departing from Ortelius.

Nevertheless, two considerations compel me to agree with Ferrarius—or rather with Balduinus. First, I can scarcely believe that so celebrated a city was omitted by the geographers, especially since it had a region bearing its own name, as is clear from Augustine’s Letter 129. Second, the great similarity of the names Milevis and Mileum, or Mireum, as Ptolemy has it, makes it difficult to doubt that they are one and the same city. I would therefore rather accuse Ortelius of placing Mileum in Caesarean Mauretania and of making the boundary between Mauretania and Numidia narrower than the river Ampsaga, since in doing so he acts against Ptolemy, than leave this city—made famous by councils and by so many bishops—without a location or geographical setting. I do not deny, however, that the *List of the African Provinces* creates a difficulty, as does the fact that a bishop of Milianum is mentioned elsewhere as well. Perhaps the name should have been Manlianum. There is a city called Manliana in Ptolemy, in Caesarean Mauretania near the Garaphian Mountains, not far from the river Savus.

But, to return to the point from which we digressed: a letter was written from the synod of Milevis to Pope Innocent in almost the same form, indeed in the same style, as that from the Council of Carthage. Hence learned men, not without a reasonable conjecture, believe that Augustine was the author of both. For immediately after the Council of Carthage he met with Aurelius and Evodius, accompanied by Alypius and Possidius, before Julius, the bearer of the synodical letters, set out for the Roman pontiff. Those five bishops also gave him other letters, which they call personal letters. We shall speak of these later. The Milevitan synodical letter runs as follows.

*(This Milevitan synodical letter too, like the Carthaginian one mentioned above, has already been printed by us in the same volume XX, at column 568.)*

Apart from this letter, nothing of the synod remains. Although there have been, and still are, those who call the eight celebrated canons of the African Church against the Pelagian heresy “Milevitan,” very few now do so as a matter of conviction; the rest retain the older and more popular designation. Learned men know that these canons were first called by that name solely because of the prejudiced authority of an ancient collector, and that there is no basis for saying that they were enacted in either of the two councils of Milevis. They were not enacted at the first, universal council, since it was convened in 402, when the Pelagian heresy had not yet arisen, or at least had not yet become known to the Africans. Nor were they enacted at the second, provincial council, since Augustine testifies that they were established at a plenary council of all Africa, the code of canons having been sent by Hadrian I to Charlemagne at the Council of Carthage.

## VI. SYNOD

Held at Carthage by five bishops, under the same consuls and for the same reason, toward the end of the same year.

The authority of Marius Mercator compels us to place, as the sixth synod, the meeting of the five bishops Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Evodius, and Possidius at Carthage. He speaks of it as follows (*Commonitorium*, chapter 13, no. 13):

> The reason why Pelagius and Coelestius were condemned by Innocent of holy memory was as follows. After the devastation of the city of Rome, Pelagius was living in Palestine. Certain zealous bishops found books of his in which many and various things appeared to have been written against the Catholic faith. These books, together with letters, were sent to the Fathers and bishops in Africa, where, after three councils had been assembled, the said books were read. Thereupon, after reports had been sent to Rome and the books themselves likewise transmitted, the apostolic decision was issued in reply; it deprived those same men, Coelestius and Pelagius, of ecclesiastical communion. We have copies of those documents in our hands.

Since we read of no council assembled in the other provinces of Africa apart from the councils of Carthage and Milevis—either one at which Pelagius’s books could have been read together with the letters of Eros and Lazarus, brought from the East to the Fathers and bishops of Africa by Orosius, or one whose report Innocent answered by depriving Pelagius and Coelestius of ecclesiastical communion—we must admit that one of the three councils mentioned by Mercator was the meeting of the five bishops, since everything fits it perfectly and fits no other. For the books of the heretics were read by five bishops; Orosius, who narrated the proceedings at Diospolis, was heard; letters from the Gallic bishops, sent from the East, were received; books were sent to Rome, both Pelagius’s *On Nature* and Augustine’s reply, *On Nature and Grace*; a letter was written to Innocent; and a response was received from him by which Pelagius was condemned. All this is established partly from the bishops’ letter to Innocent and partly from Innocent’s reply to the bishops.

Moreover, Augustine appears to support Marius when he prescribes for Valentinus and his monks the reading of what was written to Pope Innocent, Bishop of the city of Rome, concerning the council of the province of Carthage, concerning the council of Numidia, and, somewhat more fully, by the five bishops, as well as what he himself replied to those three bodies, and so forth (*Letter 215*).

Nor did Marius improperly give this meeting the name of a council, since it consisted of the foremost Fathers of all Africa, indeed of the Western Church: especially Aurelius and Augustine, the former its leader and the latter, as Prosper calls him, the intellect of councils (*Poem against the Ungrateful*, chapter 2). Certainly, when the emperor Honorius summoned from Africa eight most holy and learned bishops to the Council of Spoleto, he wrote to all these men except Possidius, whom he may have known to be Augustine’s inseparable companion (Baronius, *Annals*, under the year of Christ 419, no. 22).

The reason why those five met and, not content with the synodical letters of the two provinces, sent additional letters to the supreme pontiff—letters considerably longer, in which the entire case was explained—was, I think, this. The Pelagian party was boasting that their affairs were not judged in Rome in the same way as in Africa; that Innocent had been persuaded by their doctrine; and that the presbyter Sixtus, a man of great reputation and a distinguished light of the Roman Church, together with all the most eminent clergy, favored them. They said these and other things falsely, but so artfully and boldly that, even among good people, they produced at least a serious suspicion, if not complete belief. The supreme pontiff therefore seemed to need warning about the slander of these wicked liars, and indeed fuller instruction about the matter, lest he should suffer some human weakness in the case, or—an error that had befallen many eminent men, including Paulinus and Sulpicius Severus—extend excessive credulity to people who appeared religious and thus, as a shepherd who was not sufficiently courageous, fail to keep wolves in sheep’s clothing away from Christ’s fold.

*(Here Garnerius gives the synodical letter to Pope Innocent under the names of Augustine, Evodius, and Possidius. See it in the same volume XX of this Library mentioned above, column 572.)*

## VII. SYNOD

Held at Rome against Pelagius and Coelestius by Innocent I, under the consulship of Honorius XI and Constantius II, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the year 417.

After receiving three letters from Africa, Saint Innocent convened a synod at Rome. From there he replied to each African synod with a separate letter, which he himself calls decretal letters. All of them are worthy of so great a pontiff, whatever Erasmus may have uttered against them. All are full of the apostolic spirit: they defend the rights of the Roman see, expound the true faith, deprive the heretics of ecclesiastical communion, extend a father’s arms to those returning from error, and grant the African bishops not only the power to bestow absolution but also an express command to do so.

The date of this synod, the first Roman synod in the Pelagian controversy, is clearly stated in the letters, since they are dated on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, under the consulship of Honorius and Constantius—that is, 27 January in the year of Christ 417.

That Innocent issued his reply as the result of a synod seems to me beyond doubt. But anyone who wishes to establish this from these words of Gennadius (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 44)—“Innocent, Bishop of the city of Rome, wrote a decree given to the Western and Eastern Churches against the Pelagians”—will certainly labor in vain. For the words “of the Western Churches and of the Eastern” do not mean what would nevertheless be required: that the decree originated from the Western Churches. Otherwise it would have to be called a universal council of the West and East, which is entirely contrary to the facts. Moreover, Gennadius’s passage is plainly defective, since it lacks the word “bishops,” which is necessary—as though it said that Innocent wrote a decree of the Western Churches and gave it to the bishops of the East. Concerning this, the *Pontifical Book* undoubtedly reads: “Here he made a constitution concerning the whole Church,” that is, a constitution to be observed throughout the whole Church.

It is therefore better to prove that a synod was held from the fact that Innocent, being extremely observant of ecclesiastical custom, followed in sending his decree the same rule used in this age by the supreme pontiffs, both predecessors and successors. It was their established practice, scarcely less than a religious obligation, to write decretal letters—especially on doctrines—only in a council, and then send them throughout the world. Thus Siricius wrote to Himerius of Tarragona concerning the rebaptism of Arians; to the Church of Milan against Jovinian; and to the Africans concerning the reception of Novatians and Montensians. Anastasius wrote to John of Jerusalem concerning the errors of Origen and to Rufinus of Aquileia. Zosimus wrote to all the bishops concerning the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius. Celestine wrote to Cyril and others concerning the impiety of Nestorius. Sixtus wrote to John of Antioch and the Easterners concerning the peace of the Church. Leo the Great wrote to Flavian against Eutyches. Hilary wrote to the bishops of the province of Tarragona concerning unlawful ordinations. Finally, Felix III wrote to Peter the Fuller of Alexandria, whom he deposed on account of heresy, and to the emperor Zeno, whose *Henoticon* he rejected.

Furthermore, as Lucas Holstenius learnedly observed (*Notes on the Roman Synod under Boniface II*), the Roman pontiffs had it as an established custom to hear bishops who came to them from the provinces concerning important matters, and especially from councils, in an assembly not only of the city clergy but also of the bishops who were either in the city or summoned from neighboring places. Bishop Julius had come from the African councils with synodical letters, intending to report to the pontiff on a matter of the greatest importance, and one involving doctrine.

What was done in this synod is clear from Innocent’s letters. Two Pelagian errors were condemned and two Catholic doctrines defended: the one concerning the necessity of grace, and the other concerning the baptism of infants on account of original sin. An anathema was pronounced against the authors and followers of the errors unless they repented; pardon was offered to those who repented, and the manner in which that pardon was to be granted was prescribed.

The outcome, and how sacred Innocent’s decree was regarded by everyone, is well known: first from Augustine, who in many places likes to use Innocent’s words to refute the Pelagians, especially Julian, since Julian had been ordained by Innocent; then from the African Fathers, who determined that the sentence pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius by the venerable Bishop Innocent from the seat of the most blessed Apostle Peter should stand (*Prosper, Against the Collator*, chapter 10); indeed also from Coelestius himself, who, in order to prove himself Catholic, condemned everything charged against him in accordance with the judgment of Saint Innocent; and finally from Pope Zosimus, who vehemently pressed Coelestius to agree with Innocent’s letters as with a rule of certain faith. Zosimus followed the footsteps of his predecessor so religiously that Gennadius appears to call the letter he wrote to all the bishops of the world concerning the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius a pure promulgation of Innocent’s decree (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 43).

You will notice, reader, not without profit, that after Innocent’s decretal letters had been brought to Africa, Augustine delivered the sermon commonly called the second *On the Words of the Apostle*, largely against the Pelagians. Some were afraid to bring them before an ecclesiastical judgment, but Augustine concluded the sermon by openly expressing his view of the authority of the apostolic see:

> Wherever you find such men, do not conceal them. Let there be no perverse mercy among you. Indeed, wherever you find such men, do not conceal them; rebuke those who contradict, and bring those who resist to us. For two councils have already sent [or: have been sent] concerning this matter to the apostolic see. Replies have also come from there. THE CASE IS CLOSED; WOULD THAT THE ERROR MIGHT SOME DAY BE CLOSED AS WELL! And so forth.

You will also observe, not without some astonishment, that scarcely any decree of a supreme pontiff can be found in which the rights of the apostolic see in matters of faith and in the treatment of other major affairs are extolled more magnificently. Yet none was received by the Africans with equal praise or equal reverence—not merely greater praise, but even comparable praise. By this one fact alone the African Church sufficiently exposes the bad faith of those who boast that she supplies them with weapons against the apostolic see.

But now those noble decretal letters must be presented, cleansed of the errors with which they had hitherto been so saturated that they inspired readers either with disgust or with contempt for themselves. In purifying them we used several manuscript codices, but especially the very ancient one of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, whose use was granted to us by the most devout and learned Dom Lucas Dacherius.

*(For the letter of Pope Innocent to the bishops of Africa reproduced here, see Garnerius in the same preceding volume XX, column 582.)*

## VIII. SYNOD

Convened at Constantinople by Atticus against Coelestius, under the same consuls, in the year 417.

On account of Coelestius alone, as the ancients put it, Atticus held the eighth synod, the first Constantinopolitan synod in the matter of the Pelagian heresy. Augustine speaks of it briefly (*Against Julian*, Book III, chapter 1):

> The army of Christ, spread everywhere, conquered Coelestius at Carthage, when I myself was not present. And again: the Constantinopolitans, far removed from the African regions, and so forth.

Mercator gives a fuller account (*Commonitorium*, chapter 1, no. 4):

> Then, after several years, he went to the city of Constantinople under Bishop Atticus of holy memory. There, having been exposed in similar matters, he was expelled from that blessed city through the great zeal of that holy man, and letters concerning him were sent to the bishops in Asia, Thessalonica, and Carthage. We have copies of them and are prepared to produce them. The aforementioned Coelestius, however, after being expelled from there as well, proceeded with all haste to the city of Rome under Bishop Zosimus of holy memory, and so forth.

Three matters, however, may be questioned. First, whether Atticus truly held a synod, or merely conducted a private judgment. Second, when he held it. Finally, whether Prosper, in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, or Saint Celestine in his letter to Nestorius, mentioned this synod.

The last question will more appropriately be settled later in the negative.

As to the second, Mercator, in my opinion, answers quite clearly:

> The aforementioned Coelestius, after being expelled from here—from Constantinople—proceeded with all haste to the city of Rome.

From this it is perfectly clear that Coelestius fled from Constantinople to Rome at the beginning of Zosimus’s pontificate. Zosimus began his pontificate in March of the year 417, as we demonstrated in the notes to the *Commonitorium*, and spent a considerable period examining the case of Coelestius, which he finally concluded around May of 418. If, then, a synod was held at Constantinople, from which Coelestius fled and proceeded with all haste to Rome while Zosimus already occupied the apostolic see, it must have been held in the first year of Zosimus’s pontificate, that is, in the year of Christ 417.

The same author resolves the first doubt no less clearly when he says that Atticus sent letters concerning Coelestius to the bishops in Asia, Thessalonica, and Carthage. For in that period it was not customary for denunciatory official letters to be sent by any bishop to major sees and entire dioceses—such as Asia, Macedonia, or Africa—unless they proceeded from a council at which someone had been condemned in accordance with the canons and the sentence of condemnation was announced to the whole Church, insofar as it was concerned.

This custom, indeed this law, deserves very careful notice. It contributes greatly to the clarification of ecclesiastical history and to establishing, wherever necessary, a distinction between private letters and synodical letters. Examples establishing this custom may be found in Lucas Holstenius’s notes on the Roman synod mentioned shortly before.

Mercator had synodical letters sent to the major sees before him—letters that contained either the acts themselves or at least an abridgment of the acts—when he presented his *Commonitorium*. If only he had transmitted them to us together with the acts, as he transmitted many other things gathered at no greater cost! They would undoubtedly have shed great light on the history of Pelagianism.

## IX. SYNOD

Held at Rome by Zosimus in the case of Coelestius, under the consulship of Honorius XI and Constantius II, around September in the year of Christ 417.

Zosimus held the ninth synod, the second Roman synod, in the basilica of Clement, at the insistence of Coelestius, in the first year of his pontificate, the year of Christ 417, around the beginning of September at the latest. All these matters are established partly from Zosimus’s letters to the Africans and partly from Augustine, Marius, Mercator, and other writers of the same period; they must nevertheless be explained in greater detail.

That the supreme pontiff held an assembly of bishops, rather than merely conducting a private judgment, would easily be established if what the distinguished Marca, Archbishop of Paris, wrote were true (*On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, Book VII, chapter 6, no. 5): namely, that in matters of faith an appeal had once been made not so much to the apostolic see as to the Roman synod. Since Coelestius’s case concerned the faith, it would have had to be discussed by the judgment to which the appeal had been made. But although that learned man has supported his opinion concerning Eutyches with suitable testimony, in the case of Coelestius, Pelagius, and even Theodore, he will scarcely convince anyone except a highly credulous person, since the ancient writers do not even hint at anything of the kind.

It is therefore better to gather arguments elsewhere to prove what we maintain. The following words of the deacon Paulinus do indeed prove it (*Booklet to Zosimus*, in Baronius’s *Annals* under the year 418):

> Against these things his own teacher, Pelagius, also contends: he who condemned in the Eastern judgment the very things which this man attempts to establish IN THE ASSEMBLY OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE.

That these words must be understood of the earlier judgment instituted by Zosimus is clear from the fact that Coelestius was not present at the later one, but, despairing of his cause, withdrew and refused to submit to the examination, as Augustine says (*To Boniface*, Book II, chapter 3); or, as Mercator says (*Commonitorium*, chapter 1, no. 5), he not only failed to appear but also fled from the city of Rome.

The statements Mercator writes in the same place also prove the point, for they plainly concern the later judgment:

> He was summoned to a fuller hearing, so that he might hasten to fulfill what he had promised at the earlier hearing, and so forth.

For what is a fuller hearing if not an assembly more numerous than some earlier one? Zosimus indicates clearly enough that the earlier assembly was a substantial one and included many bishops when he says (*Letter 1 to the Africans*) that he admonished not only Coelestius but also all the priests who were present at that time from various regions, and so forth.

The place where the assembly was held also proves the point: namely, the basilica of Saint Clement. Temples were used for no other business than sacred affairs, that is, councils. See Holstenius’s notes on the Roman synod under Boniface II.

Finally, the words “acts and proceedings” prove it. Zosimus uses them, as does Augustine (*To Boniface*, Book II, chapter 3), when speaking of this very judgment.

From Augustine’s words it is plainly established that this assembly consisted not merely of several bishops, as Zosimus indicates in the passage just cited, but also of the entire Roman clergy. For he says:

> Moreover, they accuse the Roman clergy, writing that, struck by the terror of a command, they were not ashamed to admit the crime of betrayal, so that, contrary to THE EARLIER SENTENCE, by which in the proceedings they had supported Catholic doctrine, they later declared that human nature was evil, and so forth.

A little later he adds:

> For amid so many and such important ecclesiastical letters passing back and forth between the apostolic see and the African bishops, including the proceedings concerning this matter conducted in that see while Coelestius was present and responding, and so forth.

Zosimus speaks plainly about the place and the cause (*the letter cited above*):

> The presbyter Coelestius thrust himself into our examination, asking that the things which had been reported about him to the apostolic see otherwise than they ought to have been be cleared up, and so forth. On the day of the inquiry we sat in the basilica of Saint Clement, and so forth.

As for the date, the year is learned from Zosimus’s earlier letters to the Africans, while the month is learned from his later letters. The former are dated under the consulship of Honorius XI and Flavius Constantius, which was the year of Christ 417 and the first year of Zosimus. The latter are dated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. Since they followed the first letters sent from the synod, yet not immediately—for frequent professions by Coelestius intervened—it is reasonable to believe that the first letters were written around the end of August or the beginning of September, and that the synod was held at that time.

The Pontiff now writes that Pelagius’s letter and booklet, together with letters sent by Praylius to Innocent on Pelagius’s behalf, were publicly read in another assembly. They were heard with such universal rejoicing that tears flowed from some out of emotion, while many were astonished that men of such unshaken faith could have been defamed. He then adds details by which some later critics, who were more exacting and did not approve the most excellent pontiff’s more humane *οἰκονομία*—that is, his pastoral accommodation or prudential policy—thought that he could rightly have been accused and could scarcely have been adequately defended by Augustine. See what we noted on the first chapter of Marius Mercator’s *Commonitorium*.

Almost everything we have reported thus far is drawn from Zosimus’s letters to the Africans. Although Baronius reported them as obtained from the Vatican records (*Annals*, under the year of Christ 417, nos. 19 and following), the learned Marcus Antonius Cappellus of the Franciscan order rejects them as though they had been fabricated by the Pelagians in order to bring hatred upon the holy pontiff and the African Fathers. We shall dispute this matter with him when place and time permit, but first the letters must be produced as the acts of the synod—and in a form much more carefully corrected than that in which they appear in the annals. *(See also Zosimus’s letters in the volume already cited several times, XX, columns 649 and 654.)*

It is now time to address the question raised concerning these letters by the learned Cappellus, who considers them forged. The question is neither one that cannot be settled by the testimony of the ancients nor difficult, since nothing asserted by Cappellus is compelling; indeed, it collapses under its own weight. To begin with the testimony of the ancients, Marius Mercator mentions earlier letters, which are also referred to in the later ones:

> For this very reason, he says (*Commonitorium*, chapter 1), Coelestius was considered worthy of some kindness from that holy priest; and thus he obtained a certain letter full of benevolence to the African bishops, which he misused—or continues even now to misuse—for the deception of many ignorant people.

Facundus of Hermiane mentions not merely one letter, as Mercator does, but two, each written on behalf of one of the heretics. He says (*Book VII, chapter 3*):

> Finally they will find blessed Zosimus, also, the bishop of the apostolic see, praising as true and Catholic the faith of Pelagius himself and of his associate Coelestius—whom Zosimus himself had examined in the proceedings after he had been convicted in the Church of Carthage and had appealed to the apostolic see—in opposition to the judgment of his predecessor Saint Innocent, who was the first to condemn the Pelagian heresy; and, moreover, blaming the African bishops because they believed those men to be heretics, while, before the African bishops had exposed their deceptions much more clearly, he thought the aforementioned Pelagius and Coelestius to be orthodox.

To these two testimonies, so clear and weighty, a third may be added, that of Julian himself, Bishop of Eclanum. It is less clear if considered by itself, but in conjunction with the others it receives the brightest illumination.

Julian, then, in the booklet he wrote to Pope Zosimus in the name of eighteen bishops who refused to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius, sets out the reasons for their refusal and the objections to the judgment conducted at the apostolic see which the supreme pontiff had employed in his second letters, in which the earlier letters were mentioned, against the Africans. He not only sets them out but uses the very same words, to the greater reproach or insult of the apostolic see. For he writes as follows (*Booklet of Faith*, Part IV):

> We specially admonish Your Holiness not to think that it was done as a reproach to you that, out of fear of God, we did not dare to subscribe to the condemnation of absent persons. We have been taught by the Scriptures that human will must not be preferred to the commands of God, who says: “You shall not accept a vain report, nor agree with the wicked to be an unjust witness” (Exodus 23:1, according to the Septuagint). And lest anyone think that the multitude should be followed, he added: “You shall not follow the multitude in evil” (ibid.). Again: “Before you inquire, do not censure anyone” (Sirach 11:7). Again: “Speak what your eyes have seen” (Matthew 7:1). Likewise in the Gospel: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; do not condemn, so that you may not be condemned. For with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged; and with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured to you.” Likewise, in another Evangelist even the Jews confess that “our law does not judge a man unless it first hears from him and learns what he does” (John 7:51). And in the Acts of the Apostles, a similar judgment was pronounced by the Gentile Festus: that it is not the custom of the Romans to condemn anyone before the accused has his accusers present and is given an opportunity to defend himself so as to clear away the charges (Acts 25:16).

Although Cappellus may appear to be overwhelmed by this triple authority, so great and so manifest, since he can produce nothing except what is weak and feeble, he must nevertheless not be dismissed without an answer. I have often been considerably astonished that so learned a man could have been so far obstructed—whether by hatred of the heretics against whom he was arguing or by some other movement of his mind—that he failed to notice that the credibility of Zosimus’s letters is established by the very evidence through which he thought it was destroyed. He employs four arguments to prove that the letters were fabricated. First, he claims that the letters contain statements contrary to history and to Augustine’s testimony. For he says:

> If we believe the letters, there were great dissensions of mind between Zosimus and the Africans: Zosimus censuring the Africans more harshly, while the Africans in turn burdened Zosimus with an odious mass of complaints. Yet in reality the whole case of Coelestius and Pelagius was conducted with the mutual agreement of both parties, as Augustine testifies in Book II to Boniface, chapter 3, and so forth.

But Augustine testifies to the contrary, and indeed in that very passage which is cited. For while he was endeavoring to excuse Zosimus, out of reverence for the apostolic see, nevertheless, compelled by the truth, he said things that accuse Cappellus and utterly refute him. For what do these words mean? “These persons were treated somewhat more leniently than the stricter discipline of the Church required.” What do these mean? “Amid so many ecclesiastical letters passing back and forth between the apostolic see and the African bishops, and even amid the official proceedings concerning this case conducted before that see while Coelestius was present and answering questions, what letter, then, of Pope Zosimus of venerable memory, what formal pronouncement is found in which he ordered that one ought to believe that a human being is born without any taint of original sin? Nowhere at all did he say this; nowhere whatsoever did he write it,” and so forth. “His little book was called catholic because this too belongs to the catholic mind,” and so forth. What, finally, do the other words mean? “After letters had subsequently come from Africa to Rome, stating that it was not enough for slower and more cautious minds that he professed generally to agree with the letters of Bishop Innocent, but that he ought openly to anathematize what he had set down perversely in his little book; lest, if he did not do so, many who understood little should believe that those poisons against the faith in his little book had been approved by the apostolic see—because that see had said that the book was catholic—more than they believed them corrected, on account of his reply that he agreed with the letters of Pope Innocent.” And near the end: “Whatever was meanwhile dealt with more leniently in the case of Coelestius, provided only that the firmness of the most ancient and most robust faith was preserved, was a most merciful exhortation to correction, not the most destructive approval of perversity,” and so forth. Could Augustine have indicated more clearly the letters whose principal points he touches upon?

Cappellus proceeds, but the second argument which he employs is no stronger than the first, since it admits of the same solution. “Pelagius,” he says, “could not deceive the Roman Church, as Augustine writes in *On Original Sin*, chapter 8. Yet he did deceive it, if the second letters are to be believed. For what else do these words of Zosimus mean: ‘Let it be a joy to you to recognize that those whom false witnesses accused had never been separated from our body and from catholic truth’?” What do these words mean? “How great is this exultation of faith: that they are not dead, nor have perished, concerning whom false reports have been spread.”

Augustine’s passage alone must again be brought forward in response: “Pelagius deceived the Palestinian judgment, and therefore he appears to have been acquitted there. But he could not deceive the Roman Church, where you know he is so well known, *in every respect*, although he made some attempt even at this; but, as I said, he achieved nothing at all. For the most blessed Pope Zosimus *recalled* what his predecessor, worthy of imitation, had thought about him in the official proceedings themselves. He also *considered* what the faith of the Romans, renowned in the Lord, thought about him, since he saw that their united efforts on behalf of catholic truth were burning in harmonious agreement against his error.”

How ingeniously, then, are the expressions put: “he could not deceive *in every respect*”; or “he *recalled*”; indeed, also “he *considered*.” By these words Augustine quietly suggests to those who understand them that Pelagius had at some point deceived the Roman pope, though not in every respect; that Zosimus recalled what had briefly slipped from memory; and that the supreme pontiff had considered the matter somewhat more carefully than before, when he was being deceived by men of bad faith.

Cappellus adds a third argument, namely, that it is clear from Augustine’s testimony that Coelestius was neither received by Zosimus nor his faith approved; that the errors of which he was accused were not denied by him; that Paulinus was not summoned from Africa; that Eros and Lazarus were not summoned from Gaul to prosecute the case; and that no period of two months was fixed for those who had been summoned, but that this period was assigned solely to Coelestius for abjuring his errors according to a formula to be prescribed, concerning which a letter had been sent to Africa. Yet all these things are contained in the letters attributed to Zosimus, and therefore either the letters themselves are false or Augustine lied.

I admit that the letters contain the matters just mentioned: namely, that Coelestius’s faith was to some extent approved by Zosimus—whether by that name one understands his little book or the meaning of the person; that the errors laid against him were denied by Coelestius; that Paulinus was summoned from Africa to Rome so that he might appear in person as accuser on the appointed day; and that a period of two months was granted to Coelestius for repentance, since the judgment was deferred for that time. But I deny that Eros and Lazarus were also summoned from Gaul. Cappellus’s memory failed him on this point, for those two bishops never returned from Palestine to Gaul, or rather, never even returned to Africa. Nor do Zosimus’s words—“Where is Eros? Where is Lazarus? Names that ought to blush at the deeds and condemnations”—contain a summons; they are instead an accusation. Otherwise the pontiff would also have to be thought to have summoned Jacobus and Timasius. For the passage continues: “Where are the young men Jacobus and Timasius?” and so forth.

Now, the four matters which I admit are contained in the letters are confirmed as true by authorities so certain that here too the learned man has refuted himself by his own argument. To begin with the first: what else does Augustine teach than that Coelestius’s faith had been approved, when he says (*Book II to Boniface*, chapter 3) that his little book “was called catholic by the apostolic see”? How plainly does he teach the second! Namely, that Coelestius condemned his own errors under pressure from Zosimus, in these words: “Coelestius himself professed agreement with this man [Innocent], when, after his holy predecessor had said to him, ‘Do you condemn all those things that have been circulated under your name?’ he replied” (*On Original Sin*, chapter 6): “I condemn, according to the judgment of your predecessor Innocent, of blessed memory,” and so forth.

How clearly does he teach the third! “And so, as if he were delirious, so that he might rest as one lightly warmed, he was nevertheless not yet deemed to be released from the bonds of excommunication; but, after a period of *two months* had been interposed until a reply should come from Africa, an opportunity for repentance was granted him under a certain medicinal leniency of judgment” (*In the little book preserved by Baronius, under the year 418, no. 15*).

As for the fourth—that a second-month appearance had been arranged with Paulinus—Paulinus himself admits it: “For this reason I sent the little book, because, although only by word, Basiliscus the subdeacon, sent from Your Blessedness with the official documents of the apostolic see, met with me at Carthage on the fourth day before the Nones of November, so that I might appear before the apostolic see and submit to the judgment of Your Holiness,” and so forth.

Finally, Cappellus adduces, as a fourth argument intended to strengthen the others, the authority of Paulinus the deacon himself, so that he may refute an instrument drawn from the Vatican records by means of another instrument obtained from the same source. “Paulinus,” he says, “in his little book gives thanks to Zosimus because, by apostolic authority, he had condemned Coelestius, who *refused to condemn the errors* that Paulinus himself had brought against him as accuser, and because Paulinus himself had not been summoned.” Then he quotes words in which Paulinus does indeed recall that Zosimus pressed Coelestius vehemently to condemn the charges brought against him; yet he does not mention that supposed acquittal, which is recorded in the letters—something he would certainly not have omitted if it had been obtained by deception and if the apostolic see had at some point decreed what it later corrected after a fuller examination of the case.

From this he infers that the three letters circulated under the name of Zosimus—written with gall rather than ink—were fabricated by the Pelagians, both to indulge their own nature, which inclined them to slander; their anger against the supreme pontiff, whose condemnation of them they bore impatiently; and their hatred of the Africans, by whose efforts they felt themselves so pressed that, because of the Church’s thunderbolts, they could never draw breath, and, because of the imperial proscription, could nowhere stand. He further infers, or at least suspects, that two letters to Boniface and Coelestine concerning appeals were later prepared by the same craftsmen on behalf of the Africans, so that they might repay like with like—or rather return with interest whatever reproach they had first received from the city of Rome.

Such is the learned man’s position. But Baronius, as he carried many others of no small number incautiously along with him, led him into his own opinion: namely, that the little book presented by Paulinus to Zosimus had been offered in thanksgiving after Pelagius and Coelestius had been condemned by apostolic authority. Yet it had been presented several months earlier and is in reality nothing other than a carefully devised excuse for not having appeared on the appointed day—or rather, for not having had to appear—before the judgment of the apostolic see.

I do not deny that Paulinus offered some thanks to the supreme pontiff. I deny that he offered them for the final sentence passed against Coelestius—which would have been especially necessary if Baronius were to be heard—but only for this reason: that, while dealing with Coelestius, Zosimus had mentioned Paulinus, and had mentioned him all the more honorifically because he had pressed Coelestius more vehemently to condemn without evasion whatever the deacon had brought against him in his little book, provided that he wished to listen as a catholic. Paulinus interpreted such persistence by the pontiff as an honorable remission of the recognizance. For what reason would remain for him to appear at the hearing, since his faith had already been approved and the little book previously delivered to Aurelius at Carthage had been accepted as an indisputable instrument of the litigation?

But so that the whole matter—which escaped even the notice of diligent men—may become clearer, the final part of the little book should be transcribed, since it contains almost the entire affair. It runs as follows:

“Therefore I beg Your Apostolate to order that this little book of mine be received, by which I may offer thanks to so great a see and for the most just judgments passed on my behalf. For this reason I sent it, because, although only by word, Basiliscus the subdeacon, sent from Your Blessedness with the official documents of the apostolic see, met with me at Carthage on the fourth day before the Nones of November, so that I might appear before the apostolic see and submit to the judgment of Your Holiness. In response, it was stated at length that I had promised not to be absent if the judgment had been rendered against me and not on my behalf. At that time, therefore, I could do nothing, because the man who had appealed to the apostolic see was absent, although he certainly ought to have established the merits of his appeal, especially since, when the appellant does nothing, even according to human laws the victor always has the superior position. For what would it now matter to me that my case should be strengthened by the judgment of the apostolic see, if I were thereby also to appear before Your Reverence as an advocate of his perverse doctrine? I could rejoice in it if, after the things I had brought against him had been condemned, he had deserved to be acquitted, and had not allowed himself to be ordained before being cleared.”

And afterward:

“But I sent this little book to Your Blessedness through Marcellinus, subdeacon of the Carthaginian Church, delivered on the sixth day before the Ides of November.”

From these facts it is clear that Paulinus:

1. Was summoned by Zosimus: “Basiliscus met with me so that I might appear before the apostolic see,” and so forth.

2. Replied six days after the meeting: “He met with me on the fourth day before the Nones of November,” and so forth.

3. Gave his little book to the subdeacon Marcellinus for delivery on the sixth day before the Ides of November. Marcellinus also carried the letters of the council of Carthage to Zosimus, in which the procedure for conducting the judgment against Coelestius was set out. Augustine mentions these letters (*Book II to Boniface*, chapter 3), and Paulinus himself does so as well (*In the little book*) in these words: “For now he has a case not with me, but with the whole Church of God, as the letters sent to Your Blessedness attest.”

4. Wrote before Coelestius’s flight from the city of Rome, for he speaks of him (*in the same place*) as though he were present: “When he attempts to proceed against the apostolic judgment,” and “He endeavors to establish his case in the assembly of the apostolic see,” and so forth.

5. Brought forward three reasons why the recognizance was void: first, because the defendant’s earlier appeal had been disregarded: “He was absent, although he ought to have established the merits of his appeal”; second, because the summons to appear within the second month had not been communicated until the entire period had elapsed: “He met with me on the fourth day before the Nones of November”; and third, because the notice had been given not in writing, as the law required, but only verbally, which had no legal force: “Because, although only by word,” and so forth.

6. Finally, did not give thanks for the final sentence of condemnation, which was not issued before the month of May in the year 418, but only for the proceedings conducted before 8 November of the year 417. For Marcellinus, the bearer of the little book, arrived in Rome before Zosimus’s third letter to the Africans; that letter itself mentions Marcellinus’s arrival. These letters, however, were issued before Zosimus pronounced his final sentence against Coelestius, as is plainly evident from the letters themselves.

Having observed all these points, I finally reply to Cappellus that neither this last argument nor the other three preceding ones sufficiently proves that the letters which the most illustrious author of the *Annals* brought to light from the Vatican records were fabricated by the Pelagians. The authority of Mercator and Facundus gives those letters as much credibility as can possibly be afforded in matters separated from us by so long an interval of time.

## X. SYNOD

Held by Theodotus, bishop of Antioch, against Pelagius, apparently at Antioch, under the same consuls, in October of the year of Christ 417.

The tenth synod was held at Antioch by Theodotus, bishop of Antioch, as Mercator writes in these words:

“While Pelagius was still residing in Jerusalem, he was accused before a synod. At first, by evasive conduct, concealing himself behind certain ambiguous professions and pursuing or answering doubtful matters, he seems at that time to have deceived the hearing of the bishops. But later, when he was clearly detected and the accusers persisted, he was exposed by a subsequent synod over which Theodotus, bishop of Antioch and of holy memory, presided; and he was expelled even from the holy and venerable places of Jerusalem. The writings sent by that same holy Theodotus to the most reverend bishop of the city of Rome and to Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, of sacred memory, testify to this; we have copies of them in our hands as documentary evidence” (*Commonitorium*, chapter 3).

This synod was unknown to Augustine. For would he have kept silent about so important a precedent when writing against Julian, since he carefully sought out every circumstance bearing on the catholic cause and used each whenever an opportunity presented itself?

I remember no one, apart from Mercator, who mentions it—at least openly—except Marianus Victorius, unless he called the Antiochene council the Diospolitan council. “After Pelagius had vomited forth these and certain other things,” he says, “when many admonished him, fearing condemnation, he first recanted; then, falling back again into the same former errors, he was condemned by the Antiochene synod, and likewise by Innocent and Zosimus, supreme pontiffs,” and so forth (*Preface to Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon*).

I say “at least openly” because there is a passage in Photius which, if corrected—as it certainly ought to be—clearly confirms Mercator’s statement. It reads as follows (*Codex* 54):

“Moreover, this Pelagian or Coelestian heresy flourished not only in the East but also spread through the West. It was detected and convicted at Carthage in Africa by Aurelius and Augustine and condemned publicly in various councils. Those who held these views were expelled from the Church as heretics, in the time of Theophilus of Alexandria and Innocent of the city of Rome, by the Romans, the Africans, and the other bishops of the West.”

Where the Greek reads, *ἐν τοῖς χρόνοις τοῦ Θεοφίλου τοῦ Ἀλεξανδρείας*—“in the time of Theophilus of Alexandria”—one must read *ἐν τοῖς χρόνοις τοῦ Θεοδότου τοῦ Ἀντιοχείας*—“in the time of Theodotus of Antioch.” For it could not have happened that the Pelagians were expelled from the Church in Egypt during Theophilus’s time, since they had scarcely become known in the West in the year 412, when Cyril succeeded Theophilus. Yet the statements in question fit Theodotus remarkably well, since he held the synod mentioned by Mercator not long afterward—at a time when the Africans had already written from Carthage and Milevis to Innocent about Pelagius and Coelestius, or when Innocent had condemned them, as will shortly be shown.

The synod under discussion was therefore presided over by Theodotus, that celebrated bishop throughout the East, who in the year 411 succeeded Alexander in the see of Antioch: “A man distinguished for gentleness, splendidly adorned with the pearl of continence and with a carefully ordered life,” as Theodoret says (*Book I of the History*, chapter 37). He brought the Apollinarists back to the Church, while in the Council of Constantinople he expelled the Messalians from it without hope of return. He died in the year 417, according to Theodoret (*At the end of the Whole History*), after sixteen years in the episcopate; hence Nicephorus must be refuted when he assigns him only four years.

Taking occasion from Theodotus and the Messalians, observe that Binius does not state with sufficient accuracy the council held by Sisinnius and Theodotus against the Messalians. He says that it was held in the East, but at an uncertain place, in the year of Christ 427, the fifth of Coelestine, and the twentieth of Theodosius. For it is clear partly from Photius and partly from Socrates that it was held at Constantinople in March of the year 426, the fourth of Coelestine and the nineteenth of Theodosius, under the consulship of Theodosius XII and Valentinian the Younger II, both Augusti.

For Photius writes as follows (*Codex* 52):

“Sisinnius of Constantinople and Theodotus of Antioch likewise wrote a joint letter to Berinianus and Amphilochius and the other bishops in Pamphylia. The letter bears this heading: ‘To Berinianus and Amphilochius, most beloved of God, fellow members of the sacred college, and likewise to all the bishops in Pamphylia: Sisinnius and Theodotus, together with the entire holy synod assembled by the grace of God in the great city of Constantinople for the consecration of the most God-loving bishop Sisinnius, by the command and authority of our most pious and Christ-loving emperor Theodosius: greetings in the Lord,’” and the rest, as given by Binius.

Socrates’s words are these (*Book VII*, chapter 28):

“Sisinnius was ordained on the day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Theodosius XII and Valentinian the Younger Augustus II.”

This is the year of Christ 426, the fourth of Coelestine, and the nineteenth of Theodosius.

It is not equally easy to determine the date of the Antiochene synod now under discussion; nevertheless, we must try, if we can find some way to do so. Certainly, since Marius states that Pelagius was condemned in that synod by Praylius himself, and that Praylius sent letters of condemnation to the apostolic see; and since Praylius succeeded John in the see of Jerusalem after John died on 10 January 417, the synod could not have been convened before that year itself, or even before the end of the year. For Praylius wrote a letter to the Roman bishop in which, as Zosimus says in his letter to the Africans dated 11 days before the Kalends of October, he intervened as an especially earnest supporter of Pelagius’s case, since he had already been ordained bishop in place of the former holy John (*Letter 4, which is the second in the Pelagian case*). Some interval, therefore, had to elapse between this first commendatory letter, written certainly after 10 January, and the condemnatory letter mentioned by Mercator. Thus the synod cannot have been convened before the end of 417.

Nor could it have been convened before Easter, lest, when the sea became open in spring, letters in opposition to one another should arrive in Rome at the same time; nor immediately after Easter, for the same reason. Indeed, it could not have been held before the end of September, both because letters from the synod would have arrived in Rome in that year before Zosimus issued his third letter to the Africans on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April 418, and because Praylius ought not to have been absent from the Church of Jerusalem in September, when its dedication festival was celebrated on 14 September, according to Nicephorus (*Book VIII of the History*, chapter 50), with peoples assembling from throughout the world.

It remains, therefore, that Theodotus held the synod at Antioch at the earliest in October and at the latest in November. For Mercator’s and Photius’s words speak quite clearly of the bishops’ assembling at Antioch in this year, that is, 417. Mercator would not have written about the Diospolitan and Antiochene synods in the manner he actually did if one had not followed the other as soon as possible—that is, after the death of John of Jerusalem. Nor would Photius have suitably joined Innocent and Theodotus if both had not condemned the Pelagians in the same year.

Indeed, the circumstances support both authors. Since Eros and Lazarus were distressed that Pelagius had been acquitted by the Diospolitans through John’s favor and influence, and since they had consequently been accused either of slander or of ignorance for having brought charges against a man based on books which he himself had condemned, whether his own or those of others whom they had misunderstood, they pressed the matter at the first opportunity before the primate of the entire East, so that the case might be retried after the death of John, who died in the year 417.

Moreover, it is credible that neither the Gallic bishops who were the accusers nor Theodotus, who received the accusation, anticipated the customary season for holding a synod around the time of autumn, lest the prelates be wearied by an additional labor.

I think that Praylius came to the council, although it was not customary to summon him unless the whole diocese was being called together, because he had been informed by the Gallic bishops—and perhaps also by Jerome—of Pelagius’s bad faith and of the Pelagians’ boastfulness in letters sent throughout the world, as though not merely Pelagius himself but also his doctrines had been acquitted by the Palestinian Fathers. He therefore judged that it was in his interest to have the case examined more thoroughly, lest the letters he had written in commendation of Pelagius, out of reverence for his predecessor, be allowed to cause scandal throughout the world and to support heresy.

From this it can also be seen with what purpose Pelagius extracted commendatory letters from Praylius for the apostolic see and sent them, together with his associates, to Rome, along with the proceedings of the Diospolitan synod and his statement of faith. The crafty heretic wanted both to keep Praylius occupied with his own affairs at Jerusalem and to preoccupy Innocent’s mind at Rome, not yet knowing that Innocent had died, so that, if anything were attempted in the council which he perceived the Gallic bishops were pressing before Theodotus, the judgment concerning his person that had been made at Diospolis would not be reconsidered at Rome.

The records and letters sent from the synod to the bishop of the city have perished, to the great detriment of ecclesiastical history. For they would have exposed the infamous devices of the monk, and perhaps would have provided, as an example for subsequent ages, a means of convicting heretics of bad faith and compelling convicted men, after the example of Pelagius, to conceal themselves and their shame in the darkness of an unknown solitude.

## XI. SYNOD

Convened at Carthage by Aurelius, under the twelfth consulship of Honorius and the eighth of Theodosius, both Augusti, before Lent, in the year 418.

[Col. 0347A]

The eleventh synod, the third Carthaginian synod in the Pelagian case, is exceedingly obscure. Nevertheless, knowledge of it contributes considerably to the history; therefore it must be investigated somewhat more carefully, lest, when we intend to say something contrary to the opinion of learned men, we appear to assert it without serious grounds.

But since the investigation must be conducted almost entirely from Zosimus’s third letter to the Africans, I thought that I should transcribe it at once at the beginning, both to establish the credibility of what will be said and so that it may be read in a more accurate form. These third letters, together with those mentioned above, are found in volume XX of our *Bibliotheca*, column 676.

From them it is clear, first, that Zosimus wrote two letters to Aurelius and all the bishops throughout Africa. One concerned Coelestius; although it lacks an indication of the day and month, it is nevertheless dated to the consulship of Honorius XI and Flavius Constantius II. The other concerned Pelagius and followed immediately after the first, without a consular date but with the day and month: the eleventh day before the Kalends of October.

It is clear next that a response was sent from Africa to Zosimus’s letters, together with a plea that the pontiff should not judge so important a matter without the African documents. Those documents were sent with the plea, and contained partly the proceedings of the preceding synods, partly Paulinus’s little book and the letters of the Gallic bishops, as well as Pelagius’s book *On Nature*, Augustine’s reply, and various other materials.

Third, it is clear that the holy pontiff did not reply to the Africans’ plea until he had received through the subdeacon Marcellinus a synodical letter, and a lengthy one at that. For he writes, with some expression of weariness, that he had turned over the entire volume of the letter and, having eventually read it through, understood that his earlier letters had not been accepted in their intended sense.

[Col. 0347C]

Fourth, it is clear that nothing was definitively settled by a final sentence concerning Coelestius before the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, when Zosimus issued his third letter—not, as with the earlier letters, to all the bishops established throughout Africa, but to Aurelius and the others who had been present at the council of Carthage. This must be carefully noted.

Fifth, it is clear that there was some council—or rather, two councils—of the province of Carthage before the African plenary council that began on the Kalends of May. From the first, after at least Zosimus’s first letters concerning Coelestius had been received, the plea was sent together with the documents of the case mentioned above. To the synodical letter of the later council, Zosimus sent the reply which was received at Carthage on the third day before the Kalends of May, namely, two days before the general council began.

With these five points established, I maintain that, of the two provincial councils of Carthage just mentioned, one—the one to whose letters Zosimus did not reply—was held in October or even November of the year 417; the other—the one to whose Fathers Zosimus sent the letter mentioned above—was convened before Lent in the year 418. It has not seemed worth the effort to distinguish one from the other in detail, since scarcely any trace of the one remains except an extremely obscure memory, while the circumstances of the other are somewhat more fully explained.

How many bishops assembled is uncertain. That a considerable number assembled—that is, at least one of the groups mentioned in the discussion of the council of Milevis—is established by the fact that the supreme pontiff calls the gathering a council of Carthage. From this designation it is further inferred that the Fathers came only from the province of Proconsular Africa. But all this requires clarification through some knowledge of African affairs, which will also shed light on the councils that follow. For African synodal matters are often enveloped in such intricate darkness that even learned readers grow weary. It is therefore appropriate to digress briefly for the sake of this subject.

## DIGRESSION ON THE COUNCILS OF THE AFRICAN CHURCH

From ancient records it is gathered (*Cyprian, Letter 46; Augustine, Letter 110*) that four kinds of synods were held in Africa. At times, the bishop of a single city met either only with his own presbyters and deacons—an action called “contracting the presbyterium”—or he also summoned the people, which was called “drawing up the ecclesiastical proceedings”; or he further invited neighboring bishops to take part in the council.

At other times, he summoned the leading bishops of an entire province by means of a *tractoria*. This procedure is prescribed by canon 76 of the African Code:

“It has been resolved that whenever a council is to be assembled, bishops who are prevented neither by age, illness, nor any more serious necessity should attend suitably; and notice should be given to the primates of each province that, from all the bishops, either two or three groups should be formed, and that from each group in turn as many as have been chosen should attend most promptly on the day of the council. If they are unable to attend, they should record their excuses in the *tractoria*; or, if some necessity should perhaps suddenly arise after the arrival of the *tractoria*, unless they report the reason for their impediment to their own primate, they must be content with the communion of their own Church.”

At times bishops from several provinces assembled because of a common matter, though not from all of them. Such was the council of Byzacena, to which bishops were sent as legates from the province of Proconsular Africa (*Code of the African Church*, under the year 394).

Finally, at times a gathering was held from the entire diocese of Africa—that is, from all the African provinces—at the summons of the bishop of Carthage, although the method of convocation varied at different times. At first they assembled every year. Later, the timing depended on the judgment of the bishop of Carthage, or rather on the demands of the business at hand.

The first type, which corresponds to the diocesan synods of our own times, was called more a gathering or a *compresbyterium* than a council. The second took its name either from the province or from the city to which the bishops summoned by the primate came together. The third was called African, but particular, to distinguish it from the fourth, which was called universal: namely, the gathering to which either any bishops or delegates from all the provinces of Africa assembled.

In earlier times the African diocese had five provinces: Proconsular Africa, or Carthaginian Africa; Byzacena; Numidia; Mauretania; and Tripolitania. Later Mauretania was divided into two provinces, Sitifensis and Caesariensis. Some think that Numidia too was divided into two, but without substantial reason. Finally, Transfretana Hispania, or Mauretania Tingitana, was added—if the heading of the plenary council held in the year 418 is genuine, as it is read in a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Bavo at Ghent. This can, however, also be proved from elsewhere, as we shall demonstrate in the dissertation on the imperial constitutions.

[Col. 0348D]

From these facts, reader, understand which synods should be called African and which merely Carthaginian or provincial. African synods are those to which bishops assembled from several provinces. Carthaginian synods, or synods of another province, are those held by the bishops of a single province alone, whether Proconsular Africa or any other. Authority to convene the former belonged to the bishop of Carthage; authority to convene the latter belonged to the individual primates. In the former, matters concerning the whole diocese were decided; in the latter, matters concerning one province. Appeals were made to the African synods from the provincial synods, and to the provincial synods from the judgments of individual bishops.

The African synods were required to be convened annually by the prescription of the council of Hippo, as is evident from canon 18 of the African Code:

“According to the decrees of Nicaea, because ecclesiastical cases which often grow old to the ruin of the peoples must be addressed, a council shall be summoned every year. To it all the provinces that possess primatial sees shall send from their own councils two bishops as legates, or as many as they choose, so that, when the assembly has been gathered, it may possess full authority.”

Canon 73 established the time for convening them, indeed the very day:

“It has been resolved that the venerable day of Easter should be announced to all by the subscription of the formal notices, but that the day of the council should remain the same as that established in the council of Hippo, namely, the tenth day before the Kalends of September,” and so forth.

But because it was burdensome to remove so many bishops so frequently from their sees, the two aforementioned canons were abrogated by canon 95:

“Since it had been established in the council of Hippo that the plenary council of Africa should be contracted every year—not only here at Carthage, but also in the various provinces in their proper order—and this was observed so that we convened sometimes in Numidia and sometimes in Byzacena; but because this seemed burdensome to all the brothers, it has been resolved that henceforth there should not be an annual necessity for wearying the brothers. Rather, whenever a common cause, that is, a cause concerning all Africa, demands it, as soon as letters concerning the matter have been sent from anywhere to this see, a synod shall be assembled in the province where convenience recommends it. Cases that are not common shall be judged in their own provinces.”

Provincial synods were held twice a year according to the prescription of the Council of Nicaea: once before the Lent of Easter and again around the time of autumn. See canon 5 of Nicaea, quoted in the notes to the fourth synod, and from it learn at what times the several provincial councils were convened—namely, at each of these two lawful seasons, and at no other time unless necessity compelled it. Therefore, whenever councils are recorded as having been held outside the customary season, the diligent investigator should seek the reason. There was always some reason, and knowing it contributes to historical understanding.

The African synods were assembled sometimes in one province and sometimes in another, according to the established order, as was stated above from canon 95. None, however, were held outside Numidia, Proconsular Africa, and Byzacena, because the remaining provinces were less convenient on account of their distance than those provinces situated in the central part of Africa.

Provincial synods were not held in the cities where the senior bishops or primates resided, as some have thought on the basis of canon 73: “A letter should be written to the primates of each province, so that, whenever they convene a council in their own territory, they do not obstruct this day.” Rather, they were held in more convenient places within the province. This is clear from the council of Milevis and likewise from that of Cirta, which was convened by Silvanus, primate of Numidia, although he presided over the Church of Summa or Zama.

It should be noted, however, that the ancients called a synod to which all the bishops came a plenary council; hence it happened that they used this name in different senses at different times. For they called councils “plenary” not only those of all Africa, but also the provincial councils themselves, according as either all the bishops of one province assembled at the residence of their senior bishop, or bishops from all the provinces gathered at a place appointed by the bishop of Carthage. There was therefore some distinction between a plenary and a universal council: [Col. 0349D] the former could consist of only one province; the latter comprised the entire diocese, although a universal council was at times still different from a plenary council of all Africa. For to the former all the provinces were summoned only through legates; to the latter all the bishops of a single body were summoned, insofar as they wished to come. Likewise, to a non-plenary council of one province only a single body was summoned, but to a plenary council both bodies were summoned. Hence one can understand why no African Catholic synod is recorded as having had more than 220 bishops at most, although there were more than 500 Catholic episcopal churches in Africa: namely, only one body was convened from each province, that is, approximately half of them, and even from that number some had legitimate reasons for absence, concerning which there is canon 76. This arrangement was wisely established, so that churches deprived of their pastors would suffer no loss: each bishop entrusted his church to the neighboring bishop who remained behind, so that the latter might assist it. This discipline prevailed among the Catholics, whereas the Donatists lived by other practices. But I shall treat these matters more carefully at another time, if God wills, in the history of the African Church which I am planning.

Having made these observations, we must conclude the point for which we digressed: namely, that the eleventh synod was either provincial, as I rather think; or merely a particular African synod, which is not improbable. Either conclusion follows from the heading of the letters of Pope Zosimus. What was done at it is clear from what precedes; how many bishops were present is uncertain. The place, however, together with the time, president, and occasion, is certain.

## XII. SYNOD, gathered at Carthage by Aurelius from all the provinces of Africa, under the emperors Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, on the Kalends of May, in the year 418

[Col. 0350B] The twelfth synod was held at Carthage, to which bishops from all the provinces of Africa were summoned and assembled by Aurelius. Therefore, although it is commonly called Carthaginian from the place, Augustine calls it African (Epistle 215); and it is the first council of all Africa concerning the Pelagian heresy.

It was convened in the twelfth consulship of Honorius and the eighth of Theodosius, as the acts state—that is, in the year of Christ 418—not at the beginning of spring, as Binius wished, following Baronius, but only on the Kalends of May, the date given by the acts. Indeed, while ecclesiastical discipline was in force, how could 214 bishops—for that is the number said to have assembled, among them Aurelius, Augustine, Alypius, Possidius, Evodius, and other most holy prelates—have been absent from their churches during the solemn season of Easter, which that year fell on April 7, so that the completion of the feast was on April 14?

On this occasion I cannot omit what I observed [Col. 0350C] while reading the codex of the African Church and examining its general councils somewhat more carefully: that no council, except two, was held at any time earlier than at least a full month after the Easter feasts; while several are recorded as having been held in August and September. Of the two exceptions, the later—and the most famous of all, because it was convened by the necessity of the most serious affairs—was held on the Kalends of May in the year 418, when Easter fell on April 7. The earlier, which is quite obscure, is recorded as having been celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends of May in the year 399, when Easter fell on April 10. But an error must have entered this passage: either the Ides were written instead of the Kalends, or June was written instead of May, lest something so extraordinary be said to have occurred, contrary to the canons devoutly observed in the other councils.

This council must be counted among the universal synods, since it was presided over by Aurelius, together with Donatianus, bishop of Telepte and first-ranking bishop of the province of Byzacena, and 212 others, from the province of Byzacena as well as from Sitifian Mauretania, Tripolitana, Numidia, Caesariensis Mauretania, and Hispania—that is, Tingitana Mauretania, which was called Hispania beyond the Pillars of Hercules because it was subject to the vicar of the Spains.

A synodal letter was sent from it to Pope Zosimus. Prosper, addressing Cassianus, says of this letter (Book Against the Collator, chapter 10; he says the same in his Reply to the Eighth Chapter of the Gauls):

“According to your judgment, by which you assert that the beginning of holy and faithful wills does not come from God in all human beings . . . the 214 priests were mistaken, who in the letter which they placed before their decrees addressed the blessed Zosimus, bishop of the apostolic see, in these words: ‘We decree that the judgment pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius through the venerable bishop Innocent, from the see of the most blessed apostle Peter, shall remain in force until they openly confess that by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord we are assisted in each individual act, not only to know but also to do righteousness, so that without it we can possess, think, say, or do nothing that is true and holy piety.’”

But seven difficult questions arise here: four from various passages in Augustine, and three from the testimony of Prosper just cited and from another passage in the Chronicle.

The first is: which African synod was that one which is said to have recalled to the venerable Pope Zosimus what his predecessor Innocent had judged concerning the proceedings of the Palestinian synod, and after whose rescript the most just sentence was pronounced against Coelestius? (On Original Sin, chapters 7 and 8.)

The second is: which African council was that from which a rescript was sent to Zosimus before he sent his *tractoria* to all the bishops of the world? (The same work.)
