The third is: from which African assembly did the letter come to Rome stating that it was not enough for slower and more cautious persons that Coelestius professed general agreement with the letters of Bishop Innocent, but that he ought openly to anathematize the errors he had set down in his own booklet, and so forth? (Book II to Boniface, chapter 3.)

The fourth is: which was the later plenary council of all Africa [Col. 0351B] at which something brief was established against the Pelagian error? (Epistle 47 to Valentinus.)

Augustine raises these questions; Prosper raises others (Book Against the Collator, chapter 10).

The fifth, therefore, is: which councils of African bishops were those that by their decrees established that both gifts of God are involved—knowing what we ought to do and loving in order that we may do it—so that, when charity builds up, knowledge cannot puff up? For, just as it is written of God, “He is the one who teaches human beings knowledge” (Psalm 93:10), so it is written, “Charity is from God” (1 John 4:7).

The sixth is: from which synod did the African bishops write back to Pope Zosimus, praising him for the saving soundness of this judgment, and say:

“Now, as for what you wrote in your letter, which you arranged to have sent to all, saying: ‘Nevertheless, by God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—we have brought everything before the awareness of our brothers and fellow bishops’” [Col. 0351C]—“we have understood this statement,” and so forth? (In the Chronicle, under the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII.)

The seventh is: at which council held at Carthage were the synodal decrees of 207 bishops delivered to Pope Zosimus, by whose approval the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the world?

In order that so many questions may be explained and the truth made clear, insofar as possible, certain principles must be established amid such great and ancient darkness.

It is therefore established, first, that correspondence passed repeatedly between the Africans and Zosimus, and between Zosimus and the Africans, concerning the case of Coelestius and Pelagius. This is what Augustine’s words indicate (Book II to Boniface, chapter 3):

“With so many and such important ecclesiastical letters passing back and forth between the apostolic see and the African bishops, and with proceedings concerning this case also completed before that see, while Coelestius was present and answering,” and so forth.

It is further established that what Prosper attributes to the councils of the African bishops is found in exactly the same words in canon 4 of the universal African council held at Carthage on the Kalends of May, under the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII. Hence there can be no doubt that by “the councils of the Africans” he wished to mean the universal council mentioned above. Why, then, did he use the plural number? Is the reading corrupt, and should we instead read either, “The council of the African bishops was mistaken,” or, “The African bishops were mistaken”? The variant editions seem to suggest something of this sort. Or is it better to retain the ancient reading and say that Prosper, when he wrote this after the year 432, was referring to two African councils, in one of which the canons were established in 418, and in the other reviewed and approved in 419?

It is also established that the later plenary council of all Africa, at which the brief statement against the Pelagian error was made that Augustine commands Valentinus to read among other things (Epistle 215), in order to learn how the Catholic Church, relying on God’s mercy, repelled the poisons of the Pelagian heresy, is not different from the universal council held at Carthage on the Kalends of May. [Col. 0352A] For in it the entire faith of the Church against the Pelagian error, as well as the disputes arising in the monastery of Hadrumetum, was briefly contained in eight canons.

“But for what purpose,” you will ask, “and with what reference, does Augustine call this council later?” (Book I on the Pelagian Heresy, chapter 44.) Here, I think, is the obstacle at which learned men must necessarily stumble: nor can they escape in any other way than by admitting with Vossius two African councils, the later one in which the eight canons were enacted, and the earlier one from which the writings derive—both Prosper’s statement, “The 214 bishops were mistaken,” and Augustine’s words, “So that this might be done more fully and clearly.”

“But when,” you will insist, “could that earlier council have been held, if the later one met on the Kalends of May?” Here is another obstacle, at which we must remain for a while until a new light appears from what follows.

Fourth, it is established that these words of Prosper—“The African bishops wrote back to Pope Zosimus, praising him for the soundness of this judgment,” and so forth—refer to a time other than that in which the universal council now under discussion was held. For undoubtedly the Africans wrote this reply after receiving Zosimus’s *tractoria* to the bishops of the whole world. Since, therefore, that *tractoria* did not reach Africa until long after the Kalends of May, when the third letter was received, stating that nothing had yet been changed but that everything had been left in the condition in which it had long stood (Zosimus’s third letter to the Africans), the reply mentioned by Prosper must necessarily belong to approximately the month of August. Accordingly, either a new council was convened at that time, or—and this seems more probable—the same council continued until then, although the Fathers occasionally went down to visit their own churches as necessity required.

Fifth, it is established that the first three questions arising from Augustine’s words can be resolved without great difficulty, provided that the matters contained in them are said to pertain to the earlier African council, or rather to the earlier session of the universal African council. For I think there were two, or rather three, sessions or assemblies of one council; yet Augustine called each of them individually a “council,” because they were held in different months and a considerable interval of time occurred between them, as the bishops returned on the appointed day from their respective churches, at least those who had been delegated.

I therefore place the earlier assembly, or rather the earlier council, on the Kalends of May, when the council of 214 bishops is recorded; I think the later assembly, or later council, was held around the middle of June; and the final one around the middle of August.

At the first, the replies to Zosimus contained partly what is included in Augustine’s first three questions and partly what is included in Prosper’s seventh. At the second, the canons were enacted concerning which Augustine’s fourth and Prosper’s fifth questions are concerned. Finally, at the last, after Zosimus’s universal *tractoria* and his particular letter to the Africans had been received, thanks were given to the supreme pontiff, and the statement praising the *tractoria* was made which Prosper reports in his sixth question.

The reason for establishing the chronology in this way is clear. The entire affair discussed in these questions must have been completed within the interval between the end of the Easter feasts and the twelfth day before the Kalends of October—that is, from April 15 to September 21. For the 214 most holy bishops certainly celebrated the Easter feasts in their own churches, and Augustine, who attended all the assemblies, was acting in Mauretania as legate of the apostolic see on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, as is clear from his letter 190 to Optatus and from the proceedings concerning Emeritus.

Three assemblies must therefore be posited, if we are willing to follow Augustine and Prosper.

The first was the assembly at which, after Zosimus’s third letter had been received on the third day before the Kalends of May, a reply was sent to the supreme pontiff concerning the manner in which judgment was to be conducted against Coelestius. It could not have been held earlier, since only fifteen days had been granted the Fathers to assemble from their provinces. Since the Africans thought that the council’s instructions and the other documents of the case would reach Rome before Zosimus began the trial, though they would not arrive for another month, the Fathers seem to have been dismissed so that they might celebrate with their people, according to custom, the solemn feast of Pentecost and the solemn baptism, and might return immediately after the feasts were completed, in order to be present to receive and deliberate together upon any reply brought either by Marcellinus, the subdeacon acting in the affairs of the African Church, or by the supreme pontiff.

The second could conveniently have been held around the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, that is, on June 17, or even earlier, around the Ides of June. At that time the nineteen canons were enacted, eight of which concern the faith and the rest discipline.

The final canon, because it bears upon our subject, must be recalled here:

“It pleased the council that, so that all the bishops who had assembled for the council might not be detained longer by the entire council, three judges should be chosen from each province. And from the province of Carthage were chosen Vincentius, Fortunatianus, and Clarus; from the province of Numidia, Alypius, Augustine, and Restitutus; from the province of Byzacena, together with the holy old man Donatianus the primate, Cresconius, Jocundus, and Aemilianus; from Sitifian Mauretania, Severianus, Asiaticus, and Donatus; from the province of Tripolitana, Plautius, who was sent as the sole legate according to custom. Let all of them, together with the holy old man Aurelius, examine the whole matter. The entire council also requested that he himself subscribe to everything, whether the proceedings that have already been completed or the letters. And they subscribed,” and so forth.

The reason for the canon was, I think, that while a reply from Rome was awaited, and it could not be expected soon—whether because of stormy seas or contrary winds—it seemed somewhat harsh, and scarcely humane, to keep so many Fathers away from their own places until an uncertain day, especially during the hot season, when the necessities of life were not abundantly available.

A reply was nevertheless brought not long afterward—not, as I once thought, by Zosimus’s three legates, Faustinus, bishop of the Church of Potentia, and the presbyters Philip and Asellus, but by Leo, then an acolyte and later Roman pontiff. He seems at the same time to have brought an order to Augustine that he should act in Mauretania as legate of the apostolic see (Augustine, Epistle 191). Concerning the condemnation of Coelestius and Pelagius there were two letters: one universal, which Mercator calls the *tractoria*; the other a special letter to the Africans, who gave thanks in the most lavish terms (Augustine, Epistle 190).

## XIII. SYNOD, the second African synod, held there around the middle of June in the same year

From what has been discussed thus far, it seems to follow that, if we wish to speak with Augustine, the synod which he later called the plenary African council must be counted as the thirteenth, and that it was at this synod that those famous eight canons concerning the faith were enacted:

1. “It pleased all the bishops who were present at this holy synod that whoever says that Adam, the first human being, was created mortal in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die in the body—that is, depart from the body—not because of the merit of sin but by the necessity of nature, let him be anathema.

2. Likewise, it pleased the council that whoever denies that newborn infants are to be baptized, or says that they are indeed baptized for the remission of sins but derive nothing of original sin from Adam which might be cleansed by the washing of regeneration—so that it follows that the form of baptism ‘for the remission of sins’ is understood in them not truly but falsely—let him be anathema. For the Apostle’s statement, ‘Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Romans 5:12), must be understood in no other way than the Catholic Church, spread everywhere, has always understood it. For on account of this rule of faith even infants, who have not yet been able to commit any sins personally, are truly baptized for the remission of sins, so that what they have contracted through generation may be cleansed in them through regeneration.

3. Likewise, it pleased the council that whoever says that the grace of God, by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord, is effective only for the remission of sins already committed, and not also as assistance so that sins may not be committed, let him be anathema.

4. Likewise, whoever says that this same grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord assists us in not sinning only because through it the understanding of the commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we know what we ought to seek and what we ought to avoid, but that through it we are not enabled to love and to be able to do what we have recognized ought to be done, let him be anathema. For when the Apostle says, ‘Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up’ (1 Corinthians 8:1), it is exceedingly impious to believe that we have the grace of Christ for that which puffs us up, but not for that which builds us up, since both are gifts of God: knowing what we ought to do and loving in order that we may do it, so that when charity builds up, knowledge cannot puff up. And just as it is written of God, ‘He who teaches human beings knowledge’ (Psalm 93:10), so it is also written, ‘Charity is from God’ (1 John 4:7).

5. Likewise, it pleased the council that whoever says that the grace of justification is given to us for this reason: so that we may more easily fulfill by grace what we are commanded to do by free choice—as though, even if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commandments without it, though not easily—let him be anathema. For the Lord was speaking of the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, ‘Without me you can do it with greater difficulty,’ but said, ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John 15:5).

6. Likewise, it pleased the council that whoever thinks that the words of the holy Apostle John, ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us’ (1 John 1:8), should be understood as meaning that, out of humility, we ought not to say that we have no sin—not because this is true—let him be anathema. For the Apostle continues and adds, ‘But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity’ (ibid.); and here it is sufficiently clear that this is to be said not only humbly but also truthfully. For the Apostle could have said, ‘If we say that we have no sin, we exalt ourselves, and humility is not in us.’ He sufficiently shows that whoever says he has no sin speaks not the truth but falsehood.

7. Likewise, it pleased the council that whoever says that the saints say in the Lord’s Prayer, ‘Forgive us our debts’ (Matthew 6:12), for the purpose of asking this not for themselves, since this petition is no longer necessary for them, but for the sinners who are among their people—and therefore that each of the saints does not say, ‘Forgive me my debts,’ but ‘Forgive us our debts,’ so that the just person is understood to ask this for others rather than for himself—let him be anathema. For the apostle James was holy and just when he said, ‘For we all offend in many things’ (James 3:2). Why was ‘all’ added, unless so that this statement might correspond both to the psalm where it is written, ‘Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person shall be justified in your sight’ (Psalm 143:2), and to the prayer of the wisest Solomon, ‘There is no human being who does not sin’ (Ecclesiastes 7:21), and to the Book of Job, ‘He marks the hand of every human being, so that every human being may know his weakness’ (Job 37:7)? Hence Daniel, holy and just, when he said in his prayer in the plural, ‘We have sinned, we have acted wickedly,’ and so forth (Daniel 9:5), and there confessed these things truthfully and humbly, lest anyone think, as some suppose, that he had spoken them not of his own sins but rather of the sins of his people, later said, ‘While I was praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people to the Lord our God’ (ibid. 20). He did not wish to say ‘our sins,’ but said ‘the sins of his people’ and his own, because, as a prophet, he foresaw those who would misunderstand these matters so badly.

8. Likewise, it pleased the council that whoever wishes those very words of the Lord’s Prayer, in which we say, ‘Forgive us our debts’ (Matthew 6:12), to be spoken by the saints in such a way that they say this humbly but not truthfully, let him be anathema. For who could endure someone praying and lying not to human beings but to the Lord himself, who says with his lips that he wishes to be forgiven, while in his heart he says that he has no debts to be forgiven?”

It is worthy of note that in all the other councils of the African Church nothing concerning the faith was decreed; rather, they dealt solely with discipline and with the cases of individuals. Was this because provincial councils had no authority to define matters of doctrine, since the faith is a common concern, and no such matter was dealt with except in a council of all Africa? But why not even in the first universal council? Did the holy men—whose leader was Aurelius, and whose intellectual power, so to speak, was Augustine—understand that whenever a matter of faith was debated, all bishops ought to refer it only to Peter, that is, to the originator of his name and honor, and that this was an ancient tradition and an institution of the Fathers to be preserved by priestly office? (See the notes on the letter to the Council of Milevis and the Council of Carthage.)

Why, then, were canons enacted now? I think this happened because a copy of the *tractoria* had already reached the Fathers, although only through private letters and not yet through legates. Therefore, so that it might be handed to the departing bishops, I think at least the first two canons were extracted in advance from some portion of the *tractoria*. What if, grieving that the portion of the *tractoria* concerning the grace of God was missing, they thought it should be supplied by their own canons? It carried greater weight if accepted by everyone than if it came only from the delegates, whose authority perhaps did not extend so far.

How many bishops assembled has already been stated: namely, 214, provided that all who had previously assembled returned after Pentecost from their churches, which they had gone to visit. Hence an error entered Prosper’s Chronographer, which gives the number as 217. It would have been easy for scribes to write 217 instead of 214, although this error is not found in all manuscript codices.

This also requires correction of the poet Prosper’s hyperbole, when he says that the canons were issued by “three hundred tongues of nobles.” Poets customarily call a number that exceeds two hundred by the name of three hundred.

The time at which those most holy defenders of the faith assembled has also been sufficiently established: around the middle of June. It is reasonable to believe that they returned after the feast of Pentecost and the solemn baptism had been completed. Therefore, if they set out on the eighth day after the baptismal day, when the feasts concluded, and allotted fifteen days to the journey—a very short delay—it must be acknowledged that they could not have assembled before June 17. For in the year 418 the Sunday letter was F, Easter fell on April 7, Pentecost therefore fell on May 26, and the completion of the feasts on June 2.

## XIV. SYNOD, held at Rome in the same consulships by Pope Zosimus against Pelagius and Coelestius, on April 15

The fourteenth synod, which was the third Roman synod, was held by Pope Zosimus. It is the very synod which M. Mercator calls “the fuller hearing” (*Commonitorium*, chapter 1); Augustine calls it “the examination and judgment of the apostolic see” (Book II to Boniface, chapter 3, and Epistle 194); Possidius calls it “the judgment of the Catholic Church” (Life of Saint Augustine, chapter 18); the emperor Honorius calls it “the proceedings of the most blessed Church” (edict to Palladius); and Prosper calls it “the council of all the priests, subscribed by the hand of the whole world” (Book Against the Collator, chapter 41, and Poem Against the Ungrateful).

Zosimus held this synod after the arts of the heretics had been exposed and Coelestius’s bad faith had become clear. Hence [Col. 0356A] he sent throughout the whole world that celebrated letter which, as Prosper says, armed the right hands of all the bishops with Peter’s sword for the cutting off of the impious (Book Against the Collator, chapter 41).

But it is better to hear Mercator himself (*Commonitorium*, chapter 3):

“All the chapters written above, as has already been said, are contained in that letter of the blessed bishop Zosimus, which is called the *tractoria*. By it Coelestius and Pelagius were condemned; it was sent both to Constantinople and throughout the whole world, and was confirmed by the subscriptions of the holy Fathers,” and so forth.

Earlier, after mentioning the letter obtained from Coelestius by deceit, he had said:

“But when the bishops from Africa wrote back and set forth the entire case that had been dealt with among them, sending also the proceedings that had then been completed with him or concerning him, he was summoned to a fuller hearing, so that he might hasten to fulfill what he had promised—that is, so that, once the chapters mentioned above had been condemned, he might be absolved from the sentence of the African bishops by which he had been deprived of communion. He not only failed to appear, but even fled from the aforementioned city of Rome. For this reason he was most severely condemned in extensive and lengthy writings by the aforementioned bishop Zosimus of blessed memory. These writings contain the very chapters of which he had been accused, and the entire case, both that of the aforementioned Coelestius and that of his even more depraved teacher Pelagius, seems to have been narrated. We have copies of these writings here, and we suggest that similar and identical writings were sent to the bishops of the Eastern Churches, to the diocese of Egypt, Constantinople, Thessalonica, and Jerusalem.”

We have discussed the *tractoria* at greater length in the notes on the *Commonitorium*, and we shall also discuss it in the dissertation on the subscriptions required in the case of the Pelagians. There we shall show that the author of the appendix to Celestine’s letter called it canonical authority—that is, the rule of faith—and that in the case of the Pelagians it had to be subscribed just as, in the case of the Eutychian heresy, the letter of Saint Leo to Flavian had to be subscribed.

[Col. 0356C] How many bishops assembled is entirely unknown. That many assembled can be inferred from the fact that Mercator calls it a fuller hearing. Augustine reports that the urban clergy, and even a very large crowd, were present. He says this either when he relates that the presbyter Sixtus, whom rumor accused of favoring the enemies of grace, pronounced an anathema against them first, in the presence of a very large crowd (Epistle 194); or when he reports the complaints—or rather the slanders—of the Pelagians against the Roman clergy, as though, struck by the terror of an order, they had not blushed to commit the crime of treachery by later declaring, contrary to their earlier judgment by which they had supported the Catholic doctrine in the proceedings, that human nature was evil (Book II to Boniface, chapter 3).

The date has been debated, at least in part, while the African councils were being investigated. Since the assembly held on the Kalends of May sent a reply to Zosimus’s third letter, dated the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in which the pontiff stated that nothing had yet been decided by the supreme judgment; and since he issued his sentence before Honorius, who, following that judgment, issued his constitution to Palladius on the day before the Kalends of May, the synod must have assembled in the intervening period. But the greater part of that time was occupied by Lent and the Easter feasts, which fell on April 7. It is reasonable to believe that the synod was held immediately after the feast days had ended, that is, on April 15, and that, after the proceedings had been brought to Honorius, the sanction was issued on the day before the Kalends of May.

Everything fits this chronology well: Augustine’s account to Optatus of Zosimus’s letter (Epistle, in Augustine 201); Jerome’s account to Alypius and Augustine of the destruction of the Coelestian heresy, with them as collaborators and authors; and the accounts of other writers concerning Zosimus’s entire affair with the Pelagians.

Nothing remains of Zosimus’s *tractoria* except certain fragments, partly in Augustine and partly in the appendix to Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul, but these are scarcely sufficient to console us for so great a loss.

### From Augustine’s Epistle 157 to Optatus

“For, to use now the words that are found in the letter of the most blessed bishop Zosimus:

‘The Lord is faithful in his words, and his baptism, both in reality and in words—that is, in deed, confession, and the true remission of sins—possesses the same fullness in every sex, age, condition, and class of the human race. For no one is made free unless he is a slave of sin; nor can anyone be called redeemed unless he was truly captive beforehand through sin, as it is written: “If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free” (John 8:36). Through him we are spiritually reborn; through him we are crucified to the world. By his death, the document of death introduced and transmitted to all of us from Adam, contracted through descent, is torn up—a document to which absolutely no one born is not held liable before being freed through baptism.’

In these words of the apostolic see, the Catholic faith is so ancient, firmly grounded, certain, and clear that it is impious for Christians to doubt it.”

### From the authorities or judgments of the former pontiffs of the apostolic see, customarily appended to Pope Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul

#### Chapter VIII

That all the efforts, works, and merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him from any other source than from what he himself has given.

The authoritative rule of Pope Zosimus, of blessed memory, directs us toward this judgment. When writing to the bishops of the whole world, he says:

“Nevertheless, by God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—we have brought everything before the awareness of our brothers and fellow bishops.”

The African bishops revered this speech, shining with the light of the most sincere truth, with such honor that they wrote to the same man:

“But as for what you placed in the letter which you arranged to have sent to all the provinces, saying, ‘Nevertheless, by God’s prompting,’ and so forth, we have understood it in this way: that, as you passed swiftly by, you severed with the sharp sword of truth those who exalt the freedom of human choice against God’s assistance. For what did you do that was so free according to free choice as to refer everything to the awareness of our humility? Yet you faithfully and wisely recognized, and truthfully and confidently declared, that this was done by God’s prompting. This is so because the will is prepared by the Lord, and he himself touches the hearts of his children through paternal inspirations, so that they may do something good. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God (Romans 8:14). Thus we recognize that our free choice is not absent, yet we do not doubt that in every movement of human will toward good his assistance is more powerful.”

#### Chapter IX

That God works in the hearts of human beings, and in free choice itself, in such a way that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of a good will come from God, because through him we can do something good, without whom we can do nothing.

The same teacher instructed us to make this confession when, speaking to the bishops of the whole world about the assistance of divine grace, he said:

“What period of time, then, intervenes in which we do not need his assistance? In all our acts and affairs, thoughts and movements, he must be prayed to as our helper and protector. For human nature is presumptuous if it claims anything for itself, while the Apostle cries out: ‘Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers and powers of this air, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places’ (Ephesians 6:12). And as he himself says again: ‘Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (Romans 7:24). And again: ‘By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain; but I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me’ (1 Corinthians 15:10).”

What the outcome was, and what the fruit was, whether of the council or of the circular letter (*tractoria*), may be understood from all the writers of that age, [Col. 0358A] especially Augustine, Prosper, Mercator, and others, together with Possidius, whose words are these (*Life of St. Augustine*, ch. 18):

“And because those same men (the Pelagianists), in their ambition, were trying to persuade the Apostolic See to share their same perfidy, the holy African bishops most insistently arranged, through councils, that the holy pope of the city of Rome—first the venerable Innocent, and afterward his successor, the holy Zosimus—should be persuaded that that sect was to be rejected and condemned by the Catholic faith. Those bishops of so great a see, however, marking out the same men at the appropriate times and cutting them off from the members of the Church, judged by letters sent to the Churches of Africa, the East, and the West that they were to be anathematized and avoided by all Catholics. And when the most pious emperor Honorius heard and followed this judgment, pronounced against them by the Catholic Church of God, he decreed by his laws that they should be condemned and held among the heretics. Consequently, some of them returned to the bosom of Holy Mother Church, from which they had recoiled, etc.”

## XV SYNOD

Convened at Carthage by Aurelius from the whole diocese of Africa, in the same year, in the month of August.

[Col. 0358B]

The fifteenth synod—which, if we wish to speak with Augustine, ought to be called the third universal African council in the Pelagian case—was celebrated, as stated earlier, at Carthage around the middle of August. It could not have been later, since Augustine was present, and on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October he was staying at Caesarea in Mauretania.

Fifteen bishops were seated, chosen from the individual provinces, as provided in the final canon of the preceding council. It was likewise decided that, so that all the bishops who had assembled for the council would not be detained any longer, three judges should be chosen from each province by the whole council. From the province of Carthage, Vincentius, Fortunatianus, and Clarus were chosen; from the province of Numidia, Alypius, Augustine, and Restitutus; from the province of Byzacena, together with [Col. 0358C] the venerable old man Donatianus, its primate, Cresconius, Jocundus, and Aemilianus; from Mauretania Sitifensis, Severianus, Asiaticus, and Donatus; and from the province of Tripolitania, Plautius, who, according to custom, was sent as the sole legate. All of these, together with the venerable old man Aurelius, were to investigate the whole matter. The entire council asked him to subscribe personally to all the records that had already been drawn up, as well as to the letters. And they subscribed. “I, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have consented to this decree and, after it was read aloud, have subscribed.” The others likewise subscribed. Aurelius presided according to custom, together with the venerable Donatianus of the province of Byzacena. From this circumstance observe that the primates were always present in addition to the number of legates.

In the cited canon, however, only fifteen chosen men are enumerated; the names of the men chosen from both Mauretania Caesariensis and Mauretania Tingitana are missing, although it is clear from the preface of the preceding African council that the Fathers of both provinces attended. If these men were present together with the two primates, they would indeed increase the number, but not so far as to make it equal to the number [Col. 0358D] found in the commonly published councils, where the council is said to have been held by thirty-eight bishops. Or perhaps some of the Fathers remained behind of their own accord? Or was the copyist ashamed of so small a number and, by adding the mark for fifteen on either side, increased it? The reason why no legates from the two coastal Mauretanias remained seems to me not implausible: namely, that by the time the election was made—or rather, by the time the canon was composed—the bishops of both of those provinces had already departed because of the war brought by the Visigoths against the Vandals, Silingians, and Alans, who were settled in the neighboring part of Spain.

What was done in the synod is sufficiently, indeed abundantly, clear from the foregoing. Two letters of Zosimus were read, one addressed generally to all the bishops of the world, the other specifically to the Africans. Thanks were rendered in a written letter, a fragment of which is preserved by Prosper (*Against the Conference*, ch. 10):

“The African bishops went astray when they wrote back to that same pope Zosimus and praised [Col. 0359A] him in the celebration of this judgment, when they said: ‘But when you wrote in your letter, which you arranged to be sent to all, saying: “Nevertheless, at God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—we referred everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops,” we understood you to have said this in such a way that, as you passed swiftly by, you cut down with the drawn sword of truth those who exalt human free will against God’s help. For what did you do so freely with your free will as to refer everything to the conscience of our humility? And yet you rightly and wisely saw that this had been done at God’s prompting, and you said so truly and confidently. This is because the will is prepared by the Lord, and he himself touches the hearts of his children with paternal inspirations so that they may do something good. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God (Rom. 8:14). Thus we do not think that our free will is absent, yet in every good act and in each movement of the human will we do not hesitate to acknowledge that his help is the more powerful.’”

## XVI SYNOD

Convened at Carthage by Aurelius, in the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta, on the third day before the Kalends of July, in the year 419.

[Col. 0359B]

This other universal African council may, indeed must, be assigned to this place. It is recorded as having been celebrated at Carthage after the twelfth consulship of Honorius and the eighth of Theodosius, on the third day before the Kalends of July, in the secretary of the restored basilica—that is, in the year 419, on 29 June. At it the eight canons against the Pelagian heresy were reviewed and approved once more.

An imperial letter addressed to Aurelius at Ravenna on the fifth day before the Ides of June was also accepted, unless I am mistaken. It concerned the demand that all bishops subscribe to the condemnation of Caelestius and Pelagius.

Moreover, an imperial decree was sent by Aurelius on the Kalends of August to the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana. Both documents are reproduced and explained in the following dissertation, whose notes also shed considerable light on the present matters.

[Col. 0359C]

Twenty-two bishops were present, whose names are listed in the records. Faustinus, bishop of the city of Potentia, was also present, together with two other legates of the Apostolic See, the presbyters Philippus and Asellus.

The statement that 217 bishops assembled should be understood to mean that this many were said to have subscribed because, when the others returned to their own Churches, they chose that number of legates to conduct the matter in the common name.

The fact that the delegated judges held the council long after the others had returned to their Churches is attested not only by the records; the following consideration also proves it: various councils of the whole province of Africa, celebrated in past times during the episcopate of Aurelius of Carthage, were recited in this synod. They were not merely recited but, as I think, abbreviated; and this could not have been done without a considerable period of time. I therefore hold that the abbreviation was made by the Fathers, not rashly by some compiler, as certain people have thought. I refrain, however, from adducing arguments, because I see that the question is being treated somewhat more heatedly [Col. 0359D] than perhaps a stricter modesty permits.

## XVII SYNOD

Held at Anazarbus by the bishops of Second Cilicia under Maximianus against Julian, in the consulship of Asclepiodotus and Rufus, in the year 423.

Of the seventeenth synod, held by the bishops of Second Cilicia in Julian’s case, Mercator is the only witness I know of (*Preface to the Symbol of Theodore of Mopsuestia*):

“Let the aforementioned Julian acknowledge from this translation, if he is not reluctant to read it, that, while there remains in the aforementioned Theodore that by which, as we said, he had deceitfully misled Nestorius, it is even more contrary to Julian himself and to his doctrine—concerning which he composed books, wickedly swollen and unsound—and that, after Julian’s departure from Cilicia, he too was condemned by Theodore under anathema in the assembly of the bishops of his province.”

From these words, although they are extremely brief and by no means [Col. 0360A] clear and by no means clear, we have tried, by conjecture, to ascertain the time, cause, place, and names of the Fathers in the notes to the cited preface. Our reasoning was as follows, beginning with the investigation of the date.

Since the synod was held after Julian’s departure from Cilicia and before the death of Theodore of Mopsuestia; since Theodore died in the year 428, according to Theodoret (*at the end of the Ecclesiastical History*); and since Julian returned from Cilicia to Italy in the year 423, as we established in the preceding dissertation (ch. 5), the synod must be assigned to the interval of five years between those events. But to which year? To the year, I think, in which Julian left Cilicia—that is, 423. The clerics corrupted by Julian presumably began to create an uproar immediately, once the presence and authority of their teacher, which had previously restrained them, had been removed lest his unspeakable mysteries be made public. For Saint Celestine testifies that something similar happened elsewhere, in a letter addressed to Maximianus of Constantinople after the Council of Ephesus.

[Col. 0360B]

I therefore think that the reason for convening the synod was no other than what has just been stated: namely, the audacity of the heresy, which had burst into the open, although it had previously been taught only secretly by Julian and his associates—among whom, I have no doubt, Caelestius was included. The bishops of Second Cilicia, judging that this had to be suppressed, pronounced anathema against the heresy, which they easily recognized as having long since been condemned both at Antioch, to whose diocese they belonged, and in Palestine, on the island of Rhodes, and at Constantinople, with which they were connected by very frequent travel.

Since Mercator says that this assembly consisted of the bishops of the province in which Mopsuestia was located, it is reasonable to suppose that it was convened by the metropolitan of Second Cilicia, namely, by the bishop of Anazarbus, which was later called Justinianopolis. The bishops of Mopsuestia, Aegeae, Castabala, Epiphaneia, Flaviopolis, Irenopolis, Alexandria, and Rossus would have sat there. For it is clear from the Council of Mopsuestia of the year 550 that these sees were under the metropolitan of Anazarbus. [Col. 0360C]

At that time Maximianus, or Maximus, was bishop of Anazarbus; Hesychius of Castabala; Polychronius of Epiphaneia; Aurelius of Irenopolis; and Theodore held the episcopate of Mopsuestia. All these, except Theodore, are found subscribing in the Ephesian assembly convened eight years earlier (*Labbe’s edition of the Councils*, vol. 3, p. 598). Maximianus also subscribed in Nestorius’s report to the emperors, where he is called Maximus (*Acts of Ephesus*, part 2, act 2, p. 567). It is credible that these same bishops had sat in the places mentioned above eight years earlier.

It is said that Julian was anathematized in the council by all the bishops, including Theodore, who was accustomed to such tricks. What else was done is entirely unknown.

It is surprising that Julian could be anathematized by men who later supported Nestorius and had already absorbed the errors of Theodore, who misled Nestorius, since Julian and Nestorius were joined by a kinship of heresy. It must be remembered, however, that the doctrine [Col. 0360D] of Julian condemned in this council was nothing other than his teaching concerning Adam’s mortality and original sin. As for Theodore, it is clear that Nestorius must be regarded not merely as having been free from this error, but also as having opposed it. This is evident from the sermons delivered in the church, which we published after Mercator had rendered them into Latin, and which Celestine mentions (*Letter to Nestorius*, in part 1 of the Council of Ephesus, ch. 18).

From this it may be inferred why not only the Fathers who were establishing the ecumenical synod at Ephesus, but also the schismatics who had joined John of Antioch, each charged their opponents with association with the Caelestians. On both sides there were bishops from those provinces in which the Caelestian heresy had become so powerful that it had infected many among the laity and clergy, as well as not a few among the leaders of the Churches, and had deserved condemnation in ecclesiastical judgments, even [Col. 0361A] those by which bishops were deposed. Thus at Ephesus, in Palestine, at Antioch, in Cilicia, and in other places from which bishops had assembled at Ephesus, that plague had raged and then been suppressed.

It is also possible to understand why, in the petition that Saint Cyril of Alexandria and Memnon, bishop of Ephesus, presented to the synod after the schismatics had unjustly deposed them, they mentioned the doctrines of the Caelestians while rebutting the charge of various heresies brought against them. They spoke as follows (*Council of Ephesus*, part 2, act 5):

“For we have never at any time approved the teaching of Apollinaris, Arius, or Eunomius. From our earliest age, however, we learned the sacred Scriptures and were brought up in the hands of the holy and orthodox Fathers. We anathematize Apollinaris, Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Sabellius, Photinus, Paul, the Manichaeans, and every other heresy; and, in addition to these, Nestorius, the inventor of new blasphemies, together with those who [Col. 0361B] communicate and agree with him, and those who follow the teachings of Caelestius or Pelagius, whose doctrines we have never accepted. Nor do we now, after changing our will through repentance, receive ourselves back into right belief; rather, as has been said, we were nourished in the sound and apostolic doctrines of the Church.”

Memnon—or perhaps Cyril as well—could have come under suspicion of favor shown to Caelestius, since Memnon had been a presbyter of the Church of Ephesus and had sent Valerianus to Alexandria to test Cyril’s faith. Nevertheless, I think that statement may appear to bear the character of a charge rejected against the schismatics: namely, that they followed Nestorius, a supporter of Photinus of Samosata, the Manichaeans, Pelagius, and Caelestius. For there was a great association of error between the man of Samosata and Pelagius concerning Christ having earned divinity by his own merits, as we have shown in the dissertation on the authors and defenders of the Pelagian heresy.

## XVIII SYNOD

Held at Constantinople by Atticus in the case of the bishops expelled from the West, in the year 424 or 425.

[Col. 0361C]

The eighteenth synod, the second Constantinopolitan synod in the Pelagian case, was convened by Atticus in the year 424 or at the beginning of the following year.

Prosper mentions it in these verses (*Poem on the Unwarranted*, ch. 2):

> What should I say of the great care which the good priest  
> Atticus exercised in the great city,  
> With learned speech at Constantinople,  
> Refuting the envoys of the heretics by the ancient faith,  
> By which, though they concealed themselves beneath  
> A covering semblance of form,  
> Those impious hearts endured the silent torments  
> Of a rejected judgment?

Pope Celestine also mentions it when writing to Nestorius about the Pelagians, in these words (*Council of Ephesus*, part 1, ch. 18):

“For a few days of our life, after the infamous and repeatedly condemned doctrine of Pelagius and Caelestius, the Catholic faith enjoyed repose, when East and West, united in judgment, [Col. 0361D] struck them and the followers of their opinion with their weapons. The same Atticus, of holy memory, teacher of the Catholic faith and truly the successor in this matter of the blessed John, pursued them on behalf of the common King in such a way that they were not even granted the opportunity to remain there.”

And shortly afterward:

“These heretics too, about whom you wished to consult us as though unaware of what had been done, were expelled from their sees by a just condemnation, although they said that it was unjust. We do not think it surprising that they found no rest there.”

And later:

“We have read how well you hold to original sin.”

And later:

“What have those who were condemned for denying these things to do with you?”

And later:

“Why are the acts then carried out against these men being investigated, when it is certain that what was done there was communicated to us by Atticus, then the Catholic bishop? Why did Sisinnius, of holy memory, not investigate these matters? Because under his predecessor he had plainly approved that they had been justly condemned.”

From these two witnesses it is clearly evident that the synod of which both speak differs [Col. 0362A] from the earlier one from the earlier one that we placed in the eighth position. The earlier was held during the time of Zosimus; this one during the time of Celestine. In the earlier, only Caelestius’s case was heard; in the later, the case of the bishops expelled from the West. In the earlier, Mercator does not say that Caelestius was questioned, but only that he was caught in similar doctrines which he had spread at Carthage. In the later, Prosper says that the heretics were refuted by the ancient faith. Caelestius alone was present at the earlier synod; at the later, envoys of the heretics were present. After the earlier synod, Caelestius was driven from the nourishing city; after the second, those whom East and West had struck with the weapons of their united judgment were expelled. From the earlier synod letters were sent to the bishops of Asia, Thessalonica, and Carthage; from the later, to the Apostolic See. It is therefore certain that those are mistaken who not only confuse the two synods into one, but also understand Caelestius alone by the name “envoys sent by the heretics.”

[Col. 0362B]

The date of the synod can be determined without difficulty from what has just been said. Since Atticus died on 10 October 425, while Celestine began to sit in the Apostolic See on 3 November 423, Atticus must have held the synod at Constantinople in 424 or at the beginning of 425, provided that he sent the acts to Pope Celestine, as Celestine himself testifies.

What the outcome was is clear both from Prosper’s verses and from Celestine’s letter to Nestorius: the Pelagian bishops were expelled from the royal city. Atticus, teacher of the Catholic faith and truly the successor there of the blessed John, brought his glorious life—passed amid the changing turns of events—to its end, dying amid what were, as it were, his triumphs after the defeat of Christ’s enemies.

The acts have perished, to the great detriment of the Catholic cause. For if it is permissible to infer from Prosper’s words, they contained arguments drawn from the tradition of the Fathers, by which the envoys of the heretics were refuted concerning the questions on account of which they complained that they had been unjustly condemned—namely, original sin and the grace of God through Christ. Atticus, with the extraordinary skill in treating matters that was his strength, pressed these arguments vigorously in his customary manner and set them out so that all could understand [Col. 0362C] them. No Father was stronger in pressing a subject or clearer in explaining it.

## XIX SYNOD

Held at Rome by Celestine in the case of the bishops obstinately favoring Pelagius, in the consulship of Victor and Castinus, in the year 424, or in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus XI and Valentinian Caesar, in the year 425.

The nineteenth synod, the fourth Roman synod, was convened by Celestine at Rome in the case of the bishops who stubbornly refused to subscribe to the formula of faith prescribed by Zosimus.

Nestorius makes a somewhat obscure mention of the synod convened by Celestine in this matter when writing to Celestine himself on behalf of the Pelagians (*Letter 1 to Celestine*, in part 1 of the Council of Ephesus, ch. 16):

“Deign to grant us information concerning these matters, lest some people, through ignorance of the justice of truth, be disturbed by an inopportune compassion, or lest they regard the canonical indignation of Your Beatitude—which was perhaps approved against [Col. 0362D] them on account of religious sects—as something other than this.”

For what is “canonical indignation” pronounced on account of religious sects, if not a synodal judgment? For it had been established by the canons, or at least received as the custom of the Church, that judgment concerning doctrines should not be pronounced except in a synod.

Prosper speaks somewhat more clearly (*Against the Conference*, ch. 41):

“Pope Celestine, of venerable memory, to whom the Lord granted many gifts of his grace for the protection of the Catholic Church, knowing that condemned men should be granted not a judicial examination but only the remedy of repentance, ordered Caelestius, who was requesting a hearing as though the case had not been examined, to be expelled from the entire territory of Italy. So firmly did he judge that the statutes of his predecessors and the decrees of the synods had to be observed inviolably that he would by no means permit a matter once deserving severance to be reopened.”

[Col. 0363A]

The Ephesian Fathers state the matter openly (*Council of Ephesus*, part 2, act 5):

“After the records concerning the deposition of the impious Pelagians and Caelestians had been read aloud in the holy synod, together with what Your Piety had decreed and established concerning them, we too judged that these things must remain solid and firm.”

There is, however, some uncertainty concerning these testimonies: namely, whether they are to be understood of only one council or of two, one preceding Nestorius’s letter and the other following it.

For it is certain that, after receiving Nestorius’s letter, Celestine celebrated a council at Rome in which not only Nestorius’s case but also that of the Pelagian bishops was dealt with. From that council he sent letters to Nestorius, the clergy of Constantinople, Cyril of Alexandria, John of Antioch, and Juvenal of Jerusalem, containing the condemnation of Nestorius and, indeed, of others as well.

It is also certain that the acts of this council were either sent together with the letters and instructions to Cyril, or—which I consider more likely—carried by the legates of the Apostolic See, Arcadius, [Col. 0363B] Projectus, and Philippus, to the Fathers assembled at Ephesus. They were read and approved by the holy synod. Therefore either no assembly was held by Celestine before Nestorius’s letter, or the assembly we have mentioned was different from it.

Yet the existence of some earlier assembly is indicated both by the words of Nestorius’s first letter, “the canonical indignation of Your Beatitude,” and especially by these words in his later letter: “that they had been cast out from the western regions.” These expressions indicate that bishops had been deposed by Celestine in a council, since in those times it was unheard-of—or rather, considered an open violation of the canons—for a bishop to be deposed, even by the supreme pontiff, without the assembly of a council. Thus two councils were convened at different times in the case of the bishops who refused to subscribe.

But when was the first? The date of the later one is sufficiently established by the letter sent by Celestine to Cyril on the third day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, Augusti and consuls—that is, on 11 August 430. I do not think that the earlier council can be placed more suitably [Col. 0363C] anywhere than in either the second or the third year of Celestine, that is, either in the year of Christ 424, when the acts against the envoys of the heretics were brought from Constantinople to Rome, or in 425, when Atticus passed to the better life.

## XX SYNOD

The universal African synod convened by Aurelius in the same consulship, in the case of, among others, Leporius the monk, converted from error to the true faith.

In this same year a universal council was celebrated at Carthage by Aurelius. I call it the fifth African council in the Pelagian case, and I think it should be placed twentieth among the synods.

I believe that no canons were enacted there, but that the proceedings concerned either the execution of the canons already reviewed long before or cases relating to individuals that had been brought forward from the provinces.

Nevertheless, Leporius’s confession was read aloud, and it was subscribed in the name of the entire African synod by four bishops: Aurelius, [Col. 0363D] Augustine, Florentius, and Secundus. These men also sent letters to Proculus of Massilia, Cyllinius of Aquae, and the other Gallic bishops, by which Leporius’s libellus was confirmed.

This confirmation caused Leporius’s confession to be attributed to the universal African synod and to be regarded as a doctrinal definition of the bishops by the deacon Basilius, Thalassius, and other monks, who are recorded in the acts of the Council of Ephesus as having submitted a petition against Nestorius to the emperor Theodosius (*Council of Ephesus*, part 1, ch. 30). For this reason, the letter that the Africans sent to the bishops of Gaul together with Leporius’s libellus was not improperly called a synodical letter, and we therefore reproduce it. But first this whole history, since it has hitherto exercised learned men and divided them into factions, must be treated somewhat more carefully.

[Col. 0364A]

That Leporius had been infected by the contagion of the Pelagian error is attested by Cassian and Gennadius. Cassian says (*On the Incarnation*, book 1, ch. 4):

“Leporius, then a monk and now a presbyter, who, descending from the instruction—or rather, the depravity—of Pelagius, as we said above, was among the first or greatest defenders of that heresy in Gaul, was admonished by us and corrected by God. He condemned his badly conceived persuasion so magnificently that his correction is scarcely less admirable than the unshaken faith of many others. Returning, therefore, to himself, he not only confessed his error with grief and without shame in Africa, where he then was and now is, but also sent letters of tearful confession and lamentation to all the cities of Gaul, so that where his deviation had become known, his correction might also be known, etc.”

Gennadius says likewise (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 59):

“Leporius, while still a monk and afterward a presbyter, presuming upon the purity of life which he believed he had obtained solely through his own will and effort, and not through God’s help, began to follow the Pelagian doctrine. But, admonished by Gallic teachers and corrected by God in Africa through [Col. 0364B] Augustine, he wrote a libellus of his correction, in which he both made satisfaction for his error and gave thanks for his correction, etc.”

It is therefore established that Leporius erred with the Pelagians. Cassian explains in what respect his error was related to the Pelagian error, in these words (*On the Incarnation*, ch. 1):

“We certainly do not think that the following point should be passed over: it was a distinctive and characteristic feature of that heresy, which had descended from the Pelagian error, that certain people, saying that the solitary man Jesus Christ had lived without any contagion of sin, advanced so far as to assert that human beings, if they wished, could be without sin. For they considered it to follow that, if the solitary man Jesus Christ had been without sin, all human beings too could exist without God’s help, whatever that solitary man, without association with God, had been able to do; and thus they made no distinction between the whole of humanity and our Lord Jesus Christ, since any human being could, by his own exertion and industry, earn what Christ [Col. 0364C] had earned by his effort and labor. As a result, advancing into still greater and more monstrous madness, they said that our Lord Jesus Christ came into this world not to provide redemption for the human race, but to provide examples of good deeds, so that human beings, by following his discipline and walking along the same path of virtue, might attain the same rewards of virtue.”

Leporius himself explains the matter similarly when he says:

“I also consider it absolutely necessary not to conceal the following point: in the same letter, straying through a similar error, I added that Christ our Lord fulfilled all that belonged to his sufferings in such a way that, as a perfect man, he was in no respect aided by the help of divinity, etc.”

[Col. 0364D]

That monk had included his error in a letter, as he testifies in his confession:

“Where discord arose, let peace be born from there. Therefore, I ask that the letter—the cause of scandal and stumbling-block to charity—formerly written by me simply, indeed, but, as I acknowledge, unfaithfully composed in certain respects, be marked for deletion in that part or passage of the page in which it is shown to have been issued against the truth through ignorance, in accordance with the profession of this letter and the authority of your holiness; so that it may be known and evident to all, by a just judgment, that what was hostile to the faith and contrary to the truth has been cut out of the body of that same letter together with its condemnation.”

Admonished by Cassian to recognize his impiety—or rather, compelled by Proculus of Massilia to correct it—he stubbornly despised not less the command of the one ordering him than the advice of the one warning him. He was expelled either from the Church of Massilia or, more probably, from the Church of Aquae. He then departed for Africa and, having recognized the truth through Augustine’s work, professed it by submitting a libellus. All these facts are gathered partly from the cited works of Cassian and Gennadius and partly from the letter of the African Fathers to the Gallicians, which will be presented shortly.

[Col. 0365A]

After his correction, Leporius sent a letter to Proculus and Cyllinius and the other bishops of Gaul. Gennadius calls it a libellus of correction; Cassian calls it a confession, or rather a lamentation; Facundus calls it a satisfaction. Leporius asked that it be published widely throughout Gaul, so that everyone might know that, by a just judgment, that which was hostile to the faith had been cut out of the body of the same letter together with its condemnation.

This letter formerly possessed such authority that, on its account, Leporius could be called one of the defenders of the Catholic faith against Nestorius, and John Secundus could draw from it a testimony by which he confirmed the doctrine of the faith. Indeed, it was attributed to the plenary African synod, since that synod subscribed it with the hands of four bishops—Aurelius, Augustine, Florentius, and Secundus—and by subscribing made it its own.

Thus Facundus of Hermiane says (*Book 1*, ch. 4):

“Leporius wrote a libellus of satisfaction to the Gallic bishops. The venerable Fathers, Aurelius, Augustine, and the others, approved it in such a way that, to establish the truth of the matter, they added their own subscriptions to it.”

[Col. 0365B]

Cassian had already indicated the same thing at the place cited above, and had written even more magnificently when he called the letter the faith of all Catholics:

“All the African bishops, from whom he was writing, and all the Gallic bishops, to whom he was writing, approved this confession of his—that is, THE FAITH OF ALL CATHOLICS.”

John Secundus states the matter more plainly in his letter to Avienus:

“Leporius, in the letter which Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, the blessed Augustine, and the African synod confirmed.”

Leporius himself makes the point equally clear when subscribing to the libellus:

“I, Leporius, have subscribed to the libellus dictated according to my understanding, in which, wishing to express from the depths of my being the faith that, by God’s will, I shall hold to the end, after it was reread in the presence of the holy bishops in the Church of Carthage.”

Notice the place where the council was held: in the Church of Carthage.

The African Fathers not only subscribed to the libellus; they also sent a letter to the Gallic bishops, whose conclusion runs as follows:

“[Col. 0365C]

“As he was received by us through his presence, so let him be received by you through his letter. We also thought it right to subscribe to this letter with our own hands, bearing witness that it is his. We have no doubt that Your Love will gladly receive this correction of his and make it known to those for whom his error was a scandal, since those who came with him to us were corrected and healed together with him, as is expressly shown by their subscriptions, which were made in our presence, etc.”

Although Baronius considers it uncertain when the libellus was either presented to the African synod or sent to the bishops of Gaul (*Annals*, under the year 420, no. 13), others have nevertheless tried to determine the date. The author of the *Supplement to the Councils of Gaul* believes that it happened in the year 418 (*Supplement*, p. 20). P. Sirmond assigns it to the year 425 (*Gallic Councils*, vol. 1, in the notes), while P. Labbe assigns it to the following year, 426 (*General Councils*, vol. 2, p. 1684).

The author of the *Supplement to the Councils* proves his opinion by a weak argument. He thinks that the African synod mentioned by John Secundus was the same as the famous synod [Col. 0365D] held in 418 during the time of Zosimus. But this is rejected as easily as it is clearly shown that at least two African councils were assembled after that time: one around the year 423, as P. Labbe gathered from the papers of Luca Holstenius (*General Councils*, vol. 2, p. 1605); the other in 424, during the episcopate of Celestine. Leporius could therefore have presented the libellus to either of them.

Someone once argued the matter with me concerning the other two opinions as follows: Leporius was still a monk when he presented the libellus, but he was a presbyter when Cassian wrote about him in the year 429; the libellus was therefore presented before 429. Furthermore, Leporius’s error had not merely arisen but had also been condemned by its author before Nestorius taught the same doctrine, as Cassian relates; Nestorius taught it in 428; the libellus was therefore presented at least by 427. Third, it can be inferred—or at least seems possible to infer—from Cassian [Col. 0366A] that Leporius, who is mentioned in the ecclesiastical records drawn up by Augustine (*Letter 213*) when Augustine designated Eradius as his successor, was the same man whom Augustine ordained presbyter in the Church of Hippo after he had been a monk. This Leporius was counted among the presbyters of Hippo in 426, the year in which the records are dated. Since, therefore, the libellus was submitted by a monk, it must certainly have been submitted at least in 425, or even in 424, at which time, after the conclusion of Apiarius’s case, the universal council at Carthage sent a letter to Celestine, the successor of Boniface.

I cannot accept the opinion of this otherwise learned man, for two reasons. For he takes as certain what may rightly appear doubtful, if not entirely false: namely, that Leporius, whom the records list among the presbyters of Hippo, was the man now under discussion. I demonstrate that he was a different person [Col. 0366B] from the fact from the fact that Leporius is listed among those presbyters as second before Barnabas, Lazarus, and Eradius, Augustine’s longtime assistants, as is clear from Sermon 50 *On Various Matters*. He would certainly have been listed among the last if he had recently been made a presbyter from a monk.

What makes the matter still clearer is that Leporius, who is mentioned in the acts, was already a presbyter at the time when Eradius was still a young man and only a deacon—although Eradius had long since been counted among the presbyters when the acts were composed in 426, and these are numbered 110 among Augustine’s letters. Add that Leporius, whose libellus is under discussion, was not yet a presbyter but only a monk when he presented his libellus to the African synod and sent it to Gaul. For the African Fathers, in their letter to the Gauls, call him their “son,” and Cassian indicates that he was corrected before he was ordained. Indeed, who would have made a presbyter of Augustine, who held erroneous views about the faith concerning the Incarnation and had therefore been expelled from the Church? Who, then, was the Leporius mentioned in the acts? In my opinion, he was the man whom Augustine, in the sermon mentioned above, reports to have been illustrious by birth in the world and born among his people in a position of the highest honor, but who, after abandoning everything he possessed [Col. 0366C], undertook poverty for Christ.

Since Augustine subscribed to Leporius’s letter to the Gallic bishops, yet is not listed among the Fathers who wrote from the African council to Coelestine, someone might reasonably doubt whether that universal council of 424 was itself the African synod mentioned by John Secundus when he cites Leporius’s testimony. I do not deny that the force of this argument may be weakened by the fact that the African Fathers’ letter to Coelestine is somewhat severe, whereas at that very time Augustine was imploring help from Coelestine in the case of Antonius, bishop of Fussala, in letters of the greatest humility and urgency. It could therefore be said that Augustine refrained from subscribing lest, by attaching his own name, he provoke the mind of the supreme pontiff.

While my mind was wavering amid these doubts and uncertain conjectures, I happened by chance upon the supplication of Basil the deacon and archimandrite, together with other monks, who appealed to the emperor Theodosius concerning Nestorius. In it, not only is Leporius and the entire synod in Africa mentioned [Col. 0366D], but Leporius is also listed among the holy teachers of the faith who defended the truth that Christ is God against the impiety of Paul of Samosata and Photinus, and who expounded the mystery of the Incarnation in a Catholic manner (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, ch. 30). Yet until this day no African synod has been known, nor any teacher named Leporius who defended Christ’s divinity and expounded it to the faithful, apart from this monk—concerning whom Cassian, Gennadius, and John Secundus write, and who, converted by the African Fathers to a better understanding, admirably expounded Christ’s divinity in the libellus that he published as a confession of the Catholic faith, strengthened by the testimony of the African synod.

Therefore, however different Leporius the monk may be from Leporius the presbyter of Augustine—he who was noble in wealth but despised riches—the monk’s confession nevertheless seems to belong to the synod of 424 that we have mentioned [Col. 0367A]. For Basil, in the supplication that he presented to the emperor near the end of 429 or at the beginning of the following year, mentioned Leporius and the synod as matters belonging to a memory not particularly recent.

Moreover, in that same year Atticus and Aurelius, that distinguished pair of defenders of the faith, seem to have passed to heaven. The death of Atticus is recorded by Socrates on 10 October, during the consulship of Theodosius Augustus XI and Valentinian Caesar; after that time there is no further record of Aurelius—though there certainly would have been one had so eminent a bishop of the Church survived. Since, therefore, the supplication mentioned above refers both to Atticus and to the synod in which Aurelius took part, it is credible that the synod now under discussion was held during the time of Atticus.

Here we might enter into a new dispute with Cappellus, who rejects this entire African council, together with the letters sent from it to Coelestine, as some sort of fabrication invented by enemies of the Apostolic See. But quite apart from the fact that it is difficult to believe that so extensive a fiction could have remained hidden from all learned men, including those of antiquity, until this day [Col. 0367B], investigating the matter further would require a longer treatment. Since we intend to undertake that inquiry at some point in our history of the African Church, we now omit it lest we exceed the proper limits of this dissertation.

But since our present concern is with the acts of the councils relating to the Pelagian controversy, Leporius’s libellus must now be presented, together with the letter of the African Fathers to the bishops of Gaul. Both were published from the Herivall manuscript by Father Sirmondus first, and afterward by the author of the *Supplement to the Gallican Councils*. It is nevertheless not useless to transcribe both here, partly because the subject seems to require it, and partly because both have been cleansed of numerous errors that, I believe, escaped Sirmond’s exhausted diligence amid the manuscript’s inexhaustible corruptions. These errors were not so slight that they did not often divert the reader from the author’s true meaning to a false one. In addition, we observed in Leporius’s libellus several matters that are worth reading in themselves and cannot more conveniently be assigned elsewhere [Col. 0367C].

*(You now have, reader, Leporius’s libellus, together with the letter of the African Fathers to the bishops of Gaul, in volume XXXI of this* Bibliotheca*, col. 1221.)*

## XXI SYNOD

The first Gallican synod, convened, as is conjectured, by Honoratus, bishop of Arles, at Arles, during the consulship of Hierius and Ardaburius, in the year 427.

The twenty-first synod must be regarded as that large synod of the Gallican Fathers who, when aid was requested by the English Church against the Pelagian heresy—which had been spread and was growing astonishingly strong through the agency of Agricola, son of Severianus, a Pelagian bishop—sent the two most holy bishops, Germanus of Auxerre and Lupus of Troyes, to defend the Catholic faith in Britain (Prosper, *Chronicle*, under the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius).

The acts of this large synod are said to exist intact, with the names both of the bishops and of the presiding bishop [Col. 0367D]. A memorandum given by the Fathers to the two legates, Germanus and Lupus, is also said to exist. I do not doubt that these acts likewise contain the place and date, if indeed they still exist. But until they are brought to light—as I hope will happen soon—it was permissible to make some conjectures, though cautiously, and to draw from published authors something that does not appear unreasonable.

Father Labbeus did indeed make several observations worthy of attention on this subject (*Councils*, vol. II, p. 1686, and vol. III, pp. 1464 and 1676), but he states that he follows Bede and Sigebert; concerning them, judgment will have to be given later.

It is therefore safer to begin with the learned Sirmondus (*Gallican Councils*, vol. I, in the notes to p. 86):

> Just as the place of this synod is not established, so its date is also uncertain. For Sigebert, under the year of Christ 456, clearly assigns the mission of Germanus with Lupus to Britain [Col. 0368A], and Bede’s account seems to favor Sigebert. But Prosper, in his *Chronicle*, reports that Germanus was sent to Britain by Pope Coelestine in 429; following him, Baronius judged that this synod was held in that year.

Thus that most prudent man, after reporting the divergent opinions, preferred to endorse none of them. I nevertheless believe that the date of the synod is not as uncertain as it seemed to Sirmondus, although I do not think what Labbeus asserted on the authority of those two authors can be maintained. I consider greater credence due to Prosper the chronicler, to Constantius the author of the *Life of Saint Germanus*, and also to the author of the *Life of Saint Lupus*, than either to Bede or to Sigebert, since the former wrote about events that they had almost before their eyes, and certainly about matters then known to everyone, whereas Bede wrote nearly three hundred years later and Sigebert seven hundred years later.

To establish the chronology clearly, I take four points as premises. First, Prosper places Germanus’s mission to the Britons under the consulship of Florentius [Col. 0368B] and Dionysius—that is, in 429. His account is as follows:

> Agricola, a Pelagian and son of Severianus the Pelagian, corrupted the churches of Ireland by insinuating his doctrine. But at the intervention of Palladius the deacon, Pope Coelestine sends Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, in his place, so that, after the heretics had been driven out, he might lead the Britons back to the Catholic faith.

Second, Constantius writes that Germanus was sent with Lupus of Troyes by a large synod of Gallican bishops (*Life of Saint Germanus*, ch. 14, in Surius, 31 July).

Third, the author of the *Life of Saint Lupus* also writes that Lupus came to the island of Lérins for the sake of the religious life while Honoratus was still abbot; after spending one year there, he was taken away to the bishopric of Troyes, and after two years had passed he accompanied Germanus on the British expedition (*in Surius, 30 July*).

Finally, no learned person can doubt that Germanus’s mission [Col. 0368C] from the supreme pontiff to Britain is the same as his dispatch by the Gallican synod. For once Germanus’s election by the synod to the apostolic office had been approved by Saint Coelestine, and once the authority conferred upon him had also been increased, it could truly be called both an apostolic legation and a synodal mission.

From these facts it is manifest that the synod under discussion was not celebrated after 429, since it preceded Germanus’s departure for Britain, which occurred in that very year. Whether it was convened before that year or in the year itself must now be investigated.

Since Honoratus succeeded Patroclus in the see of Arles in 426, and since the words “while Honoratus was still abbot” signify the end of his abbacy, and therefore the year 425, if one adds the one year of Lupus’s religious training at Lérins—spent either under Honoratus as his teacher, which I consider more likely, or under Hilary, Honoratus’s successor, as some have thought—and then the two years completed in the episcopate, before the mission placed by Prosper [Col. 0368D] in 429, the result will be either 427 or 428. In my opinion, the synod must have been held in one of those years, and not in 429, the year to which Baronius thought it should be assigned (*Annals*, under 429).

This is confirmed above all by the fact that the view of those who, following Sigebert, postpone the great synod in question until 446 cannot possibly stand. For it is certain that at that time neither Coelestine, by whom Germanus was sent, nor Germanus himself was still alive. Coelestine died in 432, and Germanus in 443. Everyone agrees about Coelestine’s death; the date of Germanus’s death is demonstrated approximately as follows by Constantius (*Life of Saint Germanus*, book II, chs. 13–14):

> At the time when Germanus came to Ravenna to the emperor for the peace of Gaul, Peter was then governing the Church of Christ as pontiff by apostolic institution; the Roman Empire was ruled by Queen Placidia together with Valentinian, who was already a young man.

The words “Valentinian, who was already a young man” [Col. 0369A] indicate at most the ruler’s twenty-fourth year, since at that age a person is properly called a young man. Since Valentinian III was born at Ravenna in 419, on 2 or 3 July, and the year 443 was therefore Valentinian’s twenty-fourth year, Germanus must have died in 443. For in that same year he came to Ravenna and there, after the seventh day of his illness, peacefully fell asleep amid the embrace of the bishops, on the day before the Kalends of August (*Life of Saint Germanus*, book II, ch. 20).

Having established the date of the synod, we must now attempt to say something about its place—if not with certainty, at least by a plausible conjecture.

On 9 July 425, Valentinian III, on the seventh day before the Ides of July, during the consulship of Theodosius Augustus XII and Valentinian Caesar, issued a decree to Amatius, prefect of Gaul, concerning the assembling by Patroclus of various bishops who were following the wicked error of Pelagian and Coelestian doctrine.
