These are the emperor’s words: unless they returned to the Catholic [Col. 0369B] faith within twenty days of the summons, they were to be deposed from their sees and expelled from the borders of Gaul (Sirmondus, vol. I of the *Gallican Councils*).

I have no doubt that Amatius published the decree at Arles, the city in which the prefect of Gaul ordinarily resided. I likewise have no doubt that he entrusted its execution to Patroclus, insofar as it concerned the episcopal office. I do doubt whether Patroclus accomplished anything, since the times were troubled and a barbarian army was pressing Arles. But even if he did summon the bishops by letter—which is very plausible—they certainly followed the example of the obstinate men who had been expelled from Italy. Accordingly, a synod had to be assembled to depose them according to ancient custom, and it had to be a large one because of the number of the accused. It could be convened by no one other than the bishop of Arles (canon 18 of the Second Council of Arles), to whom the Apostolic See had long before entrusted its vicariate and who possessed the ancient right of convening synods in Gaul (the Constitutions of Honorius and Theodosius; see Sirmondus’s notes on Sidonius). Nor could it have been convened by Patroclus, whom a barbarian tribune, at the command of Felix, master of the soldiers, killed either near the end of 425 or at the beginning of the following year [Col. 0369C]. For Honoratus succeeded Patroclus after his death; Honoratus held the see of Arles for two years and died on 16 January 429, according to the Roman Martyrology.

The synod, then, appears to have been held by Honoratus in 428 at Arles, in the presence—or rather under the active direction—of Palladius, the deacon and legate of Saint Coelestine.

It is reasonable to believe that a large attendance of bishops from the seven provinces came to it, first because of the importance of the matter—for judgment had to be rendered concerning many bishops; second, to testify to Honoratus that no remnant remained of their former resentment against Patroclus, who had offended almost everyone through the power of his ambition; and finally, to preserve the ancient right of the canon soon to be cited and to follow the example of the secular council, which the prefect of Gaul ordinarily convened every year at Arles from the nine provinces.

[Col. 0369D] It is also credible that the English Church sent legates to the synod, both because of the similarity of the case and because they hoped to obtain easily from so great a synod the assistance for which they had come to ask.

But for this conjecture to gain greater force—whether certainty or at least credibility—it must be supported by answers to several objections that may occur to learned readers.

The first possible difficulty is that we assign the synod to 428, whereas Prosper places the mission of Saint Germanus to Britain, decreed by the synod and confirmed by Coelestine, under the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius, which occurred in 429. But Prosper’s passage supplies its own solution. It reads as follows:

> When Felix had been elevated to the rank of patrician and Aetius had become master of the soldiers, Agricola, a Pelagian and son of Severianus, a Pelagian bishop, corrupted the churches of Ireland by insinuating his doctrine [Col. 0370A]. But at the intervention of Palladius the deacon, Pope Coelestine sends Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, in his place, so that, after the heretics had been driven out, he might lead the Britons back to the Catholic faith.

Since Prosper joins together Agricola’s insinuation of the heresy, Coelestine’s sending of Saint Germanus, and Saint Germanus’s restoration of the Britons to the Catholic faith—three events that certainly did not occur simultaneously merely because they are written together, but which Prosper, as is customary, has all referred to the date of the last—why could he not similarly have referred the synod either to the conversion of the Britons, which followed the synod, or to Saint Germanus’s departure, which preceded it by one or two years, while preparations were being made and confirmation arrived from Rome after the synod’s election?

A second difficulty may also seem not without force: the author of Lupus’s life says that Lupus accompanied Germanus on the British expedition two years after obtaining the episcopate. Since he obtained the episcopate after completing one year of training at Lérins [Col. 0370B], and since Prosper testifies that Germanus departed from Gaul in 429, how could Lupus have begun his spiritual apprenticeship under Honoratus the abbot—who became bishop of Arles at the beginning of 426 or at the end of 425—and nevertheless undertaken his journey after two years in the episcopate? The solution to this doubt is the same as to the preceding one. Lupus was first assigned by the synod to accompany Germanus on his apostolic journey in 427. Then, when the proper time came, as soon as navigation was possible and everything had been suitably prepared, he set out—perhaps in 428. Finally, after the council at Verulamium had been convened, he converted the Britons to the faith in 429.

A third difficulty is raised by these words of Constantius (*Life of Saint Germanus*, book I, ch. 19):

> At that time a delegation sent from Britain announced to the Gallican bishops that Pelagian perversion had widely seized the peoples in their country and that the Catholic faith ought to be helped as quickly as possible. For this reason a large synod was assembled, and by the judgment of all [Col. 0370C], two brilliant lights of religion were sought through everyone’s prayers: Germanus and Lupus, apostolic priests, possessing the earth in their bodies and heaven in their merits. And the more arduous the need appeared, the more readily these most devoted heroes undertook it, hastening the matter by the urgings of faith.

The synod is said to have been convened because it had to receive the delegation from the English; and the saints are said to have hastened the matter, that is, to have set out immediately after the delegation. Yet we have given another reason for convening the synod and have said that the holy men spent nearly a year preparing for their journey.

This is certainly a serious difficulty. After long reflection, it finally led me, in my notes on Valentinian III’s decree to Amatius, prefect of Gaul, to suspect that the bishops whom the emperor mentions in the decree were called Gallican because they were under the prefecture of Gaul, but were in reality Britons whom Patroclus was to summon—namely, the bishop of the metropolitan city in which the prefect resided and from which [Col. 0370D] could be sent both legates to instruct the erring, and synodal decrees threatening ecclesiastical penalties to the rebels, and also the prefect’s edict with an order to the Vicar, by which he could restrain the obstinate through punishment.

Indeed, after the council had been held, some writers say that those who stubbornly persisted in their error were condemned by the magistrate (Hector Boethius, *Scottish History*, book VIII); but these men possess no great authority on this point. In any case, Constantius’s words do not deter me from my opinion; rather, they confirm it. For I ask to whom the British delegation was addressed. Was it to each of the Gallican bishops residing in his own see? That was neither customary nor would it have been effective for convening a synod and sending assistance. Was it to the first see, as was customary? Certainly. But the bishop of Arles held the primacy and by his own right could convene a synod from all the provinces of Gaul. Why, then, should it not be said that Patroclus, bishop of Arles, both received the British delegation [Col. 0371A] and informed the emperor of the entire matter, and obtained from him a rescript to Amatius, by which Patroclus himself, with increased authority, was ordered to summon the bishops? Yet he was unable to convene the synod because of the reasons previously given and left that responsibility to his successor, who, after Coelestine had meanwhile been informed of the entire affair through Palladius the deacon, was also prompted by Coelestine to send legates to Britain from the large synod he had assembled, with instructions—whether in the form of a memorandum and authority granted by himself, strengthened by imperial commands, or rather through the authority of the Apostolic See, whose legation Pope Coelestine wished the most holy men Germanus and Lupus to exercise?

Finally, Prosper raises a fourth doubt when writing against Collator (*Against Collator*, ch. 4). After recounting what Coelestine had boldly done against Coelestius, who requested a hearing after so many judgments of the Church, he writes:

> With no less diligent care he freed Britain from this same disease. When certain enemies of grace, occupying only the land of their origin, had been excluded even from that remote hiding place of the Ocean [Col. 0371B], and when he had ordained a bishop for the Scots, while striving to preserve the Roman island as Catholic, he also made the barbarian island Christian.

How, then, could Prosper fail to mention Germanus when he mentions a bishop given to the Scots, if the same pontiff sent both? This passage readily leads me, like many others, to believe that the opinion that the chronicler Prosper and Augustine’s disciple were the same person is not so firmly established that it cannot either be completely overturned or at least weakened—something that will be attempted later. Nevertheless, adhering to the common belief, I think I can also derive from this passage an argument supporting the conjecture from which it might appear to detract.

For if the pontiff expelled the enemies of grace from Britain, he expelled them with authority so great that the heretical force could not resist it. It must therefore be the case that not only were legates of the Apostolic See sent, possessing ecclesiastical power to depose bishops, but imperial orders were also issued, by which those who had been deposed were compelled to exile themselves from their homeland [Col. 0371C]. For neither could bishops be deposed without the pontiff, nor could men be expelled from their native territories without the emperor.

## XXII SYNOD

Held at Verulamium in England by Germanus and Lupus, legates of the Apostolic See, against the Pelagian bishops, during the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius, in the year 429.

The twenty-second synod must be regarded as that in which the holy Germanus and Lupus, legates of the Apostolic See, convicted the Pelagian bishops at Verulamium in England. Bede wrote about it (*Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book I, ch. 17), but he took his account from Constantius and added nothing of his own except the erroneous date, reporting that it was held in 446—that is, three years after Germanus’s death.

It is far more probably assigned to 429, when Prosper writes that, after the heretics had been driven out, the Britons were restored to the Catholic faith through the labor of Saint Germanus. For it was convened during Germanus’s first journey [Col. 0371D], as Constantius records; and in it the condemnable perversion was suppressed, its authors were refuted, and the minds of all were settled in the purity of the faith (*Life of Saint Germanus*, book I, chs. 23 and 25). Germanus’s first journey took place in 429.

I have therefore often been greatly surprised that the learned editors of the councils preferred to listen to Bede rather than either to Prosper or to the reliable chronological calculation, largely worked out by Baronius.

Since the acts themselves have perished, I think the following account of the synod by Constantius should be transcribed (*ibid.*, ch. 23):

> The authors of the sinister persuasion remained hidden away and, like an evil spirit, groaned because the peoples who were escaping from them were being lost to them. At last, after long meditation, they presumed to enter the conflict. They came forward conspicuous in wealth, resplendent in clothing, surrounded by the flattery of many; they preferred to risk a debate rather than incur shame before the people whom they had subverted by remaining silent [Col. 0372A], lest they appear to have condemned themselves by their silence.  
>   
> There, plainly, an immense multitude had gathered, stirred up together with wives and children. The people were present, destined to be both spectators and judges; the parties stood there, unequal and unlike in their circumstances. On one side was divine authority, on the other human presumption; on one side faith, on the other treachery; on one side Christ, on the other Pelagius as author.  
>   
> At first the most blessed priests gave their adversaries an opportunity to debate. Their opponents, relying solely on crude verbal display, for a long time vainly occupied both ears and time. Then the venerable bishops poured forth torrents of their eloquence with apostolic and evangelical thunder. Their own speech was mingled with the divine, and the most forceful assertions were followed by the testimonies of Scripture. Their vanity was convicted and their treachery refuted, so that, in response to each objection they raised, they confessed themselves guilty because they were unable to answer. The people, acting as judge, could scarcely restrain their hands and expressed their verdict with an outcry.

## XXIII SYNOD

Held at Rome by Coelestine in the case of the Pelagian bishops adhering to Nestorius, under the emperors Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, on 10 August, in the year of Christ 430.

[Col. 0372B]

The twenty-third synod, which was also the fifth Roman synod, was convened by Coelestine at Rome concerning Nestorius and the bishops for whom Nestorius had written in support.

Cyril of Alexandria mentions it in his letter to John of Antioch (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, ch. 2):

> Nestorius sent to Rome several quires containing his explanations. When the most devout bishops who were present in the great city of Rome had read them and had examined them through many meetings and consultations, they hissed their author with indignation; they openly declared that he had attempted a new and most pernicious heresy, one that none of the ancient heretics had ever previously devised.

Since Nestorius had written these things to Rome, I too was compelled to disclose everything that had taken place between him and me and to send, through Possidonius, the beloved deacon of the Alexandrian Church, copies of the letters that I had sent [Col. 0372C] to him. After his explanations had been read in the council, and his letters had been read—especially those that plainly bore his own signature, leaving him no opportunity for evasion—the HOLY ROMAN SYNOD immediately issued an explicit judgment against him. Concerning this, it also wrote to your Piety. Therefore, all who do not wish to fall from communion with the entire West must obey this decree in every respect. Copies of the judgment were sent both to Rufus, the most devout bishop of Thessalonica, and to several other most religious bishops of Macedonia, who are accustomed never to depart from his judgment. They also wrote to Juvenal, the most devout bishop of Jerusalem.

And in the letter to Nestorius (ibid., ch. 26):

> Behold, therefore, together with the HOLY SYNOD that assembled in the great city of Rome, under the presidency of our most holy and revered brother and fellow minister, Bishop Coelestine, we now testify for the third time in this letter [Col. 0372D].

And later:

> As for the letters that the Church of Alexandria sent to you, know that they have been judged by the SACRED ROMAN SYNOD to be free from every error and defect.

Nestorius himself also mentions it in a letter to the heretic Coelestius, whom he urges, by the example of the saints and by his own example, to remain steadfast in adversity (*Part I of the Works of Marius Mercator*):

> For letters sent by the bishops of the COUNCIL OF THE WEST, and by the bishop of Alexandria, together with many rescripts, have made our judgment clear to us, and so forth.

Coelestine issued several letters from this synod: to the clergy of Constantinople, John of Antioch, Juvenal of Jerusalem, Rufus of Thessalonica, and Cyril of Alexandria. The principal one was addressed to Nestorius [Col. 0373A]; Juvenal calls it *Περὶ τῆς Πίστεως*—“On the Faith”—at the Council of Ephesus (Part II, act 1). It is now called the constitution concerning the matter of faith. Although it deals chiefly with Nestorius, it also contains material concerning the Pelagians that contributes greatly to illuminating the synod now under discussion. Omitting what belongs to the other matter, the passages concerning the Pelagian case read as follows (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, ch. 18):

> For a certain period of our lives, after the wicked and often-condemned doctrine of Pelagius and Coelestius, the Catholic faith enjoyed peace, when the East and the West, united in a single judgment, struck them with their combined weapons, together with the followers of their opinion. Finally, Atticus of holy memory, the teacher of the Catholic faith and truly blessed John’s successor even in this matter, pursued them on behalf of our common King in such a way that they were not even granted the opportunity to remain there.

And later:

> These heretics also, concerning whom you wished to consult us as though unaware of what had been done, were expelled from their sees by a just condemnation because they spoke unjustly. We do not think it surprising that they found rest there; for they found an impious preaching in comparison with which they might consider themselves innocent.  
>   
> Since the opportunity for discussion requires it, we cannot remain silent about what astonishes us [Col. 0373B]. We have read how well you understand original sin, how you assert that nature itself is indebted, and that he rightly repays the debt who descends from a race of debtors. What have those who were condemned for denying these things to do with you? Those who are opposed to one another never come together without suspicion. They would finally have been expelled if these matters had likewise displeased you.  
>   
> Why, nevertheless, are the acts carried out against these men at that time being investigated, when it is certain that what had been done there was directed to us by Atticus, then the Catholic bishop? Why did Sisinnius of holy memory not investigate these matters? Because, plainly, under his predecessor he had approved their rightful condemnation.  
>   
> Let the wretched men lament that they were deceived by the hope they placed in human beings, when, because of their communion, only repentance could now have helped them. Behold, you are beginning to learn about these matters, if previously you knew nothing of them.

Given on 10 August, under the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, the Augusti and Caesars.

The date is established from these words; the place, from Cyril’s letters; and the outcome, from the report of the Ephesian Fathers to Saint Coelestine (Part II of the Council of Ephesus, act 5):

> After the records of the proceedings concerning the condemnation [Col. 0373C] of the impious Pelagians and Coelestians—Coelestius, Pelagius, Julian, Persidius, Florus, Marcellinus, Orontius, and those who shared their opinion—had been read through in the holy synod, together with what your Piety had decreed and established concerning them, we all reached the same judgment with you, holding them to be condemned.

From these words it can be understood that the Roman synod also concerned the Pelagians, so that those who were joined to Nestorius by fellowship in error might be struck by the same judgment.

It is remarkable, and must not be passed over without comment, that the Ephesian Fathers call this synod Western (Part II of the Council of Ephesus, act 3, in the report to the emperor), as though it ought to be regarded as representing the entire Western Church, over which the supreme pontiff presided at Rome. For we do not read that Coelestine summoned bishops from the whole Western diocese to the council, but only those who happened to be residing at Rome, as Cyril writes in his letter to John of Antioch.

[Col. 0373D]

## XXIV SYNOD

The synod of the whole world assembled at Ephesus, under the consulship of Antiochus and Bassus, on 23 June, in the year of Christ 431.

As the twenty-fourth and final synod, we place the Ephesian synod—the third ecumenical council—not because it was actually the last against the Pelagians, since other councils followed and were more numerous, but because we have bounded our dissertation within the period during which divine Providence granted Augustine life. Under his leadership, the Catholic army fought against and conquered the enemies of God’s grace (Prosper, *Against Collator*, ch. 1).

Although that outstanding defender of the faith passed to a better life in 430, on 28 August, and the Council of Ephesus did not begin before 21 June of the following year, he had nevertheless been summoned to it by the emperor in a special letter and would have constituted a considerable part of the sacred assembly had God so willed. It should therefore not be thought unreasonable that the Fathers, inspired by his spirit—and even by his books, brought by [Col. 0374A] Bassula, a deacon of the Church of Carthage—proscribed the wicked heresy.

Certainly, in the letter sent to the synod through John, the *comes* of the Sacred Consistory, the emperor mentions Augustine as though he were present, just as he mentions Coelestine and Rufus, although he knew that the latter were absent and that Augustine had died. This is because all three had been summoned by the emperor and were present at the council in different ways: Augustine by divine will, as from heaven; Coelestine by authority, through his legates; and Rufus, together with the bishops of Macedonia, by consent.

In the Roman edition of the council, and in the editions that followed Commelinus’s Greek text, the name is not Augustine but “Augustianus.” This is contrary to the testimony of the more ancient manuscript codices and, in my opinion, arose from failure to consider why the emperor wrote as he did—especially since no mention of any Augustianus occurs anywhere in the entire Council of Ephesus. The word may perhaps not be found anywhere at all, but may have originated either in the ignorance of the scribes or in the excessive learning of the editors.

Accordingly, the 274 Fathers—for that is the number given by Mercator—condemned the heretical bishops, together with Pelagius [Col. 0374B] and Coelestius, whom those bishops supported, as stated in the synodical letter to Coelestine (in the preface to Theodore’s creed, Part II of the Council of Ephesus, act 5):

> After the records of the proceedings concerning the condemnation of the impious Pelagians and Coelestians had been read in the holy synod, and after what your Piety had decreed and established concerning them had been read, we too judged that these decisions ought to remain solid and firm, and we all reached the same judgment with you, holding them to be condemned.

It should be noted, however, that the interpreter of the Council of Ephesus—whether the Roman interpreter or an earlier one—used the words “deposition” and “deposed” in place of “condemnation” and “condemned,” the terms we have used, contrary to the logic of the matter. For although the Greek word *καθαίρεσις* can mean both deposition and condemnation, it could not here have been used to signify deposition, since Pelagius was a monk who stood among the laity, and a layman cannot be deposed from a see or rank, since he holds no such position in the Church. He could only be condemned and separated from the assembly of the faithful.

[Col. 0374C] In the preface to the canons, at action 7, the following is said concerning the unmistakable sign by which Nestorians and Coelestians may be identified (Part II of the Council of Ephesus):

> These men, having no capacity at all for ecclesiastical communion, so as to be able through priestly authority to harm or benefit anyone—for some of them have also been deposed—are shown above all to follow openly the opinions of Nestorius and Coelestius by the fact that they refused to condemn Nestorius with us. The holy synod has therefore decreed by common decision that they are alienated from all ecclesiastical communion, and so forth.

Then there follow six canons altogether. Although all of them were enacted against persons belonging to the Nestorian and Coelestian parties, only the first and fourth expressly mention Coelestius. They read as follows:

1. “If any metropolitan of a province, abandoning the holy and ecumenical synod, has joined, or should in the future join, the assembly of those in revolt, whether he has agreed or should agree with Coelestius, he shall no longer be able to take any action against the bishops of the province, since from that time onward he has been deprived of all ecclesiastical communion and rendered completely useless. Rather, he shall be subject to those bishops of that province and to the neighboring metropolitans who hold the correct belief, so that he may be entirely removed from the episcopal see.

2. “If any provincial bishops were absent from the holy synod and adhered to the dissenters, or attempted to adhere to them, or, after signing the deposition of Nestorius, again returned to the assembly of the dissenters, it has pleased the holy synod that these men likewise be wholly excluded from the priesthood and have fallen from their rank.

3. “If any clerics in the several cities or regions were barred from the priesthood by Nestorius and those who conspired with him because they held the correct belief, we have judged it right that these men also recover their proper rank. In short, we order that clerics who agree with the orthodox and ecumenical synod are in no way or by no means to be subject to those bishops who have revolted or are going to revolt.

4. “If any of the clergy revolt and dare, either privately or publicly, to hold the opinions of Nestorius or Coelestius, it has been decreed by the holy synod that these men too are deposed.

5. “Whoever has been condemned by the synod, or by his own bishops, for shameful conduct, and whom Nestorius—who made no distinction among cases—and those who hold the same opinions as he, have attempted or shall attempt to restore to rank or communion contrary to the canons: we have judged that these efforts have accomplished nothing, and that such persons nevertheless remain and continue to be deposed.

6. “Likewise, if any should wish in any way to reopen the proceedings conducted by the holy Synod of Ephesus concerning individual persons, the holy synod itself has decreed that, if they are bishops or clerics, they shall fall entirely from their own rank; but if they are laymen, they shall be excommunicated.”

It is commonly said that, in the schismatic assembly led by John, bishop of Antioch, Julian and his associates were acquitted; and, as many think, this opinion originated with Gregory the Great. For he writes that a certain council—regarded by them as the schismatic Council of Ephesus—defined the following concerning Adam’s soul: because it had not died in sin, since the devil does not enter into a human heart; and that, if anyone had said this, he would be anathema (*Register*, Book V, Letter 14, and Book VI, Letter 61).

He gives a fuller account of the matter elsewhere (*Letters*, Book VII, Letter 31), and teaches that in many Constantinopolitan and Isaurian manuscripts the proceedings of the Catholic synod had been mixed together with the acts of another council. In the acts as we now possess them, however, nothing of the kind is found; nor, indeed, was anything of the kind formerly found in the manuscripts of the principal sees.

The holy pontiff argues against this definition in the two passages cited, but in such a way that in the first he interprets the death contracted through sin by Adam as spiritual death alone, whereas in the second he also understands it as bodily death. In the latter interpretation he has Augustine in agreement with him, although Augustine commonly opposes the former interpretation.

Here, however, a considerable difficulty arises: what relevance could this canon have had to the Pelagians, since they neither denied that Adam’s soul had died to God through sin, nor differed from the Catholics on this point? Moreover, how could it follow from the claim that the devil cannot enter into a human heart that Adam’s soul was not, or at least might not appear to have been, killed by sin? Should we suppose that the Eastern schismatics were so foolish that they did not realize that this reasoning would abolish every sin committed at the devil’s instigation? Some have touched upon this knot, but no one has so far explained it.

Can the deceitful heretics be believed to have wanted their patrons to define something that was, in itself, Catholic, but from which they could establish before the common people that there was no original sin? For if Adam’s soul died through sin, yet did not die for that reason because the devil, entering his heart, inflicted death upon it, then certainly no soul can die unless it sins by its own will, as little children cannot do. For no one can inflict death upon souls except one who enters into them; and no one is permitted to enter them except God, who plainly does not cause the soul’s death.

The entire history of this canon and council will be treated in the second part of the works of Marius Mercator, in such a way that the popular opinion will be refuted, if not by certain, at least by probable arguments. For the canon believed to have been enacted by the Easterners will be shown to have been fabricated by some council of Nestorius, when, at the instigation of the Pelagians, it slanderously imputed Manichaean impiety to the Catholic clergy of the imperial city. I have treated this matter at length in the notes to Nestorius’ second letter to Cyril.

## XXV. Eight synods held in the fifth century at different times in the same Pelagian controversy

Besides the synods reviewed thus far, I believe that four others were actually convened in the Pelagian controversy before the Council of Ephesus. I have nevertheless decided to omit them, because I can support my view neither with certain testimony from the ancients nor with a compelling argument, but only with a conjecture that is not implausible.

The first was held at Ephesus in Asia in the year 417. Unless I am mistaken, Prosper was speaking of it when he wrote (*Poem*, chapter 2):

> I pass over with what great commotion  
> renowned Ephesus was stirred,  
> not allowing within her own walls  
> the vessels of wrath, the blasts of disease,  
> and the seeds of death to remain.

For I believe that I have clearly demonstrated, in the notes to Mercator’s *Commonitorium* (chapter 1), that Prosper’s verses cannot be understood of the ecumenical synod.

The second was held at Syracuse in Sicily. I interpret the same author’s verse as referring to it:

> And by what faith even burning Trinacria  
> drove the viperous band from her own shores.

For, as has often been said, in former times no bishop was removed from his see without the authority of a synod. In the fifth dissertation on the book of faith published by Julian, we shall show that several such persons were deposed in Sicily.

The third was held at Rome under Boniface. The same author speaks of it (*Against the Collations*, chapter 41):

> When Pope Boniface, of blessed memory, rejoiced in the Catholic devotion of the most pious emperors, he employed against the enemies of God’s grace not only apostolic edicts but also imperial ones.

The fourth was held at Alexandria in the year 430. Cyril convened it, strictly speaking on account of Nestorius, but on that occasion also on account of the Pelagians. He may have done so because he had received from Celestine the acts of the Roman council sent to him and wished to enact measures consonant with them concerning both Nestorius and the Pelagians; or because he knew that certain disciples of the Pelagian Valerian were still hiding within his church. He had been warned to beware of this man from the time of Innocent by a certain Eusebius, whom Baronius supposed to have been a bishop of Cremona (*Annals*, year 417, no. 15).

After the Council of Ephesus, four synods were likewise held in the fifth century against either the errors or the remnants of Pelagius. I say “in the fifth century,” since I do not intend to go beyond it.

Accordingly, I pass over the Sardinian council held in the year 521 by the African Fathers while they were exiles in Sardinia; its principal spirit was Fulgentius.

I likewise omit the famous Second Council of Orange, held by fourteen bishops under the presidency of Caesarius at Orange on the fifth day before the Nones of July, in the consulship of the younger Decius—that is, in the year of Christ 529, the third year of Felix IV and the third year of Athalaric, king of Italy.

Severinus Binius, in his notes on the third canon of the Council of Riez, which was held in the time of Pope Sixtus in the year 439 by the bishops of the province of Narbonne under the presidency of Hilary, followed Baronius (*Annals*, year 430, no. 45) in supposing that the canon concerned bishops who had adhered to Pelagius and pretended repentance in order to recover sees rightly taken from them.

If this were stated truly and with probability, this council would certainly have to be counted among those convened after Ephesus in the Pelagian controversy. Indeed, it would follow that, before the Council of Ephesus, a synod had been held in the same province of Narbonne in which a sentence of deposition had been issued against bishops demanding restoration.

But I cannot accept the opinion of Baronius and Binius. Their authors neither confirm it by any testimony of the ancients or by any argument, nor do they have Father Sirmond in agreement with them in his notes on the Council of Riez. Nor can they derive from any of the eight canons—not even from the third—an argument that would furnish the slightest proof of anything similar. On the contrary, it is clear that the third canon concerns only Armentarius and those who ordained him, as well as anyone who should dare the same or something similar—namely, to ordain a bishop without the legitimate number of three bishops. For this reason they would be counted among schismatics rather than heretics.

In the year 447 Leo the Great solemnly ordered Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, to hold a synod (*Letters* 64 and 85), in order to obtain unqualified subscriptions from those who wished to return to the Church from the Pelagian heresy.

Gelasius held another synod at Rome in the year 494, at which the books of the Pelagians were proscribed, both on account of their impiety and especially because of the heresy that was attempting to revive in Dalmatia and Picenum. This was why, in the consulship of Albinus—that is, in the year 493—Gelasius wrote twice to Honorius, bishop of Dalmatia, once on the fifth day before the Kalends of August and again without a date. Indeed, on the Kalends of November he sent letters to all the bishops throughout Picenum that were filled with Catholic instruction against Pelagianism.

A synod had been held at Arles in the year 475 by the Gallic bishops. There the letter of Faustus to Lucidus was signed, and an anathema was pronounced against anyone who, among the other impieties of Pelagius, should presume to maintain, with condemnable obstinacy, that human beings are born without sin and can be saved through labor alone, and against anyone who believed that a person could be liberated without the grace of God.

At approximately the same time another synod was convened at Lyons, which approved the decrees of Arles.

## THIRD DISSERTATION. ON THE IMPERIAL CONSTITUTIONS IN THE CONTROVERSY OVER THE PELAGIAN HERESY FROM THE YEAR 418 TO 430

In the very words of Marius Mercator: “Not only by imperial laws, etc.” (*Commonitorium*, chapter 3).

After the discussion of the synods held in the Pelagian controversy, the next subject is the decrees of the rulers, which, as Possidius says (*Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 18), followed the judgment of the Catholic Church of God.

There were altogether five or six of them. Although they were enacted at different times and by different emperors—and even by the mother of Valentinian, an empress—they nevertheless display the same love for the Catholic faith and the same concern for the welfare of the Church. Thus one might reasonably think that even then Isaiah’s prophecy concerning the Church of Christ had been fulfilled:

> Kings shall be your foster-fathers,  
> and queens your nurses.  
>   
> —Isaiah 49:23

I think that each of them should be treated in the following manner: first, the texts themselves should be presented, purified of all the errors with which they have hitherto abounded; then their variant readings should be set out. These readings, which in many places have not merely failed to clarify the sense but have actually distorted it, have been corrected by us only after laborious study and comparison of several manuscripts. Next, the history of each decree should be narrated, with questions belonging to the matter resolved wherever they arise. Finally, where necessary, the decrees of the emperors, the edicts of the prefects, and other matters of that kind should be elucidated in notes.

Before this is done, however, we must respond to the apparently religious indignation of certain people, as though the emperors had not kept within the limits of their authority in this matter but had almost attempted in the Church what they once did among the pagans when they held the office of high priests of pagan impiety.

“For what is it,” they ask, “to usurp the functions of the priesthood, even in a matter of faith, if this is not it? To prescribe what ought to be believed; to declare those who think otherwise to be heretics; to command bishops to subscribe to condemned doctrines or persons, threatening them with deposition, indeed even with excommunication, if they do not obey; to prescribe to primates what belongs to their office; and so forth.”

The emperors appear to have done precisely this, especially Honorius, however religiously he may be praised, when he sent a decree either to Palladius, the Praetorian Prefect, or to Aurelius, primate of Africa.

This complaint is ancient and arose almost together with the emperors’ conversion to the faith. The holy Fathers long ago answered it sufficiently when they decreed that the world is principally governed by two powers: the sacred authority of pontiffs and the royal power. Since both were united in Christ, they were divided between pontiffs and kings as ministers of God. Thus two supreme authorities came into existence, and to each was assigned its proper measure of power. Between the two authorities a sacred covenant was established, with Christ as mediator and conciliator. Each, for his part, serves the common Lord, protects his bride, and crushes the enemies with united strength.

This is the teaching of Gelasius in his letter to the emperor Anastasius; of the Council at Theodon's estate; of Justinian in *Novel* 6; of Bernard in his letter to King Conrad; and of Hosius, as quoted by Athanasius in his letter to the solitary monks.

For, as that archbishop writes to the ruler:

> The King of kings, and likewise the Priest of priests, who alone could govern the Church that he redeemed, after raising his humanity into heaven—while remaining forever with his own through his divinity—divided his authority for governing that same Church between priests and kings, so that what holy pontiffs teach, devout kings might themselves fulfill and ensure that it was fulfilled.

And certainly, after the Church had shaken off the yoke of tyrants, been vindicated into freedom, and turned the emperors’ sword away from her own necks against those whom she had previously endured as wicked persecutors, she found in them, once they had become her children, most just assistants in carrying out her affairs.

Kings therefore do not prescribe the form of the faith, nor have they ever rightly prescribed it. They order peoples to preserve the faith received from priests, whose judgment they follow. They do not teach the Church; rather, like angels with flaming swords, they defend the gates of the city of God against heretics. They do not themselves declare those who think contrary to the form of the faith to be heretics, but subject them to the penalties imposed upon heretics. They do not personally depose bishops or exclude anyone from sacred functions—for how could they?—but they order that those deprived of office and excluded by synods be expelled from their cities, lest they create disturbances. They also order that such people be deprived of association with others, lest the contagion of their poisonous spirit cause harm.

But why should I dwell any longer on a matter already settled? The African Fathers themselves, when through legates of the synods they requested such decrees from the emperors; the supreme pontiffs themselves, however great their authority, when they employed royal edicts against the enemies of God; the entire sacred order of the clergy; indeed the whole Church, when it obeyed those same edicts—all of them forestall every objection and at the same time teach what both Christ foreshadowed before his Passion and God established at the creation of the world: that the Church needs two swords to terrify the ungodly and two lights to illuminate the spiritual world.

For, as the Fathers say, neither one light was sufficient against all the obscurities of error, nor one sword against the unrestrained boldness of the impious. A stubborn disposition both created obscurities for itself and for others, while wickedness drew boldness from the patience of the good.

What was once said with the greatest seriousness and truth is most certainly confirmed by the unhappy experience of our own age, so that Bernard’s prayer has never been more timely:

> What God has joined, let no human being separate. Let those who are joined in institutions join themselves in spirit; let them support one another, defend one another, and bear one another’s burdens.

[Note: This constitution of Honorius was first published by the Magdeburg Centuriators, *Century 5*, column 847; then by Cardinal Baronius in the *Annals* under the year 418; afterward by Salmasius in the *Eucharisticus*, p. 288; by Usserius, *On the Beginnings of the Churches of Britain*, chapter 50, p. 272; by Labbeus, volume II of the *Councils*, p. 1606; and recently by Baluzius in the appendix to Salvianus. Four of these editors attest that they consulted manuscript codices. We, however, partly by comparing the editions and partly with the help of manuscripts, have corrected the many errors that remained.]

[Note: The title differs among the editors. Magdeburg: “The sacred decree of Honorius and Theodosius against Pelagius and Coelestius.” Salmasius: “Here begins the sacred rescript issued after receiving the acts of the holy synod (of Carthage).” Usserius: “The sacred rescript issued after receiving the acts of the synod.” Baluzius: “The rescript of the emperors Honorius and Theodosius to Palladius, the Praetorian Prefect, against Pelagius and Coelestius.” History shows that this is not properly a rescript but a constitution, since the emperor is not replying either to someone who has petitioned him by letter or to someone who has consulted him in writing.]

[Note: It is scarcely possible to find any constitution in the entire body of laws containing so many statements—and statements so true—of imperial policy, almost oracular in character, that an example of an absolute sanction against heretics could be drawn from it. For what could be truer concerning the origin of heresies? A new subtlety, commended to the wind, judges it a conspicuous mark of plebeian lowliness to think with everyone and to destroy the palm of singular wisdom by what has been commonly approved. What could be more learned concerning their growth? Such things must be intercepted by timely remedy and swift action, lest, once the practice of wickedness has grown strong, they can scarcely be restrained in their youth. What could be more penetrating concerning their consolidation and, as it were, perpetuation? The path of straightforward belief has been interrupted, advocacy has been split into factions, and the material for unappeased dissension has been introduced; then, when a new stimulus to scandal has been kindled, the tranquillity of the most blessed Church—until now unshaken—trembles, as different people pursue different things through equivocal interpretation and, according to the capacity of their deceitful ingenuity, raise profane questions about new inventions.

What a sure mark by which to recognize heresy, and what a manifest sign of a heretical disposition! Abandoning the light of the common judgment, they introduce the darkness of a new dispute. They fight against the apostolic discipline and the clear, error-free judgment of the Gospel with the cunning cleverness of an untrained sect, and in their arguments they envelop the shining faith in the ambiguities of truth.

What a prudent remedy! The origin of the vice ought to be separated from public assembly, and those who are detestable not only because of their impious deed but also because their example carries a poisonous spirit should not be allowed to stand in the common gathering.

What a provident medicine for so great an evil! Therefore, wherever such people are found discussing this most abominable crime, we order that they be seized by anyone whatsoever and, brought before a public hearing, be accused indiscriminately by all, so that the public record may pursue them once convicted of the crime, while they themselves are condemned to implacable exile.]

## FIRST CONSTITUTION. OF THE EMPEROR HONORIUS TO PALLADIUS, THE PRAETORIAN PREFECT

And appended to the Emperor’s Constitution is an Edict of the Praetorian Prefects.

[Col. 0379A]

The Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, Augusti, to Palladius, Praetorian Prefect.

[Note: Here Jacobus Gothofredus should be corrected, since in the year 418 he lists Liberius as Praetorian Prefect of the West, in volume VI of the *Theodosian Code*, in the prosopography.]

To disturb the light of Catholic simplicity,

[Note: All have this word except Baronius and Baluzius. The completion of the sentence nevertheless requires it to be an epithet belonging to “splendor.”]

which always shines with pure brilliance,

[Note: It is remarkable that no one who wrote about the Pelagians in the fifth century failed to accuse them of bad faith and falsehood; indeed, no one failed to call their heresy “cunning” or by some similar name. Hence the emperor soon calls the heresy “shadowed by the lies of deceptive knowledge” and attacks the deceitful ingenuity of those who fight with crafty cleverness.

Hence Pelagius was called a serpent or snake by Orosius, Prosper, and Cassian. Hence Aurelius called the heresy a serpentine persuasion; and Paulinus the deacon, writing about Coelestius, called him a little fox intent upon his frauds.

Hence Possidius called the Pelagians crafty disputants who wrote with harmful subtlety of art. The author of the letter to Rufinus calls them sons of darkness, indeed people who transform themselves through their cunning into the likeness of sons of light.

They consistently followed this method of acting: when spreading error, testing the faith of bishops, and bringing nobles over to their side; and especially when avoiding judgments whenever they were pressed, feigning repentance if they happened to be condemned, and raising objections whenever they were required to subscribe to the definitions of the Church.

Thus Jerome writes:

> Let us take care that the most pernicious heresy be removed from the Church. It is always pretending repentance so that it may have the opportunity to teach in the churches; for if it revealed itself in the open light, it would be expelled and perish outside.

Augustine writes:

> What benefit is it to you that you weave I know not what handles and hooks of I know not what perplexity, so that simple things may not be exposed and shine in the clear light? … Pelagius thinks that he has deceived the judgment at Diospolis with these clouds, and you approve this crime with your whole head; you laugh at the fact that so many bishops were mocked by him.

Orosius writes:

> Behold, against the Church—which is pitiful—and, what is much more pitiful, within the Church itself, they hiss everywhere; impious serpents flick their tongues and lick their mouths infected with their darting tongues. For, while they expose the remaining body to mutilation and injury merely to protect the head, they consider it no loss if that part alone of themselves remains free in which they possess many and poisonous tongues, even if all their other members are cut away.

Paulinus the deacon, writing to Pope Zosimus concerning Coelestius, says:

> A little fox, always devoted to his frauds, did not know how to change his ingenuity, nor did he believe that he could be detected, since he always placed his confidence in disguises, in which he strives to hide his conscience’s buried head.

Prosper writes:

> The wickedness of such men must be resisted not so much by the zeal of disputation as by the authority of authoritative judgments, so that no member of a dogma long since overthrown may be allowed to rise again. For it is well known that the cunning of this falsehood operates in such a way that, if they are permitted, they can, under the pretext of correction, preserve for themselves some shoot of their root that finds favor with others and restore themselves wholly from a small remnant. For where the whole exists only in a part, it is not devotion to have given up almost everything, but fraud to have retained even the smallest portion.

Leo the Great writes:

> We know this to be their cunning: in whatever fragment of the accursed doctrine they distinguish themselves from the company of the condemned, they suppose that none of their opinions has been left unsalvaged. Although they pretend to reject and lay aside all their definitions, in order to make it easier to creep in, they reserve them by their entire art of deception unless they are understood.]

we have learned from widespread report that, through the ingenuity of a deceitful art, a new piece of cunning has suddenly appeared,

[Note: Baronius reads “has emerged.” Both verbs are suitable.]

which, shadowed by the lies of deceptive knowledge and raging only in a frenzied struggle, dares to assail the stable peace of heavenly faith,

[Note: Magdeburg reads “promises”; Baronius, Usserius, Labbeus, and Baluzius read “attempts.” The reading of Salmasius, which we have chosen, is better and more significant.]

while

[Note: All the authors of the same period ridicule the utterly empty boastfulness, pride, or contempt for others of the Pelagians. And not without reason. To give one example: who was more boastful of himself than Julian? Who displayed his associates more ostentatiously? Who showed greater contempt for others? He was therefore rightly called by the author of the *Chronicle* “the most boastful defender of the Pelagian error,” by Augustine “swollen with pride,” and by Mercator “a man of abusive tongue and the Catiline of his age.”

I shall offer only two testimonies, one from Vincent of Lérins and the other from Julian himself.

Vincent writes:

> What did they fall into while making their promises except some new, unknown, and unheard-of doctrine? For you may hear some of them saying: “Come, you foolish and wretched people who are commonly called Catholics, and learn the true faith, which no one except us understands, which lay hidden for many centuries but has recently been revealed and displayed. But learn it secretly and in concealment, for it will delight you. And when you have learned it, teach it secretly, so that the world may not hear and the Church may not know. For only a few have been granted the ability to grasp the secret of so great a mystery.” Are these not the words of that prostitute who, in Solomon’s Proverbs, calls passersby to herself—those who are directing their path? And so forth.

Later, in the same work, chapter 40, Vincent shows that, when writing the words just quoted, he had Julian in mind. Lest anyone, setting aside all the others, arrogate to himself alone the right to be heard and believed, he says shortly afterward:

> “Did the word of God proceed from you? Or did it come to you alone?”

And, so that this should not be taken as a casual remark, he adds:

> “If anyone seems to be a prophet, or spiritual”—that is, a teacher of spiritual things—“let him be a zealous practitioner of equality and unity,” so that he neither places his own opinions above those of others nor departs from the judgment of all.

He says that the person who does not know the commands of this matter—that is, who either does not learn what he did not know or despises what he has learned—“will not be known.” That is, he will be considered unworthy to receive the divine regard among those united in faith and made equal in humility. I do not know whether anything more bitter than this punishment can be imagined. Yet we see that, in accordance with the apostolic threat, this happened to that Pelagian, Julian, who either neglected to incorporate himself into the judgment of his colleagues or dared to remove himself from it.

How splendidly Julian vaunts himself (*Unfinished Work*, Book II, chapter 10), as a defender of truth when he inflames himself to defend the Pelagian heresy despite the Church’s thunderbolts!

> Now that evil custom has begun to be offered as a remedy, and authority has been added to pleasure, so that, by the concession of almost the whole world, obscenity—the powerful queen of minds, the conqueror of virtue, and the invincible captor of every soul—may rage: our cause of defending truth has become so much the more honorable as it has become harder, because truth and the reasoning of those who heal avail little against headlong peoples hostile to their remedies. What then? Shall we sound a retreat in consideration of these people, avenge our insults by silence, and laugh from the harbor of conscience at the shipwrecks of others? But first the kindness we owe to the human race, and then the hope and faith we have in God, oppose this hatred. Besides the fact that he has often raised the desperate ruins of the times, he has rewarded with eternal recompense the steadfastness which he willed to be exercised even to the hour of death, though it attained no effect at present.

How gloriously he extols his own party (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book II, chapter 3)!

> The teachers of our time, most blessed brother, and the authors of the accursed sedition still raging, have resolved to reach the insult and destruction of the persons whose holy pursuits burn them through the ruin of the whole Church, not understanding how great an honor they have bestowed on those whose glory they showed could not be overthrown except together with the Catholic religion. For if anyone says either that human beings possess free will or that God is the creator of those who are born, he is called a Coelestian and a Pelagian. Therefore, lest they be called heretics, they become Manichaeans; and, while they fear a false disgrace, they incur a real crime, like animals surrounded by feathers so that they may be driven into nets: lacking reason, they are forced by vain fear into real destruction.

How proudly he despises, indeed slanders, others (*Unfinished Work*, Book II, chapter 10)!

> The Church is robbed of the helm of reason, so that popular dogma may sail with horn raised. Thus, when little is permitted to the prudent but anything at all is fitting even for the base, the assessment of virtues has been excluded from the churches by a decree of sedition; and it has made us hateful among the common people that we refused to become an addition to error. I mean that common people who, weighing the worth of an opinion by its successes, judge truer that which they see has pleased more persons. For it delights them to defame every saint who has ever existed anywhere, lest they be reproved by the examples of illustrious persons. It delights them utterly, and deeply moves them, to ascribe weakness to nature; to say that the flesh is subject to inborn sins; not to locate the effect of amendment in the human will, but to call the crimes of pursuits the functions of bodily members. Such dross of the most impure dogmas flatters their ears. This nettle stirred our enemies of both sexes: while it stung some through the vice of evil custom, it was nevertheless healed, as it were, by certain ointments of salutary exhortations; but now that evil custom has begun to be offered as a remedy, etc.

“While [it], commended by the breath of novel subtlety, considers …”: thus Baronius, Usserius, and Labbeus; Salmasius and Baluzius, however, read: “The inventors of a new crime consider …” Although that reading is plausible, the other is not only more elegant in itself but also more opposed to the character of the Pelagians and more consonant with what follows. Magdeburg gives a reading with no sense: “While, commending the conspicuous mark of plebeian lowliness to the outcome of a new crime, it considers …”]

daring to assail the stable peace of heavenly faith, while, commended by the breath of novel subtlety, it considers it a conspicuous mark of plebeian lowliness to think with everyone, and a palm of singular wisdom to destroy what has been commonly approved. It has become widely known that the authors of this impious invention were Pelagius and Coelestius.

[Note: Magdeburg and Labbeus read “of this commendation,” not implausibly, because of the preceding words, “commended to the wind.”]

[Note: The reference is only to Adam’s mortality and original sin, because Coelestius’ case alone was being handled. This was the first origin and root of the entire heresy, however much it later grew.

Magdeburg, Labbeus, and Usserius read: “They assign such savage cruelty to God, the Father of all things, and especially to the most excellent and eternally omnipotent Majesty, who transcends every beginning …”

Baronius reads: “to the most excellent Majesty and thrice-omnipotent, who transcends every beginning …”

Salmasius and Baluzius read: “to the most excellent and eternally powerful Majesty, who transcends every beginning …”

None of these readings seems tolerable in comparison with the sense produced by restoring the words.]

They assign so savage a cruelty of will to God, the Father of all things, and especially to the eternally and boundlessly powerful Majesty, who transcends every beginning, that, when he undertook the task of fashioning and, in the deep conception of his spirit, weighed the condition of the human being to be formed, he set the end of the bestowed gift before its beginning and sent death before the one who was to be born.

[Note: Salmasius corruptly reads “against some people” instead of “when he undertook the work.”]

They say that this death did not flow from the snares of forbidden sin, but that the law of an unchangeable decree exacted it entirely, so that abstinence from sin would have been of no use in avoiding the fatal assault of death; and they think that its force was so tightly bound that it could not afterward be abolished.

[Note: Magdeburg reads “abolish.” The editors intended to accommodate the rules of Latin, as though the following words belonged with it. The sentence requires a division at this point.]

They say that the error of the first human being—into which he had fallen through the blindness of a captive mind, destitute of reason—did not pass down to posterity, and that the transgression of the prohibition was of consequence only in the case of the man whom the unhappy allurements of evil persuasion had carried away.

[Note: Baronius reads: “had constituted both a transgression of the prohibition and a distinction.” The conjunction entered through scribal error.]

Since the manifold authority of Catholic law plainly testifies that this error was the entrance to the destruction of all, it is clear that he who had diligently observed the divine command corrupted that command.

[Note: “Law” is used here for religion, whose authority consists in three things: the word of God, the tradition of the Fathers, and the definition of the Church. The dogma mentioned by the emperor had not only been approved everywhere by commentators generally—see Mercator in the *Subnotations*—and supported by the testimony of both Testaments and by Augustine’s tradition of the Fathers (*Against Julian*, Book I); it had also been defined by the Church, partly in particular councils, whose authority is bounded by precise limits, and partly by the decrees of two bishops of the apostolic see, Innocent and Zosimus, whose jurisdiction is to teach the whole world.]

[Note: [Col. 0383B] All except Magd. And several other things besides.] [Note: [Col. 0383C] Baron., “which, though it is continual, [one ought] to recall.” Salm., “which it is continually absent to recall.” Bal., “he took perpetually to recall.” These sentences are scarcely intelligible.]

Many other things as well, which speech rejects and the law refutes—things which it is exceedingly hateful to recall, even under the arrangement for punishment, and which ought to be cut off by timely remedy and swift speed, lest, once the practice of wickedness has grown strong, they can scarcely be restrained in youth. [Note: [Col. 0383C] Magd., “the youth of wickedness”: a tolerable reading.]

For indeed a recent report has struck the ears of Our Mildness, that within our most sacred city and other places such a pestilential poison has taken root in the hearts of certain persons that, with the path of direct belief interrupted, and with parties divided in their efforts to assert their positions, the material of irreconcilable dissension has been introduced; and, with a new fuel for scandal kindled, the tranquility of the most blessed Church, hitherto unshaken, is now wavering. [Note: [Col. 0383C] Baron., “with the direct path.”] [Note: [Col. 0383C] Magd., “the action of the most peaceful tranquility is wavering, having been attempted.” There is an obvious corruption. Salm., Uss., Labb., “the action is wavering, and tranquility, having been attempted.” Less elegant.] [Note: [Col. 0383C] Magd., with others, “one thing after another,” improbably. More probably Baron., Uss., Labb., “one path after another,” etc. Salm., “while pursuing different paths”: our reading is more correct.]

Some, namely, pursue one interpretation and others another, in an uncertain manner; and although the clarity of the sacred writings is complete, and plainly explains what the whole body of believers ought to follow, they raise a question about profane new commentaries according to the capacity of their shifting ingenuity. [Note: [Col. 0383C] Baron., Bal., “in the manner of new geese.” The comparison is scarcely worthy of a prince promulgating a law. Salm., “of new men or their own,” which has no sense. Magd., Uss., Labb., “of new authors,” etc.; nor is this reading implausible.]

[Note: [Col. 0383C]

Gothofredus long ago observed that emperors addressed the praetorian prefects in this manner, in Book II, On Episcopal Judgments, and the urban prefects in Book I, On Pacts. But he overlooked three points no less worthy of notice. First, emperors addressed bishops in the same way as well: thus Honorius addressed Aurelius of Carthage; thus Theodosius addressed Cyril even while angry, and so forth. From this it may be concluded, with no uncertain judgment, what honor emperors accorded bishops, since they equated their dignity with the highest eminence and loftiest pinnacle.

Second, not every praetorian prefect was honored with this form of address, but only those who considerably exceeded the emperors in age, as though this address had mixed causes of dignity and age. Thus, in the Novels of Theodosius, Florentius is called “the most beloved father of the Augusti”; for he was older than both Theodosius and Valentinian. Therefore correct the error that has crept into some copies, so that “prefect” may be read instead of “parent,” or that only the letter P. may be supplied. [Col. 0384B] Nevertheless, someone might reasonably have thought that those who were not older by birth than the emperors were called patricians, and that this was indicated by the letter P.

Finally, emperors used this form of address not only toward the praetorian or urban prefects, but also toward the masters of the soldiers, as is clear from Novel 13, addressed to Ariovindus, master of the soldiers, title 14, On the Removal of Military Officers from the Forum, issued at Constantinople in the consulship of Cyrus, that is, in the year 441; and also from title 24, the single Novel addressed to Aetius, master of both armies, issued at Rome in the sixth consulship of the emperor Valentinian, On the Ordination of Bishops.

The same honor was also conferred upon Eudoxius, count of the private estate, title 28, and Florentius, master of the offices, title 29. Therefore correct the other Novels in which either the letter F. or “brother” appears instead of P. and “parent.”]

“Palladius, most beloved and most affectionate father.”

For this reason, let your Illustrious Authority [Note: [Col. 0384B]

Add the words from the final part, in which the emperor orders the constitution to be promulgated throughout the whole world; and immediately wonder what the reason can be that a sanction distinguished by two such marks—perpetuity and universality—was formerly reported neither by Tribonian into the Justinianic Code, nor later by Annianus into the Breviary of Theodosius, nor recently by Gothofredus into that enormous Theodosian Code which he compiled in six volumes from all the laws of the emperors earlier than Marcian, gathered from every direction. Your wonder will be increased, I think, by the fact that in that entire threefold—if one may speak so—code there is no law against the Pelagian heresy, although there are many against other heresies, and although this very heresy was repeatedly proscribed by the emperors.

As for Tribonian, I formerly suspected two reasons why he may have wished to remain silent about the Pelagians. The first was the devices of the Pelagians themselves, if any of them still survived in the East—which I scarcely think. They had always taken the greatest care that nothing should be committed to writing by which they might at some time incur infamy or be summoned before a court. The second was that Tribonian, seeing scarcely any remnants of Pelagians in the East in his own time, may have regarded the laws enacted against them as temporary, and therefore may not have thought them suitable for inclusion in a permanent code.

I think the same should be understood of Annianus. But I have nothing to say in Gothofredus’s defense, since he could not fail to have seen those laws in Baronius, from whom he borrowed almost innumerable others; since he collected every sort of temporary law into his volumes; and since none of the four laws reported by Baronius fails to contain a great deal of learning, whether concerning chronology, the history of events, or knowledge worthy of a jurist. Did he deliberately and knowingly omit them all, lest he introduce the first and thereby be forced to recall the victory won by Sirmondus over his fellow-initiate (symmistēs), Salmasius; or lest, when remembering the second, addressed to Bishop Aurelius, he should acknowledge the great reverence with which the powers of the age honored the leaders of the Church in those early times?]

Let your Illustrious Authority know that by a law destined to endure for all time we have decreed that, once the principal authors of the detestable doctrine, Coelestius and Pelagius, have been expelled from the City, if henceforth any adherents of this sacrilege are found anywhere, or if anyone should again bring forward some statement from the condemned perversity, they are to be seized by whoever apprehends them and dragged before the competent judge. [Note: [Col. 0385C] That is, the error that would be handed down. The emperor shortly afterward orders those to be punished who are found discussing such a detestable crime. For whoever wished to impose silence upon Catholics who, in the spirit of the Church, were attacking the error might perhaps incur the censure both of Jerome, who complains that in this way “what war preserved, a fabricated peace removes” (Preface to the Dialogue against the Pelagians), and of the emperor, who condemns as sharing one and the same guilt those who either by dissembling furnish connivance or by failing to condemn furnish harmful support to error (Letter to Aurelius); and finally of Celestine, who gravely warns the bishops of Gaul that in such cases silence is not free from suspicion, since truth would come forward if falsehood were displeasing, and so forth (Letter to the Bishops of Gaul concerning Augustine). For, as Innocent I says (Letter to the Fathers of Milevis), equal punishment ought to restrain not only those who commit the acts but also those who consent to their perpetrators. There is, in fact, little difference between the mind of the person committing an offense and the favor of the person consenting.]

Everyone, whether cleric or layman, shall have the power to report them and to press the charge without any limitation, whoever he discovers to be introducing the darkness of a new dispute after abandoning the light of the common judgment, fighting against the apostolic discipline and the clear, error-free judgment of the Gospel by the cunning of a crafty and inexperienced sect, [Note: [Col. 0385D] The force of this word, *rudis*, is ambiguous. In ordinary usage it can signify ignorance or inexperience; it can also mean novelty, in which sense *rudia mancipia* in the Theodosian Code means newly acquired slaves. Neither sense is inappropriate here, since the Pelagians possessed more loquacity than knowledge, and the Fathers, especially Augustine, habitually called heretics “new” and heresy “new.”] and, by arguing in circumlocutions, wrapping the shining faith of truth in obscurities.

[Col. 0385B] Accordingly, wherever such persons are found discussing this most detestable crime, we order that they be seized by anyone, led before a public hearing, and accused indiscriminately by all, so that a public sentence may follow proof of the established charge, with them condemned to deportation into inexorable exile. [Note: [Col. 0385D] “Public style” is used for a public sentence, specifically one of deportation, as is clear from what follows, since they are condemned to deportation into inexorable exile. That *stylus* means a sentence is taught by Law 15, On Property Prescribed by Limitation, and elsewhere. Moreover, “the style of deportation” is expressly found in Law 57, On Heretics, against the Montanists; while in Law 58, against the Eunomians, in place of what this decree calls “deportation into inexorable exile,” the penalty is “deportation without anyone’s intercession.”] [Note: [Col. 0386C] Magd. corruptly, “by deportation into auxiliary exile.”] [Note: [Col. 0386C] This law seems to imitate earlier ones, for the penalty of deportation had already been decreed for other teachers of heresy as well—namely, the Eunomians, Macedonians, Arians, Apollinarians, Montanists, Donatists, and others. Concerning the first four sects, there is an express constitution of Theodosius the Great, issued at Constantinople on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Ricomer and Clearchus. Concerning the Eunomians specifically, there is a law of Arcadius, issued on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, in the fourth consulship of Arcadius and the third of Honorius, the Augusti. Concerning the Montanists and Eunomians there is also a law issued at Constantinople on the fourth day before the Nones of March, in the fourth consulship of Honorius Augustus and the consulship of Eutychius. Finally, concerning the Apollinarians there is a sanction of Theodosius the Great, issued on the sixth day before the Ides of March at Thessalonica, in the consulship of Theodosius II and Cynegius, and a law of Arcadius issued on the Kalends of April at Constantinople, in the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus.]

[Note: [Col. 0386D] The emperor agrees with Saint Innocent, who wrote to the Fathers of the Carthaginian synod: “They must be removed farther away and kept far from the Church’s entrails, lest, while the incurable error continues for too long, it grow worse and occupy many; for if they remain in this impunity for a long time, they will necessarily draw many into the disposition of their perversity and deceive the innocent—or rather, the inexperienced—who now follow the Catholic faith,” and so forth.]

For it is fitting that the source of the evil be separated from public assembly, and that those who are detestable not only for their abominable deed but also to be shunned as examples of a poisonous spirit should not remain amid the common gatherings.

Moreover, we are pleased that enactments of this kind be promulgated and disseminated throughout nearly the entire world wherever our empire extends, [Note: [Col. 0386D] Baron., Salm., Bal., “throughout nearly all our empire, wherever the world extends.” The inversion of the words reverses the sense.] lest perhaps a pretense of ignorance provide nourishment for error; and lest anyone suppose that he may safely dare what he has pretended not to know was condemned by the force of public authority. [Note: [Col. 0386D] Magd., “of ignorance,” which gives the opposite sense.] [Note: [Col. 0386D] Magd., Baron., Uss., Labb., “to hear.” The error is obvious in itself.]

[Col. 0386A] Issued at Ravenna on the day before the Kalends of May, in the twelfth consulship of Our Lords Honorius and the eighth of Theodosius, the Augusti.

## HISTORY OF THE CONSTITUTION

The constitution itself sufficiently shows by which emperor it was issued: by Honorius; on what day: the day before the Kalends of May; where: at Ravenna; in what year: in the twelfth consulship of Honorius and the eighth of Theodosius; to whom: Palladius, the Praetorian Prefect; and concerning what matter: the expulsion of Pelagius and Coelestius. But uncertainty remains as to the occasion on which it was issued; at whose request or through whose assistance it was obtained; what effect it achieved; and why it had to be repeated shortly afterward, indeed also extended. Since the last point belongs more properly to the history of Honorius’s letter to Aurelius, three other matters must now be investigated, partly from the testimony of the ancients, partly by reasoning and even conjecture.

There is indeed much in Augustine that bears upon that first decree of Honorius—namely, everything reported concerning the coercion of Julian and the other men of the Pelagian party in Italy; [Col. 0386B] but it scarcely supplies any evidence by which the matter under consideration can be established. He says that imperial authority was stirred against the authors of the heresy, that the prince had written a law against it, that the heretics had received it, and that they said the clergy at Rome had been terrified by it. “Against the authors,” he says (On Original Sin, chapter 17), “of the unspeakable error, episcopal councils and the apostolic see, and the whole Roman Church, and the Roman empire—which, by God’s favor, is Christian—were rightly stirred, until they recover from the snares of the devil.” And elsewhere (Book III against Julian, chapter 1): “Indeed, as you say, if the emperor’s response was given rather on your behalf, why do you not come forward and voluntarily bring this before the public authorities, showing that you are those whose faith the Christian prince approved? But you understand the law of faith not as it stands, but as it pleases you. What wonder, then, if you do the same with the emperor’s law?” In the same place: “Do not use the most wretched argument employed by all heretics, whom the laws of Catholic emperors restrain from pernicious license. All such people say what you yourself have said: that that side suffers from lack of reason which, when it substitutes terror in argument, wins no assent from the wise but extorts blind assent from the fearful.” Finally, writing to Boniface about the complaints of the Pelagians (Book II to Boniface, chapter 3), he says: “They even accuse the Roman clergy, writing that, struck by the terror of the command, they were not ashamed to commit the crime of betrayal.”

But since Augustine wrote all these things after Zosimus’s *tractoria*, nothing can certainly be inferred from them that resolves the question we have raised (see Dissertation 6, On the Books, etc.): was the decree obtained through the insistence of the apostolic see, or at the request of the African Church? It could have been obtained through either side.

Possidius (Life of Saint Augustine, chapter 18) offers something more significant—certainly more clearly stated, though still not sufficient to resolve the question. “Because,” he says, “those same perverse Pelagianists were attempting, through their ambition, to persuade the apostolic see of the same faithlessness, it was most earnestly enacted in the African councils of the holy bishops that the holy pope of the city of Rome—first the venerable Innocent, and afterward Saint Zosimus, his successor—should be persuaded that that sect was to be abominated and condemned by the Catholic faith. But those prelates of so great a see, condemning them at different times and cutting them off from the members of the Church, judged by letters sent to the Churches of Africa, the East, and the West that they should be anathematized and avoided by all Catholics. And when the most devout emperor Honorius heard and followed this judgment pronounced by the Catholic Church of God concerning them, he established by his laws that they should be condemned and reckoned among the heretics,” and so forth.

From this it is indeed clear that the emperor Honorius followed the judgment of the Church—that is, of the apostolic see, in which either Innocent or Zosimus was seated. But it is not clear which pontifical decree he followed; for he issued two decrees, and each pontiff pronounced judgment against the Pelagians during the time of Honorius.

Some think that Alypius of Thagaste, acting as the African Church’s envoy to the emperor, opposed the counsels of Zosimus, who had been deceived by Pelagian arts, and obtained from him a decree by which Coelestius—who seemed to have been partly acquitted by the apostolic see—was forbidden to remain in Rome and to teach freely the doctrine condemned by the Africans (Baronius, Annals, year 419). I frankly confess that I do not see how an opinion so alien to the chronology can plausibly be defended.
