For although I do not deny that the Africans bore with impatience the indulgence of the kindly pontiff—an indulgence scarcely short of excessive toward a man wholly undeserving; and although I grant that those most holy bishops tried every means by which they might, partly avert harm to the faith and partly their own disgrace; nevertheless I do not think that Alypius’s embassy and the date of the imperial decree can be reconciled with the acts of the general African council from which Alypius is said to have been sent. For if Alypius had obtained the decree, I believe he would have carried it back with him to Africa; but he could not have done so, since the decree was issued at Ravenna on the day before the Kalends of May, while on the Kalends themselves Alypius, as the acts of the plenary council show, sat with the Fathers at Carthage.

In the manuscript of the Thuaneus Codex the constitution is inscribed as follows: “Here begins the sacred rescript, issued after receiving the acts of the holy synod.” Salmasius, who saw the codex, interpreted the two letters SS. as referring to the Carthaginian synod. It would follow that Honorius’s decree was issued at the demand of the Africans, if it was indeed a rescript, since a rescript differed from a constitution in this respect: although the force and authority of both were equal, a rescript was written in reply to those who inquired or petitioned by letter, whereas a constitution was enacted by the emperor on his own initiative, as it were.

But I ask which Carthaginian synod Salmasius intended. There were several in this very case. Did he mean the first, under Aurelius, in the year 412? But that preceded the decree by six full years; or the second, from which a report was sent to Innocent? But that too preceded the decree by almost two years; or a third, somewhat more obscure, whose bishops received Zosimus’s third letter? Someone might indeed conjecture this, and perhaps not implausibly. Nevertheless, I can scarcely believe that Salmasius meant any other than the synod that composed the eight canons commonly called the Milevitan canons. If that was his view, he made one of two errors: either he thought that such canons had been composed at the Council of Milevis, an opinion than which nothing is said to be more absurd in our age; or he thought that “the Carthaginian synod” signified the universal African council, which is contrary to reason, since a synod of that kind followed the decree by at least one day, if we interpret the acts as they stand.

Nevertheless, testimony apparently favorable to Salmasius seems to come from the author of the Chronicle attributed to Prosper, from Prosper himself, from Baronius, and from the emperor Honorius. For the author of the Chronicle, under the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, says: “In those consulships, after a council had been held at Carthage, synodal decrees of 214 bishops were carried to Pope Zosimus; once these had been approved, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the world.” From this someone might perhaps infer that the decrees were first composed by the 214 Fathers assembled at Carthage—that is, the eight canons containing the condemnation of the entire Pelagian heresy—and that these were then carried not only to Rome to Zosimus for approval, but also to Ravenna to Honorius for confirmation by a sanction; that they were afterward sent throughout the world together with the tractoria of the supreme pontiff and the imperial sanction; and that, once subscribed by all the bishops, the heresy was finally overthrown everywhere.

Prosper, in his poem *Against the Ungrateful* (chapter 2):

> You, Africa, pursue the cause  
> Of our faith with fiercer zeal.  
>
> Your holy pontiffs from every city gathered,  
> And in a most renowned twofold assembly of elders  
>
> [Col. 0388C] You decree what Rome approves, what kingdoms follow.

After praising Prosper—without closer examination—as the author whom he takes to be the writer of the Chronicle, Baronius writes that the council mentioned by him was assembled at the beginning of spring; and he concludes this with certainty from the fact that Zosimus’s letters concerning the matter were addressed to it on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, and that the canons under discussion were enacted in it after the council had been extended until May. He later adds that at the same time a council was held at Carthage and judgment concerning Pelagius and Coelestius was held at Rome. He adds many other things which, although it would be tedious to report, may nevertheless be consulted with no small profit.

The emperor seems to agree with these authorities in his letter to Aurelius, for after mentioning that Pelagius and Coelestius had already been condemned by him, he says: “In this our clemency followed the judgment of Your Holiness, whom it is established were condemned by the just examination of a sentence on the part of all.” These words may be argued as follows: if Aurelius’s judgment was followed by Honorius’s first sanction, and Aurelius cannot be thought to have judged Coelestius and Pelagius together except in the Carthaginian synod, then the sanction seems likewise to have been issued after receiving the acts of the Carthaginian synod, as Salmasius thought.

But, to speak frankly about my own opinion, these testimonies have always seemed to me not merely insufficient to establish what is required, but also extremely difficult in themselves—indeed, more often contrary to the truth—unless they are assisted or rather forced by some favorable interpretation.

To begin with Baronius: if, at the beginning of spring, 214 of the most distinguished Fathers of all Africa gathered at Carthage; if the council continued until the Kalends of May and beyond; and if Zosimus wrote his third letter concerning the Pelagian case to that council, then it was certainly necessary both that so great a multitude of holy prelates should be absent from their Churches during the Paschal festivals, when the canons required the bishop to celebrate baptism; and that the end of the council should be marked by a date, while its beginning lacked one; and that the supreme pontiff should have known at Rome, on March 20—the date placed on his letter—that the council had been assembled at Carthage, indeed even dissolved, although it would not have convened before March 20. For Zosimus writes: “To Aurelius and the others who were present at the Carthaginian council.” What could be more opposed than these three points to the religious observance of the seasons, during which the canons were most scrupulously observed, especially in Africa itself; to the custom of dating councils; or finally to reason, as is self-evident?

The words of the chronicler, too, if understood in the same way as Baronius understands them, are equally difficult and confused. But if “synodal decrees” is understood to mean the eight dogmatic canons, the chronicler contradicts not only the opponent of the Collator, who mentions two councils and writes that canons were composed in one while 214 Fathers sat in the other, but also Augustine, who mentions two African councils—or rather three—of which Zosimus’s rescript came from the first, the canons were composed in the second, and Zosimus’s *tractoria* was received in the third.

What, then, shall we do with Prosper the chronicler, who, as the saying goes, was writing about events of his own time? Baronius has an easy excuse, since he was led astray by Prosper. I should scarcely hesitate, held back on one side by Prosper’s name and drawn in the opposite direction by reason, unless the thought occurred to me that I may be restrained only by the shadow of either the difficulty or the great name. For what establishes that the reading found in the commonly circulated manuscripts of the Chronicles must be preserved, rather than replaced by the reading written by Joannes Sicardus in the margin (in the edition of the Eusebian Chronicle translated by Jerome and enlarged by that same Prosper, Basel, at the press of Heinrich Petri, 1529): “The synodal decrees were brought forth by Pope Zosimus; once these had been approved, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the world”? These words, I admit, undergo some strain, but they fit the true history of events exceedingly well.

Moreover, if the common reading is retained, by what sufficient evidence is it established that the continuator of the Chronicle attributed to Prosper was not different from the Aquitanian? I know that Gennadius read a Chronicle bearing the title of Prosper (On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 54); but whether it presented the true author on its title page, or falsely named another, remains a disputed question among scholars. But even granting that the Aquitanian wrote—or rather continued—the Chronicle from the creation of the world to Valentinian’s death, is he deserving of confidence at that point when he plainly reports three falsehoods?

He writes that Boniface began his episcopate at Rome in the year 419 and held it for three years and nine months. But he began in 418 and held it for four years and ten months, less three days, since the see remained vacant for only two days after Zosimus died on December 26, and Celestine began to occupy it on December 26 of the year 423.

Next, he reports that Constantius, a servant of God, suffered at Rome at the hands of the Pelagians in the year 418; yet that holy layman [Col. 0389D] (Author of *On Predestination*, heresy 88) acted vigorously against the Pelagians without writing, before either Jerome or Augustine fought them in writing. The holy doctors, however, had been fighting them already from the year 412.

Finally, he places in the same year both Constantius’s assumption by Honorius as his partner in the empire and the death of Saint Jerome. Yet Jerome died on the day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Honorius IX and Constantius III; Constantius received the empire on February 8, in the consulship of Agricola and Eustachius—that is, in the year 421. Nor can he be excused on the grounds that he began the year with September, as did the imperial indiction, since several other testimonies by the same author contradict such an assertion.

It must therefore be admitted that the chronicler differs from the disciple of Augustine and that in this matter his memory failed. Yet even the disciple of Augustine would not deserve unquestioned confidence concerning this matter if he gave the same testimony, since, because of his extraordinary devotion to Augustine and the Africans, he was accustomed to attribute to the African Fathers as authors many things in which they actually played only the part of co-workers or even assistants.

The argument drawn from the emperor’s testimony is likewise based on an ambiguous word and is easily resolved once the meaning of that word is explained. The emperor does not say that he issued his first sanction after the judgment rendered by Aurelius in the plenary African synod—which would be necessary to confirm Salmasius’s opinion. Rather, he says indefinitely that he issued a sanction after Aurelius’s judgment, whatever that judgment may have been and whenever it may have occurred. Aurelius rendered two judgments at different times in the synods of the proconsular province: the first in 412, the second in 416. Therefore the emperor asserts that, in issuing the earlier sanction, he followed Aurelius’s judgment concerning those whom it was afterward established had been condemned by a just examination of a sentence—conducted at the apostolic see—by all those to whom Zosimus’s *tractoria* was sent and by whom the apostolic sentence of condemnation was subscribed.

Having argued these points against opinions that are not soundly established, I think that the matter can certainly be settled by reason. It is established that Zosimus wrote to the Africans concerning Coelestius in his first letters at the beginning of September in the year 417, and then shortly afterward wrote a second letter, concerning Pelagius, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. It is credible that the first letters reached Carthage before the dissolution of the synod of the proconsular province, which by custom was held around the autumn season. A rescript was sent from there to Zosimus, together with everything that had taken place in Coelestius’s presence at the Carthaginian council of 412. Along with many other documents, two petitions were also sent that had been presented to Aurelius—one by Paulinus when he brought the accusation, the other by Coelestius when he defended himself.

Armed with these materials, the pontiff began pressing Coelestius with repeated questions, so that he would condemn even those charges that Paulinus had brought in his petition. The accused maliciously evaded the issue and, with feigned intent, promised that he would subscribe to Innocent’s letter and correct those points in his petition that the apostolic see wished corrected; but at the same time he promised that, if granted the opportunity, he would convict Paulinus of heresy from Paulinus’s own petition.

Meanwhile Zosimus sent Basiliscus, a subdeacon of the Roman Church, to Africa, both to inform the African bishops about what had taken place at Rome and to summon Paulinus to judgment. After arriving in Africa, Basiliscus met Paulinus at Carthage, though not according to the requirements of the canons, since it was neither the proper time nor a procedurally valid document. Accordingly, five days after the summons, Paulinus gave Marcellinus, a subdeacon of the Carthaginian Church whom Aurelius was sending to Rome with instructions, a petition addressed to the supreme pontiff, by which he cleverly avoided judgment.

The case was taken up again at Rome with Coelestius during the winter. But the crafty man, through repeated professions and fabricated promises, continued to mock the apostolic see in almost the same way in which Pelagius had once mocked the Fathers at Diospolis. Again, before Lent, a synod of the province of Carthage was convened in Africa according to custom. From it a letter was again sent to Rome, partly concerning the need to guard against Coelestius’s frauds; partly to recall to Zosimus what his predecessor Innocent had thought concerning the proceedings in Palestine or had decreed against the heretics; and finally concerning the faithful preservation in Africa of Innocent’s decrees, and the refusal to receive Pelagius and Coelestius into communion until they had most plainly confessed that, through the grace of God by Jesus Christ our Lord, we are aided by God not only in knowing righteousness but also in doing it, through each of our acts, and so forth.

After receiving the synod’s letter, Zosimus sent a third letter to Africa on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. In it he stated that, contrary to what the Africans seemed to think, the judgment concerning Coelestius had not yet been completed, but that everything had been left in the same condition, so that there would be an opportunity for the Africans to plead their case. But immediately after sending the letter, the supreme pontiff summoned Coelestius to a fuller hearing and the highest judgment. When Coelestius realized that his devices were exposed and that no means of evasion remained, he withdrew from the examination—whether he hid in the City among his associates, fled to Ravenna to the emperor, or remained in the areas near Rome while waiting to seize an opportunity. Once his flight became known, a definitive sentence was immediately issued against both defenders of the unspeakable doctrine, and the pontiff wrote to all the bishops of the world that great letter which Mercator calls the *tractoria*. The proceedings of the Roman synod were also sent to the emperor. After he received them, the decree concerning the expulsion from the City of the condemned heretics was issued to Palladius on the day before the Kalends of May. By an edict posted by the praetor at Rome, all the clergy of the Roman Church, I think, were summoned to subscribe the *tractoria*, and they did so with the greatest willingness, with the presbyter Sixtus leading the others. At that time the days of Pentecost were being celebrated, [Col. 0391B] and a very large crowd was flocking to the Church because of the solemn baptism.

Once these points have been established according to the judgment of the ancients, the answers to the questions are straightforward and easy. It is established that Honorius’s decree was issued on the occasion of the sentence pronounced against the heretics by the apostolic see, so that imperial authority might follow the judgment of the Church. It is likewise established that it was issued at the urging of the supreme pontiff, so that, through the combined forces of both supreme authorities, the heresy might be utterly overthrown. Count Valerius provided assistance and care; Julian complains that for this reason Valerius obstructed by the weight of his dignity the granting by the emperor of a time and place for debate—perhaps Coelestius had come to request it.

How great the anguish of the heretics was is revealed by their complaint that the court had been deceived by trickery and unspeakable devices, and that a subscription had been extorted from terrified clergy who, because of fear, were betraying their own cause. The good rejoiced in a measure equal to the wicked men’s grief, when everyone saw the Pelagians’ uncontrolled audacity restrained and the violence inflicted by the heretics upon holy men—at Rome, in the case of Constantius, and at Jerusalem, in the case of Jerome—avenged by the just anger of the rulers whenever the heretics, growing insolent, thought they could act with impunity.

Nevertheless, through Coelestius’s inexhaustible devices it came about that the result did not match the hopes, but that the constitution had to be repeated, especially in order to correct the obstinacy of certain bishops who either supported the heretics’ wicked arguments by silent consent or failed to destroy them by public opposition.

[Note: [Col. 0391B] There is no constitution here, but only a copy of an edict, etc., in Garnerius, who appends this note at the end: “It is found among the cited authors as a constitution, and in the same places, except that Baronius, contrary to the chronology, assigned it to the year 421.” EDIT.]

## CONSTITUTION II

[Note: [Col. 0391C] There was a dispute between Sirmondus and Salmasius as to whether the edict of the praetorian prefects should be placed before the law of the emperors, or the law before the edict. Once the matter had been contested in their books, scholars judged that Sirmondus had prevailed; yet Salmasius, who refused to subordinate the imperial law to the edict, was not thereby spared the sharper rebuke, although he was guilty of diminishing imperial majesty. He had acted rashly, though otherwise he was a learned man, and had not paid sufficient attention to the law of Valentinian the Younger addressed to Probus—the sole law in the Code under “If through stealth,” which plainly teaches that the emperor’s law was placed before the edict. It is astonishing that Salmasius should still have companions, and even followers, in his delusion, who do not seem to have learned, either from the laws themselves or from daily usage, what it means for a prefect to publish a law beneath his own edict and proclamation.]

## COPY OF THE EDICT OF THE PRAETORIAN PREFECTS

[Col. 0392B]

[Note: [Col. 0391C] Nor is there any need here to disturb the ghosts of Salmasius—if indeed they are resting anywhere—whom Sirmond, while he was alive, decisively corrected when he supposed that an edict had been posted by four praetorian prefects, each in his own jurisdiction. Junius [Col. 0391D] divided Quartus Palladius into two persons and was mistaken twice: first, because, when he failed to recall the matter, he did not notice that all the ancients who mention Palladius’s consulship report three names together; and again, because he wrote that each prefect had posted the edict in his own jurisdiction, although each of them placed the names of the others at the head of his own edict, just as emperors place the laws of their colleagues before their own. Perhaps a third point could be added: at that time there was no praetorian prefect of Illyricum. —Magdeburgenses and Baronius, through faulty punctuation, made “Junius Quartus, Palladius, Monaxius, and Agricola” and thereby led Salmasius into the error concerning his four separate prefects.]

JUNIUS QUARTUS PALLADIUS, [Note: [Col. 0391D] He first held the prefecture of the East, as is established by several laws; he was second prefect of the Gauls, as is shown by the constitution of Honorius concerning the annual convocation at Arles of the council of the seven provinces, addressed to Agricola, Praetorian Prefect of the Gauls, in the twelfth consulship of Honorius and the eighth of Theodosius. Moreover, Monaxius entered upon the consulship with Plinta in the year 419, and Agricola with Eustathius in the year 421.] MONAXIUS, and AGRICOLA, again praetorian prefects, [Note: [Col. 0392B] Magdeburgenses, Baronius, Labbe, and Baluzius read “issued.” The verb “to issue” is the customary term.] issued the edict.

[Note: [Col. 0391C] The title of this note is not intended as a disturbance of Salmasius’s shade—if shades rest anywhere—whom Sirmond, during his lifetime, splendidly corrected for supposing that an edict had been posted by four praetorian prefects, each within his own jurisdiction. Junius [Col. 0391D] divided Junius Quartus Palladius into two persons and thus erred twice: first, because, when he failed to consult the memory of all the ancients who mention Palladius’s consulship, he did not see that they report three names together; secondly, because he wrote that each prefect had posted the edict in his own jurisdiction, although each prefixed the names of the others to his own edicts, just as emperors place the laws of their colleagues before their own. A third point might perhaps be added: at that time there was no praetorian prefect of Illyricum. —Magdeburgenses and Baronius, through faulty punctuation, “Junius Quartus, Palladius, Monaxius, and Agricola,” led Salmasius into the error of thinking that there were four separate prefects.]

Against Pelagius and Coelestius, destroying the faith of Catholic doctrine by their unspeakable discourses, [Note: [Col. 0392B] That is, by sermons addressed to the people, using the expression customary in those times. Augustine likewise calls his sermons to the people “tractates”; and, as the presbyter of Lérins testifies, those who instructed the common people were called “tractators.” See what we have noted concerning the treatises of Nestorius against the Pelagians.

The Emperor Theodosius the Great, moreover, distinguished between two words that are often confused, namely, *disceptare* and *tractare*, “to debate” and “to address.” For, in a law issued at Stobi on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Theodosius II and Cynegius, he forbade anyone going out in public to have an opportunity either of debating religion or of addressing the people, and so forth. Nor was the distinction made without reason: to debate is to dispute with someone; to address is to speak publicly to the people.] the following imperial judgment prevailed: [Note: [Col. 0392C]

“To be removed from the City” in this passage means the same as to be punished with exile beyond the whole Roman Empire. I infer this, first, from the emperor’s words, to which the prefect’s edict corresponds: “Let the public record pursue the proof of the convicted crime, with the offenders condemned to unrelenting deportation into exile,” and so forth. Secondly, I infer it from the name of all the praetorian prefects placed at the head of the edict. For the designation “in the name of all” signifies that the edict was published by one person for this reason: everyone was obliged to see that it was observed in his own jurisdiction. Finally, I infer it from Honorius’s order that the law should be promulgated: “It is useful that such a promulgation be disseminated throughout almost the whole world, wherever our empire extends.” For what purpose would there have been such universality of promulgation, or such generality of the edict, if the heretics in question were to be expelled from only one jurisdiction?

From this it can be understood that expulsion from the City has one meaning when the matter concerns the edict of a praetorian prefect, and another when it is ordered by the Urban Prefect. When the former issues the order, it signifies proscription, or deportation; when the latter does so, it signifies merely expulsion either beyond the walls of the City or to the hundredth milestone. Therefore, when Honorius issued a law to Palladius, the Praetorian Prefect, he ordered that Pelagius and Coelestius be expelled from the City in such a way that they were condemned to unrelenting deportation into exile. Constantius, however, when writing against the same men to Volusianus, the Urban Prefect, ordered that they be expelled beyond the walls of the City, but nevertheless that they should not even have permission to remain within the hundredth milestone. For the authority of the praetorian prefect was bounded by no other limits than the empire itself, whereas the power of the Urban Prefect extended only to the hundredth milestone.]

they should be removed from the venerable City and punished by confiscation of their property.

[Col. 0393A] All must therefore be warned by this edict not to lend credence to the errors of a sinister persuasion. [Note: [Col. 0393B] Salmasius reads “sinister,” less well.] Even if the person who has fallen into the obscene darkness of this obscurity is a commoner or a cleric, he will be brought before a judge by anyone who seizes him, without distinction as to the identity of the accuser; stripped of his property, he will suffer irrevocable exile.

[Note: [Col. 0393B] Baronius: “For just as supreme majesty gathers reverence from ignorance of what is secret, so it removes the injury of foolish disputation.” Salmasius and Baluzius: “Just as it does not derive an execrable ignorance from what is hidden, so it rejects the injury of foolish disputation.” A very fine thought has been corrupted by obscure wording.] For just as supreme majesty gathers reverence from ignorance of what is secret, so it [removes] the injury of foolish disputation.

[Note: [Col. 0393B] This constitution is found among the same authors as the preceding one, except in Salmasius.]

CONSTITUTION III. [Note: [Col. 0393B]

Since imperial laws had different forms according to the various causes for which they were enacted or the persons to whom they were addressed, a variety of names also came into use. They were called “constitutions” when princes issued them, as it were, on their own initiative; “rescripts” when they gave answers to consultations; and “letters,” or “sacred letters,” when they sent enactments to distinguished and honored persons. There were also mandates, orders, and other names, although the distinction of names was not always strictly observed. Indeed, the letter now before us is called a constitution by Honorius and Aurelius.

Letters, which are sometimes simply called “sacred letters,” were sent to bishops, and many of this kind are found in the acts of the Council of Ephesus. In the acts of the Fifth Council there is the celebrated letter of Justinian to Menas concerning the condemnation of Origen; it was also sent to Pope Vigilius and to the other patriarchs of Alexandria, Constantinople, and Jerusalem. This is why, unlike certain others, we have not placed “rescript” as the title, but “letter.”]

LETTER OF THE EMPEROR HONORIUS [Note: [Col. 0393C]

And indeed primate of the whole African diocese. For the province of Proconsular Africa enjoyed this privilege: the person who held the see of Carthage was primate not only of the province but also of Africa, whereas in the other provinces the senior bishop presided over his fellow bishops.

I said “of the whole African diocese,” although perhaps Mauretania Tingitana should be excepted. Just as it formerly obeyed the Vicar of the Spains, so it was subject to the primate of Nearer Baetica. Nevertheless, when the Vandals first and then the Visigoths invaded this part of the Spains, I think that something changed, and that from that time Mauretania Tingitana, or Transfretan Spain, was under the African primate. For in the acts of the African council held in 419, the representatives of Spain—namely, Transfretan Spain—are counted among the others. The Vandals, about the year 409, and the Visigoths, about the year 419, held Nearer Baetica, the Vandals having been defeated.

Aurelius was that distinguished founder of the African and almost universal Church, president of so many councils, author of so many canons, that those who preceded the primates of Africa seem to have laid only the foundations of discipline, which he completed as a model for almost the whole Catholic Church.

He held the episcopate, as I believe, for thirty-six years. He assumed it in the year 390 and died around the year 426. The date of his accession is known from the fact that in 389, while still a deacon, he witnessed with Augustine, then still a layman, a miracle performed at Carthage (Augustine, [Col. 0394A] Book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 8). In 391, however, Augustine, already a presbyter, addressed a letter to Aurelius (Letter 22). The date of his death may likewise be inferred from the fact that in 424 or 425 he subscribed, at an African synod, to Leporius’s letter to the bishops of Gaul; in 431, however, Capreolus, Aurelius’s successor, wrote to the Fathers at Ephesus through the deacon Bassula, in such a way as to show that he had already been seated for some time in the see of Carthage (Council of Ephesus, Part II, Act 1). Aurelius must therefore have died in the intervening period, and, as I believe, in 426 or 427. Nor should learned men accept Baronius’s view, when he inserts Gennadius between Capreolus and Aurelius; Gennadius preceded Aurelius.

How highly Honorius valued Aurelius is sufficiently shown by the letter under discussion. Someone might nevertheless infer the same thing from the letters by which, during the schism of Eulalius, he is said to have summoned the holy old man, together with seven distinguished African bishops, to a synod to be held at Spoleto on the Ides of June concerning the right of Boniface and Eulalius to the apostolic see. Although Cardinal Baronius inserted these letters in his *Annals* from a Vatican manuscript, some have suspected them because of their obscurity and other defects of this kind. Yet since the other defects arise from obscurity, and the obscurity from the fault of the manuscript alone, correction is not difficult. It should be read as follows:

“We had wished that another reason for your coming had arisen, so that we might enjoy the desired sight of your blessing; but since censurable ambition has initiated a contest against the pope of the city of Rome, and since we judge a holy life to be something required in a bishop, the judicial inquiry begun concerning this matter has been extended to several most learned men, whose leader is Your Holiness, in no smaller number than the custom of a synod demands. For the rewards of chastity and merit, once the vices rejected by the sacred presumption of divine religion have been removed, ought not to be revealed through men other than such as these. And although the writings of my lord and brother, the Augustus prince, would suffice, mine too will be useful, by which I have likewise added the arrival of Your Holiness. I therefore ask you, holy Lord and Father, deservedly venerable, to grant us a double benefit: both the blessing we desire from you and the necessary decision suited to the character of the case, setting aside everything else. When the Lord is in view, the labor of coming should not be refused for the confirmation of his priest. May the Divinity deign to preserve you unharmed for many years, dearest and most loving Father.”

TO AURELIUS, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE. [Note: [Col. 0394D] As far as I know, no sanction of Christian emperors concerning the assembly of all bishops had ever preceded this one in a case involving the overthrow of a heresy—whether the bishops who had been absent from a council at which a formula of faith had been established or a heresy condemned together with its authors, or even those who were quietly remaining in their own sees and were not suspected of heresy, were being required to subscribe to the sentence pronounced by the Church against someone. Certainly there is nothing of this kind in the whole Theodosian Code, nothing among ecclesiastical historians, and nothing among approved authors. The claims made concerning Eusebius and Theognis in the Arian controversy have an entirely different character. This constitution may therefore rightly be regarded as a model for many subsequent ones. A separate discussion will soon follow concerning the entire matter of subscriptions insofar as it relates to the Pelagian controversy.]

Concerning the subscription to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius.

The Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, Augusti, to Bishop Aurelius, greetings.

It had formerly been decreed that Pelagius and Coelestius, the discoverers of an unspeakable doctrine, should be expelled from the city of Rome as a kind of contagion of Catholic truth, lest they should corrupt the minds of the ignorant by a savage persuasion. In this matter our clemency followed the judgment of Your Holiness, [Note: [Col. 0395B] Magdeburgenses reads: “from which it is clear that they were condemned by all according to a just sentence,” and so forth. But can those be said to have been condemned by all against whom one bishop had pronounced sentence? Baluzius reads: “against whom our clemency followed the judgment of Your Holiness, who are known to have been condemned by all according to a just sentence,” and so forth. Our reading is much more fully expressed.] since it is clear that they were condemned by all through a just judicial examination. [Note: [Col. 0395B] That is what Prosper says—not only Prosper (*Poem on the Ungrateful*, chapter 3): “You admit that these were condemned by councils and by the judgment of the whole world,” but also Mercator in the *Commonitorium*: “The letter of blessed memory, Pope Zosimus, which is called the *tractoria*, was sent throughout the whole world and was strengthened by the subscriptions of the holy Fathers.”]

But because the stubborn evil of an obstinate crime compelled us to repeat the constitution, [Note: [Col. 0395B] Baluzius reads “against the rest, the excessively stubborn evil of the obstinate,” with the same meaning but greater elegance.] we have also decreed, by a recent [Note: [Col. 0395B] Magdeburgenses, Baronius, Ussher, and Labbe read “enactment.” The words that follow—“this definition has been prescribed for them”—show that “by a definition” should be read.] definition, that if anyone should knowingly delay either to expel or to expose them, wherever in any part of the provinces they might be lurking, he should be subjected, as a participant, to the prescribed penalty. [Note: [Col. 0395B] It is uncertain which provinces the emperor means: only the two to whose bishops Aurelius wrote; all the provinces of the African diocese; or even all those under the authority of the Praetorian Prefect to whom the earlier constitution was addressed, which is now said to be repeated. I think it more credible that all the provinces of Africa are meant. Apart from the fact that Aurelius indicates in his letter that he was giving the order to subscribe to everyone who had attended the council—and representatives of all the provinces had attended—the nature and reason of the subscription itself persuade us, since the matter was common to all the provinces, wherever the serpentine persuasion might creep in. That this order applied only to the African provinces, and not likewise to the other provinces under the praetorian prefecture, is clear from the fact that Aurelius had no authority beyond the limits of Africa. Why, then, does the text say “in whatever part of the provinces”? First, so that none of the six provinces would be excepted. Secondly, so that Mauretania Tingitana would be included, since it was subject to the Vicar of the Spains and to the Praetorian Prefect of the Gauls. For if representatives had perhaps come from that province to the plenary council—which had not previously been customary—the bishops of that province ought to have subscribed to the formula that was ordered to be subscribed by everyone present at the council.]

But especially for correcting the obstinacy of certain bishops, [Note: [Col. 0395D]

Who these men were, if Africans are meant—as in fact they are—we cannot determine. We possess no acts of the councils from which some light might perhaps emerge; nor, as far as I know, does Augustine mention any bishop in Africa who openly followed the Pelagian party, although otherwise he was a diligent investigator of this kind of matter. He does mention Vitalis, whom he rebukes rather sharply; the monks of Hadrumetum, whom he instructed in two books and as many letters; and Peter, who favored Vincentius Victor, who held erroneous views about the origin of souls. But the first was merely a deacon of the Church of Carthage; the men of Hadrumetum were monks; and Peter was a presbyter.

[Col. 0396B] If, however, the reference is not only to Africans but also to Sicilians and Italians, we shall pursue the matter at greater length, and not without sound reason, in connection with the *Memorial of Faith* that Julian, Bishop of Eclanum, wrote to Pope Zosimus in the name of eighteen Sicilian bishops (*Dissertation 5 on the Books of Faith*). This was at the time when they were being pressed more insistently to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius.]

of certain bishops, [Col. 0396A] whose perverse discussions either support by tacit consent or fail to destroy by public opposition, it will be proper for Your Holiness, dearest and most loving Father, to exercise authority, so that, [Note: [Col. 0396B] Why does the text say “the devotion of all Christians,” rather than merely that of the bishops? Because the emperor undoubtedly orders subscriptions to be obtained not only from bishops at the demand of the primate, but also from priests of the second order and from the lesser clergy, with the bishop present; indeed, even from laymen, at least those under suspicion, as may be gathered both from the Ephesian canons, which, following the imperial sanction, also concern Coelestian laymen, and from the letter of Leo the Great to Septimius concerning compelling laymen themselves to subscribe in the Pelagian case.] in abolishing the perverse heresy, the devotion of all Christians may agree.

Your Religiousness will therefore have everyone warned by appropriate letters, so that they may know from the testimony of Your Holiness that this decision has been prescribed for them: whoever, through impious obstinacy, neglects to subscribe to the condemnation of those mentioned above, so that it may be clear that his mind is pure, shall be punished by loss of the episcopate and deprived forever of communion.

[Note: [Col. 0396C] That is: “Since we are of the orthodox faith, we cannot endure heretics disseminating their error through secret discussions.” The text says “according to the Council of Nicaea,” because in those times this was almost a formula and a sure mark of orthodoxy: to profess the faith of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers assembled at Nicaea. Thus, in Law 6 on Heretics of Theodosius the Great, “the defender of the Nicene faith” and “a true worshiper of the Catholic religion” are treated as equivalent expressions. Unless this interpretation is applied to the words cited, they will scarcely bear a tolerable meaning, since the Pelagians had no particular disagreement with the Nicene faith by which the emperor could show that he was hostile to them because he himself held a correct belief concerning the *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον, “consubstantiality”).

At the end it should be noted that in the editions of the Magdeburgenses and others, the following words are read after the imperial letter: “Also given in the same form to Saint Augustine.” Someone might plausibly assert that these words were inserted by a notary, since neither in the entire law code nor among ecclesiastical writers is there any law sent by the emperors to bishops to be promulgated with authority, except to those who possessed jurisdiction over their fellow bishops either by the prerogative of their see or for some other reason. At that time Augustine, although his reputation for learning and holiness was very great, had no authority by right of his see except over a very few parishes, nor any by right of seniority, since he was not the senior of his province; Silvanus, Valentinus, Alypius, and others were senior to him.

We do indeed read of letters sent to Augustine, both by Honorius, summoning him to the synod at Spoleto in the case of Eulalius, and by Theodosius, calling him to the Council of Ephesus. But these were merely summonses, or *tractoriae*, of the sort often sent to private persons; they were not *procuratoriae*, by which an office together with authority was entrusted.]

For since we ourselves, according to the Council of Nicaea, venerate with sincere confession God, the Creator of all things, [Col. 0397A] and the author of our empire, [Note: [Col. 0397D] Magdeburgenses reads: “let them venerate the Lord, the author of our empire.” A solecism has crept into the text, either through the fault of the printers or of the notaries.] Your Holiness will not permit men of a detestable sect, devising new and unheard-of things to the injury of religion, to conceal in secret discussions the sacrilege once condemned by public authority. [Note: [Col. 0398D] Magdeburgenses reads “to be concealed in secret discussions.” The word *tractatus* is appropriate here, and the rules of Latin require an active verb.] For there is one and the same fault in those who, either by dissembling, [Note: [Col. 0398D] Magdeburgenses and Baluzius read “conformity.” This error should have been corrected from Aurelius’s letter, which uses “dissembling”; the emperor has “connivance.”] or by failing to condemn, have offered harmful support.

And in another hand: “May the Divinity preserve you unharmed for many years, dearest and most loving Father.” At Ravenna.

[Note: [Col. 0398D] Magdeburgenses reads: “Given on the Ides of June.” The numeral may have been omitted, as was also the name of the consuls, which appears everywhere else.] Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta.

HISTORY OF THE IMPERIAL LETTER.

The *tractoria* of Zosimus had arrived in Africa. It contained not only the whole case of Pelagius and Coelestius, but especially the definitive judgment of the apostolic see, to which all were required to subscribe. It was received with the greatest joy, eagerly purchased by the devout and the good, together with private letters from the supreme pontiff to the Africans. The Africans in turn gave thanks to Zosimus, accompanied by the fullest praise. The judgment was subscribed by all who were present at the council, although perhaps by some without sincerity. Copies of the *tractoria* were sent by Aurelius, the primate, to the principal sees of the provinces, so that from there they might be transmitted to the other bishops of the cities, to be subscribed both by the bishops themselves and by the clergy, and then returned with the subscriptions to the metropolitan city.

This was willingly done by many prelates, but some evaded it, especially in the provinces of Byzacena and Tripolitania. Some, as I believe, used a certain exception; others did not insist carefully enough that the lower clergy provide the required subscription; still others, following the example and perhaps the persuasion of the Sicilians, openly refused obedience to the Church.

[Col. 0397C] Since this was a common affliction of Africa and Italy, a remedy was sought from the emperors—for from whom else could it have been sought after the decrees of so many pontiffs had proved almost ineffective? Those unwilling to perform their duty voluntarily were to be compelled by fear; and those who rebelled stubbornly against the Church were to be expelled from their sees, so that at least they might benefit others by no longer possessing the power to do harm.

Honorius therefore issued a rescript not only to Aurelius, so that it might be promulgated to the bishops of his diocese, but also, as was customary, to the Vicar of Africa, so that action might be taken against the obstinate. Aurelius promulgated the imperial sanction in a letter addressed to the bishops of the province, at least of Byzacena and Arzugitana. The outcome is rightly believed to have answered the hopes of its authors, since afterward no significant disturbance is recorded as having been stirred up by the Pelagians in Africa. For the disturbances caused either by the monks of Hadrumetum or by Vitalis, the deacon of Carthage, were easily suppressed.

The matters I have briefly related thus far are of great importance for history. To prevent them from being regarded either as rash assertions [Col. 0397D] or as arbitrary inventions, they might perhaps need to be confirmed more carefully by citing the actual passages of the authors, which are cited elsewhere, were there not a danger of boring readers by such length or by the repetition of the evidence. It is therefore better, setting these matters aside, to inquire at whose instigation the emperor issued the rescript: [Col. 0398A] whether at the request of the African Church through Alypius, as the distinguished author of the *Annals* believes (under the year of Christ 419, no. 54 and following); or at that of Boniface, the supreme pontiff, as Prosper seems to suggest (*Against Cassian*, chapter 41); or at that of some other person of great influence at court through his friends.

The question can be settled by a definite argument insofar as Alypius’s embassy is concerned. He was at Carthage with two other envoys from the province of Numidia, Augustine and Possidius, on the third day before the Kalends of June, the day on which the council began, in the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta. The letter, however, was written at Ravenna on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the same consulship. Alypius therefore could not have obtained it unless—something more extraordinary than a miracle—he had completed so much travel and so much business in the space of ten days.

Nor was any other envoy sent to the emperor from Africa: not by the African synod, since none was held from the month of August in the year 418 until the third day before the Kalends of June of the following year; not by the Proconsular Province, which had no authority over the provinces of Byzacena and Tripolitania; not by Aurelius alone, who had indeed been given power to write in the name of all, but only concerning matters established in a general council; nor by several bishops conspiring together for the good of the Church, as five of them had written privately to Saint Innocent about three years earlier. An embassy so useful and so successful would certainly have been mentioned by the ancients, yet no such mention exists.

It would therefore remain to suppose that Honorius had been prompted by the supreme pontiff. This seems to be Prosper’s view when he says that Boniface, rejoicing in the Catholic devotion of the most pious emperors, used royal as well as apostolic edicts against the enemies of grace. Yet this opinion encounters a very serious difficulty: how could the pontiff, who on 25 May could scarcely breathe freely at Rome because of the schism of Eulalius, have obtained from the emperor an edict to be issued at Ravenna five days later?

[Col. 0398C] Nevertheless, I would not depart from Prosper if nothing else held me back. For why could the pontiff not have understood that many Pelagian bishops were established in Italy, indeed in Rome itself, who, after Eulalius had been expelled from the City, supported the party of Eulalius and of Antiochus, where he was residing and pressing upon the Roman see; who had conspired with the obstinate Africans against the defenders of the Catholic faith; who were deliberately preparing trouble for Boniface by name, since they were patrons of Eulalius; and who were demanding with the greatest insistence that their case be reconsidered by the emperor, as though judgment had been obtained by underhand means? And, finally, why could Boniface not have recognized that heretics customarily exploit every change in circumstances, watching for every moment? Why, I say, once he understood these things, could he not have worked through friends at court for the cause of God while he himself was suppressing at Rome the disturbances stirred up by Eulalius? I would incline to that view, as I have said, unless something else, far more probable, presented itself: namely, that the whole business was carried out by Augustine, or even by Alypius, in secret consultations with Count Valerius, with greater prudence than publicity.

[Col. 0398D] I am led to this opinion, first, by Augustine’s and Alypius’s constant determination to eradicate the heresy by every possible means. For this reason Jerome said that the Coelestian heresy had been strangled by them, its co-workers and instigators (Letter 202). Secondly, I am led by the burning zeal of Count Valerius against the heretics, despite his military duties, the distinguished position he held, and the necessary business of the state (Augustine, Book II on Marriage and Concupiscence, chapter 1). Thirdly, I am led by the Christian friendship of these three men and their frequent correspondence concerning the preservation of the purity of the faith (Preface to Book I on Marriage and Concupiscence). Fourthly, there is this complaint of Julian: “He also praises a powerful man because, when we were loudly demanding judges for this great matter and insisting that what had evidently been done by underhand means should be corrected rather than submitted to examination, he resisted us by the weight of his dignity and did not permit us to obtain either a time or a place for debate” (Book I of the *Imperfect Work*, chapter 9). Whether the person to whom he is writing acted as wickedly as the praise itself testifies, let him decide. Finally, there is Augustine’s response to this complaint, which does not altogether deny the fact (same work). “Far be it,” he says, “from the Christian powers of the earthly state to doubt the ancient Catholic faith and for that reason give its opponents a place and time for examination; rather, being certain and firmly grounded in it, let them impose the discipline of coercion upon such enemies of it as you are,” and so forth. What other coercion could be more aptly understood than that by which the emperor orders, under threat of deposition and exile, that bishops not permit men of a detestable sect, devising new and unheard-of things to the injury of religion, to conceal in secret discussions the sacrilege once condemned by public authority? (Honorius’s letter to Aurelius.)

To this must be added that violent protest of the raging Julian against Augustine and Alypius: “Why have you disturbed all Italy with such great factions? Why have you stirred up seditions at Rome by hiring crowds? Why have you fattened, from the resources of the poor, herds of horses throughout almost the whole of Africa, which, under Alypius’s direction, you assigned to tribunes and centurions? Why have you corrupted the powers of the world with the inheritances offered by matrons, so that the straw of public fury would blaze against us? Why have you stained the reign of a religious prince with the impiety of persecutions?” Such a mass of calumnious weapons hurled against both most holy bishops, as though they were the authors of the persecutions, is shown by these most abusive words: “If I summon the senate of philosophers, you will immediately set the bench-workers and the entire mob against us, shouting with women and all the camp-followers and tribunes to whom your Alypius recently brought eighty or more horses fattened throughout Africa” (Book I of the *Imperfect Work*, chapters 41 and 42).

Why Augustine pursued this matter through Valerius seems to me quite plausibly explained by the following. The holy man and his colleague saw how difficult it would be to eradicate—or even merely restrain—a heresy that was growing by so many devices and supported by the patronage of so many bishops, unless the powers of both authorities were joined together to achieve at least this much: that the faithful should be distinguished from the others by a definite mark of subscription, and that the wolves, driven away from the flocks of sheep, should no longer disturb the peace of the Church with internal and almost domestic conflicts.

Having established this concerning the person who prompted the emperor to write, we must next consider what success followed. In Africa, as I said earlier, the outcome appears to have matched the hopes, for scarcely any disturbance is recorded as having been stirred up afterward by the Pelagians. But the same did not happen in Italy, indeed not even in Rome itself. Coelestius, whether hiding in Rome or staying in its vicinity, did everything possible to increase his faction by daily insinuations (as appears in Constantius’s edict to Volusianus). Meanwhile Volusianus, the Urban Prefect, had perhaps been corrupted by the Pelagians’ schemes, or at least connived at their malicious plans, and did not assist the Christian zeal of Boniface. Hence it was necessary for Constantius to issue a second sanction, in somewhat more irate language; this will form the third chapter.

If someone investigates somewhat more carefully whether Aurelius promulgated the emperor’s constitution only to the two provinces or also to the other three, and, if only to the two, what special reason he had for doing so, I shall state openly what I think. Aurelius seems to have written to all the provinces, but directly to only two, Byzacena and Arzugitana, which was called Tripolitania and also Subventana. The reason was that the people of Hadrumetum, who cherished certain hidden germs of condemned errors, were in Byzacena; while the Tripolitans, who were few in number and came to the councils through a single representative, had to be instructed, and, because of their proximity to Libya and their contact with the East, possessed either an innate or an acquired disposition for innovation. Thus both groups had to be restrained above all others by the brake of fear, lest they dare anything against the common judgment of Africa and the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0399C] Besides the authors cited shortly afterward, we have consulted two ancient editions: one by Isidore Mercator, and the other—which is the best of all—containing certain short works of Prosper.]

CONSTITUTION IV. LETTER OF SAINT AURELIUS, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE, TO ALL BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE PROVINCE OF BYZACENA AND ARZUGITANA. Concerning the condemnation of the heretics Pelagius and Coelestius.

To the most beloved and longed-for brothers and fellow priests, [Note: [Col. 0399C]

Donatianus presided over the Church of Telepte and over the whole province of Byzacena, in which he appears to have held two synods in this year: one before Easter and the other around the beginning of autumn. At the former he received the delegation of the Proconsular Province, carried out by Vincentius of Culcita and Fortunatianus of Neapolis; at the latter he received Aurelius’s letter together with the constitution of Honorius. The acts of the former are preserved in the second volume of the great Collection of Councils; nothing remains of the latter. Yet I believe that an error has entered the record of the former. It could not have been held on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, for that would have fallen on the ninth day of Lent, with Easter falling on 30 March. In that case—something abnormal for those times—half the Fathers would have been absent from their churches for a large part of Lent. Nor would the error be adequately corrected if, as seems easy, one restored the numeral X and said that the synod was held on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March. For that would have been the first day of Lent, on which it would have been wrong for bishops to be absent from their churches. But if, retaining the numeral VI, one substitutes the Kalends of February for the Kalends of March, and says that the synod was held on 27 January, everything will fit very well: the Nicene canon requiring primates to convene the synod of their province before the Lent preceding Easter would have been observed; the synod would have begun on a Monday, as was customary; and the Fathers would have been present in their churches at the beginning of Lent.]

Donatianus, moreover, was a celebrated figure in the African Church. For he took part in the Council of Carthage before the conference of 411, presided with Aurelius over the African council in 418, convened the Council of Telepte in 419, presided in the same year with Aurelius over the African council, reviewed the canons of the preceding synods, and subscribed second after Aurelius.

On the occasion of Donatianus of Telepte, what slipped into the works of Binius and Christophorus Justellus must be corrected: namely, the claim that Donatianus obtained the primacy of his province not by right of age but by right of his city. This is wholly contrary to the truth, since in the synodical letter of the Council of Byzacena Muzonius is called “the elder” alone, just as are the others who presided over the remaining provinces, apart from the proconsular province, by the privilege of age.

Aurelius, bishop, to Donatianus of the first see, Januarianus, Felix, Palatinus, Primianus, Cajanus, the other Cajanus, Januarius, Victorinus, and the others established throughout the territory of the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana.

[Note: [Col. 0400D] Of the nine bishops whose names are inscribed in the letter, five are named in the Council of Telepte—Donatianus, Januarianus, Felix, Januarius, and Victor. No mention is made of the remaining four, Palatinus, Primianus, and both Cajani. I believe that both Cajani, and also Primianus, belonged to the province of Arzugitana or Tripolitana. Palatinus was Byzacenan. Januarianus was bishop of Tubulbacum, Felix of Segermes, Januarius of Cenculianum, Palatinus of Bosetum, and Victor of Culle or of the church of Baha.]

[Note: [Col. 0401B] Magd., *Primino Graiano*, etc. Uss., *Gaiano*. Bal., *Galano*, etc.]

Two points here deserve notice. First, Coelestius is named in the prior position, and then Pelagius, although the former was the disciple and the latter the teacher. Was it because Coelestius was a presbyter, whereas Pelagius was only a monk? Or because the entire weight of the affair, while Pelagius lay concealed at Jerusalem, had long since fallen upon Coelestius, after he had become the leader of the whole movement instead of its disciple, as Jerome says (*In epist. ad Ctesiphontem*)? Or because the Africans had no dealings with Pelagius himself, but very extensive dealings with Coelestius? Or because at that time the controversy concerned grace less than original sin, and the defense of that portion of the error had, as though by lot, fallen to Coelestius?

Second, Aurelius’ entire letter makes no mention of the eight canons established against the heresy at the later plenary council. This was certainly because the bishops were not to subscribe to the canons themselves, but to the *tractoria* of Pope Zosimus, which contained the whole case of both heretics, together with the judgment of the Catholic Church, condemning both of them along with their doctrines.

Concerning the condemnation of Coelestius and Pelagius, and of their [Col. 0401C] doctrines, [Note: [Col. 0401C] Magd., Bar., Uss., *dogmatibus* (“doctrines”): less appropriate to the history.] your holy affection, beloved and most desirable brothers, remembers that it participated in the plenary council. But since, for the honor of God, in whose hand is the king’s heart (Prov. 21:1), the authority of the most glorious Christian rulers, who guarded the true and Catholic faith, [Note: [Col. 0401D] Magd., *constituentium*, “who established.” The heterodox perhaps deliberately sinned in their flattery toward the rulers.] was added, which through my humility they wished to be made known to all their fellow bishops, [Note: [Col. 0401D] All the published codices read *voluit intimari*; but the rules of Latin required that the plural be substituted for the singular.]

[Note: [Col. 0401D] The noun *auctoritas* is used to signify a constitution, as is not uncommon in the Theodosian Code. The same word is used to signify a law (*leg. unic. de centur.*) and a rescript (*leg. 31 de petit. cap. 5*). Hence, in the collector of the appendix added to Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul, it is called *regularis auctoritas*, meaning a decretal judgment.] I hastened to instruct your honorable fraternity, by sending copies, [Col. 0402A] [Note: [Col. 0401D] Magd., *provinciarum supradictarum*. Bal., *provinciae supradictorum*: all are not unsuitable.] so that no evil might perhaps creep into any part of the province from the serpent-like persuasion of those persons mentioned above, [Note: [Col. 0401D] He says that the heresy was excluded from the universal Church, which he knew had been condemned by the Apostolic See. He did not doubt that the letters sent to all the bishops of the world would be subscribed by all the bishops of the Catholic party. In the same sense, common to everyone of that age, Possidius wrote that the emperor Honorius followed the judgment of the Catholic Church when he followed the sentence issued by the two supreme pontiffs—as though in that age the judgment of the Catholic Church and that of the Apostolic See in matters of faith were regarded as one and the same.] which has been excluded from the universal Church of the whole world.

For this reason, therefore, this constitution of the Christian rulers, so necessary, must not be hidden from your affection; [Note: [Col. 0402B] We have explained at length in a separate dissertation on this matter (chapter 2) the necessity of requiring subscription in the case of the Pelagians, which is the whole subject of the constitution, and have traced every reason for that necessity principally to the Pelagians’ obstinacy. Indeed, just as no heresy was more cunning or equipped with more malicious arts than the Pelagian, so none was more obstinate against all the powers of Church and state.] and the letters given to me by them [Note: [Col. 0402B–C] It is not sufficiently clear which letters are meant. Were they letters distinct from the constitution? The sequence of the argument favors this. Were they the same as the constitution itself? The form of the letters so teaches. Was it the first constitution, which the persistent evil compelled to be doubled, and which was sent with the letter—that is, the second constitution—to Aurelius? This is highly probable. Or finally, did there come with the letter to Aurelius at the same time either an imperial mandate to the vicar of Africa or an edict of the prefect of the praetorium, copies of either of which were sent to the fellow bishops? This is more likely.] must not be hidden either. When copies of them have been read together, your affection will learn how each of you ought to subscribe, whether you are among those whose subscription is already recorded in the acts of synods, or among those who were unable [Note: [Col. 0402C] We explained which plenary council—or rather which session of the plenary council—is meant, not without painstaking investigation, in the dissertation on synods. For we showed that in the third session of the council held in 418 a subscription was made to the *tractoria* received from Zosimus, and that thanks were offered to the pontiff for the heretics’ condemnation—thanks that were, as was proper, most ample.] to attend that same plenary council of all Africa, at which, in the condemnation of the heretics mentioned above, the subscription of all of you will have been complete: [Note: [Col. 0402C] Bal., *integrata*: less appropriate to the history and the writer’s meaning.]

[Note: [Col. 0402D] In the appendix to Salvian published by Baluze, the reading is *integrata*; in the other editors, *integra*. Both yield a not implausible sense, though the latter is better, since Aurelius addresses everyone (*Epistle* 86), and could require a complete subscription from all, but a renewed subscription from few. What subscription ought to be counted complete Leo the Great defines when writing on the Pelagians to Nicetas of Aquileia.]

[Note: [Col. 0402D]

He gives the reasons why subscription must be required from all bishops in this affair: namely, that some could justly be regarded as suspect either of dissimulation, because they allowed people devising new and unheard-of things in secret discussions to conceal a sacrilege publicly condemned by authority; or of negligence, as those who did not destroy the heretics’ perverse arguments by public opposition; or of hidden depravity, because by silent consent they supported the condemned errors. The sole means of avoiding the punishment which the emperor threatened to make most severe was a complete subscription—that is, one which made a pure mind evident. For the guilt is one and the same in those who, either by dissembling, gave connivance, or by failing to condemn, offered harmful favor.

At the end, observe what contributes to the commendation of the letter: it was written to the bishops by a man most learned in the canons, outstanding in holiness, most respectful of episcopal dignity, most closely associated with Augustine in affairs, and almost his sole equal. Thus knowledge, holiness, zeal for dignity, and association with Augustine grant Aurelius as much authority in this matter as can possibly exist, even as an example to other bishops. [Col. 0403B]]

There must be absolutely nothing [Col. 0403A] from which any suspicion might reasonably remain of either dissimulation, negligence, or perhaps hidden depravity. [Note: [Col. 0403B] Magd., *imbecillius sive dissimulationis*, “weaker or of dissimulation,” wholly corrupt.]

And in another hand: “I wish you well, brothers; live well, remembering me.” Given on the Kalends of August, at Carthage, in the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta.

## CONSTITUTION V

[Note: [Col. 0403B]

It is found in Baronius, Salmasius, Usserius, Labbe, and Baluze, in the places cited earlier, but, as I frankly admit, in a very corrupt form. Salmasius supplied this title: “Here begins the sacred letter of the emperor Constantius, father of Valentinian Augustus, concerning the banishment of the heretical Pelagian Coelestius.”

Photius calls it a decree and mentions it in these words: “The emperors Theodosius and Honorius wrote against the same heretics to Bishop Aurelius. Afterward Constantius, husband of Placidia and father of the younger Valentinian, also wrote a decree to Volusianus, prefect of the City, concerning the banishment of the heretic Coelestius. This Volusianus, the uncle of the holy Melania, at that time indeed held the pagan view with the pagans; but when death overtook him while he was serving as ambassador at Constantinople, he converted to the orthodox faith and was baptized by the blessed Proclus of Constantinople.”]

## LETTER OF THE EMPEROR CONSTANTIUS, FATHER OF VALENTINIAN AUGUSTUS III, TO VOLUSIANUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

[Col. 0403C] [Note: [Col. 0403C] Bal., “of the younger Valentinian.” Of the three Valentinians, the first is called the elder, the second the younger, and the last the little one, or the third.]

[Col. 0404A]

The Emperor [Note: [Col. 0403C]

Someone might perhaps ask why only the name of the emperor Constantius is inscribed, and not, as in other constitutions, the names of all three rulers together in this form: “The emperors Honorius, Theodosius, and Constantius, Augusti.” Were letters inscribed with only the name of their writer? Or is this a scribal error in the title, as in many other cases? Certainly, four laws issued at Ravenna during the period in which we have said Constantius ruled bear the names of the three emperors: the unique law *de repudiis*, on the sixth day before the Ides of March; law 29 *de petitionibus*, on the eighth day before the Ides of July; law 30 under the same title, on the same day; and the unique law *si certum petat de chirographis*, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. Gothofredus thinks that Constantius’ name was omitted in three other cases, and restored it in his notes to law 1 *de quinque praescriptionibus*, on the eighth day before the Ides of July; law 23 *de bonorum praescriptione*, on the same day; and law 45 *de episcopis*, on the day before the Ides of July.

I have no objection concerning the first two, since they are not different from laws 29 and 30 *de petitionibus*, but are many parts of one law. In the last case, however, the learned man’s memory certainly failed him. Since it was issued by Theodosius in the East, and, as it is reasonable to believe, at Constantinople, to Philippus, prefect of the praetorian prefecture of Illyricum, it would surely be remarkable if it bore the name of Constantius, whom Theodosius did not wish to regard as emperor. Since this is expressly reported by Philostorgius, how did it escape Philostorgius’ own commentator, Photius, in his special work? For he himself explains the entire matter in his commentary on these words of Philostorgius (Book XII, no. 10):

“Emperor Honorius raised Constantius, master of the soldiers, to the imperial scepter out of regard for their kinship, after Placidia had already borne him a son, Valentinian, to whom Honorius also granted the rank of nobility. Constantius’ images were then sent to the East, as was customary for those recently elevated to the imperial office. But Theodosius, refusing to accept the inauguration, did not receive them. Therefore, when Constantius was preparing for war on account of this insult, death, bringing his life and plans to an end, produced a change, after he had been emperor for six months.”

Olympiodorus agrees with Philostorgius in Photius (*Codex* 80): “Constantius became Honorius’ colleague in the imperial office, appointed by Honorius himself, though almost against his will. Placidia too was proclaimed Augusta by her brother and husband. Then news of Constantius’ election as emperor was sent to Theodosius, the son of Honorius’ brother, who ruled as Augustus in the eastern regions, but it was not received at all. As a result Constantius contracted an illness, repenting of the empire he had assumed, since he no longer possessed, as before, the freedom to go and return wherever and whenever he wished; nor was he, now emperor, permitted to devote himself to games, as had been his custom. Thus, in the seventh month of his reign—as a dream had indicated, ‘the sixth has passed, the seventh begins’—he died of pleurisy. His anger toward the East, and the expedition he was planning because he had not been admitted to partnership in the empire, died with him.”

The testimony of both historians refutes the chronicler Prosper, together with Hydatius and others, who thought that Constantius had assumed the empire as early as 419. I plainly do not know what drew Prosper and Hydatius to this opinion. As for what gave the others grounds for thinking so, I seem to understand it to some extent from the letter of Honorius calling Aurelius and the other African bishops to the Council of Spoleto. In that letter there is mention of writings by the emperor’s brother, who is undoubtedly Constantius. But he is called either simply “the emperor’s brother,” or “Augustus,” with the addition “his full brother,” because he was already the husband of Placidia, herself Augusta, and administered the entire empire. You will object that Olympiodorus says Placidia was called Augusta by her brother and husband. He does indeed say this, but the better historians teach that she was already called so by her brother when she was given to Constantius in marriage, in order to console the woman who resented the marriage with a title equal to that of her rival Pulcheria.

Moreover, from Constantius’ letter and Symmachus’ reply one may infer: first, that Constantius was not yet emperor on the eighth day before the Kalends of April in 419, when he wrote to Symmachus. This also demonstrates against Baronius the beginning and end of the reign assigned by us: no laws except those issued in 421 after January and before September bear Constantius’ name. Second, how great was his authority nevertheless before he obtained the empire, since he addressed the illustrious prefect of the City in no other terms than an emperor customarily used. Third, with what titles of honor he was in turn addressed, even by the prefect of the City, by whom he was called patron. Fourth, how vehemently he desired the City to be at peace, and how strongly he favored Boniface’s party, since by sending a chancellor as a faithful inspector he wished to learn, and to inform Honorius, what Symmachus, favoring Eulalius, had hitherto wished concealed.

But, whatever the cause we have proposed for the fact that Constantius’ name was not attached to Theodosius’ law, nor Theodosius’ name to Constantius’ decree, why was Honorius’ name omitted? Why do all the authors attribute the decree to Constantius alone, and not also—or rather, chiefly—to Honorius? By unanimous agreement both ruled in the West; their dominion was one and undivided; both resided at Ravenna. Indeed, Honorius’ majesty as the one who conferred the rank was greater than that of Constantius as the one who received it. We cannot resort, as before, either to scribal error or to the explanation we used concerning a privately written letter, since, as Photius makes clear, it was truly a decree, and all the manuscripts and historians commonly attribute it to Constantius as its proper author.

This difficulty leads me to think that Constantius issued the sanction not at Ravenna, where Honorius was staying, but in another city where Constantius happened to be. I also think that Honorius’ name was not added lest Theodosius be mentioned at the same time, since Constantius pursued him with reciprocal contempt. Yet another solution to the difficulty, which we touched on earlier, is much easier: the letter may simply have been written to Volusianus. For not every letter bore the names of all the emperors, but only some did; and perhaps by this device Constantius avoided the resentment that might arise from disregarding Theodosius. Photius nevertheless chose to call this letter a decree because it contained an order.

But from where, or where, did Constantius write? I suspect Rome, and the grounds for that suspicion are not slight. For when Constantius could scarcely remain in one place, as Olympiodorus says, and at the same time understood—as he says in the letter himself—that the peace of Rome was being tested, a peace he wished to preserve all the more zealously because he had established it through such great efforts, even when he could accomplish anything through favor alone with his imperial brother-in-law, he perhaps thought that the prefect of the City, who was acting too leniently, should be pressed personally, and that the prefect’s office should be intimidated by his presence, so that he would not continue to connive.

If matters stood as they may indeed have stood, the reason is clear why the writers attributed the sanction to Constantius alone; it is also clear where it was issued—namely, at Rome; at whose urging—namely, that of Boniface, the supreme pontiff; in which month—March; and for what purpose—namely, to forestall the disturbances that were usually greatest during the Easter festivals whenever the Church was divided into factions. In that year Easter fell on April 3, and the agitation of the Eulalian faction had not yet been so suppressed that it could safely be disregarded.]

## CONSTANTIUS TO VOLUSIANUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

Those matters, filled both with past superstition and with recent vanity, which we had long ago ordered to be corrected, are reported to be growing worse through daily representations. Since discord stirs the minds of peoples, we order that what was commanded long ago be repeated. [Note: [Col. 0405B] Since the law distinguishes past superstition from recent vanity, and the emperor writes that he had long ago ordered both to be corrected, it is uncertain what is indicated by “superstition” and what by “vanity.” It is likewise uncertain what orders of Constantius concerning the correction of both had preceded this one, since he had been taken into the imperial partnership only a few months, or even days, earlier. I interpret “past superstition” as Jewish superstition, in accordance with law 158 *de decurionibus*; “recent vanity,” following the usage of the Fathers, as the Pelagian heresy. Honorius had long ago issued orders against both: against Judaism, law 24 *de Judaeis* to Palladius, on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, both Augusti; against Pelagianism, partly the constitution to Palladius and partly the letter to Aurelius, discussed above. Constantius, however, since after his marriage to Placidia he managed everything in the western empire, arrogated all Honorius’ actions to himself and was accustomed to join his own letters to imperial decrees, as is clear from those he sent either to the bishops summoned to the Council of Spoleto or to Symmachus, prefect of the City, in the dispute over the pontificate between Boniface and Eulalius.]

Therefore, when these things have been read, let your Excellency diligently investigate all who show hostility to the piety of God, [Note: [Col. 0405C] That is, let him appoint investigators, as was customary in atrocious crimes such as treason. In other matters, the accused were not investigated by the office itself, but were brought to trial by accusers and punished. The first Theodosius the Great ordered investigators to be appointed to search out heretics, law 9 *de haereticis*.] and have them immediately expelled from the walls of the City, yet in such a way that they may not have permission to settle even within the hundredth milestone. [Note: [Col. 0405D] The words by which the emperor orders the penalty of exile against Coelestius to be proclaimed again leave me uncertain whether the preceding words concern people favoring recent vanity—that is, the Pelagian party—or rather others devoted to past superstition. I would readily think that the emperor was chiefly dealing with the latter and mentioned Coelestius only incidentally, were I not restrained by Volusianus’ authority, since he mentions no one but Coelestius in his edict.
