We must therefore suppose either that the prefect of the City did not issue an edict against everyone whom the emperor had sanctioned, or that the name “past superstition” also included the Pelagian heresy. The latter is made unlikely by the context; consequently, it must be admitted that, through some fault of Volusianus, the edict was less comprehensive than the sanction.]

We also command that Coelestius be expelled from the City more and more strictly. For once such people have been removed, it is clear that grace and concord retain their former stability.

[Note: [Col. 0406A]

These threatening words certainly show how earnestly Constantius wished peace to remain at Rome, but they also reveal the man’s imperious character, as do the letter written before his accession to Symmachus. Thus this letter and that one mutually provide each other with authority and credibility through their common style. It will not, I think, be out of place to reproduce the entire letter, both because we give a more correct text than has hitherto been published and because it shows with what zeal he sought the City’s tranquility and with what authority he already governed Rome, even before he had obtained the empire. The letter runs as follows:

“To ensure that we can learn each matter with certainty, and that the leaders of factions may not escape the notice of a faithful informer and inspector, we have sent our chancellor Vitulus, so that he may convey with swift haste to your Excellency and to the people the words and judgment of the invincible lord and prince. We advise you that whatever is contained in the sacred authorities must not be violated by any rashness, and that the commands issued must be put into effect with prompt execution, lest the clemency of the Augustus, which is now recognized to have delayed the matter, should not hesitate to correct it by rousing the force of his majesty.”

Symmachus replied humbly, prefacing his letter with this heading:

“To the ever-illustrious lord, magnificent in all things, deservedly sublime and exalted, Constantius: Symmachus.”

Then, after giving an itemized account of all the proceedings, he added this form of address:

“Ever most illustrious and most sacred lord, magnificent, deservedly sublime and exalted patron.”

Finally, he concluded:

“Since we believe that all these matters meanwhile ought to be reported to your virtues, whatever may be done in the days ahead for the tranquility of the City, which your felicity governs, I shall report item by item, in accordance with the truth and order of events, with better evidence.”]

Certainly, if anything of this kind is reported hereafter, know that the office of your Excellency must be subjected to capital sentence. [Note: [Col. 0406D] No one experienced in the laws is unaware that *officium* is used for the officials themselves. Honorius had earlier written the same thing, in almost the same words, to Symmachus, so that no one can doubt at whose urging—indeed, in whose spirit—the emperor was writing: “Let your Sublimity know that the chief secretary and the remaining office, which attends upon your actions, will not only be afflicted by the loss of the most severe fine, but will also incur capital punishment unless, having applied diligent effort, it hastens to give effect to the provisions of our clemency.”] For we do not permit our commands to be prolonged with impunity through negligence in their execution. Farewell, dearest and most beloved father.

And a subscription was added. [Note: [Col. 0407C] While subscribing, the emperor added this in his own hand, to give it greater force. Since Volusianus was not yet a Christian, as Photius’ account indicates, he might seem not to care greatly about matters pertaining to the true religion. Nevertheless, I seem to perceive with some clarity that at that time he was among the catechumens, already from 412, from the letters written both by Volusianus to Augustine and by Augustine to Volusianus concerning questions relating to the Christian faith, letters written more than once at that time (Augustine, Epistles 135 and 137).] “Let what we have commanded be fulfilled, because this is advantageous to your reputation.”

## HISTORY OF THE SANCTION AND THE EDICT

The sanction lacks in all published manuscripts the notation of the consuls, month, day, and even place. Until now it has not been possible to supply the editors’ omission from any manuscripts, and one must rely solely on conjecture.

But since Constantius ruled for only six months, as Philostorgius and Olympiodorus write; since he died during the consulship of Agricola and Eustathius, as all authors report; and since he died on September 2, according to Theophanes, the sanction must have been issued under those same consuls—that is, in the year 421—and specifically during the interval from February 8, when Constantius began his reign, to September 2, when he died. Concerning the month and place we may say something later; concerning the day, conjecture is not permissible.

I know that this reckoning of the period has not pleased many chroniclers, especially more recent ones, and even Baronius himself, whom the chronicler Prosper, together with Hydatius, led into his opinion concerning the three years of Constantius’ reign. But the authority of the historians Olympiodorus and Theophanes is stronger than that either of Prosper, who habitually confused everything through his desire for brevity, or of Hydatius, whose text is almost everywhere corrupt.

The reason for issuing the sanction was the one we began to describe earlier. After Coelestius had withdrawn from examination and received a sentence of condemnation, he either remained hidden among his supporters at Rome, as Augustine seems to indicate; or had returned to the City, as Baronius thinks; or had stayed nearby, as Volusianus’ edict suggests. Certainly, from his hiding place he encouraged both the Eulalian party and his own, continually watching as from a lookout to see whether he could somehow disturb either the peace of the faith or the public peace. He had clerics favorable to him in the Roman Church, and even bishops in the City, whose leader was Julianus. He encouraged them by his devices to extort from the emperor, through importunate petitions, a reconsideration of the judgment of Zosimus, who had died—whether in a plenary synod, to which they themselves had appealed, or through suitable judges who would bring no prejudgment to the case, which they falsely claimed had been imposed by their condemnors.

The timing favored their plan. Boniface, the successor of Zosimus, had scarcely secured the see after the disturbances of Eulalius, while the clergy were still divided into factions. The people had not yet sufficiently recovered from the recent riots. The prefect of the City, being a pagan, could easily be persuaded by eloquent men to believe that the dispute concerned a question of procedure, not doctrine. The praetorian office was susceptible to corruption. In the western court, Placidia, the sister of Honorius, could do anything: a woman who had experienced both extremes of fortune, as eager to rule as the men who wished to serve her were pliable and easily bent in whatever direction she desired. Finally, if these efforts did not succeed in the West, the East remained, where Theodosius had not yet shaken off the yoke of his sister Pulcheria. That virgin, pious indeed but fond of imperial power, could be deceived by the appearance both of the piety advertised by the Pelagians and of a complaint against the western empire, which she either envied with feminine feeling because of her rival Placidia or preferred to resist so as not to appear to serve Honorius.

Boniface detected this. Although the Pelagians’ activities were conducted so secretly that the pontiff could obtain the very letters by which Coelestius and Julianus instructed their supporters toward sedition only through the most vigilant diligence of the clergy, he nevertheless perceived the danger. He prevailed upon Constantius to order Volusianus to perform his office and execute the earlier sanctions against the disturbers of the divine faith and the public peace. He approached Constantius rather than Honorius, although both ruled together, partly because he had already found Constantius zealous on his side in the affair of Eulalius, when, though not yet Caesar, Constantius had vigorously pressed Symmachus into obedience to the good party; and partly because there was reason to hope that a decree against those who showed hostility to the piety of God would easily be obtained from an Augustus recently proclaimed, by which he might consecrate the beginning of his reign to God (Augustine, Book I *ad Bonifacium*, chapter 1).

This, then, may be regarded as a not implausible reason why the sanction was issued. Yet you will scarcely find anywhere in the whole Code a more imperious document, if I may speak so, whether this resulted from Constantius’ character, as Olympiodorus depicts it in his description of his appearance and as the letter to Symmachus reveals it, or rather from the justice of the cause, lest the peace established through Constantius’ great efforts should be shaken by restless enemies of God and of the empire.

## CONSTITUTION VI. EDICT POSTED BY VOLUSIANUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

Volusianus, prefect of the City, proclaimed:

[Note: [Col. 0407D] What “divine faith” did Volusianus mean? If he was a catechumen when he issued the edict, he meant faith in the true God; if he was still pagan in mind, he meant the faith followed by the emperors. For whatever belonged to the emperors was formerly called divine and sacred, even by Christians. Hence such expressions as “divine inspiration,” “divine commands,” “divine statutes,” and “most sacred sanctions” for imperial laws; hence “sacred largesses,” “sacred letters,” and the other expressions found everywhere.]

Until now, concealments friendly to defendants have withdrawn Coelestius, the disturber of the divine faith and of the public peace, from the courts. [Note: [Col. 0408C] Salm., “they have subjected sacred matters to judgments friendly to defendants.” These words are no better than Baronius’ reading, such as Salmasius boasts that he supplies.]

Now the laws and now the edicts will pursue him even in his absence: [Col. 0409A] first, residence in the eternal City is denied him, so that, even if he has stayed nearby, he may not escape the punishment he deserves, [Note: [Col. 0409B] Capital punishment is proposed for Coelestius if he has stayed even within the hundredth milestone. This is what Julianus complained about: that the blood of his supporters was being thirsted for and the public fury was being inflamed against them. We have cited the passage earlier. Reason required this passage to be emended against the testimony of the manuscripts; for what plausible sense do these words have: “that he may not escape the punishment he deserves”? “We also warn everyone by the provisions of this edict, in proportion to his rashness and audacity”?] in proportion to his rashness and audacity.

[Note: [Col. 0409B] Salmasius proposed: “so that, for anyone, a dreadful penalty of punishment may be imposed and it may be necessary to incur the sentence of proscription.” These words are much worse than those of Baronius.]

We also warn everyone by the provisions of this edict not to think that a hiding place ought to be provided for an evildoer; [Note: [Col. 0409B] I long hesitated to change the common reading, although it is faulty, because I could find no authority beyond reason on which to rely. The error is obvious, for what sense do these words make: “Now even the laws of the edict will pursue the absent man”? By what rule of Latin are “the laws of the edict” connected? What does *etiam* belong to? To *absentem*, as though the prefect were removing the accusation that he had allowed Coelestius to remain in the City? Why is it inserted awkwardly between two other words? Or does it belong to *persequendi*? With what tolerable sense? Or to “the edict and the laws,” which now for the first time pursue him, or which are being repeated? Yet neither the emperor nor the prefect pursued heretics in any other way than through laws and edicts; nor was a law and edict against Coelestius being proposed for the first time; nor could it fail to be disgraceful for Volusianus to repeat what should have been repeated. I therefore think it should be read: “Now the laws and now the edicts will pursue him.” This is the suitable speech of a man impatient of criticism and wishing to clear himself, as though he were saying: “Let it be said that Coelestius has hitherto been hidden among his friends, although in truth he has not been hidden; now the laws and now the edicts will pursue him, even in his absence.”] lest, when such a penalty has been imposed, whoever has thought that an accused person ought to be hidden from the divine and human laws should necessarily incur punishment and the sentence of proscription. [Note: [Col. 0409C] Here too an emendation was necessary, although the manuscript offers the uncertain reading *lucem*. “Divine laws” means the emperor’s sanction; “human laws,” the prefect’s edict.]

## CONSTITUTION VII. OF VALENTINIAN III TO AMACIUS, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIAN PREFECTURE OF GAUL, CONCERNING CERTAIN PELAGIAN BISHOPS TO BE SUMMONED BY PATROCLUS, BISHOP OF ARLES
[Col. 0409B] **[Note: [Col. 0409C]** Although the constitution customarily bears the name of both emperors, and Theodosius’s name indeed comes first, it nevertheless consists of three features that show it not to belong to Theodosius, as some have thought, but to Valentinian: the place from which it was issued, the illustrious man to whom it was addressed, and its subject or purpose. It was issued at Aquileia, a city belonging to the Western Empire; it was addressed to the prefect of the Gauls, who was subordinate to the ruler of the West; and it concerned bishops present in the Gallic regions who were to be summoned through Patroclus of Arles. From these indications it is usually possible to determine with certainty which emperor each law concerns, even when the names of several appear at its head, since one emperor never interfered in the affairs of the other, but each was content with his own boundaries. Nevertheless, laws enacted in one part of the Empire were also sent to the other, so that, whenever necessary, they might be observed everywhere and the unity of the Empire, consisting in several heads, might be displayed.]**

**The emperors Theodosius and Valentinian**

**[Note: [Col. 0409D]** Since this constitution was issued at Aquileia on 9 July, in the consulship of Theodosius for the eleventh time and Valentinian as Caesar—that is, in the year 425—it must have been issued by Valentinian when scarcely six years old, certainly not yet Augustus but only Caesar. For he was born in the year 419, on 2 or 3 July. Theodosius named him “most noble” at Constantinople while Honorius was still alive—that is, before 19 August 423, when Honorius died. He was called Caesar in the following year, on 24 October, at Thessalonica. Finally, he was proclaimed Augustus at Rome [Col. 0410B] by Helion, master of the offices, on 23 October, when he had entered his seventh year (Olympiodorus, in Photius, cod. 80). It therefore follows plainly that the sanction issued in Valentinian’s name must be attributed to his mother, the Augusta Placidia.

At this point I cannot remain silent about something I have often wondered at: that at that time the helm of the entire Roman world was held by two women, Pulcheria, Theodosius’s sister, and Placidia, Valentinian’s mother; and that East and West served female rule—and perhaps female designs—when formerly they had scarcely been willing to obey the great Constantines and Theodosii.]**

**CAESAR**

**[Note: [Col. 0410B]** So Sirmondus reads it, but Chifletius opposed him in his notes on Ferrandus. Relying on the authority of the Dijon manuscript, Chifletius asserted that *Almachio* should be restored in place of *Amacio*. Sirmondus argued in reply, in manuscript notes on Chifletius’s passage, that *Almachius* was a foreign word, whereas *Amacius* was written for *Amachius* or *Amachus*, just as *Pammachius* is written for *Pammachus*. Chifletius, however, forestalled this objection by denying that *Almachius* seemed so foreign a word that it could not be mentioned in the Roman Martyrology: there *Almachius* is the name of a martyr who suffered at Rome under Honorius on the Kalends of January, and of the prefect Almachius, under whom, in the time of Alexander, Cecilia suffered martyrdom on the tenth day before the Kalends of December. Baronius, however, teaches in his notes on the Martyrology that, if Theodoret is to be trusted (*Hist.* V.26), the martyr ought to be called not Almachius but Telemachus; and since Cecilia’s acts abound in errors, they could likewise have gone wrong in this name. Be that as it may, I would not presume to settle a dispute between such great men over a single name.

Gothofredus presented the first part of the law under the title “On Bishops” and the last under the title “On Heretics,” as previously, stating that it had been addressed to Bassus, *comes R. P.*; but he simultaneously warned that there was an error in the words *comiti R. P.* For what do these laws contain that concerns the count of private affairs? He therefore judged that *Basso PP.* should be restored. Four other laws are recorded as having been addressed to him at Ravenna in the same year: the first, concerning lessees and the household of the Augusta, on the day before the Nones of March; the last, concerning freedmen, on the third day before the Kalends of April; the seventh, concerning apostates, on the seventh day before the Ides of April; and the twenty-eighth, concerning Jews, on the sixth day before the Ides of April.

If the law published by Sirmondus is a combination of three laws issued by Caesar Valentinian at Aquileia, the first may be said to have been addressed to Bassus, the prefect of the praetorium, on the eighth day before the Ides of October; the third to the same man on the eighth day before the Ides of August; and the middle one to Amacius, prefect of the Gauls, on the seventh day before the Ides of July. In this way it may perhaps be possible to reconcile the conflicting opinions.]**

**To Amacius, the illustrious prefect of the Gauls.**

We restore, with willing devotion, all the privileges of the Churches and of all the clergy which the tyrant of our age had begrudged them: namely, whatever was established by deified emperors, and whatever individual bishops obtained, shall remain secured by perpetual eternity, nor shall any presumptuous person dare to tamper with it. In this matter we confess that we have rendered an even greater service to ourselves.

We also reserve for episcopal jurisdiction those clerics whom the ill-fated usurper had decreed should indiscriminately be brought before secular judges, while preserving the ancient provisions enacted concerning them. For it is not right that ministers of the divine office should be subjected to the discretion of temporal powers.

Therefore, your illustrious authority shall cause what we have ordered—orders destined to endure for all time—to be made known throughout the provinces and observed, even under penalty of sacrilege. You shall specifically include in your illustrious commands that, in every matter concerning ecclesiastical privileges, the enactments of the ancient emperors are to be preserved.

We command that various bishops who follow the wicked error of the Pelagian and Coelestian [Col. 0411A] doctrine be summoned through Patroclus, the bishop of the most holy law.

**[Note: [Col. 0411C]** By the bishop of Arles he means the man who, in the year 412, with the assistance of Constantius—then master of the soldiers and later emperor—was elevated to the see of Eros. The authors disagree as to whether Eros was expelled lawfully or unlawfully; we have followed the supreme pontiff Zosimus, who writes that he was condemned lawfully. Patroclus held the episcopate for nearly fourteen years: elevated by Zosimus and deposed by Boniface, until, by order of Felix, master of the soldiers, he left the see after being killed by a barbarian tribune, in the year 426.]**

We are confident that they can be corrected. But if, within twenty days from the time of the summons—the period during which we grant them opportunity for deliberation—they do not correct their errors and restore themselves to the Catholic faith, they are to be expelled from the Gallic regions and a more faithful priesthood is to be appointed in their place, so that the stain of the present error may be wiped from the minds of the peoples and the good of a future, more righteous discipline may be established.

**[Note: [Col. 0411C]** Someone may wonder—and, in my judgment, perhaps not without reason—whether the words “the seven provinces” refer only to those provinces in which a great council was convened each year at Arles at the summons of the prefect of the Gauls; or whether they also refer to all the others subject to the prefecture, namely the Gauls, Britain, and Spain (see Honorius’s constitution to Agricola, prefect of the Gauls, in the year 418). I think that all are meant, but especially the seven provinces. For when the emperors write to the prefect of the Gauls, “the Gallic regions” are understood with as broad a meaning as the suburban regions are when decrees are sent to the urban prefect. At that time the suburban regions were understood to extend as far as the authority of the urban prefect reached. Moreover, just as the evil probably did not prevail throughout the entire diocese of the Gauls but chiefly around Arles, so the remedy ought especially to concern that region.

I cannot, however, pass over in silence what often came to mind when I considered this history more attentively: namely, that Valentinian’s decree may also, or even chiefly, have concerned Britain, which Agricola, son of the Pelagian bishop Severianus, was disturbing by spreading the heresy, and from whose faith in the grace of Christ he had drawn several bishops into the wicked doctrine of Pelagian error.

For why should one not believe, I said to myself, that since at that time Britain formed part of the Gallic regions, as the imperial administrative register shows, and was therefore governed by the authority of the prefect of the Gauls, Caesar wrote to the prefect of the Gauls concerning the suppression of the British bishops? [Col. 0412D] Why should Patroclus not have been ordered, by the ancient right of the see of Arles, to exercise ecclesiastical judgment over them? Why should that great Gallic council not have been convened on this occasion, from which Germanus and Lupus were sent to Britain—Patroclus having meanwhile been killed and Honoratus having obtained his see and office? Why, finally, should that summons mentioned by Caesar have been anything other than a proposal to the bishops that they subscribe to the eight African canons, delivered by legates sent from the synod? For the anathemas of the Alexandrian synod were delivered to Nestorius by four episcopal legates, together with a letter from Saint Coelestine, under threat of deposition unless, within ten days, he subscribed to the anathemas and assented to the Catholic Church.]**

Certainly, religious peoples ought not to be corrupted by any superstitions (Theodosian Code, “On Heretics,” law 64). We therefore command that Manichaeans and all heretics or schismatics, astrologers, and every sect hostile to Catholics be banished from the very sight of the various cities, [Col. 0411B] so that they may not pollute them even by the contagion of their presence. We also deny Jews and pagans the license to conduct lawsuits or to serve in the army; we do not wish Christians to be subject to them, lest, through the opportunity of dominion, they alter the religion we venerate. We therefore order that all persons belonging to this disastrous error be excluded, unless timely correction comes to their aid. Issued on the seventh day before the Ides of July at Aquileia, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the eleventh time and Valentinian Caesar.

## HISTORY OF THE CONSTITUTION

No one among the ancients, so far as I know, left in writing what occasion gave rise to the enactment of this constitution. Indeed, no one even mentions it, at least in the part concerning the Pelagians. It was first published by P. Sirmondus from a manuscript of the Church of Lyons.

[Col. 0411C] I said “in the part concerning the Pelagians,” for it comprises three parts. The first and last had long before been included in the Theodosian Code: the former as law 47, “On Bishops,” and the latter as law 68, “On Heretics.”

A plausible conjecture may be made concerning the middle part. The bishops in question had their sees in Gaul, or at least within the jurisdiction of the prefect of the Gauls; for the emperor orders them to be expelled from the Gallic regions [Col. 0412A] and a more faithful priesthood to be appointed in their place. It is also credible that they held episcopal office in the seven provinces over which Patroclus exercised primacy, since Valentinian orders them to be summoned through Patroclus, bishop of the most holy law. The reason they were to be summoned and compelled to correct their errors and restore themselves to the Catholic faith was that they followed the wicked error of the Coelestian and Pelagian doctrine.

A few years earlier, the monk Leporius had followed that same doctrine in those provinces, presuming upon the purity of life which he believed he had obtained solely by his own will and effort, not through God’s assistance, as Gennadius relates (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 59). Nor was he the only one who, following the teaching—or rather the depravity—of Pelagius, fell into absurd errors. Cassian says that there was an advocate of the heresy in Gaul, either among the first or among the most prominent (*On the Incarnation*, books I.3–4).

Those who agreed with him said that the solitary man Jesus Christ had lived without any contagion of sin. They proceeded so far as to assert that human beings, if they wished, could be without sin. For they considered it a consequence that, if the solitary man Jesus Christ had been without sin, all human beings could likewise be without God’s assistance, whatever that solitary man could have been without the fellowship of God; as though they made no distinction between any human being and our Lord Jesus Christ, since the same human being could by his own exertion and industry merit what Christ had merited by effort and labor, and so forth.

Cassian admonished Leporius—or rather, Proculus of Marseilles ordered him—to condemn his error. But he was willing neither to listen to the one who admonished him nor to obey the one who commanded him. Consequently, expelled from the Church, he fled to Africa, where Augustine corrected him. He then sent a libellus of correction to the Gallic bishops, approved by the subscriptions and letters of the African Fathers.

After the libellus was received, it is not implausible that disturbances of mind arose in Gaul, and that from them came the need to restrain the tumultuous by imperial authority. Indeed, it is not unreasonable to think that Augustine both wrote to the Gauls and acted through his associates at court, so that, once the bishops had been compelled to subscribe to the condemnation of the heretics, everything in Gaul might be settled as it had been in Africa. In this way, between regions linked by such close agreement of opinion, where errors were transported along with merchandise, there might be communion not only of faith but also of the remedy against error.

This conjecture would perhaps be strengthened if that great Gallic council, from which Germanus and Lupus were sent to Britain to eradicate the Pelagian heresy, should emerge from its darkness into the desired light. For those who claim to have heard something about it say that there was in it both a memorandum given to the legates and mention of the eight canons which the common people call “Milevitan,” as though they were a formula to be subscribed by those who wished to appear to have corrected their errors and restored themselves to the Catholic faith.

Gothofredus must now be briefly challenged. In his *paratitlum* on heretics, he says that it seemed remarkable to him that no heresy anywhere in Gaul is mentioned throughout the immense six-volume Theodosian Code. He adds that, according to Jerome, Gaul had raised no monsters down to that time. But unless he intended to reject Sirmondus’s appendix, he could, without compromising Jerome’s testimony, have found in the Code—which extends down to the year [Col. 0413B] 438—a record of heretics in Gaul in the year 425.

As for why he rejected Sirmondus’s appendix, although he did not attempt to deny the authority of the Lyons and Aniciensis manuscripts—and even if he had attempted to do so, he could not have succeeded, since another manuscript from Dijon adds its authority to the others—I see no other cause than the character and prejudice of his professed party, which impatiently tolerates whatever contributes to the immunity of ecclesiastical persons. For this reason, in his discussion of law 47, “On Bishops,” he poured forth against Valentinian, the Augusta his mother, and others who did not deserve it statements which, although one might expect them from a heterodox writer, are nevertheless unworthy of an interpreter of the law—that is, of equity and goodness.

So far as I know, no edict of Amacius, the prefect, was posted at Arles, unless it is perhaps hidden in the archive of the Church of Arles. From that archive certain documents were extracted and sent to Cardinal Baronius: Zosimus’s letters concerning the privileges of the Church of Arles, and so forth. These were inserted into the *Annals*, to great benefit of chronology.

## THE CONSTITUTIONS OF THEODOSIUS THE YOUNGER AGAINST THE PELAGIANS

Thus far we have discussed the constitutions enacted in the Pelagian affair by the emperors of the West—Honorius, Constantius, and Valentinian. Next we must consider two sanctions issued by Theodosius, emperor of the East; but nothing of them survives except a memory, and that a rather obscure one.

Saint Coelestine mentions the first in writing to Nestorius, in these words (*First Council of Ephesus*, chapter 18):

“For some days of our life, after the wicked and repeatedly condemned doctrine of Pelagius and Coelestius, the Catholic faith enjoyed peace, when East and West struck them and the followers of their disputation with the weapon of united judgment. Finally, Atticus, of holy memory, teacher of the Catholic faith and truly the successor even in this matter of the blessed John, pursued them on behalf of the common ruler, so that they were not even granted the opportunity to stand there. For the bishops could not have been expelled from the royal city unless imperial authority had added force to ecclesiastical statutes and synods.”

I have shown in my dissertation on synods that a synod was held by Atticus at that time.

The second is mentioned somewhat more explicitly by Mercator (*On the Title of the Memorandum*). After writing that he had presented his *Memorandum* concerning the name of Coelestius not only to the Church of Constantinople but also to many most religious men and to the emperor Theodosius himself, he says:

“Through this Memorandum, once the most disastrous error had been learned, by imperial command both Julian, its defender and follower, together with his other associates and partners, and later Coelestius himself were driven from the city of Constantinople.”

The history of both must be sought partly in the dissertation on synods and partly in the notes on the title of Marianus’s *Memorandum*. The former was issued after the second synod convened by Atticus in the royal city concerning this matter; the latter occasioned Mercator’s *Memorandum*.

It is certain that both were issued at Constantinople, because the chronology of the laws shows that Theodosius was at Constantinople both when the synod was assembled by Atticus and when Mercator’s *Memorandum* was presented—that is, in the years 424, 425, or 429. In the consulship of Victor, which marks the year 424, the following laws were issued at Constantinople: law 3 of the Code, “On Woolen Garments”; law 7, “On an Invalid Will”; law 4, “On Public Spectacles”; law 1 of the Code, “On the Office of the Quaestor”; law 5, “On the Collation of Gifts”; law 15, “On Mines”; and law 33, “On Grain and Taxes.” In the consulship of Dionysius and Florentius, that is, in the year 429, the final law of the Code, “On Petitions,” and the final law, “On Jews,” were issued there.

We can infer to whom each was sent. Since Theodosius the Younger was accustomed to direct all his decrees concerning the defense of religion and the restraint of its enemies to no one other than the prefect of the praetorium—as is clear from law 18, “On Jews”; laws 48 and 49, “On Heretics”; law 21, “On Jews”; laws 6 and 7, “That Holy Baptism Not Be Repeated”; the final law, “On Incestuous Marriages”; law 22, “On Jews”; law 57, “On Heretics”; law 42, “On Bishops”; law 4, “That Christians Not Be Enslaved”; law 25, “On Jews”; law 59, “On Heretics”; law 26, “On Jews”; law 5, “That Christians Not Be Enslaved”; law 22, “On Pagans”; law 27, “On Jews”; laws 23 and 24, “On Pagans”; law 60, “On Heretics”; the final law, “On Pagans”; the single law, “No One May Sign and Save”; law 65, “On Heretics”; laws 4, 5, and 6, “On Those Who Flee to the Church”; the single law, “On the Property of Clerics and Monks”; and law 21, “On Bishops”—and since Asclepiodotus held the prefecture of the East in the year 424 and Florentius in the year 429, as the laws sent to them demonstrate, it is reasonable to believe that the constitutions in question were written to those same men.

I said that all decrees concerning religious matters were directed in this way, although I am not unaware that the final law “On Jews” is addressed to John, count of the sacred largesses, and the final law “On Heretics” to Leontius, urban prefect, as it is commonly read in the Theodosian Code. But since the former concerns only the collection of the ceremonial gold tax and not any religious matter; [Col. 0414C] and since an obvious error has crept into the latter law in the common editions of the Code—for in that year Leontius was unquestionably serving as prefect of the praetorium—neither law can prejudice the conclusion stated above.

From this observation I further conclude that at that time the civil forum, like the ecclesiastical one, also had certain major religious cases which were referred to the highest judgment or tribunal after the emperor, since the prefect of the praetorium possessed the highest authority after the emperor.

The month and day are completely unknown, except that the later constitution seems to belong to the end of the year 429 and the earlier to the beginning of the year 425. The former was issued after the *Memorandum* had been presented to the emperor, that is, toward the end of 429; the latter preceded by several months the death of Atticus, which occurred on 10 October 425, as established in the dissertation on synods (see the notes on the title *Memorandum*).

No part of either constitution was transferred to the Justinianic Code, partly because Tribonian regarded both as temporary, and partly because scarcely any remnants of the Coelestian error survived in the East in Justinian’s time. Whatever remained was despised among harmful heresies, both because of the small number of its adherents and, above all, because of the opinion held by many Easterners.

I say “the opinion of many Easterners,” for the Catholic faith concerning original sin had not taken deep root in the minds of all. Indeed, there were those who thought that such an assertion contained something of Origen’s poison, because through ignorance they did not know how to distinguish sufficiently between the transmission of sin and the commission of sin. They believed that no one could be born guilty unless his soul had first sinned by its own will before it fell into the body.

Certainly, when Photius criticizes Theodore of Mopsuestia’s responses to the arguments of those defending original sin, he does not depart far from Theodore’s own opinion. For elsewhere he says that there are other ways of dissolving the argument drawn from the baptism of infants in support of original sin than those used by Theodore. He speaks as follows:

“But perhaps even he was led to this without intending it, and only so that he might dissolve the difficult questions of those who inquire in this way: Why do children participate in the most holy mysteries? Why are they judged worthy of baptism, unless they too abound in sins, with sin already implanted in nature itself? For these rites are conferred for the remission of sins. Yet it was necessary to dissolve that doubt in another way, since it has many other means of resolution, and, after considering the absurd consequences that follow from the remission of sins itself, not to fabricate anything so monstrous,” and so forth.

## DISSERTATION IV. ON THE SUBSCRIPTIONS REQUIRED IN THE PELAGIAN AFFAIR

In the words of Marius Mercator:

“Julian and the other accomplices, refusing to subscribe, were deposed and deprived of office, not only by imperial laws but also by priestly statutes, and were driven from all Italy.” (*Memorandum*, chapter 3.)

[Col. 0415]

[Col. 0415A] Thus far we have seen the two supreme powers, ecclesiastical and imperial, united in the destruction of a single error: the former through synods, the latter through sanctions that followed the Church’s judgment. We must next show what that common effort was, and what common method was employed, in order effectively to carry out what had wisely been decided in the Church and at court.

There was no other method, if we believe Mercator, supported by Augustine, Possidius, and Prosper, than that a subscription be required from everyone to the decrees by which the Church condemned Pelagius, Coelestius, and the other defenders of the same impiety. This fourth dissertation will concern the subscription exacted in the Pelagian affair. It is intended to elucidate not only the words of Mercator that I have cited from the *Memorandum*, but also other passages encountered here and there in the book of *Annotations*.

### CHAPTER ONE. The reason and purpose of the dissertation on subscriptions required in the Pelagian affair

No heresy was ever, as has already been said more than once, more stubborn than the Pelagian, nor did any resist the decrees of the Church and the sanctions of the emperors more obstinately and artfully. It might be compared to diseases that grow worse through remedies, or to grasses which, when cut down, sprout again and, when burned, are sown from their own ashes.

Coelestius had been brought before the episcopal judgment of Aurelius of Carthage and deprived of communion there until he condemned his errors. But, as a heretic thoroughly trained in the arts of the courtroom, he evaded the bishop’s sentence by obtaining an appeal to the Apostolic See, which he had no intention of pursuing. Meanwhile he spread the heresy more widely, fleeing himself to Asia but, through his associates left behind at Carthage, almost overturning Africa, despite Augustine’s opposition.

Pelagius was summoned to Diospolis before a council of bishops. He came determined to deceive the Fathers by every trick available to him. He therefore condemned everything that was brought against him, fearing otherwise to be condemned (Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*). After subjecting his own person to anathema in ambiguous words, he later taught more securely and more perniciously under the falsely assumed appearance of a Catholic, had not Theodotus in the East, after convening a synod, and Augustine in the West, by sending books, opposed him.

Both had been condemned by the Apostolic See, over which Innocent I presided, after two African councils had reported the matter (Augustine, *Sermon 2 on the Words of the Apostle*, and elsewhere). Rescripts had come from Rome to Africa, and the matter would have been finished if it had been handled lawfully. The error, however, was not finished, only suppressed—and suppressed so lightly that, after remaining hidden for a while as though to regain its strength, it was accepted by far more people while creeping secretly, in proportion as its authors more boldly swore that they were being oppressed solely by the hatred and power of their enemies.

After the death of Innocent, both men once again, by means of mendacious pamphlets, had nearly persuaded Zosimus to reopen their case—or rather, to declare them Catholics while transferring the charge to their opponents. The African Fathers again referred the whole matter to the supreme pontiff; [Col. 0416B] and, once informed, he proscribed the men and their errors throughout the world (Augustine, book II *To Boniface*, and elsewhere).

The heresy might then have seemed utterly prostrate, but it nevertheless raised its head higher than before, so that what had until then muttered through two men, certainly obscure ones, dared to speak through the mouths of eighteen bishops in Italy. They began more freely to call all Catholics by the unspeakable name “Manichaeans” and to accuse the defenders of the faith of guilt in allowing moral license.

A remedy proportionate to so great an evil was sought. None could be found by Augustine and the others burning with zeal for God except that a subscription should be required from everyone—not only bishops and priests, but also minor clerics and even laypeople whose faith had fallen under suspicion—so that they might openly and plainly subscribe to the condemnation made by the Church of the heresy and of its authors, who had spread it among the people. It seemed possible in this way to counter the malicious arts of men who sometimes concealed their doctrines in ambiguous words and sometimes boasted that the authors of those doctrines had been condemned only through subreption, that is, by deceitful concealment (Nestorius, letter 2 to Saint Coelestine).

Then, I believe, it first happened that, through the combined authority of the Church and the emperors, all the faithful of whatever rank were commanded to subscribe to the definition of the Apostolic See as though it were the common doctrine of the Church, the sure rule of faith, and, as the reputed Prosper says (*Appendix to Coelestine’s Letter to the Gallic Bishops*), to the **REGULAR AUTHORITY**. In this way they were to prove their faith so that the legitimate children of the Church could be distinguished from the spurious who wished to hide in the crowd—that is, the children of light from the children of darkness.

This entire affair was carried out in the fifth century, an age in which no period was more learned or more observant of ecclesiastical discipline. I therefore thought it deserved more careful investigation—not only to clarify the words of Mercator that I cited, but also, by bringing to light what was then done by men who were at once among the holiest ever to live and among the most skilled in ecclesiastical matters, to silence those who speak unjustly and accuse our own age of the very conduct in which it follows the laws and examples of its ancestors.

In my judgment, the investigation will be appropriately organized if the second chapter explains what is meant here by “subscription,” what its purposes and usefulness are, and so forth; the third, why this remedy was so necessary against the Pelagian heresy; the fourth, whose condemnation was commanded to be subscribed—whether that of the doctrines alone or also that of their authors; the fifth, whether those men whose condemnation was subscribed admitted that they held the views brought against them; the sixth, what the formula of faith to be subscribed was and by whom it was prescribed; the seventh, by what authority the law requiring subscription was enacted—whether solely by priestly authority or also by imperial authority; the eighth, to whom subscription was required—whether only to bishops or also to others among the clergy, and even to the people—and what penalty was established for those who refused to subscribe; the ninth, what excuses the refusers offered and how their exception was received; the tenth, what other devices they used to evade the matter and what response the Fathers made to their reasons for evasion; and the eleventh, how the obstinate were subsequently treated and with what indulgence those who came to their senses were received by the Church.

After completing the investigation, I thought I should report not what I had established by argument from the statements of the Fathers, but what the Fathers themselves said in their own words. In this way, it seemed to me, the judgment of readers would be more truthful and freer, the less prejudice had been introduced.

That method, however, compelled me not only often to cite longer testimonies but also sometimes to repeat the same material in different chapters. Either practice may seem to an overly fastidious person idle and superfluous. Yet without this length the authors’ meaning would have been entirely hidden; and the nature both of the matters treated and of the testimonies is such that the former could not have been combined without confusion, nor the latter divided without loss of clarity.

### CHAPTER TWO. What is meant by “subscription,” and its purposes, qualities, and advantages

By “subscription” is understood a written guarantee or, as Saint Leo says, a written satisfaction, by which someone, according to a prescribed formula, testifies in an open and sincere profession that he obediently receives and faithfully embraces the judgment of the Church concerning some matter, as befits a son who loves unity.

From this definition one can gather the purpose of requiring subscription. The Apostle seems to have indicated it when writing to the Corinthians, who were somewhat too fond of disputes: namely, that all the children of one mother should say the same thing, that there be no schisms in the house of peace, and that each be perfect in the same understanding and in the same judgment (1 Cor. 1:11).

Since nothing is more desirable to the Church than domestic peace; since that peace is nothing other than agreement of wills; and since wills ordinarily do not agree when minds disagree, the Church strives above all that all her children should think alike and that the God of peace and love should dwell among them (ibid.). Therefore, whenever the enemy of Christ sows causes of disagreement like weeds, she immediately calls all her children to agree with her and, consequently, with one another. She compels those who refuse to approve by public testimony either their faith or their obedience, so that they may be convicted by their own written subscription if they later wish to contradict it; or, if they refuse to provide a written subscription, so that they may be distinguished from the faithful and avoided as disturbers of divine faith and public peace.

One can also gather what the form of subscription ought to be: namely, one that each person does not invent according to his own judgment but that the Church prescribes. For it belongs to the Church to prescribe the form by which faith is proved, since it is her concern that faith be proved as it ought to be. Moreover, since subscription is nothing other than a means of rendering to a superior some satisfaction, obedience, submission, or agreement, it is absurd for an inferior to satisfy or obey a superior according to his own discretion. It is likewise absurd for a son to make a law for himself concerning submission to his mother and agreement with her.

The subject matter of subscription is, in itself, the definition of doctrines, although it is sometimes any other judgment of the judging Church. For although faith is the quasi-essential bond—οὐσιῶδες, “essential”—by which the children of the Church are joined into one body, the peace of that body, which is held together by fraternal charity, is easily disturbed whenever either not all agree with the head in one judgment or they do not agree among themselves. For just as disputes never arise without disturbances of mind, so schisms always arise from great disturbances of mind.

From these considerations it is clear who can be compelled by the Church’s command to subscribe: all, namely, who are counted as children of this mother, whenever their disagreement produces any kind of scandal. I say all, whatever their rank or condition. But judging whether a sufficient cause for using this command has arisen, whether from the outcome or from fear of scandal, belongs solely to the Church. In accordance with the instruction she received from the Holy Spirit, she has used this power granted to her by God differently at different times, sometimes binding more and sometimes fewer ranks of the faithful to subscribe.

It is also clear that those whose judgment is at issue can be compelled to subscribe to a prescribed formula not only by decrees of the Church but also by imperial edicts. For since few are guided by love of justice and more are moved by fear of punishment, and since, among the two kinds of punishment, spiritual punishments frighten the obstinate less than bodily ones, it is not enough to employ the Church’s definitions, which suffice to guide the just; punishments of both kinds must also be threatened, so that they may be adequate to deter the wicked.

Subscription requires three qualities if it is to achieve its intended purpose: clarity, sincerity, and completeness. Hence Saint Leo, writing to Nicetas concerning the Pelagians (letter 86), says:

“Let them condemn, in open professions, the authors of their proud error; let them detest whatever the universal Church has abhorred in their doctrine; and let them declare, in full and open statements subscribed with their own hand, that they embrace and approve in every respect all the synodal decrees which the authority of the Apostolic See has confirmed for the destruction of this heresy. Let nothing obscure, nothing ambiguous, be found in their words,” and so forth.

Finally, experience has taught that this remedy was not merely useful and appropriate but at times necessary—especially when a certain stubborn heresy had to be eradicated, one that advanced more by fraudulently insinuating itself than by open audacity.

So it usually insinuates itself in this way: when men secretly teach impious doctrines, outwardly displaying a pious appearance but, with words contrived to deceive, saying one thing openly and another in secret; when Catholics are misrepresented among the uneducated as heretics, so that the truth suffers from personal prejudice; when defenders of error do not openly depart from the Church but strive to remain hidden among the faithful, in order to do greater harm; when such men, if expelled from the Church, falsely pretend repentance, according to circumstances and places, and by treacherous ambiguities of speech attempt to impose upon the very pastors themselves, and so forth.

Then it is necessary both to bring the impious doctrines and their authors into the open, so that they may be recognized; to vindicate the defenders of Catholic truth from calumny, so that they may fight more effectively for the faith; to drive the wolves from the fold, lest they destroy the sheep; and to hold liars to their own handwriting, so that they may either be corrected, once the hope of lying has been removed, or be convicted by their own testimony if they return to error.

The Church’s constant practice proves that what we have described can scarcely, or not even scarcely, be accomplished unless such men—as Saint Leo says in the letter just cited—“declare, in full, open, and personally signed statements, that they embrace and approve in every respect all the decrees which the authority of the Apostolic See has confirmed for the cutting out of this heresy.”

## CHAPTER III. How great was the necessity of requiring subscriptions in the case of the Pelagians

The necessity of employing the remedy of subscriptions for uprooting heresies arose at times from the excessive obstinacy of heretics. Through this obstinacy it happened that the evil not only failed to yield to ordinary remedies but actually became greater. The Pelagian heresy, however, was more obstinate than the others, to such an extent that it scarcely ever yielded, even when the forces of both authorities were joined together.

The Fathers thought that the causes of such obstinacy had to be sought nowhere else than in the manner in which the heresy either grew or defended itself against the Church’s condemnations. It grew, I say, partly through what were virtually its own means of increase, and partly through damage done to the Catholic cause: for it both employed devices by which it might itself become stronger and fabricated an unjust calumny against Catholic teachers, by which it burdened the truth with another’s ill repute. It protected itself against the Church’s condemnation in two ways—maliciously, indeed, but effectively. For the Pelagians never voluntarily made a secession; rather, they tried to remain hidden while mingling with the faithful. But if they were ever discovered and expelled from the house of peace as disturbers, then, pretending repentance, they returned by stealth to communion. Thus this great obstinacy seems rightly to have had altogether four causes: namely, their methods of spreading themselves; their calumniation of Catholics; their retention, at least outwardly, of communion; and their simulation of repentance.

It is worthwhile to explain and establish these causes one by one, using the very words of the Fathers of the fifth century. No others, therefore, seem necessary to introduce, except perhaps one or two, and then only incidentally, provided that they report something about men of the fifth century. Those who are cited will be allowed to give testimony only in their own words, so that this entire dissertation may be more a question of fact than a contentious dispute over arguments.

### § I. The first cause of the great obstinacy of the Pelagian heresy: its method of spreading and extending itself

No heresy ever strikes deeper roots, clings more obstinately to minds, or spreads more widely among peoples than when it is secretly taught: through ambiguous words; by men outwardly pious; in eloquent speeches; through letters sent into the provinces to reliable people; and when it is disseminated under the name of several bishops, through the favor of powerful persons, the devices of women—especially noblewomen—and generous almsgiving.

For at that point it derives from its secret teaching the ability to remain hidden while secretly spreading; from the piety and reputation of its authors, the ability to deceive uneducated minds more powerfully; from the elegance of its language and the novelty of its doctrine, the ability to please more alluringly; from the names of bishops and the favor of powerful persons, the ability to inspire religious people with reverence and timid people with fear; from the devices of women, the ability to creep in through flattery; and from generous almsgiving, the ability almost to enslave the minds of its recipients by a nearly justifiable servitude. Nature has created nothing more powerful than these devices for deceiving and enticing human beings, nor anything more tenacious for binding and retaining them beneath a kind of spontaneous yoke of inescapable servitude. It should therefore not seem surprising that the Pelagian heresy was so stubbornly obstinate, since it employed every one of these nine methods, all the more disastrously for the Church’s cause the more effectively they served its own.

### FIRST, IT WAS TAUGHT SECRETLY

Jerome (Preface to Book IV on Jeremiah):

“The heresy began to revive and to hiss not only in the regions of the West but also in those of the East, and to stain many people in certain islands, especially Sicily and Rhodes, and to grow from day to day, while they teach secretly and deny publicly,” and so forth.

Marius Mercator (Preface to the Book of Notes):

“The question raised against the Catholic faith among certain Syrians, and especially in Cilicia, by Theodore, formerly bishop of the city of Mopsuestia, has long since been set in motion and is now taught among a very few of them with extreme secrecy; nor is it brought forward openly,” and so forth.

Augustine (Letter 194, to Sixtus):

“They penetrate houses more secretly, and what they fear to shout openly they do not cease to sow in secret.”

And elsewhere (Letter 89, to Hilary):

“There were among us people who, wherever they could, scattered these new seeds of their error . . . but now they mutter secretly . . . . They are more numerous than we can hope; and where they are not refuted, they seduce others also into their sect, and so multiply that I do not know where they will break out.”

To this certainly belong the words of Vincent of Lérins (in the *Commonitorium*):

“What did they promise and then abandon, except some new and unknown doctrine? For you may hear some of them saying: ‘Come, you foolish and wretched people, who are commonly called Catholics, and learn the true faith, which no one except us understands, which lay hidden for many centuries but has recently been revealed and displayed. But learn it stealthily and secretly, for it will delight you.’ And likewise: ‘Once you have learned it, teach it secretly, lest the world hear and lest the Church know; for only a few have been granted the capacity to grasp the secret of so great a mystery,’” and so forth.

### THROUGH AMBIGUOUS WORDS

That is, words capable of being changed according to time and place into various meanings and turned in either direction.

Jerome (Letter to Ctesiphon concerning the Pelagians):

“You know what you teach your disciples inwardly, saying one thing with your mouth and concealing another in your conscience; to us, who are outsiders and uneducated, you speak through parables, but to your own you confess mysteries. You boast that you do this according to Scripture, because it is said: ‘Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables’ (Matthew 13:34); and to the disciples in the house he says: ‘To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given’ (ibid. 13:11).”

And afterward:

“The Eunomians, Arians, and Macedonians, different in name but united in impiety, cause us no trouble; for they speak what they think. This is the only heresy that is ashamed to speak publicly what it does not fear to teach secretly. The fury of the disciples reveals the silence of their teachers,” and so forth.

“Therefore your heresy grew, and you deceived many, especially those who cling to women and know that they cannot sin, because you are always teaching and always denying.”

Augustine (*Against Julian*, Book I, chapter 5):

“What benefit is it to you that, by some art of perplexity I cannot identify, you fasten together certain handles and hooks, so that simple things may not become evident and shine in clear light? Pelagius thinks that by these mists he deceived the judgment at Diospolis, and you wholeheartedly assent to this wickedness, laughing that so many bishops were mocked by him.”

Saint Innocent (Decretal Letter to the Fathers of the Council of Carthage):

“You rightly judge that one decision should be made for the benefit of all, so that the Church, established by its own rules and strengthened by a just decree, may not be exposed to such men. Instructed—or rather, destroyed—by the subtleties of words, they dispute under the appearance of the Catholic faith and exhale, as it were, a pestilential venom in order to pierce the hearts of those who think rightly and seek to overturn the entire discipline of true doctrine.”

And indeed, what confession of grace could appear more Catholic in appearance than the following?

That everything good which we are able to do, say, or think belongs to God (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 6); that this capacity, bestowed by God, always needs God’s help, by which he enlightens us with the manifold and ineffable gift of heavenly grace and opens the eyes of our heart (ibid., chapter 3); that such grace is given for individual acts, though not according to merits (ibid., chapter 35); that without it no good can be done; and that through it the Holy Spirit enters our hearts and works in us the very willing that is good and the very willing that is holy (ibid., chapter 10).

Pelagius confessed all these things, but not in the Catholic sense. He did so deceitfully, since he was able to explain this ambiguity of words to his disciples so as to maintain that there is no help of grace by which nature’s capacity is assisted except in the law and teaching, as Augustine says (ibid., chapter 41).

What profession of original sin could appear more explicit than this?

That Adam’s sin harmed not only Adam himself but also the entire human race (*On Original Sin*, chapter 12); that infants are not born in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression (ibid., chapter 17); that baptism is necessary at every age, and therefore no one can obtain forgiveness of sins or the kingdom of heaven unless he has received baptism (*Against Julian*, Book II); that infants themselves need Christ’s redemption (in Augustine, Letter 86); that they ought to be baptized with the same words of the sacrament as their elders (*On Original Sin*, chapter 1); indeed, that they are baptized for the remission of sins, according to the rule of the universal Church (ibid., chapter 5).

By this confession Pelagius stole an acquittal for himself, yet in the hiding places of ambiguity he was preparing refuges for falsehood and casting darkness over the truth, as Augustine says (ibid., chapter 18).

### BY MEN OUTWARDLY PIOUS

Augustine (Letter 120, chapter 37):

“They are not such as you can easily despise, but live continently and conduct themselves commendably in good works.”

Indeed, when Pelagius first began to spread his error, he was believed—and was called by Augustine himself—a good and praiseworthy man, indeed a holy man, and an outstanding Christian who had made remarkable, though not slight, progress (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, Book III, chapters 1 and 3).

Hence Zosimus vehemently accuses Heros and Lazarus of having wished to strike Pelagius, a layman striving toward a better life through long service to God, with false letters.

To fashion this appearance of piety, it was highly advantageous to prescribe so strict a discipline of conduct that they even perverted Christ’s counsels into commandments. Pelagius taught that one ought never to swear at all; that the splendor of clothing and adornments was contrary to God; that a Christian ought to possess such patience that, if someone wished to take away his property, he should gladly surrender it; that a servant of God should allow nothing bitter to come from his mouth but should always utter what was sweet and pleasant; that a priest or teacher ought to scrutinize every action and rebuke everyone confidently and boldly; that enemies should be loved as neighbors; that a rich man living in wealth could not enter the kingdom of God unless he sold everything he possessed; and that it would not benefit him even if, from those riches, he happened to perform the commandments, and so forth (Jerome, *Dialogue I against the Pelagians*, and the *Book of Pelagius’s Chapters*).

Hence Augustine, Letter 89:

“Let these men therefore cease speaking against the Scriptures, and in their exhortations let them urge people toward greater things in such a way that they do not condemn lesser things. For they cannot persuade people to holy virginity by exhorting them in any other way unless they condemn the bonds of marriage.”

And shortly afterward:

“When these men are forbidden to say such things by those who have not embraced this counsel of the Lord, they reply that the others do not wish such matters to be discussed because they favor their own vices and refuse to fulfill the Lord’s commandments” (Hilary of Syracuse to Augustine, Letter 88; Augustine to Hilary, Letter 89; and elsewhere passim).

### BY ELOQUENT SPEECH

Gelasius (Letter 7, to the bishops throughout Picenum):

“We have found Pelagius, Caelestius, Julian, and many others—men of oratorical eloquence—convicted in this assertion and struck both by ecclesiastical constitutions and by imperial commands.”

Nor was anything written more eloquently in that age than Pelagius’s letter to Demetrias (Letter 17 of the appendix among Augustine’s letters). Augustine writes to Juliana, Demetrias’s mother:

“It cannot be adequately expressed how much we desire that the writings of these men, which are read by very many because of their sharpness and eloquence, should contain an open confession of that grace which the Apostle commends,” and so forth.

Nor was anything written more eloquently than the books of Julian, which Bede advises should be read with the greatest caution (Preface to the *Song of Songs*), lest the reader fall into the mire of harmful doctrine through the abundance of his seductive eloquence.

Nor than the writings of Caelestius, who, having become Pelagius’s standard-bearer from a schoolroom rhetorician, and afterward the leader of the entire army, may rightly be thought to have turned the exceptionally keen intellect he had received from nature and trained in the arts of the law toward serving heresy to lovers of novelty in a golden cup of Babylon, as Jerome says (Jerome, Letter to Ctesiphon; Augustine, *Book II to Boniface*, chapter 3).

Nor than the translations of Annianus, concerning whom Jerome writes (Letter 143, in Jerome’s Letter 202 among the Augustinian letters):

“You ask whether I have written against the books of Annianus, the false deacon of Celeda, who feeds himself most abundantly so that he may supply the frivolous words of another’s blasphemy,” and so forth.

“He remains stuck in the same mud, and, apart from tinkling and beggarly words, says nothing else.”

### THROUGH LETTERS SENT INTO THE PROVINCES

These letters were sent through trusted men to stir the minds of the simpler people.

Jerome (*Dialogue II against the Pelagians*):

“Papyrus letters fly across the rivers of Ethiopia,” and so forth.

And elsewhere (Preface to Book III on Jeremiah):

“He sends throughout the whole world papyrus letters, formerly gold-bearing but now abusive, and interprets our patience, which comes from the humility of Christ, as a sign of an evil conscience; and he himself, though mute, barks through the dog Albinus.”

And in his Commentary on Jeremiah, on the words in chapter 23, “Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts to the prophets,” and so forth:

“Let us use this testimony against those who send letters full of lies, deceit, and perjury throughout the world, both polluting the ears of those who hear and harming the reputation of the simple, so that what is written may be fulfilled in them: ‘Pollution has gone forth from the prophets of Jerusalem into all the land.’ For it is not enough for them to devour their own iniquity and harm their neighbors; once they have hated someone, they try to defame him throughout the world and sow blasphemies everywhere.”

Augustine (*Book on the Proceedings of Palestine*, chapter 30):

“A certain letter reached our hands, said to have been written by Pelagius himself to a certain presbyter who was his friend. Among other things it said: ‘Our definition has been approved by the judgment of fourteen bishops . . . .’ This letter, full of carnal vanity and pride, flies about; produced with the tardiness of official proceedings yet preceding them in speed, it rushes ahead into people’s hands so that it may be said to have pleased fourteen Eastern bishops.”

And afterward:

“So that only the wretched, self-deceiving, victorious pride might be read in the letter.”

And elsewhere (*Book II to Boniface*, chapter 1):

“Although the new heretics are now shown more clearly to be such as must be avoided, by a more evident condemnation, they nevertheless do not cease to test the hearts of the less cautious and less educated through their writings,” and so forth.

Marius Mercator, addressing Julian (*Book of Notes*, chapter 7, section 9):

“In the letter which you dared to send to the Apostolic See, when you refused to join the universal Church in condemning Pelagius and Caelestius throughout the whole world, it is known that, before it came into the hands of the bishop of the holy Roman Church, through your agency it had been circulated through almost the whole of Italy by certain people deceived by you and insinuated into the ears of many as something of great importance.”

Hence Augustine, writing to Boniface about two letters of the Pelagians sent to him by Alypius, says that they “could have come into your hands only through the most vigilant diligence of our brothers, your sons” (*Book I to Boniface*, chapter 1).

### THROUGH THE FAVOR AND NAME OF BISHOPS

The Caelestian heresy had Theodore of Mopsuestia as its author; Julian associates him with Basil and Chrysostom (*Book III of the Imperfect Work*, chapter 113). Pelagius was also believed to have persuaded Saint Innocent himself of his position (Letter 95 to Innocent). Certainly, he insinuated himself into the friendship of John of Jerusalem and his successor Praylius, from whom he received letters of recommendation to the Apostolic See (Orosius, *Apology*). He stole a friendly letter from Augustine (Augustine, Letter 252 to John of Jerusalem), which he later displayed in order to win for himself the reputation of orthodoxy (Greek: *orthodoxias*, “orthodoxy”) (Zosimus, Letter 4). He boasted that his person and his doctrine had been acquitted by the judgment of fourteen Eastern bishops at the Synod of Diospolis (Augustine, *Book on the Proceedings*, chapter 21). Julian wrote a profession of faith to Zosimus in the name of eighteen bishops, as well as a letter to Rufus of Thessalonica, in order to draw the bishops of Macedonia over to his side (Augustine, *Book II to Boniface*, chapter 1).

Valerian sailed from the West to Alexandria so that, after insinuating himself into Cyril’s friendship, he might exploit that favor to spread the heresy. To some extent this happened, a fact which Eusebius laments in writing to Cyril:

“How did the Alexandrian Church receive this man into communion, when it alone and first among its provincial neighbors ought to have rejected him?” and so forth (in Baronius, under the year 417, section 15).

Pelagius secretly obtained friendly letters from whatever bishops he could, so that, when time and place permitted, he might produce them filled with praise of himself.

Hence Augustine (*Book on the Proceedings of Palestine*, chapter 25):

“What good do so many praises of him in bishops’ letters do him—letters which he thought ought to be recalled or even cited on his behalf—as though all those who heard his vehement and, in a certain sense, fervent exhortations to a good life could not easily know that he held these perverse opinions?”

And afterward:

“Just as I gave an account of this letter of mine, so, if necessary, those whose letters are cited should give an account of their own, saying either what they thought, what they did not know, or for what reason they wrote.”

“Therefore, no matter whose friendship among the saints Pelagius boasts of, no matter whose letters praising him he reads, and no matter what records of his own acquittal he produces, unless he proves by the testimony of reliable witnesses that he has confessed and anathematized what he wrote in his books against the grace of God by which we are called and justified, and thereafter has written and argued against those very positions, he will by no means appear corrected to those who know him more fully.”

### BY COURTING THE FAVOR OF THOSE WHO WERE DISTINGUISHED

That is, those distinguished by a reputation for holiness, by fame for learning, or by wealth and power.

When the Pelagian heresy was first taking shape, Paulinus had drawn everyone’s eyes to himself by the brilliance of his holiness (in Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 35). Pelagius nearly drew him over to his side by his letters; certainly, he won him over so completely that Augustine had to warn this holy man to beware of snares (Letter 186).

At the same time Pammachius and Oceanus surpassed the nobility of their birth by the holiness of their conduct, having converted their house into a monastery (Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapter 3). Caelestius gained access to this household through hostility to the Origenists, so that, if he could, he might introduce an error no better than theirs.

Proba, Juliana, and Demetrias had placed their Anician lineage beneath the humility of Christ. Pelagius attacked their grandmother through an appearance of virtue and their widowed mother through flattery, while praising the virgin Demetrias (Letter 17 of the appendix among Augustine’s letters); he might perhaps have conquered them had Alypius and Augustine not resisted bravely.

The household of Albina, Pinianus, and Melania at that time was no less devoted to religion than the monasteries. The British serpent tried to creep into it, but Augustine prevented its spread (*On the Grace of Christ* and *On Original Sin*), instructing these pious souls in two complete books about the devices of the deceitful heretic.

It was rumored that Pelagius had persuaded Pope Innocent, than whom no one at that time was holier. Five African bishops complained about this rumor in a letter of their own (Letter 177 among Augustine’s letters).

At Rome, Sixtus; in Africa, Augustine; in the East, John of Jerusalem; in Egypt, Cyril; and in Gaul, Severus Sulpicius, the disciple of Saint Martin, were renowned for their learning at the time when the heresy was arising. Augustine lamented that Sixtus favored the Pelagians (the letter just cited and Letter 186). Pelagius himself, invited by letter, received a reply from Augustine (*Book on the Proceedings*, chapter 24), and on that basis the heretic boasted that Augustine was his friend. Innocent, Orosius, and Augustine wrote that John had been seduced by Pelagius; Eusebius reported that Cyril had been tested by Valerian; and Gennadius testified that Severus had been deceived by the Pelagians.

Among the Romans, whose favor I previously said the Pelagians had courted, there was no one who did not abound in wealth, and these crafty men, wearing the mask of religion so that they might more easily ensnare the unsuspecting, tried to insinuate themselves into everyone’s friendship. They pursued this goal with all the greater eagerness because the reputation of holiness would prove profitable and would provide abundant sustenance even for those who wrote on behalf of the sect. They would have succeeded if, just as Jerome warned Ctesiphon, others had not warned others.

“Through you I entreat and admonish that gathering of the holy and illustrious household not to allow itself, because of one—or at most three—little men, to receive the dregs of such great heresies, or, to put it mildly, their disgrace: so that where virtue and holiness were first praised, there the shame of demonic presumption and the filthiest association may be found. Those who supply wealth to such men are shown to be gathering a multitude of heretics, making enemies of Christ, and nurturing his adversaries, while vainly professing one thing with their tongue and proving by their hand that they think another.”

The tribune Marcellinus and the count Valerius had great influence with the emperor Honorius, and indeed were also distinguished for piety, at the very time when the Pelagian error was spreading. Marcellinus was also exceptionally learned, while Valerius maintained modesty amid the highest honors and chastity at court. The Pelagians tested both men, so that Augustine had to expose the heretics’ wicked devices in books written to each of them (*Books III on the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins* and *Books II on Marriage and Concupiscence*).

To this belongs the fact that they strove with incredible determination to deceive all the Churches of the major sees by testing their bishops: the Roman Church, through Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Sixtus, and Leo, by all the leaders of the sect; the Carthaginian Church, through Aurelius, and the Ephesian Church, through Hepaclides, by Caelestius; the Thessalonian Church, through Rufus, by Julian; the Alexandrian Church, through Cyril, by Valerian; the Jerusalem Church, through John and Praylius, by Pelagius; and the Constantinopolitan Church, through Atticus, Sisinnius, and Nestorius, by seventeen bishops expelled from Italy.

### BY THE DEVICES OF NOBLE WOMEN WHO LOVED NOVELTY

These women they had won over by flattery and other wicked devices.

Jerome (in his letter to Ctesiphon):

“What do the wretched little women want, weighed down by sins, driven about by every wind of doctrine, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth? And what do the other companions of these little women want—itching for something to hear and unaware of what they hear or say? They receive the oldest mud as though it were a new mixture; like the women in Ezekiel, they plaster a wall without mortar, and when the rain of truth comes, they are scattered. Simon Magus founded a heresy with the help of Helena. Montanus first corrupted many Churches through Prisca and Maximilla, noble and wealthy women, with gold, and then polluted them with heresy. Arius, in order to deceive the world, first deceived the emperor’s sister . . . . . Each sex overthrows the other,” and so forth.

And elsewhere (*Dialogue I against the Pelagians*):

“You are so generous” (he is addressing Pelagius) “that you win favor for yourself among your Amazons, so that you have written that even women ought to possess knowledge of the law . . . . . Nor is it enough for you to have given your troop knowledge of the Scriptures unless you also delight in their voices and songs.”

Augustine, addressing Julian (*Against Julian*, Book VI, chapter 4):

“As for your followers, or your women followers, what does it matter to me what they are, whom you deceive so that you say I define that lust cannot be restrained even in a diseased body?”

One should consult the same Jerome (*Dialogue II against the Pelagians*), Augustine (*Book on the Proceedings*, chapter 6), and Mercator (*Commonitorium*, part 16 and following sections) concerning what Pelagius wrote to a widow in such abominable flattery that, out of shame, he was forced falsely to deny that the writings were his.

### BY THE DISTRIBUTION OF ALMS, AND SO FORTH

Gennadius (*Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 45):

“This Julian, by distributing alms to all the needy in a time of famine and distress, attracted many—especially noble and religious people—into association with his heresy under the appearance of compassion.”

## § II. The second cause of the same obstinacy: calumnies and lies
