The Fathers give this second reason for why the Pelagian error took such deep and stubborn possession of the minds of many: the Pelagians occupied religious people, who loved peace but were less prudent in such matters, through five kinds of lies.

They claimed that the doctrine opposed to their own—that is, the Catholic doctrine—was itself the detestable heresy of Manichaeus; that they were not disputing about doctrine but only about a question of no great importance; that they had no quarrel with the whole Church but with almost only two men, Jerome and Augustine, who, because they burned with hatred and envy against exceptionally Catholic men, were disturbing the whole world and unsettling the peace of the Church through insane tumults; that their doctrine was rejected and the contrary doctrine admitted only because the former favored the pursuit of virtue while the latter favored moral license; and finally, that from the opposing view—not merely from the whole view, but even from a single confession of original sin—almost innumerable blasphemies followed.

Thus, as the first kind of lie, they imposed the name of Manichaeans upon Catholics and attached the most execrable of all heresies to the defenders of original sin.

Pelagius, whom Jerome addresses in this way (in his letter to Ctesiphon):

“You will cry out and say that we follow the doctrine of the Manichaeans and of those who stir up wars against the Church concerning different natures, asserting that nature is evil,” and so forth.

Caelestius (in his letter to the Roman clergy, Book I to Boniface):

“Those Manichaeans say”—by whom we now mean those with whom we disagree, that is, this entire group—“that because of the sin of the first man,” and so forth.

Annianus (in his letter to the presbyter Evangelus, volume VI of Bede’s works, toward the end):

“This work ought to be more lovable to you in proportion as, shining with the light of the Scriptures, the radiance of the brightest star drives away the night of Manichaean error. For how great a consolation arises for us when we see that the truth which the Traducian attacks in us is upheld by so learned and distinguished a teacher of the East!” and so forth.

Nearly the same things appear in his letter to Horontius, the Pelagian bishop (prefixed to Saint Chrysostom’s homilies on Matthew).

Julianus (*Book I of the Imperfect Work*, chapter 59):

“This is not the faith”—by which original sin is believed—“handed down and established from ancient times, unless it was inspired in the councils of the wicked by the devil, brought forth by Manichaeus, celebrated by Marcion, Faustus, Adimantus, and all their followers; and now vomited forth by you” (he is addressing Augustine) “in Italy, to our great grief.” See similar statements in Book VI, chapter 5.

Elsewhere, in a thoroughly furious passage (in Augustine, *Book III against Julian*, chapter 17):

“One must pray to God, most blessed brother Turbantius, dearest fellow priest, that by virtues equal even to those of this present age” (he had been speaking of fertility restored to Sarah) “he may not delay rescuing the Catholic Church, the mature, fruitful, chaste, and beautiful bride of his Son, from the violation by the Manichaeans who plunder in Africa or from Africa.”

Augustine responds with due severity to this calumniator, who repeats the same charges everywhere, in four books to Boniface; but he responds most severely both in his earlier *Work against Julian* and in the later *Imperfect Work*, where he says (*Book I, chapter 22*):

“If, with a Christian heart, you considered that you claim Catholic teachers support Manichaeus, you would blush, tremble, and fall silent.”

How much this calumny favored the heresy and simultaneously harmed the truth, the holy Doctor explains in these words (*Book III to Boniface*, chapter 9):

“But because in these five matters”—the praise of creation, marriage, the law, free will, and the saints—“in which they seek hiding places and about which they weave calumnies, they are exposed and defeated by divine testimonies, they devised the detestable name of the Manichaeans in order to frighten such uneducated people as they could from giving ear to the truth against their most perverse doctrines. For the Manichaeans, by their own blasphemies, condemn three of these five matters, saying that neither human creation, nor marriage, nor the law was instituted by the supreme and true God.”

They then asserted, as the second lie, that they were not engaged in a dispute about doctrine but only about a question.

Caelestius first dared to assert this at the judgment in Carthage. Augustine (in Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapters 22–23):

“We must now examine the claim by which, wishing cleverly to avoid the odium of heresy, they assert that this is a question lying outside the danger of faith, so that, if they are convicted of having deviated in it, they may appear to have erred not criminally but, as it were, civilly. For thus Caelestius spoke at Carthage in the ecclesiastical proceedings:

‘Concerning the transmission of sin I have said that, within the Catholic body, I have heard many deny it and others affirm it, although this is a question, not a heresy. I have always said that infants need baptism and ought to be baptized. What more does he seek?’

And in the statement submitted at Rome:

‘If questions have arisen outside the faith, about which there is disagreement among many, I have not, as the author of some doctrine, established the matter by an authoritative decision. Rather, I offer for the judgment of your Apostolate what I have received from the source of the prophets and apostles,’” and so forth.

Augustine’s discussion of this matter should be consulted (ibid., chapter 24).

Later Julian asserted to Marius Mercator (*Book of Notes*, chapter 7, section 11):

“I count among undisciplined questions the claim that infants are in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression,” and so forth.

And to Augustine (*Book VI of the Imperfect Work*, chapter 1):

“I do not doubt that this opinion concerning our dispute has hitherto been regarded as pertaining more to an entangled question than to the substance of the faith,” and so forth.

Finally, the Pelagians commonly asserted before the author of the *Predestination* (*Heresy* 88):

“We are distinguished concerning a question, not concerning communion.”

They boldly claimed, as the third lie, that they had no quarrel with the whole Church but only with two men: Jerome, whom they called *Aram*—that is, “accursed”—and Augustine, whom they named “Traducian” (Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 177). They falsely claimed that these men had drawn many entire Churches over to their opinion through books and devices (Annianus, in his letter to Evangelus, and Julian everywhere).

This is established partly by the five books written by Theodore of Mopsuestia against both teachers, mentioned by Photius (*Codex* 177), from which Marius Mercator reports notable fragments (*Part II of his Works*); and partly by the testimonies of Jerome and Augustine, who make the same assertion.

Augustine, speaking of Julian (*Book II on Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 18), says:

“Coming against this most firmly established truth, so that he may not appear to attack the entire Church of Christ, he addresses me as though I were alone, and, as if correcting and admonishing me, says: ‘God made you also, but—and this must be confessed as the more serious point—error infected you,’” and so forth.

Jerome, writing to Augustine and Alypius (Letter 202, in Augustine’s collection), says:

“Through your cooperation and agency the Caelestian heresy has been strangled. It infected the hearts of so many that, although they perceive themselves to have been overcome and condemned, they nevertheless do not abandon the poisons in their minds. The only thing they can do is hate you, through whom they believe they have lost the freedom to teach heresy.”

Fourthly, they falsely claimed that Catholic doctrine pandered to vices and that, together with their own exclusion from the Church, the censure of virtues had been excluded.

Julianus (*Imperfect Work*, Book II, chapters 2 and 3):

“The rudders of reason are being torn away from the Churches, so that, with its horn raised, popular doctrine may set sail. Thus, while little is permitted to the prudent, anything whatsoever is fitting for the base; by a decree of sedition, the discipline of virtue has been excluded from the Churches. And this has made us hated among the common people: that we refused to become an addition to error—the common people, I say, who, weighing the merit of an opinion by its successes, judge it to be truer when they see that it pleases the greater number.

“For it delights them to defame whatever has ever existed, anywhere, among the saints, lest the examples of eminent men rebuke them” (ibid., chapters 5 and 6). “It truly delights them, and thoroughly affects them, to allege the weakness of nature, to say that the flesh is subject to innate sins; and not to place the effect of amendment in the human will, but to call the crimes of our efforts the duties of our members. Thus this dross of the Manichaeans panders to the ears with its most impure doctrines” (ibid., chapters 9 and 10).

“This nettle stirred up our enemies of both sexes: while it bites some with the vice of bad habit, it was nevertheless treated, as it were, with certain ointments of salutary exhortation” (ibid., chapter 11); “but now, after it began to be offered as a remedy, and authority was added to its appeal by the assent of almost the whole world, etc.” (*Imperfect Work*, Book VI, chapters 2 and 3).

[Col. 0427A] I cannot omit two replies made by Augustine. The first is against the charge that moral discipline had been relaxed (*Imperfect Work*, Book II, chapter 6):

“Why are you angry with us, who pursue the effect of amendment with all the greater certainty the more faithfully we ask it from the Lord? In vain you extend your swollen tongue with its haughty voice, etc.”

The second is against the accusation of Manichaeism brought against him (ibid., chapter 9):

“Dare, if you can, to accuse Ambrose of being a Manichaean. Consider against whom you are saying what you wish to appear to be saying against me; and if you have any fear of God or human shame, be silent. I ought to hear your insults against such men not merely patiently, but even gladly; but in tearing such men apart, you ought to feel shame before human beings and fear the divine judgments.”

Finally, as their last lie, they asserted that almost infinite blasphemies followed from the single Catholic doctrine of original sin. For when Augustine asked Julianus why he did not assent to the faith of the Church on this matter, Julianus replied (*Imperfect Work*, Book III, chapter 68 and following) that it possessed no appearance, much less any truth, of plausibility; no appearance of justice or piety; because it made the devil appear to be the creator of human beings; because it destroyed free will; because it extinguished the striving for complete moral excellence; because it provided consolation for moral obscenity and branded the work of God itself—that is, human nature—with infamy; because it subjected all the commandments of the law to the guilt of impossibility, that is, of iniquity; because it contained no less disgrace than profanity; and because, in place of sacred authorities, it swelled with accusations against God, affirming that his commandments contained tyrannical immoderation, his judgments barbarous injustice, and his oaths Punic falsehood; and because, in place of arguments and all syllogisms, it relied upon the dreams and madness of the Manichaeans.

“These, then, are the reasons that inflame us to attack the evil of nature; that make us disdain and despise association with the ruined; that make us no more terrified by the uproar of the whole world than we would be if we saw a sad forest of lupines resounding, or being shaken by filthy swine or rushing winds.”

§ III. The third reason why it was difficult to overthrow the followers of the Pelagian heresy: they refused to withdraw from the Church.

Wolves never inflict more unavoidable harm upon Christ’s sheepfold than when they hide among the sheep; nor does the darnel do more damage to the Lord’s field than when it grows among the wheat. For this reason the Good Shepherd commanded his disciples to beware of false prophets who come in sheep’s clothing, although inwardly they are ravenous wolves (Matthew 7:15). And the divine master of the household forbids the darnel to be removed until the appointed time, lest the wheat also be uprooted at the same time (Matthew 13:29).

This was the very reason why the Pelagians did not make an open separation from the Catholics, preferring instead continually to change the places in which they were unknown rather than openly, where they were known, to abstain from communion with the faithful. For they understood that in this way they would inflict great damage upon the Church and would scarcely ever be completely expelled. Let us hear the writers of that age.

Augustine (*On Original Sin*, chapter 17):

“Many followed them for this reason: because they saw that they were associated with Catholic communion.”

Marius Mercator (*Preface to the Book of Subnotations*):

“A question against the Catholic faith, raised long ago among certain Syrians, and especially in Cilicia, by Theodore, formerly bishop of the town of Mopsuestia, is still secretly handed down among a very few of them. Nor is it brought forward openly; rather, by those who trumpet it, they are meanwhile retained within the Churches as though they were Catholics, etc.”

The author whom Father Sirmond called *Praedestinatus* (*Heresy* 88):

“The Pelagians, or Coelestians, have been mixed among the Catholic people, because they have no other Church; and therefore, wherever the opportunity arises for them, they do not refuse communion, etc.”

Saint Celestine, writing to Maximianus of Constantinople concerning the Coelestians (Third Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 22):

“Through you, may the Holy Spirit oppose those men who attempt to reach whatever provinces they can, so that their impious preaching may rise again. Oppose them; for thus, wherever they arrive, they become known and are condemned. And as though the sentence so often repeated were not enough for them, they trouble distant lands and remote provinces.”

Saint Leo, writing to Nicetas of Aquileia (*Letter* 86):

“We have learned that certain presbyters, deacons, and clerics of various ranks, whom the Pelagian or Coelestian heresy had entangled, came in your province to Catholic communion in such a way that no condemnation of their own error was required from them; and, while pastoral vigilance was sleeping too deeply, the wolf covered in sheep’s skins entered the Lord’s sheepfold without laying aside its bestial dispositions.”

And afterward:

“This above all is the fruit they seek: that under the covering of communion they may visit many households and corrupt the hearts of many through knowledge falsely so called. They could certainly accomplish this only because the bishops of the Churches failed to maintain the necessary diligence in receiving such persons, etc.”

§ IV. The fourth reason why the Pelagians could scarcely ever be expelled from the Church: the pretence of repentance.

No heretics are received into the Church more dangerously than those who, after they have been expelled, pretend repentance; who, through fabricated professions, interpret their words one way publicly and another way among their confidants; or who determine the measure of satisfaction according to their own judgment. By this art they mock the Church’s kindly pastors through the lie of repentance; and through the fabrication of their professions they spread more boldly among the people the doctrine whose condemned mask they display as though it were an absolved one.

Jerome to Augustine (*Letter* 134 in Jerome, 202 in Augustine):

“Let us take care that the most destructive heresy be removed from the Churches. It always pretends repentance so that it may have the opportunity to teach in the Churches; for if it revealed itself in the open light, it would die after being expelled.”

Concerning Julianus’s feigned repentance, the following statement of the chronicler is well known:

“At this time Julianus of Eclanum, the most boastful champion of the Pelagian error, whom an immoderate desire for his long-lost episcopate was tormenting, attempted by many arts of deception to enter stealthily into communion with the Church, presenting the appearance of correction” (*Chronicle*, under the year 439, during the consulship of Theodosius XVII and Festus).

There are two books of Augustine concerning the deceitful confession of Pelagius and Coelestius: one *On the Grace of Christ*, the other *On Original Sin*. Add to these the book *On Nature and Grace*, and almost innumerable works of the same kind.

Concerning the error retained in its entirety, or in the smallest fragment that they had reserved at their discretion, by Pelagians who pretended to retract it, there is a clear passage in Saint Leo (*Letter* 86, to Nicetas):

“We know this to be their cunning: that, in whatever part of the accursed doctrine they have separated themselves from the company of the condemned, they suppose that none of their own opinions is unsound, etc.”

Long before this, Augustine had spoken of Pelagius’s confession at Diospolis and also of the document of his defense, which he sent to Africa (*On the Proceedings at Palestine*, chapter 33). When he related that something omitted from the latter had been stated in the former, he said:

“Who would not believe that this was arranged so that, as though for the sake of abbreviating those proceedings, this document might circulate everywhere, without anyone supposing that the permission to defend any of those propositions had been removed, etc.”

I cannot pass over in silence the practice of the Pelagians, who thought that nothing concerning their cause should be said without embellishment and the artifice of perplexity (Jerome, *To Ctesiphon*); that nothing written against them should be left unanswered (Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapter 19); that the matter of the controversy itself should never be treated, but that the minds of readers should be diverted elsewhere by alien questions (Augustine, *Against Julianus*, Book I, chapter 1); that their opponents should be overwhelmed by the multitude of their books, even though the same things had always to be repeated with tireless loquacity (Jerome, *First Dialogue*, no. 401); that everything should be filled with men arguing loquaciously and dragging along weak and uneducated souls as though they had been convicted, while fatiguing the strong and steadfast in faith by the very force of the dispute (*Letter of the Five Bishops to Innocent*); that they should complain without ceasing that they were being defamed, while declaring themselves thoroughly Catholic and genuinely devout (*Letter of Pelagius to Innocent*); that an impious sedition was being stirred up against them by men who were consumed with zeal for their holy pursuits and had resolved to reach their own destruction through the ruin of the whole Church (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book II, chapter 3); that innovations were being charged against them with the utmost calumny, although they brought forward nothing except what they had received from the Catholic rule, the tradition of the ancestors, and Sacred Scripture (Coelestius to Zosimus; Pelagius, *Book on Nature*; Julianus in his pamphlet); that they were insultingly called heretics, although they were concerned only with certain questions, or had promised in most holy public documents that they would condemn everything condemned by the apostolic see (the *Pamphlets of Coelestius and Pelagius’s Profession of Faith*); that the peace and tranquility of the Church were being disturbed without cause, and Christian concord and charity violated, although they themselves wished these to be preserved at any cost to themselves (Julianus and others, passim); and that the times of a religious ruler were being stained by impiety and persecution, etc. (*Imperfect Work*, Book III, chapter 34).

# CHAPTER IV. In this case, was a signature required for the condemnation of doctrines alone, or also of their authors?

It must be observed that what was formerly called subscribing to the condemnation of doctrines and authors meant nothing other than either condemning propositions—in the sense in which they were asserted by their authors, whether in speech or writing—or consenting to the Church’s condemnation of two things joined together in the propositions themselves, which are now called the legal question and the question of fact. The latter two formulas of speech, however, were devised only recently; the Fathers used only the first.

From this it is readily understood what answer was given by common agreement to the question proposed by all who either wrote about the Pelagian cause while it was being conducted or took the leading roles in conducting it. For they said that anyone who wished to be and to appear Catholic had to subscribe not only to the condemnation of the doctrines opposed to the grace of God through Christ and to original sin, but also to the condemnation of their authors, Pelagius and Coelestius.

Emperor Honorius, in the edict addressed to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, issued at Ravenna on the fifth day before the Ides of June, during the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta:

“It had indeed been established some time ago that Pelagius and Coelestius, the inventors of an accursed doctrine, should be expelled from the city of Rome as though they were certain contagions to Catholic truth, lest they pervert the minds of the ignorant by savage persuasion. . . . But because the persistent evil of an obstinate crime compelled the enactment to be repeated, we have also decreed by a recent sanction—especially for the correction of the obstinacy of certain bishops who either support their perverse disputations by silent consent or fail to destroy them by public opposition—that your Religiousness should cause everyone to be warned by appropriate writings. They will know from the declaration of your testimony that this definition has been prescribed for them: whoever, in impious obstinacy, has neglected to subscribe to the condemnation of those mentioned above, so that the purity of his mind may be evident, shall be punished by the loss of his episcopate, etc.”

Aurelius, after receiving the emperor’s constitution, wrote back to the bishops:

“For this reason, this necessary constitution of the Christian rulers ought not to have been hidden from your Charity. The letters delivered to me by them, once their copies have been read together, will enable your Love to understand how each of you ought to subscribe. . . . In that matter, since the full subscription of all of you to the condemnation of the heretics mentioned above will have been given, there must be nothing from which any suspicion can reasonably appear to have remained of either concealment, negligence, or perhaps hidden depravity.”

Julianus himself, in his *Profession of Faith* addressed to Zosimus (Part IV, no. 3):

“But we especially admonish your Holiness not to think that it was done for your reproach that, through fear of God, we do not dare to subscribe to the condemnation of absent persons, having been taught by the Scriptures that human will ought not to be preferred to the commandments of God, etc.”

Marius Mercator, in the *Memorial Presented to the Emperors* (chapter 11):

“That letter of Bishop Zosimus, of blessed memory, which is called the *Tractoria*, contains all the chapters written above; by it Coelestius and Pelagius were condemned. It was sent both to Constantinople and throughout the whole world and was strengthened by the subscriptions of the holy Fathers. Julianus and his other accomplices, however, refused to subscribe to it and were unwilling to make themselves of one mind with those same Fathers; consequently they were deposed not only by imperial laws but also by priestly decrees, etc.”

The same author, in the *Book of Subnotations* (chapter 7), addressing Julianus:

“In your letter, which you dared at that time to send to the apostolic see, when you refused to assemble with the whole Church throughout the world to condemn Pelagius and Coelestius.”

[Col. 0430B] Saint Leo, writing to Septimius concerning the Pelagians (*Letter* 85):

“Those who wish to appear corrected must acknowledge without ambiguity that they themselves condemn their error and the very authors of that error, so that no opportunity for hope may remain for perverse opinions long since destroyed, and so that no member of the Church may be violated by association with such persons, once their own profession has begun to oppose them in every respect, etc.”

Writing also to Nicetas of Aquileia (*Letter* 86), he says:

“Let them condemn by open professions the authors of their proud error, and let them detest whatever the universal Church has abhorred in their teaching. Let them declare, in full, open statements subscribed with their own hands, that they embrace and approve in every respect all the synodal decrees which the authority of the apostolic see has confirmed for the eradication of this heresy. Let nothing obscure be found in their words, nothing ambiguous, because we know this to be their cunning: that, in whatever part of the accursed doctrine by which they have separated themselves from the company of the condemned, they suppose that none of their own opinions is unsound.”

Photius (*Bibliotheca*, codex 54):

“John of Alexandria, in his apology addressed to Gelasius, bishop of the City, condemned not only the Pelagian heresy but Pelagius himself and Coelestius, together with Julianus, who was found to have succeeded them in this very sect.”

The reason why, not only in this case but in similar ones, the Church has so consistently throughout all past centuries, and especially the earlier ones, ordered people to subscribe to the condemnation both of doctrines and of their authors, and has punished those who refused as though they were heretics, was given by the emperor in these words: “so that the purity of the mind may be evident,” by condemning; and “so that no favor may be shown to the guilty person condemned for sacrilege,” by refusing to condemn. Aurelius added: lest any suspicion of hidden depravity should reasonably appear to have remained. Finally, Leo stated that this was necessary because it was known to be their cunning, etc.

For the mind of one who, when controversy arises, refuses to speak with the Church—that is, with the Bride of Christ, the teacher of truth, the truest mother of the faithful, and the judge of controversies—cannot be pure of harmful favor, free from every just suspicion, and sincerely and candidly Catholic.

It must also be observed that long ago, by men wishing to mock the Church and invalidate its judgment whenever a decision displeased them, there was devised not only the distinction between law and fact, or between doctrine and person, but also that perplexing and deceitful form of speech by which they would say that they did not indiscriminately condemn the doctrine of a particular man; rather, under a certain qualification, they anathematized whatever he had said or thought differently from what apostolic doctrine contained (*Letter to Himerius of Nicomedia* in Marius Mercator).

These are the words of Theodoretus before he returned to sound judgment, as he consoled Himerius of Nicomedia and himself after Nestorius’s condemnation by John of Antioch before the emperor Theodosius, using such deceptive language. [Col. 0431A] But how can that deception ever be avoided except by an open condemnation of both the doctrine and the person?

It is also worthy of note that the Church has always regarded as heretics those who, in matters of faith, refused to subscribe to the condemnation of persons as well, after the evidence of a case had once been examined by competent men, a legitimate judgment instituted, and it had been pronounced that the accused were guilty of the doctrines whose undisputed books had been produced—regardless of how much either the authors of the books or the patrons of their authors wished to evade the issue. For they scarcely ever failed to evade it, as is clear from the history of the councils, especially the ancient ones. Hence it happened that, likewise, scarcely ever—if indeed ever—in those universal councils were doctrines condemned without persons; that is, after making a distinction between the legal question and the question of fact.

Moreover, Pelagius, who is chiefly at issue here, is recorded as having been condemned in no judgment except on the basis of his own books or letters. Certainly he was not heard in person so that he might interpret his books; indeed, he was not even summoned to judgment so that he could answer the charges on his own behalf. For the synod of Ephesus pronounced sentence against him after rereading what had been done at Rome by Celestine. Celestine, however, did not reopen the case but followed in the footsteps of Boniface. Boniface instituted no judgment but carried out what his predecessor Zosimus had done. Zosimus heard Coelestius in person, but condemned Pelagius on the basis of his writings, following the African councils and his predecessor Innocent.

Yet Innocent did not summon Pelagius from Palestine to Rome to be heard, although the African bishops had requested this; nor did the African councils pronounce sentence against him—whatever sentence they did pronounce—except on the report of Orosius, the letters of Heros and Lazarus, and the books written by Pelagius.

I admit that Pelagius was heard once, at the assembly in Jerusalem, by John; and a second time, at the synod of Diospolis, by fourteen bishops. But in both places he was acquitted, since he denied that either the things charged against him or the sense in which they were charged were his.

He denied them, certainly, in bad faith, and for that reason he was afterward proscribed by the whole Church—and deservedly so. Therefore anyone who now wished to defend the man as though he had suffered calumny from the whole Church, which had erred in judging from his books, would deserve the same curses and anathemas as that impious Calvinist who recently, in a book published in 1645, shamelessly dared to absolve Nestorius and condemn the Council of Ephesus as heretical. He argued that, in a question of fact of this kind, each person possesses his own light, by whose guidance he may even accuse the Church itself of blindness.

# CHAPTER V. Whether those who favored the authors of the Pelagian doctrines—and the authors themselves—admitted that the things charged against them, as extracted from their books, were their own.

So far were Pelagius and Coelestius from admitting that the things charged against them were their own that they condemned them not only verbally but also in documents offered to the apostolic see.

Coelestius (*To the Roman Clergy* in Augustine, Book I, *To Boniface*, chapter 23):

“Let no one deceive you.” He is addressing the Roman clergy who belonged to his party. “Nor should the impious deny that they hold these opinions; but if they speak the truth, either let a hearing be granted, or let these very bishops who are now in disagreement condemn what I have said above—namely, that they hold these things with the Manichaeans—JUST AS WE CONDEMN THE THINGS THEY CLAIM ABOUT US; and let there be complete agreement.”

Earlier, Zosimus had been deceitfully mocked by him. Hence the holy pontiff, writing to the Africans, said (*Letter* 2 in the Pelagian case):

“We wished, therefore, to confer with you concerning the man who, among us—as you yourselves say in your letters—had been accused and who, not refusing to come to our see by appeal from the earlier judgment in order to assert his innocence, voluntarily demanded his accusers and condemned the charges that, according to rumor, he falsely said had been brought against him, etc.”

Pelagius (in Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 2):

“Anathema to anyone who either thinks or says that the grace of God, through which Christ came into this world to save sinners, is not necessary not only at every hour but also in each of our acts; and may those who attempt to take it away suffer eternal punishments.”

The whole of Augustine’s book *On the Proceedings at Palestine* must be read, and likewise the whole of *On the Grace of Christ*. Throughout these works Pelagius complains that he is being subjected to calumny, while Augustine labors intensely to expose the heretic’s bad faith.

Julianus (*Profession of Faith*, Part IV, no. 1):

“All these matters now under discussion—that is, the matters that we condemned at the end—were also condemned by the very men against whom these things are falsely alleged, who, in their own documents, testified that they had been falsely charged and condemned them.”

And shortly afterward (no. 8):

“Although, therefore, it belongs to the priestly office and to Christian charity to defend with free authority those who clear themselves in written documents, confess themselves Catholics, and condemn the things charged against them as deserving condemnation, and to form the better judgment concerning each person in matters of doubt, etc.”

Nestorius, writing concerning the Pelagian bishops (*Letter to Saint Celestine*, First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 15):

“Now, from their uncertain statements, no one has anything to which he can turn. Some call them heretics and say that for this reason they were expelled from the Western regions; but they themselves swear that they have suffered calumny and that they underwent danger for the orthodox faith through false information.”

I shall not depart from my purpose of treating only the Pelagian heresy if I cite an example from the case—or, as people now say, the fact—of Nestorius. For such is the kinship of the Pelagian and Nestorian heresies; such is their consanguinity, if I may use that expression with Cassianus (*On the Incarnation*, Book I, chapter 1), that they almost arose as one. Certainly both came forth from the same womb; struck down by the common thunderbolts of the Church, they were buried in one tomb and given one epitaph by Prosper, or by whatever other writer composed the epitaph.

Those who favored Nestorius—John of Antioch, Acacius of Beroea, Theodoretus, and many others—although they willingly pronounced anathema against all who rejected the title Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*, “God-bearer”) or divided Christ into two sons, nevertheless denied that Nestorius’s writings or statements could be understood in a sense foreign to orthodoxy. Let us hear the three whom I have named, together with Socrates, the historian of that same period.

John of Antioch, writing to Nestorius (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 25):

“Let not your Holiness now think within yourself that it is disgraceful for you to teach things that contradict one another. For if your mind understands and feels what the holy Fathers and teachers of the Church understand and feel—for this, my lord, we have learned about you from many persons and from common friends—why are you afraid to publish your pious understanding in appropriate language?”

And shortly afterward:

“Who, I ask, would find fault with you if you freely set forth what you think? Indeed, who would not extol you with praises if, for the sake of public tranquility and the common peace of the world, you accepted the name whose meaning, as we have learned, your piety possesses?”

And afterward:

“For this reason I admonish and urge you to bring this forth in an unconstrained voice. Come, do not hesitate to add to the matter that you rightly hold the name which has often been used, written, and pronounced by many Fathers, etc.”

Acacius of Beroea, replying to Saint Cyril (ibid., chapter 23):

“Many clergy and laypeople who come from Constantinople to Antioch and even to us appear to defend what has been said by Nestorius. For they say that, in its meaning, it contains nothing opposed either to apostolic doctrine or to the faith defined by the holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea to establish the ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, “consubstantial”), and handed down to the universal Church.”

Theodoretus (*Letter to Andrew of Samosata* in Marius Mercator):

“He who had been sent from Egypt demands a subscription to the condemnation made earlier and that the doctrine of the holy bishop Nestorius be anathematized. But your Holiness knows that if anyone indiscriminately anathematizes the doctrine of that same most holy and venerable bishop, it is as though he appeared to anathematize piety itself. Therefore, if we are compelled at all, we must anathematize those who say that Christ is a mere human being, etc.”

Socrates (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 32):

“In my judgment, Nestorius imitates neither Paul of Samosata nor Photinus, nor does he say that the Lord is merely human; rather, he shrinks from the word Θεοτόκος as though it were a mask and avoids it.”

And afterward:

“From his books, some of which I have read, and partly from the speech of his associates, I have discovered that Nestorius held this opinion, etc.”

# CHAPTER VI. What the formula of faith was, and by whom it was prescribed, to which subscription was required in the Pelagian case.

Just as in the Eutychian case there was no other formula of faith than the letter of Saint Leo on the Incarnation addressed to Flavian, so in the Pelagian case there was no other regular authority to which subscription had to be made, as Prosper, who is believed to be the author, puts it, than the *Tractoria* of Zosimus addressed to all the bishops of the entire world, as all the writers of the fifth century report (in the appendix to Saint Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul).

Among others, Marius Mercator most clearly testifies to this (*Memorial*, Part II):

“All these chapters written above, as has already been said, are contained in that letter of Bishop Zosimus, of blessed memory, which is called the *Tractoria*, by which Coelestius and Pelagius were condemned. It was sent both to Constantinople and throughout the whole world and was strengthened by the subscriptions of the holy Fathers. Julianus and his other accomplices, however, refusing to subscribe to it and unwilling to make themselves of one mind with those same Fathers, were not only deposed and stripped of office by imperial laws but also by priestly decrees, and were expelled from all Italy.”

Earlier he had written as follows (ibid., Part VI):

“Coelestius was condemned with an extensive, or very lengthy, writing by the aforesaid Bishop Zosimus, of blessed memory. In it the very chapters on which he had been accused are contained, and the whole case, both concerning the aforementioned Coelestius and concerning Pelagius, his still more depraved teacher, appears to have been narrated—we also have copies of these writings here. We suggest that similar and identical writings were sent to the Eastern Churches, the diocese of Egypt, Constantinople, Thessalonica, and Jerusalem, addressed to the bishops.”

From these testimonies the following six points are gathered, to which the writers of the fifth century gave corresponding testimony.

First, that Zosimus wrote a lengthy letter containing the entire case of Pelagius and Coelestius, including excerpts from their books.

Augustine (*On Original Sin*, chapter 21):

“After the rescripts of the African council, in which province that pestilential doctrine had indeed spread by creeping, although it had not occupied and penetrated it so deeply, other matters also became evident concerning him in the city of Rome, where he had lived for a very long time and where he had previously been engaged in these speeches and disputes. They had been brought forward through the care of faithful brothers, and Pope Zosimus attached them to his letters, which he composed to be carried throughout the Catholic world, as you can read, as things deserving execration. There Pelagius, as though expounding the Apostle Paul’s Letter to the Romans, argues and says, etc.”

And writing to Optatus (*Letter* 195):

“Pelagius’s argument, which, among his other condemnable statements, was also appended to the letters of the apostolic see, is as follows, etc.”

Second, that in Zosimus’s *Tractoria* the heretical doctrines were condemned together with their authors.

Augustine:

“Since Pelagius and Coelestius were the authors, or at least the most vehement and notorious advocates, of this new heresy, the vigilance of the episcopal councils, with the assistance of the Savior who protects his Church, and also the vigilance of two venerable bishops of the apostolic see, Pope Innocent and Pope Zosimus, condemned them throughout the Christian world—unless they corrected themselves and also performed penance. We have taken care to send you examples of the recent documents concerning them, whether those that flowed from that see specifically to the Africans or those sent universally to all bishops, in case they have not yet reached your Fraternity.”

[Col. 0434A] Third, that the same *Tractoria* was sent to all the bishops of the entire world.

Augustine, both in the passages previously cited and in prescribing to Valentinus what should be read against the Pelagian heresy (*Letter* 215):

“And what was written by Pope Zosimus concerning the African council, and his rescript to the bishops of the entire world.”

Prosper (*Against the Collator*, chapter 10):

“The most holy see of blessed Peter speaks to the whole world through the mouth of Pope Zosimus in this way: ‘But we, by the prompting of God, etc.’”

The author of the appendix to Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul:

“The regular authority of Pope Zosimus, of blessed memory, directs us toward this judgment, when, writing to the bishops of the entire world, he says: ‘But we, by the prompting of God, etc.’ This speech, radiant with the light of the most sincere truth, was venerated with such honor by the African bishops that they wrote back to the same man as follows: ‘But the statement that you placed in the letters which you arranged to be sent to all the provinces, saying, “But we,” etc.’”

Fourth, that this was subscribed by all the bishops.

Prosper (*Poem Against the Ungrateful*, chapter 9):

“Indeed you admit that these were condemned

by councils, and by the hand of the world.”

And elsewhere (*Against the Collator*, chapter 41):

“The Catholic army does not permit those whom it has conquered to breathe again; against whose destruction it has written one sentence by the single hand of all the priests, etc.”

And near the end (ibid., chapter 41):

“By the decrees of the African councils, Pope Zosimus, of blessed memory, added the strength of his judgment, and for the cutting down of the impious he armed the right hands of all the bishops with Peter’s sword.”

Fifth, that Julianus and his accomplices refused to subscribe.

Julianus himself, together with his sixteen fellow bishops, says—as Augustine reports (Julianus in his letter to Rufus of Thessalonica, in Augustine, Book IV, *To Boniface*, chapter 8 and at the end):

“They say that a subscription was extorted from simple bishops sitting in their own places without the gathering of a synod, etc.”

And elsewhere (*Profession of Faith*, Part IV):

“Through fear of God we do not dare to subscribe to the condemnation of absent persons, having been taught by the Scriptures that human will ought not to be preferred to the commandments of God, which says: ‘You shall not believe a false report,’ etc.”

Sixth and finally, that Julianus and his accomplices were therefore deposed, etc.

Prosper (*Book Against the Collator*, chapter 1):

“He does not permit those whom he has conquered to breathe again, against whose destruction he has written one sentence by the single hand of all the priests. Driven from the pontificate and deprived of communion, they complain as though about the happiness of our victory and arm their tongues against us—those who preferred to be exiles from the truth rather than citizens of the Church.”

I see that two objections can be made by those who might think that another formula of faith was to be subscribed: some may hold for the decree of Innocent I, others for the eight African canons, which are at times attributed to the Council of Milevis.

The following testimonies appear to support the decree of Innocent:

Gennadius (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 43):

“Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote a decree addressed to the bishops of the Western and Eastern Churches against the Pelagians, which his successor Zosimus later promulgated more broadly.”

The African Fathers (Prosper, *Against the Collator*, chapter 10):

“We determined that the sentence pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius by the venerable Bishop Innocent, from the see of the most blessed Apostle Peter, should remain in force until they openly confess, etc.”

Augustine (*On Original Sin*, chapter 7):

“Zosimus dealt with the man, Coelestius, whom the wind of false doctrine had inflated, so that he would condemn the things that had been charged against him by the deacon Paulinus, and so that he would assent to the letters of the apostolic see that had proceeded from his predecessor, of holy memory. But he refused to condemn the charges of the deacon; nevertheless, he did not dare to resist the letters of blessed Innocent, etc.”

The following testimonies appear to support the African canons:

Prosper (*Against the Collator*, chapter 10):

“With two hundred and fourteen priests, whose constitution against the enemies of the grace of God the whole world embraced with a true profession, etc.”

And in the *Chronicle* (under the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII):

“At a council held at Carthage, the synodal decrees of 214 bishops were brought to Pope Zosimus. When these had been approved throughout the world, the Pelagian heresy was condemned.”

Usserius (*On the Origins of the British Church*), following Salmasius (*On the Eucharist*), concedes this position, but more from sentiment than from reason; for each of them, being a heretic, prefers to think absurdly rather than miss an opportunity to detract something from the authority of the supreme pontiff.

But that “constitution” which the true Prosper mentions is precisely the one by which the African Fathers wished the sentence pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius through the venerable bishop Innocent, from the see of the most blessed apostle Peter, to remain in force—as no prudent person can fail to understand. [Col. 0435B] That sentence, moreover, certainly differs in no respect from the decree issued to the bishops of the Western and Eastern Churches, which Gennadius mentions, as is evident in itself. Since, therefore, Innocent’s decree differed from Zosimus’s *tractoria* only in this respect—that the former contained Catholic doctrine more compactly, the latter more fully—certainly neither Prosper, nor Gennadius, nor Augustine, nor the African Fathers disagree with Marius Mercator; rather, they wonderfully confirm his judgment and at the same time demonstrate that the ancients believed—if not always, at least at the time when a heresy was condemned without the gathering of a general synod—that, because of the breadth of its authority, the apostolic see had the right to propose to the whole Church throughout the inhabited world the form of faith.

Hence Saint Innocent wrote to the Fathers of the Council of Carthage (*Patrologia*, vol. XX, col. 582):

> [Col. 0435C] I rejoice, dearest brothers, that while you care for those Churches over which you preside, you show your concern for the benefit of all, and ask that throughout all the Churches of the entire world a decision be made for the common good of everyone, so that the Church, strengthened by its regulations and confirmed by a just decree, may not be exposed to such men, etc.

And to the bishops of Numidia assembled in the Council of Milevis (*the cited volume of Patrologia*, col. 588):

> Whenever the rule of faith is debated, I believe that all our brothers and fellow bishops ought to refer the matter only to Peter—that is, to the author of his name and honor—as your affection has now referred it, so that it may be able to benefit all the Churches throughout the world in common.

Hence also Augustine (*Sermon 2, On the Words of the Apostle*):

> On this matter—the Pelagian matter—two councils have already been sent to the apostolic see; replies have also come from there. The matter is finished.

[Col. 0435D]

## CHAPTER VII. By what authority the law requiring subscription was enacted: by priestly authority alone, or also by imperial authority

That the forces of both authorities were joined for the destruction of a single heresy, and for compelling all who resisted to subscribe to its condemnation, is clear from what has been said. For we reported the constitution of the emperor Honorius to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, concerning the enforcement of subscriptions. It is unnecessary to repeat it here; only its concluding words, which contain the necessity of requiring subscriptions, deserve more careful consideration:

> Your Holiness will not permit men of a detestable sect, devising new and unprecedented things to the injury of religion, to conceal in secret discussions a sacrilege once publicly condemned by authority. For there is one and the same guilt in those who, either by concealing their connivance or by failing to condemn, have offered harmful support.

We also reported the letter written by Aurelius, after receiving the constitution, to all the bishops of the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana. In it, just as in the constitution, this principal reason for requiring a subscription is set forth:

> [Col. 0436A] So that, once the subscription of all of you has been fully given to the condemnation of the aforesaid heretics, there may be absolutely nothing from which any suspicion might justly appear to remain—whether of dissimulation, negligence, or perhaps hidden depravity.

As was said in the preceding dissertation, imperial legislation was occasioned by the obstinacy of certain bishops who either supported the perverse arguments of the Pelagians by silent consent or failed to destroy them through public opposition, and who, either by concealing their connivance or by failing to condemn, offered harmful support. Since they refused to obey the plenary council’s demand for a subscription to Zosimus’s *tractoria*, which they had received in the preceding year, they appeared to require compulsion by imperial authority.

Indeed, as soon as Zosimus’s *tractoria* had been received, the plenary Council of Africa required a subscription from all the bishops established in the province, including those who had attended the council. For the pontiff had ordered the bishops of the entire world to do the same, and Julian himself admits this: first, in his letter to Rufus of Thessalonica, where he complains that a subscription was extorted from simple bishops sitting in their own places, without the assembly of a synod (*Augustine, Book IV to Boniface, chapter 8*); and then in his *Book of Faith* (Part IV, no. 3), in the words previously cited:

> But this matter, your Holiness, etc.

[Col. 0436B] For what else do these words signify than that the subscription had been commanded before Julian wrote either his letter or his *Book of Faith*? He wrote both while Zosimus was still alive, that is, in the year 418, at which time the imperial rescript had not yet been issued, since it is dated to the consuls of the following year, Monaxius and Plinta. The law requiring subscription, therefore, was first enacted by priestly authority and afterward by imperial authority.

[Col. 0436C] Possidius proves this admirably (*Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 48):

> Those prelates of so great a see—Innocent and Zosimus—at different times marking the same men, the Pelagians, and cutting them off from the members of the Church, decreed in letters sent to the Churches of Africa, the East, and the West that they were to be anathematized and avoided by all Catholics. When the most devout emperor Honorius heard and followed this judgment pronounced against them by the Catholic Church of God, he decreed that, condemned by the laws, they were to be regarded among the heretics.

Let us further confirm by the testimony of writers of that age the union of both authorities for this same purpose.

Prosper:

> When Pope Boniface, of blessed memory, rejoiced in the Catholic devotion of the most devout emperors, against the enemies of God’s grace he used **not only apostolic edicts but also royal ones** (*Book against the Collator*, chapter 41).

Marius Mercator (*Commonitorium*, part XI):

> Julian and his other accomplices, refusing to subscribe, were **deposed and deprived of office not only by imperial laws but also by priestly statutes**, and were driven out of all Italy.

Saint Coelestine, after the synod, to the Fathers of Ephesus (*Third part of the Council of Ephesus*, chapter 20):

> [Col. 0436D] Let them be expelled from their cities, and let them know that they will not remain in our fellowship unless, **according to the ecclesiastical constitution and that of the Christian emperors**, they condemn what has been condemned together with its authors and associates, etc.

Gelasius to Honorius, bishop of Dalmatia (*Letter 5*):

> Or perhaps you do not know that this heresy of which we speak was long ago overthrown by the apostolic see through Blessed Innocent and afterward through Zosimus, Boniface, Coelestine, Sixtus, and Leo, in continuous and unremitting judgments; and that it was condemned **not only by the laws of the Catholic Church but also by those of the Roman emperors** of that time, etc.

And writing to the bishops throughout Picenum (*Letter 7*):

> We have proved that Pelagius, Coelestius, Julian, and many other men of oratorical eloquence were convicted in this assertion and **struck both by ecclesiastical constitutions and by imperial commands**.

[Col. 0437A]

## CHAPTER VIII. To whom subscription was commanded: only to bishops, or also to others of the clergy, indeed sometimes even to laymen; and what penalty was established for those who refused

That it was commanded of bishops is attested by Julian in his letter to Rufus of Thessalonica (*Augustine, Book IV to Boniface, final chapter*):

> A subscription was extorted from simple bishops sitting in their own places, without the assembly of a synod.

And in the *Book of Faith* (Part IV, no. 3):

> But this matter, your Holiness, etc.

The emperors say in the edict to Aurelius:

> For correcting the obstinacy of certain bishops, etc.

Aurelius to the bishops of the province of Byzacena, etc.:

> How each one of you ought to subscribe, etc.

Marius Mercator (*Commonitorium*):

> Julian and his other accomplices, etc.

[Col. 0437B] That it was also commanded of presbyters and the other clergy, Augustine teaches clearly enough (*Letters 191 and 194*), when he recounts what Sixtus, a presbyter at Rome, did in the case of the Pelagians, and how, after the sentence of condemnation pronounced by Zosimus, he led the entire clergy in anathematizing not only the doctrines but also the authors of the doctrines.

That the anathema was pronounced not only orally but also in writing is clearly proved by the reproach made by Julian to the Roman clergy (*Book II to Boniface*, chapter 3), in the name of eighteen bishops. Augustine refers to it as follows:

> They even accuse the Roman clergy, writing that, struck by the terror of the command, they were not ashamed to commit the crime of treachery, so that, contrary to their earlier sentence, by which they had supported the Catholic doctrine in the official records, they afterward declared human nature to be evil.

For, as has already been shown more than once, that command was issued by Zosimus in his *tractoria*, requiring everyone to subscribe; directly, indeed, from the bishops of the major sees, but through them from the lesser sees, and through the lesser sees from the clergy of each individual Church.

[Col. 0437C] The statements that will shortly be cited from Saint Leo and the Fathers of Ephesus concerning the penalty established for those who refused to subscribe must be understood to include laymen as well. For from the penalty inflicted for violating the law it is easy to determine what the law commanded and to whom.

The statement of Prosper, so often praised above, applies to everyone in common (*Poem against Ingratitude*, chapter 9):

> Surely you confess that these things were condemned,  
> swiftly, by the hand of the whole world.

It is now understood that for bishops, presbyters, and clerics of every rank who refused to subscribe, the penalty established was deposition and expulsion from their cities, indeed also excommunication.

First, from the emperor’s letter to Aurelius (*Edict of Honorius and Theodosius*):

> Whoever, through impious obstinacy, neglects to subscribe to the condemnation of those mentioned above shall be punished by the loss of his episcopate, expelled from his cities with a perpetual prohibition, and deprived of communion.

[Col. 0437D] Next, from the *Commonitorium* of Marius Mercator (part XI):

> Julian and his other accomplices, refusing to subscribe, were **deposed and deprived of office not only by imperial laws but also by priestly statutes, and were driven out of all Italy**.

Third, from the letter of Nestorius to Saint Coelestine (*First part of the Council of Ephesus*, chapter 15), concerning those Pelagians who had refused to subscribe:

> I have often written to Your Beatitude concerning Julian, Orontius, and the others who usurp episcopal dignity, who make frequent appeals to the most devout and renowned emperor, and cut us down with continual lamentations, as though, in orthodox times, **they had been driven out of the West**, etc.

Fourth, from the letter of Saint Coelestine in reply to Nestorius (*same work*, chapter 17):

> These heretics also, about whom you wished to consult us as though ignorant of what had been done, just condemnation has expelled from their sees those who speak unjustly.

[Col. 0438A] Fifth, from canons 1, 2, and 4 of the Council of Ephesus (*second part of that council*, act 7). These establish the penalty of deposition against metropolitans, provincial bishops, and clerics who were clearly found to follow the opinions of Nestorius and Coelestius because they refused to condemn Nestorius with us. The holy synod decreed by common decision that such men **were to be excluded from all ecclesiastical communion and deprived of every priestly function** by which they could either harm or benefit anyone.

Finally, from the letter of Saint Leo to Nicetas (*Letter 86*):

> All presbyters, deacons, and clerics of whatever rank who belong to the fellowship of the Pelagians and Coelestians, etc.—if any one of them refuses to comply with salutary commands, whether he be a cleric or a layman, **let him be expelled from the fellowship of the Church**, lest, having destroyed his own soul, he plot against another’s salvation.

[Col. 0438B] Canon 7 of Ephesus also concerns laymen themselves (*second part of the Council of Ephesus*, act 7):

> Likewise, if any should wish by any means to disturb what was done concerning individuals by the holy synod of Ephesus, the holy synod itself decreed that, if they are bishops or clerics, they shall utterly fall from their own rank; **but if they are laymen, they shall be excommunicated**.

The sanction of the Caesar Valentinian must also belong here, at least insofar as bishops are concerned. It was issued at Aquileia on the eighth day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the eleventh time and Valentinian (*Book 47, On Bishops, in the Theodosian Code*):

> Since various bishops are following the wicked error of the Pelagian and Coelestian doctrine, we order that, unless within twenty days from the time of their citation—during which we grant them the opportunity for deliberation—they correct their errors and restore themselves to the faith of the Catholics, they be **expelled from the Gallic regions and a more faithful priesthood be appointed in their place**.

(See Sirmondus in the appendix to the Code.)

[Col. 0438C]

## CHAPTER IX. What objections those who refused to subscribe raised, and how the objection of the refusers was construed

Those who refused to subscribe objected partly to the judgment of the apostolic see, partly to the procedure by which subscription was demanded, and finally to the imperial sanction. They did so in such a way as to deny that they could, with a safe conscience, or ought, while observing due legal procedure, to obey the command of any authority by which they were compelled to subscribe—that is, to condemn, as they claimed, men who were pious and above all Catholic, by a rash judgment.

Against the judgment of the apostolic see they objected that the proper judicial procedure had not been observed; that suitable judges had not been present; and that the holy Zosimus, together with the Roman clergy, had committed treachery.

They attempted to establish that the proper procedure had not been observed on the grounds that the nature of judicial proceedings requires the accusers to be present, the defendants to be heard, and no one to be condemned in his absence. They claimed that neither the bishops Erotes and Lazarus, nor the deacon Paulinus, nor the two young men Timasius and Jacobus, who accused Pelagius and Coelestius, had been present at the Roman trial. Pelagius and Coelestius, they said, had not been sufficiently heard: the former had not been summoned to Rome from Palestine, while the latter, forced by fear to be absent from the trial, had been away precisely when the matter most required his presence.

[Col. 0438D] Julian raises this objection in the following words (*Book of Faith*, part IV, no. 4 and following):

> Even the Jews admit that our law does not judge a man unless it has heard from the man himself and learned what he does. And in the Acts of the Apostles a similar sentence was pronounced by Festus, a Gentile, when he said that it was not the Roman custom to condemn anyone before the accused had his accusers present and received an opportunity to defend himself and clear away the charges (Acts 25:16). Therefore Saint Paul the Apostle, establishing a rule of judgment for bishops, says: “Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter except on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (1 Timothy 5:19). Confirmed, then, by these and other testimonies, we fear pronouncing sentence upon the heads of absent men who have not been heard by us, unless they have been present and refuted.

[Col. 0439A] They raised three complaints concerning the judges.

First, that they had pronounced sentence without the assembly of a synod. Augustine says (*Book IV to Boniface*, chapter 8):

> They say that our statements were accepted by their enemies out of hatred for the truth, and that throughout the entire West a dogma no less foolish than impious was embraced; and they complain that, to confirm this, a subscription was extorted from simple bishops sitting in their own places, without the assembly of a synod.

Second, that the judges had approached the examination of the case with hostile dispositions. Augustine says (*Book III against Julian*, chapter 1):

> Concerning the judges before whom, you say, you were unable to conduct your case because no one properly deliberates about doubtful matters unless he brings a heart free from hatred, anger, and friendship—you say that those who judged your case were not such men, because they began to hate it before they came to know it. I have already answered this in the preceding book, etc.

[Col. 0439B] Third, that they lacked both the learning necessary to understand the truth and the virtue necessary to defend it. The entire final chapter of the second book against Julian concerns this matter, where Augustine responds to the heretic’s objection that his case had been condemned by ignorant men by setting against him ten exceptionally learned holy Fathers. The first and second chapters of Book V of the *Unfinished Work* likewise concern it. There Julian, after discussing at length the knowledge and courage of the judges, finally concludes:

> For it was chiefly because of this baseness of cowardly hearts that the foul doctrine of the Manichaeans sails through the shipwrecks of the Churches; for if a free and manly authority had stood firm in those who exercised the priestly office, the inventions of the Traducians would have been destroyed by public assent just as invincible reason has overthrown them.

[Col. 0439C] Concerning the accusation made by the Pelagians against Zosimus and the Roman clergy, Augustine writes (*Book I against Julian*, chapter 4):

> You accuse the successor of Innocent of the crime of treachery because he did not oppose apostolic doctrine and the judgment of his predecessor. But for the moment I say nothing about this, lest I inflame your mind—which I desire to heal rather than provoke—with praise of the man who condemned you.

And elsewhere (*Book VI against Julian*, chapter 12):

> What kind of conduct is it to accuse Blessed Zosimus, bishop of the apostolic see, of treachery so that you may persist in your perversity? He did not depart from his predecessor Innocent, whose name you were afraid to mention; but you preferred Zosimus because he initially dealt more leniently with Coelestius, etc.

And again (*Book II to Boniface*, chapter 3):

> They even accuse the Roman clergy, writing that, struck by the terror of the command, they were not ashamed to admit the crime of treachery.

There is also Julian’s tacit but malicious reproach of the supreme pontiff, as though he had committed the very fault with which Julian accused the Africans when he pronounced sentence against Pelagius and Coelestius. For the shameless heretic uses the same scriptural testimonies and the same words to incriminate the judgment of the apostolic see that the holy pontiff had used to criticize what Julian regarded as the Africans’ rash judgment.

[Col. 0439D] The letter that Zosimus sent to the Africans on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October (*Letter 4 to the Africans*) should be compared with Julian’s words (*Book of Faith*, part IV, no. 3):

> But this matter, your Holiness, etc.

When subscription was required to the condemnation not only of the doctrines but also of their authors, the bishops in whose name Julian wrote objected that such a subscription was a kind of judgment or public testimony pronounced by the subscribers against those men. They themselves, however, out of fear of God, Christian charity, and the apostolic command, neither could nor ought, no matter what persons commanded them, to subscribe to the condemnation of absent and unheard men who cleared themselves in written statements, professed themselves Catholics, and condemned the charges brought against them—men whose case was either doubtful in itself or burdened only by popular hostility.

Julian says in the *Book of Faith* (part IV):

> [Col. 0440A] All these matters now under discussion—that is, the matters we condemned at the end—were themselves condemned in their own written statements by the very men against whom these things are alleged, who testified that the charges had been falsely brought against them.

And shortly afterward:

> We do not dare, out of fear of God, to subscribe to the condemnation of absent men. We have been taught by the Scriptures that human will must not be preferred to God’s commands, and we say: “You shall not accept a false report, nor shall you agree with the wicked to be an unjust witness” (Exodus 23:1, according to the Septuagint). And lest anyone think that the multitude should be followed, he added: “You shall not join the many in wrongdoing” (ibid.). And again: “Before you investigate, do not accuse anyone.” And again: “Speak what your eyes have seen.” Likewise in the Gospel: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. Do not condemn, so that you may not be condemned; for with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged, and with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matthew 7:1–2). Therefore Saint Paul the Apostle, establishing a rule of judgment for bishops, says: “Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter except on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (1 Timothy 5:19). Confirmed, then, by these and other testimonies, we fear pronouncing sentence upon the heads of absent men who have not been heard by us, unless they have been present and refuted.

[Col. 0440B] Against the emperor’s sanction they objected, first, that it had been solicited by their adversaries because of the weakness of their case, so that those whom they could not overcome by reason they might crush by the weight of authority. Augustine writes (*Book III against Julian*, chapter 1):

> You should now repent of this whole error, lest you use the wretched argument employed by all heretics, whom the laws of Catholic emperors restrain from pernicious license. All such men say what you yourself have said: that the side which introduces terror in place of argument suffers from a lack of reason, obtaining no assent from the wise but extorting blind assent from the fearful. You are indeed new heretics, but with the others you have recognized and retained this old saying of almost all heretics.

Second, they claimed that the emperor’s favor had been purchased by gifts to powerful men. Julian says (*Book I of the Unfinished Work*, chapter 42):

> [Col. 0440C] Your colleague Alypius recently brought horses, fattened throughout Africa, to more than eighty tribunes.

And later (*ibid.*, chapter 72):

> The greatness of our case is indicated not only by consideration and weighing of the matters we defend but also by your fear. You fight against our blood by pouring out money, distributing inheritances, stirring up peoples, and corrupting authorities; you are ashamed to profess the faith which we attack, and you take refuge in the words of our position, from which you deviate.

And elsewhere:

> Why did you stir up all Italy with such factions? Why did you incite riots at Rome by hiring crowds? Why did you fatten throughout almost the whole of Africa herds of horses, which, with Alypius pursuing the matter, you assigned to tribunes and centurions? Why did you corrupt the powers of this world by offering the inheritances of matrons, so that the straw of public fury might burn against us? Why did you disturb the peace of the Churches? Why did you stain the reign of a devout ruler with the impiety of persecutions?

[Col. 0440D] Third, Julian claimed that the law had been obtained by underhand means (*Book I of the Unfinished Work*, chapter 9):

> Augustine praises a powerful man because, when we were loudly demanding that judges be appointed for our case—demanding nothing other than that what had evidently been done by underhand means should be corrected rather than exposed to examination—he resisted us by the weight of his dignity and did not allow us to obtain a time or place for debate.

Finally, they claimed that the law itself favored the Pelagians. Augustine writes (*Book III against Julian*, chapter 1):

> Indeed, as you say, if the emperor’s reply was rather in your favor, why do you not come forward and voluntarily cite this before the public authorities, showing that you are those whose faith the Christian ruler approved? But you understand the law of faith not as it stands, but as it pleases you. What wonder, then, if you do the same with the emperor’s law?

[Col. 0441A] Pelagius had set the example for his followers. When his doctrines had been condemned at the Council of Diospolis, he sent a letter to a friend, giving a false account of the entire affair, and boasted as though he had triumphed over his adversaries and his error had been approved by the bishops:

> The decision of fourteen bishops confirmed our definition, in which we said that “a man can be without sin and easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes.” This decision covered the mouth of contradiction with confusion and separated from one another the entire company conspiring for evil.

Augustine replies:

> Whether Pelagius truly wrote this letter, or whether it was fabricated by someone else under his name, who does not see how he boasts here of the error and judgment by which he was convicted and condemned as though it were a victory?

The emperor interpreted the objection of those who refused to subscribe as impious obstinacy, secret dealings, connivance, and support offered to a sacrilege publicly condemned by authority.

Aurelius regarded it as suspicious evidence either of dissimulation, negligence, or hidden depravity (*Letter to the bishops of the province of Byzacena*).

[Col. 0441B] Saint Leo judged it to be a stratagem (*Letter 86, to Nicetas of Aquileia*) by which those who refused to subscribe thought that none of their opinions could remain safe unless they either added something to or removed something from the common formula.

## CHAPTER X. What other stratagems those who refused to subscribe used for evasion

Those obstinate, suspect, and crafty men did not merely object to what we have so far described, though that in itself involved great audacity. They further demanded something that was the height of impudence: either that the case be reconsidered before suitable judges, or even that the Catholics condemn the very propositions which they themselves were accused of holding.

[Col. 0441C] Coelestius, in his letter to the Roman clergy (*Book I to Boniface*, chapter 23):

> Let no one, then, deceive you, nor let the impious deny that they hold these things. But if they speak the truth, let them either be granted a hearing, or at least let those very bishops who now disagree condemn what I have stated above—that they hold these things with the Manichaeans—as we condemn the things they allege against us, and let there be complete concord.

The words of Julian cited shortly afterward belong here, where he speaks of Augustine (*Book I of the Unfinished Work*, chapter 9):

> He also praises a powerful man, etc.

The slanderous reproach of Theodore of Mopsuestia against Augustine also belongs here. Theodore wrote five books against him (*Book II, near the end*):

> That remarkable defender of original sin could perceive none of these matters, since he had by no means been trained in the divine Scriptures and had not learned the sacred writings from childhood. Rather, whether declaiming about the meaning of Scripture or about doctrine, he frequently drew many foolish things, in his own or in common terms, from Scripture and from various doctrines. For fear of power prevented him from speaking openly against them; only those who possessed knowledge of the divine Scriptures withdrew silently.

(See the excerpt in Marius Mercator, no. 2.)

[Col. 0441D] If they could not obtain this demand, they nevertheless dared, in the customary manner of heretics, to appeal to a hearing before an ecumenical synod, as though the matter had not already been sufficiently concluded once the apostolic see had sent a renewed reply of condemnation—and one so solemn that, having been sent to all the bishops of the world, it had been subscribed, as Prosper says, “by the hand of the world.”

Julian says (*Book of Faith*, part IV, no. 2):

> We have written and sent these matters to Your Holiness as they appeared to us according to the Catholic rule. If you think they must be held otherwise, write back. But if these propositions cannot be contradicted, and yet someone wishes to stir up scandal against us, let Your Holiness be certain that we have appealed to a hearing before a plenary synod.

If even this did not succeed according to their wishes, and they were unwillingly compelled to condemn their own opinions or those of their associates, they promised to do so only with this qualification: they would conceal their impiety under words apparently religious. For they declared that they rejected the propositions brought against them according to the mind of the Church—being, of course, certain that afterward they could interpret the “mind of the Church” in whatever direction they wished.

[Col. 0442A] Pelagius first did this at Diospolis (*Book on the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 19):

> What I said were not my own opinions I reject according to the judgment of the holy Church, pronouncing anathema against everyone who opposes and contradicts the doctrines of the holy Church. For I believe in the unity of one substance, and I believe everything according to the doctrine of the holy Catholic Church. But if anyone holds an opinion foreign to this, let him be anathema.

Augustine revealed what kind of malicious or rather foolish trickery lay hidden beneath the words “according to the judgment of the Church” (*same work*, chapter 33).

Coelestius next did the same, following his teacher’s example (*Book on Original Sin*, chapter 7, and *Book II to Boniface*, chapter 3). When the supreme pontiff pressed him to condemn the charges brought against him, he replied that he agreed with the letters of Saint Innocent and rejected whatever the apostolic see rejected. Augustine should be consulted on this matter.

[Col. 0442B] Julian not only imitated both men but surpassed them. When Zosimus’s *tractoria* had to be subscribed, and five propositions were proscribed in it, he attached to each his own interpretation by which he rejected the propositions. Marius Mercator discussed this at length (*Book of Subnotations*, chapter 6), and we have explained it in our notes to Mercator.

This also pertains to the fact that in their *Books of Faith* Pelagius and Coelestius promised that they would acquiesce in the definitions of the apostolic see. But this was the trickery of faithless men, by which they evaded the sentence of a just judgment and appeared to embrace the pillar of truth at the very time when they wished to undermine it.

If even this fraud proved useless, then, when the obstinacy of their minds burst forth, they appealed with a kind of noble hypocrisy, in words full of boasting, declaring that no force could ever move them from their position, but that they would steadfastly suffer persecution for the Catholic faith even in orthodox times, following the example of those noble martyrs who, as Julian says, standing near the blazing furnace, fearlessly answered the king who compelled them:

> [Col. 0442C] “God is able, O king, to deliver us from this furnace,” etc. (Daniel 3:17).

After elaborating on the sentence of the Babylonian youths, that most vain man theatrically declaimed as follows:

> From this discipline, too, which illustrious teachers have handed down, we understand that in prosperous circumstances moderation in our desires is to be maintained, but in the doctrines of faith, steadfastness of purpose. We desire, once the swelling of persecutions has been restrained, to help the peoples as well.
