But if that does not happen, we stand ready to endure whatever is bitter—insults and dangers—rather than fail to shun the filth and foulness of the Manichaeans.

He used no less exaggerated language in the *Book of Faith* (part IV, no. 9):

> Let Your Holiness be certain that, however much this sea may swell as the winds blow and rise against us in bitter waves, it will never be able to shake the house of sound judgment founded upon the justice of Christ.

[Col. 0442D] These passages appear to be excerpts from a book *On Constancy for the Defense of the Truth against All Who Resist It*, which Julian wrote to his followers at the time when Boniface, the supreme pontiff, was using not only apostolic but also royal edicts to compel those of the clergy who wished to retain their sees, their ranks, and communion with the faithful to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius. That heretic did what others commonly do: he abused the statements of highly learned and orthodox men, indeed even the examples of the saints, to harden the minds of those who shared his error, so that they might resist the authorities of the Church and of the world, just as martyrs resisted tyrants and persecutors of the faith.

Augustine testifies that heretics were accustomed to do this in his own time, and even to call what they suffered at the hands of rulers “martyrdoms.” He says this in many places, especially in his reply to the letter of Parmenianus, in which Tichonius urged that persecution be endured rather than that the Donatist cause be abandoned. Augustine writes (*Book III against the Letter of Parmenianus*, chapter 6):

> They dare to count sacrilegious schisms or impious heresies among the martyrdoms whenever, under the lash, they are admonished to correct themselves and suffer the penalties of their error, etc.

[Col. 0443A] On this occasion I cannot refrain from reporting an observation I made while reading the history of the fifth century: at that time there were no heretics—though there were many of them, and distinguished ones—who, when they saw their sect struck by the just thunderbolts of the Church, did not immediately scatter among the people books *On Constancy*, in which they outwardly exhorted their followers to imitate the examples of martyrs, while in reality, through the wicked arts of a false comparison, they accused the defenders of the faith appointed by God of a kind of tyrannical injustice, indeed of an impiety equal to that of the pagans.

Thus Nestorius, when Coelestius and his associates had been expelled from the imperial city by the most devout ruler Theodosius, encouraged them to steadfastness in asserting the truth (*Letter to Coelestius*), citing the examples of John, who suffered under Herod, and of Peter and Paul, who suffered under Nero.

Likewise, when he pitifully described to the prefect of the Thebaid what he was being forced to endure in exile, he loaded the emperors and magistrates with curses (*Evagrius, Book I, chapter 7*).

[Col. 0443B] Likewise Theodoretus, not yet recovered, sent letters to Constantinople (*Letter to Andrew the Monk, in Marius Mercator*) and, abusing this passage of the Apostle—“God is faithful, who will not allow us and you to be tempted beyond what we are able, but with the temptation will also provide a way forward”—so inflamed his followers to obstinacy that he simultaneously accused all who had agreed with “the Egyptian”—as he called Saint Cyril—of the injustice committed against Nestorius, and accused them of having condemned that most holy man. Yet Saint Coelestine, 275 bishops in the Council of Ephesus, and the most devout emperors Honorius and Valentinian had condemned him, etc.

[Col. 0443C] Augustine had already answered the first pretext for evasion, from the time of Innocent, when he spoke to the people about the Pelagians (*Sermon 2, On the Words of the Apostle*):

> My brothers, whenever you find such men, do not conceal them; let there not be in you a perverse mercy. Rebuke those who contradict and resist, and bring them to us. For two councils have already been sent to the apostolic see concerning this matter, and replies have also come from there. The matter is finished. Would that the error might at some point also be finished!

Saint Coelestine replied (*Letter to Nestorius, first part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 17*):

> Let the wretched lament that they were deceived by the hope they placed in men, when, because of their communion, the only help that could now be offered them was repentance.

And elsewhere (Part III of the Council of Ephesus, in the letter to the Fathers of Ephesus):

“Let them be expelled from their cities, and let them know that they will not belong to our fellowship unless, in accordance with the ecclesiastical decree and the decree of the Christian emperors, they declare themselves Catholic priests, condemning the condemned teachings along with their authors and associates.””

And again (ibid., in the letter to Maximian):

“Let your vigilance resist the Coelestian error, formerly restrained and known throughout the whole world by its condemnation, so that all who are followers of this doctrine may be excluded from all human society,” etc.

Concerning these responses of Coelestine, Prosper wrote as follows [Col. 0443D] (Book Against the Conference, ch. 41):

“Coelestine, the pontiff of venerable memory, to whom the Lord granted many gifts of his grace for the protection of the Catholic Church, knowing that those who had been condemned were owed not an examination at trial but only the remedy of repentance, ordered Coelestius—who was requesting a hearing as though the matter had not been investigated—to be expelled from the whole territory of Italy. So inviolably did he judge that the statutes of his predecessors and the decrees of synods had to be observed, THAT HE WOULD NEVER ALLOW WHAT HAD ONCE DESERVED TO BE CUT OFF TO BE RECONSIDERED.””

Augustine alone sufficiently refuted the second argument (Book IV to Boniface, final chapter):

“What do they mean when they say, ‘A signature was extorted from simple bishops without the convocation of a synod’? Or was a convocation really necessary for an obvious pestilence to be condemned? As though no heresy had ever been condemned except by the convocation of a synod; whereas, rather, those heresies are very rarely found for whose condemnation such a necessity has arisen, and there are many—and incomparably more—which, once they arose, deserved to be rejected and condemned there, and thus could become known throughout other lands as things to be avoided. Yet the pride of these men, which raises itself so high against God that it does not wish to glory in him but rather in free will, is understood to be seeking this glory as well: that, on their account, a synod of East and West should be convened. Since, with the Lord resisting them, they cannot corrupt the Catholic world, they at least attempt to disturb it; whereas, after a suitable and sufficient judgment has been rendered against them, they ought rather, through pastoral vigilance and diligence, to be crushed wherever these wolves appear—whether so that they may be healed and changed, or so that others may avoid them for the sake of their own salvation and integrity, with the Shepherd of shepherds assisting,” etc.

To the third argument and the others by which they protested that they were being forcibly oppressed, Augustine replied that their declarations promising obedience to the apostolic see were fraudulent; that their profession, by which they swore that they adhered to the Church’s sentence, was false; and that what they were suffering was not [Col. 0444B] PERSECUTION, BUT THE DISCIPLINE OF COERCION. He says (Book I of the Unfinished Work, ch. 9):

“Far be it from the Christian powers of the earthly commonwealth to doubt the ancient Catholic faith and, for that reason, to grant its attackers the opportunity and time for examination. Rather, being certain and firmly grounded in that faith, let them impose the discipline of coercion upon such enemies of it as you are,” etc.

And in the second book of the same work (ch. 105), when Julian said:

“For this reason you have obtained from the powers of the world, at any cost, the denial of an examination; for you understand that you must act in this way when you are abandoned by the aid of reason,”

Augustine replies:

“Why do you still seek an examination that has already taken place before the apostolic see, and that finally took place in the episcopal judgment in Palestine, where Pelagius, the originator of your error, would have been condemned if he had not condemned those doctrines that you defend? Therefore, this heresy no longer needs to be examined by bishops, but to be restrained by Christian powers.”

And in the third book of the earlier work (Book III Against Julian [Col. 0444C], ch. 1):

“Let the whole of this error of yours now bring you remorse, lest you employ the wretched argument used by all heretics, whom the laws of Christian emperors restrain from pernicious license.”

And shortly afterward (ibid.):

“Your case has now been concluded before the competent judgment of the common bishops, and no further proceedings need be brought against you insofar as the right of examination is concerned, except that you should peacefully follow the sentence pronounced in this matter. If you refuse, you must be restrained from turbulent or treacherous agitation.”

And later (ibid.):

“Do you think that you are therefore victors because you were not granted the examination you desired? The Maximianists preceded you in such empty talk, although the Catholic Church gave you the judgment it ought to have given, where your case was concluded.”

## CHAPTER XI. How the Church dealt with those who refused and those who repented

How the Church conducted itself toward those who refused is plainly evident both from what has been said thus far concerning the statutes of Zosimus and the emperors, and from the apostolic commands of Saints Coelestine, Leo, and Gelasius.

Saint Coelestine (Part III of the Council of Ephesus, ch. 20):

“Let them be expelled from their cities, and let them know that they will not belong to our fellowship,” etc.

Saint Leo (Letter 85):

“If anyone refuses to comply with salutary instructions, whether cleric or layman, let him be expelled from the fellowship of the Church, lest the destroyer of his own soul lie in wait for another’s salvation.”

Saint Gelasius (Letter 7, to the bishops throughout Picenum):

“Let it be enough that these offenses have been committed thus far, and, so that God may be appeased, let divine matters be attended to with greater diligence than human affairs. Let the defender of the aforesaid pestilence be found nowhere at all, and let him obtain neither access to the Church nor participation anywhere in Catholic communion—he who prefers, by his wicked profession, to follow the fellowship of heretics. And those with whom he is previously shown to have mixed in harmful conversation, unless they repent and withdraw from his association, are to be removed from ecclesiastical service and punished with deserved vengeance, so that an example may be provided for the rest to avoid. Let him approach no one, nor let him anywhere any longer be permitted to utter the blasphemy long ago condemned.””

How great was the indulgence with which those who repented were received by the Church is evident partly from the decree of Innocent, which was religiously obeyed, and partly from the testimony of Possidius and Mercator. For when Innocent first condemned Pelagius and Coelestius, he exercised such apostolic foresight that, just as he prescribed the punishment of the obstinate, so he also prescribed the reception of penitents. “They must be removed,” he says (Letter to the Fathers of the Council of Carthage), “far away and kept at a distance from the Church’s inmost parts, lest an incurable error, occupying many for too long, should grow stronger. For if they remain in this impunity for a long time, they will necessarily lead many into the perversity of their own mind and deceive the innocent—or rather, the unwary—who do not follow the Catholic faith. For they will think that those people hold the right opinion whom they continue to see remaining in the Church. [Col. 0445B] Therefore let the incurable wound be separated from the sound body; and, once the breath of the raging disease has been removed, let what is sound endure more securely, and let the purer flock be cleansed of the contagion of this diseased sheep. Let the perfection of the whole body remain unblemished. But if they condemn what they have held until now, it will be within the power of the pontiffs to assist them to some extent and to care for their wounds, just as the Church ordinarily does not refuse such care to the fallen when they have repented,” etc.

He had also written to the Fathers of the Council of Milevis in the same sense (quoted by Augustine, Letter 93):

“By the authority of apostolic vigor, we decree that Pelagius and Coelestius are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion until they repent of the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive,” etc. “They must be cut off WHO DISTURB YOU AND WISH TO PERVERT THE GOSPEL OF CHRIST” (Gal. 1:7). “At the same time, we command that whoever attempts to defend this with similar obstinacy be bound by an equal punishment, since I do not think there is much difference between the intention of one who commits an offense and the favor of one who consents,” etc. “We command this because the Lord has made known by his own will that he does not desire the death of the dying, but only that he should turn back and live. If at any time, once they are restored to health, they repent after abandoning the error of their wicked doctrine, and condemn what they had condemned themselves by transgressing, the Church must not deny them their customary medicine—that is, its place of refuge—lest, while we perhaps prevent them from returning, they remain truly outside the fold and be devoured by the jaws of the waiting enemy.”

Zosimus followed this law, as Augustine testifies (On Original Sin, ch. 22):

“Since it is clear that there existed a pestilential doctrine and a heretical error, which, with the Lord’s help, the Church now avoids more openly, these two men—Pelagius and Coelestius—were either reduced to a place of repentance or, if they refused this, condemned altogether,” etc.

Prosper speaks of the same pontiff (Poem Against the Ungrateful, ch. 2):

> Thus severe goodness governed his law,
>
> so that those who wished to return from condemned error
>
> might receive peace, while those who held perversity were driven away.

Possidius reports that many truly returned to the Church (Life of Saint Augustine, ch. 18):

“Consequently, some of them—heretics condemned by the judgment of the Church and by the law of the emperor—returned to the bosom of the holy mother Church, from which they had recoiled, and others are still returning, as the truth of the right faith grows and prevails against that detestable error.”

Marius Mercator agrees with Possidius:

“Of these men—those who refused to subscribe—many, after repenting and being corrected from the aforesaid error, returned as suppliants to the apostolic see, and, having been received, recovered their churches” (Commonitorium, ch. 3).

And later (ibid., ch. 5):

“Many who had shared Julian’s position, abandoning it and Pelagius having been condemned, submitted themselves to the apostolic see and professed repentance for the things they had wrongly believed; they were deemed worthy of mercy and received by the holy shepherds.”

## DISSERTATION V. ON THE CREEDS WRITTEN BY THE AUTHORS AND PRINCIPAL DEFENDERS OF THE PELAGIAN HERESY

Regarding those words of Mercator:

“Now hear, you also, and those who will deign to read both me and you, what you yourself once pronounced against this most impious, most perverse, most shameless, and most insolent opinion of yours—namely, in that letter which you dared to send to the apostolic see at the time when you refused to meet with the whole Church throughout the world in condemning Pelagius and Coelestius” (Book of Subnotations, ch. 6, no. 9).

[Col. 0445]

[Col. 0445C] None of those whom we have mentioned as either authors or principal defenders of the Pelagian heresy failed to publish an exposition of his faith, by which he might conceal his error in Catholic words and insinuate what had been concealed to less prudent people all the more easily because he recommended it more cunningly.

Theodore of Mopsuestia wrote his, which Marius Mercator translated; Rufinus the Syrian wrote his, which Father Sirmond brought out of darkness; Pelagius wrote his, by which he might clear himself before Innocent; Coelestius likewise wrote his, which is now published in full. Julian wrote two to Zosimus, the supreme pontiff. Of these, one—which he sent under the name of the eighteen Sicilian bishops after the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius—is now published for the first time, and indeed in full; fragments of the other are found in Mercator’s *Subnotations*. A letter may perhaps also have the appearance of a profession of faith—either the one Coelestius wrote to the Roman clergy of his party, or the one Julian wrote to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica.

I thought that all of these should be presented together [Col. 0445D], so that they might more easily be compared and so that it might simultaneously become clear both how there was one spirit of error in all these men and how those who came later received from their predecessors doctrines that they nevertheless vaunted as their own.

All of them, except Theodore’s, consist of three parts: theological, economic, and ethical. The first concerns God, the second Christ, and the third humanity. The most extensive of all the confessions is Rufinus’s, [Col. 0446C] followed by Julian’s; the Pelagian and Coelestian are of medium length; Theodore’s is the briefest, since it says nothing about questions concerning humanity. In the theological section, none contains any error except concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, which Theodore openly denies, while Pelagius, Coelestius, and Julian deny it tacitly. In the economic section, Theodore clearly follows the Samosatene [Paul of Samosata] and attacks Christ’s divinity and the term Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*, “God-bearer”); the other four speak in ambiguous words, although Augustine believed that he had exposed Julian’s impiety, even though it was cunningly concealed. Theodore touched upon nothing in the ethical section; Rufinus shamelessly denies original sin, as do Coelestius and Julian. Pelagius, Coelestius, and Julian expressed their view of grace obscurely. All of them employ words wickedly contrived—partly to create hatred of their opponents by associating them with the Manichaeans, Apollinarians, and other heretics, partly to defend themselves against the charges brought against them, and partly to display piety [Col. 0446D].

## THE CREED OF THEODORE, BISHOP OF MOPSUESTIA, TRANSLATED BY MARIUS MERCATOR

It is unnecessary to annotate anything more carefully here, since earlier we explained a number of matters relating to the Pelagian controversy in the preface cited above, and we shall pursue more at length in the second part of Mercator’s works, which contains the Nestorian controversy.

It remains, therefore, to point out that this creed is mentioned here—or rather, that it is transcribed in its entirety—from Mercator’s version (he also wrote a refutation), so that by comparing it with the other confessions the reader may understand on what grounds I called suspect the statements brought forward by the Pelagians concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit and the incarnation of the Word: for they agree with the Theodorians, if not in reality, at least in wording.

### THEOLOGICAL SECTION: ON THE MOST HOLY TRINITY

1. Those who are now for the first time being instructed in the clear understanding of ecclesiastical doctrines, or who have resolved to turn from heretical error to the truth, must be taught that

2. we believe in one God, the everlasting Father—not one who subsequently began to exist, but one who exists from eternity, the everlasting God; nor one who later became Father, since he was always God, always God the Father.

3. We also believe in one only-begotten Son of God, who is of the substance or essence of the Father, truly as a Son, and of the same essence as the one whose Son he is and is believed to be.

4. And in the Holy Spirit, who is of the substance or essence of God—not one who is the Son. God is essence, since he is of that essence of which God the Father is, from whom he exists according to essence. For, as Scripture says, “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God” (1 Cor. 2:12), [Col. 0447C] thereby separating him from every creature and joining and uniting him to God, from whom or of whom he is according to essence, in a special manner indeed above every creature whatsoever. For creation is considered to be from God not according to God’s essence but according to the fact that it is made. We do not think that the Spirit received his existence either as the Son or through the Son.

5. We confess the Father as perfect in person, and likewise the Son, and likewise the Holy Spirit, while preserving for ourselves the rule of piety by which we do not regard the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as three different essences, but as one essence, which we recognize in the unity and equality of the Godhead.

### ECONOMIC SECTION: ON THE INCARNATION OF THE DIVINE WORD

6. We must also know about the dispensation which the Lord God completed for our salvation according to the Lord Jesus Christ: that the Word of God assumed a perfect human being from the seed of Abraham and David, according to the sayings of the divine Scriptures. This human being existed according to the nature shared by those from whose seed he came: a human being perfect by nature, constituted from a rational soul and human flesh, and, as a human being like us by nature, fashioned by the power and might of the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb. “Born of a woman, born under the law,” so that he might redeem us all from the curse and slavery of the law, receiving the adoption of sons that had long before been predestined (Gal. 4:4), he ineffably joined and united him to himself.

[Col. 0448A] 7. Preparing him to experience death according to the law of human beings, but then raising him from the dead and lifting him into heaven, he caused him to sit at the right hand of God. For this reason he received veneration from every creature as one worthy of worship, above every principality, authority, dominion, and power, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come (Eph. 1:21), as having an inseparable union with the divine nature, while every creature offered reverence to him as God, beyond all thought and understanding.

8. We do not say that there are two Sons or two Lords, because one Son according to essence is God the Word, the only-begotten Son of the Father. The one joined and made a participant of divinity with him shares the common designation and honor of “Son.” Nevertheless, one Lord according to essence is God the Word, and because this one is joined and associated with him, he shares honor with him. Therefore we do not say that there are two Sons or two Lords, since, this being manifest, the one who is Lord and Son according to essence has an inseparable union and association with him. For this reason, the one assumed for our salvation is referred both to the designation and to the honor of Son and Lord—not as each of us, existing independently, is called a son of God (hence, according to the blessed apostle Paul, we are called many sons of God; Gal. 3:26), but as possessing this uniquely. Therefore, because he is joined to God the Word, he shares the dignity of Sonship and lordship. This entirely removes the notion of two Lords and two Sons, while enabling us to place all faith, understanding, and contemplation in the union with God the Word. For these reasons he also receives veneration from every creature through his association with God.

9. We therefore speak of one God and Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made (John 1:3), understanding primarily God the Word, who according to essence is Son of God and Lord; and likewise understanding Jesus of Nazareth, the one received in human flesh, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power (Acts 10:38), as one who has union with the Lord Word and shares in the dignity of Lord and Son.

10. He is also called the second Adam, as the blessed apostle Paul bears witness (1 Cor. 15:45). Although he is of the same nature as Adam, he revealed to us the future state; yet he has as much difference from that Adam as there ought to be between the one who will be the giver and minister of such great future blessings and the one who brought upon us the beginning of present sorrows.

11. For this reason he is similarly called the second Adam, as one who proclaimed the second state. Since the first Adam became the beginning of mortality, suffering, and many evils, and since in him we received a likeness to that condition, the Lord Christ demonstrated the future state by appearing from heaven; he will bring us all into familiar fellowship with himself. “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is the Lord from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:47)—that is, [the reading *indevisendus* is uncertain], so that he may lead us to imitate him. Hence he adds: “As was the earthly, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (ibid., 48). In this man, he says, who appears and is seen by each of those who are to be judged, the invisible divine nature will make the judgment, according to the apostle Paul, who says: “God, having overlooked the times of our ignorance, now commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has established a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, through the man whom he appointed, giving assurance to all by raising him from the dead” (Acts 17:30).

12. This is the teaching of the ecclesiastical doctrines; therefore, let everyone who thinks contrary to these things be anathema.

## A CREED WRITTEN BY RUFINUS, A PRESBYTER OF THE PROVINCE OF PALESTINE (G)

### [PREFACE]

The Rufinus under discussion published two creeds: one longer, which is transcribed here, and another shorter, contained in the twelve anathemas relegated to the first appendix. Mercator calls those anathemas a creed, and they truly are a kind of confession. Consequently, they could have been placed here again if there were anything further to say about them.

Twenty years ago Father Sirmond publicly presented this longer book on the faith, formerly translated from Greek into Latin, with the name of its author and translator uncertain. For he did not think much credence should be given either to John the deacon, who makes Rufinus its author, or to the Corbie manuscripts, which bear the name of Pelagius. He did not trust John because Rufinus was an extraordinary devotee of Origen, whereas the author of this book was hostile to him; nor did he trust the Corbie manuscripts because in this book the principal doctrine of Pelagius appears to be overthrown—namely, that Adam would have died whether he sinned or did not sin.

The highly learned old man held this view and did not think further investigation was necessary. Nevertheless, he warned that the author of the book, whoever he was, had written it before Pelagius’s condemnation and that, for this reason—but especially because he had lived among the Greeks—he deserved pardon for attacking the Catholic faith concerning original sin. At that time nothing had yet been defined by the Church on this matter, nor, as some appear to think, was belief in this doctrine among the Greeks particularly firm or widespread.

I would certainly have refrained, out of respect for the judgment of so great a man, from investigating the author and translator more inquisitively. For how could I hope to discover what had escaped Sirmond, unless Marius Mercator had drawn attention to the author while Sirmond himself, giving no thought to the translator, had indicated him? Mercator mentions Rufinus the Syrian as the teacher of Pelagius and Coelestius; Sirmond entrusted Julian’s creed to me for more careful examination. From this arose, if not a certain conclusion, at least a conjecture about the author and translator—one neither difficult nor implausible.

The author, then, as we have shown in its proper place, appears to be Rufinus the Syrian; the translator appears to be Julian of Eclanum, who profited from it so greatly [Col. 0450A] that he wanted his own creed to be almost an abridgment of Rufinus’s. For at one point he copied nearly entire pages.

Rufinus wrote in Greek in the East before he came to Rome. He arrived in the second year of Anastasius, which was A.D. 399. He therefore wrote only a few years earlier, since he heard Theodore as his teacher, and Theodore began teaching in A.D. 390. Yet because this book attacks the Macedonians most fiercely without naming them, and attacks the Arians and Origenists openly, someone might suspect that it had been composed even before the First Council of Constantinople, which was held in A.D. 381, indeed before Macedonius was expelled from his see, which occurred in A.D. 360, and that Macedonius’s name was omitted because he had not yet been marked by the Church. But the bitterness against Origen, which is poured out through almost the whole book, sufficiently shows that the author wrote it when Jerome was angrily attacking John of Jerusalem—that is, in A.D. 393 or 394.

Julian translated the book from Greek into Latin at Rome at approximately the time when Rufinus was teaching Pelagius and Coelestius that sin was not transmitted by descent, so that the wicked doctrine would arouse less hostility and cause less horror if unwary readers believed it to be the faith of the Easterners.

The book has two parts, one longer and one shorter. The longer, which forms the body of the book, contains an exposition of the faith from the Trinity, who is God, to the resurrection of the flesh. The shorter, which is an appendix to the first, responds to the questions of the Arians. Both might appear to be completely filled with Catholic doctrine if the passages concerning our first parents, original sin, the guilt of demons, and also the incarnation of the Word were excepted. Perhaps the crafty heretic concealed Theodore’s errors beneath Catholic words out of fear of provoking hostility. Certainly, he deliberately took care to use statements that no follower of Theodore would hesitate to employ.

The whole book concerns questions which, both from the laws of the emperors and from the books of the Fathers written from A.D. 370 to 400, we know exercised the Church toward the end of the fourth century, especially in the East—whether they had then first arisen or had not yet been sufficiently extinguished. There were ten principal questions raised by different heretics, and Rufinus gives his opinion on each of them: that of the Anthropomorphites, concerning the nature of God, nos. 1 and 2; that of the Arians, concerning the consubstantiality of the Son, no. 3, nos. 9, and the entire appendix; that of the Eunomians, concerning the Holy Spirit, nos. 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, and 15; that of the Origenists, concerning the principles of things and several other matters, nos. 16, 17, 19, 20, and 51; that of Photinus and Apollinaris, concerning Christ, nos. 42, 43, 44, and 45; that of the Novatians, concerning repentance, no. 50; and those of others, concerning the creation of humanity, the human soul, the body, and the sin of the first parents: nos. 23 and 24; nos. 25, 26, 27, and 28; nos. 29–35; and nos. 37–41.

Father Sirmond published both parts—the creed, that is, and the appendix—and illustrated them with his notes [Col. 0450D], brief, as is his custom, but learned. We too publish the creed, and also the appendix, although it could have been omitted. We have not reproduced the notes of that most learned man, for they are not especially necessary for our purpose, since our entire concern is to compare with one another the confessions of the men mentioned above.

Sirmond divided the whole work into sixty-one numbered sections, whether this seemed appropriate to him or whether he found it in manuscript codices. We have preserved the numbers, since it would be irreverent not to comply with so great a man. Nevertheless, following the author, we have distributed the whole work into eight chapters, each distinguished by its own headings. The first concerns God; the second, creation and invisible creatures; the third, heavenly bodies; the fourth, the human soul; the fifth, the human body; the sixth, the sin of the first parents; the seventh, the incarnation of the Word; and the eighth, the resolution of the Arians’ questions.

## CHAPTER I. On God

[Col. 0451A]

This is our faith, which we learned from men taught by God—I mean Moses and the other prophets, who proclaimed the Old Testament to the Hebrews—as well as from the holy and blessed apostles and evangelists, who graciously made known to us the New Testament of Christ.

1. There is one God, possessing a substantial Word, equal to himself in every respect, and likewise substantial Wisdom, equal to himself in every respect. There is one substance of the Father, the only-begotten Word, and the Holy Spirit; one power; one Lord, without beginning and without end, simple and uncompounded, incorporeal, without form, without limitation; neither increasing nor diminishing, [Col. 0451B] needing nothing, undivided, infinite, invisible, incomprehensible, unchangeable, imperishable, immutable—what he is, he will always be, and will always remain the same; creator of all things, possessing authority, a benevolent provider, and just judge of the living and the dead.

And the one God the Word was born at the end of the ages from the Holy Spirit and Mary ever-virgin; he was crucified and died for us; on the third day he rose again, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of his Father; he will judge the living and the dead; and each person will receive his due in the same flesh, according to his deeds.

Sirmond observed that the name “Wisdom,” among the divine persons—a name ordinarily attributed to the Son—was formerly assigned by some to the Holy Spirit, as by our author, and before him by Theophilus of Antioch and Irenaeus of Lyons. I add Marius Victorinus. The words of Theophilus are as follows (Book II to Autolycus):

“The three days that preceded the creation of the luminaries are a type of the Trinity: of God, of his own Word, and of his own Wisdom.”

Irenaeus teaches that God did not need the ministry of angels in order to bring things into existence. “His offspring and his own formation,” he says (Book IV, chs. 17 and 37), “minister to all his works—that is, the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Word and Wisdom.” And elsewhere:

“Since Wisdom, which is the Holy Spirit, was with God before every creation, God says through Solomon: ‘Wisdom founded the earth, and Prudence prepared the heavens’” (Prov. 3:19).

Victorinus writes (Book IV On the Trinity):

“Although Christ is life, and the Holy Spirit is knowledge and understanding, nevertheless the Holy Spirit received from Christ all that he possesses, and Christ received it from the Father—that is, from the one who is being. From the one who is being there arose life, and from the one who is living there arose knowledge and understanding,” etc.

The reason for this unusual designation is that the Holy Spirit either received the name from the gift of wisdom or, as is more credible, because he is the source and origin of all virtues. What if *sophia* is used in the Platonic manner for “love of wisdom”? For the Holy Spirit is the love of his own principle, which is generating Wisdom, and of generated Wisdom—a certain subsisting love.

2. God is simple and uncompounded because divinity is not a body; composition properly belongs to bodies. He is simple and uncompounded because the Word and Wisdom are not accidents in him; for composition is understood to consist of substance together with accidents. He is simple and uncompounded because the substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not diverse but is shown to be entirely one and the same.

3. That the substance and power of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same is testified by our Lord Jesus Christ, who teaches both about himself and about the Holy Spirit. He teaches about himself when he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and again: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). By these words he plainly shows that there is one substance and the same power. For when he had said to Philip, “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father,” he wished to teach that we behold one and the same person, himself and the Father, alike in power and in substance, from the wonders that he performed. For those whose will is one and whose works are the same also have the same substance. Therefore he said to the Jews: “If I do not perform the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, even if you do not believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in me, and I am in him” (John 10:37).

He also taught wonderfully here that divinity ought to be recognized only through works, since it is naturally invisible and cannot otherwise be seen than through its own works and deeds, as Wisdom also testifies when it says: “From the greatness and beauty of created works, their Creator is correspondingly perceived” (Wis. 13:5). Likewise the blessed apostle Paul says: “His invisible attributes are understood and perceived through the things that have been made since the creation of the world, and so are his eternal power and divinity” (Rom. 1:20).

The holy apostle John again teaches that our Lord Jesus Christ openly proclaimed himself to the Jews as the Son of God according to substance, when he says: “For this reason the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18). The Jews understood this at the time: Jesus had manifested himself as the Son according to substance when he said to them: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17).

4. Our Lord Jesus Christ taught these things about himself. He also taught about the Holy Spirit: that he is of the substance of God and that the Holy Spirit does the very things that God the Father does, when he says: “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26).

Moreover, when he was casting out opposing powers, which according to human custom he called demons, he said: “But if I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 11:20). That he calls the finger of God the Holy Spirit is stated more clearly by the other evangelists in this passage. Matthew says: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. 12:28). Mark says: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven forever, but will be liable to eternal sin,” because they were saying: “He has an unclean spirit” (Mark 3:23).

When the Lord said this, he plainly taught that we should believe the substance of the Father and the Holy Spirit to be one and the same, since the finger and the one whose finger it is are understood to be of the same substance.

Moreover, when he said to his disciples: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them,” [Col. 0453A] he likewise showed that we must believe the substance of the Father and the Spirit to be one and the same.

The blessed Paul also teaches, saying: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3:16). By saying this, he plainly taught that the substance and power of God and the Spirit are one and the same, since the temple of God is recognized as such only through the Spirit of God who dwells within it.

The blessed Paul also writes about the Holy Spirit, saying: “But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. Now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:16–17). By saying this, he showed that the substance is the same, since the Spirit is Lord, and the Spirit of the Lord grants and bestows freedom.

He next argues vehemently against the Macedonians concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit and its one and the same substance with the Father and the Son. The whole of this chapter appears to have been composed first for the sake of this question.

### 5

The Son is in the Father, not as in a place—for his substance is not enclosed by boundaries—but as the word is in the mind, as the simple is in the simple, as the infinite is in the infinite, as the uncreated is in the uncreated, as the one without beginning is in him who is without beginning, and as the Lord is in the Lord, God in God, being at once of the same substance and power. Likewise, the Father is in the Son, like understanding inseparable from the word. By “understanding” I mean the Father, taking an example from ourselves, so that we may understand how the Father is held in the Son and the Son in the Father. Yet even the basis for what I have said I have drawn from divine Scripture. For when the prophets and apostles, who were taught by God, called the Son the Word, they plainly taught us to understand the Father as understanding, since the Word cannot otherwise be understood unless it proceeds from understanding or mind.

By “understanding” I do not mean something like ours, since the Word of God is not like our word, nor is his wisdom like our wisdom. Likewise, we say that the Holy Spirit is in the Father and in the Son, of the same substance or power, like wisdom existing at once in understanding and in the word. Moreover, we say that the Father and the Son are in the Spirit, of the same substance and power, and like understanding and word, which are not separated from wisdom.

The author used “mind” for the Father, as the ancient theologians commonly did, and “understanding” for mind, following the ancient philosophers. Aristotle reports them as saying: “Thinking and perceiving are the same” (*On the Soul* III.3, text 150).

### 6

That the Spirit is in God, as though it were from his substance, and as though the two were one and the same, and, so to speak, wholly in the whole, and that it knows his heights and depths, blessed Paul also teaches when he says: “But God has revealed it to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God” (1 Cor. 2:10). Then, taking an example from us—that is, from our wisdom, which penetrates more deeply into our entire understanding and knows everything that is in it—he continues: “For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the human spirit that is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:11).

Blessed Paul used an example from us in order to show how the Spirit of God knows his own depths, since he knows that the human being is the image of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For the human being is the image of God, since he is rational and possesses understanding, word, and wisdom. Thus Moses also teaches when he says: “And God said, ‘Let us make the human being according to the image,’ not according to my image alone, but according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26).

### 7

That the Holy Spirit belongs to the Son just as it belongs to the Father, blessed Paul teaches again when he says: “But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Rom. 8:9)—that is, the Spirit of God the Father. He continues: “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him.” Elsewhere he also says: “And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. 4:6).

The Holy Spirit belongs equally to the Father and the Son, since it is neither the Father nor the Son. To put it again by an example taken from us: it is neither like understanding that generates the word nor like the word that is generated by understanding, but like wisdom, which is in no way separated from understanding and the word.

The author may be understood as holding the Catholic view that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. For each person is said simply—*ἁπλῶς*, “simply”—to belong to the one from whom it proceeds. If this was his view, he certainly departed from Theodore, who expressly maintains that the Holy Spirit is neither the Son nor received existence through the Son (*Symbolum*, p. 5).

### 8

That the substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one, and their power the same, Moses, the servant of the Lord, also teaches when he says: “And God said, ‘Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness’” (Gen. 1:26). For when he ought to have said in the singular, “Let me make,” he said in the plural, “Let us make”; and he said not “according to my image,” but “according to our image.” Again he said: “And God made the human being,” not “they made.” He does this to show that the three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—have one and the same nature and an undivided divinity.

The prophet David likewise teaches that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one and the same power when he says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32:6).

### 9

Moreover, the holy apostle John, in order to teach that the Son and the Father have one and the same substance, says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him” (John 1:1).

When he said, “In the beginning was the Word,” and not “from the beginning,” nor again “the Word was with the beginning,” or “under the beginning,” he plainly teaches that the Word is without beginning, as though it were above every beginning and itself the cause of beginning. For if all things were made through him, and beginning is included among all things, then the Word itself is the head and cause both of the beginning and of the whole expanse that follows the beginning, within which times and ages are contained.

Again, when he said, “The Word was with God,” he showed that the Word is substantive, since he did not say, “The Word was in God,” but “The Word was with God.” Then, by saying, “And the Word was God,” he teaches that the Father and the Son have one and the same substance and power, since there is no difference between God and God, both being without beginning, but the substance of both is one and their power likewise the same.

Moreover, when he says, “He was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him,” he plainly teaches us that we must not believe that there are two separate substances or powers and virtues, since there is one God who establishes and creates all things through his substantive Word. For this reason we are taught not to speak of three separate substances—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—nor of powers and virtues separated from one another, since God is one, who is known to create all things by word and wisdom.

### 10

That God does everything in wisdom and with wisdom—that is, with the Holy Spirit—is testified by the holy prophet David. While proclaiming God, recounting the greatness of his power, and marveling at the riches of his wisdom, he cries out: “How greatly your works are magnified, O Lord! You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24).

Blessed Paul likewise proclaims this wisdom with the deepest amazement when he says: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. 11:33).

That the prophet David calls God’s wisdom, by which God made and makes all things, the Spirit of God, he clearly teaches in what follows, agreeing with blessed Paul in the same way. He says:

“The earth is filled with your creation. This sea is great and spacious; there are creeping things there without number. Small animals with great ones; there ships pass through. This dragon whom you formed to play in it; all these await you, that you may give them food in due season. When you give to them, they gather; when you open your hand, all things are filled with goodness. When you turn your face away, they are troubled. You take away their spirit, and they fail and return to their dust. You send forth your Spirit, and they are created, and you renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103:24–30).

In saying, “You made all things in wisdom,” and, “You send forth your Spirit, and they are created,” the prophet plainly taught that the wisdom of God and the Holy Spirit are one person.

Solomon likewise calls the Holy Spirit the wisdom of God when he says to God: “Who has known your counsel, unless you have given wisdom?” (Wis. 9:17). To show what kind of wisdom he means, he continues: “You sent your holy Spirit from on high, and thus the paths of those on earth were corrected, and human beings learned what pleases you, and were saved by wisdom” (ibid., 17–19). That is, having been taught your counsel by your Holy Spirit, they were saved.

As blessed Paul also says: “For God has revealed to us through the Holy Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God” (1 Cor. 2:10).

### 11

Since, therefore, we have such witnesses, we must not doubt that we ought to say that the substantive wisdom of God is the Holy Spirit, through whom all things created by God are known to subsist.

Some people of inadequate understanding have therefore said that the wisdom of God and the only-begotten God the Word are one and the same person, wishing to derive their arguments and grounds from blessed Paul, where he says: “But we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:23–24).

But in what blessed Paul said, he does not signify that the only-begotten God the Word is the power and wisdom; rather, he signifies the dispensation of the cross. For immediately afterward he says: “The foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings” (ibid., 25). No prudent person would dare say that the foolishness of God and the weakness of God are God the Word. Rather, as I said earlier, he signifies the dispensation of the cross: what appears foolish to unbelievers—namely, believing that Christ crucified is God—possesses the greatest wisdom; and what appears to be Christ’s weakness, because he died for us, possesses the greatest power. It is not now the time to speak of this wisdom and power.

The phrase “people of inadequate understanding” may refer either to those who assert that the Word and divine Wisdom are one person—in which case he reproaches nearly all the Fathers—or to those who drew that conclusion from the Apostle’s words. He rightly accuses the Arians of having attempted precisely this, as Theodoret testifies (*Commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians*).

### 12

Through many witnesses, therefore, we are taught by God that he has one subsistent only-begotten God the Word and one subsistent Wisdom, the Holy Spirit. Through this Spirit and through this Word, God bestows upon believers wisdom, speech, knowledge, and all the other gifts.

Blessed Paul also teaches this when he says: “I have therefore my glory in Christ Jesus before God. For I will not dare to speak of anything that Christ has not accomplished through me for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed, in the power of the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 15:17).

The apostle Paul did not alone have Christ and the Holy Spirit speaking in him; so did all the other prophets, apostles, and evangelists. Our Lord Jesus Christ also teaches this when he says: “Therefore, behold, I send you prophets and wise men and scribes” (Matt. 23:34). Likewise, concerning the Spirit of God, he says: “Therefore also the Wisdom of God says: I will send them prophets and apostles” (Luke 11:49).

### 13

That the Holy Spirit is Lord and God, and that, like our Lord, he himself bestows and grants gifts to believers, blessed Paul again teaches when he says: “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but the same God, who works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12:4).

In this enumeration of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, blessed Paul repeatedly adds “the same Lord” and “the same God,” plainly teaching that the Holy Spirit is Lord and God. He shows this even more clearly in what follows. After enumerating the gifts, activities, and ministries, he immediately adds: “But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11).

Again, wishing to teach us more clearly that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one substance, blessed Paul says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Eph. 4:5). He calls him Father of those who have been born through baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Although blessed Paul knew that there is a baptism of water and a baptism of the Spirit, he said “one baptism.” He spoke correctly, knowing that baptism is one because all are baptized and believe in the name of one Lord.

The same blessed Apostle is also accustomed to call the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit not only one Lord and one God, but also one Spirit, when he says: “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, slaves or free, and we were all given to drink of one Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:12).

### 14

When anyone hears blessed Paul saying that we were all baptized in one Spirit and given to drink of one Spirit, no one should believe that he was speaking only of the Spirit or only of the Father. Whoever believes this abolishes baptism. Those who were baptized in one Spirit were not baptized in the Father alone, nor in the Son alone, nor in the Holy Spirit alone, but in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

This is indeed one common name—not through confusion of the persons, but through the unity of nature: one Lord, one God, one Spirit. The Father is always Father, never ceasing to be Father; the Son is always Son, continuing eternally to be Son; and the Holy Spirit is always the Holy Spirit, never becoming the Father or the Son.

### 15

What, then, will those who follow the wicked doctrines of Arius and Eunomius answer us? They insist that the Son and the Holy Spirit are separated from the substance of the Father, yet, when they say, “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” they themselves do not deny that they baptize their own followers, and they believe that through baptism they are likewise deemed worthy of the remission of sins and of the sanctification of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Nevertheless, they do not cease blaspheming against the Son and the Holy Spirit, when at last, freed from their blindness, they ought to look up and understand that liberty cannot otherwise be granted to servants except by their own Lord.

But if they say that those who are baptized receive liberty or forgiveness of sins from the Father alone, and merit sanctification from the Father alone, they should know that no baptized person can be made worthy of these gifts unless he also receives gifts or graces from the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Blessed Paul is witness, writing to the Corinthians, when he says: “Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers” (1 Cor. 6), and so forth. He adds: “And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (ibid., 11).

By all these testimonies cited above, the one and the same substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is sufficiently and abundantly demonstrated.

## CHAPTER II. On Creation and Invisible Creatures

### 16

When God creates, he does not create by nature, as the fable of the deluded pagans supposes, but rather by will. For the Divinity is free and does not serve the necessity of nature, like fire, as they suppose, which is known to consume neighboring bodies not by will but through burning and conflagrating nature.

God does not act in this way. His ineffable and incomprehensible substance is above every intellectual and sensible nature, since the Divinity is visible to no one. Blessed Paul testifies to this when he says: “To the King of the ages, incorruptible, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory” (1 Tim. 1:17). Again he says: “He alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see.”

Blessed John teaches the same when he says: “No one has ever seen God. The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known” (1 John 4:12).

Since God is therefore above every sense, he creates by will, not by nature. For if God created by nature and not by will, there would be found infinitely many created worlds, including innumerable worlds created every day.

Let us therefore set aside the delirious fable of the pagans and obey divine Scripture, which plainly teaches that God creates what he creates by will or command. Thus the servant of God Moses taught when he said: “And God said, ‘Let there be light’”; and he added: “And there was light.” Again: “And God said, ‘Let there be a firmament’”; and the command was fulfilled by the order. Again: “And God said, ‘Let there be lights’”; and what had not existed before immediately came into being.

The prophet David likewise says: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5). Again: “All that the Lord willed he did, in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Ps. 134:6).

The Fathers of the same period, as many as wrote about the creation of the world, fought on this point against the pagans—or, as they say, the Greeks—that is, against Plato and Aristotle. Among them were the author of *Questions to the Greeks*, Basil, Ambrose, the author of *Questions on the New and Old Testaments*, and many others. The pagan position was this: “God creates by his being, not by his willing” (*τῷ εἶναι καὶ οὐ τῷ βούλεσθαι ποιεῖ ὁ Θεός*). See John Philoponus, *Against Proclus on the Eternity of the World*.

### 17

If, therefore, God does and creates whatever he wishes, then Origen was impious and wickedly foolish when he said as follows (*On First Principles* II): “God did not make everything he wished, but only those things which he was able to contain and comprehend.”

By saying this, he deprived the Lord of all power, as though the power to make had been granted to him only in part. For if, as Origen thinks, God does not have the ability to contain and subject to himself what he makes, then he will not have the power even to create. For whoever has the ability to create will likewise have the ability to subject created things to himself.

Let us therefore obey blessed Job, who says to God: “I know that you can do all things, and nothing is impossible for you” (Job 42:2). Let us piously and reverently believe, together with those men who were taught by God, that God can do all things; that he creates by will, not by nature; that he creates when he wills; and that he creates what he wills, as much as he wills, and of whatever kind he wills. Nothing is impossible to his will.

We say that the will of God is without beginning. For the Lord knows without beginning what he is going to create, when he is going to make it, and how much and what kind of things he intends to create.

Origen’s passage occurs in the second book of *On First Principles*, as it is cited in the excerpts appended to the letter of the emperor Justinian to Menas:

“For one must say that even the power of God is limited, and one must not, under the pretext of reverent speech, remove its limitation. For he made as many things as he was able to grasp, hold in his hand, and govern under his providence, just as he fashioned as much matter as he was able to order.”

### 18

We say that the first substances to be created were rational substances, which are regarded as heavenly, and that they are very numerous and diverse in both substance and power. Thus blessed David, placing them above the others, says: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers” (Ps. 148:1).

When he mentioned the heavens and the angels and named powers and heights, he was teaching that their substances are diverse and that their dignities and merits are likewise various.

Again, he teaches that their nature is not all the same when he says: “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103:4). When the prophet mentioned fire and spirit, he used different and distinct elements in order to teach us more clearly by an example drawn from sensible things.

Blessed Paul likewise says that they have different substances, placing the heavenly powers above earthly ones: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Phil. 2:10). By “those under the earth” he named souls released from their bodies.

Moreover, he teaches that their dignities vary and their species are different when he says: “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, because in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers” (Col. 1:15).

When he had placed the heavenly above the earthly, he immediately added human beings, who were created in Christ, saying: “And he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might hold first place in everything” (ibid., 18).

Our Lord Jesus Christ likewise teaches the diversity of substance among the spirits who departed from God—whom divine Scripture commonly calls demons, principalities, and powers—when he says: “This kind is not driven out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. 17:20). By saying “this kind” (Mark 9:28), the Lord showed that among them there are various kinds of substances and different species.

I have said all this to show the riches of God’s power. For if the Divinity is omnipotent, it must also be regarded as abundantly rich.

The author believed that the souls released from their bodies were called “those under the earth,” because the ancients held that souls awaited the last day in subterranean places, where, after judgment, they would either fly up to heaven or be thrust down into eternal punishment.

## CHAPTER III. On the Heavenly Bodies

### 19

We have also learned this from divine Scripture: God granted all the heavenly rational powers free will, just as he granted it to human beings on earth. For no one who possesses reason or understanding can serve God unwillingly or without the will to do so; rather, all obey him of their own accord.

Otherwise, if this were not so, neither praise nor blame, nor guilt, would follow them, just as happens with other irrational animals.

All of them, therefore, are capable of opposites—of good, I mean, and of evil. They are good when they do what God wills; they are evil when they do not carefully keep the Lord’s commands.

That the angels and heavenly powers receive immense praise when they do not despise God’s commands is attested by blessed David, who says: “Bless the Lord, all his angels, mighty in strength, doing his word, obeying the voice of his words. Bless the Lord, all his powers, his ministers, doing his will” (Ps. 102:20–21).

Through this praise—that is, through observance of the Lord’s commands—they enjoy blessed and perpetual life. But just as all who do God’s will obtain everlasting blessedness and receive eternal praise from God, so, conversely, all who despise the divine commands are condemned to eternal reproach.

What was numbered nineteenth and twentieth in Sirmond’s edition, we have made twenty-first and twenty-second, the logic of the matter requiring that the disorder of the manuscripts be corrected. For when Rufinus concluded his treatment of invisible substances in this way—“Enough has been said about invisible substances”—he showed clearly that he had covered everything pertaining to them.

How, then, could he afterward discuss their will, whether directed toward good or toward evil, without violating the method of his treatment? Moreover, it is reasonable to believe that Rufinus preserved the arrangement customary among all writers on this subject: to speak first about invisible heavenly substances and afterward about visible heavenly things. Finally, the very sequence of the discourse sufficiently proves the correctness of our emendation.

### 20

Therefore the one whom divine Scripture commonly calls the devil, together with those who are called his angels, envied the first human beings—Adam and Eve—and alienated themselves from the blessed life that they had first possessed. Through the deception that they themselves entirely devised, they persuaded the human being to sin and immediately turn aside from God’s command; they themselves, meanwhile, subjected themselves likewise to eternal punishment.

Our Lord Jesus Christ teaches this when he says to those who denied mercy to their neighbor: “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels; for I was hungry and you did not give me food,” and so forth (Matt. 25:41).

That the devil and those who are called his angels are heavenly creatures and rational powers is testified by blessed Peter when he says: “For if God did not spare the angels who sinned” (2 Pet. 2:4). Blessed Paul likewise teaches this when he says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3).

Therefore no one, seized by error, should suppose that they sinned before they envied human beings and that, after that sin, they came to deceive humanity, as the wicked Origen taught. Rather, as I said above, this occurred when the devil, transformed into a serpent, deceived Eve.

That from that moment the devil, having wholly abandoned the truth, immediately turned to falsehood, and that through this he killed Eve with the death of sin, is testified by our Lord, who says to the Jews who did not believe in him: “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father the devil. He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him. When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father” (John 8:44).

When the Lord said that he was a murderer from the beginning and had not stood in the truth, he plainly taught that the devil fell from the truth at the moment when, through the deceit of falsehood, he first led Eve astray and killed her by the death of transgression.

It was also said that when he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own resources, because he himself was the first to produce falsehood through fabricated deceit. Hence the others who, together with him, envied humanity were called the angels of that same devil, as though he were the first cause and head of this wickedness.

But enough has been said about them as well.

In asserting that the angels first sinned through envy of human beings, the author has some of the Fathers in agreement with him, including Irenaeus, Lactantius, Cyprian, Methodius as cited by Epiphanius and Photius, Gregory of Nyssa, and others, although their explanations are not all the same.

But in criticizing Origen for teaching that the demons sinned before they envied human beings, he disagrees with many more teachers of the Church and even with sacred Scripture itself, whose well-known statement is: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10:15). Perhaps, however, he had in mind Origen’s view that before the creation of this world many beings had sinned—both demons and souls—and that for this reason they had been hurled from heaven into bodies.

That the devil himself—that is, the prince of the demons—was transformed into a serpent and tempted Eve was the consistent opinion of the ancients. We discussed it in our remarks on Nestorius’s treatises against the Pelagians.

### 21

Enough, then, has been said about invisible substances. Now I must explain the sun and moon together with the other luminaries. Some people, deceived by an error of mind, have said that these are rational living beings.

The wicked Origen also followed their madness (*On First Principles* I.7). Wishing to draw an example from divine Scripture, he perversely dared to twist to his own liking what Scripture had said very well about the luminaries.

We must therefore understand that divine Scripture nowhere speaks of them as living beings. It says that the luminaries were made for this sole purpose: to shine over the earth and to serve human beings as signs of times, months, and years.

But if those who favor such errors say to us, “Why are the luminaries not living and rational beings, since it is written of them in this way: ‘The stars are not pure in his sight’ (Job 25:5), that is, in the sight of God?”—let them hear from us that the person who said this was not worthy of authority, since the Lord said to him: “You have spoken nothing true about my servant Job.”

Even if this had been said by blessed Job, it would still not constitute a sound proof. For the fact that they are not pure in God’s sight does not mean that they are living beings. Otherwise, let menstrual discharges of women also be called living beings, and leprous houses as well, since these too are not clean before God according to the law of Moses. We often read that many inanimate things are called unclean in a certain sense.

Origen also adds what the prophet David said: “The sun knows its setting” (Ps. 103:19), and likewise what God said to the prophet Isaiah: “I commanded all the stars” (Isa. 45:12). He does this in an attempt to confirm his wicked heresy. For he says (in the passage cited above) that the luminaries were formerly intellects and rational minds, but because they conducted themselves negligently, they were afterward deprived of their own power and condemned to these fiery bodies so that they might shine over the earth.

In many passages Origen followed Plato’s opinion, which attributed a soul not only to the world but also to the stars, and a rational soul at that, so that they might carry out their movements at God’s command. His first book *On First Principles*, chapter 7, is especially notable in this regard. Origen is reproached for it not only by Rufinus but also by Theophilus of Alexandria (*Paschal Homilies* 1 and 2), Jerome (Letters 59 to Avitus and 61 to Pammachius), Epiphanius (*Letter to John of Jerusalem*), the emperor Justinian (*Letter to Menas*), and many others. There he misuses the testimonies of Scripture, which Rufinus explains.

I wonder what reason there was for the Fathers whom I have praised, and others such as Basil and the commentators on Genesis, to attack Origen so vehemently in the East on this question, when in the West Augustine, even if he did not agree with Plato, at least remained uncertain, as is clear from several passages (*On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis* II.18; *Enchiridion* 58; and *On the Trinity* XIII.16).

This wonder is increased by the holy Thomas, who, after presenting Aristotle’s opinion concerning the soul of heaven, says: “But what has been said about the animation of heaven, we have not stated as an assertion according to the doctrine of faith, to which it makes no difference whether it is said to be so or otherwise.”

Hence Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*: “Nor do I even consider it certain whether the sun, moon, and all the stars belong to that same society, namely, that of the angels, although to some they appear to be luminous bodies, not endowed with sensation or intelligence.”

### 22

Likewise, wishing to approve the error of the pagans, Origen says that God placed the luminaries in the firmament as signs so that their movements of this kind might signify to us the things we have done.

Let those who follow Origen’s wicked heresy therefore learn not to interpret divine Scripture in this way, nor to overturn its meaning by using allegory instead of history according to their own will.

When we hear the prophet Jeremiah addressing the earth and saying, “Earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord; write this man down as rejected” (Jer. 22:29), we must not therefore say that the prophet is giving a command to the earth as though it were a rational living being.

The prophet David likewise commonly commands such bodies when he says: “Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all abysses, fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind, which perform his word; mountains and all hills, fruitful trees and all cedars” (Ps. 148:7). He does not thereby teach us to believe that all these things are rational beings.

But let Origen and his associates now be dismissed.

The passage of Origen to which Rufinus is referring seems to me to have been in his *Commentaries on Genesis*, from which Eusebius cited a fragment (*Preparation for the Gospel* IX). It reads as follows in Viger’s translation:

“It was brought about by God’s design that, from the varying arrangement of the stars, certain signs might be drawn of events that occur partly to individuals and partly to all in common. It is not human beings, certainly, who derive this knowledge—for from the revolution of the stars it is beyond human powers to understand truly and certainly whatever individuals are going to do or suffer—but rather those higher natures, which for many reasons must necessarily attain this knowledge, as we shall demonstrate later.”

Among the questions proposed for solution is this:

“How can the stars be signs, though not causes, of those events that occur to the human race? Why can human beings not possess certain and exact knowledge of those same events, while those signs are assigned to natures superior to human beings?”

## CHAPTER IV. On the Human Soul
23. When the Lord created the world—by “world” I mean heaven and earth and everything in them—he made only the human being according to his image and likeness, as Moses teaches when he says: “And God said, Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 20). And after Moses had said this in the person of God, he immediately added: “And God made man; in the image of God he made him.” Moses understood both expressions—“image” and “likeness”—as referring to one thing: having mentioned “image,” he entirely passed over “likeness.” Otherwise, if this were not so, the apostle James would never afterward have said in his Epistle, when teaching us that we ought not to use the tongue for evil, as follows: “With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse human beings, who were made according to the likeness of God” (Jas. III, 9).

God therefore placed the human being over all things that he himself created, both on land and in the sea, because the human being is his image, as blessed Paul also teaches when he says: “For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (I Cor. XI, 7). Because the human being is superior to all irrational animals over which he rules, he has by that very fact become lord of them all. For irrational animals, as Moses taught, were created from earth and water, and from these they possess both soul and body. The human being, however, appears to have the body in common with the others, but has a much more excellent soul, as Moses again says in this way (Gen. II, 7): “And God formed man from the clay of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.”

He praises human nature—something the Pelagians later did with evil intent—because it is the work of God’s hands; because it was made according to the image and likeness of God; because it rules over the other living creatures; because it participates in reason and free choice; and because it received body and soul from God, and so forth. By such lavish praises he prepares his deception.

[Col. 0464B] 24. The human being is therefore superior to all others because he is recognized as possessing a sentient and rational soul, and one endowed with free choice. Let us therefore, as prudent people, listen to Moses as he tells how God created the human being; for Moses and the other prophets speak about God in a way that we are able to understand. God is not a human being, made of soul and body, so that he might form and fashion a human being with his hands, or draw spirit from the air, breathe it into his face, and thus give him life. Rather, he does and did everything through the one Word and the Holy Spirit, by his will.

The prophets, moreover, customarily call not only the human being but also heaven and earth and the things in them—created by God’s command—the works of the Lord’s hands. The prophet David bears witness, saying to God (Ps. [Col. 0464C] VIII, 4): “I shall behold the heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars which you founded.” And again (Ps. CI, 26): “In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.” Likewise the prophet Isaiah, speaking in the person of God, says (Isa. XLVIII, 12): “Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call. I am he, I am the first, and I am the last. My hand founded the earth, and my right hand established heaven.” And again the Lord says (Isa. LXVI, 1): “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me, and what place will be my rest? For my hand made all these things.”

He proves that the human being is a work made according to the image of God not only against the Manichaeans but also against the Catholics—namely, so that from an acknowledged truth he might later craft, by stealth, the conclusion that there is no sin belonging to nature. Hence, near the end, he adds: “He does and did everything through the one Word and the Holy Spirit, by his will.” He could have said nothing more cunningly suited to his purpose. For that work appears, to those who are not sufficiently discerning, to be free from any defect if the supremely good and great God, through the Word as through an artisan’s idea, and through the Holy Spirit as the source of all good, made it not merely long ago, when he formed the human being, by a right and at once omnipotent will, but still makes it now in each conception.
