Julian may be seen to have imitated this passage when he wrote (Booklet, part II, no. 7): “We confess that the human being was made not only according to the image of God, but is also being made.” He then adduces James’s testimony, which Rufinus cited.

25. The human being is therefore, as divine Scripture has taught us, a body taken from earth, but possesses a soul created for him out of nothing, and this soul is not only sentient and rational but also immortal, as both Testaments teach us—the New, I mean, as well as the Old. For our Lord Jesus Christ also says (Matt. X, 28): “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy soul and body in Gehenna.” He called the fiery punishment destruction. For how can that which perishes completely and cannot exist anywhere at all be capable of enduring eternal punishment, when the Lord again says (Matt. XXV, 46): “And these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life”?

26. Nor should one say that the soul is a part of God, as the speech of the foolish and uneducated maintains. For [Col. 0465B] if this were so, God would never subject his own part to everlasting punishment. Indeed, the soul could not have sinned at all as a part of God, since God is always unchangeable both in nature and in will. Again, if our soul were a part of God, it would not be subdued by any bodily defect whatsoever; for the Divinity is always unconquered and has never been subjected to any bodily defect.

He does not slander Origen when he writes that Origen transmitted the pre-existence (προΰπαρξις) of souls; for nothing occurs more frequently in his other works, and especially in the books *On First Principles* (Περὶ Ἀρχῶν). But when he accuses him of impiety merely because he said that souls were made before bodies, he does not agree with Rufinus of Aquileia (*Apology to Anastasius*), nor even with Augustine, who was uncertain which of four widely circulated opinions concerning the origin of souls was the truer (Epistles 28 to Jerome and 157 to Optatus). [Col. 0465C] He does, however, agree with himself in the anathemas, with Jerome (Epistles 59 and 61), whom he follows as his teacher, and with other Eastern writers who attacked the pre-existence of souls (προΰπαρξις) more vehemently.

They might indeed appear to have attacked it rightly if they were targeting only the Origenian doctrine, about which we spoke in the notes on the anathemas, for nothing is more absurd than that doctrine. But if they understood any pre-existence whatsoever, including the view about which Augustine consistently wrote that he was uncertain, they wronged men of the greatest stature and holy defenders of the faith—although the reason for doubt has now been removed, whether by a decision of the Church, by the belief of the faithful, or by the consensus of teachers.

Moreover, Rufinus maliciously mentions the Manichaeans and Origen, plainly in order to forestall the minds of his readers and cunningly lead them into the error of believing that those who confess that Adam’s sin harmed his descendants, and that even infants are baptized for the remission of sins, either agree with the Manichaeans or with Origen.

[Col. 0465D] 27. Therefore, just as those who believe in this way are shown to believe impiously, so also those who say that souls were made before bodies are found to be far removed from piety. Hence the impious Origen, captured by the error of the gentiles and unwilling entirely to withdraw from it, while also striving to become the founder of new sects, taught their conjectures in another form of transmission. I do not think that these matters need be discussed at present, lest we spend too many words in a forest.

Since, therefore, the aforementioned Origen attempts to take examples from divine Scripture to confirm his wicked heresy, let us refute him by showing that he was entirely ignorant of divine Scripture and taught it without understanding. For although he himself said that, at the beginning of creation, heaven together with earth was not a solid body like what is visible, but that all this was a sentient and rational substance, of one and the same nature, including among these rational and sentient substances the souls of human beings, and although afterward, when mentioning the animals created on the sixth day, he found that the human being too had been created among them, he could no longer assert his own fabrication or strengthen his particular falsehood. Rather, as though he had entirely forgotten what he had previously taught, he unwillingly admits that souls were created, and once again that they are incorporeal.

Let those who venerate and cultivate Origen’s wicked heresy, and who strive to raise his interpretations of divine Scripture to the heavens with the highest praises, answer us: how can souls be understood without bodies, when Moses teaches us, saying: “And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them” (Gen. I, 27)? For it is clear to everyone that souls cannot possess the characteristics of both sexes; only bodies, which are known to be weightier, can do so.

Again, how could souls alone, without bodies, hear the statement: “Increase and multiply”? For, even according to Origen himself, the nature of incorporeal beings can neither multiply nor increase. Or how could souls created without bodies dwell in heaven, when God, blessing those whom he had made male and female, said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (ibid., 28)? But let Origen and his associates be dismissed once again.

When he says that Origen was captured by the error of the gentiles and came to the opinion that he condemns, by “gentiles” he means Empedocles, Pythagoras, and Plato, whom Origen testifies to have preceded him (*Against Celsus*, Book I). Aristotle, too, could have been included among them. He not only says (*On the Soul*, Book III, ch. 6, text 20) that the intellect comes from outside when a human being is generated, but also that it is separable, unmixed, and unaffected, and that it is essentially actuality (ἐνέργεια); indeed, that it is immortal and everlasting, existing for infinite time and subsequently entering other bodies, yet not remembering in one body what it did in another, because the remembering part is corruptible:

> “This intellect,” he says, “is separable, unmixed, and unaffected, existing in actuality in its essence. For what acts is always more honorable than what is acted upon, and the principle is more honorable than matter.”

And shortly afterward:

> “When separated, it is only what it is, and this alone is immortal and everlasting. But we do not remember, because this part is unaffected, whereas the passive intellect is corruptible, and without it nothing understands.”

28. Since, therefore, there are some who, seized by madness, say that the soul of the woman Eve was taken from the one soul of the first man, Adam; and some who say that souls were transmitted from Adam alone, through the casting of seed, into all who were born from him; while others say that souls were rather transmitted from Eve alone, and thus passed from parents to their children, we must answer them as follows.

Why, then, did Adam, who was first created from the earth according to the flesh, prophetically say in the Spirit of God concerning the rib that had been taken from him: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman, because she has been taken from her man,” and nowhere mention the soul? For if the soul too were from a soul, according to their foolish opinions, Adam certainly would never have omitted this. Just as he could say, “Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” so he could also have said, “Soul of my soul.” But he said only what he knew had been taken from him.

Moreover, the prophet Zechariah, agreeing with Moses, also says: “Stretching out heaven, founding the earth, and forming the spirit of man within it” (Zech. XII, 1). For if the flesh of the human being were not now created from pre-existing matter, just as in the case of Adam and Eve, and if afterward the soul were not created within it—not from pre-existing matter, just as in Adam and Eve—then the prophet Zechariah would never have said: “And creating the spirit of man within it” (ibid.).

Solomon teaches more plainly in Ecclesiastes that souls are supplied by God to all bodies created by him from pre-existing matter. He describes the dissolution of the human constitution when he says: “And the dust will return to its earth, and the spirit will return to God who gave it” (Eccl. XII, 7). By saying this, Solomon clearly taught that God supplied spirit to the dust that he had taken from the earth in order to create the human being, although the dust did not possess it. The spirit is said to return to God alone, although the Lord is creator of both—the flesh as well as the spirit—because he does not create the spirit from pre-existing matter, as he does the body.

Again, the human being appears to cooperate with God in the birth of the body that is to be generated, whereas God alone creates the spirit. Human beings supply the materials; God creates the human being.

That it is God who forms what is cast as seed into the womb, and who at the same time gives life to the various other things sown by farmers in the earth, is testified by blessed Job when he says to God: “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Job X, 8). The prophet David says the same. Again, God says to the prophet Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jer. I, 5). Likewise the prophet Isaiah says, among other things, concerning the people called by the name of Jacob: “The Lord who redeemed you and who formed you from the womb” (Isa. XLIV, 24).

More plainly still, blessed Paul, writing to the Hebrews, teaches that spirits—that is, our souls—do not descend by succession in the same way as bodies, when he says: “We had fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them; shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits, and live?” (Heb. XII, 9). Because God, when he blessed the first human beings—Adam and Eve—said, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. IX, 7), the Apostle called parents “fathers of the flesh.” And because we do not have souls created by God from pre-existing matter, he called God the Father of spirits.

Thus, everything is produced each day in the same way in which it was first created: some things from pre-existing matter, such as the souls of irrational animals; others not from pre-existing matter, such as human souls. But enough has now been said about the soul.

He argues against the transmission of souls, thereby preparing what he thinks is a path for attacking the faith in original sin. His disciples later followed their master’s method: Pelagius (Booklet, no. 15), Julian (Letter to Rufus), and others. To conceal themselves in the fog of obscurity, they raised an unnecessary question about the origin of the soul, so that by confusing evident matters with the obscurity of other matters they might construct a hiding place. They claimed that Catholics held the transmission of souls together with the transmission of sin.

These are Augustine’s words (*Book III to Boniface*, ch. 10), to which Julian was referring when he said to Augustine (*Unfinished Work*, Book II, ch. 178):

> “But the point that you thought you should bring against me—whether in this book to which I am now replying, or in those which you had written to Marcellinus, namely, that sin passed over when all human beings, to use your own words, were that one man—truth easily destroys and exposes to the ridicule of every sensible person. For such an argument indicates nothing besides your impiety—your impiety, I mean, by which you believe that the transmission of souls is the same as the transmission of bodies, although the former was condemned long ago in the profaneness of Tertullian and Manichaeus. This is so wicked that, when it was brought against us in the letter that we sent to the East, you attempted to ward it off by denying it in the books that you recently sent to Boniface. For you say: ‘They say that we confess the transmission of souls, but I do not know in whose books they have read this,’ as though you were swearing that you had said nothing of the kind.

> “But in order that the falsity of your claim may be exposed by comparing your own words, how can you say that the transmission of souls—a truly profane opinion—is not held in your understanding, when you profess that all human beings were that one man? If you believe that a part of the soul is attached to the seed, with what face do you write that all human beings were the one Adam, when a human being cannot exist except as soul and body together?”

Blessed Augustine, moreover, remained uncertain until the end of his life, as is clear from his response to Julian’s words just cited:

> “Therefore, from whatever part and however great a part, all who were born from him were that one man—whether according to both parts of the human being, which I confess I do not know. Nor am I ashamed, as you are, to confess that I do not know what I do not know. Yet for that reason I do not fail to know that it is written of every human being: ‘Man was made like vanity; his days pass like a shadow.’”

He replied shortly before his death, amid the clash of arms and the devastation of Africa.

Note the three passages of Scripture cited by Rufinus to prove that souls are created by God in bodies. They will frequently be used later by defenders of that opinion, as can be seen in Augustine—both elsewhere and especially in his letter to Optatus (Epistle 157) and another to Jerome (Epistle 28), which contains a consultation on this matter.

Observe also that the testimonies he uses to prove that God forms the seeds from which human beings are generated each day were employed by Julian by the same method (Booklet, part II, no. 6), namely, so that from a truth confessed by Catholics he might maliciously attack the Catholic faith in original sin and deceive minds insufficiently instructed. For nothing seemed more difficult for Augustine to understand than that both human bodies and souls come from God, while human beings nevertheless are born liable to sin.

## CHAPTER V. On the human body

[Col. 0468D]

29. Although, therefore, I have said that those first human beings—Adam and Eve—were created immortal according to the soul but mortal according to the body, they would never have tasted death if they had wished to keep God’s commandment, just as blessed Enoch merited. For although he was mortal, he was translated so that he might not see death at all (Heb. XI, 5).

That Adam and Eve were created mortal according to the body, as I have said, is testified by Moses when he says (Gen. II, 8): “And God planted a paradise in Eden toward the East, and placed there the man whom he had formed. And he caused every tree beautiful to behold and good to eat to grow from the earth, and the tree of life in the midst of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.”

God would never have planted the tree of life in paradise if Adam had been created immortal according to the flesh. Again, if Adam and Eve had been created immortal according to the flesh, they would never have heard God say to them: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. I, 28). Those who were commanded to eat, drink, marry, increase, and fill the earth could not have been completely immortal. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ also taught the Sadducees, saying (Luke XX, 34): “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage; but those who are deemed worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage; for they cannot die any more, because they are equal to the angels.”

[Col. 0469B] He takes a middle position between Augustine, who thought that the first parents were initially to be endowed by God with immortality, from which they would be deprived if they sinned, and Caelestius, who believed that they would die whether they sinned or did not sin. He holds that they were made mortal, but that, if they had not sinned, they would have been transferred, when God saw fit, to the state of immortality. This opinion pleased many Fathers of the Eastern regions and was later adopted by some Pelagians, against whom Augustine argues (*Sermon 2 on the Words of the Apostle*, ch. 6). Not without reason, since it follows from that view that death is not the punishment for sin, but that immortality is given as the reward of virtue.

30. It has, I think, been sufficiently proved that the human being was created mortal according to the flesh, since the Lord plainly teaches that those who rejoice in sexual intercourse and marriage are mortal. Thus Enoch, who pleased God, after fathering children by different wives, was translated so that he might not see death at all, as blessed Paul also says when writing to the Hebrews (Heb. XI, 5): “By faith Enoch was translated, so that he would not see death; for before his translation he is attested to have pleased God.”

We may therefore say the same concerning Adam and Eve: if they had kept God’s precept and commandment, they too, even after begetting children, would have remained continually immortal by eating of the tree of life, thereafter having no need of food, growth, or marriage.

But if some, captured by ignorance, persist in saying that Adam and Eve, once they had received permission to eat from every tree in paradise except the one prohibited by God, obtained immortality after eating also from the tree of life, they should learn that one who has become immortal has absolutely no need of food. If Adam and Eve were naturally immortal, they would never have tasted the tree from which God had forbidden them to eat, since immortals have no desire for food. Blessed Paul also testifies to this when he says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink” (Rom. XIV, 17). The kingdom of God belongs not to mortals but to immortals, as our Lord Jesus Christ also taught when he said (Luke XX, 35): “Those who are deemed worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage; for they cannot die any more, because they are equal to the angels.”

Adam and Eve, therefore, if they had kept God’s commandment, would certainly never have tasted death. But when they failed to keep the commandment, they did not become mortal from being immortal; rather, although they were mortal, they deprived themselves of the immortality promised to them by God. Hence Adam heard God say (Gen. III, 19): “You are earth, and to earth you shall go”—that is, “You are corruptible, and into corruption you shall go”—since he was already unworthy to eat from the tree of life and live forever.

To say the same thing again: if Adam and Eve had persisted in keeping God’s commandment, they would not have had the discernment to eat from the tree of life until the time when God would reveal it to them. For this reason it had also been separated from the other trees, although it had been placed in the middle of paradise, where the tree possessing the knowledge of good and evil had likewise been established, so that, fearing to touch the forbidden tree, they might also take care not to eat from the permitted one.

God himself also taught this plainly when he said (Gen. III, 22): “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest he stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever.” By saying, “Behold, he has become one who knows good and evil, and now lest he stretch out his hand,” God showed that before he experienced the knowledge of evil, Adam could not of himself understand that he should take and eat from the tree of life.

He artfully avoids, by anticipating the argument, the case by which Catholics proved from the shame of the first human beings that nature had been corrupted by sin, although, as Augustine says (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book II, ch. 9), nothing in God’s works is in itself shameful. [Col. 0470C] He says that the first human beings were not ashamed of their nakedness while they were in the condition of infants incapable of generating; but that they afterward became ashamed when nature had implanted in those who had reached maturity the desire for intercourse. This opinion pleased several Eastern writers and was later defended by the Pelagians in order to undermine the Catholic argument. See the lengthy dispute on this subject between Julian and Augustine (*Unfinished Work*, Book II). Observe also that Julian appears, in the third book of his earlier work against Augustine, to have pursued almost the same line as Rufinus, as is clear from Augustine’s reply (*Against Julian*, Book V).

31. And this is not surprising, since Adam himself also said, when prophesying about his wife, as follows: “She shall be called woman, because she has been taken from her man; and therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 23).

Not only this, but when Adam and Eve heard God say to them, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. I, 28), before their disobedience they had no knowledge whatsoever of the desire to beget children. For Moses says: “They were both naked, Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed” (Gen. II, 25).

Moses did not say this as though they, deceived by the blindness of incontinence, despised the shame of nakedness. Rather, he showed that they were like infants who did not yet possess the desire for intercourse. Therefore, after the transgression, when they perceived their nakedness—not, I mean, the whole body, but the part that Ham had also seen while Noah was asleep—only then did they acquire the desire to beget children and, understanding their nakedness, cover their private parts with fig leaves.

[Col. 0471A] 32. God therefore, taking thought for human beings, knew that they were inclined toward evil and lovers of bodily pleasures and desires, and wished instead to recall them to honorable virtue. For this reason he allows them for a certain time to be subject to the dominion of death, since he knew nothing else could restrain human beings so easily as death. For many are known to abstain entirely from wickedness through fear of death.

Thus worldly laws cannot cut away most human vices in any other way than by threatening death and punishment. For all who are held by love of this common life take care not to provide causes for sin, lest by their own wrongdoing they be compelled to be deprived of it.

We do not therefore say that death was given to human beings as recompense for evils, as the uneducated reason, but for the destruction of the mind’s perversity. For if human beings were to live forever, their wickedness would certainly never end.

Again, why should we believe that death was given as a repayment for evils, when, even if someone happened to kill a hundred people or more, no punishment could equal so many and such great murders?

It was customary for members of the Pelagian faction, out of ignorance, to accuse Catholics of ignorance, especially when the subject was mortality and original sin. Thus Theodorus in the Marian excerpts; Rufinus in other passages as well; Pelagius in his books *On Free Choice*; Julian everywhere, but especially in his later work; and Annianus in his letters.

Note, however, that the Eastern Fathers generally held the same view as Rufinus concerning the benefit of death. See Basil, Chrysostom, and the other interpreters of Genesis, although the intention of the saints was one thing and that of crafty men, who abused their agreement with the Fathers in order to seize the minds of their readers, was another. The latter wished to prevent them from perceiving the force of the argument drawn from death to prove original sin.

33. Death is therefore called good not only for wicked people, in order to destroy their perversity, but also useful for the righteous. Just as the wicked cease from sinning when deprived of this light, so the righteous, when they sleep, are freed from the continual assaults, afflictions, and miseries of the soul.

Once the righteous soul has been released from its own body, it will afterward be weighed down by no anxieties; it will not be subject to the miseries of the soul; it will encounter no necessities; it will endure no persecutions; it will suffer no further attacks from the vices of the flesh; it will no longer see day after day the host of evil suggestions; it will not be stripped for combat.

Carrying none of the anxieties of worldly affairs with it, it is no longer worn down by bodily abstinence, the cause of struggles; it no longer fights; it no longer competes in running or boxing; it no longer wrestles with principalities and powers and the spirits of wickedness. Its arena has been cleared; its contest has ceased; and, having won the victory, it immediately hastens to receive the crown of righteousness, to attain blessed and eternal life in heaven, when it has received its immortal flesh.

For this reason blessed Paul also, perceiving such battles—declared by invisible enemies against righteous people—and fearing lest the prudence of some might be changed by wickedness or their sound mind deceived by trickery, encouraged virtue by urging everyone to despise this temporal life. He says (II Cor. V, 6): “Therefore, being always courageous and knowing that while we are in the body we are away from the Lord.”

Desiring to depart from the body, hastening to bring his contest to an end, and wishing to be in God’s presence immediately, he cries out, saying (II Tim. IV, 6): “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. Henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to all who love his appearing.”

Blessed Job also frequently calls death the release from all evils, when he says: “Death is rest for a man. For God has shut him in” (Job III, 23, according to the Septuagint).

34. But if some wish to say, “How can death be rest for a human being, when blessed David says (Ps. XXXIII, 22), ‘The death of sinners is very evil’?” they should learn that it is not said in this sense: “The death of sinners is very evil,” as though an end and termination were not imposed upon their sins, but because after death they undergo the most grievous punishments on account of their transgressions.

Blessed Job likewise customarily calls death both rest and sleep when he says (Job III, 12): “Why did I suck the breasts? Now, sleeping, I would surely rest and enjoy the security of sleep with the kings and counselors of the earth who gloried in swords, or with princes who possessed much gold.”

The prophet Isaiah too, when commanded by the Lord to lament the dead king of Babylon, called this common and temporal death sleep, saying (Isa. XIV, 7): “All the earth cries out with joy, and the cedars of Lebanon rejoice over you and say: Since you have fallen asleep, no one has come up to cut us down. The underworld, seized by bitterness from below, came to meet you.”

The prophet Daniel likewise says (Dan. XII, 2): “And many of those sleeping in the earth’s dust will rise; some to eternal life, and others to reproach and eternal shame.”

Blessed Paul also teaches the same when he says (I Thess. IV, 12): “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep.”

Instructed by so many witnesses that this common death is not an evil, let us now bid a long farewell to those who call death evil.

## CHAPTER VI. On the sin of the first parents

35. We say that God gave the first man, Adam, sweat and labor from the earth for his benefit, since we cannot otherwise overcome, through reverent faith, the invisible enemies against whom we have continual struggle except by being wearied through bodily labors. Through these labors divine Scripture teaches us to free ourselves from the deceitfulness of our enemies and either preserve virtue safely or restore it once lost.

Thus blessed David, hastening to recover the virtue he had lost, teaches us when he says (Ps. L, 19): “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise.” And again (Ps. VI, 7): “I have labored in my groaning; every night I will wash my bed; with my tears I will water my couch.” And again (Ps. CVIII, 24): “My knees have grown weak from fasting, and my flesh has been changed because of oil.”

Teaching also how we ought to preserve virtue, he says (Ps. XXXIV, 13): “But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting.”

Likewise our Lord Jesus Christ taught his disciples that virtue could neither be preserved safely nor restored once lost except through bodily labors and pains. For he says (Matt. VII, 13): “Enter through the narrow gate, because the gate is wide and the way spacious that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it. For the gate is narrow and the way constricted that leads to life, and there are few who find it.”

For this reason blessed Paul, when he asked the Lord that the one who was trying to drive a thorn into his flesh might depart entirely from him, did not obtain his request. Rather, he heard the Lord say (II Cor. XII, 9): “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.” Hence afterward he said joyfully: “Therefore I will gladly glory in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me. For this reason I am pleased with myself in weaknesses, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions and distresses for Christ. For whenever I am weak, then I am strong.”

Teaching this also, he says (II Cor. IV, 16): “Therefore we do not grow faint; but although our outward man is being corrupted, yet our inward man is renewed day by day. For our momentary and light tribulation is producing for us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory in sublimity, while we do not contemplate the things that are seen but those that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal.”

We therefore say that the first human beings, Adam and Eve, were saved from their sin through the bodily labors and pains that the Lord gave them, plainly as a benefit to their souls. Hence afterward divine Scripture nowhere mentions them as having sinned.

The argument is drawn from the labors and hardships by which Catholics maintained that our first parents were punished on account of their sin, and from which they inferred the transmission of sin to their descendants, since they saw the latter afflicted with a similar punishment. Julian treats the same subject in Book V of his later Work (*Augustine, Imperfect Work*, Book VI, chapters 25 and following), and appears to have taken it from Rufinus, who expounded it at greater length. “Why,” he says, “do we think that the sole consideration of truth must be followed, when the phalanx of our enemies relies upon the very dangers of human existence and rises against us equipped with the support of hardships? For they wish, by the shame of intercourse, the pain of childbirth, and the sweat of labor, to establish the transmission of faults and punishments into offspring, so that, by these signs—of difficult births, sweating farmers, and fields overgrown with thorns—[Col. 0474A] natural guilt may be believed to exist, on account of which the human race is exercised through so many afflictions; a race which some think was made mortal through Adam’s sin,” and so forth.

### 36.

That God forgave them their sin, just as he also forgave Cain, who had first sinned, when he said to him, “You have sinned; be quiet; its return is toward you,” that is, the return of sin, “and you shall rule over it” (Gen. IV, 7)—Moses clearly demonstrates through the kindness, or mercy, which God afterward willingly extended to them. For what does Moses say (Gen. III, 21)? “And the Lord God made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them.” For if the Lord had not forgiven them their sin, he certainly would never have clothed them himself with the tunics that he himself had made for them.

Therefore, let no one think that those same tunics of skins which they wore were the [Col. 0474B] human body, as the impious Origen explained. For before those tunics of skins of which I have spoken, Adam himself showed that he possessed flesh, saying (Gen. II, 23): “This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.” We therefore say that the tunics of skins were given by God on account of the harshness of life, or because, as to those exercising themselves in virtue, he gave them what seemed appropriate, so that they might learn that invisible enemies cannot otherwise be conquered except through bodily labors. And that after the transgression which he had committed in paradise Adam thereafter persevered until the end of his life in obeying God is testified by Solomon, who, speaking of his wisdom—which preserved him in the fear of God—says as follows (Wis. X, 1): “She guarded the first-formed father of the world, when he alone [Col. 0474C] had been created, and delivered him from his offense; and she gave him strength to rule over all.”

Likewise, the blessed Paul, teaching about Eve’s salvation, says as follows (I Tim. II, 13): “For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression. Yet she will be saved through the bearing of children, if they remain in faith, love, and sanctification, with sobriety.”

No Father fails to attack Origen’s interpretation of the garments of skins—and indeed they do so sharply: Methodius in Photius, Epiphanius in the *Ancoratus* and in his letter to John of Jerusalem. “I pass over,” he says, “his frivolous interpretation of the tunics of skins, and with what effort and how many arguments he labored to make us believe that the tunics of skins were human bodies. Among other things he says: ‘Was God a leatherworker or a dealer in hides, [Col. 0474D] that he should prepare animal skins and sew from them tunics of skins for Adam and Eve?’ It is therefore clear,” he says, “that he is speaking of our bodies. And if this is so, how do we read that, before the tunics of skins, before disobedience and the expulsion from paradise, Adam spoke not allegorically but literally: ‘This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh’? Origen either spoke inconsistently, or Theodoret incorrectly interpreted him in the *Questions on Genesis*.”

### 37.

When he said “through the bearing of children,” he meant “with the bearing of children”; for divine Scripture commonly changes prepositions. The patriarch Joseph is a witness to this when, speaking of the dream to the cupbearer, he says: “Its interpretation is not through God” (Gen. XL, 8), that is, “not from God.” Likewise the blessed Paul, writing to the Hebrews, says: “Through whom [Col. 0475A] also he made the ages” (Heb. I, 2), instead of “with whom also he made the ages.” For we do not say that the Son is the Father’s subordinate on account of the statement, “Through whom also he made the ages,” but rather his co-worker.

Therefore Eve will not be saved on account of her children, nor will her offspring be condemned on account of their mother, or of their father Adam, as the opinion of the imprudent supposes. For each human being, possessing free will, will certainly be judged worthy of praise or blame according to the quality of his actions. In the same way, on the day of judgment each will either be justified or subjected to punishment, as the blessed Paul also teaches, saying (II Cor. V, 10): “For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his own body, according to what he has done, whether good, [Col. 0475B] or evil.”

He begins to attack original sin, taking his first argument from that testimony of the Apostle which he received from Theodore (*Excerpt*, 2, no. 2) and transmitted to Julian (Part II of the *Little Book*, no. 12, and elsewhere repeatedly), as though no one’s guilt could be imputed to another. He proceeds to insult Catholics, calling those whom he had previously called ignorant now “imprudent,” and later condemning them to madness. In this he followed Theodore, who in the excerpts published from Marius’ work first called defenders of original sin, ironically, “the most wise and admirable fathers of sin,” then “untrained in the divine Scriptures,” “imprudent and shameless,” and finally “mad”; Pelagius had preceded him in calling them ignorant and insane, while Julian heaped every possible insult upon them, as did other unnamed partisans whose characteristic was to praise their own side, despise others, and indeed load them with curses.

[Col. 0475C] ### 38.

That children are not punished on account of their parents, nor parents on account of their children, God again clearly taught when he said to Moses the prophet (Deut. XXIV, 16): “Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each shall die for his own sin.”

Moreover, when God reproved the imprudence of the children of Israel, at the time when they were captives among the Chaldeans according to their crimes, and they complained not entirely about themselves but about their parents, as though their parents had been the cause of all their wicked crime, they unjustly accused God concerning their captivity, saying (Ezek. XVIII, 2): “The way of the Lord is not right, because our fathers ate a sour grape and the children’s teeth were set on edge.” Through the prophet Ezekiel he says to them (ibid., 3): “As I live, says the Lord, [Col. 0475D] this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel; for all souls are mine: as the soul of the father is mine, so also the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins, it shall die.” And again (ibid., 20): “The son shall not receive the iniquity of the father, nor shall the father receive the iniquity of the son.” And again (ibid., 30): “I shall judge each of you according to his way, house of Israel, says the Lord.”

When God had said (ibid., 3), “As I live, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel,” he plainly taught them that they had persisted in the same imprudence.

The second argument specifically concerning the case of children and parents he takes from the testimony both of Moses the lawgiver and of Ezekiel the prophet. Julian introduced, or rather copied, both passages, whether in his *Little Book* (Part II, no. 11) or in his later *Work* [Col. 0476A] (*Imperfect Work*, Book III, chapter 12 and following); Theodore likewise used both in the excerpts (*Excerpt* 2).

### 39.

After these testimonies of God, therefore, those who condemn the whole world for iniquity and wickedness through the one man Adam are insane. For those who say such things either declare God unjust or at least consider the devil stronger than God, since the devil was able, through the transgression of Adam and Eve, to make evil the nature which God created good—if indeed, through the transgression of the first man Adam and his wife Eve, all human beings are subject to sin.

They ought certainly to acknowledge that they themselves are lovers of wrongdoing, since they are themselves lovers of pleasures and of the flesh; they ought not to attach the causes of their own faults to others, when they themselves appear to have been their authors.

Or else let those who consider themselves wise tell us, [Col. 0476B] although they cannot understand what they say and are not known to have any judgment concerning the subjects they discuss, why Adam and Eve, after falling once, did not fall a second time, if their nature, having been made sinful by transgression, could not completely refrain from evil. For divine Scripture nowhere records that they sinned a second time, just as it did not fail to relate that Cain sinned a second time; indeed, it clearly teaches that Abel was free from sins.

What will they also say about Enoch and Elijah? When they had pleased God, they were transferred so as not to see death at all. They were not prevented by Adam’s transgression from remaining immortal, since through them the only-begotten God clearly taught [Col. 0476C], before his carnal coming, the hope of resurrection.

What will they say also about Noah, whom God testifies to have been righteous? Moreover, with all his household he merited here the same salvation which we too merit through baptism, as the blessed Peter teaches in his Letter, saying (I Pet. III, 19): “In which also he came and preached to the spirits who were in prison, who formerly had been unbelieving, when the patience of God was waiting in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built, in which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water. This now saves you also by a similar form: baptism.”

Pelagius compressed these words—“Those are insane who condemn the whole world through one man,” and so forth—into a brief statement (*Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 7). “Those are insane,” he says, “who assert that sin comes to us from Adam by transmission.” [Col. 0476D]

Julian also wished to use the same argument. Addressing Augustine, he says (*Imperfect Work*, Book V, chapter 64): “You are insane, then, when you say, ‘God creates evil’; but you are even more insane when you attempt to prove this by evangelical testimony,” and so forth.

The third argument—“If sin is transmitted, either God is unjust or the devil is stronger than God,” and so forth—Julian himself also employed.

The fourth argument, that the opinion of original sin was invented by people greedy for pleasures, Julian expanded theatrically (*Imperfect Work*, Book II, chapters 5 and 6): “He delights in lustful souls.”

### 40.

But if, as they assert, infants die because of Adam’s sin, let them tell us why, immediately after being baptized, they are permitted to taste death, since all who have been baptized—and for this reason have become children of God [Col. 0477A]—cannot possess sin.

And if infants born of Christian parents are baptized on account of Adam’s sin, they ought not to be baptized at all; rather, they should be regarded as holy, since they were begotten of faithful parents, as the blessed Paul teaches, saying: “Otherwise your children are unclean, but now they are holy” (I Cor. VII, 14).

Likewise the blessed John says concerning children who are to be begotten, that as soon as they are born they receive the illumination of sanctification from the only-begotten Word, when he says: “That was the true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I, 9).

Infants therefore receive baptism not on account of sins, but so that, possessing spiritual birth, they may be created in Christ through baptism and become sharers in [Col. 0477B] his heavenly kingdom, as the blessed Paul teaches: “If there is any new creation in Christ” (I Cor. III, 17); and again: “But if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and fellow-heirs of Christ” (Rom. VIII, 17).

Hence Cornelius, who shone with righteousness according to God’s testimony, who had received the baptism of the Spirit just as the apostles had and was a participant in the Holy Spirit—so that, with the Holy Spirit dwelling in him, he could not possess sin at all—was nevertheless judged worthy also of that baptism which is administered through water, so that, according to the blessed Paul, having been planted in the likeness of Christ’s death, he might also become a fellow-heir of his resurrection (Rom. VI, 5).

The fifth argument—“If an infant is baptized to remove Adam’s sin, then one born of baptized parents, and thus of persons cleansed from sin, ought certainly not [Col. 0477C] to be baptized”—was employed by Coelestius in a book which, according to Predestinatus (*Heresy* 88), he published before Pelagius wrote his commentaries on Paul’s Epistles.

Pelagius included this very argument in his commentaries, as testified by Augustine (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, Book III, chapter 2), Mercator (*Commonitorium*, chapter 2), and Predestinatus (in the passage just cited), but Cassiodorus deleted it, as we have noted more than once.

For this reason Julian writes (*Little Book*, Part III, nos. 13 and 20) that he abhors those who assert that sins are not completely erased in baptism, and who deny that one born of two baptized persons, or born of a baptized woman, needs the grace of baptism.

Observe the escape route transmitted by Rufinus to the Pelagians, by which they attempted to evade the Catholics’ argument proving the sin of infants from the necessity of baptism. They said that infants were baptized not to be cleansed, since they were innocent, but to be adopted as children of God and heirs of the kingdom of heaven.

Coelestius, in the book submitted at Rome [Col. 0477D] (*Augustine, On Original Sin*, chapter 5), says: “We confess that infants ought to be baptized for the remission of sins, according to the rule of the universal Church and according to the judgment of the Gospel, because the Lord established that the kingdom of heaven can be conferred only upon the baptized; and since they do not possess the powers of nature for this, it is necessary that it be conferred through the generosity of grace.”

Julian (*Augustine, Against Julian*, Book III, chapter 3): “Christ, who is the redeemer of his own work, increases his benefits toward his image through continual generosity; and those whom he made good by creating, he makes better by renewing and adopting.”

See the lengthy notes written on this subject at chapter 8 of the *Subnotations*.

### 41.

Since, therefore, certain people, through ignorance of the divine Scriptures, dare to break out into a wicked and unjust statement concerning Christ, asserting that he assigns unbaptized children to the punishment of eternal fire—which is customarily called Gehenna in the Scriptures—let them learn from [Col. 0478A] the divine Scriptures that the punishment of eternal fire has not been prepared for the innocent and those entirely ignorant of sin, but for those known to have transgressed God’s law, as the blessed Paul teaches:

“We know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law” (Rom. III, 19);

and again: “Through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Rom. III, 21);

and again: “For where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. IV, 15);

and again: “Sin is not imputed when there is no law” (Rom. V, 13);

and again: “For without the law sin is dead. I was once alive without the law” (Rom. VII, 8–9).

Likewise, when God was giving the law through Moses concerning the young, he says: “As I live, and as my name lives, and as the glory of the Lord has filled the whole earth: because all the men who have seen my glory and the signs that [Col. 0478B] I performed in Egypt and in this wilderness, and who tested me these ten times and did not obey my voice, shall not see the land which I swore to their fathers—except their children, who are with me here today, whoever know neither good nor evil. To every inexperienced youth I shall give the land” (Num. XIV, 22 and following, according to the Septuagint).

Likewise our Lord Jesus Christ teaches concerning little children that they are free from every sin when he says: “Amen, I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 3).

And again he says to his disciples: “Allow the little children to come to me, and do not forbid them, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these. Amen, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will not enter it” (Mark X, 14).

Likewise [Col. 0478C] the blessed Paul says: “Do not become children in understanding, but be little children in wickedness” (I Cor. XIV, 20).

And again, concerning Esau and Jacob, he teaches as follows: “When they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil” (Rom. IX, 11).

Children, therefore, as divine Scripture itself has thoroughly taught, being entirely innocent, having experienced no wickedness at all, and lacking knowledge of the distinction between good and evil, are not subjected to the punishment of eternal fire—especially since eternal fire has been prepared as punishment for the impious and sinners. But let these people, together with their ignorance, be dismissed.

He opens another escape route by which [Col. 0478D] the Pelagians might withdraw when pressed by Catholics arguing from Christ’s judgment and from the sentence distributing everyone into only two places. They said that such a judgment applied only to adults who possessed reason and were guilty of violating a law they had known. See Julian’s treatment of the same testimonies as Theodore in the controversy (*Imperfect Work*, Book II).

## CHAPTER VII. On the Incarnation of the Word, or Christ

### 42.

Again we are taught that, in the last days, the only-begotten God the Word, by the will of the Father and the Holy Spirit, was pleased to become man. That he became man by the will of the Father the blessed Paul clearly taught, saying: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law, and so that we might receive adoption as children” (Gal. IV, 4).

That the Son likewise became man willingly, the blessed Paul similarly teaches, [Col. 0479A] saying: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 6).

That he became man also by the will of the Holy Spirit is testified by the angel who announced the gospel to the Virgin Mary, saying: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born will be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35).

And again, in a dream, the same angel said to Joseph: “For that which will be born from her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I, 20). Likewise the blessed Matthew says: “She was found to have conceived in the womb from the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 18).

Julian said the same thing more briefly (*Little Book*, Part I, no. 5): “In the fullness of time the Son of God was sent, not by the command of a greater power, but by a sharing [Col. 0479B] of will. The Word becomes flesh.”

### 43.

The only-begotten God the Word, therefore, having become man, received from Mary, who was ever virgin, a body, while creating for himself a rational soul of the same substance as ours. From that ever-virgin he was born as man, as Isaiah prophesied: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. VII, 14).

He called holy Mary ever virgin because, just as she conceived as a virgin, so also, remaining a virgin, she gave birth. For how will the sign given by God to Ahaz be true? If she did not remain a virgin after childbirth, then that she conceived as a virgin must not be believed at all.

For what does the Evangelist say about Joseph? “And he did not know her until she had borne her son” (Matt. I, 25)—that is, he did not know with certainty that she was the virgin who had been foretold as the one who would bear Christ, unless, after the delivery, he had recognized [Col. 0479C] that the proofs of her virginity remained intact.

There were also the subsequent announcements and signs of Christ: angels, the star, Simeon, Anna, and especially the angel’s warning, who spoke to Joseph as follows: “Rise, take the child and his mother” (Matt. II, 13). He did not say, “your wife,” so that Joseph might know that he had been given to the Virgin Mary as a servant for Christ’s sake.

Therefore, wishing to confirm the sign of virginity, the Lord, after rising from the dead, entered to the apostles when the doors were shut, showing that he possessed bones and flesh.

He argues concerning the virginity of Mary the Mother of God against [Col. 0479D] Helvidius and Jovinian, whose heresy arose before the death of Damasus. He follows Jerome, who overthrew both monsters in published books. From this discussion I conclude that this book was written while the questions of those wicked men were still raging, and thus toward the end of the fourth century.

### 44.

Christ therefore progressed in age and wisdom so that it might be proved that he had truly become man, as the evangelist Luke teaches when he says: “The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him” (Luke II, 40); and again: “And Jesus progressed in age and wisdom” (ibid., 52).

If Jesus Christ had not possessed a soul, as the wicked Arians suppose; or if, on the other hand, he had possessed a soul but not a rational one, as [Col. 0480A] the mad Apollinaris maintained, he certainly could never have progressed in wisdom, since flesh without a soul cannot progress in wisdom.

Nor does the only-begotten Son of God need an increase of wisdom, since he himself is the distributor of all our wisdom.

A suspect passage. For he distinguishes Jesus from the only-begotten Son of God, denies that the latter progressed, and affirms that the former did, in the manner of the Nestorians.

Paul of Samosata, from whom Nestorian impiety arose, says in question 5 (*Library of the Fathers*, vol. XI, among the works of Dionysius of Alexandria): “It is written in the Gospel: ‘The child grew and became strong,’ as though he were saying: Jesus, born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, grew. How then do you say that he who grew and became strong existed before the ages, had no beginning together with the unbegotten Father, and was coeternal?”

Theodore of Mopsuestia (*Excerpt from Book VI on the Incarnation*, transmitted by Mercator): “Jesus progressed in age and wisdom. But this cannot be said of the Word of God, because [Col. 0480B] perfect God was born from perfect God, wisdom from wisdom, power from power. He therefore does not progress; for he is not imperfect, so as to need increase toward perfection [These words, or similar ones, seem to be missing: ‘Jesus progressed,’ or ‘the man progressed,’ ‘for to him …’]. For he did not immediately, upon being formed or born, communicate all his proper wisdom to the deity, but imparted it gradually to the body.”

### 45.

That our Lord Jesus Christ possessed a soul just as he possessed a body the Evangelists clearly teach. The angel said to Joseph, when he was in Egypt: “Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel; for those who sought the child’s soul are dead” (Matt. II, 20).

Again, our Lord Jesus Christ said: “Now my soul is troubled” (John XII, 27); and again: “My soul is sorrowful [Col. 0480C] unto death” (Matt. XXVI, 36); and again: “As the Father knows me, and I know the Father, and I lay down my soul for the sheep” (John X, 15); and again: “For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my soul so that I may receive it again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to receive it again” (ibid., 17).

Likewise the blessed Peter, referring the testimony of the prophet David to Christ, says in Christ’s own person: “For you will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Acts II, 27).

This attacks the Arians, who admit no soul in Christ apart from the Word, and Apollinaris, who excluded only the mind. He does the same again with Pelagius and Julian in their little books; he also does so with [Col. 0480D] the Nestorians, who slandered Catholics under both names, as though they had fellowship with them.

Nestorius himself, when he was raging after receiving denunciatory letters from the apostolic see, said: “They do not call her *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος), ‘Mother of God,’ and this is all that they oppose to our convictions. For no one,” they say, “who follows the orthodox glory of faith has ever avoided this expression.”

“If you investigate,” he continues, “many tests of doctrines are supplied there, especially those belonging to the sect of Apollinaris and of Arius or Eunomius. Each of them called the holy Virgin *Theotokos*, that is, ‘Mother of God’” (in Part II of Marius Mercator’s work).

But attend, please, to what is being said here, so that you may have a fully prepared defense against these claims and against those who, placing bait on the hook, speak in this manner. You know that Apollinaris said this; you know that this expression, *Theotokos*, aroused the loudest applause with Arius.

[Col. 0481A] ### 46.

Through many testimonies divine Scripture teaches that the only-begotten Son of God became man, first of all in order to teach humility to the heavenly powers, and that the earthly human being ought never to be afflicted by the vice of pride, like the devil and his angels. Thus, seeing the Son of God possessing the form of a servant, they would never think of yielding to a proud disposition, as the blessed Paul teaches when he says (Phil. II, 5): “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.”

And what sort of form was this? He does not mean that of the heavenly powers, but that of the earthly human being, which is considered lower than all rational substances, as being created from a rational soul and an earthly [Col. 0481B] body.

Hence he adds (ibid., 7): “Being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death.” And what sort of death was it? One that among human beings is worse than all others, for he adds: “Even death on a cross.”

Regarding the reasons why the only-begotten Son of God became man, he is entirely Pelagianizing. For he gives only the six reasons which the Pelagians themselves give: to teach human beings humility; to show his love toward us; to die for sinners; to grant adoption and the inheritance of the kingdom to those who believe in him; to provide an example of the practice of virtue and the conquering of sin; and to be mediator and reconciler.

Julian (*Little Book*, Part I, nos. 7 and following): “He is therefore born for us, so that he might recall the whole world from sins by his example and redeem it by suffering; removing sin, as God, by forgiving [Col. 0481C] it, and showing, as man, through the likeness of his nature, how it might thereafter be conquered.”

Beginning with John’s baptism, by which he was baptized in order to give an example, not, as some wish, on account of his own sin, as he himself said to John: “Allow it now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. III, 15).

He subjected himself to all the passions of the flesh, enduring hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, death, and other such things: “Becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II, 8).

As the blessed Peter taught us, saying: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow in his footsteps; he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (I Pet. II, 21).

This man, therefore, suffered and was buried for our salvation according to the flesh, and on the third day rose again both to destroy death and to open for us the way of resurrection.

### 47.

But lest anyone, hearing the blessed Paul say that Christ humbled himself unto death, attach the [Col. 0481D] passion of the cross to God, as the wicked Arians think, let him understand that the only-begotten God is without passion and cannot be subject to passion at all. Whatever humble words are therefore spoken concerning Christ must all be referred to the form of the servant.

He adopts a Nestorian position when he says: “Whatever humble words are spoken concerning Christ, all these must be referred to the form of the servant.” Although these words have a Catholic meaning, they are rightly suspect when spoken by a disciple of Theodore.

### 48.

Afterward, to show how great his love was for his works, although he was Lord, he preferred, having taken the form of a servant, to become like one of us. Again, because, having become man, he deigned to undergo death for the impious and [Col. 0482A] sinners, as the blessed Paul teaches when he says (Rom. V, 6): “For why, when we were still weak, did Christ die for the impious at the appointed time? Scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps someone might even dare to die for a good person. But God commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”

Likewise, he grants spiritual adoption as children and gifts to those who believe in him, and makes them heirs of his heavenly kingdom, as our Lord Jesus Christ himself teaches Nicodemus: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John III, 3).

Hence infants, although they are not in sins, nevertheless receive the grace of baptism, so that, created [Col. 0482B] in Christ through a new birth, they may also become fellow-heirs of his kingdom, according to the blessed Paul: “If there is any new creation in Christ” (II Cor. V, 17).

### 49.

For this reason the heavenly powers also are created in Christ through faith alone, because he renewed all of them in himself as well. It is for this reason that those who believe in Christ are called a new creation: because they venerate and worship the only-begotten God the Word together with the form of a servant that he possesses.

That the heavenly powers were created in Christ is testified by the blessed Paul, who says (Eph. I, 10): “To restore all things in Christ, those which are in heaven and those which are on earth, in him.”

Again, just as he is called the head of the Church, so he is shown also to be the head of all the heavenly powers. For what does the blessed Paul say (Col. II, 9): “Because in him [Col. 0482C] the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power”?

Again, he became man so that, having condemned sin in the flesh, he might leave us an example of how each person, after overcoming carnal vices, ought no longer to be deceived by the devil’s trickery.

Again, he became man so that, through the form of a servant, he might become mediator to the Father and the Holy Spirit and to those worthy of him, and thus preserve them forever in the bond of peace, as the blessed Paul teaches: “Because in him all fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things on earth or the things in heaven” (Col. I, 19).

### 50.

Just as he himself was the cause [Col. 0482D] of so many blessings for all believers, so also he becomes a just retributor for unbelievers. Therefore the divine Scriptures teach us through many testimonies that God does not will the death of the impious and sinner, but rather that he turn and live.

As long as we are in this life, therefore, we can perform repentance and merit that future blessed and eternal life. For after the dissolution of the body no opportunity for repentance remains, as the prophet David teaches when he says to God: “For there is no one in death who remembers you; and in the underworld who will confess to you?” (Ps. VI, 6; CXIII, 17).

And again: “The dead will not praise you, nor all those who descend into the underworld.”

That Christ will judge the living and the dead the blessed Paul plainly teaches when he says [Col. 0483A] (II Cor. V, 10): “For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his own body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil.”

For this reason Christ is said to sit at the right hand of his Father as judge both of the living and of the dead. And that the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ clearly teaches (John V, 22).

He proceeds against the Novatians, as do all the writers of the same period—Nazianzenus, Ambrose, Hilary the deacon, Jerome, and others whom it would be lengthy to enumerate. But he proceeds not with the same intention as the others, but in the manner of Pelagius and Julian, when they say: “We believe that if a person falls after baptism, he can be saved through repentance”—namely, in order to stir up hostility against Catholics, who confess that a person cannot repent unless God grants it.

[Col. 0483B] **51.** We are also taught that the dead will rise in the same flesh in which they were formed in their mother’s womb, alike in body and in appearance, as blessed Paul writes to the Corinthians (I Cor. 15:35):

“But someone will say: How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come? Fool! What you sow is not brought to life unless it first dies. And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of one of the other kinds. But God gives it a body as he willed.”

When the Apostle had said that God gives it a body—not “as he wills,” but “as he willed”—he showed that, just as man was created in the beginning, so also he will rise in the resurrection, with neither his appearance nor his body changed. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ, after he rose from the dead, [Col. 0483C] did not alter either his body or his appearance at all. For just as a grain of wheat, having lost its body, is sown bare and dead, and then rises again with the same body that it had lost, so also man in the resurrection of the dead, even if he died after having lost some part of his body, will rise in that same body and appearance in which he was first created in his mother’s womb. Blessed Paul teaches this again in the following words (II Cor. 5:4):

“For we who are in this tent groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.”

And again: “For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality.”

In saying that we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed over, the Apostle shows that each of us hereafter will possess life, glory, and incorruption clothed with body, flesh, and appearance. Thus, just as red-hot iron, clothed with the glory of fire, does not at all change its proper nature, so the saints, clothed with heavenly glory, will not lay aside the body and appearance that they possess in this life. Likewise, when our Lord Jesus Christ put on glory on the mountain, he did not at all change what he was: a human being.

But concerning these matters, what has been said is sufficient for us, supported by the testimonies of divine Scripture, to establish the faith.

He holds a Catholic view concerning the resurrection of the flesh, but, following the example of Jerome, argues vehemently against Origen, John of Jerusalem, and Rufinus of Aquileia on that question (Epistle 61, and *Apology against Rufinus*).

# CHAPTER VIII, OR APPENDIX: On the Questions of the Arians

[Col. 0484A]

**52.** Since those who follow the impious heresies and doctrines of Arius or Eunomius sharpen their tongues day after day for blaspheming the only-begotten Son of God, having continually been taught to corrupt the simplicity of divine Scripture and likewise to defile the truth with certain perverse expressions that are accustomed to arise from ordinary meanings, so that they may appear to confirm their impious heresy by the dialectical portion of their sophisms, they put forward for us sophistical questions about God, attempting to estrange the only-begotten Son from the substance of the Father. I therefore consider it necessary to destroy their impious heresy by appealing to these same ordinary meanings, [Col. 0484B] so that they may themselves be refuted by the very things from which they think they derive proof.

Before I begin to enumerate their questions concerning the Son against us—questions which they regard as great and difficult—I wish to say to them that, whatever you may choose to say about the birth of the Son of God from the Father, using temporal expressions, you will not be able to establish his birth as it truly is. For the birth of the only-begotten Word of God, being natural and without beginning, cannot be comprehended as it truly is. If all words that are uttered signify time—either the present, the past, or the future—while the only-begotten God is their creator, then his birth cannot be proved by temporal expressions. Therefore, necessarily following the faith of the divine Scriptures, we must derive from it [Col. 0484C] examples for our proof.

**53.** When they ask us whether God begot the Son or not, and receive from us the answer, “He begot him,” they immediately add a question of the kind that the Greeks call a *dilemma*: “Unwillingly or willingly?” They do this so that, if we say “unwillingly,” they may at once add: “If he begot the Son unwillingly, how is it not impious to say this of God, that he was subject to the necessity of begetting?” But if we say “willingly,” they again add whatever suits their purpose: “Therefore, if he begot him willingly, and the Son was begotten by his will, no distinction at all can be maintained between him and all the other things that were likewise created by God’s will.”

We must not answer what they desire to hear, [Col. 0484D] but should rather say as follows: “He begot him neither willingly nor unwillingly.”

Once they have thereby been completely excluded from their wicked conclusion and ask us how he begot him, we shall answer them: “Naturally”—which is above every will and necessity. If they understand our answer and remain silent, all is well. But if they say that the answer is not clear, we shall in turn question them in the same manner as their own question: “Is God good willingly or unwillingly?”

They too, fearing an unlawful answer on either side, will reply to us: “Neither willingly nor unwillingly, but by that nature which is above will and necessity.” [Col. 0485A] By the answers they themselves use concerning God when they assert that he is good, we likewise establish that God begot the Son. For just as God is good neither by will nor by necessity, but by his very nature, so that he can never be found deprived of goodness, so also by nature he has the Son. For God can never be deprived of his only-begotten Son, God from God.

These statements concerning the only-begotten God would be amply sufficient if we were speaking with sensible people, since he possesses his birth from the Father naturally.

**54.** But since these people, like dogs seized by rabies, which rage even against their masters, driven by the passion of madness through ignorance and striving to blaspheme against the Son of God whenever they hear anything spoken reverently about him, and, even when excluded from their customary [Col. 0485B] blasphemy against him, do not abandon the persistence of the malice they always exercise against the Son, but try again to devise other objections, attempting to destroy the birth of the only-begotten Word from God, which is without beginning and is held to be natural, as though they always desired to fight against him—I think it necessary to answer their other vain questions as well, lest we appear to evade the force of the questions they have proposed.

They ask us, then, whether everything that ceases also began. If we answer that everything that ceases also began, they immediately add: “The Son ceased to be born; therefore he necessarily began. And if he began, there was a time when he did not exist. And if there was a time when he did not exist, it is impossible for him to have his birth from the substance of God,” since the substance of God, being without beginning and always existing in the same manner, cannot admit increase or diminution.

But we must not answer them that everything that ceases also began, because not everything that ceases now has a beginning. Nor is this the only point: not everything that has a beginning also ceases, for God, wishing to make the heavenly powers, does not have a beginning, yet once they had been made, he ceased willing to make them. Therefore not everything that ceases has a beginning.

Again, although the heavenly powers, once made, have a beginning of their substance, they never cease to exist. Consequently, not everything that began will also cease. Since, therefore, it has been proved that not everything that ceases also began, the only-begotten Son of God likewise ceased to be born, [Col. 0485D] yet does not have a beginning of his birth. For the Son’s birth from the Father is without beginning, since it is natural.

**55.** Again they ask us whether, when God was alone, he begot the Son. If we answer that he begot him when he was alone, they immediately add: “Therefore, if he was alone when he begot him, there was once a time when the Son did not exist.” But if we answer that he was not alone, they immediately add: “How can that which was always with him properly be called born?” For, as they say, the very fact that he is called born gives rise to the suspicion that he once did not exist at all.

They say this because they do not understand how much it matters that anything should be asserted about God on the basis of bodily and temporal perceptions, since the one under discussion, being without beginning, cannot be subject to the necessities of time.

Therefore let us also question them, in a way using their own question, so that their fiction—which the Greeks call a *sophism*—may become clear and evident to them. Tell us: when God was alone, did he beget mercies or not? For blessed Paul calls God the Father of mercies, saying: “Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies” (II Cor. 1:3).

If they dare to say that he begot them when he was alone, we shall answer them as follows: “Why is it not impious and sacrilegious to say that God once existed without mercies?” [Col. 0486B] For God is regarded as the fountain of mercies, and he is never believed to have been the father of wickedness, so that, having first not been the Father of mercies, he would afterward begin to become their father.

But if, avoiding this patent blasphemy concerning God, they say, “There was never a time when he was alone without mercies,” we shall answer them in the same way: “Just as God was never alone without mercy and afterward became the Father of mercies, so also he was not alone before and afterward became the Father of the only-begotten Son. For God is always the Father of his only-begotten Son, God the Word.”

**56.** But if they again persist in their folly and say that what is unbegotten signifies the substance of divinity, while God the Father is unbegotten and the Son is begotten, and therefore the substance of the Father and the Son cannot be one and the same, let them learn that “unbegotten” does not at all signify substance. For if “unbegotten” appears to be contrary to “begotten,” while nothing is contrary to substance, then plainly “unbegotten” cannot be substance.

Again, if substance is asserted in reference to what exists, while “unbegotten” refers to what does not exist—for it is unbegotten—then plainly “unbegotten” is not substance. And again, if substance is known to subsist through itself, while “unbegotten” does not subsist through itself but is spoken of a substance that was not born, then plainly “unbegotten” is not substance.

**57.** Again, if they say: “If the Father is unbegotten according to substance, while the Son is begotten, the substance of the begotten and the unbegotten cannot be one,” let them learn further that the mode of substances does not necessarily make substances different.

For because God the Father is said to be unbegotten and is likewise said to be immortal and incorruptible, he will not on that account have different substances, since “unbegotten,” “immortal,” and “incorruptible” are not one and the same thing, nor are the other similar terms. Therefore, just as these terms, when spoken of God, do not at all signify different substances, so “begotten” and “unbegotten” will never make different substances. For Adam was not begotten, whereas Seth was begotten; yet their substance is not different for that reason.

**58.** But if they persist, saying that what is without beginning is also unbegotten, and that, since the Son is begotten, he cannot be without beginning, let them learn [Col. 0487A] that not everything that is without beginning is in every respect also unbegotten, just as not everything that has a beginning is in every respect also begotten.

For God’s mercies, though possessed without beginning, are not therefore innate, since they have God as their Father. Likewise, heaven and earth, although they have a beginning, are not begotten but created. For not everything that is created is in every respect begotten. If “created” and “begotten” were the same, the evangelist John would have taught superfluously when he said: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12), since those who were once created would already possess this as well: that they should become children of God.

Therefore, just as “created” and “begotten” are not the same, so “not created” and “unbegotten” cannot be the same either, since God’s mercies, although uncreated, are nevertheless not innate.

**59.** When they again ask us: “How can God, being one, simple, and uncompounded, be at the same time Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?” let them learn that God does not thereby cease to be simple and uncompounded because he has one only-begotten substantive Word, equal to him in all things, and likewise substantive Wisdom, equal to him in all things.

But if, as they think, he is compounded because he has a will, and because this will is not equal to the substance—for substance and will are not the same—we nevertheless do not follow their opinion. Rather, we say piously and religiously that, even if God has a will and this will is not equal to the substance, he is nevertheless free from all composition.

[Col. 0487C] **60.** Since they still appear wise in their own eyes, although they have been proved utterly foolish in every respect, they ask us this also: “How can one God, one substance, be called Father and Son?” For those who say this customarily pronounce “one and only God, Son and Father” in a single part of speech, as though in Greek one said *huiopatōr* (υἱοπάτωρ, “Son-Father”).

Let them learn that they ought not to persist long in the same folly. For God should not be called *huiopatōr* merely because God the Father and his Son are one God and the substance of the Father and Son is likewise one and the same. We do not speak of one person numerically, but use a common designation for the substance.

Adam and his son Abel were one man, although one was distinct from the other and their substance was one and the same through the communion of nature; yet they were never called *huiopatōr*, nor could they even be called by that name.
