That two human beings, numerically distinct, are nevertheless called one man through communion and fellowship of nature, as I have said, is attested by God’s servant Moses, who says: “And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them” (Gen. 1:27).

Likewise, our Lord Jesus Christ calls himself and the Father one together, because of the equality and unity of their substance, saying: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God because of the unity and equality of substance.

**61.** For just as our thought cannot become speech—since thought itself is regarded as the father of our speech—so, conversely, speech can never become thought; nor is our wisdom either thought or speech. Rather, thought generates speech, but is not itself generated; likewise speech is merely generated and does not generate; and, correspondingly, wisdom neither generates nor is generated.

Our thought, being wise and possessing wisdom, as rational generates speech alone. Wisdom, in turn, does not generate speech, but exists together with thought and speech in true equality.

Thus God the Father can never become the Son, nor conversely the Son the Father; nor can the Holy Spirit become the Son or the Father. Again, God the Father did beget the only-begotten God the Word, but he himself was not born; the Son was born, but did not beget; and the Holy Spirit was neither born nor did he beget.

To put it more plainly: just as the mercies of God the Father, although born from the unbegotten Father, have generation completely conjoined to the Father’s unbegottenness, so also the substantive only-begotten Son of God has his birth completely conjoined to the Father’s ingeneration, since he is the radiance of glory and the form of God’s substance.

Thus blessed Paul, writing to the Hebrews, says (Heb. 1:3): “Who is the radiance of his glory and the figure of his substance.”

When the Apostle Paul called the Son the radiance of the Father, he plainly established that the Son is from the substance of the Father, that the Son of the Father is inseparable and undivided, and that he is always with the Father. By recalling the figure of God’s substance, he teaches that the Son has the same substance as the Father.

Again, just as the immortality of God the Father, being unbegotten together with God the Father, is not called begotten and does not itself likewise generate, so also God’s substantive Holy Spirit is neither born nor does he beget.

Therefore, while confessing three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—we believe that there is one power of the Trinity because of the unity of substance. Likewise, because of the indivisibility of nature, we confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one Lord, one God almighty, creator and providential ruler, always existing in himself and remaining the same. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# CONFESSION, OR BOOKLET OF FAITH, SENT BY PELAGIUS FROM THE EAST TO ROME, TO THE APOSTOLIC SEE

[Col. 0488D]

Baronius reported this confession, having extracted it from the Vatican records, in his *Annals*. By doing so he anticipated the plan of Father Sirmond, who intended to publish a copy written in his own hand. We present it from the copy of that most learned old man, corrected more fully than Baronius’s version (under the year of Christ 418).

## PART ONE, THE THEOLOGICAL PART

**1.** We believe in God the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible.

[Col. 0489A] **2.** We also believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were created, true God, the only-begotten and true Son of God, not made or adoptive, but begotten, of one substance with the Father—which the Greeks call *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιον, “of the same substance”)—and so equal in all things to God the Father that he cannot be inferior in time, rank, or power. We confess that the one who was begotten is as great as the one who begot him.

**3.** When we say that the Son was begotten by the Father, we do not thereby assign any time to the divine and ineffable generation. Nor do we say that the Father or the Son ever began. For we cannot otherwise confess the Father to be eternal unless we also confess the Son to be coeternal. The Father is called Father because of him, [Col. 0489B] and he who was always Father always had the Son.

**4.** We also believe in the Holy Spirit, true God, proceeding from the Father, equal in all things to the Father and the Son—in will, power, eternity, and substance.

**5.** There is absolutely no rank within the Trinity, nothing that can be called lower or higher. The whole Godhead is equal in its perfection, so that, except for the names indicating the distinct property of the persons, whatever is said of one person may most properly be understood of all three.

**6.** And just as, confounding Arius, we say that the Trinity has one and the same substance and confess one God in three persons, so, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three expressed persons according to their particular properties. We do not say that the Father is himself the Son, and himself the Holy Spirit, but that the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. We confess not merely names but also the properties of the names—that is, persons, or, as the Greeks express it, *hypostases* (ὑποστάσεις), that is, substances.

**7.** The Father never excludes the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, nor again does the Son or the Holy Spirit assume the name and person of the Father. The Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always Holy Spirit. Thus they are one in substance but distinguished in persons and names.

## PART TWO, THE ECONOMIC PART

[Col. 0489D] **8.** We say that the very Son of God, who possesses eternity without beginning together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, at the end of the ages took from Mary, ever-virgin, a perfect man of our nature, and that the Word became flesh by assuming humanity, not by changing the Godhead. Nor do we say, as some most wickedly suppose, that the Holy Spirit served as seed; rather, he acted by the power and might of the Creator.

**9.** We confess one person of the Son in Christ, but say that there are two perfect and complete substances, namely, divinity and humanity, which consists of soul and body. And just as we condemn Photinus, who confesses Christ to be merely a bare human being, so we anathematize Apollinaris [Col. 0490A] and those like him, who say that the Son of God assumed something less from human nature, and that the human being assumed—whether in flesh, soul, or understanding—was unlike those for whose sake he was assumed. We confess that he was like us, except for the single stain of sin, which is not natural.

**10.** We likewise execrate the blasphemy of those who attempt to assert, with a novel meaning, that from the time the flesh was assumed everything that belonged to the Godhead migrated into the human being, and again that everything belonging to humanity was transferred into God. Thus, by this confusion, the two substances—divinity and humanity—would appear to have been emptied of themselves and changed from their proper state into another, so that those who confess both an imperfect God in the Son and an imperfect man are judged to possess neither true God nor true man.

**11.** We say that our passible nature was assumed by the Son of God in such a way that the Godhead remained impassible. For the Son of God truly suffered, not apparently, everything that Scripture attests: hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, death, and other things of this kind.

**12.** He suffered according to that which could suffer, namely, according to the substance that was assumed. For the Son of God himself, according to his Godhead, is impassible like the Father, incomprehensible like the Father, invisible like the Father, and unchangeable like the Father.

Although the Son’s own person—that is, the Word of God—assumed a passible human being, nevertheless, through his indwelling, the Godhead of the Word suffered nothing according to its substance, so that the whole Trinity must be confessed as impassible.

**13.** Therefore the Son of God died, according to the Scriptures, in accordance with that which could die. He rose on the third day and ascended into heaven; he sits at the right hand of God the Father, while the same nature of flesh remains—the flesh in which he was born and suffered and in which he also rose. The substance of humanity was not emptied of itself but glorified, and it will remain forever with the Godhead.

**14.** Having therefore received from the Father all authority over the things that are in heaven and on earth, he will come to judge the living and the dead, both to reward the righteous and to punish sinners.

## PART THREE, THE ETHICAL PART

[Col. 0490D]

**15.** We also confess and believe in the resurrection of the flesh, so that we may say that we shall be restored in the same bodily reality in which we now exist, and that, once we have been made as we shall be after the resurrection, we shall remain so forever.

**16.** There is one life for all the saints, but the rewards differ according to their labor; conversely, the punishments of sinners also differ according to the measure of their offenses.

**17.** We hold one baptism, which we affirm is to be administered to infants in the same sacramental words as to adults.

**18.** We believe that a person, if he falls after baptism, can be saved through repentance.

[Col. 0491A] **19.** We accept the New and Old Testament in the number of books handed down by the authority of the holy Catholic Church.

**20.** We believe that souls are given by God, and we say that they were made by him. We anathematize those who say that souls are, as it were, a part of the divine substance. We also condemn the error of those who say that souls sinned previously or lived in heaven before they were sent into bodies.

**21.** We also execrate the blasphemy of those who say that God has commanded something impossible for human beings, and that God’s commandments can be kept not by individuals but only collectively by all.

**22.** We also anathematize those who, with Manichaeus, condemn first marriages, or, with the Cataphrygians, second marriages.

[Col. 0491B] **23.** We also anathematize those who say that the Son of God lied because of the necessity of the flesh, and that, because he assumed a human being, he could not do everything he wished.

**24.** We also condemn the heresy of Jovinian, who says that in the future there will be no distinction of merits and that we shall possess there the virtues which we neglected to possess here.

**25.** We confess free choice in such a way that we say that we always need God’s help. We declare both those who, with Manichaeus, say that a person cannot avoid sin, and those who, with Jovinian, assert that a person cannot sin, to be in error. Each removes freedom of choice. We, however, say that a person can always both sin and not sin, so that we may always confess ourselves to possess free choice.

**26.** This is the faith, most blessed pope, that we learned in the Catholic Church and have always held and continue to hold. If something has perhaps been stated in it with insufficient skill or caution, we desire that it be corrected by you, who possess both the faith and the see of Peter. But if this confession of ours is approved by the judgment of your apostolic office, then whoever wishes to stain me will prove himself ignorant, malicious, or even non-Catholic; he will not prove me a heretic.

The distinguished scholar Jean Launoy published a learned dissertation on Pelagius’s confession, and clearly demonstrated that it was neither sent by Jerome to Damasus, as Remigius of Lyons supposed (*Book on the Three Epistles*, ch. 39), nor spoken by Augustine in Sermon 191, as William of Paris believed [Col. 0491D] (*On Sins and Vices*, ch. 10), and that no suitable ancient or modern authority can deprive Pelagius of it. Augustine himself (*On Original Sin*, ch. 21) and Zosimus (*Epistle 2 to Africa, in the Case of Pelagius*) plainly attribute it to Pelagius.

In these three matters I willingly agree with the learned man, though not equally in the other two, which he attempts to establish separately in their respective chapters. One is that, before the time of Charlemagne, this booklet had not yet been falsely attributed by credulous antiquity to Jerome; the other is that certain passages were later added to it which concern the heresy either of Eutyches, concerning the confusion of the natures in Christ, or of Elipandus, concerning Christ’s adoptive sonship.

To begin with the first matter, I do not see how the author of the *Carolingian Work* could have cited the confession (Book III, ch. 10) as a tradition of the Catholic faith, received from the Fathers and expressed in Jerome’s words, if it were found only in more recent manuscripts [Col. 0492A] and could thus have been charged with novelty by the testimony of the ancients—and especially by the weightier testimony of their silence—at precisely the period when some had begun to inquire more carefully into the truth of manuscripts and to accuse certain works, including Jerome’s, of being spurious.

Moreover, Remigius of Lyons, a contemporary of Charlemagne (*in the place cited above*), placed the confession now under discussion alongside the three books of dialogues against Pelagius written by Jerome:

“What that holy teacher thought, in accordance with the truth of the Catholic faith, about free choice, and the dialogues that he wrote against the Pelagians under the names of Atticus and Critobulus, testify most clearly. His profession of faith, which he published most fully and perfectly to the pontiff of the apostolic see in defense of himself against certain slanderers, also sufficiently demonstrates this, where he speaks about the same free choice as follows: ‘WE CONFESS FREE CHOICE IN SUCH A WAY,’ and so forth.”

Why did he form this opinion? Certainly for no other reason than that he understood both works to be universally attributed to Jerome and had found them, in his own manuscripts—which he expressly testified were ancient—marked with the name of the same teacher.

Finally, no one would have suspected rashly that the same thing happened to this booklet as to the letter to Demetrias, which the venerable Bede states was read by his own people (*Preface to the Commentary on the Song of Songs*, ch. 5; he was writing shortly after the year 700), since they believed it to be by the holy and Catholic teacher Jerome—certainly because at that time it was commonly found among his books.

Indeed, Cassiodorus shows that the Pelagians wished to conceal the works of their teacher under the names of holy authors. He says (*Institutions of Divine and Secular Learning*, ch. 8) that the annotations of Pelagius on the Epistles of Paul were so famously held in everyone’s hands in his own age—he flourished in the sixth century—that people said they had been written through the learned efforts of Saint Gelasius, pope of the city of Rome, a most learned man. “This,” he says, “is what those commonly do who wish to defend corrupt works by the authority of a glorious name.”

[Col. 0492C] Someone could therefore conjecture, without implausibility, that as early as the sixth century, or even at the end of the fifth, Pelagius’s booklet had been inserted into Jerome’s works and placed, as it actually was in the manuscript of the Church of Lyons, alongside the three dialogues.

Thus it could have happened that at first the booklet bore Pelagius’s name at its head, through the contrivance of the Pelagians, who wished to condemn Jerome falsely in the judgment of readers, as though he had slandered his teacher concerning free choice, in opposition to the certain testimony of the confession. Then, when the author’s name was removed—as happens through the carelessness of scribes—it might have been believed to have been composed by the same person as the dialogues with which it had been joined. Something similar may be indicated by the words of Remigius.

As for the second matter—that something was inserted which pertains to the heresy either of Eutyches, concerning the confusion or even transformation of the natures in Christ, or of Jovinian, concerning human impeccability, or of Elipandus, concerning Christ’s adoptive sonship—it seems to me no less implausible.

For just as Pelagius and Nestorius did not give rise to their own heresies but only their names, Eutyches likewise did not originate his heresy, but merely gave it his name; he received it from Apollinaris. Hence Pope Leo writes (*Sermon 9 on the Forty Days’ Fast*) that in his own days some people had conceived an ancient madness from the spirit of error, once destroyed and condemned:

“They dare to deny the twofold nature in Christ, either by denying the reality of the flesh assumed or by turning the Godhead into flesh, so that, according to Manichaeus, there may be no resurrection because there was no passion, or, according to Apollinaris, the very Godhead of the Word may be mutable and itself become passible.”

Theodoret likewise writes (*Ecclesiastical Fables*, Book IV, ch. 9) that a certain Polemius, having found an opportunity in the writings of Apollinaris, both professed a confession of the substances and asserted the commingling of divinity and body; from this the heresy of the Polemians arose.

Ambrose, near the end of the fourth century (*On the Incarnation*, ch. 6), writes:

“Since these people say that the Word was changed into flesh and altered from its own nature, they are given an opportunity to twist the weakness of the flesh into a weakness of the Godhead, through a certain change made in the divine nature.”

A little later he adds:

“I have read the following stated in certain books: ‘THE ORGAN AND THE ONE BY WHOM THE ORGAN WAS MOVED WERE OF ONE NATURE IN CHRIST.’ I have included this so that the author’s name may be detected from the writings.”

Ambrose was referring to a disputational speech of Apollinaris, from which Leontius quoted this fragment (*Against the Frauds of Apollinaris*):

“The instrument and that which moves the instrument naturally accomplish one operation; and whatever has one operation also has one substance. Therefore one substance was made of the Word and the instrument.”

Why mention more? Two Gregories—Nazianzen and Nyssen—may be consulted on this matter (Oration 51; the Epistle to Cledonius; *To Theophilus on Apollinaris*).

A more straightforward answer can be given concerning Jovinian’s error regarding human impeccability. Pelagius criticized Jovinian on one point only: he saw that Jovinian’s position worked against him, namely, that a person cannot continue to sin for as long as he lives a mortal life. Pelagius held this possibility on both sides to be necessary for preserving freedom of choice; Jovinian believed that the possibility of sinning was removed by baptism—if indeed that was his belief.

This meaning is sufficiently clearly revealed by Pelagius’s words: “We, however, say that a person can always both sin and not sin, so that we may always confess ourselves to possess free choice.” Why else would the word “always” be repeated? See the lengthy dispute between Julian and Augustine concerning Jovinian’s heresy (*Imperfect Work*, Book IV, ch. 120), which each pressed upon his opponent.

Nor can I be persuaded to believe that the word “adoptive” (*adoptivum*) was added either by the Fathers assembled at Frankfurt or by anyone else of a later age. Apart from the fact that it is found in all the manuscripts, including those that appear to be older, it is not credible that such an addition could have entered all of them. Nor would it prudently have been placed here by the Fathers against the heresy of Elipandus, but in a wholly inappropriate location, since the second section discusses Christ *theologically* (θεολογικῶς), not *economically* (οἰκονομικῶς).

Moreover, with regard to the Arians, whom this passage chiefly addresses, Pelagius ought to have included this statement: “Not made or adoptive, but begotten, of one substance with the Father,” and so forth, so that the heresy denying that the only-begotten Son of God is *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιον) with the Father might be excluded, while saying that the Son is merely like one who is adopted.

Certainly, the Fathers commonly attacked this Arian doctrine of adoption (*huiothesia*, υἱοθεσία) long before the Pelagian heresy arose, and therefore also before the questions raised by Elipandus.

Finally, the Fathers assembled at Frankfurt deliberately refrained from bringing forward this testimony, although it was readily available. For, being equally learned and prudent, they understood well enough in what sense it had been spoken from the very beginning of the Arian sect and what objection it would immediately provoke from its opponents.

Furthermore, Pelagius wrote his little book of faith while he was in the East—if indeed he wrote it, and did not rather borrow it from Coelestius, with only a very few alterations. [Col. 0493D] He wrote it, I say, after the Council of Diospolis, while Theodotus was contemplating a synod at Antioch, when John of Jerusalem had already died, on 10 January 417, and Praylius had succeeded him; Praylius’s letter of recommendation for Pelagius accompanied the little book to Rome, while news of Innocent’s death—which occurred on 12 March 417—had not yet been heard in the East (Augustine, *On Original Sin*, ch. 22; Mercator, *Commonitorium*, ch. 3; Letter 2 of Zosimus to the Africans in the case of Pelagius; Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 30). The book of faith, therefore, was written—or at least sent to Rome—shortly after the Paschal feasts of 417, when navigation had again become safe. It was received by Zosimus, Innocent’s successor, and by him sent with a letter to Africa, where Augustine saw it (Book II to Boniface, ch. 2), and judged it not merely free from suspicion, as Zosimus believed it to be (Letter 2 of Zosimus on the Case of Pelagius), but also to conceal beneath evasive language a heretical opinion, which he exposed (*On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 39).

[Col. 0494A] Insofar as it concerns the questions raised by the Pelagians, the whole work is directed against either Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon or his *Dialogue*, but with such great skill that Pelagius criticizes each of the holy doctor’s statements as though he were pursuing some other matter. But insofar as it contains matters about which he had not been questioned, as Augustine says (*On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 32), it occupies people’s minds with a profession of faith concerning the Trinity and the Incarnation of the Word, for whom he is preparing a deception, and wishes falsely to pass himself off as a Catholic. Yet he too, like Rufinus the Syrian, speaks of the Incarnation in such a way that he can conceal, beneath general expressions, the impiety of Theodore of Mopsuestia, as we shall show in the notes to Julian’s confession. For the present we shall touch only upon the points by which Jerome appears to have been attacked.

**(No. 4.)** “We believe also in the Holy Spirit, true God, proceeding from the Father.” The same words occur in Coelestius and Julian. All of them, however, say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, and by their silence deny that he proceeds from the Son, since they follow their common teacher, Theodore of Mopsuestia, whose words are these: “And in the Holy Spirit, whom we do not think received his existence either from the Son or through the Son.” By this statement Pelagius attacked Saint Jerome, who, in *Dialogue* 2, after quoting Luke’s words, “When they had come to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (Acts 16:7), immediately added: “Observe that the spirit of Jesus is the Holy Spirit, who elsewhere, because of the unity of substance, is called the Father’s Spirit.”

**(No. 6.)** “That is, persons, or, as the Greeks express it, *hypostases*.” He maliciously used the Greek word in order silently to reproach Jerome for his wavering on this matter (Letter 159 to Damasus): “After the Nicene faith, after the Alexandrian decree, with the West likewise joining in, the Arian bishop and the Campensians demand of me, a Roman man, the novel term of three *hypostases*. Who, I ask, handed this down in such a way as the Apostles did? What new teacher of the nations—Paul—taught these things? We ask what they think can be understood by three *hypostases*. They say, ‘Three subsisting persons.’ We reply that we believe this. The meaning is not enough; they demand the very word, because I do not know what poison lies hidden in the syllables.”

**(No. 8.)** “Nor, as certain most wicked people suppose, was the Holy Spirit in place of semen.” I remember reading something somewhat similar in appearance in Jerome, but it can be twisted into a perverse meaning only maliciously, since, for anyone who reads it by itself, it is entirely straightforward. Hilary certainly mentions the generative efficacy of the Holy Spirit (*On the Trinity*, Book II), as does the author of the *Incomplete Work on Matthew*, whose words are these: “Thus, when the only-begotten God was about to enter the Virgin, the Holy Spirit went before him, so that, with the Holy Spirit preceding in sanctification, Christ might be born according to the flesh, the divinity entering in place of semen.” I know that Rupert denied that the Holy Spirit was in place of semen in Christ’s conception. But he himself neither explains whom he is contradicting by this denial, nor is it possible to guess any other person than the author of the *Incomplete Work*.

[Col. 0494D] **(No. 15.)** “And whatever we were made like after the resurrection, we shall remain forever.” This statement is indeed Catholic in itself, but it was maliciously directed against Jerome, who in *Dialogue* 1, and in several discussions against Pelagius concerning the purification of the faithful—including those who died in however great a number of sins—seemed to hold that only the punishments of unbelievers should be everlasting. See the fuller discussion in the notes to Rufinus the Syrian’s first anathema.

**(No. 16.)** “That there is one life of all the saints.” Pelagius appears to have inserted this phrase for three reasons. First, to make Jerome seem odious as though he were possessed of some malicious mind: Jerome, who, sharing the same opinion as he did against Jovinian concerning the inequality of rewards (Letter to Ctesiphon, *Dialogue* 2, and elsewhere), reproached him with association with Jovinian. Second, to forestall the Catholics’ objection that he made two lives for the saints: one for infants dying without baptism, and another for those regenerated. Finally, to prepare people’s minds against belief in original sin, which they would accept with greater difficulty the more firmly they were persuaded that there is no punishment except for transgressions—that is, for sins each person had committed by his own will.

**(No. 17.)** “We hold one baptism.” Augustine cites this passage (*On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 3) and exposes the heresy that was attempting to conceal itself beneath ambiguous words. Pelagius inserted it against Jerome, whose words are these (*Dialogue* 3, near the end): “I shall say only this: either we must devise a new creed, so that after the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit you may baptize infants into the kingdom of heaven; or, if you have one baptism both for little ones and for adults, you must believe that infants too are to be baptized for the remission of sins, in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, and so forth.”

**(No. 19.)** “We receive the New and Old Testament in that number of books, etc.” This was maliciously directed at Jerome, who, in listing the books of the Old Testament, appears to have followed the canon of the Hebrews rather than that of the Latin Church, at whose head Pelagius was nevertheless writing. At that time, moreover, a major question was being debated concerning the canon of the sacred books. Thus Exuperius of Toulouse consulted Pope Innocent, and in Africa the Fathers in 419 thought that a decree should be issued; it is canon 25 of the African Church’s code.

Later he wished to accuse Jerome of introducing a fifth Gospel, namely that of the Nazarenes, which he had translated from the Syriac language into Latin and from which he had cited testimony in the third *Dialogue*. Hence Julian, addressing Augustine (Book IV of the *Unfinished Work*, ch. 87), says: “He delights in agreeing with you, if only moderately. With what confidence can you, while praising Jerome’s writings, say that there was no sin in Christ, when he, in that dialogue which he composed under the names of Atticus and Critobulus with remarkable elegance, as befitted such a man, relies even upon the testimony of a fifth Gospel, which he says he translated, to demonstrate that Christ had not only natural but also voluntary [Col. 0495C] sin, on account of which he recognized that he himself needed to be cleansed by John’s baptism? He also adds to this another charge of falsification concerning a testimony of John the Evangelist. Of this work you boast in the letter that you sent to Alexandria, saying that Pelagius, crushed beneath the weight of Jerome’s Scriptures, cannot defend free choice. But that work was answered by a Catholic man who had been attacked.”

From this passage, unless Julian was lying, we learn that Augustine had read and praised Jerome’s *Dialogue*; that Augustine sent to Alexandria a letter containing praise of the *Dialogue*; and that Pelagius—or rather the deacon Anianus, who is mentioned in Jerome’s Letter to Alypius and Augustine (Letter 143)—answered it. Nevertheless, the response mentioned in the letter just cited seems to have been directed against the letter to Ctesiphon rather than against the *Dialogue*. But Anianus was almost the sole writer for Pelagius, as was stated in the first dissertation.

**(No. 20.)** “We believe that souls are given by God.” This statement too was inserted cunningly. First, to criticize Jerome, as though he were persecuting a man who agreed with him concerning the origin of souls—a question that at that time exercised the Church. Next, perhaps to reproach Augustine for his uncertainty on this matter, which he had wished to have attested by an inquiry conveyed to Jerome through Orosius. Finally, to sow a kind of prejudice against original sin, as though it could not be transmitted from parents unless the soul too were transmitted.

**(Same place.)** “We also condemn the error of those, etc.” These words were directed against Jerome, who wrote in *Dialogue* 3 as follows: “If the remission of the sins of others seems unjust to you—a remission not needed by one who could not sin—go over to your Amasius, who says that past sins in heaven and ancient transgressions are loosed in baptism, so that, in this matter too, you may follow the error of the man whose authority you follow in other respects.”

[Col. 0496A] **(No. 21.)** “We also execrate the blasphemy of those who say that God has commanded something impossible for human beings.” This whole execration is vomited by the impure man against Saint Jerome. For when Critobulus had said in the first *Dialogue*: “Either God gave possible commandments or impossible ones. If possible, it is in our power to do them if we wish; if impossible, we are not guilty if we do not do what we cannot fulfill,” and so forth, Jerome contradicts him at length and among other things says: “You see that God commanded something possible, and yet that no one, by nature, can completely accomplish what is possible. He therefore gave commandments and various virtues, all of which we cannot possess at the same time, etc.”

**(Same place.)** “And that God’s commandments can be observed not by individuals, but by everyone collectively.” Again he attacks Jerome, who in the passage just cited had said: “This is what I say in its entirety: not all of us can do everything. God commanded possible things, I admit; but each of us cannot possess all these possibilities, not because of weakness of nature—lest you bring a charge against God—and so forth.”

[Col. 0496B] **(No. 23.)** “We also anathematize those who say that the Son of God lied because of the necessity of the flesh.” This anathema too is directed against Jerome, whose difficult statement occurs in *Dialogue* 2: “You can avoid all sins, so that, while you still remain in the body, you may show yourself to be an *antitheos* [‘one opposed to God’]. He denies to his brothers and relatives that he is going to the Feast of Tabernacles. Later it is written: ‘But when his brothers had gone up, then he too went up to the feast, not openly but as though in secret’ (John 7:10). He denied that he would go, and did what he had previously denied. Porphyry barks and accuses him of inconsistency and change, not knowing that all scandals must be referred to the flesh, etc.”

**(Same place.)** “And that, because of the man he assumed, he could not do everything he wished.” Jerome is attacked again because he wrote several somewhat difficult things in the same passage. For after quoting Christ’s saying, “I can do nothing of myself, but as I hear, I judge” (John 5:30), he added: “The Arians bring forward a slander; but the Church replies that these words are spoken from the person of the man who was assumed. You, on the contrary, say: ‘I can be without sin if I wish’; whereas he can do nothing of himself, so that he may show the reality of his humanity.” And elsewhere: “Christ went away into the borders of Tyre and Sidon, and entering a house he wished no one to know it, yet he could not remain hidden” (Mark 7:24). He certainly wished to remain hidden; and why could he not do what he wished, so as to avoid the awareness of everyone at his coming? You ask the reasons why he could not remain hidden. Consider the reality of the man assumed, and you will be free of every scandal. If the Son of God is said to have been unable to do something in the flesh and because of the flesh, etc.”

**(No. 24.)** “And that we shall possess there the virtues, etc.” Under the name of Jovinian he condemns Jerome as a heretic; Jerome’s words are these (*Dialogue* 1): “As long as we have this treasure in earthen vessels and are surrounded by fragile flesh—indeed, mortal and corruptible flesh—we believe ourselves blessed if in each virtue and in each part of virtue we are subject to God. But when this mortal has put on immortality, and this corruptible has been clothed with incorruption, and death has been swallowed up in Christ’s victory, then God will be all in all; the number of the saints will rejoice in the entire choir of virtues, etc.”

**(No. 25.)** “They say with Manichaeus that a human being cannot avoid sin.” Atticus’s Critobulus made this very objection in *Dialogue* 3. For when Atticus had praised the necessity of divine assistance for performing works of piety, Critobulus replied: “I grieve that ecclesiastical men, who claim for themselves the title of teachers, should abolish free choice; once this is abolished, the sect of the Manichaeans is established.” A little later he says: “How do you preserve free choice when you say that a human being can do nothing unless God is always helping?”

**(Same place.)** “Who assert with Jovinianus that a human being cannot sin.” By this condemnation he wished to accuse Jerome of slander, since Jerome had called him an heir of Jovinian (Dialogue 2), and also a disciple (Letter to Ctesiphon), indeed even, in *Dialogue* 3, an advocate of the doctrine that a baptized person can no longer sin. For when Critobulus began to say: “Surely you will admit that those who have received Christ’s baptism do not have sin; and if they are without sin, they are righteous; and once they have become righteous, if they act carefully, they can preserve righteousness forever, and thus avoid every sin,” Jerome replies in the person of Atticus: “Are you not ashamed to follow Jovinian’s exploded and condemned opinion? He too relies upon these testimonies and your arguments; or rather, you follow his inventions, wishing to teach in the East what was formerly condemned at Rome and more recently in Africa, etc.”

[Col. 0497A] **(No. 26.)** “This is the faith, etc.” It is astonishing that for so many centuries the eyes of almost everyone should have been so captivated that they could not—or rather would not—see, despite Augustine’s repeated warnings, that this exposition of faith had either been composed by a heretic or was at least deservedly suspect. It is a particular credit of our own age, and its chief credit, that we are not rashly deceived by such merchandise. Yet care must be taken that the prudence which has escaped the excesses of credulity does not fall into an intolerable eagerness to pass judgment, and into a tyranny that almost proscribes books simply because they are displeasing.

# THE LITTLE BOOK OF FAITH PRESENTED TO POPE ZOSIMUS BY COELESTIUS, A DISCIPLE OF PELAGIUS

Some have thought that Coelestius presented two little books of his faith, one at Rome to Zosimus and another at Carthage to Aurelius, because Augustine mentions one presented to Zosimus (*On Original Sin*, ch. 5), while Zosimus mentions one presented to Aurelius. But I can scarcely approve this inference: Zosimus plainly signifies nothing of the kind. “Let those who contradict him and claim that he thinks otherwise than he set forth in his little books and confession come within two months,” he says (Letter 1 to the Africans in the case of Coelestius). By “little books” he indicates short writings, or, as I rather think, the little books of *Petitions*, which Coelestius presented several times during various judicial proceedings; not the exposition of faith, which he calls his confession. Augustine mentions only one such confession, and would certainly not have been silent about another, if one had been issued at Carthage, since it would have been more familiar to him and more carefully examined.

For when he says (*On Original Sin*, ch. 19) that Coelestius at Carthage confessed in his little book the redemption of infants, yet refused to confess that sin had passed into them from Adam, he unquestionably means the little book of *Petitions*, or a confession extorted by the force of interrogation, not a formula of faith voluntarily presented. For he says as follows (Letter 157): “Coelestius was brought before the episcopal judgment because of these very arguments against Christ’s grace; nevertheless, he was compelled to confess, concerning the infants who were to be baptized, that redemption was necessary for them also.” Although he might have said something more explicit there concerning original sin, he nevertheless prescribed no small boundary for himself by the very term “redemption.”

This interpretation must also be applied to the words of the Fathers of the Council of Carthage, who wrote to Pope Innocent (Vol. XX of our *Patrology*, col. 564): “Although Coelestius has already confessed in his little book, in the Church of Carthage, that through Christ’s baptism the redemption of infants also takes place.” By “little book” they understood a written interpretation of his opinion, presented after it had been expressed at some particular gathering.

Until the present day, it has been believed even by learned men that nothing beyond the conclusion of Coelestius’s confession survives in Augustine’s report. I think the whole confession is found in Augustine himself (*On Original Sin*, chs. 5, 6, and 23), but that its meaning escaped notice because, having been divided into two parts and scattered in distant places, the larger part could scarcely be recognized by eyes almost bewitched by a kind of mental prejudice. For since one section differs in no respect from Sermon 190 among Augustine’s sermons *On Time*, provided that its beginning is removed—the beginning added by whoever dared to fashion a Catholic treatise from the confession of a heretic—it was thought to belong to Pelagius, whereas in reality it belongs to Coelestius, because it bore considerable resemblance to Pelagius’s little book.

What I am saying will become evident if the shorter section is joined to the longer. The result will be a continuous and complete little book, precisely the kind indicated by Zosimus and Augustine. Those two witnesses are neither insignificant nor doubtful, since they did not merely glance at the little book with their eyes, but examined it with their minds attentive to nearly every syllable.

Coelestius’s little book, as Zosimus writes, was distinct from Pelagius’s, since one had been presented before the other; nevertheless, it was so similar that Pelagius’s contained everything equivalent to, and expressed in the same sense and wording as, what Coelestius had previously set forth (Letter 2 to the Africans in the case of Pelagius).

[Col. 0498B] Augustine says in it (*On Original Sin*, ch. 23): “When Coelestius had explained his faith—from the Trinity of one Godhead to the resurrection, such as the resurrection of the dead will be—with as much freedom as he wished, although no one had questioned him about these matters and no issue concerning them had arisen there, when his discourse reached the matter under discussion, he said: ‘But if any questions have arisen beyond the faith,’ etc.” He had written the same thing about Pelagius’s little book (*On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 33): “In that little book he discussed many matters about which he had not been questioned; for when he had completed, to whatever extent he wished, his discussion from the unity of the Trinity to the resurrection of the flesh—something no one had asked him about—etc., he says: ‘We hold one baptism.’”

In the same work he openly denied original sin, as Augustine testifies (*ibid.*, ch. 2): “And in the city of Rome, in his little book which he gave to the most blessed Pope Zosimus, he asserted more explicitly that original sin binds none of the little ones.”

He denied it, however, while declaring himself ready to hold whatever the apostolic see should define. Augustine says this (*Book II to Boniface*, ch. 3): “When Coelestius had included this in his little book—that a human being is born without any fault of original sin—among those matters concerning which he confessed that he still wished to remain uncertain and to be instructed, the willingness to amend was approved in a man of exceptionally keen intelligence who, if corrected, would certainly have benefited many, not the falsity of his doctrine. For this reason his little book was called Catholic: because it is also characteristic of a Catholic mind, if it happens to think otherwise than the truth requires, not to define the matter with certainty, but to reject it once it has been exposed and demonstrated.”

No one will fail to see that these six points, and others besides, agree with the little book we have mentioned, if he looks at the confessions of Coelestius and Pelagius, which we present in parallel: namely, that it is almost entirely similar to Pelagius’s confession; that it differs in a few things; that it contains extraneous questions concerning the Trinity and other matters extending to the resurrection of the flesh; that it openly denies original sin; that it nevertheless admits that infants are baptized for the remission of sins; and that it submits all its positions to the apostolic see.

## COELESTIUS

*[Note: The following texts, headed COELESTIUS and PELAGIUS, are printed in parallel in Migne.]*

**1.** We believe in God the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible.

**2.** We believe also in our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were created, true God and the true only-begotten Son of God—not made or adopted, but begotten, of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιον), and in every respect so equal to God the Father that he cannot be inferior in time, rank, or power. We confess that the one who was begotten is as great as the one who begot him.

**3.** But when we say that the Son was begotten by the Father, we do not thereby assign any time to the divine and ineffable generation; nor do we say that the Father or the Son ever began to exist. For we cannot otherwise confess the Father to be eternal unless we also confess the Son to be coeternal. The Father is called Father because of the Son, and he who was always Father always had a Son.

**4.** We believe also in the Holy Spirit, true God, proceeding from the Father, equal in every respect to the Father and the Son—in nature, will, power, eternity, and substance.

**5.** There is absolutely no rank in the Trinity, nothing that can be called lower or higher. Therefore the whole Trinity is equal in its perfection, so that, except for the names which indicate the distinctive properties of the persons, whatever is said of one person may most appropriately be understood of all three.

[Col. 0499D] **6.** Just as, while refuting Arius, we say that the Trinity has one and the same substance and confess one God in three persons, so, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons, clearly marked by their individual properties. We do not say that the Father is himself the Son, or himself the Holy Spirit, but that the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. For we confess not merely names, but also the properties of the names—that is, the persons.

**7.** The Father never excludes the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, nor in turn does the Son or the Holy Spirit assume the name and person of the Father. Rather, the Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always Holy Spirit. Thus they are one in substance but distinguished by persons and names.

**8.** We say that the very Son of God, who exists without beginning with the Father and the Holy Spirit, at the end of the ages assumed from Mary, ever-virgin, a perfect human being of our nature, and that the Word became flesh by assuming a human being, not by changing the Godhead. Nor do we say, as certain most wicked people suppose, that the Holy Spirit was in place of semen; rather, he acted by the power and might of the Creator.

**9.** Thus we confess one person of the Son in Christ, while saying that there are two complete and integral substances, namely, the Godhead and the humanity, which consists of soul and body. And just as we condemn Photinus, who confesses that Christ was merely and solely a human being, so we anathematize Apollinaris and those like him, who say that the Son of God assumed something less than the full human nature, and that the human being assumed either in flesh, soul, or understanding was unlike those for whose sake he was assumed. For we confess that he was like us, except for the sole stain of sin, which is not natural.

[Col. 0501A] **10.** We likewise execrate the blasphemy of those who attempt to assert, in a novel sense, that from the time he assumed flesh everything that belonged to the Godhead passed over into the human being, and in turn everything that belonged to humanity was transferred into God. Thus, by this confusion—something no heresy has ever dared to say—it would seem that both substances, namely the Godhead and the humanity, had been emptied of their own being and changed into something else. We would then confess the Son to be an imperfect God and an imperfect human being, and believe that we possess neither true God nor true human being.

[Col. 0501B] **11.** We say that the human being assumed by the Son of God was assumed in such a way that God nevertheless remained impassible. For the Son of God truly suffered, not merely in appearance, all the things that Scripture testifies to: hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, death, and other things of this kind.

[Col. 0501C] **12.** But he suffered according to that which was capable of suffering—not according to the substance that assumed, but according to the substance that was assumed. For the very Son of God, according to his Godhead, is impassible like the Father and incorruptible like the Father. Although the person proper to the Son, that is, the Word of God, assumed a passible human being, nevertheless, through that being’s indwelling, the Word’s Godhead suffered nothing according to its substance; and so the entire Trinity necessarily remains impassible.

[Col. 0501D] **13.** The Son of God therefore died in the same nature of flesh in which he was born and suffered, and in which he also rose again. For the substance of humanity was not emptied, but glorified, and it will remain eternally with the Godhead.

[Col. 0502B] **14.** He will come to judge the living and the dead, to reward the righteous and punish sinners.

**15.** We believe in the resurrection of the flesh in such a way that we say we shall be restored in the same reality of limbs in which we now exist, and that whatever condition we have once attained after the resurrection, we shall remain in it forever.

**16.** There is one life for all the saints, but rewards differ according to labor; and, conversely, punishments also differ for sinners according to the measure of their offenses.

**17.** We hold one baptism, which, in the same sacramental words, we say is to be celebrated for infants just as for adults.

**18.** We confess that infants ought to be baptized for the remission of sins, according to the rule of the universal Church and according to the Gospel’s teaching, because the Lord established that the kingdom of heaven can be granted only to the baptized; and because they do not possess the powers of nature, it must be granted to them through the generosity of grace.

*[Note: This was the reason Pelagius said: “I know where infants who die without baptism do not go; where they do go, I do not know” (*On Original Sin*, ch. 21). It was likewise the reason the Pelagians commonly proclaimed: “Grace has something in infants that it may adopt; the water has nothing to wash away” (*Hypognosticon*, Book V). It was also why Julian so often repeated: “Through baptism infants become not good from evil, but better from good,” etc. (*Unfinished Work*, ch. 53).]*

**19.** We say that infants are to be baptized for the remission of sins, not in order to seem to establish sin by propagation—which is far removed from Catholic understanding—because sin is not born with a human being, but is subsequently committed by the human being, and because it is shown to be not a fault of nature but of the will.

*[Note: When the Pelagians were pressed to explain how infants could be said to be baptized for the remission of sins if they were free from sin, they invented every conceivable explanation. They said that they were baptized for the remission of sins either because baptism took place in the Church, in which sins are remitted; or because it was by a sacrament that remitted whatever sins it found; or because it was in the name of Christ, who died to redeem everyone, especially sinners; or so that they might at some point obtain the remission of sins, if as adults they should commit any; or finally, so that different kinds of baptism would not be celebrated and there might not be one universal rule of the Church, etc. (*Against Julian*, Book III, ch. 3; *Unfinished Work*, ch. 53; and frequently elsewhere).]*

*[Note: He produces three arguments, to which the others used in this part against the Catholic faith may be reduced: that sin is not born but committed; that it is not a fault of nature but of the will; and that an injury is done to the Creator if evil is said to be transmitted through nature, which is God’s work.]*

And it is therefore appropriate to confess the former point, lest we appear to establish different kinds of baptism; and it is necessary to safeguard the latter, lest, under cover of the mystery, evil should be said to be transmitted to a human being through nature before it is committed by the human being, thereby injuring the Creator.

[Col. 0503C] **20.** We believe that a person who has fallen after baptism can be saved, first through reconciliation and then through penance.

**21.** We receive the New and Old Testament in that number of books which the authoritative tradition of the holy Catholic Church hands down.

**22.** We believe that souls are given by God, and we say that they were made by him. We anathematize those who say that the soul is somehow a part of the divine substance; and we also condemn the error of those who say that souls sinned previously or lived in heaven before they were sent into bodies.

[Col. 0504A] **23.** We also execrate the blasphemy of those who say that God has commanded something impossible for a human being, and that God’s commandments can be observed not by individuals but by everyone collectively.

**24.** Or those who condemn first marriages with Manichaeus, or second marriages with the Cataphrygians.

[Col. 0504B] **25.** We also anathematize those who say that the Son of God lied because of the necessity of the flesh, and that, because of the human being he assumed, he could not do everything he wished.

**26.** We also condemn the heresy of Jovinianus, who says that in the future there will be no difference in merits, and that there we shall possess the virtues which here we neglected to possess.

**27.** We confess free choice in such a way that we say that we always need God’s assistance. We say that both those who, with Manichaeus, assert that a human being cannot avoid sin and those who, with Jovinianus, assert that a human being cannot sin are in error; for each removes freedom of choice. We, however, say that a human being is always able both to sin and not to sin, so that we may confess ourselves free in choice.

[Col. 0505A] **28.** This is the faith which we learned in the Catholic Church and which we have always held; and we believe that we shall also be able to hold it from now on.

[Col. 0505B] **29.** But if questions have arisen beyond the faith, concerning which there is disagreement among many—

*[Note: These are questions on which one may affirm or deny without endangering the faith. This Pelagian trickery was sufficiently discussed in the dissertation on the subscriptions. See Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chs. 23–24.]*

—I do not, as the author of some doctrine, establish a definitive judgment on them by this authority; rather, I offer for examination by the judgment of your apostolate those things which I have received from the fountain of the prophets and Apostles,

*[Note: Those innovators impudently boasted that the whole of tradition and Scripture supported them. Augustine admirably restrains this boast, which they shared with other heretics, both throughout his works generally and especially in the first two books against Julian’s first work.]*

so that, if some error arising from ignorance should perhaps have crept into us as human beings,

*[Note: He says what everyone at that time commonly said (the Synod of the Fathers of Carthage); hence the Africans neither accused him of this statement nor rightly rejected the judgment established, but rather requested by their own decrees that the authority of the apostolic see be applied to it (the synodical letter of the Fathers of Carthage). Augustine himself publicly proclaimed in the Church that cases should be settled by apostolic replies (Sermon 2, *On the Words of the Apostle*).]*

it may be corrected by your decision.

## PELAGIUS

[Col. 0498D]

We believe in God the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible.

We believe also in our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were created, true God and the true only-begotten Son of God—not made or adopted, but begotten, of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιον), and in every respect so equal to God the Father that he cannot be inferior in time, rank, or power. We confess that the one who was begotten is as great as the one who begot him.

But when we say that the Son was begotten by the Father, we do not thereby assign any time to the divine and ineffable generation; nor do we say that the Father or the Son ever began to exist. For we cannot otherwise confess the Father to be eternal unless we also confess the Son to be coeternal. The Father is called Father because of him, and he who was always Father always had a Son.

We believe also in the Holy Spirit, true God, proceeding from the Father, equal in every respect to the Father and the Son—in will, power, eternity, and substance.

There is absolutely no rank in the Trinity, nothing that can be called lower or higher; rather, the whole Godhead is equal in its perfection, so that, except for the names which indicate the distinctive properties of the persons, whatever is said of one person may most appropriately be understood of all three.

[Col. 0499D] Just as, while confounding Arius, we say that the Trinity has one and the same substance and confess one God in three persons, so, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons, clearly marked by their individual properties. We do not say that he is himself Father, himself Son, himself Holy Spirit, but that the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. For we confess not merely names, but also the properties of the names—that is, the persons, or, as the Greeks express it, *hypostases* (ὑποστάσεις), that is, subsistences.

Neither does the Father at any time exclude the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, nor, conversely, does the Son or the Holy Spirit receive the name and person of the Father; rather, the Father is always Father, the Son is always Son, and the Holy Spirit is always Holy Spirit. Thus they are one in substance, but distinguished by persons and names.

As for the very Son of God, who possesses eternity without beginning together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, we say that at the end of the ages he assumed a complete man of our nature from Mary, ever-virgin, and that the Word became flesh by assuming manhood, not by changing his divinity. Nor, as certain men most wickedly suppose, do we say that the Holy Spirit served as the seed; rather, he acted by the power and might of the Creator.

Thus we confess one person of the Son in Christ, while saying that there are two perfect and complete substances, namely, divinity and humanity, which consists of soul and body. And just as we condemn Photinus, who confesses in Christ only a solitary and bare man, so we anathematize Apollinaris and those like him, who say that the Son of God assumed something less from human nature and that the man assumed—whether in flesh, soul, or perception—was unlike those for whose sake he was assumed. We confess him to have been like us in all things except the sole stain of sin, which is not natural.

We likewise execrate the blasphemy of those who attempt, under a novel interpretation, to assert that, from the time when flesh was assumed, everything that belonged to divinity passed over into man, and, conversely, that everything belonging to humanity was transferred into God. Thus, something which no heresy has ever dared to say would appear to follow from this confusion: that both substances—namely, divinity and humanity—were emptied of their proper nature and changed from their own state into another, so that those who confess both an imperfect God in the Son and an imperfect man are judged to possess neither the true God nor the true man.

We, however, say that the Son of God assumed our passible nature in such a way that divinity remained impassible. For the Son of God suffered, not figuratively but truly, everything that Scripture attests: hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, death, and other things of this kind.

He suffered according to that which could suffer, namely, according to the substance that was assumed. For the Son of God himself, according to his divinity, is impassible like the Father, incomprehensible like the Father, invisible like the Father, and unchangeable like the Father. Although the proper person of the Son—that is, the Word of God—assumed a passible man, nevertheless, through this indwelling, divinity according to the substance of the Word suffered nothing, so that the whole Trinity, which must be impassible, remained so.

The Son of God therefore died, according to the Scriptures, in respect of that which could die; he rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father, while the same nature of flesh remains—the flesh in which he was born and suffered, and in which he also rose again. For the substance of humanity was not emptied, but glorified, and it will remain forever with the divinity.

Having therefore received from the Father all authority over the things that are in heaven and on earth, he will come for the judgment of the living and the dead, both to reward the righteous and to punish sinners.

We also confess and believe in the resurrection of the flesh, so that we may say that we shall be restored in the same reality of limbs in which we now exist, and that, once we have been made what we shall be after the resurrection, we shall remain so forever.

There is one life for all the saints, but rewards differ according to labor; conversely, punishments also exist for sinners according to the measure of their offenses.

We hold one baptism, which we affirm is to be celebrated for infants with the same words of the sacrament as for adults.

We believe that a person who has fallen after baptism can be saved through penance.

We receive the New and Old Testament in the number of books handed down by the authority of the holy Catholic Church.

We believe that souls are given by God, and we say that they were made by him. We anathematize those who say that the soul is, as it were, a part of the divine substance. We also condemn the error of those who say that souls sinned beforehand, or lived in heaven, before they were sent into bodies.

We also execrate the blasphemy of those who say that God commanded something impossible for man, and that God’s commandments can be fulfilled not by individuals but by all collectively;

or those who condemn first marriages with Manichaeus, or second marriages with the Cataphrygians.

We also anathematize those who say that the Son of God lied because of the necessity of the flesh, and that, because of the man he assumed, he could not do everything he willed.

We likewise condemn the heresy of Jovinian, who says that there will be no distinction among merits in the future, and that we shall possess there the virtues which we neglected to possess here.

We confess free choice in such a way that we say that we always need God’s help. We therefore judge equally mistaken those who, with Manichaeus, say that man cannot avoid sin, and those who, with Jovinian, assert that man cannot sin; for each position removes freedom of choice. We, however, say that man is always able both to sin and not to sin, so that we always confess ourselves to possess free choice.

This is the faith, most blessed pope, which we learned in the Catholic Church and have always held and continue to hold. If anything has perhaps been set down in it with insufficient skill or caution, we desire that it be corrected by you, who hold both the faith and the see of Peter. But if this confession of ours is approved by the judgment of your apostolate, whoever wishes to defame me will prove himself ignorant, malicious, or even non-Catholic—not me a heretic.

## A Summary of the Letter That Coelestius Wrote to the Roman Clergy of His Party as Though It Were a Rule of Faith

[Col. 0505C]

Augustine formerly attributed this letter to Julianus (Book I to Boniface), but he was misled by a conjecture, as has often been said. We have elsewhere shown that it belongs to Coelestius (Dissertation 2, chapter 2).

It was issued immediately after the condemnation of the heresy—both the condemnation carried out by Zosimus and its acceptance by the clergy of the City, confirmed by the signatures of all. Hence the pope and the Roman clergy were accused by the Pelagians of treachery. It was issued, I repeat, immediately after the condemnation, while Zosimus was still alive (Book I to Boniface, chapter 15), at precisely the time when the Pelagians were being pressed most forcefully. For it could not have been issued after the death of Zosimus, which occurred in the same year in which the heresy was condemned. They could not have been pressed by Boniface as long as the schism of Eulalius continued; and that schism was not extinguished before July of the year 419.

I do not think that it was addressed to the entire Roman clergy, among whom were men of the highest reputation for faith, such as Boniface, Celestine, Leo, and others, but only to certain friends who were either wavering in their position or needed instruction concerning how they might retain others who were wavering. Augustine hints at this not obscurely (Book I to Boniface, chapter 1), so that through it he might find or make his own as many as possible.

It was secretly circulated among friends by hand, so that the supreme pontiff could not have obtained it and transmitted it to Augustine for refutation, had it not been for the exceptionally vigilant diligence of the brethren (ibid.).

Augustine demonstrates that it is entirely full of calumnies against Catholics, answering them one by one, so that it is unnecessary to linger longer over this point.

I was not a little surprised when I noticed that, of the seven charges brought against Catholics by the impure eunuch, none except the last, concerning the power of baptism, is absent from the account of Photius (Codex 177, in the excerpts from the five books of Theodore against Saint Augustine), who, as Mercator teaches, records the work of Theodore of Mopsuestia against Saint Augustine. So that the reader may more easily observe this, it seemed worthwhile to set fragments of both works in parallel (παραλλήλως).

### Coelestius According to Augustine

[Note: [Col. 0506B] The following texts, headed “Coelestius According to Augustine” and “Theodore According to Photius,” are printed in parallel in Migne.]

They say—the Manichaeans with whom we now have no communion, that is, the entire group with whom we disagree—that through the sin of the first man, namely Adam, free choice perished, and that man no longer has the power to live well, but that all are compelled by the necessity of their flesh to sin.

They also say that these marriages now being conducted were not instituted by God. This is found in Augustine’s book, against which I have now replied in four little books; our enemies have seized upon Augustine’s statements out of hatred for the truth.

They also say that the movement of the sexual organs and the intercourse of spouses were invented by the devil, and therefore that those who are born innocent are guilty and are produced by the devil, not by God, because they are born from this diabolical intercourse. This is unquestionably Manichaean.

They say that the saints in the Old Testament were not without sins—that is, that they were not freed from crimes through amendment, but were found under guilt and subject to death.

They also say that the Apostle Paul, or all the apostles, were always polluted by immoderate lust.

They say that Christ too was not free from sins, but lied because of the necessity of the flesh and was stained by other offenses.

They also say that baptism does not grant complete forgiveness of sins nor remove crimes, but merely scrapes them away, so that the roots of all sins remain in the evil flesh.

Against these claims we argue every day, and therefore we do not wish to lend our agreement to traitors, because we say that free choice exists naturally in all things and could not have perished through Adam’s sin; this is confirmed by the authority of all the Scriptures.

We say that these marriages now being conducted throughout the world were instituted by God, and that spouses are not guilty, but that fornicators and adulterers must be condemned.

We say that the movement of the sexual organs—that is, virility itself, without which intercourse cannot occur—was instituted by God.

We defend man as God’s work. We say that no one is compelled by God’s power toward either good or evil, but that by his own will he either does good or does evil; in a good work he is always assisted by God’s grace, while toward evil he is incited by the suggestions of the devil.

### Theodore According to Photius

The principal points of that sect are roughly these: men sin by nature, not by will. By “nature,” I do not mean that nature with which Adam was endowed and created at the beginning—for they assert that it was good and the work of the good God—but the nature which he acquired after sin, when through transgression and sin he exchanged the good for the evil and the immortal for the mortal. On this account, they say, those who had previously been good by nature also became wicked by nature, acquiring sin in their nature, not in their will.

Fifth, they assert that marriage—or at least the desire for intercourse—and the emission of semen, along with everything similar by which the human race is propagated through succession, are works of a perverse nature. When Adam fell into this nature through sin, they say, he immediately received within himself, through the defect of nature, a multitude of every evil.

They maintain that infants, although newly born, are not free from sin, since, because of Adam’s transgression, nature was established in sins and, as they themselves put it, a sinful nature is propagated to all his descendants.

Moreover, they say that no mortal is righteous; this follows in turn from what they posited at the beginning.

Fourth—O blasphemous and impious words!—they say that not even Christ, having assumed a nature infected with sins, is pure of crime. Yet, he says, in other blasphemies of theirs one can also observe that they attribute to him not a truly human nature by nature, but merely a human nature in appearance.

We say that the saints of the Old Testament passed from this life into eternal life through perfect righteousness—that is, by their devotion to virtue they departed from all sins—for we know that even those whom we read to have sinned subsequently amended their ways.

We confess that the grace of Christ is necessary for everyone, both adults and children. We anathematize those who say that one born from two baptized persons ought not to be baptized. We also condemn those who say that baptism does not erase all sins, because we know that complete purification is conferred through these mysteries.

Therefore let no one deceive you, and let the impious not deny that they hold these views. If they speak the truth, either let them be heard, or at least let these very bishops who now disagree condemn the things I have stated above, namely, that they share these views with the Manichaeans, just as we condemn the charges they spread about us, and let there be complete agreement. But if they refuse, know that they are Manichaeans, and keep yourselves from their company.

From these facts it may be concluded that the work which Mercator and Photius mention was truly written by Theodore against Augustine. It was not written before Julianus had informed Theodore by letter what had occurred at Rome in the common case—or rather, before he had met him, accompanied by Coelestius and others, and Coelestius had brought with him what was to be communicated to Theodore.

## A Booklet of Faith by Julianus of Eclanum, Sent to the Apostolic See in the Name of Eighteen Bishops Who Refused to Subscribe to the Condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius

A booklet of faith now comes to light for the first time: Julianus, bishop of Eclanum, composed it at the time when the *tractoriae* were sent from the apostolic see to all the bishops of the world. Refusing to subscribe, he preferred, as Marius Mercator says (in the second part of the *Commonitorium* and in the preface to the book *Subnotationes*), to be counted third with Pelagius and Coelestius in the condemnation rather than to show himself in agreement with the holy Fathers.

It long remained hidden in manuscript codices, partly through the same fate as Pelagius’s confession, which Cardinal Baronius brought forth from the Vatican records, and partly because, since it did not bear its author’s name openly on its front, it could for some time appear to lack sufficient evidence either to establish its origin or to give it authority.

Father Sirmond copied it out by hand from a Veronese codex while he was staying in Italy, showed it to me twenty-two years ago, and, congratulating me on my spontaneous conjecture concerning its author and date, entrusted it to me to illuminate with notes and commit to print.

At that time, however, I was occupied with the laborious task of teaching philosophy, from which I could not withdraw before undertaking the still more difficult work of treating scholastic theology. Although I have not yet laid that work aside, after twenty continuous years devoted to studies of this kind in divine matters, I am not compelled to be so anxiously occupied with it that I may never sometimes revisit, in my spare hours, the more agreeable parts of theology. This leisure made it possible for me to devote myself to illuminating Mercator’s works and to obey the instructions of that excellent old man in publishing Julianus’s confession.

## Part One: On the Most Holy Trinity, the Incarnation of the Word, and Other Articles of the Creed

### 1

[Note: Pelagius and Coelestius have the same wording. All of them, something that may perhaps surprise someone, followed not the old Roman creed, as would have been appropriate for men of the Latin nation, but the Eastern or Nicene creed. For in the old Roman creed, according to Rufinus of Aquileia (*Explanation of the Creed*), there was no mention either of the Creator of heaven and earth or of the Maker of visible and invisible things; it simply read: “I believe in God the Father almighty.” It was advantageous for the Pelagians to follow the Eastern creed, partly so that they might make themselves companions of the Nicene faith, and partly so that they might place at the beginning, against the Manichaeans, statements from which they would later maliciously attempt to derive arguments against defenders of original sin, as though on this point they favored the Manichaeans.]

We believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of all visible and invisible things.

### 2

[Note: Pelagius and Coelestius likewise express the same view in the same words, and repeat that all things were created through the Son. Thus, the more vehemently they attack the Manichaeans, who held that invisible things were made by the good God and visible things by the evil one, the greater envy they prepare against Catholics, whom they would later maliciously call by the name of Manichaeans.]

And in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, through whom all things were created; not born or made from outside, but begotten from the substance of the Father, true God from true God. Thus he who was begotten is what he who begot him is. Since the Father is God and Father without having any father of his own, the Son begotten from this Father could not be inferior to the Father. The Son has no beginning, because the Father has no development or origin.

### 3

[Note: The same words occur in Pelagius and Coelestius. They commonly say that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, and, by their silence, in my opinion deny that he proceeds from the Son. They followed, of course, their common teacher Theodore of Mopsuestia, whose words are these (*Part Four of the Creed*): “And in the Holy Spirit, whom we do not consider either to be the Son or to have received existence through the Son.”]

We believe also in the Holy Spirit, true God, proceeding from the Father, equal in all things to the Father and the Son—in will, operation, eternity, and substance.

### 4

While distinguishing the persons according to the properties of their names, we nevertheless confess the inseparable divinity of the Trinity. We believe that there is nothing in the Trinity that can be called higher or lower, because the whole Trinity is joined together by the power of divinity and the unity of substance.

### 5

In the fullness of time, the Son of God was sent—not by the command of a greater power, but through communion of will—and the Word became flesh (John 1:14).

[Note: Pelagius and Coelestius say: “By assuming man, not by changing divinity.” The Fathers use these expressions in a Catholic sense against Apollinaris, as theologians commonly interpret them. Nevertheless, in this passage they are not free from suspicion of heresy, since they are put forward by disciples of Theodore, who were concealing their teacher’s heretical meaning beneath a Catholic statement. Certainly, the term “assumption,” as it was first used by Theodore and later by Nestorius, was suspect to Saint Cyril (*Response to Theodoret* and *Letter to Successus*), since among them it signified a purely moral union. In this sense the Evangelist is said to have written that Christ “took” Peter, James, and John with him (Luke 9:28).

Accordingly, Pope Felix and martyr, praised in the Council of Ephesus, said: “The Son of God did not assume a man so that there might be another besides himself; but, while he was perfect God, he became at the same time perfect man,” and so forth (Part Two, Session 1). The scholastics say that by this form of speech the Catholic meaning was distinguished from the heretical: the Son of God did not assume a man, but humanity; for “man” signifies a person, whereas “humanity” signifies a nature. If he had assumed a man, the one assuming would be other than the one assumed; but if he assumed humanity, he truly became man, and the one assuming is not other than the one assumed.]

He did not cease to be God through conversion, but began to be man, which he had not been, through the assumption of flesh; and, so that man might ascend to God, God descended to man.

[Note: These words are used by the Fathers in a Catholic sense to signify the self-emptying of the Word and the exaltation of humanity. Nevertheless, Nestorius, together with the other disciples of Theodore, abused them in order to deny a natural union (ἕνωσις φυσική, *henōsis physikē*) and to posit a purely relational union (σχετική, *schētikē*). “God,” he says (*Sermon on the Incarnation*, in Marius Mercator), “sees the fallen nature, and by the power of divinity grasps it when it has been cast down; holding it and remaining what he was, he raises it on high.” Consider the example: “Understand what is said. If you wished to raise someone lying down, would you not touch body with body, and, joining yourself to him, raise him who had fallen, while remaining, joined to him, what you were? So too is the mystery of the Incarnation.”]

### 6

He is therefore born for us from the Holy Spirit and Mary, ever-virgin, he who according to his divinity was never absent from the Father.

[Note: Pelagius and Coelestius have the same thing in nearly the same words, except that they transmit Theodore’s poison less secretly.
