For they say: “Thus we confess one person of the Son in Christ, so that we say there are two perfect and complete substances.” Although Catholics commonly use these words against Apollinaris, they are nevertheless not free from suspicion of error when uttered by these disciples of Theodore. For Theodore and Nestorius used them to construct the heresy by which they attempted subtly to establish two sons in Christ, as Marius Mercator carefully observes (*Refutation of Theodore’s Creed*).

Indeed, when Nestorius had mentioned one person in Christ (*Letter 2 to Cyril*; *Book on the Correct Faith to the Queens*, section 12), Cyril reproached him because he used the term “person,” as they say, not in the physical sense as “hypostasis,” but in the moral sense, signifying something juridical. See the notes to the second treatise of Nestorius against Pelagius.

Moreover, the cunning man did not simply say “one person,” which should be noted, but “one person of the Son.” By this expression he could quibble in the manner of Theodore, who speaks as follows (*On the Creed*, section 8): “We do not say two sons or two lords, because there is one Son according to essence, the divine Word, the only-begotten Son of the Father. This one who has been joined and made a participant in divinity with him shares the common designation and honor of son. Likewise, the one who is Lord according to essence is God the Word; because this one has been joined and associated with him, he shares honor with him. Therefore we do not say two sons or two lords, since, while the one who is Lord and Son according to essence is manifest and has inseparable union and association with him, the one who was assumed for our salvation participates in both the designation and the honor of Son and Lord—not as each of us, existing independently, is called a son of God, whence, according to the blessed Apostle Paul, we are called many sons of God, but because he possesses this uniquely, since he is joined to God the Word. He therefore participates in the dignity of sonship and lordship, entirely removing the notion of two lords and two sons, while granting us, through union with God the Word, complete faith, understanding, and contemplation. For these reasons he also receives veneration from every creature through association with God.”]

We have therefore received Jesus Christ, the Son of God, from two wholly complete and perfect substances, God and man. We confess that according to his divinity he was like the Father, and according to his humanity like us,

[Note: Pelagius and Coelestius used the same words. All of them were thereby making a path for themselves toward denying original sin. See what has been said in the notes to chapter 2 of the *Subnotationes*.]

except for the sole stain of sin, which is not natural.

### 7

[Note: This is the distinctive error of the Pelagians, although it too was received from Theodore: that Christ came not to help but to benefit us through teaching and example. “They usually say,” Augustine states (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapters 2, 35, 37, 38, and elsewhere), “that Christ provided assistance toward not sinning because, by living justly and teaching justly, he left us an example.”]

He came, namely, for this purpose: to call the whole world back from sins by his example and to redeem it by suffering; while, as God, he removes sin by forgiving it, and, as man, by the likeness of his nature he shows how sin can henceforth be overcome.

### 8

Beginning with John’s baptism, with which he was baptized in order to provide an example,

[Note: Coelestius burdened Catholics with this calumny. Thus Augustine says (*Book I to Boniface*, chapter 12): “Accordingly, as for what this man added—that we say ‘Christ was not free from sins, but lied because of the necessity of the flesh and was stained by other offenses’—let him consider from whom he heard it or in whose writings he read it. Perhaps he did not understand it and, deceived by malice, twisted it into calumnious meanings. He thought he had read it in Jerome’s dialogue, something that escaped Augustine while he was reading his friend’s words benevolently. See what has been noted concerning Pelagius’s booklet.”]

not, as some maintain, because of his own sin, as he himself says to John (Matthew 3:15): “Allow it for now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness,” he subjected himself to every suffering of the flesh, enduring hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, death, and other things of this kind: “He became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:8). As blessed Peter taught us, saying (1 Peter 2:21): “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps”; he “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.”

### 9

[Note: Pelagius and Coelestius say: “We, however, say that he assumed our passible nature in such a way …” Julianus gives two reasons for Christ’s suffering: to destroy death and to open for us the way of resurrection, that is, for the remission of sins. He is silent about opening the way to heaven and, by his silence, in reality denies that Christ died to obtain for us the grace by which we do not sin and act well. Pelagius is plainly Nestorianizing (νεστοριανίζει, *nestorianizei*) concerning the impassibility of the Son of God and the union of the Word with human nature, which he makes a purely indwelling union (ἑνοίκησις, *henoikēsis*).]

We therefore believe that he suffered and was buried according to the flesh for our salvation, rose again on the third day, both to destroy death and to open for us the way of resurrection.

### 10

Ascending into heaven, he sits at the right hand of the Father, while the substance of humanity remains—not emptied, but glorified and destined to remain forever with the divinity.

### 11

We believe that he will come to judge the living and the dead.

### 12

By his power and example, we believe that all human flesh will be raised in the same reality of limbs in which it was made by God, so that sinners may receive punishments and the righteous glory.

### 13

[Note: Pelagius and Coelestius have exactly the same thing in the same words and with the purpose of attempting to overthrow, from Catholic doctrine, the necessity of divine grace for acting well—as though from the confession of divine grace it followed that God’s judgment was either unjust or superfluous, and that everything pertaining to piety and salvation, when divine grace is at work, occurred by fate.]

There will be one life for all the saints, but rewards will differ according to labor; conversely, punishments also exist for sinners according to the measure of their offenses.

### 14

[Note: Pelagius (*Booklet of Faith*, Part 13): “We hold one baptism, which we affirm is to be celebrated for infants with the same words of the sacrament as for adults.”

Coelestius (*On Original Sin*, chapter 5): “We confess that infants ought to be baptized for the remission of sins, according to the rule of the universal Church and according to the Gospel’s sentence, because the Lord established that the kingdom of heaven can be granted only to the baptized,” and so forth.

Julianus again (*Book II to Boniface*, chapter 5): “We confess that baptism is necessary for every age.”

This is a celebrated passage, often treated by Saint Augustine, and rightly so, for it contains the marrow of the Coelestian fraud. Although, in order to answer the arguments of Catholics who proved original sin from the baptism of infants, the heretics acknowledged these eight points—that there is one sacrament of baptism instituted by Christ; that it is necessary for every age, both for the forgiveness of sins and for obtaining the kingdom of heaven; that it is celebrated for infants with the same words as for adults; that infants themselves are baptized for the remission of sins; that this is the rule of the universal Church and the teaching of the Gospel; that little children need Christ’s redemption; and that Christ died for them also—they nevertheless denied that sin is transmitted from Adam to his descendants.

Coelestius (*Booklet Sent to Rome*, in Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapter 6): “We did not say that infants are to be baptized for the remission of sins for the purpose of appearing to establish sin by transmission,” and so forth.

Indeed, in order to evade the arguments of Catholics, they used to say that the remedy of baptism should not be changed according to causes, but operates according to persons (*Book I of the Unfinished Work*, chapter 51); that in infants grace has what adopts, but the water does not have what it washes away (*Hypognosticon*, Book V); that Christ makes those whom he made good by creation better by renewal and adoption (*Unfinished Work*, Book I, chapter 51); that little children are not baptized for the remission of sins but for the kingdom of heaven (*Book I to Boniface*, chapter 22); that this kingdom, which nature does not have the strength to obtain, is conferred by the generosity of grace (Coelestius in his booklet); and that they knew where infants who died without baptism did not go, but did not know where they went (Pelagius in Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapter 21).]

According to the example of the Church and the commandment of God, we confess one baptism, which we truly both hand down and hold as necessary simultaneously for every age. We say that no one can obtain forgiveness of sins or the kingdom of heaven unless he has received baptism.

### 15

[Note: Pelagius says the same against the Novatians. Coelestius says: “We believe that one who has fallen after baptism can be saved, first through reconciliation and then through penance.” In truth, they concealed two errors beneath a Catholic statement. The first was Coelestius’s: that forgiveness is not given to those who repent according to the grace and mercy of God, but according to the merits and labor of those who have become worthy of mercy through penance. The second was shared by all of them: from this they attempted to establish their own sinlessness (ἀναμαρτησία, *anamartēsia*).]

We believe that one who has sinned after baptism can be saved through penance.

### 16

[Note: Pelagius and Coelestius use the same words, all of them maliciously, although with an outward appearance of piety. Since the Manichaeans rejected the Old Testament entirely and part of the New Testament, the Pelagians attempted to cast the same odium upon defenders of original sin, whom they accused of association with the Manichaeans, as though on this point too they ought to hold opinions against the Pelagians. See what has been said in the notes to Pelagius’s booklet, in which he casts odium upon Saint Jerome.

It may seem remarkable to some, however, how the heretics claim that they receive Holy Scripture in the number of books handed down by the authority of the Catholic Church. For either they refer to the Roman canon, which Innocent I sent to Exuperius of Toulouse (Letter 3, chapter 7), or to the African canon, which is entirely similar to the Roman canon in the Council of Carthage commonly called the Third. Both include the Book of Wisdom among the canonical books, although it was not counted as such by those men about whom Hilary wrote to Augustine (the letter prefixed to the book *On the Predestination of the Saints).

The reason for the apparent contradiction is easily removed if the Pelagians themselves are distinguished from the Massilians. The former included the Book of Wisdom in the canon, although not with complete confidence, as is clear from the *Unfinished Work against Julianus*; the latter rejected it after they realized that it was inconvenient to their interests. Certainly, at that time one canon of the sacred books was received in one place and another elsewhere.

From this arises the question of which canon the Gallican Church followed at that time: Jerome’s, in which the Book of Wisdom was not counted, or the Roman, in which it was. I think the answer is that the same canon was not observed in all the churches of Gaul, but that Jerome’s was followed in some and another in others. For this reason Exuperius, amid such disagreement, asked Innocent which he ought to follow.

I therefore think that, at least in the region where those about whom Hilary wrote lived (the letter cited), Jerome’s canon possessed authority. For who would believe that those holy men, who at that time were opposing Augustine in Gaul, rejected the common judgment of the churches in which they lived?

If someone should ask again which canon Italy followed at that time, he will receive the answer from Innocent I’s reply to Exuperius, for Innocent lists the same number of canonical books that the Council of Trent and the Catholic Church now receive. Thus one may refute the audacity of the heretics of this period, who reject the Books of the Maccabees from the canon of Holy Scripture, although at the beginning of the fifth century they were counted within it.

The second part of the booklet answers in every respect the letter that Julianus wrote to Rufus of Thessalonica at the same time and in the name of the same bishops. For both letters contain, in Augustine’s words (*Book III to Boniface*, chapter 8), “clouds of questions” in which the impiety of the Pelagians might lie hidden from simpler or slower minds, or from those less educated in the sacred writings. These are clouds concerning praise of creation, praise of marriage, praise of the law, praise of free choice, and praise of the saints—as though any one of us censured these things, rather than proclaiming them all with the praises owed to the honor of the Creator and Savior.

It should further be observed how subtly Augustine reduces all the parts of the Pelagian heresy to three heads. To establish these, he shows that the Pelagians refer numerous statements of this kind to the following purposes (ibid.): to deny that there is original sin; to say that God’s grace, by which we are justified, is not given freely but according to our merits; and to maintain that there is sometimes such great righteousness in mortal man that he does not need the forgiveness of sins, even after the bath of regeneration, until he completes this life.

For, as he says (Book IV, chapter 2), in all these matters whatever they say in praise of creation and marriage they endeavor to direct toward this end: that there be no original sin. Whatever they say in praise of the law and free will, toward this end: that grace does not assist unless merit does, and thus that grace is no longer grace. Whatever they say in praise of the saints, toward this end: that mortal life in the saints appears to have no sin, and that they do not need to beseech God for the forgiveness of their debts. And afterward (ibid., chapter 7): “By the deceitful praise of those five goods they seduce the unwary and unlearned into these three evils. Concerning all these matters I consider that I have given a sufficient answer to their most cruel, most impious, and most arrogant vanity.”]

We accept the New and Old Testaments in the number of books transmitted by the authority of the Catholic Church.

## PART TWO. On the grace of God and the free choice of the human will; on human nature, the institution of marriage, original sin, and the saints of the Old Testament

### 1.

[Note: Pelagius echoes Julian: “We also execrate their blasphemy,” etc., in his letter to Demetrias (chapter 16): “We attribute iniquity to the Just One and cruelty to the Pious One, when we complain that he first commanded something impossible. Then we think that a person should be condemned for things he could not avoid, so that—something it is even sacrilegious to suspect—God appears to have sought not so much our salvation as our punishment,” etc. Coelestius, *Reasoning*, 15 (in Augustine, *On the Perfection of Righteousness*): “Certainly God is just; this cannot be denied. But God imputes every sin to a person; and I think this too must be confessed, because whatever is not imputed as sin is not sin. But if there is some sin that cannot be avoided, how can God be called just if he is believed to impute to anyone something that cannot be avoided?”]

We say that the commands of the divine law are possible, on account of God’s justice; and [Note: The other heretic likewise maintains the same thing; but Pelagius disclosed the mind of them all at the Council of Diospolis: “We said that a person can be without sin and keep God’s commandments if he wishes, for God gave him this possibility. We did not say that anyone is found who, from infancy to old age, has never sinned; but that, having turned away from sins through his own labor and God’s grace, he can be without sin, though even by this he is not thereafter incapable of turning back” (in Augustine, *The Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 6). When Augustine examined these words (*The Proceedings*, chapters 7 and following, and *On the Grace of Christ*), he showed that they were not merely ambiguous but also full of error.] we confess that all things can be fulfilled [Col. 0515A] through the grace of Christ, [Note: Julian wrote little about the grace of God, and even that largely on isolated occasions, except for his book *On Love*. For, as stated, he was more a Coelestian than a Pelagian (Dissertation 1 on Julian). When Augustine objected to him (*Unfinished Work against Julian*, Book I, chapter 94) that he was abolishing the grace of Christ, he replied in such a way as to reveal his mind, reducing the grace of Christ—for the sake of whose bestowal he came into this world—to creation, incarnation, adoption in baptism, example, and the remission of sins. This passage deserves consultation.] which is always the helper and companion of every good act, and through human free will, which itself too is a gift of God.

### 2.

[Note: In these and the following words Julian may appear to have cast the seeds from which Semi-Pelagianism would later arise. On this matter Prosper should be read, both in his letter to Augustine and in his book *Against the Collator*, as well as in his responses to the objections against God’s gratuitous predestination. This is not the place to discuss so extensive a subject against the uninstructed assertions of some concerning the errors of the Semi-Pelagians.]

Yet we understand this grace of God in such a way that it neither follows one who is unwilling nor abandons one who is obedient.

### 3.

But that one person is just and another unjust, we judge to occur not by the divine will but by human fault. For he denied that this difference comes from God who said that God wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4). If, then, God wills to save all, and there is no partiality with God (Rom. 2:11), sin will most justly be imputed to each person through free will, according to what is written (Eccl. 15:18): “Before a person are good and evil, life and death; whatever pleases him will be given to him” [Col. 0515B].

### 4.

It follows, therefore, that we must confess that we are sinners not because we are unable, but because we neglect to avoid sin. For this reason the day of judgment has been appointed, so that the good person may receive a reward for his labor, and the evil person may not escape punishment for his contempt.

### 5.

[Note: Augustine admirably illuminates this passage (*Letter to Boniface*, Book IV, chapter 2), where he explains what the Pelagians said in praise of human nature and for what purpose they accumulated such statements. “They express their praise of creation,” he says, “insofar as it concerns the human race, which is the present subject of controversy, in these assertions: that God is the creator of those who are born, that the children of human beings are God’s work, and that every sin proceeds not from nature but from the will. To this praise of creation they attach the claim that baptism is necessary at every age, so that this creature may be adopted as a child of God—not because it brings anything from its parents that must be cleansed by the bath of regeneration. To this praise they also add the claim that they say the Lord Christ was stained by no mark of sin, insofar as his infancy is concerned, because they assert that his flesh was utterly pure from every contagion of sin not through a distinctive excellence and singular grace, but through participation in the nature that is present in all infants. To this also belongs what they introduce concerning the origin of the soul, by which they endeavor to make all the souls of little children equal to Christ’s soul, since they wish them likewise to be untouched by any stain of sin. For this reason they also say that nothing evil passed from Adam to the rest except death—which, they say, is not always an evil, since it is even the cause of rewards for martyrs—and that it is not the dissolution of bodies, which will be raised in every class of human beings, that makes death good or evil, but the diversity of merits arising from human freedom” [Col. 0516D].]

We testify that human nature is good and whole, since it was made by the good God.

### 6.

We confess also that every human being is made by God, as the Patriarch says (Gen. 30:2): “Am I in God’s place, so that I should give you children?” And the Prophet likewise testifies (Isa. 64:8): “And now, O Lord, Abraham does not know us; for you are our Father, and we are all the work of your hands.” Hence God also says to Jeremiah (Jer. 1:5): “Before I formed you in your mother’s womb, I knew you.” Likewise in the Book of Maccabees (2 Macc. 7:22): “I do not know,” she said, “how you appeared in my womb; for I did not give you breath, nor did I myself assemble the limbs of each of you.” Job too refers the very beginning of the conceived human being to God, and says (Job 10:10): “Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese, bind me together with bones and sinews, cover me with skin, and give me life and mercy?” All the divine Scriptures are also filled with testimonies of this kind, which we have now omitted for the sake of brevity.

### 7.

We confess likewise that the human being was not only made in the image of God but is also made so, as the Lord says to Noah (Gen. 9:6): “Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed, because God made the human being in his image.” The Apostle Paul likewise asserts (1 Cor. 11:7): “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God.” The Apostle James too cries out (Jas. 3:9): “With the same tongue we bless God, and with it we curse human beings, who were made in the image and likeness of God” [Col. 0516B].

### 8.

[Note: Julian had written the same thing to Rufus, as Augustine reports in these words: “They praise marriage according to the Scriptures, because the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘He who made them from the beginning made them male and female,’ and said: ‘Increase, multiply, and fill the earth’ (Matt. 19:4), although this is not written in that place in the Gospel but in the Law. They also add: ‘Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate.’ We recognize these words as evangelical.”]

We say that marriage was established and joined together by God as its author, God saying to Noah (Gen. 9:7): “But increase and multiply, and fill the earth.” And lest anyone wish to obscure the plain history with the mists of allegory, he added (ibid.): “And multiply upon it.”

### 9.

For this reason, when the Jews asked him in the Gospel about divorce, the Lord replied (Matt. 19:8): “Moses wrote this commandment for you because of the hardness of your hearts; but from the beginning it was not so. For he who made them made them male and female, and said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’” (Mark 10:5).

### 10.

And lest one of the erring should say, “This ought to be taken as a prediction rather than a command,” he added (ibid.): “Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate.” The holy Apostle too, following Christ’s teaching, says (Heb. 13:4): “Marriage is honorable, and the marriage bed undefiled; but the Lord will judge fornicators and adulterers” [Col. 0517A]. And elsewhere (1 Cor. 7:38): “He who gives his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not give her in marriage does better.” For this is why virginity is to be praised: because it is preferred to marriage, which is good. [Note: The same judgment occurs in Book IV of the *Unfinished Work* (chapter 121), where Julian compares Augustine with Jovinian and attempts to show that Augustine is worse, in these words: “He said that necessity belongs to the good; you, to evil. He says that through mysteries human beings are restrained from error; you, that they are not even freed through grace. He dissolves Mary’s virginity by the condition of childbirth; you hand Mary over to the devil by the condition of her birth. He equates better things with good things—that is, virginity with marriage; but you call marital intercourse diseased and cheapen chastity by comparing it with something most foul. Nor do you add a degree between these things, preferring virginity not to the good but to the evil. It is the height of baseness not to be pleasing unless compared with something most loathsome,” etc.] For whatever is praised by comparison with evil lacks merit by its own dignity.

### 11.

Since, therefore, we have first spoken of the goodness of nature, and of the blessing and honor of marriage, we consequently reject [Note: The Pelagians preferred to call sin “natural” rather than “original,” so that they might arouse greater hostility against the defenders of original sin, insofar as they would seem to have a closer affinity with the Manichaeans, who said that human nature was evil. See what we have brought forward from Augustine in the notes to Part One, no. 6.

Augustine carefully collected not only testimonies from Scripture but also the arguments by which the Pelagians attacked original sin; he did so in various places and especially in Book II against Julian. “You say,” he writes (chapter 1), “that by asserting original sin we say that the devil is the creator of human beings at birth; condemn marriage; deny that all sins are forgiven in baptism; accuse God of the crime of iniquity; introduce despair of perfection,” etc.

Julian craftily placed the third part of his treatise among his condemnations of those who partly held opinions contrary to the Catholic faith concerning the Trinity and partly held views contrary to his own doctrines. But he does this so wickedly that by his deed rather than his words he slanders the Catholics who oppose him, as though they held the same views as the heretics universally hated.]

natural sin—or whatever other term it may be called—lest we inflict an injury upon God, the Creator of all, by maintaining that anything could have been made by him with sin, and lest we prove the testimonies of his Scriptures false.

### 12.

They cite what is said in the Old Testament (Jer. 31:30): “Fathers shall not die for their sons, nor sons die for their fathers; each shall die for his own sin.” And another prophet says (Ezek. 18:2): “What is this proverb that you use in the land of Israel, saying: ‘The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge’? As I live, says the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel, for all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son—they are all mine. The soul that sins shall itself die.” Likewise there (ibid., verse 20): “The son shall not bear the injustice of his father, nor the father bear the injustice of his son; the justice of the just shall be upon him” (ibid., verse 30). And again there: “I shall judge you, house of Israel, each according to his way, says the Lord.”

### 13.

And the Apostle says: “We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10). Likewise the same Apostle (Rom. 14:12): “Each of us shall give an account of himself to God.” And elsewhere (Gal. 6:5): “Each of us shall bear his own burden.”

### 14.

But we cannot accuse the saints of the Old Testament, who were justified by God and often praised in his judgment, since the Apostle says (Rom. 8:33): “Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? It is God who justifies; who is he who condemns?” And the Lord testifies in the Gospel (Matt. 23:35; Luke 11:50): “All the blood of the righteous that has been shed upon the earth shall be required from you, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah.”

### 15.

Therefore, in another passage, the Lord himself, strengthening the Apostles to patience by the example of the prophets, says (Matt. 5:12): “Rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven; for thus they persecuted the prophets who were before you” [Col. 0518A].

### 16.

And what is greater than this, he confirmed by his own testimony that those men were called “gods” by the Prophet David, saying (John 10:35): “If he called those gods to whom the word of God was spoken—and Scripture cannot be broken—do you say to him whom the Father sanctified and sent into this world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God?’”

### 17.

For it is established that they were justified through their own labor and faith in Christ, since they foresaw that God would come in the flesh, as the Lord himself asserts, saying (John 8:56): “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad.”

### 18.

And the Apostle says (Heb. 11:39): “And all these, though approved by the testimony of faith.” And again (ibid., verse 24): “By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing to suffer affliction with the people of God rather than to have the enjoyment of sin for a time. He considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, for he looked toward the reward.”

### 19.

Hence another Apostle says (1 Pet. 1:11): “Concerning this salvation those who came before us inquired, as the prophets searched into what time or what kind of time the Spirit of Christ within them was announcing: the sufferings that are in Christ and the glories that followed.”

### 20.

The Lord himself also proves that they will obtain the kingdom of heaven when he says (Matt. 8:11): “Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the sons of this kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness.”

### 21.

Therefore we choose to say with the Prophet (Ps. 138:17): “But to me your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored; their principalities have been exceedingly strengthened,” rather than, along with the erring, detract with reckless speech from the merits of the saints and from God’s testimony.

## PART THREE. Rejection of foreign doctrines

### 1.

Having duly confessed all these things according to the rule of the Catholic faith [Col. 0519A] and the authority of the divine Scriptures, we consequently condemn all heretics, and especially those who are known among the Latins both by their proper names and by their error, whose impiety we shudder at, namely:

### 2.

[Note: To show that he agreed with the Council of Nicaea and its adherents, he confesses in every respect the *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον, “consubstantial”), rejecting the heretics who attacked either the plurality of persons, as did the Sabellians; or the divinity, as did the Eunomians; or consubstantiality, as did the Macedonians and Arians. Then, from all the other heresies known among the Latins, he selects four to condemn: Apollinaris, the Novatians, Jovinian, and Mani, so that he might cast odium upon the Catholic defenders of original sin—as though defense of it necessarily implied association either with Apollinaris, who thought that souls, like bodies, were transmitted; or with the Novatians and Jovinian, who seemed to maintain the inflexibility of the human will; or with Mani, who asserted that nature was evil.]

The Arians, who impiously divide the divine substance;

### 3.

The Sabellians, who more wickedly confuse the distinct properties of the persons;

### 4.

The Eunomians, who assert that the Son of God was made from things that did not exist;

### 5.

The Macedonians, who deny divinity to the Holy Spirit;

### 6.

The Apollinarists, [Note: Observe these two expressions and similar ones, for they reveal Julian’s slanderous intention. Apollinaris made two elements of his heresy: first, that the Word took the place of a human mind in Christ; second, that soul no less than body is transmitted from parents. The heretic attributed both positions to Catholics, but one to all Catholics together with Nestorius—or rather with his teacher Theodore—and the other to Augustine and the other defenders of original sin.

From this understand one of the three reasons why Apollinaris wanted the Word to take the place of the human mind in Christ. He did not see how, if the soul were transmitted—which he considered absolutely necessary to maintain in order to defend original sin—Christ could lack original sin of his own if his soul too had been transmitted. Likewise understand why Theodore of Mopsuestia attacked Apollinaris so fiercely, though not with as much zeal for Catholic truth as with love for his own heresy, by which he denied that there was any original sin, something Apollinaris strongly opposed.]

and those like them, who say that the Son of God assumed something less than the fullness of human nature [Col. 0520A].

### 7.

[Note: Here too Catholics are maliciously attacked. For since either Novatus or Novatian likewise wanted there to be two elements in his error—one, as the Council of Trent testifies (Session 14, chapter 1), that Christ had not given the Church power to forgive sins committed after faith, that is, after baptism; the other, which is inferred from ancient writers, that not even all sins are forgiven by God, but only lesser ones, while the greater are always punished—Julian appears to have had both in view, so as to accuse the defenders of original sin as though they wished sins to be removed neither through heartfelt repentance nor through the sacrament of penance, whether all sins or any sins at all, because they maintained that, on account of the concupiscence remaining in human beings, no one in this life is free from the need to say daily: “Forgive us our debts.”]

The Novatians, who deny penance to the fallen;

### 8.

[Note: Pelagius puts it somewhat differently: “We confess free will in this way,” etc. Although he said that Jovinian asserted that a human being cannot sin, while Jovinian did not assert this without qualification but with the exception “after receiving the bath of regeneration,” he nevertheless does not seem to have understood this heresy differently from Augustine in his *Book on Heresies*, Jerome in his works against Jovinian, Julian himself in his confession of faith, and other writers of the same age. He touched upon it only verbally, in a form that could easily be understood with a restriction by all who were not unaware of the heresy, which was scarcely yet extinct.

Julian accused Augustine of sharing Jovinian’s error because Augustine had written (*Letter to Boniface*, Book I, chapter 2) that a person cannot will anything good unless he is aided by him who cannot will evil. He interpreted this statement as though the holy teacher wished the one who receives God’s grace to share not merely the good will that God possesses, but also the mode of possessing a good will—that is, necessity. On this matter see the lengthy dispute between Julian and Saint Augustine (*Unfinished Work*, Book IV, chapter 121 and following).]

the Jovinianists, who say that after baptism a person cannot sin in any way;

### 9.

[Note: Concerning the distinction of the Manichaeans’ ravings from the Catholic faith, Saint Augustine argues in both works against Julian in such a way that no greater light need be expected from elsewhere by which the mysteries of their wicked impiety may be fully discerned. Julian says that the Manichaeans believed the human soul had flowed from the good God and the flesh from the evil one, and that for this reason the one nature is always in conflict with the other. Yet Saint Augustine (*On Two Souls*) writes that the Manichaeans derive this conflict from the dissimilar nature of two souls in one human being. Julian may, however, have understood “flesh” to mean the carnal soul, which would have come from the evil god.]

The Manichaeans also, who assert two principles, namely, one good and one evil, and who say that the soul is from the good and the flesh from the evil, and therefore that there is perpetual conflict between the two natures;

### 10.

[Note: The same things occur in full in Coelestius’s letter to the Roman clergy. Julian goes further in producing nine slanders against the Catholic defenders of original sin (in Augustine, *Letter to Boniface*, Book I). He accuses them as though they asserted that marriage originated with the devil as its author; that its children are fruits of the devil’s tree; that all those conceived from marital pleasure up to Christ’s Passion were possessed by the devil by the most equitable right; that the Son of God began to benefit the human race only from the time of his Passion; that sins are not completely erased in baptism; that the saints of the Old Testament departed this life with sin; that a human being is driven into sin by necessity; that the Savior lied through the necessity of the flesh; and that, because of the impediment of the flesh, he could not do everything he wished.]

And those like them who, under the assertion of natural sin, maintain [Note: To remove this slander from the Catholics, Augustine wrote two books to Count Valerius; consult Book II of his *Retractations* (chapter 53). Julian composed four books against the first of these and eight against the second; Augustine replied in both of his works against Julian. See Dissertation I.] that marriage originated with the devil as its author, and that its children are fruits of the devil’s tree;

### 11.

And those who say that all who were conceived from marital [Note: The reading was *voluntate* (“by will”), but it should be *voluptate* (“by pleasure”). Thus Julian himself (in Augustine, *Against Julian*, chapter 12): “If the Apostle were speaking of sin transmitted by descent, he could say nowhere more appropriately: ‘For sin passed through, because all were generated from the pleasure of married couples.’”] pleasure up to the Passion of the Lord were possessed by the devil by the most equitable right [Col. 0521A];

### 12.

Or those who say that the Son of God began to benefit the human race only from the time of his Passion;

### 13.

And those who assert that sins are not completely erased in baptism;

### 14.

Or those who affirm that the saints of the Old Testament departed from this life with sin;

### 15.

And those who also say that a human being is driven into sin by necessity.

### 16.

But we likewise execrate the claim [Note: Pelagius uses nearly the same words (*Booklet*, part 17): “We also anathematize those who say that the Son of God, through the necessity of the flesh,” etc. When Julian made this very charge against Catholics in his letter to Rufus, Augustine replied (*Letter to Boniface*, Book III, chapter 6) in such a way that he showed both the passage of the Apostle from which Catholics had taken the occasion for the accusation [Col. 0521B] and how the otherwise difficult passage should be understood. “Far be it from us,” he says, “to call him a just advocate who, as these people slanderously claim, lied through the necessity of the flesh. Rather, we say that, in the likeness of sinful flesh, he condemned sin on account of sin. Perhaps because they do not understand this and, blinded by their desire to slander, do not know the various ways in which the word ‘sin’ is used in the sacred Scriptures, they boast that we affirm sin in Christ. We therefore say that Christ had no sin, either in soul or in flesh, and that by assuming flesh in the likeness of sinful flesh he condemned sin on account of sin. This, which the Apostle has expressed somewhat obscurely, is understood in two ways,” etc.]

that the Savior lied through the necessity of the flesh, and that because of the impediment of the flesh he could not do everything he wished;

### 17.

And those who condemn first marriages with the Manichaeans and second marriages with the Cataphrygians;

### 18.

And those who say that sins cannot be avoided even with the grace of God. [Note: He next proceeds to condemn those conclusions that Catholics drew from the doctrines of the Pelagians: first, that human beings can avoid sins without God’s grace or assistance; second, that little children either do not need baptism or should not receive it with the same sacramental words as adults; third, that one born of two baptized persons, or of a baptized woman, does not need the grace of baptism; fourth, that the whole human race neither dies through Adam nor rises again through Christ. He condemns these propositions in deceptive language, as Augustine demonstrates in several places from other Pelagian writings.

Before proceeding to the notes on the fourth part, I think I should discharge the promise by which I undertook to show that Julian can be convicted of the Nestorian error, or at least brought under strong suspicion of it. I establish this by five arguments. First, Julian was joined to Theodore of Mopsuestia and Nestorius by the closest intimacy. He lived familiarly with both: with Theodore in Cilicia while writing his final work against Augustine, and with Nestorius for as long as the emperor allowed him to remain in Constantinople. Both men had the same character and the same madness of people passionately devoted to their opinions: they loved no one except those who agreed with them, despised all who thought otherwise, and furiously hated their opponents [Col. 0521D].

Second, in explaining the mystery of the Incarnation, he uses the same expressions as both enemies of Christ. For he employs the term “assumption,” which at that time was deeply suspect and was used by both heretics. He contrasts that term with “conversion,” not meaning that through conversion God would cease to be God, but that through the assumption of flesh he would begin to be human. Nestorius: “If anyone says that God the Word himself was changed into the flesh which he assumed, so that he might be found as a human being,” etc. Julian: “So that the human being might ascend to God, God descended to the human being.” Nestorius: “God saw nature fallen, and by the power of his divinity he seized it when it had been cast down; holding it when cast down, and remaining what he was, he raised it on high,” etc. Why say more? He does not explain the economy of the Incarnation in words other than those used by Theodore and Nestorius—words indeed ambiguous and capable of being turned in either direction, but nevertheless constructed according to the Pelagian art, whose practitioners customarily spoke in such a way that, depending on time and place, they could accord with the minds of their hearers.

Third, he expressly rejects heretics who held views contrary to the faith of the Trinity—Arians, Sabellians, Eunomians, and Macedonians—and pronounces anathema upon them; yet he does not do the same to Paul of Samosata, Photinus, or others of that kind who blasphemously say that Christ is merely human.

Fourth, the communion of those whom he expressly execrates—Arians, Apollinarists, and Manichaeans—was repeatedly and everywhere slanderously attributed by the Nestorians to Catholics. Indeed, what deserves notice is that he condemns the Apollinarists and Manichaeans in such a way as immediately to add, “and those like them,” as the Nestorians were accustomed to do.

Fifth, he assigns no other purpose to the Incarnation than the one asserted by the Nestorians, namely, that Christ should go before the other human beings, who are like him, by his example.

Why pursue in detail the other matters that anyone can easily notice by reading? Augustine certainly presses this man hard, since, as Augustine seems to understand him, he denies that the two natures were joined in the Virgin’s womb and maintains that the union was afterward granted through the merits of the will. The passage deserves to be transcribed, although it is lengthy, for in it Augustine endeavors to show that Julian is an enemy of the Virgin who bore God (*Unfinished Work*, Book IV, chapter 83):

“You say that clear testimony fully proves that the righteousness of the assumed human being subsisted in the Son of God not from a difference of nature but from a voluntary action. Is that really so? Did Christ not even have this difference in nature: that he was born from the Virgin in such a way that he was already not only the Son of man but also the Son of God? Therefore, did this assumption—which made God and man one person—contribute nothing to that human being’s excellence of righteousness, which you say subsisted from a voluntary action? Does your defense of free will against God’s grace drive you headlong to such a degree that you even say that the Mediator himself merited by his own will to be the only Son of God, and that what the whole Church confesses is false when it professes its belief in Jesus Christ, the Son of God the Father Almighty, our only Lord, born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary? For according to you, the human being was not assumed by the Word of God in order to be born from the Virgin; rather, after being born from the Virgin, he progressed by the power of his own will and brought it about that he was assumed by the Word of God. He did not possess such and so great a will in that assumption, but preceded that assumption with such and so great a will. Nor was the Word made flesh in the Virgin’s womb; rather, afterward, by the merit of that human being and by his human and voluntary power. From this it also follows for you that, just as you believe him to have been assumed by the Word of God because he willed it, so you believe that many could have been assumed if they too had willed it, or could be assumed if they should will it. Thus human sluggishness of will would make him the only one, although there could have been many if human beings had willed it. If you say these things, where is your shame? If you do not say them, where is your heresy?”

Yet it is difficult to understand how the holy teacher could establish from Julian’s words what he attempted to establish. For he seems to have taken the words in a sense foreign to them [Col. 0523B]. Julian intended only this by his words, as is clear from the context itself: that Christ performed works of piety and righteousness not by a necessity of nature, as though he had received a nature different from ours, but by free will—which is true and entirely pertinent to the matter under discussion. Nor could he have thought otherwise, since he had to say that the union of the natures by which Christ is God and man took place in the Virgin’s womb, given that he asserts that the one who, according to his divinity, was never absent from the Father was born from Mary, ever virgin [Col. 0523C].

Someone might therefore think that Augustine understood this concerning the new followers of Paul of Samosata, as everyone commonly understood it concerning Paul himself, who taught that Christ had advanced through his own merits into the title of Son of God. For Augustine had not yet exercised himself against this class of heretics, who, although they thought Christ was merely human, nevertheless asserted that he had emerged from the Virgin joined to the Word of God, however that union might ultimately have occurred. But we shall discuss this matter more fully in the latter part of the works of Mercator, where there will be a dissertation on the heresy of Nestorius, which Cassian and the author of the epitaph of the Nestorian and Pelagian heresies, along with not a few others, did not sufficiently understand because of their preconceived opinion.

In defense of Julian, someone might produce several words from his confession in which he appears to speak against Nestorius. For he says that the Son of God was sent, born of Mary ever virgin, redeemed the world by suffering, died and rose again in order to destroy death—things that the Nestorians could not tolerate. Yet since Theodore, and even Nestorius, at times used these same words, they can conceal the heresy but cannot clear it, as will become evident in the dissertation we promised.

Nearly the whole of the fourth part is explained in Dissertation 4, which concerns the subscriptions. Accordingly, the individual points must be touched upon more briefly—or rather, only insofar as they concern history or correspond to what is found in Augustine.]

But if anyone says that human beings can avoid sins without the grace or assistance of God, we gravely detest it.

### 19.

Or if anyone denies that little children need baptism, or asserts that it should be administered with sacramental words other than those with which it is administered to adults;

### 20.

If anyone also says that one born of two baptized persons, or born of a baptized woman, does not need the grace of baptism;

### 21.

Or whoever asserts that the whole human race neither dies through Adam nor rises again through Christ.

### 22.

Or if there are any other propositions that either run contrary to the Catholic faith or belong to undisciplined disputes, we condemn them with a similar execration.

## PART FOUR. The Pelagians’ defense; appeal to a plenary synod; pretext for refusing to subscribe; criticism of the supreme pontiff; a distorted testimony of Saint Chrysostom against original sin; and epilogue

[Col. 0523B]

1. [Note: [Col. 0523D] He alludes to the booklets of Pelagius and Coelestius, and especially to Pelagius’s letters to Innocent, in which the crafty heretic wished to make it appear that he was expounding his thought in such a way as to maintain a perpetual deception—namely, through ambiguous words, which, because of their breadth of meaning, could be changed into various senses [Col. 0524B]. See Augustine’s book *On the Grace of Christ*, in which he examines both Pelagius’s booklet and his letters.] Yet all these matters now under discussion—that is, those which we condemned at the end—were themselves condemned in their own writings by the very men against whom these charges are made, while they falsely protested that the charges had been brought against them.

2. [Note: [Col. 0524B] An insolent sentence, similar to the one found in the final chapter of the first book addressed to Boniface, with which Coelestius concluded his letter to the Roman clergy [Col. 0524C].] “We have therefore written and sent these matters to Your Holiness, as they appeared to us in accordance with the Catholic rule. If you think that they must be held otherwise, write back; but if these things cannot be contradicted, and nevertheless someone should wish to stir up scandal against us, let Your Holiness be assured [Note: [Col. 0524C] Saint Augustine replied to this appeal (*On the Fourth Book to Boniface*, final chapter), and at the same time taught three points deserving the closest attention. First, that a synod is not necessary in order to condemn an open heresy; second, that far more heresies have been extinguished by particular judgments than by universal synods; finally, that heretics, out of pride, press for a synod to be convened, as though they were the sort of people on whose account the whole world ought to be disturbed.] that we have appealed to the hearing of a plenary synod.”

3. [Note: [Col. 0524C] This passage is filled with a certain malicious shamelessness. For the impure man reproaches the supreme pontiff for having sinned in the very matter in which he had chastised the Africans for sinning, since he had reproached them for their hasty judgment in the case of Pelagius and Coelestius. He also uses, to increase the insult, the same Scriptural testimonies, indeed the very same words, that Zosimus had employed in his second letter to the Africans concerning the case of Pelagius and Coelestius.] “But we particularly warn Your Holiness not to think that this was done as a reproach to you: that [Note: [Col. 0524D] Because of these and the preceding words, a question may reasonably arise: whether, in the case of another heresy also, subscription to a condemnation was imposed—not only of the doctrines but also of their authors—when some defenders of those authors, differing from the Church concerning the meaning of the books written by them, complained that, out of fear of God and obedience to the law of Christian charity, they could not condemn men whom they believed to have thought Catholicly. The answer is that the same thing occurred in the case of Nestorius, as we shall show in the observations on the second part of the works of Marius Mercator.] we do not dare, out of fear of God, to subscribe to the condemnation of absent persons, having been taught through the Scriptures that human will ought not to be preferred to God’s commands,” as God says (Exod. 23:1, according to the Septuagint):

“You shall not believe a vain report, nor agree with the wicked to be an unjust witness.”

[Note: [Col. 0524D] That passage of Exodus 23, also cited by Zosimus according to the Septuagint, reads in the commonly circulated manuscripts: “You shall not entertain a lying report, nor join your hand with the ungodly to give false testimony. You shall not follow a crowd in doing evil; nor in judgment shall you acquiesce in the opinion of the majority, so as to depart from the truth.”]

And lest anyone should think that the multitude ought to be followed, he added (ibid.): “You shall not follow the multitude in evil.” And again: “Before you have inquired, do not reproach anyone.” And again (Eccles. 11:7): “What your eyes have seen, speak.”

4. Likewise in the Gospel (Matt. 7:1): “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; do not condemn, so that you may not be condemned. For with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged; and with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.”

Likewise, in another evangelist (John 7:51), even the Jews acknowledge that “our law does not judge a man unless it has first heard from him and learned what he does.”

5. And in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 25:16), through Gentiles like Festus, the judgment was expressed that “it is not the custom of the Romans to condemn anyone before the accused has his accusers present and receives an opportunity to defend himself for the clearing away of the charges.”

6. Hence the holy apostle Paul, establishing the rule of judgment for bishops, says (1 Tim. 5:19): “Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter except on the evidence of two or three witnesses.”

7. Confirmed, therefore, by these and other testimonies, we fear to pronounce judgment against the heads of absent persons whom we have not heard, unless they have been refuted in person.

[Col. 0525B] 8. Although it is indeed the duty of priestly office and Christian charity to defend, with free authority, those who clear themselves in written statements, confess themselves Catholics, and condemn the charges brought against them as deserving condemnation, and, in doubtful matters, to interpret each person’s case for the better; nevertheless, while preserving the balance of equality between both sides that we promised long ago, we neither condemn those who have not been heard nor defend those who are absent.

9. Let Your Holiness be assured, then, that however greatly this sea may swell when the winds blow and however bitterly its waves may rage against us, it will never be able to shake the house of an upright judgment, founded upon the justice of Christ.

10. We also thought it necessary to reply, holy and venerable Brother and Father Augustine (Dear Zosimus), that [Col. 0525C]

[Note: [Col. 0525C] I think that Zosimus made three parts of his *tractoria*: the first contained the entire case of Pelagius and Coelestius, with all the arguments and opinions of each heretic [Col. 0525D]; the second, a definition of the faith for each of the parts of the controversies that had arisen; the third, the authorities of the saints with which the definition agreed. What we say about the first has been proved in Dissertation 4. What we say about the second is clear from the fragments of this decretal letter, which for that reason was called a regular authority. What we say about the third is gathered quite clearly from this passage of the booklet.

Moreover, from this *tractoria* subsequent writers—whether supreme pontiffs, Fathers, or councils—seem to have taken the practice of appending testimonies of the Fathers to doctrinal definitions, in order to prove that the faith of all ages was one. See Leo the Great’s letter to the Emperor Leo concerning Nestorius and Eutyches; Cyril’s treatises *On the Right Faith* to Theodosius and to the Empresses; his response to objections against the anathemas; the Council of Ephesus, Act 1; Theodoret in the *Eranistes*; and so forth.

[Col. 0526C] And indeed at that time, indeed always, the Church maintained this method of proceeding against emerging heresies: so that, as Capreolus of Carthage said, antiquity might be defended once novelty had been overcome; and, as Pope Sixtus wrote to John of Antioch, novelty might be permitted nothing, because nothing ought to be added to antiquity (Part II of the Council of Ephesus, Act 1). Therefore definitions were brought forward from the books of the elders, as from a kind of sacred treasury in which that divine deposit is religiously preserved, concerning which the Apostle says to his beloved disciple: “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of speech and the oppositions of falsely named knowledge, which some, professing it, have fallen away from concerning the faith” (1 Tim. 6:20). See Vincent of Lérins in the *Commonitory*, especially the part in which he expounds the Apostle’s saying: “Did the word of God go forth from you, or did it come to you alone?” and so forth (1 Cor. 14:36).]

you rightly praised in your letter: namely, that Bishop John, of blessed memory, had not destroyed the Churches but rather strengthened them. For we inserted his own words from his booklet addressed to the Neophytes concerning his opinion about the baptism of infants, so that you too, holy Brother, might know the opinion of that distinguished man on this matter.

11. [Note: [Col. 0526D] In Dissertation 1 we said that this homily of Chrysostom was read in Augustine’s time in the same version as in our own.] “Blessed be God,” he says, “let us again say: He alone has done wonders, who made all things and transformed all things. Behold, those who had shortly before been held captive enjoy the serenity of freedom; those who had been wandering in the error of exile are citizens of the Church; and those who had been in the confusion of sin now stand in the lot of righteousness. For they are not merely free, but also holy; not merely holy, but also just; not merely just, but also sons; not merely sons, but also heirs; not merely heirs, but also brothers of Christ; not merely brothers of Christ, but also co-heirs; not merely co-heirs, but also members; not merely members, but also a temple; not merely a temple, but also instruments of the Spirit. Blessed be God, who alone has done wonders. Do you see how many are the gifts of baptism? Some people think that heavenly grace consists only in the remission of sins. But we have counted ten honors. For this reason also we baptize infants, although they are not defiled by sins, so that holiness, righteousness, adoption, inheritance, brotherhood [Col. 0526B] with Christ may be added to them, so that they may be his members and become a dwelling place of the Spirit.”

12. Taught, therefore, by these divine and priestly examples, we have laid the matter before Your Holiness. It is your responsibility, having considered God’s judgment, to weigh everything with careful examination, so that the peace which we undertook to preserve, commended to us by Christ the Lord, may not be dissolved through the intervention of any scandal.

# HISTORICAL INVESTIGATION OF THE BOOKLET OF FAITH WRITTEN BY JULIAN

It is worthwhile, indeed necessary, to investigate somewhat more carefully the time at which the booklet was published and the author by whom it was written. But the question of its date cannot be resolved, at least not in every respect, until it has first become clear in whose name and to whom it was sent. Yet these matters too cannot be learned with certainty from anywhere other than the booklet itself. In its fourth part there are several points deserving notice; using them as principles, we shall thereafter establish the truth.

First, this booklet is, at least in part, a letter. “We have written and sent these matters to Your Holiness, as they appeared to us in accordance with the Catholic rule. If you think that they must be held otherwise, write back” (No. 2). And later (No. 12): “Taught, therefore, by these divine and priestly examples, we have laid the matter before Your Holiness,” and so forth.

Second, this sort of letter was written in the name of Latin, indeed Sicilian, men. “Consequently, we condemn all heretics, and especially those who among the Latins have been identified both by their proper name and by their error” (Part III, No. 1). And at the end: “Here ends the booklet of faith of S. I. C.,” that is, “of the Sicilians.”

Third, those men stubbornly refused to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius. The words of those who refused are these: “But if we do not dare, out of fear of God, to subscribe to the condemnation of absent persons, having been taught through the Scriptures that human will ought not to be preferred to God’s commands” (Part IV, No. 3). Likewise: “Confirmed, therefore, by these and other testimonies, we fear to pronounce judgment against the heads of absent persons whom we have not heard.” And later (No. 9): “Let Your Holiness be assured, then, that however greatly this sea may swell when the winds blow and however bitterly its waves may rage against us, it will never be able to shake the house of an upright judgment, founded upon the justice of Christ.”

Fourth, those who stubbornly refused to subscribe were bishops, as they show by the dignity they claim. First, when they call the bishop to whom they are writing “brother” (No. 10): “That matter also, holy and venerable brother,” and so forth. Then, when they give the reason why they refuse [Col. 0527B] to subscribe (No. 6): “Hence the holy apostle Paul, establishing the rule of judgment for bishops,” and so forth. Finally, when they claim for themselves what properly belongs to bishops alone: the right to render judgment and pronounce a decision concerning the doctrine of the faith (No. 8): “Although it is indeed the duty of priestly office and Christian charity to defend, with free authority, those who clear themselves in written statements, confess themselves Catholics, and condemn the charges brought against them as deserving condemnation, and, in doubtful matters, to interpret each person’s case for the better; nevertheless, while preserving the balance of equality between both sides that we promised long ago, we neither condemn those who have not been heard nor defend those who are absent.”

Fifth, those bishops were writing to their primate—that is, to the bishop of the greater see to whom they were subject. For when they call him both brother and father (No. 9), “holy and venerable brother and father,” they use the form by which, in those times, subordinate bishops wrote to a superior, calling other bishops, whether subordinates or equals, brothers and fellow bishops.

[Col. 0527C] Sixth, the bishops in question were replying to a letter previously received from their primate, in which they had been ordered to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius:

“We also thought it necessary to answer that matter, holy and venerable brother and father. We have written and sent these matters to Your Holiness, as they appeared to us in accordance with the Catholic rule. If you think that they must be held otherwise, write back; but if these things cannot be contradicted, and nevertheless someone should wish to stir up scandal against us, let Your Holiness be assured that we have appealed to the hearing of a plenary synod. But we particularly warn Your Holiness not to think that this was done as a reproach to you,” and so forth (No. 23, 17).

Seventh, the primate’s letters contained an honorable mention of John Chrysostom (No. 10): “You rightly praised in your letter Bishop John, of blessed memory, for having not only failed to destroy the Churches but also strengthened them,” and so forth.

From these seven observations, I think I can answer the questions and conclude, as regards the date, that the booklet was written during the interval extending from A.D. 418 to 420; indeed, approximately in the autumn of A.D. 418, as can be demonstrated in the following way.

The Book of Faith was certainly written not only after the bishops had been compelled to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius, but also before the recalcitrant bishops were expelled from their sees. Yet the bishops were not compelled to subscribe until either Zosimus’s *tractoria* had been sent to the whole world, or until the emperor Honorius, in the consulship of V ides July, Monaxius and Plinta—that is, in A.D. 419—had written from Ravenna to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage (as reported in Dissertation 3), in order to correct the obstinacy of certain bishops who either supported the perverse arguments of the Pelagians by tacit consent or failed to destroy them by public opposition. He ordered that all should be admonished to subscribe to the condemnation of the heretics [Col. 0528A], if they did not wish to be punished by the loss of their episcopate.

Since no one can be considered obstinate unless he has refused to do what he had previously been compelled to do, the bishops whose obstinacy gave occasion for the imperial letters must first have been compelled to subscribe, and by an adequate authority. Whose authority was it? Was it that of the emperor Honorius? Thirteen months earlier, at Ravenna, he had issued another sanction to Palladius, the prefect, but that sanction merely proscribed Pelagius and Coelestius; it made no provision for requiring the bishops’ subscription. Was it the authority of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, and of the African synod over which he presided? But neither does anything appear in the acts of the synod concerning a subscription to be required from all the bishops; nor, if such a provision did appear, would it have force beyond the African diocese. It was therefore the authority of Zosimus, the supreme pontiff, who, after sending his *tractoria* to all the bishops of the world, ordered that it be subscribed by everyone.

Mercator reports this (*Commentary*, chap. 2):

“For this reason Coelestius was condemned in extensive, indeed very lengthy, writings by Zosimus, bishop of blessed memory. In them were contained the very chapters of which he had been accused; and the entire case, both concerning the aforesaid Coelestius and concerning Pelagius, his still more depraved teacher, appears to have been narrated. We possess copies of these writings here, and we report that similar and identical writings were sent to the bishops of the Eastern Churches, to the diocese of Egypt, to Constantinople, to Thessalonica, and to Jerusalem.”

And later:

“All the chapters written above, as has already been said, are contained in that letter of Bishop Zosimus, of blessed memory, which is called the *tractoria*, by which Coelestius and Pelagius were condemned. It was sent both to Constantinople and throughout the whole world and was confirmed by the subscriptions of the holy Fathers. Julian and his other associates, however, refusing to subscribe and unwilling to make themselves of one mind with those same Fathers, were deposed not only by imperial laws but also by priestly decrees and driven from all Italy.”

And in another passage, addressing Julian (*Book of Subnotes*, chap. 7):

“In your letter, which you dared at that time to send to the apostolic see, when you refused to join with the universal Church throughout the whole world in condemning Pelagius and Coelestius.”

Now the *tractoria* was sent throughout the whole world in A.D. 418. For Zosimus had not yet sent it to Africa on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April in A.D. 418, when he wrote to the Africans that he had not acquitted Coelestius in his judgment but had left everything in the condition in which it stood until those who would accuse the defendant in person should come from Africa. Since Zosimus died on the seventh day before the Kalends of January of that same year, according to the Roman Martyrology and all chronologists, the *tractoria*, which contained the definitive sentence against Coelestius, must have been sent during the interval from 19 March to 26 December.

But since Augustine, as he was departing for Caesarea in Mauretania, carried this *tractoria* with him and sent it from there to Optatus (*Letter* 190), and since he was present at Caesarea on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, Augustus, as the proceedings with Emeritus record (*Augustine’s Works*, vol. VI), it must be admitted that the *tractoria* was sent from Rome at least before the beginning of September.

Finally, since this same *tractoria* was received by the African Fathers gathered in council, at which Augustine was present, as Prosper reports (*Book against the Collator*, chap. 10), it must have been sent from Rome before the month of August, indeed before the Kalends of May, as we have shown in the dissertation on the synods.

Finally, the bishops who refused to subscribe were not expelled from their sees and from Italy later than A.D. 420, as we established in Dissertation 2. For Prosper writes as follows (ibid., chap. 41):

“Pope Boniface, of holy memory, rejoiced in the Catholic devotion of the most pious emperors and used against the enemies of God’s grace not only apostolic edicts but also royal ones.”

For what else does it mean to use edicts except to put them into execution? And what edicts can be meant other than the two of Honorius that we mentioned above? Finally, what did those edicts command the bishops except subscription to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius—that is, to the letter sent by Zosimus, as was shown in the preceding dissertation?

Mercator confirms the same point (*Preface to the Refutation of the Symbol Written by Theodore of Mopsuestia*):

“Julian, after traversing lands, crossing the sea, and surveying the East, went with his associates, companions, and fellow-sufferers—συνταλαιπώροις—with great effort, as though [the text is materially defective here: *te.....ndit*] to the teacher celebrated for Christian doctrines, so that he might obtain from him confirmation of the Pelagian or Coelestian heresy which he had undertaken to defend and follow. From there, as though better instructed, he composed those eight volumes which he considers exceedingly wise, more against the Catholic faith than against Augustine of holy memory.”

Since Julian went to Cilicia in A.D. 421 or the following year, and nevertheless did not depart before he had been deposed from his see, he must have been deposed before A.D. 421. But [Col. 0529B] he wrote his booklet of faith before his expulsion, as is clear from the fourth observation. He therefore wrote it during the interval between A.D. 418 and 420. That it was written in A.D. 418 itself must be demonstrated after resolving the other question: in whose name, precisely, Julian wrote, and to whom.

Now it can scarcely be doubted that he wrote in the name of the Sicilians, since the concluding words of the appended clause clearly signify this: “Here ends the booklet of faith of S. I. C.” For who does not see that these three letters, S. I. C., abbreviate some name, and that they can mean nothing other than “of the Sicilians,” provided that—as it is easier to suppose—those three letters coalesce into a single syllable?

Nor in those times, if historians and geographers are to be trusted, did there exist among the Latins any people whose name either began with this syllable or whose bishops persisted in the Pelagian error. For the thought that these letters might indicate the Campanians and Apulians, Julian’s provincial neighbors or subjects—those who in ancient times were called Sicani and in later times Sicilians on this side of the Strait—is easily disproved by chronological considerations. For in the fifth century the new designation “Sicilians on this side of the Strait” had not yet been invented, while the ancient name “Sicani” had long since fallen out of use.

What is more, everything relevant to the present matter fits the Sicilians extremely well. Many of them followed the Coelestian heresy, which alone is almost the subject defended throughout this booklet; some were expelled from Sicily after the emperor’s edict because of their obstinacy in error; and Julian had many friends on this island, among whom he eventually died. These three points have been demonstrated in Julian’s eulogy.

Moreover, he wrote in the name of the Sicilians to the bishop who could compel the Sicilians, by his authority, to subscribe, as is clear from the sixth observation.

There were four bishops at that time—that is, during the two-year interval mentioned above—who might appear capable of doing this: two because of the dignity of the apostolic see, Zosimus and Boniface; and two because of the emperor’s edict directed to them, Aurelius and Augustine—if indeed it is true that an edict was directed to Augustine by the emperor in the same form as that directed to Aurelius. Such an edict was read in the manuscript of the distinguished author of the *Annals* (vol. V of the *Annals*, under A.D. 418). But of these four, the characteristics contained in the observations set out above fit none except Zosimus.

They do not fit Augustine, although Baronio’s manuscript appears to support him strongly. Why would the Sicilians have addressed Augustine as “Father”? Out of respect? Yet they were extremely hostile toward him because of the vigorous action he had taken against their heresy. Because of his age? But Florus, the most notable of their number, was himself of very advanced age. Because of the dignity of his see? But the city of Hippo neither held precedence in itself nor at that time possessed the primacy of Numidia, because of the seniority of its bishop.

Furthermore, it was observed that the Sicilian bishops replied to one from whom they had earlier received a letter in which Chrysostom had been praised. Yet to this day no one has reported that Augustine wrote any important letter, either concerning the condemnation of the whole heresy or concerning Pelagian questions, in which Chrysostom was said not to have destroyed the Churches but to have strengthened them. And if any such letter of such importance had been written, Augustine would not have remained silent about it when he prescribed some of his works on these questions for reading; nor would Possidius have omitted it from his catalogue, where he lists Augustine’s treatises and letters against the Pelagians with such care.

Add that the Sicilians replied to one who demanded a subscription by authority. By what authority could Augustine have demanded it? Not by any prerogative of his see, for he presided over the least important one; not by any imperial rescript, for such a rescript would have applied only to the bishops of Numidia, the province in which Augustine was located, and would not have applied to the Sicilians, who belonged to the Roman diocese.

Moreover, confidence in Baronio’s manuscript is considerably shaken: partly because at that time Augustine was not the senior bishop in the province of Numidia, and consequently was not its primate, so that, if the emperor’s mandate had been directed to him, an injustice would have been done to Valentinus, Alypius, and four other bishops senior to Augustine; partly because historians are silent about so important a matter, as are Augustine’s own eulogists—and even the Pelagians, who certainly would not have kept silent, whether the former or the latter, if something of this kind had occurred.

Finally, since Augustine left no writing by the Pelagians, especially by Julian, unanswered, he would certainly either have refuted so lengthy a confession of faith and so boldly provocative an appeal to the hearing of a plenary synod, or at least would at some time have made frequent and substantial mention of it.

[Col. 0530C] Therefore Sirmond’s copy must be corrected at the words: “That matter also, holy and venerable brother and father Augustine.” The final word was inserted by the copyist, since in the old manuscript there were two S-shaped figures joined together, by which the ancient Latins represented the Greek Ζ when they wished to use an abbreviation. He thought that it was an A, by which Augustine was indicated.

Nor do the characteristics mentioned above fit Aurelius, even though the preceding letter seems to favor him. For although he received an edict from the emperor and, after receiving it, sent a letter to the bishops ordering them to subscribe to the condemnation of the heretics, he gave the order within the limits of his jurisdiction—that is, only to the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana, or at most to the bishops of Africa. Moreover, there is no mention of Chrysostom in the letter he sent. Finally, if he had received anything of this sort from the Pelagians, he would certainly not have concealed it from Augustine; nor would Augustine himself have remained silent, since everything between those allied friends, in this matter and in other matters pertaining to ecclesiastical administration, was so entirely shared that Augustine was almost Aurelius’s mind, spirit, and hand.

Indeed, those same characteristics do not fit Boniface either, although he was the supreme pontiff. For although the Sicilians were within his jurisdiction and he could compel them to subscribe by his authority, there is no record that he wrote any letter containing either an order to subscribe or praise of Chrysostom. For if such a letter had existed, how could the writers of that period—otherwise so diligent in listing the decrees of pontiffs and councils against the Pelagians—have failed to mention it? How could Prosper, so careful an investigator of the affairs of Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, and Coelestine, have omitted it? How could Augustine himself have remained silent, when he eagerly gathered from every source arguments by which to demonstrate that the Pelagians had been condemned by the apostolic see?

[Col. 0531A] It should also be added that if Boniface had received from the Pelagians any letter as important as this one, he would certainly have sent it to Augustine for refutation, just as he sent the other two (*Books IV to Boniface*).
