Furthermore, this booklet appears to contain the first appeal by the Pelagians to an ecumenical synod. It was therefore written before the two letters of the Pelagians which Boniface sent to Africa through Alypius for Augustine to refute. For in the fourth book of the refutation, at the final chapter, mention is made both of an appeal of this kind and of a subscription exacted—or, as the heretics claimed, extorted—from simple bishops. If the subscription was indeed exacted from some bishops, it was certainly demanded by the letter to which the rebellious Sicilians replied.

But that letter was not Boniface’s, as has already been shown. Nor could it have been his; otherwise it would have had to be written before the Kalends of July in A.D. 419, when Boniface entrusted Alypius with letters to deliver to Augustine. Those letters contained the bishops’ obstinacy toward the order to subscribe—an order that had already long since been promulgated—and their appeal to a synod. Yet it could not have been written before the Kalends of July. For how could Boniface, before his authority had been sufficiently established and before he had triumphed over Eulalius, whose party the Pelagians supported, have issued so significant a decree? He scarcely held the apostolic see peacefully on the very Kalends of July in A.D. 419, after Eulalius and his supporters had been expelled.

It remains, therefore, to suppose that this booklet was presented to Zosimus. And indeed all the evidence agrees admirably with this supposition.

First, the holy pontiff had Sicilians in his diocese, among whom that particular branch of the Pelagian heresy which the booklet appears to have been written to defend was especially active.

Next, he sent a very long letter to all the bishops of the world, to which anyone wishing to have his faith approved by the Church was required to subscribe as to a rule of faith. That letter contained not only the whole case of Pelagius and Coelestius [Col. 0531C] but also the testimonies of the Fathers against the condemned heresy.

Mercator testifies to this in the *Commonitory* (chap. 1 and *Book of Subnotes*, chap. 7). Augustine agrees with Mercator in these words (*On Original Sin*, chap. 21):

“Other statements of Coelestius also, in the city of Rome where he had lived for a very long time and where he had previously been involved in these discussions and controversies, were brought to light through the care of faithful brothers. Pope Zosimus appended them to his letters, which he composed for delivery throughout the whole world, as deserving execration, as you can read there, where Pelagius,” and so forth.

Third, Julian accused Zosimus of treachery, as though he were guilty of betrayal. Augustine writes (*Book VI against Julian*, chap. 4, near the end):

“What kind of conduct is it, then, that, in order to persist in your perversity, you accuse Zosimus, bishop of the apostolic see and of blessed memory, of treachery? He did not depart from his predecessor Innocent, whose name you were afraid to mention. Rather, you preferred to attack Zosimus because at first he dealt more leniently with Coelestius, since he had said that, if anything in these opinions of yours displeased him, he was prepared to be corrected, and had promised that he would agree with Innocent’s letters.”

Finally, Julian and Augustine unanimously acknowledge that Julian sent two letters to Zosimus before writing against Augustine. For when Julian had said (*Unfinished Work*, book I, chap. 17):

“Augustine also mentions a letter which he says was sent by me to Rome; but we have been unable to recognize from the words he quoted what writing he was discussing. I sent two letters to Zosimus, once bishop of that city, concerning these questions; but I sent them at a time when I had not yet begun writing my books,”

Augustine replies:

“This letter was not addressed to Zosimus but to deceive those who in Rome might have been deceived by such persuasion. But if you do not recognize it, let it not be yours; would that those books too were not yours but someone else’s,” and so forth.

Once these points have been established, it is perfectly clear that the booklet of faith now under discussion was written in A.D. [Col. 0532A] 418, around September or even October. For it was written and sent to Zosimus after he had issued his letter to all the bishops of the world; that letter was issued on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May of the same year. Since Zosimus died on 26 December of that year, and since he received this booklet before his death but not before he had ordered the bishops of his diocese to subscribe, the time at which the booklet was written cannot more suitably be placed than in the middle of the interval between the sending of Zosimus’s *tractoria* and his death.

The following four letters, I. V. L. I., as copied by Sirmond from figures that had almost disappeared in the manuscript, speak of Julian as its author. Even if the letters themselves were silent, what other author could be indicated by the chronology, the occasion of writing, the style, the spirit of the writer, his doctrine, and the passage praising Chrysostom?

First, the chronology: firm arguments establish that this booklet was written and sent to Zosimus in A.D. 418. At that time Julian claims to have sent two letters to Zosimus concerning the Pelagian questions, while openly denying that the first of the two refuted by Augustine was his. He acknowledges the second, but neither one was addressed to Zosimus.

Next, the occasion of writing: the booklet was sent in the name of those who, although compelled by the authority of the supreme pontiff to subscribe to the condemnation of the heretics, nevertheless stubbornly refused. Marius Mercator testifies that at least one of the letters Julian sent to Zosimus was written on the same occasion. He does not merely testify to this in words; he also reports a fragment of one letter and addresses Julian as follows (*Book of Subnotes*, chap. 7):

“Now hear, you too, and let those who have kindly wished to read both you and me hear, what you yourself once pronounced against this most impious, most depraved, most shameless, and most insolent opinion of yours—in your letter, that is, which you dared at that time to send to the apostolic see, when you refused to join with the universal Church throughout the whole world in condemning Pelagius and Coelestius.”

It should also be added that Julian himself sufficiently betrays his identity, at least to learned eyes, not only through the style he uses, which abounds in metaphors, but also through the spirit of his writing, which often swells into arrogance or dissolves into boasting.

For what could be more metaphorical than this sentence?

“Let Your Holiness be assured, then, that however greatly this sea may swell when the winds blow and however bitterly its waves may rage against us, it will never be able to shake the house of an upright judgment, founded upon the justice of Christ” (*Booklet*, Part IV, No. 9).

What could be more arrogant and boastful than a man addressing the supreme pontiff and head of the whole Church in this manner? “These writings, as seemed right to us according to the Catholic rule, we have composed and sent to your Holiness. If you think they must be held otherwise, write back; but if these statements cannot be contradicted, and yet someone should wish to stir up scandal against us, let your Holiness be certain that we have appealed to the hearing of a plenary synod” (ibid., no. 2).

There is no point in discussing the doctrine, since it can be clear to anyone who even looks casually that this same doctrine is contained in this little book as in Julian’s other uncontested writings, and especially in his letter to Rufus of Thessalonica, where he is wholly occupied with praise of free will, human nature, marriage, and the saints of the Old Testament. He also uses the same scriptural testimonies, indeed the same words, as will easily be evident from the notes.

But even if all the other indications made the conjecture uncertain, the testimony of Chrysostom that has been brought forward establishes it with certainty. Julian cited this testimony against original sin first in the *Book of Faith*, and then in the fourth book against Saint Augustine; for it is set out in the same words in both places, as may be seen in Saint Augustine (*Against Julian*, book I, chapter 6).

Moreover, I have no intention of annotating the book except where matters of learning—whether historical or of some other more recondite kind—are involved, especially since several observations have already been made concerning the other *Books of Faith*, and it is neither appropriate nor permissible to linger over the exposition of doctrines. I shall nevertheless try to establish one point, in order to defend Augustine’s judgment: namely, that Julian may, if not be convicted of the Nestorian heresy, at least rightly be regarded as under suspicion of it, and that this suspicion is by no means slight.

Julian did in the first part precisely what Pelagius and Coelestius had done. He discussed many things about which he had not been questioned and brought his discussion to whatever length he wished, from the unity of the Trinity all the way to the resurrection of the flesh—matters about which no one had asked him (Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 32).

*(Garner’s notes follow, which we have placed beneath the text at the foot of the pages.)*

It will not, I think, be out of place here to cite what Mercator excerpted from another letter of Julian to Zosimus and inserted into his *Book of Notes*. Julian himself acknowledges, in Augustine’s *Unfinished Work* (chapters 6 and 9), that he wrote two letters to Zosimus. Both aim at the same objective, though not in the same way: the first contains a profession of faith, the second a condemnation of Coelestius’ five propositions, but taken in an alien sense. Thus both appear injurious to the supreme pontiff, whose judgment Julian reproaches as unjust; both excuse Pelagius and Coelestius, as though they had spoken in a sense other than that understood by their judges; and both approve the action of Julian and the other bishops associated with him, who stubbornly refused to subscribe to Zosimus’ *Tractoria*—that is, as they themselves claimed, to pronounce judgment against men who had cleared themselves by written statements, professed themselves Catholics, and condemned the charges brought against them.

The second letter may certainly be regarded as either, if not a necessary complement for carrying the matter through, at least an appendix related to it, or a note that illuminates it.

Mercator therefore excerpted the following from it (*Book of Notes*, chapter 6):

“Listen now to what you yourself once declared in the letter which you dared at that time to send to the apostolic see, when you refused to attend the assembly and, together with the universal Church throughout the whole world, condemn Pelagius and Coelestius. Before it came into the hands of that holy bishop of the Roman Church, it is known to have been circulated through almost the whole of Italy, through your agency and that of certain people deceived by you, and to have been presented to the ears of many as something of great importance. For there, among other things, you wrote:

‘Who, then, maintains that the whole human race does not die through the death of Adam, nor does the whole human race rise through the resurrection of Christ, is of a different opinion from the Apostle, who says: “As all die in Adam, so also shall all be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Rightly, therefore, is he rejected who contradicts this statement: “Through a man came death, and through a man the resurrection of the dead” (ibid., verse 21).

‘This statement also—that Adam’s sin injured Adam alone and not the human race—we rightly refute. For it must be believed that it harmed not him alone but the human race.

‘As for the claim that infants are in the condition in which Adam was before his transgression, I count it among undisciplined questions. Those who are born today are not in every respect in the condition in which Adam was before sin, although it cannot be denied that they too, like him, are God’s work.

‘Nor is it supported by reason to say that Adam was made mortal and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin. For he must be believed to have been made immortal, yet in such a way that, if he had not sinned, he could have acquired the power of immortality by tasting the fruit of the tree of life. It was therefore wrongly said that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.’”

Mercator repeats nearly the same things in chapter 9:

“In your letter which, as we have mentioned, was sent to Pope Zosimus of holy memory, you express disapproval of, and condemn, the man who believes that ADAM WAS MADE MORTAL.”

The reader should consult the notes on the sixth chapter of the *Notes*. From them he will understand why fragments of this letter had to be cited here, just as Augustine extracted other material from another letter of that same Julian, written in the name of those same bishops to Rufus of Thessalonica (*Later Books to Boniface*, books III onward). These fragments can, in a manner of speaking, be restored to the form of a letter, so that the meaning may more easily be seen once the several parts have been gathered together.

[Col. 0534B]

“To the most blessed and most holy lord, brother and fellow priest Rufus: the bishops of the West, who in orthodox times suffered persecution for the Catholic faith.

“The state of affairs taking place here, most holy brother, compels us to seek through you, for our assistance and for the Catholic faith, the agreement of the Eastern bishops against the profanation of the Manichaeans. For a question is being raised against us, and we are displeasing to powerful men because we condemn those whom the Apostle foretold would depart from the faith, having their conscience seared, forbidding marriage, and abstaining from foods (1 Timothy 4:2)—foods which they regard as unclean, since they do not believe that all things were created by God. We are compelled to deny that every creature of God is good, and that there is no substance which the supreme God did not make.

“We are compelled, I say, by the state of affairs to implore your assistance, since we may hope for nothing from this quarter. For Pope Zosimus himself has withdrawn his former judgment. Previously, after approving Coelestius’ statement as Catholic, he had ordered that it ought to be believed that a human being is born without any fault of original sin; now, whether deceived by someone’s schemes or frightened by threats, he has decreed the opposite.

“The Roman clergy, struck by the terror of the command, were not ashamed to admit the crime of betrayal together with their bishop, so that afterward they might pronounce against their earlier judgment, by which they had supported Catholic doctrine in the official proceedings, and declare that human nature is evil.

“Our adversaries, whom we are suffering, say that through Adam’s sin free choice has perished from human nature; that God is not the creator of those who are born; that marriage was instituted by the devil; and that under the name of grace they assert fate in such a way as to say that unless God inspires in a reluctant and resisting human being even the desire for good, however imperfect, that person can neither turn away from evil nor seize the good.

“They say that the law of the Old Testament was not given in order to justify those who obeyed, but in order to make the cause of sin more serious. They also maintain that baptism does not truly make people new—that is, does not grant full remission of sins—but that people become children of God in part, while in part they remain children of the world, that is, children of the devil.

“They also say that the Holy Spirit was not an assistant to virtue in the Old Testament. Indeed, they claim that all the Apostles and Prophets were not fully holy, but were less evil in comparison with worse people; and that this is the righteousness to which God bears witness: just as the prophet says (Ezekiel 16:46) that Sodom was justified in comparison with the Jews, so, by comparison with criminals, some people are said to have exercised virtue. Indeed, they went so far in blasphemy as to assert that Christ lied because of the necessity of the flesh.

“They likewise maintain that after the resurrection there will be such developments that people will then begin to fulfill God’s commandments, which they were unwilling to fulfill here.

“They hold these and other opinions with the Manichaeans. We, however, who have resolved to withdraw as far as possible from such great impiety, do not know how to heap insult upon God’s creation, but rather honor and praise worthy of its creator. We therefore confess that God is the good creator of those who are born, through whom all things were made; we confess also that human beings are God’s work, and that every sin proceeds not from nature but from the will. Thus, by the truth of this doctrine, we resist the Manichaeans when they say that an evil nature is the cause of sin.

“We say that baptism is necessary at every age, so that the creature may be adopted as a child of God—not because it brings from its parents anything that needs to be cleansed by the washing of regeneration. And from this it follows that Christ the Lord, who according to his humanity wished to be made like us, was stained by no blemish of sin, and that his flesh was utterly pure from every contagion of sin from infancy onward—not because of any personal excellence or special grace, but through the sharing of the nature common to all infants.

“But how could sin have passed from Adam to the rest, unless the soul were, as the Church abhors to say, a propagation of sin? From Adam, we say, nothing evil passed to the rest except death. Death is not always an evil, since it is even the cause of rewards for martyrs. What makes death good or evil is not the dissolution of bodies, which will be raised in the whole human race, but the diversity of merits that arises from human freedom.

“We praise marriage according to the Scriptures, because the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘He who made them from the beginning made them male and female’ (Matthew 19:4); and he said: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth’ (Genesis 1:28). He immediately adds: ‘Therefore what God has joined together, let no human being separate’ (Matthew 19:6).

“We say that the old law, which the Manichaeans curse, is, according to the Apostle (Romans 7:12), just, holy, and good for those who keep its commandments; and that for those who live justly through faith, as did all the prophets and patriarchs and saints, it was able to confer everlasting life.

“We assert that free choice did not perish, since the Lord speaks through the prophet: ‘If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land. If you are willing and do not obey, the sword shall devour you’ (Isaiah 1:19). Accordingly, we say that grace assists each person’s good purpose, but does not implant the pursuit of virtue in one who resists, because there is no partiality with God (Romans 2:11).

“We praise the saints as free from crime, since baptism renews people perfectly. For the Apostle testifies that through the washing of water the Church from the Gentiles is made holy and without blemish (Ephesians 5:27). We also assert that the Holy Spirit assisted good minds in ancient times, as the prophet says to God: ‘Your good Spirit shall lead me in the right way’ (Psalm 142:10).

“We say that all the prophets, Apostles, and saints, of both the New and Old Testaments, to whom the Lord bears witness, were righteous not by comparison with criminals but according to the rule of virtues. In the future, however, there will be a reward both for the good and for the wicked. No one can then fulfill the commandments which he despised here, since the Apostle says: ‘We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil’ (2 Corinthians 5:10).

“While we confess these things against the Manichaeans according to the Catholic faith, our enemies, out of hatred for this truth, have taken up the statements of Augustine. Throughout the whole West, a dogma no less foolish than impious has been received, and a subscription has been extorted to confirm it from simple bishops sitting in their own places without any gathering of a synod.”

## DISSERTATION VI, DIVIDED INTO TWO PARTS

### PART ONE. ON THE WRITINGS OF THE DEFENDERS OF THE FAITH AGAINST THE PELAGIAN HERESY BEFORE THE DEATH OF SAINT AUGUSTINE

In these words of Mercator:

“Against his childish attempts, Bishop Augustine of holy memory composed various books at various times,” etc. (*Preface to the Book of Notes*).

[Col. 0535]

[Col. 0535D]

After the preceding dissertation has explained what the enemies of the faith published in order, if possible, to persuade people of their errors and to deceive Catholic minds with words apparently orthodox, so that the unwary might swallow poison which, if presented openly, they would immediately have recoiled from, it seems worthwhile to set out in summary, while preserving the chronological order, everything that the defenders of the Catholic faith wrote from the rise of the heresy until Augustine’s death. In this way everyone may easily see by what successive stages the truth offered itself to view, and by what struggles it triumphed over falsehood.

There are altogether five defenders of the faith who, during a defined period, fought in writing for the Church against the heretics themselves, and whose works have come down to us: Jerome, Augustine, Orosius, Sixtus, and Mercator. Jerome, however, as the renowned leader of venerable old age, weighed down by the burden of his victories, after he had fought sufficiently, yielded his place to Augustine in order to demonstrate his former strength. Under Augustine’s leadership, for more than twenty years the Catholic army fought and conquered the enemies of God’s grace so effectively that it did not allow those whom it defeated to draw breath, and against whose destruction it composed, with the single hand of all the priests, one common sentence (Prosper, *Against the Collation*, chapter 1). The other three either fought under Augustine’s leadership or at least worked alongside him in his victory.

I have said “defenders of the faith.” For I know that Nestorius delivered sermons concerning this same heresy which Saint Celestine praised, and which Mercator transmitted down to us after rescuing them from the flames of the emperors’ vindices [official enforcers]. But it would not have been proper to count the heresiarch among the defenders of the faith.

I have also said “whose writings have come down to us.” For I am not unaware that some assert that Saint Paulinus composed a book against the Pelagians commended by Augustine. If this opinion were true, one would have to admit that the work of so great a man had either been consumed by the ravages of time or remained unburied in the darkness of libraries. But those men were deceived by the person who supplied the title to Augustine’s Letter 106 and took Paulinus’ Letter VIII to Severus for a book. For that letter contains the entire passage praised by Augustine: “I am poor and grieving, still encrusted with the squalor of the earthly image,” etc.

Finally, I have said “who, during a defined period of time,” and so forth. For Prosper, apart from the fact that he wrote almost exclusively against the Semi-Pelagians, published nothing certainly before Augustine’s death except the letter prefixed to the book *On the Predestination of the Saints* and the poem *Against the Ungrateful*, which we have shown to have been composed while Augustine was alive.

Would that Zosimus’ *Tractoria* still survived! It would lessen—or rather fully repair—the loss of the other works, since it contained not only the whole case of Pelagius and Coelestius but also the arguments both by which the heretics attacked the faith and by which they were convicted by the Church, as we learn from Augustine and Mercator.

It seemed appropriate to append to this dissertation on the books of the defenders of the faith something concerning the surviving works of the attackers of the faith, so that everyone may easily understand what remains of the whole body of material and when each item was composed. From this, one may also form a certain judgment concerning some opinions commonly received, as though the Pelagian heresy had taken on the forms and variations which Gerardus Vossius and others have cleverly devised and tried to posit as genuine stages.

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Writings of Saint Jerome against the Pelagians

Jerome wrote five letters concerning the Pelagian controversy, three books of dialogues with a common preface, and prefaces to four books of commentaries on Jeremiah. Almost nothing more. For the works he composed against Rufinus, Jovinian, and Vigilantius do not directly attack Pelagius, whom he chiefly pursues; they concern him only incidentally, insofar as he appeared to be allied with the aforementioned enemies of Jerome in some part of his doctrine.

Those labors of the holy teacher, although neither numerous nor lengthy, nevertheless contain a great deal of history, which is almost the only thing we are seeking at present. Nor are they so lacking in dogmatic teaching that the learned old man does not seem either to have anticipated everything which others later treated more fully, or to have opened the source from which the others, including Augustine, would draw abundantly.

One of the letters is to Marcellinus the tribune, concerning the origin of souls; another concerns the questions of the Pelagians and is addressed to Ctesiphon; a third is a congratulatory letter to Alipius and Augustine on the overthrow of the Coelestian heresy; the remaining two are brief letters to Augustine, which are difficult to understand because of their riddles.

The dialogues for the most part fight against the sinlessness defended by Pelagius. Only toward the end of the third book is the baptism of infants discussed, and even there the question is raised more than it is solved, while the reader is referred to Augustine’s books for instruction. The prefaces contain matters relevant to illuminating either the history of the Pelagian affair or its chronology, which is otherwise by no means clear.

### The Letter to Marcellinus the Tribune, numbered 82 in Jerome and 27 in Augustine

It was written in the year 411. For it could not have been written before Marcellinus’ arrival in Africa, since it contains a response to a letter sent by Marcellinus from Africa to Jerome. “At last,” Jerome says, “I have received a letter from your Africa expressing unanimity.” Marcellinus came to Africa either toward the end of 410—which I scarcely think possible because of the stormy sea—or in the spring that followed, which is more likely. For the edict of Honorius (*Theodosian Code*, book III, *On Religion*), by which that holy and learned tribune was ordered to attend as judge the conference to be held between Catholics and Donatists, is recorded as having been issued at Ravenna on the fourth day before the Ides of October, during the consulship of Varaneus, which marks the year 410 of Christ.

Nor could it have been written later. It appears to have been written before either the conference took place or news of it reached Palestine. Otherwise Jerome would not have kept silent about it, since he spoke of Augustine, as though he were the mind of the entire conference, with such honor that he refers Marcellinus to him as a holy and learned man who could teach orally and explain his own view—and even Jerome’s view.

In this letter five opinions concerning the origin of souls are reported: that souls either descend into bodies from heaven, where they previously existed; or flow down from the divine substance as particles; or are drawn from a treasury where they were formerly stored; or are made daily by God; or are transmitted from the parents. The first two are rejected as heretical, and the third is also rejected as the foolish belief of certain churchmen. Jerome embraces the fourth as his own position, while he attributes the fifth to the greater part of the Westerners; whether justly, he may determine for himself.

Observe that Rufinus the Syrian adhered to Jerome, disciple to master, and that Julian likewise adhered to Rufinus as his follower. Jerome, however, expounded his opinion modestly, as was fitting for a Catholic; Rufinus pronounced an anathema against those who contradicted it; Julian boasted of it as confirmed by the authority of sacred law and the Catholic Church.

### The Letter to Ctesiphon, numbered 67 in Jerome

[Col. 0538D]

Jerome wrote to Ctesiphon toward the end of 413 or at the beginning of the following year. For it cannot be said to have been written after that time. When Orosius, in the assembly of the presbyters at Jerusalem, recalled both this letter and another sent by Augustine to Hilary of Syracuse, he called both of them recently written. Since Orosius cannot have departed from Africa for Palestine later than the spring of 415, and since he carried Augustine’s letter to Hilary with him and read it at the assembly in question, it must unquestionably be acknowledged that Augustine sent it in 414 or toward the end of the preceding year. Consequently, Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon must have been written at the same time, since both were composed at the same period.

Nor can it be said to have been written before that time. Ctesiphon wrote to Jerome after Pelagius’ arrival in the East and after his considerable stay in Palestine—a stay plainly necessary for disseminating the error which at first was cautiously handed down among a few of the faithful and did not come into the open until the silence of the teachers revealed the madness of the disciples. Since Pelagius did not come to the East before the end of 411, as has been established in the account of his life; and since Jerome did not reply to Ctesiphon until after most people in the East had been deceived by the question, even before Ctesiphon’s letter arrived, and many had learned pride under the pretense of humility, it must be admitted that almost two years elapsed between Pelagius’ arrival and Jerome’s letter, since the events described could scarcely have occurred in a shorter time.

This also refutes Baronius’ opinion that the letter was written in 411. The argument he uses is refuted by Augustine’s own conduct, indeed by Jerome’s as well. Baronius says that it was written before the names of the authors of the heresy had been made public. But the names—at least that of Coelestius—were made public after the Carthaginian judgment held by Aurelius in 412. Yet Jerome wrote the dialogues, and Augustine the book *On Nature and Grace*, in 415, and neither thought it necessary to name the man against whom he was writing. Both expressly declared that they had done this deliberately.

In this letter the holy teacher argues against Pelagius’ book *On Nature*, which he cites as at least the fifth book, and against the *Book of Chapters*, which he mentions; he also refers to the fifth book and to Coelestius’ book discussed in the *Palestinian Proceedings*. He vehemently attacks Pelagius’ ἀπάθεια (*apatheia*, freedom from passions) and ἀναμαρτησία (*anamartēsia*, sinlessness), defining it as the claim that passions can be eradicated through meditation and exercise so completely that no fiber or root of vices remains at all in a human being. Thus, they say, one not only does not sin culpably, but no impulses opposed to the law of the mind arise at all. This point should not be passed over carelessly.

He refutes this notion at length, but especially with the Apostle’s testimony: “I see another law in my members, leading me captive,” etc. (Romans 7).

He then shows who the parents of the heresy of τῆς ἀπαθείας (*tēs apatheias*, “freedom from passions”) were: namely, the philosophers—Manichaeus, Priscillian, Evagrius Ponticus, Xystus the Pythagorean, Origen, and Jovinian.

He next produces four statements in which the Pelagian error is contained:

- A human being can be without sin if he wishes.
- The grace of God without which a human being can do this is free choice itself and the law of God.
- Each person is governed by his own choice.
- God’s commandments are easy.

He also recounts the madness of the Pelagians when they slander the Catholics by claiming that, because Catholics say with the Manichaeans that nature is evil, they abolish free choice through their preaching of grace.

He explains as well the methods by which the heresy advanced: it was handed down secretly and only in private rooms; among women, especially powerful women who appeared pious; through ambiguous words that could be twisted into various meanings according to the time, persons, and places; with the teacher either remaining entirely silent or speaking through disciples, so that if the listeners approved what had been said, it would be reported to the teacher’s credit, but if they disapproved, the blame would be assigned to the disciple; and by frightening those who intended to write in defense of the truth with threats of an immediate reply, and so forth.

Finally, it contains certain weighty sayings, such as these: “The Church’s victory is for heretics to say openly what they think.” “Each sex brings down the other,” and so forth.

At the end, Ctesiphon, apparently a supporter of Pelagius, receives a warning useful for all ages: “Let those who furnish resources to such men know that they are gathering a multitude of heretics, making enemies of Christ, and nourishing his adversaries. They falsely profess one thing with their tongue, when their actions prove that they think another.”

Toward the end someone may perhaps ask what these words mean: “lest one, or at most three, little men take upon themselves such filth of heresies.” Who are those three little men whom Jerome warns us to avoid?

[Col. 0540A]

I think they are Pelagius, Annianus, and Valerianus. At that time Coelestius was staying at Rhodes—or rather at Ephesus, as was shown in Dissertation I. I have almost no doubt that those three used Ctesiphon either as their supporter or as their assistant, since Pelagius had insinuated himself into his friendship. The other two followed Pelagius like shadows: one supplied his pen, the other his methods, and both provided assistance to the old man.

Enough has been said about Annianus in the dissertation cited above; Valerianus has likewise been discussed in several places. I note only here that Valerianus appears to have been so called because he was a slave, or rather a freedman, of the comes Valerius. He followed Pelagius to Palestine, went from there to Alexandria, and, after being expelled by Cyril, returned to Italy. There he gave his patron excerpts from Julian’s first book against Augustine, which Valerius sent to Augustine for refutation. From this arose the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*.

### The Three Dialogues against the Pelagians

[Col. 0540B]

The three books of the *Dialogues* were composed in 415. They were begun before 30 July and completed before December. Jerome undertook the work, as he says at the beginning of the preface, “after the repeated complaints of the brothers as to why he was delaying the fuller work promised in the letter to Ctesiphon, beyond what he had pledged.”

He was working on it on 30 July, when Orosius spoke at Jerusalem in the assembly of the presbyters on the third day before the Kalends of August, in these words: “The blessed Jerome condemned this both in his letter, which he recently published to Ctesiphon, and likewise in the book which he is now writing, in which he refutes it through an exchange of arguments arranged in the form of a dialogue.”

The work must therefore have been begun in that same year before the end of July. But since it contains no mention of the synod at Diospolis under Eulogius—of which Jerome would certainly have remembered no less than the Carthaginian synod under Aurelius—and since it speaks of the silence imposed by John and of the peace apparently made among those who were causing disturbances because of Pelagius, the dialogues were unquestionably completed during the interval between the assembly at Jerusalem and the council at Diospolis.

Since these facts are certain, I am entirely at a loss to understand why Cardinal Baronius (*Annals*, for the year 415, no. 25) wished these dialogues to have been written after the synod at Diospolis. For the fact that he adduces Prosper, who, after mentioning the synod at Diospolis, recalls writings composed by Jerome against the Pelagians (*Poem against the Ungrateful*, chapter 2), proves absolutely nothing. If that order of presentation were to establish the time at which each of the works mentioned was written, the synod at Diospolis would have followed the letter to Ctesiphon, and the judgment of Innocent would have preceded it—something no one could reasonably say. Prosper mentions the latter before the synod and the former afterward.

I am equally unable to understand why Baronius, who believes the dialogues were written after the synod, nevertheless wishes them to have been composed in 415. How could so great and elaborate a work have been completed in nine days? For no more than that number of days elapsed between the end of the synod and the end of December, as has been established by a precise calculation in the dissertation on the synods.

Moreover, the *Book of Faith* which Pelagius sent to the apostolic see after the synod is almost entirely directed against the letter to Ctesiphon and against these dialogues, insofar as it touches on the questions discussed in them, as has been observed in the notes.

This approximate chronology of the dialogues leads me to believe that a judgment concerning the causes and authors of the council at Diospolis can be proposed which, even if not certain, is at least worthy of consideration. The council appears to have assembled in itself for the ordination of the bishop of the place; but it happened that John of Jerusalem seized the opportunity to absolve Pelagius, while Jerome, through the Gallic bishops, seized the opportunity to accuse him. These three points can be established by suitable arguments.

First, that the synod in question assembled for the reason stated is clear from the fact that there were formerly two kinds of provincial synods: ordinary and extraordinary. The ordinary synods were convened in obedience to the Nicene canon ordering the bishops of each province to assemble twice every year, once before Lent and again around the autumn season. Extraordinary synods were called either for the dedication of a church, as in the case of the Second Synod of Orange; for the ordination of a bishop, which frequently occurs in ecclesiastical history; or by the command of some higher authority, which likewise often happened.

The synod at Diospolis, however, was not ordinary. It was not held at the lawful time, but at a time when the bishops were compelled by the need to celebrate the feasts of the Nativity in their own churches. Nor was it convened for the dedication of a church. It is foreign to reason that, for so slight a cause—one that could conveniently have been postponed to another time—in the middle of winter, with the more solemn feasts approaching, and even the baptism of the Epiphany imminent, the aged primate Eulogius, the old man John, the almost exhausted Porphyrius of Gaza, and other bishops should have been gathered into a council.

Nor did any command of a higher authority compel the synod. If some such command had prompted it, how could Augustine either have been ignorant of it, when Orosius had reported that he learned every detail of this affair, or have kept silent about it, when it would have been of no small importance to his case?

It remains, therefore, to suppose that the Fathers came for the ordination of a bishop. Diospolis had its own bishop, as is clear from the Council of Chalcedon and from the list of the bishops of Palestine. The Church could not be left without one with the solemn baptism approaching; and this was a reason that customarily brought extraordinary synods together. Moreover, it was the primate’s responsibility to ordain for himself a *syncellus*, that is, a bishop of his province. It is therefore clear that the first point asserted above is correct: the synod at Diospolis was convened not in itself to conduct a judgment concerning Pelagius, but to ordain a bishop.

As for the second point in the proposed division—that John seized this opportunity to clear Pelagius—it is easily established from the dissertation on the synods. From it we learn with what intention John of Jerusalem came to the synod and by what methods he tried to advance Pelagius’ cause through bishops devoted to him, even though he knew that Pelagius was hated by Jerome.

But when Jerome perceived John’s plan and methods, he wished, I think, to set bishops against bishops and to prosecute the accused by means of written charges, since John wished to preserve Pelagius’ reputation intact. I shall show how I reach this opinion, which is the third point.

The document of accusation presented by Erote and Lazarus to Eulogius of Caesarea, the primate of the province, was unquestionably composed in Jerome’s presence, with Orosius in attendance. For the charges brought against Pelagius consisted partly of material contained in that document and partly of material taken from Pelagius’ books—whether from *On Actual Conduct* or from *On the Consolation and Exhortation of a Widow*—as well as from the document which the deacon Paulinus presented against Coelestius to Aurelius of Carthage, from the letter of the monk Hilary to Augustine, and from a certain book of Coelestius divided into several chapters.

The material of the first kind is found in the first and third dialogues of Jerome, in the same words and in the same form. Orosius supplied the material of the second and third kinds, as can easily be established from the *Apology*. The material of the fourth kind is found in the dialogues, not indeed in the same words but with the same meaning.

This should nevertheless cause no difficulty, since Augustine—plainly on the testimony of Orosius—warned that at the council itself the same words from this book of Coelestius had not been reported, but only approximately the same propositions.

If these things are true, as scarcely any prudent person acquainted with the facts would deny, the causes of several events that have until now been unknown or at least uncertain become apparent.

First, this explains why Orosius did not return to Africa in the autumn, although the weather advised it and his promised undertaking required it. At the same time he was preparing an apology for himself, a lawsuit against Pelagius, and vengeance against John. Or rather, he was keeping watch for every opportunity, to see whether he could in any way thwart Pelagius’ schemes—a thing he did by accusing him secretly and through another person.

It also explains why, when Critobulus asked Jerome why he did not accuse in court the man whom he accused of heresy in secret, Jerome gave a perplexed answer, in such a way as to seem to threaten a trial. He was thinking of the Gallic bishops, both of preparing them to undertake the case and of impelling them to defend the Catholic faith.

Third, why Jerome and Orosius did not wish to accuse [Pelagius] personally, but preferred to employ the persons of two bishops: evidently, first, they feared that they might appear to be driven by ill will; and second, a bishop defending him would have to be confronted by two bishops, and those from overseas, who would be thought more knowledgeable about the affairs of Pelagius, an overseas monk. Jerome scarcely concealed this strategy—or diligence—when he later counted himself among the vanquishers of the heresy together with Augustine and Alypius, and congratulated himself on sharing with them the hatred directed against Pelagius.

[Col. 0542B] Fourth, why the two Gallic bishops did indeed present a petition to Eulogius, but nevertheless stayed away from the hearing after offering an excuse: Augustine sufficiently indicates that others at the time interpreted this excuse differently (Book *On the Proceedings of the Palestinian Synod*, ch. 1), when he says, more plausibly, that their absence occurred because one of them was ill. Nevertheless, someone might reasonably suppose that the absence was contrived: first, lest the dignity of bishops be degraded, both by appearing in the role of accusers and by contending with a monk; second, lest they engage in an unequal contest before Greek judges, since they would have to speak through an interpreter whereas Pelagius would answer in Greek himself; then, lest they offend John, Pelagius’s patron, if it should happen that they had to quarrel with him; finally, lest they be required to present a petition prepared by another’s labor, or even to press a matter with which they were not thoroughly familiar; and, in the last place, lest they be covered with shame when they heard the reasons being brought forward for rejecting their testimony—reasons which Augustine indicates were both disgraceful and very serious [Col. 0542C] (*ibid.*, ch. 16).

Now, whatever Bishop John said about our absent brothers or fellow bishops, Erote and Lazarus, or about the presbyter Orosius, or about others whose names are not expressly given there, I believe he understood that it could not count against them. If they had been present, they might perhaps—far be it from me to say, convict him of lying—but perhaps have reminded him of something he had forgotten, or of some point on which the Latin interpreter had misled him, even if without any intention to lie, certainly through the difficulty of understanding a foreign language; especially since this is not a matter being debated in official proceedings, which are usefully established so that the wicked may not lie and the good may not forget something. But if anyone should raise some question against our aforementioned brothers on this account, and summon them before an episcopal tribunal, they will attend as best they can. Why should we trouble ourselves, when not even the judges themselves wished to pronounce anything on the matter after the account given by our fellow bishop?

Fifth, why those two Gallic bishops, whose very names Pope Zosimus called unspeakable, were adorned with praise by the Africans. Orosius, a friend of the bishops, had led the Africans to this opinion, as though he were either repaying them for presenting the petition or returning a favor.

Sixth, why Jerome described the Synod of Diospolis as pitiable, when, although the faith prevailed there, John’s ingenuity nevertheless prevailed in wanting to present Pelagius as pure of heresy and, as he himself claimed, superior to his rivals.

Seventh, why, once the facts—as commonly happens—had been exposed, Jerome’s party was harassed rather severely by the followers of Pelagius; indeed, Jerome himself came into danger of his life, from which he could escape only by taking refuge in the protection of a more strongly fortified tower.

Finally, why complaints were brought to Pope Innocent about John as the author of the persecution, yet not in such a form that the pope could exercise a legitimate judgment after the persons had been named individually; for they had taken care to secure their future safety in such a way that the circumstances of the case nevertheless did not become entirely clear.

At the end one may add that, in my dissertation on the synods, I omitted the fact that the sees of the fourteen bishops of the province of First Palestine who attended the council are known, except for five—Ammonianus, the younger Porphyry, Zosimus, Nymphidius, and Chromatius. Eulogius presided over the Church of Caesarea; John over that of Jerusalem; Porphyry over Gaza; Eutonius over Jericho; Zoboenus over Eleutheropolis; Fidus over Joppa; Jovinus over Ascalon; Eleutherius over Sebaste; and Clematius, apparently, over Diospolis.

## Prefaces to the Books of Commentaries on Jeremiah

The date at which the four prefaces to the books of the *Commentaries on Jeremiah* were composed can be established with greater certainty from the prefaces themselves than from any other source.

The first was published when an unlearned slanderer had recently burst forth [Col. 0543B], with Grunnius as his forerunner—one who snored with excessive stupidity, being utterly foolish and weighed down by Scottish porridge. He even thought that Jerome’s *Commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians* ought to be censured. These details fit the Pelagian Rufinus, whom Jerome calls Grunnius: a disciple originating from Britain, a corpulent man, who criticized Jerome’s *Commentaries* for their prolixity in comparison with his own brevity.

This preface, then, was published around the year 413, when Pelagius was circulating in the East his *Commentaries on the Epistles of Paul* and, because of their simplicity and brevity, had made them more highly valued by many than Jerome’s works. This undoubtedly explains why Jerome promised brevity in nearly every preface to the books composed after that criticism. Thus he says in the second preface: “We dictate these little commentaries without extending the work to excessive length.” In the third: “I shall try to confine the broadest fields of explanation within the narrow path of a commentary” [Col. 0543C]. In the fourth: “We shall pass briefly through the fourth book, dwelling only on those matters that are obscure.”

One should note the noble spirit of the most holy old man, who thought little of the fury of his detractors—men who slandered not only words but even the syllables of words, imagining that they knew something if they disparaged the works of others.

The second preface has its own definite chronological marker, for Jerome writes:

> We dictate the second book in a rapid style, turning our ears away for a little while so that we may not hear the judgment of blood and lament the souls of those who have been slain—those who, while reputed virtuous, fall daily into pride and consider themselves like God, and so forth. We have answered their fury as best we could; and, if the Lord grants life, we shall answer more fully.

It was therefore written after the letter to Ctesiphon, where nearly the same words are found, and before the more extensive work of the *Dialogues*, which is promised; thus, in the year 414.

The third preface bears the same mark: “He barks,” Jerome says, “through Albinus the dog, large and corpulent,” [Col. 0543D] and so forth. But this belongs to a later period, when, in the fuller work—the three books of the *Dialogues*—he crushed the three heads of Cerberus. It was therefore written in the same year as the preceding preface.

The words with which the defender of the faith demonstrates by his own example the customary cunning of heretics against Catholics are altogether worthy of note. He acts day and night, both openly and by ambush, mixing falsehoods with truths, indeed coating every lie with deceitful honey, so that the one who hears the sweetness of his words does not fear the poisons in his breast. He promises peace so that he may wage more grievous wars; he laughs so that he may bite; he offers his hand so that, unexpectedly, he may kill the simple Abner. Surely this is what the Apostle also meant: “For we are not ignorant of his schemes” (2 Cor. 2:11). Here he is silent; elsewhere he accuses. He sends letters throughout the world—little books, formerly golden, now full of curses—and interprets our patience, which derives from Christ’s humility, as a sign of a bad conscience.

[Col. 0544A] The fourth preface proves by clear indications that it was composed at the same time. For it explains the origin of the Pelagian heresy and the methods of men who scatter hidden poisons, against whom the work was composed without naming them, though it had not yet been published because of the wickedness of the times and John of Jerusalem’s uncontrolled devotion to Pelagius. It is useful to present the whole passage here, since it contains much of great importance for this matter and is in itself most deserving of being known:

> Occupied by many crowds arriving from every part of the world, and by the concerns of the holy brothers and of the monastery, I dictated my commentaries on Jeremiah at intervals, so that what leisure lacked might be supplied by diligence. Suddenly, however, the heresy of Pythagoras and Zeno—ἀπαθεία and ἀναμαρτησία, that is, “impassibility” and “impeccability”—which was once slaughtered in Origen and more recently in his disciples Grunnius and Evagrius of Pontus, and in Jovinian, began to revive. It began to hiss not only in the regions of the West but also in those of the East, and to stain many people in certain islands, especially Sicily and Rhodes, increasing day by day while they secretly teach and publicly deny it.
>
> I was compelled to answer it, after long silence and swallowing my grief in silence, by the frequent complaints of the brothers. Yet I have not burst forth so far as to name the authors, preferring that they be corrected rather than disgraced. For I am not the enemy of men but of error. When they tried to strike me in requital and with the natural sting of their own grief, singing in chorus the old slanders of their teachers, they proved so speechless and wretched that they could not even curse in their own words. At that time, in books published against them, their dirges were refuted. Whoever wishes to read them will clearly see that, according to Isaiah, they are mute dogs unable to bark: they possess the will and fury to lie, but not the art of inventing and barking.
>
> To them I shall speak briefly: Either what you teach is good or it is bad. If it is good, defend it freely; if it is bad, why do you secretly slaughter wretched people with error and parade an exposition of the true faith in order to deceive the simple? If it is true, why is it hidden? If it is false, why is it written? I ask: What madness is this? The Apostle commands us to be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks us to explain the hope that is in us (1 Pet. 3:15), while the prophet cries: “I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed” (Ps. 118:46).
>
> These men avoid public discussion and whisper in the corners of the lost; they grieve as though on behalf of their own teachings, which they are afraid to confess as theirs. Whenever we speak generally against vices and heretics, they complain that they are being attacked, and, concealing their indignation for a long time, they declare that this is an evil of conscience. But if we must beware of appearing to injure an old relationship, if we cut down a most arrogant heresy with the spiritual sword, then we shall have to endure crosses for the betrayed faith and say with the prophet: “I was afflicted while a thorn was being fastened into me” (Ps. 31:4).
>
> Rather, let them hear the apostolic saying: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5:29). And again: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. 1:10). We shall pursue these matters more fully in our own work, unless they fall silent.

[Col. 0544D] In the commentaries on chapter 23 he speaks about the Pelagians, but not about Palladius the Galatian. Baronius nevertheless suspected this when he said that the reader should be warned that the preface to the sixth book of the *Commentaries on Ezekiel* appears to belong to the Pelagian controversy and to have been written after the death of Rufinus of Aquileia, as though the Pelagians had sprung from his tomb. It reads as follows (*Preface to Book VI of the Commentaries on Ezekiel*):

> I thought that, once the serpent had been pierced through the middle, the young shoots of the hydra would not revive; and, according to the fables of the poets, once Scylla was dead, the Scyllaean dogs would by no means rage against me—those who never cease barking. And when the heretics of God had been struck down by his hand, so that, if possible, even God’s elect might not be tested (Matt. 24:22) [perhaps “peace might arise” should be added], I thought the heresy itself had died. But it has left behind hereditary whelps of its hatred against us, who, while pretending to be ours, do not abandon the poisons of their ancient mother and of deceitful Ulysses. They merely coat their lips with honey, but [Col. 0545A], according to the words of Scripture, “they have softened their words more than oil,” while they themselves are arrows (Ps. 54:22)—indeed, fiery arrows, which must at once be repelled and extinguished by the shield of faith.

From these prefaces of Jerome and the other works already mentioned, one can understand the condition of the Pelagian affair in Palestine from Pelagius’s arrival until the Synod of Diospolis, and the methods by which it was advanced, especially among noble women, with Pelagius himself acting together with Annianus. A faction was being formed that would bring ruin upon the whole world, under the appearance of piety and humility, through boasting of stricter discipline, criticism of the works of others, secret meetings in private rooms, flattery of powerful widows, displays of eloquence, clever exposition of doctrine, threats against those who wrote in opposition—as though they were destined to overwhelm them beneath the weight of their replies—and the constant complaint that people devoted to the evangelical rule were suffering from envy. The clergy were divided into factions, and hatred was instilled against the saints who served God with [Col. 0545B] Jerome in the monastery, and so forth.

## The Remaining Three Letters

The letter to Alypius and Augustine was written shortly before Jerome’s death, namely, toward the end of the year 419. It mentions the Synod of Diospolis, which was convened toward the end of 415; Pinianus and Melania, who were residing in Palestine and had arrived with Albina in 416; the suppression of the Coelestian heresy, which occurred in 418; and the death of the holy Eustochium, who passed to God on 28 September 419. It also mentions the return to Africa, after a year, of the presbyter Innocent, who had been sent by the African synod to Alexandria in 418 to seek the Nicene canons. He returned in 419 and was immediately sent to Rome with the canons, to Boniface, on 26 November.

Although, to speak frankly, it seems difficult for me to believe that Innocent, having departed from holy Bethlehem some time after the repose of Eustochium [Col. 0545C]—whose death Jerome says he had previously mourned—arrived at Carthage in winter and was sent to Rome on 26 November. Therefore either Eustochium’s death must be referred to the preceding year, which I consider less likely, or the Innocent who carried Jerome’s letter was not the same person as the one sent by the Africans as legate to Alexandria. I admit this more readily because of Jerome’s words:

> The holy presbyter Innocent, who is the bearer of this discourse, did not bring my letter to your Dignity last year, as though he were never going to return to Africa.

But the Innocent who had been sent as legate was certainly going to return.

Although this letter contains a response to the questions posed by Alypius and Augustine concerning the books written by Annianus against Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon and against the *Dialogues*, most of it is nevertheless devoted to giving both men magnificent thanks, because through their cooperation and leadership the Coelestian heresy had been suppressed.

[Col. 0545D] He recalls the followers of Pelagius, who had scarcely stopped short of madness because of their master’s condemnation, in these words:

> Although they know that they have been defeated and condemned, they do not cease to spread poisons through people’s minds. They hate us—this is the only thing they can do—because they think that through us they have lost the freedom to teach heresy.

The letter contains much about Annianus that is highly useful for history and criticism, but I have included these matters in the eulogy of Annianus.

There are still two letters to Augustine, but they are extremely brief and enigmatic, as was said earlier. One is numbered twenty-five among Augustine’s letters; the other, twenty-six. The former appears to have been sent immediately after the Synod of Diospolis, when, as a certain band of depraved men was raging and striving intensely to support Pelagius, scarcely any more strongly fortified tower could protect Jerome from the attack and assault of the impious (*On the Proceedings of the Palestinian Synod*, final chapter). The latter was sent shortly after the condemnation of both heretics [Col. 0546A] in Palestine had been heard of from Zosimus; this is what the words soon to be quoted indicate.

In the first letter, this is especially remarkable:

> You are celebrated throughout the world for your virtue. Catholics honor and revere you as the restorer of the ancient faith; and, what is a sign of greater glory, all heretics detest you and persecute me with the same hatred, so that those whom they cannot kill with swords they may kill by their will.

This is also remarkable in the other:

> Many limp on both feet, and do not bend even when their necks have been broken, retaining their former affection for error, although they no longer have the freedom to preach it.

These three letters show the condition of the Pelagian affair in Palestine from the Synod of Diospolis until the year 419. The men of this faction, emboldened because Pelagius had fraudulently secured absolution from the bishops, believed that their heresy had been approved. They sent letters to the provinces and lied about the matter; they openly employed force against their opponents, so that scarcely any more strongly fortified tower could protect Jerome, and the servants and handmaids of God under Jerome’s care were subjected to a most criminal massacre [Col. 0546B], a deacon was killed, and the monastery buildings were burned (*On the Proceedings*, final chapter). But when news of the condemnation was heard, and their insolence had turned into madness, they devised and plotted everything possible against those whom they believed to be the authors of their condemnation. Restrained by fear of imperial decrees, they did not vomit out their poison, but nurtured it more secretly.

# CHAPTER II. On Augustine’s Writings against the Pelagians

Thus far concerning Jerome, who fought in the Church’s war against the Pelagians in much the same way as veteran commanders usually do—more by reputation than by hand. Augustine undertook the whole battle. Of him Pope Hormisdas spoke no less wisely than honorifically:

> What the Roman Church teaches concerning free will and the grace of God can be learned from Augustine’s various books, and especially from those addressed to Hilary and Prosper.

That is, as I interpret it: it can indeed be established from Augustine [Col. 0546C] alone what the pillar of truth and the mouth of the Holy Spirit says. Nevertheless, the opinion of so great a man should not be understood equally from all his works, but chiefly from his later ones. While this part of the pontiff’s judgment is such that nothing shorter or more comprehensive could be said in praise of any teacher, the other part contains a very serious admonition of necessary prudence: while following an authority commended in this way as a rule of Catholic understanding, we must not place equal confidence, without discrimination, in all his works, and thus, through imprudence, depart from the teacher himself. For although Augustine at times attained such an understanding of the mysteries of divine grace as perhaps no one except the apostles possessed, he did not immediately stand at the summit. Rather, by striving upward step by step, he broke through the darkness of difficulties that obstructed him, as the divine light poured itself into him.

He himself testified to this candidly and sincerely, in more than [Col. 0546D] one place and at more than one time. For this reason he instructed those devoted to him to read his works in such a way that they might progress with him and strive to approach the truth by the same, so to speak, steps (*Letter* 7; *On the Gift of Perseverance*, ch. 21; and elsewhere).

When I first applied my mind to examining the questions of grace more deeply, I thought I ought to obey the holy doctor’s instruction and draw truth from the spring which the Church, mistress of truth, pointed out to me as the purest. For that reason I investigated carefully which works were genuinely Augustine’s and which were spurious; which concerned the matter of grace in themselves and which touched it only incidentally; and, finally, at what time each had been written and with what experience on the part of the writer. In this way I might follow closely the footsteps of the guide given to me by the Church and, under his guidance and, as it were, method, arrive more easily at the destination toward which I was making my way.

Someone may perhaps think that I worked with excessive diligence [Col. 0547A], since the holy doctor himself seems to have completed this entire task by listing his works in order. Yet in the books of the *Retractations*, neither the letters nor the homilies were reviewed, but only the treatises. Even in those, however, the chronological order is not observed exactly. Anyone can readily recognize this from the single fact that scholars are still uncertain in what year the book *On Grace and Free Will* and the other book *On Eight Questions of Dulcitius* were written. Nor is this surprising, since Augustine, while revising his works, often joined together works separated in time because of the similarity of their subject matter; and perhaps it sometimes happened that, being more than seventy years old, his memory failed him.

## Before the Year 412

Three books *On Free Will* (Tome I); one book *On Two Souls* (Tome VI); *Exposition of Certain Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans* (Tome IV); two books *To Simplicianus* (Tome IV).

[Col. 0547B]

Augustine testifies that he had written nothing against the Pelagian heresy before this year. Previously, whenever circumstances required, he had acted against it not by writings but by sermons and conversations (*Retractations*, Book II, ch. 33).

Nevertheless, he appears to have stifled this monster at its birth, as it were, with the three books *On Free Will*. He began part of them while still a layman in Rome and completed the rest as a presbyter in Africa (*Retractations*, Book I, ch. 9); likewise with the single book *On Two Souls* and the *Exposition of Certain Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans*, both of which he prepared while still a presbyter (*ibid.*, chs. 15 and 22); and finally with the two books *To Simplicianus*, which he published after becoming a bishop (*Retractations*, Book I, ch. 1).

Hence it is clear that we need investigate only the dates of those works written during a period of eighteen years—the number of years that elapsed between the first work addressed to Marcellinus and Augustine’s death, which occurred in the year 430, on 28 August.

## Year 412

Three books *To Marcellinus on the Merits and Remission of Sins* (Tome VII); one book *On the Spirit and the Letter* to the same person (Tome III); *Letter to Honoratus* (Tome II).

[Col. 0547C]

These five books—for Augustine also calls a letter a book (*Dissertation on Synods*)—were written after the Carthaginian judgment concerning Coelestius, which took place before Lent in 412, and before the death of Marcellinus, who was unjustly killed by heretics under the odium of Heraclian’s tyranny in 413, on 6 April (*Jerome, Dialogue* 3, near the end).

The first two to appear were those which, although they bear the common title *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, are nevertheless called by Augustine *On the Baptism of Infants* and *On the Perfection of Human Beings* (*On the Proceedings of the Palestinian Synod*, ch. 11), and by Jerome *On the Baptism of Infants* (*Dialogue* 3, near the end)—titles taken from their principal subject.

[Col. 0547D] The reason for their composition is recounted partly in the book *On the Proceedings in Palestine* (ch. 11) and partly in the *Retractations* (Book II, ch. 33). Questions concerning Adam’s mortality, the baptism of infants, and ἀναμαρτησία (“impeccability”) were being pressed with highly contentious insistence. Marcellinus, a tribune who was suffering from extremely troublesome disputants opposed to the ancient tradition, consulted Augustine by letter. The holy doctor was compelled by the concern of charity which, through God’s grace, he possessed toward Christ’s Church to send the tribune first two books and then a third. Thus he says (*On the Merits of Sins*, Book III, ch. 1):

> A very few days after the books had been sent, I read certain writings of Pelagius, a man, as I hear, holy and a Christian of no small progress, containing very brief expositions of the Epistles of the Apostle Paul. There I discovered that, when he came to the passage where the Apostle says (Rom. 5:12), “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death,” [Col. 0548A] and thus passed into all human beings, I discovered a certain argument of those who deny that infants bear original sin, and so forth. Therefore, since I did not wish to add anything to that work which I had already completed with a definite conclusion, I thought I should insert in this letter both the argument itself, in the same words in which I read it, and what seemed to me to be a reply to it.

Augustine testifies that these books were composed after the Carthaginian judgment but before Marcellinus’s death (*Retractations*, Book II, ch. 33):

> Coelestius, his disciple, had already merited excommunication at Carthage on account of such assertions, in an episcopal judgment in which I was not present.

And elsewhere (*ibid.*, ch. 37):

> To him I had written three books entitled *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, in which the question of the baptism of infants is also discussed carefully. He wrote back to me that he had been greatly disturbed because I had said, and so forth.

The letter to Marcellinus numbered 158 should be read in the same connection.

Since these facts are certain, Baronius’s opinion must collapse—that he assigned three such books to the year 411 [Col. 0548B]; for the judgment concerning Coelestius took place in 412, before Lent.

The book *On the Spirit and the Letter* bears an unmistakable chronological mark. It was written after the books *On the Merits of Sins* and before Marcellinus’s death, and therefore either toward the end of the present year or at the beginning of the following one.

The letter to Honoratus concerning the grace of the New Testament is marked by no less evident a sign. Thus Augustine writes to Marcellinus, after sending and then, following some revision, returning the three books *On the Merits of Sins* (*Letters* 120 and 158):

> At present I have in hand a book addressed to our Honoratus, concerning five questions which he proposed to me and communicated by letter.

And elsewhere:

> At the very time when we were being vigorously occupied against the Donatists and had already begun to be occupied against the Pelagians, a certain friend sent me five questions from Carthage and asked me to explain them to him in writing, and so forth.

[Col. 0548C] (*Retractations*, Book II, ch. 36.)

## Year 413

*Sermon on the Birthday of Saint John the Forerunner* (Supplement to Tome II); *Sermon 14, On the Words of the Apostle* (Tome X).

In this year two sermons were delivered to the people at Carthage concerning the baptism of infants: the first on the feast of Saint John’s Nativity, in June (Supplement, part II, p. 338), and the second after Saint John’s Nativity, on the feast of a martyr, in July. The first was recently published from the Royal Library; the latter has long been reckoned fourteenth among the sermons *On the Words of the Apostle*.

Augustine says the following about the first (*Sermon 14, On the Words of the Apostle*):

> On the Nativity of Saint John, among the other matters that seemed to require discussion, our sermon was led to the baptism of infants. Because it was already lengthy and we were thinking of bringing it to an end, not as much was said about so great a question as ought to have been said by people concerned about so great a danger. What concerns us is not the position itself [Col. 0548D], long ago established in the Catholic Church with the highest authority, but the arguments of certain people who are now becoming more numerous and are attempting to overthrow the souls of many.

No one who wishes to glance even briefly through the sermon recently published will fail to recognize that these words refer to it.

Augustine writes as follows concerning the second sermon, after mentioning the books *On the Baptism of Infants*, to Marcellinus (*On the Proceedings of the Palestinian Synod*, ch. 11):

> Concerning this same matter, the baptism of infants, afterward, at your command—I am addressing Aurelius—in the basilica of Majorinus, holding in my hands the letter of the glorious martyr Cyprian, and reading aloud and expounding his words on this subject so that this wicked error might be removed from the hearts of certain people who had been persuaded of the things we see condemned in these proceedings, I labored, aided by your prayers, as much as I could.

It was held, as I have just said, after the feast of Saint [Col. 0549A] John’s Nativity, on the solemn day of a certain martyr—probably Felicitas, not the woman who had Perpetua as her companion and suffered at Thuburbo, but another mother of seven martyred sons, whose commemoration was also celebrated in Africa on 10 July. For after the words already quoted concerning the earlier sermon, Augustine continues (*Sermon 14, On the Words of the Apostle*):

> Today, then, with the Lord’s help, it has pleased you that we speak about this matter. We are celebrating the solemn day of a martyr, but the cause of all the faithful is greater than that of martyrs alone, and so forth.

The Apostle’s saying that was expounded was undoubtedly the one quoted in the first sermon: “Through Adam sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus passed into all, in whom all sinned.”

The subject is explained in these words (*ibid.*):

> They agree that infants ought to be baptized. Therefore the question between us and them is not whether infants should be baptized, but why they should be baptized. We say that they will not otherwise possess salvation and eternal life unless they are [Col. 0549B] baptized in Christ; but they say that it is not for salvation, not for eternal life, but for the kingdom of heaven, and so forth.

After settling the matter by many arguments, Augustine added the authority of Saint Cyprian (*Book III, Letter 8, to Fidus, on the Baptism of Infants*). He read Cyprian’s letter aloud in its entirety to the assembled people, partly in the first sermon and partly in the second. Jerome (*Dialogue* 3 against the Pelagians) appears either to have read both sermons, which Orosius brought from Africa, or to have heard Orosius recount them. For he used the authority of the same letter, which he transcribed just as Augustine did.

## Year 414

*Book or Letter to Hilary the Monk* (Tome II); *Book on the Perfection of Justice* (Tome VII).

Augustine replied by letter (*Letter* 89) to Hilary, who was asking from Syracuse about the questions raised by the Pelagians. Augustine himself calls the letter a book because of its length. Hilary, however, was merely a layman, since Augustine [Col. 0549C] calls him his “son” (*On the Proceedings*, ch. 11), while Hincmarus calls him a monk (*On Predestination*).

The date at which this letter was written can easily be established from the following facts. Orosius brought it to Palestine (*Orosius, Apology*, ch. 3), and it was read at a gathering of presbyters on 30 July 415. Jerome mentions it in the third *Dialogue*, which we have shown was completed before the Synod of Diospolis; at that synod certain matters were brought against Pelagius on its basis (*On the Proceedings*, ch. 11). Since Orosius arrived in Palestine in the spring of 415, and since, when speaking of this letter of Augustine and of another letter by Jerome to Ctesiphon, he called both recently written, the letter must certainly have been written either toward the end of 413 or at the beginning of 414. It must likewise be admitted that Augustine’s letter was written either at the end of 413, which I consider less likely, or at the beginning of 414.

Nor could it have been written earlier, since it mentions [Col. 0549D] the judgment held against Coelestius at Carthage at the beginning of 412; the books *On the Merits of Sins* and the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, which were published toward the end of 412; and finally the ecclesiastical sermons concerning the questions raised by the Pelagians, the principal ones being those two delivered around the middle of 413.

This overturns Baronius’s opinion that the letter was written in 411—that is, before the judgment against Coelestius was held at Carthage and before the books addressed to Marcellinus were written.

The book *On the Perfection of Justice* also belongs to this same period, if not to the earlier one. In it Augustine replied to a book which Paul and Eutropius, bishops of Spain, had received from Sicily and sent to him. It was said to be by Coelestius and contained sixteen definitions, or arguments, concerning ἀναμαρτησία (“impeccability”), together with their supporting testimonies from Scripture and answers to the objections. [Col. 0550A]

The date can, in my view, be inferred with reasonable probability from the following. In his consultation with Augustine concerning the Priscillianists, Orosius mentions a *Commonitorium*, as he calls it, concerning the heresies which those two bishops had sent to Augustine. The name *Commonitorium* appears to signify nothing other than the letter sent with the definitions; for if he had intended it to signify something else, Augustine would certainly not have kept silent about that, as is clear from the surrounding circumstances. Since the consultation took place a considerable time before Orosius’s departure, whether from his homeland to Augustine or from Africa to Jerome; and since the book *On the Perfection of Justice* was written both before Orosius’s return from the East to Africa and after Augustine had learned from Hilary’s reply—by which, I think, Hilary gave thanks for the letter he had received—that Coelestius was not in Sicily, it must have been composed at this time.

A serious objection, however, opposes this chronology.
