For if this book had already been written [Col. 0550B] when Orosius departed for Palestine, he would have brought it along with the other works then completed: namely, the three books addressed to Marcellinus, *Sermon 14, On the Words of the Apostle*, and the letter to Hilary. It could not have appeared less important for defending the faith against Pelagius. That it was not brought is clear from the following facts: when Jerome discussed impeccability, he did not mention it—although, when discussing the baptism of infants, he did not forget the books addressed to Marcellinus; Orosius did not read anything from it at John’s synod, although it would have been highly relevant; nothing from it was brought against Pelagius at Diospolis; and it contains much more serious and depraved material than the bishops’ petition.

This objection makes me regard my opinion as not certain, but it does not make me think it false. It could have happened that, just as Orosius either did not bring the book *On the Spirit and the Letter* or did not mention it, so too he did not bring this one, although both are highly useful for defending the faith [Col. 0550C]. It could likewise have happened that, for the same reason Augustine omitted this book when reviewing his works, although he remembered the letter to Hilary: perhaps a copy of the reply sent to Paulinus and Eutropius had either not been preserved at Hippo or had been lent to friends for copying and, along with the other books mentioned by Possidius, could not be recovered because of the common fate of such volumes.

## YEAR 415

Two Letters to Jerome (Volume II).—The Book *On Nature and Grace* (Volume VII).

Augustine sent two letters to Jerome: one (Letter 166) concerning the origin of souls, the other (Letter 29) concerning the passage of James: “Whoever stumbles in one point has become guilty of all.” Orosius carried both letters with him. Augustine writes of him:

“A devout young man has come to me: a brother in Catholic peace, a son in age, and our fellow presbyter in rank, Orosius—alert in intellect, ready in speech, burning with zeal, and desiring to be a useful vessel in the house of the Lord for refuting the false and destructive doctrines which have slaughtered the souls of the Spaniards, far more disastrously than the barbarian sword slaughtered their bodies. For he hastened to us from the shore of the Ocean, roused by the report that from me he might hear whatever he wished to know about the matters he desired to learn. Nor was his arrival without fruit. First, so that he would not place too much confidence in what he had heard about me; then I taught the man whatever I could, and, as for what I could not, I directed him to where he might learn it; and I urged him to go to you. Since he willingly and obediently accepted my advice, or rather my command, I asked him, when returning from you, to come back through us to his own country. Relying on this promise of his, I believed that the Lord had granted me an opportunity to write to you about those matters which I desire to know through you, etc.” [Col. 0550D]

He had indeed begun the book *On Nature and Grace* before Orosius departed from Hippo, but had not yet completed it. Thus in the *Retractions* (Book II, chapter 42):

“About that time a certain book of Pelagius also came into my hands, in which, with as much force of argument as he could, he defended human nature against the grace of God, by which the ungodly person is justified and by which we are Christians. The book, therefore, in which I replied to this work, defending grace—not against nature, but the grace through which nature is liberated and governed—I entitled *On Nature and Grace*, etc.” [Col. 0551A]

And in the letter to Pope Innocent in the name of five bishops (Letter 177):

“We have sent to Your Reverence a book which certain devout and honorable young servants of God delivered to us. We do not conceal their names either. As we have heard, and as you now also know, at the exhortation of Pelagius himself they abandoned the hope they had placed in this world and now serve God in continence. After, at last, they had been freed from the same error through some work of ours, with the Lord inspiring them, they produced that same book, saying that it belonged to Pelagius, and earnestly requested that a reply be made to it. This was done. The reply itself was written to them. They wrote back, giving thanks. We sent both works: the work to which the reply was made and the work in which the reply was made. And, so that we might not be excessively burdensome, we marked the passages where we ask that you not disdain to look.” [Col. 0551B]

In the book *On the Proceedings in Palestine* (chapters 23, 24, and 25), he relates the entire history of the book, as it were; he had also woven it together while writing to John of Jerusalem (Letter 179).

Thus Orosius himself writes (*Apology*, chapter 3):

“I briefly explained to Your Holiness, as best I could, that Caelestius, who had already begun to insinuate himself into the dignity of the presbyterate, was exposed, heard, convicted, and detested by the Church at Carthage, when many bishops were judging the case, and had fled from Africa; but that Blessed Augustine had replied with complete thoroughness to Pelagius’s book, after Pelagius’s disciples had exposed it and requested the reply.”

And later:

“This the African synod condemned in Caelestius. This Bishop Augustine abhorred in his writings, as you have heard. This he now condemns in Pelagius’s own writings by his reply.”

From these facts it may be concluded that the book now under discussion was begun not only before Orosius departed from Augustine and from Africa—that is, in the spring of the year 415—but even as Lent was approaching, and was completed during the summer. Thus Augustine writes to Evodius (Letter 169):

“I have also written a fairly large book against the heresy of Pelagius, compelled by certain brethren to whom he had persuaded a most destructive opinion against the grace of Christ. If you wish to have all these matters, send someone who can copy everything out for you.”

He had said earlier:

“If Your Holiness considers it worthwhile to know the matters which occupy me most, and from which I do not wish to be diverted to something else, send someone to copy them out for you. For already several works have been completed which we began this year before Easter, as Lent was approaching.”

From these facts what Baronius wrote about this book in the year 414 must be corrected, as well as what he wrote about Letter 102 to Evodius and about other works of Augustine. To say nothing of the others, the book *On Nature and Grace* had not yet been completed when Orosius departed from Africa, as Augustine himself testifies, and Jerome also testifies in his third dialogue. But Orosius departed only in the year 415.

## YEAR 416

Letter to John of Jerusalem (Volume II).—A Sermon (in Eugyppius).—Letter to Mercator (Volume IV).—Three Letters to Innocent (Volume II).—Letter to Bishop Hilary (Volume II).

[Col. 0551D]

Orosius returned to Africa in May and delivered letters (Letter 30 among Augustine’s letters)—both Jerome’s letter to Augustine and the letters of Eros and Lazarus to the African bishops concerning the proceedings at Diospolis (Acts of the Council of Milevis). The Eastern deacon Mercator, a citizen of Hippo, also delivered a written defense sent by Pelagius to Augustine (Book *On the Proceedings*, chapter 32). At the same time Pelagius’s letter to a certain presbyter friend was made public. In it he boasted that his proposition “that a person can be without sin and easily keep God’s commandments, if he wishes” had been approved by the judgment of fourteen bishops (ibid., chapter 30). [Col. 0552A]

After this, and especially after Orosius’s private report concerning Pelagius’s position with John of Jerusalem, Augustine wrote to that same bishop. First he complained that he had not received from him a written reply—the reply, of course, delivered through Orosius. Next he warned him, in brotherly charity, not to allow himself to be deceived by Pelagius, from whose book *On Nature* he produced a small sample of impiety. Finally, he offered him his book *On Nature and Grace* and requested in return, in the name of several bishops, that the proceedings of the synod at Diospolis be sent to Africa.

The letter to John—who died on 10 January 417—was therefore written after the Council of Diospolis had been held in December 415, toward the end of that year and before the two synods, Carthage and Milevis, were convened in the autumn of 416, and after Orosius’s return to Africa in May of that year. It was therefore written approximately in July 416. [Col. 0552B] Baronius must accordingly have paid insufficient attention to these chronological indications when he assigned it to the preceding year.

At about the same time the sermon was delivered from which Eugyppius cites a portion. The following words are found near its end (Volume II, chapter 288):

“Today Satan is doing this: through the poisons of heretics he is driving people out of the Church, just as through the serpent’s poison he drove them out of paradise. Let no one say that he was acquitted by the bishops. The confession was acquitted; indeed, the correction itself was acquitted, because the things he said before the bishops appeared Catholic. But what he wrote in his books was unknown to the bishops who acquitted him, and perhaps he has been corrected. For we must not despair of a person who perhaps preferred to join himself to the Catholic faith and flee for refuge to God’s grace and help. Perhaps this is what has happened. Nevertheless, it is not the heresy that has been acquitted, but the person who denies the heresy, etc.”

It was therefore delivered not only before the synods about which Augustine would not have remained silent—as he likewise did not remain silent in the second sermon *On the Words of the Apostle*—but also after the report of Pelagius’s acquittal had been spread, and after the credence produced by the letter of carnal vainglory and arrogance, which had flown ahead into people’s hands before the delay of the proceedings had been contrived (*On the Proceedings*, chapter 30). [Col. 0552C]

Moreover, from this sermon we can discern with little difficulty who that bishop was with whom Pelagius had nearly quarreled at Rome, on account of Augustine’s words addressed to God: “Give what you command, and command what you will.” For it was none other than Urbanus of Sicca, concerning whom Augustine writes:

“Our holy brother and fellow bishop, our Urbanus, who was a presbyter here and is now bishop of Sicca, had returned from the city of Rome. There, when he had come into conflict with someone who held such views—or reported that he had come into conflict with him—and when he was pressed by the force of the Lord’s Prayer—for the other man was pressing him and saying, ‘If it lies within our power not to sin, and if it lies within our power to overcome all temptations to sin by the strength of our will alone, why do we say to God, “Do not lead us into temptation”?’—what do you think he replied? ‘We ask God,’ he said, ‘not to lead us into temptation, lest we suffer some evil that does not lie within our power: lest I fall from a horse, break my leg, or be killed by a robber. These things do not lie within my power,’ etc.”

The letter to Mercator was also written in this same year, as we have shown in the notes, when Mercator had consulted Augustine about certain Pelagian questions—namely, the claim of those who deny that death was imposed as a penalty for sin (*Book of Eight Questions to Dulcitius*).

Around October three letters were sent to Innocent. One was from the fathers of the Council of Carthage, another from the fathers of Milevis, and the third from five bishops. All three, if we believe Mercator (*Commonitory*, chapter 1), were synodical letters; and all three, if one judges by their style and manner of expression, were written by Augustine. The first is Letter 90 among the Augustinian letters, now Letter 175; the second is Letter 92, now 176; the third is Letter 95, now 177. Each has been discussed at length in the dissertation on the synods.

Immediately after the letters that Bishop Julius was to carry to the apostolic see had been sent, Augustine wrote to Bishop Hilary—who is quite different from the monk of Syracuse—and first warned him to beware of heresy. He then added (Letter 178):

“When I was writing these things, we had learned that in the Church of Carthage a decree of an episcopal council had been drawn up against them, to be sent by letter to the holy and venerable Pope Innocent; and we had already written from the council of Numidia to that same apostolic see.”

These words deserve notice: “A decree of an episcopal council had been drawn up against them.” Someone might perhaps wonder what they mean, since nothing from this council survives apart from the report sent to the supreme pontiff. Yet the decree seems to be clearly indicated by these words:

“By common deliberation we judged that the authors of such a persuasion, even though it is said that the same Caelestius later attained the presbyterate, ought themselves to be anathematized unless they openly anathematize these propositions, etc. Therefore, holy lord and brother, we have thought it necessary to make this action known to Your Charity, so that the authority of the apostolic see may be added to the statutes of our unworthiness, etc.”

See what has been said in the notes on the rescript of Honorius (Dissertation 4). [Col. 0553B]

I have no doubt that Bishop Hilary, to whom Augustine wrote, was the same man who is called “of Bofetana” in the Council of Carthage. But I am entirely unable to determine in which province the Church of Bofetana should be counted, since I lack the indexes that I have hitherto used in investigating the episcopal sees and provinces of Africa. Nor have I been able to discover to this day the church or province of which Julius was bishop, the bearer of the three synodical letters, although he clearly seems to have belonged to Africa. For he could not honorably have performed this mission on behalf of two provinces, nor as some overseas foreigner, nor as an African from another province.

## YEAR 417

Three Letters of Saint Innocent (Volume II).—The Second Sermon *On the Words of the Apostle* (Volume X).—The Book *On the Proceedings in Palestine* (Volume VII).—Letter to Juliana (Volume II).—Letter to Dardanus (Volume II).

[Col. 0553C]

Innocent sent back three letters in response to the three letters received from Africa: one to the Council of Carthage, another to the Council of Milevis, and the third to the five bishops (Patrologia, volume XX, columns 582, 588, 593). All bear the same chronological note: 28 January, after the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the seventh time and of Junius Quartus Palladius, a man of consular rank. We mention them here because they are included among Augustine’s letters.

Shortly after receiving them, Augustine delivered the second sermon *On the Words of the Apostle*. He says:

“Already two councils have sent letters concerning this case to the apostolic see, and replies have come from there as well. The case is finished—would that the error might one day be finished too! Therefore we warn them, so that they may take notice; we teach them, so that they may be instructed; we pray, so that they may be changed.”

I believe that toward the end of the previous year Augustine had received the proceedings in Palestine, sent, as it is reasonable to believe, by John of Jerusalem when John replied. Accordingly, at the beginning of this seventeenth year he wrote the book to Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage, saying that the hesitation had ended which had made him uncertain about discussing Pelagius’s defense more fully and confidently. [Col. 0553D]

The chronology is established by the fact that these proceedings had not yet reached Africa when the councils were held at Carthage and Milevis, as is evident from the synodical letters. Nor had they arrived when Augustine sent his letter to John of Jerusalem, since in that letter he asks that they be sent to him. They had arrived, however, before Alypius and Augustine sent their joint letter to Paulinus of Nola, since that letter refers to very many details from the proceedings. The book *On the Proceedings in Palestine* must therefore have been completed at the time we have indicated, since the letter to Paulinus was sent late in this same year, or rather at the beginning of the following year.

Anyone can easily understand how important this book is from this one fact alone: it contains the acts of the famous synod concerning Pelagius, reviewed by Augustine, specifically to demonstrate how Pelagius had deceived the Greek fathers concerning his own person, while nevertheless being compelled to confess the Catholic doctrine that he would later attack perfidiously in his books. Certainly Augustine wishes this synod to be understood as the Church’s first victory over the heresy, even though the leader of the heretical army withdrew himself from the triumph by means of lies. [Col. 0554A]

The letter to Juliana, the mother of Demetrias, also belongs to this year, or to the beginning of the following one. It was written after Pelagius’s letters to Innocent had been received in Africa, in which he used the testimony of his letter to Demetrias in his own defense. In one of his letters, Pelagius, as Augustine reports (Letter 188), “where he most plainly gives his own name and does not conceal the name of the holy virgin, says that he wrote to her, and tries by the testimony of that work of his to prove that he openly confesses the grace of God, which he is accused either of concealing or denying.”

But the letter of Pelagius under discussion was written in the East at the beginning of the year 417; it was received by Zosimus at Rome at the beginning of September, sent to Africa on 20 September, and received in Africa around the beginning of October. Augustine therefore could not have written to Juliana before that time. Baronius nevertheless placed the letter at least four years earlier, in his *Annals* under the year 413, where he made many statements that scarcely anyone, however hard he tried, could reconcile with the true chronological order. Binius, in his notes on Innocent’s letter to Juliana, said still more that is contrary to the truth. The pontiff did not write to Demetrias’s mother after her daughter had been consecrated, but after the death of her husband, when she had professed the holy state of widowhood.

Nor could Augustine have written it much later. For he would not have kept silent about the condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius by the apostolic see if Zosimus’s *tractoria* had already reached Africa, since he could have drawn considerable support for his cause from it. The definitive sentence of the apostolic see against the heretics reached Africa only in the following year, around its middle. [Col. 0554C]

I cannot conceal the fact that this letter has often caused me astonishment. Why did Augustine write to Juliana rather than to her daughter Demetrias, whom he had inspired to undertake virginity? Why did he write to Juliana in such a way that he said nothing harsher against Pelagius, just as he had not done in the book *On the Good of Widowhood*, published for her two or three years earlier? And why did he continually persist in warning Juliana to beware of the devices and errors of the Pelagians?

My astonishment was increased by the fact that Demetrias, after professing virginity amid the congratulations of the entire world, later remained hidden in obscurity and was praised by no one at all—except perhaps by a certain Prosper, who nevertheless had to warn her again to avoid the remnants of Pelagius and to flee pride. It was as though this entire family had never ceased inclining toward Pelagius’s side, more imprudently than maliciously.

But when I considered that Julian of Eclanum was incredibly devoted to Pelagius, that he had already married a woman from the Aemilian family, that the Aemilian family was connected with the Anician family, and that Demetrias was born from it, her father being Olybrius and her mother Juliana, I seemed to see the reason for the matter that had astonished me. Julian had breathed his poison upon the related family, and Demetrias, being more fond of glory, more readily absorbed and favored it. She despised wealth and the world, but admired intellectual gifts in men who displayed the appearance of a stricter discipline while nevertheless wishing to seem to hold first place both in eloquence and in evangelical perfection. [Col. 0554D]

Moreover, Saint Paulinus himself belonged to the Anician family; he composed an epithalamium for Ia, who had been married to Julian because of their relationship; he favored the Pelagians residing at Nola in Campania; and, with Julian acting as mediator, he cultivated Pelagius’s friendship—indeed to such an extent that Augustine had to warn him gravely about the danger in which he was involved (Letter 186).

At approximately the same time, toward the end of summer, the letter to Dardanus appears to have been sent. Augustine lists it among his books (*Retractions*, Book II, chapter 49):

“Concerning the presence of God I wrote a book in which our purpose is chiefly vigilant against the Pelagian heresy, although it is not expressly named. In it I also discuss, carefully and subtly, the presence of God in nature—God whom we call the true and supreme God—and his temple.”

## YEAR 418

Letter to Paulinus of Nola (Volume II).—Two Letters to Sixtus (Volume II).—A Letter or Book to Optatus (Volume II).—Book I *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (Volume VII).—Two Books to Albina, Pinianus, and Melania (Volume VII).

Alypius and Augustine, in a joint letter to Paulinus, Bishop of Nola—a holy man, certainly, but, as has just been said, too fond of Pelagius and easily deceived by a man wearing the mask of piety—taught him about every aspect of the heresy and the particular poison of each part (Letter 186). [Col. 0555B]

That letter has a definite chronological indication, since it was written after the proceedings in Palestine had been received and before Zosimus’s *tractoria* had been brought to Africa. Augustine would have sent it, just as he sent the other letters of Innocent, if he had had the opportunity. He writes:

“Concerning this matter, reports from the two councils, those of Carthage and Milevis, were sent to the apostolic see before the ecclesiastical proceedings in which Pelagius is said to have been cleared before the bishops of the province of Palestine had reached either our hands or Africa. We also wrote to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, in addition to the reports of the councils, a private letter in which we discussed the case at somewhat greater length. He replied to everything in the way that it was right and proper for a bishop of the apostolic see to reply. You can now read all these documents, if perhaps either none of them or not all of them have reached you, etc.”

[Col. 0555C]

The proceedings in Palestine are mentioned near the end. There the principal points of the Catholic faith are briefly reviewed from those same proceedings, and the testimonies of Scripture are reported which John of Jerusalem used to establish the necessity of divine grace.

That the letter was not sent before this year is shown by these words of Augustine:

“Pelagius also deals with this in certain letters addressed to Your Reverence, where he says that he should not be thought to defend free choice without the grace of God, since he says that the ability to will and to act, without which we could will or do no good, was implanted in us by the Creator, etc.”

These words refer to what Pelagius had written in his letters to Innocent (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 35):

“Let them read the letter that nearly twelve years ago we wrote to the holy man Paulinus, Bishop of Nola. In approximately three hundred lines it confesses nothing other than the grace and help of God, and that we can do absolutely no good without God.”

[Col. 0555D]

Since Augustine did not possess Pelagius’s letters to Innocent before the end of 417—the letters were sent from Rome by Zosimus to the African fathers on 21 September—it must be acknowledged that this letter to Paulinus was written at the beginning of the present year. It could not have been written later, since it preceded the arrival of Zosimus’s *tractoria* in Africa. There is therefore no adequate reason why Baronius assigned this letter to the preceding year. His reason, as though drawn from history, is scarcely of any weight, since Augustine wrote it after Zosimus had been raised to the apostolic see.

The letter is truly outstanding and is comparable with none of Augustine’s works against the Pelagians. This is not surprising, since it was written to a man almost the holiest and noblest in the entire world, whose friend Sulpicius Severus had been imprudently deceived by Pelagius’s devices.

Someone may perhaps wish to inquire why Augustine wrote not in his own name alone but also in Alypius’s. I believe that it was because the letter would have greater power to rescue their friend from the impending danger if it came from two men bound to him by closer ties, especially from Alypius, who was both better known because of his frequent embassies from Africa to Italy and personally very dear to Paulinus, as well as possessing great authority with him because of his reputation for holiness (Pauline, Letter 98). [Col. 0556A]

After the apostolic see had condemned Pelagius and Caelestius, and after Zosimus had sent letters concerning them—both general letters to all the bishops of the world and particular letters to the Africans, through the acolyte Leo—A letter from Sixtus, a presbyter of the Roman Church, was brought through the presbyter Firmus to Alypius and Augustine together. Augustine replied to it in two letters (Letters 191 and 194): first in a shorter letter through the acolyte Albinus, and later in a longer letter through Firmus when he returned.

He seems to have written the earlier letter before his departure on the apostolic mission to Mauretania. He could scarcely have kept from expressing his joy at Sixtus’s faith, which had been demonstrated by a public example. He wrote the later letter after his return from the mission. For a work so long and learned, and dealing with so great a subject as gratuitous predestination, could scarcely—or scarcely at all—have been composed by a man so occupied. Both letters were written after June, when the sentence of the apostolic see condemning Pelagius and Caelestius was brought to Africa. [Col. 0556B]

For what else do the following words from the earlier letter (Letter 191) mean, where he sets out the manner in which one should deal with people belonging to the Pelagian party?

“Some of them may have become known to you before this pestilence was condemned even by the most manifest judgment of the apostolic see, and now you see that they have suddenly become silent. Whether they have been healed cannot be known unless they have not only kept silent about those false doctrines but have also defended the truths opposed to them with the same zeal with which they were accustomed to defend the false doctrines. Yet such people should certainly be treated more gently. Why is there any need to frighten those whom their very silence shows to be sufficiently frightened? Nor should those whose wound is hidden be passed over as though they were healthy, without the careful attention of medicine.”

Or what do the following words from the later letter (Letter 194) mean?

“I must confess to Your Charity that we were exceedingly sad in spirit when rumor spread that you favored the enemies of Christian grace. But that this sadness might be wiped from our hearts, the same rumor did not fail to report first that you had publicly pronounced an anathema against them before a very large gathering. Then, when the letters of the apostolic see concerning their condemnation had been sent to Africa, your own letter to the venerable old man Aurelius also followed. Although it was brief, it nevertheless sufficiently indicated your vigor against their error.”

During the very period of his mission, Augustine wrote at considerable length to Bishop Optatus concerning the origin of souls. After sending him Zosimus’s letters, he warned him of the condemnation of the heretics. He writes (Letter 190):

“Although I have received no letter addressed to me personally from Your Holiness, nevertheless, because the letter that you sent to Caesarea in Mauretania arrived while I was present at Caesarea, where ecclesiastical necessity had drawn us in accordance with the commission entrusted to us by the venerable Pope Zosimus, Bishop of the apostolic see, it happened that I myself also read what you had written, since the same letter was delivered to me by the servant of God, the holy Renatus. At his request, and because he pressed me very insistently, although I was occupied with other matters, etc.”

And later:

“If you willingly or patiently receive this admonition, dearest brother, I warn you not to fall through insufficient caution into a new heresy which attempts to tear down the foundations established by the ancient faith by arguing against the grace of God. Pelagius and Caelestius were either the authors, or certainly the most zealous and notorious advocates, of this heresy. Through the vigilance of episcopal councils, with the assistance of the Savior who protects his Church, they were condemned throughout the Christian world by two venerable bishops of the apostolic see, Pope Innocent and Pope Zosimus—unless, after being corrected, they should also have done penance. We have arranged for examples of recent writings to be sent to you, both those issued specifically to the Africans and those issued universally to all bishops from the aforementioned see, lest they perhaps have not yet reached Your Holiness, etc.” [Col. 0557A]

There is also the consular date under which the proceedings against Emeritus, the Donatist bishop, at Caesarea in Mauretania were recorded. They begin as follows:

“To the most glorious emperors Honorius Augustus for the twelfth time and Theodosius Augustus for the eighth time, both Augusti and Caesars; on 20 September, at Caesarea, in the major church, when Deuterius, the metropolitan bishop, together with Alypius of Thagaste, Augustine of Hippo, Possidius of Calama, Rusticus of Carteia, Palladius of Tagaba, and the other bishops, had proceeded into the apse, etc.”

From this we incidentally understand that at that time the five most distinguished bishops of all Africa were carrying out the mission of the apostolic see. This is worth noting in response to the tiresome questions of certain people.

There is someone who has called this Optatus the Optatus of Milevis; he may judge for himself on what grounds. For that celebrated author of books died around the year 370—nearly half a century before Augustine wrote this letter—and at the time Augustine was writing, Severus governed the Church of Milevis.

At the same time Augustine sent the later letter to Sixtus (Letter 194, to Sixtus) and the first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* to Count Valerius. He had received letters from Sixtus and Valerius through the presbyter Firmus (the letter to Count Valerius prefixed to Book I *On Marriage and Concupiscence*), and through that same man he replied to both, as can easily be established from the letters addressed to each.

Moreover, Augustine himself states (Book I to Boniface, chapter 5) that he wrote to Valerius after the condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius:

“I composed my book after the condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius. He recalls that he replied to it in four little books. I thought this should be mentioned because he says that my words were accepted by his enemies out of hatred for the truth, lest anyone should therefore think that the enemies of Christ’s grace were condemned as new heretics because of this book of mine. In that book, however, the defense is directed more toward marriage than toward its criticism.”

This book therefore cannot belong to any earlier period, nor to a later one. For Julian wrote four books against it. From the first of these, certain excerpts were sent to Valerius, who sent them through Alypius from Ravenna to Rome; Augustine received them from Alypius together with two letters of the Pelagians (Book II *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 1).

Since Alypius returned to Africa at the end of 419, and since Julian must have spent a considerable amount of time working on these four books—he says that he did not begin them before the autumn of 418, indeed that he composed them during the schism stirred up by Eulalius against Boniface—and since some time was necessarily required for the excerpts sent to Valerius to be made, it must certainly be acknowledged that Augustine composed this first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* immediately after completing his mission, that is, around the middle of October 418. [Col. 0557D]

Since these facts are firmly established, the two books addressed to Albina, Pinianus, and Melania—*On the Grace of Christ* and *On Original Sin*—must also have been written in this same year, around August, when Augustine remained at Carthage after the final session of the African council.

He first says that they were composed at Carthage (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 1):

“With the bearer hastening, amid our occupations—which are far denser at Carthage than anywhere else—we dictated these things as best we could, insofar as God deigned to grant it, etc.”

Next, he places them after the publication of the book *On the Proceedings in Palestine* in 417:

“What you know, and what I also included in the book that I wrote concerning the proceedings in Palestine to our venerable old man Aurelius” (*On Original Sin*, chapter 14).

Third, he places them after Pelagius’s letters had been sent to Africa by Pope Zosimus on 21 September 417:

“In the letters that he sent to Rome to Pope Innocent of blessed memory—since they did not find him alive, they were delivered to the holy Pope Zosimus and from there sent to us—he says, etc.” (*On Original Sin*, chapter 17).

Finally, he places them after the definitive sentence issued by Zosimus:

“After the Pelagian heresy and its authors had been convicted and condemned by the bishops of the Roman Church, first by Innocent and then by Zosimus, with the cooperation of the African letters, I wrote two books against it, one *On the Grace of Christ*, the other *On Original Sin*, etc.” (*Retractions*, Book II, chapter 50).

Since the definitive sentence of the supreme pontiff reached Africa around June 418 (Dissertation on the Synods), Augustine must have composed these books at Carthage after that month and before September, on the twentieth day of which he was at Caesarea in Mauretania.

The strongest obstacle to assigning them to the following year is that they were written to Albina, Pinianus, and Melania, who were living in Palestine, and were sent, as is credible, before winter closed the sea. Pinianus and Melania, however, leaving Albina behind at Jerusalem because of her advanced age, departed for Egypt in the spring of 419, as is clear from the Acts of Saint Melania, on 31 January in Surius.

I would readily believe that Pinianus and Melania gave thanks by letter for the books they had received, informing Augustine of their departure for Egypt, and that Augustine replied by a reciprocal letter addressed to Alexandria. Julian’s words strongly incline me toward this opinion (Book IV of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 87). After mentioning Jerome’s dialogues, he writes:

“Regarding this work, you boast in that letter which you sent to Alexandria, saying that Pelagius, crushed beneath the weight of the Scriptures brought against him, is unable to defend free choice. But a Catholic man who had been attacked answered that work.”

Julian’s words can, however, be understood in another sense, if—as is highly probable—Augustine wrote to Cyril concerning the expulsion of the Pelagians from his city through the presbyter Innocent, who had been sent by the Africans to Alexandria to seek the Nicene canons. At approximately that time, Eusebius of Cremona is also believed to have sent Cyril a letter on the same subject.

Finally, the widespread opinion of many who, following Baronius, have wished to read *Albinus* instead of *Albina* must be rejected. They do so both because this name is placed before that of the presbyter Pinianus and because Augustine calls those to whom he published the book “brothers.” But since Albina was Melania’s mother and Pinianus’s mother-in-law, she ought to be placed before both of them. And since one of the three names belonged to a man—and specifically to a presbyter—the appellation “brothers” was extended from him to the whole group.

## YEAR 420

Four Books *On the Soul and Its Origin* (Volume VII).—Book II *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (Volume VII).—Letter to Vitalis (Volume II).—Four Books to Boniface (Volume VII).

[Col. 0558D]

The four books *On the Soul and Its Origin* should be assigned to the year 420. The first was addressed to the monk Renatus, from whom Augustine had received the books of Vincent Victor, written against one of Augustine’s own short works concerning that question (*Retractions*, Book II, chapter 56). The second was addressed to the presbyter Peter, a praiser of Vincent; the remaining two were addressed to Vincent himself, a young man who was saying many foolish things about the origin of the soul and the baptism of infants.

The chronology is established as follows. In September of 418, while Augustine was serving as the representative of the apostolic see at Caesarea in Mauretania, Renatus visited him and read the letters received from Optatus (Letter 190, to Optatus), and consulted him about the origin of the soul, so that Augustine might reply to Optatus. At that time Vincent Victor’s two books against Augustine had not yet reached Renatus’s hands; otherwise he would certainly have delivered them to Augustine, who was present. He sent them to Hippo in the summer of the following year, as soon as he received them, but they were not handed over to Augustine until the end of autumn (Book I to Renatus, chapter 1). Augustine therefore could not have undertaken their composition before the year 420.

The second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* was sent to Count Valerius in that same year. It could not have been sent earlier; for when the first book came into the hands of Julian the Pelagian, he wrote four books against it—by no means brief books—from which someone excerpted certain passages and sent them to Count Valerius. Valerius himself sent these to Alypius, and Alypius to Augustine, who replied to those very passages in another book. Augustine says this in almost exactly these words (*Retractions* II.53).

Since, then, Alypius returned to Africa toward the end of the preceding year, as has already been stated, this second book could certainly neither have been composed nor, at least, sent to Valerius, who was then in Italy, before the beginning of the present year—indeed, not before the end of April. Alypius himself brought it to Valerius, as Julian asserts, without Augustine’s contradiction (*Unfinished Work* I.6):

> You demanded—or rather, by paternal authority commanded me—to oppose the book of the Punic expositor which Alypius, the homebred slave of his sins, recently brought to Count Valerius, and so forth.

Alypius, however, does not appear to have sailed for Italy before the spring season, or even before the Easter festivals had ended, and to have met Valerius at Ravenna. Since Easter fell that year on the twenty-third of Pharmuthi, according to Cyril—that is, on April 18 according to the Latins—and the conclusion of the festivals therefore fell on April 25, before which time the most holy bishops of old considered it a religious duty to remain with their own Churches, Valerius must have received the book as soon as possible, toward the end of May, and Augustine must have written his reply before Easter.

But why, someone may ask, did Alypius travel again to the imperial court, since he had returned from there toward the end of the preceding year? Baronius supposes that he went at the emperor’s request to obtain assistance against the Pelagians, who were causing disturbances in Africa; on this occasion he mentions Vitalis, a Carthaginian deacon, to whom Augustine’s 107th letter is addressed. But what need was there for imperial authority after Honorius’s letter to Aurelius, requiring everyone to sign the condemnation of the Pelagians and expelling from their episcopal sees those who refused?

I believe, rather, that Alypius came to Ravenna in order to obtain from the emperor a law forbidding clergy to associate with women from outside their households, and so forth—the law issued at Ravenna on May 8, under the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the ninth time and Constantius. For at that time, both frequently in other provinces and generally in Africa, that evil was spreading which Jerome, whether astonished at its origin or at its shamefulness, describes in his letter to Eustochium (*Letter* 22, *On the Guarding of Virginity*):

> From where did the plague of Agapetae enter the Churches? From where came another name for wives without marriage? And so forth.

This conjecture seems to me the more credible because Alypius and Augustine openly pursued that clerical vice with such intense hatred; because, in the general African council of the preceding year, the third and fourth canons of the Council of Carthage against clerics’ sisters, or women from outside their households, had been reviewed; because, on account of the disease’s long-established force, no remedy could be hoped for unless imperial authority restrained the wicked by penalties; because Valerius, influential with the emperor both through his own religious zeal and through his exceptional friendship with Alypius and Augustine, could obtain a rescript of such importance; and finally because the law was issued in words that appear to reflect canon 17 of the Third Council of Carthage.

That law, however, could restrain the evil for a time; it could not eradicate it. Victor of Utica bears witness that the Arians reproached the Africans for their shameful relations with clerics, even those involving virgins.

Since Baronius mentions Vitalis, and since the year in which Augustine wrote to this deacon is uncertain, it will not be out of place to speak here of the letter—almost unequalled by any other—in which the hidden mystery of prevenient grace is disclosed and twelve rules are handed down, rules that contain the Catholic judgment on this question.

I have often wondered why the eight canons of Orange differ so little from these rules, while the eight African canons differ so greatly, although the former are separated from them in time and the latter are very close to them. Could someone not infer from this either that Augustine transmitted such rules to Vitalis before the African canons were enacted, or that the error of the Gauls condemned by the canons of Orange arose from Vitalis’s teaching? I consider the first possibility not improbable, but I favor the second more strongly.

Someone may perhaps ask why I have spoken of eight canons of Orange, when twenty-five are commonly counted. The answer is easy and clear: only the first eight have the form of canons. The thirteen called the final canons can scarcely be regarded as canons in themselves so much as certain confirmations of the first eight, drawn from Augustine’s testimony.

During this same period Augustine, in four books addressed to Pope Boniface, refuted two letters of the Pelagians that the same pontiff had sent him through Alypius in the preceding year. The first was addressed to the clergy residing at Rome; the second to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica. Augustine believed both to be Julian’s (*Retractions* II.61). Julian, however, denied the first—and not without reason, since its author was Caelestius—and acknowledged the second, although he had sent it in the name of eighteen bishops, not solely in his own (*Unfinished Work* I.17). The first letter is refuted in the first book, the second in the remaining three.

The chronology is established as follows. Returning from Italy, Alypius brought these two letters to Africa together with certain excerpts transmitted by Valerius; and when he set out from Africa for Ravenna again, he received the books of Augustine’s reply to carry back (*ibid.*, I.178). Since, then, he returned from Italy to Africa toward the end of the year 429 [sic], and from Africa to Italy again in the year 420, after the Easter festivals—that is, toward the end of April—the four books must have been composed in the interval.

They are outstanding works, containing a great deal not only of dogmatic but also of historical material, especially concerning what took place with Caelestius at Rome before the supreme pontiff, and concerning the Pelagians’ complaints and their appeal from the judgment of the Apostolic See to a general synod. Augustine answered these matters so fully (*To Boniface* IV.8, 12) that there is scarcely any need for a response from anyone else.

## YEAR 421

*Handbook for Laurence* (Volume IV).—Six Books against Julian (Volume VII).

The *Handbook for Laurence* unquestionably belongs to the year 421. It is an almost divine work, and someone might rightly call it a specimen of Augustinian theology and the first outline of the scholastic, or methodical, theology that was to follow.

It belongs, I say, to this year; for it cannot belong to the preceding one, since it mentions Jerome as already dead:

> Jerome the presbyter, of holy memory, left a written work, and so forth.

(*Chapter* 87.)

Jerome died in the year 420, on the day before the Kalends of October. Nor can the work belong to a later year, since Augustine excerpted from it material with which he answered Dulcitius’s first question:

> In the book entitled *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, which I wrote for my son, your brother Laurence, these are my words on the subject, and so forth.

(*Book on Eight Questions of Dulcitius*.)

And in answer to the second question:

> I also said something of this kind to Laurence, as follows.

But the book *On Eight Questions of Dulcitius* is marked by a definite indication of the year 422, as we shall soon show.

The six books against Julian must also be assigned here, so that this year may be distinguished by two exceptional works. While the four books to Boniface were being written, four books by Julian came into Augustine’s hands, sent by Bishop Claudius. From the first of these had been excerpted the passages brought by Alypius, which Augustine had refuted in the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (*Retractions* II.61–62):

> The four books that I wrote against the two letters of the Pelagians to Boniface, bishop of the Roman Church, follow. When they came into his hands, he himself sent them to me, because he found that my name had been inserted in them calumniously at that time. This work begins: “I had indeed known you by reputation.” Meanwhile the four books of Julian the Pelagian, which I mentioned above, also came into my hands. In them I discovered that the passages excerpted from them by the person who had sent them to Count Valerius had not been written to that same count in every respect as Julian had stated them, but that some of them had been altered to some degree. I therefore wrote six books against those four.

Thus this most elaborately worked-out work, as Augustine calls it, did not appear before this year. Nor can it be pushed into the following year, since it is not credible that a man of such spirit and distinction, whose reputation seemed to sustain the name of the Catholic faith, could have patiently endured for long that he—or indeed all Catholics, of whom he was in a sense the leader—should be blamed for either fraud or negligence on the part of an excerptor. Rather, it must be certain that the heretics received a reply as soon as possible, since both of them, not without some appearance of truth, indeed with the evident authority of the books, complained before everyone that Augustine had attributed to Julian words contrary to what he had said.

I should accomplish little if I attempted to enhance the value of this work by praise, when its author, at once the most modest and the most learned of men, called it most elaborately worked out—that is, equal to all the powers of his intellect and equal to Augustine’s learning.

The first two books are devoted to refuting Julian’s calumny, by which he accused the Catholics of Manichaean impiety. The remaining four answer, one by one, Julian’s four books directed against Augustine’s first book, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*.

## YEAR 422

*Book on the Eight Questions of Dulcitius* (Volume IV).

That the *Book on the Eight Questions of Dulcitius* was written in this very year, and indeed in July, is clearly demonstrated by the words of the preface, provided they are read without the corruption found in all printed copies. They read as follows:

> As it seems to me, my most beloved Dulcitius, I was not slow in replying to your questions. For at Easter of this year, when Easter Sunday fell on the third day before the Kalends of April, I received a letter from your affection sent from Carthage. After those holy days I immediately set out for Carthage, where the excessive number of occupations that cannot be absent from that city allowed me to dictate nothing. But after I returned from there, having spent fifteen days among our people—who, after my long absence, compelled me to attend to other matters—for after three months I was permitted to return, I did not delay replying to these matters, and to the questions sent by you, which I had already treated in various works, I have drawn from those same works either my answer or, at any rate, my discussion.

I said that this passage must be read without corruption. The date of Easter must be corrected, for Easter Sunday is said to have fallen on the third day before the Kalends of April, whereas it fell on the seventh day before the Kalends. It would have been easy for an old manuscript reading *VII* to be copied as *III* after one stroke of the first numeral had been worn away.

The necessity of this correction is demonstrated as follows. The *Eight Questions* was written after the *Handbook*; the *Handbook* was written after Jerome’s death; Jerome died on the day before the Kalends of October in the year 420. We must therefore admit that the *Eight Questions* was composed after the year 420.

But Cyril’s Easter homilies and the exact calculation of the dates show that, after the year 420, Easter Sunday could not have fallen in March except in the year 430, when Augustine died, or in the year 422. Since the *Eight Questions* was not composed in 430—for it is mentioned in the *Retractions*, completed in 427—it certainly belongs to the year 422. The Sunday letter in that year was A, and therefore Easter Sunday fell on the thirtieth day of the month Phamenoth according to the Egyptians, March 26 according to the Latins.

Since Augustine replied after three months had elapsed from the receipt of Dulcitius’s letter, and since he received the letter after Easter, he must have replied in July, after April, May, and June had passed.

From these matters, established with such precision, it may perhaps be useful to draw several conclusions. First, we learn with what religious care bishops of old wished to celebrate the Easter festivals with their own people—that is, in their own Churches—and to remain there until the newly baptized had put off their white garments. Second, the expression “the days of the Easter festivals” included those days before Easter Sunday, indeed even before the vigil of Easter Sunday, on which penitents were reconciled and catechumens were initiated into baptism by the prescribed ceremonies. Finally, the order in which the books are arranged in the *Retractions* is not by itself sufficient to establish their date; for the book under discussion here has not been placed in its chronological position.

## YEAR 424

*Book on Grace and Free Will* (Volume VII).—Two Letters to Valentinus (Volume II).

I scarcely dare determine to which year the book *On Grace and Free Will* should be assigned—whether to this one or the following—together with the two letters addressed to Valentinus and the monks of Hadrumetum that belong to it. I am nevertheless certain that it must be assigned to one or the other; consequently, neither the opinion of the illustrious author of the *Annals*, who assigns it to 418, nor that of the bishop of Ypres, who believed that Baronius was mistaken by an entire decade, can stand. The former places it too early; the latter too late.

I also believe it certain that this work was composed to settle the controversies that had arisen at Hadrumetum on the occasion of Augustine’s letter to Sixtus (*Letter* 194). In that letter, the mystery of gratuitous predestination was expounded openly, as a certain means of explaining with ease the Catholic truth concerning grace. As a result, because of their lack of understanding, the minds of the monks were divided over the matter: some claimed that human freedom of will was thereby removed, while others declared Augustine’s teaching about the grace of God incredible. Accordingly, two of them, Cresconius and Felix, came from Hadrumetum to Hippo so that Augustine himself might teach them the harmony of free will and grace, enabling them, once instructed, to educate their fellow monks.

Although they were eager to return, that most kindly teacher kept them with him for some time, so that they might return better instructed after reading, with so great an interpreter, the books relevant to the question.

It is certain, finally, that both letters were sent together with the book. The first, however, was given to the monks before Easter, since they were expected to return sooner for the celebration of the feast in the monastery. The second was sent after Easter, when Augustine had changed his mind and believed that they should be detained until they had been instructed at leisure, then sent back, after the festivals had been celebrated at Hippo, better equipped by the book and by the other materials necessary for resolving the question. Augustine writes (*Letter* 215):

> I have written to you a book which, if with the Lord’s help you read carefully and understand intelligently, I do not think that any further disagreements among you on this matter will arise. They are also carrying with them other things that we believe should be sent to you, so that you may learn how the Catholic Church, through the mercy of God, repelled the poisons of the Pelagian heresy. These include what was written to Pope Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, concerning the council of the province of Carthage and the council of Numidia, and, somewhat more fully, by five bishops, together with what he himself wrote in reply to those three documents; likewise what was written to Pope Zosimus concerning the African council, together with his reply sent to all the bishops of the entire world; and what we briefly established at the later plenary council of all Africa against that same error; and my book mentioned above, which I have just written to you. We have read all these things with them here and have sent them to you through them, and so forth.

Since these three facts are certain, and since it is equally clear that Augustine’s letter to Sixtus gave rise both to the disturbances at Hadrumetum and to the book now under discussion; since it is also established that this letter was written toward the end of 418, and that the two monks of Hadrumetum came to Augustine before Easter in some subsequent year—the date of the letter—it is beyond doubt that Baronius’s opinion cannot be correct. The book *On Grace and Free Will* must have been composed during the interval between the two letters to Valentinus, one of which was written before Easter and the other after Easter, as is plainly gathered by comparing the two, which contain definite chronological indications.

The opinion of Jansenius is no more correct when he accuses Baronius of being greatly mistaken, as though it could readily be inferred from Augustine and Prosper, by indisputable arguments, that these works were written almost a decade later (*On the Pelagian Heresy* I). For Augustine testifies that the book *On Rebuke and Grace* was published after the book *On Grace and Free Will* (*Retractions* II.67; *On Rebuke and Grace* 1). The book *On Rebuke and Grace* had reached Gaul before Prosper and Hilary wrote to Augustine. Prosper says (*Letter to Augustine* 3):

> It came about, through the dispensation of God’s mercy, that when similar matters had disturbed certain people in Africa, you issued the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, full of divine authority. When it reached our knowledge at an unexpectedly opportune moment, we thought that all the complaints of those who resisted would be silenced, and so forth.

Hilary writes (*Letter to Augustine* 17):

> In addition, they are troubled that grace should be so divided—grace which was given either then to the first man or is now given to all—that Adam received perseverance, not the perseverance by which he would persevere, but without which he could not persevere through free will (*On Rebuke and Grace* 11–12). But now, for the saints predestined by grace to the kingdom, an aid to perseverance is not given of that kind, but of such a kind that perseverance itself is granted to them—not merely so that without this gift they could not be persevering, but also so that through this gift they can be nothing other than persevering. These words of your holiness have disturbed them in this way, and so forth.

The book *On Rebuke and Grace* must therefore have been published in Africa before the year 426, when Prosper and Hilary were writing, when Augustine was composing the *Retractions*, and when Honoratus had recently obtained the highest office of the Church of Arles. Augustine was composing the *Retractions* in 426, and in that same year Honoratus succeeded Patroclus, who had been killed by a barbarian tribune. Thus, if we are speaking of the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, at least three years must be subtracted from Jansenius’s decade; if we are speaking of the book *On Grace and Free Will*, four years must be subtracted.

The matter is readily established in this way. The two monks of Hadrumetum, Cresconius and Felix, returned to their fellow monks only after the festivals at Hippo had been completed and they had been instructed at leisure. Augustine therefore read with them what was written to Pope Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, and so forth (*Letter* 215). He also read with them the book of the blessed martyr Cyprian *On the Lord’s Prayer*, and showed how Cyprian taught that everything pertaining to our conduct, by which we live rightly, must be requested from our Father who is in heaven, and so forth. Finally, he read with them his own letter to Sixtus, presbyter of the Roman Church, which they had brought with them, and showed that it had been written against those who say that the grace of God is granted according to our merits—that is, against those same Pelagians.

How could all this have been accomplished by a man so occupied, with men who were neither exceptionally intelligent in themselves nor particularly well disposed toward the truth, unless several months had passed? It is therefore credible that they returned to Hadrumetum around June and brought the books with them. When the others read them eagerly but did not understand them equally well, disturbances more serious than the earlier ones arose.

From this came the renewed necessity of consulting Augustine and again sending men to the teacher who appeared to hold opinions about grace different from those they ought to hold; and again the necessity of instructing the people of Hadrumetum by a new book, lest they be deceived by the man who said that no one should be rebuked if he did not do God’s commands, but that one should merely pray that he might do them (*Retractions* II.67). Since all this could easily have occupied the remainder of that year, or even part of the following one, someone might reasonably say that the book *On Grace and Free Will* was published in 424, one year before the book *On Rebuke and Grace*.

Some objections are brought against this, but they are weak. Jansenius says that the Semi-Pelagian heresy arose as Augustine’s life was drawing toward its end, and that the book *On Rebuke and Grace* occasioned the disturbances raised by the adherents of that heresy, supposedly as Prosper testifies in his letter to Augustine. I scarcely understand how such an idea could have occurred to a man who professed to be writing a history of Pelagianism.

What did he mean by the word “heresy”? An error or a sect? If an error, he surely knew that Augustine himself had been involved in it to a considerable extent before becoming a bishop. If a sect, who does not know that the defenders of this error joined together as a sect long after Augustine’s time—if indeed they ever did so?

Furthermore, how could the book *On Rebuke and Grace* have occasioned the disturbances Jansenius mentions, if Prosper saw it as having been brought into Gaul to settle controversies that had already arisen, “through the dispensation of God’s mercy”? Finally, with what justification is Prosper cited as a witness, when these are his own words, in which he testifies that the disturbances of the people of Massilia were increased—but did not first arise—because of the book *On Rebuke and Grace* (*Letter to Augustine* 2)?

> Many servants of Christ who reside in the city of Massilia think that whatever you have discussed in your writings composed against the Pelagian heretics concerning the calling of the elect according to God’s purpose is contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and to ecclesiastical understanding. For some time they preferred to blame their own slowness rather than criticize what they did not understand; and some of them wished to request a clearer and more explicit exposition from your blessedness on this subject. It came about, through the dispensation of God’s mercy, that when similar matters had disturbed certain people in Africa, you issued the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, full of divine authority. When it reached our knowledge at an unexpectedly opportune moment, we thought that all the complaints of those who resisted would be silenced, since every question on which your holiness needed to be consulted had been answered there so fully and decisively, as though you had expressly made it your purpose to settle what had been thrown into confusion among us.

From where, then, did the first disturbances in Gaul arise? From the same source from which they first arose among the people of Hadrumetum: Augustine’s letter to Sixtus. As soon as the doctrine of gratuitous predestination was proposed, it is astonishing how the light of that doctrine dazzled the eyes of so many who were not very strong. It is equally astonishing how much trouble it caused its opponents through the passage in Wisdom in which gratuitous predestination appears to be demonstrated:

> He was taken away lest wickedness should change his understanding, and lest deceit should beguile his soul.

(*Wisdom* 4:11.)

Augustine first employed this passage when writing to Sixtus, and he argued from it closely in the works that followed (*On Rebuke and Grace* 8; *On the Predestination of the Saints* 14).

But how did the book reach Gaul? From Rome, I think, sent by Leo, then an acolyte, a close friend of Sixtus and his fellow student, and especially devoted to Cassian. Just as Leo had carried Sixtus’s letter to Augustine together with Zosimus’s *tractoria* to the Africans, so he saw Augustine’s reply to Sixtus and shared it with Cassian, whom he knew to be both knowledgeable about such matters and eager for them.

Cassian, who at that time held something like the leading position in theological teaching in Gaul, criticized certain points that supported gratuitous predestination and drew a number of bishops and presbyters over to his side. When Prosper and Hilary, together with other laymen, opposed them, disputes and disturbances arose. The arrival of the book *On Rebuke and Grace* did not settle those disturbances; it increased them.

## YEAR 425

*Book on Rebuke and Grace* (Volume VII).

The book *On Rebuke and Grace* was composed on the occasion of the book *On Grace and Free Will* and belongs to the year indicated by its title. It is an entirely admirable work and a specimen of an intellect assisted by divine grace. Its importance is shown by the dignity of its subject; the learned discussions that arose from it demonstrate how profound a doctrine it contains; and experience shows how free from prejudice and eager for progress a reader must be in approaching it.

## YEAR 426

*Two Books of Retractions* (Volume I).

After Eradius had been designated as his successor and had been admitted to share in his duties, Augustine, finding himself either partly free or at least no longer overwhelmed by the burden of affairs, began to review the works he had composed as a layman, presbyter, and bishop. The acts by which Eradius was elected (*Among Augustine’s Letters* 213) are dated under the consulship of Theodosius XII and Valentinian Augustus II, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October—that is, September 26 of the year 426.

Augustine intended the work of the *Retractions* to extend over several books, and he had already completed two, as Possidius testifies (*Life of Augustine* 28), before the Vandals invaded Africa. It is generally agreed that they invaded it in May of the year 428. While Augustine was preparing to add other books in which his letters, treatises, and similar works would be reviewed, he was prevented from proceeding further partly by the circumstances of the times and partly by the undeniable necessity of writing more urgent works. The two books of the *Retractions* therefore belong to the year 426 and the following year.

## YEAR 427

*Book on the Predestination of the Saints* (Volume VII).—*Book on the Gift of Perseverance* (Volume VII).

Two books were composed in this year: one *On the Predestination of the Saints*, the other *On the Gift of Perseverance*. In them Augustine responds, at the request of Prosper and Hilary, to the questions of the people of Massilia.

They could not have been composed earlier, since Augustine testifies that he began writing them after completing the books of the *Retractions* (*On the Predestination of the Saints* 3):

> When I was reviewing my shorter works and carrying out that review with my pen—I had already completed two books of this work before I received your more extensive writings—and so forth.

Nor could they have been composed later, since they appear to have been written before his final work, in which the most holy old man answered Julian. Otherwise, when replying to Quodvultdeus, who had requested a book on heresies, he would have used not merely one excuse—namely, Alypius’s insistence that he reply to Julian—but another as well, and no less substantial: the request of the Gauls that he compose a treatise against the people of Massilia.

## YEAR 428

*Unfinished Work against Julian* (Supplement, Part II).

The *Unfinished Work* belongs to this period. Since the matter has been discussed fully in the preface to Marius Mercator’s book *Annotations*, it is unnecessary to add more concerning its date, title, or number of books.

## YEAR 429

*Book on Heresies* (Volume VI).

The *Book on Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus, a Carthaginian deacon, was composed at this time, since Augustine began writing it after completing his response to Julian’s fifth book. Augustine writes in his letter to Quodvultdeus:

> When I have explained that matter and replied to the fifth book, if the three do not arrive in the meantime, I intend, if God wills, to begin what you request, carrying on both tasks at once—this work, namely, and that work of reviewing our shorter writings—assigning each to its own nights and days.

It should be carefully observed that in this final work of all, composed when Augustine was near death, he reviewed the errors of the Pelagians in such a way as to make this heresy consist of only five parts:

1. The grace of God, without which the commandments cannot be fulfilled, is neither different from nature nor from the law.

2. Whatever grace is granted in addition is given both on account of merits and to make action easier.

3. In mortal life a person can reach such a degree of perfection that he does not need to say to God, “Forgive us our debts.”

4. Infants are not baptized in order to remove original sin.

5. Adam, whether he sinned or did not sin, would have died.

From this observation it is clear that the whole of Pelagianism is contained in these five points. Consequently, in Augustine’s judgment, whoever condemned these very points and defended the five doctrines opposed to them would have been free from Pelagianism.

This is enough concerning Augustine’s books—briefer, perhaps, than someone might wish, but, I think, sufficient for the subject and the occasion. We did not wish to enlarge this dissertation to an extraordinary extent by adding what we once established through laborious diligence for our own benefit and that of students. We divided the works we reviewed into their several component parts; we distinguished the historical works from the dogmatic; and we asserted the strength of the arguments by which the doctrines are proved, arranging the exposition according to the laws of method. We also showed what the most holy teacher accused the Pelagians of at each period and how he advanced from day to day. But all these matters cannot be contained within the limits of this dissertation; and even if they could, they should not now be included, lest I appear to be discussing questions that tend to disturb certain people.

# CHAPTER III  
## What Paul Orosius Wrote against the Pelagians

Orosius wrote one *Apology*, and although it is not a large work, it is so full of facts and doctrines that it yields to almost no composition of its age and surpasses many, even to the envy of some. We must investigate the occasion on which it was written and the place and time of its composition, while also refuting the objections and calumnies by which it is unjustly brought under suspicion.

The entire question of its cause, date, and place is not difficult to resolve. As we explained in the dissertation on the synods, Orosius, while residing in Palestine, wrote not so much an apology for free will as an apology for himself, in the year 415, during the period extending from the end of September to December.

The chronology is established by the occasion of the writing. John, bishop of Jerusalem, who favored Pelagius and saw that the clergy were divided into factions because of his case, convened the presbyterium, so that, if possible, he might either absolve Pelagius or at least reconcile him with the others who disagreed. Orosius came to the meeting, which was held approximately five months before the Council of Diospolis, on July 30, summoned by the presbyters from his retreat at Bethlehem, to which he had withdrawn a few months earlier. Pelagius also came, introduced by John and ordered, although he was a layman, to sit among the presbyters.

Among other things, Orosius reported that he had heard Pelagius say that a person could be without sin and could easily keep God’s commandments if he wished. Pelagius replied that he had indeed said this, but not without the help of God. Nevertheless, Orosius pressed him sharply, for he knew the heretic’s evasions. John, whether maliciously or misled by the interpreter, understood Orosius’s insistence as though Orosius were claiming that the commandments could not be kept by a person even with God’s help.

Consequently, forty-seven days later, when Orosius had come to attend upon John on the first day of the *encaenia*, September 14, on account of the solemnity of the feast, he suffered rejection from the angry bishop and was ordered to withdraw far away, as one who had asserted with the utmost blasphemy that a person could not be without sin or keep God’s commandments even with God’s help.

To repel this calumny, the thoroughly Catholic man composed an *Apology*, not only on his own behalf but on behalf of the faith, especially at the urging of presbyters who held the correct view. On that occasion he admirably explained the power of the human will to act well—that is, free will. Hence the book’s title: *Apologeticus against Pelagius on the Freedom of the Will*.

Some say that the whole work is spurious and was composed as an exercise by someone who, assuming the name of Orosius, wished to write something about the events at Diospolis, although he was very ignorant of both truth and history. They make this claim partly because they believe that certain statements in the *Apology* are damaging to their own position, and partly because they do not sufficiently recognize that this book possesses great authority and reliable credibility from Augustine’s testimony (*On the Proceedings in Palestine*).

To prove the charge of forgery that they bring against it, they rely especially on four arguments. If these arguments were put forward as truthfully as they are asserted confidently, they could by no means be considered trivial. They accuse the author of the book, first, of contradicting the historical account handed down by Augustine and other witnesses no less credible; second, of being under suspicion of Nestorian impiety; third, of adhering to Novatian errors; and finally, of insulting Bishop John, a man whom they claim had an unblemished reputation.

If these charges were confirmed as they ought to be, the author of the *Apology* would indeed be guilty of assuming another’s name and of something like imposture. For the real Orosius was always far removed from every suspicion of falsehood in writing history, from every error concerning the faith, and from every neglect of the duty owed to bishops.

Jansenius of Ypres (Book I, *On the Pelagian Heresy*) brings forward part of such accusations, and Peter Vastelius (*Vindication*, Book III, section 5) another part—although the former does so briefly and cautiously, perhaps because he understood that he was fighting against the truth, while the latter does so in almost endless discourse, out of affection for John, whom he strives to present as free from error and guilt, even against all the writers of the fifth century.

The first objection commonly made by the Ypresian and Vastelius is that the author of the *Apology* writes that a synod was held at Jerusalem forty-seven days before the first day of the *encaenia*, that is, on 30 July; that John presided over it; that presbyters assembled, that he himself was present, and that he disputed verbally with Pelagius; and that John delivered a definitive judgment, while the parties were referred to Pope Innocent, so that they might abide by his decision. But all this, they say, seems to conflict with historical truth. For, in the case of Pelagius, no synod is recorded as having been assembled in the East except the one whose proceedings Augustine recounted. That synod, however, was held not at Jerusalem but at Diospolis; it was presided over not by John but by Eulogius, by virtue of his position as bishop of Caesarea; not presbyters alone were present, but fourteen bishops, whose names Augustine records; Orosius was not the accuser, but two Gallician bishops, Eros and Lazarus; Orosius was absent—indeed, so were the accusers—and the proceedings with Pelagius were conducted solely through written documents, as Augustine testifies (*Book on the Proceedings in Palestine*, ch. 11); nor is anything found in the acts concerning the case’s being referred to Pope Innocent, with the parties agreeing to this.

[Col. 0568A]

Yet this argument, however strongly supported on both sides by numerous testimonies, must collapse if its foundation is overturned—namely, if it is demonstrated from Augustine’s testimonies that two assemblies were held in Palestine, one at Jerusalem and the other at Diospolis; that Orosius was present at the former and absent from the latter. Augustine reports this in three places.

First (*Book on the Proceedings in Palestine*, ch. 14):

“Saint John, bishop of the Church of Jerusalem, when asked what had taken place in his presence before the trial, himself related it to our fellow bishops, who were presiding with him at that same trial. But when certain persons were then whispering and saying that Pelagius maintained that this could be accomplished without the grace of God—the same thing he had said above, that a human being could be without sin—he said: ‘I also brought a charge concerning this, because the Apostle, laboring greatly, but not according to his own strength, rather according to the grace of God, said: “I have labored more abundantly than they all, yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10). And again: “It is not of him that wills, nor of him that runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16). And this also: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. 126:1); and we said many other similar things from the holy Scriptures.’ But when they did not accept what we were saying from the holy Scriptures and were still whispering, Pelagius said: ‘I too believe so. Let him be anathema who says that, without God’s help, a human being can advance toward the attainment of every virtue.’”

“Bishop John related this in the hearing of Pelagius.”

Second (*ibid.*, ch. 16):

“Bishop John plainly understood this saying of the Apostle and therefore recalled it, lest Pelagius should think that anyone could avoid sin without the grace of God; and he said that Pelagius had replied: ‘I too believe so.’ Nor, when he heard this in person, did he reply: ‘I do not believe so.’ That perverse interpretation must be understood—according to which it was intended to suggest that the Apostle did not mean this but rather condemned it—so that he may either deny that it is his own, or not hesitate to correct and amend it.

“For whatever Bishop John said about our absent brothers, whether our fellow bishops Eros and Lazarus, or the presbyter Orosius, or others whose names are not expressed there, I believe he understands that it cannot count to their prejudice. For if they had been present, they might perhaps—far be it from me to say, convict him of falsehood, but perhaps remind him of something he had forgotten, or of something in which the Latin interpreter had misled him, without any intention of lying, certainly with some difficulty arising from imperfect knowledge of another language, especially since the matter was not being handled in official proceedings, which are usefully established so that wicked men may not lie and good men may not forget something.
