“But if anyone should derive some question from this against our aforesaid brothers and summon them to episcopal judgment, they will attend as best they can. Why should we trouble ourselves, when not even the judges themselves, after the account of our fellow bishop, wished to pronounce anything on the matter?”

Third (*ibid.*, ch. 30):

“Earlier, in the account of the holy Bishop John, it was likewise recalled: ‘They persisted,’ he said, ‘saying that he is a heretic. For he says that a human being can, if he wishes, be without sin.’ And when we questioned him about this, he replied: ‘I did not say that human nature permits a person to be impeccable; but I said that whoever wishes to labor for his own salvation, and strive so as not to sin, and walk in God’s commandments, has this possibility from God.’

“Then, when certain persons were whispering and saying that, according to Pelagius, this could be accomplished without the grace of God, he said: ‘I also brought a charge concerning this, because the Apostle Paul, laboring greatly, but not according to his own strength, rather according to the grace of God, said: “I have labored more abundantly than they all; yet not I, but the grace of God with me,”’ and the rest, which I have already recalled.”

From these passages, five points in particular should be noted, so closely consonant with the *Apology* that Augustine seems, while writing, to have had Orosius’s very words before his eyes.

[Col. 0569A]

1. Augustine: John, when asked what had taken place among his people before the trial, related it, and so forth.

Orosius (*Apology*, ch. 3): “I was staying in Bethlehem. From there, when you summoned me to Jerusalem, I came when called; then, at your command, Bishop John, I sat down with you in your assembly,” and so forth.

2. Augustine: “But when certain persons were then whispering and saying that Pelagius maintained that this could be accomplished without the grace of God”—that is, that a human being could be without sin—“and so forth.”

Orosius (*ibid.*, toward the end of the chapter): “To this, while he argued at length, and while our proceedings were often either distorted or suppressed because of the incompetence of an interpreter unknown to us, Bishop John said: ‘If he had said that a human being could do this without God’s help, it would have been most wicked and deserving of condemnation. But now, since he adds that a human being can be without sin, though not without God’s help, what do you say? Do you perhaps deny God’s help?’” and so forth.

3. Augustine: “But when they did not accept what we were saying from the holy Scriptures and were still whispering, Pelagius said: ‘I too believe so. Let him be anathema who says that, without God’s help, a human being can advance toward the attainment of every virtue.’”

Orosius (*ibid.*, ch. 9): “You write that a human being can be without sin and easily keep God’s commandments, if he wishes; finally, as though awakening from a very deep sleep, you add: ‘Not without God’s help.’”

4. Augustine: “Whatever Bishop John said about the presbyter Orosius, or about others whose names are not expressed there, I believe he understands that it cannot count to their prejudice,” and so forth.

Orosius (*ibid.*, ch. 3): “Bishop John said: ‘What do you say? Do you perhaps deny God’s help?’ I replied: ‘Anathema to anyone who denies God’s help; I certainly do not deny it.’” And afterward: “The bishop replied: ‘I have heard you say that, even with God’s help, a human being cannot be without sin,’” and so forth.

5. Augustine: “For if they had been present, they might perhaps—far be it from me to say, convict him of falsehood—but perhaps remind him of something he had forgotten, or of something in which the Latin interpreter had misled him,” and so forth.

Orosius (*ibid.*, ch. 5): “It should rather be granted that the interpreter seems to have erred in what he said, than that the bishop, in what he heard, seems to have invented it; and now, as though demanding payment in return for the reward he bestowed upon the heretics, he seeks false witnesses to support himself. But whether these things seem to have been rashly believed by the bishop, maliciously invented, or misunderstood by one who was ignorant, I commit the investigation to Christ the Judge. Far be it from me to dare to summon a bishop, especially the bishop of Jerusalem, before bishops—that is, to accuse him of calumny,” and so forth.

Confronted by these arguments, Vastelius finally admits that it is clear that before the trial at Diospolis certain things had taken place concerning the case of Pelagius in John’s presence, though without any formal assembly; nevertheless, he says, this occurred in the presence of the bishops Eros and Lazarus, Pelagius’s accusers, and of certain Latins who supported them, among whom Orosius also happened to be present.

But I cannot agree with his assertion that Eros and Lazarus were present, since Orosius, while recalling every detail of this gathering, gives no indication of it even in a single word.

As for the second head of accusation, Vastelius—no longer joined by the Ypresian, but proceeding alone—charges the author of the *Apology* with the Novatian heresy, in approximately these words:

“The Novatian error was that Christ had given the Church no power to remit sins other than the power of conferring baptism; and therefore that sins committed by Christians after faith could not be remitted by priests, but only by God. This error is known from the testimonies of Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine.

“But the apologist affirms the whole of this. For, addressing Pelagius, he says (*Apology*, ch. 10): ‘You say that a human being can be without sin with God’s help; you say: “A human being can”; I say: “God can.”’ And afterward (*ibid.*): ‘The scribes, not understanding the truth, murmur and say: “Who can forgive sins except God alone?” (Luke 5:21), and here he judges that those things have been abolished which he does not know God to have forgiven.’” [Col. 0570A]

And again (*Apology*, ch. 10): “‘It is possible for one who has at some time sinned to be without sin only through the grace of baptism, where, in the person of the Lord, it is said: “Your sins are forgiven you.”’ Again (*ibid.*): “‘I had power to sin; I do not have power to be freed from sin.’ Finally: ‘To sin is mine; to be absolved is not mine.’”

I can scarcely, if at all, persuade myself that Vastelius was arguing seriously when he reasoned in this manner. The Novatian error, he says, is that the ministers of the Church, rather than divine power alone, do not forgive sins committed after faith, and that no power for forgiving sins was left to the Church by Christ except the power exercised through baptism, that is, through the one sacrament of the remission of sins. But the author of the *Apology* says that a human being cannot be without sin, while God can; he attributes to God alone, and to Christ, the power by which a human being is said to be able to become without sin; he further says that no one can be certain, before the day of judgment, that he is without sin. Therefore he is held guilty of the Novatian error.

How could a learned man have failed to know either the rules of argumentation, or what the Novatian error concerning penance was, or what the Church’s doctrine was concerning impeccability and the possibility of fulfilling the commandments? Pelagius wished the commandments of God to be so easy that a human being, if he wished, could fulfill them entirely, and that he needed for this not the help of God Almighty but only his own natural strength. Orosius responds to Pelagius’s position that a human being can indeed observe, and even fulfill, the commandments, but that the power by which he can do so does not belong to him—that is, it is not implanted in him by nature—but belongs to God, who mercifully grants it according to time and circumstance.

Pelagius wished a human being to be able in this life to remain entirely free from sin, and that nothing more should be required for this than his willing it. Orosius maintains that a human being can indeed be free from sin in this life if God wills it; for God can grant this to a human being, even though thus far he has granted it to no one except Christ. But what has this to do with the Novatians?

[Col. 0570C]

Vastelius proceeds and brings forward a third head of accusation, no less astonishing than the second: he makes the author of the *Apology* guilty also of Nestorian blasphemy, apparently not content merely to accuse him of cruelty toward sinners, by denying them penance, unless he also charges him with impiety toward the redeemer of sinners, by stripping him of divinity.

“He asserts,” he says, “that Christ is called God only denominatively, and thus exists in reality as a mere human being—which is Nestorian blasphemy. For he does not wish Christ to be God in any other way than by needing God’s help, just as human beings do.”

He thinks that he can construct this incredible accusation from the following words of the apologist addressing Pelagius (*Apology*, ch. 10):

“You say that in this world a human being can be without sin with God’s help; you say: ‘A human being can’; I say: ‘God can.’”

For thus, by an extraordinary syntax of the sentence, he orders the passage to be read: “You say: ‘A human being can be without sin with God’s help’; I say: ‘God can be without sin with God’s help.’”

[Col. 0570D]

But this is mere jesting, which is unbecoming in a serious matter, since the apologist’s meaning is obvious to everyone. When it is said that a human being can be without sin with God’s help, some power is undoubtedly signified, and this power belongs properly to someone—either to God or to the human being, as though it were innate. Pelagius says that it belongs to the human being, which is heretical; Orosius says that it belongs to God, which is thoroughly Catholic.

To confirm his accusation, Vastelius adds something else, though no more seriously. “He called Christ,” he says, “by no other name than one which any Nestorian could have used; nowhere does he call him the Son of God, God Christ, or the incarnate Word.”

Let it be so, then. Yet the writers of the New Testament themselves, when speaking of Christ, used no other name than the one which the Nestorians later misused. Are they therefore immediately participants in the error? Moreover, necessity does not always require, nor do circumstances always permit, that Christ’s divinity be discussed in such explicit terms. Certainly at that time there was no reason to speak so explicitly, since neither party—I mean Pelagius and Orosius—was disputing Christ’s divinity.

Finally, Vastelius himself at last acknowledges, compelled by the truth, that these are the words of the apologist (*Apology*, ch. 21):

“This, then, is Christ our Lord; this, I say, is the Son of God, who in the power and glory of the Father—through which he created all things in the beginning, redeemed them in the middle, and will also judge them at the end—…” and so forth.

And shortly before (*ibid.*):

“He himself is the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, concerning whom John, having been introduced almost to that inaccessible light, cries out: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him’ (John 1:1).”

And shortly afterward, having explained the truth of the divine work, he adds:

“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his honor, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of glory and truth,” and so forth.

What could the Church ever have decreed, or Scripture ever said, more explicitly to demonstrate Christ’s divinity?

[Col. 0571B]

Fourth, Vastelius objects and complains that the author of the *Apology* wronged John, bishop of Jerusalem, whom Augustine honors and calls holy.

But what wrong does he claim was done? “He accused the bishop,” he says, “in somewhat harsh words.”

Let it be so. What person falsely accused of blasphemy would not deserve pardon if he spoke somewhat angrily to his accuser? But in what words did he accuse the bishop? Were they harsher and more bitter than those used either by his own teacher Jerome, in Letter 61, concerning the errors of John of Jerusalem, or by Epiphanius, in the letter sent to John himself (Letter 60 among Jerome’s letters)?

Vastelius cries out that both works are spurious. All the learned cry out in reply that both are genuine, as do those same two Fathers, whom Vastelius attempts to deprive of works that are among the things in which they take pride.

Moreover, of what crime did he accuse the bishop? That he favored a heretic? Augustine did so. That he appeared to lie? Augustine did so as well. That he had allowed himself to be mocked by Pelagius? Augustine did so. That he had inflicted calumny upon Orosius? Augustine did so too.

Finally, before whom did he bring the accusation? Before only the presbyters who knew the whole matter—not calling them judges, but merely witnesses, and finding comfort with them over the common injury inflicted by the bishop.

I therefore cannot sufficiently admire Orosius’s modesty. When necessity compelled him to clear himself of the accusation of blasphemy, he did not defend himself as fully as faith required, but, restrained by charity, complained only before the witnesses of the affair. I therefore think that this is why the book, which out of modesty he did not wish to publish lest he diminish the bishop’s reputation, remained at once rarer and less known even in his own age.

Once these matters have been discussed, it is clear and manifest that there is no reason why the apologetic book *On Free Will against Pelagius* should be denied to Orosius; on the contrary, there are very strong reasons why it should be attributed to him. It has Augustine’s testimony; its style demonstrates its author; manuscript codices bear the name of Orosius; all the learned agree; and only those resist whose interests require that weapons not be supplied by so great and so ancient a writer, and—most important—by so distinguished a disciple of Jerome and Augustine, weapons with which he himself once defeated Pelagius and with which Catholics are now in turn defeating them.

Orosius composed two parts of the *Apology*: one historical, the other dogmatic. The first contains the events conducted at the assembly in Jerusalem and, at the same time, the reason for writing; the second is altogether outstanding and worthy of its author, and it may rightly be regarded as a kind of compendium of the doctrine handed down by Jerome and Augustine.

The third part, which some have believed to extend from chapter 3 through chapter 22 and which has the character of an appendix, may not have been added by Orosius, since it is inserted awkwardly, but rather by a copyist who had read the mention of Augustine’s book *On Nature and Grace* at the beginning. Nevertheless, Orosius may have brought with him to the East some portion of this Augustinian work, since he testifies that it had been begun at the time when he departed from Africa. Whatever the truth may be, Schott did not act unwisely when he removed that addition before the entire work was published in the *Library of the Holy Fathers*.

Only two of the questions raised by Pelagius are treated in this book: one concerning the power of free will, the other concerning human perfection in mortal life. These were the only questions that Jerome was debating in the East (*Letter to Ctesiphon* and *Third Dialogue*), and he had persuaded the presbyters of his position, so that they consequently caused Pelagius great unpopularity. Both questions, however, are resolved with such subtlety—according to the school’s ἀκρίβεια (*akribeia*, precision)—and with such solidity according to the rule of faith, that I do not hesitate to say that scarcely anything better was written in ancient times, nor does anything survive among the monuments of antiquity that is more useful for later ages.

## CHAPTER IV  
### On the Six Books of the *Hypognostica*

[Col. 0572B]

At the end of the seventh volume of the works of Saint Augustine there has been placed a work against the Pelagians, comprising six books. Although Remigius of Lyons calls it a ὑπομνηστικόν (*hypomnēstikon*), that is, a memorandum or, more properly, a reminder, it is nevertheless commonly called the *Hypognostica*, as though it meant “Subnotes” or “Annotations.”

Until the present day, the author’s name, nation, and period have remained unknown. Yet, I think, it is permissible to investigate them without fear of recklessness, since their obscurity may perhaps be due to negligence. Certainly the subject with which we are engaged demands this diligence from us, so that, if possible, we may discover something—not absolutely certain, perhaps, but at least less improbable than what has hitherto been proposed.

The appropriate method of inquiry seems to be first to collect carefully from the books of the *Hypognostica* themselves all the individual details upon which an argument may rest; then, from the indications discovered, to determine who the *Hypognostes* was, in what period he lived, and on what occasion he wrote.

First, he himself explains the reason that the *Hypognostes* had for writing, immediately at the beginning, when he says (*Preface to the Hypognostica*):

“The adversaries of the Catholic faith, while striving to fight against the rule of truth with diabolical weapons, make us more cautious through our concern to respond; yet they deceive themselves before they are able to wound any of our people. For while the blind contend to empty the treasures of faith, deprived of the hope of faith, they cause the fullness of the Church’s faith, with the assistance of God’s grace, to exult.

“And while they keep watch in hypocrisy to do harm—concerning whom I think it was said through the prophet: ‘Sleep has been taken from their eyes, for they do not sleep unless they have done evil’ (Prov. 4:16)—they in a certain way awaken us who are sleeping, so that, having seized the shield of truth, our heart resisting their falsehood, we may keep watch while the evangelical trumpet resounds in our ears: ‘Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation’ (Mark 14:38).”

He then proposes the five questions of the Pelagians that must be discussed (*ibid.*):

“The blasphemy of this sort of wicked doctrine is as follows: they say that Adam would have died whether he had sinned or had not sinned; likewise, that his sin harmed no one except himself alone; that a human being, through free will, as though sufficient unto himself, can fulfill whatever he wishes, or that grace is given by God to each person in accordance with the merits of his works; that sexual desire is a natural good and contains nothing of which one ought to be ashamed; and that the infant children of baptized persons do not contract original sin, nor will they perish from eternal life if they depart this life without the sacrament of baptism.”

It should be noted, however, that Hilary of Syracuse (*Letter 156*), the deacon Paulinus (*Book on the Proceedings*, ch. 11), and Marius Mercator (*Preface to the Book of Subnotes*) had at one time listed the same number of questions, yet did not mention the fourth, concerning sexual desire—whether it is a natural good and whether it contains anything of which one ought to be ashamed. Indeed, this question does not seem to have been discussed independently, but only incidentally, before Julian undertook to defend the Pelagian cause.

Afterward, the *Hypognostes* frequently names Pelagius and Coelestius, but never Julian, although after the condemnation of the Pelagians—or at least after the year 420—no one dealt with the questions concerning original sin without mentioning Julian, as the leader of the heretical party.

Add to this that the author of the *Hypognostica*, although he frequently mentions Pelagius and Coelestius, as has been said, does not seem to attack them directly, but rather some particular individual: at times he refutes his responses to the arguments of the Catholics, at times he blocks his evasions, and at times he answers his calumnies.

What is more, that solitary adversary whom the *Hypognostes* confronts is presented as a kind of Coelestian figure, who discusses the Coelestian error at much greater length than the Pelagian error and who, out of the five questions, proposes one concerning grace and four concerning original sin. Indeed, he advances nearly all the same arguments that Julian—who was especially devoted to Coelestius—was accustomed to bring forward in his books.

Furthermore, the *Hypognostes* resolves the individual questions in a manner quite different from either Augustine or Mercator. To omit many other matters, he forcefully presses the passage from Wisdom, “God did not make death” (Wis. 1:13), against the natural mortality of Adam; yet those two authors touch on it only briefly, as though they did not place in it any great support for their case.

Again, he frequently employs testimonies from Scripture, but draws them both from the translation of the Old Testament which Jerome carefully revised from the Hebrew and from the Gospel text which that same Jerome corrected at the request of Damasus. One example will suffice. Psalm 114 reads:

“Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with me. For he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling; I shall please the Lord in the land of the living.”

These words are read differently in Augustine:

“Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you. For he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling. I shall please in the sight of the Lord, in the land of the living.”

Again, he uses the testimony of no Father, but fights solely with the authority of Scripture or with arguments, although almost no one wrote on these matters at that time without adducing the Fathers against the novelty of the error, as sacred witnesses of the faith.

Again, he mentions neither any synod nor any supreme pontiff by whose judgment the errors he attacks were condemned, although after the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius by the Church—that is, after the year 418—no one wrote on this matter who did not consider it a religious duty not to pass over so important a precedent in silence.

Again, he maintains an uneven manner of expression: at times nothing is grander than his language, and immediately afterward nothing is humbler. How lofty are these words (*at the end of the preface*):

“O evil doctrine, which the enemy of peace has devised! O doctrine by which the unity of the mother Church is torn apart from those who have been regenerated! O doctrine which, under Christ’s name, attempts to overthrow and alter Christ’s foundations! O doctrine possessing a thousand wicked names, a thousand arts of doing harm! It takes weapons against the law from the law; it attacks the Gospel from the Gospel, fighting to its own destruction; inventing falsehoods from truths, it summons truth to falsehood. But these are punishments for itself, which, uttering them in disorder, it thinks to be victory, so that in them what is written may be fulfilled: ‘By the things through which one sins, by those one is also tormented’ (Wis. 11:17).”

How humbly, by contrast, are these words expressed (*ibid.*):

“I have taken care to make this little book brief. If anyone wishes to read it, let him consider not the mediocrity of the words but the reasoning of the faith; and, if he is pleased, let him give thanks to God, who teaches human beings knowledge. If there are things in which we have erred unwillingly—if indeed there are any that require correction—let him correct them, with God as judge, out of charity; but let the one who corrects be Catholic in understanding. If, however, he is ignorant of everything or motivated by envy, let him not presume to corrupt what is sound.”

How vehement is this amplification against the praisers of sexual desire (*Book IV of the Hypognostica*, toward the end):

“Listen briefly—not to brief matters, but to matters enormous in guilt—the works of your most beloved heat, by which dulled human hearts are driven headlong into illicit intercourse; be ashamed and at last fall silent.

“Inflamed by this heat and shamefully enticed by it, a father sometimes bends toward his daughter and commits incest; a son also pollutes his father’s bed when he sometimes has intercourse with his mother or stepmother; a brother, led by desire, assaults his sister and is not ashamed to violate a female relative; a virgin cannot endure the liberty of marriage but desires intercourse at an unlawful time. A husband, not at all content with the lawful embraces of his wife, defiles the wombs of other women. Likewise, a wife, forgetful of her own husband’s bed, occupies another wife’s bed with adulterous love.

“What shall I say about the downfall of certain servants of God and sacred virgins, who in this age suffer shipwreck? What shall I say about the various impurities in which I think the devil himself, their author, is displeased with himself on your account? Behold your most beloved heat: into what filth of disgrace it unlawfully drives and hurries human minds! Behold how you have not trembled to say that such a flood of filth has existed even in the holy members of Christ! Behold what obscenity and shamefulness you are the fiercest praisers and most shameless defenders of—and, if I am not mistaken, perhaps also perpetrators, since it still does not displease you.”

How gentle, by contrast, and how abject and humble is this argument!

“As I said above, many people commonly say, when something is despised, or considered insignificant, or certainly when it does not exist at all: ‘It is nothing.’ When, therefore, we say ‘nothing,’ we name a name without substance; but when we add ‘is,’ we signify a thing. Why, then, do we call a name without substance—that is, as though it truly were something—by adding ‘is’? For whatever we say ‘is,’ we judge to be something; yet when we sometimes say ‘nothing is,’ by customary usage we add ‘is’ to ‘nothing,’ although ‘nothing’ is only a name and not a thing” (*Book I of the Hypognostica*, toward the end).

Again, he uses foreign, unusual, and even barbarous expressions, such as *protoplastus* (“first-formed”), *exsulatus* (“exiled”), *desolatus gratia* (“desolated of grace”), *refellitus* (“refuted”), *repedare* (“to step back”), and so forth.

Finally, the sixth book may appear either spurious or at least an addition, since it mentions a sixth article, although only five were proposed in the preface. Certainly the fifth book, which corresponds to the fifth article, has this conclusion, which may be called the completion of the entire work:

“But we, anathematizing you, listen to Paul, in whom Christ spoke, proclaiming and following him who said that the Catholic Church in Christ has one body and one spirit, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, through all, and in us all” (*Hypognostica*, Book V, at the end).

Moreover, that sixth book is sometimes found in both manuscript and printed codices separated from the other five. Certainly it was alone in the codex of Remigius of Lyons, who therefore stated in his preface that the *Hypomnesticum* lacked a preface; observe that he calls it in the singular number. I have more than once seen it separated from the others in an old edition of certain short works on grace. Only the first five are found in the manuscript codex of the library of Saint Victor at the walls of the city of Paris; and I have no doubt that in other codices the situation is generally the same.

From these observations, I think it may be concluded, first, that the adversary of the *Hypognostes* was none other than Julian, bishop of Eclanum. Everyone knows that Julian was especially a Coelestian, a praiser of sexual desire as a natural good, and an avowed opponent of the faith by which original sin is believed; that he spoke of grace only in passing; and that, if we believe Augustine, he was accustomed to boast of all the same things that the adversary of the *Hypognostes* adduces. Why, then, was he not named? The reason will become clear when we have dealt with the time at which the work was composed.

[Col. 0575A]

Second, this work was written after the judgment of Zosimus, issued in the year 418, but before Julian’s manifest expulsion from his see, which occurred around the year 420. That the work was written before the expulsion is sufficiently clear from the author’s silence concerning Julian’s name; that it was written after the judgment is indicated by these words (*Preface*):

“We must respond against the heretics Pelagians and Coelestians, whom the Lord, in his foreknowledge, knew would become such through their own fault before the foundation of the world, and whom, once they had arisen in the world, he condemned by a just judgment.”

For what did Julian not attempt at that time in order to have the judgment rescinded? What did he not allege against Zosimus’s Catholic definition?

This was the reason why Julian’s name was kept silent in the books of the *Hypognostica*: the author did not wish to exacerbate the bishop’s mind, since, while he had not yet been expelled from his see, Julian might still have hoped to return to the faith which he had professed under Innocent, his ordainer.

Yet this too may have been a reason for the silence: just as Julian, while attacking the Catholics, spared the name of Sixtus, so Sixtus, when attacking the Pelagians, spared Julian’s name—fear impelling Julian, and charity impelling Sixtus. Augustine says to Julian:

“You also accuse certain people,” he says (*Book VI against Julian*, ch. 4), “as though they were deserters from your doctrine, converted or returned to the Catholic faith. Yet you indicated that you feared them so greatly that you did not dare to express their names.”

From this passage, which must undoubtedly be understood of Sixtus, it may be gathered with some clarity that this presbyter had at some time shared the Pelagian position.

Third, this work was elaborated by one of the noble defenders of the faith. Certainly, if the doctrine is taken into account, no one is unworthy of that distinction. At that time the following were fighting: Jerome; Augustine; both Paulinuses, namely the bishop and the deacon; Orosius; Mercator; Pope Zosimus; Sixtus, the Roman presbyter; and perhaps certain Africans, such as Aurelius and Alypius, as well as the author either of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* or of the letter to Demetrias attributed to Prosper.

[Col. 0575C]

Fourth, it was not written by Jerome. For at that time he had ceased writing about these questions because of his extreme old age; he knew nothing of Julian’s affairs, not even by hearsay; he would have used more purely Latin diction; he would not have remained silent about the synods, which he could not omit even in a very brief letter; he would not have failed to speak of Augustine, whom, in the third dialogue, after reading a single work, he praises and exalts so magnificently; he would have sprinkled the work with some of his customary learning; and, finally, his discourse would not have been disjointed, as that of the *Hypognostes* is, but even and balanced, as is his usual manner.

### Fifth

It must likewise be excluded that the author was Paulinus, bishop of Nola, partly because of several of the arguments already presented, and partly because he did not write on these questions—though, had he attempted it, he would certainly have written in more polished Latin and in a more even style. Moreover, he had scarcely gained a clear understanding of Julian’s affairs, since he did not even know the Pelagian doctrines sufficiently, although he was a friend of Pelagius. Hence he needed to be instructed by Augustine, lest he allow the error to be persuaded upon him either by Pelagius through letters, since he was easily deceived by the appearance of piety, or by the obstinate defenders not so much of Pelagius as of the perverse doctrine, [Col. 0575D] whom he tolerated at Nola, being unable to grow angry even at wicked men.

Finally, the popular opinion that Paulinus wrote a book against the Pelagians arose from the mistake of a man who prefixed to Augustine’s Letter 106 (now 186) its subject-summary addressed to Paulinus. For he took a letter to Sulpicius Severus, which was extremely brief, for a book, and thought that the opinion which Augustine argues against the Pelagians—and praises as such—had been expressed by Paulinus against the same men, although it had been put forward by a holy man, supremely contemptuous of himself, solely for the purpose of portraying the appearance of his soul, which he believed to be wretched, and playfully deceiving his friend, who had asked that a likeness of his face be sent to him.

### Sixth

Nor can the work be attributed to Aurelius and Alypius of Africa. Although they stood firmly in the cause of the faith against the enemies of the cross of Christ—the former by holding synods, the latter by undertaking embassies—they are nevertheless reported to have written nothing except letters. In those letters, however, the [Col. 0576A] genius, learning, and style of Augustine shine so clearly that they may not unjustly be called his.

Moreover, the passage in Orosius from which someone might in some way conclude that Aurelius wrote against Pelagius—“Who are,” he says (*Apology*, chapter 1, “the pillars and foundations of the Catholic Church? Aurelius, Augustine, and Jerome have already published highly approved writings against this wicked heresy, without designating the names of the heretics,” and so forth—belongs to a much earlier period, indeed to a time preceding even the Synod of Diospolis.

I do not know whether Rivius paid sufficient attention to this passage when he wrote (*Life of Saint Augustine*) that from it we first learn that Aurelius was Augustine’s first name: “For the bishop of Carthage is there counted together with Augustine and Jerome, so that to the three defenders of the faith who had died—Cyprian, Hilary, and Ambrose—there might correspond an equal number of living pillars of the Church.”

### Seventh

The author either of the books *On the Calling of the Nations* or of the letter to Demetrias attributed to Prosper is very different from the author of the *Hypognostica*, in Latin usage, [Col. 0576B] style, and opinions. Both writers employ purer diction, a more elevated mode of expression, and a gentler judgment concerning little ones.

### Eighth

Finally, since it remains to inquire about Augustine, Paulinus the deacon, Mercator, Pope Zosimus, and Sixtus, it is easy to incline toward denying that Zosimus was the author, on the basis of the very evidence from which some prejudice might be drawn—namely, the words of Mercator (*Commonitorium*, chapter 1, no. 6):

“Coelestius was therefore utterly condemned by the writings—very extensive, or rather extremely long—of the aforesaid bishop Zosimus, of blessed memory. In them the very chapters on which he had been accused are contained, and the entire case, both concerning the aforementioned Coelestius and concerning Pelagius, his still more wicked teacher, appears to have been related,” and so forth.

For the very lengthy writings said to have been sent by Zosimus throughout the whole world certainly contained the aforementioned chapters—that is, excerpts from Pelagius’s books—which Mercator reports. Yet no such excerpt is contained in the books of the *Hypognostica*. It therefore remains to inquire about the four [Col. 0576C] others: Augustine, Paulinus the deacon, Mercator, and Sixtus the Roman presbyter.

In the ninth century it was certainly unquestioned that the books of the *Hypognostica* were Augustine’s, until the dispute arose between Hincmar and Remigius of Lyon. For when Gottschalk had praised those books as clear judges concerning grace and free will, Hincmar used them to refute Gottschalk’s Predestinarian heresy.

Remigius of Lyon accused Hincmar and declared that the books by which he felt himself seriously pressed had been falsely attributed to Augustine. He thought that this was established by the fact that they are not listed in the *Retractations* or in Possidius’s catalogue; that they lack a preface in which Augustine, in his customary manner, explains what prompted him to write or for what reason he undertook the work (*On Three Letters*, chapter 35); that a subject treated so many times in other books would have been treated anew here at no cost of effort; that the speech differs from Augustine’s; that the doctrine is discordant and Augustine’s modesty does not shine through even in the work itself [Col. 0576D]; and that scriptural testimonies are cited from Jerome’s translation, whereas Augustine was accustomed to use the old common version.

Remigius added that the work seemed to him to have been written, not long after Augustine’s death, by someone after a new calumny of the Pelagians had arisen—as though the Church taught, through the predestination of the reprobate to destruction, that God by his predestination imposed upon human beings the necessity of remaining in their wickedness and perishing eternally. He said that Augustine’s name had been placed at the beginning because the author had gathered together, in large part, Augustine’s own opinions in this brief work; but that some people, failing to understand this adequately, had thought the work itself had been composed by Augustine as a *ὑπομνηστικόν* (*hypomnēstikon*), that is, a memorandum or reminder.

Hincmar replied to Remigius and attempted to defend the public, almost universal belief on which he had relied when he used these books, received from his opponent, as [Col. 0577A] testimony (*On Predestination*). But his arguments were hardly the best, just as the arguments used against him were not the strongest.

He maintained, first, that Augustine had written the books of the *Hypognostica*, at least the sixth book, so that no one would believe that he had transmitted the doctrine of predestination to good, by which he had utterly overthrown Pelagianism with its remnants, while asserting predestination to evil—an unspeakable blasphemy. Second, Augustine had undertaken this labor toward the end of his life, at a time when he saw the Predestinarian heresy arising from his own books, which had been wrongly understood. Finally, he had mentioned in several places the work sent to Prosper and Hilary.

From this dispute between Remigius and Hincmar it is certain that the books in question had commonly been attributed to Augustine before the ninth century. At what time they began to be attributed to him is uncertain, except that the attribution must have been longstanding, since all the manuscripts presented them in this way. Remigius did not deny that this was the common belief, and Hincmar thought so as well; for Hincmar sought somewhat carefully for the causes of this popular credulity.

[Col. 0577B] Erasmus agreed with Remigius and consequently stamped the work with a similar judgment in the criticism prefixed to the books: “This work is not Augustine’s.” First, he argued that, although it is of substantial length, it is not mentioned in the *Retractations*. Next, the title *Ὑπογνοστικῶν* (*Hypognostica*) is unusual, as though one were to say “Subnotations” or “Annotations.” For Augustine does not usually give Greek titles to his books, much less titles that do not indicate the subject. Finally, the style does not agree in every respect, although it appears to belong to a learned and eloquent man. It contains more rhetorical outcry and less solid argument than Augustine. It seems to have been written by someone who undertook to draw together into one work what Augustine had discussed piecemeal against the Pelagians.

For my part, in denying these five books to Augustine, I willingly agree with Remigius and Erasmus. Nevertheless, I think that the arguments used by those three men to establish their judgment should be reconsidered, lest the truth appear to be supported by false arguments, or Hincmar, a man of great authority, appear to be condemned without a hearing [Col. 0577C].

To begin there, nothing prejudices Hincmar’s position merely because Augustine did not mention this work in his *Retractations*. How many other works did he omit! He certainly did not mention the books *On the Predestination of the Saints*, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, or *On the Perfection of Justice*. Yet who would deny that they are the genuine offspring of so great a father, though already an old man? Someone might therefore say that the *Hypognostica* met the same fate, since they were of the same age and, if we believe Hincmar, were published after the *Retractations*.

“But,” Remigius says with Erasmus, “they lack a preface in which the author gives the reasons for writing, as Augustine usually does.” On the contrary, they do have one, and an extremely lengthy one—one that must have been missing from the manuscript Remigius used. For there is no other way to excuse a falsehood that could so easily be disproved before everyone’s eyes. Moreover, what preface do the books *On the Teacher*, *On the Immortality of the Soul*, and others bear? Do they for that reason suffer from suspicion of forgery?

[Col. 0577D] Remigius continues: no mention is made of this work in Possidius’s catalogue, although Possidius, as was proper for one who had been familiar with Augustine for many years, both knew and reviewed all his works with care. But this argument is weak in itself. For Possidius first admits that he did not enumerate everything. Moreover, someone might argue that Possidius did list it, since in all the published catalogues these words are found: “one book against the questions of the Pelagianists.” What is that one book? Certainly none of those contained either in the seventh volume or in the supplement, since each is named individually in the catalogue—and that one is in addition. Let learned men assess the weight of this argument and, if they can, draw their conclusions concerning a matter that is in fact hidden from me and even torments me, unless perhaps the conjecture I shall offer later is correct.

Erasmus adds that Augustine was not accustomed to give Greek names to his minor works, especially names that [Col. 0578A] do not explain the character of their subject. In writing this, Erasmus plainly did not have in mind either the book *On Faith, Hope, and Charity* addressed to Laurentius, which Augustine called the *Enchiridion*, or the treatises addressed to the people, which he called *Homilies*—unless I am mistaken, both Greek names.

Furthermore, Erasmus himself abundantly proves that the subject of the work is adequately explained by the name *Hypognosticon*, when he interprets it as “Subnotations”: by these, he says, the author undertook to collect into one work what Augustine had discussed piecemeal against the Pelagians.

Remigius asks what necessity finally compelled Augustine to treat again material that had already been handled so often and in so many books. The author himself seems able to answer the question throughout the preface: namely, that the adversaries of the Catholic faith, while attempting to fight against the rule of truth with diabolical weapons, make Catholics more cautious through the concern of responding; while keeping watch in hypocrisy in order to cause harm, they rouse sleeping Catholics, so that, having taken up the shield of truth, they may watch with their hearts resisting [Col. 0578B] the falsehood of the adversaries, and so forth. Someone might add that it was in Augustine’s interest to remove by writing the odium arising from the Predestinarian heresy, which had emerged from his books when they were wrongly understood.

Although these arguments of either Remigius or Erasmus carry little weight for refuting Hincmar, there are seven others that completely settle the matter. For among the five principal Pelagian doctrines, the *Hypognostes* lists the claim that sexual desire is a natural good. Augustine never listed this, not even when writing about heresies toward the end of his life. The *Hypognostes* explains predestination differently from Augustine. Augustine greatly surpasses the *Hypognostes* in moderation of expression and very greatly in Latin style. Augustine cites scriptural testimonies from the old common translation; the *Hypognostes* cites them from Jerome’s Hebrew-based translation. Augustine would never have been silent about the tradition of the Fathers and the judgment of the Church in establishing the faith; the *Hypognostes* is entirely silent on these matters. Augustine, who elsewhere mentions Julian’s name so frequently, would certainly not have suppressed it here; the *Hypognostes* does suppress it, however vehemently [Col. 0578C] he attacks the man. Finally, if Augustine were the author of the work, he would certainly have published it at the time when we have shown that it was actually published; he would therefore have included it with the other works of the same period.

Someone might believe, or at least suspect, that the work should be attributed to Mercator. This suspicion might perhaps be strengthened by the following arguments. Mercator gave his book the same title as the *Hypognostes*: Erasmus himself interprets *ὑπογνωστικά* (*hypognōstika*) as “Subnotations,” and it is not implausible that a man moderately skilled in Greek would give his work a Greek title. Furthermore, both authors lived at approximately the same time, and Mercator, since he devoted himself so ardently to defending the Catholic faith, does not seem to have been free from writing for as long as the questions were burning—questions about which he carefully consulted Augustine.

It also supports the identification that both men showed the same hatred toward Julian and the same attitude toward Augustine. Their Latin is almost the same—namely, insufficiently polished. Both favor [Col. 0578D] unusual and foreign words; both frequently use exclamations and other figures of somewhat more vehement speech. Finally, both openly reproach the Pelagians for the shamefulness of their lives, in words that are indeed pointed and almost angry.

On this matter one should read chapters 4 and 5 of the *Subnotations*, where Mercator exposes Julian’s domestic disgraces. The *Hypognostes* says (*Book IV*):

“With shameless face you praise in public, in such wanton language, the movement of lustful desire, that it is plain to everyone what is done by you in secret—if, indeed, those who are not ashamed to praise such things publicly choose even secrecy.”

And later:

“Continue onward through the fields of your talkativeness, in which you do not blush to praise the heat of such great depravity, and shout, according to your custom, saying: ‘Lust is a good genital heat, and there is nothing in it of which one should be ashamed; for if it is called evil, marriage will already be condemned. Without it offspring cannot exist.’

“Let your beloved ones, most chaste assailants of chastity, take note from this—however much they delight in praising it—that they praise it so greatly. Or, if they do not delight in it, [Col. 0579A] why do you persuade them to delight in it, and why is chastity attacked by you? Why do you proclaim as good what you yourselves feel to be opposed to you? I ask you: be ashamed. No one ever delights in calling what is hostile to himself good and adorning it with praises.

“You are altogether deceived, and you deceive others; rather, you have been deceived, and you deceive. This is not a good heat, nor is it genital in the good genital members that God formed; it is evil, as has often been said, authored by the devil and preceded by sin. If through this heat the strength of your mind were not dissolved toward unlawful things, you would not praise it so freely.”

Yet although the *Hypognostes* and Mercator agree in the matters just mentioned—a point that someone might, and not without reason, call into doubt—they certainly disagree in their translation of Scripture. This is an absolutely decisive consideration when ecclesiastical writers are concerned. One of many passages from Paul will suffice, 1 Corinthians 15:54.

The *Hypognostes*: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?”

Mercator: “Death has been swallowed up into victory? Where is, O death, your goad? [Col. 0579B] Where is, O death, your contention?”

Moreover, the word *protoplast* occurs everywhere throughout the *Hypognostes*, and may therefore appear affected; it is nowhere found in Mercator, unless perhaps when he was translating Greek. Finally, Mercator wrote scarcely anything either about the grace of Christ, the natural goodness of lust, or free will, although he had frequent opportunities to write on these matters. The *Hypognostes*, however, discusses them at length in Books III and IV—and in Book VI as well, if it has the same author as the earlier books.

We possess only two works by Paulinus the deacon: the *Life of Saint Ambrose* and a short book sent to Pope Zosimus in the case of Coelestius. Neither permits us to conclude anything relevant to our question, since each treats a subject entirely different from ours. The *Life of Ambrose* certainly differs greatly in style from the *Hypognostica*, and the short book appears to belong to a man more suited to courtroom disputation than to treating a question of faith.

Moreover, Paulinus had nothing to do with Julian, but only with Coelestius. If there had been anything concerning Julian, he certainly would not have been silent about the Fathers, [Col. 0579C] the judgments of the Apostolic See, and the other synods, since even in his very short book he remembers them all so magnificently and at such length:

“Against these things, too,” he says, “his teacher Pelagius is contending, although he condemned in the Eastern judgment the very things that this man attempts to assert in the assembly of the Apostolic See. He also has against him many ancient Catholic teachers of the Churches, Eastern and Western, of the southern and northern regions, who in their books can teach him about original sin, if he desires to be healed. He has the blessed martyr Cyprian, the blessed confessor Ambrose, Gregory of Nazianzus, and blessed Pope Innocent. He still has those who struggle against him in the body—if indeed he judges them fit for so great a contest—or, at any rate, those whom he ought to follow, if he wishes to learn what is right rather than teach what is wrong. Above all, he has Your Beatitude, whose judgment he ought to have obeyed when he heard: ‘Condemn it.’ Finally, he has the infants themselves, whom he ought to pity, if he does not wish them to pity him; to whom, [Col. 0579D] to use the words of the martyr, sins are forgiven not their own but those of others.”

It remains to consider the possibility that the Roman presbyter Sixtus, who succeeded Coelestine in the Apostolic See, was the author of the *Hypognostica*. But because we were defending this opinion from the beginning as highly probable, indeed almost certain, it seemed appropriate to bring forward and submit to the judgment of readers the arguments that not only inclined me toward this conclusion but almost compelled me to it. They arose from careful attention to everything bearing on the whole matter. Although each argument could perhaps be weakened by a contentious person, all of them taken together can scarcely fail to obtain the assent of a reasonable person.

The first consideration that moved me was this. According to Augustine’s testimony, Sixtus had once favored the Pelagians and had extended his patronage to them for some time. This was of great importance—not merely at Rome, where he held power, but throughout the world, to which Rome’s example [Col. 0580A] extended.

Augustine testifies to this when he congratulates Sixtus on having undertaken the cause of the faith against the enemies of grace (*Letter 191*): “What could be more pleasing to read or hear than so beautiful a defense of God’s grace against its enemies, from the mouth of one who had formerly been proclaimed a patron of great importance to those same enemies?”

And elsewhere (*Letter 194*): “I must confess to your Charity that we were exceedingly saddened in spirit when rumor spread that you favored the enemies of Christian grace. But, so that this sadness might be wiped from our hearts, the same rumor did not fail to report that you had first pronounced an anathema against them before a very large gathering. Then, together with the letters of the Apostolic See,” and so forth.

The second consideration is this. Three things in particular gave the patronage that he had extended to the Pelagians the importance that Augustine mentions: Sixtus’s distinguished name and doctrine; the office he held, teaching the people about matters of faith; and the authority by which, through the power of Zosimus, he governed almost the whole Church. Augustine clearly teaches these three things in both of his letters to Sixtus.

In part, he writes that in Sixtus’s letters the faith of the Roman Church itself was speaking (*Letter 194*):

“But now, since you have explained more openly and fully what you thought about and against that doctrine, [Col. 0580B] so that through your letters the faith itself of the Roman Church might speak with us. To whom above all the blessed Apostle Paul spoke much and in many ways about the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord,” and so forth.

In part, he refers everything to Sixtus as to the governor of affairs (*Letter 191*):

“Therefore, venerable lord and holy brother, worthy of honor in the love of Christ, although you are doing very well when you write about this matter to the brothers among whom they are accustomed to boast of your friendship with them, a greater responsibility nevertheless remains for you: not only must those who dare to chatter too freely about that error, which is most hostile to the Christian name, be punished with salutary severity, but those who continue to whisper it—more cautiously and timidly, yet without ceasing—must also be guarded with the greatest pastoral vigilance, for the sake of the weaker and simpler sheep of the Lord. They enter houses, as the Apostle says, and do the other things that follow, acting with practiced impiety [Col. 0580C].

“Nor are those to be neglected who suppress in profound silence, through fear, what they think, yet do not cease to hold the same perversity. Some of them, before this pestilence was condemned even by the most manifest judgment of the Apostolic See, may have become known to you; now you see that they have suddenly become silent. Whether they have been healed cannot be known unless they have not only ceased to speak those false doctrines, but have also defended the true doctrines opposed to them with the same zeal with which they formerly defended the false ones. Such people, however, must certainly be treated more gently. Why should those be frightened who are shown to be sufficiently frightened by their very silence? Yet they should not be passed over as though they were healthy, without the careful attention of medicine, since their wound lies hidden.

“Although they are not to be frightened, they must nevertheless be taught; and, as I think, they can be taught more easily, since in them fear of severity assists the teacher of truth. Thus, with the Lord’s help, once they understand and love his grace, they may by speaking also overcome what they no longer dare to say.”

In part, Augustine also relates that Sixtus’s letter was sent to Aurelius, primate of Africa, together [Col. 0580D] with the Apostolic See’s letters, so that the same bearer, Leo the acolyte, carried Sixtus’s letter and the papal *tractoria* (*Letter 191*):

“For when we copied your very brief letter concerning this matter, which you sent through Leo the acolyte to the most blessed old man Aurelius, with exultant eagerness, and read it with the greatest attention we could give, in it you explained to us what you thought about that most pernicious doctrine, and what, by contrast, you thought about the grace of God, which he bestows upon little and great alike, and to which that doctrine is utterly hostile. How much, then, do you think we read your longer writings with joy, and how eagerly we offered them to others to read, and continue to offer them to those to whom we are able?”

Finally, Augustine urges the presbyter to teach with pastoral care those whom he had hitherto sufficiently frightened by his power, and attributes to him what had been done in the name of the supreme pontiff (*Letter 194*):

“We speak with you at somewhat greater length, admonishing you to persist in teaching those whom, as we have learned, you have persisted sufficiently in frightening. [Col. 0581A] For there are some who think that impieties justly condemned should still be defended more freely; and there are others who secretly enter houses and do not cease to sow in secret what they fear to shout openly. There are also those who have been entirely silenced, crushed by great fear, but who still retain in their hearts what they no longer dare to utter with their mouths. Yet, from their earlier defense of that doctrine, they may be well known to the brothers.

“Accordingly, some must be restrained more severely, others must be investigated more vigilantly, and others must indeed be treated more gently but taught no less diligently, so that, if they are not frightened lest they be lost, they may nevertheless not be neglected lest they perish.”

The third consideration was of this kind. Sixtus sent brief letters to the three pillars of the African Church—to Aurelius, and longer ones to Alypius and Augustine—in which he sought both to remove from himself the odium of having favored heretics, to clear himself of suspicion of agreement with them, to acquit his reputation before the Catholics, and to close the mouths of the Pelagians who boasted of his friendship.

“Then, together with the letters of the Apostolic See concerning their condemnation, your own letter to the venerable old man Aurelius also arrived in [Col. 0581B] Africa. Although it was brief, it nevertheless sufficiently indicated your vigor against their error” (Augustine, *Letter 194*).

The fourth consideration is that the longer letters contained a defense of God’s grace against its enemies—an excellent defense, certainly, but not yet one that Augustine thought befitted the supreme pontiff’s representative. Thus, although the holy bishop displayed Sixtus’s letter to everyone in his joy, as the Catholic confession of a man of great distinction explaining what he thought about the most pernicious doctrine and, by contrast, about the grace of God, which he grants to little and great alike (*Letter 191*), he nevertheless thought it necessary to disclose to Sixtus the deepest mysteries of predestination. In this way, after explaining the meaning of Scripture, Sixtus could easily resolve the questions of the Pelagians that he had presented in his letters as difficult.

Augustine carried this out with ingenuity and prudence—or, rather, with deliberate skill. While showing by strong [Col. 0581C] arguments how justly the heretics had been defeated and condemned through Sixtus’s efforts, he cleverly supplied the victor with weapons by which he could complete the victory in every respect. For a victory could not rightly be called complete so long as it seemed to have been produced by the enemy’s flight and the form of the law rather than by either the teaching of the judges or the assent of the defeated.

“They must be taught no less diligently,” he says, “so that, if they are not frightened lest they be lost, they may nevertheless not be neglected lest they perish”—and so forth, by which he resolves the questions of the Pelagians: “For they think that free will is taken away from them if they do not concede that a human being can possess even a good will without God’s help.”

The fifth consideration is that Augustine warned Sixtus—and warned him sharply, although under the guise of speaking about another person—that he was not adequately fulfilling his duty. Although he had formerly defended Pelagius’s error with great vehemence and afterward condemned Pelagius himself, he was not devoting as much effort to asserting the truth once known as he had previously devoted to defending falsehood.

“Some of them, before this pestilence was condemned even by the most manifest judgment of the Apostolic See, may have become known to you; [Col. 0581D] now you see that they have suddenly become silent. Whether they have been healed cannot be known unless they have not only ceased to speak those false doctrines, but have also defended the true doctrines opposed to them with the same zeal with which they formerly defended the false ones” (Augustine, *Letter 191*).

By these words the most holy man undoubtedly addressed Sixtus himself under another name, either as one among them or as the principal one. He warned him that, since he had assisted the error not merely by favor but also by speeches and even writings, he must now attack it not only by word and anathema but also through treatises and books. For otherwise, as Augustine teaches elsewhere, the Apostle’s command could not be fulfilled—a command whose meaning extends far beyond the words themselves:

“Just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Romans 6:19).

[Col. 0582A] This opinion had been deeply fixed in Augustine’s mind; it did not first occur to him when he wrote to Sixtus. Since he regarded Pelagius’s purification at Diospolis as suspect, because it was in fact full of malicious deception, Augustine wrote:

“However much Pelagius may boast of the friendship of any saints, however many letters he may read praising him, and however many acts of his purification he may produce, unless he anathematizes, as having been confessed on the trustworthy testimony of competent witnesses, the things that he put in his books against the grace of God by which we are called and justified, and thereafter writes and argues against those very things, he will by no means appear corrected to those who know him more fully” (*On the Proceedings at Palestine*, chapter 29).

The sixth consideration persuaded me that Sixtus supported the Pelagian error in writing because the three books *On Riches*, *On the Works of Faith*, and *On Chastity*, published nearly a hundred years ago from the Vatican Library by Salvator of Salona, are not only works of our Sixtus—as Salvator proves apart from the testimony of ancient manuscripts—but also contain Pelagian errors, as scholars recognized long ago.

[Col. 0582B] I know that Baronius denies these books to Sixtus. I also know that Bellarmine and others reject Salvator’s judgment and the testimony of the ancient manuscripts. But the sole reason hitherto advanced for doing so is that the books contain Pelagian errors.

But what follows from that? Is it really a matter of religious principle to suppose that a man who was eventually elevated to the supreme pontificate might once have written something that he later condemned and ensured was condemned by everyone—long before he ascended to the Apostolic See and the summit of the pillar of truth? Did Augustine himself not, before becoming bishop, follow an error that he later condemned in the Massilians?

The seventh consideration, then, is that Sixtus appears to have written books after Augustine had both warned him in friendship and fully instructed him. In part, he wrote them to fulfill his duty and make clear to everyone how far he had withdrawn from his earlier errors; in part, to attack Julian, whom he knew had been made the leader of the whole host, as a representative of all, even without mentioning his name; in part, to approve Zosimus’s *tractoria*, which had been composed at his urging and perhaps by his hand and assistance [Col. 0582C], by adding what were virtually commentaries; and finally, to make amends, through books added to his letters, for the letters written in Zosimus’s name to the Africans in favor of Coelestius and Pelagius—not merely by letters sent to Aurelius, Alypius, and Augustine, but by correcting all that had been done wrongly in fuller fashion through the addition of books.

I shall soon explain why I have said that Zosimus’s letters to the Africans were composed by Sixtus, when we come to examine the style in which the books of the *Hypognostica* were written.

I am entirely convinced that the books Sixtus wrote are the *Hypognostica*. To continue making this opinion persuasive, note, reader, that the *Hypognostes*—something that may perhaps seem surprising to someone—began his book at the point where Augustine ended his longer letter to Sixtus (*Letter 194*). It is as though, by his action, he were saying what he left unsaid in words: that he obeyed Augustine’s admonitions, followed him as his guide, and published a book corresponding to the letter.

“If you know of anything else that they devise against the Catholic faith,” Augustine says (*ibid.*) [Col. 0582D], “and whatever arguments you yourselves, with faithful and wholly pastoral love, discuss against them, lest they devastate the weak members of the Lord’s flock, make it known to us. For through the restlessness of heretics we are, as it were, roused from the sleep of our negligence, so that we may search the Scriptures more vigilantly and find means by which their attacks may be resisted, lest they harm Christ’s sheep. Thus, through the manifold grace of the Savior, God turns even what the enemy contrives for destruction into assistance.”

The *Hypognostes* writes in the preface to Book I of the *Hypognostica*:

“The adversaries of the Catholic faith, while attempting to fight against the rule of truth with diabolical weapons, make us more cautious through the concern of responding; but they deceive themselves before they can wound any of our people. For when the blind strive to empty the treasures of the faith, emptied of the hope of faith, they cause the fullness of the Church’s faith, with the help of God’s grace, to exult. And while they keep watch in hypocrisy in order to cause harm, I think that what was said through the prophet applies to them: ‘Sleep has been taken away [Col. 0583A] from their eyes; for they do not sleep unless they have done evil’ (Proverbs 4:16). In a certain sense they rouse us who are sleeping, so that, having taken up the shield of truth, with our hearts resisting their falsehood, we may keep watch while the evangelical trumpet sounds in our ears: ‘Watch and pray, that you do not enter into temptation’ (Mark 14:38).

“Therefore the heretics, attacking the Catholic faith, trust in their own strength—that is, in the boldness of their hearts—desolate of grace, and in the abundance of their riches, glorying in the works of their own will. But God has scattered the bones of those who pleased themselves; they have been confounded, because the Lord rejected them (Psalm 52:6). Let us also trust as we resist them in the grace of the Lord, which is our glory, redeeming us from those who surround us, giving us understanding, and instructing us in this way on which we walk, confirming his eyes upon us, because in God is our salvation and our glory; God is the God of our help, and our hope is in God.”

Next, consider whether time, place, subject matter, and the other circumstances do not draw the mind of one who reflects toward Sixtus.

### [Col. 0583B]

The *Hypognostes* wrote at approximately the time when Augustine’s letters were delivered to Sixtus, since the work was composed around the year 419, and Augustine’s later letters to Sixtus were sent either toward the end of 418 or at the beginning of the following year (chapter 2 of this dissertation).

He wrote at Rome, since he uses the version of Scripture that at that time was in use only at Rome; and he wrote about the very questions that were troubling the Roman Church and were contained in Zosimus’s *tractoria*.

Finally, he wrote against Julian, who had not yet been deposed, but was nevertheless one of those residing at Rome whom Augustine complains (*Letter 194*) were still defending, with excessive freedom, impieties that had been justly condemned.

Since, then, nothing prevents these books from being attributed to Sixtus—not place, not time, not subject matter, nor any other circumstance—and since many considerations recommend attributing them to him, including Augustine’s admonition, Sixtus’s duty, the correspondence of the preface of the *Hypognostica* with the conclusion of Letter 105, and so forth [Col. 0583C]; indeed, since Augustine’s authority compels this conclusion, for when he attributes Zosimus’s acts to Sixtus he indicates clearly enough that Zosimus’s letters were written by that same Sixtus; and even if he did not indicate this, the identical style of both works, a kind of single spirit, the same opinions, and almost the same expressions demonstrate that the author of the two works was the same—for example:

“Before the tribunal of Christ we shall all stand,” and so forth (*Letter 2 to the Africans*);

“Along with me will stand before the tribunal of Christ, to render an account, whoever he may be,” and so forth (Preface to the *Hypognostica*);

it is exceedingly probable, if not certain, that the books of the *Hypognostica* were composed by Sixtus.

I am not unaware that two objections may be raised against what has been advanced thus far. The first is that the three books we mentioned—*On Riches*, *On the Works of Faith*, and *On Chastity*—do not appear to have been written in the same style as the *Hypognosticon*, and that consequently either one work or the other must be denied to Sixtus, thereby weakening to some extent the foundation of our argument. The second is that Sixtus could scarcely ever have cleared himself of the suspicion of being favorably disposed toward the Pelagians, since, even after he had become supreme pontiff, twelve years later, some said—and many believed—that he favored Nestorius, a friend of the Pelagians; yet he would have utterly removed this suspicion if he had published a work so vehemently opposed to them.

But as regards the first point, I do not deny that there is some dissimilarity between the two works, both in style and in spirit. Yet no one will refuse to concede to me in turn that one kind of writing is polemical, as employed in the *Hypognosticon*, and another didactic, as employed in the other books. The former must be more vehement, the latter gentler; and no one becomes angry with an adversary in the same words with which he instructs a friend. Once the differences arising from the nature of the subject are removed, scarcely any disparity remains either in Latin usage or in expression.

The second objection, however, is scarcely of any importance. For Sixtus may have endured this slander from certain men deceived by Pelagian cunning. Although, before the condemnation, they had boasted of his friendship, afterward they falsely claimed that he did not oppose them inwardly but only with his tongue, in order to serve the times and avert from his own head the danger then hanging over it, from the anger both of the emperor and of the supreme pontiff.

For this is how the matter must be understood: Sixtus, who after the death of Zosimus—under whose pontificate nothing was impossible—had been reduced by his successor Boniface, so to speak, to the ranks, ought to have been careful lest, in the eyes of a supreme pontiff especially devoted to the Africans, the suspicion that he favored the Pelagians should increase the odium accumulated through his former authority. For that reason he wrote more angrily against them, and this did not escape the leaders of the Pelagian party, Julian and Coelestius, who interpreted Sixtus’s action as though he were not dealing with the matter seriously. Thus, at some later time, he might be reconciled with them, provided that in the meantime he was neither named among those who attacked the Catholics nor otherwise provoked; provided, rather, that what he himself said more harshly was borne with greater patience, and that only the Africans were assailed. The Africans were not otherwise especially well disposed toward the Romans, and toward Sixtus above all, because of the affair of Apiarius and because Zosimus’s letters had been written by Sixtus.

Augustine’s words addressing Julian (Book VI *Against Julian*, chapter 4) clearly confirm this conjecture:

> “I do not know whom you accuse as having been converted, or returned, to the Catholic faith, as though they were deserters from your doctrine. Yet you have indicated that you fear them so greatly that you did not dare to express their names, lest perhaps, when they heard from you their false crimes, they should immediately return to you accusations which, if not true, would at least be more credible. Whoever these men are—men of serious judgment—they would not do this, and, in accordance with the Apostle, they would spare you: ‘Not returning abuse for abuse.’”

These words concern Sixtus, who held power in Rome at the time when they were written, shortly after the death of Zosimus.

Perhaps this is also why Prosper, after magnificently recounting what four predecessors of Sixtus had accomplished against the Pelagians, says:

> “We trust that, by God’s protection, what he accomplished through Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine, he will accomplish through Sixtus; and that, in the guardianship of the Lord’s flock, this portion of glory has been reserved for this shepherd: just as those men drove away the manifest wolves, so may he drive away the hidden ones, while there resounds in his ears the speech of that most learned old man, by which he encouraged his fellow-laborer, and so forth.”

This prudent form of speech and this artful manner of expression reveal, unless I am mistaken, that Prosper’s mind was somewhat doubtful about whether his predecessors had shown equal zeal in the cause he was pursuing.

Someone may find it astonishing that the ancients made no mention of books of this kind—whether Sixtus’s friends, such as Augustine; the critics of his works, such as Gennadius; or his contemporaries and near-contemporaries, such as Prosper and Fulgentius.

Yet Augustine was a friend of Jerome. When, however, did he mention either the letter to Ctesiphon or the *Dialogues*, works than which nothing better had been published against the Pelagians? Gennadius did indeed list Sixtus’s works, but carelessly and almost in passing, just as he did the works of Celestine, touching only upon those that were directed against Nestorius. Prosper, finally, is wholly devoted to his Augustine, and Fulgentius likewise; each of them seems to have forgotten the others. Nor is this unreasonable, since disciples ought to be devoted admirers of their master.

Moreover, Gennadius did not wish to speak about Sixtus, while Augustine was obliged to remain silent. For Gennadius was accustomed either to pass over in silence authors who had fought against Pelagius—or at least against the remnants of Pelagius’s teaching—however distinguished they might be, as in the case of Jerome; or to mention them reluctantly, as in the case of Prosper; or to honor them with malicious praise, as in the case of Augustine. Augustine himself, however, behaved differently toward Sixtus at different times. His praise of Sixtus while the latter held power in Rome was compelled by the needs of the times. His later abstention from praise was suggested by the change in circumstances after the death of Zosimus. The reason why he did not strongly commend Sixtus’s books was the character of the *Hypognosticon*: if he ever wished to recommend books to be read against the Pelagians, he could produce something better.

Add to this that a man as great as Augustine undoubtedly was—although, as that writer said, capable of every kind of praise—nevertheless, being born in Africa, seems to have retained to the very end of his life something, I know not whether of native poison or rather of native genius, by which Africans were accustomed to praise their own people and their own works above those of others. I do not recall having read anywhere that Augustine spontaneously praised any writer except his own Cyprian. He praised others once or twice, but only under the pressure of necessity: when he was answering Pelagius, who claimed that his doctrine was confirmed by the authority of the saints (*On the Grace of Christ*, and elsewhere); or when he was answering Julian, who objected that the Easterners agreed with him and that the doctrine of original sin was new and had recently been fabricated in Africa (*Books in Reply to Both*).

At the conclusion, a conjecture must not be omitted which, although it may appear slight at first sight, nevertheless truly possesses some weight. When Possidius lists Augustine’s works, he mentions one book against the questions of the Pelagianists. The question is: which single book was it? We know that Augustine wrote several short works on the questions of the Pelagianists: three books to Marcellinus; one letter to Hilary; the book *On the Perfection of Justice* to Paul and Eutropius; one letter to Optatus; two books to Albina, Pinianus, and Melania; one letter to Paulinus; another to Mercator; and two books to Count Valerius. These and other works contained in the second part of the seventh volume are listed in the *Index*, along with one book against the Questions of the Pelagianists.

Yet we know of no book on the questions of the Pelagianists other than the *Hypognosticon*, which is wholly devoted to resolving them. Possidius, in my opinion, counted this book among the others because he found it among Augustine’s works without an author’s name, and therefore thought that all had the same author. He found it there, as one may conjecture, because it had been sent by Sixtus to Augustine as to a friend—that is, without the author’s name, since the author was sufficiently well known by other means.

I believe that from this action of Possidius there arose the popular error by which, from that time onward, the *Hypognosticon* was regarded by less careful critics as an Augustinian work.

I understand that the contrary may be objected: in the manuscripts and printed editions there is not one book entitled *Hypognosticon*, but six, whereas Possidius mentions a single book. Yet the manuscripts themselves dispel the objection, since the better manuscripts show no division into books, but merely parts separated under that title: “On the First Article,” “On the Second Article,” and so forth.

## PART TWO. ON THE WRITINGS OF THE ENEMIES OF THE FAITH, IN DEFENSE OF THE PELAGIAN HERESY, DURING THE LIFETIME OF SAINT AUGUSTINE

[Col. 0585]

[Col. 0585B] Thus far we have examined what the five most holy defenders of the faith wrote against the Pelagian heresy during Augustine’s lifetime and at what times they wrote it; for it is necessary to count Mercator among the other four.
