We must next consider what six enemies of the faith published in the meantime, and what God has willed to survive from their books, as though a trophy had been erected from the rich spoils of the enemies, in honor of Christ’s grace.

The whole labor involved in gathering from every quarter the fragments, as it were, of broken weapons may yield some benefit, since it will thereby become clear at what times particular questions were agitated, on what occasions the books were written, and through what stages the heresy increased. The third of these matters, however, belongs more properly to the following dissertation, for which this appendix will provide sufficient material.

The first thing to be noted concerning the writings of the enemies of the faith is that various works were published by various authors and at different times, yet that one spirit pervades them all: a spirit that is proud, deceitful, and crafty. None of these men fails to boast of himself and his associates; none fails to despise others; none fails to heap insults upon his opponents; none fails to flatter the powerful; none fails, through querulous falsehoods, to claim that he suffers the injury which he himself inflicts; none fails to conceal his true mind and to invoke the tradition of the Fathers; none fails to claim for himself an understanding of Scripture while attributing ignorance, dullness of intellect, madness, and depravity of character to those who disagree with him.

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Writings of Theodore, Bishop of Mopsuestia, and Rufinus, Presbyter of the Province of Palestine, a Disciple of Theodore and Teacher of Pelagius

Of the works which either author composed in support of Pelagian doctrines, nothing survives except Theodore’s five books—or rather, fragments of books—against Augustine, and Rufinus’s *Little Book of the Faith* together with twelve anathemas. For the fragments of Theodore that we shall present in the latter part of Mercator’s works were collected from fifteen books *On the Incarnation* and on related matters.

Since enough has been said in the appropriate place concerning Rufinus’s confession and the other short works of both heretics, I think that the following five points should now be briefly observed.

First, although the Pelagians raised four principal questions—whence comes the mortality of the human race; whether the sin of the first parent is transmitted to posterity; what human nature by itself can accomplish toward a good work; and whether God’s grace is given on the basis of merits—only the first two were discussed by Theodore and Rufinus. Rufinus did, however, touch somewhat upon the perfection of justice in his second anathema, in which he condemned those who affirmed that any holy man, whether prophetic or apostolic, could be perfect without God’s help. In this he seems to have anticipated Julian and others who later attributed the beginning of justice to free will and its perfection to God’s assistance.

Second, Theodore and Rufinus forged and handed over to their followers the weapons with which the Catholic defenders of the two doctrines mentioned above were to be attacked: whether arguments distorted from Scripture into perverse meanings, or arguments derived from human reasoning. Thus Theodore was rightly called the teacher of Pelagius, Coelestius, and Julian, both by Mercator and by John Maxentius; and Mercator was likewise right to call those three men disciples of Rufinus.

Third, in later times the Pelagians scarcely attempted any objections or evasions that they had not learned from Rufinus. Theodore may therefore rightly be called the author of Pelagian impiety, and Rufinus the author of its craftiness.

Fourth, before the Pelagian heresy came to the West, its condition in the East was such that the first two principal doctrines were maintained with great vehemence, while the third was treated more mildly. Such, then, was the state of affairs in the East before the year 400.

Finally, although Theodore composed a five-book work (*opus πεντάβιβλον*) against Saint Augustine a few years before his death, he had nevertheless transmitted his doctrines either in writings that have perished or in private conversation among his disciples. From these Rufinus and others after him derived their teaching. On closer consideration of Theodore’s work, I judge that it was written against Augustine alone; yet in such a way that Theodore made Jerome the author of the doctrine and Augustine its defender. On this interpretation, whatever conflict and disagreement appears between Mercator and Photius is removed. See the notes on the fragments of the work.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the Writings of the Monk Pelagius, a Disciple of Rufinus and Teacher of Coelestius

What Pelagius wrote, and on the testimony of which authors the individual works are attributed to him, has been stated elsewhere (Dissertation I, chapter 4). We must now present what survives and assign to each work its chronological indications.

### Three Books on the Trinity

[Col. 0587B]

Gennadius, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* (chapter 42), says:

> “Pelagius, the heresiarch, before he was exposed as a heretic, wrote three books on the faith of the Trinity, necessary for learned men,” and so forth.

From this we have gathered, as far as possible, the time at which they were written (the dissertation cited above): namely, before the arrival in Rome of Rufinus the Syrian, whom Pelagius used as a teacher of error, and therefore before the time of Pope Anastasius; but not before Siricius, nor while Damasus was still alive and there was a close relationship between Jerome and Pelagius. Otherwise Jerome would not have omitted the name of his friend Pelagius from the catalogue of writers which he completed in the year 392—that is, in the fourteenth year of Theodosius and the eighth of Siricius. At that time Pelagius had not yet revealed his heresy, but enjoyed a reputation for holiness and learning.

Nothing survives from these three books except Gennadius’s testimony. At that period, however, all ecclesiastical writers who wished to be heard were publishing books on the Trinity, because the two heresies, Arianism and Macedonianism, had not yet been entirely extinguished. Each man longed to defend the Nicene and Constantinopolitan creeds and thereby prove himself orthodox. For at that time, as the testimony of the ancients shows, the confession of the *ὁμοούσιον*—the consubstantiality—was the established and public profession of orthodoxy.

Pelagius, moreover, made his view of the Trinity clear enough in his *Little Book of the Faith*. He agrees with Theodore of Mopsuestia concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, although he conceals the error. “We believe,” he says, “also in the Holy Spirit, true God proceeding from the Father.” See the notes on the *Little Book of the Faith*.

### Brief Expositions on All the Epistles of the Apostle Paul

Augustine mentions this work in Book III of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapters 1 and 12, and in the book *On the Proceedings at Palestine*, chapter 16; Mercator mentions it in chapter 2 of the *Commonitorium* and in the preface to the *Annotations*; the author of the *Predestined Heresy* mentions it under heresy 88; and Cassiodorus mentions it in chapter 8 of the *Divine Readings*. They attributed it to Pelagius as to its indisputable author, and this attribution is now beyond controversy.

At one time, however, it was attributed to Gelasius, as some people seem to have inferred from Cassiodorus’s words. Certainly credulous antiquity attributed it to Jerome and inserted it among his works, as it did most of the other works of Pelagius, including the *Little Book of the Faith* and the letter to Demetrias. In this way it transmitted the work to us, although it would otherwise easily have perished, had it not falsely claimed a name worthy of eternity.

Nor was this credulity or false attribution a crime of a later age. Primasius seems to me to have assigned these brief commentaries to Jerome without ambiguity. Primasius lived in the sixth century. In commenting on Paul’s words in Romans 3, “As it is written, ‘That you may be justified in your words,’” and so forth, he introduces David as speaking in this way:

> “While you accuse me as guilty of an enormous transgression, through the prophet you prove that you are concerned with our works, and you overcome those who judged you indifferent to human actions.”

He adds:

> “Therefore, concerning this sense of the Apostle, I have set down the entire exposition of a certain holy man, so that the reader’s concern might be more fully instructed; and wherever I found it in this form, I have inserted full pages here for the sake of instruction.”

The man whom he praises, whose full pages he inserted into his work, was neither Ambrose—for Ambrose said nothing of this kind—nor Augustine, either for the same reason or because Primasius usually names him explicitly. Jerome, therefore, seems to have been intended. Primasius wished to derive his commentaries from these three writers.

Yet the words he quoted are found in Pelagius, in his exposition of the same passage. Pelagius wrote as follows:

> “You have proved that you are concerned with human beings, since through the Prophet you have revealed my hidden things, and you have overcome those who pretend that you are indifferent to human actions.”

Thus Primasius took Pelagius for Jerome and attributed the exposition of one writer to another—not, I believe, on private judgment, but in accordance with common belief. By the sixth century, therefore, those brief expositions of Pelagius had already been attributed to Jerome.

This conjecture is supported by the fact that he calls the work from which he transferred the quoted sentence “expositions,” which is the title under which Pelagius’s scholia are known. He also says that he repeatedly inserted full pages from it; and he did in fact insert complete passages from Pelagius.

I have said that Augustine read this work, and read it carefully, since at different times he quoted several passages from it. Yet he criticized only two things: the first, a statement made in another person’s voice against original sin (*Book III to Marcellinus*, chapter 1); the second, a statement made in Pelagius’s own voice concerning the meaning of the apostolic sentence, “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (*On the Proceedings at Palestine*, chapters 15 and 16). He raises no objection concerning grace and free will, nothing concerning the law and the perfection of justice, and nothing concerning the thicket of sinful concupiscence. It is therefore astonishing that Vossius, and those who almost copied Vossius, should have been more clear-sighted than their supposed master, and should have boldly written that the doctrines for which Pelagius was reproved are contained, most of them in the clearest words and without any ambiguity, in these very brief expositions.

The work was also read, unless my opinion deceives me, by Jerome. How could a diligent man have failed to know of a work so widely praised by Pelagius’s followers, especially one whose brevity was set against Jerome’s prolixity? Yet nothing was excerpted from it for inclusion in the book of accusation, which was certainly composed at Jerome’s house—either because the readers saw nothing worthy of criticism, or because there was another reason, especially this: that Pelagius’s complaint could have had force concerning these books, which had not been reviewed by Anianus—that some short works of his had either been secretly taken away or extorted from him by entreaty before they were corrected.

The work was certainly read and partly corrected by Cassiodorus, as we have shown in the notes on chapter 2 of the *Commonitorium*. For this exceptionally learned man removed from the commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans whatever Pelagius held against the Catholic faith. He thereby gave his successors an example, and almost an instruction, to do the same in the expositions of the other epistles, so that the work—at once highly subtle and very brief—might be read with greater security.

It is credible, if not certain, that the commentaries we possess, whether in printed editions or manuscript codices, were copied from the corrections of Cassiodorus and his disciples. I was astonished when I considered that some people call these very expositions on the Epistle to the Romans, even after they had been purged by Cassiodorus, a man especially Catholic, a kind of Hydra of Pelagian heresies and a sewer of filth vomited forth by that impure heresiarch. What is more, Primasius of Saint Augustine, as devoted a disciple as Fulgentius, transferred or rather copied into his own commentaries a great many passages from those very places that are accused of error.

No one can read the work without easily judging that it is written in a humbler style than either the book *On Nature*, the letter to Demetrias, or the books *On Free Will*. Pelagius published these in another person’s style, but the former in his own, as we have shown in several places. Thus Jerome’s judgment concerning Pelagius’s childishness does not conflict with the praise others gave him for eloquence. Jerome judged what the barbarian from Scotland could accomplish by himself in the Latin language; the others judged what shone forth in the works mentioned above.

This work must have been completed by Pelagius before the year 412, since Augustine read it when he wrote to Marcellinus in the year 412. Mercator reports that it was published before the devastation of Rome, which occurred in 410; indeed, he says that it was composed immediately after Pelagius had been taught by Rufinus the Syrian the doctrine opposed to Catholic teaching concerning the mortality of the human race and the transmission of sin—something that occurred in the time of Pope Anastasius.

To make clear how much alteration Cassiodorus introduced, I thought it appropriate to set out *παραλλήλως*—in parallel—the text found in the commonly circulated manuscripts, after Cassiodorus’s correction, and the text written by Pelagius, as reported by Marius and also by Augustine.

[Note: The following texts, headed “PELAGIUS ACCORDING TO MERCATOR” and “PELAGIUS IN THE MANUSCRIPTS CORRECTED BY CASSIODORUS, AS THEY NOW EXIST,” are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### PELAGIUS ACCORDING TO MERCATOR

“Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death” (Romans 5:12). He says that he used an example or image: just as, when sin did not exist, it entered through Adam, so also, when righteousness had remained in no one, life was restored through Christ.

[Col. 0589D] “And death passed to all human beings” (ibid.). He says: Since those who sin likewise die, death did not pass into Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob, concerning whom the Lord says, “For all live to him” (Luke 20:38). Here, he says, he calls all dead because, amid the multitude of sinners, the few righteous are not excepted, just as he says there, “There is none who does good, not even one” (Psalm 52:2, 4). And again he says, “Every man is a liar” (Psalm 115:11). Or certainly death passed to all who lived according to human custom, not heavenly custom.

[Col. 0590D] “But death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Romans 5:14). Either, he says, when there was no one to distinguish between the just and the unjust, death thought that it ruled over everyone; or it reigned over those who transgressed a commandment as Adam did—that is, among the sons of Noah, who were commanded not to eat the soul in the blood, and among the sons of Abraham, who were commanded to practice circumcision—but also over those who, apart from a commandment, had despised the natural law.

[Col. 0591B] “Who is the form of the one to come” (ibid.). He says: Just as Adam was formed by God without sexual intercourse, so Christ proceeded from a Virgin, the Holy Spirit fashioning him. Or, as some say, he is a form by contrast: just as the former is the head of sin, so the latter is the head of righteousness.

[Col. 0591C] “But not as the transgression, so also the gift” (ibid.). He says this lest equality be thought to exist in the form.

“For if, through the transgression of one, many died, much more did the gift and grace of God abound to many through one man, Christ” (ibid. 15). The Apostle says that grace was more powerful in giving life than sin was in killing, because Adam killed not only himself but also his descendants, whereas Christ liberated both those who were then in the body and those who would exist afterward.

[Col. 0592A] He says: Those who hold a contrary view concerning the transmission of sin attempt vehemently to attack those who defend its transmission. “If,” they say, “Adam’s sin harmed even those who do not sin, then Christ’s righteousness also benefits those who do not believe, since the Apostle says in the same way—or rather, even more—that through one man people are liberated than previously perished through one man.” Then they say:

[Col. 0592B] “If baptism cleanses that ancient and long-standing sin, then those born from two baptized parents ought to be free from this sin; for they cannot transmit to their descendants what they themselves did not possess. Moreover, they add: If the soul is not transmitted by descent, as indeed it is not, but only the flesh possesses the transmission of sin, then only the flesh deserves punishment. For it is unjust that a soul born today, not from Adam’s stock, should bear another’s ancient sin. Indeed, it is reasonable that God, who forgives personal sins, should not impute another’s.”

And again, in another discourse, Pelagius says:

“If a sinner begot a sinner, so that the original sin of his infant might be absolved when the child received baptism, then a righteous man ought to beget a righteous man. If parents, after their conversion, do not harm their own children through their personal sins, then much less can they harm their children through those sins. If it happened to the first man that he was the cause of death, then after Christ’s coming no one ought to die. If death arose through Adam’s sin, we would never die after the remission of sins which our liberator granted us. Adam’s sin therefore had greater power in killing absolutely all human beings than Christ’s grace had in saving them, since grace benefited not everyone but only believers; for not all who are born from Adam are reborn in Christ.”

### PELAGIUS IN THE MANUSCRIPTS CORRECTED BY CASSIODORUS, AS THEY NOW EXIST

[Col. 0589B]

“As through one man, and so forth. If through one person, Eve, sin entered into the world, those who say that sin existed in the world before the devil deceived Eve are insane. Likewise, here he wishes to show that Christ suffered for this reason: so that we, who by following Adam had departed from God, might be reconciled to God through Christ. ‘Into this world sin,’ and so forth. ‘By example or form.’ Just as, when sin did not exist, it came through Adam, so also, when scarcely any righteousness remained in anyone, it was recalled through Christ; and just as death entered through the former’s sin, so life was restored through the latter’s righteousness—future life, not present life.

[Col. 0589D] ‘And so into all,’ and so forth. While they sin in this way, they likewise die; for death did not pass into Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, concerning whom the Lord says, ‘For all those live.’ Here he says ‘all dead’ because among the multitude of sinners the few righteous are not excepted, as in the passage, ‘There is none who does good, not even one,’ and ‘Every man is a liar.’ [Col. 0590A] Or it passed into all who lived according to a human, not a heavenly, manner. Likewise, the Apostle now signifies the death of the soul, because Adam died when he transgressed, just as the prophet also says: ‘The soul that sins shall itself die’ (Ezekiel 18:4). For it also passed into all human beings who transgressed the natural law.

‘In which,’ and so forth. That is, in that all sinned; he sins after the example of Adam [perhaps: ‘of Adam who sinned’].

‘Until the law,’ and so forth. The law, the avenger of sin, arrived; before its arrival, they sinned more freely [perhaps: ‘because they enjoyed the length of the present life,’ etc.]. Sin existed before the law, but it was not considered to be sin to the same extent, because it had already been almost obliterated from human nature. Likewise, by saying ‘until the law,’ he signifies Moses; and by adding ‘sin is not imputed when there is no law,’ he again indicates the natural law, through which Cain transgressed, and after him those who transgressed the natural law.

‘But sin,’ and so forth. How did death reign if sin was not imputed? Unless one understands that it was not imputed in the present life.

[Col. 0590D] ‘But death reigned,’ and so forth. Either, while there was no one to distinguish between the just and the unjust, death thought that it ruled over everyone; or it reigned not only over those who transgressed a commandment as Adam did—that is, among the sons of Noah, who were commanded not to eat the soul in the blood, and among the sons of Abraham, who were commanded to practice circumcision—[Col. 0591A] but also over those who, without a commandment, despised the law of nature.

‘Even over those who did not sin in the likeness,’ and so forth. These are those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression: [Col. 0591B] they transgressed through the natural law and not, like Adam, through a commandment.

‘Who is,’ and so forth. He was a form of Christ either because, just as Adam was made by God without sexual intercourse, so Christ proceeded from a Virgin through the operation of the Holy Spirit; or because some say that he was a form by contrast: just as Adam was the head of sin, so Christ was the head of righteousness. Likewise, Adam was made a form of Christ: for just as the first Adam, transgressing God’s commandment, is an example to those who wish to transgress God’s law, so Christ, fulfilling the Father’s will, is an example to those who desire to imitate him.

‘But not,’ and so forth. This is said lest equality be thought to exist in the form.

‘For if many died through the offense of one, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of one man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many,’ and so forth. Here he plainly teaches that he is not speaking generally about every human being, saying, ‘Many died through the offense of one’; for by the common and natural death not only sinners but also the righteous die.”

### One Book of Testimonies

[Col. 0593A]

Gennadius, in the place cited shortly before, says:

> “He also wrote, for the practical conduct of life, one book of Eulogies drawn from the divine Scriptures, marked out by an index of chapters in the manner of Saint Cyprian the martyr.”

Seven points seem to deserve attention concerning this work.

First, Pelagius professed himself an imitator—or rather, a fulfiller—of the work of the blessed martyr Cyprian, who wrote to Quirinus. Hence Augustine says (*Book IV to Boniface*, chapter 8):

> “Pelagius, the heresiarch of these men, certainly mentions Cyprian with the honor due to him. When writing a book of testimonies, he asserts that he is imitating him, saying that he is doing for Romanus what Cyprian did for Quirinus.”

Pelagius therefore set out sentences under individual headings and proved them by appended testimonies from Scripture, following the method of the holy martyr. This is why the work is sometimes called *Eulogies*, sometimes *Testimonies*, and sometimes *Titles and Chapters*.

Second, since Cyprian wrote three books of *Testimonies*, it appears that Pelagius added a fourth, completing the martyr’s third book and combining them all into one finished work, to be read by those devoted to a holier life as a compendium of heavenly precepts (Cyprian, preface to his work). For Cyprian’s first two books argue against the Jews concerning the faith, whereas the third concerns religious discipline, or, as Gennadius puts it, practical conduct.

Third, Pelagius did all this maliciously, gradually and imperceptibly drawing unwary minds toward his own party through their reading of Cyprian. He twisted into a perverse meaning many statements made by the holy martyr in a Catholic but ambiguous sense. Such statements include the twelfth title, “That one must not swear”; the forty-second, “That faith benefits entirely, and that we can do only as much as we believe”; the forty-ninth, “That even enemies must be loved”; the fifty-second, “That the freedom to believe or not to believe is placed in the will”; the sixty-first, “The desire to possess, and that money must not be desired”; and the sixty-fifth, “That all sins are laid down in baptism”; the seventy-seventh, “That the sinner must be rebuked publicly,” and so forth. For at that time he was giving birth to a heresy that would spread throughout the entire world.

Fourth, the same book contained two statements which Augustine refutes in his letter to Hilary: that one must never swear at all, and that a rich man living in his wealth cannot enter the kingdom of God unless he sells all that he possesses, and that it does him no good if he happens to fulfill the commandments from those riches. Pelagius wished both statements to appear to have been taken from Cyprian, and the first indeed was taken in the same words from the third book, title 12, though the sentence was somewhat twisted and even corrupted.

Fifth, a large part of what the Gallic bishops charged Pelagius with was drawn from this same book. It is therefore astonishing that Gennadius wrote that this work was necessary for learned men. Did Gennadius not thereby rather reveal his own partiality toward Pelagius and make his own reliability suspect?

Sixth, the statements drawn from that work and charged against Pelagius had been explained by him so craftily that they seemed to the Fathers at Diospolis to have a tolerable meaning, although in reality they had an exceedingly perverse one, as Augustine perceived with subtle insight. For this reason, Pelagius’s interpretation will be placed under each title wherever it has been preserved.

Finally, Gennadius entitled this work *Eulogies*, or *On Practical Conduct*—that is, on the active life or on the duties of the virtues, which at that point concerned not God but one’s neighbors. Julianus Pomerius used the word in this sense in the second book of the work commonly called *On the Contemplative Life*. The work is still attributed by some, remarkably, to Prosper, despite the clear authority both of Isidore and of the manuscript evidence.

The number affixed to the titles in Jerome (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 42) is certainly corrupt; yet it cannot be corrected without a laborious comparison of manuscript codices, for which the reward seems very small. It is not insignificant, however, if one considers more carefully Jerome’s observations on each title. One will perceive, not without intellectual pleasure, that they are still greatly useful in our own time. It will also be quite helpful to consult Augustine’s observations on each of Pelagius’s interpretations in the book *On the Proceedings at Palestine*.

### TITLE

**That no one can be without sin unless he has knowledge of the law** (Jerome, *Dialogue* 1).

**Pelagius’s Interpretation** (Augustine, *On the Proceedings at Palestine*, chapter 1):

> “I did indeed say this, but not in the way they understand it. I did not say that whoever has knowledge of the law cannot sin, but that through knowledge of the law one is helped not to sin, as it is written: ‘He gave them the law for assistance’ (Isaiah 8:20, according to…
the Septuagint (LXX).

# TITLE

Women too ought to possess knowledge of the law and ought also to sing psalms to God (Jerome, same work).

# TITLE XIV

A servant of God ought to let nothing bitter proceed from his mouth, but should always [Col. 0594C] utter what is sweet and agreeable (same work).

# TITLE XXI

A priest or teacher ought to watch over everyone’s conduct and rebuke sinners boldly, lest he have to render an account for them and their blood be required from his hands.

# TITLE XXXI

A priest or teacher ought to flatter no one, but should rebuke everyone courageously, lest he destroy both himself and those who listen to him.

# TITLE LXXII

Everyone is governed by his own will, and each person is left to his own desire (Augustine, *Book on the Proceedings at Palestine*, chapter 2).

On this very subject, the Wisdom of Solomon says (Wisdom 7:1 and following) [Col. 0594D]:

> I too am a mortal human being like everyone else, and descended from the earthly one who was formed first; in my mother’s womb I was fashioned as flesh for a period of ten months, coagulated in blood from human seed and the pleasure of sleep that accompanies it. And when I was born, I received the common air, and fell upon the similarly formed earth, uttering my first cry like everyone else. For no king has had any other beginning of birth. There is therefore one entrance into life for all, and a similar departure. For this reason I prayed, and understanding was given to me; I called, and the spirit of wisdom came to me.

And the Psalmist says (Psalm 108:18):

> He loved cursing, and it shall come upon him; he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him.

And Ecclesiasticus says (Ecclesiasticus 15:17):

> He has set before you water and fire; stretch out your hand toward whichever you wish. Before a human being are good and evil, life and death; whatever pleases him shall be given to him.

**Pelagius’s interpretation:** I said this on account of free choice, for which God is the helper of the person choosing good; but when a person sins, he himself is at fault, as belonging to free choice.

# TITLE LXXIII

On the day of judgment, the wicked and sinners are not to be spared (Jerome, same work; Augustine, same work, chapter 3), but are to be consumed by eternal fires. For it is written in Psalm 103:

> Let sinners perish from the earth, and the wicked, so that they are no more.

And in Isaiah:

> The wicked and sinners shall be burned together, and those who abandon God shall be utterly consumed.

**Pelagius’s interpretation:** I said this according to the Gospel, where it is said of sinners:

> These shall go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Matthew 25:46).

And if anyone believes otherwise, he is an Origenist.

# TITLE LXXXI

No one can know wisdom and the understanding of the Scriptures unless he has learned them; and an uneducated person ought not to usurp knowledge of the law (Jerome, same work).

# TITLE LXXXIII

A Christian ought to possess such patience that, if someone wishes to take away what belongs to him, he willingly gives it up; and the display of clothing and ornaments is contrary to God.

> To the one who wishes to go to court with you and take your tunic, leave him your cloak as well.

# TITLE CLXIV

Enemies are to be loved as neighbors. Luke 5:

> Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you; bless those who curse you, and pray for those who slander you.

# TITLE CLXV

One must never trust an enemy.

# TITLE CXXIII

The kingdom of heaven was also promised in the Old Testament (Jerome, same work; Augustine, same work, chapter 5).

**Pelagius’s interpretation:** This too can be proved from the Scriptures. Heretics deny it in order to insult the Old Testament; but I, following the authority of the Scriptures, said it because it is written in the prophet Daniel (Daniel 7:18):

> And the saints shall receive the kingdom of the Most High.

# TITLE C

A human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments, if he wishes (Jerome, same work; Augustine, same work, [Col. 0595D] chapter 6).

**Pelagius’s interpretation:** We said that a human being can indeed be without sin and can keep God’s commandments, if he wishes, for God gave him this possibility. But we did not say that anyone is found who, from infancy to old age, has never sinned. Rather, after turning away from sins, a person can, through his own labor and God’s grace, be without sin, though even on this account he is not thereafter incapable of turning back.

# TITLE CXXIII

One must not sin even lightly.

# TITLE CXXXI

Evil ought not even to be thought.

Matthew 5:

> Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

**Pelagius’s interpretation:** We did not state this in that way [Col. 0596A], but said that a Christian ought to take care lest he think evil. The Gallican bishops had objected as though he had said that evil must not even enter one’s thoughts.

# Letter to the holy bishop Paulinus of Nola

Augustine mentions this letter when writing to Paulinus in these words (Letter 106):

> He also deals with this in a certain letter addressed to Your Reverence, where he says that he ought not to be considered to defend free choice without the grace of God, since he said that the possibility of willing and acting—without which we are unable to will or do anything good—was implanted in us by the Creator. Thus, according to the author himself, this is understood as the grace of God that is common to pagans and Christians, to the impious and the pious, to believers and unbelievers.

He also refers to it in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 35, where the following seems worth transcribing:

> Let them read, he says, the letter that we wrote nearly twelve years ago to the holy man Bishop Paulinus. In perhaps three hundred lines it confesses nothing other than the grace and help of God, while nevertheless maintaining that we are able to do good without God. I therefore read this letter and found that throughout almost the whole of it he dwells on the power and possibility of nature, and establishes the grace of God almost nowhere except there. But he touches upon Christian grace with such brevity, merely mentioning the name, that he seems to have feared to speak of it at all. Whether, however, he wishes it to be understood as the forgiveness of sins, or also as the teaching of Christ—where there is also the example of his conduct, which he presents in several places in his brief works—or whether he believes that some assistance in doing good is added to nature and teaching through the inspiration of the most ardent and luminous charity, is not at all clear.

From this the date of the letter is established. For Pelagius wrote what we have just quoted in the year 417; therefore the letter he had written nearly twelve years earlier must have been written in the year 405.

It is also established that at that time Pelagius concealed his mind and opinion concerning the grace of Christ so carefully [Col. 0596C] that not even Augustine was able to understand what he had in mind. Hence one may rightly wonder at the perspicacity of those who discerned errors in Pelagius’s expositions that neither Augustine detected nor Pelagius wished to reveal, even many years later. Thus, when Augustine appears to criticize him in writing to Paulinus, he is in fact making a suspicion based on some prejudice arising elsewhere rather than from the letter itself.

It is likewise clear on what occasion Augustine wrote to Paulinus. He saw, evidently, what danger Pelagius posed to a man easily captivated by an appearance of piety. As he loved Paulinus both for his faith and for himself, Augustine thought this danger had to be forestalled and employed a precaution all the more necessary because Paulinus could reasonably have been suspected: he had long concealed from a friend, despite repeated letters, what relationship he maintained with Pelagius, and at Nola he tolerated Pelagius’s disciples, even the most obstinate, freely defending their doctrines. Yet because there was nothing in Pelagius’s letter that openly attacked the grace of God, Augustine did not undertake to refute it point by point. Instead, content to explain the profound mystery of gratuitous predestination, he warned Paulinus about the condemnation of Pelagius by the Fathers at Diospolis and by the apostolic see, and about the doctrines that must be confessed if the Catholic faith was to be preserved.

Finally, the condition of the Pelagian heresy in the year 405 is clear. The treatment of grace was cautious, and ambiguous words were employed to test people’s minds. After they had become somewhat entangled in questions concerning the beginning of faith and other matters apparently less serious, they were gradually and imperceptibly led into error concerning the powers of nature for works of piety, because of what Augustine calls the inescapable chain of doctrines that mutually fit together by their own logic.

# Letter to Bishop Constantius

As far as I know, this letter is mentioned nowhere [Col. 0597A] except in *On the Grace of Christ*, whose chapter 36 contains these words, whether Pelagius’s or Augustine’s:

> Let them also read what I wrote to the holy Bishop Constantius, where I joined God’s grace and assistance briefly but plainly to human free choice.

As I said above, I have not read this letter. But if it is not unlike the others that he mentions and that are known to me, it too contains nothing of what we are seeking.

Who Constantius was, and over which church he presided, no one can determine, since no synods held in Italy at that time are known whose acts have come down to us. I nevertheless conjecture that he was distinguished either by nobility of birth or by a reputation for holiness. For Pelagius wrote to such men in order— as we have noted more than once—either to secure for himself the reputation of a good man or to obtain a patron for his impiety.

It should be noted, however, that the slippery heretic, in pretending to hold the true faith, appealed to letters that he had given to three men whose renown would strike the eyes of his opponents; but he kept silent about the books by which he could easily [Col. 0597B] have been convicted. The letters had evidently been composed with such art that, being capable of being bent toward opposite meanings, they presented him as Catholic to Catholics and as a heretic to heretics.

This letter must have been written after the letter to Paulinus but before the book *On the Institution of a Virgin* addressed to Demetrias. The chronological order seems to have been preserved in the recension. It therefore appears to have been written before Pelagius began his flight from the city of Rome in 408, for at that time he had begun to speak more openly. It must therefore date from approximately 406. Since nothing of the letter itself survives, the condition of the still-concealing heresy cannot be disclosed from it.

# One book, or perhaps two, consolatory and exhortatory, addressed to a widow

Hieronymus mentions this work in his third dialogue; Augustine in *The Proceedings at Palestine*, chapter 6; and Mercator in the *Memorandum*, chapter 4. At that place we have noted many matters relevant to it, which you may consult.

From this you will recognize that the widow to whom the work is addressed was called Livania by Mercator, but was believed by some to be either Melania the Elder or Juliana, the wife of Memorius. You will likewise recognize that the widow was praised with such lowly flattery that Pelagius himself, whatever the reason, was ashamed to admit the work as his own; indeed, he condemned its author for foolish speech. Nevertheless, that he lied in this was demonstrated by books consulted by Augustine and by trustworthy men who were friends of Pelagius.

A not implausible conjecture concerning the widow has now arisen: namely, that she was either Juliana, the mother of Demetrias, or Albina, the mother-in-law of Pinianus. As for Juliana, it is credible that she asked Pelagius to provide the instruction of a virgin for her daughter Demetrias because she had previously received from him a rule for widows. Moreover, several men distinguished for learning and piety wrote to Juliana about widowhood, among whom Pelagius wished to be seen—partly because of his own vanity and partly because of a certain rivalry with Augustine.

Albina, for her part, was already connected with Pelagius when he was established at Rome [Col. 0597D], by a kind of pious bond of necessity. Therefore, as soon as it became possible for her to address him in person at Jerusalem, she insistently urged him to remove the odium of heresy that had been fastened upon him; from him she obtained not only the confession contained in the first chapter of the first book of *On the Grace of Christ*, but perhaps also the whole of the defense that he sent to Rome.

What if there were two books addressed to the widow, one consolatory and the other exhortatory, and both were said to have been sent to some Juliana—but the consolatory one to the wife of Memorius, and the exhortatory one to the mother of Demetrias? Certainly the widow’s name was inscribed on neither book, as is clear from the manuscript that Augustine read. Nevertheless, this entire conjecture about two books may seem weak, since one book could at the same time have been consolatory on the death of her husband and exhortatory toward a life worthy of a Christian widow.

But there is another matter of far greater weight—indeed, of such importance that it almost compels me, abandoning my former opinion that the widow was Juliana, the wife of Memorius and mother of the heretic Julian, to adopt the contrary view that she was the parent of Demetrias, whose husband Olybrius died before the destruction of the City, according to Jerome. If this conjecture appears probable—as it very much does—this work addressed to the widow must be said to have been composed either at Rome, before Pelagius left there with the others in fear, or in Sicily, where he first arrived. On this reckoning it belongs either to the year 408 or to the following year.

## What survives of this book in authors of the same age

It befits a maidservant of Christ to follow simplicity—not the sort that is more folly than simplicity, but that of which Scripture says (Proverbs 11:25, according to the Septuagint):

> Blessed is every simple soul.

And elsewhere Scripture says (Deuteronomy 27:26 and Galatians 3:10):

> Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them.

From this it is shown that true simplicity is not that which scorns God’s commandments with senseless security, but that which guards the precepts of the law with wise fear. For when Scripture says that the one who does not remain in the things written there is accursed, it does not, conversely, wish the one who has not kept all the commandments to be called blessed. And if every simple person is blessed, then the simple person is one who has fulfilled all the precepts of the law.

To hate, curse, envy, lie, slander, and believe those who slander is considered a light or even no sin. But those who think this have forgotten that we read that people are liable to be consigned to Gehenna even for violating a light commandment. For it is clear that the Lord said (Matthew 5:22):

> Whoever says to his brother, “Fool” or “Raca,” shall be guilty of Gehenna.

Let piety find a place with you where it has found one nowhere else; let justice, an exile everywhere, find a dwelling with you (Book on the Proceedings at Palestine, chapter 6). Let truth, which no one now knows, become domestic and friendly to you; let the law of God, which almost everyone despises, be honored by you alone.

O how fortunate and blessed you would be if justice—which is believed to exist only in heaven—were found on earth in you alone!

For that person rightly raises his hands to God, and that person pours forth prayers with a good conscience, who can say:

> For you know, Lord, how holy, how innocent, how pure of every fraud, injury, and robbery are the hands that I stretch out to you; how just and undefiled, and free from every lie, are the lips with which I pour out prayers to you, that you may have mercy on me.

These words are found somewhat differently in *The Proceedings at Palestine*:

> That person raises his hands worthily to God, and that person pours forth prayer with a good conscience, who can say: You know, Lord, how holy and innocent and clean of every wickedness, injustice, and robbery are the hands that I extend to you; how just and clean, and free from every lie, are the lips with which I offer supplication to you, that you may have mercy on me.

# Book on Nature

Augustine mentions this work especially in three books: *On Nature and Grace*, *The Proceedings at Palestine*, chapter 33, and *Retractions*, chapter 4. Orosius also mentions it briefly in his *Apology*, as does Jerome in his third dialogue.

Pelagius composed it in Sicily, either through the work of Anianus or of Coelestius, and it was secretly delivered into the hands of trusted men. Accordingly, it was sent to Augustine by James and Timasius, two young men whom Pelagius’s exhortation had converted to the pursuit of a holier life, and who, after having imbibed error together with their commitment to piety, had been led out of it.

Five African bishops sent this book, together with their letter, to Pope Innocent for his examination:

> We have sent to Your Reverence a book which certain religious and honorable young servants of God gave us. We do not conceal their names, for they are called Timasius and James. As we have heard, and as Your Reverence already knows, they abandoned the hope they had in the world at the exhortation of Pelagius himself, and now serve God continently. When, by some effort of ours, with the Lord inspiring us, they had finally been freed from the same error [Col. 0599B], they produced this very book, saying that it was Pelagius’s, and urgently requested that a response be made to it. A response was written to them. They sent back a letter of thanks. We have sent both documents: the one to which the response was made and the response itself. And, so that we would not be excessively burdensome, we marked the places at which we ask that you not hesitate to inspect how, when challenged on the point that he denied the grace of God, he replied in such a way as to say that grace was nothing other than the nature in which God created us.

The supreme pontiff replied and branded the book he had read with the gravest condemnation (Patrologia, volume XX, column 593):

> We opened and examined the book said to be his, which Your Charity sent us. In it we found much blasphemy and nothing pleasing—nothing that was not utterly displeasing—so that it ought to be condemned and trampled upon by anyone. No one except the person who wrote such things could receive and entertain anything like them in his mind.

We present an excerpt from Saint Augustine’s *On Nature and Grace*, adding a preface from Sallust, from whom Augustine says it was taken, and also adding a very few other passages that seemed necessary to complete the meaning. These additions themselves are marked in a different typeface so that they would not mislead.

### Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 1

There are people who, although they ought to accuse the human will for their sins, instead accuse human nature and try to excuse themselves through it. Meanwhile they do not listen to Scripture, which praises God on every page, declares his work complete, and proclaims nature free from accusation.

If only they would at least listen to the words of a pagan:

> The human race, he says, falsely complains about its nature, claiming that it is weak and short-lived and governed more by chance than by virtue (Sallust, preface to the *War with Jugurtha*). For, if you reflect on the matter, you will find nothing greater or more excellent, and you will find that human beings lack industry more than they lack strength or time. Yet the mind is the guide and commander of mortal life. When it advances along the path toward the glory of virtue, it is sufficiently strong, powerful, and illustrious, and it has no need of fortune, since fortune can neither bestow nor take away uprightness, industry, or the other good arts. But if, captured by depraved desires, it is cast down into inactivity and bodily pleasures, and after indulging for a little while in destructive lust, its strength, time, age, and intelligence have ebbed away through negligence, then the weakness of nature is blamed: each person transfers his own fault to circumstances. [Col. 0599D] It is much less wicked to transfer the causes of one’s faults to circumstances than to transfer them to human nature, since circumstances are for the most part entangled by chance or by human thoughtlessness, whereas God, who is good and just, created nature.

### The same work, chapter 7

Accordingly, against those who seek a defense for their sins in the weakness of human nature, I say that a human being can be without sin, and that nature was so created by God that a person does not sin by necessity but by will. To treat the question rationally, one must distinguish at the outset between asking whether something can exist—which concerns possibility alone—and asking whether it actually exists. We are dealing only with possibility. Unless this has first been established with certainty, to pass on to another matter is highly improper and out of order.

I repeat the same point. I say that a human being can be without sin. What do you say? You say that a human being cannot be without sin. Neither do I say that a human being is without sin, nor do you say that no human being is without sin. We are arguing about can and cannot, not about is and is not. For “no one is clean from defilement” (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint), and “there is no human being who does not sin” (3 Kings 8:46), and “there is no righteous person on earth,” and “there is no one who does good” (Psalm 13:1), and other similar statements, prove nonexistence, not impossibility.

Such examples show what certain people were like at a particular time, not that they could not have been otherwise; hence they are rightly found to be culpable. For if they were such because they could not have been otherwise, they would be free of guilt.

### The same work, chapter 10

“You can indeed be without sin,” you will say, “but through the grace of God.” I thank your humanity for not merely failing to oppose or simply confessing my assertion, which you previously attacked, but also for not refusing to confirm it. For to say, “He can indeed be, but through this or that,” what else is it than not only agreeing that he can be, but also showing how or in what manner he can be? No one proves the possibility of anything more clearly than the person who also acknowledges its quality, since quality cannot exist without the thing itself.

“But here,” you will say, “because you do not mention the grace of God, you appear to reject it.” Do I reject it, when by confessing the thing I necessarily confess also that by which the thing can be brought about? Or do you reject it, when by denying the thing you unquestionably deny whatever it is through which the thing is brought about? Whether it is called grace, assistance, mercy, or whatever it is through which a human being can be without sin, whoever confesses the thing itself also confesses it.

### The same work, chapter 11

For if I say, “A human being can argue, a bird can fly, a hare can run,” and do not also mention what makes these things possible—that is, the tongue, wings, and feet—have I denied the qualities of these activities, when I have confessed the activities themselves?

### The same work, chapter 12

“But there are certain light sins,” you will say, “which, because they occur so frequently, cannot all be avoided.” Certainly they ought not to be reproved, not even with a light correction, if they cannot be avoided at all.

### The same work, chapter 13

“But are you yourself without sin?” you will say. Certainly not. But the fact that I am not without sin ought to be attributed to my negligence rather than to impossibility.

### The same work, chapters 14–15

What some people say—that the words “a human being can be without sin” are nowhere written in precisely this form, whereas it is written that no one can tame the tongue, and therefore that no one can be without the sin of the tongue—is easily refuted. The question is not what words are used to express each proposition.

When the apostle James says, “No human being can tame the tongue” (James 3:8), he speaks reproachfully, as though he were saying: “So, no human being can tame the tongue?” He is rebuking them and saying: “You can tame wild beasts, but you cannot tame tongues?”—as though taming the tongue were more difficult than taming wild beasts.

### The same work, chapter 17

“But,” you will say, “the Apostle said: ‘The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be; and those who are in the flesh cannot please God’” (Romans 8:7–8). But the Apostle plainly indicates that by “the wisdom of the flesh” he means not the wisdom that descends from above, and that by “being in the flesh” he means not those who have not departed from the body, but those who live according to the flesh.

You will continue to object: “At least the sins of ignorance cannot be avoided, whatever may be said about the possibility of avoiding other sins.” I admit that sins of ignorance cannot be avoided as long as a person is ignorant. But he ought to be vigilant beforehand so that he does not remain ignorant. Ignorance is therefore blameworthy because, through his own negligence, a person does not know what he ought to have known had he applied diligence.

### The same work, chapter 18

You will also add: “Certainly a human being cannot remove sins that have already been committed; rather, they must be expiated, and the Lord must be entreated on their behalf.” I willingly admit this, because what has been done cannot be made undone by the power of nature or by human will.

### The same work, chapter 19

But to overturn the position in which those who oppose us place their defense, we must first discuss the claim that nature is said to have been weakened and changed through sin. Therefore, before everything else, I think we must ask what sin is. Is it some substance, or is it a name entirely lacking substance, by which not a thing, not an existence, not some body, but an act wrongly performed is expressed? I believe that it is so. And if it is so, how could something lacking substance weaken or change human nature?

### The same work, chapter 21

Moreover, this sickness that each person experiences ought not to have been contracted through sins, lest the punishment of sin consist in committing more sins. Nor was the first human being condemned to death because he contracted a necessity of sinning through his first sin, for afterward he did not sin. His descendants too are not weaker than he was; indeed, they fulfilled more commandments, whereas he neglected to fulfill one.

### The same work, chapter 22

Moreover, sin ought not to have been punished in such a way that the sinner would commit more sins as a result of the punishment. Punishment would then be the material of sin, if the sinner were weakened for the purpose of committing more sins.

### The same work, chapters 24–25

Furthermore, the Lord could die without sin; no evil can be the cause of some good; nor was sin necessary, as they claim, in order that it might become the cause of God’s mercy.

### The same work, chapter 26

God does indeed apply his mercy to this matter too, whenever it is necessary, because it is necessary that a human being receive such assistance after sin—not because God wished to be the cause of such necessity. A physician, too, must be ready to treat someone who has already been wounded; but he ought not to wish that a healthy person be wounded so that he may treat him.

### The same work, chapters 27–28

It is utterly absurd and foolish to say that it was necessary for a human being, in order to remove the occasion for pride or glory, to be unable to exist without sin. “But,” they say, “God can heal everything.” Certainly he can. Yet it is absurd to say that God tells a human being: “You must sin so that you may not sin.” What more can I say, except that one might believe that fires are extinguished by fires if one can believe that sins are cured by sins?

### The same work, chapter 29

But how shall we separate pride itself from sin? To sin is as much an act of pride as to be proud is to sin. Ask what any sin may be, and see whether you can find one without the name of pride. Every sin, unless I am mistaken, is contempt of God; and every contempt of God is pride. For what is so proud as to despise God? Therefore every sin is pride, as Scripture also says: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclesiasticus 10:15).

### The same work, chapter 30

Moreover, how could someone be subject to God on account of the guilt of a sin that he knows is not his own? It is not his own if it is necessary; or, if it is his own, it is voluntary. And if it is voluntary, it can be avoided.

### The same work, chapter 33

“But,” they say, “a human being is compared with God if he is asserted to be without sin”—as though an angel, because he is without sin, were thereby compared with God.

### The same work, chapter 34

They also say: “What you assert appears reasonable, but it is proud to say that a human being can be without sin.” Yet in which side should humility be placed? Without doubt, if the side that is proved to be truth is considered proud, then humility would belong to falsehood. Humility must therefore be placed on the side of truth, not on the side of falsehood.

### The same work, chapter 35

They add this as well: “We know the sins of many of the saints.” It is not only true that many saints sinned; it is also reported in the sacred writings themselves—not so that their examples might serve to make us despair of not sinning, nor so that they might somehow provide us with security in sinning, but so that we might learn either the humility of repentance or that salvation must not be despaired of even after such falls.

But how are we to believe that these saints departed from this life? With sin, or without sin? If with sin, how are they saints? If without sin, then they could be without sin.

### The same work, chapter 36

In those same sacred writings, many are reported not merely not to have sinned but also to have lived righteously: Abel, Enoch, Melchizedek, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Joshua son of Nun, Phinehas, Samuel, Nathan, Elijah, Elisha, Micaiah, Daniel, Azariah, Hananiah, Mishael, Ezekiel, Mordecai, Simeon, Joseph, to whom the virgin Mary was betrothed, and John.

Add to these the holy women: Deborah; Hannah, the mother of Samuel; Judith; Esther; the other Hannah, daughter of Phanuel; Elizabeth; and the very mother of our Lord and Savior, whom piety requires us to confess to have been without sin.

### The same work, chapter 37

Perhaps they will say: “Could Scripture have mentioned the sins of everyone?” This can properly be said concerning those whose good or evil deeds Scripture does not mention at all. But concerning those whose righteousness it records, it would certainly also have mentioned their sins if it had known that they had committed any.

But let us grant that at other times, because of the multitude of the crowds, Scripture refrained from recounting the sins of everyone. What shall we say of the very beginning of the world, when there were only four human beings? Why did it not wish to mention the offenses of all? Was it because of the vast multitude, which did not yet exist? Or because it remembered only those who had committed offenses and could not remember the one who had committed none?

Certainly, at the beginning, Adam and Eve, from whom Cain and Abel were born, are reported to have been only four human beings. Eve sinned, and Scripture reported it; Adam also transgressed, and the same Scripture did not keep silent. Cain likewise sinned, and Scripture itself testified to it, indicating not only their sins but also the character of their sins.

If Abel too had sinned, Scripture would unquestionably have said so. But it did not say so. Therefore he did not sin; indeed, it presents him as righteous. Let us therefore believe what we read, and let us consider it impious to assert what we do not read—an argument that is sufficient even when applied to everyone.

### The same work, chapter 41

Those against whom we are speaking object: “For all have sinned” (Romans 3:23). But it is clear that the Apostle was speaking about those who existed at that time, that is, Jews and Gentiles. Indeed, it is the custom of Scripture that when “all” are mentioned, it does not always mean absolutely everyone, without exception.

Thus the Apostle says (Romans 5:12):

> Just as through the offense of one judgment came upon all human beings unto condemnation, so through the righteousness of one came upon all human beings unto justification of life.

Yet it is beyond doubt that through Christ’s righteousness not everyone, but only those who chose to obey him and were cleansed by the washing of his baptism, were sanctified.

### The same work, chapters 42 and following

But let me grant the point and agree that Scripture testifies that all were sinners. It says what they were, not that they could not have been otherwise. Therefore, even if all human beings could be proved to have been sinners, this would in no way harm our definition, since we defend not so much what human beings are as what they could be.

Certainly God, who is as good as he is just, made a human being capable of being free from the evil of sin, if he had wished. What nature can do is not a matter of will. But the present question is not whether there have been or are any human beings in this life without sin, but whether they could have been or can be without sin.

“But this,” you will say, “is what troubles many people: you defend the claim that human beings can be without sin without the grace of God.” O blindness of ignorance! O sluggishness of an untrained mind, which thinks that something is being defended without God’s grace when it hears that it must be attributed solely to God!

For when it is said that the very possibility belongs not at all to human free choice but to the author of nature—that is, to God—how can it be understood apart from God’s grace when it is judged to belong properly to God? But to make this clearer, we must discuss the matter at greater length [Col. 0604B].

We say that the possibility of each thing rests not so much in the power of human choice as in the necessity of nature. For example, I can speak. That I can speak is not mine; that I speak is mine—that is, it belongs to my own will. And because what I speak is mine, I can do either: speak or not speak.

But because the fact that I can speak is not mine—that is, it does not belong to my choice and will—I must always be able to speak, even if I should wish not to be able to speak. Yet I cannot be unable to speak unless perhaps I remove the bodily member by which the function of speaking can be carried out. For whatever is constrained by natural necessity is deprived of the freedom of the will and of deliberation.

### The same work, chapters 47 and following

The same can be perceived with hearing, smell, and sight. Hearing, smelling, and seeing are within our power; but the ability to hear, smell, or see is not within our power, but rests in natural necessity.

In the same way, the possibility of not sinning must be understood: not sinning is ours, but the ability not to sin is not ours. Because not sinning is ours, we can sin or not sin. But because the ability not to sin is not ours, even if we wished not to be able not to sin, we cannot be unable not to sin, since no act of will can remove what is shown to be inseparably implanted in nature.

### The same work, chapter 51

The possibility of not sinning itself rests not so much in the power of free choice as in the necessity of nature. Whatever is placed in the necessity of nature is unquestionably attributed to the author of nature, namely God. How then can it be thought to be stated apart from God’s grace when it is shown to belong properly to God?

### The same work, chapter 52

“But according to the Apostle,” you will say, “the flesh is opposed to us” (Galatians 5:17). How can the flesh be opposed to any baptized person, when, according to the same Apostle, that person is understood not to be in the flesh? For he says:

> But you are not in the flesh (Romans 8:9).

## (The same work, chapter 54)

Indeed, by many words of the Apostle it is shown that he so often speaks of “flesh” that he wishes not the substance, but the works of the flesh, to be understood. Moreover, who made the human spirit? Without doubt, God. Who created the flesh? The same God, I believe. Is God, who created both, good? No one doubts it. And is everything that the good Creator made good? This must be confessed. If, therefore, both spirit and flesh are good, since they were created by a good Creator, how can two good things be contrary to one another?

## (The same work, chapter 58)

“But the devil opposes us,” say our opponents; “let us resist him, and he will flee.” “Resist the devil,” says the blessed Apostle, “and he will flee from you” (James 4:7). Hence we must consider what harm he can do to those from whom he flees, or what power he should be understood to possess if he can prevail only over those who do not resist.

## (The same work, chapter 61)

They also say that I alone defend these things. But what will they do with Catholic interpreters who defend precisely the same position?

Lactantius (*Divine Institutes*, book IV, chapter 14): “It was necessary that the teacher and instructor of virtues should become like a man, so that, by conquering sin, he might teach man that he is able to conquer sin.” And again: “So that, when the desires of the flesh had been subdued, he might teach that sinning is not a matter of necessity, but of purpose and will.”

## (The same work, chapter 62)

The blessed Hilary (*On Matthew 5: Blessed are the pure in heart*): “For only when we have been perfected in spirit and transformed by immortality—which has been prepared for those alone who are pure in heart—shall we behold with immortality that which is in God.” And again: “What writings of Job had he read, that he might abstain from every evil thing, since he revered God with a mind uncontaminated by vices? To worship God is properly the duty of righteousness.”

## (The same work, chapter 63)

The holy Ambrose, however, says:

“They apply this [passage] to those who, preferring consolation for their sins, think that a human being cannot exist without frequent sins, and who use the verse written in Job: ‘No one is pure from uncleanness, not even if his life upon earth is but a single day; his months are numbered by him’ (Job 14:5). They should first be asked to define what it means for a human being to be without sin: whether it means never to have sinned at all, or to have ceased sinning. If they think that to be without sin means never to have sinned at all, I too agree. For ‘all have sinned and lack the glory of God’ (Romans 3:23). But if they deny that a person who has corrected his former error and transformed himself into such a condition of life that he abstains from sin can refrain from transgressions, I cannot agree with their opinion, since we read that ‘the Lord loved the Church so much that he might present it to himself glorious, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, but that it might be holy and without blemish’ (Ephesians 5:25–27). For since the Church has been gathered from the nations—that is, from sinners—how can it be made spotless from those who were spotted, unless first, through Christ’s grace, it has been cleansed from sin, and then, through the quality of not sinning, it abstains from transgressions?”

## (The same work, chapter 64)

John, bishop of Constantinople, likewise says that sin is not a substance but a wicked act; and because it is not natural, a law was given against it, and it derives from freedom of choice.

The most blessed Sixtus, bishop of the Roman Church and martyr of the Lord:

“Because God permitted human beings the freedom of their own will, so that, flourishing purely and without sin, they might become like God.” And again: “A pure mind is a holy temple for God, and a clean and sinless heart is for him the finest altar.” And again: “The chaste and sinless man has received from God the power to be a son of God.”

## (The same work, chapter 65)

The venerable presbyter Jerome, when expounding what is written, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8), says that those whose conscience accuses them of no sin, and who are pure in heart, behold the Pure One; the temple of God cannot be polluted. Likewise (*Against Jovinianus*, book II): “God created us with free choice; we are drawn neither toward virtue nor toward vices by necessity. Otherwise, where there is necessity, there is no crown.”

## (The same work, chapter 67)

Bishop Augustine likewise says in his books *On Free Choice* (book III, chapter 18):

“Whatever that cause of the will may be, if it cannot be resisted, one yields to it without sin; but if it can be resisted, one should not yield to it, and one will not sin. Or does it deceive the unwary? Then let him beware lest he be deceived. Or is its deception so great that it cannot be avoided at all? If that is so, then there are no sins. For who sins in what cannot in any way be avoided? But sin is committed; therefore it can be avoided.”

## First Letter to Saint Augustine

Pelagius wrote two letters to Saint Augustine: the first when he departed from Africa, so that he would not leave without greeting him; the second after the Palestinian synod, to announce that he had been acquitted. Both are mentioned incidentally in the book *On the Proceedings in Palestine* (chapter 26), and nowhere else, so far as I know. Something of the second survives; nothing of the first. We have shown that this letter was written in the year 412 (*Dissertation 2*, chapter 3). Augustine replied, and Pelagius produced the reply at the trial of Diospolis in his own defense, together with the letters of several other bishops, who, as commonly happens, praised him familiarly. Augustine interpreted his own letter (in the passage cited shortly afterward), lest it seem to favor them; concerning the others he wrote:

“Moreover, just as I gave an account of this letter of mine, so, if it were necessary, those whose letters are cited would give an account of their own, saying either what they thought, or what they did not know, or for what reason they wrote.”

Someone might perhaps conjecture—and in my opinion not absurdly—which bishops’ letters Pelagius read on his own behalf and even arranged to have inserted in the proceedings: namely, those who mentioned Paulinus, Constantius, Memorius, and eighteen bishops, whether of Italy or Sicily. Paulinus in particular was dear to him, and he wrote to him; he also wrote to Constantius; and Julian’s friendship clearly proves that he had been on familiar terms with Memorius, Julian’s father. The remaining prelates, although they preferred to surrender their sees rather than subscribe to Pelagius’s condemnation, nevertheless undoubtedly adorned him with praises, and with those praises magnified his reputation as unimpaired.

## Letter to Demetrias, or Book on the Institution of a Virgin

Pelagius called this work *On the Institution of a Virgin* a letter; Bede called it a book; Augustine used both designations. It was, however, falsely attributed to Jerome from Bede’s time onward. For Bede writes as follows (*Preface to the Canticles*, chapter 5):

“But also in the book that he wrote to Demetrias, the virgin of Christ, *On the Institution of a Virgin*, he reveals what he thinks about this same power of free choice. Some of our people, reading this book diligently, rashly supposed it to be by the holy and Catholic doctor Jerome; they failed entirely to perceive that both the sweetness of its captivating eloquence and the perversity of its seductive heresy clearly prove that this little work is not his.”

I do not think any other cause for the misattribution need be sought than a certain fate of Jerome, together with the ignorance or negligence of scribes who inserted several heretical works into the works of the Catholic doctor. This is why works that, because of their author’s impiety and detestation, would otherwise have perished have come down to us intact.

Some also think that it was falsely attributed to Augustine. I nevertheless believe that it was merely included among Augustine’s letters as number 142. Perhaps the reason was that it is mentioned in the letter written by Alipius and Augustine to Demetrias’s mother, which follows it. Thus those who immediately attributed to Augustine whatever they found among Augustine’s letters must have suffered from no small lack of judgment.

Bede himself attributes this work to Julian (in the passage cited shortly afterward), which I find astonishing if he had read either Augustine’s Letter 188 or the book *On the Grace of Christ*. He must have read them if he is indeed the author of the *Collectanea on the Letters of Paul*, drawn from the works of Saint Augustine, for that book is praised more than once in this very passage. Hence I am scarcely able not to agree with Baronius, who rejects this work as Bede’s and attributes it to Peter, abbot of Tripoli, about whom Cassiodorus writes (*Divine Readings*, chapter 8):

“Peter, abbot of the province of Tripoli, is said to have annotated the Letters of Saint Paul with excerpts from the little works of Saint Augustine, so that through another’s mouth he might reveal the secret of his own heart. He fitted these excerpts appropriately to each passage, so that you might rather believe that the whole work had been completed through the labor of blessed Augustine. For it is astonishing how he so elucidated one text by means of another that, without any addition of his own words being mixed in, he appears to have fulfilled the desire of his own heart. Through God’s favor, this work is to be sent to you from the African region among other books.”

Bellarminus does indeed protest against Baronius; but what he adduces in opposition does not seem to me sufficient to accomplish what he intends. For he produces these words from the *Catalogue of Bede’s Works*, compiled by Bede himself:

“Whatever expositions I found in the little works of Saint Augustine on the Apostle, I took care to transcribe in their entirety and in order, lest the holy man should appear a liar and a plagiarist, unless he were the author of the work in question.”

He then adds that it is not believable that Bede wrote nothing on the Letters of Paul, since he wished it to be understood that he had expounded the whole of Scripture, of which the Apostle’s Letters are an especially important part. Finally, he concludes that there is no reason why two men, at different times and in different places, could not have labored with the same zeal to explain Paul from Augustine’s writings.

Yet when he produces this catalogue, he does not greatly advance his own case. In it Bede mentions no works other than those he had published before the fifty-ninth year of his life. It is certain, however, that someone supplemented it with works written later. Therefore Bede cannot be called either a liar or a plagiarist, even if he was not the author of the *Collectanea*.

Now, after hearing Cassiodorus’s testimony, it will appear considerably less credible that two men should have engaged in producing *Collectanea* of the same kind, with the same zeal and in the same manner, than that Peter’s work, perhaps found among Bede’s books, should have been attributed by his disciples to their master, so that they could boast that he had expounded the whole of sacred Scripture.

I scarcely understand, however, how Bellarminus concluded from a catalogue inserted into the *Ecclesiastical Annals* that Bede had expounded the whole of Scripture, since the catalogue makes no mention of an exposition either on Matthew or on John. Yet since both works are found among Bede’s published writings, they may have been added by later men.

Indeed, there is perhaps no more difficult judgment concerning the works of any author than that concerning Bede’s, for several reasons, but especially because of the variety of style and the character of the age that immediately followed Bede. The men of that period knew few names of distinguished writers and were accustomed to attribute indiscriminately and without taste to those famous authors known to them everything they found without an evident author.

Anyone who compares the books on the *Canticles*, especially the preface, with other books that may be called into question will certainly agree with me concerning the variation in style I have mentioned. Such a person would immediately reject either these books or those as Bede’s—unless he wished to maintain that Bede deliberately disguised his style in order to confuse his readers.

Add that the author of the *Collectanea* must have been thoroughly versed in Augustine’s works, as the labor itself shows, whereas Bede was not particularly so. For Bede wrote about Julian things that conflict with Augustine: namely, that Julian was the author of the letter to Demetrias and that he had been raised as a boy by Pelagius when Jerome was writing the *Dialogues*. Yet Augustine attributes the letter to Pelagius in several places and teaches that, when Jerome was writing, Pelagius was in the East, while Julian had become a deacon long before that time and had lived in the house of Memorius, a most holy man. But enough of this.

In the book *On the Institution of a Virgin*, Pelagius so cleverly concealed his opinion beneath a certain ambiguous generality of language that, by softening hostility through the word “grace” and avoiding offense, he almost seemed to confess to Augustine the very grace in question—the grace by which we are helped to do something (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 39). His deception would not have been exposed to a man otherwise so perceptive, unless Pelagius’s mind had betrayed itself in his other books.

Accordingly, Augustine censured only two manifest enormities in his doctrines. The first was that, by doing God’s will, we merit divine grace. The second was that we are helped by the grace of the Holy Spirit not because, without the Spirit, we cannot resist the tempter even by the mere possibility of nature, but so that we may resist more easily.

He did not expressly condemn the remaining doctrines, but he nevertheless regarded them with suspicion, since they speak of grace in such a way that they could be understood either of nature, or of the remission of sins, or of the revelation of doctrine (Letter 187). He mildly corrected one somewhat arrogant statement, as well as something immodest in Orosius. Bede, however, identifies twelve points of accusation against Julian; these may be consulted in Bede himself, in the passage cited shortly afterward.

This ambiguous manner of writing that Pelagius employed in his letter had several effects.
