It ensured not only that Jerome did not wish to extract from it anything that could be brought against Pelagius in an episcopal court, but also that Pelagius confidently produced this book as a witness to his faith. Since everything could be conveniently explained because of the ambiguity of the words, a man otherwise regarded as virtuous ought prudently not to have been convicted of an uncertain crime. Nor could he be pressed vigorously by the testimony of a witness whose words the judge’s kindness could take in a favorable sense and whose credibility was enhanced by the name of Demetrias.

Nothing of this book is presented here, because it is found complete after the letters, whether of Jerome or of Augustine, among the rejected works.

## Pelagius’s Second Letter to Saint Augustine, or the Brief of Purgation Sent through the Deacon Carus

No ancient writer, so far as I know, mentions this brief except Augustine, who writes the following in his book *On the Proceedings in Palestine* (chapter 32):

“There is another matter about which I must not remain silent. In the brief of his defense, which he sent to me through a certain Carus, a fellow citizen of ours from Hippo but a deacon from the East, he did something that differs from what is contained in the episcopal proceedings. What the proceedings contain, however, is much better and firmer, and altogether clearer in support of Catholic truth against the pest of that heresy. For when I read the brief, before the proceedings had reached us, I did not know that he had used in it the very words he used at the trial when he was present. There are only a few differences, and they are not very significant, so I do not greatly concern myself with them.”

In the following chapter Augustine shows how cunningly this abridgment of the proceedings at Diospolis had been fabricated. He produces two examples by which Pelagius, sometimes removing words from the proceedings and sometimes adding words to them, wished to suggest to credulous readers that his own opinions could still be defended, however much the teachings of Coelestius had been proscribed. The passage deserves to be read, for it exposes the deceitful as well as arrogant methods of heretics after their condemnation, by which the less careful are easily deceived.

## Letter to a Certain Presbyter Friend after the Synod of Diospolis

Augustine alone likewise mentions this letter, in the following words (*On the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapter 30):

“A certain letter came into our hands, said to have been written by Pelagius himself to one of his presbyter friends, who, as the same letter states, had kindly admonished him in writing not to cause anyone, on his account, to separate from the body of the Church. Among other things, whose insertion would be too lengthy and is unnecessary, Pelagius says:

‘By the judgment of fourteen bishops our definition has been approved, in which we said that a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes. This opinion has covered the mouth of contradiction with confusion and has separated from one another every association conspiring for evil.’

Whether, then, Pelagius truly wrote this letter, or whether it was fabricated by someone under his name, who does not see how this error boasts of the judgment in which it was convicted and condemned as though it were a victory? For he set down these words as they are read in his book called the *Book of Chapters*, not as they were brought forward in the trial, or repeated in his own reply. Indeed, those who brought the charge, through I know not what negligence, omitted a word over which there is no small controversy. For they reported that he had said, ‘A human being can, if he wishes, be without sin’; nothing was said about ease.

“And shortly afterward:

‘Nevertheless, that letter, full of carnal boasting and arrogance, flies abroad, and, outrunning the proceedings’ delay through its speed, rushes into people’s hands, so that it may be said to have pleased fourteen Eastern bishops: not merely that a human being can be without sin and keep God’s commandments, without God’s help even being named, but only if he wishes. Thus, by silently excluding the divine grace for which the fiercest struggle was being waged, human pride alone is read in the letter—wretched and deceiving itself, yet acting as though victorious.’

See what has been observed concerning the letters sent into the provinces by the Pelagian faction in the third dissertation, where the reasons are discussed why Pelagianism resisted ecclesiastical and royal authority with such obstinacy.

It can scarcely be doubtful that Pelagius sent both the letter to his friend and the brief of defense to Augustine either before Orosius’s departure from the East or at least when Orosius was returning from Palestine to Africa. For as soon as navigation became possible after the synod of Diospolis, both should have been sent immediately: partly so that the brief might serve as an abridgment of the proceedings, which were being intentionally delayed; partly so that the faction’s members might have something with which to undermine the credibility of Orosius and of the Gallican bishops’ letters, while at the same time encouraging the timid through the repeatedly promised agreement of the Eastern bishops.

Both, therefore, belong to the spring season of the year 416, when the sea first became navigable; thus they either preceded or accompanied Orosius’s arrival in Africa. From this one may infer what Augustine reports: that the letter to the friend was lengthy, so as to instruct the faction concerning the whole matter; full of boastful vanity, so as to serve as an official messenger of victory; and an uncontrolled display of victorious arrogance, so that the insolent faction would have something with which to taunt its opponents as though they had been subdued.

## The Book of Faith Sent by Pelagius to the Apostolic See

This has been discussed sufficiently in the preceding dissertation. One point may be added, which the headlong haste of the workmen omitted after the end of the discussion, following these words:

“Nor, as certain men most wickedly suppose, was the Holy Spirit the seed.”

[Though a malicious interpreter could twist this statement of Ambrose (*On Luke*, book I, chapter 2):]

“For it was not a man’s intercourse that opened the secrets of the virgin’s womb; rather, the Holy Spirit poured himself—the immaculate seed—into the inviolate womb.”

Thus it should be read, not as it appears in the common manuscripts, without the little word *se* (“himself”); for there is an allusion to the angel’s words: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you,” and so forth.

I admit that the immense praises with which Pelagius adorned Ambrose seem to prevent us from saying that Pelagius had Ambrose in mind. Yet the character of the Pelagians was certainly such that they did not refrain from insulting anyone whom they found opposed to them, sometimes leaving names unmentioned when they feared unpopularity, and sometimes stating them openly when they thought they could do so with impunity.

## Letter to Innocent I, Supreme Pontiff

The letter is not preserved in its entirety, but Augustine retained a substantial portion of it in his book *On the Grace of Christ*. It has been excerpted there, with certain words distinguished in a different typeface so that it would retain the appearance of a letter.

“Most blessed pope, there are two matters concerning which people try to defame us. The first is that we deny the sacrament of baptism to little children and promise some of them the kingdom of heaven without Christ’s redemption. The second is that we say a human being can avoid sin in such a way as to exclude God’s help, and that we trust in free choice to such an extent that we reject the assistance of grace.

“These are the charges that the presbyter Jerome, who envies me as a rival, brings against me; these are the charges brought by another young man sent from Africa by my enemies; these are the charges that two bishops, deservedly expelled from their sees in Gaul, never cease to bring, although they were ordered to remain silent in an episcopal judgment and although the holy synod declared that we belong to Catholic communion.

“Indeed, I have never heard even an impious heretic say what I have proposed concerning little children. For who is so ignorant of the Gospel reading that he would dare to affirm this—or even be able lightly to say or think it? Moreover, who is so impious as to wish little children to be excluded from the kingdom of heaven, and to think that they should not be baptized and reborn in Christ, when Christ openly says: ‘Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God’ (John 3:5)? Who is so impious as to deny a child of any age the common redemption of the human race, and to be unwilling that one born into an uncertain life should be reborn into a perpetual and certain life?

“Let this letter, then, clear me before your blessedness. In it we say plainly and simply that we possess complete free choice both to sin and not to sin, and that in every good work it is always assisted by divine help.”

We say that human beings were created by God in his image and likeness, and that, when God created them, he gave them the power of free choice—that is, the possibility of sinning and not sinning—so that they might live commendably. We say that this power of free choice exists generally in all people: in Christians, Jews, and Gentiles alike.

Free choice exists equally in all by nature, but only in Christians is it assisted by grace. In the others it is the good of their condition, naked and unarmed; in those who belong to Christ, it is fortified by Christ’s help. The former are to be judged and condemned because, although they possess free choice, through which they could come to faith and merit God’s grace, they misuse the freedom granted to them. The latter, however, are to be rewarded because, using free choice well, they merit the Lord’s grace and keep his commandments.

This was consistently our opinion even before we suffered persecution. If our enemies themselves wish to examine it, let them read our *Book of Faith*, which we send to your blessedness. In it we maintain one baptism, which we say is celebrated with the same sacramental words for infants as for adults; and we confess free choice in such a way that we say that we always need God’s help.

Let them likewise read the letter that we wrote nearly twelve years ago to the holy man Paulinus, bishop. In approximately three hundred lines it confesses nothing other than God’s grace and help, and declares that we can do absolutely no good without God. Let them read another letter to the holy bishop Constantius, in which, briefly but clearly, we joined God’s grace and help to human free choice.

Let them also read what we composed in the East for the sacred virgin of Christ, Demetrias, and they will find that we praise human nature in such a way that we always add God’s grace as its help.

Let them also read my recent little work, which we were recently compelled to publish in defense of free choice. They will recognize how unjustly those who have eagerly tried to defame us by denying grace have acted, since throughout almost the entire text of that work we confess both free choice and grace perfectly and completely.

## Four Books on Free Choice

### [Column 0611C]

The work on free choice composed by Pelagius is mentioned with complete clarity by Pelagius himself (in his letter to Saint Innocent):

“Let them also read my recent little work, which we were recently compelled to publish in defense of free choice.”

Augustine also mentions it (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 3):

“In the books that he published in defense of free choice, which he mentions in the letter he sent to Rome,” and so forth.

Jerome refers to it less explicitly in his letter to Alipius and Augustine (Letter 143), and Julian likewise in his final work against Augustine (*Unfinished Work*, book IV, chapter 72).

Augustine reports that the whole work consisted of four books:

“There are four books of this work; I read them, and from them I selected what I proposed to treat and discuss, and, as far as I could, I dealt with it before we came to this letter of his, which he sent to Rome; but in these four books as well,” and so forth.

## From the First Book

### [Column 0611D]

(*On Grace and Original Sin*, book I, chapter 18):

“We possess the possibility of either alternative, implanted in us by God like a certain fruitful and fertile root, so to speak, which, according to the human will, produces and brings forth different things, and which, according to the choice of its cultivator, can either shine with the flower of virtues or bristle with the thorns of vices.”

(*The same work*, chapters 22–23):

“He who runs toward God and desires to be governed by God—that is, who suspends his will upon God’s will—he who, by continually cleaving to him, becomes one spirit with him, according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 6:17), accomplishes this through no other means than freedom of choice. Whoever uses it well surrenders himself entirely to God and mortifies his whole will, so that with the Apostle he can say: ‘I live, yet it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me’ (Galatians 2:20). He places his heart in God’s hand, so that God himself may incline it wherever he wills (Proverbs 21:1).”

(*On Grace and Original Sin*, book II, chapter 13):

“Every good or evil by which we are praiseworthy or blameworthy does not arise with us, but is enacted by us. We are born capable of either, not full of either, and we are begotten without virtue just as without vice. Before the action of our own will, the only thing in a human being is what God created.”

(*On Grace and Original Sin*, book I, chapter 28):

“Since we possess within us free choice so powerful and so firm for not sinning, which the Creator of human nature implanted generally in human nature, we are nevertheless, through his immeasurable kindness, armed day by day with his help, so that what human beings are commanded to do through free choice they may more easily accomplish through grace.”

## From the Third Book

(*On Grace and Original Sin*, book I, chapter 4):

“We distinguish these three things in this way and divide them as though arranged in a definite order. First we place ‘being able,’ second ‘willing,’ and third ‘being.’ We assign ‘being able’ to nature, ‘willing’ to choice, and ‘being’ to inclination. The first of these—that is, being able—belongs properly to God, who bestowed it upon his creature. The other two, namely willing and being, must be referred to the human being, because they descend from the source of choice.

“Therefore, in a good will and a good work, praise belongs to the human being—or rather, to both the human being and God, who gave the possibility of that will and work and who always assists that possibility with the help of his grace. But the fact that a human being can will and accomplish the good belongs to God alone. Thus the one thing can exist even if the other two do not; but the latter two cannot exist without it.

“Accordingly, I am free not to have a good will or a good action, but I cannot in any way fail to possess the possibility of the good. It is present in me even if I do not wish it, and nature never at any time permits it to rest from its activity.

“Let some examples make this meaning clearer to you. The fact that we can see with our eyes is not ours; but whether we see well or badly is ours. To embrace the whole matter in general terms: the fact that we can do, say, or think every good thing belongs to the one who gave and assists this ability. But whether we act, speak, or think well belongs to us, because we can also turn all these things toward evil.

“Hence—and this must often be repeated because of your slander—when we say that a human being can be without sin, and when, by confessing the possibility we have received, we praise God who granted us this ability, there is no occasion there for praising the human being, where the matter concerns God alone. For the discussion is not about willing or being, but only about what can be.”

(*The same work*, chapter 7):

“Here the most ignorant of men think that we do injury to divine grace because we say that it can by no means perfect holiness in us without our will—as though God had commanded something of his grace and did not also supply the help of his grace to those whom he commanded, so that what human beings are commanded to do through free choice they may more easily accomplish through grace.

“We confess that grace, contrary to what you think, exists not only in the law but also in God’s help. For God helps us through his teaching and revelation: he opens the eyes of our heart; he shows us future things so that we may not be occupied with present things; he discloses the devil’s snares; and he enlightens us with the manifold and ineffable gift of heavenly grace. Does the person who says these things seem to you to deny grace? Or does he confess both God’s free choice and God’s grace?”

(*The same work*, chapter 39):

“What you wish to understand from the Apostle, all ecclesiastical writers assert that he said in the person of the sinner who was still under the law, held, as it were, by a certain necessity of sinning because of an excessive habit of vices. Although he desired the good by his will, habit nevertheless drove him headlong into evil.

“In the person of one human being he designates the people still sinning under the old law, whom he says must be freed from this evil habit through Christ. Christ first forgives all sins through baptism to those who believe in him; then, by imitation of himself, he urges them toward perfect holiness and conquers the habit of vices by the example of virtues.”

(*The same work*, chapter 10):

“How, then, will the Apostle’s statement stand: ‘For it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish’? God works in us the willing that is good, the willing that is holy, when he inflames us—devoted as we are to earthly desires and loving present things like dumb animals—with the greatness of future glory and the promise of rewards; when, through the revelation of wisdom, he rouses our sluggish will to desire God; and when he persuades us of everything that is good, something which you elsewhere do not fear to deny.”

(*The same work*, chapter 43):

“The blessed bishop Ambrose, in whose books the faith of Rome shines forth especially, who gleamed among Latin writers as a kind of beautiful flower, whose faith and most pure understanding of the Scriptures even an enemy did not dare to criticize.”

No one who reads Augustine’s and Julian’s words, which I shall quote shortly, can deny that Pelagius was the author of this four-part work. Nevertheless, Augustine may appear at one point to have attributed it to Annianus, when he was writing to Jerome; nor did Jerome disagree with Augustine when he replied in these words (Letter 143):

“As for what you ask—whether I have replied against the books of Annianus, the false deacon of Celeda, who is abundantly supplied with material so that he may frivolously furnish words of another’s blasphemy—you should know that I received the books themselves, sent in notebooks by the holy brother Eusebius the presbyter, not long ago. Then, whether because illnesses overtook me or because of the death of our holy and venerable daughter Eustochium, I was so grieved that I almost considered them unworthy of attention.

“For he remains stuck in the same mud and, apart from tinkling and beggarly words, says nothing else. Nevertheless, we took great pains that, while attempting to reply to my letter, he should expose himself more openly and make his blasphemies clear to everyone. Whatever he denies saying in that wretched synod of Diospolis, he professes in this work; and it is no great task to answer the most foolish ditties.

“If, however, the Lord grants me life and we obtain a sufficient number of scribes, we shall reply in a few brief compositions—not to refute a heresy already dead, but to rebut his ignorance and blasphemy in our own words. Your holiness would do this better, lest I be compelled to praise ourselves against a heretic.”

It is credible, although not certain, that the letter to Ctesiphon and the three *Dialogues* were answered in one and the same work, which, because it was composed in the sense of Pelagius and in the style of Annianus, could justifiably be attributed to both. After considering the matter more carefully, I think this more probable than what I seemed to have established in the first dissertation with arguments that were strong, though not conclusive.

First, Jerome reports that Pelagius replied to the letter, in the words quoted above. Julian also plainly says that Pelagius replied in three *Dialogues*, when he addresses Augustine as follows (*Unfinished Work*, book IV, chapter 87):

“With what confidence do you, relying on Jerome’s writings—which he composed under the names of Atticus and Critobulus with remarkable and, as befitted such a man, charming elegance—also attempt, by the testimony of the fifth Gospel, which he says he translated, to show that Christ possessed not only natural but also voluntary sin, for which he recognized that he needed to be cleansed by John’s baptism?

“Regarding another testimony of John the Evangelist, he also fastens upon him the charge of falsification. Concerning this work, in the letter that you sent to Alexandria, you boast in such a way as to say that Pelagius, overwhelmed by the mass of the Scriptures, cannot defend free choice.

“BUT THAT WORK WAS ANSWERED BY A CATHOLIC MAN WHO HAD BEEN ATTACKED.”

Who was this Catholic man who had been attacked in the *Dialogues*? Who was overwhelmed by Jerome with the mass of the Scriptures, if not Pelagius?

It is then concluded quite plainly from the fact that Julian says that Pelagius opposed the Dialogues that the four books On Free Will, whose author is Pelagius, contain a response to the Dialogues; nor did Pelagius write anything else after the Dialogues had been published, apart from two or three letters, a little book of faith, and the books On Free Will. Add that the celebrated passage of the Apostle in Romans 7—“For I do not do the good that I want,” etc.—which Jerome pressed in Dialogue 2, is laboriously twisted in Book III of [Col. 0614C] On Free Will, if it can in any way be explained. What is more, in the same book Ambrose is lavishly praised, and mention is made of the enemy by whom Ambrose’s faith could not be reproached; but this was maliciously done to arouse ill will against Jerome, whom almost everyone knew to have been less than fair to Ambrose. Add that in the Dialogues the question περὶ ἀναμαρτησίας—“concerning sinlessness”—is said to be raised not only regarding whether it is possible, but also regarding whether it exists; this statement is vigorously attacked in the books. Add that the Dialogues as a whole are devoted to explaining the weakness of free will, while the books as a whole are devoted to exalting its powers, so that with good reason both Works could be entitled On Free Will, just as I remember having seen the Dialogues sometimes entitled that way. For this reason I think that Pope Gelasius said that Jerome had disputed about free will.

Now it becomes clear that the letter to Ctesiphon and the three Dialogues were answered in one and the same Work, from the fact that the Dialogues are nothing at all other than the more extended and more fully supported exposition which Jerome had promised [Col. 0614D] in the letter; and from the fact that nothing is reported as having been written against the letter except after the Palestinian synod, at which time it is established that the books under discussion were composed.

Finally, the considerations that seemed to carry weight in the opposite direction have a suitable resolution—or rather, a suitable reconciliation with these later conclusions. For if the four books On Free Will are attributed jointly to Pelagius and Annianus, though for different reasons, Pelagius and Annianus will nevertheless not be one and the same person, contrary to what the bishop of Ypres wished. Yet the writer will truly be said to have been abundantly supplied with material for furnishing the words of another’s blasphemy, as Jerome reports; and the author will appear to be wallowing in the same mire as before, which Jerome also says; and in these books Pelagius will profess what he had condemned at the synod, as Augustine demonstrates; and our emendation of the passage in Jerome [Col. 0615A] will stand; and, as the matter actually is, Augustine did not so much answer the four books On Free Will as extract from them a few passages—without failing to praise Jerome—which served his own purpose. Since these points are certain, or highly probable, the books On Free Will must have been sent to the West before they were published in the East. Thus they must first have reached Africa under Annianus’s name, before they were sent from the West to Jerome. Jerome left them unanswered because the burdens of advancing age and the occupations that overwhelmed a man nearly ninety years old with grief prevented him from replying.

## CHAPTER III. What Coelestius, the disciple of Pelagius and teacher of Julian, wrote

Gennadius counts Coelestius among ecclesiastical writers on account of three little works published before the heresy. “Coelestius,” he says (Book On Ecclesiastical Writers, ch. 44) [Col. 0615B], “before he joined Pelagius—or rather, while he was still a young man—wrote three letters to his parents from the monastery, in the manner of little books, necessary for everyone who desires God. Their discourse is indeed moral; nothing of the vice later revealed in him appears there, but the whole work is directed toward encouraging virtue.”

Nothing of works of this kind survives, unless perhaps they are read under another’s name, as I think may be the case, or unless they are identical with a certain book of Chapters, about which I shall speak shortly.

After he joined Pelagius, he first wrote against original sin. This work, which must have been published around A.D. 401 or 402, is indicated by Mercator, Vincent of Lérins, and the author of the *Predestined*. Nothing of it survives except what Pelagius inserted in his expositions of the Epistle to the Romans and what Augustine, in Book III of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, Mercator in the *Commonitorium*, and the author of the *Predestined* reported; we have presented it in the preceding chapter. I think that six statements were excerpted from the same book [Col. 0615C]—first objected to Coelestius at the trial in Carthage and then to Pelagius at Diospolis—and indeed a seventh as well, in which he allegedly said that the Church was without spot or wrinkle. All of them have a close affinity with the argument of the book; the seventh, however, may have contained something more malicious, since it sought the alliance of the Donatists, who still possessed considerable power at Carthage. Augustine may be seen to have perceived this when he says (*On the Proceedings at Palestine*, ch. 12): “Pelagius was accused of saying that the Church here is without spot or wrinkle; hence the Donatists also had a long conflict with us in our conference,” and so forth. He then adduces the arguments by which he had convicted the Donatists.

Afterward he wrote another Work divided into many chapters, in which he seems to have attacked divine grace just as he had previously attacked original sin. From this work the following ten statements were extracted and brought against Pelagius, as though the teacher had taught these things to his disciple.

[Col. 0615D]

1. Since we do more than is commanded in the Law or the Gospel.

2. That God’s grace and assistance are not given for each individual act, but exist in free will, or in the Law and teaching.

3. That God’s grace is given according to our merits, as though, if God gave it to sinners, he would appear unjust. Therefore grace itself has been placed in my will, whether I should become worthy or unworthy. For if we do everything through grace, then, when we are overcome by sin, it is not we who are overcome but God’s grace, which wished to help us and could not. If it is God’s grace when we conquer sins, then he himself is at fault when we are overcome by sin, because he either could not or would not preserve us altogether.

4. That each individual person can possess all the virtues and graces.

5. That people cannot be called children of God unless they have become entirely without sin.

6. That forgetfulness and ignorance are not subject to sin, because they occur not according to the will but according to [Col. 0616A] necessity.

7. That there is no free will if it needs God’s assistance, since each person has it in his own will either to do something or not to do it.

8. From Peter’s statement that we are partakers of the divine nature, it follows that the soul can be without sin in the same way as God. For how could anyone become a participant in something whose condition and power he is defined as being alien from?

9. That our victory comes not from God’s assistance but from free will, since we took up arms by our own will. Conversely, when we are defeated, that is ours, because we refused to arm ourselves by our own will.

10. That forgiveness is not granted to penitents according to God’s grace and mercy, but according to the merits and labor of those who through repentance became worthy of mercy.

From the same book Jerome took what he has [Col. 0616B] in his letter to Ctesiphon:

“One of his disciples—or rather, now already his teacher and leader of the whole army, and a vessel of destruction against the Apostle—running through thickets of solecisms and not, as his followers boast, of syllogisms, philosophizes and argues as follows:

“‘If I do nothing without God’s assistance, and in each individual work everything that I accomplish belongs to him, then it is not I who labor but God’s assistance in me that will be crowned; and he gave me free will in vain, since I cannot fulfill it unless he is always helping me. For the will that needs another’s aid is destroyed. But God gave free will, and it will not otherwise be free unless I do what I want. Accordingly, either I use once the power given to me so that free will may remain free, or, if I need another’s aid, freedom of will will be destroyed in me.’”

And afterward:

“Listen, I beg you, listen to the sacrilegious man: ‘If I wish to bend a finger, move a hand, sit, stand, walk, run about, spit, wipe the filth from my nostrils with two fingers, relieve my bowels, or discharge urine, I shall always need God’s assistance.’” [Col. 0616C]

With regard to all these matters, whether those brought forward from the *Proceedings at Palestine* or those produced from Jerome’s letter, it is worthwhile to observe, first, that what Jerome reported pertains to the third chapter, in which Coelestius denies that any grace is needed for individual acts other than the grace placed in free will, or in the Law and teaching. Second, it is correctly said in general that Coelestius runs through thickets of syllogisms; for in all his books he used a syllogistic method of reasoning. What Pelagius extracted from the book against the transmission of sin consists of mere arguments: “If Adam’s sin harmed even those who do not sin, then Christ’s righteousness benefits even those who do not believe,” and the seven other consequences. The *Book of Definitions*, to which Augustine opposed his book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, contains only sixteen compressed arguments, accompanied by Scripture testimonies brought forward contentiously. That in these two Works there was an equal and identical form of style [Col. 0616D] is understood from the fact that Augustine detected the author of the *Definitions* by the intellectual character that he had observed in this book of Coelestius.

Third, Coelestius wrote books on the whole of the heresy—on Original Sin, on Grace, and on Sinlessness—but they were brief and compressed, so that he seems to have armed his faction against the bosom of the Church with certain murderous daggers. Fourth, this book against grace was published before the synod held at Diospolis in A.D. 415; before the book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, perhaps written in A.D. 410; before Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon, sent in A.D. 413; indeed, before the trial at Carthage in A.D. 412 and the conference with the Donatists held in A.D. 411. It seems to have been carried by Pelagius to the East, where Jerome read it. It was therefore published, at the latest, when Coelestius was staying with Pelagius in Sicily—that is, from A.D. 408 to 411. Fifth, Augustine’s statement is true: Pelagius wrote about his heresy more timidly and obscurely, while Coelestius [Col. 0617A] wrote more openly and boldly. For what could be clearer or more shameless than the three books mentioned above? Sixth, before any ecclesiastical judgment was instituted, or even at the very beginning of the fifth century, this was the condition of the Pelagian heresy: it was reduced to three points, and the heretics did acknowledge the true grace of Christ, but a grace given according to merits and not necessary for human beings, though merely useful.

Finally, when the third chapter of Coelestius was brought against Pelagius, Pelagius replied (*On the Proceedings at Palestine*, ch. 14): “Whether these statements belong to Coelestius, let those who say that they are Coelestius’s see to it; but I have never held this view, and I anathematize anyone who holds it.” To these words Augustine replies:

“Behold, he does not wish the nature of free will, nor the Law and teaching, to be understood as the grace by which we are assisted in each individual act. What then remains, except that he understands the grace of which the Apostle speaks as the administration of the Holy Spirit?” and so forth.

By these words he shows that Pelagius appeared to acknowledge the true [Col. 0617B] grace at issue. Nevertheless, in the book *On the Grace of Christ* he either makes Pelagius suspect of lying or actually convicts him of it. For he says (ch. 3):

“Since Pelagius had condemned, without any refusal, in the episcopal proceedings, those who say that God’s grace and our assistance are given for individual acts but exist in free will, or in the Law and teaching, we thought that all evasions on this matter had been exhausted. He had also condemned those who teach that God’s grace is given according to our merits. Yet in the books that he published in defense of free will, he is shown to hold nothing other than what he had appeared to condemn,” and so forth.

## The Book of Definitions

To what we said in the observations on Augustine’s book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, we shall add the following. Augustine writes to Eutropius and Paul, bishops of Spain, concerning this little work of Coelestius:

“Your Charity asked me to answer the definitions said to be Coelestius’s [Col. 0617C]. For the same little document that you gave me was headed as follows: ‘DEFINITIONS, AS THEY ARE SAID TO BE, OF COELESTIUS.’ I believe that this heading belongs not to him but to those who brought the document from Sicily, where Coelestius is reported not to have been. We too may suppose that these are the doctrines of that man, or even of some of his followers. For these brief definitions—or rather arguments—are not unlike the intellectual character of the work that I examined elsewhere and of which he is certainly the author; and I do not think without reason that the brothers who brought this material from Sicily had heard that he had taught or written these things.”

From this we learn what title the book bore; where it came from to Spain; by whom it was sent to Augustine in Africa; how Augustine recognized it as Coelestius’s; and by what method he refuted it—namely, by presenting each argument as it stood in the document and adding a response to each. Its subject is clear, since the entire work concerns sinlessness. It is divided into three parts and runs as follows in full.

## The Definitions of Coelestius, or Arguments Concerning Sinlessness

[Col. 0617D]

Before everything else, the person who denies that a human being can be without sin must be asked what any sin is: something that can be avoided, or something that cannot be avoided? If it cannot be avoided, it is not sin; if it can be avoided, a person can be without the sin that can be avoided. For no reason—or at least no justice—allows something to be called sin that cannot in any way be avoided.

Again, it must be asked: Is sin a matter of the will or of necessity? If it is a matter of necessity, it is not sin; if it is a matter of the will, it can be avoided.

Again, it must be asked what sin is: natural [Col. 0618A] or accidental? If it is natural, it is not sin; but if it is accidental, it can depart; and what can depart can be avoided; and what can be avoided is something without which a person can exist.

Again, it must be asked: What is sin—an act or a thing? If it is a thing, it must have an author; and if it is said to have an author, someone other than God will appear to be introduced as the author of some thing. But if it is impious to say this, sin must necessarily be an act, not a thing. If, then, it is an act—or rather, because it truly is an act—it can be avoided.

Again, it must be asked whether a person ought to be without sin. Without doubt, he ought. If he ought, he can; if he cannot, then he ought not. And if a person ought not to be without sin, he ought therefore to be with sin; and sin will [Col. 0618B] no longer be sin if it is established that one ought to have it. But if this too is absurd to say, it must be confessed that a person ought to be without sin. Yet it is established that he ought to do nothing other than what he can do.

Again, it must be asked whether it is commanded that a person be without sin. Either he cannot be without sin, and then it is not commanded; or, because it is commanded, he can. For why would something be commanded that could not possibly be done?

Again, it must be asked whether God wishes a person to be without sin. Without doubt he wishes it, and without doubt he can bring it about. For who is so mad as even to doubt that something can happen which he does not doubt God wishes to happen?

Again, it must be asked: How does God wish a person to exist—with sin or without sin? Without doubt he does not wish him to exist with sin. One must consider how great an impiety [Col. 0618C] and blasphemy it is to say that a person can exist with the sin that God does not wish, while denying that he can exist without the sin that God does wish him to lack—as though God had created someone for this purpose: that he could be what God did not wish and could not be what God did wish, and that he should exist contrary to God’s will rather than according to it.

Again, it must be asked: By what means does a person become sinful—through the necessity of nature or through freedom of will? If through the necessity of nature, he is without guilt; if through freedom of will, it must be asked from whom he received freedom of will. Without doubt, from God. But it cannot at all be denied that what God gave is good. By what reasoning, then, is it proved to be good if it is more inclined toward evil [Col. 0618D] than toward good? It is more inclined toward evil than toward good if through it a person can exist with sin and cannot exist without sin.

If God made a human being good, and, in addition to making him good, commanded him to do good, how impious it is to confess that the human being is evil, although he was not made evil and was not commanded to be evil, and to deny that he can be good, although he was made good and commanded to be good.

Again, it must be asked: In how many ways is all sin constituted? In two, unless I am mistaken: either when the things that are forbidden are done, or when the things that are commanded are not done. Everything that is forbidden can certainly be avoided, just as everything [Col. 0619A] that is commanded can be carried out. For something would be forbidden or commanded in vain if it could neither be avoided nor fulfilled. And how shall we deny that a person can be without sin, when we must confess that he can avoid everything that is forbidden just as he can do everything that is commanded?

Again, it must be asked: How is it that a person cannot be without sin—by will or by nature? If by nature, it is not sin; if by will, the will can very easily be changed by the will.

Again, it must be asked: If a person cannot be without sin, whose fault is it—his own or someone else’s? If it is the person’s own fault, how can it be the person’s fault if this condition is one that he cannot avoid?

Again, it must be asked: If human nature [Col. 0619B] is good—as no one except Marcion or Manichaeus will dare deny—how is it good if it is impossible for it to be free from evil? For who would doubt that every sin is evil?

This too must be said: God is certainly just, for this cannot be denied; yet God imputes every sin to the human being. I think this too must be confessed, because whatever is not imputed as sin is not sin; and if there is some sin that cannot be avoided, how can God be called just if he is believed to impute to anyone what cannot be avoided?

But if someone says, “Give me a person without sin,” the answer should be: “I give you one who can exist.” If he continues to ask, “Who is that person?” the answer should be: “You yourself.” If he says, “I cannot be such a person,” the answer should be: “Whose fault is that?” If he says, “Mine,” one must [Col. 0619C] say: “How is it your fault if you cannot yourself be without sin?” If he continues, “Are you yourself without sin, since you say that a person can be without sin?” the answer should be: “If I am not without sin, whose fault is that?” If he says, “Yours,” the answer should be: “How can it be mine if I cannot be without sin?”

## Testimonies by which it is proved that a person is commanded to be without sin

In Deuteronomy: “But you shall be perfect before the Lord your God” (Deut. XVIII, 13). Likewise there: “And there shall not be one who is incomplete among the children of Israel.”

Likewise the Savior in the Gospel: “Be perfect, just as your Father who is in heaven is perfect” (Matt. V, 48).

[Col. 0619D]

Likewise the Apostle in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “Finally, brothers, rejoice; be perfect” (II Cor. XIII, 11).

Likewise to the Colossians: “Admonishing every person and teaching every person in all wisdom, so that we may present every person perfect in Christ” (Col. I, 28).

Likewise to the Philippians: “Do everything without murmuring and hesitation, so that you may be blameless and simple, like immaculate children of God” (Phil. II, 14–15).

Likewise to the Ephesians: “Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and immaculate in his sight” (Eph. I, 3–4).

[Col. 0620A]

Likewise to the Colossians: “And although you were once alienated and enemies in mind through evil works, you have now been reconciled in the body of his flesh through his death; present yourselves holy, immaculate, and blameless” (Col. I, 21–22).

Likewise to the Ephesians: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, but that it might be holy and immaculate” (Eph. V, 27).

Likewise in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “Be sober and righteous, and do not sin” (I Cor. XV, 14).

And in the Epistle of Saint Peter: “Therefore, girding the loins of your mind, being sober and perfect, hope in the grace that is offered to you, as obedient children, not conforming yourselves to the former desires of [Col. 0620B] your ignorance, but according to him who called you, the Holy One, be holy yourselves in all your conduct, because it is written” (Lev. XI, 46): “You shall be holy, because I am holy” (I Pet. I, 13).

Hence blessed David also says: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest on your holy mountain? The one who walks without blemish and practices righteousness” (Ps. XIV, 1–2). And elsewhere: “And I shall be blameless with him” (Ps. XVII, 24). And elsewhere: “Blessed are the blameless in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. CXVIII, 1).

Likewise in Solomon: “The Lord loves holy hearts; but all the blameless are acceptable to him” (Prov. XII).

## Testimonies of Scripture that must be set forth from the opposite side against those who foolishly think that they can destroy free will or the possibility of not sinning by the authority of Scripture

[Col. 0620C]

They commonly object that holy Job said: “Who is clean from sin? Not even an infant whose life on earth is a single day” (Job XXVI, according to the Septuagint). One must oppose to this what Job said: “For I am a righteous and blameless man; I have become an object of ridicule” (Job XIV, according to the Septuagint); and: “Behold, I am near my judgment, and I know that I shall be found righteous” (Job XIII, according to the Septuagint); and: “For I have kept his ways and have not turned aside from his commandments, nor shall I depart” (ibid. XXIII, 11); and: “I was clothed in righteousness, and I surrounded myself with judgment like a cloak” (ch. XXIX, 14); and: “My heart did not reproach me throughout my life, and there was nothing unjust in my works, but my prayer was pure” (ch. XXVII, 6).

[Col. 0620D]

Again, they commonly propose: “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV, 2). To them one must answer with what is written in the Book of Numbers: “A truthful man” (Num. XXV, according to the Septuagint). And this is what is read about holy Job: “There was a man living in the land of Ausitis, named Job, truthful, blameless, righteous, a worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil thing” (Job I, 1). Likewise in Job himself: “And the wonder held fast the truthful man.” Likewise in Solomon, concerning Wisdom: “Lying men will not remember her, but truthful men will be found in her” (Ecclus. XV, 8). Likewise in the Apocalypse: “And no lie was found in their mouth, for they are without blemish” (Apoc. XIV, 5).

Again, they propose: “There is none who does good, not even one” [Col. 0621A] (Ps. XIII, 3). To them one must answer with what holy David says: “Hope in the Lord and do good” (Ps. XXXVI, 3). And holy Tobit says: “Do not be afraid, my son. We lead a poor life, but we shall have many good things if we fear God, turn away from every sin, and do good” (Tob. IV, 23).

Likewise they say that the Savior said: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” (Luke XVIII, 19). The answer should be that the same Lord elsewhere said: “The good person brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart” (Matt. XII, 35). And again: “Who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” (ibid. V, 45). And elsewhere it is written: “Good things were created for the good from the beginning” (Ecclus. XXXIX, 30); and again: “Those who are good shall be inhabitants of the earth” (Prov. II, 21).

Likewise they say: “Who can boast that he has a pure heart?” [Col. 0621B] (Prov. X, 9). The answer should be that the Savior says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8); and that David says: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? The innocent in hands and pure in heart” (Ps. XXIII, 3); and elsewhere: “Do good, Lord, to those who are good and upright in heart” (Ps. CXXIV, 4); likewise in Solomon: “Good is the substance of the person whose conscience has no sin” (Ecclus. XIII, 30); likewise there: “Turn away from wrongdoing, direct your hands, and cleanse your heart from every offense” (ibid. XXXVIII, 10); likewise in the Epistle of John: “If our heart does not reproach us, we have confidence before God, and whatever we ask, we shall receive from him” (I John III, 20, 22).

Likewise they commonly say: “There is no righteous person on [Col. 0621C] earth who does good and does not sin” (Ecclus. VII, 21). The answer should be that the Lord says of holy Job: “Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him on earth, a blameless man, a true worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil work” (Job I, 8).

Likewise they say: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII, 2). To them one must answer with what the Evangelist testifies concerning holy Zechariah: “Now Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord” (Luke I, 6). And the blessed Apostle says: “That we might be holy and immaculate in his sight” (Eph. I, 4).

Likewise they say: “If we say that we have no sin, [Col. 0621D] we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John V). The answer should be that the same holy John says in the same Epistle: “But I write this, brothers, so that you may not sin. Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him, and he cannot sin” (I John III, 9); likewise there: “The one who is born of God does not sin, because God’s generation preserves him, and the Evil One will not touch him” (ibid. V, 18); likewise there, where he speaks of the Savior: “For he appeared in order to take away sins. Everyone who remains in him does not sin. Everyone who sins has neither seen him nor known him.” Likewise there: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is; and everyone [Col. 0622A] who has this hope in him sanctifies himself, just as he too is holy” (I John III, 2–3).

Likewise they say: “It is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 16). To them one must answer with what the same Apostle says elsewhere concerning a certain person: “Let him do what he wishes” (I Cor. VII, 36). Likewise to Philemon concerning Onesimus: “I wanted to keep him with me, so that he might serve me on your behalf; but I wished to do nothing without your counsel, so that your good deed might not be as though compelled, but voluntary” (Philem. 13–14). Likewise in Deuteronomy: “I have set life and death before you, good and evil; choose life, so that you may live” (Deut. XXX, 15). Likewise in Solomon: “God established the human being from the beginning and left him in the hand of his own counsel; he added commandments and precepts. If you wish, the commandments will preserve [Col. 0622B] you, and afterward you will make a pleasing covenant. I have set before you water and fire; stretch out your hand toward whichever you choose. Before the human being are good and evil, life and death; poverty and honor come from the Lord God” (Ecclus. XV, 14).

Likewise in Isaiah: “If you are willing and listen, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and do not obey me, the sword shall devour you. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. I, 19).

Finally, if someone says, “Can it happen that a person does not sin even in speech?” the answer should be: “If God wills it, he can; God does will it, therefore he can.”

Likewise, if someone says, “Can it happen that a person does not offend even in thought?” the answer should be: “If God wills it, he can; God does will it, therefore he can.”

## The Little Book of Faith Presented to Zosimus, Supreme Pontiff

[Col. 0622C]

We have discussed this confession sufficiently in the preceding dissertation; nothing needs to be added.

## Letter to the Roman Clergy

This too has been discussed sufficiently in the same place.

## CHAPTER IV. What Julian, Bishop of Eclanum, wrote

Gennadius speaks as follows about Julian’s books:

“Julian, a bishop, a man of keen intellect and learned in the divine Scriptures. A scholar in both Greek and Latin, before he revealed Pelagius’s impiety in himself, he was distinguished among the teachers of the Church. Later, however, when he appeared to defend Pelagius’s heresy, he wrote four books against Augustine, its opponent, and then again eight books. There is also a book of an altercation between the two men defending their respective positions.”

I readily agree with Gennadius when he calls Julian a man of keen intellect, learned in the sacred Scriptures, and skilled in both languages [Col. 0622D]. The sharpness of his intellect is displayed by his works; his skill in both languages by the translation of Rufinus the Syrian’s *Faith* and by other works; and the power—rather, the violence—with which he treated or, better, tortured Scripture is shown by his final Work. I do not agree with him equally when he adds that Julian had been distinguished among the teachers of the Church, if by “teacher” he means a writer. For how could the works of a distinguished writer have escaped the diligence and almost inquisitiveness of either Augustine or Mercator? But if by “teacher” he means, according to the custom of that age, one who taught the people in the Church, I shall not strongly object, since there are some traces in Augustine that lead in this direction. No one disagrees with Gennadius concerning the books against Augustine, except that the altercation between the two should not have been distinguished from the final Work, unless perhaps—what I think he may have wished to indicate—he meant that in his own time the final Work was sometimes preserved by itself and sometimes accompanied by Augustine’s responses to several of its books.

## The Book of Rufinus, a Priest of the Province of Palestine, On Faith, Translated from Greek into Latin

[Col. 0623A]

We demonstrated without obscurity in the fifth dissertation that Julian was the translator of this book; we also showed for what purpose and at what time the whole work of translation was undertaken. That passage should be consulted, and at the same time attention should be paid to the reason Gennadius wrote these words: “Before he revealed Pelagius’s heresy in himself.” For he indicated that Julian, before Pelagius’s heresy openly emerged, had revealed it in another person—in Rufinus, namely, whose confession he had made available for Latin readers. From this two conclusions follow. First, Julian published such a translation while he was still very young. Second, the part of the Pelagian error concerning original sin was first transmitted by the Pelagians as though it were the faith of the Easterners. I even add a third conjecture: Julian was converted from married life to a stricter way of life by Pelagius’s exhortations; and from this, as Julian’s father Memorius wrote, Augustine learned [Col. 0623B] about Pelagius’s praise, which he later reported in his books.

## First Letter to Zosimus, Supreme Pontiff

We have discussed this letter sufficiently, and more than sufficiently, both in the notes to chapters 6 and 9 of the *Subnotations* and at the end of Dissertation 1, where we gathered fragments scattered here and there in Mercator, who alone mentioned the letter, although Julian acknowledges it as his own (*Book I of the Imperfect Work*, ch. 17). It was written in approximately the autumn of A.D. 417; it shows what the condition of the heresy was at that time, since, at least in the matter of the Coelestian position, it was contained in approximately five propositions.

## Letter, or Little Book of Faith, Sent to Zosimus, Supreme Pontiff, in the Name of Eighteen Bishops

Mercator mentions this little book, and Julian does so as well, though somewhat more obscurely. We established that it belonged to its author in Dissertation 5 and published it in full with notes; nothing needs to be added. We showed [Col. 0623C] that it was written in A.D. 417.

## Letter to Rufus of Thessalonica in the Name of Eighteen Bishops

We discussed this letter in Dissertation 5, where fragments scattered through Augustine’s three later books to Boniface were gathered together in the form of a letter. It was written in the same year as the preceding two, or perhaps at the beginning of the following year. Julian acknowledged it as his own; Augustine refutes it in his three later books to Boniface.

## Four Books to the Bishop Turbantius, Against Augustine’s First Book On Marriage and Concupiscence

We composed the history of these four books when reviewing Augustine’s second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. Therefore only two matters remain to be observed: first, the fragments that survive in Augustine; second, the books from which the fragments must be extracted. Regarding the fragments, it is certain that substantial portions are found from the first book [Col. 0623D] and small portions from the remaining three. Augustine first refuted the first book in his own second book *On Marriage*, reproducing verbatim everything contained in the document excerpted from this first book and presented to Count Valerius, who sent it to Augustine through Alypius. From this document we know the title of the books: “Against Those Who Condemn Marriage and Assign Its Fruits to the Devil.”

Fragments of this Work are found in three of Augustine’s works: in the second book *On Marriage*, where the document of excerpts is refuted; in the six books against Julian, whose four later books oppose Julian’s four books so closely that not only books correspond to books, but chapters also correspond to chapters; and in the *Imperfect Work*, in which the section belonging to Julian is entirely devoted to attacking Augustine’s second book *On Marriage*. We refrain from presenting the material we collected with care, partly because it occurs [Col. 0624A] in books that everyone is accustomed to wear out through constant use, partly to prevent the appendix from growing beyond measure, and partly because it contributes little or almost nothing to the subsequent dissertation, since the first three defenders of the Pelagian sect provide more than enough material for resolving the questions at issue.

## Eight Books to Florus of Beneventum, Apparently a Bishop, Against Augustine’s Second Book On Marriage and Concupiscence
We have discussed this work at greater length in the preface to Marius Mercator’s *Book of Subnotations*, where it was shown what title it ought to bear, contrary to Vignier’s opinion; when it was composed, where, and with whose assistance; when it was read to Mercator; and so forth. The first five books, or even the first six in their entirety, are preserved in Augustine’s final work, during which he died. They clearly show the state of the Coelestian heresy at that time—Coelestian, I say, for grace is scarcely touched upon except in passing.

## The Book on Love, or Commentary on the Song of Songs

[Col. 0624B]

Only Bede (*On the Song of Songs*) mentions this work; he makes it consist of two books, one *On Love*, the other a *Commentary*—unless, indeed, both concerned love, which Julian endeavored, on the basis of the example of the sacred book, to distinguish from the most shameful lust. In the first book Bede argues against five, or six, of its innumerable propositions.

1. Through the choice of free will we can do the good things we wish, although with the help of God’s grace we may accomplish them more easily.

2. The mysteries concealed in the Law can be perceived only by those whom sight and learning have rendered discerning, and whom piety has made so.

3. A holy and noble love, implanted in us by nature from the very beginning of the light, which nature conciliates for us, can persist with undiminished vigor down to the extremity of old age, relying solely upon the powers of the soul, [Col. 0624C] without any loss of its own strength.

4. Our love derives from the soul what it derives from the body: from the body, that it is disturbed and impetuous; from the soul, that it is elevated and continuous.

5. The same love, so long as it desires nothing from the Gentile inclination, moves as though at the discretion of the soul alone; and in its actions it possesses delight, being not only free from disturbance but also rejoicing in liberty.

6. The assistance of the Holy Spirit is given in response to our preceding efforts and merits, and is given for this purpose, that we may love the human race more closely. For he said:

> When, therefore, the mind of the wise man—which subjects pleasure to the dignity of love and both arouses and orders desire—never goes beyond the limits of duty, but advances through efforts and merits toward such greatness [Col. 0624D] and beauty that the grace of the Holy Spirit begins to fan its noble flame, then that charity comes into being which strives to embrace in its bosom not only relatives or fellow citizens, but the human race itself.

In the later book:

On the words, “Your breasts are better than wine” (Song of Songs 1), he maintained that our opinions lead us into precisely these foaming floods of error, so that we turn the accusation against the author himself; and, in order to remove the charge which the crimes of the will evidently branded upon us, we subjected the very nature of the body to disgrace, swearing that we enter this light incapable of goodness and full of iniquity. Finally, scarcely anyone could be led to righteousness—not, I say, by reason, but not even by the discipline of the sacred Law. [Col. 0625A] For this opinion disparaged the nature of flesh and blood. But after the mediator of God and human beings had taken upon himself the saving mystery, so that, in giving an example of consummate virtue, he might assume the nature of mortal humanity, he showed that all crimes belonged to conduct, not to seed: when wills were turned toward better things, the commands not only of the Law but also of the Gospel could be fulfilled. By his very assumption of flesh he condemned the sins of conduct—not, that is, by changing the nature of the flesh, but by changing its works, so that the righteousness of the Law might be fulfilled in us under his example.

On the words, “Your neck is like necklaces”: when a beautiful neck, beautiful by nature, is adorned with the decoration [Col. 0625B] of jewels, industry unquestionably increases its good fortune; and, as though worthy of each other, the honor of the necklaces and the beauty of the neck come together. So also in you, whose nobility instruction shapes, so that the virtues which nature begins, discipline may perfect.

Again, on the words, “I will seize you and bring you into my mother’s house; there you will teach me” (Song of Songs 8): already in infancy he shows many things that we ought to learn. First, that the very creator of all those born from the union of male and female was the one who fashioned for himself a body from a virgin without the ministry of a man. Next, that no sin is congenitally present in a human being, since he existed both clothed in the reality of flesh and free from stain. Finally, that our origin cannot, except impiously, be attributed to the works of the devil, since it rejoices in God not only as its true creator but also as its indwelling inhabitant.

Observe that Julian composed this work on the occasion of his, as Bede says, contest with Augustine—that is, as I interpret it, after completing his first work of four books, and indeed even later. For the whole of this elaborate composition appears to have been made in imitation of Theodore of Mopsuestia, who wrote amorously on the Song of Songs, as the excerpts of the Fifth Synod demonstrate.

## The Book on the Good of Constancy, against the Perfidy of the Manichaean

This is the constancy which above all asserts the power and goodness of free choice, and the freedom of nature and of the movements of the human soul, while showing that every good of the mind is voluntary and subject to no accident.

And shortly afterward:

> For it arms each person’s intelligence [Col. 0625D] and kindles the spirit, continually reminding it of its liberty, and driving every fear away from it.

And after much else:

> For if, as the most learned and orthodox have brilliantly argued, no one can ever truly be harmed except by himself, and there is absolutely nothing by which anyone can be made miserable against his will, what then will virtue fear except its own failure, by which a human being is harmed forever? It belongs to divine grace to assist and strengthen constancy, so that it may guard the other virtues and defend itself against all the vices that resist it.

And near the end:

> The Manichaean is scandalized because, while denying the fictitious god, we fear offending our Lord, who is true: because we assert that nature is good, and that human beings possess free choice.

Only Bede mentions this book; we have shown elsewhere that it was written after Julian’s expulsion from his see.

# CHAPTER V. What Annianus, deacon of Celeda and Pelagius’s secretary, wrote

Scarcely anything can be added to what was said in Dissertation I about Annianus, Pelagius’s “squire,” as Orosius calls him. He wrote all of Pelagius’s works except the brief expositions; he also wrote two letters under his own name, which he prefixed to homilies of Chrysostom translated by him into Latin.

## Letter Prefixed to the Homilies on Matthew

To the truly holy and most blessed Lord Orontius, bishop, Annianus.

[Col. 0626B]

You exercise upon me equally the affection of a most devout father and the skill of a most wise teacher: amid these storms of trials which we endure together for love of the faith, you draw my spirit away both from grief and from torpor, and send my mind, languishing under anxiety, back to the study of the Scriptures. For, most blessed sir, you command me to pour into the Latin language, in whatever speech I am able, the commentary of Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, in which he explained the evangelist Matthew in ninety-one books. Would that we might accomplish this as conveniently as you command it opportunely and profitably. For what could be offered to our ears more learned for prudence, more ardent for exercise, or more purified for doctrine [Col. 0626C] than these splendid monuments of so distinguished a mind and intellect? Especially at this time, when, on the pretext of certain exceedingly difficult questions, opposition is offered with sufficient insolence to the edification of morals and ecclesiastical discipline. For blessed John rises up in defense of that cause, both in his other works and in this one, with such greatness and ardor that, by interpreting the evangelist’s sayings, he seems to fight alongside us for evangelical perfection.

For what does he impress upon human beings more than the nobility of their nature, which, against the rage of Manichaeus, is praised by the unanimous agreement and harmony of all right-minded thinkers? It is praised either for the glory of its admirable creator, or to arouse the pursuit of virtue, or to chastise the vices of pleasure. What, I say, does he commend more insistently [Col. 0626D] than the dignity of the freedom implanted in us by God, the confession of which is the principal distinction between us and the pagans? They so unhappily believe that the human being, created in the image of God, is bound by the violence of fate and the necessity of sinning that he is forced even to envy the animals.

What does he insinuate against these same teachers more effectively than that God’s commandments are possible, and that the human being is capable of every virtue which God either commands or counsels? By this alone injustice is driven away from the one who commands, and guilt is produced in the transgressor.

And when this glory of learned men discusses God’s grace, with what abundance and what caution does he celebrate it! He is neither careless nor excessive in either respect [Col. 0627A], but moderate in both. He shows human wills to be free, yet everywhere acknowledges that divine grace is necessary for carrying out God’s commands; he commends the continuous assistance of divine grace in such a way that he does not destroy the efforts of the will.

In nearly every part of doctrine, and especially in moral exhortation and in all the rules of ecclesiastical discipline, he agrees throughout so closely with our writers that he might be thought to have instructed our own people, whom he never saw at all, in the whole understanding of Scripture. How strongly he is held by love for exhorting—that is, correcting, and even adorning—human beings, he chiefly demonstrates in this work. Having undertaken the role of one who commends, he completes a definite portion of each book by exposition [Col. 0627B], while bringing the remainder forward with an exhortation friendly to himself and as perfect as he can make it.

Even in the passages of exposition, which are full of acumen, weight, coherence, learning, and substance, he has no other principal aim than not to pass over even the smallest point of morality, as though he alone had almost completely perceived the purpose of the divine Law. Although that Law is woven through innumerable matters, he reduces everything to one end: namely, that it should kindle those to whom it has been given to love God and pursue virtue.

That he does not do this for a kind of display or for that stinking vanity of glory is testified not only by the whole restraint of his doctrine and character, which also shines through his writings, but by the very end of his life. Indeed, in all his speech he not only corrects but also arms the listener’s spirit [Col. 0627C]. His entire principal aim is not so much to teach that private honesty which lies hidden amid the shadows of prosperity, as to establish a virtue that fights daily as though in battle array, and that, without any loss to itself, is beaten by the showers of tribulation and scorched by its fires.

That virtue this distinguished teacher of the Church and true disciple of Christ fulfilled so completely that all he discussed concerning the assertion of virtue even through death seems to have been impressed upon no one so much as upon himself alone. Finally, he adorned a life shining with holiness from adolescence and decorated in the priesthood with a thousand marks of perfection by adding sufferings endured for the love of righteousness. Certainly, for such a thing to befall someone living in peace among the churches requires a great spirit, a mind far removed from all human glory, and altogether rare virtue.

What is indicated in the seventh book of this work is that, while still a presbyter at Antioch, he composed these writings with which he then built up that Church. From this it becomes increasingly clear that, when he later held the episcopate in the imperial city and stirred up those notorious and immense conflicts against himself, he did not act from some rashness or from a liberty discordant with his character. Rather, he had always formed himself in this way and had sworn so consistently and firmly on the side of truth and justice against all the hosts of the wicked that, although the names of priests or the weapons of kings might combine against him, they could drive him from his priestly [Col. 0628A] throne, but never from the truth.

Thus, carrying out the best reflection in the circumstances, he preferred to crown the honor of a bishop with the dignity of a confessor rather than corrupt it with the shamefulness of a flatterer.

There is also something almost distinctive and proper to him, by which you in particular, because of the similarity of your pursuits, may love him: always concerned, always watchful, always hostile to harmful complacency—or rather, to deadly torpor—he recommends everywhere the usefulness of compunction, himself deeply moved. Accordingly, his speech is scarcely ever raised into pompous display; rather, it is entirely adapted to the benefit of the listener.

His very style, as can be observed more clearly in his own work, is exceedingly well suited to the ears of the Church. It expresses that ancient but learned mode of speaking: [Col. 0628B] moderate, even, mature, chaste; free from every fault of carelessness and every luxuriant display of ornament; not squalid, yet not florid; not unpolished, yet not smoothed by excessive refinement; not bristling with harshness, yet not wanton with pleasantness. Everywhere it indicates the greatest abundance and admirable ability, but nowhere an ambition to speak. Hence the simple reader understands him more readily, while the eloquent reader praises him.

Certainly, as you may also have heard from many others, after all the varied and splendid riches of the ancient writers and after the brilliant light of so many distinguished teachers, all the ecclesiastical libraries of the Greeks are now especially adorned by his volumes. Finally, you can easily understand that the marvelous care with which Basil speaks, [Col. 0628C] the applauded magnificence of Antiochus, and the lofty buskin of Gregory are readily surpassed by this moderation of John.

For he has imbued and tinged his style, which reigns with the unimpaired ability we have mentioned, everywhere with the flavor and color of the Scriptures, so that the former seems to relax somewhat in the adornment of eloquence, while the latter appears to flash with the majesty of the Scriptures. Perhaps he alone is less pleasing to the ears of adolescents who are placed in the school of letters and prefer what is painted to what is solid, who pursue what is beautiful rather than what is useful, who love things that merely sound rather than things that act, and who take greater delight in being sprinkled with the pleasantness of flowers than in being nourished by the richness of fruits.

If, therefore, I have made him appear sufficiently diminished in Latin, you must attribute this not so much to me, venerable lord, as to yourself. [Col. 0628D] You urged me to translate him with such authority of command and such an entreaty of affection that I preferred to take something—or rather, very much—away from his stylistic honor than to incur guilt against you by refusing any longer.

For whatever this work of mine may be worth, I ask in return the most generous gift of your prayers, so that you may help us by your prayers as well as by your example to imitate something of that man’s virtue. Remember me always in Christ, my deservedly most blessed lord.

## Letter Prefixed to the Homilies on the Praises of Paul

To the holy Lord Evangelus, Annianus sends greetings.

[Col. 0629A]

Recent experience has taught me how useful the commands of good men are to those who obey them: entering by a more direct path of kindness, they confer benefits under the appearance of commands. For what more pleasant or more fruitful thing could you have commanded me than to translate into our language something from the works of the blessed John—namely, the seven little books which he once delivered in the Church on the praises of the apostle Paul?

Although my language is extremely rough in this foreign speech, I have nevertheless derived more pleasure and benefit than labor. For while I tried to translate him from Greek for you, it happened that I myself absorbed him more closely and enjoyed more fully the truth of so distinguished a doctrine, especially since his rich intellect everywhere treats an even richer subject.

This blessed Paul is portrayed not with the shadowy colors of some fabricated praise [Col. 0629B], but formed by the inviolable truth of his virtues. His distinguished praiser asserts him everywhere with such completeness and solidity—now from the greatness of his deeds, now from the illumination of his words, at one time from the variety of his counsels, at another from the depth of his dispensations, then from the endurance of his sufferings and from the splendor of his signs—that he seems not merely to have painted him but, as it were, to have raised him again to offer once more an example of perfection.

For when the merits of other people are praised by others, the result is usually something commonplace and meager; and, in speech wandering about on the surface, the virtues themselves seem to come forward more in their names for commemoration than in their realities. But blessed John, by looking more deeply at Paul and bringing him clearly before us, seems to me to have examined [Col. 0629C] and expressed the very veins and marrow of his virtues. They all live so vividly in this praise, and are adorned with their flowers and fruits so fully, that we almost seem to admire them no less as explained by this man with such sublimity than as possessed by the Apostle himself.

This work ought to be all the more lovable and pleasing to you because, shining with the light of the holy Scriptures like a most brilliant star, it assails the darkness of Manichaean error. What consolation arises for us when we see so learned and illustrious a teacher of the East building up that truth which the Traducianist attacks among us? Blessed John guards, arms, and kindles this truth here as in all his books, fortified on every side, so that he seems to have prepared assistance for us against the assault upon the true faith rather than to have instructed only his present disciples. [Col. 0630A]

How powerfully does he rise against necessity! How powerfully does he rise in defense of free choice! How, agreeing everywhere with our books, does he commend the supports of divine grace while preserving the right of the will? How brilliantly does he set against the darkness of all vices, and in defense of all virtues, the most splendid vessel of election as their mirror?

First, by placing blessed Paul before all the saints and comparing him with the angels. Second, by asserting the goodness of nature from his virtues and sayings. Third, by proving his charity to be most fervent for the salvation of all. Fourth, by speaking of his calling and of the truth of the Gospel confirmed everywhere by him. Fifth, by discussing his sufferings and the variety of his dispensations [Col. 0630B]. Sixth, by resolving all those questions with which the Traducianist, in opposition, stains blessed Paul with the obscurity of vices, in order to reconcile sins to his faithful by apostolic example. Seventh, by extolling above all others his fire of zeal for Christ and his fervor for teaching even before the dignity of the apostolate, so that it may be perfectly clear that the necessity of sinning has been extinguished, since both the Apostle’s teaching and his life wage war against the Manichaeans.

Yet in translating so excellent a work, although, as I think, we have lost nothing of the truth of its meaning, [Col. 0630C] we have nevertheless lost no small amount of the beauty of its eloquence, since we have been unable to reproduce the splendor of so noble a style and the grace of its expressions. But even so, you should not regret having commanded this work. You need not fear that, offended by the roughness of the translation, you will be deprived of the pleasure of reading it. Whatever has been lacking to us in refinement and verbal ornament is entirely compensated by the magnificent inventions of the man whom we have translated.
