For the whole of Saint John is so bright and radiant that, through the light of his thoughts, he can easily flash even amid the clouds of our language.

Reader, observe how close is the relationship among these letters and the book *On the Institution of the Virgin* addressed to Demetrias—in their Latin, their thoughts, their figures of speech, and their vocabulary—so that it is plainly evident that Annianus is the author of both compositions. Observe likewise with what justification Annianus has been called, both in Dissertation 2 and in the discussion of the letter to Demetrias, “Pelagius’s squire,” as Orosius says, and, as Jerome suggests, something like his tongue.

# DISSERTATION VII. ON THE ORIGIN AND GROWTH OF THE HERESY THAT TOOK ITS NAME FROM PELAGIUS

On these words of Marius Mercator: “The five chapters generate one most impious and abominable doctrine”; and these: “The entire substance of Julian’s foolish and still more impious labor appears to be reducible to one depraved doctrine, namely, that the transgression of Adam and Eve did not make them mortal,” and so forth (*Preface to the Book of Subnotations*, nos. 4 and 9).

[Col. 0629]

## CHAPTER ONE. What is to be undertaken in this dissertation, and by what method

[Col. 0629D]

At the time when the monk Hilary, at Syracuse, consulted Augustine about the questions which Pelagius and Coelestius were raising in Sicily, the heresy, according to Hilary—or rather, what was believed to constitute the heresy—consisted of these five points (Letter 88 among Augustine’s letters): that a human being can be without sin and easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes; that an unbaptized infant cannot justly perish, because it is born without sin; that a rich person remaining in his wealth cannot enter the kingdom of God unless he sells all that he possesses, and that it cannot benefit him if he happens to fulfill the commandments from those riches; that one ought never to swear at all; and that the Church as it now exists has neither wrinkle nor stain and can be without sin.

The final point, if indeed it was a distinct one, was easily referred back to the first. The two later points concerning the rich and oaths, because of their incredible absurdity—or astonishing character—were rejected by everyone and abandoned even by their own adherents. The remaining two [Col. 0631A] caused immense trouble for the Catholic Church, since their authors defended them stubbornly and they were more easily persuaded upon minds insufficiently educated, because faith—which teaches the necessity of divine grace and the reality of original sin—surpasses human understanding.

All the writers of the fifth century who touched upon this heresy teach that the entire heresy which took its name from Pelagius was contained, as it were, in these two heads. Augustine thought he had comprehended the whole of it in this one statement (*On Nature and Grace*, chapter 6):

> Human nature needs neither a physician in little children, because it is sound, nor the assistance of grace in adults, because it is sufficient for itself for righteousness.

Vincent of Lérins:

> Who before that profane man Pelagius ever presumed so much upon the power of free choice that he did not think God’s grace necessary to assist it in good actions one by one? [Col. 0631B] Who before his prodigious disciple Coelestius denied that the whole human race was bound by the guilt of Adam’s transgression? (*Commonitory against Heresies*, chapter 564).

The Fathers of the Council of Carthage:

> Whoever in general teaches and affirms that human nature can be sufficient for itself to overcome sins and fulfill God’s commandments, and is thereby found to be an adversary of God’s grace—which is more clearly manifested in the prayers of the saints—and whoever denies that little children are freed from perdition through the baptism of Christ and receive everlasting salvation, let him be anathema (*Patrologia*, vol. XX, 564).

The Fathers of the province of Milevis:

> These are the two things by which they seek utterly to overturn everything on which we Christians stand. What faithful hearts could endure that God should not be asked to be our helper against the evil of sin and in the practice of righteousness, and that the sacrament of Christian grace should not assist little children in attaining eternal life? (*Letter 92 among Augustine’s letters).

[Col. 0631C]

Pelagius himself, writing to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, says—these are Augustine’s words—that there are two charges “by which people try to defame him: one, that he denies the sacrament of baptism to little children and promises the kingdoms of heaven to some without Christ’s redemption; the other, that he says a human being can avoid sin in such a way as to exclude God’s help, and that he trusts so much in free choice that he rejects the assistance of grace” (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 30).

Coelestius too, summarizing his entire calumny against Catholics—or his empty talk in concealing the heresy—said:

> We confess that the grace of Christ is necessary for everyone, both adults and little children, and we anathematize those who say that someone born of two baptized parents ought not to be baptized (*Book I to Boniface*, chapter 22).

Julian’s complaint also belongs here (*in Augustine, Book III against Julian*, chapter 1):

> If anyone says either that human beings possess free choice or that God is the creator of those who are born, he will be called a Pelagian and a Coelestian.

[Col. 0631D]

Pelagius and Coelestius defended both parts of the error, though not, as we noted earlier, with equal zeal. Each had his own position, as though he had undertaken it for himself, which he defended in preference to the other. Pelagius fought against the grace of God and for human will; Coelestius fought against original sin and for nature. Hence it happened that, according as each of their followers adhered more closely to one or the other leader, he was called either Coelestian or Pelagian.

Each of these parts was further divided into two. The first, which was Coelestian, embraced two questions: Adam’s mortality and original sin, each with its own appendices. The second, which was Pelagian, likewise embraced two: the assisting and prevenient grace of God, again with their related points. The fifth position, which might appear to concern impeccability—or, as the Greeks say, ἀναμαρτησία (*anamartēsia*, sinlessness)—belongs to the necessity of grace, as Augustine proves everywhere, not so much by word [Col. 0632A] as by deed.

It is our plan to compose the history of the Coelestian heresy by itself, since this is the one which Mercator, to whose work we are devoting our labor, touched upon, and from it the Pelagian heresy was propagated, as will be seen later. We thought it appropriate to relate its history in the manner naturalists usually do when they are said to write the history of a tree: they report the soil in which it grows, the time and causes of its birth, the manner of its growth, and the spreading and wooded multitude of its branches. For this heresy was like a certain unhappily fortunate tree which, born in an obscure place and from an ignoble sower, nevertheless grew through deceptive growth and the unremitting labor of its cultivators into such a multitude of offspring that it seems a prodigy for so vast a growth to have arisen from a single slender root.

That slender root was nothing other than the claim that Adam would have been mortal whether he sinned or did not sin. From this arose, as Mercator teaches, the denial of original sin—that is, as Jansenius of Ypres says [Col. 0632B], the origin of the whole of Pelagianism.

Since Pelagianism is contained, as it were, in two denials—one of original sin, the other of the necessity of inward grace, whether assisting grace for each individual act of piety or prevenient grace for free choice in the matter of salvation—I shall, unless I am mistaken, clearly show that it arose from the root I have mentioned, if I establish from reliable testimonies of the ancients, first, that the question whether Adam was created mortal was the very first of all; next, that from its agitation arose another question, concerning sin and the baptism of infants; then, from that one, a third, concerning the weakness of nature for works of piety and the necessity of divine grace for each individual act; finally, from the third, a fourth, concerning prevenient grace.

But before these points are proved by the testimonies of the ancients, the logic of the discussion seems to require that we set out what Mercator records about the questions proposed, lest a failure of memory prevent the reader from receiving from this dissertation the greatest benefit he ought to derive from it.

[Col. 0632C]

A question contrary to the Catholic faith, raised long ago among certain Syrians—especially in Cilicia—by Theodore, formerly bishop of the city of Mopsuestia, is still secretly handed down among a few of them, and is not openly produced. Rather, those who vaunt it, while posing as Catholics, retain it for the time being within the churches.

> NAMELY, THAT THE PROGENITORS OF THE HUMAN RACE, ADAM AND EVE, WERE CREATED MORTAL BY GOD; THAT THEY DID NOT INJURE ANY OF THEIR DESCENDANTS BY THEIR TRANSGRESSION, BUT HARMED ONLY THEMSELVES; THAT THEY MADE THEMSELVES GUILTY OF TRANSGRESSING THE COMMANDMENT BEFORE GOD, WHILE ABSOLUTELY NO ONE ELSE WAS GUILTY.

This foolish question, no less hostile to the right faith, was first brought to Rome under Anastasius, of holy memory, supreme pontiff of the Roman Church, by a certain Rufinus, a Syrian by nationality.

Being shrewd, and protecting himself against the odium attached to it, he did not dare to advance it himself. Instead, he deceived Pelagius, a monk from Britain, and thoroughly imbued and instructed him in the impious absurdity mentioned above [Col. 0632D]. Soon afterward, when Pelagius ventured to compose commentaries on the apostle Paul and came to that famous passage of the Letter to the Romans, which reads, “Therefore, just as through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings,” and so forth (Romans 5:12), he said that only those were guilty and held bound by that transgression who wished to imitate Adam in transgressing God’s commandments—not everyone generated from his seed through the succession of generations.

From this point he argues and declares at greater length concerning the passages that follow in the letter:

> No human being at all has been injured, or is injured, by the transgression of Adam’s sin through generation, but by imitation, he says, because Adam was the first to sin in the human race; and that person becomes guilty and liable who imitates him by his own will—not by being born, but by sinning.

Coelestius, noble by birth and at that time a legal scholar in the courts, adhered to this Pelagius. Yet he had been born a eunuch from his mother’s womb through a defect of nature [Col. 0633A]. Instructed by the aforementioned Pelagius, he absorbed this most impious view in a purer form and, with incredible loquacity, made many people participants and accomplices in this madness of his. He dared to disseminate the same view openly and publicly among the people in the following statements:

> “Adam was made mortal, and whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died;

> “Because Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race;

> “Because infants who are born are in the same condition in which Adam was before the transgression;

> “Because the whole human race does not die through Adam’s death, since the whole human race does not rise again through Christ’s resurrection;

> “Because infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.”

These five chapters generate one most impious and abominable doctrine.

He added:

> “A human being can be without sin [Col. 0633B] and can easily keep God’s commandments;

> “Because even before Christ’s coming there were human beings without sin;

> “And because the Law sends people to the kingdom of heaven in the same way as the Gospel.”

These and similar teachings pleased Julian himself and his other comrades. Once they had become known and had been exposed, they were condemned by ecclesiastical authority along with the persons named above; and Julian defended them by the sheer number of his books. He was consequently content to be counted as a third, along with Pelagius and Coelestius, in their condemnation.

From this account by Mercator it is possible to understand several things, neither few in number nor insignificant in importance. But before they are explained individually, it is worthwhile to warn the reader to pay somewhat closer attention to the words with which Mercator in reality makes the Coelestian heresy consist of only two parts: one concerning Adam’s mortality, the other concerning the powers of human nature [Col. 0633C] to fulfill the commandments. For the six other propositions which he adds he plainly does not intend to have been chapters of the error, but merely certain proofs of the chapters—four belonging to the first doctrine and two to the second. This is indicated, I think, not obscurely by the two causal conjunctions, *quoniam* and *quia* (“because”), prefixed to the individual propositions.

The same point should also be observed in the *Book on the Proceedings in Palestine* (chapter 11), where Pelagius is confronted with the propositions which the deacon Paulinus had earlier brought against Coelestius at the Council of Carthage. The same conjunctions are used with the same propositions, so that it should not be thought to have happened accidentally in either passage, but deliberately, to signify that four questions arose from the first doctrine and two from the second. For, as happens, in order to confirm a doctrine placed in controversy, people produced propositions which, because of the reciprocal surges of contradiction, developed into a new question.

From what Mercator reports, it is now clear that, before the time of Pope Anastasius, the Coelestian heresy arose at Mopsuestia in Cilicia Secunda, with Theodore as its author [Col. 0633D]. For Rufinus, who had long before been instructed by Theodore, came to Rome in the year 399, which was the second year of Anastasius’s pontificate.

Indeed, it is credible that it first arose when Theodore began to occupy the see of Mopsuestia—that is, in the year 390—if, having either received it from Diodore of Tarsus, whom he had as his teacher, or fabricated it himself, he later became a teacher of the Church and wished immediately to hand it on to others, as the lust for innovation is incapable of restraint.

If this is certain—as what Mercator reports undoubtedly is—it follows that John Maxentius truly wrote of Theodore of Mopsuestia (*Second Confession*) that the opponents of original sin were disciples of Coelestius, Pelagius, and Theodore. Likewise, Coelestius truly asserted before Aurelius that, when he was in Rome, he had learned from Rufinus the presbyter that there was no transmission of sin (in Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapter 3). Likewise, Augustine truly said of Pelagius and Coelestius (Letter 190, to Optatus) that they were either the authors of, or certainly the most zealous and well-known advocates of, the error by which the grace conferred through Christ upon little and great alike is attacked [Col. 0634A]. Finally, Photius truly wrote that the Coelestian heresy first flourished in the East and was then propagated from there into the West. All these points had previously been less clear.

And from this the following other passage of Augustine receives its light, though otherwise somewhat obscure. For after speaking of Pelagius and Coelestius, condemned because they denied original sin, he continues in these words (On Original Sin, ch. 22):

> Those who are either said or proved to be the authors of this perversity—or, at any rate, if they are not its authors but learned it from others, are nevertheless its defenders and teachers—are proclaimed as having caused it to creep and grow more widely through their words, writings, appropriate indications, and the reputation arising and spreading from all these things.

Here too the popular opinion concerning Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia, is dispelled—as though he had been the author of the [Col. 0634B] Coelestian heresy concerning original sin. Jansenius of Ypres, like certain more recent writers on Pelagian history, defends this opinion in more than one place (Book I, On the Pelagian Heresy, ch. 12), evidently forgetting that none of the ancients ever charged Rufinus of Aquileia with denying the transmission of sin. Jerome would certainly have made that charge if the matter had been so; and he also forgets that Pammachius was no less hostile to Rufinus than devoted to Jerome, and did not offer Rufinus hospitality, but arranged for him to be expelled from the Church by the supreme pontiff. But these matters have been discussed elsewhere at greater length (Dissertation 1).

Augustine, moreover, John Maxentius, and Photius return to Mercator the authority that they derive from him, their testimonies agreeing with his. Photius especially (Codex 177), when he reports that he had read five books in which Theodore of Mopsuestia attacked those who said that human beings sin by nature, and therefore that infants are washed clean by baptism. The testimonies [Col. 0634C] of both men are given in their own words in the notes, partly in the preface to the *Subnotations*, and partly in Mercator’s excerpts from the books of Theodore of Mopsuestia against Saint Augustine, the defender of original sin.

But observe, reader, how Mercator, as did the other writers mentioned above, reduced this entire heresy to two main points. The first of these concerned original sin, as they expressed it because that was how the matter was commonly reported. Mercator himself, as a man especially engaged in this question, led the stream back to its very source and said that the issue concerned human mortality.

Observe also that, from Mercator’s recension of the errors of Coelestius, one must correct what appears in the *Palestinian Proceedings*, where the charges brought against Pelagius from Coelestius’ doctrine are reported. For, with no mention being made of the error concerning the powers of free will, the two proofs that follow are rashly mixed with the others, and thus five arguments for a single error are presented in this form (Book On the *Palestinian Proceedings*, ch. 11):

> Adam was made mortal, so that whether he sinned, [Col. 0634D] or did not sin, he would die; because Adam’s sin harmed him alone and not the human race; because the Law sends one to the kingdom in the same way as the Gospel; because before Christ’s coming there were human beings without sin; because newborn infants are in the condition in which Adam was before his transgression; because neither does the whole human race die through Adam’s death or transgression, nor does the whole human race rise through Christ’s resurrection.

Finally, observe that our dissertation ought to have two principal parts: the first concerning the doctrine—how it grew prodigiously from a slender root into so great a multitude of branches; the second concerning the doctrine’s first author—how Mercator’s opinion about Theodore of Mopsuestia can be reconciled with the opinion of the writers on Pelagian history. For, following Jerome, they mention Cassian and the poet who composed an epitaph for the Nestorian heresy, along with many others, and [Col. 0635A] much earlier figures as well, such as Paul of Samosata, Origen, Photinus, Jovinian, and others.

## CHAPTER II  
### How the other three principal errors derived their origin from one error

We showed in the preceding chapter that the Pelagian heresy had four principal doctrines. Prosper ingeniously described the origin of all of them when he arranged each according to its apparent manner of birth (*Poem Against the Ungrateful*, ch. 1):

> The doctrine that the ancient serpent,  
> the British snake, sated with the dragon’s gall,  
> spewed forth in a pestilential utterance:
>
> By this principle, he maintained, the first human beings were created,  
> so that whether they transgressed the prescribed commandment,  
> or remained blameless by keeping the law,  
> they would in any event suffer that death  
> by which life leaves the flesh—  
> a death not produced by sin,  
> but fixed as the companion of created beings  
> by God himself, its institutor.
>
> Therefore those begotten from their fathers had drawn  
> no guilt [Col. 0635B] from them; nor are their descendants now born  
> unlike the first human beings in origin—those who sinned  
> through the evil use of their freedom, harming their offspring  
> by example, not by seed.
>
> All the innocent, moreover, could live  
> in the citadel of virtue and preserve  
> the beauty implanted in the mind  
> by their own choice, since the natural honor  
> of one who wills rightly endures,  
> and the law implanted within their hearts  
> admonishes them of what is written outwardly.
>
> To this was added the grace of Christ,  
> which established in itself a general refuge  
> for those who had fallen, if they wished  
> to be renewed in the sacred font,  
> so that, when the guilt voluntarily incurred  
> had been dissolved by pardon, nature might of its own accord  
> return to its own powers.
>
> Whatever strength it had lost through errors,  
> once cleansed and restored it could preserve  
> for the future.
>
> So rich, however, is this gift of baptism,  
> and so much is bestowed upon human beings  
> through this covenant, that it is fitting  
> even for little ones entirely free from fault,  
> so that those who have been well born  
> may become better, and nature’s good  
> may be illumined by an added honor.
>
> Yet no one among all human beings is born  
> deprived of this gift by God’s judgment;  
> rather, each person by his own freedom deserves  
> to receive the promises of the One who calls—  
> [Col. 0635C] promises owed to the upright  
> but not owed to those who have turned away.

How, in fact, what Prosper asserts actually came about may perhaps become clear from the following.

Almost in every age people have asked where evil comes from—whether the evil of the mind, which is sin, or that of the body, which is death, that is, the separation of the mind from the body. The Manichaeans held that sin arises from nature; Catholics held that it arises from human will (Augustine, in the books *On Free Choice* and elsewhere throughout).

Next it was asked where death, or the common necessity of dying among human beings, comes from: whether from nature, whose creator is God, or from sin, whose parent is the will. Theodore of Mopsuestia held that it arose from nature; Catholics, from sin. Consequently, when the question was brought back to the first human being, Theodore said (in Mercator’s excerpts and in the Fifth Synod) that Adam was made mortal in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die. Catholics, on the contrary, said that he was made in such a way that, unless he had sinned, he would not have died at all (Augustine, Book I, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins* [Col. 0635D], ch. 2).

Theodore maintained that the necessity of dying is common to everyone, but that sin is not common, since infants often die innocent, even in their mothers’ wombs. Catholics held that these persons too, though only a few days old, are held by the sin of their first parent, and therefore are not born as innocent as the first human being was created. They also held that human nature was indeed granted immortality at the beginning of creation, but was deprived of it in the death of sinful Adam and would receive it again in Christ’s resurrection.

To this Theodore replied (in Mercator’s preface to the *Subnotations*) that the first parents harmed no one through their transgression, but made only themselves guilty; that infants are begotten by their parents as innocent as the first human being created by God; that Adam, when he was created, possessed no greater innocence than infants who lack every possibility [Col. 0636A] of sinning; that the whole human race does not die through Adam’s death, since the whole human race does not rise through Christ’s resurrection, but only the devout; and that infants, if they die before receiving baptism, are not deprived of eternal life.

When Catholics argued that the first human being’s sin is transmitted by origin to his descendants, and that they are therefore called children by nature of the paternal wrath, and that little children are born liable to the punishment of death because they share in their father’s guilt, Theodore’s followers proceeded into open heresy (in Mercator’s fourth excerpt from the five books of Theodore against Saint Augustine). They asserted that the Church’s tradition concerning original sin either belonged to the madness of Manichaeus, who said that nature is evil; or to Origen’s fantasies about the *pre-existence* (*προϋπάρξει*) of souls and their sin before embodiment; or to Tertullian’s error concerning the transmission of souls. From this arose three questions: whether those who defend original sin are Manichaeans; whether souls are created daily by God or existed before embodiment; and whether the transmission of souls occurs just as does that of bodies. But those questions arose incidentally. [Col. 0636B] This one arose in its own right.

For, the Catholics said, why are infants baptized if they have no stain? Why are they baptized for the remission of sins if they are innocent? “So that they may become better from being good,” the heretics replied; “so that children of human beings may be adopted as children of God; so that they may be heirs of the kingdom of heaven.” For if they die by their own fate before baptism, they will not be deprived of eternal life, but only of the kingdom of God. Although they are certain innocent images of God and therefore, because of the immortality of their souls, ought to possess eternal life, they have nevertheless not been made coheirs of Christ through the sacrament of faith. It pleased the Father to give the kingdom only to those of that kind.

Then one question multiplied into several, but all gradually coalesced into a single one: whether Adam’s descendants are born children of wrath, or, as they put it, whether there is a transmission of sin. Catholics affirmed it; the heretics denied it. Both parties fought as though for the very heart of the matter, with the full contention [Col. 0636C] of their minds and all the force of their arguments. The astonishing abundance of arguments, however, also produced innumerable questions, as the statements of the respondents were turned, as commonly happens, into material for dispute.

The heretics pressed two points above all. First, the transmission of sin could not be admitted without condemning marriage. Second, even if it could be admitted, it nevertheless ought not to be, because of the boundless absurdity that would follow from it—and indeed the multitude of blasphemies.

The Catholics immediately distinguished the use of marriage from lust, or sexual desire. The former, as it comes from God, is honorable, and constitutes the natural origin of children; the latter, as it arose from sin, is vicious and is the transmission of sin. The heretics, by contrast, maintained that lust, or, as they called it, the pleasure of married couples, was not merely honorable and praiseworthy but a work of God, since none of God’s works is imperfect or shameful. Here was the sixth branch of the heresy: that lust is a natural good.

[Col. 0636D] The Catholics, in confirming faith in original sin, relied not only on the authority of Scripture, the tradition of the Fathers, the common mind of the Church, and the rite of baptism, but especially on the argument that the nature existing in us is not of the same kind as the nature Adam possessed before sin: free from fault, upright, inclined toward the good, an unimpaired image of God, and a work worthy of its craftsman. Rather, ignorance of truth, difficulty in doing what is right, blindness of mind, weakness of will, slavery under the power of the devil, and other such conditions seem to discolor the image of God and demonstrate its corruption. Yet nothing could have corrupted it except sin, which either became in some manner part of nature or at least is propagated through the condition of birth.

Here again the stubborn pride of the heretics broke out into manifest heresy. They dared to assert that Adam was created in no other condition than that in which we are now procreated, since both have the same origin, whether the Creator made one from clay or the procreator produced the other from seed. [Col. 0637A] They claimed that ignorance of truth and difficulty in doing what is right are primordial features of nature, yet that the author is not thereby to be blamed, since both can be corrected, indeed entirely removed, through the use of reason. For, they said, a law is implanted by nature in human minds, and whoever fulfills it is pure from every crime, upright in life, and *sinless* (*ἀναμάρτητος*); and everyone can easily keep this law if he wishes (Pelagius, on Romans 11, no. 17).

The Catholics insisted that God’s grace is necessary to overcome temptations, fulfill the law, and perfect righteousness. This is confirmed by the testimony of all Scripture, by the prayers of the Church, and by the agreement of all the faithful. The heretics evaded the point, however, and, in order to avoid the odium attached to the word, admitted that none of these things is accomplished without God’s assistance—indeed, assistance is needed for each individual act—but claimed that this assistance does not differ from nature, law, and teaching. For, they said, only three things are needed for doing good: power, guidance, and impulse. Innate freedom of choice supplies the power; instruction supplies the guidance; and the will [Col. 0637B] supplies the impulse, since it is born to follow reason, with which it is connate.

The Catholics pressed that this kind of grace is not the grace which Christ came to obtain, the grace by which the Holy Spirit works in us both to will and to accomplish; the grace which every saint, following Paul’s example, implores with groans against temptations; the grace we ask for when, taught by Christ, we say: “Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil.”

The heretics answered each point. First, Julianus said (in the *Booklet of Faith*, part I, no. 7):

> Christ came to call the whole world back from sins both by his example and to redeem it by his suffering: while, as God, he took sin away by forgiving it, and, as man, he showed through the likeness of human nature how sin could thereafter be overcome.

Next Pelagius said (in Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 10):

> The Holy Spirit works in us to will what is good and to will what is holy when he sets us, devoted to earthly desires and loving only present things like dumb animals [Col. 0637C], on fire with the greatness of future glory and the promise of rewards; when, through the revelation of wisdom, he rouses a sluggish will to desire God; and when he persuades us to do everything that is good.

Then he said (ibid., ch. 8):

> God helps us when we labor through his teaching and revelation: when he opens the eyes of our heart; when he shows us future things so that we may not be occupied with the present; when he exposes the devil’s snares; and when he illuminates us with the manifold and ineffable gift of heavenly grace.

Finally he said (from Book II of Eugippius, ch. 288):

> We ask God, when we say, “Do not bring us into temptation,” not to suffer us to undergo some evil that is not in our power—for example, that I should fall from a horse or break my leg, that a robber should kill me, or something of that sort. These things are not in my power. But if I wish, I can overcome the temptations of my sins, and I can do so without God’s assistance.

When the Catholics pressed still more forcefully that the grace proclaimed by the heretics was not a grace that kindled the will [Col. 0637D], but one that merely enlightened the mind; not one poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, but one that remained external; not one by which the children of God are moved to act holily, but one by which only the manner of acting is shown, the Pelagians, overwhelmed by the weight and number of the testimonies of divine Scripture, finally confessed this grace as well. But they refused to admit that it is given except according to merits, lest God be a respecter of persons; and they held that it is given only so that what would otherwise still be accomplished, though with greater difficulty, may be done more easily and readily. Pelagius himself once answered in this way, while he was still in Rome—that is, before the year 408.

When the Catholics objected that, for Christ’s sake, God grants human beings a certain grace entirely out of mercy—that is, without preceding merits (Augustine, *On Grace and Free Choice*, ch. 13)—the heretics held that this grace was the remission of sins, but then divided into opposing positions. Pelagius [Col. 0638A] affirmed that sins are forgiven freely for Christ’s sake (on Ephesians 1); Coelestius denied that pardon is given according to the grace and mercy of God, but according to the merit and labor of those who have become worthy of mercy through repentance (Book On the *Palestinian Proceedings*, ch. 21).

When the Catholics insisted that a grace must be admitted by which sins are not merely forgiven, but by which sin is prevented; indeed, by which right conduct is brought about; indeed, which goes before the wills, both preparing them so that they may act and moving them so that their ability is not fruitless, the heretics obstinately resisted. They acted as though confession of such grace removed free choice from human beings, attributed iniquity to God, and made all good things occur by fate. Here the battle was fought fiercely over prevenient grace, its power, and its harmony with free choice, as well as over its cause, namely, the eternal predestination of God.

These errors, and many others too numerous to review, were born from the first error like luxuriant branches from a trunk. They did not all arise spontaneously, but [Col. 0638B] as the varying heat of disputation compelled them. Yet none of them, a point especially worthy of note, arose at a time when any judgment had yet been held—either in Africa concerning Coelestius, in the East concerning Pelagius, or at Rome concerning both. Rather, they arose while Pelagius and Coelestius were advancing their cause either through discussions and controversies at Rome or through loquacious arguments and conversations in Sicily. Since this is established by a definite chronology, it plainly demonstrates, I think, that those are mistaken who, while proclaiming that they have grown pale over Augustine’s books, nevertheless write—against Augustine—that Julian invented the final theory concerning grace only after Zosimus had condemned the heresy: namely, that grace is given either on account of merits or merely to make works of piety easier to perform. The truth will later become evident through incontrovertible arguments.

## CHAPTER III  
### The question of Adam’s mortality [Col. 0638C], the first of all the Pelagian questions: debated by disputants, reviewed by fifth-century writers, and refuted by Catholics of the same age; with eleven particular appendices

The question of human death—whether it arose from nature, whose creator is God, or from sin, which arises from the human will—was already being raised long before the time of Theodore. Almost none of the ancient interpreters of Genesis omitted it, especially when they were discussing the leather garments that God is said to have put on the first human beings after the sin (Genesis 3:21), which many thought signified the mortal body. Yet while this question was being debated, no one believed that either position could be defended at the peril of faith, provided that the body was not said to have been given to human beings as a prison in which they might expiate their former offenses.

At that time, moreover, everyone commonly thought that the human body had been made from dissoluble [Col. 0638D] parts, but that immortality had been promised by God the Creator—on the condition, however, that human beings not make themselves unworthy of so great a benefit. When that condition was violated and the promise was forfeited, the human being immediately became mortal.

Soon, however, it was debated whether death was inflicted on the guilty as a punishment or given to the wretched as a benefit. Many thought it was bestowed as a benefit; many, as a punishment. The dispute was still innocent, although it had been placed, as it were, on slippery ground. For among those who defended death as a punishment, some said that it belonged to individual sinners, so that, remarkably, no one would die except by the merit of his own sin. Others, on the contrary, said that it was common to everyone, since it arose from the guilt of the common parent.

But these people, according to what they wished to believe about the sin of the first human being, were again divided into two opinions. Some defended the transmission to Adam’s descendants of punishment alone; others, of guilt as well. From this the heresy arose, as it were, two-formed: [Col. 0639A] some maintained that nothing at all was transmitted from Adam, not even punishment; others maintained punishment without guilt. Both groups denied original sin. The first error was proper to the Pelagians; the second long remained among those who professed themselves enemies of the Pelagians.

Before these matters are established by the testimonies of the ancients, it is worth noting that original sin, in the sense in which this expression began commonly to be used in the fifth century and is understood in our own times, was not debated until the fourth century was drawing to a close. Earlier, at least in the East, even the designation “original sin” was unpopular, as though it suggested Origen’s error concerning the pre-existence of souls and their descent into bodies to expiate the sins of their former life. This was why the opponents of Catholic doctrine so vehemently attacked Origen, the defender of *pre-existence* (*προϋπάρξεως*).

But it is now time to prove through the testimonies of the ancients that the question concerning the cause of human mortality was raised in those earlier times, and that three [Col. 0639B] principal opinions were adopted: namely, that Adam was made either actually immortal but potentially mortal; actually mortal but potentially immortal; or actually neither, but potentially both, according as by his merit he either maintained his condition or changed it.

Theophilus of Antioch—he was the seventh bishop of the Church of Antioch after Peter—writes:

> Someone may ask: Was the human being created mortal? Certainly not. What then? Was he immortal? Not that either. From the beginning of his creation he was made neither mortal nor immortal. If God had made him immortal from the beginning, he would have made him God; if he had formed him mortal from the beginning, God could rightly have appeared to be the author of human death. It is therefore evident that the human being was made by God neither mortal nor immortal, but, as we indicated above, a participant in both in a certain manner: so that, by keeping God’s commandment, he might advance toward immortality and finally become God himself by receiving this reward; but if he turned toward sin and disobeyed God [Col. 0639C], he would become the author of his own death (Book II, *To Autolycus*).

Origen, quoted by Theodoret (Question 39 on Genesis), writes:

> What should we think those leather garments were? It is extremely foolish, childish, and wholly unworthy of God to suppose that God took the skins of slaughtered or otherwise dead animals and, sewing those skins together like a leatherworker, fashioned them into clothing. Again, to avoid this absurdity, it is certainly plausible and effective for eliciting assent to say that those leather garments were nothing other than bodies; but it is not evident that this is true. For if the leather garments are flesh and bones, how could Adam previously have said: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh”? Overwhelmed by these ambiguities, some assert that the leather garments are the mortality with which Adam and Eve were clothed, having been consigned to death on account of sin. But such people cannot easily explain how God, rather than sin, produces mortality in the successor. Moreover, they must say that flesh and bones by their own [Col. 0639D] nature are not corruptible, since afterward our ancestors received the condition of mortality because of sin.

Methodius (*On the Resurrection*, quoted by Photius, Codex 234):

> When almighty God had made Adam immortal, but knew that he had been made evil through the devil’s snares, just as the devil who deceived him was evil, he therefore fashioned leather garments for him, as though clothing him with mortality, so that through the dissolution of the body everything evil that was in him might die.

The author of *Questions from the Old Testament* (Question 19, quoted by Augustine, volume IV):

> It must be asked whether Adam, when he was made, had an immortal or a mortal body. God made the human being in such a way that, so long as he did not sin, he would flourish in immortality, so that he himself would be the author of life or death for himself; so that, by guarding himself from sin, he might rejoice in his own labor and in being immortal, but, by neglecting that duty, might himself be held responsible for having become mortal. For as long as he remained in the law of the [Col. 0640A] Creator, he was worthy to eat from the tree of life, so that he could not die. His body was not of such a kind that it seemed impossible for it to dissolve; rather, the taste of the tree of life restrained the body’s corruption. Finally, even after the sin he could have remained indissoluble, if the Lord had permitted him to eat from the tree of life. For how could he have had an immortal body if it was sustained by food? An immortal being has no need of food or drink. Food supplied strength, while the tree of life, like a medicine, prevented corruption. Thus it was for the human being like an impregnable wall.

Gregory of Nazianzus (Oration 42):

> After, through the envy of the devil and the assault of the woman—an assault which she endured because she was more yielding and brought forward because she was more suited to persuasion—he forgot the commandment he had received and was overcome by that bitter taste (O my weakness! For it is the weakness of my first parent). At once he is expelled, because of his sin, both from the tree of life and from paradise [Col. 0640B] and from God himself, and he puts on leather tunics, that is, a coarser and mortal flesh. He first recognizes his nakedness and hides from God, and even here he gains death and the cutting off of sin, so that evil might not be immortal. Thus punishment itself turned into mercy; for this is how I judge God to inflict punishments.

Ambrose (*On Paradise*, ch. 7):

> Again another question arises: from where did death come to Adam? From the nature of such a tree, or from God? If we attribute this to the nature of the tree, the fruit of this tree seems to have prevailed over God’s life-giving breath, since the fruit of this tree brought to death the one whom the breath had given life. Or, if we say that God was the author of death, they claim that we accuse him in a twofold way: either that he was so harsh that he refused to forgive when he could have done so, or, if he could not, that he appears weak. Let us therefore see how this may be resolved.

We must next show, likewise through the testimonies of the ancients, how the question of the manner in which death arose from sin—whether as the result of punishment or as an occasion of benefit granted to the wretched—long remained within the bounds [Col. 0640C] of a certain innocent and religious dispute. All agreed unanimously that the mortality to which Adam’s descendants are now and have always been subject arose from the sin of the first human being. They nevertheless asked whether death, after Adam and his offspring had been expelled from the place of happiness into the land of misery, should be called a benefit that ended their miseries, or a punishment that the offspring born in exile would endure with their father.

Catholics generally thought that death had been given to human beings as a benefit in place of immortality: partly because of the authority of Scripture, which says that God made leather garments for human beings and expelled them from paradise so that they would not live forever by eating the fruit of the tree of life; partly so that they might distance themselves more from the error of the pagans, who dreaded death as the supreme evil and the total destruction of the human being; and partly because of a certain prejudice akin to Origen’s opinion concerning death, namely, that it is the separation of the mind from the body, as though from a prison. It is enough to name four of the many who held this view.

[Col. 0640D] Gregory of Nazianzus (Oration 42):

> After, through the envy of the devil and the assault of the woman, he forgot the commandment he had received and was overcome by that bitter taste, and so forth; and even here he gained death and the cutting off of sin, so that evil might not be immortal. Thus punishment itself turned into mercy; for this is how I judge God to inflict punishments.

Ambrose (*On the Good of Death*, ch. 4):

> If we recall that God did not make death, but that, after the human being fell into the crime of transgression and fraud, the sentence overtook him so that earth might return to its own earth, we shall find that death is the end of sin, lest the longer life continued, the more numerous the guilt should become. Therefore the Lord allowed death to enter, so that guilt might cease, and so forth.

Epiphanius (*Heresies* 64):

> For this reason God made those leather tunics: to clothe him, as it were, with a kind of death, so that through the dissolution of the body whatever evil had been produced in him might die together with him.

[Col. 0641A] Chrysostom (Homily 26 on Genesis):

> God inflicted the punishment of death on Adam for this reason: so that, after he had become subject to sin through disobedience, he would not sin perpetually thereafter. Do these things not seem to you to display the greatest clemency—that he should be expelled from paradise and punished with this punishment?

But while the dispute, as we said, had long remained among Catholics within certain limits, human curiosity, incapable of moderation, eventually broke out. Some bold men began asking whether death had really arisen from sin, or whether, on the contrary, Adam would have died whether he sinned or did not sin—not on account of guilt, but by the fate of nature.

At first the common opinion of the Church was challenged rather timidly, and these curious men proceeded, if not in reality, at least in words, to the position of those who said that death had not been inflicted as a punishment but bestowed as a benefit. They claimed that death was in itself either indifferent or even good, and certainly not evil, since it is the end of sinning, the end of evils, secure rest after labor, an exit into a more blessed life, and often a gift [Col. 0641B] of God. Their boldness then advanced further, and, in the manner of the pagans, they said that death is a pure necessity of nature, to which the human race must be subject, whatever the condition of individuals with respect to the habits of their will.

Rufinus the Syrian followed the first part of this opinion; Coelestius followed the second. Rufinus concludes a long and intricate discussion of the matter, extending from no. 32 through no. 35, with these words:

> Taught, therefore, by many witnesses that this common death is not an evil, let us now bid farewell to those who call death evil.

Coelestius, however, if we believe Augustine, Mercator, Sixtus, and the author of the *Predestined*, asserted this as his capital doctrine: “Adam was made mortal, so that whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die.”

But since this seemed to conflict with the sacred Scriptures, whose authority had until then been supreme, the matter was debated fiercely—not now as an arbitrary question, as previously, but as a doctrine of faith. This was the first [Col. 0641C] error of the Pelagians, from which, as we shall show, many others derived their origin. This was why, when Pelagian doctrines were being discussed, this error was formerly regarded either as the only one or as the first of all.

Mercator certainly mentions it first (Preface to the *Subnotations*). He dared openly and publicly to disseminate among the peoples, everywhere, this same view in these verbal formulations:

> “Adam was made mortal, so that whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died” (see chapter 2 of this dissertation).

Prosper likewise placed this first among the doctrines of the others (*Poem Against the Ungrateful*, ch. 1):

> By this principle, he maintained, the first human beings were created,  
> so that whether they transgressed the prescribed commandment,  
> or remained blameless by keeping the law,  
> they would in any event suffer that death  
> by which life leaves the flesh—  
> a death not produced by sin,  
> but fixed as the companion of created beings  
> by God himself, its institutor.

Augustine also listed it first among the matters brought against Pelagius at Diospolis [Col. 0641D] from the proceedings drawn up at Carthage with Coelestius. He says (Book On the *Palestinian Proceedings*, ch. 11):

> The charges brought against Pelagius follow—charges reported as having been found in the teaching of Coelestius, his disciple: “Adam was made mortal, so that whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die; because Adam’s sin harmed him alone and not the human race,” and so forth.

The *Hypognostes* likewise numbered it first (in the preface to the books of the *Hypognostes*, volume VIII of Augustine’s works):

> The unspeakable blasphemy of such a doctrine is as follows. “Adam,” they say, “whether he sinned or did not sin, would die.” Likewise, “his sin harmed no one except himself alone,” and so forth.

The deacon Paulinus charged Coelestius before Aurelius with this first point: that he had perversely taught that Adam would have died whether he sinned or did not sin. For, after the words cited above from the book *On the Palestinian Proceedings* [Col. 0642A], the following is added:

> These charges were brought in such a way that they were also said to have been heard and condemned at Carthage by Your Holiness and by the other bishops who were with you (Book On the *Palestinian Proceedings*, ch. 11).

Augustine refuted this point first, and in the very work with which he began to combat the Pelagian heresy in writing. After promising in the preface that he would resolve the questions proposed by Marcellinus, he begins the second chapter as follows (Book On the *Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, ch. 2):

> Those who say that Adam was created in such a way that he would have died even without the merit of sin—through no punishment of guilt but through the necessity of nature—plainly attempt to refer what is said in the Law, “On the day you eat of it, you shall die,” not to the death of the body but to the death of the soul that occurs in sin, and so forth.

He continues on the same argument through chapter ten, where he begins to discuss original sin, although earlier he had already shown how the second question arose from the first.

Following Augustine’s example, the *Hypognostes* began [Col. 0642B] its first book from this point:

> “Adam,” they say, “whether he sinned or did not sin, would have died.” We answer: “You are deceived, heretic; you are deceived,” and so forth.

The African synod condemned this first. For although it has eight canons against the Pelagian heresy, the first of all is:

> It has pleased all the bishops who were present at this holy synod that whoever says that Adam, the first human being, was made mortal in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die in the body—that is, depart from the body—not on account of the merit of sin but through the necessity of nature, be anathema.

Long after these events, the later Council of Orange enacted its first canon concerning death contracted by all through Adam’s sin.

He mentioned only one in his decree, chiefly because he seemed to himself to have included the rest in that heading and to have indicated there the origin of the second error. For he says:

> It became widely known that Pelagius and Coelestius were authors of an impious speculation. [Col. 0642C] They assign to God, the parent of all things and to that supreme Majesty, always of unlimited power and transcending every beginning, so savage an inclemency of will that, when he undertook the creative care of forming the world and weighed, in the profound conception of his spirit, the nature of the man he was to construct, he set the end of the established gift before its beginning and sent death before the one yet to be born—not death flowing from the ambush of forbidden sin, but death exacted entirely by the law of an immutable decree—so that, in avoiding the deadly onset of death, abstaining from sin would be of no avail; and they think that its force is so tightly bound that it cannot subsequently be abolished. They say that the error of the first man, into which he had rushed in the blindness of a captured mind and impoverished reason, did not descend to his descendants; and that, in the case of the man whom the unhappy allurements of ill-advised grace had carried away, there existed only the transgression of the prohibition as a distinction, whereas the manifest authority of Catholic teaching in every respect testifies that he was the vestibule of the destruction of all, since it is clear that he assiduously corrupted the command of the divine precept.

[Col. 0642D] Nestorius thought that only this point required refutation—although perhaps there was another reason also why he mentioned only one—and he devoted to it a considerable portion of the discourses preserved by Mercator, as anyone can easily recognize by reading them.

If, however, the doctrines of the Pelagians were sometimes reported by the ancients—not, for the present, taking account of more recent writers—in a different order, as they truly are by Augustine in his *Book on Heresies*; or if some omitted the question of Adam’s mortality, as Jerome and afterward several others did, I think this should be attributed either to the period in which they were writing or to the particular occasion, which varied from time to time. For different questions prevailed at different times, and it was not always necessary to discuss each one so exactly and so carefully as the nature of the matter either seemed by a kind of right to require or had secured from the authors mentioned above.

Indeed, after it had been demonstrated by so many and such clear testimonies of Scripture that the origin of human death lay in sin, the Pelagians abandoned their former doctrine that mortality arose from the necessity of nature—if not in reality, which I scarcely think, at least verbally—[Col. 0643A] at the time when Augustine was either delivering Sermon 7 *On the Words of the Apostle* or writing to Boniface. For there the Pelagians are introduced as sinning through excess and saying (*Book IV to Boniface*, ch. 2) that all human beings die according to their merits, because they have sinned; for death would not occur unless it came from sin. In that passage they are represented as saying that nothing evil passed from Adam to the rest except death, which is not always an evil, since it is even the cause of rewards for martyrs, and since it is the diversity of merits arising from human freedom—not the dissolution of bodies, which will be raised in every class of human beings—that makes death good or evil.

But it is now necessary to show, by the testimonies of the ancients, whether they stood for the Catholic faith or on the opposing side, how eleven other, less fundamental questions arose from this first question.

[Col. 0643B] The authors in question, whose works at least we possess, are about eight. Of those who explicitly wrote against the Coelestians when we bring our discussions of Adam’s mortality to an end are Augustine, Hypognostes, Mercator, and—if he may be numbered among such great and Catholic men—Nestorius. An equal number wrote on behalf of the heresy: Theodore of Mopsuestia, Rufinus of Palestine, Coelestius, and Julian.

When the Coelestians therefore said that Adam had been made mortal by God in such a way that he would eventually die, not as punishment for guilt but by necessity of nature (Augustine, *Book I on the Merits and Remission of Sins*, ch. 2), the Catholics immediately brought forward the words of the divine law threatening: “On the day when you eat of it, you shall die” (Gen. II, 17). These words undoubtedly indicate that Adam would not have died if he had not violated the law. For who, if he has any sense, would threaten someone whom he wished to deter with only that evil which both parties know would otherwise certainly occur?

[Col. 0643C] The Coelestians replied (Augustine, ibid., ch. 3) that God’s threats should be understood as referring to the death of the soul, since this alone could be proportionate to so great a sin; that they did not concern bodily death, which is either itself part of human nature or at least a necessity of nature.

But when the Catholics insisted that the threats of the one who commands must be understood in accordance with the sentence of the one who condemns, they replied that God had said to Adam, after he violated the law: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return.” This sentence certainly concerns bodily death alone. They also added the testimonies of two Apostles, so clear that they required not an interpreter but a reader, as Augustine says (ibid., ch. 4). The first is from the Epistle to the Romans:

> “If Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of justification. But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. VIII, 10–11).

The second is from the Second Epistle to the Corinthians:

> “Through one man came death, and through one man the resurrection [Col. 0643D] of the dead; and just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (I Cor. XV, 21–22).

The heretics were forced to abandon their first objection, since it was plainly contrary to Paul. They therefore admitted that the words of the divine command must be understood of bodily death, but not of natural death, which occurs by fate, rather of premature and violent death, such as is inflicted upon criminals by human judgment (Theodore, excerpt 1). They applied to this the words both of God throughout Scripture and of human beings, who often threaten lawbreakers with death, although they do not thereby make those who are immortal mortal.

They also applied the following consideration to the same point: God, as punishment for sin, commanded Adam to cultivate the earth—not simply, since from the beginning he had been commanded to cultivate paradise, but with many labors, through which the ungrateful earth would turn itself into thistles and thorns (ibid.). [Col. 0644A] They likewise added the example of the sentence pronounced upon Eve, by which she was made subject through sin not simply to childbirth, for which she had been born, but to the pains of giving birth, which she would suffer with the greatest intensity.

“Therefore,” they said, “just as nature assigned the man to agriculture and the woman to childbirth, while punishment added the man’s labors and the woman’s birth pangs, so God, on account of sin, made both subject not to death of just any kind, but to premature death.”

From this arose a threefold question, which Julian and Augustine debate with great vehemence (*Unfinished Work*, throughout): whether death itself, or only the premature character of death, was the punishment of sin; whether laborious childbirth would have existed in paradise; and whether the man would have subdued the earth by difficult and arduous farming.

After the Coelestians had continued to evade the issue, they finally came to the Apostle’s decisive testimony:

> “Through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12).

[Col. 0644B] From this it is most clearly established that death arose not from the necessity of nature but as punishment for the guilt committed by that man, in whom the others also existed. Hence arose the question of original sin and of the baptism of infants. Although this question obscured the one from which it took its beginning, it nevertheless continued to be joined to it by more careful investigators, so that the origin of so great an evil would not remain hidden.

Augustine explained the origin of one question from the other, and the transition between them. But before his words are copied, the remaining arguments should be presented: those which Hypognostes uses against the Coelestians, as well as those which the Coelestians and their parent in doctrine, Theodore, used on their own behalf.

First (*Book I of Hypognostes*), Hypognostes argues from death itself, which, they say, God neither made nor wills by an antecedent will:

> “Do not court death through the error of our life, for God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living; for he created all things so that they might exist, and he made all the nations of the world healthful” (Wis. I, 12).

Second (*Book I of Hypognostes*), he argues from the human being, whom God created indestructible and made in his own image:

> “But through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. II, 23).

Other interpreters did touch upon both points, but they did not think that a major defense of the cause rested there. Nevertheless, when the Coelestians felt themselves gravely pressed by these arguments, they arrived at the most absurd position of saying that everyone is born immortal, just as Adam was, and that no one dies except through the merit of his own guilt—even infants, they said, suffer death because of their sins, whether sins committed by the infants themselves in their mothers’ wombs.

Jerome, Augustine, and Mercator do not so much refute this insanity by the force of argument as present it for ridicule; for to set out such dreams is already to refute them.

[Col. 0644D] Coelestius advanced two arguments on behalf of his cause. The first (*Book against the Transmission of Sin*, cited by Augustine, *Book II on the Merits of Sins*, ch. 30) was:

> “If it was made the case through the sin of the first man that we should die, then through Christ’s coming it would be made the case that those who believe in him should not die; for the transgression of the offender did not harm us more than the incarnation or redemption of the Savior benefited us.”

The second (ibid., ch. 33) was:

> “If this bodily death had occurred because of sin, surely we would not die after the remission of sins which the Redeemer has granted us.”

Mercator explains both arguments (*Commonitorium*, ch. 2) as coming from Pelagius’ book. But although Pelagius included them in his commentaries, he did not present them in his own person; rather, he presented them as statements of the opponents of original sin, that is, of Coelestius, whom we have often noted as the first to write on that question against the Catholic faith. Augustine responds to both lines of reasoning in the passage cited above.

[Col. 0645A] Theodore advanced two further arguments. Namely, if human beings died because of sin, then Christ, since he was free from sin, ought not to have died; and Enoch, holier than the other saints, ought not to have been granted immortality. Augustine responds to the first. The second is in itself weak, since God has countless other reasons for wishing to preserve Enoch and Elijah free from death (*Book II on the Merits of Sins*, chs. 29–30).

Finally, certain people with whom Mercator contended—and whose questions he even referred to Augustine—seem to have reasoned approximately as follows. If mortality was contracted through the sin of the first man, then, just as everyone descended from Adam, no one ought not to die, especially since Christ himself experienced the fate of death. Yet the Apostle teaches that, at the end of the world, some will go to meet Christ while still living in their bodies:

> “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air. And so we shall always be with the Lord” [Col. 0645B] (I Thess. IV, 15–16).

But enough has now been said about the principal question, whose appendices were the eleven controversies between the Pelagians and the Catholics:

1. Whether diseases arise from guilt or from nature.
2. Whether the pains of childbirth would have existed in paradise.
3. Whether farming would have been laborious without sin.
4. Whether God is the author of death.
5. Whether death ought to be counted among evils.
6. Whether each person dies through his own personal guilt.
7. Why the righteous die, if death is the punishment of sin.
8. Why Christ himself eventually suffered death.
9. Whether all are destined to die, since all are held by the same original sin.
10. Whether all ought to rise through Christ’s resurrection, or only the righteous.
11. Whether resurrection in itself ought to be counted among good things.

## CHAPTER IV

The question of original sin, arising from the preceding question, produced very many others, and especially the greatest of them: the question of the baptism of infants and their redemption through Christ.

[Col. 0645C] Augustine explains the origin of the second question from the first in the work with which he first fought against the Pelagians (*Book I on the Merits and Remission of Sins*, ch. 9). After he had discussed mortality and proved by several testimonies of Scripture that it arose from the sin of the first man, he finally brought forward this last, almost decisive testimony:

> “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12).

He did not, however, bring it forward first himself. For since the Catholics had already used it for a long time, he reports that the Coelestians replied (in the passage soon to be cited) that the death mentioned there was not bodily death, which Adam did not deserve through sin, but the death of the soul, which occurs in sin itself; and that sin passed to other human beings not by propagation but by imitation. They also said that original sin is not removed in infants through baptism, since they insist that there is no original sin at all in those who are born.

[Col. 0645D] They understood the Apostle’s testimony to assert four points. First, that sin entered the world through one man; second, that death also entered through sin; third, that this death passed to all human beings—a generality of words that must include infants; and finally, that all sinned in one man.

They readily admitted the first point but attempted to obscure the remaining three through perverse interpretations. The Church, however, checked the rash efforts of those who attempted this by its condemnation.

For that reason, whoever among the ancients either recounted or opposed the doctrines of the Pelagian heresy placed second the doctrine concerning original sin. To pass over Mercator and Prosper once again, Paulinus made this the second objection against Coelestius: that Adam’s sin injured Adam alone and not the human race (*Book on the Proceedings of Palestine*, ch. 11).

[Col. 0646A] In these words, and likewise in Mercator, observe again that the causal conjunction *because* (*quoniam*) is prefixed to the proposition in question in Paulinus’ testimony. This indicates that the proposition serves as proof of some earlier proposition. Therefore, just as the question of proof, whenever it arises, proceeds from the question for whose solution the proof is assumed, so the question of original sin must unquestionably have arisen from the question of the mortality of the human race, because the latter is proved from the former.

Hypognostes counted this as the second point:

> “Likewise, that Adam’s sin injured no one except Adam himself” (*Preface to Hypognostes*).

Again:

> “They say: Adam’s sin injured no one except himself. We respond: If the sin of the first human beings harmed only them and none of us, etc.” (*Hypognostes*, Book II, ch. 1).

He also mentioned it.

Augustine certainly refutes this second point in the work in which he first exercised himself against the Pelagians. Hypognostes likewise refutes it in his second book, after treating the origin of death in the first; Augustine does so in *Book I on the Merits of Sins*, chapter 9 and following.

[Col. 0646B] The African synod condemned it in canon 2, after having spoken first about mortality:

> “Likewise, it has been decided that whoever denies that newborn infants are to be baptized from their mothers’ wombs, or says that they are indeed baptized for the remission of sins but derive nothing of original sin from Adam which is cleansed by the bath of regeneration—so that it follows that in them the form of baptism for the remission of sins is understood to be not true but false—let him be anathema. For the Apostle’s statement, ‘Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Rom. V, 12), must be understood in no other way than as the Catholic Church, spread everywhere, has always understood it. For on account of this rule of faith, even infants, who could not yet have committed any sins in themselves, are truly baptized for the remission of sins, so that what they have contracted through generation may be cleansed in them through regeneration.”

[Col. 0646C] Thus Jansenius of Ypres, after saying that the capital doctrine of the Pelagians, and the hinge, as it were, of their other doctrines, was that Adam had been made mortal in such a way that he would die whether he sinned or did not sin (*Book I on the Pelagian Heresy*, ch. 13), shortly afterward says that the following was like the foundation of all the rest: Adam’s sin injured Adam alone and not the human race. Consistent with this was the claim that infants newly born are in the state in which Adam was before his transgression, and therefore are held by no original sin (*Book III*, ch. 1).

The authority of this writer does not, however, seem great in this matter, since he speaks inconsistently and, carried away by the heat of disputation, makes the foundation of the Pelagian heresy now one thing and now another.

From this you may refute Vossius, who (*History of the Pelagian Controversy*, Book II, Part I) holds that the question of original sin did not arise from the question of mortality, but that the latter arose from the former. He was misled by the authority of certain ancients who prove that Adam’s sin was propagated to his descendants from the fact that even infants, although guilty of no personal fault, die; yet no one under a just God dies except by the merit of sin.

It seemed to Vossius—if one may put it this way—that his insufficiently prudent genealogy showed what question arose from what question, but not what matter arose from what matter, although these two things are very different. Vossius’ error imposed itself upon many others, whom he led away from the truth along with himself.

It is incredible how many questions sprang from this second question, like shoots from a root. For while the struggle was being waged fiercely on both sides—through Scriptural testimonies, compelling arguments, and especially the consequences and connections associated with either opinion—the Coelestians, in order to evade the force of their Catholic opponents, were compelled to say many things. Some of these were afterward condemned in councils; others were rejected by the Fathers as contrary to the ancient doctrine received by the Church.

But the Catholics, in turn, were compelled by the Coelestians [Col. 0647A] to investigate more carefully the instruments of the cause, which had been somewhat concealed, as commonly happens when peaceful possessors neglect what they have; and to draw weapons from their proper places with which to defend the faith under attack.

The Catholics therefore fought for original sin with three arguments: the authority of sacred Scripture; reasoning drawn both from infants and from adults; and the testimonies of the Fathers, by which either the continuity or the universality of the Catholic position is demonstrated.

The heretics opposed them with an equal number of arguments. They abused the sacred writings, assembled arguments, and attempted to twist the words of the Fathers into support for their own position.

Each of these types of argument must be discussed briefly, but in such a way that those arguments which began to be advanced after Augustine—or rather after the judgment of Zosimus—are scarcely touched upon. What should chiefly be recalled are the arguments employed after the beginnings of the rising heresy and before its condemnation by the Apostolic See.

### § I. The Scriptural testimonies with which the Catholics fought; the replies offered by the Pelagians; and the questions arising from the conflict

[Col. 0647B]

It should be observed that in the earliest period the Catholics fought with only four Scriptural testimonies, while the heretics chiefly used three. Jerome gathered the former, as it were, into a single bundle; Rufinus of Palestine gathered the latter.

Thus Jerome (*Book XIV on Ezekiel*, ch. XLVII), in the year 410:

> Who among human beings can boast that he has a pure heart (Prov. XX, 9), or into whose mind, through the windows of the eyes, will the death of desire not enter—and, to say too little, the titillation of the soul? “The world is placed in the evil one” (I John V, 19), and “the heart of man is inclined to evil from childhood” (Gen. VIII, 21), so that the human condition is not without sin even for a single day from the beginning of its birth. Hence David also confesses in the Psalm: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. L, 7). Not in the iniquities of my mother, or certainly in my own, but in the iniquities of the human condition. Hence also the Apostle: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. V, 14).

He had written the same thing twenty years earlier in Book II *Against Jovinian*, when he was vigorously attacking that heretic’s doctrine of sinlessness (*ἀναμαρτησία*, anamartēsia), so that the prudent reader may incidentally observe how closely related the question and the doctrine of original sin are to the question and doctrine of impeccability.

Rufinus, however, in his little book *On the Faith* (nos. 37–39), before the year 400:

> Therefore Eve will not be saved on account of her children, nor will her offspring be condemned on account of their mother or their father Adam, as the opinion of the foolish supposes. For each human being, as possessing free choice, will be judged worthy either of the highest praise or of blame according to the quality of his own deeds. In the same way, on the day of judgment each will either be justified or subjected to punishment, as blessed Paul also teaches when he says: “We must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil” (II Cor. V, 10).

> That children are not punished for their parents, nor parents for their children, God taught plainly again when he said through the prophet Moses (Deut. XXIV, 16): “Fathers shall not die for sons, nor sons for fathers; each shall die in his own sin.”

> Moreover, when God was rebuking the imprudence of the children of Israel, who at that time were captives among the Chaldaeans according to their crimes, and who complained not entirely about themselves but about their parents, as though their parents had been the cause of all their abominable wickedness, they unjustly accused God concerning their captivity, saying: “The way of the Lord is not right, because our fathers ate a sour grape, and the teeth of the children were set on edge” (Ezek. XVIII, 2).

> Through the prophet Ezekiel he says to them (ibid., 3): “As I live, says the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel, for all souls are mine; as the soul of the father is mine, so also is the soul of the son; the soul that sins shall itself die.”

> And again (ibid., 20): “[Col. 0648A] The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father bear the iniquity of the son.”

> And again (ibid., 30): “I will judge each of you according to his way, O house of Israel, says the Lord.”

> When God said, “As I live, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel,” he plainly taught that they were not to remain in the same imprudence. After these testimonies of God, therefore, those who condemn the whole world of iniquity and wickedness through the one man Adam are insane.

[Col. 0648B] It should likewise be observed that Augustine employed eight other testimonies, which Julian partly left unanswered and partly attempted to twist into alien interpretations convenient to himself. Julian also employed certain testimonies which Augustine interpreted. But neither Julian’s passages nor Augustine’s were much discussed by the other disputants of the earlier period, either because they were considered inferior to the others or because they had not yet occurred to them.

Photius, certainly, in his synopsis of Theodore’s five books against Augustine, explicitly mentions only one of them, from Psalm L:

> “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me.”

He writes as follows:

> “They also bring forward that statement: ‘Behold, I was conceived in iniquities,’ and anything else of the same kind”; although in his final words he plainly indicated other passages as well.

Third, it should be observed that it is unknown how the Pelagians responded to the later Scriptural testimonies brought forward by Augustine.
