We possess nothing written by them on this subject except what Julian reported from Augustine’s books: either the three books addressed to the tribune Marcellinus, the two addressed to the Count Valerius, or the four addressed to Pope Boniface. Even there he contradicted only the two books addressed to Valerius directly and opposed the others merely in passing.

He was silent about the rest, including the especially elaborate six-book work in which Augustine refutes four books of Julian—either because he had never seen them, which he perhaps falsely claims in Mercator (*Preface to the Subnotations*), or, as is more reasonably thought, because he concealed the matter on account of the difficulty of responding.

[Col. 0648C] Ambrose, therefore, in his book *On the Ark and Noah*, and Jerome, in his commentary on chapter 47 of Ezekiel, argued from these words of Genesis:

> “God saw that the wickedness of man was great upon the earth, and that every thought of his heart was intent upon evil continually” (Gen. VI, 5).

They emphasized that it cannot be understood how every thought of the heart of a human being whom God created upright from the beginning could be directed toward evil continually, unless nature had been corrupted, and unless human beings of such a kind as the first man, created by God from the dust, were no longer born from human seed.

Pelagius seems to have objected to this passage in his book *On Nature*, when he wrote that one must first discuss the claim that nature is said to have been weakened and changed through sin, etc. (cited by Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 19). He made the objection without naming his opponent, out of reverence, I think, for Ambrose, whom he was accustomed to praise. [Col. 0648D] He denied, at least implicitly, that this was the meaning of Scripture, since nature itself cannot be changed by sin, which has no substance in itself.

This passage from Genesis, however, does not seem to have been considered important by the Catholics; Augustine certainly neglected it. Nevertheless, it may have given rise to a question debated more frequently afterward: whether sin possesses some substance. Augustine, Hypognostes, and others discussed this.

Augustine believed that God’s command concerning the circumcision of infants on the eighth day was of greater importance for this matter:

> “The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant” (Gen. XVII, 14).

But this passage was neither produced by the earliest disputants nor explained by Augustine in such a way as to win the agreement of other interpreters, including Catholic ones. [Col. 0649A] Nor did it seem to Julian worthy of a response, although he had read it, since it was cited by him in the second book *On Marriage*. Consequently, it generated no question concerning the purpose of circumcision.

As for the passage from Job, which according to the Septuagint reads:

> “For who is clean from uncleanness? No one, even if his life upon the earth is but one day” (Job XIV, 4),

Jerome used it in his commentary on chapter XLVII of Ezekiel, and Augustine used it in Book VI *Against Julian*, chapter 12, and elsewhere frequently. But I think that this passage from Job did not receive a response from the Pelagians, nor could it then have been pressed very forcefully, since the interpreters of the Church almost unanimously understood these words in another sense.

Thus Ambrose writes (*Book I on the Interpretation of Job*, ch. VII):

> Truly wretched is the human condition, that a person should be compelled to render an account of his sin, which he cannot avoid; to enter into the presence of the Lord and undergo the judgment of the Almighty; to give reasons for his deeds, which he has carried through so many stages of his life, when no one can be free from sin, so that guilt creeps in from the very cradle of infancy before there is any awareness of error. And how wretched it is that his life is brief, a sweet enticement, a manifold misery, daily anger! Thus in a small pleasure there is perpetual bitterness.

[Col. 0649B] In his commentary on the Psalmist’s words, “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities” (Ps. L, 7), he also uses the testimony from Job, but, in keeping with the circumstances of the time, he treats the matter obscurely, since it had not yet been sufficiently explained.

The famous passage of Psalm L, “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. L, 7), was brought forward by nearly all the Catholics: by Hilary in his commentary on Psalm CXVIII; by Ambrose, Book I *On Repentance*, chapter 2; by Jerome in his commentary on chapter XLVII of Ezekiel; and by Augustine in Book II of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 73, and Book III, chapter 12.

But when this passage was customarily cited, as we learn from Theodore through Photius, it is not clear what response the Pelagians gave.

[Col. 0649C] Augustine, both often elsewhere and especially throughout both works *Against Julian*, argues with the full force of his speech from the passage in Ecclesiasticus:

> “A heavy yoke lies upon the sons of Adam from the day of their departure from their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all” (Eccli. XL, 1).

He also argues from this passage in Wisdom:

> “He was not unaware that their nation was wicked, and that their malice was natural, and that their thinking could not be changed forever; for their seed was accursed from the beginning” (Wis. XII, 10).

He says:

> “In any case, whoever he may be speaking about, he is speaking about human beings. How, then, is the malice of every human being natural, and the seed accursed from the beginning, unless reference is made to the fact that through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned?” (*Book II on Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 8).

Julian (*Book IV of the Unfinished Work*, ch. 123) fiercely attacks Augustine’s argument and tries to impose upon him the impiety of the Manichaeans concerning an evil nature. He denies that original sin is proved by this passage, because the Wise Man calls the seed of the Canaanites accursed from the beginning just as Isaiah calls the seed of the Israelites blessed (Isa. LXV, 22, according to the Septuagint).

From this he concludes that those conditions of seed, since they are opposites, cannot pertain to original sin, which must be universal and arise from one common cause in all.

[Col. 0649D] These, then, are approximately the arguments which the Catholics brought from the Old Testament in those early times to defend the faith in original sin. From the New Testament they produced five others (Rom. VII, 17). Two of these, however—drawn partly from the general law of baptism and partly from sin dwelling in the members—seem to belong more to the construction of arguments than to establishing the matter by their own weight.

The third, concerning the death of all in Adam and the resurrection of all in Christ, mentioned earlier (I Cor. XV, 22), did not establish the matter by itself but served only as an aid to reasoning, by which, as they say, [Col. 0650A] the common sin of all mortals was inferred from the common punishment, which is death.

The fourth was drawn from the fact that we are called by the Apostle “by nature children of wrath” (Eph. II, 3). No one before Augustine employed this testimony. Augustine himself used it before he had heard anything about the Pelagian heresy, in a work which he completed while he was still a presbyter. He also used it in his earlier writings against the heresy (*Book III on Free Choice*, ch. 19). Therefore it could not have been unknown to Pelagius, who is known to have seen Augustine’s books *On Free Choice*, for he praises them in his book *On Nature*. Yet it is unknown what response Pelagius or his followers explicitly gave.

Pelagius, however, when interpreting this passage, led the Apostle’s meaning in a very different direction. He says (*Commentary on chapter II of the Epistle to the Ephesians*):

> When our mind clung to earthly and carnal things, we not only desired but also did whatever evil thought suggested. The custom of ancestral tradition had so possessed us that we all seemed to have been born for condemnation. But God, who is merciful, etc.

This may be viewed as a kind of response to the passage from the Apostle brought forward in the books *On Free Choice*, since Pelagius’ commentaries were written at least twelve years after those books.

[Col. 0650B] The Catholics therefore fought invincibly with the Apostle’s testimony:

> “Just as through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12);

and:

> “But death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (ibid., 14);

and:

> “Just as through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one act of righteousness justification unto life came upon all human beings. For just as through the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners, so through the obedience of one many will be constituted righteous,” etc. (ibid., 18–19).

[Col. 0650C] From this three conclusions were drawn. First, death passed to all on account of Adam’s sin because sin passed to all—that is, because it was propagated. Second, sin passed even to those who did not sin by imitation but only by propagation. Finally, many arrive at destruction through Adam’s offense, just as many are constituted righteous through Christ’s righteousness.

This argument was already employed from the earliest period of the rising heresy, that is, before the fifth century. It became like the foundation by which the Church afterward wished to establish its Catholic judgment and definition. The Council of Milevis certainly brought it forward in its letter to Innocent I; the African council in canon 2; the Second Council of Orange likewise in canon 2; the Council of Trent in its fifth session; Pope Zosimus in his *Tractoria*; and Gelasius in his decretal letter to the bishops of Picenum—all as an evident testimony of the faith.

[Col. 0650D] And indeed, when the Pelagians felt themselves vehemently pressed by its force, they devised and said everything possible by which they might appear both to extricate themselves from the passage and to persuade simpler minds that the question there concerned not the transmission of sin, as they then called it, but imitation.

They therefore pursued each individual word and argued from each accompanying expression in their own interest. First, they said that the Apostle compares Adam’s sin with Christ’s righteousness and equates the two; therefore Adam’s sin did not pass into all, because Christ’s righteousness likewise did not pass into all. They wished this to be indicated by the word “many,” which the Apostle used deliberately, abstaining from the more general term. Next, they said that sin passed into these many not by propagation but by imitation: Adam harmed his descendants just as Christ benefited them, namely, by the example of an evil work that Adam provided and of a good work that Christ provided. They said afterward that, had the Apostle wished to speak of propagation, he would not have said that sin entered through the transgression of one man, since propagation is the work of two. Julianus discusses this at length in the second book of his later work against Augustine [Col. 0651A]; but Pelagius had already set out these arguments in his commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans, and Coelestius in his book *Against the Propagation of Sin*, since the Catholics refuted them before the year 422, when Julianus undertook to write this work.

From this arose five questions: whether Christ benefited human beings by example alone, and whether that was either the sole or the chief reason for his coming, so that he might display in himself a pattern for the conduct of the rest of life; by what means Christ’s righteousness benefits infants, who cannot imitate an example; how infants can be called believers, since Christ’s righteousness benefits believers alone; in what sense Christ can be called the infants’ Redeemer, Savior, and Jesus; and whether he died for them. In a word, what do human beings of only a few days owe to Christ? These questions were also discussed on another occasion, namely, in connection with the baptism of infants.

## § II. What testimonies of Scripture the Pelagians produced; what answer the Catholics gave; and what questions arose from them

[Col. 0651B]

To the testimonies of Scripture brought forward by Catholics, the Pelagians thought that other scriptural testimonies should be opposed, by which they might somehow persuade others of their own position. In this respect they did what they habitually did in every other matter: thus Coelestius, in the third part of his book of *Arguments*, when dealing with sinlessness, set testimonies against testimonies. There is no doubt that he observed the same procedure, as he was exceptionally attached to his method, in his book *Against the Propagation of Sin*. It is unknown, however, which passages he used, although it is clear that he used some, from the fact that several are touched upon indirectly in the fragments. He undoubtedly obtained them from the same source as Pelagius and Julianus: from Rufinus the Syrian’s book, from which the Coelestian heresy drew its substance as though from a spring.

Pelagius adduces Paul’s statement: “Without the law sin [Col. 0651C] was dead.” From this he concludes: “If, when the law did not exist, sin did not exist, those who assert that sin comes to us from Adam by propagation are insane” (*Commentary on Romans* 7:8). It is as though he were saying: Sin cannot exist in those who have no knowledge of the law; but there is no knowledge of the law in infants. Sin, therefore, is in them as though dead.

Julianus produced several passages, partly in his statement of faith and partly in his two works against Saint Augustine; but he borrowed almost all of them, just as Pelagius borrowed that argument of his, from Rufinus. Rufinus was thus the first writer of this wicked doctrine—not indeed its teacher, since he learned it from Theodore, but its writer, since he wrote in Greek before the heresy had been exposed to Latin readers.

Rufinus therefore first used the words of God addressed to Moses: “The fathers shall not die for the children, nor the children for the fathers; each one shall die in his own sin” (Deut. 24:14). Julianus transferred the same passage, unchanged, into his statement of faith and treated it theatrically in the third book of his later work (ch. 12 and following). Its force lay in [Col. 0651D] the proposition that God must be believed to judge in the same way as he commands judgment to be conducted, since he is the source and model of all justice, which ought to govern judgments.

Augustine nevertheless replied (ibid.) that this law applies to children already born and to human judges, but not likewise to children condemned in their first parent, in whom they sinned just as they die; nor does it apply to God, who, whether he judges directly himself or through human representatives, has not bound his own judgments by this law. This is evident from the example of the infants who perished in the Flood, those who perished in the destruction of Sodom, and those who were killed in the punishment of Achan.

From this arose the question whether justice forbids one person to be punished for another person’s offense, even by God.

Next he uses the words of God spoken through Ezekiel in response to the complaint of the Israelites that they were suffering for their parents’ sins and that their teeth were being set on edge when their fathers had eaten sour grapes. “As I live,” says the Lord, [Col. 0652A] “this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel: for all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son, they are mine. The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18:3). Again: “The son,” he says, “shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of the son” (ibid., 20). And again: “I shall judge each one of you according to his way, house of Israel, says the Lord” (ibid., 30). The force of this passage was the same as that of the earlier one. Julianus himself not only reproduced it in exactly the same words in his statement of faith but also argued it at great length in the fourth book of his earlier work and the third book of his later work.

Augustine replied that the prophetic statement was a promise of the New Testament and of the spiritual inheritance belonging to the age to come. The work of the Redeemer’s grace is to erase the paternal bond of indebtedness and at the same time to ensure that no one is guilty by another’s will, but that each person afterward gives an account for himself (Book VI of the earlier work against Julianus, ch. 12, and Book III of the later work, ch. 38 and following). He confirms this [Col. 0652B] with Jeremiah’s testimony. After saying nearly the same things, Jeremiah adds: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers” (Jer. 31:31). In the New Testament, therefore, once the paternal bond of indebtedness has been erased by the Mediator’s blood, a person, by being reborn, begins no longer to be liable for paternal debts to which he had been bound by birth.

He likewise uses the Apostle’s testimony, which Julianus also inserted into his own confession of faith (Book IV of the earlier work, ch. 4): “For we must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive what is proper to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10). Julianus asked how this could apply to any infants, since they had done nothing evil, especially those who died prematurely; nor, he argued, is judgment exercised except concerning one’s own evil deeds.

Augustine replied in both works against [Col. 0652C] Julianus. In the earlier one (Book VI, ch. 4), he asks whether infants are to be made manifest or not. “If they will not be made manifest,” he says, “what assistance does this statement give you, when it does not apply to those whose case is now under discussion? But if they will be made manifest, how does each one receive what he has done, when he has done nothing—unless what is done through the hearts and mouths of those who act, whether they believe or do not believe, pertains to them? For he said ‘what is proper to his body,’ meaning what pertains to each person already living in himself,” and so forth. In the later work (Book III, ch. 109), he says:

“Tell me, then, what good they did through the body by their own free will, so that they should receive the kingdom of God, so great a good; or what evil they did by their own will, those infants who are to be alienated from this life of God? But if, as you must, you acknowledge that they are made alive in Christ without any works of free will that each person performs through the body, why do you not acknowledge that these others die in Adam, since you know that Adam, conversely, is a type of Christ who was to come?” And so forth.

Here the questions began to arise that later, on another occasion, became more heated. [Col. 0652D] How could infants who die prematurely belong to Christ’s final judgment, whether they had been baptized or had not, when judgment is exercised concerning their own good and evil deeds? To what destination will those who were not baptized depart after the judge’s sentence? Do they withdraw to some intermediate place?

It should also be noted that certain other passages were brought forward, both by Rufinus and by his copyist Julianus. These included passages concerning the natural use of sexual intercourse (Rom. 1), the salvation of mothers through the bearing of children (1 Tim. 2), the sanctification of children by their parents (1 Cor. 7), and the justification of human beings through Christ’s obedience (Rom. 5). But since these passages served more to confirm arguments and resolve objections than to establish by themselves the matter under discussion, they should be deferred until the arguments are treated.

[Col. 0653A]

It should further be noted that scarcely any testimonies were produced by either side that the opposing party did not attempt to turn back against the author who had cited them; nor was there any testimony that was not subjected to careful examination. The Catholics had to labor all the more because many of the older interpreters seemed to have spoken in favor of the Pelagians, since they had inveighed more vehemently against the Manichaeans. Indeed, the most celebrated among the Greeks—Origen, Diodore of Tarsus, and Theodore of Mopsuestia—actually adopted Pelagian positions; Basil and Chrysostom could appear to favor them in their wording. Among the Latins, two men of the highest authority, Ambrose and Hilary, had expressed their views with the carelessness appropriate to the times—that is, with words not sufficiently guarded—so that statements directed against Jovinianus and Manichaeism lay open to the treacherous attacks of future heretics.

It should also be noted that Jerome, whose authority in interpreting Scripture was then supreme, was initially praised by the Pelagians, so long as he seemed capable either of being drawn over to their side [Col. 0653B] or of being restrained by the influence of distinguished women and the entreaties of friends, so that he would not oppose their schemes. But after he began to fight more openly for the faith, he suffered calumny: partly from Pelagius, as though envy toward an old friend had moved him (Jerome, Preface to the *Dialogue*); partly from Julianus, as though he had made Christ guilty of falsehood and of sin (Book IV of the later work, ch. 87); and partly from Theodore, as though Jerome were either a Manichaean, because he said that human beings sin by nature (Photius, *Codex* 177), or a corrupter of Scripture, because he introduced a fifth Gospel; or an ignorant man, because he distorted the Old Testament with the assistance of some foolish Hebrew; or a plague upon the churches, which he infected with his absurd opinions.

It should likewise be noted that Jerome wrote many things before the questions raised by the Pelagians, things that might be thought to assist heretics, at least by the less learned, had he not elsewhere sufficiently demonstrated a Catholic mind. For in those passages of Scripture on which the Pelagians placed their support and the foundation of their opinion, he interpreted them in such a way that, [Col. 0653C] because of certain prior prejudices and his intense hatred of heretics, he might appear closer to the Pelagians than to Augustine. Jansenius of Ypres observed this (Book VII, *On the Pelagian Heresy*, ch. 4) in the question of prevenient grace and the beginning of faith. He also seems to acknowledge the same concerning nearly all the other mysteries of grace, when he writes that the Pelagian errors on this matter were drawn from Origen’s commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans—commentaries that no one now reads except in Latin, and which Jerome translated in his customary manner, that is, not so much translating them as interpreting them. Thus he willingly wished the statements to be believed to be his own by right, as though he had adopted them from Origen and adorned them as he pleased.

Finally, attention should be drawn to what Photius says (*Codex* 177) about Theodore of Mopsuestia, who attacked the defenders of original sin. “Theodore,” he says, “does rightly in detesting and rejecting these very things, and at times refutes their absurd and blasphemous opinions most excellently and forcefully. He also adapts his own meanings to the passages of sacred Scripture [Col. 0653D] that they have misused, so that he may altogether expose their ignorance. But this is not consistent throughout his work. For he also seems in many matters to be giving birth to the sect of Nestorius, and at least concerning the end of punishments he appears to mutter Origen’s opinion.”

From these facts it is clear, first, that Theodore answered all the testimonies produced by the Catholics, but that his answers have perished, to the great detriment of history. Next, the fragments transcribed by Mercator are authentic, since the fourth excerpt contains something related to Origen’s opinion, of which Photius makes mention. Finally, it is clear that the Pelagians commonly reproached the Catholics with ignorance. Augustine frequently complains of this, while Pelagius and Julianus frequently did it. In the last place, it was customary for the Pelagians to allow nothing that was brought against them to pass without an answer. See Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon.

## § III. What arguments the Catholics produced to establish original sin; what evasions the heretics employed; and what questions arose from them

[Col. 0654A]

Now that it has been shown by which testimonies of Scripture the two sides fought, and how fiercely each side debated this question, it is next necessary to demonstrate what arguments, and how powerful a set of arguments, the Catholics used to constrain the obstinate heretics, as we proposed secondarily. These arguments can easily be reduced to two headings, since some were drawn from the case of infants and others from that of adults. Pelagius, however, subtly perceived that both headings depended upon this one point: that nature is said to be corrupted in all human beings (*Book On Nature*). Augustine also perceived this when he objected to the Pelagians that they said human nature needed neither a physician in infants, because it is sound, nor the help of grace in adults, because it is sufficient for salvation by itself (*Book On Nature and Grace*, ch. 6).

The Catholics therefore drew their argument from the case of infants approximately as follows. If nature is not corrupted, [Col. 0654B] even in infants themselves, and if there is no original sin at all, infants neither need Christ’s baptism nor belong to Christ in any sense, nor ought they to suffer under the just God the miseries to which they are seen to be subject. But that infants need Christ’s baptism has been, and has always been, the constant faith of the whole Church. That they are afflicted by miseries is shown by experience, both obvious and daily. Therefore original sin exists in infants, and nature is corrupted in them as well. This reasoning must, however, be explained point by point, beginning with what concerns baptism.

The Catholics therefore asked the opponents of original sin for what reason infants need Christ’s baptism, and why they are carried so anxiously to the church in the arms of those who bear them to be cleansed, if they are not guilty of sin transmitted from their parents. Since the baptism administered by the Church is Christ’s baptism, and is a washing, a regeneration or inner renewal [Col. 0654C] of the inner human being, for the remission of sins and in the death of Christ, and since it is celebrated throughout the whole Church with fixed rites and the same sacramental words, they drew from this seven arguments, all of them especially offensive to the Pelagians.

For if the baptism that the Church confers on infants belongs to Christ—that is, to Jesus, who saves his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21); to the Redeemer, who gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Tim. 2:6); to the liberator, who rescued his own from the power of darkness (Col. 1:13); and to him of whom there are many similar statements, all of which Mercator pursued with the greatest care—if, I say, the baptism in which infants are immersed belongs to Christ, then they must either not need this baptism, or, if they need it, they must by its benefit be saved from sins, redeemed from captivity, rescued from the power of darkness, and so forth. Since they had neither sinned nor entered captivity or the power of the devil by the merit of their own will, they certainly sinned by another’s will, entered captivity by another’s will, and fell under the power of darkness [Col. 0654D] by another’s will. The sin of the first man, therefore, whose punishment—that is, death—they suffer, is imputed to them.

Further, if baptism is a kind of washing, as it certainly is, and if no one can enter the kingdom of heaven unless he has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit (John 3:5), then unquestionably the sacraments of Christ, because they are certain divine and truthful symbols, must accomplish inwardly what they signify outwardly. Thus, through the washing of water in the word of life (Eph. 5:26), the souls of infants are cleansed from a stain. But from what stain, unless from sin? And from whose sin, unless from that which is both alien, as Cyprian says, because of its commission, and one’s own, as Augustine says, because of its contagion?

Next, if baptism has the power of a kind of regeneration in Christ and renewal according to the Spirit, infants must previously have been dead in the first Adam before they could be reborn in Christ, the new Adam. They must likewise first have fallen into old age [Col. 0655A] before they could be renewed, clothed with Christ, and made a new creation in Christ. That preceding death is certainly not bodily but spiritual, namely, sin; nor can any other old age be conceived than that by which the image of God, impressed upon the human being when God fashioned him, has been discolored, as it were, by sin.

Fourth, the Apostle truly said: “All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death, and we have been buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. 6:3). Since being baptized into Christ’s death means nothing other than dying to sin, just as Christ died in the flesh, infants unquestionably die to sin when they are baptized. But to what sin, if they have inherited no sin by origin?

Fifth, the Church confesses one baptism for the remission of sins. It therefore cannot be conferred on anyone else—unless one says that it is a certain empty and deceptive symbol—than on a sinner. Infants, therefore, are sinners, not by will but by origin.

Finally, when infants are exorcized and breathed upon in baptism [Col. 0655B], either the rites employed by the Church of God are empty, or the devil is driven away from infants, under whose power they had until then been, either as children of divine wrath or as slaves under the lordship of death and sin. Thus Augustine, addressing the Pelagians while treating this argument (Book III of the earlier work against Julianus, ch. 3), says:

“Go on, then, and say, as you do: ‘They are baptized in the sacrament of the Savior, but they are not saved; they are redeemed, but they are not liberated; they are washed, but they are not cleansed; they are exorcized and breathed upon, but they are not rescued from the power of the devil.’ Say also: ‘Blood is poured out for them for the remission of sins, but they are not cleansed by the remission of any sin.’ What you say is astonishing; what you say is new; what you say is false. We are astonished at what is astonishing, we guard against what is new, and we refute what is false.”

Observe how the holy teacher reinforces his argument with the weight of tradition when he accuses the Pelagian theories of novelty.

Finally, since the baptism conferred on infants [Col. 0655C] and that conferred on adults is one and the same, and since it is celebrated in both ages with the same sacramental words, it likewise has the same force in persons of both kinds. Thus, no less in infants than in adults, it washes the soul from the stain of sin and accomplishes what the symbol of washing declares.

Because of these arguments, the Pelagians, already from the earliest period when the questions arose, were inflamed by an intolerable resentment. They tried to evade the force of the arguments by their own devices—that is, by quibbles, falsehoods, and the general ambiguity of words—partly by turning their own weapons back against the Catholics and partly by weakening, through subtle distinctions, whatever could not be turned back.

The first parent of the error, Theodore, when asked why children shared in the most holy mysteries and why they were judged worthy of baptism, if not because they too abounded in sins, since these mysteries are conferred for the remission of sins, asserted that [Col. 0655D] “there are two remissions of sins: one, indeed, of sins committed; the other, the very state of sinlessness, or no longer sinning, a complete pardon and the absolute destruction of sin.” This latter remission began to reveal itself when Christ the Lord assumed flesh, and is given to us “in the manner of a pledge” (*ἐν ἀῤῥαβῶνος τάξει*); but it is given perfectly, both in return for good works and in the restoration after the resurrection. To obtain this, both we and infants are baptized (Photius, *Codex* 177).

Rufinus, Theodore’s disciple, before the year 400, says the following (*In the Statement of Faith*, ch. 6, no. 40):

“But if, as they themselves assert—the Catholics who oppose us—that infants die because of Adam’s sin, let them tell us why they are immediately permitted to taste death after being baptized, since all who have been baptized, and for this reason have become children of God, cannot have sin. And if infants are baptized because of Adam’s sin, those born of Christian parents should by no means need to be baptized; rather, they should be regarded as holy, since they were begotten of faithful parents, just as blessed Paul teaches when he says: ‘Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy’ (1 Cor. 7:14).

“Similarly, blessed John also says concerning children who are to be begotten that, as soon as they are born, they receive the illumination of sanctification from the only-begotten Word, when he says: ‘He was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into the world’ (John 1:9). Infants therefore receive baptism not because of sins, but so that, possessing a spiritual birth, they may be created in Christ through baptism, and become participants in the kingdom of heaven itself, as blessed Paul teaches in these words: ‘If [there is] a new creation in Christ’ (2 Cor. 5:17). And again: ‘But if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ’ (Rom. 8:17).

“Thus Cornelius (Acts 10), who, according to God’s testimony, excelled in righteousness, who had received the baptism of the Spirit just as the Apostles had, and who shared in the Holy Spirit—so that, with the Holy Spirit dwelling in him, he could not possibly have sin—was nevertheless judged worthy also of that baptism which is administered through water, so that, according to blessed Paul, having been planted in the likeness of Christ’s death, he might also become [Col. 0656B] a fellow heir of Christ’s resurrection (Rom. 6:5).”

Later (ch. 7, no. 48), he says:

“To those who believe in him he grants spiritual adoption and gifts, and makes them heirs of his heavenly kingdom, as our Lord Jesus Christ himself teaches when he says: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God’ (John 3:3). Therefore infants, who are not in sins, nevertheless merit the grace of baptism, so that, created in Christ by a new birth, they may also become fellow heirs of his kingdom, according to blessed Paul: ‘If [there is] a new creation in Christ’ (2 Cor. 5:17).”

When Pelagius complained in a letter to Saint Innocentius that he was being defamed as denying the sacrament of baptism to infants and as promising the kingdom of heaven to some without Christ’s redemption, he said:

“I have never heard even an impious heretic say what they allege that I have said about infants. For who is so ignorant [Col. 0656C] of the Gospel reading that he would attempt to assert this? Indeed, who could even lightly say or think such a thing? Further, who is so impious as to wish infants to be excluded from the kingdom of heaven, and not to think that they should be baptized and reborn in Christ, when Christ openly says: ‘Unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God’ (John 3:3)? Who is so impious as to deny to an infant of any age the common redemption of the human race and to refuse to have reborn into perpetual and certain life one who has been born into uncertainty?”

And in his *Statement of Faith* (Part III, no. 17):

“We hold one baptism, which we affirm is celebrated in infants with the same sacramental words as in adults.”

Moreover, when he was questioned by certain pious and Catholic friends, he replied (*Book On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 32) that infants receive baptism for the remission of sins. After Augustine reports this, he adds:

“He does not here say, ‘in the words “for the remission of sins,”’ but he confessed that they are baptized into remission itself. [Col. 0656D] And yet, if you were to ask him what sin he believed was remitted in them, he would maintain that they had no sin.”

In his *Statement of Faith*, Coelestius, after using exactly the same words about baptism as Pelagius, added the following of his own (no. 18):

“We confess that infants ought to be baptized for the remission of sins, according to the rule of the universal Church and according to the teaching of the Gospel, because the Lord established that the kingdom of heaven can be conferred only upon the baptized. Since infants do not possess the powers of nature for this, it is necessary that it be conferred through the generosity of grace.

“But we do not say that infants are to be baptized for the remission of sins in order to appear to affirm sin by propagation, which is wholly foreign to Catholic understanding: for sin is not born with a human being; it is afterward committed by the human being. It is shown to belong not to nature but to the will. It is therefore fitting to confess the former, lest we appear to create different kinds of baptism; [Col. 0657A] and it is necessary to safeguard the latter, lest, under cover of the mystery, an evil be said to be transmitted to a human being by nature before it has been committed by that human being, to the injury of the Creator.”

Julianus, in his *Statement of Faith* (Part I, no. 13), says:

“We confess and teach, according to the example of the Church and the commandment of God, one baptism, which is truly necessary for all ages alike; and we say that no one can obtain remission of sins and enter the kingdom of heaven unless he has received baptism.”

In his earlier work against Augustine, after complaining bitterly that the question of baptism had been made odious to his party among the ignorant through the lies of its opponents, he says:

“We say that the grace of baptism is not to be changed according to the causes involved, because it distributes its gifts according to the capacity of those who approach it. Therefore Christ, who is the redeemer of his own work, continually increases his benefits toward his image; and those whom he made good by creation he makes better by renewal and adoption.”

For these words, see what Augustine brings forward (Book III against Julianus, ch. 3), and also what Mercator adduces in his *Subnotations* [Col. 0657B].

In his later work, revising this same passage from the earlier work, he says (Book I, ch. 53):

“When I had said that God is the author of heaven and earth and of everything in them, and therefore also of human beings, for whose sake all things were made, it did not escape me, I said, that when we say these things, the claim must be spread abroad about us that we do not think the grace of Christ the Lord necessary for infants. This greatly and deservedly offends Christian peoples, unless they should not regard us as the authors of the statement, which is in itself wicked. For in that way they would neither incur guilt by believing false things about their brothers nor demonstrate their zeal for the love of the faith.

“Therefore this part of our position must be defended against the assault of vanity, and the mouths of those who revile us must be closed by a brief confession. We therefore confess the grace of baptism to be useful to all ages to such an extent that we strike with an eternal anathema all who think it unnecessary even for infants. But we believe this grace to be rich in spiritual gifts, [Col. 0657C] abundant in many gifts and venerable virtues, and, according to the various kinds of infirmity and the differences among human conditions, to heal by one power both as a consolation of remedies and as a bestowal of gifts.

“When this grace is applied, it is not to be changed according to the causes involved, for it already distributes its gifts according to the capacity of those who approach it. Just as all the arts, despite the diversity of the materials they take up for cultivation, do not themselves suffer either deterioration or increase, but, remaining always the same and in one mode, are adorned with diverse effects, so also, according to the Apostle, one faith and one baptism are multiplied and extended in gifts, yet are not changed in the orders of the mysteries.

“But this grace does not oppose justice, which washes away the stains of iniquity; nor does it create sins, but cleanse them; it absolves the guilty and does not accuse the innocent. For Christ, who is the redeemer of his own work, continually increases his benefits toward his image; and those whom he made good by creation he makes better by renewal and adoption.”

A little later (ch. 54), he says:

“Behold, by the light of this confession [Col. 0657D] I have condemned both those who would deny baptism to infants and you, who dare to stain God’s justice by prejudice against it. I have declared that I hold nothing other than that the established mysteries are to be administered in every age with the same words in which they were delivered, and that they ought not to be changed according to the variety of circumstances.

“But the sinner is made perfectly good from evil; whereas the innocent, who possesses no evil of his own will, is made better from good—that is, best—so that both, consecrated, may pass into the members of Christ, but one having been found in an evil life and the other in a good nature. The former corrupted by wrongful action the innocence he had received at birth; the latter, without praise and without the guilt of will, possesses only what he received from God the Creator. Happier in his unstained original condition, he could not corrupt the goodness of his simplicity.”

With regard to these statements of the heretics, it seems to me that the following should first be observed: the Pelagians turned the argument drawn from baptism to establish original sin against the doctrine of original sin itself [Col. 0658A], not only in the manner of Rufinus but also in that of Coelestius. If a sinner begot a sinner, so that his original sin might be removed from the infant when the infant received baptism, then a righteous person ought to have begotten a righteous person. And again: if baptism cleanses that ancient and long-standing sin, those born of two baptized persons ought to be free from that sin; for they could not transmit to their descendants what they themselves had not possessed at all.

Thus, by various forms of expression, they stated one and the same opinion. But they thereby brought great odium upon themselves, as though they themselves were asserting that the children of the faithful did not need baptism. At the same time, however, they turned this odium back upon the Catholics, as though it followed from the doctrine of faith that the children of the faithful did not need baptism. Hence this mutual dispute appeared to contain the substance of the entire controversy, but in a way hostile to the Pelagians. For this reason Innocentius is said to have decreed against Pelagius and Coelestius (in the *Book of the Popes*) that anyone born of a Christian woman must be reborn through baptism. For the same reason Julianus curses anyone who says that a person born of two baptized parents, or born of a baptized woman, [Col. 0658B] does not need the grace of baptism (in the *Statement of Faith*, Part III). By this curse he attempted to throw back upon his opponents the charge brought against him.

It should likewise be observed that, when the Catholics asked the Pelagians why infants, if they lacked the original stain, needed the washing of baptism, and pressed them with powerful arguments, the Pelagians responded by attempting to weaken the force of those arguments through distinctions. They wished these distinctions to appear to have been taken from Chrysostom’s homily to the newly baptized. In that homily Chrysostom, arguing against certain people who confined the heavenly grace of baptism to the remission of sins alone, after counting ten other benefits, says:

“For this reason we baptize infants, although they are not defiled by sins: so that holiness, righteousness, adoption, inheritance, brotherhood with Christ may be added to them; so that they may be his members and become dwelling places of the Spirit.”

Chrysostom delivered this homily at Antioch, and therefore before the year 398, when he ascended the throne of the Church of Constantinople [Col. 0658C]. The Pelagians themselves used Chrysostom’s words, especially Rufinus, but Julianus above all, who forces this homily upon us in all his works.

It should also be observed that these same heretics, in order to escape the common offense of all the faithful, admitted many things that appeared thoroughly Catholic: namely, the common redemption by Christ of all people, including infants—Pelagius; that Christ also died for infants and shed his blood for them—Julianus; that they are regenerated through baptism—Rufinus; that they are reborn—Pelagius; that they become a new creation in Christ—Rufinus; that all need Christ’s washing—all of them; even the righteous, as Cornelius did—Rufinus; even those born of the faithful—Julianus; that Christ established one baptism for adults and infants—Pelagius, Coelestius, Julianus; that it ought to be celebrated in both ages with the same words and rites—Pelagius; that it is received for the remission of sins—Theodore, Coelestius; and that this is done according to the rule of the Church and the form of the Gospel—Coelestius. [Col. 0658D]

It should further be observed that, when the Catholics asked for what reason the Pelagians asserted that infants needed baptism, the Pelagians gave no other answer than Chrysostom’s: so that holiness, righteousness, adoption, and brotherhood with Christ might be added to them; so that they might become his members and temples of the Holy Spirit; so that they might become heirs of God and the people of Christ; so that they might attain the kingdom of heaven, which, because they do not possess the powers of nature, must be conferred through the generosity of grace. That is, as they say in the schools, so that they might be raised from the natural state to the supernatural state.

Finally, it should be observed that the slippery heretics defended themselves against the Catholics’ arguments chiefly by six distinctions.

Against the first, they recalled a twofold redemption: one by which captives are properly redeemed, and another by which something is said properly to be purchased, such as a house intended for habitation. They maintained that Christ redeemed by his blood both sinners, as captives, and infants, as temples which he would inhabit through faith. They also maintained that people may be said to be saved both when they pass from bad to good, as adults do, and when they pass from good to better, as infants do. They even admitted that Christ paid the price by shedding his blood, but that some thereby became merely rich, as infants did, while others were also liberated from the slavery of sin, as adults were.

Against the second, they ordered that two things be considered in baptism: that it is a washing with water, and that it is the grace of adoption. Both benefit adults, but only the latter benefits infants. Hence they proclaimed this statement (*Hypognostes*, book V): “In infants water has nothing to wash away; grace has something to adopt.”

Against the third, they said that one person’s twofold generation must be considered: one carnal generation, by which he is a son of the old Adam; the other spiritual, by which he is a son of God, a new creature in Christ, and a member of the new Adam. They said that the latter occurs in baptism, which is therefore called regeneration, renewal, procreation, and new birth.

Against the fourth, they admitted that those who receive baptism are planted together in the likeness of Christ’s death, but not in such a way that all die on account of sin as Christ did; rather, all simply become co-heirs of Christ’s resurrection. Rufinus touched upon part of this position in a word; Julian treated the whole matter at great length, with Augustine protesting.

As for the fifth—that the Church confesses one baptism, and specifically one conferred for the remission of sins—the Pelagians did not give a single answer. For, divided into opposing parties, some, such as Julian, denied that baptism was conferred upon infants for the remission of sins, saying that it was so conferred only upon adults. The power of heavenly grace, they held, bestows different gifts according to the differences among human conditions: upon some gifts alone, upon others remedies as well. Others, such as Theodore, invented a twofold remission of sins: one consisting in pardon for sins committed, which concerns adults; the other consisting in sinlessness, which is granted to all in baptism, even infants. In this life it is granted only imperfectly and as a pledge; in the kingdom of heaven it is granted in itself and perfectly, since the inheritance of that kingdom is perceived in baptism. Some indeed admitted that one could say that infants were baptized for the remission of sins, but only for this reason: through the sacrament of regeneration they became children and members of the Church, outside which no one attains remission of sins, and within which they might at some future time obtain pardon if they sinned after receiving faith. Thus they said that infants were baptized for the remission of sins—indeed, of their own sins—but of future sins. Others said that the sins were committed either in an earlier life, before souls slipped into bodies, as Theodore seems to indicate to Photius; or in their mothers’ wombs, or immediately after birth, as certain others say in Augustine.

To the sixth and seventh arguments, drawn from the unity both of baptism itself and of the words and rites with which it is celebrated throughout the Church, Julian responded in both of his works against Augustine. He explained at great length what he had stated briefly in his little treatise: that he truly transmitted and maintained one baptism, according to the Church’s example and God’s command, because, as he says elsewhere, one baptism suffices to produce different effects according to the diversity of those who receive it.

I would be endless and excessive if I wished to pursue everything that was raised and rejected on both sides. Augustine is wholly occupied with these matters, partly in developing them and partly in reporting them; so is the whole of the *Hypognostes* of Sixtus, and the whole of Marius Mercator. Mercator treats them in his book of *Subnotations*; Sixtus in the books of the *Hypognostica*; Augustine in three books *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, in the book *On Original Sin*, in the six books of the earlier work against Julian, in as many books of the *Imperfect Work*, and in numerous sermons and letters.

Moreover, I have observed that none of the ancients employed the argument from infant baptism to demonstrate that nature itself is corrupted by sin even in infants who lack the use of reason.

Augustine discovered another argument, which, I think, he taught to Mercator, Hypognostes, and the author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, and which he drew from chapter 40 of Ecclesiasticus, which says that a heavy yoke was imposed upon the sons of Adam from the day they came forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all. Explaining this passage with reference to infants, he says (*Letter* 166): “They languish under illnesses, are tormented by pains, afflicted by hunger and thirst, weakened in their limbs, deprived of their senses, attacked by demons, and so forth. How do they justly suffer these things without any fault of their own?” And elsewhere (*Imperfect Work*, book I, chapter 50):

“If you are pleased with the innocence of infants, remove from them, if you can, the heavy yoke that is upon the sons of Adam from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all. But I think that Scripture, which said this, knew better than you what the innocence of a creature is and what the justice of the Creator is. Who, then, does not see that, if infants possess the innocence you proclaim, God’s justice is absent from their heavy yoke? Since divine justice is present in their heavy yoke, they do not possess such innocence as you proclaim—unless perhaps, as you struggle with this question, your just but weak God can somehow come to your aid: a God who could not assist his own images lest innocent beings be crushed beneath a heavy yoke of misery. Thus you would say that he wished to help them because he is just, but could not because he is not omnipotent. In this way you would escape these difficulties, but lose the chief article of faith by which we first confess in the Creed that we believe in God the Father almighty. Therefore your God, amid the many and great evils that infants suffer, will lose either his justice, his omnipotence, or his very care for human affairs. Whichever of these you assert, consider what you have done.”

The entire force of the argument turns on this one principle: that it is unjust for infants to be afflicted by such miseries unless there is something in them that displeases God and is being punished. For this age, being in itself an innocent work of God, can possess corruption from no other source than from something opposed to God—namely, the sin of an evil will. Since that alone, not being from God, is opposed to God, and since it cannot be found in infants on account of their age, it must have passed from the parent of the whole race to his descendants.

How substantial and certain this argument is, I demonstrated long ago in the schools; the present occasion does not permit me to say more. So far as I know, none of the ancients before Augustine employed this reasoning. I do not remember having read what Julian answered, but he was certainly not unaware of it, since Augustine had brought forward the testimony of Ecclesiasticus in book II *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, against which Julian contends in his later work.

Earlier writers answered that these things were not punishments of a guilty nature, but the original conditions of a pure nature. For that reason Christ, who assumed flesh from the Virgin without any sin, also assumed many infirmities of infancy, just as he assumed mortality and the other conditions common to all human beings (*apud* Augustine, book I *On the Merits of Sins*, etc., chapter 27).

From this very response, however, the Catholics drew added strength for their argument. For if God, as the Apostle testifies (Romans 8:3), sent his Son “in the likeness of sinful flesh, in order to condemn sin in the flesh,” it must be admitted that there is some sinful flesh, since there can be no likeness of a thing that does not itself exist. Yet there is no sinful flesh if human nature in all people is such as it was created in Adam. Certainly Christ was not like human beings in the flesh if they had defiled their flesh with vices.

The heretics then seized upon this as an opportunity to bring a charge against the Catholics, as though they attributed to Christ, with Manichaeus, merely a phantom flesh and only an image of our flesh: for ours, they said, is sinful, whereas Christ has merely the likeness of sinful flesh. Thus Theodore (*apud* Photius, codex 177), when he had said that the Catholics did not even exempt Christ from sins, adds that in their other blasphemies one may observe that they attribute human nature to him not truly and naturally, but merely in appearance. Hence Pelagius, Caelestius, and Julian, in their professions of faith, so carefully proclaim that Christ was conformed to us according to his humanity, except for the sole stain of sin, which is not natural.

From this arose, first, the question why Christ, who wished to be born from a Virgin by a non-common birth, nevertheless wished to assume the common infirmities of the flesh. Next came the question why, if suffering and dying are the punishment of sin, the innocent Lamb suffered and died. Then: why do infants after baptism remain subject to such evils, especially demonic harassment, when they are just and children of God? Finally: whether, in the place of innocent nature—the paradise planted by God—there would have been the groans of women in labor, miscarriages, and the unhappy toils of farmers.

Related to this argument is another, which is drawn from the condition of adults. They suffer their own miseries, not only those they share with infants but many more that are peculiar to them, which Augustine vividly depicts in book XXII of *The City of God* (chapter 22):

“The fact that the entire race of mortals was condemned is testified by this very life—if it ought to be called life—which is filled with so many and such great evils. For what else does the depth of ignorance indicate, from which every error arises, which receives all the sons of Adam into a kind of dark bosom, so that no human being can be freed from it without labor, pain, and fear? What else does love itself of so many vain and harmful things indicate?” And shortly afterward: “These, indeed, are the evils of human beings, yet they come from that root of error and perverse love with which every son of Adam is born.” Then, in the following chapter: “In addition to these evils of this life, which the just and the wicked share, the just also have certain labors peculiar to themselves, by which they struggle against vices and are engaged in the temptations and dangers of such battles. For sometimes more vigorously, sometimes more weakly, the flesh nevertheless does not cease to desire against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh,” and so forth.

It is therefore clear that the particular miseries of adults may be reduced to two categories. Some concern the soul, such as concupiscence, ignorance of what is right, and difficulty in doing good; others concern the body, such as mortality, diseases, the laborious cultivation of the earth, the difficult childbirth of women, and so forth. The cause of these evils must be either God’s injustice or inability, or the punishment of the first and ancient sin. For no one can be miserable under a just God unless he deserves it.

So far as the first category is concerned—namely, the evils of the soul—Augustine, so far as I know, was the first to draw an argument. The defenders of the ancient faith had already drawn arguments from the second category from the earliest times. Rufinus tacitly answered them as follows:

“We say that God bestowed on the first man Adam, for his good, both the sweat and the labors that he would endure from the earth, since we cannot otherwise overcome, by venerable faith, the invisible enemies against whom we wage continual warfare unless we are wearied by bodily labors,” and so forth.

He discusses this at greater length, citing passages from both Testaments. It appears all the more plausible because ancient interpreters of Genesis, such as Chrysostom and Ambrose, wrote of labor just as they wrote of death: they said that these had been bestowed upon human beings by God as a benefit rather than as a punishment.

Augustine placed great confidence in this point as support for his cause, as though everything contrary to the happy condition of our first parents that we suffer plainly demonstrated that human nature had been corrupted. His reasoning seems to have proceeded as follows.

First he formed in his mind the idea of a certain perfect life, which innocent humanity would lead in a most delightful dwelling: the highest part of the soul would be subject to God, the lower part to the higher, and the body to both. Every irrational nature would obey its ruling human master, and the earth itself would obey its cultivator at his command.

He then concluded that humanity ought to have been constituted in this way partly because a work of the infinite Craftsman ought to be worthy of its author and therefore perfect in every respect; partly because the image of God ought to correspond to its exemplar—namely, the most beautiful creature to the best Creator, and the mistress of itself and of the lower nature to the Lord of all.

But when he saw that the present condition of human beings was far different from Adam’s former condition—that misery had replaced happiness, rebellion subjection, mortality everlasting life, and corruption perfection—he concluded that the whole human race was held under sin. For he was convinced that corruption could not have entered God’s work unless human sin had opened the way, that is, through humanity’s voluntary turning away from God.

“For,” he said, “from what other source could the omnipotent God be compelled to abandon his work, so that another, more powerful and envious being might harm it? Or how, if he were not compelled, would he—as a good God—take back benefits he had bestowed except from one unworthy of them; or—as a just God—deprive a human being of benefits already granted, which is certainly to punish him, unless he deserved it; or—as one who loves humanity most dearly—place a heavy yoke upon the sons of Adam from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all (Ecclesiasticus 40:1), unless they were guilty of a common fault?”

There must therefore be some fault, and a common fault of all, which the ancestor of the whole race committed by his will when all were that one man; and which his descendants contract when they are begotten from sinful flesh—that is, flesh stripped of its gifts on account of sin—and pay for in the place of misery, excluded from the place of innocent happiness.

Augustine valued this reasoning so highly that, when the Pelagians asserted that the things we suffer were the original conditions of nature, he did not so much refute them as ridicule them, as though they had been convicted of a still greater folly. He says that the Pelagians should paint paradise, where Adam was created, as a place of great blessedness in which its inhabitants enjoyed such a happy peace that, within themselves, they had to fight an internal war against the impulses of concupiscence lest they fall into consent to unlawful or dishonorable intercourse.

There, even if concupiscence itself—secretly stirring chaste hearts—could not be represented by any painter’s art, pregnant women could nevertheless be painted rejecting useful foods with disgust, craving harmful ones with foul delight, feeling nauseated, vomiting, growing pale, sometimes expelling immature fetuses by miscarriage, and, even in childbirth, protesting their misery through the punishment that the mother Eve received. Though the painting could not make a sound, it could imitate the faces of the sorrowful, groaning, and weeping as best it could, and so forth (*Imperfect Work*, book III, chapter 163).

He continues:

“Anyone who, unaware of the matter, looked at this painting and read its title and asked for its explanation would receive from you, obviously—but contrary to what he wished to hear—this excellent answer: ‘Such would have been the condition of the human race even there, because it is such here, where no origin of sin is drawn from human offspring.’ If he agreed, he would become a Pelagian; but if he refused to agree with this foolishness, which is without effect, you would accuse him of being a Manichaean,” and so forth (*ibid.*, chapter 199).

Augustine’s entire line of reasoning, however, did not satisfy everyone. There are some among the scholastics who seem either to encounter or to create a certain difficulty in it. Let them look to that matter themselves; we are engaged in something else. One may read both works against Julian on this subject, where Augustine, gathering the powers of intellect that he had employed everywhere, fights for the faith in original sin not only through the testimonies of Scripture, as a theologian, but also through arguments, as a philosopher. In passing, I think it worth observing that arguments, if confirmed by the Church’s tradition and by the common judgment of the faithful, possess very great and unconquerable force; but if considered in themselves and treated by the art of philosophers, they may seem to some capable of being weakened.

## § IV. The arguments by which the Pelagians attacked the faith; what the Catholics replied; and what questions arose from these matters

Just as the Pelagians thought testimonies should be opposed by testimonies, so they thought arguments should be opposed by arguments. There was this difference, however: they opposed few testimonies with many, but very many arguments with only a few. Nor is this surprising, since nothing is more ingenious than human pride when it resists the yoke by which it is to be held captive, and nothing is more fertile than the human mind when it undertakes the defense of pride.

It was shown earlier that all the Catholic arguments were directed toward proving that nature had been corrupted by the first man’s sin. The Pelagians aimed in the opposite direction, lest nature be believed to have been corrupted by sin and sin to be natural, as they put it. For they seemed to themselves to see contradictory propositions in the claim that sin was natural. Whatever is sin, they said, must be voluntary for a human being and must be punished by a just God. Whatever is natural, however, cannot pertain to the will, since the will follows nature; nor can it be punished by God, whose justice judges merits and whose wisdom is the author of natural things.

They further said that neither any efficient causes of this sin nor any means by which it could be transmitted could be conceived. From these two points, therefore—namely, the nature of sin and the mode of its transmission—they drew very many arguments and very many consequences that possessed the force of arguments. Theodore, Rufinus, Pelagius, Caelestius, and Julian drew them, although Pelagius perhaps should scarcely be included, since he discussed the whole matter only through the persona of another. The Catholics resolved each of the Pelagians’ arguments, and from this arose almost innumerable questions.

Rufinus first, then. “They are mad,” he says (*Booklet of Faith*, chapter 8, no. 39), “who condemn the whole world to the guilt of crimes through the one man Adam. For those who say this either declare God unjust, or certainly judge the devil stronger than God, because the devil was able, through the transgression of Adam and Eve, to make evil the nature that God created good—just as, through the transgression of the first man Adam and his wife Eve, all human beings are subject to sin.”

Then (*ibid.*):

“If the nature of Adam and Eve, having been made sinful through transgression, was unable to abstain completely from evils, why, when they fell the first time, did they not also fall the second time? And whence came so many righteous people afterward—Abel, Enoch, Noah, Elijah, and others?”

Again (no. 40):

“If infants die because of Adam’s sin, let them tell us why they are permitted to taste death immediately after baptism, since all who have been baptized—and for this reason have become children of God—cannot possess sin.”

Afterward (*ibid.*):

“If infants born of Christian parents are baptized because of Adam’s sin, they ought not to be baptized at all, but should be regarded as holy, because they were begotten from faithful parents, just as blessed Paul teaches when he says: ‘Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy’ (1 Corinthians 7:14).”

Finally (no. 41):

“If infants possessed any sin, then, unless they were washed from it before a premature death, they ought certainly to be assigned to the punishment of eternal fire, which Scripture usually calls Gehenna. Let them learn from the divine Scriptures that the punishment of eternal fire was not prepared for the innocent and for those entirely ignorant of sin, but for those who are known to have transgressed God’s law.”

Pelagius (*On Nature*, in Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 19):

“First, we must discuss the claim that nature is said to have been weakened and changed by sin. Therefore, above all, I think it must be asked what sin is: whether it is some substance, or altogether lacks substance—a name expressing not a thing, not an existence, not some body, but an act wrongly performed.” He then adds: “I believe this is so. And if it is so, how could something lacking substance weaken or change human nature?”

Caelestius, partly in Augustine (*On the Merits of Sins*, book III), partly in Mercator (*Commentary and Subnotations*), and in the author of the *Predestined* (*Heresy* 88):

“If Adam’s sin harmed even those who do not sin, then Christ’s righteousness also benefits those who do not believe, since the Apostle says that through one person people are liberated in a similar—indeed, greater—way than they had previously perished through one person.

“If baptism cleanses that ancient and aged sin, those born from two baptized people ought to be free from this sin. For they cannot transmit to their descendants what they themselves did not possess.

“If the soul is not transmitted by descent—as indeed it is not—but only the flesh possesses the transmission of sin, then only the flesh deserves punishment. For it is unjust that a soul born today, not from Adam’s mass, should bear another’s sin, so ancient. Indeed, it is reasonable that God, who forgives personal sins, should not impute another’s.

“If a sinner begot a sinner so that original sin might be remitted to his child upon reception of baptism, then a righteous person ought to have begotten a righteous person.

“If parents, after conversion, are not harmed by their own former sins, much less can their children be harmed through them. If it happened that the first human being was the cause of death, then after Christ’s coming people ought no longer to die.

“If death arose through Adam’s sin, we would never die after the remission of sins that our Deliverer granted us. Adam’s sin therefore proved more powerful in killing absolutely all human beings than Christ’s grace in saving them, since grace benefited not everyone but only believers. For not all who are born from Adam are also reborn in Christ.

Julian first raised two objections explicitly: first, that the defenders of original sin condemn marriage; second, that they assign its offspring to the devil. Both, without doubt, are Manichaean. This objection gave Augustine the occasion to write book I *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. When Julian refuted it, he again introduced many more arguments in four antirrhetic books, some of which he later expanded and others established in eight books against Augustine’s second book *On Marriage*. If one wished to pursue every point individually, one would have to transcribe the whole works.

All these arguments tend toward the following questions. First, how could sin exist in God’s work—in marriage and in marriage’s aids or offspring? Next, how can marriage be excused when all its offspring are under the devil’s power, merely because they arise from the union of a man and a woman? Then, how can that be called sin which does not arise from the will of the human agent but from nature, whose author is God? Fourth, how can the necessity of sinning be reconciled either with the justice of God, who punishes what cannot be avoided, or with the pursuit of virtue, by which people, inspired to do so, try to fulfill the law? Finally, how does the opinion that sin is transmitted differ from the madness of Manichaeus, when both consist of the same elements and the same propositions? Julian confirms this by producing a letter of Manes to his daughter Menoch, recently discovered at Constantinople.

To the first of these questions Augustine replied (*Imperfect Work*, book III, chapter 174) that, in the use of marriage, one must distinguish what is good by divine institution from what is corruption belonging to the devil. Sin is found in this work of God on account of lust or concupiscence, which is not from God but from the devil, the author of sin.

From this arose an endless dispute about concupiscence:

1. Whether it is a disease or a force of nature.
2. Whether it is poison breathed in by the devil or a benefit once bestowed upon human beings by God.
3. How and why it remains in the baptized, in whom there is no condemnation.
4. How it propagates the guilty when it has ceased to be guilty through baptism.
5. How it can be called a vice in human beings when it is shared with animals.
6. How the saints, when they beget children, can make good use of this evil.
7. How it arose from eating the forbidden tree and, if it arose from there, how it is not good when God created the tree.
8. Whether shame commanded that the parts upon which it resides should be covered.
9. Why those parts are not moved in accordance with the command of reason, as other parts are.
10. Whether they would likewise have been under their own control in paradise.
11. Whether concupiscence is shown to be evil by the fact that all devout people struggle against it.
12. What that law of sin is which dwells even in the limbs of the saints and resists the law of the mind.
13. How the good of marriage must be distinguished from vice, fertility from lust, and the guilt of concupiscence from the act itself.
14. Whether Christ was free from the common stain because he was born of a virgin by a non-common birth.
15. Whether everyone begotten through the union of a man and a woman is born guilty.

These and other matters were debated on both sides with such intense passion that the dispute often turned into declamation, whether praising the generative power of offspring or accusing the lust of the flesh.

Augustine resolved the third question by admitting that all sin arises from the will of a creature and none from nature, whose author is God. Yet, although this confession placed him at a great distance from the Manichaeans, he distinguished two kinds of sin in order to show that sin can arise from the will in different ways. One kind is committed by each person’s own will; the other is contracted by anyone born from a sinner through another’s will. Original sin, insofar as it concerns Adam, he said belongs to the first kind; insofar as it concerns his descendants, to the second. Yet he held that the descendants are guilty because they were that one man who first sinned, and in him violated God’s covenant.

On this occasion Augustine’s earlier definition of sin was examined with greater subtlety: “the will to admit or retain what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain.” The question was asked what notion of sin is impressed upon all minds; there was discussion of God’s justice as judge of wills; Manichaeism was carefully examined; the essence of sin was explained; and some even debated the origin of souls. If souls were transmitted through descent, the difficulty of understanding how sin passes along with seeds would be eased; but if they are created daily by God in bodies, or sent from elsewhere, there is immense difficulty in discovering how sin is transmitted.

As for the fourth question, concerning the necessity of sinning contracted by everyone after nature was corrupted, the Catholics provided an adequate answer, but in such a way that two other immense questions were raised. One concerned free choice: whether that great sin had destroyed it from the human race. The other concerned ἀναμαρτησία (*anamartēsia*, sinlessness): whether a human being can be without sin in this life. Each in turn generated many other, far smaller questions, but together the two produced the most important question of all: the necessity of divine grace’s assistance for performing works of piety and overcoming temptations. That question will be treated in the following chapter.

The first question generated only a few subsidiary questions: how it can be said that the freedom of choice was lost through sin; and how, if freedom of choice was lost, God’s justice can be defended when he punishes what cannot be avoided, and so forth.

The second generated more questions, which it would take too long to discuss individually. From this came Caelestius’ fifteen propositions and Pelagius’ book *On Nature*. Augustine answered the former in his entire book *On the Perfection of Righteousness*; Jerome answered the latter in his letter to Ctesiphon and in three dialogues; Augustine in his book *On Nature and Grace* and other writings; and the African synod refuted it in its last three canons.

It should further be observed that the question of sinlessness had, as it were, three ages or stages, for it first concerned morals alone and was ethical; then it became dogmatic; and finally it belonged to both categories.

In the first stage it existed before the controversies about the transmission of sin and the corruption of nature had been raised—whether when Evagrius of Pontus and others were writing περὶ Ἀπαθείας (*Peri Apatheias*, “On Impassibility”), or when Pelagius was writing his book *On Testimonies*. It was in the second stage when controversy began to be stirred up on account of the transmission of sin. Finally, it existed in the third stage when the African canons were composed and when Augustine, the author of those canons, fought against Pelagius partly in letters and partly in books.

Augustine judged this error to be, in the first stage, at least somewhat tolerable, provided that its defenders did not boast that they themselves were ἀναμάρτητοι (*anamartētoi*, sinless); in the second, a wicked contention; and in the third, a heresy deserving anathema.

That holy teacher should be consulted, among other places, especially toward the end of his book *On the Perfection of Righteousness*, where he writes:

“Finally, if, apart from our Head, the Savior of his body, some people are asserted either to have been or to be just in this life without any sin—whether because they never consent to its desires, or because what is so small [that is, so very slight] is not to be counted as sin, since God does not impute it to piety—I do not think we ought to resist very strongly. For I know that this has seemed so to certain people, whose opinion on the matter I do not dare to criticize, although I cannot defend it either.
