“But plainly, whoever denies that we ought to pray, ‘Do not lead us into temptation’—and he denies it who contends that God’s grace is not necessary for a human being in order not to sin, but that the human will, once the law has been received, is sufficient—must, I do not doubt, be removed from the ears of all and anathematized by the mouths of all.”

Pelagius’ ἀναμαρτησία was opposed by certain ecclesiastical writers through arguments that Jerome and Orosius explain, and also through various scriptural testimonies, but above all through two decisive passages:

“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8); and, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12). The Apostle’s words and Christ’s words addressed everyone: the former teaching trust in Christ the mediator, the latter teaching the common form of prayer.

The Pelagians replied: The words of both passages are spoken with one meaning by the ordinary faithful and with another by the perfect. The ordinary faithful speak them truly and for themselves; the perfect speak them humbly and for others who are sinners among their people.

The Fathers refuted this sort of quibbling not only by producing scriptural testimonies such as “In many things we all offend” (James 3:2), “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm 143:2), “There is no one who does not sin” (Ecclesiasticus 7), and “He marks every human hand, so that every person may know his weakness” (Job 37:7), but also by anathematizing it.

To the arguments brought forward by the heretics belong certain odious consequences that they claimed followed from the transmission of sin. For while the Catholics proved this transmission from the fact that nature had been corrupted, they admitted three consequences from their doctrine. The opponents of the faith, offended by them, seized upon them as opportunities both for accusation and for argument.

The Catholics admitted that their doctrine entailed that, through the first man’s sin, nature had become both sinful and the begetter of sinners; that, because of Adam’s sin, some necessity of sinning had been contracted by his descendants; and that all who are born from marriage remain under the devil’s power until they are reborn in Christ.

From this the heretics commonly inferred that the transmission of sin did not differ from the Manichaean error, which holds that nature is evil. They therefore labeled the Catholics “Manichaeans” and “Traducians.” No designation seemed more intolerable to Augustine, and not without reason, since less educated people might easily suspect that something of his former error still clung to so great a teacher—an error in which he had been entangled, as he had openly admitted in writing.

For this reason, with all the force of his intellect, eloquence, and learning, he rejected this charge both from the Catholics and from himself, especially in three works.

Theodore brought forward the following five charges (*apud* Photius, codex 177):

That human beings, who were naturally good before, had been made wicked by nature, and now sinned by nature rather than by the will;

That infants, although newly born, were not free from sin, since, because of Adam’s transgression, a sinful nature was propagated to all his descendants;

That no mortal was just, and that not even Christ, having assumed a sinful nature, was free from guilt;

That marriage, or at least its use, was the work of the perverse nature into which Adam fell through sin, and that immediately, through the defect of nature, he took upon himself a multitude of evils.

Caelestius brought forward the same number (*apud* Augustine, book I to Boniface), and they were not greatly different:

Through the sin of the first man, that is, Adam, free choice had perished, so that no one now possessed the power to live well, but all were compelled to sin by the necessity of their flesh.

The marriages now practiced had not been instituted by God; the intercourse of spouses had been invented by the devil; and therefore those who were born were innocent but became guilty and were made by the devil, not by God, because they were born from this diabolical intercourse.

The saints of the Old Testament were not free from sin; even the Apostle Paul, or all the apostles, had always been polluted by immoderate lust.

Christ had not been free from sins, but had lied through the necessity of the flesh and had also been stained by other offenses.

Baptism did not grant complete forgiveness of sins or remove crimes, but merely scraped them away, so that the roots of all sins remained in the evil flesh.

[Col. 0667B] Julian also introduced five points, as Augustine reports in these words (*Book II against Julian*, chapter 1):

“You say that, by asserting original sin, we call the devil the creator of human beings at birth; condemn marriage; deny that all sins are forgiven in baptism; accuse God of the crime of injustice; and instill despair of perfection. For you insist that all these consequences follow if we believe that infants are born bound by the sin of the first man and therefore are under the devil unless they are reborn in Christ. ‘The devil creates,’ you say, ‘if they are created from this wound which the devil inflicted upon human nature, originally created sound; and marriage is condemned if it is believed to possess something from which those born are made liable to condemnation. Nor are all sins forgiven in baptism if some evil remains in baptized spouses from which evil offspring are generated. Nor indeed is God unjust when, although he forgives baptized people their own sins, he condemns an infant because, though created by him and neither knowing nor willing it, it contracted others’ sins even from those parents whose own sins had been forgiven. Nor can a virtue understood as contrary to vice be believed capable of being perfected, because it is incredible that inborn vices can be eradicated—vices which should no longer even be considered vices. For someone who cannot be anything other than what he was created to be does not sin.’”

Impure men even dared to charge the holiest of men with having adopted their position for no other reason than that, by accusing nature and God, they sought to absolve themselves of their own crimes.

Rufinus (*Booklet of Faith*, chapter 8, no. 39):

“They should certainly recognize themselves as greedy for wrongdoing, since they themselves are lovers of pleasures and of the flesh; they ought not to attach to others the causes of those things of which they themselves appear to have been the authors.”

Pelagius (*Book on Nature*):

“There are those who, although they ought to accuse the human will for their sins, instead accuse human nature and attempt to excuse themselves through it. But the human race falsely complains about its own nature, and so forth.”

[Col. 0667D] Julianus (*Book II of the Unfinished Work*, chapters 5, 6, 7, and 8):

“For it is altogether pleasing to those who overflow with passion to defame everything that has ever belonged to the saints, anywhere and at any time, lest they be corrected by the examples of renowned works. It is altogether pleasing, and deeply satisfying, to allege the weakness of nature; to say that the flesh is subject to innate sins; and not to place the achievement of correction in the human will, but to call the crimes of one’s desires the functions of one’s limbs. Their Catholic faith is supposedly this: that it confesses free choice, but choice by which a human being is compelled to do evil and cannot will the good. They call vain and heretical the statements of those who assert that the just Lord created human beings free for good works and that it lies within each person’s power to withdraw from evil and shine through the pursuit of virtue. Thus those who throw their crimes back upon the necessity of the flesh may be pierced by the goad of anxiety and fear.

“Finally, in churches possessing a great abundance of good people and a large congregation, it is proclaimed that sin has such force that, before the form of the limbs, before the beginning and arrival of the soul, it flies over the seed already cast and escapes into the mother’s secret place; that it makes those who will be born guilty; and that guilt, older than birth itself, awaits the substance. This is the law of sin which thereafter dwells in the limbs and compels the captive human being to serve crimes, being more worthy not of chastisement for shameful acts but of mercy, since what we call the vice of a perverse will is named in the Church by men and women, and by great pontiffs, ‘original suffering.’”

§ V. Which Fathers’ testimonies were brought forward on both sides; the replies made in turn; and the questions that arose from them

To prove impeccability, Pelagius produced testimonies from seven authorities: Lactantius, Hilary, Ambrose, John of Constantinople, Pseudo-Christ, Jerome, and Augustine. Against original sin, Julianus praised Basil, John of Constantinople, and Theodore of Mopsuestia—or rather Diodore of Tarsus, Theodore’s teacher.

Observe that Julianus appealed to Greeks, whereas Pelagius appealed only to Latins. Julianus never mentions Ambrose except incidentally; and what Pelagius brought forward from Chrysostom is neither impressive in itself nor contained in the express wording of the testimony, nor easily found in the author. Julianus praised the Greeks partly as a display of learning before scholars, by whom he wished to be approved alone, and partly as a fabricated claim of agreement with the Easterners before the common people. Pelagius used the testimony of Latins chiefly because he was writing to his “Amazons,” that is, noble Roman women unacquainted with a foreign language.

Augustine satisfied both sides with the testimonies they had produced, explaining not only any statements expressed obscurely by such eminent men but also showing, in the Fathers’ own words, that the teachers of the Church had testified on behalf of the common belief of the faithful.

He himself, in turn, produced two witnesses against Coelestius, Cyprian and Ambrose; and twenty-five against Julianus: Irenaeus of Lyons, Cyprian of Carthage, Reticius of Autun, Olympius the Spaniard, Hilary of Poitiers, Ambrose of Milan, Innocent of Rome, Gregory of Nazianzus, Basil of Caesarea, John of Constantinople, Jerome the presbyter of Stridon, and the fourteen Fathers of Diospolis. He produced so many and such eminent men partly to repel from himself the odium of Manichaeism, since he agreed with teachers so thoroughly Catholic, and partly to show that the five consequences by which the Pelagians frightened the less educated away from firmly holding the faith of original sin were both novel and contrary to truth. For those Fathers, celebrated throughout the world, while following the faith of original sin, nevertheless condemned each of these consequences; nor can they be believed to have been so slow—indeed, so foolish—that, although they were teachers of the peoples, they failed to see what followed from what, especially in a matter of such importance.

[Col. 0668D] At this point, I think, one should observe particularly, first, that Augustine used the testimonies of the ancients so artfully that by one act he demonstrated that he held the doctrine believed everywhere, always, and by everyone, and that he therefore followed universality, antiquity, and consensus—the three marks of the Catholic faith. He cited seventeen Greeks: Gregory, Basil, John, and the fourteen Fathers of Diospolis; six Latins: Cyprian, Reticius, Olympius, Hilary, Ambrose, and Innocent. He praised two as intermediaries of both Churches, Irenaeus and Jerome, in such a way that he might appear to have produced witnesses to the faith from every region and period. Yet he introduced no others except those who had died piously in communion with the Church. Hence it is clear that that earlier, highly elaborated work against Julianus was composed in the year 421, as was demonstrated in the sixth dissertation. For Jerome, the last of all the teachers, died in the year 420.

Second, Augustine must have labored considerably to collect suitable testimonies from the ancients concerning the transmission of sin. For, since the faith concerning this matter was still enveloped in complete darkness, scarcely anyone expressed the relevant judgment clearly. Catholics commonly acknowledged that we are born children of wrath and that the first parent, when he sinned, harmed not himself alone but also his descendants. They also acknowledged that, because of disobedience, Adam condemned his race—that is, the whole human race—and that consequently all of us who have come from him are held liable to our father’s debt, or, in the Apostle’s expression, to the bond of indebtedness.

Yet the transmission of sin did not clearly emerge from this, since many of the ancients said that only the punishment had passed on: bodily mortality with what might be called its accompanying features. The Pelagians seized upon this statement in order somehow to escape the arguments of the Catholics. At last they confessed—almost as though forced by torture—that Adam had harmed his descendants not by example alone but also by sin, though not through guilt passing on, but through punishment.

Augustine closed this escape by asserting his own principle: under a just judge, punishment cannot pass on without guilt. As far as I know, he was the first to employ this principle, though not without difficulty, since he repeatedly quoted God’s declaration, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children,” while refusing to hold children liable for the guilt of their fathers.

Third, it should be observed that Augustine introduced Ambrose as a witness with all the greater zeal because Ambrose possessed greater authority among everyone, owing to the recent memory of his extraordinary holiness and unvanquished constancy in defending the faith. The Pelagians could less easily reject him, on account of the integrity of his doctrine, which they themselves had praised; and Augustine could introduce him more honorably in defense of the faith than if he had received that faith from Ambrose at baptism.

[Col. 0669C] To this testimony Julianus first replied that Augustine himself had diminished the authority of the ancients when he wrote that he was not troubled by them but only by the canonical books. Next, it seemed astonishing that statements should be brought forward as Ambrose’s which Manes had written in his books and which Augustine had absorbed. Then he said that mere little phrases were being produced, and doubtful ones at that, when clear judgments were required. Finally, some things had occasionally slipped carelessly and incautiously from Ambrose and others; if they were alive, they themselves would condemn those statements after perceiving what consequences followed from them. In the end, Augustine, having found nothing more authoritative, had fled in despair to these passages, from which he might perhaps derive comfort through companionship but could obtain no defense, since no writings by disputants could take precedence over the law and work of God.

But since this is, as far as I remember, the only place where the Pelagians replied to Catholics who used the testimony of the Fathers, may it not—and indeed must it—be inferred from this how great was the shamelessness of such men? When the names of the Fathers favored them, they exalted them to heaven; when their judgments contradicted them, they condemned them as impious. They added the name of holiness to the men whom they praised, but disparaged the most renowned figures whenever those figures seemed to oppose them. This has always been the characteristic of every partisan heresy.

Fourth, Julianus was as zealous for Chrysostom as Augustine was for Ambrose; yet Julianus did not conduct himself toward Ambrose as Augustine did toward Chrysostom. Julianus neither explained anything by Ambrose nor turned anything from Ambrose against his opponent, as though he despised the author himself. Augustine, however, explained every statement of Chrysostom that was brought against him and drew from the same author material with which either to refute his opponent or to defend the Catholic faith.

The two adversaries each drew Chrysostom over to his own side: Julianus in his *Booklet of Faith* and in the fourth book of his earlier work; Augustine in the first book against Julianus. Julianus, however, argued almost exclusively from one passage of the homily to the newly baptized, whereas Augustine used four others: the letter to Olympia, the homily on the Raising of Lazarus, Homily 9 on Genesis, and Homily 10 on the Epistle to the Romans.

From that very homily on which Julianus relied for support, Augustine took the following passage in defense of the faith:

“Christ came once and found us bound by our father’s bond, which Adam wrote. He showed the beginning of the obligation; our sins increased the interest.”

After introducing this passage, Augustine says:

“Do you hear a man who is both learned in the Catholic faith and a teacher of it, distinguishing the debt of the father’s bond, which has adhered to us as an inheritance, from those debts whose interest has increased through our own sins? Do you hear what is remitted to infants in baptism, who have not yet contracted their own debts and nevertheless could not be exempt from their father’s bond?”

For his words, untranslated, read in Greek as follows:

> Ἔρχεται ἅπαξ ὁ Χριστὸς, εὗρεν ἡμῶν χειρόγραφον πατρῷον, ὅ τι ἔγραψεν ὁ Ἀδάμ. Ἐκεῖνος τὴν ἀρχὴν εἰσήγαγεν τοῦ χρείους, ἡμεῖς τὸν δανεισμὸν ηὐξήσαμεν ταῖς μεταγενεστέραις ἁμαρτίαις.

Word for word, these words mean:

> “Christ came once; he found our father’s bond, which Adam wrote. He introduced the beginning of the debt; we increased the interest through later sins.”

“Was he content to say ‘the father’s bond,’ unless he added ‘our,’ so that we might know that, before we increased the interest through our later sins, the debt of that father’s bond already belonged to us?” (*Augustine, Book I against Julianus*, chapter 6).

When I read this and reflected that the homily in question had been translated into Latin by Annianus, I wondered why Augustine, who had observed so precisely—and not without reason—that the translator had earlier used *peccatum* (“sin”) for *peccata* (“sins”), had not likewise noticed that in this passage the word *ostendit* (“showed”) had been used for *induxit* (“introduced”), thereby suggesting that the obligation had passed to us not by transmission but by imitation.

[Col. 0670C] Julianus, in turn, could have taken from the homily on the Epistle to the Romans a passage that seemed to conflict with Augustine’s more expansive argument from it, indeed to weaken each of its parts. The statement that “many were made sinners through the disobedience of one” seems to present a considerable problem. For if Adam sinned and became mortal, and those who arose from him were likewise mortal, there is nothing absurd in that. But that another should have become a sinner through his disobedience—what, I ask, is the coherence or consequence of that? On this reasoning, even punishments would not be owed by one who was such, since he did not become a sinner through himself.

What, then, does the word “sinners” mean in this passage? It seems to me to mean no more than “liable to punishment and condemned to death.” Moreover, that all became mortal after Adam died, he demonstrates clearly and at length, and so forth.

CHAPTER V. The origin of the question concerning the necessity of God’s grace through Christ from the preceding question; also the origin of other questions from it, especially that concerning the power of free choice

[Col. 0670D]

The origin of the third question, which concerns the assistance of divine grace, is so clearly derived from the second that it scarcely requires laborious demonstration. For once the corruption of nature had been proved on the basis of original sin, nothing was more straightforward than to demonstrate the corruption of nature from the remedy of grace and the disease from the medicine. Two things show that this is what happened. First, in the earliest period no controversy arose concerning the assistance of divine grace; the whole dispute concerned the cause of mortality, original sin, and also impeccability, as is clear from the works of Theodore and Rufinus the Syrian. Second, the ancients made the question of the assistance of grace the third question after the two already explained, both in word and in deed, following the order of origin. If they had wished to follow any other order, the course of the treatment would have been entirely different, as everyone can see.

Hypognostus therefore counts as the third error, in his preface, the Pelagian error by which they say that a human being can fulfill whatever he wishes through free choice, as though free choice were sufficient in itself; and in his third book, after the preceding two errors rejected in the earlier books, he attacks it.

Mercator, after recounting the doctrines connected with natural mortality that Coelestius defended, adds, he says (*Preface to the Subnotanda*): that a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes. He gives two reasons for this error: first, because before Christ’s coming there were people without sin; and second, because the Law sends people to the kingdom of heaven in the same way as the Gospel. The force of the proof lies in this: if the Law once had the power both to make people righteous and to send them into the kingdom of heaven, it must still have that power; and thus the inward grace of the will through Christ would not be especially necessary—a grace which at that time was almost the sole subject under discussion.

[Col. 0671B] Prosper, after explaining the same two errors concerning the mortality of the human race and the transmission of sin, continues in these words (*Poem against the Ungrateful*, chapter 1):

> “That all the innocent can live upon the citadel of virtue,
>
> and preserve the beauty implanted in the mind,
>
> since the natural dignity of one who wills rightly rests upon free choice,
>
> and the law planted within the heart teaches
>
> what is written outwardly, and so forth.”

When the African synod had established, in its first two canons, the Catholic faith concerning the mortality of the human race and original sin, it immediately struck with an anathema, in its third canon, anyone who said:

“If anyone says that the grace of God, by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord, has power only for the remission of sins already committed, and not also for assistance so that they may not be committed, let him be anathema.”

The Council of Orange, following the African synod one hundred and twenty years later, transmitted the Church’s teaching in order: concerning the corruption of nature, both body and soul, in its first canon; concerning the transmission of sin, in the second; and concerning grace, in the third and the remaining canons.

Augustine understood well that the reason for disputing with the Pelagians about God’s grace had arisen partly from the Apostle’s passage in Romans 5, where a comparison is established between the two heads of human nature, Adam the corrupter and Christ the restorer—and from which original sin is most incontrovertibly proved—and partly from the impeccability proclaimed by the Pelagians. For both these reasons he began to write about grace: in the books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, in the work that followed, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, in the book *On Nature and Grace*, and in the book *On the Grace of Christ*, and elsewhere.

Pelagius himself indicated the same thing in his book *On Nature*, when he wrote that one must first discuss the claim that nature had been weakened and changed through sin.

“First,” he says—that is, before controversy is raised concerning the assistance of grace for healing nature.

At this point Augustine’s argument should be read (*On Nature and Grace*, chapter 19), where he concludes corruption and disease from the remedy:

“What is healed if nothing has been wounded, nothing injured, nothing weakened, and nothing corrupted? Further, if there is something to be healed, there is something from which it has been corrupted. You hear a person confessing; what more do you want from one who argues? ‘Heal my soul,’ he says. Ask him from what it has been corrupted, since he asks to be healed, and hear what follows: ‘For I have sinned against you.’”

It would next be necessary to see by what arguments the faith was defended by Catholics and attacked by heretics. But the whole matter has been treated sufficiently by us for the present purpose (chapter 2 of this dissertation) and abundantly by others for the sake of learning. I therefore think that only a few observations need be made before proceeding to the second part of the dissertation.

There should, however, be some distinction, in relation to this historical discussion, between the grace of God, which is called simply God’s grace, and grace through Christ. The question concerning the former was less extensive; that concerning the latter was greater. This, unless I am mistaken, clearly shows the reason for the inquiry: namely, the corruption of nature. Jerome seems to have confused the two, as perhaps did Orosius and other ancients; but Augustine subtly distinguished one from the other and disputed almost exclusively about God’s grace through Christ.

For, as he repeatedly observed (*On Original Sin*, chapter 24), the Christian faith properly concerns the case of two men: through one we were sold under sin, through the other we are redeemed from sins; through one we were cast down into death, through the other we are freed for life. The first ruined us in himself by doing his own will rather than the will of the one by whom he was made; the second saved us in himself by doing not his own will but the will of the one by whom he was sent. The Christian faith, therefore, properly rests upon the case of these two men.

Why Jerome proceeded one way and Augustine another seems readily apparent. Jerome treated the question as it arose from the assertion of impeccability; Augustine treated it as arising from the Apostle’s passage just mentioned. Pelagian impeccability, relying proudly upon its own powers, rejected every form of divine assistance; but the Apostle’s passage compared the new Adam with the old in such a way as to show the grace of the new Adam superior to the sin of the old.

From this anyone can easily understand both why different writers use different arguments against the Pelagians—for different writers were attacking different doctrines—and why Augustine himself argued one way in *On Nature and Grace* and another way in *On the Grace of Christ*. In the former he was fighting against impeccability; in the latter, for the benefit of Christ the Savior.

But three things must again be distinguished in God’s grace through Christ: that it is through Christ, that it is supernatural, and that it is gratuitous. It is conferred because of the mediator between God and human beings; it restores the powers of nature that have been lost; and it precedes free choice, being granted without regard to merits. Insofar as it is conferred because of Christ, it is called healing grace; insofar as it supplies power, supernatural grace; insofar as it precedes merits, gratuitous and prevenient grace.

Nearly all Augustine’s books against the Pelagians concern healing grace, especially the one entitled *On the Grace of Christ*. The earlier works concern assisting grace, except for certain letters; the later works concern stimulating or awakening grace. Jerome wrote extensively about assisting grace, but scarcely anything worth mentioning about awakening grace. Indeed, some say that in this area he did not proceed without blame.

§ I. Which questions arose, and how they arose, concerning God’s grace insofar as it is through Christ and heals corrupted nature

First, it should be observed that, when the African canons were composed, the Church chiefly defended three points against the Pelagians concerning God’s grace through Christ.

First, that the grace of God, by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord, is effective not only for the remission of sins already committed but also for assistance so that sins may not be committed.

Second, that this same grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord assists us not merely because through it the understanding of the commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we know what we ought to seek and what to avoid, but also because through it we are enabled and disposed to love and to accomplish what we have recognized ought to be done.

Finally, that the grace of justification is not given so that we may more easily fulfill by grace what we are commanded to do by free choice—as though, even if grace were not given, we could still, though not easily, fulfill the divine commands without it.

From this it can be known that at that time the dispute was not, at least κυρίως (“properly” or “in the principal sense”), about God’s assistance insofar as it is gratuitous, but insofar as it is merely supernatural—that is, insofar as it assists nature’s inability to perform works of piety. It is also clear from this that Letter 107 was not written until after the period of the African synod, whose canons we have cited.

Second, on the occasion of the Apostolic passage in which the two Adams are compared, a very serious controversy arose between Catholics and Pelagians: why Christ came into this world; why he suffered and died; how he benefited humanity; whom he benefited and to what extent; and by what means he redeemed us either from sins or from the curse of the Law.

No Pelagian failed to reveal his mind: Theodore, though more obscurely, in his creed (*near the end*); Rufinus the Syrian more openly in his *Booklet of Faith* (chapter 7, no. 46); Pelagius in his commentaries on the Apostle’s passage (part I, no. 7); and Julianus in his *Booklet of Faith* (books II, III, and IV) and in many passages of the *Unfinished Work*.

Theodore:

“The second Adam came in order to reveal to us the future state of immortality and to lead us to imitate him.”

Rufinus the Syrian:

“He came to teach humility even to all the heavenly powers; to show his love toward human beings; to die for sins; to grant adoption and the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven to those who believe in him; to provide an example of practicing virtue and avoiding sin; to be the mediator between God and human beings; and to bind them together forever by the bond of peace.”

Pelagius:

“He came both to forgive sins by his death and to grant righteousness, and to teach us the manner of love by which we should love God and Christ himself. For why did Christ die for us undeservedly, unless to manifest his love, since we were still weighed down by the sicknesses of sins and crimes? He died for the ungodly in order, through contemplation of his benefits, to commend his grace; to show, in the marketplace of sin, how much we ought to love him; and to let us see, in view of so great a benefit, whether anything should be preferred to him, since toward us, the ungodly, he preferred neither his own life nor refused the death that was necessary for us.”

Julianus:

“Christ was born to call the whole world back from sins both by his example and by suffering, removing sin as God, by forgiving it, and showing as a human being, through the likeness of his nature, how sin could thereafter be conquered. Beginning with the baptism of John, by which he was baptized to give an example—not, as some wish, on account of his own sin—he subjected himself to every suffering of the flesh, enduring hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, death, and other things of this kind: ‘He became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross’ (Philippians 2:8). The blessed Peter taught us this when he said: ‘Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps; he committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth’ (1 Peter 2:21). Thus, having suffered and been buried in the flesh for our salvation, he rose on the third day, both to destroy death and to open for us the way of resurrection.”

Observe further, careful reader, that Rufinus said nothing, nor Pelagius or Julianus anything in more words, than Theodore had said in fewer. The fact that they additionally wrote that Christ died for sinners and that human beings were redeemed by Christ’s death does not undermine this observation. For, as the testimonies cited make clear, by such magnificent expressions they meant nothing other than that Christ loved us to the point of death and by that example urged us to love him in return with equal love. They also meant that, by dying undeservedly—as Pelagius puts it—Christ wished to triumph over death and to show in himself both how death could be conquered and what our resurrection to immortality would be like.

Third, it should be observed that the Pelagians called nature and free choice, which was granted to human beings by God the Creator at their creation, by the name “grace.” In addition, however, they acknowledged grace of six kinds.

The first was adoption, conferred in baptism.

The second was the remission of sins, given to penitents.

The third was the Law and external instruction, which showed the way of salvation.

[Col. 0674A] The fourth was the example given by Christ, which displayed, as in a mirror, the manner of life that ought to be lived worthily under the Christian name.

The fifth was illumination, by which the Holy Spirit entered the soul, opened the eyes of the heart, and supplied understanding.

The sixth was the grace by which the Holy Spirit worked even within the wills themselves.

They said that the first three were entirely necessary for doing good, while the later three were merely useful. This, apparently, was how they arranged their reasoning.

No one can perform anything worthy of the kingdom of heaven—the inheritance promised to sons and the reward promised to the holy—unless he is a son, a friend of God, and knowledgeable about the commandments. Yet the fathers of the Old Testament did good works worthy of the kingdom of heaven before Christ had provided his example and given the Holy Spirit. Therefore neither Christ’s example nor the operation of the Spirit given by Christ is necessary for doing good, but only advantageous.

Moreover, no one can be said to be equipped with free choice if he does not know what he ought to do and cannot both will and accomplish what is commanded, since free choice is the power to do the good that is commanded and to turn away from the evil that is forbidden. Every believer is commanded to live worthily before God and to attain the inheritance of the children of God.

Fourth, Julianus reduces whatever benefit God has conferred upon human beings through Christ—interpreting, I suppose, the mind he knew the others to possess—to ten headings. For he says (*Book I of the Unfinished Work*, chapter 94):

“We confess the manifold grace of Christ. His first gift is that we have been made from nothing; the second, that just as we are endowed with sensation as living beings, so we surpass beings endowed with sensation by reason, which has been impressed upon the soul so that it might be called the image of the Creator. The freedom granted to free choice likewise pertains to this dignity. We also reckon among the benefits of grace the increases in benefits that it never ceases to bestow upon us.

“The same grace sent the Law as an aid, since it was its function to awaken through manifold instruction and foster by its invitation the light of reason, which examples of depravity and the habit of vice had dulled. The fullness of this grace—that is, of the divine benevolence which gave things their cause—therefore required that the Word become flesh and dwell among us.

“For God, demanding from his image a return of love, made clear how immeasurably he had acted toward us, so that, even if late, we might love in return the one who, commending his love to us, did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us (Romans 8:3). He promised that, if thereafter we wished to obey his will, he would make us coheirs of his only-begotten Son.

“This grace, therefore, not only forgives sins in baptism but also, through the benefit of pardon, elevates, adopts, and consecrates the human being, and so forth.”

After Julianus’s lengthy confession, Augustine complains that one thing had been omitted, by which the confession could have been made convincing. He then adds:

“Pelagian, love wills the good, and love is from God; and it is not through the letter of the Law but through the spirit of grace,” and so forth.

[Col. 0674D] At this point I will not conceal what has often occurred to me: that the Pelagians once held nothing different from the Calvinists of our own time concerning what they call the formal cause of justification. Both agree that people are justified either by the sole imputation of Christ’s righteousness or by the sole remission of sins, with grace and love excluded—grace and love which are poured into their hearts by the Holy Spirit and adhere to them—or else that the grace by which we are justified is merely God’s favor.

The Calvinist position is established by the words of the Council of Trent (*Session 6, canon 11*). The Pelagian position is evident from the fact that they admitted five propositions which are almost the principles of the Calvinist view:

1. Through baptism people become members of Christ, are adopted as children of God, and are thereby appointed coheirs of Christ; indeed, when baptized, they become temples and instruments of the Holy Spirit (*Julianus, Booklet of Faith*, part VI, no. 11; and Augustine, *Book I against Julianus*, chapter 6).

2. We receive the remission of sins because of Christ’s death, since he suffered for sinners as though they themselves had suffered: Rufinus and Pelagius in the passages cited shortly above.

3. People are justified by Christ’s obedience: Pelagius in chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Romans.

4. Both sins are forgiven freely and the Holy Spirit is given freely: Pelagius in the same passage.

5. Although all these things take place in justification, love is nevertheless not poured into our hearts in justification itself, and therefore the inner person is not renewed. Augustine attributes this position to the Pelagians in *Book III of the Unfinished Work*, chapter 108.

Indeed, if they had confessed that this gift was conferred upon people by the Holy Spirit when they are made righteous, they would certainly have acknowledged that free choice by itself is not sufficient to perform works of piety but requires assistance that inheres in the person. For “to inhere” means the same as “to be poured into the hearts,” and it is by this indwelling that the Holy Spirit dwells within the righteous person. They would also have acknowledged that Adam’s sin deprived humanity of the possibility of blessed good, which must be restored through the work of Christ.

They would have perceived these and many other matters that Augustine alone, for the most part, discusses with the Pelagians. For at that time sanctifying grace, distinguished from love and understood as inert in itself, had not yet been conceived.

Sixth, it should be observed that in those early times, when inquiry was being made into the manner in which Christ freed us from the curse of the Law—not merely the Mosaic Law, whose yoke he removed, but any law that threatens violators with eternal destruction—some Catholics, carried away by the heat of their opposition, did not keep within proper limits. They carried the force of right belief so far that they dared to deny that anyone could perish eternally if he died with right faith and, as Ambrose puts it, “clothed with Christ,” no matter what crimes held him bound.

They said that this was precisely what the Apostle intended when he wrote: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us” (Galatians 3:1).

Who these men were, and how eminent they were who held such an opinion, we have shown partly in the notes to Rufinus’s *Faith* (Anathema 1) and partly in the notes to Mercator’s *Commonitorium* (chapter 4). That question was entirely the same as this one: whether Christians who follow the right faith but are sinners should at some point be spared after a suitable purification by fire.

Finally, it should be observed that, during Augustine’s lifetime, nothing concerning the grace of God through Christ was defined either by the Apostolic See or by councils beyond what is contained in the three canons of the African synod cited above. Nevertheless, two questions were debated—not now with the Pelagians on behalf of the faith, but among Catholics, for the sake of understanding: first, the predestination of human beings in Christ; second, the distinction between the grace bestowed upon an innocent nature and that by which fallen nature necessarily has to be assisted. Augustine wrote at length and with equal accuracy on each question: on the first, in Letter 105 (now 194), addressed to Sixtus; on the second, in the book *On Rebuke and Grace*. But since these questions concerned a deeper understanding of grace, they were passed over both by the supreme pontiffs, by the African council, and by Augustine when he identified the principal points of the Pelagian heresy—although in the book *On Heresies* the term “predestination” is used.

## § II. The origins and nature of the questions concerning the grace of God through Christ, insofar as it is called supernatural and assisting grace

Concerning that grace by which God assists human weakness, and which differs from nature, from the law, from adoption as children of God, from the remission of sins, and even from Christ’s example—and indeed from the interior teaching called illumination—the Pelagians raised three principal questions: first, whether some such grace is necessary for doing good and avoiding evil; second, what it accomplishes when it is present, whether it gives the very power to act piously or only facility; third, how it operates in the will, whether merely by inclination or also by acting efficaciously.

As to the first question, the Pelagians thought that human beings possessed from God an innate possibility of either alternative, like a certain fruitful and fertile root which, from the human will, produces and gives birth, and which, according to the choice of its own cultivator, can either shine with the flower of virtues or bristle with the thorns of vices (Pelagius, *On Nature*).

Likewise, as to the second, they thought that God gives human beings his grace so that what they are commanded to do through free choice they may more easily fulfill through grace (Pelagius, ibid.).

Regarding the third, they slandered Catholics as though, under the name of efficacious grace, they were introducing fate. This is sufficiently clear both from the books of the heretics, from the African canons, and from Augustine’s writings—especially the book *On the Grace of Christ*—as well as from Julian’s complaint, whether in the letter to Rufus or in the fourth book of the *Unfinished Work*.

[Col. 0676B] First, it should be observed that the Pelagians believed that the powers of free choice which God the Creator had once given to Adam were daily bestowed by God the Creator upon each human being at birth. For it was practically a fundamental dogma of the Pelagians that infants are born in the condition in which Adam was before he sinned. Therefore, since among Catholics opinions differed concerning the powers of free choice with which an innocent human being was endowed, while the matter—as often happens—had not yet been sufficiently examined, there was also a difference in the way various Catholics fought the Pelagians concerning God’s assistance: Jerome’s approach was easier, Augustine’s more difficult.

Jerome did not posit any distinction—at least not one that he transmitted in his books—between the assistances given to the two conditions. Augustine, however, distinguished them in such a way that he admitted that what the Pelagians asserted concerning the powers of our free choice, at least for overcoming temptations, was true of the first human being. “This was not so,” he said, “in the powers of free choice as they now are—namely, not to depart from God in temptation—as it was in the human being before the fall” (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, [Col. 0676C] ch. 7).

Yet this question concerning the distinction between the assistances was debated not so much between the Pelagians and the Church as within the Churches, by interpreters who examined the mystery with greater curiosity.

Second, it should be observed that careful inquiry was then made into the quality and powers of free choice, and also into the notion of divine justice, human sin, and even the force of the law, since the Pelagians drew from these four matters their arguments against the necessity of the assistance of divine grace. For it seemed to them that either free choice, upon which God’s judgment is established; or the justice of God, which consists entirely in rendering account according to human merits; or the nature of sin, which cannot arise from anywhere except the will; or the holiness of the law, which God himself proclaims—all these would be eliminated if whatever is done piously necessarily had to be done by the interior grace of God.

Several testimonies of Scripture were therefore examined, but especially three which the Pelagians misused [Col. 0676D] to persuade people of their opinion concerning the freedom of choice:

“I have set before you life and death, good and evil; choose life, that you may live” (Deut. 30:14);

and:

“God created human beings from the beginning, and left them in the hand of their own counsel,” etc. (Sirach 15:14);

and:

“If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and do not obey me, the sword shall consume you,” etc. (Isa. 1:19).

It was then debated: first, whether the freedom of choice, both for sinning and for doing good, is a power in such a way that both alternatives equally reside in the innate powers of the human will—what is commonly celebrated as the equilibrium of free choice; second, whether the power to sin is part of freedom and therefore derives its origin from God; third, whether the need for divine grace is incompatible with the freedom of our will—or, as they put it, whether there is free choice if it needs God’s assistance (*On the Proceedings of the Palestinian Synod*, ch. 7); fourth, whether someone who asserts that human beings have nothing of their own except falsehood and sin, and cannot act as they ought unless assisted by him who cannot act wrongly, thereby agrees either with Manichaeus, who dreamed that nature was evil, or with Jovinian, who attributed impeccability to the truly baptized, or even holds an opinion worse than either heretic; fifth, whether every kind of necessity is harmful to freedom; sixth, in a word, by what reasoning the freedom of choice and the necessity of grace can be reconciled. Augustine wrote a separate book on this subject, *On Grace and Free Choice*.

The question concerning divine justice was subsequently examined: first, whether a just God can command an action which a human being lacks the power to perform; second, whether, from the fact that we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ so that each may receive according to his works, it follows that an innate common power exists in all, by which everyone is able to fulfill whatever God, of whatever kind or manner, has either advised or commanded; and thus whether the authority of the one commanding and the proper power of the one obeying are equal, so that what Augustine wrote when addressing God could not be said: “Give what you command, and command what you will”; third, whether sin, which is punished by God, must be so voluntary that neither forgetfulness nor ignorance can be involved in sin, since they occur not according to the will but according to necessity (*On the Proceedings of the Palestinian Synod*, ch. 18); fourth, whether sin can be the punishment of sin, and whether it is a suitable division of sin to distinguish between what is merely sin and what is also the cause of sin.

Finally, the question was examined what power the law possesses for producing good, whether the law implanted in human minds or the law inscribed on tablets—that is, the natural law and the Mosaic law. The Pelagians exalted the law wonderfully; the Catholics lowered it: the former in order to destroy the grace of Christ, the latter in order to establish it.

The Pelagians said that, according to the Apostle, the ancient law, being just, holy, and good, could confer everlasting life upon those who kept its commandments and lived justly by faith, such as the Prophets, Patriarchs, and all the saints (*To Boniface*, book IV, ch. 2). The Catholics replied [Col. 0677C] that the law was being praised against grace through a very cunning choice of words. For it was not that law, although just, holy, and good, which could confer everlasting life upon all those people of God, but the faith that is in Christ. This faith works through love, not according to the letter which kills, but according to the Spirit which gives life. By frightening people concerning transgression, the law leads them to this grace of God like a pedagogue, so that what the law itself could not confer may be conferred upon a person (ibid., ch. 5).

The Pelagians attributed to the law whatever properly belongs to grace. The Catholics warned that the letter of the law must be distinguished from the Spirit: the letter shows what must be done; the Spirit assists in carrying it out.

The Pelagians—something worth noting—fought all the more stubbornly because they seemed to themselves to be speaking more openly in agreement with Chrysostom. The Catholics’ struggle was correspondingly more laborious, because it was less possible to persuade ordinary people of the appropriate distinction, whether between Spirit and letter or between the law of works and the law of faith, since even discerning minds scarcely recognized it. For this reason Augustine composed the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, and so forth.

Third, it should be observed that controversy also arose here concerning: first, faith in Christ; second, the saints of the Old Testament; third, the virtues of the philosophers; fourth, even the works of the Gentiles. The Pelagians maintained that, without faith in Christ, the first human beings before the law, the Jews under the law, and even the Gentiles after the law had performed many good works, either by the assistance of the law alone or by the knowledge of the true God which they had received by nature.

It was also debated: first, whether the law led to the kingdom of heaven in the same way as the Gospel; second, whether the kingdom of God was promised in the Old Testament. From the promise, they said—understanding it as a sending, that is, as the power of leading people to the kingdom of heaven—the heretics drew their conclusion; third, how Christ benefited the people of old; fourth, whether anyone, anywhere or at any time, had attained salvation without faith in Christ. Inquiry was also made, fifth, into the sanctifying power of the ancient sacraments, and whence they possessed it; sixth, whether there had been any sacraments before the law of circumcision. Augustine even thought it necessary to investigate the distinction between the two Testaments and to discuss more subtly the grace of each.

Moreover, because the weakness of the law was shown with respect to perfecting righteousness, the Catholics suffered the following calumnies, as though they were saying: first, that the Holy Spirit had not assisted good minds in ancient times (*To Boniface*, book IV, ch. 2); second, that the law of the Old Testament had not been given in order to justify those who obeyed, but in order to make the cause of sin more serious (*To Boniface*, book III, ch. 2); third, that scarcely anyone could be led to righteousness by reason, and not even by the institution of the sacred law; fourth, that they rejected the Old Testament with Manichaeus, denying that it possessed any power in itself for sanctifying human beings (Julian, cited by Bede, book I *On the Song of Songs*). When the Catholics refuted these four calumnies and the heretics defended them, they generated an equal number of questions.

## § III. Concerning God’s assistance through Christ, in what respect it is grace, or a gratuitous benefit, and in what respect it is called prevenient

After the tractoria of Zosimus and the African canons, the question of the grace of God insofar as it assists our weakness and is therefore called assisting grace died down. Another question revived and burned fiercely, even among the enemies of the Pelagians: concerning God’s assistance in the sense in which it is grace. For Scripture calls it grace, as when the Apostle says: “Unhappy man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24); and: “I labored more abundantly than all; yet not I, but the grace of God with me,” etc. (1 Cor. 15:10).

First, it should be observed that this question was chiefly proposed in four ways: first, whether grace is given on the basis of merits—merits which precede grace, and which must therefore be natural, since nothing except nature precedes grace; second, whether the grace of God precedes human wills, or follows them after they have moved spontaneously; third, in the conversion of a human being, whether the action of God converting the human being to himself precedes, or the action of the human being turning from the world toward God; fourth, what kind of grace God’s grace is: prevenient or subsequent; the guide of free choice or its attendant (Celestius, *Book of Chapters*, ch. 3).

Second, it should be observed that, from the earliest days of the rising heresy, Celestius wrote in his *Book of Chapters* (ch. 3) that God’s grace is given according to our merits, because, if he gives it to sinners, he appears to be unjust. He added these words: “Therefore grace itself has been placed in my will, whether I should become worthy or unworthy. For if we do everything through grace, when we are overcome by sin, it is not we who are overcome but God’s grace, which wished to assist us in every way and was unable.” He says again (*On the Proceedings of the Palestinian Synod*, ch. 14): “If it is God’s grace when we conquer sins, then he himself is at fault when we are conquered by sin, because he either could not or would not preserve us altogether.”

Third, it should be observed that Pelagius did not state an open position on this question either in his commentaries on Paul’s Epistles, in his *Eulogies*, or in his book *On Nature*. At Diospolis, indeed, he condemned the statement of Celestius which had been brought against him and declared that he had never held such a position. Augustine tried to convict him of bad faith in his condemnation and of lying in his declaration, both from what he had said at the synod and from his books *On Free Choice* and his letter to Demetrias.

For how could Pelagius sincerely declare in December 415 that he had never held this position, when in 413 he had written the contrary to Demetrias? After introducing the testimony of the Apostle James, who says, “Submit yourselves to God, and resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7), he explains, he says (*Letter to Demetrias*, ch. 5), how we must resist the devil if we are truly subject to God; and by doing his divine will, we may also merit grace and, with the assistance of the Holy Spirit, resist the wicked spirit more easily.

How could he sincerely have condemned an error which he later revealed that he retained in his mind, in 417, in the books *On Free Choice*, in these words?

“He who runs to God and desires to be governed by God—that is, who hangs his will upon God’s will—who by continually cleaving to him becomes, according to the Apostle, one spirit with him, does this only by the freedom of choice. Whoever uses that freedom well surrenders himself wholly to God and mortifies his entire will, so that he can say with the Apostle: ‘I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me’ (Gal. 2:20). He places his heart in the hand of God, so that God himself may incline it wherever he wills (Prov. 21:1).”

Indeed, he seems to have inadvertently disclosed his mind at the council itself. When it was objected that they asserted that every human being could possess all virtues and graces, and removed the diversity of graces which the Apostle teaches, we replied—though they maliciously and incompetently criticized us—“We do not remove the diversity of graces; we say that God grants all graces to the one who is worthy to receive them, just as he granted them to the Apostle Paul.”

Augustine’s arguments, however, may perhaps not persuade everyone. In the last passage he understood the word “worthy” as though it signified some preceding merit of work or deed, although it could in some way be taken to mean one whom God had deigned to favor with graces, without any unusual use of the word, whether among the Fathers of that period or in Augustine himself. Nor should the conjecture seem far-fetched, since Pelagius answered the Greek judges in Greek and may appear to have used the word ἀξιοῦσθαι (*axiousthai*), which can mean either “to be adorned” or “to be generously endowed with dignity by another.”

In the earlier passage, Augustine thought that a favorable interpretation could be applied, the one he himself supplied (*On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 22), as though Pelagius had said: “By doing the divine will of God we may merit grace, just as grace is added to believers who live piously, by which they may resist the tempter courageously,” even though they had initially also received grace in order to do God’s will. Since he distrusted this testimony, Augustine added another, although that passage too could tolerate the same interpretation if it were not otherwise clear what the Pelagians commonly thought concerning the power of free choice.

Pelagius therefore appears to have concealed his mind on this matter, whether because he was more timid or more cunning than Celestius, on account of the unpopularity it might bring him, and to have used ambiguous words by which, as Jerome says (*Letter to Ctesiphon*), “he would say one thing in private to his disciples and another openly before the people.”

Fourth, it should be observed that, although this controversy arose together with the heresy, it became more fiercely inflamed only after the African canons had been established, and therefore after the year 418. For if matters had stood otherwise, Augustine would not have failed to explain, in the canons he composed, the Church’s position on a question which he later considered as important as this one, when he called it the most pernicious of all dogmas. Yet I hesitate to adhere too strongly even to this otherwise plausible reasoning, chiefly because there may have been another just reason for Augustine’s silence: namely, that he knew very well that not all Catholics were yet sufficiently convinced of the entire mystery of gratuitous predestination and of the hidden calling according to God’s purpose—a mystery which Augustine himself had not understood before becoming a bishop.

The question therefore arose together with the heresy, but its danger was not immediately recognized. Indeed, for a long time it deceived many people, including men of great reputation, and, if we believe some, even Jerome. This is nevertheless surprising, since in his first work against Pelagius (*Letter to Ctesiphon*) he so expressly and gravely cites Paul’s testimony by which Augustine confesses that he himself was recalled from error: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

Fifth, it should be observed that this error, as I have said, flowed both from a false notion of divine justice—as though it excluded all grace—and from a perverse interpretation of the Apostle’s statements: “There is no injustice with God” (Rom. 9:14); and, “There is no partiality with God” (Rom. 2:11). They understood it as though to bestow unequal benefits upon equals were to show partiality, and as though this were the very vice which God forbids human beings (Deut. 1:17), and which he would not wish to express in his own actions as examples set before us for imitation. How this presumed opinion drove Origen headlong into his delusions, deceived eminent men, and gave birth to the error later called Semi-Pelagianism, we have shown in the notes to Rufinus’s *Confession of Faith*.

Sixth, it should be observed that Catholics and Pelagians agreed that some necessary beginning of good action is freely bestowed upon human beings by God, whether it effects action, as they say, physically, or whether it acts morally and gives the action value and dignity. They differed, however, in that the Pelagians did not distinguish this efficient principle from nature, from the innate powers of free choice, or from the law; whereas the Catholics asserted that something different from all three is diffused in our hearts by the Holy Spirit.

They likewise agreed that the principle from which an action receives its value, and the dignity equal to the kingdom of heaven—the power they call meritorious—is itself the grace of adoption and reconciliation, by which we become children and friends of God. But they differed in this very point: the Pelagians thought that this entire grace—by which I mean adoption and the remission of sins—was merely God’s favor; the Catholics held that it consisted in inherent righteousness and charity, by which God truly makes us righteous and lovers of himself.

There was not, however, one unanimous opinion among the Pelagians concerning the forgiveness of sins which God grants to the penitent. Pelagius himself consistently asserted that sins are forgiven freely (*Commentary on Romans*, ch. 5). Celestius, by contrast, said that forgiveness is not given to the penitent according to the grace and mercy of God, but according to the merits and labor of those who, through repentance, have become worthy of mercy (*On the Proceedings of the Palestinian Synod*, ch. 18).

I have said that Pelagius consistently remained in this position. I cannot agree with the very learned Petavius, who accuses Pelagius of inconsistency on this point (vol. III, *On Dogmas*, book *On the Pelagian Heresy*, ch. 3). He clearly taught the same thing in 402, in his commentary on Romans 5; in 410 or 411, in the book *On Nature*; in 415, if we believe Augustine, at the Palestinian synod; and in 417 or 418, before Albina, Pinianus, and Melania in Palestine, who urged him to acknowledge grace. “Anathema,” he said (*On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 1), “to whoever thinks or says that the grace of God, through which Christ came into this world to save sinners, is not necessary not only at every hour or every moment, but also in each of our acts; and may those who try to take it away receive eternal punishment.”

Add to this that Augustine acknowledges this to have been Pelagius’s position in both books against Julian, and thus in 422 and 428, and in the book *On Grace and Free Choice* in 424. Indeed, he recognizes it everywhere as the distinctive position of the Pelagians, so that Celestius’s opinion must evidently not have pleased his associates.

Nevertheless, Petavius correctly observed that it is by no means easy to understand how Pelagius, if he wished to write coherently, could have said that sins are forgiven freely, since he believed that no one is justified except by faith, yet did not wish faith to be given by God, but held that it arose from free choice. Whether he spoke inconsistently is a question for another place. In the position I have mentioned (*ibid.*, nos. 3 and 5), he certainly remained consistent, and it is not difficult to answer Petavius’s arguments from the chronology of the works cited above.

Seventh, it should be observed that among those who wanted free choice to precede the operation of the Holy Spirit, and who said that something on the human side precedes grace, there was not one common opinion. Some maintained that this always occurs, as did the Massilians; others, only sometimes, as did Cassian. The former may be called the stricter, the latter the milder, Semi-Pelagians.

Furthermore, some held that works themselves precede grace; others, only faith and prayer; still others, something less than faith—namely, an inclination to believe, an effort to rise, or something similar. Although these errors were condemned much later by the Council of Orange in 529, they had already arisen in Augustine’s time, partly in Africa and partly in Gaul, as is clear both from Augustine’s letter to Vitalis and his books addressed to the monks of Adrumetum, and from the letters of the Gauls Prosper and Hilary to Augustine.

Eighth, it should be observed that from the error that grace is given on the basis of merits many consequences were drawn, whether by the Pelagians themselves or by the remnants of the Pelagians, and that as many questions arose from them: first, that grace is placed in each person’s power, provided that he becomes worthy or unworthy; second, that every human being can possess all virtues and graces; third, that Christ was made God as the reward of merits, works, and labors; fourth, that no one can, by merit, begrudge Christ his dignity, since anyone can be what Christ is, provided that he is equally willing to strive; fifth, that infants themselves attain the grace of adoption in baptism on the basis of merits, whether past merits in another life, present merits—as though they themselves believe—or future merits foreseen by God; sixth, that either not all predestination is grace, or none of it is grace, but all or almost all of it is justice; seventh, that there is no calling according to God’s purpose, and so forth.

# CHAPTER VI. The words of Saint Jerome concerning the leaders of the Pelagian heresy are examined, as they appear to conflict with the opinion of Marius Mercator

Thus far we have woven together the history of the heresy itself and of its dogmas—or rather, of its questions—and at the same time, I think, have clearly shown both how one question produced a monstrous multitude of others and how rightly Mercator wrote that the entire sum of the foolish and, still more, impious labor of Julian could be reduced to one perverse proposition: “THEY SAY THAT THE TRANSGRESSION OF ADAM AND EVE DID NOT MAKE THEM MORTAL” (*Preface to the Book of Subnotations*).

Next we must say something which may seem to remain from the first dissertation, concerning the inventors of the heresy and the earliest leaders of Pelagius, as Jerome calls them. From this it will likewise become clear what Mercator reports: that Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, was the first to raise this question against the Catholic faith (ibid.).

For, as has been pointed out more than once, when Mercator writes in this way, men otherwise of great reputation seem to be in conflict—especially Jerome himself. Turning his address to Pelagius, he says (*Letter to Ctesiphon*): “I shall briefly set out the names of your leaders and associates, so that you may notice the sort of company in which you glory.”

“Manichaeus says that his elect, among whom he places Plato’s souls in heavenly regions, are entirely free from sin and cannot sin even if they wish to. For they have risen to such heights of virtue that they mock the works of the flesh. Priscillianus, a branch of Manichaeus in Spain, says the same thing. His disciples are especially devoted to you because of his obscenity, rashly claiming for themselves the word of perfection and knowledge; they shut themselves up alone with women, and so forth.

“You share a part in the Gnostic heresy derived from the impiety of Basilides. Hence you also assert that those who are without knowledge of the law cannot avoid sins.”

A little later he says: “Do you still wish to know another leader of your error? Your teaching is a little branch of Origen’s, and so forth. Nor should you be ashamed of association with such men, while rejecting the names of those whose blasphemies you share. The second question of Jovinian is the discipline of your own ingenuity,” and so forth.

It is worth briefly investigating these words of Jerome concerning Origen, Manichaeus, and Jovinian, which more recent writers habitually seize upon without examination—not only because this investigation contributes to the history for which we are publishing the materials, but also because of the place in which we now stand and the defense of Mercator that we have undertaken. It may be that truth suffers some harm from the prejudice of popular opinion; if not, at least the darkness in which it is enveloped may be dispersed.

The period of the people under discussion prescribes the order of the inquiry. We should therefore begin with Origen, since he is the oldest of the three. The bishop of Hippo was mistaken in memory when he made Manichaeus older than Origen, since Manichaeus was in fact about thirty years younger.

## § I. Concerning Origen and the Origenists, such as Evagrius Ponticus, Palladius of Galatia, and others

When it is asked whether the doctrine of the Pelagians arose from that of Origen, I think the question can, and indeed must, be understood in three ways.

First, it is asked whether Origen once taught the condemned dogma which the Pelagians later taught. Second, whether the dogmas which Origen and the Pelagians commonly followed were received by the Pelagians from Origen’s books. Third, whether the defenders of the Pelagian heresies learned from the Origenists—if not from books, at least through speech and tradition—the doctrines which they later collected, as it were, into one body of teaching and spread throughout almost the entire world.

Jansenius of Ypres answers the question understood in these three ways (*On the Pelagian Heresy*, chs. 13 and following). First, he asserts that Pelagius taught nothing different—apart from one exception—from what Origen had taught nearly two hundred years earlier. Second, he says that Pelagius drew all his dogmas chiefly from two of Origen’s works: the commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans and the books *On First Principles* (*Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*). Third, he says that Pelagius learned the mysteries of the sect from Evagrius Ponticus, Palladius of Galatia, and the Origenist monks, partly in Egypt and partly in Palestine.

He establishes the first part of his assertion (ibid.) by comparing the dogmas which each author taught concerning free choice and its natural power, the law of nature and of Moses, grace and merit, divine predestination, and so forth. He easily proves the second by citing testimonies from both of Origen’s works, whose very words the Pelagians used in explaining their error.

Relying on his own authority, he affirms the third and says (ch. 17): “Since many of them—the Pelagians and Massilians—pursued the perfection of religious life as monks, they lived among the Origenist monks in Egypt and Palestine. Having drawn their errors from Evagrius Ponticus, Palladius of Galatia, and similar associates, they themselves became leaders for the others in their descent into ruin.”

From all this, he says, one can see how correctly Saint Jerome calls Origen the “darling” (*amasium*) and ἀρχαῖος (*archaios*) of the Pelagians—that is, the author of the books *On First Principles*, their teacher, and Pelagius’s doctrine a little branch of Origen.

Whether Jerome is rightly summoned as a witness, and with what learning Origen is thought to have been called ἀρχαῖος because he wrote the books *On First Principles*, or “friend” of the Pelagians because the Pelagians loved him, let him—or anyone else who wishes—see to it. Certainly learned men think otherwise.

I admit that Origen wrote against the faith of the Church that free choice possesses as much power as is sufficient, together with the mere revelation of truth or the assistance of the law, to believe in God and to merit that grace by which it may then be assisted in performing works of piety. I also do not deny that he thought the predestination of the saints belonged to justice, but not likewise to grace.

Nevertheless, I maintain that on both matters he differed greatly from the Pelagians, and agreed only with the people of Adrumetum or the Massilians. For concerning the inability of nature to fulfill the duties of Christian piety and attain salvation, he spoke so openly that no one who has read even his works superficially could hold him guilty of agreement with the Pelagians.

As is well known, the Pelagians denied that, in order to fulfill righteousness, overcome temptations, rise from sin, persevere in the good, and attain salvation, the grace called “of the will”—that is, interior grace—was necessary. They held that only the use of free choice was necessary, so that whatever a person could do by himself, even if sometimes with difficulty, he might accomplish with the assistance of grace more pleasantly and easily.

Origen taught quite differently, and did so in more than one place. I shall offer a few passages from many, together with the learned author of the Origenist collection (vol. I of Origen’s works, book II, *Origenist Questions*, question 7).

When Origen had mentioned Peter’s fall because of his overconfidence, he said (*Treatise 35 on Matthew*): “Through this we are instructed never to promise anything without reflection, beyond our human condition—as though we were able, from ourselves, to fulfill the confession of Christ or any of God’s commandments.”

And elsewhere (*Homily 4 on Psalm 36*): “You see, therefore, that we always need the Lord’s assistance: first, lest we fall; then, even if we have fallen, so that we may rise again.”

Again (*On Psalm 4*): “We must now say what good things are ἀπροαίρετα (*aproaireta*), that is, independent of choice, since this statement is true: ‘Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain’; and, ‘Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain’ (Ps. 126:1). Whoever advances builds a house; whoever is perfect guards a city. But the work of the builder is vain, and the watch of the guardian vain, unless the Lord builds and the Lord guards.

“Good will be outside our free choice: the virtue of the Lord, which assists and helps the building of the builder, and builds together with him who cannot complete the building by himself.”

A little later he says: “Therefore our will, together with divine assistance, which insofar as it concerns us is not arbitrary, is necessary not only for someone to become honorable and good, but also for one who has become honorable and good to persevere in virtue. For even a perfect person is about to fall into ruin if, having become proud in his uprightness, he claims this as his own achievement and does not render the due glory to him who contributed far more to acquiring and retaining it,” and so forth.

But, as the proverb says, I would only be doing what has already been done if I lingered longer on this point. I ask the reader who loves sincere truth to consult the passage from the Origenist collection which I cited. From it, no doubt, he will derive no less pleasure than usefulness, as truth reveals itself—truth which, against its will, had been oppressed by the foreign darkness of prejudices.

I shall mention only one matter which the learned man omitted. The Pelagians did indeed agree with Origen in certain respects, but they could not have borrowed anything from him deliberately, since they not only rejected him but also pursued him with deadly hatred, and whenever they could, heaped personal abuse upon him.

It is recorded that Theodore of Mopsuestia sharpened his pen against Origen as a corrupter of Scripture. Rufinus the Syrian impiously and abominably called him a fool who had followed the madness of certain people deceived by an error of mind (no. 17), impious and ignorant of divine Scripture (no. 19), teaching it without understanding (no. 23), and so forth. Pelagius treated “being an Origenist” as equivalent to a charge deserving anathema (ibid.).

The Pelagians commonly, whenever an opportunity arose (*On the Proceedings of the Palestinian Synod*, [Col. 0683D] ch. 2), condemned in their confessions of faith Origen’s doctrines concerning the pre-existence of souls, the necessity of the creation of the world for God, the animation and significance of the stars, original sin, the impeccability of the perfect, the impossibility of conversion for the wicked, the temporality either of punishments or of blessedness, the nature of the bodies that will rise, and other matters of this kind, calling them ignorant, mad, impious, abominable, and accursed.

And where is the “darling”?

Nevertheless, I do not deny that all the Pelagians read Origen, who was the most celebrated of interpreters of Scripture, and read him in the language in which he wrote, since they both affected a reputation for expertise in handling the Scriptures, and no Latin of this sect was without knowledge of Greek—or at least wished to appear to possess it. Pelagius certainly, if we believe Augustine, used the Greek language at the synod of Palestine. Caelestius, having spent a long time in the East—teaching [Col. 0684A] at Ephesus and Rhodes, managing the affairs of his faction at Constantinople, and conferring with Theodore at Mopsuestia—was, I believe, speaking Greek, since Easterners despised the Latin language in comparison with their own. Julian, besides being involved with Caelestius in the same business dealings and conferences, and having made Rufinus’s Latin his own authority, boasted of his reading of the Greeks to such an extent that he wished to make his doctrine acceptable to Easterners. Finally, Annianus left to posterity proof of what he knew of Greek in his translations of Chrysostom’s homilies.

I contend only this: that Origen differed very greatly from the Pelagians, even in the matter in which he is commonly said to have agreed with them—namely, concerning ἀπάθεια (*apatheia*, freedom from passions), ἀναμαρτησία (*anamartesia*, freedom from sin), and the powers of nature for soliciting divine grace.

For Origen attributed sinlessness solely to the aids of grace, through which a certain highest degree of perfection could be attained; they attributed it solely to the powers of nature, to which it would indeed be desirable that divine help be joined, but would not be necessary.

[Col. 0684B] Origen held that the powers of nature were sufficient merely for believing God when He promised gifts, and for restraining oneself amid temptations by knowledge of the law and love of what is right; they held them sufficient also for perfecting either faith or righteousness.
