Origen taught that no one could enter the kingdom of God without the true grace of Christ, an inward grace and not merely an external favor of God; they taught that many could enter without it.

At the beginning I acknowledged what is plainly true: that Origen, concerning grace as following upon free will, appeared to have written what the presbyters of Massilia defended nearly two hundred years later. Yet I can scarcely be brought to believe that the Massilians derived from Origen’s books their own doctrine, which pleased the bishop of Ypres, especially from his *Commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans* and from the books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*).

For who would assert that what is said to have been drawn from the *Commentaries* was taken from Origen himself, and not rather from Rufinus—if he notices what no learned person is unaware, namely, that the *Commentaries* in question were [Col. 0684C] translated into Latin by Rufinus? Because of the many things either explained or supplied, many people of that age believed that they ought to be called Rufinus’s rather than Origen’s; nor would Rufinus himself strongly resist those who held this opinion, and he would have adopted the entire work, had he not considered it envious and full of arrogance to assume for himself, as he says, so great an honor.

On this subject one should read both his preface, where he states what he was asked to do, and his conclusion, where he openly confesses how much he added from himself. “They say,” he writes, “in what you write, since a great deal of your own work is contained in it, ‘Give it the title of your name and write: *Jerome’s*”—read *Rufinus’s*—“books of explanations of the Epistle to the Romans. For, they say, among secular authors too, the title bears the name not of the one whose work has been translated from Greek, but of the one who translated it.’ But they grant all this to me, not out of love for me, but out of hatred for the author. Yet I, who defer more to my conscience than to my name, even if I seem to add certain things, fill out what is lacking, or shorten what is lengthy, do not think it right to steal the title [Col. 0684D] from him who laid the foundation of the work and supplied the material for constructing the building. Let it be in the reader’s discretion, once he has approved the work, to ascribe the merit of the work to whomever he wishes.”

He had written earlier: “Although there was no lack of very great labor in the other parts as well, while we wished to supply what Origen had delivered extemporaneously in the assembly of the Church, with the intention not so much of exposition as of edification, etc. We undertook the labor of completing what was lacking so that questions that had been raised and left unresolved—for this often happens with him because of his homiletic manner of speaking—would not produce weariness for the Latin reader, etc.”

I believe the same judgment should be made concerning the books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*. For the work in the form in which we now possess it has been interpolated by Rufinus in many places, especially in those dealing with the question under discussion. One example, among many, and a particularly conspicuous one, will suffice. In Book III [Col. 0685A] of *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, chapter 1, Origen had discussed free will; and that entire discussion was translated word for word in chapter 21 of the *Philocalia*. Yet that chapter does not contain the following words, which must have been inserted by Rufinus:

“God wished to expose excuses of this kind for such complaints, and to show that it is not the concealment of divine providence but the choice of the human mind that becomes the cause of its own destruction. He also bestowed the graces of His beneficence upon the unworthy and unbelieving, so that truly every mouth might be stopped, and the human mind might recognize that everything comes from itself and nothing from God.”

These words, I say, are not contained in the *Philocalia*, although the sequence of the discourse is preserved there; indeed, it is far more suitable without this addition by Rufinus.

Since these things are so, and since the doctrine contained in the books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* may, indeed ought, with good reason to be called Rufinus’s rather than Origen’s—unless it is clearly transmitted elsewhere, a point I do not obstinately deny—it cannot immediately be said, merely because the Massilians made progress from the books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, that they made progress from Origen.

[Col. 0685B] Yet I do not think that they took their opinion even from the books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*. For, if we believe Prosper, this error had become widespread in Gaul before those books were brought there. They did not come to the West before the time of Anastasius, as Jerome relates; and yet Prosper and Hilary say that this opinion is found in the works of earlier interpreters.

“From whom, then,” you will ask, “did the Massilians of that period imbibe their poison?” What if someone were to answer that they imbibed it from books written by Augustine before his episcopate? For he himself admits that at that time he was entangled in the same error and disclosed it in his books. It is credible—indeed certain, given the fame of the man celebrated throughout the world and the proximity of Spain, where they were read, as Augustine testifies (*On Predestination*, 35, chapter 3)—that those books were brought into Gaul.

[Col. 0685C] Or perhaps someone else might say that Augustine himself received the cause of his error from the books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*. But how could that have happened, when he had neither read the Greek works himself nor been able at that time to see them translated into Latin? He was ordained bishop in the year 395, the eleventh year of Siricius; yet Rufinus did not return to the West with his ship full of blasphemies until after Anastasius had succeeded Siricius.

It would be more plausible for someone to conjecture that the Massilians learned from Cassian, Cassian from Chrysostom, and Chrysostom from certain earlier interpreters of Scripture, to whom God had not yet revealed the most obscure mystery of grace. For a certain preconceived opinion of divine justice had generally taken root in their minds: they believed that God would be a respecter of persons if He gave grace neither to those who asked nor to those who willed it; if He loved one person more than others whose condition was the same; or if election arose from foreknowledge rather than foreknowledge from election, and so forth.

[Col. 0685D] Although Cassian himself, when he taught that in the matter of salvation grace sometimes claimed the first place and sometimes free will, had begun to undermine the foundation of this general opinion, he still could not reach the whole truth which God wished to disclose through Augustine, because part of the old prejudice remained in force.

[Col. 0686A] But it is now time to discuss what the bishop of Ypres wrote: that the Pelagians had drawn their poison from Origenist monks, from Evagrius Ponticus, and from Palladius of Galatia. Since the same case applies to Evagrius as to Palladius—for Evagrius is said to have been Palladius’s teacher—it will be enough to speak of Palladius. But from which Palladius did Pelagius receive the doctrine handed down orally? For we know that three men of that name existed at that time, all either Galatians or not far removed from Galatia: namely, the Helenopolitan of Bithynia, the author of the *Lausiac History*, who adhered to Chrysostom and fled to Rome in 404 when Atticus was persecuting him; another Helenopolitan, of Palestine, who converses with Theodore, a deacon of the Roman Church, in a dialogue on the life of Chrysostom; and a third, the accuser of Jerome, whom Jerome charges with servile wickedness and with the heresy of a revived ἀπάθεια. Baronius, confusing his memory, reports that this man came to Rome on Pelagius’s behalf in 417. Which of the three could have taught Pelagius at Rome? For the popular story of Pelagius’s journey to Egypt and the East before he came to Rome has, I believe, been plainly disproved.

Which Palladius, I ask, was Pelagius’s instructor? The first? Pelagius could indeed have seen him at Rome, as the chronology shows; but he could not have been taught his errors by him first, since Palladius came to the City in 404, whereas Pelagius had already completed his book *On Actual Conduct*, in which those errors are contained.

Was it, then, the other interlocutor in the dialogue? But when that man came to Rome, after the city’s siege, he could not have met Pelagius, who had fled before the siege. And even if we grant that he could have met him, Pelagius could not have been instructed by him in this way, since he had gathered disciples long before that time.

[Col. 0686B] Or, finally, was it the third? But he was rather Pelagius’s disciple than his teacher, since he did not know Pelagius until Pelagius had come to Palestine, after the errors had been spread through Italy and Sicily.

Nevertheless, something that cannot be denied creates a difficulty—and not a slight one—in the authority of Jerome, when he teaches that the heresy of ἀπάθεια was propagated by Origen, and that Evagrius Ponticus, the teacher of Palladius, preceded Pelagius. From this it appears that Pelagius learned from Origen, Evagrius, and Palladius the doctrines of the Origenists. But to precede is one thing, to teach another; ἀπάθεια itself, or ἀναμαρτησία, is one thing, and the method of attaining the degree at which a person is never disturbed by any thought of vice is another. Jerome defines ἀπάθεια in this latter sense. In proclaiming ἀπάθεια, Origen and Evagrius Ponticus did indeed precede Pelagius; they did not hand down the doctrine to him. Otherwise the two would have had the same understanding of the manner of acquiring ἀπάθεια, whereas in fact one differs greatly from the other.

[Col. 0686C] It is not difficult to demonstrate this. Until now, no one has imagined that it is possible to arrive at the summit of the virtues just described except in five ways: either by the powers of nature alone, without any assistance of grace; or by the powers of nature, aided by inward grace so as to rise more easily; or by the efforts and, as it were, aspirations of nature, promoted by grace, without which perfection may indeed be desired but cannot be possessed; or by the powers of grace alone, which both precedes and arouses the wills, but is not some singular benefit granted to only a few; or finally by the powers of grace alone, but of a certain exceptional grace granted either only to the Mother of God or perhaps also to John the Baptist and the holy apostles.

The pagans followed the first method, together with the philosopher Xystus, whose work Rufinus falsely attributed to the martyr Sixtus. Pelagius and his followers followed the second; Origen the third; certain others, whose error Augustine considers tolerable, the fourth; and the faithful generally the fifth. Thus all agree in defending ἀναμαρτησία, but each proposes a different method of acquiring it; and Origen is farther from Pelagius than Pelagius is from Xystus.

[Col. 0686D] From what has been established in this discussion, it is plainly evident that Origen had indeed thought, many years earlier, what the Massilians—at least the stricter among them—thought, but not what Pelagius thought, since Pelagius differed from the Massilians, as they say, “by the whole heavens.” It is also evident that the Pelagians themselves did not learn from Origen, nor did the Massilians. The former oppose Origen in explaining the powers of free will with respect to works of piety; the latter neither saw Origen’s books nor were Origenists.

## § II. On Manichaeus, Priscillian, the Messalians or Euchites, and the Enthusiasts

[Col. 0687A] It is certainly astonishing that Jerome calls Manichaeus and Priscillian, along with others, Pelagius’s leaders, when he himself testifies that the name “Manichaeans” was attached to Catholics by Pelagius, and Julian openly charged Augustine with disguising Priscillian’s fate under the name of efficacious grace. How can opinions that contradict one another agree in one and the same position?

I admit that Augustine once reproached Julian for the ways in which Manichaeism assisted his doctrines; but I do not remember reading that Augustine ever wrote that Julian had learned those doctrines themselves from Manichaeus.

It is therefore reasonable to suppose that when Jerome called Manichaeus Pelagius’s leader, or teacher, he intended only this: since he was an accuser of errors no less than of morals, he meant that Pelagius, like Manichaeus, recognized certain ἀναμάρτητοι (*anamartetoi*, sinless persons), who could safely associate with women and, although they loved them and boasted that they had no desire, even when surrounded by companies of virgins. He therefore charged them not so much with a fellowship of doctrine as with a fellowship of morals, knowing that there was the greatest difference between the doctrines of the two heretics, but none in their morals; and understanding that both had arrived at the same destination of disgrace by different roads. On this subject it is worth reading what Jerome wrote about the “Amazonian women” of the Pelagians, either in his letter to Ctesiphon or in his dialogues, since those writings make what we have said perfectly clear.

[Col. 0687B] Four questions arise here. The first is why Manichaeism was turned into an accusation against Catholics, and especially against Augustine, under whose leadership the Catholics were fighting. I believe this happened for seven reasons:

1. Because Catholics asserted original sin, whereas the Pelagians preferred to call it natural.

2. Because of the manner in which sin was transmitted—by propagation from Adam to his descendants—so that Catholics appeared to condemn marriage and the intercourse of man and woman itself.

3. Because they defended the necessity of having contracted sin through Adam’s sin, and of the nature of his descendants having been made sinful until it was healed.

4. Because Catholics said that the flesh of us all is the flesh of sin, whereas Christ came only in the likeness of the flesh of sin; by saying this, they appeared to deny that Christ’s flesh was consubstantial with ours.

5. Because they said that individual human beings are born under the power of the devil and remain so until they are reborn in Christ.

6. Because they diminished the force of the law, exalted faith against it, and commended the grace of Christ, as though the Old Testament were thereby rejected and the patriarchs slandered.

7. Because of the gratuitous election of some rather than others, by which a twofold mass of human beings seemed to be established, one powerless for evil and the other powerless for good.

These were the seven doctrines of the Manichaeans, made all the more odious at that time because the sectarians were plunging into greater moral depravity. The Pelagians dared, with the utmost impudence, to call the Catholics—and even Augustine himself—suspect of, or actually guilty of, this. For that reason Julian called Augustine the Epicurus of his age, the violator of the Church and corrupter of morals.

[Col. 0687D] The matters I have mentioned are established partly from Caelestius’s letter to the Roman clergy, and partly from the books of Theodore, Julian, and Annianus.

Caelestius writes (*In Augustine, Book I to Boniface*, chapters 2 and 5):

> “Those Manichaeans”—with whom we now have no fellowship, that is, all those with whom we disagree—“say that through the sin of the first man, that is, Adam, free will perished, and that no one now has the power to live well, but that all are compelled by the necessity of their flesh to sin. They also say that the marriages now being contracted were not instituted by God; they say that the movement of the sexual organs and the intercourse of married persons were invented by the devil, and therefore that infants who are born are guilty and are made by the devil, not by God, because they are born from this devilish intercourse. This is unquestionably Manichaean.”

[Col. 0688A] Theodore, in Photius (*Codex* 277), writes:

> “They say that not even Christ, having assumed a sinful nature, is free from crime; although in their other blasphemies too one may observe that they attribute human nature to Him not truly and by nature, but only figuratively.”

Julian makes the same point throughout almost all the pages of his works, but most shamelessly when he extracts from a fictitious letter of Manes to his daughter Menoch what he can cast against Augustine as something related to it:

> “Listen now,” he says (*Imperfect Work*, Book III, chapter 17), “and recognize what your father writes to a certain daughter of his, your sister, etc.”

Annianus writes in the letter to Orontius prefixed to his homily on Matthew by Chrysostom:

> “What does he impress upon human beings more strongly than the nobility of their nature, which is praised, by the unanimous agreement and harmony of all right-minded people, against the madness of Manichaeus? What, I ask, does he commend more insistently than the glory of the freedom implanted in us by God, the acknowledgment of which is the chief distinction between us and the pagans? What does he press upon us against those same teachers more strongly than that God’s commandments are possible, and that man is capable of every virtue commanded or urged by God?”

[Col. 0688B] The second question is whether all the Pelagians generally brought against Catholics the charge of Manichaeism, and at what time each did so, and which of them was first. The answer is plainly established by what has just been presented: Annianus, Julian, and Caelestius made this accusation after the year 418, but they learned it from their teacher, whom Jerome addresses in his letter to Ctesiphon with these words:

> “You will cry out and say that we follow the doctrine of the Manichaeans and of those who construct wars against the Church from different natures, asserting that the nature which cannot in any way be changed is evil, etc.”

The same point is relevant to what appears in the Commentaries written in the year 402 (*On Chapter XV of the First Epistle to the Corinthians*), concerning the error of the Manichaeans and Apollinarists regarding the nature of each Adam. For the Pelagians were accustomed to reproach Catholics for not attributing to Christ true flesh consubstantial with ours, since they said that ours was the flesh of sin, but that Christ possessed the likeness of the flesh of sin. They had learned this impudent and unjust reproach [Col. 0687C] from Theodore of Mopsuestia, as is evident from the words cited shortly above.

[Col. 0688C] The third question is why Augustine drove away this accusation so carefully and laboriously whenever an occasion arose. I believe there were four reasons. First, the accusation had some appearance of truth, at least to simpler people, because of the assertion of original sin and of the corruption of the human race resulting from it. Second, at that time no name was more hateful than that of the Manichaeans, because of the imperial laws against them and the sect’s abominable crimes. Third, Julian pressed this point with all the force of eloquence at his command, portraying the defenders of original sin, through rhetorical embellishment, as worse than the Manichaeans. Finally—and this was a singular consideration—there might arise a suspicion that some remnant of his former error, in which he had once admitted that he was entangled, still clung to Augustine; this would have been all the more damaging to the Catholic cause because Augustine surpassed the other defenders of the faith.

[Col. 0688D] The fourth question—how Augustine either defended himself against the accusation by the agreement of the saints, or defended the saints and the faith of the Church through the testimonies and tradition of Scripture, or demonstrated that the errors of the Manichaeans were supported by the opinions of the Pelagians—is easily resolved. Anyone can see what answer must be brought forward in the works written on this matter: namely, the two books *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, the four books to Boniface, the six books against Julian, and the *Imperfect Work*, in which that outstanding defender of the Church died. These works would virtually have to be copied in their entirety if the battle were to be fought with the testimonies in their explicit and complete wording.

Moreover, what Jerome said about the Pelagians’ fellowship with the Manichaeans in the doctrine of sinlessness and the moral filth that followed from it should properly be understood also of their kinship with the Messalians, the Enthusiasts, and the Euchites. For there could have been no other relationship, nor was any other one in fact alleged by Jerome.

[Col. 0689A] Near the end, it is useful to observe that Orosius (*Apology*, chapter 1), following the example of his teacher Jerome, also charged the Pelagians with agreement with Origen, Priscillian, and Jovinian—an agreement so complete that those ancient heretics, though long dead, still lived in these men, and even spoke through them. For he says:

> “This abhorrence of the most poisonous doctrines still has living dead men and dead living men. For Origen, Priscillian, and Jovinian, once dead in themselves, live in these men; and they not only live but also speak. But now Pelagius and Caelestius, if they persist in these things, behold them—living dead men—against the Church, which is grievous, and, what is much more grievous, openly hissing within the Church, etc.”

Taking occasion from the words of Orosius that I have quoted, I will frankly state what I remember having pointed out once before: where the popular belief arose concerning the first name Aurelius, which is attributed to Augustine. It seems to have arisen from Orosius’s preceding words, because readers did not consider them carefully and scribes did not punctuate them as they should have. [Col. 0689B] They read as follows:

> “It is the will and ordinance of God that the evil which had been tolerated through patience should necessarily be exposed, and that, through the conflict of fury, those receiving the reward of their error that they deserved should not merely bring about the designation of the worst doctrines, but also the disclosure of the persons who must be corrected. For the Fathers, and those martyrs and confessors who have now found rest—Cyprian, Hilary, and Ambrose—and those who even now must remain in the flesh, who are the pillars and foundations of the Catholic Church—Aurelius, Augustine, and Jerome—have already published many highly approved writings against this wicked heresy, without naming the heretics. Although this abhorrence of the most poisonous doctrines, etc.”

[Col. 0689C] Since Orosius contrasts three living men with the three pillars of the Church who had died, copyists, through carelessness, believed that only Augustine and Jerome were being contrasted, and thus fused Aurelius and Augustine into one person. They did so because they thought that only those two had written against the Pelagians and did not remember either the Council of Carthage, at which the judgment of Caelestius had been instituted, or Aurelius’s place among ecclesiastical writers.

“But when,” you will ask, “did this opinion, which is found in many manuscripts, become widespread?” I confess that I can scarcely conjecture, unless perhaps it should be referred to the time of Aurelius Cassiodorus. The conjecture could be strengthened, weakened, or confirmed by collating ancient manuscripts.

## § III. On Jovinian

[Col. 0689D] When Pelagius defended his ἀναμαρτησία, Jerome charged him with being in this respect the successor and heir of Jovinian and with reviving a condemned heresy, whether he did so unwittingly through ignorance or knowingly through impudence. Whether the holy doctor made this charge rightly or wrongly is worth investigating, partly because the purpose of the present dissertation requires it, and partly—and especially—because some accuse Jerome as though he had not sufficiently understood the mind of either heretic, namely Jovinian or Pelagius.

They say that this happened to so great a man because he did not know the force of the Greek word ἀναμάρτητος (*anamartetos*, incapable of sinning), and for that reason did not sufficiently distinguish the impossibility of sinning asserted by Jovinian from the possibility of not sinning defended by Pelagius, although “not being able to sin” and “being able not to sin” differ enormously.

An astonishing accusation indeed—especially when brought by those who least ought to bring it, since they look up to Augustine and almost worship him. Augustine says that Jerome must not be despised, for he was learned in Greek, Latin, and even Hebrew eloquence; having passed from the Western Church to the Eastern, he lived to an advanced age in the study of sacred letters, and his eloquence shone from East to West like a lamp (*Against Julian*, Book I, chapter 7). What is contempt, then, if not what those men are practicing?

[Col. 0690A] To make the whole question clear, Jovinian’s error must first be explained, and then Pelagius’s, so that when one has been compared with the other it may be evident what injury Jerome either inflicted or suffered.

Although it may perhaps not be as easy as it seems to grasp Jovinian’s mind, the ancients wrote as follows about his error.

Jerome (*Against Jovinian*, Book I):

> “Jovinian said that virgins, widows, and married women who have once been washed in Christ, if they do not differ from the others in their other works, are of equal merit. He attempts to prove that those who have been reborn in baptism with full faith cannot be overthrown by the devil. He proposes as a third point that there is no difference between abstaining from food and receiving it with thanksgiving. Fourth, and finally, he says that all who preserve their baptism have one and the same reward in the kingdom of heaven.”

[Col. 0690B] The holy doctor says this in the first book, which he devoted entirely to refuting the first chapter of the heresy; he then begins the second:

> “Jovinian’s second proposition is that those who have been baptized cannot be tempted by the devil; but whoever has been tempted is shown to have been baptized with water and not with the Spirit, etc.”

Augustine (*On Heresies*, heresy 82):

> “Jovinian said, like the Stoic philosophers, that all sins are equal, and that a person cannot sin after receiving the washing of regeneration.”

The author of the *Predestined* says the same thing (*Heresy* 82).

Pelagius interpreted Jovinian’s mind in the same sense when he wrote in Part III of his *Book of Faith*:

> “We confess free will in such a way as to say that it does not always need God’s help, and that those who say with Manichaeus that man cannot avoid sin are as much in error as those who assert with Jovinian that man cannot sin. For each of them removes the freedom of the will.”

Julian refers to baptism somewhat more clearly (*Part III of the Book of Faith*, no. 8):

> “We condemn the Jovinianists, who say that after baptism a person cannot sin in any way.”

[Col. 0690C] It should further be observed that before Jerome no one attributed this error to Jovinian. It was attributed neither by Pope Siricius in his letter to the Church of Milan, in which his other errors are proscribed, nor by Ambrose in the synodical reply of the Council of Milan to Siricius. This is surprising, since Jovinian’s second book was read at the Roman and even at the Milanese synod, as the synodical documents testify; yet in this book, if we believe Julian, the error of ἀναμαρτησία was contained (*Imperfect Work*, Book I, chapter 97). Hence someone might conjecture either that the doctrine of Jovinian *περὶ τῆς ἀναμαρτησίας*—“concerning sinlessness”—was disregarded by both synods as being of little importance compared with the other matters, which I scarcely believe; or that it was received in a tolerable sense, which is less improbable.

[Col. 0690D] Jovinian appears to have arrived at, or rather to have driven his followers toward, this position partly through a desire for a pleasure-loving life, so that they might be thought able to move without danger among banquets and crowds of virgins; and partly through a false estimation of the virtue contained in the sacred mysteries. They reasoned as though no one were truly regenerated in Christ through baptism, no one truly stripped off the old man and died to sin, and no one were truly reborn from the Holy Spirit and set free into the liberty of the children of God unless thereafter he ceased to be subject to the temptations either of error, the devil, or concupiscence. From this they could infer that no baptized person was able to sin, since each person sins either by being deceived through error or struck by one of the two forms of temptation.

Two passages in Jerome support this reasoning; in them the presumption of this sect openly reveals itself. In one, Jovinian himself is introduced; in the other, Jovinian’s heir—that is, Pelagius.

In the first, Jovinian speaks as follows (*Against Jovinian*, Book II):

> “John says: ‘Everyone who has been born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he has been born of God. By this the children of God and the children of the devil are manifest’ (1 John 3: [Col. 0691A] 9). And at the end of the Epistle: ‘Everyone who has been born of God does not sin; but the generation of God preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him’ (ibid., 5:18).”

In the second, Pelagius says (*Dialogue* 2):

> “I am entirely without sin,” he says; “I have no filthy garments; I am ruled by my own will; I am greater than the Apostle. He does what he does not wish and does not do what he wishes; I do what I wish and do not do what I do not wish. The kingdoms of heaven have been prepared for me—indeed, I myself have prepared them for myself by my virtues. Adam is held liable, as are the others who consider themselves guilty in the likeness of Adam’s transgression; I alone, with my company, am not held liable. Others, shut up in cells and not seeing women, are tormented by desires because they are wretched and do not hear my words; but even if I am surrounded by crowds of women, I have no concupiscence. For it has been said of me: ‘The holy stones roll upon the earth’ (Zechariah 9:16); and therefore I do not feel it, because by the power of free will I carry the trophy of Christ.”

[Col. 0691B] Add to this what Julian says when comparing Augustine with Jovinian (*Imperfect Work*, Book IV, chapter 121):

> “Jovinian says that through the mysteries man is freed from error; but you say that he is not freed even through grace.”

From these three passages it is clear how Jovinian wished those who were truly reborn from the Spirit to be freed through baptism from error, the devil, and concupiscence, and therefore to be sinless.

Someone might perhaps ask how all that has been reported should be understood concerning ἀναμαρτησία. For it can be conceived in two ways, according to the different source from which it appears to arise: namely, from an inability to perform a wicked action, whether physical, as they say, or moral. The latter too is twofold, since it arises either because God protects a person by a singular grace with respect to each individual act—a benefit granted to those who are said to be confirmed in grace—or because the error of the mind has been removed and the tempter restrained, whether the external tempter, namely the devil and the world, or the internal one, namely concupiscence.

[Col. 0691C] If the heretic believed that regeneration entirely removes the possibility of sinning, which in the schools they call physical; or if he believed that all who are baptized are confirmed in grace, or that they can never at any time be overcome by temptations, then the man must have been either monstrously stupid, shamelessly impudent, or incredibly indifferent to his reputation. What greater stupidity could there be than not knowing the deed of the Apostle Peter—certainly baptized by Christ—which is described so explicitly in the Gospel? What greater impudence than to excuse an act which Peter himself condemns with his tears? What greater contempt for one’s reputation than not fearing that everyone would bring against him what no one can fail to know?

He therefore seems to have spoken, at least on the surface, in another and more probable sense. But what sense? Perhaps none other than this: that the power of sacred baptism is so great that whoever has become a new creature in Christ, having been an old creature in Adam, can sin only by his will—whether by a will as free as Adam’s or even freer; that is, without being taken captive by error, tempted by the devil, drawn away by concupiscence, or led astray by mistake.

[Col. 0691D] Several considerations can persuade us that this was Jovinian’s meaning. First are the words of both Jerome and Julian quoted above, in which the threefold instigator of sin is excluded.

The devil: “Jovinian’s second proposition is that those who have been baptized cannot be tempted by the devil, etc.”

Concupiscence: “Even if I am surrounded by crowds of women, I have no concupiscence, etc.”

Finally, error: “He says that through the mysteries man is freed from error.”

For whoever lacks these three sources of sin can rightly be said to lack what they call the proximate possibility of sinning, and thus to be unable to sin, since no one sins except through ignorance of the truth—which is error—or through the suggestion of the devil, which is external temptation—or through the enticements of concupiscence, which is internal temptation.

Second, at that time, when the question was being asked whether a person could be without sin, the issue was not merely consent, which is called guilt, but especially the movements of concupiscence. Because of these movements Paul lamentably [Col. 0692A] desired to be freed from the body of death and released from the law of his flesh. Thus at that time a person was called ἀναμάρτητος and ἀπαθής—“sinless” and “without passion”—if he did not suffer those disturbances.

Third, when Jovinian said that all sins were equal, he was also openly admitting that good works were equal. He therefore allowed two things: first, that there were some sins among the faithful, for he contrasted sins with works performed after baptism; second, that the sins of the faithful, just like good works, were of equal merit, since the latter were performed with equal holiness and the former with equal wickedness—pure, as they say, that is, without weakness or error. For Jovinian appeared to believe that through baptism a person returned to the condition from which he had fallen through Adam’s sin: a condition in which there was no error or weakness at all, but a perfect power and possibility of not sinning.

Fourth, Jovinian acknowledged that the faithful committed certain sins—and serious ones at that. For I do not think Jerome maliciously introduces him, in exhorting virgins to marry, as saying the following (Book II *Against Jovinian*, near the end) [Col. 0692B]:

“Do not fear fornication: whoever has once been washed in Christ cannot fall; for he has the remedy of marriage to disperse his lusts. But if you fall, repentance will restore you,” and so forth.

Thus, if Jerome is to be trusted at all, Jovinian acknowledged the power of repentance—not merely of that inward repentance which consists in contrition of heart, but also of that outward repentance which is contained in the sacrament and in the power of forgiving sins granted by Christ to the Church. But if he had believed that baptism brought about an absolute impossibility of sinning, he would certainly have had to deny that Christ granted the Church any power to forgive the sins of the faithful, at least their more serious sins, since there could be no such sins to forgive.

Fifth, just as none of the ancients charged Jovinian with Novatianism, so neither did they charge him with Donatism—that the Church on earth is without “spot or wrinkle.” Yet defenders of the faith ought to have brought both heretical errors against him, since he constituted the Church solely from those incapable of sinning.

[Col. 0692C] Sixth, likewise none of the ancients condemned Jovinian for the error which Augustine is said to have imputed to Pelagius: that the Church consists solely of the predestined. They ought to have condemned him for this, if the Church consisted only of saints who had acquired perfect impeccability through baptism.

Seventh, that heretic unquestionably defended no other ἀναμαρτησία, or “sinlessness,” than that which the Stoic philosophers devised and called ἀπάθεια, “freedom from passion.” For he acknowledged no other sinlessness than that which, in his view—as in that of the Stoics—arose from the removal of error. But the Stoic ἀπάθεια consisted solely in this: that the wise man would neither be deceived by error, nor be persuaded by others to incline toward evil, nor suffer from disturbances of the soul.

Eighth and finally, the Pelagians themselves seem to have indicated clearly enough that their opinion concerning ἀναμαρτησία and ἀπάθεια differed in words from Jovinian’s doctrine but agreed with it in reality. For they defended Jovinian’s second book almost as their own, drew from it the arguments for their own opinion, and answered several [Col. 0692D] testimonies of Scripture which Jerome had brought against them, partly through Pelagius in his book *On Nature* and partly through Caelestius in his *Ratiocinations*. Jerome had cited these passages:

“We all offend in many things, according to the Epistle of James” (James 3:2), and “No one is clean from sin, not even if his life should be but one day” (Job 14:4). “For who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will claim that he is clean from sins?” and so forth (Proverbs 20:9).

He had also cited this:

“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

Caelestius addressed these same passages in objections 1, 5, and 13. Indeed, to strengthen his own opinion, he transcribed the words with which Jovinian, according to Jerome, attempted to establish his own position:

“John says” (ibid. 5:18): “Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him”; and, “Whoever is born of God does not sin, because God’s generation preserves him; the evil one does not touch him.”

[Col. 0693A] These eight arguments have no slight appearance of truth and might lend credibility to the conjecture concerning Jovinian’s view of impeccability, if the testimonies of the ancients to the contrary did not appear so explicit. But those ancients, whether all or most of them, were Pelagians, who may have lied according to their customary practice; and in my judgment they possess little authority. They do, however, create a powerful suspicion that Jovinian, from the earliest period, had already anticipated the invention of the heretics of our own age concerning indefectible grace—that is, grace which cannot be lost by one who has truly been baptized and has professed the true faith.

Thus far concerning Jovinian’s error. Pelagius, however, is accused of having said that a human being can be without sin and can keep God’s commandments if he wishes; and of holding that he can do both in such a way that he is easily able not merely to avoid individual sins but to avoid all sins, and not merely to fulfill individual commandments but to fulfill all commandments. This is what it means to be ἀναμάρτητος, “sinless.”

Pelagius held this view first in the *Book of Eulogies*, when he was preparing to spread his heresy; then in the book *On Nature*, when he began to write in its defense; and finally in the books *On Free Will*, after the Synod of Diospolis, when he was defending what had been condemned. The author of the *Ratiocinations*—whether that was Caelestius or Julian—held the same view. So did the Catholic writers who reported on the Pelagian errors: the deacon Paulinus, Jerome, Augustine, and Orosius.

[Col. 0693B] By these expressions, “if he wishes,” he signified such power in our will that a human being would possess sufficient strength to live rightly and would need no other grace of God than either his own freedom, which was granted at birth, or knowledge of the law, which accompanies reason, or even the adoption of the children of God and the forgiveness of sins, which is conferred through baptism.

Indeed, Pelagius was compelled to adopt this position because he simultaneously held two beliefs: namely, that Adam’s descendants are born in the same condition in which Adam was originally created, and that Adam was created by God—as is indeed the case—with every aid necessary for living piously, if he wished. Yet he did not understand these aids in the Catholic sense [Col. 0693C], that is, as divine gifts and aids added to a nature powerless of itself. He wanted them to be nothing other than the innate power of free will, assisted by the law and adorned by a certain favor of God.

Pelagius’ error therefore had two parts: first, that a human being can be without sin if he wishes; second, that he can achieve this without God’s grace, through the powers of his own nature. In the first respect he agreed with Jovinian; whether he agreed with him in the second is uncertain, since Jovinian’s view of divine grace remains obscure.

Pelagius was therefore rightly pressed by Jerome in the *Dialogues* with the same arguments by which Jovinian had been pressed in his second book, since both heretics held the same view. Pelagius was also rightly accused of fellowship with Jovinian by that renowned defender of grace. Nor was he ignorant of the force of the Greek word ἀναμάρτητος, “sinless”; in knowledge of languages he was second to none among the Fathers. This may appear to be an adequate solution to the question, provided that Jovinian is believed to have held the view conjectured above.

[Col. 0693D] But if in reality he introduced another kind of impeccability—such as that of the heretics of our own age, which is far more probable, if not certain—then Pelagius must be said to have changed his opinion and, in his earliest period, to have adhered to Jovinian, as Caelestius did also; afterward, when they perceived how disreputable that agreement was, they withdrew from him.

At first, therefore, they asserted that a person who had truly received baptism could no longer sin. Pelagius himself transmitted this assertion in his *Expositions of Paul*, while Caelestius transmitted it in his *Book of Chapters*. Later they said—as Julian did also in his *Brief Statement of Faith*—that a person after baptism could refrain from sinning. By this statement they softened Jovinian’s impeccability, which was in itself too harsh and too extraordinary, and made it more credible.

Jerome had read the earlier opinion in the works of Pelagius and Caelestius known to him, and therefore rightly associated Pelagius with Jovinian. [Col. 0694A] Jerome’s accusers encountered the later opinion in the statements of faith published by both heretics, and from these they took the opportunity to accuse him.

This distinction was not invented by me out of a desire to defend a doctor of the Church, although there would have been good reason to devise it. Rather, both parts are transmitted by the heretics themselves in unmistakable words, especially the latter part, which appears openly in all the statements of faith.

“We confess free will,” they say, “in such a way that we declare that we always need God’s help. We say that both those who, with Manichaeus, declare that a human being cannot avoid sin and those who, with Jovinian, assert that a human being cannot sin are in error; for each removes freedom of choice. We, however, say that a human being can always sin and can refrain from sinning, so that we always confess ourselves to possess freedom of choice.”

The earlier position appears in Pelagius’ note on Paul’s words: “For how shall we who died to sin still live in it?” (Romans 6:2). Since Paul is speaking of baptism, and since the interrogative expression signifies a certain ἀδυναμία, or “impossibility,” Pelagius added in a brief note: “He wishes the baptized person to be as firm as one who is perfect”—words, [Col. 0694B] as well as their meaning and form of expression, that are purely Jovinian.

Then Caelestius, in chapter 6 of the book just mentioned, asserted that people could not be called children of God unless they had been made entirely without sin. In that book it is clear that “children of God” means the baptized, since baptism is the sacrament of adoption; and that “without sin” means “perfect.” For immediately after an objection is raised, the Synod of Diospolis is said to have inferred, on his authority, that even the Apostle Paul was not a child of God, since he says: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect” (Philippians 3:12).

Caelestius therefore held the same opinion as Pelagius, and both held the same opinion as Jovinian.

“But at what time,” you will ask, “is Pelagius first found to have changed his opinion?” In my view, it was when the Synod of Diospolis charged him with saying that a human being could be without sin and observe God’s commandments if he wished. He replied in these words (*Acts of the Palestinian Synod*, chapter 6):

“We did say that a human being can be without sin [Col. 0694C] and keep God’s commandments if he wishes, for God gave him this possibility. But we did not say that anyone is found who, from infancy to old age, has never sinned. Rather, having turned away from sins, a person can, through his own labor and God’s grace, be without sin; yet even by this he does not become incapable of turning away afterward.”

You see, reader, that Pelagius again agrees with Jovinian, who urged his virgins away from their holy purpose toward an impure life by offering the hope of obtaining forgiveness through repentance and returning to moral integrity. You likewise see that Jovinian and Pelagius agreed concerning ἀναμαρτησία, “sinlessness,” insofar as it harms morals and permits men to associate more familiarly with groups of women; yet they did not agree concerning the other doctrines, whether those relating to the transmission of sin or those relating to other consequences. Thus you understand that Jerome did not contradict Mercator concerning the first authors of the Pelagian heresy.

## CHAPTER VII. An Inquiry into Certain Verses Attributed to Prosper Concerning the Association of the Pelagian Heresy with the Nestorian Heresy

[Col. 0694D]

The following epitaph of the Nestorian and Pelagian heresies is widely known. It is said to have been inscribed by Prosper upon their common tomb, and it contains something resembling a riddle: one heresy is said to have been at once the mother and daughter of the other. The Nestorian heresy is said to have given birth to the Pelagian, and to have received back from it, in turn, the birth it had given. For when the Nestorian heresy taught that the Lord Jesus had attained his dignity—according to what the poet seems to mean—through the merits of nature, the Pelagian heresy, arising from this much later as though from a root, dared to assert that individual human beings received by the same merits of nature the grace by which they become children of God.

When this assertion gained strength, the Nestorian heresy, almost worn out by the years and already dead, began to revive from it. Thus the error that had flowed from the head, Christ, into the members—that is, into human beings—[Col. 0695A] afterward seemed to return from the members to the head. This is what the author of the epitaph sings; but the poet himself must be heard:

> The Nestorian plague succeeded the Pelagian,
>
> Though it was begotten in my womb.
>
> Unhappy mother and daughter of the wretched child,
>
> I came forth from the very seed that I had borne.
>
> For I first began to found a citadel upon proud merits,
>
> And wished to lead the work from the head to the body.
>
> But while my offspring arms itself from the lowest places against the highest,
>
> It had no suitable time for battle.
>
> Yet after the grievous wounds of kindred deceit,
>
> I joined harsh battles with an equal end.
>
> One judgment alone gave me, defeated, over to death;
>
> Willing to rise again, she fell twice.
>
> With me she rises, with me she dies, and with me enters
>
> The tomb and descends to the depths of the prison of hell.
>
> To which our mad pride plunged us headlong,
>
> Stripped of gifts and swollen with merits.
>
> For wishing Christ, through the piety and reward of works,
>
> To be God, we did not remain within the covenant of the head.
>
> [Col. 0695B] And hoping for a crown from the freedom of the soul,
>
> We lost the righteousness that grace gives.
>
> Therefore, whoever pities the tombs of this double ruin,
>
> Beware lest you be joined to us in our destruction.
>
> For if you acknowledge only belatedly certain gifts of the Lord,
>
> But believe that these are owed to humanity, you will be one of us.

I admit that these verses are ingeniously and sharply expressed; but whether they are true or otherwise must be investigated more carefully. This is required both by the plan of the dissertation undertaken and by the popular opinion in which Cassianus, in his seven books *On the Incarnation of the Word*, agreed with the poet, as did other Western Fathers who at first understood the Nestorian heresy less clearly.

The careful labor will not be without considerable reward, if, during the investigation, the true kinship of the two heresies—something not widely known—should become evident.

[Col. 0695C] The author of the epitaph therefore teaches six things altogether concerning the Nestorian heresy: that it gave rise to the Pelagian heresy; that it in turn received its origin from the Pelagian; that it wished a human being to become God through piety and the reward of works; that it fought after the wounds of kindred deceit; that it was destroyed by a single judgment; and that, together with the Pelagian heresy, it was left unburied and thrust down to hell.

I maintain that all these things were stated elegantly by the poet but either confusedly or falsely by the historian. To make this clear, three matters must be observed somewhat more attentively.

First, the question concerning Christ’s divinity arose in the East and was proposed in nearly the common formula by which it was asked what name should be given to Mary, the mother of Jesus: whether merely ἀνθρωποτόκος, “bearer of a human being,” or Λογοτόκος, “bearer of the Word,” or Χριστοτόκος, “bearer of Christ,” or Θεοτόκος, “bearer of God.” The dispute was not about a mere word, but the principal controversy of the Christian faith was being formulated in its customary terms.

Second, the heresy that denies that God was born from Mary assumed different forms at different times. The first form, insofar as it concerns our subject, was given to it by Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch; the second by Photinus, who presided over the Church of Sirmium; the third by Leporius, [Col. 0695D] a monk; and the fourth by Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople. Thus the one heresy received different names, just as it assumed different forms, from its different authors. It was called Pauline, Photinian, Leporian, and Nestorian.

In the third century Paul went so far in his madness that, because he asserted that the one whom Mary bore was a mere human being, he said that Mary could properly be called only ἀνθρωποτόκος. He added that Mary’s son had earned through his own works a certain special union with God, on account of which he could in some sense be called the Son of God. But he understood the union as merely relational and as a union with God himself in his entirety, if one may speak in that way. For, being devoted to Jewish unbelief, he did not acknowledge the Trinity of divine persons in the Catholic manner, but only in name. Thus he wished Mary to be called neither Λογοτόκος, nor Θεοτόκος, nor Χριστοτόκος, except improperly.

[Col. 0696A] In the fourth century Photinus taught that Christ, that is, a human being joined to the Word of God, had indeed been born from Mary. Therefore he held that Mary was not merely ἀνθρωποτόκος but also Χριστοτόκος. He did not want the union to be purely moral; but he is said to have denied that the Word was truly God, making it instead something uttered or emitted, which at one time proceeded from God for an assigned task and returned to God after the task had been completed. He denied that Mary was truly Θεοτόκος, but held that she was only Λογοτόκος.

At the beginning of the fifth century Leporius agreed with Paul that the one whom Mary bore was a mere human being and that, through his own works, he had earned union with the Word, who was of the same substance as God. Yet Leporius did not wish the union to be perpetual, since he held that it had been removed on the cross, although it was resumed after the resurrection. Therefore he asserted that the Virgin ought properly to be called only ἀνθρωποτόκος, and not Χριστοτόκος, Λογοτόκος, or Θεοτόκος.

In the year 428 Nestorius began to preach that Mary had borne [Col. 0696B] Christ and therefore ought to be called not merely ἀνθρωποτόκος but also Χριστοτόκος. Yet he held Christ to be a mere human being who had been assumed by the Word of God—that is, by the second person of the Trinity—not on account of his merits but by grace, from his mother’s womb. He did not, however, think that the assumption was καθ’ ὑπόστασιν, “according to person,” by which the human being would become God, but merely σχετική, “relational,” by which the human being would be God’s instrument, garment, temple, or image. Consequently, he admitted that the Virgin could be called Θεοτόκος, but not properly; only in the same way that Elizabeth could be called Πνευματοτόκος, “bearer of the Spirit,” because she bore John, in whom the Holy Spirit was present.

Third, the heresy that received its name from Pelagius likewise assumed different forms from different authors who held erroneous opinions about the grace of God in the work of salvation. One form came from Leporius, who held that Christ, and other human beings as well, had earned by the merits of nature all that divine grace with which they had been endowed. Another came from Pelagius, who said that human beings could earn whatever grace they possessed, but that [Col. 0696C] Christ had received the grace by which he became the Son of God as a gift. Another came from certain Pelagians who asserted that neither Christ by any merits of his own, nor other human beings, could merit the grace with which they had been endowed. Rather, they said, human beings, through their own efforts and their own faith in God, could induce divine benevolence to grant them the grace by which they could perform works of piety.

In view of these matters, the defenders of the epitaph must be asked what the poet means by the name “Nestorian plague”: whether he means the entire heresy, consisting as it were of its four parts, or rather one part, namely the Nestorian heresy in its proper sense.

If he means the entire heresy, how can it be said to have been defeated and put to death by a single judgment, when the Pauline heresy was condemned by two councils at Antioch, the Photinian at Sirmium, the Leporian in Africa, and the Nestorian at Rome, Alexandria, and Ephesus?

If they wish the name to signify Nestorianism strictly so called, how can Christ be said to have been made God through the piety and [Col. 0696D] reward of works, when Nestorius both denied that Christ was truly God and asserted that a union of the natures, of whatever kind he admitted, had taken place in the Virgin’s womb?

They must likewise be asked how they understand the Pelagian heresy as viewed by their poet: whether in its entirety or only in part.

If in its entirety, with what truth did he sing that this heresy, wishing to rise again, had fallen twice? For it was struck with anathema more than once in Pelagius and Caelestius—whether at Diospolis, Rome, Carthage, or Ephesus—and in Leporius in Africa.

If only in part, how could he assert that Pelagius wished Christ to have become God through merits? Julian, in his *Statement of Faith*, which agrees with the statements of the other two, confessed the union of the natures in the Virgin’s womb in the very words used by Leporius, with the approval of the African council and the subscription of Augustine, when he set out the Catholic faith opposed to his former error.

Leporius says:

> “Therefore Jesus Christ, God-man, the Son of God, is born for us properly from the Holy Spirit and Mary [Col. 0697A] ever Virgin,” and so forth.

Julian says:

> “Therefore he is born for us from the Holy Spirit and Mary ever Virgin, he who according to his divinity was never absent from the Father. From two complete and perfect substances, therefore, God and man, we have received Jesus Christ, the Son of God.”

But if the error of the Massilians is also included under the name of the Pelagian heresy, how many errors must there be in the history? For Cassianus, the leader of the Massilians, vehemently attacks this supposed mercenary divinity of Christ arising from merits in his books *On the Incarnation*. Nor was the doctrine of the Massilians proscribed together with the Nestorian heresy at the Council of Ephesus, but nearly a hundred years later at the Second Council of Orange.

Why pursue the matter further? The poet unquestionably mistook the Leporian heresy for the Nestorian, although there is a great difference between them. Yet the poet deserves the more readily granted pardon because Cassianus himself made the same mistake and drew his friend Leo the Great, as well as many others afterward, into his opinion; [Col. 0697B] they followed the authority of both men.

Cassianus evidently thought that Nestorius agreed in all respects with Samosata, the author of meritorious dignity, since he agreed with him in the fundamental doctrine that Christ was in reality a mere human being. But he was mistaken in this opinion because he had lived in the East before Nestorius’ heresy had been exposed and was writing in the West, at Massilia, where the doctrine of Samosata was publicly known because of the monk Leporius.

At that time Nestorianism was still obscure in Gaul and even in Italy. It had become known through rumor that Nestorius was reviving the heresy of Samosata, but the sermons and letters of Nestorius, sent to Cassianus by Leo—then a deacon—at the command of Celestine, did not reveal the heretic’s mind concerning this matter. Anyone can readily understand this, provided that he reads Nestorius’ letters to Celestine together with our notes on them.

[Col. 0697C] “What then,” you will ask, “was there no association between the Pelagian and Nestorian heresies?” There certainly was, and it was far greater than is commonly believed. For Nestorius does not seem to have held sound views concerning original sin itself, as it is distinguished in thought from the debt of dying contracted through Adam’s sin; nor concerning the grace of Christ, which he did not distinguish from law and teaching; nor concerning the purpose of the Incarnation, which he held to be merely the example of right living that Christ was to provide for other human beings. These are the three principal points of the Pelagian controversies.

Julian, partly in his profession of faith and partly in his final work against Augustine, openly reveals—as Augustine himself thought—that he and his teachers Pelagius and Caelestius agreed with Theodore of Mopsuestia and Rufinus the Syrian concerning the Incarnation of the Word. (See the notes on the profession of faith and the dissertation on the Nestorian heresy below, in Part II of the fourth book of Mercator’s works.)

[Col. 0697D] However much the Pelagians attempted to conceal their position and disguised their heretical mind under words that appeared Catholic, they are exposed by adequate indications. Thus Jerome was not without reason in calling Pelagius the Antichrist, a name by which the Fathers commonly called Nestorius and others who fought against Christ.

It is therefore no wonder that the followers of Pelagius clung so obstinately to Nestorius that the Council of Ephesus issued the same canons against the Nestorians and the Caelestians, and that both names—associated with the same odium and the same impiety—existed at that time.

Someone may perhaps wonder that we make this assertion concerning the Pelagians, since Jerome, Augustine, Orosius, [Col. 0698A] Mercator, and the Fathers assembled in so many and such great councils neither burdened them with this accusation nor charged them with this impiety. For how could such careful and perceptive defenders of the faith have failed to notice what others’ eyes have detected?

This is certainly a serious objection, but it can be answered from the very point from which it seems to derive its force.

The Nestorian troubles had not yet arisen when the Pelagian heresy broke into public view. Theodore’s reputation had not yet begun to suffer, nor had his impiety, concealing itself beneath Catholic or at least ambiguous expressions, been detected, when Pelagianism seemed everywhere to have been struck down by the Church’s thunderbolts and to have died.

At that time everyone execrated Samosata and Photinus as guilty of twin blasphemies: the violation of the Trinity and the violation of the Incarnation. Whatever those men had uttered impiously, Theodore had partly softened by his explicit confession of ὁμοουσία, “consubstantiality,” and partly concealed under the pretext that he used better expressions concerning Christ. Thus the Pelagians’ faith concerning the Incarnation appeared sound on the surface, while they concealed the plague [Col. 0698B] within and, speaking with Theodore—or rather with Catholics—were believed to think inwardly what they expressed outwardly.

Their credulity was all the more inclined in this direction because other errors were exposing themselves more clearly—errors that held minds captive by their appearance and turned those inflamed with zeal for the true faith against themselves.

Although Augustine was exceptionally perceptive in detecting the hiding places of error, he regarded Julian with suspicion because of certain imprudent expressions concerning the doctrine of Christ’s mercenary divinity.

From the principle maintained by the Pelagians—that grace is given only on account of merits, lest there be injustice and partiality with God—it necessarily followed that Christ’s divinity had been earned by human merits. Once that principle, which was a kind of foundation of the entire heresy, was granted, this consequence could not be denied by a person who wished his opinions to be consistent with themselves.

[Col. 0698C] But it is one thing to suffer from the defect of ἀνακολουθία, “inconsistency,” and another to defend a consequence in its own right. If the matter were otherwise, no heretic could ever be refuted by reasoning; for from what else could he be refuted except from something he admits to be true? I admit that the Pelagians violated the rules of dialectic; I deny that they violated the faith concerning the Incarnation. I think that Cassianus accused the Pelagians more from prejudice than from reliable evidence.

Indeed, Pelagius may appear to have believed that the Blessed Virgin was Deipara, “Mother of God,” in that very book (*On Nature*) in which he attacked grace most vigorously. For when he was listing holy women, he added as a crowning example “the mother of our Lord and Savior himself, whom piety requires us to confess to have been without sin.”

If Mary is truly called the mother of the Lord and Savior, then surely the one whom she bore neither obtained dominion over other human beings through merits of his own nor received it as a reward for works, so that he could save his people from their sins. Otherwise the Church’s conclusion would be weak when it draws from the Creed, where the Son of God is said to have been born from the Virgin Mary, that Mary is properly Deipara, “Mother of God.”

[Col. 0698D] In sum: Cassianus did not understand the doctrine of Nestorius or of the Pelagians; the author of the epitaph did not sing truthfully; the two heresies were not related in the way alleged, namely that both denied the name Θεοτόκος, “Mother of God,” to the Virgin Mary; the Massilians, whose leader was Cassianus, did not think that Christ had been made God by the reward of works; Augustine did not prove gratuitous predestination from any other source than the example of Christ, which was admitted even by them; and the popular opinion concerning two heresies confederated against the Θεοτόκος rests upon no adequate authority.

# THE LATER PART OF THE EXTANT WORKS OF MARIUS MERCATOR, CONTAINING THOSE MATTERS THAT CONCERN THE NESTORIAN HERESY

[Col. 0699]

## HISTORICAL PREFACE

The second part of the works of Marius Mercator concerns the Nestorian cause, than which scarcely any cause in the ecclesiastical records is more famous. Since it presents nearly all the instruments of that cause, many of which until this day have either been obscure or entirely unknown, it will not, I think, be unwelcome to students of ecclesiastical affairs; indeed, it may be expected to please them because of its novelty and because it sheds the long-desired light.

Yet it does not seem possible to read it with as much pleasure and benefit as it can provide unless the history of the eight years that elapsed from Nestorius’ ordination to his deportation to the Oasis has first been understood.

This consideration led me to think that such a history ought to be prefixed. Yet it should not be taken from writers other than those who either conducted the affair themselves—such as Celestine, Cyril, Nestorius, Cassianus, Theodoretus, and the Fathers at Ephesus—or were able to observe with their own eyes what was taking place—such as Socrates and Sozomen—or appeared shortly afterward, such as Gennadius, the author of the *Predestined*, Evagrius, and others, whether they followed the Catholic side or the opposing side.

The more what is said is supported by such witnesses and their words, rather than by doubtful conjectures or superficial arguments, the greater credibility it will possess.

I know that a summary of the Nestorian affair was prefixed to the Council of Ephesus. I also know the history of the same affair written by Father Petavius, and I am not unaware that Christian Lupus recently published a dissertation and added to it an appendix concerning the holy Synod of Ephesus.

Yet neither the summary I mentioned, nor Petavius’ history, although extremely accurate, nor the labor of the other learned man deterred me from my undertaking, as though I were engaging in superfluous work and doing what learned men had already completed.

For, apart from the fact that it was necessary to explain the order in which we arranged Mercator’s works and to show readers the time and occasion in which each item originated, the summary prefixed to the Council of Ephesus is certainly shorter than it should be; Petavius’ history contributes little to our purpose; and Christian Lupus, overwhelmed—almost to the point of being buried—by the immense wealth of learning that he gathered in his scholia on the canons published by the eight councils, was unable to attend to certain subtler matters that we have observed with greater care while pursuing fewer topics and dwelling upon a single council, that of Ephesus.

These matters are nevertheless worth reporting at considerable cost, since they involve no little subtlety and have great importance for history. For they overturn many popular opinions by the weightiest authority and clearly show how much the learned world owes to Marius Mercator.

## YEAR 427

Sisinnius, the successor of Atticus, had occupied the episcopal seat of the imperial city for not quite two years when he died on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Hierius and Ardaburius. That year was 427 after Christ, the fifth of Pope Celestine, the twentieth of Theodosius the Younger, and the third of Valentinian III (Socrates, Book IV, chapter 26).

After Sisinnius’ death, the clergy of Constantinople became so divided while considering his successor that, while some obstinately supported Proclus—whom Sisinnius had placed over the Church of Cyzicus—and others Philip the presbyter, scarcely any hope of agreement appeared. It therefore seemed good to the Emperor Theodosius, in order to settle the dispute, to summon Nestorius from the Church of Antioch. Even if he should not be acceptable to both parties, he would at least be offensive to neither.

Apart from his desire for peace, three considerations moved the emperor to this decision. First, the memory of Chrysostom was sacred in the imperial city. Chrysostom had been summoned from Antioch to the see of Constantinople and had fulfilled every requirement of a perfect bishop.

Second, at that time the Church of Antioch abounded in presbyters distinguished not only by the reputation of their holiness but also by their learning and eloquence.

[Col. 0701] Third, among so many eminent men, Nestorius either truly excelled by merit or had at least acquired a greater reputation than the others.

He was born at Germanicia, a small town in Syria, although Marcellinus reported that he was born at Antioch. Cassianus adds that he was brought up and baptized as an infant in the same city. Evagrius writes that he embraced the monastic life in the laura of Saint Euprepius near Antioch and, after exercising himself there for a long time with John and Theodoret as companions, was made a presbyter by Bishop Theodotus.

Others report that, as soon as he became a presbyter, he was placed in charge of catechesis and expounded the faith in the Church not only to those preparing for baptism but also defended it against heretics. These were the two duties of a presbyter-catechist.

By nature he possessed a proud spirit and a desire for honor, an opinionated mind, and an ability readily to employ every kind of deceptive art. Solitude cultivated these seeds of vice, making a man already vain by nature esteem and love himself. The discipline of Theodore of Mopsuestia greatly increased them. From that teacher he learned first to hold erroneous opinions concerning the Incarnation of the Word, then to despise the orthodox as ignorant, and finally to insinuate heresy eloquently among unwary people, according to the time and place. For he turned his native eloquence and his facility in extemporaneous speech to wicked uses.

Formed by such a disposition and training, he first cultivated an appearance of holiness. Even among the least imprudent, this appearance was made credible by his avoidance of public gatherings, his seclusion among books, his dark clothing, the pallor of his face, his visible abstinence from food, the solemn gravity of his thoughtful brow, a certain modest sadness, and other disguises by which wickedness commonly pretends to be virtue.

Deceiving the eyes and minds of people in this way, he next employed other devices, almost conjuring tricks, by which he might win the goodwill of people of every rank. First, even while he was staying at Antioch, he presented himself not merely as an admirer of Chrysostom but also as an imitator of him, especially in that Asian style of speaking which is more pleasing to the populace than any other. Afterwards, in order to gain the goodwill of all who were distinguished and zealous for the faith, he displayed deadly hatred toward the heretics who were then especially detested—the Apollinarists, Arians, Origenists, and others. Finally, after he came to Constantinople, he dared, with the help of his favorable reputation, to insinuate himself into the esteem of the great and into the favor of the emperor himself and of the imperial virgins. Nor did hope deceive this bold man, to the great detriment of the Christian cause; for he was contriving everything with the single purpose of revealing the heresy conceived in his mind only when he would be able to support it by authority.

The circumstances of the times, the condition of the court, and the character of the emperor Theodosius favored the schemes of this man, fraudulent and wicked though he was. The excellent prince had a gentle disposition and loved peace and religion, but he was easily captivated by the appearance of piety and by the prejudices of those who occupied positions of influence. He had long lived under the rule of his sister Pulcheria, indeed a holy virgin but an imperious one; and, wishing eventually to assert his freedom as though from servitude, he wanted to appear to manage affairs himself. Nevertheless, he remained subject to the counsels of the courtiers, who possessed the greatest license to dare anything whatsoever in the name of the emperor.

## In the Year 428

Nestorius, therefore, summoned by Theodosius after the see had remained vacant for three months, arrived at Constantinople during the consulship of Taurus and Felix. He brought with him from Antioch the presbyter Anastasius, his companion in every secret plan and deliberation, whom he later used as an instrument of his impiety and of his professed hatred toward the God-bearer.

He was ordained on 10 April, with great favor from the bishops, the clergy, the court, and the people. “Immediately,” says Socrates, “when he was delivering an address before the emperor, he put forward this maxim, which is often on people’s lips, before the whole populace: ‘Give me, emperor, the earth cleansed of heretics, and I will give you heaven. Help me in overthrowing the heretics, and I will help you in overthrowing the Persians.’ By this utterance he seemed to have revealed not so much zeal for the faith as untimely boldness of spirit and a desire for empty glory” (Book VII, chapter 29).

Five days later he arranged for the church of the Arians to be demolished. But the Arians themselves, driven by the impotence of their anger, threw torches onto the roof of their church; the fire caught the neighboring buildings and would have defiled the city with conflagration had God not restrained the force of the flames. At this, the people, enraged against Nestorius as though he were prophesying, gave him the name “the incendiary.”

Nor did he persecute only the Arians, but also the Macedonians, Novatians, and Quartodecimans, and even the Coelestians—these more mildly, the others so severely that the emperor had to warn him to observe moderation. Nevertheless, at his instigation the emperor issued at Constantinople, on 30 May, during the consulship of Felix and Taurus, a law against all heretics addressed to Florentius, the Praetorian Prefect (Socrates, Book VII, chapter 29). These actions might have seemed the duties of an excellent bishop, had he not, as Vincent of Lérins says, persecuted the blasphemies of every heresy in order to open a path for his own particular heresy (Commonitory, no. 11).

Moreover, he made the name of Chrysostom—already restored by Atticus to the sacred diptychs, but still disliked at court because of the former hostility of Theodosius’s parents—acceptable to everyone. By serving as mediator of such a great peace, he bound to himself not only the courtiers but also the populace, and especially those who, because they had separated in great numbers from the others on account of John Chrysostom, were called Johannites.

While by this strategy he was occupying the minds of all the secular orders, he was at the same time laying traps for each of the other two orders, so that, once he had disclosed the heresy, he might frighten the clergy, monks, and fellow-bishops—whom he undoubtedly understood would resist him—partly by the power of the court and partly by the violence of the multitude.

[Col. 0703] When matters had thus been arranged, he believed that he could now safely insinuate the heresy, but still deceitfully, through trusted agents alone and under another person’s name. If the agents’ words were received favorably, he himself would use the popular enthusiasm to advance further; but if minds were disturbed, he could withdraw from the unpopularity and, by a timely explanation, bend the words scattered among the people toward a milder meaning.

Different writers recount the first occurrence differently. Cyril says:

“There was a certain bishop named Dorotheus at Constantinople, who held the same opinions as Nestorius—a man devoted to flattery for the sake of profit and whose tongue was ready for rashness. While a large crowd was present in the church and Nestorius was seated on the throne of the church of Constantinople, he rose and dared to shout in a loud voice: ‘If anyone says that Mary is the God-bearer [Deipara], let him be anathema.’ Immediately there arose a great uproar among the people, followed by a withdrawal, and so forth” (Letter to Acacius of Beroea).

Socrates gives a different account:

“The cause was of the following kind. The presbyter Anastasius, who had come there with him from Antioch, was always in his company, was held in great honor by him, and served as his adviser in conducting affairs. At a certain time he taught in the church that Mary ought to be called God-bearer by no one, for she was a human being, and God could not be born from a human being. These words greatly disturbed the minds of everyone, both clergy and laity” (Book VII, chapter 32).

However the matter finally occurred—whether in the way Cyril reports, or in the other way reported by Socrates, or even in both ways, which I consider more likely: Anastasius first arguing, and Dorotheus first pronouncing the anathema against the Θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”—Nestorius certainly resisted neither of them but rather supported them in his preaching. For when Anastasius had stirred up a disturbance in the church by his sermon, “Nestorius,” says Socrates, “endeavoring to confirm the opinion of Anastasius—for he did not wish to rebuke the man whom he held in such high regard for casting blasphemies against Christ—very frequently discussed the controversy in the church before the people; and he vigorously raised questions about it, and entirely rejected the term ‘God-bearer’” (ibid.).

Similarly, he either incited Dorotheus—which is nevertheless more like the truth—or at least, as Cyril writes, allowed him to utter publicly in the church, while the sacred rites were being performed, in reckless boldness: “If anyone says that Mary is the God-bearer, let him be anathema” (Letter to Acacius of Beroea).

Nor did he merely tolerate the impious words of Anastasius and Dorotheus. When he had resolved at last to disgorge the poison long conceived within him, he delivered in the great church, where a large assembly of people of every order had gathered in expectation, a sermon on the Lord’s incarnation, or on the virginal birth. Marius Mercator rightly calls it an utterly foolish treatise (*Against the Eleven Anathemas*); Cassian calls it pestilential (*On the Incarnation*, Book VII, chapter 6); Cyril calls it a compendium of every blasphemy.
