For it contains the whole poison of the impiety first disclosed by Nestorius, especially these words, which almost all writers report with abhorrence:

“God has a mother; therefore paganism is excusable when it introduces a mother to the gods. No, excellent man, Mary did not give birth to God, and so forth; she gave birth to a human being, an instrument of the Godhead, a human being who bore God [Θεοφόρον], and so forth.”

The beginning of the sermon is: “The intention of the discerning in the church is the doctrine of piety; and the doctrine of piety is knowledge of providence,” and so forth.

At such blasphemy everyone shuddered, and the indignation of the hearers and the agitation of the faithful were so great that some did not refrain from protesting before him in the most holy church. On the very day on which the sermon on the incarnation was delivered, a certain simple monk, burning with zeal for the faith, came forward immediately after the sermon into the middle of the church while the assembly was being celebrated. He attempted to prevent the herald of impiety, as a heretic, from entering. But Nestorius had him beaten and handed over to the high officials; after he had again been torn by scourging and publicly flogged, with a herald preceding him and crying out, he expelled him into exile. Nor did this tragedy end there. For those who followed the party of the man who was conducting everything by force, after his impious sermon, would have perpetrated a massacre in the very holy church of God itself, had God not prevented it. Thus the monks of Constantinople stated in the supplication presented to the emperor (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 30).

The event reported by Cyril also occurred: the people of Constantinople abstained from the assembly, except for certain frivolous and vain persons and those who flattered Nestorius. Nearly all the monasteries likewise abstained, as did their archimandrites and even a large part of the senate, fearing that they might suffer some injury to the faith from the bishop himself and from those whom he had brought with him when he departed from Antioch, if they should pour forth any perverse teaching (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 14).

## In the Year 429

Nestorius, partly raging with anger and partly relying on the power of the court, delivered shortly afterward a second sermon, ostensibly against the Arians and Macedonians but in reality against the Catholics. In it he appeared both to confirm his earlier sermon, whether by branding the Catholics with a false accusation or by twisting the authority of the Nicene Creed to support his own meanings.

At that time an extraordinary and audacious deed occurred, which Cyril relates concerning Eusebius, who, because of his exceptional learning and piety, became bishop of Dorylaeum. At that time he was still living among the laity, yet he dared publicly to rebuke in words the bishop who was speaking impiously before the assembly; thus he gave an outstanding example of his faith and of courageous firmness against heresies.

He also delivered a third sermon shortly afterward, ostensibly against the Apollinarists, on dogma or Θεογνωσία—“knowledge of God”—that is, on the unconfused union of the two natures in Christ and the reciprocal sharing of names. In this sermon he concealed the poison somewhat more artfully and poured it into the people all the more harmfully, since he appeared to be attacking the Apollinarists, who confused the natures in Christ, a name detested by Catholics at that time. Nevertheless, he could not keep silent about his own heresy concerning Christ as a mere human being, distinguished from the saints and other human beings only by excellence.

[Col. 0705] Thus several people courageously resisted the heretic raging against Christ. But what is worthy of admiration is that the laity resisted first, then the monks, afterwards the presbyters, and finally the bishops. Nor did these high-minded defenders of the faith think that the matter should be handled by word alone; they also used writing and the pen, so that knowledge of so important and religious a cause might reach more people.

Eusebius was the first of all. Inflamed by the divine Spirit, he publicly presented a protest against Nestorius, and by this act kindled everyone’s zeal for the faith against the bishop who was renewing the heretical doctrines of Paul of Samosata. The protest reads as follows:

“I adjure and beseech all who are going to receive this document, by the most holy Trinity, to show it to the bishops, presbyters, deacons, and readers, and also to the laity living in Constantinople, and to distribute a copy of it to them, for the evident confusion of the heretic Nestorius; for he holds precisely the opinions held by Paul of Samosata, who was condemned by the Catholic bishops with an anathema one hundred and sixty years ago” (Leontius, Book III *Against Eutyches and the Nestorians*).

At that time, it seems to me, Marius Mercator wrote a letter on the same subject as Eusebius’s protest and in almost the same form—namely, on the distinction between the heresy of Nestorius and the doctrines of Paul of Samosata, Ebion, Photinus, and Marcellus of Galatia. For the question was then burning among everyone: whether Nestorius agreed with the Samosatene. Each person gave his opinion according as he seemed to himself clever or learned. Hence Socrates too, although a layman, and knowledgeable in theological matters, wished to offer his judgment, as a man of the court (Book VII, chapter 31). Mercator’s letter begins:

“This is the doctrine, no less impious than vain, of Paul of Samosata and Nestorius,” and so forth.

At the same time, presbyters, inflamed by the example of the laity, had attacked the perverse doctrine in the church called Irene Maritima. They were immediately ordered to be silent by the threats and authority of the bishop, who was raging with anger. As a result, the people, demanding the customary preaching of the faith, publicly shouted: “We have an emperor; we do not have a bishop” (Supplication of Basil, First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 30).

Nor did the people conduct the matter only by complaints, but also by threats and public reproaches of the crimes that Nestorius concealed under the appearance of piety. They accused him of neglecting the needy and of distributing the resources of the poor to greedy men. Then they threatened to throw him into the sea and to kill the shepherd who had become a wolf (Cyril, *Encomium of the Virgin*).

Threats would have been followed by action had the power of the magistrates and the fear inspired by the emperor himself, who favored Nestorius, not held them back. The monks themselves, with free simplicity, charged both matters against Theodosius. For after they had exposed Nestorius’s weakness and his license to rage against anyone whatsoever, they said:

“Inflated by pride, by which he despises everyone, relying on money and on the power of certain corrupt men, and, to speak frankly about the matter, relying also on your own domination, he does these things” (Supplication, First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 30).

While everything was boiling with hostility—hostility on both sides, though not equally just on both sides—Proclus, who had been ordained bishop of Cyzicus by Sisinnius, continued to perform his former office at Constantinople and to teach the people in the church. He was distressed that weeds were being scattered in place of good seed in the field of Christ, which he had undertaken to cultivate. Thus, when a very large assembly was being held, urged by the love of Christ that filled his truly apostolic breast, he delivered before a great gathering of people of every order a panegyric discourse on the Virgin God-bearer against Nestorius. Although he did not name his adversary, out of respect for the presiding bishop, he nevertheless refuted the heresy known to everyone, to the greatest applause of the hearers.

Theophanes and Cedrenus recount the event in these words:

“On one Sunday, while Nestorius was presiding, Proclus was invited to give an exposition and said: ‘A homily on the God-bearer, whose beginning is: “Today is a virginal festival, brothers,”’ and so forth.”

On the more solemn feast day, while Nestorius was presiding, Proclus turned to preach and said: “A homily on the God-bearer, whose beginning is: ‘Today is a virginal assembly, brothers,’” and so forth.

Vincent Ricardus, from an old Greek manuscript chronology, reports the event somewhat differently:

“On one Sunday Nestorius appointed Proclus to teach; and immediately Proclus said in a loud voice: ‘A homily on the Lady God-bearer: “Virginal ...,”’ and so forth.”

Nestorius had appointed a more solemn feast for Proclus, on which he was to teach the people. But Proclus suddenly said in a loud voice: “A homily on the Lady God-bearer: ‘Virginal ...,’” and so forth.

That celebrated homily, praised by everyone, was delivered in the year of Christ 429, the first year of Nestorius, on a more solemn feast, either of Christ or of the Blessed Virgin. Such feasts were called κυριακαὶ ἑορταί, “Sunday feasts.” It must therefore have been delivered either at the Theophany, Θεοφάνεια, on 6 January—which I consider less likely—or at the Annunciation, ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγελισμῷ, which we call the Annunciation, on 25 March, as the subject of the discourse and the context itself indicate.

The applause given to the speaker by everyone was as great as the dignity of the speech and the hearers’ piety toward the God-bearer and hatred of Nestorius could possibly produce. Nevertheless, Nestorius himself immediately dared, as was his custom, to address the people and, with the utmost shamelessness and impiety, to criticize the principal points of Proclus’s speech, indeed to condemn them as blasphemy. The beginning of the discourse is:

“Christ-loving peoples giving the applause to those who perform the service of speech on behalf of the blessed Mary is not surprising. For the very fact that she became the temple of the Lord’s flesh surpasses everything most worthy of praise,” and so forth.

Nor was he content with having spoken once against the defender of the God-bearer. He delivered three further sermons, at three successive assemblies after the Paschal celebrations, in each of which he attacked at greater length three principal propositions of Proclus: that God suffered and died; that God is our high priest; and that the Blessed Virgin ought to be called Θεοτόκος, “God-bearer.” Since assemblies were formerly held on Sundays and Saturdays and also on the commemorations of martyrs, it is scarcely possible to determine on which day each sermon was delivered. Nevertheless, I scarcely believe that any was delivered on the feast of a martyr or of another saint, for I know of none that fell within that period.

He delivered one sermon above all the others before a huge crowd assembled by his own supporters. It was more harmful than the rest both because it is longer and because it explains more fully what had been stated briefly and less openly in the others. The subject of the sermon was: “Against those who, on account of the union, either mortify the divinity of the Word or deify the humanity.” Its beginning is:

“I laugh at the insults of the heretics against me, as the contrivances of madmen, and at their threats of casting me into the sea, and at their desire for disturbances, and at the new schemes of persecution they are now directing against us, and at the neglect of the needy which they charge upon us, and at the ravings of others’ chatter against us, as at the croaking of frogs; or at least I tremble before them as before the darts or camps of infants,” and so forth.

In this speech he did not mention Proclus’s name, as in the three earlier ones. But while arguing against each of his propositions, especially those that implied that God had died for us, he attacked a man already sufficiently known to everyone, branding him as wretched, heretical, a calumniator, Apollinarist, and Arian.

The unspeakable heretic had sent his first treatise on the Incarnation, together with several other homilies, into the provinces through trusted men, so that the plague might be spread more widely. When these writings reached Egypt and were secretly and maliciously introduced into the monasteries, Cyril, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, was compelled to write to the monks in order to confront the danger that could be feared because of the ignorant simplicity and credulous fickleness of some into whose hands the writings had come. For it was easy for the agitation of minds, which had already arisen, gradually to increase—as usually happens—through disputation and to turn into obstinate error and heresy.

Cyril himself reports this to Pope Celestine:

“When the homilies of Nestorius had been brought into Egypt, I learned that certain frivolous people had been led into error and were anxiously investigating among themselves whether he thought and spoke correctly or otherwise. Fearing that the contagion of the disease might gradually strike deeper roots in the minds of the simpler, I wrote a general letter to the monasteries of Egypt and strengthened those who were wavering in the true faith” (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 14).

The letter must have been sent not around the feast of the Theophany, at which time the date of Easter was announced to the monks—for otherwise it would have had its solemn conclusion indicating the time of Easter—but after the Paschal feast. At that feast, some members of each monastic community were accustomed to come to Alexandria to celebrate with the bishop, serving as representatives of all.

Cyril says that copies of that distinguished letter to the monks were brought to Constantinople through the efforts of certain persons—certainly sent by Cyril through his representatives—and read there. They were so helpful that many officials sent Cyril letters of thanks on that account. But this very fact supplied Nestorius with fuel for the anger he had conceived against Cyril (Letter to Celestine).

Nestorius therefore ordered a certain Photios to reply (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 12). But the reply, which Cyril had at some point seen (Second Letter to Nestorius), has not, as far as I know, survived to our times. Nor was he satisfied with that reply; he first practiced secret and then open hostility against Cyril.

When certain Egyptians were staying in the imperial city, men against whom the Alexandrian bishop had taken action under the prescriptions of the canons because of the infamy of their lives, Nestorius suborned them to bring accusations against Cyril and to submit petitions to himself and to Theodosius. These accused Cyril not merely of administering the Church badly but also of nearly seizing tyrannical control over Egypt against the emperor and, at the very least, of stirring up disturbances against the magistrates. This calumny later burst into the open, as did another charge which, in the view of some, was stamped upon the Alexandrian clergy accompanying him, as though they held the opinions of the Manichaeans.

The whole East, not merely Constantinople, was thrown into turmoil on account of Nestorius’s sermons, as Cyril reports. When the Roman pontiff Celestine received them from somewhere, together with reports of disturbances in the churches of the East, he was offended and considered it necessary to consult Cyril on the matter with the other bishops, to whom he had caused a report to be made about everything in their assembly, asking whether matters were really as rumor proclaimed.

Celestine’s letters have perished, but Cyril mentions them when writing to Nestorius in these words:

“What, finally, shall I do? For it is time to speak and to confer with Your Reverence. The most reverend and most religious bishop of the Romans, Celestine, together with all the venerable bishops who are with him, has indicated certain documents that I do not know how were brought to Rome. It is uncertain whether they belong to your religious teaching or not; for they write to us that they are exceedingly offended on account of them.”

At one and the same time, as it is reasonable to believe—that is, toward the end of April—Cyril sent a letter against the homilies of Nestorius both to the monks, so that they might be instructed, and to the Alexandrian clergy in Constantinople, so that they might disseminate it. Cyril had sent several of his clergy there, not merely to conduct the customary affairs of the churches of Egypt in the imperial city, but also to keep watch on behalf of the faith and to inform their bishop precisely about each of Nestorius’s schemes and plans.

When these men reported that Nestorius, with an embittered spirit, was moving every stone in order to offend the author of the letter and to make him hated by everyone else, Cyril wrote to Nestorius. In the letter he cleared himself of the charges, traced the causes of the disturbances back to their author, explained the complaints of the Roman pontiff about the treatises sent to him, urged repentance, and promised his own steadfastness in advancing the cause of the faith. The letter begins:

“Reverend and trustworthy men who came to Alexandria reported to us that Your Reverence is greatly distressed and is moving everything in order to injure me and striving by every means to do so. When I wished to learn the causes of your distress, they said that certain Alexandrians were circulating my letter to the holy monks,” and so forth.

[Col. 0709] After receiving the letter, Nestorius replied through the presbyter Lampon, briefly indeed, but not without a serious accusation against Cyril, namely, that he had written to him earlier with excessive intemperance.

This was the beginning of the open conflict between the two bishops of the principal sees, Alexandria and Constantinople. Since their authority was then immense, both because of the dignity of their sees and because of their individual persons, almost the entire world followed their respective parties, agitated itself incredibly, and even became divided. From that point onward the matter was conducted with great heat of spirit, while the two leaders of the parties attempted everything by which each might overthrow his adversary.

Nestorius fought with malicious tactics, as was natural to his character; Cyril fought in open battle, for his spirit was lofty and upright and, unless restrained by the bridle of Christian virtue, almost ambitious. He had indeed imitated the holy character of his uncle Theophilus, whose see he had inherited. Hence, even among prudent people, he acquired an ambiguous reputation in this matter. Love for his see, second only to Rome; burning zeal for the faith; hatred of heresy; and impatience at the injury inflicted upon Christ gave his actions a variety of apparent faces. Even his speeches, outstanding in doctrine and eloquence, sometimes seemed to rise beyond proper bounds and almost to be inflamed by anger.

At the same time Nestorius, intent on every device, tried to discover some means by which he could occupy the mind of Celestine. He had learned from Cyril’s letters that the supreme pontiff had been greatly offended after reading certain treatises circulated under Nestorius’s name. He therefore wrote to him, ostensibly on account of the Pelagian bishops living at Constantinople, but in reality to alarm the pontiff and, if possible, draw him over to his own party.

He wished to appear to have explained his own mind in the letter, although he concealed it with the greatest cunning. He also sent through Antiochus, an illustrious man, several treatises that contained poison hidden beneath many coverings of true doctrine. At least three such treatises, as can be gathered from Celestine’s letters and Cassian’s books, were delivered by Antiochus. The first was on the Incarnation, the cause of the disturbances; the second was ostensibly against the Macedonians and Arians; the third, ostensibly against the Apollinarists, was in reality directed against the Catholics. The letter begins as follows:

“We owe one another fraternal conversations,” and so forth (see above, col. 173).

Around this time Mercator appears to have presented to Theodosius his *Memorandum against Julian and Caelestius and the other Pelagian bishops*, and to have published it to everyone else, whether of the clergy, the administration, or the court (see above, col. 63). In it he exposed the entire case of such men in a way that made it clear to everyone what sort of men Nestorius was favoring with his friendship. Thus each person could understand the spirit in which Nestorius had previously persecuted heretics, while preparing a path for error.

A supplication was also presented to Theodosius by Basil, deacon and archimandrite; Thalassius, reader and monk; and other holy monks. After setting forth what they had hitherto suffered indignantly and continued to suffer daily at the hands of Nestorius, and after freely charging the emperor with protecting the heretic, they made two principal requests: first, that a synod be convened to remove disagreements concerning the faith; second, that the uncontrollable boldness of the Nestorians be restrained, lest they meanwhile continue to rage unchecked.

The date can be determined from the fact that in this supplication the Nestorian affair is said to stand just as it does in Nestorius’s letter to Celestine—namely, to be increasing and gaining strength daily. Nestorius claimed that he was teaching many people to abandon error, though this was a lie; the monks, more truthfully, said that he was terrifying them with threats and beatings.

At that time Cyril also replied to certain people who complained that, when he had heard Nestorius’s impious doctrine becoming worse, he had not restrained himself and allowed it to perish by itself through silence. Instead, they said, he had sent to Constantinople the letter he had written to the Egyptian monks, and by its dissemination among the people had provoked Nestorius and virtually compelled him, impatient of foreign criticism, to harden his resolve.

In writing, Cyril explained both the reasons for his action and the importance of the matter, which did not permit silence. He began as follows:

“Since Your Reverence has written to me that you are distressed because the most God-fearing Nestorius is grieving that I wrote the letter to the monks,” and so forth.

Not long afterward Cyril, following his custom of announcing the date of Easter, sent to all the churches, but especially to the church of Constantinople, a Paschal homily—his seventeenth—in which he explained the dogma of the faith concerning the incarnation of the Word in such a way as admirably to refute Nestorius’s first sermon on the virginal birth, touching upon each of its parts in no superficial manner.

Since this homily says nothing about God having been made priest, it is a clear sign that by that time neither Proclus’s speech nor Nestorius’s criticisms of it had yet reached Alexandria. For after Cyril learned of the controversy, he habitually omitted no opportunity to defend Proclus in this matter. It is also certain that Cyril wrote this Paschal homily before he received the letters from his agents in Constantinople. Those letters spoke of the fourth sermon against Proclus, in which the matter of God having been made priest was treated.

Meanwhile, from his own people staying in Constantinople, and especially from Bupha Martyrius, a deacon acting in the affairs of the Alexandrian Church, Cyril received a copy of the reply made by Photios to the letter addressed to the monks. At the same time he received Nestorius’s fourth sermon against Proclus. He also learned by whom and through what instigators he was suffering calumny in the city. He further discovered that those who supported Nestorius were speaking of peace and attempting to arrange harmony between the two leaders of the parties.

Accordingly, Cyril wrote from the Alexandrian synod, which according to custom was held before Lent, a second letter to Nestorius. In it he complained that he was suffering injury from Nestorius’s wicked flatterers; he refuted the fourth sermon against Proclus, though as if treating another matter; and he set forth the Catholic faith, knowing well that his opponents were employing deceit. For who, otherwise, would appear to love disturbances if he were to irritate a man desirous of peace?

The letter begins with these words:

“Certain people, as I hear, are chattering about my reputation before Your Reverence, frequently seeking suitable opportunities during processions or assemblies.”

The letters are said to have been issued at the Council of Chalcedon in the month Mechir, in the twelfth indiction—that is, from 26 January to 26 February—for the Egyptians defined the month Mechir by this interval of time.

At about the same time, indeed by the same route, Cyril instructed those representatives of his, sending them a memorandum about how they should conduct themselves with the Nestorians if peace were discussed; on what conditions they might come to terms; what they should answer to questions; what they should say in meetings; what they should testify to be the disposition of their minds; and so forth. The writing begins:

“I have read the letters sent by you, from which I learned,” and so forth.

He also sent a letter to a certain friend of Nestorius, with whom he himself likewise maintained a familiar relationship—I believe it was Acacius of Melitene. In it he testified that he did not reject proposals for peace, provided that the faith remained safe and the offense to the faithful was removed; otherwise, he was prepared to endure anything rather than abandon the cause of God. It begins as follows:

“I know the sincerity of your affection, and I have not failed to recognize your zeal,” and so forth.

While men of the Nestorian party were speaking of peace, Nestorius himself was treacherously contriving a calumny, either against the Alexandrian clergy themselves or rather against others who agreed with Cyril. He had them, when a council had been convened—under the instigation, as is reasonable to believe, of the Pelagians—prosecuted as guilty of Manichaean impiety, deprived of office, and struck with an anathema.

Thus he himself writes to Cyril:

“Know that you have been led astray by the clergy of your disposition, perhaps, by those who have been deposed here by the holy synod on the ground that they hold the opinions of the Manichaeans,” and so forth.

Marius Mercator ambiguously translates these words as follows:

“Know, however, that you have been led astray by those who were deposed by the holy council because they were filled with the disease of the Manichaeans, or—and this is the more important point—by clergy attached to your faction.”

A council of this kind must have been held in that year, around the month of August. At it the decree on behalf of the Pelagians was made which, down to the present day, has been believed by the eastern schismatics to have been enacted at Ephesus.

Meanwhile the supreme pontiff Celestine, after receiving from Nestorius the letters mentioned above, together with the three treatises, having consulted Leo the deacon, whom he employed as his chief assistant in governing the Church, decided to send the whole of Nestorius’s writing to Cassian, a friend of Leo. It was to be not only translated from Greek into Latin but also refuted. For, in addition to his knowledge of both languages, Cassian was then distinguished by the highest reputation for learning, and he pursued the Church of Constantinople—of which he had been ordained deacon by Chrysostom—with exceptional devotion.

After receiving the treatises, Cassian immediately undertook the outstanding work *On the Incarnation of Christ*. In seven books he refuted the heresy of Nestorius, though without naming him, since Nestorius still held the see of Constantinople. Cassian included in this work many propositions, both from Nestorius’s letter to Celestine and from the first sermon on the Incarnation and the other sermon against the Arians and Macedonians.

During Lent, Nestorius in turn answered Cyril’s second letter with his own second letter. When it was read at the Council of Ephesus, the Fathers judged that it contained a doctrine contrary to the Catholic faith—and not without reason, since it contradicted Cyril’s second letter, which was a sincere exposition of the faith received from the ancestors.

Throughout his letter Nestorius aimed to prove that the Son of God could not be said to have been born, suffered, or died. He pursued this purpose not less maliciously than artfully. He used the term “divinity” for God—that is, as they say, he used an abstract term for a concrete one—and twisted the testimonies of Scripture into foreign meanings. Finally, he gave merely verbal assent to Cyril’s doctrine concerning the union of the natures into one hypostasis, through a deceitful abuse of the term “person.” The letter begins:

“Insults against the admirable letter,” and so forth.

Toward autumn the slippery heretic again reported to Pope Celestine concerning the case of the Pelagians, but, as was his custom, he was less concerned with another person’s affair than with his own. The letter was delivered by Valerius, an illustrious man, whose rank would lend it weight and establish credibility not only for Nestorius’s writings—for Valerius was his most faithful friend—but also for what he was going to say about affairs at Constantinople: namely, about the complaints of the Pelagians before the emperor and about Nestorius’s disputes, partly with Cyril and the clergy of the imperial city and partly with others who had been offended by his teaching.

The beginning of the letter is:

“I have often written to Your Blessedness concerning Julian, Orontius, and the others who usurp episcopal dignity,” and so forth.

When Cyril was reading Nestorius’s second letter, he weighed these concluding words with particular attention:

> “What pertains to our Church is daily increasing for the better; and what pertains to the people, know that it is extending toward greater progress through the grace of Christ, to such an extent that this multitude cries out in the words of the prophet: ‘THE EARTH SHALL BE FILLED WITH THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE LORD, AS ABUNDANT WATER COVERS THE SEAS.’ Know also that the imperial household, its doctrine having been clarified, lives in great joy; and, to bring the page to an end, see that the saying about the Church which is here among us, concerning all the heresies that contend against God, is being fulfilled: ‘THE HOUSE OF SAUL WENT ON, AND GREW WEAKER; THE HOUSE OF DAVID WENT ON, AND GREW STRONGER’ (2 Sam. 3:1).”

When he had considered these words more carefully—or rather, when he had learned from his own people that matters truly stood as Nestorius had written, namely, that the ardor of the faithful was cooling while the spirits of the Nestorians were being inflamed, and that an opinion was gaining strength among many that the issue was not about doctrine but merely about a single word—he feared, as that outstanding defender of the faith, lest the cunning heretic should deceive both the supreme pontiff by letters, the emperor by flattering speeches, and the other Churches [Col. 0713] through trustworthy agents. He therefore resolved to meet so great a danger by sending letters to Celestine and, to the others, writings setting forth the orthodox faith. He sent two books on the true faith, one to the emperor Theodosius and the other to Pulcheria Augusta. He also wrote, as was customary, a homily to all the principal Churches. This was the eighteenth, in which, in accordance with the prescription of the Council of Nicaea, he announced the date of Easter for the year 431. In it he used the allegory of a battle to be undertaken against the depraved movements of the soul; he could be seen to sound the trumpet and kindle the faithful to fight bravely in the Lord’s battle. And lest their minds remain uncertain about what battle he was calling them to fight, he explained the mystery of the Incarnation in such a way as clearly to set out how God is said to have died—the very point over which Nestorius chiefly slandered the Catholics. Toward the end he gave particular exhortation to the relief of the needy, whose neglect Nestorius had accused him of. By that exhortation he returned to Nestorius a serious, though not undeserved, reproach.

At the beginning of the new summer, or even in the waning spring, Cassian completed his work *On the Incarnation* and sent it to Rome. At that time Possidonius, a deacon of the Alexandrian Church, brought Cyril’s letters there. Celestine indicates this when writing to Nestorius:

> “Some time ago we received your letters, to which, because of the urgency of the matter, we were unable to give any reply; for the statement had to be translated into Latin. While we are now doing this, although late, through my son Possidonius the deacon, we have received from the holy brother and fellow-bishop Cyril, that most approved priest, writings about you of such a kind that we grieve that the testimony of those who had reported concerning your ordination has perished.”

That Possidonius certainly came to Rome around the beginning of summer is established by the fact that he brought to Cyril Celestine’s letter dated 11 August; it is not credible that he was kept waiting for more than two months before a reply was given, since the turn of events and the nature of the case ruled out every delay. Yet he could scarcely have reached Rome at the time just mentioned unless he had left Alexandria no later than about the middle of April. At that time Cyril sent a letter to Acacius of Beroea, in almost the same sense as the one to Pope Celestine. He cannot be said to have sent it earlier, since he testifies that he had written about this matter to Celestine before writing to any other of his fellow priests; nor later, since he makes no mention in it of letters sent by him to the apostolic see, as he certainly would have done if he had known that his own letters had been received by Celestine. For he had instructed Possidonius not to deliver them to Celestine until he knew that Celestine had received the letters sent to him by Nestorius.

Acacius replied immediately upon receiving the letter, but in keeping with his character, and therefore craftily. He praised Cyril for his zeal for the faith while excusing Nestorius as having merely slipped in a word. Yet he condemned both for imprudence: when a dispute had arisen over a single word, one of the Fathers, he said, refused to speak in the customary manner, while the other pressed the matter more forcefully than reason allowed. Although he did not expressly take the side of either, to a more attentive observer he may nevertheless appear inclined toward the Nestorian position.

## YEAR 430

At Rome, near the beginning of August, a synod of bishops was held by Celestine, consisting of those then found in the city or summoned from its vicinity. At it, I suppose, Cassian’s work was read; the confession of the Alexandrian synod, contained in Cyril’s letters, was also read; Nestorius’s books, together with his letter to Cyril, were examined; and Nestorius was then condemned and ordered, if he wished to avoid the penalty of deposition within ten days of the notification, to retract his error and subscribe to the Alexandrian confession. Those who had been raised up on account of the faith were then restored to communion with the Church. The Alexandrian bishop was charged with carrying out the sentence. The matter of the Pelagians received by Nestorius was also dealt with, and their earlier deprivation was confirmed. Finally, seven letters were written by the supreme pontiff in the name of the synod: to Cyril, so that he might act in this affair as representative of the apostolic see; to Nestorius, so that he might return to repentance; to the Constantinopolitan clergy, so that they might remain steadfast in the faith; and to John of Antioch, Rufus of Thessalonica, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Flavian of Philippi—that is, to the bishops of the principal sees of the East—so that they might prosecute the cause of the faith energetically. All are assigned the same date, 11 August, during the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III.

The papal letters were carried by Possidonius, first to Cyril at Alexandria and then to the other Eastern bishops, each in his own city. Cyril wished his own letters to John of Antioch and Juvenal of Jerusalem to accompany the papal letters, in order to test the disposition of each of them toward Nestorius and to discover what hope for the cause of the faith might be expected from them.

He had written to both before the Alexandrian synod, from which four bishops were sent through the imperial city as executors. This is clear because no mention of the synod occurs in their letters, and those letters could not have been received by the persons to whom they were addressed before the end of October. Possidonius could not have reached Alexandria before the middle of September, nor Jerusalem—or at least Antioch—before late October, because of the distances involved.

When John of Antioch first received the letters of the supreme pontiff and of Cyril, he shared them with the bishops who happened at that time to be with him—there were perhaps six, one of whom was Theodoret—and immediately sent copies of each to Nestorius, together with friendly and holy admonitions that he should avert, by whatever means he could, the storm hanging over his head, and remove the offense of the whole Church by confessing the term Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*, “God-bearer”). He employed many arguments, but especially the example of their common teacher Theodore, who had sometimes retracted a word that had escaped him, lest the tumult arising from it should continue to disturb the peace of the Church. John’s letter could not have been brought to Constantinople before the middle of November [Col. 0715]. What Nestorius replied is unknown; but the outcome showed that he remained obstinate in his position.

Meanwhile, in Egypt Cyril convened a council from the whole diocese, although it is reasonable to think that this was the ordinary synod held around the autumn season according to the prescription of Nicaea. From it he sent Nestorius a synodical letter containing three things: an exposition of the faith, twelve anathemas to be subscribed, and notification of the sentence pronounced by Pope Celestine. It begins: “When our Savior said, etc.” The synod sent four bishops as legates to deliver Celestine’s letters and the synodical letter to Nestorius: Theopemptus, Daniel, Potamon, and Macarius, whom some incorrectly call Comarius. I do not understand why Baronius counts only Theopemptus and Daniel as bishops among the legates, while reducing Potamon and Macarius to the rank of ministers of the Alexandrian Church. In an ancient manuscript we find the date on which the synodical letter was sent, and therefore also the date on which the synod was held: 3 November.

Together with the synodical letter Cyril sent two other letters, one to the clergy and the other to the archimandrites of the imperial city, informing them of the whole matter and at the same time inflaming them to defend the faith, to persevere steadfastly, and meanwhile to maintain communion with those whom Nestorius had unjustly separated from the assembly of the faithful.

Meanwhile Nestorius, having received John’s letter in which he was warned, and having seen copies both of the apostolic sentence and of Celestine’s and Cyril’s letters to John, understood what a storm threatened his head. Yet, because of his lack of self-control, he was unwilling to avert it by the only lawful means—an appropriate retraction of his statements and a public confession of Θεοτόκος. Having summoned his friends, or rather his flatterers, as he later complained, he attempted to turn the storm against Cyril. After accusing Cyril before Theodosius both of impiety toward God and of a crime against the emperor, he requested that a general council be convened at which judgment might be rendered against the accused.

He later regretted that this had been done. He had hoped by this means to retain and, as it were, suspend the blow of the apostolic sentence until a synod could be held, at which, through the power of the imperial officials and the multitude of the Antiochenes and his own supporters, he might easily overwhelm Cyril and his Egyptians. It turned out otherwise, after many changes of circumstance, with God turning everything toward a better outcome. He charged Cyril with having sent Pulcheria and her sisters a special book on the true faith, not content with writing to Theodosius on the same subject, as though he were seeking the Augusta’s favor against her imperial brother, to whom his sister’s influence had begun to seem offensive and almost like a yoke he wished to shake off.

At Nestorius’s instigation Theodosius summoned a general council and called bishops from all the dioceses to Ephesus for Pentecost of the following year. He sent letters to the bishops of the principal sees: Celestine of Rome, Rufus of Thessalonica, Cyril of Alexandria, John of Antioch, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Capreolus of Carthage. Just as he ordered each of them to come without excuse or delay, with those of his clergy whom he knew to be suitable, so he forbade anyone meanwhile, before the synod had been convened and its common judgment concerning all matters had been given, to introduce any private innovation. He was evidently acting in Nestorius’s interest, since otherwise the sentence of the apostolic see would have cast Nestorius from his throne. The edict was issued at Constantinople on 18 November, during the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, Augusti and consuls.

The emperor wished private letters to Cyril to accompany the common summons. In them he charged him with disturbing the Church, attempting to disrupt the harmony of the imperial household, prying into matters belonging to others, an uncontrolled desire to rule, a harsh and ill-considered manner of acting, and other accusations no less serious. He threatened that, if Cyril continued to stir up disturbances, he would experience the anger of a prince whose benevolence he had abused.

Cyril did not think that he should clear himself before Theodosius of the charges brought against him until the synod had been completed, lest he appear either to beg pardon or to avoid judgment. The charge brought by the emperor concerning a desire to rule, moreover, somehow adhered to almost all the Alexandrian bishops. Athanasius himself, before Constantine, was accused of usurping secular power in Egypt; and Socrates says of Theophilus and Cyril alike:

> “After the death of Theophilus, Cyril was placed in the episcopal see. He gained power over the bishops and assumed for himself an even greater authority than Theophilus had ever possessed. From that time the bishop of Alexandria acquired, in addition to dominion over the sacred clergy, authority also over secular affairs.”

Nestorius anticipated the emperor’s edict with letters of his own to Celestine. In them he attacked Cyril, as though, conscious of wrongdoing, he feared the synod’s judgment concerning the pamphlets submitted against him; and he accused him of a certain malicious evasion and tedious inconsistency, by which he would at one moment reject the term Χριστοτόκος (*Christotokos*, “Christ-bearer”) and at another admit it at will. He then craftily urged the pontiff to settle the dispute between the parties contending over Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*) and ἀνθρωποτόκος (*anthropotokos*, “man-bearer”), ordering that each side, abandoning its own term—which could signify either pure God or pure man—should use the third term, Χριστοτόκος, which contained within itself the force of both alternatives. Finally, he informed him of the general synod summoned by Theodosius, doing so cunningly, as though taunting the pontiff for having declined to accept his judgment.

The fear that Nestorius pretended to attribute to Cyril, he himself had conceived in immense measure because of his conscience. Yet, despite the resistance of his pride, he could not restrain himself from revealing it to Celestius, the leader of the Pelagian party. Consoling Celestine over the exile imposed on him by Theodosius by citing the example of saints who had suffered persecution, Nestorius wrote that he too was sustained by that example against the storm of evils descending upon him:

> “For the letters sent to the bishops by the council of the West, and by the Alexandrian [council] through many replies, have made our sentence known to us, etc.”

[Col. 0717] While these things were taking place at Constantinople, the bishops sent by the Alexandrian synod arrived there and, on Sunday, delivered to Nestorius Pope Celestine’s apostolic letters and Cyril’s synodical letters as his representative, in the presence of a great crowd of clergy and distinguished men. Theopemptus, one of the legates, narrated the sequence of events to the Fathers at Ephesus:

> “On Sunday, after the synaxis had been completed, we went up to the episcopium. There, with the entire clergy and almost all the distinguished men present, we delivered to Nestorius the letters in question. After receiving them, he appointed the following day for us to speak with him. We therefore departed. But when we returned on the next day, he did not admit us, nor did he give any satisfaction concerning the letters. Instead, publicly before the assembly, he proposed the same doctrines as before, and doctrines even worse than those.”

Marius Mercator shows that the Sunday fell on 7 December, since he reports that Nestorius received the letters on 7 December, during the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, Augusti and consuls.

Six days later, in the Church of Saint Sophia, after a presbyter κατηχηστής (*katēchistēs*, “catechist”) had delivered a lengthy discourse on charity, Nestorius raged against Cyril without mentioning his name. Challenging him to a single combat over doctrine and alleging the ancient hostility of the Alexandrians toward the Antiochenes and Constantinopolitans, he attempted to remove from himself the suspicion of sharing the opinions of Paul of Samosata and Photinus, while trying to prove that Cyril agreed with Apollinaris and Arius. The sermon begins:

> “Our preceding teacher has set before us a sweet table of charity; for it has no bitterness of fraternal hatred, no poison of envy, no rust of feigned brotherhood, etc.”

On the following day, which was Sunday, he delivered another sermon, shorter in words but equal in impiety. He preached before a large gathering, whether curiosity or partisan enthusiasm had brought the listeners together. Its subject was the same as that of the preceding discourse, of which it is virtually a summary. It begins:

> “In other lands lies the usefulness of other things, etc.”

I believe that Nestorius craftily failed to add anything after the catechist’s discourse on the knowledge of piety, as was customary. Instead, pretending to be exhausted by the previous day’s labor, he remained silent so that the people would ask him to speak about the controversy, at least in summary form. Thus he says:

> “What, then, is the knowledge of piety? If anyone wishes to learn it in summary—for I spare both myself, who am tired, and you, who are suffering from crowding—what, then, as I was saying, is the knowledge of piety, if anyone wishes to learn it in summary? It is to inquire into the divinity of the consubstantial Trinity, and that the divine nature assumed an embodied man. You press upon matters that have often been discussed as though they had not been discussed, and insist vehemently upon exactness. Since, therefore, it is necessary to yield to your violence, which exercises a pious tyranny over us, we shall once again repeat the same words before you. Preserve, then, in summary, this knowledge of piety.”

After receiving the letters of both synods, Nestorius immediately sent a copy to his friend John at Antioch, asking him to arrange for two of the most learned bishops of his council, Andrew of Samosata and Theodoret of Cyrrhus, to write against Cyril’s twelve anathemas, on the grounds that they contained the heresy of Apollinaris and Arius. Each fulfilled this request in such a way that Cyril refuted the objections of both before Easter.

## YEAR 431

Since Cyril’s letter, together with its twelve chapters, had not been delivered only to Nestorius, so that he might be pressed by it, but generally to everyone, as a complete rule of faith useful to all; and since Nestorius saw his own doctrine attacked by the twelve anathemas as though by twelve weapons, he too composed twelve anathemas, each corresponding to one of Cyril’s, and gave them to his followers for publication, as weapons by which, as he boasted, the attacks of Apollinaris and Arius might be beaten back and shattered.

Marius Mercator was then staying at Constantinople. As he was a vigorous defender of the faith and had begun courageously to resist the rising heresy, he could not bear with patience that Nestorius’s anathemas should be read by everyone without answer and should harm many people. Inflamed, therefore, with zeal for the truth, he wrote an outstanding work entitled *Book of Contradictions against the Twelve Chapters of Nestorius’s Blasphemies*, in which he contradicts the twelve chapters through letters sent to him by the holy Celestine, bishop of the city of Rome, and the holy Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and, replying in very brief arguments, endeavors to refute the twelve chapters of the faith that had been sent to him. The two verbs in the present tense—“he contradicts” and “he endeavors”—clearly indicate that the work was composed at the time just mentioned, and not at another.

During the winter Cyril labored over three works, partly to defend his anathemas and partly to defend Proclus’s sermon. In the first he answered the objections made by Andrew of Samosata in the name of the Easterners; in the second he resolved Theodoret’s objections; in the third he contradicted a certain book by Nestorius against Proclus. All are full of outstanding learning, but especially the third. Cyril argues with the full force of his mind against those who reject Θεοτόκος and divide Christ into two sons, and who deny that God suffered and died and became our priest.

After the Easter celebrations had ended, Nestorius immediately set out from Constantinople for Ephesus, and Cyril from Alexandria, each with his own companions and each resolute in spirit: the former to manipulate intrigues, the latter to defend the faith courageously. The reason for their hurried departure was partly the distance between the places, but much more the fear or prudence of each. Their fear was that either of them might appear not to have obeyed the emperor’s appointed day literally, or might in some way delay or evade the council’s judgment in his own case. Their prudence was that, if one preceded the other, he might meanwhile receive the arriving bishops and bind them to his side through acts of service.

Two companions came with Nestorius, Candidian and Irenaeus. Candidian came with instructions from the emperor to maintain order [Col. 0719] in the synod; Irenaeus came as Nestorius’s private friend, although the outcome also showed that Candidian himself strongly favored Nestorius. The emperor said:

> “We have ordered Candidian, the most distinguished count of the sacred domestics, to attend your holy synod; but on this condition and with this limitation: that he have no involvement whatever in the questions and controversies arising concerning the doctrines of the faith. Finally, let this also not be hidden from you: the most magnificent Count Irenaeus must have no participation either in the deliberations of your most holy synod or in the matters entrusted by us to our distinguished legate Candidian, since he has gone to Ephesus solely out of friendship with Nestorius, the most pious bishop of this celebrated city.”

When Nestorius came to Ephesus with a large retinue, he brought with him ten of his own bishops, whose names are appended to the report Nestorius made to the emperor concerning the affairs of the synod. Cyril brought many more bishops—fifty, if we believe John of Antioch—and their names can readily be identified from the signatures in the acts. I think that the whole Alexandrian synod, or almost the whole of it, accompanied its bishop. Before the synod Cyril wrote twice to his people in Alexandria: once while on the journey, from the island of Rhodes; and again from Ephesus, after he had arrived before Pentecost. In the latter letter he speaks of Nestorius’s machinations:

> “That perverse and ever-watchful beast is running everywhere, etc.”

Cyril therefore reached Ephesus four or five days before Pentecost, whose Sunday that year fell on 7 June. Juvenal arrived with the Palestinians five days later. When Flavian, who represented the Macedonians, arrived is unknown. John of Antioch deliberately delayed on the road with the Easterners. Nevertheless, while he was only five or six days’ journey away, he wrote to Cyril through two bishops, Alexander of Apamea and Alexander of Hierapolis. Cyril stated that he had replied to him on 20 June.

Evagrius, or whoever else he may be among those he mentions, attempts to excuse John. He says:

> “John, the bishop of Antioch, was absent with his followers on the appointed day, not voluntarily, as it seems to many who wish to defend his action, but because he could not summon his bishops so quickly. For some of the cities over which they presided were twelve days’ journey or more from Antioch for a swift and energetic traveler, while Ephesus was about thirty days’ journey from Antioch. But when John consistently declared that he could not be present on the appointed day—that is, on the new Sunday (for that is what it is called)—all his bishops remained at their own sees.”

This passage is wholly corrupt and confused, but it can be corrected and restored from Nicephorus as follows:

> “He also affirmed that he would not have come on the appointed day if his colleagues had remained at their sees on the new Sunday, as it is called.”

In the Greek text one reads νέα Κυριακή (*nea Kyriakē*, “new Sunday”). This was the conclusion of the Easter celebrations, before which bishops were not accustomed to depart from their Churches, in order to bless the newly baptized after they had laid aside their white garments.

John’s excuse would indeed have been sufficient, if matters stood as described. Since Easter that year fell on 19 April, the conclusion of the celebrations, or νέα Κυριακή, fell on the 26th. If the bishops who lived farther from Antioch spent fifteen or even sixteen days making the journey to their metropolitan, and several more days restoring their bodies after the fatigue of travel, John could not have left Antioch with his followers before the middle of May. Since Ephesus was thirty days’ journey from Antioch, so large a company could certainly not have reached Ephesus before 14 June, seven days after the appointed date, even if it traveled as quickly as possible. That, however, could not have been done at all by men burdened with old age, and could scarcely have been done even by the strong. John could hardly have reached Ephesus with his followers before the end of June. Nevertheless, it is better to think that John’s excuse was unjust than to condemn the Fathers at Ephesus for excessive haste, which would amount to judging the first and most celebrated action of the council defective.

While they awaited the arrival of everyone and the beginning of the synod, Liberatus says, the bishops who were present raised the question of blessed Mary, the Mother of God; Cyril, meanwhile, was making certain excerpts from Nestorius’s books, wishing to disturb him. By “excerpts” he means selections that Mercator translated under this title:

> “Chapters excerpted by Bishop Cyril from various books or treatises of Nestorius, translated by us from Greek into Latin.”

These differ both from the excerpts presented to the Council of Ephesus by Peter, chief of the notaries, and from those contained in the *Book of Contradictions*. They nevertheless shed great light on the other materials, indeed on the whole history.

The historical preface might end here, since nothing is found in our author—at least nothing certain and relevant to the Council of Ephesus. Yet because Mercator presents certain writings of Theodoret composed after the council, and writings of considerable importance, it seemed worthwhile briefly to summarize what happened up to the time when Theodoret wrote the letters or books mentioned above. I shall admit what is true: nothing is more complicated than the chronology of the many events contained in the second part of the Council of Ephesus; nothing is more confused than the arrangement of the writings. I cannot sufficiently marvel at the compiler’s intention—or negligence—by which he mixed everything together so thoroughly that he seems to have wished to amuse himself by twisting the minds of the curious.

While the Fathers who had arrived earlier were waiting for the others, who were expected shortly, the time was spent not only in greetings, friendly conversations, and discussions of the matters to be handled, but also in hearing men who were among the most eloquent and learned in almost the whole world: Cyril, Acacius of Melitene, Theodotus, and others. At that time Cyril delivered a discourse on Jeremiah’s allegorical partridge and on the praises of the Virgin Deipara; Acacius of Melitene delivered an entirely remarkable speech on the unity of Christ [Col. 0721]; and two homilies of Theodotus were read, beside which nothing was written in so learned an age.

Those same two outstanding bishops, Theodotus of Ancyra and Acacius of Melitene, attempted, because of their long-standing association, to bring Nestorius through conversation to agreement with the Church, but in vain. For three days before the synod began they heard from him those impious words that later filled everyone with horror:

> “I do not worship a God of two or three months, nor him who fled into Egypt.”

They also heard these other words from his companions:

> “It is one who suffered, another who is the Word of God; the Jews crucified a man, not God.”

When the Fathers complained about John’s delay to the two bishops whom he had sent ahead, they said to them not once but repeatedly:

> “HE INSTRUCTED US TO INFORM YOUR PIETY THAT YOU SHOULD NOT PROLONG THE SYNOD IF HE SHOULD HAPPEN TO DELAY ANY LONGER; RATHER, WHAT NEEDS TO BE DONE SHOULD BE DONE.”

When they had reported this, and it was certain, both from the delay and from what had been announced in his name, that John was avoiding the assembly—either because he was indulging the friendship that existed between him and Nestorius, or because Nestorius had been a cleric of his Church, or even because he was complying with the pleas of some who were interceding for him—the holy synod held its session in the great church at Ephesus called Mary.

When the Fathers had been summoned to the church called Mary—which Cyril appears to teach was called Holy and Deipara—Nestorius requested that the church of the holy apostle John be opened for his party, so that they might meet there. Memnon, the bishop of Ephesus, refused and the people, devoted to the Virgin, opposed him. Hence Nestorius’s frequent complaints, as though he had been rejected through a riot. He says:

> “The author and leader of this great sedition was Memnon, bishop of Ephesus. For he closed against us the holy churches, the houses of the holy martyrs, and the most sacred basilica of the apostle, so that no refuge in them was open to us even when we were being treated with hostility. But he opened the great church to them and prepared there a suitable place for their assembly; to all of us, however, he threatened death.”

The first session proceeded as follows. Sixteen days after the date fixed by the emperor, Nestorius, having been lawfully summoned but refusing to come, first the faith of the Council of Nicaea was read; then the emperor’s sacred letter; afterward Cyril’s second letter to Nestorius and Nestorius’s second letter to Cyril; then Celestine’s letter to Nestorius and Cyril’s denunciation with the anathemas; finally excerpts from Nestorius’s books and contrary testimonies from twelve earlier Fathers. At the end, after Capreolus of Carthage’s letter to the synod had been read, and with the sun already setting, the following sentence of deposition and excommunication was pronounced against the contumacious man:

> “The holy synod said: Since, among his other impieties, the most impious Nestorius has refused both to obey our summons and to admit the most holy and devout bishops whom we sent to him, we could not refrain from turning our attention to an examination of what he impiously taught. We have therefore discovered, partly from his letters and writings, partly from the sermons that he most recently delivered in this metropolis of the Ephesians and that have been established by testimony, that he thinks and proclaims impiously. Compelled by the sacred canons and by the letter of our most holy brother and fellow minister Celestine, bishop of the Church of Rome, and repeatedly overcome with tears, we have necessarily come to this sorrowful sentence against him. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ, whom he has attacked with his blasphemous words, defines through this most holy synod that Nestorius himself is deprived of episcopal dignity and separated from the entire fellowship and assembly of priests.”

The same sentence was announced on the following day in these terms:

> “The holy synod, gathered by the grace of God in the metropolis of the Ephesians in accordance with the decree of our most devout and Christian emperors, to Nestorius, the new Judas: Know that, because of your impious preaching and your contumacy contrary to the canons, on the twenty-second day of the present month of June, in accordance with the decrees of the ecclesiastical sanctions, you have been deposed by the holy synod and separated from every ecclesiastical rank.”

On that very day Count Candidian reported to the emperor on what had been done at the council; Nestorius also reported, and both reports were false. Nevertheless, they moved Theodosius, whose mind was already inclined toward Nestorius and hostile to Cyril, against the entire synod. Candidian’s report has perished, but that it agreed entirely with Nestorius’s report is clear from the sacred letter sent by the emperor through Palladius. Nestorius complained that the emperor’s orders had been disregarded; that John of Antioch’s arrival had been obstructed; that Memnon had closed the church against him and his followers; that violence had been inflicted upon them by the clergy and monks; and, finally, that everything was being conducted in a disorderly and seditious manner. He therefore made two urgent requests: first, that what had been done should be rescinded; second, that rules for holding the synod should be prescribed so that each metropolitan should have only two bishops present with him. He pressed this request maliciously, since he knew that in Egypt there were no metropolitans as there were in the East, Asia, Thrace, and the other dioceses favorable to him.

On the same day the synod wrote a very brief letter to the most distinguished Eucharius, defender of the Constantinopolitan Church, and to the presbyters, stewards, and other clergy. It informed them that Nestorius had been deposed and that therefore everything belonging to the Church was to be guarded until a bishop had been elected to whom an account of all things could be rendered. Cyril also wrote to Dalmatius the archimandrite and to his own people stationed at Constantinople, so that they might understand what action was required amid this reversal and disturbance of affairs, which Candidian was contriving so that the truth would not become known to the emperor:

> “Since, as I understand, reports have been delivered by the most magnificent Count Candidian, be cautious and vigilant, and make it known that the record of the proceedings concerning Nestorius’s deposition has not yet been fully written. Consequently, we have not yet been able to send our report to our devout and victorious emperors; [Col. 0723] and, with God’s favor, it will be sent together with the record, provided we are allowed to send someone capable of carrying it. But if the sequence of the record and the report is delayed, know that we are being prevented from sending them.”

At that time Dalmatius was regarded as the holiest of all monks, since he had not set foot outside his monastery for forty-eight whole years and led a life comparable to that of the angels. He was devoted to Cyril in an exceptional degree, for the common service of Christ joins holy men together; and through this minister God accomplished the most difficult of all tasks, as will later be said.

The address of Cyril’s letter shows to whom he wrote: to the bishops Macarius and Potamon, and to the presbyters Timothy and Eulogius. This allows one to refute Baronius’s opinion that Macarius and Potamon were not bishops. Of the four Egyptian bishops sent by the Alexandrian synod from Alexandria to Nestorius at Constantinople, two went on to Ephesus for the council, Theopemptus and Daniel; two remained at Constantinople to manage affairs, Macarius and Potamon. Eulogius is the very man to whom Cyril later gave the memorandum mentioned below.

Before John of Antioch arrived with his followers—which occurred five days after Nestorius’s deposition—the synod reported to the emperor on the events at Ephesus and wrote to the clergy and people of Constantinople concerning Nestorius’s condemnation. At that time Cyril also wrote to the clergy and people of Alexandria and to the Fathers of the monks. He delivered a speech to the Fathers, apparently on 23 June, when seven of the schismatics came down to Saint Mary and joined the synod. The beginning of the speech is:

> “I see the radiant assembly of all the holy ones, etc.”

He also delivered another speech on Saturday, apparently while the synaxes were being held, after Rheginus, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, and others had spoken.

On that same Saturday, toward evening, John arrived with his party. The synod had sent bishops with clerics to meet him outside the city; only Cyril among them was admitted to embrace him. The rest were driven back by his attendants. No one was allowed to explain the synod’s instructions; indeed, at the command or with the permission of Count Irenaeus, even the bishops themselves were beaten by the attendants. That count had come to Ephesus with Nestorius and had gone out to meet John in order to forestall the synod’s envoys and embitter the Antiochene bishop against the Fathers—as though he himself had been slighted because the proceedings had been hastened, or a friend had been unjustly injured by the deposition, or both sees had been harassed because of their ancient disputes with Alexandria.

As soon as the Antiochene leapt down from his carriage, before the dust had even settled, he summoned the synod to his lodging. Count Candidian, who lied about everything in the assembly of the bishops just as he had in his report to the emperor, presided. After some proceedings conducted according to the prescriptions of the canons, John pronounced the judgment he and Irenaeus had devised on the road: deposition against Cyril and Memnon—the former, allegedly, because he taught the heresies of Arius, Apollinaris, and Eunomius in his chapters; the latter, because he conducted everything in the city by violence—and excommunication against all the other Fathers unless, by the appointed day, they abandoned Cyril and Memnon and crossed over to his side. Forty-three bishops subscribed the judgment. It was not made public until letters had been sent to the emperor and the empresses, and to the clergy, senate, and people of Constantinople, lest the catholic writings reveal both the character of the precipitous judgment and the falsity of the complaints.

The reason why John acted in this way is readily understood. Since he wanted to preside over the council and rule the city at his pleasure, he certainly had to refrain from deciding anything about Nestorius, so that the accused man could not sit as judge; to remove Cyril from the position he occupied by the authority both of the apostolic see and of his own see; to depose Memnon, so that he could no longer exercise any authority in the Ephesian Church. He was not very concerned about Juvenal of Jerusalem, whose see had always been subject to Antioch. Finally, John had to forestall the arrival of the envoys of the supreme pontiff, lest they bring from him any instructions that might obstruct his plans.

Meanwhile Candidian’s report had been brought to Constantinople. After reading it, Theodosius immediately sent a rescript through Palladius the Magistrian and ordered everything to be annulled as improperly done; all things were to be restored to their former state, so that the matter might proceed in due order; the doctrines were to be examined by common deliberation, so that all might agree more readily; and no one was to be permitted to leave Ephesus, whether for his homeland or for the imperial court, before everything had been properly completed, so that the matter might be brought to a conclusion. Indeed, he declared that he had written to the provincial governors ordering them neither to admit to their homeland nor to their own city anyone who departed without authorization.

The emperor’s rescript, which is said to have been issued at Constantinople on the third day before the Kalends of July, arrived at Ephesus seven or eight days later—that is, on the fourth or fifth of July. It was read to both parties, and, since Palladius was pressing them, a response was given both by the synod and by the Orientals. The response given by the holy synod is dated in the commonly circulated copies “on the Kalends of July,” but this is an error too obvious to require elaborate refutation. How could a letter issued by the emperor at Constantinople on the third day before the Kalends of July have reached Ephesus, so far away, within two days? “The Kalends” must therefore be restored to “the Nones”; nothing is more credible than that the response was given to the courier who was hurrying on his way, on the second day after his arrival—that is, on the Nones of July.

In its response the synod complained that Candidian’s tactics had so far concealed the truth from the emperor: he had not merely forestalled the synod’s envoys with his report, but had also delayed them on the road by improper means. The synod therefore asked that the emperor summon the count, together with five bishops who could explain in his presence what had been done by each side and in what manner. John of Antioch complained in his reply to the holy synod that men actually sent by the synod to Constantinople had hastened along the road in order to forestall Count Irenaeus, whom he had sent.

[Col. 0725] John therefore replied, together with his synod, to the same imperial letters. After giving an account of the proceedings against Cyril and Memnon, he requested that it be decreed that no more than two bishops be attached to each metropolitan when they came into the assembly, and that they dispute the doctrines. He also complained that the Church of Saint John had been closed to him even after the emperor’s letters, although he said that he and his party had gone there to pray for the emperor. But he deceitfully concealed the true circumstances: the doors of the church had been closed by the people and clergy because he wanted, contrary to law and justice, to install a bishop in Memnon’s place. Ephesus did not belong to the Antiochene diocese, since it was autocephalous; nor had Memnon been lawfully deposed, since he had neither been heard nor judged except by a precipitate judgment, and by a man who had no authority in the matter.

John was not content merely to reply in writing. A few days later he sent Count Irenaeus—the friend of Nestorius and the bitterest enemy of the holy synod—with new letters, so that he might oppose the synod’s envoys in the emperor’s presence.

Meanwhile, on the tenth of July, envoys from the apostolic see and the Western synod arrived at Ephesus: the presbyter Philip and the bishops Arcadius and Projectus. On the same day the second session was held, not at Saint Mary’s, as the first had been, but in the episcopal residence, since it was less a conciliar session than a reception of guests and an examination of the instructions of the apostolic see. Accordingly, nothing else was done except that, after greeting the synod, Philip requested—and the other two immediately requested on their own—that the letters of the supreme pontiff to the synod be read and that the proceedings of the earlier session be privately made available to them for examination.

Celestine’s letters were read first in Latin, out of respect for the Roman Church, and then in Greek, so that everyone might hear them. The Fathers acclaimed Celestine, and the proceedings were finally communicated to the envoys.

On the following day the Fathers met with the envoys at Saint Mary’s. First, the proceedings previously conducted in the deposition of Nestorius were read publicly. Then each of the three envoys pronounced his judgment against Nestorius separately, and the proceedings were signed. Afterward the synod reported to the emperor the arrival of the envoys and the unanimous agreement of both Churches in condemning Nestorius. It therefore requested permission to depart, as though everything had been completed. Finally, it wrote to the clergy and people of Constantinople.

The fourth session took place five days later, namely on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August. The Fathers sat at Saint Mary’s, with the deacon Hesychius of Juvenal acting as secretary; for Peter, Cyril’s presbyter, could no longer advance the synod’s business in a matter concerning his own bishop. Cyril and Memnon therefore presented a petition in which they complained before the holy synod of the injury inflicted upon them by the Orientals, and asked that John be summoned to give an account of his conduct and to prove before the synod whether he thought that either of them was chargeable with any crime or heresy.

Bishops were sent once and again to summon John. After being repulsed, they reported that his house was surrounded by soldiers who prevented access. The Fathers therefore declared that the proceedings conducted by John’s synod against Cyril and Memnon were void, and decreed that the emperor be informed of this and that John be summoned for a third time before proceedings were lawfully taken against him.

On that same day, after the summons, John ordered a document full of insults and lies to be posted in contempt of the synod—not only against Cyril and Memnon, but also against the entire assembly of the Fathers. It stated that Cyril and Memnon had been deposed for heresy, while the synod itself had been excommunicated for showing favor to heretics, until it agreed with the Orientals. By this declaration he hoped to provoke a riot by stirring up the common people; but his hope deceived him.

On the following day, while the Fathers were seated in the same place, Cyril first reported the document publicly posted by the Orientals, by which he had been brought into popular hatred on account of the heresy of Apollinaris, of whom he was said to be, together with Memnon, the chief. He then condemned Apollinaris, Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Sabellius, Photinus, Paul, the Manichaeans, and Nestorius himself, together with those who followed either Nestorius or Pelagius and Celestius. Finally, he requested that John be summoned for a third time, so that he might prove before the synod whatever he had alleged in writing.

The synod approved the request and sent three bishops with a notary to deliver its instructions to John. But John arrogantly refused to hear the envoys in person and sent his archdeacon, a man worthy of contempt, to report that it was useless to send messengers back and forth, since they would be dealing with a matter that, having been referred to the emperor, was no longer within the authority of either party. Nevertheless, the envoys were to inform two presbyters of their instructions, so that John would not be unaware of them. The synod therefore pronounced a sentence of excommunication against John and his bishops, again declared void everything done against Cyril, Memnon, and the others, and informed the emperor of the whole matter.

Nor was the matter reported only to the emperor; it was also reported to the supreme pontiff. After recounting the sequence of events, the synod further informed him of the sentence pronounced against the Celestian and Pelagian bishops. The proceedings of the Roman synod concerning those same bishops were then read. Whether they were read on this very day, while the bishops sent to John were returning—which I consider more probable—or on an earlier day, before the apostolic see had yet been informed, Cyril delivered an address against John in that assembly of the Fathers. It might seem that he had yielded somewhat to anger, unless one may reasonably believe that a mind devoted to Christ, when inflamed with zeal for the faith, could rightly pass beyond ordinary rules of speech, as the prophets did.

As affairs took this turn, John resorted to his customary tactics. He tried to occupy the emperor’s mind by means of letters, knowing him to be both a defender of the laws and a most determined avenger of disturbances. He therefore wrote that the synod had violated ecclesiastical laws; that the Fathers continued to communicate with bishops who had been deposed for heresy; that they had publicly celebrated the sacred mysteries although they had been barred on account of excommunication; and that, although they had been deprived of every legal right, they had pronounced both a sentence of absolution in favor of Cyril and Memnon and a sentence of condemnation against John and his associates, whom the counts had praised; and that men of this sort did and dared everything with unrestrained arrogance.

He therefore requested that the synod be summoned either to Constantinople, where the emperor’s presence would compel everyone to act peacefully, or at least to Nicomedia, from which messages could be conveyed more quickly to the imperial city. He also renewed his earlier request, craftily, that no more than two bishops be added to each metropolitan. He asked that the Nicene faith—an exemplar of which he placed before his letter, together with the proceedings of his own synod condemning Cyril’s chapters as imbued with heretical meaning—be subscribed by everyone in its pure form, and that no one be permitted to say either that Christ was merely a man or that the deity was passible.

Two facts are established by this letter and the associated proceedings.
