First, the holy synod had already sent bishops to the emperor. “Constantly observing the decrees of Your Piety,” John says, “we did not send the most pious bishops there, as those men did who readily dare everything; rather, we communicated what was necessary by letter.” Second, a third set of letters had already arrived from the emperor. John continues: “When, in the second and third letters sent by our most pious emperors, it was commanded that the Churches of God everywhere be joined together by the bond of peace,” and so forth.

John also wrote one letter to the prefect, another to the master of offices, and a third to the praepositus Scholasticus. From this we can understand which patrons the Nestorian faction had at court and what sort of men they were: Antiochus, the *patricius* and consul; Valerius, master of the offices, who held the consulship in the following year; and Scholasticus, praepositus of the sacred bedchamber. Nestorius had an old relationship with the first two, for he had entrusted to them his letters to Saint Celestine when they were being sent from the East to the emperor Valentinian. Both of John’s letters contain several matters worthy of notice.

Count Irenaeus, whom John had sent to the emperor, seems to have reached Constantinople around the twentieth of July. He did indeed arrive as quickly as possible, but the envoys sent by the synod had preceded him by three days and had meanwhile brought most of the leading men over to the better side. Nevertheless, through Irenaeus’ contrivances, the truth was obscured by clouds of lies, and many wavered in the opinion they had formed. Various disputes arose on both sides, and people’s judgments shifted as the partisanship of the factions drove the undecided now here, now there.

In the end, many thought it best that those sent by the synod and Irenaeus should appear together before the emperor to debate the dispute; this was done by order of Theodosius. But what actually came of it was not disclosed by the envoys. Irenaeus certainly congratulated himself on the outcome of the hearing in a letter to the Orientals, as though he had succeeded in ensuring that, of the three men whom one side or the other had deposed, only Cyril would remain deprived of office—or even that the emperor had immediately sent his deprivation to the holy Church of God, which amounted to a form of publication.

But when John the physician and Cyril’s syncellus arrived—sent, I think, to announce John’s deposition—another great change in circumstances and opinions took place, so that the leading men were now drawn into various judgments. “Some,” Irenaeus writes, “affirm that what has been done on both sides ought at present to remain valid, and therefore that not merely two persons, as had sometimes seemed the case, but three depositions ought to be confirmed. Others think that the deprivation of all should be annulled equally, but that some of the most pious bishops ought to be summoned here, so that the doctrine of the faith may be carefully examined by the rule of truth and the things done at Ephesus contrary to law and justice may be investigated. There are also men who are exerting themselves with the greatest zeal and moving every stone so that they may be allowed to leave Ephesus with definite decrees from the most pious emperor, claiming that they will learn everything and settle it as far as they can. Those who love you earnestly plead that this not happen, knowing for certain what sort of minds are behind these efforts and not being unaware from whom they received this plan.”

The last proposal prevailed: someone from among the leading men was to be sent with suitable decrees and instructed in Theodosius’ name to order that three men—Cyril, Memnon, and Nestorius—had been deposed, and to compel all of them to meet in a single synod and peacefully settle the remaining matters.

Count John of the Sacred Office was therefore sent, bearing letters from the emperor individually addressed to all the bishops of both parties, so that, since they were to be heard by everyone together, the process of assembling one synod might begin. A letter from Acacius of Beroea to the emperor was also sent with the imperial letters. Acacius had offered advice for establishing peace, suited to his own character, his inclination toward Nestorius, and his hatred of Cyril. The emperor’s letter bears no date, but it must have been issued a few days before the end of July.

On the twenty-second of July the Fathers met with the envoys in the episcopal residence. They decided that the testimonies extracted from various Fathers by Peter, chief of the notaries, ought to be entered into the proceedings. These testimonies concerned the interpretation of the Nicene faith, insofar as it was relevant to the question under discussion.

Then Charisius, presbyter and steward of the Church of Philadelphia, complained before the synod and presented a petition requesting that the judgment of his bishop Theophanes be reconsidered. He had been barred from communion because he had opposed the presbyters James and Antony, who had been sent by Anastasius and Photius, the assistants of Nestorius, with letters to the bishops of Lydia. These men were spreading the thoroughly impious creed of Theodore and were demanding that it be signed by those returning to the Church from the heresy of the Quartodecimans.

Charisius was acquitted by the synod, and Theodore’s creed was condemned. That famous law was enacted which in later centuries provoked so many disputes: no other formula of faith was to be composed apart from the one issued by the Fathers at Nicaea. The holy synod decreed that no one might produce, write, or compose another faith apart from that defined by the holy Fathers who had assembled at Nicaea with the Holy Spirit. If anyone dared either to compose another faith or to produce or offer one to those wishing to turn to the knowledge of the truth—whether from paganism, Judaism, or any heresy whatsoever—the synod decreed that, if they were bishops or clerics, they should be alienated from the episcopate or clergy; if they were laymen, they should be subjected to anathema.

On the day before the Kalends of August—in the commonly circulated copies, the day before the Kalends of September—before Count John had arrived at Ephesus, the Fathers were seated in the church called Saint Mary’s. Rheginus, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, seizing a suitable opportunity, presented a petition to the synod complaining that the Church of Antioch was arrogating to itself, contrary to the Nicene canons, authority over the island of Cyprus, although from apostolic times the metropolitan had been ordained by the synod of the entire province. The synod prohibited any innovation and ordered that the sixth Nicene canon be observed, with everyone content within the boundaries of his own diocese.

Yet Rheginus does not seem to have acted in good faith with the Fathers, nor do the Fathers appear to have been particularly concerned to preserve the rights of John of Antioch, whom they saw obstinately clinging to the enemy of Christ.

Meanwhile, Count John of the Sacred Office reached Ephesus with remarkable speed. After greeting the bishops of both parties, he summoned everyone to his lodging for the following day. To prevent an outbreak of violence at the entrance, since tempers had already been inflamed, he prescribed the order in which they were to enter.

John of Antioch and Nestorius arrived with their parties almost at dawn. Cyril also arrived with other bishops; illness kept Memnon at home. At first an argument, almost a battle, arose. Some denied that Nestorius ought to be present when the emperor’s letters were read; others insisted on the contrary and rejected Cyril. But the count forcibly removed Cyril and Nestorius, read the letters, and, while the parties were by no means quiet, announced the deposition of Nestorius and handed him over to Count Candidian for custody. Cyril and Memnon were entrusted to Count James. He immediately informed the emperor of everything done on the first day and added that the bishops’ minds appeared irreconcilable and impossible to pacify. The report was made on the day after his arrival.

The holy synod was extraordinarily disturbed by the count’s action and wrote two letters to the emperor. The first begins: “Your Majesty, wishing to confirm piety…” The second begins: “Your Most Christian Majesty, most pious emperors…”

In the second letter the synod first complained that the emperor had been falsely informed that the deposition of Cyril and Memnon had been approved by the holy synod and that the names of Catholics had been mixed with the names of schismatics in the superscription. It then declared that it could in no way communicate with the Orientals until they themselves subscribed to the deposition of Nestorius and withdrew the accusations they had maliciously brought against the synod. Finally, it requested that Cyril and Memnon be restored to it, that the faith be clearly explained and preserved in the written records, and that more men not attached to either party be sent to advise the emperor sincerely.

The same synod also sent a letter to the bishops residing in Constantinople and to the other presbyters and deacons of the city. It complained above all that it was not permitted to write to Constantinople so that the truth might become known:

“Let Your Piety know that we inhabit Ephesus altogether as though it were a prison. For three months now we have been confined here so tightly that we cannot freely and without danger send anyone, whether by sea or by land, either to the pious court or to any other place. Whenever it has happened that the messages we sent have been delivered, the messengers, in order to escape six hundred dangers to their lives, have been forced to disguise themselves in one form after another.”

The letter then recounts the calumnies fabricated against the synod by its opponents:

“But the reason why we are guarded with such care is nothing other than that everything against us is falsely reported to the most pious emperors. Some, as we understand, accuse us before the pious ears of the Augusti as though we were authors of sedition. Others have dared to suggest that our ecumenical synod had deposed Cyril, the most holy and God-beloved archbishop of Alexandria, and our most holy and God-devoted fellow bishop Memnon. Some perhaps have not been afraid to add that we wished to enter into friendly conversation with the assembly of secession, whose leader is John of Antioch. We are therefore guarded with such diligence lest these things become known.”

Finally, after praising the steadfastness of all his companions, who preferred to follow the exiled Cyril rather than cling to John, the letter urged the recipients to ask the emperor either to summon some of the bishops who might speak openly or to dismiss everyone to their own Churches, lest they perish from the grievous sufferings weighing upon them:

“Inform the emperor and entreat him, so that, taking pity on us, he may at last recall us from this splendid prison. If we are indeed worthy to see the face of the most pious and Christ-loving emperor, let him order this to be done; but if we are judged unworthy of such a privilege, at least let him permit us to return to our Churches, lest we all perish here, some consumed by illness and others by grief.”

A memorandum was added, addressed by name, I think, to Dalmatius the archimandrite. It could move even the hardest heart to compassion:

“We are being destroyed by the heat, since the air is oppressive, and almost every day someone is buried,” and so forth.

That the synod wrote two letters to the emperor—something which some have called into question—and the order and content of each are not as commonly known, is clearly shown by letters that Cyril sent from his confinement: one to the clergy and people of Constantinople, in which he chiefly warned two of his friends, Dalmatius the most holy archimandrite and Alipius the presbyter of the apostles, both men of great authority with the emperor, about what was being prepared and what needed to be done; and another to three bishops of his own diocese who were staying in the imperial city, Theopemptus, Daniel, and Potamion.

These are the letters which, enclosed with the memorandum, a beggar carried concealed in a reed, in order to evade the tactics of the Orientals, who through their friends were preventing anything from being brought from the holy synod to Constantinople that might harm their interests.

[Col. 0731] What the count of bribes accomplished afterward is clear from Cyril’s letter to the clergy and people of Constantinople:

“When the aforesaid most magnificent man tried everything in order that John and those with him might be received into communion with the holy synod, they have not endured even to hear such a proposal down to the present day. Rather, they resist completely and say: ‘It is impossible for us to come to this unless what they have done contrary to law is annulled, unless they come as suppliants to the synod as men who have committed an offense, and unless they anathematize in writing Nestorius and his doctrines.’ The entire insistence of the synod rests upon these demands.

“When that most magnificent man whom we mentioned was disappointed in this hope, he devised another plan. He asked the holy synod to provide him with a written exposition of the faith, so that, when they too had agreed and subscribed at his urging, he might return and say: ‘I have reconciled men who were divided by personal offenses.’ When the holy synod understood this, it rose again and declared plainly: ‘We do not wish to inflict this insult upon ourselves. We were not summoned here as heretics; we came to establish the faith, which was wavering and under attack, and we have established it. Nor is it necessary for the emperor now to learn the faith, since he knows it and was baptized in it.’ Thus even this plan did not succeed with the Orientals.”

Cyril gave this letter after it became known at Ephesus that Count John had not reported everything accurately, but before the seven men from each side had been summoned to Constantinople—therefore around the middle of August. About this time the summons ought to have been brought to Ephesus, and Nestorius should have been given permission to go wherever he wished and to relieve the pain of his deposition in whatever retreat pleased him. Cyril and Memnon, however, were to remain in custody while their case was investigated and judged by the emperor after bishops from both parties had debated it.

Theodosius adopted this plan partly because Count John himself had reported that Nestorius had been lawfully deprived of office; partly because those who wielded influence in the palace, unable to rescue Nestorius from the sentence he deserved, were trying by courtly artifices to involve Cyril and Memnon in the same disgrace and to lessen their friend’s dishonor through association with men who were not guilty; and finally because of the emperor’s religious disposition, which had been moved by the counsels of the most holy archimandrite Dalmatius and by the most serious appeal of the clergy of Constantinople.

Envoys from both sides were therefore ordered to come to the imperial city. They do not seem to have delayed setting out, and probably departed around the twentieth of August, for the Orientals state in their letters to their associates that they were at Chalcedon on the fourth of September.

The holy synod chose the presbyter Philip and the bishops Arcadius, Juvenal, Flavian, Firmus, Theodotus, Acacius, and Evoptius. To these men, as they were about to depart, it gave a letter to the emperor and four instructions to observe.

First, they were to secure the safety of Cyril and Memnon. Second, they were not to join John and his associates, since those men had refused to depose Nestorius with the synod, had dared to condemn Cyril and Memnon contrary to the canons, had defended Nestorian and Celestian doctrines to no small extent, and had not hesitated to stigmatize the synod of the whole world as heretical. Third, if Theodosius ordered them to communicate with the Orientals, they were to obey, but on these conditions: that the Orientals subscribe to the condemnation of Nestorius; ask forgiveness in a petition for what they had done against the presidents of the synod; condemn the doctrines of Nestorius and his followers; and cooperate with the synod in restoring Cyril and Memnon to their dignity. Fourth, they were not to promise communion before the presidents had been restored, and meanwhile were to report everything to the synod. At the end it was added that, if they did not obey these instructions, the synod would neither regard what they did as valid nor admit them afterward into its communion.

The Oriental faction sent the same number of bishops from its side: John of Antioch, a second John of Damascus, Himerius, Paul, Macarius, Apringius, and Theodoret. Although it granted them full authority to conduct the proceedings, it nevertheless instructed them to ensure by every means that Cyril’s chapters were rejected as heretical and alien to the catholic and apostolic Church.

Attached to the instructions was a petition to the emperor, in which they implored him, by everything sacred, not to permit anyone to subscribe with impunity to any other formula of faith besides the Nicene Creed. They also asked that each man submit his opinion on the disputed questions in writing to the emperor, so that, if he later asserted anything contrary, he could be challenged by his own statement. In this way there would be one agreement among all, and two free opinions about the questions would not be permitted; rather, the entire matter would be settled by debate. If this could not be achieved in the emperor’s presence, they claimed that they should be free to return to their Churches.

They further accused Juvenal of Jerusalem of trying by improper means to bring Phoenicia Secunda and Arabia over to Cyril’s side. They were distressed that this one patriarch in particular had not been formally accused.

A letter survives written on 13 August to the holy synod by the seven bishops Eulalius, Eutrechius, Acacius, Chrysaphius, Jeremiah, Theodulus, and Isaiah, who were staying in Constantinople. In writing they testified to their zeal in defending the faith before the Fathers, as men who were vigorously conducting the matter in the city, encouraging the Fathers at Ephesus to bring the victory courageously to completion, and prepared to request permission to come to Ephesus and provide assistance if the synod wished. They therefore asked that instructions be sent to them for carrying on the common cause.

Dalmatius also wrote to the holy synod in the same sense. Since the letter has not yet been published, it seems appropriate to reproduce it in full, first in Greek as it appears in the Vatican manuscript and then in Latin. It runs as follows.

### Letter sent to the holy synod in the city of Ephesus by Dalmatius, the most holy archimandrite

I received the letter sent to me by the holy synod, and, learning what it contained, I was first of all deeply grieved on account of the circumstances and afflictions that have befallen you. For it was written in the letter that some of the holy Fathers living there had died because of the confinement.

But know this: I am ready to fulfill every command of yours, and in no respect have I overlooked, neglected, or disregarded anything—especially since the matter concerns the orthodox faith and is pleasing to God. For no one can depart from the living God and devise other plans. Those who rightly handle the word of God’s truth possess life both in this age and in the age to come; but those who depart from God’s grace are accursed and cast into the outer darkness, as are Nestorius and those who share his mind.

For God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ has made the whole holy synod radiant and built it up, and has accepted our labors and our sweat. We therefore give thanks to God, who has prospered your way and granted you victory on behalf of the faith. Pray for me, I beg your holiness.

### Latin version

I received the letter sent to me by the holy synod, and, reading what it contained, I was first of all deeply grieved because of the evils that have befallen you. For it was written in the letter that some of the holy Fathers living there had perished because of the confinement.

For the rest, know that I shall promptly fulfill any commands of yours, and that until now I have passed over nothing. I neither carelessly neglect anything nor am I unconcerned, especially since the matter concerns the orthodox faith and God. No one can fall away from the living God and adopt other plans.

Those who rightly handle the word of truth (2 Tim. 2:15) possess the life of God both in this age and in the future; but those who fall away from God’s grace are cast into the outer darkness (Matt. 8:12), as are Nestorius and those who share his opinions. For God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, has been pleased with the holy synod and cares for it all as his own building; he regards your labors and sweat as pleasing. We therefore give thanks to God, who has led you along the right path and granted you victory on behalf of the faith. Pray for me, I beg your holiness.

In the same Vatican manuscript there is also the synod’s reply to Dalmatius. It is brief if considered by itself, but it contains an inserted passage, as it were an appendix, concerning the supreme administration of the monasteries of the imperial city, which had been conferred upon Dalmatius. I have thought it should be disregarded because of its historical unreliability (*anistoria*). The synod replies as follows.

### Copy of the letter sent by the holy synod to the lord Dalmatius

The holy and ecumenical synod assembled in the metropolis of the Ephesians at the command of Theodosius and Valentinian, the most pious and Christ-loving emperors, received the letter sent by Dalmatius, the most holy archimandrite and father of the monks. It learned that he had been moved with great zeal, had left his cell after forty-eight years, gone to the most pious and Christ-loving emperor, and instructed him concerning everything that had followed and been accomplished by the holy synod regarding the deposition of the impious Nestorius.

We gave thanks to Christ, our true God, who moved you in this way to support the sound doctrine of our faith and to make our labors and sweat manifest, not only to the most pious emperors, but also to the most holy archimandrites and to all the Christ-loving clergy and people. For what other human being contributed to us except your holiness? The truth was revealed by no one other than you—that is, by the lord Dalmatius. For this reason we all extend our hands in prayer to the humane and good God, asking for the flourishing life and safety of our most pious emperors and of your holiness.

We therefore exhort you to continue to contribute more fully to our cause and to take our place there in the matters concerning the faith that arise. For we have learned that, even before Nestorius appeared in Constantinople, God revealed to you what was in his heart, and that you used to say to all who came to your cell: “Take heed to yourselves, brothers, for an evil beast has come to this city and is about to injure many by his teaching.”

May the holy and consubstantial Trinity preserve you sound in soul and body as you praise Christ, our God. Pray earnestly for us, most holy brother.

### Copy of the letter sent by the holy synod to the lord Dalmatius

When the holy and ecumenical synod, assembled in the metropolis of the Ephesians at the command of Theodosius and Valentinian, the most religious and Christ-loving emperors, received the letter sent by Dalmatius, the most holy archimandrite and father of the monks, and learned that he had been moved by great zeal, had left his cell after forty-eight years, gone to the most pious and Christian emperor, and taught him everything that had followed and been accomplished by the holy synod concerning the deposition of the impious Nestorius,

we gave thanks to Christ, our true God, who moved you in this way to support the sound doctrine of our faith and to make our labors and sweat manifest, not only to the most pious emperors, but also to the most holy archimandrites and to all the Christ-loving clergy and people. For what other human being brought us assistance apart from your holiness? Since the truth was made manifest by no one except you—that is, by the lord Dalmatius—we all therefore stretch out our hands in supplication to the benevolent and good God for the prosperous life and safety of our most pious emperors and of your holiness.

We exhort you, therefore, to join us in accomplishing still more and to take our place there in the matters concerning the faith that arise. Although no exhortation is necessary, we know that God revealed to you what Nestorius was harboring in his heart before he openly ravaged Constantinople, and that even then you were accustomed to say to all who were in the monastery: “Take heed, brothers, for an evil beast is ravaging this city and infecting many with his teaching.”

May the holy and consubstantial Trinity preserve you safe in mind and body as you proclaim Christ, our God. Pray for us, most holy brother.

When the envoys of the parties reached Chalcedon toward the end of August, they were ordered to remain there because of the monks who were causing disturbances—if Theodoretus is to be trusted in giving this explanation. There they learned by report that Nestorius had been dismissed from Ephesus eight days before their arrival and permitted to go wherever he wished. Since this was no slight prejudice to the case, it brought as much joy and good hope to the Catholics as it brought grief and fear to the Orientals, because Theodosius seemed to be inclining toward the better side.

“After we came to Chalcedon—for neither we nor our opponents were permitted to enter Constantinople because of the disturbances caused by the good monks—we learned by report,” Theodoretus says, “that eight days before we appeared, the lord Nestorius had been dismissed from Ephesus to go wherever he wished. We were therefore deeply grieved, since the things done there unlawfully and without judgment now appeared to have gained strength.”

On the fourth of September, the legates of the Easterners wrote to their associates at Ephesus. On that day the emperor was expected to pass from Chalcedon to the Rufinian estate, where he had decided to hear the case. And indeed, after summoning them there, he heard them not once but a fourth time, indeed even a fifth, and apparently with sufficient benevolence. Hence they prematurely congratulated themselves on victory in letters sent to their associates at Ephesus.

For they reported that the matters they had presented had been accepted by the emperor, while those presented by the synod’s legates had been rejected; that they themselves had reproached Acacius for saying that the Godhead was passible, and that Theodosius had recoiled from so great a blasphemy; that he had ordered each party to submit its opinion in writing, and that they had proposed no other faith than that of Nicaea; that, with the emperor’s approval, the people were flocking to him from Constantinople and earnestly begging them to fight vigorously for the faith, and that they could scarcely restrain them from harming their opponents.

The Easterners in the city of Ephesus congratulated their legates on so happy an outcome of the struggle. At the same time, they warned them that the Fathers of the Catholic synod—whom they called the Egyptians—were conducting themselves just as before: judging cases, of which many were being brought before them; providing for various churches; and so forth. They also sent them two copies, subscribed by themselves, of the Nicene confession of faith, together with an exposition of the chapters recently composed by Cyril, and also a petition to be presented to the emperor.

In this petition, after thanking the emperor humbly for the favor he had shown them, they pleaded abjectly on behalf of Nestorius, whose name they concealed because they had heard that it was displeasing to the emperor. What could be more abject than these words?

> We pray and prostrate ourselves before your feet, that your piety may receive us as we humble ourselves with long-suffering, and as we make a just petition on behalf of the injured person against those who have accepted Cyril’s heretical chapters, etc.

They further instructed their legates to do everything in their power on Nestorius’s behalf and never, in their own name, to consent to the restoration of Cyril and Memnon unless the chapters were condemned. They execrated them to such a degree that they would not accept even one of them, even if death were threatened.

After several days, the surge of their thoughtless rejoicing was checked. When the emperor returned to the city, the legates of the Catholic synod were ordered to accompany him, so that they might ordain the bishop of Constantinople, while the Easterners were left at Chalcedon. The latter sent a petition to Theodosius, asking that no ordination take place before the doctrines had been examined; otherwise, they predicted, great evils would arise from what they were perhaps plotting. They said:

> We have judged it necessary to inform your piety by the present letter, before God and Christ himself and the Holy Spirit, that if anyone is ordained before the orthodox doctrines have been examined by those who hold heretical opinions, the whole Church must necessarily be divided, with clergy and people alike at variance. For none of the devout will endure that communion be granted to those who worship heresy, and that their own salvation be annihilated.
>
> But if these things are to occur, your piety will then be compelled to act contrary to your own intention. For schism will grow despite your decision, and it will grieve those who contend for piety, since they cannot endure that their souls should perish and that the impious doctrines of Cyril, which they seek to justify, should prevail among contentious men.
>
> Many who are devoted to piety—and all of us from the Eastern diocese, as well as those from your province, from the dioceses of Pontus, Asia, Thrace, Illyricum, and Italy—will not permit Cyril’s doctrines to be admitted. They have also sent your piety the book of the most blessed Ambrose, which teaches against this superstition now springing up.
>
> Therefore, lest this happen and your piety be further disturbed, we beg, entreat, and implore you to decree that no ordination take place until the orthodox faith has been established.

The petition received no other response than that the legates of the Easterners and their associates at Ephesus were given permission to return to their own churches. When they learned this, they sent the emperor a third petition, filled not only with anger but also with irrational reproach and even shameless threats.

They dared to accuse Theodosius, first, of having deceived them:

> We were summoned to confirm the faith of the holy Fathers; yet we have been detained at Chalcedon until the present day, and now we are being dismissed to our own places.

Second, they accused him of despising the Easterners more than others:

> Moreover, you are not merely their king but ours as well; for the East is no small portion of your kingdom.

Third, they accused him of betraying the faith for political reasons:

> Let your majesty not despise the faith which is being adulterated, into which both you and your ancestors were baptized, and which you now need in the war by which you are pressing Africa.

[Col. 0737] Fourth, they accused him of making himself liable to eternal condemnation:

> Those who have been permitted to retain their churches are killing the souls of those who approach them, and of anyone who wishes to listen to them.

Finally, they accused him of behaving as one who ought to be treated like those who reject the word of God and persecute the apostles:

> If, after this our supplication, your piety does not accept this teaching given before God, we too shall shake the dust from our feet and cry out with blessed Paul: “We are pure from your blood” (Acts 20:26).

This petition also accomplished nothing. Therefore, after receiving permission to depart, they informed their associates at Ephesus of the state of affairs: the cause of Nestorius was plainly desperate, since no one could tolerate his name; the Cyrillians had deceived everyone by tyranny, frauds, flattery, and gifts; and they had scarcely obtained from the emperor, by their entreaties, permission to return to their own churches—but on the condition that both the Egyptian and Memnon of Ephesus should remain in their respective places.

For, they said:

> In this way the Egyptian will be able to blind everyone with his gifts; in this way, although he has committed countless evils, he will return to his throne, while this innocent man will scarcely be dismissed to his own dwelling.

Before departing from Chalcedon, however, Theodoret delivered a highly virulent speech in which, in the name of the legates, he bade farewell to the supporters of Nestorius who had crossed to Chalcedon to hear him speak. He said:

> You have dared to cross the terrifying waves of the Propontis in order to hear our voice, which you regard as the likeness of the voice of your shepherd. You desire to hear the pleasant melodies of your shepherd’s pipe—the shepherd whose fellow shepherds have slain him with their reeds, etc.

John, who was present, according to custom took up the speaker’s words. In bidding the audience a final farewell, he inflamed them to obstinacy in their error, slandering the Catholics as though they said that the Godhead was passible and that the nature of the body and the Godhead had become one—an accusation which Theodoret had also made earlier.

> It is a sacred law, said John, that what belongs to sons should be credited to their fathers. Gilead, therefore, is mine, and Manasseh is mine; indeed, they are not mine but God’s, who has brought your Church together with ours and has bestowed this zeal for piety, together with other gifts. I rose among you for this reason: to greet you while also bidding you farewell. For we are with you as we contend against our brothers.

What the ecumenical synod received from its legates has not, so far as I know, been reported in writing. Yet it can be understood from the fact that, after their difficult struggle with the enemies of Christ, the Fathers returned to their churches like victorious commanders, crowned with laurels after winning the battle. Cyril himself arrived at Alexandria on 30 October, which, according to the Egyptians, was the third day of the month Athyr, where he was received by his people as the leader of a triumphant army.

Indeed, in his nineteenth homily, in which he announced the date of Easter for the year 432, he seems to have sung a kind of victory hymn for himself. Yet, out of a concern for modesty, he softened it with allegorical figures, just as he had done with the previous year’s trumpet-call. He said:

> Appropriately, we too shall once again employ for you what the lyre of the Psalmist sang in ancient times: “Clap your hands, all nations; shout to God with a voice of rejoicing” (Psalm 46:2).

That is, let us sing a song of victory to Christ, for he has conquered the world on our behalf (Colossians 2:15), since he himself says—and has triumphed over—“the principalities, the authorities, and the rulers of this world’s darkness, the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (1 Corinthians 15:24). In this way he rescued us from their cruelty and freed us from our ancient crimes, nailing to the cross “the bond that stood against us” (Colossians 2:14), so that, rejoicing for this very reason, we may say: “Where is your victory, O death?” (Hosea 13:14).

Four months after Nestorius’s abdication had elapsed. On 25 October, the eighth day before the Kalends of November, which was a Sunday, a synod of bishops ordained Maximianus bishop of the imperial city. Some had been sent from Ephesus by the Catholics; others had perhaps been found at Constantinople or had come from the province itself. Maximianus had been a monk and a presbyter, not especially cultivated in literary studies, but proven in faith, devoted to peace, and dedicated to works of piety.

He was displeasing to no party among the clergy; indeed, he was especially acceptable to the Apostolic See, whose legates were present, because he had laid the first foundations of his sacred service in the Roman Church. This was why he was preferred to Proclus and Philip—men otherwise outstanding in learning and piety, but favored by rival parties among the clergy.

Immediately after the ordination, the synod sent letters, as usual, to the principal sees and also to the bishops of Old Epirus, whom the schismatics were attempting to deceive, as though they enjoyed communion with the holy synod although they had not withdrawn from their former position. For this reason, the canons read in the seventh session were sent to them, so that they might be informed of what had been decreed against the schismatics and Nestorians and of the penalty subsequently established for those who dared to communicate with them.

Together with the synod’s letter addressed to Cyril at Alexandria, the new bishop appended a personal letter in which he praised the holy confessor of Christ according to his merits and asked either to be strengthened by the prayers of so great a prelate, instructed by his counsel, or bound to him by an everlasting bond of charity.

He also added his own letters to both the synodal and imperial letters addressed to the most exalted pontiff, Saint Celestine. John the presbyter and Epictetus the deacon undertook to deliver all of them. So far as I know, those three letters no longer exist; nevertheless, they are mentioned in Celestine’s replies to each of them. From this we learn that the bearers of the letters arrived in Rome by the Lord’s Nativity; that the emperor’s letters, and others as I suppose, were read before the great assembly at Saint Peter’s; and that they were received with the highest rejoicing of all.

> We received my devout sons, John the presbyter and Epictetus the deacon, messengers of so great a matter, with the rejoicing of the whole Church. After your piety’s letters had been read before the entire assembly of the Christian people at the blessed Apostle Peter’s, we offered vows to our God on your behalf. For, by the Lord’s action, they reached us in such a way that they arrived on the very day on which we celebrate the birth, according to the flesh, of Christ our God—the very matter that was being disputed—and the whole assembly refuted the impiety of those who had been convicted.

When the Easterners learned that no account had been taken of their protest and that Maximianus had been ordained, [Col. 0739] each departed for his own province, resolved never to enter into communion either with the Alexandrians or with the Constantinopolitans. For they alleged that Cyril had been lawfully deposed by them, as it seemed to them, and that Maximianus had been improperly ordained after his predecessor had been unlawfully driven out. Hence, whereas until then only two conditions for making peace had been required—agreement to Nestorius’s deposition and condemnation of his errors—a third was added as well: approval of Maximianus’s ordination.

## Year 432

Why, then, did the clergy of the imperial city wait nearly three months for the pontiff’s reply? The cause was undoubtedly Celestine’s illness: twenty-two days after writing the letters, he departed to God.

In these letters the vigilance of the most holy pontiff shines forth in advancing the peace of the Church; his apostolic vigor in overthrowing heresies; his devotion to discipline against minds stubborn in error; his gentleness toward penitents; and his paternal affection toward all.

Yet one thing was lacking to the prayers of the excellent old man, who desired to depart and be with Christ: something like the necessary completion of his victory, namely, peace for the Church, communion between the Antiochenes and the others, and Nestorius’s removal beyond the limits of future danger. He requested this from the emperor in words as forceful as those of the supreme pontiff:

> We beseech and ask, invoking him whom you worship through your faith, that you provide the weapons which you are accustomed to provide. Now every safeguard must be set in place, lest the ravenous wolf, excluded from the sheepfolds of the Lord’s flock after raging against them, return by a serpent’s winding path to the destruction of souls, digging tunnels wherever he can. For he cannot rest, since in his fury he longs to lie upon his prey.
>
> Provide protection for the healthy and remedies for those who are being healed. Enclose the truth of the Catholic faith within the walls of your religious devotion, so that believers may be protected by them and the followers of so great an error may not dare to enter. This is the full fruit of your victory: to leave nothing that the Church of God must again fear.
>
> Therefore, let your clemency remove from every association the man whom the judgment of all the priests has expelled, yet who persists in sacrilegious preaching, so that he may have no opportunity to destroy anyone.

The pious prince ought not to have allowed the prayers of the excellent Father to be ineffectual. Therefore, after consulting Maximianus and other bishops, as well as the clergy of the Church of Constantinople, he wrote [Col. 0741] to John of Antioch, Acacius of Beroea, and Symeon Stylites concerning the establishment of peace with Cyril: to John, that he should enter into harmony; to the other two, that by their prayers before God and their counsels they should press the matter forward.

Aristolaus, a tribune sent with authority, delivered the emperor’s letters. He was to compel both bishops either to agree personally to the terms of peace or to come to Nicomedia, where they would remain without hope of seeing the emperor until they became reconciled.

The imperial decree bears no precise date. It is nevertheless clear that it was issued in April, because when it was issued the death of Celestine—which occurred on 6 April—had not yet been heard of at Constantinople. The emperor said:

> While the bishops mentioned above were promising that, if you subscribed to the deposition of Nestorius and anathematized his teaching, every cause of dispute would immediately be removed, Cyril, the most holy bishop of Alexandria, together with his people, and the most holy Celestine, bishop of glorious Rome, and all the other priests of the orthodox faith everywhere would return to communion with your piety, etc.

Upon receiving these commands, John convened a council at Acacius of Beroea’s residence. Either Acacius was then at Antioch, as was his custom, or John himself went to Beroea with his bishops to visit the old man. We have inferred this in its proper place from Theodoret’s words.

When the imperial documents were read in the council—documents ordering agreement to Nestorius’s deposition and the condemnation of his doctrines, and thus acknowledging Cyril’s victory—the minds of the Easterners were astonishingly disturbed. After deliberation, however, they decided not to carry out the orders until every art of deception had been exhausted.

It was therefore determined that John himself should conduct the business of peace and should not, on any account, allow himself to be compelled to go to Nicomedia. Cyril, meanwhile, was to be cunningly forced into conditions that would safeguard the honor of the Easterners: namely, that all his writings should be abolished and that all should subscribe to the single Nicene confession.

Cyril says (Letter to Acacius):

> After the imperial decree had been presented to the Easterners, and after they had represented it as issued according to the opinion of those bishops from their party who were at Constantinople, they assembled in some council—I do not know what council—with the most holy and pious bishop Acacius of Beroea, and arranged to have written to me the terms of the agreement, that is, of the peace of the holy Churches. They claimed that peace ought not to be made except in the manner which they themselves prescribed.
>
> Their demand, however, was burdensome and troublesome. They wanted everything I had published in letters, tomes, or books to be abolished, and they wanted to agree only with the faith issued by our holy Fathers at Nicaea.

Such absurd conditions seemed designed to be proposed in private letters written by Acacius of Beroea to Cyril, as though he were acting as an intermediary for peace. If accepted, Cyril would appear to have lost his victory because of the authority of the writer; if rejected, there would be an opportunity to slander Cyril as an enemy of peace and to attempt another route by which he could be compelled, even against his will.

Acacius wrote as had been decided. Cyril says:

> I replied to those proposals as follows: We all adhere to the exposition of faith issued by the Nicene Fathers, without in any way weakening anything contained in it; for everything in it has been handed down rightly and blamelessly, and after that exposition of the faith it is not safe to investigate anything further with excessive curiosity.
>
> But what we have rightly written against the blasphemies of Nestorius is of such a character that no argument can persuade us to deny that it was rightly written. It is therefore more necessary that they themselves, in accordance with the decree of the most pious and Christ-loving emperor—or rather, with the decree of the holy synod of Ephesus—should expel the man who fought against the glory of Christ the Savior, attack his impious blasphemies with an anathema, consent to his deposition, and approve the ordination of the most holy and pious bishop Maximianus.

When the Easterners had been frustrated in their hope, they again resorted to stratagems. Cyril relates them as follows:

> After receiving these letters, they sent to Alexandria the most religious and pious bishop Paul of Emesa. He discussed those matters with me at length, namely, the things that had been said and done at Ephesus contrary to justice and duty.
>
> Since those matters seemed better consigned to oblivion, and attention ought rather to be devoted to matters of greater importance and weight, I asked whether he had brought any letter from the most pious bishop John. Immediately he handed me a letter, but it did not contain what it ought to have contained, nor had it been dictated in an appropriate manner. It conveyed irritation rather than exhortation.
>
> I therefore did not accept it. For although they ought to have softened by some apology the distress of mind which I had suffered because of what had preceded and of what they themselves had done at Ephesus, they did the opposite: they said that they too had been rightly angered against me because of their zeal for the sacred doctrines.
>
> But they heard from me that divine zeal had not moved them, nor had they drawn up their battle line against me because they were fighting for the doctrines of truth. Rather, they had yielded to the flatteries of men and sought the friendships of those who then seemed powerful.

Nor did Paul himself abstain from fraud. Although he brought letters filled with complaints, he nevertheless presented himself as prepared, in his own name and in the name of all the Easterners, to fulfill the three things Cyril demanded. He did so cunningly, however, so that Cyril would appear to have obtained pardon for what had been done rather than to have granted it, and so that the Easterners could claim that they were concealing Paul’s action rather than approving or authorizing it.

Cyril explains how he exposed the fraud in these words (Letter to Donatus):

> When I had sent these letters, they realized that they could not receive communion unless they first completed what they ought to do. Therefore they sent to Alexandria Paul, the most reverend and religious bishop of Emesa, to bring me a letter concerning the restoration of communion. The letter, however, was not properly composed, for it presented certain complaints against us, as though some things had been said or done in the holy council neither rightly nor properly.
>
> I did not accept such a letter but replied: Since they ought to have asked pardon for their former offenses, how do they dare to inflict new insults?
>
> When [Col. 0743] the aforementioned most pious bishop excused what had occurred and affirmed under oath that this was not their intention, but that they had proceeded to write in this way out of the simple sincerity of their hearts, I accepted the apology for the sake of charity.
>
> Nevertheless, I did not receive him into the assembly until he had presented a petition in which he anathematized Nestorius’s doctrines in writing, confessed that he regarded Nestorius as deposed, and assented to the ordination of the most religious bishop Maximianus.
>
> He asked that, since these petitions had been offered by him in the place of all the most religious bishops of the East, I should demand nothing further. I would not allow this in any way. Instead, together with my distinguished lord, the tribune and notary Aristolaus, I sent two of our clergy to Antioch and gave them a document, ordering them that, if John, the most reverend bishop of the Church of Antioch, subscribed it and accepted it, only then should they deliver to him letters concerning communion.

Paul then employed another stratagem, worse than the first, either to overturn the synod’s decrees or to throw the causes of the obstructed peace back upon Cyril. He insisted that Nestorius’s deposition alone was sufficient to quiet the disturbances which Nestorius alone had stirred up; that the other bishops should be restored to their sees, especially the four who had been named and deposed: Helladius, Eutherius, Himerius, and Dorotheus.

Cyril writes to Donatus:

> Let your sanctity know this also: at the beginning the most religious and pious bishop Paul strongly insisted on behalf of the deposed Helladius, Eutherius, Himerius, and Dorotheus, and earnestly begged that the decrees issued against them be abolished. For he asserted that peace among the Churches could not otherwise be established unless this too were added.
>
> I replied that he was attempting something impossible, since we would never permit it. Thus they remained in the same schism in which they still persist, and no mention of them was made in the terms proposed for peace among the holy Churches.

When the Easterners saw all their devices being defeated, they finally obeyed the emperor’s commands and Cyril’s demands. Yet they added another element of fraud, so that they might appear to have obtained what they had contended for at Ephesus: that the question of doctrine should be addressed before that of persons; that each party should submit its confession of faith in writing; and that the twelve chapters should not be mentioned.

Cyril had indeed granted this, perhaps acting with greater generosity than was appropriate toward deceitful men because of his desire for peace. From it the Easterners took the opportunity to spread among the people the falsehood that Cyril had retracted his chapters and adopted the position of the Easterners.

John therefore wrote to Cyril, but in ambiguous language, appearing less to reveal his mind than to conceal it. He declared that he had not entered into concord voluntarily but by order of the emperor; that he was sending a confession of faith for no other reason than to silence those who wished to attack him; that he did not admit a natural (*φυσική*) union of the natures, but only union; that he did not simply call the Virgin *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”) according to this conception of the unconfused union (κατὰ ταύτην τῆς ἀσυγχύτου ἑνώσεως ἔννοιαν); and that he did not condemn Nestorius’s doctrines but only new and profane expressions.

All these statements could bear an ambiguous meaning, since he expressed his position in words which Nestorius himself would have used willingly. For Nestorius had confessed that the holy Virgin was **Θεοτόκος**; that the natures were united without confusion; that Christ was one Son and Lord; that the Word had become flesh; that from the moment of conception he had united to himself the temple which he assumed; and other things which John likewise set forth.

While the business of peace was being conducted partly at Antioch and partly in Egypt, Theodoret, distressed that matters were not turning out according to his own wishes, wrote letters to the two Andrews: one a Constantinopolitan monk, the other bishop of Samosata. He also wrote to John of Antioch and Himerius of Nicomedia. In these letters he declared that he had found nothing in Cyril’s letter that appeared contrary to sound doctrine, since it contained statements opposed to the chapters. Nevertheless, even if every extreme danger threatened, he could not consent either to Nestorius’s deposition—whom he praised with extraordinary encomiums—or to the condemnation of his doctrines without an exception indicating that he condemned the doctrines whoever might hold them, so that Nestorius’s person might be spared.

> For, he says, whoever anathematizes the doctrine of that most holy bishop indiscriminately appears to anathematize piety itself.

When the tribune, weary of delay, returned from Alexandria—where he had gone to hasten the business—to Antioch in order to press John, Cyril sent two of his clergy with him. He gave them a document and ordered them that, if John subscribed and accepted it, only then should they deliver to him letters concerning communion.

The document contained three conditions of peace. Cyril writes to Donatus:

> When the most pious John had subscribed, and the other more distinguished men who were with him; when they had anathematized Nestorius’s doctrine, confessed that they regarded Nestorius as deposed, and approved the ordination of the most religious and pious bishop Maximianus, we restored communion to them.

Theodoret, just as he had not been present with John when peace was established, so did not subscribe with the others. Instead, in his retirement he plotted disturbances—or rather stirred up the minds of the bishops of his province, whom he even compelled to assemble as though in synods wherever it seemed convenient. For this reason, the emperor later ordered him, as a disturber of the public peace, to remain within Cyrrhus.

After matters had been settled on both sides, Paul of Emesa presented Cyril with a petition in which he agreed to all the conditions of peace. He not only received communion but was also granted permission to preach to the people. Cyril presided in the great church on 25 December, and Paul spoke Catholic doctrine concerning the incarnation of the Word and the Virgin who bore God. He received such loud applause from the acclaiming people that he was forced not only to interrupt his sermon but also to postpone part of it until 1 January.

In the published editions, observe that the words toward the end have been corrupted. They should be restored as follows.

The people said:

> Son of Theophilus, of Athanasius, and of Cyril.

Bishop Paul said:

> Let us hear the wisdom of the Father, which rouses the minds of us orthodox believers but casts down the ranks [Col. 0745] of the Church’s enemies, etc.

Cyril, as was customary, took up the speaker’s words, commending the sermon:

> We have drawn water for you from the sacred fountain—the fountain, I mean, of the teacher who spoke before us. Enlightened by the light of the Holy Spirit, he has explained to us the great and venerable mystery of our Savior, etc.

## Year 433

When Theodoret learned that the matter had been completely settled and that John of Antioch had written not only to the principal sees but also to the emperor, testifying that he condemned Nestorius’s doctrines and consented both to his deposition and to Maximianus’s ordination, he wrote again to Himerius. In these letters he revealed both his own lack of self-control and the frauds of his faction.

He also sent a letter to Nestorius himself, as a kind of pledge of his obstinacy in defending the heretic’s cause:

> Against the things unjustly and wrongfully done against your veneration, even if someone were to cut off both my hands, I shall not be able to give my consent—God’s grace undoubtedly cooperating with me and supporting the weakness of my soul. I have also made this certain in writing to those who demand these things, and I have sent your sanctity copies of what I wrote to them, so that you may recognize that no passage of time will change us by divine grace.

Theodoret even spread the report through the neighboring provinces in letters of his own that the Easterners’ apology did not differ from Nestorius’s position, and that Cyril had not remained in his former opinion but had instead adopted the contrary position—indeed, that he had accepted a new exposition of the faith while rejecting the Nicene one.

It is established by certain evidence that Theodoret spread these and other claims, although Cyril concealed his name when replying to Acacius, who had warned him about the matter. Nor was Theodoret content to test the neighboring regions with these lies. He wrote the same things to Constantinople, and even to Epirus; as before, he also wrote to Italy, to the bishops of Ravenna, Aquileia, and Milan.

To refute these claims, Cyril was compelled to write to Acacius in Cappadocia, to Eulogius in Constantinople, and to Donatus in Old Epirus. For this peace was not approved by everyone: at Antioch, according to Liberatus, some of the bishops still hesitated to communicate with Cyril, believing that he had erred and later recognized the truth, and blaming John for not demanding the condemnation of Cyril’s chapters from him.

At Constantinople also, Liberatus continues, certain men from the imperial court, through Eulogius the presbyter and representative of the Alexandrian Church, blamed Cyril for having accepted from the Eastern bishops a confession of two natures—what Nestorius had said and taught.

In Alexandria also some, out of ignorance or even because of their wickedness, raised objections, as though either John of Antioch himself had not written things consonant with Paul’s sermon, or Cyril had inclined toward the Oriental party through some excessive *οἰκονομία* (“accommodation” or “policy”). Therefore, after delivering a sermon in the church, Cyril ordered both letters of peace to be read publicly. “The most God-loving bishops established there,” he said, “confessed the right faith, without profanation. What the most God-loving and reverend bishop John of Antioch wrote to me, and what I wrote back to him, you shall hear, God willing.” An error has crept into the date transmitted by the published manuscripts; for the sermon was delivered not on the twenty-eighth of Pharmuthi, but on Tybi—that is, not on April 23, but on January 23. For once peace had been arranged at the beginning of January, how could Cyril either have delayed reporting it to the people for so long, or have failed to remember the reason why the report had been delayed so long?

As soon as peace had been arranged, Cyril and John each reported it in letters to the supreme pontiff Sixtus. The legates, returning to Rome toward the end of April, gave an account consistent with those letters. Certainly, at Saint Peter’s, both the letters were read in the assembly and the legates were heard by the bishops who had gathered for Sixtus’s birthday. That day was April 26. “O report,” said the pontiff (Letter to Cyril), “worthy of the one who sent it, worthy of the assembly! A matter of heavenly joy ought to have such judges; and since both the matter and the case demand it, the place too should not be left unmentioned. The entire brotherhood gathered at the blessed apostle Peter. Behold an auditorium suited to its hearers and appropriate to what was to be heard. Our fellow bishops had that witness of congratulation which we possess as the beginning of our honor. For he himself presided over the holy and venerable synod which, with the Lord’s favor, my birthday had gathered, since this must be believed, seeing that he is shown to have been absent neither in spirit nor in body. He was present at the victory, who was not absent from the contest; he aided the wishes of our hearts, who sees the symbol first handed down among the apostles being diminished; he did not allow the impious head to rejoice in consolations, nor did he permit the purity of that clear fountain to be long disturbed by a muddy whirlpool.” And elsewhere: “The entire brotherhood which had gathered for my birthday heard,” and so forth.

Meanwhile Nestorius, in his retreat at the monastery of Euprepius, did not cease causing disturbance. Though arrogantly miserable, he dared, despite the ruin of his affairs, to hope for his former dignity. Accordingly, by assembling groups of friends and collecting resources supplied by them, he prepared the means by which he might someday recover the favor of the courtiers whom he had lost; and so he continued to foster the heresy and to retain in his faction the bishops of the province and many clergy. Indeed, he won over not a few, especially those whom either hatred of Cyril, jealousy toward John, or weariness of the peace that had been concluded inflamed.

He had now spent almost four years, without relaxing his impious efforts to advance the affair, when John, weary of the disturbances by which he saw his province being divided, and indignant that Nestorius stubbornly disregarded his admonitions—and, as many report, also moved by zeal for the faith, which he had at last recognized as being attacked—turned his former friendship with Nestorius into a just vengeance on behalf of peace and faith. He therefore asked the emperor that the author of these evils be sent far away, and he obtained this without difficulty, with the support of Proclus, who had succeeded Maximian in the see of Constantinople.

[Col. 0747] The edict of deportation is found in the fifth part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 12 of the Peltan edition; it is absent from the Binian and Royal editions. Baronius cites it under the year 436, but it lacks a date. Hence it happened that Baronius, when he read in the heading of the Peltan edition, “Copy of the imperial decree sent to Isidore, prefect and consul of the praetorium, concerning the exile of Nestorius,” assigned it to the year in which Isidore held the consulship. But since Nestorius spent only four years in the monastery of Euprepius before his exile, and since it is highly probable that the sanction ordering the burning of Nestorius’s books was not issued before the decree ordering Nestorius’s deportation, the edict in question must belong to the beginning of the year 435, since the other decree, concerning the burning of the books, is dated in the Theodosian Code to August 3 and in the Justinian Code to July 30, in the fifteenth consulate of Theodosius and the fourth of Valentinian, Augusti and consuls.

After Nestorius had been deported to the Oasis and his books condemned to the flames, those who adhered to the heretic nevertheless attempted, by whatever means they could, to make it believed that Nestorius had suffered an injustice and to compensate for the loss of his books. Since he had been condemned either chiefly or even solely because he taught a new doctrine concerning the incarnation of the Word, contrary to the Fathers, they circulated the books of Diodore of Tarsus and Theodore of Mopsuestia—men famous for their reputation and dead in communion—or at least collections corresponding to Cyril’s individual chapters and agreeing with the Nestorians. They also translated these works into the languages of the Syrians, Armenians, and Persians, so that they could be read by everyone. They employed this strategy first so that the affair might be conducted far from its original centers and therefore not easily overturned; then, little by little, once the doctrines seemed to be strengthened by their widespread acceptance, they would infiltrate the greater Churches.

The principal authors of this plan were two men: Theodoret and Ibas, closely united by their scholarly interests and distinguished for their learning—the former a bishop, the latter still a presbyter—and both equally hostile to Cyril. Theodoret, a bishop, devoted himself to corrupting Phoenicia; Ibas to translating the books into a foreign language. Both worked to disturb the peace of the Churches.

Acacius, bishop of Melitene, and Rabbula, bishop of Edessa, warned the Armenians in writing to beware of the poison of the Nestorian heresy, which they had learned had been administered to them through Theodore’s books. Having been warned, they assembled and sent from their synod two presbyters, Leontius and Aberius, to Proclus in Constantinople, with petitions and Theodore’s volume. They requested instruction as to which doctrine was better—that of Theodore or that of Acacius and Rabbula—for the bishops of Cilicia had caused them to doubt by alleging that Acacius and Rabbula had written out of envy. After carefully examining the matter, Proclus sent the Armenians his celebrated letter on the incarnation, and also sent it to John of Antioch for approval. In it, although he refuted Theodore’s doctrines—which he also reported—both by arguments of his own and by the appended testimonies of the Fathers, he nevertheless thought that Theodore’s name should be left unmentioned because of the man’s reputation, celebrated throughout the entire East.

From this arose serious disturbances. Monks from Armenia brought into the East, and even into the imperial city, certain excerpts from Theodore’s books, arguing that if Nestorius had rightly been condemned, those passages too could not fail to be condemned together with their author. Hence the Churches were also stirred by the question of Theodore’s name. For it is said that Cyril wrote three books against Theodore and one against Diodore, in which he reported and refuted by name the statements of both men. John of Antioch convened a synod, from which he issued three letters defending Theodore. Proclus remained firm in his judgment, and the spark then appeared to have been extinguished. The bishops of the three great sees—Cyril, John, and Proclus—died not long afterward; but eventually the spark burst into a conflagration, which only the Fifth Synod proved capable of extinguishing, when the names of Theodore, Ibas, and Theodoret were struck with anathema.

Mercator excerpted some passages from Theodore’s books *On the Incarnation* and inserted them, translated into Latin, into his own Works. For this reason the matter has been preserved in the historical record. Why, then, should Mercator not have undertaken this labor at that time, when either Proclus was composing his tome, or dogmatic letter, or when the Armenian monks later filled Constantinople with their complaints?

Thus the impious enemy of Christ, deported to the Oasis, wrote there a long history of his sufferings. Forced repeatedly to change his dwelling because of the incursions of barbarians, he was at last worn down by his misfortunes and died miserably, while worms devoured his detestable tongue.

[Note: [Col. 0747A] From this preface it is clear how much is missing from the published editions of the Council of Ephesus, including the Roman and Royal editions, indeed even the more recent one, although these missing materials belong no less to this council and are even more necessary than those that have been preserved. It is also clear how disorderly almost everything is arranged in the aforementioned editions, and by what method the disorder can be removed and everything restored to its proper order.

The entire work, therefore, appears to require division into four parts. The first contains the events preceding the announcement of the council and giving rise to its convocation; the second, the events from the announcement of the council up to the first session; the third, the events throughout the period of the council; the final part, the events that followed, extending to the peace of the Churches, the deportation of Nestorius, and the disturbances that arose in Armenia.

The entire work should therefore contain the affairs of approximately ten years: the first part, namely, what was written from the end of the year 428 to November of the year 430; the second, what occurred from that November to June 22 of the year 431, on which day the synod began; the third, what took place during the four succeeding months of the council; and the fourth, what occurred from the end of the year 431 almost to the year 437, or even 438. Items missing from the published editions are marked with asterisks.]

## BOOK ONE

Containing thirteen sermons of Nestorius, together with one of Proclus; three letters of Nestorius, together with four of Saint Cyril; one letter of Mercator concerning the heresy of Nestorius; and excerpts made by Saint Cyril from Nestorius’s works.

[Col. 0753]

## THE SERMONS OF THE IMPIOUS NESTORIUS

### MARIUS MERCATOR, SERVANT OF CHRIST,

[Note: [Col. 0753C] From these words it is clear that Mercator combined in a single codex three kinds of writings: the sermons of Nestorius; the letters of Nestorius and Saint Cyril; and certain excerpts of statements taken by Saint Cyril from Nestorius’s books, which Liberatus calls “selections.” We have likewise combined these materials in a single book. But since Mercator’s codex lacks order, it seemed appropriate, after removing the confusion, to restore each item to its proper time.]

### PREFACE TO VARIOUS SERMONS OF THE IMPIOUS NESTORIUS ON THE INCARNATION OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST

Translated from Greek, together with certain letters of the same Nestorius and Cyril, and chapters excerpted by Saint Cyril from various books of Nestorius.

[Col. 0753C] [Note: [Col. 0754C] This prefatory letter was written after the Council of Ephesus, as the words “Nestorius, formerly bishop” show; yet it was not written much later. For Mercator wrote it so that both the condemnation of Nestorius and the complete documentary record of the case might simultaneously come to the knowledge of the Westerners, [Col. 0755A] so that each person could understand for himself how deservedly he had been deposed by the universal synod who had either spoken or written such great blasphemies.]

Marius Mercator, servant of Christ, sends to his fellow servant and reader, his equal [Baluz. “and kinsman”], in the Lord, greetings in the faith.

Moved by the fervor of the Catholic faith, I have taken care to translate from Greek into Latin certain sayings or writings of Nestorius, formerly bishop of Constantinople, addressed to the people and containing blasphemies, so that they might be known and avoided by the faithful who share my language. In these passages I have tried, insofar as possible, to express the words word for word, lest I should later be judged a true translator only after first being proved a falsifier.

Therefore, devout reader, grant pardon if either the expression is less polished [Baluz. adds “than it is”], or if the novelty of words adopted in some places should perhaps strike your ear. I have chosen rather to expose myself to the tongues of detractors than to wander farther from expressing the truth of the meaning; for where the danger of falsification is greatest, I have preferred not to depart more widely.

Let those eloquent little men of ours therefore occupy themselves from this moment [Baluz. “the same men”] with examining our individual syllables and prying into our words. I do not care about this, nor do I value it highly, confident that no one will impose upon me the name of falsifier on account of this work.

[Note: [Col. 0755A] He perhaps has in mind Julian and others among the Coelestians, whose most eloquent interpreter was Annianus, translator of certain homilies of Chrysostom [Col. 0755B]. They laughed at Catholics as though they were less eloquent, and by the elegance of their writing and their skill in translation insinuated their error into the minds of inquisitive readers. Julian certainly despised Augustine, and Annianus others, as unskilled in more refined Latin; but Augustine charges the translator of Chrysostom’s homilies with falsification (*Against Julian*, Book I, chapter 6), and Jerome makes the same charge against Pelagius (*Dialogue* 3, near the end, and Letter to Ctesiphon, and elsewhere), complaining that Pelagius lies in wait for him in each individual syllable.]

I also know that these men will reproach us for certain defective expressions which the need to preserve the peculiar character of the Greek forced from us. Let each person say whatever he wishes about this and think whatever he pleases; I rely on the judgment of the wise, for, without the enticement and cosmetic coloring of words or the trifles of schoolmen, the simple beauty of truth is always pleasing.

Now here [Note: [Col. 0755B]

There can be no doubt that this sermon on impiety truly belongs to Nestorius. Almost all writers of his own age attribute it to him, namely Marius Mercator—partly here, partly in his refutation of the eleventh anathema, where, after calling it “the most foolish treatise,” he says: “Why are we surprised that he did this with the testimony of the Gospel, when he also violently twisted another passage in the same way and abused it to the impiety of his own meaning, thinking that authority from the Gospel gave it strength, where it is said: ‘What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the spirit is spirit’ (John 3:6)? For he employed this testimony in that most foolish treatise in which he first argued about the virginal birth. In that place he said as follows (No. 7): ‘Mary did not give birth to God, my good man, for what is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the spirit is spirit; but she gave birth to a man, the instrument of divinity, and a man carrying God.’”

It is found throughout Cassian’s books *On the Incarnation*, but especially in the seventh book (chapter 6), where he calls it “a pestilential treatise.” “In a certain pestilential treatise of yours,” he says, “you wrote as follows (No. 5): ‘Since man is the image of the divine nature, the devil cast this image into corruption. God grieved for it as for his image, just as the emperor grieves for his statue, and he restores the corrupted image; and without seed he formed a nature from a virgin, according to him who was born without seed, Adam, and through man he raises up human nature. For just as death came through man, so also the resurrection of the dead comes through man.’”

Saint Cyril refers to it in his first letter to Nestorius (No. 7): “For certain men have almost reached the point where they no longer allow it to be confessed that Christ is God, but rather call him *ὄργανον καὶ ἐργαλεῖον τῆς Θεότητος*—‘an instrument and tool of divinity,’—and a man who carries God (*θεοφόρος*).” And in his third letter (same place): “Nor do we say that the Word of God dwelt as if in an ordinary man, born of the holy Virgin, lest Christ be believed to be a man who carries God (*θεοφόρος*).”

Eusebius, then an advocate in the case and later bishop of Dorylaeum, refers to it in the protestation which he publicly submitted after this sermon had been delivered (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 13): “Paul of Samosata says: ‘Mary did not give birth to the Word.’ Nestorius, not departing from this meaning, says (No. 7): ‘Tell me, good sir, did Mary not give birth to Divinity?’” Theodoret also refers to it (same place)—or, if someone else was the author of the letter to Sporatius: “In the church of the orthodox he uttered many such statements: ‘Mary did not give birth to God, good sir, but she gave birth to a man, the instrument of Divinity; [Col. 0756B] the pagan is free from blame who introduces a mother for the gods’” (No. 6).

The author of the *Predestinate*, heresy 88, says: “Mary gave birth only to a man. For if we say that she gave birth to a man, we make her the mother of a god, like the pagans. Therefore Mary gave birth to a temple for God, not to the one who dwells in the temple” (same place).

The author of the *Conflict of Arnobius with Serapion* says: “Serapion said: ‘This doctrine belongs to Nestorius.’ Arnobius said: ‘I have before me the assertions of Nestorius; if the judges command, I shall read them.’ The judges said: ‘Let what Arnobius offers be read, so that, if Serapion’s objection is true, it may be demonstrated.’ When the homily had been received, it was read at the relevant place as follows: ‘The most holy Mary did not give birth to the Godhead, for what is born of the flesh is flesh. The creature did not give birth to the Creator, but she gave birth to a man, the ministry of the Deity. The Holy Spirit did not build God the Word; for what was born from her is from the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Holy Spirit built a temple for God the Word from the Virgin.’” [Col. 0756C] And shortly afterward: “‘The one who was born in the womb is not God in himself.’” And shortly afterward: “‘Let us honor the form that bears God’ (*Θεοδόχον*).”

Finally, Gennadius says (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 53): “After Nestorius had been granted the pontificate of the Church of Constantinople, he wrote a book apparently on the Lord’s incarnation, filled with his perverse interpretation and containing sixty-two testimonies from divine Scripture. What he asserted will be shown in the catalogue of heretics.”

But these words of Gennadius raise a serious question. For ancient writers mention this sermon on the Incarnation composed by Nestorius, but, as far as I know, none mentions another book on the same subject; and yet the work we possess, whether sermon or treatise, contains scarcely more than five or six testimonies from divine Scripture in support of the heretical meaning. The question, although exceedingly difficult, will be resolved in its proper place (in the dissertation on the books of Nestorius).

Add that three outstanding men wrote against this sermon [Col. 0756D]: Proclus, a panegyrical address on the praises of the Virgin who bore God; Cyril, a letter to the Egyptian monks, his seventeenth Paschal homily, and several other works; and Cassian, seven books, which he entitled *On the Incarnation* precisely because in them he fought against Nestorius’s treatise *On the Incarnation*. In all these works they concealed Nestorius’s name, because when they wrote, he had not yet been condemned, nor had he even been formally accused of heresy in a public judgment.

For this reason I have thought that almost nothing else need be done in the notes than to compare the individual statements of such eminent men with the individual statements of Nestorius and to correct the places where defective readings occur.]
