His [Note: [Col. 0756D] If this is the first sermon—as it truly is—addressed to the people against impiety, it must have been delivered after the impious statements of the presbyter Anastasius [Col. 0757A] or of Bishop Dorotheus, so that Nestorius might approve the words of either or both and the agitated people might somehow be appeased. Yet it might occur to someone that this sermon does not differ from the homily which Theophanes writes was read by Nestorius and delivered to his own syncellus Anastasius. “Theophanes says (in the *Chronographia*), ‘He ordered the homily delivered to his syncellus on matters of faith to be read publicly in an assembly of the Christian people. It contained the following: “Let no one now call Mary Mother of God; for Mary was a human being, and it is impossible for God to be begotten by a human being.”’”] is the first sermon of impiety in the church addressed to the people, in which he unhappily fell into error concerning the Lord’s Incarnation and disastrously collapsed.

## FIRST SERMON. On the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ

[Col. 0757A]

### 1. [Note: [Col. 0757C] Nestorius divided his sermon into two parts: one on Providence, which appears almost wholly Catholic, although Cassian criticizes it in some respects; and the other on the Lord’s Incarnation, which was the source and origin of all his impiety.]

The Church’s concern for pious doctrine is the concern of thoughtful people; and pious doctrine is knowledge of Providence. For whoever knows God knows God’s providence, since he knows God to be the creator of bodies and souls. [Note: [Col. 0757C] “To be their guardian.” The reading we have received from the Beauvais manuscript is confirmed by what follows: “my first and greatest protection in preserving me.” Likewise below: “how great our protection is.” Nevertheless, Garnerius removed the word *tutorem* (“guardian”) here and substituted *creatorem* (“creator”), while Gerberon substituted *auctorem* (“author”). —Baluze.] Therefore, it is clear that all who worship God without knowing this are ignorant of the truth: for they profess to know God, but by their deeds, as it is written, they deny him (Tit. I, 16). [Col. 0757B]

### 2.

Now the creator must care for those whom he created; the lord must show solicitude toward those over whom he rules; the head of a household must be the defender of his own house.

### 3.

Our life is unequal to the dignity of so great a government. God the craftsman fashions me in my mother’s womb, and in those hidden recesses of my mother’s womb he is my first and greatest protection in preserving me. I am born, and I find fountains of milk. I begin to need the cutting of foods, and I am found armed with certain knives—namely, teeth. I conduct myself as a man, and creation becomes my tributary: for the earth below feeds me, and in heaven the sun is lit for me as a lamp; he assigns to me the spring season, [Note: [Col. 0757C] “The spring season.” When Garnerius printed *vernum* here, while Gerberonius printed *veris*, they did not remember that *vernum* can also be used substantivally. Pliny, book XIX, chapter 3, says that truffles are most tender in spring. See Du Cange’s *Glossarium*. —Baluze.] summer brings me ears of grain, winter produces rains, and autumn pays tribute in wine. [Col. 0758A]

### 4.

What an uneven life we lead, composed of poverty and riches! Mortals could not otherwise have been sustained. For observe in these very things how great our protection is. The easy spoilage of grain forces the rich, out of fear of corruption, to sell it to the needy; the changeable nature of wine compels its owner to enter into commerce through fear of loss. [Col. 0758B] Gold is therefore imperishable and resistant to time because, when hoarded, it harms no poor person. For what harm do riches do to me if they restrain their gold, when the rich are compelled to sell the things that feed me? [Baluze: “For what harm do they do to me?”]

### 5.

The human race, honored with ten thousand gifts, has been adorned at the end and culmination by the gift of the Lord’s Incarnation. Since the human being is an image of the divine nature, [Note: [Col. 0757D] Cassian translated this passage from the Greek and refuted it in these words (*On the Incarnation*, book VII, chapter 6): “Since the human being is an image of the divine nature,” and so forth, as quoted earlier.] and since the devil drove this image into corruption, [Note: [Col. 0757D] Cassian (*ibid.*): “Thus you also say: ‘The human being is an image of the divine nature; but the devil cast it into corruption. God grieved for it as for his image, just as an emperor grieves for his statue.’ You introduce the name of God so that you may lie under the name of religion. You put holy things first so that you may persuade us of perverse things; and by confessing God you bring it about that you deny the very one whom you confess,” and so forth.] he grieved as a king does for his own statue, and [Note: [Col. 0758C] Cassian (*On the Incarnation*, book VI, chapter 6; see also book VII, chapter 6): “Have you perhaps said anything from those fantasies with which you now rave about the symbol? Did you yourself also say: ‘Where is the statue here, where is your instrument? Your instrument, I say—for far be it that this should belong to anyone other than you. Where is that passage in which, affirming the Lord Jesus Christ to be like a statue—not because he is God, but because he is the image of God—you think he should be worshiped, and making the Lord an instrument of majesty, blasphemously claim that he should be honored not for his own sake but for the sake of the one who supposedly breathes and resounds through him?’”] renews the corrupted image, fashioning a nature from the Virgin without seed, just as Adam too was formed without seed, and effects the restoration [Baluze: “resurrection”] of the human race through a human being. [Col. 0758C] [Note: [Col. 0758D] Cassian (*On the Incarnation*, book VII, chapter 7): “‘Since, you say, death came through a human being, therefore also the resurrection of the dead comes through a human being’ (I Cor. XV, 21). Are you even trying to prove your perversity and crime by apostolic testimony, and to disgrace the chosen vessel through the contagion of your impiety? Clearly, because you do not understand the author of your salvation, you make the Apostle too appear to have denied God. Yet if you wished to use apostolic testimonies, why, content with one of his statements, did you suppress all the rest and fail to add immediately: ‘Paul the Apostle, not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ’ (Gal. I, 1)? Or: ‘We speak wisdom among the mature’ (I Cor. II, 6). And afterward: ‘Which none of the rulers of this age knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory’ (ibid., 8)? Or: ‘In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily’ (Col. II, 9). And: ‘One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things’ (I Cor. VIII, 6). Do you approve the Apostle in one part and reject him in another, receiving him only where, in accordance with the economy, he calls Christ a human being, but rejecting him where he calls him God? Paul does not deny that Jesus is a human being; yet he confesses that this same human being is God. Thus he proclaims that resurrection came to the human race through a human being, while nevertheless confirming that God himself rose in that human being. For see whether he does not proclaim as God the one who rose, when he testifies that the one who was crucified is the God of majesty.”] For, he says, “through a human being [came] death, and through a human being the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV, 12).

### [Col. 0759A] 6. [Note: [Col. 0759B] Thus far Nestorius has spoken, in a way, as a Catholic; now he rages with a heretical spirit against the divinity of Christ [Col. 0759C] and the dignity of the Virgin Mother of God. For, as Cassian observes (*On the Incarnation*, book VII, chapter 6), Nestorius acted like certain poisoners who mix honey with poison in the cups they prepare, so that what is harmful may be concealed by sweetness, and while someone is captivated by the sweetness of the honey, he may be destroyed by the plague of the poison.]

Let those who, blinded in the economy of the Lord’s incarnation, do not understand either what they say or what they affirm about the subjects of their claims hear these things (I Tim. I, 7). As we have just learned, they repeatedly ask one another whether Mary should be called Θεοτόκος—that is, *God-bearer* or *Mother of God*—or ἀνθρωποτόκος, that is, *mother of a human being*. [Col. 0760A] Does God have a mother? [Note: [Col. 0759C] The author of these and many other statements on the same subject is found either in the letter to Sporatius or in chapter twelve of book four of the *Heretical Fables*; likewise the author of the *Praedestinatus*, as stated in the notes to the preface.] Then paganism, which introduces mothers among the gods, is excusable. [Note: [Col. 0759C] Cassian reports and also refutes this argument (*On the Incarnation*, book VII, chapter 14): “You therefore use the sacred Scriptures against God and attempt to make his own witnesses testify against him. But how? Truly, so that you may be not only a transgressor against God but also against the testimonies themselves. It is no surprise, of course, that because you cannot do what you wish, you do only what you can: since you cannot turn the sacred testimonies against God, you pervert the testimonies themselves. For you say: ‘Then Paul also lies about Christ when he says: “Without mother, without genealogy.”’ I ask you: of whom did Paul intend this to be said—to the Son and Word of God, or to Christ, whom you separate from the Son of God and blaspheme as a mere human being? If indeed of Christ, whom you call a solitary human being, how could a human being be born without a mother, without a genealogy of maternal origin? But if of the Word and Son of God, what shall we do with the fact that the same Apostle, whom you sacrilegiously regard as your witness in the same place and testimony, testifies that the one whom you assert to be without a mother is also without a father, saying: ‘Without father, without mother, without genealogy’? Therefore, since you use the Apostle’s testimony to assert that the Son of God is without a mother, you also blasphemously assert that he is without a father.”] So Paul is a liar concerning Christ’s divinity when he says— [Note: [Col. 0760A]

Cassian (*ibid.*, and chapter 15): “What madness, then, compelled you to cite that testimony, where, by saying that he did not have a mother, you appear also to have denied his father? For since in the same testimony he is said to be without a father just as he is without a mother, it is necessary that, in the same way in which he is understood there to be without a mother, he should also be believed to be without a father. But that precipitous madness bent on denying God did not understand this. When it presented what is written in truncated form, it did not see that, once the sequence of the sacred volume had been opened, its shameless and obvious lie could be refuted. O foolish blasphemy and madness! While it does not itself see what ought to follow, it did not even understand what could be read—as though, because it deprived itself of understanding, it could deprive everyone else of the reading; or as though everyone would therefore lose the eyes of their heads for reading because it had already lost the eyes of its mind.

“Hear, then, heretic, what you stole; hear the complete and whole passage that you presented in weakened and truncated form. The Apostle, wishing to reveal to everyone the two births of God, so as to show that the Lord was born in divinity and in the flesh, says: ‘Without father, without mother.’ One of these belongs properly to the birth according to divinity, the other to the flesh. For just as he was generated without a mother in divinity, so in the body he was without a father; and thus, since he is neither without a father nor without a mother, he must nevertheless be believed to be both without a father and without a mother. For if you consider him as born from the Father, he is without a mother; if you consider him as born from his mother, he is without a father. Thus, in each birth he possesses one of the two, but in each he does not possess the other: for the birth according to divinity needed no mother, and for the birth of the body he sufficed for himself without a father.

“Therefore, the Apostle says, ‘without mother, without genealogy.’ How does he say that the Lord was without genealogy, when the evangelist Matthew began his Gospel with the genealogy of the Savior, saying: ‘The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham’ (Matt. I, 1)? Thus, according to the evangelist, he has a genealogy; and according to the Gospel, he has one from his mother; according to the Apostle, he does not have one from his father. Therefore the Apostle rightly says: ‘Without father, without mother, without genealogy.’ Where he declared him to have been born without a mother, there he also mentioned that he was without genealogy.

“Accordingly, in the Lord’s two births, the evangelical and apostolic writings agree with each other: according to the evangelist, he has a genealogy, born in the flesh without a father; and according to the Apostle, he does not have one, the Lord having been generated in divinity without a mother, as Isaiah says: ‘Who shall declare his generation?’ (Isa. LIII, 8).”

**Proclus.** How, according to Paul, is he without father and mother? If he is merely human, then he is certainly not without a mother, for he has a mother. Again, if he is merely God, then without doubt he is not without a father, for he has a father. But now one and the same person is ἀμήτωρ—“without mother”—insofar as he is creator, and ἀπάτωρ—“without father”—insofar as he is human.

—The sacred Hebrew text has ἀγενεαλόγητος in Heb. VII, 3. On this passage see Wesseling, in his letter on fragments of Aquila in the writings of Philo Judaeus, p. 30. —Gallandi.

ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἄνευ γενεαλογίας (Heb. VII, 3), that is, “without father, without mother, without an account of genealogy.”

### 7. [Note: [Col. 0760D] This passage is cited in Mercator’s refutation of the eleventh anathema; then in Eusebius’s appeal; next in the monks’ petition to the emperor; and finally in the letter to Sporatius and in book four of Theodoret’s *Heretical Fables* (chapter 12). The following words of the petitioning monks should be noted: “After being put off once and again to another time, at last he [Nestorius] came forth and said, ‘State briefly what you want.’ But after he heard from us what he had taught—namely, ‘Mary gave birth to nothing other than a human being consubstantial with herself; and nothing can be born from flesh except flesh’—and learned that these things were not consonant with the orthodox faith, he immediately ordered us to be arrested,” and so forth. When we were brought before him again, we were beaten. Finally, after composing a speech by deceit, he assented, as later became clear, to the natural Son of God having been born from holy Mary the Mother of God, adding that “there is also another son,” and so forth.]

“No, excellent man, Mary did not give birth to God. For what is born from flesh is flesh, and what is born from spirit is spirit” (John III, 6). [Note: [Col. 0761B] Cassian had this passage in view when he wrote (*On the Incarnation*, book VII, chapter 24): “Where is that statement of yours: ‘A creature could not give birth to the Creator; what is born from flesh is flesh,’ and so forth?”] [Col. 0761A] A creature did not give birth to the one who is uncreated; the Father did not recently beget the Word God from the Virgin. “In the beginning was the Word” (John I, 1), as John says. A creature did not give birth to [Note: [Col. 0761B] Baluze restores *the Uncreated* in place of *the Creator*, adding this note at the foot of the page: “The old books read *the Uncreated*. Garnerius, however, restored *the Creator*, doubtless following Cassian’s authority, who writes as follows in book VII of *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, chapter 24: ‘And where is that statement of yours: “A creature could not give birth to the Creator”; and: “What is born from flesh is flesh”?’ —Editor.] the Creator [Baluze: “the Uncreated”], but she gave birth to a human being, [Note: [Col. 0761C] Mercator, in his refutation of the eleventh anathema, adds: “a God-bearing human being,” *anthrōpon theophoron*. Cyril seems to have aimed at this expression, either when he composed his fifth anathema in these words: “If anyone dares to say that Christ is a God-bearing human being, *anthrōpon theophoron*, rather than truly God, as the one Son who naturally, in that the Word became flesh, shared in flesh and blood as we do, let him be anathema”; or when he had earlier written thus to Nestorius (*Letter* 1): “Some have come close to not permitting it to be confessed that Christ is God, but instead [call him] an instrument and tool of the divinity, *organon kai ergaleion tēs Theotētos*, and a God-bearing human being.” And in his letter to the monks (part 19), after citing Isaiah (Isa. LIX, 3): “See how, as though speaking in the Spirit, he calls him Emmanuel and Lord, and names him God, because he knew him not as a merely God-bearing human being, *theophoron*, or as one assumed in the capacity of an instrument, but as God incarnate.” And later (part 20), having cited John’s testimony: “To these I add the great Baptist John, who, when he began to preach Christ, did not call him an instrument of the divinity or, according to some, a merely God-bearing human being, but God incarnate, that is, made human.” Again (part 21): “If anyone should contend that he was nothing other than a bare instrument of God, he would, even unwillingly, deprive him of the true status of Son.” And (part 23): “We by no means say that the temple assumed from the sacred Virgin was taken in the capacity of an instrument,” and so forth. Finally (part 26): “But if Christ is neither the true Son of God nor God by nature, but, like us, nothing other than a human being or an instrument of divinity, we have by no means obtained salvation through God.”] an instrument of the divinity. The Holy Spirit did not create God the Word: “What is born from her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I, 20); rather, he fashioned for God the Word a temple from the Virgin, in which he might dwell. [Note: [Col. 0761D] Proclus (*Panegyrical Oration*, part 2): “Where the serpent had poured in his poison through disobedience, there the Word, entering through obedience, built for himself a living temple.”]

### 8. [Note: [Col. 0762B] Although Garnerius printed this passage in an emended form, he nevertheless appended to it a note as though he had reproduced the ancient reading of the manuscripts, which is: “The incarnate God is and is not dead.” “Although,” he says, “the reading is the same in both manuscripts, it is nevertheless faulty and confused. It may be restored in this way: ‘God is indeed incarnate; he is not dead.’ Proclus vigorously attacks this passage (*Panegyrical Oration*, part 5 and following).” Baluze followed the manuscripts. —Editor.]

God is indeed incarnate, but he is not dead; rather, he raised the one in whom he was incarnate. He bent down to raise what had fallen, but he himself did not fall: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men” (Ps. XIII, 2). [Note: [Col. 0762C] “Lest, bending down, I.” This passage appears corrupt. Garnerius wrote *inclinans eum*, “bending him”; Gerberonius, *nec me indignans reum levare qui cecidi*, “nor, disdaining me, raise the guilty one who had fallen.” I would suggest reading *nec me inclinans reum levare qui cecidit*, “nor, bending down, raise the guilty one who fell,” so that the sentence seems to be constructed as follows: “nor, bending down, raise the guilty one who fell”—that is, me—“as though he himself had fallen.” —Baluze.] In bending down to raise the guilty one who had fallen, he is reproached as though he himself had fallen. God saw the fallen nature and, by the power of his divinity, took hold of it when it had been struck down; holding it while it lay prostrate, and remaining what he was, he raised it on high. Understand the example that is given. If you wished to raise someone lying on the ground, would you not touch body with body and, joining yourself to him, raise the fallen person, while remaining yourself what you were by being joined to him? Consider the mystery of the Incarnation in the same way.

### 9. [Note: [Col. 0762C] I believe that the material contained in sections nine, ten, and eleven was inserted here from the seventh sermon (parts 26, 27, and 28), except for the following brief passage: “Because of the one who uses that garment which he uses.” The reason for this opinion is that if Cassian had read these words in the sermon he possessed, he would not, I believe, have passed over them without strong condemnation, since they are filled with the most unspeakable impiety. He carefully follows the rest insofar as he judged that the error was contained in it.]

Because of the wearer, I worship the garment which he wears; because of the one who is hidden, I worship what is visible outwardly: God is inseparable from the one who appears outwardly. [Baluze: “adoring.”] [Note: [Col. 0762C] Gallandius prefers *quod utitur*, “which he uses.” “Correctly,” he says, “the translator uses *utitur* instead of *quo utitur*. Cicero, *Ad Atticum*, letter 31, book XII: ‘Silius does not use anything either.’”]

### 10.

How, then, would I dare to separate the honor and dignity of the one who is not divided? I divide the natures, but I join the reverence.

### 11.

Attend to what is being said. The one who was formed in the womb is not God in himself; for if that were so, we would truly be worshipers of a human being. But because God is in the one who was assumed, the one who was assumed has been called, and is called, God from the one who assumed him.

### 12. [Note: [Col. 0762D]

The Beauvais manuscript is no less corrupt than the Vatican manuscript. For it reads as follows: “Therefore let us tremble at the Lord’s Incarnation, let us receive the form that receives God, with one and equal reverence with which we honor God the Word, as the divinity’s …” The fault in both manuscripts ought to be corrected partly from Cassian and partly from Cyril.

These are Cassian’s words in the commonly circulated manuscripts (*On the Incarnation*, book VII, chapter 8): “Yet, so that you would not believe the Lord Jesus to be one of the common people, you granted him some dignity, giving him honor as a holy human being, but not divinity as a human being and true God. For what do you say? ‘God formed the Lord’s Incarnation; let us honor the form of the *Theotokos* with God, as one form of the divinity, as the inseparable statue of the divine will, as the image of the hidden God.’ Earlier you said that Adam was the image of God; here you call Christ an image; him a statue, and this one a statue. Yet thanks are evidently owed to you for the honor shown to God, because you grant that the form of the *Theotokos* should be honored with God. In this there is not so much honor as insult. For even in this you do not grant the Lord Jesus Christ the honor of divinity, but deny it: by a subtle art of impiety you say that he is to be honored with God, so that you may not confess him to be God; and by the very thing by which you seem deceitfully to have joined him, you separate him. For when you blasphemously say that he should not be worshiped as God but honored as though with God, you assign him a conjunction with divine proximity in order to remove the truth of his divinity. Most impiously and cunningly, enemy of God, you wish to accomplish the crime of denial under the name of confession. ‘Let us honor him,’ you say, ‘as the inseparable statue of the divine will, as the image of the hidden God.’ The honor of our Creator and Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, has evidently advanced among us through his benefits. If we were redeemed by him from eternal destruction so that we should call our Redeemer a statue, we strive to respond to his kindness and goodness with worthy obedience and worship if we also try to take away the majesty which he did not refuse to humble for our sake.

“Nevertheless, this very passage of Cassian also requires correction; it should be read as follows: ‘God formed the Lord’s Incarnation; let us honor the form that receives God, Θεοδόχον, with God, as the living form of the divinity, as the inseparable statue of divine majesty, as the image of the hidden God,’ and so forth.

“Not only does the following argument, as is evident, show that it should be read in this way, but Cyril also does so in his letter to those of his followers who were in Constantinople (first part of the Council of Ephesus). ‘Since,’ he says, ‘he complains that an unfamiliar expression is being demanded—namely, that the holy Virgin be called Mother of God, θεοτόκον—let him answer us when asked where Scripture speaks of a mother of Christ, that is, χριστοτόκον. Is there any episcopal council that has called Christ Θεοδόχον, that is, “receiver” or “bearer” of divinity? For in that fourfold statement which he sent here and which greatly offended us, the wording is τὴν Θεοδόχον,’ and so forth.

“From this testimony of Cyril one may infer that the sermon of Nestorius with which we are dealing is defective in part in Mercator, since its concluding words are missing there and, as is probable, much more besides.”

—Baluze, disagreeing with Garnerius, restored the whole passage as follows: “Therefore let us tremble at the Lord’s Incarnation: τὴν Θεοδόχον τῷ Θεῷ λόγῳ συνθεολογῶμεν μορφήν, that is, ‘the form that receives God.’” At the foot of the page he adds: “We have restored this passage, which is very corrupt in the other editions, in accordance with the evidence of the Beauvais manuscript; our emendation is confirmed by Cyril’s words quoted below on p. 107. That it was already corrupt in Cassian’s time may be inferred from the fact that he too quoted it in a very faulty form in book VII of *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, chapter 8: ‘God formed the Lord’s Incarnation. Let us honor the form of the *Theotokos* with God, as one form of the divinity,’ and so forth. It should also be noted that the word *formed* seems to belong to the preceding clause, as though Nestorius were saying: ‘But because, in the one who was assumed, the one who was assumed is called God from the one who assumed or formed him: let us honor the Lord’s Incarnation, the form of the *Theotokos*.’ It should further be noted that in the Royal manuscript *theotocon* is written where Cassian’s editions have *theotoci*; this confirms the opinion of those who think that Θεοδόχον should be read here in Cassian. See Mercator’s words below, p. 69.” Thus far Baluze. [Col. 0764D] Then, taking up the words τὴν Θεοδόχον individually, he attacks them as follows: “From these words—which also occur in Cyril’s letter to his clergy stationed at Constantinople, but which Garnerius omitted there because the passage is very confused in the Beauvais manuscript—from Cyril’s words, I say, Garnerius inferred that this sermon of Nestorius is in part defective in Mercator and that much is missing from it. This is not true after we have restored the passage. See also below, at the end of Sermon 7.” —Editor.]

Therefore let us tremble at the Lord’s Incarnation. [Col. 0763A] Let us reverence the form that receives God with the one and equal reverence with which we honor God the Word, [Note: [Col. 0764D] Baluze gives this differently, namely: “with one and equal reverence with which we honor God the Word in his divinity, as …” He nevertheless notes that *una* is read in Cyril’s letter to his clergy, which may be consulted below. —Editor.] as the truly inseparable image of the divinity, as the image of the hidden Judge. Let us confess and adore the double as one: [Note: [Col. 0764D] Marius Mercator vigorously argues against this statement in the appendix to his refutation of the twelfth anathema (parts 2 and following).] for the one double is one because of unity. Hear Paul proclaiming both: the eternity of the Only-Begotten according to divinity and the single dignity produced by association or conjunction: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb. XIII, 8). Amen.

## SERMON II. On the doctrine, or Θεογνώσια—that is, on the unconfused conjunction of the two natures in Christ and the communion of names, directed against the Apollinarians

[Col. 0763B]

Cyril teaches that this was delivered in the church (*Letter to Acacius of Melitene*). The titles of the excerpts from the Council of Ephesus show that it was entitled “On Doctrine.” The opening shows that by the name of doctrine Θεογνωσία is understood, and therefore knowledge of Christ’s humanity together with his divinity. Anyone who compares with one another the passages from which the individual sections were taken will easily recognize that their sequence was not invented arbitrarily by us but is genuine.

I do not prove our devotion toward me by shouting, but I praise your desire concerning the doctrines and the fact that you remember the Lord’s divinity and humanity.

And shortly afterward:

I see that the peoples possess great reverence and very prudent piety, but that through ignorance they are blind concerning Θεογνωσία. This, however, is not the fault of the people; but, to speak modestly, it is because the teachers have not had time to set before you something about the doctrines with greater refinement and clarity. [Col. 0764A]

You remember quite clearly what I have often said to you when I distinguished two natures in Christ the Lord: there are two if you consider nature; if dignity, there is one. For the authority of the natures is one because of the conjunction, although the natures always remain in their own order, while, as I have already said, they are joined in dignity into a single authority.

Therefore I want you to be more cautious in your approval or applause: there is no division of the conjunction, the power, the sonship, or of that which is Christ. There is no division in these things; but there is division in divinity and humanity. Christ, insofar as he is Christ, is undivided; and the Son, insofar as he is Son, is undivided. For we do not have two Christs or two sons; there is not among us a first Christ and a second, nor one and another, nor again one Son and another Son. Rather, the same one is double—not in dignity, but in nature.

But just as we call God the maker of all things “God,” and Moses “God”—for he says, “I have appointed you as God to Pharaoh” (Exod. VII, 1)—and Israel “the Son of God”—for he says, “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. IV, 22)—and just as we call Saul “the anointed one”: “I will not lay my hand upon him, because he is the Lord’s anointed” (I Sam. XXIV, 7); and likewise Cyrus: “Thus says the Lord to my anointed one, Cyrus” (Isa. XLV, 1); and the Babylonian “holy”: “For I command those who have been sanctified, and I lead them” (Isa. XIII, 3)—so we call the Lord Christ, God, Son, and holy. But although the communion of names is similar, the dignity is not the same. [Col. 0765A]

Whenever, therefore, Holy Scripture is going to speak either of Christ’s birth from the blessed Virgin or of his death, it nowhere calls him God, but either Christ, Jesus, or Lord, because these three names indicate the two natures: sometimes one, sometimes the other, sometimes both. What I am saying is this: whenever Scripture recalls the birth from the Virgin, what does it say? “God sent his Son” (Gal. IV, 4). It does not say, “God sent the Word,” but uses the name that indicates the two natures. Since the Son is human and God, it says, “God sent his Son, born of a woman.” When you hear “born of a woman,” you should immediately consider that the name used indicates the two natures and that it is the Son’s birth from the blessed Virgin that is being named. For the Virgin gave birth to the Son of God, Χριστοτόκος: since the Son of God is double in natures, she did give birth to the Son of God because she gave birth to the human being who is the Son of God by reason of the Son of God joined to him. [Col. 0765B]

We have shown that in the birth from Christ’s Virgin Mother, Holy Scripture uses the name “Son.” Now hear also about the death, and see whether the name “God” is ever placed there, so that we might introduce a suffering God. “When we were enemies,” he says, “we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. V, 10). He does not say, “through the death of God the Word.”

God the Word was indeed God, Son, and God with the Father before the Incarnation; but in the last times he took the form of a servant. Since he was Son before and is so called after the assumption, he cannot be called a divided Son, lest we establish two sons. But because the one who was Son from the beginning is joined to him, the dignity of sonship cannot undergo division. I speak of dignity of sonship, not of natures. Therefore God the Word is also called Christ, because he has an enduring conjunction with Christ; nor is it possible for God the Word to do anything without humanity, for humanity has been brought to the highest degree of conjunction, though not to deification, as the more recent teachers of doctrine assert. [Col. 0765D] [Col. 0766A]

Thus we also call Christ according to the flesh “God,” because of the conjunction which he has with God the Word, while knowing that he is a human being who appears. Hear Paul proclaiming both: “From the Israelites is Christ according to the flesh, who is above all gods” (Rom. IX, 5). First he confesses him to be a human being; then, by his conjunction with God, he calls the one who appears “God,” so that no one may think that Christianity is a worshiper of a human being.

Hear also this name, “Lord,” used at one time of Christ’s humanity, at another of his divinity, and at another of both. “Whenever you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death” (1 Cor. 11:26). Hear from the preceding words the ignorance of those who object: they read that the usefulness of this mystery is very great, and what remembrance it brings to human beings; and hear not me saying this, but blessed Paul: “Whenever you eat this bread.” He did not say, “Whenever you eat this divinity,” but, “Whenever you eat this bread.” See that what is set before them is the Lord’s body: “Whenever you eat this bread,” of which the body itself is the antitype. Let us therefore see whose death it is. “Whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death.” Hear more clearly in what follows: “until he comes.” But who will come? “They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with great glory” (Matt. 24:30). And, what is more, the prophet had shown him coming more plainly before the apostles and cries out concerning the Jews: “They will look upon him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12:10). What, then, was pierced? The side. But the side belongs not to God, but to man.

Let us therefore preserve the conjunction of the natures without confusion; let us confess God in the man; let us worship the man, who through a certain divine conjunction with almighty God is worthy of adoration.

Say of the one who assumes that he is God; add of the one assumed that he is the form of a servant; then assert the dignity of the conjunction: that the authority of the two is shared, that the dignity of the two is the same; and, while the natures remain, confess the unity.

[Note: [Col. 0765D]

As we said at the beginning, apart from Marius Mercator, five witnesses affirm this.

Cyril (Book Against [title uncertain], ch. 9): For he writes again in this way, when he had undertaken a discussion against the Arians: “They absurdly assert that the Word of God himself is more recent than the Divinity, which is greater; but these men make him later than blessed Mary and place a temporal mother before the divinity, the creator of time.” And elsewhere (Book IV, ch. 1): “The Word of God became flesh and dwelt among us. The Father made the humanity he had assumed sit with him,” and so forth. And later (ch. 3): “This good man dares to diminish the Word of God, consubstantial with God the Father, as though he did not know that he became man—not by casting away what he is as God, but rather by assuming what he was not. For while, as has been said, he takes the Holy Spirit’s part, he injures the Son when, against the followers of Arius, he says: ‘Inflicting a greater injury upon him and separating from the divine nature the Spirit who formed his humanity,’” and so forth.]

Cassian (Book VII, On the Incarnation, ch. 17): “You say, then, in another discussion—or rather, in another blasphemy of yours: ‘They separate from the divine nature the Spirit who created his humanity.’ For he says that what was born from Mary is from the Holy Spirit,” and so forth, up to these words: “This Spirit, finally, who bestowed such great glory upon Christ.”

Eusebius, in his protestation (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, ch. 13): Nestorius says: “They assign a temporal mother to the divinity that established the ages.” Again Paul says: “Mary received the Word, and is not older than the Word.” Nestorius says: “How could Mary have given birth from herself to one older than she?” Paul says: “Mary brought forth a man like us.” Nestorius says: “The one born from the Virgin is a man.” Paul says: “Yet he is superior to us in every respect, for he is from the Holy Spirit, brought forth through divine promises, and, according to Scripture, grace was given to him.” Nestorius says: “I saw the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, and also giving him the power of ascent; for, when he commanded the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up through the Holy Spirit. This, then, is the one who bestowed such great glory upon Christ.”

Peter, first secretary of the notaries (Act 1 of the Council of Ephesus): “How can he be a servant,” he says, “who cooperates with the Son and the Father? And if anyone investigates the works of the Spirit, he will find them neither different from nor unlike the works of the Father and the Son,” and so forth, up to these words: “For when the Spirit of truth comes, he will glorify me.”

The author of the dispute between Arnobius and Serapion. Also in another sermon, whose beginning is: “Often, as I turned over in my mind the waves of life, the manifold mutability of earthly things, and the snares scattered throughout life, I cried out in perplexity: ‘Who can be delivered?’” And a little later he says: “They separate from the divine nature the Spirit who created his humanity. For what was born from Mary is from the Holy Spirit,” and so forth.

Since it is plainly established that this sermon is Nestorius’s, someone may perhaps ask when it was delivered. It was certainly before Nestorius sent his first letter to Pope Celestine: for it was sent to Rome together with that letter, and from there to Cassian, who excerpted what we have reported above; indeed, it was before the protestation presented by Eusebius, since he himself proved from it Nestorius’s agreement with Paul of Samosata; and, with still greater reason, before Cyril’s books of contradictions were written and the blasphemies excerpted at Alexandria and brought to Rome by Possidius, Nestorius’s deacon. For these two events occurred after the aforementioned letter and the presentation of the protestation.

Since Nestorius sent his first letter to Celestine in the year 429, in the autumn, while the protestation appears to have been presented before the panegyric delivered by Proclus in the year 429, on March 25, this sermon must have followed immediately in December of 429 and thus have been delivered around the beginning of January.]

## SERMON III. Delivered by Nestorius

[Note: [Col. 0766D] Nestorius divided his treatise into two parts: the first against the Macedonians, the second against the Arians. Yet in each he argues against them with such craft—or malice—that, while indeed exaggerating the impiety of the heretical doctrines, he does not go so far that they could not appear more tolerable than the opinions of Catholics. This is why Mercator, and also Cyril, say that the sermon was not delivered simply against the Arians. It is reasonable to believe that the surviving fragments of both parts are exceedingly small in comparison with the whole. For in the first part he refutes only the Macedonian blasphemy by which they asserted that the Holy Spirit was Christ’s servant; in the second he touches only lightly upon the Arian cause.] Ostensibly against the Arians and Macedonians, but in reality against the Catholics who defended the true union of the natures in Christ.

[Col. 0767A]

[Note: [Col. 0768C] The impiety of the Macedonians concerning the Holy Spirit as Christ’s servant is indeed refuted, but by means of another no less serious impiety, in which Christ himself is said to be inferior to the Holy Spirit: by that Spirit, namely, he was formed in the Virgin’s womb, adorned with righteousness, made terrifying to demons, consecrated as the temple of the divinity, and endowed with the glory of ascension.]

“Those men, devising an even greater injury against Christ, cut off the Holy Spirit from the divine nature—the Spirit who fashioned Christ’s humanity in the Virgin’s womb. For, as Scripture says, ‘What was born in her is from the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. 1:20); he reformed what had been fashioned according to righteousness: ‘He was manifested in the flesh and justified in the spirit’ (1 Tim. 3:16); he made him terrible and fearful to demons: ‘For I cast out demons by the Spirit of God’ (Luke 11:20); he fashioned his flesh as a temple: ‘For I saw the Spirit,’ he says, ‘descending like a dove and remaining upon him’ (John 1:32); he granted him his ascent into heaven: ‘For,’ Scripture says, ‘after commanding the apostles whom he had chosen through the Holy Spirit, he was taken up into heaven’ (Acts 1:2). This Spirit, I say, who bestowed such great glory, they assert to be Christ’s servant.

“But how can he be a servant who cooperates with the Son and the Father? For if anyone investigates the works of the Spirit, he will find them neither different from nor unlike the works of the Father and the Son—not because the one divinity is divided, but because divine Scripture distributes among the individual substances things that belong to one power, so that the likeness of the Trinity may be demonstrated. Consider this, beginning with the works performed in their proper time: ‘The Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1:14). The Father made the man who had been assumed sit with him: ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand’ (Ps. 109:1). The Spirit glorified the one who had been assumed: ‘For when the Spirit of truth comes, he will glorify me’ (John 16:13).”

Would you like us to add another manifestation of the Trinity’s activity to these? The Son dwelt in the body. The Father commended the baptized one. The Spirit formed him in the Virgin. The Son chose the apostles: “I chose you,” he says (John 15:19). The Father sanctified them: “Father,” he says, “sanctify them in your truth” (John 17:17). The Spirit made them proclaimers (Acts 2:4).

[Note: [Col. 0768D] As I said, he touches lightly but wickedly upon the Arian cause, so that he may represent what the Catholic defenders of the Incarnation say as something more impious than what the Arians say. For he says that both groups abase the Word, but in such a way that the Arians subject him only to the divinity, asserting him to be inferior, whereas the Catholics subject him also to the creature, saying that he is more recent.]

“And these men” (the Arians), “although in their madness they say that the Word, God, is lesser than the majesty of the Father’s divinity, nevertheless do not confess him to be recent; but these others declare him also to be second and later than blessed Mary, and assign a temporal mother to the divinity, the creator of time.”

[Note: [Col. 0768D] The Nestorians greatly favored this argument, so that scarcely anyone failed to use it. It is certainly found in Eutherius (Sermon 3): “Moreover,” he says, “according to them, the Virgin was not even a mother. For if the Word made himself flesh, he did not come forth from flesh assumed from her. For how can she be the mother of one whose birth has no part in her? How can that be called birth—the inappropriate passage, as it were, through a channel? They therefore make the holy Virgin not a mother, but a vessel.”]

Indeed, they do not even grant that she is Christ’s mother. For if it was not the nature of man but the Word of God whom she bore, she who gave birth is by no means found to be the mother of the one born. For how can she become the mother of one who is alien to the nature of his mother? But if she is truly called his mother by them, then the one who was born is not of the nature of the divinity but is man, since it is proper to every mother to give birth to one consubstantial with herself.

Therefore she will not be a mother who did not give birth to one consubstantial with herself. Therefore, since they call her mother, she gave birth to one who is like her in substance. And who will be like him in substance? Without doubt, the one who came into being through the work of the Holy Spirit: “What was born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20), with whom the Word, God, was continually present.

The Word, God, therefore, was not born from Mary, but remained in the one who was born from her. He did not receive his beginning from the Virgin, but was inseparably joined for all time to the one who, growing and gradually taking shape over the course of months, was in the Virgin’s womb. It is one thing to say, “He remains with the one who was born,” and another to say that the one who remains with the person born is himself the one who needed the passage of months in order to be born.

When Nestorius was using profane novelties of expression in the midst of the Church—by which he attacked both the title Theotokos (Θεοτόκος, “Mother of God”) and Christ’s twofold birth—

[Note: [Col. 0769C]

That man, said to be upright, remarkably learned, and inflamed with zeal for the faith, who at that time was still among the laity when he opposed Nestorius, and who afterward—as the word “still” indicates—was elevated to a higher rank, was undoubtedly none other than Eusebius, later bishop of Dorylaeum. For at the time when he first of all detected Nestorius’s heresy, he not only flourished in the praise of virtue, the reputation of learning, and zeal for the faith, but was also counted among the advocates of the imperial city.

From this it is plainly understood why Eusebius publicly presented his famous protestation at Constantinople, by which he demonstrated the agreement of Paul of Samosata and Nestorius. Since he had openly resisted the heretic and had been badly treated by him as though he had spoken impiously, he felt that it was in the interest of his reputation—and indeed of the Catholic faith—to reveal to everyone, but especially to the clergy, how justified he had been in doing so.

The time when the protestation was published is also understood: it followed Nestorius’s sermon against the Arians and preceded Proclus’s oration, and thus fell approximately in the middle of January. For what Leontius wrote is true: that Nestorius’s heresy was first detected, indeed publicly rebuked, by Eusebius. No one before him had dared openly to accuse the bishop of the imperial city, a man dear to the emperor.

Someone may ask why we so confidently attribute to Eusebius the protestation which, in the commonly circulated manuscripts of the Council of Ephesus, is assigned to the clergy of Constantinople, despite the opposition of all editors of the councils. I reply that we do so on the basis both of reason and of the authority of the ancients. First, the person who presents the protestation is a single individual. “I adjure,” he says, “all who will receive this document by the holy Trinity, and I entreat them,” and so forth. Then he asks that the document be communicated to the bishops, presbyters, deacons, readers, and also the laity living in Constantinople, for the manifest confusion of the heretic Nestorius. These two facts, although they might perhaps be made to fit the clergy of Constantinople, fit perfectly a single individual who was counted neither among the bishops, nor among the presbyters, nor even among the deacons and readers living in Constantinople. There is also the clear testimony of Leontius the Scholasticus: “The refutation of both men, Paul and Nestorius, was presented from the publicly circulated testimony said to have been issued by Eusebius, who at that time was distinguished by authority in judgment; afterward he became prefect of the Church of the Dorylaeans. Inflamed, as they testify, by divine zeal, he was the first to detect and convict the heresy of Nestorius and Eutyches, having been exposed to countless dangers for the sake of piety. Hear, therefore, with what sort of blasphemies collected from Paul of Samosata he joined Nestorius’s blasphemies, and demonstrated that the mind of both was equally insane,” and so forth (Book III Against the Nestorians and Eutychians, vol. IV of Ancient Readings).]

A certain man, truly upright, who was still among the laity but had nevertheless acquired remarkable learning, moved by fervent and religious zeal, cried out in a louder voice: “He says that the Word himself, before the ages, underwent a second generation—that is, the generation according to the flesh and from a woman.” When the crowd became tumultuous at this, and the greater and sounder part raised him to the highest praises as an especially pious and wise man, not ignorant of correct doctrine, while others nevertheless grew angry against him, Nestorius himself intervened. At once he approved those whom he had ruined by his teaching; but he sharpened his tongue against the man who had not endured his doctrines, and against the holy Fathers who had established for us the pious definition of the faith, and said:

“I rejoice when I see your zeal, for by it the things shamefully spoken by that wretched man can plainly be refuted. For where there are two generations, there must necessarily be two sons; but the Church recognizes one Son, the Lord Christ himself.”

We, however, ought to understand what has just come to mind concerning the Nicene Council, which nowhere dared to say that the Word of God was born from the Virgin Mary. For it says: “We believe in one almighty Father and in one Lord Jesus Christ.”

[Note: [Col. 0770C] Among the people of Constantinople no other creed was in use than the Nicene Creed, although the Antiochenes used another, and one considerably different. When Nestorius was arguing against the Catholics at Constantinople, he brought forward the Nicene Creed; Cassian, against Nestorius, used the Antiochene Creed (Book VI throughout). To make the difference between the two known, it seemed worthwhile to set one against the other in parallel (παραλλήλως).]

Pay attention: although the Fathers first placed “Christ,” which demonstrates the conjunction of two natures, they did not say “the one Word of God”; rather, they used a name that signified both, so that, by descending step by step, when you hear of death you may not be troubled by anything novel, and when you hear of crucifixion and burial you may not be wounded in hearing, as though the divinity itself had suffered.

[Note: [Col. 0770D] Cassian vigorously attacks this passage (Book VI, chs. 9–12). “What do you say?”—he addresses Nestorius. “Why is the one born from the Christotokos (Χριστοτόκος, ‘Mother of Christ’) not considered the Son of God? ‘If we say,’ you declare, ‘I believe in God, the Word, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father, consubstantial with the Father, who descended and was buried,’ the hearer immediately receives a blow.” You therefore consider the faith of our salvation and the mystery of the Church’s hope a blow to your hearing and ears. And how, when you once ran to baptism, did you hear these mysteries with sound ears? How, when the teachers of the Churches instructed you, were your ears not wounded? Then, certainly without any wound, you performed the double function of mouth and ears, both repeating what you had heard from others and hearing yourself as you spoke. Where then were these wounds of your ears? Where was this blow to your hearing? … The blow to your hearing and the wound of your ears is therefore “God born” and “God suffering.” And where is that saying of yours, O Apostle Paul: “We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1)? … Their ears were therefore wounded by the preaching and passion of God, just as yours are now. They thought this was a blow to their hearing, just as you do. And for this reason, when the Apostle preached Christ as God, they closed the ears of their heads at the name of God and Lord Jesus Christ, just as you close the ears of your mind.]

Then let us see what they add: “We believe also in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of the Father, who for us descended and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit.” They did not say that he was born from the Holy Spirit. See how they interpret the matter by descending step by step, since they said that he was made man. “We say,” they declare, “that God was incarnate, not that the divine nature underwent a change into flesh, but we indicate the indwelling which he maintained in the man.”

And after a little: “Hold on to this: although they omitted saying, ‘We believe in God the Word, his only-begotten Son,’ they said, ‘We believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, consubstantial with the Father, true God from true God, through whom all things were made, who for us human beings and for our salvation descended and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit, from the Virgin Mary, and was made man.’ They nowhere said, ‘was born.’ Why, we ask? So that they would not introduce two births of the divinity.”

And after a little: “For Scripture says: ‘God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law’ (Gal. 4:4). Here it demonstrates two natures. But it narrates what concerns only the man. Ask the contentious man, certainly, who was made under the law. The Word of God? Certainly not.”

What, then, were we saying? “Do not fear to take Mary as your wife; for what has been born”—whether we say “born” or “made,” it does no harm to the meaning—“what has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20). If we say that the Word of God was born in the womb—for it is one thing to be together with the one who is being born, and another to be born—then, “what,” he says, “has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit”; that is, the Holy Spirit created what is in her. The Fathers therefore saw, as those who knew the holy Scriptures, that if we call the one who was incarnate “born,” the Word of God the Son will be found to be the Son of the Holy Spirit, or to have two Fathers. But if we say “made,” the Word of God will be found to be a creature of the Holy Spirit. Avoiding, therefore, the expression “generation,” they said this: “He who descended for our salvation and was incarnate.” What does “incarnate” mean? Not that he was changed from divinity into flesh.

In saying “incarnate from the Holy Spirit,” they followed the evangelist. For when the evangelist came to the incarnation (ἐνανθρώπησις), he avoided speaking of a generation of the Word and said “incarnation.” Hear him: “And the Word became flesh” (John 1:14); he did not say, “The Word became through flesh.” For whenever the apostles or evangelists mention the Son, they say that he was born from a woman. Observe, please, that whenever they use the name “Son,” they say that the one who was born was born from a woman. But whenever they mention the Word, no one dares to speak of generation through humanity.

Hear blessed John the evangelist when he came to the Word and his incarnation (ἐνανθρώπησις). Hear what he says: “The Word became flesh”—that is, he assumed flesh—“and dwelt among us”—that is, he put on our nature—“and we saw the glory of the Son himself.” He did not say, “We saw the generation of the Word.”

[Col. 0772A]

And after a little: “If they had said, ‘We believe in one God, the Word,’ it would have followed that death was attributed to the divine nature. Therefore they take a common name, namely Jesus Christ, so that they might signify both that he died and that he did not die. Thus, just as someone may say that a man has died, although the soul is immortal, nevertheless, because he has used a name that signifies two natures—the body that dies and the immortal soul—there is no danger in the expression. For both the body and the soul are called ‘man.’ So, then, that great chorus also spoke of Christ.”

## The Nicene Creed, which is also the Constantinopolitan Creed

[Note: [Col. 0772A] The following texts, headed “The Nicene Creed, which is also the Constantinopolitan Creed” and “The Antiochene Creed,” are printed in parallel in Migne.]

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, creator of all things visible and invisible.

And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father; through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth.

[Col. 0772C]

Who for us human beings and for our salvation descended, and was incarnate and made man, and suffered, and rose again on the third day; he ascended into heaven and will come to judge the living and the dead.

And in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and “Before he was born, he was not,” or that he came from things that did not exist, or from another substance or essence, or who assert that the Son of God is subject to change or alteration—the Catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them.

## The Antiochene Creed

[Col. 0772A]

I believe in one and only true God, the almighty Father, creator of all visible and invisible created things.

And in our Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son and firstborn of the whole creation, born from him before all the ages and not made, true God from true God, ὁμοούσιον (consubstantial) with the Father, through whom the ages were also joined together and all things were made.

[Col. 0772C]

Who came for us, and was born from the Virgin Mary, and was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures, and ascended into heaven, and will come again to judge the living and the dead.

## EPISTLE

[Note: [Col. 0773B] The occasion on which it was written and the time are stated in the historical preface: namely, in the second year of Nestorius, at the beginning of January, after the three earlier sermons in which Nestorius had delivered his impiety in the Church, so that, while the clergy remained silent through fear, this layman too might accuse the wicked heresy. Thus, just as it is paired with Eusebius’s protestation, so the two are bound together in their relation to life, each shedding light upon the other; they should not be separated, but the protestation should be placed after it, as though it were its explanatory title. The text is not taken from the more recent version, whether the Peltan or the Roman, but rather from the older one, which, although inferior to the other in Latin style, surpasses it in fidelity and even appears to be Mercator’s own, since it does not depart from the method of translation which Marius professed to follow in the preface to Nestorius’s sermons against the Pelagians; it is full of expressions which Marius almost deliberately favors, and it includes Nestorius’s words, which Mercator translates in the same way in his other works.]

### OF MARIUS MERCATOR

On the Difference between the Heresy of Nestorius and the Doctrines of Paul of Samosata, Ebion, Photinus, and Marcellus.

[Col. 0773A]

Marius Mercator, [Note: [Col. 0773C] He designates himself by this name, as laymen were accustomed to do, so that it may be clear that at that time he had not been appointed to any rank of the clergy. For in that age no cleric failed to take pride in bearing the name of his rank.] servant of Christ, greeting to his fellow servant, the reader [Note: [Col. 0773C] Since the letter was to be scattered among the people and passed from hand to hand to anyone who encountered it, it was addressed not to any particular person but generally to his fellow servant, who, like himself, declared himself a servant of Christ, whose glory was endangered by the heretic. I think that it was first written in Greek and then in Latin, or in both languages simultaneously by Mercator, so that it might pass over no people of any nation. Marius did something similar in the Commonitorium.]

1. [Note: [Col. 0773D] On this comparison of Nestorius with the man of Samosata, besides Eusebius’s protestation, it is worthwhile to consult Nestorius himself and Mercator: Nestorius in the last two sermons, in which he attempts to remove from himself the charge of agreement with the man of Samosata and with Photinus; Mercator in his contradiction of Nestorius’s twelfth anathema, near the end. We shall discuss the matter at length in a separate dissertation on the Nestorian heresy.] This is the no less impious than vain doctrine of Paul of Samosata and Nestorius.

Nestorius, concerning the Word of God [Baluz. adds “indeed”], does not hold the same view as Paul, who defines the Word not as substantial but as an uttered, effective expression of God’s power; [Note: [Col. 0773D] Baluz.: Nevertheless, Nestorius does confess that the Son himself is in the substantial Word, rarely, albeit subtly [reading uncertain], since he does not expressly say that the Word is the Son from eternity. EDIT.] yet Nestorius does not acknowledge that the substantial Word is naturally the Son of God himself. Rather, he says—cleverly, because not explicitly—that from eternity he is not the Son but only the Word, who, remaining in the Father’s substance, is God [Note: [Col. 0774C] Garnerius, in the margin: “consubstantial.” EDIT.], consubstantial, which the Greeks call ὁμοούσιον; but he asserts that the Son is and must be called the one who was born from Mary.

2. In this way he separates the eternal from the temporal, assigning to the one—God and the Word of God—the things that belong to majesty, and to the other the things that belong to human weakness. But because of their indivisible and inseparable connection, he says that the latter was considered worthy to receive the designation “Son of God,” since he has this by merit and adoption, not by nature.

[Note: [Col. 0774C] This admonition must be observed, lest Mercator appear to misrepresent Nestorius, who seems to affirm that the Word was, before the incarnation, both Son and God (Sermon 3). But since he repeatedly says that the name “Son” signifies two natures (Sermon 2), Mercator rightly infers that Nestorius asserts that the Word was not the Son from eternity but only the Word. The whole passage, however, is so involved—not to say corrupt—that its meaning can scarcely be reached. Perhaps, in this novel matter, Nestorius did not sufficiently explain his thought, as often happens, and Mercator did not sufficiently understand from ambiguous words the opinion of a man who was trying to conceal it.]

3. But when the Catholics object to him that, according to this interpretation, he regards there being two Christs and two Sons, he answers on his own behalf as follows: “I define one Christ, who must be called the anointed one, from chrism; this same one is the one Son of God, because, as was said above, he is joined to God the Word by an indivisible fellowship. Sometimes, because of this very inseparable conjunction, or connection, that Word also is called by the same titles, although they are completely alien to his nature. Finally, because of his merit, this Jesus Christ, of singular birth and incomparable life, was considered worthy, as a temple containing the entire fullness of divinity, to be inhabited by this God and Word of God.”

[Note: [Col. 0774A] Baluz. adds “Jesus” after “two” (thus, “two Jesus Christs”); reads “who” for “because”; and adds “indeed” after “sometimes.” In §2, Baluz. omits “since”; in §5, reads “Into that which indeed” for “But in that”; and in §6 adds “nevertheless” after “Lord Christ.”]

4. In this respect, therefore, he is joined to Paul of Samosata: he separates the indweller and the dwelling-place according to merits, dividing what is proper to each of them according to the diversity of nature. This is shared by both of them with Ebion, Photinus, and the Galatian Marcellus.

5. But in confessing the substantial Word of God and asserting that he is God from eternity with the Father, he rightly differs from the men mentioned above and is joined to the true faith.

6. But because he again says that the same Word, God, is not naturally the Son of God the Father but only the Word, as we explained above, and divides in the Lord Christ the merits of each substance, he incurs the great crime of impiety and hence, as one alien and expelled from the ecclesiastical faith, rightly—

[Note: [Col. 0774C] By Eusebius, certainly, in the protestation, and by the other faithful who withdrew from the bishop. See Sermon 5.]

[Col. 0774D]

Publicly presented protestation at Constantinople against the impious sermons of Nestorius.

I adjure the recipient of this document, by the Holy Trinity, to make it public to bishops, presbyters, deacons, lectors, and laypeople living in Constantinople. Moreover, let him provide them with a copy, for the reproof of Nestorius, because he holds opinions like those of Paul of Samosata, who was anathematized by the orthodox bishops 160 years ago. The statements made by each of them are as follows:

—Paul said: “Mary did not give birth to the Word.” Nestorius said correspondingly: “Mary did not give birth to the Godhead, most excellent” (*Sermon 1*).

—Paul said: “For he did not exist before the ages.” Nestorius said: “And they assign a temporal mother to the Godhead, the maker of the ages” (*Sermon 3*).

—Paul said: “Mary received the Word, and she is not older than the Word.” Nestorius said: “How, then, did she give birth to one older than herself?” [Col. 0775A] (*Sermon 1*).

—Paul said: “Mary gave birth to a man equal to us.” Nestorius said: “He is a man, who was born from the Virgin” (*ibid.*).

—Paul said: “Yet he is better in every respect, because grace is in him from the Holy Spirit, from the Scriptures, and from the promises.” Nestorius said: “For I saw,” he says, “the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him—the one who granted him his ascension. ‘Giving commands,’ he says, ‘to the apostles whom he had chosen through the Holy Spirit, he was taken up’ (Acts 1:2)—the one, evidently, who granted Christ such great glory” (*Sermon 3*).

—Paul said: “Neither is the one born from David alien to Wisdom, nor does Wisdom dwell in another in this way. For it was in the prophets, and more particularly in Moses, and in many lords [κυρίοις, eminent men]; rather, in Christ, as in a temple.” Elsewhere he said that Jesus Christ was one thing and the Word another. Nestorius said: “Is it possible that the one born before all the ages should be born another time as something else [ἄλλο ἅπαξ], and this with respect to the Godhead? Behold, he has clearly been proved a transgressor by saying: ‘The one born of the Father was not born of Mary.’ Behold, he agrees with the heretic Paul, who says that the Word is one and Jesus Christ another, and that they are not one, as the true faith proclaims.”

“Therefore I have indicated to you, zealous defender of the holy faith, a portion of the anathema of the Church of Antioch [in the commonly circulated manuscripts: ‘a portion of the doctrinal statement’ (μέρος τοῦ μαθήματος)]—the Church from which, in the first place, we received even the name ‘Christians’—because it does not recognize one Son of God as one person and another as another, but one and the same: the one born before all the ages, God from God the Father, consubstantial with the Father, and the same one born from Mary under Caesar Augustus. For it expressly declares: ‘True God from true God, consubstantial with the Father, through whom the ages were created and all things perfected; who came for us and was born from holy Mary the Virgin; and was crucified under Pontius Pilate.’ And the rest of the creed.

“Blessed Eustathius also agrees with these things. He was bishop of Antioch and one of the 318 bishops present at the holy Great Council, and he says as follows: ‘He is not merely man, but also God, just as the prophet Jeremiah says (Baruch 3:36): “This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. He discovered the whole way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings.”’ When, then, did he live among human beings, except when he was born among them from the Virgin, and was an infant with them, and grew, and ate, and drank? And other things.

“Therefore, if anyone should presume to say that there is one Son, the only-begotten one before the ages, who was born from the Father, and another born from the Virgin Mary, and that they are not the same one Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema.”

He has therefore been condemned.

[Note: [Col. 0775C] Since Proclus refuted Nestorius’s first sermon on the virgin birth in a panegyrical address to the Virgin Θεοτόκος, and Nestorius in turn attacked Proclus’s address in his fourth sermon, this discourse had to be placed here—not merely to show why Nestorius later said almost nothing concerning the matter of the incarnation without raging against Proclus, but also, and especially, because it appears to have had Marius Mercator as its translator, as will soon be stated.]

## HOMILY

[Note: [Col. 0775C] He was indeed bishop of Constantinople in his own time, having been appointed after Maximian, who was installed after Nestorius had been deposed. Yet he is here called Cyzicene because, when he delivered the address, he was commonly known by that designation. He had been elevated to the see of the Church of Cyzicus by Sisinnius, Nestorius’s predecessor, but was rejected by the Cyzicene clergy. Although they respected his virtue, they wished to retain the authority of electing their own bishop, an authority which the bishop of the imperial city was attempting to assume contrary to canon and custom. Thus, after rejecting Proclus, whom Sisinnius had ordained, they appointed Dalmatianus for themselves; Proclus, however, remained in Constantinople with the title of bishop but with the office of presbyter, as he had previously held.]

He lived for a long time in the Church of Constantinople before obtaining its see. While still a young man he attached himself to Chrysostom as a secretary and, after becoming a lector, served him in the transcription of books. Later, Atticus—who succeeded Chrysostom after Arsacius—ordained him deacon and presbyter, and he then began to instruct the people, enjoying a great reputation for eloquence and an even greater one for piety.

These qualities caused him, whenever the see became vacant, to be summoned into competition for the episcopate with the most distinguished presbyters of that Church. After Atticus’s death, he competed with Sisinnius and Philip; after Sisinnius’s death, again with Philip, while the clergy were stubbornly divided; after Nestorius’s deposition, his virtue once more competed with Philip and Maximian. Yet each time he was rejected—not unwillingly, because of the man’s exceptional modesty and holiness of life.

The causes of his rejection are said to have been partly the machinations of Chrysostom’s enemies at court; partly the people’s excessive enthusiasm, from which arose either suspicion or envy in the emperor; and partly the favor enjoyed by his competitors among the city clergy, together with the clergy’s fear that Proclus, following Chrysostom’s example, would observe ecclesiastical discipline more rigorously. After so many rejections, he finally obtained the see upon Maximian’s death (A.D. 434), when the former obstacles had been removed. The court had returned, as it were, to friendly relations with Chrysostom; Proclus’s virtue, proven by long experience, had transformed the emperor’s suspicion into esteem; Philip had damaged the opinion formed of him by his untimely disparagement of good men; and the Nicene canon prohibiting the translation of bishops had received, through a letter of Pope Celestine, so convenient an interpretation that, if Proclus were appointed to the see of Constantinople, he could no longer seem to be doing what Jerome once described as despising the companionship of a poor virgin and seeking the embraces of a richer adulteress.

What he accomplished during the entire twelve years in which he presided over the episcopate—that is, until the year 446, when he died—is narrated by Socrates; consult him.

## OF PROCLUS, BISHOP OF CYZICUS

[Note: [Col. 0776B] If the title stated the time as precisely as it states the other circumstances, it would shed considerable light on the history. Nevertheless, certain statements by the authors and certain expressions in the discourse [Col. 0776C] can make up for the title’s silence. We said (*Preface to the History*) that it was delivered in A.D. 429, the second year of Nestorius, on March 25, when the εὐαγγελισμός—the Annunciation—was being celebrated. For, if we believe Theophanes, it was delivered ἐν μιᾷ Κυριακῇ, “on a certain Lord’s feast.” The word Κυριακή has such force that, when used absolutely, it signifies some more solemn feast day, with ἑορτή, “feast,” understood; but when it denotes one day of the week, it always—or almost always—has the word ἡμέρα, “day,” added. Since in former times no ἑορτὴ Κυριακή, “Lord’s feast,” was named except one belonging to Christ or the blessed Virgin, and since the feast in question was not Christ’s but the Virgin’s—for Proclus says, “Today the virginal solemnity summons our tongue to proclamation,” etc.—and since, from December, when Nestorius delivered his first sermon, until the feast of Easter, during which period the address must have been delivered, there was no such feast except the εὐαγγελισμός, on which all agree, the panegyrical sermon in question was unquestionably delivered at that time.

As for what someone might allege from certain words of the Tenth Council of Toledo [Col. 0776D] and from these words of the title, “On the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ” (M. Mercator, Part I of the Works), claiming that Proclus spoke in the church on behalf of the Virgin Deipara on December 18, a day celebrated as the εὐαγγελισμός, this carries little weight with me. Although I admit that the same solemnity was at one time called εὐαγγελισμός when it concerned the Virgin, and ἐνανθρώπησις when it concerned Christ, I nevertheless know that the opinion that the εὐαγγελισμός was formerly celebrated by the Greeks in December is neither certain, as we established in that place, nor, even if it were true, sufficient to remove the difficulty, since the historical evidence prevents Proclus’s panegyrical sermon from being assigned to another time.]

Delivered while Nestorius was seated in the great church of Constantinople, on the incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ, and that the blessed Virgin Mary is the Deipara, and that the one born from her is neither God alone nor a mere man, but Emmanuel, God and man without confusion and without change.

[Col. 0777A]

[Note: [Col. 0777D] The first reason why this seems so, against the opinion of some who attribute the translation of the address to Dionysius Exiguus, is that no one believed Dionysius Exiguus to be the author of this ancient translation before Vincent Richard, who recently published all the works of Proclus, and the learned Labbe, who agreed with Richard. Yet neither of them asserts this forcefully: the former says that perhaps the matter is so, while the latter does not wish to endorse Vincent’s statement, being content to write of Dionysius in these words (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Dionysius”): “The address of Proclus on the praises of the Virgin is said to have been rendered from Greek by the same author.”

A further reason is that Richard’s argument from style actually overturns the very point for which it is offered: the style of the ancient translator and that of Dionysius are not the same, although the diction of both may be humble or careless. The translator may appear to have aimed at expressing the author’s meaning all the more faithfully by departing as little as possible from the Greek phraseology, just as Mercator admits of himself in a similar case (*Preface to the Various Sermons of Nestorius*).

Finally, since the ancient manuscripts, especially the Vatican manuscript (Vatic. MS 2836), from which Richard transcribed, call the translator unknown, room remains for conjecture. Since this version is not inconsistent with the method of translation followed by Mercator when rendering, as he says, Nestorius’s and Cyril’s Greek writings “word for word,” he may plausibly be regarded as the author of this version. The probability may be increased by the fact that, unless Mercator translated Proclus’s address into Latin, he would certainly have failed in the purpose by which he wished Nestorius’s blasphemies to be known and avoided by the faithful who shared his language. For the contents of the fourth and fifth sermons—and even those that follow—as well as of Cyril’s letters and other books, could scarcely be understood unless Proclus’s address, against whom Nestorius chiefly directed himself, had first been understood; for all these writings drew their subject matter, either wholly or chiefly, from it.]

Apparently translated by Marius Mercator.

### 1

Today the virginal solemnity, brothers, summons our tongue to proclamation, and the present festival, with great propriety, becomes for those who have assembled a provider of benefit. For it has the substance of chastity and the glory of the female sex, on account of her who is a mother in time and forever a virgin.

### 2

Behold, both earth and sea offer gifts to the Virgin: the former quietly spreading its back beneath the waves, the latter directing the steps of those who walk without hindrance. Let nature rejoice, let women be honored, let humanity lead the dances, let virgins be glorified: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5:20).

The blessed Mary has summoned us—the spotless vessel of virginity, the rational paradise of the second Adam, the work of the union of natures, the solemnity of salutary exchange, the bush which the fire of divine birth did not consume, truly the light cloud that bore in the body him who is above the cherubim.
