O fleece most pure of the heavenly rain, from which the Shepherd clothed himself with a sheep!

### 3

Mary: mother and handmaid, Virgin and heaven, the only bridge of God to human beings, the terrifying loom of the dispensation, on which the tunic of the ineffable incarnation was woven. The Holy Spirit is the over-weaver of this work; the power from on high, overshadowing, is the weaver; the garment is the clothing of the ancient Adam; the threads are the flesh from the immaculate Virgin; the shuttle is the immeasurable grace of the one who puts it on; the craftsman is the Word, which entered through obedience.

Who has seen, who has heard, that the uncircumscribed God dwelt in a womb, and that the womb of the Virgin contained him whom heaven could not contain?

### 4

God was born from a woman, but not naked; a man was born, but not a mere man. The one who was born showed the gate of salvation where the gate of ancient sin had been. For where the serpent poured out poison through disobedience, there the Word, entering the temple through obedience, fashioned it into a living being. From where Cain, the first disciple of sin, emerged, there Christ, the liberator of our race, sprang forth without seed.

### 5

The lover of humanity was not ashamed of a woman’s birth pangs, for the business being conducted concerned life. He who had fashioned the wombs without dishonor was not defiled by dwelling within them. If the mother did not remain a virgin, the one born is merely human and the birth was not miraculous; but if she remained a virgin even after giving birth, then he was ineffably born from her who entered through closed doors without hindrance. Recognizing the union of the natures, Thomas exclaimed: “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28).

### 6

Do not be ashamed, O man, of birth; it itself became for us the occasion of salvation. If he had not been born from a woman, he would certainly not have died; if he had not died, he would not through death have destroyed “the one who has the power of death” (Heb. 2:14), that is, the devil.

It is no insult for the architect to remain in the things he himself built; the potter is not defiled by renewing the clay he had fashioned. Thus the undefiled one is not defiled by proceeding from the Virgin’s womb: he was not defiled when he fashioned it, and, passing through it, he was not polluted.

### 7

O womb in which the guarantee of our common freedom was prepared! O womb in which weapons against death were forged! O threshing floor in which Christ, the cultivator of nature, sprang forth like an ear of grain without seed! O temple in which God became priest—not changing his nature, but, out of compassion, clothing himself with the one who is according to the order of Melchizedek!

### 8

“The Word became flesh” (John 1:14), even though the Jews do not believe in the birth. God assumed the form of a human being, even though the pagans disparage the miracle. For this reason the mystery is “a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles” (1 Cor. 1:23), because the miracle surpasses reason.

If the Word had not dwelt in the womb, flesh would never have sat upon the throne. If it were an insult to God to enter the womb, it would also be an insult to angels to minister to human beings.

### 9

He who by nature is ἀπαθής, “impassible,” being God, became πολυπαθής, “subject to many sufferings,” out of compassion. Christ God did not become God through advancement—far be it—but, as we believe, became man out of compassion.

We do not proclaim a man made divine; we confess God incarnate. He made his own handmaid his mother. He who according to essence is without a mother is, according to the dispensation, without a father. For how, according to Paul, is he “without father and without mother” (Heb. 7:3)? If he is merely human, he is not without a mother; if he is naked God, he is not without a father. But now he is himself without a mother as creator, and without a father as the one fashioned.

### 10

Be ashamed even of the archangel’s name, O man: the one who announced Mary is called Gabriel. And what does Gabriel mean? “God and man.” The name came beforehand so that the dispensation might be believed.

### 11

Learn the reason for his presence and glorify the power of the incarnate one. The human race owed much and was unable to pay the debt. Through Adam we had written the whole account of sin, and the devil kept us as slaves. He produced our instruments against us, using our suffering body as though it were many sheets of parchment. The evil counterfeiter of sufferings stood shaking the debt against us and demanding judgment.

One of two things was therefore necessary: either death had to be imposed by judgment, since all had sinned, or someone had to be given in compensation who would become the justification for the recovery of all. A human being could not save, for he was subject to the debt; an angel could not redeem, for he was insufficient as the price of liberation. The one without sin had to die for sinners, for this, and this alone, was left as the solution to evil.

### 12

What, then? He who had brought the whole of nature into being from nothing, who lacked nothing in any gift of goodness, devised both life as the most certain answer to those sentenced to death and the most fitting release from death. He becomes man, as he himself knows—for speech cannot interpret the miracle—and he dies by virtue of having become man; and by virtue of what he had previously been, he liberates, according to Paul’s words: “In whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins, through his blood” (Eph. 1:7).

### 13

O astonishing thing! He traded immortality to others, for he himself was immortal. No other such one existed, exists, or will exist according to the dispensation. He alone is the God and man born from the Virgin—not merely possessing a dignity that could be set in opposition as a price to the multitude of the guilty, but surpassing every judgment.

As Son, he preserved what is unchangeable in relation to the Father; as creator, he possessed unfailingly what belongs to power; as one who loves to show mercy, he displayed the things belonging to compassion without any comparison; and finally, as priest, he offered what was suitable for representation. No one will find anything comparable or even approaching these things in any respect.

### 14

Consider his love for human beings. Voluntarily sentenced to death, he dissolved the death that stood against those crucifying him and turned the iniquity of those killing him into the salvation of the wicked.

### 15

It was not possible for a mere human being to save, since he himself also needed a savior, according to Paul’s statement: “All have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:28). Since sin handed man over as guilty to the devil, the devil drove the one handed over toward death. What concerned us was in great danger, and the release from death was impossible.

### 16

The physicians who had been sent accused us. What, then? When the prophets saw that the wound exceeded human skill, they cried out to the heavenly physician.

One said: “Lord, bow down your heavens and descend” (Ps. 144:5).

Another: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed” (Jer. 17:14).

Another cried: “Stir up your power and come, that you may save us” (Ps. 80:3).

Another said: “Alas for me! My soul, because the merciful one has perished from the earth.”

Another said: “If truly God has dwelt among human beings.”

Another: “Let your mercy, Lord, quickly come upon us.”

Another: “God, attend to my help; Lord, hasten to help me” (Ps. 70:2).

Another: “The one who is to come will come, and he will not delay” (Hab. 2:3).

Another: “I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost; seek your servant” (Ps. 119:176).

### 17

He who by nature is king and God did not despise the oppression of human nature. Rather, he came who was always present, paid the ransom with his own blood, and gave for the human race a body, assumed from the Virgin, as compensation to death. He redeemed the world from the curse of the law. Hence Paul cries: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law” (Gal. 3:13).

### 18

The one who redeemed us, therefore, was not a mere man, O Jew, for human nature was enslaved to sin; nor was he naked God, O Manichaean, for he had a body. If he had not clothed himself with me, he would not have saved me. Rather, he who had passed sentence in the Virgin’s womb clothed himself with the guilty one, and there a fearful exchange took place: while giving the Spirit, he received flesh; he himself was with the Virgin and from the Virgin. The Spirit overshadowed her, and he himself became flesh from her.

### 19

If Christ is one person and God the Word another, there will no longer be a Trinity but a quaternity. Do not tear apart the garment of the dispensation, woven from above. Do not be a disciple of Arius. He impiously divides the essence; do not divide the unity, lest you be divided from God.

### 20

Tell me: who appeared to those “sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1:79)? A man? And how could this be, if he lived in darkness, according to Paul’s statement: “He delivered us from the power of darkness” (Col. 1:13), and again: “For you were once darkness” (Eph. 5:8)?

Who, then, shone forth? Let David teach you, saying: “The Lord is God, and he has shone upon us” (Ps. 118:27). The natures came together, and the unity remained without confusion.

### 21

He came to save, but he also had to suffer. How, then, could both occur? A mere man could not save; naked God could not suffer. He himself, existing by nature as God, became man: by what he was, he saved; by what he became, he endured.

### 22

Therefore, when the Church saw the Synagogue crown him with thorns, she lamented its presumption and said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, go out and see the crown with which his mother crowned him” (Song 3:11).

He himself bore a crown from thorns in order to dissolve the sentence of thorns. He was himself in the bosom of the Father and in the womb of the Virgin, between his mother’s arms and above the wings of the winds. Above, he was worshiped by angels; below, he reclined with tax collectors. The Seraphim did not look upon him out of reverence, while Pilate questioned him. A servant struck him, while creation was held captive. He was nailed to the cross, while the throne of glory was not empty. He lay in the tomb, while he stretched out heaven like a skin. He was reckoned among the dead, while he despoiled Hades. Below, he was slandered as a deceiver; above, he was glorified by the saints. O astonishing mystery!

### 23

I see the miracles and proclaim the deity; I behold the sufferings and do not deny the humanity. But Emmanuel opened the gates of nature as man, while as God he did not break the virginal seal. He came forth from the womb just as he entered through the ear. He was born as he was conceived: impassibly he entered, incorruptibly he came forth, according to the prophet Ezekiel, who says:

“The Lord turned me toward the outer way of the sanctuary gate that faces east, and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate shall be closed; it shall not be opened, and no one shall pass through it, because the Lord God alone shall enter through it, and it shall remain closed’” (Ezek. 44:1).

### 24

Behold the manifest confirmation of holy Mary, the Mother of God. Henceforth let every contradiction be dissolved, and let us be enlightened by the teaching of the holy Scriptures, so that we may obtain the kingdom of heaven in Christ Jesus our Lord. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON IV

On the incarnation. The first and extemporaneous sermon against Proclus’s panegyrical address to the Virgin Θεοτόκος.

[Note: [Col. 0781C] Socrates testifies that Nestorius possessed the ability to speak extemporaneously, and his display of it is evident from his fourth sermon against the Pelagians. That he did so here is demonstrated by the entire sermon, and especially by these words: “I have greatly admired the division made above by the preceding teacher,” etc. (No. 4). By the designation “preceding teacher,” one ordinarily meant the speaker whose sermon the presiding bishops succeeded. Thus Nestorius says in his penultimate sermon: “The preceding teacher of charity has set before us a sweet table,” etc. And in his fourth sermon against the Pelagians: “When my tongue pressed me toward another sermon, the preceding teacher, mindful of my promises, admonished me,” etc. So also Cyril, after Paul of Emesa’s address: “We have drawn water for you from the sacred fountain, namely from the teacher who spoke before us,” etc. Others use the same expression, but it is unnecessary to list them.]

### 1

It is not surprising that peoples who love Christ applaud those who devote their speech to the blessed Mary. For the very fact that she was made a temple of the Lord’s flesh surpasses everything most worthy of praise.

But your affection must attend to this point: when we speak about the honor and praise of that blessed woman more than is proper or fitting, we must take care not to appear to confuse the dignity of God the Word by making him born twice.

And so that you may understand the matter, let us use a simpler manner of speaking and an expression easy for everyone to grasp, lest what is said exceed the hearing of the listeners.

[Note: [Col. 0781D] Before “lovers,” Baluze has “applause”; since the word is repeated shortly afterward, the repetition seems quite acceptable. EDIT.]

[Note: [Col. 0781D] He is directing this against a statement by Proclus, who, addressing the Virgin, exclaimed: “O temple in which he became priest!” Nestorius attempts to correct him by briefly suggesting that the blessed Virgin is a temple only in this respect, and that uniquely sacred: she contained the Lord’s flesh, than which nothing created is holier.]

[Note: [Col. 0782C] Nestorius attacks with extraordinary vehemence the two births of Christ: one eternal, from the Father, insofar as he is the Word; the other temporal, from his mother, insofar as he is man. Hence he became vehemently enraged against Eusebius, who publicly argued that all his sophistries were dissolved by distinguishing the two. See the notes on the second sermon.]

### 2

Anyone who simply says that God was born from Mary first prostitutes the nobility of the doctrine before the Gentiles, exposing it publicly and presenting it as something to be blamed and mocked. For immediately a pagan, hearing with disapproval that God was born from Mary, will bring this objection against the Christian:

“Necessarily, the one who simply says that God was born from Mary—and does not understand that one who was born through the conjunction of two natures, divine and human, is God—will hear: ‘I cannot worship a God who was born, died, and was buried.’”

The clear division of the doctrine is this: the one who was born, who required the stages of growth and was carried in the womb through the appointed months, has a human nature, but one certainly joined to God.

[Note: [Col. 0782D] He criticizes the obscurity of Proclus’s address, which scarcely could have been understood by the audience except by a few, and those more learned, because of the grandiloquence, so to speak, of its thoughts, the brevity of its sentences, and the remarkable metaphors and other similar figures of speech with which it abounds. The more pleasantly such figures tend to seize the mind when spoken or read, the more easily they escape the understanding of a mind held in suspense and, as it were, astonished.

—Baluze: “And so, using simpler speech, lest what is said exceed the hearing of the listeners, I shall use an expression easiest for everyone to understand.” EDIT.]

### 3

It is one thing to say that, when one was born from Mary, that God who is the Word of the Father was joined to him—something entirely clear, firm, and irreproachable even to the Gentiles—and another thing to say that the Godhead itself needed a birth unfolding through the months. For God the Word is the maker of times, not fashioned within time.

### 4

I have therefore been greatly astonished at the division made on this subject by the preceding teacher, who says (Part 3): “The one born from a woman is neither naked God nor a mere man.”

For one must not say that God was born nakedly and in some undifferentiated fashion: no one generates one who is older than himself. Nor should one profess a naked humanity; rather, the humanity was generated in conjunction with God.

[Note: [Col. 0782D] These are Proclus’s words, as noted above (No. 3): “God was born from a woman, but not naked; a man was born, but not a mere man. The one who was born showed the gate of salvation where the gate of ancient sin had been. For where the serpent poured out poison through disobedience, there the Word, entering the temple through obedience, fashioned it into a living being. From where Cain, the first disciple of sin, emerged, there Christ, the liberator of our race, sprang forth without seed. The lover of humanity was not ashamed of a woman’s birth pangs.”]

[Note: [Col. 0783C] Baluze omits the words: “The one born from a woman is neither naked God nor a mere man.” EDIT.]

[Note: [Col. 0783C] He uses the same argument in writing to Saint Celestine. Nevertheless, the term Θεοτόκος can be tolerated on account of this very consideration, and because the word is applied to the Virgin alone, on account of the inseparable temple of God the Word derived from her—not because she is the mother of God the Word. “For no one gives birth to one older than herself” (Letter 1 to Saint Celestine).

Cassianus excerpted this statement and refuted it vigorously (*Book VII, chapter 2*). I do not think that Nestorius sent this sermon to Celestine, since it was extemporaneous and therefore of lesser importance; even if he had sent it, and Cassianus had received it, he would have taken more from it for refutation, since it contains things worse than those he refutes.]

### 5

I want you, who are attentive examiners of religion—for I hold the same opinion of you as of the Antiochenes—to be drawn toward this point, as I was saying: that God became high priest. I cannot tolerate this. For if God is both creator and high priest, to whom must an embassy be presented by the high priests?

[Note: [Col. 0783D] These are Proclus’s words, as stated above (No. 3): “O womb in which the guarantee of our common freedom was prepared! O womb in which weapons against death were forged! O threshing floor in which Christ, the cultivator of nature, sprang forth like an ear of grain without seed! O temple in which God became priest—not changing his nature, but, out of compassion, clothing himself with the one who is according to the order of Melchizedek!”]

### 6

I have spoken these things to your affection, and I would say more, except that this thought entered my mind: I seem to be arguing contrary to the teachers of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0783D] He undoubtedly means those who taught the people in the Church, as he himself had done at Antioch before being elevated to the episcopate of Constantinople, and as Proclus had also done—the man against whom he was declaiming. From this one can infer how greatly the more distinguished presbyters of the Church of Constantinople differed from Nestorius concerning the Lord’s incarnation. This is also evident both from the letters of Celestine and Cyril, and from the letters of those Constantinopolitan clergy to various persons, as well as from the complaints of the monks before the emperor. It is not improbable, however, that Nestorius was also referring to the earlier Fathers of the Church, from whom Eusebius had accused him of differing in his protest and had expressly praised Eustathius, bishop of the Church of Antioch, citing his splendid testimony.]

I therefore want you to be discerning in examining doctrines: neither confuse the humanity that was assumed with God the Word, nor call the one who was born a naked man; but neither say that God the Word, having been tempered or mixed with humanity, lost his own essence.

[Note: [Col. 0784C] He is referring to Proclus’s words: ἄλλ’ ἐκ γυναικὸς ἐγεννήθη Θεὸς οὐ γυμνὸς, καὶ ἄνθρωπος οὐ ψιλός, “From a woman he was born—not naked God, nor a mere man” (Part 2). Ὁ τοίνυν ἀγοράσας ἡμᾶς οὐ ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος, ὦ Ἰουδαῖε, “The one who redeemed us, O Jew, is not a mere man” (Part 8). And: ἄνθρωπος ψιλὸς σῶσαι οὐκ ἴσχυε· Θεὸς γυμνὸς παθεῖν οὐκ ἠδύνατο, “A mere man could not save; naked God could not suffer” (Part 9).]

7. For this reason, when the disciples were standing in amazement at the time when he was being lifted up into heaven, and were reasoning among themselves, as one may suppose: “Do you think that human nature has been dissolved? Do you think that in heaven it remains in the same essence?”—and while they were astonished at this sight, angels came and said: “This Jesus who is seen, [Col. 0784A] this one who required the increase of months, this one who died, this one who endured the cross, will come in the same way as you saw him ascending into heaven” (Acts 1:11). And again blessed Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles: “By a man,” he says, “whom God appointed to judge the world, granting assurance to all by raising him from the dead” (ibid. 17:31). Did God the Word rise from the dead? But if the giver of life was put to death, who will be the one to confer life?

8. Besides this, we are thereby very much open to reproach from the Arians. For if we simply and without qualification name God the Word as the one who was born, see what follows from this. You say simply: “He who was born of Mary is God.” At once the heretic replies in accusation:

[Note: This is once again an attack on Proclus’s statement (Part 2), and an attempt to show that Proclus presents the mystery of the incarnation as something to be mocked no less by Arians than by pagans.]

[Note: Some words were missing that seemed necessary to the sense and could be supplied in this way: “Therefore you accuse us unjustly when you say that the Son is lesser than the Father and created, since among you too this is included in your confession,” etc. Nestorius himself says something similar in his third sermon, when he says that the catholic defenders of the incarnation hold a worse view than the Arians in this respect: the Arians made the Son lesser than God the Father alone, whereas the catholics made him more recent than a created mother.]

“Therefore you accuse us unjustly when you say that the Son is lesser than the Father and created; for among you too this is included in your confession,” he says, “that he who was born of Mary is God the Word.”

9. Hear what that same God the Word himself testifies concerning himself: “Go and announce to my brothers: I am going to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17). When he said this, the one who was born of blessed Mary was consubstantial with us in his humanity; but inasmuch as he was joined to God, he was far removed from us, because God is the superior substance.

10. Then you will free yourself from their blasphemy, and you will easily and briefly state the mystery of the faith in this manner:

[Note: He alludes to these words of Proclus: “If Christ is one and God the Word another, then there is no longer a Trinity in the divine nature, but a quaternity.”]

“One is God the Word, who was [Note: Proclus. ‘Where the serpent poured out poison through disobedience, there the Word, entering the temple through obedience, gave life to what he had fashioned’ (Part 2). Nestorius contradicted these words because Proclus had previously contradicted the following words spoken by Nestorius: ‘The Holy Spirit did not create God the Word, but fashioned for God the Word a temple, from the Virgin, in which he might dwell’ (Sermon 1, no. 7).] in the temple which the Spirit fashioned, and another is the temple apart from the God who dwells within it. It belongs to the temple to be dissolved by death; it belongs to the one inhabiting the temple to raise it up. This is not my own saying, but the Lord’s voice: ‘Destroy this temple,’ he says, ‘and in three days I will raise it up’” (John 2:19).

11. Let us therefore confess the unity of the conjunction [Baluz. “dignity”], but two natures and substances; otherwise the Word [Baluz. adds “God”] will be found to be a creature of the Holy Spirit. For what does the evangelist say?

[Note: Baluz.: “For what does the evangelist say concerning him who was created in the womb?” EDIT.]

“What has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20). But if God the Word was naked and alone when he was born [Baluz. adds “created”], and if, as the evangelist says, the Spirit did not create his temple in blessed Mary, God the Word will be found to be the work of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0785B] 12. Let us therefore flee the error of this confusion. Let us say that our Lord Christ is twofold according to nature, but one according to the fact that he is the Son.

13. When certain people reported even this to me, I often laughed with delight, because, they say, “The bishop thinks what belongs to Photinus,” not knowing either what they are saying or about whom they are making their claims (1 Tim. 1:7). For what I say is found to be the overthrow of Photinus’s [Baluz. adds “doctrine”] teaching. Photinus’s position gives God the Word his beginning from Mary’s giving birth, whereas I say that God the Word has always existed before the ages.

[Note: Although agreement with Paul of Samosata was chiefly alleged, as is clear from Eusebius’s protestation, Nestorius also mentions Photinus. Since Photinus’s memory was more recent and therefore more hateful, the allegation of association with him was correspondingly more painful. As far as can be known from the records of antiquity, this charge was first made by Marius Mercator in a letter that he circulated publicly at the time when Eusebius issued his protestation (see the notes to that letter).]

14. For them, a proverbial saying will suffice for me: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly” (Prov. 26:4). But I want you to be perceptive examiners of doctrines,

[Note: He again criticizes the applause given to Proclus and the remarkable elegance of the panegyric speech, by which the people were extraordinarily captivated and had applauded the speaker, to Nestorius’s disadvantage.]

not to use applause, nor to be carried away by the charm of speech, nor to suppose that any doctrine or reasoned argument, once examined, is presumptuous merely because it is new, but rather to judge it the glory of truth.

## SERMON V. On God Born and the Virgin Θεοτόκος, the second [Note: When Nestorius had briefly attacked three statements of Proclus in an extemporaneous speech—namely, that the Virgin was Θεοτόκος (“Mother of God”); that God had suffered and died; and that he had been made high priest—he later decided that each should be attacked at greater length in a separate sermon. He dealt first with the present sermon, which we have extracted from the collections both of Cyril and of the Ephesian material translated by Mercator, not without some care and success.

He devoted the whole sermon to explaining in what sense the Virgin could be called Deipara, “Mother of God,” without prejudice to his own doctrine. He makes a serious accusation against the catholics, as though they said—or at least believed—that the Virgin was the parent of the Godhead itself, indeed a goddess; or at least as though, with Arius, Eunomius, and Apollinaris, they confused the natures in Christ. He also arouses no less resentment by suggesting that they had adopted the opinion that she was Θεοτόκος for two reasons, and those very trivial ones.

In refuting this sermon, Cyril devoted almost his entire first and second books of the five in which he opposed the blasphemies of Nestorius (Books I and II of the *Contradictions*). Someone might rightly call this outstanding work an apology for Proclus, since Cyril responds there almost exclusively to the sermons Nestorius delivered against Proclus. The first and second books concern the Virgin Θεοτόκος and God born; the third concerns God as priest; the fourth and fifth deal for the most part with God suffering and dying. This is why we have assigned the same order to the sermons. Only the two later portions of the sermon are found in Mercator; the rest have been supplied from Cyril’s work just mentioned. All are preserved in Greek.]

against Proclus.

1. I have often asked those who defend the title Θεοτόκος: “Do you say that the Godhead was born from the holy Virgin?” At these words they immediately recoil: “Who,” they say, “is afflicted with so great a disease of blasphemy as to say that the one who gave birth to the temple, through the work of the Holy Spirit, gave birth to God himself?”

Then, when I add: “What absurdity, therefore, is being said by us, when we urge that this word should indeed be uttered, but that we should proceed to its common meaning as applied to the two natures?”—then they think it blasphemous when we say: “Either openly confess that the Divinity was born from blessed Mary; or, if you flee from this expression as blasphemous, why do you pretend that you do not say what you say just as I do?”

2. If you were to pronounce “Deipara,” “Mother of God,” in simple faith, I would feel no hostility toward the expression while seeking its meaning. But because I see that, under the pretext of honoring blessed Mary, you are confirming the blasphemy of the heretics, I carefully fortify myself against the utterance of the word, since I regard the danger hidden in that expression with suspicion.

[Col. 0786B] 3. To state this more clearly, and so that it may be more easily understood by people: those who followed Arius, Eunomius, and Apollinarius, and the choirs of all such people, endeavored to introduce the designation Θεοτόκος, in order that, through a mixture and the complete failure to distinguish the two natures, nothing that is lowly might be understood as spoken of the humanity. Thus they would already have an opening against the very Divinity, as though everything were said of one [subject], not on account of the dignity resulting from the conjunction itself, but on account of nature itself.

For there is one Christ and one Lord. But in Christ—yes, in the only-begotten Son—the name “Christ” and the name “Son” are spoken sometimes of the Divinity, sometimes of the humanity, and sometimes of the Divinity and humanity together.

4. I have already said many times: if someone among you who is more simple-minded, or anyone else whatever, takes pleasure in the word Θεοτόκος, I have no hostility toward the word, provided that he does not make the Virgin a goddess.

5. “If Christ is God,” they say, “and Christ was born from blessed Mary, why is the Virgin not the mother of God?” I conceal nothing of what they object. For the lover of truth brings forward against himself everything that can be said by falsehood.

An infant is formed in the womb, but until it has received its shape it does not yet have a soul; once it has been formed, however, the soul is already fashioned by God. Thus, although a woman gives birth to a body and God grants the soul, the woman is not for that reason called the mother of the soul because she gave birth to an ensouled being, but rather the mother of a human being. Likewise, although blessed Mary gave birth to a human being, with God the Word passing through together with him, she is not for that reason the mother of God. For the Divinity of the Word did not take its beginning from blessed Mary; rather, he was God by nature.

6. Concerning blessed John the Baptist, the holy angels proclaimed that he would be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb (Luke 1:15); and thus blessed John the Baptist was born possessing the Holy Spirit. What then? Will you call Elizabeth the mother of the Spirit? Direct your minds to this, and if there are any among you who are disturbed by what is being said as though it were unheard-of and unusual, grant allowance to their ignorance.

[Col. 0787B] 7. Hear also another testimony from Scripture: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” Behold, it calls him “the Lord of glory.” It does not call the humanity by this name, but the Divinity. Yet this is what those people do who tear apart the great union: when you say that this one is not Lord but that one is, you make Christ a mere man.

What then do you say, heretic, while speaking in the person of the Church? Is that man himself also Lord, or is he not? If he is Lord, then the things said of him share a common reference. If not, then do not, when you make Christ a bare and simple man, fasten this reproach upon me.

Let us hear blessed Paul crying out plainly to identify the one who was crucified. Hear, then, his clearest words: “For he was crucified through weakness, but he lives through the power of God.” If he was crucified through weakness, who was made weak, heretic? Was it God the Word?

8. See what follows, heretic. I do not begrudge the Virgin the name Χριστοτόκος, “Mother of Christ.” For I confess that she is worthy of reverence, she who conceived God; through whom the Lord of all passed; through whom the sun of righteousness shone forth. For the Word was God, joined to the man and dwelling in him. But I suspect the applause.

How did you understand what I said about his having passed through? I did not say “he passed through” in the sense of “he was born”; for I do not so easily forget my own position. That God passed through the Virgin Χριστοτόκος, “Mother of Christ,” I have learned thoroughly from Scripture; that he was born from her, I have not learned.

9. Nowhere does divine Scripture assert that God was born from the Virgin Χριστοτόκος; rather, it asserts that Jesus Christ, the Son, the Lord, was born.

Let us all confess this. For whoever does not immediately accept what divine Scripture has taught is wretched. “Arise, take the child and his mother” (Matt. 2:13). These are the words of the angels—indeed, your own words. Perhaps the archangel knew his generation. “Arise, take the child and his mother”; he did not say, “Arise, take God and his mother.”

## SERMON VI. On the Words of the Apostle’s Epistle to the Hebrews: “Consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus,” etc. (Heb. 3:1)

1. When they hear the title “apostle” applied to Christ, they misunderstand it and think that God the Word is an apostle. Likewise, when they read the word “high priest,” they imagine, with astonishing folly, that God is a high priest. For who, on hearing of the office of an apostle, would not immediately see that a man is being indicated? Who, on hearing the name of high priest, would call the nature of the Divinity to the ministry of priesthood?

2. For if God is high priest, who will be the one to be honored through his office? If God is going to offer sacrifices as a high priest, there will be no one to whom God can offer them. What dignity would remain to the Divinity if, as an inferior, he offered sacrifices to one superior?

3. Why, then, did God appear to them to be called high priest, when he has absolutely no need of sacrifice according to the rite of priesthood for his own advancement? He is, after all, the perpetual possessor of the Divinity. “Chosen from among human beings and appointed as high priest, he is established on behalf of human beings before God” (Heb. 5:1).

[Col. 0788B] 4. “He did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. 2:16). Is the seed of Abraham itself the Divinity? Hear also the following statement: “Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect” (ibid. 2:17). Was this said of the Divinity? For what brothers could God the Word have who were like him?

5. Consider also what is joined to these words: “so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God; for because he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted” (ibid. 2:17–18). The one who suffered, therefore, is the merciful high priest; the temple is capable of suffering, not the one who is God, the giver of life.

6. The seed of Abraham is the one who is “the same yesterday and today,” according to the words of the apostle Paul (Heb. 13:8), not the one who said, “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58).

[Col. 0788C] “Like his brothers in every respect” (Heb. 2:17) is the one who assumed the fellowship of a human soul and body, not the one who said, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

7. The one who is consubstantial with us was sent, anointed, and proclaimed release to captives and sight to the blind: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to proclaim good news to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind” (Isa. 61:1).

8. When he was speaking of Christ as having been sent to announce release to captives, the Apostle added this as well and said: “This one, who was made a faithful high priest to God” (Heb. 2:17). For he was made this; he had not been so eternally beforehand. This one, heretic, gradually advanced to the dignity of high priest.

[Col. 0788D] Hear a voice crying out this to you even more clearly: “In the days of his flesh,” he says, “he offered prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence. Although he was a Son, he learned obedience from what he suffered; and, having been perfected, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him” (Heb. 5:7).

That which gradually advances is brought to completion, heretic. Luke also proclaims this in the Gospel: “Jesus advanced in age, wisdom, and grace” (Luke 2:52). In agreement with this, Paul says: “Having been perfected, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him, being called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek” (Heb. 5:6).

[Col. 0789A] This is the one compared with Moses in the type of leading armies; the one called the seed of Abraham; the one made like his brothers in every respect; the one made high priest in time; the one perfected through sufferings; the one who, because he suffered and was himself tempted, is able to help those who are tempted; the one called high priest according to the order of Melchizedek. Why, then, do you think differently from Paul? Why, by joining the impassible God the Word to an earthly body, do you make him a suffering high priest?

Since, then, this one alone is our compassionate, related, and steadfast high priest, never be driven away from faith in him. For he was sent to us through the promised blessing, from the seed of Abraham, offering the sacrifice of his body both for himself and for his own race.

## SERMON VII. The fourth against Proclus

[Note: There can be no doubt that this is a genuine offspring of the heresiarch. For the credibility of those who not only mention him but also report lengthy fragments from him does not deceive us.

Cyril says: “They sent to this deacon, who administers ecclesiastical affairs, two little documents: one perhaps composed by Photius, or by someone else, against my book which I published for the monks; and another, as if in the form of a quire, bearing even an unsuitable title, as follows: ‘Against those who, because of the conjunction, either put the Divinity of the Word to death or deify the humanity.’ Its preface runs as follows: ‘Insults,’ etc. Then he attempts to show that the body suffered and not God the Word, etc.” (*In the Letter to His Clergy in Constantinople*, Part 3.)

From the same work, lengthy fragments are reported in extracts 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12 in Mercator. They are also reported in Book I of the *Contradictions*, p. 14; Book II, pp. 52, 54, and 58; and Book V, pp. 134 and 138 of the Paris Greek-Latin edition. They are likewise reported in the response to the objections of the Easterners against the third anathema. From these passages we have taken the Greek text.

At the Council of Ephesus (Part 2, Act 1), certain excerpts from the books of Nestorius were presented. Those numbered 7, 8, 14, and 19 belong to this sermon; from these as well we obtained the Greek.

The title, as has just been stated, must be taken from Cyril’s letter to his own clergy.]

### Against those who, because of the conjunction, either put the Divinity of the Word to death or deify the humanity

[Col. 0789B]

1. I consider the insults of the heretics against me to be the devices of madmen and their threatened drownings in the sea, the desires for disturbances, the new schemes of persecution that are being directed against us, and the negligence toward the needy which they charge us with, together with the ravings of others’ chatter against us. I laugh at them as at the croaking of frogs, or at least I despise them as infants’ missiles or encampments, such as the prophet once mocked when he said: “The arrows of little children have become their wounds” (Ps. 63:8).

[Note: Both manuscript codices read *infantium rapinas* (“robberies of infants”), plainly an error which we think should be corrected from Cyril’s passage cited below, although Cyril’s own text is not entirely reliable, whether one consults the Greek text of the Council of Ephesus or the Marian translation. It reads as follows: “The preface, however, intensifies the insults from the heretics, as having been made by hardened men or by madmen.” The Roman translator renders it: “But the preface attacks the insults of the heretics as having been made with excessive insolence.” Mercator’s preface reads: “Against the insults inflicted by the heretics with the greatest harshness,” with neither translator conveying, or at least supplying, the proper sense. I believe it should read: “I consider the insults of the heretics against me to be the devices of madmen,” or “as having been made by madmen,” or “as having been made by hardened men,” according as one reads either ἐπὶ σκληρῶν or ἐπὶ λήρων. We have chosen the first reading, as being more consistent with the corrupt words of the manuscript codices.—“Infants’ trifles.” In the old books *infantum rapinas* was written. When Garnerius understood this to be seriously corrupt, he restored *delirantium machinas* (“the devices of madmen”). The true reading was indicated to us by Rev. Father Joannes Commirius of the Society of Jesus. The ancients used *apinae* and *tricae* for futile and trifling things, a metaphor drawn from Apina and Trica, two little towns of Apulia which Diomedes destroyed. Pliny, Book III, chapter 11: “There Diomedes destroyed the peoples of the Moradores and Dardanians, and two cities which became proverbial jokes, Apina and Trica.” Martial, Book I, epigram 114:

“Whatever I once played with as a young man and a boy,  
and my little trifles.”

The same author, Book XIV, epigram 1:

“They are trifles and inanities, and anything cheaper than these.”

See Erasmus’s *Adages*. BALUZ.—“I did not understand what *apinae* had in common with drownings. I consulted Baluzius’s notes; I saw the reading of the old books, *rapinas*; I understood and accepted it. Mothers commonly frighten their little children with threats of being carried off and drowned, by a wild beast and by similar μορμολύκεια, that is, bogeymen. There is no doubt that the heresiarch had this in mind.” COTELER, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, vol. III, p. 600.]

2. There is nothing more pitiable than that shepherd who boasts of the praise of wolves. If he wishes to please them and chooses to be loved by them, he will thereby become a great danger to the sheep. No shepherd, therefore, can please both wolves and flocks of sheep. I shall accordingly despise their voices, as I said, bringing against them the Lord’s words: “Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil?” (Matt. 12:34).

3. Nevertheless, it is necessary to resist and oppose the opinions with which they arm themselves against the Lord. For they call the life-giving Divinity mortal, and dare to drag God the Word into theatrical dramas, as though the same one were wrapped in rags and dead—horrible to say! In order that the Lord Christ might extend his kindness toward us, according to them he is in danger of falling from the dignity of the Divinity.

[Note: Cyril was aiming at this passage when he wrote: “Shall we therefore suppose that, because he became flesh, he divested himself of the dignity and glory of his primordial existence? By no means. Rather, we shall wisely consider that the Son, although he became flesh, was not deprived by the Father of those prerogatives which naturally belong to him; but that, nevertheless, he was recognized by him as his own, although he had presented himself to be seen in human form. For the Only-begotten, God the Word, did not become human for the purpose of falling away from the Divinity, but rather, even in the assumption of flesh, retained his excellence and glory” (*Paschal Homily* 17).]

[Col. 0791A] 4. Listen, most wretched man, and although you are raging, admit a concern for your sanity: Pilate did not kill the Divinity, but the garment of the Divinity. God the Word was not wrapped in a shroud by Joseph and placed in a tomb. For how could that one suffer this, who holds the circle of the earth and all who dwell in it as though they were locusts, as the prophet says (Isa. 40:22)?

[Note: He turns his speech to Proclus, without naming him, out of consideration for the favor of the people, over whom Proclus had great influence. Proclus had said: “For he himself carried a crown from thorns, in order to dissolve the sentence of thorns; he himself was in the Father’s bosom and in the Virgin’s womb; in the arms of his mother and upon the wings of the winds; above he was worshiped by angels, and below he reclined with tax collectors; the seraphim did not look upon him because of reverence, and Pilate questioned him; a slave struck him, and creation was terrified; he was fastened to the cross, and the throne of glory was not bare; he lay in the tomb, and he stretched out heaven like a skin; he was reckoned among the dead, and he despoiled Hades; below he was slandered as a deceiver, and above he was glorified by the saints. O astonishing mystery!”—On the reading *ponens lauda*, Baluzius notes: “Thus the Bellovacensis codex. Gerberonius published *Accedas*; Garnerius, *Audi*, who thinks that the speech is addressed to Proclus without naming him.” EDIT.]

5. But who is the one wrapped in burial linen? Hear the Gospel voices resound: “There came a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, who himself had also become a disciple of Jesus. He approached Pilate and requested the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered that the body be handed over; and Joseph took the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth, and placed it in the tomb” (Matt. 27:57–60). Three times he said “body,” and not once did he mention the Divinity. For the soldiers did not pierce the Divinity with a spear.

[Col. 0791B] But what was wounded by them? John teaches us: “One of the soldiers,” he says, “pierced his side with his spear” (John 19:34). And hear still another argument by which it is established that the Divinity was not wounded at all: “Immediately,” he says, “blood and water came out” (ibid.).

[Note: Theodoret copied this passage in almost the same words, and even expanded it (*On the Impassibility*). “When it was already late, a certain rich man came,” etc. Observe how often he mentions the body, in order to silence the mouths of those who blaspheme the Divinity. Blessed Mark did the same, and so on. Marvel, therefore, when you see the agreement and the consistent and continuous repetition of the word “body.” The celebrated Luke likewise narrated that Joseph asked for the body. The most divine John added other details as well: “Joseph of Arimathea asked Pilate,” etc. Observe how often the body is mentioned, and that after saying that it had been fastened to the cross, that Joseph had asked Pilate for it, and that he had taken it down from the wood and wrapped it in linen with myrrh and aloes, he then used the name of the person and said that Jesus had been placed in the tomb. For this reason the angel also said: “Come, see where the Lord was laid,” using the common designation “body.” We too customarily speak in this way: “So-and-so was buried in this place,” and do not say “his body,” although everyone of sound mind knows that we are speaking of the body. Holy Scripture is accustomed to speak in this way. “Aaron died,” it says, “and they buried him on Mount Hor,” etc. (Num. 33:37); “Samuel died, and they buried him at Ramah” (1 Sam. 25:1); and countless similar examples. The divine Apostle observed this custom when speaking of the Lord’s death: “For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Cor. 15:3–4), and what follows. The same passage is repeated in Book V, chapter 15, of the *Haereticarum Fabularum Compendium*.]

6. The one who gives life did not himself die. For who would have continued to exist? Who would have raised the dead? He came to raise dead human beings; for he is found bringing help to those lying dead, not himself lying there as one deprived of help.

God was not changed by the conjunction or association with a human being. For he himself cries out through the prophet: “I am, I am, and I have not changed” (Mal. 3:6). And again: “But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Ps. 101:28).

[Col. 0792A] But, united to human nature and embracing it with the arms of the Divinity, he raised it on high while remaining what he was.

[Note: He had misused the same example in his first sermon: “God saw nature fallen, and by the power of the Divinity he grasped it when it had been cast down; holding it and remaining what he was, he lifted it on high. Understand the example of what is being said: if you wished to raise someone lying on the ground, would you not touch body with body and, joining yourself to him, raise up the fallen person, while remaining yourself what you were because you had been joined to him? Understand the mystery of the incarnation in the same way” (Sermon 1, no. 8).]

7. For this reason Peter himself, preaching about our firstfruits and recounting the exaltation which God bestowed upon this visible nature, says: “God raised up this Jesus” (Acts 10:40). God, therefore, did not die, but raised him up.

8. Hear Peter speaking, O Apollinaris. With Apollinaris, hear also the impiety of the Arians. “God,” he says, “raised up this Jesus”—this one who is visible; this one whom the eyes behold; this one who was fastened to the wood; this one who was touched by the hands of Thomas, who cried out to him: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).

[Note: It is worthwhile to consult Cassian on this subject. He treats this passage in order to prove the Divinity of Christ and overturns Nestorius’s position. He also reports other passages worthy of reading, although they do not concern this sermon, which he did not see, but rather the first. He writes as follows: “What did he cry out? ‘My Lord,’ he says, ‘and my God!’ Did he say what you say: ‘A man, and not God; Christ, and not the Divinity’? Certainly he touched the body of his Lord and answered that he was God. Did he introduce any separation between the man and God? Or did he call that flesh Θεοδόχος, ‘God-bearing,’ as you say, that is, an image receiving the Divinity? Or, in accordance with your impiety, did he say that the one he touched should be venerated not for his own sake but because of the one whom he had received within himself? Perhaps the apostle of God did not know this subtlety of your distinction” (*On the Incarnation*, Book III, chapter 15).]

Having been made more certain by these words—by the resurrection of the very body that had been touched and crucified—he glorified God for performing these astonishing deeds, saying: “My God and my Lord” (John 20:28). He was not calling what he had touched God; for the Divinity is not investigated by this touching. If Thomas had begun to recognize or learn that God the Word was God through this touching, the Lord would undoubtedly have said to him: “Touch and see, because I am spirit and God.” But instead he says the opposite: “Touch and see, because I am not a spirit; for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39). He means: “Me, whom you see to be composed according to what is visible and apparent, and whom you perceive to be touchable according to the substance of the body.”

[Col. 0793A] 9. For the Divinity of the Father’s Word is not bones and flesh, O Apollinaris. Of this touchable one Peter cries out: “God raised up this Jesus” (Acts 10:40). Therefore he was exalted by the right hand of God, though the Word was not assisted by a right hand. O Arian madness! Having also received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father (Acts 2:33), he poured out this one whom you see and hear.

10. Hear Paul also reasoning about God and explaining the unchangeable conjunction of God and man. “Being in the form of God,” he says, “he did not deem it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7). Likewise, he says elsewhere: “He spoke to us in the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages, who is the radiance of glory” (Heb. 1:2–3).

He very carefully calls him “Son,” “the radiance of glory,” and an appointed (*positivum*) heir.

[Note: From this it is clear why Elipandus is said to have inclined toward Nestorianism. He is convicted of admitting two sons just as Nestorius did, since he acknowledged one who was natural and another who was adopted. For to be made an appointed (*positivus*) heir is to be adopted. He is convicted on this basis, since it is impossible for both kinds of sonship from the same parent to belong simultaneously to one and the same person.]

He is an appointed (*positivus*) heir according to the flesh, but the radiance of the Father’s glory according to the Divinity, since, even after becoming incarnate, he did not depart from the likeness which he shares with the Father. Therefore Paul also says: “who is the radiance of glory,” so that no one, upon hearing “he was in the form of God,” might suppose that he was a nature passing away or changed.

11. John, in describing the co-eternity of the Word and the Father with one another, used these words: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), omitting *is*. For he did not say, “In the beginning the Word is, and the Word is with God,” but, “In the beginning the Word was with God, and God was the Word.” The question concerned the first existence, or essence, of the one who assumed humanity.

[Note: This passage is the source of what is cited in seventh place at the Council of Ephesus, and in ninth place in Cyril, as well as in the response to the objection of the Orientals against the third anathema. Nestorius has nearly the same wording in his second letter to Cyril: “When Paul was recalling the divine incarnation and began to add what concerns the Passion, he first placed ‘Christ,’ a common name, as I said shortly before, for the natures. Then he introduces an appropriate statement, or account, of each: for he says, ‘Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God’ (Phil. 2:5). But, not to speak of each point: ‘He became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross’ (ibid.). Since, therefore, he had begun to mention death, so that no one might consequently suppose that the Word God was passible, he placed ‘Christ’ as a significant designation of a passible and impassible essence in the singularity of the person, so that the impassible and passible Christ might be named without danger: impassible in his Deity, but passible in his bodily nature” (Nestorius, *Letter 2 to Cyril*, §§6–7).]

12. Paul, however, recounts all that occurred together: both the incarnate essence and the unchangeable and everlasting union of the incarnate Deity. Therefore, writing, he cried out: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being constituted in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:5). He did not say: “Let this mind be in you which was also in God the Word, who, being constituted in the form of God, took the form of a servant.” Rather, the Apostle, taking the name “Christ” as a designation signifying two natures, calls him, without danger to himself, both the form of a servant and God, without reproach—keeping distinct the expressions that signify the twofold nature. And he does not proclaim to Christians only that Christ God is unchangeable, but also that he is benevolent, taking the form of a servant, and existing as the one who subsisted, so that you may know that he was not changed after the union, but was seen at once as benevolent and just. For his death on behalf of the ungodly, without sin, belongs to the flesh; and the fact that he did not shrink from dying for enemies is a grace of immeasurable benevolence. For, according to Paul, “hardly for a righteous person will anyone die” (Rom. 5:7).

13. That the human race should be taken up through a human being, and Adam reconciled, displays great circumspection in justice. For it was just that the nature which had offended should again be made acceptable to God; and it is just to absolve the formerly liable nature that incurred the debt. The human race ought indeed to have offered God an irreproachable and blameless way of life, but it was deficient in discharging the debt.

[Note: Perhaps one should read, “For the passions are neglected.” Gerberonius published *passiones*. Garnerius thinks one should read, “For the passions are neglected.” What if we read *pensionis* (“of the payment”), as the metaphor concerning debt and discharge continues? — Baluze.]

For the passions of negligence, dragging the soul this way and that, drove it naked of virtues; and there were few professors of piety and justice.

[Note: Baluze corrects this to *possessores* (“possessors”), and notes at the end: “The older books prefer this reading both here and shortly afterward, and it seems to be confirmed by the words found below, ‘when nature had possessed the firstfruits of its own lump.’ Garnerius restored *professores* (“teachers”) in both places.” — Editor.]

And then, amid the poverty of that age, who were those who seemed or were thought to be teachers? [The printed wording is difficult.] Throughout the whole world, however, the debt was present: “For all,” he says, “have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23). The interest on sin also continued to grow.

14. What, then, did the Lord Christ do? Seeing the human race bound by sins and unworthy of redemption, he discharged the debt—not by command, lest benevolence injure justice. The Apostle Paul bears witness to this when he cries out: “Christ, whom God put forward as a propitiatory sacrifice through faith in his blood, to demonstrate his righteousness” (Rom. 3:25); that is, so that benevolence might be shown to be just, not bestowed indiscriminately and arbitrarily without judgment. Therefore Christ assumed the person of the indebted nature and, through it, paid the debt as the son of Adam.

[Col. 0795A] 15. [Note: Saint Celestine had this passage in mind when he wrote to Nestorius: “At this point, since the occasion of the discourse requires it, we cannot remain silent about what astonishes us. We read how well you understand original sin, how you assert that nature itself is indebted, and that the one who descended from the race of the debtor rightly repays that debt. What are you to make of those who have been condemned for denying these things?” (*Letter to Nestorius* 11, p. VI, Council of Ephesus, ch. 18.) Yet in the notes to Nestorius’s sermons against the Pelagians, we clearly showed that Nestorius spoke only of the debt of dying contracted through Adam’s sin—at least explicitly—and not likewise of the death of the soul, which Catholic faith nevertheless requires. Indeed, human nature is introduced praying before God and asking through Christ to be freed from the miseries contracted from Adam (no. 18); yet no other death is mentioned than that which concerns the body. From this, what we said about the council convened at Constantinople also receives illumination: there those who agreed with the Manichaeans were condemned because they said that the first man died in his soul through the devil’s work.] It was necessary that the one paying the debt should be descended from the race of him who had once contracted it: the debt through a woman, release through a woman. But learn the debt, so that you may learn the repayment.

Adam became liable to punishment because of food. Christ paid this debt in the desert when he hungered and rejected the devil’s proposal concerning the restoration of food.

16. He incurred the guilt of desiring the Divinity against God when he heard the devil say, “You will be like gods” (Gen. 3:5), and eagerly seized the food. Christ paid this debt when, rejecting the voice of the demon who promised him power—for the demon said to him, “I will give you all these things if you will fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9)—he answered: “Go away, Satan; you shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (ibid., 10).

[Col. 0795B] 17. Through disobedience on the tree Adam became liable to the punishment; Christ also paid this debt by becoming obedient on the tree (Phil. 2:8). Therefore Paul says: “He took out of the way the bond against us with its ordinances, which was contrary to us, nailing it to the cross” (Col. 2:14). And the one who paid on our behalf is Christ; in him, however, our nature paid the debt. For he had assumed the person of that same nature, whose sufferings he paid in his own suffering, because, as Paul says, “we have redemption through his blood” (Eph. 1:7; Col. 1:14).

18. See now our nature in Christ pleading its case before God against the devil and employing these just arguments:

“I am oppressed by injustice, most just Judge; the wicked devil attacks me and exercises against me, openly, the tyrannical power of impotence. Granted that he handed the first Adam over to death because he was the occasion of his sin: why did he crucify the second Adam, whom, O King, you fashioned from a Virgin? Why did he hang the thieves with him? Why was he numbered with the wicked, though he committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth?” (1 Pet. 2:22; Luke 22:37).

“Or is his accursed intention not evident? He openly envies me as your image, Lord. Attacking me without any cause, he tries to overthrow me; but grant me that you are a just judge. You were angry with me because of Adam’s transgression; for his sake, if you have Adam joined to you without sin, I entreat you to be reconciled. Granted that because of him you handed me over to corruption; because of this one, grant me a share in incorruption. Both belong to my nature. As I shared in the death of the first, so shall I share in the immortal life of the second. I am fortified by indisputable and unconquerable arguments. In every respect I overcome my adversary. If he raises a dispute concerning the corruption that came upon me from Adam, I shall plead in opposition from the life of the one who committed no sin. And if he accuses me on account of that one’s disobedience, I shall establish his guilt by this one’s obedience.”

19. As Christ celebrated this triumph over the devil, he said: “Now is the judgment of this world; now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12:31). For just as the devil held a charge against the whole posterity of the first-formed man and had an original claim, so, when nature had possessed in Christ the blameless firstfruits of its own lump, Christ, striving against the devil, defeated him by the very defenses on which the adversary relied. For in Christ he most justly brings forward against the devil the blameless origin of his own firstfruits, if the devil introduces the causes of guilt inherited from Adam. This is what Paul says: “Christ died for our sins; indeed, he also rose, who is at the right hand of God and intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:34).

[Note: “Garnerius,” says Baluze, “corrected this by restoring *potestatem* (‘power’) and *posteritatem* (‘posterity’), and I think his correction is sound. Nevertheless, I did not dare depart from the wording of the old books.” — Editor.]

20. [Note: There can be no doubt that this passage is excerpted from Cyril and is reported as number eleven. For it is evident that both what precedes and what follows are excerpted from here; and in the eleventh place it is read as follows: “And after more in the same book.” It is nevertheless remarkable that the two passages differ so greatly both in meaning and in wording. Cyril’s eleventh excerpt reads as follows:

“Our nature intercedes for us in Christ’s use, established as a garment and relying on the defenses of its blameless origin; and because the sin of the one first fashioned became the cause for the whole race, there was, O man, an occasion for the assumption of this man, so that the corruption which had occurred through the flesh might be destroyed through the flesh. It is of this flesh, not of the Deity, that the burial on the third day took place. Its feet were held by nails; this flesh the Holy Spirit fashioned in the womb. Concerning this the Lord said to the Jews, ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up’ (John 2:19). Do I alone call Christ twofold, and does he not himself call both the temple destructible and God its raiser? But if it was God who was destroyed, O Arian—an accusation that would rightly rebound upon his own head—he ought to have said, ‘Destroy this God, and in three days he will be raised.’ If God died, if he was committed to burial, then that saying in the Gospel is meaningless: ‘Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you?’ (John 8:37). But now he says: ‘Why do you seek to kill me, a man upon whose head a crown of thorns has been placed; a man who says, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:47), and who endured a three-day death?’ Yet I adore him together with the Deity, as a co-worker of divine authority.”]

For our human stock, clothed by Christ, intercedes, wholly free from every sin, and a just defense arises against the punishment imposed upon us from the beginning by the one who was first formed in figure upon his own race. This was the occasion for the assumed human being to destroy through the flesh the corruption which he had merited through the flesh.

[Col. 0797A] 21. It is the burial on the third day of this man, not of the Deity. His feet were held by nails. This man the Holy Spirit fashioned in the womb. Concerning this flesh the Lord said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

22. Am I alone calling Christ twofold? Does he not himself call both the temple that is to be destroyed and the Lord who raises it? But if it was God who was being destroyed—an accusation that should be turned upon Arius’s own head—the Lord would have said: “Destroy this God, and in three days he will be raised.” If God was put to death in the tomb, Christ lies when he said: “Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you?” (John 8:40).

23. But Christ is not merely a man, O slanderer; he is man and God together. If he existed as God alone, then, according to Apollinaris, he ought to have said: “Why do you seek to kill God, who has spoken the truth to you?” But now he says: “Why do you seek to kill this man, who has been crowned with thorns; this man who said, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ (Matt. 27:46 ff.); this man who endured a three-day death?”

24. Yet I adore him together with the Deity, as a co-worker of divine authority. For Scripture says: “Let it be known, brothers, that through Christ the forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to us” (Acts 13:38).

25. I venerate him as the instrument of the Lord’s goodness. For he says: “Be kind and compassionate toward one another, as God in Christ also forgave us” (Eph. 4:32).

[Col. 0797C] 26. I honor him as the council chamber of God’s purposes: “For I want you to know the knowledge of the mystery of God the Father and of Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:1).

27. I receive him as the form that pledges for God on our behalf. He says: “The one who sent me is true, and I speak to the world what I have heard from him” (John 8:26).

28. I bless him as the pledge of eternal peace. “For he is our peace, who made both one and broke down the dividing wall of hostility in his flesh,” and so forth (Eph. 2:14).

29. I worship him as the propitiatory sacrifice of divine indignation. “God,” he says, “put Christ forward as a propitiatory sacrifice through faith, through his blood” (Rom. 3:25).

30. I love and revere him as the beginning of immortality for mortals. “For he,” he says, “is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead” (Col. 1:18).

31. I embrace him as the mirror in which divinity shines forth. For he says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19).

32. I adore him as the living purple robe of the King. For he says: “Being constituted in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and being found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:6).

33. I praise him as the hand of the Deity rescuing me from death into life. For he says: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, then I will draw all people to myself” (John 12:32). And showing what “lifted up” means, the faithful evangelist says: “He said this to indicate by what death he was going to die” (ibid., 33).

34. I marvel at him as the door through which there is entry into divine things. For he says: “I am the door; whoever enters through me will be saved, and will go in and out and find pasture” (John 10:9).

35. I adore him as the image of the almighty Deity. For God, he says, “highly exalted him and granted him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Phil. 2:9).

36. Because of what is hidden, I adore what appears to the eyes. God is inseparable. I do not separate the dignity of the one who appears, for he is inseparable; I distinguish the natures, but unite the reverence.

37. That which was fashioned in the womb is not God by itself; that which was created by the Holy Spirit is not God by itself; that which was buried in the tomb is not God by itself. For otherwise we would plainly be worshipers of a human being and of one who was dead.

38. But because God is in the assumed one, the one assumed is called God from the one who assumes, as joined to the one who assumes. Therefore the demons shudder at the designation of God joined to the crucified flesh—not as suffering together with it—recognizing God. Therefore this one, who appeared to sight, will also come as judge, because he is joined to the almighty Deity. For he says: “Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory” (Matt. 24:30).

39. For just as a king, having won victory, is seen in the cities with the weapons with which he overcame the enemy in battle, and wishes to be seen with those same weapons, so the King and Lord of all will come into his creation with the cross and the flesh, to be seen with the weapons by which he overcame impiety. He will judge the world in the form of a man, with almighty power, in accordance with Paul’s proclamation, who says: “God overlooked the times of ignorance, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has established a day on which he will judge the world in the man whom he appointed, having given assurance to all by raising him from the dead” (Acts 17:30–31). This was said so that no one might suppose that the Deity was dead.

[Col. 0798D] 40. For even if you search through the whole of the New Scripture together, you will nowhere find in it that God died. Rather, when death is mentioned, it is assigned to Christ, or to the Son, or to the Lord. In Scripture, “Christ,” “Son,” and “Lord,” when understood of the Only-Begotten, are designations signifying two natures; sometimes they indicate the Deity, sometimes the humanity, and sometimes both together. For example, when Paul writes and proclaims: “While we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:10), he indicates his humanity. When he again says to the Hebrews: “God spoke to us in his Son, through whom he also made the ages” (Heb. 1:2), he indicates the Deity of the Son as well. For the flesh is not the creator of the ages, having been fashioned after many ages.

[Note: He alludes to the concluding words of the panegyrical oration which Proclus ends as follows: “Behold, manifest proofs of the holy and God-bearing Mary” (ἰδοὺ ἀποδείξεις ἐναργεῖς τῆς ἁγίας καὶ Θεοτόκου Μαρίας).]

Behold a fitting demonstration of the designation “Son of God,” and of the essence of his Deity and humanity.

41. Let us now ask whether this name—that is, “Christ”—is also understood as “Son,” and whether it too pertains to the designation of both. “Jesus Christ,” he says, “is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb. 13:8). For, existing as God and as man, he is the same person: according to Paul, both the last and before the ages; as man, recent; but as God, before the ages.

42. It has therefore been shown to you that the designation “Christ” sometimes indicates the temple and sometimes God dwelling in it. Now demand where “Lord” too is applied in the person of the Son and indicates sometimes that man and sometimes God. “Come,” he says, “see the place where the Lord lay” (Matt. 28:6). Again, the women, weeping as though the Lord’s body had been stolen away by the Jews, say: “They have taken away my Lord” (John 20:13). And to the Galatians Paul says: “I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord’s brother” (Gal. 1:19). Again, he himself says to the Corinthians: “Whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. 11:26). And again: “Lord, I see that you are a prophet” (John 4:19). All these are proofs of the Lord’s incarnation, because God the Word was not thrown into the tomb. For how could the one who sustains the universe by the word of his power have risen if, according to Arius, he was lying there? Nor did the women weep over the essence of God, as though it could have been stolen from the tomb. For who could suppose that the Deity was graspable by thieves’ hands? Nor was James the brother of the Deity; nor do we proclaim the death of God the Word when we are nourished by the Lord’s body and blood. For the nature of God receives the sacrifice; it is not itself sacrificed in the sacrifice. Nor is God a prophet, but the giver of prophecy. Thus, in this passage, “Lord” is, as I said, an expression for the flesh as possessing the Lord’s dignity, although by no process or mixture has it passed into the substance of the Deity.

43. Elsewhere “Lord” is a demonstrative designation of the Deity, as in: “There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Cor. 8:6). For Christ is the maker of all things through his Deity, not through his humanity, which is found to have been created after creation itself.

[Col. 0800A] 44. Elsewhere, however, as I said, “Lord” signifies both realities, as in: “Lord Jesus, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59). And: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name?’” (Matt. 7:22). And Paul says: “The Lord, the righteous judge, will award me on that day—not only me, but also all who have loved his appearing in godliness” (2 Tim. 4:8). You have seen how he is Christ, Son, and Lord. When Scripture mentions the Only-Begotten, it intends these designations to signify sometimes humanity, sometimes divinity, and sometimes both.

45. Why, then, do you confuse what is not confused? Why do you assign the name of God to death, when divine Scripture nowhere uses it in mentioning death? Why, when you hear Paul crying out, “In the man whom God appointed … raising him from the dead” (Acts 17:31), do you, through an empty imagination, judge the Deity to have been born and died?

46. Paul also rightly designates as the one who will come as judge this man who was visible, since the devil prepared for the worms a human being fashioned by God in his own image and honored with the kingdom of the earth.

[Note: The passage is perplexing and, unless I am mistaken, corrupt; nevertheless it can perhaps be emended as follows: “Christ, almighty, came according to Scripture in the form of a man, so that the devil himself might also learn by experience that he too, along with all others, was under God’s dominion. Since man was made in the image and likeness of God, and appointed king and lord of the earth, he was rightly raised by his creator even to the kingdoms of heaven.” Garnerius considers this passage perplexing and corrupt and thinks that *futurum* (“future”) should be replaced by *Scripturam* (“Scripture”). This emendation nevertheless seems unnecessary, because Mercator appears to refer to what he had said shortly before: that Paul designated this visible man as the judge who was to come. — Baluze.]

Christ comes—“according to the future, in the form of an almighty man” [the corrupt printed wording is uncertain]—so that the devil himself may learn by experience that he too, along with all others, was under God’s dominion, because man was truly made in the image and likeness of God, appointed king and lord of the earth, and rightly exalted by his maker even to the kingdoms of heaven.

[Col. 0800C] 47. But your audience surpasses our discourse, and, confessing myself defeated, I take refuge in silence, always wishing to be separated from this desire of your audience.

48. [Note: This passage too is corrupt. It should be restored partly from Cassian, *Sermon* 1, and partly from Cyril’s letter to those of his followers residing in Constantinople. “Let us therefore worship the assumption of the Lord’s humanity. Let us exalt the mystery of the incarnation with unceasing hymns. Let us venerate the Virgin who received God with the same and equal honor as God the Word. Let us not raise the Virgin who received God together with God to divine things—I mean *Theodokhon* [Θεοδόχον], etc.” Cotelerius, *Monumenta Ecclesiae*, vol. III, p. 595, corrects and completes the passage as follows: “Let us not reason about the Virgin who received God together with God …,” wishing the letters δ and χ to be written instead of τ and κ. — Galland.]
