Let us therefore worship the assumption of the Lord’s humanity; let us exalt the mystery of the incarnation with unceasing hymns; let us reason about the Virgin who received God together with God; let us not raise her together with God to divine things—I mean *Theodokhon* (Θεοδόχον), not *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκον), wishing the letter δ to be expressed, not κ. For there is one, as I may say according to their own terminology, Father God, *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος), that is, “begetter of God,” who has this compound name.

Let us therefore regard the visible form joined to the invisible as belonging with God to divine things: “Let us honor the nature that is borne with the one who bears it” (τὴν φορουμένην τῷ φορώντι συντιμῶμεν φύσιν), that is, let us honor the nature which is God’s garment together with the one who uses it, as a ray, so to speak, of the incarnate Deity.

[Note: There is a double fault in the sentence, for the entire phrase should be deleted, since it contributes nothing to the sense and indeed obstructs it considerably. How well everything reads once it is deleted: “Let us honor the nature which is God’s garment together with the one who uses it, as a ray of the Deity, as the inseparable image of divine authority,” and so forth. If the sentence is retained, it should be corrected according to what was said in the notes to this first sermon, as follows: “And thus let us fear the Lord’s incarnation.” For it was easy for *et* to be changed into *ut*, and *Dominicam* into *dicam*.]

Let us fear it as the inseparable image of divine authority, as the image or statue of the hidden Judge. Distinguishing the natures, let us unite the honor; let us confess him as twofold and adore him as one: for the one composed of two natures is one according to unity.

49. If a heretic, speaking in an ecclesiastical capacity, reproaches you with your dead God, answer the statement angrily: “It is God who raised from the dead the great Shepherd of the sheep” (Heb. 13:20); he himself was not put to death and raised up. If a Jew says that you worship a man, answer with the apostolic tradition: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). If a Gentile asks the reason for the humanity that was assumed, affirm that it is the remission of sins.

Answer him with Paul’s words: “Since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead also came through a man; for as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:21). To him be glory for ever and ever.

## FIRST LETTER OF SAINT CYRIL

[Note: Cyril wrote altogether three admonitory letters to Nestorius. One begins, “Venerable men”; another, “Some are babbling”; and the last, “When our Savior.” All are now published in the translation of Marius Mercator. I have called them three admonitory letters; for I think he also wrote a congratulatory letter when Nestorius was ordained, as well as a paschal letter at the appropriate time. The former is clearly indicated by Celestine’s letters to Nestorius himself, and also by Cyril’s apology to Theodosius; the latter is supported by custom. This, then, is the first of the admonitory letters, since it is mentioned in the second (no. 3): “I will also admonish you now,” and both are mentioned in the third (no. 2): “Behold, by these writings we have now addressed you for the third time.”

The first contains complaints and little else besides an exhortation to repentance. The second also contains an exposition of the faith as it is formulated from the Nicene Creed; the third authoritatively declares what must be done and what faith must be subscribed in order to retain communion with the Church. It is remarkable, however, that although the second yields much to the third, and both were read at the Council of Ephesus, only the second was approved by the Fathers’ judgments; it alone was also read at the Council of Constantinople under Flavian and reread at Chalcedon. (See above, dissertation 3.)

It must have been sent in the year 429, around August, for Nestorius replied to it briefly through the presbyter Lampo. After receiving the reply, Cyril wrote his second letter, which is recorded in the fifth synod as having been written in the month of Mechir, in the thirteenth indiction—that is, near the end of January in the year 430. Cyril’s letter could not have been sent from Alexandria to Constantinople, nor Nestorius’s reply in turn from Constantinople to Alexandria, without a suitable interval of time.

From it we learn three things useful to history.

1. Cyril’s letter to the monks was written around the summer or even spring of 429. For, if it was to provoke Nestorius, it had to be carried from Egypt to Constantinople and circulated there by certain Alexandrians; likewise, news of Nestorius’s agitation had to be brought from Constantinople back to Alexandria, and that was the occasion for this letter. These things cannot happen without some interval of time, and not a short one. Therefore, since this first letter of Cyril to Nestorius was sent around August, one must acknowledge that the letter to the monks was written either in summer or even in spring. Nor could it have been written earlier, since the occasion for writing it arose nowhere else than from Nestorius’s treatises, especially the sermon on the virgin birth that had been brought to the monks; and that sermon could not have been delivered at Constantinople before Christ’s birth, nor sent to Alexandria—if we believe the author of the *Praedestinatus* (Heresy 89)—unless it had first been read at the Easter festival. That this very sermon stirred up disturbances among the monks is abundantly clear from this first letter of Cyril to Nestorius (no. 1), in which Cyril writes that some people asserted that Christ was merely an instrument of the Deity and a God-bearing man (*Theophoros*, Θεοφόρος); these words are found in the aforementioned sermon (no. 5).

2. Nestorius’s treatises had already been brought to Rome before this time (no. 2) and had caused offense to Celestine and the other bishops who were with him. Celestine had also written with the bishops—by which I understand synodical letters—to Cyril concerning Nestorius’s case before this time: “For they write to us,” he says, “being greatly offended by these things” (ibid.).

3. Nestorius became an object of hatred, chiefly because he had denied that the Virgin was *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος). His words of denial are found in the treatise on the virgin birth (no. 5): the issue was not merely a dispute over the word itself, but because, according as it was affirmed or denied, the word briefly showed which side each person followed in the greatest question after the Trinity: the true Deity of Christ.]

CYRIL, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, TO NESTORIUS, translated from the Greek sermon by Marius Mercator

1. Venerable and trustworthy men who came to Alexandria reported to us that your Reverence was greatly troubled by something, was stirring everything up in order to injure me, and was striving by every means to do so. When I wished to learn the causes of your distress, they told us that certain Alexandrians were circulating my letter to the holy monks and had made it the cause of hatred aroused against me and of your displeasure.

2. I was therefore astonished that your own reverence did not take greater account of the fact that it was not my letter, written later, but certain statements of your Reverence that had provided the occasion for disturbance concerning the faith. For many people circulate not only little written notes but also your expositions, and we are laboring to correct all those who have been corrupted by them. Some were nearly brought to the point of no longer tolerating the confession that Christ is God,

[Note: He refers to Nestorius’s first sermon, which contains these words: “The creature did not give birth to the Creator, but gave birth to the instrument of the Deity, and to a God-bearing man” (Θεοφόρον).]

but instead to call him “an organ and tool of the Deity, and a God-bearing man” (ὄργανον καὶ ἐργαλεῖον τῆς Θεότητος, καὶ ἄνθρωπος Θεοφόρος)—which we may render in Latin as “an instrument or tool of the Deity, and a man clothed with God, using God, or bearing God.” What in all this is not utterly absurd?

3. It was therefore our responsibility to be angry over what your Reverence said—or did not say, for I place very little confidence in the written notes that are being circulated. How, I ask, could we remain silent when the orthodox faith is being wounded and so many people are being corrupted every day? Shall we not stand before the tribunal of Christ, or shall we not give an account, as those appointed to speak, for our inopportune silence?

4. What, finally, should I do? For it is time either to speak or to confer with your Reverence, asking about certain written notes that have somehow been brought to Rome to the revered and most religious bishop of the Romans, Celestine, together with all the venerable bishops who are with him, since it remains uncertain whether or not they belong to your Reverence. For they write to us from there, greatly offended.

5. In what way shall we also satisfy those who come from all the Churches of the East, and care for those who murmur against the same written notes? Do you think that little disturbance has arisen in the Churches from such treatises? We are all in anxiety and prepared for labor in correcting those whom I do not know how have been persuaded to think otherwise, so that they may be recalled to the right path.

6. Since, then, your Reverence has caused and occasioned these rumors, how do you suppose that we can rightly be blamed? Or by what right do you shout against me in vain, rather than correct your own discourse, so that the offense of the whole world against you may subside?

7. If a statement has slipped out before the people, let it be corrected by a retraction. Deign to offer one expression to offended ears by declaring the holy Virgin to be the childbearing mother of God—that is, *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκον)—so that, after you have healed those whose minds are darkened by sorrow, while maintaining before all the true glory of your religious confession, we may celebrate in peace and unanimity the assembly of the people.

[Col. 0803C] 8. Let your Reverence have no doubt that we are prepared to endure everything for the faith that is in Christ—to undergo chains and prisons, and gladly to submit even to death.

9. But I say in truth that, while blessed Atticus was still alive, a book concerning the holy and consubstantial Trinity had already been composed,

[Note: In the first part of volume four of the Paris Greek-Latin edition of the works of Saint Cyril there are nine dialogues in which two persons, Cyril and Hermias, are introduced as interlocutors. The eighth is entitled *On the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten, and that Christ is One and Lord, according to the Scriptures*; the ninth, *That Christ is One, by way of opposition*. The sixth, however, contains a great deal on the same subject. It is uncertain which treatise is meant here; I myself think it more likely that the sixth dialogue is intended. For the entire work on the consubstantial Trinity seems to have been completed in seven dialogues, and the ancients list no more; moreover, what is contained in the sixth concerning the Incarnation agrees especially well with the writings addressed to the monks. Furthermore, the eighth and ninth dialogues are not entirely free from suspicion of being spurious, as we shall show elsewhere (*In the dissertation on Cyril’s books*).]

in which there is also a fuller treatment of the Lord’s incarnation, and it is found to agree with what I have now written. I reread it to the bishops and clergy, as well as to the attentive members of the congregation; but I published it to no one. Perhaps, if I publish it, I shall again be accused,

[Note: Nestorius did not complain for the reason that a book published at that time was not being read. Rather, he complained about this letter, as though it had been written immoderately and therefore deserved no reply; he predicted that greater disturbances would arise from it. Yet the insistence of the presbyter Lampon caused him to change his mind. That presbyter was an Alexandrian, an energetic man in the conduct of affairs, as is clear from a letter Cyril later sent to him while he was residing at Constantinople. He had been sent by his bishop to carry letters and to deal with Nestorius concerning the disturbances that had arisen. Nestorius himself hints at this in his letters. Since they are brief and reveal the whole sequence of events with considerable clarity, I have thought it appropriate to append them.]

although I composed the book even before Your Reverence’s ordination. Greet the brotherhood that is with you; those who are with us greet you in the Lord.

To the most religious and most holy fellow-minister Cyril, Nestorius sends greeting in the Lord.

Nothing is more powerful, surely, than Christian modesty; nothing is more steadfast. It moved us to write at this time through the most religious presbyter Lampon. For when he reported many things about your piety, and in turn heard many things, he finally never ceased pressing us until he obtained this letter from us. Therefore we yielded to the man’s persistence; for, to confess frankly what is true, the modesty of any Christian man—for God dwells in his breast—usually inspires me with no small fear.

Accordingly, as far as we ourselves and our own affairs are concerned, although not a few things have been pointed out by Your Piety that are scarcely compatible with brotherly charity—for one ought to speak modestly—we have nevertheless resolved to preserve an unshaken gentleness of spirit and to continue in our former practice of greeting you by letter with goodwill and friendship. How much fruit that vehement urging of the most religious presbyter Lampon will bring us, experience itself will show. I and all who are with me wish to salute the entire brotherhood that is with you.

[Note: At the Council of Chalcedon (Act 2), this letter is said to have been given in the Egyptian month Mechir, in the thirteenth indiction. The Egyptian month Mechir extends from 26 January to 25 February. The thirteenth indiction fell in the year 430. It seems to have been delivered on the very first day of Mechir and from the synod that, according to the Nicene canon, preceded Lent. This is clear, first, because the ancients customarily designated the first day of a month by no other indication than the name of the month itself; second, because in that year the fast began on 19 Mechir, that is, 14 February; and finally, because the ordinary synod before Lent was held at a time when the Fathers could conveniently return, each to his own church, before the fast began. That Cyril wrote from the synod will be demonstrated clearly in the notes to the third letter.

This second letter, moreover, is almost entirely opposed to Nestorius’s sermons against Proclus, especially the fourth, which begins, “Although the insults …,” so that it may rightly be called *Proclus’s defense*. It also contains some statements at variance with the first sermon, which concerned the virgin birth and preceded Proclus’s other two homilies.]

THE SECOND LETTER OF SAINT CYRIL, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, TO NESTORIUS; TO WHICH THE SAME NESTORIUS, IMPIOUSLY CONTRADICTING IT, THOUGHT A REPLY NECESSARY. Translated from Greek into Latin.

1. As I hear, certain men are chattering about my reputation in Your Reverence’s eyes, and doing so repeatedly,

[Baluz. adds: “namely, by seeking opportune times for processions”]

seizing suitable occasions for assemblies,

[Baluz. “occupying”]

perhaps thinking that they are pleasing your ears by uttering crude accusations against us. They have suffered no injury from us at all, but have been rebuked by us, and that gently: one because he was unjustly harassing the blind and the poor; another because he had drawn his sword against his mother; a third because he had stolen another man’s gold with a maidservant, and because he had always enjoyed such a reputation as no one would wish even his most serious enemies to acquire.

[Note: Cyril had learned from letters sent by his people residing at Constantinople what calumny he was suffering from three Alexandrians—he later acquitted the fourth—and at whose instigation these wicked men dared to accuse their most holy bishop. I do not know what misled Baronius and others who followed him into thinking that the crimes Cyril charged against those depraved men had instead been charged against Cyril by those same men. See the notes to the letter Cyril wrote to his clergy.]

2. But I am not speaking about such men, lest the measure of my lowliness exceed what is fitting, either above the Lord and Master or above the Fathers. For it is not easy for anyone, even if he keeps his life under careful watch, to avoid the curses of wicked men; but those who have a mouth full of cursing and bitterness (Ps. 13:3) will one day render an account to the Judge of all.

3. I shall now turn to what chiefly concerns me, and even now, as a brother in Christ, I shall remind you of the rule of doctrine and of the sense of faith that must be preached to the congregations with every precaution. I shall also urge you to consider that, if one of those little ones who believe in Christ is offended (Mark 9:41), God’s anger is intolerable. But if the injured are a multitude, how, I ask, can one fail to strive by every means to remove the offense wisely and to make sound faith known to those who seek the truth?

4. This must be done rightly: if, while reading the books of the holy Fathers, we acknowledge their great authority, and if we test ourselves to see whether we are in the faith (2 Cor. 13:5), then, as it is written, we must thoroughly and properly strengthen our own understanding by their words and irreproachable definitions.

[Note: Nestorius is accused by ecclesiastical writers of having been little acquainted with the books of the holy Fathers and of despising them because of his swelling pride. This factional spirit moved Eutherius, in his first and second sermons, to attack those who judge the truth by numbers alone and who command each person to be content with his own faith, without examining the Scriptures or speaking according to their prescription.]

5. Therefore that holy and great council of the Fathers defined that the only Son, begotten according to nature from God the Father, God from true God, light from light, through whom the Father created all things, descended, was incarnate, became man, rose on the third day, and ascended into heaven.

[Note: Cyril uses this argument both here and in his letter to the Egyptian monks because Nestorius had abused it in his third sermon, when he said: “But you must know that what has now come to mind is the Council of Nicaea, which nowhere dared to say that the Word God was born from the Virgin Mary. For it says: ‘We believe in God the almighty Father,’ and so forth.”]

6. Following these decrees also in this way, let us see what it means that the Word of God from God was incarnate. We do not say that the nature of God was transformed and became flesh, nor that it was changed wholly into the man composed of soul and body. Rather, we hold that the Word of God, uniting to himself substantially, or essentially, flesh endowed with a rational soul, became man ineffably and inscrutably and was called the Son of Man—not merely according to will or good pleasure, nor as though there were only an assumption of a person—but because diverse natures came together into a true unity, and one Christ and Son arose from both.

[Note: In Greek it is καθ’ ὑπόστασιν, which the translator Mercator rendered by two words very common in this matter, to which, among other Fathers, especially the later ones, the Greek οὐσιωδῶς ordinarily corresponds. Mercator will say toward the end: “The Word united to the flesh according to essence.” It should be noted that, since these expressions were new and therefore less understood, they gave heretics an opportunity to fabricate calumnies against the defenders of the Catholic faith, as though they agreed with Apollinaris or Arius in thinking that the two natures in Christ had merged into one nature, with the Word giving form to the flesh in place of a soul.]

This does not mean that the distinction of the natures was abolished by the union; rather, the same natures, divinity and humanity, by an ineffable and secret conjunction into unity, perfected for us one Lord, Christ, and Son.

[Note: Baluzius, omitting the words “divinity and humanity” above, added here from a Vatican manuscript “of divinity and humanity,” so that the text read: “but rather, the same natures, perfecting … one Lord and Christ and Son of divinity and humanity.” This is not correct. The Bellovacensis manuscript had more reasonably omitted both clauses, for the words “the same natures” are entirely sufficient to convey the meaning; nevertheless Garnerius restored the words so that the Latin might agree more closely with the Greek, which reads: “Not as though the distinction of the natures had been abolished through the union, but rather as though the natures had perfected for us the one Lord Jesus Christ and Son of divinity and humanity through an ineffable and unspeakable conjunction toward unity.” EDIT.]

7. Thus, although he has existed before the ages because he was born from God the Father, he is nevertheless said to have been born also from a woman according to the flesh. This does not mean that his divine nature—in which he is consubstantial, or coessential, that is, ὁμοούσιος, with the Father—received its beginning in the holy Virgin in order to exist; nor that, of necessity and for his own sake, he required a second birth after the first from the Father.

[Baluz. “after the Father”]

For it is impious and ignorant to think that one who existed before the ages and was coeternal with the Father needed a second beginning in order to exist. Rather, because for our sake and for our salvation he proceeded from a woman after uniting to himself substantially, or essentially, the man, he is said in this way to have been born also according to the flesh.

8. For he was not first born as a man from the holy Virgin, nor conceived in her, with the Word of the Father subsequently coming upon the man so born. Rather, he is believed and said to have sustained a carnal birth, united from the beginning and in the very womb, assigning to himself the birth proper to that flesh.

[Note: Since Nestorius’s opinion had not yet been sufficiently understood, many thought that he agreed in every respect with the Samosatene and thus held that the union of the two natures had not occurred in the Virgin’s very womb, but much later, when the man had earned that benefit solely by his own works. This opinion concerning Nestorius attached itself to almost all Westerners—Cassian, Prosper, and others—and indeed to many Easterners as well, before Nestorius disclosed his view that the union of the Word occurred in the very conception of the man. See the dissertation on the Nestorian heresy. This observation is extraordinarily helpful for understanding statements of the Fathers which appear to conflict both with one another and with the truth.]

[Baluz. omits “first”]

8. In the same way we say that he himself suffered and rose again—not because the Word of God suffered in his own nature, or felt the force of wounds or nails, or endured the other torments of wounds—for the Divinity is impassible, since it is also incorporeal—but because the body that became his own suffered. He is therefore said to have suffered these things himself for us, since the impassible one was in the body that suffered.

9. In this way we also understand that he died, although according to nature the Word of God is immortal, incorruptible, life itself, and the giver of life.

[Baluz. adds: “of God”]

But because, again, his own body, by the grace of God, as the apostle Paul said, tasted death for everyone (Heb. 2:9)—not that these things pertained to his nature (for to think or say this is the height of madness), but because, as I said shortly before, his flesh tasted death.

10. Likewise, when the flesh rose again, his resurrection is also spoken of—not because it fell into corruption, far from it, but because what rose was his body.

[Baluz. omits “was”]

11. Thus we confess one Christ and Lord, not as though we were worshiping a man together with the Word of God, lest through the occasion of a single syllable—that is, the word “with”—some fictitious division or conception should creep into our understanding. Rather, we worship one and the same in both, because the body is not alien to the Word, with whom it sits at the right hand of the Father. Nor do we worship as though two sons were sitting there, but as one according to the union with the flesh.

For if we avoid that substantial union as either impossible or improper, we begin to confess two sons. For it becomes entirely necessary to separate them and to say that the man was honored with the special name of “son,” whereas the Word of God truly and naturally possesses the name “Son” in its proper sense.

12. One and the same Lord Jesus Christ must not therefore be divided into two sons. For no one who holds and thinks this way is in any manner assisted by the right rule of faith.

[Baluz. adds: “in any respect”]

Even if someone should think that the unity of persons ought to be proclaimed,

[Note: In Greek: εἰ καὶ προσώπων ἕνωσιν τινὲς—“even if some, however much, proclaim or boast publicly of a unity of persons.”]

the Scripture did not say that the Word of God united to himself the person of a man, but that he became flesh. For the Word’s becoming flesh means nothing other than that he became similar and comparable to us, sharing in flesh and blood,

[Note: The expression “is said to have been compared” is somewhat daring, used instead of “was made equal.” Mercator seems to have expressed the Greek sense paraphrastically rather than literally. The Greek reads: “But for the Word to become flesh means nothing other than that he shared in flesh and blood in a manner similar to us.” He also omitted several things that follow, apparently gathering Cyril’s statements into a summary.]

and made our body his own; and he came forth as man.

[Baluz. omits “similar and”]

13. The sound and perfectly clear rule of faith everywhere serves as a kind of embassy on this matter.

[Note: He has devoutly retained the force of the Greek word πρεσβεύει, “acts as ambassador”; although it is not entirely exact Latin, it is well suited to expressing Cyril’s meaning.]

Thus we find that the holy Fathers held this view; thus they confidently pronounced the holy Virgin to be the bearer of God, that is, Θεοτόκος.

[Note: He has in mind the first and fifth sermons. In the former Nestorius openly denies that the Virgin ought to be called Θεοτόκος; in the latter he is afraid to use the term, as dangerous because heretics had abused it, and because agreement with them had to be avoided even in language. Hence Cyril reports that Θεοτόκος was pronounced by the Fathers, and pronounced confidently.]

This does not mean that the nature of the Word of God, or his Divinity, received from her its beginning in order to exist. Rather, it means that, having taken from her a body endowed with a rational soul,

[Baluz. “endowed with reason”]

to which the Word of God was united according to essence, he is believed to have been born from her according to the flesh.

14. I write these and similar things out of the charity of Christ, entreating you as a brother, adjuring you before God and the chosen angels, and exhorting you to think and teach these things with us, so that the peace of the Churches may be preserved and the indissoluble bond of charity may remain among the priests of God.

[Note: Among the letters of Saint Cyril relating to the Council of Ephesus, some are historical, some dogmatic, and some mixed. I call “historical” those that shed light on events; “dogmatic,” those that expound the faith; and “mixed,” those that combine both forms. This letter is almost entirely historical. Nor is that surprising, since it has the form of a memorandum given to faithful men for the conduct of affairs in the imperial city according to the circumstances of time and place.

Moreover, as it is read here in Mercator’s translation, it differs astonishingly from the version found in both editions of the Council of Ephesus—the Peltan and the Roman—and from both the old Latin and the more recent Greek-Latin editions of Cyril’s works. Someone might therefore think it a different letter, were it not that the earlier and larger portion is the same, with only a few alterations. I am consequently almost persuaded to believe that the Greek text as it now stands is corrupt and should be corrected from the translation of Marius Mercator. The Mercator version certainly sheds far more light on the history than the common version and contains less confusion, as will become clear from the observations that follow.]

LETTER OF SAINT CYRIL, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA,

[Note: In the common edition of the Council of Ephesus it is entitled: “To the Constantinopolitan clergy engaged in mutual dissensions.” Whether this or the following title is false is uncertain; substantial conjectures can be offered on both sides.

The common title is supported, first, by the fact that it is found in all the Greek manuscripts, both those consulted by Peltanus and those used by Autbertus in preparing the Greek-Latin edition of Cyril’s works. Second, the beginning of the letter may suggest that the Constantinopolitan clergy had written to Cyril complaining about Nestorius, and no other response seems to appear. Third, whenever Nestorius is mentioned, he is twice called the bishop of those to whom the letter is addressed. Finally, mention is made of a certain pamphlet composed against Nestorius by those to whom the letter is addressed and intended to be presented to the emperors. Someone might believe this to be the same document that is reported to have been submitted by the Constantinopolitans (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 3).

There are, however, far more numerous and weightier reasons for restoring the title that has been displaced by the Marian title:

1. Cyril always had his own representatives—whether *apocrisiarii* or agents in the affairs of the Egyptian diocese—in the imperial city. Especially during those turbulent times, he needed trustworthy and energetic men who could prudently investigate both the direction of events and the means by which Nestorius’s schemes might be avoided—schemes aimed at the destruction not only of Cyril but also of the faith.

2. The letter has the form of a memorandum, and it corresponds exactly to the memorandum Cyril gave to his presbyter Eulogius, who was staying in the city after the council had ended (Third Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 37). It surpasses all credibility that a foreign bishop would give a memorandum, or indeed a commission, to the clergy of another church, especially of a church hostile to Alexandria, where many still certainly remained attached to Chrysostom, whose name Cyril had only recently accepted.

3. Cyril speaks of his Alexandrian calumniators as men well known to those to whom he is writing. Could Alexandrians really have become so familiar to men living so far away that they could be indicated by a mere word?

4. Although several letters of Cyril to the Constantinopolitan clergy survive, no other has the form of a reply except the one written in the year 430, around autumn, from the Alexandrian council (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 27). Indeed, no other could have had such a form, since that very letter seems to say that Cyril had not yet replied to the complaints of the imperial city’s clergy. The letter before us was sent an entire year earlier.

5. In this very letter, as it is read in Mercator’s translation, Nestorius is not called the bishop of those to whom it was written. Rather, in one place Cyril explicitly speaks of himself and calls himself the bishop of those to whom he is writing.

6. No petition is recorded as having been presented to the emperor by the clergy of the imperial city; rather, it was presented by monks, whose leader was Basil the archimandrite. Therefore, if it were necessary to admit that Cyril wrote to those who were going to present the petition, one would have to admit that he wrote not to the Constantinopolitan clergy—for that general expression means either the whole clergy or at least its better part—but to monks, some of whom were deacons, just as some were readers. Finally, Greek manuscripts copied long afterward deserve less credence than Marius Mercator, who translated the letter almost at the time it was written.

The date of its composition is easily understood from the following facts. The letter itself mentions Cyril’s letters to the Egyptian monks, which had been circulated throughout the city and had exasperated Nestorius; the reply published by Photius to that letter; the petitions handed to Nestorius by the Alexandrian calumniators against Cyril; and the sermon delivered by Nestorius beginning, “Although the insults … .” It must therefore have been written after these events, and consequently not before February of the year 430, when they had all occurred. Indeed, since it contains the same subject matter as Cyril’s second letter to Nestorius but does not mention that letter—although it would have been necessary to mention it, if the truth allowed—it must have been written either before that letter or at the same time as it. Cyril warned Nestorius at the beginning of the year 430, in the month Mechir, or February; this letter therefore belongs to the period mentioned above.]

to his clergy stationed at Constantinople; translated from the Greek sermon by Marius Mercator.

1. I have read the letter sent by you, from which I learned that our enemies, when they met with you, pretended to seek peace and friendship and said,

[Note: In the Greek text, Anastasius is named instead of “our enemies”—that impure presbyter, Nestorius’s *syncellus*, associate in his counsels, and agent in spreading the heresy. Having accompanied Nestorius from Antioch, he was the first, if the Greek historians are to be trusted, to dare publicly to deny in church that the blessed Virgin was the Mother of God. He may have blurted this out during a dispute, carried away by the heat of argument, as Socrates suggests (Book VII, chapter 37), or he may have read a homily written by Nestorius, as Theophanes reports (*Chronology*, under the year 428).

I say “if the Greek historians are to be trusted,” because Cyril says that the blasphemy was uttered by Dorotheus, bishop of Marcianopolis, in Nestorius’s presence and without his disapproval. The dispute can perhaps be reconciled if Anastasius is said to have been the first to deny that the Virgin was the Mother of God, while Dorotheus was the first to pronounce an anathema against those who asserted it.

That Anastasius is the man whom Charisius reported to have written, together with Photius, who was likewise an agent of Nestorius, letters of recommendation to James and Antony for the Philadelphians, in order to recall them from the heresy of the Quartodecimans (Second Part of the Council of Ephesus, Act 6). Yet he did not recall them to the Catholic faith, but to Nestorius’s party, through the rash subscription of a creed fabricated by Theodore of Mopsuestia, about which we shall speak later.]

“As I wrote to the monks, so they hold the faith”; then, turning to their own interpretation, they said that I myself had declared that the holy council did not remember that expression which is Θεοτόκος.

[Baluz. adds after “expression”: “I mean ‘Mother of God,’ that is …”]

2. But I wrote that, even if the council did not use this word, it nevertheless acted appropriately.

[Baluz. omits “nevertheless acted appropriately”]

For at that time none of these matters had been stirred up, nor was it necessary to introduce what was not then being sought. Nevertheless, by the power and force of its meaning, I think that the holy Virgin was called by that council the Mother of God, that is, Θεοτόκος. For it says that the one who was born from God the Father, through whom all things were made, became incarnate, became man, suffered, rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and will come as judge.

3. This does not mean that the Word who was begotten according to nature from God should be believed to have died in every respect, or to have been pierced in the side by a lance—for what side does an incorporeal nature possess, or how did the Life of lives die?

[Note: Baluzius published: “But because this Word was united to the flesh, therefore, when that flesh suffered, he recalls the suffering into himself, as though his own body were undergoing it.” Gallandius repeated this reading in the text, but corrected it in the notes: “The passage is corrupt. The Greek reads: ‘But because the Word, having been united in the flesh, and then while it was suffering, as though his own body were suffering, appropriates the suffering to himself.’ That is: ‘Because the Word united himself to the flesh, when the flesh suffered, as though his own body were undergoing the suffering, he transferred the body’s suffering to himself as his own.’ See Cyril’s works, volume V, part II, page 33. EDIT.”]

Rather, because this Word was united to the flesh, when that flesh suffered, he takes the suffering upon himself, as though it were his own body that was suffering.

[Baluz. “the suffering that his own body endured”]

4. They therefore argue sophistically and deceive themselves when they say that they want peace while lying about their intentions. It is easy to understand that they harbor their own poison in their hearts. They sent two pamphlets to this deacon who administers ecclesiastical affairs: one composed by Photius,

[Baluz. “Photinus”]

or by someone else, against my book published for the monks;

[Note: He was, as we have said, the associate of the presbyter Anastasius, with whom he sent letters to the corrupters of the Philadelphians, mentioned in the case of Charisius (Second Part of the Council of Ephesus, Act 6). The reply he wrote to Cyril’s book for the monks, unless I am mistaken, was destroyed by the flames in which Theodosius ordered the Nestorian books to be burned by an edict (Third Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 48). It is said to have been read to the monks on 23 Pharmuthi, in the first indiction, in the 164th year of Diocletian—that is, in the forty-first year of Theodosius, the twenty-fourth of Valentinian, and the year 448 of Christ—under the consulship of Zeno and Postumianus, on 18 April. An earlier edict on the same matter had nevertheless preceded it; this is recorded in the Theodosian Code as having been issued at Constantinople on 3 August, in the fifteenth consulship of Theodosius and the consulship of the man who was announced with him, that is, in the year 435.]

and another in the form of a small book, bearing even an unsuitable title, as follows: “Against those who, because of the conjunction, either mortify the Divinity of the Son or transfer the humanity into God.”

[Baluz. “either mortify the divinity or fellowship of the Son”]

[Baluz. “who have been mortified”]

Its preface runs as follows: “Although the insults of the heretics against me … .”

[Note: That pamphlet, apparently in the form of a quaternion, bore the title: “Against those who, because of the conjunction, either mortify the Divinity of the Son or transfer the humanity into God.” It is in no way different from the fourth sermon against Proclus, which begins, “Although the insults … .”]

5. Then they try to show that the body suffered, and not the Word of God, as though either we or anyone else could have said that the impassible Word was capable of suffering. No one is so insane. Rather, as we have often said, the holy council declared that the very Word through whom all things were made suffered in his own flesh, according to the Scriptures. For when his body suffered, he himself is said to have suffered, just as, although nothing suffers in its substance and nature, the human mind is nevertheless said to suffer when its body suffers.

6. But since their purpose is to introduce two sons and two Christs—one specifically a man and the other properly God—they make the union exist only in the persons,

[Baluz. adds: “or understand it”]

refusing to acknowledge that the Word of God was properly and substantially united to man, became man, and assumed manhood. Therefore they equivocate and, as it is written, invent excuses in sins (Ps. 140:4).

[Baluz. adds: “of God”]

[Note: See the separate dissertation on this opinion of Nestorius.]

7. When you meet with them, say this: They are doing wrong by introducing certain talkative and babbling men against us and, by encouraging and defending them, making themselves responsible for their wickedness.

[Note: Cyril complains of this very thing to Nestorius: “As I hear, certain men are chattering about my reputation in Your Reverence’s eyes, and doing so repeatedly, seizing suitable occasions for processions or assemblies, perhaps thinking all the more that they are pleasing your ears by uttering crude accusations against us. They have suffered no injury from us at all, but have often been rebuked by us, and gently: one of them because he was unjustly harassing the blind and the poor; another because he had drawn his sword against his mother; a third because he stole another man’s gold with a maidservant, and because he had always enjoyed such a reputation as no one would wish even his most serious enemies to acquire” (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 6).]

8. But this is not the cause of our own injury. Tell them that I am not an enemy even of this man who resides there and presides over it;

[Note: No one fails to see that Nestorius is indicated here. BALUZ.]

but that the venerable bishops of both East and West are injured because the correct doctrine concerning Christ is not being proclaimed, but a thoroughly perverse one.

9. The following evidence is sufficient to refute them: no one has ever said in the Churches anything like what is contained in his expositions, which run as follows:

[Note: These very words are read in the twentieth excerpt from Ephesus; they contain, in my opinion, the beginning of the second sermon. See the observations on that sermon.]

“I do not approve your zeal for me on account of your shouting, but I praise your longing concerning doctrine, in which you have remembered the Lord’s divinity and humanity.”

And shortly afterward:

“I see that the peoples possess great reverence and very prudent piety, but are blind through ignorance of doctrine. This, however, is not the fault of the congregations, but, to put it modestly and decently,”

[Note: Cassianus presses this passage (Book VII, chapter 30): “And you, most impious and shameless man, defiler of the illustrious city, grievous and deadly contagion of the Catholic and holy people—you dare to stand in the Church of God and speak, and with your blasphemous and frenzied words to defame priests of uncorrupted faith and Catholic confession. Is it because of the fault of earlier teachers that the people of Constantinople go astray? You, then, are the corrector of earlier bishops; you, the condemner of ancient priests; you, superior to Gregory; you, more approved than Nectarius; you, greater than John; you, greater than all the priests of the cities of the East?” Cassianus must have seen this letter, since Cyril sent it to Celestine through Possidonius together with other documents concerning the same affair. Or Nestorius may have sent his second sermon to Celestine through Antiochus, which I consider more likely.]

because the teachers did not have time to add something to you that was more polished and lucid concerning doctrine.

10. I ask that it be explained how his predecessors did not have time to teach. Is he more eloquent than John, or can he be compared with blessed Atticus? Is he found to be their equal, or wiser than they?

[Note: [Col. 0813C] Socrates accuses Nestorius of arrogance, but also of ignorance. For he writes as follows (Book VII, chapter 32): “When I read the books published by Nestorius, I find a man unlearned and utterly devoid of education.” And shortly afterward: “He shrinks from the word Θεοτόκος [Theotokos, ‘God-bearer’] as though from a specter; and this happened to him through extraordinary ignorance and lack of understanding. For although he was naturally eloquent in speech and was therefore thought learned, in reality he was uneducated; indeed, he disdained to study thoroughly the writings of the ancient interpreters. Exalting himself insolently through the fluency and elegance of his speech, he both almost entirely disregarded the ancients and considered himself superior to everyone.”]

What could be more arrogant than this? [Baluz.: “What could be more haughty?”] Or how does he not plainly confess, by saying these things, that he is introducing a new and unfamiliar doctrine, wholly unknown to his predecessors, and—what is utterly impious—that he wishes to introduce it into the Church?

11. For my part, I have no argument against him concerning other matters; but may he come to repent and at some point confess the right faith. As for what he contrives against me, provoking and inciting enemies, may he render an account [Col. 0813B] to God.

[Note: [Col. 0813C] This agrees with what is contained in Nestorius’s third letter to Celestine concerning the memorials submitted against Cyril [Col. 0813D]. “I have learned,” he says, “that the most honorable Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, frightened by the memorials submitted against him, is seeking hiding places for himself, in order to avoid the holy synod that is to be held on account of these very memorials; meanwhile he is devising certain other verbal schemes,” and so forth.]

12. It is no wonder [Note: [Col. 0813D] Nestorius brought their accusations before the emperor; hence the holy prelate was compelled to write a defense to Theodosius. “The advocates of Nestorius’s doctrines,” he says (Third part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 13), “bending against me the bow of envy and hatred, and devising in various ways acts of their own uncontrolled madness against me, hired and equipped as accusers certain men whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame, as blessed Paul says (Philippians 3:19), and arranged that they should frequently cause trouble for your imperial authority,” and so forth.] if they speak ill of us.

[Note: [Col. 0813D] Their abominable crimes were reported shortly before from Cyril’s letter to Nestorius [Col. 0814B]. Yet the most holy Victor ought to have been removed from the number of the slanderers; Cyril himself later wrote his defense to the emperor (Third part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 13). “The beloved solitary Victor,” he says, “also experienced with me the darts of an unbridled tongue. For certain habitual liars had spread about him that he too had uttered some absurd nonsense against me, so that when he came to me at Ephesus, some members of the holy synod accused him at length. Indeed, everyone, hating him as though he were one of the impious, turned away from him and persisted in calling him a parricide, fratricide, and by other such names. When that old man learned of this, with many very holy bishops standing around him, he raised his hands to heaven and, contrary to his usual practice, swore by the most sacred baptism and the venerable mysteries of Christ that he was conscious of none of these crimes. Finally, by this means, I and he together were scarcely able to appease the minds of those who had been offended.”

Regarding these men, Christian Lupus is not consistent with himself. At one point he makes them Constantinopolitan presbyters, when he associates them with Photius against Cyril; at another he makes them Alexandrians, when he believes that the crimes genuinely charged against them by Cyril were instead charged by them against Cyril. I have been unable, although I have pondered the matter for a long time, to discern what caused this belief, so alien to the truth—although Lupus shares it with certain others. For Cyril’s words plainly point in the opposite direction (Letter 2 to Nestorius, First part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 8).]

Chaeremon and Victor, and Sophronas, the filth of the city, and the bankrupt Flavian’s slave [Baluz adds “and”]; for they were always worthless both in their conduct toward themselves and in their dealings with others. Let the man who provokes them know that we have never feared undertaking a journey [Baluz omits “undertaking”], nor answering their accusations [Col. 0814A], if the present circumstance should require it. For it may happen, through the dispensation of our Savior, that a council is ordered to be convened, perhaps even for slight and utterly insignificant reasons, in order to cleanse the Church.

13. Let that wretched man therefore not hope [Baluz omits “that wretched man”] that, even if more numerous and more trustworthy witnesses should still accuse us, he will become our judge. For even if we are ordered to come to him, we shall refuse his hearing [Baluz adds “or judgment”] and, by God’s favor, make it clear all the more how he ought to give an account for his own blasphemies.

[Note: [Col. 0814D] We shall refuse—that is, we shall reject. Thus, at the Council of Chalcedon, where the old interpreter, speaking about the case of Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, wrote “I appeal from you,” the deacon Rusticus translated it “I reject you,” as noted in the new collection of the Councils, page 1154. Alexander, bishop of Hierapolis, in his synodical letter against the tragedy of Irenaeus, chapter 6, page 694. There are also other excerpts from Nestorius in the Lateran Council of Pope Martin and in the acts of the Sixth Council. BALUZ.]

14. We do not therefore reject peace; indeed, we desire it, provided that the right faith is announced and professed, or that he finally cease preaching such things. For his quire [Col. 0814B] contains such great perversity [Note: [Col. 0814D] This is the fourth sermon against Proclus, which Cyril says he presented to his deacon in the form of a quire (no. 3 of this letter); in Greek it is properly called “the quire of Nestorius’s blasphemies.”] that it is rightly said of those who wrote it that they hold the primacy in blasphemies.

15. Since he complains that an unfamiliar expression is being demanded—“Mother of God” [Dei genitricem; Baluz: “the woman who gave birth to God”], that is, Θεοτόκος [Theotokos], the holy Virgin, a title neither Scripture nor a holy synod has put forward, let him answer us when questioned: where does Scripture speak of the mother of Christ, that is, Χριστοτόκος [Christotokos, “Christ-bearer”]? Is there any episcopal council that has called Christ a θεοδόχος [theodochos], that is, a “God-receiving form” or form capable of receiving deity?

[Col. 0815A]

16. [Note: [Col. 0815B] He understands the first sermon to concern the incarnation, or the virginal birth, in which these very words occur (no. 12): τὴν θεοδόχον τῷ Θεῷ Λόγῳ συνθεολογῶμεν μόρφην—that is, “let us accord equal theological honor to the God-receiving form with God the Word.”

These and other passages provide considerable support for the account—although an unusual one—given by the author of the *Predestined* concerning the beginning of the dispute between Cyril and Nestorius (Heresy 89): “Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, is said to have fallen into the eighty-ninth heresy. For it is customary that the bishop of Alexandria send one of his treatises to Constantinople, where it is read at Easter, and that the bishop of Constantinople send his treatise to Alexandria, where it is read. In his treatise the Constantinopolitan Nestorius wrote that Mary was not Θεοτόκος but Χριστόκος [Christokos], that is, that she did not give birth to God but to a human being. For if we say that she gave birth to God, we make her the mother of gods, like the pagans.”

Observe that the phrase “at Easter” is not to be understood as meaning that the treatise was read on Easter Day, but “at Easter,” that is, in preparation for proclaiming the Nativity of Christ.]

For in the quire that he sent here and that greatly offended us, he wrote: τὴν θεοδόχον τῷ Θεῷ Λόγῳ συνθεολογῶμεν μόρφην—that is, “let us accord equal theological honor to the God-receiving form with God the Word.” Likewise, concerning that ever-venerable Virgin, he wrote: τὴν θεοδόχον παρθένον τῷ Θεῷ μὴ συνθεολογῶμεν—that is, “let us not raise the God-receiving Virgin together with God to divine status.”

17. Yet he does not know what he is saying. For if the Virgin, as he maintains, did not give birth to God and is not Θεοτόκος, nor could she receive God in her womb, who is Christ, [Col. 0816A] how at least is she θεοδόχος [theodochos, “receptive of deity”], as he again wishes?

[Note: [Col. 0815C] This occurs in another sermon than the one just mentioned. It is the fourth against Proclus, in which these words appear: “For there is one, as I shall say according to them, the Father God, Θεοτόκος—that is, ‘begetter of God’—who bears this name” (no. 47).]

18. Why does he prefer that the Father be called Θεοτόκος [Theotokos], rather than that holy Virgin, whom he ought more correctly and suitably to have called θεογεννήτορα [theogennetora, “begetter of God”; in Latin, *Dei genitorem*]? Let him therefore tell us where he has read these words or from whom he heard them. There are many charges arising from his expositions, but they will be reserved and brought forward at the appropriate time—unless, perhaps, some repentance follows.

[Note: [Col. 0815D] These and other matters down to the end are lacking in the Greek. In their place there are some passages concerning a supplicatory memorial that was to be presented to the emperor Theodosius. It is said to have been read and corrected by Cyril and sent back with instructions that, if necessity did not otherwise compel it, it should be suppressed; but if Nestorius continued in his madness, it should be presented. I believe that some have said it was to be presented in Cyril’s name because Cyril appears in it to ask the emperor not to have Nestorius as judge in the matter of the memorials submitted by the accusers.

But to state fully what I think about the matter, I first assert that those who suppose this book to be identical with the protest displayed at Constantinople concerning Nestorius’s agreement with the Samosatan are mistaken, as are those who make Cyril the author of the protest. For that protest was published almost a year before the letter under discussion was written, by Eusebius of Dorylaeum—later bishop—and was publicly used to demand that Nestorius be prosecuted for heresy. Since Cyril, however, says in the Greek text that he suppressed the memorial, dictated it in altered wording, and had it corrected by others, so that Nestorius might not complain that he was being prosecuted for heresy before the emperor, how could the protest have been composed by others? Moreover, the protest has no appearance of a supplicatory memorial to the ruler, nor was it presented to the emperor; rather, it was publicly displayed to everyone residing in the imperial city.

I further assert that the whole history of this memorial may reasonably appear suspect to some, since it is mentioned nowhere else. For if someone should happen to think that all this must be understood of the supplication submitted to Theodosius by Basil and the other monks [Col. 0816C], that view has no resemblance to the truth. The memorial stipulates that Nestorius should not appear to be accused of heresy before the emperor, whereas he is openly accused in the supplication. In the memorial Cyril rejects Nestorius’s judgment, explicitly expressing hostility; nothing of this sort is found in the supplication. In the memorial Cyril was to speak in his own name; in the supplication the monks act on their own behalf.

If, nevertheless, anyone should think that everything written about the memorial pertains to the monks’ supplication, let him say that the Constantinopolitans appeared to have omitted Cyril’s correction because of Nestorius’s insane persistence, both in spreading error and in harassing his opponents—persistence for which he ought openly to have been charged with heresy.

Let him also say that the demand for an ecumenical council was a suitable way of declining a case that was to be heard before Nestorius, and that it showed extraordinary prudence—not only to request judgment in the name of the monks, and not likewise in Cyril’s name, but also to number Cyril among the Fathers as a witness to the faith, thereby declaring him Nestorius’s adversary and consequently subject to another’s judgment. The fact that he is called without the grand titles customary in such circumstances may perhaps appear an unmistakable indication that the supplication was seen by Cyril but, out of modesty, was cleansed, as it were, of his own praises.

Finally, I think, not without reason, that the letter was actually written by Cyril just as it was translated into Latin by Mercator, but that the Greek addition is nothing other than a memorandum or note which Cyril attached to the same memorial, as is customary, when he returned it. Someone who did not understand it well may have thought that it was part of the letter and, so that it would not have two conclusions, removed its proper ending and inserted another’s.

But so that none of the material ordinarily read may be missing at this point, we present the note in Greek and Latin, although inscribed under its own title.]

I must make my intention clear to you. Therefore I write again: although I am peaceful by nature and quite unfamiliar with litigation, I nevertheless desire the Churches to enjoy peace and the priests of God, living in peace, to remember us, as our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of all, says: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

20. [Note: [Col. 0817C] Baluz: “If there is anything by which stability may be strengthened—for I truly say that I so desire health for myself and to be found upright before God, as well as all the bishops—in conversations,” and so forth.]

In your conversations, then, say this: many things have indeed proceeded from them that would injure us; nevertheless, there will be peace when he ceases either to teach or to think such things. For when the faith is injured, it arouses enmity, indeed it intensifies it. [Col. 0817B]

21. If he professes the right faith, complete and very firm peace will be established. If he holds this as his desire, let him write the Catholic faith and send it to Alexandria. If these things are written from the inmost disposition of his heart, I too am ready, to the best of my ability, to write and publish similar things, and to say that none of our fellow priests ought to be burdened, since we learn that his words have a right intention and a clear purpose. But if he remains in perversity and empty glory, and asks for peace, nothing remains except that we resist with all our strength, lest we be thought to agree with him [Baluz adds “and to hold the impious things that he holds”]. For, on behalf of the faith that is in Christ, to labor, to live, and to die is my greatest desire.

## MEMORANDUM ATTACHED TO THE LETTER

I received and read the supplicatory memorial sent by you to me, which is to be presented to the emperor, though not without our opinion. But because it inveighs at length against the man who is active there, whether he is called “brother” or by any other name, I have so far suppressed it, lest, rising up against us, he should complain that through us he had been reported to the emperor as a heretic [Col. 0817C]. Accordingly, we dictated it in different words, while also rejecting him as our judge and explicitly expressing hostility, and requesting that the present dispute be transferred to another tribunal if they should persist in being altogether unreasonable.

When, therefore, you have read the memorial, deliver it if necessity requires. If you observe that he persists in these intrigues and is plotting nothing but hostility against us, report it carefully [Col. 0818A]. For I shall choose pious and prudent men, both bishops and monks, and send them to you at the earliest opportunity. For, as it is written, I shall give no sleep to my eyes, nor slumber to my eyelids, nor rest to my temples (Psalm 131:4), until I have completed the struggle for the salvation of all. Therefore, now that you have learned my position, act courageously. As soon as possible, letters will be prepared by me, both of the kind that is necessary and for those to whom they ought to be sent. For I have resolved, on account of the faith of Christ, to undergo any labor and endure every torment, even those counted among the gravest punishments, until I have endured the death undertaken for this cause and found it joyful.

## NESTORIUS’S SECOND LETTER

[Note: [Col. 0817C] This letter was sent in the year 430, after Easter. For it responds to Cyril’s second letter, which Cyril sent from Alexandria to Constantinople in the month Mechir, in the thirteenth indiction [Col. 0817D].

Concerning this same letter, Nicephorus writes as follows—though the matter requires more exact examination: “When Cyril received Nestorius’s letters, vomiting forth enormous waves of heresy, together with certain other quires, he assembled the provincial synod of Alexandria and presented copies of the letters exchanged by both men. He sent copies of them and the decrees of the synod to Celestine, bishop of ancient Rome” (Book XIV, chapter 33, *Dissertation on the Synod*).

A copy of it was sent first by Cyril through the deacon Possidonius and then by Nestorius to the holy Celestine; the former fact is established from Cyril’s letter to Celestine, the latter from Nestorius’s third letter to the same man.

It was read at the Council of Ephesus and rejected, with an anathema against its author, first by the metropolitans, who pronounced their judgments individually; afterward by the others, who cried out together in these words: “We all anathematize Nestorius’s letter and doctrines; we all anathematize Nestorius the heretic” (Second part of the Council of Ephesus, session 1). It was likewise reread and condemned at the Council of Chalcedon.

From this letter, and from the words of those who mention it, many things may be understood that contribute to a deeper understanding of the Nestorian heresy [Col. 0818D] and its history; these will be explained individually in their appropriate places.]

## LETTER TO SAINT CYRIL, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, IN REPLY; TRANSLATED FROM THE GREEK INTO LATIN BY MARIUS MERCATOR

[Col. 0818B]

1. I shall leave the insults contained in your remarkable letter against us to a forbearance deserving of medicine and appropriate to the matter and the occasion. But what cannot be passed over in silence, because silence would bring danger, I shall attempt to answer briefly and concisely, as I am able and as opportunity permits, to the prolixity of your discourse, avoiding and rejecting [Note: [Col. 0818D] He attacks Cyril’s letter as though it were defective in four respects: obscurity, disorder, prolixity, and the harshness of its expression. At the same time he flatters himself by contrast, as though his own speech were clear, well arranged, brief, and perhaps excessively polished. As for his charge, Asians were accustomed to reproach Alexandrians on this point.] the darkness, confusion, and horror of lengthy speech.

2. I shall begin with the exceedingly wise words of your charity, inserting them—or rather setting them out word for word: “The holy and great council,” you say, “defined that the only-begotten Son, begotten naturally from God the Father, true God from true God, light from light, through whom the Father created all things, descended, became incarnate and human, suffered, and rose again.”

3. These are the words of your piety, and you surely recognize them as your own. [Note: [Col. 0818D] He attempts, by means of a fabricated exhortation, to return against Cyril the charge that Cyril had brought against him, but not with equal justification. For everyone accuses Nestorius of negligence in handling the books of the Fathers, indeed even of contempt for them, as Socrates reports. Cyril, by contrast, is praised as πολυμαθέστατος [polymathestatos, “most learned”] and as the most careful follower of the Fathers. Nestorius accuses Cyril in such a way as to say that Cyril reads the Fathers’ statements only superficially and does not understand them.]

Now hear us also, as we offer a brotherly exhortation in the interest of piety—namely, the exhortation that that old man Paul declared to his beloved Timothy when he said: “Attend to reading, exhortation, and doctrine; for by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you” (1 Timothy 4:16). What, then, tell me, does this word “attend” mean? You have read only superficially the tradition of those holy men, and, supposing that they said that the Word who is coeternal with the Father was passible, you have remained unaware of an ignorance deserving pardon.

4. Therefore, if you please, examine these words more attentively, and you will find that that divine gathering of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0819D] In order to slander Cyril, he used, as they say, an abstract noun in place of a concrete one. Since the former signifies nature and the latter person, and since the communication of properties cannot take place with abstract nouns because of the unconfused distinction of the natures, but only with concrete nouns because of the identity of the person subsisting in two natures, he maliciously represented the Catholic teacher as though he were asserting that the Word suffered in his own nature. His claim became all the more persuasive because the Fathers, speaking without fear when no heretics were lying in wait, often appear to have used abstract expressions when they ought to have used concrete ones.]

did not say that the consubstantial Deity was passible, nor that this Deity, which is coeternal with the Father, had recently come into being, nor that this Deity rose again—the Deity that raised up the temple after it had been destroyed.

If you lend an ear to me as I offer fraternal medicine, I shall insert before you the very words of those Fathers and, through them, free you from the bond of slander that you strive to impose upon them and, through them, upon the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0820D] From this I conclude that the reading in the Council of Ephesus should be “I shall free” rather than “I have freed.” BALUZ.] [Baluz adds “which you strive to impose”].

5. “We believe,” they say, “also in our Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son.” Observe how, first establishing as common foundations the names “Lord,” “Jesus Christ,” and “only-begotten Son,” names belonging to both divinity [Baluz adds “and humanity”], they then build upon them the tradition concerning the assumed human being, the resurrection, and the passion. Thus, by establishing certain names common and significant of both natures, neither are those things that belong properly to the Son’s generation and lordship divided [Baluz: “distinguished”], nor are those things that belong properly to the natures, in the singularity of the Son’s birth, endangered by the abolition [Baluz: “resolution”] of any confusion through the name of union [Col. 0819C].

6. In this matter Paul became their teacher. When he recalled the divine incarnation and began to add what concerns the passion, he first placed “Christ,” the common name of the natures, as I said above; then he introduced an appropriate statement, or account, of both. For he says: “Let this be felt among you, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as robbery; but”—not to speak of each point individually—“he became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5).

7. Since he had begun to mention death, so that no one might consequently suppose that the divine Word was passible, he used “Christ,” a term signifying the singularity of the person composed of passible and impassible essence [Note: [Col. 0820D] This passage, as well as another preceding it (no. 5), and indeed the one that follows (no. 8), led some less discerning people into the error of saying that Nestorius asserted a single person in the Catholic sense. They attempted to support this claim with many testimonies, whether from Nestorius or even from Cyril. But when they saw that Catholic teachers protested against it, they set out their view in writing in such a way that they effectively retracted it. Concerning that Nestorian singularity of person, see the dissertation on the Nestorian heresy, where we expose the very sources of the poison concealed under this appearance.] so that Christ might safely be called both impassible and passible: impassible in respect of his deity, but passible in respect of his bodily nature.

8. I could say much about this, and first of all I could demonstrate that those holy Fathers remembered not the divinity’s role in the dispensation but only the assumption of humanity. But I remember the brevity promised in the preface, and I feel it restraining my speech.

9. I now come to the second point raised by your charity. In it I praised the distinction made between the natures according to the account of deity and humanity, and their fellowship in one person. I also praised your statement that God the Word did not at all need a second birth from a woman, and that you professed the deity incapable of suffering; for these things are truly Catholic and wholly opposed to all sects that attack the Lord’s natures.

10. But as for the rest, if you present to the ears of your readers some hidden, profound, and incomprehensible explanation, let your prudence examine it. For you seemed to me cleverly to destroy your earlier statements when you introduced again as passible and newly created the one who had first been proclaimed impassible and incapable of receiving a second birth. It would be as though the properties naturally belonging to God the Word had been corrupted through their association with the temple, or as though human beings ought perhaps to consider that temple itself—free from sin and inseparable from the divine nature—as nothing, because it had not endured birth and death for sinners; as though one ought not to believe the Lord’s words addressed aloud to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). He did not say, “Destroy my deity, and in three days it will be raised.”

11. Again, as I wish to expand my discourse here, the recollection of the promised profession of brevity calls me back. Yet I shall say something. Throughout the divine Scriptures, whenever they mention the Lord’s dispensation, they transmit not the passion and birth of Christ’s deity but of his humanity. Therefore, according to the clearest and most suitable reasoning, the holy Virgin ought to be called not the mother of God, that is, Θεοτόκος [Theotokos], but the mother of Christ, that is, Χριστοτόκος [Christotokos].

12. The evangelist also cries out: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1). It is evident that God the Word was not David’s son. Take, if you please, another testimony: “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ” (ibid., 1:16). Attend to another statement: “Now the generation of Christ was in this way. When Mary his mother had been betrothed, she was found to have conceived in her womb from the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 1:18). Who could or ought to suppose that the deity of the Only-begotten was created by the Holy Spirit? What more needs to be added to these things? Hear again: “And the mother of Jesus was there” (John 2:1). And again: “With Mary, the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). Also this: “That which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20). And again: “Take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt” (Matthew 2:13). And this: “Concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3). And again, concerning his passion: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and on account of sin condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans 8:3). And again: “Christ died for our sins” (1 Corinthians 15:3). And once more: “Christ having suffered in the flesh” (1 Peter 4:1). And this: “This is my body, and this is my blood” (Luke 22:19). He did not say, “This is my deity.”

13. There are ten thousand other passages, expressed in many different ways, testifying that the human race must not think of the Son’s deity as recent or novel, or as capable of bodily sufferings, but that the flesh joined to the divine nature is that from which Christ calls himself the son of David. For what does he say? “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” They answered, “David’s.” Jesus replied and said: “How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying: The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand” (Matthew 22:42)? He is certainly David’s son according to the flesh, but according to his deity he is Lord. It is entirely certain that the body is the temple of the Son’s deity, and that this temple was united through an exceptionally exalted and divine conjunction, so that it is good and worthy of the evangelical tradition to confess that the divine nature takes to itself and refers to itself the things that belong to God.

14. But to attribute to God, under the name of this intimacy, the properties of the united flesh—namely, birth, suffering, and mortality—is, brother, either the reasoning of erring paganism, or that of the mentally deranged Apollinaris and Arius, or that of the remaining heretical plagues, and something worse than these. For such men, being drawn in by the name of intimacy, would make God the Word a participant in nursing because of that intimacy, and a sharer in the growth of age, which advanced little by little, and, at the time of his passion, in need of angelic assistance because of fear.

15. I say nothing of circumcision, sacrifice, sweat, and hunger, which indeed befell the flesh for our sake. Yet, when these things are joined to him, they are also to be adored. But when they are attributed to the deity, they are now received falsely and bring upon us, as though we were slanderers, just grounds for condemnation.

16. These are the traditions of the holy Fathers; these are the commands of the holy Scriptures. Thus they reason about the things of divine mercy and authority according to God: “Meditate on these things; be occupied with them, so that your progress may be evident” (1 Timothy 4:15). Paul said these things to everyone.

17. You do well to take care of those who are offended by us [Note: [Col. 0821C] Nevertheless, he accused Cyril before the emperor on this very ground, as though he took an overly inquisitive interest in others’ affairs. Hence Theodosius, somewhat angrily, wrote to Cyril: “He who is separated from us by so great a distance of places cannot altogether escape blame for inquiring too inquisitively into our affairs,” and so forth (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 31).] and to be concerned about the matters that exist among us. I am grateful for your unanimity; but know that you have been misled [Note: [Col. 0821C] “By those who”—that is, by Philip, a presbyter of the Church of Constantinople, whom Nestorius deposed on the charge of Manichaeism, as the memorandum of Saint Cyril given to Possidonius when he was going to Rome to Pope Celestine teaches; published in the new collection of the Councils, page 379. BALUZ.] by those who were deposed by the holy council.

[Note: [Col. 0821D] But by what council, after all? I am astonished that no one to this day has investigated these words, although Nestorius’s letter has been in the hands and repeatedly before the eyes of all learned men. In so obscure a matter, one must attempt to draw from the individual circumstances something that, if not certain, is at least not improbable. This refutes the popular opinion that has taken root in many minds concerning Pelagian bishops received by the Eastern faction at Ephesus.

The council in question, whatever its nature, was certainly held at Constantinople, since Nestorius was writing from there, as the Greek word ἐνταῦθα—“here, in this place”—indicates. It was also undoubtedly held according to custom, that is, in accordance with the fifth canon of Nicaea, either before the Lent of Easter or around the autumn season. For if it had met contrary to custom, the writers who were so meticulous in recording every smallest detail of Nestorian history would certainly have mentioned it. Ordinary synods, however, are usually passed over in silence, unless something worthy of note happened in them.]

Nestorius presided; for who else in the imperial city, whose see he occupied, and which was ἀυτοκέφαλον [autocephalous]? The bishops of the province assembled, for that is what the Nicene canon prescribed. That they assembled either in the year 429, in the autumn, or—what seems to me far more credible, indeed certain—in the year 430, before the Lenten fast of Easter, that is, at the beginning of February, is demonstrated by the strongest reasoning. For it could not have been held in the preceding year, 428, since at that time the disputes between Nestorius and Cyril had not yet become heated in the autumn; nor in the following year, since Nestorius’s letters mention the council, and Cyril’s letters to Rome were sent together with his writings to Nestorius, while the pope replied to Cyril on August 11, 430.

At the council proceedings were conducted against the Manichaeans and Marcionists, or certainly against those who were said to suffer from the disease of the Manichaeans, as Nestorius himself testifies. Some were deposed by the council’s sentence because they professed “to hold the opinions of the Manichaeans” (τὰ τῶν Μανιχαίων φρονεῖν). But who were these clerics? Alexandrians, as the Roman translator indicates? Rather, Constantinopolitans, as Mercator suggests? Or both, as someone might perhaps think? Certainly the Greek text favors Mercator more; nor would Cyril have endured, without the gravest complaint, an injury inflicted upon his own clergy.

The reason why the synod dealt with this matter seems quite credible. Toward the end of 429, Mercator had presented to the emperor a memorandum against Julian and other bishops of the Coelestian faction, who, having been expelled from the West, had fled to the imperial city. After reading the memorandum, the emperor expelled from Constantinople the whole group of such men, and Coelestius above all, as though their leader.
