Nestorius, displeased that men who had taken refuge with him—and whose complaints he had brought before the emperor—should be expelled, whether to obey those urging him on or to offer some consolation to the afflicted, judged that those who had stirred up the storm against the head of their friends should be condemned in his council for the impiety of the Manichaeans. It is known to everyone that the Coelestians, or the patrons of the Coelestians, were accustomed to level this very accusation against Catholics; and it is known to all who have read Augustine’s books attentively that Pelagius threatened the Catholics, and Julian the Eastern Churches, with condemnation on account of the doctrine of original sin.

In this council one may reasonably believe that the canon mentioned by Gregory the Great was enacted: the canon that declared anathema against anyone who asserted that Adam’s soul had died in sin, since the devil does not enter the human heart. But in order that this conjecture of ours may become more probable, the history of the Isaurian monks, which gave Gregory occasion to write what is found in Letters 114 and 195 and elsewhere, must apparently be reconstructed.

Two Isaurian monks and priests, John and Anastasius, were brought before John, bishop of Constantinople—called the Faster—on charges of the heresy of Manichaeus and Marcion. He appointed investigators and judges for the case. After the Isaurians had been condemned by them, they appealed to the apostolic see, over which Gregory the Great presided. One of them, John, was acquitted in the Roman council; the other was found to be infected with the Manichaean stain. But in order to defend his judgment, John the Faster sent to Rome a book written by Anastasius. A conspicuous mark had been added to it—whether by John himself or by someone else—to indicate which statements in it appeared deserving of condemnation. Among these was the following: “When Adam sinned, his soul died, because he lost the blessedness of his original condition.” When Gregory read this in the council, he was astonished at the great ignorance of the annotator and judges, who had condemned a Catholic doctrine as Manichaean.

When John, bishop of Constantinople, learned this, he sent Rome once more a book bearing the title of the Ephesian synod and containing several canons, among them one in particular in which anathema was pronounced against anyone asserting that Adam’s soul had died in sin, and so forth.

The pope was even more astonished at this second matter. He ordered the Ephesian books kept at Rome to be examined, and some very ancient, uncorrupted copy to be brought from the Church of Ravenna; he also ordered Count Narses to seek out the oldest copies possible at Constantinople, so that any fraud might be detected. Meanwhile, he convicted the Pelagian doctrine of the canon and demonstrated that Adam must be said to have died in soul because of sin, lest the truth of the divine sentence be undermined: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall surely die.”

What Narses found at Constantinople is unknown. Certainly the Roman and Ravennese copies contained nothing in the definition of the anathema and condemnation except what they reported as the chapters of Cyril of blessed memory.

Three years later, when Cyriacus had succeeded John the Faster in the see of Constantinople, Gregory wrote to the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch about the case of the Isaurians—not because he suspected Cyriacus of heresy, for from his synodical letters he knew him to be Catholic, but so that the bishops of those great sees might be cautious on behalf of others, and so that the seeds of error might be trampled down before they emerged publicly. These words of the pope deserve attention:

“That synod which contains a canon and was held under the appearance of the First Council of Ephesus asserts that certain chapters submitted to it were approved; these are the propositions of Coelestius and Pelagius. But since Coelestius and Pelagius were condemned in that synod, how could those chapters be accepted by it, when their authors were condemned?”

When dealing with the case of the Isaurians (*Ad annum* 593 and 595), Baronius writes that the canon in question was issued at Ephesus in the schismatic council, and that it was the second canon. As the first, I suppose, he placed the canon by which Cyril and Memnon were deposed. But he does not show from where he either inferred or received this.

Christian Lupus, perhaps wishing to assist Baronius in his difficulty, ventures a bolder opinion (*Scholia on the Canons of the Council of Ephesus*, p. 417): namely, that those Pelagian canons had been submitted to the Ephesian council of John of Antioch by the deposed bishops Julian, Orontius, and the other four, together with Coelestius, but had not been approved by it; rather, they had been inserted by the artifice of the Pelagians into the acts of the Ephesian synod as they were being copied for distribution among the public. Hence, when such a corrupted copy was presented, it imposed upon John the Faster and his judges, who must have been extremely ignorant; and from them it was later transmitted to the pope in Rome.

This entire history is drawn from the letters of Gregory the Great. It is better, however, to hear the pontiff speaking in his own words, for they contain much worthy of notice and are full of a certain profound ecclesiastical learning.

Gregory therefore wrote to Count Narses:

“Your Charity, concerned for our opinion, took pains to write what you thought about that book which was sent against the priest Anastasius. We examined it carefully in part and found that it had fallen into the doctrine of Manichaeus. But the one who indicated by an opposing mark that certain passages were heretical also falls into the Pelagian heresy, because he marked as heretical certain passages that were stated in a Catholic and entirely orthodox manner. For where it is written that, when Adam sinned, his soul died, the writer explains below in what sense he called it dead: because Adam lost the blessedness of his original condition. Whoever denies this is not a Catholic.”

And shortly afterward:

“The person who marked this passage in the same book sent to me by my brother John, the bishop, as heretical, is therefore a Pelagian, because this statement is plainly Pelagius’s, and the apostle Paul openly refuted it in his Letters. I omit mentioning each of the passages in his Letters, for I am speaking to one who knows them. Pelagius, however, who was condemned at the Ephesian synod, adopted this position in order to show that we had been redeemed by Christ in vain.”

And afterward:

“Your Charity should therefore seek out entirely ancient copies of that same synod and see whether anything of this kind is found there; then send me the copy you discover, and as soon as I have read it I will send it back. Do not readily trust the new copies, for this has made me doubtful, and I have not yet wished to write anything about this matter to my aforesaid brother John, the bishop. The Roman copies are much more reliable than the Greek, because ours possess neither subtleties nor frauds. Concerning the priest John, know that his case was decided by a SYNOD. There I clearly learned that his adversaries wanted to make him a heretic. They tried for a long time, but were completely unable to do so.”

To John of Constantinople:

“We were greatly astonished that those whom you appointed as judges against John, a priest of the Church of Chalcedon, in a matter of faith, should have carelessly trusted an opinion rather than the truth, and should have refused to believe a man who professed his faith with determination—especially since, when the accusers themselves were questioned about the Marcionist heresy they had mentioned, and by which they were attempting to make him guilty, they openly declared that they did not know what it was. From this it is plainly evident that, without regard for God, they wished to burden his person not justly but against their own souls, relying solely upon their will.

“We therefore held a COUNCIL, as the record of the proceedings conducted before us shows, carefully investigating and considering everything necessary. Since we could find no guilt at all in the aforesaid priest, and especially since the statement of faith that he presented to the judges delegated by you agrees in every respect with the sincerity of the true faith, we rejected the judgment of those same judges and declared, by our own decision, that he was Catholic and free from every charge of heresy, by the mercy and grace of Christ our God and Redeemer, which had revealed this to us.”

Likewise to the emperor Maurice:

“When, therefore, the acts conducted against John, a priest of the Church of Chalcedon, were reported in the council, together with the sequence of the judgment, we learned that he had suffered a still greater injustice: although he cried out and demonstrated that he was Catholic, he was crushed not by the guilt of an offense but by a long and unfounded accusation. Indeed, his accusers openly declared that they did not know the Marcionist heresy they had mentioned.”

And afterward:

“Since, therefore, after carefully examining and considering everything, the decision I shared with the sacred COUNCIL declared the aforementioned priest John Catholic, by the grace of divine power revealing this to us,” and so forth.

To Theoctistus, a relative of the emperor:

“We therefore inform you that John the priest, the bearer of this letter, has been found free from the charges of which he had been accused. After holding a COUNCIL and examining his faith with careful scrutiny, as he requested, we found no fault in him arising from an erroneous confession. But since, by God’s mercy, he appeared to be a professing adherent and worshiper of the true faith, we acquitted him by our decision—especially since his accusers professed that they did not know what the Marcionist heresy was that they had mentioned.”

And to Eulogius of Alexandria and Anastasius of Antioch:

“Three years ago, compelled by the case of the Isaurian monks, who were accused of heresy, my former brother and fellow priest, the Lord John, sent me a letter in which he appeared to demonstrate that they contradicted the definitions of the Ephesian synod. As though from that same synod, he sent us certain chapters against which they were said to have objected. Among other things, the following was written there concerning Adam’s soul: ‘that it did not die in sin, because the devil did not enter the human heart; and if anyone said this, let him be anathema.’

“When this was reported to me, I was greatly saddened. For if the soul of Adam, who sinned first, did not die in sin, how is it that it was said to him concerning the forbidden tree: ‘On whatever day you eat of it, you shall surely die’?

“And afterward:

“That the devil enters the human heart is not denied if one believes the Gospel. For it is written there: ‘And after the morsel, Satan entered into him.’ And again it says there: ‘When the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas that Judas should betray him.’ Whoever denies this falls into the Pelagian heresy.

“Since, therefore, upon examining the Ephesian synod, we found nothing of this kind contained in it, we also had a very ancient copy of that same synod brought to us from the Church of Ravenna. We found it to agree so closely with the synod we possessed that it differed in no respect and contained nothing else in its definition of anathema and condemnation except what the twelve chapters of Cyril of blessed memory condemn.

“We have given the whole account much more fully and precisely to his aforesaid representatives, who are present here, and have satisfied him completely. Therefore, lest either these or similar matters creep in there and scandalize the holy Church, it was necessary for us to report these things to Your Holiness. Although we know our brother and fellow bishop Cyriacus to be orthodox, we must nevertheless be cautious on account of others, so that the seeds of error may be trampled down before they emerge publicly.”

Finally, to Anastasius of Antioch:

“When Your Fraternity was speaking about the preservation of the holy councils, you professed that you guarded the holy First Synod of Ephesus. But because, from the annotation of a heretical book sent to me from the imperial city, I learned that certain Catholic chapters had been condemned together with heretical ones—and because some people think that this First Ephesian Synod is the same one that is said to have been composed there by heretics—it is entirely necessary that Your Charity seek out that same synod from the holy Churches of Alexandria and Antioch and discover how it truly stands; or, if you prefer, we can send from here what we have preserved from antiquity in our archives.

“For that synod which was held under the appearance of the First Ephesian Synod asserts that certain chapters submitted to it were approved, and these are the propositions of Coelestius and Pelagius. Since Coelestius and Pelagius were condemned in the Ephesian synod, how could those chapters be accepted by it, when their authors were condemned?”

From what Gregory the Great wrote, much can be concluded concerning the present matter. First, one must depart from the opinion of those who separate the case of the Isaurian monks from that of the two priests. Second, canons belonging to another council had been inserted into the book containing the Ephesian synod. Third, chapters had been submitted to this inserted council and approved by it. Fourth, those chapters made the Isaurians guilty of agreement with Manichaeus and Marcion. Fifth, one of the chapters contradicted the Catholic doctrine concerning Adam’s soul, which died through sin, and contradicted Anastasius’s judgment; it was therefore Pelagian or Coelestian. Sixth, that council was distinct from the ecumenical Ephesian synod, since in the ecumenical synod Pelagius and Coelestius were condemned, whereas in that council their doctrines were approved. Seventh, Gregory the Great heard the case of the Isaurians in a council and wished this to be known both to the emperor, Count Narses, John the bishop of Constantinople, and the emperor’s relative, so that none of them would be unaware of it. Finally, that council was not identical with the council of the Eastern schismatics; for, as Lupus rightly argues, Coelestian doctrines were not approved there. If they had been, Catholics certainly would not have passed over so great a crime without the gravest complaint; for the chapters submitted to the council were likewise approved by it.

And since these points are certain, a probable conjecture may be drawn from them, by which the six propositions containing, unless I am mistaken, the solution of the entire question—and the explanation of a very confused matter—may be confirmed.

1. The council mentioned by Gregory was none other than the council convened by Nestorius, which we have just mentioned; for those who clung to the opinions of Manichaeus and therefore of Marcion are said to have been condemned there. The two heretics shared one opinion concerning the evil nature of man.

2. The chapters in question were submitted to the Nestorian council, and they were opposed to the Catholic faith concerning the corruption of human nature—that is, corruption with respect to the soul, not the corruption affecting the body, for in this matter Nestorius held the Catholic position.

3. Those same chapters were easily approved by Nestorius, since, as we have shown elsewhere, he held the Catholic position concerning bodily death contracted through sin, but appears, with respect to the death of the soul transmitted from Adam to his descendants, to have followed his teacher Theodore of Mopsuestia, the most vehement opponent of original sin.

4. That approval of the chapters was included among the anathemas of the synod; for it would be difficult to find examples from ancient times of people being deposed on account of a doctrine whose advocates had not been anathematized.

5. Those very anathemas were transferred into a copy together with the Ephesian synod, at first with an inscription distinguishing them; then the inscription was either omitted through the negligence of copyists or erased through the devices either of the Coelestians, who persisted in great numbers in the East until the time of Photius, or of the Nestorians, who wished to fabricate a charge against the Ephesian synod.

6. Perhaps it is true, as Christian Lupus conjectured, that the Coelestians—and Nestorius himself—attempted to win the support of the Easterners so that they would approve such anathemas, motivated by a desire to contradict the orthodox Fathers who had approved Pope Coelestine’s judgment concerning the Pelagians. For it is not without significance that, at the time when the Fathers reported the case of the Pelagians to the apostolic see, the Easterners wrote a three-part confession of faith. In the first they professed the Nicene Creed; in the second they struck with anathema only seven heretics by name, among them Manichaeus and Marcion; in the last they proscribed Cyril’s twelve chapters. This perhaps explains why Baronius said that the second canon enacted by the Easterners concerned Adam’s soul, and so forth. Nor is it without significance that the schismatics rejected the charge, brought by Catholics, of association with the Coelestians only by returning a similar accusation, though undeserved.

Someone might perhaps ask why the schismatics ultimately refused to approve Nestorius’s aforementioned anathemas in express terms, contenting themselves with stating the judgment implicitly and covertly. The answer may readily be drawn from the fact that Theodosius had recently expelled the Coelestians and Pope Coelestine had just condemned them. It would not have been safe to oppose openly the judgment of either one or the other; rather, it was necessary to retain the favor of both. For Nestorius, already condemned, did not yet possess such authority that he could drive the Easterners so far, especially since John of Antioch wished to diminish that very authority elsewhere, so that he might hold the primacy of the council more securely, if possible. Indeed, whatever prevented the Easterners from openly approving the anathemas made by Nestorius against the followers of Cyril—however openly they themselves had rejected those followers as heretics—must likewise, unless I am mistaken, have prevented them from openly confirming the anathemas that Nestorius had once composed, in the weakness of his spirit, against men entirely free from the Manichaean heresy, whom he had regarded as Pelagians.]

[Fragment:] …because they had been filled with the disease of the Manichaeans; or, what is most important, by clerics more devoted to your affection. For the matters concerning our Church are daily improving; and as for those concerning the people, know that they are extending toward ever greater progress, through the grace of Christ, so much so that this multitude cries out in the words of the prophet: “The earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as many waters cover the sea” (Isaiah 11:9).

### 18.

[Note: We once observed that this passage gave Cyril occasion to write two books *On the Right Faith*: one to the emperor Theodosius, the other to Pulcheria and her virgin sisters. Hence he was later subjected to the accusation that, by this diversity of books, he had attempted to stir up some disturbance in the imperial family. Nestorius obscurely suggests that the imperial family agreed with him; the emperor, much more clearly, does so even after receiving the books in the sacred document already cited. Therefore, lest you be unaware of the state of our affairs, know that the Churches and the empire are united, and that, with our authority contributing and the providence of Christ the Savior assisting, they will from now on be increasingly joined together.]

Know also that the imperial household, its doctrine having been clarified, is living in great joy. And, to bring this page to an end, see that the saying concerning the Church among us, regarding all the heresies that contend against God, is also being fulfilled: “The house of Saul grew weaker and weaker, while the house of David grew stronger” (2 Samuel 3:2). These are our counsels, as from brother to brother. But if anyone wishes to be contentious, Paul will cry out through us to him: “We have no such custom, nor does the Church of God” (2 Corinthians 11:16).

## SERMON VIII. On Judas, against the heretics

[Note: By the name “heretics” he formally means the Apollinarists, but in reality Catholics who opposed him, whom he falsely accused of Apollinarianism.

It is reasonable to suppose that this sermon was delivered during Holy Week, when the account of Christ’s Passion was customarily read and expounded in the Church. In which year of Nestorius is uncertain; I nevertheless suspect that it was delivered in his third year, 431 in the Christian era, because it clearly contradicts the third, fourth, and twelfth of Cyril’s anathemas, which Nestorius received together with the synodical letters in December 430.

This may perhaps be connected with that saying of Nestorius reported by Socrates: “Do not boast, Jew; you have not crucified the Lord of glory.”]

1. I willingly ask those heretics who mix and blend the nature of the Godhead and the nature of humanity into one essence: who, in this passage, is the one who is betrayed and handed over to the Jews? For if a blending or mixture of the two has taken place, which one was seized by the Jews? God the Word, or the nature of humanity? Who appears to have been killed? I am compelled to use more elementary language so that what is said may be clear to everyone.

2. Tell me, please, to whom do the things that occurred apply? Is it to the nature of God, which you presume to confuse and blend by mixing the two together? Then God the Word is passible, though He has nothing in common with the flesh in the killing. Or was He led by the Jews to be killed?

3. Why, then, if according to you the two natures have been blended, did we recently hear Scripture recounting the power of the sacrament that the Lord handed down to His disciples, saying: “On the night on which He was betrayed, He took bread, gave thanks, and gave it to His disciples, saying: Take and eat of this, all of you, for this is my body”? Why did He not say: “This is my Godhead, which will be broken for you”? And again, when He took the cup and offered it, why did He not say: “This is my Godhead, which will be poured out for you for the remission of sins,” but rather: “This is my blood, which will be poured out for you for the remission of sins” (Matthew 26:28)?

Separate the nature, but join the union. Confess Christ the Son of God, but a twofold son—man and God—so that the passion may indeed be attributed to the human nature, while the release from the passion, which took place in the man who suffered, may belong solely to the Godhead.

## SERMON

[Note: It is not established at what time this sermon was delivered. I can affirm only that it was delivered after the controversies had arisen, and therefore in the year 429, during Lent. From its subject, however, someone might perhaps suspect that it belongs to the period when Nestorius was accused of holding the views of Paul of Samosata and Photinus, and many consequently withdrew from him; he appears to urge them to return to fellowship with him, after offering satisfaction, before they approach the altar.

Observe from this sermon, and from Cyril’s refutation of it, that the faith of the fifth century concerning the real presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist is plainly recognized. For what could be clearer than this question of Nestorius: “Whom, then, do we eat? The Godhead, or the flesh?” Or this statement of Cyril (*Book IV, Against the Contradictions*, chapter 4): “Just as that life-giving body of the Word Himself, which He made His own through a true union that surpasses both understanding and speech, is life-giving, so we too, who partake of that holy flesh and His blood, are entirely given life, since the Word dwells in us—not only in a divine manner through the Holy Spirit, but also in a human manner through that holy flesh and His precious blood.” Or these words that follow: “He dwells in us and makes us victors over corruption, descending into our bodies, as I have said, even through His own flesh, which is true food.”]

### IX. On the passage: “If you remember that your brother has something against you” (Matthew 5:23), as though against the heretics

1. Listen attentively to what is said: “Whoever eats,” He says, “my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” Remember that what is said concerns the flesh: “As the living Father sent me, me who am visible.” Surely I have not added the term “flesh” to give them grounds for complaining that I interpret me badly: “Whoever eats,” He says, “my flesh and drinks my blood.” Did He say: “Whoever eats my Godhead and drinks my Godhead”? Rather: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

And after other matters:

“But let us come to the point. ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.’ Remember that we speak of the flesh: ‘As the living Father sent me,’ me who appear; but perhaps I am not interpreting correctly. Let us examine what follows: ‘As the living Father sent me,’ and so forth. He speaks of the Godhead, I of the humanity. Let us see who is the perverse interpreter. ‘As the living Father sent me’: the heretic says that the Godhead was sent, and claims to confess that he is speaking of God the Word when he says, ‘As the living Father sent me.’ Therefore, according to them, this too must be understood in this way: ‘I, God the Word, live by the Father.’ After this, it seems to say: ‘And whoever eats me, he also will live.’ Whom, then, do we eat? The Godhead, or the flesh?”

I shall also mention the words that caused that scandal. The Lord Christ was speaking with them about His flesh: “Unless you eat,” He says, “the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you will not have life in yourselves.” Those who heard the sublimity of these words could not bear them; in their ignorance they thought that He was recommending cannibalism.

## SERMON X

[Note: We have supplied the title, compelled by the subject of the sermon itself. For the consubstantiality of the Holy Spirit is proved from the unity of operation, but in such a way that Christ is denied to have been glorified by Himself and is said to have been glorified by the Spirit, as though by one greater. For this reason the Ephesian Fathers condemned this fragment of the Nestorian treatise as blasphemous; and Cyril judged that it must be contradicted as something said foolishly, impiously, and audaciously against the doctrines of piety. Although what Nestorius says can be understood in a Catholic sense, it appeared to the Fathers to contain heresy—not because of the words in themselves, which are ambiguous and evasive, but because they considered them as uttered by their author, according to the ancient practice by which not persons in dogmas but dogmas in persons were condemned.]

As though against the Macedonians, but in reality against Catholics who defended the true incarnation.

[Column 0829C]

“I still have many things to say to you,” and so forth (John 16:12). And after a little:

“The operations of the Trinity are common, and are divided only with respect to the substances. Why, then, is the glorification of the Only-Begotten sometimes attributed to the Father, as in the statement, ‘My Father is He who glorifies me’ (John 8:54), while at other times it is attributed to the Spirit? For He says: ‘The Spirit of truth, who will glorify me’ (John 16:13). Sometimes it is assigned to Christ’s power, as it is written: ‘They went out and preached the word everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the signs that accompanied them’ (Mark 16:16).

“And there is clear evidence of this cooperation: the Son became man; the Father placed Him upon the throne; the Spirit honored Him with signs; the Son dwelt in the body; the Father commended Him when He was baptized; the Spirit formed Him in the Virgin.”

[Note: I would readily believe that this was said before the heresy was revealed, indeed at the very beginning, when, while fiercely attacking the Arians, he pretended to be Catholic, if three things did not restrain me: the opinion of the third party, the testimony of Marius Mercator, and the authority of the Ephesian Fathers. For the applause given by the people at these words—“For He Himself was both an infant and the Lord of the infant”—and Nestorius’s own correction or interpretation of the statement seem to me to indicate plainly enough that by that time a popular opinion had already arisen concerning Nestorius, namely, that he divided Christ into two persons. Moreover, Mercator vehemently attacks these very words, which provoked the applause, as though they contained the whole heresy and introduced a fourth person into the Trinity. Finally, once the chief notary had recited them, the Ephesian Fathers considered these words, like the others, equally dreadful and blasphemous, although Cyril praised them as Catholic while refuting Nestorius in his own words. Or have we perhaps forced into one sermon statements delivered at different times?]

## SERMON XI. Against the Arians, on Isaiah’s words: “A child is given to us, and a son is born to us” (Isaiah 9:6)

1. Truly great is the mystery of so great a gift. For this one who appears to be an infant, this one who now appears as newly born, this one who in bodily fashion needs swaddling clothes, this one who has recently been brought forth according to visible essence, is the Son, as Scripture teaches: the eternal Son, the Son who is the maker of all things, the Son who binds the dissoluble nature of creation with the swaddling clothes of His own power.

2. For the infant is God, possessing His own power. Far be it from you, Arius, to say that God the Word is under God’s power. We therefore recognize the humanity of the infant and the divinity; we preserve the unity of sonship in the nature of the Godhead and the humanity.

3. I say this so that you may know what a surpassing and supreme union of the Godhead existed even in the infant himself, when the Lord’s flesh was seen. For He Himself was both an infant and the Lord of the infant. You applauded the statement, but do not applaud it without careful attention; for I said that the same one was both the infant and the inhabitant of the infant.

4. Thus it may be demonstrated even more clearly who it was whom they worshiped and to whom the grace of the Holy Spirit led them: not to a merely ordinary infant visible to the crowd, but to a body ineffably joined to God.

5. Who can now behold so immense an ocean of kindness: nature ruling together with its creator, and the Godhead joined to humanity, commanding nothing without Him and judging no one without Him; caring for the living with Him in supreme providence, and raising the dead together with Him?

## LETTER

[Note: This is that celebrated letter which was once regarded as standing for the whole Council of Ephesus, so fully and clearly does it set forth the Catholic doctrine of the incarnation of the Word against Nestorius. The twelve anathemas appended to it, which the ancients called “chapters,” brought Cyril great unpopularity and caused the Catholics much difficulty for a long time, so that he had repeatedly to give satisfaction—whether to friends requesting an explanation or to opponents raising further objections. When peace between the Churches was being discussed and the faith was being established at the Council of Chalcedon, the Catholics were compelled to remain silent about them because of the offense they caused.]

In the manuscript codex of the convent of the Discalced Carmelites in Paris, the date is given as November 30, in the fourteenth indiction. Unless these chronological indications are corrected, they cannot agree. For Cyril undoubtedly wrote to Nestorius last in the year 430, and Nestorius received Cyril’s letter at Constantinople on December 7. If the codex is to be trusted, the letter would have been received at Constantinople seven days after it had been written at Alexandria—something altogether incredible.

Everything will easily fit if it is said that it was written at Alexandria on November 3 and received at Constantinople on December 7, and that the indiction, as is proper, is reckoned not from January, in which case it would be the thirteenth, but from September, in which month the fourteenth began.

It can conveniently be divided into three parts. In the first, the legation from the apostolic see is narrated in something like a historical account; in the second, the doctrine of the faith and the position opposed to Nestorius are set forth; the third contains the twelve anathemas.

In the latter two parts nothing could have been written with greater caution, skill, or rather prudence, so that if Nestorius had subscribed—as he was ordered to do—no one could fail to see that by those very words he had plainly contradicted and retracted what he had taught.

It can scarcely be read profitably unless the letter of Saint Coelestine, sent to Nestorius from the Roman synod, has first been carefully considered. It is found in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 18, and we shall reproduce it in our dissertation on the synods held in the case of Nestorius.

# Third Synodical Letter of Saint Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, addressed to Nestorius, Bishop of the Church of Constantinople, containing twelve chapters of anathemas

[Col. 0831B] To the religious and God-beloved fellow priest Nestorius: Cyril, and the synod assembled at Alexandria from the Egyptian diocese, sends greeting in the Lord.

1. Since our Savior plainly declares, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37), what shall we suffer, when your Reverence demands that we love you more than Christ, the Savior of all? For what benefit will this bring us on the day of judgment, or what defense shall we be able to find, if we maintain such prolonged silence concerning the blasphemies you have uttered against him? And if you alone were being harmed by teaching or holding these opinions, our concern would be less. But since you have scandalized the whole [Col. 0831C] Church and mixed among the peoples the leaven of an unprecedented perversity and a new heresy—not only among those present there, but among those established everywhere, since books of your expositions have been circulated throughout the world—what further account, or argument of excuse, can suffice for our silence? Or how could it not be necessary to remember Christ the Lord saying: “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword; for I have come to separate a man against his father and a daughter against her mother” (Matt. 10:34)? For when the faith is injured, reverence for parents is despised as useless and dangerous, and love toward children and brothers is avoided. Finally, even death after this life [B: “rather, death above life itself”] is chosen by pious men, so that, as it is written, they may obtain a better resurrection (Heb. 11:35).

2. Behold, then, we have now addressed you in writing for the third time, together with the holy synod assembled in the great city of Rome under the presidency of our most holy and venerable brother and fellow priest, Coelestine, bishop. We urge you to abstain from the corrupt and distorted doctrines which you are known both to hold [Col. 0832B] and to teach, and instead to receive the sound faith handed down from the beginning to the Churches by the blessed apostles and evangelists, who both saw these things with their eyes and are shown to have been ministers of the Word.

3. But if your Reverence delays doing this, in accordance with the deadline fixed in the letter of our most holy and venerable fellow priest Coelestine, bishop of the Roman Church, know that you have no share with us, nor any place or fellowship with the priests and bishops of God. For it is not lawful for us to disregard Churches so disturbed, peoples so scandalized, the most upright faith violated, and even the flock dispersed which you ought to have guarded—if indeed you had been, in our judgment, a lover of sound doctrine, piously following the footsteps of the holy Fathers.

[Col. 0832C] 4. Accordingly, all those whom your Reverence removed from communion on account of the faith, or deposed from their rank, whether laymen or clergy, we receive into our communion. For it is not right that those should be oppressed by your decrees who know how to think correctly and who, even while doing you good, wisely resisted you. You yourself took care to signify this in the letter which you sent to the holy bishop of the great city of Rome and our fellow bishop, Coelestine, [Col. 0833A] by writing the same thing.

[Note: [Col. 0832D] Although this letter is exceedingly famous and contains much material, both historical and doctrinal, we have appended only a few notes to it, since it must be examined more carefully again in the dissertation on the synods held in the case of Nestorius. This is undoubtedly the first letter Nestorius sent to Coelestine, in which the following words are read: “Finding no slight corruption of orthodoxy here among certain people, we daily employ both anger and gentleness toward the sick,” etc. From this it is clear that Coelestine sent Cyril the letters he had received from Nestorius, just as Cyril had entrusted to Possidonius the letters written to himself by Nestorius, so that he might carry them to Rome [Col. 0833C]. See these letters of Nestorius in the first part of the works of Marius Mercator.]

5. Yet it is not sufficient for your Reverence merely to confess the creed expounded at that time, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, by the venerable and great council assembled at Nicaea. For you have neither understood [Col. 0833B] nor correctly interpreted it, although you have uttered the same words in the sound of your voice, however orthodox they may appear. Rather, it follows that you must swear that you anathematize your polluted and profane doctrines, and that you hold and teach what all of us—bishops, teachers, and leaders of the peoples, throughout both East and West—believe and teach.

[Note: [Col. 0833C] Here, namely, where he says: “We ought to know that what has now come to mind is the creed of Nicaea, which nowhere dared to say that God the Word was born from the Virgin Mary,” and the other points which he pursues at length (Sermon 3, apparently Against the Macedonians and Arians). Consult the passage itself and understand why Cyril expounded the faith after first setting forth the creed of the Council of Nicaea: he refuted by that very means the fraud which Nestorius practiced upon the uninstructed.]

6. [Note: [Col. 0833C] This passage is obscure, and, so far as I know, no one has attempted to explain it. What letters sent by the Church of Alexandria should be understood? Those containing the appended anathemas? But those are precisely the letters with which we are now occupied. Or the first two? How can they be said to have been sent by the Church of Alexandria—that is, by the synod—when they are inscribed in the name of Cyril alone, rather than in the name of the Alexandrian synod, as is the third? Light will be shed upon the hidden truth in the dissertation on the synods held in the case of Nestorius.]

The Church has given its assent to the letters sent from Alexandria to your Reverence, both the holy synod assembled at Rome and all of us, as having been correctly and irreproachably composed. We have appended to this letter what you ought to hold and teach, and what it is appropriate for you to avoid.

7. For this is the faith of the apostolic and catholic Church, to which all orthodox bishops throughout East and West give their assent:

“We believe in one God, the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten as the only-begotten from the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον] with the Father—that is, of one substance with the Father—through whom all things were made in heaven and on earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down, was incarnate, and was made man; he suffered, and, rising on the third day, ascended into the heavens, from which he will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit.”

“But those who say, ‘There was a time when he was not,’ and ‘Before he was begotten he did not exist,’ and ‘He was made from things that did not exist,’ or who say that the Son of God is from another substance or essence, or is changeable and alterable—the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.”

8. Accordingly, following in every respect the confessions of the holy Fathers, which they uttered while the Holy Spirit spoke through them, adhering with equal steps to the intention present in their understanding, and walking along the royal road, we confess that the only-begotten Word of God himself, God, born from the very essence of the Father, true God from true God, light from light, through whom all things were made, whether in heaven or on earth, descended for our salvation and deigned to humble himself to the point of self-emptying. Having been incarnate and made man—that is, having received flesh from the holy Virgin and made it his own—he endured our birth from the womb, proceeding as man from a woman, without abandoning what he was. For although he came to be in the assumption of flesh and blood, even so he remained what he was: God by nature and in truth.

9. [Note: [Col. 0833D] Nestorius everywhere, and especially in his letter to the holy Coelestine, falsely attributed this to the Catholics: “They openly blaspheme God the Word as consubstantial with the Father, as though he had taken the beginning of his existence from the Virgin who is Christ-bearer [Χριστοτόκος], as though he had been built together with his temple and buried with the flesh,” etc. See also the title of the seventh sermon: “Against those who, on account of the union, either put God the Word to death or deify the humanity.” Cyril is aiming at both passages.]

Accordingly, we do not say that the flesh was changed into the nature of the Godhead, nor that the ineffable essence of God the Word was changed into the substance of flesh. For he is unconvertible and unchangeable, remaining continually the same, according to the Scriptures (Ps. 101:28). He was seen as a little child, or rather [Baluz.: “placed”] still in the cradle and lying in the Virgin Mother’s arms, yet as God he filled the whole creation, existing undivided with his begetter. For what is divine is understood without quantity or bulk and is contained by no boundaries.

10. Therefore, confessing that the Word was united to the flesh [Note: [Col. 0833D]

The Greek is καθ’ ὑπόστασιν, “according to hypostasis.” I again point out that this one expression was formerly an indisputable mark of orthodoxy [ὀρθοδοξία]. All the others can be twisted into erroneous meanings, and in fact have been distorted by the Nestorians; this one alone never could be. Hence it is astonishing how hateful it became to the heterodox, and how many accusations were brought against it. This is why, when the expression ἕνωσις καθ’ ὑπόστασιν, “union according to hypostasis,” had been omitted by Cyril and John in the exposition of the faith that they composed here and there while peace between the Churches was being established, that peace appeared suspicious to many Catholics, and John was said by his own people to have won the case. Cyril therefore had to clear himself, both before his friends—Acacius of Melitene, Successus, Valerian, and Donatus—and before his representatives in Constantinople, as though he had either agreed with the Easterners while they remained in their position, or had not defended the cause of the faith with sufficient courage because of some timid accommodation.

Moreover, what I said—that this expression was almost a fixed token of the faith—is proved by Cyril’s action. When he had written, “Confessing that the Word was united to the flesh according to substance,” he immediately proceeds to refute all the opinions of Nestorius, skillfully indeed, but nevertheless irresistibly.

It should be noted that the Roman translator departed from Cyril’s meaning, which Mercator understood. For the Greek words, “Confessing, then, that the Word has been united to the flesh according to hypostasis, we worship one,” etc., he translated: “Although we confess that the Word was united to the flesh according to hypostasis, nevertheless we worship one,” etc., as though the confession of union according to hypostasis appeared opposed to worshipping one, rather than as though it necessarily entailed it. Mercator’s translation is therefore much better: “Confessing, then, that the Word was united to the flesh according to substance, we worship one,” etc. This is why we have often said that, although Mercator yields to others in matters of Latin style, he nevertheless surpasses them in faith and understanding.]

according to subsistence [Col. 0835A], we worship one Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, not setting apart and distinguishing man and God as though they were joined to one another solely by a unity [Baluz.: “to themselves”] of dignity and authority. For this is merely a novelty of expression and nothing else. [Note: [Col. 0835C] He rejects the moral union, which they call τῆς ἀξίας καὶ αὐθεντίας ἑνότητα, “the unity of dignity and authority,” since it is not καθ’ ὑπόστασιν, “according to hypostasis,” but joins two independently existing persons only by a relation [σχέσει].]

Nor do we separately designate Christ as God the Word who is from God, and another Christ separately, who was born from a woman. Rather, we recognize one Christ alone, the Word of God the Father, together with his own flesh. Then, as man, according to us, he was anointed, although he himself bestowed the Spirit upon those worthy, and not according to measure (John 3:34), as the blessed evangelist John declared.

[Note: [Col. 0835D] He also rejects the opinion of two Christs, one from the Father and the other from the mother, joined only by homonymy [ὁμωνυμίᾳ]. Cyril often attacks this elsewhere—not as though Nestorius had ever expressly stated it, but because it necessarily follows in reality from his opinion concerning a relational union [ἕνωσις σχετική], however much he himself disguises it.]

11. [Note: [Col. 0835D] He also refutes a third form of relational union [σχετικὴ ἕνωσις], namely, pure indwelling [ἐνοίκησις], or the dwelling of the divine Word in the man by which the man is not actually God but merely belongs to God, or is God-bearing [Θεοφόρος], an expression pleasing to Nestorius. Cyril opposes to this form of union another, which he calls union according to nature [ἕνωσιν κατὰ φύσιν], and says is like the union by which the soul is joined to its own body, leaving aside, as theologians point out, the imperfections involved.]

Nor do we say that the Word of God dwelt in an ordinary man who was born from the holy Virgin, lest Christ the man be thought to possess God as an inhabitant. For although the Word dwelt among us (John 1:14), and it is said that all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in Christ (Col. 2:9), we do not understand that, having become flesh, [Baluz. adds “not”] he dwelt in it in the way in which he is said to dwell in the saints, nor have we attempted to define that such an indwelling took place in him. Rather, being united according to nature, without being wholly changed into flesh, he made such an indwelling his own as the soul of a human being is believed to have in its own body.

12. Therefore Christ, the Son and Lord, is one, [Note: [Col. 0835D] In Greek: ὡς συνάφειαν ἁπλῶς, etc. Among the Greeks συνάφεια means either the coupling of male and female; or, in Basil, the association of married persons and the communion of civic life; or, in Chrysostom, the joining of limbs; or finally, in Cyril, the fitting together of things capable of being connected, and παράθεσις, that is, juxtaposition. Whatever meaning the word may bear, it is more suitable for concealing heresy than for expounding the faith. Hence Cyril everywhere attacks the term sharply as being filled with poison. Indeed, Theodore of Mopsuestia, and Theodoret himself while he was still in error, compared the conjunction of the two natures in Christ to the union of spouses.]

not as though by some conjunction consisting in a unity of dignity and authority which a man has toward God. For equality of dignity alone cannot unite natures. Peter and John, for example, are equal to one another in dignity, and for this reason they are shown to be apostles and holy disciples; nevertheless, neither is one with the other. Nor do we understand the mode of conjunction according to association or connection, for this is insufficient for a NATURAL unity. Nor do we understand it according to the effect of participation, as when we too, clinging to the Lord, are one spirit with him (1 Cor. 6:17).

[Col. 0836A] 13. Rather, we avoid the name “conjunction” as unsuitable for signifying the mystery of unity.

14. [Note: [Col. 0836D] He argues against Nestorius’s statement concerning Christ, whose Word made him Lord and God, as though Christ himself were not God and Lord. For the relative expression “whose,” like the oblique cases, has the power to establish a distinction, even opposition, between the extremes related by the expression. Thus, although God is truly Lord of the humanity, he is not Lord of Christ unless two persons are asserted in Christ.]

Nor do we assert that God the Word of God the Father is the God or Lord of Christ, lest we once again divide the one Christ, the Son and Lord, more openly into two, and fall into the crime of sacrilege by making that one God his own God and Lord. For, as we said above, God the Word was united to the flesh ACCORDING TO SUBSTANCE. As God, he is indeed the God of all and ruler of the universe. Yet he is not servant or Lord to himself, since it is foolish, or rather impious, to think or say this. Although he called God his Father, since he too is God by nature and is from his essence, nevertheless we are in no way ignorant that, while remaining God, he also became man, existing under God according to the law proper to human nature. But how could he himself be God or Lord to himself?

Therefore, as man, insofar as this appropriately corresponds to the measure of his self-emptying, he declared that he was with us under God. In this way also he was made under the law (Gal. 4:4), although he himself promulgated the law and existed as God, the lawgiver.

15. [Note: [Col. 0836D] The words which he is careful not to utter are Nestorius’s, from the first, or rather the seventh, sermon. He rejects, as something dreadful, a mere unity according to homonymy and worship [καθ’ ὁμωνυμίαν καὶ προσκύνησιν], since such a unity entirely dissolves Christ into two persons.]

We are also careful not to say of Christ: “Because of the one who assumed, I honor the one who was assumed,” or, “Because of the invisible one, I worship the visible one.” But even more dreadful than this would be to add: “The one who was received is called God together with the one who received him.” For whoever says these things again divides into two Christs the one who is one, establishing the man separately on one side and God likewise separately on the other. He plainly denies the unity according to which one is not worshipped together with another, nor is one called God together with another; rather, one Christ is understood, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, to be honored with one act of service together with his own flesh.

16. [Note: [Col. 0836D] Here the confession that God suffered is open, as is the refutation of the calumnious Nestorius and the defense of Proclus. Nestorius had slandered the Catholics as though they asserted that the Word suffered by nature or in his divinity; Proclus had been brutally beaten by Nestorius because of his confession of the faith.]

We also confess that the very one who was born from God the Father as the only-begotten Son, God, although according to his own nature he was beyond suffering, nevertheless suffered in the flesh for us, according to the Scriptures (1 Pet. 4:1), and was in the crucified body of his own flesh, IMPASSIBLY appropriating the sufferings. “By the grace of God he tasted death for everyone” (Heb. 2:9), handing over his own body to death, although by nature he himself is life and the resurrection of the dead.

For, in order by ineffable power to trample down death and to become the firstborn from the dead in his own flesh, and the firstfruits of those who sleep, [Baluz. adds: “and to make a way”] for human nature’s return to incorruption, “by the grace of God,” as was said above, “he tasted death for everyone” (ibid.), and, rising on the third day, he stripped hell.

17. Therefore, although it is said that the resurrection of the dead came through a man (1 Cor. 15:21), we understand this to mean the Word who became man, the one who is from God, and that through him the dominion of death was destroyed [Col. 0837B] (Heb. 2:14). He will come at the appointed times, as the one Son and Lord in the glory of the Father, to judge the world in righteousness (Acts 17:31), as Scripture testifies.

18. Accordingly, we necessarily add this as well. Proclaiming the death according to the flesh of the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, and likewise confessing his resurrection and ascension into heaven, we celebrate in the Churches the unbloody service of sacrifice. Thus also we approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, becoming participants in the body and precious blood of Christ, the Redeemer of us all—not as though we received ordinary flesh, God forbid; nor as though we received the flesh of a sanctified man joined to the Word according to a unity of dignity; nor as though it belonged to one possessing a divine indwelling [Col. 0837C]. Rather, we receive it as truly life-giving and as having been made the proper flesh of the Word of God [Baluz. omits “of God”]. For, since he exists naturally as life, because he is united to his own flesh, he declared it life-giving.

Therefore, although he says to us [Baluz. adds “coming to us”], “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood” (John 6:53), etc., we must not regard it as the flesh of merely one human being among us. For how could human flesh be life-giving according to its nature? Rather, it is the flesh truly made his own who, for our sake, both became and was called the Son of man.

19. We do not divide the sayings which our Savior uttered in the Gospels between two subsistences or persons. For the one and only Christ is not double, although he is understood to have come together into an undivided unity from two different realities [Col. 0837D], just as a human being, consisting of soul and body, is not rather two but one from both.

Accordingly, we rightly understand that human and divine sayings alike were spoken by the one Christ. When he speaks in a manner most worthy of God concerning himself, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9), and, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), we understand his divine and ineffable nature, according to which he is one with his Father because of their one and the same substance, existing as his image, character, and radiance of glory [Col. 0838A] (Heb. 1:3).

But when, without in any way dishonoring the measure of human nature, he addresses the Jews: “Now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you” (John 7:1), we no less recognize God the Word, who is in the likeness and equality [Baluz.: “equity”] of the Father, even within the measures of his humanity.

If it is necessarily believed that he who exists by nature as God became flesh, or rather a man endowed with a rational soul, what reason is there for anyone to be ashamed of these sayings, if he uttered sayings proper to a man? If he were to reject speech appropriate to a man, who, according to us, compelled him to become man? But since for our sake he mercifully and willingly humbled himself to self-emptying, for what reason would he avoid sayings worthy of self-emptying?

We therefore attribute all his sayings in the Gospel to one person, to the one subsistence—namely, that of the incarnate Word—because, as it is written, the Lord Jesus Christ is one.

20. Scripture calls Christ “the apostle and high priest of our confession” (Heb. 3:2), as one who offers to God the Father the confession of our faith, which is continually offered by us to him and through him to God the Father. Again, we say that the one who is by nature the only-begotten Son from God is the one to whom the name and office of priesthood belong, and we assign neither the name nor the office of priest to another man besides him.

“For there is one mediator between God and human beings” (1 Tim. 2:5), and a reconciler to peace, offering himself for us to God the Father as a fragrant offering (Eph. 2:5). Therefore he said: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire; burnt offerings and offerings for sin did not please you; but you prepared a body for me. Then I said, ‘Behold, I come; in the heading of the book it is written concerning me, to do your will, O God’” (Heb. 10:5).

He offered his own body, not for himself but for us, as a fragrant offering. For he does not need offering or sacrifice for himself, since as God he is free from every sin. But if all have sinned and lack the glory of God (Rom. 3:23), since we have become especially prone to excess through mutability and human nature has been weakened by sins, whereas he was not so, and therefore we need his glory, who could still doubt that the true Lamb was sacrificed for us and on our behalf?

But whoever says that he offered himself both for himself and for us cannot escape the charge of impiety, since he committed absolutely no fault and in no way sinned. What offering, then, would he need, when he had committed no crime of his own for which, had it existed, an offering might appropriately have been made?

21. When he also says of the Spirit, “He will glorify me” (John 16:14), we rightly understand this and confess that the one Christ and Son received glory from the Holy Spirit—not as one needing another’s glory, for his Spirit is neither better nor superior to him, but because, while performing wondrous works to demonstrate his divinity, he used the power of his own Spirit and is therefore said to be glorified by him.

This is like someone saying of human beings that one person’s virtue or discipline glorifies him. Although the Spirit exists in his own subsistence and his personal property is understood according to the fact that he is Spirit and not Son, nevertheless he is not alien to the Son. For the Spirit is called the Spirit of truth (John 16:13), and Christ is the truth (John 14:6). Therefore he proceeds FROM HIM IN THE SAME WAY AS FROM GOD THE FATHER.

Finally, this same Spirit, performing glorious miracles through the hands of the holy apostles, glorifies the Lord Jesus Christ after he has ascended into heaven. For Christ, believed to exist by nature as God, worked powers through his own Spirit, and therefore said: “He will receive from what is mine and announce it to you” (John 16:14). The same Spirit is not said to be wise or powerful through participation in another, since he is perfect in every respect and entirely lacks nothing good. He is believed to be the Spirit of the Father’s power and wisdom—that is, of the Son—and therefore is shown in reality and in subsistence to be power and wisdom itself.

22. [Note: [Col. 0839D] From the fact that the Word was united to the flesh according to hypostasis [καθ’ ὑπόστασιν], he establishes the central point of the question, as it was commonly debated: whether the holy Virgin was God-bearer [Θεοτόκος]. He establishes it in such a way as to answer the two calumnies which Nestorius directed against the Catholics, especially against Proclus and Eusebius. The first was that they held what Photinus held, namely, that the Word derived the beginning of his existence from the Virgin; the second was that the Word needed this second birth in order to exist.]

Therefore, because the holy Virgin bodily gave birth to God united to flesh according to subsistence, we confess that she is the Mother of God [Dei genitrix]. This does not mean that the nature of the Word received from the flesh the beginning of its existence. For “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), and he is the creator of the ages, coeternal with the Father, and the creator of the universe.

Rather, as we said above, because he united human nature to himself according to subsistence and endured bodily birth from that very womb, this does not mean that he necessarily needed this birth on account of his own nature—a birth which took place at the end of the ages—but that he might bless the firstfruits of our substance. When a woman gave birth to him united to flesh, the curse pronounced against the entire human race might cease, and our bodies might no longer be consigned to death.

And by himself undoing also what was said, “In sorrow you shall bear children” (Gen. 3:16), he might demonstrate to be true what had been foretold in the prophet’s voice: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Cor. 15:34). And again: “God has taken away every tear from every face” (Apoc. 7:17).

For this reason we say that, in accordance with the divine economy, he also blessed marriage itself when, at Cana of Galilee, he deigned to be present after being invited with the holy apostles.

[Note: [Col. 0840D] Cyril appears to have read Nestorius’s first sermon against the Pelagians and to be aiming at it here, since this passage from Genesis and the praise of marriage are treated at length by Nestorius.

No observation is made here concerning the anathemas, since the many matters worthy of note belong entirely to the dissertation on the synods, where it will be shown which treatise of Nestorius each one attacks.]

23. We have been taught to hold these things by the holy apostles and evangelists, by every divinely inspired Scripture, [Col. 0839D] and also by the blessed confessions of the Fathers, which are supported by the truth. It is now appropriate for your Reverence to agree with all these things and to consent without any deceit. What your Reverence must anathematize is appended to this letter.

[Col. 0840A] I. If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is truly God, and therefore that the holy Virgin is the Mother of God—for she bore according to the flesh the Word of God who became flesh—let him be anathema.

II. If anyone does not confess that the Word of God the Father was united to flesh according to subsistence, and that there is one Christ together with his own flesh, the same at once God and man, let him be anathema.

III. If anyone divides the substances in the one Christ after the union, joining them only by a connection based on dignity, or even on authority or power, and not rather by the coming together effected through natural unity, let him be anathema.

IV. If anyone divides between two persons or subsistences the sayings contained in the apostolic and evangelical writings, which the saints speak concerning Christ or which he himself speaks concerning himself, assigning some to a man understood separately apart from the Word of God, and assigning others, as worthy of God, solely to the Word of God the Father, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0840B] V. If anyone dares to say that Christ the man is God-bearing [Θεοφόρον], that is, bearing God, and does not rather confess that he is truly God, as one Son by nature, according to the fact that the Word became flesh (John 1:14) and likewise shared, as we do, in flesh and blood (Heb. 2:14), let him be anathema.

VI. If anyone says that the Word of God the Father is the God or Lord of Christ, and does not rather confess that the same one is at once God and man, because the Word became flesh according to the Scriptures, let him be anathema.

VII. If anyone says that Jesus the man was assisted by the operation of God the Word, or was energized [ἐνεργούμενον] by him, and attributes to him the glory of the only-begotten as though it belonged to another existing separately from him, let him be anathema.

VIII. If anyone dares to say that the assumed man must be worshipped together with God the Word, glorified together with him, and called God together with him, as one with another—for the additional syllable [“together”] always compels this meaning—and does not rather worship Emmanuel with one act of supplication and render him one glorification, according to the fact that the Word became flesh, let him be anathema.

IX. If anyone says that our one Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Holy Spirit as though he had used an alien power through the Spirit and had received from him the ability to act against unclean spirits and to perform divine signs among human beings, and does not rather say that it was his own Spirit through whom he completed the divine signs, let him be anathema.

X. Divine Scripture recalls that Christ became the high priest and apostle of our confession (Heb. 3:2) [Col. 0841A]: “He offered himself for us as a fragrant offering to God and the Father” (Eph. 5:2).

Therefore, if anyone says that our high priest and apostle became not the Word of God himself when he became flesh and, according to us, man, but rather a man other than him, specifically born from a woman; or if anyone says that he offered himself as an offering both for himself and for us, and not rather for us alone—for he had no need of an offering, since he knew no sin at all—let him be anathema.

XI. If anyone does not confess that the flesh of the Lord is life-giving and the flesh proper to the Word of God the Father himself, but says that it belongs to another joined to him by dignity, or as though he possessed a divine indwelling, and does not rather confess, as we have said, that it is life-giving because it was made the flesh proper to the Word who can give life to all things, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0841B] XII. If anyone does not confess that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, tasted death in the flesh, and became the firstborn from the dead, according to the fact that as God he is life and the giver of life, let him be anathema.

# Letter of Nestorius, Bishop of Constantinople, [Note: [Col. 0841C]

Nestorius wrote two letters to Coelestine concerning the case of the Pelagian bishops who, having been expelled from the West, had taken refuge in Constantinople; we published them in their proper place. This third letter, which is wholly concerned with the case of Nestorius, now appears for the first time and sheds much light on the history, so that it may rightly be regarded as a reliable standard by which many things may be examined that even learned men have either expressed obscurely or not entirely accurately.

It must have been written toward the end of November, namely after the emperor had announced the general synod but before Coelestine’s decree-bearing letter to Nestorius had been brought to Constantinople. For, first, it mentions the synod announced by the emperor. The decree concerning the indiction is dated the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, Augusti, that is, 19 November in the year 430. In the second place, it does not mention the letter of the holy Coelestine, which certainly could not have been omitted if it had already been received.

Since that letter was sent to Nestorius by four bishops from the Alexandrian synod on Sunday, which was the seventh day before the Ides of December, this letter must have been written during the interval from 19 November to 7 December. See the historical preface.]

to Pope Coelestine.

1. I have learned that the most honorable Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, [Note: [Col. 0841D]

See the notes on Cyril’s letter to his representatives in Constantinople, and add to what is said there the following passage from Cyril’s letter to Acacius of Beroea concerning the slanderers suborned by Nestorius: “Turning against the hostile enemy, he does not cease gathering together certain magicians and men of desperate character, and suborning them to scatter lies about me among the populace” (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chap. 22).]

Nestorius, moreover, when he attempted to divert the storm hanging over his own head onto Cyril—or rather, when he wished to preside over the judgment that was to be exercised against himself—and when he understood that, because of the condition of his see, he could not arrogate this to himself, since the authority established in the synod at Constantinople was not accepted at Rome, and since it was not lawful for a greater see to be judged by a lesser one, induced the emperor to convene a synod. He hoped that, in the absence of the archbishop of Old Rome, either through the emperor’s favor or through the compliant silence of the humble John of Antioch, he would preside over it, with Cyril placed among the accused. Indeed, he had long boasted that he would preside, as we understand from Cyril’s letter to his representatives at Constantinople.]

because of the written accusations brought against him to us, frightened and seeking hiding places for himself, in order to avoid the sacred synod that was to be held on account of these very written accusations, meanwhile devised certain other verbal stratagems and embraced the expressions *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος, “Mother of God”) [Col. 0841C] and *Christotokos* (Χριστοτόκος, “Mother of Christ”). Of these, he admits the one but excludes the other from the Gospels at one moment, and then again admits it—namely, *Christotokos*—according, I believe, to an excessive subtlety of prudence.

2. I do not resist those who wish to use the expression *Theotokos*, provided that it is not uttered for the confusion of the natures according to the madness of Apollinaris and Arius. [Note: [Col. 0842C] Marius Mercator might seem to suggest to someone that Nestorius used the expression *Theotokos* only after being admonished by John of Antioch; but the history of the period teaches otherwise. For in his fifth sermon, and in the letters that he sent to the holy Celestine on behalf of the Pelagians, Nestorius protested that nothing prevented anyone from applying the name *Theotokos* to the blessed Virgin, provided either that the impiety of Apollinaris and Arius was avoided or that the holy Virgin was not therefore thought to be a goddess. Accordingly, the admonition mentioned by Mercator must be understood as referring to the reproach made against him, both publicly by the faithful and privately by his friends.]

Nevertheless, I do not doubt that this expression, *Theotokos*, yields to that expression, *Christotokos*, as having been uttered by angels and evangelists. [Note: [Col. 0842D] Namely, in those passages where, when the Lord’s birth is discussed, he is called Jesus, Savior, and Christ, and where the blessed Virgin is called the mother of Jesus and of the Lord, and so forth. Nestorius argued above all from this: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ,” etc.; “of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ” (Matthew 1:1, 16).] Unless I were saying this to Your Holiness, who already knows it, I would need a long and extensive discussion of this very matter.

3. But even apart from this, Your Beatitude also knows perfectly well that, if we suppose two opposing factions to be standing against one another, and if one of them uttered only the expression *Theotokos*, while the other uttered only the expression *Anthropotokos* (ἀνθρωποτόκος, “Mother of Man”), and if each faction drew the other over to its own confession, so that, if it could not accomplish this, it would risk falling away from the Church, then the person appointed to handle this matter, having concern for both factions, would have to remedy the danger threatening both sides by means of the expression handed down by the evangelists, which signifies both natures.

For, as I have said, the expression *Christotokos* moderates their assertion: it removes the blasphemy of Paul of Samosata, namely, the claim that Christ, the Lord of all, was merely a man; but it also drives away the wickedness of Arius and Apollinaris.

4. [Note: [Col. 0842D] Namely, the second letter, which begins: “Although the insults against us contained in the remarkable letters,” etc. From this we learn that the two letters read at the Council of Ephesus, session 1—one from Cyril to Nestorius and the other from Nestorius to Cyril—were sent to Celestine by both writers, each fearing that his letter might be altered by his opponent.]

I also wrote these very things to the most honorable bishop of the Alexandrians, as Your Beatitude can learn from the copies that I have attached to this letter of mine, or from those that were written to us by him.

[Col. 0842C] 5. [Note: [Col. 0842D] The expression “without excuse,” together with the emperor’s sacred letter to the metropolitans, indicates clearly that the synod was convened at Nestorius’s request, and that even the form of the summons was communicated to him.]

It also pleased the most devout emperors [Baluz. [Col. 0843A] omits “most devout emperors”], with the Lord’s help, to summon without excuse a synod of the entire world, for the investigation of other ecclesiastical matters. [Col. 0844A] For I do not think that the ambiguity of the terms will require a difficult inquiry or will prove an impediment

[Note: [Col. 0843A]

The abrupt manner in which the letter ends seems to indicate that something is missing, at least the customary formal conclusion, which was appended to the other two letters to Celestine and to the others addressed to various recipients: “To all the brotherhood in Christ,” etc.

### Short Dissertation on the Opinion of the Most Illustrious Marca, Who Holds that the Apostolic See’s Sentence against Nestorius Was Suspended by Theodosius and that the Earlier Acts of the Council of Ephesus Were Lawfully Rescinded

The passage at which we have arrived, and the matter under discussion, require that we examine somewhat more carefully what has been written, partly by certain learned men and partly by the most illustrious Marca, concerning Theodosius’s action in the case of Nestorius (*On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire*, Book IV).

I therefore think that four questions must be debated: by whom the synod of Ephesus was convened; at whose request or prompting; what the reason for convening it was; and whether the Fathers exceeded the limits prescribed to them by the emperor.

As to the first question, there are those who believe that it was convened by Celestine, the supreme pontiff, and that the imperial letters were nothing other than executory instruments of an apostolic mandate, and therefore merely *tractoriae*.

They argue this from several considerations, admittedly general ones, but ones that can scarcely persuade the learned, since they are drawn from writings that, even if they are not spurious, are at least not free from suspicion. They are refuted, first, by the letter that we have before us: for the summons is said to have been decreed before it became known to Celestine. Next, they are refuted by the entire sequence of the Acts, in which the Fathers, gathered from almost every part of the world, repeatedly testify that they assembled at the emperor’s command, without mentioning an apostolic mandate even once. They are also refuted by the testimony of all the historians of that age, as well as of every other kind of writer: they commonly remain silent about a command from the apostolic see, while speaking openly of an imperial command. Finally, they are refuted by the confession of the supreme pontiff himself, who, when writing to the emperor through his three legates sent to Ephesus, does not mention his own mandate but does mention the imperial command. “In accordance with our priestly office,” he says, “we have devoted our service, insofar as we are able, and to this synod which you ordered to be held we present our presence in the persons whom we have sent.” Moreover, Theodosius the emperor mentions his own command everywhere in the four sacred letters—whether those sent to the metropolitans in the provinces or those directed to the synod—yet nowhere mentions an apostolic command.

[Col. 0843D] Someone, however, raises three objections. First, that Pope Gelasius, in his first Roman synod, testified that the Council of Ephesus had been convened with Celestine’s consent. Second, that the Fathers say in their reports that they assembled according to the canons. Finally, that Hincmar wrote that general synods had always formerly been held by order of the apostolic see and through imperial convocation.

But Gelasius does indeed say that Nestorius was condemned with Celestine’s consent; he does not say that the synod was convened with it. Again, the Fathers’ statement that they assembled according to the canons means precisely that they followed the custom of the Church—a custom observed at the Council of Ephesus just as at Nicaea and Constantinople—Theodosius the Younger following the example of Constantine, who convened Nicaea, and of Theodosius the Elder, who convened Constantinople. Finally, Hincmar left a record of what was done in his own age and in neighboring times; the question here concerns the custom of the fifth century and of earlier periods.

Theodosius therefore convened the council and summoned the Fathers to Ephesus for the day of Pentecost. But at whose prompting, or at whose request, did he do this? That was the second question.

Christian Lupus wrote not long ago (*Scholia on the Canons of the Councils*, vol. I, p. 388) that Julian of Eclanum, the leader of the Pelagians, had requested this from the emperor, at the time when, in the name of himself and of other bishops expelled from Italy, he was pressing an appeal from the apostolic see to an ecumenical synod.

I myself do not know where that author learned or inferred this. But I do not doubt that Mercator overturned such a [Col. 0844B] fiction or conjecture by the very title of his *Memorial against Julian*. For he reports that these bishops were expelled from the imperial city immediately after the time when the memorial was presented, that is, around the end of the year 429. How, then, could Julian, in the following year, have attempted or even carried out so important a matter at Constantinople?
