Moreover, Julian is not mentioned at all either in Theodosius’s sacred letters, in the Acts of the council, or in the reports of either the orthodox or the schismatics, except in the letter written by the holy synod to the holy Celestine after the legates’ arrival at Ephesus, when through them the Acts of the Roman synod were received, read, and approved. Indeed, there is no discussion of the Coelestians except as men whose case had already been entirely prejudged.

Once this singular opinion has been rejected, the common opinion of all is that the council at Ephesus was convened at the urging and request of Nestorius. He had certainly been threatening to do this ever since the written accusations against Cyril had been received. From that same time Cyril himself had desired it; indeed, perhaps he arranged for it to be demanded through Basil and other monks especially devoted to him, by means of a petition that they presented.

Nestorius certainly sought and obtained it through the counsel of his flatterers. But afterward he deeply regretted that he had taken advantage of the ruler’s readiness and favor for this purpose. For by this means he did not evade the sentence of the apostolic see, which was the one thing—or at least the principal thing—he had hoped for; rather, he experienced it as all the more severe, insofar as it received greater weight from the authority of more than two hundred bishops.

Now, as to the third point in the question, the reason for convening the synod was, if I am not mistaken, twofold: one reason openly displayed, and another hidden in the mind. The first is easily learned from Theodosius’s sacred letter: namely, the peace of the Church, the confirmation of the faith, and the reconciliation of the two dissenting sees.

Opinions differ concerning the second. The most illustrious Marca holds approximately the following: Nestorius, after he had been condemned by two synods, the Roman and the Alexandrian, unless he repented within ten days, seems to have appealed to the emperor, and to have obtained from him a rescript by which the sentence of both synods was either suspended until judgment could be rendered by the ecumenical synod that Nestorius was arranging to have convened, or entirely annulled, with the case restored to its original condition (*On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire*, Book IV, chap. 4, no. 1).

I believe that the most learned prelate supposes that Nestorius was informed of the sentence of both synods before he either complained to the emperor or had a council summoned at his request. For unless he holds this view, I do not see how he could infer from this event the point over which he is chiefly concerned: namely, that rulers had sometimes, after summoning a synod to settle controversies, suspended the execution of an earlier sentence issued in an ecclesiastical judgment; and that they did not act unjustly in doing so, since the decree of suspension was neither judged unjust by the Fathers of old nor rejected, but rather willingly accepted and entered into the Acts as the rule of judgment.

After citing a substantial portion of the sacred letter, he says: “I certainly do not see how Theodosius could have decreed this suspension unless we allow a place for the petition of Nestorius, who complained that he had been condemned without a hearing, and, if one wishes, for his appeal, which prompted Theodosius to convene the council, so that meanwhile, while the appeal was pending—or, if you prefer, while the case was being restored to its original condition—nothing would be changed. Yet so far from the Fathers’ having raised a complaint about this suspension at the Council of Ephesus, they rather ordered the rescript to be inserted into the Acts and took full account of the reason for the suspension,” etc.

But the opinion on which this very learned man wished to base his reasoning is contradicted partly by Theodosius’s own sacred letter, partly by Mercator’s authority, and partly by Nestorius himself. The sacred letter is dated the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, while Mercator writes that the letters of the synods were delivered to Nestorius on the seventh day before the Ides of December. Yet when Nestorius wrote to the supreme pontiff after the council had been summoned, he wrote as though he had learned nothing about the sentence of the apostolic see.

Therefore Nestorius did not appeal to the emperor after he had lawfully learned that he had been condemned by the synods, nor did Theodosius suspend the sentence of the apostolic see by an edict. For no one, I believe, lawfully appeals from a judge’s sentence before that sentence has been lawfully announced, nor can an appeal be maintained until the sentence of which one complains has been produced.

I admit that Nestorius requested the council’s convocation through private petitions to Theodosius, who was favorably disposed toward him. He did not request a judgment from the emperor acting according to the requirements of law. Therefore, since the sentence of the apostolic see was not announced until after the synod had been summoned, it ought rather to be regarded as having been forestalled than suspended by an edict—if we are to speak precisely.

Since, however, mention has been made of Theodosius’s sacred letter, I think it will not be beside the point to investigate *more precisely* (ἀκριβέστερον) the opinion of the most illustrious Marca, who believes that the Fathers at Ephesus exceeded the limits prescribed to them in two principal respects by the imperial letter brought by Candidianus to the synod already convened by the emperor, and that therefore the Acts preceding the arrival of Count John were rightly rescinded.

The first point is that, in Candidianus’s absence, they completed the judgment against Nestorius. The second is that, although the emperor had declared to the synod that no civil or criminal case, even if ecclesiastical, was to be brought against any bishop, either in the synod or in a public court, but that all such matters were to be summoned to Constantinople, nevertheless the subsequent condemnations of Cyril, Memnon, John, and the Orientals had violated the law that had been issued.

These two matters—I do not conceal it—formerly caused me no small difficulty when I examined the records of Ephesus more attentively, and, much as I wished to do so, I was never able to accept them as credible.

As to the first point, Candidianus was undoubtedly present on the very first day on which the Fathers assembled, and he read aloud in the public meeting the emperor’s mandate. I admit that he was not present when the matter under discussion was doctrine and the case of Nestorius connected with that doctrine—but this happened through his own fault. He was not expelled by the Fathers, as he later dared to lie to John of Antioch; rather, he withdrew voluntarily, when the Fathers, following the emperor’s mandate, were unwilling either to postpone the synod or to heed his appeal. By fraud, in order to favor Nestorius, he urged that the beginning of the synod be deferred until John’s arrival. He was certainly not unaware that the bishop of Antioch was deliberately delaying on the road, according to the plan of Count Irenaeus, who had gone to him carrying instructions from the entire faction.

Moreover, neither Nestorius, when he complained to the emperor about the Fathers of the synod, nor the Oriental schismatics, when they protested to the same emperor about the proceedings before their arrival, nor the emperor himself, when he criticized the synod’s actions, alleged Candidianus’s absence. This is a strong indication that Candidianus himself did not dare to report to the emperor that he had been expelled in the manner he falsely claimed.

I am therefore readily persuaded to believe that the words of a man who was thoroughly mendacious—just as they once deceived the Orientals when they heard them—also recently deceived the most illustrious Marca when he read them.

As for the imperial law that was violated, after Cyril, Memnon, and the others condemned had been acquitted—which was the second point of the accusation against the Fathers of Ephesus—I do not think it should be examined before the actual words of the imperial edict have been set forth. They read as follows:

“Above all, the same most magnificent Candidianus has been instructed to observe with the greatest care that he allow no other ecclesiastical controversy whatsoever, wherever it may have arisen or been initiated, which does not pertain to the proposed examination of doctrine, to be brought forward before the ambiguity of all the matters now called into question has been resolved and those matters that contribute to the investigation of truth have been examined with the most exact judgment and have reached an outcome consistent with the orthodox religion. Moreover, Your Piety has also been informed that it has seemed good to Our Serenity that no pecuniary or criminal case whatsoever be brought against anyone in your sacred synod or even in the public court of the Ephesians. If any such matter should arise or occur to anyone, We wish its complete investigation to be reserved to Our great city.”

From this it is clear that the emperor distinguished causes of three kinds: first, causes of faith, which he orders to be treated before all others; second, ecclesiastical causes, wherever they may have arisen or been initiated, which he forbids to be brought forward before the matter of faith has been settled; and finally, pecuniary or criminal causes, the investigation of which he forbids both to the synod and to the court of Ephesus.

It is also clear from the fact that ecclesiastical causes are forbidden to be brought forward before the settlement of the faith that they are immediately permitted to be brought forward after the faith has been settled. Since, then, no causes can more properly be called ecclesiastical than those concerning the judgment of bishops on account of erroneous doctrines, there is no doubt that the judgment of Cyril, Memnon, and the others was not forbidden even by the words of the imperial letter—words to which Marca added whatever he pleased.

Furthermore, even if the case of Cyril, Memnon, John, and the Orientals had not been of this ecclesiastical kind, but had pertained to those pecuniary or criminal causes whose investigation Theodosius reserved to the great city, it would not for that reason follow that anything had been done beyond the limits prescribed by the emperor. For if there was any prohibition, it is contained in the sacred letter brought by Palladius; but the condemnations of Cyril, Memnon, John, and the Orientals took place before that letter was brought.

Cyril and Memnon were deposed by the Orientals on the fifth day after Nestorius had been deposed by the synod, that is, on June 27. The sacred letter brought by Palladius, however, since it was nothing other than a rescript responding to Candidianus’s report, was not issued at Constantinople until Candidianus’s report had arrived there. That report was sent from Ephesus on the day after Nestorius’s deposition, that is, on June 23.]

to the discussion of the Divinity of the Lord Jesus.

## Letter of Nestorius, Replying to Coelestius, Translated from Greek into Latin by Marius Mercator

[Col. 0845A]

1. To the honorable and most religious presbyter Celestius: Nestorius sends greetings in the Lord.

Do not take offense, venerable brother, at enduring these things from those who ought to carry out what is imposed, especially from those who assert the truth and refuse communion with the polluted or defiled. For the sufferings endured by the holy men who existed before our time were pleasing to them, while the sufferings themselves were temporary and the truth eternal.

Thus John the Baptist, when he reproved Herod for his sin—although Herod was a king—was condemned to death by beheading; but he was not afraid, for he had Christ as his head, which could not be cut off. In the same way Paul and Peter were also killed. And what more need be said? This has always been the way things have happened, as devotion has advanced through various trials.

2. Therefore, do not, by falling away from the truth, betray it to prudent persons, namely those of the same orthodox confession (for the letters sent to the bishops by the Western and Alexandrian councils, together with many replies, have made our position clear to us). Perhaps, with the Lord cooperating, something useful will come to the Churches of the right faith.

[Col. 0848A] We greet all the brotherhood.

3. And in another hand: “May you remain safe, steadfast in spirit, and pray greatly for us; may you be granted to us, most religious brother.”

[Note: [Col. 0847A]

There can be no doubt that this sermon is genuine, since Mercator mentions it elsewhere, something from it seems to have been reported by Baronius, all its circumstances agree perfectly, and the reason for its delivery, which is contained in the title, is clearly related in the first session of the Council of Ephesus.

Peter, presbyter of Alexandria and chief of the notaries, said: “Not only were the letters that Celestine, the most holy and most sacred bishop of the Roman Church, had written to the most reverend Nestorius sent and delivered to him, but also those that Cyril, the most holy and most devout bishop of the Alexandrian Church, and the entire synod of Egypt had sent to him through Theopemptus, Daniel, Potamon, and Macarius, most religious bishops. Therefore, I ask that Theopemptus and Daniel, most religious bishops who are present here, be questioned on this matter.”

Flavian, bishop of Philippi, said: “Let Theopemptus and Daniel, our most religious fellow ministers who are present, explain whether they delivered such letters.”

Theopemptus, bishop of Cabasa, said: “On Sunday, when the assembly was being held, we went up to the episcopal palace, and there, in the presence of the entire clergy and almost all the illustrious persons standing by, we delivered to Nestorius the letters about which we are speaking.”

Daniel, bishop of Darnis, likewise confirmed the same.

Flavian, bishop of Philippi, said: “Did he then answer the letters?”

Daniel, bishop of Darnis, said: “Then he answered us that we should come the following day and meet with him privately. But when we returned, he shut off the entrance and did not deign to give us an answer.”

Theopemptus, bishop of Cabasa, said: “After receiving the letters of which we have just spoken, he arranged that we should have a discussion with him on the following day. We therefore departed; but when we returned the next day, he did not admit us, nor did he give satisfaction concerning the letters. Instead, he publicly proposed in the assembly the same doctrines as before, and doctrines even worse than those. Indeed, he not only taught these things before the letters were delivered, but taught much worse things after he received them, and to this day he does not cease teaching them.

The sermon was delivered on Saturday, the day on which assemblies were customarily held frequently, as is evident from the case of Proclus, who ordained Thalassius, when, among other senators, he had come to the bishop in the church on a Saturday. It was delivered, I say, on Saturday, the thirteenth day of December. For the letters of the apostolic see and of Cyril were delivered to Nestorius by four bishops of the Egyptian diocese on Sunday, as is clear from the report of the bishops themselves; they were received on the seventh day before the Ides of December, as Mercator records; and the sermon was delivered six days after the letters had been received, as the same Mercator testifies.

It is therefore necessary to hold that it was delivered on December 13. For in the year 430 the Dominical Letter was E, and consequently the month began on Monday; thus the seventh day was Sunday and the thirteenth was Saturday.

Furthermore, although Nestorius raged especially against Cyril, in the violence of his spirit he also attacked John of Antioch, despite his being a friend. Yet he did so in such a way that, although he attempted to refute the substance of the admonition, he nevertheless followed its advice and publicly confessed *Theotokos*.

There is no speech from which one could learn more about matters pertaining to Nestorianism. Almost every word has been carefully selected, whether to conceal his opinion, to slander his opponents, or to deceive unwary hearers—as that slippery heretic actually accomplished, according to Mercator, and indeed according to the outcome itself. See the notes that were needed for almost every passage.]]

## Sermon XII

Delivered in the church in which he received the letters of Celestine, bishop of Rome, and the denunciation of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, on the seventh day before the Ides of December [Note: [Col. 0848B] Baluzius gives the eighth day before the Ides instead of the seventh and explains the correction as follows: “We have emended it in accordance with the authority of the ancient books, since previously it read ‘the seventh day before the Ides.’ How important this emendation is was stated in the first volume of the new collection of the Councils, p. 422; there is no need to repeat it here.” EDIT.], in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, Augusti, six days after he had received those same letters.

1. [Note: [Col. 0848B]

While Nestorius was presiding, a presbyter had instructed the people according to custom, speaking either generally about the duties of charity, in order to prepare their minds for the bishop who was about to preach, or specifically about providing a meal for the poor, and also for strangers and friends, following the example of Christ, who received his disciples at the mystical supper when he was about to take leave of them.

Nestorius took up the presbyter’s words (no. 1). After praising both the speaker and charity—while maliciously criticizing the beginning of the letters he had received either from Cyril or from John of Antioch—he first set forth the doctrine of the Incarnation, concerning the two natures and the indivisible union of each (nos. 2 and 3). Then, without naming him, he raged against Cyril (nos. 4 and 5), whom he challenges to a contest of disputation. He complains spitefully against John of Antioch that a dispute is being made with him over one expression that anyone may use, provided that he avoids a heretical meaning (nos. 6 and 11).

Next he attempts to clear himself of the charge of agreement with Paul of Samosata and Photinus (nos. 12 through 19). Afterward he discusses at length *Theotokos* and *Christotokos* (nos. 22 and 31). Finally, driven once again into his intemperate language, he provokes Cyril (no. 27). At the end he urges his hearers patiently to tolerate those who wish to use the expression *Theotokos* (no. 32). This sermon may rightly be called a compendium of the entire Nestorian doctrine.

The beginning of Cyril’s letter was as follows: “Since our Savior openly declares: ‘Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me’ (Matthew 10:37), what will become of us, who are asked by Your Religion to love you more than Christ, the Savior of all?” etc.

John, however, began his letter in this way: “I have sincerely disclosed my opinion of Your Piety, through my lord and magnificent Count Irenaeus in every respect, to your affection, without any deception whatsoever. And because, having used a genuine purification, I am, as I think, free from every suspicion before you, I have decided henceforth to give counsel freely and frankly to your sincerity. From what I am about to advise, you will be able to derive no small proof of our candor toward you, and at the same time to perceive how greatly that charity which is according to God concerns us.

Those who pursue this charity obey the divine laws; but those who neglect it and devote themselves to impostures destroy themselves by their own weapons before they destroy those whom they attack.”]

Our preceding teacher set before us a sweet table of charity. It has neither the bitterness of fraternal hatred, nor the poison of envy, nor the rust of feigned brotherhood. So sweet are the things of charity that the Lord of all also loves them. God loves charity as the innate goodness of his own benevolence; and from it he establishes beneficial necessities for all peoples.

Because many things divided human friendship, God implanted necessities among unwilling people that would join them together in mutual friendship. The lands of the Dalmatians possess one kind of agricultural produce; the Goths possess an abundance of their native resources; the Spanish land has its own fertility; Africa possesses another broad and wealthy expanse of land. This arrangement exists so that each person may receive from his neighbor what he lacks, and so that the needy person, seeking elsewhere what he does not possess, may through necessity be bound in friendship with his neighbor.

[Col. 0849B] 2. Therefore the Lord of all also put on our nature, the garment of Divinity that can never be removed, the inseparable clothing of the divine substance, the mirror of the Lord of all, which, although it had lost its own dignity of nature, even though he should be angry ten thousand times upon hearing—

[Note: [Col. 0849B]

The passage is corrupt, for “Manichaeus” has been substituted for “Marcellus,” and “natural use” for “temporal use.” For Manichaeus is nowhere read as having held the opinion about Christ attributed to him here; he said that Christ’s flesh was phantasmal and not a true garment. Marcellus, however, as the ancient writers report, maintained in his delirium that human nature had been assumed by the Word for a time, but would be laid aside after the judgment of human beings.

The passage should therefore be emended as follows: “Even though Marcellus should be angry ten thousand times upon hearing it, he did not receive this garment for temporary use, but forever, so that he might make it sit at the right hand of his Divinity.”

There are several reasons for the emendation, most especially those drawn from the history of Marcellus. But, in my opinion, the most certain reason is that Nestorius, as was his custom, imitated Chrysostom at this point as well (*Homily 11 on John*, on the words “And he dwelt among us”). Chrysostom says:

“Consider for me the fearful and mysterious dignity of that mystery. For he dwells in this tabernacle perpetually; he put on our flesh, not as one who would again abandon it, but so as always to have it dwelling with him. For if this were not so, he would certainly not have deemed it worthy of the royal throne, nor would he, while bearing it, be worshiped by the entire heavenly host,” etc.]

Manichaeus did not receive this garment for natural use, but forever, so that he might make it sit at the right hand of his Divinity; [Note: [Col. 0849D] Nearly the same passage is found in Cyril’s thirteenth excerpt. “Who now could behold so immense an ocean of benevolence: nature reigning with its creator, and Divinity joined to humanity; commanding nothing without it, judging no one without it, caring for the living with it in supreme providence, and raising the dead together with it? Heretics weaken and overthrow all these hopes, which are governed for all by the strongest and most benevolent Lord.] he gives nothing to the living without this garment of his; he does not judge the dead without it; he willed the kingdom of his Divinity to be one with it.

[Note: [Col. 0849D] Baronius reports these words—or words very similar to them—under the year 428, no. 32, but does not say where he obtained them. He does, however, show by the note he adds, etc., that he borrowed them from a longer sermon.

Since he wished to produce something that might in some degree support Socrates’ claim that Nestorius did not share the views of Paul of Samosata, he writes as follows: “For the defense of Socrates, it may be suggested that the slippery heresiarch Nestorius, knowing that the name of Paul of Samosata was ill-regarded in the Church and rejected by all the orthodox, pretended likewise to detest that Paul and to profess the Council of Nicaea, in order by this means to win over the minds of his hearers. Hence it happened that Nestorius himself uttered the following against Paul: ‘So may Paul of Samosata perish, who deliriously taught us that the Lord’s humanity was naked,’ etc.”

Baronius had, I think, read the works of Marius Mercator, which had been brought from Heidelberg to Rome, while he was accustomed to examine the codices of the Vatican library, of which he was curator. For a copy was transmitted from there both to us and to certain others. But that Palatine codex was disfigured by so many errors and interspersed with so many lacunae that scarcely a few of the passages reported by Baronius could have been extracted from this sermon.

Garnerius, in his annotation elucidating this passage, cites a fragment from Baronius’s *Annals* in which Nestorius is read as having uttered the following against Paul of Samosata: “So may Paul of Samosata perish, who deliriously taught us that the Lord’s humanity was naked.” Garnerius therefore concluded that, in Baronius’s view, the codex of Mercator brought from Heidelberg had been placed in the Vatican library.

But apart from the fact that the words reported by Baronius differ greatly from those reported by Mercator, that Palatine codex had not yet been brought to Rome while Baronius was alive. BALUZ.]

Let Paul of Samosata remain stupefied at his teeth, for he deliriously declares that the Lord’s humanity is naked of Divinity; he fabricates that it is alone, apart from Divinity, although it is always joined and united with it, and although it can do the same things, equally, as God. For God “gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).

### 3

And lest anyone be astonished to hear of a kingdom belonging to the flesh together with the Divinity, he anticipated this through the Scripture of the Spirit, demonstrating that he who dwells in the dwelling-place is one, and showing from whom and whence the honor surrounding that which is seen and appears increased:

“He bestowed upon him,” he says, “the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess to God that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (ibid.). [Col. 0850B]

He did not, he says, diminish the divine substance in relation to that which is invisible—the honor surpassing all things—for it is demonstrated how the Son is loved by the Father; for there is one Son, both the visible and the invisible; one Christ, both he who makes use and that which he uses; the natures are two, but the Son is one.

> **Note:** [Col. 0850D] What Catholic words, apparently, could fail to deceive in this way? They certainly deceived the hearers when they were spoken, as Mercator records. Hence they called sycophants and envious persons those who accused Nestorius, and they openly burst out in these words: “Behold, he said ‘one’; what more do you want?” See Mercator’s passage, where Nestorius’s deception is exposed.

### 4

Why do you turn the speech into a slander? Why do you secretly shoot me with golden arrows?

> **Note:** [Col. 0850D] This was maliciously charged against Cyril, first by Nestorius and afterward by Nestorius’s followers: that he conducted his affairs through gifts and drew bishops over to his side by promises. Theodoretus, speaking for the Easterners—or rather in the name of the Easterners, says: “Know that, seeing the Cyrillians deceive everyone, so to speak, by tyranny, fraud, flattery, and gifts, we often beseeched the most pious emperor,” etc. (*Second part of the Acts of Ephesus*, near the end). And shortly afterward: “Thus the Egyptian will be able to blind everyone with his gifts,” etc. And in his letter to Rufus of Thessalonica: “Since they were deprived of piety, they necessarily devised another power for themselves, namely, the strongholds of men, thinking that by pouring out money they would overcome the faith of the Fathers” (*Last letter of the schismatics to their associates, Second part of the Acts of Ephesus*, in the proceedings against Cyril). Moreover, the plunderer of the poor spitefully throws his own crime back at the most holy man. The people openly accused Nestorius of this offense, as did the monks in their petition to the emperor, and Cyril himself repeatedly, although Cyril’s reputation was harmed by the wealth that he left at his death to his relatives and that Dioscorus thought should be reclaimed; indeed, Theophilus, Cyril’s predecessor and uncle, was also burdened by suspicion of avarice. See the letters of Athanasius (*Act 3 of the Council of Chalcedon*), Socrates (*Book VI, chapter 7*), and Baronius (*under the year 445*), where he observes that wealth left by prelates—even holy ones—to their nephews, from the Church’s revenues, had always been a cause of vexation, whether justly or unjustly.

> “What against me.” This clause seems to have to be deleted, since it is merely another version of the preceding sentence. **Baluzius.**

Why do you secretly send golden arrows against me? [Col. 0851A] Let us test our own contests; let us produce, one against the other, the grounds of our life and religion.

> **Note:** [Col. 0851B] He alludes to the pamphlets given to him against Cyril, mentioned in the observations; then to Cyril’s letter to his clergy residing at Constantinople; and also to Nestorius’s final letters to Saint Celestine. He likewise alludes to the complaints made against him, both publicly and privately before the emperor, discussed in the observations on the beginning of the seventh sermon.

> **Note:** [Col. 0851C] By his arts he had tried to win the confidence of the court, and had almost drawn Pulcheria, together with her brother the emperor and her virgin sisters, to his side, as he himself boasts vaingloriously (*at the end of the second letter to Cyril*). This caused Cyril to write two books on the mystery of the incarnation, one to the emperor and the other, separately, to Pulcheria and the royal sisters. I say separately, since the other work commonly read in the published manuscripts of the Council of Ephesus is not Cyril’s, but Theodotus’s and also Atticus’s, as will be shown in the dissertation on Cyril’s books. For Nestorius’s devices for deceiving the imperial household and the magnates of the court, see the monks’ petition to Theodosius (*First part of the Acts of Ephesus*, chapter 30, no. 4).

The emperor is pious; the queens love God. Be a brave man in debate: what prevents you from entering into discussion? Why do you try to bring disturbances with bestial roars? I too know how to cry out with the prophet: “I am ready, and I am not disturbed” (Psalm 118:60).

### 5

Moses also taught me not to be disturbed, since Egyptian despair received proof in the prophet mentioned above; nor did you terrify the once-blessed Flavian when you sent letters in a tyrannical spirit.

> **Note:** [Col. 0851C] He complains of the two Antiochene bishops, Meletius and Flavian, and of the two Constantinopolitan bishops, Nectarius and John Chrysostom, who suffered harsh treatment from the Alexandrians Peter, Timothy, and Theophilus. He uses this to prove that, having been made bishop of Constantinople from an Antiochene presbyter, he was persecuted by Cyril of Alexandria not on account of his own deserts, but as though because of the native jealousy or hatred of one people toward another. What Meletius suffered from Peter and Timothy, and what Flavian, Nectarius, and John suffered from Theophilus, may be seen in the writers of those times.

> **Note:** [Col. 0851D] He throws back at Theophilus the charge of a certain overbearing tyranny, on account of which Flavian was accused before the emperor by a Roman bishop at Theophilus’s instigation. Thus Theodoretus says (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 23): “When the Roman bishops—not only that admirable Damasus, but also Siricius after him, and Anastasius, the successor of Siricius—had inveighed vehemently against the emperor, saying that he ought to suppress those who attempted to exercise tyranny against him, but to grant impunity to those who sought through tyranny to overturn the laws of Christ, the emperor again summoned him and tried to compel him to go to Rome. Then the most wise Flavian answered him freely, to the greatest praise of all: ‘If anyone, O emperor, accuses me of professing a faith that is not entirely sincere and sound, or says that I lead a life unworthy of the priesthood, I will gladly submit to the sentence pronounced by those very judges whom I shall use. But if they are disputing about the see and the episcopate, I will neither go to judgment with them nor oppose those who desire to obtain that dignity; rather, I will willingly yield and resign the episcopate myself. Therefore, give the Antiochene see to whomever you wish.’ But the emperor, greatly admiring this greatness of spirit and wisdom, ordered him to return to his homeland and shepherd the Church entrusted to him. After a long interval, when the emperor again came to Rome, the bishops once more summoned him on the same charge—namely, that he had not restrained Flavian’s tyranny. Then the emperor ordered them to say what sort of tyranny it was; for, he said, ‘I myself shall take Flavian’s side and plead his case at the trial.’”

> **Note:** [Col. 0852B] I think he is speaking of the letters that Theophilus wrote to Flavian after the Council of Capua had entrusted him with the investigation of the case of Evagrius and Flavian, the Antiochene bishops who were in dispute, summoning Flavian to judgment. But Flavian evaded the summons by appealing to the emperor, as Ambrose testifies (*Letter 78*).

nor did you disturb Meletius, who came before him and is now numbered among the saints.

> **Note:** [Col. 0852C] Almost all the Egyptians, they say, opposed Meletius and favored Paulinus; Athanasius and Peter also did so for a time, following the example of the Roman pontiffs. Nor was Timothy ever reconciled, not even at the time of his death, although both were at Constantinople. Such is the testimony of the writers of those times.

Amphilochius, as is believed, praised Meletius in a funeral oration, as did Gregory of Nyssa, whose words are these: “A new apostle has increased the number of apostles for us,” etc. Five years later Chrysostom praised him in a panegyric at Antioch, relating that the citizens loved the holy man so greatly that they gave the name Meletius even to their infants and not only had his image painted in their homes but also engraved it on the bezels of their rings.

You possess and give what you have—“the good man brings good things out of his good treasure” (Matthew 12:35)—and you gave blessed Nectarius a taste of such gifts of yours.

> **Note:** [Col. 0852C] He governed the Church of Constantinople partly during the time of Timothy and partly during that of Theophilus. What trouble he caused those Alexandrian bishops is sufficiently clear; what he suffered from them remains obscure.

> **Note:** [Col. 0852D] Whoever has the leisure may consult Nicephorus, who, drawing on the history of Nicetas the philosopher, relates how Cyril, as soon as he assumed the Alexandrian Church, was advised by a letter from Atticus to restore John’s name to the sacred diptychs; how he replied harshly and in the opposite sense to Atticus, who had been compelled by necessity to do precisely that; how he was likewise strongly urged by Isidore of Pelusium in letters to do the same, but still did nothing, since his mind had not yet settled after the former disturbances; and finally how, terrified by certain nocturnal visions, he convened a synod at which he honorably entered John’s name in the sacred records.

I say nothing of John, whose ashes you now, against your will, venerate with adoration.

> **Note:** [Col. 0852D] Garnerius has in the margin: “Correct to ‘whom you adore.’” Baluzius adds at the foot: “See whether this passage may be useful against those who deny that honor should be shown to the relics of the saints.” **Editor.**

> **Note:** [Col. 0852D] In a letter to Scholasticus, the eunuch of the emperor Theodosius, Nestorius himself testifies that he cares little for episcopal honor and that he would very readily lay it down if by that means the strengthening of the orthodox faith could be secured. It is preserved in the *Synodicon against the Tragedy of Irenaeus*, chapter 16. **Baluzius.**

No concern for the episcopate troubles me, nor do I have any discussion about it; so long as I breathe, I support sound doctrine. [Col. 0853A]

### 6

But I shall remove from them their elegant and specious pretext.

> **Note:** [Col. 0853C] He refers to the words of the letter of John of Antioch (*First part of the Acts of Ephesus*, chapter 25, section 4), in which John admonishes him to calm the disturbances of the Church by a public confession of Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*, “Mother of God”)”: “Come, do not hesitate to add the name that has rightly been used, written, and pronounced by many Fathers concerning the matter that you rightly hold; and do not continue to reject a word that expresses a pious and correct conception of the mind. For no ecclesiastical teacher has ever rejected this name, Θεοτόκος. Those who have used it are numerous and highly distinguished; those who have not used it have never accused of error those who did use it. Certainly, when we are driven by a superfluous curiosity directed only toward the vain opinions of heretics and stubbornly reject the name whose meaning we rightly hold, we seem to do nothing other than consider it unimportant to offend severely, rashly, and without any benefit, the consciences of our brothers. For if we do not accept what is offered by the meaning of the name, it remains that we fall into the gravest error—or rather, that we deny the ineffable economy of the only-begotten Son of God. Once this name has been removed, or rather once the meaning of this name has been rejected, it immediately follows that he who undertook that marvelous dispensation for our salvation is not God; and then that the Word of God neither emptied himself nor, lowering himself into the form of a servant, displayed to the human race an ineffable greatness of goodness.”

“They say he does not say Θεοτόκον, that is, ‘mother of God,’ and this is the whole matter that they raise against us. For no one,” they say, “who follows the true glory of the faith has ever avoided this expression.” There are many indications there of doctrines, especially those belonging to the sect of Apollinaris and to Arius or Eunomius. If you investigate, each one of them called the holy Virgin Θεοτόκος, that is, “mother of God.”

> **Note:** [Col. 0853D] A related passage is cited by Cyril from Nestorius’s second treatise to Proclus. It reads as follows: “If you were to use Deipara—‘God-bearer’—in simple faith, I would have no objection to the expression while investigating the meaning of the word. But because I see that, under the pretext of honoring blessed Mary, you are confirming the blasphemy of the heretics, I cautiously fortify myself against the utterance of the word, since I regard the danger concealed in the expression with suspicion.”

“To make this clearer and easier for all to understand: those who followed Arius, Eunomius, and Apollinaris, and all the choirs of people belonging to that sort of family, sought to introduce the title ‘Mother of God,’ so that, through a mixture and the failure to distinguish the two natures, nothing of what is lowly would be understood as spoken of the humanity, and an opening would thereby be made for them against the Divinity itself—as though everything were said of one entity, not according to the dignity resulting from the union but according to the nature itself. For there is one Christ and one Lord; but in Christ—in the only-begotten Son, I mean—the name Christ and the name Son are spoken now of the Divinity, now of the humanity, and now of both humanity and Divinity.”

### 7

But attend, I ask you, to what is being said, so that you may have a ready defense against these arguments and against the very bait that they attach to the hook when they speak. Do you know that Apollinaris said this? Do you know that this expression, Θεοτόκον, arouses the greatest applause among the followers of Arius? Do you know that it is also frequently used by Eunomius?

“Yes,” you say, “but I utter this expression not according to their meaning” [Baluzius: “the Son,”]. I praise your denial, but meanwhile I accuse you concerning what you say: that this expression alone preserves the truth. For there are people who say Θεοτόκον and yet, according to your own confession, are certainly heretics.

But since those who say Θεοτόκον derive from it a mixture or blending of the two natures, so that what is lowly does not appear to have been said of the substance of the flesh, nor what is exalted to have been spoken of God and Lord of all, condemn those who say “mother of God” according to the meaning of Apollinaris and Arius. And I cry out with you: Θεοτόκον; but I say Θεοτόκον and also add “mother of a human being,” that is, ἀνθρωποτόκον (*anthropotokos*). [Col. 0854A] For the heretic does not tolerate this being said, because of the division that also results from the distinction of the words.

### 8

> **Note:** [Col. 0854D] I believe he wishes to appear to comply with the admonitions of John of Antioch, who urged a public confession of Θεοτόκος, and to follow the example proposed to him by the friend of their common teacher, Theodore of Mopsuestia, who had publicly retracted a similar statement. But in order to lessen the embarrassment of the retraction, he invokes an example far more illustrious—namely, the Apostle Paul, who, for the sake of the οἰκονομία (*oikonomia*, “economy”), also adopted Jewish rites.

Therefore, in order to surpass even their elegant and rather palatable speeches, let us say Θεοτόκον. For Paul also knew how to do such things, lest divisions arise through some ostensible righteousness, while he was preaching grace and boldly arguing against the uselessness of the law. But when he came to Jerusalem, he was taught by the apostles that he ought to accommodate himself to those dwelling there, so that divisions would not arise in the Church—something that appears to possess the semblance of piety.

What, then, does he do? He adopts observance of the law, so that he might both be purified and shave his head, doing everything for the edification of the Church. Later, explaining this very matter in his instruction on the establishment of the Churches, he said: “To the Jews I became as a Jew, so that I might gain the Jews; to those who are under the law, as though I were under the law, although I myself was not under the law, so that I might gain those who are under the law; to those who are without the law, as though I were without the law—not being without the law of God, but under the law of Christ—so that I might gain those who are without the law. I became all things to all, so that I might gain all” (1 Corinthians 9:20).

### 9

Therefore, if you proclaim Mary Θεοτόκον not according to the disease of Apollinaris, concealing Apollinaris’s rage beneath a Catholic persona, confess with me what all Catholics say. But this is proper to Catholics who utter this expression, Θεοτόκον: they also pronounce the holy Virgin ἀνθρωποτόκον, that is, “mother of a human being.”

> **Note:** [Col. 0854D] Nestorius employed many expressions to conceal the heresy that was tolerated among Catholics because the expressions were used in a Catholic sense. They were not tolerated in Nestorius because he used them in a heretical sense. Such expressions include Χριστοτόκος (*Christotokos*, “mother of Christ”), ἀνθρωποτόκος (*anthropotokos*, “mother of a human being”), συναφεια (*synapheia*, “conjunction”), ἀνάληψις (*analepsis*, “assumption”), ἕνωσις τοῦ προσώπου (*henosis tou prosopou*, “union of person”), and so forth. These matters are treated fully in the dissertation on the Nestorian heresy.

### 10

She is Mother of God, not on account of Divinity bare of humanity [Col. 0855A], but on account of God the Word united to the temple.

> **Note:** [Col. 0855C] There is more than one reason why Nestorius more frequently calls Christ’s humanity a “temple” than by any other name. First, he thought that this name was better suited to explaining his heresy; for it could not be rejected, since Christ himself used it, according to the Evangelist, when he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”—but “he was speaking of the temple of his body” (John 2:19). Second, it was suitable for signifying the mode of union that they wished to be a pure ἐνοίκησις (*enoikēsis*, “indwelling”), since God dwells in a temple. Third, it seemed appropriate for explaining a σχετική ἕνωσις (*schedikē henōsis*, “relative union”), by which the Word and the human being would be worshiped with one veneration, since God and the temple are worshiped with one religious devotion. Fourth, the passage in John appeared, as the Nestorians themselves thought, to express both the distinction of the natures and the non-operation of one in the other, even though there were no ἕνωσις καθ’ ὑπόστασιν (*henosis kath’ hypostasin*, “union according to hypostasis”).

But she is the mother of a human being, that is, ἀνθρωποτόκος, on account of the temple that is naturally consubstantial with the holy Virgin.

> **Note:** [Col. 0855C] He strove with all his strength to call the Virgin Χριστοτόκος, so that, by an otherwise Catholic expression, he might conceal his heresy. For although he said in good faith, before Evagrius (*Book I, chapter 7*), that he had introduced the expression Χριστοτόκος for Mary—“so that I might not sin in either direction, either by asserting that Christ was not subject to death or, by inclining to the other side, by depriving him of immortality”—the defenders of the Catholic faith nevertheless resisted him vehemently, because they understood Nestorius to signify by the name Christ a mere human being. Accordingly, Χριστοτόκος had no other force of signification in Nestorius than ἀνθρωποτόκος.

Although to call her Χριστοτόκον, that is, “mother of Christ,” is likewise nothing other than to confess what is common to the Divinity and the humanity.

And Paul teaches this, who, proclaiming one and the same person, says: “Jesus is the same yesterday and today, himself for the ages” (Hebrews 13:8).

> **Note:** [Col. 0855D] Here again we find the supremely Catholic word “PERSON” uttered in a heretical sense. In speaking of the union, Nestorius shunned no Catholic expression except this one: ἕνωσις καθ’ ὑπόστασιν, “union according to hypostasis.” Whoever deliberately avoids it is in reality afflicted by Nestorius’s disease, or at least under suspicion of it—and not without good reason. This is said with reference to Theodoretus, whose faith will be examined according to this rule in its own separate dissertation, and also with reference to certain bolder men of our own age who do not approve what the entire Church approves.

### 11

Let this opportunity of theirs, which appears to have the semblance of reason, meanwhile be dissolved and removed. Confess both, calling the holy Virgin Θεοτόκον and likewise ἀνθρωποτόκον. But do not call her Θεοτόκον alone [Baluzius adds: “For this is what Apollinaris cries out”], for Arius preaches and venerates this. Instead, add the expression equally belonging to Catholics, which safeguards the understanding of “mother of God”:

“The holy Virgin is Θεοτόκος according to the unity, and ἀνθρωποτόκος, that is, mother of a human being, according to the corresponding nature.”

Thus you will proclaim what belongs to the apostles and prudently avoid what belongs to the heretics—especially what belongs to Paul of Samosata and Photinus, whom you pretend to know but entirely fail to understand.

### 12

For Paul and Photinus do not know the Divinity of the Son. You, beloved, ought to know these things, so that you may not be carried away by what the aforementioned men say. Paul and Photinus, the most foolish of men, do not know the two natures of the Son; they do not know God and man.

They disagree with one another, and I disagree with Paul in this: he says that Christ is merely a human being and that he has a beginning only from the time when he was born of the Virgin. [Col. 0855C] But I resist you here precisely so that you will not dare to make the Divinity, which is eternal, contemporary with the flesh.

> **Note:** [Col. 0856C] This passage is reported by Marius Mercator in the appendix to the contradiction of the twelfth anathema, part XII. Nestorius, as I have observed with particular care, inveighs especially forcefully—and even with abusive language—against three heretics, Marcellus, Paul, and Photinus, in order to prove that he is alien both to their company and to their opinion. As far as I know, Mercator alone had charged him with this association of the three.

### 13

Why do you accuse him as though he were asserting Paul’s doctrine, when he overturns what belongs to Paul? Who is it here that asserts Paul’s meaning? Is it the one who says that the Divinity is contemporary with the body, or the one who says that the essence of the Divinity in the Son was begotten from the Father before the ages?

### 14

This, then, is the very evil sect of Paul of Samosata. Photinus differs from it in this respect: not because he says that the Son possesses Divinity, but because he says that there is another Word besides the one who came in the last times; for he says that there is a Word apart from the temple.

### 15

But it is necessary to speak more plainly, so that you may recognize more clearly and openly the disease of each sect.

Paul and Photinus differ from one another in this: one of them says that Christ is merely a human being; the other does indeed speak of the Word, but does not confess that this Word is God. Rather, he says that this Word is at one time called by the name of the Father and at another time called by the name of the Word. Hence he also calls it Λογοπάτορα (*Logopatora*), that is, “Word and Father,” or, if one may say so, “Word-Father,” perversely applying to this purpose, according to the wickedness of his understanding, what is rightly said in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

> **Note:** [Col. 0856C] Garnerius corrects this in the margin to “Father and Word-Father.” **Editor.**

> **Note:** [Col. 0856D] I think Nestorius took those words from some writing of Photinus, of which not even the memory seems to survive. Photinus held this opinion about the Word: when it was extended toward creatures and thus brought forth, it was called the Word, and for that reason he also called it “uttered” or “operative”; but when it remained in itself and was, as it were, gathered together, it was simply God. Thus, for this heretic, God working in creatures was the Word, while God remaining in himself was simply God. Hence he said that the rational principle of the Word was temporal, and therefore that the Word, insofar as it is the Word, received its beginning from the Virgin. For this reason he denied that God had been joined to humanity, but said that the Word, insofar as it is the Word—that is, insofar as it is a certain divine operation—had been joined to it. Nothing could be more confused than this man’s fantasies.

“You see,” he says, “that he sometimes calls God the Word ‘God’ and sometimes ‘Word,’ as though extended and gathered together.” But he does not introduce God the Word as having become man. For he does not know the Divinity of Christ; he does not know that the divine substance assumed a human being; he entirely fails to recognize the Divinity of the Word existing before the ages.

### 16

Photinus therefore differs from Paul in this respect. Sabellius differs from Photinus in the following: Sabellius says Υἱοπάτορα (*Yiopatora*), calling the very Son the Father and the very Father the Son, whereas Photinus says Λογοπάτορα (*Logopatora*).

Photinus, as I said, does not possess the Divinity of the Word. Sabellius, however, does speak of the Son, but does not say that the substance of the Son exists in its own distinctness. Hence he says Υἱοπάτορα, that is, that the very Father is the Son, because he dreams of one substance.

But for this reason divine Scripture, guarding against their disease, sets forth the incarnation of the Word: “In the beginning,” it says, “was the Word” (John 1:1), and the rest that follows. Then, descending [Baluzius: “ascending”], it says: “And the Word became flesh” (ibid. 14), so that it might show the substance of the Son existing in its own distinctness, apart from the substance of the Father.

Finally, Photinus, driven into a corner, is compelled to speak of the Word, but he does not confess this Word to be the Son. The Spirit, foreseeing this, entered the heart of the Evangelist so as to fortify the souls of Catholics. And what does it say? “And the Word became flesh.”

### 17

Behold, for the moment you have recognized the proper substance of the Word. How, then, may we also recognize the Only-begotten, since according to Photinus he is not the Father, nor Λογοπάτωρ, but God the Word and Son?

“And the Word,” he says, “became flesh and dwelt among us”—that is, he dwelt in our nature.

“And the Word became flesh” is also an excellent designation of the expression itself, so that the vanity of all empty anxieties may be removed from every side: “And the Word became flesh”; he assumed, he says, our nature.

Then, so that the goodness and wonder might be greater, he names the assumption of humanity from the lowlier part of nature, saying that the Word became flesh. This does not mean that he departed from his own essence; for this reason he added: “And he dwelt among us,” so that he might show the indwelling of the assumed humanity. “And the Word,” he says, “became flesh.”

### 18

Since, by saying “became,” he does not demonstrate a change, we can recognize the Evangelist’s meaning from other words of divine Scripture. Let the Apostle Paul be heard crying out concerning the Lord: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

Certainly, if “became” were understood according to mutability, that which is a curse could not bestow a blessing, nor could a curse free anyone from a curse.

What, then, is τὸ factum est, “became”? He himself assumed in himself the curse owed to us. “To us,” he says, sinners, the punishment of the cross was owed; judicial condemnation awaited us; every kind of punishment was due to us; every excess of torment awaited us. But he came and assumed in innocent flesh the punishment that was owed to us, so that he might condemn sin itself as unjustly rushing upon him, crying out these words to the devil, the father of sin:

“YOU HANDED THIEVES OVER TO THE CROSS AS THOUGH THEY WERE GUILTY OF SIN; BUT FOR WHAT REASON DID YOU FASTEN ME TO THE GALLOWS WITH THIEVES?”

### 19

Paul also demonstrates this, namely, the condemnation of sin through the Lord’s body: “God,” he says, “sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8:3).

It is rightly said “in the likeness of flesh,” because the body that appeared bore about it the likeness of sinful flesh.

“God sent his Son”—a common name for the natures, namely, for man and God. He did not say, “God sent God the Word,” lest the heretic seize upon the expression and say: “You see how one sends and another is sent.”

The Son, O Arian, is sent according to the nature of humanity; but he is not sent according to the essence of the Divinity, for no place is separated from the power of God.

### 20

Meanwhile, amid the applause, Photinus should not escape when he is being accused. For, while disputing this matter, I introduced the teaching of the Apostle Paul, showing [Baluzius: “considering”] that the Word is the Son: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.”

He did not say, “God sent God the Word.” Certainly, the Word of God was not separate in nature from the temple.

Immediately, through ignorance, they break into shouting, saying: “How did he say that God the Word is one and the Son who was sent another?”

I did not say that the Son was one and God the Word another. Rather, I said that God the Word and the temple are naturally another Son, [yet] one by conjunction. Thus elsewhere also I said, in the beginning [Col. 0857D]—

> **Note:** [Col. 0857D] The editors have understood this word differently. Cotelerius (*Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, vol. III, p. 601) writes: “The most learned men believe that the word *subripio* is corrupt; yet it suffers only from faulty conjunction, and should therefore be restored as follows: ‘Thus elsewhere also I said: Bring forward and challenge these expressions.’” Baluzius writes: “There is no doubt that this word is corrupt. Nevertheless, we have retained it because it is found in the ancient manuscripts. Garnerius restored it as *sub principio*.” **Editor.**

### 21

Bring them forward and challenge these expressions. Do not wound me with golden arrows.

> **Note:** [Col. 0857D] He repeats the slander that he made in section 3 concerning Cyril’s bribing of Constantinople with gold. Compare this passage with Cyril’s corresponding charge against Nestorius: “That impious and blasphemous man, seeing himself defended by his companions, grew bold through their support; indeed, while hoping to inspire us with terror, he encouraged us. Come, let us say according to custom, with sighs and tears: ‘It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes’ (Psalm 117:8). For this man—this execrable man—having emptied his golden quiver, stirred up consuls and companions, magistrates, and the chorus of queens. But let us employ the prophetic saying: ‘Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we in the name of the Lord our God’ (Psalm 19:8),” and so forth.

I have no golden arrows. I say to you in the words of blessed Peter: “I have neither gold nor silver; but what I have I give you: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ of Nazareth” (Acts 3:6). Learn the human being and God.

### 22

But, as I was saying, divine Scripture nowhere attributes the sending from the Father to the divine Word; rather, it attributes it to the Son, who is God the Word and man. Thus elsewhere also: “God sent his Son” (Galatians 4:4).

> **Note:** [Col. 0858D] He attacks this passage of the Apostle in every possible way and strives, through an improper but plausible interpretation for the uneducated crowd, to bring discredit upon the person who had used this testimony, in the irrational violence of his mind. Without naming him, he rages against John of Antioch, who otherwise loved him greatly; for he alone among those from whom he had received letters had argued from this passage of Paul to prove Θεοτόκον. He wrote as follows (*First part of the Acts of Ephesus*, chapter 25): “Since the divine Scriptures chiefly confirm God’s mercy toward us by showing that his one eternal Son, born before all the ages in an impassible manner, also came forth from the holy Virgin, the divine Apostle directs attention to this when he says: ‘God sent his Son, born of a woman’ (Galatians 4:4). Here he clearly shows that the Only-begotten of God himself came forth into the light through a wondrous birth from the Virgin, as I said shortly before. And if the holy Fathers call the Virgin Deipara—‘God-bearer’—because of this birth, I do not know why it was necessary, with your permission, to undertake this entirely unnecessary question against us ourselves and against ecclesiastical peace, as you see.”

He did not say, “God sent God the Word”; for, if he had said this, both would be found to be local and confined to a part. If the nature of the Divinity was the one sent, and the one sending, then it is local and confined to a part; for the one who is sent is sent to a place where he is not.

### 23

“God sent his Son” (Galatians 4:4), because it was unfitting for the nature of the Divinity to appear among those who were sent. Paul the elder, possessing Christ, the Lord of all, who knows himself more truly and clearly:

“God,” he says, “sent his Son, born of a woman” (ibid.).

The Son of God was born, God the Word and man. Therefore, because of the unity, let the woman who gave birth be called the mother of God, that is, Θεοτόκος; but because of the nature of man, let her be called mother of a human being, that is, ἀνθρωποτόκος.

And since you refuse to say both in one expression, I say “God and man”; do not say Χριστοτόκος—behold, I distinguish myself from you only by this word.

But when you call her mother of God, that is, Θεοτόκος, remember also to call her mother of a human being, that is, ἀνθρωποτόκος, lest you remove the economy [Col. 0859B], which is the head of our salvation.

> **Note:** [Col. 0859C] He alludes to these words of Saint Celestine: “We lament that you have removed from the creed handed down to the apostles the words that promise us the hope of our entire salvation.” And afterward: “What part of honor shall I reserve for him, when the matter concerns the removal from me of the cause of my entire salvation?” (*Letter to Nestorius, First part of the Acts of Ephesus*, chapter 18).

### 24

“God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law” (ibid.).

Who was made under the law? The nature of the Divinity? How? As though it could observe the precepts of the law? How? As though it could demonstrate to the priests that it had not transgressed the law? Was it also the nature of the Divinity that had to undergo the legal purifications, ascend into the temple, and offer sacrifices?

And who could persuade the priests that the nature of the Divinity had not transgressed the law? [Baluzius: “had transgressed the law.”]

### 25

Thus the Son was made under the law, and was not made under the law: he was made, indeed, through the humanity he assumed; he was not made through the majesty of the Divinity.

For the Divinity, which promulgated the law, to whom else, as legislator, did it have to offer the things prescribed by the law?

### 26.

God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. For this reason he made him who knew no sin to be sin for us (ibid.). Likewise, “He was made a curse for us” (Gal. III, 13): the writer did not explain to us that the blessing belonging to the nature of the Godhead was turned into a curse; rather, because he took upon himself the sin of our nature, he indicated that an unjust punishment had fallen upon him. So also, by saying that “he made him to be sin for us,” he caused him to appear before human eyes as enduring what was equal to the guilty, and as being crucified equally with the robbers—but not on his own account. But for whom, O Paul? “He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us”?

### 27.

But the question is: how is the Word the Son? We say this especially to convict Photinus, who confesses the Word but does not call the Word God the Son: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14). See how he also demonstrates the assumption of a human being when he says, “And he dwelt among us, and we saw his glory.” Whose glory? Without doubt, the Word’s: “glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father.” You see that the Only-begotten is not one, while the one from the Father is another; therefore the Word of God is the Son. How then, Photinus, do you overturn the substance of the Godhead [Baluz.: “of the deity”]?

### 28.

But if we attend to the eagerness of your zeal, the sun itself will fail us here, and perhaps we shall not be able to proceed to another doctrine. Preserve these things, therefore, among yourselves; for the devil knows how to contrive harm for human beings even from good things. Discussions about God are indeed good, for they pour forth within themselves the fragrance of life; but discussions generate quarrels, quarrels stir up anger, anger provokes the hands, provoked hands are moved to wounds—and what wounds do, and what end they have, may experience—God forbid—be kept far from this very speech. For sometimes they even produce ultimate death.

### 29.

[Note: He maliciously foretells that the very violence he himself was exercising was to be feared from Cyril; and in fact he persuaded many that hostility toward him was being pursued, not on account of any merit of the case.

Hence the emperor Theodosius wrote as follows (In the sacred letter to Cyril, I part, concerning Ephesus, ch. 31): “It is the mark of the same disposition—turbulent and audacious—and of the same zeal, to wish to confuse all ecclesiastical and imperial affairs and to tear them apart from one another, as though every other opportunity for you to seek praise and glory were lacking.” And near the end, when ordering him to come to the synod: “By this course, you will be considered neither to have been deceived by some private distress of mind, nor to have acted with excessive hostility toward anyone, in the harsh and ill-considered measures you have already undertaken in defense of your opinion” [Col. 0860C].

Hence Theodoret, after Cyril’s death: “There is no longer any contention; envy has died, and the heresy has been buried with it” (Sermon before Domnus).

Hence also Eutherius (In the preface to the Sermons): “How shall I be able either to match in my speech the fervent zeal of your piety, or to repay in full measure the duty owed to truth, or to restrain the assaults of falsehood, which now throws everything into confusion, when everything that is said is full of rashness and madness? They are said with the utmost impudence and arrogance, so that now they dare to do what previously they had not dared: to such an extent that the wickedness of the heretics will no longer lie in wait for the simpler people secretly and lightly, but, as though it possessed supreme power over all, will perpetrate every crime, assume authority over everyone, prescribe laws according to its own decisions, drag anyone it wishes toward its own purposes, demand immediate obedience, hear cases, exact penalties from the more diligent worshipers of piety, envelop this man in insults, drive another from his homeland, weave nets of accusation for one, cast another down from his rank of dignity, overthrow another by audacity, and drag yet another by the nose with the inflated bubbles of empty words. I say nothing of chains, prisons, fines, disgrace, scourges, and the pitiable spectacle of slaughter.”

And later: “They condemn without a trial; they reject those whom they have never convicted of falsehood; they call audacity courage; they name cruelty zeal; they regard fraud as wisdom. What tragedian could express all these things even in a sustained voice?” Liberatus, relating what Cyril was doing while the day of the future synod was awaited, says: “He was making certain excerpts from Nestorius’s books, wishing to unsettle him; for he was, as they say, his enemy.”]

This, however, will not occur among us, provided that the Egyptians are concerned with it; for no opportunity for insolence is given them in the city that rules. Their sole concern is to disturb everything everywhere. But let us contend against them with other weapons, taking up the commands of Paul. “It is necessary,” he says, “that a bishop be blameless, the husband of one wife, sober, chaste, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, holding fast the faithful word that is according to the doctrine, so that he may be able both to exhort with sound teaching and to refute those who contradict” (I Tim. III, 2). He did not say that he should be able to wound those who contradict, but that he should be able to refute those who contradict, and to defend and embrace sound doctrine.

“But what if he provokes him?” you will say. “It is necessary to instruct those who contradict with gentleness: ‘Perhaps God may grant them repentance, so that they may recognize the truth and recover from the snare of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will’” (II Tim. II, 26).

### 30.

[Note: He had recalled at the outset the tyrannical spirit of the Alexandrian bishops; accordingly, he likes to employ this term in order to cast odium upon Cyril, who, like his predecessors—indeed more than they—had come under suspicion of having usurped secular power in Egypt, and thus of tyranny, as Socrates relates.]

No one calms disturbances by disturbances; no physician heals wounds with wounds. For the sake of peace I tolerate the audacity of tyranny; I do not kick back against one who kicks. Christ was once kicked, but he himself did not kick back. What did he say to the one who kicked? “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts V, 5).

### 31.

Let us therefore preserve these things among ourselves in memory, as I said. Let us turn away from every heresy and hate it; with Paul of Samosata, let us abhor Photinus; with Apollinaris, let us detest Arius; and toward every sect of perverse faith let us be implacable, while embracing the faith of the Church, and let us not be disturbed with respect to our own members.

Those who say only Θεοτόκος (“God-birther”), even though they lack what they might perhaps accept later and limp with regard to the right faith, are nevertheless members of the Church. And those who say only “mother of a human being,” that is, ἀνθρωποτόκος (“mother of a human being”), are also members of the Church, but are lacking spiritual medicine.

Let brotherhood therefore not rush upon brothers: “A brother helping a brother will be exalted like a fortified city” (Prov. XVIII, 9). And again Paul says: “Brothers, even if someone is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. VI, 1).

Suppose that the one who says Θεοτόκος also says Χριστοτόκος (“Christ-birther”), a name signifying two natures. And everything must be done for the edification of the Church.

### 32.

As I said, this expression—Χριστοτόκος—is indeed significative of two natures, both of the Godhead and of humanity. But when dealing with simpler people, a clearer expression is necessary. What prevents one from saying Χριστοτόκος, Θεοτόκος, and ἀνθρωποτόκος? Just as one who says “Christ” confesses that he is God and man, so if you say Θεοτόκος and ἀνθρωποτόκος, you have confessed both.

### 33.

[Note: It was perhaps to these words, or at least to this speech, that ancient historians referred when, following Socrates, they said (Book VII, ch. 33): “When affairs were then disturbed and confused, Nestorius, realizing that the plague of contention was spreading more widely among the people, was brought to repentance and called Mary ‘God-bearer,’ speaking as follows: ‘Let Mary be called God-bearer, and let the offenses of minds be calmed.’” Yet no one thought that he had said this because he was moved to repentance, although Nicephorus records this statement as having been made by Nestorius (Book XIV, ch. 35) after the Council of Ephesus, when the Church was being torn apart by the terrible schism caused by him.]

Let us therefore, I beg you, lay down on both sides the battle-line of contention against our own members. If anyone has been more shameless, let us forgive him; and if anyone speaks more subtly, let him likewise be considered worthy of pardon. Let us look only to this: that no one call God the Word a creature, or call the humanity that was assumed imperfect.

If anyone says these things, let righteous anger be taken up against him. But if he introduces distinction into those things that you confess, what should you say to him except: “If my expression offends my brother, I will never utter it again”? If [Baluz. adds: “I”] I seem to someone less suited to give counsel for peace, hear Paul crying out to you: “What you have learned, received, heard, and seen in me—do these things, and the God of peace will be with you” (Phil. IV, 9).

## SERMON XIII. On the following day, that is, Sunday

[Note: Nestorius delivered this sermon on the fourteenth of December in the year 430, when he was tired from the previous day’s labor and yet was being pressed to convey the knowledge of piety more forcefully and concisely. It is possible either that he had cunningly arranged for his own people to impose this demand upon him—which is the more probable explanation—or that he was genuinely compelled by others, in a kind of pious tumult, to disclose his mind concerning a doubtful matter.

He divides the knowledge of piety into two parts: the confession of the consubstantial Trinity and the assumption by God the Word of a perfect human being. He deals only with the latter, since this was the matter over which the controversy was raging. He passes over the first as already confessed by his hearers. Marius Mercator attacks this sermon, as he did the preceding one, in the appendix to his Refutation of the Twelfth Anathema.

—On Sunday: that year Sunday fell on the seventh day of the month of December, not the fourteenth, as Garnerius thought. See the new collection of the Councils, pp. 422, 689. BALUZ.]

The said sermon.

### 1.

[Note: This sermon exists in another version in the Synodical against the Tragedy of Irenaeus, chapter 3, where it is noted that Nestorius delivered it when he had entered late for the tables—that is, for the Masses at which the mysteries were celebrated—as stated in volume I of the new collection of the Councils, pp. 689 and 1323. BALUZ.]

In other lands, different occupations have different advantages. To some, serving in the army seems greatly advantageous; to others, commerce in the marketplace is suitable; to others, it is desirable to devote themselves to the maritime art; and to some, to undertake the business of any other earthly way of life. But the knowledge of piety is useful and necessary in common to all human beings—to kings and priests, to ordinary people and the powerful.

### 2.

What, then, is the knowledge of piety? If someone wishes to learn it concisely—

[Note: The Fathers often mention the crowding of hearers at sacred sermons—ὠθισμόν, θλῖψιν, στενοχωρίαν. For that reason, together with Christian Lupus, I understand these words of Nestorius as follows: “For I spare you, since I too am very tired, and you are altogether constricted, or, according to another version, are suffering from crowding.” The Greek was doubtless σφιγγόμενοι, “being constricted.” COTEL.

“Are suffering from crowding.” In the Synodical: “constricted.” The reference is to the impatience of the hearers. BALUZ.]

—for I spare both myself, who am tired, and you, who are suffering from crowding. If, then, as I was saying, someone wishes to learn it concisely, the knowledge of piety is to adopt a correct account of the consubstantial Godhead of the Trinity, and to confess that the divine nature assumed a human being.

[Note: From this point up to the words “What, then, is this?” these words are not found in the Synodical. BALUZ.]

You press us concerning things that have often been said, as though they had not been said, and insist vehemently upon exacting them. Since, therefore, it is necessary to yield to your violence—which possesses a pious [Baluz.: “impious”] tyranny over us—we shall repeat the same words before you once again. Preserve, therefore, this knowledge of piety in concise form.

### 3.

What is this, then, except ὀρθολογία (“right reasoning”)—of the consubstantial divine Trinity, of the divine nature that assumes a human being, and of the flesh assumed in the virgin womb—

[Baluz.: “And hence the assumption of a human being by the perfect Godhead, of the perfect [human being],” etc. EDIT.]

—and of the perfect human being assumed by the Godhead; and thereafter, the more excellent contemplation of the perfect Godhead and perfect humanity joined together in one Son, the right of two natures coming together in one authority through divine reason.

### 4.

For this reason we have often told you how “Christ” is an appellation signifying both names, that is, humanity and the divine nature. Therefore, if anyone expressly says only “Christ,” let him know that in this name both natures are signified and jointly named.

### 5.

For this reason blessed Matthew, the writer of the Gospels, when he came to the mystery of the generation, did not give an account of the generation from either nature, but rather from the name “Christ.” It is necessary, however, to speak explicitly, so that understanding may be made easier for all: “The book,” he says, “of the generation of Jesus Christ” (Matt. I, 1).

He did not say: “The book of the generation of God the Word,” nor “the book of the generation of a human being.” For if he had said “the book of the generation of a human being,” he would have shown Christ to us as merely human. Likewise, if he had said “the book of the generation of God the Word,” he would have introduced the Godhead to us as wholly without humanity.

[Note: Hence the Synodical should be corrected, where it reads “on the human side” instead of “without a share.” BALUZ.]

In the appellation “Christ,” therefore, he embraces both natures, so that neither can be understood without the other.

### 6.

For this reason we also suitably apply to the holy Virgin, because we call her the mother of Christ, a name of twofold designation: Θεοτόκος, which means “mother of God,”

[Note: The words “and ἀνθρωποτόκος, that is, mother of a human being,” are absent from Baluz. He admits that Garnerius correctly restores them, but was nevertheless unwilling to depart from the wording of the ancient copies, in which they are absent. EDIT.]

and ἀνθρωποτόκος, that is, “mother of a human being.”

### 7.

Since, however, it is necessary—especially for those who seek a clearer understanding, since they are sons of the Church—to use more explicit language, I therefore now proclaim in a louder voice, with more evident speech, the same definition by which I previously spoke briefly of that blessed Mary ever-virgin: the holy Virgin is the mother both of God and of a human being, that is, Θεοτόκος and ἀνθρωποτόκος.

She is mother of God because the temple created in her by the Holy Spirit was united to the Godhead; she is mother of a human being because of the first-fruits of our nature assumed by the nature of the Godhead.

### 8.

These are, in concise form, the doctrines of piety. Retaining all these things in memory, preserve them everywhere, turning away from the perverse glory of the heretics.

One must not suppose that the Church says Θεοτόκος in the same sense in which Θεοτόκος is a worn-out expression among them. For neither, when they call him “Son,” does the Church confess “Son” with them in such a way that the understanding of “Son” is equal and similar among both. Among them, the word “Son” is bare, possessing nothing consubstantial with the Father; among us, however, the appellation “Son” is accompanied by its cause, reality, or work.

Likewise, among them Christ, the Lord of all, is called God; he is also called God among us. But among them he is created, whereas among us he is uncreated together with the one who begot him.

### 9.
