Let us not, therefore, be led by the same appellation to a single understanding with the heretics. Rather, let us confess together that humanity and the Godhead are joined in the one generation of the Son.

Nor did the Godhead descend into flesh—for the Godhead is immutable, and in this God revealed himself to the Jews, saying: “I am, I am, and I have not changed” (Mal. III, 6)—nor was the flesh changed through the incarnation.

God is not ashamed of the nature that he assumed; he is not ashamed to possess that which reigns with him. For if he were ashamed of it, he would not have assumed it. Having assumed it, because of his love for the human race, he possesses our nature as an inviolable garment of the Godhead.

Hold these things in memory in every respect in Christ, to whom be glory for ages of ages.

## EXCERPTS FROM VARIOUS TREATISES OF NESTORIUS, DISTRIBUTED INTO FOUR COLLECTIONS

### NOTICE

There are several collections of excerpts from the treatises of Nestorius. The first and more famous, though not the fullest, is the one that Peter, chief secretary, presented to the Fathers at the Council of Ephesus. A second is found in Cyril, in the work sometimes called the *Refutation* and sometimes the *Contradiction against Nestorius*. Marius Mercator rendered a third, made at Ephesus by Cyril, into Latin; we now publish it for the first time.

The first, which may be called the Ephesian collection, contains twenty chapters; the second, the Cyrillian collection, forty-three; the third, which Liberatus calls the “excerpting,” twenty-two—although the same chapters occur in different collections. It will soon become clear that Cyril is the author of all the collections, and that Mercator is the translator of the last two.

As Mercator suggests, all the excerpts were taken from a codex composed from many gatherings, arranged by a certain method, although the individual treatises do not seem to have been contained separately in each gathering, as is plainly demonstrated in the notes.

That codex, which Marius mentions, was certainly not different from the book mentioned by Cyril when he says (Book I of the *Contradiction*, preface):

“I came upon a certain book composed by a certain person, in which many sermons had been collected according to the letters and arranged as though in order, and nothing was lacking to make it worthy of preservation. If something had been said by its author that would fade away through being consigned to oblivion, I might perhaps have decided both that I ought to remain silent and that I ought to advise others to do the same, lest such absurd and imprudent statements become known to many others and to our descendants. But since a multitude of blasphemies has been collected in that book, and much has been proclaimed and barked against the doctrines of truth, how could it not have been almost necessary for us to gird ourselves and fight for the salvation of the readers, so that they might suffer no harm from it? For the same fragments are read both in the book and in the codex.”

Indeed, it may seem to some that the codex was not even different from the book on the Incarnation which Gennadius reports (Book on Ecclesiastical Writers, ch. 53) that Nestorius wrote for his heresy, filled with sixty-two testimonies from sacred Scripture:

“After he had been appointed bishop of the Church of Constantinople, displaying himself openly as the enemy of the Church whom he had concealed, he wrote a book, supposedly on the incarnation of the Lord, constructed from sixty [perhaps fifty] and two testimonies of divine Scripture according to his perverse understanding. Whatever he asserted in it is demonstrated in the catalogue of heretics.”

We compared those three collections with no small labor and indicated where they agree and where they differ. For this is by no means insignificant for understanding the affair of the Nestorian heresy. We therefore thought that they should all be published together: partly because the first two are found in Marius Mercator, whose works we are publishing; partly because the third supplies the actual Greek words of Nestorius for many fragments that are found only in Latin in Mercator.

We added a fourth collection from various books of both Cyril and other writers, so that everyone might be able to behold the heretic’s opinions at a single glance and judge from them how undeservedly certain people in the past—and some even today—have dared to say that Nestorius fell through words rather than in reality, and that he therefore received a sentence of condemnation because of obstinacy rather than heresy.

## ACT VI OF THE SYNOD OF EPHESUS

[Note: From this act of the Council of Ephesus, at which Nestorius was condemned, Garnerius produced nothing except fragments of the books of the heresiarch that the Fathers brought forward in his accusation. Since, however, as Baluz noted, the whole act has been copied in both copies among the works of Marius Mercator, we have taken care to restore it here in full, informing the reader, as is proper, where the fragments excerpted by Garnerius occur. EDIT.]

In it is contained the FIRST COLLECTION OF EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOK OF NESTORIUS, presented to the Fathers of the Ephesian synod by Peter, chief secretary, translated, as may be believed, by Marius Mercator.

Metrodorus of Leontopolis, Macarius of Antaeopolis, Peter of Oxyrhynchus, Strategius of Athribis, Athanasius of Paralus, Sylvanus of Cophritis, John of Hephaestus, Aristobulus of Thmuis, Theon of Sethroïtis, Lampetius of Casium, Cyrus of the Achaeans, Publius of Olbia, Samuel of Dysae, Zenobius of Barca, Tenon of Tentyra, Sopater of Septimiaca, Eusebius of Nilopolis, Heraclida of Heracleopolis, Chrisadrius of Aphroditopolis, Andrew of Hermopolis Magna, Sabinus of Panopolis, Abraham of Ostracine, Hierax of Aphnau, Alypius of Sela, Alexander of Cleopatris, Isaac of Tuna, Ambon of Bouto, Heracleus of Thynis, Isaac of Elearchia, Heraclius of Thmuis, Theon of Psinca, Ammonius of Panephysus, Bessula, deacon of Carthage, Arcadius and Projectus, most holy bishops and legates, and the most holy presbyter Philip, legate of the apostolic see of the Romans, Peter, presbyter of Alexandria and chief secretary, said:

“Your holy and great synod, exercising every care for the right and apostolic faith and for the doctrines of truth, and consulting the peace and condition of the Churches, has issued a definition. Since we have it in hand, if it pleases your holiness, we shall read it.”

The holy synod said: “Let the definition issued by the holy and universal synod be examined and inserted into the present acts.”

The Council of Nicaea set forth this faith:

“We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father, only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of the same substance as the Father, through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth; who for our salvation descended, was incarnate and made man, suffered, and rose again on the third day, ascended into the heavens, and will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit.

“But those who say, ‘There was when he was not,’ and ‘Before he was born he was not,’ and who assert that he was made from nothing or from another substance, and who say that the Son of God is either created or changeable, the apostolic Church anathematizes.”

All ought indeed to agree with this holy faith. For it contains, properly and sufficiently, what is useful for the whole world. But since there are certain people who pretend to confess and assent to it while nevertheless corrupting the force of its statements, interpreting them according to their own judgment, and corrupting the truth—sons of pestilence and error—it was necessary also to bring forward the statements of the holy and orthodox Fathers, which could show how they themselves understood the faith and trusted themselves to proclaim it to others, so that it might become clear that all who hold the right and undefiled faith must understand, interpret, and proclaim it in that manner.

Peter, presbyter of Alexandria and chief secretary, said: “Since we have in hand the books of the holy and most religious Fathers and bishops, and of various martyrs, and since we have excerpted a few chapters from them, we shall read them if it pleases you.”

Flavian, bishop of Philippi, said: “Let these also, once read, be inserted.” And they were read as follows.

### From the book *On the Godhead* by Peter, most holy bishop and martyr

“Certainly grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I, 17); hence also “we have been saved by grace” (Eph. II, 8–9), according to the apostolic saying: “And this is not from yourselves, nor from works, lest anyone should boast.”

By his will the Word became flesh (John I, 14), and was found in appearance as a human being (Phil. II, 7). Yet he was not deprived of the Godhead. For it was not so that he might cease from his own glory and power that, “though he was rich, he became poor” (II Cor. VIII, 9); rather, it was also so that he himself might endure death for us sinners: “the just for the unjust, so that he might offer us to God, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit” (I Pet. III, 18).

And after other statements:

Hence the evangelist also asserts the truth, saying: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14)—namely, from the time when the angel greeted the Virgin, saying: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you” (Luke I, 28).

When Gabriel said, “The Lord is with you,” he meant that God the Word was with you. For he demonstrates that he was born in the womb and became flesh, according to what is written: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born will be called the Son of God” (ibid., 35).

And further, after other statements:

God the Word, while no man was present, by the will of God, who easily accomplishes all things, became flesh in the Virgin’s womb, requiring neither the activity nor the presence of a man. For the power of God overshadowing the Virgin was more effective than a man, while the Holy Spirit also came upon her at the same time.

[Note: Besides the Vatican and Bellovacense manuscripts, which we used in correcting the works of Marius Mercator, I found another old copy of these testimonies in manuscript 1868 of the Colbert Library. BALUZ.]

### From the book *Against the Arians* by Athanasius, most holy bishop of Alexandria

[Note: Colbert has “Against Arius.” BALUZ.]

“Many saints, therefore, were holy and free from every sin. Jeremiah, however, was sanctified even from the womb; and John, while he was still in the womb, leaped for joy at the voice of Mary the Theotocos [Perhaps: “Theotocu.” GALLAND.] (ibid., 44).

“And yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression (Rom. V, 14). Thus, nevertheless, human beings remained corruptible and mortal and capable of the sufferings belonging to their nature.

“But now, when God the Word became human and made his own the things proper to our flesh, sufferings no longer affect the body because of the Word who was in the body; rather, they were crushed by him. Human beings, however, are no longer sinners and mortals according to their own sufferings, but according to the power of the Word they rise immortal, incorruptible, and eternal.

“Hence, although flesh was born from Mary the Theotocos, he himself is said to have been born who grants that others might be born, so that he might transfer our generation into himself, and so that we might no longer merely depart from earth into earth, but, joined to the heavenly Word, might be raised by that Word itself into heaven.

“Rightly, therefore, he also transferred the other sufferings of the body into himself,

[Note: Colbert has “into himself.” BALUZ.]

“so that we might become [The same manuscript: “we might become.” BALUZ.] partakers of eternal life, not as human beings, but as those who cling to the Word.

“For we no longer die in Adam according to the former generation, but, with our generation and all carnal frailty transferred into the Word, we rise from the earth,

[Note: Here we have followed the authority of the Bellovacense book. The Vatican copy has “but with our generation”; the Colbert copy has “but according to our generation.” BALUZ.]

“with the curse of sin dissolved because of him who was made a curse for us.”

[Note: The Vatican and Colbert copies read this way; the Bellovacense has “having been passed over.” BALUZ.]

### From the same author’s Letter to Epictetus

“How, then, did those who are called Christians dare even to doubt whether the Lord who came forth from Mary is indeed the Son according to the substance and nature of God, but according to the flesh from the seed of David and from the flesh of holy Mary?

“How, moreover, were they so audacious as to say that Christ, who suffered and was crucified in the flesh, is not the Lord, Savior, God, and Son of the Father?

“Or how do they wish to call themselves Christians who say that the Word came upon a holy human being, just as it came upon each of the prophets, rather than that he himself became human when he took a body from Mary,

[Note: Colbert has “not another.” But this reading is not good. BALUZ.]

“and that Christ is one person while the Word of God who existed before Mary and before the ages was another, the Son of the Father?

“Or how can they be Christians who say that the Son is one thing and the Word of God another?”

And after other statements:

“Far be it from us to say that these things happened merely in appearance, as some have thought. For when the Savior truly became human, the salvation of the whole human being was accomplished.

“For if the Word had been in the body merely in appearance, as they say—and what is said to exist merely in appearance is only a kind of fantasy—our salvation and the resurrection of human beings would be found to have occurred through δοκήσις [opinion], not in reality, according to the utterly wicked Manichaean. [Note: Mercator retained the Greek term. Δοκήσις means “opinion.” The Colbert manuscript incorrectly has “diocesin.” BALUZ.]

“But if our salvation did not occur through fantasy, and if salvation was accomplished not merely for the body but for the whole human being, soul and body, then the human nature that came from Mary was, according to the Scriptures, truly the Savior’s.”

[Note: [Col. 0870D] The ancients, among them our Marius Mercator, regarded this excerpt from the letter to Prosdochius as a genuine work of Julius. But Leontius, in Book 8 of *On the Sects*, Act 8, did not hesitate to assert, on the testimony of several copies, that the letter from which this excerpt was taken belonged not to Julius but to Timothy, who had Apollinaris as his teacher. On this matter the most learned Constantius says more in the appendix to the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 71, where he also presents the entire letter, wrongly attributed to Julius, which G. L. recovered from an ancient English manuscript, and appends this same excerpt from that letter in a threefold version. Moreover, Mercator repeats below, p. 239, the same fragment, falsely attributed to Julius. GALLAND.]

## Letter of Julius, Most Holy Bishop of Rome, to Prosdochius

He is proclaimed for the completion of the faith—the Son of God, incarnate [Col. 0870D] from the Virgin Mary, who dwelt [Col. 0871A] in human beings, not one who merely operated in a human being. For this is said of the prophets and apostles. Perfect God in the flesh, and perfect man in spirit. Not two sons: one, indeed, the natural Son who assumed a human being, [Note: [Col. 0871D] Colbert reads “and one natural man assumed by God.” Baluz. reads otherwise. GALLAND.] and the other a mortal man assumed by God; but one only-begotten Son in heaven, the only-begotten God on earth.

## From a Letter of Felix, Most Holy Bishop of Rome and Martyr, to Maximinus, Bishop, and to the Clergy of the Church of Alexandria

[Note: [Col. 0871D] Read “Maximinus”; for this is how it appears in the inscription of this fragment among the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, Act 1, p. 1055, vol. III of the Venetian edition of the Councils by Labbe. It is also found in Cyril, *Apology against the Orientals*, under Anathema 4, at the cited place, p. 1379, or among the works of the same holy Father, vol. VI, p. 174, but without the name of the bishop to whom the letter was addressed. The aforementioned Coustantius observes in *Roman Pontiffs’ Letters*, p. 294, that there were indeed some who attributed this fragment to Saint Felix, pope and martyr. Indeed, Lequien, in Dissertation 2 on Damascus, no. 7, considers that nothing now remains to prevent us from not only removing this fragment from this holy pontiff but also from attributing it to heretics. The learned man examines and refutes that opinion, and finally concludes: “Since Cyril and the Council of Ephesus judged this fragment not unworthy of the most holy pope and martyr Felix, and since Marius Mercator, Vincent of Lérins, Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, and other Catholics subsequently accepted it as his, it would be a matter of conscience for us to remove it from him so long as something else has not been established.” GALLAND.]

Concerning the incarnation of the Word and concerning faith: we believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary. For he is the eternal Son and Word of God, and not a man assumed by God in such a way that he was someone other than himself. For the Son of God did not assume a man so that he might be someone other than himself; rather, while he was perfect God, he simultaneously became perfect man, incarnate from the Virgin.

## From the Fifth Paschal Letter of Theophilus, Most Holy Bishop of Alexandria

For there now remain traces of the ancient miracles, lest people believe too little that the power of God can cause a virgin to give birth, in whom the living Word of God was present for the sake of our likeness. For otherwise he himself could not address us in a manner more suited to us; nor did he receive a body from pleasure and [Note: [Col. 0872D] This expression is used metaphorically for intercourse. Thus Solomon says in *Wisdom* 7 that he was coagulated in blood from human seed and in the pleasure of sleep that accompanies it. BALUZ.] sleep, as happens with other human beings, but he received a body like hers, born from a Virgin—appearing indeed as a human being like us and in the form of a servant, but proved by his deeds to be the maker and Lord of all, performing the works of God.

## From the Sixth Paschal Letter of the Same Author

[Col. 0871C] Just as the greatest craftsmen display the power of their art not only in precious material, but also, if they demonstrate their skill in mud or wax, appear all the more worthy of praise, so also God the Word, the best craftsman of all, living and effective, who ordered all things in fitting arrangement, came to us not by assuming some heavenly material for a body, but by displaying in clay the greatness of his art. Correcting the human being fashioned from clay, he himself came forth from the Virgin as a new human being—unlike us in the manner of his generation, but in every other respect like us without sin (Hebr. 4:15): born, wrapped in swaddling clothes, nourished with milk, [Col. 0872A] laid as an infant in a manger, enduring the frailty of our nature for the sake of the earlier causes; yet, while still an infant, he terrified Satan and his army, calling the magi to repentance and arming them to despise the king who had sent them.

## From the Book of Cyprian, Most Holy Bishop, *On Mercy*

There are many and great benefits, dearest brothers, by which the abundant and lavish clemency of God the Father and of Christ has worked and continues to work for our salvation: that the Father sent the Son to preserve and bring us to life, so that he might restore us; [Note: [Col. 0872D] Thus the ancient Vatican and Colbert manuscripts read, except that they also read *quoque* for *quodque*. The Bellovacensis has: “that the Son of God also …” This reading is not good. BALUZ.] and that the Son was sent and wished to become the Son of Man, so that he might make us sons of God. He humbled himself so that he might raise up the people who had previously lain prostrate. He was wounded so that he might heal our wounds. He served so that he might draw servants out into freedom. He endured death so that mortality might bring forth immortality.

## Ambrose, Most Holy Bishop of Milan

If they do not believe me, let them believe the Apostle, who says: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law” (Gal. 4:4). “His Son,” he says—not one of many, not a common son, but his own. By saying “his own,” he signified the distinctiveness of the eternal generation. Later he added that this one was made from a woman, so that the making might be attributed not to the divinity but to the assumption of the body. “Made from a woman” refers to the reception of flesh; “made under the law,” to observance of the law. That heavenly generation was before the law; this one was after the law.

## The Same Author

[Col. 0872C]

Let empty disputes about words therefore be silent, since, as it is written, the kingdom of God is not in persuasive speech but in the demonstration of power (1 Cor. 2:4). Let us preserve the language concerning divinity and flesh. One Son speaks in both, because both natures are in the same one, and he does not always speak in one and the same manner. Consider in him now the glory of God, now the sufferings of a human being: as God he speaks divine things, because he is the Word; as a human being he speaks human things, because [Note: [Col. 0872D] Colbert reads “in him.” BALUZ.] he spoke in my substance: “This is the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51). This bread is flesh, as he himself said: “The bread that I will give is my flesh” (ibid., 52). “This is the one who came down; this is the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into this world” (John 10:36). The very text teaches us that it was not the divinity that needed sanctification, but the flesh.

## Gregory the Great, Bishop of Nazianzus

Let people neither deceive nor be deceived by supposing that the “Dominical” man, as they call him—or rather our Lord and God—lacks a mind. For we do not separate him, the human being, from the divinity; instead, we affirm one and the same person: formerly not a human being but God and Son alone, before the ages, without a body and without anything bodily; afterward also a human being assumed for our salvation, passible in the flesh, impassible in divinity, comprehensible in body, incomprehensible [Col. 0873B] in divinity; the same earthly and heavenly, visible and intelligible, capable of being contained and incapable of being contained; perfect man and likewise God, so that the whole human being who had fallen into sin might be restored.

If anyone does not consider Mary to be Theotokos—“God-bearer”—he is far from the divinity. If anyone says that he passed through the Virgin as through a conduit and was not formed in her by both a divine and human process—divine because without a man, human because according to the manner of birth—or if anyone says that a human being was formed and later clothed himself with God, let him be accursed. For this is not the generation of God but a flight from generation.

If anyone introduces two sons, one from God the Father and the other from the mother, rather than one and the same Son, let him fall away from the adoption promised to those who rightly believe. There is a twofold nature, God and man, because there are soul and body. But there are not two sons, nor two gods. For here there are not two human beings, although Paul called what is within a human being and what is outside a human being by these terms (2 Cor. 4:16).

And, to put it briefly, the things from which the Savior comes are one thing and another—for the visible is not the same as the invisible, nor is what belongs to time like what is before time—but there are not two persons, one and another; far from it. For both are joined in the union: God incarnate and man consecrated by divinity, or whatever name one may wish to give it.

I say “one thing and another” in contrast to the Trinity. There, there is one person and another, lest we confuse the substances; but there are not three things and another three things. For the three are one and the same, alike in divinity.

If anyone says that he worked as in a prophet, by grace, and not that he was joined and united by substance, let him be empty of divine operation—or rather, full of its opposite.

If anyone does not worship the crucified one, let him be accursed and be counted among the Theoctonoi [Note: [Col. 0873D] That is, “killers of God,” as the ancient translator of the Council of Ephesus explains it. BALUZ.].

If anyone says that he attained perfection through works, or that he merited adoption after baptism or after resurrection from the dead, according to the pagans who introduce [Note: [Col. 0873D] The Bellovacensis manuscript reads *naperpapot*. The Vatican manuscript has *ΠΑΡΕΓΡΑΠΡΟϹ*. The old version of the Council of Ephesus has *parengraphtos*, that is, “inscribed.” The Greek text has *παρενράπτας*, which Peltanus translates “ascribed,” while the old translator of the Synod of Chalcedon has “fabricated.” BALUZ.] *naperpapot*, let him be accursed. For whatever comes into being, grows, or is perfected is not God, even if it is described in that way on account of gradual growth.

## From Basil, Most Holy Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, First Letter

Neither heaven and earth alone, nor the breadth of the seas [Note: [Col. 0873D] Below: “height.” EDD.], nor the things that live in the waters, nor terrestrial animals, nor the stars, nor the air, nor the seasons, nor the varied and diverse ordering of the elements, can prove the excellence of divine power as much as this: that God, who cannot be contained, was able to be joined to death without suffering in the flesh, so that by his suffering he might give us impassibility.

## Gregory, Most Holy Bishop of Nyssa

[Col. 0874B]

“Have this mind among yourselves,” he says, “which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:5–7).

What is poorer than the form of a servant in God? What is more humble for a king than willingly to descend to share in our most wretched nature? The King of kings and Lord of lords puts on the form of a servant. The Judge of all pays tribute to rulers [Note: [Col. 0873D] It seems that *pensat* should be read: “and pays.” BALUZ.], and the Lord of creation is brought into a cave. He who contains all things finds no place in an upper room but is thrown into a manger among mute animals. The pure and undefiled one suffers the filth of human nature, and, walking through all our [Col. 0874C] poverty, reaches even the experience of death.

You see the measure of voluntary poverty. Life deigns to taste death; the judge is brought to judgment; the Lord of all life submits to the verdict of a judge; the King of the heavenly powers does not repel the hands of executioners. “In these things,” he says, “let him see the example and measure of humility.”

## Atticus, Bishop of Constantinople

Today Christ the Lord assumed a birth of mercy. For he had already possessed divine dignity, and afterward added mercy. The Word is emptied, although by nature [Note: [Col. 0873D] We have emended the corrupt reading of the edition of Baluz, *exinanibile* (“capable of being emptied”). Or, if you prefer, you may read *per me licet*, “it is permitted by me,” not *exinanibile*. In any event, Mercator must have written one or the other. I would nevertheless believe the former word to have been rendered by the translator, just as shortly afterward he translates *incarnabilis*. The Greek of this fragment is found among the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, Act 1, p. 1062, in the cited volume, and in Cyril’s *Apology against the Orientals*, under Anathema 4, at the same place, p. 1378. In both places, however, we read *ἀκένωτος, ἄσαρκος*, “not capable of being emptied, bodiless.” After writing these observations, I noticed that Mercator rendered it *inexinanibile*, “incapable of being emptied,” below, p. 239, where this fragment is again quoted. GALLAND.] incapable of being emptied. He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (ibid., 7). The one incapable of incarnation becomes incarnate. For “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14). He who cannot be handled because of his incorporeal nature is handled. [Col. 0874D] He who has no beginning comes under a bodily beginning. The perfect one grows; the immutable one progresses; the rich one becomes poor in an upper room. He who encompasses the heavens with clouds is wrapped in swaddling clothes. The King is laid in a manger.

## The Bishop of Iconium

[Col. 0875A]

Since he is both King and God, and tasted mortality for the sake of the bodily dispensation, the gifts are signs of the mystery. They offer gold, for they recognize a king. They offer frankincense, for he to whom they offer it is God. They also add myrrh, because of the mortality of suffering contained in the mystery.

## The Same Author

For unless he had been begotten bodily, you would never have been reborn spiritually; and unless he had endured the form of a servant, you would never have attained the glory of adoption. Therefore the heavenly one came to earth [Note: [Col. 0875D] The translator adds here, “he descended,” a word absent from the Greek and consequently omitted by Mercator. The Greek reads: “For this reason the heavenly one is on earth, so that …” GALLAND.], so that you, an earthly being, might be received into heaven. Therefore Christ emptied himself, so that we might all receive from his fullness (ibid., 16). His death became your immortality. The Lord’s suffering became the servant’s exaltation. Yet you seize the benefit and turn it into blasphemy.

## Atticus, Bishop of Constantinople

[Note: [Col. 0875D] Read “if indeed.” For the Greek at the cited place, p. 1062, reads: *Εἴ τινα διακρίνει*, “if he separates anyone,” where the old translator has, “if he separates anyone from us.” Shortly afterward we have corrected *communia*, the corrupt reading, to *communio*, “communion.” The Greek has *καὶ παθῶν κοινωνία καὶ σταυρός*, “and communion in sufferings and the cross.” The old translator has, “and communion in sufferings and the cross.” GALLAND.]

If the incarnation of the Only-Begotten and the birth from a Virgin and communion in sufferings and the cross and death and suffering cause doubt, let the doubter be taught and know that all these things were causes of the world’s salvation, and that not even these things are unworthy of divine mercy.

For if it is shameful for God to dwell in her, it is even more shameful to make a virgin. But if he did not consider it an insult to fashion a virgin, neither did he judge it disgraceful to dwell in her. And if suffering evil is a misfortune, how great a thing is it to free others from sufferings?

Therefore the immortal also died by death, condemned death by death, and rose again, granting us resurrection. He endures all these things not in the nature of divinity [Col. 0875C] but through the assumption of flesh: remaining untouched in divinity according to his own nature, yet enduring and suffering everything so that he might become for us the guide and author of eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0875D] Baluzius added this title, as he himself states in his notes; for he found no title in the ancient copies of Mercator. In the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, Act 6, p. 1202, in the cited volume, where this and what follows are found, the following inscription is given: “Here begin the acts concerning the report of Charisius, when he approached the holy synod against the Quartodecimans.”

Peter, presbyter of Alexandria and chief of the notaries, said: “Holy,” and so forth. GALLAND.]

## ACT OF THE CONFESSION OF CHARISIUS THE PRESBYTER

[Note: [Col. 0876D] This passage is defective. Baluzius testifies below in his notes that the manuscript copies read *jus*, which is undoubtedly corrupt. But it would be easier to emend it to *jussu*, “by order,” than to *juxta*, “according to,” or at least to add *decretum*, “decree.” The Greek reads *κατά θέσπισμα*, “according to the decree.” GALLAND.]

By decree of the most pious and most august emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, this most holy synod of deeply religious bishops from all the holy churches of nearly the entire world was assembled in the metropolitan city of Ephesus. The council was being conducted and it was decreeing that the faith expounded through the Holy Spirit by the holy Fathers who had then assembled at Nicaea, numbering three hundred and eighteen, should remain firm, while arranging by appropriate means whatever pertained to this matter.

A certain presbyter named Charisius [Note: [Col. 0875D] The name Amphilochius may have fallen out of the manuscript; it appears in the cited volume, p. 1063, where a fragment of this kind occurs. GALLAND.] [Col. 0876A] and administrator of the holy Church of the city of Philadelphia asserted that certain heretics originating from Lydia had indeed wished to abandon their error, to turn to the light of truth, and to be instructed in the pious and correct doctrines of the Catholic Church; but that those who were to be led to the truth had instead been brought into a worse error, falling, as it were, from a pit into a deeper pit.

For he asserted that Antony and James, bearing the names of presbyters, had come down from Constantinople with commendatory letters from Anastasius and Photius, who at that time adhered to the heretic Nestorius and likewise bore the names of presbyters. Although the apostolic and evangelical tradition of the faith, which the Fathers who assembled at Nicaea had also expounded, ought rather to be preferred to those who are turning from error to truth and who desire to come from darkness into light, they had offered some exceedingly impious exposition of doctrines, composed as though it were in the form of a creed, and had compelled those wretched men to subscribe to it, thereby exceeding every measure of impiety.

And so that what has been said may appear more clearly, there is also copied below the document presented by the aforementioned presbyter Charisius, together with the impious and utterly evil exposition of faith concerning the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God, including the subscription of those who had been deceived.

## Document of Charisius

To the most holy and God-beloved universal synod [Note: [Col. 0876D] Thus in the manuscripts of Justellus; that is, “ecumenical,” as the Greek has, *συνόδῳ οἰκουμενικῇ*. GALLAND.] assembled in the metropolitan city of Ephesus, from Charisius, presbyter and administrator of the Church of Philadelphia.

[Col. 0876C] It is indeed desirable for all wise people always to render due and fitting honor to fathers, especially to spiritual fathers and teachers. But if it should happen that those who ought to teach babble to their students about the faith things capable of injuring everyone’s ears and minds, it is necessary to reverse the order and for the disciples rather to rebuke those who persist in teaching perversely.

But since Nestorius must be numbered among such people, he has reaped the fruits of his evil opinion; and because he has thought and taught extremely badly concerning the faith of Christ, often teaching what it was not fitting for him to teach, he has disturbed the entire world. Thus even the pious emperors have been compelled to decree that your most holy synod should assemble and confirm the doctrines of the true faith. The Lord God in his mercy has also granted this, so that for the aforementioned reason you, most holy Fathers, might all assemble here. [Col. 0877A]

For this reason I prostrate myself at the knees of your holiness and affirm that not only Nestorius himself but also Anastasius and Photius, presbyters and participants in his impiety, wishing to disseminate the same evil faith in other cities as well, have shown and continue to show favor to a certain James, like themselves, admitting him to their table and fellowship in conversation. They also commended him by letters as an orthodox man to the most glorious bishops of Lydia, although he accepts things that will move your holiness, once you learn of them, to impose just and appropriate punishments upon him, and also upon those who defend and favor him.

For when he arrived at the city of Philadelphia in Lydia, he deceived certain simpler clergy. Rejecting the faith that the Fathers had set forth at Nicaea, he compelled them to subscribe to another faith—or rather, to treachery—and in their simplicity they did this and subscribed in the following manner [Note: [Col. 0877D] It seems that one should read: “They did this and subscribed.” The Greek reads: *καὶ δὴ τοῦτο πεποιήκασιν, ὡς ἁπλούστεροι καθυπογράψαντες*. The old translator has: “And indeed they, being simple, did this, subscribing in the following manner.” GALLAND.]: “We assent to this correct faith.”

This exposition, full of heretical blasphemy, is complete with the subscription of those who were deceived. I ask that it be read before your holiness, so that it may be understood how they attempted to pervert the true faith. I also ask that the letters of the aforementioned men be read, in which they testify that James, the heretic who dared such things, is orthodox, while they excluded me, as though I were a heretic, from communion and ministry, although I retain the doctrines of piety, as will appear in what follows.

When these things have been read, your holiness will discover what crimes they have committed against the true faith; and through your holiness God will utterly destroy them. [Col. 0877C]

## Confession of Charisius

I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker and creator of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, [Note: [Col. 0877D] Mercator read *ὁμοιούσιον*, “of similar substance,” in his copy. But in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, in the cited volume, p. 1205, the correct reading is *ὁμοούσιον Πατρί*, “consubstantial with the Father.” GALLAND.] of similar substance with the Father, who for us and for our salvation came down from heaven, was incarnate, was born of the holy Virgin, became man, was crucified for us, died, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead.

And in the Spirit of truth, the Paraclete, [Note: [Col. 0877D] In the same Acts the reading is *ὁμοούσιον Πατρὶ καί Υἰῷ*, “consubstantial with the Father and the Son.” GALLAND.] of similar substance with the Father and the Son. And in the holy catholic Church, and in the resurrection of the dead, [Note: [Col. 0878D] Thus the Vatican manuscript. The Bellovacensis has “and in eternal life.” See the ancient version of the Council of Ephesus, p. 531. BALUZ.] and in eternal life.

I, Charisius, presented the document as stated above, and subscribed it in my own hand.

## NESTORIAN CREED

[Note: [Col. 0878D] Composed by Theodore of Mopsuestia, as stated above, p. 41, and in Collections 4 and 5 of the Fifth Council. See Facundus, Book III, chapters 2 and 5. BALUZ.]

Whoever is now being instructed for the first time in the knowledge of ecclesiastical doctrines, or desires to move from any heretical error into the truth, ought to learn and confess the following:

We believe in one God, the eternal Father, who did not begin to exist later but was God beforehand and always, nor later became Father, since he was always God and Father.

We also believe in one only-begotten Son of God from the substance of the Father, so that he is truly Son and is from the substance of the one whose Son he is and is believed to be.

And in the Holy Spirit, who is from the substance of God. He is not the Son but God by substance, being of the same substance as the one who is God and Father, from whom he exists by substance. “For,” he says, “we have not received the spirit of the world but the Spirit who is from God” (1 Cor. 2:12), separating him from every creature and joining him to God, from whom he exists by substance in a singular and proper manner distinct from every other creature. We believe that the creature was made by God not from substance but by the cause of his operation.

Nor do we consider him to be the Son, nor that he received his essence through the Son [Note: [Col. 0878D] The Greek at the cited place, p. 1208, has *τήν ὕπαρξιν*, “subsistence,” according to the old translator. GALLAND.].

We confess that the Father is perfect in his own person, and the Son likewise, and similarly the Holy Spirit, while preserving for us the rule of piety, so that we do not believe the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be three different substances, [Note: [Col. 0878D] The Greek reads: *Ἀλλὰ μίαν τῇ ταυτότητι τῆς θεότητος γνωριζομένην*. The old translator has: “But one, to be recognized by the identity of divinity.” GALLAND.] but one and the same likeness of divinity.

It is also necessary to know concerning the dispensation that the Lord God fulfilled in the Lord Christ for our salvation: that God the Word assumed a perfect man from the seed of Abraham and from David, according to the proclamation of the holy Scriptures, of the same nature as those from whose seed he was; a man perfect by nature, composed of a rational soul and human flesh.

This man, like us in nature, fashioned and made by the power of the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb, born of a woman and born under the law (Gal. 4:4), so that he might redeem all from slavery to the law and bring about the adoption long ago promised, was joined to himself in an incomprehensible manner. He caused him to experience death in the human manner, raised him from the dead, lifted him into heaven, and made him sit at the right hand of God.

Therefore, since he is above every principality, power, and dominion, and above every name that can be named, not only in this age but also in the age to come (Eph. 1:21), he received veneration from every creature, which renders it to him.

Nor do we say that there are two sons or two lords: one, the Son by substance, God the Word, the only-begotten Son of the Father, to whom this man was joined and, sharing in sonship, also shares the name “son”; and one, the Lord by substance, God the Word, to whose honor this man, being joined to him, also contributes.

Therefore we do not say that there are two sons or two lords, because, while the one who is Lord and Son by substance is manifest and has an inseparable union with him, this one also, who was assumed for our salvation, is referred to him—that is, *συναναφέρεται*—in the designation “Son” and “Lord.” This does not happen as with each of us, who is a son in himself—for this reason, according to blessed Paul, there are many sons (Gal. 3:26)—but only this man, possessing a special union with God the Word and sharing in sonship and lordship, removes the notion of two sons and two lords, while granting us union with God the Word, so that we may hold every faith and opinion concerning him; and on account of these things he also receives veneration, [Note: [Col. 0879D] The Greek passage reads in full: *Ὑπὲρ ὧν δὴ καὶ τὴν προσκύνησιν, καὶ [perhaps κατὰ] ἀναφορἀν θεοῦ, παρὰ πάσης δέχεται τῆς κτίσεως*. The old translator has: “Therefore he also receives adoration from the whole creation, on account of the relation referred to God.” GALLAND.] as one related to God.

We therefore say that there is one Son and Lord, Jesus [Col. 0879B] Christ, through whom all things were made. First we understand God the Word, who is Son of God and Lord by substance; then we introduce also the son assumed from Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Spirit and with power (Acts 10:38), as sharing in sonship and lordship through his union with God the Word.

He is also called the second Adam, according to blessed Paul (1 Cor. 15:45), as being of the same nature as Adam but showing us the condition of the future age, and possessing from him a difference as great as that which must exist between the one who supplied the hidden blessings of the future state and the one who initiated present evils.

In the same way he is also called the second man (ibid., 47), as the one who showed us the condition of the future, since Adam was the founder of the former condition—mortal, passible, and full of every sorrow—in whom we also received his likeness.

The Lord Jesus, who will appear from heaven in the future, showed us the second condition and will lead us all into communion with himself. “The first man,” he says, “is from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly” (ibid.), that is, he will come from there in order to lead us all into likeness with himself. Therefore he adds: “As was the earthly, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (ibid., 48–49).

Appearing in him and making himself visible in him to all who are to be judged, the divine nature will render judgment, although it is hidden and invisible. For “overlooking the times of ignorance, God now announces to human beings that all should repent, because he has established a day on which he will judge the world in the man whom he has appointed, giving assurance to all by raising him from the dead” (Acts 17:30–31).

This is the affirmation of ecclesiastical doctrines; and whoever believes contrary to these things, let him be accursed. Whoever does not accept saving repentance, let him be accursed. Whoever does not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the custom of the Catholic Church, let him be accursed.

[Note: [Col. 0879D] The Greek has *Ῥοὑδιος Ἰκονικοῦ*, “Rudius of Iconium.” Another reading is *Βούδιος Ἰουνικοῦ*, “Budius of Junicus.” Before these words the following heading appears at the cited place, p. 1210: “The subscription of those who had been deceived.” GALLAND.]

## Budius of Junicus, of Philadelphia, a Quartodeciman

I have acknowledged the true faith of orthodoxy, and I asked the most holy bishop Theophanius, and I approached the most holy Catholic Church. I anathematize every heresy, especially that of the Quartodecimans, in which I previously erred, and I assent to the exposition of the true faith written above. I also anathematize those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the custom of the Catholic and Apostolic Church.

And I swear by the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and by the piety and victory of the lords Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinianus, perpetual Augusti. If I should violate any of these things, I shall be subject to the severity of the laws. Since I did not know letters, I subscribed to the exposition read to me through Hesychius of Philadelphia, a curial official [Note: [Col. 0879D] The Greek has *διὰ Ἡσυχίου*, “through Hesychius.” Likewise shortly afterward one should read, as in the text, “Hesychius, son of Cerdanepius,” rather than “Esytius, son of Cerdanepius.” GALLAND.].

## Esytius Cerdanepius, of Philadelphia, a Curial Official and Quartodeciman

I have acknowledged the true faith of orthodoxy, and I approached the holy Catholic Church with a request. I anathematize every heresy, especially that of the Quartodecimans, and I assent to the exposition of the true faith written above. I also anathematize those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the holy, Catholic, and Apostolic Church.

And I swear by the holy and consubstantial Trinity, by the piety and victory of the Christ-loving rulers Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinianus, perpetual Augusti. If I should violate any of these things, I shall be subject to the severity of the laws. And I subscribed in my own hand.

## Rufinus of Philadelphia, a Quartodeciman

I have acknowledged the true faith of orthodoxy, and I approached the holy Catholic Church with a request. I anathematize every heresy, especially that of the Quartodecimans, and, together with my entire household, I assent to the exposition of the true faith written above. I anathematize those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the holy, Catholic, and Apostolic Church.

And I swear by the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and by the piety and victory of the Christ-loving rulers Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinianus, perpetual Augusti. If I should violate anything, I shall be subject, together with my entire household, to the severity of the laws. [Col. 0880D] After the exposition had been read to me and had pleased me, I subscribed according to my own judgment and will.

[Note: [Col. 0879D] The Acts, p. 1211, add *οἰκείᾳ μου χειρὶ*, “with my own hand,” which I would consider to have been omitted through the carelessness of a copyist rather than of the translator. Again, before the word “I subscribed,” one should read *et placita*, “and having pleased me,” as in the following subscription. For the Greek in both places reads *καὶ ἀρεσάσης μοι*. GALLAND.]

## Eugenius of Philadelphia, a Quartodeciman

[Note: [Col. 0880D] Thus the ancient copies of Marius Mercator, both here and shortly afterward; the Greek and Latin editions also simply have “of Philadelphia,” as do the manuscript copies of the Royal Library and the ancient copies of the old version of the Council of Ephesus. But in the ancient Latin interpretation of the Council of Chalcedon, both here and shortly afterward, the reading is “of the second Philadelphia,” which shows that this reading in Marius Mercator is ancient. [Col. 0881D] See the first volume of the new collection of the Councils, pp. 1137 and following. This Philadelphia was in Lydia. Ammianus Marcellinus mentions another, which was in Arabia, in Book 14. BALUZ.]

I, Eugenius of Second Philadelphia, a Quartodeciman, have acknowledged, together with my entire household, the true faith of orthodoxy, and I asked the most holy bishop Theophanius, and I approached the most holy Catholic Church. I anathematize every heresy, especially that of the Quartodecimans, and those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the holy, Catholic, and Apostolic Church.

I assent, together with my entire household, to the exposition of the true faith written above. And I swear by the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and by the piety and victory of the Christ-loving rulers Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinianus, perpetual Augusti. If I should violate anything, I shall be subject, together with my entire household, to the severity of the laws. After the exposition had been read to me and had pleased me, I subscribed in my own hand.

Faustinus, a layman of Disphiladelphia, a Tessarescaedecatite, [Col. 0881B] acknowledged the true faith of orthodoxy; and I asked the most holy bishop Theophanius, and I approached the most holy and catholic Church; and I anathematize every heresy, especially that of the Tessarescaedecatites, in which I had previously erred. And I assent to the exposition of the right faith written above, also anathematizing those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the custom of the holy Catholic Church. And I swear by the holy, consubstantial Trinity, and by the piety and victory of the emperors Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinian, the perpetual Augusti. But if I should undermine anything of these declarations, I shall be subject to the severity of the laws. After the exposition had been read to me, I approached with my entire household and subscribed with my own hand.

Damalius and Alexander, through the hand [Col. 0881D] of Euprepius, son of Theodorus, the most reverent deacon, [Col. 0881C] acknowledged orthodoxy; and we asked the most holy bishop Theophanius, and approached the Catholic Church, anathematizing every heresy, especially that of the Tessarescaedecatites, in which we had previously erred, and those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the custom of the orthodox. After the exposition had been read to us, we swore by the venerable oath of the most holy Trinity, and by the victory and salvation of our lords Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinian, the perpetual Augusti, that we would undermine nothing of the declarations written above. And, believing together with our households, we subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 0881D] This reading is confirmed by the manuscript codices of the ancient version of the Council of Ephesus. But in the Greek manuscripts and in the Council of Chalcedon, “of Eutropius” is read. BALUZE.]

Flavius Nymphidianus, a scholasticus of Disphiladelphia, I renounce all the doctrines and practices of the Tessarescaedecatites, who do not accept the doctrines of the orthodox, [Col. 0881D] and declare that I share in the faith of the orthodox in all things and accept it.

Polychronius, son of Tatianus, and a Philadelphian, through the hand of Flavius Hesychius [Note: [Col. 0881D] This is the reading of the old copies of Marius Mercator. The ancient version of the Council of Ephesus has simply “Cerdali.” [Col. 0882D] In the Council of Chalcedon, and in Danihel, it reads “Cerdaliheli.” The editions have “Cerdanepius.” BALUZE.] son of Cerdaliheli, a Philadelphian court official, because I was writing late, acknowledged orthodoxy; and [Col. 0882A] asking the most holy bishop Theophanius, I approached the Catholic Church, anathematizing every heresy, especially that of the Tessarescaedecatites, in which I had previously erred, and those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the custom of the orthodox. After the exposition had been read to me, I swore by the venerable oath of the most holy Trinity, and by the victory and salvation of our lords Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinian, the perpetual Augusti, that I would undermine nothing of the declarations written above. And I believe together with my entire household, and all the declarations written above are pleasing to me. I, Polychronius, borrowed the hand of (Hesychius).

[Note: [Col. 0881D] The Greek manuscripts have “of Neotarius.” A little earlier they have “Marinus, son of Syntheus.” GALLAND.]

Eustathius, son of Marcellus, [Note: [Col. 0882D] In Greek it is διὰ Φιλαδέλφου, “through Philadelphus,” which the interpreters rendered “Philadelphus.” Here too the Council of Chalcedon incorrectly has “of the second Philadelphia,” likewise in the subscription of Julian below, p. 199. BALUZE.] a Philadelphian goldsmith and a Tessarescaedecatite, acknowledged orthodoxy; and asking the most holy bishop Theophanius, I approached, by my own judgment and will, the most holy Church of God, the Catholic [Col. 0882B] and orthodox Church, anathematizing every heresy, especially that of the Tessarescaedecatites, and those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the custom of the orthodox. And I swore by the holy Trinity, and by the piety of the Christ-loving emperors Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinian, the perpetual Augusti, that if I should undermine anything of the declarations written above, I would be subject to the severity of the laws. And I subscribed with my own hand.

[Note: [Col. 0882D] Greek: Εὐτύχιος, “Eutychius.” GALLAND.]

Eutytius of Disphiladelphia acknowledged orthodoxy; and asking the most holy bishop Theophanius, I approached, by my own judgment and will, the most holy Church of God, the Catholic and orthodox Church, anathematizing every heresy, especially that of the Tessarescaedecatites, and those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the custom of the orthodox. And I swore by the holy [Col. 0882C] Trinity, and by the piety of the Christ-loving emperors Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinian, the perpetual Augusti, that if I should undermine anything of the declarations written above, I would be subject to the severity of the laws. And I subscribed with my own hand.

Stratonicus, son of Emonius, a Philadelphian and a Tessarescaedecatite, acknowledged orthodoxy; and asking the most holy bishop Theophanius, I approached the holy Catholic and apostolic Church of God, anathematizing every heresy, especially that of the Tessarescaedecatites, and those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the custom of the orthodox. And I swore by the holy Trinity, and by the piety of the Christ-loving emperors Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinian, the perpetual Augusti, that if I should undermine anything of the declarations written above, I would be subject [Col. 0882D] to the severity of the laws. And I subscribed through my nephew Alexander, because I did not know letters.

Theodoretus and Alexander and [Note: [Col. 0882D] Read “Philadelphus,” as in the cited Acts, p. 1217, Φιλάδελφος. GALLAND.] Philadelphus subscribed through one of us, Alexander, and acknowledged [Col. 0883A] orthodoxy; and asking the most holy bishop Theophanius, we approached the holy Catholic, apostolic, and orthodox Church of God. And we anathematize every heresy, especially that of those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the custom of the orthodox. And we swore by the holy Trinity, and by the piety and victory of our lords Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinian, the perpetual Augusti, that if we should undermine anything of the declarations written above, we would be subject to the severity of the laws. After this exposition had been read to us, we subscribed.

Marinus, son of Evethus, through the hand [Note: [Col. 0883D] The Greek has Νεωταρίου, “of Neotarius.” A little earlier: Μαρῖνος Συνθίου, “Marinus, son of Syntheus.” GALLAND.] of Neorius, lector of the orthodox, acknowledged orthodoxy; and asking the most holy bishop Theophanius, I approached the holy Catholic and apostolic Church of God. And I anathematize [Col. 0883B] every heresy, and those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the custom of the orthodox. And I swore by the holy Trinity, and by the piety and victory of our lords Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinian, the perpetual Augusti; and I swore by the venerable oath that if I should undermine anything of the declarations written above, I would be subject to the severity of the laws. And I subscribed.

Padicius the Philadelphian subscribed with my own hand, and acknowledged orthodoxy; and asking the most holy bishop Theophanius, I approached the holy Catholic and apostolic Church of the orthodox, anathematizing every heresy, especially that of the Tessarescaedecatites, and those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the custom of the orthodox. And I swore by the venerable [Col. 0883C] oath that if I should undermine anything of the declarations written above, I would be subject to the severity of the laws. After the exposition had been read to me, I subscribed with my own hand.

Cyriacus the Philadelphian, one of the Novatian heresy, acknowledged orthodoxy; and asking the most holy bishop Theophanius, I approached the holy Catholic and apostolic Church of God, anathematizing every heresy, especially [Note: [Col. 0883D] Greek, Καθαρῶν, “of the Cathari.” GALLAND.] that of the Cathari. And I swore by the venerable oath that if I should undermine anything of the declarations written above, I would be subject to the severity of the laws. After the exposition had been read to me, I subscribed through Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0883D] In the Council of Chalcedon there is added: “and especially that of the Novatians. And I assent together with my entire household to the aforesaid exposition of the Catholic faith. And swearing by the venerable sacrament to the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and to the piety and victory of the lords emperors Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinian, the perpetual Augusti, if I should transgress any of these declarations, I shall be subject together with my entire household to the severity of the laws. And after the exposition had been read to me and had pleased me, I subscribed with my own hand.” At this point Rusticus the deacon, p. 1140, notes that this addition [Col. 0884D] is not found in the Greek codices, which contain only the words translated by Mercator. See the New Collection of the Councils, p. 652. BALUZE.—The Greek reads as follows: Διὰ Εὐσεβίου τοῦ Καλλιοπίου Σύρου, “through Eusebius Calliopius the Syrian.” GALLAND.] Galliopistrus.

Eusenius the Philadelphian, a sailor, acknowledged orthodoxy; and asking the most holy bishop Theophanius, I approached the holy Catholic and orthodox Church of God, [Col. 0883D] anathematizing every heresy. And I swore by the venerable oath that I would undermine nothing of the declarations written above. And I subscribed with my own hand.

[Col. 0884A] Diomedes, living in the village of Caccaba, acknowledged orthodoxy; and asking the most holy bishop Theophanius, I approached of my own will the holy Catholic and apostolic Church of the orthodox, anathematizing every heresy, especially that of the Tessarescaedecatites, in which I had previously erred. And I swear by the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and by the victory and piety of the lords [Note: [Col. 0884D] The Greek adds τῆς οἰκουμένης, “of the inhabited world.” GALLAND.] that I will persevere in the declarations written above, undermine nothing, and preserve the faith of the orthodox in all things. And if I should be caught undermining anything of the agreements, I shall be subject to the severity of the laws. After hearing the exposition, I subscribed with my own hand.

Julian of Disphiladelphia acknowledged orthodoxy and approached the holy Catholic and apostolic [Col. 0884B] Church of God, anathematizing every heresy, especially that of the Tessarescaedecatites. And I swore by the venerable oath that if I should undermine anything of the declarations written above, I would be subject to the severity of the laws. And [Note: [Col. 0884D] In Greek, the Council of Chalcedon reads ἀρεσθείς, “being pleased,” which seems better. BALUZE.] being ill, I subscribed through Martyrius the lector.

[Note: [Col. 0884D] In the same council, Eutychius, chorepiscopus of Aulaca, is called the leader of the heresy of the Quartodecimans. BALUZE.]

Eutychius of the village of Aulacis, leader of the heresy of the Tessarescaedecatites, acknowledged the true faith of orthodoxy; and asking the most holy bishop Theophanius, the most reverent [Note: [Col. 0884D] In the same source, “chorepiscopus.” BALUZE.] bishop Jacobus, and the most reverent presbyter and steward Charisius, I approached the holy Catholic and apostolic Church, anathematizing every heresy, especially that of the Tessarescaedecatites, in which I had previously erred; and I assent to the exposition of the right faith written above, anathematizing those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter [Col. 0884C] according to the custom of the Catholic and apostolic holy Church. And I swore by the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and by the piety and victory of the lords Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinian, the perpetual Augusti: but if I should undermine anything of the declarations written above, I shall be subject to the severity of the laws. And I subscribed with my own hand.

Patricius, presbyter from the village of Parazioxili, through the hand of Maximus, my fellow presbyter, because I did not know letters, acknowledged the true faith of orthodoxy; and I asked the most religious bishop Theophanius and the most reverent presbyter Charisius, and I asked to communicate as soon as possible with the holy Catholic and apostolic Church of the orthodox; and I anathematize every heresy, especially that of the Tessarescaedecatites, and those who do not [Col. 0884D] celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the custom of the Church. And I swore by the holy and life-giving Trinity, and by the piety and victory of our lords Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinian [Col. 0885A] the perpetual Augusti, that if I should undermine anything of these declarations, I would be subject to the severity of the laws.

Zenon, [Note: [Col. 0885C] Thus the codices of Marius Mercator, except that the Vatican manuscript has “poetha.” In Greek there is ποθε, which makes no sense. From this, or from a similar reading, the word found in the copies of Mercator arose. In the ancient version of the Council of Ephesus, p. 535, it has “Pithatae.” Justellus’s codex, cited by Labbe in the margin of p. 688 of volume three of the Councils, has “potia.” The author of the ancient version of the Council of Chalcedon used a codex in which nothing of this kind was present. Perhaps περιοδέτης should be read. Concerning this word, see Marca, book II of On Concord, at the end of chapter 13. BALUZE.—In Justellus’s manuscript: “from the territory of Acaripotia.” Greek: χωρίου Σαγορου πύθε, thus. GALLAND.] from the territory of Sagaris, a poet and a member of the Tessarescaedecatite heresy, acknowledged the true faith of orthodoxy; and asking the most holy bishop Theophanius, the most reverent chorepiscopus Jacobus, and the most reverent presbyter and steward Charisius, I approached the most holy and Catholic Church, anathematizing every heresy, especially that of the Tessarescaedecatites, in which I had previously erred. And I assent to the exposition of the orthodox written above [Note: [Col. 0885C] Greek, προγεγραμμένη, “written above.” GALLAND.], anathematizing those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the custom of the Catholic Church. And I swear by the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and by the victory of our lords Flavius Theodosius and Flavius Valentinian, the perpetual Augusti. [Col. 0885B] But if I should undermine anything of the declarations written above, I shall be subject to the severity of the laws. I, Flavius Palladius, lent him my hand because, being present, he did not know letters.

After these matters had been read out, the holy synod decreed that no one might present, write, or compose any other faith besides that which was established by the holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea in the Holy Spirit. But those who should dare either to compose or to present another faith to persons wishing to be converted to acknowledgment of the truth from paganism, Judaism, or any other heresy—if they are bishops or clerics—shall be deprived, bishops of the episcopate and clerics of the clerical office; and if they are laymen, they shall be anathema. Likewise, if any should be found—whether bishops, clerics, or laymen—believing or teaching those things [Col. 0885C] that are written in the exposition brought forward by Charisius the presbyter concerning the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God, or indeed the impious and perverse doctrines of Nestorius, which are also written below, they shall be subject to the judgment of the holy and universal synod. Thus it shall be clear that a bishop will be deprived of the episcopate and deposed; a cleric will likewise be removed from the clerical office; and if he is a layman, he too will be anathema, as was said above.

## EXCERPTS

[Note: [Col. 0885C] Here begins, in Garnerius, the first collection of excerpts from Nestorius. The same Garnerius prefixes the following notice: “This collection is placed before the other two [Col. 0885D] because of the chronological order, in which it precedes the others. For it is mentioned in the letters that Cyril wrote concerning the case of Nestorius to the holy Celestine, where it says: ‘So that Your Holiness may clearly perceive both what he says and thinks and what our blessed and great Fathers handed down, I have sent volumes containing the statements of the chapters’ (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 14). Since the letters were sent in the year 430, at the beginning of spring, the collection must have been made at the beginning of the year 430, and indeed, as I think, at a synod of the Church of Alexandria convened before Lent, from which the second warning letter to Nestorius was sent. Some doubt may nevertheless remain, but it will be removed in the preface to the third collection. The translator may be believed to be Marius Mercator, first because these excerpts are found in the same codex as his other works; second, because their Latin is not different from that which Marius testifies in the preface to the Sermons of Nestorius that he translated word for word from Greek into Latin. Add that the version is extremely ancient. Two considerations nevertheless oppose this opinion. The first is that, in works whose translator is certainly Mercator, there is a different version from that found here of the same statements of Nestorius. The second is that Cyril of Alexandria writes to Celestine that he translated into Latin the same statements that I too, as far as it was possible through others who are in Alexandria, took care to render in Latin. Yet it often happens that at different times the same author expresses the same passages, περικοπαί, of a discourse in different words. Further, it is certain, or at least highly probable, that the version which survives from the Greek Acts of the Council of Ephesus [Col. 0886C] was prepared from them and therefore differs from the Alexandrian version. The Greek text seemed worth setting against the Latin version, so that the latter might appear all the more faithful in proportion as it was more genuine and straightforward. It also seemed useful to note in the margin from which work of Nestorius the passages, περικοπαί, had been taken, and in what other places they were used.” EDIT.]

From Nestorius’s own book, quire XVI, on doctrine.

Whenever Holy Scripture is going to speak either of Christ’s birth from the blessed Virgin or of his death, it nowhere calls him God, but either Christ, Jesus, or Lord, since these three names indicate two natures: now one, now the other, now both. What I say is as follows. Whenever Scripture recalls to us the birth from the Virgin, what does it say? “God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4). It does not say, “God sent the Word.” Rather, it uses the name that indicates two natures. Because the Son is human and God, it says, “God sent his Son, made from a woman.” Thus, if you hear “made from a woman,” you should be ashamed even of the name used, which indicates two natures, so that by his birth from the blessed Virgin you call him Son. For the Virgin, Christ-bearer (Χριστοτόκος), gave birth to God’s Son. But since the Son of God is twofold in natures, [Note: [Col. 0886D] Baluze, followed by Gallandius, rejects the negative particle.] she did not give birth to the Son of God; rather, she gave birth to the man who is Son because of the Son joined to him.

The same, from quire XXI.

See what follows, heretic. I do not begrudge the Virgin the name Χριστοτόκος, “Christ-bearer.” For I confess that she who conceived God is worthy of reverence, she through whom the Lord of all passed, through whom the sun of righteousness shone forth; but further [Note: [Col. 0886D] That is: “But I suspect that you are applauding me without fully understanding my meaning. What did I intend to express by the word ‘passed’? Hear this. I did not say ‘passed’ instead of ‘was born,’ etc.” The Greek reads: Πάλιν ὑποπτεύω τὸν κρότον· πῶς τὸ Προσῆλθεν ἐνοήσατε; Οὐκ εἴρηταί μοι τὸ Προσῆλθεν ἀντὶ τοῦ Ἐγεννήθη, etc. It is found in Baluze, followed by Gallandius: “But further I suspect how you have understood the applause concerning what I said, ‘passed.’ I did not say, etc.” EDIT.] I suspect applause. How did you understand this that I said, “passed”? I did not say “passed” in place of “was born.” For I do not so quickly forget my own words. I have been thoroughly taught by Scripture that God passed through the Virgin Χριστοτόκος, “Christ-bearer”; [Note: [Col. 0887D] Baluze, followed by Gallandius, has: “But I have never learned that God was born from her.” “Nowhere,” etc. EDIT.] but I have not been taught that he was born.

Again, after other matters. Nowhere does divine Scripture assert that God was born from the Virgin Χριστοτόκος, “Christ-bearer,” but rather Jesus Christ, the Son, the Lord. Let us all confess this. For whoever does not immediately accept what divine Scripture has taught is wretched: “Arise, and take the child and his mother” (Matt. 2:13). This is the voice of the angels, indeed your own. Perhaps the archangel knew the circumstances of his birth [Note: [Col. 0887D] The same distinguished men have: “the archangels knew the events of the birth,” more consonant with the Greek, Τὰ κατὰ τὴν γέννησιν ᾔδεσαν οἱ ἀρχάγγελοι.] : “Arise, and take the child and his mother.” He did not say, “Arise, and take God and his mother.”

The same, from quire XIX.

What, then, were we saying? “Do not be afraid to take Mary your wife; for what has been born in her” (whether we say “born” or “made,” the meaning suffers no harm), “what has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20). If we say that God the Word was born in the flesh, there is a difference between being together with the one being born and being born. “What has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit”; that is, the Holy Spirit created what is in her. The Fathers therefore saw, as those who knew the holy Scriptures, that if we call the one who became incarnate “born,” God the Word will be found to be a creature of the Holy Spirit, or to have two fathers. But if we call him “made,” God the Word will be found to be [Note: [Col. 0887D] So also shortly afterward. But here the Vatican codex has “or the Son.” BALUZE.] a creature of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, avoiding the language of birth, they said this: “Who descended for our salvation and became incarnate.” What does “became incarnate” mean? Not that he was changed from divinity into flesh. When they said that he became incarnate from the Holy Spirit, they followed the evangelist. For when the evangelist came to ἐνανθρώπησις, “becoming human,” he avoided speaking of birth concerning the Word and spoke of incarnation. Hear where: “And the Word became flesh” (John 1:14). He did not say, “The Word became through flesh.” For wherever the apostles or evangelists mention the Son, they do not say that he was born from a woman. Observe, I ask, where they use the name “Son”; and what was born from a woman, they call “born.” But where they mention the Word, no one dares to speak of birth through humanity. [Note: [Col. 0887D] The codices mentioned above have: “Hear: blessed John the evangelist, when he had come to the Word [and] his ἐνανθρώπησις, hear what he says,” etc. The Greek exemplar reads: Ἄκουε· ὁ μακάριος [Col. 0888D] Ἰωάννης ὁ εὐαγγελιστὴς ἐλθὼν εἰς τὸν Λόγον καὶ τὴν ἐνανθρώπησιν αὐτοῦ, ἅκουσον οἷά φησιν. EDIT.] Hear the blessed John the evangelist when he had come to the Word and his ἐνανθρώπησις, “becoming human”; hear what he says: “The Word became flesh,” that is, he assumed flesh; “and dwelt among us,” that is, he put on our nature; “and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory,” the glory of the Son. He did not say, “We saw the birth of the Word.”

From quire XV.

Thus we also call Christ, according to the flesh, God, because of the conjunction that he has with God the Word, knowing that he is the man who appears. [Note: [Col. 0888D] We have emended this with the help of the Greek text and the ancient version of the Council of Ephesus; for the copies of Marius Mercator read “And having been heard.” In the Council of Chalcedon: “Hear, therefore.” See the New Collection of the Councils, p. 1143. BALUZE.] Hear Paul proclaiming both: “From the Jews,” he says, “is the Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all” (Rom. 9:5). First he confesses the man; then, by the conjunction with God, he calls the one who appears “God,” lest anyone should think that Christianity worships a man.

The same, from quire XXVII.

But just as we called God the maker of all things and called Moses “god”—for he says, “I have appointed you god to Pharaoh” [Col. 0888B] (Exod. 7:1)—and called Israel the son of God—for he says, “Israel is my firstborn son”—and just as we call Saul “christ”: “I will not lay my hand upon him,” he says, “because he is the Lord’s christ” [Note: [Col. 0888D] Read “the Lord’s christ,” as the Vulgate and the Septuagint have it. The Acts of the Council of Ephesus, session 1, p. 1067, where these Nestorian statements are found, likewise have this reading. GALLAND.] (1 Sam. 24:7); and likewise Cyrus: “Thus says the Lord to my christ, Cyrus” (Isa. 45:1); and the holy Babylonian: “For I command those who have been sanctified, and I lead them” (Isa. 13:3); so also we call the Lord Christ God, Son, and holy. But although the communion of all is similar, their dignity is not the same. [Note: [Col. 0888D] Although the Greek text and the ancient version of the Council of Ephesus indicate that “names” should be read here, we have not altered the text, because this reading is constant in two copies of Marius Mercator and in Julian’s codex of the ancient version of the Council of Chalcedon. BALUZE.]

The same, from quire XV.

“Let this mind be in you,” he says, “which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:5–7). He does not say: “Let this mind be in you which was also in God the Word, who, though he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant.” But since he calls Christ, as a designation of two natures, he safely called him both the servant-form that he assumed and God, since this can be said without sin concerning the twofold and separable character of the natures.

The same, from quire XVI.

“So that at the name of Jesus,” he says, “every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (ibid., 10–11). Because of the one who carried, I honor the one who was carried; because of the invisible one, I venerate the one who appears. God is never separated from the one who appears. Therefore I too do not separate the honor. I separate the natures, but I make the veneration one.

The same, from quire XVII, on doctrine.

God the Word was indeed Son and God with the Father even before the incarnation. But in the last times he assumed the form of a servant. Yet since he is Son both beforehand and so called after the assumption, he cannot be called a divided Son, lest we establish two sons. But because he is joined to the one who was Son from the beginning, [Note: [Col. 0889D] Baluze does not have the words “who is joined to him,” and immediately adds a note under the word “sonship”: “This passage is mutilated. See the ancient version of the Council of Ephesus, p. 474.” EDIT.] and because he is joined to him, he cannot be so according to the dignity of sonship, I say, not according to the natures. Therefore God the Word is called Christ, because he has an everlasting conjunction with Christ.

The same, from quire XV.
