[Col. 0889B] [Note: [Col. 0889D] Another similar passage of Nestorius occurs in the fifth session of the Lateran Council under Pope Martin, where it is said to be taken from the second book written by Epiphanius of Myasa, and likewise in the fourth session of the Sixth Ecumenical Council, where the older editions before the Roman edition have “Epiphanius of Myse.” This reading originated in Merlini’s edition, who, having read in the old book of the Church of Beauvais—which, I think, he was using—“epifans mq; es eos,” and lacking the Greek text, patched together the reading presented by the old editions. The Roman editions replaced “which Epiphanius of Myse wrote” with “which he entitled the distinguished initiation.” The Greek text of the Sixth Council can further be used to correct the Greek text of the Lateran Council. BALUZE.]

Let us therefore preserve the conjunction of the natures without confusion; let us confess God in the man, and let us worship, by a certain divine conjunction, the man who is to be worshiped together with God almighty.

The same, from quire VI.

Consider also what follows immediately from these words: “So that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, able to help the one being tempted, since he himself was tempted in what he suffered” (Heb. 2:17–18). Therefore the one who suffered is a merciful high priest. But the temple is passible, not the life-giving God of the temple that suffered.

The same, from quire XVII.

“So that you may know,” he says, “how great was the conjunction of the Divinity, even when the Lord’s flesh could be seen in an infant.” For the infant and the Lord of the infant were the same. You have praised the statement, but do not praise it too carelessly. For I said that the infant and the inhabitant of the infant were the same.

The same, from quire I.

For the works of the Trinity are common and are to be divided only among the substances. But the splendid glory of the Only-begotten is sometimes assigned to the Father: “For it is my Father,” he says, “who glorifies me” (John 8:34); sometimes to the Spirit: “For the Spirit,” he says, “of truth will glorify me” (John 16:14); sometimes to Christ’s power.

The same, from quire XVI.

This is the one who says: “God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). This is the one who tasted death for three days. But I adore him together with the Divinity, as a fellow worker of divine authority.

And after other matters. Because of the one who carried, I honor the one who was carried; and because of the hidden one, I venerate the one who appears. God is never separated from the one who appears. Therefore I too do not separate the honor from him. I separate the natures, but I make the veneration one. He who was fashioned from the Spirit is not God in himself; he who was buried in the tomb is not God in himself. For if this were so, we would certainly be worshipers of dead men and of the dead. But because God is in the one assumed, the one who has been assumed is called God from the one who assumed him, as joined to the one who assumed him.

The same, from quire three, against the heretics, when he was speaking about the Spirit.

“For how,” he says, “can he be a servant who works together with the Son and the Father?” And if anyone should inquire into the works of the Spirit, he will find that they are not different from the works of the Father and the Son—not because the one Divinity is divided, but because divine Scripture distributes among the individual substances the things that belong to one power, [Note: [Col. 0890D] Greek, καθ’ ἑκάστην ὑπόστασιν, “to each hypostasis.” A little earlier, in the passages cited from quire I, Mercator translated καὶ μόναις ὑποστάσεσι, “and only to the subsistences,” as “and only among the substances.” Cyril repeats this passage below, p. 242. The Greek is found in volume III of the Councils, p. 1381. Shortly afterward in the text, p. 1069, appears καί μοι σκόπει τὸ ὅμοιον (τῆς τριάδος) ἐκ τῶν ἐν ἔργοις καιρῶν ἀρξάμενον. The ancient translator has: “That this is true may be observed from those works that were undertaken in time.” In general, our author regularly renders ὑπόστασις as substantia, whereas Cyril’s translator usually renders it as subsistentia and sometimes as hypostasis. It is enough to have noted this once here. GALLAND.] so that the likeness of the Trinity has begun from the times of its works. God the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). The Father made the assumed man sit with him (Eph. 2:6). For he says, “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1). The Spirit glorified the glory of the one who was assumed: “For when the Spirit of truth comes, he himself will glorify me” (John 16:14).

The same, from quire VI.

When he said concerning Christ that he had been sent to proclaim release to captives (Luke 4:18), he added this as an apostle and said: “This one who was made a faithful high priest” (Heb. 2:17). For this one was made; he had not previously been so perpetually. This one who gradually advanced to the dignity of high priest, heretic. Hear the voice proclaiming this to you more clearly: “In the days of his flesh,” he says, “offering prayers and supplications to the one who was able to save him from death, with a loud cry and tears; and having been heard because of his reverence, although he was a Son, he learned obedience from the things he suffered; and having been perfected, he became for all who obey him the cause of eternal salvation” (Heb. 5:7–9). But what gradually advances is perfected, heretic. [Col. 0891A] [Note: [Col. 0891D] The Greek likewise has, περὶ οὗ καὶ Ἰωάννης, “concerning whom John also.” Here Nestorius suffered a lapse of memory, for the passage is Luke 2:52. GALLAND.] Concerning him John also cries out in the Gospels: “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom and grace” (Luke 2:52). To this Paul also appropriately refers when he says: “Having been perfected, he became for those who obey him the cause of eternal salvation, having been called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek” (Heb. 5:9–10).

And after other matters. “He is called high priest,” he says. Why, then, do you think differently from Paul? Why, by mingling the impassible God the Word with an earthly body, do you make the high priest passible?

The same, from quire VII.

“Therefore, brothers, partakers of a holy heavenly calling, consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus, faithful to the one who made him” (Heb. 3:1–2).

And after other matters. Since this one high priest is therefore ours, compassionate, or related to us, and steadfast, do not ever depart from faith in him. For he was sent to us from the promised blessing, from the seed of Abraham, as one offering sacrifice for himself and for his own bodily kindred. It should be noted that he confesses that every high priest needs a sacrifice; and when he makes an exception for Christ as though he did not need one, he says that in these matters he offers [Note: [Col. 0891D] An error of the copyists or typesetters. Mercator must have written “and for his kindred.” The Greek, p. 1071, reads: ἐν τούτοις ὑπὲρ ἑαυτοῦ φησιν προσφέρειν, καὶ τοῦ συγγενοῦς, θυσίαν, “in these matters he says that he offers a sacrifice both for himself and for his kindred.” The ancient translator has: “He affirms that he offered a sacrifice both for himself and for his kindred.” GALLAND.] and bears the sacrifice.

The same, from quire IV.

Hear, then, and examine the words carefully: “Whoever eats,” he says, “my flesh” (John 6:56). Remember that we are speaking of flesh, and that the name “flesh” is not invented by me, lest I appear to them a false interpreter. “Whoever eats,” he says, “my flesh and drinks my blood.” Did he perhaps say: “Whoever eats my Divinity [Col. 0891C] and whoever drinks my Divinity”? “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

And after other matters. But let us come to the προκείμενον (*prokeimenon*), that is, the subject or argument. [Note: Baluze, followed by Galland, reads *procimenum*. EDIT.] “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” Remember that we are speaking about flesh: “Just as the living Father sent me” (ibid., 58)—me, who appear visibly. But perhaps I am not interpreting correctly. Let us examine what follows. “Just as the living Father sent me.” He says that this concerns the Divinity; I say that it concerns the humanity. Let us see who is the false interpreter. “Just as the living Father sent me.”

[Note: The passage is defective and must be restored by comparison with the Greek. For we read there as follows: “The heretic also says: ‘Here he speaks of the Divinity. “He sent me,” he says, that is, God the Word, etc.’ That is, according to the old translation: ‘The heretic also says: “Here he expresses the Divinity”; for the meaning, according to them, is: “God the Word sent me: just as the living Father sent me, and I, God the Word, live because of the Father.” Then what follows immediately: “Whoever eats me will also live.” What, I ask, are we eating—the Divinity or the humanity?’” GALLAND.]

The heretic says that here the Divinity sent me, God the Word. “Just as the living Father sent me,” according to them, “and I, God the Word, live because of the Father.” What comes next? “Whoever eats me will also live.” What are we eating—the Divinity or the flesh?

## From the same author, from gathering XVI

And yet, he says, if you investigate the whole of the New Testament, nowhere in it will you find death attributed to God, but either to Christ, or to the Son, or to the Lord. For when Christ, Son, and Lord are spoken of by Holy Scripture concerning the Only-Begotten, it indicates two natures: sometimes it signifies the Divinity, sometimes the humanity, and sometimes both. Thus, when Paul writes and declares, “When we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. V, 10), he signifies the humanity of the Son. Again, when the same apostle says to the Hebrews, “God spoke to us in the Son, through whom he also made the ages” (Hebr. I, 2), he signifies the Divinity of the Son. For the flesh did not make the ages, since it came into being after many ages.

And after other matters. The Divinity did not have James as a brother; nor do we proclaim the death of God the Word when we eat the Lord’s blood and body.

## From the same author, from gathering XXIII

I see, he says, that our people possess immense reverence and the most ardent devotion, but that they stumble through ignorance in the dogma of the knowledge of God (θεογνωσία).

[Note: The old translator of the Council of Ephesus renders this “the dogma of piety.” The old translator of the Council of Chalcedon renders it “divine knowledge.” GALLAND.]

But this is not the people’s fault; rather, to speak honorably, their former teachers did not have time to demonstrate the doctrines to you accurately.

[Note: These words belong to Peter, presbyter of Alexandria, and therefore should have been separated from what precedes. BALUZE.]

Behold, here he plainly admits that no one before him had preached such things to the people.

[Note: Before these subscriptions, the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, session 1, p. 1077, read: “The sentence of deposition issued by the holy synod against Nestorius.” GALLAND. — The subscriptions are not found in Garnerius, who, as we said above, presents from this session of the synod nothing except excerpts from Nestorius. EDIT.]

# SECOND COLLECTION

Its title in Mercator here is: “Excerpts from various books or treatises of Nestorius, chapters excerpted by Bishop Cyril and translated by us from Greek into Latin.”

[Col. 0897]

### 1. From the completed codex, gathering XXVI

Among other things:

We ought to know this; for just now I recall the Council of Nicaea, which nowhere dared to say that God the Word was born from the Virgin Mary. For it says: “We believe in one almighty Father, and in one Lord Jesus Christ.” Observe that, after first naming Christ—a designation that demonstrates the conjunction of two natures—they did not say “in one God the Word,” but adopted a name that signified both, so that, when you hear of death, you would not be disturbed by any novelty through their condescension, nor would your hearing be wounded when you hear that he was crucified and buried, as though the Divinity itself had suffered.

Then let us see what they add: “We also believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Only-Begotten, who was born from God the Father, consubstantial with the Father, who for us came down and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit.” They did not say that he was born from the Holy Spirit. You see how they interpret by condescending, since they said that he was made human. “This one,” they say, “we call incarnate,” not indicating a change in the divine nature through its receiving flesh, but the indwelling that he exercised in the human being.

### 2. And after some intervening material in the same work

Hold on to this, he says: Omitting the words, “We believe in God the Word, his Only-Begotten Son,” they said instead: “We believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, consubstantial with the Father, true God from true God, through whom all things were made, who for us human beings and for our salvation came down and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit, from the Virgin Mary, and was made human.” They nowhere said, “was born.” Why, we may ask? So that they would not introduce two births of the Divinity.

### 3. Again, in the same work, after some intervening material

Wishing to demonstrate clearly that, when the name “Son” is used, the word does not invariably signify the one who is God, but is introduced as a common designation, he says: Thus Scripture says, “God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law” (Gal. IV, 4). Here it certainly demonstrates two natures; but it narrates what occurred only with respect to the human being. Ask the contentious one who was made under the law: God the Word? Certainly not.

### 4. Again, from another codex, in the first gathering

Its beginning is as follows: “I still have many things to say to you.” And after some intervening material:

The glorification of the Only-Begotten is sometimes attributed to the Father, as in the saying, “My Father is he who glorifies me” (John VIII, 54); sometimes it is attributed to the Spirit, for he says, “The Spirit of truth will glorify me” (John XVI, 13); and sometimes it is assigned to Christ’s power, as it is written: “They went out and preached the Word everywhere, the Lord cooperating and confirming the Word through the accompanying signs.”

### 5. Again, in gathering VIII, concerning passages from the Apostle’s Epistle to the Hebrews

For when they hear the name “apostle” in Christ, they wrongly understand God the Word to be an apostle. Likewise, when they read the title “high priest,” they imagine God to be a high priest—an astonishing madness. For who, on hearing the office of an apostle, would not immediately see that a human being is indicated? Who, on hearing the name of high priest, would summon the nature of the Divinity to the ministry of priesthood? If God is a high priest, who will be the one who ought to be worshiped through his office? If God is going to offer sacrifices as a high priest, there will be no one to whom they are offered—what, after all, is now worthy of the Divinity, if he offers sacrifices as an inferior to one superior?

And he adds: Thus, then, he says, how did God appear to them as one who should be called high priest, when he has absolutely no need of sacrifice, according to the rite of priesthood, for his advancement? For he is the everlasting possessor of Divinity. “For a high priest is chosen and taken from among human beings and appointed on behalf of human beings before God,” etc. (Heb. V, 1).

### 6. And he adds

“He did not take hold of angels,” he says, “but of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. II, 16). Is the Divinity the seed of Abraham? Hear also the following words: “Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect” (ibid., 17). Is this said of the Divinity? For what brothers like himself could God the Word have? Consider also what is added to these words: “So that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God; for in that in which he himself suffered and was tested, he is able to help those who are tested” (ibid., 18). Therefore, the one who suffered is the merciful high priest; but the temple is passible, not the one who gives it life, namely God. The seed of Abraham is the one who is “the same yesterday and today” (Heb. XIII, 8), according to the words of the apostle Paul—not the one who said, “Before Abraham was, I am” (John VIII, 58). He is the one who was made like his brothers in every respect and assumed the brotherhood of a human soul and body (Heb. II, 17), not the one who said, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9).

### 7. Again, in gathering XIX, when he was speaking, as it were, against Arius

Those people, although in their madness they declare God the Word to be lesser than the Father’s greater Divinity, nevertheless do not acknowledge him as a recent being. But these others even pronounce him to be second and later than blessed Mary, and declare that a temporal mother is greater in Divinity than her maker.

[Note: Manuscript B reads: “they assign him to the divinity that makes the times.” EDIT.]

Indeed, they do not even concede that she is the mother of Christ. For if it was not a human nature but God the Word whom she gave birth to, she who gave birth is in no way found to be the mother of the one who was born. For how could she be in any way the mother of one who is alien to the nature of the woman who gave birth? But if she is called a true mother by them, then the one brought forth is a human being, not the Divinity.

[Note: The old books read “born of the Divinity”; Baluze agrees with them, except that he thinks “Divinity” should be emended. EDIT.]

For it is proper to every mother to give birth to one consubstantial with herself. Therefore, she will not be a mother who did not give birth to one consubstantial with herself. Since they call her a mother, she gave birth to one who was similar to her according to substance.

[B. “who was her own.”]

But who will be similar to him according to substance? Without doubt, the one who came into being through the work of the Holy Spirit. “For what has been born in her,” Scripture says, “is from the Holy Spirit,” with whom God the Word was continually present.

[Baluze omits “God the Word.”]

God the Word was not born from Mary, but remained in the one who was born from her. He did not have his beginning from the Virgin, but was inseparably joined for all time to the one who, growing and gradually taking shape over the course of months, was formed in the Virgin’s womb.

But it is one thing to say, “The one who was born remains with him,” and another to say that the one who remains with the one born is the same one who, in order to be born, required the passage of months.

[Note: B reads: “to remain with the one who was born”; and another thing is to say that the one who remains with the one born is this same one who, in order to be born, needed the course of months. EDIT.]

### 8. Again, from another treatise, gathering XV [B: XX]

“This Jesus,” he says, “God raised up; God did not die, but raised him up.” Apollinaris, hear the words of the apostle Peter; and you too, Arian impiety with Apollinaris, hear them. “God raised up this Jesus” (Acts X, 40), the one who appeared visibly to human eyes; this one who was crucified on the wood;

[B: “fastened to the wood.”]

this one whom Thomas touched with his hands, who cried out to him, “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke XXIV, 39). And when the disciple believed these words and, after touching him, became certain of the resurrection of the flesh that had been crucified, he glorified God, the maker of wonders, saying, “My Lord and my God” (John XX, 28)—certainly not calling the thing he had touched “God.”

### 9. Again, in gathering XXIX

[Note: Baluze: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” The question was which was the first substance of the existence that bore the human being. Paul, however, narrates from the Law what occurred, etc. EDIT.]

Paul narrates both the essence that was incarnate and the unchangeability of the incarnate Divinity, which remained after the union. For this reason he also cries out in writing: “Have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, although he was established in the form of God, took the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 5).

But the Apostle, taking the name “Christ” as a designation signifying two natures, can irreproachably call him both one who took the form of a servant and God, dividing the things that are said to signify the twofold nature.

### 10. And after much else, in the same book

For our nature, he says, intercedes for us in the use of Christ, established as a garment, relying on defenses for its blameless origin. And because that sin—which was previously figured—became the cause of the entire race, it provided the occasion, O human being, for the assumption of humanity, so that through flesh the corruption that had occurred through flesh might be destroyed.

[Note: B: “Just as he was the occasion for sin.” EDIT.]

The burial on the third day belongs to this flesh, not to the Divinity. Its feet were held by nails. The Holy Spirit formed this flesh in the womb. Concerning this flesh the Lord said to the Jews, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II, 19).

Do I alone call Christ twofold, when he himself calls both the temple destructible and God the one who raises it? But if it was God who was being destroyed, O Arian—and may this rightly be turned against the head of blasphemy—

[Note: Baluze emends *blasphemiarum* to *blasphemium*, but thinks the following note is needed: “*Blasphemium*, that is, *blasphemia*. The letter of the bishops of the Council of Sardica to Pope Julius in a very old Saxon manuscript of the Colbertine Library: ‘Or certainly the serpent devil would pour out the poison of blasphemies.’ Hilary of Poitiers, in his book *Against Constantius Augustus*, already dead: ‘I found a synod of the eastern bishops at Seleucia, where there was as much of blasphemies as pleased Constantius.’ The letter of Pope Celestine to Nestorius in the ancient version of the Council of Ephesus, p. 425: ‘How did it occur to you to direct words toward these questions, which it is blasphemy even to consider?’ The Council of Chalcedon, session 10: ‘because of the mass of blasphemies.’ Thus I read it in the Paris manuscript, as I recently noted, instead of what the editions have, *blasphemiarum*. The Council of Pope Martin at the Lateran, session 4: ‘not indeed fearing the blasphemy by which it is said.’ So the old manuscript of the Church of Beauvais reads, whereas the editions have *blasphemiam* where it is said. See the most learned Charles du Fresne, sieur du Cange, in his annotations on Anna Comnena, p. 335, and in his Glossary.” EDIT.]

—it would have been necessary to say, “Destroy this God, and in three days he will be raised.” If God died, if he was consigned to burial, then that saying in the Gospel is empty: “Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you?” (John VIII, 40).

But now he says: “Why do you seek to kill me, a man upon whose head a crown of thorns has been placed; a man who says, ‘God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’” (Matt. XXVII, 46), and who endured a death lasting three days. Worship this one together with the Divinity, as the associate of divine authority.

### 11. Again, after some intervening material in the same work

I worship him, he says, as the image of the Almighty: “God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II, 9).

Because of the one who uses it, I worship the thing that he uses; because of the one who is hidden, I honor what appears outwardly. In the one who is inseparable, I do not separate dignity, but I separate the natures and unite reverence.

God is not, in himself, what is to be laid in the tomb; otherwise we would plainly be worshipers of a human being, and of a dead human being. But since, in the assumed one, God is called God through the one who assumes, because the assumed one is joined to the one who assumes, therefore the demons also shudder at the name of the crucified flesh, knowing that God is joined to the crucified flesh but has not suffered together with it.

For this reason, too, the one who appeared visibly will come as judge, since he is joined to the Almighty Divinity.

### 12. Again, after much else in the same place

The Divinity, he says, did not have James as a brother; nor do we announce the death of God the Word when we are nourished by the Lord’s body and blood.

[B: “For the divine nature receives the sacrifice.”]

The divine nature receives the sacrifice; it is not itself sacrificed in the sacrifice.

### 13. Again, in another treatise against the Arians, gathering XIV

Who now could behold such an immense sea of benevolence: nature ruling together with its maker, the Divinity joined to the human being, commanding nothing without him, judging no one without him, caring for the living with him in supreme providence, and raising the dead together with him?

[B adds: “The heretics weaken and tear apart all these hopes, which are governed for all by the most powerful and benevolent Lord.” Baluze restores this passage.]

### 14. Again, in another treatise by the same author, in gathering V, concerning the passage of Holy Scripture where it says, “If you remember that your brother has something against you” (Matt. V, 23)

“Whoever eats,” he says, “flesh.” Remember that what was said, “Just as the living Father sent me” (John VI, 55), concerns flesh, since I am visible. But perhaps I am interpreting the saying wrongly; therefore let us hear from what follows: “Just as the living Father sent me, and I live through the Father” (ibid., v. 58). He understands the Divinity here; I speak of the human being.

Let us see who is the sound interpreter.

[Baluze: “the devious interpreter.”]

“Just as the living Father sent me.” Here the heretic says that the Divinity was sent and professes that he is speaking of God the Word: “Just as the living Father sent me.” Therefore, according to them, this too must be understood in the following way: “And I, God the Word, live through the Father.”

[Baluze: “I, God’s Word.”]

For after this it appears to say: “And whoever eats me will live.” Whom, then, are we eating—the Divinity or the flesh?

### 15. Again, in gathering VI of the same author, against the heretics, concerning Judas

Willingly I would inquire here about those heretics who, by mixing and blending the nature of the Divinity and the humanity into one concept, ask who it is who is betrayed and handed over to the Jews in this passage. For if a blending or commixture of both has taken place, which of the two was seized by the Jews—the Word of God or the nature of humanity? Who appears to have been killed? For I am compelled to use simpler expressions so that what is said may be clear to everyone.

Tell me, if you will, upon whom do the things that occurred fall? Surely not upon the nature of God, which you presume to confuse and blend by merging both together.

Therefore, is God the Word passible?

[Baluze: “the Word of God.”]

He has nothing in common with the flesh in the killing. Or was he led by the Jews to be killed? Why, then, now that you have blended both natures according to your own view, did we just hear Scripture narrating the power of the sacrament that the Lord handed over to his disciples, saying: “On the night on which he was betrayed, he took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and said to his disciples, ‘Take and eat from it, all of you; for this is my body’” (1 Cor. XI, 23)?

Why did he not say, “This is my Divinity, which will be broken for us”?

[Baluze: “for you.”]

And again, taking the cup and offering it, he did not say, “This is my Divinity, which will be poured out for you for the forgiveness of sins,” but rather this: “This is my blood, which will be poured out for you for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. XXVI, 28).

Separate the nature, but join the union. Confess Christ as the Son of God, but as a twofold Son, human and divine, so that the suffering may indeed be attributed to the human nature, while the release from suffering—which took place in the human being who suffered—may belong to the Divinity alone.

### 16. Again, elsewhere, in gathering IX, against the Jews

Separating, he says, the proper dignity of the natures from the one union.

### 17. Again, from another treatise, in gathering XXV

For this reason I want you to be cautious in approving or applauding. Division is not a union of the Divinity, nor of the power. When the Son is Christ, there is no division in these matters; but there is division in the Divinity and humanity according to what Christ is.

The Son is undivided; according to what he is as Son, he is undivided. For we do not have two Christs and two Sons, nor is there among us a first Christ and a second, nor one and another, nor again one Son and another Son. Rather, the very same one, the very same Son, is twofold—not in dignity, but in nature.

### 18. Again, in gathering XXVI, as though against Apollinaris

The reverence due to the two natures, he says, we call one dignity—that of the one who joined both.

[Baluze: “one, because of the dignity of the one who, etc.” EDIT.]

### 19. Again, elsewhere, from another treatise, in gathering XXXII, he says the same concerning Christ

Although we call Christ a temple, he is in no way separable from the Divinity, but is joined to God, possessing the whole divine operation, both God’s fellow-worker in creation and exercising dominion over all things together with him.

[Baluze omits “Concerning Christ.”]

### 20. Again, in another treatise by the same author, on the passage written, “If you remember that you have something against your brother,” as though against the heretics

Hear attentively to the words, he says: “Whoever eats,” he says, “my flesh.” Remember that what is said concerns flesh. Surely I did not add the name “flesh” myself, so that they might complain that I interpret the matter incorrectly.

“Whoever eats,” he says, “my flesh and drinks my blood”—surely, also, “whoever drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him”?

### 21. Again, from another treatise, gathering XXXI

I say this so that you may know how great and supreme a union of the Divinity existed even in the infant himself, when the Lord’s flesh is seen. For he himself was both an infant and the Lord of the infant himself.

You praised the expression, but I do not want you to approve it without examination. For I said: “He himself was the infant and the indweller of the infant.”

Again, from another codex, gathering II, as though against the Arians and Macedonians:

Devising an even greater insult against Christ, they sever the Holy Spirit from the divine nature, although he formed Christ’s humanity in the Virgin’s womb. For, as Scripture says, “What was born from her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I, 20). He restored, according to righteousness, what had been formed: for, as Scripture says, “He was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit” (1 Tim. III, 16).

He made Christ terrifying and dreadful to the demons: “For I cast out demons,” he says, “by the Spirit of God” (Luke XI, 20). He fashioned his flesh into a temple: “For I saw the Spirit,” he says, “descending like a dove and remaining upon him” (John I, 32). He granted him his ascension into heaven: for, as Scripture says, “After giving instructions through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up into heaven” (Acts I, 2).

This Spirit, I say, who granted such great glory, is asserted by them to be a servant—

# THIRD COLLECTION

Excerpts from various treatises of Nestorius, cited by Saint Cyril in the five books of the Contradictions.

[Col. 0903]

[Col. 0903B] Concerning these five books of the *Contradictions* of Saint Cyril, Photius writes as follows (*Codex* 169): “The five books of Saint Cyril against the blasphemies of Nestorius were read. The first refutes ten principal charges of Nestorius; the second, thirteen; the third, six; and the fourth and fifth, seven each,” and so forth.

## From Book I

1. “I often asked them: Do you say that the Godhead was born from the holy Virgin? At these words they immediately recoil,” etc. *Sermon 5.*

2. “See what follows, heretic. I do not begrudge this expression to the Virgin who gave birth to Christ,” etc. *Sermon 5.*

3. “Thus also elsewhere he says: ‘He has spoken to us in the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages; who, being the radiance of his glory,’” etc. [Col. 0903C] *Sermon 7.*

4. “‘If Christ is God,’ he says, ‘and Christ arose from blessed Mary, why should the Virgin not be the Mother of God?’” etc. *Sermon 5.*

5. “Concerning blessed John the Baptist it is proclaimed by the holy angels that the infant was to be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother’s womb,” etc. *Sermon 5.*

6. “‘For I rejoice,’ he says, ‘when I see your zeal,’” etc. *Sermon 3.*

7. “But we must pay attention to what has now come to my mind: even the Council of Nicaea nowhere dared to say that God was born from Mary,” etc. *Sermon 3.*

8. “They followed the evangelist. For when the evangelist came to narrate the humanization, he avoided saying ‘generation’ [Col. 0903D] in connection with God the Word and instead used ‘incarnation,’” etc. *Sermon 3.*

9. “Yet they foolishly assert that the Word of God, which is certainly greater in divinity, is more recent,” etc. *Sermon 3.*

10. “I have already said many times: If anyone among you is rather simple-minded,” etc. *Sermon 5.*

## From Book II

1. “If you put forward *Theotokos* in simple faith, I would have no objection to the expression, while seeking the meaning of the word,” etc. *Sermon 5.*

2. “Therefore, whenever the sacred Scriptures expound the birth of Christ from the blessed Virgin, they nowhere say ‘God,’ but either ‘Christ’ or ‘Lord,’” etc. *Sermon 2.*

[Col. 0904B] 3. “For he says: ‘God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law,’” etc. *Sermon 3.*

4. “But just as we call that one the God who created all things, and Moses himself ‘God,’” etc. *Sermon 2.*

5. “Say of the one who assumed that he is God,” etc. *Sermon 2.*

6. “Therefore I want you to hold firmly and cautiously,” etc. *Sermon 2.*

7. “That glorification of the Only-Begotten is sometimes ascribed to the Father,” etc. *Sermon 10.*

8. “He was indeed God the Word even before he became human, Son and God, and consenting with the Father,” etc. *Sermon 2.*

9. “Therefore, so that it might be demonstrated to them more clearly who this is whom they have worshiped,” etc. *Sermon 11.*

10. “Nor is Christ merely a man, O slanderer, [Col. 0904C] but man at once and God,” etc. *Sermon 7.*

11. “I venerate him as the image of almighty divinity,” etc. *Sermon 7.*

12. “What was formed in the womb is not God in itself,” etc. *Sermon 7.*

13. “But this one is, according to the flesh, a kinsman of Israel,” etc.; “this one is, according to his observable nature, a man”; “this one, in Paul’s words, was born from the seed of David,” etc. *Sermon 2.*

## From Book III

1. “For when they hear the name of ‘apostle,’ they understand God the Word himself as the apostle,” etc. *Sermon 6.*

2. “He did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham,” etc. *Sermon 6.*

3. “The seed of Abraham is the one who is the same yesterday and today, as Paul says,” [Col. 0904D] “not the one who said: ‘Before Abraham came to be, I am,’” etc. *Sermon 6.*

4. “This one, the faithful high priest made so by God, was made such; for he did not exist from eternity,” etc. *Sermon 6.*

5. “Since therefore this one alone is for us a merciful, kindred, and steadfast high priest, beware lest you be moved away from his faith,” etc. *Sermon 6.*

6. “You certainly remember what I have often said to you, when I distinguished two natures in Christ,” etc. *Sermon 2.*

## From Book IV

1. “God the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. The Father made the assumed humanity sit with him,” etc. *Sermon 3.*

[Col. 0905A] 2. “And the evident proof of this cooperation is,” etc. *Sermon 10.*

3. “Building a greater insult, he says, against him, and separating the spirit from the divine nature, which formed his humanity,” etc. *Sermon 3.*

4. “‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him,’” etc. *Sermon 9.*

5. “I shall also mention the words of that scandal,” etc. *Sermon 9.*

6. “Hear also this name, ‘Lord,’ used sometimes of Christ’s humanity, sometimes of his divinity, and sometimes of both,” etc. *Sermon 2.*

7. “But why also, as we heard shortly before, if both have been mingled, as you suppose, does our Lord, when he was handing on the power of the mystery to the disciples, say thus?” etc. *Sermon 8.*

## From Book V

[Col. 0905B] 1. “We have shown that in the birth from Christ’s mother, the Virgin, divine Scripture uses the name ‘Son.’ Hear now also how, in the account of his death, the name ‘God’ is placed somewhere, so that we may introduce a suffering God: ‘When we were enemies,’ he says, ‘we were reconciled to God through the death of God the Word.’” *Sermon 2.*

[Col. 0906A] 2. “Hear also another testimony of theirs. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory,” etc. *Sermon 5.*

3. “Although I am in the form of God, I assumed the form of a servant; although I am God the Word, I am seen in the flesh; although I am Lord of the universe, I assumed the person of a poor man for your sake; although I visibly hunger, I supply food to those who hunger.” *Sermon 5.*

4. “I would gladly ask the heretics who mingle the nature of divinity and humanity into one essence: who is the one now handed over by the traitor to the Jews?” etc. *Sermon 8.*

5. “This is the one around whom a crown of thorns was placed,” etc. *Sermon 7.*

6. “Therefore, when blessed [Col. 0906B] Peter was speaking about those first fruits of ours and recounting the exaltation of the visible nature, accomplished by the power of divinity,” etc. *Sermon 7.*

7. “Since, however, if they had said, ‘We believe in one God the Word,’ it would have followed that death was attributed to the divine nature,” etc. *Sermon 3.*

# FOURTH COLLECTION OF SAYINGS OF NESTORIUS FROM VARIOUS TREATISES OR BOOKS, Scattered through the Works of Saint Cyril

[Col. 0905]

## From the book *On the Right Faith*, addressed to the Emperor Theodosius

[Col. 0905B]

[Col. 0905C] “This one, who was born from God, is the true and natural son; that one, who was born from the Virgin, is called Son of God equivocally.” And shortly afterward again: “Certainly God the Word is not a man, but assumed a man, since the Only-Begotten, from the beginning, is in himself the Son of God, the maker of all things; but the man whom he assumed, since he is not God by nature, is called by the same name on account of the one by whom he was assumed, who is the true Son of God. The statement, ‘No one knows the Son except the Father,’ shows the true and natural Son of God the Father; but Gabriel’s statement, ‘Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor with God; and behold, you will conceive in the womb and bear a Son, and you will call his name Jesus,’ applies to the man.” *Sermon 3.*

[Col. 0905D] “The people’s devotion toward me is not expressed by the acclamations of the crowd,” etc. *Sermon 2.*

**Anathema 1.** “I often asked them: Do you say that the divinity was born from the blessed Virgin?” etc. *Sermon 7.*

**Anathema 3.** “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, emptied himself,” etc. *Sermon 7.*

In another exposition (same place): “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow,” etc. *Sermon 7.*

In another (same place): “Say of the one who assumed him that he is God,” etc. *Sermon 2.*

[Col. 0906B] **Anathema 7.** “For the operations of the Trinity are common,” etc. *Sermon 10.*

[Col. 0906C] **Anathema 8.** “We confess God in the man; by the divine union we worship the man as co-worshiped.” *Sermon 2.*

**Anathema 10.** “He was sent to proclaim release to captives,” etc. *Sermon 6.*

**Anathema 11.** “Listen, paying attention to the words,” etc. *Sermon 9.*

**Anathema 9.** “The one who bestowed such great glory on Christ, who made him terrifying to demons and granted him his ascent to heaven.”

**Anathema 10.** “This faithful high priest made so by God,” etc.

“I have learned from divine Scripture that God proceeded from the Virgin who bore Christ; but I have nowhere learned that God was born from her. Therefore nowhere does divine Scripture say that God was born from the Virgin who bore Christ, but rather Jesus Christ, the Son, the Lord.

“Therefore he is also called Christ, God the Word, because he has an abiding conjunction with Christ. Let us therefore retain the unmixed union of the natures,” etc. (Same place.)

“God is inseparable from the visible one. Therefore I do not separate his honor, since he is not separated; I separate the natures, but I join the worship.” (*Sermon 7*, same place.)

# BOOK TWO

Containing: **THE TWELVE CHAPTERS OF THE BLASPHEMIES OF NESTORIUS**, with the *Contradictions* of Marius Mercator; **THE RESPONSE OF SAINT CYRIL TO THE OBJECTIONS OF THE EASTERNERS**; **THE RESPONSE OF THE SAME TO THE CRITICISMS OF THEODORET**; **THE SCHOLIA OF SAINT CYRIL ON THE INCARNATION OF THE WORD**; translated by Marius Mercator.

[Col. 0907]

# THE TWELVE CHAPTERS OF THE BLASPHEMIES OF NESTORIUS

In these writings, sent to him by the holy Coelestine, bishop of the city of Rome, and by Cyril of Alexandria, Nestorius contradicts them and, replying in very brief arguments, attempts to refute the twelve chapters of faith that had been sent to him. We have placed first Cyril’s chapters, which the Roman Church approved by true judgment, and afterward Nestorius’s, both translated from Greek into Latin.

[Col. 0909]

# NOTICE ON THE TWELVE CHAPTERS OF THE BLASPHEMIES OF NESTORIUS

This little work is plainly exceptional, and all the more worthy of esteem because it is unique: no one among the ancients, indeed not even among more recent writers, other than Mercator, is reported to have refuted the anathemas of Nestorius.

No room for doubt concerning its author remains for anyone willing to read the contradiction of the final anathema (*Appendix to the Contradictions*, no. 13). Its contradictor mentions a codex in which that treatise of Nestorius occupied the fourth place and whose beginning is: “Sweet to us,” etc. It is in fact contained in the collection of materials relating to the affair of Nestorius that we possess from Mercator.

Moreover, it is possible not merely to conjecture but also to determine with certainty the time when Mercator wrote, partly from the title, in which Nestorius is said to have attempted to contradict the letters of the holy Coelestine and Cyril through twelve chapters of his blasphemies and to refute the catholic anathemas; partly from the sequence of the entire work, in which there is no mention either of the condemnation of Nestorius or of the approval of Cyril’s chapters by the Council of Ephesus, but only of the approval of those same chapters by the Roman Church. It therefore follows that the work was composed during the interval between the seventh day before the Ides of December in the year 430, when the letters of Saint Coelestine were received by Nestorius, and the tenth day before the Kalends of July in the year 431, when the Ephesian synod began.

This interval may again be narrowed somewhat. Since the appendix refutes two later sermons of Nestorius, one delivered on the thirteenth of December and the other on the fourteenth, and since Mercator did not reply immediately, this work must be assigned to the following year.

The title explains the subject of the work: it is a contradiction of the twelve chapters of the Nestorians, although, as I have said, a criticism of two later sermons of Nestorius is appended. For this entire composition consists of two parts: the first is dogmatic; the second, which follows, is critical.

From this many things previously hidden until our own day become known. First, Mercator was the translator of the anathemas of Nestorius, which are absent from the Peltan edition of the Council of Ephesus; they are found, however, in other subsequent material, by the same translator, but neither together with Cyril’s catholic anathemas nor with the contradiction of the catholic writer—indeed, with many errors from which they now emerge purified on the basis of the Vatican and Beauvais manuscripts.

Second, Mercator translated Cyril’s anathemas twice: once with the third letter and again in this work. The meaning is the same in both places, though the wording is not identical. It is more careful in the letter, where the anathemas were considered in themselves; here it is somewhat more negligent, since they are cited incidentally.

Third, Dionysius Exiguus appears to have borrowed the translation of the anathemas from Mercator. It is the same in both, apart from a few words, although Mercator preceded Dionysius by a full century.

Fourth, Cyril’s anathemas were approved by the Roman Church “by true judgment”—that is, in my opinion, at the Roman council from which Coelestine wrote his letter to Nestorius. Mercator’s testimony thereby confirms our position concerning the Alexandrian synods discussed in Dissertation 2.

Fifth, at the same time Nestorius, through the height of his folly, both proclaimed *Theotokos* and pronounced an anathema against the one who proclaimed it. For at approximately the same time he delivered his final sermon and wrote his anathemas. In the sermon he openly confesses *Theotokos*, while in the anathemas he condemns the one who confesses it. It is therefore plainly evident that neither Nestorius nor perhaps the Easterners devoted to Nestorius ever made a sincere confession of *Theotokos*.

Sixth, Bonosus, who was condemned by Pope Damasus, held the see of the Church of Sardica—a fact which learned men had sought in vain down to the present day. This greatly assists in clarifying the otherwise sufficiently obscure history of the case of Bonosus, which was entrusted to the Macedonian bishops.

Seventh, Ebion was a Stoic philosopher; and Macedonius held the same view as the Arians concerning Christ’s flesh, for which the Word served in place of a soul. It was not Arius himself but the Arians who made this heresy. Those who denied that Christ was God were called “Homuncionites” by the Roman Church.

Eighth, Apollinaris was the first to teach that Christ had no soul other than the Word. He fell into this error all the more readily because he read in the Scriptures that angels, having assumed bodies, and, as he himself thought, even animated bodies, performed the functions of life on equal terms with the other human beings.

It should further be observed that Mercator prepared a codex for himself containing five especially famous sermons of Nestorius. The first begins: “The doctrine of piety.” The second: “Peoples who love Christ.” The third: “The insults of the heretics against me.” The fourth: “Our preceding teacher was sweet.” The fifth and final one: “In other lands it is situated.” In other places, however, and even in this work, he mentions other sermons that we have published, collected from various sources. The reason why he selected the five mentioned above rather than others is, I think, not obscure: Nestorius possessed them both to disseminate his heresy openly and to defend himself against the objections of his opponents.

# FIRST ANATHEM OF SAINT CYRIL

[Col. 0909A]

Cyril said: “If anyone does not confess that the one who is Emmanuel is truly God, and for this very reason that the holy Virgin is Mother of God—for she gave birth in the flesh to the Word who is from God, made flesh, according to what is written, ‘And the Word became flesh’ (John 1:14)—let him be anathema.”

# ANATHEM OF NESTORIUS

## In the manuscript codices

[Note: The following texts, headed “In the manuscript codices” and “In the published books,” are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Against these words Nestorius said: “If anyone says that the one who is Emmanuel is God the Word, and not rather God-with-us—that is, that he inhabited the nature which is ours, through his union with our mass, which he assumed from the Virgin Mary—and calls the holy Virgin the mother of God the Word, rather than the mother of the one who is Emmanuel, and says that God the Word himself was changed into the flesh which he received for the display of his divinity, so that in appearance he might be found to be a man (Philippians 2:7), let him be anathema.”

## In the published books

“If anyone says that the one who is Emmanuel is true God, and not rather God-with-us—that is, that he inhabited the nature which is ours, through his union with ours, which he assumed from the Virgin Mary—and calls the holy Virgin the mother of God the Word, rather than the mother of the one who is Emmanuel, and says that God the Word himself was changed into the flesh which he received for the display of his divinity, so that in appearance he might be found to be a man, let him be anathema.”

# CONTRADICTION OF MARIUS MERCATOR

[Col. 0909C]

1. The catholic writer contradicts these perverse statements as follows:

[Note: Mercator appears to have interpreted Nestorius’s statement as though he had said that Emmanuel is not God the Word, but the one who is called God-with-us—not because he is God, but because he is with us and inhabited the human nature that he assumed from the Virgin. Hence he accuses him of multiple crimes: first, impiety, because he denied that the Word dwelt among us; then paganism, because he admitted two gods, one eternal and the other temporal; next, bad faith, because at the same time he affirmed and denied that the blessed Virgin is *Theotokos*; afterward, agreement with Paul of Samosata concerning a non-substantial Word; then ignorance, because, from Cyril’s words, he concluded that when the Word became flesh, it was said that the Word was changed into flesh; and finally association with Manichaeus, who wanted the Word to have assumed flesh not in reality but in appearance.]

“This man speaks as though God the Word had not dwelt among us, which is sufficiently foreign to pious understanding. Yet it is filled with singular folly and impiety to say that the Word of the Father is not Emmanuel, but that the one born from Mary, who inhabited the nature of our mass, which he assumed from the Virgin, is Emmanuel. For the whole human race understands Emmanuel in its confession, as we learned—not by inventing it ourselves, but from Scripture, our teacher and interpreter—to mean ‘GOD WITH US’ [Baluz.: ‘God’].”

2. Again, who could doubt that this must be understood as “God with us”? For when we desire and invoke God’s being with us, what else do we wish than that the majesty of his power be present [Baluz. omits: “be present”]? Although it is wholly everywhere and nowhere divided, nevertheless we ask and desire to be aided by his help, so that he may be with us, assisting us.

3. Therefore, if this does not apply to God the Word according to that excellent—or rather perverse—teacher, namely, that he is the one who is invoked as being with us, let him see for himself the blasphemy he has uttered. But if, as he wishes, the one with us to whom the name Emmanuel applies is the one who possessed the first fruits of our mass, then, according to his exceedingly wise—or rather senseless and impious—definition, there were undoubtedly two gods [Baluz. omits “gods”]: one who is not Emmanuel, that is, not God with us; and another who [Note: From this it may be inferred when this work was written—namely, in the fifth century, when nearly one-third of it had already elapsed. The author’s age may likewise be inferred clearly enough, even if it is established more plainly by other evidence.] began, four hundred years ago and somewhat more, to be a certain new and recent god with us.

4. He also adds that if anyone calls the holy Virgin the mother of God the Word, let him be anathema. But [Baluz.: “very much”], as his supporters wish, after being admonished this man corrected his first criminal statement, by which he had scandalized the whole world, denying that she is *Theotokos*. For they say that after the admonition he said or proclaimed *Theotokos*. [Note: Before the Council of Ephesus Nestorius was repeatedly admonished canonically to confess the blessed Virgin as *Theotokos*: first by Cyril in his earlier synodical letters; then by John of Antioch, although this was rather the counsel of a friend; and finally by Saint Coelestine, exercising the authority of his see. It is impossible to determine which of these admonitions is meant.] It has therefore become clear to you both how he spoke then and how far he has now advanced for the worse.

5. Therefore, as he wishes, the Virgin is not the mother of God the Word but of Emmanuel. Consequently, according to his most wise argument, he wants this one to be called “with us” because he was united to our mass, which he assumed. What will he do when he is called God? [Note: Baluz.: “For he was not called only Emmanu, not also El, that is, ‘with us and God.’”] For he was not called merely *Emmanu*, that is, “with us,” but also *El*, that is, “God.” Therefore this god [Baluz. omits “god”], whom the erroneous teacher compels us to confess, will be of what authority, of what power—temporal and recent? Scripture cries out: “There shall not be in you a new and recent god” (Psalm 80:8).

6. Next, does he call that ancient god of his, whom he does not want to be with us, the Word alone of the Father? Perhaps he understands it as non-substantial, but, like Paul of Samosata in former times, as a word that is expressed and commanding. Who, then, would not understand from this, who would not notice, that he clearly savors the heresy of that same Paul? Under the pretext of proclaiming one God—that is, a monarchy—he defines God the Father alone as the true God, while his Word is a word that presides over operations by command, like a human word expressed in speech, which accomplishes the works it has determined.

7. He says that Emmanuel is God not by nature but by the grace of God, through participation in or association with that Word, and, as he more expressly tends to say, through conjunction, or even union, and sometimes unity. When he very rarely speaks of this unity in order to deceive inexperienced hearers while preserving his own meaning, he understands it in the same way as the statement in the Gospel: “Holy Father, make these also one in us, just as we are one” (John 17:21). When this subtle unity of his has sounded in the ears of the uninstructed crowd, and we are called sycophants and envious men, they applaud and say: “‘BEHOLD, HE SAID ‘ONE’; WHAT MORE DO YOU WANT?”

[Note: From this I infer three things: first, that the author of this work wrote at a time when Nestorius was still preaching in Constantinople; second, that Mercator himself, the author of the work, was regarded as his public accuser and therefore was ill spoken of among the populace, which had been deceived by the bishop’s devices; finally, that Nestorius abused the place from John the Evangelist, understanding it, in the manner of the Arians, of agreement of wills, although it should be understood of unity of nature.]

8. There follows his empty argument by which he thinks to exclude the catholic faith, which, following John the evangelist, says and holds: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14). [Note: Cyril was attacked by almost everyone on account of the first anathema, as though he had suggested in it that the Word had passed over into flesh. He dispelled the charge in six hundred places, yet could not completely establish himself free from suspicion.] From this he thinks it follows that, if this is said, God the Word is declared to have been changed into flesh—which is indeed very far from right faith.

[Note: Eutherius attacks Cyril on this passage, or another similar one. Since Eutherius, like Nestorius, interpreted the conjunction of the Word with humanity as a union *according to good pleasure* (*καθ’ εὐδοκίαν*), and maliciously tried to bring the catholics into disrepute as though they asserted that the Word had been changed into flesh, he added these words: “What, then, are the subtleties of the opponents? ‘What he was, he remained; what he was not, he became.’ Therefore either the indivisible nature was divided, and one part remained while the other was changed; or the whole was changed; or it came to be only in opinion; or these things ought indeed to be said but ought not to be understood. What, then, is the use of a word that signifies nothing?”]

“For while God the Word always remained in the nature and essence of the Father, in the one and the same essence in which he was and is unchangeably, for our salvation he became man, what he was not, so that he might make us, each of us who were not sons, his sons. This is what the rule of the creed and the faith of Nicaea held; this is what the definition of all the ancient interpreters maintained and handed down to us.”

9. He also adds, for the display of himself, that God the Word assumed our mass—that is, as he says, so that in appearance he might be found to be a man, while God was displayed. His Greek wording declares this empty and impious notion:

> “If anyone should say that God the Word himself was changed into flesh, which he received in the display of his divinity, so that in appearance he might be found to be like a man, let him be anathema.”

This means: “If anyone says that God the Word was changed into the flesh which he received for the display of his divinity, so that in appearance he might be found to be a man, let him be anathema.”

All Greeks recognize the difference between *σχηματισμός* and *σχῆμα*. By *σχηματισμός* the Greeks understand a case in which there is not truth but rather an imitation or fiction assumed to deceive the senses [Baluz.: “a deception”]; *σχῆμα*, however, signifies the actual truth of appearance. We might express these two terms by “display” and “appearance,” so that “display” is deceptive, whereas “appearance” is the manifestation of the whole nature.

10. We should like to know, then, what this new and vain teacher is aiming at. In what *σχηματισμός* did this new god of his cause himself to be seen? For he must be said to belong to him, not to Christians. By what appearance, then, was he found to be like a man? Do you see that he has fallen into the opinion of Manichaeus, whether through his exceedingly wicked will or through foolish ignorance? For he does not wish God to be a true man, but believes in a fantastic—that is, merely apparent—Christ, the Son of God.

# SECOND ANATHEM OF SAINT CYRIL

[Col. 0912C]

Cyril said: “If anyone does not confess that the Word of the Father was substantially united to the flesh [Baluz.: ‘flesh’; ‘one’], and that Christ is also one with his own flesh, and that the same one is unquestionably both God and man, let him be anathema.”

# SECOND ANATHEM OF NESTORIUS

## In the manuscript codices

[Note: The following texts, headed “In the manuscript codices” and “In the published books,” are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Nestorius said:

[Note: Petavius saw that the reading was corrupt, and, by the force of his understanding, inferred the meaning expressed by Mercator. He corrected it as follows (*Dogmatics*, vol. IV, book VI, chapter 17): “If anyone should say that in the conjunction of the Word of God with the flesh a change of the divine substance from place to place took place, and should say that the flesh was capable of the divine nature and was partially united to it; or should again extend the flesh of the uncircumscribed nature infinitely so as to receive God, and should say that the same one is by nature both God and man, let him be anathema.” Some words are nevertheless still missing, which Petavius did not supply because he lacked the following contradiction, from which they must be taken: “But one Son and Christ”; and therefore the final part of the anathema should be read: “And should say that the same one is by nature both God and man, and not one Son and Christ; let him be anathema.”]

“If anyone should say that in the conjunction of the Word of God which was made with the flesh, a change of the divine essence from place to place took place, and that the flesh was capable of his divine nature, or was partially united to the flesh, or should again extend the flesh to receive God, together with the divine nature, which is infinite and uncircumscribed, and should say that the same one is by nature both God and man, let him be anathema.”

## In the published books

“If anyone should say that in the conjunction of the Word of God which was made with the flesh, a change of the divine sentence took place, and should say that the flesh was capable of his nature and partially united to the flesh, or, with the uncircumscribed nature, should extend the flesh infinitely in order to receive God, and should say that the same one is by nature both God and man, let him be anathema.”

# CONTRADICTION OF MARIUS MERCATOR

1. The catholic writer contradicts him:

“He acts as though the following were implied and had to be understood: if anyone says that the Son of God was substantially united to our mass, then he is immediately burdened by the absurdity that compels him to confess a change in God according to the manner of bodies, together with extension and enclosure. But this is not so, since not even a human soul suffers this in its own body [Baluz. adds: ‘of a man’]; how much less should this be thought of the divine nature.

2. Next he says that the same Christ is not naturally God and man, but one Son and Christ. What is this novelty, so unheard of, obscured by such labyrinthine twists? He defines that there must be one Son, yet despite him—or rather, despite the suffocation produced by his clever argument—two emerge. For if Christ, whom he also wants to be Emmanuel, is not naturally the Son of God, while the Word of the Father is the Son by nature, there are undoubtedly two sons [Baluz. omits “sons”]: one by nature [Baluz.: ‘naturally’], the other not by nature but by grace; one eternal, the other temporal. ‘But there is one,’ he says, ‘because the one who is Son by nature has taken the other into association or conjunction’ [Baluz. adds: ‘the other by the one’]. Let any catholic reader recognize how vain and impious all this is.

3. For according to right and true faith there is one Son [Col. 0913D] of God: God the Word with his man, whom, when he willed, he assumed from a rational soul and a true, solid body. He is neither divided nor double, as this man dreams, but one—whole and the same, so to speak—God and man; or, to speak more significantly, God-man and man-God.

# THIRD ANATHEM OF SAINT CYRIL

[Col. 0914A]

Cyril said: “If anyone divides the substances in the one Christ after the union, connecting them only by association according to dignity, authority, or power, and not rather by their coming together into a natural unity, let him be anathema.”

# THIRD ANATHEM OF NESTORIUS

## In the manuscript codices

[Note: The following texts, headed “In the manuscript codices” and “In the published books,” are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Nestorius said:

[Note: The reading is defective everywhere, though less so in Mercator. With Mercator’s imperfect assistance, and aided by the history of the events, we can, unless I am mistaken, restore what Petavius did not correct to its true and original state. It should therefore be read as follows: “If anyone says that Christ, who is also Emmanuel, is one not according to conjunction but according to nature, and does not confess that both substances—the substance of God the Word and that of the man assumed by him—are even now preserved without confusion in the one connection of the Son, let him be anathema.” For Nestorius here presents his heresy concerning a mere *συνάφεια* of the natures and a purely moral assumption of the man, while disguising his proclamation of one Son; at the same time he accuses the catholics as though they said that the natures were confused, or at least changed after the resurrection.]

“If anyone says that Christ, who is also Emmanuel, is one not according to conjunction but according to nature, and does not confess that from both substances—the substance of God the Word and that of the man assumed by him—there is one connection of the Son, which is even now preserved without confusion, let him be anathema.”

## In the published books

“If anyone says that Christ, who is also Emmanuel, is one not according to conjunction but according to nature, and does not confess that from both substances—the substance of God the Word and that of the man assumed by him—there is one connection of the Son, which we even now preserve without confusion, let him be anathema.”

# CONTRADICTION OF MARIUS MERCATOR

He is contradicted. He follows himself completely and never departs from his own exceedingly bad intention, by which he attempts to introduce one Son naturally and another joined by association, who is said to be either Son or God not naturally but positively, and yet is not so in truth [Baluz. adds: “God”].

# FOURTH ANATHEM OF SAINT CYRIL

Cyril said: “If anyone distinguishes between two persons or substances those expressions that are contained both in the Gospels and in the apostolic writings, or even those that are spoken about Christ by the saints or by Christ himself about himself; and if he believes that some of these should be applied to the man, considered separately from God the Word, as though he were to be understood in a particular way, while others, as worthy of God, he assigns to the Word of God the Father alone, let him be anathema.”

# FOURTH ANATHEM OF NESTORIUS

## In the manuscript codices

[Note: The following texts, headed “In the manuscript codices” and “In the published books,” are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Nestorius said: “If anyone accepts as referring to one nature those expressions that have been written in the Gospels and in the apostolic writings concerning Christ, who is from both natures [Baluz. omits “nature”], and attempts to attribute sufferings to God the Word himself, both according to the flesh and according to the divinity, let him be anathema.”

## In the published books

“If anyone accepts as referring to one nature those expressions that have been written in the Gospels and in the apostolic letters concerning Christ, who is from both, and attempts to attribute sufferings to God the Word himself, both according to the flesh and according to the divinity, let him be anathema.”

# CONTRADICTION OF MARIUS MERCATOR

1. He is contradicted. He thinks that it follows that one is forced to confess the divine nature to be passible if one says that the Son of God, God, suffered for us. Does he not know that the whole common man, consisting of soul and body, when he suffers in the nature of the body [Baluz. omits “in the nature of the body”], suffers nothing from pain in the nature of the soul?

### 2.

Moreover, he is no wiser than the Fathers assembled at the Council of Nicaea, who, expanding more fully the confession of faith handed down to us by the apostles because of the impiety of Arius that had then arisen, declared as follows: [Col. 0915B]

“We believe,” they said, after the confession of God and the Father, “in one Lord of ours, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, true God from true God, light from light, consubstantial with the Father”—which the Greeks call ὁμοούσιον—“born, not made, through whom God the Father made all things; who for us and for our salvation, in the latter times, descended from heaven, was incarnate, suffered, was crucified, died, was buried, rose again on the third day, and will come to judge the living and the dead,” and so forth.

### 3.

By no means [Baluz. “Did they?”] did they understand another [Baluz. omits “another”] Jesus Christ, who would be Emmanuel and passible, and another, the impassible Word of the Father [Baluz. *impassibilem*, “the impassible one”]; rather, they understood one and the same eternal God, who, together with his body assumed in the latter times, was impassible in his divinity but passible [Col. 0915C] in his body. In that body, for us and with it, as with what was his own, he was born, seen, suffered, and rose again on the third day; and again, with it, he will come from heaven to judge the living and the dead.

## FIFTH ANATHEMATISM OF SAINT CYRIL

Cyril said: If anyone dares to call Christ ἄνθρωπον Θεοφόρον—that is, a man using God, or carrying God—and does not rather confess him to be truly God, as the one Son who, naturally, inasmuch as the Word became flesh, shared with us in like manner flesh and blood, let him be anathema.

## FIFTH ANATHEMATISM OF NESTORIUS

### In manuscript codices

[Note: [Col. 0909] The following texts, headed *In manuscript codices* and *In printed books*, are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Nestorius said: If anyone dares to say that, after the assumption of the man, the Son of God is naturally one, although he is Emmanuel, let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0915D] I suppose that Nestorius originally wrote *Jesus* instead of this word, *one*; nevertheless, the sense can remain intelligible, provided that it means what exists from the assumption of the man by God and from the union of both natures—that is, Emmanuel, “God with us.” For otherwise Nestorius would be understood to introduce two Sons, one by nature, the other by grace or by designation, as Mercator says.]

### In printed books

If anyone dares to say that, after the assumption of the man, the Son of God is naturally one, although he is Emmanuel, let him be anathema.

## CONTRADICTION OF MARIUS MERCATOR

The Catholic contradicts: Therefore, according to you, most foolish and most impious man, there are two Sons [Baluz. omits *Sons*: *Filii*]: one who is so by nature, and another who is so by designation. And how is this not impious?

## SIXTH ANATHEMATISM OF SAINT CYRIL

Cyril says: If anyone says that the Word of the Father is the God or Lord of Christ, and does not rather confess that this very same one is God and man simultaneously, as the Word made flesh, according to the Scriptures, let him be anathema.

## SIXTH ANATHEMATISM OF NESTORIUS

### In manuscript codices

[Col. 0916B]

Nestorius said: If anyone, after the incarnation, names anyone other than Christ “God the Word,” and attempts to say that the form of a servant had no beginning together with God the Word, and that it is uncreated, as he himself is, and does not rather confess that it was created by him, as by its natural Lord, Creator, and God—he who also promised to raise it by his own power, saying to the Jews, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it” (John 2:19)—let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0915D] I do not believe that Nestorius used the word ἐνσαρκώσεως, “incarnation,” but rather ἐνανθρωπήσεως, as it were “inhumanation.” He rarely uses the former, apparently to avoid it as more consonant with Catholic doctrine; he uses the latter more frequently, in order to conceal, under an otherwise Catholic word, his error concerning a purely ἐνοικήσεως, or “indwelling,” union between the Word and the man.]

### In printed books

If anyone, after the incarnation, names anyone other than Christ “God the Word”; if he attempts to say that the form of a servant indeed has no beginning with God the Word and is uncreated, as he is, and does not rather confess it to have been created by him, whom it acknowledges as Lord, Creator, and God by nature, and whom he promised also to raise by his own power, saying, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it”—let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0916D] This passage, otherwise obscure because of a faulty reading that entered both the manuscript codices and the common edition, had to be explained. It should therefore be read: “that the form of a servant had no beginning together with God the Word, and that this form,” etc. In the first part of his chapter Nestorius spoke Catholicly; in the second he falsely charged Catholics with holding that Christ’s flesh was coeternal with the Word. Hence Mercator accuses him both of inconsistency and of slander.]

## CONTRADICTION OF MARIUS MERCATOR

### 1.

The Catholic contradicts. This speech appears to belong to foolish ostriches [Note: [Col. 0916D] Baluzius adds *recelare*, which he explains in this note: “That is, I believe, to imitate. For Pliny says in Book X, chapter 1, that ostriches have this stupidity: although the rest of their body is so tall, when they hide their necks in a bush, they think themselves concealed. Garnerius omitted this word in his edition.” EDIT.], who think themselves hidden up to the neck while exposing the rest of their bodies to danger. He says that Christ is one, yet does not see his own earlier impious statements, having quickly forgotten his Emmanuel.

### 2.

Finally, from whom has he ever heard that the Lord’s body is coeternal with him? (Although, from the time when he deigned to assume it, it is everlasting.) Does he mean that what belongs to him is therefore also coeternal with him? Would that he might here [Baluz. “thus”] understand that, according to the symbol of faith, the one Son of God, God the Word, together with the perfect man assumed by him—composed of a rational soul and a body—[Col. 0917A] is one. As it is written: “He himself bore our infirmities, and for us he suffers” (Isaiah 53:4), suspending them, that is, in his body upon the tree (1 Peter 2:24). Then he would not descend into this empty impiety of Paul of Samosata by dividing the merits of the two natures and persons!

## SEVENTH ANATHEMATISM OF SAINT CYRIL

Cyril said: If anyone says that, in Jesus as in a man, God the Word was inactive, and that the dignity of the Only-Begotten should be attributed as to another existing besides him, let him be anathema.

## SEVENTH ANATHEMATISM OF NESTORIUS

### In manuscript codices

[Note: [Col. 0909] The following texts, headed *In manuscript codices* and *In printed books*, are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Nestorius said: If anyone says that the man who was created from the Virgin [Col. 0917B] is the Only-Begotten who was born from the Father’s womb before the morning star (Psalm 109:4), and does not rather confess that, because of his union with him who is naturally the Father’s Only-Begotten, he was made a participant in the title “Only-Begotten”; and if he says that Jesus is someone else besides Emmanuel, let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0917D] We restored this exceedingly corrupt passage in both places. For even in the manuscript codices that we used it could not be read with any intelligible sense: “let him confess him by the title of the Only-Begotten, and that he was rather made a participant.”]

### In printed books

If anyone says that the man who was created in the Virgin is the Only-Begotten who was born from the Father’s womb before the morning star; and does not rather confess that, because of the union, he was made a participant in the title of the Father’s naturally Only-Begotten Son; and if he says that Jesus is someone else besides Emmanuel, let him be anathema.

## CONTRADICTION OF MARIUS MERCATOR

The Catholic contradicts. Turning over the same things by the same means [Col. 0917C] [Baluz. *volens*, “willing”], he settles the same account in the same mud [Note: [Col. 0917D] To “settle an account” (*versuram solvere*), as found in Terence, means precisely to make no progress despite expectation, even if one turns in various directions seeking where to avert the impending evil.] For once again he brings forth, hissing from the twisted caverns, his father, in the manner of a serpent. He produces the Only-Begotten, whom he wants to be understood as the Son of God by nature; yet he does not consider him to be God with us, because he does not grant him the natural name of Emmanuel, but only the descriptive designation of the word itself. Likewise, he grants his temporal Emmanuel no naturally proper title of Only-Begotten; rather, because of the joining or conjunction of that natural Only-Begotten, he leaves him an empty designation.

## EIGHTH ANATHEMATISM OF SAINT CYRIL

Cyril said: If anyone dares to say that the assumed man ought to be worshiped together with God the Word, and called God as one alongside another—for the addition of the syllable “with” would compel this interpretation—and does not rather venerate Emmanuel with one reverence and offer one glorification, according to the fact that the Word became flesh (John 1:14), let him be anathema.

## EIGHTH ANATHEMATISM OF NESTORIUS

### In manuscript codices

[Note: [Col. 0909] The following texts, headed *In manuscript codices* and *In printed books*, are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Nestorius said: If anyone says that the form of a servant is to be worshiped for its own sake—that is, according to the character of its own nature—and that it is Lord of all things, and does not rather venerate it because of [Baluz. “through”] the fellowship by which it has been joined and united to the blessed and naturally sovereign nature of the Only-Begotten [Col. 0918B] [Baluz. *Dominicae*, “of the Lord”], let him be anathema.

### In printed books

If anyone says that the form of a servant is to be worshiped for its own sake—that is, according to the character of its own nature—and not as Lord of all things, and does not rather venerate it through the fellowship by which it has been joined to the blessed and naturally sovereign nature of the Only-Begotten, let him be anathema.

## CONTRADICTION OF MARIUS MERCATOR

The Catholic contradicts. No Christian has ever separated and divided the one and same God, the Son of God, Jesus Christ, by a distinction or difference of merits, so as to display him as double within himself, possessing diverse and thus [Baluz. *si*, “if so”] unequal dignity.

## NINTH ANATHEMATISM OF SAINT CYRIL

Cyril said: If anyone says that the one Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Holy Spirit as by an alien power, by which he operated through him, and that he received from him the ability to work against unclean spirits, and through him performed divine signs, and does not rather say that the Holy Spirit is his own, just as he is the Spirit of the Father, through whom he worked signs, let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0917D] It must be acknowledged that Dionysius Exiguus and several others were deceived, Dionysius by Mercator, and Mercator by a fault in the Greek exemplar. No fraud has hitherto been detected by scholars; the difficulty arose from faulty punctuation and perhaps from a premature judgment concerning the anathematisms, as though they were oracles that created reverence for themselves through their obscurity.
