The correctly punctuated Greek text is therefore as follows:

Εἴ τις φησὶ, τὸν ἕνα κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν δοξάζεσθαι παρὰ τοῦ πνεύματος, ὡς ἀλλοτρίᾳ δυνάμει, τῇ ἰδίᾳ αὐτοῦ χρώμενον, καὶ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ λαβόντα τὸ ἐνεργεῖν etc.

That is: “If anyone says that the one Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Spirit as by a power alien to him, and that he used the Spirit’s own power, and received from him the ability to act,” etc. Mercator, however, read ὡς ἀλλοτρίᾳ δυνάμει τῇ διὰ αὐτοῦ χρώμενον, “as using an alien power operating through him.”]

## NINTH ANATHEMATISM OF NESTORIUS

### In manuscript codices

[Note: [Col. 0909] The following texts, headed *In manuscript codices* and *In printed books*, are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Nestorius said: If anyone says that the form [Baluz. “of the form”] of a servant is consubstantial with the Holy Spirit [Baluz. “the Holy Spirit”], and does not rather say that, through the mediation of that Spirit, it had from its very conception the union or conjunction with God the Word [Col. 0918D] through which it sometimes performed among human beings [Col. 0919A] common and wondrous [Baluz. *miserandas*, “piteous”] healings, and from which there arose the power to drive out spirits, let him be anathema.

### In printed books

If anyone says that the form of a servant is consubstantial with the Holy Spirit, and does not rather say that, through the mediation of the Holy Spirit, it had from its very conception the conjunction with God the Word, through which it sometimes performed wondrous healings among human beings, and from which there arose the power to cure spirits, let him be anathema.

## CONTRADICTION OF MARIUS MERCATOR

The Catholic contradicts. What mediation between God the Word and the Holy Spirit does he introduce—a mediation unknown throughout all the ages and to all human beings? We cannot understand it, since the divine Scriptures testify that there is one mediator, in the words of the apostle Paul: “For there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). And again: “For he himself made both one, breaking down the middle wall of partition, the hostility, in his flesh, abolishing the law of commandments in decrees, in order to create the two in himself as one new man, making peace” (Ephesians 2:14). And the other passages, which it would take too long to insert. What, then, does this unheard-of novelty mean, unless he wishes also to separate Christ from the substance of the Holy Spirit, and to say that he could not himself work signs and powers without the mediation—or even the assistance—of the Spirit?

## TENTH ANATHEMATISM OF SAINT CYRIL

Cyril said: Holy Scripture designates Christ as having been made the high priest [Baluz. adds “and apostle”] of our confession: “For he offered himself to God the Father for us as a fragrant offering” (Ephesians 5:2). If anyone therefore says that our high priest and apostle was made someone other than God the Word himself, when he became flesh and, according to us, man, but as though a particular man besides him had been made from a woman; and if anyone says that he offered himself as an offering for himself, and not rather for us alone—for he who knew no sin had no need of an offering—let him be anathema.

## TENTH ANATHEMATISM OF NESTORIUS

### In manuscript codices

[Note: [Col. 0909] The following texts, headed *In manuscript codices* and *In printed books*, are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Nestorius said: If anyone says that the Word who was in the beginning was made the high priest and apostle of our confession and offered himself for us, and does not rather say that the apostolate belongs to Emmanuel, and divides the offering according to the same distinction between the one who united and the one who was united, not assigning to the one common fellowship of the Son—namely, to God the things that belong to God and to man the things that belong to man—let him be anathema.

### In printed books

If anyone says that the Word who was in the beginning was made the high priest and apostle of our confession and offered himself for us, and does not say that he was the apostle of Emmanuel, and attributes the offering according to the same distinction to the one who united, if there was one who was united, assigning to the one commonality of the Son the things that belong to God and the things that belong to man, let him be anathema.

## CONTRADICTION OF MARIUS MERCATOR

[Col. 0920A]

The Catholic contradicts. Behold how clearly he has once again appeared with his Emmanuel—for Emmanuel must always be said to be his own [Baluz. “Emmanuel”]. To him he assigns individual merits separately, as though he were the lowest and far inferior to that other whom he determines not to be God with us; yet naturally God, who makes him God by the favor of conjunction, by title or designation, but not by nature.

## ELEVENTH ANATHEMATISM OF CYRIL

Cyril said: If anyone does not confess that the Lord’s flesh is life-giving, as the very flesh of God the Word himself, but regards it as belonging to someone else besides him, joined indeed [Baluz. “whom he joined to himself”] according to dignity, or according to the fact that it possessed only a divine indwelling [Col. 0920B], and does not rather confess it to be life-giving, as we have said, because it became the proper flesh of the Word of God, to whom it is possible to give life to all things, let him be anathema.

## ELEVENTH ANATHEMATISM OF NESTORIUS

### In manuscript codices

[Note: [Col. 0909] The following texts, headed *In manuscript codices* and *In printed books*, are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Nestorius said: If anyone says that the flesh united to God the Word [Baluz. “to God”] is life-giving by the capacity of its own nature, while the Lord and God himself declares, “It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing,” let him be anathema. [Col. 0920C]

### In printed books

If anyone says that the united flesh is life-giving by the capacity of its own nature, while the Lord and God himself declares, “It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:63), let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0919D] Without doubt all of this, although it appears in the printed editions, should have been deleted. For it does not belong to the Catholic contradiction of the anathematism, nor is it formulated in the same manner as the preceding material, nor does the Catholic contradictor make any mention of it.]

And he adds: “The Spirit is God” (John 4:24), although this was not stated. If anyone therefore says that God the Word became flesh according to the substance of flesh, and that he preserves it in this manner and particularly in the Lord Christ after his resurrection, when he said to his disciples: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see me have” (Luke 24:39), let him be anathema.

## CONTRADICTION OF MARIUS MERCATOR

[Col. 0920D]

### 1.

The Catholic contradicts. Christian ears must be closed, lest they hear such great and manifest blasphemy. For he says that Christ’s flesh is not life-giving by its own nature, and he adduces evangelical testimony, imagining that it supports his impiety, although the evangelical truth itself strikes his eyes with the wickedness and violence with which he has wrested it to his purpose. For it was said there at that time, “It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing,” [Col. 0921A] when Christ [Baluz. omits “Christ”] was teaching the apostles that they ought to live according to the inner man—that is, not carnally but spiritually—and that they ought accordingly to understand what they were hearing. In that context the saying, “It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing,” is entirely appropriate.

### 2.

And this utterly insane man [Baluz. *sanctissimus*, “most holy”], in order to persuade people that Christ’s flesh is useless, fragile, and weak, violently dragged this saying of the Savior into his blasphemous meaning, as though he had spoken of his own flesh when he said that the flesh profits nothing. And where is that saying of the Lord: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54)? We considered it necessary, and more than useful, to insert the entire evangelical context in order to refute him [Col. 0921B] and his followers.

### 3.

Jesus therefore said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, Moses did not give you bread from heaven; for the bread of God is that which descends from heaven and gives life to the world.” They therefore said to him: “Lord, always give us this bread.” Jesus then said to them: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me will not hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst. But I told you that you have both seen me and have not believed. Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will not cast out, because I have descended from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me, so that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.”

The Jews therefore murmured about him [Col. 0921C] to Jesus, because he had said: “I am the bread that descended from heaven.” And they said: “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he say, ‘I have descended from heaven’?” Jesus answered and said to them: “Do not murmur among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up on the last day. For it is written in the Prophets: ‘And they shall all be taught by God.’ Everyone therefore who hears from the Father and learns comes to me—not because anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father. Amen, amen, I say to you, everyone who believes in me has eternal life. I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate manna in the desert and died; this is the bread that descends from heaven, so that whoever eats of it may not die. I am the bread of life that descended from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever; and the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.”

The Jews therefore argued with one another, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” Jesus said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day; for my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. Just as the Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will also live because of me. This is the bread that descended from heaven—not as your fathers ate manna in the desert and died; whoever eats this bread will live forever.”

He said these things while teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum. Many of his disciples, therefore, when they heard this, said: “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were murmuring about this, said to them: “Does this offend you? What then if you see the Son of Man ascending into heaven where he was before? It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6).

### 4.

But why should we be surprised that he did this with the testimony of the Gospel, when he similarly dragged another passage into his argument by force and abused it in support of his impious meaning, thinking that he could strengthen his position by evangelical authority? The passage says: “What is born of flesh is flesh; and what is born of spirit is spirit” (John 3:6). [Note: [Col. 0921D] These words, like the others, occur in the first sermon (No. 7).]

For he used this testimony in that most foolish treatise in which he first argued about the virgin birth. In that passage he said: “Mary did not give birth to God, my good man” (ibid.); “for what is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit; but she gave birth to a man who was an instrument of divinity, and to a man carrying God.”

[Note: [Col. 0921D] Θεοφόρον, that word is everywhere attacked by Cyril as being full of poison (see *Paschal Homily* 17). See the dissertation on the Nestorian heresy, where the expressions are explained which, although they were accepted in a Catholic sense by the Fathers of earlier times, had to be rejected by defenders of the Catholic faith against Nestorius because he twisted them into a perverse meaning.]

At that time the discourse was addressed to Nicodemus, the ruler of the synagogue, who did not yet believe the Savior’s words and who, because he understood carnally, when he heard, “Unless someone is born again, he cannot be saved” (John 3:3), replied: “How can this happen? Can I enter my mother’s womb again and be born?” (ibid.) Then, having noted his foolishness—for, as I have said, he understood not spiritually but carnally [Baluz. *separet*, “separates”—an apparent corruption]—he plainly heard: “Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God”; or, as it is written elsewhere, “Unless someone is born again.” Then he added: “What is born of flesh is flesh.”

### 5.

Since this is so, where and when did he think that this saying, “What is born of flesh is flesh,” should be applied? Clearly, so that he might deny that God Christ was born from the Virgin. For what benefit does this testimony bring him except that the one who was born flesh from the Virgin’s flesh is merely [Baluz. “as”] a man, in whom God the Word [Col. 0922D] deigned to dwell?

## TWELFTH ANATHEMATISM OF SAINT CYRIL

Cyril said: If anyone does not confess that God the Word suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, and tasted death in the flesh, and that he became the firstborn from the dead, inasmuch as he is also life and life-giver as God, let him be anathema.

## TWELFTH ANATHEMATISM OF NESTORIUS

[Col. 0923A]

### In manuscript codices

[Note: [Col. 0909] The following texts, headed *In manuscript codices* and *In printed books*, are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Nestorius said: If anyone, while confessing the sufferings of the flesh, also attributes them without distinguishing the dignity of the natures to the Word of God and to the flesh in which he was made, let him be anathema.

### In printed books

If anyone, while confessing the sufferings of the flesh, also attributes them to the Word of God as though he had applied them to the flesh in which he was made, without distinguishing the dignity of the natures, let him be anathema.

## CONTRADICTION OF MARIUS MERCATOR

### 1.

The Catholic contradicts. Why does he rage in vain? Why is he senselessly mad? No one [Baluz. omits “except”] except a mentally deranged person, provided that he is still a Christian, attributes to that ineffable divine nature—in accordance with its own living essence or nature—the sufferings that our flesh undergoes, or the emotions and movements that the soul experiences from things joyful or sorrowful. For he does not assign bodily pains even to the human soul; in these matters it is impassible, because it is immortal, although, as we mentioned above, it has its own passions arising from movement.

Nevertheless, so long as it dwells in fellowship with its flesh, it must share in its pain through sorrow, while itself suffering no pain [Baluz. “pains”], as we have said, in its own essence or nature. Thus, in a manner incomparable, immeasurable, and ineffable, the Word, the Son of God, bearing a composite man [Baluz. *passus*, “having suffered”] consisting of soul and body, is rightly said to have suffered whatever that assumed humanity endured. For that entire human substance, which he had assumed in order to heal it, was his own; joining it to himself, he made himself wholly one with it. Remaining God with it as what he was, he also existed as man.

### 2.

The man who is God will also come to judge, according to the saying of the prophet [Baluz. “by which”], who declares that he will come visibly: “They will see him whom they pierced” (Zechariah 12:10). Another prophet says: “And he is man, and who knows him?” In the Acts of the Apostles, the angels said to those same apostles: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:14).

# DISSERTATION OF MARIUS MERCATOR, OR APPENDIX TO THE CONTRADICTION OF THE TWELFTH NESTORIAN ANATHEMATISM

This is a refutation of the second sermon and of the subsequent two, together with a retraction of the second anathematism.

[Col. 0924A]

### 1.

Moreover, what he says in the preceding sermon or treatise—which is near the end of the gathering of four leaves, at the place marked by the sign of the asterisks—must not remain unexamined, since he attempts to introduce unheard-of meanings of great absurdity. He wishes Christ to have been declared by Matthew to belong to neither nature. If that is so, which may it never be, then he will belong to no one—unless perhaps, at the peril of his own head, he belongs to the nature of a beast.

[Note: [Col. 0923D] That sermon was the fifth in Mercator’s codex, but in reality it is the very last of all. In its fourth part these words are found: “Hence blessed Matthew, the author of the Gospels, when he came to the mystery of the generation, gives an account of the generation from neither nature, but rather from the title ‘Christ.’” Mercator may appear to be laboring over the words “from neither nature” with excessive fastidiousness; but what can one do with a man whom love of Christ urges and inflames against the Antichrist?]

[Note: [Col. 0923D] The ancients used certain marks to indicate special places in their books, as is still done today; most commonly they used asterisks, as is clear to those who handle handwritten books. I have also seen labyrinths of such marks occupying the place. Hence below the reader will find the signs of the labyrinths inserted. BALUZ.]

### 2.

This final madness of his, accompanied by impiety, is produced by his perverse understanding, by which he declares Christ to be double, as though man and God were separated from one another by nature, while he presents himself as a highly cautious and clear-minded disputant. [Note: [Col. 0924D] He alludes to these words of Nestorius in Sermon 4: “The clear division of this doctrine is as follows: he who was born, who required the passage of time for growth and was carried in the womb for the appointed months, has a human nature, but one certainly joined to God. It is one thing to say that, when the one who is the Word of the Father was born from Mary, that God was joined to him; this is perfectly clear, firm, and beyond reproach even to the Gentiles,” etc.]

Yet he does not see another heretic, approaching him with still more foolish caution, who presents him with a Christ fabricated as threefold—consisting, namely, of soul, body, and God.

[Note: [Col. 0924D] Nestorius calls Christ “double” in many passages, but especially in Sermon 1 (No. 12): “Let us confess and worship the double one as one; for the double of the natures is one because of the unity.” Observe that Mercator used “nature” in place of “hypostasis.”]

### 3.

What if Apollinaris should also confront him, defining every ordinary man as τριυπόστατον, “three-hypostatic,” consisting of soul, body, and mind? He wanted mind, or reason, to be one thing, and soul to be another, of a different nature and substance. Although he impiously raved that Christ had no mind or reason, but a soul without a mind, and that the Word of the Lord took the place of the mind, nevertheless, if his view had prevailed—which may it never do—an ordinary man would, as we have said, have been believed to be threefold. Would not this utterly insane teacher have thereby introduced a fourfold Christ for us, consisting of soul, body, mind, and God?

### 4.

Leaving aside these ravings, we confess Christ to be God, the eternal Word who was with the Father and was made flesh—that is, made man—consisting of a rational soul and a body, while remaining in him unchangeable and unaltered, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. His divine nature is one undivided whole with his flesh and, as we have said, rational soul. He must not be called double or triple, because no ordinary man, one consisting of a rational soul and a body, could ever be called double or triple; rather, in the singularity of his state [Note: [Col. 0924D] *Substance* is used for ὑπόστασις, or subsistence (*On the Categories*, chapter “On Substance”); for even among philosophers hypostasis is primary substance, and it is also called by Aristotle substance simply speaking (*Metaphysics*, Book VII). Hence Mercator immediately continues: “Thus also that ineffable majesty of the divine Son of God is one in its person and substance with his assumed soul,” etc.], he is one and one substance.

Likewise, that ineffable divine majesty of the Son of God is one in its person and substance with his assumed soul, endowed with his own mind or reason, and with his solid and perfect body. It admits none of these absurd and impious designations of “double” or “triple,” because of the unity or singularity in which it was pleased to assume and bear man, and from itself and that man to make one Lord, Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0925D] Mercator calls Jesus Christ “one of the Trinity.” This statement divided even Catholics into various positions, when they debated whether one of the Trinity should be said to have suffered], remaining, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God in the Trinity forever.

Concerning him the apostle John says in his First Epistle (1 John 1:1): “What was from the beginning, what we heard and saw with our eyes, what we contemplated and our hands touched concerning the Word of life—and the life was made manifest, and we saw and bear witness, and proclaim to you the eternal life that was with the Father and appeared to us—what we saw and heard we proclaim to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us, and our fellowship may be with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.”

### 5.

The cautious and prudent reader should also attend to what he is said to have written on the second leaf of the ninth gathering of this codex, where this sign appears. Since this man is possessed of astonishing foolishness and insanity, as well as utterly absurd impiety, it is astonishing that he could have had followers or hearers capable of understanding anything.

Let us therefore carefully examine what the empty-headed man says, so that he may not confess the holy Virgin Mary as Θεοτόκον, “God-bearer”: [Note: [Col. 0925D] These words are found both in Cyril’s excerpts (*Excerpt* 1) and in the first book of Cyril’s *Contradictions* (Chapter 7); they are taken from Sermon 4.]

“Nowhere,” he says, “did the Council of Nicaea dare to say that God the Word was born from the Virgin Mary. For it says: ‘We believe in one Lord Jesus Christ.’ [Col. 0925C] Observe that, although the Fathers first set down ‘Christ,’ which demonstrates the conjunction of two natures, they did not say ‘in one God the Word,’ but adopted a name that signifies both,” and so forth.

### 6.

Since, therefore, Jesus Christ is for this same council nothing other than the Lord—and the Lord is undoubtedly God the Word and the Son of God—who, together with his assumed body and rational soul, became a complete man, formed and brought forth in the womb of that holy woman, and, proceeding from it already wholly God and man, is wholly and entirely one and one inseparably, where does this mad teacher get the authority even to call Jesus Christ “Lord,” if he is not the Word of God? For dominion belongs to no one except God alone.

Does this excellent teacher not know this? If, therefore, Jesus is not also God in his view from conception and birth, so that she might rightly be the Mother of God—that is, Θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”—according to the entirely correct definition of the ancient Fathers? From where, then, did he at least appear to be Lord to him?

### 7.

[Note: He brings back for examination matters contained in the final sermon (No. 4): “Hence we have often told you how Christ is a designation significant of both names, that is, of humanity and of the divine nature. Hence, if anyone expressly says ‘Christ’ only, let him know that in this name both natures are signified and conjoined.”]

Then who told him that the name “Christ,” or where did he dream, that it is a name signifying two natures, [Col. 0926A] when this name rather expresses a human being among human beings? For it must be understood that it is said *ἀπὸ τῆς χρίσεως*, that is, “from anointing,” as though “anointed”—something that did not belong to the nature of God.

### 8.

There is also that feature of his immeasurable stupidity whereby he says that the holy council said: “We believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten, who was born from God the Father, consubstantial—that is, ὁμοούσιον—with the Father, who descended for our sake.” Jesus, certainly, according to his own view, is a man. Tell me, please, how is he, or in his view, consubstantial with God the Father, unless as God begotten from God the Father? Or again, how is he not God who is from Mary? If he was born in this way, how did the Council of Nicaea understand and proclaim the matter, and why did it consent to confess this only to such an extent? What, then, is solid? [Col. 0926B] What is sound? What is whole in his account?

### 9.

There is also another delirium of impiety: he says that those Fathers neglected to declare that they believed in God the Word, the only-begotten Son; but, he says, they declared that they believed in one Lord Jesus Christ, consubstantial with the Father, God from true God, light from light, through whom all things were made—as though God the Word were not the Son in his view, as is more plainly declared in his earlier sermon.

What is this man’s vanity? What madness is this? What is this mockery in so inconsistent a discourse, no less foolish than impious? God’s Word is not the Son of God for him; Jesus is God in one half and man in the other, and yet the same person cannot be the Word of God and the Son? At one moment he is consubstantial, born from God the Father, true God [Col. 0926C] from true God, light from light; afterward, however, possessing none of these things naturally, but sharing in divine dignity only by another’s designation, like a man born in time.

### 10.

Christian ears must surely be closed when it is said that the name “Son” does not signify that Word of the Father who is from him and in him. Let the reader attend to this testimony: “God,” he says, “sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4:4); evidently because, since he was born of a woman and is not God, the Word is not his Son, but someone else who could be born by a woman’s childbirth.

### 11.

Earlier, certainly, he had approved the opinion of the Fathers that Jesus Christ is consubstantial with God the Father, God from true God, light from light; and he had approved it most rightly. [Col. 0926D] What did he suddenly think about the Word of God, which was in the beginning with God and was God, so that it should again not be the Son of God? Or did he think that the Nicene Fathers had defined Jesus Christ—who is consubstantial with God the Father, true God from true God, and light from light, just as he had most favorably understood it—not to be God, so that everything, and the whole person, one and the same, and whatever is said of him and whatever manner of expression is used concerning him, should be understood and regarded in this way?

Although he became man, as the most faithful and truthful witness, John the Evangelist, testifies, saying, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14)—and this is beyond doubt—it must not be denied that he became under the law and assumed in himself all those things which, having become man, he ought to bear as man. But this must not be denied in such a way; rather, it must be confessed with all our strength, so that, while the impassible nature of his divinity remains wholly with him, these things may be believed to have been assumed by him.

### 12.

Who, moreover, could calmly endure this other delirium of his, in which he says that Christ Jesus is his own Lord? His words are these: “I say this,” he says, “so that you may know how exalted and extraordinary a conjunction existed, even in the infant himself, when the Lord’s flesh was seen; for he himself was both an infant and the infant’s Lord.” Who has ever been called lord of himself? But this man, wishing and attempting to introduce a fourth person and substance into the holy Trinity, displays extraordinary stupidity and is stained with the marks of impiety.

### 13.

We advise that his fourth treatise, also contained in this volume, be considered with greater care and attention. Its beginning is: “The teacher who preceded us has set before us a sweet table of charity,” and so forth. To identify the passages that we have undertaken to explain here, the reader will find signs of labyrinths—that is, asterisks—placed there.

For there he attempts to show what distinction he has contrived between Paul of Samosata and Photinus, his teachers, striving to clear himself as though he were alien to their doctrine; and he says as follows: “Paul, indeed, in saying that Christ is man alone and that he first began to exist when he was born of the Virgin,” and so forth. [Col. 0928A]

[Note: He was bishop of Sirmium, which is known to everyone; but it is not equally well known that the author whom Sirmond named *Praedestinatus* appears to have originated from that same city. For he writes (Heresy 44): “The heresy of the Samosatenians was restored by Photinus, our bishop,” and so forth. And (Heresy 45): “I said that Photinus was our bishop, just as Judas Iscariot our apostle was ours,” and so forth. Since Photinus was bishop of Sirmium, that author appears to have been a man of Sirmium. Yet in Heresy 44 he calls Optatus “ours,” although it is established that Optatus was from Milevis. For he says: “Parmenianus went about all Africa, composing books against us and making new psalms; against him our Optatus wrote.” But he called Optatus “ours,” just as he said that Parmenianus composed books “against us,” because of their religious allegiance and party affiliation: Optatus wrote on behalf of the Catholics, while Parmenianus wrote against the Catholics. But concerning the author of this book, whom a not very learned critic has harassed, we shall speak more fully sometime, if God provides the opportunity.]

All this evil of Photinus’s impiety [Col. 0927C] was derived rather from Ebion, the Stoic philosopher.

[Note: Concerning Ebion, Mercator reports some things that partly agree with the writings of others and partly may seem new. It agrees with all heresiologists that Christ was an ordinary man, born from Joseph and Mary, who surpassed other human beings by the merit of his life and was therefore adopted as the Son of God. It also agrees with Jerome (*On Illustrious Men*, chapter 19) that the Gospel according to John was written especially against Ebion. But, so far as I know, no one has previously reported that this heretic followed Stoic philosophy or that he employed the testimony of the three evangelists Matthew, Mark, and Luke to establish his heresy. For the generally accepted view, supported indeed by great authorities, has been that the Ebionites received only the Gospel of Matthew; indeed, the author of *Praedestinatus* writes that they were condemned by Luke at Antioch. Mercator may have written about Ebion’s profession of Stoicism where others were silent; he may also have called Ebion a philosopher because, despising wealth, he followed voluntary poverty, as the writers report. It is indeed credible that Ebion himself made use of the authority of Matthew, Luke, and Mark once these three Gospels already existed. Later the Ebionites rejected Mark and Luke: the former because they regarded him as opposed to that man, the latter because he had written things agreeing with Luke.]

### 14.

This man arose while the Apostle John was still alive in Asia, and dared to preach that Christ was an ordinary man born from Joseph and Mary, that he had surpassed the whole human race by the merit of his life, and that for this reason he had been adopted as the Son of God. He asserted that he followed the authority of the evangelists Matthew, Mark, and Luke.

At that time the Apostle John composed a Gospel against him, in which he declared at the outset that the Word existed in the beginning, that the Word was with the Father, and that the Word was God (John 1:1). Then, descending from this introduction, in order to show that the man whom those three Evangelists had written about was also God, he says: “What was made in him was life” (ibid., 1:4). And shortly afterward: “The Word became flesh” (ibid., 1:14).

### 15.

Marcellus the Galatian therefore followed this philosopher Ebion. Photinus also followed him, as did, in the final period, Bonosus of Sardica, who was condemned in advance by Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome.

[Note: Concerning this passage, observe first the time in which the opponent lived—namely, approximately fifty years after Bonosus had been condemned by Damasus—and thus more than four hundred years after Christ’s birth. Next, observe which city Bonosus held as his episcopal see, something unknown to Baronius, Petavius, and other writers of great reputation: it was Sardica. Finally, observe how Bonosus, whom Anysius of Thessalonica and the bishops of Macedonia condemned in the time of Pope Siricius, is nevertheless said to have been condemned in advance by Damasus, namely under the names of Marcellus and Photinus, whose heresy he revived. For at the Roman synod, from which Damasus’s profession of faith was sent to Paulinus of Antioch, they were proscribed.]

### 16.

As for Paul of Samosata, who was bishop of Antioch during the reign of the emperor Aurelian, it is true that he defined Christ, in common with others, as a man born from both parents. But he understood and proclaimed the Word of God the Father not as substantial but as uttered or commanding—not, as the Catholic faith holds, the Word in substance or essence, consubstantial—that is, ὁμοούσιον—with God the Father’s Son.

### 17.

Photinus, however, held a view equal to that of the utterly insane Nestorius. He did not deny that the Word of God existed in substance, but he maintained that this Word dwelt externally and peculiarly in Jesus, who had been born from Mary according to the ordinary manner of married couples, and that through him he performed on earth all those miracles that we read in the Gospels.

[Note: He accuses Nestorius of ignorance or thoughtlessness because Nestorius said λογοπάτορα instead of υἱοπάτορα, a word which Praxeas invented in order somehow to explain his opinion concerning the Trinity. See Tertullian’s separate book *Against Praxeas*, which he wrote after already being infected with the errors of Montanus. Moreover, Mercator’s statement that Montanus also used υἱοπάτορα and thus adhered to Praxeas contradicts Epiphanius, who writes (*Against Heresies*, book 2, heresy 48) that Montanus agreed with the Catholics concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Yet Socrates opposes Epiphanius by counting Montanus among the followers of Sabellius and even producing ancient writers who held that view. Since the matter is somewhat more complicated and would require more leisure, I wished to mention this so that no one might accuse Mercator.]

But Praxeas was the first to utter υἱοπάτορα—which this utterly insane man calls Λογοπάτορα, not knowing what he says—and, not long afterward, Montanus with his Prisca and Maximilla uttered it as well.

### 18.

After this, Sabellius and Marcellus, at the time when the most impious Arius arose, thought that they ought to preserve monarchy in the substance of divinity. Deceived by an unspeakable error, they dared to say that God the Father himself was his own Son, himself his own Father, himself the Holy Spirit, himself incarnate, himself suffering and crucified, himself enduring all things from the Jews, rising from the dead, and accomplishing everything that we believe and confess Christ performed in his own person for the salvation of the human race.

[Note: He mentions monarchy, which Sabellius and Marcellus maintained because of their desire to preserve it, though they were deceived by error. On this occasion it should be observed that both heretics and Catholics used the term “monarchy” when discussing the Trinity, but in different senses. The heretics used “monarchy” partly to exclude the unity of the persons and partly to exclude consubstantiality. The Catholics used it to lead the faithful away from a plurality of gods and to show that there is one unbegotten being in the Trinity, who is ἀρχὴ τῆς Θεότητος, “the source of divinity,” as the Greek Fathers express it.]

### 19.

The sole difference, then, between the man of Samosata and Photinus is this: Paul understood the Word of God as προφορικόν, καὶ πρακτικὸν λόγον καὶ ἐνεργητικόν—that is, a Word uttered and effective in power—but not as substantial, which the Greeks call οὐσιῶδες.

[Note: It is remarkable that this is said concerning Photinus’s difference from the man of Samosata, as though the former acknowledged the substantial Word of God while the latter acknowledged only the uttered and effective Word. For if this is so, how does Mercator not appear to contradict himself when, in his letter concerning the distinction between the heresy of Nestorius and the doctrines of Paul of Samosata, Ebion, Marcellus, and Photinus, he says: “In confessing the substantial Word of God and asserting that he is God eternally with the Father, Nestorius rightly differs from those mentioned and is joined to the orthodox faith”? Moreover, the most learned Petavius reports from Epiphanius (*Dogmatic Theology*, vol. 4, book 1, chapter 3) that Photinus affirmed that the Word, which lacked hypostasis in the same way as our own, proceeded from God and was changed into flesh. But since there will be a fuller discussion of Photinus’s error in the future, in Dissertation 1, where it will be compared with the Nestorian position and Mercator’s view of Photinus will be supported by testimonies from the ancients, it is enough here merely to indicate the question.]

Photinus, however, the teacher of Nestorius, denies that this Word of God exists in substance, and does not wish it to be the Son of God. In his impiety he raves that the Word dwelt peculiarly in, or adhered to, Christ Jesus, born from Joseph and Mary, and that this man was nothing more than a human being, although he surpassed all human beings by the merit of his life.

### 20.

The Roman Church calls Photinus and those who share this kind of depravity “Homuncionites.”

[Note: I remember reading in Augustine (vol. 10, fragment 26) that heretics who knew Christ only as a man were called by this name. I have also read in the author of *Praedestinatus* (Heresy 76) of the heresy of the “Homuncionites,” but it was different from the one Augustine mentions: they were people who said that the image of God exists in the human body, not in the soul. Philaster, however, reports this heresy without naming its followers in chapter 49, and Augustine follows Philaster in Heresy 76. Therefore this term, “Melitonians,” unknown to everyone, must have entered Augustine’s catalogue of heresies through a copyist’s error. Epiphanius attributes this heresy concerning the image of God to the Audians in Heresy 70; the author of *Praedestinatus*, Heresy 50, agrees, as does Augustine in Heresy 50, where they are called “Vadians” through the error of copyists.]

But it calls Sabellians, together with their ancient kindred, “Patripassians.”

[Note: Some deny that Sabellius held that the Father himself suffered. See Epiphanius in the *Anacephalaeosis* of book 2, on heresy 30. But Athanasius should be heard instead; his words agree with those of Marinus: “Such are those who among the Romans are called Patripassians, but among us Sabellians” (*On the Synods*).]

For, as has been said, they understand the Father himself and the Son himself under the name of unity: at one time he is Father, at another Son, one and the same person, himself to himself even the Spirit.

### 21.

[Note: It is also remarkable that the only difference between Nestorius and Photinus should be that the former said Christ was born from a virgin, while the latter said he was born from a marriage. Their chief commonality, however, is that both denied that the Word of God could be called the Son before the incarnation; Nestorius appears to deny this in several passages. The whole matter must be examined more carefully in the dissertation on the Nestorian heresy.]

Nestorius differs from Photinus, his teacher, only in this: he asserts that Christ was born from the Virgin Mary. In all other respects he is wholly Photinus’s follower, standard-bearer, and champion, especially in the point mentioned above: that the Word of God is not the Son of God, ought not to be called the Son, and that no one except Jesus, born from Mary, should be called the Son of God.

He says that Jesus merited this name because he became the temple of the one dwelling within him, through the undivided fellowship and conjunction between himself and the Word of God. Yet he does not say that he is by nature the Son of God, since he obtained the privileges of divinity from this union by grace, not possessing them by nature.

### 22.

This species of his impiety is not contained and read here in this chapter, but in other writings and treatises inserted in this same volume. Hence the Catholic reader must be cautious concerning the inconsistency and variation that he displays. Whether he employs it through cunning or through madness in order to attract his hearer is not easy to determine; nevertheless, in whatever way it is taken, it is clear that he is inconsistent and contradictory to himself.

Who would not recognize that such a man must either be avoided as a cunning captor of souls, or, as one senselessly contradicting himself and confused by his inconsistency, must in no way be followed?

### 23.

In those twelve chapters in which the holy Bishop Cyril, writing to this same Nestorius, set forth the true and sound faith, and in which Nestorius thought it necessary to respond to each point in opposition, the second of his objections must now be reconsidered.

There he says: “If anyone says that, in the conjunction of the Word of God with the flesh, a change or conversion from place to place of the divine substance took place; or says that flesh was capable of the divine nature; or says that the divinity was partially united to the flesh; or again extends flesh infinitely and without limitation along with the divine nature so that it may contain God; and says that the same person is by nature both God and man—let him be anathema.”

As though some madman like him could fail to consider at least the angels, who, as Scripture says, are spirits of fire. For it is said of them: “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning flame” (Psalm 103:4).

### 24.

[Note: Eutherius discusses this argument, drawn from angels assuming bodies, in Sermon 11, whether he found it in Mercator’s works—which one might suppose without rashness—or in Cyril, where it is also found.]

It is therefore certain that the angels whom, as we read and also believe, God frequently sent to the saints at different times assumed human appearance, taking bodies so that they could be visible to those to whom they were sent.

But whether they merely assumed bodies in which those spirits temporarily dwelt, fulfilling the ministry of rational souls; or whether, like prophets, they externally inspired animated bodies, one must not easily or rashly affirm either alternative.

### 25.

This presumptuous opinion, treating uncertain matters as certain and things not at all expressed in Scripture as though they were, deceived Apollinaris of Laodicea and afterward the Arians—not Arius himself—and also Eunomius and perhaps the later Macedonius. From this they came to believe and proclaim that Christ the Son of God assumed only a human body, not a soul as well, and that in place of a soul the Word, the Son of God the Father, dwelt in the body he had assumed.

[Note: Here a popular opinion is overturned which attributes to Arius what was devised by the Arians. On this matter much has been said in the dissertation.]

### 26.

But if this is so, they were truly deceived by the foolish error of their own judgment. For the human assumption of the Savior is found to be incomparable with that of the angels—far beyond any estimation, and beyond even that by a great distance.

Since this assumption was to take place for the redemption of the entire human race, it was necessary that the Savior assume the whole and complete human nature that was to be saved, raised with him into heaven, and remain inseparable from him in eternal life. I repeat: he had to bear the whole human nature.

The bodily assumption of the angels, however, was temporary and took place in order to display a divinely commanded service. Whichever of the two alternatives occurred—whether they are said to have had animated bodies or bodies without souls—the Catholic faith is in no way harmed.

### 27.

Later Apollinaris, as though correcting his position but actually making it worse, confessed that there was indeed a soul in Christ, but impiously raved that the human faculty of reason or mind was not present in it, and that in its place there was God, the Son of God.

### 28.

So many times, and at so many different periods, as we have said, did angels appear—whether merely taking bodies or assuming bodies that were also animated. Could anyone ever say or believe that they were changed and transformed from their spiritual and angelic nature into corporeal or even ensouled beings? Certainly not.

What, then, is this insane teacher attempting to thrust forward here in order to spread clouds before the ignorant? If anyone says that the Son of God, God the Word, according to the Gospel became flesh, or became man, he is immediately accused, as though he were utterly impious, of proclaiming that the divinity was changed into flesh.

### 29.

Let us consider how impious and vain is the final statement that he placed in this very chapter. He says: “If anyone says that the same person is by nature both God and man, let him be anathema.”

Wishing to introduce a double Christ, or simply thinking incoherently, he did not understand what he had said. For he failed to see that it could immediately be objected to him that no one had said that Christ was not by nature God or man.

The same Christ, since he is God and man—or, to speak more precisely and cautiously, since he is man-God and God-man—is nothing other than what he is by nature. If, as he thought, he is not by nature—which statement, being so impious, may recoil upon his own head—then he cannot be anything at all, because whatever cannot exist by nature cannot exist in any way whatsoever.

[Col. 0931]

## APOLOGETICUS FOR THE TWELVE CHAPTERS

### PREFACE TO ST. CYRIL’S APOLOGETICUS

[Col. 0931] Cyril had appended to his third letter to Nestorius twelve chapters concerning errors. Because each has an anathema attached, they are commonly called “anathemas,” although the ancients preferred to call them chapters. On receiving them, Nestorius immediately sent them to John, bishop of Antioch, asking him to arrange for their refutation, and for the condemnation of the errors of Apollinaris and Arius, by the two most eminent men of his diocese, Andrew of Samosata and Theodoret of Cyrus.

Both did what was requested, and each issued a writing equally bitter and acrimonious: Andrew in the name of the Orientals, Theodoret in his own name; for the former wrote at Antioch, the latter at Cyrus. John’s synod approved Andrew’s objections and, I suppose, sent them to Alexandria through the deacon Possidonius himself, who had brought John the letters of Celestine and Cyril. Theodoret circulated his censures through Phoenicia and the neighboring regions, and even sent them to the imperial city, in order to oblige his friend Nestorius. When Evoptius, bishop of Ptolemais in Pentapolis, received them, he sent them to Cyril.

Both wrote before the Council of Ephesus. Theodoret himself attests this in the preface to his *Pentalogium*. Cyril replied to both before the council, as is clear from the fact that he nowhere mentions Nestorius’s condemnation by the synod, although so weighty a judgment of the Church would have been highly material to his case.

At that time Andrew was renowned among the Orientals for his learning and piety. Three of Theodoret’s letters to him survive: the first is numbered twenty-four among those published by Sirmond; the second is found in the Fifth Synod; the third is in Marius Mercator, by whose translation it is now published for the first time. From the first one learns the high esteem in which Andrew was held by all; from the second, that he did not come to the Council of Ephesus because of ill health; from the third, that he clung obstinately to Nestorius and never consented to his condemnation, even when Theodosius exerted pressure through the tribune Aristolaus.

It is certainly remarkable that Baronius writes (*Annals*, year 431, no. 183) that, after the council had been dissolved, Andrew was induced by John of Antioch to write against Cyril’s chapters, and that he received this reward for his impiety: from being a monk at Constantinople, he became bishop of Samosata. First, however, when Theodoret wrote to him after the peace of the Churches, that Constantinopolitan was still a monk. Next, Liberatus relates that, immediately upon receiving Cyril’s letters, Nestorius asked John to have his own men criticize the chapters; and Baronius himself reports this from Liberatus under the year 430. Finally, Theodoret testified that he wrote before the council, and we have shown that Cyril replied to both men before that same council. Cyril certainly answered Theodoret as a man unknown to him; but could this have been after the council, when Theodoret had promoted the cause of the schismatics, whether alone or among the foremost? Finally, Theodoret addressed Andrew in letters from Ephesus as a bishop, and indeed as one not long since made bishop.

How long he lived is uncertain. For what Theodore the Reader says—“Rabbulas, bishop of Edessa, was blind; but Andrew of Samosata accused him of having written against Theodoret’s twelve chapters” (*Collectanea*, book II, vol. II of the *Library of the Fathers*)—can contribute nothing to chronology, since nothing is more confused than that man’s *Collectanea*. He certainly did not survive until the year 451, when the Council of Chalcedon was held. For there the name of Rufinus of Samosata is read; and, since he gave his opinion in the one hundred and twenty-first place among more than six hundred bishops, he cannot have governed the Church of Samosata only recently, since it is credible that the Fathers were listed according to the order of their ordination. I therefore think that Andrew scarcely lived as late as the year 440.

The method he follows in this work is roughly as follows. He charges Cyril less with error than with having spoken inconsistently, with using ill-considered and ambiguous expressions, and with perhaps maliciously concealing some latent error.

He draws the passages which he opposes to the anathemas from only two works of Cyril: namely, the letter to the Egyptian monks and the seventeenth Paschal homily; he calls the former the first tome and the latter the second. For these two were, as it were, the first open signs of the quarrel with Nestorius and the trumpets of war; and they were widely known everywhere, both because of the homily’s general relevance and especially because the letter had been deliberately disseminated through the cities, above all at Constantinople, to which Andrew was writing.

Finally, it should be observed that Andrew advances very few assertions that cannot bear a sound interpretation. Thus he does not differ so greatly from Cyril that they could not readily be reconciled if contentiousness were absent. I say “advances,” because he repeatedly sets out the position of the Orientals, attacked in the anathemas under, as it were, Nestorius’s name. Thus this composition may seem not so much an attack on any one man as either a defense and judgment of the Oriental synod, or an opinion on the anathemas as mutually contradictory.

This was why Cyril, although sometimes angered by the importunity of his detractors, nevertheless treated Andrew more mildly than Theodoret: in the former he saw an entire province, in the latter an individual person, and indeed one unknown to him.

## APOLOGETICUS OF ST. CYRIL, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, FOR THE TWELVE CHAPTERS AGAINST THE ORIENTAL BISHOPS, IN WHOSE NAME ANDREW OF SAMOSATA HAD WRITTEN OBJECTIONS

Translated by Marius Mercator.

[Col. 0933]

[Col. 0933A] Those who hasten to devote their mind to God thrice holy [Baluz. omits *thrice holy*], and who desire to adhere to the doctrines of truth, indeed reject the profane and empty discourses of wicked heretics [Baluz.: “new”]; but, directing the inward and secret eye of the mind toward divine Scripture and arming it therefrom with sound judgments, they rise steadfastly against those who pervert what is right, almost crying out: “We have been exceedingly zealous for the Lord” (3 Kings 19:10).

Therefore, while Nestorius was pouring forth many and diverse blasphemies against Christ, the Savior of all, and, as it were, utterly overthrowing the great and venerable mystery of the incarnation, we judged that it would be a grave danger to keep silent about matters so great and such as these. Accordingly, we repeatedly admonished him to refrain from blasphemies of this kind. But after we made no progress whatever, we necessarily undertook to defend the doctrines of piety. We therefore marked certain chapters drawn from his own blasphemies and usefully anathematized them—that is, those who think the same things as he—obeying blessed Paul, who says: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than that which you received, let him be anathema. But even if we, or an angel from heaven, preach to you a gospel other than that which we preached to you, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1:9).

But I do not know how [Note: That is, Andrew, bishop of Samosata, and Theodoret of Cyrus, as Cyril’s memorandum addressed to the presbyter Eulogius shows. This apologetic work of Cyril is directed against Andrew’s censures. In another book Cyril subsequently replied [Col. 0934A] to Theodoret, below, in Cyril’s response. On Andrew’s censures, see also what we have recently said in the first volume of the *New Collection of Councils*, p. 748. BALUZE.] some persons took this ill—whether they were companions in and like-minded with the same madness, or whether, while concealing that they thought the same things as he, they nevertheless assisted him by every means [Baluz.: “him by all means”] and tried to make hateful those who wished to speak for Christ. Yet they ought to have reflected that, had they more strongly rebuked false teachers, that very act would have gained for them Christ’s love and favor. Instead, they did what they ought by no means to have done: they declared hostile to themselves those whose imitators, had they been, they would have crowned their heads with everlasting glory along with those very persons.

They therefore censured the anathemas as though they had not been rightly composed; then, against each one, they set their own inventions and certain absurdities, hoping to creep in upon [Baluz.: *subripere*, “steal in upon”] the unlearned and those who receive their words carelessly.

[Col. 0935B] It was therefore necessary that we too set truth against them, repel their utterly empty accusation, and prove that they are revilers and censors rather than investigators of the whole truth. Accordingly, after setting out each anathema and also placing beneath it what they had objected, we added our own replies, making those skilled in holy Scripture judges and seeking the just verdict of those who possess knowledge of the truth.

### FIRST ANATHEMA

If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is truly God, and therefore that the holy Virgin is *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”), for she bore according to the flesh the Word of God made flesh, let him be anathema.

### CENSURE OF THE HERETICS

[Col. 0935C] Who confesses that the Word of God made flesh was born ACCORDING TO THE FLESH? For if the mother [Baluz. omits *mother*] gave birth according to the flesh, how is she still a virgin? Further, where shall we place that saying: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35), if, according to him, the holy Virgin gave birth carnally and not in a divine manner? And how did the star, appearing in wondrous ways, point him out? How did the Magi come from Persia under the star’s guidance, seeking him who had been born, and, when they found him, offer gifts appropriate to his intelligible and visible natures (Matt. 2:11–12)? How did angels descending from heaven sing among the shepherds of his birth, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke 2:14)? Are these signs of a carnal birth, or rather of a divine one?

Otherwise, if we receive the words themselves carelessly and without consideration, we shall imagine that a conversion of the Word and a change into flesh took place, and thus suppose that he himself became both sin and curse—unless we examine both what follows and what precedes in the books, the customary usage of Scripture itself, and understand the Word’s being born according to the flesh as indwelling in flesh, in accordance with the sense of the Gospels.

### RESPONSE OF THE ORTHODOX

The most wise John clearly shows the mystery of the only-begotten Son of God’s dispensation according to the flesh, saying: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” [Col. 0936A] (John 1:14). Correctly understanding this, the most blessed Fathers who were assembled at Nicaea in their time [Baluz.: “then”] said that the Word himself was born of God the Father, through whom [Baluz.: “whom”] and with whom the Father made all things: light from light, true God from true God, incarnate and made man; that is, united to flesh possessing a rational soul, and yet, though made man, remaining God.

That union was made without conversion and without confusion cannot be doubtful to anyone, since the Word of God remained what he had been before, although he became flesh. For what is said to be incarnate is not converted into the nature of flesh; rather, something other than flesh, though united to flesh, is understood.

Id being their conviction, the blessed Fathers called the holy Virgin Θεοτόκος [God-bearer] [Col. 0936B]. For they believed that she had borne the Son—incarnate and made man—through whom the Father made all things. But Nestorius, inventor of new blasphemies for us, opposes this opinion and censures it, as though she ought not truly to be called Θεοτόκος; for he says:

“I have often asked them: ‘Do you say that the Godhead was born from the holy Virgin?’ They immediately evade the answer. And who,” they say, “is so blasphemous as to say that God was created by the Spirit in her who bore the temple?” Then, when I add: “What absurdity, therefore, are we committing by persuading people to avoid this expression and to come instead to the common meaning of the two natures?” what I say then appears blasphemous to them. “Either openly confess that the Godhead was born from the holy Virgin; or, if you flee this expression as blasphemous, why, while agreeing with me in the same opinion, do you pretend not to agree?” (Cyril’s Letter to Acacius of Beroea, Sermon 5).

Since he was therefore pressing the matter violently—or rather wickedly provoking those who call the holy Virgin Θεοτόκος to confess that the Godhead was the offspring of the flesh and that God the Word had received from a woman the beginning of his existence [Baluz. substance], we, wishing to prove that we utterly reject such an opinion—for we are not so deranged as to think anything so impious—said that the Virgin had borne the Word of God made flesh, that is, made man, according to the Scriptures. She bore him carnally, that is, according to the flesh; for God the Father also begot God the Son from himself in a divine manner. But since that which is born from flesh is flesh (John 3:6), the Virgin, being as it were flesh, bore him carnally [Col. 0936D]. Nor do I abolish the miracle of the generation, nor deny the operation of the Holy Spirit, through which he fashioned in the womb that which was born; rather, I demonstrate that just as God begets divinely, and as befits God, according to his nature, so also man begets humanly, and flesh carnally.

Since, therefore, the Word is God by nature, although he became flesh, he came forth divinely and as truly befitted God. For he alone had an unmarried mother, and preserved her as a Virgin—the woman who bore him according to the flesh. And I marvel at this: although they are reluctant to call the holy Virgin Θεοτόκος, they nevertheless assert that she bore him in a divine manner; for an ordinary man is not born divinely.

[Col. 0937A] Next they say that the gifts offered by the Magi corresponded to both the intelligible and the visible. Thus they again divide the one Lord Jesus Christ into two after the conjunction. For he became intelligible and visible, not by a conversion of nature, but by the conjunction of the body, which is visible. Certainly, holy Scripture has taught that the apostles themselves were spectators and ministers of the Word, since it is clear to all that the Word of God the Father is incorporeal and intangible. Yet I hear the holy disciples say: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen, which we have contemplated with our eyes, and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). The gifts, then, corresponded to the one person, Christ; for in the one there is God and man together. Therefore, when he was born, choirs of angels and hosts of spirits proclaimed him Savior and Deliverer [Col. 0937B].

But since the Evangelist says, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14), they say that they fear lest, if τὸ ἐγένετο retains its proper meaning, some conversion should be understood to have occurred in the divine nature of the Word. I commend the fear, but I marvel that, while rejecting the expression and its true and necessary meaning, they say that the Word became flesh in the same way as it is said that he became a curse and sin (Gal. 3:13; 2 Cor. 5:21). Why, then, when they consider themselves exceedingly shrewd, do they not see that the blessed Evangelist, by saying ἐγένετο, excludes every notion of conversion, immediately adding: “And he dwelt among us”?

Moreover, it is absurd to dare to say that the Word became flesh in the same way as he is said to have become a curse and sin [Col. 0937C]. For he did not truly and properly become a curse and sin; rather, the righteous one was reckoned among the wicked (Mark 15:8; Isaiah 53:12), in order to destroy sin. He was called accursed who blesses the creature, in order to dissolve our curse and free from punishment those who believe in him. He was not therefore truly a curse and sin; but he was called both, in order to destroy the curse and sin.

Therefore, if he became flesh in a similar manner, he destroyed flesh also, just as he destroyed the curse and sin; and he neither truly became man nor was truly incarnate, but the mystery existed only in δοκήσει, in mere appearance, and the reality and manner of the Incarnation would be found only in bare names.

The hope of the resurrection is also utterly removed. “Into whose death, then, were we baptized?” (Rom. 6:3) [Col. 0937D]. Where is the word of faith that we preach? “For if we confess that Jesus is Lord and believe that God raised him from the dead, we are saved” (Rom. 10:8). Is our faith in one who is merely like us, an ordinary man? Or do we not rather adore the Word who, for our sake, became man in human form? He therefore did not receive the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7), he who was free—that is, God. He did not humble himself, he who shines with the heights of dignity [Baluz. deity], and who exists in equality with the Father and in his form. He did not enter into self-emptying [Col. 0938A], he who from his fullness distributes all good things to creation [Baluz. apportions them].

Away with this madness! The most blessed Fathers taught us otherwise. They truly called the Word of God the Father incarnate and made man, without corruption [Baluz. without conversion] and without confusion. The manner of the dispensation, however, is hidden and ineffable. I shall call their own statements as witnesses to what I have said.

### Of Peter the Martyr, Bishop of Alexandria

The Evangelist speaks the truth: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14)—from the time, namely, when the Angel greeted the Virgin, saying: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28). “The Lord is with you,” Gabriel said, meaning, “God the Word is with you”; for this signifies that he would be born in the womb and become flesh, according to what is written: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35) [Col. 0938B].

### Of Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria

Hence also, when his flesh was born from Mary Θεοτόκος, he himself is said to have been born—he who grants that others may be born—in order to transfer our generation into himself [Baluz. so that we might be born].

### Of the Same, from the Letter to Epictetus

[Note: [Col. 0937D] See what we recently said in the first volume of the *Nova Collectio Conciliorum*, pp. 466, 596, 599, 606, 757, 922. — BALUZ.]

How, then, did those who are called Christians dare even to doubt whether the Lord who proceeded from Mary is truly the Son of God in substance and nature, while according to the flesh he is from the seed of David and from the flesh of holy Mary? How, moreover, could they be so bold as to say that Christ, who suffered and was crucified in the flesh, is not Lord, Savior, God, and Son of the Father? Or how do they wish to be called Christians when they say that the Word came upon a holy man—as upon one of the prophets—instead of saying that he himself became man by taking a body from Mary? Or that Christ is one, and the Word who existed before Mary and before the ages as the Son of the Father is another? Or how can they be Christians who say that the Son is one and the Word of God another?

We follow this opinion and faith of the holy Fathers. But if anyone teaches differently and introduces new expressions, he appears to be wandering outside the straight and trodden path [Col. 0938D]. That it is neither unusual nor unfamiliar for the holy Fathers to say that he was born CARNALLY, but rather that this expression is frequent and repeatedly employed, the statements written below will demonstrate. They are as follows.

[Note: That is, of Amphilochius, Bishop of Iconium. See above, p. 471. — Baluzius.]

### Of Amphilochius, Bishop of Iconium

“For unless he had been begotten CARNALLY, you would never have been spiritually reborn; and unless he had endured the form of a servant, you would never have obtained the glory of adoption” [Col. 0939A]. Here too, “carnally” is used for “according to the flesh,” just as “divinely” means “according to divinity.”

The objection of the Easterners to the second anathema, and Cyril’s response, is nowhere found in the codices—whether printed or manuscript—that I have seen. That there nevertheless was some such objection is clear from the fact that, in his objection to the third anathema, Andrew says that he is again opposing Cyril with words taken from Cyril’s own statements, although in the objection to the first anathema he opposed nothing of the kind. Moreover, the whole issue turned on the second anathema, since the discussion concerned ἕνωσις καθ’ ὑπόστασιν, that is, the principle which, once granted, overthrew the whole of Nestorius’s heresy and established the Catholic faith. It is hardly credible that nothing was said about the main point of the entire matter by a man who had undertaken the defense of Nestorius.

## THIRD ANATHEMA

If anyone divides the substances in the one Christ after the union, and joins them by conjunction alone according to dignity, authority, or dominion, rather than by a certain joining effected through a natural ἕνωσις [union], let him be anathema.

### Refutation of the Heretics

Again we shall remind him of his own words, convicting him of having spoken of two substances in what he wrote in the first volume, as follows:

“Therefore, insofar as it pertained to his proper nature, the Word of God the Father was not sanctified in himself; but if anyone believes that he who was born from the holy Virgin was anointed and sanctified, himself alone and by himself, and for that reason was called Christ,” and so forth (Letter to the Monks, §§15–16).

How, then, forgetting his own words, does he compress the matter into one substance, confusing the natures by calling the divine ἕνωσις natural?

And who could ever accept a natural divine ἕνωσις in the mystery of the dispensation? For if that union is natural, where is grace? Where is the divine mystery? For natures, once established by God, serve necessary laws. Will the order of the dispensation again arise through ἀνακύκλησις [recurrence] and the law of nature, in accordance with that fabulous χιλιονταετηρίς—“thousand-year period”—invented by Apollinarius [Baluz. Apollinaris]?

The heresiologists—Epiphanius, Philastrius, Augustine, Theodoret, and the author of the *Praedestinatus*—make no mention of Apollinarius’s ἀνακύκλησις and χιλιονταετηρίς [Col. 0939D]. Yet three very weighty writers do: Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Jerome. Jerome writes the following about Papias:

“He is said to have published a Jewish δευτέρωσις [repetition or secondary exposition] of a thousand years, followed by Irenaeus and Apollinarius, who say that after the resurrection the Lord will reign in the flesh with the saints” (*On Illustrious Men*, ch. 28).

Indeed, when Dionysius of Alexandria had written against Irenaeus, who was entangled in this error, Jerome testifies (*Preface to Isaiah*, ch. 65) that Apollinarius replied in two volumes.

### Orthodox Response

The divine Paul, as the steward of God’s mysteries, makes clear to everyone how the only-begotten Word of God became man, himself having Christ speaking in him:

“For he did not take hold of angels,” he says, “but he took hold of the seed of Abraham. Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God” (Heb. 2:16).

But, affirming this statement with proper assent, following holy Scripture everywhere, and admiring the words of the divine teachers—or rather, judging them to be most holy laws—we do not say that the Word of God the Father took hold of the holy angels or of his own nature; rather, as the divine writings prescribe, we believe that he overshadowed the holy Virgin, since he is the power of the Most High Father, fashioned a body for himself from her through the operation of the Holy Spirit, became man, and was called the Son of Abraham and David. He had not ceased to be truly the Son of God and the Father [Col. 0940B], but had remained in his own nature, majesty, and glory of deity, although he became flesh; for God is unchangeable and stronger than every conversion.

There is therefore one and the same Son and Lord, both before the Incarnation and after the Incarnation. To divide the one into two, to undermine the true ἕνωσις, to separate him into parts, and to speak of man separately and God separately is a crime of enormous impiety.

He calls it a true ἕνωσις, which elsewhere he calls φυσική [natural]. For no union is true unless it joins the things themselves, or φύσεις [natures], and not merely the qualities of things. Every ἕνωσις makes one thing out of many; but if that which results is something substantial, it is a true and simply stated ἕνωσις. If it is some quality or something other than substance, it is not a true union, but merely a κατὰ τι [according to some respect] and σχετική [relative] ἕνωσις; for, as the Philosopher says, substance, insofar as it is being ἁπλῶς [simply], is also one ἁπλῶς [simply].

Therefore every ἕνωσις that is not, as they say in the schools, into unity of substance—whether substance is taken as nature or as hypostasis—is not, according to Cyril, κατὰ ἀλήθειαν [according to truth], but only κατὰ σχέσιν [according to relation]. Hence in this matter the following expressions are synonymous: ἕνωσις ἁπλῶς [union simply], ἕνωσις φυσική [natural union], ἕνωσις καθ’ ὑπόστασιν [union according to hypostasis], and ἕνωσις κατ’ ἀλήθειαν [union according to truth]. Conversely, the following are equivalent: ἕνωσις κατά τι [union according to some respect], ἕνωσις σχετική [relative union], ἕνωσις κατ’ εὐδοκίαν [union according to good pleasure], ἕνωσις κατὰ τὴν ἀξίαν [union according to dignity], and συνάφεια ἡ ἔξωθεν [an external conjunction], and so forth.

What is more remarkable is that in Cyril, where the discussion concerns ἕνωσις, φύσις [nature] is taken for ὑπόστασις [hypostasis]. This will be explained later.

But, disregarding all these considerations, Nestorius dared to utter the following words (Sermon 7, §12):

“Have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, although he was in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” He did not say: “Have this mind in yourselves which was also in God the Word, who, although he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant.” But when he said “Christ,” as an appellation of two natures, he safely named him both the form of a servant that he took and God, since these expressions can be said without sin of the twofold and separable relation of the natures.

And again, in another treatise (Sermon 1, §9):

“‘At the name of Jesus,’ he says, ‘every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord’ [Baluz. adds: ‘in the glory of God the Father’]. Because of him who carried, I worship him who was carried; because of the invisible, I venerate the visible. God is never separated from him who appears; therefore neither do I separate the honor. I separate the natures, but I make one veneration.”

And again in another treatise (Sermon 2, at the end):

“Call him who assumed, because he is God; call him who was assumed, because he is a servant. Then add the dignity of the conjunction, because the authority of the two is common; because the dignity of the two is the same. While the natures remain, confess the unity of dignity.”

You see that everywhere he separates the natures, but makes, as he himself says, one veneration, speaks of a common authority, and posits only a unity of dignity, ἐνήτης. But whatever is common cannot be common to one alone; it must be common to two or more, understood separately and individually. For what reason, then, have they censured the sermon in which we anathematize these things? What crime have we committed if, opposing the impious doctrines of Nestorius—profane and novel inventions—with doctrines of piety, we have properly taken account of the defense of our brothers?

But since they say that I contradict myself in my sermons, and, to prove this, recite part of my letter written to the holy monks, I have thought it appropriate to answer this also in words suited to the matter. For they say that I too spoke of two substances, and they suppose that this is sufficient proof. Having therefore set out that part of the letter, I shall immediately add the words by which they will be convicted everywhere of falsehood and empty speech.

**Letter:** “Therefore, insofar as it pertained to his proper nature, the Word of God was not sanctified by himself alone; but if anyone should think that he who was born from the holy Virgin was anointed and sanctified by himself alone, and therefore called Christ, let him come forward and prove that anointing alone is sufficient to show that the one who is anointed is like the glory of the Father and shares the same throne with God, who is supreme over all” [Col. 0941C].

Because Nestorius, inventor of new blasphemies, asserts that the Word of God, named Christ separately, is one, and that another Christ, who was born from the Virgin, is separate and distinct, we censure this opinion of his as unsuitable, incongruous, and outside the bounds of truth. We neither affirm that the Word of God the Father, considered alone and in himself, was anointed with the oil of gladness, nor, on the other hand, that the man, considered alone and in himself, is one Son and the Word of God the Father another, distinct from him who was born from the Virgin. Rather, we affirm that all should confess one Christ, the only-begotten Word of God, incarnate and made man [Col. 0941D]: “For there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4:5). It is therefore not obscure to anyone who wishes to think rightly that they distort the meaning of what I have written and here too slander the truth.

This is also correct for another reason and entirely free from blame. We know, of course, that the flesh is something other than the Word born from the Father, according to the particularity of its nature; and that the only-begotten Word of God is something else according to the character of its nature [Col. 0942A]. Yet to know that this is so is not to divide the natures after the union.

He used “natures,” or φύσεις, for hypostases; this is something to be carefully observed. By the term φύσις he understands nothing other than what in the schools is called a natural reality, opposed, as they say, to a moral entity or even to an accident. Accordingly, the word φύσις, as it is determined by its accompanying expressions, acquires various meanings. Thus in Cyril φύσις τοῦ λόγου [the nature of the Word] is the same as the hypostasis of the Word; whereas φύσις τοῦ Θεοῦ [the nature of God] is the common divinity of the persons. Likewise, φύσις τοῦ Κυρίλλου [the nature of Cyril] is properly his own individuality, as they say; and φύσις τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [the nature of man] is the common nature, and so forth.
