But if anyone wishes to contemplate the force of the mystery with a discerning mind and easily understand it from what we said at the beginning, namely, that God the Word did not take hold of his own nature [Col. 0942B], but of the seed of Abraham [Note: [Col. 0941] Baluzius adds here: “Nor is the holy body, which is from the seed of Abraham, like the Word of God in substance; by which, etc.” — EDIT.], then, taking it from the blessed Virgin, he came forth as man, so that he might be made like his brothers and be called the firstborn, although he is the only-begotten Son.

Yet although the body is of another nature, distinct from the Word of God the Father, nevertheless there is one Christ, one Son, one God, and one Lord, although he became flesh. It is dangerous to undermine the reality of the true unity and to separate the substances into two sons [Baluz. into two parts], saying that they are indeed diverse and separate from one another by their own properties, while maintaining that they have only an external and honorific conjunction.

If, then, we say “natural ἕνωσις,” we shall be speaking truly, especially since divine Scripture uses this expression so frequently. The blessed Paul writes somewhere: “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3). No one, however, would say that divine wrath has substance by nature, so that sinners would also be called its children. For if we say this, we shall be like the fury of the Manichaeans. Rather, he used “by nature” for “in truth.”

Therefore, without confusing the natures, and without mixing them together as the opponents allege, we call the ἕνωσις natural because we everywhere affirm that one Christ, Son, and Lord was made from two dissimilar realities—that is, from divinity and humanity. The doctrines of Apollinarius are of no concern whatsoever to us [Baluz. “no cause for concern”]; for those who have once been condemned as corrupters of the truth ought to be shunned.

[Col. 0942D] From two natures, as they say, dissimilar in kind, there was made one hypostasis, one Christ, one Son, one Lord—one, I say, substantially and καθ’ ὑπόστασιν [according to hypostasis], not merely one morally and κατὰ σχέσιν [according to relation].

## FOURTH ANATHEMA

If anyone distributes between two persons or substances the expressions found in the evangelical or apostolic writings, or those spoken by the saints concerning Christ, or by Christ himself concerning himself, assigning some to the man, understood separately apart from the Word of God [Col. 0943A], and others as divine to the Word of God alone, let him be anathema.

### Refutation of the Heretics

Here too it is appropriate to remind him of his own doctrines, in which he says (Homily 17, Paschal):

“If you hear that he advanced in age, wisdom, and grace, do not suppose that the Word of God became wise through advancement (Luke 2:52); but do not even dare to say that we assign the advancement in age, wisdom, and grace to the man. Even if Scripture denies its own testimony, teaching that advancement occurred according to the visible flesh of the Lord, it is not now the time to convict him of this, since we are hastening to the chapter before us. For, to prove that he speaks of two substances and contradicts himself, we have set out what he said earlier” [Col. 0943B].

It is not fitting to apply expressions to two persons, two substances, or two sons—separating the ἕνωσις, or the one Son. For that highest ἕνωσις is indivisible and inseparable, and there is one Son in every respect and in every way. Therefore, with the unity preserved, and with one Son, Christ, and Lord demonstrated, the things that are said must be applied to the one and same Son. Not to divide the evangelical expressions, or those spoken by the Lord himself concerning himself, or those set down in the apostolic writings, is the mark of extreme madness.

For if we do not divide the expressions, with what eyes shall we look upon the Eunomians or Arians, who are accustomed to refer everything that is said to one nature and to elevate the humble expressions of humanity to the height of divinity? Or how shall we understand the Lord’s words, which he spoke because of the visible nature of the flesh: “I have not come to do my own will” (John 6:38); and: “I received a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak” (John 12:49); and: “I do nothing of myself” (John 8:28); and: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17), and other expressions of this kind?

For if the expressions are indivisible, as are the natures, God the Father will be the God of the only-begotten Son by himself, while the Son, according to his deity, will be the minister and intermediary of the Father’s commands. And if we refer the humble expressions to the nature of deity, to whom shall we ascribe: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and: “He himself does the same things as the Father”; and: “Just as the Father raises the dead, so also the Son gives life to those whom he wills” (John 5:19, 21)?

Yet, according to the Lord’s own word [Note: Baluz. reads: “The Father is indeed God of the flesh that in the last times was made from the seed of David. The Father…”], the Father is both his Father and his God: God, indeed, of him who in the last times was made from the seed of David according to the flesh; but Father of the Word, who was eternally and impassibly and always born from him—his sonship being preserved and made manifest in one manner [Baluz. “to be preserved”]. For how shall we understand: “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58); and: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3) [Col. 0944A], if the expressions are indivisible? Shall we ascribe the natural expression [Baluz. “the expression of nature”] to that which in the last times was made from the seed of David, saying that it existed before Abraham and before David and that all things were made through it?

Or rather, with due regard for piety, while the natures remain without confusion and the unity remains undivided, shall we assign the expressions according to the power of the conjoined natures, as stated above, to the one Son, Lord, and Christ, referring everything not to one nature but to one Son? Thus, from the one name we understand both natures, because of the supreme and incomprehensible ἕνωσις:

“No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven” (John 3:13);

and again:

“If you see the Son of man ascending where he was before” (John 6:63).

Do we not, from the designation “Son of man,” understand both him and the one who is joined to him without confusion and inseparably? [Note: Baluz. reads: “For even if he called himself Lord of man because of…”] For although he called himself the Son of man because of the nature of the flesh he had assumed and which was visible, he nevertheless showed by his deeds that he was God. And further: “Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (Heb. 2:10); and again: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb. 13:8). If he is “yesterday and today,” how are all things through him? And if all things are through him, how is he “yesterday and today”?

Yet both that all things are through him is true, and that he is yesterday and today must be believed, and that he is the same forever is certain—if we apply the expressions according to the diversity of the natures conjoined without confusion and inseparably. We understand “yesterday and today” according to what is visible, “forever” according to what is intelligible, and, according to the conjunction of sonship, we understand him to be one and the same.

### Orthodox Response

Their purpose, plainly, is this: those who thoughtlessly and recklessly undertake to accuse the anathemas that we formulated so usefully and necessarily have nothing right either to think or to say, but merely show themselves to be slanderers and detractors. For if they had carefully directed the eye of their mind to the writings, they would certainly recognize that they themselves more strongly confirm the anathema by their assent and clearly demonstrate from what they criticize that it was not ineptly composed by us [Note: “I shall say how they do this,” Baluzius does not have this wording. — EDIT.].

When the good Nestorius was preaching in the Church, he said this (Sermon 5, the second against Proclus):

“To make this clearer and more evident to everyone—the Arians, Eunomians, Apollinarians, and all who belong to the same flock—it is their endeavor to say Θεοτόκος, as though, by some mixture having occurred and the natures not being divided [Baluz. “not to be divided”], the humble expressions would not be understood of humanity and would find a place against the deity, as though everything that is said were said of one and the same thing.”

After these words, our anathema was most appropriately formulated [Col. 0945A], since it does not permit the one Lord Jesus Christ to be divided into two persons or two substances.

That they themselves also agree with our statements is clear from what they have tried both to think and to write. Their words are as follows:

“It is not fitting to apply expressions to two persons, two substances, or two sons—dividing the unity, or the one Son. For that supreme ἕνωσις is indivisible and inseparable, and there is one Son in every respect and in every way. Therefore, with the supreme unity preserved, and with one Son, Christ, and Lord demonstrated, the things that are said must be applied to the one and same Son. Furthermore, according to the power of the conjoined natures, the things that are said must be applied to the one Son.”

Therefore, if that supreme ἕνωσις must be preserved, what opportunity for division can break in [Baluz. interrupt]? And if anyone dares to divide, he appears to be wandering far from the straight path and to be opposed to the doctrines of piety.

[Note: “What, then, does the anathema say?” So read the older books. In the Bellovacensis, however, there is additionally a title-like insertion: “Fifth Anathema.” But no title should be added, since no refutation of the heretic follows. — BALUZ.]

What, then, does the anathema say?

“If anyone divides the expressions in such a way that he assigns some to the man, understood separately apart from the Word of God, and others as divine to the Word of God alone, let him be anathema.”

Therefore, if those who divide and separate the man by himself and the Word of God by himself do not divide the one Christ and do not speak of two sons, let my accusers rightly be angry with me. But if this is their view, then it is plainly division for which they have accused my statements—especially since they themselves, from what they say, confess Emmanuel to be indivisible and one through the supreme unity.

I too gladly and fully agree with all who habitually think rightly that each of the individual expressions—whether spoken about Christ or by Christ [Col. 0945C]—must be understood prudently and wisely. Some are divine, while others are more suited to the dispensation of the flesh. But since the one and same person is God and man together, he now speaks divinely and now humanly. Nevertheless, we affirm that both kinds of speech belong to the one Jesus Christ. We neither strip the temple born from the Virgin of divinity, nor say that the Word of God the Father exists without flesh after the secret and ineffable union.

I marvel, however, that although they appear to scrutinize my writings carefully and, as they themselves suppose, examine my letters subtly, they deliberately pass over whatever in them is useful and necessary and pertains to the proof of sound doctrines [Col. 0945D]. But they seize upon anything that seems to them to offer even the faintest suspicion by which they might bring a charge against us, with sufficient agility and zeal.

I shall recall my own statements. For I wrote to Nestorius in my letter as follows (Letter 3, §19):

“We do not divide the expressions of our Savior found in the Gospels between two substances or two persons. For Christ is not twofold, but one and alone, although he is understood from two different realities to have been brought into one inseparable unity. Thus also, although man is understood to consist of soul and body, he is not for that reason two, but one from both.

“Yet we most rightly confess that the human expressions, and likewise the divine expressions, were uttered by him. For when, as God, he teaches about himself: ‘Whoever sees me sees the Father also’ (John 14:9); and: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30), we understand his divine and ineffable nature, through which he is one with his Father because of the ταυτότης [identity] of substance. For he is his image and figure and the radiance of his glory.

“But when, without dishonoring the measure of humanity, he addresses the Jews: ‘Now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you’ (John 7:1), we nevertheless recognize from the other conditions of his humanity the same one who is in equality and likeness with the Father, God the Word [Note: Baluz. reads: ‘We recognize God the Word from the measure of his humanity. For…’].

“For if it is necessary to believe that, although he is God by nature, he became flesh, or man, with flesh animated by a rational soul, why should anyone be ashamed of his expressions if they were spoken in a human manner? For if he rejects the words that appear to suit a man, who compelled him to become a man like us? And if for our sake he voluntarily entered into self-emptying, why should he reject expressions appropriate to that self-emptying?

“All the evangelical expressions, therefore, must be said of one person and of one substance, the incarnate Word: ‘There is one Lord Jesus Christ’ (1 Cor. 8:6), according to the Scriptures. We are not thereby shown to be ignorant of the dispensation appropriate to each expression [Baluz. ‘to each word’]; rather, we refuse to permit those who are ψυχικοί [natural, soulish] and do not possess the Spirit [Baluz. ‘Christ’] to call there two sons or to say that the substances are divided from one another after the inseparable unity.”

Since at the beginning of their statements they placed only a very brief part of our letter, threatening that they would at some time convict us as though we were committing no ordinary offense against the Word of God the Father, recklessly attributing to his nature an increase appropriate to the flesh, let us now say what must also be answered on this point, setting down the whole passage of the letter. For, fearing the truth and hastening to insinuate themselves into the minds of their hearers, they quoted only that part which seemed useful to them, by which they could bring against us a specious accusation. The text runs as follows:

“And if you hear that Jesus was advancing in age, grace, and wisdom, do not suppose that the Word of God had been wise by way of advancement; rather, remember that the blessed Paul wrote in this way: ‘Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God’ (1 Cor. 1:18). But do not rashly dare to say that we assign the advancement in age, wisdom, and grace to the man; for that is nothing other than dividing the one Christ into two parts. But, as I said earlier, although he is Son before the ages, in the last times he is said to have been the Son of God, making the generation of his flesh his own by dispensation. Likewise, although he is the wisdom of the Begetter, he is said to advance in wisdom: he who is most perfect, being God, receives into himself, through the supreme union, what properly belongs to humanity, in a familiar manner. Why, then, when God says, ‘Judge with righteous judgment’ (Deut. 1:16), do they themselves corrupt the truth? For we do not assert a division of substances after the union, nor do we say that the nature of the Godhead needed increase and advancement. Rather, we say that through the dispensation he made his own the things proper to the flesh, since he became flesh, according to Scripture.”

[Col. 0946D]

He calls the Paschal Homily a “letter,” not because it is not a discourse—indeed, it is an extended and carefully composed one—but because it was truly sent throughout almost the whole world, and especially through the Eastern Empire, to all the principal and autocephalous (*αὐτοκεφάλαι*) sees, from which it would pass to the lesser sees and announce the day on which Pascha was to be celebrated.

That the chorus of the holy Fathers also assents to this faith and opinion I shall prove by adding a passage from a treatise delivered by Atticus of blessed memory, which runs as follows.

### Atticus, Bishop of Constantinople

[Col. 0947A]

Today Christ the Lord assumed a birth of clemency, for he already possessed the birth that belongs to divine dignity. And further he said:

“The Word of clemency is emptied, although by nature it cannot be emptied: ‘He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant’ (Phil. 2:7). Without flesh, he comes to be in flesh, for ‘the Word became flesh’ (John 1:14). He who cannot be handled because of his incorporeal nature is handled. He who has no beginning enters upon a bodily beginning [Baluz.: ‘comes to be under a beginning’]. The perfect one grows; the unchangeable one advances; the rich one comes to be in a lodging [Baluz.: ‘in an upper room’]. He who encompasses heaven with clouds is wrapped in swaddling clothes; the King is laid in a manger.”

### That the Division of Substances after the Union Is a Great Sin

[Col. 0947B]

That dividing the substances after the union is a great sin, or rather that it overturns the venerable mystery of the Incarnation, we shall nevertheless understand if we examine the passages set forth below from Julius and Felix, who presided over the Roman Church.

### Julius, Bishop of Rome

[Col. 0947C]

It is proclaimed for the consummation of faith that the Son of God, incarnate from the Virgin Mary, dwelt in us—not that he worked in a man; for that has its place in the prophets and apostles. He is perfect God in flesh, perfect man in spirit: not two sons, but one; not one natural Son who assumed a man, and another mortal man assumed by God, but one only-begotten Son in heaven and one only-begotten Son on earth, God.

### Felix, Most Holy Bishop and Martyr of Rome

[Col. 0947D]

#### On the Incarnation of the Word and the Faith

We believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, born from the Virgin Mary. For he is the eternal Son of God and the Word, not a man assumed by God so that there might be another besides him; but, while he was perfect God, he simultaneously became perfect man, incarnate from the Virgin.

On the letters of Julius and Felix, the supreme pontiffs, see the very learned Petavius—not so much his discussion as his doubt—in volume IV of *Dogmata ecclesiastica*, book IV, chapter 6, § 9.

[Note: [Col. 0947D] Therefore the sixth has been omitted. —Baluzius.]

### Seventh Anathema

[Col. 0948A]

If anyone says that Jesus, as a man, was assisted by the operation of the Word of God [Baluz. adds: “the Son”], and assigns the glory of the Only-begotten to someone other than him, let him be anathema.

### Refutation of the Heretics

No one confesses that our Lord Jesus Christ was assisted by the operation of the Spirit as merely a man, or as a prophet, or as an apostle. Nevertheless, we can neither deny nor erase the apostolic statements spoken of him on account of the visible nature of his flesh, provided that we say: “According to the operation of the might of his power, which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead” (Eph. 1:19). And again: “Whom God raised from the dead, having loosed the pains of death” (Acts 2:24). And again: “Exalted by the power of God” (ibid., 33), and other similar passages.

But although these things are said on account of what is visible, let no one suppose that he was assisted by operation as merely a man, or as a holy man, or as a prophet, or as an apostle. Therefore we neither erase nor deny the divine statements, nor do we anathematize them through ignorance or blasphemy: they were spoken and set down on account of the visible nature of the flesh. Nor do we say that he was assisted by operation as merely a man, or as a holy man, or as a prophet, or as an apostle. For he did not say, “Thus says the Lord,” but, as Son and lawgiver, “I have said to you” (Matt. 5:32).

[Col. 0948B]

Andrew should be observed speaking so confusedly that he seems to follow Nestorius’s error, namely, that the Incarnation is merely the dwelling of the Word in a man. Although he asserts that the Holy Spirit—or rather the Word, for the question did not in fact concern the Spirit—worked in him differently from the way he worked in other men, he nevertheless does not explain the different mode. Thus, in wording, he does not sufficiently depart from Paul of Samosata, who asserted that Christ was indeed a mere man, but one in whom God worked in a special manner. In fact, Cyril objected to the Easterners, until the time when peace was concluded, that they agreed in reality with Nestorius, even though they concealed their mind under ambiguous expressions.

These final words—“For he did not say, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ but, as Son and lawgiver, ‘I have said to you’”—although to some they seem to absolve the Easterners, arouse suspicion in me. For what else do they signify than either *υἱοθεσία* (“adoption”) or *κοινωνία τῆς αὐθεντίας* (“participation in authority”)?

[Col. 0948C]

### Orthodox Response

Now, too, we must answer them in the same words and by the same reasoning. For certainly there is one Lord Jesus Christ, who is believed to be both the Word eternal from God the Father and existing before the ages [Note: [Col. 0949D] Baluzius: “And who in the last times of the age became man, and who,” etc.], and the man who was made in the last times of the age and who had a unique and immeasurable generation according to the flesh. Yet there is one Son, both God and Lord, who worked signs and powers surpassing man, demonstrating that, although he had become flesh, he was nevertheless also truly God and the power of the Father. For, having become man, he did not cease to be what he had been.

[Col. 0949A]

Finally, he performed wonders: at one time rebuking demons, at another crushing Satan, at another bringing light to the blind, raising the dead, and calming the sea raging in its depths by a single word—not glorifying some man or another Christ besides himself, as one of the prophets or apostles, but producing glory for himself, so that all might believe that he was God by nature, although he had become man.

[Col. 0949B]

Is it not therefore the most shameful thing to tolerate Nestorius saying (Sermon 10, apparently in the Macedonian controversy): “The operations of the Trinity are common, and only the substances are to be divided; but the splendid glory of the Only-begotten has at one time been assigned to the Father, at another to the Spirit, at another to the power of Christ”? Let the objectors therefore prove either that Christ is to be understood as another, separately and apart, upon whom the only-begotten Word of God imposed his power, as though there were another son separately besides himself; or, if he is not another but one and the same—both the only-begotten from the Father and a man according to the flesh from a woman—for what reason would it have been better for us to remain silent, rather than oppose the force of truth to his ravings and declare the splendor of the true doctrines?

[Col. 0949C]

He was and is God the Son. But since he once assumed the measure of humanity, he did not dishonor the dispensation, and he voluntarily endured everything for our sake because of the self-emptying. Therefore, although according to his nature he himself is life, he is said to be given life by the Father; and although he is Lord of glory, he is said to have received glory. For the Hebrew of Hebrews, learned in the law [Baluz.: “lawgiver”], truly from the tribe of Benjamin, the Apostle Paul, says: “Not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead, giving him glory” (Gal. 1:1).

[Col. 0949D]

But although he is said to have received glory from the Father because this belongs to the measure of the Incarnation, he nevertheless knows that, because he is God, he possesses a dignity that surpasses the measure of the whole creation. For he says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27).

[Col. 0950A]

Let someone who desires to learn ask: “If all things have been handed over to you by the Father, as though you had needed glory and ought, on account of humanity [Baluz.: “the human mode”], to possess dominion over all, how do you say that it is impossible for human minds to know you, just as they know the Father?” He replies: “Knowledge of me is not contained only in visible things. I am God in flesh and blood, to be known according to the flesh; according to the nature and glory of the Godhead, I am equal and like to God the Father, transcending every thought and word.”

Therefore, to return to the subject, we do not empty the apostolic statements—far from it—nor, while thinking as we ought, do we oppose the logic of the *ἐνανθρώπησις* (“becoming man”). Rather, everywhere following the sacred Scriptures and confirming the statements of the divine teachers, we rise up [Baluz.: “we advance”] against those who pervert the Church’s sound doctrines.

[Col. 0950B]

That the Father is said to have raised the Lord Jesus Christ from the dead—namely, because that event was accomplished with respect to his flesh—can be doubted by no one. He himself, however, since he is the life-giving and effective power of the Father, gave life to his own temple, according to the saying: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). Therefore that body which was to be given life was not alien, nor the body of one of our fellow human beings, but the Word’s own body.

### Eighth Anathema

[Col. 0950C]

If anyone dares to say that the assumed man ought to be co-worshiped with God, and co-glorified, and called God together with another as one alongside another, rather than worshiping Emmanuel with a single veneration and assigning him one glorification, because “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), let him be anathema.

### Refutation of the Heretic

We do not speak of co-worship and co-glorification as though they concerned persons, substances, or two sons—as though veneration were offered to the flesh in one way and to God the Word in another—but rather we offer one veneration and the rest to the one Son, and so also with what has been stated [Baluz. omits: “and so with what has been stated”].

[Note: [Col. 0949D] In the first volume. That is, in Paschal Homily 17, which is called Cyril’s first volume, also below on pp. 260 and 261 (*Refutation of the Heretic*, Anathema 11); nevertheless, below on pp. 249 and 266 (*Refutation of the Heretic*, Anathemas 8 and 12), the first volume refers to the letter that Cyril likewise wrote to the Egyptian monks against Nestorius. It must nevertheless be acknowledged that it is called the second volume on p. 260. —Baluzius.]

As he himself says in another volume (Paschal Homily 17):

“For although, as Word, he sat with his Father, and is from him and by nature in him, nevertheless he heard him saying also with the flesh: ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet’ (Ps. 109:1). Thus we also say that he is worshiped, both by us and by the holy angels.”

[Col. 0950D]

To this we reply that he rebuked very ignorantly and incompetently those who wish the one and same Son to be worshiped with the flesh, as though *σὺν* (“with”) and *μετά* (“with”) were altogether different, although he himself used the expression in precisely this way, saying, as mentioned above, that he ought to be worshiped with the flesh, while denying that the flesh should be co-worshiped with the Godhead.

### Orthodox Response

The divine Paul has made us most discerning by saying: “Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith” (2 Cor. 13:5). For human understanding, even if it is carried outside the straight path by a certain arrogance and self-love, and possesses a movement that recoils from the doctrines of truth, fears recognizing its own novel and foolish thoughts. Nevertheless, it will very easily correct itself by examining the labors and writings of the holy Fathers, who are memorably praised by all because of their most correct knowledge of doctrine; and then it will properly test its faith. For it is established for all who are sound in mind that they should follow the opinions of those men, since they too, filling out their understanding with the apostolic and evangelical tradition and rightly and irreproachably forming the rule of faith from the sacred writings, were lights in the world, holding the word of life (Phil. 2:16), as it is written.

[Col. 0951A]

Our father Athanasius, bishop of eternal memory, therefore writes about Christ, the Savior of all (*On the Incarnation of the Word*, volume II):

[Col. 0951B]

“We confess that he himself is the Son of God and God according to the spirit, and the son of man according to the flesh—not two natures of one Son, one to be worshiped and the other not to be worshiped, but one incarnate nature of the Word, worshiped [Baluz.: ‘to be worshiped’] with his flesh in one veneration; nor two sons, one truly the Son of God and to be worshiped, the other from Mary, a man not to be worshiped, made a son of God by grace like human beings.”

And further on:

“He who was born from the Virgin Mary is Son [Baluz. adds: ‘is’] of God by nature and truly God, not by grace or participation; according to the flesh he was born a man from Mary, but according to the spirit he himself is the Son of God and God.” [Baluz. adds: “And again.”]

[Col. 0951C]

“If anyone, contrary to these things, teaches as though from Holy Scripture, saying that one is the Son of God and another is he who was born from Mary, made a son by grace like us, and that there are two sons—one by nature the Son of God, from God, and one by grace a man from Mary—or if anyone says that the flesh of our Lord came from above and not from the Virgin Mary, or that the Godhead was changed into flesh, or confused, or altered, or that the Godhead of our Lord [Baluz. adds ‘our Lord’ here and below] was passible, or that the flesh of the Lord is not to be worshiped as the flesh of a man, or is not to be worshiped as the flesh of the Lord and God, the holy and catholic Church anathematizes him, obeying the divine Apostle who says: ‘If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema’ (Gal. 1:9).”

[Col. 0951D]

While he thought and wrote these things for us, Nestorius, the enemy of Christ’s glory and his rebellious opponent, unleashing an unbridled tongue against him, says as follows (Sermon 2, toward the end):

“Let us confess the God who is in the man. Let us worship the man who is to be co-worshiped with God through the divine conjunction with God the Word.”

Does he not plainly call Christ a man bearing God, *Θεοφόρος*? Does he not say that merely a conjunction of the man with God has taken place, according to what is recorded in Paul’s words: “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17)?

[Col. 0952A]

Yet the truth is that Christ, one and the same, was rather God and man together—not some man to be understood separately and apart, merely clinging to God through conjunction. For after that ineffable union, whether one calls Emmanuel God or names him man, it is necessary to understand the Word of God as made man and incarnate; yet we know that he is also the Word of the Father.

Thus it is one thing to say that the Word, the Son of God the Father, is one with the flesh joined to him, and another to say that God is in a man, as he was also in the prophets or in us through the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0952B]

Without danger and without reproach, as I think, you may say that the incarnate Word of God, being one Son, is to be worshiped not without his own flesh but together with it. In the same way, every soul is honored in its body, and what is composed of two is designated by one name, as one animal.

When, therefore, you speak about Christ, the Savior of all, and divide him who is one into two, declaring that the man is to be understood separately and apart, and then dare to say that he ought to be co-worshiped and called God together with another, as though there were another Son of God besides himself, who can endure this or pass over in silence such insolence of speech? You ought rather to have said: “Let us worship God the Word, who became man and is called God, and who is worshiped in his humanity, because he is God by nature and was born from God the Father.”

[Note: [Col. 0951] Baluzius: “But perhaps those on the opposite side will say: You too will be guilty,” etc.]

[Col. 0952C]

But perhaps those on the opposite side will say: “You too will be guilty, since you write in your letter that the Son sat with the Father together with his flesh, and then rebuke the one who says that the man ought to be co-worshiped with God the Word and called God together with another. For saying *σὺν* and saying *μετά* amount to the same thing.”

Let us refute them, since they do not understand the force of the statements and pay no attention to the nature of things. Whenever, in one person and one nature or substance, discourse explains the elements from which it is naturally composed [Baluz. adds: “the person itself”], and adds either *τὸ σὺν* (“the with”) or *τὸ μετά* (“the with”), it preserves the meaning of unity and defines that the thing is not divided into two parts. But whenever the substances have first been divided into two parts, and *τὸ σὺν* or *τὸ μετά* is used to signify each separately and apart, then certainly the meaning is of two or more, and not of one through composition.

[Col. 0952D]

For example, if I say that the soul of a man is to be co-honored [Baluz.: “co-worshiped”] with its body, when honor is paid to the man who is composed of both; or if someone says that the soul is one animal with its body, he certainly does not divide one man into two. Rather, it is clear that he understands the elements from which a man either is or is composed.

[Col. 0953A]

But if I say, “Peter and John are called men,” or if I say, “John was going up into the temple with Peter,” *τὸ σὺν*, or *τὸ μετά*, no longer has the meaning of one. For Peter is not composed with John, nor are both reckoned as one man.

Why, then, do they corrupt the truth by dividing the one Christ into two through ignorance? Or if they think that, when we say that the Son sat with the Father together with his body, we have made two sons understood, let them inquire more carefully whether, by saying “one Son,” we also say that he is to be honored in one sitting with the Father, and not in two: not so that one is assigned separately to the body and another again to the Word. They will never prove this. For we assert that the one Son, together with his flesh, God and man at once, is honored in one sitting with the Father.

But to say “co-honored” and “called God together with another” plainly means confessing that two are to be co-honored and called God together with another. This is full of madness and alien to the sound doctrines of truth.

[Col. 0953B]

Thus an anathema was made against those who divide Emmanuel in every way and by every means, separately into a man and separately into God the Word. For the teachers of divine things preached him to us as one, according to the sincere and incorrupt knowledge of the sacred writings.

### Ninth Anathema

If anyone says that the one Lord Jesus Christ, glorified by the Spirit and by its power as though by something alien, uses it and receives power from it so that he may work against unclean spirits and perform divine signs among human beings [Baluz. omits “among”], rather than saying that the Spirit through whom he worked divine signs is his own proper Spirit, let him be anathema.

### Refutation of the Heretics

[Col. 0953C]

Let us once again bring forward what he himself said earlier and remind him, perhaps forgetful of his own statements. For he said not only that the Lord performed signs in the Spirit, but also that he himself, having died, was given life through the Spirit. For in the first volume (*Letter to the Monks*, chapter 25) he says:

“If, then, he did not suffer because he died in the flesh, according to the Scriptures, neither was he given life in the Spirit.”

[Col. 0953D]

But one must consider how contrary to himself he speaks: in his anathemas denying that the Lord casts out demons in the Spirit of God and performs other signs, and making false the Lord’s saying set down in the Gospels: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. 12:28).

We, however, confess that our Lord Jesus Christ performs wonders both by his own proper power and through the operation of the Spirit—not because he himself lacks proper power and therefore needs the power of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0954A]

Whoever says that the Holy Spirit is not present denies the sacred Scriptures. For even if divine Scripture says somewhere that the Father performs works of wonder, as when it says, “The Father who remains in me, he himself does the works that I do” (John 14:10), it is nevertheless the Son who acts; for everything that belongs to the Father belongs to the Son.

And if Scripture says that the Spirit acts, as when it says, “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. 12:28), it is nevertheless the Lord who acts in the Spirit [Baluz. omits “nevertheless”]. For the Son is not alien either to the Father or to the Spirit, nor are the operations of the Trinity divided or set apart from one another. Rather, the operation of each substance of the Trinity is proper to it, as it is mentioned in Scripture.

[Col. 0954B]

Thus Scripture sometimes records that the whole creation is the work of the Son, saying, “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 32:6), and sometimes of the Holy Spirit; for it adds, “and by the breath of his mouth all their power” (ibid.). But this is not because the Father is unable to do everything and therefore the Son also acts, nor because the Son is weak for creating and the Spirit is consequently taken up [Note: [Col. 0953] Baluzius omits the words: “nor likewise is the Spirit taken up because the Son is weak for creating.”]. For it is true that “all things were made through him” (John 1:3).

Rather, Scripture expresses to us the one substance, the one honor, and the one power of the Trinity by saying at one time that things were made by the Father, at another by the Son, and at another by the Holy Spirit. In this way we understand that everything depends upon one divine substance [Baluz. omits “divine”].

For just as the consubstantial (*ἐνούσιον*) and enhypostatic (*ἐνυπόστατον*) Only-begotten Word was born from that substance without suffering, so the Spirit proceeded from that substance, and he too exists in his own substance. Thus one essence (*οὐσία*) is designated in three substances, and none is recognized as alien to another according to the account of substance; rather, the individual substances are declared only through their distinguishing properties or distinctions.

In what way, then, is the operation proper to those whose substance, power, and will are common? For whatever things are common to them certainly have one operation.

### Orthodox Response

[Col. 0954C]

Do I need the voices of witnesses to prove that the adversaries want to engage in frivolous and foolish fables and recklessly tear us apart with insults? I think their own words alone can demonstrate this.

In the anathema under discussion we affirmed that the Holy Spirit is plainly the Son’s own Spirit, and that the Son performs divine signs through him. Yet the adversaries, who so frequently accuse me of forgetting my own statements, have fallen into such stupidity and madness that they suppose I am saying that the Son does not cast out demons through the Spirit.

[Col. 0954D]

Is this not an obvious slander? For if they do not deign to admit that the expulsion of demons belongs among the divine signs, let them say whatever they wish and accuse me in every way, as though I had not said that these are divine signs [Baluz.: “as though I had said that these are not divine signs”]. But if, among the other miracles, the expulsion of demons is also to be numbered, why, while avoiding the truth as though it involved some great loss, do they make a point of honoring the disease of their loquacity and refuse to despise a matter hateful both to God and to human beings?

[Col. 0955A]

They seem to have forgotten Christ, who says: “How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me cast out the speck from your eye,’ while you yourself do not see the beam in your eye? Hypocrite, cast out first the beam from your own eye, and then you will see how to cast out the speck from your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7:3–5).

That the divine Trinity [Baluz.: “divinity”] is one substance, with equal power and operation, we have not learned from your speech; rather, we believe from the divine Scripture that this is so. Nor is it difficult to see that the anathema in question does not obstruct right faith but rather benefits it.

[Col. 0955B]

For it does not permit those who divide and separate the one Lord Jesus Christ, as we have often said, separately into a man and separately into God the Word, so that two persons and two substances divided from each other are understood [Baluz. omits “divided from each other”], to say that the Son, as a common man, was assisted by the operation of the Spirit so that he could perform wonders.

For if this is so, he differs in no respect from the holy apostles or prophets, who, filled by God’s kindness with divine gifts, said: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10). This statement may properly apply to holy men, in whom the distribution of divine gifts shines forth; but it does not apply to Christ. For the Holy Spirit is his own, just as he is the Spirit of God the Father; and just as the Father works through the Spirit, so he too works through the Spirit.

[Col. 0955C]

Finally, when he said to the Jews, “I have shown you many good works from my Father” (John 10:32), and, “I do not speak from myself, but the Father who remains in me performs the works” (John 14:28), he again said: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. 12:28), attributing the operation through the Spirit both to himself and to the Father, because of their same [Baluz. adds: “and similar”] substance.

A great and very lengthy treatise could indeed be composed on these matters, but it would belong to a more suitable occasion to develop them at greater length.

[Col. 0955D]

Therefore we do not say that Emmanuel was assisted by the Spirit as by an alien power. Rather, we say that he used the Spirit as his own divine power and that he possesses as his own the power of the consubstantial Spirit [Baluz.: “of the substance of the Spirit”]. For when the blessed disciples performed signs, they said: “Men, brothers, why do you look at us as though by our own power or authority [Baluz.: ‘devotion’] we had made the lame man sitting at the Beautiful Gate walk?” (Acts 3:12). But Christ’s Spirit is his own.

To those who hasten to disparage our teaching I shall say this: if it does not seem terrible [Baluz.: “horrible”] to their minds to divide the indivisible Son and to say that Jesus, as a common man, was assisted by the Spirit, then we recoil from those who believe this. But if they confess one Christ, Son and Lord, and the same one to be God and man together, let them believe with us that he is not assisted as though by a spirit alien to him and possessing a better power; rather, let them believe that he himself performs divine signs through his own Spirit, in whom also is the power of all things that are born. In this way they will eventually cease to slander us without cause and gnash their teeth against us in envy.

### Tenth Anathema

[Col. 0956A]

Divine Scripture records that Christ was made the high priest and apostle of our confession and that he also offered himself for us as a fragrant offering to God and the Father. [Note: [Col. 0955] Baluzius: “If anyone therefore says that our high priest and apostle was not the Word of God himself, then,” etc.]

If anyone therefore says that the Word of God himself was not made our high priest and apostle—that is, when he became flesh and man like us—but that it was another man, separate from him, born from a woman; or if anyone says that he offered offerings for himself and not rather for us alone—for he who knew no sin had no need of a sacrifice—let him be anathema.

### Refutation of the Heretics

If God the Word is the high priest, to whom does he offer sacrifice, his own God, or what sort of sacrifice does he offer? But he has forgotten the blessed Paul, who says: “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been tempted in every respect without sin” (Heb. 4:15).

[Col. 0956B]

Who, then, was tempted? God the Word, or rather human nature, the seed of David?

And again: “No one takes the honor for himself, but he who is called by God, just as Aaron was; so also Christ did not wish [Baluz.: “did wish”] to glorify himself as high priest” (Heb. 5:4).

Who, then, is compared with Aaron in priestly dignity, with him who does not take the honor for himself but is called by God, and with him who ascends to the rank of priesthood? Is it the divine nature, co-eternal with the Father, which possesses as its own everything that belongs to the Father?

[Col. 0956C]

And to what dignity, higher than itself, was it ascending? Shall we say that priesthood is more glorious than the divine nature, into which it ascended not by itself but, like Aaron, when called by God, and by which it was glorified?

Or rather, is it that nature which was made from the seed of David and appointed beforehand? To it, according to the Psalmist, God also swore that he would give an eternal priesthood: “For the Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4).

[Col. 0956D]

Was the Godhead of the Only-begotten receiving promises from God under oath that it would receive an eternal priesthood and through it become glorious?

Who could tolerate us, either thinking or saying such things, rather than reproving us when we remember that God is ordained high priest, receives promises under oath, is called to the dignity of the priesthood, and does not receive honor by himself but is called to it and compared with the one who first received the priesthood?

And further: “As it is also said elsewhere, ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Heb. 5:7).

[Col. 0957A]

Who, then, has been made like Melchizedek in priesthood? Does the rule of piety require us to think that it is God the Word, or rather the flesh assumed from us, which has been joined to him inseparably and without confusion?

And further he says: “In the days of his flesh, he offered prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard” [Baluz. omits: “offering, he was heard”], and so forth.

Was God the Word offering prayers and supplications with a loud cry to someone else who was able to save him, and was he heard because of his piety, and did he learn from what he himself suffered, and was he brought to completion?

[Col. 0957D]

[Note: [Col. 0957D] Baluzius omits the words: “If therefore God the Word is the high priest, he certainly learned from what he suffered in himself, and was also brought to completion.”]

If, therefore, God the Word is the high priest, he certainly learned from what he suffered in himself, and was also brought to completion.

[Note: [Col. 0957D] Baluzius: “But let your mind not be frightened when you hear of him who suffered and of him who remained impassible. For he who is from David’s seed was not separately and apart from the other named Son, just as neither was the divinity, after the union, etc.” EDIT.]

But let your mind not be frightened when you hear of him who suffered—and indeed, while he was the Son. For we do not posit two sons: the one who suffered and the one who remained impassible. Nor was that which is from David’s seed named “Son” separately and apart, just as neither was the divinity, after the union, called “Son” without visible flesh. Sonship after the ἕνωσις [union] is common to both natures, since they are not to be separated from one another. For after the ἕνωσις there is no separation whatsoever; rather, that ἕνωσις remains eternal.

Likewise, even in the sufferings of the flesh, the deity was inseparable, though it remained impassible; and through the flesh it accomplished the divine signs. Therefore we confess one and the same Son, while the natures remain unconfused—not another and another, God forbid, but saying that one and the same Son, according to the divine Scriptures, our Lord Jesus Christ, was made our High Priest and Apostle. Yet we confess him not as a man born of a woman separately and apart from the Word of God the Father, but as one such that that which was made from David’s seed, joined unconfusedly and inseparably to God the Word, was a High Priest tempted in all things without sin, taught obedience by the things he suffered [Baluzius: “obedience”], and offering his own flesh to God and the Father, not for himself but only for us. For the Father is not the God of the Only-Begotten’s deity, but his Father.

## ORTHODOX REPLY

Let us appropriately say again to our adversaries: “How long will you limp on both feet?” For you ought to bring to the knowledge of Scripture a sound and upright understanding, and not, as though limping with a double mind and weakened in spirit, refuse to use straight footsteps (III Kings XVIII, 21). For all who are double-tongued and unstable in all their ways are restless and will receive nothing from the Lord (James I, 8).

I say this while greatly astonished at our adversaries: they reproach this anathema with such shamelessness and insolence, because they do not want us to call the Word of God and Father “the Apostle and High Priest of our confession” (Hebrews III, 1), however much he became man. Those who attempt to malign his generation according to the flesh, and who dare to reject it as though it were something new, and who flee from calling the holy Virgin Θεοτόκος [God-bearer], how could they not easily deny the reality of the dispensation? Let them therefore hear the voice of Isaiah: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah VII, 9).

The divine evangelist John proclaimed something great and pre-eminent throughout the world when he said that the Word became flesh (John I, 14). But those who steal away the force of the truth say that he became flesh in the same way that he is said to have become both a curse and sin (Galatians III, 13). We have already said enough about these matters that could demonstrate how exceedingly feeble their argument concerning them is.

To the men who rebuke us we now say this: Learn to listen to those who groan in distress [Baluzius: “who are afflicted”]; understand with us the mystery that is according to Christ, the foundation, the principal causes of the dispensation, and, so to speak, his very coming upon the scene. Or rather, give support to the truth of the sacred writings, confessing that the Only-Begotten Word of God, who is in the bosom of the Father, through whom all things exist and in whom all things are, became flesh—not undergoing conversion or confusion, but rather remaining by nature forever what he was, is, and will be.

He became flesh by undergoing birth from the holy Virgin—I mean according to the flesh—and was called the Son of Man. Likewise, he shared with us in flesh and blood (Hebrews II, 14). For those who believe this and hold the venerable and most true faith, everything that follows will be perfectly clear, and none of it will appear difficult or obscure. For it is written: “All things are plain to those who understand, and right to those who find knowledge” (Proverbs VIII, 8).

[Col. 0958C] I think it necessary to explain the reasons for which the anathema was composed. Nestorius, who mixed low things with high and confused everything, said something of this kind somewhere (Sermon 6, the third against Proclus) about Christ, the Savior of all:

“He who was made a High Priest faithful to God was sent to announce release to captives; for he was made such—he was not always so. This is the one who gradually advanced, O heretic, by grace, to the dignity of High Priest.”

He added many other statements revealing the same impiety and kindred audacity. When someone heard such words, who would not think that he ought to endure anything rather than maintain, in matters such as these, a silence hateful to God? Christ died for us, disregarding every insult; he endured the cross and, according to the flesh, death. Shall we fail to repay our Savior even with a return of words, but sleep in deep silence while hearing such abominable blasphemies? Shall we not also become participants in crimes of this kind?

What do you say: “He gradually advanced to become High Priest”? Yet, although he was God, he emptied himself and assumed the form of a servant, though by nature free; he humbled himself, although he surpasses every created thing and glories in the heights of deity. If he was advancing when he was emptied, how did he humble himself? Shall we say that his self-emptying was the cause of honor and glory for him? And then, how could he already have been emptied?

“If the Word of God the Father himself became High Priest,” he says, “who is greater than he, and who is to be honored by the service of the priesthood?”

I shall therefore say further: Believe that, although he is God by nature and the Son in the form of the Father, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped [Baluzius: “as something equal”], but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Thus he became man, and thus he took the form of a servant, not considering it vile or incompatible with the dispensation to be called both Apostle and High Priest. He did not disdain the measure of our humanity; how could he despise what belongs to humanity?

It is not difficult or arduous for us to proceed with more words and set forth the proofs of this matter in a longer treatment. But, leaving that aside for the present, I shall cite the words which they themselves composed. For they wrote as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0959D] Baluzius: “But let your mind also not be frightened when you hear of him who suffered and of him who remained impassible. For that which is from David’s seed was not separately and apart named Son, just as neither was the divinity, after the ἕνωσις, without flesh, etc.” EDIT.]

“But let your mind not be frightened for the moment when you hear of him who suffered—AND INDEED, WHILE HE WAS THE SON. For we do not speak of two sons: the one who suffered and the one who remained impassible. For that which is from David’s seed and was named Son was not separately and apart from the divinity, just as neither was the divinity, after the ἕνωσις, called Son without visible flesh.

“Moreover: ‘Therefore we confess one and the same Son, while the natures remain unconfused, not saying another and another, God forbid, but one and the same; and no one, according to the divine Scriptures, can fail to confess that our Lord Jesus Christ was made our High Priest and Apostle.’ Yet he was not a man born of a woman, separated and apart from the Word of God the Father.”

If, then, they say that there is one Son, not dividing into two the one who is from David’s seed and the Word of God the Father—

[Note: [Col. 0959D] Baluzius: “... not dividing into two that which is from David’s seed and the Word of God the Father; they injure the mystery by dividing [the] dispensation, etc.” EDIT.]

—how do they not injure the mystery by dividing the dispensation between God and man? Why do they not rather say that he is one and the same, both God and man, so that everything—both divine and human—belongs to him? For if something divine is said of his divinity, we entirely believe that it is most true.

[Note: [Col. 0959D] Baluzius: “For we know that he is God, and if something human is also attributed to him, we shall likewise assent. For we confess, etc.” EDIT.]

For we know that he is God, even if something human is said of him. We shall likewise assent to this: for we confess that God is in flesh and blood, and through human things we recognize the measure of his humanity. A million myriads of angels [Baluzius: “holy angels”] minister to him, and Seraphim surround his divine throne.

[Note: [Col. 0960D] Baluzius: “But since he became man, he was also called High Priest—not in order to offer sacrifice to a greater God, but to himself and to the Father, the confession of our faith, rather to the Father.” EDIT.]

But when he became man, he was also called High Priest—not in order to offer sacrifice to a greater lord, but to himself and to the Father, and to secure the confession of our faith. If you say that it is not worthy of God to minister in the priesthood, I too say so—and if the Word were alone and without flesh, you would be right to say it.

[Note: [Col. 0960D] The words “and in dignities above creation, as God,” and what follows, are omitted by Baluzius. EDIT.]

But since he became man, observe that he ministers because of his humanity, while in dignities he is above creation, as God. For he sits with God and the Father. Thus see him offering sacrifice as man and sitting with God. For what does blessed Paul say? “We have such a High Priest, who has sat at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens.”

Knowing, therefore, that although he is God he became flesh—and that he is one and the same—we shall attribute everything to him as one, and we shall not be ignorant of the modes of the dispensation, wisely and skillfully referring the force of the statements always to his obedience.

[Col. 0960B] I have frequently pointed out that the whole question concerning God as High Priest arose from Proclus’s panegyrical homily. Nestorius endured so impatiently Proclus’s statement that the Virgin’s womb was the temple in which God became priest that he immediately attacked it publicly in an improvised speech and later condemned it vehemently in an entire discourse. Cyril vigorously defended Proclus, although without naming him, both in the *Book of Contradictions* and in the synodical letter and in the defense of the tenth anathema.

That question, however, having arisen from the particular zeal of certain individuals, did not develop into a public—or rather, a general—controversy, but was abandoned by the other disputants. The reason Nestorius attacked Proclus’s statement with such zeal, and Cyril defended it, was no other than an emotional inclination: Nestorius’s aversion and Cyril’s affection for Proclus. Nestorius regarded Proclus as an avowed enemy, while Cyril regarded him as a defender of the faith and the leader of the Catholic clergy of Constantinople.

## ELEVENTH ANATHEMA

If anyone does not confess that the Lord’s flesh is life-giving and the proper flesh of God the Word himself, and not the flesh of anyone else apart from him, even if that other is joined to him either by dignity or merely by divine indwelling; and does not rather confess it to be life-giving, as I have already said, because it was the proper flesh of the Word, who can give life to all things—let him be anathema.

## REFUTATION OF THE HERETICS

It must be confessed that the Lord’s flesh was the proper flesh of the Word through the ἕνωσις. Yet it must also be understood that it was assumed from us. It is superfluous to add, “and not to anyone else apart from him,” unless perhaps he denies that it was assumed from us. For to call the Lord’s flesh “proper” so repeatedly is the language of one who denies that it is of our nature.

And where is our ground for boasting? Through whom does Paul say, “He raised us up together and made us sit together” (Ephesians II, 6)? For what human being has flesh that belongs to someone else? Does not each one of us have flesh that is common, in respect of similarity of substance, with everyone else [Baluzius omits “with everyone else”], but proper to himself because each person’s flesh belongs not to another but to the one whose it is?

What, then, does he mean by saying “proper,” as though he were saying something different? For if he understands that the Lord’s flesh was assumed from our flesh, and understands that each person’s flesh is proper to the one whose it is, and not to another, why does he mention as though it were something new that it was proper?

Does he perhaps, under cover of this expression, deny that it was assumed from our nature, as he says more explicitly in his second tome [Baluzius: “first tome”] (Homily 17)?

“The child,” he says, “was not according to us—that is, not in a bare or merely similar likeness to us—but human indeed because of the flesh, and divine, as though above us and from heaven.”

And again, in another tome (*Letter to the Monks*), he says:

“For it was a body, not belonging to another in the manner in which it belongs to us, but rather the proper body of God [Baluzius adds: “the Father’s”] Word, which was born from her.”

For who has ever said that the Lord’s flesh belonged properly to any human being—whether Abel, Noah, Elijah, or some other of the ancient figures? We say not only that the Lord’s flesh did not belong to any other of the ancient human beings, but rather that it belonged properly to the Lord himself and was joined to God the Word unconfusedly and inseparably.

Nor has the flesh of any one of us ever become the flesh of someone else, as we said above, except of the one whose flesh it becomes. Since this is confirmed by the tradition of the Church, why does he say “proper” so frequently, unless perhaps he denies that it is of our nature?

Why, moreover, does he forbid saying that it was “joined to him according to dignity and authority,” when he himself says in his second tome [Baluzius: “first tome”] (Homily 17):

“For thus we became rich through his poverty, when human nature was raised up in him into the divine nature [Baluzius: “divine dignity”]”?

But let us also respond to one who places propositions contrary to one another. If the natures remain unconfused, while the ἕνωσις remains, and if we say that veneration, power, dignity, and authority ought to be offered to the one Son, while the natures remain unconfused ἐν τῇ ἑνώσει [in the union], show what else is lacking that could confirm the ἕνωσις, and we shall agree and grant it—yet without confusion of the natures.

But apparently, for proof of the supreme ἕνωσις, nothing is sufficient for him unless it confuses the natures. We, however, preserve the natures unconfused and confess the supreme and divine ἕνωσις, incomprehensible to us [Baluzius: “intelligible to us”], offering everything to his glorification, as to God and the one Son, and saying to him in the words of blessed Peter: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew XVI, 16).

## ORTHODOX REPLY

At times the wretched Jews, wounded in spirit by the weapons of envy, were stirred to impious madness. But when they also laid their criminal hands upon Christ, the Savior of all, he compelled them to give an account of the causes of their audacity and crimes, saying:

“I do many good works for you from my Father; for which of these works do you stone me?” (John X, 32).

But they advanced to such recklessness and impiety in their thoughts that they even attempted to accuse him of blasphemy, saying:

“We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God” (ibid., verse 33).

The Savior said to them:

“Is it not written in your law, ‘I said, You are gods’ (Psalm LXXXI, 6)? If he called those gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be annulled—do you say to him whom the Father sanctified and sent into this world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (John X, 34 and following).

[Col. 0962B] As we investigate the manner of the apostleship by which he is said to have come to us, we derive our understanding from the sacred writings. For he himself said through Isaiah:

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me. He has sent me to evangelize the poor, to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind” (Isaiah LXI, 1).

We say that the Son was sent by God and the Father after becoming man. For the account and name of apostleship most perfectly accord with the measure of his self-emptying. He was sent, as I said earlier, not as the bare Word of God the Father, without flesh, but after undergoing birth according to the flesh, or receiving a body from holy Mary, and ineffably and unconfusedly joining it to himself, as has very often been said: “God the Lord has shone upon us, according to the Scriptures” (Psalm CXVII, 26).

[Col. 0962C] We say, therefore, that the body belonged properly to the Word, not to some particular and separate human being other than himself who is to be understood as Christ and Son. Just as each one’s body is said to belong particularly to the one whose it is, so also this must be understood of the body of the one Christ.

For although it is like and related to our bodies, since it was made from a woman, nevertheless it is understood and called his proper body, as we said earlier. Since the Word of God the Father is naturally life, he made his own flesh life-giving. In this way it became for us a life-giving blessing. Therefore Christ said:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: I am the living bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world” (John VI, 38).

And further:

“If anyone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he remains in me and I in him” (ibid., verse 33).

Observe how everywhere he calls the body that came from a woman his own, because of the supreme ἕνωσις.

Since the matter of the mystery stands thus, Nestorius says again in his treatise (Sermon 9):

“Listen,” he says, “and attend carefully to what is written: ‘Who eats my flesh.’ Remember that what is being said concerns flesh, and that I am not inventing the name ‘flesh,’ lest I seem to interpret one thing as another: ‘Who eats my flesh and drinks my blood.’ Does he perhaps say, ‘Who eats my deity and drinks my deity’? But ‘who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.’ Remember that what is being said concerns flesh: ‘As the living Father sent me’—me who appear.

“But perhaps I am interpreting one thing as another. Let us hear what follows: ‘As the living Father sent me.’ He said ‘deity’; I say ‘humanity.’ Let us see who is the perverse interpreter: ‘As the living Father sent me.’ The heretic says that he speaks here of deity, that is, ‘The living Father sent me, God the Word, according to them, and I, God the Word, live because of the Father.’ Then he adds, ‘Who eats me will also live.’ What do we eat—deity or flesh?”

We have certainly treated at greater length these statements, which he made so outrageously and insolently. But I cannot see what he wishes to understand when he says that God the Word was not sent, but incarnate and made man, while setting aside and separating, as he himself says, “the one who appears.” Indeed, his invention is all the more obvious and evident [Baluzius: “present”], for he undermines the account of the ἕνωσις, making Christ’s body appear common rather than the proper body [Baluzius: “truly”] of him who is powerful to give life to all things.

This is a longer discussion in the fourth book of the *Contradictions*, in whose fourth chapter these very words of Nestorius are quoted and discussed at length. Hence it is clear that the work of the *Contradictions* was composed before Cyril replied to the Orientals; and from this what is said in the Preface on page XXII receives illumination.

All human things appear small and exceedingly insignificant to the Word of God. Yet after he deigned, for our sake, to endure the self-emptying that brought salvation to the world, even if he is said to have been sent to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind, he is nevertheless glorified in this respect, as having endured the humility of the dispensation according to the flesh. Let no wise person reproach him for enduring these things for our sake.

Does he not therefore, by affirming that there is another Son and Christ besides God the Word, and that the one who appears is that other one, to whom alone he attributes the office and name of apostleship, call our mystery ἀνθρωποφαγία [anthropophagy, “human-eating”], and wickedly turn the minds of his hearers toward destructive thoughts, subjecting to human reasoning what is believed solely and with undemonstrated faith [Baluzius: “human reasonings”]? For one must not say that, because deity is not eaten, the holy body of Christ is therefore common.

It is necessary to know, as we have often said, that the body is the proper body of the Word who gives life to all things. Since it is the body of life, it is life-giving. Through it the Son pours life into our mortal bodies and destroys the dominion of death. The holy Spirit of Christ also gives us life in a similar way, for, according to the Savior’s own voice, “It is the Spirit who gives life” (John VI, 64).

Nothing prevents us from bringing forward examples from the holy Fathers as well, so that I may not appear to be the only one who calls the body the proper body of the Word, and so that our adversaries may recognize that they have cried out against us without cause, since we everywhere follow the voices of the Fathers.

Our most renowned Father and bishop Athanasius says in his book *On the Holy Trinity*:

“It was shown that he truly had a body, not one existing merely in appearance. It was fitting that the Lord, when putting on human flesh, should put on the whole of it together with its sufferings, so that, just as we say that the body was his proper body, so also the sufferings of the body should be said to be his proper sufferings, though because of his deity the sufferings did not touch him.”

And again:

“We necessarily discussed these matters beforehand, so that if we see him acting or speaking divinely through his own body as through an instrument, we may understand that, as God, he performs these things.”

Such, then, are the words of our blessed Father Athanasius.

Yet although it is called the proper body of the Word, it is nevertheless from a woman, since it is understood to be flesh. Blessed Paul says:

“The first man was from the earth, from clay; the second from heaven” (I Corinthians XV, 47).

Christ himself says:

“No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man” (John III, 13).

We say, however, that the Word does not say these things while carrying down from heaven a body joined to himself,

[Note: [Col. 0963D] Baluzius omits the words: “But that, existing above and from heaven.” EDIT.]

but that, existing above and from heaven, he ineffably, incomparably, immutably, and unconfusedly made the body joined to himself. Therefore he says that he is from heaven even when he had become the Son of Man.

Since our statement, which gave the rebukers occasion to curse, was thus rightly made and entirely without fault, if the anathema opposes the blasphemies of certain persons by setting truth against falsehood,

[Note: [Col. 0964D] Baluzius: “I think that I have in no respect done wrong if I have said, etc.” EDIT.]

I think that I have done no wrong in saying that Christ was born above us. For although God the Word became man, he is nevertheless not only above us in this way but also above every creature. For he is understood to be not merely a man like us, but the same one is also from above and from heaven.

## TWELFTH ANATHEMA

If anyone does not confess that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, tasted death in the flesh, and became the firstborn from the dead, since he is, as God [Baluzius omits “as God”], both life and life-giving—let him be anathema.

## REFUTATION OF THE HERETICS

Again we remind his own followers that he explicitly called the divine nature wholly impassible in his first tome (*Letter to the Monks*). For he says:

“There is one, therefore, who is more worthy and superior to all: he laid down his life for all, and, in accordance with the dispensation, permitted the flesh for a short time to be brought low by death, and, being life, destroyed death; he did not endure anything contrary to his nature.”

Let us therefore address him as he contradicts himself: How can the one who permits the flesh for a short time to be brought low by death, and who, being life, destroys death, without enduring anything contrary to his nature, now, as you yourself say, suffer in the flesh?

In fact, God did not suffer together with the flesh to which he was joined. Rather, the flesh that was joined to God the Word suffered, by his permission, the things proper to it. For neither death nor suffering could have occurred without his permission. If death cannot intervene while the soul is present, how could death or suffering disturb his temple while God was present—not merely present in a simple way, but joined to it by a supreme union known to him alone—unless by his permission? The deity did not suffer together with the flesh; rather, by the permission of the deity, the flesh suffered the things proper to it.

That he maliciously inserted the words “SUFFERED IN THE FLESH,” for the deception of the simple, can be understood from this: he certainly would not have preserved the impassibility of the divine nature if he had said “SUFFERED IN THE FLESH.” For whoever says “SUFFERED IN THE FLESH” is saying that he himself suffered together with the flesh. Although, then, he suffered together with the flesh, he is nevertheless shown to be passible.

Either he suffered according to his nature, because he was capable of suffering, or contrary to nature. If he suffered according to nature, then the Father will also be passible, since he is like the Son. For everything that is in the one who is born must necessarily be in the one who begets. Or we shall confess that he suffered, possessing a nature capable of suffering, while the Father cannot suffer. But if we say this, we shall think the same as the heretics who say that the deity of the Only-Begotten is passible, while the Father cannot suffer. Hence they also say that he is ἑτεροούσιον—that is, of another substance.

But if he says that he suffered contrary to nature, we shall ask: What suffering could be stronger than the divine nature, so as to bring low within himself the one who is impassible by nature? He will say: “This belongs to his will.” We shall answer: His will is impassible. We are asking for something passible that transferred the impassible nature into its own passibility; otherwise the divine will also wills what is appropriate to itself.

“What is more fitting,” he says, “than to preserve the human race?”

But how could the human race be preserved by transferring him into passibility, when that passibility would have transferred the divine and impassible nature into suffering? Certainly, as the stronger thing, it transferred into its own passibility that which was impassible. And what benefit will there be for what is passible if what is impassible also becomes passible? This addition is rather an increase of evil than its removal. For no thing is diminished when something similar is added to it; rather, it is increased.

What salvation, then, is there for a passible nature [Baluzius: “passion”], as we have said? Certainly not the communion of the impassible with the passible, but the migration of the passible to the impassible [Baluzius: “the passible”]. This is what the Lord Christ also accomplished. He was not himself, according to his deity, led into suffering; rather, through the holy flesh he raised all of humanity to the heights, lifted it from its prostrate condition to heaven, and deigned to confer adoption upon it, though previously subject to slavery [Baluzius omits “to slavery”].

Who, then, owed death because of disobedience? Surely human nature, not the divine. What death of disobedience, then, had to be returned or paid?

## ORTHODOX REPLY

The power of the truth is certainly great and marvelous, as experience itself testifies [Baluzius: “as the matters themselves testify]. For I shall not need a longer discourse to satisfy those who have been deceived and have supposed that we said the divine nature of the Word was passible, since the adversaries themselves have voluntarily conceded and most clearly confessed that we are very far removed from such accusations.

But since they set forth the matter without any proof, in their madness, as they please, and attempt to demonstrate their own cleverness and acumen by sharp inventions of interpretation, they act with sufficient ingenuity when they say that God the Word is impassible according to his nature. Let them hear from us that they are fighting without cause and striking the air, since no one on the opposite side is striving against them, or holding contrary or divergent views. Why, then, do they labor in vain? Why do they contend without cause? Who is so stupid, who so bewildered, as to say that the most excellent of all natures is passible, and dare to place it among the weaknesses of creation, when it is incorporeal and superior to every creature?

Since, however, the account of the mystery recognizes that the Only-Begotten Son of God became man according to the dispensation, and we affirm that the holy body assumed from blessed Mary belongs properly to him, we rightly say, because of the property belonging to the dispensation, that the sufferings of the flesh are his, while preserving everywhere the impassibility of his nature. For he is God who was born from God.

Whenever, then, he is said to have suffered in the flesh, he is understood to have suffered not in his nature but in the flesh. Rather, he makes the sufferings of the flesh his own [Baluzius: “its sufferings”], for the body joined to him became his, as I said earlier. Therefore the divine Paul says that he, through whom and in whom the Father made all things, became the firstborn from the dead, when he wrote:

“We give thanks to the Father, who made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in the light; who rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins. He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, because in him all things were created in the heavens and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities. All things were created through him and in him; and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him.
