He is also the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might hold first place in all things. For in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things on earth or the things in heaven” (Colossians I, 12 and following).

Observe how he recalls that all things, visible and invisible, thrones and principalities, were made through him; says that he was given as head of the Church; affirms that he became the firstborn from the dead; and declares that all things were reconciled through him and that he made peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things on earth or in heaven.

Who, then, can doubt any longer? Or who would fear that the account of the mystery might show the Son’s nature to be passible if he is said to have suffered in the flesh? For, as I said earlier, he regards the sufferings of his body as his own sufferings.

Blessed Peter approved this understanding when he said: “Since Christ suffered for us in the flesh” (I Peter IV, 1). It is one thing for us to say that he suffered in the flesh, and another to say that the nature of the deity suffered. For when the same one is both man and God, he is impassible with respect to his divine nature but passible with respect to his humanity. What evil or novelty is there if he is said to have suffered in the part that could suffer, while the part that could not suffer remained impassible?

That the chorus of the blessed Fathers also shone forth with this faith we shall again learn from what they themselves wrote, following the Savior’s command. For they remembered him saying: “You received freely; give freely” (Matthew X, 8).

## OF THE MOST BLESSED GREGORY, BISHOP OF NYSSA

“Have this mind among yourselves,” he says, “which was also in Christ Jesus [Baluzius: ‘in Christ Jesus the Son’], who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians II, 5).

What is poorer in God than the form of a servant? What is humbler in a king than voluntarily to descend to participation in our exceedingly poor nature? The King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule pays tribute. The Lord of creation is brought into a cave. He who contains all things finds no place in an upper room, but is laid in a manger for mute animals. The pure and undefiled one suffers the filth of human nature, and, passing through all our poverty, reaches even the experience of death.

You see the extent of voluntary poverty: Life deigns to taste death; the Judge is brought before the judgment seat of life; the Lord of all submits to the verdict of the judge; the King of the heavenly principalities does not repel the hands of executioners.

## OF THE MOST HOLY BASIL, BISHOP OF CAESAREA

Neither heaven, earth, the height of the seas, the creatures living in the waters, terrestrial animals, stars, trees, air, the hours of time, nor the varied and diverse ordering of the elements can demonstrate the majesty of his power as much as this: that God, who cannot be contained, was able, while remaining impassible, to be joined through the flesh to death, so that by his suffering he might grant us impassibility.

## OF THE MOST BLESSED ATHANASIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA
And it was shown that he possessed a body not merely in appearance but truly. It was fitting, moreover, that the Lord, when clothing himself in human flesh, should assume it in its entirety together with its passions, so that, just as we call the body his own, so also the passions of the body might be said to be his own—even though, because of his divinity, the passions did not touch him. But if the body belongs to another, let the passion also be said to belong to another; whereas if the flesh is the Word’s—for “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14)—it is necessary that the passions of the flesh be said to belong to the one whose flesh it is. For whose are the passions—condemnation, scourging, thirst, the cross, death, and the other bodily sufferings? His also are the victory and the grace. It is therefore right and fitting that such sufferings be said to belong not to another but to the Lord himself, so that the grace also may be his, and so that we may not appear to worship one in place of another, but to be worshipers in true religion: since we pray to the true and natural Son of God, who became human, and nevertheless remains God and Savior.

I think, therefore, that what has been added should be sufficient to satisfy prudent readers, especially since the divine law plainly states: “Every word shall be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Matthew 18:16). If anyone, then, wishes to argue further, let him hear us say to him: “Go on your way.” But we, who are devoted to the truth, shall follow the sacred Scriptures and the faith of the holy Fathers; for thus we shall attain the prize of the heavenly calling in Christ, through whom and with whom glory be to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0967D] [Note: While these pages were being sent to press, I happened by chance upon the book of Anastasius of Sinai, called *The Guide of the Way*, and, while looking for something else, encountered chapter twenty-two, in which Andrew of Samosata is mentioned and a moderate-sized fragment from a work relating to the anathemas is transcribed. I thought that it ought to be compared with this passage, both because of the kinship of the subject and on account of the author, whose views can thereby be known somewhat better than from the preceding work. Since Anastasius wished to prove that many statements had subsequently been falsely attributed to the holy Fathers, that many things they had piously said were twisted by heretics into false meanings, and, more remarkably, that different people had twisted them in opposite directions, he gives as an example Andrew of Samosata. Andrew—an utterly astonishing thing!—attempts to make Saint Cyril a patron of Nestorius, and produces words by which he seems to admit in Christ not only two natures but also two hypostases, although the Eutychians, utterly opposed to the Nestorians, were trying to draw him over to their own side. Thus Anastasius.]

While the Gaianites, Theodosians, and Eutychianists were accusing Cyril up and down, as though he said that there was one nature in Christ, Andrew of Samosata argues in his writing that Cyril rather supports Nestorius—even if he does so unknowingly—and is caught in the snare he himself set, precisely because he quotes these words from the beginning of the fourth chapter written by blessed Cyril: “If anyone divides Christ into two persons or hypostases, let him be anathema.”

Andrew responds to this as follows:

“What an excellent judgment! How pious this exposition by Cyril of the doctrines! Behold, following the usage of the Fathers, and especially of the councils, he teaches that hypostases are persons, following the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea, who say that there are three hypostases, or persons, in the most holy and consubstantial Trinity. If, then, he rightly asserts that hypostases are persons, why does he himself, in almost all his writings, call natures hypostases? For when he calls natures hypostases, and hypostases persons, what else does he profess except that there are different persons in Christ, when he says that the natures, or hypostases, remained unmixed?

“Whose hypostases, O outstanding Cyril? Clearly, Christ’s, if you define hypostases in this way. But if this definition—that persons are hypostases—did not originate with you, someone might perhaps have defended you by saying that, by the term *hypostases*, Cyril does not understand persons, but certain subsistences of substantial realities. But since you yourself have brought forward that definition against yourself, no room for defense remains. Therefore, when you say that Christ’s natures, or hypostases, remained unmixed, you say nothing other than that hypostases, or persons, remained unmixed.

“From this law laid down by you—namely, that natures are hypostases or persons—it follows that there are three natures in the three persons of the most holy Trinity, as the Arians contend, but two persons in the two natures of the Only-begotten Son. Thus, when you say in your treatise *On Worship* that the ark was a figure of Christ’s two natures, or hypostases, and elsewhere, in these very words, that Christ is constituted from two natures, or hypostases, or persons, it is not obscure that you confess Christ’s body to have first existed and been formed in the Virgin’s womb, and only afterward to have been united with the person of the divine Word. You also affirm this in the third chapter in the following manner: ‘If anyone divides the hypostases after the ineffable union.’ And since in countless other passages you call natures hypostases, you contradict yourself in your books addressed to Hermias, and disagree with yourself, asserting that nature is one thing and hypostasis, or person, another.

“And how is it that, when Theodoret undertook to refute your twelve chapters, you never defended what you assert about such hypostases in the third chapter? Thus you contradict yourself inconsistently and cut down your own vineyard, sometimes asserting one nature of Christ, sometimes two persons.

“For in your scholia also, when interpreting the stater which Peter found in the fish’s mouth, you write as follows: ‘Therefore Christ is the true stater. For he himself is the double image.’ Great thanks are owed to the eloquent Cyril, who everywhere confesses different images and hypostases in Christ.”

You have heard, brothers, the insults of that most wicked dragon Andrew, which he spewed forth against the most wise teacher Cyril from a breast filled with Nestorian poison, because Cyril said that the natures are hypostases.

[Note: From this fragment it can be understood: (1) that Andrew was an ardent partisan of Nestorius; for this reason Anastasius calls him both accursed and a most wicked dragon; (2) that Andrew’s chapters were attacked in a written work distinct from the *Objections*. For this entire fragment is not found in the *Objections*, nor did it ever belong there. For how could Cyril have failed to answer such serious objections, when he resolved even the smallest points? (3) that this book was written after Cyril had refuted Theodoret’s criticisms, and therefore after his response to the objections of the Easterners; for both the refutation, in part four of the fragment, and the response to the objections are mentioned in the preface to the refutation; (4) that Andrew’s book appears to have been written either toward the end of the Council of Ephesus, after letters had been received from Theodoret concerning Nestorius’s situation, or after the council had been dissolved, when the schismatics, having returned to the East, confirmed by synod the sentence of deposition passed against Cyril, as Liberatus relates. At that time the Easterners dared everything against the twelve chapters, which were not even approved by all Catholics; the supporters of Nestorius, through impatience at their afflicted cause, dared everything, since they still had patrons at court; (5) that Cyril’s scholia *On the Incarnation of the Only-begotten* were published before the Council of Ephesus, if what Andrew writes is true. For he speaks of them as a work already long in circulation, although the passage about the stater which he cites is not found in the scholia now extant. Therefore either Anastasius, having suffered a lapse of memory, called another work by the name of the *Scholia*, or the passages written about the stater are missing from them; (6) finally, that Cyril’s statement in Anathema III is harassed throughout this fragment: “If anyone divides the hypostases in the one Christ after the union, and connects them with one another only by a conjunction according to dignity,” and so forth. For the hypostases seem to have been put in place of the natures. If only the natures are united, and if there are two natures, it follows that Cyril says there are two hypostases in Christ—which is Nestorian; but if there are not two, it follows that one has passed into the other—which is Arian. Andrew is mistaken, however, in his reasoning. Cyril means nothing other than that, once the natures have been united without confusion and without conversion, two hypostases must no longer be admitted—“for this is what it means to divide the hypostases” (*διαιρεῖν τὰς ὑποστάσεις*)—which are joined only by a relational union (*σχετικῇ ἑνώσει*).]

[Col. 0969]

THE APOLOGETIC OF SAINT CYRIL, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, AGAINST THEODORET, OR RESPONSE TO WHAT THEODORET SAID AGAINST THE ANATHEMAS

[Col. 0969C] Cyril sends greetings in the Lord to Evoptius, his most reverend and beloved brother and fellow priest. [Note: Bishop of Ptolemais, mentioned above on pages 173 and 216. This short work of Cyril was published in another version in 1628, in a book entitled *Antidote against Heresies*. Baluzius.]

I have read what your Holiness sent me some time ago, and I have admired your affection and the sincerity of your love in Christ. I think, however, that now too I ought to cry out with the greatest propriety what is written in the Book of Proverbs: “A brother helped by a brother is like a well-fortified city” (Proverbs 18:19). It seems to me that love has been especially honored by the praises of divine Scripture, and rightly so, since it contains in itself the fullness of the law (Romans 13:10), is to be preferred to the other virtues, and appears wonderful to the souls of the saints. I mean the love which, as we say, is not fulfilled by bare and isolated words, but which receives testimony from realities themselves. For just as the precious stones said to come from India are not admired by the eyes of those who behold them merely because someone speaks of their beauty, but because they themselves are beautiful, so the splendid glory of love appears from actual examples, surpassing all good things.

Your Reverence values this love highly, as you are always accustomed to observe the footsteps of the saints and to follow the praises of their most approved way of life. I therefore received the volume that had been sent, so that I might once again learn the affection of your Holiness. It is said to have been composed against the anathemas by Theodoret of Cyrus—for so, I hear, that town is called. After reading it, I gave the greatest thanks to God and did not cease saying: “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Psalm 119:2).

[Col. 0971B] For I found myself everywhere, and in each individual chapter, subjected to calumnies. I was therefore astonished that a man not unfamiliar with letters, as some have reported of him, and perhaps endowed with no small knowledge of the sacred writings, should have been so ignorant of the force of the chapters that I began to suspect that, by feigned ignorance, he was gratifying the desires of others—lest he should appear to disparage us rashly and without any plausible pretext. Especially since, unless I am mistaken, there is absolutely nothing difficult or obscure in our statements, nothing hard to understand. But since it has become necessary to answer him briefly as well, although we have already written on these matters, lest anyone think that we remained silent because we were convicted, I shall proceed to the response, observing brevity insofar as the matter permits.

[Col. 0971C] It would especially have been proper for him, since he possesses knowledge of the divine Scriptures and wished to dispute with us concerning sacred mysteries, to mention only the sacred writings and not to bring forward rotten and filthy fables. [Note: Baluzius has *cariosas* and thus supports this reading: “Thus Jerome, in his letter to Nepotian, said *pene jam cariosis artubus* [‘with limbs already almost decayed’]. Moreover, that *cariosas*, not *curiosas* as in Garnerius, ought to be read here is also clear from another version, where we find ‘old wives’ tales.’ EDIT.] For he deigns to liken my discourses to the APPLE OF DISCORD, and perhaps thinks this proves his learning. Thus we too have admired his excessive learning: clearly, on account of his profound and immense erudition, he was not ignorant of the APPLE OF DISCORD, nor of Paris, the son of Priam.

For in the letter, after other matters: “Moreover, he himself not only asserted these things, but also dared to anathematize those who were unwilling to obey his blasphemies. Yet if these inventions are his, and not rather something hostile to the truth that someone cast into public circulation as though written by him, such as that fable of the APPLE OF DISCORD, which kindles a flame.” [Note: Baluzius moves these words to the beginning of the following refutation of the heretic; he explains his reasoning in the next note. EDIT.]

But, setting these matters aside for the moment, let us continue with the subject before us.

## FIRST ANATHEMA

If anyone does not confess that God is truly Emmanuel, and therefore that the holy Virgin is *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος, God-bearer)—for she gave birth bodily to the Word of God who became flesh—let him be anathema.

## HERETIC’S REFUTATION

[Note: Here Baluzius transferred the words mentioned in the preceding note and adds: “Garnerius, thinking that these words were Cyril’s, moved them from this place to before the first anathema, and made the beginning of Theodoret’s words read: ‘But we, who follow the evangelical tradition.’ We restored them to the place they occupy in the ancient copies. For it is certain that they are Theodoret’s, not only because in Mercator’s manuscripts they are said to be his, but also because they occur in the same place in the old version mentioned above, and because they are also found in Greek in the same order in volume four of Theodoret’s works, p. 706. What led Garnerius to make this alteration was, I think, that, seeing Theodoret’s preceding words depend on others and that Cyril’s preface mentions Theodoret’s words about the apple of discord, he thought those words should be joined to Cyril’s. But if he had noticed that some things from Theodoret’s preface are missing here, though they occur in the Greek text and in that old version, Garnerius would have done what we did—that is, he would not have moved them from the place they occupy in Mercator’s manuscripts.” EDIT.]

But we, who follow the evangelical tradition, do not say that God the Word became flesh by nature and was converted into flesh; for God is unalterable and immutable. Of him the prophet David also says: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Psalm 102:27). Paul, the great preacher of the truth, asserts in his Letter to the Hebrews that this was spoken of the Son (Hebrews 1:11); and elsewhere God says through the prophet: “I am, I am, and I have not changed” (Malachi 3:6). Therefore, if God is unalterable and immutable, he cannot undergo conversion or change; and if it is impossible for the unalterable to be converted, God the Word did not become flesh by conversion, but assumed flesh and dwelt among us, according to the words of the Gospels. Divine Paul himself, explaining this, says in his Letter to the Philippians: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ the Son, who, being in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:5–7).

It is therefore evident from these statements that the form of God was not converted into the form of a servant, but that, remaining what it was, it took the form of a servant. Therefore, if God the Word [Baluzius: “the Word of God”] did not become flesh, but assumed living and rational flesh, he himself was not naturally born, conceived, fashioned, and formed from the Virgin, receiving from that point a beginning of existence—he who existed before the ages, who is God, who was always with God, who clings to the Father and is to be acknowledged and worshiped with the Father. Rather, when he fashioned a temple for himself in the virginal womb, he clung to what had been fashioned, conceived, formed, and born. For this reason also we call the holy Virgin *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος), not because she naturally gave birth to God, but because she brought forth a human being joined to God, who had fashioned him. [Note: In the letter of Pelagius: “whom he himself formed.” In the old version cited above: “who fashioned him.” Baluzius. Pelagius II copied this portion into his third letter to the bishops of Istria. Baluzius.]

This entire paragraph is cited in the Fifth Council among the statements of Theodoret against Saint Cyril that were condemned by anathema. His offense, however, is that he contradicts Saint Cyril on the point in which the rule of faith was established: namely, that the blessed Virgin gave birth to the Word who became flesh, and not merely to a human being joined to God.

But if it was not a human being who was fashioned in the Virgin’s womb, but God the Word, who existed before the ages, then God the Word is a work of the Holy Spirit. For Gabriel says: “That which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20). But if the Only-begotten Word of God is uncreated and of the same substance as the Father, [Baluzius adds: “and coeternal with the Father”] he is not a work of the Holy Spirit. If, however, the Spirit did not form God the Word in the Virgin’s womb, it remains that we must understand the form of a servant to have been naturally formed and fashioned.

But since it was not merely the form of a servant, but a temple containing God the Word as its inhabitant, according to Paul’s words—“For in him all the fullness of deity was pleased to dwell bodily” (Colossians 1:19)—we call the holy Virgin not merely *Anthropotokos* (ἀνθρωποτόκος, human-bearer), but also *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος, God-bearer): *Anthropotokos* because of the fashioning and formation, and *Theotokos* because of the union (*ἕνωσις*). Therefore the child who was born was called Emmanuel: neither God separated from human nature, nor a human being stripped of divinity. For Emmanuel means “God with us,” according to the words of the Gospels; and “God with us” signifies both the one who was assumed from us for our sake and God the Word who assumed him. Therefore the child is Emmanuel because of God, who assumed him; and the Virgin is *Theotokos* because of the joining of the form of God to the form of a servant. God the Word was not converted into flesh; rather, the form of God assumed the form of a servant.

## ORTHODOX RESPONSE

We have often and at great length accused those who refuse to confess that God is truly Emmanuel and that the holy Virgin is *Theotokos*, because she gave birth according to the flesh to God the Word when he became flesh—that is, became human. But if the man who so correctly accuses us does not know that God is truly Emmanuel; if God the Word, having become flesh, was not born bodily from the holy Virgin according to the Scriptures, why did he not cry out more openly: “What are you doing, good man [Baluzius adds: ‘Ambrose’]? You pour forth unspeakable statements; you trample upon the doctrines of truth. God is not truly Emmanuel, nor is the holy Virgin *Theotokos*”? Then, while he shouted and said such things, we could wisely have opposed him with the statements of divine Scripture, setting before him the tradition of the apostolic and evangelical faith and the confession of the holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea in their time, and could have persuaded him that he was attempting to criticize our statements neither rightly nor honorably, indeed that he was hastening to resist the divine Scriptures.

[Col. 0974A] But the prudent and clever interpreter, leaving aside what he ought and was required to say, and having touched none of these matters, turned altogether in another direction. He immediately began to say that God the Word is stronger than conversion, and that he was not transformed into the nature of flesh, as though he thought or asserted that this was the meaning of the anathema.

Let him hear, then, this man who does not know how to answer another’s speech: “Man, you exercise vain words without cause and resist an opinion that is hateful either to us or to yourself. We too know that that divine and transcendent nature does not suffer even the shadow of conversion, and that God the Word did not pass over into the nature of flesh after laying aside his divinity.”

[Col. 0974B] But when he recalls that the form of a servant was assumed from the form of God, let him teach us [Baluzius adds: “if”] whether forms, existing without substances and by themselves, came together with one another. I think that he himself will not confess that this was so. For it was not merely appearances without substances, and forms among themselves, that came together through an economic union (*ἕνωσις*); rather, there was a coming together of the realities themselves, or substances, so that the reality of the incarnation [Baluzius: “of humanity”] might truly be believed to have occurred. Therefore, even if we say that God the Word became flesh, we do not thereby say that confusion, mixture, conversion, or change occurred in him; rather, we say that he was joined, by a hidden and ineffable manner, to a holy body possessing a rational soul. For whatever is said to be united is not confused, but assumes something else into itself.

We therefore affirm that the Word of God the Father assumed holy and ensouled flesh and was truly and without confusion united to it from the womb; that a human being came forth from it, while nevertheless remaining true God. For this reason also the holy Virgin is *Theotokos*. I think it superfluous, however, that she should also be called *Anthropotokos*. For if there were people so deranged in mind as to say that the nature of the Word had its origin from flesh as from its source, and had received from it the beginning of its existence [Baluzius: “substance”], perhaps those who showed that she ought to be called *Anthropotokos* would not seem entirely unreasonable. But since such an opinion is hateful to everyone, and the holy Virgin cannot be understood to be *Theotokos* in any other way than by first believing that God the Father’s Word became flesh—that is, became human—for the Virgin did not give birth to bare divinity, what advantage will those who contend that she must also be called *Anthropotokos* gain from this dispute?

But, as it appears, they have contrived for themselves an opportunity to speak against Christ. For they cannot endure either to believe or to say that the Word of God the Father, who was the Son before the ages, was united without confusion and without conversion, from the womb, to flesh possessing a rational soul, and thus became a human being like us. Instead, just as they mention one of the saints as having had God dwelling in him, they also urge others to think in this way, failing to consider that in us too God, through the Holy Spirit, dwells as in holy temples. For it is written: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Corinthians 3:16–17). Yet although we are called temples, having God dwelling in us through the Spirit, we know another mode of the mystery according to Christ. For we say that flesh possessing a rational soul was truly united to God the Word.

I would gladly ask him whether he truly confesses that the unity of God the Word with humanity, or with the holy body rationally ensouled, was accomplished—or whether he too, following the example of certain people, holds that there was only a relational conjunction (*συνάφειαν σχετικήν*) of a servile and *anhypostatic* form (*ἀνυπόστατος*) with the divine form, which is *enhypostatic* (*ἐνυπόστατος*); or, in another way, only through the homonymy of sonship (*ὁμωνυμία*) and equality of dignity; or whether he understands some other mode of conjunction.

But perhaps I am troubling him without cause and asking questions unnecessarily. For I possess his own words and his clearest confession. In this first chapter he said: “Therefore the child who was born is called Emmanuel; neither is God separated from human nature, nor is the human being stripped of divinity.” He ought indeed to have treated the subtle exposition of these words with greater care and refinement; nevertheless, this much must certainly be noted. For in explaining the unity, he himself denies that God is separated from human nature by the unity, and confesses the same one to be both God and human. Why, then, is he not ashamed to criticize our statements? [Note: Baluzius adds here: “and unjustly condemns the second anathema, which reads as follows.” EDIT.]

## SECOND ANATHEMA

If anyone does not confess that the Word of God the Father was united to the flesh according to substance, and that Christ is one with his own flesh—that is, the same one both God and human—let him be anathema.

## HERETIC’S REFUTATION

We confess one Christ, obeying the divine traditions of the apostles, and we call him both God and human because of the union (*ἕνωσις*). But we entirely reject a union according to substance (*ἕνωσις per substantiam*) as something new and foreign to the divine Scriptures and to the Fathers who interpreted them.

This entire passage too was cited and condemned in the Fifth Council, because it rejected the union according to hypostasis (*ἕνωσις καθ’ ὑπόστασιν*), whose confession is the sole, certain, and fraud-free rule of right belief. Hence, in canon 13, anathema is pronounced against anyone who defends the impious writings of Theodoret, which he composed against the true faith, against the holy First Council of Ephesus, against Saint Cyril and his twelve chapters, and against everything he wrote in defense of the impious Theodore and Nestorius and of others who held the same opinions as the aforesaid Theodore and Nestorius—defending them and their impiety, and for this reason calling those teachers of the Church impious who confess the UNITY ACCORDING TO SUBSISTENCE of God the Word with the flesh, and so forth.

But if the person who finds these words wishes to say that “union according to substance” means a mixture of divinity and flesh, we shall oppose him with all energy and prove it to be blasphemy. For mixture must necessarily be followed by confusion; and confusion, once it has occurred, removes the distinct property of nature. Things that are mixed do not preserve what they were before. But to say this of God the Word and of the seed of David is utterly disgraceful.

We must instead obey the Lord, who demonstrates two natures when he says to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). But if a mixture had occurred, God would no longer have remained God, nor would the temple be recognized as a temple; rather, God would be the temple and the temple God. For this is what the nature of mixture requires. And the Lord would not have rightly said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” He ought instead to have said: “Destroy me, and in three days I shall rise again,” if there had truly been a mixture and confusion. But now he shows both that the temple is to be destroyed and that God will raise it up.

A union according to substance (*ἕνωσις per substantiam*) is therefore superfluous, since they use it, as I think, in place of mixture. It is sufficient to say “union” (*ἕνωσις*), which both displays the properties of the natures and commands that the one Christ be worshiped.

## ORTHODOX RESPONSE

Behold again this noble [Note: This word does not correspond to the Greek word *γεννάδας*, which Cyril uses here. For that reason Garnerius added the word “noble” and read: “Behold again this noble barbarian.” But either “noble” should be read by itself or “barbarian.” Marius Mercator appears to have understood these words of Cyril as ironic, and therefore translated *γεννάδας* as “barbarian,” just as below, on page 288, for Cyril’s *ὁ θρασύς*, which he ought to have translated “audacious” or “rash,” he used *strenuus* (“vigorous”), which is a word of praise rather than blame. Here, in place of “barbarian,” the old version mentioned earlier has “strong.” Baluzius.] barbarian, seeking an opportunity for abuse from the smallest causes, criticizes the expression because we said “according to substance,” declares it unusual, and asserts that we introduced it in a novel manner. He does not consider that the force of words [Baluzius omits: “the force of words”], when it opposes the truth to the arguments of impious heretics, overturns what appears to stand in its way.

Since Nestorius everywhere abolished the generation of God the Word according to the flesh, establishing for us only a unity of dignities and saying that the human being joined to God was honored by the homonymy of sonship (*ὁμωνυμίᾳ*), it was necessary for us, acting against his statements, to say that a union according to substance (*ἕνωσις per substantiam*) had occurred. This expression signifies nothing other than this: that the nature, or substance, of the Word—that is, the Word himself—was truly united to human nature, without any conversion or confusion, as we have often said, so that he is understood to be and is one Christ, himself both God and human.

Cyril’s words should be carefully noted:

“We say that a union according to hypostasis (*τὴν καθ’ ὑπόστασιν ἕνωσιν*) has occurred. The expression ‘according to hypostasis’ signifies nothing other than this alone: that the nature of the Word, or the hypostasis—that is, the Word himself—was truly united to human nature,” and so forth.

We say that a uniting according to hypostasis has occurred. This expression signifies nothing other than this alone: that the nature of the Word, or the hypostasis—that is, the Word himself—was truly united to human nature, and so forth.

From this comes that famous statement of Athanasius and Cyril: “After the union there is one incarnate nature of God the Word.” For “nature” has been put in place of “hypostasis,” and this is not peculiar to Catholics. Nestorius himself also, if we believe the Fathers of the Fifth Council, used “natures” in place of “hypostases,” when he said:

“Because of him who put on the garment, I worship him who was clothed; because of him who is hidden, I worship him who appears. God is inseparable from him who appears; therefore I do not separate the honor of him who is inseparable. I separate the natures, but unite them in worship” (*Sermon* 7, no. 37).

Theodoret, however, confused one term with another in his refutation of the following anathema, when he said:

“Since the divine form has taken the form of a servant, it is pious to confess one person, one Son, and one Christ; but it is not improper to speak of two hypostases that have been united, or rather of two natures” (*τῆς τοῦ θείου μορφῆς λαβούσης τὴν τοῦ δούλου μορφήν, ἕν μὲν πρόσωπον, καὶ ἕνα υἱὸν καὶ Χριστὸν ὁμολογεῖν εὐσεβές· δύο δὲ τὰς ἑνωθείσας ὑποστάσεις, εἴτουν φύσεις, λέγειν οὐκ ἄτοπον*).

Theodoret himself, I think, appears to mean by this that God was not separated from human nature, nor can humanity be understood apart from divinity. Therefore we neither say that the forms of the servant and of God were joined apart from substances, nor define that a common human being, honored merely by equality of dignity, was relationally joined (*σχετικῶς*) to the Word. Rather, as I said above, we say that the Only-begotten Son of God himself, who truly assumed flesh possessing a rational soul, became human while nevertheless remaining God.

But that vehement man, powerful in speech and exceedingly sharp in thought, declares that such an expression signifies mixture, and dares to say this, bringing forward the consequences of a mixture of natures as though we did not know them. Perhaps he boasts with some insolence and thinks that no one except himself can extend a speech as far as he wishes, provided that he presents as truly said something that no one has said, so that he may appear to have something to offer among those who cannot distinguish the empty talkers and liars from those who hold to the right path of truth and exercise themselves in prudent and necessary discourse.

I confess that at first I thought he was by no means ignorant of the force of the chapters, but was pretending ignorance and gratifying certain people. Now, however, I have discovered that he truly was ignorant.

## THIRD ANATHEMA

If anyone divides the substances in the one Christ after the union, and joins them by a conjunction according only to dignity, authority, or dominion, and not rather by a certain coming together accomplished through a natural union (*ἕνωσις*), let him be anathema.

## HERETIC’S REFUTATION

The meaning of the statements is obscure and shrouded in darkness, but their impiety is plain to the devout. For whom is it not obvious that “conjunction” and “coming together” differ in no respect? [Note: For a coming together is of things that were previously separated, while a conjunction is of things that were previously divided. EDIT.] For a coming together is of things that were previously divided. But this most prudent inventor of words, as though placing contrary words together, set down terms that agree with one another: “It is not necessary,” he says, “to join substances by a conjunction, but by a combination and a natural coming together”—perhaps not knowing what he says, or knowingly blaspheming.

Nature is something commanding and compelling one to do certain things, not by will. This is what I mean: we hunger by nature, suffering this not by choice [Baluz. *sitientes*, “being thirsty”], but by necessity; and if this were not so, the poor would be freed from begging, since they would have it within their will not to hunger. We naturally perceive, naturally sleep, naturally draw breath. Yet none of these things, as I have said, occurs by will; for if anyone refuses any one of them, he will necessarily experience the end of life.

Therefore [Note: [Col. 0977D] “If natural.” This segment is cited in the epistle of Pelagius II mentioned above. GALLAND.] if the natural conjunction of the servant’s form took place [Note: [Col. 0978D] “The conjunction of the form of God and the form.” These words also occur in the same epistle. From this one may conclude that they were rightly restored from the manuscripts of Marius Mercator, for they had fallen out of Garnerius’s edition. GALLAND.] through some compelling necessity, and if God the Word was joined to the servant’s form not by his own clemency, then the lawgiver will be found serving necessary laws. But blessed Paul did not teach us this; rather, he taught the contrary, namely, that “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 6). By saying “he emptied himself,” he signifies will.

If, therefore, he was joined by his own decision and will to the nature assumed from us, the expression “natural conjunction” is superfluous; for it is enough to confess a *henōsis* (ἕνωσις, “union”). *Henōsis*, moreover, is understood of things that have been divided; for if there is no division, *henōsis* can never take place, and whoever admits *henōsis* also admits a prior division [Baluz. om. *praeviam*, “prior”].

Why, then, does he say that substances, or natures, ought not to be divided, especially since he knows that the substance of God the Word was perfect, and that the servant’s form assumed by him was perfect—and therefore he said “substances,” not “substance”? Thus, if each nature is perfect, and both have come together into one—the form of God, namely, assuming the servant’s form—piety requires us to confess one person, “one person” (ἓν μὲν πρόσωπον), and likewise one Son and one Christ. But to say that two united substances [Col. 0978D], or natures, exist is not foolish; rather [Baluz. add. *ex causa*, “for good reason”], it is more consistent.

For if in one human being we distinguish the natures, calling the mortal part the body and the immortal part the soul, but both together “the human being,” then much more is it fitting to distinguish the properties of the natures of the One who assumes and of the man who is assumed. We also find blessed Paul dividing one and the same human being into two human beings: at one time saying, “Although our outer man is being corrupted, our inner man is being renewed” (II Cor. IV, 16); at another, “I delight in the law of God according to the inner man” (Rom. VII, 22); and immediately afterward, “That Christ may dwell in the inner man” (Eph. III, 17).

If, therefore, the Apostle distinguishes the natures existing in a natural conjunction at the same time (ὁμοχρόνων), why does he charge with impiety those who distinguish the properties of the natures—the nature of the eternal God and that of his man, who was assumed in the last times? I say that this is the charge made by the man who teaches us commixture under other names.

## ORTHODOX RESPONSE

Observe how that wise man first falsely claims that our statements are obscure; although he himself possesses a darkened and clouded mind, he calls obscure what is plain to the wise and most evident in its expression.

He supposed that our argument maintains that it should be called a “convention” rather than a “conjunction.” Then, wishing to display his cleverness, he says that we mean the same thing whether we say that a convention or a conjunction has taken place. Here too I admire the acumen of his mind: perhaps he alone has learned what no one has ever been ignorant of, and what has been so trampled underfoot that it appears well known even to those entirely alien to secular learning and literature—indeed, even to those who have acquired only a slight and uncertain knowledge by hearing stories.

Admiring his learning, therefore, I say this to him: Wake up at least a little, as though from drunkenness or sleep, since you attempt to open so great a mouth against us; and carefully and sharply attend to the mystery of the unity that is spoken of concerning Christ. Some bring an accusation against this unity [Baluz. *in foeditate*, “in baseness”], transferring the statements of the sacred Scriptures to whatever interpretation pleases them. For they say that the natures are divided from and separated from one another, each existing separately and in its own part; but they maintain that the man was joined to God *relationally* (σχετικῶς), according to dignity alone, or authority, and according to the homonymy of sonship (ὁμωνυμία).

This anathema opposes that opinion and resists such profane novelties of expression. For it affirms that the Word was united by nature—that is, not *relationally* (σχετικῶς), but truly—to flesh possessing a rational soul; and that he must in no way be divided, lest by dividing the indivisible we understand two sons.

But he, not understanding what natural union—that is, true union—is, a union that neither confuses the natures nor produces commixture, so that each begins to be something other than what it was, adopts something childish and frivolous as proof of what he believes to be sound.

Finally, he says: If the union was natural, then the Word’s emptying was not voluntary, but occurred as though by necessity and compulsion, for nature is a commanding force. To this anyone could say to him: Hunger, thirst, and the other things you mentioned are natural weaknesses of the flesh, and in us they possess movement because we have a nature subject to passions. But the divine and mysterious nature of the Word is subject neither to necessity nor to passion; it was compelled by no one—not even by itself—to become flesh against its will, or to assume the measure of humanity and take hold of Abraham’s seed.

That his argument is violently ill-considered is not difficult for those who wish to discover. For he says categorically and without doubt that all natural things are subject to the laws of necessity. As proof of this he brought forward the fact that we hunger and thirst against our will, nature impelling us to this even if someone does not wish it—although a learned man, practiced in these matters, ought to have discerned other and more substantial causes of such things, causes worthy of a fuller argument—unless it is perhaps false that the rational human being is rational by nature. If so, he was compelled against his will to be rational.

Tell me next: Is almighty God not God by nature? Is he not by nature holy, just, good, life, light, wisdom, and power? Is he too, against his will and under compulsion, what he is? To think so is certainly the clearest proof of insane stupidity.

What, then, is he presenting to us as an impregnable and invincible rampart—a lie—and employing arguments so feeble that, when he hears that a natural union has occurred, that is, a true, voluntary, and wholly unconfused convention of substances, he attempts to twist the force of the statements so that they may be thought to have been improperly expressed? Nor does this vigorous man shudder [Baluz. add. *exemplo nostro*, “by our example”] when he declares that the nature of the Word is subject to unavoidable necessity.

“He emptied himself”—not against his will, but willingly the Only-Begotten became human. Yet he did not, as you claim, assume a man, granting him a *relational* conjunction and honoring him with the privilege of sonship, as though he were one of us.

Therefore, even if we understand the substances to have been united, and the Word of God to have become man and been incarnate, and thus seem in some way to speak of a natural union—one that excludes that union which is not true but *relational* (σχετική), such as we too have through faith and sanctification because we have become partakers of the divine nature—for, as Paul says, “The one who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17)—nevertheless we do not subject the impassible and free Word of God to natural necessity and compulsion.

As for our unwillingness, after the union [Baluz. add. “divine”], to regard the things united as separated from one another: unless I am mistaken, this is neither criminal nor blameworthy, especially since the distinguished man Theodoret himself, proposing one of us as an example, does not allow a human being to be divided into two, although, insofar as it concerns the theoretical consideration of a human being (θεωρία), he may be capable of division, in the sense that we understand the soul to be one thing by nature and the flesh another according to its own nature.

Therefore, inquiring more carefully by a similar method, we say that the union understood to have taken place in Christ is, according to the theoretical consideration (θεωρία) of divinity and humanity, a true convention effected through *henōsis* (ἕνωσις). We do not fail to recognize that the Word of God is one thing apart from the flesh, and that the flesh according to its own nature is another thing apart from the Word. But to divide what has once been united is criminal; nor does right reason permit us to separate the one Christ, Son, and Lord into two Sons. For holy and divine Scripture leads us to this understanding.

Yet he has no concern whatsoever for the truth of the doctrines, nor does he take pains to learn anything necessary or even moderately useful to him [Note: [Col. 0981D] “He avoids it as something that could harm him. Nevertheless.” This is the reading of the Vatican manuscript. Bellovacensis has *cudat*. The old translation of the *Antidote* has *festinat*. BALUZ.], but only what could harm him. Nevertheless, while he boasts in his lie and flaunts his cleverness at slander, let him hear from us: “Why do you boast in wickedness, you who are mighty in iniquity? Your tongue devised injustice all day long” (Ps. LI, 3).

## FOURTH ANATHEMATISM

If anyone distributes among two persons, or substances, the expressions found in the evangelical or apostolic Scriptures—whether those spoken by the saints concerning Christ or spoken by Christ himself concerning himself—and assigns some of them to him as a man understood separately from the Word, while assigning others as divine to God the Word alone, let him be anathema.

## REBUKE OF THE HERETIC

This too is related to what was said above. For he wishes, as though a commixture had taken place, that there be no distinction among the expressions spoken in the holy Gospels or apostolic books, although he especially boasts of being an enemy of Arius, Eunomius, and the other founders of heresies.

Let the teacher most skilled in divine doctrines say, then, how he can refute the blasphemy of the heretics when he assigns to God the Word the lowly expressions appropriate to the form of a servant [Col. 0981C]. For by doing this they assert that the Son of God is lesser, created, made, a servant, and made from nothing.

To whom, then, shall we—who think differently from them and confess the Son, consubstantial and coeternal with God the Father, the maker, creator, arranger, governor, most wise arbiter, and almighty ruler of all things—indeed, the very power itself [Baluz. *ipsum* here and below, “the very one”], life itself, and wisdom itself—assign these words: “God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. XXVII, 46); and: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI, 39); and: “Father, save me from this hour” (John XII, 27); and: “No one knows that hour, not even the Son of man” (Mark XIII, 32); and the other things spoken humbly by him and written about him by the holy apostles? [Note: [Col. 0981D] In the Fifth Council it reads: “To whom shall we apply hunger and thirst?” The old translation of the *Antidote*: “To whom shall we apply hunger and thirst?” The Greek words show this to be better. BALUZ.]

To whom shall we ascribe hunger and thirst? To whom fatigue and sleep? To whom ignorance and fear? Who is the one who needed the assistance of angels?

If these things belong to God the Word, how did wisdom not know? Or how can that be called wisdom which possesses the defect of ignorance? Or how will he appear to have spoken truthfully when he declares that he possesses everything belonging to the Father, while he does not possess the Father’s knowledge? For he says, “The Father alone knows that day” (Matt. XXIV, 36). Or how is he the image most like his begetter if he does not possess everything belonging to his begetter?

If he does not lie when he says that he is ignorant, what will anyone think about him? But if he knows the day and, wishing to conceal it, says that he is ignorant, you see what sort of blasphemy follows from this: the truth is lying. But how can that be called truth which has the opposite of truth? If the truth does not lie, neither is God [Baluz. “God’s”] the Word ignorant of the day that he himself appointed, on which he will judge the world; rather, he possesses the Father’s knowledge, being his most exact image.

Therefore the ignorance belongs not to God the Word, but to the form of a servant, which at that time knew only as much as the indwelling divinity revealed.

[Col. 0982B] Almost the entire passage contained in the paragraph was also reported in the Fifth Synod as expressing the Nestorian error concerning two sons, as Cyril observed.

The same may be said about other similar matters. For what rational sense is there in saying that God the Word said to the Father, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. XXVI, 39)?

For many irrational consequences again follow from this. First, the Father and the Son would be in disagreement, the Father willing one thing and the Son another; for he says, “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” Then again we shall find enormous ignorance in the Son, since he is found saying in ignorance, “If it is possible, let the cup pass.” But to say this of God the Word is impious and full of blasphemy. For he who came for this very purpose, who willingly assumed our nature, who emptied himself, certainly knew the outcome of the mystery of the dispensation, for whose sake he proclaimed to the holy apostles: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of man will be handed over to the Gentiles, and will be scourged and crucified, and on the third day he will rise again” (Matt. XX, 1).

How, then, would he who announced these things, and who rebuked Peter when he pleaded that they should not happen, have pleaded that they should not happen if he plainly knew everything that was to occur? How is it not absurd that Abraham, many centuries beforehand, saw his day and rejoiced; that Isaiah likewise foretold the saving sufferings, as did Jeremiah, Daniel, Zechariah, and the entire chorus of prophets; but that he himself was ignorant, sought deliverance, and pleaded against what was destined to benefit the salvation of the world [Col. 0982D]? [Note: [Col. 0982D] This too is found in the Fifth Synod. BALUZ.]

Therefore these words belong not to God the Word, but to the form of a servant, which feared death because death had not yet been undone. God the Word permitted it to say these things, giving room for fear to appear, so that the nature of the one born might be evident and so that we might not suppose that what came from Abraham and David was a mere appearance and phantasy (δόκημα and φαντασία), on account of the profane heretics [that is, the Manichaeans] whose faction produced such blasphemy.

Therefore let us ascribe to God the Word the things spoken or done divinely, but let us assign the things spoken humbly to the form of a servant, lest we imitate the blasphemies of Arius and Eunomius.

## ORTHODOX RESPONSE

Would it not have been much better, I ask, for him to investigate the force of the statements himself, keeping his mind free from hatred and prejudice? But he does not deign to do this at all. He turns everything according to his own will and says: “This too is related to what was said above. For he wishes, as though a commixture had taken place, that there be no distinction among the expressions written in the holy Gospels or apostolic sayings, although he especially boasts of being an enemy of Arius, Eunomius, and the other founders of heresies.”

So far as he is concerned, this is what he says. But I am as far from saying that the natures were confused with one another and underwent confusion, commixture, or conversion as he is from thinking rightly.

Nor have we abolished the distinction of expressions. For we know that some things were done divinely and others humanly; some are appropriate to the most exalted glory, while others are more suited to the measure of the emptying. But we assert that these things must not be assigned to two persons utterly divided from one another. For if our Lord Jesus Christ is one, one is the faith in him, and one the baptism (Eph. IV, 5); therefore there will rightly be one person, the person of that one being.

And if he is at once God and man, it is certainly fitting that he should utter expressions both divine and human, since his divine and mysterious nature is in no part made inferior to the majesty of the Father, and since we must believe that the dispensation with the flesh took place: being God, he is also said, as one of us, to have become human.

Everything, then, belongs to the one Christ, both the divine and the human. For if the Word of God the Father did not become human, let him not speak humanly as one of us; but if it is true that he likewise shared in flesh and blood with us, becoming like his brothers in every respect—that is, like us—why do those who do not allow a human voice, and who hasten to assign the humility of speech, produced on account of the dispensation, to the form of a servant as though to another Son existing separately, foolishly criticize the entirely proper order of the dispensation?

It is foolish for them to say that they shrink from the wickedness of the heretics while refusing to follow the tradition of the right faith. It would be more excellent and far more learned to assign the human expressions not to another person, understood as a Son existing separately, nor to the form of a servant, as they are accustomed to say, but rather to the measure of humanity itself. For since he was at once God and man, he ought to proceed through both kinds of speech [Baluz. om. *procedere*, “to proceed”].

I marvel that he too pretends to confess that Christ is one—the same being at once God and man—and then, as though he had forgotten what he rightly held, divides the one again into two. For he introduces the Savior’s statement: “But concerning that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, except the Father” (Mark XIII, 32).

Then, affirming that the Word of God the Father is wisdom and foreknows all future things, he adds: “Therefore it is not the ignorance of God the Word, but of the form of a servant, which at that time knew so much” [Note: [Col. 0983] Baluz. adds: “as much as the divinity dwelling in him revealed.” EDIT.]. The same may be said about other similar matters.

Therefore, if you do not falsely [Baluz. “erroneously”] say that Christ is one, and God the Son, the same being at once God and man, why do you divide him, and why are you not ashamed to say that there are two Sons? Unless perhaps the one who possesses foreordained knowledge and the one who knows everything, the one who receives a particular revelation and the one who is perfect in wisdom, the one who knows only so much and the one who knows as much as the Father, do not seem to be two at all.

But if he is one and the same, on account of the most genuine reality of the union, and not one person and another divided and separate, it belongs altogether to him both to know and to appear not to know. He knows divinely, therefore, as the wisdom of the Father. But because, in the economy, he takes upon himself the measure of human ignorance [Baluz. “ignorance”], he makes this too familiar to us along with the other things, although, as we recently said, he is wholly ignorant of nothing, but knows everything together with the Father.

For what reason, then, is he said to have hungered and to have become weary from the journey, since he is life and life-giving, being God, and since he himself is the living bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world (John VI, 51), and since he is himself the Lord of powers (Ps. XXIII, 10)? Clearly, it is so that he may truly be believed to have become human. He regards human experiences as familiar, never exceeding the goods of his nature, but retaining them unmoved, in which he always was, is, and will be.

But the one who says that a revelation was given to the form of a servant by the indwelling God, and that this revelation had been predetermined, presents Emmanuel to us as a prophet and a man bearing God (θεοφόρος)—and nothing more.

Yet he thinks that he is saying something clever and impregnable: “If it is God the Word,” he says, “who cried out, ‘FATHER, IF IT IS POSSIBLE, LET THIS CUP PASS FROM ME’ (Matt. XXVI, 39), then he first disagrees with the Father and improperly refuses to drink the cup, although, he says, he knows that the passion was destined to be salvific for the world. Therefore, such expressions do not belong to God the Word.”

Let him hear our reply on this matter as well, since he totters and stumbles on such weak arguments. Since, then, it seems to you that such expressions ought to be removed from God the Word and assigned solely to the servile form, do you not divide one into two sons? And to whom does this seem obscure among the wise?

Someone might perhaps follow your arguments and say that it is neither plausible nor rational for the form of a servant to refuse the passion, to disagree with the Father and with the Word that indwelt it [Baluz. “the Word”], while knowing that the passion would be salvific for the world and the cause of life for those who had been conquered by death. “Therefore,” he would say, “it ought to be seen as superior to fear and obedient to the divine commands.”

Do you not realize, then, that you are chattering pointlessly? Where did this commonplace invention of arguments come from?

Therefore, I readily confess that all human things appear small and insignificant in comparison with God the Word. But I ask whose emptying this is understood to have been, and who willingly endured it.

If, as they say, it was the form of a servant, or that which was from the seed of David, how and in what manner was it emptied, since it was assumed by God? But if the Word himself, who was in the form and equality of God the Father, is said to have emptied himself, how and in what manner was he emptied if he refuses the emptying?

The emptying of God the Word, who cannot suffer conversion, consists in doing or saying something human for the sake of the dispensatory convention with the flesh.

And even if he became human, the logic of the mystery in no way violates his nature. For he remained what he was, even when, for the salvation of the world and for the sake of life, he descended into humanity.

Therefore we shall assign the evangelical expressions and those of the holy apostles not to two persons, but to the one Christ, Son, and God. We shall neither diminish his divine nature and glory on account of the human, nor reject the dispensation; rather, we shall believe that the Word’s incarnation (ἐνανθρώπησις) took place for our sake.

## FIFTH ANATHEMATISM

If anyone dares to say that Christ is a man bearing God (θεοφόρος), and does not rather confess him to be truly God, as one Son by nature, because the Word became flesh and shared in flesh and blood in the same way as we did, let him be anathema.

## REBUKE OF THE HERETIC

We confess that God the Word shared in flesh, blood, and an immortal soul in the same way as we did, because these things have been united to him. But we do not say that God the Word became flesh by conversion; rather, we accuse of impiety those who say this.

How contrary this is to what was said previously may be seen from the following. For if the Word was converted into flesh, he certainly did not share in flesh and blood; but if he shared in flesh and blood, he shared in them as another existing beside them. If the flesh is something other than himself, then he was not converted into flesh.

Therefore [Note: [Col. 0985D] These things are found in the same epistle of Pelagius II. BALUZ.] using the term “sharing,” we worship one Son, both the one who assumes and the one who is assumed, while nevertheless recognizing the distinction of the natures.

[Col. 0985D] [Note: [Col. 0985D] “And to call him a man bearing God,” as stated by many. Some material seems to be missing here, material that is present in that epistle of Pelagius, where it reads as follows: “We do not refuse to call Christ ‘a man bearing God,’ that is, a man carrying God or clothed with God, as he was called by many holy Fathers” [Col. 0986D]. But in the ancient translation of the *Antidote* it is read almost exactly as in Mercator. BALUZ.]

We do not refuse to call him “a man bearing God” (θεοφόρος), that is, “God-bearing,” as he was called by many holy Fathers. One of them was that great Basil, who used this name in his discourse to Amphilochius on the Holy Spirit and in his interpretation of the fifty-ninth psalm.

We call him *theophoros* (θεοφόρος), not as though he received some particular divine grace of which I know not what kind, but as possessing the entire divinity of the Son united to him. Explaining this, blessed Paul said: “See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty glory, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ; because in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. II, 8).

## ORTHODOX RESPONSE

It is not difficult to show that here too he is occupied with empty fables. We assert that Christ ought not to be called a man bearing God (θεοφόρος) by anyone, lest he be understood as having been like one of the saints; rather, he should be called the truly God who became man, the incarnate Word of God.

Again he rebukes what has been correctly said, deceives in various ways, and lies. He says that we claim that God the Word was converted into the nature of flesh, and he draws arguments from afar by which he attempts to prove that God the Word is not subject to change.

But what I have said so often I must say again now: no one says that the divine and immortal nature of the Word was converted into earthly flesh; rather, everyone confesses that it is unchangeable. Cease at last from expending empty labor to demonstrate to those who have been deceived in no respect that God the Word is by nature unalterable and immutable. For who is so stupid or mentally deranged that he would wish to think and say things so disgraceful and perhaps abhorrent even to fools?

Yet I greatly marvel that, while he everywhere affirms that Emmanuel is God, he is convicted of assigning to him the measure of a prophet [Col. 0986C]. For he says that he is a man bearing God, so that he appears to be like us, who have God dwelling in us through the Holy Spirit. He dwells in our hearts, and we are temples of God.

But it is by no means the same thing to say that the Word became man and to say that God dwells in a man. For although blessed Paul’s statement is true—“For in him it was pleased that all the fullness of divinity should dwell bodily” (Col. II, 8), that is, not *relationally* (σχετικῶς)—nevertheless he says that there is one Father and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.

Let someone then say that Christ and his Spirit also dwell in a man, and that it is written concerning certain people, “Those who dwell in houses of clay” (Job IV, 19), from the same clay as which we too are made. Nevertheless [Col. 0986D], one human being is understood and exists through the composition of flesh and a rational soul dwelling in the flesh [Baluz. om. “dwelling in the flesh”].

Why, then, does he persist in disturbing the sound and stable rule of faith? At one moment he says that Christ, Son, and Lord is one, the same being at once God and man; at another he places him among the prophets, calling the man himself *theophoros* (θεοφόρος), perhaps not realizing that he thereby makes him equal even to us, if he is not truly God but rather a temple in which the Word dwells, just as he does in us.

But that these things are not so, divine Scripture has taught with complete clarity: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14), so that no one might suppose that he was converted and changed into the nature of flesh.

The one who became flesh, or man, is not a man bearing God (θεοφόρος), but rather God, who entered into a voluntary emptying and made his own flesh from a woman—flesh not soulless and without sensation, but ensouled and rational.

We also remember that he called the temple his body. He did not, however, establish a *relational* indwelling, as in us through the Spirit; rather, through the union Christ, Son, and Lord is understood as one.

## SIXTH ANATHEMATISM

If anyone says that the Word of God the Father is the God or Lord of Christ [Baluz. adds “or”], and does not rather confess that he is the same being at once God and man, because the Word became flesh according to the Scriptures, let him be anathema.

## REBUKE OF THE HERETIC

Blessed Paul calls that which was assumed by God the Word the form of a servant. But since the assumption preceded the union, and blessed Paul, discussing the assumption, called the assumed nature the form of a servant, the name “servitude” has no place once the union has taken place.

For if blessed Paul, writing to those who believed in him, said, “Therefore he is no longer a servant but a son” (Gal. IV, 7), and the Lord likewise said to the disciples, “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John XV, 15), then much more has the source of our nature, through which we too have merited the grace of adoption, been freed from the designation “servant.”

Therefore we confess the form of a servant to be God, because the form of God has been united to it. We agree with the Prophet when he calls Emmanuel a child, the messenger of great counsel, wonder, counselor, mighty God, ruler, prince of peace, and father of the age to come (Isa. VII, 14; IX, 6).

The same prophet, even after the union, while proclaiming the nature of the one assumed, calls what is from the seed of Abraham a servant, saying: “You are my servant, Israel, and in you I will be glorified” (Isa. XLIX, 3); and again: “Thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb as a servant for himself” (ibid. 5). A little later: “Behold, I have given you as a covenant of the race, as a light of the Gentiles, that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth” (Isa. XLII, 7; XLIX, 6).

That which was formed in the womb is not God the Word, but the form of a servant. For God the Word was not converted into flesh; rather, he assumed flesh possessing a rational soul.

## ORTHODOX RESPONSE

The mystery of the dispensation of the Only-Begotten, which took place with the flesh, will now make our statements no less common to us and will readily show that they have been made reasonably. For the Only-Begotten Son who is in the form of God and the Father, who is in every respect equal [Baluz. “equal and like”] to his begetter, who shares the same glory and is free, took the form of a servant and was called the brother of those who bear the yoke of servitude—that is, our brother.

Thus, as one of us, he paid the double-drachma to the collectors of tribute, and as a human being he became subject to the law, although as God he is the lawgiver. He taught his disciples that he is truly Son and, because of the flesh, in the form of a servant, while by his own nature he is free, being from God and being God. Nevertheless, possessing his own form of a servant because of the measure of the emptying, he paid tribute to the collectors.

Therefore, even if someone says that he was called a servant by the voice of the holy prophets, no one should in any way take offense. For they knew, when the Holy Spirit revealed it to them [Baluz. adds “to them”], that he who had become human, the Word from God the Father, was nevertheless, even in this respect, the free Son. Yet he did not cast aside the measure of the most wise emptying; rather, for our sake, who are under the yoke of servitude, he assumed a similar form.

Thus he also calls the Father himself God, although he is God by nature and from the Father, and is in no respect inferior to the Father in majesty.

Therefore, when Nestorius writes about Christ as follows—“Therefore the one who suffered is that merciful high priest, not the God who gives life to the one who suffered”—and calls the Word of Christ “God,” adding, “He himself was both the child and the Lord of the child” (*Serm.* 6, no. 6)—we emphatically affirm that these statements were made neither correctly nor appropriately, but impiously.

For if the God of Christ [Baluz. “Christ, God’s”] is the Word of God and the Father, then there must be two beings, absolutely and unquestionably. But how can the same person be understood as both child and Lord of the child? Therefore Emmanuel must not be called both God of himself [Baluz. “his God”] and Lord, if he is the same being at once God and man, as the Word of God became human and was incarnate.

No one, however, can doubt that divinity is one thing by its own nature and humanity another. Nevertheless, Christ is from both—from divinity and humanity—according to the dispensatory union.

## SEVENTH ANATHEMATISM

If anyone says that Christ, as a man, was assisted by the operation of God the Word [Baluz. adds “the Son”], and assigns to him the glory of the Only-Begotten as to someone other than the Only-Begotten himself, let him be anathema.

## REBUKE OF THE HERETIC

If human nature is mortal, while God the Word is life and life-giving, and he raised up the temple that had been destroyed by the Jews and lifted it into the heavens, how was the form of a servant not glorified through the form of God? For if the nature that is mortal became immortal through the union of the Word and God, then what it did not possess it received; and in receiving what it did not possess, it was glorified by the one who gave it glory. For this reason the Apostle cries out: “According to the working of the power of his might, which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead” (Eph. I, 20).

## ORTHODOX RESPONSE

[Col. 0989A]

Those who name Christ do not designate to their hearers one ordinary man like us, but the Word of God made man and incarnate. Therefore, even if it is said that he fulfilled certain marvelous and divine works through his own body, which provided him with the service of an instrument, nevertheless it is he himself who acts—the Lord Christ, the Lord of powers [Baluz. omits “of powers”]—not granting the primacy to another so that he might be able to act; just as he gave the blessed disciples authority over unclean spirits, so that they might cast them out and heal every disease and every infirmity among the people. Hence blessed Paul said: “For I will not dare to speak of anything that Christ did not accomplish through me, in word and deed, in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Holy Spirit” (Rom. XV, 18). The blessed disciples also once approached Christ rejoicing and said: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name” (Luke X, 17).

We say that the saints were helped by Christ in the Spirit, as though they were other persons besides him. Are we to understand, in the same way and by the same reasoning, that Jesus himself was helped by the Word in the Spirit, as though he were another Son besides the only-begotten Son of God? The union shows us that he is one and the same, and we refuse to divide him into two: for even if the Word became flesh, according to the Scriptures, nevertheless he is also in this way the only-begotten Son, according to the true union, which no human mind can comprehend.

He, therefore, is the one and only Christ Jesus who, through his own body, as through an instrument, performed the divine signs. Nor do we say that Christ himself was helped in his activity after the manner of the saints; for this is impious and greatly blameworthy. But if he raised his own body from the dead, since he himself is life and life-giving, and glorified it, demonstrating that his nature is life-giving, he did not grant this glory to anyone else besides himself. Certainly he said to the heavenly Father: “Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John XVII, 5), although he was also God, by nature from God, and Lord of glory. How, then, does he, as though lacking the glory that he possessed before the world, ask for glory again? For after he became man, also through his flesh, “by the grace of God he tasted death for everyone,” as blessed Paul says (Heb. II, 9). [Note: [Col. 0989] Baluz.: “As blessed Paul says, not refusing the reproach of earthly dishonor,” etc. EDIT.] Thereafter, refusing the reproach of the insults inflicted upon him, he foretells the resurrection, through which it is recognized that he is both life and life-giving, since he is God; and in this way too we believe in him.

He therefore glorified not someone else, but himself, indicating that the temple truly joined to him was stronger than death; and we do not believe that the body united to him was lifeless or without perception and mind [Baluz. omits “and mind”].

## Eighth Anathema

If anyone dares to say that the assumed man ought to be co-worshiped with God the Word, and co-glorified and jointly named God, as one distinct person alongside another; and does not rather worship Emmanuel with one worship and assign him one glorification, because “the Word became flesh” (John I, 14), let him be anathema.

## Refutation of the Heretic

We offer one glorification to the Lord Christ, as I have often said, and confess him to be the same God and man. This is what the principle of the union has taught us; nevertheless, we shall not refuse to speak of the properties of the natures. For God the Word was not changed into flesh; nor, conversely, did the man lose what he had been and become transformed into the nature of God. Therefore, while declaring the property of each nature, we worship Christ the Lord.

## Orthodox Response

[Col. 0990B]

But we, accustomed to think what is better and truer, and examining subtler meanings for a more certain explanation and a more correct understanding of the mystery, in accordance with the teaching of the sacred writings and the practice of the holy Fathers, do not say that a man was assumed by God the Word [Baluz. “by the Word”], and joined to him through an externally understood σχέσις (*schesis*, “relation”); rather, we define that he himself became man. For this reason we judge those who dare to say that a man was assumed to be outside the boundaries of the doctrines of piety: they assert that he ought to be co-worshiped with the Son of God, as one distinct person alongside another. For if he is the same God and man at once, he is worshiped as one, with one worship; he is not co-worshiped and jointly named God, lest Emmanuel be believed to be merely an ordinary man like us, made a participant in divine glory by favor. Rather, he is believed to be God truly made man in the flesh for our sake—not by conversion or alteration of nature, but by a providential union.

## Ninth Anathema

If anyone says that the one Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Spirit through its power, as by an alien force, and received from it the ability to act against unclean spirits and perform divine signs; and does not rather say that the Spirit through which he performed the divine signs was his own proper Spirit, let him be anathema.

## Refutation of the Heretic

Here he has clearly dared to anathematize not only those who preserve piety in this age, but also those who came before—the preachers of truth, the writers of the divine Gospels, the choir of the holy apostles—and, in addition, the archangel Gabriel. For that Christ was made according to the flesh from the Holy Spirit, Gabriel first foretold to Mary before the conception [Baluz. omits “to Mary”], and after the conception taught Joseph. To Mary, who asked, “How will this be, since I do not know a man?” (Luke I, 35), he said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born will be called the Son of God.” To Joseph he said: “Do not be afraid to take Mary your wife, for what has been begotten in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I, 20). And the Evangelist says: “When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 18).

The Lord himself also entered the synagogue of the Jews, received the prophet Isaiah, and read the passage in which he says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Luke IV, 18); and, adding what follows, he said: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your ears” (ibid., 21).
