Blessed Peter also said this when speaking to the Jews: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit” (Acts X, 38). Isaiah had proclaimed it many centuries earlier: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him—the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety; the spirit of the fear of God shall fill him” (Isa. XI, 1). And again: “Behold my son whom I have loved, my beloved, in whom my soul has been well pleased. I shall place my Spirit upon him, and he shall announce judgment to the nations” (Matt. XII, 18). The Evangelist also included this testimony in his writings. The Lord himself said to the Jews in the Gospels: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has certainly come upon you” (Luke XI, 20). And John says: “The one who sent me to baptize with water himself said to me: ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’” (John I, 33).

[Col. 0991C]

Thus that most diligent examiner of divine doctrines anathematized not only the prophets and apostles, nor merely the archangel Gabriel; he also extended his blasphemy against the Savior of all. For we have shown that Christ himself, at one time speaking to the Jews after reading, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me,” said: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your ears” (Luke IV, 18); and at another time, speaking to those who said that he cast out demons by Beelzebul, said that he cast out demons by the Spirit of God (Luke XI, 20).

We do not say that God the Word, who is of the same substance as his Spirit and coeternal with it, was formed by the Holy Spirit and anointed; rather, we say this of the human nature that was assumed from us by him in the last times.

[Col. 0991D]

But if he said that the Son’s own Spirit is of the same nature and proceeds from the Father, we shall agree and accept the statement as pious. If, however, he means that the Spirit derives its existence from the Son or through the Son, we shall reject this as blasphemy and impiety. For we believe the Lord when he says: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father” (John XV, 26); and likewise the divine Paul when he says: “We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from the Father” (I Cor. II, 12).

## Orthodox Response

[Col. 0992A]

I have already said that the force of the chapters contradicts the vanities—or rather, the blasphemies—and the statements [Note: [Col. 0991D] In the Bellovacensis manuscript it reads: “ipsius est praedixit aliis ne igitur est Christus secundum carnem vehementer incultis.” I do not know from where these words were transferred here, unless [Col. 0992D] they migrated here from what is read on the following page. BALUZ.] of Nestorius himself, which are exceedingly uncultivated. For when he said concerning the Holy Spirit (Sermon 2): “This is the one who bestowed such glory upon Christ, who made him terrifying to demons, who granted him his assumption into heaven”; and when he babbled in this way about Christ as though about some ordinary man like us, the anathema was necessarily composed. It was directed not against those who say that Jesus, that is, the man made by God the Word, was glorified by the Holy Spirit, but rather against those who shamelessly claim that he used the power of the Holy Spirit as something alien. For we clearly remember him saying of the Holy Spirit: “He will glorify me” (John XVIII, 14). [Col. 0992B] We also know that by the operation of the Holy Spirit he himself subdued unclean and evil spirits.

But we do not say that he used the power of the Holy Spirit as something alien, like one of the prophets. For the Holy Spirit was and is his own, just as it is the Father’s. The divine Paul made this unmistakably clear when he wrote: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. IV, 9). The Holy Spirit proceeds from God the Father, according to the Savior’s saying, but it is not alien to the Son; for it has everything in common with the Father. The Son himself also showed this concerning the Holy Spirit: “All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said to you that he will take from what is mine and announce it to you” (John XVI, 15). [Col. 0992C] The Holy Spirit therefore glorified Jesus as he performed miracles; nevertheless, it was his own Spirit—not by an alien power, nor as something superior to him, since he is understood to be God.

We have not therefore blasphemed against the holy angels or the prophets, as the man who has learned only to curse dared to say. But since he and those like him are still intent on dividing the one Christ into two—namely, into the one who is glorified and the one who assists the activity—[Note: [Col. 0992D] Baluz.: “and to say that the one who is glorified and helped in his activity is one, and the one who glorifies and helps the activity is another,” etc. EDIT.] they foolishly attack every principle of piety that could turn them away from so perverse an opinion [Baluz. “seduce”].

Finally, mentioning blessed Gabriel, the accuser says: “He was the first to foretell, before the conception, that Christ according to the flesh would be made from the Holy Spirit.” Therefore there is one Christ according to the flesh and another Christ specifically, the Word from God the Father. Where, then, is the union? And what benefit would result if there were two Christs, each understood and named separately?

Even if, then, they pretend to fashion for themselves the appearance and persona of piety and say that Christ is one, let them hear from us that they believe in two: “How long will you limp on both feet?” (III Kings XVIII, 21). It is better to walk in straight paths, preserving a right and steadfast faith, not wavering through foolish thoughts.

## Tenth Anathema

Divine Scripture records that Christ was made the high priest and apostle of our confession. For he offered himself for us as a fragrant offering to God the Father. If anyone therefore says that it was not God the Word himself—when he became flesh and man like us—who was made our high priest and apostle, but another man separately from him, born of a woman; or if anyone says that he offered the offering for himself and not rather solely for us—for he had no need of a sacrifice, since he knew no sin—let him be anathema.

## Refutation of the Heretic

[Col. 0993B]

The unchangeable nature was not changed into the nature of flesh; rather, he assumed human nature and placed it above ordinary high priests, as blessed Paul teaches when he says: “Every high priest taken from among men is appointed on behalf of men in matters pertaining to God, so that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, being able to have compassion on those who are ignorant and erring, since he himself is also surrounded by weakness. For this reason he ought to offer for sins on his own behalf as well as on behalf of the people” (Heb. V, 1). Immediately afterward, explaining the same point, he says: “So also Christ, as Aaron” (ibid., 5). Then, showing the weakness of the assumed nature, he says: “In the days of his flesh, he offered prayers and supplications to the one who was able to save him from death, with a loud cry and tears; and he was heard because of his reverence. Although he was a Son, he learned obedience from what he suffered, and, having been perfected, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him, being called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek” (ibid., 7).

Who, then, was perfected through the labors of virtue, since he was not perfect by nature? Who learned obedience through experience, which he did not know before experience? Who lived with reverence? Who offered supplications with a loud cry and tears, unable to save himself, but imploring the one who could save him and seeking deliverance from death? Not God the Word, immortal, impassible, incorporeal. According to the Prophet, the remembrance of him is joy and the lifting away of tears; for “he will wipe away every tear from every face” (Isa. XXV, 9, according to the Septuagint). And again the Prophet says: “I remembered God” (Ps. LXXVI, 4), and I rejoiced; that he crowns those distinguished in piety (Dan. XIII, 2); that he possesses everything belonging to the Father (John XVI, 15); that he is the very likeness of his begetter (Col. I, 15, 39); that he displays the Father in himself (John XIV, 10). Rather, these things pertain to the one who had been assumed by God from David’s seed, mortal and passible; who trembled before death, although afterward he destroyed death’s dominion through the divinity of the one who assumed him; who walked in all righteousness; who said to John, “Permit it now, for it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. III, 15); who received the designation of high priest according to the order of Melchizedek (Heb. V, 10). For he bore the weakness of nature, whereas almighty God the Word did not. Therefore blessed Paul had said earlier: “We do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been tested in every respect like us, without sin” (Heb. IV, 15).

Almost the whole of this περικοπή (*perikopē*, “section”) is read in the Fifth Synod, Collation 6. Theodoret and Cyril contend over this passage with great force of argument, but with still greater partisan zeal. The issue concerns Proclus, as I have noted more than once: Theodoret disliked him, since he was a distinguished opponent of Nestorius, while Cyril valued him as the leader of those fighting for the faith at Constantinople. Theodoret charges Cyril with converting the Word into flesh; Cyril, in turn, reproaches him with deplorable folly, ignorance of the mystery under discussion, an assertion of ἐνώσεως σχετικῆς (*henōseōs schĕtikēs*, “a relational union”), agreement with Nestorius, impiety, and contradiction. This entire speech of Cyril can drive a great wedge into the position of Theodoret’s defenders.

The nature assumed from us and for us experienced our passions, without sin; not the one who assumed it for our salvation. At the beginning of this chapter he again teaches: [Note: [Col. 0993D] In the letter of Pelagius II: “Consider,” the Apostle says, “Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, faithful to the one who made him,” etc. BALUZ.] “Consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, faithful to the one who made him, as Moses also was in all his house” (Heb. III, 1). Who, if he thinks correctly, would ever call the uncreated and coeternal God the Word with the Father a creature? Rather, he means the one who was from David’s seed, who, free from all sin, was our high priest and offered himself as a victim for us to God, having in himself, certainly, God the Word united to him and inseparably joined to him. [Note: [Col. 0993D] In Pelagius’s letter: “and true God.” For this is how it is read in the Colbertinus manuscript, from which the letter was published, instead of what the editions have, “and I shall add ‘true.’” But in the version of the *Antidote* it reads “God the Word.” The Greek text likewise. BALUZ.] [Note: [Col. 0994D] In Pelagius’s letter: “offered.” BALUZ.]

## Orthodox Response

When Israel had offended God and provoked him to anger, the prophet Jeremiah said sorrowfully: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may mourn this people day and night?” (Jer. IX, 1). And I think such words apply no more to Israel [Baluz. “to them”] than to those who always have an open and insolent mouth against Christ—those who, according to what is written, audaciously and arrogantly insult even ineffable glory (II Peter II, 10). They are most worthy of weeping and lamentation: in their boundless madness they neglect the straight and blameless path of piety toward Christ, pursue a crooked track and winding ways, and stain the beauty of truth with the perverse inventions of their thoughts.

[Col. 0995A]

Let those, therefore, who think what is hateful to everyone hear—those who err in their knowledge of the Scriptures and do not know the great and venerable mystery of the Incarnation. For the divine Scriptures proclaim that Emmanuel, the Word of God and the Father, became a man like us and shared in flesh and blood as we do. They also affirm that he became flesh, that is, man—not by conversion or alteration, but through the power of the secret union. Therefore we call Jesus Christ one Lord, and profess one faith and likewise one holy baptism.

But these men, abhorring correct doctrines and insolently setting up a harsh interpretation against the sacred writings, look only to what seems good to them and speak of a man assumed by God the Word, perhaps according to what one of the prophets said: “I was not a prophet, nor a prophet’s son; but I was a shepherd, tending sycamores, and God took me from the sheep” (Amos VII, 14); or perhaps as blessed David says: “The Lord takes up the meek” (Ps. CXLVI, 6). They mean a σχέσις (*schesis*, “relation”) and spiritual familiarity of the sort that we too have with him by will, grace, and sanctification: for by adhering to the Lord, “we are one spirit,” as it is written (I Cor. VI, 17). But this does not at all signify that God became man, nor that he shared in flesh and blood as we do; rather, it means that he assumed a man in no other way than it is said that he assumed the apostles, the prophets, and all the other saints.

Does the divine Paul deceive those sanctified by faith when he says most clearly of the Only-Begotten that, “although he was rich, he became poor” (II Cor. VIII, 9)? Far from it; the greatest preacher of truth will never lie. But let us now examine more carefully who is rich and how he became poor. For if, as they confidently say and believe, a man was assumed by God, how did the one assumed by God become poor, when he has been adorned with the higher dignities of his nature? He was glorified. But if that is not true, they will criticize the assumption, since it cast him down to a lower and less glorious condition of humanity. Yet such a view is foolish. Therefore it was not the one assumed who became poor; it remains for us to say that God the Word, although rich, descended into our poverty.

But how did he become poor? Let us attend as necessary. He is unquestionably unchangeable by nature and did not abandon what he was to pass into the nature of flesh; he remained what he was, that is, God. Where, then, shall we see the humility of poverty? In the fact that God assumed one ordinary man like us, as the impious parasites of Nestorius dared to say? And what sort of poverty and self-emptying would this be? Is it merely that he perhaps wished to honor some man like us? Yet the almighty God is in no way diminished by bestowing benefits. How, then, did he become poor? Because, although he was God by nature and the Son of God and the Father, he became man from David’s seed; he was born according to the flesh and assumed a servile condition, that is, a human one, although he is the maker of all things. Having become man, he is not ashamed to assume the human condition. For if he did not refuse to be like us, how could he refuse those things by which he could show that he had truly become a man like us? If, therefore, we remove him from human actions and words, we differ in no way from those who, if they could, would strip him even of his flesh—those who do not believe the divine Scripture and entirely overturn the mystery of the Incarnation, the salvation of the world, hope, faith, and the resurrection.

Someone may say that it is unfitting and in no way appropriate for God the Word to weep, fear death, refuse the cup, or undertake the office of priest. I too gladly agree that these things are least suited to the divine nature and glory. Nevertheless, in these things I see the poverty that he willingly endured for our sake. If the dishonor of his self-emptying seems grievous to you, marvel all the more at the Son’s love toward us: what you call so unfitting and insignificant, God made precious to himself for your sake.

He wept in the manner of human beings, so that he himself might restrain your tears [Baluz. “observe your tears”]. He was afraid, providentially permitting the flesh at times to suffer what belongs to it, so that we might become utterly confident. He refused the cup so that the cross might expose the impiety of the Jews. He is said to have been weakened according to his humanity, so that he might free you from weaknesses. He offered prayers and supplications so that he might make his ear readily attentive also to your supplications, and so that you might learn not to become drowsy at all in temptations, but rather to devote your mind to prayer. Therefore he rebuked the holy apostles when they were sleeping, saying: “Could you not watch with me for one hour? Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. XXVI, 4). By presenting himself as a restoration of blessed life, he benefited the world; therefore he made the weaknesses of humanity familiar to himself, so that he might also truly be believed to have become man, while nevertheless remaining what he was, that is, God.

But I do not know how those who pretend to call Christ one, and Son, and Lord, and the same God and man, can say that God the Word was not named the high priest and apostle of our confession when he became man. Instead, they assert that someone else—I do not know whom—an isolated man in himself, who was from David’s seed, was called to this office. Perhaps they fear that, if they think correctly, they will appear to have defected from the impiety of Nestorius. For he says as follows (Sermon 6, the third delivered against Proclus): “This one who was made a faithful high priest to God—for he was made, and had not always been—this one who gradually advanced in the dignity of high priest, heretic.” Then, wishing, as he thinks, to confirm the truth of his statements, he says: “Concerning him Luke also cried out in the Gospels: ‘Jesus advanced in age, wisdom, and grace.’” And again: “But since this one high priest is compassionate toward us, related to us, and trustworthy, do not be led astray by his nature; for he was sent to us from the promised blessing and seed of Abraham, bringing with him a victim for himself and for his bodily lineage.”

But Theodoret, that excellent imitator of his madness, does not blush to say: “He assumed human nature and appointed it above ordinary high priests, as Paul also says: ‘Every high priest taken from among men is appointed on behalf of men in matters pertaining to God, being able to have compassion on those who are ignorant and erring, since he himself is also surrounded by weakness; and for this reason he ought to offer for sins on his own behalf as well as on behalf of the people.’” Did he not, as far as it depends on him, make Emmanuel an ordinary man like us? Are not these statements also akin to those quoted above, giving birth to the same blasphemy? What do you say? You fear the manner of priesthood in Christ, the Savior of all, and it does not seem suitable for God the Word to minister in human fashion because of the dispensation? Uncover your face, lay aside your persona, and openly deny the incarnation of God the Word, on account of which he was also called a high priest. Do you see him offering sacrifice as though to another and greater God, the Father? Have you observed him offering sacrifices in the manner of those who are assumed from among men and who can have compassion on the ignorant and erring because they too are subject to our weaknesses? Have you not considered that he consecrates the faith of all—or the confession of faith—to the Spirit and the Father? [Note: [Col. 0997D] Baluz.: “Consecrates it to himself and to the holy Father. Is this,” etc. EDIT.] Is this the manner of human ministry: to demand faith from those who have been offered in the Spirit as a fragrant offering? Observe how he is said to minister in a different manner: although he is God, he ministers in human fashion because of the dispensation; for he sits with God the Father and is seen upon the exalted thrones.

Does the fact that he is human terrify you, while what is divine does not free you from fear? You cannot discern from the facts themselves that Emmanuel is both God and man. Yet with such insolence and thoughtlessness—indeed, going beyond every boundary of impiety—you say that he was perfected through labors and virtue and gradually advanced in the dignity of high priest. If he advanced, where is his self-emptying, and where did he become poor? [Note: [Col. 0997D] The words “If he was perfected … he was made perfect” are not found in Baluze’s text. EDIT.] If he was perfected through virtue, then he was made perfect in time from a state of imperfection. Whatever is not perfect in virtue is contained in fault and defect; and what is contained in defect is in sin. How, then, is it written of him that he committed no sin (I Peter II, 22)?

He dared to say the following, which is written below: “Who, then, was made a priest? Who was perfected through virtue, since he was not perfect by nature? Who learned obedience through temptations, which he did not know before the temptations? Who lived with reverence, and, crying with a loud voice and offering supplications, was unable to save himself but implored the one who could save him?” O most audacious and criminal statement! What tears could erase the sins of those who believe so impiously? If you accept the union, how could you fail to understand that you are speaking of God who became man? He humbled himself for your sake, and you impiously cry out: “Be propitious, Lord; this will never be fitting for you.” Therefore you shall hear him say: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me” (Matt. XVI, 22).

In the conclusion of his statements, however, he said: “Therefore the one who is from David’s seed is the high priest, having within himself, namely, God the Word, united to him and inseparably joined to him.” How can he say that what is from David’s seed is united to God the Word if he assigns the priesthood only to the one who is from David’s seed? For if the union is true, there are certainly not two, but one and only one is understood as Christ from both.

[Col. 0998B]

It is therefore clear that they confess the union deceptively, assailing the minds of the simpler believers [Baluz. “enticing”]. For they believe the conjunction to be σχετικὴ (*schetikē*, “relational”) and externally effected—the kind of union that we too have when we become participants in the divine nature itself through the Spirit. We must not therefore follow their vanities, but the upright and blameless faith and the evangelical and apostolic decrees.

## Eleventh Anathema

If anyone does not confess that the Lord’s flesh is life-giving and the proper flesh of God the Word, but says that it belongs to someone else, joined to him by dignity or by mere indwelling; and does not rather confess it to be life-giving, as I said earlier, because it is the proper flesh of the Word, who is able to give life to all things, let him be anathema.

## Refutation of the Heretic

As is apparent, the man who shares the same opinions as the heretics is devoted to obscurity in order to conceal his impiety. But nothing is stronger than truth, which can reveal the darkness of falsehood with its rays. Enlightened by it, let us expose his manifestly ἑτερόδοξος (*heterodoxos*, “heterodox”) faith. First, he nowhere mentions a rational soul, nor does he confess the perfect man who was assumed; everywhere he speaks of flesh, following the doctrines of Apollinaris. Next, while expressing the opinion of mixture in other words, he sprinkles it throughout his statements. For here he openly calls the Lord’s flesh lifeless when he says: “If anyone confesses that the Lord’s flesh is not the proper flesh of God the Word, but belongs to another besides him, let him be anathema.” It is therefore apparent that he does not confess that God the Word assumed a soul, but only flesh, while he himself stands in the place of the soul for the flesh. We, however, call the Lord’s flesh life-giving, ensouled, and rational, because the life-giving divinity has been united to it [Baluz. omits “to it”].

He too, although unwillingly, confesses a distinction of natures by naming flesh and God the Word and saying that the flesh was his own proper flesh. Therefore God the Word was not changed into the nature of flesh; rather, he has flesh proper to himself—the assumed nature—and made it life-giving through the union.

## Orthodox Response

Those who through ignorance have fallen away from upright and true thoughts almost say: “We have made falsehood our hope, and we shall be covered by falsehood” (Isa. XXVIII, 15). For they recklessly put forward whatever judgment they please, and they do not remember the divine Scripture, which says: “Judge with righteous judgment” (Zech. VII, 9). And again: “A false witness shall not go unpunished” (Prov. XIX, 5).

We say that the holy body of Christ, the Savior of all, is life-giving. It is not merely the body of an ordinary man like us, a common body; rather, it is truly the proper body of the Word, who gives life to all things. It is proper in the same way that each of us is said to possess his own proper body.

This fine fellow has left no device of his verbosity against us untried, although he agrees with our statements. Once again he brands us with the infamy of Apollinarian impiety and is not ashamed to say that I conceal the matter of mixture or confusion under different words and call the flesh joined to the Word lifeless. But perhaps someone might say to him: “My good man, will you also accuse blessed John of the same crimes? For he says: ‘The Word became flesh’ (John I, 14). Go on, then, and insolently say of him also that he did not mention a rational soul, but called the Lord’s flesh lifeless.”

What if you also hear Christ, the Savior of all, say: “Amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John VI, 54). Insult the Word himself too, if you wish: he names only flesh and nowhere in these passages mentions a rational soul.

But if you were intelligent and wise, you would not fail to recognize that often even the mention of flesh alone designates the living being composed of soul and body—that is, the human being. For it is written: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. XL, 5). Therefore the one who says that the Word became flesh is not wholly unaware that he is also mentioning a rational soul.

But, as I said at the beginning, lacking proof, he has found falsehood as a covering for himself and tries to bring an accusation so that he may appear to be saying something.

Yet the holy Fathers do not think that a man was assumed by God [Baluz. adds “not”]. For they never believed in this way; rather, they said that God the Word himself became man and was united to flesh possessing a rational soul. The union is entirely unconfused and without conversion; for God the Word is unchangeable, and this is what we believe.

## Twelfth Anathema
If anyone does not confess that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, and was crucified in the flesh, and tasted death in the flesh, and was made the firstborn from the dead—for, as God [Baluz. omits “as God”], he gives life and is life-giving—let him be anathema.

## REFUTATION OF THE HERETIC

The sufferings of a passible nature belong properly to it; the impassible nature is superior to sufferings. Therefore the form of a servant suffered, while the form of God was also joined to it, permitting it indeed to suffer for the sake of the salvation that was to result from the sufferings; and he calls its sufferings his own because of the union [Baluz. “leading”]. Therefore, he says, it was not God who suffered, but the man who was assumed from us by God. For this reason blessed Isaiah, proclaiming it beforehand, cries out: “A man in affliction, and knowing how to bear weakness” (Isaiah 53:3). And the Lord Christ himself said to the Jews: “Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you?” (John 8:40). It is not life itself that is killed, but he who possesses a mortal nature. Teaching this elsewhere, the Lord said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” Therefore, the one who is from David was indeed destroyed; but the only-begotten Word of God, who was born impassibly from the Father before the ages, raised up what had been destroyed.

## RESPONSE OF THE ORTHODOX

The nature of the Word is certainly impassible, and, as I think, this is uncertain to no human being. No one would sink into such insane folly as to say that this mysterious nature, superior to sufferings, is held by our weaknesses. But since the suffering was destined to be saving for the world, and since it was impossible for God the Word to suffer anything in his own nature, he wisely entered into the dispensation: he made a body of his own that could suffer, so that, while the body suffered, he himself might be said to have suffered, although he remained impassible according to his own nature.

But since he willingly suffered in the flesh, for this reason he is and is called the Savior of all. As Paul says: “By the grace of God he tasted death for everyone” (Hebrews 2:9). The divine Peter also bears witness, saying most wisely: “Since therefore Christ suffered for us” (1 Peter 4:1). This refers, of course, not to the nature of the Godhead, but to the flesh. Finally, how is the Lord of glory said to have been crucified? And likewise, how was he through whom all things exist, and in whom all things have been ordered (1 Corinthians 2:8; Hebrews 2:10), as blessed Paul says, given by God the Father as head of the body, the Church, and made the firstborn from the dead? He suffered the sufferings of the flesh as belonging familiarly to himself; but the Lord of glory was in no way a man like us and of the common kind.

Perhaps you will say that the unity is sufficient to prove that Christ and the Lord who was crucified are one. Then let everything be said to belong to him, and let it be believed that the Word of God is the Savior, remaining impassible according to the nature of the Godhead but suffering in the flesh, in accordance with what Peter said: the body that tasted death was his own through the true union. Finally, how is Christ, according to the flesh, from the Jews, and God over all, blessed forever, amen (Romans 9:5)? In whose death were we baptized? By confessing whose resurrection are we justified? [Note: [Col. 1001A] Baluz.: “Yet according to his nature the Word of God is superior to death—or rather, he is life itself. Were we therefore baptized into the death of an ordinary man? [Col. 1002A] We are justified by believing in Jesus; or rather, by what follows, etc.” EDIT.] Of some ordinary man? Or, what is truer, do we proclaim the death of God made man and suffering in the flesh for us, and, confessing his resurrection, cast off the burden of sins? For we were bought with a price—not with perishable silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a pure and spotless lamb (1 Corinthians 6:20; 1 Peter 1:19).

It would not be difficult to recall many other things concerning these matters and to set forth examples from the holy Fathers. But I think these will be sufficient for the more teachable; for it is written: “Give an opportunity to the wise, and he will become wiser; instruct the righteous, and he will add to his understanding” (Proverbs 9:9).

[Col. 1002A] These words—“HE SUFFERED WILLINGLY,” πέπονθεν ἕκων—were attacked by Eutherius in Sermon 8, as were these: “THE WORD SUFFERED IN THE FLESH,” ἔπαθεν ὁ Θεὸς Λόγος σαρκί. Moreover, the affinity of subject matter and the similarity of wording between the Eranistes and the Refutations of the chapters or propositions are so great that they show not only that they have the same author, whom everyone acknowledges, but also the same opponent, whom few notice to be Cyril. I think we shall demonstrate this in the supplement to Theodoret’s works that we are preparing to publish shortly, if it be God’s will. There, after Theodoret’s life has been distinguished by his deeds, and after his faith has been examined, judgment will be passed on each of his works in such a way that several works—part of which Mercator has supplied—will be shown to be missing from the Sirmondian edition, and the history of each, namely its date, causes, and character, will be narrated.

[Col. 1001]

# SCHOLIA OF SAINT CYRIL, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, ON THE INCARNATION OF THE ONLY-BEGOTTEN

## INTRODUCTORY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING WORK

This treatise, entitled *Scholia on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten*, is not more distinguished than it is useful. It contains not only an explanation of three words difficult to understand—Christ, Emmanuel, and Jesus—the prior knowledge of which is necessary for treating the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, but also a solution to the complicated question of how two natures came together, without confusion or conversion, into the unity of the divine person, and how that unity is not relational and moral (*σχετικήν*), but natural and substantial (*φυσικήν*): the pivotal issue of the whole controversy that agitated the entire world with such violence.

There can be no doubt about its author, since Theodoret, in the second dialogue called *Inconfusus*; Leo the Great, in Letter 97; the Council of Chalcedon, at the end of Act 2; Facundus of Hermiane, in Books VII and XI; Leontius the Scholastic, in Book I *Against the Nestorians and Eutychians*; and others not only mention this work as published by Cyril, but also draw testimonies from it to confirm the faith. Add that in the Royal Library at Paris a substantial portion exists in Greek under Cyril’s name, which John Aubert translated into his Greek-Latin edition of Cyril’s works, volume V, part I.

It is possible to conjecture the time at which it was composed from the fact that, although the holy defender of the faith argues against Nestorius, he does not call him by name—though otherwise he was not accustomed to remain silent about him after his condemnation, or even before his condemnation, as soon as the dispute had, so to speak, been initiated and legal proceedings had begun; that is, after the synodical letter from the Egyptian synod, together with the pope’s letters containing the sentence of deposition and the twelve chapters called anathemas, had been sent. It must therefore be said to have been composed before the Council of Ephesus.

But where, and at what more precise time? Someone might suppose that it was at Ephesus, when Cyril, compelled by the Catholics’ insistence, had to explain certain things in the anathemas that seemed somewhat too harsh or obscure, especially to repel the hostility that his adversaries had stirred up against him, as though he agreed with the Apollinarists that there was one nature in Christ and that the divine Word had been changed into flesh.

I, however, think that it was written at Alexandria, long before that. For before responding either to Andrew of Samosata or to Theodoret, who criticized the anathemas, Cyril undertook this work in order to equip those who would argue for the faith with an account of the preliminary meanings of the terms, as it were, and of several other matters that he would use in the course of the debate. He composed it, unless I am mistaken, when the controversy had first begun to burn among the Alexandrians, who were not yet sufficiently trained by intellectual exercise, and when Cyril himself was first entering the struggle for Christ against Nestorius, having sent his earlier admonitory letters of official character. This treatise was therefore written at approximately the same time as the letter to the Egyptian monks, that is, around the middle or at least toward the end of the year 429. The subject of both works is the same, and the only difference seems to be one of method: the method of the letter is more rhetorical, while that of the *Scholia* is almost scholastic.

Three considerations drive me to this conclusion. First, the *Scholia* were written before the Council of Ephesus, as has already been established; yet they were written some considerable time before it, since Andrew of Samosata, in Anastasius of Sinai, mentions this work as widely known. Second, the work appears to present elementary instruction delivered to minds inexperienced in the controversy: it consists of explanations of terms, distinctions necessary for resolving objections, and examples devised to clarify the matter. Third, throughout the work there is no explicit mention of the pope himself, but only of matters read in Nestorius’s first, second, and third sermons against the rule of faith, although this question deserved treatment on account of either its subtlety or its necessity. Yet it arose from Proclus’s homily, which Nestorius criticized with particular harshness; and nothing concerning that homily could have been brought to Alexandria before the time thus determined.

The question of the translator is somewhat more difficult. Whoever he was, he must have written in the fifth century, indeed during Cyril’s lifetime, since from this very version—as it now exists—Leo the Great, immediately after Cyril’s death, as though from a commonly available text, as well as the Council of Chalcedon and Facundus of Hermiane, extracted the passages they cite in the places mentioned above. Someone might reasonably believe that this work should be attributed to one of those Alexandrians whose Latin Cyril excused to the holy Coelestine when he sent papers translated by them. Yet it seems more plausible to identify the translator as Marius Mercator, a man otherwise well versed in better Latin. The work is found among his works in both manuscript codices that we used; he lived in the period when it was written; moved by zeal for the faith, he rendered into Latin what the Greek defenders of the faith wrote; and in his preface to the sermons of Nestorius he declared that, in translating the works of Nestorius and Cyril, he had disregarded the rules of Latin style.

> “In these works,” he says, “as translator I have attempted, as far as possible, to render word for word, lest I should be proved a falsifier first rather than a true interpreter later. Therefore, pious reader, grant pardon if either the speech is less polished or the novelty of words used anywhere should perhaps strike your ear. I have chosen to expose myself more to the tongues of detractors than to depart farther from expressing the truth of the meanings, where every danger of falsification lies.”

We had to expend no small labor in correcting so ancient a translation, which had accordingly been corrupted by copyists, as commonly happens. Manuscript codices and printed books were indeed helpful. But since there is one version shared by all, and since it has been corrupted no less by scribes than neglected by the translator, whenever the Greek did not illuminate the text—and it illuminated it only rarely—we had to conjecture and restore, as best we could, the words the translator had used. For we regarded it as a matter of conscience to change nothing; nor, even if it had been permissible from another source, could we have done so, since the Greek text is lacking in many places. The Greek text we possess is drawn either from Theodoret, the Council of Chalcedon, or the Royal Library.

This distinguished work now appears, praised most highly by the holy Fathers, not only more accurately corrected—which is certainly no small matter—but also almost one quarter fuller than it is found either among the editors of Cyril’s works or among the collectors of the councils. We shall indicate what is missing from the commonly circulated books wherever necessary.

The commonly circulated codices contain twenty-eight chapters of the whole work; the Marianus manuscript contains thirty-five; Photius counts only nineteen, having reduced to this number all the material that others separate, though not, to be sure, for the best reason. It is worthwhile to transcribe Photius’s words:

> “Another book was likewise read, entitled *Scholion on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten*. It explains approximately the following: what Christ is; how Emmanuel is to be understood; what Jesus Christ is; in what sense the Word of God is called man; in what sense the Word of God is said to have emptied himself; how Christ is likewise one; how Emmanuel is also one; what we call the emptying. It also treats the fiery coal seen by Isaiah, and ten other chapters related to these matters. This book can be of very great benefit to its readers.”

Facundus of Hermiane may appear to have found a different division in the codex he used. For what Photius identifies as chapter eight, Facundus himself calls chapter seven; and what Photius places as chapter eleven, Facundus calls chapter ten. He writes as follows:

> “Cyril, in the book he called *Scholia*, in the seventh title, [asks] what we call the union; ‘the soul,’ he says, ‘all the things that belong to the body,’ etc.” (Book XI, chapter 7).

And afterward:

> “Let us again observe what he said in the same book, in the tenth title, or what the title alone presents at first sight; for he promised that he would demonstrate this in it, saying” (ibid.) “that, even when the Word of God had been truly united to humanity, the substances nevertheless remained unconfused. And to prove this he added the following: ‘The holy tabernacle was erected through the desert according to God’s will,’ etc.”

Although an error could easily have crept into both places, if, as is credible, the number was written in Roman letters as VII and XI, for careless copyists could easily have removed the third stroke in one place and added it in the other, I think Facundus’s reading should be corrected and Photius’s retained, with the two chapters concerning the coal or the lily nevertheless combined into one. These examples serve equally to prove the point proposed in the title.

It is also reasonable to believe that each chapter originally had its own title indicating the subject to be treated. It is not equally likely that what is found in the published books was the original arrangement, namely that individual chapters were assigned, awkwardly and without method (*ἄμεθοδος*), to individual testimonies or examples. Mercator’s codex was unable to provide any assistance in confirming either view, since it has titles without any numbers.

Therefore, although the division of the chapters that has become customary must be carefully preserved, it nevertheless seemed worthwhile to place the numbers of Photius’s individual chapters alongside those of the commonly circulated version and, by presenting here the titles of the individual chapters from Mercator, to display the whole work in synopsis.

### Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten

Chapter I. What Christ is.  
Chapter II. How Emmanuel should be understood.  
Chapter III. What Jesus is.  
Chapter IV. Why the Word of God was called man.  
Chapter V. Why the Word of God is said to have emptied himself.  
Chapter VI. How Christ is one.  
Chapter VII. How Emmanuel is one.  
Chapter VIII. What we call the union.  
Chapter IX. That the flesh itself, possessing a rational soul, became the body of the incorporeal Godhead; and that, if we attempt to separate these from one another, we shall unquestionably undermine the dispensation understood in Christ.  
Chapter X. That, when the Word of God was united to true humanity, the substances nevertheless remained unconfused.  
Chapter XI. That, although the Word of God was God, he became man; and that he was not, as some think, simply a man honored by a bare conjunction and called to the equal dignity or authority of the Word of God.  
Chapter XII. That Christ Jesus, made man, is called God the Word.  
Chapter XIII. That Christ is not a man who bears God (*Θεοφόρος*), nor did the Word of God simply dwell in a man; rather, according to the Scriptures, he became flesh, or a perfect man.  
Chapter XIV. Apostolic statements in which Christ is called God.  
Chapter XV. How one must understand “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us”; how the Word, who is God, is sent; and how the body is called his own.  
Chapter XVI. How the holy Virgin is understood as *Θεοτόκος*, “Mother of God.”  
Chapter XVII. That the Only-Begotten, appearing as both God and man, is called God and man.  
Chapter XVIII. On Christ’s passion, and its usefulness; that the same person is spoken of in different respects, and that we do not divide him into two.  
Chapter XIX. Against those who say that the human things befit the Word of God by relation alone.

Although the Marianus codex supplies five chapters, and those lengthy ones, that are commonly missing, I scarcely dare guarantee that the work is even now published in its entirety, if Anastasius of Sinai is to be trusted. For he cites a passage concerning the coin found in the fish’s mouth, which is not found in the *Scholia* as they now exist. Yet I strongly suspect that Anastasius, having lapsed in memory, assigned the title *Scholia* to another work. This suspicion seems all the more probable because he testified that he composed his book, the *ὁνὴγου* [reading uncertain], more from recollection than from reading of authors, and therefore warns the reader to verify or even restore the testimonies.

On the occasion of the *Scholia*, from which Theodoret brought three testimonies in the second dialogue of the *Eranistes*, I cannot omit what I have conjectured about the testimonies appended to the letter of Saint Leo at the Council of Chalcedon. Namely, I conjecture that they were added by Theodoret, since they are all found in exactly the same words in the dialogue I mentioned, while nowhere in the whole letter is there either mention or promise that such testimonies would be brought forward. Add that Facundus says Theodoret asserted the letter of Leo against the Palestinians and Illyrians who protested against it, bringing forward, as the acts of the Council of Chalcedon have it, the testimony that appears among those appended. But there would have been no need to bring it forward if it had already been appended to the letter; it would certainly have been read at the same time, together with any others that existed then. Moreover, it is evident that the letter was translated into Greek either by Theodoret or at least by those who supported Theodoret’s party—and was even corrupted by the translators, a matter about which Leo himself complains to the emperor Marcian. Furthermore, in the letter the pope sets out several articles of faith, not only against Eutyches but also against Nestorius; yet no testimonies are appended except those useful for asserting the distinction of the natures, which had been used in the dialogue called *Inconfusus* to refute those suspected by Theodoret of Apollinarianism. No testimonies are brought from the books written against Nestorius, although they are also read in the dialogue cited.

The value of this little work may be estimated especially from the fact that scarcely any later writer who wished to use Cyril’s authority in explaining the mystery of the Incarnation failed to draw some testimony from the *Scholia*. Add that Cyril himself may appear to have commended this work when he wrote to Eulogius:

> “The same book,” he says, “contains toward the end certain brief explanations of Christ’s dispensation, very beautiful and useful.”

The explanations he mentions must differ neither from the *Scholia*, nor from the subsequent treatise *On the Incarnation of the Word*, nor from the dialogue appended to it; for Cyril wrote nothing else about which there could be doubt. Yet the work certainly differs from the subsequent treatise, which is in fact a single sermon; and it also differs from the dialogue just mentioned. Who would call a dialogue by the proper name *ἔκθεσις*, “exposition”? Nevertheless, the dialogue could have been appended to the *Scholia* as a kind of epitome or *ὑπόμνημα*, “memorandum.”

The precision of its method is clear from its sequence. Cyril begins with the interpretation of simple terms, explaining what Christ is, what Emmanuel is, what Jesus is, what “one” is, and what “union” is. He then turns his discourse to the propositions commonly used in this subject and explains how Christ is one, how Emmanuel is one, and how Jesus is one—that is, one Lord, and so forth. Then he explains how the Word is said to have emptied himself, to have been united to flesh, to have become man, and yet not to have been changed or deprived of his Godhead. From this he proceeds to show how Christ is not a man who bears God (*θεοφόρος*), or one inspired by a divine power, but truly God-man; then how the Word is said to dwell among us, to be sent to us, and to possess a body of his own; and how the holy Virgin is understood as *Θεοτόκος*. Finally, he explains how the Only-Begotten, appearing visibly in the flesh, is called God and man, how he suffered, and refutes those who think that human attributes befit God in no other way than by mere relation. As I have already noted, nearly every chapter is filled with distinctions useful for warding off the objections of the heterodox.

Before I conclude this preface, I think it should be noted that Eutherius, whose work circulates under the name of Athanasius, wrote nearly all his twenty sermons against this book—if not exclusively, at least chiefly. For the propositions he attacks in bitter language are found almost all at length in Cyril’s *Scholia*. We shall demonstrate this in the supplement to Theodoret that we are shortly to publish. We shall join Eutherius to Theodoret both because of the kinship of their subject matter and because of the identity of their faith (*ταυτότητα*).

# CHAPTER ONE. What Christ Is

[Col. 1005A]

The name “Christ” possesses neither the force of a definition nor the meaning of a substance of a particular kind, as, for example, “man,” “horse,” or “ox” might; rather, it signifies something enacted in someone. For certain people of earlier times were anointed with oil, according to what pleased God at that time, and anointing was a sign of kingship for them. Prophets too were invisibly anointed by the Holy Spirit, and for this reason they were also called “christs,” that is, anointed ones. Finally, blessed David sings in the person of God and says: “Do not touch my christs, and do not act wickedly against my prophets” (Psalm 104:15). The prophet Habakkuk also says: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your christs” (Habakkuk 3:13, according to the Septuagint).

[Col. 1005B] In Christ, the Savior of all, we say that an anointing took place; but it was neither symbolic, as one performed with oil, nor like the anointing involved in prophetic grace. Nor was it the kind that is understood to take place for the completion of some such task, as we say occurred in Cyrus, king of the Persians [Col. 1006A] and Medes. He led an army against the Babylonians, God Almighty impelling him to do so. For it is said: “Thus says the Lord to my anointed, Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped” (Isaiah 45:1). Although that man was a worshiper of idols, he was called “anointed” because, as though anointed for kingship, he was appointed by heavenly approval and ordained by God to overthrow Babylon with great force.

But the following applies more properly to Christ. Because sin had reigned over all on account of Adam’s transgression (Romans 5:14), and the spirit had departed from humanity (Genesis 6:3), and for this reason humanity was involved in every evil, it was necessary that, restored once more through God’s mercy to its former state, it should become worthy of the Spirit. The only-begotten Word of God became man and appeared among earthly beings with an earthly body. [Col. 1006B] He was also free from sin, so that in him, and in him alone, human nature, crowned with the praises of innocence, might be enriched with the Holy Spirit and thus be restored to God through sanctification. For the grace begun by Christ, who is [Baluz. adds “in”] our firstborn, also passes to us. Teaching us this, blessed [Col. 1007A] David sings to the Son: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Psalm 44:8).

The Son was therefore anointed after our example with the praises of innocence; and, as I said earlier, in him human nature was illumined and made worthy to receive the Holy Spirit, which would no longer depart from it as before but would rather remain in it. Hence it is written that the Spirit descended upon him and remained upon him (John 1:32). The Word of God is therefore called Christ because, for our sake and in our likeness, he became man and took the form of a servant. He is anointed humanly, according to the flesh; but he anoints divinely, with his own Spirit, those who believe in him.

# CHAPTER TWO. How Emmanuel Should Be Understood

[Col. 1007B]

The Word of God is called Emmanuel because he took hold of Abraham’s seed and likewise shared in flesh and blood with us (Hebrews 2:14). Emmanuel is interpreted as “God with us.” We confess that the Word of God was with us, not locally—for in what place is God not present, since he fills all things? Nor was he with us merely in the sense of appearing to be present for the sake of assistance. For it was said in this way to Jesus the son of Nave [Baluz. omits “the son of Nave”]: “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you” (Joshua 1:5). Rather, he became present in what belongs to us, that is, in humanity, without abandoning his own nature; for the nature of the Word of God is immutable.

[Col. 1007C] But why, when it is plainly said to Jesus the son of Nave [Baluz. omits “the son of Nave”], “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you” (ibid.), was he nevertheless not called Emmanuel? The reason is this: although he is said to have been with one of the saints, we do not say that the Word of God became “with us” except at the time when, according to what Baruch says, he appeared on earth and lived among human beings, finding the whole way of knowledge and giving it to Jacob his servant and to Israel beloved by him: “He is our God, and no other will be compared with him” (Baruch 3:38).

As far as the nature of God is concerned, he was not yet with us, for there is a great distinction between Godhead and humanity, and the difference between the natures is exceedingly great.

[Col. 1007D] Therefore divine David, in a mystical reference to proximity [Alternative: “the closest union”], called the Word of God, who had not yet come to us, saying in the Spirit: “Why, O Lord, have you departed far away?” (Psalm 10:1). [Note: [Col. 1007] Baluz.: “He departed, yet was with us; who, etc.” EDIT.] Therefore he no longer departed, but was with us: while remaining what he was, he took hold of Abraham’s seed, as I said; he also took the form of a servant and appeared as a man on earth.

“Christ” and “Emmanuel” both designate for us the same Son, partly because he was anointed according to our custom, receiving the Spirit as a human being [Col. 1008A] according to human nature, so that in himself and as the first [Alternative: “with human nature receiving the Spirit in him, so that he might be first”] he was established as the beginning of the race, while himself again, as God, anointing with the Holy Spirit those who believe in him; and partly because he was with us for the reasons I have just given. The prophet Isaiah makes us certain of this concerning him, saying: “Behold, the Virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name will be called Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7:14). When the holy Virgin became pregnant by the Holy Spirit and gave birth to a son according to the flesh, he was then also called Emmanuel: he was with us, the incorporeal one, through carnal birth. This is what was signified by David’s voice: “God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent” (Psalm 49:3); and, I think, by this statement: “I who speak am present.” Having spoken through the prophets while still the incorporeal Word, he also came bodily.

# CHAPTER THREE. What Jesus Is

In terms of the intentions by which we ought to call the Son of God one, Christ, Emmanuel, and Jesus signify the same thing; and the name was formed from the reality itself. “For he,” it says, “will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Just as Emmanuel signified that the Word of God became with us through birth from a woman, and Christ signifies that, having become man, he is called anointed according to us in a human manner, so also Jesus signifies that he saved us, his people. This most clearly demonstrates that he is truly and by nature Lord of all [Col. 1008C]. Let no one say that he is the creation of an ordinary man; rather, it is more fitting to say that everything belongs to the Only-Begotten, even though he became man.

Someone might say: “But Israel was called the people of Moses.” We answer that they were indeed called the people of God, and this was true. But since they were led into apostasy and made a calf in the wilderness, they were dishonored by God. He no longer deigned to call them his people, but assigned them to a man. This is not so with us: we are his own children, because he is God and all things were created through him. Thus David says: “For he made us, and not we ourselves; but we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture” (Psalm 49:7). Finally, he himself also said concerning us: “My sheep hear my voice, and they follow me” [Col. 1008D] (John 10:27). And again: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must gather them also, and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (ibid. 10:16). He also commanded blessed Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my lambs; feed my sheep” (John 21:17).

# CHAPTER FOUR. Why the Word of God Was Called Man

He was called man, although by nature he is God, the Word of God the Father, because he likewise shared in blood and flesh with us (Hebrews 2:14). [Col. 1009A] Thus he appeared among earthly beings, [Note: [Col. 1009D] Baluz.: “Without abandoning the nature of humanity, perfect in its own account.” EDIT.] not abandoning what he was, but assuming the nature of humanity, perfect in its own account. Nevertheless, he remained God in his humanity and Lord of all, since by nature and in truth he was born from God the Father [Baluz. “from God and the Father”]. The most wise Paul demonstrates this to us most clearly: “The first man,” he says, “was from the earth, made of dust; the second from heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:47).

The holy Virgin gave birth to a temple united to the Word; yet he is said to be from heaven, and rightly so, Emmanuel. For his Word was born from above, from the substance of God the Father; he descended to us when he became man, yet even so he is from above. John testified concerning him, saying: “He who comes from above is above all” (John 3:31). Christ himself also said to the Jewish people: “You are from below; I am from above” (John 8:23). And again: “I am not from this world” (John 14:16), although, as a man, he was called a part of the world; nevertheless, as God, he was also above the world. For we clearly remember him saying: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man” (John 3:13). We say that the Son of Man descended from heaven through the unity of the dispensation, the Word granting his own flesh the glory and splendor of his divine majesty.

# CHAPTER FIVE. Why the Word of God Is Said to Have Emptied Himself

The Word of God is full by nature and perfect in every respect, distributing from his fullness his good things to creation, as he says: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Isaiah 44:3). We say that he emptied himself without anything in his own nature being violated, without being changed so as to become otherwise, and without becoming inferior in any respect. For he himself is immutable and unchangeable, just as is his begetter, [Note: [Col. 1009D] Baluz.: “and never will he ever become capable of suffering.” [Col. 1010D] EDIT.] and he was never capable of any suffering. When he became flesh, that is, man, he made the poverty of humanity his own. First, because he became man once for all, although he remained God; and second, because he took the form of a servant, although according to his own nature he is free, since he is the Son. Thus, although he is himself the Lord of glory, he is said to receive glory; although he himself is life, he is said to be given life; and he receives authority over all, although he himself is king of all; and although he is equal to God the Father, he became obedient, suffering the cross, and so forth. Although these things correspond to the measure of humanity, he nevertheless regards them as belonging familiarly to the flesh and fulfills the dispensation while remaining what he was.

# CHAPTER SIX. How Christ Is One [Baluz. omits “is”]

The divine Paul writes: “Although there are many gods and many lords in heaven and on earth, yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we are from him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we are through him” (1 Corinthians 8:5). But the most wise John said of the Word of God that “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). The blessed Gabriel proclaimed to the holy Virgin, saying: “Behold, you will conceive in the womb and bear a Son, and you will call his name Jesus” (Matthew 1:26). Since divine Paul recalls that all things were made through Christ Jesus, and confirms the force of his statement by proclaiming God to be the maker of all things, the divine Evangelist speaks truly; and since the angel’s voice also indicates that Jesus Christ was truly born from the holy Virgin, we do not understand the Word of God without humanity. Rather, we say that one resulted from both: God made man, the same one born divinely from the Father as the Word, and humanly from a woman as man—not as though he were called at that time into existence as a second beginning of substance when he is said to have been born according to the flesh, but as one born before all the ages who, when the appointed time for fulfilling the dispensation arrived, was also born from a woman according to the flesh. [Therefore, although others were called “christs” by a similar designation, there is one through whom all things exist, Jesus Christ—not because he became the maker of all things as man,] but because the Word of God, through whom all things were made, likewise shared in flesh and blood with us (Hebrews 2:14) and was called man, without losing what he was. Thus he is rightly understood to be the maker of all things even in the flesh.

# CHAPTER SEVEN. How Emmanuel Is One
[Col. 1010C] [Baluz. adds: “Once”] In the last ages God the Word is said to have become man [Baluz. reads: “the Word of God is said to have been made man”], and, as the divine Paul says, he was manifested through his sacrifice (Heb. IX, 27). And what sacrifice was it? He offered his own body for us to God and the Father as a fragrant offering, and entered once for all into the holy place, not by the blood of goats or bulls, but by his own blood. For in this way he obtained eternal forgiveness for those who believe in him (Eph. V, 2; Heb. IX, 13).

Therefore, many saints existed before him; but none of them was called Emmanuel. Why was this? The time had not yet come when he who is superior to every creature was to be with us—that is, was to come into our nature through the flesh. There is therefore one Emmanuel, for the Only-Begotten became man only once, when he underwent carnal birth through the holy Virgin. For it was also said to Jesus son of Nave [Baluz. omits “son of Nave”]: “I shall be with you” (Josh. I, 5). Yet he was not Emmanuel. He was also with Moses, but neither was he called Emmanuel. Accordingly, whenever we hear that the name “God with us” was given to the Son, let us understand it wisely: he was not with us in the last times in the same way in which he is sometimes said to have been with the saints. For he was merely their helper; but he was with us—that is, he became one of us—without losing his own nature, since, as God, he is unchangeable.

## CHAPTER VIII. What We Understand the Union to Be

[Note: [Col. 1011D] Autbert wished to emend Mercator’s version from the Greek.] Union is accomplished in many ways. Some who are separated in feeling or will and are at variance with one another are said to be united through social reconciliation, when hostility has been laid aside. We also call things united when they are glued together, or joined in other ways, whether through composition, mixture, or blending.

Whenever, then, we say that God the Word has been united to our nature, the manner of his union seems to surpass every human conception of union. For that mysterious union—entirely unknown except to him who knows all things—was not accomplished through the methods written above [Col. 1011B].

Nor is it surprising that we are overcome in such an inquiry, since, when investigating how our own things are constituted, we acknowledge that they surpass the discovery of our minds. In what manner, for example, do we suppose that the human soul is united to its body? Who can express it? But if those who scarcely understand small matters—or rather, even those who are capable of understanding them—must conjecture such subtle things, which transcend every account, we say that it is fitting to conceive the union of Emmanuel as resembling the union that one understands the human soul to have with its body, although the explanation falls short of the truth.

[Note: [Col. 1011D] Facundus, Book XI, chapter 7, reports this passage in nearly the same words.] For the soul considers all that belongs to the body to be its own, although by its proper nature it is free from [Note: [Col. 1011D] Facundus: “the body’s passions, both natural and those that occur externally,” which is better. BALUZ.] the body’s passions, both natural and those that come from outside. The body is moved toward natural desires, and the soul consents; although in no way itself participating in the desire, it nevertheless regards the fulfillment of the desire as its own pleasure. And if the body should happen to be struck with a sword or subjected to torture, the soul suffers with it because its own body is suffering; yet it itself, in its own nature, undergoes no torment at all.

Nevertheless, we also say that the union accomplished in Emmanuel is of this kind. For it was necessary that the soul united to his body should grieve with it [Note: [Col. 1012D] Facundus: “in order that, through fear, he might submit his neck to God.” BALUZ.], so that, while he feared the passions, he might submit his neck to God.

But concerning God the Word, it is impious to say that he suffered with the passions. God is impassible and utterly unlike our condition. Yet he was united to flesh possessing a rational soul; while that flesh suffered, he himself remained impassible, but as God he knew what happened to the soul and, as God, he subdued the infirmities of the flesh. Nevertheless, he regarded them as his own, since they belonged to his body. Thus he is said to have hungered, to have been wearied, and to have suffered for us.

Therefore, the union of the Word with humanity may not irrationally be compared with our own condition [Col. 1012A]. For just as the body is of a different nature from the soul, yet one human being is made and called from both, so also from the perfect subsistence of God the Word [Baluz. reads: “substance”] and perfect humanity there is one Christ, the same being God and man simultaneously in one and the same person. And God the Word, as I said before, regards as his own those things proper to the flesh, because the body is his, not another’s. He makes the operations of his divine majesty common with his flesh as with his own, so that he can also give life to the dead and heal the sick.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the Coal

[Note: [Col. 1012D] Here again Autbert interpolated Mercator’s version, as he did in the following passages, for which he had the Greek text.] But if it is appropriate to demonstrate the union also by examples from divine Scripture, as it were through a figure, come, let us speak as we are able [Col. 1012B].

Blessed Isaiah says: “One of the Seraphim was sent to me, and he had a coal in his hand, which he had taken from the altar with tongs. He came to me, touched my lips, and said to me: ‘Behold, this has touched your lips, and it will take away your iniquities and cleanse your sins’” (Isa. VI, 6).

We say that the coal presents to us a figure and image of the Word made man. If it touches our lips—that is, if we confess faith in him—then he makes us pure from every sin and frees us from our former offenses.

Moreover, in the image represented by the coal, one may see God the Word united to humanity, yet not having cast off what he was. Rather, he transformed the nature he assumed into his own glory and operation. For just as fire attached to wood and penetrating it takes hold of it, and, although the wood does not cease to be wood, changes its power and appearance, pours itself wholly into the wood, and is now regarded together with it as something almost one, so understand this of Christ.

God was ineffably united to humanity: he preserved it as what it was, and he himself remained what he was. Yet, once united, he is regarded as one with it, making its properties his own, while also imparting to it the operation of his own nature.

## CHAPTER X. That the Flesh Itself, Possessing a Rational Soul, Became the Body of the Incorporeal Divinity; and that, if We Wish to Separate These from One Another, We Will Certainly Undermine the Dispensation Understood in Christ

[Col. 1012D] In the Song of Songs our Lord Jesus Christ himself is introduced as saying: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II, 1).

Just as a fragrance is an incorporeal reality but has, as it were, a body of its own in that in which it exists, so the lily is understood as one thing made from both. Its account as one thing would be destroyed by the separation of either part, for the fragrance exists in the underlying body.

So also in Christ we understand the nature of divinity, which spreads its surpassing majesty throughout the world like a most sweet fragrance, to exist in the body of humanity as in an underlying substance. And that which is incorporeal by nature may, through the economic union, almost be said to have become corporeal, because he wished to make himself known through the body; for in it he performed divine signs. Thus that which is incorporeal may be understood as existing in its own body, just as fragrance exists in the flower that bears it. Yet the lily is now called both fragrance and flower.

## CHAPTER XI. That, Although God the Word Was United to True Humanity, the Substances [That Is, Subsistences] Remained Unconfused

[Note: [Col. 1013D] Facundus also cites this passage from this version in the same place.] The holy tabernacle was erected through the desert according to God’s will, and in it Emmanuel was represented in many ways [Col. 1013B].

Almighty God said to the divine Moses: “You shall make for me an ark of testimony from incorruptible wood, two and a half cubits long; and you shall overlay it with pure gold; inside and outside you shall overlay it” (Exod. XXV, 10).

The wood, since it is incorruptible, is a figure of the incorruptible body, for cedar is incorruptible. Gold, however, as a material more precious than others, indicates to us the majesty of the divine substance.

Observe, then, that the whole ark was overlaid with pure gold, outside and inside. God the Word had been united to the holy flesh, and this, I think, is what it means for the ark to have been overlaid with gold on the outside. That he also made the rational soul inhabiting the body his own is shown by the command that the inside of the ark likewise be overlaid with gold.

[Note: [Col. 1013D] Facundus also cites this passage from the same version in the same place. Leontius of Byzantium also cites it at the end of Book I Against the Eutychians.] The fact that the natures, or substances, remained unconfused we know from this: the gold laid upon the wood remained what it was, and the wood was adorned with the beauty of gold; nevertheless, it did not cease to be wood. That the ark is understood as an image of Christ can be demonstrated by many proofs.]

For it went before those who were of Israel, seeking rest for them. Christ also says somewhere: “I will go and prepare a place for you” (John XIV, 3).

## CHAPTER XII. That, Although He Was God the Word, He Became Man; and That Man Was Not Simply Honored by a Bare Conjunction and Called to the Equal Dignity or Authority of God the Word, as Some Think

[Col. 1013D] The divine Paul says that the mystery of godliness is great (I Tim. III, 16). And so it truly is: he was manifested in the flesh, although he is God the Word, and he was justified in the Spirit. He was in no way confined by our infirmities, although he became man like us, for he committed no sin. “He appeared” [Col. 1014A] also to the angels. For they were not ignorant of his birth according to the flesh. “He was proclaimed also among the Gentiles,” as God made man; “he was believed on in the world.”

The divine Paul proved this when he wrote: “Therefore remember that formerly you Gentiles in the flesh, who are called uncircumcision by what is called circumcision in the flesh made by hands, were at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope of the promise and without God in this world” (Eph. II, 11).

The Gentiles were therefore in the world without God, since they were without Christ. But once they recognized that he was truly and by nature God, they too were recognized by him, confessing the faith; and he was received into glory—certainly divine glory. For blessed David sings: “God has ascended with a shout of triumph” (Ps. XLVI, 6). He certainly ascended with the body, and not in bare divinity, for God had become incarnate [Col. 1014B].

We therefore believe not in a man like us who was honored by grace with divinity, lest we be exposed as worshipers of a man, but rather in the Lord, who appeared in the form of a servant, who truly became like us, yet remained God in his humanity. For God the Word, having assumed flesh, did not lay aside what he was; nevertheless, the same one is understood to be both God and man.

This, then, is the rule of faith, and rightly so. But if someone should say, “What harm is there if a man like us is understood to have grasped divinity, rather than God’s becoming man?” we shall answer that a thousand considerations can be opposed to the contrary view, even, as it were, signaling with a nod that we must steadfastly resist it and not believe it to be so.

Let us begin with what comes first. Let us examine the manner of the dispensation accomplished with the flesh and investigate more closely the nature of our condition. Human nature had been endangered and found [Baluz. [Note: [Col. 1013D] So the old edition of Cyril’s Scholia and the Vatican codex. Bellovacensis has “deprehensa.” The Vatican reading is confirmed by the following passages from the objections of the Orientals against Cyril’s anathemas above, p. 267 (Cyril, Apology for Anathema 12, Response to the Heretics): “How he who permits the flesh to be briefly brought low by death,” etc.; and p. 268 (ibid.): “so that in himself he might bring low him who is impassible by nature.” Likewise in Cyril’s eighth scholion, p. 379: “And if it should happen to be brought low or tortured through its own body.” BALUZ.] brought low] under the extremity of evils. It had been condemned by the curse and by death, entangled in the snares of sin, wandering and existing in darkness. It did not know God, who is God by nature and in truth; instead of the Creator [Baluz. “instead of the Creator”], it worshiped the creature.

How, then, could it be freed from such evils? Shall we say that it was possible for humanity to grasp the divine nature, although it had no knowledge at all of what the dignity of the heavenly nature was, being overwhelmed by the darkness of ignorance and polluted by the filth of sin? How could it grasp the holy nature and receive a glory that no one can find unless he has received it? Let us grant that it perhaps understood [Baluz. “merely”] and knew how to grasp God [that is, divinity]. Who taught it? “How will they believe unless they hear?” (Rom. X, 14). Yet to grasp divinity is not the same as receiving the glory appropriate to it.

It is therefore more fitting, and indeed correct, to think as follows: wishing to save what had perished, God the Word, through whom all things exist, descended to us and entered into what he was not, so that human nature might become what it was not. Through the union it became manifest to the dignities of the divine majesty, and was raised beyond nature rather than bringing the immutable God down below nature.

It was fitting that the incorruptible nature should grasp the corruptible, in order to free it from corruption. It was fitting that he who did not know sin should be conformed to sinners, in order to restrain sins. For just as, wherever light is present, the darkness of night perishes, so, when immortality is present, every form of corruption will certainly flee away. And when he who knows no sin is present—he who also made the sinless body his own—every sin will yield.

That the Word, although he was God, became man, and that Christ is not rather understood as a man “deified” (τεθεοποιημένος), I shall also endeavor to demonstrate from the sacred writings.

Blessed Paul says of the Only-Begotten: “Who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II, 7).

Whom, then, shall we say was in the form of God and in equality with the Father, who did not regard this as something to be grasped, but rather descended into self-emptying and into the form of a servant, humbling himself and being made in our likeness?
