If he was merely and solely a man made from a woman, how did he possess the fullness from which he could be understood to have emptied himself? Or from what height is he said to have humbled himself? Or how was he made in the likeness of human beings, when by nature he already was what he was, even though he perhaps would not be said to have been made such? And where was he emptied, if he assumed the fullness of divinity [Col. 1015D]? Or how could he not have been made most high, since he ascended into heavenly glory?

We therefore say that it was not a man who was made God, but rather that God the Word, who existed in equality with the Father and in his form, was made in self-emptying on account of humanity. He was emptied in this manner, because of our likeness, while remaining full as God. He was humbled because of the flesh, yet did not descend from the height of the divine majesty, for he possesses the highest throne. He was made in the likeness of human beings, although he has the same form as the Father, being the one who is the figure of the substance.

But since he once became like us, he is said to have ascended, with the flesh, into the glory of divinity, which he possesses openly as his own, although he was in it in another manner because of his humanity. For he is believed to be Lord of all, even with the flesh [Col. 1016A].

Every knee bows to him, not to the grief or dishonor of the Father, but rather to his glory. The Father rejoices and is glorified when the Son is worshiped by human beings, even though the Son has been made like us.

It is written again: “For he did not take hold of angels, but of the seed of Abraham; therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect” (Heb. II, 16). Behold, God the Word took hold of the seed of Abraham; it was not some unknown man like us who grasped divinity. He himself is made like us and is called our brother [Baluz. omits “our brother”] as man, not insofar as concerns the nature of divinity.

Since the children shared in flesh and blood, he likewise shared in them [Col. 1016B], so that through death he might destroy the one who holds the power of death—that is, the devil—and free those who throughout their lives were held in natural slavery by fear of death (ibid., v. 14).

Here again he himself, just as we do, shared in blood and flesh, and this fact has an immediately connected and proximate cause. For it is written: “What was impossible for the law, in that it was weakened through the flesh, God did: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and because of sin he condemned sin in the flesh” (Rom. VIII, 3).

Observe again that it is not a man striving after the divine nature and ascending to its dignity who is shown, but rather God the Father sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh in order to destroy sin. Therefore, although the Word is God, he entered into self-emptying by becoming man; Christ is not seen as merely a man striving after divine glory.

## CHAPTER XIII. That Christ Jesus Is Called God the Word Made Man

Considering more closely the mystery of the dispensation of the incarnate Only-Begotten, we assert, preserving the true and correct faith, that the very Word of God the Father—true God from true God and light from light—was incarnate, became man, descended, suffered, and rose from the dead. For this is how the great and holy council defined the confession of faith.

As we investigate and wish to discern what it finally means for God the Word to have been incarnate and made man, we see that it does not mean that he assumed a man through a conjunction accomplished by equality of dignity or authority, or merely through the homonymy of sonship (ὁμωνυμία). Rather, he became man like us, without any conversion or change taking place, and at the same time raised up with his own nature the one who, in the assumption of flesh and blood, was present economically [Baluz. “dispensationally”].

There is therefore one who, before the Incarnation, is named by divine Scripture the Only-Begotten, the Word, God, image, light, figure of the Father’s substance, life, glory, radiance, wisdom, power, majesty, Lord of Sabaoth, and by other such names that truly belong to divinity.

After the Incarnation he is called man [Baluz. omits “man”], Christ, Jesus, propitiation, mediator, firstfruits of those who sleep, firstborn from the dead, the second Adam, and head of the body of the Church, although the former names also remain attached to him.

[Note: [Col. 1017D] Baluz. reads: “all things in the last times.” EDIT.] Everything belongs to him, both the former things that are his own and those that were made in the last times.

There is therefore one and the same person: the one who was true God before the Incarnation, and who remained, remains, and will remain what he was in his humanity. The one Lord Jesus Christ must not therefore be divided into one who is separately man and another who is separately God. We say that he is one and the same Jesus Christ, not ignoring the difference of the natures, but preserving them unconfused with one another.

Whenever sacred Scripture says that “the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily in Christ” (Col. II, 9), we do not therefore say that God the Word dwelt in another Christ, in a man considered separately [Col. 1017B]. Nor, by dividing what has been united, do we understand two sons. Rather, we understand that Scripture sometimes names Christ according to one aspect, and that it has placed the humanity of God the Word, which he possesses as his own, in the position of a temple.

It is also written concerning human souls: “Those who dwell in houses of clay, of which we too are made from the same clay” (Job IV, 19).

[Note: [Col. 1017D] Baluz. reads: “It names human bodies and asserts that souls dwell in them,” etc. EDIT.] Since it names human bodies “houses of clay” and asserts that souls dwell in them, shall we divide one human being into two human beings? Indeed, it is not at all unreasonable to say that a man’s own spirit dwells in him.

Therefore, even if speech proceeds through such figures of expression, since it cannot proceed otherwise [Baluz. reads: “which cannot be done otherwise”], the natures of things must not for that reason be corrupted. Rather, they must be preserved according to the sound rule of truth [Col. 1017C].

Whenever things that have different natures are gathered together and appear to be united through composition, and one is then said to dwell in the other, they must not be divided into two, since the agreement of the union is in no way violated [Baluz. “must in no way be violated”], even though we name the things that have been united separately by their own names.

For, as I said before, one’s own spirit is said to dwell in a man, yet a man is not thereby called one thing and his spirit another, nor his body a separate thing. The divine Paul also mentions something of this kind through an indirect signification [that is, obscurely and almost enigmatically], saying: “Even though our outer man is being corrupted, yet the inner man is renewed day by day” (II Cor. IV, 16).

If someone should say that our inner man dwells in the outer man, he would speak truly, yet he would not thereby appear to divide one into two. The prophet Isaiah also says somewhere: “By night my spirit keeps vigil for you, Lord” (Isa. XXVI, 9). Is his spirit said to keep vigil for God as though it were something other than himself? Would that not be utterly absurd? It is therefore necessary to understand the figures of speech, but not to depart from the appropriate meaning. Rather, we must refer the force of the statements to the sense fitting each thing.

[Col. 1018A] Although Jesus is said to advance in age, wisdom, and grace (Luke II, 52), this belongs to the dispensation. For God the Word allowed his humanity to advance in its customary manner, and wished gradually, as it were, to reveal the glory of his divinity and to extend it along with the growth of the body, so that nothing might seem strange and so that such excessive novelty might not frighten certain people. Especially since they were saying things such as: “How does this man know letters, when he has not been taught?” (John VII, 15).

Bodily growth, therefore, and advancement in grace and wisdom belong to the measure of humanity. But we confess God the Word himself to be perfect in his nature, lacking neither growth, nor wisdom, nor grace. For he bestows wisdom, grace, and every good thing upon the creature.

[Col. 1018B] If Jesus is said to have suffered, the suffering belongs to the dispensation; nevertheless, it is rightly said to be his, because his own body suffered, and he who could not suffer was himself in the suffering body. For he is impassible as God. Yet, insofar as it concerned the insolence of his revilers, he would have suffered if he were capable of suffering.

Therefore, since the Only-Begotten became like us, whenever he is called man by divine Scripture, let us attend to the dispensation and confess that he is also God by nature.

## CHAPTER XIV. Examples from Divine Scripture That God the Word, Having Become Man, Remained God: Concerning the Propitiatory

God says somewhere to the priest Moses: “You shall make a propitiatory of pure gold, two and a half cubits in length and one and a half cubits in width. You shall make two adorned golden Cherubim and place them on its two sides. One Cherub shall be on this side and one Cherub on that side of the propitiatory. You shall make two Cherubim on its two sides. The Cherubim shall stretch out their wings above, overshadowing the propitiatory with their wings; their faces shall look toward one another, and they shall look toward the propitiatory” (Exod. XXV, 17).

Let this be a most certain enigma: God the Word remained God even in his humanity, in his glory and majesty, although through the dispensation he became like us. For he became Emmanuel for us as a propitiatory through faith (Rom. III, 25).

The most wise John also confirmed this for us, saying: “My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin; but if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins” (John II, 1).

Paul likewise says: “God set him forth as a propitiatory [Baluz. ‘as a propitiator’] through faith in his blood” (Rom. V, 25).

Observe, moreover, the Cherubim standing around the propitiatory and overshadowing it with their wings, turned toward the propitiatory and almost fixing their eyes upon it at the Lord’s command. For the holy multitude of the heavenly spirits looks only to God’s will and is never satisfied with beholding God.

Thus the prophet Isaiah says that he saw the Son on a lofty and exalted throne, with Seraphim standing around him and serving him as God (Isa. VI, 1).

## CHAPTER XV. Another Example from the Rod of Moses

The divine Moses was once appointed to free Israel from the violence of the Egyptians. But because it was necessary first to teach those who were under the yoke of an unfamiliar slavery that God had already been reconciled to them, he was commanded to perform signs; for a miracle often leads us to faith.

Moses therefore said to almighty God: “But if they do not believe me or listen to my voice, and say, ‘The Lord has not appeared to you,’ what shall I say to them?”

Then the Lord said: “What is that which is in your hand?”

He answered: “A rod.”

And he said to him: “Throw it upon the ground.” It became a serpent, and Moses fled from it.

And the Lord said to Moses: “Stretch out your hand and seize its tail.” He stretched out his hand, seized its tail, and it became a rod in his hand.

And he said to him: “So that they may believe you, because the Lord, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you” (Exod. IV, 1).

Observe in these things the Son of God in nature and in truth, as though he were a kind of rod of the Father. The rod is a sign of kingship, and the Father gave the Son authority over all things (John XVII, 2). Hence the divine David also says: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, and the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. XLIV, 7).

But he threw it upon the ground—that is, he surrounded it with an earthly body, or sent it into the earth through humanity. At that point he was made in the likeness of wicked human beings, since the serpent is a sign of wickedness.

That this is true we know from the following [Baluz. “you will know”]. Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, in image and figure, because of the dispensation accomplished with the flesh, is represented by the bronze serpent that Moses raised to ward off the serpents’ bites (Num. XXI, 8).

For he says: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John III, 14).

Just as the serpent made of bronze became a cause of salvation for those in danger—for they were healed when they looked upon it—so also the Lord Jesus Christ will be a cause of life for those who see him indeed in the likeness of the wicked, because he became man, yet do not fail to recognize that he is the life-giving God. He gives them the power to avoid poisonous creatures, that is, hostile powers [Col. 1019D].

This too may be a figure of the matter: Moses’ rod devoured the other rods that the magicians had thrown upon the ground (Exod. IV, 2).

The rod was therefore thrown upon the ground, but it did not remain a serpent forever [Baluz. “it did not always remain a serpent”]. When it was taken up again, it became what it had been. For although, as I said, the rod of the Father—the Son, through whom he has authority over all things—was made in our likeness, nevertheless, when the dispensation had been fulfilled, he flew back into heaven and was again as the rod of uprightness and of the kingdom in the Father’s hand.

For he sits at the right hand of his begetter in his own majesty, occupying the highest throne, even with the flesh (Ps. XLIV, 7).

## CHAPTER XVI. Another Example from Moses’ Leprous Hand, Which Was Completely Healed

The Lord God said to him again: “Put your hand into your bosom.” He put his hand into his bosom, and when he brought it out, his hand had become like snow. And he said again: “Put your hand into your bosom.” He put his hand into his bosom, brought it out, and it was restored again to the color of his flesh (Exod. IV, 6).

Divine Scripture names the true Son of God the hand at the right hand of God the Father. For it introduces him as saying: “With my hand I established the heavens” (Isa. XLVIII, 13). The divine David also sings: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. XXXII, 6).

Observe, then, that while Moses’ hand was still hidden in his bosom, it had not yet become leprous; but once it was brought out, it immediately became leprous. Then it was put back at once, brought out again, and thereafter was no longer leprous. For he says: “It was restored to the color of his flesh.”

Therefore, as long as God the Word was in the bosom of the Father, he shone with the splendor of divinity. But when, in some manner, he went outside through incarnation or enfleshment (ἐνανθρώπησις), he was made in the likeness of sinful flesh and was reckoned among the transgressors (Rom. VIII, 3; Isa. LIII, 12).

The divine Paul says that he who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him (I Cor. V, 21). I think this signifies leprosy, for according to the law the leper is unclean [Col. 1020C] (Lev. XIII, 2).

But since he was again in the bosom of the Father—having been taken up in the resurrection from the dead—the hand appeared clean when brought out again. For our Lord Jesus Christ will come after the appointed times in the purity of divinity and glory, although he will not cast off our likeness.

Blessed Paul says of Christ: “Because he died once for the taking away of the sins of many, he will appear a second time, without sin, to those who await him for salvation” (Heb. IX, 28).

Therefore, whenever sacred Scripture names Christ Jesus for us, do not suppose that he is a man considered separately, with God the Word not truly united to him. Rather, understand that Jesus Christ is the Word from God the Father, even though he became man.

## CHAPTER XVII. That Christ Was Not a Man Bearing God (θεοφόρος), Nor Did God the Word Simply Dwell in a Man, but That He Rather Became Flesh, or a Perfect Man, According to the Scriptures

[Col. 1020D] Those who possess an undefiled faith in Christ, confirmed by every sound affirmation, should say that he himself, God the Word from God the Father, descended into self-emptying, taking the form of a servant and making his own the body born from the virgin; that he became like us and was called the Son of man.

He is God according to the Spirit, but the same person is man according to the flesh.

Then the divine Paul addressed the people of the Jews, saying: “In many parts and in many ways, God formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in his Son” (Heb. I, 1).

And how are we to understand that God the Father spoke in the Son in these last days? He spoke in earlier times through him when he gave the law, and for this reason the Son says that the words spoken through the most wise Moses are his own [Baluz. omits “spoken through the most wise Moses”].

For he says: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets. I have not come to abolish but to fulfill. For I say to you: not one iota or one stroke will pass from the law until all things come to pass. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. V, 17).

Add also the prophet’s voice: “I am present—the one who was speaking” (Isa. LII, 8).

Therefore, when the Son was made flesh, the Father spoke to us in him, as blessed Paul says, in these last days (Heb. I, 1). But lest we believe too little that he is the one who was also the Son before the ages, Paul immediately adds: “Through whom he also made the ages” (ibid., v. 2), declaring him also to be the radiance of glory and the figure of the Father’s substance.

The one through whom God the Father made the ages therefore truly became man. He was not, as some think, present in a man, so that we should understand him as a man who had God dwelling within him.

For if they truly believe that these things are so, the blessed evangelist John will appear to have spoken unnecessarily when he says: “And the Word became flesh” (John I, 14). Where, then, is the necessity of enfleshment (ἐνανθρώπησις)? Or why does he say that God the Word became incarnate, if he did not become flesh?

The force of enfleshment signifies that he became like us, yet remained even so above us—indeed, above the whole of creation itself [Col. 1021C].

I think, however, that what I have said ought also to be confirmed and demonstrated by examples: namely, that the Only-Begotten became man and is God even with the flesh, and did not merely dwell in a man, thereby making him a God-bearer (θεοφόρος), as though there were others who had shared in his divinity.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That Emmanuel had God dwelling in him in a manner different from ours

God says somewhere concerning us: “I will dwell in them, and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Apoc. III, 20). Our Lord Jesus Christ himself likewise says: “Behold, I am coming; and if anyone opens to me, I will enter, and I will dine with him, and the Father and I will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 16). We are also called the temple of God: “For you are,” he says, “the temples of the living God” (I Cor. III, 17). And again: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God?” (I Cor. VI, 19).

But if they say that Emmanuel likewise had God dwelling in him, and that, like each one of us, he had God dwelling within him, let them openly confess this. When they see him being worshiped by us and by angels, equally in heaven and on earth, let them be ashamed, as people who hold opinions that are different and alien, and who do not understand the intention of the sacred writings, nor possess within themselves the faith handed down to us by those who, from the beginning, both saw and ministered to the Word.

[Col. 1022A] But if they say that he is God, and is glorified as God, for the reason that the Word of God the Father merely dwelt in him, and not because he became man, they will again hear from us: If it is enough for those who have God dwelling within them to make them truly gods and worthy of worship, then all angels and human beings must be gods and worthy of worship, for God dwells in the holy angels. We too have had him within us through the Holy Spirit; but this is not enough to show that those who possess the Holy Spirit are gods by nature and worthy of worship.

Therefore Emmanuel is not God and worthy of worship because God the Word dwelt in him as in an ordinary man, understood as a separate entity [Baluz.: “and, in part, God the Word”]; rather, he is so because he became flesh, that is, man. For he remained [Col. 1022B] both God and worthy of worship.

## CHAPTER XIX. Apostolic statements in which Christ is called God

Speaking of the mystery according to Christ, he says: “Which in other generations was not made known to the sons of men, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles” (Eph. III, 5). And: “The mystery which was hidden from ages and generations, but has now been made manifest to his saints, to whom he willed to reveal the riches of the glory of this mystery among the nations, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory, whom we proclaim” (Col. I, 26).

If, therefore, he is a God-bearer (θεοφόρος), and not truly God, how is he himself the riches of the glory of the mystery that is proclaimed to the nations? Or how is God proclaimed at all?

## CHAPTER XX. Another passage

[Col. 1022C]

“For I want you to know what concern I have for you and for those who are in Laodicea, and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh, so that their hearts may be comforted, instructed in love and in all the riches of the fullness of understanding, unto the knowledge of the mystery of God, Christ” (Col. II, 1).

Behold: he calls the mystery of God the mystery of Christ, and wishes some to understand it fully, unto the knowledge of him. What understanding, then, would those need who wished to learn Christ’s mystery, if they were going to hear merely that God dwelt in a man? Great understanding is required to know how the Word, since he is God, became man.

## CHAPTER XXI. Another passage

[Col. 1022D]

“For from you the word of the Lord has sounded forth, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but in every place your faith toward God has gone out” (I Thess. I, 8).

Here again he mentions that faith was directed toward God, while Christ also says: “He who believes in me has eternal life” (John VII, 25). By “the word,” however, he means the preaching concerning himself.

## CHAPTER XXII. Another passage

“For you yourselves know our entrance among you, that it was not in vain; but after suffering much and being treated with insults, as you know, at Philippi, we had confidence in our God to speak to you the gospel of God” (I Thess. II, 2).

[Col. 1023A] Behold: while speaking in God, he mentioned the gospel of God—the one who preaches Christ to the nations.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Another passage

“Remember, brothers, our labor and hardship, working night and day so that we might not burden any of you; we preached the gospel of God among you” (I Thess. II, 4). And again: “Therefore we also give thanks to God without ceasing, because when you received from us the word that you heard from God, you welcomed it not as the word of men, but as truly the word of God, which is at work in you who believe” (Ibid. v. 13).

Does he not clearly refer to the gospel of God and the word of God as the preaching concerning Christ? Indeed, this is entirely manifest to everyone: “For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all, instructing us that, denying impiety and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this present age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus II, 11).

[Col. 1023B] Behold: our Lord Jesus Christ is named fully as God, and great. For it is he whose glorious coming we await, hastening to live soberly and irreproachably. But if he is a God-bearing man (θεοφόρος), how is he the great God? Or how can the blessed hope be placed in him? For surely Jeremiah is right when he says: “Cursed is the one who places his hope in man” (Jerem. I, 5). Nor can the fact that he bears God make him God himself, as I said earlier.

Finally, let them teach us what prevents all the others who have had God within them from also being gods and worthy of worship. [Col. 1023C] But blessed Paul calls Christ God, great and blessed, possessing illumination, when he is found saying concerning the Jews and Emmanuel: “To them belong the fathers, and the covenant, and the promises, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, blessed for ever and ever. Amen” (Rom. IV, 9).

That he was preaching according to divine revelation becomes clear from his own words: “Then, after fourteen years, I again went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also. I went up according to revelation, and I set before them the gospel that I preach among the nations; but privately before those who seemed to be something, lest perhaps I should be running, or had run, in vain” (Gal. II, 1).

Preaching Christ to the nations as God, he everywhere calls his mystery divine. He went up to Jerusalem by revelation and set it before those who seemed to be something—that is, the holy apostles or disciples—lest he should be running in vain. But when he had gone down from Jerusalem and again joined the assemblies of the nations, did he correct anything from what he had said before? Did he not persist in confessing Christ as God? For this reason he writes to certain people: “I marvel that you are so quickly transferring yourselves from him who called you to another gospel—which is not another, except that there are some who trouble you and wish to pervert the gospel of Christ” (Gal. I, 6).

And again he says: “But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you anything beyond what you received, let him be accursed” (Ibid.). For what reason, then, leaving aside all the others—even if they had God dwelling within them—did he alone preach Jesus as God?

## CHAPTER XXIV. Another passage

It is written concerning Christ: “When he was in Jerusalem during the feast, many believed in his name, seeing the signs that he performed; but Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people and had no need for anyone to testify concerning man: for he himself knew what was in man” (John II, 23).

If he were a God-bearing man (θεοφόρος), how were the many who believed in his name in Jerusalem not deceived? [Col. 1024B] Or why does he alone know what is in man, when especially no one else knows? For it is said that God formed our hearts individually (Ps. XXXII, 15). Or why does he alone forgive sins? He says: “The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins” (Matt. IX, 6). Why does he alone, apart from the others, sit beside God the Father? Why do angels serve him alone? Why did he teach us to regard as common the Father who is in heaven, while he described him as his own in a special sense?

But perhaps you will say that such statements must be attributed to the Word who dwelt within him. Was it not then necessary for him, according to the measure appropriate to the prophets [Baluz.: “according to the prophets”], also to say: “Thus says the Lord”? Yet when he wished to establish commands above the law, assuming for himself the authority appropriate to a lawgiver [Baluz.: “the lawgiver”], he said: “I say to you” (Matt. V, 32).

[Note: [Col. 1023] Something seems to be missing here; I think it is what Anastasius of Sinai mentions concerning the coin paid as tribute. EDIT.]

How does he say that he is free and not subject to God? Is it because he is truly the Son? And if he were a God-bearing man (θεοφόρος), would he also be free by nature? For God alone is free and unbound: he alone, as it were, demands tribute from all, and receives religion from everyone as though in place of debts. Although Christ is the fulfillment of the law and the prophets, if he is a God-bearing man (θεοφόρος), may we not say that the fulfillment of the prophetic proclamations has brought upon us the crime of worshiping a man (ἀνθρωπολατρία)?

Moreover, the law proclaimed: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deut. VI, 13). By what instruction, then, did it lead us to Christ as to a superior recognition for those who had been in the shadows? Shall we therefore despise and cease to worship the God of the Law and the Prophets [Baluz. omits “of the Law and the Prophets”], and worship a man who has God dwelling within him? Where was it more excellent to understand God: in heaven or on earth [Baluz.: “or rather in a man”]? In the seraphim or in an earthly body?

If he were a God-bearing man (θεοφόρος), how did he share almost as we do in flesh and blood (Heb. II, 14)? For if the fact that God dwelt in him is sufficient for him to share in flesh and blood in the same way as we do, and to share in these things is itself the same as becoming man, then—since God also dwelt in many saints—he became man not once but very often. Why, then, is he said to have appeared once, at the consummation of the ages, for the destruction [Baluz.: “the removal”] of sin through his sacrifice (Heb. IX, 26)? And if he were a God-bearing man, how do the divine Scriptures proclaim one coming of the Word? If he too became a temple of God, how is Christ also in us? Is it as a temple among temples? Or rather as God in temples through the Spirit? If he were a God-bearing man, why is his body alone life-giving? The bodies of the others in whom Almighty God dwelt ought also to have been such.

The divine Paul also wrote somewhere: “Anyone who sets aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by one who has trampled upon the Son of God and regarded as defiled the blood of the covenant?” [Col. 1025B]

Yet the law was divine, and its commandments were spoken through angels. How, then, will the one who has regarded the blood of Christ as defiled be worthy of a worse punishment? Or how is faith in Christ superior to the religion according to the law?

But, as we have already said, Christ is not, like the other saints, a God-bearing man, but is rather truly God, possessing a glory higher than that of the whole world. Since he is God by nature—the Word of God—he became flesh, or a perfect man. For we believe that the body united to him is animate and rational, and that the union is altogether real.

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Baluz.: “He is not a God-bearing man like the other saints, but …” EDIT.]

## CHAPTER XXV. How one must understand “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” and how his body is called his own

[Col. 1025C]

Blessed Paul states that the Only-Begotten Word of God “took hold of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. II, 16), and also that he shared almost as we do in flesh and blood (Ibid. 14). We also remember John, for he says: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14).

Was it therefore the purpose of these spiritual men to teach that the Word of God is subject to transformation, or that it is lawful for him to undergo a change, which is more appropriate to a creature? Thus, perhaps, he might of his own accord become what he was not, or someone else might drive him against his will into another nature [Baluz.: “might be driven”]? Far from it. For he remains the same, excluding every change from his nature and knowing nothing of the shadow of transformation. That heavenly and celestial nature is always firmly established in its own properties.

How, then, did the Word become flesh? This must be considered. First, sacred Scripture often calls flesh “man” [Baluz. omits “man”], and uses a part to signify the whole living creature; at other times it also uses the soul alone to signify the same whole. For it is written: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke III, 6). And the divine Paul himself says: “I did not consult flesh and blood” (Gal. I, 16). The pontiff Moses also addressed those who were from Israel: “Your fathers went down into Egypt with seventy-five souls” (Deut. X, 22).

But you should not therefore say that naked souls without flesh went down into Egypt, nor that God granted his salvation to lifeless bodies and flesh alone. Therefore, whenever we hear that the Word became flesh, we understand a man composed of soul and body. The Word, being God, became a perfect man, receiving an animate and rational body, and truly uniting it to himself in a manner known to him. Such things cannot in any way be perceived by our senses, and he was called the Son of Man.

But if, looking as into a mirror, we must speak by analogy, human understanding can conjecture to some extent that the Word was united to a body possessing a rational soul, just as the soul of a human being—although of a different nature from the body—receives communion and union with its body. Thus it almost seems not to be something other than the body, because through the composition of both, one living creature is produced [Baluz.: “we are made”], while the soul nevertheless remains, as I said earlier, in its own nature.

Therefore we do not say that God the Word became man through change or transformation, nor at all that he ceased to be God. Rather, receiving flesh from a woman and being united to it from the womb, he came forth as the same person, simultaneously man and God. He did not cast aside the eternal generation from God the Father [Baluz. omits “eternal”] and undergo a temporal one [Baluz.: “a hidden one”], receiving from a woman the beginning of his existence as man.

He permitted his own flesh [Baluz.: “his own nature”] to be born according to its laws, so far as the manner of birth was concerned. In other respects, he possesses something unlike human nature: he was born of a Virgin and alone had an unmarried mother.

[Note: [Col. 1025D] That is, one who had not been defiled by the embraces of a man. The term “to marry” (nubendi) is often found in obscene contexts. For example, in the Gospel of Saint Mark: “They neither marry nor are given in marriage.” And in Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 209: “If he nevertheless remains unmarried, or she remains unmarried.” BALUZ.]

The Evangelist also records that he himself became flesh and dwelt among us [Baluz. omits “the Evangelist”], so that he might establish both that he became man and that he did not lose what was his: for he remained what he was.

For it is certainly understood as one thing dwelling in another—that is, the divine nature in humanity—without undergoing mixture, confusion, or change, so as to become what it was not. Whatever is said to dwell in another does not itself become like that in which it dwells; rather, one thing is understood as being in another. In the case of the nature of the Word and of humanity, however, their different natures indicate only a distinction. For one Christ is understood to exist from both.

Therefore, as I said earlier, with the absence of confusion preserved, he says that the Word dwelt among us. For he knows that there is one Only-Begotten Son, made flesh and man.

[Col. 1027A] [Note: [Col. 1027D] What follows, up to Jacob’s struggle with the angel and the words in chapter 31, “the breadth of his thigh,” is absent from the common editions and is now published for the first time. —Baluz., [Col. 1028D] “Observe how the divine Evangelist wisely crowns the whole nature of human beings. He says, etc.” EDIT.]

The divine Evangelist seems to me, by “flesh,” wisely to name the whole nature of human beings. For he says that the Word dwelt among us, recalling that the incarnation of the Word took place not, as I suppose, for any other reason than that we too, enriched by participation in him through the Holy Spirit, might gain the benefit of adoption.

Therefore we believe that the highest and true unity was brought about in Christ. But if Christ is said to dwell in us, he will establish a relational dwelling (σχετική). It is not in this way that God is said to have dwelt in Christ: “For in him the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” (Col. II, 9)—not by participation or by a simple relation (σχέσις), as when the sun shines upon something or fire communicates its inherent heat to other things, but, so to speak, by the very sincere divine nature making for itself a dwelling, according to the entirety of what it is, through a true union, as we said earlier, in the temple born of the Virgin. Thus Christ Jesus both is and is understood to be one.

I will not deny that our speech is overcome when it attempts to express this fully. But for that reason the mystery of Christ is not to be disbelieved; rather, it is all the more wondrous. For the more it surpasses every mind and every word, the more it must be placed beyond all wonder.

We do not say that the Word, having become flesh—that is, a perfect man—is contained within the measure of a body; that would be utterly foolish. Rather, we believe that he also fills all things, as he habitually fills heaven and earth and what lies beneath them. For all things are full of God, and all things are small in comparison with him. But how he is wholly present both in each individual thing and in all things is difficult to comprehend and express—indeed, impossible. In my opinion, he possesses this because he is incorporeal and indivisible.

We call the body the Word’s own body, not in the way that laughter is a man’s own or neighing is a horse’s own, but because, having become his through true union, it serves him as an instrument for carrying out what he ordinarily performs, apart from sin alone.

But if it should perhaps be said that God the Word was also sent, let none of you be frightened by thinking: Where will the incorporeal one go, or to what place will he withdraw, when all things are full of him? Let him rather know that there is another mode of being sent. The one who is sent does not change place from one location to another; rather, he assumes a sacred ministry, which we learn was also entrusted by Christ, the Savior of all, to his disciples.

Finally, the divine Paul says concerning Christ: “Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession” (Heb. III, 1). Observe that when he presents him as ministering in the manner of human beings, although he is God by nature, he also attributes to him the office of apostleship. Nothing is absurd, as I said earlier, if God the Word is also said to be sent by the Father. For he most certainly fills all things and is wholly absent from no place. We, however, interpreting divine realities through human expressions, customarily understand the dispensation of the immortal nature by bodily figures.

Finally, although the Holy Spirit fills all things, blessed Paul writes and says: “And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. IV, 6). The Savior himself also says: “It is expedient for you that I go; for if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John XVI, 7). We must therefore refer everything to the rule of piety and follow it with firm understanding; in doing so, we shall benefit ourselves above all.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How the holy Virgin is understood to be Θεοτόκος (Theotokos, Mother of God)

[Col. 1028B]

The Word of God the Father was born in an ineffable manner. This generation surpasses every sense and thought, and is appropriate to an incorporeal nature. Nevertheless, what is born is understood to be the proper offspring of the begetter and of the same substance with him. Therefore it is also called “son,” the name indicating [Baluz. adds “as it were”] a true and genuine offspring. But since the Father is living eternally, it is necessary that he also live eternally for whom he is Father.

Thus, as the wisest Evangelist records: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God, and the Word was also with God” (John I, 1). But at the consummation of the ages, for us human beings [Baluz. adds “and for our salvation”], he became incarnate and became man—not abandoning what he was, but retaining his unchangeable nature, always established upon the summit of divinity. Yet for our sake, in accordance with the divine dispensation, he accepted an act of self-emptying, and did not disdain [that is, “did not despise”] the poverty appropriate to human nature. For although he was rich, he became poor, as it is written: “so that by his poverty we might become rich” (II Cor. VIII, 9).

He therefore became man, and is said to have undergone birth from a woman. Because he truly received from the holy Virgin a body united to himself, we call the holy Virgin Θεοτόκος, since she gave birth to him according to his humanity, or according to the flesh, although he had, before the ages, a generation from the Father.

To suppose that the Word received his beginning from this point, when he became man, is full of impiety and madness. For the Savior himself showed that such people are utterly foolish when he said concerning himself: “Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am” (John VIII, 58). How could he otherwise have existed before Abraham, when he was born according to the flesh many ages later? The divine John sufficiently refutes them, I think, when he says: “This was he of whom I said: After me comes a man who has come before me, because he was before me” (John I, 30).

Let us therefore cease contending without cause over such a trivial matter and turn instead to something that can bring benefit, lest some people be troubled when they hear that the holy Virgin is Θεοτόκος, and fill their minds with Jewish unbelief—or indeed with pagan impiety. For the Jews attacked Christ, saying: “We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because, being a man, you make yourself God” (John X, 23).

The children of the pagans, however, ridicule the Church’s doctrines when they hear that God was born from a woman. But they will reap the fruits of their own madness, and they will hear from us: “A fool speaks foolishly, and his heart understands vain things.” For although the account of our mystery is a stumbling-block to the Jews and foolishness to the nations, it is nevertheless, for us who know it, truly wondrous, saving, and most worthy of belief.

If anyone dared to say that this earthly flesh was the mother of bare divinity, and that from a creature there was born a nature superior to every creature, that would be madness and frenzy. For divine nature was not made from earth; the corruptible will never become the root of incorruption; mortality will not give birth to life; a bodily, tangible thing will not become the source of an incorporeal offspring; the uncreated will not be born from the created; nor will that which is without beginning be born from that which has a beginning.

But since we affirm that the Word of God became like us and took a body like our bodies, truly uniting it to himself by a hidden and ineffable manner, and that thus he became man and was born according to the flesh, what is absurd or unworthy of belief? Especially since the human soul, as we have said very often, although of a nature other than the body, is nevertheless born with it because it is united to it. No one should suppose that the nature of the body gives the soul the beginning of its substance. Rather, God inserts the soul into the body in an ineffable manner, and it too is born with the body. Nevertheless, we define the one living creature produced from both as a human being.

Therefore the Word was God, but also became man; and because he was born according to the flesh, it is necessary, on account of his humanity, that she who gave birth to him be Θεοτόκος. For if she did not give birth to God, then certainly the one begotten by her will not be called God. But if the divine Scriptures call him God himself, she gave birth to God made man, since man could not otherwise become man except through birth from a woman. How, then, can she who gave birth to him not be Θεοτόκος? That the one born from her is true God, we learn from the divine Scriptures.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Statements concerning Christ

“Behold, the Virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel” (Isa. VII, 14, according to the reading of Matthew and Cyril).

How, then, is what was born from the holy Virgin called Emmanuel, when Emmanuel, as I said earlier, signifies that the Word who is true God from true God was, on account of the flesh, in our nature [Baluz. omits “true”]? He became Emmanuel, for he emptied himself, undergoing our birth and becoming like us, and thus lived among us.

Therefore he is God in the flesh, and she who bore him carnally, or according to the flesh, is truly Θεοτόκος.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Another passage

“For they will all gather a garment collected by deceit and put away a robe with alteration, and they will wish that these had been burned; for a child has been born for us, and a son has been given to us, whose rule has been placed upon his shoulder, and his name is called Messenger of Great Counsel” (Isa. IX, 5, according to the Septuagint).

You hear that he was called a child and that he underwent a birth like ours. Yet heaven indicated this child through the most brilliant star; the Magi came from the furthest limits of the earth and worshiped him; angels proclaimed the good news to the shepherds, saying that a Savior had been born, and announcing peace as well as the Father’s good pleasure: “Messenger of Great Counsel.”

For he manifested to us the Father’s will, who was well pleased in him to save the world [Col. II, 20] and through him and in him to reconcile the world to himself. Having been reconciled through Christ, we have been reconciled to God; for the Son is truly God, of God the Father.

What the Father’s counsel was, then, of which he was the messenger, he himself teaches when he says: “For God so loved the world that he gave his Only-Begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John III, 16).

That Only-Begotten Son is the one begotten from the holy Virgin. For he is the Word himself, made man, who was God in the flesh and thus appeared to earthly beings. Finally, he said: “He who believes in me has eternal life” (John VI, 47).

That through him and in him we believe in the Father, he explained when he said: “He who believes in me [Baluz. adds: ‘does not believe in me’], but in him who sent me” (John XII, 44); and: “He who sees me sees him who sent me” (Ibid. v. 45).

[Note: [Col. 1029D] Baluz.: “He who has seen me has seen him who …” EDIT.]

“Listen to me, islands, and attend, nations. After a long time he will stand,” says the Lord; “from the womb of my mother they will call my name” (Isa. XLIX, 1, according to the Septuagint).

Although the Word is God, he did not fail to know that he would undergo birth, having become incarnate from a woman for our sake. He knew that he would be called Christ Jesus by God the Father, proclaiming to all of us the new name of the Son, which is blessed on earth.

Observe that he names his own mother, who gave birth to his body. Therefore, if he knows himself to be God [Baluz. adds “true”], she who gave birth to him according to the flesh is rightly called Θεοτόκος. But if he is not God—as some boldly, or rather wickedly, think—then the holy Virgin must be deprived of the title by which she is called Θεοτόκος.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That the Only-Begotten, appearing as man, is called God

[Col. 1031A]

Solomon says in prayer: “And now, Lord God of Israel, let your word be made credible, which you spoke to your servant David. Is it indeed credible that God dwelt with human beings on earth?” (II Paralipomenon VI, 17, according to the Septuagint).

Observe that he marvels at the incarnation of the Word: for he dwelt with human beings on earth when he became man, since the event appeared incredible. Otherwise, how would this be something exceptional or worthy of wonder, when God does not depart from the things he himself created, sustaining them and containing those that already exist, while creating those that do not yet exist?

The truly exceptional miracle is that God, having become man, dwelt on earth with human beings, in accordance with the promises previously given to the divine David. For it is written: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not annul it” (Ps. CXXXI, 11). What did he swear? “From the fruit of your womb I will place one upon your throne.”

Although David believed that Almighty God would never deny his promise, he nevertheless inquired more carefully about the place of the generation, and therefore said: “If I ascend upon the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Ibid. v. 3).

Then, having also discovered this through the Spirit and learned the place of the Only-Begotten’s carnal generation, he proclaimed it and said: “We heard of it in Ephrata”—that is, in Bethlehem—“we found it in the fields of the forest.” That by “Ephrata” he means Bethlehem, the prophet confirms: “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrata” (Mic. V, 2).

Observe how he calls him whom he believed had been created like us in Ephrata the God of Jacob, whose dwelling was in the tabernacle. For there the holy Virgin gave birth to Jesus.

He also calls him the God of Abraham elsewhere, saying: “The princes of the peoples have gathered together with the God of Abraham” (Ps. XLVI, 10). For, almost as though instructed by knowledge of the future through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, he saw with the eyes of his mind the princes of the peoples—that is, the holy apostles—in the service of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore, since the one born from a woman has been called the God of Abraham and the God of Jacob, why should the holy Virgin not be Θεοτόκος? [Col. 1031D]

## CHAPTER XXX. Another passage

The prophet Habakkuk says: “Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid. I considered your works, and I was terrified. You will be known in the midst of two living creatures; you will be revealed when the time comes; when my soul is troubled, you will remember mercy in wrath. God will come from Theman, and the Holy One from Mount Pharan” (Hab. III, 1).

See how he will be known in the midst of two living creatures. For when he was born from a woman and lived until the time of the precious cross, by the grace of God, as blessed Paul says, he tasted death for everyone through his body (Heb. II, 9). But because he was God by nature, he rose again to eternal life.

Thus the one who endured the precious cross for us was known in the midst of two living creatures. For he himself says somewhere to the Jews: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am” (John VIII, 28).

Observe also how, calling him God, he declares that he will come from Theman and from Mount Pharan. Theman is interpreted as “the south.” For Christ appeared not from the regions of the north, but from southern Judea, in which Bethlehem also lies.

Therefore, since the one who was called Lord and God came from southern Judea—for he was born in Bethlehem—how can the holy Virgin not be Θεοτόκος?

## CHAPTER XXXI. Another passage

[Col. 1032B]

It is written in Genesis: “Jacob, however, remained alone, and a man wrestled with him until morning. When he saw that he could not prevail against him, he touched the breadth of his thigh [Note: [Col. 1031D] What follows is lacking in the common editions.] while he was wrestling with him, and said to him: ‘Let me go, for the dawn has risen.’ But he said: ‘I will not let you go unless you bless me.’” And after other words: “He blessed him there and called the name of that place ‘the face of God’: ‘For I have seen God face to face,’ he said, ‘and my soul has been saved.’ The sun rose, and he passed beyond the face of God; but he himself limped on his thigh” (Gen. 32:24). The sense of the Scriptures is indeed mystical: it seems to indicate the struggle of the Jews, which they carried on with Christ [Baluz. omits “with Christ”], [Col. 1032C] almost wrestling with him; yet they were overcome, and would themselves also obtain his blessing if, through faith, they had turned to him in the last times. Nevertheless, that man who wrestled was certainly a man, and yet Jacob called him the face of God; and not only that, but he knew him to be God in truth: “For I have seen God face to face,” he says, “and my soul has been saved” (ibid., v. 30). Emmanuel is God by nature. He is also called the face of God. For he is “the figure of the Father’s substance” (Heb. 1:3), and he thus spoke of himself to the Jews when he said concerning God and the Father: “You have neither seen his face, nor do you have his word abiding in you, because you do not believe him whom he sent” (John 5:38).

That the man who wrestled [Col. 1032D] with Jacob was truly God, sacred Scripture will again establish. For it says: “The Lord said to Jacob: ‘Rise, go up to Bethel, dwell there, and make there an altar to God, who appeared to you when you fled from the face of your brother Esau’” (Gen. 35:1). Returning from Mesopotamia at God’s command [Baluz. omits “at God’s command”], and fearing Esau, Jacob transported his children and all his possessions: “But he remained alone, and a man wrestled with him” (Gen. 32:24).

## CHAPTER XXXII. Another.

The blessed Daniel, explaining a terrifying vision for us, says: [Col. 1033A] “I saw in the vision of the night, and behold, one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven; he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they brought him before him. And to him was given honor and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His authority is an everlasting authority, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Dan. 7:13). You hear how he does not simply recall having seen a man, lest he be thought to be one of us, and Emmanuel merely like us; but “like a son of man.” [ [Note: [Col. 1033D] This passage is reproduced near the end of the first book of Leontius of Byzantium Against the Eutychians. BALUZ.] For although the Word is God by nature, he was made in the likeness of human beings and was found in appearance as a man (Phil. 2:7), so that both might be understood in the same one: that is, neither a mere man nor the Word without humanity and flesh.] Nevertheless, he recalls that the principality and honor which he always possessed were given to him: for he says that all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. Since, therefore, the created order serves the only-begotten Word of God even when he is situated in humanity, and since he has the principality of the Father and his own, while the holy Virgin bore him according to the flesh, how is she not understood to be Θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”? 

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Christ’s Passion; and that it is useful that different things are said of one and the same person according to different aspects, and that we do not divide him into two.

Saint Paul explains the saving Passion to us, for he says: “Now by the grace of God he tasted death for all” (Heb. 2:9); and likewise: “For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures; that he was buried; and that he rose again on the third day” (1 Cor. 15:3). The most wise Peter also says: “Christ having suffered for us in the flesh” (1 Pet. 4:1). Since, therefore, we believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, that is, God the Word seen in human form, or made a man like us, how can we attribute the Passion to him and nevertheless preserve him as impassible, as God?

The Passion, then, belonged to the dispensation: God the Word himself making what belongs to the flesh his own because of the ineffable union; yet he remained outside suffering insofar as this pertains to his own nature, for God is impassible. Nor is this surprising, since we also see that the human soul itself, if the body has suffered something, remains outside suffering insofar as this pertains to its nature; yet it is not understood to be wholly outside suffering, because the body that suffers is its own. [Note: [Col. 1034D] Baluz.: “although it is inseparable from the savior of all, I shall use it,” etc. EDIT.] Although it is non-contiguous and simple, nevertheless what suffers is not alien to it. Understand the same concerning Christ, the Savior of all. I shall use examples that may show us, as though through an enigma, that the Only-begotten shared in the Passion insofar as this pertains to the familiarity of his body, yet remained free from suffering as God.

[Col. 1034A] Thus almighty God commanded the most wise Moses to perform miracles, so that Israel might believe that he had been sent by God [Baluz. adds “not”] and that they might be freed from oppression. He says: “You shall take water from the river and pour it upon the earth, and the water which you take from the river shall become blood upon the earth” (Exod. 4:9). We say that water is a figure of life, and that the Son is by nature life, proceeding from the Father as from a river, of the same substance; therefore he gives life to all things. “But when,” he says, “you pour the water upon the earth, it shall become blood.” When the Word became flesh from the earth—that is, when he clothed himself with flesh from the earth—he is then said to have suffered death like ours in it, although by nature he is life.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Another.

[Col. 1034B]

In Leviticus God signifies [Baluz. omits “God”] that the leper is polluted and unclean (Lev. 13:1 ff.), and thus commands that he be expelled from the camp, and that, if the disease has been healed, he be cleansed in this manner: “And taking two clean birds, and cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop, the priest shall command; and having killed one bird in an earthen vessel, over living water, he shall take the living bird and wash it in the blood of the bird killed over the living water, and sprinkle it seven times upon the one who has been cleansed from leprosy, and he shall be clean.”

The most precious blood of Christ and the sanctification of holy baptism make us clean, wash away the filth of our pollution, and drive away the mortality of carnal desire. But consider this: omitting for the present a detailed examination of the force of the words of the writers, we shall recall what is useful for the mystery. Christ is compared with two birds, not because there are two sons, but because there is one composed of two things—divinity and humanity brought together into unity. The birds are clean, for our God Jesus Christ committed no sin; rather, he was the holy Word, both in respect of divinity and in respect of humanity [Baluz. omits “in respect of humanity”]. He is compared with birds because he is, as it were, above the earth in the heights, and from heaven above: Christ is from heaven as man, although the holy Virgin bore his flesh; in this way, therefore, he is from above and from heaven. For God the Word, who is from above and from the Father, receiving flesh from the holy Virgin and considering it his own and proper flesh, as though he had brought it from above and from heaven, said: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). He always attributes to his own flesh the things that are his; and once united, it is considered one with him.

But observe that, after one bird has been killed, the other is washed in its blood and nevertheless does not die. What does this mean? The Word lived, although his own flesh had died, and he called the suffering common to both because of the union and the intimacy he had with the [Col. 1035A] flesh. Thus he himself lives as God, while he made the body his own and received the body’s sufferings intimately into himself, although he himself suffered nothing in his own nature. It is therefore beneficial and necessary, if in the one Christ we accept what is constituted according to different aspects concerning one and the same person, and what may not be divided into two, although the things spoken of may be different from and entirely unlike one another in their actual character.

This is what I mean. We say that God the Word was born according to the flesh from a woman, although he grants birth to all things and calls into birth things that are not yet born. He was born according to different aspects, insofar as he is understood to be a man like us; yet he calls all things into birth because he is God by nature.

It is also written of him: “The child grew and became strong, and was filled with wisdom and grace” (Luke 2:52). Since he is perfect by nature as God, and from his fullness bestows spiritual gifts upon the holy, since he himself is the giver of wisdom and grace, how does the child grow and become filled with wisdom and grace? According to different aspects: for since he is at once the same man and God, because of the union he speaks of what is proper to humanity [Baluz. “leads”]; yet he is perfect, and the giver of wisdom and grace, as God.

He is also named both firstborn and only-begotten. But if someone wishes to examine the force of the words themselves, the firstborn is the one who is firstborn among many brothers; the only-begotten, however, is only-begotten, no longer firstborn and not among many brothers. Yet he is both this and that. How, then? According to different aspects: he is firstborn as one among many brothers, because of his humanity; but he is the same only-begotten one as the one born alone from the one Father, and as God.

He is said to have been sanctified by the Spirit, although he ordinarily sanctifies those who approach him; he was baptized according to the flesh, although he baptized in the Holy Spirit. How, then, is the same person both sanctifying and sanctified, baptizing and baptized? According to different aspects: he is sanctified humanly, just as he is baptized; but he sanctifies divinely and baptizes in the Holy Spirit.

Although he himself raises the dead, he rose from the dead; although he is life by nature, he is said to be given life. How is this to be understood? According to different aspects: he rose from the dead and is said to be given life according to the flesh; but he gives life and raises the dead as God. He suffers and does not suffer according to different aspects: he suffers humanly in the flesh, because he is man; but he remains impassible divinely, as God.

He worshiped with us: “You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know” (John 4:22); and he is also to be worshiped: “Every knee shall bow to him” (Phil. 2:10). This too is according to different aspects. He worships because he assumed a nature that ought to worship; but he is worshiped as one greater than the nature that worships, because he is understood to be God. In worship, he must not be divided into a man separately and God separately; nor do we say that, as though joined to God by an equality of dignity and with the substances divided, the man is worshiped together with him—for that is full of the utmost impiety. Rather, the one Word of God, made man and incarnate, is to be worshiped; yet we must believe that the body united to him possessed a rational soul like ours. For almighty God did not command two firstborn to be worshiped by us and by the holy angels. There is one who was introduced into the inhabited world (Heb. 1:6); and if we examine more carefully the manner of this introduction, we shall find the mystery of the dispensation according to the flesh. He was introduced into the inhabited world when he became man, although by his nature he appears to be exceedingly distant from the world and is believed truly to exist in the eminence of divinity: for he is another, beyond the elements, their creator. Therefore, by nature he is above the things he himself created, since he is God by nature. Yet one is to be worshiped, as I said earlier, even when he is among many brothers; for it was then that he was called firstborn.

The man blind from birth worshiped one Son when he was healed in a singular and wondrous manner. For when Jesus found him in the temple, he said: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” He replied: “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” (John 9:38). But Christ, showing him himself together with the body, said: “You have indeed seen him, and he who speaks with you is he” (ibid. 37). You see that he uses the singular number, not permitting God and man to be understood separately; indeed, even if someone names Emmanuel a man, he does not signify an ordinary man at all, but the Word of God united to our nature. The blessed disciples worshiped him as one man when they saw him walking in wondrous fashion upon the waters, and worshiped him, saying: “Truly you are the Son of God” (Matt. 14:35).

But if we say that a man is worshiped together with God, we introduce an enormous division. For σύν, which in Latin is cum, unless it is used with the meaning of unity that exists through composition, compels us to understand two. Just as no one is said to agree with himself, or to dine together, or to worship together, or to walk together with himself—for the preposition placed before the verb indicates two persons—so also, if someone says that a man is worshiped together with God, he plainly speaks of two sons, separated from one another. For the principle of unity, if it is understood merely as equality of dignity or authority, is shown not to be true; and we have already proved this at greater length elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Against those who say that human things befit God the Word only by relation.

Some chatter about the carnal dispensation of the Only-begotten and, by reducing to fragile human senses the venerable and great mystery, beloved even to the spirits above, through which we too have been saved, they stain the honor and beauty of the truth. They ought not to try to strengthen whatever seems right to them, but rather to examine, with the subtle and penetrating eye of the mind, the intention of the sacred Scriptures, and thus enter upon the straight path, following what the most holy Fathers examined. Instructed by the illuminations of the Holy Spirit, they established for us the symbol of faith, saying that he who was ineffably born from the substance of the Father, God the Word, through whom all things were made, those in heaven and those on earth, descended for us human beings and for the sake of our salvation, became man [Baluz. adds “became flesh”], suffered, ascended into heaven, and would come after the appointed times to judge the living and the dead.

Yet there are some who think themselves learned and knowledgeable, puffed up with arrogance and conceit. When they hear these words, they mock them, and consider words spoken so correctly to be mere ravings, even though we believe that the knowledge of the truth was opened to the holy Fathers by the illumination of the Holy Spirit. But these people, as though they alone were capable of better understanding, do not think that the only-begotten Son of God, who is from his substance, God the Word, suffered in his flesh for us humanly, although, insofar as he is understood to be God, he has in his own nature the property of being unable to suffer. Instead, they place separately and apart from him the man who was begotten from the holy Virgin. Then, assigning him, as they suppose, a measure of glory, they say that he was united to the Word of God the Father; and explaining the manner of the union, they say that equality of dignity or authority was granted to him by God, so that by a similar designation both Christ and Son, and also Lord, might be named. But if it is said that the man they devise also suffered something, they claim that this must be referred to God the Word himself, because he is joined to him by equality of dignity, while the natures remain divided and each is what it is.

I shall explain the force of their views as far as I am able, setting forth examples from the sacred Scriptures. Christ hungered, was wearied by the journey, slept, entered a boat, was struck with blows by attendants, was scourged by Pilate, received the soldiers’ spitting, and, when they pierced his side with a spear, they offered his mouth vinegar mixed with gall. He also tasted death, suffered the cross, and endured other insults from the Jews. They say that all these things happened to a man, but that they must be referred to the person of the true Son. But we believe in one God the Father, almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; likewise in one Lord Jesus Christ, his Son. We refuse to divide him into Emmanuel the man separately and the Word separately. Knowing that the Word became man like us, we truly call the same one God from God; and humanly, a man like us from a woman. We further affirm that, because of the intimacy of the union, he endured the weaknesses of the flesh, while preserving the impassibility of his nature, since he was not merely man but also God by nature; and just as the body was his own, so too were its natural and blameless sufferings, as well as the injuries inflicted upon him by the insolence of certain people.

[Col. 1038A] He suffered impassibly, because he did not humble himself merely to become like us, but because, as I said earlier, he preserved for himself what belongs to his nature, namely, that he is superior to all. But if we said that through a conversion or change of his nature he passed into the nature of flesh, we would necessarily have to confess, even against our will, in every possible way that the hidden and divine nature was passible. If, however, although he became man like us, he remained unchanged [Baluz. “unchangeable”], since it belongs to the heavenly nature not to be able to suffer; and if, through his union, the body became passible, then he must suffer because the body suffers, since the body is said to be his own. Yet he himself remains impassible, since it belongs to him not to be able to suffer.

If Emmanuel was glorified through suffering, as he himself said when he was about to suffer the precious cross for us—“Now the Son of Man has been glorified” (John 13:31)—why are they not ashamed to attribute the glory of the Passion to a man who has only a connection with him through equality of dignity? For, according to their view, he simply joined to himself, in accordance with the will and good pleasure of the Father, a man, made him equal to his own glory, and granted that by a similar designation he should be called Christ, Son, God, and Lord.

Therefore the Word was not truly incarnate, nor did he become man at all. Or perhaps they may say that the holy teachers of the whole world were false and deceitful, without this causing any harm? Let them either say—and come forward to prove it—that the manner of union introduced by them possesses the force of incarnation, and that this is what it means for the Word to have become man. Or, if they think that these things are not so, why do they devise for us a manner of union that is no union, neglecting the truth? They ought to say that the Word of God and the Father was united to our humanity. In this way he will be understood to have suffered humanly in his own flesh, while, insofar as this concerns the nature of divinity, he is free from every affliction, as God.

I shall further prove that, by naming a “relation”—which I do not know how they discovered—they diminish Emmanuel’s glory; that they scarcely make him one of the holy prophets; and that they rank him among the many. I shall set forth examples from divine Scripture.

[Col. 1038D] At one time in the desert the people of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying: “Would that we had died, struck down by the Lord in Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate our fill” (Exod. 16:3). Then the most wise Moses spoke—for it was fitting to refute such reckless impatience: “But what are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against God” (ibid. 7). For during that period almighty God also reigned among the people of Israel through the holy prophets.

The Jews [Baluz. “They”], being fainthearted in this matter as well, approached the divine Samuel and said: “Behold, you have grown old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint over us a king to judge us, as all the other nations have” (1 Sam. 8:5). The prophet was deeply distressed by this. But almighty God said: “Hearken to the voice of the people, as they have spoken to you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, so that I should not reign over them” (ibid. v. 7).

Christ also said somewhere to the holy apostles: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Luke 9:48). He also promises that he will address the merciful from his tribunal: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34). Recognizing intimately their virtuous conduct, he says concerning those for whom they had acted benevolently: “As long as you did it for one of these least ones, you did it for me” (ibid. v. 40).

[Col. 1039B] Behold, the nature of relation is clearly recognized in these examples. The people of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, and although the matter had reference to God, Moses and Aaron were nevertheless human beings like us. You will understand the same way in the other examples we recently mentioned: they were holy and admirable men, certainly, but still human beings like us. Is it then in this way that the man joined to God the Word, as they claim, has a relation in respect of his sufferings? And how is he not then an ordinary man, separate and nothing else? Therefore he is not truly God Emmanuel, not the only-begotten Son, not God by nature.

Furthermore, why has no other person honored by God the Word received equality of dignity or authority? Why do they insist that this one alone has obtained equality in all things, especially since God the Savior of all does not judge according to persons, but with just judgment, as he himself declares? Why, then, does he alone sit in judgment? How will he come as judge, with the angels attending him? And why alone is he worshiped both by us and by the spirits above?

“But indeed,” he says, “we find that you also do this, for you confess that he suffered, insofar as you attribute the sufferings of the flesh to him, although you preserve him as impassible as God.” But we, excellent man, after first uniting the Word and the man, attribute the sufferings to the flesh, while preserving him as impassible as God. For although he became like us, we must nevertheless recognize the majesty of the heavenly dignities and of his divine eminence.

Having therefore established the unity beforehand, as though laying down a foundation of faith, we confess that he suffered in the flesh, while he remained outside suffering, since he possesses the property of being unable to suffer. But if we divide God and man into parts, separating the natures from one another, and say that the Word bore what happened to the body only by relation, then Emmanuel, who was begotten from the holy Virgin, has the status of Moses and Aaron. Emmanuel means “God with us.”

Therefore, although he says through the holy prophets: “I gave my back to scourging, and my cheeks to blows; I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isa. 50:6); and again: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Ps. 21:18); and again: “They gave me hyssop for food, and in my thirst they offered me vinegar” (Ps. 68:22), we attribute all these things to the Only-begotten, which he suffered in the flesh for us according to the dispensation, in accordance with the Scriptures: “By his bruise we were healed, and he was weakened because of our sins.” Yet we know that he is impassible by nature. For if, as I said earlier, the same person is at once man and God, his sufferings certainly belong to his humanity, while it belongs to God to be understood as impassible.

Thinking in this way, we shall preserve piety, and proceeding by right thoughts and understanding, we shall reach the prize of the heavenly calling in Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# BOOK THREE

Containing Excerpts by Marius Mercator from the books of Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret of Cyrrhus, and Euthenius of Tyana, bishops of the Nestorian party.

[Col. 1039]

## ADMONITION

No heresy was ever more eager than the Nestorian to spread its doctrine among the peoples. One might believe that the devil, the father of all heresies, cultivated this one above the others so that he might more fully satisfy his hatred of Christ the God-man and of human beings redeemed by Christ’s blood.

It promoted its cause not so much through sermons as through written books, undoubtedly at the devil’s prompting. For impiety, at which Christian ears recoil when it is openly proclaimed, is sometimes tolerated more patiently when it withdraws from curious eyes into concealment: while eloquence lends charm to the discourse, it both pleases through another’s poison and harms through its own.

From the time when Nestorius openly declared war on the Church until Cyril’s death, which occurred in the year 444, three books appeared, as though they were three emblems of the faction. Each arose from the destruction of the preceding one and displayed the same impiety in three forms. The first contained Nestorius’s sermons, arranged in a certain artful order so as to insinuate error. The second contained excerpts from the works of Diodore of Tarsus and Theodore of Mopsuestia, men scarcely surpassed in renown at that time. The third contained the Pentalogy of Theodoret and the sermons of Eutherius, as well as the dialogues of the Eranistes. Others followed others, so that when one had been proscribed, or at least had lost its power to do harm because some learned work had been composed and published against it as an antidote to the poison, another was substituted, bearing a less hated name but possessing no less pestilential a power.

Cyril refuted the first in five books of Contradictions; Proclus refuted the second in his Tome to the Armenians; and Mercator refuted the last in the work whose portion we now publish, for I do not think that it survives complete.

Photius mentions this third book, which we have said contained the Pentalogy of Theodoret, the sermons of Eutherius, and the Eranistes, in codex 49. In doing so, however, he made one mistake in counting the books and another in naming the author.
