For he counts twenty-seven books and makes Theodoret alone the author of all of them, although Mercator demonstrates that there were two authors; and Mercator is the more worthy of belief because he wrote at the time when those men were alive. In this volume, then, there were only five books of Theodoret, inscribed under the single title Pentalogy, and altogether twenty sermons of Eutherius, together with a letter prefixed in the manner of a preface. It is worthwhile to transcribe Photius’s words:

“Twenty-seven books of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, against various propositions were read.

“The first book is directed against those who assert that God the Word was of one nature and that he took his beginning from David’s seed, and likewise against those who attribute sufferings to the divinity. The second book contends more vigorously from Scripture against the same people. The third discusses the same matter. The fourth contains the teaching of the holy Fathers concerning the glorious incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God. The fifth collects the opinions of heretics, which it compares with the opinion of those who entirely refuse to acknowledge two natures in Christ, and shows that they have great affinity with one another. The sixth establishes that our Lord Jesus Christ is one Son. The seventh takes the place of a letter, with which the first volume concludes. The eighth is against those who judge the truth merely by numbers. The ninth is against those who boast that one ought neither to speak nor inquire from the Scriptures, but that their faith is sufficient for them. The tenth is against those who wrongly object to the statement, ‘The Word became flesh.’ The eleventh is against those who forbid acknowledging two natures in the incarnation. The twelfth is against those who assert that to say ‘the Word is one thing and the flesh another’ is to profess two sons. The thirteenth is against those who say that to acknowledge Christ as a man is the same as placing one’s hope in a man. The fourteenth is against those who declare: ‘He suffered without suffering.’ The fifteenth is against those who say: ‘He suffered as he wished.’ The sixteenth is against those who assert that the words themselves must be accepted, but not their meanings, on the grounds that the meanings exceed everyone’s understanding. The seventeenth is against those who say: ‘The Word suffered through the flesh.’ The eighteenth is against those who assert: ‘What punishment would the Jews have deserved if they had not crucified God?’ The nineteenth is against those who affirm that he is a Jew who asserts that God was not crucified. The twentieth is against those who say that the angels who ate food with Abraham did not consequently also assume the nature of flesh. The twenty-first is against those who diminish the miracles one by one while denying the flesh. The twenty-second is against those who inflict harm upon the human race by refusing to admit that the beginning was taken from our nature. The twenty-third is against those who boast that they simply believe what is said and do not consider what is fitting or unfitting. The twenty-fourth is against those who abolish the difference of the natures after the Passion and Ascension. The twenty-fifth repeats in summary what has hitherto been handed down in parts. The twenty-sixth concerns the composition, or consubstantiation, manifested afterward. The twenty-seventh concerns what is according to the common man as an example.

“It is clear even from the titles alone which of the books listed above reinforce orthodox doctrine and which depart from it.

“Moreover, in the same volume I read three books of his, longer than those mentioned above. They bear the title ΕΡΑΝΙΣΤΗΣ ἢ Πολύμορφος, that is, ‘Companion’ or ‘Multiform.’ The first of these teaches that God the Word is immutable; the second, that the union is unmixed and entirely unconfused; the third, that God the Word is impassible or undisturbed. There is also a fourth, in which he reworks these same arguments through syllogisms.”

From Photius’s words five points may be gathered: first, the time when the Eranistes was written, concerning which there will be a fuller opportunity for discussion in the supplement to Theodoret that we shall soon publish; second, how many of Eutherius’s sermons are missing from the second volume of Athanasius’s works—for only seventeen are found, together with the prefixed letter or preface, and thus the final three are missing; third, what the subject of the Pentalogy was, and also its purpose, which was the same as that of the Eranistes, since in both works the same propositions of Catholic teachers are attacked, and in almost the same manner; fourth, what opinion was held of Theodoret’s faith, even in Photius’s time, although Photius praises him immensely; fifth, that the volume mentioned by Photius contained three works of exactly the same character. For the same poison is contained in Eutherius’s sermons as in the Pentalogy, except that it is more harmful in the sermons because it is more eloquently expressed. These matters, however, will be explained more fully in the aforementioned supplement to Theodoret’s works.

Now concerning Mercator’s antirrhetic work against the third book I have mentioned, and also, at least in part, against the second. I would believe—or rather, I would conjecture—that Mercator composed a three-part work or codex concerning the Nestorian affair. The first part contained everything concerning Nestorius and Cyril; the second, everything concerning Theodore of Mopsuestia; and the third, everything concerning Theodoret and Eutherius. We divided the first into two because of its exceptional length. We joined the second and third because of the opposite consideration. It would have helped considerably in gaining a deeper understanding of Nestorius’s doctrine to add to Marius’s excerpts from Theodore the other passages found scattered elsewhere: in Leontius the Scholastic, who accuses Theodore; in Facundus of Hermiane, who defends him; and in the decree of Pope Vigilius and in the Fifth Council, where he is condemned.

As for the names of the three authors from whose works Mercator excerpted what is published here, there is little point in offering a preliminary discussion, since the history of Theodoret—and also of Eutherius—is to be woven into the supplement, a matter neither unworthy of curious readers nor of little use for ecclesiastical affairs. Theodore has already often been mentioned, both in the first dissertation on the earlier part of Mercator’s works and in the notes to various passages; and he must again be discussed at greater length in the first dissertation on this latter part.

[Col. 1041]

# I. THEODORE OF MOPSUESTIA

## MERCATOR’S PREFACE

[Col. 1041] Marius Mercator, servant of Christ, sends greetings to his fellow servant, the reader.

1. The work of Theodore, formerly bishop of the town of Mopsuestia in the province of Cilicia, is in Greek. I have attempted, to the best of my ability, to transfer it into Latin, word for word, wishing to impress upon Latin ears that his perverse and Catholic-faith-opposed teaching concerning the Lord’s dispensation, and the sufficiently extravagant sense by which he maliciously deceived Nestorius, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, along with himself, must be avoided in every way and not followed.

2. At the same time, wishing to admonish Julian, the heretical Pelagian or Coelestian, formerly bishop of the town of Eclanum, that Theodore was his model, Julian traveled across the lands, traversed the sea, and explored the East, making his way with his associates, companions, and fellow συνταλαιπώροις [fellow sufferers], with great exertion—as though toward a teacher renowned for proclaiming Christian doctrine—in order to obtain from Theodore himself confirmation concerning the Pelagian or Coelestian heresy which he had undertaken to defend and follow, and then, as though better instructed, to compose those eight volumes which he considers most prudent, directed more against the Catholic faith [Col. 1043B] than against Augustine of holy memory.

[Col. 1044A] 3. Therefore, if the aforesaid Julian does not disdain to read it, let him recognize from this translation that the same bad faith remains with the aforementioned Theodore by which, as we said, he wickedly deceived Nestorius along with himself, and that it is even more opposed to Julian and to his own doctrine—the doctrine about which, puffed up and deranged, he composed his books—and that even after Julian’s departure from Cilicia, Theodore condemned him by an anathema at the assembly of the bishops of his province.

4. Let him therefore not grow angry or resentful toward us if we expose, convict, and lament him as alien to the Catholic faith and justly condemned, together with Theodore, whom he praises without limit in his books and whose authority and judgment he boasts of relying upon in his error—for he is more deserving of lamentation than of persecution by any hatred.

## EXPOSITION OF THEODORE’S PERVERTED FAITH

[Col. 1043]

[Col. 1043B] 1. Those who are now first being instructed in the clear understanding of ecclesiastical doctrines, or who have resolved to turn from heretical error to the truth, ought to be taught that we believe in one God, the eternal Father—not one who later began to exist, but one who is eternally God from eternity; nor one who later became Father, since he was always God and always Father.

2. We also believe in one only-begotten Son of God, who is from the substance or essence of the Father, truly as Son, and of the same essence with him whose Son he is and is believed to be [Gerb.: “with him, whose”; Baluzius: “in that which is”].

3. And in the Holy Spirit, who is from the substance [Col. 1043C] or essence of God—not that he is the Son, but God in essence, since he is of that essence of which God the Father is, and from whom he is according to essence. For Scripture says: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit which is from God” (1 Cor. 2:12). By this it separates him from every creature and joins and unites him to God, from whom, or of whom, he is according to essence—specifically, in a manner superior in every way to every creature, which is said to be from God not according to God’s essence, but according to the fact that it is a created thing and has its cause. We do not think that he received his existence either as Son or through the Son.

4. We confess the Father perfect in person, and likewise the Son, and likewise the Holy Spirit, while preserving for ourselves the rule of piety by which we do not regard the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as three different essences, but as one, which we recognize in the unity and equality of the Godhead.

5. We must also know about the dispensation which the Lord God [Baluzius, with the old books: “God”] completed, for our salvation, according to the Lord Jesus Christ: that God the Word assumed a man, perfect from the seed of Abraham and David, according to the declarations of the divine Scriptures—one existing according to nature as did those from whose seed he came; a man perfect by nature, constituted of a rational soul and human flesh; and this man, naturally a man like us, fashioned by the power and might of the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb, made from a woman, made under the law, so that he might redeem us all from the curse and slavery of the law, receiving the adoption of sons predestined long ago (Gal. 3:13). He joined and united him to himself in an ineffable manner. He prepared him to experience death according to the law of human beings; but, raising him from the dead and lifting him into heaven, he made him sit at the right hand of God. Therefore, although he exists above every principality, authority, dominion, and power, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come (Eph. 1:21), he received worship from every creature, as one having an inseparable union with the divine nature, and as the entire creation offers him reverence as God beyond every thought and understanding.

6. We do not say that there are two sons, nor two lords, because one Son according to essence is God the Word, the only-begotten Son of the Father, with whom this man is joined and, as a participant in the Godhead, shares the common designation and honor of Son. Likewise, the Lord according to essence is God the Word; this man, joined and associated with him, shares his honor. Therefore we do not say that there are two sons or two lords, because, while the one who is Lord and Son according to essence is manifest, the one assumed for our salvation, having an inseparable [Col. 1044D] union and association with him, is counted together with him, both in designation and in the honor of Son and Lord—not as each of us, existing from himself, is called a son of God, whence we are also called many sons of God, according to the blessed apostle Paul (Gal. 3:26). Rather, this man, possessing this singularly because he is joined to God the Word and sharing in the dignity of Son and in dominion, entirely removes the conception of two lords and sons; and he grants us, through our union with God the Word, every faith, understanding, and contemplation, and for this reason receives veneration from every creature through his association with God.

7. Therefore we call Jesus Christ one God and Lord, through whom all things were made, understanding primarily God the Word, who according to essence is Son of God and Lord; and likewise also considering the one who was assumed, Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power (Acts 10:38), as having union with God the Word and sharing in the dignity of Son and Lord.

8. He is also called the second Adam, as the blessed apostle Paul bears witness (1 Cor. 15:45). As though he were of the same nature as Adam, he revealed to us the future state, while having as great a difference from that Adam as ought to exist between the one who will be the giver and minister of such future blessings and the one who introduced the beginning of present sorrows for us. For this reason he is similarly called the second Adam, as one who proclaimed the second state.

And because the Lord Christ, appearing from heaven and destined to bring us all into familiar communion with himself, revealed the future second state in contrast to that former state—mortal, subject to suffering, and full of many evils—in which we received likeness to him and of which Adam became the beginning. “The first man,” he says, “was from the earth, earthly; the second man, the Lord, from heaven” (ibid., 47)—that is, he is to be seen from there so that he may lead us to imitate him. Hence he adds: “As was the earthly, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (ibid., 48).

In this man, he says, who appears and is seen by all, the divine nature will render judgment upon those who are to be judged, according to the apostle Paul, who says: “God, having overlooked the times of our ignorance, now commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has established a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, by the man whom he appointed, giving assurance to all by raising him from the dead” (Acts 17:30).

9. This is the doctrine of ecclesiastical teachings; and therefore let anyone who thinks contrary to these things be anathema.

## REFUTATION OF THE THEODORIAN CREED BY MERCATOR

[Col. 1045]

[Col. 1045B] 1. Rather, we Catholics declare to you and to all who agree with you an unending anathema—you who have uttered such things with the foulest mouth and most wicked tongue. Consider, if you are willing to awaken, what evil you are attempting to introduce. Whether through ignorance or malice, you must decide.

2. These words of yours are perjured, with their most perverse meaning hostile to Catholic truth. You say that God the Word assumed a man, perfect from the seed of Abraham and David, constituted from a rational soul and body; and that this man, naturally a man like us, was fashioned by the power and might of the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb, made from a woman, made under the law, so that he might redeem us all from the curse and slavery of the law, receiving the adoption of sons predestined long ago (Gal. 3:13); that he joined and united him to himself in an ineffable manner, preparing him to experience death according to the law of human beings, but raising him from the dead, lifting him into heaven, and making him sit at the right hand of God (ibid.). And shortly afterward: “He received worship from every creature, as one having an inseparable union with the divine nature.”

3. Do you therefore intend to construct from this meaning—which, indeed, you should recognize as being spoken against your own head [Correction: “which you should know was spoken against your own head”]—that Christ, already born from the Virgin through the Holy Spirit, adhered or was joined, as you constantly babble, to the Word of God, God; and that from his association he acquired merit and the designation; and that he should be called Son of God in name only, not by nature, possessing the other privileges not as genuine ones but as bestowed by grace? You suppress what is written: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

When this is brought against you, you slander your opponents as though they believed that God had been changed into flesh. Far be it from anyone—even the most deranged—to say or think this. For God the Word, who was not man, became man, the Son of God, without laying aside what he was, but remaining God in the substance or nature of the Godhead, with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

4. For does a soul—even that of any human being—when mixed and joined to a body lose either the immortality of its nature or the fact that it is invisible and incorporeal? Certainly not.

[Col. 1046C] 5. To this most empty and futile slander we must also oppose the utterly faithful and sacred account of the three angels who descended at the destruction of Sodom. It shows that Abraham received them, and that they ate and washed their feet (Gen. 18:1). Are they to be said, in assuming those bodies, to have been changed and transformed from an angelic substance into the nature of bodies? May God avert such madness! Certainly not. Remaining in their immortal and incorporeal nature and substance, they were temporarily present in bodies and fulfilled the divinely commanded duty assigned to them.

6. Who, then, could tolerate someone babbling such things, and hear him verbally protest—merely to deceive the simple—that he does not say there are two sons, while in his explicit statements plainly displaying two: of different merit, different dignity, different condition, and different nature?

7. Yet, as we said, he deceives and misleads the ignorant. For how does he say that he neither speaks of nor believes in two sons, while separating one from the other—one temporal, the other eternal according to essence and nature—and claiming that the temporal one is to be honored through participation and in name only, but is not by nature the Son of God and God? For he separates their respective conditions [Col. 1047A] and merits, wishing one to be by nature what the other is through union and association with the one who is by nature God and Son of God.

8. He ought surely to have remembered the saying of the apostle Paul: “I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites. To them belong the adoption, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, the glory, and the promises; to them belong the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, Christ was born, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:3).

He is certainly God over all, who according to the flesh has his origin among the Israelites, from the seed of Abraham and David, through the Virgin’s womb. For we have learned from the Gospel that “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14). From that time onward, neither the weak and fragile things of humanity nor the divine, sublime, and eternal things are to be separated from any person or substance [correction: “one”].

9. He ought to have heard Isaiah proclaiming: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us, whose rule is upon his shoulder; and he will be called Wonderful, Messenger of great counsel, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His kingdom will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace; upon the throne of David his father and over his kingdom, to establish and strengthen it in judgment and righteousness, from now and forever. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this” (Isa. 9:6–7).

10. This is the mighty God—namely, the one who was a child, unquestionably the one wrapped in swaddling clothes at Bethlehem and placed in a manger, the one worshiped by the Magi, the one who afterward went to Egypt with his parents, so that, according to another prophet’s proclamation, he might be called from Egypt. The prophet says: “Out of Egypt I called my Son” (Hos. 11:1).

11. Jeremiah, too, should be thrust into his face as he cries out: “This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him. He discovered every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:35–38).

12. Let us be told, I ask, who this one is who afterward appeared on earth and lived among human beings. Certainly it is the Word of God, God man and man God, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of the Father. While he was present on earth in the flesh and visibly lived among human beings in that same flesh, he suffered from human beings in it, was crucified in it, died in it, and rose again in it on the third day; in that same flesh he will come as judge to judge the living and the dead.

The whole of this is by nature the Son of God, from God the Word and man, with a rational soul and solid, perfect flesh. These three substances are now one substance and likewise one person. For God substantially assumed and bore the man, having thereby become flesh without change; he neither laid him aside nor will he ever lay him aside—the one who reigns and exercises lordship with him.

13. What duality of natures, what diversity of substances, is being brought before us with great and impious loquacity in the one Lord Christ? Clearly, so that we may hear that there are two Christs and two different sons of God.

And certainly an ordinary human being, constituted from soul and body—from unquestionably different substances and natures, namely bodily and spiritual, gross and subtle, visible and invisible, mortal and immortal—comes together into one, not contrary to nature but naturally and by God’s institution. God decreed and arranged that he should be so once and from the beginning and forever. Therefore, when a human being exists and is called a human being, there is one nature, one substance, and one person.

14. Nor did the apostle Paul, when he said, “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man, the Lord, from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:47), and elaborated further on the other matters in the same context, indicate that he was double or that there were two natures in him. Nor did the one who said, “When a man was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13), mention two natures in him.

15. Nor must we omit what was said in Genesis: “Jacob went down into Egypt with his sons, all seventy-five souls” (Gen. 46:27). Likewise the prophet: “All my souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins, it alone shall die. And the one who has eaten the sour grape—his teeth shall be set on edge” (Ezek. 18:4, 20).

Another prophet says: “Bless the Lord, my soul” (Ps. 145:1), and “all my bones shall speak praise to you” (Ps. 35:10). On the side of the body: “My Spirit,” he says, “shall not remain with these human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3). Another says: “My flesh rejoiced in hope” (Ps. 15:9), and elsewhere: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6).

Would these things happen to them without souls? Or, because only souls were mentioned above, were they separated from the association of the body in good or bad merits? What utterly deranged person would say this? Certainly not. Rather, as long as the two are joined and connected to one another, the nature—that is, human nature or the nature of a human being—is stated and signified naturally, not in duality but in unity.

16. Therefore, no person of sound mind, when a living human being suffers adversity or rejoices in fulfilled desires, should say that he is not constituted from both, or that he suffers pain or rejoices in happiness, since no one doubts that the soul, in its own nature and proper substance, is not affected by pain. Divine Scripture also teaches us this more clearly, saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28).

17. What need is there to heap up more testimonies? Or what end will there be to searching them out? Or who ever was or will be able to examine everything and mention everything by which it could be proved that this man has spoken impiously not in a novel way, but in the manner of the ancient teachings—partly of Paul of Samosata, partly of Ebion, partly of Marcellus of Galatia, and of Photinus?

Let him nevertheless hear, in place of innumerable testimonies, one Gospel passage of massive force [Gerb. “let him hear it cry out”; Baluzius deletes “passage”]: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

And certainly Christ said this while he was still to be crucified: “The Son of Man who descended from heaven,” he says, “and who is in heaven.” Thus God the Word-man and man-God the Word is one, just as he is one in the glory and majesty of God, so also he is one in the things that are lowly according to man.

And there is one Lord Jesus Christ from the womb, who substantially, as Son of God, is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit: one God in the Trinity, forever and ever.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE CREED AND ITS REFUTATION

[Col. 1049]

[Col. 1049A] 1. Two general councils remembered this creed: the Council of Ephesus, in its sixth session, and the Second Council of Constantinople, in its fourth session. Among the ancients, besides Mercator, it was also remembered by Cyril in his letter to John of Antioch and to the Eastern Synod; by Pope Vigilius in his Constitutum; by the Emperor Justinian in his book for the Acephali; by Facundus of Hermiane in Book 3, chapters 2 and 5; by Leontius Scholasticus in Book 3 Against the Nestorians, section 18; and by others.

Among more recent writers it was likewise remembered by Manuel Calecas in Book 2 Against the Greeks; Bellarmine in Book 3 On Christ, chapter 5; Petavius in volume 4 of the Dogmas, Book 1; and Christian Lupus in volume 1 of his Scholia on the Canons of the General Councils, in several places, but especially on page 774.

2. Yet no one remembers it without also rejecting it: either as containing nothing sound, as Cyril did; or as impious, Judaic, and criminal, as Leontius did; or as composed by Satan, as did the Fathers of the Fifth Synod, and so forth.

The Third Synod, that is, the Council of Ephesus, proscribed it in its sixth session:

“If any persons are found—whether bishops, clerics, or laypeople—either to hold or to teach the doctrines contained in the exposition presented by Charisius the presbyter concerning the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God, and so forth, let them be subject to the sentence of this holy and universal synod.”

The Fifth Synod also proscribed it. For after the impious creed had been read, the holy synod exclaimed: “Satan composed this creed. Anathema to the one who composed this creed. The First Synod of Ephesus anathematized this creed together with its author,” and so forth.

Cyril, in his letter to Proclus, says: “Let your holiness know that, when the exposition composed by him was presented before the holy synod, as those who presented it said, containing nothing sound, the holy synod rejected it as being full of perverse interpretations and as full of perverse interpretations and as gushing forth (πηγάζουσαν) Nestorian impiety.”

[Col. 1049C] When Mercator prepared to refute the creed, whose concluding clause was: “This is the doctrine of ecclesiastical teachings, and therefore let anyone who thinks contrary to these things be anathema,” he immediately added: “Rather, we Catholics declare to you and to all who agree with you an unending anathema—you who have uttered such things with the foulest mouth and most wicked tongue.”

The Emperor Justinian—or whoever wrote under Justinian’s name the book against the Acephali that Facundus refuted—says: “Nevertheless, so that all Christians, recognizing Theodore’s madness, may not be carried away by his impious doctrines, we have inserted in this present book, from the blasphemies he composed in the creed fabricated by him, the passages that stand in his own discourses” (apud Facundus, Book 3, chapter 5).

Leontius says: “It stands against the original instruction of the Christian religion and removes from those who are regenerated their deifying creed—that is, the faith of the Council of Nicaea—not merely mutilating it, but utterly destroying the whole faith and handing down another in its place, treating as nothing those great lights and having no horror of so audacious a crime. For, as I have said, he publishes another creed of faith—or rather, I should call it of faithlessness.”

The doctrines of the creed that destroy the original faith of the Christian religion are sufficiently demonstrated by the authors just mentioned. Since the faith chiefly consists in the Trinity of the divine persons, the incarnation of the Word, and the grace of Christ, some accuse it of three errors concerning the Trinity of the divine persons; others, of an equal number concerning the incarnation of the Word; and in the final dissertation on the first part of Mercator’s works, we identified a third kind of error concerning the grace of Christ, or the purpose and effect of the incarnation.

Recent writers almost universally accuse the words found in section 3 concerning the Holy Spirit: “We do not think that he is the Son or that he received his existence through the Son.” Manuel Calecas attempts to draw these words into a favorable meaning, as though they said that the Holy Spirit did not receive his existence through the Word in the same way as every created thing does, but his kindly interpretation—or violence—achieved very little.

Others accuse the creed, though Facundus does not mention their names, because it seems to introduce a fourth person into the Trinity. For although section 5 had said, “We believe in God the Father, and in the only-begotten Son of God, and in the Holy Spirit,” it then speaks of the Lord Jesus Christ, in whom we are certainly required to believe as though he were different from the other three. But the objection is futile.

In the book published under Justinian’s name, Sabellianism is charged against the author of the creed, as though he now introduced not a fourth person but contracted the other three into one. The words in section 4 appear to have supplied the occasion for the objection: “We confess the Father perfect in person, and likewise the Son, and likewise the Holy Spirit,” and so forth. After quoting these words, the author of the book adds: “The hearer must observe that, when he says SIMILARLY and LIKEWISE with reference to the person of the Holy Trinity, he appears, according to the madness of Sabellius, to assert one person of the three names of the Holy Trinity.” Facundus easily dispelled an objection of this kind, which is certainly not particularly serious.

The Council of Ephesus condemns the entire creed as contrary to the Catholic faith concerning the incarnation of the Only-Begotten, and, in Cyril’s words, as the source from which Nestorian impiety springs. Hence Mercator hands down that its author spoke impiously not in a novel way, but partly in the manner of Paul of Samosata, partly of Ebion, partly of Marcellus of Galatia, and of Photinus.

[Col. 1050C] Mercator therefore censures Theodore, first, because in the creed he makes Christ a mere man and a son of God, saying that he is not Son by nature but by adoption or grace; second, because he openly proclaims two actual Christs; third, because he denies that the evangelist’s words, “The Word became flesh,” can be received in their proper sense unless the Word is said to have been changed into flesh.

He demonstrates these points at length, but adds another, arising, I think, more from an anticipated opinion than from a firm collection of evidence. For he charges the author of the creed with asserting that the man was first formed by the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb and existed before he adhered to the Word, and that through his union with the Word he became worshipful to every creature.

Yet it is established by sound reasoning and by Theodore’s unquestionable testimonies that, at the very conception, there existed a συνάφεια [union] of the Word and the human nature, of precisely the kind Theodore admitted. For what could be clearer than either that statement of Theodore which Mercator himself adduces in excerpt 3: “He was secretly joined to the same one, for he was not absent when he was formed; he was not divided when he was born,” and so forth; or the statement Facundus uses to repel the accusation (Book 3, chapter 5): “It is especially good at this point to conclude what force belongs to the things that have been said, whether ‘living together,’ or ‘being baptized,’ or ‘being crucified,’ or also ‘dying,’ or ‘being buried,’ and ‘rising again.’ We do not apply these things to some mere man. For in demonstrating each of the things mentioned, we do not hesitate to add this, so that we may provide no opportunity for slanderers to speak evil; but the Word, having indeed indwelt him, did so from the very formation in his mother’s womb.”

Finally, from the words of section 8 we inferred that Theodore indicates, not obscurely, that the grace of Christ, on account of which he came into this world, is nothing other than either teaching or example.

As far as I know, Facundus was the first to raise the question of the author. Since the judgment of the ancients concerning Theodore was established, Facundus dared to dissent, lest the man whom he was attempting to clear of heresy should immediately be convicted from the creed itself, against the Fifth Synod. I am surprised that men of great reputation—Manuel Calecas, Bellarmine, and Petavius—followed Facundus in making Nestorius the author. How could they either disregard the judgment of the Fifth Synod, when Facundus scarcely produced anything in his own defense, or fail to heed Leontius, who carefully pursued each of Theodore’s statements? I say nothing about Mercator, whose works [Col. 1052A] were hidden at that time but, now published, no longer permit doubt.

Nestorius used his teacher’s creed to spread his heresy. He arranged for it to be subscribed by people returning from heresy to the Church, as though it were a mere exposition of the Nicene or Constantinopolitan faith. He carried this out through two agents of his impiety, Anastasius and Photius, who sent two other presbyters, Antonius and James of Philadelphia, to reconcile the Quartodecimans and induce as many as they could to subscribe.

But Charisius, presbyter and steward of the Church of Philadelphia, having detected what was happening, reported the entire matter to the Council of Ephesus. The whole story is narrated at length in its sixth session.

## THE WORDS OF MARIUS MERCATOR

[Col. 1051]

Let us demonstrate from his writings, which we translated from Greek, what kind of faithlessness the aforementioned Theodore also possessed.

## EXCERPTS FROM THEODORE OF MOPSUESTIA

[Col. 1051]

### FIRST EXCERPT

From the fourth book of the second volume of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, on folio 10, against Saint Augustine, who defended original sin and argued in Catholic fashion that Adam was made mortal through transgression.

[Col. 1051B]

1. Although there are so many things demonstrating that Adam was formed from the earth in such a way that he was entirely mortal, he nevertheless chose to engage in a discussion concerning the food proper to him. Unable thereafter to perceive the truth, he attached a defense based on a deceptive falsehood in place of doctrine. God did not say, “You will be mortal,” but, “You will surely die” (Gen. 2:17).

2. Since they were entirely mortal by nature, God threatened to impose upon them the experience of death, which, in accordance with the customary manner of his kindness, he also delayed bringing about. For when he says, “Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed in return” (Gen. 9:6), he does not mean that whoever kills a human being will become mortal, but that he is worthy to be condemned to such a death.

So also here he said, “You will surely die,” not that they would then become mortal, but that through transgression they would be worthy to receive the sentence of death [Baluzius: “on account of transgression”].

3. But observe also the divine sentence which God appears to impose upon Adam after the sin. For he says: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I commanded you, saying, ‘From this alone you shall not eat,’ you have eaten from it; cursed is the earth in your labors. In sorrow you shall eat it all the days of your life. It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the grass of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread until you return to the earth” (Gen. 3:17–19).

By these words he threatened that Adam would lead a sorrowful life, thereafter obtaining with labor from the earth the fruits by which he would be nourished and sustained, no longer possessing, as previously, so great an abundance as he had enjoyed from the plenty of paradise.

For God did not impose working the earth as a punishment, as though transferring human beings from an immortal nature into mortality, since he had also assigned paradise to him “to work it and keep it” (Gen. 2:15). Rather, in place of his former great abundance and the pleasure of paradise, he threatened that his sustenance from the fruits of the earth would be sorrowful.

For he was already entirely mortal and then needed the fruits of paradise, just as now he seeks the fruits of the earth; and as punishment, deprived of his former delights, he is chastised by this most sorrowful and laborious way of life.

4. Hence, in conclusion, he added consistently: “For you are earth, and you will return to earth” (Gen. 3:19). Here too he signifies the mortality of his nature. He did not impose this name upon one who was immortal and only then beginning to receive a sentence of death, as those most wise defenders of original sin—or rather, those remarkable fathers of sin—assert.

Rather, divine Scripture indicated that this designation appropriately belongs to one who was naturally made mortal from the beginning. It repeatedly applies this term to human beings to display their corruptible and dissoluble nature. For it says: “He remembered that we are dust. A human being’s days are like grass; like a flower of the field, so he will blossom, because the spirit has passed through him, and his place will no longer be” (Ps. 102:14–16).

It means that we are all corruptible and dissoluble, like grass that blossoms briefly and soon perishes. For we live only a short time, and thereafter arrive altogether at nonexistence.

So too Abraham says: “I am earth and ashes” (Gen. 18:27), as though he were saying: “I am not worthy to converse with so great a God—a man made from earth and destined to become entirely this.”

Therefore, if human nature were only then becoming mortal, he ought rather to have said, “You will be earth, and you will return to earth.”

### SECOND EXCERPT

From the same Theodore, from the third book of the second volume, four folios before the end of the book.

1. But that remarkable defender of original sin could perceive none of these things, since he had never been trained in the divine Scriptures, nor from childhood learned the sacred writings, in accordance with the words of the blessed Paul (2 Tim. 3:15). Whether declaiming about the meanings of Scripture or about doctrine, he frequently and shamelessly brought forth many foolish statements concerning the Scriptures themselves and numerous doctrines, both in particular and generally.

For the influence of authority [Baluzius: “fear”] permitted no one to speak against him; only those who possessed knowledge of the divine Scriptures silently criticized him [perhaps: “withdrew themselves”].

Finally, he fell into this novel doctrine, saying that God, in anger and fury, had decreed Adam to be mortal, and that on account of his one offense he had condemned all human beings—even those not yet born—to death.

In arguing this way, he is neither ashamed nor embarrassed to hold views about God that no one has ever attempted to attribute even to human beings of sound judgment who possess some concern for justice.

Nor did he remember that divine utterance which says that this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth have been set on edge”; for thus says the Lord God: “The teeth of the one who has eaten the sour grape shall be set on edge” (Ezek. 18:2). By this he demonstrates that God does not at all punish one person for another’s offense, according to the error of certain people, but that each person must render an account for his own sins.

2. The blessed Paul also adds statements agreeing with these: “God,” he says, “will repay each person according to his works” (Rom. 2:6). And: “Each of us will bear his own burden” (Gal. 6:5). And: “Why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ” (Rom. 14:10).

[Col. 1053C] 3. Yet this remarkable man thought that God had been so violently enraged on account of one sin that he subjected Adam to the most terrible punishment and promulgated an equal sentence against all his descendants. Among them there have been so many righteous people that no one could easily count them.

He ought especially to have considered how utterly incongruous it would seem for Noah, Abraham, David, Moses, and the countless other righteous people to have been made liable to punishment on account of his [perhaps: “one”] offense; and that, because of one sin established merely by the tasting of a tree [perhaps: “sin”], God had extended his anger beyond every measure of justice, casting aside all the virtues of so many righteous people and subjecting them to such a punishment—
might enslave.

4. For even if he considered nothing else, at least by reflecting on Abel he ought reasonably to have judged that he—the first to be righteous—was the first to die; and if God had ordained death as a punishment for human beings, how could it not have been the height of impiety that the one who had been the cause of sin should live, and that Eve, the discoverer of wickedness, should live with him as well? I pass over the devil, who has continued to enjoy immortality down to the present, while the first righteous man, the discoverer of virtue and the first to undertake the care of divine worship, was struck down before all sinners by punishment.

5. It was also necessary for that most wise man to consider carefully Enoch, who did not die. For he was not endowed with such virtue or piety that he surpassed everyone else—Moses, I mean, and the prophets, and the apostles, or all the others of whom the most blessed Paul says, “of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. XI, 37)—so that, while they had died, he alone should continue without experiencing death. Rather, from the beginning God had determined this within himself: that mortals should first become mortal, but afterward rejoice in immortality; and he himself arranged this for our benefit.

And a little later:

6. “God,” he says, “showed these same things more plainly when he transferred Enoch and made him immortal. For if God had brought death upon humanity as the cause of punishment on account of sin, and had not long ago determined this within himself, ordering everything ineffably for our sake according to his own wisdom, Enoch certainly would not have been immortal, but the Lord Christ would have come to experience death.”

And a little later:

7. “For this reason,” he says, “the Lord became the author of all good things for human beings: just as Adam was the initiator of the first and mortal condition, so he himself, existing as the initiator of the second and immortal condition, first preserved the natural features of the former Adam, being born of a woman, being wrapped in swaddling clothes, and gradually receiving the increases of age. For Jesus,” he says, “advanced in age and wisdom and grace before God and human beings” (Luke II, 52). He received circumcision; according to legal custom he stood before God in the temple; he was subject to his parents and devoted to the lawful manner of life. In the same way, in order to complete the remaining things, he finally accepted death, as something owed to nature, so that, dying according to the law of human nature and rising from the dead by divine power, he might become the beginning for all human beings who accept death according to their own nature, so that they may rise from the dead and be transformed into an immortal substance.

8. For just as we have all been made conformed to Adam according to the present condition, so in the future we shall be made conformed to Christ the Lord [Baluz. adds: “according to the flesh”]. “He will transform the body of our humiliation, so that it may be conformed to the glory of his body” (Philipp. III, 21). And: “As is the earthly one, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly” (I Cor. XV, 48). And: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly.” He thereby shows that, having become partakers of Adam’s first condition, we necessarily also attain a share in the future condition of the second Adam, Christ the Lord, according to the flesh: for he arose from this same nature and received everything that belonged to nature. For this reason he endured death, so that, accepting death as something belonging to nature and rising from the dead, he might perfect nature as free from death.

9. He accepted death for this reason, but by no means sin; rather, he remained entirely free from it. For whatever belonged to nature—that is, death—he unquestionably assumed; but sin, which did not belong to nature but to the will, he accepted in no way. And if sin had been in nature, then, according to the statement of this most wise man, he would necessarily have assumed sin as something wholly existing in nature.

### THIRD EXCERPT

The same Theodore, from the second codex, book three, folio eighteen.

[Col. 1055A]

1. “If God did not know that Adam would sin” [Baluz. “truly knew”], “let the answer of these most wise men be that it is utterly insane even to conceive such a thing in thought. It is clear that he knew Adam would sin, and therefore undoubtedly that he would die. How, then, is it not the height of madness to believe that at first he made him immortal” [Baluz. “mortal”] “for six hours—for that was the length of time from his creation until the transgression, since he was made from earth on the sixth day and, having eaten contrary to the divine command, was expelled from paradise—and that afterward he displayed him as mortal through sin?” [Col. 1055B]

2. For it is certain that, if he had wished to make him immortal, even the intervening sin would not have changed God’s judgment, since God did not make the devil mortal from immortal, although the devil was the source of all evils.

### FOURTH EXCERPT

The same Theodore, from the second codex, book three, folio twenty-five.

[Col. 1056A]

1. “For,” he says, “if he hands over to punishments without end and without correction those who lived from Adam until the coming of Christ the Lord amid such impieties and injustices as the blessed Paul expressed in his own words, as has been demonstrated above from his statements, what great reward of resurrection will he be thought to confer? For when will resurrection be regarded as a gift, if punishment without correction is inflicted upon those who rise?”

And a little later:

2. “Who is so mad as to believe that so great a good becomes the material for infinite punishment for those who rise? It would have been more beneficial for them not to rise at all than, after the resurrection, to endure the experience of such and so many evils under infinite punishments.” [Col. 1056B]

### FIFTH EXCERPT

The same Theodore, from some other book [Note: [Col. 1055B]

Theodore wrote almost innumerable works, as we learn from Facundus, Leontius, and other ancient writers, and from Theodore himself. Nevertheless, Mercator excerpted what he now presents from three works: namely, from the books written against Augustine, from the book *To the Baptized*, and from the books entitled *On the Incarnation*. The first work, since it pertains to the Pelagian controversy, was discussed in the first part of Mercator’s works; nevertheless, it seemed appropriate to publish it again here, so that the sequence of Mercator’s words might be clearer. Nothing of particular relevance is known about the second. The last is now under consideration.

Baluzius transcribes this title differently, namely: “The same Theodore, from the eighth catechetical sermon, folio seven,” and adds the following notes:

“The same Theodore. The following material is not found in the Italian edition. This title was added from the Vatican codex, since it is absent from the Bellovacensis. Nevertheless, Garnerius set down this title as though it existed in ancient copies: ‘The same Theodore, from some other book against the Lord Jesus Christ and his incarnation.’ He immediately notes that Theodore entitled these last books *Περὶ ἐνανθρωπήσεως τοῦ Μονογενοῦς*—‘On the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten’—but since in them the basis of the true incarnation is not explained but overturned, Mercator preferred to write ‘against the Lord and his incarnation.’ Yet the truth of this is disproved by the genuine title of the following fragment, recovered from the Vatican codex.”

“*Catacismi*, or *catechismi*, as is clear from Facundus, who in book IX, chapter 3, reports the opening lines of this fragment from another version and says that they were taken from the *Book to the Baptized*. But in the fourth collation of the fifth council, *Ad baptizandos*—‘To Those Being Baptized’—is consistently written, not only in the editions but also in ancient manuscripts written by hand; this seems preferable.” EDIT.]

from some other book [Note: [Col. 1055D]

Theodore entitled these last books *Περὶ ἐνανθρωπήσεως τοῦ Μονογενοῦς*—“On the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten”—but since in them the basis of the true incarnation is not explained but overturned, Mercator preferred to write “against the Lord and his incarnation.”

That work was indeed dense and extensive, comprising fifteen thousand lines in fifteen books. Facundus is witness to the number of books; Theodore himself gives the number of lines in the preface to his work *On Apollinarius and His Heresy* (Book IX, chapter 3), where he recounts the whole history of this labor and complains that his opponents corrupted it by inserting material that would provoke hostility against the doctrine of the two sons. “Nearly thirty years ago,” he says, “we composed a book on the incarnation of the Lord extending to fifteen thousand lines, in which throughout the whole work we examined Arius’ and Eunomius’ errors on this matter, as well as Apollinarius’ vain presumption, so that, in my judgment, I might omit nothing that pertained either to strengthening ecclesiastical orthodoxy or to convicting their impiety.

“But those who rashly presume everything, and who had moreover been instructed by Apollinarius, the founder of this heresy, made our work known to everyone, in case they could find anything capable of refuting what was written in it. Since no one dared to undertake the contest against us in writing, they imitated weak and cunning athletes who, unable to contend against stronger opponents, try to overthrow them by whatever ambushes and devices they can.

“For they themselves undoubtedly wrote among one another certain foolish things that we would never have said. Finally, they inserted these very things into a certain section of our writings and showed them to their associates, and sometimes also to our people, who in their simplicity listened to everything with receptive minds. They offered this as evidence, as they thought, of our impiety. One of these written statements was that there are two sons.

“Thus it was necessary for those writings to appear not only foolish but also weak to their hearers, since they could be demonstrated neither by sound reasoning nor by appropriate argument; and for that reason they had been written by those weak men, so that the one who had written them might more easily be convicted on their basis.

“One of our own, because of his excessive simplicity, believed that these writings were ours. For this reason they considered him trustworthy enough to read them, and he reported to us what had been written. When we heard this, we did indeed rebuke him for having believed statements made against us concerning matters about which he had often heard us speak both in church and privately; he ought to have judged our spoken word more trustworthy than the writings, as evidence of our position, which it is our purpose to preserve in matters of doctrine” (Facundus, Book X, chapter 1).

From this it may be understood what Gennadius relates concerning Theodore, presbyter of the Church of Antioch, who wrote fifteen books against the Apollinarians and Eunomians on the incarnation of the Lord, comprising fifteen thousand lines. In them, with the purest reasoning and testimonies from Scripture, he demonstrated that the Lord Jesus possessed the fullness of humanity just as he possessed the fullness of divinity. He also teaches that a human being consists of only two substances, namely soul and body, and that sensation and spirit are not another substance but innate functions of the soul, by which it breathes, is rational, and makes the body capable of sensation. He devoted the fourteenth book of this work specifically to discussing the uncreated, solely incorporeal, and sovereign nature of the holy Trinity, and the nature of created things, explaining it in a pious sense and with the authority of the holy Scriptures. In the fifteenth volume he confirmed and fortified the entire body of his work, citing also the traditions of the Fathers.

For he could not have been speaking of any other work or author, since the characteristics of the work that he reports correspond remarkably with those reported by Facundus and by Theodore himself.

It is therefore untrue that some, following Miraeus, say that this work should be attributed to Theodore of Raithu. For the Theodore of Raithu lived in the time of Maximus the martyr, that is, in the seventh century, whereas Gennadius lived at the end of the fifth; thus nearly 168 years intervened between them.

Nor is it true, as certain learned men think, that Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, was different from Theodore, presbyter of the Church of Antioch, whom Gennadius and Photius mention. For it is certain that the books which Gennadius and Photius attribute to the Antiochene were written by Theodore of Mopsuestia. Why, then, you may ask, is he called a presbyter of the Church of Antioch? It was the customary practice of that period to identify authors in books by the rank in which they had composed those books.

From these observations I conclude, first, that Theodore wrote the books *On the Incarnation* not only before he became bishop, and therefore before the year 394, when he first took his seat—for he wrote them as a presbyter and held the episcopal see for thirty-six years—but also before the year 390, since he testifies that he composed this book thirty years before writing *On Apollinarius and His Heresy*. He produced that work several years before his death; he died in the year 428, as Theodoret reports.

I further conclude that the account of Hesychius, presbyter of Jerusalem, in ecclesiastical history should be corrected. A fragment of it is quoted at the fifth synod (Collation 5). He says:

“Already weakened by advanced old age, if any spark of piety had perhaps existed in him, and that spark having grown old, he presumed to compose books against the manifestation of the Lord God. Passing over their multitude—for it is not lawful to reread impious discourses—let us now mention one.” He is in fact dealing with this very work, since he reports something of Theodore in the mystical discourses; and the mystical discourses undoubtedly do not differ from the book *On the Incarnation*, since Facundus quotes from the thirteenth mystical book what was written in the book *On the Incarnation* concerning Paul of Samosata.]

against the Lord Jesus Christ and his incarnation.

1. [Note: [Col. 1056C]

Facundus shows which book Mercator excerpted for the material that he attributes to Theodore. He says as follows (Book IX, chapter 3):

“This man”—Theodore—“knew that Christ, coming in the manifestation of the flesh, was the maker of the world and its rightful Lord. By saying that Christ has two natures, he did not say that there are two sons, or two lords, or two Christs, as the heretics falsely claim. For he spoke plainly in the *Book to the Baptized*:

‘For if we say that there are two natures, no necessity compels us either to say that there are two sons, or two lords, or two Christs, since to think this is the height of madness.’

It should further be observed that Mercator follows Theodore’s footsteps. Just as Theodore does here in this book what he did in the creed, so Mercator now does the very thing he did in his refutation of the creed. He demonstrates that Theodore introduces two sons of God: one by nature, who is eternal; the other by adoption, who is temporal. Thus the Son of the Virgin, or Emmanuel, or Christ, is in reality a mere human being, united to the Word by *σχέσις* (*schesis*, relational association) alone, just as the saints and prophets are united to God.”]

“For,” he says, “if we say that there are two natures in Christ, it does not necessarily follow that we assert two sons or two lords, since to think this is rightly judged the height of madness. For all things that are two in one respect and one in another are not, by their unity, deprived of the distinction between the two: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John X, 30). Yet because they are one, the distinct property of each is not to be denied.

“And elsewhere, speaking of man and wife, he says: ‘They are no longer two, but one flesh’ (Matt. XIX, 6). Yet because man and wife are one flesh, they are not thereby no longer two [Baluz. adds: ‘but one flesh’]. They remain two insofar as they are two, and one insofar as they are one.

“In this way, here too there are two by nature, but one by conjunction: two by nature, because there is a diversity of natures [read: ‘of natures’]; but one by conjunction, because what has been assumed shares an undivided veneration with the one who assumes it, remaining his indivisible temple.”

2. [Note: [Col. 1058C]

Nothing more cunning could have been said for dialectical purposes. The teachers of that art say that things do not enter into a number unless they have the same denomination, and that they do not have the same denomination unless they possess the same form in the same way; Aristotle calls this *οὐσία κατὰ τοὔνομα* (*ousia kata t’ounoma*, “substance according to the name”). From this principle Theodore infers: therefore, although the Word and the human being are not united *καθ’ ὑπόστασιν* (*kath’ hypostasin*, “according to hypostasis”), but only *σχέσει* (*schēsei*, “by relation”), nevertheless they cannot be called two sons or two lords. For although they possess the same form of sonship and denomination, they do not possess it in the same way: the Word possesses it by nature, the human being by conjunction alone. Hence, when the expression “Son of God” or “Lord of all” is heard, the Word is understood in himself, *κυρίως* (*kyriōs*, “properly”) and simply, while the human being is understood *κατά τι* (*kata ti*, “in a certain respect”) and *ὁμωνύμως* (*homōnymōs*, “equivocally/homonymously”).]

“For all things that are called two contain the notion of two when one is believed to be indifferent from the other, in accordance with which they receive the name and enumeration of two. For example, divine Scripture mentions four beasts (Dan. VII): a bear, a leopard, a lion, and another that surpasses these in ferocity. They are four because each beast is shown to exist, in substance, as no less than the other beasts.

“‘The testimony of two men is true’ (John VIII, 17), because each is by nature what the other is. Likewise: ‘No one can serve two masters’ (Matt. VI, 24), because, for the one who renders service as to a master, each is no less a master.

“Thus here too, if each were by substance both son and lord, they could in some way be called two sons and two lords, according to the number of persons. But since one exists by substance as son and lord, while the other is not shown by essence to be either son or lord, yet is recognized as having shared in those things through the conjunction made between him and the other, we therefore speak of one son and one lord.

“Primarily, when we understand ‘son’ and ‘lord,’ we mean the one who is believed and proved truly to be both according to substance; but in our thought we also embrace the one who is inseparably joined to him and is considered, through an ineffable union with him, to share in sonship and lordship.

“Thus, wherever divine Scripture mentions this son who has been assumed, we say, by reference to the one who assumes him and in accordance with the unity, that he is called son.” [Col. 1059A]

[Note: [Col. 1059A]

In the fifth synod this section (*περικοπή*, “extract”) is said to have been excerpted from Theodore’s book *To Those Being Baptized*; Facundus writes *To the Baptized*. The fifth synod itself favors Facundus, for in excerpt 36 it says: “He was reborn and became another, no longer the changeable part of Adam,” and so forth; these words are in the past tense, not the future.

Since this kind of fragment is connected in an unbroken sequence of discourse with the first fragment, which Facundus excerpted from the same book, it is clear that everything intermediate belongs to the book *To the Baptized*.

See what judgment Pope Vigilius delivers concerning this fragment of Theodore in his *Constitutum*, no. 35.]

“For when he says, ‘Concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh’ (Rom. I, 3),” [Note: [Col. 1059B] “It is clear from the same *Constitutum* of Pope Vigilius and from the fifth council that *Deum*—‘God’—should not be read.” BALUZ.] “he does not yet mean the Word, but the form of a servant that was assumed. For he is not God according to the flesh, nor was God made from the seed of David—the one whom the blessed Paul clearly calls ‘Son.’

“We understand him as Son, not because he is called Son in himself, but because, through the conjunction that he has with the one who truly is Son, he is called this.”

3. [Note: [Col. 1059B]

I conclude that this fragment too belongs to the book *To the Baptized* because, after words of this kind and, with the connection preserved without interruption, these words undoubtedly follow: “so that he might take great care of him,” and so forth. In the fifth synod these are said to have been excerpted from the same book as the preceding material, namely, the book *To the Baptized*. We therefore thought they should be appended here (Excerpt 37):

“so that he might take great care of him; might make everything belonging to him his own and endure it; might lead him through all the passions by which he perfected him according to his own virtue; and, not departing from the dead according to the law of his nature, might by his presence, operation, and grace free him from death and the evils that arise from it; and might raise him from the dead and bring him to a better end.”]

“The Creator had mercy on the ruined creature and, without commixture, formed an infant; he brought him to mature age, introducing the likeness of nature through the progression of growth, according to the measure of belief. Yet, while secretly existing as joined to the same one, he was not absent when he was formed, was not divided when he was born, was joined to him while he spoke [Baluz. adds: ‘and’], remaining present in his actions and preserving there his connection without sin.”

4. [Note: [Col. 1059C]

A related passage is reported by Facundus from Book XIII *On the Incarnation*:

“It is good at this point above all to conclude what force the things that have been said possess, whether ‘to live,’ ‘to be baptized,’ ‘to be crucified,’ ‘to die,’ ‘to be buried,’ or ‘to rise again.’ We do not say these things by applying them to some ordinary human being. For in each demonstration of the things said we do not delay to add this, so that we may provide no opportunity for slanderers to speak evil.

“Rather, he was inhabited by God the Word from the very utterance in the womb of his mother; yet he was inhabited not according to ordinary inhabitation, nor according to the grace understood to exist in many, but according to a certain excellence, according to which we also say that the two natures were united and that, according to the union, they became one person.”

Leontius adduces another related passage from Book VII *On the Incarnation*:

“He possessed union with him immediately from the beginning, when he was being formed in the womb.”

And a little later:

“He also possessed an extraordinary inclination toward better things through the union with the Word, by which he was deemed worthy, through the foreknowledge of the Son of God, who united him to himself from the beginning.”

And afterward:

“It is clear that he exercised virtue with so much greater perfection and ease than the other human beings could exercise it, insofar as God, who had united him to himself at the beginning of his formation, supplied him with greater cooperation.”

From these passages—whether the one Mercator adduces in the text, or those adduced by Leontius or Facundus—it is clear that those who composed, in the name of the emperor Justinian, the book refuted by Facundus (Book III, chapter 2) were deceived. In it they wrote:

“For it is necessary to consider mentally that when the Apostle says of the one who signifies the person of the Word that he was in the form of God, which is in the essence of the Father, he did not say that the one who was in the form of a servant received this, so as to demonstrate the Word united to a preexistent human being according to the madness of Theodore and Nestorius.”

It is also clear that a popular opinion arose concerning the teaching of Theodore and Nestorius on this matter, either from certain statements of both that were not correctly understood, or, as I rather think, from the prejudice that both agreed with Paul of Samosata in this part of their error, since both agreed on the principal point: that Christ was in reality a mere human being.

“He advanced,” he says, “in age,” and so forth. I conjecture that this fragment, as well as the following one, was taken from Book X *On the Incarnation*, in which Theodore is abundant in gathering testimonies from Scripture to prove that a distinction must be maintained not only between the natures in Christ but also between the persons—or rather, the hypostases. For he often abused the term “person,” or *πρόσωπον* (*prosōpon*), which formerly among the Greeks, and indeed among the Latins, pertained more to conduct than, as they say, to physical realities.

For this reason he willingly confessed one person in Christ, although in reality he taught two hypostases, as is plainly evident from this fragment, both in Leontius’ frequently cited book and in the fifth synod, Collation 5:

“It is clear that unity is appropriate, for through it the natures brought together have formed one person according to unity. For just as it is said of a man and a woman that they are no longer two but one flesh, so let us also reasonably say, according to the principle of unity, that there are not two persons but one, with the natures distinct.

“For just as there it does not harm the number two that they are called one flesh—for it is certain that they are called one according to the respect in which they are one—so here too the unity of person does not harm the difference of the natures. For when we distinguish the natures, we speak of the perfect nature of God the Word and the perfect person; nor can one speak of a perfect subsistence without a person. Likewise, we speak of a perfect human nature and a perfect person. But when we look to the conjunction, then we speak of one person.”

See also the following fragment in Leontius, in which the same impiety is repeated by the same deception.

Moreover, it is clear from the fragments brought forward by Leontius, by the fifth synod, and by Facundus that Theodore was doing in Book X *On the Incarnation* what we have described.

Baluzius places before this fragment the title: “Diodore, bishop of Tarsus, dividing the divinity of Christ from his humanity,” and adds the following note:

“Diodore of Tarsus. This title, like the following ones”—the fragments that follow under numbers 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9 are also found under the name of the same Diodore in Baluzius—“was added from the Vatican codex. Since they were absent from the Bellovacensis, Garnerius consequently published what follows as though it belonged to Theodore of Mopsuestia, although it belongs to Diodore of Tarsus. Consequently, when that same Garnerius thought that the two preceding fragments were by Theodore of Mopsuestia, he conjectured that they had been taken from his tenth book *On the Incarnation*. But this conjecture now disappears.” EDIT.]

“Jesus,” he says, “advanced in age and wisdom” (Luke II, 52). But this cannot be said of the Word God [Baluz. “of God”], because perfect God was born from perfect God, wisdom from wisdom, power from power. He therefore does not advance, for he is not imperfect and does not need growth in order to attain perfection. [Note: [Col. 1061C] These words, or similar ones, seem to be missing: “Jesus advanced,” or “the human being advanced”; for otherwise, etc.] The Deity did not immediately bestow all its own wisdom upon him when he was formed or born; rather, it bestowed this wisdom upon the body little by little.

5. [Note: [Col. 1061C]

I suspect that this was taken from Book XV *On the Incarnation*, with which the entire work concludes, as Facundus says. Indeed, as Gennadius wrote, it was supported and strengthened by citations from the traditions of the Fathers; and, as may be gathered from other fragments, answers were supplied to certain customary questions.

I infer this from a fragment found in the fifth synod, where it is called a work without a book number; but in Leontius it bears the title “The Same, from Book XV.” It runs as follows:

“Let no one be deceived by the artifice of questions. For it is disgraceful to set aside such a cloud of witnesses, in accordance with what the Apostle said, and to be deceived by cunning questions into joining the party of one’s opponents.

“What are the questions they ask with skill? ‘Is Mary the mother of a human being or the mother of God?’ ‘Was the one who was crucified God or a human being?’ But these questions certainly have a settled answer,” and so forth.]

“Say to them,” he says, “‘The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me’ (Deut. XVIII, 15). God the Word is not from among the brothers. For a prophet is one who receives the grace of the Spirit and foretells the future, serving the Spirit in announcing what is to come. Who, then, is God the Word to whom he rendered service, or whose prophet was he shown to be? You see, therefore, that divine Scripture speaks cautiously.”

6. “I ask you,” he says, “pay attention. They say to us: ‘Why, then, do you separate?’ You answer, you who do not separate. Is God the Word in the last times? What do they say? Do you suppose they say this? Certainly not; he exists before the ages.

“And if he is before the ages, then that which is from David’s seed is before the ages, and David himself, from whom the seed comes, much more so. But David does not exist before the ages, for he is proved to be later than many human beings; and what is from David’s seed comes after twenty-eight generations from David.

“But if what was formed in the womb is before the ages and is not from the seed of David, then divine Scripture lies.”

7. [Note: [Col. 1061C]

Eusebius presents the portion of this fragment concerning the Virgin in his *Obtestation*, but Leontius reproduces it in full; both, however, derive it from Paul of Samosata. How, then, did Mercator attribute it to Theodore? Or perhaps Theodore copied it from Samosata? For it seems customary among the members of this faction to borrow from one another what they say.]

“The human being is anointed, Jesus our Lord; the Word is not anointed. For the Word is greater than Christ, since Christ was made great through wisdom. The Word is from above, but Jesus Christ the human being is from here below. Mary did not give birth to the Word,” [Note: [Col. 1061D] Garnerius, seeing that the sense was incomplete, supplied: “for Mary was not God.” Leontius has a better reading: “for Mary did not exist before the ages.” BALUZ.] “for Mary was not God” [Baluz. omits “God”], “but she gave birth to a human being like us, though better than us in every respect, because he was from the Holy Spirit.”

8. [Note: [Col. 1061D]

Leontius attributes this fragment to Diodore of Tarsus and says that it was excerpted from Book I *Against the Synousiasts*. From its Greek text Franciscus Turrianus translates as follows:

“Let me urge you to be fortified and firm for the careful examination of doctrines. The Son was perfect before the ages; the one whom he assumed from David was perfect—the Son of God, the son of David.

“You will say to me: ‘Then do you proclaim two sons?’ I do not say two sons of David, for I did not say that God the Word was the son of David. Nor do I say two sons according to substance; for when I say that God the Word dwelt before the ages in the one begotten from the seed of David, I do not say that there are two from the substance of God.

“Observe what is brought forward in the fifth synod, Collation 5, in first and second place, from Cyril’s books against Theodore; Leontius attributes them to Diodore. Yet Cyril composed this work against both of them, as is clear from Facundus (Book III, chapter 3, and elsewhere).

“Marvel at the maneuver of a man abusing both the subtlety of his own intellect and the patience of his readers. From this also consider how Theodore’s teacher Diodore, and Theodore himself with his successors, could confess one Son. Likewise observe what kind of conjunction Diodore admitted between the Word and Christ: namely, one like the Word’s conjunction with the prophets, through *ἐνέργεια* (*energeia*, “operation”), but with three differences: it was perpetual with Christ, it enabled him to perform greater offices, and it involved a greater sharing either in honor or in an abundance of virtue.

“Let Facundus now strive to defend the disciple of a man so wickedly cautious and impiously subtle, a disciple who followed his teacher most closely.”]

“We lead you,” he says, “to a careful and cautious examination of doctrines.” [Note: [Col. 1062D] This clause is absent from Leontius’ excerpt. BALUZ.] “We labor on your behalf, lest we have to render an account to the Lord for our silence.

“The Son was perfect before the ages; he assumed the perfect one who is proved to be from David—the Son of God, the son of David.

“You will say to me: ‘Then you proclaim two sons.’ I do not say two sons of David. Did I assert that God the Word is the son of David? Nor do I say two sons of God according to substance.” [Note: [Col. 1062D] In place of this, Leontius has: “For I do not say two from the substance of God, when I say that God the Word dwelt before the ages in the one begotten from the seed of David.” BALUZ.] “For do I assert that two sons were begotten from the substance of God before the ages? Rather, I say that the Word of God dwelt in the one who is proved to be from the seed of David.”

[Col. 1062B]

9. “Not in the same way,” he says, “did God the Word dwell in the one who is from the seed of David as he dwelt in the prophets. They enjoyed the grace of the Holy Spirit in a particular and limited measure [Baluz. ‘measured’]; but this one remained continually in those things in which they were only at times, and was filled with the glory and wisdom of the Word.

“Another is undoubtedly to be understood as existing besides him, subsisting [Baluz. ‘sustaining’] as a son in his own right and separately. For the Word did not fill himself with wisdom and glory, but rather bestowed these distinguishing qualities upon another.”

10. “We adore the purple because of the one clothed in it, and the temple because of its inhabitant; the form of a servant because of the form of God; the lamb because of the high priest; the one assumed because of the one who assumes; the one formed in the Virgin’s womb because of the creator of all things.

“Having confessed these things, offer one veneration. One act of adoration will do no harm, provided that you have first confessed the realities.”

[Note: [Col. 1062D]

The reading *pontifex*—“high priest”—seems suspicious to me, indeed it should be deleted, and the word *pastor*—“shepherd”—should be written in its place. For “lamb” and the noun joined to it are distinguished in the same way as “purple” and “the one clothed,” “the one assumed” and “the one who assumes,” “the one formed in the Virgin’s womb” and “the creator of all”—that is, the human being and the Word.

Yet every Nestorian recoiled from saying that the Word was the high priest, as is clear both from Nestorius’ Sermons 4 and 6 and from the criticism of the tenth anathema, whether by Andrew of Samosata or by Theodoret. No member of that faction could recoil from the Word as the one bearing the lamb, that is, the human being, since they claimed to adore the one carried because of the one carrying him, and so forth.
