Moreover, the question of whether God is high priest does not seem to have been raised before the panegyric sermon addressed by Proclus to the Virgin as Mother of God in the year 429.

Observe, too, the source from which Nestorius had advanced. He regularly borrowed many things partly from Chrysostom and partly from Theodore: from Chrysostom, good things that he corrupted; from Theodore, bad things that he enlarged.]

11. You say “one veneration,” but through this one veneration you introduce blasphemy, so that, if there is one adoration, there is also one substance.

12. [Note: [Col. 1063A] This impious statement is not read everywhere in precisely the same form as at present. At the Council of Tyre, when the bishops acting as judges were speaking, it is reported by the accusers of Ibas of Edessa as follows: “I do not envy Christ who was made God; for insofar as he was made so, I too was made so.” Οὐ φθονῶ τῷ Χριστῷ γενομένῳ Θεῷ· ἐφ’ ὅσον γὰρ αὐτὸς ἐγένετο, κἀγὼ ἐγενόμην (“I do not envy Christ who became God; for insofar as he became so, I too became so”). But in the Instruction of the Edessene Clergy it appears thus: “I do not envy Christ who was made God, since I too, if I wish, can become so, according to him.” Οὐ φθονῶ τῷ Χριστῷ γεγονότι Θεῷ, ἐπειδὴ κἀγὼ, εἰ βούλομαι, γίνομαι κατ’ αὐτόν (“I do not envy Christ who became God, since I too, if I wish, become so according to him”). In the former passage it is attributed to Ibas, bishop of Edessa, by four presbyters of that same Church. In the latter, the accusation of the presbyters is dissolved by the testimony of sixty-five ministers of that same Church. Moreover, Ibas cleared himself of so heinous a charge, with his emotions stirred—as was proper—in the following words: “Anathema to him who said it, and to him who brought the accusation; ten thousand times over I would endure being cut to pieces rather than say this word. Far be this from me, even to think of it,” and so forth.

Words of this kind can admit not merely one interpretation, [Col. 1063C] but as many interpretations as the different ways in which they are reported. If they are read as they stand in the Instruction of the Edessene Clergy, the interpretation we gave in Dissertation 7 on the first part is not inappropriate, namely: “I do not envy Christ that he became God; for I too can likewise become God if I wish.” For by his own works and by the native powers of his free will he merited divinity, and I too, as a participant in the same common nature, can perform such works. But if the words of the accusing presbyters are understood according to their plain sense, this meaning will immediately present itself: “I do not envy Christ that he became God; for insofar as he became so through assumption, I too became so through baptism”—that is, both became adoptive sons of God.

Yet someone might interpret the words reported by Marius more leniently in this way: “I do not envy Christ that he became man; for what he became, I too likewise became”—namely, because such honor, proceeding from him, overflowed upon me on account of our sharing the same nature. Nevertheless, although this third interpretation contains much piety, Ibas himself, together with the others, recoiled from the words when they were first uttered; it therefore cannot be the true one. The words must consequently have been understood in one of the other two ways; but in either case they contain dreadful impiety and arrogance: in the first, the doctrine of Paul of Samosata and of Pelagius; in the second, that of Theodore.

Whether Ibas ever uttered this impious statement is uncertain. For the Fathers of Chalcedon declared that the charges brought against Ibas had not been sufficiently proved, and nothing of this kind was brought against him at the Fifth Synod, although he was condemned there together with his letter. I nevertheless consider it certain that, if he ever uttered it, he did not do so at the time first alleged by the accusing presbyters, namely in the year 445, since Marius wrote this little work before that date. I therefore think that we should believe Mercator, who attributes it either to Theodore of Mopsuestia, or rather to Paul of Samosata, whose two earlier περικοπαί (passages) he had cited.

The reason why I am inclined to attribute it rather to Paul of Samosata is that Theodore denied that the assumed man attained this through merits, but held that it was by a singular grace when he was first formed in the Virgin’s womb; whereas Paul of Samosata asserted this. Furthermore, although Theodore actually taught that Christ was the adoptive Son of God, he nevertheless maintained that Christ had been adorned with such dignity and raised to such honor as no creature, however much it might strive, could attain.---In Baluzius this fragment appears under the name of Ibas, bishop of the Edessenes [Col. 1064C], with this annotation: “We also owe this title to the Vatican codex, since it was lacking in the Bellovacensis. Consequently Garnerius, seeing that Ibas denied having said the things reported immediately below, and thinking that Marius Mercator attributed them to Theodore of Mopsuestia, judged that Mercator should be believed, though strongly inclined to think them more readily those of Paul of Samosata. In reality, however, they are those of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, as Marius Mercator testifies. See the final constitution of Pope Vigilius, published by us in the new edition of the Councils.” EDIT.] “I do not envy Christ,” he says, “when he was made [Col. 1064A] God; for what he himself was made, I too was made, because it belongs to my nature.”

13. [Note: [Col. 1064C] This fragment too is preceded by a title which, as it stands, reads: “The same Ibas, addressing the people at Easter.” “From this,” says Baluzius, “it is clear that this fragment can be joined to the preceding one. For from the booklet of the Edessene presbyters against Ibas it appears that he uttered the preceding statements about Christ while preaching in the church, according to custom, on the holy day of Easter. The same presbyters testify that he also said the following.” EDIT.] “Today Jesus has become immortal. When Mary approached him after the resurrection, he said to her: ‘Do not touch me’; for she thought that he was still the Lord he had been, and she did not know that after the resurrection he had been made perfect.”

[Col. 1063]

## II. THEODORET OF CYRRHUS

### PREFATORY NOTICE

No one is unaware who Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, was, or how outstanding his learning was. It is equally well known to all how devoted he was to Nestorius before, compelled by affliction, he returned to a better mind. We have said enough about this, insofar as concerns the present undertaking, in the historical preface; we shall speak at much greater length in the supplement to Theodoret that we are preparing, where we shall undertake a more detailed discussion of his life, faith, and works.

We now publish Mercator’s collections, in the form in which they are found in manuscript codices, intending to provide more extensive material in its proper place—not from Mercator, but gathered from elsewhere, and not without labor. These collections contain, as the title states, letters and certain excerpts, whether from books or from sermons. We shall deal with the letters later; for now, with the five books mentioned by Mercator.

They are in fact the first six of the twenty-seven books against heretics which Photius says he read from Theodoret—one book having been divided into two. But although the whole matter contains much obscurity, it requires a more extended explanation. First, however, we must transcribe what Photius says (Codex 46):

“Twenty-seven books of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, against various propositions were read.

“The first book is directed against those who assert that God the Word had one nature and that he took his origin from David’s seed; likewise against those who attribute sufferings to the Divinity. The second book engages more forcefully with the same people from Scripture. The third discusses the same subject. The fourth contains the teaching of the holy Fathers concerning the glorious incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God. The fifth collects the opinions of the heretics and compares them with the opinion of those who do not at all acknowledge two natures in Christ, showing that they have a close affinity with one another. The sixth establishes that our Lord Jesus Christ is one Son.”

Before the Council of Ephesus, Theodoret had written against Cyril’s twelve anathemas. John of Antioch had urged him to write and had assigned the same task to Andrew of Samosata, so that, by the authority of the two most learned men in the whole East, minds might be forestalled from believing Cyril, who, in the anathemas—as though in a kind of epitome—was presenting the Catholic faith. That first attempt failed when the anathemas were read at the council and not rejected; indeed, the Catholic Fathers went over to Cyril’s side against Nestorius. Theodoret therefore tried again, after the dissolution of the synod, to confirm by whatever means he could the objections he had previously raised and to undermine what had been established at the council. He undertook this attempt either because he was actually erring together with Nestorius, or because, blinded by emotional attachment, he did not sufficiently perceive how impiously Nestorius thought and how Catholicly Cyril thought.

He divided this work, whose excerpts we have before us, into five books. In the first three he attempted to show that Catholic doctrine was opposed to the Gospels and to the teaching of the Fathers; in the fourth he wished to prove that the judgment of the Ephesian Fathers was akin to the opinions of the heretics; and in the fifth he finally explained how Christ is one Son.

Although the individual books were divided into many chapters, I infer that they were not particularly lengthy from the fact that Photius writes that the three books of the *Eranistes* were longer than these, though even those were not very large individually.

That the second and third books were in reality joined together seems to be indicated by Photius’s words: “The third discusses the same subject.” I nevertheless think that they were divided according to this distinction: the second contained testimonies chiefly from the New Testament, while the third contained testimonies from the Old.

That the entire work was entitled *On the Incarnation* (περὶ ἐνανθρωπήσεως) is inferred from a substantial portion of it, which we shall present in both Latin and Greek in the supplement to Theodoret, since it bears this title in a book from the Royal Library. It is likewise established from the same book that it bore the name *Pentalogium* (Πενταλόγιον). The first designation was taken from its subject, the second from the number of books.

Moreover, the learned Father Combefis thought that the *Pentalogium* was identical with the five books of heretical fables. Nothing could have been more poorly conjectured by a man who lacked Mercator’s evidence distinguishing the two works, namely the *pentabiblon* (πεντάβιβλον).

The time of composition can be concluded with reasonable probability from the first letter to Himerius of Nicomedia, if the following words are indeed to be understood in this connection: “Having read the letters sent from Egypt and repeatedly discussed with us, we found them consistent with the Church’s doctrine, but we proved that they were contrary to the twelve chapters, which up to the present we have continued to oppose.” The work must therefore have been composed during the interval between the departure of the Easterners from Ephesus for their homeland and the negotiations for peace among the Churches—that is, in the year 432.

Several writers of antiquity mention this work, first among them Irenaeus, bishop of Tyre, when, in letters written to Theodoret, he complained that Theodoret had omitted Theodore of Mopsuestia, and even Diodore of Tarsus, Theodore’s teacher, when producing Fathers as witnesses to his own opinion. Theodoret really did omit both in this work, although he brought forward very many others; and he seems to have forestalled the objection in the fourth book, at its conclusion, where the matter will again be discussed. The reason it appears so is, first, that Irenaeus wrote to Theodoret at approximately the time when we said this work was published, namely when the negotiations for peace among the Churches were under way and expositions of faith, deliberately composed in somewhat ambiguous language, were being sent back and forth.

Moreover, the emperor Justinian, in his address to the Fathers of the Fifth Synod, complains that the impiety transmitted by Nestorius was being reintroduced through Theodore of Mopsuestia, the teacher of Nestorius, and also through Theodoret’s impious writings, in which he set forth matters contrary to the true faith, to the First Council of Ephesus, and to Cyril of holy memory, and so forth.

The Fathers of the Fifth Synod, canon 13: “If anyone defends the impious writings of Theodoret, which he set forth against the true faith, against the First Council of Ephesus, against holy Cyril, and against his twelve chapters, and everything that he wrote in defense of the impious Theodore and Nestorius, let him be anathema.”

Mercator attempts to demonstrate nothing else in these collections than that Theodoret held the same views as Theodore and Nestorius—that is, that he distinguished in reality two sons and two lords, and therefore judged the son of the Virgin to be in reality a mere man, however much he wished to appear to hold the contrary opinion. Mercator achieves this through two arguments: the agreement of Theodoret’s words and opinions with those of the two men mentioned above, and his avowed devotion to both of them, together with his hatred of holy Cyril and the Ephesian Fathers, whom he disparages under the names of Arians and Apollinarists.

You should not be surprised, reader, that Mercator constructs so serious an accusation against a man of such great reputation as Theodoret, and in such weighty terms. The outstanding defender of the faith preferred to adhere to the whole Church rather than to a man somewhat more enamored of disturbances than true and prudent zeal for the truth would permit. Marius certainly wrote at a time when Theodoret’s faith was doubtful among the saints, and before it had yet been vindicated at the holy Council of Chalcedon.

Gregory the Great approved Mercator’s judgment—if, as learned men acknowledge, Gregory, while still in minor orders, wrote under the name of his predecessor Pelagius a letter, or book, to Elias of Aquileia and the other schismatic bishops of Istria who did not consent to the condemnation of the Three Chapters. For he levels against Theodoret the same charges as Mercator, using the testimonies from the same excerpts and the same—indeed, the very same—words. We shall present each item in its proper place. See letter, chapter 20, from which you will understand four things.

First, that Gregory the Great had seen Marius Mercator’s codex; for he copied from it everything that he cites at considerable length in the passage mentioned shortly. Second, that in the same codex, together with Theodoret’s letters, there were also criticisms of Cyril’s anathemas and excerpts from the books now under discussion, just as they actually occur in our manuscripts. Third, that Mercator himself was the interpreter of all these materials; for Gregory cites them in precisely the same words. Fourth, what opinion Gregory had formed of Theodoret before Theodoret professed the faith at the Council of Chalcedon: Gregory says that he wrote against the true faith, held opinions contrary to the holy Church, came to think rightly after his error, destroyed the unity of the Divinity and humanity in Christ, and composed writings that were corrupt, heretical, and full of every impiety. To this he adds Mercator’s defense, which addresses Theodoret with even greater severity. Who does not see how rash it is to defend Theodoret’s writings in their arrogance, when it is clear that Theodoret himself later condemned them by professing the truth? And later: “Rejecting only his heretical writings, we continue, together with the synod, to pursue him as still Nestorian; and together with the synod we venerate Theodoret when he professes the truth.”

Whether Pope Pelagius himself wrote these words or Gregory while still a deacon wrote them in the pope’s name, they possess very great authority—at least greater authority than those who hold views contrary to my Mercator.

Observe, reader, that when Gregory wrote in the letter about the Three Chapters, he set down regarding two of them what he had taken from the Fifth Synod; but when he came to the third, concerning Theodoret, he took the collections solely from Mercator. Although certain matters are also read in the Fifth Synod—such as those relating to the first anathema—in these passages he nevertheless preferred Mercator’s version, abandoning the text of the Fifth Synod.

## EXCERPTS FROM THEODORET

From the five books that he wrote against the blessed Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, and against the holy Council of Ephesus, by which Nestorius was condemned, at the instigation of the devil.

[Col. 1067]

### EXCERPT ONE

From Theodoret’s preface to the five books against the blessed Cyril and the holy Council of Ephesus.

### EXCERPT ONE

[Col. 1067A]

Before the assembly was held at Ephesus, we resisted the twelve chapters briefly and openly, so that their meaning might become known even to the less capable and those without reasoning. But because the man who put these things forward openly declared himself in the council, and because many of those who had assembled—through ignorance [Baluzius: “ignorance”], rather than through any knowledge of doctrine—considered them pious, it seemed worthwhile to contend again, to extend the discourse, and to refute in many ways the curtailed [Baluzius: “following”] blasphemy, so that we might demonstrate more clearly to the ignorant how the things now especially advanced by these men are shown to be contrary to the Gospels. [Col. 1067B]

### EXCERPT TWO

From the first book of the same work. [Note: [Col. 1067B] Observe how, in the excerpts from the first book, he writes that he dealt with those who assert that God the Word had one nature and that he took his origin from David’s seed, and likewise with those who attribute sufferings to the Divinity.]

For this reason Emmanuel was called “the child” long ago, even before many ages had passed from his birth from the Virgin [Baluzius: “of the Virgin”]. But “Emmanuel” indicates both the nature of the one who took and of the one who was assumed; [Col. 1068A] for it is interpreted “God with us”—that is, God in our nature, God in man, God and man, God made man, God clothing himself, without limitation, with the nature of man, God in a human temple, God with us, God on account of the unity of the one whom he took from us. [Note: [Col. 1067B] These expressions, although very Catholic in themselves, are not free from suspicion because of the character of the speaker and the words that follow: “God on account of the unity of the one whom he took from us.” For this was a familiar formula of the Nestorians: on account of unity, a man is called God, just as through affection a friend becomes a lover. I also regard as suspect the statements “God in our nature,” “God in man, God and man,” “God clothing himself with the nature of man,” “God in a human temple,” and “God with us,” since they signify a pure indwelling and clothing, and therefore the Nestorian σχετικὴ ἕνωσις (“relative union”). Thus Mercator was not rash in adducing these statements to prove that Theodoret asserted two sons.] Therefore Emmanuel is not only God but also man; and he himself was called Christ, named Jesus, and called Savior.

Again, from the same first book.

[Note: [Col. 1067C] This is directed against Cyril’s statement that the incarnate Word has one nature. To some people this appeared to be a symbol of the true faith, as can be seen from Cyril’s letters written after peace had been made among the Churches to friends who complained that he seemed to have departed from orthodoxy (ὀρθοδοξία), since he had conceded to the Easterners that there were two natures in Christ after the union. Earlier they had accused him on this account of adhering to the Apollinarists, who deliriously imagined that the union had produced a confusion of natures. I say “the Apollinarists,” not Apollinaris himself; for Theodoret reports that a certain Polemius—called Polemion by others—was the first author of the confusion. “A certain Polemius,” he says, “having found an opportunity in the writings of Apollinaris, declared that a confusion of substances and a commingling of Divinity and body had taken place.” From this arose the heresy of the Polemians (*Heretical Fables*, book IV, chapter 9).]

If there were a commingling or confusion, and one substance were produced from the two, neither would God remain God, nor would the temple remain a temple; rather, God would be the temple and the temple would by nature be God, for that is what admixture produces. And if this were so, the Lord would not appropriately say, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). For he ought to have said, “Destroy me, and in three days I will rise again,” since the two natures would have made one through the adjustment produced by commingling.

### EXCERPT THREE

Likewise from the second book of the same work. [Note: [Col. 1068C] Observe, reader, and recognize in all the excerpts from the second book the character of the second book described by Photius, in which he says that Theodoret engages more forcefully with his opponents from sacred Scripture.]

[Note: [Col. 1068C] We shall soon publish this entire excerpt in a fuller form, in Greek and Latin, in the supplement to Theodoret. Gregory the Great copied a large part of it and transferred it into the letter praised in the preface. After quoting the angel’s words to the Virgin, he has the following: “Consider here also that everything is spoken in human terms. ‘He will be great,’ it says; it does not say, ‘He is.’ ‘He will be called the Son of the Most High’; it does not say, ‘He is called.’ ‘The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father’; it does not say, ‘He has it,’ but ‘The Lord God will give it to him.’ ‘And he will reign’; it does not say, ‘He reigns.’ And over whom? ‘Over the house of Jacob’; it does not say, ‘over angels and archangels.’”]

But Gabriel too, when he evangelized the Virgin, as blessed Luke explains, said: “Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High; and God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end. Therefore also the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:31–35).

Consider that here too everything is spoken in human terms. “He will be great,” he says (ibid., verse 35); he does not say, “He is.” “He will be called the Son of the Most High”; he does not say, “He is called,” or “He is.” He does not say, “He has the throne of David his father,” but, “He will give it to him.” And “he will reign”; he does not say, “He reigns.” Over whom? “Over the house of Jacob”; he does not say, “over angels and archangels.” And again, “He will be called the Son of God”; he does not say, “He is called.”

[Note: [Col. 1069C] Great audacity, and impiety as well! Audacity in accusing the ecumenical synod of betraying the truth because of its perversity; impiety in openly dividing the Son of God from the son of the Virgin, the natural son from the adoptive, and joining the one to the other only by a unity of veneration and glory, and so forth.]

What do you say to this, you who, assigning proper sufferings to the Truth, have presumed, because of human disputes, to wage war against God? To whom do these things belong—to God, who always is [Baluzius adds: “and to the Lord”], and to the king, and to the holy one, and to the Son of God? Or rather to the temple, which was taken from David’s seed [Baluzius: “which is holy”] and, on account of the unity of God the Word, earned these very things?

Again, shortly afterward in the same book:

Therefore he did not foretell that God the Word would become great after the Virgin’s birth, but that the temple which was made holy from the Virgin, assumed, united, and itself also called “son,” would become great—not so that we should adore two sons, but so that, beholding the invisible God in the visible temple, we might render to him one glory of veneration.

[Col. 1069C] Again in the same second book.

[Note: [Col. 1069C] Gregory copied this together with the title: “In the same second book he says: ‘But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan.’ And again: ‘Jesus departed in the power of the Spirit into Galilee.’ Do not suppose that God the Word needed the cooperation or assistance of the Spirit; rather, the visible temple enjoyed the various gifts of the Holy Spirit.” He copied it to prove the very point Mercator also sought to prove—namely, that Theodoret asserted two persons in Christ.]

As you find it written: “But the Lord, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4:1). And again: “Jesus departed in the power of the Spirit into Galilee” (ibid., verse 14). Do not suppose that God the Word needed the cooperation or assistance of the Spirit; rather, the visible temple enjoyed the various gifts of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1070A] Again, somewhat later in the same place:

But so that you may clearly perceive the division of the two natures, let us come to the teaching of the Lord himself. The Jews approached him, saying: “What sign do you show us, since you do these things?” (John 2:18). Jesus answered: “Destroy this temple,” drawing them by his demonstrative expression toward the visible thing; and, “in three days I will raise it up” (ibid., verse 19), manifesting to his hearers the power of the Divinity.

From the same book:

“God exalted him as author and Savior” (Acts 5:31). Who, then, was exalted? Not the one who is exalted by nature, but the nature that the Divinity exalted [Baluzius: “raised up”], which the Jews killed by hanging it on the wood. For this nature was exalted [Col. 1070B] through the conjunction of the one who took it and dwelt in it.

From the same book:

“It is evident,” he says, “who rose on the third day and who raised him up, according to the Savior’s promise: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will rebuild it’” (John 2:19). What rose on the third day, the Jews hung on the wood. “This one God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:38). For God the Word did not need an anointing or the operation of the Holy Spirit; rather, he took the temple from David’s seed and joined it to himself. [Note: [Col. 1069D] Baluzius adds here: “and bestowed healing upon all who believed.” Shortly afterward, when he again recalls the passage, he adds “and the anointing of the Nazarene,” and attempts to justify these final words as follows: “These words have been added from ancient codices.” It seems, however, that one should read: “recalling the anointing of the Nazarene,” and so forth. For he is clearly referring to the tenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles. EDIT.] The Apostle clearly demonstrates this by recalling the anointing that was performed by God, the Holy Spirit with which he was anointed, the power that he enjoyed, and how he worked healing: “because God was in him” (Mark 6:14).

From the same book:

“We see Jesus, made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor, so that apart from God he might taste death for everyone” (Hebrews 2:9). He separates him from the suffering, so that [Note: [Col. 1069D] The edition, whether the Latin Vulgate or the Greek, has something quite different: “so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone,” ὅπως χάριτι Θεοῦ ὑπὲρ παντὸς γεύσῃ τοῦ θανάτου. Some Greeks, however, read ὅπως χαρὶς τοῦ Θεοῦ (“so that the grace is of God”), and so forth. The reading followed by Theodoret supports the heresy of those who say that the man was abandoned by God at the time of the Passion. That heresy was produced by another faulty rendering of Colossians 2:15. Where we read: “Blotting out the bond written against us in decrees, which was contrary to us, and he took it away from the midst, nailing it to the cross; and stripping principalities and powers, he led them openly in triumph, triumphing over them in himself,” certain ancient writers read: “stripping off the flesh.” Thus Hilary in book *On the Trinity*; Ambrose in his *Treatise on the Creed*, chapter 13; and Augustine both in *On Christian Combat*, chapter 2, and elsewhere throughout. That heresy, which appeared to Capreolus to be a branch of Nestorianism, began to spread in Spain and compelled the Spanish laymen Vitalis and Constantius to consult Capreolus, bishop of Carthage, about how it should be opposed. Father Sirmond published the letter of the questioners and Capreolus’s reply in 1630. Both were included in the collection of general councils, whether by those who prepared the royal edition or by those who prepared the larger and more accurate one. The questioners’ words in the published books are: “They also say that a mere man hung on the cross after being seized. They say: ‘God withdrew from him.’ To this our smallness replies: ‘God never withdrew from the man he had assumed, except when he said from the cross: Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”’ From this I draw three conclusions: first, that these Spaniards supposed the Word withdrew from the man as death approached; second, that the common reading is corrupt, as is sufficiently shown by the incoherent sentence, ‘after being seized. They say: God withdrew from him’; finally, how the corruption ought to be corrected. Vitalis and Constantius argue that the error of those who say that the man was abandoned by the Word not only on the cross but throughout the entire Passion, and therefore from the moment of his seizure, is worse than their own. I therefore think that it should be read: ‘They also say that a mere man hung on the cross; for after he had been seized, they say, God withdrew from him,’ and so forth—that is, ‘after the seizure.’

“Vitalis and Constantius were the more excusable in their error because they had perhaps been misled by the example of a great man, namely Ambrose, whose words are these: ‘This blessed soul, which cried out to the Divinity on the cross, saying, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”—the man cried out, about to die through separation from the Divinity. For since the Divinity is free from death, death could not exist unless life departed, because the Divinity is life, which never suffers either death or corruption, for it is always immortal and incorruptible. God, however, who is Word and Spirit, who breathes where he wills, did not unwillingly abandon the human flesh and soul he had assumed; rather, because he willed it, where he willed, how he willed, and when he willed, he laid it down, leaving it, and again assumed it. Therefore he was not stripped of the flesh by anyone’s right or power; he himself stripped himself. For he who could not have died if he had not wished to, undoubtedly died because he wished to. The Apostle proves this to be so when he says: “Stripping himself of the flesh, he stripped principalities and powers, triumphing over them in himself”—that is, through the death of the man he had assumed.’---“Apart from God,” Hebrews 2:9. The text of both the Vulgate and the Greek has “by the grace of God,” χάριτι Θεοῦ. Theodoret read χωρὶς Θεοῦ, “apart from God.” Mercator therefore censures him, in the heading prefixed to this excerpt, for corrupting the Pauline text. But unjustly. For Saint Jerome, near the beginning of book II of his Commentary on Galatians 3:10, writes of both readings: “Scripture bears witness that Christ died for all by the grace of God, or, as is read in some copies, WITHOUT GOD.” This latter reading was certainly not unknown to Origen in his Exegesis on John 1:1 and 11:49, nor was it unfamiliar to the Latin Fathers. To omit others, Saint Ambrose, On Faith II.8, writes: “How well the Apostle put it: ‘That WITHOUT GOD he might taste death for all,’ lest we should think that passion belonged to the Divinity rather than to the flesh.” Again, ibid. V.8: “The mystery of God’s incarnation is the salvation of all creation, according to what is written: ‘That WITHOUT GOD he might taste death for all’; that is, that all creation is to be redeemed by the price of the Lord’s blood without any suffering of the Divinity.” Nevertheless, Mill contends at Hebrews 2:9 in his Greek New Testament, on the agreement of all Greek manuscripts and of most Latin ones, that the common reading χάριτι Θεοῦ, “by the grace of God,” should be retained. On this passage Wetstein treats at length after Mill in volume II, page 392, of his Greek Testament. That thick work, produced with excessive and laborious toil, contains much that is useful, learned, and worth knowing, but also many things discordant with the faith and absurd, which its author, carried away by excessive license and party spirit, allowed himself, and which may someday, with God’s help, be corrected. GALLAND.]

“apart from God,” he says, “he might taste death for everyone” [Col. 1071A]. For he says that this one was made a little lower than the angels; but God the Word is not lower than the angels, but is the creator of angels, powers, dominions, and every invisible and visible creature.

From the same book:

Adding one testimony to all these, I shall bring the discourse to an end: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” How, then—we wise men must attend to this—how is he himself the same yesterday and today and forever, both temporal and eternal, both in time and beyond time? For if he is eternal, he is not temporal; and if he is in time, he is not beyond time.

[ [Note: [Col. 1072C] We supplied this entire passage from Baluzius, who copied it from a Vatican codex. It is absent from Garnerius, who followed the Bellovacensis. EDIT.] Words of Marius Mercator.]

[Col. 1071B] Again, from the fourth book of the same work, after the testimonies of the holy Fathers, which that wicked and impious man attempts to twist to his own criminal meaning, [Note: [Col. 1072D] These words are evidently corrupt and can be corrected only with the help of manuscripts. GALLAND.] after he had dared to mention certain heretics—including Theodore—and had attempted to extol them with the highest praises, he uttered the following words in insult to the holy Fathers who condemned Nestorius at Ephesus, exclaiming:] [Col. 1072A]

[Note: [Col. 1072D] He is directing his attention to Cyril’s fourth anathema, which reads as follows: “If anyone distributes between two persons or substances (ὑποστάσεις) the expressions found in the evangelical or apostolic Scriptures, whether spoken by the saints about Christ or by Christ himself about himself, assigning some to the man understood separately apart from the Word and others to God the Word alone, let him be anathema.” Consult Theodoret’s criticism of this anathema and compare it with these passages; from the kinship between them you will understand how great Theodoret’s hatred was toward all the anathemas, and especially toward this one. Hence Mercator was not unjustified in writing what follows with somewhat greater agitation.]

“Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind! And who is blind and deaf except one who is out of his mind, who does not wish to attend to the truth, closing his eyes against the rays and depriving himself of light? Hear, then, the teacher of truth, who rightly commands that the evangelical and apostolic expressions be divided, attributing the lofty ones to the Divinity and assigning the lowly ones to the humanity. Finally, cease resisting this pious division, and do not, through fear of an anathema, instill terror in the simpler people. For we attend to the things you put forward as terrifying, as though they were refuse, and we preserve the teachings of the holy Fathers.”

### Words of Marius Mercator

[Col. 1072B] By these words this profane man attempts to weaken, as he supposes, the sentence rightly pronounced under the imposition of an anathema both against Nestorius and against those like him [Baluzius adds: “his”], lest his followers and accomplices, out of fear of present and future punishment, abandon their perverse doctrines and strive to return to the path of unity. Finally, so that the wickedness of his heart might become evident, in the last [Col. 1073A] part of the fourth book he celebrates in his praises Theodore, bishop of the city of Mopsuestia [Baluzius: “Mamsuestia”], whom almost all Catholics recognize as a heretic, in the following manner.

# FOURTH EXCERPT

From the final part of Theodoret’s fourth book.

[Note: [Col. 1073B] This passage may appear to belong to this book. When Theodoret, in reply to Bishop Irenaeus, who reproached him for having passed over Diodorus and Theodore in the *Eranistes*, says (Letter 16):

“With what honor I should pursue such great men, the book which I composed about them bears witness. In it I dissolved the accusation brought together against them, fearing neither the power of their accusers nor the snares laid against us. For the book of the *Pentalogy* differs in no respect from the *Apology for Diodorus and Theodore*.” This is clearly demonstrated by what follows in Mercator’s words.

The same point appears in Dialogue 1 of the *Eranistes*: “I would also bring before you the accounts of Diodorus and Theodore, those strongest defenders of the truth, unless I saw that you are hostile toward them and that Apollinaris’s hatred and malevolence have taken their place in you. For you would see that they too wrote things consonant with the others, drew streams from the divine fountain, and themselves also became channels, indeed spirits. But I shall pass them over, because you have undertaken implacable war against them.”]

He says:

“For this reason I deliberately omitted the great Theodore, champion of piety and defender of the evangelical proclamations: because you are also attacking him, for some reason or other, together with us. After very many sweat-filled exertions and accumulated labors, after so many struggles and numerous studies, he is being assailed not by the calumnies of outsiders, but by those of his own people and fellow believers. For I ought, together with Paul, to have enumerated the dangers arising from the gentiles, from robbers, and finally from false brothers (II Corinthians 11:26). For this reason we wished to pass over so great a man.”

# FIFTH EXCERPT

Likewise, from the fifth book, which is the last of his entire work. Words of Marius Mercator.

This despicable man attempts to construct this calumny against the holy synod that justly struck down Nestorius, daring to say that the blessed Fathers who assembled at Ephesus pronounced that sentence not with the intention of upholding correct doctrine, but rather through fear [Col. 1074A] [Baluz.: resentment], so that it might appear that the long-buried impiety of Apollinaris had been renewed through them. He intensifies this insult against the holy bishops of God in the following treacherous words.

## From Theodoret’s Fifth Book, for Theodore

[Note: [Col. 1073C] He now pours out against the holy bishops of God the same things that he had earlier written against Cyril, when he sent his criticisms of the anathemas to John of Antioch [Col. 1073D]:

“I was deeply distressed when I read the anathemas that you sent, instructing us to refute them in writing and to expose their heretical meaning plainly to everyone. I was distressed because a man who has received the office of feeding, to whom so great a flock has been entrusted, and who has been commanded to care for weak sheep, is not only himself sick—indeed, severely so—but also strives to fill the sheep with sickness, and tears apart what is to be fed more savagely than wild beasts. For those beasts seize and rend what has been scattered and separated from the flock. But this man, standing in the midst of the flock and regarded as its savior and guardian, introduces hidden error among those who obey him. What he openly attacks is easy to observe; but one who lays an ambush under the appearance of friendship finds his opponent off guard and easily inflicts injury upon him. This grieves me much more: that under the name and appearance of piety, and in the dignity of a shepherd, he breaks out into heretical and blasphemous utterances and renews the empty as well as impious teaching of Apollinaris, long since extinguished,” and so forth.]

“Such was the force of the envy to which you have surrendered yourselves that what Apollinaris once spoke through one or two men, and those secretly, he now presents through many leaders of the Church in the sacred assemblies of the churches; and such [Baluz.: deadly] herbs are offered to the flocks by their shepherds, while the bites of wolves are inflicted upon rational sheep through the ministry of their rulers. The man who used to address a few people outside the walls of two or three cities, and who even led them astray by various songs, now dances through the midst of the cities because of you. For you proclaim his errors and adorn yourselves with novelties of speech, restoring his blasphemy, which had already been consumed by time.”

Words of Marius Mercator.

What unity of Deity and humanity this same Theodoret acknowledged is necessarily made clear by the words in which he wrote.

# SIXTH EXCERPT

From the same book.

[Note: [Col. 1074B] These passages contain the deceitful subtlety of the Nestorians. Abusing the term “person,” they confessed, indeed, one person in Christ after the union of the natures, but one of the kind found in a man and a woman after marriage: σχέσει (*schesei*, by relation), certainly, not φύσει (*physei*, by nature); or, as they say, not one physically and substantially, but one morally and legally.

Someone might perhaps believe either that Theodoret learned this from Theodore, whose complete opinions he occasionally copies, or that Marius Mercator was deceived by the similarity of their names, or that the matter arose from some other fault—whether on the part of those copying what belonged to Marius or of those excerpting what belonged to Theodore as reported in the Fifth Synod, as has happened more than once elsewhere.

For in the aforesaid synod, Collation 4, and in Leontius, these very words are attributed to Theodore, as excerpts from Book Eight *On the Incarnation*. I would adopt that view were I not restrained by Gregory the Great, who attributes this περικοπή (*perikopē*, passage) to Theodoret—and does so in a letter written in the name of the supreme pontiff to Theodoret’s supporters, who might have complained of the slander stamped upon Theodoret, if something spurious had merely been inserted under his name.

Therefore I think that Theodoret took from Theodore the part presented by Mercator, though not without altering certain things so that the distinction could be recognized. To establish this, and at the same time preserve Mercator’s credibility, it is useful to present what is found either in Leontius, or in the Fifth Synod, or in the letter of Pelagius II written by Gregory the Great.]

In Leontius, therefore:

“It is manifest in every respect that confusion is superfluous, unbecoming, and contradictory, since each nature remains indivisibly in itself. Again, it is manifest that the union is fitting and appropriate; for through it the united natures constituted one person according to the union.

Therefore, concerning what the Lord says of man and wife, ‘For this reason they are no longer two, but one flesh,’ we may appropriately say, according to the principle of union: ‘They are no longer two persons, but one,’ namely, with the natures remaining distinct.

For just as there the number two is not impaired by their being called one flesh—for it is clear in what respect they are called one flesh—so here the union of the person does not impair the difference of the natures.

When we distinguish the natures, we speak of the perfect nature of God the Word and the perfect person; for it is not permissible to speak of a hypostasis without a person. Likewise, we speak of the perfect nature of man and of his person. Yet when we consider the joining together, we then speak of one person.”

In the Fifth Synod (Collation 5, no. 29):

“It is manifest that unity is appropriate; for through it the collected natures formed one person according to unity. For just as it is said of a man and a woman that they are no longer two but one flesh, so let us reasonably say, according to the principle of unity, that they are no longer two persons but one, namely, with the natures remaining distinct.

For just as there the number two is not harmed by their being called one flesh—for it is certain in what respect they are called one—so here the unity of the person does not harm the difference of the natures.

For when we distinguish the natures, we speak of the perfect nature of God the Word and of the perfect person; nor is it possible to say that there is a perfect subsistence without a person. Likewise, we confess the perfect nature and person of man. But when we look to the conjunction, we then speak of one person.”

In the letter of Pelagius II to Elias of Aquileia, and so forth:

“We distinguish the natures of God the Word; we call the nature complete and the person without doubt perfect, for it is not lawful to affirm a substance without a person. Likewise, we confess the perfect human nature together with its person. But when we look to the conjunction, only then do we rightly call it one person.”

“What the Lord says of man and wife,” he says, “that they are no longer two but one flesh (Matthew 19:6),” [Col. 1075A] [Note: [Col. 1076C] Baluz.: “The natures unquestionably remain established under distinction,” and so forth. EDIT.] “with the natures unquestionably remaining, but possessing distinction; and just as there the number two in no way prevents them from being called one flesh—for it is certain in what manner they are called one—so here the unity of the person in no way harms the difference of the natures.

Finally, when we distinguish the natures, we speak of the nature of God the Word as complete and of the person as unquestionably perfect; for it is not lawful to affirm a substance without a person. Likewise, we confess the perfect human nature together with its person. But when we look to the conjunction, only then do we rightly call it one person.”

# SEVENTH EXCERPT

Likewise, from chapter fifteen of the same book.

“These things,” he says, “refute the folly of Apollinaris, who asserts that God the Word dwelt in the assumed flesh in place of reason or mind. For if the assumed nature did not possess a human mind, then it was God who contended against the devil, and God also who accomplished the victory. But if God accomplished the victory, I have received no benefit from that victory, since I could have contributed nothing to it; and I am also deprived of the joy that arose from this event, rejoicing in another’s triumphs.

But the devil exults, is lifted up, and boasts and glories, as though he had wrestled with God; for it is a great thing for him even to be defeated by God.”

Likewise, from chapter sixteen of the same book.

[Note: [Col. 1076C] From this passage, which is said in the Greek codex of the royal library to have been taken from the work *On the Incarnation* (περὶ ἐνανθρωπήσεως), a widely held opinion is overturned. Certain men renowned for their reputation for learning, having been deceived by corrupt codices of Gennadius, believed that the work on the Incarnation of the Lord which Gennadius says Theodoret composed was not different from the four books of the *Eranistes* written against Eutyches and Dioscorus. This excerpt—or rather, the entire account of the Lord’s temptation, of which it is a part—would be sought in vain in the books of the *Eranistes*.]

“Using this defense also, the devil could rightly have said to God:

‘I, Lord, creator of all things, did not undertake a contest against you. For I know your dignity, understand your power, recognize your dominion, and confess my servitude, although I am known as a rebel. But I yield the victory both to the angels and to the entire heavenly multitude, among whom I too, wretched as I am, once was.

Against this man, however, I undertook the contest—the man whom you formed from clay, made in your image, honored with reason, appointed a citizen of paradise, and established as lord of land and sea. I deceived him by seduction, not by necessity; to this day I do not cease to overcome him, cast him down, and hand him over to death.

I persist in bringing him into the arena and ordering him to wrestle with me [Baluz.: receiving him]. Stand by as spectator; show him wrestling even with the skill athletes employ; demonstrate also the rules of the contest; anoint him [Baluz.: with a claw] as you wish; [Col. 1076B] only do not give him assistance. For I am not so bold and bereft of mind as to attempt to contend against you, the creator.’

The devil would rightly have said these things to Christ the Savior if he were not man, but God, contending on behalf of man.”

## On chapter twenty-nine

“The Son of God, inseparably joined to man, taught him the discipline of supreme virtue, guarded him unharmed from the darts of sins, and showed him to be whole and superior to the devil’s deceit. Allowing him to taste death for a short time, he immediately freed him from its tyranny, granted him participation in his own life, raised him to the heavens, made him sit at the right hand of the Majesty, and bestowed upon him the name that is above every name—conferring upon him his own dignity and assuming the designation of his nature.”

# EXCERPTS FROM THE LETTERS OF THEODORET

[Col. 1075]

[Col. 1075D] Thus far concerning the book *On the Incarnation*, or the *Pentalogy*. Now concerning the letters, beginning with the one that Theodoret wrote to Nestorius, for which Mercator, after translating it into Latin, prefixed the following preface.

[Col. 1076D] [Note: [Col. 1075D] By the term “exile” he means withdrawal to the monastery of Saint Euprepius, which we discussed in the historical preface. For it cannot signify deportation to the Oasis, which occurred four years after the Council of Ephesus had been dissolved—whether this letter was given while the matter of reconciling the Churches of Alexandria and Antioch was being discussed, or shortly afterward, when peace had been established, namely, toward the end of 432 or immediately at the beginning of the following year.

—“To Nestorius in exile.” Garnerius thinks this should be understood as his withdrawal to the monastery of Saint Euprepius near Antioch. But this withdrawal is nowhere called exile, and it is more readily believed that this letter was written when Nestorius had been deported to the Oasis. See what we have said on this subject at chapter 24 of the synodical work against Irenaeus’s *Tragedy*. BALUZ.]

Theodoret wrote to Nestorius, who had been assigned to exile because of his impiety, a letter in which he makes clear that he had approved the doctrine of the blessed Cyril, whom he calls [Note: [Col. 1077D] After Theodoret began to act more angrily in Nestorius’s case against Cyril, he calls him by this name—“the Egyptian”—especially in all the writings, whether treatises or letters, that bear his name, partly in the second part of the Council of Ephesus and partly in the Fifth Synod. From this it is easy to determine under whose authorship particular passages that might otherwise be doubtful were genuinely written.] “the Egyptian,” not because of love of honor, but compelled by the truth itself; yet that he in no way consented to the condemnation of Nestorius.

## Letter

[Note: [Col. 1077D] This letter is reported in the Fifth Synod, but by another translator. It is said there to have been given after unity had been established between the Orientals and the most holy Cyril. At that time, as is evident from the following letter, John of Antioch was demanding that those subject to him accept the conditions of peace, condemn the doctrines of Nestorius, and give their written consent to his deposition and to the ordination of Maximian.]

[Col. 1078B] There is, moreover, no reason to think it spurious, because Leontius reports that forged letters of Theodoret and Nestorius were being circulated by heretics. For if he means that statement to refer to these letters themselves, he may be refuted by Mercator’s testimony. Since Mercator recorded events of his own time, he has greater authority than Leontius, who wrote at least fifty years later.]

## Theodoret to Nestorius

“To my truly God-loving lord and venerable holy Father, Nestorius, bishop: Theodoret sends greetings in the Lord.

I think your holiness knows that urban society, service, and glory do not overcome me, and that I have no need of lofty sees. If nothing else, at least the solitude of the city whose administration I seem to have received has sufficiently taught me this philosophy: that even solitude is known to contain an accumulation of affairs capable of delaying many people, including those who take excessive delight in such matters.

Let no one, therefore, persuade your holiness that, because I desired to be a bishop, I received the Egyptian writings with closed eyes, as though they contained correct doctrines. For, I confess, after repeatedly rereading and carefully examining them, I found them free from heretical perversity and feared to place any stain upon them. Yet this was not done as though the one who had become a cause of disturbance to the whole world should thereby be approved; and I hope that on account of this I shall be subject to no guilt on the day of judgment, because the just Judge examines the intention of each person.

But concerning the things unjustly and wickedly done against your veneration, not even if someone were to cut off both my hands could I give my consent—divine grace unquestionably cooperating with me and raising up the weakness of my soul.

I have also made this certain in writing to those who demand these things, and I have sent your [Baluz.: “your”] holiness copies of what I wrote to them [Note: [Col. 1078C] Theodoret did not attend the council held by John of Antioch at Beroea concerning the arrangement of peace with the Alexandrians. First he was questioned by letter about his opinion of the conditions of peace and the profession of Cyril; then he was summoned so that he might subscribe to the agreed conditions. He rejected the conditions as unjust but accepted Cyril’s profession as a recantation of his earlier position; yet, because of his love for Nestorius and his impatience with Cyril’s victory, he refused to subscribe. We have shown all this at length in the dissertation on the Life of Theodoret to be prefixed to the supplementary collection of his works.], so that he may recognize that no passage of time will change us through God’s grace [Baluz.: *commutavit . . . ostendit*, “has changed … has shown”], nor will it show us to be octopuses or chameleons [Al.: “shape-shifters”], which imitate rocks in one case and leaves according to their respective colors in the other.

I and those who are with me warmly greet all the brotherhood that is with your veneration in the Lord.”

## Words of Marius Mercator

[He wrote] another letter in favor of the Nestorians.

[Note: [Col. 1078C] I do not think anyone will be an excessively rash conjecturer who supposes that this letter was written to Andrew, a Constantinopolitan monk favorable to Nestorius. Sirmondus included in his edition another letter to him, numbered 143. The subject matter of the two is not dissimilar, although in the letter preserved by Marius Theodoret expresses his meaning more openly, while in Sirmondus’s letter he conceals it through calculated brevity.

For it reads as follows (Letter 143):

“You write to a man who does not hold another opinion, but who has been trained in the discipline of the apostles and who defends the Trinity, not a quaternity. For I have judged those equally impious who dare to force the two natures of the Only-Begotten into one, and those who attempt to divide our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, God the Word made man, into two sons—if indeed there are any such people, for I do not think there are. But this calumny has always been shamelessly attached to the Church by those who follow Arius and Eunomius and those who adopt the party of Apollinaris.

Yet it is easy for those who pay careful attention to see that our most renowned Fathers, the lights of the Churches, suffered this very accusation from the enemies of truth, which at the present time we endure from the best defenders of the new heresy. Their impiety the all-wise Lord exposed, not permitting the wicked heresy to be strengthened by prolonged endurance.

Therefore, rest assured, lord, that you are writing to fellow believers, as you can easily learn from our many night-long labors. Return a letter; for, if God wills, these letters will again provide encouragement toward charity.”]

Concerning the two letters we have compared, first observe that the one found in Sirmondus’s collection is not placed in the wrong period, as some have thought. It belongs to later times, when Theodoret was accused of heresy and even condemned by Dioscorus at the Robber Council of Ephesus; it does not belong to the earlier period, when the troubles surrounding Nestorius had not yet subsided. This is shown by the words:

“It is easy to see that our Fathers, the lights of the Churches, suffered this very accusation from the enemies of truth, which at the present time [Col. 1079C] we endure from the best defenders of the new heresy.”

Next observe from the other letter, which Mercator excerpted, how Theodoret not only believed that Cyril had recanted his position, but even boastfully congratulated himself on this victory because Cyril’s anathemas had been criticized and their author, as he claimed, had been compelled to adopt Nestorius’s position.]

He sent another letter to Constantinople [Col. 1079A], in which he says that the Egyptians confessed two natures and the other doctrines of piety, but that no correction followed concerning the injustice committed against Nestorius.

[Note: [Col. 1079C] Baluz.: “The same Theodoret, from the letter that he sent to Constantinople for the consolation of the Nestorians, in which he says that the Egyptians confess two natures and the other doctrines of piety, but that no correction followed concerning the injustice committed against Nestorius,” and so forth.

And in a note:

“Garnerius conjectured here that this letter was written to Andrew, a Constantinopolitan monk; but in the supplementary collection of Theodoret’s works, p. 96, he presented this as a certainty. It is certain that it was written to the Constantinopolitans for the consolation of the Nestorians, just as, for the consolation of the same people, he wrote those letters to them that are found in the synodical work against the *Tragedy of Irenaeus*, chapters 40 and 47.” EDIT.]

## Theodoret to Andrew, a Constantinopolitan Monk

And after other material:

“But faithful is God, who will not allow either us or you to be tempted beyond what we can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that we may be able to endure (I Corinthians 13:10); and he will refute falsehood. Indeed, even now, with falsehood refuted, the assertion is proved and the power of truth has been demonstrated.”

[Note: [Col. 1079D] From this it is inferred that the letter was given after Cyril’s profession of faith had been sent to John of Antioch, that is, toward the end of 432. Cyril either sent two professions—one before the profession of faith presented by Paul of Emesa on John’s behalf, and another in the letter subsequently delivered to John—or he sent the same profession at different times or in different words.

The first of these two possibilities is more credible. Hence some have rashly accused Cyril of imprudence, because he sent the profession of faith first, as though it were the part of the accused to offer satisfaction before receiving it. From this arose Theodoret’s empty, taunting calumny, contained in the following words.]

“For behold, those who had confused the natures of Christ the Savior by impious reasoning, and had dared to preach one nature and to attribute sufferings to the Deity, had also insulted the most holy and venerable high priest of the supreme God, Nestorius [Baluz.: “had rebounded”]. [Note: [Col. 1079D] Compare this passage with another similar one in the letter incorrectly said in the Fifth Synod to have been sent to John [Col. 1080B], when in fact it was sent to Domnus, John’s successor. From the comparison you will understand that Binius and others had little reason for rejecting this very letter to Domnus as spurious. We have clearly demonstrated this in the critique prefixed to the supplementary collection of Theodoret’s works, against certain earlier authorities as well.]

But, like a bit and bridle (Psalm 31:9), according to the prophet, with their jaws completely broken and led from crooked ways to straight ones, they learned the truth again, using the assertion of the man who endured wars for the sake of truth.

For instead of one nature they now confess two (anathematizing those who preach mixture or confusion), they venerate the Deity of Christ as impassible [Baluz.: “in passibility”], they explain that the sufferings belong to the flesh, and they divide the evangelical utterances, assigning the sublime and God-worthy things to the Deity and the humble things to the humanity. For such things have now been sent in writings from Egypt.”

## Words of Marius Mercator

“He also wrote another letter to Andrew, bishop of Samosata, after reading the letter of the holy Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, sent from Beroea.”

[Note: [Col. 1080B] It is thereby established with considerable clarity that the synod said to have been held by John of Antioch while the matter of peace was being negotiated took place at the house of Acacius in Beroea, and not at Antioch, as the editors of the Councils and many others commonly suppose. It is also gathered—something otherwise certain—that Theodoret did not attend this synod, either because he impatiently endured the negotiations concerning peace, that is, concerning the condemnation of Nestorius and the reception of Cyril, being intensely devoted to the former and excessively hostile to the latter, or because he was prevented by some other obstacle.]

## Theodoret to Andrew, Bishop of Samosata

[Note: [Col. 1080C] This letter is said in the Fifth Synod to have been written after peace had been restored to the Churches. Another letter of Theodoret to the same man is read as having been given at Ephesus, where Andrew had not assembled because of illness, after Cyril and Memnon had been deposed by the Orientals and restored by the holy synod—that is, around the end of July 431.]

“The distinguished Aristolaus sent from Egypt Magisterianus [Col. 1080B] [Baluz.: ‘Magisterianus’] with a letter from Cyril. In it Cyril anathematizes Arius, Eunomius, Apollinaris, those who say that the Deity of Christ is passible, and those who assert confusion and mixture of the two natures. We rejoiced at this, although he avoided our proposal.

[Note: [Col. 1080C] What proposal was this? The one concerning which Cyril wrote to Acacius of Melitene:

‘At a certain council held with the most holy and pious Bishop Acacius of Beroea, they arranged that a letter be written to me concerning the terms of the agreement—that is, that peace between the holy Churches should not be made except in the manner prescribed by them. They wanted everything I had published, whether in letters, treatises, or books, to be abolished, and wanted us to consent only to the faith issued by the Fathers of Nicaea.

I replied to them as follows: We all adhere to the exposition of the faith issued by the Fathers of Nicaea, undermining nothing whatever contained in it; for all those things have been correctly and blamelessly handed down, and it is not safe to investigate anything further after that exposition of the faith.

But what we correctly wrote against the blasphemies of Nestorius is such that we cannot be persuaded by any means to deny that it was correctly written. Therefore, what was needed was that they should, in accordance with the decree of the most pious and Christ-loving emperor—or rather, in accordance with the decree of the holy synod of Ephesus—expel the man who fought against the glory of Christ the Savior, attack his impious blasphemies with an anathema, consent to his deposition, and approve the ordination of the most holy and pious Bishop Maximian.’]

[Col. 1081A] “He demands a subscription to the condemnation made some time ago, and that the doctrine of the holy bishop Nestorius be anathematized. But your holiness knows that if anyone [Note: [Col. 1081B] That is, without making any restriction and without distinguishing between doctrine and person. From this you may understand how ancient is that κρησφύγετον (*kresphýgeton*, hidden refuge), which certain people have sometimes abused, and which that impious man recently dared to use in a written book accusing Cyril and the Council of Ephesus of the Eutychian heresy. We shall discuss this matter more fully elsewhere, when we undertake a dissertation on subscriptions in the case of the Pelagians.] anathematizes the doctrine of that same most holy and venerable bishop indiscriminately, it is the same as though he appeared to anathematize piety.

Therefore, if we are compelled at all, we ought to anathematize those who say that Christ was a mere man, or who divide our one Lord Jesus Christ into two sons, or who deny his Deity, and so forth.”

[Note: [Col. 1081C] Baluzius separates the following material from what precedes it under this heading:

He proves the matter as follows:

Pelagius II, in the letter mentioned shortly before, says in writing to Alexander, bishop of the Palestinian Syrians: ‘I think,’ and so forth. This letter of Theodoret to Alexander exists complete in the synodical work cited above, chapter 66.”

“I think that my most holy and venerable lord, Bishop John, has been satisfied above all because I in no way consent to the condemnation of my most holy and venerable lord, Bishop Nestorius” [Col. 1081B].

[Note: [Col. 1081C] “To give consent” is the reading found at Tarsus. Seeing that this passage was mutilated, Garnerius interpolated it as follows: “to give consent, nor to violate the common promise made at Tarsus,” and so forth.

But from the letter of Pelagius cited above it is evident that originally nothing else stood there in the books of Marius Mercator than what is still read by us. It is certain, however, that some things are missing in this passage and must be supplied and corrected from the synodical work, as follows:

“to give consent, because he remembers what was done at Tarsus, Chalcedon, and Ephesus.” BALUZ.]

“—to give consent, nor to violate the common promise made at Tarsus, Chalcedon, and Ephesus.”

[Note: [Col. 1081D] The Orientals had resolved never to consent either to the deposition of Nestorius or to the restoration of Cyril, and they had made this resolution not once or in one place only, but first at Ephesus, when the legates departed from there for Constantinople after receiving their instructions; again at Chalcedon, when they presented a petition to the emperor; afterward at Tarsus, when they returned to the East after being dismissed; and finally at Antioch, before they separated from one another and returned individually to their own cities.]

“For he also remembers what was recently brought forward by us many times at Antioch after our return. Let no one, therefore, deceive your holiness into thinking that I will ever do this, God unquestionably cooperating with me and strengthening me.”

## Theodoret’s Letter to Himerius, Bishop of Nicomedia

[Note: [Col. 1082B] This was unquestionably written at the time when Paul of Emesa, as envoy of the Eastern synod, was conducting negotiations for peace at Alexandria and, according to his instructions, was trying to settle the matter under the most honorable conditions—namely, that only assent to the Nicene faith should be demanded; that no subscription to the deposition of Nestorius should be required, but that it should be confirmed by silence alone; and that the bishops deposed by Maximian—Himerius, Helladius, Eutherius, and Dorotheus—should recover their sees.]

Among other things:

“We make our settled intention known to your holiness [Col. 1082A]: having read the letters sent from Egypt and repeatedly discussed among us, we found them consonant with the doctrine of the Church; [Note: [Col. 1082C] That is, what he writes to the monk Andrew: that Cyril, led from crooked ways to straight ones, finally learned the truth. It is worthwhile to compare both letters together.] but we judged them contrary to the Twelve Chapters, which we have persisted in opposing to the present day.

[Note: [Col. 1082C] He himself opposed Cyril’s chapters not only in the five books *On the Incarnation* mentioned above, but even to the point of death; he also transmitted them to others as objects of execration. Hence Gennadius, successor of Anatolius in the see of Constantinople, shortly after Theodoret’s death—and therefore after the Council of Chalcedon and the condemnation of Dioscorus together with Eutyches—broke out against Cyril’s anathemas in these words:

‘Woe is me because of evils! Alas, alas! For where else could anyone now begin? What and how many blasphemies of Cyril the Egyptian have I encountered? How many blasphemies have I heard?’ and so forth. (In Facundus, Book I, chapter 4.)]

[Note: [Col. 1082D] In his letter to Donatus, Cyril recounts the history of that entire undertaking for the restoration of the four bishops—Himerius of Nicomedia, Helladius of Tarsus, Eutherius of Tyana, and Dorotheus of Marcianopolis—who had been deposed by the synod of Maximian. We discuss this same history at length in the dissertation on Eutherius, whose works we shall join to the appendix to Theodoret because of their connection.]

It therefore seemed good to us that, if your Holinesses receive the Churches divinely entrusted to you, you should communicate with the Egyptians and the Constantinopolitans, and with others who are known to have fought against us together with them, since they have professed that they possess our faith—or rather, that of the apostles—but should not consent to the condemnation of the venerable and most holy Nestorius, which is said to have taken place. For we truly judge it unjust and impious that, although he was guilty of the same crimes of which his associate had also been convicted, pardon should be granted to the one while the door of repentance is closed to the other; and much more unjust and more impious that an innocent man should be delivered to death.

Let your Holiness therefore know that we judge that we ought not to communicate with them before you receive your Churches. This was decreed not by me alone, but by all the most holy bishops of our region, after a council had been held. [Note: [Col. 1082D] In Baluzius, what follows is separated from the preceding material under this title: “Another letter of the same Theodoret to Alexander of Hierapolis.” See the complete letter from which this passage is taken in the *Synodicon*, chapter 99, p. 806. EDIT.] And I already told your Holiness that, if the doctrine of my lord, the venerable and most holy Bishop Nestorius, is condemned, neither shall I communicate with those who do this. If it pleases your Holiness to insert this very point into the letter that will be sent to Antioch, let it be done. Therefore, I beg you, do not delay, while I cling to your footsteps.

[Note: [Col. 1083B] Baluzius entitles this fragment: “Another letter of the same Theodoret to the same Alexander, after he learned that John, Bishop of Antioch, had anathematized the doctrine of Nestorius.” He adds in his notes: “This letter is preserved in full in the *Synodicon* cited above, chapter 128, p. 849.” EDIT.]

**To the same, after he learned that John had anathematized the doctrine of Nestorius.**

After other matters:

“Let it not escape your Holiness,” he says, “that, after I read the letter addressed to the emperor, I was deeply grieved in spirit, because I clearly recognize that the person who wrote it, while holding the same opinion, condemned him indiscriminately and unjustly—him who knew and taught nothing except sound doctrine [Baluzius: ‘taught nothing new’]. But although the anathema inserted in it—while more than sufficient to disturb the reader because of the agreement in his condemnation—was nevertheless set down not indiscriminately but with a certain qualification, it provided consolation. [Col. 1083B] For he did not say, ‘We anathematize his doctrine,’ but ‘Whatever he said or thought contrary to what apostolic doctrine contains.’”

[Note: [Col. 1083C] Theodoret was either extremely blind if he did not see the blasphemies of Nestorius, or in some measure a Nestorian if he regarded these blasphemies as sound doctrine. I therefore cannot sufficiently wonder that many approved the opinion of Agobard, who said that Theodoret had discovered a middle position between the heretic Nestorius and the Catholic Cyril, and that, while fighting for the truth, he fought against the truth, etc. [Col. 1084B]]

### Words of Marius Mercator

Likewise, from the acts written against Domnus, Bishop of Antioch, in which the same Domnus is accused because, in his presence, that most wicked Theodoretus dared to say openly in the Church, after the death of Cyril, the holy pontiff of Alexandria, insulting his blessed repose, as follows.

### From a sermon delivered at Antioch by Theodoret after the death of Saint Cyril

[Note: [Col. 1084B] Because of this sermon, and perhaps other similar statements, Theodoret was accused of dividing Christ into two sons. For this was the substance of the entire accusation brought against him, as he testifies in Letters 93, 101, and 105, although he complains everywhere that this charge was made against him, and in Letter 84 attributes its origin to the fact that certain people in the East held this opinion. This letter is addressed to the bishops of Cilicia, to which the city of Mopsuestia, Theodorus’s see, belonged. He suspected that some among them held this view and requested that they be corrected, lest some odium from the crime of his friends rebound upon him.]

“No one now compels anyone to blaspheme. Where are those who say that it is God who was crucified? God was not crucified, but the man Jesus Christ was crucified. God, however, raised up his temple from David, just as David himself foretold: ‘Man begets man.’ By nature the Son of God is God the Word; Christ, however, is the son of David. But the Son of God is not a temple” [Baluzius: “the temple of the Son”]. “There is no longer any dispute. Egypt and the East have come together under one yoke; envy has died, and heresy has been buried with it. Those who preach that God suffered now rest,” etc.

### Another version in the Fifth Synod, differing not only in wording but also in certain meanings

“No one now compels anyone to blaspheme. Where are those who say [Col. 1084B] that it is God who was crucified? God is not crucified; the man Jesus Christ, who is from the seed of David, the son of Abraham, was crucified. It is the man Jesus Christ who died. God the Word raised up his temple, which is from David, just as David said: ‘Man begets man.’ He who by nature is the Son of God is God the Word. Christ, however, is the son of David; but he is the temple of the Son of God. There is no longer any dispute. The East and Egypt are under one yoke; envy has died, and dispute has been buried with it. Let the theopaschites rest.”

## III. EUTHERIUS OF TYANA

### PREFACE OF MARIUS MERCATOR

[Note: [Col. 1085A] We shall add a dissertation on both his person and his works in the appendix to the supplement to Theodoret. For the present, the following may suffice. He was metropolitan of Tyana, in the diocese of Constantinople, and especially devoted to Nestorius. He subscribed, in seventh place, to Nestorius’s report concerning the first session of the Council of Ephesus; and, in twenty-sixth place, to the deposition of Cyril and Memnon. He is also mentioned in the emperor’s letter to the Council of Ephesus, in the synod of John of Antioch, read by John, the imperial official, and in all the places where Catholics enumerate the names of the schismatics. When the conditions for restoring peace to the Churches were being debated, the Easterners fought for the restoration of him, Helladius of Tarsus, Himerius of Nicomedia, and Dorotheus of Marcianopolis. The Alexandrians, however, resisted vigorously, and those four men therefore did not enjoy the benefit of peace. See the letter written by Cyril to Donatus after the disturbances of the Churches had been settled.]

On Eutherius, a bishop of the Nestorian party, and on his sermons against the opinions of Saint Cyril and certain Catholics.

[Note: [Col. 1085B] To this day, the sermons in volume II of the Works of Athanasius entitled *Against Various Heresies*, published in Scultetus’s translation with an uncertain author, have been variously attributed: some thought them Athanasius’s, others Maximus the Martyr’s, and others the work of an unknown author. Mercator establishes their author all the more certainly by citing a notable fragment of the sermon. But much more concerning Eutherius’s sermons will be said in the dissertation just mentioned. ]

[Col. 1085A] [Note: [Col. 1085C] We have restored, as far as conjecture based on what precedes and follows permits, the material lacking in the manuscript copies; for that reason we have distinguished it in a different type, lest anyone perhaps accuse us of the fault of interpolation.]

Now that the blasphemies of Nestorius, Theodorus, and Theodoretus have been exposed, let us demonstrate from the sermons he wrote against the opinions of certain Catholics that Eutherius’s impiety was the same as theirs, though insinuated into the minds of the faithful more subtly and therefore more perniciously. Let us begin especially with the opinion of the blessed Cyril, pontiff of Alexandria, concerning Christ, which he expressed by saying:
