[Note: [Col. 1085C] Cyril expressed this proposition both in his third letter to Nestorius and in various other places, as well as in the *Scholia*; he also alludes to it in his defense of the twelfth anathema against the Easterners, on the authority of the great Basil, who says that God was joined impassibly to death through the flesh: τὸν Θεὸν διὰ σαρκὸς συμηλακῆναι τῷ θανάτῳ ἀπαθῶς, “that God was joined to death through the flesh impassibly.” In *The Impassible*, Theodoret’s *Eranistes* admits this form of speech as though it were common among Catholics: “We say that he suffered impassibly.” Theodoret derides this statement as ridiculous: “Who in his right mind could endure these ridiculous circumlocutions of words? For no one has ever heard of an impassible passion or an immortal death. For what is impassible has not suffered, and what has suffered does not remain impassible.” Earlier he had also mocked Cyril’s statement, “The Word suffered in the flesh”; from this it is sufficiently clear that by the name *Eranistes* not Eutyches—as many credulously suppose—but Cyril is in fact meant.]

### HE SUFFERED IMPASSIBLY

This statement, supported by the authority of Catholic truth, seeks to assert that the one and same Son of God is to be believed impassible according to his divinity and passible according to the flesh; just as Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, explains in his book *On the Incarnation of Christ* in these words (Book *On the Incarnation*, chapter 5):

“He was dying, and he was not dying; he was being buried, and he was not being buried; he was rising, and he was not rising, because he was raising his own body; because what fell is what rises, and what did not fall does not rise.”

[Note: [Col. 1086B] Observe carefully that Theodoret took his testimony from Ambrose’s book *On the Incarnation*, specifically from chapter 5, to use it for his own purpose. Yet he did not quote the words that Mercator gives, although they greatly assist in distinguishing the natures in Christ. He omitted them, evidently because that chapter contains a remarkable passage relevant to the matter under discussion and capable of convicting Theodoret—or at least Nestorius. “Against all heresies this is the general faith: that Christ is the Son of God, eternal from the Father, and born from the Virgin. Saint David the prophet describes him as a kind of giant, because, while being one, he is a participant in divinity and body, possessing a twofold and double nature. He, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, rejoiced like a giant to run his course: bridegroom of the soul according to the Word, giant of the earth, because, while carrying out the functions of our nature, he—being always eternal as God—assumed the mysteries of the incarnation; not divided, but one, because both are one, and one is in both, whether in divinity or in body. For one is not from the Father and another from the Virgin; rather, the same one is from the Father in one manner and from the Virgin in another. One generation does not prejudice the other, nor does flesh prejudice divinity, because neither is the pledge opposed to the Father, nor the will to the passion, nor the passion to the will.”]

But the followers of Nestorius, dividing the one into two sons, separate the will of one from the sufferings of the other. They do not believe that God was born from the Virgin according to the flesh, nor do they say that he endured the insult of the cross according to the flesh. Instead, by asserting that these humiliations belonged to a man, they separate the mystery of the saving dispensation from the Word of God, and thus prove themselves ungrateful for such great benefits.

### Words of Marius Mercator

But now let the crafty depravity of the aforementioned Eutherius, which will have no further force among the faithful, be exposed.

## FRAGMENT FROM A SERMON OF EUTHERIUS THE NESTORIAN AGAINST SAINT CYRIL, TRANSLATED BY MARIUS MERCATOR

[Col. 1087]

“O well-considered playful doctrine of unconsidered wisdom [Note: [Col. 1087B] A playful construction. We restored this from the Vatican manuscript in place of what Garnerius, following the Bellovacensis manuscript, published as *luxuria et disciplina* (‘extravagance and discipline’). We have shown in the notes to chapter 21 of Lactantius’s *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* that *lusoria* was sometimes written elsewhere for *luxuria*. The Greek words of this fragment, which survive in volume II of Saint Athanasius’s works, p. 305, and hence in the appendix to Theodoret’s works, p. 701, confirm this correction. BALUZ.]—extravagance and discipline, building and destroying at the same time, as we see children playing in the sand:

‘He suffered impassibly.’

Before I hear what he suffered, the meaning of what he suffered escapes me; for the addition ‘impassibly’ does not allow what he suffered to remain” [Baluzius adds: “impassibly”]. “If he suffered, how did he suffer impassibly? If impassibly, how did he suffer? Let us speak ineffably and think insensibly. Who has ever seen someone falling without a fall, rising without a resurrection, grieving without grief, being wise without wisdom, helping without assistance, or releasing something in an unreleaseable manner? And I shall accept it: ‘He suffered impassibly.’”

Paul, he says, ascending to the third heaven and hearing unspeakable words in heaven [Baluzius: “in paradise”], uttered nothing of the sort, perhaps leaving such a sublime interpretation to these men. For he did not say, “He suffered impassibly,” but: “He learned obedience from the things that he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8); and: “Tempted in every respect according to likeness, without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). In this way he completely removed such delirious expressions. For he who was tempted in every respect according to likeness, if he suffered, suffered passibly [Baluzius: “impassibly”], so that the likeness might be preserved in every respect; or else let others be shown to have suffered impassibly, so that the likeness which he bore may be preserved.

Therefore, either the Savior must be confessed to have truly suffered, or others must likewise be believed to have suffered impassibly, according to whose likeness the Lord is said to have been tempted.

What demonstration of patience would there be if he suffered impassibly? How could Christ’s patience be proclaimed if, in suffering pain, he did not feel it? How would Christ’s ineffable and incomparable love toward human beings be shown if his passion took place without pain? Who would not choose to suffer, not only for friends but even for enemies, if it were possible to suffer impassibly?

[Col. 1088B] Why, moreover, did the Lord say, “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:42), if he was beginning to endure his passion without pain? Why did he also cry out to the Father, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (ibid., verse 39)? Why, too, did he offer prayers and supplications to the one who could save him from death, with a loud cry and tears (Hebrews 5:7)?”

## EPILOGUE

[Col. 1087]

[Col. 1087C] We have set these things down hastily for the present, lest we seem to exceed the limits of the book. At a suitable time, with God’s favor, we shall expose more fully the poisonous contagions of many people who deceive the simplicity of the faithful [Baluzius adds: “with a simple witness”].

But now, at the conclusion of this work, it is possible to refute this very Nestorian perfidy with several examples.

“Say, ungrateful, cruel, and impious heresy, which rejects the voluntary self-emptying of Christ our Lord for our sake [Baluzius: ‘which regards it as shameful’], and considers the humility of divine condescension unworthy; which, together with Jews and Gentiles, reckons Christ’s cross a scandal and folly, and does not confess that God made man endured sufferings impassibly: if, while the Nile remained in its own nature, it was blood to the Egyptians (Exodus 7:20), but drinkable water to the Hebrews; if daylight gave light to the Israelites (Exodus 10:23; Wisdom 18:1), but poured out upon their enemies the darkness they deserved; if the Babylonian furnace refreshed the three youths with dew but consumed the Babylonians with fire (Daniel 3:24); why should it seem to you unworthy or impossible that one and the same Son, on account of both natures, should have suffered impassibly for us? If this is the power and capacity of a creature, why could the Creator not accomplish the same, he who did everything he wished in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses (Psalm 134:6)?”

[[Note: [Col. 1087D] In Garnerius, the material enclosed in brackets is absent. We restored it from Baluzius, who thus censures Garnerius’s omission: “These passages fell out of Garnerius’s edition. Fell out, I say: for in his general preface, p. VI (Supplement, cols. 15–16), he cites part of them and says that the book ends with them. All these passages are of great importance.” [Col. 1088D] EDIT.]]

But lest the followers of Nestorius, in their customary slander, accuse as Eutychians those who resist their wicked doctrine, it must be said that both heresies share this characteristic: whenever a Catholic disputant rises against either one, he escapes neither accusation. While we refute the madness of Eutyches, they do not cease calling us Nestorians; and, conversely, when the accomplices of Nestorius are convicted by Catholic truth, they falsely claim that their refuters are Eutychians. We therefore judged it necessary to expose both forms of depravity, which creep through the ignorance of many, by means of the sermons of the most blessed Father John, bishop of the city of Tomi in the province of Scythia. [Note: [Col. 1088D] Excerpts from the works of John of Tomi followed; they have been lost. BALUZ.]

# BOOK FOUR

Containing **TWO DISSERTATIONS**:

The first, **ON THE HERESY AND BOOKS OF NESTORIUS**;

the second, **ON THE SYNODS HELD IN THE CASE OF NESTORIUS**, from the time when the disturbances began until peace was restored to the Churches.

[Col. 1089]

## FIRST DISSERTATION: ON THE HERESY AND BOOKS OF NESTORIUS

On these words of Marius Mercator:

“Thus Nestorius is joined to Paul of Samosata in that he separates the indweller and the dwelling according to their respective merits, dividing what belongs properly to each of them according to the difference of nature; and this is common to both of them with Ebion, Photinus, and Marcellus of Galatia” (*Letter on the Distinction*, no. 17).

[Col. 1089A] After the works of Nestorius, Theodorus of Mopsuestia, Theodoretus, and Eutherius, which Mercator collected, have been presented in the preceding books, it will not, I think, be useless or irrelevant to our subject—although perhaps by no means a light undertaking—to set forth the Nestorian heresy clearly and openly. By Nestorius himself bearing witness, we shall show what kind of impiety it was that disturbed the whole world and attempted to cast Christ down from the throne of divinity.

Different writers present it in different ways, and it is certainly woven from such intricate errors—or from such deceptive modes of speech—that it has deceived not only later observers, who stand far removed from it, but also the ancients and people of its own age.

This undertaking will help establish confidence in Mercator, and all the more so because it will become clearer from it how subtly he detected the heresy hiding in its concealments, exposed it, and brought it into the light, even when it repeatedly assumed many forms and eluded the keenest minds.

[Col. 1089B] It will also help strengthen the authority of the Church. In former times there were a few people—and in our own time there are many more—whose conviction is equally important for faith and truth, since they think that Nestorius either did not err at all, which is impious to say, or erred only slightly, which is rash, or was condemned beyond measure, which is unjust.

Theodoretus certainly considered Nestorius so free from error that he believed condemning his doctrine to be the same as pronouncing an anathema against piety itself. Socrates wrote that the controversy had arisen merely over a word used by Nestorius. Anyone who placed an epitaph upon the Nestorian heresy—asserting that Christ became God through the merit and reward of his works and labors—was likewise charged with the same fault. Neither Theodoretus piously, nor Socrates prudently, nor the poet justly seems to have judged.

Yet even in our own age some adhere to them: many to Theodoretus among the Sacramentarians, which is less surprising; to Socrates, men of an excessively heated age and contentious mind, which is not unusual; and to the poet, many men of great reputation and learning, which is regrettable. Although their opinions differ, their injustice is the same, since it is both a crime to acquit the enemy of Christ and an injustice to burden a most wicked man with the crimes of others.

How honorable, and how useful, it is to engage in this work is matched by how arduous and difficult the undertaking itself appears. In this question there are prejudices in favor of the authors cited—many in number, highly damaging to truth, and by no means hostile to the faith—which, however much weight they possess from age and influence from numbers, must nevertheless be removed from minds occupied by credulity, as usually happens.

To accomplish this, it is first necessary, after presenting the ancient errors concerning the incarnation—that is, the union of the two natures in Christ—to establish the question raised by Nestorius.

[Col. 1090A] Next, Nestorius’s own heresy must be set forth from unquestionable testimonies, that is, testimonies taken from no source other than Nestorius himself.

Then we must explain what opinion Arius, Apollinaris, and Eunomius held, which Nestorius attributed to the Catholics; and how, when he wished to distance himself from it, he fell into error.

Afterward this same error must be compared with the doctrines of Ebion, Paul of Samosata, Marcellus of Galatia, and Photinus, whose association with Nestorius was reproached by the Catholics, or whose association with the Catholics was reproached by Nestorius.

Finally, we must show what expressions this wickedly clever man misused either to conceal or to insinuate his heresy.

Lastly, certain popular opinions concerning this matter must be overthrown—opinions introduced partly by great authorities and partly confirmed by common habits of hearing and speaking.

At the end, we must investigate the remainder of Nestorius’s faith and his books.

## CHAPTER ONE

### The nature of the celebrated question that Nestorius raised in the Church, and on account of which a general council was necessary to resolve it

[Col. 1090B]

There are three doctrines of the Christian faith: the consubstantiality of the divine persons, the truth of the incarnation, and its fruit, which is the salvation of human beings. From the earliest times the Church has labored to establish these doctrines. Whenever heretics have attacked one of the three, it has stirred the entire world; each has compelled the Church to fight with all her strength and to purchase her victories over her enemies not only with the labors but also with the blood of the saints.

The war against the enemies of the *homoousion*—the consubstantial—was indeed renowned. But, if one may say so, it yields in consequence to the later war against the enemies of the incarnation, or the destroyers of the true incarnation. The former war was therefore concluded by two general councils; the latter scarcely by four, and those so numerous that at times the entire Christian world seemed to have flowed together into a single city, Chalcedon. The first of the councils I mentioned was held at Ephesus in the case of Nestorius, so that the great question on which the salvation and dignity of the Christian name depended might be resolved.

To understand the nature of so great a controversy—which is what this chapter must accomplish—we must first explain what the ancient heresies were concerning the joining of the two natures in Christ; then the Catholic doctrine opposed to those heresies; and finally the points on which Nestorius agreed with the Church and those on which he disagreed.

### § I. The ancient heresies concerning the joining of the natures in Christ, and the Church’s doctrine opposed to those heresies

All who have been counted by the Christian name down to the present day have unanimously asserted that two natures, divine and human, were joined in Christ to some degree. But as soon as the question was asked either what divinity and humanity were in themselves, or in what manner the two were joined, heresies suddenly arose that were as opposed to one another as they were hostile to the Catholic faith.

It is neither possible nor necessary to list them individually and briefly. Two outstanding Fathers, Cyril and Leo the Great, undertook this task: Cyril when writing to Theodosius concerning the right faith, and Leo when instructing the Church against Eutyches. In our own age Dionysius Petavius also performed it, with great distinction both for learning and for diligence (Volume IV of the *Dogmatics*, book I).

We may, unless I am mistaken, approach the matter appropriately as follows. Whoever considers the conjunction of the natures in Christ immediately distinguishes by the power of understanding the natures themselves, which are joined, from the manner of their conjunction. He distinguishes two natures, while considering both the kind and the permanence of the conjunction.

Some have erred in all these matters; others concerning the natures, others concerning the manner of conjunction; and even among these errors there has not been complete uniformity. Some of them were deceived concerning the divinity, others concerning the humanity. Of the latter, some fell into error concerning the kind of conjunction, others concerning its permanence.

From this arises a fourfold division. It is especially relevant to our subject because, in explaining its several parts, we need mention by name scarcely any heretics other than those whose association was attributed either by the Catholics to Nestorius or by Nestorius to the Catholics.

In explaining the mystery of the incarnation, Sabellius sinned against the divinity, as though by excess, since he asserted that the whole divinity was incarnate in itself, distinguishing the persons of the Trinity not in reality, as was proper, but only by name or even by operation.

Samosatene and Arius, by contrast, sinned through defect. Samosatene said that the Word of God joined to human nature was *anupostatos*—without individual subsistence—and merely uttered, almost like our own word. Arius, on the other hand, although he made the Word hypostatic, nevertheless refused to confess him consubstantial (*homoousios*) with the Father. He regarded him merely as one of the creatures, indeed the first and most excellent of all, but still far inferior to God.

Against these, the Catholic Church established the doctrine that the Word, the second person of the Trinity and the Son consubstantial with the Father, joined himself to humanity.

But concerning humanity, Manichaeus fell into error by asserting only the appearance of flesh; Apelles by asserting flesh received from heaven; the Arians by asserting a humanity lacking a soul; and Apollinarius by asserting that a humanity without a mind had been assumed.

Against these heretics the Church defined that the whole of humanity was assumed by the Word consubstantial with the Father, so that the whole might be saved.

Concerning the kind of conjunction, some likewise sinned through defect, others through excess. The former included Theodorus of Mopsuestia, who admitted only a moral or relational union (*schetikē*); the latter included those who imagined the conversion of one nature into the other: either of divinity into flesh, as some Apollinarians held; or of humanity into God, as the Theopaschites held; or of both into some third mixed entity, as Eutyches is reported to have believed.

In opposition, the Church defined that two natures, unmixed and unconfused, came together in a union according to hypostasis (*henōsis kath’ hypostasin*), or natural union, and, as it is commonly expressed, substantial union.

Finally, concerning the permanence of the union, those erred not only who denied that it would always endure, but also those who denied that it was formed in the Virgin’s womb. Thus Paul of Samosata is said to have imagined that it was earned through works by the adult Jesus; thus Leporius and others are said to have taught that it was laid aside during the three days of death, or at least when Christ complained from the cross that he had been abandoned, or even throughout the entire time of the passion; and thus Marcellus of Galatia is said to have taught that it would be discarded after the work of redemption had been completed.

[Col. 1092A] Opposed to these errors stands the Church’s unshaken faith: the two natures came together from the very beginning of conception, and they have never lost, nor will they ever lose, their union. All the faithful profess in the Creed that they believe in Christ “whose kingdom shall have no end.”

It is therefore clear that the Catholic doctrine has five parts: namely, that the Word, consubstantial with the Father, was joined inseparably in the Virgin’s womb to an integral human nature by a substantial union. These five points may be reduced to three questions: what kind of natures were joined in Christ, how long the union lasted, and in what manner it occurred. We must examine what Nestorius testified that he believed concerning each.

## § II. What Nestorius believed concerning the natures joined in Christ

Nestorius consistently confessed that the divine Word, whom the Evangelist teaches to have been joined to human nature, was neither something merely uttered and *anupostatos*, which Photinus is said to have intended after Samosatene, nor something subsisting that was less than the Father, as Arius asserted, but consubstantial with the Father and *homoousios*.

He attacks Photinus and Samosatene in both of his final sermons, and with greater force because, by this criticism, he was trying to withdraw himself from association with both men, an association of which he was accused:

“Paul and Photinus differ from one another in this,” he says (Sermon 12, no. 15): “one of them says that Christ is merely a man; the other indeed speaks of the Word, but does not confess that the Word is God. Rather, he says that this Word is sometimes called by the name of the Father and sometimes called by the name of the Word. Hence he also calls him *Logopatōr*, which means ‘Word and Father,’ or, if one may say so, ‘Word-Father,’ perversely applying to this purpose what is properly said in the Gospel: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God’ (John 1:1). You see,” he says, “that he sometimes calls the Word God and sometimes the Word, as though extended and gathered together; but he does not introduce God the Word as having become man. For he does not know the divinity of Christ; he does not know that the divine substance assumed a man; he altogether does not know the divinity of the Word existing before the ages.” And shortly afterward: “Photinus, as I have said, does not possess the divinity of the Word.”

In the final sermon (no. 2):

“The science of piety is to set forth a right account of the divinity of the consubstantial Trinity and to confess that the divine nature assumed a corporeal man.”

And shortly afterward (no. 3):

“Having preserved this knowledge of piety in summary form. What else is it than *orthologia*, a right account of the consubstantial divine Trinity and of the divine nature that assumes a man? See Sermon 7, no. 11, in the same sense.”

In these passages he likewise attacks Arius, although he does not name him. For what else is it to confess *homoousios* than to contradict Arius? Moreover, the hatred toward the Arians that we said had burned in Nestorius—whether when he set fire to their church in the imperial city or when he listed them as the first of the heretics in the law that he urged Theodosius to enact against the entire class of heretics—clearly shows how far he stood from the error of those who thought that the Word was a creature or at least something inferior to the Father.

Finally, his sermons contain passages that expressly attack Arius, such as these from Sermon 4 (nos. 8–9):

“For this reason we are also greatly blameworthy in the eyes of the Arians. If we simply and without qualification call God the Word ‘born,’ see what follows from this. You say simply: ‘God is the one who was born from Mary.’ Immediately the heretic objects: ‘Then you accuse us unjustly when we say that the Son is less than the Father and created, since even in your confession there is this: that the Word who was born from Mary is God.’ Hear what this same God the Word testifies concerning himself: ‘Go and announce to my brothers: I am going to my Father and your Father, my God and your God’ (John 20:17). But when he said this—he who was born from blessed Mary—he was indeed consubstantial with us according to his humanity; but in that in which he was joined to God, he was far removed from us, because he was God, of a superior substance.”

To this may be added the Creed of Theodorus, which Nestorius made his own when he proposed it to the people as something to be believed. It contains an explicit confession of the *homoousion*. We may also add Mercator’s testimony concerning Paul of Samosata, when he distinguished Nestorius’s heresy from Paul’s:

“Nestorius,” he says (*Letter on the Distinction*, etc., no. 1), “concerning the Word of God does not think as Paul does. Paul defines the Word not as substantial but as uttered, and as an effective power of God. Yet Nestorius does not confess of the substantial Word that he is naturally the Son of God. Rather, he says—cleverly, though not explicitly—that from eternity he is not the Son but only the Word, who, while remaining in the substance of the Father, is God consubstantial with him, whom the Greeks call *homoousios*.”

So much for Nestorius concerning the divinity of the Word. We must now consider his view of human nature. He demonstrated not merely in explicit words but above all by his conduct that the whole of humanity was assumed by the Word—not flesh lacking a rational soul, as the Arians held, nor flesh lacking a mind, as Apollinarius wished. He did so especially when he continually charged the defenders of the hypostatic union—that is, the Catholics—with agreement with Apollinarius and Arius on this point, as though no one could conceive a substantial union of the natures unless he said that the Word took the place either of the whole soul or at least of the mind.

To repel this slander, Cyril, when presenting the rule of right faith to Theodosius, wrote that the whole nature of man had been assumed by the Word so that the whole might be healed. When he defended his own faith and that of Memnon at Ephesus, he was compelled, in a written statement, to condemn Arius, Apollinarius, and Eunomius.

Andrew of Samosata had made this accusation against Cyril in the name of the Easterners. Theodoretus had also made it, charging Cyril with having burst forth in his anathemas into heretical and blasphemous expressions and with having revived the empty and impious doctrine of Apollinarius, which had long since been extinguished.

[Col. 1093C] Nor did he impose that charge upon Cyril alone, but also upon all the Fathers of the Council of Ephesus, forgetting modesty and himself; for, when in his uncontrolled anger over the condemnation of his Nestorius, who had been condemned, he sharpened his venomous pen against the most sacred council, he addresses the holy teachers of the faith as follows (Book V of the *Pentalogus*):

“Envy, to which you have enslaved yourselves, has prevailed to such an extent that what Apollinaris once uttered through one or two men—and those secretly—is now displayed by many prelates of the Church in the sacred assemblies of the Churches; such herbs are offered to the flocks by shepherds, and the bites of wolves are inflicted upon rational sheep through the ministry of their leaders. He who once addressed a few people in two or three cities, outside the walls, and seduced them even with various songs, now dances through the middle of cities by your agency; for you proclaim his errors and adorn yourselves with novelties of expression, restoring his blasphemy, which had already been consumed by time.”

§ III. What Nestorius thought concerning the beginning and duration of the union of the natures

[Col. 1093D]

Just as Nestorius did not depart from the Church’s judgment concerning the two extremes of the union, so neither did he think anything opposed to the Church concerning the time at which the union first existed, continued thereafter, or was to continue. For he held that it had already come into existence when the Holy Spirit was at work in the Virgin’s womb and was building a temple for the Word—that is, at the very conception of the man. He teaches this so openly and so frequently that I cannot sufficiently marvel at those who attribute another opinion to Nestorius.

Sermon 3 (Nos. 5–6): “Who, then, will be like her according to substance? Without doubt, he who came into existence through the work of the Holy Spirit. For what was born in her is from the Holy Spirit, with whom the Word God was continually present. Therefore the Word God was not born from Mary, but remained in him who was born from her. He did not receive his beginning from the Virgin, but was inseparably joined for all time to him who, growing and gradually being formed over the course of months, was in the Virgin’s womb.”

Sermon 4 (No. 4): “Nor ought one to say that God was generated nakedly and in some undetermined manner, for no one generates one who is older than himself; nor, again, should one profess a naked humanity, but rather that humanity joined to God was generated.”

Sermon 5 (No. 5): “Thus, just as a woman gives birth to a body, while God bestows the soul—and therefore the woman is not called the mother of the soul because she has given birth to an animate being, but rather the mother of the human being—so also the blessed Virgin, although she gave birth to a human being, with the Word of God passing through together with him, is not for that reason the mother of God.” And afterward (No. 8):

“See what follows, heretic. I do not begrudge the Virgin the name *Christotokos* (Χριστοτόκος); for I confess that she is worthy of reverence, since she received God, through whom the Lord of all passed, through whom the sun of righteousness shone forth. For the Word was God, joined to the human being and dwelling in him. But I suspect applause. How did you understand this expression, ‘passed through’? I did not say ‘passed through completely’ (*pertransiit*) in the sense of ‘was begotten’; for I do not so easily forget my own doctrine. I have learned from Scripture that God passed through the virgin *Christotokos*; I have not learned that he was born.”

Sermon 13 (No. 3): “What else is this knowledge of piety than *orthology* (ὀρθολογία), concerning the consubstantial divine Trinity, the divine nature that assumes the human being, and the flesh received in the virgin womb, etc.” And afterward (No. 5):

“I proclaim with the loudest voice that the holy Virgin is mother both of God and of a human being—mother of God, indeed, because the temple created in her was united to the Divinity, etc.”

Moreover, in Letter 1 to Saint Celestine he says that the humanity was born joined to God through the Spirit, and in Anathema 9 that it had union from the very conception. What more is needed? The very term *Christotokos*, which he introduces everywhere, settles the matter plainly: if the Virgin gave birth to Christ, God and man were joined in her womb. For Christ, according to Nestorius, is a “God-bearing man” (ἄνθρωπος θεοφόρος) and an instrument joined to the Divinity.

[Col. 1094C] And indeed Theodorus himself, Nestorius’s teacher, teaches in the Creed that the Word assumed the human being, formed in the Virgin’s womb by the power and might of the Holy Spirit, and joined him to himself ineffably. He explains this more clearly in his book *To the Baptized*, when he says: “The Creator was secretly joined to him; he was not absent when he was being formed; he was not divided when he was being born,” etc.

Nestorius also did not depart far from the truth concerning the perpetual connection of the natures—that is, a connection which had neither been interrupted up to that time nor was ever to be dissolved afterward. For he calls the humanity the Divinity’s “garment that cannot be stripped off” (Sermon 13), and asserts that the union of the incarnate Deity is unchangeable and enduring forever (Sermon 7). He says that the human being is the perpetual possessor of the Divinity, and that the Word of God is continually with him (Sermon 6). Against Marcellus of Galatia, who thought otherwise, he inveighs at great length (Sermon 12, No. 2):

“The Lord of all has put on our nature—a garment of the Divinity that is obviously never to be stripped off, an inseparable clothing of the divine substance, the mirror of the Lord of all. Although it had lost the dignity proper to its nature, even if Marcellus becomes ten thousand times angry on hearing this, he did not receive this garment for ordinary use, but forever, so that he might make it sit at the right hand of his Divinity. He gives nothing to the living without this garment of his; he does not judge the dead without it. He willed that the kingdom of his Divinity should be one with it.”

From what has been set forth thus far, it is perfectly clear that the question raised by Nestorius concerned in every respect the kind or mode of the union by which the two natures in Christ are joined. Since he introduced the union of the natures into controversy, as is known to all; and since the Catholic doctrine concerning this union had altogether five parts, as we showed earlier; and since Nestorius agreed with the Church in the four already explained, as has been established, it remains that he disputed concerning the one remaining doctrine—that is, concerning the kind and mode of the union, which the Church called substantial, while Nestorius called moral.

And indeed Leontius, a man especially learned and skillful in discerning doctrines, writes that the whole controversy was raised over this matter. Yet he warns (*Against Nestorius*, Book III, etc.) that the dispute was not about words, but about the mode of the entire mystery of Christ, which ought not to be approved or rejected simply on the basis of this or that word, or of certain expressions, but from first principles. The principles, however, are the mode of union according to hypostasis and according to relation (κατὰ σχὲσιν). The Fathers, he says, transmitted the former; heretics the latter, and thereby introduced the worship of a human being (ἀνθρωπολατρεία).

# CHAPTER II. What Nestorius’s heresy was concerning the kind of union by which the two natures in Christ are joined

To make Nestorius’s meaning concerning the question clear, we must first examine in what forms, or rather in what expressions, it was formerly proposed, and by what rules the answers of any writers are to be tested, so that it may be seen whether they are correct or contrary to the faith. Then we shall consider what Nestorius thought. Afterward, the words in which he expressed his opinion, and by which he himself convicted himself of heresy. Next, what Nestorius’s defenders bring forward to weaken the force of the testimonies cited. Finally, what those same defenders adduce to prove that Nestorius in fact followed the true faith—and how weak such arguments are.

## § I. The former ways in which the question of the union of the natures in Christ was proposed, and the nature and force of the twofold union brought into controversy

The question of the kind or mode of the union by which divinity and humanity are joined in Christ is in reality one; nevertheless, over time and according to place, it was proposed in several forms, or rather in several formulas of speech.

First, it was asked whether the union of the natures was so great that Christ was not merely a human being, but a human being deified (ἄνθρωπος τεθεωποιημένως).

Second, whether the *economy* (οἰκονομία) by which the Word became flesh and dwelt among us was merely some indwelling (ἐνοίκησις), clothing (ἔνδυσις), conjunction (συνάφεια), operation (ἐνέργεια), etc., or rather the true and natural union (ἕνωσις) of the two natures.

Third, what kind of union it was that admirably joined the natures in Christ: whether it was like that which exists between spouses, or rather like that which joins soul and body in a human being.

Fourth, whether that singular union should be called physical or merely moral; substantial or only affective; according to hypostasis (καθ’ ὑπόστασιν) or only according to relation (κατὰ σχὲσιν).

Fifth, whether through the Incarnation it came about that God truly is man, and man in turn truly God.

Sixth, whether there is a double person in Christ, and a double Son and Lord; or whether Christ is truly one.

Seventh, whether the divine person assumed not only the human nature but also a person, in the manner in which one human being is said to assume another into partnership in some undertaking, work, or even life.

Eighth, whether the one begotten from the Father before the ages is one person, and the one born from his mother in the fullness of time another.

Ninth, whether Christ had two births: one eternal, by which he proceeded from the Father, and the other temporal, by which he came from his mother.

Tenth, whether the blessed Virgin is truly the Mother of God, or *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος), or only the mother of Christ, and also the mother of a human being—that is, *Christotokos* (Χριστοτόκος) or *Anthropotokos* (ἀνθρωποτόκος).

Eleventh, whether Christ should be called God-bearing man (θεοφόρος), or God-borne (Θεόφορος); “Deifer,” or one carried by God; belonging to God, or God himself.

Twelfth, whether the one who was crucified is God or man.

Finally, whether one of the Trinity can be said to have suffered.

No one will be surprised that one question was proposed in so many forms who considers carefully what is subtly disputed in the schools concerning the *exchange* or *communication of properties* (ἀντιδόσις or κοινωνία τῶν ἰδιωμάτων) between the natures united in Christ. For it will readily be understood that whenever something one is made from two things, the attributes proper to each—the Greeks call them *idiomata* (ἰδιώματα)—are communicated reciprocally, though not indiscriminately, but according to the mode of the union. If the union is physical and substantial, then not only moral properties, such as being worshiped, ruling, possessing authority, surpassing in dignity, exercising judgment, etc., but also physical properties, such as being born, suffering, dying, etc., become common, so that, as the logicians say, they may also be predicated in the direct case. But if the union is merely moral and relational (σχετική), the properties of each are indeed communicated reciprocally, though not all in the same way: the moral properties in the direct case, as they say, and the physical properties only obliquely, if the expression is to remain proper.

These two rules of the schools are demonstrated partly by the example of spouses and of the human being himself, and partly by theological reasoning. For when there is a physical or substantial union, as they say, into one hypostasis—and since a hypostasis is nothing other than a suppositum, that is, in Greek, the first underlying subject (πρῶτον ὑποκείμενον) of which all things are predicated—it is necessary that all attributes without distinction, whether physical or moral, can be attributed to one suppositum. Conversely, since a moral union does not result in one hypostasis, but only in an affection or in things dependent upon an affection, it can produce only what is akin to it: namely, that moral attributes become common and undivided, and that this very indivision is indicated by words even in the direct case. Physical properties, however, are communicated in such a way that their division is signified at the same time, which occurs through relative or oblique predication.

If, therefore, the two natures of Christ come together by a substantial bond into the unity of the Word’s hypostasis, it is necessary not only that there be one dignity, one authority, and one veneration of God and man, etc., but also that God truly be called man and man in turn truly God; that God be said to have been born of the Virgin, to have suffered in the flesh, to have been crucified, to have died, etc. But if the two natures just mentioned are joined to one another only by affection or relationally (σχετικῶς), then there must indeed be one veneration of God and man, one dignity and authority, because the man is worshiped on account of God, etc. Nevertheless, the properties called physical cannot be communicated except obliquely. Thus the man is not called God, but God’s temple, statue, instrument, garment, working-instrument (ἐνεργαστήριον), etc.; nor is God properly man, but merely the indweller of the man, etc.

From what has just been said, everyone can easily see that all the forms in which the question may be proposed reduce to the one issue stated by Leontius: whether the union of the natures took place according to hypostasis (καθ’ ὑπόστασιν) or according to relation (κατὰ σχὲσιν).

If the union was of the former kind, Christ must not be merely man, but truly God—not merely God-bearing, but God himself. The Incarnation must not be mere indwelling, but true union. The union of the natures must be more like that which joins soul to body than that which joins spouses. It must unite the substances themselves, not merely their affections; join the natures, not the persons; and there must be one Son of God and one Lord of all, the same one born before the ages and in time, the same one possessing a twofold birth, the same one who was crucified and who is God. Finally, the blessed Virgin must truly be *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος), just as any woman is the mother of her own son.

But if the union was of the latter kind—that is, according to relation (κατὰ σχὲσιν)—the opposite must necessarily follow: Christ would properly be something belonging to God and merely God-bearing (Θεόφορος), not God by nature; the Incarnation would be mere indwelling; the natures would be joined like spouses, and their person would be one morally but two physically; there would truly be two sons in Christ, one by adoption and the other by nature; the one born in time would not be the same as the one born from eternity; the one crucified would not properly be the same as God; no one of the Trinity would have suffered; and God would not have become the high priest and apostle of our confession. The blessed Virgin, finally, should not properly be called *Theotokos*, but at most *Christotokos*.

From this also appears the remarkable artistry with which Cyril composed his anathematisms, each directed against one of the chapters of the Nestorian heresy. Although there will be another occasion for discussing this in the following dissertation, it should nevertheless be observed in passing that in the first anathema Cyril responds to the question as it was debated in his own time, on the occasion of Isaiah’s prophecy, which was on everyone’s lips: “Behold, the Virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7:14). The question was whether the one called Emmanuel by the prophet is truly God, and whether the Virgin who bore Emmanuel is truly *Theotokos*.

From this, finally, a rule is established by which the statements of any writer may certainly be examined, so that it may be determined whether he thinks correctly or otherwise concerning the union of the natures in Christ, or, as people formerly said, concerning the unity of Christ. We must see whether he denies or grants that the physical properties of God may properly be predicated of man, and those of man of God. If he denies this, he recognizes only a moral union, such as exists between God and the saints; he makes Christ merely a man, etc. If he grants it and understands in its proper sense the Evangelist’s statement, “The Word became flesh”—that is, that through the Incarnation the Word truly became man—then he thinks correctly concerning the mystery of the Incarnation.

This rule cannot appear either fallacious or doubtful, however much it may seem to presuppose that the laws of the communication of properties (ἀντίδοσις) were known to the author whose writings are being examined; and although those laws involve considerable subtlety and are not easily understood by everyone, so that a writer might have been ignorant of them. I repeat: this rule is neither fallacious nor doubtful, since the laws of the communication of properties cannot be hidden from anyone who is at least reckoned among the learned, insofar as they bear upon understanding the state of the question under discussion. For the various ways of proposing the question depend entirely upon some understanding of the communication of properties. How, then, could those whose office is to teach others—bishops, presbyters, catechists (κατηχισταί), and interpreters of divine matters—be ignorant of the state of a question about which they must speak both to the people and in discussions, especially when that question is neither newly raised nor disputed with only slight contention, as was the Nestorian question? For nearly two hundred full years before Nestorius became bishop, it had been examined in every direction by the most learned men of the Church, through conciliar definitions, books, and disputations.

## § II. What Nestorius thought concerning the question

When everything set forth in the preceding chapter has been carefully considered, it is easy to explain what Nestorius actually thought concerning the Incarnation—that is, concerning the joining of the Word to human nature—however much, as he was a marvelous craftsman of concealment, he tried to hide his mind beneath words devised for deception.

He adhered very closely to Theodorus of Mopsuestia, whom he had used as his teacher, so that he often borrowed not only his opinions but even his words. Therefore he denied that the union of the natures was hypostatic, by which man is called God and God man—that is, by which the physical properties of man are attributed to God and those of God to man. He admitted a moral and relational union, which can communicate to man the moral properties of God, but cannot communicate the physical properties except relationally—that is, as they say, in the oblique case.

He therefore maintained that the whole mystery of the Lord’s economy consisted in this: that the Word, consubstantial with the Father and descended from heaven for the salvation of human beings, descended into the man whom the Holy Spirit formed in the Virgin’s womb; that he dwelt in this man as God dwells in a temple; that through this man he offered himself to be seen, as through a mirror, or represented himself as through an image; and that he assumed the person of the man and used him as an instrument, almost as a spirit is accustomed to use a body, whether a wicked spirit uses a possessed person or a good spirit an assumed body.

For this reason he called the Lord’s economy—which he preferred to call *becoming human* (ἐνανθρώπησις) rather than *incarnation* (σάρκωσις), although he did not always refrain from the latter term—sometimes indwelling (ἐνοίκησις), sometimes clothing or assumption (ἔνδυσις), assumption (ἀνάληψις), operation (ἐνέργεια), and conjunction or adaptation (συνάφεια); that is, indwelling, clothing, assumption, operation, and a kind of joining. These terms, unless they exclude the hypostatic union (ἕνωσις καθ’ ὑπόστασιν), can certainly be used in a Catholic sense and were in fact used by the Fathers. But if they reject that union and signify only indwelling, only clothing, and only assumption, they are the proper words and, as it were, the watchwords of Nestorian impiety.

This was also why he said that the man was indeed worshiped by the angels and adored by us, but only together with God—that is, co-adored. For, on account of the relation and the worship due to the divinity, religion extends to the temple; the veneration of a ruler pertains to his statue; and a garment is ordinarily held in esteem because of the one who wears it.

For the same reason, he rejected, between the incarnate and assumed man and the Word, any unity greater than one according to grace, operation, dignity, equality of honor, relation, affection, or power. Such a unity, since it can exist between two perfect persons, did not prevent Nestorius from acknowledging two persons in Christ in reality; indeed, if he wished to think coherently, it compelled him to confess those two persons, although he concealed this with all his strength. For he said that through the Incarnation the person of the Word and the man became one because the dignity of both was one, their right was one, and their operation one—not otherwise than because of marriage a husband and wife are one person in the affairs and conduct of life, however much they truly remain two hypostases. For the wife receives from her husband both her name, as it were her civil name, and the dignity by which she surpasses others, and authority in conducting affairs.

[Col. 1098C] For this reason also he refused to admit that certain lowly things proper to the man could be attributed to the Word after the Incarnation. Thus he avoided saying that God was an infant, wrapped in swaddling clothes, three months old, a fugitive into Egypt, wearied from the journey, seized by the Jews, suffering, crucified, or dead. For, as was said earlier, no union can communicate such attributes unless it is physical and according to hypostasis (καθ’ ὑπόστασιν), and he rejected every such union.

If, however, he was sometimes compelled to use these expressions in the manner of ordinary people and even of Sacred Scripture, he denied that they were true in any other way than according to equivocation (καθ’ ὁμωνυμίαν) and relationally (σχετικῶς), because the Word dwelt in the infant and suffering man and acted through the man just as a spirit acts through a possessed person. This was why he admitted that the Word referred human sufferings to himself and, as it were, assumed them—just as a deity may regard the violation of its temple as done to itself, a ruler the mockery of his statue, or a spirit the actions performed through a possessed person as its own.

[Col. 1098D] For the same reason he forbade that the Virgin be properly called *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος). For how could she truly be so called unless God were properly said to have been born from her? But being born is a natural property of man, which only hypostatic union communicates. He preferred that she be called *Christotokos* (Χριστοτόκος), as one who had given birth to a man in whom God had dwelt from the very first conception; or *Theodochos* (Θεοδόχος), “receiver of God,” because she received God into the temple which the Holy Spirit prepared from her for the coming Word. Hence it is clear why he refused to admit two births of the divine Word, an eternal birth from the Father and a temporal birth from his mother; otherwise the Virgin would necessarily have to be called *Theotokos*.

If, however, the authority of Scripture sometimes compelled him to confess that the Virgin’s son was God, he insisted that this could be said only in the sense in which Moses was called the god of Pharaoh, and in which many others to whom this name is attributed in the sacred writings are so called—namely, by catachresis and because of a certain sharing in authority.

[Col. 1099A] If it were also objected that the Creed of the Council of Nicaea calls him one and the same Son of God and of the Virgin, or that the authority of the Church acknowledges neither two sons nor two Christs and Lords, but only one, he replied that there is one Christ, so called from anointing, and that the Virgin’s son is likewise the Son of God—not by nature, but by adoption; not essentially (οὐσιωδῶς), but relationally (σχετικῶς).

How he fortified all these parts of his opinion by reasoning, or at least asserted them in explicit words—and rather, how he testified against himself—will be seen in the following section. We shall reduce the material to five headings, lest an endless accumulation of testimonies weary the reader.

## § III. The arguments by which Nestorius tried to establish his opinion, and the words in which he expressed it—or rather testified against himself

Those who think that Nestorius did not transmit his doctrine, by which he opposed Catholic dogma, in any orderly method must have carelessly read through the speeches and other writings of this subtly wicked man; for no heretic was more dialectical (διαλεκτικώτερον) than he.

To make this clear, it should first be observed that in this controversy, with the opposing sides contending against one another, it was commonly thought that the dispute could be settled in no better way than by carefully investigating in what sense John had said, “The Word became flesh.” When this was investigated, it immediately occurred to them that one thing could become another in only five ways: either the mind becomes a human being by informing the body; or water is said to have been made wine by Christ through conversion; or the elements become a mixture through blending (κρᾶσις) and confusion; or, when two perfect natures are mutually united, the individual of one is said to have become the individual of the other through hypostatic union; or finally, a man becomes his wife’s husband and a woman her husband’s wife through relationship and relation (σχέσις).

Apollinaris interpreted the Evangelist’s statement, like the Arians, according to the first mode, by informing; Eutyches, as is believed, according to the second, by conversion; Polemius according to the third, by confusion; the Catholic Church according to the fourth, by hypostatic union (ἕνωσις ὑποστατική); and Theodorus, Nestorius’s teacher, according to the fifth, by mere relationship. Nestorius therefore seemed to himself to demonstrate Theodorus’s opinion, which he had adopted, only when he assumed as an acknowledged principle that the Incarnation had to take place in one of the five modes just mentioned, and then by the force of argument showed that none of the first four could be admitted. Once that had been established, he understood that the remaining possibility was that the Word was said to have become flesh in the fifth mode, through mere relation (σχέσις).

With all the force of reasoning he could muster, therefore, he attempted to attack each of the first modes, but especially the fourth. In rejecting the first three he agreed with the Church. But he attacked the fourth for two reasons: partly because he thought it did not differ from the preceding modes—in which he revealed the blindness of his mind—and partly because it followed from it that the physical properties, whether human properties attributed to God or divine properties attributed to man, would also be communicated. Thus one could say that God suffered and died, etc.; that there were two births of the one Word; that God was born, was three months old, fled into Egypt, etc.; that the blessed Virgin could truly be called *Theotokos*; that the Word was the Virgin’s son, etc.; and that the Word, although God by nature, had become the high priest and apostle of our confession. He argued that these four consequences conflicted with the divinity and eternity of the Word, indeed with his equality with the Father and his supreme authority over all creatures. The first argument will be treated in the next chapter; how he handled the second will become clear from what follows.

It should therefore be observed, second, that the term “passion” signifies everything that happens to a human being contrary to the proper condition of body and soul, such as weariness, thirst, hunger, sorrow, death, crucifixion, etc. Thus, wherever Nestorius denies that the Word of God truly suffered, he must also be understood to deny all the other things that have the force of passion and are included under that category. Conversely, whenever he asserts that one of the things mentioned is incompatible with the incarnate Word, he affirms that all the others are likewise incompatible. This had to be stated beforehand so that the weight of the testimonies could be assessed as it ought.

Sermon 1 (No. 2): “God was indeed incarnate, but he did not die; rather, he raised up the one in whom he was incarnate.”

Sermon 2 (No. 7): “We have explained why, in the birth from Christ’s Virgin mother, divine Scripture uses the name ‘Son.’ Now listen also concerning death, and see whether the name of God is placed anywhere in such a way that we introduce a suffering God: ‘When we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son’ (Romans 5:10). It does not say, ‘through the death of God the Word.’” And afterward (No. 10):

“Who, then, will come? ‘They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with great glory’ (Matthew 24:30). And what is even more important, the prophet showed him coming more clearly than the apostles did, and cries out concerning the Jews: ‘They will look upon him whom they pierced’ (Zechariah 12:10). What, then, was pierced? The side. But the side does not belong to God, but to man.”

Sermon 3: “If the Nicene Fathers had said, ‘We believe in one God the Word,’ death would have been attributed to the divine nature. Therefore they take a common name, namely Jesus Christ, so that they might signify both the one who died and the one who did not die. It is just as if someone said, ‘That man has died,’ although the soul is immortal. Yet because he used a name signifying two natures—the body that dies and the immortal soul—there is no danger in the expression; for both the body and the soul are called man. Thus that great chorus also spoke of Christ.”

Sermon 4 (No. 2): “I cannot adore God as born, dead, and buried.” And afterward (No. 7): “Did God the Word rise from the dead? But if the life-giver was put to death, who will be the one to give life?”

Sermon 5 (No. 7): “Let us hear blessed Paul openly proclaiming who it was that was crucified. Listen, then, to his clearest statement: ‘He was crucified through weakness, but he lives through the power of God’ (2 Corinthians 13:4). If he was crucified through weakness, heretic, who was weakened? Was it God the Word?”

Sermon 6 (No. 9): “Why, then, do you think differently from Paul? Why, mixing the impassible God the Word with an earthly body, do you make him a suffering high priest?”

Sermon 7 (No. 3): “They call the mortal the life-giving Divinity, and dare to drag God the Word into theatrical stories, as though the same one were wrapped in swaddling clothes and dead. What an outrage! So that the Lord Christ might extend his kindness toward us, his dignity as God is put at risk among them.” And afterward (No. 6):

“It was not he himself who died, the one who gives life; for who would continue to exist? Who would raise the dead? He came to raise dead human beings; for he is found bringing aid to the dead as they lie there, not himself lying there and being without aid.” And shortly afterward (No. 7):

“Therefore God did not die, but raised him up.” And (No. 40):

“For even if you search through the entire New Testament, you will nowhere find in it that the death of God is mentioned; rather, it is assigned either to Christ or to the Lord.” And (No. 42):

“We do not proclaim the death of God the Word when we are nourished by the Lord’s body and blood. For the divine nature receives the sacrifice; it is not itself sacrificed in the sacrifice. Nor is the prophet God, but the giver of prophecy.” And (No. 45):

“Why do you attribute the name of God to death, when Sacred Scripture nowhere brings it forward in mentioning death? When you hear Paul crying out, ‘He has appointed a man by whom he will judge, having raised him from the dead’ (Acts 17:31), why do you, in your empty imagination, judge the Divinity to have been born and to have died?” And finally (No. 49):

“If a heretic reproaches you, speaking as though from the person of the Church, with having a dead God, respond angrily to the statement: ‘It is God who raised from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep’ (Hebrews 13:20). He himself was not put to death and then raised up.”

Letter 2 to Saint Celestine (Nos. 13, 16): “To attribute to God, under the name of this familiarity, the properties of the joined flesh—namely, birth, suffering, and mortality—is, brother, either the opinion of misguided paganism, or of Apollinaris and Arius, who were out of their minds, or of the remaining heretical plagues, and something worse than these. For such men must make God the Word, under the pretext of familiarity, a companion of suckling and, because of familiarity, a participant in the growth of age that gradually took place, and a participant in suffering in time, needing the assistance of angels because of fearfulness. I say nothing of circumcision, sacrifice, sweat, and hunger, which indeed happened to the flesh for our sake. Yet when these things are joined to him, they must also be adored; but when attributed to the Divinity, they are not only accepted falsely, but bring upon us, as though we were slanderers, just grounds for condemnation.”

Three other sermons, 8, 9, and 10, should be read in the same sense. After the passages we have brought forward, can anyone still doubt that Nestorius maintained this proposition to be false: “God has suffered”? We must now examine the other proposition, “God has been born,” by the same method.

It should therefore be observed, third, that the expression “God born” includes absolutely everything that either precedes birth—such as being carried in the womb and being formed over a number of months—or follows it—such as being wrapped in swaddling clothes, suckled, growing, being two or three months old, advancing in age—and, when the divine Word is under discussion, undergoing two births and having a female parent. We shall therefore have clearly demonstrated that Nestorius denied that God could be said to have been born if we show that he rejected even one of the things listed above.

Sermon 1 (Nos. 6–7): “God has a mother; therefore paganism, which introduces mothers among the gods, is excusable. Paul, then, is a liar concerning Christ’s divinity when he says, ‘without father, without mother, without genealogy’ (ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἄνευ γενεαλογίας). No, excellent man, Mary did not give birth to God,” etc.

Sermon 3 (No. 6), among many other statements: “Therefore the Word God was not born from Mary, but remained in him who was born from her. He did not receive his beginning from the Virgin, but was inseparably joined for all time to him who, growing and gradually being formed over the course of months, was in the Virgin’s womb. It is one thing to say, ‘He remains with the one who was born,’ and another to say that the one who remains with the one born is himself the one who would have required the passage of months in order to be born.”

Eusebius, still a layman in the Church, openly opposed this, maintaining that the Word himself, who existed before the ages, had undergone a second birth, according to the flesh, and by so devout yet audacious an outcry stirred the assembly and split it into opposing factions. But he would have been overwhelmed by the partisans of Nestorius, despite the resistance of the good men, had not Nestorius suppressed the uproar of the rioters. Then he said:

“I rejoice” (No. 7), “as I behold your zeal; for by it the things shamefully uttered by that wretched man can plainly be refuted. For those who have two generations must necessarily have two sons. But the Church acknowledges one Son, the Lord Christ himself.”

And later, when he had spoken of the Fathers of Nicaea [Col. 1101D] (No. 9):

“Nowhere did they say, ‘He was born.’ Why, we ask? So that they would not introduce two births into the Godhead.”

And again (No. 11):

“They saw, therefore, as men knowledgeable in the sacred Scriptures, that if we call him who was incarnate ‘born,’ God the Word, the Son of the Holy Spirit, will be found [to have been born].”

Finally (No. 12):

“They followed the evangelist; for when he came to ἐνανθρώπησις [‘incarnation’], he avoided speaking of a generation of the Word and said ‘incarnation,’ etc.”

### Sermon 4

(No. 2):

“He who simply says that God was born from Mary first of all prostitutes the nobility of the doctrine to the Gentiles, placing it before them for censure and ridicule. For a pagan, immediately taking up the objection that God was born from Mary, will bring this charge against the Christian: ‘I cannot worship a God who was born, died, and was buried.’

“But the division of the doctrine is clear. He who was born, who required time for the stages of growth, and who was carried for the proper number of months in the womb [Col. 1102A]—he possesses a human nature, though truly joined to God.”

And immediately afterward (No. 4):

“I have greatly admired the division made on this subject by my predecessor, who said: ‘He who was born from a woman is neither God alone nor a mere man,’ because one must not say that God was generated nakedly and in some ordinary fashion; for no one generates one who is older than himself.”

And finally (Nos. 8–9):

“You say simply: ‘It is God who was born from Mary.’ Immediately the Arian heretic objects in reproach: ‘Then you accuse us unjustly when we say that the Son is lesser than the Father and created, since among you too this is included in the confession: that the Word is God, who was born from Mary.’

“Hear what that same God the Word himself testifies concerning himself: ‘Go and report to my brothers: I am going to my Father and your Father, my God and your God’ (John 20:17). But when he said this, he who was born from blessed Mary was indeed consubstantial with us according to his humanity; yet, in that he was joined to God, he was far removed from us, since God is the superior substance.”

### Sermon 5

(No. 8), which is entirely about God born and about the Virgin Θεοτόκος [‘God-bearer’]:

“See what follows, heretic; I do not begrudge the Virgin the name Χριστοτόκος [‘Christ-bearer’]. For I confess that she is worthy of reverence, since she received God, through whom the Lord of all passed, through whom the Sun of righteousness shone forth. For the Word was God, joined to man and dwelling in him.

“But I suspect that you applauded when you heard how I understood what I said, namely, that he ‘passed through’ her. I did not say ‘passed through’ in the sense of ‘was begotten’; for I do not so easily forget my own position. I have learned from Scripture that God passed through the Virgin Χριστοτόκος; I have not learned that he was born from her. Nowhere does divine Scripture assert that God was born from the Virgin Χριστοτόκος; rather, it says that Jesus Christ, the Son and Lord, was born.”

### Sermon 7

(No. 37):

“God is not, in himself, that which was formed in the womb; God is not, in himself, that which was created by the Holy Spirit.”

It should be observed, fourth, that the question concerning the conjunction of the natures in Christ was presented at different times in different words, as we have said: when Nestorius began to preside, the question was whether Emmanuel was truly God and whether the Virgin was truly Θεοτόκος [‘God-bearer’]. Thus he himself says in Sermon 1 (No. 6):

“People frequently ask us whether Mary should be called Θεοτόκος [‘God-bearer’] or ἀνθρωποτόκος [‘man-bearer’].”

And in Letter 3 to Saint Celestine (No. 3), when he wished to set out the formal character of the question:

“Let us suppose,” he says, “that two opposing parties are standing against each other. Let one of them utter only this word, Θεοτόκος; and let the other utter only that word, ἀνθρωποτόκος. Let each party draw the other over to its own confession, so that, if it does not achieve this, it risks falling away from the Church, etc.”

Hence Dorotheus and Anastasius, the first trumpeters of impiety, used no other form of words than this, which answered the common question:

“If anyone says that Mary is Deipara [‘God-bearer’], let him be anathema.”

Indeed, Cyril testifies that almost the whole struggle undertaken for the faith concerned the assertion that the Virgin was Deipara. For this reason, when John of Antioch wrote a friendly letter to Nestorius, he demanded this one thing of him: that he call her Θεοτόκος [‘God-bearer’]. And when he presented his statement of faith, he first called the Virgin Θεοτόκος, wishing by this, as though by a token of confession, to show himself Catholic.

But the action of Paul of Emesa in this matter is outstanding. When he was seeking to restore the peace of the Churches, which had been disturbed on account of Nestorius, and was about to prove his faith in the Church of Alexandria before an immense assembly, he spoke as the occasion then required. After the prophetic passage had been read—“Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb,” etc.—he burst out with these words:

“Therefore the Mother of God gives birth to Emmanuel.”

Then the people acclaimed:

“Behold, this is the faith! This is God’s gift! Orthodox Cyril, this is what we wished to hear. Let anyone who does not speak thus be anathema.”

Then Paul continued:

“Therefore Mary the Deipara [‘God-bearer’] bore Emmanuel for us; and Emmanuel means God made man. For God the Word, who before the ages was begotten from the Father in a mysterious and ineffable manner, was born from a woman in the last times.”

[Col. 1103A] Just as in the time of Athanasius the man who confessed ὁμοούσιον [‘consubstantial’] appeared to be following the right faith, so in the age of Nestorius did the man who openly said Θεοτόκος [‘God-bearer’]. Conversely, just as anyone who refused to confess ὁμοούσιον was counted among the Arians, so anyone who rejected Θεοτόκος was assigned to the party of Paul of Samosata. Nestorius rejected it as openly as anyone could have done.

### Sermon 1

(Nos. 6–7):

“Let those who, blinded in the dispensation of the Lord’s renewal, do not understand either what they say or about what they make assertions (1 Tim. 1:7), hear this. For, as we have just learned, they frequently ask one another whether Mary should be called Θεοτόκος [‘God-bearer’] or ἀνθρωποτόκος [‘man-bearer’].

“Does God have a mother? Then paganism is excusable for introducing mothers among its gods. Paul, then, is a liar when he says of Christ’s divinity that he is ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἄνευ γενεαλογίας—that is, ‘without father, without mother, without an account of generation.’

“No, my good man, Mary did not bear God. For that which is born from flesh is flesh, and that which is born from spirit is spirit (John 3:6). A creature did not bear him who is uncreated; the Father did not beget God the Word, newly appearing from the Virgin: ‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John 1:1), as John says. A creature did not bear the Creator; she bore a man, the instrument of the Godhead.”

### Sermon 2

(No. 2):

“Whenever sacred Scripture is about to speak either of Christ’s generation from the blessed Virgin or of his death, it nowhere says ‘God,’ but either ‘Christ,’ ‘Jesus,’ or ‘Lord,’ etc.”

### Sermon 3

(Nos. 4–6, etc.):

“The Arians, although in their madness they make God the Word lesser than the majesty of the Father’s Godhead, nevertheless do not confess him to be recent. These men, however, declare him even to be posterior to blessed Mary and consign a temporal mother to the Divinity who created time, etc.”

And afterward:

“Therefore God the Word was not born from Mary, but remained in him who was born from her. He did not have his beginning from the Virgin; rather, he was inseparably joined for all time to him who, growing month by month, was gradually formed in the Virgin’s womb, etc.”

[Col. 1103C] ### Sermon 4

(No. 2):

“He who simply says that God was born from Mary first of all exposes the nobility of the doctrine to the Gentiles, etc.”

### Sermon 5

(Nos. 5–6), which is entirely directed against Θεοτόκος [‘God-bearer’], presents the argument of the Catholics against itself:

“If Christ is God,” they say, “and Christ was born from blessed Mary, why is the Virgin not the Mother of God?”

“I conceal nothing of what they object. For the lover of truth sets before himself everything that can be said by falsehood.”

Then he replies:

“An infant is formed in the womb; but, until it has received its shape, it does not yet have a soul. Once it has been formed, however, the soul is immediately fashioned by God. Thus, although a woman gives birth to the body and God supplies the soul, the woman is not for that reason called the mother of the soul because she has borne an ensouled being; rather, she is called the mother of the man. In the same way, blessed Mary, although she bore a man, while the Word of God passed through together with him, is not for that reason the Mother of God. For the divinity of the Word did not take its beginning from the blessed Virgin; rather, he was God by nature.

“The holy angels proclaim concerning blessed John the Baptist that the infant would be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb (Luke 1:15); and thus blessed John the Baptist was born possessing the Holy Spirit. What, then? Will you call Elizabeth the mother of the Spirit? Direct your minds to this, and if there are any among you who are disturbed by what is being said as though it were unheard-of and unusual, grant indulgence to their ignorance.”

### Letter 1 to Saint Celestine

(Nos. 4–6):

“Some have even now dared to call the Virgin Χριστοτόκος [‘Christ-bearer’]; yet they do not recoil from calling her Θεοτόκος [‘God-bearer’], although those holy Fathers of Nicaea, who surpass all praise, are recorded to have said nothing more concerning the holy Virgin than that our Lord Jesus Christ was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.”

And afterward:

“I say nothing of the Scriptures, which everywhere proclaim the Virgin as the mother of Christ, not of God the Word, through both angels and apostles. I think that the reputation preceding your blessedness has taught you how many struggles we have endured on this account, while you also recognize that we did not struggle in vain. For many of those who were in error have been corrected by the grace of the Lord [Col. 1104A], learning from us that the birth must be ὁμοούσιος [‘consubstantial’] with the one who gives birth; that there is no commixture of God the Word with man, but rather a union of the creature and of the Lord’s humanity, joined to God through the Spirit from the Virgin.

“But if anyone proposes this name, Θεοτόκος, on account of the humanity born and joined to God the Word, not on account of the woman who gave birth, we say that this term is not properly applicable to the woman who bore him. For a true mother must be of the same essence as that which is born from her; nevertheless, the term can be tolerated because of the consideration itself, and because this Word is the only one named in connection with the Virgin, on account of the inseparable temple of God the Word derived from her. It is not because she is the mother of God the Word—for no one gives birth to one who is older than himself.”

And in Letter 2 to Saint Cyril (No. 11):

“Everywhere in the divine Scriptures, whenever they mention the Lord’s dispensation, the passion and birth of Christ’s humanity, not of his divinity, are handed down. Thus, according to the clearest reasoning, it is more fitting and appropriate for the holy Virgin to be called not the mother of God, that is, Θεοτόκος, but the mother of Christ, that is, Χριστοτόκος.”

From these passages it is evident that Nestorius rejected Θεοτόκος [‘God-bearer’] not merely verbally, but also for multiple reasons.

First, he argued that one must not speak without the rule either of Scripture or of tradition; yet neither Holy Scripture, nor the Council of Nicaea, nor anything else, he said, remembered Θεοτόκος.

Second, he argued that the confession of Θεοτόκος favored paganism, which introduced mothers among its gods.

Third, he argued that this same opinion made Paul a liar, since Paul had said that Christ was ἀπάτωρ and ἀμήτωρ, “without father” and “without mother.”

Fourth, he argued that it entirely conflicted with the incorporeality, immutability, eternity, and consubstantiality of the Word with the Father. For, he said, that which is from flesh is flesh; that which the Virgin carried was created by the Holy Spirit; no one gives birth to one older than himself; whoever is born is ὁμοούσιος [‘consubstantial’] with the one who gives birth; and every mother is consubstantial with the one whose mother she is called.

[Col. 1104C] Fifth, he argued that this very opinion contradicted itself: while asserting the Deipara, it denied the mother of Christ. For if it was not the nature of man, but God the Word, whom she bore, the woman who gave birth would in no way be found to be the mother of him who was born. For how could she become the mother of one who is alien by nature to the one who gives birth?

Sixth, he argued that those who preach Θεοτόκος were more foolish than the Arians. For although the Arians make God the Word lesser than the majesty of the Father’s Godhead, they nevertheless do not confess him to be recent. These men, however, declare him to be even posterior and secondary to blessed Mary, and assign a temporal mother to the Divinity who created time (No. 4).

Seventh, he argued that the very defenders of Θεοτόκος exposed the excellence of the incarnation and the nobility of the doctrine to the Gentiles, making them objects of ridicule and calumny; indeed, they favored the Arians by undermining the arguments of the Catholics.

[Col. 1104D] Eighth, he argued that they agreed with Arius, Eunomius, and Apollinaris, who had sought to introduce the designation Θεοτόκος, so that, once a commixture had been made and the two natures had not been distinguished, nothing of what was inferior would be understood as having been said of the humanity; and so an opening would already be available to them against the Godhead itself, as though everything were said of one subject, not on account of the dignity resulting from the union, but on account of the nature itself (Sermon 5, No. 3).

Ninth, he argued that once the confession of Θεοτόκος was made, it followed first that the very Godhead itself had been born from the Virgin; second, that every woman was the mother of her son’s soul; and finally, that Elizabeth was the parent of John, πνευματοτόκος [‘Spirit-bearer’]. These three consequences were plainly either impious or full of ignorance.
