He inferred them from the fact that the Virgin brought forth a man to whom the Godhead was joined, that the woman brought forth a son who received his soul from God, and that Elizabeth brought John into the world already filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb.

Tenth and finally, he argued that the Virgin could not be called Θεοτόκος [‘God-bearer’] [Col. 1105A] because she bore Christ, in whom was God the Word, unless she were likewise said to have borne the Father and the Holy Spirit, since both were also in Christ, just as they are in all the righteous. Indeed, if she is called Θεοτόκος and not Λογοτόκος [‘Word-bearer’], the very word sufficiently reveals that she ought not to be called the mother of one person, but of the entire Trinity, which is God.

At this point one is moved to question the patrons of Nestorius, and Albertinus especially, who wishes to appear learned: are these the words of a man who slipped into error inadvertently, or did he say them deliberately? Are these the arguments of some thoughtless person, to whom a single word escaped, or of a malicious contradictor who, after much reflection, carefully weighed each circumstance of the matter? Finally, is this elaborate speech merely a defect of a tongue carried away by passion, or rather the expression of a mind everywhere consistent with itself and always steadfast in its purpose?

It should be observed, fifth, that when Proclus, in his panegyrical oration (No. 7), exclaimed concerning the Virgin’s womb:

“O temple in which God became priest, not changing his nature, but, out of compassion, clothing himself with the one who is according to the order of Melchizedek!”—

Nestorius was not merely offended by the statement, but also revealed, through his response to the temporal oration, his impatience. Indeed, afterward, when his anger ought to have subsided, he attacked Proclus’ statement in Sermon 6, after explaining Paul’s words, “Consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus,” as though all the properties of a high priest, which the Apostle had so carefully sought out and expounded, were unfitting to the divinity of the Word, even when incarnate.

Thus, in Sermon 6, he says:

“When they hear the name ‘apostle’ applied to Christ, they wrongly understand God the Word to be an apostle; likewise, when they read the title ‘high priest,’ they imagine God to be a high priest—an astonishing madness! For who, on hearing of the office of an apostle, would not immediately see that a man is being indicated? Who, on hearing the name of the high priest, would call the nature of the Godhead to the ministry of a priest?”

Then, after enumerating more than fourteen characteristics [Col. 1105C] of that priest of whom Paul speaks, and arguing through each one, he gathers his argument together:

“This is the one who, in the manner of leading armies, was compared with Moses; this is the one called the seed of Abraham; this is the one made like his brothers in every respect; this is the one who became high priest in time; this is the one perfected through sufferings; this is the one who, in that very thing in which he suffered, was himself tested and is able to assist those who are tested; this is the one called high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

“Why, then, do you think differently from Paul? Why, by mixing the impassible God the Word with an earthly body, do you make him a passible high priest? Since this, then, is our one high priest—both compassionate toward us and akin to us, and steadfast—never be driven away from faith in him. For he was sent to you according to the promised blessing, from the seed of Abraham, offering a sacrifice of the body both for himself and for his own kind” (Sermon 6, Nos. 9–10).

Those who have chosen to defend Nestorius against the judgment of the Church do not yield to such numerous and manifest testimonies. Instead, they first try to weaken the force of the arguments [Col. 1105D] just brought forward. Then they produce witnesses whose authority, they claim, proves that Nestorius actually stood for the truth and merely slipped in his wording. Finally, they seem to themselves able to explain the cause of his lapse: namely, that his zeal for the faith had been kindled, and his ardor inflamed against the Apollinarians and Arians; and that, carried away by excessive passion—as was his habit against all heretics—he neither maintained moderation in speaking nor wished, through impatience at disgrace, to correct the words he had rashly uttered. These three points must be examined individually.

## § IV. What the defenders of Nestorius reply to the arguments brought forward in the preceding section, and what kind of replies theirs are

We are addressing only those who profess to retain the faith of the Council of Ephesus, not Socinians or other openly avowed antichrists of that kind—that is, those who have openly declared war on the divinity of Christ. Among these men [Col. 1106A], therefore, all who undertook the cause of Nestorius easily understood that they could not defend him unless they accused as ignorance and also condemned as inconsistency the very man whom they were trying to absolve from heresy—as though he had fought against those with whom he did not know how to speak in the language of the Fathers, and as though, in explaining his own opinion, he had used at different times different expressions containing ambiguous and perplexing meanings.

They therefore distinguish two parts, as it were, in the doctrine of the incarnation: faith and understanding. Faith, they say, believes that Christ is God and man, and that the two natures have been joined in one person by a certain divine and ineffable manner, etc. Understanding perceives certain subtler consequences of faith—for example, what and how great a communication of properties arises from the manner of the union; in what way the things belonging to God extend to man, and those belonging to man to God, etc.

They say that Nestorius, being a man approved for instructing the faithful, undoubtedly perceived what was sufficient for carrying out his office—namely, the things that properly and, so to speak, essentially belong to the faith: that Christ is one Son of God and one Lord of all; that he is not divided into two persons; that he is not merely man in himself; and so forth. But, they say, such is the weakness of the human mind that he became confused over the consequences of faith and therefore recoiled from certain expressions received in the Church, such as “God born,” “God suffered,” “high priest,” “the Virgin Deipara,” and so forth.

They add that the same thing happened to him as commonly happens to men distinguished by rank: when they are accused of error or even warned about it, they prefer to defend the error rather than admit it, lest by confession they either cast away their dignity or at least diminish it. They therefore say that Nestorius obstinately persisted in the position into which he had fallen thoughtlessly, and that he was struck with an anathema either unjustly, as certain Calvinists babble, or merely because of obstinacy of mind, as some Catholics have imprudently let slip.

This defense has two parts. The first is properly a defense; the second is rather an excuse. They construct the former [Col. 1106C] partly from the testimony of the ancients and partly from reasoning; they merely ask us to believe the latter. The first will be examined in the following section; the second is considered here.

They say, then, that Nestorius did indeed sin against the laws of ἀντίδοσις [‘exchange’ or ‘communication’ of properties], but that this in no way prevented him from otherwise holding the right faith. For the same thing happened to certain Fathers, whom the Church nevertheless venerates as teachers of the faith, especially to those who admitted a communication of properties in abstract terms—something more intolerable than anything else in this question, since it plainly indicates a confusion of the natures. If, then, they could sin by excess while preserving the faith, why should Nestorius not likewise be said to have sinned by defect while preserving the faith?

Yet the very distinction employed by the patrons of Nestorius itself shows sufficiently why the case of the Fathers is not the same as that of Nestorius.

First, it did not follow from the opinion of the Fathers that the union of the natures καθ’ ὑπόστασιν [‘according to hypostasis’]—the central point of the question—was abolished; it did follow from the Nestorian position.

Second, the sayings of the Fathers can easily be restored through a favorable interpretation of their manner of speaking, by removing what is superfluous. Nestorius’ words could not endure this, since, once what was lacking had been added, it would be necessary to acknowledge the very things that Nestorius had openly professed himself unable to tolerate.

Further, the Fathers added something by which the license of their expressions could be restrained: namely, an anathema against the heretics with whom they might seem to agree, and specifically against that aspect in which the heresy was οὐσιωδῶς [‘essentially’] contained. Nestorius, by contrast, added nothing by which suspicion of error might be lessened, but rather something by which it was strengthened and often even increased. For he did not pronounce an anathema against the heretics with whom he was thought to agree in the respect in which it was necessary, but in another respect that was not at issue. What else could this be than an actual admission of agreement?

Moreover, the Fathers had expressed an unequivocal position elsewhere in defense of the faith. Indeed, where they might have been thought to need indulgence, they used expressions that demonstrated the sincerity of their faith, such as that the Godhead suffered in the flesh, etc. After Nestorius had once revealed the poison hidden in his mind, he brought forward nothing that was not consistent with error, nothing that did not cohere with it.

Finally, some of the Fathers used Nestorius’ expressions—συναφείας [‘association’], ἀναλήψεως [‘assumption’], ἐνοικήσεως [‘indwelling’], Θεοφόρου [‘God-bearing’], etc. Indeed, as Leontius noted, they used several of the same statements and nevertheless did not thereby fall under suspicion of error. This was partly because the state of the question had not yet restricted freedom of speech by quasi-temporal laws, and partly because Nestorius had deliberately sought out the individual expressions he used, even from Scripture itself, where the words could easily be twisted to opposite meanings for the purpose of deception, so that a single little word could turn Catholic expressions into heretical ones.

For example, he called the incarnation ἐνοίκησις [‘indwelling’]; the Catholics also used that word, but he used it alone, whereas they did not use it alone. He called Christ a man Θεοφόρος [‘God-bearing’]; Basil also used that term. But Nestorius refused to add that Christ was simultaneously God by nature, whereas Basil added this [qualification], etc.

But in order to uncover the foundation of the excuse, it must be examined more carefully whether Nestorius despised the laws of ἀντίδοσις [‘exchange’ or ‘communication’ of properties] rather than failed to understand them. It was certainly in his interest to despise them, so that he could make the accusation against the Catholics more plausible to the common people. For when he reproached them as though they were saying that the Godhead itself was born from the Virgin, suffered in the flesh, remained unburied in the tomb, and other things of that sort, he could accuse them all the more credibly of agreement with Arius and Apollinaris, and present himself as a Catholic, since he appeared to be fighting against heretics and enduring the hostility stirred up by the allies of heretics.

Could a man not dull of mind, placed in charge of instructing the people and trained by frequent controversies, thoroughly versed—as he himself boasted—in reading the Fathers, have been ignorant of what the parties believed in a question on which it had often been necessary to speak? Could he have been unaware of the state of a controversy that had been debated for nearly two hundred years? Did he, a man from the learned Church of Antioch, raised to the throne of the imperial city on the reputation of his teaching, not understand what the opposing parties thought in a dispute of such persistent notoriety? Did the veteran disputant fail to see the devices by which each side avoided objections and explained its own position? He brought forward nothing that Samosata had not previously objected to Dionysius of Alexandria; nothing that Dionysius and the Antiochene Fathers had not refuted by explaining the faith concerning the attributes of Christ that appeared to conflict. Certainly he used no arguments except those he had taken from Photinus, though expounded with the skill of Theodore.

What more is there to say? Was his mind so disturbed when he spewed forth the poison of impiety that he forgot what he had previously known about the communication of properties, and what he taught in the Church, when he openly said concerning Christ (Sermon 9):

“This is truly the great mystery of so great a gift. For this one who appears to be an infant, this one who has newly appeared, this one who requires bodily swaddling clothes, this one who has recently been born according to visible essence, is the Son, as Scripture teaches—the eternal Son, the Son who is the maker of all things, the Son who binds the dissoluble nature of the creature with the swaddling clothes of his own power. For the infant is God, possessing his own authority. So far is it from being the case, Arius, that God the Word is subject to God’s power.

“We therefore know the humanity of the infant and the divinity; we preserve the unity of sonship in the nature of the Godhead and of humanity. I say this so that you may know how surpassing and supreme a union of the Godhead existed even in the infant himself, when the Lord’s flesh was seen. For he himself was both an infant and the Lord of that infant.”

Before his heresy was exposed, he certainly knew the correct forms of speech. But when those forms invalidated the sophistical arguments that alone he employed, he did not wish to preserve them while attacking the faith. This is not surprising, since no one wishes to appear to know what he understands to be detrimental to his own cause.

## § V. What the defenders of Nestorius bring forward to prove that he actually followed the right faith

[Col. 1108A]

Now, in order to prove that Nestorius followed the right faith, those defenders produce six testimonies, clear, as they themselves think, and entirely beyond doubt. The first is that of Nestorius himself, not only professing the right faith in explicit and unambiguous words, but also complaining that he was being falsely accused in this respect. The second is that of John of Antioch, a man praised by the holy Fathers not only for the holiness of his life but also brought forward as a witness in matters of faith. The third is that of almost all the bishops of the East, among whom were many distinguished for their reputation for holiness and learning. The fourth is that of Theodoret, whom Photius and other Greeks call divine. The fifth is that of the historian Socrates, who wrote the events of his own times. The sixth is that of Diodore of Tarsus and Theodore of Mopsuestia, whom many Fathers extolled with extraordinary praise, including praise for their faith, even though they nevertheless said the same things as Nestorius.

This, then, is how they argue. Since orthodox faith [Col. 1108B] in this matter is contained either wholly or chiefly in four propositions—namely, that Christ is not merely man; that he exists as one, that is, that there are neither two sons nor two lords nor two Christs; that both natures have come together in one hypostasis of the Word; and that the blessed Virgin is called Deipara—Nestorius did not absolutely deny even one of these points, but asserted each of them in explicit words.

He clearly asserted the first in Sermon 7 (No. 23):

“Christ is not a mere man, O calumniator, but man and God together. If he existed as God alone, he ought, according to Apollinaris, to have said: ‘Why do you seek to kill God, who has spoken the truth to you?’ But now he says: ‘Why do you seek to kill this man, who has been crowned with thorns?’ This man who said, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ This man who endured death for three days, etc.”

In Sermon 12 (No. 2):

“Let Paul of Samosata remain in astonishment, gnashing his teeth, since in his madness he declares the Lord’s humanity to be bare and separate from the Godhead. He speaks of this humanity, which is always joined and connected, as though it were alone apart from the Godhead, although it can do the same things and equally possess the same power as God. For God gave him the name that is above every name.”

He stated the second no less clearly in Sermon 2 (No. 5):

“There is no division of this—neither of conjunction, nor of power, nor of sonship, nor of that which is Christ. In these there is no division; but in divinity and humanity there is division. Christ, insofar as he is Christ, is undivided; and the Son, insofar as he is Son, is undivided. For we do not have two Christs or two sons; there is not among us a first Christ and a second, nor one and another, nor again one son and another son. Rather, the same one is twofold, not in dignity but in nature.”

In Sermon 11 (Nos. 1–3):

“This is truly the great mystery of so great a gift! For this one who appears to be an infant, this one who has newly appeared, this one who requires bodily swaddling clothes, this one who has recently been born according to visible essence, is the Son, as Scripture teaches—the eternal Son; the Son who is the maker of all things; the Son who binds the dissoluble nature of the creature with the swaddling clothes of his own power. For the infant is God, possessing his own authority. So far is it from being the case, Arius, that God the Word is subject to God’s power.

“We therefore know the humanity of the infant and the divinity; we preserve the unity of sonship in the nature of the Godhead and of humanity. I say this so that you may know how surpassing and supreme a union of the Godhead existed even in the infant himself, when the Lord’s flesh was seen. For he himself was both an infant and the Lord of that infant.”

In Sermon 12:

“One Son: both that which is visible and that which is invisible; one Christ: both he who makes use and that which he uses. The natures are twofold, but the Son is singular. Why do you turn the statement into a calumny?”

He seems to explain the third part of the Catholic faith without obscurity in Letter 2 to Cyril (No. 5):

“Once certain names common to both natures and certain meanings have been established, neither the things belonging to the Son’s generation and lordship are to be divided, nor are the things proper to the natures to be endangered by any abolition of distinction in the singularity of the Son’s birth.”

In Letter 2 to Saint Celestine (No. 3):

“Much labor is also devoted by us to this matter, as we strive to drag out of the Church of God the most filthy impiety of the worst opinion of Apollinaris and Arius. For I do not know how certain men, conceiving from the Godhead and humanity of the Only-Begotten a kind of ecclesiastical image of commixture, are afflicted with the disease of those heretics, daring both to pour the passions of the body over the Godhead of the Only-Begotten, and to pretend that the immutability of the Godhead passed over into the nature of the body, and to confuse both natures—which, because of their supreme and unconfused union, are worshiped in the one person of the Only-Begotten—by the mutability of commixture.”

In Cyril himself (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, ch. 4), in the book *On the Right Faith to the Queens*, chapter 12:

“Moreover, certain people, I do not know in what manner, assert that this name, Christ, applies also separately and by itself to the Word of God the Father—that is, as he is conceived by the mind as existing outside the flesh. Then they contend that it applies in a similar way to the one who was born from the holy Virgin, insofar as he too is considered to subsist separately and by himself. Finally, they teach that it applies equally to both together as to one, on account, as they themselves say, of the conjunction binding them into one person.”

In the letter to Alexander of Hierapolis (in the Fifth Ecumenical Council, Collation 6):

“The natures must remain in their own properties, and thus, through a marvelous unity surpassing every explanation, one glory must be understood and one Son confessed.”

And again:

“We do not make two persons into one person; rather, by one designation of Christ we signify both natures together.”

In an unnamed sermon preserved by Cyril (*Book V of the Contradictions*), Christ is introduced as speaking:

“Although I am in the form of God, I put on the form of a servant; although I am God the Word, I am seen in the flesh; although I am Lord of the universe [Col. 1109C], I put on the person of a poor man for your sake; although I visibly hunger, I supply food to those who hunger.”

Finally, concerning the fourth point, in Sermon 6 (No. 4):

“I have already said many times: If any simpler person among you, or anyone else, takes pleasure in this word Θεοτόκος [‘God-bearer’], I have no objection to the word itself, provided only that he does not make the Virgin a goddess, etc.”

In Letter 3 to Saint Celestine (No. 2):

“But I too do not resist those who wish to use this word, Θεοτόκος, provided that they do not utter it according to the madness of Apollinaris and Arius, for the confusion of the natures.”

In Sermon 12 (No. 7):

“Condemn those who, according to the view of Apollinaris and Arius, call her the Mother of God; and I join you in crying out, Θεοτόκος.”

And afterward (No. 22):

“The Son of God was born as God the Word and man. Therefore, because of the unity, let the woman who gave birth be called the Mother of God, that is, Θεοτόκος.”

Sermon 13 (No. 7): “Since, however, for the sake of those who seek a clearer understanding—especially since they are sons of the Church—we ought to use more explicit language, therefore [Col. 1109D] now also, in the same definition with which I previously spoke briefly about that blessed Mary, ever-virgin, I proclaim in the clearest possible terms, with the loudest voice, that the holy Virgin is the mother both of God and of man.”

Thus far Nestorius has spoken for himself. Now let us consider John of Antioch, who was thoroughly acquainted with Nestorius’s faith, whether because of their long association at Antioch and their common studies and teacher, or because, after the disturbances caused by the withdrawal, he diligently investigated the entire matter concerning his friend. Writing, therefore, to Nestorius, he says (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chap. 25):

“For if your mind thinks and feels what the holy Fathers and teachers of the Church think and feel—for this, my lord, we have learned about you from many people and from common friends—why do you hesitate to make your pious understanding public in suitable language?” And later: “Who, I ask, would find fault if you freely explained what you think? Indeed, who would not praise you if, for the sake of public [Col. 1110A] tranquility and the common peace of the world, you accepted the name whose meaning, as we have learned, your piety possesses?” And again: “Many, as I understand, have quite frequently heard from you that you reject the expression itself alone, not also its pious meaning; yet if certain ecclesiastical authorities of more distinguished reputation should urge you, so that, once the name itself had been admitted, you would call the holy Virgin Mary Deipara [θεοτόκος, ‘Mother of God’], you would by no means refuse to do so.”

The testimony of that bishop is all the more weighty because he was regarded as especially knowledgeable in orthodox faith, both by the highest pontiffs and even when questions of faith were under discussion.

In this matter the whole diocese of the East followed its bishop. Although it abounded in bishops distinguished equally for holiness and learning, it nevertheless undertook Nestorius’s cause and, if we trust Theodoret, never departed from his opinion except verbally—namely, by softening Nestorius’s harsher expressions and employing, in explaining the mystery of the Incarnation, that economy of language which Nestorius had rejected out of sheer pride and obstinacy.

When, therefore, the synod of the East, for the sake of restoring peace among the Churches, had agreed [Col. 1110B] to Nestorius’s deposition, and John, in the name of the synod, had written not only a confession to Cyril—which Cyril declared irreproachable—but also a letter to the emperor, Theodoretus says of it (Letter 2 to Alexander of Hierapolis):

“I have learned that the man who wrote this letter to the emperor, holding the same opinion, condemned unjustly and without discrimination the man who knew and taught nothing except sound doctrine. Yet although the anathema inserted in it, even if sufficient, disturbs the reader more than the agreement concerning the condemnation, nevertheless, since it was not placed there without discrimination but with a certain qualification, it brought consolation. For he did not say, ‘We anathematize his doctrine,’ but, ‘Whatever he said or thought otherwise than the apostolic doctrine contains.’”

Theodoret himself made clear what he thought about the matter, both by words that are not obscure and, most clearly, by these statements (Letter 2 to the same person):

“I have already declared to your holiness that if the dogma of my lord, the venerable and most holy [Col. 1110C] bishop Nestorius, is condemned, neither shall I communicate with those who do this. If it pleases your holiness to insert this very point into the letters being sent to Antioch, let it be done. Therefore, I beg you, as I follow in your footsteps, do not let it be delayed.”

He reveals his mind no less openly in writing to Andrew of Samosata:

“Aristolaus demands subscription to the condemnation made some time ago, and that the dogma of the holy bishop Nestorius be anathematized. Your holiness knows that if anyone anathematizes, without qualification, the doctrine of that same most holy and venerable bishop, it is as though he appeared to anathematize piety. Therefore, if we are compelled at all, we ought to anathematize those who say that Christ is merely a man, or who divide our one Lord Jesus Christ into two sons, and those who deny his divinity.”

The historian Socrates, moreover, after carefully examining Nestorius’s books, as he himself testifies, nevertheless wrote as follows (Book VII, chap. 32):

“Nestorius came to be thought by many to say that the Lord was merely a man and to be introducing [Col. 1110D] the doctrine of Paul of Samosata and Photinus into the Church. Hence such a great dispute and such a storm arose that an ecumenical council was required. But when I examine his books, I find him to be an unlearned man, etc.; nevertheless, he does not seem to me to imitate Paul of Samosata or Photinus, or to say that the Lord is altogether merely a man. Rather, he seems to fear the single expression ‘Deipara’ [θεοτόκος] as though it were a specter.”

And later:

“He appears to be ignorant of the writings of the ancients and therefore, as I said, attacks this expression. For he does not call Christ merely a man, as Photinus and Paul of Samosata did. The homilies published by him also show that he in no way removed the person of the divine Word, but everywhere acknowledges it as subsisting and indwelling, etc. This is how I find him thinking, both from the books of his that I have read and from what his admirers say.”

Finally, Diodore, who taught Theodore, and Theodore, who taught Nestorius, can disclose the mind of their common pupil by revealing their own. For Nestorius clung to them just as Theodoret, the other of the pupils, did, [Col. 1111A] and Cyril openly confirms this, reporting that both of them shared Nestorius’s views.

But Facundus, after proving by the testimony of Athanasius, Peter of Alexandria, Timothy, Basil, Chrysostom, and Epiphanius that Diodore was of upright faith, concludes his defense in this way (Book IV, chap. 2):

“Who, however, could tolerate Diodore’s being accused by Julian because he confessed that God was born of the Virgin, and his being accused even by Christians as though he had denied this? Or who, on hearing Julian threaten Diodore because he proclaimed Jesus the Galilean to be the eternal God—although he could not deny that he had died and been buried—and therefore say that he was punished by his gods with the greatest punishment because, miserably imbibing the error of the theologizing fishermen, he proclaimed such things, would also judge him deserving of expulsion from the Christian community, as though he had believed Jesus the Galilean to be merely a man and not also God?”

Facundus also brings forward passages from Theodore (Book III, chap. 2), excerpted with such precision that nothing seems capable of being produced more significant for orthodox faith. In the thirteenth book of *On the Incarnation*:

“It is good at this point above all to conclude [Col. 1111B] what force the things that have been said possess—whether it is a matter of living, being baptized, being crucified, dying, being buried, or rising again. We do not attach these things to some merely ordinary man. In each demonstration of the things mentioned, we do not delay adding this point, so that we may provide no opportunity for slanderers to speak maliciously. But we say that God the Word dwelt in him from the very formation in his mother’s womb—not by a common indwelling, nor according to the grace understood to exist in many, but according to a certain excellence, by which we also say that the two natures were united and that one person was effected according to the union.”

It is worthwhile to see how Facundus argues each of Theodore’s statements in his defense.

## § VI. How Weak Are the Arguments Produced on Behalf of Nestorius

These, then, are the arguments of Nestorius’s defenders. Although they possess some appearance of truth, by which they deceived Albertinus the Calvinist and others of that sort, in reality [Col. 1111C] they are exceedingly vain and derive whatever weight they may seem to possess only from the thoughtlessness, or even the ignorance, of those who employ them.

To expose the disguise in what Nestorius said on his own behalf, it must be noted that this heretic—than whom nothing was ever more artful or deceitful—was accustomed, following the example of his teacher Theodore, to conceal his meaning beneath Catholic words. From Theodore he learned not so much the doctrines he was to follow as the frauds by which he could protect himself.

Next, it must be observed that the whole heresy to which Nestorius gave his name consisted in denying that the two natures in Christ were united *according to hypostasis* [καθ’ ὑπόστασιν], but affirming that they were united only by a moral bond, such as ordinarily exists between spouses, or at least would exist between those thought to be joined by a perpetual and indissoluble bond. Each would always belong to the other, and neither could ever be separated from the other; but there would be one perpetual dignity belonging morally to both, one authority, and one moral person. Indeed, the same parent would be said to belong to both, but in different [Col. 1111D] ways: the parent of the one by nature, of the other as though by adoption, and so forth.

Thus, when Nestorius complained that he was being slandered and wished to appear angry with the Samosatenian who affirmed that Christ was merely a man, he concealed his real position. For he was not accused of wishing Christ, like the Samosatenian, to have existed for some time without the Word and to have merited his union with the Word by his works. Who had not repeatedly heard him proclaiming that the natures had been joined in the Virgin’s womb, indeed from the very conception? But—and rightly—he was blamed for saying that these very natures were joined only by a moral bond. The result would be that God was indeed the God of man and man the man of God, but not that God was man and man God; that the evangelists’ words would be understood neither in their proper nor, if one may speak thus, their direct sense, but only figuratively and *relationally* [σχετικῶς]; that the Word had not become flesh but was merely an inhabitant of flesh; that God had not died, [Col. 1112A] but the temple of God; that the Virgin was not *Deipara* [θεοτόκος, ‘Mother of God’] but *Anthropotokos* [ἀνθρωποτόκος, ‘mother of man’], and so forth.

Nor is Nestorius’s fraud any less evident when he proclaimed Christ to be one, and one Son and Lord. For he made Christ one not by hypostasis but by mere conjunction, after the manner of spouses, who are one morally. This example is repeatedly thrust forward both by Theodore, Nestorius’s teacher, and by Theodoret, his associate in the school.

He also made Christ one Son of God and of the Virgin, but by a remarkable twist. For he said that the man was the Son of God not by nature but by union; not because he himself was the Only-Begotten, but because he was joined to the Only-Begotten. That is, as they put it, he was a son because of the Son, not in the direct but in the oblique sense. Likewise, the Word was called the Virgin’s son only in an oblique sense, because he dwelt in the Virgin’s son. This was his claim that everything belonging to the Word and to the man was communicated by *equivocation* [καθ’ ὁμωνυμίαν].

Cyril exposed the tricks of this wicked quibbler’s use of the word “person.” He showed that the heresy was being concealed beneath “unity of person,” and that nothing else was signified except that, through the Word’s *incarnation* [ἐνανθρώπησις], [Col. 1112B] the dignity of God and man had become one, as had authority, power, and whatever other moral terms of this kind there might be.

For the great trickster took the word “person” as a legal term, by which spouses, as has often been said, are one person. Yet if he had acted in good faith, he ought to have taken it as something belonging to nature and as meaning hypostasis itself; in that sense, spouses are actually two persons and two hypostases.

That transparent fellow also allowed the Virgin to be called Deipara, provided that she was not thought to be a goddess. With no less treachery he lay in wait for his hearers when he ordered that she be called *Theotokos* [θεοτόκος], provided that she was not understood in the sense of Apollinaris and Arius.

For his heresy held that no woman could be called a mother unless she were consubstantial with the one whose mother she was, considered in himself and separately. Thus no woman could be called the mother of the Word, since no woman could be consubstantial with the Word considered in himself unless she had become a goddess; nor had the Word [Col. 1112C] become consubstantial with a woman through conversion.

The wicked man disclosed his own meaning when he wrote to the supreme pontiff in these words (Letter 1 to Celestine, no. 6):

“If anyone proposes the name *Theotokos* [θεοτόκος] because the humanity born was joined to God the Word, and not because of the woman who gave birth, we say that this word is not properly applicable to the woman who gave birth. For a true mother must be of the same essence as the one who is born from her; nevertheless, because of the consideration involved, and because this word is applied to the Virgin alone on account of the inseparable temple of God the Word derived from her, it can be tolerated—not because she is the mother of God the Word, for no one gives birth to one older than herself.”

Such, then, is the emptiness of the testimony Nestorius produced on his own behalf. The evidence brought forward by John of Antioch is worth no more, whether one considers the time at which the letter was written, the person who wrote it, or Nestorius himself.

At that time Nestorius’s mind, although exceedingly embittered, was not to be driven into madness by a denunciation of heresy, but rather gently handled by a sort of diplomatic [Col. 1112D] flattery. Moreover, when the letter was written, there was not yet one settled opinion among all concerning Nestorius’s faith, for he deliberately spoke in a confused and ambiguous manner. Some interpreted his slippery words in a more favorable sense; others interpreted them in the opposite—and truer—sense.

Finally, it is believable that John’s own faith at that time was not altogether sincere. Indeed, it is scarcely doubtful that he retained in his mind the doctrine he had imbibed from their common teacher Theodore, and cherished it for so long, until he either laid it aside after being instructed by the controversy or frightened by the upheaval of the world.

Although, to speak frankly, I have always regarded—and still regard—the confession of faith that John published for the peace of the Churches with suspicion, Cyril’s prudent acceptance of the confession and his kindly *economy* [οἰκονομία] have not yet been able, despite my strong desire, to lessen this suspicion.

First, Acacius of Beroea appears to have been the author [Col. 1113A] of the confession, a man who, in my judgment, was ill-disposed toward Christ. Second, Nestorius could subscribe to this confession without prejudice to any of his own dogmas. Finally, Cyril may appear, wearied by the disturbances, to have thought that the Churches should be pacified by such means.

But we shall return to this matter on another occasion. For now, observe that Acacius’s testimony could also have been produced on behalf of Nestorius. For when he wrote to Cyril, he seems, like John, to excuse Nestorius. But, also like John, he can rightly be regarded with suspicion for both reasons: because his faith is doubtful and because his attitude toward the accused is certain.

The case of the Eastern bishops is the same as John’s. Theodoret’s testimony unquestionably ought not to be heard as authoritative, since it comes from a man either in agreement with Nestorius or joined to him by extraordinary friendship. Either consideration removes all credibility from it, or at least greatly diminishes it.

Add that the very testimony of Theodoret that has been brought forward establishes the contrary. For how could he persuade Catholics of Nestorius’s innocence when he shows himself acting [Col. 1113B] against the judgment of the Church?

What authority can Socrates possess in a theological matter, since he was either a scholasticus from the law courts or a writer from the imperial court? And even if some authority is granted him, Nestorius’s cause will nevertheless not emerge better from it. What Socrates writes is certainly true, but irrelevant.

He says that Nestorius does not call Christ merely a man, as Paul and Photinus did. Certainly: they denied that the man was joined to the Word, which subsists in itself and is consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος] with the Father—something Nestorius certainly confessed. They denied that a union had existed from the conception of the man; Nestorius affirmed this. They denied that the Virgin was *Christotokos* [Χριστοτόκος, ‘Mother of Christ’]; Nestorius contended that she was.

What more need be said? They openly professed Christ to be merely a man; Nestorius did not profess this. But in reality he did not admit a union *according to hypostasis* [ἕνωσιν καθ’ ὑπόστασιν], and in this he agreed with them.

Thus he deceived Socrates when, in his fourth and twelfth sermons, he declared [Col. 1113C] that he was far removed from Paul and Photinus. Socrates believed the speaker, being ignorant of the fraud that needed to be exposed and of the mystery that needed to be understood more deeply.

But to call Diodore of Tarsus and Theodore of Mopsuestia as witnesses by whom Nestorius’s orthodox faith might be proved—what else is that than an attempt to prove someone free of a crime by producing his accomplices, or even his leaders? Cyril exposed both as Nestorius’s instructors, one closer and the other more remote, and the Church condemned them. Nor has Facundus ever adequately absolved either of the two, however hard he strives, since each, by his own words, both exposes and condemns himself.

For what is more heretical than this statement of Diodore (Book I *Against the Synusiasts*)?

“Let no one think that the Son of Mary is God the Word. [Col. 1113D] For a mortal naturally gives birth to a mortal, and generates a consubstantial body; nor does God the Word undergo two births, one before the ages and the other in later times.”

What could be more shameless than this statement from the same work?

“The perfect Son before the ages assumed the perfect one who was from David—the Son of God assumed the son of David.”

“You say to me: Then do you proclaim two sons?”

“I do not say two sons of David. For I did not say that God the Word is the son of David. Nor do I say that there are two sons of God according to substance. For I do not say that there are two from the substance of God when I say that God the Word dwelt before the ages in the one begotten from the seed of David.”

Theodore copied these words into his books *On the Incarnation*. For the same statements are found there, and he adds:

“God the Word did not dwell in the one who was from the seed of David in the same way as in the prophets. They enjoyed the grace of the Holy Spirit in a certain partial and limited measure, whereas in this one the things that were sometimes in them remained continually. He was filled with the glory and wisdom of the Word. The other, plainly, existed apart from the Word and was properly a subsisting Son, separately. For the Word did not fill himself with wisdom and glory; rather, he conferred these distinguishing qualities upon another.”

Once these points have been demonstrated, who would not be astonished at the audacity of Albertinus and the Symmysts—especially Albertinus, that glutton for books—who defend Nestorius against [Col. 1114A] the Third General Council, whose authority the Calvinists themselves accept in their confession, and whose judgment twelve centuries of reverence have approved; against the Fathers of the fifth—that is, learned—century, the most illustrious lights of the whole Church; against the faith of all devout worshipers of Christ?

They defend a man crushed by the thunderbolts of the Church, convicted by the disputations of the Fathers, detestable throughout all succeeding ages, and abominated by all who love Christ. They assert as free from error one whom the laws declare to be the leader of monstrous doctrine; one whom the emperors considered unworthy even of his own name; one whom his own conscience condemned as guilty and whom a world in turmoil judged; one whose tongue nature, avenging his Lord, gave over to be consumed by worms before his death.

Indeed, however much some may try to conceal it, their audacity was driven to this point by the fact that one of them committed to print the hatred toward the name of Deipara professed by men with too much leisure.

# CHAPTER III. On the Three Heretics Arius, Apollinaris, and Eunomius, Whose Association Nestorius Falsely Imputed to Catholics

[Col. 1114B]

Although Nestorius’s mind and opinion concerning the Lord’s dispensation are clearly revealed by the preceding chapters, they will become still more evident and clearer if the reason is disclosed why Nestorius attacked Cyril and Cyril’s Catholic followers with such vehemence.

That reason was, unless I am mistaken, the appearance of affinity between the Catholic opinion and the Arian and Apollinarian opinions—an affinity so great that the difference between one and the other could be discerned only by perceptive eyes in the light of faith.

Since there are two forms of *physical union* [φυσικὴ ἕνωσις], one more difficult to understand, by which two natures are joined into the unity of a single hypostasis, and the other very familiar, by which two things are joined [Col. 1114C] even into unity of nature, as soul and body, Nestorius and others thought that no one could defend any *physical union* except the kind we have said belongs to the second mode.

Since many absurd and impious consequences follow from this, those who defended the union of the first kind were easily brought into popular hatred. For they could not readily be distinguished from Arius and Apollinaris, and yet those two men were universally detested.

This, then, was why Nestorius and others who defended union *according to hypostasis* [καθ’ ὑπόστασιν] accused Cyril of association with Arius, Apollinaris, and Eunomius, and branded Catholics with the name of heretics.

It is therefore useful to make some observations concerning each of these three heretics, so that Nestorius’s opinion concerning the mystery of the Incarnation, and his slander against Catholics, may be increasingly exposed. For the wicked man reveals his own mind all the more clearly the more vehemently he condemns another’s opinion as heresy, or at least as error.

## § I. On Arius and the Arians

The ancients have handed down [Col. 1114D] that there were two principal elements in the Arian impiety concerning the divine Word. The first was that the Word was less than the Father and created; the second, that the Word had taken the place of a soul for the flesh.

The Arians omitted the former when discussing the Trinity and the latter when discussing the Incarnation; nevertheless, the two were connected, as will soon become clear.

Concerning the latter, Athanasius says in his book *On the Coming of Christ*:

“Arius confesses that the Word took flesh alone in order to conceal the Divinity; and, in place of our inner man—that is, in place of the soul—he says that the Word existed in the flesh, daring to attribute to the Divinity the experience of suffering and the resurrection from the dead.”

And elsewhere (*On the Incarnation of Christ*):

“Therefore the Arians fashion their dreams in vain, asserting that the Savior assumed flesh alone, so that they impiously transfer the experience of suffering to the impassible Divinity.”

Epiphanius likewise teaches this about Arius’s followers in *Heresy* 69 and, in summary, as Augustine reports (*Book of Heresies*, nos. 49–50). So do the two Gregorys: Gregory of Nazianzus in Letter 1 to Cledonius, and Gregory of Nyssa in the book [Col. 1115A] *Against Eunomius*. Cyril of Alexandria also teaches it in his apologetic letter to Acacius of Melitene.

Theodoretus writes (*Book V of the Heretical Fables*, chap. 11) that Arius and Eunomius thought that a body had been assumed, while the Divinity had taken the place of the soul.

Mercator observes that this fiction was not invented by Arius himself but by the Arians, so that, in my opinion, they might more easily escape questions that had not yet arisen in Arius’s time. Nevertheless, it is attributed to Arius, partly because of the customary practice of burdening teachers with the discredit of their disciples, and partly because it appeared to have been derived from his principles or at least to agree closely with them, as we shall explain later.

The Arians arrived at this opinion partly because of certain prejudices, whether their own prejudices concerning the Word or common prejudices concerning man and the soul; and partly because, once this hypothesis was granted, they seemed able easily to explain everything the Church’s faith maintained concerning Christ against Photinus. I believe that this Arian fiction arose in Photinus’s time.

At the time [Col. 1115B], the question was whether Christ was merely a man in whom the Word dwelt, and how the Word dwelt in man: whether merely by operation, as the Holy Spirit dwells in the righteous, or also by a *physical union* [ἕνωσις φυσική], by which the Word could properly be said to have become flesh rather than merely to be an inhabitant of flesh.

Those who resisted Photinus, who introduced mere indwelling, divided into two groups. Some kept within the proper bounds, like the Catholics; others went beyond them, like the Arians and Apollinarists.

For all of them, seeing that they had to defend a substantial union if they wished to take the evangelist’s words according to their proper meaning, and understanding that there were two kinds of substantial union, which we explained above, the Catholics were satisfied with hypostatic union, while the Arians wanted the greater kind, such as exists between soul and body. Therefore they said that in Christ the Word supplied to the flesh what the soul usually supplies: life, motion, and sensation.

If Epiphanius (*Heresy* 69) and the author of the *Dialogue Against the Apollinarists*—attributed by some to Athanasius and by others to the martyr Maximus—are to be believed, they appear to have reasoned in this matter almost as Aristotle usually reasons in physical questions (*Physics*, Book II):

“What is now occurring could have happened both completely and well; otherwise it could have happened neither well nor completely; therefore it happened in this way.”

They inferred that it could have happened in this way for the Word to become flesh—that is, man—because man is a soul using a body, and because any created mind can be changed into a soul, infused into a body, and become a man.

Since, therefore, they said that the Word was one of the created minds, they maintained that it could be united to flesh in the manner of a soul and thus become a man.

They accepted the first principle—that is, the definition of man—as though it were already granted by the widespread Platonic doctrine of that time. They borrowed the second from Origen, whose offspring they were in a certain sense. The third they claimed as their own.

They then proved that everything cohered beautifully [Col. 1115D] if the Word were said to have become flesh in this way by the example of every ordinary man, whose soul, when infused into the body, becomes a man. The following consequences were connected with this reasoning:

1. Christ would not be a man such as any one of us, but truly God using an assumed body just as a soul uses its body.

2. The blessed Virgin would as truly be called *Theotokos* [θεοτόκος, “Mother of God”] as any other woman who gave birth to a man would be called *Anthropotokos* [ἀνθρωποτόκος, “mother of man”].

3. The Incarnation would not be merely a *relational* [σχετική] union of the two natures, such as exists between spouses, but rather a *physical* and *essential* [οὐσιώδης] union, such as exists between soul and body.

4. There would indeed be two natures in Christ, as there are in us, but nevertheless a single hypostasis of both, likewise as in us.

5. The one who is Son from the Father would not be different from the one who is from the mother; rather, he would be one and the same from both. For in us [Col. 1116A] the man created by God is not one man and the man procreated by parents another.

6. There would be two births of the one divine Word: one eternal birth from the Father, the other temporal birth from the mother. In the same way, two births can exist in any human being: one from God, by which the mind is created—and, if we believe Origen, before the ages—and the other by which the man is procreated at a fixed time.

7. The Word could not be called Christ’s Lord, nor could Christ be said to be less than the Holy Spirit.

8. God would be asserted to have been born, suffered, died, and so forth, as truly and properly as individual human beings are said to be born and to suffer.

9. Finally, Christ’s flesh would have been deified, and the Word incarnated.

Why pursue the remaining points? One example of an ordinary man is enough to make the whole matter clear.

It followed from this doctrine that, when the Word became incarnate, he was changed into a soul, mixed with the flesh, and made passible. For when a mind is incarnated and becomes a man, the Origenists said that it was changed into a soul, [Col. 1116B] mixed throughout the body, made subject to suffering, and assumed all the names applied to man.

They also seemed to infer that the entire work of the Incarnation could not have been accomplished otherwise because only two ways of resolving the matter remained. One was asserted by the Samosatenian: a purely *relational* or moral union. The other was attributed by some to Photinus: a union that was indeed hypostatic, but by which not the man subsisted in the hypostasis of the Word; rather, the Word subsisted in the hypostasis of the man, since it was in itself *without a hypostasis* [ἀνυπόστατος] and merely an utterance.

Neither alternative could be admitted. This was demonstrated not only by the common faith of the Church against both heretics, but also by the two Antiochene synods against the Samosatenian, by the two synods of Sirmium, and by other synods that had defined matters against Photinus.

They then pressed forcefully the evangelist’s statement, “The Word became flesh,” as well as the familiar question: “Why would there be a soul where the Word is present, and indeed physically united to it?” Finally, they invoked [Col. 1116C] the arguments of the Apollinarists, both those reported by Cyril (*On the Right Faith to Theodore*, chap. 17) and the many arguments accumulated in Dialogues 4 and 5 *On the Trinity*, among the works of Athanasius.

Such was the Arian heresy concerning the Incarnation, arising from the other heresy concerning the Trinity. For by calling the Word the first of the created minds, they made him suitable to enter a body and become a soul.

No one, perhaps, will be surprised that Cyril was suspected by the Easterners of this heresy if he considers either the circumstances of the times, when the mystery of the Incarnation still lay concealed beneath all its darkness, or the disposition of those whose envy consumed them.

For the *physical* and *hypostatic* union [ἕνωσις φυσικὴ καὶ καθ’ ὑπόστασιν] that Cyril defended in a Catholic sense appeared to have the same consequences as, and to conflict in the same ways with, the Arian heresy—especially to men who were partly moved by envy and partly bewitched by the insane love of their own Nestorius.

This suspicion had taken such deep possession of their minds that, although Cyril never neglected [Col. 1116D] an opportunity either to anathematize Arius, to attack the conversion, confusion, and mixture of the Word, or to teach emphatically that the whole of humanity, and indeed the soul itself, had been assumed, he could scarcely ever persuade them of his sincerity.

Indeed, when peace was being established among the Churches, he was at times compelled to remain silent concerning his anathematizations, as though they were causes of discord. So obscure was the distinction between the two opinions at that time, and so visible only to the most clear-sighted.

To show that I am not making this claim rashly, it is worthwhile to compare the Arian doctrine with each of Cyril’s anathematizations.

In the first, Cyril said that Emmanuel was God *in truth* [κατὰ ἀλήθειαν], an expression he elsewhere interprets as meaning “God by nature.” This very expression belonged to the Arians: Emmanuel was as truly God by nature as each of us is a man.

Cyril added that for this reason the blessed [Col. 1117A] Virgin was *Theotokos* [θεοτόκος]. The Arians also loudly proclaimed this very thing, and Nestorius frequently cast it as a charge against Proclus and Cyril.

In the second, Cyril taught that the Word of God the Father had been united to the flesh *according to hypostasis* [ἡνῶσθαι καθ’ ὑπόστασιν], and that Christ was one with his flesh. The Arians explained their own position in these very words when they used the example of the soul, which is one man with its body.

In the third, he hurled an anathema at anyone who did not confess the *physical union* [φυσικὴ ἕνωσις] of the Word and the flesh. The entire poison of the Arian doctrine was contained in these two words, “physical union,” of the sort that unites soul and body.

In the fourth, he forbade anyone to divide between two hypostases the expressions concerning Christ that occur throughout the sacred Scriptures, whether spoken by Christ himself or by the apostles. The Arians likewise forbade this, again abusing the example of man.

In the fifth, he declared that, when the Word became flesh, he shared in flesh and blood just as we do. The Arians kept saying nothing else; [Col. 1117B] indeed, this was the brief explanation of the whole heresy.

In the sixth, he denied that the Word was Christ’s Lord. The Arians denied this as well—and not only denied it, but also gave a clear reason for doing so: the Word united to the flesh is Christ in no other way than the soul infused into the body is a man. But no one is properly called his own lord.

In the seventh, he likewise rejected the claim that the Word operated in Christ as in a man who was not the Word himself. The Arians also rejected this, saying that the Word was this man, Jesus Christ, in the same way that a soul is some particular man—for example, Peter.

In the eighth, he prohibited saying that the assumed man was worshiped together with the Word, as though there were two beings to be worshiped, man and Word; otherwise, as is argued elsewhere, a quaternity would be introduced in place of the Trinity. The Arians likewise prohibited this for the same reason as the one they had first devised.

He also prohibited, in the ninth, anyone [Col. 1117C] from asserting that Christ was aided by the power of the Holy Spirit as by something external, since the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son and Christ is that very eternal Son of God from whom the Spirit proceeds. The Arians likewise prohibited this, and for the same reason, since they asserted that the Holy Spirit was created by the Father through the Son.

The two subsequent anathematizations—the first concerning anyone who denied that the Word, by the Incarnation, became the high priest and apostle of our confession and offered himself for us, though not for himself, to the Father; the second concerning anyone who denied that the life-giving flesh of the Lord, that is, the flesh that gives life to the world, was proper to the Word—contain a doctrine which, although I do not recall reading it expressed among the Arians in precisely the same words, can nevertheless clearly be derived from Arian principles. For if the Word stood in place of the soul by which the man Jesus Christ existed, one must unquestionably admit that every office of Christ, and thus his priesthood and apostleship, [Col. 1117D] belonged to the Word.

One must likewise conclude that the Word offered himself to the Father for us and made his flesh—which he animated—the life-giving bread set forth on the sacred table.

The final anathematization, concerning the Word of God suffering, being crucified, dying, and becoming the firstborn from the dead, offended the Nestorians above all others. It therefore appeared not merely akin to the Arian heresy but identical with it, and consequently seemed to be condemned by the Nicene Creed, in the passage that anathematizes anyone who asserts that the Son of God is subject to change and alteration.

These and other considerations sufficiently brought Cyril under suspicion of agreement with the Arians. Yet two things increased the suspicion, and these would later become the seeds of a great controversy.

The first was that Cyril often used the word “nature” [φύσις] in place of “hypostasis” [ὑπόστασις]. Thus, when he proclaimed a single hypostasis [Col. 1118A] in Christ, he seemed to acknowledge a single nature in Christ.

But this could scarcely, if at all, be understood without the Arian fiction that the Word occupied the place of the soul.

The second point was that he openly said that after the ἕνωσις [union] there was one nature of the incarnate Word: a position which, being obscure in itself, was therefore easily taken in the worse sense by people ill-disposed toward Cyril.

The Arian heresy, moreover, was refuted chiefly by four arguments.

I. That the Word is of the same essence as the Father, and is the ἀληθινὸς Θεός [true God], whom the Arians admitted, on account of the excellence of his essence, to be ἄτρεπτος καὶ ἄναλλοίωτος [immutable and unchangeable], and therefore incapable of being reduced to the condition of a soul informing a body.

II. That in the Gospel Christ spoke of his soul, which at one time had been troubled and sorrowful unto death, and which he himself had laid down and had again taken up at will.

III. That unless the Word had also assumed the mind of a human being, he would certainly not have saved the whole human being: for he saved only that which he assumed; and he ought especially to have undertaken to heal that part in which the root of evil, namely sin, lay. [Col. 1118B]

IV. That Christ would not have died in obedience, nor by his death have merited anything for human beings, nor consequently have been their mediator with God. For these three things belong only to one who was at once rational and inferior.

§ II. On Apollinaris and the Apollinarists

There was no small affinity between the teaching of Apollinaris and that of the Arians. The difference, however, was this: whereas the Arians granted Christ no soul besides the Word, Apollinaris granted him the soul by which the body is animated, moved, and endowed with sensation. He therefore asserted that only the functions of the mind were fulfilled by the Word. From this single difference many consequences arose; yet it seems that they should not be considered before certain points concerning Apollinaris himself have been observed—points which may perhaps bring some light to a matter of extraordinary obscurity. [Col. 1118C]

There were two Apollinarii, father and son. When the father had migrated from Alexandria to Laodicea, he begot the son, who, like his father, devoted himself entirely to rhetoric and sophistry. Both served the Church of Laodicea: the father in the rank of presbyter, the son as lector. They created their heresy, if we believe Socrates, during this period.

Only the son’s name became especially famous; yet the ancients transmit contradictory accounts of him, some pouring out praises and others abuse.

Jerome writes that he was bishop of Laodicea; Theodoret, that he was bishop of Antioch. Socrates relates that he created his heresy while he was still a lector, because, being unable to control his anger, he was plotting revenge against Bishop George, by whom he had been suspended. Epiphanius says that he fell into error through thoughtlessness when he held the episcopate. Socrates attributes his suspension by George to excessive intimacy with a pagan philosopher; Sozomen maintains that it happened because Apollinaris had communicated with Athanasius when the latter was passing through Laodicea. Theophilus, and also Jerome, testify that Apollinaris wrote innumerable volumes against the Arians, Eunomians, and Origenists. Nazianzen accuses him of agreement with such heretics. Basil and Theodoret make him guilty of Sabellian impiety; Vincent of Lérins and Leontius Scholasticus declare him orthodox. Some of the ancients report that he taught three propositions strongly opposed to the faith: first, that the Word did not assume flesh from Mary but brought it from heaven; second, that the divinity of the Word, if not wholly, at least in part, was converted into flesh; finally, that for a thousand years after the judgment the saints would reign on earth with Christ, and that at length there would arise an Origenist ἀνακύκλησις [cycle or recurrence]. Epiphanius contends that these and similar monstrosities were opinions rather than doctrines, devised by the disciples, and that the master, as often happens, suffered from the odium incurred by his disciples. But why should I pursue other matters no less contradictory to these?

[Col. 1119A]

Amid such disagreement among the authors—produced either by the bias of the writers, which is not incredible, or by the perplexity of the matter, which is more reasonable to suppose—I would rather adhere to Epiphanius and the Lirinensian. Although they lament the unhappy fall of a man whom they greatly praise, they nevertheless charge him with one error alone, though a most serious one: that he taught that the Word existed in Christ in place of the mind, while everything else was like that of a human being.

He came to this opinion, if not for more, at least for three reasons. Mercator reports the first in his dissertation on the twelfth anathema of Nestorius. After mentioning angels who had sometimes appeared in bodily form, and denying that anything should be affirmed easily and rashly when the question is (no. 24) whether they had assumed only bodies in which those spirits temporarily dwelt, performing the ministry of rational souls, or whether they had externally inspired animated bodies, as prophets do, he continues as follows:

> This presumed and uncertain opinion, taken as certain although nowhere expressed in Scripture, deceived Apollinaris of Laodicea, and afterward the Arians—but not Arius himself—and Eunomius, and perhaps the later Macedonius, so that from this they believed and declared that Christ the Son of God assumed only a human body, not also a soul; and that, in place of a soul, the Son of God, the Word of the Father, dwelt in that assumed body.

And later:

> Although afterward Apollinaris, as though correcting his position for the worse, confessed that there was indeed a soul in Christ, he nevertheless deliriously asserted that the human reason or mind was not in him, but that God, the Son of God, existed in its place.

(Mercator, *On the Twelfth Anathema of Nestorius*, nos. 25, 27.)

Nemesius gives the second reason (*On the Nature of the Human Being*):

> Certain men, among them Plotinus, establishing that the soul is one thing and the mind another, wish the human being to consist of three elements: body, soul, and mind. Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea, followed them; and, having laid this foundation of his position, he built upon it the rest of his doctrine accordingly.

Cyril indicates a third and a fourth reason in his book *On the Correct Faith to Theodosius* (chap. 17). After expounding the Catholic faith concerning the unity of Christ against Photinus, he adds concerning Apollinaris:

> They too openly establish one Christ alone, and they vehemently abhor as something joined with the utmost impiety the division of one Emmanuel into two. Yet they proclaim that the Word was united to flesh which was human—that is, endowed with reason—but deprived and bereft of a rational soul. They assert that they have discovered an entirely plausible reason why they ought to teach this. For they say that those things which by composition concur in constituting one complete being are parts and possess the character of incomplete things; whereas what is complete in itself, and exists in its own nature, does not need to enter into a partial composition. Therefore, they say, one must carefully avoid exposing to deserved slander that exact unity which is recognized to have occurred in Christ, by admitting that the temple united to the Word became a complete human being.
>
> Indeed, I suspect that they will add this also: if we say that Emmanuel was formed from a complete human being and the Word of God the Father, we shall run into a great and plainly unavoidable danger, namely, that whether we wish it or not we shall be compelled to hold and profess two Christs and likewise two sons.

The author of the fourth and fifth dialogues *On the Trinity*, included among the works of Athanasius, reports several other arguments.

Nothing better can be brought forward concerning this entire heresy than the conversation which Epiphanius held at Antioch with Vitalis, a disciple of Apollinaris, when he wished to reconcile Vitalis and Paulinus—both then bishops of that city and opposed to each other over the faith. He says that he received from Paulinus a statement of faith corrected by Athanasius’s own hand, but questioned Vitalis in the following manner (*Heresy* 77, concerning the Dimaerites):

“Do you profess that Christ properly assumed flesh?”

“I do,” he replied.

“Did he receive that same flesh from the Virgin Mary without human generation and through the Holy Spirit?”

He did not deny this either.

“Do you regard the Word of God himself and the Son of God as having descended from heaven and assumed flesh from the Virgin?”

He assented with great solemnity.

Asked again by us whether he had also received a soul from the same source, he confessed with equal solemnity and constancy that he had; and he said that nothing else should be asserted, but that the truth should be stated in every respect. Thus Vitalis confessed that Christ had assumed a human soul. For he spoke as follows:

“Christ was altogether a complete human being.” Then, after we had questioned him about the soul and flesh, we finally asked him: “Did Christ the Lord receive a mind?” Without any hesitation he denied it. We then replied: “What, then, do you think made him a complete human being?” To this he disclosed to us the innermost convictions of his mind. “We say,” he replied, “that he was a complete human being if we assign divinity to him in place of a mind, and add flesh and soul, so that the complete human being consists of flesh, soul, and divinity, which functions as a mind.”

Apollinaris therefore occupied an intermediate position between the Catholics and the Arians. He agreed with both in the points on which they opposed the Docetists (Δοκήται), the Photinians, and those whom Cyril seems to call σχετικοί [relationalists]. For against the Docetists he confessed Christ’s true flesh, and against the σχετικοί he confessed a real—that is, physical—ἕνωσις [union] of the flesh with the Word.

He agreed with the Arians in failing to preserve the proper manner of explaining the essence of the union; that is, he posited a union no greater than that which exists between the flesh and the rational part of a human being. Consequently, his position had all the implications by which it falsely claimed kinship with the Catholics, just as the Arian position did. Yet he differed from the Arians in declaring the Word consubstantial with the Father and in attributing to Christ, in addition to human flesh, a soul. In this way he avoided, if not all, at least part of the odium that had accumulated against the Arians.

For he could explain without difficulty the passages of Scripture that mention Christ’s soul as troubled, sorrowful, laid down, and so forth. He interpreted these passages as referring to the sensitive soul. [Col. 1120C] Nor was he compelled to admit the three particular enormities of the Arians: namely, that when the Word became incarnate he was confused and mixed with the flesh, that he was converted into it, or that he was passible in his own nature. For, apart from the fact that confusion, mixture, conversion, and passibility belong only to the soul, into which the mind enters when it is joined to the body, certainly, although Aristotle calls the νοῦς [mind] of the human being incorporeal (*On the Soul*, book III), he nevertheless calls it χωριστὸς, καὶ ἀπαθὴς, καὶ ἀμιγὴς [separable, impassible, and unmixed]. Much more, then, could the divine mind, or the Word, become incarnate without any confusion, mixture, or passion affecting itself, and perform the function of a mind.

No one will be surprised that Apollinaris joined Aristotle to Plato if he remembers that Apollinaris was taught by his father, and that his father was taught by Ammonius of Alexandria, who combined the doctrines of both philosophies.

Before bringing this discussion to an end, it is worthwhile to resolve certain questions and, by resolving them, shed light on what has been related partly about Apollinaris himself and partly about his doctrine.

[Col. 1120D]

I. Why did Nestorius more than once, and the Nestorians frequently, charge Cyril—with such agitation and anger—with agreement with Apollinaris?

I think this happened for three reasons. First, because the uneducated populace did not perceive the ambiguous distinction between the Apollinarian doctrine and the Catholic doctrine defended by Cyril. Second, because the sect of the Apollinarists was extraordinarily hated at Constantinople, either on account of the absurd opinions attributed to them or because of the recent law enacted by Theodosius, at the urging of Nestorius, against all heresies. At the head of that law, to increase their disgrace, were written the names of the Arians, Macedonians, and Apollinarians. Their alleged crime was that, deceived by a guilty design, they believed lies instead of the truth’s fountain; and therefore they were forbidden to possess a church within any city (*Theodosian Code*, law 65, *On Heretics*). This had long before been prohibited by Theodosius the Great and Arcadius. Finally, the name of Apollinaris was habitually made odious by all devout people and by the most distinguished bishops, lest, since he possessed immense authority, he should—“as that man says”—draw the whole world over to his side.

II. Why did the name of Apollinaris become so odious, although he was otherwise a distinguished man who had suffered exile from the Arians for the faith, whom Epiphanius celebrates as exemplary in character, Jerome as highly renowned for his published books, and Vincent of Lérins as a teacher of the world?

I think that Apollinaris suffered, as Epiphanius relates in the passage cited, not so much from his own as from his disciples’ odium. He experienced what teachers often experience when the populace pours upon masters—who otherwise are not blameworthy—the hatred properly owed to their worse disciples.

Nevertheless, there had doubtless been great offense aroused against Apollinaris’s own position, and not without reason, since it entirely removed the true redemption of our race. For Christ healed what he assumed. If, therefore, he did not assume the mind, by which sin is chiefly committed, but only the body, which is subject to death, then it certainly cannot be said that he freed the human race from sin, which is the death of the soul, but only from corruption, which is the death of the body. And how small and meager a redemption would that be? For this reason Apollinaris could appear either—although no controversy had formerly arisen on this point—to have acted injuriously toward Christ by refusing to acknowledge him as the redeemer of souls, or to be guilty of Pelagian impiety by denying that souls needed redemption, as though they were pure from original guilt and sufficient by their own natural powers to attain salvation.

III. What, finally, were the distinctive inventions of the Apollinarists?

I find six principal ones among the ancient authors (Theodoret, book IV, *Heretical Fables*).

The first was συνουσίωσις [co-essential fusion], that is, the confusion of the natures, whose inventor was Polemius. He gave his name to the sect of the Polemians, or Synusiasts.

The second was κρᾶσις τῆς θεότητος καὶ τοῦ σώματος [the tempering and mixture of divinity and body], whose inventor was likewise Polemius. From this arose the heresy of the Eutychians. Saint Thomas correctly interprets συνουσίωσις, σύγχυσις, and κρᾶσις as the informing of the body by the soul.

The third was the conversion of the Word into flesh when he became human, and again of the flesh into the Word after the ascension. These were called the Word’s σμίκρωσις [diminution] and the flesh’s ἀποθέωσις [deification]. In reality, these two conversions are nothing other than the two states, as they express it, of the soul in the body: one in a mortal body, in which the soul is in some way subject to the body, and the other in an immortal body, in which it rules over the body in every respect.

The fourth was that the Word did not assume flesh from the Virgin but brought it from heaven. Thus the Virgin could not truly be called Θεοτόκος [God-bearer]; indeed, she could not even be called ἀνθρωποτόκος [human-bearer], except merely in appearance, since she had not truly given birth to a human being united to the Word but had only transmitted him, as water passes through a conduit. I think this fiction was devised by those Apollinarists who, finding themselves unable to withstand the enemies of the Mother of God or to answer their arguments, preferred, in their delirium, to say that the Virgin had become pregnant from heaven and had done nothing more than receive from there the body she was to give birth to.

The fifth was that the flesh brought from heaven was eternal and had been created together with the Word. Those who deliriously held this position must have defected from Apollinaris to Arius insofar as they said that the Word was created, and to Origen or at least the Origenists insofar as they said that the flesh had been created together with the Word. For the latter maintained that, apart from the true God, who alone is the Father, nothing incorporeal exists.

The sixth was that this flesh, although consubstantial with the Word, just as our flesh is consubstantial with us, was nevertheless ἑτεροούσιος [of a different essence] from our flesh. Those who followed this delirium openly turned toward the Docetists. For if Christ had neither a soul nor flesh ὁμοούσιον [of the same essence] with ours, he was not truly human but only appeared to be so.

The seventh was that the divinity of the Word was passible in itself. This too was an impiety by which the Apollinarists, departing from their teacher, fell toward the Arians, because they had not sufficiently understood the difference between soul and mind, although Apollinaris had made that distinction the foundation of his position. Once this distinction between mind and soul was removed, they supposed that the Word in Christ occupied not merely the place of the mind but also that of the soul, which experiences grief and undergoes the movements produced by the body’s affections. These are called παθὴ [passions] by the Greeks. Yet one should not suppose that men had become so insane as to believe that the divinity of the Word could in itself be scourged, fastened with nails, pierced by a lance, buried, and so forth. They therefore called the Word παθητὸν [passible], no doubt because he could suffer in the manner of a soul joined to a body, which is shaken and disturbed by the body’s movements because of their kinship and, as they said, their συνουσίωσις [co-essential fusion].

IV. What proves that these are not the inventions of Apollinaris himself but of his disciples?

Several solid arguments prove this.

First, Apollinaris himself greatly praised the letter of Athanasius to Epictetus, bishop of Corinth, in which all these positions were refuted. He wrote as follows (*Letter to Serapion*, in vol. V of the *Ancient Readings* of Henricus Canisius, p. 112):

> We have strongly approved the letter of my lord Athanasius sent to Corinth. We condemned the great madness of those who say that the flesh is consubstantial with God.

Next, he denies that these very enormities can justly be charged against him (*Letter to Dionysius*, ibid.):
