> It is clear that no one can charge us with those things which were said against certain men, from what we have always written: namely, that the Savior’s flesh is not from heaven, and that his flesh, insofar as it is flesh, is not of the same substance as God.

Finally, he expressly condemns these same positions, as well as the Arian doctrine from which they generally arise—namely, that the Son of God is a creature—not only in his own name but also in the name of his true disciples (*ibid.*, p. 116):

> Apollinarius and those who are with me hold this concerning the incarnation: the Word of God assumed from Mary flesh ὁμοούσιον [of the same essence] with our flesh, uniting it in union with the divinity from the beginning of conception in the Virgin. Thus he became human, since, according to the Apostle, a human being is flesh and Spirit. This is what it means for the Word to become flesh, to be united with flesh as a human spirit. He is called a human being of flesh like us; but the Lord is a human being above us. Therefore he is also heavenly, on account of his own heavenly Spirit, against which the prudence of the flesh was opposed. In this way sin was destroyed in Christ, and death, which arose from sin, was dissolved. We become participants in this work and are saved through faith; and although we are descended from an earthly father, we become like the heavenly one. Therefore let him be anathema who does not say that the flesh is from Mary; who says that this flesh is of an uncreated nature and ὁμοούσιον [of the same essence] with God; who says that the divinity is passible; or who says that the passions of the soul arise from the divinity itself.

The reader should finally be reminded that although the Pelagians may perhaps have been joined to the Apollinarists by considerable necessity, they nevertheless anathematized them in their own statements of faith. See Theodoret in the Creed; Rufinus, chapter 45 of the *Faith*; Pelagius, *Statement*, no. 7; Caelestius, in the same place; and Julianus, *Statement*, part III, no. 6. We have set out the reasons in the notes to the passages cited; it will be worthwhile to consult them.

§ III. On Eunomius

Eunomius’s error concerning the Trinity of the divine persons is extremely well known and familiar to everyone; the other error, concerning the incarnation of the Word, is not equally so. For which of the ancients has not reported that Eunomius held the same views as Arius concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit? But I do not remember reading anyone who, in the fifth century, wrote that Eunomius agreed with the Arians in making the Word occupy the place of a soul in Christ, except Mercator, Theodoret, and Nestorius. Those three, while always joining Eunomius to the Arians because of their shared error, also teach that nothing can be brought forward concerning his error that would not already have been dealt with in the discussion of Arius. We shall therefore dispatch the matter of this man easily, once a few points have been observed.

First, it should be observed that Mercator added Macedonius as a companion of Eunomius, a connection reported either by none or by very few of the ancients. Yet it is not surprising that one heretic should agree with another, as though by a conclusion, when they agreed concerning the principle. Both admitted that the Son of God is a created mind, and therefore suited to put on flesh in the manner of a soul. From this principle the Arians said—according to Epiphanius (*Heresy* 69, no. 52)—that the Son had put on flesh because he was inferior to the Father. Yet that holy man did not understand the statement in precisely the same way as its authors. They were offering a reason why the Son, but not the Father, could put on flesh. Epiphanius understood them as asserting that the Son had in fact put on flesh precisely because he was inferior to the Father, as though the necessity, rather than merely the possibility, of assuming flesh arose from the Son’s inferiority. Hence he argues from the example of the Holy Spirit and the angels, whom the Arians admitted to be inferior to the Father but nevertheless did not say had assumed flesh. But this may be said incidentally concerning Epiphanius’s passage.

It should next be observed that the disciples of Eunomius departed so far from their teacher that, if the philosopher Nemesius is to be trusted, they said that the divine Word had been united with the body not in substance but through the powers of each. They did not say that the substances were united or tempered with one another, but that the powers of the body were mixed with the divine powers (*On the Nature of the Human Being*, chap. 3, toward the end). [Col. 1123B]

I confess that I do not understand the cause which produced so great a delirium. Nevertheless, I seem to see here the origin of Monothelitism in Eutychianism: what the Eutychians said concerning substances, the Monothelites said concerning powers alone. Hence I have always suspected that the question concerning one will and one operation in Christ also concerned the mind, though it received its name from the operation of the will because that operation was more important when Christ’s merit and obedience were under discussion. But this entire matter belongs elsewhere.

Third, it should be observed that in the East Eunomians were punished by the gravest laws enacted by Theodosius the Great, beginning in the year 381, when Eunomius was still alive. They were neither permitted to have churches in the cities nor to hold assemblies nor to ordain priests. Moreover, books full of perfidy were to be burned before the eyes of their authors, in the fire of judgment, as the law says (*Theodosian Code*, *On Heretics*, laws 6, 8, 11, 12, 13). Later the Eunomians were frequently called, as though they were the standard-bearers of heretics, the first among them.

Fourth, it should be observed that Mercator, being highly skilled in law, had law 13 of the *Theodosian Code*, *On Heretics*, in view when he joined Arius, Apollinaris, Eunomius, and Macedonius as companions in error. For the emperor himself wrote as follows:

> “Eunomians, Macedonians, Arians, and likewise Apollinarians are notorious names among the offices of the sacred religion,” and so forth.

As I considered why the emperor had joined these four names together, a highly plausible reason occurred to me: namely, that they agreed in some one heresy, but not in any other than the claim that the Word with his flesh was not merely one person but also one nature. If this is indeed the case—and it is almost certainly so—let the students of law determine whether this law may not receive light from Mercator and reveal more clearly than jurists have hitherto believed either its character or its occasion.

[Col. 1123D]

Fifth, it should be observed that by law 63, *On Heretics*, of the *Theodosian Code*, which Theodosius the Younger issued to Florentius, prefect of the praetorium, in 428 at the urging of Nestorius against all heresies, the Eunomians were forbidden every opportunity to assemble and pray on Roman soil. Other penalties were also imposed, penalties which they shared with the Manichaeans and other plagues of the world and which carried no less disgrace than inconvenience.

In this law it is worth noting that the Eunomians are separated from the Arians, Macedonians, and Apollinarians, who are treated more mildly, although previously they were usually joined with them. Instead, the Eunomians are counted with the Valentinians, Montanists or Priscillianists, Phrygians, Marcionists, Borborians, Messalians, Euchites or Enthusiasts, Donatists, Audians, Hydroparastatae, Ascodrogites, Photinians, Paulinians, Marcellians, and those who had reached the very depths of wickedness, the Manichaeans.

This was not because they taught worse things than the Arians, Macedonians, and Apollinarians, whether concerning the Trinity or the incarnation, but because they had grown more powerful in the city and had resisted more stubbornly the bishops of the imperial city—Gregory, Nectarius, John, and Atticus. Nestorius, the author of the law, sought either to celebrate their virtues not so much by praise as by imitation and by following in their footsteps, or at least wished to appear to do so.

Finally, it should be observed that the statement of Vincent of Lérins (*Commonitorium*, chap. 16) is entirely true and is confirmed by this law: in order to open a path for his own heresy, Nestorius attacked the blasphemies of all the heresies. Yet the exceedingly crafty man did this in such a way that he attacked most vehemently those heresies whose odium either he himself or his opponents would have used to burden his adversaries or him; toward others he acted more mildly and even more leniently. Thus he arranged for the Arians, Macedonians, and Apollinarians to be mentioned at the beginning of the law, and for the Photinians, Paulinians, and Marcellians at the end. He was going to charge Catholics with association with the former; he was attempting to ward off the association with the latter that had been charged against him, and to do so with the considerable prejudice already established by the law.

# CHAPTER IV. Nestorius Compared with the Earlier Heretics and with All the Others Whose Association Was Charged Against Him by the First Defenders of the Faith

[Col. 1124B]

Thus far we have heard Nestorius as he himself explained, in his own words, the heresy to which he gave his name. We have also examined the arguments by which his defenders supported him. We have even dealt with the question of the three heretics into whose company he attempted, maliciously, to draw the Catholics. Now he should be compared with those earlier men, especially the heretics, from whom he was said to have revived the error he had received and to have bestowed upon it his own name.

Eusebius, who at one time governed the Church of Dorylaeum, while he was still a layman serving among the legal scholars of the imperial city, was the first of all to charge Nestorius with agreement with Paul of Samosata. Mercator further charged him with the heresy of Ebion, Marcellus the Galatian, Photinus, and Bonosus; Proclus charged him with Judaism and also with the ἀθεότης [godlessness] of the pagans; Cassian charged him with association with Leporius and the Pelagians; and finally Cyril charged him with the συμφωνία [agreement] of Diodore of Tarsus and Theodore of Mopsuestia. Each of these must now be considered, following the chronological order in which they arose, although considerable material concerning the Pelagians and Leporius was written earlier in the seventh dissertation on the first part.

§ I. On the Pagans, the Jews, and Manichaeus, whose association and criminal agreement were charged against Nestorius by Proclus, Cyril, the Emperor Theodosius, and others

No one, as we mentioned earlier, was ever counted under the Christian name who did not acknowledge some union of the divine and human nature in Christ. Therefore those who posited no union at all were counted among the pagans and Jews. This applied not only to them but also to those who defended a merely σχετικὴ [relational] union while rejecting a hypostatic one. For this is, according to the Apostle (1 John 4:3), to “dissolve Jesus,” and thus to profess oneself an Antichrist—an identifying and common mark of pagans and Jews.

Hence paganism, in which divine worship is offered to human beings, and Judaism, in which the Messiah is believed to be merely human, were charged by the Fathers against Nestorius. It likewise happened that, after a law had been enacted, the emperor later forbade Nestorius’s followers to abuse the name of Christians.

Cyril therefore made Nestorius guilty of pagan impiety and ἀνθρωπολατρεία [the worship of a human being], because Nestorius simultaneously confessed that Christ was to be worshiped by angels and human beings at God’s command, yet maintained that he could be called God of all only in the same sense in which Moses was the god of Pharaoh. From this it necessarily followed that he asserted that a mere human being was to be worshiped—a position that is sheer paganism, since the honorary divinity attributed to Moses did not remove him from the human order.

[Col. 1125A]

Proclus made the same accusation, and Nestorius bore it so impatiently that he charged Cyril with νεκρολατρεία [the worship of a dead man] in sermon 7 and Proclus with agreement with the pagans in sermon 4. His reason was that Cyril had asserted that God was dead in his third letter, while Proclus had said in his panegyric oration that the Virgin was the Mother of God. The pagans, moreover, worshiped the dead with divine worship and assigned mothers to their gods.

So much for paganism. As for Judaism, Proclus deservedly cast Nestorius under the odium of that name when, in his homily on the Virgin Θεοτόκος [God-bearer] (no. 18), he addressed him in the following words without naming him:

> Who, then, redeemed us? Not a mere human being, O JEW; for human nature was enslaved to sin, and so forth.

Nestorius perceived the allusion. Wishing to remove such an odious disgrace from himself, he uttered a statement by which he appeared to cast the charge back upon its author:

> Do not boast, JEW, for you did not crucify God.

Thus, by means of unspoken names, they attacked one another.

The Jews held three opinions concerning Christ that were contrary to the truth. First, that he was Joseph’s son by Mary his wife: “Is this not the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary?” (Matthew 13:55). Second, that he was an ordinary man from the crowd; hence they rebuked him as though he had spoken impiously of God as his own Father: “Though you are a man, you make yourself God” (John 10:33). Finally, that he performed miracles by magical art: “He casts out demons by the prince of demons” (Matthew 9:34).

Nestorius indeed confessed that Christ was born from the Virgin, and he also confessed that he performed wondrous works by divine power, although that power was not proper to him. Yet in reality he asserted that Christ was substantially a naked human being, and in this he certainly agreed with the Jews. He was worse than they, however, because, while acknowledging a redeemer, he nevertheless deprived him of the sole power of redemption—which is the true incarnation of God—as Proclus subtly indicated, by taking divinity away from him.

Add to this that he corrupted, like the Jews, the two testimonies of Isaiah which more clearly establish Christ’s true divinity: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7:14); and, “A child is born to us,” and so forth (Isaiah 9:6). He did so in the anathemas directed against the Cyrillians in the first passage and in sermon 11 in the second. In the former he explains what power belongs to the word “Emmanuel”; in the latter, how the child given to us is God. In both passages he introduces a mere ἐνοίκησις [indwelling] in place of a true ἕνωσις [union].

Anathema I:

> If anyone says that he who is Emmanuel is truly God, and not rather God with us—that is, that he inhabited the nature that is ours, by having been united to the mass of our nature which he assumed from the Virgin Mary—and if anyone calls her the mother of God the Word, rather than the mother of him who is Emmanuel, let him be anathema, and so forth.

In sermon 11 (nos. 2–3), on the words of Isaiah, “A child is given to us,” and so forth, he says:

> The infant is God, sovereign over himself. Far be it from you, Arius, to say that the Word of God is under God’s power. We therefore recognize the humanity of the infant and the divinity; we preserve the unity of sonship in the nature of divinity and humanity. I say this so that you may know how an exceedingly exalted and supreme conjunction of divinity existed even in the infant himself, when the Lord’s flesh was seen; for he himself was both an infant and the Lord of that infant. You praised the statement, but do not praise it without careful attention. For I said that the infant and the inhabitant of the infant were the same.

From this it is clear why the heresy of Nestorius was called Jewish impiety; why that wicked presbyter Anastasius, the enemy of the Θεοτόκος [God-bearer], was called an advocate of Jewish impiety; why Nestorius, steeped in Jewish opinions, was also called by Anastasius of Sinai a Chaldaean Assyrian pig (*The Guide of the Way*, chap. 14); and why Theodosius the Younger wished the participants in this monstrous and impious superstition to be called Simonian, so that, because they had imitated the crime of Simon in abandoning God, they might rightly seem to have inherited his name (*Law* 66, *On Heretics*).

[Col. 1126A]

Indeed, the more each of the ancient heretics was devoted to the rites of Jewish superstition, the more hostile he was toward the divinity of Christ. This will become clear from examples of the heretics who followed.

Meanwhile, one should consider how great, formerly and even in our own age, have been the audacity, ignorance, and even wickedness of certain men who, despite Nestorius’s having been charged with pagan and Jewish impiety by such eminent men, nevertheless boast that he was entirely free from guilt. Thus they either accuse Cyril, Proclus, and the other Fathers of ignorance—an act of incredible audacity—or, after long and careful study of Nestorius’s works, they were unable to perceive his mind—an instance of ignorance and intellectual dullness—or, because of a perverse disposition, they wished to contradict the truth once they had recognized it—an astonishing wickedness.

Let us join him to the Manichaeans; for he is scarcely different from them. For what remains of the Christian name in one who asserts that Christ—whose name he bears—is some empty mockery, which he wished to appear to human eyes, deceiving them, [Col. 1126B] to be a man, although he was no man? Mercator called Nestorius under suspicion of Manichaean madness in these words (Against the Contradictions of Nestorius’s Anathemas):

> Moreover, this man adds, for his own display, that the Word of God assumed a mass of flesh, that is, as he says, “so that in appearance he might be found as a man, but in display as God”; and his Greek wording declares these things to be vain and impious: “If anyone should say that the very Word of God was changed into flesh, which he assumed in the outward representation of his divinity, so that in appearance he might be found as a man, let him be anathema.”

That is: “If anyone should say that the very Word of God was changed into flesh, which he assumed for the display of his divinity, so that in appearance he might be found as a man, let him be anathema.”

All Greeks recognize a difference between σχηματισμός (*schēmatismos*) and σχῆμα (*schēma*). By σχηματισμός the Greeks understand that in which there is not truth but rather a simulation or fiction assumed to deceive the senses; σχῆμα, however, signifies the reality of the outward form itself. We might render the two terms “display” and “appearance”: display is deceptive, whereas appearance is the manifestation of the whole nature. What, then, does this new and empty teacher mean? We should like to know by what σχηματισμός this new god of his caused himself to be seen—for he must be called his god, not the God of Christians. And in what σχῆμα was he found to be like a man? Do you see that this man, whether through the most wicked will or through foolish ignorance, has slipped into the opinion of the Manichaeans, who do not wish God to be a true man but believe Christ, the Son of God, to be fantastic—that is, merely apparent?

Yet although Mercator’s ἀκρίβεια (*akribeia*, precision) may perhaps not be approved by all students of purer Greek, this suspicion, just as it should not be dismissed because of the authority of such a man, so likewise need not necessarily be imitated because of its excessive subtlety.

§ II. Concerning Ebion, whose association with Nestorius was alleged by Marius Mercator

The ancients did not all write the same things about Ebion; rather, they transmitted certain contradictory accounts, which no one can reconcile without difficulty. Mercator writes as follows (Dissertation on the Twelve Anathemas of Nestorius):

> The entire evil of Paul’s impiety was drawn from Ebion the Stoic philosopher. He arose while the Apostle John was still living in Asia, and dared to proclaim that Christ was an ordinary man, born from Joseph and Mary; that he had surpassed the whole human race by the merit of his life; and that for this reason he had been adopted as the Son of God. He claimed to have followed the authority of the evangelists Matthew, Mark, and Luke. At that time the Apostle John composed his Gospel against him, in which he stated at the outset that “in the beginning was the Word,” that “the Word was with the Father,” and that “the Word was God” (John 1:1). After this preface, descending to what followed in order to show that the man whom those three evangelists had written about was also God, he said: “What was made in him was life.” And shortly afterward: “And the Word was made flesh.”  
> 
> Following this philosopher Ebion was Marcellus the Galatian. Photinus also followed him, as did, in the final period, Bonosus of Sardica, who was condemned in advance by Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome.

Epiphanius says the following (Against the Heresies 30.18):

> The Ebionites, so far as Christ is concerned, consider him to be a prophet of truth, and hold that Christ became the Son of God through a certain progression of virtue and conjunction with God, insofar as he was raised to sublime and heavenly things. They thought that the prophets were prophets not of truth but of understanding. Accordingly, they held Jesus to be merely a prophet and a man, yet also the Son of God, although he was a mere man, as we have already said, who had deserved to be called the Son of God because of his outstanding virtue.

He later indicates that the assertion that Christ was born from the mingling of his parents belonged not to the disciples but to Ebion himself, their teacher. For after he had extensively proved, by adducing the testimony of Isaiah, Jeremiah, the angel, and Mary, that Christ was not begotten from human seed but from the heavenly Father, he continues in these words:

> Truly, the unhappiness of those who depart from the truth is incredible. Abandoning the testimonies of the prophets and angels, they preferred to cling to the heretic Ebion, who, embracing Jewish observances according to the inclination of his own mind, nevertheless separated himself from the Jews.

[Col. 1127B] Theodoret writes (Ecclesiastical Fables II.1):

> The leader of this group was Ebion—for the Hebrews call a beggar “ebion.” He taught that there is one unbegotten being, as we do, and that this being was the creator of the world. But he said that the Lord Jesus Christ was born from Joseph and Mary and was a man, although he surpassed all others in virtue and innocence and ordered his life according to the Mosaic Law. These people alone accept the Gospel according to the Hebrews, while they call the Apostle an apostate. Symmachus was one of them; he translated the Old Testament from Hebrew into Greek.  
> 
> There was another class bearing the same name. They too are called Ebionites, and in all other respects agree with the former group; but they say that the Savior and Lord was born from a virgin. They use only the Gospel according to Matthew; they observe the Sabbath according to the Jewish Law, and they sanctify the Lord’s Day in our manner.

The author of *The Predestined* writes (I.10):

> The Ebionites assert that the Lord Jesus Christ was merely a man, [Col. 1127C] and they establish that the commandments of the Law are to be observed in the Jewish manner. The evangelist Luke encountered them in the Church at Antioch and condemned them, teaching that the angel had said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

I omit the testimonies of Philaster and Augustine because they contain virtually nothing beyond what is found in Epiphanius’s summary, which both of them generally reproduce as a single account.

From these writers we learn the whole history of Ebion. He was a disciple of Cerinthus and lived in Asia during the time of the evangelist John.

Through an extraordinary metamorphosis he was first a pagan, then a Jew; next, from a Jew a Christian; soon afterward, from a Christian a Stoic philosopher; finally, from a philosopher a heretic, and even the leader of a heresy bearing his own name.

He taught four things about Christ: that he was born from the marriage of Joseph and Mary; that he was merely a man, but exceptionally holy; that, having earned divine favor by the integrity of his conduct, a certain divine power descended upon him, as it commonly did upon the prophets; and that this power was not given according to an ordinary measure but with almost the entire fullness of divine effectiveness, so that he became the Son of God through a unique adoption.

This perversion of doctrine was no less serious than his insistence that Jewish rites should be retained and mixed with Christian practices. Indeed, still more things are attributed to him, plainly impious and detestable, but Epiphanius suspects that these were peculiar to the Ebionites (in the place cited).

Nestorius disagreed with Ebion in almost innumerable places concerning the first head of his impiety, namely, the claim that Christ was born from the mingling of parents. He likewise disagreed concerning the third, since he asserts that the flesh assumed by the Word was in the Virgin’s womb and existed from the very conception. In reality, however, he agreed with him on the remaining two points, as has been demonstrated, although he tried to conceal his mind with all the power of his considerable skill in deception. Therefore, when he first began to disclose his heresy, Mercator rightly charged him with agreement with Ebion in that part of the question which was then being debated—namely, whether Christ was merely a man.

Before the discussion moves elsewhere, I think it should be noted that Mercator was the first—or rather, that no other ancient writer was the first—to write two things about Ebion: namely, that he was devoted to Stoic philosophy and that he abused the authority of the three evangelists, Matthew, Mark, and Luke, to prove his heresy. We have discussed the former in the notes on Mercator’s passage.

The latter requires somewhat more careful treatment, for Mercator has Theodoret contradicting him. Theodoret writes that Ebion accepted only the Gospel κατὰ Ἑβραίους (*kata Hebraious*, “according to the Hebrews”). But what Gospel was that? Was it the one mentioned by Theodoret himself when he wrote about the Jews or Nazarenes, namely, the Gospel κατὰ Πέτρον (*kata Petron*, “according to Peter”), which they used and in which they honored Christ as a righteous man? Or was it the one Epiphanius calls κατὰ Ματθαῖον (*kata Matthaion*, “according to Matthew”), which was written first in the Hebrew language? [Col. 1128B] Or was it one that some call κατὰ Μάρκον (*kata Markon*, “according to Mark”), because, as Jerome reports, Mark is believed to have written down what Peter related orally? Or rather was it the one Jerome discusses (Commentary on Matthew II, on chapter 12):

> In the Gospel used by the Nazarenes and Ebionites, which we recently translated into Greek from the Hebrew language, and which most people call the authentic Gospel of Matthew?

This last opinion is by far the more probable.

Someone may perhaps object that the three authors just mentioned contradict Mercator on the very point on which they agree: that there was one Gospel of the Nazarenes accepted by the Ebionites. For Mercator reports that Ebion used the authority of three evangelists. The dispute can easily be settled, however, if either Mercator is understood to mean Ebion, while the others mean the Ebionites, or if Ebion himself is said to have followed the authority of the three evangelists—not simply, as though he revered their authority, but, as the expression goes, *ad hominem*, because he was employing an authority accepted by his opponents.

But why did Theodoret say that the Gospel accepted by the Nazarenes was κατὰ Πέτρον, if it did not differ from that fifth Gospel mentioned by Jerome, which he says some believed to be Matthew’s authentic Gospel? I think this question can scarcely be resolved unless we say either that a textual error entered Theodoret’s text—which is not impossible—or that Theodoret suffered a lapse of memory, which is more likely. Jerome’s authority is preferable on this point, since he read the Caesarean codex, in which the true title was found, and translated it into Latin.

§ III. Concerning Paul of Samosata, whose heresy was alleged against Nestorius by Eusebius and Mercator

The first person, so far as I know, to charge Nestorius with the heresy of Paul of Samosata was that Eusebius about whom we wrote earlier. For when he had publicly rebuked a bishop in the Church for teaching impious doctrines, and when the bishop’s faction was denouncing him as a slanderer, he publicly presented a formal protest in which, by comparing the opinions of Paul and Nestorius, he showed that both held the same views.

Mercator either immediately followed Eusebius’s example or accompanied it, spreading among the public a letter concerning the difference between the heresy of Nestorius and the doctrines of Samosata. He did not do this in order to establish a distinction concerning the question at issue, but rather to expose the agreement between them by revealing the artifices of the heretic who wished to remain concealed.

I believe that Socrates took up Nestorius’s cause against these two defenders of the faith—whom he otherwise detested—because envy, as often happens, spurred him to diminish the glory of a man who had come from the public forum or the imperial court to the honor of defending the faith, an honor gathered by his equals in public life.

I do not remember reading in Cyril any part of this accusation—not because it was unknown to such a great man or seemed false to him, but because he considered it superfluous against a man whom the odium directed against Photinus, who held the same views as Paul, already overwhelmed. It is remarkable, moreover, that neither Cassian nor the Fathers at Ephesus attributed this fault—whatever it may be—to Nestorius.

[Col. 1129A] Nestorius attempted to repel the accusation, but only in his final period, when, after receiving the letters of Pope Celestine, in which Samosata was mentioned, he delivered his twelfth sermon. Earlier, although Mercator and Eusebius accused him, he seems, in his arrogance, to have looked down upon the laymen who were accusing him, as people meddling in matters outside their sphere and forgetful of their own status.

In Sermon 12 he repelled the charge with all his strength and also tried to throw it back upon his accusers. Mercator, however, showed that his defense was full of vanity, ignorance, and suspicion (in the dissertation on the twelfth anathema of Nestorius), and he did so learnedly. Yet in doing so he introduced points which, either because of their novelty or for some similar reason, create difficulties. Before these are examined, Paul of Samosata’s doctrine must be set forth as it is reported by the ancients; indeed, something must also be said about the life and character of the man whom even Theodore of Mopsuestia, because of his impiety, calls an angel of the devil—one who, plainly, begrudged Christ his divinity (On the Incarnation XIII, in Facundus III.2).

[Col. 1129B] The ancient writers transmitted the following facts about Paul of Samosata, facts that clearly demonstrate that the spirit of heresy and wickedness has been the same in every age, even in the earliest period, when the Church had not yet been asserted in freedom but, while the pagans ruled, groaned beneath the blows of executioners (from the letter of the Fathers of the Second Synod, in Labbe’s Councils I).

From a man of the lowest station he became bishop of Antioch, and he ascended the third throne of the Church by the same devices by which heretics ordinarily rise: the influence of a powerful woman, an appearance of piety, a reputation for learning, facility of speech, and the favor of a factious multitude.

For, as the Fathers of the Second Synod of Antioch say:

> Although before becoming bishop he was poor and a beggar, and had received no resources at all either left to him by his parents or acquired by the exercise of any trade, afterward he attained unbelievable wealth through crimes and sacrilege and by extorting from his brethren, etc., thinking that piety was a source of profit, etc. (ibid.).

[Col. 1129C] He was no less unscrupulous in pursuing glory than in scraping together money. In ecclesiastical assemblies he assiduously pursued a certain ambitious vanity, seeking nothing but empty glory and aspiring to pomp; by such arts he drew the minds of the inexperienced into admiration of himself. He went so far as to arrange, through his supporters, for those who did not applaud him when he spoke to be subjected to insults. These are the words of the same Fathers (ibid.).

They continue by describing the arrogance of a man who despised everyone else:

> During sermons delivered to the people, he was accustomed to criticize and insolently attack teachers who had long since died. Meanwhile, he himself was μεγαλοῤῥημονῶν καθάπερ οὐκ ἐπίσκοπος, ἀλλὰ σοφιστὴς καὶ γόης—speaking grandiloquently as though he were not a bishop but a sophist and a charlatan. He subjected the bishops of neighboring regions, as well as the presbyters who flattered him, to himself, and they too praised him in their sermons as though he were an angel fallen from heaven.

They express his openly shameful way of life in these words:

> He even took with him wherever he went two women in the bloom of youth and conspicuous for their beauty; he lived amid luxury, was fond of banquets, and also permitted presbyters and deacons to keep such “sisters” and συνείσακτοι (*syneisaktoi*, “female companions brought into the household”), not without danger of scandal and suspicion. Although good men privately grieved, sighed, and groaned, they did not dare to accuse him because of the power of his supporters (ibid.).

He attached himself to Queen Zenobia, a woman otherwise praised by the ancients, but Jewish and imperious. In order to serve her, he introduced Jewish impiety into Christian doctrine and denied the divinity of Christ, indeed even the Trinity of persons, babbling something incoherent about the Word and the Holy Spirit as ἀνυπόστατον (*anypostaton*, “without subsistence”) (Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History II.8; Athanasius, Letter to the Solitaries; Chrysostom, Homily 8 on John).

Two synods were held against Paul at Antioch. The first took place in the year of Christ 265, when several bishops assembled from every direction, one of whom was Gregory Thaumaturgus. They carefully investigated Paul and his faith. But he cunningly and deceptively paraded a Catholic doctrine, concealing by ambiguous words what he really thought in his mind. Thus he sent the bishops, deceived—or rather congratulating themselves on having discovered in him the integrity of Catholic faith—back to their own churches (Eusebius VII.27).

A second synod was convened five years later, when Paul’s impiety burst into the open. The ancient writers do not agree on how many Fathers assembled. Eusebius writes that almost innumerable bishops gathered (VII.30); a letter of Basil and the monks to the emperors against Nestorius fixes the number at 180, although Athanasius reduces it to seventy in his book on the synods.

Once again the slippery heretic attempted to deceive the Fathers by his usual arts, but without success. For Malchion—a man raised from the sophistic schools to the rank of presbyter, learned and exceptionally skilled in disputation—convicted him; and the synod deposed him from his see. The emperor Aurelian himself, although a pagan, ordered him, once deposed, to be expelled from the city and at the same time commanded that the church be handed over to someone who was in communion with the bishop of Italy and of Rome (Peter the Deacon, *On the Incarnation*, in Fulgentius).

The Fathers sent a synodical letter to Dionysius, bishop of Rome, and to Maximus of Alexandria, as well as to the other bishops throughout the world. A large portion of it is preserved in Eusebius (in the place cited shortly above), from which we have extracted nearly everything said thus far.

So much for Paul’s person. We now turn to his heresy, whose principal points Augustine makes three (Heresy 44): first, that Christ had not always existed; second, that he received his beginning from birth of the Virgin; and finally, that he was nothing more than a man. The author of *The Predestined* has the same points in exactly the same words; Nestorius has them as well.

Epiphanius adds a fourth point (Heresy 65): namely, that the Word of God who descended upon Jesus was something prolatitious and ἀνυπόστατον, “without subsistence.” Philaster agrees with Epiphanius (Sermon 12), as does Mercator, both in his letter concerning the difference between Nestorius’s and Paul’s doctrines and in his dissertation on Nestorius’s twelfth anathema, except that Mercator adds that Paul said Christ was begotten from both parents. In this statement he disagrees with everyone else, including Nestorius, who himself departs from the others; for by comparing Paul with Photinus, Nestorius appears to attribute the heresy of the prolatitious Word to Photinus alone.

Athanasius reports the error of Samosata in these words (On the Saving Advent):

> Paul of Samosata confesses God from the Virgin, God brought forth into the light at Nazareth, and says that from this point he received the beginning of his existence and his reign. Nevertheless, he acknowledges in him the effective Word and wisdom from heaven, and thinks that by predestination he existed before the ages but first began to exist at Nazareth, so that, as he says, the Father alone is the supreme God.

The consistency of everyone’s opinion causes me all the greater astonishment because it seems more plainly to conflict with the letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Paul himself and with the words of Paul that Dionysius cites. From these it appears that Paul thought that the Holy Spirit formed in Mary’s womb a man whom it intended as a temple to be inhabited by the Word in due time; that this man advanced by living a diligent life and for that reason pleased the Word more than other men; and that he attracted the Word to dwell within him.

Thus the Word of God dwelt in him, but in such a way that the one and only Christ had two hypostases, two persons, and two Sons of God: one by nature, who existed before the ages, and one καθ’ ὁμωνυμίαν (*kath’ homonymian*, “by homonymy”), Christ and son of David, who did not exist before the ages but came into existence in time and received the name “Son” according to God’s good pleasure—just as a city receives the name of its lord and a house the name of the person who built it. Thus Christ was another man besides God the Word, differing from the substance and dignity of the other Christ; and there was one Christ who inhabited and performed works of divine justice (in Dionysius’s letter to Paul).

To remove, if possible, the contradiction that seems to exist in the statements of the writers cited thus far, several important questions arising from them must be resolved. Their explanation contains nearly everything that has been transmitted by the ancients and must be discussed by us concerning Samosata:

1. What sort of Word of God did Paul in reality acknowledge? Was it the Word that Paul himself describes as ἀνυπόστατον, or the Word that several others report as ἀνυπόστατον?

2. Did he say that Christ was born from both parents, as Mercator seems to write, or from the Virgin alone, as others say?

3. What do Athanasius’s words, cited shortly above, mean: “God brought forth into the light at Nazareth, and from this point received the beginning of his existence and his reign”?

4. Did Paul teach that the Word dwelt in the man from the very beginning of his formation, as Athanasius seems to indicate, or, as is commonly asserted, only after he had lived a holy life and earned so great a benefit through works of piety?

5. In what respect did Nestorius agree or disagree with Paul?

6. How accurately did Mercator write that the two heretics agreed in saying that the Word had not been the Son from eternity but only the Word—a statement that constitutes the very marrow of the Paulian heresy?

With regard to the first question, there is an old opinion, extending from remote times down to our own age, that Paul of Samosata abolished the Trinity of divine persons and called the Father alone “God,” while nevertheless attributing to him a coeternal Word, but merely a prolatitious and ἀνυπόστατον Word, similar to our own. The origin and the complete truth of so widespread an opinion are not clear.

When I investigated who among all writers first attributed this doctrine to Paul, I found no Latin writer earlier than Philaster and no Greek writer earlier than Epiphanius—at least none who explicitly revealed his meaning, although even these two do not speak with complete clarity.

Philaster writes (volume 4 of the *Library of the Fathers*, at the beginning):

> There was a certain Paul of Samosata in Syria after these men. He denied that the Word of God—that is, Christ, God’s substantive, personal, and eternal Son—was eternal with the Father. Rather, he called it prolatitious, as though it were a kind of air; nevertheless, he did not teach that one should believe in a living, eternal person of the Son together with the eternal Father.

[Col. 1131C] Epiphanius writes (Heresy 65):

> Paul’s opinion is that God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God. The Word of God and his Spirit perpetually exist in God, just as we see that a man’s own word exists in his heart. The Son of God has no subsistence of his own but subsists in God. In addition, the Word of God descended to earth and dwelt in Jesus, who was merely a man. Thus, he says, there is one God: neither is the Father truly Father, nor the Son Son, nor the Holy Spirit the Holy Spirit. Rather, the one God is the Father, and the Son of this Father is in him, as speech is in a man.

Mercator followed both of these writers (Letter on the Difference, etc., no. 1):

> Nestorius, he says, does not think about the Word of God as Paul does, for Paul defines it as not a substantive but a prolatitious and effective Word of God’s power.

And elsewhere (Dissertation on Nestorius’s Twelfth Anathema, no. 19):

> Paul understood the Word of God as προφορικὸν καὶ πρακτικόν, λόγον δὲ ἐνεργετικόν—that is, prolatitious and effective of power—but not substantive, which the Greeks call οὐσιῶδες.

The truth of the opinion is no less uncertain than its origin. For how can these things, transmitted by the ancients and accepted by later writers, cohere with Paul’s own words, in which he speaks of two hypostases in Christ, two persons, and even two sons—one by nature, who existed before the ages, and the other καθ’ ὁμωνυμίαν, who came into existence in time? If the Word and the man are two hypostases in Christ, a point which Paul proves at length in ten entire questions, how can the Word be ἀνυπόστατον? Or perhaps the Father’s hypostasis really was in Christ, but it was not called such—what Sabellius believed? Yet if the matter were so, how could Paul not have been a Patripassian like Sabellius, although none of the ancients reports this and several deny it? Or is the letter of Dionysius of Alexandria spurious—a possibility that may have occurred to someone who had despaired of solving the problem? But what then shall we do with Jerome, who says (On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 69) that, only a few days before his death, a notable letter of Dionysius was circulated against Paul of Samosata?

The solution to this extremely tangled question must be extracted from the very mysteries of Paul’s delirium. He imagined God as resembling the sun, in which three things should be considered: the shape, or disk itself, as it is called, and two energies, that of illuminating and that of heating. He said that the Father was like the shape and substance, the Word like the power of illuminating, and the Holy Spirit like the power of heating. But he maintained that the Word—and the same must be understood of the Holy Spirit—could be considered in two different states, according as it was either ἐνδιάθετον or προφορικόν. In the schools these are called “immanent” and “transient.”

As long as it remains in God, it has no hypostasis other than that of the one who understands it, if we believe Paul—just as our own word has no separate hypostasis when it is conceived inwardly. But when it is uttered externally and sent forth, it begins to have a hypostasis distinct from the one who utters it; nevertheless, it loses that hypostasis as soon as it returns to God from whom it proceeded, having fulfilled its task.

Paul therefore made the divine Word ἐνυπόστατον, “possessing subsistence,” when it had departed from God, and ἀνυπόστατον, “without subsistence,” when it remained in God: thus ἀνυπόστατον before the ages, but ἐνυπόστατον in time. He added that the Word then became a son when it was uttered and began to possess its own hypostasis, for the utterance itself was the son’s coming forth into the light. He further added that at that moment a god came into being—not ἀΐδιος, eternal, and subsisting by himself from eternity—for how could one become what one already was? Rather, he was a recent and new god, since he began at Nazareth.

He also held that the Word, having become the Son and already existing as God in its own right, descended into Jesus and performed in him works that aroused wonder. Yet when suffering, or at least death, was imminent, it abandoned him and flew back to the Father. For this reason, neither could the Word be said to have suffered nor could God be said to have died. He considered the clearest proof of this abandonment to be that, while expiring, Jesus cried out: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

Such is the fiction of a deranged mind. Nevertheless, from it everything transmitted by the ancients about Samosata can readily be understood.

First, then, he asserted that the Word was ἀνυπόστατον when it was uttered and ἐνυπόστατον when it was with God.

Second, he held that the same Word was eternal when it was merely the Word in God, but temporal when it emerged as the Son.

Third, he held that there was one true and eternal God, namely the Father, but in addition two other temporal gods, the Word and wisdom, when they were sent forth.

Fourth, he held that two Sons of God existed in Christ: one by nature, the other by adoption; and that the latter suffered, while the former did not.

From these points we can also understand in what respect he agreed with Sabellius concerning the Trinity and in what respect he opposed him. Both in reality abolished the Trinity, but Sabellius said that the Word and Wisdom were merely names of one God acting in different ways. Paul did not want the Word and Wisdom to be something ἐνδιάθετον, “immanent,” from eternity, something that could be sent forth in time and exist independently. Hence Sabellius said that the Father had become incarnate and even suffered; Paul denied this. Thus the former was called a Patripassian by all the ancients, while the latter was called so by none.

This occasion also permits us to observe another difference between Sabellius and Paul. The former acknowledged a union of natures καθ’ ὑπόστασιν, “according to hypostasis”; for how else could he say that the Father suffered when Christ suffered? The latter rejected such a union altogether, since his claim that Christ had two persons and two Sons of God was entirely incompatible with hypostatic union.

The second question can be resolved more easily and straightforwardly. For when Mercator says that Paul defined Christ as an ordinary man born, like other men, from both parents, this does indeed seem contrary to the words of Athanasius cited above—“Samosata confesses God from the Virgin”—and to Paul’s own words: “Jesus grew, born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary” (Question 5). In reality, however, there is no contradiction.

The controversy did not concern Christ’s mother—whether she gave birth as a virgin or from a man—but, in Athanasius, concerned the recent and new god of whom they spoke. In Paul’s fifth question, the issue was the two persons in Christ, which he labored throughout ten questions to prove; and in that context it mattered very little what sort of mother was being described—whether Mary alone, a virgin, or a woman who had conceived from a man. Athanasius seems to have spoken of her as he was accustomed to do; Paul, in accordance with the sense of his opponents; Mercator, as the facts stood.

Mercator is supported by the accepted rule that those heretics who followed Jewish rites more closely than others generally denied that Christ was born from a Virgin and twisted Isaiah’s prophetic prediction about this matter into meanings as foreign as those of the Jews.

It is not so easy to answer the third question, since Athanasius’s words under discussion contain the mystery of the Samosatene heresy, of which almost nothing is less commonly known.

He therefore thought about the Trinity in the following way—if this can be called thinking rather than delirium. There is one God who is simply God and eternal, yet he has his own λόγος (*logos*, “Word”) and his own σοφία ἐνδιάθετος (*sophia endiathetos*, “immanent wisdom”), both of which he would at some point send forth from his bosom to fulfill a command and, once the task was completed, summon back to himself. When those two had been sent—that is, when the λόγος had been uttered and the σοφία extended—as they departed from the one who sent them and thus began to exist independently and χωρίϛ (*chōris*, separately), they began to be certain hypostases and even gods in their own right, but πρόσκαιροι (*proskairoi*), temporary.

Thus, if we believe Samosata, both came to the Virgin: Wisdom as the fashioner of the temple, and the Word as its inhabitant. Consequently, God came into existence from Mary, and God was brought forth into the light at Nazareth, receiving from that point the beginning of his existence and his reign.

He nevertheless said that this god, although in reality temporary, was eternal by predestination. By this distinction he avoided the passages of Scripture that attribute eternity to the person of the Word. This is the interpretation of Athanasius’s words, which can be gathered partly from Epiphanius, partly from the letters of Dionysius, and partly from other ancient writers.

No one will be surprised that Samosata called the Holy Spirit by the name “Wisdom” if he has either read our notes on Rufinus’s book or remembers what Basil the Great and the author of the exposition of faith called ἡ κατὰ μέρος (*hē kata meros*, “the exposition in detail”), attributed to Gregory Thaumaturgus, report about the Sabellians.

Basil writes (Homily 27):

> They think that Wisdom is in God as human wisdom is in a man, by which he is wise; and they interpret the Word as similar to the word spoken by the mouth or conceived in the mind, without any hypostasis.

The author of the *Faith* writes:

> When the Sabellians confess the Word, they compare it with the inner word. They say that Wisdom is like the disposition formed in the soul of educated people; and for this reason they say that the Father and the Son are one person, since one man is not divided from that which exists together with him as Word and Wisdom.

The fourth question concerning Samosata is whether he believed that the man Jesus, as he put it, was not joined to the Word and made God καθ’ ὁμωνυμίαν, “by homonymy,” until he had reached mature age and had acquired such dignity for himself through the merit of his works and the reward of his labors.

In the first dissertation, in the earlier part, we produced witnesses who said that Samosata held this opinion. That view has long prevailed, and we have generally followed it in popular accounts—or rather, we have assumed it. Yet Athanasius appears to transmit the opposite view in the words cited while resolving the first question. For if Samosata confesses God from the Virgin, God brought forth into the light at Nazareth, and says that from this point he received the beginning of his existence and his reign, he unquestionably admits that the Word and the man were united when the angel Gabriel was first sent by God to the city of Nazareth and the Virgin there conceived from the Holy Spirit.

The conflict between these opinions will easily be removed if we listen to Theodore of Mopsuestia as he explains his teacher’s views; for it is credible that the disciple agreed with his teacher’s opinion. In Book VII *On the Incarnation*, after saying that the Word was joined to Jesus in the Virgin’s womb, and that from that point Jesus possessed a more developed use of reason, an admirable disposition toward virtue, and an inclination toward the pursuit of what was right, while the Word was continually present, impelling, guiding, and assisting him in the accomplishment of every honorable deed, he says:

> He attained perfect virtue with the greatest ease, whether he observed the Law before baptism or, after baptism, lived an ordinary life in a state of grace, providing us with its pattern and becoming for us in this way a kind of path toward it. Then, after the resurrection and ascension into heaven, he demonstrated by his own will that he was worthy of the union which he had previously assumed at his formation, according to the good pleasure of the Lord.

There were, therefore, according to Samosata, two distinguishable modes of the union of the Word with Jesus, of the Son of God with the Virgin’s son. One existed from the time of formation until the perfection of complete virtue; the other remained afterward, at least until the Passion. The former was like the Word lodging in Jesus; the latter was properly the Word’s indwelling. The former was a matter of gratuitous benefit, the latter of reward. Athanasius spoke of the benefit; the others, of the reward.

Now, the fifth question—on the point in which Nestorius agreed with Paul regarding the mystery of the Incarnation—is resolved by Mercator in the frequently cited letter. For he says (Nos. 4–5):

“In this respect Nestorius is joined to Paul of Samosata: that he separates the indweller and the dwelling-place according to their merits, dividing what belongs properly to each of them on account of the diversity of nature. This, indeed, they both share with Ebion, Photinus, and Marcellus of Galatia. But in this respect—that he confesses the substantial Word of God and asserts that He is God from eternity with the Father—he rightly differs from those men just mentioned and is joined to the orthodox faith.”

[Col. 1134C] Attend to these final words: “He asserts that He is God from eternity with the Father.” For they show how truly we have explained Paul’s fiction concerning a recent God—that is, one who began to exist when the Word was uttered or sent forth by the Father. Hence Mercator immediately mentions the “uttered” or “prolative” Word. Nestorius does not indeed think of the Word of God as Paul does: Paul defines the Word not as substantive, but as the effective, prolative Word of God’s power. Yet at the same time Mercator exposes another outrage of Nestorius, one shared with Paul. Nestorius nevertheless does not confess, concerning the substantive Word, that He is naturally the Son of God; rather, he says—cunningly, though not explicitly—that from eternity He is not the Son, but only the Word, who, remaining in the substance of the Father, is God consubstantial with Him, whom the Greeks call ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*). But he asserts that the one who was born from Mary is the Son, and ought to be called the Son. Thus he divides the eternal from the temporal, assigning to the former—God and God’s Word—the things belonging to majesty, and to the latter—the other one—the things belonging to human weakness. Yet, because of their indivisible [Col. 1134D] and inseparable connection, the latter was considered worthy to be designated the Son of God, since he possesses this status on account of his merits and by adoption, not by nature.

The principal and evident distinction between one heretic and the other, therefore, was that the former called the Word ἀνυπόστατον (*anhypostatos*, without hypostasis), whereas the latter called Him ἐνυπόστατον (*enhypostatos*, possessing hypostasis). He omitted speaking about the virginity of the mother and about other matters of this kind, as though they were incidental.

He also supplied the central point of their agreement, from which the remaining points could easily be seen as corollaries. For he said that Paul and Nestorius agreed in asserting that Christ is the Son of God, not by nature but by adoption; and that both separated the indweller and the dwelling-place according to their merits—that is, according to ἀξία (*axia*, worth or dignity). For this is the crux of the question: since, if there are two Sons of God in Christ, and if the dignity of the indwelling God differs from that of the man, two persons must be acknowledged in Christ, divine and human.

[Col. 1135A] From this, in turn, follow all the remaining parts of Paul’s doctrine, which are contained in the ten questions proposed to Dionysius. For if there are two hypostases in Christ, it follows that Christ is not by nature the God of the apostles, Question 1; that He is by nature a man like us, Question 2; that the hypostasis of the Word is not the same as that of the one who was crucified, Question 3; that Christ’s body is neither ζωοποιόν (*zōopoiōn*, life-giving) nor incorruptible, because life is substantially united to it, Question 4; that the son of Mary did not exist before the ages and with the unbegotten Father, Question 5; that, as a child fleeing with his mother into Egypt, he neither existed from eternity nor was present everywhere, Question 6; that the Word did not assume the form of a servant without a hypostasis, Question 7; that the one who is truly said to have been twelve years old cannot be called eternal, Question 8; that the great God was not the one who hungered and labored, Question 9; and that the one who truly said, “I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17), is not God at all, Question 10.

But in order that these matters may be seen still more distinctly, we must recall the five parts of Catholic doctrine [Col. 1135B] which we distinguished in Chapter 1. In the first of these—that the Word is consubstantial with the Father—Nestorius differed from Paul, and Mercator noted this.

As for the second, namely, that the Word assumed the whole of human nature, and not flesh alone lacking either a soul or a mind, both agreed with the Catholics. Regarding the third, that the assumption was accomplished in Mary’s own womb, both held the correct view. In the fourth—the claim that the Word joins human nature in an indissoluble bond—Nestorius diverged from Paul: Nestorius is reported to have thought in the Catholic manner, whereas Paul thought otherwise, namely, that the man was at some point abandoned by the Word. As for the fifth, concerning the mode of union καθ’ ὑπόστασιν (*kath’ hypostasin*, according to hypostasis), both departed from the truth, but Paul openly and Nestorius covertly. For Paul plainly said that there were two sons; Nestorius did everything possible to avoid appearing to admit two persons in Christ, and two sons and lords.

Now, concerning what Mercator has just said, we must examine the final point in the division: how accurately it was said that Nestorius did not confess that the consubstantial Word was naturally the Son of God, but that from eternity He was only the Word, etc.; and that the Son was the one who was born from Mary (Letter on the Distinction, no. 1). For Nestorius himself seems to contradict Mercator in explicit terms. “Before the incarnation,” he says, “God the Word was both Son and God with the Father; but in the last times He assumed the form of a servant.” Yet since He was already the Son beforehand, and is so called after the assumption, He cannot be called a divided son, lest we constitute two sons. Rather, because he is joined to the one who was Son from the beginning, he cannot, according to the dignity of sonship, undergo a division of sonship.

Mercator himself resolves the difficulty by the way he presents the matter. For in the letter he charges Nestorius with seeking evasions in his manner of speaking, and elsewhere with contradicting himself. There is also another delirium of impiety in his statement that the Fathers had neglected to declare that they believed in God the Word, the only-begotten Son; instead, he says, they declared that they believed in one Lord Jesus Christ, consubstantial with the Father, [Col. 1135D] God from true God, light from light, through whom all things were made—as though, for this man, God the Word were not the Son, as is made clearer in his preceding sermon.

What is this man’s vanity? What madness? What mockery is more appropriate to such an inconsistent discourse, no less foolish than impious? The Word of God is not, for him, the Son of God; Jesus is for him half God and half man, and yet the same Jesus cannot be the Word, the Son of God. At one moment He is consubstantial, born from God the Father, true God from true God, light from light; afterward He has none of these things naturally proper to Him, but only by another’s designation shares in divine dignity, like a man born in time.

Christian ears must surely be closed when it is said that the name “Son” does not signify that Word of the Father who is from Him and in Him. To this testimony, reader, pay close attention: “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” [Col. 1136A]—plainly because, since the one born of a woman is not God, the Word is not his Son, but someone else who could be born through a woman’s delivery (Dissertation on the Twelfth Anathema, nos. 9–10).

Mercator later demonstrates this same point much more clearly and again warns the reader not to allow himself to be deceived. This form of impiety is not contained here, in this chapter, but in other writings and treatises inserted and read in this same codex. Hence a Catholic who reads must be cautious about the variability and inconsistency—whether they arise from cunning, or from madness intended to attract the hearer, it is not easy to know. In any event, however, it is clear that he is inconsistent and contradicts himself. Who would not recognize that such a man must either be avoided as a cunning captor, or, as a senseless man who contradicts himself and is confused by his inconsistency, in no way followed? (Ibid., no. 22.)

Since Mercator so carefully warns the reader to pay attention, the reader may perhaps ask how important this accusation ultimately was. It was certainly of the greatest importance, since it contained the summary of the entire case: for one who denies that the Word was the Son of God before the incarnation, and thus asserts that the name “Son” designates both natures, first conflicts with Scripture, which proclaims the eternal Son whom the Father begot before the morning star. Next, he contradicts the Nicene faith, by which the Son is believed consubstantial with the Father and the Father is believed to be eternally Father. Then he displays not merely the appearance of Samosatene impiety, but its proper emblem. Further, if Christ became the Son of God in time, it is easy either for two sons in Christ to be admitted, or for the eternal generation of the Word to be rejected, or for the Word’s conversion into a man to be introduced, or for Christ to be made the adoptive Son of God. These are the outrages of Paul, Sabellius, Polemius, and the man of Mopsuestia.

Finally, if both natures are signified by the name “Son,” the force of almost all the arguments drawn from Scripture and the Council of Nicaea to prove that God was born, suffered, and died, etc., is evaded; and thus the foundation of the Catholic faith concerning hypostatic union [Col. 1136C] is undermined, etc.

But the reader may ask again why Nestorius wished to appear, in this question, to follow now one side and now the other.

Certainly, while refuting the Nestorian anathemas, Mercator sometimes shows that Nestorius introduces two sons in the second, third, fourth, and fifth anathemas, one eternal, existing by nature, and the other temporal, existing by adoption and, as he says, by καθ’ ὑπόστασιν (*kath’ hypostasin*) alone. At times he casts suspicion on him for association with the Samosatene, who raved about a prolative Word; at other times he also charges him with the offense of converting the Word into a man. These are not merely conclusions drawn by a man sharply forcing his adversary toward paradoxes, but assertions. For why was Nestorius so anxious and concerned to remove from himself the suspicion of Sabellius, Paul, and Photinus, if there were no plausible basis for it? Why did he devote a large part of his twelfth sermon to this argument, and do so carefully and laboriously, if he was not troubled by this accusation?

## § IV. On Marcellus of Galatia, whose agreement with Nestorius Mercator alleged

[Col. 1136D]

Mercator is, so far as I know, the only ancient writer who brought this charge against Nestorius, because Marcellus’s case appeared to him to be the same as that of Samosata and Photinus. Yet he did not press the charge vigorously, since this very matter was considered so perplexing by the others that accusing Nestorius of association with Marcellus might seem more a defense than an accusation.

Mercator, who counts Marcellus among the heretics, is supported by men of great name and authority: Hilary, in his book to Constantius; Basil, Letter 293, etc.; Chrysostom, Homily 2 on the Epistle to the Hebrews; Marius Victorinus, Book I Against Arius; Theodoret, Book II of the *Heretical Fables*, the penultimate chapter; and several others. Yet I would not wish to number Athanasius and Epiphanius among them (*Haeresis* 72). This is so, first, because a speech has been falsely attributed to Athanasius in which Marcellus is joined with Samosata, and because Hilary of Poitiers and Sulpicius Severus did not write with sufficient credibility about Marcellus’s condemnation by Athanasius; and secondly, because Epiphanius is uncertain on this matter and produces two confessions of Marcellus, one of which is entirely Catholic, while the other admits of various interpretations.

Marcellus is acquitted by Pope Julius, by the Council of Sardica in its synodical letter, and by Athanasius in his letter to the solitaries. Above all, he is acquitted by his endurance of every kind of bitter persecution from the Arians, and almost martyrdom, on behalf of the faith in the ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*). Therefore, when I weigh these testimonies, I can scarcely bring myself to think that Eusebius of Caesarea’s five books *Against Marcellus* do not have greater force for refuting the charge than for bringing it against that man who, since he was one of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers who condemned Arius, deserves pardon if he inadvertently allowed something to escape him, or unfortunately fell under suspicion of Sabellianism—as even Basil the Great unjustly did.

With matters standing thus, I would rather, with Epiphanius, mourn the wretched fate of this man, as also of Apollinaris, than pass judgment with others in a matter so difficult and obscure. In this I seem to be following the example of the great Athanasius, who, when Epiphanius asked him about Marcellus, is said to have remained silent and, with an indignant and faintly smiling nod, given an ambiguous sign of a mind angry either with his detractors or with human weakness.

However the matter may stand, Mercator attributes to Marcellus (*Dissertation on the Twelfth Anathema*) the claim that he followed the heresy of Ebion and Samosata; Nestorius (*Sermon 12*) says that Marcellus believed that the Word would at some point lay aside the human nature; Eusebius (*Five Books Against Marcellus*) says that Marcellus claimed Christ began from Mary; and Theodoret (*Book II of the Heretical Fables*, chapter 10) says that Marcellus claimed that a kind of extension of the Father’s divinity came into Christ and called this extension God the Word. If these reports are true, Nestorius agreed openly with Marcellus in the first point; in the third, somewhat obscurely; and in the remaining two he opposed him. Nor are any arguments needed to prove this beyond those already used to demonstrate Nestorius’s association with the other heretics.

Turn your mind, reader, to the ancient defenders of the Nicene ὁμοούσιον and wonder that so many fell under suspicion of Paulianism—either because, inflamed by hatred of Arianism, they did not maintain sufficient restraint in their speech, which is a weakness of the human mind, or because they were overwhelmed by the calumnies of the Arians, which reflects the injustice of the times in which the world was astonished to find itself Arian.

## § V. On Photinus, with whom Mercator first said that Nestorius agreed

Nestorius once complained publicly in the Church that he was being branded with the heresy of Photinus:

“When,” he says (*Sermon 4*), “some people reported this also to me, I often laughed with delight, because, they say, ‘The bishop thinks what belongs to Photinus,’ not knowing either what they are saying or what they are affirming. For what I say is found to be the overthrow of Photinus. Photinus’s teaching gives the Word His beginning from Mary’s childbirth, whereas I say that the Word, God, has always existed before the ages.”

In saying this, he had in mind Mercator’s letter (*On the Distinction*), in which he was publicly charged with this crime for the first time. For in that letter (nos. 4–5), Mercator had explained in what respect Photinus and Nestorius agreed and in what respect they differed:

“He is joined to Paul of Samosata in this respect: that he separates the indweller and the dwelling-place according to their merits, dividing what belongs properly to each on account of the diversity of nature. This, indeed, they both share with EBION, PHOTINUS, AND MARCELLUS OF GALATIA. But in this respect—that he confesses the substantial Word of God and asserts that He is God from eternity with the Father—he rightly differs from those men just mentioned and is joined to the orthodox faith.”

[Col. 1138A] As is clear, Mercator had divided his position into two parts, one concerning agreement and the other concerning disagreement. Nestorius used the second part in his deceitful defense, as is clear from the words quoted at the beginning. To the first part he responded as follows (*Sermon 4*, no. 10):

“Then you will be freed from their blasphemy, and you will easily and briefly state the mystery of religion in this way: God the Word is one, the one who was in the temple which the Spirit fashioned, and the temple is another, apart from the God who indwelt it. It belongs to the temple to be dissolved by death; but it belongs to the indweller of the temple to raise it up. This is not my statement, but the Lord’s voice; I read it: ‘Destroy this temple,’ He says, ‘and in three days I will raise it up’ (John 2:19). Let us therefore confess the dignity of the conjunction, but two natures and substances.”

Then (no. 11):

“Let us therefore flee the error of this confusion. Let us say that our Lord Christ is double according to nature, but one according to what He is as Son.”

Observe in passing that Nestorius plainly confessed two hypostases in Christ, united only by συναφεία (*synapheia*, conjunction). For he had undoubtedly said in Greek: τῆς συναφείας τοίνυν ὁμολογῶμεν τὴν ἑνότητα, τὰς δὲ φύσεις καὶ τὰς ὑποστάσεις διπλᾶς—“Let us therefore confess the unity of the conjunction, but the natures and the hypostases as two.” Mercator, however, in his customary manner, translated συναφεία as “conjunction” and ὑπόστασις as “substance.”

He attempted to dissolve the same accusation in his twelfth sermon, where he first demonstrates the agreement of Samosata and Photinus, then their difference, and finally their divergence from himself. He says (nos. 12, 15):

“Paul and Photinus do not know the divinity of the Son; they do not know the two natures of the Son; they do not know God and man. Yet they differ from one another in this: one of them—Paul—calls Christ merely a man; the other—Photinus—does speak of the Word, but does not confess that the Word is God. Rather, he says that this Word is sometimes called by the name of the Father and sometimes designated by the name of the Word. He does not introduce God the Word as having become man, for he does not know the divinity of the Son; he does not know that the divine substance assumed a man; he utterly fails to recognize the divinity of the Word existing before the ages.”

[Col. 1138C] Observe that Nestorius says three things about Photinus: first, that he wishes the Word to be signified by the name “Christ”; second, that he denies that this Word is God, saying instead that He is called at one time by the name of the Father and at another by the name of the Word; third, that he does not introduce God the Word as having become man. He infers the third point from the claim that Photinus knows neither the divinity of the true Son, nor that the divine hypostasis assumed a man, nor the divinity of the Word existing before the ages.

“Paul differs from me in saying that Christ is merely a man and that He has His beginning only from the time when He was born of the Virgin. But I resist you here for this reason: so that you may not dare to make the eternal divinity contemporary with the flesh” (no. 12).

Observe here also that Nestorius explicitly explains the point on which he differs from the Samosatene, but not the point on which he differs from Photinus. Whether he did this deceitfully or ἀτεχνίᾳ (*atechnia*, through ineptitude) is uncertain. Nevertheless, three grounds of disagreement can be understood from the preceding words—namely, those which he attributes to Photinus—and two can be gathered from what follows: that Photinus does not possess the divinity of the Word, and that he does not confess that the Word was the Son before the incarnation. Nestorius assumes that he himself taught the opposite of all these things openly in the Church, as though they were evident to everyone. How accurately he makes this assumption must now be examined, especially because the matter concerns the full extent of Nestorian wickedness and Mercator’s good faith in making the accusation.

Mercator, refuting the defense of Nestorius just described and defending his own accusation, writes as follows (*Dissertation on the Twelfth Anathema*):

“Photinus held a doctrine equal to that of this most insane Nestorius: he does not deny that the Word of God exists in the substance, but says that this Word dwelt from without in a peculiar manner in this Jesus who was born from Mary, according to the ordinary custom of married people, and that through him He performed all those miracles on earth.”

And afterward (no. 19):

“Photinus, the teacher of Nestorius, does not deny that this Word of God exists in substance, but he does not wish it to be the Son of God. He raves impiously when he says that the Word dwelt in a peculiar manner in Christ Jesus born from Joseph and Mary, or adhered to him, and that this man was nothing more than a man, although by the merit of his life he surpassed all men.”

And again (no. 21):

“Nestorius truly differs from Photinus, his teacher, only in asserting that Christ was born from the Virgin Mary. In all other respects he is entirely Photinus’s follower, standard-bearer, and champion, and especially in the point already mentioned: that the Word of God is not the Son of God, ought not to be called the Son of God, and that no one except Jesus born from Mary should be called the Son of God.”

In order that it may appear how truly Marius wrote that Nestorius differed from Photinus only in asserting that Christ was born from the Virgin, while agreeing with him in all other respects, it must be understood that at that time there were several questions concerning the incarnation of the divine Word from Mary, the betrothed of Joseph. Some concerned the Word who assumed flesh; others the flesh that was assumed; others the assumption itself; others Christ; and others Christ’s mother.

Concerning the Word assuming flesh, four questions were asked: whether He was the true God, ὁ ἀληθινὸς (*ho alēthinos*), against Arius; whether He was distinct from the Father in hypostasis, against Sabellius; whether He was God in Himself from eternity, against the Samosatene; and whether He was the Son from eternity, against the same man.

Concerning the flesh, three questions were likewise asked: whether it was real and ὁμοούσιος (*homoousios*, consubstantial) with ours, against the Phantasiasts; whether it was taken from Mary, against the Apellites; and whether it possessed a soul and mind, against the Arians and Apollinarists.

Concerning the assumption, an equal number of questions were debated: whether the union of the natures in Christ was καθ’ ὑπόστασιν (*kath’ hypostasin*, according to hypostasis), or merely κατὰ σχέσιν (*kata schesin*, according to relation), against the Samosatene; whether it existed from the time of conception, against Leporius; and whether it was continuous and destined to remain eternal, against Marcellus.

Concerning Christ, more matters were indeed brought into question, but chiefly three: whether He was merely a man, against Ebion, etc.; whether there were two persons in Him, against the Samosatene; and whether He began to exist from His mother, against Photinus.

[Col. 1139C] Finally, concerning Christ’s mother, two matters were disputed: whether she was truly Deipara, “God-bearer,” against Theodore of Mopsuestia; and whether she gave birth as a virgin or from a man, against Helvidius and other Antidicomarianites of that kind. Thus fourteen questions in all were proposed. Any others that arise either arose incidentally or can easily be reduced to these.

It is established by incontrovertible arguments, first, that Nestorius and Photinus partly agreed and partly disagreed concerning Christ’s mother. They agreed insofar as both denied that she was Deipara; they disagreed insofar as Nestorius asserted that she gave birth as a virgin, whereas Photinus asserted that she gave birth from a man.

Second, both in reality agreed concerning Christ in the common view that He was merely a man, that He began to exist from the Virgin, and that there were two hypostases or persons in Him.
