For the last two points do not differ from the first; and therefore all defenders of the faith demonstrate by the same arguments as those used for the first point that Nestorius truly asserted them.

Third, both likewise agreed concerning the union of the natures. Neither admitted a substantive union, since both denied that Christ was God; and neither is accused by the ancients of agreeing either with Leporius, or rather with the Samosatene and Marcellus of Galatia, concerning the duration of the union.

Fourth, both likewise taught the same things concerning Christ’s flesh. No ancient writer ever accused them of agreement with the Phantasiasts, Apellites, Arians, or Apollinarists; on the contrary, all recount the hostility of both men toward those heretics.

The dispute with Marius, therefore, can concern only the questions relating to the Word, as though he had unjustly charged Nestorius with agreement with Photinus on this point. But since there are four such questions, no one will have accused Marius concerning the first. For Nestorius confessed the consubstantial Trinity, as is clear from his final sermon, and Photinus consistently held the faith of the ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*). Indeed, this was what aroused the fury of the Arians against him. When he had been deposed by them at the Council of Sirmium, he could have recovered his see if he had subscribed to the confession they offered against the ὁμοούσιον.

The controversy therefore reduces to the remaining three questions, although the last two in reality coincide. For if the Word is not the Son from eternity, then He is certainly not God in Himself from eternity; and conversely, if the Word is not God in Himself from eternity—which Mercator calls being God in substance—then He cannot be the Son from eternity, but must be the Son in time, since no one can truly be the Son unless he differs from the Father by τρόπος τῆς ὑπάρξεως (*tropos tēs hyparxeōs*, the mode of existence). But all the ancients report that Photinus taught that the Word was not the Son from eternity, but only became so in time. And when we were discussing the Samosatene, we established that Nestorius was rightly charged with agreement with the Samosatene on this point.

It remains, therefore, to show that Nestorius and Photinus alike departed from Sabellius’s position. Once this has been established, it will plainly be evident that Marius was right to write these words (*Dissertation on the Twelfth Anathema*, no. 21):

“Nestorius [Col. 1140B] differs from Photinus, his teacher, only in asserting that Christ was born from the Virgin Mary. In all other respects he is entirely his follower, standard-bearer, and champion, and especially in the point already mentioned: that the Word of God is not the Son of God, ought not to be called the Son of God, and that no one except Jesus born from Mary should be called the Son of God—he who, having been made the temple of the one dwelling within him, deserved to be called this through the undivided association and conjunction between himself and the Word of God, yet was not by nature the Son of God, since he obtained the privileges of divinity from this union, possessing them not by nature but by grace.”

Yet no one will doubt that Nestorius was alien to Sabellius after reading his final sermon and remembering the Theodorian creed, which he adopted as his own by adoption, so to speak. For in it Sabellius’s συναίρεσις (*synairesis*, conflation), as Nazianzenus calls it, is openly condemned.

Nor will anyone deny that Photinus departed from Sabellius who agrees with Nestorius himself, and also with Epiphanius and Philaster, when they write that Photinus thought about the Word in the same way as the Samosatene. For the Samosatene differed from Sabellius only concerning the Word’s distinction from the Father, so much so that no ancient writer counted the Samosatene among the Patripassians, whose leader Sabellius is said to have been.

But these matters, which have been stated more briefly under the pressure of logical necessity, seem better expanded and confirmed by the testimonies of the ancients.

We said first that Photinus consistently remained in the confession of the ὁμοούσιον. Socrates testifies to this (Book II, chapters 24–25). For he relates that Photinus was condemned by the Arians assembled at Sirmium and expelled from his see. Then, after presenting the creed composed by those same men, he adds:

“They attempted, after his deposition, to persuade Photinus to agree to these propositions and subscribe to them, and promised that they would restore his episcopate to him if he would come to his senses, condemn with an anathema the doctrine he had devised separately, and thus embrace their opinion. He rejected the condition and challenged them to debate; but, being defeated, he was condemned. Thereafter, living in exile, he composed a book in both Greek and Latin. He wrote against all the heresies while striving to disseminate his own doctrine.”

From this passage of Socrates we learn, first, what Photinus’s heresy was, since it is condemned in these words of the creed:

“If anyone says that Christ Jesus, the Son of God, who served the Father in the creation of all things, did not exist before the ages, but that He was Son and Christ only from the time when He was born from Mary, and that He then began to be God, just as Paul of Samosata asserted, let him be anathema.”

Next, we learn that Photinus followed the doctrine of the Samosatene. Third, that his name was not explicitly included in the creed, so that he might more easily subscribe to it. Fourth, that Photinus wrote against all the heresies in order to disseminate his own more credibly. In this he anticipated his disciples Theodore and Nestorius, who sought to make access to their own doctrine easier by attacking all the other heresies. Finally, it follows from this book that the statements which Nestorius and others report as having been made by Photinus were taken from it.

We said next that the last two questions concerning the Word reduce to one. Apart from the fact that the reasoning drawn from an understanding of the Samosatene doctrine sufficiently proves this, it is demonstrated by Audentius, an ancient writer whom Gennadius mentions (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 14):

“He wrote with particular purpose against the Photinians, who are now called Bonosians, a book entitled *On the Faith Against All Heretics*, in which he showed that the antiquity of the Son of God was co-eternal with the Father, and that He did not then receive the beginning of His divinity from God the Father when, through God’s creative action, He was conceived and born as a man from the blessed Virgin Mary.”

For he joined the two propositions as though one were an explanation of the other. For this reason, when the ancients explain the heresy of Photinus, some report one proposition and some the other; indeed, often the same writer reports one at one place and the other elsewhere.

We took as the starting-point of our argument the claim that the Samosatene—and therefore Photinus, the Samosatene’s follower—did not teach the same thing as Sabellius. Theodoret objects to this. Yet Nestorius himself (*Sermon 12*, no. 16) not only admits what we previously stated, but also supplies two differences between Sabellius and Photinus, in his own words:

“First, Sabellius calls the Father Υἱοπάτωρ (*Huiopatōr*, Father-Son), whereas Photinus calls Him Λογοπάτωρ (*Logopatōr*, Word-Father). Second, Sabellius asserts the divinity of the Word but denies His subsistence; Photinus denies the divinity of the Word but asserts His subsistence.”

That very confession of Nestorius, although it requires examination, nevertheless resolves the objection drawn from Theodoret. For both heretics—by “both,” I mean Sabellius and Photinus—sin against the true faith of the Trinity, as Theodoret testifies; yet they do not do so in the same way, as Nestorius says.

We have established that Photinus agreed with the Samosatene concerning the matter under discussion. The Arians at Sirmium state this in their creed, and Philaster, Epiphanius, and Augustine report it. Nevertheless, Nestorius (*Sermon 12*, no. 15) and Mercator (*Dissertation on the Twelfth Anathema*, no. 19) oppose it. Their statements must therefore be examined, beginning with those of Nestorius.

“Paul and Photinus,” he says, “differ from one another in this: one of them calls Christ merely a man; the other does speak of the Word, but does not confess that the Word is God. Rather, he says that this Word is sometimes called by the name of the Father and sometimes designated by the name of the Word. Hence he also calls Him by the name Λογοπάτωρ, that is, ‘Word and Father,’ or, if it may be said, ‘Father of the Word,’ perversely applying, according to the wickedness of his understanding, the statement properly made in the Gospel: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God’ (John 1:1). ‘You see,’ he says, ‘that he sometimes calls the Word God and sometimes Word, as though extended and gathered together.’ He does not introduce God the Word as having become man, for he does not know the divinity of Christ; he does not know that the divine substance assumed a man; he utterly fails to recognize the divinity of the Word existing before the ages.”

His statement that the Samosatene calls Christ merely a man is true if “merely a man” means one who is not at the same time man and God. But from this Nestorius himself is convicted of agreement with the Samosatene. If, however, he means that the Samosatene did not posit two natures in Christ, joined by a perpetual bond, he falsely attributes this to the Samosatene, as is clear from § 4.

Furthermore, when he says that Photinus does not introduce God the Word as having become man, and gives as the reason that Photinus does not know Christ’s divinity, does not know the divine substance or ὑπόστασις (*hypostasis*) to have assumed a man, and entirely fails to recognize the divinity of the Word existing before the ages, he either does not know Photinus’s position, or knowingly misrepresents it, or contradicts himself. For he reports Photinus’s words in interpreting the Evangelist:

“You see that he calls the Word God at one time and Word at another, as though extended and contracted.”

Photinus therefore knows the divinity of the Word existing before the ages, although he does not regard it as subsisting in itself, or in its own property. Nevertheless, he considers it to possess a subsisting property when it is extended and brought forth; and this certainly occurred when it was sent to work in Jesus. Photinus therefore knew that the divine hypostasis had assumed a man. He also knew Christ’s divinity, if calling Christ “God” means nothing other than that the Word was joined to human nature by συναφεία (*synapheia*, conjunction), ἐνοίκησις (*enoikēsis*, indwelling), ἐνέργεια (*energeia*, operation), and other equivalent modes which Nestorius acknowledges. Nestorius’s interest was to lie, lest everyone immediately recognize him as the one whom Mercator called “the follower, standard-bearer, and champion of Photinus, his teacher.”

Mercator establishes this as the sole difference between Photinus and the Samosatene (*Dissertation on the Twelfth Anathema*, no. 19): Paul understood the Word of God as προφορικὸν καὶ πρακτικὸν λόγον καὶ ἐνεργετικὸν (*prophorikon kai praktikon logon kai energe­tikon*), that is, a prolative and practical Word, efficacious in power, and not a substantive Word, which the Greeks call οὐσιῶδες (*ousiōdes*). But Photinus, the teacher of Nestorius, does not wish this Word to be the Son of God.

Earlier he had said (no. 17):

“Photinus held a doctrine equal to that of this most insane Nestorius: he does not deny that the Word of God exists in the substance.”

He had also said in the frequently cited letter (no. 5) that Nestorius, in confessing the Word as substantial and asserting that He is God from eternity with the Father, rightly differed from those men mentioned—Ebion, Paul, Photinus, etc.—and was joined to the orthodox faith.

How do these statements cohere? How did Photinus not deny that the Word existed in the substance? How could Paul agree with Photinus concerning the Word, as the ancients report, if Photinus did not assert the Word to be prolative in the same manner as Paul? A difficult knot! Nevertheless, the answer to the first part of the difficulty is easy: the negative particle has been omitted in one place in the manuscript copies, and the passage should be read as the syntax of the contrasting terms itself requires:

“Photinus does not deny that this Word of God exists in the substance, but he does not wish it to be the Son of God.”

As for the latter difficulty, I confess that I remain perplexed, unless perhaps we may conjecture that Photinus, in order to soften somewhat Paul’s position—which he understood to be hated by everyone—devised something resembling Tertullian’s fantasy: namely, that the Word, together with its hypostasis, sometimes lies hidden in the Father’s bosom and is joined to the Father, while at other times it comes forth from there and is separated.

## § VI. On Bonosus, whom Mercator numbers among Nestorius’s predecessors

[Col. 1142C]

Mercator reports three things about Bonosus: first, that he presided over the Church of Sardica; second, that he was condemned in advance by Damasus; third, that he followed the heresy of Ebion. From these follows a fourth point: he must be counted among Nestorius’s predecessors.

The first of these facts was until now not merely unknown to the general public but concealed from nearly all the most learned men, Baronius and Petavius among them. Both acknowledge this concerning themselves: the former in his *Annals*, under the year of Christ 389; the latter in the fourth volume of his *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, book XIV, §37.

Mercator’s view is confirmed by the decree of the Council of Capua, by which the case of Bonosus, who had been brought to trial, was entrusted to Anysius of Thessalonica and the Macedonian bishops—plainly in accordance with the canons of the Church, which provide that any bishop accused of wrongdoing should be judged by neighboring fellow bishops, but not by his own subjects, if he is a metropolitan. Sardica, moreover, is a metropolitan city of Dacia and neighboring Macedonia. [Col. 1142D]

The second point likewise was unknown, or at most doubtful, even to men otherwise outstanding in learning. Nevertheless, many statements by Mercator support it, especially the second part of the letter that Damasus wrote from the Roman synod to Paul of Antioch:

“If anyone says that the Word operated in the Lord’s flesh with a human mind, the Catholic Church anathematizes him; and likewise those who confess two sons in the Savior—that is, one before the incarnation and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin—and who do not confess the same one to be the Son of God both before and afterward. Whoever wishes to subscribe to this letter, provided that he has previously subscribed to the ecclesiastical canons, which you know very well, and to the Nicene faith, you shall receive without any ambiguity.”

Concerning this letter, observe first that it is presented by the supreme pontiff as a synodal statement possessing canonical [Col. 1143A] authority, to which one ought to subscribe as to a rule of orthodoxy (*ὀρθοδοξία*). Zosimus said the same about his synodal letter in the Pelagian case, and Leo the Great about his in the Eutychian case.

Observe next that Bonosus chiefly erred in confessing two sons in Christ, one eternal and the other temporal. He did not, however, fall under the other condemnation by which Damasus strikes the Apollinarists and Arians—that is, the Dimaerites—with an anathema.

Finally, observe that Bonosus is rightly numbered among Nestorius’s predecessors, since he confessed two sons in Christ—a characteristic stain of this heresy.

Although Gennadius wrote that the Bonosians differed from the Photinians only in name:

“Audentius, a Spanish bishop, wrote against the Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians; and especially, with particular attention, against the Photinians, who are now called Bonosians.”

From this last observation it is clear what Mercator reports as the third fact about Bonosus: namely, that he followed the heresy of Ebion in that respect in which Christ was said to be merely human. For whoever confesses two sons must believe that one is God alone and the other, in reality, merely human. [Col. 1143B]

Whether he embraced the other aspect as well—namely, that Christ’s mother gave birth by a man—is not equally certain. Indeed, a fairly strong argument for denying it may be drawn from the fact that, when he maintained that Mary had received other children after Christ’s birth, he was condemned for that reason by the Macedonian bishops under the presidency of Anysius of Thessalonica, as one who had defiled the womb consecrated to Christ’s lodging and the palace of the eternal king with human seed (in the letter to the Illyrians).

Furthermore, since Mercator says that Bonosus was condemned in advance by Damasus—that is, condemned before he revealed his heresy—the inference is drawn that, if all else failed, Damasus’s letter to the Illyrians, which we have just mentioned, would have to be rejected. For the pontiff could not truly be said to have condemned Bonosus in advance, since the author of the letter leaves him, in his own judgment still untouched, to be judged by judges selected by the synod.

## § VII. On the Pelagians, whose friendship with Nestorius was charged not only by Mercator but also by other ancient writers

[Col. 1143C]

It was counted as a fault in Nestorius by several of the ancients that he had received into his friendship Caelestius and the Caelestian bishops, who had fled from the West to Constantinople. Cassian was the first of all to reproach him for this, in his books *On the Incarnation of the Word*. Pope Celestine reproached him afterward, in his letter to Nestorius; then Mercator, in the preface to Nestorius’s sermons; and finally Cyril and the Fathers of Ephesus.

Not merely friendship but also agreement in doctrine was briefly charged by Pope Celestine in the letter just mentioned:

“What have you in common with those who have been condemned for denying these things? Things opposed to one another never come together without suspicion; and if they were equally displeasing to you, they would finally be expelled.”

The Ephesian Fathers likewise condemn, though obscurely, in the same canon, those who dare either privately or publicly to hold the opinions of Nestorius or Caelestius (canon 4 against the Ephesians). [Col. 1143D]

Cassian, however, does so at length and openly throughout nearly all the books mentioned earlier. He alleged that for this reason Nestorius, by his intercessions, encouraged the complaints of the Pelagianists and defended their cause in his writings:

“He subtly—or, to speak more accurately, deceitfully—acts as their patron, and with a wicked affection lends wicked support to a depravity akin to his own, knowing that he shares their mind and their spirit, and therefore grieving that a related heresy has been separated from the Church, although he knows that it is certainly joined to himself by its perversity.”

The history of the monk Leporius is well known in this connection. Comparing him with Nestorius, Cassian says:

“If Christ who is from Mary is not the same as he who was born from God, you unquestionably make two Christs” (book VI, chapter 14). “This is in accordance with that crime of Pelagian impiety which, asserting that the man born alone from the Virgin was merely human, said that he was a teacher of the human race rather than its redeemer, because he gave human beings not redemption of life but [Col. 1144A] an example of living, so that people, by following him and doing similar things, might attain similar results.

“Your impiety therefore has the same origin and the same root of error. They assert that a solitary man was born from Mary, and you do the same. They separate the Son of Man from the Son of God, and you do the same. They say that the Savior was made Christ through baptism; you say that he was made a temple of God in baptism. They do not deny that he was made God after the passion; you deny that he was God even after the ascension. Your perversity therefore differs from theirs in only one respect: they seem to blaspheme the Lord on earth, while you do so also in heaven. You have surpassed and gone beyond those whom you imitate—we do not deny it.”

Gennadius, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, and the Chronicler believed to be Prosper, under the year 431, in the consulship of Taurus and Bassus, report the same agreement between Leporius and Nestorius.

Nothing is more commonly cited in this connection than the epitaph that a certain poet inscribed on the common tomb of the Nestorian and Pelagian heresies. In it the unhappy shades are introduced saying:

[Col. 1144B]

“Into what depths has mad pride plunged us,

stripped of gifts and swollen with merits?

For desiring Christ to be God

by the piety of works and the reward due to them,

we did not stand firm in the covenant of the Head.

Hoping for a crown from the freedom of the mind,

we lost the righteousness that grace gives.”

In the earlier volume of Mercator’s works, however, we have overturned the popular opinion on this subject, partly in the notes to Nestorius’s sermons, partly in the second dissertation on synods (on the twentieth synod, chapter 7), and finally in the section on the Pelagian heresy, where the true affinity of the two heresies has been entirely exposed. Nevertheless, we shall say something more before this dissertation itself is completed, when we investigate Nestorius’s faith concerning five other points of Catholic doctrine besides the incarnation.

For the present, it is useful to observe that no Nestorian, if he wishes to think consistently, can defend original sin, the true grace of Christ the Redeemer, and human inability to perform works of piety. [Col. 1144C] Nor can any Pelagian, unless he is willing to utter propositions that are at least mutually contradictory, uphold the true divinity of Christ and the necessity of the hypostatic union for the purpose of redemption. This is not obscurely established by Cassian’s words, and it follows easily from the principles set down by the Fathers.

In conclusion, I cannot conceal what occurred to me after I had published the dissertation on the synods convened in the Pelagian controversy, concerning Leporius and the great city of the Belgians, where Cassian writes that Leporius’s error originated. At that place I interpreted this as Trier, since the expression “the great city” signifies a metropolis, and Trier was, so to speak, the political metropolis of Gaul, since the prefect of the Gauls long maintained his residence there.

A conjecture concerning Cologne Agrippina now seems to me more credible, or at least not less implausible. Euphratas once governed its Church; he is said to have denied the divinity of Christ. Although he was deposed on account of blasphemy at the Council of Agrippina, held in the year 346, after the consulship of Amantius and Albinus, it could nevertheless have happened that the seed of impiety he had scattered remained buried for a long time and finally burst into the light in Cassian’s day.

Certainly Valerian of Auxerre, while delivering his sentence, attributes to Euphratas precisely those errors that Leporius later defended: namely, that Christ was neither God nor existent before his birth from Mary, and that consequently it was not God but a human being who suffered.

Yet something remarkable is reported about Euphratas, which presents a serious difficulty to investigators of ecclesiastical history: the very man who is said to have been deposed in the year 346 at the Council of Agrippina on account of his errors is said to have sat among the Fathers at the Council of Sardica in the following year, and even to have served, together with Vincent of Capua, as the synod’s envoy to the emperor Constantius, who was staying at Antioch, as Athanasius testifies (in his letter to the solitaries).

It is astonishing that a man—and indeed a bishop—should have been an envoy [Col. 1145A] sent by Catholics under a synodal decree against the Arians when he had been deposed and condemned the previous year. The Arians would have had to be absurdly malicious to attempt to build an accusation against a man by introducing a prostitute, when they could have overwhelmed him with a genuine accusation.

Many consider this an insoluble knot, and it is indeed quite perplexing. To untie it, Baronius shifted the Council of Agrippina to the year 350 or 351 and supposed that Euphratas had swallowed the poison of the Samosatenian during his embassy. When he later revealed this, Baronius thought, the bishops of Gaul condemned him; but so far he has persuaded only a few of his opinion.

Binius offers something more plausible (in his notes on the Council of Agrippina): two councils were held at Cologne Agrippina in the case of Euphratas, one in the year 346 and the other in 375, as Trithemius reports. At the first, Euphratas was either cleared of suspicion of heresy or corrected by an admonition. At the second he was deposed. The collectors of the councils, however, combined both into one—a thing that may [Col. 1145B] perhaps have happened elsewhere as well.

On this account, the same thing would have happened to Euphratas as to the Samosatenian: after pretending to reform at the first Antiochene synod, he was convicted of heresy and deposed at the second, with another man substituted in his place.

## § VIII. On Diodore of Tarsus, against whom Cyril wrote as though against Nestorius’s teacher

After Nestorius had been banished to the Oasis and his books proscribed by imperial law, certain people who thought that the condemned heresy ought not merely to be retained but even promoted first secretly circulated, through the hands of trustworthy men, certain excerpts from Diodore of Tarsus and Theodore of Mopsuestia that agreed with Nestorian doctrine; afterward they openly spread them among the public (Liberatus, *Brief Account*, chapter 10).

They acted with this purpose: since those two men possessed the highest authority among all on account of their reputation for sound doctrine and pious faith, either to overwhelm the men who condemned Nestorius [Col. 1145C] by their own weight, or at least to suppress them, and to repair the loss of Nestorius’s books with the opinions of distinguished writers.

How excerpts of this kind came into the hands of Cyril of Alexandria and Proclus, bishop of the imperial city, and what disturbances they caused, has been partly related in the historical preface and will partly be explained where the question of the Constantinopolitan synod arises. From that synod Proclus sent a volume to the Armenians, and on this occasion Cyril wrote books of his own. Each bishop refuted these writings: Proclus in a volume that still exists, Cyril in two books of which nothing survives except a very few fragments.

I think they perished by the same fate as the books written by Theodoret in defense of Diodore and Theodore. We shall deal fully with Cyril’s and Theodoret’s works in the supplement to Theodoret, which we are preparing.

Proclus appended the excerpts to his volume without the authors’ name, lest, if it had been included, it might either have diminished Proclus’s credibility or aroused enormous resentment among good men [Col. 1145D], so deeply had everyone’s opinion of Diodore taken root in their minds. And indeed, who would not suspect the man whom none of the Fathers of his age failed to praise highly, whom Athanasius called a herald of the truth, Timothy—Athanasius’s successor after Peter—called a man of apostolic faith, Chrysostom called a man of angelic life and a living martyr, and Epiphanius declared equal to the prophet Elijah?

Almost nothing remains of Diodore’s works except certain statements found in Greek chains, and also in Mercator, Leontius, and the Fifth Synod. But the chains present flowers; the others present poison. The former introduce him as an interpreter of Scripture, while the latter present him as Theodore’s and Nestorius’s teacher.

Yet that great man, when he had grown old, fell into error while recklessly pursuing the heresy of Apollinaris. For he asserted every part of that blasphemy which Theodore and Nestorius later defended, so that he was rightly called Theodore’s father and Nestorius’s grandfather. [Col. 1146A]

He taught that there were two sons of God in Christ: the one who was from Mary was not the Son except by adoption or grace; the Word had neither two births nor been born from Mary; the Word was not Christ but Christ’s lord; and God could not be said to have suffered or been crucified. In these six propositions, either wholly or for the most part, Nestorianism is contained.

He scattered such errors throughout the work he wrote *Against the Synusiasts* (*πρὸς τοὺς Συνουσιαστάς*), that is, against Apollinaris. Apollinaris, while fighting against Photinus, who erred through deficiency in explaining the union of the Word with flesh, himself erred through excess and confused and mixed the Word with flesh in the same way that the human mind, infused through the limbs, is mixed with the body that it moves and informs. From this work Diodore’s character could have been recognized, had the appearance of piety not almost bewitched the eyes of the world.

[Col. 1146B]

He wrote against Apollinaris at a very advanced age. He was an abbot of great renown when Chrysostom came to him in the year 376, eager to cultivate monastic life and to learn. From being abbot of the monks he became bishop of Tarsus through Meletius, already an old man, in the year 378. He attended the Second Synod in 381. Chrysostom praised him publicly in Antioch after the year 386, when he was already almost exhausted by old age.

Nevertheless, he had not written at that age—or at least had not yet published the work—in the year 392, when Jerome completed his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; otherwise Jerome would have remembered so distinguished a composition. Perhaps he died while engaged upon this work, for by the year 394 Phalerius had succeeded him in his see, as is understood from the acts of the Constantinopolitan synod held under Nectarius in that same year.

It is worthwhile to present fragments of the work. In this way, the source of Nestorian blasphemy—or at least the stream nearest to its source—will be revealed, and Cyril will at the same time be defended against Facundus of Hermiane, Diodore’s patron. [Col. 1146C]

Before presenting them, however, it will be useful to point out that the excerpts read by the ancients as coming from Theodore’s books *Against the Synusiasts* actually belong to Diodore, who gave his books this title, whereas Theodore entitled his work on the same subject *Against the Impious Apollinaris and the Apollinarists*.

Indeed, what Leontius, an especially careful author, attributes to Diodore, others assign to Theodore, as will become clear from what follows. Leontius does note, however, that Theodore was accustomed to borrow many things from other writers and from the Samosatenian himself in the same words, transferring them into his own work, so that his books seem not written but copied (book III, *Against the Eutychians*, near the end).

### From Diodore’s first book against the Synusiasts

[Col. 1146D]

“We are bringing you to a careful and cautious examination of doctrines. We labor for your sake, lest we have to render an account to the Lord for our silence. The Son, perfect before the ages, assumed him who is shown to have come from David, perfect: the Son of God assumed the son of David.

“You will say to me: ‘Are you proclaiming two sons?’ I do not say two sons of David. Did I assert that God the Word was the Son of David? Nor do I say, in terms of substance, that there are two sons of God. For do I assert that two sons were begotten from God’s substance before the ages? I say that the Word of God dwelt in him who is proved to come from David’s seed” (in Mercator, book III).

### From the same work

“If anyone wishes, by an abuse of language, to call the Son of God, God the Word, the son of David, let him call him so on account of God the Word’s temple, which is from David; and let him call him who is from David’s seed [Col. 1147A] the Son of God by grace, not by nature. Let him not be ignorant of natural fathers, nor overturn the order, nor call him who is incorporeal a body, nor say that he is both from God before the ages and from David, both suffering and impassible.

“A body is not incorporeal; what is below is not above; what is before the ages is not from David’s seed; what has suffered is not impassible. These things cannot be referred to one and the same meaning. The things belonging to the body do not belong to God the Word, and the body does not possess what properly belongs to God the Word. Let us confess the natures and not deny the dispensations” (in the Fifth Synod, Session 5; in Leontius, book III, *Against the Eutychians*).

### From the same work

“By grace is the Son who is man from Mary; by nature, [Col. 1147B] God the Word. What is according to grace is not according to nature, and what is according to nature is not according to grace: there are not two sons.

“Let sonship, glory, and immortality according to grace be sufficient for the body that is from us, because it has been made the temple of God the Word. Let it not be elevated above nature, and let it not insult God the Word by the thanksgiving owed by us. And what is the insult? To join him with the body and suppose that he needs the body for perfect sonship.

“God the Word himself does not wish to be David’s son but his lord. He did not begrudge this body being called David’s son; rather, he was present for that reason. Those who look rightly agree that, since we seek natural fathers, we should not call God the Word the son of David or Abraham, but their maker; nor should we call the body, which was born from Mary, from the Father before the ages, but [Col. 1147C] the seed of Abraham and David.

“And when the question concerns births according to nature, God the Word must not be thought to be the son of Mary. For a mortal generates a mortal, according to nature and according to the body, one like himself. God the Word did not undergo two births, one before the ages and another in later times. Rather, he was begotten from the Father according to nature, while he fashioned for himself from the very womb the temple that was born from Mary.”

A little later:

“But when the discussion concerns the saving dispensation, man is called God—not because he was made this, but because he assumed this—and God is called man, not as though he had been made circumscribed or existed everywhere. For he was a body, tangible even after the resurrection; and such as it was, it was received into heaven, and in this form he will come, as it was received.” [Col. 1147D]

### From the same work

“But if it was flesh,” says Apollinaris, “that was crucified, how did the sun turn away its rays, darkness cover the entire earth, earthquakes occur, rocks split apart, and the dead rise?

“What, then, do they say about the darkness that occurred in Egypt in the time of Moses—not for three hours but for three days? What about the other miracles performed through Moses, and those performed through Jesus son of Nave, who made the sun stand still? What about the sun which, in the time of King Hezekiah, contrary even to nature, turned backward? And what about the remains of Elisha, which raised a dead man?

“For if they demonstrate that God the Word suffered [Col. 1148A] by pointing to what occurred at the cross, and do not allow that these things happened on account of the human being, were not the events in the time of Moses for the sake of Abraham’s race, and those in the time of Jesus son of Nave, and those in the time of King Hezekiah? But if those things were wondrously done for the sake of the Jewish people, how could the things that occurred at the cross not have been done even more for the sake of God the Word’s temple?”

### From the same work

“The Son of God was for no one; the flesh was Son for the sake of the Son. And why do I say ‘for the sake of the son’? The flesh was for our sake. And lest you think the Word blasphemous, seek the demonstrations.

“If human beings had not sinned, there would have been no need for the law, for the law is not laid down for the righteous. [Col. 1148B] If those who were under the law had not increased sin, there would have been no need for grace. Since the law could not kill sin, did he not assume flesh for our sake, so that by being crucified, dying, and raised up he might bring a remedy to death and to the sentence of death?

“If deceit and the sentence of death had not advanced against us, what need would there have been for this economy of the Savior? What need would there have been to put on a body? Did he not receive flesh for our sake?”

Reader, observe:

1. Cyril wrote three books against excerpts of this kind, as Liberatus reports (*Brief Account*, chapter 10). In the first he refuted what concerned Diodore, and in the second and third what concerned Theodore. Yet he suppressed the name of either or both, as can sufficiently be understood from his letter to Proclus.

2. Nothing survives of Cyril’s entire work except the fragments read in the Sixth Session of the Fifth Synod. The circumstances of their disappearance are very obscure, since the fourth book, which Liberatus calls *On the Incarnation*, survives intact under the title *Dialogue: That Christ Is One, by Way of Opposition* (tome V, part I, edition of G. L.).

Nothing more exact or more carefully elaborated did Cyril write on the history of doctrine. The work appears to be the achievement of a craftsman who had reached full learning through his preceding labors, and the final effort of the most learned man on this subject. For Cyril wrote it three years before he departed to the heavenly realms.

3. Facundus of Hermiane (books III, IV, and VIII) called into question, at least apparently, whether this work had been written by Cyril or by someone else under his name. Liberatus agrees with Facundus in these words:

“Cyril wrote four books: three against Diodore and Theodore, as authors of Nestorian doctrine, and another book on the Incarnation. In them are contained incorrupt testimonies of the ancient Fathers, namely, of Felix, the Roman pope; Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop of Corinth; and Gregory called the Wonderworker (*Θαυματουργός*). Although in those books the statements Theodore published against the Arians are praised, they nevertheless maintain that he himself was Nestorius’s teacher.

“Against them, the Catholic defenders of the truth, the Acephali, responded as follows: those books are not Cyril’s, because although he is said to have placed in them testimonies against the dead, he did not use them against the living Nestorius, either at the synod or in any of his letters. Hence they say that Cyril neither dictated nor published those books.”

[Col. 1148D]

4. The Fifth Synod made no mention of Diodore, although Theodore is named explicitly and excerpts from Diodore (*περικοπαί*) are reported without his name. Facundus makes an argument from this silence and constructs an accusation against the holy synod on that basis.

But it does not seem that he explains sufficiently what exactly he is alleging. Is it that Diodore’s name was suppressed while Theodore’s was expressed? This was done for a proper reason: reverence was to be shown to the former, whereas a mark of disgrace was to be imposed on the latter.

Or does he mean that Diodore was spared out of reverence and therefore not condemned? Yet the second and third anathemas concern excerpts from Diodore’s books and consist of words that Diodore himself used. They read as follows:

[Col. 1149A]

“2. If anyone does not confess that God the Word has two births, one before the ages, timeless and incorporeal, from the Father, and the other in the last days, from that same one who descended from heaven and was incarnate and born from the holy, glorious, God-bearing and ever-virgin Mary, let him be anathema.

“3. If anyone says that the God Word who worked miracles is one person and Christ who suffered another; or that God the Word was with Christ when he was born of a woman; or that he was in him as one person in another; and does not confess our one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, the incarnate and made-man Word of God, together with his miracles and the sufferings which he voluntarily endured in the flesh, let him be anathema.”

5. Diodore’s memory was spared because of the extraordinary opinion formed about him and wondrously increased by the praises of the saints.

6. Theodoret, Diodore’s perpetual praiser, must either have clung obstinately to Diodore’s doctrine until he renounced Nestorius, or else have been incredibly blind in mind: after approving Cyril’s faith as [Col. 1149B] free from every heretical corruption and consonant with the Church, he nevertheless praised the orthodoxy (*ὀρθοδοξία*) of Diodore, who taught contrary things.

7. When Diodore speaks of Christ’s mother, he always calls her Mary and never Virgin. This can arouse suspicion of a Judaizing opinion, and not without reason, since Diodore adhered to Photinus and to Marcellus of Galatia, his fellow countrymen, who were infected with Judaic poison on this subject.

8. In his first letter to Succensus, Cyril wrote about Diodore things that agree with the excerpts, so that they appear to have been taken from them. They may therefore usefully be added here:

“A certain Diodore, formerly, as they say, an opponent of the Holy Spirit, entered into communion with the orthodox Church. After, as he supposed, laying aside the stain of Macedonian heresy, he fell into the power of another disease.

“For he thought and wrote that the one born from David’s seed, from the holy Virgin and Mother of God, was one Son separately, while the Word from God the Father was another Son, considered separately. [Col. 1149C]

“Concealing the wolf beneath a sheep’s skin, as it were, he pretends to call Christ one. But although he refers this name only to that sole-begotten Son, the Word begotten from God the Father, he also calls the one from David’s seed ‘son,’ yet he grants him this name as a matter of grace, since he is united to that true Son.

“He says that he is united not as we assert, but according to dignity alone, authority, and equality of honor. Nestorius became his disciple. Thus, darkened by Diodore’s books, Nestorius pretends to confess one Christ, one Son, and one Lord; but he too divides the one into two and sets them apart, saying that the human being is joined to God the Word by a sharing of name, equality of honor, and dignity.”

## § IX. On Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, Nestorius’s teacher

In the first dissertation, in its first part, we stated what Theodore was like: the character, habits, and disposition of a man waging war against Christ. [Col. 1149D] There was no one more changeable, assuming whatever form circumstances of time and place required; no one more adept at putting on the appearance of piety; no one more artful at bewitching minds and more cunning at stealing glory; no one more audacious in spreading errors, perverting Holy Scripture, and writing faith into the minds of the people; and finally no one more disastrously successful in his disciples, since before his death he saw many of them presiding over the Churches of the East, including two bishops of the greatest cities—Nestorius of Constantinople and John of Antioch—and two men celebrated above all for their reputation for learning, Andrew of Samosata and Theodoret of Cyrus, and others.

But why should I labor over an encomium of such a man, when Leontius the scholastic has discharged this task, though vainly, and with all the greater credibility because this highly learned man is treating a subject especially familiar to him (book II, *Against Eutyches and Nestorius*)?

When he was a young man, he had been drawn over to their side by Theodore’s followers [Col. 1150A] and had remained with them for a long time. At last, when divine light shone upon him, he exposed the frauds of the wicked faction and eventually revealed them to everyone, lest they continue harming the unwary, in a book entitled *A Triumph over the Secretly Transmitted Impiety of the Nestorians at the Beginning, and over Its Parents*.

He divided it into four parts. In the first he explains the wicked arts of Theodore’s followers; in the second, Theodore’s character and books; in the third, Nestorius’s agreement with Theodore; and in the last, fragments from Theodore’s books that confirm these statements.

### 1

After invoking God as witness to the truth and giving the reasons for writing, he relates the following about Theodore’s followers:

“The first artifice of their hypocrisy, worthy of their malice, is this: although they do not accept the holy teachers of the Church who were given by God, they verbally pretend that they do not accept either Theodore or Diodore, the first sources of their impiety.

“Next, among those to whom they set traps, they verbally praise and recommend acceptance of the great [Col. 1150B] synod, although in their hearts they reject it, as do certain others.

“After the synod has been accepted, they ask which of the Fathers each person is accustomed to read and to which he is especially devoted. If men other than their own have been praised, however distinguished those men may be, they do not oppose this at the first encounter, although they cannot even bear to have the others named; they do this lest the person they wish to ensnare take fright and fly away.

“‘These Fathers are good,’ they say, ‘but they are no better than our own.’

“If the simple man then asks for their names, they say: ‘Read first, and then you will learn what sort of men they are and how important, although in your misery you have not even learned their names.’

“Then they add other gifts to the books. They promise assistance and the support of the court if he is in need, even advancement in public office and companionship with the learned men they possess. They do not desist until the person succumbs either to ignorance, poverty, flattery, or whatever else they commonly use to ensnare those who do not guard their hearts with complete vigilance.

[Col. 1150C]

“When they now hold him captive and have made him dependent upon their services, if he is a monk, they instill in him disgust with his profession and promise to enroll him among the clergy, or to assist him in some other way, if he becomes a participant in their doctrine. If he is a layman, they offer suitable benefits; but by postponing the gifts, they make him long for them, so that, bound for the moment by a false hope, he may remain in their faction.

“When they saw that righteous hatred of the impious doctrines and of their author was increasing daily among the faithful, they said in their personal conduct: ‘Let Nestorius go; we shall follow the father of those same doctrines, from whom he himself drew.’ For just as the Manichaeans divide people into the elect and the ordinary, so these men divide them into worshipers and condemners of Nestorius.

“While pretending to share in the Church’s communion, they use the Church as though it were a praetorium and the clergy as an army, where everything is done by deceit. When someone who had been drawn over to their side once complained that it was impossible to share communion [Col. 1150D] in the sacred mysteries with them and at the same time with the Church, they said:

“‘You must not be troubled by this arrangement. The bread set forth as a type of Christ’s body has received no greater blessing than the bread sold in the marketplace, or than the loaves that the Philomarianites offer in Mary’s name.’

“If they have difficulty defending the leader of their doctrine, they say that he was praised by distinguished men and that Basil the Great, the two Gregories, and other Fathers—even Cyril—held the same opinions as he did. They scrape together the Fathers’ words with their fingernails, as it were, but refuse to hear from them those expressions in which the whole substance of the matter is contained, such as ‘natural union’ (*φυσικὴ σύνοδος*), ‘deification,’ ‘the blood of God,’ ‘the cross,’ and ‘the passion,’ and, above all, ‘according to the generation of the Word’ and ‘hypostatic union’ (*ἕνωσις καθ’ ὑπόστασιν*).

“They do not refuse these expressions because, as they habitually lie, there is a dispute with them about words, but because of the realities and doctrines themselves, which all the divine teachers of the Church unanimously [Col. 1151A] rejected together, and especially the latest of all the synods, the Council of Chalcedon—the union, seal, and confirmation of all the preceding synods. That synod utterly overthrew the fortress of impiety and celebrated in illustrious praises the supreme pontiff Leo, who dispersed and extinguished the hidden impiety.

“When they are pressed more closely, they deny that the man they follow was condemned by the great synod and claim that he was defended by a learned man. But in the anathema against the most wretched Nestorius, that man himself was expelled as well; and the defense brought a more abundant argument for the prosecution.”

### 2

Thus far Leontius on the followers; now he turns to Theodore, the bishop and leader of the sect.

“They say that he is the very man whom the great John rescued from the depths of intemperance after he had fled from the monastery; who, scarcely out of childhood, dared to handle the sacred writings; whom Theophilus rejected when he sought the see of Tarsus and compelled to confine himself to the Church of a middling town; who, in a public address in the Antiochene Church, did not hesitate to stir up the entire crowd [Col. 1151B] openly by his disapproval of the title *God-bearer* (*θεοτόκος*); and who, finally, in every perverse interpretation of Scripture, never ceased mocking and ridiculing the labors of the holy teachers who had worked upon it.

“He rejected Job from the canon of the sacred books as though it were a pagan fable; the books of Chronicles and Ezra as empty rhapsodies; the Song of Solomon as a love poem; and he despised the canonical Epistles as works falsely attributed to the apostles. He referred the Psalms, in a Judaizing manner, to Zerubbabel and Hezekiah, assigning only three of them to the Lord.”

And these things he did against the Scriptures inspired by the Holy Spirit; and against traditions, he raged no less impiously against the other breathing of the Holy Spirit. And lest he wear himself out by attacking each item individually, he takes his stand against the first instruction of the Christian religion and removes the Creed of those who are regenerated; I mean, the faith of the Nicene Council—not merely mutilating the Creed itself, but utterly destroying the whole faith and handing down another in its place.

[Col. 1151C] He dares another evil, no less serious than those already mentioned: for he has babbled forth another Mass, in addition to that which the Fathers handed down to the Churches. He showed no reverence either for the Mass of the apostles or for that of Basil the Great, composed in the same spirit; in this Mass he filled the *τελετή* (*teletē*), that is, the mystery of the Eucharist, with blasphemies rather than prayers.

Moreover, he removed the fear of judgment and of hell. Hence Leontius, burning with indignation, says: “For these things they love you, wretch, who belong to your sect. You have concocted for them this truly bitter and lamentable drug as a means of removing the fear of God. These things are set down in your books, which men of your faction translated into the Chaldaic and Armenian languages, so that each person might more easily swallow the poison as though it were native to him.”

After many charges had been brought concerning grace and free will, the origin of sin, and the condition of the angels, Leontius turned his speech to Theodore and said: “You imagine that your Christ is another animate idol created by the Trinity itself, and you slander the Trinity as though it taught that a creature should be worshiped. For you do not teach the worship of God made man, but the eternal worship of a man honored with the name of God. You ascribe to this man an honored and splendid birth and upbringing, and a birth scarcely more exalted than a prophetic one. You say, namely, that the Word of God, according to foreknowledge, wished to grant him union at the very formation taking place in the womb, knowing that he would never depart from his purpose concerning the virtues.

“You also cover him with the darkness of ignorance, saying that he knew nothing except what appeared to him through the Word united to him according to dignity. You say that he was so ignorant that, when he was tempted, he did not know who was tempting him; and you concede that he was not even free from sin *κατὰ διάνοιαν* (*kata dianoian*), that is, from sin of thought—let alone the saints. Yet you do not think that even sin of thought is sin. You do not shudder to teach that the passions of the soul were more troublesome to him than those of the body; for you say plainly: ‘And by stronger reason he subdued the pleasures.’ You concede that he was gradually purified through progress in the virtues and made daily more capable of receiving the divine blessings that were to come to him as a man. You baptize him so that from that time, and not before, he might be called perfect according to the virtue of the law, Christ perfect, and might undertake the evangelical life and complete it. Do you not also say that, for this reason, his time was shortened? For he might have grown weary over a longer period of time; and therefore, as though unwilling, you make him devise the short way of salvation—that is, the cross—and die for himself no less than for the whole world.”

Toward the end, Leontius reproaches Theodore for his fifteen books on the incarnation of the Word, which he calls invented and feigned wars against heretical opponents, but in reality undertaken against the truth. Since Theodore had resolved to attack the truth, and recognized that he could not complete the undertaking, he changed the title “War against the Truth” into the title “War against the Heretics.”

### 3.

After this he concludes the comparison between Nestorius and Theodore in a word. For he says that both denied the *Θεοτόκος* (*Theotokos*, “God-bearer”), and that from this denial both began to disclose their impiety. After the *συνουσίωσις* (*synousiōsis*, consubstantiality) of Apollinarius and Arius had been condemned, this one word alone contained both the whole substance of the faith and the distinction between the Catholic party and the heretical one. It is well known, moreover, how Nestorius revealed his heresy in his first sermon, namely by renouncing the title *Θεοτόκος*. Leontius reports that when this very title *Θεοτόκος* was condemned by Theodore at Antioch, the entire Church was thrown into turmoil, as was Nestorius himself, who was present—if we believe John of Antioch (*In epist. ad Nest.*).

Theodore, however, either out of reverence for the Church or in service to the times, issued public signs of repentance. Nestorius remained obstinate and retracted at Ephesus the false confession of *Θεοτόκος* that he had made in a public address at Constantinople, when he protested that he could not worship a God who was three months old.

### 4.

Now Leontius, about to bring forth excerpts from Theodore’s books against the incarnation, as he puts it, first speaks of his other works. He says that Theodore composed many perverse expositions of the sacred Scriptures of both Testaments, but more virulently of Paul’s Epistles and of the three Gospels of Matthew, John, and Luke. He also mentions an apology published for Basil against Eunomius, though it could appear to be an accusation of Basil and a defense of Eunomius. He further mentions an elaborate book against the Magi, that is, the Persian magicians, in which their portents are exposed as delusions. He passes over the remaining works in comparison with the books either entitled “On the Incarnation” or written against Apollinarius, and remarks that these could be obtained only with great difficulty, so carefully were they concealed. Perhaps for this reason Facundus and Hesychius of Jerusalem call them “mystical.”

The excerpts collect the points by which Theodore is convicted of blasphemy in five propositions:

1. That the Word did not truly become man, but merely appeared to do so.
2. That Christ is merely a man in whom the Word dwelt, from the very first formation.
3. That this man is the Son of God only by adoption.
4. That Christ’s mother is not the *Deipara* (“God-bearer”).
5. That two hypostases exist in him, even though unity of person is mentioned to satiety—but a unity such as exists between a man and his wife.

Having convicted Theodore by his own words, Leontius adduces statements agreeing with those of Diodore and Paul; then the composition concerning Paul and Nestorius proposed by Eusebius at Constantinople; and finally the statements of the Council of Antioch, of both Gregory—Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa—of Ephrem, Cyril, and Isidore the Hermit, all opposed to the heretics.

Before I finish speaking about Nestorius’s teacher, I cannot refrain from depicting, in its native colors, the idol which, according to Leontius, Theodore himself substituted for the true Christ—yet with no colors other than those employed by Theodore or Nestorius themselves.

One must therefore first imagine a man who, chosen by God as the savior of the whole human race, received—besides an outstanding natural disposition and the greatest inclination toward what is honorable—as much of God’s grace as God had determined to bestow upon any one human being, or even upon all human beings together.

One must next imagine this man, endowed with such grace, being continually governed by some divine person standing beside him, so that he might neither stray from what is true and right nor lead others into error, but might precede others on the way as their guide, by example and word.

One must also imagine a God who commands a man adorned with all the gifts commonly called charisms appropriate to him to devote himself ardently to works of piety and to transfer whatever merit he might thereby have acquired to the benefit of others. The Nestorians, however, do not speak of merit, but only of example: such a holy man would show what human power, with divine assistance, could accomplish, and by this demonstration would give the rest of humanity hope of completing virtue.

Such a leader of life, if one existed, could rightly be called the Son of God—not by nature, however, but by grace; not by generation, but by adoption. He would be called not merely “Son,” but also “only-begotten,” because he had been chosen through exceptional grace; indeed, he would also be called “first-born,” because he would stand out among many brothers and adopted sons of God.

He would likewise rightly be called Christ in an eminent sense: first, because, in comparison with the other saints who are called christs, he would have been anointed with a singular anointing upon the head as king, judge, and priest of the whole human race; and second, because he had been chosen by God for the greatest of all works, namely, the salvation of all.

With no less right he would be called Lord of all, even though he addressed others as brothers. For he would give his precious blood on behalf of all and, by paying the price, make the people already given to him his own.

He could also truly be called Emmanuel above the other saints, since God would work in him—as in a special *ἐργαστήριον* (*ergastērion*, workshop or instrument)—and dwell in him as in a uniquely holy temple.

He could also be called God: first, because he would be worshiped with the same honor as God, on account of *σχέσις* (*schesis*, relation) and *ἀναφορά* (*anaphora*, reference); and second, because he would act in God’s place, and indeed more excellently than Moses, since he would receive the judgment and governance of the whole human race.

This is the form of Christ sketched by Nestorius and Theodore; this is the idol that the Fathers cast down, using not only weapons taken from Scripture but also those furnished by reason. “No one,” says Proclus (*On the Right Faith*, ch. 2), “can save human beings except God; but this one would be a mere man.” Cyril says (*On Psalm 129*): “No one can save the human race from sins except one who is by nature incapable of sin; but this one would be capable of sin, because he is a creature.” “He was able to redeem,” Augustine cries (*Homily 6*), “who was unable to sell himself; but any creature can sell itself.” Eusebius, called Emisenus (*Book V Against Eutyches*): “He cannot intervene for slaves, being bound by the laws of slavery.” Vigilius Afer (*Book II to Thrasamund*, ch. 2): “In order that opposites might be brought together and the things above and below restored, this could happen in no other way than if such a mediator existed as, coming from heavenly things, might be united with earthly ones.” Fulgentius (*On Psalm 48*): “How could he be the universal giver of beneficence whom nature showed to be in need of another’s help?” Basil: “Only the God-man can give God propitiation for sins. What could anyone possess in this world so great that it could serve as a sufficient price for a soul?”

Those who say that some man could have been endowed by God with as much grace as he was capable of receiving, or as much as God had ever decided to bestow upon all human beings together, may appear to introduce something similar to the Nestorian fiction. They may further say that a man so munificently endowed could be made the head of his entire race and receive a mandate concerning the good works of each individual, to be referred to its members, and that he could thereby merit for them—even “condignly,” as they say—the grace by which they would be sanctified and released from sins, including that great sin by which Adam corrupted the whole nature in himself.

To this man, by excellence the Son of God through adoption, all the honors that the Nestorians heap upon their Christ can be applied, and all the offices prescribed by which the work of human restoration would be fulfilled.

Nevertheless, these doctors differ extraordinarily from the Nestorians—namely, as potentiality differs from actuality, as the schools say; that is, as what is formed by the mind alone differs from what is asserted to have been made in reality. The Socinians do not differ in this way; rather, they agree completely with Nestorius, whose heresy they have recalled from the underworld.

## CHAPTER V. On the Works of Nestorius

The whole of this volume speaks of the works of Nestorius that Mercator presents—works that are now to be set forth by four writers of the fifth century and one of the sixth: Cassian, Cyril, Arnobius the Younger, Gennadius, and Evagrius. Although the words of several of them have sometimes been introduced elsewhere when occasion arose, as in the preface to the excerpts and in various other places, I think they will not improperly be brought together here, so that the points requiring observation may be understood more easily in proportion as the matters to be observed have been laid more clearly before the eyes.

Not all those whom I have cited list all of Nestorius’s works; some mention more, others fewer. Cassian mentions three: the first letter to Pope Celestine and two sermons, the first and the second. See the notes on each of these three. For there we explained what Cassian quoted from each work and in which books he refuted the material quoted; nothing further need be added to his statements.

Cyril mentions several in one work. Thus he says in the preface to the first book of the *Contradictions*:

“I came upon a certain book composed by someone, in which many sermons had been gathered, arranged alphabetically and set out as though in order; nor was there any reason why it should not be preserved, if something of the sort had been said by its author that would otherwise disappear into oblivion. Perhaps I would have decided that I ought to remain silent and advise the others to do the same, so that such absurd and imprudent statements might not become known to many others and to our descendants. But since a multitude of blasphemies has been collected in that book, and much has been proclaimed and barked against the doctrines of the truth, how could it not have been almost necessary for us to gird ourselves and fight for the salvation of the readers? We had to ensure that they suffered no harm from the matter, but rather learned vigorously to repel the damage arising from wrongly spoken words.”

1. Concerning this testimony, observe first that the book mentioned by Cyril is the very one called by Mercator, in the Cyrillian excerpts, a codex composed from many quires. The excerpts were taken from the same book and codex. It is likewise the very book mentioned by Peter, chief secretary, when he says: “We also have before us the books of the most reverend Nestorius’s blasphemies, from one of which we have selected chapters which, if this holy council approves, we shall read aloud” (*Second Part of the Council of Ephesus*, act 1). For nearly everything read aloud at the council is found in Cyril’s five books of the *Contradictions*, in which the excerpts from the book in question are refuted. Nor should anyone find this agreement surprising, since the three items I have mentioned—the books of the *Contradictions*, the excerpts or extracts, and the chapters read aloud at the Council of Ephesus—are by the same author, namely Cyril, whose presbyter Peter, chief secretary, was.

2. Observe next that this same book was indicated by Gennadius when he wrote about Nestorius (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 53):

“After he had been endowed with the pontificate of the Church of Constantinople, his eloquence and abstinence commending him, he revealed himself as the open enemy of the Church whom he had long concealed. He wrote a book apparently on the incarnation of the Lord, constructed according to his perverse sense from sixty-two testimonies of divine Scripture; in it, whatever he asserted is shown in the catalogue of heretics.”

The book of which Cyril speaks was undoubtedly entitled *Περὶ ἐνανθρωπήσεως* (*Peri enanthrōpēseōs*, “On the Incarnation”). What Gennadius says concerning sixty-two testimonies of divine Scripture—or, as we have emended it, fifty-two, or at most seven—will be explained in the dissertation on Cyril’s books.

3. Observe, third, that this book contained only sermons assembled together, and not letters—neither those written to Pope Celestine nor those written to Cyril. Cyril, otherwise a diligent extractor, took nothing from the letters, although they contain much that is neither better than the sermons nor less opposed to sound faith. It is clear, moreover, that not all the sermons we possess were included in the book, because nothing from the twelfth or the following sermon is found in any of the excerpts, although both were infected with Nestorian poison—indeed, much worse than those preceding them—as appears in the report of the bishops who were sent from Alexandria to Nestorius with apostolic and synodal letters. Thus Theopemptus, bishop of Cabasa (*Council of Ephesus*, part II, act 1):

“After receiving the letters, he was not satisfied, but publicly, in a speech before the assembly, set forth the same doctrines as before, and doctrines even worse than these. Nor did he teach these things only before the letters were delivered; after he received them, he taught much worse things, and to this day he does not cease teaching them.”

4. Observe, fourth, that it is doubtful whether the first sermon, which was the worst of all, was contained in such a book. For nothing is known to have been extracted from it except perhaps what is read in section 9. It was observed in the notes that, on the basis of the passage itself, which seemed to me to disclose the matter by direct inspection (*αὐτοψία*, *autopsia*), these fragments had been drawn from the seventh sermon, from which Cyril extracted much else and incorporated it into the sermon. But the place of Arnobius, read subsequently and soon to be cited, compels me to correct the observation already printed.

Although it may seem strange that the first sermon, the head and source of the others, was not included in the codex under discussion, this may perhaps have happened because the book was published to lessen the odium that the first sermon had aroused. It should therefore have been without the very incentive and fuel of the evil being mitigated. I think the same reason caused the fourth sermon also to be absent, since none was more odious on account of its criticism of Proclus’s homily, which had been celebrated with immense praise. Its absence is inferred from the fact that nothing from it appears in the excerpts, although the extractors could have taken from it certain capital points relevant to the matter then at issue.

Arnobius the Younger mentions, besides the first sermon, two others, which we have confused with the third. He nevertheless reports much that is either missing from the printed texts or can shed light on our notes to those texts. For this reason the entire passage of Arnobius seemed worth transcribing as published by Fevardentius, while noting the errors that escaped the diligence of learned men.

“I have before me what Nestorius asserts. If the judges command it, I shall read it.”

The judges said: “Let what Arnobius offers be read, so that Serapion’s objection, if it is true, may be demonstrated.”

When the homily had been received, it was read at the relevant place as follows:

“Most holy Mary did not give birth to the Godhead; for what is born of flesh is flesh (John 3:6). A creature did not give birth to the Creator, but she gave birth to a man, a minister of the Godhead. The Holy Spirit did not build God the Word; for, he says, what was born from her is of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 1:20). Therefore, the Holy Spirit built a temple for God the Word from the Virgin.”

And shortly afterward:

“What was formed in the womb is not God in itself and according to itself.”

And shortly afterward:

“Let us honor in God the form of the *Θεοτόκος* [*Θεοδόχος*]”—that is, “God-bearer” [“God-receiver”].

Likewise, in another preaching, whose beginning is:

“Often, as I revolved in my mind the waves of life, considered the manifold mutability of earthly things and the snares scattered throughout life, I cried out in perplexity: ‘Who will be able to escape?’”

And shortly afterward:

“The divine nature separates the Spirit [the Spirit from the divine nature] who created his humanity; for whatever was born from Mary is of the Holy Spirit, he says. He also filled, according to righteousness, what had been created; what was manifested in the flesh was justified in the spirit (1 Timothy 3:16). He made him feared by demons, concerning whom the Lord himself says: ‘I cast out demons by the Spirit of God’ (Luke 11:20). He himself made his flesh a temple, whence the Baptist said: ‘I saw the Holy Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon him.’”

Likewise, shortly afterward:

“He who gave him elevation in heaven [into heaven]—for he says that he gave commandments to the apostles whom he chose through the Holy Spirit, and afterward he was taken up into heaven (Acts 1:2). This one, therefore, who bestowed such a dispensation upon Christ [bestowed glory upon him; he is said by these men to be Christ’s servant, who think him born merely in the flesh], they separate from the divine nature.”

Likewise, in another preaching, whose beginning is:

“No illness is worse for human minds than ignorance.”

And shortly afterward:

“But these people make God second after blessed Mary, when they assign the temporal mother to the creator of the ages, the Godhead [assign her to the creator of the ages, the Godhead]. Indeed, they do not even permit her to be the mother of Christ, although she is *Χριστοτόκος* (*Christotokos*, “Christ-bearer”). For, as they say, it was not human nature but God the Word who was born from her, and she who gave birth is not the mother of the one born. For how can she be the mother of one alien to her nature? If she is a mother, then what was born is humanity, not the Godhead. It is proper for a mother to give birth to something like her own essence [for the essence to give birth to something like itself]; otherwise she will not be a mother if she has not given birth to something like her own essence; or, if she is a mother, she has given birth to something like her own essence.”

Likewise, after other statements:

“For he is the God and creator of the months, and is not the offspring of months; he is the maker of holy Mary, not one later fashioned from the Spirit within her. But without my instruction, hear the angel saying to Joseph himself: ‘Take the child and his mother’ (Matthew 2:13). Therefore he said ‘of the child,’ not ‘of the Godhead.’”

Likewise, after these words:

“Do you want another testimony added for you? ‘The days were completed for her to give birth, and she gave birth to her firstborn Son’ (Luke 2:6). Behold whose mother the *Χριστοτόκος* was: the mother of the child whom Mary bore, not of the Godhead, which encompasses all things. Hear another testimony: ‘When the magi saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy, and entering the house they found the child with Mary his mother’ (Matthew 2:11). Everywhere the Virgin is proclaimed the mother of the child, not of the Godhead. Why, then, do you assign flesh as the mother of the Godhead?”

And shortly afterward:

“It befell the Virgin *Χριστοτόκος* to give birth to humanity, a ministry of the Godhead for God the Word [joined to God the Word].”

When the judges heard these words, they said: “The statements of Nestorius given thus far are sufficient.”

Before the words just cited, Gennadius had written:

“Nestorius the heresiarch, while he was a presbyter in the Church of Antioch and was regarded in teaching as an outstanding, extemporaneous declaimer, composed countless treatises of various *hypotyposeis* (outlines or expositions). In them, even then, he subtly and wickedly infused the poisons of the impiety later revealed—poisons that moral exhortation sometimes concealed” (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 52).

The countless treatises he mentions were consumed either by the shameful fate of their name or by the avenging flames of the emperors. Yet if they were all consumed—and it is not unbelievable that some, having falsified their lineage, may have substituted themselves for better parents—two sermons certainly attributed by Combefis to Athanasius (*Bibliotheca Patrum*, Greek and Latin, vol. I), on the resurrection and ascension of Christ, reveal themselves by the character of Nestorius: florid and at times almost poetic, elevating itself through metaphors and animated, as it were, by apostrophes, with testimonies from Scripture, generally taken in their literal sense except when twisted toward heresy, and periodically marked by a distinctive style.

Other sermons possess this same character, perhaps more of them than is commonly supposed: whether those attributed to Asterius, Amphilochius, and Basil of Seleucia; those rejected among Chrysostom’s spurious works, which bear no author’s name; or finally those concealed among the genuine treatises of Chrysostom through fraud, even from the learned censors of Chrysostom’s works. Nor is this surprising, since Nestorius attempted with the greatest zeal to imitate Chrysostom’s style and made himself more commendable to the people by that imitation. But neither does the place permit us to linger longer over this matter, nor does the scope of the argument. Perhaps we shall undertake the task at some future time.

Evagrius Scholasticus (*Ecclesiastical History*, book I, ch. 7) mentions three letters previously unknown to others. He calls them books and reports that Nestorius wrote them while in exile in the Oasis.

He mentions the first in these words:

“By chance I came upon a certain book published by Nestorius himself, in which an account of his affairs is contained. Thus Nestorius, the father of blasphemy, writes the following, among other things, to those who had brought charges against him—both because he had rashly attempted innovations and because he had imprudently demanded that a council be convened at Ephesus—and wished by other means to defend and justify his blasphemy:

‘I was compelled by necessity to undertake this. For when the Church was being torn apart, with one party affirming that Mary should be called *ἀνθρωποτόκος* (*anthrōpotokos*, “man-bearer”) and the other insisting on *Θεοτόκος* (*Theotokos*, “God-bearer”), I myself, so as not to offend on either side—either by affirming that Christ was not subject to death or by inclining to the other side and depriving him of immortality—invented this term *Χριστοτόκος* (*Christotokos*, “Christ-bearer”), by which Mary should be called.’”

Evagrius continues to relate from the same book matters that shed much light on the history. In that book he also shows that Theodosius initially refused to ratify Nestorius’s deposition because of the affection with which he embraced him. Later, when certain bishops from both factions had been sent from the city of Ephesus to Theodosius, Nestorius was granted permission to return to his monastery, which was situated before the gates of Antioch.

Nestorius himself also relates that he stayed in that place for four years, receiving various honors and various rewards, but was later banished to the Oasis by an edict of Theodosius. What was the chief matter, however, he completely concealed. Certainly, while living in that place, he did not cease from his blasphemy, to such an extent that John, bishop of Antioch, brought forward the opinion openly that Nestorius should be punished with perpetual exile.

He mentions the second and third in these words:

“Moreover, Nestorius writes another treatise, sharply and subtly, addressed to a certain Egyptian, concerning his relegation to the Oasis; in it he discusses these matters more fully, and so forth.”

[Col. 1157C] From a letter written by Nestorius concerning the matters that had long ago been agitated at Ephesus regarding the most holy religion, and sent to the prefect of the Thebaid:

“By the emperor’s decree we have been compelled to move to the Oasis, otherwise called Ibis.”

After inserting certain intervening material, he adds:

“After the Oasis mentioned above had been captured by barbarians and utterly devastated by fire and slaughter, we were released by those same barbarians, who, I do not know for what reason, suddenly took pity on us. Certain threatening declarations were added to terrify us, so that we might leave that region as quickly as possible; for, they said, the Mazices would immediately occupy it once we had departed.
