We therefore came into the Thebaid with certain captives whom the barbarians, out of mercy—for what they intended I cannot say—brought with us. Finally, each of these men was sent away to his own beloved home, while we hastened to Panopolis. For we feared that someone, since we were captives, might seize the opportunity to cause us trouble, either fabricating against us the charge of fugitives or trying to entangle us deceitfully in some other kind of accusation—for malicious people usually have an abundant supply of various calumnies.

“Therefore we beseech your Excellency to take care of our captivity, as the laws require, and not allow any captive to be handed over to crafty men for destruction; lest all posterity should sing this as a tragic refrain: that it is better to be led captive by barbarians than to flee to the Roman government for help.”

After adding an oath, he further requested this of him:

“Please allow us to remain in this dwelling to which we came from the Oasis when we had been released by the barbarians, so that whatever God has decreed concerning us may now befall us.”

From another letter of Nestorius written to the same man:

“Whether you regard this letter, written by us to your Magnificence, as a token of my affection for you or as a warning sent from father to son, I ask you to attend to the matters explained in it. They are indeed very many, though we have compressed them into as few words as possible.

“The Oasis, which is also called Ibis, was long ago utterly devastated when a multitude of nomads made an incursion into it.”

And shortly afterward:

“When these things had happened, your Magnificence, moved by I know not what reason or having seized upon what opportunity, ordered that we be taken by barbarian soldiers from Panopolis to a certain region called Elephantine, situated at the farthest edge of the province of the Thebaid. We were miserably dragged there by the soldiers I have mentioned. When we had been broken and crushed by the length of the journey, we again received from your Magnanimity an unwritten order to return to Panopolis. Thus, weakened by the hardships that befell us on so long and arduous a journey, our bodies afflicted by illness and weakened by old age, with our hands and sides also broken, we came once more to Panopolis, where, cut down by adverse circumstances and the bitter bite of pain, we almost breathed our last.

“Again, another written order from your Excellency brought us from Panopolis to a certain border of that region. When we thought that the orders issued against us had now reached their end and were awaiting the will of the most illustrious emperors concerning us, another truly cruel order was unexpectedly issued: that we should now be punished with exile for the fourth time.

“And somewhat farther on:

“Please be satisfied with these actions; let it be enough to decree so many exiles against one body. I beg you to rest content with the hardships that we have already received from your Magnificence. I ask you to leave the inquiry that must be conducted concerning us to our invincible emperors, before whom our case ought to have been set forth, as equity requires. These counsels are written by us to you as from a father to a son. But if you should again, as before, take these matters badly and with an embittered spirit, do what your will commands, provided that reason cannot overcome your will.”

Besides these letters, two others are found in the acts of the Council of Ephesus and of the Fifth Council. The first is Nestorius’s report to the emperor concerning the proceedings of the council on the day when he was deposed. It contains nothing unusual requiring it to be reproduced here, since it is readily available to anyone handling the records of the councils. Of the second, which was addressed to Alexander of Hierapolis, this brief fragment survives:

“The natures must remain in their own properties, and thus one glory must be understood in a manner marvelous and surpassing every rational account, and one Son confessed.”

And again:

“We do not make two persons into one person, but by one designation we signify two natures.”

## CHAPTER VI. On the Faith of Nestorius with Respect to Five Other Doctrines

Besides that notorious impiety of which Nestorius was convicted at Ephesus by his own testimony and condemned by the judgment of the entire Church, he was once suspected—and still is by some, neither few nor unlearned—of other errors. There are at least five such errors. The first concerns the procession of the Holy Spirit; the second, what I may call the mercenary divinity of Christ; the third, original sin; the fourth, the grace by which one lives well; and the last, the body of Christ in the Eucharist.

For he appeared to have asserted that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone; that a man merited union with the Word by his own works; that only the punishment of death passes into Adam’s descendants; that grace consists solely in the law, teaching, and example of Christ; and finally, that Christ’s body is indeed truly present in the Eucharist, but is not made present through that astonishing conversion which the Church calls transubstantiation, but solely through *συνάφεια* (*synapheia*, conjunction) or *συνουσίωσις* (*synousiōsis*, consubstantial union), which is more commonly called “impanation.”

### § I. What Nestorius Thought Concerning the Procession of the Holy Spirit

Nestorius was once thought guilty of denying the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, and even in our own age he is believed to have done so by men of great name and outstanding learning. The reasons why he was and is believed to have held this position were, first, that he had heard Theodore as his teacher; second, that he had Theodore’s fellow student and closest friend Theodoret as his associate; third, that he was joined to the Pelagians by a communion of doctrine, as the confessions of the Pelagians show; fourth, that he handed down Theodore’s creed to the peoples as a certain rule of faith, and even made it his own when he wished it to be the token of his communion; fifth, that he approved Theodoret’s criticism of Cyril’s anathemas all the more certainly because he had taken pains both to have it made and to disseminate it among the people; and finally, that he attacked the Arians and Macedonians as though they were his most bitter enemies—in his customary manner, that is, with an uncontrolled passion for contradiction.

For Theodore is regarded as the father and author of this heresy. Theodoret openly and vigorously defended it after receiving it from his teacher Theodore. The Pelagians undoubtedly followed it; in their statements concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit in their professions of faith, they used no words other than those copied from Theodore’s creed. Theodore’s creed indicates this clearly when it says:

“*καὶ οὔτε Υἱὸν νομίζομεν, οὔτε διὰ Υἱοῦ τὴν ὕπαρξιν εἰληφός*.”

“But we do not consider him [the Holy Spirit] to be the Son, nor to have received his subsistence through the Son.”

The criticism of the ninth anathema reveals the same doctrine openly, when it rejects as something impious and blasphemous the statement:

“*ἅγιον Πνεῦμα ἐξ Υἱοῦ, ἤδε δι’ Υἱοῦ τὴν ὕπαρξιν ἔχειν*.”

“[That] the Holy Spirit is from the Son, or has his subsistence through the Son.”

Finally, the Arians together with the Macedonians stated the Catholic proposition, though not in a Catholic sense: namely, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Someone may ask in passing why the Arians and Macedonians either held, or rather professed among Catholics, this view concerning the matter. In my opinion, they did so in order that they might establish their error—classifying the Holy Spirit among creatures—by means of three assumed principles. First, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Word, as the tradition of the forefathers held; next, that all things except the Son himself and the Father were made through the Word, according to the Evangelist’s statement; finally, that it is a common human notion that whatever has been made is a creature. For they concluded: “Therefore, if the Spirit proceeds from the Word, and whatever proceeds from the Word has been made, and everything made is a creature, then the Spirit is certainly a creature.”

Although these considerations arouse no slight suspicion—and the very weighty authority of great men such as Bellarmine, Petavius, and Allatius [Col. 1160A] considerably increases it—I am nevertheless far from readily assenting to the view. For I do not remember ever having read anything in Nestorius’s books that could confirm the opinion of such eminent men; indeed, I seem to see something that weakens it. In his contradiction of the ninth anathema, Nestorius could have attacked that Cyrillian statement which Theodoretus rebuked in such insulting terms; instead, he preferred to introduce something obscure concerning the mediation of the Holy Spirit, or the agency by which Christ was joined to the Word and by which he performed miracles among human beings and exercised power over demons, rather than say anything at all about the procession of the Spirit from the Son—a matter on which Cyril had openly expressed his opinion, not only in that anathema but also in the letter to which the anathemas were appended. For he had written:

> “Although the Spirit exists in his own individual subsistence, and is understood as having his own personal property according to what he is as Spirit and not as Son, nevertheless he is not alien to him. For he has been called the Spirit of truth, and Christ is the truth; hence he proceeds from him just as he proceeds from God the Father.”

[Col. 1160B]

§ II. What Nestorius thought concerning the union with the Word bestowed on Christ in recompense for his works

We absolved Nestorius, in the first chapter, from suspicion regarding the second of the errors that consisted in division, where we showed that the popular accusation arose from the belief that Nestorius held precisely the same opinion concerning the manner of the Incarnation as Paul of Samosata and Leporius, although he differed from them extraordinarily with respect to the time at which the natures were united.

Nor did this false opinion about Nestorius deceive only Westerners, apparently under the influence of Cassian; it also misled not a few Easterners and, astonishingly, at one point even Cyril himself. For Nestorius seemed to Cyril to deny that the Virgin should be called the Mother of God (*Theotokos*, Θεοτόκος) for the reason that he believed Christ had earned his union with the Word through his works, as a reward for his labor. This, however, happened at the beginning, when the heresy was still obscure and was revealing itself piecemeal, timidly or rather craftily, and thus deceiving everyone of sound judgment, including Cyril himself. Once the matter had subsequently become clearer, Cyril abandoned this opinion. See what was said in the seventh dissertation on the first part of the *Works of Mercator*, when a certain epitaph attributed to Prosper was brought back under examination—an epitaph which the poet wrote, with greater elegance than truth, as an inscription for the common tomb of the Nestorian and Pelagian heresies.

§ III. Nestorius’s opinion concerning original sin investigated

It is not equally easy to reach a judgment concerning Nestorius’s mind in this third area as in the preceding ones. The charge of the third error—that there is no transmission of sin, but that only the punishment of death, without guilt, passes from Adam to his descendants—can neither easily be dismissed nor clearly confirmed. There are conjectures on both sides, neither few nor slight; and there are also conflicting testimonies from very weighty authorities on either side.

In defense against the charge stands, first, the testimony of Pope Celestine, who wrote to Nestorius: “We have read how well you hold the doctrine of original sin: how you have asserted that nature itself is liable, and that he who descends from the race of the debtor rightly pays the debt” (*First Part of the Council of Ephesus*, ch. 15).

Next stands that very statement of Nestorius to which Celestine directed his attention in writing: “Christ assumed the person of a debt-bearing nature, and through it paid the debt as Adam’s son; for the one who pays the debt had to be descended from the race of him who had once contracted it” (*Sermon* 7, no. 14).

Then there are these words from the same sermon (ibid., no. 19):

> “In achieving this triumph over the devil’s victory, Christ says: ‘Now is the judgment of this world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out’ (John 12:31). For just as the devil held the guilt of the first-formed man against all his posterity and had an original claim, so nature, having possessed in Christ the guiltless first-fruits of its own mass, strove against the devil and conquered him by the very defenses on which the adversary relied. For in Christ it most justly brings forth against him the guiltless origin of its first-fruits, if the devil introduces the earlier grounds of guilt derived from Adam. This is what Paul says: ‘Christ died for our sins; indeed, he also rose again, who is at the right hand of God and intercedes for us’ (Rom. 8:34).”

Finally, there are the four sermons against the Pelagians. In the first, the offspring of human nature are called accursed and condemned; the difficulty of childbirth, once natural, is also said to have become a curse in human bodies because of sin. Even the earth itself is charged with something like iniquity because it does not answer the sweat of those who cultivate it, and this too is attributed to Adam’s sin. Moreover, the catechumen is urged to receive the grace of baptism for this reason: “Lest, bound by the same evils by which Adam was bound, he too should be plunged into the same and even greater ones, and carry away with him the punitive sentences pronounced against nature” (*Sermon* 1 against the Pelagians).

In the second sermon (no. 7) we find the following:

> “The devil brought forth sin from Adam like a bond of indebtedness; Christ, on the other hand, from flesh without sin, strove to cancel this debt. The devil was rehearsing the condemnation that had proceeded through Eve against the whole of nature; Christ, however, was setting forth the mortification that had come upon the human race through blessed Mary.”

And later (ibid., no. 10):

> “The catechumen remains a debtor, as one alien to him who cancelled the bond. When his soul has departed from the flesh, the devil, mingling with the angels who escort souls, says: ‘Why are you taking away this soul of mine, which is still in existence? You are invading my right, my possession; you are invading my debtors.’ And if what happens among human beings also seems relevant, this plea concerning the catechumens will prevail, with the devil adding: ‘They close the doors of the churches to them on earth, while you come from heaven to meet them and receive them. You are trying, O angels, to use force against my right. What common relationship do you seem to have with catechumens? They have not been reborn of water and the Spirit, so that you may lead them to the kingdoms of heaven; they have not renounced the inheritance that is subject to me.’”

In the third sermon (no. 2):

> “A twofold mortality was raging against us: one affecting the mortal nature made through sin; the other arising from the rejection of knowledge. For ignorance of God bears the likeness of the insensibility that results from death. The devil therefore became the author of both deaths; Christ, overthrowing him, lifted our life from both through mortification.”

In the fourth sermon (no. 4):

> “Just as human nature, taking its foundation in Adam, collapsed when that foundation fell and came under the hand and power of the devil who cast Adam down, so, since the faith of the Church has the Lord Christ as its foundation, the power of that same foundation remains immovable, secure, and unshaken through the firmness of its head, which cannot be torn away.”

And near the end:

> “Let us love the restorer of fallen nature; let us embrace him who cut down the strength and sinews of our common enemy,” etc.

These arguments appear extremely strong at first sight, but they themselves reveal their weakness if what is said is examined somewhat more carefully.

To begin with Celestine’s words: however much they may seem to praise Nestorius’s faith, they nevertheless show that the pontiff had not entirely removed every suspicion from his mind. For he says: “What have you in common with those who have been condemned for denying these things? Things opposed to one another never come together without suspicion. They would finally be expelled if they also displeased you.”

Next, Nestorius himself may increase the pontiff’s suspicion, for he clearly indicates that the debt of death by which he says the whole nature is bound belongs to the body, not to the soul. Thus, he says (*Sermon* 7, no. 20):

> “Our liberated mass, clothed by Christ, intercedes, entirely free from every sin, and an unjust defense arises against our punishment, which the one who was first formed imposed upon his race from the beginning. This is the function of the assumed man: that a human being might dissolve through the flesh the corruption he had earned through the flesh.”

Moreover, what else do the four sermons against the Pelagians accomplish than to say that bodily death, the sufferings of women in childbirth, and the labors of farmers originated in the sin of the first human being? Nowhere, however, does he teach that this is transmitted to later generations.

Add that, when he mentions the bond brought by the devil against human beings, he remembers only death (*Sermon* 2 against the Pelagians, no. 5):

> “The devil, however, brought forth that which is against nature—the bond that is written: ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall go’ (Gen. 3:19). And from this he pressed on, consuming the generations of human beings by death.”

Indeed, he is not obscurely Pelagianizing concerning the reception of baptism for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (*ibid.*, no. 9):

> “The necessary sacrament of the saving bath confers this benefit upon all. For whoever has been washed in baptism becomes the household member, the bodily sharer, and the intimate of him who cancelled that bond, and becomes with him an inhabitant of heaven. ‘Where I am,’ he says, ‘there also is my minister.’”

And later:

> “They [the catechumens] have not been reborn of water and the Spirit, so that you may lead them to the kingdoms of heaven.”

Finally, in the third and fourth sermons he does indeed mention a twofold death, of body and soul, whose author is said to be the devil; and he also teaches that nature collapsed through Adam like the ruin of a foundation. These statements seem to contribute greatly to establishing belief in original sin. Yet in reality they accomplish nothing more than this: that the first human being sinned, and that the death which was the punishment of sin passed to his descendants together with the example of sinning; that the human race became subject to the tyranny of the devil, the prince of death; and that Christ rescued us from this tyranny and made us participants in immortality and the kingdom of heaven. Augustine testifies that many Pelagians confessed all these things after the decree of Honorius and the *Tractoria* of Zosimus.

[Col. 1162C]

Although these and other considerations produce an uncertain conjecture through their mutual collision, in my judgment the synod of which we spoke in the notes to Nestorius’s second letter makes Nestorius’s conviction certain and explicit. For at that synod, with Nestorius presiding, an anathema was pronounced against the defenders of original sin, and the Catholic dogma was rejected among the impieties of Mani and Marcion. And indeed, what else could have been expected either from the disciple of Theodore or from the patron of the Coelestians?

“Why, then,” someone may ask, “did he speak publicly, in the presence of the very people with whom he agreed in the Church, not merely once or in passing, but three or four times, in extended discourse, against men whose opinion he shared?” I think that this wily man did so for several reasons.

First, lest he should turn against himself the anger that the Western Church—where the Pelagians had been expelled and whose favor he was seeking—had conceived against obstinate heretics. Second, lest he should appear to offend against the decree of the emperor Honorius, written against such men and also published in the East. Third, lest he should be thought to disapprove the sentence pronounced against Pelagius by Theodotus, bishop of Antioch, by whom he had been ordained. Fourth, lest he should do anything contrary to the memory either of Atticus, his predecessor, who had refuted the envoys of those same bishops and expelled Coelestius from the imperial city, or of Sisinnius, who had followed Atticus’s judgment. Fifth, lest he should alienate the minds of the bishops of Cilicia Secunda, whose goodwill it greatly concerned him to secure, since they had assembled a synod and pronounced sentence against Julian. Sixth, so that, as Mercator suggests (*Preface to the Sermons of Nestorius*), he might imitate the bad faith of the Mopsuestene, who had warmly loved and agreed with those men—even publishing books in agreement with them—but had condemned them verbally in the aforementioned synod of his province, in order to avoid envy. Seventh, so that he might afterward make use of the Coelestians’ assistance with greater security, the less he seemed outwardly to favor them. Finally, lest he should have to bear the odium of two errors at once, since he was almost overwhelmed by suspicion of one of them.

§ IV. What Nestorius’s opinion was concerning the means of divine grace through Christ

[Col. 1163A]

We discussed the fourth error, which concerns the means of divine grace, in the notes to the third sermon against the Pelagians. There we observed that Nestorius remembered a twofold death contracted through sin and destroyed by Christ, and defined one as the soul’s separation from the body, the other as its separation from God.

> “A twofold mortality was raging against us: one affecting the mortal nature made through sin; the other arising from the rejection of knowledge. The devil became the author of both deaths; Christ, overthrowing him, lifted our life from both through mortification, raising the soul through life-giving commandments and, through the resurrection, renewing and restoring what is mortal” (*Sermon* 3 against the Pelagians).

Concerning these words, it should be noted that when Nestorius defines the death of the soul as the rejection of knowledge, he places the soul’s life not in charity but in knowledge. Thus he limits Christ’s grace to life-giving commandments—not to the diffusion of charity, that is, to the law and illumination of the mind, rather than to grace and the inspiration of the will. All of these are plainly Pelagian doctrines.

For this reason he said that the Word became incarnate and dwelt in the human being whom he assumed in order to restore the human being—that is, the image of the divine nature cast down into corruption. What corruption he meant, however, he immediately explains by adducing the Apostle’s testimony: “For by a man came death, and by a man the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15:12). It was likewise for this reason that, when he showed that the curses God had cast upon the human race had been removed by Christ, he mentioned most of the curses as pertaining to the body, but none as pertaining to the soul.

This, finally, was why he nowhere in his Works mentioned inward grace. Nor could he have done so. For whoever believes that Christ is merely a human being must, as Cyril often repeats, deny the true redemption of the human race by which we are freed from sin, and place the whole fruit of the Incarnation in Christ’s example. This is the most destructive poison of the Pelagian plague.

§ V. Whether Nestorius erred concerning the manner in which Christ’s body is made present under the Eucharistic symbols

Just as the investigation of the fifth error, concerning the Eucharist, will be more remarkable because of its novelty, so it also appears more laborious because of the preconceived opinion of certain people. Nevertheless, it is necessary both for Nestorius’s case and for that of others. For Nestorius, because, as Cyril says:

> “Nestorius and those who think as he does foolishly destroy the power of the mystery” (Νεστόριος καὶ οἱ τὰ αὐτοῦ φρονοῦντες παραλύουσιν ἀμαθῶς τοῦ μυστηρίου τὴν δύναμιν).

For others, because among controversialists and scholastic theologians there have been some who said that the Nestorians held the correct opinion concerning the Eucharist, although they erred concerning the union of the flesh with the Word. It is not difficult to understand the meaning either of Cyril’s words or of the doctors I have mentioned; it will certainly become clear shortly, after the remaining matters, which belong to a more recondite doctrine, have been explained.

To explain them, it should first be observed that Cyril both held among his own people and persuaded the Fathers at Ephesus that three unions must be considered in participation in the Eucharist: one of Christ’s flesh with the Word, immediate and physical; another of our flesh with Christ’s flesh, likewise immediate and physical; and finally, a mediated union of our body with the Word, from whom, as from the source of all life, there would flow not only spiritual life into the soul but also immortality into the body.

Accordingly, Cyril placed the power and efficacy of the Eucharist in this: that we truly eat flesh made life-giving (ζωοποιός) through its union with the Word, who is capable of giving life to all things (τῷ τὰ πάντα ζωοποιεῖν ἰσχύοντι). He therefore rightly accused Nestorius of weakening the life-giving power (ζωοποιός) of the Eucharist by removing the natural union of the flesh with the Word (ἑνώσει φυσικῇ).

[Col. 1164A]

For if there is no true union of the flesh with the Word, the source of life, then there is no true union of the Word with our flesh either; and thus immortality does not flow from the Word into our body through communion. Yet the theologians whom I praised did not say without reason that the Nestorians held the correct opinion concerning the Eucharist and had not departed from Cyril’s view. Cyril was speaking of the Eucharist’s effective power, which he complained Nestorius had weakened; they were speaking of the real presence of Christ’s flesh with the symbols, a presence which Nestorius, together with the whole Church of his own time and of earlier times, confessed.

Nestorius’s faith on this point is demonstrated by many other things, but especially by what is contained in Sermons 2, 8, and 9. There he says that Christ’s flesh is eaten by us, though not in the same way as the invisible food of minds, the Divinity. For, when explaining Christ’s statement, “Whoever eats me shall live,” he asked whom we should eat: the Divinity or the flesh. His purpose was to show that the natures had not been confused or converted through the Incarnation, since one is eaten—namely, the flesh—while the other is not eaten, namely, the Divinity. He therefore takes it as an acknowledged and unquestionable fact that Christ’s flesh is eaten by us at the sacred table. Otherwise, from the fact that the Divinity is not eaten and the flesh is eaten, he would have concluded very foolishly that the natures in Christ had not been confused or changed into one another through the Incarnation. The immediate reply would have been that both are eaten only by the mouth of the mind, and neither by the mouth of the flesh.

This is also supported by what is found in Sermon 7, where Nestorius treats the same argument and says:

> “Nor do we proclaim the death of the Word of God when we are nourished by the Lord’s body and blood; for the nature of God receives the sacrifice, but is not itself sacrificed.”

At that point he concludes that the natures are unconfused (ἀσύγχυσις) and unaltered (ἀμεταβλησία), from the fact that the Divinity is not sacrificed but the flesh is sacrificed in the offering that takes place when we are nourished by the Lord’s body and blood. For how could one be sacrificed and the other not, if either both had come together into one or one had passed into the other? He took as the starting point of his reasoning the fact that Christ’s body is daily both sacrificed and eaten amid the sacred mysteries. Unless he had assumed this as indisputable and accepted in his own age, he would certainly have incurred the criticism of all his hearers.

Finally, that Nestorius agreed with Cyril concerning the real presence of Christ’s body with the symbols is clear from this: otherwise Cyril, who was an energetic defender of such a presence, would have sharply rebuked him for dissenting. Everywhere, after all, Cyril derived from the eating of Christ’s flesh an argument to establish his own position.

Moreover, what I have said about Cyril’s being an energetic defender of the real presence requires little proof, since he was sometimes criticized for it even by the Calvinists themselves. Who could have stated the position more clearly than Cyril, either in his exposition of the eleventh anathema or in his response to Nestorius’s question about whom we eat, the Divinity or the flesh?

> “Just as that life-giving body of the Word himself, which he made his own through a true union surpassing both understanding and speech, gives life, so we too, who enjoy participation in that holy flesh and his blood, are altogether given life. The Word dwells in us not only in a divine manner, through the Holy Spirit, but also in a human manner, through that holy flesh and his precious blood.”

And later:

> “He dwells in us and makes us conquerors of corruption, while he descends into our bodies, as I have said, also through his flesh, which is true food” (*Book IV of the Contradictions*, ch. 5).

Since these things are so, I cannot sufficiently marvel at the audacity of Albertinus, the Calvinist Sacramentarian, who attempted to draw Nestorius, however unwillingly, over to his own side. After first making Nestorius a Catholic instead of a heretic with respect to the doctrine of the Incarnation, he then tried to transform him from a defender of the real presence into a Sacramentarian like himself, on the basis of these words from Sermon 2 (no. 10):

> “Look at what is set forth concerning his lordly body: ‘Whenever you eat this bread, of which the body is the antitype’” (βλέπε περὶ τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ τοῦ δεσποτικοῦ τὸ πρόκειμενον, Ὁσάκις ἂν ἐσθίητε ΤΟΝ ΑΡΤΟΝ ΤΟΥΤΟΝ, οὗ ἐστι τὸ σῶμα ἀντίτυπον).

He argues as follows (*Book II on the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, p. 772, latest edition):

> “By ‘THIS BREAD’ he must necessarily understand either the accidents of bread without the substance of bread, or true bread in its substance, or the Lord’s own body. For no fourth possibility can be imagined here. He cannot designate the first, both because it would be utterly absurd to say, ‘Whenever you eat these accidents,’ since accidents are not food, and because the passage concerns that bread which the Lord had called his body; yet it was not accidents that he had said were his body, as even the adversaries themselves admit. Nor can he mean the third. For when he says that the LORD’S BODY is the ANTITYPE OF THAT BREAD—that is, the thing or reality represented by that bread as its type—and since, as Cyril notes, a TYPE IS NOT THE REALITY THAT IT REPRESENTS but its image, by THAT BREAD he cannot mean the Lord’s own body. It remains, therefore, that he means true substantial bread, which consequently, when it is eaten—that is, after consecration—remains substantially what it was before.”

There seem to me to be three faults in this reasoning: the first a fault of logic; the second, bad faith; and the third, a perverse understanding either of the Nestorian position or of the question at issue.

Is it not a fault of logic, when enumerating what can be signified by the expression “THIS BREAD,” to list three possibilities while omitting a fourth which is obvious to everyone in this matter and completely settles the question—namely, Christ’s body clothed in the symbols, or Christ himself hidden under the appearance of bread and wine? Hence Christ himself said that he was eaten: “Whoever eats me shall live”; and that he was the bread he would give: “I am the bread that came down from heaven.”

Is it not likewise bad faith to know perfectly well that Nestorius maintained only this much: that the Eucharistic bread was not the Divinity but a figure of the body, whatever kind of figure it might be, and yet to conclude from this that Nestorius said this same bread was not merely a figure—which alone would have served the argument—but that it was an empty figure, which was less relevant to the matter? Moreover, why should ἀντίτυπον in this passage be said to mean something other than “sign,” and τύπος something other than “figure,” when the one is substituted for the other and the passage requires no meaning other than that of τύπος? Add that a thing can at times be its own ἀντίτυπον if it assumes a twofold appearance and one appearance is the sign of the other; hence arose the distinction between an empty and a full sign.

Finally, does he not understand the Nestorian opinion and question poorly when, although the controversy concerns the real presence, he speaks about the manner of the presence; and although Nestorius was an “impanator,” as will shortly be shown, he maintains that Nestorius did not defend the marvelous conversion that the Catholic Church upholds against the Consubstantialists (Συνουσιασταί)?

But it is now time to demonstrate what I have just said: although Nestorius believed that Christ’s body was actually present under the symbols, offered in sacrifice and eaten in communion, he nevertheless erred concerning the manner of its presence, believing that Christ’s body was joined to the bread through mere conjunction (συνάφεια) and consubstantiation (συνουσίωσις), which is now commonly called impanation.

To make this clear, I think two matters must be observed more carefully. First, there is a close relationship between the Incarnation and the Eucharist, so that the Fathers call the latter a kind of extension and continuation of the former. For just as through the Incarnation the Word is united to humanity, so through consecration Christ’s body is united to the symbols. In both cases, through an ineffable union, there is one person of God and man and one hypostasis of Christ’s body and the symbols. In both, God and Christ’s body are hidden: God under the appearance of a human being, and Christ’s body under the appearance of the symbols. Through the former God truly becomes man; through the latter Christ’s body truly becomes food. In the Incarnation, because of the marvelous union of the two natures (ἕνωσις), their properties are mutually communicated, so that God is said to have suffered, and the human being to be omnipotent, and so forth. In the Eucharist, because of the sacramental conjunction of Christ’s flesh with the symbols, the flesh is said to be touched and the symbols to give life, and so forth.

[Col. 1166A]

To demonstrate true faith in the Incarnation, this one statement is sufficient, if understood in its proper sense: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14). Likewise, to establish faith in the Eucharist, this single saying of Christ is sufficient when accepted in its proper sense: “This is my body.” Why should I pursue the other points more closely, when everything is readily apparent from these to anyone?

It should next be observed that there is a considerable affinity between the Nestorians and the Sacramentarians, the opponents of transubstantiation. In my view, it consists in four respects: both use the same principles, are pressed by the same arguments, seek the same evasions, and express their error in the same formulas.

These principles are certainly common to both groups:

1. Neither acknowledges any union—whether of the natures in Christ or of the parts in the Eucharist—other than a moral union, called conjunction (συνάφεια) and a mere relation (σχέσις), lest a greater union should produce, as they suppose, a confusion (σύγχυσις) of the things united.

2. Each admits two hypostases in its respective composite, lest the things united should either become imperfect or suffer damage to their essence.

3. Each denies that anything can rest upon an alien subsistence, lest either humanity should be believed to be substantially assumed by the Word or accidents to exist without a subject.

4. Each rejects every union greater than a relational union (σχετική), lest Christ’s flesh should either be coextensive with the Word or be immense.

Both are pressed by numerous arguments, but especially by one drawn from these words of the Evangelist and of Christ: “The Word became flesh” and “This is my body”—provided that these statements are understood, as they ought to be, both properly and according to the tradition of the Fathers, the common opinion of the faithful, and their agreement with the other passages of Scripture in which the same matter is treated.

They pursue the same evasions. First, both obstinately defend the view that the scriptural passage brought against them is figurative; and, astonishingly, both allege the same figure. Next, both, if they do not openly despise the authority of the Fathers, at least diminish it. Finally, both wish the dispute to be settled by Scripture alone. Yet they bring forward the same passages from it, and—what is astonishing—corrupt them by fraud and twist them by force. It is neither difficult nor necessary to demonstrate this point one by one, since anyone who reads the books of both groups will encounter testimonies that establish what I say by their evident force no less than by their number.

Both speak in the same manner: the former about Christ, the latter about the Eucharist. The Nestorians of old denied that, when Christ was shown, one could properly say, “This is God”; rather, they said, it was merely an image of God, or something of that sort. When the Eucharist is displayed, the Sacramentarians forbid anyone to dare assert that it is properly Christ’s body, calling it instead a sign, figure, antitype, and so forth. The Nestorians admitted that Christ could be called God, but only homonymously (ὁμωνύμως); the Sacramentarians likewise say that the Eucharist may indeed be called Christ’s body, but only homonymously, and so forth.

[Col. 1166D]

Finally, it should be observed that although Nestorius acknowledged two complete, unconfused, and unmixed natures in Christ—which was Catholic—he nevertheless joined them only by relation (σχέσις), and not according to hypostasis (καθ’ ὑπόστασιν), which is foreign to the faith. He thus stood midway between the advocates of hypostatic union and the advocates of confusion, and therefore carefully avoided appearing to approach either side, even in a single word. Since he clearly understood that nothing is more closely related or more similar than Christ and the Eucharist, he thought that both should be understood and discussed in the same way. He feared that, if he said anything incautious about one mystery, it might damage his position concerning the other.

Thus, either he was in reality a Sacramentarian of the kind now represented by the Lutherans, or at least he can be regarded as laboring under the gravest suspicion of being one. Accordingly, Cyril did not write without reason that Nestorius and others who held the same opinion as he did “destroy the power of the mystery” (παραλύειν τὴν τοῦ μυστηρίου δύναμιν), since that power lies not only in the real presence of the body but also in its almost substantial union with the symbols, comparable to a hypostatic union—a union that cannot occur without transubstantiation.

Four considerations remarkably strengthen this suspicion.

First, there is what is read in Leontius (*Book III Against the Nestorians and Eutychians*, no. 6) concerning the followers of Theodore of Mopsuestia. As has often been said, Theodore was the common teacher of Nestorius and Theodoretus. When someone took offense at the manner they followed and complained that it was impossible to maintain communion both with them and with the Church, since the Church treated the sacred mysteries one way and they treated them another, they replied:

> “You should not be troubled by this arrangement. For the bread set forth IN THE TYPE OF CHRIST’S BODY did not participate in any greater blessing than the bread sold in the marketplace, or than the twisted cakes offered by the Philomarianite women” (Epiphanius treats of the Philomarianites in *Heresy* 78, no. 23), “who offer them in the name of Mary.”

You see how those Nestorians eventually declined little by little toward the Sacramentarians, such as the Calvinists. Once one has fallen into a single error, the descent into others is easy.

We have restored this passage, which had been corrupted through the carelessness of copyists, by adding the negative particle that the sense plainly requires concerning the bread set forth as a type, the twisted cakes of the women who sacrifice to Mary, and the speakers’ purpose.

Second, Theodoretus, who was especially devoted to Nestorius and, when writing the *Eranistes*, was likewise erring with him concerning the mystery of Christ, seemed to men of great name and learning—Cardinals Cusanus and Alanus, the theologians Gregory of Valencia and Gamachaeus, and even the Roman editors who were the first to publish the Greek text of the dialogues of the *Eranistes*—not to have held a sufficiently clear opinion concerning the union of Christ’s body with the symbols in favor of the Catholic truth of transubstantiation. Indeed, carried toward the opposite position by the impulse of a related error, he seemed to incline in that direction.

Third, the Calvinist Sacramentarians, weighed down by the burden of their own error, in turn incline toward Nestorius—if not all of them, at least most. I learned of this by reputation and then, through the report of a man distinguished no less by learning than by rank, read it stated without concealment in a work published by a Calvinist minister. For he expressly denies, and not without several arguments, that the Virgin can properly be called the Mother of God, and he asserts that his own people today refrain from calling her the Mother of God.

Fourth, Hilary states in Book VIII of *On the Trinity* that the flesh and blood, once received and consumed, bring it about that we are in Christ and Christ in us. He then adds:

> “Is this not the truth? Let it certainly not be true for those who deny that Christ Jesus is truly God,” etc.

It is as though he were saying: No one can deny that the true flesh and true blood of Christ—that is, of the God-man—are received and consumed, unless he likewise denies that Christ Jesus is truly God.

[Col. 1167]

# SECOND DISSERTATION: ON THE SYNODS HELD IN THE CASE OF NESTORIUS, FROM THE TIME WHEN NESTORIUS STIRRED UP DISTURBANCES UNTIL HE WAS DEPORTED TO THE OASIS AND DIED THERE

[Col. 1167B]

Far more synods of bishops were held in Nestorius’s case before his deportation to the Oasis than is commonly believed. I think I can demonstrate fifteen, or even sixteen, although I shall remain within the period specified in the title. Four were convened at Rome, an equal number at Alexandria, and two at Ephesus—the ecumenical synod and the schismatic one. Four were held at Constantinople. There were at least two held by the Easterners: the first at Antioch, before the peace of the Churches, when they continued to rage against Cyril; and the later one at Beroea, at the house of Acacius, when they deliberated about peace at the emperor’s command. Some of those included in this enumeration may, however, have been ordinary meetings, or may even have been summoned for other reasons.

Concerning each of them, I think that nothing need be noted briefly except what escaped the diligence of others, exhausted by extensive works, or what careless writers let slip contrary to the truth of history.

I. Synod held at Rome by Celestine, supreme pontiff, on the occasion of Nestorius’s letters sent from Constantinople, in the consulship of Dionysius and Florentius, in the year of Christ 429, after the paschal celebrations.

This synod is obscure, and, I believe, there is no mention of it anywhere except in Cyril’s first letter to Nestorius:

> What shall I do at last? For it is time to speak—or rather, to confer with Your Reverence—when the most reverend and most religious Coelestine, bishop of the Romans, asks about certain papers which somehow reached Rome, together with all the venerable bishops who were with him, since it is uncertain whether they are regarded as belonging to Your Religion; for they write to us in a state of intense indignation, etc.  
> (*Letter 1 of Cyril to Nestorius*)

That these venerable bishops had assembled in synod, and had not merely happened to form some casual gathering with Coelestine, is shown clearly enough by these words: “when Coelestine, bishop of the Romans, asks, together with all the bishops who were with him.” But the following words prove it explicitly: “For they write to us in a state of intense indignation.” They indicate that a joint letter had been written to Cyril by the bishops who were then with Coelestine. And what else could this mean than that a synodical letter had been issued? For letters jointly written with the supreme pontiff were not ordinarily sent except by bishops lawfully assembled.

The date of the synod is established by the fact that, after receiving the Roman letters, Cyril wrote to Nestorius in the autumn, as will become clear in the following chapter. The synod, therefore, must have been convened at Rome either at the beginning of summer or thereabouts.

It was not an ordinary synod, of the kind convened before Lent and in autumn; yet neither was it an extraordinary synod—that is, one summoned by a *tractoria*. Otherwise it would not have remained unknown. Rather, it was an *ἐνδημοῦσα* synod, consisting of bishops who happened at that time to be present at Rome together with the city’s clergy. Such synods were often held whenever some matter of importance arose.

At it, those papers of Nestorius were read and rejected which had been brought from Constantinople to Rome and had given occasion for the synod. They contained Nestorius’s first three sermons, from which had arisen disturbances in the imperial city as great as those described by Socrates (Book VII) and Cyril (in his letter to Pope Coelestine).

[Col. 1168D]

It is uncertain who sent the papers to the apostolic see: perhaps the *apocrisiarii* either of the apostolic see or of the Alexandrian Church, or some other person inflamed by zeal for the faith. What if it was Marius Mercator himself? He was certainly residing at Constantinople at that time; he was then presenting the case against Nestorius, a supporter of the Pelagians, in whatever way he could; and he was then translating Nestorius’s sermons into Latin, so that the impiety of the heretic might become known to the men of his own people.

The papers were sent translated into Latin; otherwise judgment would not have been passed on them immediately, as it later was not passed on others brought by the illustrious Antiochus, a friend of Nestorius. For, as Coelestine gives as his reason, it was necessary to wait until the discourse had been translated into Latin.

However the matter may stand, it may certainly be said, not without justification, that this was the Church’s first victory over Nestorius. For in this synod he was condemned for the first time—not by name, since it was uncertain, or at least not sufficiently established according to the requirements of a lawful judicial proceeding, who was the author of the papers—but generally in respect of his doctrines. Just as those doctrines had provoked offense, and indeed vehement offense, so they were condemned by the unanimous agreement of the Fathers.

A letter was therefore written to Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrian Church—not merely to inform him of anything certain concerning the author of the papers. For who could have remained hidden as the author amid such great disturbances in the Church? Nor was it written, as some suspicious person might suppose, to discover whether Cyril himself agreed with Nestorius; for Cyril was regarded as unimpeachable in reputation and free from every error. Rather, the letter was written so that the bishop of the see already regarded as second after Rome might be stirred up to perform his proper part in due season and to advance the matter that was being prepared, although he was already laboring with sufficient vigilance to defend the faith—indeed, to the point of risking the reproach of excessive diligence.

The letters written to Cyril, whether by Coelestine or by the bishops, have perished—if there were two sets of letters, rather than one, as was customary with the apostolic see and perhaps with the greater sees, whose bishops generally subscribed their own names to synodical letters whenever they were issued by a provincial council. I say “by a provincial council,” for the practice was different when they wrote from the whole of their diocese, or whenever several bishops of the greater Churches were present.

Here someone inquisitive may ask why the letters were sent from Rome to Cyril of Alexandria, who was far from Constantinople, rather than to John of Antioch, who was nearer. The answer is easy and straightforward. First, John could have appeared suspect, since he had been a presbyter of the same Church as Nestorius, the Church of Antioch, and a disciple of the teacher Theodore. Moreover, John’s industry and energy in conducting affairs had not yet been tested, since he had scarcely completed a year in the episcopate. In addition, the see of Antioch was only third after Rome; indeed, for several years it had yielded precedence to Constantinople, although the Roman pontiffs refused to approve this. A greater see, however, was not ordinarily judged by a lesser one. Cyril, on the other hand, whether because of his personal disposition or because of the public interest of his see, could not be suspected of favoring Nestorius; and his diligence and vigorous spirit had been demonstrated by seventeen years in the episcopate, years both difficult and full of affairs.

Even if these two considerations had carried less weight, the Alexandrian see was in reality the first of the greater sees after Rome, and was regarded as virtually first among those recognized by the Roman pontiffs, who opposed the Constantinopolitan Council on this point. According to ancient custom, therefore, it possessed the right to judge the other three sees, and exercised that right whenever it did not please the apostolic see to retain judgment for itself. Hence, whenever a case of this kind arose, the bishop of Alexandria was ordered by the Roman bishop to act on his behalf; furnished with this twofold authority, he completed the matter, since by the institution of the Church he was the first judge under the supreme pontiff.

This explanation of the authority possessed by the bishops of Alexandria seems all the more probable because it reconciles the conflicting opinions of the authorities on the subject. It preserves the rights of both sees, the apostolic and the Alexandrian, and does not resort to some extraordinary delegation granted to Cyril, supposedly indicated by the *phrygium*, or pallium, and the mitre sent from Rome—an explanation which Nicephorus and Theodore Balsamon could scarcely have persuaded men of anything but extraordinary credulity to accept.

## II. The Synod that was the First Alexandrian Synod, under the bishop Saint Cyril, in the same year and under the same consuls, in autumn

[Col. 1170A]

The letters of the supreme pontiff, and any others that may have been issued by the Roman synod, reached Alexandria at the beginning of autumn. After receiving them, Cyril sent his first letter to Nestorius by Lampon, a presbyter and monk. When Lampon returned with Nestorius’s reply, Cyril supplemented its brevity with another letter that followed soon afterward—one that, in the words of Nicephorus (Book XIV, chapter 33), spewed forth mighty waves of heresy. Cyril issued his refutatory letter in the Egyptian month Mechir, that is, at the very end of January or the beginning of February.

I believe that both of Cyril’s letters—the one he entrusted to Lampon for delivery and the one by which he replied to Nestorius—were written from a synod. Not, indeed, from a universal synod, that is, one of the whole diocese of Egypt, but from a particular Alexandrian synod, or one of the first province alone. Nor do I think that both letters were issued from the same synod; rather, I believe that each was issued from its own. Thus I seem to discern two provincial synods before the universal Egyptian synod, and I support this conjecture, or opinion, with arguments that are not implausible.

At the time when Cyril wrote each of these letters—he wrote the first in autumn and the second before Lent—he was holding an ordinary synod, that is, the synod which the Nicene canon commands to be held annually. For, though he observed ecclesiastical discipline in few respects, he cannot be thought to have neglected a precept that no one anywhere in the world failed to observe religiously.

In synods of this kind, judgments were not rendered only concerning persons, nor was only such disciplinary action decided as was advantageous to the Church. If matters of greater importance arose, the bishop also took counsel with his brethren, since such matters concerned the see itself rather than the person of the bishop. For they were considered major cases—cases which, in former times, were decided not so much by the bishop personally as by the see itself, that is, by the bishop together with his council.

The matter at hand was, moreover, of the greatest importance: to investigate the case of the bishop of the imperial city, who was stirring up disturbances throughout almost the entire world; whom trustworthy men arriving from Constantinople accused of error; concerning whom the supreme pontiff had ordered an inquiry as a man laboring under suspicion of heresy; who was condemning himself through writings scattered everywhere; and whom Cyril was canonically obliged to admonish and summon to sing a recantation.

I therefore do not see how the statement of the most learned Petavius can stand—namely, that Nestorius was first summoned by Cyril through two private letters and then through one synodical letter (Volume IV of *Dogmatics*, Book I). For how can legal reasoning allow those letters to be called private which are said to have been sent by the Alexandrian Church itself, which served as the first and second canonical admonitions, and the second of which was expressly called synodical at the Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon? Yet it is established by clear testimonies that the letters in question were of this character.

For Cyril says of both letters (Letter 3 to Nestorius):

> “The holy synod that assembled at Rome, and all of us, agreed that the letters sent by the Alexandrian Church to Your Reverence were correct and had been written without reproach,” etc.

The Church agreed with the letters sent from the Alexandrian Church to Your Reverence—both the holy synod that assembled at Rome and all of us, since they had been written correctly and irreproachably.

Since, therefore, in the ancient ecclesiastical manner of speaking, for letters to be sent on such matters by the Alexandrian Church means nothing other than that they were sent by the Alexandrian synod, both of Cyril’s letters to Nestorius must certainly be said to have been written by a synod.

That these letters also functioned as the first and second admonitions is clearly taught by Pope Coelestine when he wrote to Nestorius:

> “Therefore, although our brother Cyril asserts in his second letters that you have been summoned, I wish you to understand that, after his first and second letters, and after this correction of ours—which is clearly already the third—you have been completely separated from the entire college and assembly of Christians, unless you promptly correct what has been wrongly said,” etc.

Cyril teaches the same thing in his letter to the same Nestorius (Letter 3):

> “Behold, therefore, together with the holy synod assembled at the great city of Rome under the presidency of our most holy and venerable brother and fellow priest, Coelestine, bishop, we have now summoned you for the third time by this letter. We advise you to abstain from the corrupt and distorted doctrines which you are known both to hold and to teach. Instead, receive the true faith handed down from the beginning to the Churches through the blessed apostles and evangelists, who both saw these things with their eyes and are shown to have been ministers of the Word. If Your Reverence delays doing this, then, according to the period fixed in the letter of our most holy and venerable fellow priest Coelestine, bishop of Rome and head of the Church, know that you have no share with us, nor any place or conversation with the priests and bishops of God.”

[Col. 1171B]

Cyril says the same thing in his letters to the monks of Constantinople: Nestorius was already being admonished by him through three letters (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 28).

Since, therefore, Cyril’s first letter to Nestorius is itself synodical, as we have clearly established, it is necessary to admit that a synod was held at Alexandria in the year 429, in autumn, at precisely the time when the letter was sent; and that this synod was provincial and ordinary.

Nothing remains of it except the letters to Nestorius and to the monks of Egypt, together with Paschal Homily 17, by which the date of Easter for the following year, 430, was announced. The homily is, moreover, concerned with the same subject as the letter to the monks, for in both all the doctrines of Nestorius contained in his first three sermons are thoroughly refuted.

I am convinced that the homily, together with the doctrinal letter to the monks, belonged to the synod. I have no doubt that the paschal homilies, since they were of the greatest importance, were read beforehand in the synod—and that this occurred at the autumnal synod, since they were customarily sent from Alexandria in autumn so that they might reach the other Churches in time, where Easter was announced on the day of the *Theophany*.

Nor do I doubt that the letter to the monks was written by the same synod. For it was intended more for Constantinople than for the monasteries themselves. Yet it was useful to place the address to the monks upon it, so that the conflict would not be waged before it had been lawfully proclaimed.

In the homily, the argument proceeds both defensively and offensively. The doctrines attacked by Nestorius are defended: the two births of the Word (sermon 3), the divinity of Emmanuel (sermon 2), the unity of Christ (the same sermon), and the Virgin as *Theotokos*—Θεοτόκος, “God-bearer” (sermon 1). In turn, the doctrines defended by Nestorius are attacked, such as Christ as *Theophoros*—Θεοφόρος, “God-bearing” (sermon 1), and the co-adoration of Christ (sermons 1 and 2), and so forth.

The passages of Scripture which Nestorius abused are also explained, such as “motherless” (*ἀμήτωρ*) and “fatherless” (*ἀπάτωρ*) in sermon 1, and “God sent his Son,” and so forth, in sermon 3. Finally, the accusations that the same heretic directed against Catholics are rejected, such as *anthropolatria*—ἀνθρωπολατρεία, “the worship of a man”—in sermon 1, and so forth.

If anyone has the leisure to examine this matter carefully, let him compare the aforesaid homily with the letter to the monks of Egypt, and both of them with Nestorius’s first three sermons. He will observe, not without some pleasure, first, the state in which the Nestorian cause then stood; second, how prudently Cyril began to fight against Nestorius under another person’s name; third, how Cyril nevertheless could not conduct the matter so covertly that Nestorius would not realize that he was being attacked, and therefore attempted to refute the letter under the false name of a certain Photius, answering like with like; and finally, how cleverly Cyril, at the end of the paschal homily, delivered this exhortation:

> “Therefore, since we have been bought at a price and are not our own, let us serve the Buyer according to his rights. Let us tame the rebellious movements of the flesh, drive far away the utterly wicked crimes, and, conspicuous in every moderation, fight the good fight, finish the course, keep the faith, relieve the sufferings of the needy, comfort orphans, defend widows, procure remedies for the sick, visit prisoners, and show ourselves kind and steadfast in mutual charity.”

For he seems to sound a trumpet call by which the faithful might be inflamed to fight for Christ against a man who, besides godlessness (*ἀθεότης*), was charged with plundering the Church’s property and indeed with robbing the patrimony of the poor.

## III. The Synod that was the Second Alexandrian Synod, under Cyril the bishop, in the year of the consuls Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, in the year 430, before Lent

The Council of Chalcedon mentions this synod when it explicitly calls Cyril’s second letter to Nestorius synodical. It names it in the definition of the faith:

> “But concerning those who attempt to corrupt the mystery of the dispensation and shamelessly rave that a mere man was born from the holy Virgin Mary, the synodical letters of the most blessed Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, to Nestorius and to the Easterners,” etc.  
> (Act 5, in the definition of the faith.)

The reference is to the letters that had been read in the second session, as is clear to anyone who examines the matter. Only two had been read: namely, the second letter to Nestorius, which begins “Some are objecting,” and that celebrated pacificatory letter beginning “Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult,” and so forth.

Indeed, Cyril himself calls his first two letters to Nestorius not so much his own as letters of the Alexandrian Church:

> “The Church agreed with the letters sent from the Alexandrian Church to Your Reverence, both the holy synod that assembled at Rome and all of us, since they had been written correctly and irreproachably.”  
> (Letter 3 to Nestorius.)

As for the second Alexandrian synod, from which Cyril’s second letter to Nestorius was issued, the testimony of Nicephorus may appear to make the matter clear (Book XIV, chapter 33):

> “The divine Cyril, when he heard Nestorius’s blasphemies, sent him one letter and then another. In them he declared in explicit terms that those who did not openly confess Christ as God, but in blasphemous language called him a man who bears God—*Theophoros*—and an organ or instrument of the Divinity, were anathema. Nestorius answered him in writing, conducting the matter with insults and blasphemies as well. When these letters of Nestorius, spewing forth mighty waves of heresy, had been received, Cyril gathered a provincial synod at Alexandria with four others, and presented before it the letters exchanged between them. He sent copies of these letters and the decrees of the synod itself to Coelestine, bishop of Old Rome. In addition, he sent Nestorius a third letter, to which he attached the much-celebrated Twelve Chapters together with the anathemas.”

It is useful to observe the following points in these words of Nicephorus. First, Cyril wrote two letters to Nestorius before the universal synod of Alexandria was convened. Second, this synod was held before Cyril’s and Nestorius’s exchanged letters were sent to the supreme pontiff. Third, the decrees of the synod were also sent to Rome, evidently by Possidonius, a deacon of the Alexandrian Church, as is known from another source.

Since the letters which Nicephorus says were sent to Rome are quite different from the third letter, which has the anathemas appended to it—for that letter was written at the universal synod assembled after Possidonius’s return—it is necessary to conclude that the synod mentioned by Nicephorus, whose decrees were carried by Possidonius to the apostolic see, was different from the Egyptian, or universal, synod from which the delegation of four bishops was sent to Nestorius with the pontifical letters and Cyril’s anathemas. This is why Nicephorus calls the former synod provincial, in order to distinguish it from the Egyptian synod, which was universal.

Again, it must be observed from Nicephorus’s testimony that two extremely obscure questions arise, and that because of them someone might perhaps think that the whole narrative should be deprived of credibility. The first question is: which was the one letter and which the second in which Cyril explicitly declared anathema against those who did not openly confess Christ as God, but in blasphemous language called him a man who bears God and an instrument of the Divinity? The second question is: which were the four letters received together with Nestorius’s letters?

I have called these questions obscure because the letter said to contain an explicit anathema against anyone who professed Christ to be a man who bears God and an instrument of the Divinity is neither Cyril’s first nor his second letter to Nestorius. Nothing of the kind is read in either.

Furthermore, in Nestorius’s first letter to Cyril no part of the doctrine is touched upon, not even in a word. The second letter now preserved is indeed full of blasphemies, but it was written after the Alexandrian synod mentioned by Nicephorus. What, then, are the letters of Nestorius that spewed forth heresy and were presented to the synod from which Cyril’s second admonitory letter to Nestorius was written, when Nestorius appears to have answered that second letter of Cyril with a letter spewing forth heresy?

To bring light to these matters, it seems necessary to set out the whole testimony of Nicephorus by way of a paraphrase (First Letter, no. 2):

Cyril, when he heard Nestorius’s blasphemies—reported by trustworthy men who had arrived from Constantinople at Alexandria, and by the *apocrisiarii* who brought warning—sent him one letter and then another. The second was apparently addressed to the monks of Egypt, but in reality to the people of Constantinople and, under another person’s name, to Nestorius himself. In these letters he explicitly declared anathema against those who did not openly confess Christ as God, but in blasphemous language called him a man who bears God, and an organ or instrument of the Divinity.

Nestorius, after first replying briefly through Lampon, answered him again in writing—writing that contained the heads of the blasphemies to which Cyril later replied in his second letter. He conducted the matter with insults and blasphemies.

When these letters of Nestorius, spewing forth mighty waves of heresy, had been received, Cyril gathered a provincial synod at Alexandria—not the universal synod of all Egypt—with four others: members of the Constantinopolitan clergy, monks of the city, agents of the Alexandrian Church, and his own deacon Bupha. Before it he presented the letters exchanged between them—his first letter and Nestorius’s two letters. He sent copies of these letters and the decrees of the synod itself to Coelestine, bishop of Old Rome, through Possidonius, a deacon of the Alexandrian Church.

By “the decrees,” understand the letter which Cyril issued to Nestorius as the second letter from the synod and sent to Constantinople, together with replies to the other letters of other persons.

In addition, after Possidonius’s return from Rome, Cyril sent Nestorius a third letter from the universal council of all Egypt, together with the letters of Coelestine, the supreme pontiff, delivered by four bishop-legates. To this letter he attached the famous Twelve Chapters together with the anathemas.

The same synod is also mentioned by Vigilius in Book V against Eutyches. When he cited a passage of Cyril contained in the second letter to Nestorius, section 8 and following (Volume IV of the *Library of the Fathers*), he wrote in these words, than which nothing clearer could be said in support of our position:

> “The blessed Cyril also said this in the letter of the whole synod to Nestorius.”

I do not think that we should listen to otherwise very learned men who interpret the synod mentioned by Vigilius as the Ephesian synod merely because this letter is inserted in the Acts of Ephesus. For who could rightly conclude from that fact that it was itself the letter of the whole synod to Nestorius? Otherwise Coelestine’s letter to Nestorius, which is likewise inserted in the Ephesian Acts, would also be called the letter of the whole synod to Nestorius.

In sum, this synod was held at Alexandria in the year 430, before Lent, in the month Mechir. It was provincial, and Cyril presided over it. From it a letter was sent to Nestorius, which appears to have been delivered to him by agents of the Alexandrian Church.

## IV. The Synod that was the Second Roman Synod, under Coelestine the supreme pontiff, in the same year and under the same consuls as the preceding synod, in August

[Col. 1174A]

After receiving Cyril’s letters concerning Nestorius—which the deacon Possidonius had brought, together with copies of the letters exchanged between Cyril and Nestorius, the decrees of the synod, and also excerpts of statements from Nestorius’s works—Pope Coelestine convened a synod at Rome of a great many bishops. From it he sent Nestorius letters announcing his condemnation, beginning “After a few days of our life,” and so forth (Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 18).

Cyril mentioned this synod when writing to John of Antioch:

> “Moreover, after his expositions and letters had been read in the council—and especially those bearing his explicit signature, so that no room for evasion remained—the holy Roman synod immediately pronounced a clear judgment against him. Concerning this it also wrote to Your Piety. Those who do not wish to be cut off from communion with the whole of the West must obey that decree in every respect. For they sent copies of the expositions both to our most pious brother Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica, and to several other most religious bishops of Macedonia, who are not accustomed ever to depart from his judgment. They also wrote to the most pious Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem. It is now for Your Piety carefully to consider what will serve the cause; for we shall follow what they have indicated.”

Cyril likewise mentions it in his third letter to Nestorius:

> “Behold, therefore, together with the holy synod assembled at the great city of Rome under the presidency of our most holy and venerable brother and fellow priest, Coelestine, bishop, we have now summoned you for the third time by this letter. We advise you to abstain from the corrupt and distorted doctrines which you are known both to hold and to teach. Instead, receive the true faith handed down from the beginning to the Churches through the blessed apostles and evangelists, who both saw these things with their eyes and are shown to have been ministers of the Word. If Your Reverence delays doing this, then, according to the period fixed in the letter of our most holy and venerable fellow priest Coelestine, bishop of Rome and head of the Church, know that you have no share with us, nor any place or conversation with the priests and bishops of God.”

Nestorius himself also mentions this council in a letter to Coelestine, calling it the council of the bishops of the West:

> “Do not, therefore, betray the truth by departing from it—for the letters sent to the bishops by the council of the West and by the Alexandrian council, through many replies, have made our judgment plain to us”—addressing, evidently, prudent men of the same orthodox profession, and so forth.

Arnobius the Younger does not merely mention it in his dispute with Serapion; he also reports part of the speech delivered by Coelestine as presiding bishop. He writes as follows (Volume XV of the *Library of the Fathers*):

> Arnobius said: “The holy Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, a man of apostolic memory, having learned that the Nestorian doctrine, contrary to the faith, was spreading, wrote throughout Egypt and sent word to the holy Coelestine, a bishop of apostolic memory, saying that it would redound to his praise if something were corrected by the man who held the citadel of the pontificate.  
>   
> “Holy Coelestine became so much his encomiast—*ἐγκωμιαστής*—that he pronounced a sentence of condemnation against Nestorius. He proclaimed Cyril’s praise both in the sight of God and before all, asserting that Cyril’s understanding was strengthened by the preaching of the distinguished bishops of our province; and he clearly explained that this had also been the understanding of Damasus, Ambrose, and Hilary.  
>   
> “For he said in the council itself: ‘I remember that Ambrose of blessed memory, on the day of the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ, caused the whole people with one voice to sing to God: “Come, Redeemer of the nations; show forth the Virgin’s birth; let every age marvel; such a birth befits God.”’  
>   
> “Does such a birth befit a man?  
>   
> “And he added: ‘Therefore, the understanding of our brother Cyril, in calling Mary *Theotokos*, agrees completely with the words: “Such a birth befits God.” The Virgin brought forth God in her childbirth, through the power of him who is full of omnipotence.  
>   
> “‘Hilary also, a man of keen intellect, writing to the emperor Constantius concerning the Lord’s incarnation, says: “The Son of God became man.” Then, repeating himself with reversed order, he says: “God became the Son of man.” But man did not become God, nor did the Son of man become the Son of God. For the greatness of the Lord overcame the lowliness of the servant’s form, so that the servant’s form itself, which he assumed, ceased to be servile through the Lord who assumed it.  
>   
> “‘If those who by nature are not sons of God are made sons of God through him, how much more did he who by nature is the Son of God exalt into God the one with whom, by his own will, he was conceived and born in the virgin womb, so that at his name every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Philippians 2:10)?  
>   
> “‘My predecessor Damasus, writing to Paulinus, bishop of the Church of Antioch, says among other things: “We anathematize those who assert that there are two Sons of God: one who was begotten from the Father, and another who was born from the Virgin through the assumption of flesh.”  
>   
> “‘The same Damasus, a man of apostolic memory, says in another letter to Paulinus: “We anathematize those who confess two sons in the Savior: one before the incarnation and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin, and who do not confess that the same one, both before and afterward, is the Son of God, the same Christ—not to mention that they refuse to confess that the Son of God himself was born from the Virgin.”’”

These words also shed light on the statement of Gennadius concerning Coelestine (Book on Illustrious Men, chapter 54):

> “Coelestine, bishop of the city of Rome, dictated the decrees of the synod against the aforementioned Nestorius. He published a volume setting forth the synod’s proceedings and gave it to the Churches of the East and West, affirming that, although two natures remain perfectly in Christ, one person of the Son of God must be believed. For the aforementioned Nestorius was shown to be opposed to this doctrine.”

From all these sources, some sort of history of the council in question can be pieced together. It was convened at Rome by Pope Coelestine at the beginning of August, in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, the most august consuls. The bishops assembled included those who could conveniently be summoned from the cities of Italy after the arrival of Possidonius, deacon of the Alexandrian Church, as well as those who had perhaps come from more distant regions, as was customary for the anniversaries of the apostles or who happened to be staying in the city for some other reason.

A considerable number must have assembled, since the Ephesian Fathers, Nestorius, and others elsewhere repeatedly call it the synod of the West. It is credible that Possidonius, Cyril’s *apocrisiarius*, was present, just as Bessula, a deacon of the Carthaginian Church sent by Bishop Capreolus with letters, attended the Ephesian council. The purpose of the summons was the restoration of peace to the Church troubled by Nestorius.

Nestorius’s expositions, brought by the illustrious Antiochus, were therefore read, as were the two letters which Nestorius had sent to the apostolic see in defense of the Pelagians. Valerius, the chamberlain, had delivered the first of these to Coelestine, and Antiochus the second. The letters exchanged between Cyril and Nestorius were also read. Indeed, certain excerpts were read either from Nestorius’s works, in conflict with the faith, or from the books of the Fathers, contrary to Nestorius. Perhaps Cassian’s work on the Incarnation was also examined—the work in which Nestorius’s heresy had been refuted in seven books at the urging of the archdeacon Leo.

The business occupied several sessions while the matter was carefully conducted with the dignity appropriate to the case and to the faith. The supreme pontiff delivered a speech to the Fathers of the synod in which he showed that Cyril agreed with Ambrose, Hilary, and Damasus. He also showed that the case had already been prejudged by such great teachers in Cyril’s favor, since Cyril’s faith had been approved, and against Nestorius, whose error had been condemned by an anathema.

A sentence was likewise pronounced against the author of the error: unless he sang a recantation within ten days of the announcement, he would lose not only his own see but also communion with the faithful.

[Col. 1176A]

The form of the sentence was as follows:

> “Understand clearly that this is our judgment: unless you preach concerning Christ our God those things which the Roman, Alexandrian, and entire Catholic Church believes—and which the Church of Constantinople, too, has hitherto held most excellently, according to the faith set forth at the Council of Nicaea—and unless, within ten days counted from the first day on which this summons becomes known to you, you lay aside this impious innovation by which you endeavor to separate what venerable Scripture joins together, and condemn it by an open and written confession, know that you have been cast out from communion with the universal Catholic Church and are wholly unfit for any function belonging to priestly authority.”

A decree was subsequently made concerning the restoration to communion of all those who had been expelled from the Church because of the faith by Nestorius—whether bishops, clerics, or anyone else.
