Indeed, it was declared that they had never been separated from communion with the apostolic see. This was communicated both to Nestorius, whose unjust sentence was being rescinded, and to the clergy of Constantinople, so that they might communicate with those persons more freely.

Yet lest it appear that the sentence of one who had already provoked the divine sentence against himself could remain in force for a time, the authority of our see expressly decreed that no bishop, cleric, or Christian of any kind who, from the time Nestorius or his associates began to preach such things, had been expelled from his place or from communion by Nestorius or by those like him should be regarded as either expelled or excommunicated. Rather, all such persons both have been and continue to be in our communion, because no one who faltered by preaching such doctrines could expel or remove anyone.

And so, in order that the council’s decrees might achieve their effect, the supreme pontiff entrusted his own authority to Cyril for the execution of the sentence and for making provision, by apostolic authority, for the Church of Constantinople—not, as some have thought, for convening an ecumenical council. For these are the words of the delegation:

“Accordingly, having invoked the authority of our see, and exercising our power in our place and stead, you shall execute such a sentence with no lack of rigorous severity: namely, unless within an interval of ten days, counted from the day of this our admonition, he anathematizes in explicit words his impious doctrine and promises that henceforth he will confess that faith concerning the generation of Christ our God which both the Roman Church and the Church of Your Holiness, and finally the whole Christian religion, proclaim, let Your Holiness immediately make provision for that Church. Let him understand that he has in every respect been separated from our body: for, having rejected every effort at healing and, like a pestilential disease, having spread insanely through the whole body of the Church, he has now sought to hurl himself and all the others entrusted to him into utter destruction.”

Three other letters were written by the council: one to Nestorius, summoning him to repentance and threatening him if he hardened his mind; another to the clergy of Constantinople, to admonish them concerning the whole matter and the preservation of the faith of their predecessors; and a third to John of Antioch, and likewise to Juvenal of Jerusalem, Rufus of Thessalonica, and Flavian of Philippopolis [Col. 1176D], so that they might labor steadfastly with the apostolic see in defense of the faith. Although all of them bear the name of the supreme pontiff, if we believe Cyril, the three latter belong to the synod, whereas the first, which is addressed to Cyril, belongs to Celestine, the president of the synod. The former contain an exhortation and an announcement of the sentence that had been passed—matters belonging to the synod; the latter contains the conferral of authority, which belongs to apostolic jurisdiction.

Gennadius confirms this account (in the passage cited immediately above), while both shedding light on it and receiving light from it. For the decrees of the synod which he says were dictated by Celestine are those very three final letters, which, although they were issued by the synod, nevertheless bear Celestine’s name. Likewise, when he says that a document was prepared by the same pontiff and given to the Churches of East and West, he means these same letters: those sent to John, Juvenal, and Cyril, bishops of the East, and to Rufus and Flavian, bishops of the West [Col. 1177A]. Finally, the definition of faith according to which, while two natures remain in Christ, one person of the Son of God is to be believed, may have been nothing other than the condemnation of Nestorius, who held the contrary view. Hence Gennadius added: “The aforesaid Nestorius was shown to be opposed to this sentence.”

### V. The Synod that was the First Constantinopolitan Synod, Convened by Nestorius, under the Same Consuls and in the Same Year, during the Autumn Season

The memory of this synod is exceedingly obscure. It is known from no other source than Nestorius’s letters to Cyril, commonly called the second, although in reality they are the third.

“You do well to take care of those who are offended at us and to be concerned about what is taking place among us. I thank Your Unanimity; but know that you have been led astray by those who were deposed by the holy council because they were filled with the disease of the Manichaeans—or, what is especially the case, by the clergy who enjoy your special affection” [Col. 1177B].

We have said more about Nestorius’s council in the notes to Nestorius’s own letters. Although it would be superfluous to reproduce them here, it will be useful to reread them: they contain not a few matters relevant to the history of the synods and shed considerable light on a very obscure affair, namely, the anathema pronounced in favor of the Pelagians.

No one, after weighing the words of the letter cited and remembering the ancient custom of not writing doctrinal letters except in a synod, will deny that this letter to Cyril was issued from this synod.

### VI. The Synod that was the First Universal Synod of All Egypt, under the Same Consuls and in the Same Year, at the Beginning of the Month Athyr according to the Egyptians

When Possidonius brought letters from the West, Cyril immediately sent him to the East to carry Celestine’s synodical letters to Juvenal of Jerusalem and John of Antioch. In the meantime Cyril convened a synod, called by some Alexandrian, after the city in which it assembled, but by others—and more correctly—Egyptian, because the bishops of the entire diocese of Egypt were summoned. Nevertheless, it is scarcely credible that bishops were summoned from Lower Egypt, as we shall explain below.

The synod was held toward the end of October, when the month Athyr begins, or perhaps at the beginning of November. For the synodical letter sent from it to Nestorius is dated 3 November, which was a Monday; and thus the synod began at that time, since scarcely any synod in former days is found to have begun except on a Monday. Nor could it have been held later, since the four bishops sent from it were present at Constantinople and delivered the synodical letter to Nestorius on 7 December, which was a Sunday. Nor could it have been held earlier, since Possidonius did not leave Rome before 11 August, the date borne by all Celestine’s letters brought by him; and at least two months were required [Col. 1177D] both for Possidonius to return from Rome to Alexandria and for the bishops, summoned from the entire diocese by official writ, to assemble at Alexandria.

The reason for the convocation is clear: letters had been received from the Roman synod, together with the pontiff’s mandate and a difficult as well as laborious task. On this depended not only the tranquility of the Churches but also the stability of the imperiled faith. The bishop of the royal city, who was especially dear to the emperor, would either have to be compelled to retract what he had taught or be driven from the see to which he had been elevated by Theodosius with the support and assistance of the courtiers.

It cannot be determined who attended or in what number, since the synod is scarcely mentioned anywhere except in three letters sent from it by Cyril and in one of Nestorius’s letters to the heretic Celestine. Nevertheless, it would not be implausible to suspect that many of those who went with Cyril to Ephesus also attended this council [Col. 1178A]. For it is reasonable to suppose that Cyril summoned to Alexandria the most learned men of his diocese and then brought them to Ephesus. Fifty were in fact brought to Ephesus, as appears in the report sent by Palladius from the Easterners to the emperor (Second Part of the Council of Ephesus, in the acts against Cyril). If this suspicion is not dismissed—as indeed it ought not to be—the consequence is that the bishops of the cities of Lower Egypt must be said to have been summoned to the Egyptian synod, either alone or for the most part. For many, if not all, came from there to Ephesus, as anyone will readily notice who compares the Ptolemaic lists with the Ephesian subscriptions.

A delegation of four bishops was appointed. They were to travel to Constantinople and deliver the Roman and Egyptian synodical letters to Nestorius, the Constantinopolitan clergy, and the archimandrites. The legates were Theopemptus of Cabasorum, Daniel of Darnis, Potamion, and Macarius, bishops (Second Part of the Council of Ephesus, act 1).

I do not know what reason the illustrious author of the Annals had for reducing the latter two to the rank of presbyters of the Alexandrian Church [Col. 1178B]. Such an action is contradicted by the words of Peter, the chief notary (ibid.):

“But also those things which the most holy and pious bishop of the Alexandrian Church, Cyril, and the entire synod of Egypt had sent to him through Theopemptus, Daniel, Potamion, and Macarius, the most religious bishops, and so forth.”

It is also contradicted by the heading which Cyril placed on the letter he sent to Constantinople after the deposition of Nestorius:

“Cyril, archbishop of Alexandria, to Macarius and Potamion, bishops, and to the lord Dalmatius, archimandrite of the monasteries, and so forth” (ibid., act 1 of the Council of Ephesus).

Finally, it is contradicted by the ancient custom of summoning bishops of the greater sees, when they were to be called to judgment, through at least three bishops.

Thus Nestorius was summoned to the ecumenical council. First: Hermogenes of Rhinocurura, Athanasius of Paralia, Peter of Parembolae, and Paul of Lampsae, bishops. Second: Theopemptus of Cabasorum, Theodulus of Elusa, and Anderius of Chersonesus in Crete, bishops. Third: John of Haephestus, Anysius of Thebes, Domnus of Opus in Hellas, and Daniel of Darnis, bishops.

Likewise John of Antioch was summoned. First: Archelaus of Myndus in Caria, Paul of Lampsae, and Peter of Parembolae in Palestine. Second: Timothy of Termessus, Eustasius of Docimium, and Eudoxius of Choma in Lycia, bishops. Third: Daniel of Colonia, Commodus of Tripolis in Lydia, and Timothy of Terma on the Hellespont, together with Musonius the notary (ibid., act 5).

Likewise Dioscorus was summoned to the Council of Chalcedon. First: Constantine of Bostra, Acacius of Ariarathia, and Atticus of Zela, together with Himerius the reader and notary. Second: Pergamius of Antioch in Pisidia, Cecropius of Sebastopolis, and Rufinus of Samosata, together with Hypatius the notary. Third: Francion of Philippopolis, Lucian of Byzus, and John of Germanicia, together with Palladius the deacon and notary (Council of Chalcedon, act 3).

This custom appears to have originated from Christ’s words: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Matthew 18:16). The Apostle likewise says: “Against an elder do not receive an accusation except under two or three witnesses” (1 Timothy 5:19). The Church wished, in the judgment which it exercised over bishops, to maintain the greatest possible strictness of discipline.

The four legates arrived at Constantinople before 8 December. On that very day, after the completion of the synaxis, they delivered the letters to Nestorius in the presence of a large gathering of clergy and a multitude of distinguished persons. The letters nearly drove Nestorius into a frenzy; nevertheless, they achieved no success because a general council had already been announced, beginning on 19 November, and because the emperor had forbidden anyone to introduce any change before the council’s definition.

Of the legates, Macarius and Potamion remained at Constantinople to conduct affairs as circumstances required, though under the counsel of Dalmatius, the most holy archimandrite [Col. 1179A]. The other two, Theopemptus and Daniel, returned to Alexandria, despite the stormy sea, in order to report on their embassy to the synod that was to be held before Lent and to assist Cyril with their counsel concerning the emperor’s communications received, whether rescripts, private letters, or official warrants. For they had themselves seen the condition of the court and the attitude of the city, and had learned thoroughly from others devoted to Cyril about the affairs of Nestorius.

We have already discussed the published copy of the synodical letter and the public anathemas, and the disturbances they caused in the royal city, not only in the historical preface and at the beginning of the second book but also in many other places. It is now time to fulfill what we promised there concerning the anathemas, or twelve chapters, by observing certain matters relevant to history. There is nothing to say about the letter to which they are appended, apart from what we have included in the notes to that letter and this brief point: in it Cyril speaks not in his own name but in the name of the whole diocese.

[Col. 1179B] Concerning the anathemas, then, I have the following to say: where and when they were composed; with what skill; how they oppose Nestorius’s statements; with which opinions of the earlier Fathers they agree; who opposed them and who at times defended them; who was their first Latin interpreter; and whatever else may arise.

First, the words of both Celestine and Mercator raise a question concerning the time and place. Celestine (Letter to Nestorius, near the end) mentions the faith which he sometimes calls that of the Alexandrian Church and sometimes Cyril’s, and which he himself approved and prescribed for Nestorius to hold. Mercator writes (In the title of the Refutation of Nestorius’s Anathemas) that Cyril’s chapters had been approved by the judgment of the Roman Church. The question therefore arises: what was this judgment of which Mercator speaks, and what was the faith of the Alexandrian Church’s priest of which the Pontiff speaks?

It is certain that by “judgment,” exercised by the Roman Church, a synod is meant in which Cyril’s chapters were both carefully examined and solemnly approved. This synod must be understood as having been held before the ecumenical Council of Ephesus, before Mercator wrote against Nestorius’s anathemas.

It is equally certain that the faith mentioned by the Pontiff was approved before he wrote to Nestorius. Since the letter to Nestorius was written from the second Roman synod, that faith must be said to have been composed at Alexandria before the second Roman synod, and then brought to Rome by the deacon Possidonius; and so it belongs to the second Alexandrian synod.

The question, therefore, is whether that faith is identical with the anathemas or something else. I thought it was the anathemas when the preface to the second book was at press; but after considering the matter more carefully, I perceived that they differ, and that it is nothing other than the confession of faith contained in Cyril’s second letter to Nestorius, from number 5 through number 14. This confession is rightly called that of the Alexandrian Church and of Cyril himself, since it was composed at the Alexandrian synod over which Cyril presided [Col. 1179D]. It was carried to Rome by Possidonius together with the mutual letters of Cyril and Nestorius; it was approved at the second Roman synod; and it differs from the anathemas in no respect except that the anathemas speak of the divinity of our High Priest and of Christ’s life-giving flesh, whereas the letter says nothing of these matters. Moreover, the anathemas are properly antirrhetic, or refutational, whereas the faith is a certain affirmative confession.

This, it seems to me, explains why Mercator said that Cyril’s chapters were approved by a true judgment of the Roman Church: namely, when the faith was approved. It explains why the supreme pontiff sometimes called this faith that of the Alexandrian Church and sometimes that of its bishop, since it was written at a synod presided over by Cyril. Finally, it explains why the Egyptian Fathers wrote to Nestorius:

“Moreover, the Church both of the holy synod that assembled at Rome and of all of us has given its assent to the letters addressed from Alexandria to Your Religion, as having been correctly and irreproachably composed” [Col. 1180A].

For those letters contained the faith, and the writers signify that they too agreed with it.

Once these points have been established, it becomes clear that the anathemas were composed at Alexandria in some synod: in the particular second synod, they were drafted, as it were, in the year 430, in the month Mechir; in the universal Egyptian synod, in the same year and in the month Athyr, they were published. Thus Mercator’s words must be understood in a manner consistent with the truth. For it is hardly credible that the title was inserted at a later time, since it greatly serves to discredit Nestorius by saying that he opposed chapters which the Roman Church had approved by a true judgment.

The anathemas were composed with an admirable art and an almost geometrical method, in which nothing could be more exact. This is evident from the fact that they contain first the theorem to be proved, then the principle of proof and two lemmas, and finally nine corollaries.

The question was whether Emmanuel, whom Isaiah mentions and whom the whole Church interprets against the Jews as Christ Jesus, is truly God, and whether Emmanuel’s mother is truly the Mother of God (*Deipara*). Cyril answers (Anathema 1) that Emmanuel is truly God and that Emmanuel’s mother is truly the Mother of God. He establishes the former as the theorem to be demonstrated and at the same time sets down as the firmest principle of demonstration the Evangelist’s saying: “The Word became flesh.”

He then establishes the first lemma: that the natures are united καθ’ ὑπόστασιν (*kata hypostasin*, according to hypostasis), and that Christ is one and the same God and man (Anathema 2). He next concludes the second: that the natures are not joined by σχέσις (*schesis*), that is, by a merely moral union (Anathema 3).

He does not construct a demonstration from the lemmas, although this would be easy, because the law of the anathemas does not permit it. Instead, he immediately draws nine consequences.

The first corollary: things said of Christ are not to be divided in such a way that some belong only to the man and others only to God, with not all of them attributed to one and the same person (Anathema 4).

The second: Christ is not “of God” but God himself; for that oblique case signifies distinction as well as relation (Anathema 5) [Col. 1180C].

The third: the Word is not the man’s “Lord,” for example, but the man himself (Anathema 6).

The fourth: reverence is not owed to Christ merely because the Word operates in him and communicates dignity to him as to one distinct from himself (Anathema 7).

The fifth: Christ is to be worshiped in no other way than God himself (Anathema 8).

The sixth: he performed miracles by no other power than that by which God performs them (Anathema 9).

The seventh: the High Priest of our confession is truly the Word, and he did not offer a sacrifice for himself but only for us (Anathema 10).

The eighth: the flesh offered for us is life-giving because it is the Word’s own flesh, that is, the flesh of essential Life (Anathema 11).

The ninth and last: the Word truly suffered in his own flesh, and Christ rose from the dead by his own power (Anathema 12).

[Col. 1180D] Observe further that all nine consequences are concerned with two things to be established: the unity of Christ and the redemption of humanity. Since there are three kinds of unity—of person, of dignity, and of operation—the first and second consequences establish unity of person; the third and fourth, unity of dignity and worship; and the fifth and sixth, unity of operation and power.

There are likewise three parts of redemption: the sanctification of the soul, the vivification of the body, and satisfaction for sins. The first is asserted in the seventh consequence, which concerns Christ’s priesthood; the second in the eighth, which concerns his life-giving flesh and the power of the Eucharist; and the third in the ninth, which concerns the death of God suffered in the flesh, against those who contradict it.

Cyril employed another technique by which he ensured that not only all the chapters as a whole would oppose Nestorius’s entire doctrine, but that each chapter would oppose a corresponding part. He set theorem against theorem, principle against principle, lemmas against lemmas, and consequences against consequences. His ingenuity lay in reducing the adversary’s confused and scattered doctrine to order, so that by an exquisite method both Catholic doctrine might be expounded and each component of the error expelled [Col. 1181A]. This will be clear to anyone, provided only that Nestorius’s error is presented in an orderly fashion, together with the indicated passages of his works in which each opinion or part of the error is contained.

Cyril demonstrated this splendidly: first, in the part of the synodical letter which I would rightly call negative, since there he denies that Catholics say what Nestorius asserted; second, in his defense of the anathemas, where he explains the necessity of each; and finally in that admirable dialogue *That Christ Is One*, in which the renowned champion, as though gathering his strength against the remnants of Nestorius, wished to display a model of the art of conquering and, being soon to die, to raise for himself an immortal trophy.

This admirable defender of the faith used a third technique as well. He intended his anathemas to be nothing other than the opinions of the Fathers, but cast as though into thunderbolts [Col. 1181B]. He therefore employed testimonies from ten Fathers: four Latins—Julius, Felix, Cyprian, and Ambrose; three Egyptians—Peter, Athanasius, and Theophilus; and three Greeks—Gregory of Nazianzus, Basil, and Gregory of Nyssa. All except one were bishops of the greater Churches and αὐτοκέφαλοι (*autokephaloi*, independent heads). Three were from the West, three from the East, and four from the South; all were distinguished for holiness, and four were renowned for the palm of martyrdom for the faith. He wished his chapters to be tested by a certain rule of ὀρθοδοξία (*orthodoxia*, orthodoxy), so that they might contain nothing except what all, everywhere, and always had taught. On this subject see Vincent of Lérins in his customary manner—that is, treating the matter explicitly, subtly, and in defense of the truth (Commonitory, chapter 42).

Observe further that, from the testimonies of the Fathers which he adduces, Cyril constructed scarcely more than four propositions:

1. That the Son of God truly became man.
2. That the same, and not another, is the Son of God and the son of man; and thus that God was born from a woman, and that the Word had two generations.
3. That the Virgin is the Mother of God.
4. That the immortal endured death, and that the one who was crucified is the one who is to be worshiped.

From these four all the other propositions at issue in the anathemas are easily derived. Indeed, the four themselves could readily be reduced to Athanasius’s single proposition: that the Son of God truly (*ontos*) and in truth (*aletheia*) became man.

Someone may ask—perhaps more out of curiosity than usefulness—why Cyril praised no Father from the Antiochene diocese and none from Constantinople, although he could have cited men from both, neither less numerous nor less weighty as witnesses to the truth than the others. The testimonies of Atticus and Amphilochius do not undermine this question, since they are believed to have been added in the commonly circulated copies of the Council of Ephesus. For writing three years after the council, the Lirinensian counts only ten Fathers and wishes the number to appear mystical.

Why, the curious questioner may ask, was the great Eustathius of Antioch, one of the 318 Nicene Fathers, not included by Cyril among the witnesses to the truth? Why was John of Constantinople omitted? Why Atticus, John’s successor? Why Ammonius of Adrianople, Severianus of Gabala, and Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium? Why Antiochus of Ptolemais and Vitalis, whose testimonies Cyril cites in his book *On the Right Faith to the Queens* (chapter 9 and following)? Why, likewise, were the anathemas of Gregory Thaumaturgus and Pope Damasus omitted, although they are extremely similar to Cyril’s and could have added weight to them? Concerning Gregory Thaumaturgus the answer is straightforward: the anathemas issued under his name seem, according to Bellarmine and Petavius, to have had another author. As for the others, it is not even possible to guess, since matters of this kind depend on the discretion of the person producing the witnesses. For the notion that some suspicious person conceived—that Chrysostom was not praised by Cyril because remnants of resentment remained stored in his mind—is wholly absurd, since Cyril employed John’s testimony in his book addressed to the Queens.

[Col. 1182A] It will be useful to compare the anathemas, whether those of Damasus to Paul of Antioch, those of Gregory Nazianzen to Cledonius, those attributed to Gregory Thaumaturgus, or those of subsequent councils, with Cyril’s. From such a comparison an admirable theology of the incarnation of the Word and the divinity of Christ could be constructed.

Nestorius was the first of all to fight against Cyril’s anathemas, setting twelve antirrhetic, or refutational, chapters against them. Andrew of Samosata and Theodoret then fought against them, and Cyril answered them. The Ephesian Fathers themselves may appear to have opposed them insofar as they required an exposition of each one. Gennadius certainly fought against them—while he was still a presbyter, as can be gathered from Facundus (Book II, chapter 4)—and later became that most holy bishop of Constantinople after Anatolius, when the controversy was still raging. Indeed, he answered each of them in exceedingly harsh words.

To these must be added all the Easterners, who both passed a sentence of deposition against Cyril on account of the chapters and made the authority given to their envoys to the emperor conditional upon their using every effort to have the chapters rejected as heretical. After the council was dissolved, they again proscribed them at Antioch; and when terms of peace were proposed, they insisted that the chapters must be retracted or at least buried in silence. The latter course was desired and obtained from Cyril, wearied by the disturbances, by the Constantinopolitan synod itself, over which Maximianus, Nestorius’s successor, presided. In this matter that synod too appeared to be insufficiently fair toward the chapters. Finally, Ibas, still a presbyter of the Church of Edessa, fought against them in his famous letter to Maris the Persian.

It should be noted that the Constantinopolitan synod which ordained Maximianus may be regarded as the Ephesian synod, as will be shown later, when there is occasion to discuss that very synod. For there was present in it Philip the presbyter, the legate of the supreme pontiff; there was also Arcadius, bishop and one of the legates of the Western synod; and one of the patriarchs, Juvenal, who alone among them was free to act for the Catholic party [Col. 1182C]. There were also other legates of the ecumenical council and bishops of the greater Churches, together with the remaining bishops who were then to be found in Constantinople, as well as others summoned from neighboring cities.

Therefore, since all of them judged that the chapters ought to be passed over in silence, it is not surprising if it is said that the Ephesian synod entered Cyril’s third letter into the Acts because it had been publicly read, but treated only the second as the rule of faith. Since this is established with complete certainty from the individual bishops’ opinions, it ought carefully to be noted by anyone interested in such matters, as a point useful for resolving numerous historical questions.

It has been sufficiently shown with what disposition those who opposed the chapters during Cyril’s lifetime did so. But apart from Cyril himself, who defended them in three separate books, and Marius Mercator, who overthrew the Nestorian antirrhetic writings, no ancient writer, so far as I know, has handed down the name of anyone who defended them. Nor is this surprising, since in that period minds were not yet sufficiently pacified to perceive how far the confession of ἕνωσις καθ’ ὑπόστασιν (*henosis kata hypostasin*, union according to hypostasis)—the principle and, as it were, the root of all the chapters—stood apart from the Apollinarian heresy [Col. 1182D].

This may also explain why, at the Council of Chalcedon itself, held in the fifth year after Cyril’s death, the third letter was passed over in silence, although it seemed that the matter should have been discussed all the more carefully because that deranged monk Eutyches and Dioscorus, the leader of the Ephesian robbery, were abusing it in an intolerable manner.

Here a question arises: at what time were Cyril’s chapters approved and received by the Church as canons of faith? When we were explaining certain words of Mercator, we said that they had been approved at the second Roman synod, but only as a root—that is, insofar as they differ from the profession of faith contained in Cyril’s second letters in form alone. But when were the chapters themselves, in their own form, received?

Some think that this occurred at the Ephesian synod itself, at which legates of the Roman Church were present (Christopher Lupus, notes on the Council of Ephesus, chapter 5). They produce three arguments in support of their opinion. First, that John of Antioch, who had judged Cyril worthy of deposition because of the chapters, was condemned by what they call a contradictory judgment. Second, that the synod issued no other doctrinal decree, although the whole Church believes that it issued some such decree. Third, that Cyril, writing in his apology to the emperor, testifies that both the Roman Church and the holy synod assembled from the whole world bore witness to the rectitude of his faith. A fourth argument may be added: the Easterners objected to the Catholic synod’s subscription to the chapters; Theodoret complained that they had been accepted by all; and Ibas caused trouble for the clergy of Osrhoene concerning the same matter.

These arguments, however, carry little weight. To begin with the last, the members of the Nestorian party told many lies, especially the claim that the Catholics agreed with Apollinaris. Among them, this was equivalent to subscribing to the chapters. Next, when Cyril says in his letter to the emperor that he has the testimony of the Roman Church and of the holy synod concerning the rectitude of his faith, understand him to mean the faith contained in his second letters and approved at the second Roman synod, not the chapters composed after that synod, as we have clearly demonstrated [Col. 1183B].

Third, no decree of faith was issued by the whole synod except the approval of Cyril’s second letter and the rejection of Nestorius’s opposing letter. This is clear from the sentence of each individual bishop, from the reading of the first session in its entirety, and from the histories of the fourth and fifth councils: in them Cyril’s second letter is said to have been read, but not the third.

Finally, John of Antioch was not condemned by a contradictory judgment. For how could a man who had contumaciously deserted his appointed hearing have been judged? And even if he had been, the chapters would not thereby have been received; rather, the hasty, injurious, and illegitimate deposition of an author who had not been heard would have been rejected.

When, then, did they first acquire the force of canons? Gregory the Great seems to imply that they acquired it at some point when he writes that in the Roman and Ravenna copies of the Council of Ephesus there is nothing else in the definition of anathema and rejection except what the chapters of Cyril of blessed memory reject (Letter 195, which is the third letter of Book VI).

But this passage from Gregory establishes very little. It signifies only that the aforesaid copies contained no anathema against those who asserted that Adam’s soul had not died in sin, but only Cyril’s anathemas. I do not see how one can conclude from this that the chapters were then received as canons of faith. Nevertheless, I would not deny that the matter can be established from elsewhere—namely, from the fact that the fifth and sixth councils were later admitted, and that in both of them the chapters were received.

I would readily believe, however, that at that time the Acts of Ephesus preserved at Rome and Ravenna were very mutilated and contained nothing more than what Dionysius Exiguus translated into Latin. Certainly, in the Beauvais manuscript which we used, only the few items listed in the general preface—and which we wholly rejected—are included under the name of the Council of Ephesus [Col. 1183D].

It is still impossible to determine who first translated Cyril’s letter into Latin, since Mercator translated the anathemas before the Council of Ephesus itself and, not long afterward, translated the letter into Latin. Thus Dionysius Exiguus had little reason, in the sixth century, to boast that he had translated the synodical letter of Saint Cyril, pontiff of Alexandria, from Greek into Latin speech, so that the apostolic faith of so great a teacher—already well known to the Greeks but hitherto unknown to the Latins—might become known:

“So that the Nestorian stain may be clearly recognized by men and rightly rejected for its wickedness; for under the pretext of faith it never ceases to insinuate faithlessness, and with Jewish fury joined to error it strives to disturb the tranquility of the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world.”

For before Dionysius, Mercator, inflamed by the fervor of the Catholic faith, had taken care to translate Nestorius’s and Cyril’s letters from Greek into Latin so that they might be known by the faithful brethren of his own language (Preface to the Sermons and Letters of Nestorius and Cyril).

### VII. The Synod that was the Third Roman Synod, under the Same Consuls, on the Nones of May

After Nestorius had been informed by a letter from John of Antioch that Celestine’s letter would shortly arrive, announcing the sentence of condemnation passed at the Roman council, he left no stone unturned to avert the great danger threatening his head. He thought no remedy more effective or more immediate than to obtain from the emperor the convocation of a general synod, to whose judgment everything would be referred and in the meantime no one would be permitted to attempt anything.

He obtained this from the emperor without great difficulty, since he could bend him in whatever direction he wished, both through his own arts and through the power of the courtiers, especially in the direction toward which the emperor was inclined by the urging of the monks and by his rivalry with Constantine and the great Theodosius, who had convened synods from throughout the world.

Theodosius therefore issued an imperial summons to all the bishops of the greater sees. He prefaced it by saying that religion and the empire were so closely related that each received increase from the successes of the other; that kings were intermediaries between God’s providence and humankind, ministers of the former and guides of the latter toward a pious and upright life; and that the ecclesiastical order would finally become what it ought to be when the clergy of every rank had been freed from blemish and fault and united in harmony and agreement (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 32).

He then ordered all the metropolitans to be present at Ephesus by Pentecost of the following year and to bring with them the most learned bishops of their provinces. He next explained the reasons for convening the synod: namely, that the disturbances arising here and there from many disagreements and disputes might be quieted according to the ecclesiastical canons [Col. 1184C], that those matters which had hitherto been admitted in an insufficiently seemly manner might be corrected, and that the stability of the piety owed to God and of the public welfare might finally be secured.

He further forbade anyone, before the most holy synod had been convened and had given its common judgment concerning all matters, to introduce privately any innovation whatsoever. Finally, declaring that he would accept no excuse for absence, he ordered everyone to be present diligently on the appointed day.

Since this imperial rescript was issued at Constantinople under the consulates of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III Augusti, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, it could not have been brought to Rome before the end of December or even the beginning of January. Hence Celestine was obliged to deliberate about sending legates to Ephesus who would represent the Roman Church and the apostolic see.

Since this was customarily done in a synod, especially when the faith of the Western Church was to be set forth, the pontiff convened bishops at Rome—not a small number, nor merely those from neighboring cities [Col. 1184D]. For an assembly had to be gathered which could properly be called a synod of the entire Western Church.

I know of no one who explicitly mentions this synod. Philip the presbyter, Celestine’s representative, refers to it somewhat obscurely when he says that the priests of the Eastern and Western Churches were present at the Ephesian priestly assembly, either in person or through their legates (Second Part of the Council of Ephesus, act 3).

A little more clearly, Cyril declared in an interlocutory statement that the legates had deposed Nestorius, acting in place of the apostolic see and of the entire synod of the most holy and God-beloved Western bishops (ibid.).

The whole Council of Ephesus plainly says this in its report to Theodosius concerning the legates’ arrival (ibid., in the report to the emperor):

“God, accepting as grateful and pleasing the care and zeal of Your Most Christian Majesties for piety, also stirred the hearts of the holy Western bishops with zeal, so that they might vindicate Christ, who had been subjected to insult. For although the immense distance of the journey prevented that entire multitude of most holy bishops from reaching us, nevertheless, having assembled there together under the presidency of Celestine, the most holy and devout bishop of great Rome, they have even now proclaimed our judgment concerning the faith with complete agreement, and have determined that those who hold divergent opinions are wholly excluded from every lot and rank of the priesthood. Indeed, even before this most holy synod assembled, Celestine, the most holy bishop of great Rome, had indicated these things in his letters and had entrusted them to Cyril, the most holy and God-beloved bishop of the great city of Alexandria, so that he might act in his stead.

“But now, also by other letters, he again made these matters known to the holy synod which Your Majesty ordered to assemble in the metropolis of the Ephesians. He sent these letters through Arcadius and Projectus, the most holy bishops, and Philip, the most devout presbyter of great Rome, who supply the presence of Celestine, the most holy and God-beloved bishop. Since, therefore, these men who have come have explained to this synod of ours by letter the judgment of the entire holy Western synod, declared to us a view concerning faith and piety consonant with our own, and decreed the same things as we have decreed—both in their letters and in the matters entrusted to them, which they also submitted in writing—we have necessarily reported to Your Majesties, as duty required, with their agreement, so that Your Piety may be certain that the judgment which has just proceeded from us is one common judgment of the whole world.”

These words—whether spoken by the presbyter Philip, by Cyril, or by the Fathers—cannot properly, indeed cannot at all, be understood of the second Roman synod. At that synod nothing could certainly have been deliberated concerning the sending of legates to the ecumenical synod who would represent the entire synod of Western bishops, since the ecumenical synod had not yet been convoked. Nor could anything concerning the faith have been defined by bishops whose zeal God had kindled, confirming the emperors’ earnest purpose, since the emperors’ earnest purpose had not yet become known.

Furthermore, do not these words of Cyril—that the judgment of the East was still being proclaimed by those assembled bishops—clearly demonstrate that the Westerners had assembled in synod twice? This is especially so since the agreement of the Westerners with the Easterners is said to be contained in the instructions which the legates had received from the synod of Westerners.

Moreover, of the three legates, the presbyter Philip is said to hold the place of Pope Celestine, while the bishops Arcadius and Projectus perform the legation of the Western Church. The Western Church, then, had been gathered into a council; for how otherwise could it have sent legates?

The cause, place, and president of the council are plainly established by what has been said. There can scarcely be any controversy about the time. For Celestine’s letters are recorded as having been issued on the eighth day before the Ides of May, or the day before—that is, on the seventh day before the Ides of May. Nor could the council have been convened before that time. By what means could the emperor’s decree have been brought to Rome before the end of December, or even the beginning of the following January; or the pope’s circular letter have reached the more distant Churches at a suitable time; or the bishops have left their Churches during Lent, when, according to ancient custom, they were occupied with preparing catechumens for baptism; or the bishops have been allowed less than three weeks to complete the journey? Since Easter fell this year on 19 April, the council could not have assembled until approximately the seventh day before the Ides of May.

Earlier I said that the number of bishops was uncertain, and it was uncertain from which cities they had been summoned. For scarcely anything remains in the Acts that could establish a definite view, but only material that can provide room for conjecture. Nevertheless, the number must have been considerable, and they must not have been gathered only from neighboring cities, since the synod is called that of the Western Church. I would readily believe that bishops also assembled from more distant regions, such as Insubria and Sicily; and certain acts of the saints seem to indicate this.

The principal matter discussed was the sending of legates to Ephesus. It is also credible that the faith was discussed—whether the definitions of the two preceding synods were reviewed, or the letters of Nestorius and Cyril were once more summoned for examination, or the faith of the Western Church was presented in some other way and incorporated into the instructions given to the legates.

Three men served as legates: the presbyter Philip and the bishops Arcadius and Projectus. To them was added Siricius, notary of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome.

What their instructions contained can be understood both from Celestine’s letters and from the speeches of the legates to the Ephesian Fathers during the council. One instruction concerned Nestorius: that they should execute what Celestine had long before determined. The other concerned the synod: that they should confirm the council’s decrees and add to them the weight of apostolic authority.

**Pope Celestine** (in his letter to the synod):

“We have sent, in accordance with our pastoral concern, our holy brothers and fellow priests, men of one mind with us and highly approved, Arcadius and Projectus, bishops, and our presbyter Philip, to be present at what is being done and to execute what we previously determined.”

Philip, requesting that the proceedings conducted before his arrival be produced, gives this reason: “so that, in accordance with the judgment of our blessed pope and of this present holy assembly, we too may CONFIRM the proceedings.”

**Arcadius:** “Following the instruction of Celestine, the most holy pope of the apostolic see, who has deigned to send us as his EXECUTORS in this matter, and so forth.”

**Projectus:** “I also, as EXECUTOR of the judgment, together with my brothers, by the authority of the legation of the apostolic see, determine, and so forth.”

Nothing remains of the Acts, so far as I know, except three letters of the supreme Pontiff: one to the ecumenical synod, another to the emperor Theodosius, and a third to Cyril. The first two are recorded as issued on the eighth day before the Ides of May; the third on the seventh day before the Ides of May.

In the first letter, the pope exhorts the Fathers to preserve the faith harmoniously, especially in that place where the apostle John was then present, the herald of Christ’s divinity and of singular charity; he then commends the legates.

In the second, after praising Theodosius’s constancy in defending the Catholic faith, he earnestly beseeches him, under the solemn appeal of divine judgment, not to permit turbulent innovation any license, nor to grant any opportunity to those who seek to confine the power of the divine Majesty within the framework of the human dispensation, thereby disturbing ecclesiastical peace. The cause of the faith ought to be greater than that of the kingdom; whatever labor is undertaken for the peace of the Church or the reverence due to holy religion is undertaken for the safety of the Empire.

From the last letter we learn that Cyril had consulted Celestine about whether Nestorius should be received if he condemned his own doctrines, since, after the period of the truce had elapsed, the sentence previously issued seemed to be taking effect. The pope replies, in accordance with the custom of the apostolic see, that an accelerated correction of any person is never displeasing to God, since he wills every human being to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. He says that he is concerned for the peace of the Catholic Church and for the salvation of the one who is perishing—provided that the man is willing to acknowledge his illness, and so forth.

Before I finish speaking about this synod, I think that certain points should be noted concerning the legates, the presbyter Philip and the bishops Arcadius and Projectus, but especially concerning Philip.

1. He was a presbyter of the Church of the Apostles (Council of Ephesus, act 3), and Baron believes—and not implausibly—that he was the man of the same name, rank, and office who, thirteen years earlier, served as legate of Zosimus in Africa together with Faustinus, bishop of the Church of Potentia, and the presbyter Aselus, to handle the matter of the appeals.

2. Although all three together, and at times each individually, are called legates of the apostolic see, or of the Roman Church, and are said to supply the place of the apostolic see and of the entire synod of Western bishops, Philip alone is expressly said to hold Celestine’s place. This is stated both in the Fathers’ report to the emperor concerning the arrival of the legates and in the mandate which the ecumenical synod gave to its own legates to Theodosius.

3. Conscious of his own authority, he speaks in the council of the pre-eminence of the supreme pontiff in words more exalted than any perhaps ever used.

4. He was the first of the legates to address the holy synod (Act 2); the first to pronounce the sentence of condemnation against Nestorius; and the first to sign the condemnation (Act 3).

5. He was the first, and outside the number of legates to the holy synod prescribed by the emperor—though Arcadius was one of those legates, as was the patriarch Juvenal—to depart for the emperor (Act 6).

6. In the mandate he is named first among the legates, in these words: “To Philip, the most devout and God-beloved, holding the place of Celestine, the most holy bishop of the apostolic see of the great city, and to the most devout bishops, and so forth” (ibid.).

7. He himself also seems to have raised Maximian, with whom he had served in the Roman Church together with Celestine and Sixtus, presbyters of the same generation who later became supreme pontiffs, to the throne from which Nestorius had been cast down. Hence Celestine says of Maximian, a foster son of the Roman Church:

“Rome, which always counted him among her own, bears witness to him as to a part of her own body” (Third Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 22, in the letter to the emperor).

And elsewhere, when he was exhorting the clergy of the Church of Constantinople to honor Maximian:

“Listen from him to what, while he was associated with us, he often heard from our predecessors. Our colleague speaks to you with our voice, because one faith must necessarily be proclaimed in unity. He does not borrow from us, in his person, the testimony of someone else; he was given by us, and was chosen from among our own,” and so forth (ibid., chapter 24).

8. Finally, he suffered calumny from the supporters of Nestorius, who circulated a letter under his name, as though he had said that Sixtus, Celestine’s successor, had been displeased by the deposition of Nestorius (ibid., chapter 35). We have explained the origin of the calumny elsewhere (First Part of Mercator’s Works, Dissertation 6), in the discussion of the author of the books of the *Hypognosticon*.

Concerning the other two legates, the bishops Arcadius and Projectus, we can conjecture only this: that they were men both learned and industrious, worthy of so important a legation; that they were called legates of the Western Church and of the apostolic see; and, finally, that Arcadius preceded the other either in ordination or in age.

The see and homeland of both are uncertain. For what Baronius conjectures—that Arcadius held a see in Gaul and Projectus at Forum Cornelii—is undermined by the very evidence from which it seems capable of being established. The distinguished writer says that in Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul, concerning the defense of Saint Augustine against his slanderers, the name of Arcadius is included among those to whom the letter is addressed. But from this it is plainly concluded that the Arcadius to whom Celestine wrote was a different man from the one he sent to Ephesus. For Celestine was writing in the year 431 to Arcadius, bishop of Gaul, at the time when Arcadius the legate was staying at Ephesus.

Baronius then adduces a sermon of Peter Chrysologus delivered at the ordination of Projectus of Forum Cornelii, in order to prove that the legate of the same name perhaps presided over the Church of Forum Cornelii. But the sermon he cites was delivered by Chrysologus when he was already a bishop, since he was speaking at the ordination of a bishop whom he himself was to consecrate. Yet Peter Chrysologus himself was ordained by Sixtus, who succeeded Celestine in the year 432. He therefore could not have preached at the ordination of a man who had been bishop before the year 431 and who thus would have preceded him in pastoral care by three years.

On the occasion of the legates, something brief should be said about Petronius, who is said to have been sent by Theodosius to Pope Celestine in the matter of Nestorius and to have brought the emperor’s letters. To these the pope replied that, so that the heresy might not spread more widely, he would, as was customary, convoke an ecumenical synod. This synod was celebrated at Ephesus in the following year, with a large gathering of two hundred bishops.

If such Acts deserved credence, Theodosius would have arranged for the synod to be convened not at Nestorius’s urging but out of hatred; he would not himself have convoked it, but Celestine would have done so; the pope would not have issued the sentence of condemnation at the time when the synod was convoked, but would have entrusted its issuance to the synod; and he would not have appointed Cyril to execute the sentence, but the entire synod. Yet the credibility of the Acts is unstable, however much Sigonius has attempted to strengthen it by interpolating ancient records. For Nestorius himself acknowledges that he had requested the synod; hence he is also called by Celestine the petitioner for the synod.

The legates of the apostolic see—and especially Philip, the most zealous defender of pontifical dignity—testified that the council had been convoked not by Celestine but by the emperors. It was convoked at the time when the pope’s sentence against Nestorius was to be put into execution. And Celestine entrusted the execution to Cyril, not to the ecumenical synod, as is clearly established by the letters of Nestorius and Celestine and by the Acts of the council.

## VIII. The Synod that was the Ecumenical Council of Ephesus, under the consulship of Flavius Antiochus and Anicius Bassus, or after the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III Augusti, in June, on the 22nd, a Monday

Since the matters relating to the Council of Ephesus occupy almost the entire third volume of the more recent collection of Councils, and since everything in it—whether preceding the synod, occurring during it, or following it until peace was established among the Churches—is distributed into three parts, I would be laboring in vain if, apart from the historical preface, I wished to write anything more about this synod. I cannot do so either better or more briefly. I have therefore thought it worthwhile to add only two matters which perhaps will not be unwelcome to the reader: namely, what we first learned about the Council of Ephesus from Mercator, and what I observed while reading both the works of ancient and of more recent writers on Ephesian affairs—whether something singular that may be learned, or something that, contrary to certain rules established elsewhere, ought to be avoided.

A third matter could have been added: a synopsis of the material relating to the Council of Ephesus, showing what is missing from the commonly circulated editions, supplying it, and restoring to their proper places what is presented in disordered sequence. But this has already been done at the end of the preface.

### § I. What We First Learned from Mercator about the Council of Ephesus

Mercator supplies us with:

1. Five sermons of Nestorius against the Pelagians, and thirteen concerning his own heresy, in which he openly reveals himself as a heretic;

2. Extracts by Cyril from the works of Nestorius, far more extensive than those found in the Ephesian material;

3. A refutation of the anathemas of Nestorius, which no one had previously attempted and which contains many things unknown down to the present day;

4. A refutation also of the creed composed by Theodore of Mopsuestia, by which the opinion of Facundus of Hermiane and of others who attribute that creed to Nestorius is overthrown;

5. Certain extracts from Theodore’s books on the Incarnation, in which the whole poison of Nestorian impiety is contained;

6. Fragments of five books written by Theodoret against the holy Council of Ephesus, from which many matters previously obscure are illuminated;

7. A short work against Eutherius, a man of the Nestorian faction, by which Photius is refuted for attributing foreign sermons to Theodoret;

8. A letter of Theodoret to Nestorius, published in a far more corrected form;

9. Letters of the same man to various persons, in which he reveals his impatience with the restoration of peace among the Churches;

10. Also a sermon, or rather a fragment of a sermon, in which the same man insults Cyril. From this many popular opinions are erased, with Mercator holding the torch before us.

He further teaches the number of Fathers who assembled at Ephesus, previously uncertain: he reports that 274 assembled. He also shows that Theodoret wrote against Cyril’s chapters before the synod, something that had remained doubtful until the present day. Finally, he records that, after their memorial had been submitted, the Pelagian bishops were condemned by the Ephesian Fathers.

These and other matters should be credited to Mercator. Through his assistance, moreover, the great disorder found in the works relating to the Council of Ephesus in the first and third parts of the commonly circulated editions can be removed. Anyone who reads the synopsis appended to our historical preface will recognize how easily the order can be restored.

It should further be observed that the Acts contained in the second part are not complete, but were abridged by Saint Cyril, with many things omitted that did not concern the Nestorian affair. Cyril suggests that he himself wrote the Acts in a letter to Eulogius, his *apocrisarius* at Constantinople:

“Present to the most magnificent prefect the two booklets which I sent to him: one written against the blasphemies of Nestorius; the other containing the Acts of the synod against Nestorius and his adherents” (Third Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 37).

That many things were omitted is demonstrated by this one fact: Leo the Great writes that Juvenal attempted at the Council of Ephesus to claim for himself the primacy of Palestine through fabricated documents (Letter 62 to Maximus of Antioch, chapter 4), yet nothing of this kind is found in the Acts.

The Eastern schismatics complain in their embassy to the emperor that their opponents did not cease, down to the present day, to exercise their accustomed tyranny, since they had suffered no punishment at all. “For everywhere sending unlawful depositions into the Churches, they disturb both clergy and people” (Second Part of the Council of Ephesus, in the Acts against Cyril and in the letters of the schismatics). The Acts are completely silent about those depositions.

Someone may bring forward the passage found in Gregory the Great concerning the Pelagians absolved by the assembly of the Easterners, and the anathema pronounced against those who defended the view that Adam’s soul had died through sin. But we have shown that Gregory was deceived by John the Faster, who sent the pope, as though they were the Ephesian Acts, proceedings conducted by Nestorius in his own synod against the Manichaeans. We discussed this in the notes to Nestorius’s second letter to Saint Cyril.

### § II. Observations Made in the Individual Historians of the Council of Ephesus

The history of the Council of Ephesus was written by the following ancient authors: Socrates (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII), Evagrius of Epiphanea (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book I), the deacon Liberatus (*Breviary*), Theophanes (*Chronography*), and Nicephorus Callistus (Book XIV). Among more recent writers are Baronius (under the year 431), the editors of the Councils, Petavius (*Dogmatic Theology*, volume I, book IV), and Christian Lupus (in his scholia on the general canons of the councils). In each I have noted what exceptional and distinctive material they contribute, and where, in my judgment, they present views contrary to certain arguments established elsewhere.

### On Socrates the Scholastic of Constantinople

Apart from what is commonly found in all the authors, the following points are notable:

1. In ancient Greek copies the same reading was found as in the commonly circulated version of 1 John 4:3. This is useful for strengthening the authority of the Vulgate and for refuting the recent admirers of Greek manuscripts.

2. Nestorius very frequently preached against the *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”), and his distance from Paul of Samosata and Photinus is evident from the sermons he delivered. These facts lend credibility to the sermons of Nestorius translated into Latin by Mercator. In those sermons Nestorius frequently disputes against the *Theotokos*, and he tries to demonstrate his distance, as he puts it, from Paul and Photinus in the highly agitated sermon he delivered after receiving the letters of Celestine and Cyril.

3. Nestorius was still living in the Oasis when Socrates committed these matters to memory—that is, in the year 439, up to which point he had extended his history from Constantine the Great through the seventeenth consulship of Theodosius, a span of 140 years.

These points deserve notice. Nearly everything else is presented in a confused manner, or even falsely—not to say ineptly—by a forensic writer dealing with theological matters.

Socrates writes:

1. That Nestorius did not assert, together with Paul of Samosata and Photinus, that Christ was merely human, but differed from Catholics only in words, and that he recoiled from the single word *Theotokos* because of the ignorance and negligence of the ancients. The entire preceding dissertation demonstrates how far this is from the truth.

2. That after the famous blasphemy, “I will not call God the one who grew to maturity through menstrual intervals,” Nestorius withdrew from the gathering of the bishops. This conflicts with the Ephesian Acts, for Theodotus, bishop of Ancyra, reported it in the first session as something Nestorius had said three days before the Fathers held their assembly.

3. That Nestorius was condemned on 28 June by the leaders of Cyril’s party, and that conversely Cyril was deposed by the bishops of Nestorius’s party before the arrival of John of Antioch. Both statements plainly conflict with the Acts: the Fathers deposed Nestorius on the 22nd, while John deposed Cyril in a tumultuous council on the very day of his first arrival.

4. That John was angry with Cyril at Ephesus but did not depose him until he had returned to Antioch. The entire claim is disproved as false by the Acts of the Eastern conciliabulum.

5. Finally, that both bishops, after their friendship had been restored, returned each other’s sees. Yet there were only three conditions of peace: the condemnation of Nestorius’s doctrines, agreement regarding his deposition, and agreement likewise concerning the ordination of Maximian. This is clear from the letters of Cyril, John, and Theodoret.

### On Evagrius the Scholastic of Epiphanea

We owe to Evagrius the preservation of Theodulus’s letter concerning the affairs of Nestorius after his deposition. If he had not torn it into sections, but had inserted it into his history intact, he would undoubtedly have earned greater gratitude from posterity.

He took much from Socrates and more from the Acts of the synod, yet he also added not a little from himself that conflicts with the truth, even where that truth is confirmed by certain testimonies.

1. He writes that, when Nestorius was traveling from Antioch to Constantinople, he met Theodore in the city of Mopsuestia and, after hearing his teaching, departed from true piety. This conflicts with John of Antioch’s letter to Nestorius, in which John speaks of Theodore as a common teacher whom they had once heard.

2. He suggests, or even declares, that Celestine’s and Cyril’s letters had been received by Nestorius before he requested from the emperor that a council be convoked. Yet the synod was convoked on 19 November, the date on which the imperial decree is recorded, whereas Celestine’s letters were received on 8 December following, as Marius Mercator demonstrates.

3. He excuses John of Antioch’s delays on the journey, as though they had not been intentional but had been caused by necessity. Yet from the “new Sunday” (*νέα κυριακή*), that is, from 27 April of that same year to 21 June, fifty-five days elapsed, and no bishop of the Antiochene diocese was more than a little over forty stages—or days of travel—from Ephesus, according to Evagrius himself, and indeed according to John.

4. He asserts that Cyril’s and Memnon’s memorials were accepted by all the bishops of both parties assembled together, and that John and his followers were summoned and excommunicated. The Acts openly contradict this. Even if they did not, he would still be speaking inconsistently: how could the leaders of both parties have assembled together, while John’s priests were nevertheless excluded as though they were contumacious?

5. Finally, he places the restoration of friendship between Cyril and John before Paul of Emesa arrived at Alexandria. But unquestionable records prove this false, since Paul himself was the mediator of the peace, and the mutual letters of John and Cyril say so (Third Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapters 30 and 34).

### On Liberatus, Deacon of the Church of Carthage, in the *Breviary of the Cause of the Nestorians and Eutychians*, the First Ten Chapters

Liberatus, deacon of the Church of Carthage and defender of the Three Chapters, writes that he obtained everything he treated in the *Breviary* of the Nestorian heresy partly from Socrates, partly from the Acts of the councils, and partly from the letters of the Fathers. It would have been desirable for him to have transmitted the material as sincerely and systematically as he had received it from the Acts of the councils and the letters of the Fathers of the Catholic party. He would have departed less often from the truth, committed fewer errors of arrangement, and certainly would not have revealed his own inclination toward the men of the Nestorian party.

Nevertheless, his work contains material useful for correcting certain ancient writers, illuminating matters belonging to Nestorian history, and even restoring to their proper order what is heaped together confusedly, especially in the third part of the Council of Ephesus.

1. After writing that Nestorius differed from the Samosatenian because, while confessing the existence of the divinity of the Son of God, Nestorius taught Christ to be a mere man, conceived and formed, and afterward advanced into God—that is, a deified man—and not the Word made flesh who dwelt among us (chapter 2), Liberatus shows the source from which he drew this account:

“For this reason Lucentius places the following in the epitome of his *Chronicles*, and says: ‘In the consulship of Felix and Taurus, Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, attempts to introduce a new error into the Churches, preaching that Christ was born from Mary as man only and not also as God; and he says that divinity was conferred upon him according to his merit.’”

He is indeed wrong to attribute Leporius’s error to Nestorius. Yet at the same time he provides something useful when he calls Lucentius the author of the annotation attributed to Prosper, and likewise teaches that the second part of the *Chronicles*, commonly inscribed with Prosper’s name, is nothing other than a continuation added by Lucentius. Thus he shows how the almost limitless *ἀνιστορησία*—“unhistorical treatment” or “lack of historical method”—and the confusion of the chronology, which runs almost continuously through this entire addition, can be removed from Prosper, a man of great learning and outstanding judgment.

Lucentius was bishop of Asculum, one of the four legates sent by Saint Leo to the Council of Chalcedon; he brought his epitome down to the year 455. But this belongs elsewhere.

2. He reports that, after a sermon delivered by Paul of Emesa in the Church of Alexandria concerning the two natures of Christ in one person (chapter 8 of the *Breviary*), and after the words of John, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), Cyril, as was customary, responded to the sermon and said among other things:

“What could be said more clearly than this? What explanation do these words require? He taught us that the one who dwells is one thing, and the one in whom he dwells another; human nature is one thing, divine nature another.”

And when he concluded his sermon, he repeated Paul of Emesa’s words:

“Behold,” he said, “John proclaiming two natures and one Christ: two natures of the Only-Begotten and one person. For when he said, ‘And he dwelt among us,’ he proclaimed two natures; then he added: ‘And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.’”

After reporting these words, Liberatus says:

“Cyril discussed these matters in the presence of Paul and taught the Church of Alexandria to believe concerning Christ as it had previously learned when Paul had discussed the matter.”

From this it may be inferred that Saint Cyril spoke after each of Paul of Emesa’s two sermons, for he delivered two. The words just reported belong immediately after the second; those found in the third part of the Council of Ephesus (chapter 3) belong after the first. For the sentence of John was not treated in the first sermon, but it is treated at length in the second. The commonly circulated edition of the Councils must therefore be corrected: Cyril’s sermon, which is placed after the second sermon of Emesa, should be attached to the first; while the fragment preserved by Liberatus should be attached to the second.

3. He also reports a fragment of the letter in which John of Antioch replies to the emperor’s letters brought by Aristolaus the tribune. Theodoret mentions this letter in his letter to Himerius (chapter 8):

“Because of those chapters of his, I will send my faith to Cyril; if he receives it and subscribes to it, I will communicate with him; otherwise I cannot be at peace with him.”

Many conclusions can be drawn from this passage. Elsewhere it sheds light on obscure matters and confirms doubtful ones. On these points, see the notes to this letter of Theodoret.

Yet how much he wrote against the unquestionable testimony of others, and how much against the sequence of events! I shall pass over the statement concerning the ordination of Nestorius, which he says occurred on the first day of April, although it occurred on the tenth. It could be a mistake by the copyist, who, finding “10 April” in the book from which he was copying, may have written “1 April.”

Certainly through his own fault he says (chapter 4 of the *Breviary*):

1. That John’s letter to Nestorius was written before Cyril sent his letter to Celestine concerning Nestorius’s affairs. Yet it is established that Cyril first wrote to the pope concerning Nestorius’s affairs; then the pope wrote to Nestorius and John; and finally John, after receiving Celestine’s and Cyril’s letters, wrote to Nestorius. Hence Celestine writes to Nestorius:

“We received, through my son the deacon Possidonius, such a letter concerning you from my holy brother and fellow bishop Cyril, a most approved priest, that we grieved that the testimony of those who had reported concerning your ordination had perished.”

Hence also John writes to the same Nestorius:

“Clerics from Alexandria have brought us, with great zeal, various letters concerning your piety: some from the most devout bishop Celestine, and all the others from the most holy bishop Cyril. Sending copies of these, I earnestly ask your Charity to read them in this way,” and so forth.

2. That the emperor’s decree sent to Cyril was dispatched at Nestorius’s request, after Nestorius had received Cyril’s letter to which the twelve chapters were appended (ibid., toward the end). Yet the decree preceded that letter by almost three weeks: the decree is dated the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, whereas the letters were received on the seventh day before the Ides of December.

3. That, after one decree had been written to Cyril, another was sent to all the bishops, by which they were summoned to Ephesus for the council. Yet the former decree itself mentions him:

“You too will have to be present at the appointed time, which is indicated in another letter sent to all the metropolitans” (First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 31).

4. That Celestine, in the letter beginning, “The letters of Your Holiness have caused sadness to our holiness,” gave Cyril his own authority to conduct the council. Yet Celestine’s letter preceded the decree announcing the synod by three months. It is dated on the third day before the Ides of August of that same year, and messengers announcing the convocation of the synod did not arrive in Rome before December, when that month was already waning. At that time Nestorius first informed Celestine about the matter:

“It pleased the most devout emperors, with the Lord’s help, also to convoke without excuse a synod of the whole world, for the investigation of other ecclesiastical matters. For I do not think that an inquiry will find the ambiguity of the words difficult, nor that it will be an impediment to the discussion of the divinity of the Lord Jesus.”

5. That John of Antioch came to Ephesus two days after the council had deposed Nestorius. This conflicts with the report of the comes Candidianus to John and his synod (in the Acts of the Ephesian conciliabulum):

“When, during the preceding five days, the most reverend bishop Cyril, and Memnon, bishop of this city, and the most reverend bishops who are with them had assembled in the holy Church, I forbade them to hold a session together contrary to the decrees of our lords and most devout emperors, and I instructed them to await the arrival of all of you. They nevertheless urgently requested that I read the imperial decree to them. When I refused, because of Your Holiness’s absence,” and so forth.

Candidianus made this report on the very day John arrived (in his synodical letter to Celestine):

“For as soon as he entered Ephesus, before he had shaken off the dust gathered on the journey, before he had removed his clothing, he gathered certain men who had withdrawn with Nestorius, who spoke blasphemous words against his own head and all but mocked the glory of Christ; and, as though he had assembled a college of men numbering about thirty, who bore the name of bishops,” and so forth.

6. That the Orientals published their judgment against Cyril and Memnon by posting a public notice before the arrival of the legates of the Western Church. This is contrary to the evidence of the Ephesian Acts. For the legates arrived on 9 July, and on the following day they were heard in the synod, when the second session was held. At that time, however, nothing had yet been learned about the schismatics’ judgment against Cyril and Memnon. For as soon as Cyril and Memnon first learned of this judgment by popular rumor, they submitted petitions to the holy synod on 16 July [Col. 1193B]. On that same day John, together with his supporters, was summoned once and again to give an account of his conduct; before he could be summoned a third time, he published on the walls of the theater, on a posted sheet, the sentence of deposition against Cyril and Memnon, but of excommunication against the entire synod. Thus Cyril said in his statement during the fifth session:

> Your Piety, acting through the most reverend and most religious bishops, summoned them at the first and second citation, as the faithfulness of the Acts records. But when they could neither defend their rashness by any arguments nor find any means of making a legitimate excuse, they committed an act disgraceful and worthy of mountebanks and street-peddlers. For if they had wished to make anything public before this great synod, they ought rather to have approached modestly and decorously—as Christian men should—and set out in person what they considered appropriate, then listened to the responses. Indeed, nothing prevented them from doing so—for soldiers had not yet been stationed before the holy synod, as they were before their houses. Instead, by composing a little document [Col. 1193C] full of arrogance and ignorance, and publicly posting it, they condemned this entire city—not so much to rioting as to the condemnation of their own ill-considered rashness.

The reason why the schismatics then published a judgment that they had suppressed for seventeen days is also obvious. It was in their interest to establish before the people that they had defaulted on their undertaking to appear, lest they be roughly treated by the rioting crowd. They sought to prove this by the publication, showing that they had been summoned to judgment by judges possessing no authority, since they were excommunicated. But why did they publish the judgment by means of a posted notice, rather than in the canonical manner through ecclesiastical officials? So that, by means of their own soldiers keeping watch before John’s house, they might pretend that the violence they had inflicted on others had been inflicted upon themselves, and thus claim that they were being prevented from acting according to the canons—especially since they could have alleged that the document which John’s archdeacon had submitted in the name of the synod of the Orientals had been rejected by the bishops summoning John for the third time.

7. That, after the synod had been dissolved and Maximian had been installed, the bishops wrote from Constantinople to Cyril because the proper measure of friendship and peace among the Churches could not otherwise be achieved unless everything Cyril had written in the matter—in letters, tomes, and books—were annulled (III part. conc. Eph. cap. 35). In fact, Cyril reports that this had been demanded by Acacius of Beroea and the Orientals (Epist. ad Acac. Melit.):

> The emperor therefore summoned to himself the most reverend and most pious bishop of the Church of Constantinople, Maximian, together with several others who happened at that time to be present there, and earnestly deliberated with them by what means the dissension of the Churches might be removed and the ministers of the divine mysteries brought back to concord and peace. They declared that this could never be accomplished in any other way, and that those concerning whom the dispute existed would not first come to concord until the bond of unanimity and agreement in faith had been set before them and, as it were, placed at their head. They said that the most pious John of Antioch ought to anathematize the doctrines of Nestorius and confirm his deposition in writing. They also said that the bishop of Alexandria would consign private offenses to oblivion and, because of charity, would regard as nothing the insults—which had indeed been extremely grave and serious—that he had suffered at Ephesus. When the most religious emperor agreed with them and took great pleasure in this plan, my most illustrious lord, the tribune and notary Aristolaus, was sent to carry it out. After the imperial decree had been explained to the Orientals, and had been represented as having been issued on the advice of the bishops who were present at Constantinople, they gathered, I know not by what arrangement, with the most holy and pious bishop Acacius of Beroea, and had them write to me setting out the terms of the agreement—namely, that the peace of the holy Churches ought not to be effected except in the manner which they themselves prescribed. Their demand, however, was severe and burdensome: they wanted everything I had published either in letters, or tomes, or books to be abolished; they were willing to agree only to the faith set forth by our holy Fathers at Nicaea [Col. 1194B].
