8. That John assembled a synod at Antioch for the sake of the peace negotiations. Cyril states in the passage just cited (p. 274, col. 2) that it was assembled at Beroea in the presence of Acacius; Mercator likewise states this in the preface to Theodoret’s letter to Andrew of Samosata.

9. That Cyril, after peace had been established, replied to Theodoret when he criticized the chapters, and explained his own chapters (Cap. 9 Brev.), and that peace and unity were thereby restored to the Churches. The entire passage should apparently be transcribed:

> These are the things that Cyril wrote in defense of the Oriental bishops concerning the two natures of the one Christ. I think that those who at that time did not at all accept this teaching were the founders of the Acephali, who neither have Cyril as their head nor show whom they follow. At that time Evoptius, bishop of Ptolemais in the region of the Pentapolis, received a copy of Theodoret’s letter, which had been written against Cyril’s Twelve Chapters, and sent it to Cyril so that he might reply to it and explain his chapters. Cyril received it with the greatest gratitude and produced an interpretation of his chapters, adding twelve explanations, so that he might appear to give a full account in their defense. Thus, when Cyril accepted and defended the faith of the Oriental bishops and explained his own chapters, peace and unity were restored to the Churches.

This is contradicted by Cyril, who makes no mention of the condemned Nestorius in the three apologies that he composed in defense of the chapters. Surely, if he had intended to do so, he would at least have written two of them before the synod and the third—as we said in the preface—while he was being held in custody, when his own case and that of Nestorius were still pending because of the imperial decree suspending every proceeding until the entire matter had been more carefully investigated and decided. That he wrote two before the synod—one against Andrew and the other against Theodoret—is clear from the fact that he replied first to Andrew and then to Theodoret, as though to a man not yet known. But how could Theodoret have been unknown to Cyril after the synod, when he had been virtually the mind and intelligence of the conciliabulum?

10. Finally, so as not to delay any longer in examining Liberatus’s statements with excessive care, I shall pass over several matters of lesser importance and add only this: through want of thought, Liberatus accepted as having been written by Socrates what he found annotated by someone in Socrates’ manuscript, or transferred from the margin into the text—although the annotator ought to have been in conflict with himself through intolerable madness. For the annotator denies that Nestorius said that Christ was God; Socrates affirms it.

The passage seems worth transcribing, since it gave several people occasion to err, along with Liberatus—Nicephorus, Evagrius, and others. It reads as follows:

> In his *Ecclesiastical History*, Socrates distinguishes Nestorius from Paul and sets out their difference in this way: “It is evident,” he says, “that Nestorius was ignorant of the readings of the ancients; therefore, as I have said, he remained occupied only with the word.”

[Note: [Col. 1193] The words that slipped into the text from the margin plainly conflict with Socrates, who says that Nestorius held the Catholic view.]

> But he subjected not only the word to examination [Col. 1195A], but also altogether denied that he who was born was God. We, however, confess that he who was born of the holy Virgin and was crucified is the Lord of glory, as the Apostle says: “For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.” Moreover, Nestorius says: “Do not boast, Jew; you did not crucify God,” as though the Lord of glory himself were not also God.

For he does not say that Christ was a mere man, as Photinus did, and so forth.

### On Theophanes Cerameus in the *Chronography*

Theophanes records five matters passed over by the earlier historians. First, that Nestorius was rebuked by Eusebius, then *scholasticus* of the imperial city (*σχολαστικῷ τῆς βασιλίδος*), when hitherto no one had dared to accuse the bishop of the royal city, who enjoyed favor at court and was able to undertake anything through the support of the powerful. I said “by the earlier historians,” for Leontius of Byzantium had already long before recorded this (Book III *Against the Nestorians and Eutychians*). Secondly, that this same Eusebius resisted the presbyter Anastasius when he pronounced an anathema upon the defenders of the *Theotokos* (*Θεοτόκου*, “Mother of God”). Thirdly, that Proclus delivered, while Nestorius presided in the Church, a panegyrical discourse on the Virgin Mother of God. Fourthly, that this very discourse was delivered *ἐν μίᾳ κυριακῇ* (“on one Sunday”), on some more solemn feast-day—namely, that of the Virgin’s annunciation, as we said in the notes on the discourse. Lastly, that Nonnus, bishop of Edessa, wrote to John of Antioch in these words: “Cleanse the Church, man of God, from the tares of Nestorius and their perfidy.” From this we understand that Nonnus succeeded Rabbula, and that Ibas succeeded Rabbula [as the printed Latin states, though the succession is irregular].

But he erred not in five matters only. For:

1. He assigns the ordination of Nestorius to the year of Christ 423, the eighth of John of Antioch, the thirteenth of Saint Praylius of Jerusalem, and the seventh of Coelestine the supreme pontiff. All these dates are far from the truth, whatever beginning of the year Theophanes may have adopted—whether September, as he actually did, or January, as others are accustomed to do. For by the unanimous judgment of all, Nestorius was ordained in the consulship of Taurus and Felix, and thus in the year of Christ 428, since he succeeded to the see of Constantinople when Sisinnius died toward the end of 427. Next, John was made bishop of Antioch in place of Theodotus, who ceased to live in 428, according to Theodoret (*Ecclesiastical History* V.39). Certainly Acacius of Beroea, replying to Cyril in 430, calls John newly ordained (I part. conc. Ephes. cap. 23). Thereafter Praylius governed the Church of Jerusalem after John; but John died in 416. Indeed, Praylius had already yielded the see of the holy city to Juvenal when he died before 428, as is clear from the same Theodoret (ibid.), who mentions Juvenal together with Sisinnius. Finally, Coelestine began to occupy the apostolic see, vacant through the death of Boniface, on 3 November 423; consequently he did not precede Nestorius by seven years, Nestorius having been installed in the see of the royal city on 10 April 428.

2. He writes that Coelestine gave letters concerning Nestorius’ case to John of Antioch and Praylius of Jerusalem together. Coelestine himself and Cyril contradict this. For the former, speaking of letters concerning John and Juvenal sent through Possidonius to Cyril, says: “We have also written these same things to our holy brothers and fellow bishops John, Rufus, Juvenal, and Flavian” (I part. conc. Ephes. cap. 15). The latter, concerning these very letters of Coelestine, writes to Juvenal: “When the most reverend and most pious bishop of the Roman Church, Coelestine, had learned about him and had written, and had given the letters themselves to me, I judged that I ought in turn to send them to you,” etc.

3. He relates that, after receiving the emperor’s letter of rebuke, Cyril wrote concerning the orthodox faith to Theodosius and to the empresses, his sisters, to clear himself. But the emperor’s letter proves Theophanes false. For in it Theodosius reproves Cyril because, by addressing one work to him and another to Pulcheria, he had sought, by directing one work to him and another to Pulcheria, to test the harmony of the imperial household and reconcile brother with sister:

> Unless you had thought that there was some dissension between us, or at least hoped that something of that kind would arise from your letters, why, I ask, had you written one thing privately to us and to my most religious wife Eudoxia, and another to my sister Pulcheria Augusta, who is herself most zealous for piety?

(I part. conc. Ephes. cap. 31).

4. He says that Coelestine excused his absence because of the hardships to be endured at sea in winter weather. But the excuse is neither adequate in itself, since the journey was to be made in spring, after that season had advanced—for the meeting had been appointed for Pentecost, that is, 7 June—nor true, since the supreme pontiff, through his legates, gave another reason: that the matter was no longer one of pronouncing a sentence, which belongs to authority, but of carrying it into execution, which belongs rather to obedience (Council of Ephesus, session 2).

5. He wishes the synod to have begun on 20 June, sixteen days after the appointed date. But how do these things accord either with themselves or with the Acts of the council? For the appointed date was Pentecost Sunday, which fell on 7 June, as the certain calculation of dates establishes; while the Acts expressly state that the synod began on 22 June—and it ought to have done so, since that day was Monday, on which it was customary for synods to begin.

6. He constructs the story—if it is history and not fable—of the beginning of the synod as follows:

> Accordingly, on the twentieth day of June the council began to be celebrated, with Nestorius, Cyril, and Praylius presiding over the assembly, Cyril holding the place of the Roman pontiff. While all were speaking about theology, Nestorius said with great arrogance: “I shall not call one who is two or three months old God; therefore I am clean from the blood of you all, and I shall not come to you hereafter.” Having said this, he left, accompanied by six bishops who adhered to his opinion. Cyril’s followers, assembling the next day, sent three bishops to summon Nestorius, etc.

For all this conflicts with the Acts of the council (II part. conc. Eph. act. 1), from which it is clear that the synod began on 22 June; that Nestorius never came to it, much less presided in it; and that the blasphemy uttered by Nestorius was spoken in a private meeting with Acacius of Melitene and Theodotus of Ancyra, who left Nestorius’ lodging, detesting the sacrilegious utterance.

Here a question arises which must briefly be resolved: how did it happen that, although the synod began on 22 June, the bishops nevertheless reported to the synod on that very day that they had been sent the day before—plainly by the synod—to summon Nestorius? Thus it had already assembled the day before. But since the twenty-first day was Sunday, the Fathers had to meet for the synaxis. Nestorius being absent, he was invited by four bishops to come to the synod on the following day, but was not legally cited, since it was a feast-day and the bishops had not yet made a lawful beginning of the council. Hence he was afterwards summoned a third time according to the canons, since the first summons did not have the force of canonical procedure, but was merely an admonition and invitation.

7. He relates that John of Antioch arrived with his party on the third day after the synod had begun. By this error he involved later writers in error too, contrary to Cyril’s clear testimony previously cited.

8. He likewise relates that Nestorius sat with John and the other schismatics when the sentence of deposition against Cyril and Memnon was pronounced. Yet no Acts contain this; indeed, by their silence they contradict it. In fact John’s synod did not restore Nestorius. It could not do so, being inferior to the one that had deposed him; nor, had it been able, would John have allowed it, since he was seeking the presidency of the synod, an ambition which Nestorius, by the privilege of his see—established by the Council of Constantinople as second after Rome—would have thwarted.

9. He speaks of Theodoret criticizing Cyril’s chapters, and Cyril refuting Theodoret, as though that criticism and reply had been composed during the synod. Theodoret contradicts this:

> Before the assembly at Ephesus was held, we briefly and plainly opposed the twelve chapters, so that their meaning might become known even to the unlearned and those without understanding, etc.

(Preface to the Five Books against the Council of Ephesus).

10. He says that Nestorius was taken away with the Orientals when they returned to their Churches. In fact he had left Ephesus for Chalcedon before the legates arrived.

11. He writes that peace was restored to the Churches when Cyril and John met, by the emperor’s command, after Nestorius had been deported to the Oasis, in the fourth year after his deposition. Yet, as certain chronological markers establish, peace was reconciled in the second year after the Ephesian synod. Nothing is more confused than this author.

### On Nicephorus Callistus, Book XIV of the *History*, chapters 32–37

Nicephorus took almost everything from Socrates, whose words he copies and whose name he even mentions. He likewise took from Evagrius and Theophanes, whom he does not name at all, although he uses their writings, retaining even the first person of the speaker—a fact that may occasion astonishment. Therefore the observations made about those three writers apply here as well: Nicephorus agrees with his masters both when they are right and when they err.

His own particular error, nevertheless, is that he maintains (chapter 34) that the Ephesian synod was held in the forty-first year after the second. For fifty years elapsed between the two: the second met in 381, the Ephesian in 431.

This too is his own error: that the Orientals forcibly retained Nestorius in the episcopate for the third year after the Ephesian synod. For before the peace John and his party did not even regard him as a bishop.

Yet he contributes two points of use for the history. First (chapter 33), concerning the decrees of the Alexandrian synod sent to Coelestine the supreme pontiff, a matter which we discussed while treating the second Alexandrian synod. Secondly (chapter 34), concerning the injunction of the great and holy man Euthymius, by which he ordered Peter, bishop of the Saracens, to adhere to Cyril of Alexandria and Acacius of Melitene as pillars and chief authorities of the orthodox faith. He took this from Cyril the monk, who wrote the *Life of Euthymius*.

### On the Most Illustrious Cardinal Baronius, Writer of the *Annals*, and Other Modern Writers, etc.

The most illustrious writer of the *Annals* wrote on the affairs of Nestorius with his customary judgment, learning, and diligence. If everything said by the ancients that he either collected carefully, corrected felicitously, or conjectured subtly had to be adduced, almost the entire history of five years would have to be transcribed. Yet there are some points on which, however much I might wish otherwise out of reverence for so great a man, I cannot agree—whether through slowness of mind, or because they seem to me either to conflict with certain preconceived judgments or to be reconcilable with them only with difficulty. I think these points should be set forth here and compared with the conflicting arguments, so that I may show the more learned the difficulty I experience in this matter.

And, to omit what is referred to the year 428 (no. 20)—whether concerning Nestorius as Paul of Samosata’s nephew by blood—an opinion arising from words of Suidas understood in an alien sense; or concerning the origin of the Nestorian heresy in the Pelagian doctrine of the merits of nature, an error of Leporius attributed to Nestorius by Cassian (Book I *On the Incarnation*, etc.) and thence popularly believed; or concerning a certain history of Nestorius (no. 27), attributed to Theodoret of Cyrrhus (Book IV of the *Heretical Fables*, chapter 11); or concerning the protest of Eusebius against Nestorius, falsely attributed to Cyril (no. 31).

For the year 429 the most illustrious cardinal maintains that Nestorius sent letters to the Egyptian monks (no. 22) in order to test their faith. Yet Cyril does not testify to this (Epistle 1), nor does any ancient writer. Rather, all commonly report that Nestorius’ expositions reached the monks and that some persons circulated them in order to deceive the minds of the simpler people.

He further maintains that Cyril’s letter to the monks was written before Nestorius disclosed his heresy (no. 22). Yet that letter is wholly concerned with refuting Nestorius’ first discourse, indeed also his second, as is clear from comparison of the letter and the discourses themselves. But the most illustrious cardinal could not have seen either discourse.

It does not seem more probable to me that the books *On the Right Faith* addressed to Theodosius and to the empresses, his sisters, were composed before Cyril’s first letter to Nestorius (ibid.). For the occasion for composing them was furnished by Nestorius’ second reply to Cyril’s second letter, as we demonstrated in the notes on Nestorius’ letter.

What he says concerning Cyril’s letter to the clergy of Constantinople, their petition, and the accusations brought against Cyril by four men serving the furious Nestorius (nos. 38 ff.) is in part refuted by Mercator, who gives the true heading of the letter; and in part it arose from a faulty Latin translation of the letter, which caused charges that Cyril made against those wicked men to be thought charges made by them against Cyril.

For the year 430 (no. 46), Julian, a follower of Pelagius, is said to have been Capuan by origin and bishop of Atella. This was commonly asserted by many because the manuscripts of the chronographers Gennadius and Prosper had been corrupted; but after the manuscripts were corrected, almost no learned person believes it.

It is said that Cyril sent to Coelestine the tomes he had written against Nestorius (no. 11), and Cyril himself is called as witness. But Cyril’s words (Epistle 1 to Coelestine) seem to contradict this:

> So that Your Holiness may clearly perceive both what he says and thinks and what those blessed and great Fathers of ours handed down, I have sent several tomes containing fragments of certain chapters; I also took care to have them translated into Latin by persons living at Alexandria.

[Col. 1198C] I see absolutely no way in which what follows (no. 12), concerning a Roman synod convened after Cyril’s letters were received through Possidonius—a synod, I say, which Cyril mentioned in his first letter to Nestorius—can be defended. For in this letter Cyril does indeed write to Nestorius about some Roman synod; but, just as that synod preceded this first letter of Cyril to Nestorius, which is evident in itself, so it also preceded Cyril’s letter to Coelestine, to whom he sent through Possidonius the very second letters of Nestorius as well.

Further, I am wholly unaware—and it seems incredible—whence comes the assertion that the letter of Coelestine to Nestorius (no. 13), in the form in which it is now extant, was translated from Latin into Greek and then again from Greek into Latin. For whatever Ephesian materials have been translated from Greek into Latin are read differently in different editions; but the letter in question is everywhere the same and in the same words, which plainly retain a Latin mode of expression. I admit, however, that the Contius edition of the Council of Ephesus (1574, Paris, at Nivellius) contains something supporting the most illustrious cardinal’s opinion; but that edition is so incomplete that no one has followed it.

I do not dwell on the distinctive insignia of vicarial power which Coelestine the supreme pontiff is said to have sent Cyril—that is, a Phrygian cap or pallium, or head-covering, which they call a mitre. Since these are reported by modern Greeks without the testimony of the ancients, they carry little credibility. And since the same authors at the same time say that both the title of pope and that of judge of the whole world were assigned to the Alexandrian, they find scarcely any belief, even with Baronius himself (no. 26). Finally, since these same modern Greeks assert that all these things were transmitted to Cyril’s successors, the whole story appears almost like a fable to persons who are not exceedingly credulous. For who does not know from all ancient images that Greek bishops of every rank, at least metropolitans, wore a pallium of the sort Western bishops receive as a gift from the supreme pontiff? Who is unaware that the title “pope” was applied to bishops generally, but that “judge of the whole world” was assigned to no one? Or who would suppose that a mitre of the kind commonly used is a sign of that supreme power—or indeed that the kind now worn by supreme pontiffs was worn by the ancients or transmitted to a vicar, if one were ever appointed? Had this happened, the ancients would have remembered it, either as an extraordinary thing in this single case now under discussion, or as an ordinary thing whenever vicarial power was conferred by supreme pontiffs.

I entirely fail to see the reasoning that led Baronius (no. 30) to assert that Cyril, before the cognizance of Coelestine the supreme pontiff, was unwilling to hold any synod in Nestorius’ case. For it has already been shown at length that he held two before writing to Coelestine (chapter 2 of this dissertation). I greatly wonder that the most illustrious cardinal adduces Cyril’s letters to Coelestine as witness for this assertion; the words he quotes seem to me to have a very different sense:

> I confess that I had intended to warn him by synodical letters that we could not remain in communion with one who taught and thought such things. Yet, judging that a hand should be offered to the fallen and that those cast down should be raised up as brothers, I have not done this to the present day; nevertheless, lest I should do nothing here, I exhorted him by letter.

Cyril does not deny that he warned Nestorius by synodical letters, since there he admits that the letters sent to Nestorius were those of the Alexandrian Church. But he says only that up to that point he had not said “anathema” against those denying the *Theotokos*, as Nestorius had said it against those affirming it, nor had he withdrawn from Nestorius’ communion. This is clear from the very words of the letter to certain Constantinopolitans cited by Baronius:

> What prevented us too from writing and thinking things contrary to his utterances: “Anathema, if anyone denies that Mary is Mother of God”? But up to now I have been unwilling to do this, lest there be persons who say that the bishop of Alexandria or the Egyptian synod has pronounced a sentence of anathema against Nestorius.

(I part. conc. Eph. c. 9).

I also wonder considerably why two bishops, Theopemptus and Daniel, and besides them two ministers of the Alexandrian Church, Macarius and Potamion—whom Baronius elsewhere makes archimandrites (no. 113)—are said to have been sent from the Egyptian synod to deliver to Nestorius the letters of the apostolic see and of Cyril (ibid.). For Cyril writes to the latter two, who remained at Constantinople, a letter headed:

> To Macarius and Potamion, bishops, and to Lord Dalmatius, archimandrite, etc.

(II part. conc. Eph. act. 1, among the catholic letters). Later, after the former two had been sent among the synod’s legates to the emperor, he wrote another letter to his fellow ministers Theopemptus, Potamion, and Daniel.

I do not so much wonder that the most illustrious writer of the *Annals* adopted the popular opinion (no. 60) that the Council of Ephesus was requested by Nestorius’ entreaties and convoked by the emperor Theodosius after the letters of the apostolic see had been brought to Constantinople by four bishops of the Egyptian diocese. For Mercator alone could refute that opinion—which even the most illustrious de Marca embraced—by making known the day on which the letters were delivered to Nestorius. For from this it is clear that the synod was convoked nineteen days before the letters were presented, although, as we have shown in the historical preface, the common opinion can in some measure be excused and brought within the bounds of truth.

It cannot so readily be excused that the synod is said to have been convoked on the advice of Coelestine the supreme pontiff (nos. 62, 63). For, to pass over much else, Coelestine would have had conflicting intentions at the same time: on the one hand, he would have pronounced a definitive sentence of condemnation against Nestorius and sent executors; on the other, he would have referred the case to a council. Certainly, in his letters to the synod, he would have mentioned something of any advice of his, if there had been any, etc.

I cannot understand how the most learned cardinal can maintain that Cyril explained his chapters before Andrew of Samosata and Theodoret of Cyrrhus, at Nestorius’ request and by John of Antioch’s command, wrote against them. For the exposition contained in the third part of the Council of Ephesus, distinct from the replies to the objections of each of the two aforesaid bishops, was composed by Cyril, at the synod’s request, while he was held in custody, as was established in the notes on the anathematisms and is demonstrated by the letter of the schismatic synod to its legates sent to the emperor.

I do not recall reading among the ancients that judicial proceedings were ever conducted on Sundays, especially in councils, but only on lawful court-days. Therefore I find difficulty in Baronius’ statement (no. 48) that on 21 June four bishops were sent by the Fathers to Nestorius to summon him legally to the synod. For since in 431 the dominical letter was D, 21 June was Sunday. In fact, that first mission of four bishops to Nestorius was a friendly invitation to the synaxis rather than a judicial citation to the synod. For that reason no notary went with the bishops, as always occurred in citations; nor was the citation framed in prescribed words and committed to writing, as the canons command. Consequently, when Juvenal understood that someone might complain that procedure was not lawful and that the case was being heard before the defendant had received the threefold canonical citation, he shrewdly intervened in these words:

> Although ecclesiastical enactments determine that it is enough if defendants are cited three times to answer the charges brought against them, we were nevertheless prepared to summon the most religious Nestorius by a fourth citation through the bishops beloved of God. But since his house is besieged on every side by bands of guards, and since, as the most reverend bishops returning from there testified, he grants no one access to himself, it is clear that with a conscience by no means clean he refuses the sight of this holy synod. Therefore, in accordance with the canonical enactments now before us and conducive to confirming our orthodox and pious faith, let the necessary measures be taken.

(Council of Ephesus, part II, session 1). For he feared that the day would be consumed in citations and that the affair could not be brought to an end; yet it was necessary for it to be completed, in order that the things desired might be brought to their outcome.

I understand well why the most illustrious Baronius (no. 78) commonly accepted the opinion concerning Pelagian bishops restored by the Oriental synod of schismatics and a canon enacted against original sin. He trusted Gregory the Great, who held that opinion, and, burdened by the immense labor of universal history, did not investigate the particular matter more attentively. Unless I am mistaken, we have attained the truth, if not by a certain argument, at least by a highly probable conjecture, in the notes on the so-called second letter of Nestorius to Cyril.

Nor do I understand equally why (no. 83) the presbyter Philip is said to have addressed the synod before the two episcopal legates and to have subscribed to Nestorius’ condemnation, because cardinal presbyters, though inferior to bishops in dignity, nevertheless, by their closer connection with the head, formerly possessed grounds on which they might sometimes be preferred to bishops. For, to say nothing of the eminence of cardinals, there was certainly another reason why Philip spoke and subscribed before Arcadius and Projectus: he represented Coelestine, whereas they represented the Western synod. This also explains, as we have already observed, why, when the emperor commanded seven legates from each synod—the Catholic and the Oriental—to be sent to Constantinople, Philip went in addition to the number, while Arcadius the bishop was included in that number. For Philip, because of the authority of Coelestine, whose legation he discharged, was regarded not, like Arcadius, as one member of the synod, but as bearing the person of its head, and was counted on his own account.

What Cyril relates in his apology concerning Victor the monk should indeed be accepted. But I am wholly ignorant how it could have been learned (no. 86) that the Nestorians lied anything else about him than what they charged against three other Egyptian calumniators of Cyril, whose monstrous crimes Cyril recounts, as was said above.

But what Prosper says in verse (*Carm. de Ing.*, chapter 2)—namely, that the Pelagians condemned at the Council of Ephesus were expelled from Ephesus in a tumult—must unquestionably not be accepted (no. 100). For, unless my judgment deceives me, it has been clearly demonstrated in the notes on the *Commonitorium* and in various other places that, during Augustine’s lifetime, there was a tumult at Ephesus against Coelestius, ordained presbyter in that Church, and his clerical followers.

The synod’s report to the emperor, beginning, “Concerning your solicitude and zeal for piety,” does not seem to have been placed in its proper location. Baronius believes that by it dismissal was requested from the emperor after everything had been concluded, including the matters dealt with in the seventh session. But it was written in the third session, as Cyril’s subscription as president plainly shows; yet before the seventh session he had been placed in custody by Count John.

[Col. 1201B] When speaking of Count John, sent to Ephesus to settle affairs, Baronius writes as follows (no. 128):

> The man sent to Ephesus by the emperor was John, who, they say, was almoner to Theodosius himself and whose more proper title was *comes sacrarum largitionum* (“Count of the Sacred Largesses”), etc.

I wonder at this not a little. For to this day I do not recall reading that the Count of the Sacred Largesses was an almoner; rather, he was one of the second fourfold rank of the *illustrissimi*, whose offices are described at length in the *Notitia Imperii*.

Nor does it arouse in me any less astonishment (No. 154) that the work is described as an apology composed by Cyril at Ephesus while he was being held in custody; for it ends with words that plainly indicate that Cyril wrote it at Alexandria after his return, when he was already enjoying peace, as though safe in a harbor from storms:

> You preserved us, as though snatched from a blazing furnace, by your most tranquil commands, so that, together with the holy bishops and monks scattered throughout your Egypt, [Col. 1201C] we might continually offer thanksgivings to the most holy Christ for your empire, victory, and stability (III part. Conc. Eph., chap. 13).

Theodoretu­s might perhaps be excused (No. 170) for having called the bishop of Milan, from whom Ambrose’s book *On the Incarnation* had been sent to Theodosius, Martinus, although at that time no one of that name governed the Church of Milan. Theodore­tus, I say, might be excused for this: a man living so far away could easily have slipped into error amid such a close resemblance of names as existed between Martinus and Martinianus, which was the name of the bishop of Milan at that time. It could also have been a scribal error, a copyist abbreviating the longer name into another that was shorter and more familiar to him.

Baronius reports (No. 183) that, after returning to his own Church, John of Antioch was the instigator and prompter of Andrew, so that Andrew might attack Cyril’s chapters in the name of the Orientals; and that Andrew performed this task, receiving as his reward that John should make him, though previously a monk at Constantinople, bishop of Samosata. [Col. 1201D] The similarity of the names perhaps led astray a man otherwise most prudent. For the Andrew who wrote against the chapters was, at the time when he wrote, one of the members—if we believe Liberatus—of John of Antioch’s council; that form of expression indicates that he was a bishop. Certainly he governed the Church of Samosata at the time of the Council of Ephesus, as Theodoret shows; and he still governed it when Aristolaus the tribune first came to Antioch to negotiate peace between the Churches.

Furthermore, that Andrew of Constantinople was still a monk when Theodoret wrote him a letter in the year 449 (*Epistle* 123), after suffering an injury from the president of the Ephesian robber council. Add that in that century it was unusual to ordain a man to another diocese, and such an action, carried out with so much arrogance—especially by the Antiochene against the rights of the bishop of the imperial city—would not have been passed over without serious complaint. The whole matter is treated more carefully [Col. 1202A] in the historical dissertation prefixed to the *Anathematiz­ms*.

Baronius also reports (*Annals*, year 432, No. 57) that John held a synod at Antioch after the tribune’s arrival, and that from it he wrote first to Sixtus of Rome and then to Cyril, expressing his agreement with the condemnation of Nestorius and the ordination of Maximianus. He even claims that John behaved differently toward Cyril than toward Sixtus: that he immediately disclosed his mind to the latter, but concealed it from the former, as though bargaining by strategy.

The facts, however, seem to have been the reverse. Two synods must be distinguished, or two stages of one synod. John first wrote to Cyril at Beroea, where he held a synod at the house of Acacius, and from there sent the bishop of Emesa. Then, after matters had been settled at Alexandria and Cyril’s replies had been received, John subscribed at Antioch, together with his adherents, to the faith of Ephesus and sent, as was customary, a joint letter to Sixtus, Cyril, and Maximianus, by which he showed himself to be in Catholic communion.

I say that John subscribed with his adherents—but not [Col. 1202B] with all of them. Some had withdrawn in indignation because this condition of peace had not been stipulated: namely, that Cyril should expressly retract his chapters. Others had not been present; among them was Theodoret, who impatiently endured the condemnation of Nestorius and Cyril’s victory. Since both Theodoret and Liberatus bear witness to this, I cannot sufficiently marvel that Baronius (No. 80) says that Theodoret had subscribed to the terms of peace and accepted Cyril’s faith at that time, especially since he is later compelled, in several places, to reveal Theodoret’s troubled mind concerning the matter.

These and many other things caused me difficulty when I was reading the *Annals*—all the more because I would gladly avoid disagreeing with the illustrious author of the *Annals*, if the other authorities permitted it. Their testimony, however, appears so clear that, against my will, it draws me over to its side.

I can say the same of Father Petavius, whose fourth volume [Col. 1202C] of the *Dogmas* contains a most learned account of Nestorius, of the heresy bearing his name, and of the Council of Ephesus. Since that account was compiled from ancient authorities, it can readily be judged from the observations made on each of those authors individually.

A *History of the Council of Ephesus* has also recently appeared from Christian Lupus, a Louvain doctor of the Augustinian order. It is indeed learned, but not sufficiently exact either in chronological matters or in its treatment of the definite testimony of the ancients, as though the immensity of his learning had overwhelmed the careful precision—*akribeia* (ἀκρίβεια)—required in the investigation of truth. Whenever occasion arose, whether in the dissertations or in the notes, I have corrected whatever in this author appeared to conflict with the indisputable testimony of the ancients.

## IX. The synod called the schismatic Council of Ephesus, begun under John of Antioch five days after the Catholic council

In the third volume of the latest collection of the councils, the acts of the schismatic synod are joined to the acts of the ecumenical council in such a way that the first part is placed after the first session and the second [Col. 1202D] after the sixth. The former contains an account of the proceedings concerning the deposition of Cyril and Memnon; the latter contains a confession of faith and the homilies of Theodoret and John. Both parts also contain various reports to the emperor and letters to different persons, comprising much that is useful for clarifying the history.

John of Antioch, having deliberately delayed on the journey, arrived at Ephesus on Saturday, that is, on 27 June, the twenty-seventh day after the appointed date and the fifth after the deposition of Nestorius.

He excused his delay to the emperor on the grounds that it was the rainy season, that the journey had to be made overland, that the arrival of bishops from distant places had to be awaited at Antioch, and that Antioch itself was partly suffering from famine and partly in danger from overflowing rivers (II part. Conc. Eph., session 1, in John’s report to the emperor).

[Col. 1203A] Cyril accused John in his *Apology* of deliberately delaying because of his devotion to Nestorius, lest he be compelled to pass judgment on one whom his own Church had submitted to the Church of Constantinople (III part. Conc. Eph., chap. 13).

Facundus of Hermiane seems to have understood the matter more shrewdly. He observes (*Book* VII, chap. 5) that John deposed Cyril and Memnon in such a way that Nestorius nevertheless was not restored; and by this observation he intimates plainly enough that the delay had no other cause than John’s ambition, since he was attempting to seize the presidency of the synod. For if events had turned out according to his wishes and intrigues, then, once two patriarchs had been deposed—Cyril by his own synod and Nestorius by the other—while the Roman legates had not yet arrived and the bishop of Jerusalem possessed scarcely anything beyond the name of his dignity, John alone would have remained able to preside over the entire synod. He hoped, evidently, that through the artifices of the counts Irenaeus and Candidianus he would induce the emperor to order all [Col. 1203B] the bishops of both parties to assemble together (Report to the emperor).

He therefore proceeded slowly until Nestorius had been deposed by those who had assembled with Cyril. But when he heard that this had happened, he flew forward like a winged creature, so that he might forestall the legates of the West and, now secure, overthrow Cyril.

Nevertheless, he deceitfully sent two metropolitans ahead to inform the synod that his arrival would soon take place and, at the same time, to urge those who were weary of the prolonged delay, in ambiguous words, to do—before he arrived unexpectedly—whatever seemed necessary; that is, as he himself understood it, to depose Nestorius. By this maneuver he both advanced his own interests, since others removed Nestorius, whom he himself could not remove because of their friendship; created an opportunity for accusing the synod of having acted precipitately; secured a means of appearing to console his afflicted friend, as though he were attempting everything on his behalf; and, through their ignorance, compelled even the counts who favored Nestorius to serve his own ambition. This, as far as conjecture can determine, seems to have been the true cause [Col. 1203C] of the deliberate delay.

A delegation went out to meet him beyond the city gates, not only consisting of several clerics and bishops but also of Cyril himself, the president of the synod. John embraced Cyril in friendship, but treated the others with contempt and even allowed them to be mistreated by the counts. He knew that the synod had sent men to report on Nestorius’s affairs and to warn them to avoid meeting with the deposed man.

What John did on that very day—or rather that evening—at his lodging, still covered with the dust of the road, is contained in the acts (II part. Conc. Eph., after session 1).

I have thought five matters worthy of particular examination.

First, what role Theodoret played in the assembly: whether merely that of one bishop among many, or rather that of some kind of agent and, as it were, director, at whose nod and prompting John acted, while the other bishops were less distinguished either in learning or in practical experience.

I was led to this second opinion first by John’s initial inclination toward Theodoret [Col. 1203D], by his admiration for Theodoret’s ability, and by the extent of his praise, as though nothing could equal him. I was led to it also by the fact that Theodoret himself speaks of the events then taking place just as he usually speaks of his own affairs; and finally because the acts of the assembly plainly reveal Theodoret’s bold and self-confident spirit, his resentment toward Cyril for disregarding the objections to the anathematisms, his criticism of the form and style of Cyril’s language, and his customary accusations against Cyril concerning fellowship with Apollinaris and other heretics of that kind.

Second, whether Ibas, that famous bishop of Edessa, attended John’s synod. Christian Lupus affirms that he did, on the basis of these celebrated words from the letter to Maris the Persian:

> Two days after this condemnation, we came to Ephesus. When we learned that, at the deposition of Nestorius, those who carried it out had proposed and confirmed twelve chapters composed by Cyril against the ordinances of the true faith, and had assented to them as consonant with the true faith, [Col. 1204A] all the bishops of the East deposed Cyril himself and decreed excommunication against the other bishops who had agreed with the chapters (Schol. vol. I, p. 410).

In support of this he cites Facundus of Hermiane, who nevertheless asserts the contrary in explicit words: “Ibas, however, was not present at the Council of Ephesus in which Nestorius was condemned” (*Book* VII, chap. 3).

Two unanswerable arguments support Facundus. First, the names of the Eastern bishops belonging to the schismatic synod are listed in the acts of the Council of Ephesus not once but repeatedly. In session 1, forty-three are named who subscribed to the sentence pronounced by John of Antioch. They are counted again in session 5, when the Fathers report to the emperor concerning the Easterners; again in another report, which is the response to the sacred document brought by Palladius; and finally in the synodical letter prefixed to the canons. Yet nowhere is there any mention of Ibas.

Second, [Col. 1204B] Nonnus, the predecessor of Rabbula, governed the Church of Edessa at the time of the council, and Rabbula had occupied the see before Ibas. Rabbula was still alive in the year 435, when he wrote to the bishops of Armenia and to Saint Cyril concerning Diodore of Tarsus and Theodore of Mopsuestia, and received letters from Cyril. Ibas therefore was not a bishop at the time of the Council of Ephesus, but only a cleric—and one who was not especially well disposed toward his bishop. Thus Liberatus writes (*Breviary*, chap. 10):

> When Acacius of Melitene and Rabbula, bishop of the city of Edessa, learned this—concerning whom Ibas, his successor, says in his letter: “This man, who presumes everything, presumed openly to anathematize him in his own Church,” speaking above of Theodore of Mopsuestia—they wrote to the bishops of Armenia that they should not accept the books of Theodore of Mopsuestia, as those of a heretic and the author of Nestorian doctrine.

Some attempt to undermine Christian Lupus’s argument from the letter by rejecting the letter itself as spurious, alleging that its falsity is betrayed especially by the fact that it contains statements conflicting with the acts [Col. 1204C] of the Council of Ephesus—for example, that John arrived at Ephesus two days after the deposition of Nestorius. Although this opinion pleased some, even before Facundus’s time, it long ago disappeared as a trivial fiction.

It is better, therefore, to acknowledge the following points. First, that the letter is genuine, despite having generated so many disputes. Second, that Ibas was at Ephesus at the time of the Council of Ephesus, lest the letter be accused of falsehood. Third, that he came there in John of Antioch’s retinue—or rather in Theodoret’s company, since he was connected with Theodoret by a shared intellectual and scholarly association. Fourth, that at that time he did not yet preside over the Church of Edessa and therefore did not subscribe among the bishops. Fifth, that he deliberately misstated John’s arrival as having occurred two days later, in order to agree with John, who was telling almost the same story to the emperor. Finally, that he briefly touched upon the remainder of Nestorius’s history, lest he be compelled to say what he preferred to leave unspoken, and that he wrote to Maris the Persian before becoming a bishop—that is, before the year 439.

All these points can be established without difficulty: partly from the words of the letter itself, in which [Col. 1204D] Ibas speaks of Nestorius’s condemnation as something carried out by others; and partly from Facundus and Liberatus themselves, who call Ibas “venerable” but speak of him, at most, as a presbyter.

Third, whether this synod had several sessions. Although the acts of only one session are preserved, there must nevertheless have been several, since the Easterners remained at Ephesus for three continuous months and were not idle, but carried out many actions belonging to an assembly of bishops. For, first, a common response was given to both of the emperor’s sacred communications: the one brought by Palladius and the one brought by John, count of the sacred largesses. Then seven bishops were sent to the imperial court and were given instructions. Add that a confession of faith and a petition to the emperor were composed. Finally, letters were received from their legates and letters were sent back to them—things that cannot be carried out without a conciliar assembly.

[Col. 1205A] On the occasion of the legates of the schismatic synod, it should be observed that one of them was John of Antioch, and that he was sent with the intention that, if the legates of both parties should meet—as was expected to happen—the Antiochene, by virtue of his see, would preside and would ordain the bishop of the imperial city, should someone have to be appointed in place of Nestorius, whose affairs appeared desperate. The Easterners omitted no opportunity to claim for themselves the judgment over Cyril and Nestorius and, at least once, to dominate the other Churches. For the bishop of the New Rome was burning with resentment at having been preferred to the Antiochene by the Council of Constantinople.

Fourth, what was done concerning the Coelestians at this synod? It is astonishing how differently different people conjecture about this, because of several letters of Gregory the Great in which he relates what business he had with John the Faster, bishop of Constantinople, concerning certain monks accused of heresy. But since we have overturned the popular opinion on this matter in more than one place, especially in the notes to the second [Col. 1205B] letter of Nestorius, I think that at present the only question requiring discussion is why the Catholics cast upon the Easterners the odium of association with the Coelestians, and why the Easterners in turn attributed the same fault to the Catholics.

I believe the reason was that at that time no name carried greater odium, since the entire Church and the entire empire had recently condemned the Coelestians as no heretics had ever been condemned before. For all the bishops of the principal sees had proscribed this kind of heretic by letters of denunciation sent to the whole Church: Theodotus of Antioch together with Praylius of Jerusalem in the year 416; Zosimus, the supreme pontiff, in 418; Atticus of Constantinople in 423; Cyril of Alexandria in 430; and again the Apostolic See under Coelestine, once and again. In the West, Honorius, and in the East, Theodosius, had also pursued these same men through edicts sent to the praetorian prefects.

[Col. 1205C] Fifth and finally, what was the reason that the Eastern bishops separated from the others? Was it because they really held the same opinions as Nestorius, or merely because they were ill disposed toward Saint Cyril and those who agreed with him—in other words, was the synod of the Easterners genuinely heretical, or merely schismatic?

The Fathers of Ephesus certainly regarded John, the leader of the Easterners, with suspicion because of his agreement with Nestorius:

> Our suspicion concerning John, that most religious bishop, was neither groundless nor singular. For as soon as he arrived, he openly declared to the holy synod that he adhered to the opinion of Nestorius—whether this happened because he wished to gratify friendship, or because he shared Nestorius’s error in doctrine.

[Col. 1205D] Cyril condemned them all as heretics:

> Some of them grant the holy Virgin the title *Theotokos*—“Mother of God”—and even confess that she is the mother of a human being; but others altogether deny it and add that they are more ready to offer their hands to be cut off than to subscribe to such a term. Everywhere they conduct themselves shamefully, declaring themselves heretics.

This was not true only during the synod, when passions were stirred, but also beforehand, when the matter had not yet been pursued with such intensity—and even afterward, when the minds of both parties had revealed themselves more plainly in words, as usually happens.

Before the synod, when Cyril was defending his chapters and replying to Andrew’s objection in the name of the Easterners, he in turn brought three charges, which were unmistakably *tekmēria* (τεκμήρια), proofs, of Nestorianism. First, that they rejected *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκον) (Anathematism 1, 10). Second, that they interpreted figuratively John’s statement, “The Word became flesh,” just as Paul’s statement, “He was made a curse for us” (Anathematism 1). Finally, that they refused to acknowledge two births of the Word (Anathematism 10).

In opposition to Theodoret, who claimed to be setting forth the faith of the Easterners, [Col. 1206A], Cyril brought six further charges, no less impious: namely, that they defined the incarnation as a mere *enoikēsis* (ἐνοίκησις), indwelling, and *analepsis schetikē* (ἀνάληψις σχετική), a merely relational assumption (Anathematism 11); that they rejected *henōsis kath’ hypostasin* (ἕνωσις καθ’ ὑπόστασιν), union according to hypostasis (Anathematism 2); that they actually acknowledged two sons in Christ (Anathematism 4 and 9); that they called Christ a *theophoros* (θεοφόρος), a God-bearing man (Anathematism 5); and that they denied that God was the one who is the apostle and high priest of our confession (Anathematism 10), or the one who suffered in the flesh (Anathematism 12).

After the synod, when peace was being discussed, Cyril demanded that the Easterners condemn the doctrines of Nestorius and set forth the faith in writing—something ordinarily demanded only of those who either abjure an error or at least labor under the gravest suspicion of error. He did indeed accept the faith they set forth, but, as he later sincerely admitted to his friends, he interpreted the doubtful points *oikonomikōs* (οἰκονομικῶς), “by accommodation,” and out of love for peace, in the better sense.

What is more, the Easterners themselves seem to have convicted themselves of heresy: heresy defended at the time when the synod was being held, retained when they set forth their faith, and again disclosed after peace had been made. For, when setting forth their faith, [Col. 1206B] they said:

> We shall speak briefly, just as from the beginning we have drawn from the divine Scriptures and the tradition of the holy Fathers, adding absolutely nothing to the faith set forth at Nicaea by the holy Fathers. For that faith, as we said before, is fully sufficient for every knowledge of piety and for the rejection of every perverse heretical doctrine.

What do the expressions “from the beginning” and “as we said before” refer to? Certainly to nothing else, since the entire letter contains no antecedent relative reference, than to these words of the instructions given to the legates:

> Let this be certain: the chapters, together with the anathematisms added by Cyril of Alexandria to the faith of the Fathers who assembled at Nicaea, must be rejected in every way as heretical and alien to the Catholic and Apostolic Church.

By these words they sufficiently indicate that they were then following the very faith they had followed earlier in the synod—the faith opposed to the chapters, not merely to some of them but to each one, so that they were unwilling to agree with even a single chapter, even if they had to be torn apart piece by piece. Yet no one could accuse the third chapter of heresy except a heretic. For who but a Nestorian would assert that the natures in Christ are joined by a merely moral union?

[Col. 1206C] Furthermore, in their exposition of their faith they do not themselves condemn Nestorius’s doctrines, but only “his wicked and profane innovations” (φαύλας αὐτοῦ καὶ βεβήλους καινοφωνίας), as though that Antichrist had indeed sinned in words, as John had once written to him, but in reality followed the Catholic faith as they understood it—even though that faith was contrary to the Westerners, to the supreme head of the Church, and to the greater part of the East.

What is more, they gave an exposition of the faith more deceptive than anything could be. Therefore Theodoret, unable, because of his distress, to conceal the matter, sincerely admitted what was really happening and accused his own associates of wicked deception: they condemned in Nestorius what they themselves actually believed.

But when a mind, agitated and unable to bear a prolonged concealment, can no longer contain itself, they once again, after peace had been established, gradually disclosed their former opinions. They circulated the books of Diodore and Theodore among the people, as though either the teachers of the East had to be condemned in Nestorius or Nestorius had to be acquitted in those teachers. Cyril almost came to regret [Col. 1206D] having approved the faith sent to him; he partly excused his action to friends who disapproved of it and partly consoled himself inwardly with the conviction of *oikonomia* (οἰκονομία), accommodation, and with his desire for peace.

These matters will be treated at greater length in the supplement to Theodoret, where his methods for disturbing the peace will be exposed. For now, several statements by Cyril should be briefly set out, so that the foregoing may be believed. Thus he writes in his letter to Acacius of Melitene:

> I have read the letter of your holiness, written to the most religious and reverend bishop John of Antioch [Col. 1207A], full of the greatest confidence and, at the same time, of love for God. I too wrote letters of this kind to him; but, as it seems, worse things prevail. For while pretending to hate the things that belong to Nestorius, they introduce them again in another form, admiring the things that belong to Theodore—and certainly possessing an equal, or rather a much worse, disease of impiety. For Theodore was not the disciple of Nestorius; rather, Nestorius was his disciple. They speak as though from one mouth and vomit forth from their own heart the same poison of evil doctrine.
>
> The Easterners therefore wrote to me that the things belonging to Theodore ought not to be condemned, lest, as they said, the sayings of blessed Athanasius, Theophilus, Basil, and Gregory also be condemned. For they say the same things as Theodore. I could not tolerate their writing this, but I declared confidently that Theodore had a blasphemous tongue and a pen that served it, whereas those other men were teachers of the whole of orthodoxy and shone within it.
>
> They nevertheless persuaded the Easterners to such an extent that the people began shouting in the Churches, “May Theodore’s faith increase!” Once, when he had been stoned in his own Church, he dared mutter something brief. But as the teacher thinks, so the flock understands.

See also the letter to Lampon and Gennadius, *On Accommodation* (περὶ τῆς οἰκονομίας), which expresses the same view.

## X. The synod called the second Council of Constantinople, concerning the ordination of Maximianus, under the same consuls, on 25 October

[Col. 1207B] When the emperor Theodosius learned from the most holy archimandrite Dalmatius that he was being deceived by the counts sent to Ephesus, who were preventing reliable messengers from Constantinople from bringing news of the affairs at Ephesus, he ordered bishops from both parties to be sent to him, so that they might report the truth openly. He heard them at the villa of Rufiniana near Chalcedon. The Easterners numbered five; but when he had been informed about the whole matter, he dismissed them to their Churches and brought the Catholics to Constantinople, in order to appoint a bishop over the imperial city (II part. Conc. Eph., in the letter of the Catholics and schismatics).

They therefore assembled at Constantinople on 25 October in the year 431. The synod consisted of Philip the presbyter, representing Pope Coelestine; [Col. 1207C]; the seven bishops sent by the ecumenical council—Arcadius, Juvenal, Flavian, Firmus, Theodotus, Acacius, and Evoptius; four Egyptians—Daniel, Theopemptus, Macarius, and Potamion; and seven others who happened then to be present at the imperial court—Eulalius, Eutrechius, Acacius, Chrysaphius, Jeremiah, Theodulus, and Isaiah—together with the others customarily present from the neighboring cities subject to the see of Constantinople.

While they were deliberating about the bishop to be appointed, controversy arose again concerning Philip, the presbyter of the Church of Constantinople, and Proclus, the encomiast of the Mother of God. Philip once again easily lost his case. The dispute over Proclus was more serious: some members of the clergy eagerly desired him, while others, and especially those with influence, brought forward the old reason for rejecting him—namely, his previous occupation of the bishopric of Cyzicus.

The zeal of a large part of the clergy and people for Proclus was reinforced by the favor of the ecumenical synod and of the supreme pontiff, and even by a kind of claim of right, since Proclus had fought vigorously for the faith and had suffered from Nestorius, whose impious doctrines he had openly denounced, what tyrants commonly inflict on martyrs.

Yet this very consideration restrained Theodosius and the leading men from inclining toward him. They feared that Proclus might either, following the example of Chrysostom, use [Col. 1207D] the people’s love to dare what was displeasing to the imperial court; or, because of his hatred of Nestorius, obstruct the plans for peace that the emperor desired, even if the peace were fictitious; or, finally, driven by zeal for truth and faith, expose the schemes of the powerful men who favored Nestorius and who had until then secretly but disastrously harmed religion (Liberatus, *Breviary*, chap. 7).

This conflict of considerations and disagreement led everyone, once both aforementioned presbyters had been passed over, to agree upon Maximianus. The legate Philip worked for this outcome in favor of his fellow soldier in the Roman Church.

Maximianus had been a monk of the Church of Constantinople and then a presbyter and administrator of the poor; nevertheless, he had been brought up in the Roman Church. He was pleasing to everyone: to the supreme pontiff, because he had lived for a long time with him in the Roman Church; to the emperor, who revered Dalmatius, Maximianus’s spiritual father, [Col. 1208A] above all others; to the Council of Ephesus, which he had supported, together with Dalmatius, before Theodosius; to Saint Cyril, who was closely connected with Dalmatius and the other monks; to the Catholic party of the Constantinopolitan clergy, with whom he had worked vigorously; and even to those who favored Nestorius, because his religious simplicity and lack of learning would fulfill Nestorius’s desire. He was also pleasing to the court and to the men who held power because of his peaceable disposition, and finally to the entire people because of his reputation for holiness and his care of the poor.

For, as the supreme pontiff testifies (III part. Conc. Eph., chap. 20), he was not raised up by the glory of wealth, nor by an ambition for power such as usually exists in those who seek office, nor by the inflation of honors. By the vote of the poor, to whom, as a faithful and prudent servant, he gave food at the proper time, he was placed over all the goods of his Lord (Matthew 24:47).

After these words of Coelestine, the following is added:

> And yet, even if he desired the episcopate, he desired it only for the sake of good work, as the Apostle says (1 Timothy 3); he desired a good work. Thus our God observes both what we desire and why we desire it. Who could doubt that a man presiding might accomplish more than he was able to accomplish while subject to another? A hateful and blasphemous man could not hold this office [Col. 1208B]—that is, the care of bodies—since he was striving to wound souls, and so forth.

These words plainly indicate that Maximianus had suffered from envy because he had sought the dignity, but that the pontiff defended him because Maximianus wished to restore to their proper uses the resources of the poor that Nestorius had squandered.

From this synod three letters were sent: one to the supreme pontiff, one to the bishops of Old Epirus, and one to Cyril. This is known only from the response, for the third letter, which is read in the third part of the Council of Ephesus (chapters 16 and 17), is a personal letter written by Maximianus alone to a friend.

The letters to the pontiff, carried by the presbyter John and the deacon Epictetus, were accompanied by a letter from the emperor to the same pontiff. The letters to the Epirotes were accompanied by the canons enacted by the ecumenical synod against the supporters of Nestorius and Coelestius. Nothing remains of the former except their memory in the pontiff’s response; the latter are contained in the third part of the Council of Ephesus.

Both sets of letters mention [Col. 1208C] the ordination of Maximianus in place of Nestorius, an ordination that was a complete victory in matters of faith concerning error and, in the matter of Christ, a victory over Nestorius. The letters sent to Rome contained praise of Maximianus. Those sent to Old Epirus contained warnings about avoiding the practices of the schismatics and the lies of those who boasted that they enjoyed fellowship with the ecumenical council, although they had been separated and expelled from it by a sentence of excommunication.

Moreover, the synod used the same Ephesian canons that it sent to Epirus against four metropolitans of the diocese of Constantinople: Himerius of Nicomedia, Helladius of Tarsus, Eutherius of Tyana, and Dorotheus of Marcianopolis. It deposed them from their sees because they continued to adhere to Nestorius and, as is credible, appointed others in their places. The sentence is obscurely mentioned, but it is nevertheless certain, as we have shown in its proper place.

[Col. 1208D] What reply was given by the Macedonians is unknown. Coelestine sent his reply on the Ides of March through the presbyter John and the deacon Epictetus. They had come to Rome during the days of the Lord’s Nativity and returned to Constantinople by Easter.

The excellent old man sent four paternal letters: to the synod, to Theodosius, to Maximianus, and to the clergy and people of Constantinople. To the synod he sent congratulations on the completion of the victory, that is, on the ordination of Maximianus. To Theodosius he sent not merely congratulations but also exhortations, urging him, once Nestorius had been driven far away, to procure peace among the Churches. To Maximianus he sent admonitions, urging him to gather again Christ’s flock, which had been scattered by the wolf, and, following in the footsteps of his predecessors, to restore the Church entrusted to him to its former splendor.

Finally, to the clergy and people of the imperial city he sent a very lengthy letter [Col. 1209A] concerning Christ’s victory over the enemy Nestorius; the steadfastness of the Constantinopolitan Church in preserving the faith against the tyranny of a shepherd turned into a wolf; the praises of Cyril, who was fighting for Christ; his own eagerness to provide assistance to those in danger; Nestorius’s evasion of the judgment of the synod he himself had requested; the Coelestians who adhered to him; the need to hear Maximianus’s teaching, which he had imbibed at its source in Rome; and, finally, the need to preserve religion steadfastly.

These letters of the most holy pontiff possess all the more authority and deserve all the greater reverence because they breathe more fully the apostolic spirit: the spirit of a soul rejoicing in a victory won, and of an excellent old man seeking from God his release after exhausting himself in the labors of a most difficult war and obtaining that departure, together with the legitimate crown of justice, from the just Judge.

For although he wrote on the Ides of March, he departed to heaven on the third day before the Nones of April, obtaining from God what he had requested from the emperor: concord among the Churches and the removal of Nestorius, the cause of discord, far from human society.

## XI. The second schismatic synod, held by the Easterners immediately after the Council of Ephesus had been dissolved, approximately in November of the year 431

The Easterners had determined that they would never agree either to the deposition of Nestorius, which they claimed had been unjustly carried out and to their own contempt, or to the restoration of Cyril, whom they boasted they had rightly deprived of office on account of heresy.

They did not begin this opposition only once or in one place. They began at Ephesus, when the legates, having received their instructions, were preparing to depart for Constantinople; again at Chalcedon, when they presented a second and third petition to the emperor; a third time at Tarsus, when they returned to the East after being dismissed; and finally at Antioch, where they had gathered from Ephesus and Chalcedon before dispersing from one another and returning individually to their own Churches.

This account is supported not only for the most part by the acts of the Council of Ephesus but also by Theodoret’s testimony [Col. 1209C] in the writings of Mercator. For Theodoret wrote to Andrew of Samosata:

> I think that, above all, my most holy and venerable lord Bishop John has been especially satisfied that I in no way consent to the condemnation of my most holy and venerable lord, Bishop Nestorius, nor violate the common pledge made at Tarsus, Chalcedon, and Ephesus. For he also remembers what we repeatedly brought forward recently at Antioch after our return.

There can be no doubt that the synod at Antioch was convened at Theodoret’s prompting, since he bore with the greatest bitterness of spirit the fall of his friend Nestorius and the victory of his opponent Cyril, as he understood it.

It is reasonable to believe that the bishops who had returned either from Chalcedon or from Ephesus assembled there, as well as several others who had remained in the East during the time of the council, such as Andrew of Samosata and others.

From the testimony of two ancient writers who mention this gathering, it is possible to ascertain, at least to some extent, what took place [Col. 1209D]. Socrates writes (Book VII, chapter 33): “When John had returned to Antioch, he gathered many bishops together and deposed Cyril, who had already returned to Alexandria.” Liberatus writes (Brief Account, chapter 6): “After learning these things, the emperor ordered them—the legates of the ecumenical synod—to enter the church and ordain another bishop in place of Nestorius; and afterward he ordered all the bishops to depart, each to his own region. Thus John set out with his followers for Antioch, where, gathering very many bishops, he again condemned Cyril, although Cyril was already in Alexandria.”

## XII. The synod that was the third Constantinopolitan synod—or rather, the consultation of the bishops in the palace before the emperor—concerning the establishment of a basis for peace among the churches, in the consulship of Flavius Valerius and Flavius Aetius, in the year of Christ 432.

Theodosius, after receiving a letter from Saint Celestine urging the settlement of the dispute between the Eastern and Alexandrian Churches [Col. 1210A], and after likewise reading the apologetic book in which Cyril easily defended himself before the emperor—who had already taken the side of the ecumenical synod—against the calumnies of the Easterners, summoned Maximian, bishop of the imperial city, together with the other prelates found in the imperial retinue and even the clergy of the city, in order to deliberate on the means of establishing peace and removing the discord between those two major churches, which were drawing the government of the East into their respective factions, as well as Constantinople itself, where the clergy and people were still afflicted by factions, whether voluntarily or under the influence of Nestorius’s friends.

Nor was the matter either insignificant or easy to handle. For the bishop of each of the two greatest cities—Alexandria and Antioch—possessed great and especially weighty authority, not only because of the dignity of his see, but also because of his own individual reputation.

Neither had acquired a slight reputation for holiness; both were joined in friendship to men of the greatest sanctity: John to Simeon the Stylite, Cyril to Dalmatius [Col. 1210B]. Both were distinguished by learning and zeal for the faith. Each fought against the other with correspondingly greater vehemence because he thought himself compelled to fight for the more honorable cause—or rather, by necessity itself.

Nevertheless, the Antiochene bore nearly the whole odium of the dispute, since he had been excluded from communion with both Romes; and because Cyril enjoyed that communion, he prevailed by the merit of his cause. Yet Cyril himself was suspect to many for this reason: he was believed to wish to avenge the injuries he had received at Ephesus and his old resentments. Moreover, the Antiochene was weighed down by the suspicion that he agreed with Nestorius, whom he seemed to have defended beyond the limit permitted by reason in the assistance owed to a friend in danger.

Cyril, on the other hand, was heard as the defender of the faith chiefly because of the presumption that he remained in communion with the apostolic see and with the whole synod.

Since these and other considerations were pulling the assembly toward differing opinions, the emperor decided first to write to both prelates, but in different letters. Nevertheless, in both letters [Col. 1210C] he ordered them to come to Nicomedia and not to leave until they had settled the matter of peace by mutual agreement.

He then imposed these conditions of peace: that the Antiochene should consent to the condemnation of Nestorius and his doctrines, as well as to the ordination of Maximian; and that Cyril should forget the injuries he had suffered. Next, he pressed Acacius of Beroea and Simeon the Stylite by letter to moderate John’s spirit and incline him toward peace.

Fourth, he forbade Cyril and John to bring any bishops with them to Nicomedia for the discussion, allowing them only a few clerics whose services they might require. Fifth, while the matter was being conducted, he forbade any ordination, deposition, or other appointment whatsoever of any bishops. Finally, he sent the tribune Aristolaus, who was to advance the matter not merely by letters and instructions but also by the authority entrusted to him (Third Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 24).

All these measures were carried out. The letters sent by the emperor to John and to the Stylite have reached us (ibid., chapter 26). Those sent to Cyril have entirely perished [Col. 1210D], and those to Acacius have survived only in part.

Nor can the opinion of certain people stand who think that the emperor’s letters which, in the third part of the Council of Ephesus, are addressed to the blessed Simeon the Stylite were either addressed to Simeon alone, or to Acacius alone, or were common to Simeon and Acacius. For those who hold this view must not have read the letters with sufficient attention: they contain nothing that concerns Acacius and nothing that does not properly apply to Simeon (ibid., chapter 25).

It will not be out of place to extract something from these three letters. From the first, addressed to John, come words worthy of a most Christian prince:

> We are presented with a grave occasion of distress and great sorrow by the fact that the teachers of ecclesiastical peace, and the very fountains of concord, have fallen into such disagreements that they require others to remind them, by their exhortations, of what they ought to have proclaimed in accordance with their office (Third Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 24).

Also worthy of attention is this statement [Col. 1211A]:

> Meanwhile, while the desired agreement of peace, concord, and mutual friendship between you is being confirmed even on the journey to our conference, no ordination, deposition, or any other appointment whatsoever of any bishops shall be attempted. But if anything of this kind should meanwhile happen, let it remain unmoved and undisturbed until the Catholic Church’s settlement has been achieved; for devout clerics may suffice for the performance of the divine ministries until perfect union is attained (ibid.).

From the second letter, addressed to the Stylite:

> Contention and discord disturb us so greatly that we consider them the principal cause of all our calamities. We are confident that the affairs of our kingdom will proceed according to the will of God’s goodness if the members of the Church and of the orthodox faith are joined and united (ibid., chapter 25).

Finally, from a fragment of the third letter:

> It is fitting that your holiness should ask these things of God with every diligence and zeal, that he may declare the priests of the ROMAN RELIGION approved (ibid., chapter 26).

## XIII. The synod that was the third synod of the still-schismatic Easterners, held at Beroea under Acacius, after the emperor’s instructions had been delivered by the tribune Aristolaus, in the same year, toward the end of June.

[Col. 1211B]

After the tribune Aristolaus arrived in Syria and delivered the emperor’s letters to John of Antioch, Acacius of Beroea, and Simeon the Stylite, John summoned bishops from his entire diocese, so that, since the matter concerned everyone, everyone’s judgment might also determine what had to be done and how the royal commands were to be obeyed.

The time at which the synod was held can plausibly be determined as follows. Everyone agrees that it was held in the year 432, and this is established by indisputable evidence. The emperor’s letters, although they lack a date, nevertheless mention Pope Celestine; they must therefore have been written before the middle of April, when, as is clear, the messengers announcing Celestine’s death—which occurred at Rome on 6 April—had not yet [Col. 1211C] reached Constantinople. Aristolaus therefore cannot have arrived in Syria—or travelled there by land—before the middle of May had passed.

Now, in that year Pentecost fell on 22 May. Therefore, even if the imperial dispatch is said to have arrived immediately after the letters were received or after the festivals had ended, it could not have reached all the bishops—some of whom lived twelve stages from Antioch—before the beginning of June. Consequently, the bishops could not have assembled at the appointed place before June was already advancing.

Although it is commonly believed that the synod was held at Antioch, Cyril and Mercator nevertheless undermine that popular belief with definite testimony. Cyril, writing to Acacius of Melitene, says:

> After the imperial decree had been explained to the Easterners, as having been issued according to the judgment of those bishops who were present at Constantinople, they gathered in some council—I do not know what council—at the house of the most holy and devout bishop Acacius of Beroea, and arranged for a letter to be sent to me, etc.

Mercator, on the other hand, reports a letter written by Theodoret to Andrew of Samosata after Cyril’s letter, sent from Beroea, had been read. Nevertheless, it may not implausibly be said that the synod began at Beroea and ended at Antioch, as will be explained later.

We have discussed this synod at sufficient length in the historical preface, and also in the notes to the aforementioned letter of Theodoret. There we have explained most of what Cyril sincerely and fully relates in his letters to Acacius of Melitene and Donatus, bishop of Nicopolis, as well as what Liberatus wrote partly from Cyril and partly from other sources.

It is credible that ten metropolitans of the Eastern diocese assembled, each with two bishops subject to him. The matter was common to all, and John had often sought that form of assembly. Rabbula of Edessa, however, seems to have avoided this [Col. 1212A] gathering with his suffragans, just as his predecessor Nonnus had withdrawn himself from the synod of Ephesus. This synod was, as it were, a completion of the Ephesian synod, since Rabbula was thoroughly Catholic and united with Cyril in doctrine.

Theodoret was certainly absent. He was deeply distressed either that a deliberation should be held about the condemnation of Nestorius and reconciliation with Cyril, or that the measures he had striven so hard to establish should be rescinded.

After the imperial letters had been read, it seemed that the matter ought not to be conducted at Nicomedia between only two bishops deprived of all counsel. That would be dangerous, since John, who had only recently been ordained, could not be considered the equal of Cyril, a bishop of twenty years’ standing, either in learning or in experience of affairs. The matter therefore had to be arranged where it could be handled more securely.

It also seemed that, since Nestorius’s cause was hopeless, the emperor’s command should indeed be obeyed, but that the tribune should be wearied by delay.
