They should deal cunningly with Cyril, so that the honor of the Easterners might be preserved and Cyril might be made to appear either hostile to peace or, if he accepted it, to have obtained it from John rather than to have won a victory.

[Col. 1212B]

That crafty old man Acacius therefore wrote to Cyril that peace among the churches could not be achieved unless Cyril abolished everything he had published in letters, tomes, or books and assented only to the faith issued by the holy Fathers at Nicaea. In other words, he had to retract his first two letters to Nestorius, his third letter together with the twelve chapters and the defenses of those chapters, and the five books he had published against the blasphemies of Nestorius. By “letters” the first two letters were meant; by “tomes” were meant both the third letter with the anathemas and the writings on the right faith, although the five books contradicting the blasphemies of Nestorius are also entitled “tomes.”

When Cyril rejected these absurd conditions, Paul of Emesa was sent to Alexandria to fight the matter face to face. John sent Cyril two sets of letters: one set contained complaints and offered what was almost an apology; the others were more submissive and equitable, and were to be used provisionally to deceive Cyril, if possible, by whatever means [Col. 1212C].

The synod also dealt with the formulation of a statement of faith, but with such artifice that it was composed in words Cyril had not used but had not rejected either—words that seemed to contradict Nestorius but could in reality be reconciled with him, and that, if Catholics accused them of a perverse meaning, could immediately and easily be turned into a Catholic meaning consonant with the judgments of the saints. Such a formula is contained both in John’s letter to Cyril and in Cyril’s letter to John (Third Part of the Council of Ephesus).

The synod likewise dealt with pressing for the restoration of the four schismatic bishops—Helladius, Himerius, Eutherius, and Dorotheus—who had been deposed by Maximian’s synod.

It also dealt, after Cyril’s letters had been received—letters in which he consented to the conditions of peace—with the form of faith to be subscribed by everyone.

Finally, a report concerning the whole matter was again sent to the emperor, and also to Sixtus, who had succeeded Celestine in the apostolic see. Thus peace was established—or, if not established, at least feigned [Col. 1212D].

The formula of faith was as follows:

> We therefore confess our Lord Jesus Christ to be the only-begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man, consisting of a rational soul and a body. Before the ages he was begotten from the Father according to his divinity; but in the last times the same one, for us and for our salvation, was born from the Virgin Mary according to his humanity. The same one is consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity and consubstantial with us according to his humanity. For a union of two natures has taken place; therefore we confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord.
>
> According to this understanding of an unconfused unity, we confess the holy Virgin to be the Mother of God—θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”—because God the Word became incarnate and became man, and from the very conception united to himself the temple that he assumed from her.
>
> We know that serious theologians use the evangelical and apostolic statements about the Lord in different ways. Some they make common, as belonging to one person; others they utter separately because of the diversity of the two natures. Those that befit God they customarily refer to Christ’s divinity, while the humble ones they refer to his humanity.

When Theodoret carefully examined this statement of faith, he confidently asserted that it was the same as Nestorius’s and that Cyril could not have accepted it except after renouncing his earlier position, contained in the twelve chapters.

I think he attempted to prove this judgment in his *Pentalogium*, or in the books written on behalf of Diodore and Theodore. But since nothing remains of the entire work except the fragments presented in the third book, it is neither difficult nor perhaps useless to supply this loss—if indeed it is a loss—by comparing the wording of the faith with the wording of Nestorius. This is not intended to condemn John’s faith, which was praised by the Fathers; such a judgment would be rash and exceptionally audacious. It is intended merely to show that the complaint of Cyril’s holy friends was not without foundation, as equity and respect may seem to require [Col. 1213B]. Since anyone can readily make such a comparison for himself, I shall note only a few points.

First, the Eastern synod wished its faith to have three parts: one concerning Christ, another concerning the Virgin Θεοτόκος, “Mother of God,” and a third concerning ἀντίδοσις, that is, the communication of properties. In the first two parts it speaks affirmatively; in the third it maintains that it knows how serious theologians speak about the matter.

By this statement it may appear to regard the ἀντίδοσις τῶν ἰδιωμάτων—the “communication of properties”—as something indifferent, although it alone is the certain, or at least the principal, rule among the certain rules by which statements about the incarnation of the Word must be examined, so that it may be clear whether they are Catholic or not (see Dissertation 1, chapter 2).

Second, Nestorius’s heresy consisted in his joining the two natures in Christ by a merely moral union and thus positing two hypostases or persons in Christ, one of which belonged to the other: for example, God was the inhabitant of the man [Col. 1213C], while the man was God’s temple. For this reason he called that union a union of σχέσεως, “relation.”

Accordingly, he posited three terms signifying both natures—“Son,” “Christ,” and “Lord”—which, when speaking about Christ, signified now one nature in the grammatical subject, as they say, and now the other, according to the attribute being predicated. For example, when it is said that Christ died, Nestorius interpreted “Christ” as the man in whom God dwelt, and so forth.

These and other considerations show what deception he concealed under those three terms. That deception itself cannot be exposed without the rules of ἀντίδοσις set out in Dissertation 1. Thus someone who refuses to disclose his mind on this question may either in reality agree with Nestorius or, with good reason, be suspected of agreement.

Third, the faith of the Easterners could not without cause have appeared suspect to Cyril’s most learned friends, and Nestorian to Theodoret. For its first and second parts are such that, if one attends only to the words, Nestorius could readily subscribe to them without sacrificing his doctrine.

Anyone can clearly see this who wishes to reread the passages of the first dissertation in which either Nestorius and his advocates defend him, or we show that he held Catholic views against the Arians, Apollinarists, Marcellus, and Leporius. Cyril perceived this, and therefore, when he cleared himself and the Easterners before Acacius of Melitene, he added to the formula of faith the sermons of the man from Emesa, which were much more conformed to Catholic truth [Col. 1213D].

Finally, one may reasonably conjecture that the man from Emesa preached once and again in the Alexandrian Church while Cyril presided over it for this reason: that each sermon might supply what was lacking in the statement of faith and that the later sermon might shed light on the earlier one.

This is why, at the very beginning of the first sermon, answering the solemn question in express words and adducing the testimony of Isaiah, he said: “Therefore the Mother of God gives birth to Emmanuel.” By saying this, he seemed to assert to the people precisely what Cyril had asserted in the first chapter.

In the second sermon, however, he spoke more clearly about the Word’s double birth, the one person of the two natures, the communication of properties, and God’s suffering. He did so in such a way as to testify that he was transmitting Cyril’s doctrine, and he ended his speech as follows:

> We have set before you what is yours. For this is the teaching of your father; this is your ancestral treasure. These are the doctrines of blessed Athanasius; this is the teaching of the great Theophilus; they are pillars of the orthodox faith.

## XIV. The synod that was the second universal Egyptian synod, concerning the establishment of peace among the churches, in the same consulship, around autumn.

Just as the East held its synod, partly at Beroea and partly at Antioch, so Egypt held its own at Alexandria while the matter of peace was being conducted. The reason for meeting was the same for both synods, but their intentions and their methods of handling the matter were not the same. The Eastern synod employed devices by which it might deceive its opponent; the Egyptian synod devoted all its strength to the work desired by all good men: the defense of truth and the concord of the churches [Col. 1214B].

That the synod we have mentioned was in fact held at Alexandria is established beyond doubt by the fact that Cyril’s letters to John of Antioch, beginning “Let the heavens rejoice,” which were read at the Council of Chalcedon, are called *synodical* in the Fifth Synod (Fifth Synod, Session 6).

It lasted for several months. It must have begun around autumn, when the emperor’s sacred letter ordering the establishment of peace was brought to Alexandria. It could not have ended before the middle of January, when the matter of peace also appears to have been completed, namely when Paul of Emesa, the legate of the East, returned to the East. He had preached in the Alexandrian Church at the beginning of January and, on his return, carried Cyril’s letters with him.

At the beginning, a formula of faith was drawn up and sent to Antioch by Alexandrian clerics. What its wording was cannot be determined, since it does not survive. Nor [Col. 1214C] can it be said to be part of that famous letter beginning “Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult,” and so forth. For the faith now under discussion preceded John’s letter to Cyril, whereas that letter followed it. Moreover, most of what Theodoret reports about this faith is not found in the letter.

Theodoret read this statement of faith and, compelled by the truth, approved it. I have no doubt that he is speaking of this very statement when he writes to Nestorius:

> Let no one, therefore, persuade your holiness that I, desiring to be a bishop, accepted the EGYPTIAN WRITINGS with closed eyes as though they contained correct doctrines. For, I confess, after reading them repeatedly and examining them carefully, I found them free from heretical perversity and was afraid to place any stain upon them.

He likewise writes to Andrew, a Constantinopolitan monk, in these words:

> For those who had confused the natures of Christ the Savior by impious reasoning, who had dared to preach one nature and to attribute sufferings to the Godhead, have now—because they had insulted the most holy and venerable supreme priest of God, Nestorius—had their jaws completely broken, like a bit and bridle, according to the prophet (Psalm 31:9), and have been led from perverse ways to the right path. They have learned the truth again, using the assertion of the man who endured battles for the truth. For at present they confess two natures instead of one, anathematizing those who preach mixture or confusion; they venerate the Godhead of Christ as impassible; they explain that the sufferings belong to the flesh; they divide the evangelical statements, assigning the sublime and God-worthy statements to the Godhead and the humble ones to the humanity. Such, then, are the writings now brought from Egypt.

See the notes on both passages.

The faith of the Easterners was also read, and men fervent in charity, perhaps weary of the disturbances, interpreted it favorably and benevolently.

Not all the bishops of the other provinces approved this accommodation—not even all holy men, such as Isidore of Pelusium [Col. 1215A]. Certainly Cyril was almost accused of treachery by his friends and even by the outstanding defender of the faith, Acacius of Melitene, and therefore had to write an apology to Acacius, Valerian of Iconium, Donatus of Nicopolis, and Successus, bishop of Diocaesarea, as well as to his own representative Eulogius in the imperial city, so that he might satisfy the courtiers who complained that Cyril had betrayed the faith (Third Part of the Council of Ephesus).

At least three synodical letters were then issued: a communion letter to John of Antioch; a letter of notification to Sixtus, the pontiff; and, as is credible, one to Maximian, bishop of the imperial city. The first has reached us; the second is mentioned in Sixtus’s reply.

What else was done at Alexandria with Paul of Emesa and with the tribune Aristolaus has been sufficiently related in the historical preface.

This kind of peace pleased both supreme authorities, Sixtus and Theodosius, because they were weary of the disturbances; it did not please others of either party to the same extent [Col. 1215B].

Each side accused its own bishop of excessive accommodation. The Easterners accused John because he had not demanded the condemnation of the chapters. Catholics accused Cyril because he had confessed two natures in Christ after the union, and thus seemed to have abandoned these two doctrines of orthodox faith: that the union of the natures is καθ’ ὑπόστασιν, “according to hypostasis,” and φυσική, “natural”; and that after the union there remained one incarnate nature of the Word.

Theodoret slandered John and persuaded many others to do so. Not only an order of bishops or clerics, but even the imperial court itself, and indeed the most holy monks, including Isidore of Pelusium, called Cyril into suspicion. Cyril called Isidore “father.”

Isidore writes (Book I, Letter 323):

> You, O admirable man, must always remain firm and constant, so that you neither betray heavenly things through fear nor appear to fight against yourself. For if you weigh what has now been written by you against what was written earlier, you will appear either subject to flattery or the servant of fickleness, as one who succumbs to empty glory.

What Cyril replied to Isidore is unknown. What he replied to the other three is clear from the letters read in the third part of the Council of Ephesus. But we shall discuss these matters at greater length in the supplement concerning the author of Theodoret’s calumnies.

## XV. The synod that was the fourth Roman synod under Sixtus, the supreme pontiff, in the consulship of Theodosius XIV and Maximus, in the year of Christ 433, on 26 April.

After receiving Cyril’s letter concerning the peace established among the churches, Sixtus, rejoicing with incredible joy, replied to Cyril in these words (Third Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 41):

> O report worthy of the sender, worthy of the assembly! Such things ought to have had witnesses of heavenly joy; and since the matter and the cause demand it, the place also ought not to be left unmentioned. The entire brotherhood gathered to the blessed apostle Peter. Behold an audience suited to its hearers, an assembly suited to what was to be heard. Our fellow bishops had him as witness to their congratulation whom we have as the beginning of our honor.
>
> For he himself presided over the holy and venerable synod which, with the Lord’s favor, my birthday had gathered, since we must believe that he was absent neither in spirit nor in body. He was present at the victory, who was not absent from the contest. He aided the wishes of our hearts, since he sees the symbol first handed down among the apostles being diminished. He did not allow the impious head to rejoice in consolations, nor did he permit the purity of that clear spring to be long disturbed by a muddy whirlpool.
>
> The brothers have returned to us—to us, I say, who, pursuing the disease with common zeal, have cared for the holiness of souls.

And later:

> Rejoice, therefore, dearest brother, and rejoice victoriously with the brothers gathered again to us. The Church was seeking those whom she has received. For if we wish none of the little ones to perish, how much more ought we to rejoice over the health of the rulers! We read how much joy the one sheep brought back produced, and therefore we must understand what praise belongs to the restoration of so many shepherds. Flocks are seen in each individual; and the cause of one person is never treated when the health of many is at issue.
>
> We rejoice that we have done nothing premature, since we are congratulating ourselves on the fruit of our judgment. We endured for the brothers, confident that they would gather not thorns but grapes.

Then:

> We are therefore expecting and desire the clerics of our aforementioned brother John to come. We know that he will give an answer for both your honor and your labor.

And near the end:

> This holy brotherhood writes these things with me to your veneration, approving and confirming your labors in every respect. Yet those labors could not have been burdensome or bitter, because they were undertaken for him whose light burden and easy yoke we bear.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Theodosius XIV and Maximus.

From these words of the holy pontiff we can understand several things.

1. We can understand how great was the joy with which the apostolic bosom of Peter’s successor was filled when he saw the concord of the churches restored, and what sentiments Christ’s vicar held toward Nestorius, the enemy of Christ. This refutes the calumny of the Nestorians, who with the utmost shamelessness had spread among the people that letters had been forged in the name of the legate Philip, in which Sixtus was said to have taken the deposition of Nestorius badly [Col. 1216B].

2. Cyril’s letter was read at the synod in Rome, and the synod was held at Saint Peter’s. This was not because the receipt of the letter was the reason for convening the synod, but because, as was customary, the bishops had gathered for Sixtus’s birthday—that is, for the anniversary of his accession.

3. We can determine the day on which the synod was celebrated: namely, 26 April. For Sixtus was himself installed on that day, since he succeeded Celestine—who departed this life on 6 April—after the see had been vacant for twenty days.

The chronological notice found in Baronius and in the councils must therefore be corrected. It could not have happened that this synodical letter was delayed until the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, since in the letter itself the pontiff writes that he had not yet received messengers from John of Antioch, although another letter of Sixtus to John is said to have been given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October.

[Col. 1216C]

4. Sixtus’s letter was in fact synodical, since it is said that the holy brotherhood wrote it together with the pontiff presiding.

5. We can determine which bishops came to the synod: namely, those who were accustomed to celebrate the pontiff’s birthday in their assembly. This was customary not only for bishops of neighboring cities but also for more distant bishops who wished on that occasion to recognize what Innocent I calls “the fountainhead of the churches” and what Cyprian calls “the principal church,” from which priestly unity arose.

Thus Leo the Great, Sixtus’s successor, after praising Peter’s universal care for Christ’s sheep in his successor, says:

> Hence the desired and honored presence of my venerable brothers and fellow priests is all the more sacred and devoted, if, through the piety of the duty in which they have deigned to be present, they pay their principal respect to the one whom they know to be not only the bishop of this see but also the primate of all bishops (Sermon 2, on the anniversary of his accession).

6. We can determine the origin of the Nestorians’ calumny that Sixtus was displeased by the deposition of Nestorius [Col. 1216D]. Cyril had pressed Sixtus in his letters to issue an apostolic judgment against John of Antioch, the patron of Nestorius. But the pontiff withheld that judgment. Hence he says that he rejoiced because he had done nothing premature and had received the fruit of his patience. The Nestorians interpreted this kindly patience according to their own meaning.

Add that, according to Gennadius (Book on Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 54), Sixtus also sent a letter to Nestorius himself, in which he attempted, if possible, to restore him to a right mind, broken or at least subdued by his misfortunes:

> Likewise Sixtus, Celestine’s successor, sent judgments concerning the same matter both to Nestorius himself and to the bishops of the East, in order to cut down his error.

Sixtus himself bears witness to this in his letter to John of Antioch:

> I believe that the course and order of events have been reported to your charity: how we wished to come to his aid by our admonition; we restrained him as he rushed headlong, when he was about to be plunged into the depths by the weight of his blasphemies, etc. (Third Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 41).

Observe, reader, that in this letter Sixtus is not replying to the letter of John which is read in the third part of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 27, and which is addressed:

> To the most holy and most beloved brothers of God and fellow ministers, Sixtus, Cyril, and Maximian: John and all the others who are with me.

Rather, he is replying to another letter, which does not survive and whose opening allegedly called Sixtus “the light of the Church shining everywhere.” For nothing similar to these words is found in the letter placed in chapter 27.

[Col. 1218A]

Since what follows concerns a different matter from that of Nestorius, I shall bring to an end my discussion of the many synods subsequently held concerning Cyril’s chapters, which Theodoret mentions (Letter to Domnus). I do so partly because Theodoret himself was the instigator of those synods, whose history we shall publish shortly; and partly because, for the synods whose treatment we would wish to undertake, we have fixed the period at the lifetime of Nestorius. From the time he was expelled to the Oasis, we regard him, in the customary manner, as among the dead—although he was to return by imperial command, had God’s death of the impious man not forestalled such an unjust indulgence.

[Col. 1217]

## Garnerius’s Notice to the Reader

There are three matters about which I wish to warn you, reader, before I bring the work to an end.

First, the third dissertation was promised in the title of the fourth book [Note: [Col. 1217] In fact, in the argument of the fourth book Garnerius had promised another dissertation, which would treat of books written at the same time—namely, during the Nestorian heresy—by defenders of the faith. Since no trace of this work existed, we did not think its mention should be made in the title of the book cited. EDITOR.]: concerning the writings composed during the lifetime of Nestorius, whether on behalf of the faith by Proclus, Cyril, Cassian, Theodotus, and Atticus, who forestalled the heresy that was about to arise, together with other distinguished defenders of Catholic doctrine; or on behalf of the heresy by Nestorius, Andrew of Samosata, Theodoret of Cyrus, Eutherius of Tyana, and the other patrons of Nestorius, as well as the opponents of the anathemas.

The promise would have been fulfilled if two obstacles had not intervened. The first was that the whole volume had already grown to a greater size than had been expected, while the dissertation, already lengthy in itself, still needed to be enlarged by certain ancient documents that we are still awaiting from elsewhere. The second was that, since the dissertation concerns a subject related to that which must be treated in the examination of Theodoret’s books, it seemed that the dissertation should be postponed until Theodoret’s supplement, where it will have both a convenient and a necessary place.

Second, I shall for the present remain silent about the places from which I expect the ancient documents, although it would be useful to say so, so that some benevolent person might perhaps lend similar materials. I was afraid that the same thing might happen to them as happened to Mercator.

At one time, when I was speaking about him among certain people—as the laws of friendship require—openly and frankly, I said that I was using two manuscript codices, the Vatican and the Bellovacensis: I possessed one of them itself and a copy of the other. It happened that someone conceived the desire to seize the labor I had undertaken. It also happened that, through the kindness of an excellent prince, what I had said I had received from the Vatican was transcribed from the Vatican, and that the favour shown me by the chapter of Beauvais was assailed through the devices of anonymous persons; so that an unjust authority was almost fraudulently obtained from the supreme magistrate, the commands of superiors who resisted were held in little account, and the fidelity of the workmen was solicited. What could not be done lawfully under the rule of France was carried out with impunity in that part of the world where war is now being waged covertly.

Third, in the Bellovacensis manuscript certain Acts of the Council of Ephesus have been mixed among Mercator’s works. They are extremely incomplete and scarcely of any importance. Although Lucas Holstenius thought that Mercator had translated them, anyone who reads them will nevertheless judge them unworthy of being attributed to so great a man. Two features encountered in the course of reading plainly prove them spurious.

For they contain Theodore’s creed, written in a Latin that is much different and worse than the Latin used by Mercator in his translation. Moreover, the author of these rejected materials counts 193 bishops as condemners of Nestorius, whereas Mercator counts 275.

Add that, apart from the testimonies of the Fathers cited in the first session, the affair of Charisius, which belongs to the sixth session, and the thoroughly defective subscriptions of the bishops, these Acts contain almost nothing that would give them value. I therefore decided to omit the whole of them—not only because of their worthlessness, but also so that the volume would not be burdened by even two additional sheets.

**Caecilia:** Her martyrdom, 410.

Eunuch by a defect of nature, ibid. When he was born, ibid. When he joined Pelagius, 279. When he wrote to his parents from the monastery, 280. He was never a monk, 278. His obstinacy, ibid.

He openly denied original sin, 159. He was the first to write against the transmission of sin, 280. At what time, 68, 112, 280. He taught the heresy independently in Sicily, ibid. He won over the clergy of Carthage, 282. In the Carthaginian trial under Aurelius he confessed that he had received his error concerning original sin from Rufinus, 86. The better clergy resisted Coelestius when he sought the rank of presbyter, 282.

Coelestius was summoned to the judgment of the Apostolic See, 77. He declined examination by the Apostolic See, 78. He was condemned at Rome, and a letter of condemnation was sent to the principal sees, 77. When he was first proscribed by Honorius’s edict, 283. He stirs up disturbances from his hiding places at an opportune moment, 408. He was condemned at Ephesus in the ecumenical council, 285. He asks Coelestine to reopen his case, 284. He abused the letters sent by Zosimus to the Africans in the Pelagian controversy, 76. He was expelled from the royal city by an imperial sanction issued to Florentius, prefect of the prefecture, 65. He complained to Nestorius about his expulsion from the royal city, 181. He accompanied Julian into Cilicia, 284.

The Coelestians’ understanding of the divine command concerning Adam’s bodily death, 643 ff. Arguments against original sin, 644.

**Conference with the Donatists:** 282, 321.

The outcome of its presentation, 65.

**Compsa:** A city, 128.

**Concupiscence:** The transmission of original sin, 134. The origin of the fourteen questions concerning concupiscence, 664.

**Consequences:** Whether Pelagian or Semi-Pelagian, arising from the error that grace is given on account of merits, 679 ff.

Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 54, elucidated in his account of Celestine, 1175. A passage of Hesychius of Jerusalem in the Fifth Synod, *Collation* 5, corrected, 1058. Concerning Cyril’s response to Theodoret’s criticisms, 1194. [Col. 1238] Concerning words falsely attributed to Socrates, ibid.

A passage of Mercator, Nestorius’s Sermon I, restored, 760. A passage in Nestorius’s Sermon I corrected, 762. A passage in Nestorius’s Sermon 12 corrected, 848. A passage in Nestorius’s refutation of the anathemas corrected by Petavius, 912. A passage of Nestorius’s Sermon 7 corrected, 789. A passage of Nestorius’s Sermon 7 elucidated from Cyril’s seventeenth Paschal Homily, 790. Nestorius’s statement concerning the “uttered Word” examined, 1140. The opinion of those who assert that the Ephesian synod was summoned by Saint Celestine is discussed, 843. The popular accusation against Theodore—that the human being was formed before being assumed by God—is refuted, 1060. The Roman interpreter of the Council of Ephesus corrected, 834. A passage of the Fifth Synod, *Collation* 5, section 35, corrected, 1059. A passage of the Fifth Synod, *Collation* 5, excerpt 37, elucidated, 1059. A passage of the Fifth Synod, *Collation* 5, in the first and second place, elucidated, 1061.

Socrates, book VII, chapter 31, criticized concerning matters relating to Nestorius, 759. Book VII, chapter 33, elucidated, 861. He is criticized for asserting that Nestorius differed from the Catholics only in words, 1190. Concerning Nestorius’s withdrawal from the assembly of bishops after the blasphemy concerning the three-month-old God, ibid. Concerning the date of Nestorius’s condemnation by the bishops of Cyril’s party, ibid. Concerning Cyril’s deposition by John of Antioch, ibid. Concerning the mutual restoration of their sees after friendship was reconciled, ibid. A passage of Theodoret elucidated from a passage of Cyril, part III of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 35, 1080. Theophanes criticized concerning the date of Nestorius’s ordination, 1194. Concerning the letters of Pope Celestine to John of Antioch and Praïlius of Jerusalem, 1195. Concerning the date when Cyril wrote the book *On the Right Faith*, ibid. Concerning the reason Celestine did not come to Ephesus, 1196. Concerning the day on which the Ephesian council began, ibid. Concerning how the council began and who presided, ibid. Concerning John of Antioch’s arrival at Ephesus, ibid. Concerning Nestorius’s attendance at the schismatic synod, ibid. Concerning Theodoret’s criticism of the chapters, ibid. Concerning Nestorius’s departure with the Eastern bishops, 1197. Concerning the date of the peace that was concluded, ibid. A passage of Vincent of Lérins in the *Commonitory*, chapter 16, elucidated from law 63 *On Heretics* of the Theodosian Code, 1124.

# INDEX OF NOTABLE PERSONS AND SUBJECTS MENTIONED IN THE LATTER PART OF THE WORKS OF MARIUS MERCATOR

[Note: [Col. 1235] This index refers to the works of Marius Mercator between columns 699 and 1218 of this volume.]

## A

Acacius of Beroea, ill-disposed toward Christ, 1112. Acacius of Melitene unsuccessfully attempts to bring Nestorius’s mind around to the Church’s understanding, 721. The first universal synod of Egypt against Nestorius: why and when it was held, 1177. Agobard’s opinion concerning Cyril, 1083. The First Alexandrian Synod against Nestorius: why and when it was held, 1170. The right of the Church of Alexandria, 1169. Almost all the Alexandrian bishops accused of usurping lay authority, 715. Anastasius the Sinaite teaches much concerning Andrew of Samosata, 967. Anastasius, presbyter and first *syncellus* of Nestorius, denied that the Virgin was the *Deipara* (“God-bearer”), 810. Where and when Cyril composed the anathemas, 1179. The art and method of Cyril’s anathemas, 1180, 1181.

Andrew of Samosata: who he was, 931. He does not depart from Paul of Samosata concerning the Incarnation, 948. His teaching concerning God the bishop is refuted, 958, 959. He refutes Cyril’s chapters in a book distinct from the objections, 968, 969. He charges Cyril with contradicting himself, 941, 942. Andrew of Samosata’s method in arguing against Cyril, 933. The distance from Antioch to Ephesus, 719.

Apellis’s error concerning Christ’s humanity, 1091. The dispute among authors concerning Apollinaris, 1118. What Apollinaris’s error was and from where it arose, 931. His true heresy, 1118. The causes of the heresy, ibid. His error concerning Christ’s humanity, 1091. Who mentioned *anakyklesis* (ἀνακύκλησις, “cycle”) and *chiliōntaetēris* (χιλιονταετηρίς, “thousand-year period”), 939. Both affinity and conflict with the Arians, 1118, 1119. The name is odious, 1121. The error is refuted, 932.

The Apollinarists’ error concerning the joining of the natures in Christ, 1091. Their six principal inventions, 1121. Why Nestorius so spitefully charged Cyril with Apollinarianism, 1120. Arguments advanced in defense of Nestorius, 1106, 1107. Arius sinned against Christ’s divinity as though through deficiency, 1091. [Col. 1239] It was the Arians, not Arius, who devised the heresy concerning Christ’s flesh, 907. Why they agreed with the Catholics concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, 1159. Why and when they invented the claim that the Word had taken the place of the soul in the flesh, 1114. How they would say that the Word became flesh, 1115. The Arian error concerning Christ’s humanity, 1091. Its origin concerning the Incarnation, 1116. Doctrine reconciled with Cyril’s anathemas, 1117. The Arian heresy attacked chiefly with four arguments, 1118. The Arian heresy concerning the divine Word has two principal points, 1114.

Augustine charges the translator of Chrysostom’s homilies with the crime of forgery, 755. Although a pagan, the emperor Aurelian ordered Paul of Samosata to be deposed from his see and expelled from the city, 1130. The origin of the author whom Sirmond called *Praedestinatus*, 927.

## B
Baronius the cardinal praised, 1197. He seems to have read the twelfth sermon of Nestorius, 849. Basil the archimandrite, having presented a petition to Theodosius, complains of the cruelty of Nestorius, 709. Bonosus presided over the Sardicensian Church, 907 and 1142. He followed the heresy of Ebion, ibid. Bonosus renewed the heresy of Marcellus and Photinus, 928. He was condemned in advance by Damasus, ibid. and 1143. By whom he was condemned in the time of Pope Siricius, 928. Bupha, deacon of Martyrius and *agens in rebus* of the Alexandrian Church at Constantinople, warns Cyril about Nestorius’s affairs, 710.

## C

Count Candidian and Nestorius falsely report the proceedings of the Council of Ephesus to the emperor, 721. The canon declaring anathema against anyone who asserted that Adam’s soul had died in sin, since the devil does not enter the human heart: in which council it was written, 823. Cassian writes a work on the Incarnation of Christ against the heresy of Nestorius, 711. Why he entitled seven books *On the Incarnation*, 756. At what time he sent them to Rome, 713. In opposition to Nestorius he used the Antiochene Creed, 770. He presses Nestorius severely, 770. In Book VII, chapter 30, he sharply rebukes the same man, 812. He saw Cyril’s letter to his clergy, 813. The five parts of Catholic doctrine concerning the Incarnation, 1092. Catholics and heretics used the term “monarchy” in different senses when speaking of the Trinity, 929. The cause of the disagreement between Cyril and Nestorius, 815. When the Council of Chalcedon was held, 1182. Where and when the case of Charisius was discussed, 727. How Christ is without a father and without genealogy, 759. How he is called an apostle, 962. How he was made a curse and sin, 937. How he knows and does not know the day of judgment, 984. He is called “double” by Nestorius in many passages, 923. How he is one according to Nestorius, 1111. To dissolve Christ is characteristic of the Gentiles and the Jews, 1124. How Christ’s body gives life to our bodies, 963. Chrysostom visited Diodore out of zeal for cultivating the monastic life, 1146. Pope Celestine is stirred when Nestorius’s homilies are brought to Rome, 707. He sends Cyril the letters Nestorius had written to him, 832. He sends Nestorius’s writings to Cassian, so that he may answer them, 711. At Rome he convenes a synod in the case of Nestorius; from there seven letters were conveyed by Possidonius to the principal sees, together with Cyril’s letters to John of Antioch and Juvenal of Jerusalem, 713. He delegates his authority to Cyril for carrying out the sentence issued against Nestorius, 1176. The subject of the three later letters, 1186. His death, 739.

Three collections of excerpts from Nestorius’s treatises, with a fourth added from various books by other writers, 865. When the first collection of excerpts from Nestorius’s books, presented to the Fathers of the Council of Ephesus, was made, 865. The confession of union *καθ’ ὑπόστασιν* (“according to hypostasis”) was formerly the single unquestioned mark of right faith, 834. When the First Council of Constantinople was held in the case of Nestorius, 1177. How the Constantinopolitan synod concerning Maximian’s ordination can be regarded as an Ephesian synod, 1182. The Constantinopolitan populace withdraws from Nestorius when he reveals his heresy, 703. The Constantinopolitans used the Nicene Creed, 770. The dispute among the Constantinopolitan clergy, while they were deliberating over a successor after Sisinnius’s death, was settled by Theodosius, 699. The custom of citing bishops of the principal sees: its nature and origin, 1178. How Christ’s body is proper to the Word, 962.

Cyriacus succeeded John the Faster in the see of Constantinople, 823. Cyril’s character, 709. Cyril observed ecclesiastical discipline [Col. 1240] in only a few matters, 1170. Atticus warns him to restore Chrysostom’s name to the sacred diptychs, 852. Great disputes arose between Cyril and Nestorius, 707. Cyril seems to have read Nestorius’s sermons against the Pelagians, 840. A vigorous defender of Christ’s real presence in the Eucharist, 1003. He wrote much against Nestorius’s first sermon, 755. In letters sent to Nestorius he urges repentance and promises his own steadfastness in advancing the cause of the faith, 707. He convened a council in Egypt concerning Nestorius’s case and sent him a synodal letter, 715. From the Alexandrian synod he wrote a second letter to Nestorius, ibid., 713. When Cyril’s first letter to Nestorius was sent, 801. By whom it was delivered, 1170. It contains three useful historical points, 802. He had earlier written a letter to the Egyptian monks, 810. Against Nestorius’s first homily, 707–708. When Cyril’s second letter to Nestorius was sent, 804. It alone was approved by the judgments of the Fathers of Ephesus, and alone was read at the Second Council of Constantinople and at Chalcedon, 801. Why it was called a “synodal letter” by the Council of Chalcedon, 1171. Why Cyril prefixed the Nicene Creed to his third letter, 833. He refutes Nestorius’s slander, ibid.

Cyril could scarcely remove from himself the suspicion of Arian heresy, 1116. Cyril’s three admonitory letters to Nestorius, apart from the congratulatory letter on his ordination and the festal letters, 801. They are said to have been written by the Alexandrian Church itself, 1171. They possessed the force of a legitimate admonition, ibid. After reading Nestorius’s second letter, he writes books *On the Right Faith* to Theodosius and the empresses, 713. He replies to certain complainants that, by remaining silent, he would not have allowed Nestorius’s doctrine to fall into something worse, ibid., 709. Before the Council of Ephesus he refused to refute the charges Theodosius had brought, 715. He mentions Nestorius’s seventh sermon, which is the fourth against Proclus, 789. Why he prefers that God the Father be called *Θεογεννήτωρ* (“God-begotten”) rather than *Θεοτόκος* (“God-bearer”), 815. He rejects the unions in Christ of dignity, equivocation, indwelling, *συνάφεια* (“ conjunction”), and *προσκύνησις* (“worship”), 835. Having suffered the slander that he implied the Word had entered into flesh, he could scarcely prove himself free from suspicion, 911. In what sense he said that the Virgin had carnally given birth to the Word made flesh, 936. Why he composed an apology against the Orientals, 933. Accused before the emperor of curiosity, 821. He acted one way toward Andrew of Samosata and another toward Theodoret, 933. He thanks Evoptius for sending Theodoret’s work against the anathemas, 969. He accuses Theodoret of feigned ignorance and displayed learning, 971. And also of contradiction and inconsistency, 986. In five books of *Contradictions* he defends Proclus against Nestorius, 786. He sent letters to Acacius of Beroea, to which Acacius craftily replies, 713. When he went to Ephesus, 717. Before the synod began, he excerpted certain passages from Nestorius’s books, ibid. Why he praised no Father from the Antiochene or Constantinopolitan diocese at the Council of Ephesus, 1181. He rejects the unjust terms of peace proposed by John, 741. He dismantles the frauds of Paul of Emesa, who had been sent by the Orientals to Alexandria, ibid. He wrote an apology for the monk Victor to the emperor, 813. He refutes excerpts from Diodore’s books used to defend the Nestorian heresy, 1145.

Cyril and Memnon are acquitted by the Council of Ephesus, 725. Cyril warns his representatives about how they should conduct the matter with the Nestorians, ibid., 711. Cyril’s letter to those stationed at Constantinople, with Marius Mercator as interpreter, 809. When it was written, 810. It should be corrected from the Marian version, 809. What title it bears, 808. It is almost entirely historical, 808. As published from Mercator, it differs greatly from the letter read in the general council, ibid. When the seventeenth festal homily was sent throughout the world, 709. Its subject is the same as that of the letter to the monks, 1171. When and where the *Scholia on the Incarnation* were written, 969, 1001. What they contain, 1001. Who their translator was, ibid. Their division, 1003. Their synopsis, ibid. The twelve chapters by which they were attacked, 1182. By whom, under what title, and when they were refuted, 931. By whom they were defended, 1179. By whom they were first rendered into Latin, 1183. With what skill they were composed, 1179. Why they are said to have been approved by the Church’s true judgment, ibid. When they were regarded as rules of faith, 1182. Cyril’s death, 1039.

## D

Who Dalmatius the archimandrite was, 723. The letter of Dalmatius the archimandrite sent to the Council of Ephesus, 731. The form of the decree concerning the reception of those expelled by Nestorius, 1176. Diodore of Tarsus praised by the Fathers, 1145. When he became bishop of Tarsus, 1146. His errors, ibid. What union of the natures in Christ he acknowledged, 1062. Diodore of Tarsus’s testimony on behalf of Nestorius is worthless, 1113. What remains of his works, 1145. Excerpts from his books against the Synusiasts, 1146.

Dionysius Exiguus seems to have borrowed his translation of Cyril’s anathemas from Mercator, 907. *Disertulus* [reading uncertain] concerning Marius Mercator, 755. [Col. 1241] A short dissertation on the opinion of the most illustrious Marca, who thinks that Theodosius suspended the apostolic see’s sentence against Nestorius and that the earlier acts of the Council of Ephesus were lawfully rescinded, 843 and following. Dorotheus first pronounced an anathema against *Θεοτόκος* (“God-bearer”), 703 and 810.

## E

Ebion was a Stoic philosopher, 907, 927, 1126. Ebion denied Christ’s divinity, 928. Ebion’s opinion concerning Christ is reported differently by different writers, 1126–1127. Ebion’s four doctrines concerning Christ, 1127. Ebion misused the authority of the three evangelists Matthew, Mark, and Luke to prove his heresy, 927, 1128. Ebion’s teacher and period, 1127. Ebion’s inconsistency, ibid. The Elionites accepted only Matthew’s Gospel, 928.

The Church’s first victory over Nestorius, 1169. Elipandus’s heresy exposed, 793. What the true *ἕνωσις* (“union”) is, 940. What *ἕνωσις φυσική* (“natural union”) is, ibid. The Council of Ephesus was convoked at Nestorius’s request, 841–842. When it was held, 1188. Where and when it began, 721. It reports Nestorius’s deposition to the emperor, ibid. It writes to the clergy of the imperial city concerning Nestorius’s condemnation, 723. The Council of Ephesus complains to the emperor about Candidian’s actions, 723. The Council of Ephesus warns Eucharius, defender of the Constantinopolitan Church, that Nestorius has been deposed, 721. The sentence of deposition and excommunication issued against Nestorius by the Council of Ephesus, and when it was announced, 721. Where the second session of the Council of Ephesus was held, 725. It writes to the bishops stationed in the city and to the clergy so that the truth may become known, 729. It reports the condemnation of John and the others to the emperor and the supreme pontiff, 725. In a letter to the emperor it complains about Count John’s action and attests its own steadfastness, 729. It writes to Dalmatius, 733. The Council of Ephesus sends envoys with instructions to Theodosius concerning Cyril’s and Memnon’s case, 731. When the envoys of the Council of Ephesus reached Chalcedon, 735. The envoys of the Council of Ephesus are admitted into the city to ordain a bishop, while the schismatics remain at Chalcedon, ibid. The Council of Ephesus customarily writes to the principal sees concerning Maximian’s ordination, 737. The order of the acts of the Council of Ephesus restored, 747. The second part of the Council of Ephesus’s proceedings is entirely confused, 719.

The four bishops delegated to Constantinople to defend Nestorius’s synodal letters: when they arrived, 1178. Formerly it was impious to transfer a bishop from one see to another, 1077. Cyril’s third letter to Nestorius was formerly regarded as representing the entire Council of Ephesus: when it was written, 831. The three parts of Cyril’s third letter to Nestorius, 832. When the *Eranistes* was written by Theodoret, 1041. Who is designated by the name *Eranistes*, 1086. The relationship between the Eucharist and the Incarnation, 1165. Two errors of Eunomius shared with the Arians, 1122.

What the heresy of Euphratas of Agrippina was, 1144. Who Eusebius the layman, later bishop of Dorylaeum, was, 769. He was the first to detect Nestorius’s heresy and publicly rebuke it when detected, ibid. He was the first of all to inflame hearts with zeal for the faith by publicly presenting a protest against Nestorius, 705. When he presented his protest against Nestorius, 768–769. Eusebius’s protest against Nestorius’s impious sermons, 769, 773.

Eutherius, metropolitan of Tyana, was especially devoted to Nestorius, 1085. How he became known, ibid. He wrote twenty sermons to Eustathius, bishop of Parnassus, against the Council of Ephesus, 739. He attacked Cyril’s *Scholia*, 1005. Several sermons were attributed to Eutherius by Marius Mercator, 1085. Eutyches’s error concerning the conjunction of the natures in Christ, 1091. The origin of the Eutychian heresy, 1121.

Evagrius tries to excuse John of Antioch for deliberately delaying on the road, 919. In what sense the evangelist’s statement “the Word became flesh,” and so forth, was understood by the heretics, 1099. What the Gospel *καθ’ Ἑβραίους* (“according to the Hebrews”) is, 1128. What the Gospel *κατὰ Πέτρον* (“according to Peter”) is, ibid. Cyril praises Evoptius’s affection, 969. The embassy to the emperor Constantius explained, ibid. Excerpts by Marius Mercator from the books of Theodore of Mopsuestia, 1051 and following. From several letters and five books of Theodoret against Cyril, 1067. Excerpts by Leontius convict Theodore on five propositions, 1152. The excuse offered by Nestorius’s defenders is worthless, 1106–1107.

## F

The name “Son” signifies two natures for Nestorius, 773. What *Φόσις* [probably *φύσις*, “nature”] is, 942.

[Col. 1242]

## G

Gennadius, successor of Anatolius in the see of Constantinople, 1082. The period of Gennadius of Massilia, 1057. The origin of paganism and Judaism, 1124. What the grace of Christ, because of which he came into the world, means for Theodore of Mopsuestia, 1051–1052. Gregory the Great saw Mercator’s codex, 1065. Gregory the Great’s opinion that Theodoret had not yet professed the faith at the Council of Chalcedon, 1065.

## H

The *History of the Isaurian Monks*, which gave Gregory the Great occasion to write, 823 and following. Proclus’s homily, delivered while Nestorius was seated in the great church of Constantinople, on the Incarnation of the Word, 775 and following. Comparison of the seventeenth festal homily with Cyril’s letter to the monks, 1171. Who were called “Homuncionites” by the Church, 907. Who the Homuncionites were, 929–930. What “hypostasis” meant among the philosophers themselves, 924.

## I

The inquiry into the council of which Nestorius speaks in his second letter to Cyril, where he says that Cyril was deceived by those who had been deposed by the holy council, 821 and following. Count Irenaeus either orders or permits the bishops who had attended the council, when they encounter John, to be beaten by his guards, 723. Irenaeus arranges for the condemnation of Cyril by John to be publicly announced in the Church at Constantinople, 727.

## J

Jesus Christ is called “one of the Trinity” by Mercator, 925. After receiving the letters of Celestine and Cyril, John of Antioch amicably warns Nestorius, but in vain, 713. As he travels to Ephesus, he deliberately delays on the road, 719. When he reached Ephesus, 723. Having convened a synod of forty-three bishops, he deposes Cyril and Memnon, 723. He attempts to win the emperor’s mind by means of letters, 725. After the third summons he is condemned as contumacious by the Catholic synod, 725. After receiving Theodosius’s sanction, he convenes a synod at Beroea, 741. His testimony on behalf of Nestorius is weakened, 1112 and following.

Count John S. L. is sent to Ephesus to order, in Theodosius’s name, that Cyril, Memnon, and Nestorius be deposed, 727. Why and when he came to Ephesus, 727 and following. He attempts to reconcile the parties, but in vain, 729. Why Judaism was charged against Nestorius, 1124. The Jews held three opinions about Christ contrary to the truth, 1125. When Juvenal of Jerusalem went to Ephesus, 719.

## L

Who the presbyter Lampo was, 803. Where and when the envoys of the West to the general Council of Ephesus were chosen, 1185–1186. The envoys of the apostolic see subscribe to Nestorius’s condemnation, 725. Leo the Great, while still a deacon, was Pope Celestine’s administrator in governing the Church, 711. Leporius’s error concerning the perpetuity of the union of the natures in Christ, 1091. The petition to be presented to Theodosius differs from the protest submitted at Constantinople, 815. Libels full of accusations against Cyril were given to Nestorius, 810.

## M

Macedonius shared Eunomius’s error, 1122. He held the same opinion as the Arians concerning Christ’s flesh, 907. Why the Macedonians held the same opinion as the Catholics concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, 1159. The principal cases that were held, 1170. The Manichaean error concerning Christ’s humanity, 1091. The Manichaean heresy concerning Christ, 849. The Manichaeans and Marcion shared one opinion concerning the evil nature of man, 826. Why Manichaeism was charged against Nestorius, 1126. The heresy of Marcellus of Galatia concerning Christ, 849. The disputed opinion of Marcellus of Galatia, whose agreement was charged against Nestorius by Mercator, 1136.

Maximian was ordained bishop of the imperial city, 737. By whom he was raised to Nestorius’s throne, 1187. Which bishops he deposed in his synod, 1082. Meletius praised by Chrysostom in a funeral oration, 852. [Col. 1243] Memnon forbids the Nestorians to open the Church of Saint John at Ephesus, 721.

What Mercator’s codex contains and when it was written, 753. The second part of his works contains the entire case of Nestorius, 699. Mercator’s admonition against the Pelagians, 709. His letter on the distinction between Nestorius’s heresy and that of Paul of Samosata, ibid., 706. Mercator was still a layman when he wrote the letter on the distinction between Nestorius’s heresy and Paul of Samosata’s, 773. Deceived by a fault in the Greek exemplar, as were many after him, 917. He presents certain writings of Theodoret composed after the council, 719. What he intended in the excerpts from Theodoret’s five books, 1065. He seems to be the translator of the first collection of excerpts from Nestorius’s books, 865. He was regarded as Nestorius’s public accuser, 911. He accuses Nestorius of many crimes, 909. He charges Nestorius simultaneously with inconsistency and slander, 916. He refutes Nestorius’s twelve anathemas, 717. When he refuted Nestorius’s anathemas, 907, 911. He is the true translator of Nestorius’s anathemas, which he rendered into Latin twice, 907. He used “nature” for “hypostasis,” 924. He differs from Epiphanius concerning Praxeas, 929. He teaches many things about the Council of Ephesus that had hitherto been unheard of, 1188. Mercator’s age, 910. Gregory the Great’s testimony confirms the defense of Mercator’s attack on Theodoret, 1065. How his work against Nestorianism was divided, 1041. The statements concerning Nestorius’s agreement with Photinus regarding the Incarnation are examined, 1138 and following. Dissertation on the twelfth anathema, 924.

Monothelitism arose from Eutychianism, 1123. Montanus was classed with Sabellius by Socrates, 929.

## N

Nestorius was made a presbyter from a monk by Theodotus of Antioch, 701. He was placed in charge of catechesis, ibid. He was summoned from Antioch to Constantinople by Theodosius, ibid. He brought the presbyter Anastasius with him from Antioch to Constantinople, ibid. When he was ordained bishop, ibid. He addressed the emperor arrogantly, ibid. He arranged for the Arian church to be destroyed, ibid. His methods for winning the favor of both the powerful and the imperial family, ibid.

Nestorius’s methods for spreading his heresy, 702. His assistants in spreading the heresy, 1052. When he teaches the heresy on his own, 703. He obtains a law from Theodosius against all heretics in order to make way for his own heresy, 702. A simple monk contradicts him while he is spreading his heresy, 703. Those who first resisted him when he raged against Christ, 705. He rages against Eusebius, who openly contradicts his heresy, ibid. He used the creed of his teacher Theodore, 1052. He misused the Nicene Creed, 770.

He attempts to win Celestine’s favor by sending, through Antiochus, letters concerning his own case and that of the Pelagians, together with three treatises, 709. Whether the first sermon was merely spoken or was written by Nestorius, 755. He is sent into Egypt to the monasteries to spread his heresy, 707. The second sermon, on doctrine or *θεογνωσία* (“knowledge of God”), 703. The third sermon, against Catholics who defended the true union of the natures in Christ, attributed to him, 766 and following. When it was delivered and what parts it contains, 766, 768. He refutes the blasphemy of the Macedonians and of the Arians, 766.

The fourth sermon, on the Incarnation against Proclus, when it was delivered, 782 and following. It was not sent to Celestine, 783. The fifth sermon, on the Virgin *Θεοτόκος* (“God-bearer”), the second against Proclus, 785. The sixth sermon, on the Apostle’s statements, 787. The eighth sermon, against the heretics, on Judas, when it was delivered, 827. The ninth sermon, apparently against the heretics, when it was delivered, 828. The tenth sermon, apparently against the Macedonians but actually against the Catholics, 829. The eleventh sermon, against the Arians, when it was delivered, 830. The twelfth sermon: when, on what subject, and with what skill it was delivered, 848 and following. It may be called a compendium of the entire Nestorian doctrine, 847. The thirteenth sermon, when it was delivered, 862.

Nestorius’s first letters to Celestine, when they were sent, 768. He again attempts to win Celestine’s favor by sending letters concerning his own case and that of the Pelagians, 711. When his third letter to Pope Celestine was sent, 841. Nestorius was not satisfied by Celestine’s letters, which the bishops of the Alexandrian synod had delivered, 717. He immediately answered Cyril’s first letter through the presbyter Lampo, 801. He replies to Cyril’s second letter with a second letter of his own, which the Fathers of Ephesus judged contrary to Catholic doctrine, 711.

Why Nestorius attacked Cyril so vehemently, 1114. Why he complained about Cyril, 803. Enraged by Cyril’s letter to the monks, he orders a certain Photius to reply and suborns accusers against Cyril, 707. He tries to turn back against Cyril the charge Cyril had brought against him, 818. He charges Cyril with tyranny, 861. He criticizes Cyril’s letter and praises his own, 818. He answers Cyril’s twelve anathemas with twelve of his own, 717. Marius Mercator refuted twelve chapters of Nestorius’s blasphemies, 907.

Which men Nestorius calls teachers of the Church, 783. A despiser of the holy Fathers, 805. Accused both of pride in despising other teachers and of ignorance, 813. He corrupted the testimonies of the Old Testament [Col. 1244], 1125. By sophistry he evaded the testimonies of Scripture in which Christ is called God and Son of God, as well as the authority of the Council of Nicaea, 1098 and following. Why he frequently mentions the temple when explaining the Incarnation, 855. He directly slanders Theophilus and Cyril, and indirectly the Roman pontiff, 850–851. He attacks the words of Pope Celestine, 859. After convening a synod, he charges his opponents with Manichaeism, 711. He criticizes Proclus, 785. He contradicts Proclus, who spoke of the Virgin Deipara, and in three sermons attacks the principal points of that speech without naming Proclus, 706–707. He possessed an ability to speak extemporaneously, 781. He made contradictory statements concerning *Θεοτόκος*, 907. He conceals his opinion concerning *Θεοτόκος*, 842. He rages against Christ’s divinity and the dignity of the Virgin Deipara, 759. He slanders the Catholics as though they believed the Virgin to be a goddess, 786. Before the Council of Ephesus he was repeatedly admonished to confess the Virgin as *Θεοτόκος*; he rejected the admonition, 910. He is compared with Sabellius, 1140. He is compared with Leporius by Cassian and others, 1143. He is compared with Ebion, 1127. He is compared with sorcerers, 759. He complains that violence is being done to him, although he had done the same to others, 859. Why he attacks Marcellus, Paul, and Photinus abusively, 856.

Nestorius’s disagreement and agreement with Photinus concerning the Incarnation, 1138 and following. He attacks Photinus and Samosata, and Arius, 1092. He indicates two points of disagreement with Photinus, which Mercator refutes, 1138. Yet there was one difference, 929–930. He held the correct opinion concerning the time when the union first existed and concerning the perpetuity of the union of the natures in Christ, 1093. He uses all the Catholic terms in a heretical sense but refuses only to admit a union *καθ’ ὑπόστασιν* (“according to hypostasis”), 855. He actually admitted two hypostases in Christ, 1098, 1138. He conceals the heresy of two sons, 854. After the union he divides the hypostases, 941. What he thought concerning the natures joined in Christ, 1092. In many passages he teaches that the natures were joined in the Virgin’s womb, 774. He denies that the Word was Son before the Incarnation, 925.

Nestorius’s heresy concerning the kind of union of the natures in Christ, 1095 and following. The arguments by which he attempted to establish his view of the union of the natures in Christ, 1099 and following. What his defenders answer to the arguments proving that he held an erroneous view of the union of the natures in Christ, 1105 and following. Why some believed him to assert one person in the Catholic sense, 820. In bad faith he denies that he disagrees with Samosata, 1128–1129. When he attempted to reject agreement with Samosata, ibid. He uses abstract terms in place of concrete ones in order to slander Cyril, 819. He held the Catholic view concerning the death of the body contracted through sin, but concerning the death of the soul propagated from Adam he followed Theodore of Mopsuestia, 826. What he thought concerning original sin, 1160 and following. In what sense he understands the evangelist’s words “the Word became flesh,” and so forth, 1099. He improperly abuses the Apostle’s statement in Galatians 4, 858. He held the correct view concerning the integrity of the assumed human nature, 1093.

What he thought concerning the manner in which Christ’s body is made present through the Eucharistic symbols, 1163 and following. Why he seems to have departed from the Church’s faith concerning the Eucharist, 1166. He truly was an “impanator,” one who held that Christ is present in the bread, 1165. What he thought concerning the union of Christ’s works with the Word, by which those works were rewarded, 1160. What he thought concerning the aids of divine grace through Christ, 1163. Concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, 1159.

His second letter to Cyril, read in the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon and condemned, 817. By whom Nestorius’s papers were sent to Rome, 1168. Why Nestorius wrote against the Pelagians, with whom he agreed, 1162. His association with the Pelagians, charged by whom, 1143. He wrote back to Caelestius the Pelagian, 845. He plundered what was owed to the poor, 790.

Nestorius’s character, 701. His homeland, ibid. His inconsistency, 930. The methods by which he attempted to win the court’s allegiance, 851. Nestorius asks Theodosius to summon an ecumenical council in order to avert the storm hanging over his head; afterward he regretted what had been done, 715, 844. He hoped that he would preside over the council, 842. He easily obtained from Theodosius that it be summoned, 1184. He writes to Pope Celestine about the council’s convocation as though taunting him, 715. When he went to Ephesus, 717, 719. After his condemnation he withdrew to the monastery of Saint Euprepius and continued to cause disturbances from the monastery, 745. By Theodosius’s decree he was deported to the Oasis, and his books were burned, 747. When he was deported, 1076. By whom Nestorius’s works were catalogued apart from Mercator, 1154. Why Nestorianism was called Jewish impiety, 1124. The history of the Nestorian case: from which authors it was taken and why it was written after the works of others, 699. The first two agents of Nestorian impiety, 1102. Through whose books the Nestorian heresy was disseminated, 1039 and following. By which authors it was attacked, ibid. The patrons of the Nestorian faction at court, 727. The members of the Nestorian faction habitually borrowed from one another what they said, 1061. The Nestorians cannot defend original sin or true grace in Christ, 1144. How they would call the Son of God one, 1062. The affinity between the Nestorians and the Sacramentarians consists in four points, 1164 and following.

The Nicene faith is confirmed by the Fathers of Ephesus, 727 and following. The Nicene Fathers did not indeed call the Virgin *Θεοτόκος*, but many others did, whom Nestorius opposes, 936.

Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus: who he was, 1063. Suspected of Nestorianism, 973. Explains in what sense Christ may be called Θεοφόρος (“God-bearing”), 985. The Creed is condemned by all who have mentioned it, except Facundus, 1049. Translated into Latin by Marius Mercator, 1042. Condemned at the Council of Ephesus, 727. What is the book *To the Baptized*? 1059. Dialectical subtlety, 1058. His opinion concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, 1159. Character of Theodore of Mopsuestia’s followers, 1149. Theophanes reports five matters concerning the Council of Ephesus omitted by other writers, 1194. Many testimonies of Gregory the Great concerning the history of the Isaurians demonstrate matters worthy of notice, 826. Testimonies of the Fathers explaining what it means for the Word to have become flesh—that is, to have been born from the Virgin, 938. The Church defends three doctrines as foundations, as it were, of the Incarnation, 1090.

## U

Physical union does not subject the Word either to necessity or to violence, 980. There are two kinds of physical union, 1114. [Col. 1248] What is the effect of substantial union? 1095. How the word ἐγένετο (“became” or “came to be”) is to be understood, 937. ## SECOND DISSERTATION

On the councils held in the case of the Pelagians during the lifetime of Saint Augustine, 319.

### FIRST COUNCIL

Held at Carthage by Aurelius against Coelestius, in the ninth consulship of Honorius and the fifth of Theodosius, the Augusti and consuls, in February of the year of Christ 412, 321.

### SECOND COUNCIL

Convened at Jerusalem by John the bishop in the case of Pelagius, in the tenth consulship of Honorius and the sixth of Theodosius, the Augusti and consuls, on 30 July in the year of Christ 415, 323.

### THIRD COUNCIL

Convened at Diospolis by Eulogius of Caesarea against Pelagius, in the tenth consulship of Honorius and the sixth of Theodosius, the Augusti and consuls, on 20 December in the year of Christ 415, 327.

### FOURTH COUNCIL

Called together at Carthage by Aurelius against Pelagius and Coelestius in their absence, during the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the seventh time and Junius for the fourth time, around the autumn of the year of Christ 416, 331.

### FIFTH COUNCIL

Assembled at Milevis by Silvanus the Elder, or primate of the province of Numidia, against the same heretics, under the same consuls, toward the end of October in the year of Christ 416, 333.

### SIXTH COUNCIL

Held at Carthage by five bishops, under the same consuls and for the same reason, toward the end of that year, 335.

### SEVENTH COUNCIL

Held at Rome against Pelagius and Coelestius by Innocent I, during the consulships of Honorius XI and Constantius II, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the year 417, 336.

### EIGHTH COUNCIL

Convened at Constantinople by Atticus against Coelestius, under the same consuls, in the year 417, 338.

### NINTH COUNCIL

Celebrated at Rome by Zosimus in the case of Coelestius, during the consulships of Honorius XI and Constantius II, around September of the year of Christ 417, ibid.

### TENTH COUNCIL

Held by Theodotus, bishop of Antioch, against Pelagius, apparently at Antioch, under the same consuls, in October of the year 417, 344.

### ELEVENTH COUNCIL

Convened at Carthage by Aurelius, during the twelfth consulship of the Augusti Honorius and the eighth of Theodosius, before Lent, in the year 418, 347.

### TWELFTH COUNCIL

Gathered at Carthage by Aurelius from all the provinces of Africa, during the twelfth consulship of Honorius and the eighth of Theodosius, the Augusti and consuls, on the Kalends of May in the year 418, 350.

### THIRTEENTH COUNCIL

The second African council held there, in the same year, around the middle of June, 353.

### FOURTEENTH COUNCIL

Celebrated at Rome by Pope Zosimus against Pelagius and Coelestius, under the same consuls, on 15 April, 355.

### FIFTEENTH COUNCIL

Convened at Carthage by Aurelius from the whole African diocese, in the same year, in August, 358.

### SIXTEENTH COUNCIL

Called together at Carthage by Aurelius, during the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta, on the third day before the Kalends of July, in the year 419, 359.

### SEVENTEENTH COUNCIL

Held at Anazarbus by Maximian against Julian, involving bishops of the Second Cilicia, during the consulship of Asclepiodotus and Rufus, in the year 423, ibid.

### EIGHTEENTH COUNCIL

Convened at Constantinople by Atticus in the case of the bishops expelled from the West, in the year 424 or 425, 361.

### NINETEENTH COUNCIL

Held at Rome by Coelestine in the case of bishops obstinately favoring Pelagius, during the consulship of Victor and Castinus in the year 424, or during the consulship of Theodosius Augustus XI and Valentinian Caesar in the year 425, 362.

### TWENTIETH COUNCIL

A universal African council convened by Aurelius under the same consuls, in the case both of others and especially of the monk Leporius, converted from error to the true faith, 363.

### TWENTY-FIRST COUNCIL

The first Gallican council, convened by Honoratus, bishop of Arles, apparently at Arles, during the consulship of Hierius and Ardaburius, in the year 427, 367.

### TWENTY-SECOND COUNCIL

Held at Verulamium in England by Germanus and Lupus, legates of the Apostolic See, against Pelagian bishops, during the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius, in the year 429, 371.

### TWENTY-THIRD COUNCIL

Held at Rome by Coelestine in the case of Pelagian bishops adhering to Nestorius, during the thirteenth consulship of Theodosius and the third of Valentinian, the Augusti and consuls, on the fourth day before the Ides of August, in the year of Christ 430, 372.

### TWENTY-FOURTH COUNCIL

The council of the whole world, assembled at Ephesus, during the consulship of Antiochus and Bassus, on 23 June in the year of Christ 431, 373.

### TWENTY-FIFTH

Eight councils held in the fifth century, at various times, in the same Pelagian case, 375.

On the emperors’ constitutions in the case of the Pelagian heresy, 377.

## FOURTH DISSERTATION

On the subscriptions required in the case of the Pelagians, 415.

### CHAPTER I
